units.la: NIVERSAM quidem Helvetiae gentem, Viri clarissimi ac celeberrimi, multis nominibus plurimi faciendam esse non ignoro, eos tamen ex illa non immeritò singulari quadam observantia prosequor, & amantius complector, quibus me veritatis Euangelicae communicatio, ac syncerae fidei societas arctius aliquanto in communi Seruatore Christo Domino coniunxit. Horum celebritati & existimationi, si qua in re cumulum aliquem adijcere possem, eius me officij debitorem haud grauatim agnosco, & ad id quod debeo, propensum esse profiteor, praestaremque ex animo quicquid huc facere possit, si tanta esset ingenij facultas, quanta est animi in id officij propensio. In horum autem albo haud postremo mihi loco est urbs vestra vere Basilea, id est, Regia, non iuxta saeculum tantum longe lateque clara, sed & propter Christianae religionis ac fidei puritatem Regi Regum Christo Domino cu primis sacra. In hac praeter alia dona Dei valde suspicienda est, primùm insignis Ecclesia ad Canonem Euangelicae doctrinae pientissimorum virorum opera ac ministerio per gratiam Dei reformata: qua in re alij plantando, alij rigando fideliter cooperati sunt Domino, & adhuc cooperantur fratres aliquot pij & eruditi, & haud poeniten dis dotibus ad id muneris instructi, quorum laboribus benedictionem apprecor à Domino. Post Ecclesiam de praedicanda venit Academiae vestrae omnis generis disciplinis instructae celebritas, in qua per eximios cum artiu tum sacrae Theologiae professores, ingenia adolescentu non vestratium tantum, sed & exterorum haud infeliciter excoluntur, & ut olim Ecclesijs ac Rebuspublicis prodesse queat instituuntur. Et hoc beneficij genus in filium meum Abrahamum Musculum collatum, haudquaquam dissimulare debeo. Is enim non modò magnà eruditionis suae partem, sed & Magisterij sui gradum Scholae vestrae debet. Est ea quidem à Pio secundo Romano Pontifice, secundum Historicorum commentarios, erecta & confirmata: verum singulari dono Dei factum est, ut seruiat iam non Romano, sed coelesti Pontifici Christo. De Typographia quid dicam, cuius inuentione Dominus Germaniam nostram tum temporis decorare coepit, cum in propinquo esset, ut & barbariem, errorum matrem, eliminaret, & mysterium iniquitatis, quod in Ecclesia saeculis iam aliquot omnium licentiosissimè grassatum est, detegeret? Propter luculentissima Typographiae commoda urbem vestram merito amant, & laudibus extollunt omnes, cum eruditi, tum pij. In hac enim illa potiorem quam habet in Germa-
units.tr: I am well aware that the whole Swiss nation deserves the highest regard on many grounds, yet I cherish and embrace with particular affection, and not without good reason, those whom the sharing of the Gospel truth and the fellowship of sound faith have joined somewhat more closely to me in our common Saviour, Christ the Lord. If I could add anything to the fame and reputation of these men, I acknowledge that I am bound to that duty, I declare that I am ready to discharge what I owe, and I would gladly do from my heart whatever I could do here, if my talent were as great as my willingness to serve. Among these men your city, truly Basel, the royal city, holds no minor place. It is famous far and wide, and not only for its age; it is also dear, above all, to Christ the Lord, King of kings, because of the purity of the Christian religion and faith. In this city, besides the other gifts of God, we must greatly esteem, first, the distinguished Church, reformed by the grace of God through the labour and ministry of most devout men, according to the rule of the Gospel teaching. In this work some have planted, others have watered, and faithfully cooperated with the Lord, and still some pious and learned brethren, not unworthy of their office and equipped with fitting gifts, continue to cooperate. For their labours I pray the Lord's blessing. After the Church, I come to the renown of your Academy, furnished with every kind of discipline, in which, through its outstanding professors of the liberal arts and of sacred theology, the talents of young men, not only of your own citizens but also of foreigners, are cultivated with no little success and trained so that they may in time be of service to the churches and the commonwealth. This benefit, conferred on my son Abraham Musculus, I must by no means pass over in silence. For he owes to your school not only a large part of his learning but also the degree of his master's office. This school was indeed founded and confirmed by Pius II, Roman Pontiff, according to the records of the historians; but by a singular gift of God it has come about that he now serves not the Roman pontiff but Christ, the heavenly Pontiff. What shall I say of printing, by whose invention the Lord began at that time to adorn our Germany, when it was near at hand that it should both eliminate barbarism, the mother of errors, and expose the mystery of iniquity, which for several centuries had raged most unrestrainedly in the Church? Because of the most excellent advantages of printing, both learned and pious men rightly love your city and extol it with praise. For in this city printing has long ago fixed a seat more prominent than it has in the rest of Germany, not without a singular counsel of God.

units.la: Germania sedem iam olim nō sine singulari consilio Dei fixit: cui eximiā operam suam non solùm Frobeniana domus, singulari artis huius industria ac sedulitate clara, sed & multi alij industrij ac præstantes Typographi sedulo contulerunt: è quibus haud postremus extitit Ioannes Heruagius, piæ recordationis, uir eximius, mihiq; à multis annis admodum amicus, cuius uestigijs hæredes Ioannem Heruagium & Bernardum Brand, amicos clarissimos, dextrè in bæsuros spero. Quis autem condignè explicuerit quàm multis illi, quàm uarijs, quàm præclaris & utilibus monumentis omnes artis suæ cōpendio repleuerint ac ditarint nationes, effecerintq;, ut non in plateis tantùm, sed & in toto passim orbe Sapientia clamare, & ad disciplinam suam rudes & imperitos uocare coeperit? Quid aliud doctissimum Erasmum Basileam pellexit, quàm insignis Typographiæ commoditas? Delectatus quidē est & cœli uestri puritate, urbis q; amoenitate: uerū quàm sit Typographicis emolumentis sedulò ac feliciter usus, haud opus est ut commemorem. Quid de insigni Christi organo dicam, qui haud nomine tantùm, sed & re ipsa Oecolampadius erat, uir pius & doctus, uir clarus nomine utroq;, Lampas clara domus ô Basilea tuæ? Duobus hisce rectè coniunxero eruditissimū Simonem Grynæum, cuius ingenium & eruditionem in conuentu VVormaciensi Anno millesimo, quingentesimo, quadragesimo, multi boni, & haud indocti uiri exosculabantur. Trium istorum cineres sub eodem apud uos tecto nō sine singulari munere Dei asseruātur. Celebratur iamdiu nescio quis locus, in quo triū Magorum corpora quiescere dicuntur. Quod si Magi sunt quos singularis sapientia reddit illustres, reuera felix poteris Basilea uideri, omnino Magis nobilitata tribus. Verùm ne, quod nemini non est manifestum, studiosius persequar urbis uestræ felicitatem doctioribus, & ad hanc causam prosequendam instructioribus permittens, præsentis instituti mei consilium paucis expediā. Ambas Apostoli Epistolas ad Corinthios scriptas, in Scholæ nostræ collegio hic Bernæ ęs potui, feliciter explicui, & explicationem illarum in hosce quos uidetis Commentarios redegi. Et quoniam ante annos aliquot scripta mea in urbe uestra per supradictum Heruagium imprimi, uulgariq; cœperunt: hæc quoque usum est consueto prælo subijcere, & publico usui destinare. Ne uerò perpetuò commodis urbis uestræ, quibus ego quoq; cum multis alijs bene sum usus, ingratus uidear: uisum est, Viri præstantissimi, laborem hunc meum nomini uestro ad hoc nuncupare, ut aliquasaltem ratione animi mei erga Ecclesiam, Rempublicam, Academiam, & uniuersam simul urbem uestram, propensionem ac gratitudinem declarem. Hoc consilium meum ut æqui boniq; consulatis, & nuncupatum uobis opus, qua estis humanitate præditi, amanter complectamini oro. Christus Dominus, communis noster Seruator, concedat Vobis, Vrbi, Ecclesiæ & Academiæ uestræ, rerum omnium in hisce exulceratis temporibus tranquillitatem ac prosperitatem, cum primis uerò constantem in ueritate Dei, ac uera pietate progressum. Bernæ Heluetiorum, Anno millesimo quingentesimo, quinquagesimo nono, ultima Ianuarij.
units.tr: Diligent work has been contributed to this art, which is famous for its singular skill and industry, not only by the Froben house but also by many other busy and excellent printers. Among these, no small figure was Johannes Herwagen, of pious memory, an outstanding man and for many years a very close friend of mine. I hope that his heirs, Johannes Herwagen and Bernhard Brand, illustrious friends, will skilfully follow in his footsteps. But who could fully explain how many, how varied, and how splendid and useful monuments they have filled and enriched the nations with, in brief summary of their whole art, and how they have brought it about that Wisdom has begun to cry out not only in the streets but throughout the whole world, calling the untrained and unskilled to her discipline? What else drew the most learned Erasmus to Basel, but the notable convenience of printing? He was indeed delighted both by the purity of your sky and the pleasantness of your city; but how diligently and successfully he made use of the advantages of printing, there is no need for me to recount. What shall I say of that remarkable instrument of Christ, who was Oecolampadius not only in name but in fact, a man pious and learned, a man renowned in both names, O Basel, bright lamp of your house? I rightly add to these two the most learned Simon Grynaeus, whose talent and learning many good and by no means unlearned men embraced with kisses at the Worms conference in the year 1540. The ashes of these three are preserved under one roof with you, not without a singular gift of God. For a certain place, I know not which, has long been celebrated as the resting place of the bodies of the three Magi. But if those are Magi whom singular wisdom makes illustrious, you may truly be thought fortunate, Basel, ennobled by three Magi indeed. However, lest I pursue at too great length what is plain to everyone, the happiness of your city, leaving its further praise to abler men better equipped for the task, I shall briefly set out the purpose of my present undertaking. I have been able to expound, with success, in the college of our school here at Bern, the two Epistles of the Apostle to the Corinthians, and I have put that exposition into these commentaries which you see. And since some years ago my writings began to be printed and circulated in your city through the aforesaid Herwagen, I have also resolved to submit this work to the usual press and to make it available for public use. So that I may not seem ungrateful for the advantages of your city, of which I too have made good use together with many others, I have thought fit, most distinguished sirs, to dedicate this labour of mine to your name, so that at least in some measure I may declare my affection and gratitude toward your Church, Commonwealth, Academy, and the whole city of yours together. I beg you to take this my purpose in good part, and to embrace kindly the work dedicated to you, as you are endowed with your accustomed courtesy. May Christ the Lord, our common Saviour, grant to you, to your city, Church, and Academy, tranquillity and prosperity in all things in these troubled times, and above all, steady progress in the truth of God and in true piety. At Bern in Switzerland, in the year 1559, the last day of January.

units.la: PRAEFATIO VVOLFGANGI MVSCVLI DE ARGVMENTO Epistolae.
units.tr: Preface of Wolfgang Musculus on the Subject of the Epistle.

units.la: [I]Clesiam Corinthiorum Paulus tāto fructu ac studio plantauerat, ut potissimam Apostolatus sui gloriam in illis haberet, illosque sibi praecipuè uendicaret, dicens: Etsi alijs non sum, uobis tamen sum Apostolus. Apud hos egerat annum & menses sex, quòd diuina esset uisione admonitus, in ea ciuitate magnum esse eorum numerum, qui ad dominum essent accessuri: qua de re in Actis cap.18. legere licet. Seditione uero per obstinatos & improbos Iudaeos aduersus ipsum mota, ubi fratres in doctrina & fide Christi confirmasset, discessit. Post discessum uero ipsius, circumuenti à pseudopostolis à syncera pietatis conuersione, in sectas & uaria uicia defecerant. Itaque ut ad institutum illos reuocaret, & emendaret, hanc epistolam ad eos admodum argumentosam scripsit ut quidam uolunt, ex Epheso, quemadmodum habet & Graeca praefatio, & ea quoq; quae Hieronymo datur: uel, ut alij sentiunt, nempe Graecorum codices, è Philippis per Timotheum, Stephanam, Fortunatum, & Achaicum. Erant autem, quae in Corinthijs hac epistola corrigenda putauit, nec modica, nec minuta, sed multa, uaria & haud dissimulanda uicia, adeo ut mirum sit, quomodo ecclesia à tam insigni Apostolo, tam diligenter ac prolixè instituta, tot potuerit modis tam breui absentiae ipsius spacio labefactari & corrumpi. Sed uideamus ex ordine singula.
units.tr: The Apostle Paul had planted the church of the Corinthians with such fruit and zeal that he took his greatest glory in his apostleship from them, and he claimed them especially for himself, saying: "Even if I am not an apostle to others, I am nevertheless an apostle to you." He stayed among them for a year and six months, because a divine vision had told him that in that city there was a great number of those who were about to come to the Lord. You may read about this in Acts chapter 18. But when a rebellion was stirred up against him by obstinate and wicked Jews, he left, after strengthening the brothers in the teaching and faith of Christ. After his departure, however, they were drawn away by false apostles from the sincere conversion to godliness, and they fell into factions and various vices. So, in order to call them back to their duty and correct them, he wrote this very closely argued letter to them. Some hold that he wrote it from Ephesus, as the Greek preface states, and as the one attributed to Jerome also says. Others think, as the Greek manuscripts have it, that it was sent from Philippi through Timothy, Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus. The faults he thought needed correcting in the Corinthians in this letter were not small or trivial, but many, various and not to be passed over. It is remarkable how a church so carefully and fully instructed by so distinguished an apostle could be shaken and corrupted in so many ways in such a short time of his absence. But let us look at each matter in order.

units.la: 1 Primùm contentione, dissidijs & sectis tanquam carnales, & nimium inflati laborabant, ita ut in diuersas partes diuisi, quasi capita quaedam sectarum erexerint, à quibus pendebant, & quibus nominetenus quoque accenseri uolebant: utpote quasi à Paulo pendentes quidam dicerēt, ego sum Pauli: alij à Cepha, ego sum Cephae: alij ab Apollo, ego sum Apollo: ita scilicet à pseudapostolis pendedant in partes miserè scissi, ac de illis quique gloriabantur, à quibus erant uel baptizati, uel alias denentati, perinde ac si non essent satis perfectam doctrinam ab Apostolo suo consecuti. Huc plurimùm faciebat opum abundantia, morum corruptio, & ingeniorum curiositas: deinde & philosophiae studium, quòd in ea urbe, ut Chrysostomus annotat, multi essent oratores & philosophi. Vrbs erat magna, opulenta & celebris. Quare & mores illic, sicuti fieri solet, corruptio res erant, & incolatum illius amplectebantur cupidè oratores, sapientes ac philosophi, uerbis splendidis magis, quàm factis pijs & honestis studentes: quorum uerbis & hypocrisi fiebat, ut integritas ecclesiae rumperetur. Duae nanque magnę sunt ecclesiarum pestes, philosophi & pseudapostoli. Isti pesti occurrit primo loco, & merito. Est enim omnium exitiosissima. Hoc facit capite 1. 2. 3. & 4.
units.tr: 1. First, as carnal and overly puffed up, they were labouring under contention, dissensions and factions. They were divided into different parties, and as if they had raised up certain heads of sects, they depended on these and wished even to be named after them. Thus some said, as if they depended on Paul: "I am of Paul"; others, "I am of Cephas"; others, "I am of Apollos." In this way they were wretchedly torn into parties, depending on the false apostles, and each boasted of the one by whom he had been baptised or otherwise instructed, as if they had not obtained a sufficiently complete teaching from their own apostle. The abundance of wealth, the corruption of morals and the curiosity of minds contributed greatly to this. Next there was the study of philosophy, since in that city, as Chrysostom notes, there were many orators and philosophers. The city was large, wealthy and famous. Hence morals there, as usually happens, were corrupt, and orators, wise men and philosophers eagerly made it their home, pursuing splendid words more than pious and honourable deeds. Through their words and hypocrisy the unity of the church was broken. For there are two great plagues of churches: philosophers and false apostles. The Apostle rightly confronts this plague first, since it is the most destructive of all. He does this in chapters 1 to 4.

units.la: 2 Deinde, quoniam opulentiam plerunq; sequitur delicatae uitae mollities, maximè in scortationis impuritate: ususueniebat, ut Corinthij etiam Christiani facti ueterem & consuetā immunditiem retinerent, ita ut talis scortatio, qualis apud ipsos erat, ne inter gentes quidem audiretur. Qua in re uidemus quàm sit facilius, externas religionis formas mutare, quàm consuetas uitae corruptelas abijcere. Id mali corrigit capite quinto & sexto.
units.tr: 2. Next, since wealth is generally followed by the softness of a pampered life, especially in the impurity of fornication, it happened that the Corinthians, even though they had become Christians, kept their old and customary uncleanness, so that such fornication as existed among them was not heard of even among the Gentiles. In this we see how much easier it is to change the outward forms of religion than to cast off the habitual corruptions of life. He corrects this evil in chapters 5 and 6.

units.la: 3 Tertiò, ut fieri solet inter eos qui opibus colligendis student, uigebat inter Corinthios Christianos lites iudiciariae, idq; sub impijs, & à Christo alienis iudicibus, ad opprobrium Christianae religionis, dum alius alij fraudem faciebat, & quisque ius suum persequebatur, nec erat, qui iniuriam à fratre illatam patienter ferendam esse cogitaret. Hoc emendat cap. 6. Et utin m id mali sic emendatum esset ab Apostolo semel, ut postea non esset in ecclesias postliminio reductum.
units.tr: 3. Thirdly, as usually happens among those who strive to gather wealth, lawsuits were rife among the Christian Corinthians, and these were brought before impious judges who were alien to Christ, to the reproach of the Christian religion. One defrauded another, and each pursued his own right, and there was no one who thought that an injury done by a brother should be borne patiently. He corrects this in chapter 6. And this evil was corrected by the Apostle once for all, so that afterwards it was not brought back into the churches.

units.la: 4 Quartò, & hoc agebat Satan, ut publicam legitimi coniugij honestatem labefactando religionem Christi Gentibus & Iudaeis etiam hoc nomine odiosam ac detestabilem redderet. Sic induxit quosdam è numero credentium, qui religionis & continentiae praetextu uxores suas, pertaesi forsan, relinquerent, quasi maximè in impari coniugio, illicitum esset Christiano cohabitare uxori ac liberis. Et hac de re uidetur Corinthiorum quidam Paulo scripsisse. Instruit igitur & hic illos, docens matrimonia non esse conuellenda, ne imparia quidem, nisi nolit cohabitare infidelis fideli. Et consulit quidem de uirginitate amplectenda, sed id ea cautione, ne quem laqueum simplicioribus inijciat. Hanc causam tractat cap. 7. idque non sine singulari consilio spiritus sancti magna diligentia ac fuse. Erat enim ea correctio non modò Corinthiorum tum temporis ecclesiae necessaria, sed & omnibus caeteris in posterum contra Satanae studia admodum utilis futura.
units.tr: 4. Fourthly, Satan was also at work here, so that by undermining the public honour of lawful marriage he might make the religion of Christ hateful and detestable both to Gentiles and to Jews on this account. Thus he led some of the believers, who perhaps grew weary of their wives under the pretext of religion and continence, to abandon them, as if it were unlawful for a Christian to live with a wife and children, especially in a mixed marriage. It seems that some of the Corinthians wrote to Paul about this matter. So he instructs them here too, teaching that marriages must not be dissolved, not even mixed ones, unless the unbelieving partner is unwilling to live with the believing one. He does indeed give counsel about embracing virginity, but with such caution that he does not cast a snare for the simpler sort. He treats this matter in chapter 7, and does so with great care and at length, and not without the singular counsel of the Holy Spirit. For this correction was not only necessary at that time for the church of the Corinthians, but would also be very useful in future for all others against the designs of Satan.

units.la: 5 Quintò, quoniam Christiani inter Gentes incredulos & eidololatras sub impijs magistratibus habitabant, & templa celebria adhuc erant in usu & potestate eidololatrarum, quibus moris erat mactare pecudes dijs suis, coramque illorum imaginibus in ipsis templis conuiuari: usuueniebat, ut ad gentium impia conuiuia uocarentur, & Christiani partim per ignorantiam, quod nondum quòd Christiani essent, cognosceretur, partim dolo, ut quales essent probarentur, uel etiam à Christianismo reuocarentur. Hic qui de libertate Christiana gloriabantur, & quacunque ratione, ne offenderent, gratificari studebant amicis, & forsan, ut & crucem declinarent, iungebant se templarijs Gentium conuiuijs, praetexentes eidolum nihil esse, eidolis immolare bonas Dei creaturas, & res externas, quæ neminem interne polluant, esse ad uescendum liberas, atque hoc præpostero libertatis usu grauiter offendebant infirmiores, fidemq; suam & conscientias maculabant, & interim infideles in errore confirmabant. Hos reuocat ad faniora cap. 8. 9. 10.
units.tr: 5. Fifthly, since Christians lived among unbelieving Gentiles and idolaters under impious magistrates, and since famous temples were still in use and under the control of idolaters, where it was customary to slaughter cattle for their gods and to feast before the images of those gods in the temples themselves, it happened that Christians were invited to the impious banquets of the Gentiles. Some did this out of ignorance, since it was not yet known that they were Christians; others did it by deceit, in order to prove what sort of people they were, or even to be called back from Christianity. Those who boasted of Christian liberty, and who, for whatever reason, eagerly sought to please their friends so as not to give offence, and perhaps also so as to avoid the cross, joined in the feasts of the Gentiles in their temples. They pretended that an idol is nothing, that the good creatures of God and external things, which do not inwardly defile anyone, are free to be eaten even when offered to idols. By this perverse use of liberty they gravely offended the weaker brothers, stained their faith and consciences, and meanwhile confirmed the unbelievers in their error. He calls these people back to sounder views in chapters 8, 9 and 10.

units.la: 6 Sextò, pro more Mercurialium delicatorum, in quo erant & nati & educati, & cui in templis eidolorum assueuerant, uiri comas nutriebant, & tectis capitibus in ecclesia precabantur: mulieres uero nudis capitibus in ecclesijs comparebant, quod & naturæ & decoro sexus reclamabat. Hoc arguit cap. 11. Hieron. in prologo secundi libri Commentariorum quos in Epistolam ad Galatas scripsit, hæc usque adeo non esse Apostolica correctione emendata scribit, ut ad suam usque ætatem in ecclesijs Achaiæ duraverint.
units.tr: 6. Sixthly, after the manner of the effeminate devotees of Mercury, in whose habits they had been born and brought up, and to which they had become accustomed in the temples of idols, men were letting their hair grow long, and praying in the church with covered heads. Women, on the other hand, appeared in the churches with bare heads, which was contrary both to nature and to the dignity of their sex. He argues against this in chapter 11. Jerome, in the preface to the second book of his Commentaries which he wrote on the Epistle to the Galatians, writes that these things were not corrected by the Apostle's instruction to such a degree that they lasted in the churches of Achaia even down to his own time.

units.la: 7 Septimo, quoniam non modò abiecta philadelphia, dissidebant animis interne, sed & externe scisi erant in sectas, ne in ipsa quidem dominica Cœna concordiam seruabat, sed quasi ad carnale quoddam epulum & seculare conuiuium collecti, alius inebriabatur, alius esuriebat, & qui ditiores erant, seorsum suas cœnas contempta ecclesia Christi præsumebant: atq; ita efficiebant, ut nihil ipsi de Cœna domini nisi solum nomen restaret, & conuentus ecclesiastici non in melius sed in deterius abirent. Iltam dominicæ Cœnæ corruptionem per authoritatem ac declarationem institutionis Christi corrigit, adiectis minis contra eos qui de hoc pane manducabant & de calice domini bibebant indigne. Id facit cap. 11. magno serio, pro magnitudine mali, exprobrando, redarguendo, exponendo, comminando & hortando. Antiqua planè est ista dominicæ Cœnæ prophanatio, quæ non ab Apostolo tantum, sed & multis pijs patribus reprehensa, nunquam emendari sustinuit, sed perpetuo in peius abiens, tandem supremas obtinuit, & omnem correctionis spem exclusit.
units.tr: 7. Seventhly, since brotherly love was not only cast aside, but they were also divided inwardly in their minds and outwardly split into factions, they did not even keep harmony at the Lord's Supper. Gathered as if for some carnal feast and worldly banquet, one became drunk, another went hungry, and the richer ones presumed to hold their own suppers apart, despising the church of Christ. And so they brought it about that nothing of the Lord's Supper remained but the name, and the ecclesiastical assemblies went not for the better but for the worse. He corrects this corruption of the Lord's Supper by the authority and declaration of Christ's institution, adding threats against those who eat of this bread and drink of the cup of the Lord unworthily. He does this in chapter 11, with great earnestness, in proportion to the magnitude of the evil, by rebuking, refuting, explaining, threatening and exhorting. This profanation of the Lord's Supper is truly ancient, and it was condemned not only by the Apostle but also by many pious Fathers. It never allowed itself to be corrected, but, going steadily downhill, it at last gained the upper hand and shut out every hope of correction.

units.la: 8 Octauò, propter charismata quædam peculiaria, maximè linguarum, plerique in ecclesia Corinthiorum ad contemptum reliquorum insolescebant, & conuentus ecclesiasticos confundebant, ac inutiles planè reddebant, alienis linguis psallentes, & prophetantes. Contra hunc abusum declarat rationem & usum donorum spiritus, potissimum linguarum, & per occasionem adpotiora charismata, uidelicet fidem, spem & charitatem hortatur. Hoc facit cap. 12. 13. 14. Hoc loco uehementer mirandum est, quid sibi uoluerint Romani, quòd linguam suam Germanis in religione obtruserunt, cum nihil in ea esset, nec hodie sit eius charismatis, quo tempore apostolorum plerique per miraculum alijs atque alijs sunt linguis usi. Nunquam hoc in animum suum inducere potuissent, si tantopere doctrinæ Apostolicæ acquieuissent, quantopere Apostolici uideri uolunt.
units.tr: 8 Eighthly, because of certain special gifts, especially tongues, many in the Corinthian church grew arrogant toward the rest, threw their assemblies into confusion, and made them quite useless, singing psalms and prophesying in foreign tongues. Against this abuse he explains the purpose and use of the gifts of the Spirit, especially tongues, and on that occasion he exhorts them to the more excellent gifts, namely faith, hope and love. He does this in chapters 12, 13 and 14. Here one must marvel greatly at what the Romanists meant by forcing their own language on the Germans in religion, when there was nothing of that gift in it, nor is there any today, whereas at the time of the apostles many used different foreign tongues by miracle. They could never have brought this into their minds if they had acquiesced as much in apostolic doctrine as they wish to appear to do.

units.la: 9 Nonò, & hoc licentiæ accesserat, ut fieri solet, ubi omnia pro quorumuis libidine in ecclesia turbantur, ut mulieres conuentibus ecclesiasticis unà cum uiris ex æquo publicæ doctrinæ functionem usurparent, contra status & conditionis muliebris subiectionem ac decorum. Ab eo illas reuocat cap. 14. Accidebat hoc exuberantia spiritus, de qua prædictum erat, Prophetabunt filiæ uestræ. Nos cogitemus quanto serio humanarum adinuentionum luxuries restringenda sit, quando ubertas spiritus, si exorbitet, Apostolica diligentia refrenetur.
units.tr: 9 Ninthly, this licence had also crept in, as usually happens when everything in the church is thrown into disorder at the whim of anyone, so that women, together with men, claimed for themselves the office of public teaching on equal terms, against the subjection and propriety of the female state and condition. He recalls them from this in chapter 14. This came from an excess of the Spirit, of which it had been foretold: "Your daughters shall prophesy." Let us consider how seriously the luxuriance of human inventions must be restrained, when the abundance of the Spirit, if it runs to excess, is curbed by apostolic diligence.

units.la: 10 Postremò, quoniam philosophiæ studio quidam ex illis addicti erant, coeperant & resurrectionem corporum negare. Tales fructus gignit humanæ sapientiæ acumen. Resurrectione mortuorum paucissimi ex sapientibus huius mundi credunt. Nam eam ratio humana comprehendere nequit, quæ philosophiæ quasi quidam fons est: contra istos asserit fidem resurrectionis, eamq; potissimum ex morte & resurrectione Christi affirmat, & quomodo futura sit describit. Hoc agit cap. 15. Argumentis utitur multis & pregnantibus, tanquam in causa, sine qua omnis nostra fides, & uniuersa Christi dispensatio prorsus inutilis sit oportet.
units.tr: 10 Lastly, since some of them were devoted to the study of philosophy, they had begun to deny the resurrection of the body. Such fruits are produced by the subtlety of human wisdom. Few of the wise of this world believe in the resurrection of the dead, for human reason, which is as it were a kind of fountain of philosophy, cannot grasp it. Against these people he asserts faith in the resurrection, and affirms it chiefly from the death and resurrection of Christ, and describes how it will be. He does this in chapter 15. He uses many weighty arguments, as though it were the cause without which all our faith and the whole dispensation of Christ must of necessity be utterly useless.

units.la: Hæc sunt uicia Corinthiorum, quæ necessario corrigenda ueniebant. Ea plenius adhuc sic recenseri possunt, 1 Contentiones & schismata inter se habebant.
units.tr: These are the vices of the Corinthians, which were bound to be corrected. They can be listed more fully as follows:

units.la: 2 Carnales carnaliter sapiebant.
units.tr: 1 They had contentions and schisms among themselves.

units.la: 3 Temerè iudicabant ante tempus.
units.tr: 2 Carnal men thought in a carnal way.

units.la: 4 Alius contra alium inflabatur.
units.tr: 3 They judged rashly before the time.

units.la: 5 Scortationem habebant, qualem nec gentes admittebant.
units.tr: 4 One was puffed up against another.

units.la: 6 Peccatum illud nec corrigebant, nec deplorabant.
units.tr: 5 They tolerated fornication of a kind not even the Gentiles allowed.

units.la: 7 Iudicijs coram incredulis certabant.
units.tr: 6 They neither corrected that sin nor lamented it.

units.la: 8 Iniurijs alius alium lædebat.
units.tr: 7 They brought lawsuits before unbelievers.

units.la: 9 Eidolothyta edendo infirmos offendebant.
units.tr: 8 One wronged another with injuries.

units.la: 10 Mulieres non uelatæ Ecclesiam intrabant.
units.tr: 10 Women who did not veil themselves were entering the Church.

units.la: 11 Schismata etiam in Cœnam dominicam inferebant, seipsi non probabant, corpus Domini non dijudicabant, alius ebrius erat, alius esuriebat, inuicem non expectabant.
units.tr: 11 They also introduced schisms into the Lord's Supper: they did not test themselves, did not discern the body of the Lord, one was drunk, another was hungry, and they did not wait for one another.

units.la: 12 Donis spiritus abutebantur.
units.tr: 12 They abused the gifts of the Spirit.

units.la: 13 Linguis operam dantes, charitatem negligebant.
units.tr: 13 Devoting their efforts to tongues, they neglected love.

units.la: 14 Mulieres in ecclesia docere præsumebant.
units.tr: 13 While they busied themselves with tongues, they neglected love.

units.la: 15 Ordinem prophetandi in Ecclesia confundebant.
units.tr: 14 Women presumed to teach in the church.

units.la: 16 Resurrectionem mortuorum nonnulli negabant.
units.tr: 15 They threw the order of prophesying in the church into confusion.

units.la: Ignorantiam Dei quidam habebant. Et ultra hæc omnia uocat eos Ecclesiam Dei, & uocatos sanctos. Quid uocarent hodie talem Ecclesiam Anabaptistæ?
units.tr: 16 Some denied the resurrection of the dead.

units.la: Vltimo capite de collectis in usus sanctorum faciendis quædam commemorat, & præterea Timotheum illis, Stephanam, Fortunatum & Achaicum commendat, ac pro exemplaribus, quos imitentur, proponit, atque ita suo more salutandi adiecto officio Epistolam claudit.
units.tr: Some had no knowledge of God. And beyond all these things he calls them the church of God and the called saints. What would the Anabaptists today call such a church?

units.la: Nemo debet igitur exigere, ut certus quidam scopus ac status huius Epistolæ tradatur, cum in ea Apostolus de rebus tam uarijs differat.
units.tr: In the last chapter he mentions certain things concerning the collections to be made for the needs of the saints, and besides, he commends to them Timothy, Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus, and sets them forth as examples for them to imitate. Thus, adding a greeting in his usual manner, he closes the Epistle.

units.la: Nobis tamen ex istis quæ paucis perstrinxi, obseruandum est, quàm cito status Ecclesiæ, etiam ab Apostolo institutæ, corrumpatur: ut cauti simus, nec credamus illis, qui hodie asserunt Ecclesiam errare non posse.
units.tr: Therefore no one ought to demand that some fixed aim and state of this Epistle be laid down, since in it the Apostle discusses matters so various.

units.la: Quod autem hæc Epistola ei quæ ad Romanos est, ordine subijcitur, non ideo factum est à ueteribus, quòd tempore quoque illam subsequatur, cum eam magis tempore præcedat. Nam ea quæ ad Romanos est, nullas alias præcedit, nisi eas quas ex vinculis Romæ scripsit: ut sunt, ad Philippenses, ad Timotheum, ad Ebræos, ut Chrysostomus sentit, & ad Philemonem. Præposita autem est reliquis Epistola ad Romanos, quod in ea potissimum totius Christianæ fidei scopus aliquanto dexterius ac diligentius traditus est.
units.tr: Yet from these things which I have touched on briefly, we must observe how quickly the state of the church, even one established by the Apostle, becomes corrupted, so that we may be cautious and not believe those who today assert that the church cannot err.

units.la: Hæc paucis præfari libuit, quo Lector statim initio Epistolæ huius argumentum sic in compendio habeat, ut simul potiora illius membra singulatim & ex ordine intelligat. Sic enim praemonitus, certiorem poterit inter legendum retinere cursum: & quę legerit non modo intelligere facilius, sed & ex præmonstrata dispositione memoriæ certius & minori negocio commendare.
units.tr: That this Epistle is placed in order after the one to the Romans was not done by the ancients because it follows it in time, when it rather precedes it in time. For the one to the Romans precedes no others except those which he wrote from the chains at Rome, such as those to the Philippians, to Timothy, to the Hebrews, as Chrysostom holds, and to Philemon. But the Epistle to the Romans was placed before the rest because in it the aim of the whole Christian faith is set forth somewhat more skilfully and carefully.

units.la: Est hæc Epistola omnium accommodatissima Ecclesijs uel schismate, uel malis moribus, uel ritibus adulterinis corruptis. Quare nostra hac ætate diligenter est ac sedulò uersanda, illis præsertim, quorum est ex officio curam gerere Ecclesiarum, & quæ in illis corrigenda ueniunt corrigere. Verùm (proh dolor) tam abest hodie, ut sic animati sint Ecclesiarum præsides, ut nemo magis prolapsæ religionis reformationem auersetur & impediat: cuius necessitatem plerique illorum ne agnoscere quidem sustinent, partim ne hactenus erasse uideantur, partim ne non ritus tantum tam fœde corruptos, sed & seipsos cum primis emendare, & in ordinem redire cogantur. Quare orandus est Dominus, ut ipse gregis sui quem sanguine suo redemit, curam gerat, & pastores largiatur syncEros ac fideles, quibus maior sit cura præstandi officij, quàm uel proprij nominis uel quæstus.
units.tr: I have been pleased to say these few things by way of preface, so that the reader, from the very beginning of this Epistle, may have its argument in summary, and at the same time understand its principal parts one by one and in order. For thus forewarned he will be able to keep a surer course while reading, and to commit to memory what he has read not only more easily understood, but also more certainly and with less effort, from the arrangement previously shown. This Epistle is most suited to churches either disturbed by schism, or corrupted by bad morals, or by adulterated rites. Therefore in our own age it must be studied diligently and earnestly, especially by those whose office it is to bear care for the churches and to correct what needs correcting in them. But (alas!) so far is it today from being the case that the presidents of the churches are so inspired, that no one resists and hinders the reform of a fallen religion more: most of them cannot bear even to acknowledge its necessity, partly lest they seem to have erred hitherto, partly lest they be compelled not only to amend rites so foully corrupted, but also themselves first, and to return to order. Therefore the Lord must be prayed to, that he himself may take care of his flock, which he redeemed with his own blood, and grant sincere and faithful ministers, for whom the care of performing their office is greater than that of their own name or gain.

units.la: PRAEFATIONIS DE ARGVMENTO EPISTOLAE FINIS.
units.tr: The End of the Preface on the Argument of the Epistle.

units.la: COMMENTARII VVOLFGANGI MVSCVLI DVSANI, IN PRIOREM EPISTOLAM PAVLI AD CORINTHIOS.
units.tr: COMMENTARIES OF WOLFGANG MUSCULUS OF DIEUZE, ON THE FIRST EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM CAP.
units.tr: ARGUMENT OF THE CHAPTER

units.la: {1}OC capite Apostolus post salutatio nis officium primũ Corinthios, quos erat propter sectarum studium ob- iurgaturus,per encomiũ gratiæ Dei quam in Christo acceperant, comen dat,quam se tanti facere dicit, ut perpetuas illius nomi ne Deo gratias agat. Deinde illos per obsecrationem & nominis Domini Iesu Christi obtestationem ad stu- dium concordiæ hortatur. Tertio, cur huius admo- neat,per narrationem subiungit,quomodo audierit se- ctas inter ipsos esse, ad quarum studium amoliendum, contra supercilia humanæ sapientiæ & falsæ sanctimo niæ, extollit Euangelicæ doctrinæ & uocationis sim- plicitatẽ,per quam Deus & credentes seruare, & pru dentes, potentes ac nobiles huius mundi pudefacere uoluerit.
units.tr: In this chapter the Apostle, after the customary greeting, first commends the Corinthians, whom he was about to rebuke for their zeal for factions, by praising the grace of God that they had received in Christ. He says he values it so highly that he gives God unending thanks for it. Then he exhorts them by entreaty and by invoking the name of the Lord Jesus Christ to pursue concord. Third, he explains by narrative why he gives this admonition: he has heard that there are factions among them. To remove their zeal for these, he sets the simplicity of the Gospel doctrine and calling against the haughtiness of human wisdom and false holiness, by which God wished to save believers and to shame the wise, the powerful and the noble of this world.

units.la: CAPVT PRIMVM.
units.tr: CHAPTER ONE

units.la: PAVLVS uocatus Apostolus Iesu Christi per uoluntatem Dei, & Sosthenes frater Ecclesiæ Dei, quæ est Corinthi, sanctifica- tis per Christum Ie- sum, uocatis sanctis, unà cum omnibus qui inuocãt nomen Domini nostri Iesu Christi, in quouis loco, uel suo uel no- stro. Gratia uobis & pax à Deo patre nostro, & Domino Iesu Christo.
units.tr: Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother, to the Church of God which is at Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, together with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, both theirs and ours: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: 1 VOCATVS Apostolus.] Nõ idem est, atq; nominatus uel dictus Apostolus, uel qui uo- cor Apostolus: sed uocatus ad munus Aposto- licũ, ut & Eras. Rom.1. uertit. Neq; enim quid nominetur, quisue dicatur apud homines, ad- modum commendat: sed ad quam functionẽ à Deo uocatus sit, nusquam nõ inculcat. Nam hoc plurimum ad authoritatẽ doctrinæ Euan gelicæ faciebat, non ultro cucurrisse, sed à Deo uocatum & missum esse. De pseudoprophetis traditur, quod neq; uocati, neq; missi cucurre- rint, adeoque ex Deo non prophetauerint. Vt itaq; persuadeat doctrinam suam esse ex Deo, mox initio epistolæ contra pseudoapostolos commendat Apostolatus sui uocationem.
units.tr: 1 CALLED to be an apostle. This is not the same as being named or said to be an apostle, or as being an apostle by my own description; it means called to the apostolic office, as Erasmus also translates it in Romans 1. For he does not much commend what he is named or what people call him; but he never fails to stress to what office God has called him. For this contributed greatly to the authority of the Gospel doctrine: that he had not run of his own accord, but had been called and sent by God. Of false prophets it is recorded that they ran without being called or sent, and therefore did not prophesy from God. So that he might persuade them that his doctrine is from God, at the very start of the epistle he sets forth, against the false apostles, the calling of his apostleship.

units.la: 2 PER uoluntatem Dei.] Hoc ferè in omni- bus epistolis inculcat. Et merito. Neque enim ab hominibus uel per homines, sed per Iesum Christum magno miraculo cœlitus uocatus e- rat, unde de uoluntate Dei certus erat factus. Tam enim aberat ut hác dignitatem ambiret, ut magis totam hanc religionem conatus sit pro uiribus subuertere. Hac de re uidere est Act. 9. ubi sic legimus: Saulus autẽ adhuc mi- nas ac cædes spirans in discipulos Domini, ac- cesit ad principem sacerdotum, & petijt ab eo epistolas in Damascum ad synagogas, ut si quos inuenisset huius uiæ uiros ac mulieres, uinctos perduceret in Hierusalem. Et cum iter faceret, contigit ut appropinquaret Damasco. Et subito circumfulsit eum lux de cœlo. Et ca- dens in terram, audiuit uocem dicentem sibi: Saule Saule, quid me persequeris? Hæc ibi, un- de satis apparet, in eo ipsum magis fuisse, ut fi- dem in Christum euerteret, quàm ut Apostolatum illius ambiret.
units.tr: 2 BY the will of God. He stresses this in nearly all his epistles, and rightly so. For he had been called not by men or through men, but by Jesus Christ, by a great miracle from heaven, and so he was certain of the will of God. He was so far from seeking this dignity that he rather strove with all his strength to overthrow this whole religion. On this matter see Acts 9, where we read as follows: "But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any men or women of this Way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. And as he journeyed, it happened that he drew near to Damascus. And suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. And falling to the earth, he heard a voice saying to him: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" From this it is sufficiently clear that his aim was rather to overthrow faith in Christ than to seek the apostleship for himself.

units.la: 3 ET Sosthenes frater.] De illo legimus Act. 18. quomodo apud proconsulem Achaiæ Gal- lionem, facto tumultu Corinthi sit à Græcis percussus, cũ esset princeps synagogæ. Quam- obrem uero percussus sit à Græcis, à Luca non memoratur: unde & diuersa hic est opinio, qui busdam putantibus hoc factum esse in gratiam Pauli, eo quòd aduersum hunc pro Iudæis fe- cerit: cuius sententiæ est Chrysostomus, ex eo forsan motus, quod seditio memoratur à Iu- dæis contra Paulum mota, & quod ille fuerit synagogæ princeps: alijs uero arbitrantibus il lum percussum esse ut Christianũ, & qui Pauli partes iuuerit, adeoq; seditioni causam dederit. Et qui id sentiunt, mouentur ex eo, quod Apostolo in hac epistola in subscriptione iun- ctus est, id quod uerosimilius est. Apparet au- tem illum fuisse uirum pium & cordatum, & qui pro nomine Christi suis relictis & bonis & domesticis Apostolum sit fideliter ac con- stanter in prædicatione Euangelij comitatus. Non est autem præter rationem, quod hunc si- bi initio huius epistolæ coniungit. Reuocat e- nim in memoriam illis qui erant ex circumci- sione fideles, quid hic uir, olim princeps Iudai cæ synagogæ, à sua gente fuerit propter Do- minum perpessus: & proponit illius ipsis exé- plum, quo & ipsi in fide Christi constanter ac fideliter perseuerent. Et uide modestiam Apo- stoli. Quamuis conuerterit hunc Sosthenẽ ad Dominum, haud tamen uocat eum discipulũ, sed fratrem, longe diuersus à pseudapostolis, qui toti in eo erant, ut discipulos post se trahe- rent. Agnoscebat quidem hic Sosthenes Pau- lum pro suo doctore & Apostolo, eamque ob causam illum comitabatur: uerum Paulus illū non habet pro discipulo, sed pro fratre.
units.tr: 3 AND Sosthenes the brother. We read of him in Acts 18, how, when a tumult was raised at Corinth, he was struck by the Greeks before the proconsul of Achaia, Gallio, although he was the leader of the synagogue. Why he was struck by the Greeks is not recorded by Luke; hence opinions differ here. Some think this happened to gratify Paul, because he had acted against him on behalf of the Jews; Chrysostom holds this view, perhaps moved by the fact that the sedition recorded was stirred up by the Jews against Paul, and that Sosthenes was the leader of the synagogue. Others think he was struck as a Christian who had supported Paul's cause, and so had given cause for the uproar. Those who hold this view are moved by the fact that he is joined with the Apostle in the greeting of this epistle, which is the more likely explanation. It appears that he was a pious and sensible man, who, for the name of Christ, left behind his possessions, his goods and his household, and faithfully and steadfastly accompanied the Apostle in preaching the Gospel. It is not beside the point that Paul joins him with himself at the beginning of this epistle. For he recalls to the memory of those who were believers from circumcision what this man, once the leader of a Jewish synagogue, suffered from his own people for the Lord, and he sets his example before them, so that they too may persevere constantly and faithfully in faith in Christ. And observe the modesty of the Apostle. Although he converted this Sosthenes to the Lord, he does not call him a disciple but a brother, quite unlike the false apostles, who were wholly intent on drawing disciples after themselves. Sosthenes indeed acknowledged Paul as his teacher and apostle, and for that reason accompanied him; but Paul does not regard him as a disciple, but as a brother.

units.la: 4 ECCLESIAE Dei, quæ est Corinthi.] Hæc est epigraphe. Non scribit quibusdā separatim, sed communiter toti ecclesiæ. Nam pertinebant ad omnas ex æquo, de quibus scribebat. Qui delinquebāt, erant corrigendi, qui adhuc sani erant, in ea erant integritate, quam retinebant, confirmādi. Ideo communiter omnibus eius ecclesię fidelibus epistolam hāc inscribit. Non agit seorsum cum schismaticis, sed horum morbum in totius ecclesię conscientia curandum esse censet. Pulchrè autem ab inscriptione statim sese accommodat ad caussam quam initio epistolæ tractaturus erat, ecclesiam illos uocans, idque Dei, duplicin omine ad concordiam hortans. Nam ipsum ecclesiæ nomen, unitatem & concordiam includit, sectis repugnans: & quod ecclesiam Dei illos uocat, centra id quasi antidoton est, quod alius, Ego sum Pauli: alius, Ego sum Cephæ, &c. dicebat, cum nullius essent hominis ecclesia, sed Dei.
units.tr: 4 OF the Church of God which is at Corinth. This is the superscription. He does not write to some people separately, but to the whole Church in common. For what he wrote concerned all alike. Those who were going astray had to be corrected, and those who were still sound had to be strengthened in the integrity they maintained. Therefore he addresses this epistle in common to all the faithful of that Church. He does not deal with the schismatics apart, but judges that their disease must be cured within the conscience of the whole Church. Moreover, from the very superscription he aptly adapts himself to the cause he was about to treat at the beginning of the epistle, calling them the Church, and that of God, exhorting them to concord by a double sign. For the very name of Church includes unity and concord, and is opposed to sects. And that he calls them the Church of God is, as it were, an antidote against the saying of one party, "I am of Paul," of another, "I am of Cephas," and so on, when the Church belonged to no man, but to God.

units.la: 5 SANCTIFICATIS p Christū Iesum, uocatis sanctis.] 1 Exponit hac periphrasi, quosnā p ecclesiā Dei intelligat. Erat Corinthi synagoga Iudæorū, quemadmodum Act. 18. patet. Illi se ut populum Dei, ita & ecclesiam esse Dei gloriabantur. Quare ne synagogæ Iudaicæ scribere putetur, mox atque scripsit: Ecclesię Dei, quæ est Corinthi, ad differentiam illius Christianæ ecclesiæ specificationem subiecit dicēs, Sanctificatis per Christum Iesum, uocatis sanctis. In quibus uerbis expressit, quid sit ecclesia Dei. Multitudo uidelicet sanctificatorum per Christum Iesum, ac uocatorum sanctorū. De hac non est ut in præsenti dicamus. Erit de illa ex professo in Locis nostris dicendum. Ad idem autem propositum cōtra sectarios facit, quod sanctificationis per Christum & uocatio nis ad sanctimoniam meminit. Per sanctificationem Chrysostomus intelligit baptismi lauacrum, in quo per Christum sanctificamur, hoc est à mūdo prophano in fidem ac cultum Dei segregamur. Et quoniam ea sanctificatio, & ad sanctimoniam uocatio non fit in nomine ministri alicuius uel docentis uel baptizantis, sed in nomine Christi: ideo commodum contra sectarum studia sanctificatos illos & uocatos sanctos uocat in Christo Iesu, ut est in Græco. Hac ratione & infra dicit, Gratias ago Deo meo, quod neminē uestrum baptizaui, nisi Crispum & Gaium, ne quis dicat quod in nomine meo baptizatus sit.
units.tr: 5 SANCTIFIED in Christ Jesus, called to be saints. By this periphrasis he explains which people he means by the Church of God. At Corinth there was a synagogue of the Jews, as Acts 18 makes clear. They boasted that they were the people of God and so also the Church of God. Therefore, lest it be thought that he was writing to the Jewish synagogue, as soon as he wrote "the Church of God which is at Corinth," he added a specification to distinguish it from the Christian Church, saying "sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints." In these words he expressed what the Church of God is: namely, the multitude of those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be saints. We need not discuss this here at length; it will be treated expressly in our Loci. But what he mentions, sanctification in Christ and the calling to holiness, serves the same purpose against the sectarians. Chrysostom understands by sanctification the washing of baptism, in which we are sanctified through Christ, that is, set apart from the profane world into the faith and worship of God. And since this sanctification and calling to holiness do not happen in the name of some minister, either teaching or baptizing, but in the name of Christ, for this reason, against the zeal of the sects, he calls those sanctified and called to be saints "in Christ Jesus," as it is in the Greek. For this same reason he says below, "I thank God that I baptized none of you, except Crispus and Gaius, lest anyone should say that he was baptized in my name."

units.la: 2 Pulchrè autem commendat gratiam Dei, quod nō simpliciter illos sanctos uocat, quod soli Deo competit: sed sanctificatos, & uocatos sanctos, id est, ad sanctimoniam & gratiam Dei uocatos. Nam hic non prædicatur meritum fidelium, sed magis gratia Dei in Christo. Est enim uocatum sanctum, uel sanctificatum esse, non uirtutis nostræ, sed gratiæ diuinæ titulus & professio. Hac de re Augustinus super illud Psal. 86. Custodi animam meam, quoniā
units.tr: 2 Paul commends the grace of God beautifully here. He does not simply call them saints, which belongs to God alone, but "sanctified" and "called saints," that is, called to holiness and to the grace of God. For this passage does not proclaim the merit of believers but rather the grace of God in Christ. To be called holy or to have been sanctified is a title and a confession of divine grace, not of our own virtue. On this point Augustine, on Psalm 86, "Keep my soul, for I am holy," writes thus:

units.la: sanctus sum, sic scribit: Et hæc quidem fuistis, inquit Apostolus, sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis. Si ergo eos sanctificatos dicit, dicat unusquisque fidelium, sanctus sum. Non est ista superbia elati, sed confessio non ingrati. Si enim dixeris te sanctū esse ex te, superbus es. Rursus fidelis in Christo, & membrum Christi, si te non dixeris esse sanctum, ingratus es. Dic Deo tuo, sanctus sum, qa sanctificasti me, quia accepi, non quia habui: quia tu dedisti, non quia merui. Etenim ex alio latere incipis iniuriam facere ipsi domino nostro Iesu Christo. Si enim Christiani omnes & fideles & baptizati in illo ipsum induerunt, sicut Apostolus dicit: Quotquot in Christū baptizati estis, Christum induistis, si membra facti sunt corporis eius, & dicunt se sanctos non esse, capiti ipsi faciunt iniuriam, cuius membra sancta nō sunt. Iam uide ubi sis, & de capite tuo dignitatem cape. Ergo dicat unusquisque Christianus, imò dicat totum corpus Christi, clamet ubiq; patiens tribulationes, diuersas tentationes & scandala innumerabilia: Custodi animā meam, quoniam sanctus sum. Hæc ille. Non est igitur sanctificatum esse idem, quod iustum ac sine peccato esse.
units.tr: "You were these things indeed, says the Apostle, but you have been washed, you have been sanctified. If, then, he calls them sanctified, let each of the faithful say, I am holy. This is not the pride of one who exalts himself but the confession of one who is not ungrateful. For if you say that you are holy of yourself, you are proud. Again, if you are a believer in Christ and a member of Christ, and do not say that you are holy, you are ungrateful. Say to your God, I am holy, because you have sanctified me: I have received, I have not possessed; you have given, I have not merited. For otherwise you begin to do wrong to our Lord Jesus Christ himself. For if all Christians, both faithful and baptized, have put on him himself, as the Apostle says, 'As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ,' and if they are made members of his body, and yet say that they are not holy, they do wrong to the head itself, whose members are not holy. Now see where you are, and take your dignity from your head. Let therefore every Christian say, nay, let the whole body of Christ say, crying out everywhere amid tribulations, various temptations and countless scandals: Keep my soul, for I am holy." Thus far Augustine. Being sanctified, therefore, is not the same as being just and without sin.

units.la: 3 Notandum ergo ecclesiam tam misere corruptam & scissam, adhuc ab Apostolo uocari ecclesiā Dei, sanctificatos & uocatos sanctos, ut & Christus Act. 18. dixit: Ne timeas, &c. quoniam populus est mihi multus in hac ciuitate. Licet admodū esset ea ecclesia corrupta, erant tamen adhuc in illa synceri ac probati fideles, quorum gratia hic illi titulus competebat.
units.tr: 3 We should note, then, that the Church, so wretchedly corrupted and torn apart, is still called by the Apostle the Church of God, and its members are called sanctified and called saints, just as Christ also said in Acts 18: "Do not be afraid, for I have many people in this city." Although that Church was very corrupt, there were still in it sincere and approved believers, on whose account this title was rightly applied to it.

units.la: 6 VNA cum omnibus, qui inuocat nomē domini nostri Iesu Christi in quouis loco, & ipsorum & nostro.] 1 Non est hoc ita intelligendū, quasi diuidat inuocatores nominis Christi à sanctificatis & uocatis sanctis. Sunt enim planè ijdem. Verūm hoc agit. Ostendit unum esse corpus omnium sanctificatorum in Christo, ubicunq; locorum sint, quod & ipsum fortiter contra sectarū studium pugnat, per quod fit ut etiam unius loci Christiani à se inuicem scindantur ac dissideant, cum corpus Christi, quamuis multis locis dispersum, sit unitum.
units.tr: 6 "Together with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, both theirs and ours." 1 This should not be understood as if he were separating those who call upon the name of Christ from those who are sanctified and called saints. For they are plainly the same people. Rather, his purpose is to show that there is one body of all the sanctified in Christ, wherever they may be, and this also strongly opposes the zeal of the sects, through which it happens that even Christians of a single place are split from one another and at odds, although the body of Christ, though dispersed in many places, is one.

units.la: 2 Illud. Q VI, inuocant nomē domini nostri Iesu Christi.] Diligenter notandum est. Nam aperte tribuit Apostolus Christo diuinitatem, ubi illi dat inuocationem. Omnino nanq; non licet inuocare nisi uerum & unicū Deum. Poterat aliud proferre elogium Christianorum, uerum hoc uoluit ueros ac synceros Christianos uerę ecclesiæ membra exprimere. Hac se nota probent hodie, qui inuocationem diuorum docent. Quare admonemur hic, qua in re censenda sit Christi ecclesia, nempe in inuocatione nominis domini. Quid autem sit inuocare nomen domini, in Rom. cap. 10. declaratum est. Plane adulterinū est, quod hic in commētarijs Hieronymo adscriptis legitur ad hūc modum: Proprie sacerdotum est inuocare dominū, quib. dicitur: Sic benedicite filijs Israel, inuo-
units.tr: 2 "Who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ." This must be carefully noted. For the Apostle plainly ascribes divinity to Christ when he gives him invocation. For it is altogether unlawful to invoke anyone but the true and only God. He could have used some other description of Christians, but he wished to express that true and sincere Christians are the members of the true Church. Those today who teach the invocation of the saints should test themselves by this mark. Hence we are reminded here by what sign the Church of Christ is to be judged, namely by the invocation of the name of the Lord. What it is to call upon the name of the Lord has been explained in Romans 10. It is plainly a spurious addition that is read here in the commentaries ascribed to Jerome, in this manner: "It is properly the work of priests to invoke the Lord, to whom it is said: 'Thus shall you bless the sons of Israel, invoking'"

units.la: Augustinus. inuocantes nomen meum super illos. Ignorabat Apostolus hoc genus sacerdotum in ecclesia Christi. Simpliciter scripsit ecclesiae Corinthiorum, & unà cum illa fidelib. omnibus, qui syncera fide nomen Christi inuocant.
units.tr: Augustine. "invoking my name upon them." The Apostle was unaware of this kind of priest in the Church of Christ. He simply wrote to the Church of the Corinthians, and together with it to all the faithful who call upon the name of Christ in sincere faith.

units.la: 3 IPSORVM' QVE & nostro.] In Graeco ita posita est hęc particula, ut uel ad dominum Iesum, uel ad locum pertinere posit. Chrysostomus uidetur ad dominum referre, quasi admoneat Apostolus communem esse fidelium omnium dominum Christum, ubicunque illi locorum constituti sint. Nam sic scribit: αἰ αγιων ... Ex ista lectionis ordinatione, conspicuum est, Chrysostomum uerba haec ita intelligere, ut Christus dicatur, communis omnium credentium & inuocantium se dominus, ubicunq; illi sint. Proinde quod dicit, Qui inuocant nomen Domini nostri Iesu Christi, in omni loco, & ipsorum & nostro: ita legendum est, Qui est in omni loco, & ipsorum & noster dominus. Quidam tamen legunt in genitiuo, Ipsorum & nostri.
units.tr: 3 "Both theirs and ours." In the Greek this particle is so placed that it can refer either to the Lord Jesus or to the place. Chrysostom seems to refer it to the Lord, as if the Apostle were reminding them that Christ is the common Lord of all the faithful, wherever they are situated. For he writes thus: the saints' ... [αἰ αγιων ...]. From this ordering of the words it is clear that Chrysostom understands the passage so that Christ is called the common Lord of all believers and invokers of himself, wherever they may be. Accordingly, the words "who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, in every place, both theirs and ours" should be read as "who is in every place, both theirs and our Lord." Some, however, read the genitive, "of theirs and of ours."

units.la: Prouocat ergo Corinthios hac particula suo exemplo ad affectum mutuae & catholicae charitatis ac concordiae, non solum erga & inter seipsos, sed simul omnes ubique locorum Christianos, quos colendos & diligendos in Christo uel hoc nomine admonet, quod nomen Domini Iesu Christi inuocant.
units.tr: Therefore by this particle the Apostle urges the Corinthians, by his own example, to a feeling of mutual and catholic love and concord, not only toward and among themselves but at the same time toward all Christians everywhere, whom he admonishes to be cherished and loved in Christ, and on this very ground, that they invoke the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Hieronymus sic exponit: in omni loco, ipsorum & nostro. Quia sacerdotes & suo & apostolorum loco funguntur, propter quod etiam ecclesiarum apostoli nuncupantur. Sic exponit, quoniam praemissa ad sacerdotes pertinere iudicat. Et quoniam uacillat, addit. Item aliter: Vniuersis ecclesijs prouinciae Achaiae ostendit se has literas mittere. Et hanc sententiam Lyranus sequutus sic exponit: Cum omnibus qui inuocant nomen domini, &c. quantum ad fideles habitantes, non solum in ciuitate, sed etiam in tota dicecesi. Ideo subditur: In omni loco ipsorum, id est, subiecto iurisdictioni episcopi, & aliorum ecclesiae illius ministrorum. Et nostro: Per hoc enim quod subijciebantur episcopo ciuitatis, nō erant exempti à potestate Apostoli. Haec ille. Expositio haec non conuenit statui illius ecclesiae, qui tū erat, cum haec Apostolus scriberet, quare nec menti Apostoli conuenit. Et ualde dubito commentarios illos esse Hieronymi, qui illi inscribuntur.
units.tr: Jerome explains it thus: "in every place, both theirs and ours. Because priests perform the office of both their own and the apostles' place, on account of which the apostles are also called the churches' apostles." He explains it so because he judges that what precedes pertains to priests. And since he wavers, he adds another explanation: "Likewise otherwise: he shows that he is sending this letter to all the churches of the province of Achaia." Following this opinion, Lyra explains: "With all who call upon the name of the Lord, etc., as far as the faithful dwelling not only in the city but throughout the whole diocese. Therefore it is added: 'in every place of theirs,' that is, subject to the jurisdiction of the bishop and the other ministers of that church. 'And ours': for by the fact that they were subject to the bishop of the city, they were not exempt from the power of the Apostle." Thus far Lyra. This explanation does not suit the condition of that church, which then existed when the Apostle wrote these things, and therefore it does not fit the Apostle's mind either. And I greatly doubt that those commentaries are Jerome's, which bear his name.

units.la: Ambrosius exponit ad hunc modum: Cum Iudaeis ueris iungit & gentes, quia salus ex Iudaeis est. Vt in omni loco ubi gentes quae inuocant nomen domini nostri Iesu Christi, & ubi Iudaei supra memorati sunt, similiter sint omnes unum. Neq; haec expositio placet. Si Chrysostomi non probatur, puto simpliciter sic esse intelligendum: Vnà cum omnibus qui inuocant nomen domini nostri Iesu Christi, nec re-
units.tr: Ambrose explains it in this way: "He joins the Gentiles with the true Jews, because salvation is from the Jews. So that in every place where Gentiles are who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and where the Jews mentioned above are, all are likewise one." Nor does this explanation please me. If Chrysostom's is not approved, I think it should be understood simply in this way: "Together with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,

units.la: fert quo illi loco hoc faciant, ac tales existant, siue apud nos in hac prouincia, siue alibi, ubicunque agant.
units.tr: it makes no difference in what place they do this or what sort of people they are, whether among us in this province or elsewhere, wherever they act."

units.la: 7 GRATIA uobis & pax à Deo patre nostro, & domino Iesu Christo.] 1 Hęc est salutatio initio epistolae pro more praemissa. De ratione salutandi amicos & fratres alibi dixi-mus, utpote in comentarijs nostris super Matthaeum cap.5. & 10. Ponit autem salutationem uere piam & Apostolicam, quam optarim tam esse mentibus nostris uera fide & charitate per spiritum Dei insitam, quàm chartis est nota & familiaris. Vsurpat hanc omnibus ferè epistolis, nec frustra. Non enim potest quicquam uel salubrius, uel suauius, aut certè necessariū magis excogitari, quàm est haec gratia & pax à Deo patre nostro, &c. De hac salutatione quae dam annotauimus in epistolam ad Romanos, ubi eadem habetur. Competenter optat illis gratiam & pacem, non irae, sed gratiae ac pacis ministerLid̃ à Deo patre & domino Iesu Christo, cuius erat minister & Apostolus, & cuius nomine ad ipsos scribebat. Sic cordis affectu spirat & apprecatur fidelibus, quód ex officio Apostolatus praedicabat. Non solum optat salutando, sed & praedicat annunciando.
units.tr: 7 "Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." 1 This is the greeting, placed at the beginning of the letter according to custom. I have spoken elsewhere about the manner of greeting friends and brothers, namely in our commentaries on Matthew, chapters 5 and 10. He sets forth a greeting that is truly pious and Apostolic, and I could wish that it were as firmly implanted in our minds by true faith and charity through the Spirit of God as it is familiar and well known to the pages. He uses it in almost all his letters, and not in vain. For nothing more salutary, more sweet, or indeed more necessary can be imagined than this grace and peace from God our Father, etc. We have made some observations on this greeting in our commentary on Romans, where the same words occur. He fittingly wishes them grace and peace, not wrath but the grace and peace that is the ministry of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, whose minister and apostle he was, and in whose name he wrote to them. So he breathes out and invokes upon the faithful the feeling of his heart, which in the office of the apostleship he preached. He not only wishes it in greeting but also proclaims it in announcing.

units.la: 2 Gratiam quidam exponunt, condonationem admissorum: Pacem uero quietē ac gaudium conscientiae. Illi uidentur respicere ad id quod gratia potitum solemus dicere eum, qui cum reus esset libere dimissus, nec punitus est ut iure debuisset. Sed hic sensus non est proprius huius dictionis. Nam haec significatio magis exprimit declarationem & effectum gratiae, quàm ipsam gratiam, quae est fauor animi benigni ac beneuoli erga aliquem, unde, ubi opus fuerit, prouenit illa delictorum condonatio. Non semper ergo gratia peccatorum remissionem significat, peccatorum uero remissio semper gratia uocari potest. Beata uirgo dum ab angelo salutaretur, uocabatur κεχαριτωμένη, ubi non statim exponendum est, quod propter peccatorum condonationem sit dicta gratiosa. Quemadmodum & eleemosyna, id est, misericordia, aliquando quidem id quod ex misericordia impenditur misero significat, sed non proprie. Nam ita non effectū, sed magis affectum animi alienae miseriae condolentis significat. Ita & pax Ebraeis est, quando salua sunt omnia. Sic Iosephus ad fratres suos dicebat, שלום אביכם. Est ne pax patri uestro? Quoniam uero conscientiae pax non est, nisi ex fide gratiae Dei, recte pax gratiae subiungitur, & pro conscientiae pacatione ponitur. Quanquam haudquaquam negarim Apostolum etiam Ebraeo more per pacē externi quoque statur tranquillitatem intelligere. Hieronymus uidetur illam intelligere de concordia ecclesiastica. Sic enim hoc loco annotat: Pax gratiam seruat, quà quidam habere nolebant, intelligens de schismaticis, qui pacem ecclesiae rumpentes gratiam etiam Dei, quantū in ipsis erat, excludebant. Lyranus ad hunc modum:
units.tr: 2 Some explain "grace" as the forgiveness of sins, and "peace" as the quiet and joy of conscience. They seem to have in mind the usual sense of the word "grace", as when we say of a man who was accused and freely released, and not punished as the law required, that he received grace. But this meaning is not the proper sense of the word. For this sense expresses the declaration and effect of grace rather than grace itself, which is the kindly and benevolent favour of the mind towards someone. From that favour, where it is needed, the forgiveness of offences arises. So grace does not always mean the remission of sins, but the remission of sins can always be called grace. When the blessed Virgin was greeted by the angel, she was called [κεχαριτωμένη], and there is no need to explain at once that she was called "gracious" because of the forgiveness of her sins. Likewise "almsgiving", that is, mercy, sometimes denotes what is given out of mercy to the wretched, but not in the proper sense. For in that way it signifies not the effect but rather the affection of a mind that feels with another's misery. So too "peace" among the Hebrews means that all is well. Thus Joseph said to his brothers, [שלום אביכם] "Is your father at peace?" Since there is no peace of conscience except from faith in the grace of God, "peace" is rightly joined to "grace" and set in place of the calming of conscience. Yet I would by no means deny that the Apostle, in the Hebrew manner, also understands by "peace" outward tranquillity. Jerome seems to understand it of church concord. For he thus remarks on this passage: "Peace keeps grace, which some did not want to have," understanding this of the schismatics, who by breaking the peace of the Church also shut out the grace of God, so far as they were concerned.

units.la: {a} Gen. 43. Gratia uobis, in præsenti, & pax, id est, gloria {A}in futuro, in qua pax perficitur. Nos cogitemus dum pax gratię subiungitur, non posse uecram contingere pacem nisi ex gratia Dei.
units.tr: {a} Gen. 43. Grace to you in the present, and peace, that is, glory {A} in the future, in which peace is brought to completion. Let us consider that, when "peace" is joined to "grace", a true peace cannot come except from the grace of God.

units.la: 3 A'Deo patre, &c.] Id est, ueram & sempiternam uobis gratiam & pacem opto. Multa sunt etiam temporaria bona à Deo comuniter omnibus concessa. Verum hic de illis specialiter loquitur, quæ fidelibus Christi & uera ac sempiterna proueniunt, cum dicit: à Deo patre nostro, & domino Iesu Christo. Vide quomodo Christum, & qua in re Deo patri coniungat, ac dominum nostrum uocet.
units.tr: 3 "From God the Father, etc." That is, I wish you true and everlasting grace and peace. There are many temporal goods that God grants in common to all. But here he speaks specially of those that come to the faithful of Christ and are true and everlasting, when he says: "from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." Note how he joins Christ with God the Father, and in what respect, and calls him our Lord.

units.la: Gratias ago Deo meo semper pro uobis, super gratia Dei quæ data est uobis per Christum Iesum.
units.tr: I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God which has been given to you through Christ Jesus.

units.la: Hoc est exordium, affectum Apostolici pectoris exprimens, ad insinuandam simul & captandam benevolentiam accommodatum. Nam tam suam Apostolus erga Corinthios beneuolentiam insinuat, quàm illorum, ut attenti sint, captat. Rhetorum quidem hic mos est, sed non omnibus est Apostoli affectus. Illi ex ostentatione humanæ scientiæ, in qua sunt instituti, & de qua gloriantur, animos auditorum titillare conantur: Apostolus uero magis quæ rit quomodo prosit, quomodo placeat. Itaque licet & ipse utatur commodis subinde exordijs, quibus sibi benevolentiam auditorum conciliet: non huius tamen duntaxat gratia hoc {B}facit, licet etiam hoc quærat, sed ut per id illis possit prodesse, & doctrinam suam acceptiorem reddere.
units.tr: This is the exordium, expressing the feeling of the Apostle's heart, and well suited to insinuate and at the same time win goodwill. For the Apostle both shows his own goodwill towards the Corinthians and seeks to make them attentive. This is indeed the custom of the rhetoricians, but it is not the feeling of the Apostle in every case. They, out of the display of human learning in which they are trained and of which they boast, try to tickle the minds of their hearers. The Apostle, however, seeks rather how he may benefit and how he may please. So although he too sometimes uses the customary exordia, by which he wins the goodwill of his hearers, he does not do this for that purpose alone, though he does seek it, but so that by it he may be of use to them and make his teaching more acceptable.

units.la: Et hoc tum potissimum facit, quando eos quibus scribit aliqua in re castigaturus est, ut hac est epistola facturus, ne per subsequentem correptionem exacerbati animos erga admonentem obturent. Sic solent parentes liberos correpturi, sic & qui pueros in scholis prudenter instituunt. Plurimum momenti habet ad erigendum animos etiam eorum, qui delinquere coeperunt, si quid in se lau dari adhuc & alicuius fieri senserint. Nisi enim hoc fiat facili momento ad desperationem adiguntur, sic ut nunquam in uiam redire cogitet.
units.tr: He does this especially when he is about to rebuke those to whom he writes in some matter, as he will do in this letter, so that they will not, angered by the correction that follows, close their minds against the one who admonishes. So parents do when they are about to correct their children, and so do those who wisely train boys in schools. It matters greatly, for raising the spirits even of those who have begun to go astray, that they feel something still to be praised in themselves and something of worth in them. For unless this is done, they are driven with little effort to despair, so that they never think of returning to the right way.

units.la: 2 Habet autem exordium hoc duo quæ ad conciliandam benevolentiam potissimum faciunt. 1 Primum est, quod ostendit quo sit erga illos charitatis præditus affectu. Hoc facit in eo quod dicit: Gratias ago Deo meo pro uobis semper. Qui gratias agit, pro re hoc facit si bi chara ac desiderata. Pro Corinthijs hoc facit Apostolus. Ergo erant sibi chari ac desiderati. Nec facit hoc cum discrimine aliquo, sed in genere. Non dicit, pro ijs qui adhuc sani inter uos sunt: sed simpliciter, pro uobis. Non excludit eos quos erat correpturus, sed communi hac mitigatione animos eorum ad emendationem prouocat.
units.tr: 2 This exordium has two features that especially help to win goodwill. 1 The first is that it shows the affection of charity he has towards them. He does this when he says: "I give thanks to my God for you always." He who gives thanks does so for something dear and desired to him. The Apostle does this for the Corinthians. Therefore they were dear and desired to him. Nor does he do this with any distinction, but in general. He does not say, "for those among you who are still sound," but simply, "for you." He does not exclude those whom he was about to rebuke, but by this common softening he provokes their minds to amendment.

units.la: Auxetis est charitatis, quod dicit, Semper. Aliquando memore esse amicorum, potest & modica quædam dilectio, semper uero uehementis sit amoris oportet. Quoties ad Deum orabat, illiq; ecclesias Christi commendabat, simul gratias illi agebat de singulari in eas gratia collata. Sic memor erat Romanorum, & hic Corinthiorum, & aliarum ecclesiarum indesinenter.
units.tr: The increase of charity is in what he says: "always." To be mindful of friends at some times may come from a moderate love, but to be so always must come from a vehement love. As often as he prayed to God and commended the churches of Christ to him, he at the same time gave thanks to him for the singular grace bestowed on them. So he was mindful of the Romans, and here of the Corinthians, and of the other churches, without ceasing.

units.la: 2 Alterum est, quod nonnihil eos commendabiles reddit propter gratiam Dei, quam acceperant per Iesum Christum, quàm declarat nō solum per continuam erga Deum gratiarum actionem: sed & subiectam amplificationem, præclaram fuisse. Nec putet quisquam nihil habere commendationis hanc partem exordij, quæ concernat Corinthios, propterea quod non ipsorum commendat uirtutes, sed diuinā gratiam. In hoc sæculo quidem uerum est, encomia non ab alienis, sed proprijs esse uirtutibus sumenda: in regno Christi uero maximum est encomium, & plurima commendatio, diuina gratia & benevolentia potiri. Et beatam uirginem angelus non ab ipsius proprijs uirtutibus, sed à diuina gratia commendat, dum gratiosam uocat, id est, diuinam gratiam adeptā. Quid enim charius nobis esse debet gratia & fauore Dei? Cur nobis non essent commendati, qui beneuoletia diuinæ gratiæ potiūtur, quos Deus ipse amplectitur & charos habet? Quanquam & in aulis principū reperias forsan hoc usuuenire, ut aulicis reliquis, duntaxat probis, commendatiores quidā hoc nomine sint, quod principi præ alijs sint chari.
