units.tr: 2 The second feature is that it makes them somewhat commendable on account of the grace of God which they had received through Jesus Christ, which he shows not only by his continual thanksgiving to God but also by the following amplification, which is most excellent. Let no one think that this part of the exordium, which concerns the Corinthians, has nothing of commendation, because he does not commend their virtues but the divine grace. In this age it is indeed true that commendations are to be taken not from outsiders but from one's own virtues. But in the kingdom of Christ the greatest commendation, and the most praise, is to possess the divine grace and favour. The angel also commends the blessed Virgin not from her own virtues but from the divine grace, when he calls her "gracious," that is, one who has obtained divine grace. For what ought to be dearer to us than the grace and favour of God? Why should not those be commended to us who enjoy the goodwill of divine grace, whom God himself embraces and holds dear? Although perhaps you may find in the courts of princes that this happens, that some courtiers, though the rest are only upright, are more commendable by this title, namely that they are dearer to the prince than the others.

units.la: Ita debet comparatum esse & inter fratres, ut reliquis sit commendatior, qui parentibus est gratior. Sed hoc rarissime inuenias. Notum est exemplum fratrum Ioseph. Illorum odijs ob id ipsum erat expositus Ioseph, quod à patre plus ipsis haberetur in precio ac singulari uelte ornaretur. Vide Gen. 37.
units.tr: So too it ought to be arranged among brothers, that the one who is more pleasing to the parents is more commendable than the rest. But you will find this very rarely. The example of Joseph's brothers is well known. Joseph was exposed to their hatred for this very reason, that he was held in higher esteem by his father than they were, and was adorned with a singular robe. See Gen. 37.

units.la: 3 Illud, DEO meo.] Quod & Rom. 1. posuit, quo quod & aliorum commune est suum facit, indicium habet. uox enim est eorum qui singulari quadam familiaritate & fiducia erga Deum tenentur. Vnde crebra est in Psalmis, & plerūque erumpit, ubi ardenti & pleno cordis affectu Dei fit mentio, ut maximè solet in tentationibus & anxijs precationibus fieri.
units.tr: 3 "To my God." He has this sign, which he also used in Rom. 1, by which he makes his own what is common to others as well. For it is the voice of those who are held by a certain singular familiarity and trust towards God. Hence it is frequent in the Psalms, and it bursts out most often where the mention of God is made with a burning and full affection of heart, as is most especially the case in temptations and anxious prayers.

units.la: Nec ulla iniuria afficiuntur reliqui pij, quasi non & ipsorum sit Deus, cum eadem charitate, fiducia & familiaritate & illis uti liceat: fratribus suis nihil præscribit, nec fiducia quæ filiorum est, erga patrem illis aufert, qui communem patrem, suum uocat patrem. Non est autem hac loquutione usus Apostolus præter rationem. Erat enim singularis Dei minister, & hunc inter gentes prædicabat, quæ ad id usque temporis alienæ fuerant à uero Deo. Potè rat adijcere, Cui seruio, & quem uobis prædicaui, sicut in Rom. cap. 1. dixit: Testis est mihi Deus, cui seruio in spiritu meo. Perinde est ac si legatus regis dicat, Gratias ago regi meo semper pro uobis, pro singulari gratia quā in uos contulit, &c.
units.tr: Nor are the other godly harmed in any way, as if God were not theirs too, since it is permitted for them to use him with the same charity, trust and familiarity. He does not prescribe anything to his brothers, nor does he take away from them the trust that belongs to sons towards the father, since he calls the common Father his own Father. The Apostle has not used this way of speaking beyond reason. For he was a singular minister of God, and preached him among the nations, which until then had been alien from the true God. He could have added, "whom I serve, and whom I have preached to you," as he said in Rom. chap. 1: "God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit." It is just as if the envoy of a king were to say: "I give thanks to my king always for you, for the singular grace which he has bestowed upon you," etc.

units.la: OBSER. I.
units.tr: Observation I.

units.la: 4 Quod gratiarum actionem ad Deum praemittit, Corinthios docet suo exemplo, ut nunquam obliuiscantur gratiae acceptae, sed perpetuo illius memores grati sint. Est enim gratitudo coseruatio acceptorum beneficiorum, & conciliatio futurorum.
units.tr: 4 In that he places thanksgiving to God before everything else, he teaches the Corinthians by his own example never to forget the grace they have received, but always to be mindful of it and grateful. For gratitude is the preservation of benefits received and the means of securing those to come.

units.la: Docet autem nos ut non solum eorum gratia quę nobis, sed & quę alijs à Deo datur, gratias illi agamus. Verū hic animus opus habet uiuo ac iugi sensu beneficiorum Dei, tam quæ alijs, quàm quæ nobis ab illo impenduntur.
units.tr: He also teaches us to give thanks to God not only for the grace given to us but also for the grace given to others. Yet this attitude needs a lively and constant awareness of God's benefits, both those bestowed on others and those bestowed on us.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: 5 Quanquam in omnibus quoq; alijs epistolis, demptis Galat.1. Tim. & ea quæ est ad Titum, ad cōmendationem gratię Dei animi sui gratitudinem uel laudando uel gratias agendo, mox initio declarat: ad Corinthios tamen hoc maiore necessitate facit, ut & Chrysoft. annotauit. Sentiebat enim gratiam Dei quam illi per suum ministerium acceperant in Christo, à pseudapostolis eleuari, quasi in Christo non satis fuerint imbuti: quemadmodum solent, qui selectas aliquas & nouas reuelationes pollicentur, ut præsentem Dei gratiam contemptam reddant, & ex animis fidelium auferant spe & expectatione longe sublimiorum. Hac potissimum ratione gratiam Dei quam acceperant per suum ministerium, illis commendatam reddere cupiens, incipit à gratiarum actione: imò ostendit se continuo illius nomine Deo gratias agere, tantum non confundens eos quod eius tam cito sustinuerint obliuisci.
units.tr: 5 Although in all his other epistles, except Galatians, 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus, the Apostle at the very beginning declares his thankfulness of mind, either by praising or by giving thanks for the commendation of God's grace, he does so with greater urgency to the Corinthians, as Chrysostom also noted. For he perceived that the grace of God which they had received through his ministry in Christ was being belittled by the false apostles, as if they had not been sufficiently instructed in Christ. This is what those do who promise certain select and new revelations, so as to make the grace of God now present seem contemptible and to remove from the minds of believers the hope and expectation of things far more sublime. Wishing above all to render the grace of God that they had received through his ministry commended to them, he begins with thanksgiving. Indeed, he shows that he continually gives thanks to God on its account, almost rebuking them for having so quickly allowed it to slip from their memory.

units.la: Hoc & hodie inculcandum est ijs qui per Euangelium Christi ab erroribus liberati, ueritatis cognitionem acceperunt. Videmus enim gratiam hanc Dei tam multifariam, quam Germaniæ nostræ ecclesijs præ cæteris concessit, à maiori parte eorū qui illius facti sunt participes, susque deque fieri, indeque illis accidere, quod alij in sectas abduci se sinunt: alij ad Babylonem, unde fuerant liberati, redeūt, alij uarijs uitijs uitam suam conspurcant, quorum nihil facerent, si gratiam Dei agnoscerēt, & de amplitudine illius cogitarent: quod facile possent, si memores essent Babylonicę capti uitatis, seruitutis, cæcitatis, tyrannidis, & impietatis, unde beneficio Euangelicæ sunt ueritatis præter spem omnem sola bonitate diuinæ gratiæ erepti. Omnino nostris hodie accidit per acceptæ gratiæ contemptum, quod Corinthijs accidisse uidemus, quos alio in loco Apostolus eam ob causam monet, ut uideant ne gratiam Dei in uanum acceperint.
units.tr: This must be pressed upon those today too who, freed from error through the Gospel of Christ, have received the knowledge of the truth. For we see that this grace of God, which he has granted in such abundance to the churches of our Germany above others, is for the greater part of those who have become its partakers held cheap, and that as a result some allow themselves to be led away into sects, others return to Babylon, from which they had been freed, and others defile their lives with various vices, none of which they would do if they acknowledged the grace of God and reflected on its greatness. They could easily do so if they remembered the Babylonian captivity, the servitude, blindness, tyranny and impiety from which they were rescued, beyond all hope, by the sole goodness of divine grace through the benefit of the Gospel truth. Certainly what we see the Corinthians suffered through contempt of the grace received is happening today among us as well, and in another place the Apostle warns them for this reason to see to it that they have not received the grace of God in vain.

units.la: QVAE data est uobis per Christū Iesum.] Et Chrysosto. illud ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, idem est atque per Chtistum Iesum. Quamuis non displicet, quod nonnullis magis placet ut quemadmodū in Græco est, legamus, in Christo Iesu. Neq; enim per Christum tantum, sed & in illo, hoc est, illi insiti, donis gratiæ Dei ditamur & instructi reddimur. Generalius erat, quod dixit,
units.tr: "Which was given to you through Christ Jesus." Chrysostom takes the phrase ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ [en Christō Iēsou] to mean the same as "through Christ Jesus." Still, it does not displease me that some prefer to read, as the Greek has it, "in Christ Jesus" [en Christō Iēsou]. For we are enriched and equipped with the gifts of God's grace not only through Christ but also in him, that is, when we are grafted into him. What he said was more general:

units.la: A Super gratia Dei. Nam quicquid boni uspiam est, ex gratia & bonitate Dei est, etiam apud eos qui in Christo non sunt.
units.tr: A Concerning the grace of God. For whatever good there is anywhere comes from the grace and goodness of God, even among those who are not in Christ.

units.la: Ex gratia Dei est uiuere, hominem esse, sanum esse, opulentum esse, sapientem esse, &c. Bonitate nanque domini plena est terra. Et qui huius generis gratia Dei potiuntur, debēt & ipsi illam agnoscere & grati esse. De hac uero non loquitur Apostolus hoc loco. Ideo per subiectam expositionem declarat de qua loquatur, cū dicit: Quæ data est uobis per Christum, uel in Christo. Hoc est, quam in Christum credentes adepti estis. Licet & diuites fuerint, & mundana sapientia præditi, nihil tamen horum commemorat, ea tantum commendans quæ in Christo acceperant per fidem. Et merito hoc facit. Quid enim sunt reliqua omnia huic gratiæ comparata?
units.tr: It is by the grace of God that we live, that we are human, that we are healthy, wealthy, wise, and so on. For the earth is full of the goodness of the Lord. Those who enjoy this kind of grace of God ought also themselves to acknowledge it and be grateful. But the Apostle does not speak of this kind here. Therefore, by the explanation that follows, he makes clear what he means when he says: "which was given to you through Christ," or "in Christ." That is, the grace which you have obtained by believing in Christ. Although they were rich and endowed with worldly wisdom, he mentions none of these things, commending only what they had received in Christ through faith. And he does this rightly. For what are all other things compared with this grace?

units.la: Chrysostomus hanc particulā sic exponit, ut tātum respiciat ad hoc, quod per Christum gratiam Dei non per aliquem hominem acceperint Corinthij, quod in se uerum est, & pulchre quoque ad propositum facit: ut admoneantur Corinthij, ne adhæreant pseudapostolis, sed Christo & illius Euangelio. Mihi uero uidetur Apostolus magis exponere gratiam Dei quæ illa sit, cuius nomine Deo semper gratias agat.
units.tr: Chrysostom explains this phrase so that it refers only to the fact that the Corinthians received the grace of God through Christ and not through any human being. This is true in itself and also fits the purpose well: the Corinthians are warned not to cling to the false apostles, but to Christ and his Gospel. But it seems to me that the Apostle rather sets out more fully what that grace is, on whose account he always gives thanks to God.

units.la: Quod in omnibus ditati estis per ipsum, in omni sermone & cognitione, quemadmodum testimonium Iesu Christi cōfirmatum est in uobis, adeò ut nō destituamini ullo dono, expectantes reuelationem domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: That in all things you were enriched in him, in all speech and knowledge, just as the testimony of Jesus Christ was confirmed among you, so that you lack no gift, awaiting the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Exponit quod dixit, De gratia Dei quæ data est uobis in Christo Iesu. Facit autē hoc non simpliciter, sed cum illius amplificatione, per quam & gratiam in Christo acceptam amplificat, & simul Apostolatus sui efficaciam contra pseudapostolos commendat, idq; duplici argumento.
units.tr: He explains what he said: "concerning the grace of God which is given to you in Christ Jesus." He does this not simply, but with an amplification, by which he both enlarges the grace received in Christ and at the same time commends the efficacy of his own apostleship against the false apostles, and he does so with a twofold argument.

units.la: 1 Primum à sufficientia & plenitudine, tali ac tanta ut nihil posset in illa desiderari. Hoc quidem clanculum hic facit per amplificationem acceptæ in Christo gratiæ, in posteriore uero cap.12. apertius sic dicit: Nulla in re inferior fui summis apostolis, tametsi nihil sum. Signa quidem apostoli peracta fuerunt inter uos cum omni patientia, & signis & prodigijs & potentibus factis. Nam quid est in quo fueritis inferiores cæteris ecclesijs? Quod si malum prima hac & moderata fuisset admonitione emendatum, haud opus fuisset ea quæ hic uno & altero uerbo attigit, & moderate intelligenda cogitandaq; propositum, in ea quam posteriorem ad ipsos scripsit pluribus & apertioribus uerbis inculcare. Qua in re & modestiam apostolicam, & simul irremissum studium corrigendi mali uidemus.
units.tr: 1. The first is from sufficiency and fullness, of such a kind and so great that nothing could be desired in it. He does this here only covertly, by amplifying the grace received in Christ; but in the later chapter 12 he says it more openly: "I was in no way inferior to the chief apostles, though I am nothing. The signs of an apostle were wrought among you with all patience, by signs and wonders and mighty deeds. For in what were you inferior to the other churches?" If the evil had been corrected by this first and moderate admonition, there would have been no need for what he touched on here in one or two words to be pressed home in the later letter, which he wrote to them at greater length and in plainer words, to be understood and considered in the same measured way as the present purpose. In this we see both the apostolic modesty and at the same time his unrelenting zeal for correcting the evil.

units.la: 2 Alterum est à constantia & perennitate ad finem usque duratura. Pertinet enim & illa ad perfectionem doni. Primus defectus est, non esse acceptum donum plenum & sufficiens: alter, non esse cōstans ac perpetuum. Licet enim perfectum sit in se donum, omnibusq; suis numeris absolutum, ei tamē perfectum nō est qui illo suapte socordia nō ad finem usq; cōstanter utitur. Sed de hoc altero defectu in sequentib.
units.tr: 2. The second is from constancy and perpetuity, lasting to the end. For this too belongs to the perfection of a gift. The first defect is not to have received a gift that is full and sufficient; the second, not to have it constant and lasting. For although a gift may be perfect in itself and complete in all its parts, it is not perfect for the one who, through his own carelessness, does not use it constantly to the end. But of this second defect we shall speak in what follows.

units.la: 2 QVOD in omnibus. Hoc est, in quauis re. Germanissimus est. Nam ita solemus nos Germani dicere, In allem.
units.tr: 2. "That in all things." That is, in every matter. It is very German; for we Germans are accustomed to say, In allem.

units.la: Amplificat autem acceptam iam gratiæ plenitudinem in duobus. Primum in eo qd̄ quantum ad Christi cognitionem & gratiam pertinet, nullo dono spiritus destituti sint. Huc pertinet quod dicit, In omnibus: & mox, Adeo ut non destituamini ullo dono. Quod sane nō est ultra metem Apostoli & statum præsentis cau sæ diuexandum, & ad omnia spiritus sancti dona in uniuersum rapiendum. Neq; enim staret hoc uerbum, si eo sensu acciperetur.
units.tr: He amplifies the fullness of grace already received in two respects. The first is that, as far as the knowledge and grace of Christ are concerned, they were lacking in no gift of the Spirit. To this belongs what he says, "in all things," and soon after, "so that you lack no gift." This certainly must not be stretched beyond the intention of the Apostle and the state of the present cause, and extended to all the gifts of the Holy Spirit in general; for the word would not stand if it were taken in that sense.

units.la: Deinde in eo quòd accepta dona abundantia & copiosa sint, quòd non solum omnia spiritus dona acceperint, sed singula copiose ac opulente acceperint. Ad id facit, quod dicit:
units.tr: Then, in that the gifts received are abundant and copious, not only did they receive all the gifts of the Spirit, but they received each of them richly and plentifully. To this points what he says:

units.la: DITATI estis. Diuitiarū enim dictio copiā rerū ac thesauros exprimit. Sic alibi thesauros scientiæ ac sapientiæ Dei in Christo esse dicit.
units.tr: "You were enriched." For the word "riches" expresses an abundance of things and treasures. So elsewhere he says that the treasures of the knowledge and wisdom of God are in Christ.

units.la: Illud, PER ipsum. In Græco est ἐν αὐτῷ, id est, in ipso. Potest simpliciter sic exponi: qd̄ in omnibus ditati estis ab eo tempore quo in Christū credere coepistis, illiq; inserti estis. In Christo esse, primum generaliter est in illius esse religione ac nominis professione: deinde est illi uera esse fide & unitate spiritus insitum & incorporatum, quemadmodum palmes est in uite, & membrum in corpore. Prior modus complectitur omnes, qui nomen ac religionē Christi profitentur: posterior uero electorum & uerorum fidelium est tantum.
units.tr: As to "through him": in Greek it is ἐν αὐτῷ, that is, "in him." It can be explained simply thus: you were enriched in all things from the time when you began to believe in Christ and were grafted into him. To be in Christ is first, in general, to be in the profession of his religion and name; then it is to be implanted and incorporated into him by true faith and the unity of the Spirit, as a branch is in the vine and a member in the body. The former mode embraces all who profess the name and religion of Christ; the latter belongs only to the elect and true believers.

units.la: 3 IN omni sermone & cognitione. Potest quidē uideri illud, in omni sermone, quod est in Græco, ἐν παντὶ λόγῳ, dictum esse per Ebraismum בכל דבר, ut possit uerti, in omni re. Verū quoniam quod præcesssit ἐν πα·ντὶ, id est, in omni, generaliter dictum est: existimo non conuenire, ut hanc quoq; particulam generaliter positam esse sentiamus. Quare pro specificatione præcedentis accipienda uidetur, & legenda, non in omni re: sed, in omni sermone. Hoc est, in omnis generis sermone & cognitione. Loquitur autem de donis spiritus, de quibus infrà tractabit ca. 12. & partitur illud quod dixit, Ditati estis in omni, in sermonem & scientiam. Per sermonem exponit Chrysostomus, differendi, & quę sententias exponendi facultatem. Scientia uero cognitio est illa diuinæ uoluntatis in Christo per Euangelium reuelata.
units.tr: 3. "In all speech and knowledge." It may indeed seem that the phrase "in all speech," which in Greek is ἐν παντὶ λόγῳ, was said by a Hebraism, בכל דבר, so that it could be rendered "in every matter." But since what preceded, ἐν παντὶ, that is, "in all," was said generally, I think it not fitting that we should understand this particle also as put generally. Therefore it seems to be taken as specifying the preceding, and it should be read not "in every matter" but "in all speech": that is, in all kinds of speech and knowledge. He speaks, however, of the gifts of the Spirit, of which he will treat below in chapter 12, and he divides what he said, "you were enriched in all things," into speech and knowledge. Chrysostom explains "speech" as the ability to discourse and to expound opinions. "Knowledge," however, is that knowledge of the divine will which has been revealed in Christ through the Gospel.

units.la: 4 QVEMADMODVM testimonium Iesu Christi cōfirmatum est in uobis. Testimonii Iesu Christi, est Euangelij prædicatio. Ita apostoli dicti sunt testes Christi Act. 1. In Græco est καθὼς, quod uulgatus interpres uertit, sicut & nonnulli recentiores, quemadmodū Erasmus: quibus rebus, composita uox est, ex καὶ κατὰ & ὡς
units.tr: 4. "Just as the testimony of Jesus Christ was confirmed among you." The testimony of Jesus Christ is the preaching of the Gospel. So the apostles are called witnesses of Christ in Acts 1. In Greek it is καθὼς, which the Vulgate translator renders "sicut" (as), as do some more recent writers, such as Erasmus; the word is compounded of καὶ κατὰ and ὡς.

units.la: quasi dicas, Secundum sic: uel, secundū quod, id est, quatenus, uel quo tempore testimonii Iesu Christi confirmatū est in uobis. Erasmus intellexit testimonium Iesu Christi cōfirmatum fuisse in Corinthijs uel per sermonem & scientiam Apostolicę prædicationis, tanq; per organa, uel per dona sermonis & scientię, ipsis Corinthijs concessa. Sane testimonium Iesu Christi confirmatū fuit bifariam. Primum doctrina apostolorū & portentis, quę facta sunt ab Apostolo in uirtute Christi. Nam id datur signis ac portentis Marci ultimo. Domino sequente, inquit, & sermone cōfirmante sequentib. signis. De signis illis in posteriore ca. 12. cōmemorat. Deinde in animis credentium & donis ab illis acceptis. Sunt qui Græcam uocē μαρτύριον, quæ testimoniū sonat, intelligunt de morte Christi, quo sensu & mortem eorum, qui pro ueritate Christi moriūtur, μαρτύριον uocare solemus. Verum exquisitior est hic sensus, quàm ut conueniat causæ quam hic agit Apostolus.
units.tr: As if you were to say, "according to how," or "according to which," that is, "in so far as," or "at what time the testimony of Jesus Christ was confirmed among you." Erasmus understood that the testimony of Jesus Christ was confirmed among the Corinthians either through the speech and knowledge of apostolic preaching, as through instruments, or through the gifts of speech and knowledge granted to the Corinthians themselves. Certainly the testimony of Jesus Christ was confirmed in two ways. First by the teaching of the apostles and by the wonders which the Apostle performed in the power of Christ. For this is given in the last chapter of Mark: "The Lord working with them and confirming the word with the signs that followed." Of those signs he speaks in the later chapter 12. Then in the minds of believers and in the gifts received from them. There are those who understand the Greek word μαρτύριον, which means testimony, of the death of Christ, in which sense we are accustomed to call the death of those who die for the truth of Christ μαρτύριον. But this sense is too far-fetched to fit the cause which the Apostle is handling here.

units.la: 5 ADEO ut non destituamini ullo dono. Charisma est Græce, id quod ex affectu gratiæ datur, unde plerunq; donum uertitur. Intelligit autem de donis non quibusuis, sed ut dixi, de illis quorum infrà 12. mentionem faciet.
units.tr: 5. "So that you lack no gift." Charisma is the Greek word, that which is given from the disposition of grace, whence it is commonly translated "gift." He understands it, however, not of any gifts whatever, but, as I have said, of those whose mention he will make below in chapter 12.

units.la: QVAESTIO I.
units.tr: QUESTION I.

units.la: 6 Sed quæritur hic quare de illis donis, quæ neminem saluant, loquatur, & non magis de fide, spe & charitate, sine quibus nemo saluatur, etiamsi cętera dona habeat innumera, & in quibus potior est Apostolatus gloria.
units.tr: 6 But it is asked here why he speaks of those gifts which save no one, and not rather of faith, hope and love, without which no one is saved, even if he has countless other gifts, and in which the glory of the apostleship is greater.

units.la: Respondeo. Ita exigebat propositum, in qd̄ tendebat. Nam in eo est, ut declaret Apostolatui suo nihil deesse, ut impar debeat haberi reliquis apostolis. Ideo usurpat non occulta illa spiritus dona fidem, spem & charitatem: sed manifesta, quę & infrà uocat manifestationem spiritus, cap. 12. dicens: Vnicuiq; uero datur manifestatio spiritus, ad id quod expedit. Nam huic quidem per spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ, alij uero per spiritum sermo scientiæ, &c. Et præterea tam aberat ut Corinthij negare uel uellent uel possent confirmationem hanc testimonij Christi, & spiritus manifestationem, ut etiam donorum istorum gratia insolescerent plurimum. Quod uero ad potiora illa attinet, admonebit illos infrà. Hoc ideo admonendum putaui, ne quis putet diuitias regni Christi esse in sermone & scientia proprie, quod Apostolus hic sermonem ponit & scientiam. Egregia dona sunt spiritus, sed talia, quæ sine fide nemo saluent. Seruiunt quidem ecclesiæ in cognitione Christi ac uera pietate edificandę: uerum interea non saluant eos, quibus sunt, tanquam organis, per miraculosam spiritus sancti operationem data. Notum est illud Christi: Dicent multi in illo die, Domine, nōne in nomine tuo prophetauimus, &c. at tu confitebor illis, nunquam noui uos. Matth. 7.
units.tr: I answer: the purpose he was pursuing required it. For his aim is to show that nothing is lacking in his apostleship, so that he ought not to be considered inferior to the other apostles. So he cites not those hidden gifts of the Spirit, faith, hope and love, but the manifest ones, which he also later calls the manifestation of the Spirit, in chapter 12, saying: "But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, and to another the word of knowledge," and so on. Moreover, the Corinthians were so far from wanting or being able to deny this confirmation of the testimony of Christ and this manifestation of the Spirit, that they even grew very proud because of the grace of these gifts. As for the greater gifts, he will admonish them later. I thought this should be noted, so that no one supposes that the riches of the kingdom of Christ consist properly in speech and knowledge, which is why the Apostle here mentions speech and knowledge. These gifts of the Spirit are excellent, but they are of such a kind that no one is saved by them without faith. They indeed serve the Church in building up knowledge of Christ and true godliness; yet they do not save those who possess them, since they were given through a miraculous operation of the Holy Spirit, as instruments. That saying of Christ is well known: "Many will say to me on that day, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and so on? But then I will declare to them, I never knew you." Matth. 7.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: 7 Quæritur etiam à quibusdam, (mouet eam quæquæstione & Chrysost.) quomodo Corinthij, cum nullo dono spiritus destituti fuerint, potuerint esse carnales, quod infrà illis objicit. Nunquid carnales estis? Et: Non potui uobis, inquit, loqui, quasi spiritualibus, sed tanq; carnalibus. Respondetur hic à plerisq;, quod duæ fuerint eius ecclesiæ partes. Vna eorū quæ probati manebant, de quibus infrà ca. 11. Oportet enim hæreses esse, inquit, ut qui probati sunt manifesti fiant. Hanc partem cócernere dicūt, quæ aliquid habent encomij. Altera eorum, q degenerauerant. Ad ista referēda uolunt, quæ corriguntur & reprehendūtur. Chrysost.cum ista & alias rationes assignat, cur prædicentur Corinthij donis spiritus ornati, & tamē in multis reprehēdantur. Vtpote, uel quod initio qui dem tales facti fuerint, ditati uidelicer in omni sermone & scientia, cum dona hæc primum accepissent: postea uero facti per socordiā remissiores opes hasce spiritus amiserint, atq; rursus carnales esse coeperint. Verum & premissa gratiarum actio, & quæ infrà cap. 12 & 14. sequuntur, huic sententiæ non fauent. Vel, quod dicta sint hæc ab Apostolo hyperbolicæ, qua sermonis figura quæ amplificata uolumus, magis facere solemus, quam in se existant. Vel, quod de suis ipsius donis sermonis & scientiæ loquatur Apostolus. Dicā quod mihi uidetur. Ea quæ illis hic tributa talia sunt, ut nihil prohibeat quin simul carnales fuisse credi queat. Spiritalem enim hominem non faciūt dona il la spiritus miraculosa, quæ ad Euangelij confirmationem in ecclesijs apostolorū uiguerunt, sed regeneratio animorum quæ est per fidē, qua corda purgantur, illa demum spiritale reddit è carnali. Imò tam abest, ut hæc dona, quantumuis miraculosa, p se reddāt hominem ex carnali spirituale, ut si desit regeneratio, quæ est per spiritū Christi, magis reddant hominē inflatū & arrogantem, unde & Apostolus infrà dicit: Scientia inflat, charitas ædificat.
units.tr: 7 Some also ask (Chrysostom too raises this question) how the Corinthians, since they lacked no gift of the Spirit, could have been carnal, which he later objects to them: "Are you not carnal?" and "I could not speak to you," he says, "as to spiritual people, but as to carnal people." Most answer here that the church had two parts. One consisted of those who remained approved, of whom he speaks later in chapter 11: "For there must be heresies," he says, "so that those who are approved may become manifest." They say that this part is what he commends, since it has something praiseworthy. The other part had degenerated, and they want the things which are corrected and rebuked to be referred to this part. Chrysostom, with these and other reasons, explains why the Corinthians are praised as adorned with the gifts of the Spirit and yet are rebuked in many things: either because they were indeed such at the beginning, made rich in all speech and knowledge when they first received these gifts, but afterwards, through carelessness, became more lax, lost these riches of the Spirit and began again to be carnal. But neither the preceding thanksgiving nor what follows in chapters 12 and 14 favours this opinion. Or, the words were spoken by the Apostle hyperbolically, by a figure of speech which we usually employ when we wish to magnify things, rather than as they actually stood. Or, the Apostle speaks of his own gifts of speech and knowledge. I will say what seems to me to be the case. The things attributed to them here are such that nothing prevents us from believing they could at the same time have been carnal. For those miraculous gifts of the Spirit, which flourished in the churches of the apostles for the confirmation of the gospel, do not make a man spiritual; it is regeneration of souls through faith, by which hearts are cleansed, that finally makes a spiritual person out of a carnal one. Indeed, these gifts, however miraculous, are so far from making a man spiritual instead of carnal by themselves, that if regeneration, which is through the Spirit of Christ, is lacking, they rather make a man puffed up and arrogant. Hence the Apostle also says later: "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up."

units.la: 8 EXPECTANTES reuelationem domni nostri. Et hoc facit ad priorem amplificatæ gratiæ Christi partē, quæ sita est in plenitudine & sufficiētia eorū quæ in regno Christi cognoscenda sunt, & quæ ad Euangelij administratio nem & confirmatione requiruntur. Tantundē enim est ac si dicat, nulla alia reuelatione opus habetis, q ea quæ Christū ipsum in die iudicij reuelabit, usq; adeò nullo dono spiritus destituti estis. De hac Christi reuelatione meminit & ad Coloss.cap.3. Hoc apertius aliquato contra pseudapostolos positum est, qui prætextu sublimiorū reuelationū, Euangelij simplicitatem traducebant, & Corinthios seducebāt. Diligenter aut obseruandū est, quod non simpliciter dicit: Expectantes dominū, sed expectantes reuelationem dñi nostri Iesu Christi. Est enim Christus ad finē usq; mundi abscōditus ab oculis huius mūdi, in fine uero apparebit conspicuus, ubi nō erit amplius tēpus fidei, quod iam est. Abscondito Christo non possumus ad herere nisi fide ac spiritu: mādus fide hac desti tutus Christo addici non potest. Quàm est autē illæ abscōditus, tam est & uita nostra, quæ in illo est & uniuersa felicitas p ipsum nobis parta in oculis mūdi abscondita, reuelanda demū quando ipse reuelabitur. Sit & nobis hoc dictum, qui doctrinæ apostolicæ fidē damus ne si namus nobis fucū fieri quasi extra illā desint adhuc, nescio quæ sublimiū rerū speculationes ac reuelationes. Hoc tantū curemus, ut pietatis studio reuelatæ p Euangeliū Christi cogniti oni respōdeamus. Hoc si fecerimus, secure poterimus Christi seruatoris expectare aduentū.
units.tr: 8 "Waiting for the revelation of our Lord." This serves the first part of the magnified grace of Christ, which lies in the fullness and sufficiency of what is to be known in the kingdom of Christ, and which is required for the administration and confirmation of the gospel. For it is as if he said: you have need of no other revelation than that which Christ himself will reveal on the day of judgement; so entirely are you lacking in no gift of the Spirit. He also mentions this revelation of Christ in Colossians chapter 3. This was stated somewhat more openly against the false apostles, who, under the pretext of higher revelations, belittled the simplicity of the gospel and led the Corinthians astray. We must observe carefully that he does not simply say "waiting for the Lord," but "waiting for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ." For Christ is hidden from the eyes of this world until the end of the world, and at the end he will appear visibly, when there will no longer be the time of faith, which is now. While Christ is hidden, we can cling to him only by faith and spirit; the world, destitute of this faith, cannot be attached to Christ. As our life, which is in him, and all the happiness obtained for us through him, are hidden from the eyes of the world, so much is Christ hidden; they will be revealed at last when he himself is revealed. Let this also be said to us, who give faith to the apostolic teaching, lest we deceive ourselves, as if, outside it, there were still some speculations and revelations of higher things that we lack. Let us take care only to respond, through a zeal for godliness, to the things revealed in the gospel and known in Christ. If we do this, we can securely await the coming of Christ the Saviour.

units.la: 9 Et obserua quod nō simpliciter dicit, Vsq; ad reuelatione domini nostri Iesu Christi: sed expectātes reuelationē, &c. Quo admonemur Christianorū esse, ut cū gaudio expectēt reuelationem Christi. Expectatio Christi nonnihil habet desiderij. Beati quib. expectatus ac desideratus reuelabitur. Sic Christ̃ dixit: Et uos similes estis hominibus expectantib. dominū suum, &c. & id desiderij pulchre exprimit uerbum ἀπεκδεχόμενοι, quod significat quidem proprie excipio. Quia uero excipi dicuntur, qui expectati cum gaudio suscipiūtur, fit ut ἀπεκδέχεσθαι sumatur pro expecto. Cōmodum aut, quoniam reuelatio Christi de cœlis expectatur, posuit ἀποκαραδοκία, quo usus est & ad Phil.3. quod significat alicunde aliquid expectare cum gaudio. Vel certe significat uehementē expectationem. Nam ἀπό aliquando intendit significatū, ut si dicas ex corde expectare. Existimo autem haud esse incōueniens, si participium hoc, expectantes, positum esse sentiamus hoc sensu. Vt nō destituamini ullo dono, intellige, uobis necessario, si expectaueritis reuelatione domi ni nostri Iesu Christi. Sic enim promittit illis copiam & sufficientiā donorū Dei indefinentem, si fideliter adhæserint domino, & omni impatientia & scrupulositate abiecta reuelationem domini nostri Iesu Christi constanter ad finem usq; expectent. Hanc expectationē sciebat firmissimam esse conseruationem & custodiam sinceræ erga Christū fidei, & optimum antidoton contra tentationes defectionis, & quarumuis sectarum.
units.tr: 9 And observe that he does not simply say "until the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ," but "waiting for the revelation," and so on. By this we are reminded that Christians should await the revelation of Christ with joy. The waiting for Christ has some element of longing. Blessed are those to whom he will be revealed when he is awaited and desired. So Christ said: "And you are like men waiting for their lord," and so on. The word ἀπεκδεχόμενοι [apekdechomenoi] expresses this longing beautifully; properly it means "to receive from", and since those who are awaited are said to be received with joy, ἀπεκδέχεσθαι [apekdechesthai] comes to be used for "to expect". Fittingly, since the revelation of Christ is awaited from heaven, he used ἀποκαραδοκία [apokaradokia], which he also uses in Philippians 3, and which signifies to wait eagerly for something from somewhere with joy; or certainly it signifies an intense expectation, for ἀπό [apo] sometimes intensifies the meaning, as when you say to await from the heart. I think it is not inappropriate to take this participle, "waiting", in this sense: "that you may lack no gift," understand: for you, necessarily, if you have waited for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. For so he promises them an abundance and sufficiency of the gifts of God that never fails, if they cling faithfully to the Lord, and, casting off all impatience and anxious scruple, constantly await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ to the end. He knew that this expectation is the most firm preservation and guard of sincere faith in Christ, and the best antidote against the temptations of apostasy and of any sects whatsoever.

units.la: Qui & cōfirmabit uos usq; in finē inculpatos, in die domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: Who will also confirm you to the end, blameless, on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Fidelis Deus, p quem uocati estis in cōsortiū filij ipsius Iesu Christi dñi nostri.
units.tr: Faithful is God, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

units.la: Hoc alterum est, quo gratia Dei q in Christo Corinthij acceperant, commendat. Videlicet ab illius constantia & perennitate [quæ durare posit ad finem usq. Et hoc commodum subiecit ei quod dixit, Expectātes reuelationē domini nostri Iesu Christi. Caute tamē, non dicit, permanebitis enim usq; in fineminculpati. Nam hoc non erat futurum. Iā tū enim degenerare coeperant: sed, qui & confirmabit uos usq; in finē, magis potentiam & fidē Christi q Corinthiorū cōstantiam cōmendans. Posuit aut hoc, ut admoneret eos primū nō opus esse noua aliqua reuelatione, sed cōfirmatione in gra
units.tr: This is the second thing by which he commends the grace of God that the Corinthians had received in Christ: namely, its constancy and perpetuity, which can endure to the end. He adds this benefit to what he said, "waiting for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ." Yet he speaks cautiously. He does not say "you will remain blameless to the end," for that was not going to happen; they had already begun to degenerate. Instead he says, "who will also confirm you to the end," commending the power and faithfulness of Christ rather than the steadiness of the Corinthians. He says this first to remind them that they do not need some new revelation, but confirmation in the grace

units.la: A Ad ista referēda uolunt: B quod ἀπεκδέχεσθαι. Act.15. tia illa Dei quam plenam ac sufficientem acce perant, ut in illa in finé usq; perfistere posint.
units.tr: A They want these things referred to: B the word ἀπεκδέχεσθαι [apekdechesthai], Acts 15. ...the grace of God, which they had received full and sufficient, so that they could persevere in it to the end.

units.la: Deinde confirmationem eam paratá quoq; esse in Christo, à quo sit petenda. Et huius gratia dicit: Qui confirmabit uos. Non enim tam dicit, quid futurū esset hac in re, q; quid à Christo petere deberent, & quid ille paratus sit suis præstare, si, quemadmodum præmisit, reuelatio nem ipsius constanter expectaurerint.
units.tr: Next, this confirmation is also prepared for them in Christ, and it is to be sought from him. For this reason he says, "who will confirm you." He is saying less what would happen in this matter than what they ought to ask of Christ, and what he is ready to grant his people, if, as he has said beforehand, they constantly wait for his revelation.

units.la: INCVLPATOS.] Hoc est, qui cōdemnari nequeatis. Pertinet ad hoc quod dixit, Cōfir mabit uos, ut scias quatenus confirmet suos dominus. Alias in multis deficiunt, & miserijs innumeris exponuntur. Vel expone, sine crimine, utpote perfidiæ & defectionis. Alioqui peccatis nemo liber est.
units.tr: BLAMELESS. This means "those who cannot be condemned." It belongs to what he said, "will confirm you," so that you may know how far the Lord confirms his people. Otherwise they fail in many ways and are exposed to countless miseries. Or explain it as "without blame," namely of faithlessness and defection. Otherwise no one is free from sins.

units.la: IN die domini nostri Iesu Christi.] Exponit quod dixit, In finem usq;. Nempe quo desinente hoc mundo dies domini aderit. Vel quod magis placet, referēdum est ad proxime præce dēs, inculpatos: ut intelligamus eum loqui de eo quod per cōfirmationem domini in die domini sint inculpati futuri, quicquid de ipsis interea mundus iudicet. Magna hinc est consolatio ueris Christianis, qui non à mūdo tantum, sed & à falsis fratribus & ecclesia maligne agentium cōdemnantur in hoc mūdo, quod sciunt se in die domini nostri Iesu Christi habendos esse pro inculpatis. Ad hoc etiam facit, quod fidem Dei adducit ad cōfirmandam hanc sperandę à Christo cōfirmationis fiduciā. Fidelis Deus inquit. Nō sumit argumentū ab ipsorum probitate aut aliqua alia prærogatiua, sed ab eo quod omniū est certissimū & constantissimum, qd' nemo piorū negare potest, & quod tale est, unde hoc quod asserit absq; ulla cōtradictione colligitur: & quod Deū, si non confirmemur in bono, ab omni culpa liberat, nostrā uero socordiā damnat. Fidelis est Deus inquit. Quasi dicat: Nemo addubitet de fide ac bonitate Dei. Non potest suos deserere. Est enim fidelis. Apud Eras.uide quomodo Apostolus di ctione hac utatur. Vtitur hoc elogio Dei & infrà ca.10. quo talem nobis Deū commendat, qui non modò uerax sit in promissis: sed qui nec fidem expectantium se, & à se pendentium irritam & inanem fieri sinat, totus ad nostram salutem propensus.
units.tr: ON THE DAY OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST. He explains what he said, "to the end." That is, when this world ends, the day of the Lord will arrive. Or, what pleases me more, it should be referred to the immediately preceding word, "blameless," so that we understand him to be speaking of this: that by the Lord's confirmation they will be blameless on the day of the Lord, whatever the world meanwhile judges about them. Hence great consolation comes to true Christians, who in this world are condemned not only by the world but also by false brothers and by the Church acting maliciously. They know that on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ they will be regarded as blameless. This also serves the point that he brings in the faithfulness of God to confirm this confidence, hoped for from Christ, of being confirmed. "Faithful is God," he says. He does not draw his argument from their uprightness or any other privilege, but from what is most certain and constant of all, which none of the godly can deny, and which is such that what he asserts follows from it without any contradiction. And God, if we are not confirmed in good, sets us free from all fault, but condemns our carelessness. "Faithful is God," he says, as if to say: let no one doubt the faith and goodness of God. He cannot desert his own, for he is faithful. Look, in Erasmus, how the Apostle uses this expression. He uses this title of God also in chapter 10 below, commending to us a God who is not only true in his promises, but who also does not allow the faith of those who wait for him, and who depend on him, to become void and empty, being wholly inclined to our salvation.

units.la: PER quem uocati estis. ] Declaratio est fidei Dei ab eo quod iam præstitit. Nam beneuolentiæ futuræ argumentū merito ex præteritis beneficijs colligitur. Ideo uocationem in Christo adducit, in qua agnoscendā proponit fidem Dei. Amplificat eam p hoc quod dicit, In consortium filij sui. Satis esset in cōsortiū angelorū uocari. Vocari aut in cōsortiū filij Dei, quid aliud est, q; non simpliciter assumi ultro uenientes & quærentes: sed etiam nihil huius cogitantes spontanea & ultronea philanthropia Dei ex summis miserijs in cōmunicationē omniū bonorū uocari, quorū unigenitus Dei hæres est constitutus. Hinc est quod infrà disturus est, omnia uestra sunt, uos Christi, Christus uero Dei. Et illud obserua, quod nō dicit, Iesu Christi fratris nostri: cum sic dicendum uideatur, postq; nos in consortium filij Dei uocatos esse dixit, sed Iesu Christi, inquit, domini nostri. Neq; ipse adimit filio suo dominij prærogatiuā quam illi dedit in omnia, etiam in consortes suos: neq; nobis licet sic trāsire in cōsortium unigeniti Dei, ut non agnoscamus eū amplius p domino nostro. Vocat ipse quidā nos fratres suos, dicens: Narrabo nomē tuū fratribus meis, uerū nobis cōuenit sic hāc dignatioē amplesti reuereter & humiliter, ut simul ipsum dominū nostrū agnoscamus & colamus.
units.tr: THROUGH WHOM YOU WERE CALLED. This is a declaration of God's faithfulness from what he has already done. For an argument of future goodwill is rightly drawn from past benefits. So he brings in the calling in Christ, in which he sets out that the faithfulness of God is to be acknowledged. He magnifies it by adding, "into the fellowship of his Son." It would be enough to be called into the fellowship of angels. But to be called into the fellowship of the Son of God is nothing other than not simply being taken up when we come and seek of our own accord, but being called, even though we were thinking of none of this, out of the deepest misery, by the spontaneous and voluntary love of God for mankind, into the sharing of all good things, of which the only-begotten Son of God has been appointed heir. Hence he is about to say below, "all things are yours, and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's." And observe that he does not say "Jesus Christ our brother," although that might seem to be the fitting way to speak, since he has said that we were called into the fellowship of the Son of God. Instead he says "Jesus Christ our Lord." Nor does he take away from his Son the prerogative of lordship which he gave him over all things, including his co-heirs. Nor are we permitted to pass into the fellowship of the only-begotten Son of God in such a way that we do not any longer acknowledge him as our Lord. He himself does call some of us his brothers, saying, "I will declare your name to my brothers." Yet it becomes us to embrace this favour reverently and humbly, so that at the same time we acknowledge and worship him as our Lord.

units.la: Obsecro aut uos fratres, per nomen domini nostri Iesu Christi, ut idē loquamini oēs, & non sint inter uos dissidia, sed sitis integrum corpus eadem mente & eadem sententia.
units.tr: I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be perfectly joined together in the same mind and the same judgment.

units.la: Post insinuatione & captatione beneuolentiæ, iam aggreditur primū caput huius epistolæ, quo Corinthios à sectarū studio ad concordiam ecclesiastica reuocare statuit. Et quoniā materia ipsa schismaticis iniucūda futura erat, caute illā & ita ingreditur, ut q; fieri possit tolerabilem reddat admonitionem: & hoc est, qd' ab obsecratione orditur. Est aut principalis p positio, ut unanimes sint, eadem mente & eadem sententia perfecti & integri.
units.tr: After the introduction and the winning of goodwill, he now approaches the first chapter of this letter, by which he resolves to recall the Corinthians from their eagerness for factions to ecclesiastical concord. And since the subject itself was bound to be unwelcome to the schismatics, he approaches it cautiously, so as to make the admonition as tolerable as possible; and this is why he begins with an entreaty. The main proposition is that they should be of one accord, perfect and whole, in the same mind and the same judgment.

units.la: OBSECRO aut uos fratres.] Iterū pathos in uerbo obsecrandi, quo amicus exprimitur affectus, dū qui bene consulit, etiā obsecrat, ut pdesse possit. Quanquā uerbū etiā hortari & admonere significat: & nihil uetat, quo minus ita hic exponatur. Verū quoniam cōmuniter ita exponunt, & uetus quoq; p uerbum obsecrandi reddidit, & suauius aliquid à pectore Apostolico eructat uerbū obsecrandi quam adhortandi, maxime initio tractationis, uolo & ipse legere, Obsecro uos fratres.
units.tr: "I beseech you, brethren." Again there is emotion in the word "beseech," by which a friendly feeling is expressed: the one who advises well also entreats, so that he may be of use. Yet the word also means to exhort and admonish, and nothing prevents it from being explained in that way here. But since commentators commonly explain it so, and the old translator also rendered it by the word "beseech," and since a word of entreaty bursts more sweetly from the Apostle's heart than one of exhortation, especially at the beginning of the discussion, I too wish to read it as "I beseech you, brethren."

units.la: FRATRES.] Quāuis uulgare sit Apostolo Christianos uocare fratres, hoc tamen loco id opportunissime facit. Primum, studio nō eos aperte, qui in culpa erant, ac sectis studebant (erant enim probati quidā inter Corinthios, ad quos hæc non pertinebant, de quibus infrà cap.11.) sed cōmuniter omes, appellatione fratrum alloquitur. Est enim tolerabilis ijs qui in culpa sunt, si non nominatim arguantur, sed in genere ita corrigantur quasi ipsorū uitiū, omnium fit commune. Et licet aliquid hic iniuriæ fiet probatis & insontibus, ferendum tamen hoc illis est: & hoc pacto seruiendū infirmis fratribus ad ędificationē, cū sciant uniuscuiusque innocētiam esse Deo conspicuā. Deinde & appellatione fratrum charitatis & cōcordiæ fraterne illos admonet in loco, cum proposuerit animos eorum ad illā impellere. Non enim poterunt locū habere schismata, ubi regnat charitas fraterna: & rursus ubi schismata obtinent, necesse est uel nullā uel modicā haberi fraternæ charitatis ratione. Quid enim minus cōuenit charitati, eiq; staterne, quā in sectas diuidi.
units.tr: "Brothers." Although it is common for the Apostle to call Christians brothers, here he does so most opportunely. First, by design he does not openly name those who were at fault and devoted to sects (for there were some approved men among the Corinthians to whom these things did not apply, about whom see below, chapter 11), but addresses them all together with the name of brothers. A rebuke is more tolerable for those who are at fault if they are not accused by name, but are corrected in general, as though their fault were shared by all. And although some injury will be done here to the approved and innocent, they must bear it, and in this way the weak brothers are served for their edification, since the innocence of each is plain to God. Second, by the name of brothers he also admonishes them, in this place, to brotherly love and fraternal concord, since he has set out to drive their minds towards it. For schisms cannot have a place where brotherly love reigns; and conversely, where schisms prevail, it must be that little or no account is taken of brotherly love. For what is less consistent with love, and with brotherhood, than to be divided into sects?

units.la: Athoc fiebat Corinthi. Ideo satis in loco fratres A illos appellat, non quòd uerè fratres uel frater ne inter se animati & affecti esset, sed ut ad cha ritatē illis fraternā redeundum esse admoneat.
units.tr: And this was happening at Corinth. Therefore he rightly calls them brothers in this place, not because they were truly brothers, or were minded and disposed towards one another as brothers, but so as to admonish them that they must return to brotherly love.

units.la: PER nomé dni nostri Iesu Christi.] Quanq; tāti debuerat esse apostolica authoritas, ut per illius reuerentiā ad cōcordiā se reduci sinerent Corinthij: modestia tu usus, illā nō obijcit, sed lóge potiore, nempe nominis dni Iesu Christi. Q.d. Quod si ego uobis tanti non habeor, Christus tamen dominus nester tanti sit, cuius gratia permoueamini, ut quod peto, praestetis.
units.tr: "Through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ." Although the apostolic authority ought to have been so great that the Corinthians would allow themselves to be brought back to concord out of reverence for it, he, out of modesty, does not put this forward, but a far greater one, namely the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. As if to say: if I am not held in such esteem by you, yet let our Lord Christ be held in such esteem, by whose grace you may be moved to grant what I ask.

units.la: Quę est aut uis huius obtestationis? an satis est, magná esse Christi authoritate, ut illius respectu obtemperet Apostolo? Si satis est, ergo per nomen dni Iesu Christi quiduis inter Christianos obtineri debet. Nequaq;. Sed exigitur, ut hoc quod petitur, tale sit, quod Christo placeat, quod nomini illius gloriosum sit, in quo si obedias, Christo gratificeris. Alioqui absurdū & impiū fuerit, ea uelle per nomen Christi obtinere, quae Christo displiceat. Quod autē Corinthij sectis studebant, Christo utiq; displiceba t. Et quod Paulus exigebat, ut ad concordia redirent, prorsus nomini Christi cōgruebat & gloriosum erat, Christoq; placebat. Erat enim cōmunis illorū dās. Quis dās æquo animo tolerat suorū disidia? Huc pertinet quod dicit, Dni nostri Iesu Christi. Deinde & nomini Christi fiebat iniuria, quod Christiani à Christo sic appellati, aliorū nominibus censeri incipiebat, ut alius diceretur Pauli, alius Cephæ, &c. Hāc contumeliam deprecatur, dicens: Per nomen dni Iesu Christi. Q.d. Ipsum Christi nomē, quo insigniti estis, debebat uos à sectarum cohibere studio, & unitatis admonere. Et huc putatur pertinere, quod in exordio huius epistolæ tonties, nempe, ad hunc usq; locum decies, mentionem Christi Iesu inducit, quod nusquam in tam breui uidetur contextu facere.
units.tr: What, then, is the force of this entreaty? Is it enough that the authority of Christ is great, so that out of regard for him they obey the Apostle? If that were enough, then anything at all ought to prevail among Christians through the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. By no means. Rather, what is asked must be such that it pleases Christ and is glorious to his name, so that in obeying you please Christ. Otherwise it would be absurd and impious to wish to obtain through the name of Christ things that displease Christ. But that the Corinthians were pursuing sects certainly displeased Christ, and that Paul required them to return to concord was wholly fitting to the name of Christ, glorious to it, and pleasing to Christ. For he was their common Lord. Who bears with equanimity the dissensions of his own? To this pertains what he says: "of our Lord Jesus Christ." Moreover, an injury was also being done to the name of Christ, since Christians who were called by Christ's name began to be named after other men, so that one said "I am of Paul," another "I am of Cephas," and so on. He deprecates this insult when he says: "through the name of the Lord Jesus Christ." As if to say: the very name of Christ, with which you are marked, ought to restrain you from the pursuit of sects and remind you of unity. And it is thought that this is also why, at the beginning of this letter, he brings in the mention of Christ Jesus so often, namely ten times up to this place, which he seems not to do anywhere else in so brief a passage.

units.la: VT idem loquamini omnes.] Paucis uerbis exprimit quid petat. Quid est autē idē loqui omnes? Primū cū cōcordiā exigat, quid estquod eadē uerba exigit? Quid situ est in uerbis? Deinde quomodo idē omnes loqui possunt etiā? sequentia declarant hanc particulam. Nam ubi dicebat, alius, ego sum Pauli: alius, ego sum Cephæ, &c. certe non idem loquebantur omnes. Hoc est, nō ijsdem appellationibus seipsos censebant, cum essent omnes Christiani. Proinde idem omnes loqui quod hic exigit, est idē profiteri de se omnes, eidem authori se accēsere omnes, eodem de se praedicato uti omnes. Quid est autem, quod omnes uult de se prędicare, ui delicet ut quisq; se dicat esse Christianū. Hoc sci licet ut facere nequeunt qui in sectas diuidun tur: ita qui faciunt, qui de se idē praedicat, haud facile in sectas sese diuidunt. Idem dicere, po test etiam exponi pro eandem doctrinam profiteri, opinionibus uarijs non dissentire, ut idē sit cum eo quod dicit, eadem sententia.
units.tr: "That you all speak the same thing." He states in a few words what he asks. But what is it for all to speak the same thing? First, since he demands concord, why does he demand the same words? What is there in words? Then, how can all of them speak the same thing? The following clauses explain this phrase. For when they said, "I am of Paul," "I am of Cephas," and so on, they were certainly not all speaking the same thing. That is, they did not describe themselves by the same appellations, though they were all Christians. Therefore, to speak the same thing, as he requires here, is for all to profess the same about themselves, to attach themselves to the same authority, and to use the same description of themselves. What, moreover, does he want all to say of themselves? Namely, that each one is a Christian. Those who are divided into sects cannot do this; but those who do it, who say the same of themselves, do not easily divide themselves into sects. To speak the same thing can also be explained as professing the same doctrine, not dissenting in differing opinions, so that it means the same as what he says next: the same judgment.

units.la: ET non sint inter uos schismata.] Id est, sectæ uel scissurae. Iam per contrarium declarat, quid sit quod dixit, Vt idem dicatis omnes. Ergo contraria sunt inter se, idem de se praedicare omnes, uel eādem profiteri doctrinam omnes, & in sectas diuidi. Itaq; schismatici sunt, qui nō idem de se praedicant, qui se non Christo uni authori salutis, sed alijs atq; alijs addicūt, & qui non eandem doctrinę sententiam profitentur. Nam ideo alterum ponit, ut alterum excludat, quod certe absurde & absque neruis faceret, si fieri posset, ut schismatici non sint, qui nō idem de se praedicant, nec idem docent, aut profiteantur: ut qui se uocant Augustinianos, Benedictinos, Franciscanos, magis q Christianos. Item qui opinionibus diuersis inter sese dissident Thomistæ, Scotistæ, Albertistę, &c. Itē nominales, reales, &c. Illi nolunt pro schismaticis haberi, cū tn nō idē de se prędicet. Si isti possunt excusari, quòd dicūt se nihilominus Christum agnoscere pro Seruatore, licet interea patronos elegerint, quib. accenseantur, quid uetat & Corinthios ita excusari potuisse? Nō enim credo illos ita diuersa de se praedicasse, quòd Christo prorsus abiecerint, aut patronos illos & magistros suos pro uitæ authoribus habuerint. Quod si & Corinthij hoc pacto recte excusantur, non uideo quomodo Paulus hic defendi queat, ne nugarū ac delirij argui possit. Proinde necesse est Apostolo schismaticos esse, & nō idem de se praedicare, pro eodem usurpari.
units.tr: "And that there be no schisms among you." That is, sects or splits. Now he declares by the opposite what he meant by "that you all say the same thing." So these are opposed to each other: all saying the same of themselves, or all professing the same doctrine, on the one hand, and being divided into sects on the other. Thus those are schismatics who do not say the same of themselves, who attach themselves not to Christ alone, the author of salvation, but to this man and that, and who do not profess the same doctrine and judgment. For he sets down the one so as to exclude the other; he would do this absurdly and without force if it were possible that those who do not say the same of themselves, nor teach or profess the same things, were not schismatics, such as those who call themselves Augustinians, Benedictines, or Franciscans rather than Christians. Likewise those who disagree among themselves in diverse opinions: Thomists, Scotists, Albertists, and so on; likewise nominalists, realists, and so on. These do not want to be regarded as schismatics, though nonetheless they describe themselves differently. If these men can be excused on the ground that they nonetheless acknowledge Christ as Saviour, although meanwhile they have chosen the patrons by whom they are named, what forbids that the Corinthians too could have been excused in the same way? For I do not believe they described themselves so differently that they utterly cast off Christ, or regarded those patrons and masters of theirs as the authors of life. But if the Corinthians are rightly excused in this way, I do not see how Paul can here be defended against the charge of trifling and raving. Therefore it must be that, for the Apostle, those are schismatics who do not say the same of themselves and are not reckoned as one and the same.

units.la: SED fitis integrū corpus, eadem mente & eadem sententia.] Et hoc ad prioris particulæ expositionē facit, ut ostēdat se exigere in Christo perfectam concordiam, quà hic collocat in eandem mentem & eandem sententiam.
units.tr: "But that you be a whole body, with the same mind and the same judgment." This too serves to explain the previous clause, showing that he demands in Christ a perfect concord, which he here places in the same mind and the same judgment.

units.la: Et hanc omnimodam & perfectam concordiam uolūt quidam exigi commodum per hoc quod dicit καταρτισμένοι, quod exponunt perfectos uel integros. Significat enim aliquando καὶ ταρτίσω idem quod absoluo & perficio. Nam ἀ- πὼ aliquando integrum significat, unde desumptum est uerbum κατ' ἐπιτ. Et sanè hoc sensu accipitur Lucæ 6. ubi sic legimus, καταρτισμένος ἔσται ὡς ὁ διδάσκαλος αὐτοῦ.
units.tr: Some people want this complete and perfect agreement to be required by the word they render καταρτισμένοι [katartismenoi], which they take to mean perfect or whole. The verb sometimes means the same as to complete or perfect, and the noun for completeness comes from it. In this sense it is used in Luke 6: "Everyone who is perfect [καταρτισμένος ἔσται ὡς ὁ διδάσκαλος αὐτοῦ] will be like his teacher."

units.la: Quoniam uero καταρτίζω non hoc solum significat, sed simul usurpatur pro componere, conglutinare, conciliare, utpote, quando quæ antea luxata erant, in sua loca restituuntur (unde Galeno, annotante Budæo, καταρτισμὸς ἐστὶ μετάθεσις ... ) & quæ diuersa erant, in unam quasi massam coadaptantur (ut apud Dioscoridem καταρτισμένα ἐδέσματα edulia significant, ex uarijs rebus composita) Videtur haud absurdum esse, si hoc loco intelligamus Apostolum ista dictione, cum de concordia loquatur, exigere partium quasi luxatarum &dissidentium compositionem & conciliationem.
units.tr: But καταρτίζω does not have only this meaning. It is also used for to put together, to join, to reconcile: for example, when things that were dislocated are restored to their places (so Galen, as Budaeus notes, says that καταρτισμός is a replacing), and when things that were different are fitted together into one mass, as in Dioscorides, where καταρτισμένα ἐδέσματα means foods made up of various ingredients. So it does not seem absurd to understand the Apostle here, since he is speaking of agreement, to demand the joining and reconciliation of parts that have been, as it were, dislocated and at odds.

units.la: Et hoc sensu pulchrè illos admonet gratiæ Christi, qua antea prorsus luxati ac dissipati, in unum fuerant corpus compositi, & non solum erga Deum, sed & inter seipsos conciliati.
units.tr: In this sense he admirably reminds them of the grace of Christ, by which they, once utterly dislocated and scattered, were joined into one body, and reconciled not only to God but also to one another.

units.la: Quomodocūq; hāc uocē siue cōglutinationis siue integritatis sensu accipiamus, puto parum rū referre. Nā earū rerū integritas, quæ ex partibus sunt ueluti membris compositæ, ex indiuulsa partium cohæsione & compositione constat, unde & hoc uerbū utroq; sensu accipitur. Et hic apte schismati ecclesiæ opponitur, per quod illa integritatem & compactionē sui ueluti membris luxatis amiserat. Nihil itaq; incomodi fuerit, si legam⁹, Sed sitis integri (corpus non est in Græco nec in uulgata uersione) in eadem mente, & in eadem sententia.
units.tr: However we take this word, whether in the sense of being joined together or of being whole, I think it makes little difference. The wholeness of things made up of parts, like limbs of a body, consists in the unbroken cohesion and joining of the parts, and so the word is taken in both senses. Here it is rightly set against the schism of the Church, through which the Church had lost its wholeness and cohesion, as if its limbs were dislocated. So there is no harm in reading, "But be whole [corpus is not in the Greek, nor in the Vulgate version] in the same mind and in the same judgement."

units.la: Satis aūt conuenienter, cum dixisset, Vt idem dicatis oēs: subiecit, Sed sitis integri in eadem mente & in eadē sententia, significans eos non esse eadem mente ac sententia præditos, ideoq; non dicere idē. Requirit igitur à fidelibus eam mentis ac sententiæ unitatē, quæ & foris cum uerbis tū factis declaratur. Quod Corinthij in sectas diuidebātur, nō erat aliunde, q̄ quod animo ac mēte diuisi erāt. Concordia spiritus externæ quoq; uitæ concordia & unitate confert. Sanè nihil potest excogitari & iucundius & decētius in ecclesia Christi, q̄ si omnes eadē sint mente ac sententia, atq; ita idē dicant oēs, & eandē pietatis regulam mutuo consensu sequent, ut nō sit præter rationē, quod non hic tantum, sed & alijs locis unitas ista corporis ecclesiastici ab Apostolo urgetur. Corpus est ecclesia. Corporis autē unius lingua est una, anima una, spiritus unus, cor unū, mēs una, uoluntas una, caput unū. Nisi hæc sit in corpore unitas, nō poterit illius integritas salua cōsistere. Quæ cōditio nō magis est animati nostri corporis, q̄ ecclesiastici. Et hinc est quod Satan tam impro be satagit, ut unitatem ecclesiæ, ueram illam, quæ in Christo est, uarijs modis scindat, & falsam, quæ sit in erroribus & mendacijs statuat & cōseruet. Quare quod hic Apostolus dicit, Sed sitis integri in eadē mēte, & in eadem sentētia, non est indiscriminatim de quauis mentis ac sententiæ unitate: sed de ea intelligendū quæ ad corporis Christi, ecclesiæ uidelicet, integritate omnino requiritur. Ea aūt nō potest esse alia, q̄ quæ sit in Christo ac per spiritū Christi. Recte uocabis hāc unitatem fidei, & spei dilectionis Christianæ, quæ ex ueritate & unitate spiritus Christi proueniat, per quā idē credamus & dicamus omnes, idē sperēmus omnes, idē diligamus & amplectamur omnes, ubi hæc est unitas, ibi nulla schismata locū habere possunt. Aliam unitatē nō quærit Apostolus, sed hāc omnino seruatā cupit. Vrgent hodie unitatem, qui dominium in ecclesia exercēt. Intelligūt aūt non hāc quā intelligit Apostolus, sed eā q̄ ecclesias Christi Rom. pontifici subijciat, quē eaput uni uersalis ecclesiæ cōstituerūt. Hūc agnoscere p capite ecclesiarū & uicario Christi, qui plenam habeat omniū rerū tā cœlestiū q̄ terrestriū potestatē scrinio pectoris sui inclusam, & hoc illi nomine in omnibas sese subijcere, nec latū digitū à cōstitutionibus illius, mādatis, sanctis & ritibus quoq; ab ipso approbatis, ne ad manifestā quidē & cognitā Christi ueritate discedere, id demū uocāt ueram ecclesiæ unitatem.
units.tr: Quite fittingly, having said, "that you all say the same thing," he added, "but be whole in the same mind and in the same judgement," meaning that they were not endowed with the same mind and judgement, and therefore did not say the same thing. He therefore requires of the faithful that unity of mind and judgement which is shown outwardly both in words and in deeds. The Corinthians were divided into factions for no other reason than that they were divided in spirit and mind. Agreement of spirit also brings agreement and unity to outward life. Indeed nothing can be imagined more pleasant and fitting in the Church of Christ than that all should be of one mind and judgement, and so all say the same thing, and follow the same rule of piety by common consent. It is no wonder that the Apostle insists on this unity of the church body not only here but also in other places. The Church is a body. A body has one tongue, one soul, one spirit, one heart, one mind, one will, one head. Unless there is this unity in the body, its wholeness cannot remain safe. This condition belongs no less to the church than to our living body. And so Satan labours so wickedly to tear apart, in various ways, the true unity of the Church that is in Christ, and to establish and maintain a false unity that exists in errors and lies. Therefore what the Apostle says here, "But be whole in the same mind and the same judgement," does not refer indiscriminately to any unity of mind and judgement, but to that which is wholly required for the wholeness of the body of Christ, that is, the Church. This cannot be any other than the unity that is in Christ and through the Spirit of Christ. You may rightly call it the unity of faith, of hope, and of Christian love, which comes from the truth and unity of the Spirit of Christ, through which we all believe and say the same, all hope the same, all love and embrace the same. Where this unity is, schisms can have no place. The Apostle seeks no other unity, but wishes this one to be kept entirely. Today those who exercise dominion in the Church press for unity. But they understand by it not what the Apostle understands, but that which subjects the Churches of Christ to the Roman pontiff, whom they have made the head of the universal Church. They want him acknowledged as the head of the Churches and the vicar of Christ, who holds the full power over all things, heavenly and earthly, enclosed in the casket of his breast; and they want everyone to submit to him in all things, and not to depart a finger's breadth from his decrees, commands, holy things and rites, even when these have been approved by him; and they call this the true unity of the Church, even when they plainly know that it departs from the manifest truth of Christ.

units.la: Quātumuis diuersa studia, diuersæ opiniones, diuersa instituta tā diuersarū sint in Papatu sectarū, propter unā tamen hāc unitatem, qua se omnes cōformiter Rom. pontifici tanq̄ capiti suo subijciunt, ac sua omnia ad pedes illius uel probanda uel reijcienda deferunt, nō modo tolerātur, sed & sanctificātur. De his cogitādū est hodie, quoties plausibiles hæ uoces unitatis, pacis, cōcordiæ ac mutui consensus ab aduersa rijs iactātur, & odiosa illa nobis schismatam & hæresum uocabula obijciūtur. Pacē & unitatē uolumus & nos, sed eā q̄ sit Christi, in Christo, & sub Christo, in spiritu ac ueritate Christi, nō q̄ nos Babyloni subijciat, unde exire iubemur.
units.tr: However many different pursuits, different opinions and different institutions there are among the sects within Papacy, they are not only tolerated but even sanctified, for the sake of this one unity, by which all conform to the Roman pontiff as their head and submit all their affairs to his feet, to be approved or rejected. We must think about this today, whenever those plausible words of unity, peace, concord and mutual consent are thrown at us by our opponents, and those hateful names of schisms and heresies are flung at us. We too desire peace and unity, but the peace and unity that belong to Christ, in Christ and under Christ, in the Spirit and truth of Christ, not that which subjects us to Babylon, from which we are commanded to go out.

units.la: IN eadē, inquit, mente, & in eadē sententia. Vulgata uersio sic habet, In eodē sensu, & in eadem sciētia. Sic legit & Ambrof. & exponit ad hūc modū: Perfectos eos uult esse in eodē sensu quē illis tradiderat, ut nō discreparent. Adiiorū enim exēplū, quos supra laudat, hos prouocat, ut hoc sentiāt ac defendāt. In Græco est ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ νοΐ, ἢ ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ γνώμῃ. Apparet interpretē per νοῦν, id est mente, intellexisse sensum, & per γνώμην scientiā, quæ Græcis uocatur γνῶσις. Chrysost. intelligit per γνώμην, uolūtatem, quēadmodū & nonnulli recētiores, per νοῦν uero intelligentiā ac sententiā iudicij. Et sanè sunt hæc duo in anima principalia, unde omnis uita nostra uel bene uel male dirigitur, mens uidelicet & uoluntas. Græca uox νοῦς, rationale & purissimam partē animæ significat, qua sentimus, intelligimus & iudicamus, ad quā pertinet sciētia, intelligentia, sapiētia & prudētia, secundum quā uel prudentes uel stulti iudicantur, hāc mentem uocamus: γνώμη uero mentis est sententia, iudicij ac decretū. Et quoniā hinc plerūq; est uolūtas, fit ut sæpenumero γνώμη pro uoluntate & affectu accipiatur. An aūt Apostolus hāc duarū iftarū uocum discretionē hoc loco spectarit, nolim affirmare. Potuit illis uti simpliciter eo sensu quo alibi dicit, Vt uno spiritu unoq; animo decertātē fidē adiuuetis. Et: Sitis eodē modo affecti, unanimes, idem sentientes, &c. sicut in Actis legimus, Erat illis cor unū & anima una, & quēadmodū Germanice dicimus, Eins sins Vndgmyets.
units.tr: "In the same mind," he says, "and in the same judgement." The Vulgate version has, "in the same sense and in the same knowledge." Ambrose also reads it this way and explains it thus: he wants them to be perfect in the same sense that was handed on to them, so that they do not disagree. For he urges them, by the example of the others whom he praised above, to think and defend this same thing. In the Greek it is ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ νοΐ [in the same mind] or ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ γνώμῃ [in the same judgement]. It appears that the translator understood by νοῦς, that is mind, sense, and by γνώμη, knowledge, which the Greeks call γνῶσις. Chrysostom takes γνώμη to mean will, as do some more recent writers, and by νοῦς understands the understanding and judgement of the sentence. And indeed these are the two principal faculties of the soul by which our whole life is directed either well or badly, namely the mind and the will. The Greek word νοῦς signifies the rational and purest part of the soul, by which we perceive, understand and judge, and to which belong knowledge, understanding, wisdom and prudence, by which people are judged either prudent or foolish; we call this the mind. γνώμη, however, is the opinion, judgement and decision of the mind. And since this is often bound up with the will, γνώμη is often taken to mean will and inclination. I would not venture to affirm whether the Apostle had in view this distinction between the two words in this place. He could have used them simply in the sense in which he says elsewhere, "that you may strive with one spirit and one soul for the faith," and, "be of the same disposition, of one mind, thinking the same," and as we read in Acts, "they had one heart and one soul," and as we say in German, "Eins sins Vndgmyets" [one in mind and in heart].

units.la: Illud optarim ex animo, ut quoniā nostra hac ætate soluta est conscientiarū captiuitas, & passim libere sentitur & iudicatur de fidei nostræ ac religionis rebus, ac scripturæ sacræ libere legūtur & exponuntur, unde prorsus necesse est uariare sententias: hactenus saltē unitate in ecclesia seruemus, ut uno & eodē simus corde & animo in Christo domino, aliusq; aliū uere diligat, nec iudicet quisq̄ & condemnet à se in quibusdā dissentiente. Prorsus iniquum est, propterea dānare fratrē, quod libere sentit, nec iurat in ullius, quisquis sit, uerba magistri, nisi solius Christi: cū uideamus eos q̄ sic à se dissentientes dānāt, hoc iure libertatis uti, ut sententia suā nullius potestati subijciāt, sed liberā retineant.
units.tr: I would heartily wish that, since in our age the captivity of consciences has been loosened, and people freely feel and judge everywhere about the matters of our faith and religion, and the Holy Scriptures are freely read and expounded, from which opinions must necessarily differ, we would at least keep unity in the Church so far that we are of one and the same heart and mind in the Lord Christ, that each truly loves the other, and that no one judges or condemns another for disagreeing with him on certain points. It is wholly unjust to condemn a brother because he thinks freely, and does not swear by the words of any master, whoever he may be, except Christ alone; since we see that those who condemn others who dissent from them use this right of liberty, namely that they do not subject their own opinion to anyone's power, but keep it free.

units.la: Significatum enim mihi de uobis est fratres mei, à familiaribus Chloæ, quod coucõtentiones sint inter uos.Dico autē illud, quod unusquisq; uestrū dicit, alius quidem:Ego sum Pauli,ego uero Apollo,ego uero Cephæ,ego uero Christi.
units.tr: For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by the household of Chloe, that there are quarrels among you. I mean this: each of you says, one, "I am of Paul," and another, "I am of Apollos," and another, "I am of Cephas," and another, "I am of Christ."

units.la: Quamobrem unitatis seruandæ admoneat, hac quasi narratione quadā aperit. Significatū est mihi,inquit.quasi dicat:Quod ista scribo,& concordia à uobis exigo,non est ex inani quadam de uobis suspicione, qua laborare solent animi sinistri:sed ex eo, quod quorundam relationibus accepi,contentiones inter uos obortas esse,interea dū à uobis abusum,&huius gratia,animo plane paterno,& ut decet Christi Apostolum, ab istis uos contentionibus dehortor. Et amicum huc affectum iterum exprimit cum dicit,Fratres mei,ut ostendat se illos nondum habere pro deploratis, sed agnoscere pro fratribus, eiusdem spei ac salutis consortibus. Videmus etiam eos, de quorū peccatis sumus instructi,recte à nobis uocari fratres.
units.tr: Therefore, in order to urge the keeping of unity, he discloses this by way of a kind of narrative. "It has been reported to me," he says, as if to say: what I write, and the agreement I demand from you, do not arise from some groundless suspicion about you, of the sort that sinister minds are wont to harbour. They come from what I have received through the reports of certain people, that contentions have arisen among you, while I warn you away from these contentions with the plainly fatherly feeling that becomes an Apostle of Christ, and for the sake of this.
