He expresses his friendly feeling again when he says, "my brothers," to show that he does not yet regard them as beyond hope, but acknowledges them as brothers, sharers in the same hope and salvation. We also see that those whose sins we have been told about are rightly called brothers by us.

units.la: A familiaribus Chloæ.] Quia dixit:Nuncia tum uel significatum est mihi, ne fictum putet, addit à quibus hoc acceperit. Et tamē nomina tim eos non exprimit, quod studio factum plerique exponunt,ne inuidiam relatoribus suscitaret. Sanè prudentiæ est quod relationem hanc non tribuit uni certæ personæ, sed generaliter familiaribus Chloæ. Quid autē per Chloen sit intelligendum,ambigunt quidam, è quorū numero est Ambrosius,an sit uir,uel fœmina, uel locus aliquis.Ex odis tū Horatij annotate Erasmo Chloe reperitur sexu fœmineo,ut cū dicit: Me nunc Cressa Chloe regit, Dulces docta modos,& citharæ sciens.
units.tr: "From the household of Chloe." Because he said, "It has been reported to me," lest they think it invented, he adds from whom he received it. Yet he does not name them individually, which most expositors say was done deliberately, so as not to stir up hatred against the informants. Surely it was prudent of him not to attribute the report to one particular person, but to speak generally of the household of Chloe. Some are in doubt about who Chloe is, among them Ambrose: whether she is a man, or a woman, or some place. But in the odes of Horace, noted by Erasmus, Chloe is found to be of the female sex, as where he says: "Now the Cretan Chloe rules me, skilled in sweet measures and the lyre."

units.la: Apparet hanc familiā fuisse ex ijs,quos infrà probatos uocat cap.11. qui certè ægre tulerunt istam ecclesiæ Corinthiorum diuisionē,adeoq; illam Apostolo,ut corrigeretur,infinuarunt.
units.tr: It appears that this household was among those whom he later calls approved, in chapter 11, who certainly were grieved by this division in the Corinthian Church, and so made it known to the Apostle, so that it might be corrected.

units.la: QVOD cõtentiones sunt inter uos.] Quod suprà uocauit nō idem omnes dicere,itē schismata, hoc iam uocat contentiones. Est autē contentio, æmulatio quædā & zelus,quādo quisq; suā sententiā mordicus tuetur. Vnde lites oriūtur & rixę,quod fieri solet ubi sectarū studium in ecclesia uiget,ita ut contentiones fructus qui dam sint schismatū,quibus nō elanguida iā,sed adhuc calida & feruētia schismata notātur. Reperies enim schismata inueterata iā & quasi emortua, in quibus nullus apparet cōtentionis feruor,q nō queas rectè contentiones uocare.
units.tr: "That there are contentions among you." What he earlier called not all saying the same thing, and schisms, he now calls contentions. Now contention is a kind of rivalry and zeal, when each person defends his own opinion stubbornly. From this lawsuits and quarrels arise, which usually happens where a spirit of factions thrives in the Church, so that contentions are in a sense the fruit of schisms, by which schisms are marked not yet languid but still hot and fervent. For you will find schisms that are already long-standing and almost dead, in which no heat of contention appears, which you could not properly call contentions.

units.la: Intelligimus ergo in ecclesia Corinthiorum fuisse nō simpliciter schismata, sed contentiosa & feruida schismata,quę nomine contentionū ad Apostolū sint à familiaribus Chloæ delata.
units.tr: We understand therefore that in the Church of Corinth there were not simply schisms, but contentious and fervent schisms, which the household of Chloe reported to the Apostle under the name of contentions.

units.la: DICO autem illud, quod unusquisq;] Expositio est.Quasi dicat: Quod dico de contentionibus, quæ inter uos esse feruntur, ne me putetis de triuialibus quibusdam uel iudiciarijs rixis loqui,hoc est
units.tr: "Now I mean this, that each one" is an explanation. As if to say: what I say about the contentions that are reported to be among you, do not think I am speaking of some trivial or litigious squabbles; this is what I mean.

units.la: Quod unusquisque uestrū dicit.] Legendum est ad hūc modum: Quod unusquisq; uestrū dicit, alius,Ego sum Pauli, alius, Ego sum Apollo,&c.Non enim unusquisque illorū se & Pauli,& Apollo, & Cephæ & Christi esse dicebat.Nā qui se alicui addixerat,alijs se non accē sebant.Qui se dicebant esse Pauli, illi non dicebant simul se & Apollo esse & Cephæ & Christi.Alioqui nulla fuissent inter ipsos disidia & schismata nullæ contētiones,si quisq; se omnibus istis addixisset.Quia uero istis exponit, de quibus contentionibus dicat, manifestum est quod contentiose alius se Pauli, alius Apollo, alius Cephæ esse dixerit.
units.tr: "That each one of you says." It should be read in this way: each one of you says, one, "I am of Paul"; another, "I am of Apollos," and so on. For each of them did not say that he was of Paul, and of Apollos, and of Cephas, and of Christ all at once. For whoever had devoted himself to one did not join himself to the others. Those who said they were of Paul did not at the same time say that they were of Apollos, or of Cephas, or of Christ. Otherwise there would have been no discord or schisms among them, no contentions, if each had devoted himself to all of these. But since he sets out by name which contentions he means, it is plain that, quarrelsomely, one said he was of Paul, another of Apollos, another of Cephas.

units.la: EGO quidē sum Pauli.] Hoc, ut pleriq; exponūt,nō ita intelligendū est, quod uere se alij Paulo,alij Apollo, alij Cephæ addixerint, cū à pseudapostolis pependerint:sed quod hoc pacto uoluerit Apostolus absurditate contentionū in se Apollo & Cephæ declarare. Nā si schismatici essent, si qui se uel Paulo uel Petro primis illis apostolis acceserent,quāto magis erat qui se pseudapostolis adnominabant. Et hoc colligitur infrà cap.4.ex eoquod dicit:Hæc per figurā transtuli in meipsum, & Apollo propter uos, ut in nobis disceretis ne quis supra id qd̄ scriptū est de se sentiat, ut ne hic illius, ille huius nomine inflemini alius aduersus alium.
units.tr: "Indeed I am of Paul." This, as most expositors explain it, is not to be understood as meaning that some truly devoted themselves to Paul, others to Apollos, others to Cephas, since they depended on false apostles. Rather the Apostle wished, by this manner of speaking, to show the absurdity of the contentions by putting himself, Apollos and Cephas forward as examples. For if there were schismatics who joined themselves to Paul or to Peter, those first apostles, how much more were there those who named themselves after the false apostles! This is gathered from what he says later in chapter 4: "I have transferred these things by figure to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that in us you might learn not to think of anyone above what is written, that none of you be puffed up in favour of one against another, one on behalf of this man and another on behalf of that."

units.la: Quanq; credibile est fuisse etiā qui se Pauli, uel Apollo,uel Cephæ esse dicerent,cū Paulus eos ad fidē cōuerterit,& Apollo quoq; ibi Christū docuerit post Paulū, homo doctus in scripturis ac distertus. Licet enim hoc sancti nō quārant, ut ipsorū nomine quisq; ad contētionem abutatur:cōsilio tamē Satanę hoc fieri uidem9, ut quo quisq; sanctior est, hoc ad schismata & cōtetiones contentiosis magis seruiat.Exēplum huius habemus in discipulis Iohānis Matth.9. Io.3.licet Iohāni & Christo optime cōuenerit.
units.tr: Yet it is credible that there were also those who said they were of Paul, or of Apollos, or of Cephas, since Paul had converted them to the faith, and Apollos also taught Christ there after Paul, a man learned in the Scriptures and eloquent. For although the saints do not seek this, so that anyone should abuse their names for contention, nevertheless by the counsel of Satan it is seen to happen that the more holy someone is, the more he serves schisms and contentions in the hands of the quarrelsome. We have an example of this in the disciples of John, Matthew 9 and John 3, although it agreed very well with John and with Christ.

units.la: De Petro aut & Christo quid dicemus? Quo modo quidā se Cephę esse dixerūt, cū nō legam9 illū uenisse Corinthū? Arbitror fuisse pseudapostolos qui Petri authoritatem Paulo opponētes,aliena sub illa doctrinam introducere, se seq; uenditare conati sint, unde factū sit, ut odio Pauli sectatores illorum Cephistas sese uocarint. Dubium non est, iam tum fuisse pseudapostolos,qui Petri nomine abuterentur,& illorum credo esse successores,qui Romę sub nomine Petri inualuerunt.
units.tr: But what shall we say about Peter and Christ? How could some say they were of Cephas, when I do not read that he came to Corinth? I suppose there were false apostles who, setting the authority of Peter against Paul, tried to introduce their own doctrine under his name and to promote themselves, whence it came about that, out of hatred for Paul, his followers called themselves Cephasites. There is no doubt that already at that time there were false apostles who abused the name of Peter, and I believe they are the successors of those who gained ground at Rome under the name of Peter.

units.la: De illis qui dixerunt se Christi esse,quid statuemus? an & illi schismatici fuerūt? Ambros. intelligit eos qui in ueritate Christi ac fide per seuerabant,& contentiones istas detestabātur. Cur ergo coniungit illos Apostolus schismatici? Chrysost.dicit hoc non ideo factū, quòd ipsos reprehēdat,quasi nō debuerint se Christo accēsere: sed quod à quibusdam tantum hoc diceretur,cum debuerit dici ab omnibus.
units.tr: What shall we decide about those who said they were of Christ? Were they also schismatics? Ambrose understands them to be those who persevered in the truth and faith of Christ and detested these contentions. Why then does the Apostle join them with the schismatics? Chrysostom says this was not done because he rebukes them, as if they ought not to have attached themselves to Christ, but because this was said only by some, when it ought to have been said by all.

units.la: Mihi pace aliorū uidetur fieri posse ut nō minus schismatice Christi esse se quisquā dicat, q si se dicat esse uel Pauli uel Petri. Quomodo? Si cōtenciose hoc & peruerse faciat. Vtpote si unitatē & concordiā hoc nomine rūpat, & sub illo peruersam aliquam opinionem mordicus tueatur, & reliquos diuersum sentiētes à Christo exsto excludat, seque ab illis separet. Qui hoe facit, male se Christi esse dicit, licet in se bonum sit esse Christi. Ita Euangelicum dici in se bonum est, & commune omnium Christianorū. Iam si qui appellatione Euangelij aduersum alios inflati propter diuersas aliquas sententias peruerse intellectas, à reliquo Christianorum consortio discederent, charitatem rumperent, corpus Christi diuiderent, nunquid schismatici Euangelicos se dicerent?
units.tr: With due respect to others, it seems to me that someone can say he is of Christ no less schismatically than if he said he was of Paul or of Peter. How so? If he does this quarrelsomely and perversely. For instance, if under that name he breaks unity and concord, and stubbornly defends some perverse opinion, and excludes from Christ himself those who think otherwise, separating himself from them. The one who does this wrongly says he is of Christ, although to be of Christ is good in itself. So too to be called evangelical is good in itself, and common to all Christians. Now if some, puffed up against others under the name of the Gospel because of some diverse opinions wrongly understood, were to withdraw from the fellowship of the rest of the Christians, breaking charity and dividing the body of Christ, would they not be schismatics even if they called themselves evangelicals?

units.la: Finge uenisse Corinthū post discessum Pauli inter reliquos pseudapostolos, qui ut Pauli authoritatem eleuarent, discipulos se Christi peculiares fecerint, utpote quod Christum uidissent, cum illo circuissent, & doctrinam suam ab ipso coràm accepissent, quodque Christus ipse & circumcisus esset, & legem custodisset, cum Paulus Christum non uiderit, discipulusque ipsius non fuerit. An non hac uia fieri potuit, ut qui istorum doctrinam acceperint, contentiose Christi se, contra doctrinam Apostoli initio traditam, dixerint?
units.tr: Imagine that after Paul's departure there came to Corinth, among the other false apostles, men who, in order to diminish Paul's authority, made themselves peculiar disciples of Christ, on the ground that they had seen Christ, had gone about with him, and had received their doctrine from him in person, and that Christ himself was circumcised and kept the law, whereas Paul had not seen Christ and was not his disciple. Could it not have happened in this way that those who received the teaching of these men said, contentiously, that they were of Christ, against the doctrine of the Apostle first handed down?

units.la: Quod si essent, qui uitam Christi perfecte, ipsorum opinione, expressuri, nec uxores ducerent, nec facultates proprias haberent, nec eodem loco consisterent, ob id quod Christus nec uxorem, nec liberos, nec domum, nec terrenam aliquam facultatem habuisse legitur, quotquot uxores habent, & res proprias possident, & uno loco consistunt, à Christo excludentes, ac se uere Christi esse iactantes, an isti uere Christi essent, & non schismatici ipsissimi? Schismatici utique, quemadmodum & olim quidam hoc nomine se apostolicos uocantes, quod nec uxores haberent, nec res proprias possiderent (ut in Augustino est de haeresibus) à consortio omnium Christianorum uxores & propriam facultatem habentium secedebant, idque duplici nomine. Primum, quod peruerse uitam Christi exprimeret, cum ista & plerique philosophi ante Christum praestiterint, deinde quod peruersius istorum nomine à communione se ecclesiae seiungerent.
units.tr: Suppose there were people who, in their own opinion, would perfectly express the life of Christ: who would not take wives, nor have private property, nor remain in one place, because it is read that Christ had neither wife, nor children, nor home, nor any earthly possession; and suppose they excluded from Christ all who have wives and possess private property and remain in one place, boasting that they alone are truly of Christ. Would these truly be of Christ, or would they not rather be the most genuine schismatics? Certainly schismatics, just as some formerly did who, calling themselves apostolic under this name, because they had no wives and possessed no private property (as is found in Augustine's book on heresies), withdrew from fellowship with all Christians who had wives and private property. And this for a twofold reason: first, because they expressed the life of Christ perversely, although many philosophers before Christ also attained this; second, because, more perversely still, in that name they separated themselves from the communion of the Church.

units.la: Proinde licet in se bonum sit dicere Christi sum, Euangelicus sum: uidendum tamē etiam atque etiam est, ut hoc Christiane ac uere, deinde non schismatice praeter rationem dicatur: praeter rationem inquam, propterea quod ratione iusta & necessaria, non solum malum non est, sed laudabile, à reliquis diuidi, ut est in exemplo Thobiae. Haec uolui alijs cogitanda proponere, quae ut non affero sic esse facta inter Corinthios, ita non dubito sic apud illos fieri potuisse.
units.tr: Therefore, although it is in itself a good thing to say "I am of Christ" or "I am an Evangelical," we must nonetheless look again and again whether this is said in a truly Christian way, and not schismatically and beyond reason. I say "beyond reason," because it is not only not evil but commendable to separate oneself from others for a just and necessary reason, as in the example of Tobias. I wished to put these things before others for consideration; and although I do not assert that they were so done among the Corinthians, I do not doubt that they could have been done so among them.

units.la: Num diuisus est Christus? Num Paulus crucifixus est pro uobis? Aut in nomine Pauli baptizati fuistis?
units.tr: Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?

units.la: Qui liberos suos corripiunt & emendant, primum illis perpetratum facinus exponunt, ut sciant qua de causa reprehendantur: deinde admissorum absurditatem opprobrant, ut illa cognita auocentur à proposito malo, & ad resipiscentiam permoueantur. Ad hunc planè modum, & Apostolus hic primum quid de Corinthijs audierit mali, exponit, id quod in praecedentibus fecit, ibi: Narratū est mihi ab illis, &c. cui expositioni statim subiungit facti reprehensione, cū dicit, Nū diuisus est Christus?
units.tr: Those who correct and amend their children first set out the wrong that has been committed by them, so that they know the reason for their rebuke; then they reproach the absurdity of what was done, so that, once it is recognized, they may be turned away from the evil purpose and brought to repentance. In exactly this way the Apostle here first sets out what evil he has heard of the Corinthians, as he did in what precedes, there: "It has been reported to me by them," etc. To this exposition he immediately adds the rebuke of the deed, when he says, "Is Christ divided?"

units.la: Instituit autem talem ἀνγκὴν, qui & absurditatem illam schismatum breuiter & conspicue absque ulla contradictione ob oculos ponat, & nonnihil propter indignitatem rei commotum reprehendentis animum resipiat. Et hoc facit acribus illis & crebris interrogantiunculis (quas Graeci ἐρωτήματα uocant) instando & urgendo. Erat enim adeo absurdum & aperte contra Christum, quod in Corinthijs reprehendit, ut non habuerit opus ulla probatione uel disputatione.
units.tr: He employs a kind of examination [ἀνάκρισις] which both places before their eyes, briefly and plainly and without any possibility of denial, the absurdity of those schisms, and in some measure stirs the mind of the one rebuking, moved by the indignity of the matter. He does this by pressing and urging with sharp and frequent little questions (which the Greeks call erotemata [ἐρωτήματα]). For what they were doing was so absurd and so openly against Christ that he had no need of any proof or disputation.

units.la: NVM diuisus est Christus? Non dicit male facitis, quod Christum diuiditis, qui unitate gaudet, nec diuisionem agnoscit: sed, Num diuisus est Christus? quod aliquanto uehementius est. Quomodo autem Christum diuiserant Corinthij? Chrysostomus & Hieronymus de eo intelligunt, quod corpus Christi diuiserat. Ambrosius de eo, quod gloriam Christi diuiserant, & in alios deriuarant. Deinde quod diuersa quoque de Christo à diuersis doctoribus acceperant.
units.tr: "IS Christ divided?" He does not say, "You do wrong in dividing Christ," who rejoices in unity and acknowledges no division; but, "Is Christ divided?" which is a good deal more forceful. But how had the Corinthians divided Christ? Chrysostom and Jerome understand it of the body of Christ, that they had divided it. Ambrose understands it of their dividing the glory of Christ and transferring it to others. And further, of their having received different teachings about Christ from different teachers.

units.la: 1 Ergo Christum diuidunt, quotquot ecclesiam in partes & studia scindunt. Et hoc fit primum, quando eadem manente doctrina, iuxta Christum eriguntur alia capita, inter se non diuersa: quibus datur, quod uni Christo competit, ut iam non sub uno, sed multis capitibus sit corpus Christi. Et hoc forsan est, quod Ambrosius vocat diuidere gloriam Christi. Gloriam Christi diuidebāt discipuli Iohannis, qui illam Iohanni magistro suo tribuebant, licet inter Christum & Iohannem nihil esset diuisi dij. Ita si Corinthij reuera pars à Paulo, pars ab Apollo, pars à Cepha, pependerunt, hoc pacto gloriā capitis Christi diuiserunt, licet nec Paulus, nec Apollo, nec Cephas hoc quaesierint, & nihil inter illos diuisidij fuerit. Ita olim ecclesiam scindentes, caput Christi & gloriam illius diuidebant, qui de primatu inter se contendentes, ad se rapiebat quod erat Christi, ut patriarchae illi Romani, Alexandrini, Ierosolymitani, & Constantinopolitani, quasi sorti tunicam Christi inconsutilē subijcientes, & suo quisque iuri uendicare cupientes.
units.tr: 1. Therefore, all who tear the Church into parties and factions divide Christ. This happens first when, while the doctrine remains the same, other heads are set up alongside Christ, not different from him in doctrine; to them is given what belongs to Christ alone, so that the body of Christ is no longer under one Head but under many heads. This is perhaps what Ambrose calls dividing the glory of Christ. The disciples of John divided the glory of Christ when they ascribed it to their master John, although there was no division at all between Christ and John. So, if the Corinthians really hung, some on Paul, some on Apollos, some on Cephas, in this way they divided the glory of the Head, Christ, although neither Paul, nor Apollos, nor Cephas sought this, and there was no division among them. In the same way, in former times, those who tore the Church apart divided the Head, Christ, and his glory, when they contended with one another over primacy and snatched to themselves what belonged to Christ, like those patriarchs of Rome, Alexandria, Jerusalem and Constantinople, who, as if casting lots for Christ's seamless tunic, each wanted to claim it for his own right.

units.la: 2 Deinde Christum diuidunt, qui non solum diuersis capitibus corpus illius assignant, sed & qui diuersa de illo tradunt aut etiam accipiunt, quasi in seipso quoque iam, nō solum in membris suis sit diuisus. In seipso autem diuisus est, qui non idem sentit, cuius doctrina in seipsa diuersa est. Non quod Christus in seipso ita sit diuisus, cuius sermo simplicissima veritas est & amen: sed quod qui diuersa de illo inter Corinthios praedicabant, quantum in ipsis erat, Christū in se diuisum praedicarent. Vtpote dum alij circumcisionem & legis obseruantiam
units.tr: 2. Second, they divide Christ who not only assign different heads to his body, but also those who hand down or receive different teachings about him, as if Christ were already divided within himself, not only in his members. He is divided within himself who does not think the same, whose teaching is inconsistent with itself. This is not to say that Christ is divided within himself, whose word is the simplest truth and "Amen"; but that those who preached different things about him among the Corinthians, as far as lay in them, were proclaiming Christ divided in himself. For while some taught circumcision and observance of the law in the name of Christ,

units.la: tiam
units.tr: ...tiam

units.la: tiâ sub nomine Christi docebât, alij verò illarû tire de Christo, merito ab Apostolo urgentur abrogatione tradebât, alij ciborum delectum, alij promiscuos cibos probabât, atq; ita dupli ci nomine Christũ diuidebât, primũ in seipso, quasi sibi ipsi disidentem: deinde in corpore ipsius in partes iam scissum. Itaq; quicunq; alia ecclesiæ capita assignant, à quibus penden dum sit Christianis, & qui diuersa à doctrina Christi & apostolorum tradunt, Christum diuiduunt.
units.tr: ...and others taught the abrogation of these observances concerning Christ, and are rightly urged by the Apostle; others approved the selection of foods, others approved eating anything indiscriminately. And so, in a twofold way, they divided Christ: first within himself, as if disagreeing with himself, and then in his body, now torn into parts. Therefore, whoever assign other heads to the Church, on whom Christians must depend, and whoever hand down things contrary to the teaching of Christ and the apostles, divide Christ.

units.la: 1 Diuisus est Christus, quando cum olim di xerit: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis & oneratis estis, & ego reficiam uos. iam contrà, Nõ ad me, inquit, sed ad sanctos meos currite qui laboratis, illi uos reficient.
units.tr: 1. Christ is divided when, having once said, "Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you," now, on the contrary, he says, "Not to me, but run to my saints, who labor; they will refresh you."

units.la: 2 Diuisus est, quando iam dicit: qui non manet in Romano pontifice, eijcietur foras sicut palmes & arescet, cũ olim dixerit, qui non manet in me, mittetur foras & arescet.
units.tr: 2. He is divided when he now says, "Whoever does not remain in the Roman pontiff will be cast out like a branch and will wither," whereas once he said, "Whoever does not remain in me will be cast out and will wither."

units.la: 3 Diuisus est Christus ubi iam dicit: Nõ solû Deũ adorate & colite, sed & sanctos meos, cum aliquando dixerit: Dominum deũ tuum adorabis, & illum solum coles.
units.tr: 3. Christ is divided where he now says, "Adore and worship not only God, but also my saints," whereas once he said, "You shall adore the Lord your God, and serve him alone."

units.la: 4 Diuisus est Christus cum olim dixerit: Sine me nihil potestis facere, iam uerò uiribus humanis hoc dat, ut posint proprijs motibus & sua ipsorum facultate quod bonũ est facere & appræhendere.
units.tr: 4. Christ is divided when once he said, "Without me you can do nothing," but now, by human strength, he grants that people can by their own motions and their own powers do what is good and lay hold of it.

units.la: 5 Diuisus est Christus iam dicés, Non bibite ex eo omnes: sed hęresis est, si hoc doceatur cũ olim dixerit, Bibite ex eo omnes. Quid ad hæc omnia aliud dicem?, quàm quod hic Paulus cœlestis instar fulminis ad disipationem sectarum cœlitus illapsus dicit: Nunquid diuisus est Christus?
units.tr: 5. Christ is divided when he now says, "Do not drink of it, all of you"; but it is a heresy if this is taught, whereas once he said, "Drink of it, all of you." What more can I say to all this than that here Paul, like a thunderbolt from heaven, falling down from heaven for the scattering of sects, says: "Is Christ divided?"

units.la: Tametsi scissi essent Corinthij in partes: tamen quæq; pars nihilominus uolebat Christi esse, & doctrinam Christi recte tenere uideri, cum tamen plurimũ inter se & per acoluthiam doctorum & capitum, deinde & doctrinæ diuersitate disiderent. Cum itaq; fieri nequeat, ut caput disidentiũ partium esse queat Christus, illi autem Christiani uideri uellent: quid aliud sequebatur quàm quod omnium absurdissime, quantum in ipsis erat, Christum diuiderent in Paulinianos, Apollonistas & Cephistas, hoc est in authorem sectarum. Disidentium autè partiũ caput esse nequit, quia communis est omnium Dominus, quod partes negant, dum quæque ita sibi Christum adscribit, ut alijs auferat. Is autem nõ uult tantum Paulinianorum Dominus esse, sed & aliorũ. Illi au tem disident à Paulinianis, & talé Christum uolunt, qui non sit Paulinianorum quoq; Dominus. Rursus Pauliniani Christum, ita suũ ef se uolunt, ut non sit simul & aliorum. Hoc itaque pacto sequitur uel schismaticos extra Christum esse, quando ille nõ uult cuiusquam tantum esse partis, sed communiter omnium, & illi nolunt commune cum alijs Christum, sed proprium & peculiarem sectę suę Dominum, uel Christum, siquidem Christiani sunt schismatici, esse diuisum, quod cum sit impium sen
units.tr: Although the Corinthians were torn into parties, nevertheless each party still wanted to be Christ's and to seem to hold the teaching of Christ rightly, although they disagreed very much among themselves, both in their succession of teachers and leaders and also in the diversity of their doctrine. Since therefore it cannot be that Christ is the head of disagreeing parties, while yet they wished to be seen as Christians, what else would follow but that, most absurdly of all, as far as lay in them, they divided Christ into Paulinians, Apollonians and Cephasites, that is, into the author of sects. But Christ cannot be the head of disagreeing parties, because he is the common Lord of all, which the parties deny, since each one so claims Christ for itself as to take him away from others. He, however, does not wish to be the Lord only of the Paulinians, but of others also. Those others disagree with the Paulinians and want a Christ who is not also the Lord of the Paulinians. Again, the Paulinians want Christ to be so much their own that he is not also of others. In this way it follows either that the schismatics are outside Christ, since he does not wish to belong to any one part only but to all in common, and they do not want Christ in common with others, but as the Lord proper and peculiar to their sect; or, if Christians are schismatics, that Christ is divided, which, since it is impious...

units.la: NVM Paulus crucifixus est pro uobis? Primum absurdum quod committebant Corinthij, erat contra unitatem Christi, qui diuidi nequit. Alterum erat contra ipsam redemptionis prærogatiuam. Ea est, ut redemptus alterius nõ sit quàm redẽptoris. Sic infra cap. 7. Empti estis precio magno, nolite fieri serui homines. Et 2. Cor. 5. Et pro omnibus mortuus est, ut qui uiuunt, posthac non sibi uiuant, sed ei qui pro ipsis est mortuus, & resurrexit. Et Rom. 8. Siue uiuamus siue moriamur, Domini sumus. In hoc enim Christus & mortuus est & resurrexit ac reuixit, ut mortuis ac uiuis dominetur. Iam qui se uel Paulinianos uel Apollonistas, uel Cephistas uocabant, hanc Christo prærogatiuam infringebant, hoc ipso quod aliorũ quàm Christi esse se dicebant. In alterius enim transfire nomen, nõ potest filius sine contumelia patris, nec uxor sine contumelia & in iuria uiri. Hoc faciebant schismatici dicentes: Ego sum Pauli, ego sum Apollo, ego sum Cephæ. Aliud est dicere: Ego audio Paulum prædicantem, ego à Paulo sum in nomen Domini baptizatus, quod ferendum fuisset, & schisma nõ resipuisset: & aliud, Ego sum Pauli. Audire possumus omnes Christi ministros, esse uero non debemus ullius nisi solius Christi, qui pro nobis est mortuus. Hoc scilicet est quod urget Apostolus, dicens: Num Paulus crucifixus est pro uobis?
units.tr: Was Paul crucified for you? The first absurdity the Corinthians committed was against the unity of Christ, who cannot be divided. The second was against the very prerogative of redemption. This is that the one redeemed belongs to no one but his redeemer. So below, chapter 7: "You were bought with a great price; do not become slaves of men." And 2 Corinthians 5: "And he died for all, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and rose again." And Romans 8: "Whether we live or die, we are the Lord's. For to this end Christ both died and rose and revived, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living." Now those who called themselves Paulinians, or Apollonians, or Cephasites, were infringing this prerogative of Christ, by the very fact that they said they belonged to someone other than Christ. For a son cannot pass into another's name without dishonour to his father, nor a wife without dishonour and injury to her husband. The schismatics did this when they said: "I am of Paul, I am of Apollos, I am of Cephas." It is one thing to say, "I hear Paul preaching, I was baptized by Paul in the name of the Lord," which might have been tolerated and would not have implied schism; and another to say, "I am of Paul." We may all hear the ministers of Christ, but we ought to belong to no one but Christ alone, who died for us. This is clearly what the Apostle presses when he says: "Was Paul crucified for you?"

units.la: AVT in nomine Pauli baptizati estis? Insurgit ab occultioribus ad manifestiora. Primum quod de Christo diuiso dixit, occultius erat eo quod subiecit, Num Paulus pro uobis crucifixus est? (Occultius inquam quod attinebat ad captum sectariorum.) Deinde quod subiecit: Nũ Paulus pro uobis crucifixus est? occultius isto quod dicit: Nũ in nomine Pauli baptizati est? Hoc enim apertius erat, in quo minus poterant tergiuersari. Non solum apertum erat, in cuius nomen baptizati essent, sed & id quod inde colligitur, nèpe eius esse quem que fidelium, in cuius nomen baptizatus est. Finge inter oues oboriri schismata, ita ut pars huius se, pars alterius esse serui dicat, cum sint omnes unius Domini, & nulla alicuius serui: Illis si dixeris: Nũ diuisus est Dominus uester, satis quidem declararis schismatis absurditatem: apertius uerò hoc feceris, si dixeris, Num seruus ille cuius esse uultis, uos data pecunia coemit? Et rursus multo apertius isto, si subieceris, Num serui huius signaculo obsignatæ estis? Quod si hoc ignoratis, Dominum uerum non esse diuisum, nec aliquâ ferre diuisionem: deinde eius uos esse à quo estis coemptæ, uel signacula quibus obsignatæ estis cõsulite. Unde statim discetis cuius nomini deputari debeatis. Tale quid uelle mihi uidentur istæ percontationes Apostoli.
units.tr: Or were you baptized in the name of Paul? He rises from the more obscure to the more manifest. First, what he said about Christ being divided was more obscure than what he added, "Was Paul crucified for you?" (I mean more obscure in the sense that it was harder for the sectarians to grasp.) Then, what he added, "Was Paul crucified for you?", is more obscure than what he says next, "Were you baptized in the name of Paul?" For the latter was plainer, and there they could evade less. It was not only plain whose name they had been baptized into, but also what follows from it, namely that each believer belongs to the one into whose name he was baptized. Suppose schisms arise among the sheep, so that one part says it serves this man and another part says it serves that one, though they all belong to one Lord and to no servant of anyone. If you say to them, "Is your Lord divided?", you certainly show the absurdity of the schism well enough; but you would do it more plainly if you said, "Did that servant whom you want to belong to buy you with money?" And again, much more plainly than that, if you added, "Were you sealed with the seal of this servant?" But if they are ignorant of this, consult that the true Lord is not divided and does not bear division, and then that you belong to the one by whom you were bought, or whose seals you bear. From these you will learn at once to whose name you ought to be credited. Such, it seems to me, are the questions the Apostle wishes to pose.

units.la: Quod autem non dicit: Num Petrus cruci-
units.tr: Now as to his not saying, "Was Peter cruci-

units.la: fixus est pro nobis vel in nomine Petri baptizati estis? Sed, Num Paulus cruci&c. Et num in nomine Pauli bapt? seipsum non alium aliquem ponens, prudentia repsit apostolicam, ne videatur non tam Christi quærere gloriam, quàm alios ad hoc deprimere, ut solus ipse potiores habeat. Hoc facit & infrà cap. 3. ubi seipsum ante alios abijcit, ut Christum extollat, cum dicit: Quis igitur est Paulus? Quis est Apollo? Item: Omnia vestra sunt, sive Paulus sive Apollo sive Cephas.
units.tr: fied for you, or were you baptized in the name of Peter?" but "Was Paul cruci-fied?" and "Were you baptized in the name of Paul?", setting himself forward and no one else, the Apostle's prudence crept in, lest he seem to seek not so much Christ's glory as to bring others down so that he alone might hold the higher place. He does the same below in chapter 3, where he casts himself beneath the others in order to exalt Christ, saying: "Who then is Paul? Who is Apollos?" Likewise: "All things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas."

units.la: Admonemur ergo hoc exemplo, ut quotiescunq; deprimenda est humana authoritas, ut salva sit authoritas Christi, ut hoc ea faciamus cautione, ne liuore ducti magis nostra quàm Christi gloriam quærere, vel magis nostram ignominiam quàm Christi ulciscì videamur. Nam ita comparatum est ingenium hominis, ut pleruncq; sub prætextu nominis Christi suâ quærat gloriam, vel dum alios sibi præferri videt, oppressos cupiat, non ut solus obtineat Christo, sed ne sint quib. posthabeatur, etiamsi priores occupare nequeat.
units.tr: We are therefore admonished by this example that whenever human authority must be lowered, it is to be done so that Christ's authority remains intact, and that we take such care not to appear, driven by spite, to seek our own glory rather than Christ's, or to avenge our own disgrace rather than Christ's. For the human mind is so constituted that it very often seeks its own glory under the pretext of Christ's name; and when it sees others preferred to itself, it wishes them crushed, not so that it alone may hold Christ, but so that there may be no one over whom it is placed second, even if it cannot seize the first place.

units.la: Deinde notandum est hoc loco, quàm non deceat Christianos alicui se addicere, nisi uni Christo, qui pro nobis est crucifixus, & in cuius nomen baptizati sumus. Hieronymus hoc loco taxari eos quoq; putat, qui suis iam temporibus in ecclesia diuitiis colligendis operam dates, exemplo se Abrahæ & Iob tuebantur, quibus dici posse arbitratur, Num Abraham crucifixus est pro vobis? Num in nomine Iob baptizati estis? Quasi ne imitari quidè liceat aliû præter unum Christum. Si peccant qui imitantur Abraham & Iob, hoc est, qui quod Abrahæ & Iob licuit, hoc ipso sibi quoq; licere putant quod ipsis licuit: quid de illis dicemus qui nô solum pro exemplaribus instituendæ vitæ sanctos sibi alios alij proponunt, ut faciunt Monachi & Nonnę, Benedictini & Franciscani, Dominicastri, Bernardini, deinde & qui in doctrina quoq; & opinionib. alios atq; alios authores sectantur, ut Scotistæ, Albertistæ, Occamistæ, Thomistæ: sed & patronos sibi quisque peculiarem deligunt, quorum se fidei committant, cui per omnem vitam seruiát, quasi Christiani sint instar pupillorû & orphanorum à Deo patre & Christo domino relicti ac deserti, quibus opus sit humanû patrocinium & quædam ne pereant. An non hic dicere possumus multo uerimus, quàm ubi Hieronymus dicit: Nunquid sancti pro nobis crucifixi sunt? uel in nomen sanctorum baptizati sumus? deinde & cum Hieronymo etiam istis dicere licebit, Num Benedictus pro vobis crucifixus est? Num in nomen Francisci baptizati estis? &c. Num Thomas pro vobis crucifixus est? vel in nomen Scoti vel Alberti baptizati estis?
units.tr: Next, it must be noted here how unfitting it is for Christians to attach themselves to anyone except Christ alone, who was crucified for us and in whose name we have been baptized. Jerome thinks that those are also rebuked here who in his own time devoted effort to gathering riches in the Church, and who defended themselves by the example of Abraham and Job, to whom, he thinks, it could be said: "Was Abraham crucified for you? Were you baptized in the name of Job?" As if it were not even permitted to imitate anyone besides the one Christ. If those sin who imitate Abraham and Job, that is, who think that what was permitted to Abraham and Job is permitted to themselves by the same token, what shall we say of those who not only set before one another holy men as patterns for ordering their lives, as do the monks and nuns, the Benedictines and Franciscans, the Dominicans and Bernardines; and then also those who follow one author after another in doctrine and opinions, as the Scotists, Albertists, Occamists and Thomists do; but each one also chooses for himself a particular patron to whose faith he entrusts himself, to whom he serves all his life, as if Christians were like orphans and wards left behind and abandoned by God the Father and Christ the Lord, who need human protection and some guardians lest they perish? Can we not say here, with much more truth than where Jerome says, "Were the saints crucified for us? Or were we baptized in the name of the saints?" And then, with Jerome, it will also be permissible to say to these people: "Was Benedict crucified for you? Were you baptized in the name of Francis?" etc. "Was Thomas crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Scotus or of Albert?"

units.la: Tertio. Notandum obiter & hoc est, quid sit baptizari in nomen patris & filij & spiritus sancti, ut habeamus quasi quandam eius formulæ, qua baptizamus, expositionem, in eo quod dicit: Nunquid in nomen Pauli baptizati estis? inde colligens non licere, ut quisquam dicat se Pauli esse, cum non sit in nomen Pauli baptizatus. Quare nô licet? Quia se iam non potest alij addicere, qui Christo dicatus & obsignatus est. Hoc autem est, qui in nomen Christi baptizatus est. Ergo baptizari in alicuius nomen, est quasi in illius obsignari pecunia, ut ad ipsum proprie pertineas, illiusque te esse profiteare solius. Est itaque baptizare in nomen patris & filij & spiritus sancti, inter eos aliquem obsignare, qui in gratiam sunt patris & filij & spiritus sancti ita assumpti & sanctificati, ut nullum præterea patrem, nullum Dominum, nullum sanctificatorem, paracletum, aduocatum, cuius se fidei committat, quæ colat, cui obediat ac seruiat, agnoscere liceat. Quid vero ista per baptismum sanctificatio, obsignatio, & adoptio secum adferat, non huius est loci, ut commemoremus.
units.tr: Third, it should be noted in passing what it is to be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, so that we may have, as it were, an explanation of the formula with which we baptize, in what he says: "Were you baptized in the name of Paul?" From this he gathers that it is not lawful for anyone to say that he belongs to Paul, since he has not been baptized in Paul's name. Why is it not lawful? Because he who has been dedicated and sealed to Christ can no longer devote himself to another. But he who has been baptized in the name of Christ is dedicated to Christ. Therefore to be baptized in someone's name is, as it were, to be sealed with that person's money, so that you properly belong to him and profess that you belong to him alone. Thus to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is to seal someone among those who are taken into the favour of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit and sanctified in such a way that he may acknowledge no other father, no other Lord, no other sanctifier, comforter or advocate, to whose faith he entrusts himself, whom he worships, obeys and serves. But what this sanctification, sealing and adoption through baptism brings with it is not the place for us to recount here.

units.la: Gratias ago Deo meo, quod neminem vestrum baptizauerim, nisi Crispum & Gaium.
units.tr: I give thanks to my God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius.

units.la: Hoc loco, & ex consequentibus apparet, pseudapostolos duabus rationibus discipulos post se traxisse, & inter Corinthios sectarum studia mouisse. Vna erat baptismus. Altera, eruditioris & elegantioris sermonis ad normam mundanæ sapientiæ compositi plausibile studiû fieri poterit, ut & alijs nonnullis rationibus usi ad hoc sint, ut suppressa autoritate Apostoli, ecclesiam in partes scinderent. Tamen quoniam de istis hoc loco loquitur Apostolus, nô perscrutabimur reliquas curiosius, sed istas cô siderabimus.
units.tr: From this place and from what follows it appears that the false apostles drew disciples after themselves by two means and stirred up factions among the Corinthians. The first was baptism. The second was the plausible pursuit of a more learned and elegant speech, composed according to the standard of worldly wisdom. They may also have used other devices to the same end, so that, with the Apostle's authority set aside, they could split the Church into parties. However, since the Apostle speaks of these matters in this place, we will not investigate the rest too closely, but will consider these.

units.la: De prima ratione loquitur hic, cum dicit: GRATIAS ago Deo meo, quod neminé vestrûm baptizauerim, &c.] Liquet pseudapostolos baptismate usos contentiose, & ad fomentum & corroborationem sectarum, ita ut quemadmodum Galat. ultimo legitur de doctoribus circumcisionis, cogunt uos circumcidi, ut in carne vestra glorientur, & isti ad hoc baptizauerint doctrinæ suæ quisque sectatores, ut eos quasi in suum nomen haberet obsignatos, qui interea baptizatos ab alijs quærèrentur. Ea nanque erat astutia Satanæ, ut hoc symbolo baptismatis, quo filios Dei obsignari uoluit spiritusfanctus in unum corpus, abuterentur ministri ipsius ad disipationem corporis Christi. Tale studium fuisse etiam in Donatistis & Nouatianis in Amhrosio & Augustino uidere est. Nam illi suæ tantum sectæ potestatem baptizandi uindicabant, reliquorum ab alijs baptizatorum neminem suæ communioni admittentes. Ad quem modum & nostris temporibus pestem hæc Catabaptistæ renouarunt. Cum itaq; studium hoc baptizandi peruersum obtineret iam inter Corinthios, ut pseudapostoli baptizando, non Christo, sed sibi ipsis & suæ gloriæ mystas obsignarent, atq; isti qui baptizabantur, baptistarum fuorû nomina inducerent: ut ab hoc se studio alienum ostenderet Apostolus,illudq; traduceret,scribit ad hũc modũ: Gratias ago Deo meo quod neminem,&c. Non dicit simpliciter, quod nemine m: sed quod neminem Corinthiorũ baptizauerit,nisi &c.uidelicet ne quisquam se in hoc studio, quasi sua queat authoritate tueri, neue aliquam huius mali occasionem dedisse uideri possit.
units.tr: He speaks of the first means here, when he says: "I give thanks to my God that I baptized none of you," and so on. It is clear that the false apostles used baptism contentiously, to foment and strengthen the sects. In the last chapter of Galatians we read of the teachers of circumcision: "they compel you to be circumcised, that they may glory in your flesh." In the same way these men baptized, each his own followers, so that he might have them sealed as his own, while those who were baptized were sought out by others. This was the cunning of Satan: the ministers of baptism, by which the Holy Spirit wished the sons of God to be sealed into one body, would abuse that sign to scatter the body of Christ. That this same zeal existed among the Donatists and Novatians can be seen in Ambrose and Augustine. For they claimed the power of baptizing for their sect alone, admitting none of those baptized by others into their communion. In our own times the Catabaptists have renewed this same pestilence. Since this perverse zeal for baptizing already prevailed among the Corinthians, so that the false apostles, by baptizing, sealed initiates not to Christ but to themselves and their own glory, and those who were baptized took up the names of their baptizers, the Apostle, to show that he was alien to this zeal and to disparage it, writes thus: "I give thanks to God that I baptized none," and so on. He does not say simply "that I baptized no one," but "that I baptized none of the Corinthians except," and so on, namely so that no one could defend himself in this zeal as if by his own authority, or so that it could not seem that he had given any occasion for this evil.

units.la: De Crispo & Gaio habetur in Actis.De Crispo Act. 8.legimus, ubi archisynagogus fuisse scribitur. Et de Gaio Act. 20. & in ea quæ ad Romanos est,cap.ultimo.
units.tr: Crispus and Gaius are mentioned in Acts. We read of Crispus in Acts 8, where he is said to have been the ruler of the synagogue. Gaius is in Acts 20, and in the letter to the Romans, the last chapter.

units.la: Ne quis dicat, quod in meo nomine baptizauerim.
units.tr: Lest anyone say that I baptized in my own name.

units.la: Hic assignat rationẽ, cur Deo gratias agat, quod nõ multos Corinthiorum baptizauerit. Videlicet ne quis dicat, quod in nomine suo baptizauerit. Sed quomodo Apostolo timendum hoc fuisset,si plures baptizasset,quod baptizarit in suo nomine? Ergo qui multos baptizant, uideri possunt in suo ipsorum nomine baptizare: & qui paucos baptizant, suspicione illa liberi sunt? Expendendę sunt circumstantiæ. Per se non sequitur,hic multos baptizat, ergo suspicandum est, quod in suo nomine baptizet, cum & Iohannes baptista multos baptizasse legatur,de quo tamen nemo dicere potest, quod in suo nomine baptizarit. Notatur,ut supra dixi,studium eorũ qui per baptismum sibi ipsis discipulos obsignabant,adeoq; multi erant in baptizando, quia multi erat in augendis suis sectis. Quoniã itaq; hic morbus ecclesiam Corinthiorũ obtinebat,gaudet Apostolus, quod non multos baptizauerit Corinthi, ne hoc studio laborasse & ipse uideri possit. Quemadmodum itaq; dum sectæ urget, & per baptismum augentur, ij qui multi sunt in baptizando,etiam si non dicant,Baptizo te in nomen meum:uidentur tamen in suo nomine baptizare,hoc est,non Christo, sed sibi ipsis discipulos creare, ita qui paucissimos baptizat, ab eo uitio alieni uidentur.Sic baptizabant in suo nomine Donatistæ & Nouatiani, hoc est, per baptismum faciebant ex Christianis Donatistas & Nouatianos, non regnũ Christi,sed suas sectas augentes.
units.tr: Here he gives the reason why he thanks God that he baptized few of the Corinthians: lest anyone say that he baptized in his own name. But how would the Apostle have had reason to fear this, if he had baptized more, that he baptized in his own name? Are those who baptize many to be thought to baptize in their own name, and those who baptize few free of that suspicion? The circumstances must be weighed. It does not follow in itself: "here he baptizes many, therefore it must be suspected that he baptizes in his own name," since John the Baptist too is read to have baptized many, and yet no one can say that he baptized in his own name. As I said above, this is pointed out: the zeal of those who by baptism sealed disciples for themselves, and there were many baptizing because there were many increasing their sects. Since this disease held the Corinthian church, the Apostle rejoices that he baptized few at Corinth, lest he too might seem to have labored at this zeal. Just as, while factions press on and are increased through baptism, those who baptize in great numbers seem to baptize in their own name, even if they do not say "I baptize you in my name" (that is, they create disciples not for Christ but for themselves), so the one who baptizes very few seems free of that fault. Thus the Donatists and Novatians baptized in their own name: by baptism they made Christians into Donatists and Novatians, increasing not the kingdom of Christ but their own sects.

units.la: Baptizaui autẽ & Stephanæ domũ, præterea haud scio, num quem aliũ baptizauerim.
units.tr: I baptized also the household of Stephanas; besides this, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.

units.la: De Stephana isto illiusq; familia habemus infrà cap.ult. Diligenter declarat etiã studiose recolendo se nõ multos baptizasse,nec aliquo baptizãdi studio laborasse, cũ potuisset in tãta ecclesia baptizare q plurimos, de qua dñs dixerat: Est mihi populus multus in hac ciuitate.ubi ergo dixerat,Neminẽ baptizaui,nisi Crispum & Gaium, quia occurrebat cogitanti & Stephanæ domus,addit & illá: & quia nõ erat sibi de aliquo alio coscius,subdit,Præterea nescio num quem alium baptizarim,non dicens, Nullum alium baptizaui: sed nescio an aliũ ali quem baptizarim,simul & cautius,& tamẽ cõ
units.tr: We have more about this Stephanas and his household below, in the last chapter. He also carefully declares, by recalling it deliberately, that he did not baptize many and did not labor under any zeal for baptizing, although in so great a church he could have baptized very many, of whom the Lord had said: "I have a great people in this city." Where he had said, "I baptized none except Crispus and Gaius," the household of Stephanas came to mind as he thought, so he adds that as well. And because he was not aware of any others, he adds: "Besides, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else." He does not say "I baptized no one else," but "I do not know whether I baptized anyone else," which is at once more cautious, and yet in such a way

units.la: mode hoc cõmemoras, ut ostendat se tã nullo baptizandi studio laborasse, tamq; nullos suo nomini discipulos baptizãdo parasse,ut quam uis paucos baptizarit, eos ipsos tamen in memoria non tenuerit.
units.tr: as to show that he labored under no zeal for baptizing and had gathered no disciples for his own name by baptizing, so that, though he baptized few, he did not keep even those few in memory.

units.la: Nõ enim misit me Christus ut baptizarem,sed ut Euangelium prædicarem.
units.tr: For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the Gospel.

units.la: Iam rationẽ reddit,quare tã nullo baptizãdi studio præditus fuerit inter Corinthios,ut tam paucos baptizarit,ne uideatur hoc fecisse cõtĕ ptu baptismatis. Nã absq; dubio pseudapost. plurimũ pietatis præferebát in sedulitate baptizãdi,ut ad ipsos cóparatus hac in re Paulus uideri potuerit ad augẽdũ cœtũ Christianorum negliges. Quid rationis ergo reddit? Nõ dicit, Quia nihil est baptismŏ, quia ad regnũ Christi nõ pertinet baptismŏ: sed, Non enim misit me Christus ut baptizaaem, sed ut Euangelium prædicarem. Rationem desumit ex cõditione uocationis suę ad apostolatũ, quã dicit nõ sitã esse in baptizãdo,sed ineuãgelizãdo:se missum esse à domino nõ baptistam, sed euangelistam, adeoq; studium suum fuisse ut quàmplurimos Christo per Euangelij prædicationem lucrifaceret,baptizandi officio alijs permisso.
units.tr: Now he gives the reason why he was so little concerned with baptizing among the Corinthians that he baptized so few, lest it seem that he did this out of contempt for baptism. For without doubt the false apostles placed great piety in their eagerness to baptize, so that, compared with them, Paul might seem negligent in increasing the Christian assembly. What reason, then, does he give? He does not say, "Because baptism is nothing, because it does not pertain to the kingdom of Christ," but: "For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the Gospel." He draws the reason from the nature of his calling to the apostleship, which he says lies not in baptizing but in preaching the Gospel. He was sent by the Lord not as a baptizer but as an evangelist, and so his zeal was to win as many as possible to Christ through the preaching of the Gospel, leaving the office of baptizing to others.

units.la: Et hic uidemus expositionẽ duorum locorũ Matt.& Marc. ult.ubi suos Christus emittit ad euangelizandũ Matth. ult.dicens: Euntes docete oẽs gentes,baptizantes eos in nomẽ patr. &c.& Marc.ult.Ite in mundũ uniuersum,prædicate Euangeliũ omni creaturę,quicunq; crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit. in quibus licet mentio fiat baptismi, tamen uis eius mandati non est sita in baptismo,eo quod non det suis hoc loco mandatũ baptizandi,sed euã gelizandi, unde nulla potest argumentatio ex his locis de baptismate sumi, nisi quod forma in nomẽ patris ac filij & spiritussanẽti baptizandi præscribitur.Et hoc est quod hic Apostolus dicit se non esse missum ad baptizandum, sed ad euangelizandum, nisi uelimus dicere Paulum aliud accepisse mandatũ à Domino quàm reliqui Apostoli, quod temerariũ est asserere.
units.tr: Here we see the explanation of two passages, Matthew and Mark at the end, where Christ sends his disciples out to evangelize. In Matthew at the end he says, "Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, etc.," and in Mark at the end, "Go into all the world, preach the Gospel to every creature; whoever believes and is baptized will be saved." In these passages, although baptism is mentioned, the force of the command does not lie in baptism, because in this place he does not give his disciples a command to baptize but to evangelize. Hence no argument about baptism can be drawn from these passages, except that the form of baptizing in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is prescribed. This is what the Apostle means here when he says that he was not sent to baptize but to evangelize, unless we wish to say that Paul received a different command from the Lord than the other apostles, which is rash to assert.

units.la: Sed quæret forsan aliquis,si non erat missus ad baptizádum, cur ergo omnino baptizauit? Ergo fecit quod nõ licuit?Respõdeo.Euãgelij prædicatio & baptismŏ, nõ sunt res cõtrarię,ita ut q alterũ obit,hoc ipso nequeat,si necesse sit, alterũ administrare. Qui Euangeliũ prædicat, nõ est missus ad dispensandá eleemosynã pauperũ.Et tamẽ,ubi necesseerat,fecerũt hoc Apostoli: uerũ quia is apostolatus erat prędicatio Euangelij,ideo relicta eleemosynæ administratione adhęrebat prædicationi uerbi. Ita & Paulo usuuenit in præsenti caussa. Per seipsum noluit baptizare, nisi ita exigeret necessitas, quemadmodum & de Petro legimus Act. 10. quod per seipsum Cornelium cum suis nõ baptizarit ipse,sed iusserit eum baptizari
units.tr: But perhaps someone will ask: if he was not sent to baptize, why did he baptize at all? Did he therefore do what was not permitted? I answer: preaching the Gospel and baptizing are not opposed things, so that whoever undertakes one cannot, for that very reason, administer the other if necessity requires it. He who preaches the Gospel is not sent to distribute alms to the poor. And yet, where necessity required, the apostles did this too; but because their apostleship was the preaching of the Gospel, they left the administration of alms and clung to the preaching of the Word. So it also happened to Paul in the present case: he was unwilling to baptize in person unless necessity demanded it, just as we read of Peter in Acts 10 that he did not baptize Cornelius and his household himself, but ordered them to be baptized.

units.la: Per hanc collatione prędicationis & baptismatis uidemus expressam Euãgelicæ prędicationis dignitate,quomodo illa excellat officiũ baptibaptizádi,& ita fit iniunſta apostolis & Euan{A}gelíſtis,ut ue illis fit niſi euágelizét, ue aút non lit fi nó p fe baptizét. Vtitur hoc loco Chrysost. pulchra similitudine ad declarandá Euágelicę prædicationis respectu baptismi dignitate, ita tamé ut baptismo interea nihil decedat. Dicit Euágelicá pdicatione perinde habere atq; inſtructionē athletę, q sane opus habet certandi scientia & exercitio, nec est cuiuis pstitu pofsi bilis.Baptismi officiū minusexigere industrię, exercitij & laboris,& esse instar eiꝰ officij, quo in certaminibus quidá uictoribus coronas im ponebât: q res talis erat, ut quiuis facile posset pstare, & tamen sua gloria nó carebat.Ita dicit suo tępore munus baptizádi in ecclesia cómis sum fuisse senibus quibusdá aliàs ad functionę uerbi inutilibus.Iá si eadem est ratio cœnę do minicę quę est baptismi, quid est qꝶ nostri epi scopi oēm suá functione collocant in celebra tione aliquot missarū & quasdá alias cæremo nias humanitus institutas, neglecta Euangelij prędicatione,quá cómiserunt interea,si tamen cómiserunt, insimæ eruditionis hominibus ?
units.tr: From this comparison of preaching and baptizing we see expressed the dignity of evangelical preaching, how it surpasses the office of baptizing, and so it is laid upon the apostles and evangelists that either they evangelize or, if they do not, that they baptize only if they do not do it through themselves. Chrysostom uses a beautiful similitude here to show the dignity of evangelical preaching in comparison with baptism, yet in such a way that nothing is taken away from baptism meanwhile. He says that evangelical preaching is like the training of an athlete, which certainly needs the knowledge and practice of contending and is not possible for just anyone. The office of baptizing, he says, requires less diligence, practice and labour, and is like the office by which in contests certain men placed crowns on the victors: a task of such a kind that anyone could easily perform it, and yet it did not lack its glory. So he says that in his time the duty of baptizing in the Church was entrusted to certain old men who were otherwise useless for the function of the Word. Now, if the reason for the Lord's Supper is the same as that of baptism, what is it that our bishops do, who place their whole function in the celebration of several masses and certain other ceremonies instituted by human authority, neglecting the preaching of the Gospel, which they have meanwhile entrusted, if indeed they have entrusted it, to men of the lowest learning?

units.la: NON erudito sermone.] Trăsit hic ad alte rū pseudapostolorū studium puersum suppri mendū, quo nó solū sectas instituebát & foue bant,sed uirtutem quoq; crucis Christi enerua bant, quam in sequentibus uindicabit magno studio,usque ad caput quintum.
units.tr: NOT IN LEARNED SPEECH. He now turns to the other endeavour of the false apostles, which was to be suppressed. By it they not only set up and fostered sects, but also weakened the power of the cross of Christ, which he will defend with great zeal in what follows, up to the fifth chapter.

units.la: Viderát pseudapostoli,nec ferre pōterát scā dalū crucis Christi, apud sapiētes huius mūdi. Hoc fugere cupiētes, filiū pdicádi Christi cru cifixi,quo utebâtur apostoli,mutarút in doćtri næ gen⁹,qꝶ nó redoleret stulticiá crucis Chri sti &irrisioni pateret:sed quod redoleret gustū philosophiæ, essetq; plausibile iudicio ratióis, &alienū ab eo qꝶ Paulus prędicauerit de mor te & resurrectione Christi, quo pleriq; sapien tū offensi fuerât. Hoc esse puto,quod dicit,Nó in sapientia sermonis,ut intelligat hanc ἀναλογίαν de doćtrinę pseudapostolorum materia, phi losophię studiū resipiente. Quod si quis intelli gere uoluerit cum Chrysost. & Erasmo de ser monis cócinnati & cópositi elegátiore structu ra,ut σοφίαν sit hoc loco idé qꝶ elegâs,quasi Apo stolus hoc taxet in pseudapostolis,quod rhe toricati sint in Christo pdicádo,neglecta Euan gelij prędicandi simplicitate,p me licebit. Arbi trór aút illos doćtrinā suá etiá hoc quoq; qua si condimento ab irrisione mundanę sapientię uindicasse, cū in posteriore epistola appareat Paulo ab illis contemptibilis sermonis obie ćtam esse uilitatem.
units.tr: The false apostles had seen, and could not bear, the scandal of the cross of Christ among the wise of this world. Wishing to avoid this, they changed the kind of teaching in which the apostles preached the crucified Christ into one that did not smell of the foolishness of the cross and was not exposed to ridicule, but that smelled of philosophy, was pleasing to the judgment of reason, and was foreign to what Paul had preached about the death and resurrection of Christ, by which many of the wise had been offended. I think this is what he means when he says, "Not in wisdom of speech," so that he understands this relation [ἀναλογίαν] as concerning the matter of the false apostles' teaching, which savoured of the study of philosophy. But if anyone wishes to understand it, with Chrysostom and Erasmus, as referring to the more elegant structure of a speech polished and composed, so that wisdom [σοφίαν] here means the same as elegance, as if the Apostle were rebuking in the false apostles that they had used rhetorical art in preaching Christ, neglecting the simplicity of preaching the Gospel, I will allow it. Yet I judge that they also protected their teaching from the ridicule of worldly wisdom by this kind of seasoning, since in the later epistle it appears that the lowliness of his speech was thrown at Paul as an object of contempt by them.

units.la: Agnoscit ergo, imo uocationi suæ uindicat sermonis simplicitatem,q sibi ab pseudapostolis ꝑbro dabatur,tā abest ut huiꝰ gratia pudesiat, cū dicit se nó solū missū esse ad euágelizandū: sed ita quoq; missū esse, ut q simplicissime, re iećta omni sermonis compositione & elegan tia sine omni mundanæ sapientiæ facultate & subsidio, sermone crucis Christi Gętibus ꝑpo neret.Et hoc facit p negatiuá,dum dicit,Nó in sapiétia sermonis. Ergo in simplicitate sermo-
units.tr: He therefore acknowledges, indeed claims for his calling, the simplicity of speech which was thrown up to him as a reproach by the false apostles. So far is he from being ashamed of it that he says he was not only sent to evangelize, but was also sent in such a way that he would set forth the word of the cross of Christ to the Gentiles most simply, rejecting all composition and elegance of speech, without any faculty or support of worldly wisdom. And he does this by a negative statement, saying, "Not in wisdom of speech." Therefore, in simplicity of speech.

units.la: nis. Nā ista est cōtrariorū natura, ut ubi alterū negatur, alterū affirmetur. Negat se missū esse ut euágelizet erudito sermóe, igitur indicat se missū esse,ut euágelizet sermóe rudi ac simpli ci.Nó hic cóparatū est, ut supra, cū Euangelio & baptismo,ubi dixit,Nó ad baptizandum,sed ad euangelizandū.Nam baptismus Euangelio non pugnat,licet sit separata actio, & non pro prie apostolica.Pugnat autem studium eruditi sermonis,quod hic à se reijcit apostolus,studio sermonis rudis ac simplicis, quod uidemus có suetum esse sacræ ubiq; scripturæ.
units.tr: For it is the nature of opposites that where one is denied, the other is affirmed. He denies that he was sent to evangelize with learned speech; therefore he indicates that he was sent to evangelize with rough and simple speech. This is not compared here, as above, with the Gospel and baptism, where he said, "Not to baptize, but to evangelize." For baptism does not conflict with the Gospel, although it is a separate action and not properly apostolic. But the study of learned speech, which the Apostle here rejects from himself, does conflict with the study of rough and simple speech, which we see to be customary throughout holy Scripture.

units.la: NE inanis reddatur crux Christi. ]
units.tr: That the cross of Christ not be made empty.

units.la: Crucé Christi uocat morte Christi & redem ptione nostrá,quæ est per mortem Christi.Illá cómendaturus à uirtute,contra studiū Aposto lorū,nó simpliciter dicit, ne inanis sit nostra re demptio : sed,ne inanis reddatur crux Christi. Conatur enim etiá ipsum mortis genus, myste rij gratia, cómendare & extollere,adeoq;,ut & supra cœpit, aperte ac fortiter meminit crucis Christi,de qua erubescebát sectarij. Sic & alibi dicit,Ego autem nihil uolo scire nisi Christum Iesum & hunc crucifixum. Item, à me absit glo riari nisi in cruce Domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: By the cross of Christ he means the death of Christ and our redemption, which is accomplished through the death of Christ. Wishing to commend this by its power, and against the studied eloquence of the Apostles, he does not simply say that our redemption would be empty, but that the cross of Christ would be made empty. For he also seeks to commend and exalt the very kind of death, for the sake of the mystery, and, as he began to do above, he openly and boldly calls to mind the cross of Christ, which the sectarians were ashamed of. So he also says elsewhere: "For I determined not to know anything among you, except Jesus Christ and him crucified" (1 Cor. 2.2). Likewise: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ" (Gal. 6.14).

units.la: NE inanis reddatur.] ἵνα μὴ κενωθῇ.Ne euacue tur. Quæ euacuátur inania reddútur, ut inania oua & inanes nuces sunt, in quibus nihil est so lidi.Ita per hac metaphorá ꝑponit nobis cru cé Christi,id est morte Christi,uelut plenú co pię cornu,unde hauriamus cognitione diuinę uoluntatis,dilećtionis immensæ, uitá ac felicita tě uerá & sempiterná, iustificatione, pacem & gaudiū : quæ omnia in hanc crucē thesauri in star collocata sunt,ita ut qui ista tollat & obscu ret,recte dicatur euacuare crucé Christi, quan tum in se est, licet interea sit omniū cælestibus bonis plenissima credentibus.
units.tr: "That it not be made empty" [ἵνα μὴ κενωθῇ], that is, that it not be emptied. What is emptied is made empty, as empty eggs and empty nuts are, which contain nothing solid. So by this metaphor he sets before us the cross of Christ, that is, the death of Christ, as a horn of plenty, from which we draw the knowledge of the divine will, immense love, true and everlasting life and happiness, justification, peace and joy. All these things have been laid up in this cross as in a treasury. Therefore whoever removes or obscures these things is rightly said to empty the cross of Christ, as far as he is concerned, even though it remains full of heavenly blessings for all believers.

units.la: Iá ergo caussam reddit, quare non sit missus ut erudito sermone prædicet Euangeliū Chri sti,sed rudi ac simplici,uidelicet,ne inanis red datur crux Christi: quod iá nó esset agere Apo stolū Christi,sed Satanę: nó Euágelij doćtorē, sed falsificatorem.Quid enim aliud est, qui uel ut marsupium suum refertum reddat,uel men tē inani gloria tumidam,ita prędicat Christum ut inanem faciat illius crucē, unde mortalibus omnis constat spes salutis ac uitæ.
units.tr: Now he gives the reason why he was not sent to preach the Gospel of Christ in learned speech, but in plain and simple speech; namely, "that the cross of Christ be not made empty." This would no longer be the work of an apostle of Christ, but of Satan; not a teacher of the Gospel, but a falsifier. For what else is it, when someone preaches Christ so that he makes the cross empty, whether to fill his own purse or to swell his mind with empty glory, than to make void the cross from which all hope of salvation and life comes to mortals?

units.la: Docet ergo,quaten⁹ nó agnoscat studiū ele gantis & compositi sermonis,& quale,ne pute mus usum & artificiū eloquetiæ ab Apostolo prorsus dānari. Non agnoscit etiá opes & poté tiá,cū tamé sint bonæ Dei creaturæ.Hactenus in ministerio nó agnoscit eloquentiá, & asse rit sermonis simplicitaté,quatenus nó euacue tur,sed probe dispensetur gloria & uirtus cru cis Christi. Vbi res agitur nó Euágelij & regni Christi, sed mundi huius negocia dispesantur, ibi certe locum habet fucus & uis eloquentiæ, locū habent rationes & persuasiones humanæ sapiętiæ,ut quod res ipsa forsan,sua ueluti nu ditate absq; ullo fuco & artifico ꝑposita obti nere nó potest, obtineat belle cōposita & eleganter structa. Vbi uero proponédū est Euangelium Christi, crucis mysterium, opus diuinę uirtutis in Christo, ibi non habet locum artificium eruditi sermonis, sed simplicitas rudis & incópositæ dictionis: ubi exigitur fides in Christum, ibi locum non habent humanę sapientię λογισμοί, & enthymemata. Quare, Ne euacuetur gloria crucis Christi, & statuatur gloria sapientiæ carnis: ne fides nostra in Christū debeatur magis rhetoricis persuasionib. quàm uirtuti gratiæ Christi. Defectus & infirmitatis indicium est, ubi opus est externo & accessorio appa ratu. Mulier uenusta & honesta, quæ natiuo decore commendatur, nihil opus habet, ut fucis ornetur. Turpis uero & inhonesta, opus habet ut belle cōpta, fucata & composita procedat, ut quod nō potest naturali & propria pulchritudine obtinere, obtineat aliena & emendicata: cui si demas ascititiū ornatū, nihil aliud relinquitur quàm ipsa turpitudo & deformitas.
units.tr: He therefore teaches to what extent he does not acknowledge the study of elegant and polished speech, and what kind of speech it is, lest we think that the use and art of eloquence are utterly condemned by the Apostle. Nor does he acknowledge its resources and power, although these are good creatures of God. So far, in the ministry he does not acknowledge eloquence, and he asserts simplicity of speech only insofar as the glory and power of the cross of Christ are not emptied but are duly set forth. Where the business at hand is not the Gospel and kingdom of Christ, but the affairs of this world are being handled, there indeed the veneer and force of eloquence have their place; there the arguments and persuasions of human wisdom have their place, so that what the matter itself, presented in its bare nakedness without any veneer or artifice, perhaps cannot obtain, may be obtained by being finely composed and elegantly constructed. But where the Gospel of Christ, the mystery of the cross, and the work of divine power in Christ are to be proposed, there the artifice of learned speech has no place, but the simplicity of plain and unadorned utterance does. Where faith in Christ is required, there the reasonings [λογισμοί] and enthymemes of human wisdom have no place. Therefore, "lest the glory of the cross of Christ be made empty, and the glory of carnal wisdom be established; lest our faith in Christ be owed more to rhetorical persuasions than to the power of the grace of Christ." It is a sign of weakness and infirmity when external and added apparatus is needed. A beautiful and honest woman, who is commended by her natural charm, has no need to be adorned with cosmetics. But an ugly and dishonourable woman needs to go forth finely adorned, painted and arranged, so that what she cannot obtain by natural and proper beauty she may obtain from something borrowed and begged for. If you take away her added ornament, nothing remains but her very ugliness and deformity.

units.la: Interea tamen nō est putandum locum hic dari ineptæ illi barbariei, cui affine fuit, imò de ditum præteritum sæculum, quam magis uocare licet sermonis confusionem ac corruptionem, quàm simplicitatem. Vt enim non est probandum in ministro Euangelij, si studeat rhetorico dicendi artificio, ut magis rationi humanæ plausibilem quàm homini Christiano credibilem sermonem componat, quo non tam Christo quàm sibi gloriam quærat: ita pro bandúnon est si impurè, incondite, confuse, corrupte ac peruerse dicat, ita ut neq; seipsum probe intelligere queat. Candor & puritas sermonis, uocum scilicet & sententiarum, ut intelligi possis quid dicas, tam abest ut reijciatur ab Euangelio Christi, ut magis requiratur. Neq; enim hoc quærit Apostolus à ministro Christi, ut sit barbarus & ineptus, sermone corrupto & obscuro: sed ut simpliciter & pure Euangelij & crucis Christi doctrinam proponat.
units.tr: Yet meanwhile we must not think that room is given here to that inept barbarism, to which the preceding age was closely related, or rather was steeped in; one may call it more a confusion and corruption of speech than simplicity. For just as it is not to be approved in a minister of the Gospel if he strives after the rhetorical art of speaking, so that he composes a discourse more pleasing to human reason than credible to a Christian, by which he seeks glory not so much for Christ as for himself, so it is not to be approved if he speaks impurely, incoherently, confusedly, corruptly and perversely, so that he cannot even properly understand himself. Clearness and purity of speech, of words and of sentences, so that you can be understood as to what you are saying, is so far from being rejected by the Gospel of Christ that it is rather required. For the Apostle does not ask this of a minister of Christ, that he be barbarous and inept, with corrupt and obscure speech, but that he set forth the doctrine of the Gospel and of the cross of Christ simply and purely.

units.la: Cauendum itaq; omne studium non solum dicendi sed & quodcunq; aliud, quo crux Christi euacuatur. Astutia Satanę nobis nōdū satis est obseruata. Nō est putandū nullā illi esse methodum euacuandi crucem Christi, nisi per studium eloquetię. Euacuatur mille modis. Quisquis Christianam religionē fundat opibus & potentia mundi, quod iam olim cœperūt & fecerunt Rom. Pontifices, is certe euacuat crucē Christi. Quisquis humanas uires & humana merita docet, in religione Christi, euacuat crucem Christi. Quisquis nostram satisfactionem pro peccatis docet, euacuat crucem Christi.
units.tr: Therefore every study must be guarded against, not only of speaking but of anything else whatever by which the cross of Christ is made empty. We have not yet sufficiently observed the cunning of Satan. Let no one think that he has no method of emptying the cross of Christ except through the study of eloquence. It is emptied in a thousand ways. Whoever founds the Christian religion on the wealth and power of the world, as the Roman Pontiffs began long ago to do and did, certainly empties the cross of Christ. Whoever teaches human strength and human merits in the religion of Christ empties the cross of Christ. Whoever teaches our satisfaction for sins empties the cross of Christ.

units.la: Quisquis ueritatem carnis Christi negat, qd' plerique hæreticorum fecerunt, euacuat crucem Christi. Quisquis etiam id quod in ipso Christo gloriosum est & cœleste ita admiratur, complectitur & prædicat, ut interea negligat crucē Christi, in qua unā gloriatus est Paulus, ut sensim credentiū animos à uirtute crucis Christi, per quam saluamur auocat, ita mirabili consilio Satanæ præpostera gloriæ Chri-
units.tr: Whoever denies the truth of the flesh of Christ, as many heretics have done, empties the cross of Christ. Likewise, whoever so admires, embraces and proclaims what is glorious and heavenly in Christ himself that he meanwhile neglects the cross of Christ, in which alone Paul gloried, thus gradually drawing the minds of believers away from the power of the cross of Christ, through which we are saved, by a wonderfully crafty plan of Satan, empties the glory of the cross of Christ by a perverse commendation of the glory of Christ,

units.la: sti commendatione gloriam crucis Christi euacuat, & in ipso Christo Christum destruit.
units.tr: and in Christ himself destroys Christ.

units.la: Nam sermo crucis, iis quidem qui pereunt, stultitia est, & nobis qui seruamur, potentia Dei est.
units.tr: For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.

units.la: Per distinctionem declarat quatenus sit sermo crucis stultitia, quatenus uirtus & sapientia Dei. Potest etiam exponi per ἀνδυνασφορὰν, uel per concessionē. Fugiebāt pseudapostoli scandalum crucis Christi, malentes mundo quàm Christo placere, adeoq; nouam & doctrinā & doctrinæ formam, quæ plausibilis esset humanæ sapientiæ, introducebant. Hanc illorū stultitiam notans, concedit primum, sermonē crucis stultitiam esse quibusdam: uerum talibus, quorum nulla debebat esse ratio ministro Christi, idq; non ex uicio doctrinæ crucis, sed eorū quibus illa pro stultitia reputatur, alioqui uirtutem esse Dei, ijs qui saluantur. Vt si uelis uino laudem uindicare, cōtra illius calumniatores, dicas: Vinum quidem noxiū est, sed febricitantibus: sanis autem plurimū adfert & utilitatis & iucūditatis. Aut si honesti uiri nomen & gloriam cōtra illius ofores asserturus dicas: Displicet quidē & male audit, sed apud reprobos, probis uero admodum cōmendatur. Hic duplici nomine cōmendatur uir honestus. Primum in eo quod bonis placet, deinde nón minus in eo quod malis displicet, quibus displiciuisse multa est laudis portio. Ita & hoc loco Apostolus quod putabatur cedere ad ignominiā crucis Christi, declaratiōe ac diuisione sua conuertit in illius gloriā. Quasi enim obiecturi essent: Quid iactat nobis doctrinam crucis, quasi magnus in illa reconditus sit sapiētię thesaurus, cum sit stulta: occupat dicens: Nam sermo crucis, iis quidem qui pereunt, stultitia: & nobis qui saluamur, potentia Dei est.
units.tr: He explains by distinction how the message of the cross is foolishness and how it is the power and wisdom of God. This may also be explained by way of anthypophora [ἀνδυνασφορὰν], or by concession. The false apostles shunned the scandal of the cross of Christ. They preferred to please the world rather than Christ, and so they introduced a new teaching and a new form of teaching that would be pleasing to human wisdom. Noting their foolishness, the Apostle first concedes that the message of the cross is foolishness to some, but to those whose judgment should carry no weight with a minister of Christ. The fault lies not in the teaching of the cross but in those who count it foolishness. Otherwise it is the power of God to those who are saved. It is as if one wished to defend the reputation of wine against its slanderers and said: wine indeed is harmful to the feverish, but to the healthy it brings much usefulness and pleasure.
