Or if one wished to vindicate the name and glory of an honest man against his accusers and said: he is indeed displeasing and ill spoken of among the wicked, but he is highly commended among the good. An honest man is commended on two counts: first because he pleases the good, and then no less because he displeases the wicked, and to have displeased them is itself a great part of his praise. So too in this place the Apostle turns into the glory of the cross what seemed to tend to its disgrace, by his own explanation and distinction. It is as though his opponents were about to object: why does he boast to us of the teaching of the cross, as if a great store of wisdom were hidden in it, when it is foolish? He anticipates them, saying: for the message of the cross is foolishness to those who perish, but to us who are saved it is the power of God.

units.la: Tuetur ergo gloriam & uirtutē crucis Christi, quam innuerat dicens, Ne inanis reddatur crux Christi. Quod aliūde inane potest reddi, in se utile sit necesse est. Quod enim in seipso est inutile, extrinsecus non potest reddi inutile. Scelestus homo à nemine potest scelestus reddi. Ideo declarandi eius gratia, scandalum stultitiæ quod cruci Christi aliunde impingebatur, amolitur, imò in laudem & gloriam illius uertit dicens: Nā sermo crucis, fateor, stultitia quidem est, sed periturisi, &c.
units.tr: He therefore defends the glory and power of the cross of Christ, which he had hinted at when he said: lest the cross of Christ be made empty. What can be made empty by something else must in itself be useful. What is useless in itself cannot be made useless from outside. A wicked man can be made wicked by no one. So, to make this clear, he removes the scandal of foolishness that was being thrust upon the cross of Christ from elsewhere, and indeed turns it into the praise and glory of the cross, saying: for the message of the cross, I admit, is foolishness to those who perish, etc.

units.la: I Illud, POTENTIA Dei est.] bifariam potest exponi. Aut enim intelligendū est, Sermonem crucis haberi, p uirtute Dei, ab ijs qui saluantur, sicut habetur, p stultitia à perεutibus, atq; ita & Hieronymus & Ambrosius exponūt: aut intelligendum est, quod ijs qui saluantur reipsa sit Dei potentia, non solum æstimetur, secundum illud Rom. 1. Non me pudet Euangelij Christi. Potentia siquidem est Dei, ad salutē omni credēti. Nā utrūq; uere de Euangelio Christi dicitur, non solum quod in se ipsa sit uirtus Dei crux Christi: sed quod qui saluan tur, per uirtutem illā Dei, quæ in prædicatione Euangelij operatur, saluentur. Et hoc sensu poterimus sic legere, At potetia Dei nobis est, qui salutem per illum consequimur. Sicut statim dicit, Placuit Deo, ut per stultitiam praedicationis saluos faciat credentes.
units.tr: 1. The words "is the power of God" can be explained in two ways. Either it must be understood that the message of the cross is held to be the power of God by those who are saved, just as it is held to be foolishness by those who perish; and so Jerome and Ambrose explain it. Or it must be understood that it is in fact the power of God for those who are saved, and not merely thought so, in keeping with Romans 1: "I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ, for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes." Both statements are truly said of the gospel of Christ: not only that the cross of Christ is in itself the power of God, but that those who are saved are saved by that power of God which works in the preaching of the gospel. In this sense we may also read it thus: "But the power of God is to us, who obtain salvation through him," just as he says immediately after: "It pleased God, through the foolishness of the preaching, to save those who believe."

units.la: SERMO crucis.] Notandum hic est quomodo uocet Euangelij praedicationem sermonem crucis, id est sermone de cruce Christi. Quod enim de cruce Christi praedicatur, id uocatur sermo crucis. Epitheton hoc Euangelij diligenter obseruandum est, & penitius omnium Christianorum mentibus insculpendum, ut sciant quando uere uel praedicent uel audiant Euangelium Christi, nempe quado sermone crucis Christi, quo uisum est Deo saluare credentes, praedicat uel audiût, ne se ullo pacto abduci sinat uel ad splédidiora uel ad sublimiora, quod Corinthijs p pseudapostolos usuuenerat, q re licto sermone crucis plausibiliora pponebát.
units.tr: THE MESSAGE of the cross. It must be noted here how he calls the preaching of the gospel the message of the cross, that is, a message about the cross of Christ. For what is preached about the cross of Christ is called the message of the cross. This epithet of the gospel must be carefully observed and more deeply engraved in the minds of all Christians, so that they know when they truly preach or hear the gospel of Christ: namely when they preach or hear it as the message of the cross of Christ, through which God has chosen to save believers. They must never allow themselves to be led away, in any way, to things more splendid or more lofty. This had happened to the Corinthians through the false apostles, who, abandoning the message of the cross, put forward more pleasing things.

units.la: STVLTITIA est pereuntib.] Qua in re ui debatur sermo crucis stultitia pereûtibus: Nã oportet illi aliquid inesse, quod incredulorum iudicio stultitiá sapiat. Crucifixus ille praedicabatur ab Apostolo filius Dei, praedicabatur saluator mundi. Iam utrunq; uidebatur mûdi sapientibus summam referre stultitiâ, uel hoc sci licet credere de filio Dei, quod crucifigi sustinuerit ac potuerit, uel credere de homine per infirmitate cruci facto obnoxio, qd' esse posit aliorû saluator, quum seipsum saluare nequiuerit. Ita enim & Iudæi dicebant, Alios saluos fecit, & seipsum nõ potest saluare. Offendebat ergo omnino incredulos, mundi sapientes, sermo iste crucis, utroq; nomine, cũ prędicans de crucifixo, quod sit filius Dei: tũ affirmás, quod sit saluator mundi. Si Deus est, inquiunt, quid poterit stultius excogitari, quàm Deum cruci affixum, se nõ potuisse liberare è manibus mortaliũ? Si homo est, & ita infirmus, ut crucé effugere nequiuerit, quid & hic stultius fingi potest, quá credere homine crucifixũ, omnes mortales saluare posse, etiamsi quàm maxime iustus fuerit, cum sibi ipsi saluator esse nequiuerit?
units.tr: FOOLISHNESS to those who perish. In this matter the message of the cross is said to be foolishness to those who perish, for something must be in it that, in the judgment of unbelievers, tastes of foolishness. The crucified one was preached by the Apostle as the Son of God, and preached as the Saviour of the world. Now both of these seemed to the wise of the world to contain the greatest foolishness: either to believe that the Son of God could suffer and be able to be crucified, or to believe that a man made liable to death through weakness could be the saviour of others, when he could not save himself. The Jews too said as much: "He saved others, himself he cannot save." So this message of the cross offended the unbelieving wise men of the world on both counts, since it preached the crucified one as the Son of God and affirmed him to be the Saviour of the world. "If he is God," they say, "what could be thought more foolish than that God, fixed to a cross, could not free himself from the hands of mortals? If he is a man, and so weak that he could not escape the cross, what could be imagined more foolish than to believe that a man who was crucified could save all mortals, however very just he may have been, when he could not be his own saviour?"

units.la: QVI pereunt, & qui saluamur.] De discrimine electorum & reproborum, hoc est, pereuntiũ & saluandorum, notādus est hic locus, quomodo queat utraq; pars agnosci: pereuntibus dicit sermone crucis esse stultitiam, ijs qui saluátur, Dei potentia. Cupis scire ad utrâ partę pertineas, expende quid tibi uideatur sermo crucis. Si stultitia, signũ est quod de pereuntibus sis. (Qui omnem medicinâ &cibũ respuit, faci le moriturus intelligitur.) Si potentia Dei, indicium est, quod ad salutę ptineas. Et unde aliàs habet Apostolus istâ certitudine quod dicit, no bis q saluamur, nisi ex eo quod fide Christi Iesu credentes agnoscũt in cruce Dei potentiâ? Tam abest ergo, ut odio habeamus Euangelio reluctantes, ut magis cõmisereamur, tanq; manifesto indicio pereuntes. Videmus prēterea hic fieri nõ posse, ut sermone crucis agnoscât, qui electi non sunt. Verum de electis ac reprobis peculiaris locus in Locis nostris erit.
units.tr: WHO perish, and WHO are being saved. This passage must be noted for the distinction between the elect and the reprobate, that is, between those who perish and those who are to be saved, and for how each part may be recognised. He says that the message of the cross is foolishness to those who perish, but the power of God to those who are saved. If you wish to know to which part you belong, consider what the message of the cross seems to you. If it is foolishness, that is a sign that you are among those who perish. (Whoever rejects all medicine and food is easily understood to be about to die.) If it is the power of God, that is evidence that you belong to salvation. And from where else does the Apostle have this certainty in saying "to us who are being saved," except from the fact that believers in Jesus Christ recognise in the cross the power of God? So far, then, are we from hating the gospel and resisting it, that we should rather pity those who perish, as clear evidence of their condition. We see moreover that it cannot happen that those who are not elect recognise the message of the cross. But a special place on the elect and the reprobate will be given in our Loci.

units.la: Scriptũ est em: Perdã sapientiã sapientium, & intelligentiã intelligetiũ reijciam. Vbi sapiens? ubi scriba? ubi disputator seculi huius? Nonne infatuauit Deus sapientiam seculi huius?
units.tr: For it is written: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and will bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent. Where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the disputer of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?"

units.la: Per scripturas fidem facit uerbis suis. Citat duos locos ex propheta Esaia. Primus ex capite 29. alter cap. 33. Quid ergo confirmat eorum quæ præmisit? Præcedentia duo habuerunt, unum, quod sermo crucis stultitia sit pereuntibus. Alterum, quod potentia Dei sit ijs qui saluátur. Ex his uero sequitur, quod doctrina crucis quæ prædicatur ad salutem mortalium tantis sit, ut iudicio sapientiæ humanæ comprehendi & agnosci nequeat. Iam qui Euangelio reluctantur, iniquũ putant talem institui uiam ad salutem, quam humanus intellectus assequi nequeat, adeoq; putant hoc deo adscribi non debere. Et hodie quoq; Iudæi dicunt se credere non posse, quod Deus tam occulto & obscuro modo mittere uoluerit filium suum, ut non potuerit agnosci: cũ hoc nihil sit aliud, quàm illudere mortalibus, promissiones scilicet itaseruare, ut nemo uoluerit eas agnoscere. Necesse ergo habuit Apostolus scripturarum testimonio probare hoc esse prędictum per spiritum sanctum, quod in illis diebus, ubi opus redemptionis perficeretur, ratio saluádi talis futura esset, quá sapientia seculi huius non agnosceret. Ideo hos prophetę locos inducit, ne quisquá cũ iunari queat quod è suo capite ista confingat.
units.tr: He confirms his words by Scripture. He cites two passages from the prophet Isaiah, the first from chapter 29, the other from chapter 33. What, then, does he confirm of what he has said before? The two preceding statements were: first, that the message of the cross is foolishness to those who perish; second, that it is the power of God to those who are saved. From these it follows that the teaching of the cross, which is preached for the salvation of mortals, is of such a kind that it cannot be grasped or recognised by the judgment of human wisdom. Now those who resist the gospel think it unjust that a way of salvation should be instituted which the human intellect cannot attain, and so they think that this should not be ascribed to God. Even today the Jews say that they cannot believe that God would wish to send his Son in so hidden and obscure a manner that he could not be recognised; but this is nothing other than mocking mortals, since it keeps the promises in such a way that no one would wish to recognise them. The Apostle therefore needed to prove by the testimony of the Scriptures that it had been foretold by the Holy Spirit that in those days, when the work of redemption was to be accomplished, the manner of saving would be such that the wisdom of this world would not recognise it. So he brings forward these passages of the prophet, lest anyone could suspect that he was inventing these things from his own head.

units.la: PERDAM sapientiá.] Quod ad historiam attinet, minatur Deus populo suo tá intolerabile exitiũ per Assyrios, ut nihil sint inventuri remedij etiam sapientes & intelligentes inter ipsos. Et illud, ubi sapiens? cap. 33. insultatio est liberatorum contra obsessores urbis Ierosolymæ. Nam pollicetur propheta liberationé populo ab obsidione ista graui regis Sancherib, ita ut sint liberati iam insultaturi illis, quos antea metuerant, ac dicturi, Vbi iá est scriba? ubi est quæstor? ubi est scriba palatiorũ? Nam antea dederant regi Assyriorũ tributũ, quo negato per Ezechiam, ortũ erat id belli. Sed hac de re in Comentarijs nostris super Ieshaiá. Quod ad lectionẽ attinet posterioris huius loci, Apostolus neque Ebræa neq; Septuaginta sequutus est, sed magis sensum pro sua libertate expresit quàm uerba. Nã in Ebraeo ita habetur ... i. ubi scriba? ubi pŏderator? ubi scriba turriũ? Septuaginta uero sic ... Proinde quidã putát hęc Apostoli esse uerba non alicuius scripturę. Nã nisi unica interrogatiuncula est quę quadrat, nempe, ubi est scriba? reliqua diuersa sunt. Quod enim dicit, ubi est sapiens? nec est in Ebreo nec in Greco. Iterũ, ubi est inquisitor sæculi huius, nec est in Ebreo, & ipsum nec in Greco. Et præterea etiá id qd' cõgruere uidetur, uerbo tatũ cõgruit non sensu. Nã scriba ... Ebr. & Græce, ... τιας in propheta nō ad sapientiā, sed ad officiū illud situræ pertinet, quod magis potestatis quàm sapientię authoritate ualebat: in Apostolo uero γραμματεύς, idé est quod literatus & doctus, ut cōgruat precedenti, ubi est sapiēs: & sequenti, ubi est disputator seculi huius? His de causis prope assentior illis, q putant hāc insultationē cōtra mūdi sapientes mere esse Apostoli nō scripturę uerbis cōtextā, quam præmisso scripturę loco cōmodū subiecit, tanquā ex illo natā. Instat enim, & urget, ueritatē huius prophetę conspicue adimpletā euincens. Quasi di cat: An non cōspicuū est quod propheta dicit, hoc nostro tēpore, in hac Euāgelij Christi cau sa? Nēpe qđ sapientiū Deus sapientiā perdiderit. Date mihi aliquē sapiētē, date literatū, date So phistā aliquē & acutū disputatorē, quæso quid adfert in hac causa? Primum, nō intelliget, sed magis explodet. Deinde q adferet ex sapientię penetralib. plane stulta erūt, nec quicquā faci ent ad uerā salutē. Et hoc est, qđ propheta dixit, quod ad oculos iā adimpletū uidemus, ut sapientiam mundi huius Deus infatuauerit.
units.tr: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise" (Isa. 29:14). As far as the historical sense goes, God threatens his people with such intolerable ruin through the Assyrians that even the wise and intelligent among them will find no remedy. "Where is the wise man?" in chapter 33 is the taunt of those who were delivered against the besiegers of Jerusalem. The prophet promises the people deliverance from the grievous siege of King Sennacherib, so that those who had once feared their enemies would now be free to mock them and say: "Where now is the scribe? Where is the collector? Where is the scribe of the towers?" For they had previously paid tribute to the king of Assyria, and when Hezekiah refused it, the war arose. But I have treated this matter in our commentaries on Isaiah. As for the wording of this latter passage, the Apostle followed neither the Hebrew nor the Septuagint, but expressed the sense more freely than the words. In the Hebrew it reads: "where is the scribe? where is the weigher? where is the scribe of the towers?" The Septuagint reads differently. Hence some think these words of the Apostle are not taken from any Scripture. Indeed, only one little question, "where is the scribe?", fits; the rest differ. For "where is the wise man?" is found neither in the Hebrew nor in the Greek. Again, "where is the inquirer of this world?" is found neither in the Hebrew nor in the Greek. Moreover, even the word that seems to agree agrees only in wording, not in sense. For the Hebrew and Greek word for "scribe" in the prophet pertains not to wisdom but to that office, which carried more weight by authority of power than of learning; but in the Apostle, γραμματεύς means one who is literate and learned, so that it fits the preceding "where is the wise man?" and the following "where is the disputer of this world?" For these reasons I rather agree with those who think this taunt against the wise men of the world is wholly the Apostle's own, not framed in the words of Scripture, and that he added it after the scriptural passage as if arising from it. For he presses and urges the point, proving the truth of this prophet clearly fulfilled. As if he said: Is it not plain that what the prophet says is happening in our own time, in this cause of the gospel of Christ, namely that God has destroyed the wisdom of the wise? Give me some wise man, give me a learned man, give me some sophist and sharp disputer; I ask you, what does he contribute to this cause? First, he will not understand, but rather will scoff. Then whatever he brings out of the innermost recesses of wisdom will be plainly foolish and will achieve nothing toward true salvation. And this is what the prophet said, which we now see fulfilled before our eyes: that God has made foolish the wisdom of this world.

units.la: Nō est aūt putādum quod iudiciū hoc Dei, quo mūdi sapiētes in cognitiōe Christi appre hēdēda infatuātur, iā olim finē ceperit, cū ipsa causa adhuc duret, & sapientia mundi eadē sit quæ tū fuerit. Proinde quemadmodū suo tem pore Corinthios Apostolos cōtra hoc scanda lum, quod Euangeliū crucis à sapiētibus mun di reprobatur, hoc prophetæ loco muniuit: ita & nos hodie cōmuniendi sumus similibus lo cis, ne offendamur, cū uidemus neminē ita re lustari doctrinæ Euangelicæ atq; mūdi huius sapientes, quales eos hic describit Apostolus, uocans literatos & disputatores. Deinde uide mus etiam hic quàm sit periculosum homini Christiano eximium fieri in mundana sapiētia & eruditione, cuius nostro quoq; tēpore con spicua sunt documenta. Et præterea, quá non sit sperandum causam religionis suo fore loco per literatos & disputatores restituendam.
units.tr: Yet we must not suppose that this judgment of God, by which the wise men of the world are made foolish in grasping the knowledge of Christ, has long since ended, since the cause itself still endures and the wisdom of the world is the same as it was then. Therefore, just as the Apostle at that time fortified the Corinthians against this stumbling block, that the gospel of the cross is rejected by the wise of the world, by this prophetic passage, so we too today must be fortified by similar passages, lest we be offended when we see that hardly anyone is so instructed in the Gospel doctrine by the wise of this world, such as the Apostle describes here, calling them learned and disputers. Next, we see here also how dangerous it is for a Christian man to become eminent in worldly wisdom and learning, of which our own time also furnishes clear examples. And besides, we must not hope that the cause of religion will be restored to its place by learned men and disputers.

units.la: Illud, NONNE infatuauit Deus sapiētiam huius mundi? Bifariam exponitur. Primū, ut idē sit, atq; infatuatā ostēdit. Sic exponit Chry sost. Nec insoles est illa loquutio, ut dicatur in fatuare aliquē, qui fatuū esse declarat & cōuin cit. Ita nos Germani dicimus: Du must mich zum dieb machen. hoc est, probādū tibi erit, quā uere me sure uoces. Ad hūc modū psermone crucis declarauit Deus & manifestū fecit sapiētiā mū di huius prorsus stultā esse in rebus diuinis ad salutē ptinentibus: ubi cōpertū fecit, eos potis simum offendi cruce Christi, qui reliquis sunt sapientiores. Deinde ita exponitur, ut nō solū declarauerit hoc Deus per sermonem crucis, sed & ipse effecerit, id est ipsam sapientiā excæ cauerit singulari iudicio, dum studio consilii um uoluntatis suæ ab ipsis abscondit, Matth. 11. ut uidentes non uiderent. Iohan. 9.
units.tr: As for the phrase "Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?", it is explained in two ways. First, so that "making foolish" means the same as "showing to be foolish." Chrysostom explains it so. Nor is this way of speaking unusual, to say that someone is made foolish when he is shown and convicted as a fool. So we Germans say: "Du must mich zum Dieb machen" ("you will have to make a thief of me"), that is, you will have to prove how truly I speak. In this way God by the word of the cross declared and made manifest that the wisdom of this world is utterly foolish in matters divine that pertain to salvation, when he showed that it is especially those who are wiser than the rest who are offended by the cross of Christ. Second, it is explained in such a way that God not only declared this through the word of the cross but also himself brought it about, that is, by a singular judgment he blinded wisdom itself, while he hid from them the counsel of his will through study, Matt. 11, so that seeing they might not see, John 9.

units.la: Nec emphasi caret, quod non dicit, Nōnne Deus sapiētes huius mūdi infatuauit: sed nōn ne sapiētiā, &c. Nā si dixisset sapiētes, mox co-
units.tr: Nor is the emphasis lacking in the fact that he does not say "Has not God made foolish the wise men of this world?" but "has not God made foolish the wisdom...," etc. For if he had said "the wise men," someone would straightway think that the Apostle was speaking not of all but perhaps only of the more stupid wise men of his own time.

units.la: gitaret aliquis, Apostolū nō de omnib. sed de sui tātū tēporis sapientib. forsan stupidioribus loqui. Vbi uero dicit ipsam sapientiā infatuatā esse à Deo p sermonē crucis, apertū est stultitię damnari in reb. diuinis uniuersam sapiētiam, quā & Cicero lib.2. de Finib. uocari posse dicit rerū diuinarū humanarūq; scientiā. Et Basilius homelia de proverbijs Salomonis sic definit: ἐστι ἀληθὴς ... Huc etiā pertinet quod dicit sapientiā mūdi huius, & nō sapiētiā aliquorū philosophorum: ut includat omnem ætatē, omne sapientiæ genus, & nihil relinquat planè iudi cio & intelligentiæ rationis humanæ: ut uerū sit illud Christi, Nemo cognouit patrem nisi fi lius, & cui uoluerit filius reuelare.
units.tr: But where he says that wisdom itself has been made foolish by God through the word of the cross, it is plain that all wisdom in divine matters is condemned as folly, which Cicero, in book 2 of De Finibus, says can also be called the knowledge of things divine and human. And Basil, in his homily on the Proverbs of Solomon, defines it thus: [ἐστι ἀληθὴς ...]. To this also pertains his saying "the wisdom of this world" and not "the wisdom of certain philosophers," so that he includes every age, every kind of wisdom, and leaves nothing at all to the judgment and understanding of human reason; so that that saying of Christ holds true: "No one has known the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him."

units.la: Nam quoniam in sapientia Dei non cognouit mūdus per sapientiā Deum, uisum est Deo per stulticiam prædica tionis saluos facere credentes.
units.tr: For since in the wisdom of God the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe.

units.la: Rationem assignat, cur Deo uisum sit talem salutis uiam inducere, quam mundi sapientia non agnosceret. Quoniam, inquit, mundus in sapientia Dei, per sapientiam suam Deum non cognouit. Habet autem ista ἀπόδειξιν duas partes. Primùm quid Deo uisum sit, deinde quare hoc uisum sit.
units.tr: He gives the reason why it pleased God to introduce such a way of salvation as the wisdom of the world would not recognise. "Since," he says, "the world, in the wisdom of God, did not know God through its own wisdom." This proof [ἀπόδειξιν] has two parts. First, what pleased God; second, why it pleased him.

units.la: VISVM est Deo, inquit, per stulticiam prædicationis saluos facere credētes.] Stulticiam prædicationem. (intelligit autem sermonem crucis) quam non ideo sic uocat, quod sit stulta: sed quod uel stulta uideatur sapiētibus huius mundi, uel quod stultos iuxta mundum exigat, quos saluet, ut & infra cap. 3. admonebit, cum sit ipsa sapiētia Dei & uirtus Dei. Et huic stultitiæ pulchre conuenit, quod non dicit, saluos facere intelligentes, scientes, sapiētes, exquirentes, disputantes: sed credentes, hoc est stultos, iuxta rationem mundi. Nam illius iudicio stultum est aliquid pro certo apprehendere, ubi nullæ assignantur rationes & persuasiones, sed simpliciter exigitur, ut credas. Et re uera in rebus mundi ita habet, unde & plerunque huiusmodi stulti, omnia credentes, facile falluntur: in rebus uero diuinis ubi Deo creditur, non ita. Nam illic Deo creditur omniū uera-cissimo, qui neminem fallit.
units.tr: IT PLEASED God, he says, to save those who believe through the foolishness of the preaching. He calls the preaching "foolishness" (by which he means the word of the cross), not because it is foolish in itself, but because it seems foolish to the wise of this world, or because it requires those whom it saves to be foolish by the standard of the world, as he will remind us below in chapter 3, though it is the very wisdom and power of God. The word "believing" fits this foolishness beautifully. He does not say "to save those who understand, know, are wise, inquire or dispute," but "those who believe," that is, those who are foolish by the reckoning of the world. For by its judgment it is foolish to grasp something as certain when no reasons or persuasions are given, and one is simply required to believe. In the affairs of the world it is indeed so, and that is why such credulous fools are often easily deceived. In divine matters, however, where we believe God, it is not so, for there we believe the most truthful of all, who deceives no one.

units.la: Deinde, Cur ita Deo uisum est? Quoniam in sapientia Dei, &c. Sapientiam Dei uocat, constitutionem istam cœli ac terræ & omnium quæ in illis sunt, quæ omnia sapientissime sunt condita, siue res ipsas, siue rationem & causas earum, siue effectus & utilitatem, siue ordinem, harmoniam & constantiam, siue magnitudinem multitudinemque infinitam: deinde & splendorem ac pulchritudinem, unde & κόσμος, id est ornatum uocarunt, respicias: ut nihil aliud expendenti occurrat, quàm immensa quædam & incomprehensibilis opificis huius & sapientia & potentia, quam admirari & suspicere posis, perscrutari non posis. Per huius sapientiæ Dei prædicatio nem, quæ egreditur etiamnum in universum orbem, mundi sapientia Deum non cognouit, nec ut Deum coluit ut seruaretur: ideo aliam inuenit rationem, ut seruaret uel credentes & stultos, posteaquā sapientes per suam sapientiam sapientem Deum non cognouerunt. Et hæc saluandi stultos credētes ratio, licet cedat ad infatuationem sapientiæ mūdi, deinde ad excæcationē eorū qui illa in reb. diuinis utūtur, ut posit uideri iudicii quoddā irati Dei, quatenus perdūtur sapientes in sua sapientia: tamen in seipsa est ipsissima misericordia & gratia beneuolentis Dei, & cōsultum cupientis humano generi. Vnde ut uerbo εὐδοκία usus est Apostolus, quē significat beneuolētiæ cuiusdā consilii, quā beneuolētiaDei erga homines expressērunt & angeli in natiuitate Christi. Qua in re perinde fecit Deus, atq; si ciuitas quædā longo tēpore liberalitate regis p quā fuisset in libertate cōstituta, nō sustinuerit agnoscere, ut & gratia esset, & regē ex animo coleret, adeoq; digna iā esset, quæ ingratitudinis & socordiæ merito periret: Rex uero quia nondū iuberet uniuersam delere, sed quouis modo ad meliora reducere, cōsilio mutato libertate adimeret, & salutem ita pmitteret, ut in seruitutem redacti obedietes seruarentur. Quis nō regis huius simul & sapientiā & beneuolētiā iuste deprędicaret? Quis diceret factū esse animi irati, etiā si posteā inobedientes, & libertate pristina p rebellionem utentes merito perirēt? Ita plane uidetur habere cōsiliū hoc Dei, cuius Apostolus hic meminit. Ex hoc ergo colligimus ista duo. Primum, non esse aliā saluādi rationē, quàm istam quæ est per stultitiā prędicationis, qua saluantur credentes: ut merito pereant, quicunq; alia uia salutem quærunt.
units.tr: Next, why did it please God to act thus? "Since in the wisdom of God," and so on. He calls wisdom of God the very constitution of heaven and earth and of all that is in them, all of which were made most wisely, whether you look at the things themselves, or their reason and causes, or their effects and usefulness, or their order, harmony and constancy, or their vast magnitude and multitude; and then at their splendour and beauty, which is why they called the world [κόσμος], that is, adornment. If you weigh these things, nothing else meets you but the immense and incomprehensible wisdom and power of this Maker, which you can admire and revere but cannot search out. Through the preaching of this wisdom of God, which even now goes out into the whole world, the wisdom of the world did not know God, nor did it honour him as God so that it might be saved. Therefore he found another way to save fools who believe, after the wise had not known God through their own wisdom. And this way of saving the foolish believers, although it leads to the making foolish of the wisdom of the world and then to the blinding of those who use it in divine matters, so that it may seem a kind of judgment of an angry God, insofar as the wise are destroyed in their own wisdom, is nevertheless in itself the most genuine mercy and grace of a kindly God who desires the good of the human race. Hence the Apostle uses the word "good pleasure" [εὐδοκία], which signifies a kind of benevolent plan, the kindness of God toward men which the angels also expressed at the birth of Christ. In this matter God acted just as if a city, which a king's generosity had long before set free, would not acknowledge it, so that the favour was known and the king was honoured from the heart; and the city had by then deserved to perish for its ingratitude and carelessness. But the king, since he did not yet wish to destroy the whole city, but to bring it back to better things by some means, changed his plan, took away its liberty, and allowed it to be saved in such a way that, reduced to servitude, it would be preserved by obedience. Who would not justly praise this king for both his wisdom and his kindness? Who would say that he acted out of an angry mind, even though those who afterwards were disobedient and, through rebellion, misused their former liberty, rightly perished? This seems to be exactly the plan of God, of which the Apostle speaks here. From this we gather two things. First, there is no other way of salvation than that which is by the foolishness of the preaching, by which those who believe are saved; so those who seek salvation by another way rightly perish.

units.la: Alterū, in causa salutis nostræ exigi stulticiā hanc, qua nō scrutemur, nec rationes exquiramus eorū quę per Euangelij prędicationē pro ponuntur: sed captiuato omni rationis intellectu, imò repugnante, cedamus in obsequium & seruitutem fidei.
units.tr: Second, that this foolishness is required for the cause of our salvation: that we do not scrutinise, nor seek the reasons for those things that are set forth through the preaching of the Gospel, but, with all the understanding of reason taken captive, or rather resisting, we yield to the obedience and servitude of faith.

units.la: Hęc duo considerata, adimunt credentibus offendiculū illud quod in sermone crucis per mundi sapientiam Corinthijs obijciebatur, & perpetuò obijcitur, ita ut iam nemo Christianus offendatur, si uideriт Euangelicam doctrinam, stultitiæ instar, à sapiētibus mundi huius explodi: sed magis stupeat & admiretur, si uideat aliquem ex sapientibus illam amplecti.
units.tr: These two points, once considered, remove from believers that stumbling-block which was once, and is still constantly, thrown at the Corinthians by the wisdom of the world in the word of the cross. So no Christian should now be offended if he sees the evangelical doctrine rejected by the wise of this world as foolishness. Rather he should be astonished and marvel if he sees some of the wise embrace it.

units.la: Videamus etiā hoc loco, q; iustū iudiciū iræ Dei maneat eos, qui doctrinam Euangelij respuunt, & hanc diuinæ beneuolentiæ rationē ad humani generis salutem propositam explo dunt, sicut & Iohānes dixit: Qui non credit, ira Dei manet supra ipsum. Nullam enim possunt habere excusationem increduli, siue sapientes siue stulti iuxta sæculum. Sapiētes quia dono Dei abutūtur, & in sapientia sua Deū nō agnoscunt nec colunt, sed summam Dei sapiētiā cō-temnūt. Stulti quia cōsilium Dei, ad hoc temperatum, ut ad salutem accedere liceat, absque ullo sapiētię carnis adminiculo, nec quicquam exigatur quàm ut credatur: ad quam rem appositissima est stultitia iuxta mundum, & ipsi cōtemnunt. Vt ergo rex ille cuius supra memini, merito perderet inobedientem ac rebellem ciuitatem, quæ nec libera, nec serua dominum suum agnosceret: ita & mūdus à Deo omnium iustissime damnabitur.
units.tr: Let us also see at this point that the just judgment of God's wrath remains upon those who spurn the doctrine of the Gospel and reject this plan of divine kindness proposed for the salvation of mankind, just as John said: "He who does not believe, the wrath of God remains upon him." For unbelievers, whether wise or foolish by the standard of this age, have no excuse. The wise, because they abuse God's gift and do not acknowledge or honour God in their wisdom, but despise the supreme wisdom of God. The foolish, because the plan of God is so arranged that one may approach salvation without any help from fleshly wisdom, and nothing is required except that one believe. For this matter the foolishness of the world is most suitable, and these very people despise it. Therefore, just as that king I mentioned above would justly destroy a disobedient and rebellious city which, being neither free nor enslaved, did not acknowledge its lord, so the world too will be most justly condemned by God.

units.la: QVAESTIO I.
units.tr: QUESTION I.

units.la: Sed quærat forsan aliquis, quomodo mundum dicat Apostolus Deum in sapiētia sua per sapientiam nō cognouisse, cum idem ipse Apostolus Rom.1. dicat sapientes Deū per uisibilia opera illa cognouisse? Notādum est hic, duplicem esse cognitionem Dei. Vnam, generalem illam quæ est communis omnibus ex opificio Dei omniū illustrissimo. De ea loquitur Apostolus Rom.1. Illa non saluat, licet excusationē adimat. Alterum, specialem hanc, quæ est diuinæ uoluntatis in Christo cognitio, & ad salutem facit. Hanc scilicet non cognouit mundus per sapientiam suam in sapientia Dei, de qua hic locus est.
units.tr: But perhaps someone will ask how the Apostle can say that the world did not know God through its wisdom, when this same Apostle says in Romans 1 that the wise knew God through His visible works. It must be noted here that there are two kinds of knowledge of God. The first is general, which is common to all from the most illustrious work of God's creation. The Apostle speaks of this in Romans 1. It does not save, although it takes away excuse. The second is special, which is the knowledge of the divine will in Christ, and it leads to salvation. It is this that the world did not know through its own wisdom, in the wisdom of God, and this is the knowledge the passage is about.

units.la: QVAESTIO II.
units.tr: QUESTION II.

units.la: Deinde quæri potest, quomodo dicat Deū consilium hoc stultæ prędicationis tum inijsse, posteaquam mundus per sapientiam suam Deū in sapientia Dei non cognouit, cum alibi consilij huius mysterium fuisse ab æterno absconditum in Christo Iesu, & electos ante constitutionem mundi ad uitā in Christo prædestinatos esse doceat, Ephef.1. Respondeo. Loquitur de Deo humano more, ut & scriptura facit Genef.6. & multis alijs locis. Sic quoniam ubi cœpit Euangelium, tum primum uisa est mutata saluandi ratio, ideo dicit Deum consilium hoc cepisse: cū tamen ita prædestinarit à sæculo, ut infra 2. Loquitur ergo hoc loco Apostolus secundum temporis rationē, de eo quod in tempore cœpit, & secundum ordinem dispensationis diuinæ, non secundum abditissimam œconomiam filiorum Dei abyssum, in qua latet huius consilij principium.
units.tr: Next, one may ask how the Apostle says that God then undertook this plan of foolish preaching, after the world through its own wisdom had not known God in the wisdom of God, when elsewhere he teaches that the mystery of this plan had been hidden from eternity in Christ Jesus, and that the elect were predestined to life in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1). I answer: he speaks in human fashion, as Scripture also does in Genesis 6 and in many other places. So, since the Gospel began, when the manner of saving first appeared changed, for this reason he says God then undertook this plan, although He had predestined it from the beginning of the age, as he says below in chapter 2. The Apostle therefore speaks in this place according to the reckoning of time, and of what began in time, and according to the order of the divine dispensation, not according to the most hidden economy, the abyss of the sons of God, in which lies the origin of this plan.

units.la: Quandoquidem & Iudęi signum postulant, & Græci sapientiā querūt. Nos aūt prædicamus Christum crucifixum, Iudęis quidem offendiculū, Græcis uero stultitiam: sed ipsdem uocatis, Iudæis pariter & Græcis Christum Dei potentiam ac sapientiam.
units.tr: Since both the Jews ask for a sign and the Greeks seek wisdom. But we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block indeed to the Jews, and foolishness to the Greeks; but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks alike, Christ is the power and wisdom of God.

units.la: 1 Declaratio est superiorum. Dixerat sermonem crucis stulticiam esse pereuntibus, deinde per stulticiā prędicatiōis saluos fieri credētes. Iam declarat qua ratione prędicatio Euangelij, sermoq; crucis perituris sit stulticia, quos diuidit in Iudæos & Græcos. Quoniā inquit Iudæi increduli signum postulant, & Græci sapientiā querūt. Nos aūt prædicam⁹ crucifixū Christū, in quo Iudæi quæ petunt signa, nō inueniunt, nec Græci quà quærunt sapientiam, ideoq; Iudæi in eo offenduntur, & Græci pro stultitia habent, quod de Christo prædicamus. Et hac ratione impediuntur ne Christū fide apprehendant. Obserua, quod eos quos uno uocabulo perituros uocauit, iā uocat Iudæos & Græcos, p quos nō modo & ceterarū nationū incredulos coprehendit, sed & omnē totius mundi sañ stimoniā pariter & sapientiam pstringit, eiusq; dementiæ damnat, quod Christū sapietiam ac potentiā Dei, ppostero certitudinis studio seducti, signaq; & sapientiā quærētes, respuāt & auersentur. Quid ergo prēterea habet in se mū dus hic eximium, quod accómodum sit regno Dei, quādo potissimæ illius nationes, Iudæi ac Græci, cū sanctitatis, tū sapietiæ nomine cōspi cuæ, offendiculum ac stulticiā inueniunt in eo in quo Deus summā uoluit esse potentiam ac sapientiam omnibus in ipsum credentibus? Quid est autē signum & sapientiā quærere? Est nolle credere uerbo Dei, sed uelle certitudine habere tale, quā ratio queat apprehēdere. Ergo qui signa & sapientiā quærūt, fide crucis Christi respuunt, in qua ipsorum iudicio inueniunt stulticiā & impotentiā, atq; ita offenduntur et pereunt. Vocati uero, id est credentes, in cruce Christi inueniūt sapientiam & potentiam Dei, dū credunt se morte Christi à morte liberatos, & ad uerā uitā assertos, q Dei sapientia & potētia ab incredulis intelligi non potest: quia non humana ratione, sed fidei sensu capitur, iu xta illud, Nisi credideritis, non intelligetis.
units.tr: 1. This is an explanation of what has gone before. He had said that the word of the cross is foolishness to those who perish, and then that through the foolishness of the preaching those who believe are saved. Now he explains by what reasoning the preaching of the Gospel, and the word of the cross, is foolishness to those who perish, whom he divides into Jews and Greeks. For, he says, the unbelieving Jews ask for a sign, and the Greeks seek wisdom. But we preach Christ crucified, in whom the Jews do not find the signs they ask for, nor do the Greeks find the wisdom they seek. Therefore the Jews are offended by him, and the Greeks regard as foolishness what we preach about Christ, and by this reasoning they are prevented from grasping Christ by faith. Observe that those whom he called, in one word, "those who perish," he now calls Jews and Greeks. By this he includes not only the unbelievers of the other nations, but also he takes in equally all the testimony and wisdom of the whole world, and condemns its madness, because, led astray by a perverse zeal for certainty, it seeks signs and wisdom, and rejects and turns away from Christ, the wisdom and power of God. What, then, is there in this world that is remarkable and fitted to the kingdom of God, when those most powerful nations, the Jews and the Greeks, renowned both for holiness and for wisdom, find a stumbling block and foolishness in that in which God wished to have his supreme power and wisdom for all who believe in him? What is it to seek a sign and wisdom? It is to be unwilling to believe the Word of God, but to wish to have such certainty as reason can grasp. Therefore those who seek signs and wisdom reject the faith of the cross of Christ, in which, by their own judgment, they find foolishness and weakness, and so they are offended and perish. But those who are called, that is, those who believe, find in the cross of Christ the wisdom and power of God, since they believe that they have been freed from death by the death of Christ and brought to true life. This wisdom and power of God cannot be understood by unbelievers, because it is grasped not by human reason but by the sense of faith, according to that saying: "Unless you believe, you will not understand."

units.la: 3 Quid est autē quod Iudæis signa petētibus in Christo ter miraculis referto non potuit satis fieri? Hoc scilicet est, qď signa uel nō quærūt ex animo, uel nō ea quærūt q uirtute Dei facta sunt in Christo sermonem suū confirmante sequentibus portentis: sed peculiaria quædā, ut ab ipso Christo quoq; signū de cælo petebant. Matth.16. id quod nihil erat aliud q hypocritica & subdola cōtra ueritatis agnoscēdæ lucem tergiuersatio, cui nullis etiam signis, utut immensis & infinitis, satisfieri poterat.
units.tr: 3. But why could the Jews, who asked for signs, not be satisfied in Christ, who was so rich in miracles? This is clearly because they either did not seek signs in earnest, or they did not seek those signs which were done by the power of God in Christ, confirming his word by the portents that followed. Instead they sought certain peculiar signs, such as they asked of Christ himself, a sign from heaven (Matthew 16). This was nothing other than a hypocritical and deceitful evasion, set against the light of recognising the truth, and no signs, however great and countless, could satisfy it.

units.la: Videmus ergo, q aĩimis excæcatis ac perti nacibus nequeat uillis quantūuis magnis signis & portētis ad hoc satisfieri, ut lucem ueritatis agnoscát & amplectátur. Quid ergo querūt hodie, q ad pdicatione Euágelij signa postulant?
units.tr: We see, therefore, that to minds blinded and obstinate no signs or portents, however great, can satisfy the demand that they recognise and embrace the light of truth. What, then, do those today seek who ask for signs when the Gospel is preached?

units.la: Dicet quisq̄: Ergo ne usq; adeo illicitū est signa quærere, ut hoc nomine digni sint qui pereant, quotquot ad certitudinē ueritatis acqui renda signa poscūt? Quid est ergo quod Achas spterea in scripturis culpatur, qď signū à Deo petere nolebat? Respondimus ad hāc quæstionem in commentarijs nostris super Ieshaiam cap.7. Multū refert quare & quomodo signum petas à Deo uel nō petas. Si ut Iudei incredula, facis rem illicitā: si ut Ezechias & Gideon, tam non peccas, ut etiam quod petis impetres.
units.tr: Someone will say: "Is it then so unlawful to seek signs, that all who ask for signs in order to acquire certainty of the truth deserve to perish for this reason? What then is the reason that Ahaz is blamed in the Scriptures for being unwilling to ask God for a sign?" We answered this question in our commentaries on Isaiah, chapter 7. It matters greatly why and how you ask God for a sign or do not ask. If you do so like the unbelieving Jews, you do something unlawful; if you do so like Hezekiah and Gideon, you do not sin, and even obtain what you ask.

units.la: 4 Illud, Christum Dei sapiētiā & uirtutē, de Christo crucifixo, deq; illius cruce & morte in telligē. Nā, ut & Hieron. hic admonet, non loq̄tur de Christi diuinitate, sed de mysterio, dif- pēsatione, & uirtute crucis, in qua & Iudæi offenduntur, & Græci stulticiā inueniūt: credētes uerò Dei sapiētiā & uirtutē, ad saluādū uideli cet. Quod dicit, ijsdē uocatis Iudæis pariter & Græcis, facit ad discretionē earūdē gentiū incredulorum & fideliū, ne ipsos populos totos reprobatos esse putemus. Fideles uocat uocatos, cū tñ in genere uocari uoluerit oēs, ipseq; Christ dixerit, multi uocati, pauci uero electi: unde constat, nō uenile ad fidem Christi, quot quot sunt uocati. Vocatos ergo hic intelligit eos, quos Deus ad salutē destinauit, ideoq; singulari gratia ad regnū suum uocati uoluit, quo modo & Ro.8.legim⁹, quos pdestinauit, hos & uocauit: quos uocauit, hos & iustificauit, nō eos de qbus dictū est, q uocati sūt nō erāt digni.
units.tr: 4. The phrase "Christ, the wisdom and power of God" must be understood of Christ crucified, and of his cross and death. For, as Jerome also reminds us here, he does not speak of the divinity of Christ, but of the mystery, the dispensation, and the power of the cross, in which the Jews are offended and the Greeks find foolishness, while those who believe find the wisdom and power of God, which saves. What he says, that Jews and Greeks alike are called, serves to distinguish between those unbelieving nations and the faithful, so that we do not think the peoples themselves are wholly rejected. He calls the faithful "the called," although he wished all in general to be called, and Christ himself said, "Many are called, but few are chosen." From this it is plain that not all who are called come to the faith of Christ. Therefore by "the called" here he means those whom God appointed to salvation, and whom he wished to call to his kingdom by singular grace. In this way we read in Romans 8: "Whom he predestined, these he also called; whom he called, these he also justified," not those of whom it was said that they were called but were not worthy.

units.la: Quoniam stulticia Dei sapientior est quàm homines, & imbecillitas Dei robustior est quàm homines.
units.tr: Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.

units.la: 1 Hoc pertinet ad id qď dixit uocatis Iudæis pariter & Græcis Christū crucifixū esse uirtutē & sapientiā dei. Ratio est, inq̄t, quòd id qď stultum putatur in Deo & infirmū, uidelicet quòd pdicamus filiū Dei crucifixū: q res Iudeis infirmitas, Græcis stulticia uidetur, sapietius est & potetius q sit ulla sapientia & uirtus humana. Quare? Quia qď nulla potuit pstare sapientia nullaq; potentia mūdi, hoc pstitit crux Christi. Morte, peccatum & regnū satanæ destruxit, iu sticiā & uerā felicitatē cū sempiterna uita inue xit, qď nec Iudæorū sanctimonia, nec Græcorū philosophia unq̄ potuisset efficere. Sed ista crucifixi sapietia & uirtus incredulis est absco dita, & tamen à credentibus agnoscitur.
units.tr: 1 This relates to what he said to the called, both Jews and Greeks, that Christ crucified is the power and wisdom of God. The reason, he says, is that what is thought foolish and weak in God, namely that we preach the Son of God crucified, appears to the Jews as weakness and to the Greeks as foolishness, yet it is wiser and mightier than any human wisdom or power. Why? Because the cross of Christ accomplished what no wisdom and no power of the world could accomplish. By death it destroyed sin and the kingdom of Satan, and it brought in righteousness, true happiness and eternal life, which neither the holiness of the Jews nor the philosophy of the Greeks could ever have achieved. But this wisdom and power of the crucified One is hidden from unbelievers, and yet it is recognised by believers.

units.la: 2 Exponunt quidam hunc locū etiā de sapiē tia & uirtute p̄dicati Euágelij, quo totus orbis innouat⁹ est, & cóferūt hic imbecillitate philo sophię in ipsis capitibus Platone & Sacrate, cū uirtute Euágelij, declarantes q illa nihil, ista tā immensa effecerit. Vide hoc loco Chrysost.
units.tr: 2 Some expound this passage also of the wisdom and power of the preached gospel, by which the whole world has been renewed. They compare the weakness of philosophy in its chief men, Plato and Socrates, with the power of the gospel, declaring that the former achieved nothing while the latter achieved so immense a thing. See Chrysostom on this passage.

units.la: Videtis enim uocationem uestram fratres, quod non multi sapientes.
units.tr: For consider your calling, brothers, that not many are wise.

units.la: 1 Probat qď dicit p cōditionē eorū quos uo catos suprà dixit i.credētes in Christū. Expo nunt aūt ista bifariā. Primū, de cōditione mini strorū Euágelij, quales illi fuerint, nēpe homines idiotę: qď ad seculū attinet, rudes, tenues, imbecilles, ignobiles, quorum tū ministerio & doctrina tāta ad fidē Christi hominū multitudo cōuersa & saluti ac uitæ æternæ asserta est, de quib. nemo suspicari potest, qď ullis huma næ sapietiæ persuasionibus aut potentiæ uiri bus res tātas in toto orbe effecerint, quib. nec potētia, nec sapientia mūdi resistere potuit, ut cōspicuū sit argumētū diuinæ sapientiæ & po tētiæ in cruce Christi declaratę. Hic scilicet de claratū est, quomodo stulticia Dei sapiētior, & ībecillitas Dei robustior sit hoinib. Quadrat huc pulcherrimū illud exęplū cuiusdā philoso phi, q cū nullis potuisset disputatiōib. & syllo gisṁorū retinaculis ad fidē Christi duci, simpli cissima Euangelij Christi prędicatione p rudē quendem quendam episcopũ persuasus credidit, de quo Euseb.in histor.Eccl.lib.10.cap.3. Eufeb.in hiftor.Eccl.lib.10.cap.3.
units.tr: 1 He proves what he says from the condition of those whom he called above, that is, those who believe in Christ. They explain this in two ways. First, of the condition of the ministers of the gospel, what sort of men they were: unlearned men, as far as the world is concerned rude, humble, weak and lowborn. Yet through their ministry and teaching so great a multitude of people was converted to the faith of Christ and assured of salvation and eternal life. No one can suspect that such great results were achieved throughout the whole world by any persuasions of human wisdom or by the strength of men, to which neither the power nor the wisdom of the world could offer resistance. So it is a clear proof of the divine wisdom and power declared in the cross of Christ. Here it is plainly shown how the foolishness of God is wiser, and the weakness of God stronger, than men. That famous example of a certain philosopher fits here well: though he could not be led to the faith of Christ by any disputations or chains of syllogisms, he was persuaded by the simplest preaching of the gospel of Christ, delivered by a certain unlearned bishop, and believed. Concerning him see Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 10, chapter 3.

units.la: 2 Quidam uero exponunt non de ministrorum qualitate, sed in genere, de qualitate Christianorum, quos Deus uocauerit rudes, paupe res, ignobiles, infirmos, & nullos quod attinet ad sæculum & ad collationem eorum, qui veritate Euangelij potisimum reluctabantur, sapientes, potētes, nobiles, &c. Et hoc sensu pulchre medetur Apostolus ei scandalo, quod patiebantur credentes, propter uilitate ac tenuitatem conditionis suæ, & splendorem aduersariorum, dũ ostendit ita uisum esse Deo, ut tales potisimum eligat, in quibus per prædicationis Euangelicę stulticiā, suam declarat sapientiam & potentiam.
units.tr: 2 Others, however, explain it not of the quality of the ministers but in general of the quality of the Christians whom God has called: rude, poor, lowborn, weak, and nothing as far as the world is concerned, in comparison with those who most stubbornly resisted the truth of the gospel, namely the wise, powerful, noble and so on. In this sense the Apostle skilfully remedies the scandal that believers suffered on account of the lowliness and meanness of their condition and the splendour of their opponents. He shows that it has pleased God to choose especially such people, in whom, through the foolishness of the evangelical preaching, he displays his wisdom and power.

units.la: 3 Illud βλέπετε uetus reddidit per modum imperandi, uideret: Erasmus uero, modo indicandi, uidetis, & addit etiam rationem, cur melius sit uidetis quidete. Videlicet quod non fuerit necesse admonere ut uiderent, quod alioqui ui debant, sed quod uoluerit Apostolus re perspicuam & claram argumenti uice ob oculos exponere. Verum nihil puto quicquid id est rationis impedire, quo minus queamus legere uidete æque atq; uidetis. Nō enim simpliciter admonet ut uideant quod manifestū est, sed ut diligentius considerent, & in eo diuini consilij ratione: & hoc ipsum, de quo loquebatur, expendant, ad quem sensum non male quadrat si legamus, Videte uocationem uestram.
units.tr: 3 The old version rendered [βλέπετε] in the imperative mood, as uideret ("let him see"). Erasmus, however, rendered it in the indicative, uidetis ("you see"), and adds a reason why uidetis is the better reading: namely, that it was not necessary to urge them to see what they ought in any case to see, but that the Apostle wished to set before their eyes, as it were by way of argument, something plain and clear. Yet I think no such reasoning prevents us from reading "see" (videte) just as well as "you see" (uidetis). For he does not simply urge them to see what is evident, but to consider more carefully and to weigh in it the reasoning of the divine plan, and to ponder that very matter of which he was speaking. To this sense it fits well if we read: "Consider your calling."

units.la: 4 Notandū interea est, quod nō dicit nullos sapientes, potentes, nobiles, &c. elegit Deus: sed nō multos, ne putemus in uniuersum omnes tales esse abiectos. Aliquos enim certe tales elegit, sed non multos. Rationem subiunget.
units.tr: 4 It should be noted meanwhile that he does not say that God chose no wise, powerful or noble men, and so on, but that he chose not many, lest we think that all such people in general were rejected. For he certainly chose some such people, but not many. He will give the reason below.

units.la: 5 Ad hæc & illud est notandum, quod uerbo eligēdi utitur, ubi de uocatione loquitur fidelium, ut intelligas eum loqui, non de ea uocatione quā Christus innuit dicēs, Multi uocati, pauci electi: sed de ea, quam hic idē Apostolus Rom.8. ponit, cum dicit: Quos prædestinauit, hos & uocauit: quos uocauit, hos & iustificauit, quæ est electorum tantū, quemadmodum & iam antea annotauimus.
units.tr: 5 It should also be noted that he uses the verb "to choose" where he speaks of the calling of believers, so that you understand him to be speaking not of that calling which Christ indicated when he said, "Many are called, but few are chosen," but of that which the same Apostle sets out in Rom. 8, when he says: "Whom he predestined, them he also called; whom he called, them he also justified." This calling belongs to the elect only, as we noted earlier.

units.la: Vt pudefaceret sapientes, potentes, & obliteraret ea quæ sunt, ne gloriaretur ulla caro coram ipso.
units.tr: That he might shame the wise and the powerful, and bring to nothing the things that are, so that no flesh should glory before him.

units.la: Rationem reddit diuini consilij, cur tales uocari uoluerit. Vt pudefaceret, inquit, sapientes, potentes & nobiles & qui aliquid esse uidetur. Et ut intelligamus quis sit ille pudor, quo per uocationem humiliū, rudium & imbecilliū affici uoluit mundi sapientes, potētes ac nobiles, addit uerbum καταισχύνω, quod quasi exponit istum pudorem. Significat enim ignauum, inertes, otiosum & inane reddere. i. ἀργὸν ποιῆσαι, quod fit, quando aliquid prorsus inutile redditur, ut nō præstet quod ex eo sperabatur. Est itaq; pudor iste qui mundi sapientiæ, potētiæ ac nobilitati per uocationem istam humiliū & rudium offusus est, nihil aliud quàm manifesta declaratio.
units.tr: He gives the reason for God's counsel, why he wished such people to be called. "That he might shame," he says, "the wise, the powerful, the noble, and those who seem to be something." So that we may understand what kind of shame he wished the wise, powerful and noble of the world to suffer through the calling of the humble, unlearned and weak, he adds the word καταισχύνω [katalschynō], which as it were explains this shame. For it means to make idle, inert, useless and empty, that is, ἀργὸν ποιῆσαι [argon poiēsai], which happens when something is rendered entirely useless, so that it does not produce what was hoped from it. Therefore that shame which has been poured over the wisdom, power and nobility of the world through this calling of the humble and unlearned is nothing other than a plain declaration.

units.la: ad ueram iustitiam ac salute non hoc præstare posse quod sperabatur, sed prorsus inutilem ac stultam esse mundi sapientiam, uanā & imbecillem esse mundi potentiam, quemadmodum per uocationem publicanorum & peccatorum pudefecit sanctimoniā pharisæorū, scribarum, & omnium iusticiariorū: ubi declaratū est, ueram iusticiā ac salutem fide apprehendētibus publicanis ac peccatorib. iusticiarijs uerò & sanctulis operarijs respuētibus, ad ueram iusticiam & salutem non facere sanctimoniam & iusticiam carnis, sed magis animi deiecti humilitate, peccati cōfessione, & fidei stultę obedientiam. Ita & hic per uocationē hominū abiectorum, rudium & imbecilli & uicisim neglectum sapiētium, potentum, nobiliū, &c. declaratum est ad cognitionem, & κατὰ ἰδιον ueræ iusticiæ & salutis id præstare non posse sapien tiam & potentiam mundi, quod putabatur, sed plane inutilem esse & uanam.
units.tr: That the wisdom of the world cannot accomplish for true righteousness and salvation what was hoped, but is wholly useless and foolish, and that the power of the world is vain and weak: just as through the calling of tax collectors and sinners he shamed the holiness of the Pharisees, scribes and all the self-righteous. There it was made plain that tax collectors and sinners, who grasp true righteousness and salvation by faith, are the ones who receive it, while the self-righteous and the sanctimonious workers reject it; that holiness and righteousness of the flesh do not contribute to true righteousness and salvation, but rather the humility of a cast-down spirit, the confession of sin, and the obedience of foolish faith. So also here, through the calling of abased, unlearned and weak men, and conversely the neglect of the wise, powerful, noble and so on, it has been declared, for our knowledge, and κατὰ ἴδιον [kata idion], that the wisdom and power of the world cannot do for true righteousness and salvation what was supposed, but are plainly useless and vain.

units.la: 2 Et hæc est gradis illa confusio, quā mũdus nunquā sustinet agnoscere. Nam & hodie rerũ diuinarum cognitione & ueră felicitatem, non quærit apud rudes, idiotas, imbecilles & abiectos Christianos, quibus magis stultitiā depu tat & ɛrumnosam calamitatē: sed apud sapientes, doctos, potētes & nobiles. Verū ubi reuelabuntur electi, & manifesta erit gloria fidelium in reuelatione Christi & filiorum Dei, tum erit & ista confusio sapientū, potentum, nobilium, non solum ipsis, sed uniuerso orbi quoq; conspicua, cum dicent: Ecce quos habuimus derisui, quorum uitam ęstimauimus esse insaniam, quomodo computati sunt inter electos Dei?
units.tr: 2 This is that confusion of rank which the world never allows itself to acknowledge. For even today it does not seek the knowledge of divine things and true happiness among the unlearned, the simple, the weak and the despised Christians, whom it regards as foolish and as a wretched calamity, but among the wise, the learned, the powerful and the noble. But when the elect are revealed, and the glory of the faithful is made manifest at the revelation of Christ and the sons of God, then this confusion of the wise, powerful and noble will be visible not only to themselves but to the whole world, when they say: "Behold, these are the ones we once held in derision, whose life we considered madness. How are they counted among the elect of God?"

units.la: 3 Cur autem ad hunc modum cōfundi ac pudefieri uelit Deus mūdi sapiētes, potētes ac nobiles, adhuc ampliꝰ declarat, cũ subdit, Ne gloriatur ulla caro coram ipso. Isti ratiōi duo insunt.
units.tr: 3 Moreover, he declares still more clearly why God wishes the wise, powerful and noble of the world to be thus confounded and shamed, when he adds: "that no flesh should glory before him." This reason has two parts.

units.la: 1 Vnum, quod superbiā carnis supprimere uoluerit Deus, illiq; omnem adimere gloriam sapientiæ, potētiæ ac nobilitatis: hoc est, quod dixit, Vt pudefaceret, ut si dicas eū non esse ui détem cui quidem oculi sint, uerum licet foris aperti, intus tamē uirtute uidēdi destituti, &c. Quæ est enim ista sapientia, potentia & nobilitas, quæ ad ueram iusticiam, ueram scientiam, ueram potentiā & nobilitatem nihil præstare potest? Tollitur ergo carni omnis gloria sapientiæ, dum proditur esse stulta: potentiq, dumma nifestatur esse imbecillis: nobilitatis, dū declaratur esse prorsus ignobilis.
units.tr: 1 First, God wished to suppress the pride of the flesh and to take away from it all glory of wisdom, power and nobility. This is what he said, "that he might shame," as if you were to say that a man is not a seer who has eyes, but though they are open outwardly, lacks the power of seeing within, and so on. For what sort of wisdom, power and nobility is it that can contribute nothing to true righteousness, true knowledge, true power and true nobility? All the glory of wisdom is therefore taken from the flesh, since it is shown to be foolish; of power, since it is made plain to be weak; of nobility, since it is declared to be utterly ignoble.

units.la: Et notāter adiecit, Coram ipso, quod non solum indicat carni ademptā esse gloriam non in mundo, ubi & sapientiæ & potentiæ & nobilitatis nomine tumet & adoratur: sed corā Deo, ubi & stulta & imbecillis & ignobilis est: uerū etiam notat gloriam carnis non esse ueram, sed umbratilē tātū & falsam, ideo quod corā Deo, qui est ipsa ueritas nullam habet gloriam, iuxta illud, Non enim qui seipsum commendat probatus est, sed quem Deus commendat. Nam coram Deo aliquid esse, hoc demum est uere esse. Exuit ergo carnem uniuersam ueræ sapientiæ.
units.tr: And he pointedly added "before him," which not only indicates that the flesh has been stripped of glory, not in the world, where it swells with pride and is admired under the names of wisdom, power and nobility, but before God, where it is foolish, weak and ignoble; it also shows that the glory of the flesh is not true but merely shadowy and false, because before God, who is truth itself, it has no glory, according to that saying: "For he who commends himself is not approved, but whom God commends." For to be something before God is at last to be truly something. Therefore he strips the whole flesh of the glory of true wisdom.

units.la: Coram ipso.
units.tr: Before him.

units.la: sapientiæ, potentiæ & nobilitatis gloria, cum dicit, Coram ipso, & nihil illi aliud relinquit, nisi inane spectrum quoddam eius glorię quâ habet in hoc sæculo.
units.tr: the glory of wisdom, power and nobility, when he says "before him," and leaves to it nothing but a certain empty phantom of that glory which it has in this age.

units.la: 2 Alterum est, quod uoluerit Deus omne gloriâ sapientiæ & potetiæ sibi soli uindicare, per hanc rationē saluandi, & ad salutem uocan di humiles, imbecilles ac rudes, neglectis sapietibus & potetib. Et hoc sensu posset illud, CORAM ipso exponi p iuxta ipsum: ut intelligas Deum nolle communicationem gloriæ huius permittere carni, ut aliquid uideatur cō ferre de sua sapientia & potentia & nobilitate ad rationem salutis & uerę iusticiæ ac felicitatis: sed causam hanc ita instituere, ut carni maneat confusio, sibi uero soli omnis honor & gloria: caro deprehendatur stulta, imbecillis & ignobilis, ipse uero solus sapiens & potens &c. Sic alibi, soli sapienti Deo, inquit Apostolus, ubi de ista ineffabili sapientia saluandi mortales loquitur.
units.tr: 2 The other reason is that God willed to claim for himself alone all glory of wisdom and power, by this method of salvation, and by calling to salvation the humble, weak and unlearned, while neglecting the wise and powerful. In this sense the words "before him" could be explained as "beside him," so that you understand that God does not wish to allow the flesh any share in this glory, so that it might seem to contribute anything of its own wisdom, power or nobility to the plan of salvation and of true righteousness and happiness. Rather, he so arranges the matter that confusion remains for the flesh, and all honour and glory for himself alone; the flesh is found foolish, weak and ignoble, while he alone is wise, powerful, and so on. So the Apostle says elsewhere, "to the only wise God," where he speaks of this ineffable wisdom of saving mortals.

units.la: 4 Notandum hic est, quomodo Apostolus dictione carnis notet, & superbiæ, Deo intolerabilis, arguat omnes eam sapientiam, potentiam, iusticiam, sanctimoniam, omnes eas uires, quæ sunt extra Christum. Proinde uniuersa nostra iustitia & sanctimonia nihil est aliud quàm immunda caro, uniuersæ nostræ uires & uirtutes, nihil aliud sunt quàm imbecillis caro, & præterea detestabilis superbia, gloriam Dei, quantum in nobis est, obscurans, dum illius sapientiam, sanctimoniam & iusticiam, in Christo respuit reipsa, quicquid uerbis & externa specie simulemus.
units.tr: 4 It must be noted here how the Apostle, by the term flesh, marks and charges with pride, intolerable to God, all that wisdom, power, righteousness and holiness, all those strengths, which are outside Christ. Accordingly, all our righteousness and holiness is nothing other than unclean flesh, and all our strengths and virtues are nothing other than weak flesh; and besides, there is detestable pride, which obscures the glory of God as far as it lies in us, while in fact it rejects his wisdom, holiness and righteousness in Christ, whatever we may pretend by words and outward show.

units.la: Ex eodē autē uos estis, in Christo Iesu, qui factus est nobis sapietia à Deo, iut sticiaq; & sanctificatio, & redemptio, ut sicut scriptū est: Qui gloriatur, in domino glorietur.
units.tr: "But of him are you in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption; that, as it is written, He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord."

units.la: Illud ἵνα αὐτὸ bifariam exponitur. Quidam legunt, ex ipso, & exponūt, Deo patre, uel per ipsum Deum patrē, uos estis in Christo, uidelicet uocati. Quidam uero legūt, ex eodem, & exponunt per modum uel rationem uocatiolnis, id est, ex eodem modo, eadem ratione, eodem consilio Dei & propositio, uocati estis in Christo Iesu. Nā supra dixit: Videte uocationē uestram, quę expositio mihi germanior uidetur. Apparet enim iuxta argumenti materiam, Apostolum nō hoc agere, ut admoneat Corinthios à Deo uel per Deum esse uocatos, quod alioqui sciebant, & absque dubio ipsi quoque pseudapostoli haud quaquam dissimulabant, adeoq; ad institutū nihil faciebat. Sed hoc magis admonere ut intelligant quo Dei consilio & propositio ad Christum uocati sint rudes & humiles neglectis sapientibus & potentibus mundi, uidelicet eo, de quo iam dixit, ut pudefierent sapientes & potentes mundi, nec habeat caro ulla gloriam apud Deum alicuius uel sapientiæ uel potentiæ.
units.tr: The phrase [ἐξ αὐτοῦ] is explained in two ways. Some read "from him" and explain it as "from God the Father," or "through God the Father," by whom you are in Christ, that is, called. Others read "from the same" and explain it as "in the manner or reason of the calling," that is, in the same way, by the same reason, and by the same counsel and purpose of God you were called in Christ Jesus. For above he said, "Consider your calling," and this explanation seems to me the more accurate. For given the subject matter, it is clear the Apostle is not here intending to remind the Corinthians that they were called by God or through God. They already knew that, and the false apostles certainly did not deny it either, so it would contribute nothing to his purpose. Rather, he means to make them understand by what counsel and purpose of God the lowly and humble were called to Christ, while the wise and powerful of the world were passed over: namely, the purpose he has already mentioned, that the wise and powerful of the world might be put to shame, and that no flesh might have any glory before God on account of any wisdom or power.

units.la: Et huc pertinet, quod amplioris declaratio
units.tr: And to this belongs what he adds by way of a fuller explanation,

units.la: A nis, imò magis cōsolatiōis gratia subijcit, memori mēte prorsus uniuersis fidelibus retinendum. Qui factus est nobis à Deo sapientia, &c. id quod non solum ad propositum eorum dictū est, quibus Christus crucifixus stulticia est, iniusticia, immūdicia & perditio, cū sit & credentibus nobis habeatur sapiētia Dei, iusticia, sanctificatio & redēptio: sed multo magis ad hoc, ut doceat ad quid & quo cōsilio missus sit à patre, quod plurimum faciebat ad institutū. Nam ex eo patebat, locum in Christo non habere studium & gloriā humanæ sapientiæ, iusticiæ & sanctimoniæ, ideoq; pseudapostolos illos magis opprimere q̃ promouere gloriam Christi. Dicit igitur: Qui factus est nobis à Deo. Intellige de humanitate & omnib. illius agnatis, & uniuersa dispensatione. Secundum diuinitatem non est factus, nec factura, sed secundum humanitatem. sic & alibi: Vbi uenit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus filium suum, factū ex muliere, factum sub lege. Qui factus est nobis. Non simpliciter, Qui factus est à Deo: sed nobis, uidelicet credentibus. Quid enim nobis prodesset, Christum esse à Deo factum sapientiam, iusticiam, &c. Nec simpliciter, Qui factus est nobis sapientia: sed, Qui à Deo, inquit, nobis est factus sapiētia. Neq; enim sine isto quoque plena esset consolatio & salus. Verum ubi utraq; coiungit, & à Deo esse factum, & nobis esse, id est, nostrum plane factum, nihil potest adhuc desiderari ad nostrā salutē, cū Christus fit noster, & à Deo nobis datus, quātus quātus est. Iuxta illud: Puer natus est nobis, & filius datus est nobis.
units.tr: He adds this for the sake of consolation, or rather, as something all the faithful must hold firmly in memory. "Who was made to us by God wisdom," and so on. This was said not only with regard to those to whom the crucified Christ is foolishness, unrighteousness, uncleanness and destruction, whereas to us who believe he is the wisdom of God, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. It applies much more to this purpose: that he teaches for what end and by what counsel Christ was sent by the Father, which greatly served his intention. For from this it was plain that there is no place in Christ for the pursuit and glory of human wisdom, righteousness and holiness, and therefore those false apostles were rather oppressing than advancing the glory of Christ. He says, then, "who was made to us by God." Understand this of the humanity and all its circumstances, and of the whole dispensation. He was not made according to his divinity, since he is not a creature, but according to his humanity. So also elsewhere: "When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law" (Gal. 4). "Who was made to us": not simply "who was made by God," but "to us," that is, to believers. For what good would it do us that Christ was made by God wisdom, righteousness, and so on? Nor is it simply "who was made wisdom to us," but "who was made wisdom to us by God." For without the latter also the consolation and salvation would not be complete. But when Paul joins both, that he was made by God and that he was made to us, that is, plainly made our own, nothing further can be desired for our salvation, since Christ is ours and given to us by God, however great he is. This accords with that text: "A child is born to us, and a son is given to us" (Isa. 9).

units.la: 3 Deinde addit, ad quid nobis sit datū, qd in illo habeamus. Sapiētia, inquit, iusticiaq; & sanctificatio & redemptio. Non dicit ut per illum redderemur sapientes, iusti, sanctificati, & redempti, cū tamē hæc nobis per Christū contingunt, & non solum hæc, sed prorsus omnia per illū nostra sint facta, infra cap.1. & Rom.8. ubi dicit: Quomodo nō omnia nobis cum illo donauit? Sed ut ipse esset nobis, id est nostra sapientia, iusticia, sanctificatio & redemptio, quod magno consilio in loco posuit, ut obtineat nobis, tāquam carni, nihil aliud relinqui quàm stulticiam, iniusticiam, immundiciam & perditionem: & omnem nostram sapientiam, iusticiam, sanctificationem & redemptionem esse in capite Christo, ut cōnectat nos Christo tanquam capiti perpetua necessitate, ita ut hactenus simus, & tamdiu iusti, sancti, sapientes & redēpti, quatenus & quamdiu fide permanserimus in Christo ad sapientiā, iusticiā & sanctificationē & redēptionē nobis à Deo dato. Duo itaq; hic innuitur. Vnū, omnē nostrā sapiētiā, iusticiā, &c. esse in uno Christo, ne qdq; nobis hic adscibere queam. Alterū, & nos esse sapientes & iustos & sanctificatos & redeptos, quatenus in Christo sumus. Nec datur itaq; locus hic temeritati cuipiā & superbię carnis, cū ois gloria sapientiæ & iusticiæ reijcitur in unū Christū: nec negligētiæ quasi nobis liceat esse stultis, iniustis & immūdis in Christo, ubi Chri stus dicitur nostra esse sapientia, iusticia, &c̨ę̨t. Quemadmodum enim hominis sensus in capite sunt, ita ut nihil huius possit adscribi pedibus uel manibus, uel reliquis membris, nisi quantum sunt capiti coniuncta, & tū ipsa non sunt insensata: sic & nobis usuuenit in Christo ut in illo habeamus quidem omnem sapientiam & iusticiā, &c.tanquā in capite, uerum ita, ut in illo nō simus ipsi stulti & iniusti, &c. hoc est, prorsus omni sapientia & iusticia Dei destituti, sed redempti, iustificati, sanctificati ac sapientes.
units.tr: 3 Next he adds in what respect Christ has been given to us, namely that we have in him wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. He does not say that through him we are made wise, righteous, sanctified and redeemed, although these things do come to us through Christ, and not only these but absolutely all things have been made ours through him; see below in chapter 1 and Romans 8, where he says: "How will he not also give us all things with him?" Rather, he says that Christ himself is our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption, and he has put this in that place with great purpose, so that it may hold us to this: that nothing else is left to flesh but foolishness, unrighteousness, uncleanness and perdition. And all our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption lie in Christ as the head, so that he binds us to Christ as to the head by a perpetual necessity; so that we are, and for as long as we are, righteous, holy, wise and redeemed, only insofar as and for as long as we remain by faith in Christ, to receive from God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption given to us. Two things are therefore indicated here. First, all our wisdom, righteousness, and so on, is in Christ alone, so that we can ascribe nothing of it to ourselves. Second, we are wise, righteous, sanctified and redeemed insofar as we are in Christ. Thus no room is given here to anyone's rashness or the pride of the flesh, since all the glory of wisdom and righteousness is taken away and placed in Christ alone; nor to negligence, as if we might be foolish, unrighteous and unclean in Christ, since Christ is said to be our wisdom, righteousness, and so on. For just as the senses of a man are in the head, so that nothing of them can be ascribed to the feet or hands or other members except insofar as they are joined to the head, and even then they are not without sense; so it happens to us in Christ, that in him we indeed have all wisdom and righteousness, and so on, as in the head; yet in such a way that in him we ourselves are not foolish and unrighteous, that is, utterly destitute of the wisdom and righteousness of God, but redeemed, justified, sanctified and wise.

units.la: Vt quemadmodum scriptum est: Qui gloriatur, &c. Applicat istam sententiā ad propositū, contra pseudapostolos, qui in propria sapientia & iusticia extra Christum gloriam in hoc sæculo quærebant. Respicit autem ad locū prophetæ Hiere.cap.9. Sic dicit Dominus: Non glorietur sapiens in sapientia sua, &c.
units.tr: So that, as it is written: "He who glories, and so on." He applies this saying to the matter at hand, against the false apostles, who in this world sought glory outside Christ in their own wisdom and righteousness. He looks back to the passage of the prophet Jeremiah, chapter 9. Thus says the Lord: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, and so on."

units.la: Coplexus est itaq; Apostolus breui sententia summam prædicationis & fidei nostrę, cū dicit: Qui factus est nobis à Deo sapientia, iusticia, sanctificatio & redemptio quæ: quia demolitur omnem carnis gloriam, bellum sustinebit à doctis, sapientibus & potentibus huius mundi prorsus ἀσεβείαν, usq; ad sæculi consummationem: qui quoniam ipsi sibi uolūt esse sapientes, potētes, iusti, sancti, Christi participes esse non possunt, nec habet in illis locum consilium hoc Dei.
units.tr: The Apostle has therefore summed up in a brief sentence the sum of our preaching and faith, when he says: "who has been made to us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption"; because it overturns all the glory of the flesh, it will sustain, from the learned, the wise and the powerful of this world, utterly impious war, until the consummation of the age. Since they wish to be wise, powerful, righteous and holy themselves, they cannot be partakers of Christ, nor does this counsel of God have a place in them.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Summa capitis huius duo habet. Primum ad memoriam Corinthijs reuocat Apostolus, qualis ad eos uenerit quàm non munitus eloquentia & sapietia mundi, qualisq; apud eos egerit, nempe infirmus, ac tremebundus. Deinde, uindicat prædicationem Euangelij ab ignominia stultitiæ, asserens illi sapientiam Dei, animali homini incognitam & incomprehensibile: soli autem spiritui Dei & spiritualibus notam.
