units.tr: The summary of this chapter has two parts. First, the Apostle recalls to the Corinthians how he came to them, how unarmed he was with eloquence and worldly wisdom, and how he behaved among them, namely as a weak and trembling man. Then he defends the preaching of the Gospel against the charge of foolishness, asserting that it contains the wisdom of God, which is unknown and incomprehensible to the natural man, but known only to the Spirit of God and to spiritual men.

units.la: Tego cum uenirē ad uos fratres, nō ueniebam cum eminentia sermonis aut sapientię, annunciáns uobis testimonium Dei.
units.tr: When I came to you, brothers, I did not come with excellence of speech or of wisdom, announcing to you the testimony of God.

units.la: Pertinere mihi uidetur capitis huius prima portio usq; ad eum locum ubi dicit: Porro sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos, &c. ad ea quæ primo capite de conditione & qualitate uocationis Euangelicæ adduxit, per quā Deus uoluerit mundi sapientiam, potentiam & nobilitatem pudefacere, & carni omnem gloriam adimere, ut qui gloriatur, in Domino tantum glorietur, qua uocationis qualitate se quoque comprehensum esse iam commemorat, ad memoriam Corinthijs reuocans, qualis ad eos uenerit Apostolus, per quem ad fidem Christi essent uocati. Quasi dicat: Expendite uel in me,
units.tr: The first part of this chapter, up to the place where he says, "However, we speak wisdom among the perfect," etc., seems to me to pertain to what he set out in the first chapter about the condition and quality of the Gospel calling, by which God willed to put to shame the wisdom, power and nobility of the world and to take away from the flesh all glory, so that whoever boasts may boast only in the Lord. He now recalls that he himself is included in this quality of calling, reminding the Corinthians what kind of apostle came to them, through whom they were called to faith in Christ. It is as if he were saying: "Weigh well, even in my case,

units.la: quæ dico, quàm nolit Deus ad promotionem regni sui opera mundanæ sapientiæ, potentiæ & nobilitatis uti. Sed ut istam carnis gloriam inanem reddat & cōfundat, elegerit humiles, rudes, imbecilles & ignobiles, &c.Cū ego ipse uerter Apostolus, primum ad uos uenirem, scitis quàm non uenerim cum sermonis aut sapientiæ mundanę eminentia, annuncians uobis testimoninm Dei, & quæ sequuntur, &c.
units.tr: what I say, and how little God wishes the works of worldly wisdom, power and nobility to be used to advance his kingdom. But in order to make this empty glory of the flesh vain and to confound it, he has chosen the humble, the unskilled, the weak and the lowly," etc. "When I, the Apostle, first came to you, you know how I came not with excellence of speech or of worldly wisdom, announcing to you the testimony of God," and what follows, etc.

units.la: Magno autē consilio reducit Corinthios ad ipsum Apostolatus sui apud eos exordiū & ingressum, ad conuersationis suæ, prædicationis & periculorum conditione & formam, in qua nihil apparuit de qua aliquoufq; caro gloriari posset, cum nec sapientiam, nec eloquentiam, nec nobilitate mundi attulerit, sed magis imbecillitatem, cuius iam recordabitur, & timorem ac tremorem multum ostēderit: & tamen utut ista omnia fuerint conteptibilia, ipsa persona, sermo rudis, doctrina in speciem stulta, utpote de crucifixo quodam saluatore, deinde persequutio, metus ac tremor, nihilominus tamen Dei potentia sese exeruerit, & inter ipsos operata sit, ut immutatis mentibus & relicto Gentili errore ad fidem Christi suscipiendam sint permoti. Hoc scilicet est, cuius gratia illos ad principiū uocationis suæ reuocat, ut in ipso discant cōsilium Dei, cuius supra meminit, ut postea non ufqueadeo mirentur gloriam illam mundanæ sapientiæ, cuius nomine pseudapostoli plurimum tumebant, & simplicitatem doctrinæ Euangelij corrumpebant. Ad errorem plurimum facit, si obliuiscare, unde sis ad veritatis uiam ingressus. Proinde Satanas astute conuersionis principia Corinthijs per pseuda postolorum splendorem abscondit, ut eo illos longius ab ipsa ueritate abduceret, quo magis à typo Apostolicæ formæ considerando auerteret.
units.tr: With great purpose he brings the Corinthians back to the very beginning and entrance of his apostleship among them, to the manner and condition of his conduct, preaching and dangers, in which nothing appeared of which the flesh could boast at all. He brought neither wisdom, nor eloquence, nor worldly nobility, but rather weakness, which he will now recall, and he showed much fear and trembling. And yet, however contemptible all these things were, the person himself, the rude speech, and the doctrine which seemed foolish, since it concerned a crucified Saviour, and then the persecution, fear and trembling, nevertheless the power of God displayed itself and worked among them, so that their minds were changed and, having abandoned Gentile error, they were moved to receive the faith of Christ. This is certainly the reason why he leads them back to the beginning of their calling, so that in that very beginning they may learn the counsel of God, of which he spoke above, and so that afterwards they may not so greatly admire that glory of worldly wisdom in whose name the false apostles were much puffed up and corrupted the simplicity of the Gospel doctrine. It greatly fosters error if you forget from where you entered the way of truth. Therefore Satan cunningly hid the beginnings of conversion from the Corinthians by the splendour of the false apostles, so that he might lead them further away from the truth itself, the more he turned them from considering the type of the apostolic form.

units.la: Illud, ANNVNCIANS uobis testimoniū Dei, bifariam exponunt, actiue & passiue.
units.tr: The words "ANNOUNCING to you the testimony of God" they explain in two ways, actively and passively.

units.la: 1 Actiue, ut intelligas de testimonio quod Deus ipse per ministerium. Euangelicū dabat filio suo, per potentiam spiritus, cuius recorda bitur iam in sequentibus, de quo & Christus Ioan.15. Cum uenerit paracletus spiritus ueritatis, &c. ille testimonium perhibebit de me. Hoc sensu annunciare testimoniū Dei, est præ dicare uirtutem Dei in Christo Iesu crucifixo, filio Dei, & è mortuis excitato, declarata. Certe ad hanc prædicationē non conuenit humanæ sapientię persuasio. Absurdum enim est, testimonium Dei cōfirmare uelle authoritate rationis ac sapientiæ humanæ.
units.tr: 1. Actively, so that you understand it of the testimony which God himself gave to his Son through the Gospel ministry, by the power of the Spirit, of which he will remind them in what follows. Of this Christ also speaks in John 15: "When the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, has come, etc., he will bear witness concerning me." In this sense, to announce the testimony of God is to proclaim the power of God displayed in Christ Jesus crucified, the Son of God, and raised from the dead. Certainly the persuasion of human wisdom does not fit this preaching. For it is absurd to wish to confirm the testimony of God by the authority of human reason and wisdom.

units.la: 2 Passiue uero, ut intelligas de testimonio quod ipse Apostolus dedit Deo, ac filio eius. Apostolos enim fuisse utriusq; & patris ac filij testes liquet. Patris, infra cap.15. Reperimur autem & falsi testes Dei, quoniam testificati sumus de Deo, quod excitauerit Christū, quem non excitauit, uidelicet, si mortui nō resurgūt. Filij, Act.1. Sed eritis mihi testes, non solū Hierosolymis, uerum etiam in uniuersa Iudæa. Et Lucæ ult. Vos estis testes horum. Et Ioh. 15. Et uos testimonium perhibebitis.
units.tr: 2. Passively, however, so that you understand it of the testimony which the Apostle himself gave to God and to his Son. It is clear that the apostles were witnesses of both the Father and the Son. Of the Father, below in chapter 15: "We are found also to be false witnesses of God, because we testified of God that he raised up Christ, whom he did not raise up, namely if the dead do not rise." Of the Son, Acts 1: "But you will be my witnesses, not only in Jerusalem but also in all Judea." And Luke last chapter: "You are witnesses of these things." And John 15: "And you will also bear witness."

units.la: Sunt autem quibus testimonium Dei annũciare apostolum, hoc loco idem est atq; mandatum Dei annunciare, hoc est, nomine Dei testificari, & ad poenitentiam & fidem Christi uocare, quo sensu aliquid sanè legimus Actorum 20, ubi sic loquitur Apostolus: Quin annũciarem uobis & docerem uos, publicè ac per singulas domos testificans Iudæis simul & Græcis, eam quæ erga Deum est poenitentiam, ac idem quæ est erga Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Est enim Euangelium Christi duplici nomine mandatum Dei. Primũ, quod apostolis est mandatum, ut prædicent. Væh enim mihi est, inquit, nisi euangelizauero: nam necessitas mihi incumbit. Deinde, quòd omnibus in illo denunciatur ac mandatur, nisi uelint æterna morte perire, ut resipiscant & credant Euangelio, adiecta promissione uitæ æternæ his qui credunt. Et hac ratione doctrinam Euangelij, quam prædicabat ex mandato & nomine Dei, uocat testificatione omnium & Iudæorum & Græcorum: quæ quia fiebat nomine Dei, haud immerito poteit dici testimonium Dei.
units.tr: Now, that the apostle announces the testimony of God, in this place means the same as announcing the command of God, that is, testifying in God's name and calling to repentance and faith in Christ. In this sense we certainly read something in Acts 20, where the Apostle speaks thus: "But I announced to you and taught you, testifying publicly and from house to house, both to Jews and to Greeks, the repentance which is toward God, and the same faith which is toward our Lord Jesus Christ." For the Gospel of Christ is commanded by God in a twofold way. First, because it is a command laid on the apostles to preach: "Woe to me," he says, "if I do not preach the Gospel, for necessity is laid upon me." Then, because it is declared and commanded to all in it, unless they wish to perish with eternal death, that they should repent and believe the Gospel, with the promise of eternal life added for those who believe. And for this reason he calls the doctrine of the Gospel, which he preached by the command and in the name of God, a testimony given to both Jews and Greeks. Since it was done in the name of God, it can not undeservedly be called the testimony of God.

units.la: Non enim me iudicaui quicquam scire inter uos, nisi Christũ Iesum, & hunc crucifixum.
units.tr: For I did not judge myself to know anything among you, except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.

units.la: Græcè est, ... Hic pronomen Me, non est, & articulus fere ab omnibus negligitur. Omnino subaudiendum est aliquid. Vtpote, dignum esse me & sufficiente, non iudicaui eius gratia, quòd scirem aliquid inter uos, uel aliquid aliud eiusmodi. Agit enim hoc, ut ostendat se non uenisse ad Corinthios fiducia humanæ sapientiæ & eloquentiæ, cũ nihil professus sit inter eos quàm Christum Iesum, eumq; crucifixũ. Sic & illud supra, Non ueniebam cum eminentia sermonis, idem esse uidetur atq;, Non ueniebam fiducia eminentiæ sermonis & sapientiæ permotus.
units.tr: In Greek it reads "... ". The word "me" is not there, and the article is almost always overlooked. Something must be supplied. Thus: "I did not judge myself worthy and sufficient, for the sake of knowing anything among you, or anything else of this kind." For he is doing this to show that he did not come to the Corinthians relying on human wisdom and eloquence, since among them he professed nothing but Jesus Christ, and him crucified. In the same way, the earlier statement "I did not come with excellence of speech" seems to mean the same as "I did not come, moved by confidence in excellence of speech and wisdom."

units.la: Emphasis autem in eo est, quòd non dicit se non plurimum scire, sed nihil nisi Christum Iesum. Nam in eo est, ut ostendat se nulla prorsus scientia & sapientia confisum ad eos uenisse, nisi de unius Christi cognitione. Nec frustra est, quod dicit, Inter uos. Quasi dicat: Vobis comparatus, usq; adeò sapientibus planè nullus fui: nec qua in re gloriari potuissem, nisi de uno Christo Iesu crucifixo, quem uobis annunciare ueni. Et præterea id quoque emphasi nõcaret quòd non contentus dixisse, Nisi Christum Iesum: addit, Crucifixũ, idq; cum singulari quadã denotatione, id est Et hûc crucifixũ. Vsq; adeò scilicet diuerso modo à pseudapostolis Christũ se prædicasse ostendit Corinthijs, ut cuius ipsos pudebat, nempe crucis Christi, de ea ipse sit plurimùm gloriarus, & præter eam nihil scire se professus: & rursus in quo ipsi plurimùm gloriabantur, huius nihil ipse sibi uindicauerit, nec concupierit.
units.tr: The emphasis lies in the fact that he does not say he knows not very much, but that he knows nothing except Jesus Christ. For his point is to show that he came to them relying on no knowledge or wisdom at all, except knowledge of Christ alone. Nor is the phrase "among you" there without purpose. It is as if he said: "Compared with you, who are so wise, I was utterly nothing. Nor could I have boasted of anything except of the one Christ Jesus, crucified, whom I came to announce to you." Moreover, the emphasis is also heightened by the fact that, not content with saying "except Jesus Christ," he adds "crucified," and does so with a particular stress, that is, "and him crucified." So plainly he shows the Corinthians that he preached Christ in a manner quite different from the false apostles: he himself gloried most of all in that cross of Christ, which they were ashamed of, and professed to know nothing apart from it; and conversely, what they gloried in most of all, he claimed nothing of for himself and did not desire.

units.la: Sit nobis obsecro per Deum hoc Apostoli exemplum noctes atq; dies ob oculos positũ, quibus testimonium Dei mudo est annunciandũ. Incredibilis uanitas uerè occupat omnes hodie Christi ministros, ut nihil minus scire se ostendant, quàm quòd solum scire debebat: & quæ ad Euangelij Christi prædicationem non adeò exiguntur, tanquam summè necessaria, prope sola affectent. Non quòd respuedę sint omnes artes, ista admoneo. Et Apostolus hic non dicit, Non enim quicquam iciui: sed, non iudicaui sciendum mihi quicquam esse inter uos, nisi Christum Iesum. Aliud est nihil scire & aliud scire quidem, uerũ non iudicare sciendum esse aliud quàm Christum Iesum. Absque dubio omnino stupidus & aliarum rerum ignarus non fuit, ut multis locis apparet (nam unde alioqui uersiculum Epimenidis poetę ci taffet in ea quæ est ad Titum, ...). Verum omnia pro nihilo ducebat respectu cognitioìs Christi crucifixi, nec iudicabat secularem eruditionem ad testimonium Christi Iesu requiri.
units.tr: I beg you, by God, let this example of the Apostle be set before our eyes night and day, by which the testimony of God is to be announced to the world. An incredible vanity truly possesses almost all the ministers of Christ today, so that they show they know far less than what they alone ought to know, and they aim almost exclusively at those things which are not so much required for the preaching of the Gospel of Christ, as if they were the most necessary. I do not mean that all the arts are to be rejected; I am only giving a warning. Nor does the Apostle here say, "For I have known nothing," but "I did not judge that I ought to know anything among you except Jesus Christ." To know nothing is one thing; to know indeed, but not to judge that anything is to be known except Jesus Christ, is another. Without doubt he was not utterly dull and ignorant of other things, as appears in many places (for otherwise, from where would he have quoted the little verse of the poet Epimenides in the letter to Titus?). But he regarded all things as nothing in comparison with the knowledge of Christ crucified, and he did not judge that worldly learning was required for the testimony of Jesus Christ.

units.la: Quòd aũt de scientia Christi crucifixi meminit, non intelligit simpliciter de historia crucifixionis Christi, quam certè & Iudæi incredauli sciebant & uiderant: sed de mysterio crucis, omnibus incredulis abscondito, in quo abditi sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ ac scientiæ Dei. Itaq; in speciem quidem ista extenuationis gratia dicta uidentur, quasi parũ sit & modici momenti, scire Christum Iesum & hunc crucifixum: uerum reipsa gloriationem habet infinitæ cuiusdam sapientiæ ac scientiæ, utpote, quam uniuersus orbis sua sapietia nunquam assequi potuit. Perinde est, ac si dicat quisquã: Hodie inter opulentissimos aliquos magnates & optimates constitutus, Ego me nihil habere iudico inter uos nisi diuitias cœlestes, & eas infinitas & sempiternas. Et positus inter potentes huius mundi, deq; potentia sua plurimum præsumentes dicat, Ego me nihil posse inter uos iudico, nisi apud Deũ omnia per eum qui me confortat. Et inter sapientes, Ego nihil me scire iudico inter uos sapientes, nisi recondi-tissimam consiliorum Dei sapientiam, quam totus mundus apprehendere nequit. Omnino tale est reipsa, licet in speciem nõ uideatur, quod hic dicit: Nihil me scire iudicaui inter uos nisi Christum Iesum, & hunc crucifixum. Hoc est, nisi filium Dei, Saluatorem mundi, dominum cœli ac terrę, & simul uictoriam illius de morte, satana & inferno, & totius humani generis redemptionem, liberationem, reconciliationem cum Deo ac restaurationem omnium eorum quæ sunt in cœlo & in terra: & in summa, reparationem uerę ac sempiternę felicitatis. Nam hæc omnia in se complectitur cognitio Christi, idq; crucifixi.
units.tr: But when he speaks of the knowledge of Christ crucified, he does not mean simply the historical fact of Christ's crucifixion, which even the unbelieving Jews knew and had seen; he means the mystery of the cross, hidden from all unbelievers, in which all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God are hidden. So indeed these things seem to be said by way of self-depreciation, as if it were a small and trifling matter to know Jesus Christ and him crucified; yet in reality they contain a boast of a certain infinite wisdom and knowledge, which the whole world, by its own wisdom, could never attain. It is just as if someone were to say: "Standing today among the richest magnates and nobles, I judge that I have nothing among you except heavenly riches, and those infinite and everlasting." And placed among the powerful of this world, who presume much on their power, he might say: "I judge that I can do nothing among you, except before God, all things through him who strengthens me." And among the wise: "I judge that I know nothing among you who are wise, except the most hidden wisdom of God's counsels, which the whole world cannot grasp." Indeed, what he says here is altogether of this kind, although it may not appear so on the surface: "I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified." That is, except the Son of God, the Saviour of the world, the Lord of heaven and earth, and at the same time his victory over death, Satan and hell, and the redemption of the whole human race, its deliverance, its reconciliation with God, and the restoration of all things in heaven and on earth; and in sum, the restoration of true and everlasting blessedness. For the knowledge of Christ, and indeed of Christ crucified, embraces all these things within itself.

units.la: Itaq; ista scientia Apostoli, de qua dicit: Nõ enim iudicaui me quicquam scire inter uos, nisi Iesum Christum, & hunc crucifixum, duo habet. Vnum, hûc Iesum, quem prædicabat, esse bet. Christum. Alterum, esse crucifixum, id est, con filio Dei esse crucifixum ad salutem ac redemptionem humani generis. Apostoli aliquâdiu credebant quidem hunc Iesum esse Christum filium Dei, mysteriū tamen crucis ipsius ignorabant. Matth.16. Et Iudęi ad Christū dicebant Ioh.11. Nos audiuimus ex lege quòd Christus manet inæternum: & hinc colligebant, Christo non competere quod de morte sua ibi dicebat, nimirum ignorantes mysterium crucis.
units.tr: Therefore this knowledge of the Apostle, of which he says, "For I did not judge that I knew anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified," has two parts. The first is that this Jesus whom he preached is the Christ. The second is that he was crucified, that is, that as the Son of God he was crucified for the salvation and redemption of the human race. The Apostles for a time indeed believed that this Jesus was the Christ, the Son of God, but they were ignorant of the mystery of the cross itself (Matt. 16). And the Jews said to Christ (John 11): "We have heard from the law that Christ remains forever," and from this they concluded that what he said there about his own death did not fit Christ, plainly because they were ignorant of the mystery of the cross.

units.la: Et ego per infirmitatem, & cū timore ac in tremore multo apud uos uersatus sum, & sermo meus & prædicatio mea, non erat in persuasoriis humanæ sapientiæ uerbis, sed in ostensione spiritus ac potentiæ: ut fides uestra non sit in sapientia hominum, sed in potentia Dei.
units.tr: I was with you in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling. My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might rest not on human wisdom but on the power of God.

units.la: 1 Et hæc pertinent ad primam capitis huius partem. In memoriam illis reuocauit, quàm humili sermone ad ipsos uenerat: iam subiungit, qualis apud ipsos egerit. Amplificationem autem habent humilitatis Apostolicæ, ad declarandum consilium illud Dei, contra sapientiā & gloriam carnis. de quo supra egit cap.1.
units.tr: 1 These words belong to the first part of this chapter. He calls to their memory how humbly he had come to them, and now he adds how he had conducted himself among them. He also amplifies the humility of the apostle, to set out that purpose of God against the wisdom and glory of the flesh, of which he treated above in chapter 1.

units.la: 2 PER infirmitatem. ] Infirmitatem putant eum uocare suo more pericula, insidias, persequutiones. Sic alibi. Si gloriandum est, de ijs q infirmitatis meæ sunt gloriabor. ubi & præmittit & subiungit periculorum commemorationem. Item, libenter igitur gloriabor in infirmitatibus meis, &c. Ita & hoc loco statim subiungit, Et cum timore ac tremore multo. Verùm quoniam aliud est periculum externum, & aliud periculo esse obnoxium, malo per infirmitatem hoc loco intelligere còditionis uel mentis Pauli in becillitatem, qua fiebat multorum odijs & infestationib. obnoxius, perq; illa ad timorem ac tremorem permouebatur. Videtur enim ista, Cū timore ac tremore multo, quasi expositionis uice subiunxisse: ut intelligamus illum loqui de eo, quòd nulla fuerit mundi potentia & subsidio suffultus, sed omnium probris, insidijs & improbitati expositus & obnoxius. Nam & nos Germani impotentes ac nullis uiribus præditos infirmos uocamus, utpote si pauperi negocium sit cum diuite, hic dicimus, Er ist im zuo schwach. Significat se nullis uel personæ uel potentiæ subsidijs suffultum prædicasse apud ipsos Christum, ne qua id cannis fiducia tentasse putetur, quo omnis ipsius & labor & efficacia & fructus soli diuinæ operationi tribuatur. Quanto magis pseudapostoli subsidijs carnis nitebantur, tanto illa ipse aliena à se fuisse gloriatur: ut admoneat Corinthios, cursum Apostolatus sui non carnis uiribus ac subsidijs, sed operationibus & efficacia spiritus fuisse apud ipsos suffultum, atque ita studia pseudapostolorum tanquam carnalia & mundana suspecta reddat, uitandaq; esse moneat. Prędicauerat ipse Christum apud Corinthios primus, ac primos satanæ & impiorum
units.tr: 2 IN WEAKNESS. Some think that by "weakness" he means, in his usual way, dangers, plots and persecutions. He speaks so elsewhere: "If I must boast, I will boast of the things that concern my weakness." There he both introduces and adds a mention of dangers. Likewise: "I will gladly boast in my weaknesses," and so on. So here too he immediately adds, "and with much fear and trembling." But since external danger is one thing and being exposed to danger is another, I prefer to understand by "weakness" here the weak condition of Paul's body or mind, by which he was made liable to the hatred and attacks of many, and was moved by these to fear and trembling. For it seems that he added "with much fear and trembling" almost as an explanation, so that we understand him to speak of the fact that he was supported by no power or help of the world, but was exposed and liable to all the reproaches, plots and wickedness of men. For we Germans too call powerless men who have no strength "weak," as when a poor man has a dispute with a rich one we say, "He is too weak for him" (Er ist im zuo schwach). He means that he preached Christ among them supported by no help of person or power, lest anyone think he had attempted this with some fleshly confidence, so that all his labour, effectiveness and fruit might be ascribed to divine operation alone. The more the false apostles relied on the help of the flesh, the more he boasts that these things were far from him, so that he may warn the Corinthians that the course of his apostleship among them was supported not by the strength and aids of the flesh but by the operations and efficacy of the Spirit. In this way he makes the efforts of the false apostles appear carnal and worldly and suspect, and advises that they be avoided. He himself had been the first to preach Christ among the Corinthians, and he endured the first assaults of Satan and of the impious stirred up against the doctrine of truth, as usually happens to those who are the first in some place to refute old and entrenched errors by the doctrine of truth, and bring light into the darkness of the world. Afterwards the false apostles came in, and by accommodating themselves to the carnal Corinthians they made their first and true apostle seem contemptible, and began to introduce a doctrine that would be conspicuous for the splendour of worldly wisdom, and so would make the teachers themselves less exposed to all kinds of afflictions, fear, trembling and anxious cares.

units.la: impetus aduersus doctrinam ueritatis excitatos sustinuit, quemadmodum ufuenire solet illis, qui primi alicubi catholicos & inueteratos errores doctrina ueritatis redarguunt, & lacem tenebris mundi inferunt. Postea subingresi sunt pseudapostoli, ficq; carnalibus sese Corinthijs accommodarunt, ut præ illis sorderet primus ac uerus ipsorum Apostolus, & doctrinam inuehere cœperunt, quę splendore mundanæ sapientiæ spectabilis esset, ideoque ipsos doctores minus redderet omnis generis afflictionibus timoriq; ac tremori curis ac foli citudinibus obnoxios.
units.tr: Trials and attacks against the teaching of truth were stirred up against him, as usually happens to those who are the first in any place to refute long-standing and widely accepted errors by the teaching of truth and bring light into the darkness of the world. Afterwards the false apostles crept in and accommodated themselves to the Corinthians' carnal inclinations, so that their own true apostle seemed contemptible in comparison. They began to introduce a teaching that was impressive with the splendour of worldly wisdom, and this made its teachers less exposed to all kinds of afflictions, fears, trembling and anxieties.

units.la: 3 ET in timore ac tremore multo.]Ecce non solum eam infirmitatem comemorat, quæ est ab externæ potentię inopia, sed & eam quę est animi. Poteit enim esse ut imbecillis quisquam fit, adeoq; multis afflictionibus obnoxius, & tamen animo firmus nec timeat nec tremat, aut certè non multum tremat. Hic autem etiā animo imbecillis est timens ac tremes admodum. Tanti scilicet est Apostolo per propriam infirmitatem declarare potentiam Christi, ut audiemus.
units.tr: 3 And in fear and much trembling. Here he mentions not only the weakness that comes from lack of external power but also that of the mind. For it can happen that a man is weak and exposed to many afflictions, and yet is firm in spirit, does not fear or tremble, or at least does not tremble much. But here he is weak in spirit as well, fearing and trembling greatly. Clearly it matters so much to the Apostle to declare the power of Christ through his own weakness, as we shall hear.

units.la: 4 Nec putet quisquam ista Apostolo parum adferre laudis. Nam hinc potissimum laudandus est, quòd cum esset & externè & internè infirmus, nequiuerit tot periculis & afflictionibus impediri, quo minus circumquaque crucem Christi prædicaret. Hinc & Chrysost. ista annotat hoc loco: [Greek text] ita, quæ attribuitur. [Greek text].
units.tr: 4 Let no one think that these things add little praise to the apostle. For he is to be praised chiefly for this: that although he was weak both outwardly and inwardly, he was not hindered by so many dangers and afflictions from preaching the cross of Christ on every side. Hence Chrysostom also notes this in this place: [Greek text], so it is attributed: [Greek text].

units.la: 5 Sed oritur hic quæstio, quomodo dicat se hic in multo timore ac tremore fuisse apud Corinthios, imò quomodo fuerit in timore ac tremore (credimus enim illum uera dicere) cum Act. 18. legamus Dominum Corinthi illi uisum esse ac dixisse: Noli timere, sed loquere, ne taceas. Nam ego sum tecum, & nemo adoriatur te ut affligat te, quoniam populus est mihi multus in hac ciuitate. Quomodo igitur timuit ac tremuit? An non credidit cœlesti uisioni? Credidit utiq;, & tamen timuit. Verba Domini non hoc uolebant, ne prorsus timeret, sed ne timeret ut taceret. Timorem carnis non ademit illi, uerùm ne illo uictus taceret, hoc erat scilicet quod exigebat. Et Apostolus igitur timuit, & tamen non tacuit. Et hoc itaque loco discendum est, quomodo fides uerbi Dei, prote-
units.tr: 5 But here a question arises: how can he say that he was in great fear and trembling among the Corinthians? Indeed, how could he be in fear and trembling (for we believe he speaks the truth), when we read in Acts 18 that the Lord appeared to him at Corinth and said: "Do not fear, but speak and do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one shall attack you to harm you, because I have many people in this city." How then did he fear and tremble? Did he not believe the heavenly vision? He certainly believed it, and yet he feared. The words of the Lord did not mean that he should not fear at all, but that he should not fear so as to be silent. He did not take away his fear of the flesh, but he did not want him, conquered by that fear, to be silent; that, clearly, was what he required. So the apostle both feared and yet did not keep silent. And so in this place we must learn how faith in the word of God and in divine protection does not exclude fear and trembling, except that kind which detracts from the fear of God.

units.la: Act.18. protectionis etiam diuinæ, nó excludat timorem ac tremorem, nisi talem, qui derogat timorem Dei. Ita & illud Matth. 10. Nolite timere eos qui corpus occidunt, animam autem non possunt occidere: non ita est intelligendum, quòd exigat à suis Christus quandam animi stupiditatem & Stoicam ἀπαθείαν in aduersis, sed ne ue lint homines plus timere quàm Deum. Ideo subijcit ibi, Sed eum potius timete qui potest & animam & corpus perdere in gehennam. Horrorem carnis, quem sentiunt sancti quoq; in periculis, non eximit: sed corrigit & moderatur, ne superiores habeat, ideo illi timorem Dei opponit.
units.tr: Acts 18. So also that saying in Matthew 10: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul," is not to be understood as if Christ required of his people a certain numbness of mind and Stoic apatheia in adversity, but rather that men should not fear more than God. Therefore he adds there, "But rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell." He does not remove the dread of the flesh, which even the saints feel in dangers, but he corrects and moderates it, so that it does not gain the upper hand; for this reason he sets the fear of God against it.

units.la: 1 ET sermo meus & prædicatio mea.] Hoc repetit, propter sequetem particulam. Nequit autem alioqui satis inculcare ruditatem prædicationis suę, ut deijciat glorias pseudapostolorum & declaret uirtutem crucis Christi.
units.tr: 1 AND MY SPEECH AND MY PREACHING. He repeats this on account of the following particle. Otherwise he could not sufficiently impress the plainness of his preaching, so as to cast down the boasting of the false apostles and to show the power of the cross of Christ.

units.la: 2 IN persuasorijs.] ἐν πειθοῖς λόγοις. Sermones persuasorij sunt, quibus auditor in sententiam dicetis, animo persuasus abducitur. Eam uim uocant quidam Suadam, quidam Suadelá, aliqui ψυχαγωγίαν flexanimam, quæ tante̊ est uirtutis, ut diuinos illi ueteres honores dederint. Apud Corint. Pytho Diana colebatur. Et Ægialenses ad flumen Sythām ψαλτής sacellum habuisse leguntur. Pinxerunt nonnulli ingetem populum ab unius dicentis ore pendentem, & quasi cathenula aurea per aures transmissa alligatum & attractu. Huius in hoc seculo magna laus, adeoq; & ingens studium est. Gloriatur autem Apostolus nihil huius attulisse se, nec habuisse in sua prædicatione.
units.tr: 2 IN PERSUASIVE WORDS. en peithois logois. Persuasive speeches are those by which the hearer, persuaded in mind, is led into agreement with what is said. Some call this power Suada, some Suadela, others psychagogian, soul-leading, which is of such great power that the ancients gave it divine honours. At Corinth Pytho was worshipped as Diana. And the Aegialenses are read to have had a shrine by the river Sythas, psaltes. Some have painted a great crowd hanging on the lips of a single speaker, bound and drawn along as if by a little golden chain passed through their ears. In this age such eloquence is greatly praised and eagerly pursued. The apostle, however, boasts that he brought none of this to his preaching and had none of it in his teaching.

units.la: 1 SED in demonstratione spiritu & uirtutis.] Huc ibat. Ideo reliqua omnia quæ carnis sunt, reiecit, nec erubuit propriam infirmitatem, timorem ac tremorem, sermonisq; humilitatem ad memoriam Corinthijs reuocare, ut totum quod gestum erat, daretur operationi & efficaciæ spiritus.
units.tr: 1 BUT IN DEMONSTRATION OF THE SPIRIT AND OF POWER. This is what he was aiming at. Therefore he rejects all the other things that belong to the flesh, and he is not ashamed to recall to the Corinthians his own weakness, fear and trembling, and the humility of his speech, so that everything that was done might be given to the operation and efficacy of the Spirit.

units.la: 2 Spiritum autem uocat donū spiritus Dei, cui addit uirtutem, id est efficaciam & operationem spiritus. Nec simpliciter dicit, In spiritu & virtute: sed, In demonstratione spiritus & virtutis.
units.tr: 2 He calls the Spirit the gift of the Spirit of God, to which he adds power, that is, the efficacy and operation of the Spirit. He does not simply say "in Spirit and power," but "in demonstration of the Spirit and of power."

units.la: Quę illa sit demonstratio, aliter atq; aliter exponitur. Potest enim intelligi de eo, quòd ex spiritu Dei loquutus sit, iuxta quod Christus apostolis suis Mat. 10. pollicitus est, quòd non ipsi loquuturi sint, sed spiritus patris ipsorum in ipsis. Et donum spiritus per apparitionē linguarum id significabat. Loquutus est autem ex spiritu Dei non frigide & ociose, sed efficaciter: ideo addidit, Et uirtutis. Spirabat enim sermo Apostolicus in seipso diuinum quid, energiam etiam habens ad immutandas mortalium mentes adiunctam, per spiritus operationem & efficaciam, cuius gratia Euangelium Christi Rom. 1. & cap. præced. uocat uirtutem Dei. Ita & de Iohanne baptista dicebat angelus ad Zachariam: Et spiritus S. replebitur iam inde ab utero matris suæ, multosque filiorum Israël conuertet ad Dominum Deum ipsorum.
units.tr: What this demonstration is, is explained in different ways. It can be understood as referring to the fact that he spoke from the Spirit of God, in accordance with what Christ promised his apostles in Matthew 10, that they would not be the ones speaking, but the Spirit of their Father speaking in them. The gift of the Spirit was signified by the appearance of tongues. He spoke from the Spirit of God not coldly and idly, but effectively; therefore he adds "and of power." For the apostolic word breathed something divine in itself, having an energy joined to it for changing the minds of mortals, through the operation and efficacy of the Spirit. For this reason the gospel of Christ in Romans 1, and in the preceding chapter, he calls the power of God. So also the angel said of John the Baptist to Zechariah: "And he shall be filled with the Holy Spirit already from his mother's womb, and he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God."

units.la: Et ipse præcedet ante illum cum spiritu & uirtute Heliæ. Et ut exponeret quid intelligeret per spiritū & uirtutem Heliæ, addebat: Vt conuertat corda patrum in filios & inobedientes ad prudentiam iustorum, ut paret Domino plebem perfectam. Quid autem illud erat aliud quàm demonstratio spiritus & uirtutis, quam hic sermoni & Euangelio suo tribuit Apostolus? Quidam uero propter dictionem δυνάμεως exponūt de patratione miraculorum & portentorum, quæ ab Apostolo uirtute spiritus Dei patrata sunt, quorum & in posteriore ad Corinth. cap. 12. ipse meminit dicens: Signa quidem apostoli perácta sunt in uobis, cum omni patientia, & signis & prodigijs & potentibus factis. Et certè δύναμις plerunque ita accipitur, maximè in historijs Euangelicis. Complectamur igitur omnia per demonstrationem spiritus & uirtutis, quæ spiritus Christi in Apostolis & per apostolos, ipsorumque prædicationem operatus est, loquendo, efficaciter, & cum uirtute loquendo: sicut de Stephano legimus, cuius sapientiæ & spiritui resistere non poterant aduersarij, iuxta promissum Christi, Dabo uobis os & sapientiam, cui non poterūt resistere omnes aduersarij uestri, corda audientium permouendo, illuminando, immutando & regenerando, manifestationem spiritus per uaria dona dando, de quibus infra. 12. miracula; & portenta patrădo. Nam ista spiritum & uirtutem Dei exprimebant.
units.tr: And he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah. To explain what he meant by the spirit and power of Elijah, he added: "to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people." What else was this than a demonstration of the spirit and power that the Apostle here attributes to his preaching and to his gospel? Some, however, on account of the word power [δυνάμεως], explain it of the working of miracles and portents, which were performed by the Apostle through the power of the Spirit of God. He himself mentions these in the second letter to the Corinthians, chapter 12, saying: "The signs of an apostle were wrought among you, with all patience, by signs, wonders and mighty deeds." And indeed power [δύναμις] is very often understood in this way, especially in the Gospel histories. Let us therefore embrace everything under the demonstration of the Spirit and power, which the Spirit of Christ worked in the Apostles and through the Apostles and their preaching, both by speaking effectively and by speaking with power. So we read of Stephen, whose wisdom and spirit his opponents could not resist, according to the promise of Christ: "I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries will not be able to resist." This power works by moving, enlightening, changing and regenerating the hearts of hearers, and by giving the manifestation of the Spirit through various gifts, of which more below in chapter 12: miracles and portents performed. For these things expressed the Spirit and power of God.

units.la: 3 Vide autem quomodo humanæ sapientiæ detSuadelam compositi sermonis, quæ sita est in probabilibus rationibus, tâ incertis, ut quæ astruunt, alijs uicissim ac diuersis destruatur: Euangelio uerò suo, sermoni rudi & humili, tribuat ἀπόδειξιν, hoc est certam & firmam demonstrationem, uidelicet spiritus & uirtutis Dei. Et in eo quod spiritum & uirtutem Dei opponit sapientiæ humanæ, traducit illam, ac reprobat propter carnem & infirmitatem. Vnde & subdit:
units.tr: 3 See how he assigns demonstration [ἀπόδειξιν], that is, a certain and firm proof, namely of the Spirit and power of God, to his gospel, a plain and humble speech, while he denies such proof to the persuasive power of composed speech, which rests on probable arguments so uncertain that what one set of them establishes is overturned in turn by others. In setting the Spirit and power of God against human wisdom, he disparages and rejects it on account of the flesh and its weakness. Hence he adds:

units.la: Vt fides uestra non sit in sapientia hominum, sed in potentia Dei.
units.tr: That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.

units.la: 1 Quasi dicat: Vt fides uestra non sit fundata supra arenam, sed supra petram: non sit dubia & incerta, sed firma, certa & immota. Vt in aedificijs plurimum refert quo quid fundamento nitatur, ne ruinæ sit obnoxium: ita & in fide plurimum, imo totum refert, quo nitatur fundamento, ne sit fluctuans & dubia, sed firma & solida. Iam qui persuasorijs humanæ sapientiæ sermonibus ad credendum aliquid inducuntur, quid illi aliud habent quàm fidem supra humanam sapientiam fundatam? Quomodo autem poterit illa cōstans esse & impetum carnis, ipsius quoq; rationis, mundi & satanæ sustinere & excipere?
units.tr: 1 As if he said: that your faith should not be founded upon sand, but upon rock; that it should not be doubtful and uncertain, but firm, sure and immovable. In buildings it matters greatly what foundation a thing rests upon, lest it be liable to collapse; so in faith it matters greatly, indeed everything, what foundation it rests upon, lest it be wavering and doubtful, and instead be firm and solid. Now those who are brought to believe something by the persuasive speeches of human wisdom, what else do they have than a faith founded upon human wisdom? But how can such faith be steadfast, and withstand and bear up under the assault of the flesh, of reason itself, of the world and of Satan?

units.la: 2 Vide quàm potenter impugnet studium humanæ sapientiæ, & commendet simplicitatem doctrinæ Euangelicæ. Suprà dixit: Ne euacuētur crux Christi. Ergo humana sapientia evacuat crucē Christi, Euangelica ruditas tuetur gloriam crucis Christi.
units.tr: 2 See how powerfully he attacks the pursuit of human wisdom and commends the simplicity of the Gospel teaching. Above he said: "lest the cross of Christ be made void." Therefore human wisdom empties the cross of Christ, while Gospel plainness guards the glory of the cross of Christ.

units.la: 2 Deinde. Ne glorietur apud Deum ulla caro. Item, ut q; gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. Ergo humana sapientia dat carni gloriā, & admit Deo. Simplicitas Euangelicæ doctrinæ admit carni gloriam, & adscribit Deo.
units.tr: 2 Next: "that no flesh may glory before God." Likewise: "let him who glories, glory in the Lord." Therefore human wisdom gives glory to the flesh and takes it from God. The simplicity of Gospel teaching takes glory from the flesh and ascribes it to God.

units.la: 3 Et hoc loco, Ne fides vestra fit in sapientia hominum, sed in potentia Dei: igitur sermones persuasorij fundant fidem supra arenā humanæ sapientiæ, citò ruituram, simplicitas doctrinæ Apostolicæ, supra potentiæ diuinæ petram, immotè pmāfurā, & omnes satanę, mūdi & carnis tentationes & incursus superaturam.
units.tr: 3 And in this place: "that your faith may not be in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God." Therefore persuasive speeches found faith upon the sand of human wisdom, which will soon fall; the simplicity of apostolic teaching founds it upon the rock of divine power, which stands immovable and will overcome all the temptations and assaults of Satan, the world and the flesh.

units.la: Porrò sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos, sapientiam autem non seculi huius, neque principum seculi huius qui abolentur: sed loquimur sapientiā Dei in mysterio, quę est recondita, quā præfinieratDeus ante secula, in gloriam nostram, quam nemo principum seculi huius cognouit.
units.tr: Yet we speak wisdom among the perfect, but a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are brought to nothing; but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which is hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory, and which none of the rulers of this age has known.

units.la: Hęc est altera portio capitis huius, qua prædicationem Euangelij liberat à contumelia & ignominia stulticiæ, tribuens illi, licet occultā, diuinam tamen sapientiam: arcanam quidem seculi hominibus, notam uero spiritalibus. Agnouit quidem sermonis, personæq; suæ humilitatem, uerūm cui coniuncta sit uirtus spiritusfanctì, ita agnouit quidem prædicationis Euangelij stulticiam coram sæculo: uerū quæ habeat sapientiam reconditam, nulli sapienti comprehensibilem. Vt igitur humilitate personæ suę, conditionis imbecillitatem, & sermonis ruditatem à contemptu uindicauit per id quod dixit, sed in ostensione spiritus & uirtutis: ita hic & ipsius materiæ quæ de cruce Christi per Euangelium prædicatur, gloriā tuetur, cum dicit, Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos, &c. De qua hæc duo ad finem capitis usq; agit. Primum, esse absconditam in mysterio, ignotam mundo & principibus mundi, nec posse apprehendi cognitione animalis hominis. Alterum, reuelari illam per spiritū Dei credentibus & spiritalibus.
units.tr: This is the second part of this chapter, in which he frees the preaching of the Gospel from the reproach and disgrace of foolishness, ascribing to it a divine wisdom, though hidden: indeed secret to the men of this age, but known to the spiritual. He acknowledged the humility of his speech and of his person, but he also acknowledged that the power of the Holy Spirit was joined to it. So he acknowledged that the preaching of the Gospel is foolishness before the world; but that it holds a hidden wisdom, comprehensible to no wise man. Thus, just as he defended his person's humility, the weakness of his condition and the plainness of his speech from contempt by what he said, "but in demonstration of the Spirit and power," so here he also defends the glory of the very matter that is preached through the Gospel concerning the cross of Christ, when he says, "We speak wisdom among the perfect," and so on. On this matter he treats two points up to the end of the chapter. First, that it is hidden in a mystery, unknown to the world and its rulers, and cannot be grasped by the knowledge of the natural man. Second, that it is revealed by the Spirit of God to believers and the spiritual.

units.la: INTER perfectos.] Græcè est, ἐν τοῖς τελείοις: In perfectis. Vt ambiguum sit quò referas. Et uetus & Erasmus habent, Inter perfectos. Intelligunt enim ferè omnes, Apostolum loqui de ijs, quibus competat prædicatio Euágelij quibusq; habeatur pro sapientia Dei, quos opponit filijs huius seculi, quibus illa stultitia uidetur. Puto autem non admodum errare eum, q legens in perfectis, intelligat de sermonibus aut uerbis spiritus, de quibus infrà dicet, Quæ loquimur non sermonibus quos docet humana sapientia, sed quos docet spiritusfanctus, spiritalibus spiritalia comparantes: ut opponat spiritales loquēdi modos, alienos ab humanæ sapientiæ imbecillitate, persuasorijs humanæ sapientiæ sermonibus, de quibus supra memi-nit, quorum gratia tumescebant pseudapostoli, & Euangelicæ doctrinæ simplicitatem, ut sermone rudem obscurabant, ne quis putet abs re esse quod hoc sensu ista ab Apostolo dicuntur.
units.tr: "Among the perfect." In Greek it is among the perfect [ἐν τοῖς τελείοις], that is, "in perfect things," so that it is ambiguous to what one should refer it. The old version and Erasmus have "among the perfect." Almost everyone understands the Apostle to speak of those to whom the preaching of the Gospel belongs, and for whom it is held to be the wisdom of God, whom he sets against the children of this age, to whom it seems foolishness. I think, however, that he is not greatly wrong who, reading "in the perfect," understands it of the words or speech of the Spirit, of which he will say below: "which things we speak not in words which human wisdom teaches, but which the Holy Spirit teaches, comparing spiritual things with spiritual." Thus he sets spiritual modes of speaking, foreign to the weakness of human wisdom, against the persuasive speeches of human wisdom, of which he spoke above, by which the false apostles were puffed up, and which they used to obscure the plainness of Gospel teaching as if it were rude in speech. Lest anyone think it is beside the point that these things are said by the Apostle in this sense.

units.la: Quod si quis putauerit inconuenientius esse ad hunc sensum, quod no dicit, Sapientiam autem loquimur sermonibus perfectis, sed in perfectis, quod inusitatum sit Latinis dicere, Loquor in sermonibus perfectis, cum sit dicendum, Loquor sermonibus perfectis: hic uideat infrà eandem phrasim, ubi dicit, ἀ λαλοῦμεν ... id est, Quæ & loquimur non in sermonibus quos docet humana sapientia, sed quos docet spiritus sanctus. Deinde & commodius est, quoniam omnino aliquid subintelligere oportet, ut id subintelligamus quę & proximè præcedit, & subnectitur etiam, quàm aliud quid, cuius hoc loco non fit mentio, licet capite superiore de ijs dixerit, quibus prædicatio Euangelij sapientia Dei sit.
units.tr: But if anyone thinks that it fits this sense less well that he does not say, "we speak wisdom in perfect words" but "among the perfect," which would be unusual in Latin (one would say "I speak in perfect words" when one ought to say "I speak perfect words"), let him look at the same phrase below, where he says which things we also speak [ἃ λαλοῦμεν], that is: "which things we speak not in words which human wisdom teaches, but which the Holy Spirit teaches." Moreover, it is more suitable, since one must necessarily supply something, to supply what immediately precedes and what follows, than some other thing that is not mentioned in this place, although in the previous chapter he spoke of those for whom the preaching of the Gospel is the wisdom of God.

units.la: Si uero legerimus, Inter perfectos, intelligendi sunt credentes, quos supra uocatos dixit ex Iudæis & Græcis, qnos non comparatione minoris intelligentiæ Christianorum hic perfectos uocat, quod quidem alibi facit: sed per collationem incredulorum, qui humanæ sapientiæ iudicio impediuntur, ne τέλειοι sint perfecti & accommodati ad percipiendam hanc sapientiam Dei. Suspicor enim si hic sensus retinendus est dictionem derfectionis Ebraico esse more positam, quo perfecti uocantur תמים, id est, integri, synceri, simplices: quales sunt qui abnegata sua sapientia, simpliciter prædicato Dei uerbo assentiuntur.
units.tr: If, however, we read "among the perfect," those who are believers must be understood, whom above he said were called from among Jews and Greeks. He calls them perfect [τέλειοι] here not by comparison with a lesser understanding among Christians, as he does elsewhere, but by comparison with unbelievers, who are hindered by the judgment of human wisdom from being perfect and fitted to grasp this wisdom of God. For I suspect that if this sense is to be kept, the word for perfection is used in the Hebrew manner, by which the perfect are called tamim [תמים], that is, whole, sincere, simple: such as those who, having renounced their own wisdom, simply assent to the preached Word of God.

units.la: Reijciendus autē prorsus est sensus illorum qui intelligunt Apostolum loqui de sublimio re quadam sapientia, quàm sit sermo crucis, quam seorsum perfectioribus communicauerit. Licet enim infrà initiò cap. tertij in eum sensum aliquid dicere uideatur, non tamen loquitur de alia sapientia sublimiore quàm sit Euangelicæ prædicationis, cum illa habeat in se omnem thesaurum sapientiæ & scientiæ Dei. Licet prudenter sit iuxta captum auditorum dispensanda, quod & Apostolus ipse coactus fuit facere apud Corinthios.
units.tr: The view of those who understand the Apostle to speak of some wisdom more sublime than the message of the cross, which he communicated apart to the more mature, must be utterly rejected. For although at the beginning of chapter 3 below he seems to say something in that sense, he does not speak there of another wisdom higher than the preaching of the Gospel, since that preaching contains in itself all the treasure of the wisdom and knowledge of God. Although it must be dispensed prudently according to the capacity of the hearers, which the Apostle himself was also compelled to do among the Corinthians.

units.la: SAPIENTIAM autem nō seculi huius.] Suggillat sapientiam humanam hoc loco bifariam. Primum, quòd illam uocat sapientiam huius seculi, includens eam quasi carceri cuidam rebus huius seculi, inanibus acfluxis, quo reijciat & excludat à rebus spiritalibus & futuri seculi, in quibus prorsus nihil habet loci. Deinde quòd dicit, Qui abolentur, siue intelligas de principibus solis, siue simul & de seculo isto præsenti, quemadmodum secundum Græcam phrasim intelligi potest: ostendit hic inutilitatem mūdanæ sapientiæ, quę nequeat possessores suos ab interitu uindicare, nec res eas in quibus tanquum artificis scientia in materia, teria, exercetur. Quemadmodum si medicina depreciaturus dicas. Non de medicina ista corporum, neque medicorum, qui abolentur: sed de spirituali medicina loquor. Quid hic aliud dares medicinae corporali quàm eam inutilitatem, ut nec ægrotos nec medicos ipsos conseruare queat, ne intereant? Tale quid uidetur esse in hac negatiua, qua dicit non sapientiam seculi huius, nec principum seculi huius, qui abolentur.
units.tr: "Not of this age's wisdom." Paul disparages human wisdom here in two ways. First, he calls it the wisdom of this age, shutting it up as in a prison among the empty and fleeting things of this world, and so shutting it out and excluding it from spiritual things and the things of the age to come, where it has no place at all. Second, when he says "who are being brought to nothing" (whether you take this of the rulers alone, or of this present age together with them, as the Greek phrasing allows), he shows how useless worldly wisdom is. It cannot save its possessors from ruin, nor can it preserve the things in which it is exercised, as the skill of an craftsman is exercised in its material. It is like someone who, meaning to disparage medicine, said: "I am not speaking of this medicine of the body, nor of the physicians, who are brought to nothing, but I am speaking of spiritual medicine." What more would you be granting to bodily medicine than this uselessness, that it cannot keep the sick or the physicians themselves from perishing? Something of this kind seems to lie in this negative statement, in which he says not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing.

units.la: Vocat autem principes seculi huius, non stultos illos tyrannos, bestias magis quàm homines, cum loquatur non de potentia, sed de sapientia seculi huius: sed sapientes, & prudentes, apud Gentes philosophos, apud Iudaeos sacerdotes, scribas & pharisaeos. Nam ita ipse imperandi ratio & necessitas exigit, ut uel phi losophi imperet uel imperatores ac principes philosophentur. Certè nostro seculo hic locus non bene conuenit, nisi forsan quatenus adi-mit principib. huius seculi sapientiae Dei, quae in Christo praedicatur, cognitionem.
units.tr: He calls them rulers of this age not those foolish tyrants, more beasts than men, since he is speaking not of power but of the wisdom of this age: he means the wise and prudent, among the Gentiles the philosophers, among the Jews the priests, scribes and Pharisees. For the very logic and necessity of ruling demands that either philosophers rule or rulers philosophize. Certainly this passage does not fit well with our own age, unless perhaps insofar as it deprives the rulers of this age of knowledge of the wisdom of God, which is preached in Christ.

units.la: QVI abolentur.] Graecè est καταργούμενων, quod uetus reddidit, Qui destruuntur: Erasmus, Qui abolentur. Sensus huius particulae quem iam exposui, aliorum est, non meus. Nam plerunque ita exponunt, ut intelligatur de omnimoda illa perditione uel abolitione magis principum, de qua infrà capite decimoquinto, quae futura est in iudicij die. Verùm quia Apollo-lus non loquitur in futuro, Qui abolebuntur, aut destruentur, sed in praesenti: suspicor aliud ab illo agi quàm de futura illa abolitione principum & totius seculi, quae accidet illis per uiri tutem secundi aduentus Christi. Hic uerò uidetur loqui de praesenti aliqua abolitione prin-cipum, idque quod attinet ad illorum sapien-tiam, quae illis accidat per praedicationem Euangelij: quam Hieronymus quoque innuere uidetur, cum dicit, Qui cum sapientia sua per nostrum Euangelium destruuntur. Quomodo ergo destruuntur principes uel abolentur per Euangelij praedicationem? Confugiamus ad Graecae dictionis proprietatem, quae expensa, pate-facit nobis, quod quaerimus. Suprà capite pri-mo, ibi: Vt pudefaceret sapientes, potentes, & obliteraret ea quae sunt, uim uerbi huius καταργῶ expendimus, quod proprie significat ἀργὸν ποιῶ, id est, ociosum, ignauum, iners, inutile & uanum reddere, & tale esse ostendere. Vt hic illud τὴν καταργουμένην proprie sit, qui uani, ina-nes, inutiles & ignaui declarantur. Quomodo? Vt suprà dixi, Quoniam scientiam salutis, quae est in cruce Christi, ignorát, nec uiam unquam inuenire potuerunt uerae salutis, ut ut sapien-tes habiti fuerint.
units.tr: "Who are being brought to nothing." The Greek is καταργουμένων, which the Old translator rendered "who are being destroyed," and Erasmus "who are being brought to nothing." The sense of this phrase, which I have just set out, belongs to others, not to me. For most commentators explain it as referring to that total destruction or abolition of rulers which is to come on the day of judgment, discussed below in chapter fifteen. But since Paul is not speaking of the future, "who will be brought to nothing or destroyed," but of the present, I suspect he is dealing with something other than that future abolition of rulers and of the whole age, which will befall them at the coming of Christ in glory. Here he seems to speak of some present abolition of the rulers, in respect of that wisdom of theirs which is taken from them through the preaching of the gospel. Jerome also seems to hint at this when he says: "who with their wisdom are destroyed by our gospel." How, then, are rulers destroyed or brought to nothing through the preaching of the gospel? Let us take refuge in the proper meaning of the Greek word, which, once examined, makes plain what we seek. Above in the first chapter, where Paul says "to shame the wise, the mighty, and to bring to nothing the things that are," we considered the force of this verb καταργῶ, which properly means ἀργὸν ποιῶ, that is, to make idle, lazy, sluggish, useless and vain, and to show oneself to be such. So that the participle τῶν καταργουμένων properly means those who are declared vain, empty, useless and idle. How so? As I said above, because they do not know the knowledge of salvation, which is in the cross of Christ, and they could never find the way of true salvation, however wise they were held to be.

units.la: Quod si iam inaudita quaedam medicandi ratio ab idiotis & rudibus, nulla opinione artis eius praeditis, introduceretur, qua tamen ægro-ti palsim ac solidè curarentur, deque illa dictu-rus contra consuetam opinionem magis quàm artem quae nunc est in usu, diceres: De medi-cina autem loquor, non de ea quae nunc est in usu apud celebres illos medicos τῶν καταργουμένων, qui inanes, ociosi, ac uani redduntur, per nouam illam scilicet & ueram medendi artem recens inductam, quis non intelligeret, quid diceres?
units.tr: Suppose that some unheard-of method of healing were introduced by laymen and untrained persons, with no reputation for the art, and yet the sick were cured completely and soundly by it; and suppose you were to speak of it against common opinion rather than of the art now in use, saying: "I am speaking of medicine, not of that which is now in use among those famous physicians who are rendered vain, idle and useless (τῶν καταργουμένων), namely through that new and true art of healing lately introduced." Who would not understand what you meant?

units.la: SED loquimur sapientiam Dei.] Hic ordi-tur ea quae pertinent ad sapientiam Euangeli-cae praedicationis, cui principio dat, quòd sit sa-pientia Dei. Non potest eam amplius & com-pendiosius praedicare, quàm quòd uocat eam sapientiam Dei. Quid enim homo est comparatus Deo? Tantundem scilicet humana sapien-tia est, comparata sapientiae Dei.
units.tr: "But we speak the wisdom of God." Here begins what pertains to the wisdom of the evangelical preaching, to which he first gives this: that it is the wisdom of God. He could not preach it more fully or more briefly than by calling it the wisdom of God. For what is man compared with God? Human wisdom, compared with the wisdom of God, is just as much as that.

units.la: IN mysterio.] Infinita est sapietia Dei, quae ubique in mortalium oculos, ex conditione creaturarum incurrit. Ostendit autem se loqui non de manifesta illa, sed de abstrusiore: ideo ubi dixit in genere, Sed sapientiam Dei: adie-cit specificandi, uel magis discernendi gratia, In mysterio, &c. Mysterij dictio non in nostra religione tantum, sed & multis aliis in usu est, quasi peculiaris secretiorib. sacris, quae in uul-gus spargere pro piaculo habetur. Volunt autem μυστήριον idem esse atque ἀπὸ μυστῶν ἐπὶ ἀδύτων, id est, occultandum est, intusque reconditum seruandum. Visus eius est, ubi aliud uidetur, au-ditur, alijsque sensibus percipitur, aliud uerò creditur. Hac de re uide Chrysostomum hoc loco. Crucis Christi praedicatio, mysteri-um est. Non enim in ea uidetur quod gestum est, nec in illius superficie patet, quod credi-tur. Iudaeus uidit in cruce ac morte Christi in-firmitatem hominis, unde offenditur: fidelis credit uirtutem Dei, unde saluatur. Ita sacra-menta illa noui Testamenti mysteria dicuntur, baptismus & Eucharistia, ubi incredulus igno-rat quid sit aqua, quid panis & uinum: fide-lis uetò intelligit per fidem, & adorat. Vnde illud ueterum: Norunt fideles, quid hic degu-stetur.
units.tr: "In a mystery." The wisdom of God is infinite, and in its effects it meets the eyes of mortals everywhere, from the condition of creatures. But he shows that he is speaking not of that manifest wisdom but of a more hidden one. So where he has said in general "But the wisdom of God," he adds, to specify or rather to distinguish, "in a mystery," and so on. The word mystery is in use not only in our religion but in many others, as a term for peculiar and more secret rites, which it is held a sin to spread among the common people. They hold that μυστήριον means the same as ἀπὸ μυστῶν ἐπὶ ἀδύτων, that is, something to be concealed and kept hidden inwardly. It is a thing that is seen where something else appears, is heard, and is perceived by the other senses, but is believed in its inner meaning. On this matter see Chrysostom on this passage. The preaching of the cross of Christ is a mystery. For in it what was done is not plainly seen, nor is what is believed apparent on its surface. The Jew sees in the cross and death of Christ the weakness of a man, and is offended by it; the believer trusts the power of God, and is saved by it. So those sacraments of the New Testament are called mysteries, baptism and the Eucharist, where the unbeliever does not know what water is, or bread and wine, but the believer understands through faith and adores. Hence that saying of the ancients: "The faithful know what is tasted here."

units.la: QVAE est recondita.] Commendationem habet, quod hic dicit, praedicationis Euange-licae, quòd non uulgaris cuiusdam sapientiae doctrinam adferat, sed abscondita. Quod ab sconditur à uulgo, selectum est. Nam praecipua bona, ut sunt filiorum & amicorum, non om-nibus obijciuntur. Facit ergo sapientiam E-uangelij in cruce Christi, selectam aliquam & praecipuam, quae non uniuersis destinata sit, sed selectis tantum Dei filijs. Est autem ita ab-scondita, ut nec angelis nec archangelis neque ulli creaturae patuerit, antequàm adimplere-tur, quod & Chrysostomus annotat, citans lo-cum illum Pauli ubi dicit: Vt innotescat prin-cipatibus & potestatibus in coelestibus per ec-clesiam multiformis sapientia Dei.
units.tr: "Which is hidden." Here he commends the preaching of the evangelical doctrine, in that it brings forward not some common wisdom but a hidden one. What is hidden from the common people is chosen, for the principal goods, such as those belonging to sons and friends, are not offered to everyone. Therefore he makes the wisdom of the gospel in the cross of Christ something select and outstanding, which is destined not for all but only for the chosen children of God. It is so hidden that it was not disclosed to angels, archangels, or any creature, until it was fulfilled. Chrysostom also notes this, citing Paul's passage where he says: "that now to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places might be made known through the Church the manifold wisdom of God."

units.la: QVAM praefinierat Deus ante secula. ] An-te secula, idem est atque ab aeterno. Nam om-nia consilia Dei ab aeterno sunt, non tempora-ria. Duo dat haec particula Euangelio Christi. Primum, quòd non sit fortuiti euentus, sed cer-tum & praefinitum à Deo. Nemo disputet er-go, cur ista doctrina non sit olim allata. Habuit
units.tr: "Which God predestined before the ages." "Before the ages" is the same as "from eternity." For all the counsels of God are from eternity, not temporal. This phrase gives two things to the gospel of Christ. First, it is not a matter of chance outcome, but certain and predetermined by God. Let no one argue, then, why this doctrine was not brought forth long ago. It had

units.la: {A} ... suos fines, fines scilicet latendi, deinde & fines progrediendi. Præfinitum enim est à Deo quàdo deberet reuelari, & quibus. Alterū est, quòd ab æterno sit prædestinatum. Non est ergo noua quædam doctrina, ut libera sit à probro & suspicione καινοφωνίας.
units.tr: {A} ... its own limits, namely limits of concealment, and then also limits of advance. For it was predetermined by God when it ought to be revealed, and to whom. The second thing is that it was predestined from eternity. It is therefore not some novel doctrine, so that it is free from the reproach and suspicion of novelty of speech [καινοφωνίας].

units.la: Expendit hic Chrysostomus emphasim diuinę dilectionis erga genus humanū, quod ante illius conditionem prædestinarit rationem salutis ipsorum. Sic solent parentes liberis, antequam nascantur etiam, prædestinare quædā quibus opus sint habituri.
units.tr: Chrysostom here weighs the emphasis of divine love toward the human race, in that before their creation God predestined for them the means of salvation. Just so parents are accustomed to predestine for their children, even before they are born, certain things they will need.

units.la: Accommodetur hæc particula, ei quod supra dixit capite primo. Nam postquam in sapientiaDei non cognouit mundus per sapientiā Deum, uisum est Deo, per stulticiam prædicationis saluos facere credentes. Ne putes hæc ita esse dicta, quòd sapientiam istam crucis Christi pater tum demum excogitauerit, ubi uidit se à mundo per sapientiam suam non agnosci: prohibet quod hic dicit, Quā præfinierat Deus ante secula.
units.tr: Let this phrase be applied to what he said above in the first chapter. For after the world did not know God through God's wisdom, in the wisdom of God, it pleased God to save those who believe through the foolishness of the preaching. Do not suppose that these things are said as if the Father had devised this wisdom of the cross of Christ only then, when he saw that he was not acknowledged by the world through his own wisdom. What he says here, "which God predestined before the ages," prevents that.

units.la: IN gloriam nostram.] Hoc est, credentium. Quæ est autem illa gloria nostra? Chrysostomo idem est atq; salus nostra. Alij adoptionem filiorum Dei assignant, quæ est per Christum. De gloria ista filiorum Dei uide Rom. 8. Simpliciissimè expone, ad glorificandū nos. Vt intelligas Deum ante secula ita præfinijsse, ut per crucem filij sui eos quos elegit, glorificaret. Consolatur humiles & abiectos Christianos in eo quod ab æterno destinatam habent in Christo gloriam, ut hoc quod mundo uidetur ignominiosum, ipsis fit loco summæ & æternę gloriæ.
units.tr: IN OUR GLORY. That is, of believers. But what is that glory of ours? For Chrysostom it is the same as our salvation. Others take it to mean the adoption of the sons of God, which comes through Christ. On this glory of the sons of God, see Rom. 8. Explain it most simply as "to glorify us," so that you understand God to have so foreordained before the ages that through the cross of his Son he would glorify those whom he chose. He comforts the humble and despised Christians with the fact that they have in Christ a glory destined for them from eternity, so that what appears shameful to the world becomes for them the place of the highest and eternal glory.

units.la: QVAM nemo principum seculi huius cognouit. ] Quid est, quòd nominatim principibus dat ignorantiam cœlestis huius sapientiæ? An isti soli non cognouerunt? Non id agit, sed eorum meminit, quia soli uidebantur diuinorum habere cognitionem, eo quòd pro sapientibus haberentur. Vbi illis adimit sapientiæDei cognitionem, conspicuum est, quod omnibus mortalibus illam adimat. Adimit autem omnibus, dicens: Nemo principum. quod plus est, quàm si diceret, Quam principes seculi huius non cognouerunt. Quòd autem omnibus illam mortalibus deneget, infrà patet, ubi dicit, Animalis homo nō percipit ea quæ sunt Dei.
units.tr: WHICH NONE OF THE PRINCES OF THIS AGE KNEW. Why does he name the princes in particular and deny them knowledge of this heavenly wisdom? Did these alone fail to know it? He is not saying that. He mentions them because they alone seemed to have knowledge of divine things, since they were held to be wise. Where he takes from them the knowledge of God's wisdom, it is plain that he takes it from all mortals. He takes it from all by saying "none of the princes," which says more than if he had said "which the princes of this age did not know." That he denies it to all mortals is clear below, where he says, "The natural man does not perceive the things of God."

units.la: NAM si cognouissent, haudquaquā dominum gloriæ crucifixissent. ] Probat quod dixit, ex ipso facto principum seculi huius. Quis enim prudenter ac scienter filiū Dei crucifigere sustineret? Crucifixerunt eum autem principes huius seculi. Ergo non cognouerunt eū. Illum ubi non cognouerunt, sapientiam Dei non cognouerūt. Christus ipse testatus est, quod hic Paulus dicit: Neq; me nouistis, inquit, neq; patrem meū. & in cruce, Ignosce illis, quia nesciunt quid faciunt. Et Petrus in Actis dicit: Et nunc fratres, scio quòd per ignorantiam fecistis, sicut & principes uestri.
units.tr: FOR HAD THEY KNOWN, THEY WOULD NEVER HAVE CRUCIFIED THE LORD OF GLORY. He proves what he said from the very deed of the princes of this age. For who would knowingly and deliberately dare to crucify the Son of God? Yet the princes of this age did crucify him. Therefore they did not know him. And where they did not know him, they did not know God's wisdom. Christ himself bore witness to what Paul says here: "You know neither me," he says, "nor my Father." And on the cross: "Forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." And Peter in Acts says: "And now, brothers, I know that you did it in ignorance, as did your rulers."

units.la: Obiter hic notandū est, quā non debeat om-
units.tr: Incidentally, it should be noted here that not everything in parables ought to be applied to the matter under discussion.

units.la: nia in parabolis applicari ad causam de qua agitur. Nam Matth. 21. & Marc. 12. dat Christus agricolis talem sermonem, ut dicant: Ecce hic est hæres, uenite occidamus eum, & occupemus hæreditatem eius. Licet enim hæc ad sacerdotes, scribas & pharisęos, crucifixores suos loquatur, tanquā ad ipsos pertinentia: tamē non debet inde colligi, quòd cognouerint ipsum esse filium Dei, & heredem uineę. Nam alioqui male conueniet ei particulę cum hoc & similibus alijs locis. Satis erat ex eo colligere, quòd occisuri essent filium, & hereditatem ipsius sibijpsis uindicaturi. Hoc faciebat ad propositum parabolę: quòd autem eum cognouerint esse filium Dei, non ita. Sunt tamen qui dicant principes Iudęorum non cognouisse dominum glorię, quia non plenè & efficaciter illum cognoscebant. Et rursus cognouisse eum, quòd aliquam illius cognitionem ex miraculis nollent uellent hausisse. Verùm sententia quam posui, simplicior esse, & minus quæstionis habere uidetur.
units.tr: not everything in the parables should be applied to the matter under discussion. For in Matthew 21 and Mark 12 Christ gives the husbandmen a speech in which they say: "This is the heir; come, let us kill him and seize his inheritance." Although he speaks this to the chief priests, scribes and Pharisees, his crucifiers, as if it pertained to them, it should not be inferred from this that they had recognised him to be the Son of God and heir of the vineyard. Otherwise that phrase would not fit well with this and similar passages. It was enough to gather from it that they were going to kill the son and claim his inheritance for themselves; this served the purpose of the parable. But that they recognised him as the Son of God is not so. Yet there are some who say that the rulers of the Jews did not know the Lord of glory, because they did not know him fully and effectively; and again, that they did know him, since they had drawn some knowledge of him from the miracles, though they were unwilling to. But the view I have put forward seems simpler and to raise less question.

units.la: Sed quemadmodū scriptum est: Quæ oculus non uidit, & auris nō audiuit, & in cor hominis nō ascenderunt, quę præparauit Deus diligentibus se.
units.tr: But as it is written: What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and what has not entered into the heart of man, these things God has prepared for those who love him.

units.la: Locus hic ex Esa. ca. 64. desumptus est. Ambiguum est aut quomodo precedentibus connectatur, licet satis liqueat illum ad hoc inductum, ut probet per Scripturas, sapientiam Dei principibus huius mūdi esse incognitā, nec ulla posse ratione ab animali homine comprehendi. Potest itaque referri uel ad id quod dixit, Quam nemo principum seculi huius cognouit: ut uelut consequenter ratione adiūgat ex propheta, uidelicet, quòd abscondita sint, quę Deus suis præparauit: & illud, Nam si cognouissent, dominum gloriæ haud quaquam crucifixissent, sit uelut per parenthesim positū, uel ad id quod dixit, Sapientiam loquimur nō huius mundi, sed sapientiam Dei in mysterio, quę est recondita: ut non solum huc respiciat, quòd eam sapientes huius mundi non cognoscunt, sed ut ostendat, de qua sapiētia & de quibus arcanis ipse loquatur, uidelicet de illis quę Deus ante secula præfiniuit ad nostrā gloriam. Nam utraq; ista insunt huic loco, & quod sapientia Dei sit abscondita sapientibus mūdi, & quòd abscondita illa sapientia Dei ea contineat, quę ad nostram gloriam diuinitus ante se eula prædestinata sunt. Primum in eo, quod dicit: Oculus non uidit, curis non audiuit, in cor hominis nō ascenderūt. Nam omnis cognitio hominis his uelut instrumentis constat. Aut enim per externos sensus aut per internos ad rerum cognitionem peruenitur. Per oculos & aures, externos: per cor, internū sensum complexus est. Ita & alibi de incredulis Iudęis dicitur, quòd nec uidentes uideant, nec audientes audiant, nec corde intelligant. Tres crasio res sensus corporis gustum, tactum & olfactū non potuit propheta, eo quòd ad rerum sublimitatem mium cognitionem, maximè in religione locum non habent. Si ergo nec oculis nec auribus, nec cordi mortalium innotuit cõsilij Dei arcanum, ergo exclusa est omnis illius cognitio naturalis, quæ scilicet esse posit ex ordine rationis & naturæ. Alterum in eo ponitur, quod additur, Quæ præparauit Deus diligentibus se. Verbo præparandi respondetur ei quod dixit, Quam præfiniuit Deus ante secula: & illud, Diligentibus se, refertur ad id quod ibi adiecit, Ad gloriam nostram.
units.tr: This passage is taken from Isaiah 64. It is unclear how it connects with what precedes it, though it is quite plain that Paul brings it in to prove from Scripture that the wisdom of God is unknown to the rulers of this world, and that the natural man cannot grasp it by any reasoning. It can therefore be referred either to what he said, "which none of the rulers of this age knew," so that the words from the prophet follow as a logical consequence, namely that the things God has prepared for his own are hidden, and the words "for had they known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory" stand as a parenthesis; or it can be referred to what he said, "We speak the wisdom not of this world, but the wisdom of God in a mystery, which is hidden." In that case the point is not only that the wise men of this world do not know this wisdom, but also that Paul shows what wisdom and what secrets he himself is speaking of, namely those things which God predestined before the ages for our glory. For both of these are contained in this passage: that the wisdom of God is hidden from the wise of the world, and that the hidden wisdom of God contains those things which were predestined by God for our glory before the ages. The first is seen in what he says: "Eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and they have not entered into the heart of man." For all human knowledge consists of these instruments. Indeed, we reach knowledge of things either through the external senses or through the internal. He has comprehended the eyes and ears as the external senses, and the heart as the internal sense. So also elsewhere it is said of the unbelieving Jews that seeing they do not see, hearing they do not hear, and they do not understand with the heart. The prophet did not mention the three grosser senses of the body, taste, touch and smell, because they contribute least to the knowledge of lofty things, and least of all in religion. If then the secret of God's counsel has been made known neither to the eyes, nor to the ears, nor to the heart of mortals, then all natural knowledge of it is excluded, that is, the knowledge which could arise from the order of reason and nature. The second is found in what is added: "which God has prepared for those who love him." The word "prepared" corresponds to what he said, "which God predestined before the ages," and the phrase "who love him" refers to what was added there, "for our glory."

units.la: Sequutus est autè Apostolus hoc loco non Septuaginta, sed Ebreos, quamuis non planè, si uerba expendas. Septuaginta nanq; sic habent: ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος οὐκ ἤκουσαν, οὐδὲ οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ ἴδον, θεὸς πλὴν σοῦ, καὶ τὰ ἔργα σου ἃ ποιήσεις τοῖς ὑπομένουσιν αὐτόν. Hoc est: A seculo non audiuimus, neque oculi nostri uiderunt Deum, præter te & opera tua, quæ facies his qui misericordiâ expectant. Ebræa uerò ad hunc modum: ומעולם לא שמעו לא האזינו און לא ראתה עין אלהים זולתך יעשה למחכה לו, id est: Et à seculo non audierunt, auribus non perceperunt, oculus nô uidit Deum præter te, qui sic faceret expectantì se.
