Ergo Apostolus adiecit primum illud: Et in cor hominis non ascenderunt: deinde uerbum Faciet mutauit in uerbū Præparauit: tertio quod Ebræus habet, Expectàti se, ipse reddidit, Diligêtibus se: ut appareat ipsum legisse pro למחכה לו, id est, expectàti se, לממחכה לו id est, diligêti se. Significat enim חבב per beth, diligere: מחכה uerò per caph, expectare. Et præterea ordinem inuertit, dum illud, Oculus nô uidit, primùm posuit, deinde de auditu subiecit. Ista libertas citandi Scripturas sit Apostolis conueniens, nobis non ita, quorum est magna cautione in citandis Scripturis uti.
units.tr: The Apostle followed here not the Seventy but the Hebrew text, though not exactly, if you weigh the words. The Seventy have it thus: "From the age they have not heard, nor have their eyes seen God, except you, and your works which you will do for those who await him" [ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος οὐκ ἤκουσαν, οὐδὲ οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ ἴδον, θεὸς πλὴν σοῦ, καὶ τὰ ἔργα σου ἃ ποιήσεις τοῖς ὑπομένουσιν αὐτόν]. The Hebrew runs in this way: "And from of old they have not heard, nor perceived with the ears; the eye has not seen God besides you, who will act for him who waits for him" [ומעולם לא שמעו לא האזינו און לא ראתה עין אלהים זולתך יעשה למחכה לו]. So the Apostle first added "and has not entered into the heart of man"; then he changed the word "will do" into "has prepared"; thirdly, what the Hebrew has, "who wait for him," he rendered as "who love him," so that it appears he read לממחכה לו, that is "loving him," for למחכה לו, "waiting for him." For חבב with beth signifies to love, while מחכה with caph signifies to wait. Moreover he inverted the order, putting "the eye has not seen" first and afterwards adding what concerns hearing. This freedom in citing Scripture suits the Apostles, but not us, who must use great caution in citing the Scriptures.

units.la: OBSER. QVAE PRAEPARAVIT Deus diligentibus se.
units.tr: Observation. What God has prepared for those who love him.

units.la: Solet hic locus citari de immensis futuræ uitæ bonis, quòd illa captu & intellectu sint incomprehensibilia. Nec immeritò licet enim per fidem in Christum dignitatem illorum cognouerimus in multis, nondum tamen omnia, imò nec ista quæ cognoscimus, luculèter: sed obscurè adhuc & in ænigmate cognoscimus. Quàm uerò magna sint & inæstimabilia, uel ex eo nobis conieciurandum proponitur, quòd quæ in terris uisuntur & audiuntur, & corde percipiuntur ampla satis & splendida, imparia sint cœlestib. & futuris bonis: quæ certè non solum ob id quòd occulta sunt, sed & quòd infinita sunt & magnitudine & multitudine & diuturnitate, nullis possunt sensibus mortalium apprehendi: ne illis quidem, qui sunt alioqui omnium capacissimi. Quid enim cordis desiderio, ut de intellectu tacea, capacius & insatiabilius? Et tamen nec illud ad cœlestium bonorum amplitudinem sufficit siue intelligendam siue desiderandâ. Iam sanè am-
units.tr: This passage is commonly cited concerning the immense good things of the future life, which surpass human capacity and understanding. The citation is not unjustified. Although through faith in Christ we have come to know their worth in many respects, we do not yet know everything, and not even those things we do know clearly; we know them still obscurely and as in a riddle. How great and inestimable they are may be conjectured from this: the things seen and heard on earth, and perceived in the heart, are quite ample and splendid, yet they are unequal to the heavenly and future goods. These cannot be grasped by any of the senses of mortals, not only because they are hidden but because they are infinite in greatness, multitude and duration, and not even by those who are otherwise most capacious of all. For what is more capacious and more insatiable than the desire of the heart, to say nothing of the understanding? Yet even this does not suffice to comprehend or to desire the greatness of the heavenly goods. Indeed, the things we read in the Scriptures are very ample, the things we hear through the preaching of the gospel are ample, and the things we perceive by believing with faith are ample. Yet when we come to the actual possession of them, so that what is in part ceases and we possess what is perfect, what else will happen to us than what is read in the figure of the queen of Sheba? Seeing much greater things with Solomon than she had heard by report, she was astonished and dismayed and said: "The word is true which I heard in my own land about your words and your wisdom. I did not believe those who told me until I came and saw with my own eyes, and found that the half had not been told me. Your wisdom and your works are greater than the report I heard."

units.la: plissima sunt, quæ in Scripturis legimus, quæ per Euangelij prædicationem audimus, quæ fide credentes percipiimus: & tamen ubi ad ipsam illorum possessionem peruenerimus, ut cessante quod ex parte est, possideamus quod perfectum est: quid aliud nobis ususueniet, q quod per figuram de regina Saba legitur, quæ multo ampliora cernens apud Salomonem quàm rumore perceperat, stupebat & consternata dicebat: Verus est sermo, quem audiui in terra mea super sermonibus tuis & super sapientia tua. Non autem credebam narrantibus mihi, donec ipsa ueni: & uidi oculis, & probaui quod media pars nunciata mihi non fuerit. Maior est sapientia tua, & opera tua maiora sunt quàm rumor quem audiui. Hoc enim interest inter terrena & spiritalia, quod terrena auidius expetûtur absentia, & citius uilescunt præsentia, quia in se uilia sunt, & de se opinionum nostrarum uicio plura & maiora promittunt, quàm præstare queant: cœlestia uerò minus desiderâtur absentia, & plus amantur posse sessa, nec tædium sui pariunt, eo quòd maiora præstent possessa quàm absentia promiserant.
units.tr: For this is the difference between earthly and spiritual things: earthly things are desired more eagerly when absent, and they quickly become worthless when present, because they are worthless in themselves, and through the fault of our opinions they promise more and greater things than they can deliver. Heavenly things, on the other hand, are less desired when absent, and are loved more once possessed, and they do not breed weariness of themselves, because when possessed they deliver greater things than they had promised when absent.

units.la: I I.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Notandum & hoc, quomodo Apostolus sapientiam illam Dei mundo abscônditam, & cœlestia arcana, quæ per Euangelium prædicatur quidem, omne tamen sensum superant, in ea collocat, quæ nobis sint à Deo præparata. Quemadmodum si quis regis alicuius splendorem & diuitias inexhaustas commendatus de illis dicat, Quas populo suo pararit. Certè hic non tam gloriam & diuitias regis quàm summam in suos beneuolentiâ, & uicisim in æstimabilem ciuium eius regni felicitatem prædicaret. Huc & illud pertinet quod supra dixit, Quam præfiniuit ad gloriam nostram.
units.tr: We should also note how the Apostle places in the things that God has prepared for us that wisdom of God which is hidden from the world, and the heavenly mysteries which are indeed preached through the Gospel but nonetheless surpass all understanding. It is as if someone, commending the splendour and inexhaustible riches of some king, were to say of them: "which he has prepared for his people." Surely such a speaker would be proclaiming not so much the glory and riches of the king as his supreme goodwill towards his own, and in turn the inestimable happiness of his kingdom's citizens. To this also belongs what he said above: "which he predestined for our glory."

units.la: I I I.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Tertio loco expendendum est summopere, quibus bona illa infinita sint à Deo præparata. Non dicit omnibus in uniuersum, sed qui busdam tantum. Et illos connotat indicio tali, quod nobis queat esse cognitum. Ideo non dicit, Quæ præparauit Deus diligentibus suis, quos ipse ab initio dilexit: sed, Diligentibus se. Notius enim nobis est, an diligamus Deum, quàm num diligamur à Deo. Quanquam enim innumeris modis Deus suam erga genus humanum bonitatem declaret, non tamen inde poterit colligi, quinam sint quos ita diligat, ut æterna illis bona destinarit, eo quòd solem suum oriri faciat supra malos æquè ac bonos. Et illud in propheta: Expectantibus se, similiter notam habet nobis cognitam. Nam ad fidem pertinet ista expectatio Dei, iuxta illud: Qui fidit illi, non festinabit. Ergo expectabit. Cuiq; uerò credenti, fides sua nota est, ut Apostolus 2. Corinth. 13. scribit, d.cens: Vosipsos probate num sitis in fide.
units.tr: In the third place, we must weigh very carefully to whom those infinite goods have been prepared by God. He does not say to all in general, but to certain people only. And he marks them by a sign such that it can be known to us. Therefore he does not say "which God has prepared for those whom he has loved from the beginning," but "for those who love him." For it is better known to us whether we love God than whether we are loved by God. For although God declares his goodness towards the human race in countless ways, it cannot from this be gathered who they are whom he so loves that he has destined eternal goods for them, since he makes his sun rise upon the evil as well as the good. And the saying in the prophet, "for those who wait for him," likewise has a sign known to us. For this waiting upon God belongs to faith, according to that saying: "He who believes in him will not hasten. Therefore he will wait." And to the believer his faith is known, as the Apostle writes in 2 Corinthians 13, saying: "Test yourselves whether you are in the faith."

units.la: Non dico ignorare fideles, quòd diligâtur à Deo. Alias unde dixisset hic Apostolus: Qui dile-
units.tr: I do not say that the faithful are ignorant that they are loved by God. Otherwise how would the Apostle here have said: "who

units.la: A 1.Reg.10.
units.tr: A 1 Reg. 10.

units.la: B dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me: sed licet fide sciamus nos charos esse Deo, minus tamen ignorare possumus, ipsi ne illum diliga mus, uel secus, cum ea de re uniuscuiusq; possit conscientia indubitato testari, nec ulla specialis reuelatio ad cognitionem illius reqratur.
units.tr: B loved me and gave himself for me" (Gal. 2)? But although we know by faith that we are dear to God, we can hardly be ignorant whether we love him, since on this matter each person's conscience can bear witness without doubt, and no special revelation is required for the knowledge of it.

units.la: Quid igitur? Tantine est dilectio nostra, ut illius respectu Deus ab aeterno praeparárit nobis tantam gloriam? Ergo non est electio Dei libera, sed eligendorum probitati alligata? Deinde non ex bonitate Dei, sed ex futuro merito eorum qui dilecturi erant Deum, ortum habens? Ista no sunt ex hoc loco colligenda. Neque enim hic traditur quid Deus eligedo suos respexerit, sed simpliciter quae sit nota eorum, qui ad aeternam felicitatem electi sunt. Alioqui omnes iusticiae nostrae, etiam tum cum sunt, ita sunt imperfectae, ut Scriptura eas comparet panno mulieris menstruatae. Esa. 64. & Augustinus recte dicat: Vae universae iusticiae nostrae, si remota misericordia iudicetur. Et Paulus Ro. 5. Cum essemus peccatores, inquit, & inimici, &c. Quod ergo corruptum est & prauum, & ubi aliquid boni diuino munere accipit (quid enim habes quod non accepisti?) imperfectū & illud est, quomodo potest tantae electionis esse causa, cum nondum est, quasi melius sit futuru ubi esse incipit, q; antea sit à Deo pscitū?
units.tr: What then? Is our love so great that God from eternity prepared such great glory for us on account of it? Then is God's election not free, but bound to the goodness of those who are to be elected? And does it arise not from the goodness of God but from the future merit of those who were going to love God? These things are not to be gathered from this passage. For it is not here taught what God looked to in choosing his own, but simply what the mark is of those who are chosen to eternal happiness. Otherwise all our righteousness, even when it exists, is so imperfect that Scripture compares it to the cloth of a menstruating woman (Isa. 64). And Augustine rightly says: "Woe to all our righteousness, if it is judged apart from mercy." And Paul, Romans 5: "When we were sinners," he says, "and enemies," and so on. Therefore what is corrupt and perverse, and where it receives anything good by divine gift (for what do you have that you have not received?), that too is imperfect. How can it be the cause of so great an election, when it does not yet exist, as if it would be better once it begins to be than it was before, foreknown by God?

units.la: NOBIS autem Deus reuelauit per spiritū suum.] Supra praedicationi Euangelicae elogium sapientiae Dei tribuit, dicens: Sed loquimur sapientiam Dei in mysterio, quae est recondita: haec uero ad alteram particulam pertinent, quam illi tradit, nempe, quod per spiritus reuelationem acquiratur. Habent autem occupationem. Nam quasi quis dicat: Si sapientiam Dei praedicas talem, quam nemo principum huius seculi cognouit, imo ea doces, quae nec oculus quisquam uidit, nec auris audiuit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt, unde tibi horum est cognitio? Respondet: Nobis Deus ipse reuelauit per spiritum suum. Ergo cognitio Dei nulla alia ratione potest apprehendi quam per reuelationem Dei. Matth. 11. Datur reuelatio cognitionis horum mysteriorum & patri & filio. Hic & spiritui sancto. Ergo pater reuelat, filius reuelat, spiritus reuelat. Sol illuminat, radius solis illuminat, splendor solis illuminat.
units.tr: "But God has revealed to us through his Spirit." Above, the Apostle attributed to the Gospel preaching the praise of the wisdom of God, saying: "But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which is hidden" (1 Cor. 2). This sentence pertains to the other part, which he sets forth, namely that it is acquired through a revelation of the Spirit. Now they have an objection. For it is as if someone were to say: "If you preach a wisdom of God such that no prince of this age has known it, indeed you teach things which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and which have not entered the heart of man, from where do you have knowledge of these things?" He answers: "God himself has revealed them to us through his Spirit." Therefore the knowledge of God cannot be apprehended by any other means than through the revelation of God. Matthew 11: "The revelation of the knowledge of these mysteries is given both to the Father and to the Son." Here also to the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Father reveals, the Son reveals, the Spirit reveals. The sun illuminates, the ray of the sun illuminates, the brightness of the sun illuminates.

units.la: Spiritus enim omnia scrutatur, etiā profunditates Dei. Quis enim hominum nouit ea quae sunt hominis, nisi spiritus hominis, qui est in homine? Sic & ea quae sunt Dei, nemo nouit, nisi spiritus Dei.
units.tr: For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him? So also no one knows the things of God, except the Spirit of God.

units.la: Ista probandi gratia ad proximè praecedentia subijciuntur. Dixit: Nobis autem Deus reuelauit per spiritum suum, quibus tria insunt.
units.tr: He adds these words to prove what has just gone before. He said: "But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit," and there are three parts to this.

units.la: 1. Deus autem reuelauit.
units.tr: 1. But God has revealed.

units.la: 2. Nobis.
units.tr: 2. To us.

units.la: 3. Per spiritum suum.
units.tr: 3. Through his Spirit.

units.la: De primo nihil subijcit. Neque enim opus erat. Nec de altero rationem reddit, cur sibi & quibusdam alijs, non autem omnibus. Superest ut tertiam particulam probare instituerit. Videlicet quod spiritus Dei reuelet ista ineffabilia arcana regni Christi. Probat autem duo necessaria. Primum, quod possit. Huc pertinet quod dicit: Spiritus enim omnia scrutatur, etiam profunditates Dei. Ad reuelandi facultatem, hoc est docendi & illuminandi, requiritur scientia eorum quae docenda sunt. quia ergo dixit, Nobis reuelauit Deus per spiritum suum, dat illi scientiam arcanorum Dei, idque omnium: ad quod utitur uerbo scrutan di, quia loquitur de arcanis Dei, de mysterijs mundo incognitis. Qui autem omnia nouit, eaque arcana, adhęc profunditates Dei, id est abditissima & secretissima Dei consilia, certè is aptus est ad reuelandum quodcunq; secretum.
units.tr: He says nothing about the first, for there was no need to. Nor does he give a reason for the second, why it was revealed to himself and certain others and not to all. It remains that he set out to prove the third part, namely that the Spirit of God reveals these unspeakable secrets of the kingdom of Christ. He proves two things that are necessary. First, that the Spirit can do so. To this belongs what he says: "For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God." The power to reveal, that is to teach and enlighten, requires knowledge of the things to be taught. Since he had said, "God has revealed to us through his Spirit," he gives the Spirit knowledge of the secrets of God, and of all of them. For this he uses the word "search," because he is speaking of the secrets of God, mysteries unknown to the world. Whoever knows all things, including those secrets and moreover the depths of God, that is, the most hidden and most secret counsels of God, is certainly fit to reveal any secret whatever.

units.la: Verbum Scrutandi nemo diuexet, quasi humano more spiritus Dei res antea ignotas diligenti scrutinio, cogitatione, inquisitione ac ratiocinatione demum cognoscat: id quod humanae infirmitatis est, non omniscientiae diuinae. Nihil aliud agit hoc uerbo Apostolus, q; quod Scriptura facit, cum de Deo dicit, quod scrutetur corda & renes. Hoc est, omnia secreta intelligat & penetret sua scientia. Accomodauit uerbum scrutandi causae, de qua loquitur. Loquitur enim de mysterio abscondito, more humano pro more Scripturae, quae de Deo perinde atq; de homine loqui solet.
units.tr: Let no one take offence at the word "search," as if the Spirit of God, in human fashion, came to know things previously unknown through careful scrutiny, thought, inquiry and reasoning at last. That belongs to human weakness, not to divine omniscience. The Apostle does nothing with this word except what Scripture does when it says of God that he searches the hearts and the reins: that is, that by his knowledge he understands and penetrates all secrets. He has adapted the word "search" to the matter he is speaking of. For he speaks of a hidden mystery in human terms, according to the manner of Scripture, which is accustomed to speak of God just as it speaks of man.

units.la: Alterum, quod Apostolus probat, quod & propius ad propositum facit, est, quòd non solum sciat omnia spiritus Dei, ideoque reuelare queat: sed quòd solus omnia sciat. Exclusit enim omnem mortalium cognoscendi & intelligendi naturalem facultatem, deditque reuelationem arcanorum Dei spiritui Dei: atq; ideo necesse fuit, ut no solum declararet, quod reuelare ista possit, sed quod solus etiam possit. Et hoc declarato, declaratum est & prius illud. Prius est, ut scias aliquid: posterius, ut solus scias, quod alij ignorant. Vbi de posteriore constiterit, de priore nemo dubitare poterit. Non potest enim non sapiens esse, qui solus sapiens est. Hanc itaque particulam quomodo probat? Quis enim, inquit, hominū nouit ea quę sunt hominis, nisi spiritus hominis, qui est in homine? Sic & ea quae sunt Dei, nemo nouit, nisi spiritus Dei. Hic no colligit, spiritum Dei scire, quae sunt Dei: sed neminem praeter illum scire, quae sunt Dei. Sicut in hypodigmate quod probandi gratia adducit, no id tantum est, quod spiritus hominis sciat ea quae sunt in homine: sed quòd praeter illū nemo ea sciat, nisi cui per illum reuelentur.
units.tr: The second thing the Apostle proves, and this bears more directly on his purpose, is that the Spirit of God not only knows all things and so can reveal them, but that he alone knows all things. For he excludes every natural capacity of mortals to know and understand, and gives the revelation of God's secrets to the Spirit of God. Therefore it was necessary that he should declare not only that the Spirit can reveal these things, but that he alone can. And once this is declared, the former point is declared too. The former is that you know something; the latter is that you alone know what others do not. Once the latter is established, no one can doubt the former, for he who alone is wise cannot but be wise. How, then, does he prove this part? "For who among men," he says, "knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him? So also no one knows the things of God, except the Spirit of God." Here he does not infer that the Spirit of God knows the things of God, but that no one except him knows the things of God. In the comparison he brings in to prove the point, the meaning is not only that a man's spirit knows the things that are in a man, but that no one else knows them, unless they are revealed to him through that spirit.

units.la: Abludunt autem à propósito, qui quaerunt de Satana, an non & ille quae hominis sint cogitata, sciat? Si scit ea, ergo non est Deus solus cardiognostes: deinde non est uerum quod hic dicit Apostolus.
units.tr: Those who ask whether Satan also knows the thoughts of a man stray from the point. If he knows them, then God is not the only searcher of hearts, and then what the Apostle says here is not true.

units.la: Est autem argumentum à minori, omnium forfortissimũ: Si homo hominis secreta scrutari non potest, par paris, quomodo homo secreta Dei, minor omnium maximi scrutari poterit? Si reconditum quid habet homo, quod soli illius notum sit spiritui, quomodo secretũ Dei extra illius spiritum cuiquam notum esse poterit? Si quod uicinum est & cognatum, inscrutabile est, quomodo scrutabitur caro quę sunt Dei? terra, quæ sunt cœli?
units.tr: The argument is from the lesser to the greater, the strongest of all. If a man cannot search the secrets of a man, equal with equal, how will a man be able to search the secrets of God, who is the greatest of all, far beyond him? If a man has something hidden that is known only to his own spirit, how can the secret of God be known to anyone outside that Spirit? If what is near and kindred is unsearchable, how will flesh search the things of God, or earth the things of heaven?

units.la: Quoniam autem irrefragabile est primum, neminem hominum scire quæ sunt hominis nisi spiritum hominis, qui in eo est: deinde & qd ex eo infertur, uidelicet nec quæ Dei sunt, nota esse cuiquam nisi spiritui Dei: ideo audeter interrogat, dicens, Quis enim, &c.
units.tr: But since it is unquestionable, first, that no man knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him, and secondly, what follows from this, that the things of God are likewise known to no one except the Spirit of God, he therefore boldly asks, saying, "For who among men," etc.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Primum hic notādum est, quàm nihil possint in rebus Dei liberi arbitrij uires, quamqʼ ratio humana cæca sit ad cognoscendam ueritate Dei, quæ est in Christo Iesu. Sic Christus ad Petrum dicebat Matth.16. Caro & sanguis nō reuelauit tibi, sed pater meus qui est in cœlis. Et Iohan.6. Nemo uenit ad me, nisi pater meus traxerit eum. Et erunt omnes doćti à Deo. Igitur nulla scientia, nulla sapientia, nulla rationis humanæ industria quicquam poterit ad cognoscendam uolŭtatem Dei, nisi accesserit reuelatio Dei, cuius hic meminit. Si enim nemo hominum, ne sapientissimus quidem scire potest quæ sint hominis alicuius, etiam stultissimi, cogitationes, nisi accipiat eas per reuelationem: quomodo poterit quisquâ scire cogitationes Dei, nisi accesserit reuelatio Dei? Hinc tamen non debet colligi, inutile esse ministerium uerbi, quod humanitus administratur. Nam ita dispositum est à Deo, ut per auditum sit fides & ministri uerbi sint ministri spiritus, & dispensatores mysteriorum illius. Ideo Paulus erat positus ad illuminandas gentes. Sic Galatas parturit in Christo. Et apostolos suos misit in orbem Christus, ut docerent omnes gentes. Et Ioh.17 dixit: Nō pro istis tantū rogo, sed & pro illis qui per sermonem eorum crediturí sunt in me. Magna est utilitas ministerij uerbi, per cuius stultitiam salui fiunt credentes. Sed si accesserit numinis afflatus, & referatio cordium, ut est in exemplo Lyddæ purpurissæ, Act.16. Alioqui qui plantat, nihil est.
units.tr: First, it must be noted here how little the powers of free will can do in the things of God, and how blind human reason is in knowing the truth of God which is in Christ Jesus. So Christ said to Peter, Matt. 16: "Flesh and blood have not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." And John 6: "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him. And they shall all be taught by God." Therefore no knowledge, no wisdom, no effort of human reason can achieve anything toward knowing the will of God, unless the revelation of God comes, of which he here speaks. For if no man, not even the wisest, can know the thoughts of any man, even the most foolish, unless he receives them by revelation, how can anyone know the thoughts of God unless the revelation of God comes? Yet from this it should not be concluded that the ministry of the Word, which is administered by men, is useless. For God has so ordained that faith comes by hearing, and that the ministers of the Word are ministers of the Spirit and dispensers of his mysteries. So Paul was set apart to enlighten the Gentiles, and so he labours in Christ for the Galatians. And Christ sent his apostles into the world to teach all nations. And John 17: "I do not pray for these alone, but also for those who will believe in me through their word." Great is the usefulness of the ministry of the Word, through whose foolishness believers are saved. But this holds if the breath of God comes, and opens the hearts, as in the example of Lydia the seller of purple, Acts 16. Otherwise, "he who plants is nothing."

units.la: Notandum autem est, quòd Apostolus loquitur de uera & uiua uoluntatis Dei cognitione, nō de ea quæ per exercitium Scriptura rum est tantū, sine singulari reuelatione: quæ magis opinio quædam est, ad tempus durās, incerta & fluctuans quàm certa scientia, unde & inefficax est, nec cor mutans, nec uitam innouás, nullam fidem, nullam dilećtionem uel Dei, uel proximi, nullum timorem Dei adferens: cum ea scientia quæ est per reuelatione Dei hoc est, per afflatum spiritus Dei hæc omnia secum adferat. Adiungatur igitur exercitio Scripturarum, precandi sedulitas, adiunga tur anim' humilitas, adiungatur desideriu im-
units.tr: It must be noted, however, that the Apostle is speaking of the true and living knowledge of the will of God, not of that which comes only through the practice of the Scriptures without a singular revelation. The latter is rather a certain opinion, lasting only for a time, uncertain and wavering, than sure knowledge. Hence it is also ineffective, neither changing the heart nor renewing life, bringing no faith, no love either of God or of neighbour, no fear of God. The knowledge that comes through the revelation of God, that is, through the inspiration of the Spirit of God, brings all these with it. Let there therefore be added to the practice of the Scriptures earnest prayer; let humility be added to the soul; let there be added a desire for the righteousness of God,

units.la: sticiæ. Nam spiritus Dei supra humiles & Deū timentes conquiescit.
units.tr: righteousness. For the Spirit of God rests upon the humble and those who fear God.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Deinde in hypodigmate notandū est, quod non dicit, Nemo nouit quæ sunt in homine: sed, Quis hominum nouit quæ sunt in homine? Licet enim cogitationes hominis sint inscrutabiles hominibus, Deo tamen sunt apertitissimæ. Magno quidem Dei consilio factum est, ut abditissimæ sint nostræ cogitationes, nec cuiquam mortalium possibile sit illas cognoscere: quod ad conuićtum nostrū, posteaq ita corruptis sumus affećtibus, summopere ne cessarium est. maxima tamen prouidentia sibi soli reseruauit, ut sciat hominũ cogitationes, qui omnium est moderator. De hoc posterio-re non cogitant filij huius seculi, & priore abu tuntur, pro sua prauitate, iuxta illud: Prauum est cor hominis, & inscrutabile, quis cognoscet illud? Et Esa.29. Vę qui profundi estis cor de, ut à Domino abscondatis consilium, quorum opera sunt in tenebris, & dicunt: Quis ui det nos?
units.tr: Next, in this example it must be noted that he does not say, "No one knows the things that are in a man," but, "Who of men knows the things that are in a man?" For although the thoughts of a man are unsearchable to other men, they are most plainly open to God. By the great counsel of God it has come about that our thoughts are most hidden and that it is not possible for any mortal to know them. This is very necessary for our common life, since we have been so corrupted in our affections. Yet with the greatest providence he has reserved for himself alone the knowledge of men's thoughts, since he is the governor of all. The sons of this age do not consider the latter, and they abuse the former to suit their own depravity, according to that saying: "The heart of man is depraved and unsearchable; who will know it?" And Isaiah 29: "Woe to you who are deep of heart, hiding your counsel from the Lord, whose works are in darkness, and who say: Who sees us?"

units.la: Præterea & eos arbitror non esse bono ingenio præditos, qui aliorum secreta curiose inuestigant, cum Deus ita ordinarit, ut densis-simis tenebris sint hominibus hominum cogitationes opertæ: curiosum scilicet hominum genus scire laborat, quod curare nec uult nec potest: imo de quo ubi cognouerit, magis doleat quàm gaudeat: uel si gaudeat, peruersé gaudeat.
units.tr: Moreover, I think that those are not endowed with a good disposition who curiously investigate the secrets of others, since God has so ordained that the thoughts of men are covered by the thickest darkness. Plainly the curious tribe of men labours to know what it neither cares nor is able to know. Indeed, once it has learned it, it will grieve more than it rejoices, or if it rejoices, it rejoices perversely.

units.la: Nos uero non spíritum mundi accepimus, sed spíritum qui est ex Deo.
units.tr: But we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is from God.

units.la: Redit ad id quod dixit: Nobis autem reuelauit Deus per spiritum suum. Quæ nanque subijciuntur, nihil aliud agunt, quàm quod do cent arcana Dei nulli hominum, sed soli spiritui Dei scrutabilia esse: ideoq; illum solū posse reuelare, quæ Deus prępararit diligentibus se. Iam resumit illud quod dixit, Nobis reuelauit Deus per spiritum suum, latius explicandum. Quomodo reuelauit Deus per spiritum suum? Per id scilicet, quod spiritum suum nobis dedit: hoc est, gratiam & operationem spiritus sui qua docemur, quæ sint & quanta quę à Deo donata sint nobis.
units.tr: He returns to what he said: "But God has revealed to us through his Spirit." For what follows does nothing else than teach that the hidden things of God are knowable to no man, but only to the Spirit of God, and therefore that he alone can reveal what God has prepared for those who love him. Now he takes up again what he said, "God has revealed to us through his Spirit," to be explained more fully. How has God revealed through his Spirit? Namely, by giving us his Spirit; that is, by the grace and working of his Spirit, by which we are taught what and how great are the things that have been given to us by God.

units.la: Quid est autem quòd non simpliciter dicit, Nos autem spiritū qui ex Deo est accepimus: sed, Nos autem non spiritum mundi accepimus, &c. Et quid uocat spiritum mundi? Dixit, neminem scire quæ Dei sunt, nisi spiritum Dei, ut nec quæ hominis sunt, nisi spiritū hominis: ita nunc dat mundo, hoc est mundanis hominibus, suum spiritum, uelut homini cuipiam, per quem intelligit eam partem, qua cöstat rerum cognitio, sapientia & intellećtus (hoc enim loco de sapientia Dei & de humana loquitur) ut spiritus mundi sit sapientia & intellećtus mundi. Alioqui per spiritum & affećtus aliquādo, animus & uoluntas intelligūtur. Verū hic Apostolo non agitur de affećtib.
units.tr: But why does he not simply say, "We have received the Spirit which is from God," but rather, "We have not received the spirit of the world," and so on? And what does he call the spirit of the world? He said that no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God, just as no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man. So now he gives to the world, that is, to worldly men, his own spirit, as if to some man, through which he understands that part by which the knowledge of things consists, wisdom and understanding (for in this place he speaks of the wisdom of God and of human wisdom), so that the spirit of the world is the wisdom and understanding of the world. Otherwise, by "spirit" and "affections," sometimes the mind and will are understood. But here the Apostle is not dealing with the affections.

units.la: Notat autem clanculum pseudapostolos, contra quorum peruersum studium ista scribit, qui magis mundi spiritū referebant, quàm spiritum Dei, per sapientiæ humanæ studium non Christi, sed suam gloriam quærentes: crucem Christi non prædicantes, sed euacuantes. Horum gratia dicit: Nos autē non accepimus mundi spiritum, sed Dei. Quid ergo mirum, si desideratur in nobis, & suspicitur in illis humana sapientia? Glorietur de mundi huius sapientia, qui mundi spiritum acceperunt: quærant humanā sapientiam, si qui illam affectāt, non ab apostolis Christi, sed ab illis qui principis huius mundi sunt ministri, adeoq; & mundi spiritum acceperunt.
units.tr: Now he secretly points at the false apostles, against whose perverse zeal he writes these things. They more readily referred to the spirit of the world than to the Spirit of God, seeking by the study of human wisdom not Christ but their own glory, not preaching the cross of Christ but emptying it. For their sake he says: "But we have not received the spirit of the world, but that of God." Why then is it a wonder if human wisdom is desired among us, and admired in them? Let those who have received the spirit of the world boast of the wisdom of this world. Let them seek human wisdom, if any desire it, not from the apostles of Christ, but from those who are ministers of the prince of this world, and who have therefore received the spirit of the world.

units.la: VT sciamus quæ à Deo donata sunt nobis.]
units.tr: That we may know the things that have been given to us by God.]

units.la: 1 Quæ sunt illa? Quæ per Christum accepimus. Dedit nobis filium, & cum filio dedit omnia, Rom. 8. & infrà: Omnia uestra sunt. Nec satis est quòd omnia nobis dedit, sed uult ut sciamus etiam istam ipsius erga nos paternam beneuolentiam. Et huius scientiam largitur per spiritum suum. Nam ille testificatur cordibus nostris, quòd sumus filij Dei, & docet nos omnia. Ergo cognitio donorum Dei est per spiritum Dei.
units.tr: 1 What are those things? Those which we have received through Christ. He has given us his Son, and with the Son he has given all things (Rom. 8), and below: "All things are yours." Nor is it enough that he has given us all things; he also wills that we know his own fatherly goodwill toward us. And he grants the knowledge of this through his Spirit. For he bears witness to our hearts that we are children of God, and teaches us all things. Therefore the knowledge of the gifts of God is through the Spirit of God.

units.la: 2 Rursus scientia quæ est ex spiritu Dei, scientia est non rerū mundi, sed donorum Dei. Non enim est mundi, sed Dei spiritus, non in hoc datus (licet illi omnia etiam quæ mundi sunt, nota sint) ut mundi nos sapientiam: sed ea doceat, quæ à Deo nobis sunt donata.
units.tr: 2 Again, the knowledge that comes from the Spirit of God is knowledge not of the things of the world, but of the gifts of God. For it is not the Spirit of the world but of God, and it has not been given in order to teach us the wisdom of the world (although all things that are of the world are also known to him), but in order to teach those things that have been given to us by God.

units.la: 3 Tertiò ista scientia quæ ex spiritu Dei est, per reuelationem arcanorum Dei, licet sit omnium amplissima: limitata tamen est, non ad omnia in uniuersum quæ in Deo sunt sese extendens, sed ad ea tantum, quæ nobis necessaria sunt, ad cognitionem eorum quę à Deo nobis donata sunt. Alioqui infinita est diuinæ sapientiæ & consiliorum illius profunditas, magis adoranda quàm ad perfectum usq; cognoscenda. Licet propensissimus sit erga filiolum pater, non tamen illi omnia sua secreta reuelat: sed ea tantum illi insinuat, quæ ipsi sint necessaria ad cognitionem paternæ dilectionis & beneuolentiæ. unde commodum hic Apostolus non dicit, Ut sciamus omnia Dei consilia: sed, Quæ à Deo donata sunt nobis.
units.tr: 3 Thirdly, this knowledge which comes from the Spirit of God, through the revelation of the hidden things of God, although it is the fullest of all, is nevertheless limited. It does not extend to all things in general that are in God, but only to those things which are necessary for us, for the knowledge of what has been given to us by God. Otherwise the depth of the divine wisdom and of his counsels is infinite, to be adored rather than known fully to the end. Although a father is most inclined toward his little son, he does not reveal to him all his secrets, but only those things which are necessary for him to know the fatherly love and goodwill. Hence the Apostle here does not say, "That we may know all the counsels of God," but, "What has been given to us by God."

units.la: 4 Quartò, notandū est, quòd nō dicit, Quæ à nobis exigantur per Deum, quæ illi debeamus, quo studio, quo timore debeamus illi obedire, cum tamen & ista cognitio ad pietatē pertinet, & ex spiritu Dei fit: sed quæ à Deo donata sint nobis. Et quòd non dicit, Quæ à Deo nobis sunt acquisita & emerita: sed, dona ta, χαρισθέντα, hoc est, gratuitò data. Licet enim magno precio, non tamen nostro, sed filij Dei, qui & ipse nobis donatus est, redēpti sumus.
units.tr: 4 Fourthly, it must be noted that he does not say, "What is required of us by God, what we owe him, with what zeal and what fear we ought to obey him," although this knowledge too pertains to piety and comes from the Spirit of God; but, "What has been given to us by God." And he does not say, "What has been acquired and earned by us from God," but "given" (charisthenta), that is, given freely. For although we have been redeemed at a great price, it was not our price but that of the Son of God, who was himself given to us.

units.la: Ergo primarium est in scientia Dei, quę per spiritū Dei est, ut cognoscamus quæ per Deū donata sint nobis in Christo Iesu. Alioqui & mundi huius spiritu præditi, tradunt Deum esse timendum, colendum, idque non tempo-
units.tr: Therefore the chief thing in the knowledge of God, which comes through the Spirit of God, is that we know what has been given to us by God in Christ Jesus. Otherwise those who are endowed with the spirit of this world also teach that God is to be feared and worshipped, and this not with fleeting

units.la: rarijs dohis: sed puræ mentis affectibus, ut uidere est in Catone: Si Deus est animus, nobis ut carmina dicunt, Hic nobis pura mente colendus erit. Et in Persio Satyra secunda: Dicite pontifices, in sacro quid facit aurum? Nempe hoc, quod Veneri donatæ à uirgine puppæ. Quin damus hoc superis, de magna quod dare lance Non posit magni Messalæ lippa propago Compositū ius fasq; animi, sanctosq; recessus Mentis, & incoctū generoso pectus honesto.
units.tr: gifts but with the affections of a pure mind, as one may see in Cato: "If God is a mind, as the verses say, he is to be worshipped by us with a pure mind." And in Persius, Satire 2: "Tell me, priests, what does gold do in the sacred vessel? Surely this: it is given to Venus by the virgin girl's doll. Indeed we offer this to the gods, what the bleary-eyed offspring of great Messalla could not offer on a great dish: the composed law and right of the mind, the sacred recesses of the spirit, and a breast steeped in noble honesty."

units.la: Item quid debeamus quisq; proximo, pleni sunt philosophorum & poëtarum libri: quæ uero nobis à Deo sint per Christum donata, prorsus sunt spiritui mundi incognita, à quorum tamen cognitione omnis uera & solida pietas cūm erga Deum, tum erga proximum ortum & uim suam habet.
units.tr: Likewise, the books of philosophers and poets are full of what each of us owes to his neighbour; but the things that have been given to us by God through Christ are altogether unknown to the spirit of the world. Yet from the knowledge of these things every true and solid piety, both toward God and toward our neighbour, has its origin and its strength.

units.la: Quæ & loquimur, non sermonibus quos docet humana sapientia: sed quos docet Spiritus sanctus, spiritalibus spiritalia comparantes.
units.tr: Which things also we speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in those taught by the Holy Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual.

units.la: QVAE & loquimur.] A scientia Dei, quæ per spiritum Dei est, transit ad doctrinæ ministerium, uel magis regreditur. Nam suprà de illo loqui coepit. Illud duo habebat.
units.tr: "Which things also we speak." The Apostle passes from the knowledge of God that comes through the Spirit of God to the ministry of teaching, or rather returns to it, for he had begun to speak of that knowledge earlier. That knowledge had two parts.

units.la: Primum doctrinæ genus mundo incognitum, & illius iudicio stultam prædicans redemptionem, quæ est per crucem Christi. De hoc est quod dicit: Quæ & loquimur. Quasi dicat: Quid aliud loqueremur spiritu Dei imbuti, perq; illum scientiam eorum quæ à Deo donata sunt nobis adepti, quàm hoc ipsum qd ex spiritu Dei didicimus? Didicimus autem non sapientiam mundi huius, sed eam quæ à Deo data est nobis, ut sciremus donorum illius munificentiam. itaq; de illis & loquimur. Ergo doctrina Euangelij est, loqui quæ à Deo donata sunt nobis. Hanc doctrinæ primariam partem qui non tradit, nihil minus agit quàm doctorem Euangelicum.
units.tr: The first kind of teaching is unknown to the world, which judges the redemption through the cross of Christ to be foolishness. This is what he means by "which things also we speak." As if he said: What else should we speak, being imbued with the Spirit of God and having through him gained knowledge of the things given to us by God, than this very thing we have learned from the Spirit of God? We have learned not the wisdom of this world, but that which is given to us by God, so that we might know the bounty of his gifts. Therefore it is of these things that we speak. The doctrine of the gospel, then, is to speak of the things given to us by God. Whoever does not hand on this primary part of doctrine is doing nothing less than acting as an evangelical teacher.

units.la: Deinde doctrina Apostoli & hoc habebat, quòd non humanæ sapientiæ persuaforijs uerbis, sed rudi ac simplici sermone tradebatur, qui auribus eorum quos delectabant rhetorum flosculi & enthymemata, uilis & contemptus habebatur. Ignorabant enim, preciositatem eorum quæ docebantur, è qua sola rudi sermoni apostolorum suauitas omniū iucundissima accedit. Huc respicit, ubi dicit: Nō sermonibus quos docet humana sapientia, sed quos docet spiritus. Quasi dicat: Quòd prædicatio nostra non respipit humanam sapiētiam, in causa est, quòd non mundi, sed Dei spiritu imbuti sumus: quem habemus non solum cordis nostri illuminatorem & doctorem, sed & oris gubernatorem, & uerborum informatorem. Habent mundanæ sapientiæ mystæ suas loquendi formulas, bene illis utantur. Quę autem insania est, ab illis qui è spiritu Dei loquūtur tur, exigere mūdani spiritus idioma: quod nihil aliud est, quàm mundi huius spiritum constituere spiritus Dei doctore ac praeceptore. Quod si pseudapostoli illi malunt esse munda ni quàm diuini spiritus discipuli, quid mirum si & mundani spiritus loquelam exprimant? Nos autem quoniam illum non accepimus, neque illius magisterio utimur, libenter patimur desiderari in nobis istam humanae sapientiae elegantiam, quam uelut spiritus Dei mystae non immerito repudiamus, non solū quae à spiritu Dei didicimus, sed & quomodo ad loquendum ab illo instituimur, loquentes.
units.tr: Then the teaching of the Apostle also had this feature: it was delivered not in the persuasive words of human wisdom, but in a rude and simple style, which seemed cheap and contemptible to the ears of those who were delighted by the rhetoricians' flourishes and enthymemes. For they did not know the preciousness of the things taught, from which alone the sweetest charm of the apostles' plain speech arises. He looks to this when he says: "not in words which human wisdom teaches, but which the Spirit teaches." As if he said: That our preaching does not depend on human wisdom is because we are imbued not with the spirit of the world but with the Spirit of God, whom we have not only as the illuminer and teacher of our heart, but also as the governor of our mouth and the shaper of our words. The initiates of worldly wisdom have their own forms of speech; let them use them well. But what madness it is to demand from those who speak by the Spirit of God the idiom of the worldly spirit, which is nothing other than to set the spirit of this world up as teacher and instructor of the Spirit of God. If those false apostles prefer to be disciples of the world rather than of the divine Spirit, is it any wonder if they also express the language of the worldly spirit? But we, since we have not received that spirit and do not use his instruction, gladly suffer that elegance of human wisdom to be missed in us. We rightly reject it, as initiates of the Spirit of God, not only in what we have learned from the Spirit of God but also in how we are trained by him to speak.

units.la: SPIRITALIBVS spiritalia cōparantes.
units.tr: Comparing spiritual things with spiritual.

units.la: Hæc particula licet omnino ad praecedentia pertineat, trifariam tamen exponitur.
units.tr: Although this phrase pertains entirely to what precedes, it is explained in three ways.

units.la: 1 Primum, ferè omnes per spiritalia intelligunt doctrinam spiritus, & per spiritalibus, in masculino genere, spiritales homines spiritu Dei imbutos, ut sit sensus: Hi qui spiritū Dei acceperunt, intelligunt ex nobis spiritalem pa riter & doctrinam & sermonem. Et huic sententiae uidetur astipulari quod sequitur: Animalis autem homo non accipit ea quae sunt spiritus Dei.
units.tr: (1) First, almost everyone understands "spiritual things" to mean the doctrine of the Spirit, and "to the spiritual," in the masculine, to mean spiritual men imbued with the Spirit of God, so that the sense is: those who have received the Spirit of God understand from us both the doctrine and the speech, which are equally spiritual. This view seems to be supported by what follows: "But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God."

units.la: 2 Deinde Chrysostomus exponit ad hunc modum: Spiritalia per spiritalium collationē probantes & declarantes, non per humanae sapientiae persuasionē, rationes ac syllogismos. Vtpote partum uirginis, per id quod Adam & Eua non ex aliquo cōcubitu: sed Adam ex terra, & Eua ex Adam sunt conditi, & per sterilis Sarae, item Elizabet Zachariae partum, & resurrectionē Christi ex figura Ionae. Ergo Chrysostomo spiritalia spiritalibus cōparare, est p spiritalium rerū testimonia, figuras & demonstrationes, quae obscura sunt in fide nostra illustrare ac confirmare. Verùm arbitror Apostolum huc non respexisse, hoc maximè loco.
units.tr: (2) Next, Chrysostom explains it thus: comparing and declaring spiritual things by means of spiritual things, not by the persuasion of human wisdom, reasonings and syllogisms. For example, the birth of the virgin is shown by the fact that Adam and Eve were not formed by any sexual intercourse, but Adam from the earth and Eve from Adam; and by the birth of Sarah, who was barren, likewise the birth of Elizabeth to Zechariah; and the resurrection of Christ from the figure of Jonah. Thus for Chrysostom to compare spiritual things with spiritual is to illustrate and confirm, by testimonies, figures and demonstrations drawn from spiritual matters, what is obscure in our faith. Yet I think the Apostle did not have this in view here, especially in this place.

units.la: 3 Preterea Erasmus in Annotationibus suis (licet in Paraphrasi priorem sententiam sit sequutus) dictione Spiritalibus, non homines, sed res spirituales intelligit, quibus & spiritalia coaptari & conferri dicit: ubi illae non munda naे sapientię, sed spiritus Dei uerbis tradūtur, ut generi sapientiae ac doctrinę respondeat, & genus sermonis, & sit conformitas & συγκρισις. Et hic sensus conuenit ipsi argumento. nā hac de re adhuc loquitur Apostolus. Collatio est & conformitas, quando dialectica dialecticè, mathematica mathematicè, rhetorica rhetoricè, mundana mundanè traduntur. cui rei plurimum studetur à singularum disciplinarū alumnis, ita conforme est ut & spiritalia spiritaliter seruata collatione tradantur.
units.tr: (3) Furthermore, Erasmus in his Annotations (although in his Paraphrase he followed the former opinion) understands by "spiritual" not people but spiritual things, to which he says spiritual things are fitted and compared: where those things are delivered not in the words of worldly wisdom but in the words of the Spirit of God, so that the kind of speech corresponds to the kind of wisdom and teaching, and there is conformity and comparison [συγκρισις]. This sense also suits the argument itself, for the Apostle is still speaking of this matter. There is comparison and conformity when dialectic is taught dialectically, mathematics mathematically, rhetoric rhetorically, and worldly things in a worldly way. Students of each discipline strive greatly for this, so that spiritual things too may be taught in a conformable way, the comparison being kept spiritual.

units.la: Iterum ergo nouo argumento perstringit humanę sapientiae studiosos pseudapostolos, simulq; nostros magistros magis Aristotelem quàm spiritum Dei spirantes, ostendens studium illud eloquentiae & sapientiae humanae referre, non Dei, sed mundi spiritum: & collationem & conformitatem nō spiritalium, sed humanarum rerum respere: simul defendens
units.tr: So again, with a new argument, he rebukes the false apostles who are devoted to human wisdom, and at the same time our own teachers, who breathe Aristotle more than the Spirit of God. He shows that this zeal for human eloquence and wisdom belongs to the spirit of the world, not of God, and that the comparison and conformity concern not spiritual but human things. At the same time he defends the rudeness of the evangelical speech against the shame of contempt with which the false apostles and the wise of the world burdened it.

units.la: A sermonis Euangelici ruditatem contra contemptus ignominiam, qua per pseudapostolos & mundi sapientes grauabatur. Adiunge ista ad ea quae supra dicta sunt, ibi: Vt fides uestra non sit in sapientia hominum, sed in sapientia Dei, & habebis quatuor fortissima argumenta contra humanae sapientiae in rebus fidei studium. Videlicet, quod sapientia mundi euacuet crucem Christi, quod det carni gloriam coram Deo, quod fidem nostrā fundet in persuasorijs rationis humanę uerbis: & hic, quod resipiat spiritum nō Dei, sed mundi. Vicissim ruditas sermonis Apostolici commendat uirtutem crucis Christi, admit carni, & dat Deo omnem gloriam, fidem nostram fundat in potentia Dei, & resipit spiritum Dei mentiū nostrarum doctorem, & linguae moderatorem.
units.tr: Add these words to what was said above, namely: "that your faith may not rest in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God" (1 Cor. 2:5), and you will have four very strong arguments against the pursuit of human wisdom in matters of faith. Namely: that worldly wisdom empties the cross of Christ; that it gives the flesh glory before God; that it founds our faith on the persuasive words of human reason; and here, that it savours of the spirit not of God but of the world. Conversely, the rudeness of the apostolic speech commends the power of the cross of Christ, abases the flesh, gives all glory to God, founds our faith on the power of God, and savours of the Spirit of God, the teacher of our minds and the governor of our tongue.

units.la: Animalis autem homo nō accípit ea quæ sunt spíritus Dei. Stultícia siquidē illi sunt, nec potest cognoscere, quoniā spiritaliter dijudicantur. At spiritualis dijudicat quidem omnia, ipse uero à nemine dijudicatur.
units.tr: But the natural man does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness to him, neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned. But he who is spiritual judges all things, yet he himself is judged by no one.

units.la: 1 Faciunt ista ad latiorem declarationem eius, quod ostendit sapientia Dei à nemine cognosci, nisi ab illis quibus ea per spiritum Dei reueletur. Confert autem utrinque cūm homi nem animalem, tum spiritum Dei, & docet ita esse comparatū hominem animalem, ut quae spiritus Dei sunt, nequeat cognoscere, quemadmodum si bestiā dicas cognoscere non posse quae hominum sunt. Plus enim interest inter animalem hominem & spiritum Dei, deinde & inter intellectum hominis, & ea quę sunt spiritus Dei, quàm inter hominem & bestiam.
units.tr: 1 These words serve to explain more fully what he shows, namely that the wisdom of God is known by no one except those to whom it is revealed through the Spirit of God. He compares the natural man with the Spirit of God on both sides, and teaches that the natural man is so constituted that he cannot know the things of the Spirit of God, just as if you were to say that a beast cannot know the things of men. For the difference between the natural man and the Spirit of God, and again between the human understanding and the things of the Spirit of God, is greater than the difference between a man and a beast.

units.la: 2 Vocat autem hominem ψυχικὸν animalem à potiore hominis parte, anima scilicet: ut admoneat, totum hominem ineptum esse ad res spirituales amplexandas. Si enim dixisset, Carnalis autē homo non accipit ea quae sunt spiritus Dei: uisus fuisset eam tantum hominis partem, quae affectibus carnis corrupta est, & rationi repugnat, à cognitione & approbatione rerum spiritualium & diuinarum reijcere, nō autem eam quam rationem uocamus, ita ut uiderentur notari tantum hi homines, qui propterea quòd toti carnis rapiuntur affectibus, carnales uocari solent, quod ipsi tantum spiritalia approbare nequeant. Secus uerò illi, qui quoniam rationis imperio obedire uidentur, non carnales, sed rationales & sapientes uocantur: quasi isti queant pro rationis industria de rebus iudicare diuinis, ut ita Sardanapalus & diues epulo in Euangelio ueluti carnales excluderentur à cognitione eorum quae spiritus Dei sunt, Plato uerò & scribae Iudaeorum tanquam rationales & sapientes non excluderentur. Ne hoc quisquam suspicetur, non dicit, Carnalis homo non accipit ea quae Dei sunt. sed, Animalis homo. Id est, is qui iuxta animae cognitionem & affectus uitam, & maxime ximè iuxta seculum sapienter, instituit, quales suprà intellexit per principes huius mundi.
units.tr: 2 He calls the man ψυχικὸν, natural, from the nobler part of man, namely the soul, so as to warn that the whole man is unfit to embrace spiritual things. For if he had said "the carnal man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God," he would seem to be excluding from the knowledge and approval of spiritual and divine things only that part of man which is corrupted by the desires of the flesh and resists reason, and not the part which we call reason. In that case only those men would seem to be marked out who, because they are wholly swept away by the desires of the flesh, are usually called carnal, since they alone cannot approve spiritual things. But those who seem to obey the rule of reason, and are therefore not called carnal but rational and wise, would be thought able to judge divine things by the cleverness of their reason. In that way Sardanapalus and the rich man who feasted in the Gospel would be shut out from the knowledge of the things of the Spirit of God as carnal men, while Plato and the scribes of the Jews would not be shut out as rational and wise. So that no one may suspect this, he does not say "the carnal man does not receive the things of God," but "the natural man." That is, the man who orders his life according to the knowledge and desires of the soul, and above all wisely according to this world, the kind of man he described above as the rulers of this world.

units.la: 3 NON accipit.] Vetus habet, Non percipit: quod idem illi esse uidetur atq;, Non intelligit. Græcè est, ἀχνοεῖ, quod hoc loco magis est, Nō amplectitur, non approbat, quàm non intelligit aut non percipit. Non enim loquitur hic de perceptione quę intellectu fit, quam infrà tanquam huius particulæ rationem subijciet: sed de acceptatione & approbatione, quæ fit affectu. Aliud est amplecti affectu, quod sæpenumero absq; iusta rerum cognitione fit: & aliud intellectu percipere, quod sæpe affectu nō acceptatur. Neq; enim omnia intelligimus, quę affectamus & amplectimur: nec rursus omnia amplectimur, quæ qualia sint, uerè cognoscimus. Animalis autem homo nec amplectitur nec agnoscit ea quæ sunt spiritus. Vtrunq; illi dat Apostolus hoc loco: primù uerò, quòd nō amplectatur, non approbet ea quæ sunt spiritus: deinde, quòd nō cognoscat etiam, imò ne possit quidem cognoscere.
units.tr: 3 "Does not receive." The old version has "does not perceive," which seems to mean the same as "does not understand." The Greek is ἀχνοεῖ, which in this place means "does not embrace" or "does not approve" more than "does not understand" or "does not perceive." For he is not speaking here of that perception which comes through the understanding, which he will afterwards set out as the reason for this particle, but of acceptance and approval, which come through the affections. It is one thing to embrace something with the affections, which often happens without a sound knowledge of the matter, and another thing to perceive it with the understanding, which often is not accepted with the affections. For we do not understand everything that we desire and embrace, nor on the other hand do we embrace everything whose nature we truly know. The natural man neither embraces nor acknowledges the things of the Spirit. The Apostle gives him both faults in this place: first, that he does not embrace or approve the things of the Spirit; then, that he does not know them, or rather cannot even know them.

units.la: 4 EA quæ sunt spiritus.] Intellige nō solum ipsam doctrinam spiritus, sed & illius idiotismum rudem ac simplicem: utrunq; non approbat animalis. Nam humanarum rerum & scientia tumet, & affectu languet: quia animalis est, & carnalis. In ipsa natura utrinq; diuersitas est, ut nec spiritus animalia: nec quod animale est, spiritalia probet. Nam caro concupiscit aduersus spiritum, & spiritus aduersus carnem.
units.tr: 4 "The things of the Spirit." Understand not only the doctrine of the Spirit but also its plain and simple manner of speech: the natural man approves neither. For human learning puffs up, and in the affections it grows weak, because it is natural and carnal. In their very nature there is a difference between the two, so that the natural things do not approve the spiritual, nor does what is natural approve what is spiritual. For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh.

units.la: 5 Nec præter rationem est, quod non dicit, Ea quæ sunt Dei: sed, Quæ sunt spiritus Dei. Nam & animalis homo multa sanè approbat & amplectitur, & nouit etiam quæ Dei sunt, ut uidere est in scriptis philosophorum, & in ipso communi mortalium sensu. Mysterium uerò regni Christi, & quæ Deus præparauit diligentibus se, quæ per doctrinam spiritus & intelliguntur, & prædicantur in Euangelio Christi, non intelligit, nec approbat animalis homo. I. deo quasi exponens superiorem particulam, qua dixit, Quæ sunt Dei, nemo nouit nisi spiritus Dei: pro eo quod ibi dixit, Quæ sunt Dei: hic posuit, Quæ sunt spiritus Dei.
units.tr: 5 Nor is it without reason that he does not say "the things of God," but "the things of the Spirit of God." For the natural man certainly approves and embraces many things, and he also knows the things of God, as may be seen in the writings of the philosophers and in the common sense of mortals. But the mystery of the kingdom of Christ, and the things God has prepared for those who love him, which are understood and proclaimed through the teaching of the Spirit in the Gospel of Christ, the natural man neither understands nor approves. In other words, he is explaining the earlier clause, where he said "the things of God no one knows except the Spirit of God," by putting "the things of the Spirit of God" in place of "the things of God."

units.la: STVLTICIA siquidem illi sunt.] Hæc est ratio, cur animalis homo non amplectatur ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei: quia uidelicet illi stulta uidentur.
units.tr: "For foolishness they are to him." This is the reason why the natural man does not embrace the things of the Spirit of God: namely, that they seem foolish to him.

units.la: 1 Et hic uidemus primum, quod per animalē hominem hoc loco intelligat hominem sapientiæ studio deditum, & quæ sapientiæ uidentur amplexantem: quę uerò stulta, reijciente. Nam indicat hac rationis redditione, ea quæ spiritus Dei sunt, ideo non acceptari ab animali homine, quòd illi stulta uideantur. Alioquihomo carnalis & magis ex affectibus quàm rationis iudicio uiuens, quæ respuit, magis ob id respuit, quòd sapientiá uel resipiunt uel exiguntquàm quòd stulta uideantur. Nam ille non minus auersatur philosophiæ studium propter sapientiam quam non affectat, quàm animalis doctrinam spiritus, propter opinionem stulticiæ, quam fugiendam putat.
units.tr: 1 Here we see first that by the natural man in this place he means the man devoted to the study of wisdom, who embraces what seems to be wisdom and rejects what seems foolish. For by giving this reason he indicates that the things of the Spirit of God are not accepted by the natural man because they seem foolish to him. Otherwise, a carnal man who lives more by the desires than by the judgment of reason rejects them more because they taste of wisdom or demand it, than because they seem foolish. For that man is no less averse to the study of philosophy on account of its wisdom, and does not desire it, than the natural man is averse to the teaching of the Spirit on account of the opinion of its foolishness, which he thinks must be avoided.

units.la: 2 Deinde uidemus hic uerbum illud ἀχνοεῖ, ut iam monui, non esse de intellectu, sed de affectu exponendum. Non enim ideo sapientes huius mundi doctrinam Euangelij non intelligunt, quòd ea uideatur ipsis esse stulta: sed quoniam eam non cognoscunt, ideò stultam reputant: & quia stultam reputant, ideo non acceptant, sed respuunt, ut opinio stultitiæ fit fructus ignorantiæ, reprobatio uerò Euangelij apud sapientes ex eo nascatur, quod doctrinam illius stultam esse putant. Igitur animalis homo, sapiens huius mundi, non acceptat, nō approbat Euangelium, quia stultum illi uidetur: stultū aut illi uidetur, quia non intelligit.
units.tr: 2 Second, we see here that the word ἀχνοεῖ, as I have already said, must be explained not of the understanding but of the affections. For the wise men of this world do not fail to understand the doctrine of the Gospel because it seems foolish to them; rather, because they do not know it, they think it foolish, and because they think it foolish, they do not accept it but reject it. So the opinion of foolishness is the fruit of ignorance, and the rejection of the Gospel among the wise arises from this, that they think its doctrine foolish. Therefore the natural man, the wise man of this world, does not accept or approve the Gospel, because it seems foolish to him; and it seems foolish to him because he does not understand it.

units.la: 3 Tertiò patet etiam ex hac particula, quòd quæ spiritus Dei sunt, à sapientibus mundi huius non solum non approbentur, sed & explodantur, & cum irrisione reijciantur. A sapientibus enim quæ stulta uidentur, summè fugiendapŭtantur. Est enim stultitia sapientiæ exopposito cóntraria, ut tolerabilius sit philosopho, quod molestum est, seuerum ac durum, triste & iniucundum, quàm quod stultum est. Nam illius profesioni nihil adeò repugnat, atque doctrina stulta. Quemadmodum igitur diuitiæ nihil est aduersum magis paupertate, arrogantiā nihil inuisum magis humilitate, & homini uoluptatibus carnis dedito, nihil ingratius continentia & uitæ seueritate: ita sapientiæ studio so nihil magis ridiculum est doctrina talì, quæ stultitiam resipere uidetur. Ergo illud ἀχνοεῖ non solum hic Apostolo sonat, non amplectitur: sed magis politum est pro auersatur, respuit, explodit, & irridet. Nec id frustra est, quòd non dixit, Siquidem illi stulta uidentur, sed stultitia illi sunt. quod apparet per auxesim distum, ut ostendat ea quæ spiritus Dei sunt, à sapientibus huius mundi stultissima uideri, imò ipsam esse stulticiam. Sicut hominem scelestissimum significantes dicimus, Scelus est: pro, scelestissimus est.
units.tr: 3 Third, it is also clear from this clause that the things of the Spirit of God are not only not approved by the wise of this world, but are also hooted down and rejected with mockery. For the wise regard what seems foolish as most to be avoided. Foolishness is in fact the opposite of wisdom, so that for a philosopher it is more bearable to be troubled, harsh, severe, sad and unpleasant than to be foolish. For nothing is more contrary to his profession than foolish teaching. Just as wealth is nothing more opposed to poverty, pride nothing more hateful than humility, and for a man given over to the pleasures of the flesh nothing more distasteful than self-restraint and a strict life, so nothing seems more ridiculous to one devoted to wisdom than a teaching that seems to savour of foolishness. So ἀχνοεῖ here means not only "does not embrace" for the Apostle, but more properly "turns away from, rejects, hoots down, and mocks." Nor is it without purpose that he did not say "if indeed they seem foolish to him," but "they are foolishness to him." This is put by way of an intensified expression, to show that the things of the Spirit of God seem most utterly foolish to the wise of this world, indeed that they are foolishness itself. Just as when we describe a most wicked man we say, "He is wickedness," meaning, "he is most wicked."

units.la: OBSER.
units.tr: OBSERVATION.

units.la: Hic locus summopere notandus est. Non enim priuatum quid & temporarium uel personale, sed generale & perpetuum tradit, quòd non minus nostro quàm Apostoli seculo uerum est, ut non magis hodie sperandum sit Euangelium Christi placiturum hominibus animalibus, quàm unquam. Est enim animalis ipse homo sibi perpetuò similis, & rursus ea quæ spiritus Dei sunt, sibi ipsis quoque perpetuò concordant. Vbi autem animali homini, & nihilominus carnali, Euangelium adeò displicet, quid non irrisionis & molestiæ illius nomine expectandum est Christi, & spiritus Christi ministris.
units.tr: This passage must be carefully noted. For it does not teach something private, temporary or personal, but something general and lasting, which is no less true in our age than in the Apostle's: the Gospel of Christ is no more likely to please natural men today than it ever was. For man, being natural, is always like himself, and likewise the things of the Spirit of God are always consistent with themselves. Where the Gospel so greatly displeases natural and yet carnal man, what else is to be expected but mockery and harassment, in the name of Christ and of the ministers of his Spirit?

units.la: 1 NEC potest cognoscere.] Velut rationem assignat, cur ea quæ spiritus Dei sunt, adeoq; & sapientissima, ab animali homine, id est hominis ratione & intellectu tanquam stultissima reijciuntur. Quia illa, inquit, non intelligit. git. Alioqui non uiderentur esse stulta, si ea intelligeret.
units.tr: 1 NOR CAN HE KNOW THEM. Here he gives the reason why the things of the Spirit of God, and therefore the wisest things, are rejected as the height of foolishness by the natural man, that is, by human reason and understanding. Because, he says, the natural man does not understand them. Otherwise they would not seem foolish to him, if he understood them.

units.la: 2 Et ne culpa huius detur hominis animalis desidiæ & negligentiæ, quasi possit ea iudicio rationis, si uires illius intendat, cognoscere, adimit illi prorsus non solum intellectum diuinorum, sed & intellectus facultatem dicens: Nec potest cognoscere.
units.tr: 2 And lest the fault be put on the natural man's laziness and carelessness, as if by the judgement of reason he could know them if he exerted his powers, he takes away from him altogether not only the understanding of divine things but also the faculty of understanding, saying: Nor can he know them.

units.la: Quid ergo hic relinquitur uiribus rationis in cognoscendis rebus Christianæ fidei: Scilicet duobus uerbis, uelut fulminibus, pternitur omnis conatus sapientiæ huius mundi in rebus Dei. Nec potest, inquit, cognoscere.
units.tr: What, then, is left to the powers of reason for knowing the things of the Christian faith? In two words, like thunderbolts, every effort of the wisdom of this world in the things of God is struck down. He cannot know them, he says.

units.la: Ergo ubi animalis homo conatur ad cognitionem pertingere regni Christi, frustra laborat: ubi de rebus spiritus disputat, garrit: ubi pronunciat, mentitur: ubi in religione statuit, temerarius est: ubi docet, seducit: ubi sectatores reperit, perdit. Quare? Quia non potest cognoscere. Quid igitur expectabimus in fidei Christianæ negocio decisionem animalium, imo nonnunquam & carnalium?
units.tr: Therefore, when natural man tries to reach the knowledge of the kingdom of Christ, he labours in vain; when he disputes about the things of the Spirit, he chatters; when he pronounces, he lies; when he decides in matters of religion, he is rash; when he teaches, he misleads; when he finds followers, he destroys them. Why? Because he cannot know. What, then, can we expect as the decision in the business of the Christian faith from natural men, and indeed sometimes from carnal men?

units.la: 1 QVONIAM spiritaliter dijudicantur.] Si quæras quare nequeat animalis homo cognoscere ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei, respondet, quia spiritaliter dijudicantur. Quid est spiritaliter aliquid fieri? Est ex sententia, instinctu & iudicio spiritus fieri. Et quoniam hic de cognitione eorum quæ sunt spiritus Dei loquitur, spiritaliter res diuinas cognoscere, est eas cognoscere iudicio, ductu, & illuminatione spiritus: sicut animaliter aliqd uel rationaliter cognoscere, est ex iudicio rationis cognoscere. Idem ergo est ac si diceret, Animalis homo non potest cognoscere ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei, quoniam non animaliter & cum iudicio rationis dijudicatur, sed ex instinctu & iudicio ductuq; spiritus.
units.tr: 1 BECAUSE THEY ARE JUDGED SPIRITUALLY. If you ask why natural man cannot know the things of the Spirit of God, he answers: because they are judged spiritually. What does it mean for something to be done spiritually? It means to be done according to the mind, by the prompting and judgement of the Spirit. And since he is speaking here of the knowledge of the things of the Spirit of God, to know divine things spiritually is to know them by the judgement, guidance and illumination of the Spirit, just as to know something animally or rationally is to know it by the judgement of reason. So it is the same as if he said: the natural man cannot know the things of the Spirit of God, because they are not judged in a natural way and by the judgement of reason, but by the prompting, judgement and guidance of the Spirit.

units.la: 2 Dijudicatur, inquit. Dijudicare non est cognoscere, sed ut cognoscas indagare, scrutari, discutere, examinare, ut fieri solet à sapientibus, qui causarum, effectuum & circumstantiarum scrutinio ad rerum cognitionem rationis uiribus & iudicio peruenerunt. Et hoc uerbo in loco utitur, ut indagationes & scrutinia philosophorum traducat & reijciat, doceatq; impossibile esse, ut hac uia perueniatur ad cognitionem eorum quæ sunt spiritus Dei, eo quod illa non rationis, sed spiritus Dei iudicio & scrutinio cognoscantur.
units.tr: 2 They are judged, he says. To judge is not the same as to know; rather, in order to know, one investigates, searches, sifts and examines, as wise men usually do, who by the scrutiny of causes, effects and circumstances have arrived at knowledge of things by the powers and judgement of reason. He uses this word here in order to disparage and reject the investigations and inquiries of the philosophers, and to teach that it is impossible to reach the knowledge of the things of the Spirit of God by this route, because those things are known not by the judgement and scrutiny of reason but by the judgement and scrutiny of the Spirit of God.

units.la: 3 Cauendum est hoc loco commentum eorum, qui particulam hanc exponunt de allegorijs abstrusioribus, quas putant esse spiritale dijudicationem per quam ueniatur ad cognitionem eorum quæ sunt spiritus Dei, cum illæ plerunque magis rationalem industriâ & discussionem scripturæ animalem respiciant quàm iudicium spiritus. Spiritaliter dijudicare, non est allegorice scripturam exponere, sed ex reuelatione spiritus mentem Dei cognoscere.
units.tr: 3 At this point we must beware of the invention of those who explain this phrase as referring to more abstruse allegories, which they think are a spiritual judgement by which one comes to the knowledge of the things of the Spirit of God, whereas these allegories for the most part depend on rational cleverness and the natural reasoning of Scripture rather than on the judgement of the Spirit. To judge spiritually is not to expound Scripture allegorically, but to know the mind of God by the revelation of the Spirit.

units.la: AT spiritualis dijudicat quidè omnia, ipse uero à nemine dijudicatur.] Discernit spiritualem ab animali. Vocat autem spiritualem eum qui spiritu Dei illuminatur, qui spiritus
units.tr: BUT the spiritual man judges all things, yet he himself is judged by no one. He distinguishes the spiritual man from the natural. He calls spiritual the one who is illuminated by the Spirit of God, who has a taste not for the judgement of reason but for the things of the Spirit, who lives by the guidance of the Spirit and not by carnal affections.

units.la: A iudicio non rationis sapit, qui spiritus ductu non affectuum carnalium uiuit. Nihil hic loci est illis, qui ecclesiastici tantum ordinis gratia spirituales uocantur.
units.tr: Nothing here applies to those who are called spiritual only by reason of their ecclesiastical office.

units.la: 2 DIIVDICAT omnia.] Dijudicat, nō rationis indagatione, sed spiritaliter, iudicio spiritus, per quem in cognitionem rerū spirituallium ducitur.
units.tr: 2 HE JUDGES ALL THINGS. He judges not by the investigation of reason but spiritually, by the judgement of the Spirit, through whom he is led into the knowledge of spiritual things.

units.la: Omnia. Non intellige uniuersaliter de quibusuis, sed de ijs, quæ sunt spiritus Dei, de quibus Euangelium Christi prædicat, & quæcunque ad illa pertinent.
units.tr: All things. Do not understand this universally of anything whatever, but of those things which belong to the Spirit of God, of which the Gospel of Christ preaches, and of whatever pertains to them.

units.la: 3 IPSE uero à nemine dijudicatur.] Nemo animalis potest dijudicare, æstimare & cognoscere spiritalem hominem. Vt est Iohan.3. Spiritus spirat ubi uult, & uocem eius audis, & nescis unde ueniat aut quo uadat: sic est omnis qnatus est ex spiritu. Spiritalem enim esse, spiritaliter intelligere, spiritaliter uiuere, talia sunt, quæ non possunt rationis iudicio comprehendi. Ideo illud, A nemine, non est uniuersaliter de omnibus hominibus, sed de ijs tantum accipiendum, qui non sunt spirituales. Mundus, inquit Iohannes, non nouit uos, quia non nouit Deum.
units.tr: 3 YET HE IS JUDGED BY NO ONE. No natural man can judge, estimate or know the spiritual man. As in John 3: The Spirit blows where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes; so is everyone who is born of the Spirit. For to be spiritual, to understand spiritually, to live spiritually, these are things which cannot be grasped by the judgement of reason. Therefore that phrase, by no one, is not to be taken universally of all men, but only of those who are not spiritual. The world, says John, does not know you, because it does not know God.

units.la: 4 Hæc uerba à nonnullis aliter exponūtur. Ambrosio uerbum dijudicandi idem est atq; condemnandi: ut, Quoniam spiritaliter dijudicatur (nam in singulari legit, & ad animale hominem refert) idem fit atq; Spiritaliter condenatur. Sic spiritalis iudicat omnia, id est, per illius exemplum condemnantur increduli. Et ipse à nemine iudicatur, id est, condemnatur. Ita & Hieronymus. Theophylactus illud, Spiritalis dijudicat omnia: intelligit de eo quod omnia quæ mundi sunt, spiritalis tanquam una iudicet. Et ipse à nemine dijudicatur. Id est, inquit, à nemine arguitur. Est ex recentioribus qui hanc particulam, Et ipse à nemine dijudicatur, referat nō ad spiritalē hominem, sed ad ipsum spiritum Dei propter sequentia, quod licet in se uerum sit, uerborū tamen contextui non admodum congruit.
units.tr: 4 Some expound these words differently. For Ambrose, the verb to judge means the same as to condemn, so that, "since it is judged spiritually" (for he reads it in the singular and refers it to the natural man), it amounts to "is condemned spiritually." Thus the spiritual man judges all things, that is, through his example unbelievers are condemned; and he himself is judged by no one, that is, is not condemned. So also Jerome. Theophylact understands the phrase, the spiritual man judges all things, to mean that the spiritual man, as one, judges all the things that are of the world. And he himself is judged by no one, that is, as he says, is accused by no one. Some of the more recent writers refer this phrase, and he himself is judged by no one, not to the spiritual man but to the Spirit of God itself, on account of what follows; which, although it may be true in itself, does not agree very well with the context of the words.

units.la: Quis enim cognouit mentem domini? Quis consilium dabit illi? Nos autē mentem Christi tenemus.
units.tr: Who has known the mind of the Lord? Who will give him counsel? But we have the mind of Christ.

units.la: 1 Locum desumit ex propheta Esa.cap.40. quo & in Romanis cap.11. usus est. Probat autem hic illud quod suprà dixit, Quæ sunt Dei nemo nouit, nisi spiritus Dei: &, quod iam primum posuit, Spiritalis dijudicat omnia, ipse uero, ut spiritalis, à nemine dijudicatur. Si enim nemo cognouit mentem Dei, nisi spiritus Dei: certe firmum est, quod nemo cognoscat illam per rationis iudicium, & quod soli spirituales eam cognoscant, & quod illi à nemine cognosci queant. Quæ hic notanda sunt, uide in Commentarijs nostris super Epist.ad Rom.
