units.tr: 1 He takes this from the prophet Isaiah, chapter 40, which he also used in Romans, chapter 11. Here he proves what he said above, that "the things of God no one knows except the Spirit of God," and what he has already laid down first, that "the spiritual man judges all things, but he himself, as spiritual, is judged by no one." For if no one has known the mind of God except the Spirit of God, then it is certainly firm that no one knows it by the judgment of reason, that only the spiritual know it, and that they cannot be known by anyone. What is to be noted here, see in our commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans.

units.la: 2 Nos autē mentem Christi tenemus. Mens Christi est mens Dei, secretum illud cōsilium Dei. Christū aūt ponit, quia p illius fidē datur spiritus, & per spiritum reuelatio mentis Dei.
units.tr: 2 "But we have the mind of Christ." The mind of Christ is the mind of God, that secret counsel of God. He names Christ because through his faith the Spirit is given, and through the Spirit the revelation of the mind of God.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Tego fratres nō potuí lo qui uobís ut spiritalibus, sed loquendū fuit ut carnalibus, ut infantibus in Christo. Lactis potu uos alui, & nō cibo. Nondum enim poteratis, imò ne nunc quidē adhuc potestis. Nam adhuc carnales estis. Siquidē cū in uobis sit æmulatio & contentio, & factiones, nonne carnales estis, & secundum hominem ambulatis? Etenim cū dicat aliquis, ego quidem sum Pauli, alter uero ego sum Apollo, nonne carnales estis?
units.tr: And I, brothers, could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but I had to speak to you as to carnal people, as to infants in Christ. I fed you with milk, not with food. For you were not yet able, nor even now are you able; for you are still carnal. Since there is among you jealousy and strife and factions, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to man? For when one says, "I am of Paul," and another, "I am of Apollos," are you not carnal?

units.la: Redit hoc capite ad id quod primo coeperat, ut διχοστασίαι quas inter se Corinthij alebat, corrigat. Calumniæ pseudapostolorum & omnium mundi sapientium obnoxia erat cū doctrina Pauli, tum ipsa personæ humilitas, & sermonis rūditas, qua doctrinam stultitiæ nomine eleuabant, sermonem uerò uelut rudem & abiectum explodebant, cui calumniæ obuiam perrexit capite secundo. Nam ex isto contemptu crucis Christi & humilitatis Apostolicæ, uelut ex fonte fluxerat ὁ διχοστασίων ἀφορμή, insinuantibus sese Corinthiorum animis pseudapostolis, nomine sapientiæ & eloquentiæ, ut contempta simplici crucis Christi doctrina, discipulos post se traherent, & ecclesiam Christi scinderent. Iam quoniam & hoc pluri mū ad id mali faciebat, quod doctrinā pseudapostolorum, cum simplicitate eius quam initio ut elementariam ab Apostolo acceperant conferentes, illam admirabantur uelut sublimem & perfectiorem, istam uerò uelut rudem & humile fastidiebant, & ob eam causam maiora de pseudapostolis quàm par erat sentientes, in illis gloriabantur, seque illorum discipulos esse iactabant: primum isto capite imperfectioris doctrinæ causam per translationem in auditorum qualitatem conijcit. deinde subiungit, quàm nemo debeat etiam de ministris Christi sentire & gloriari ultra quàm condignum sit, nedum de illis qui sapientiæ nomine turgent.
units.tr: This chapter returns to the matter he had begun with, namely to correct the divisions [διχοστασίαι] that the Corinthians were fostering among themselves. The false apostles and all the wise men of the world were ready to slander both Paul's teaching and his personal humility and plain speech. They lifted their doctrine up in the name of folly, and they scorned his speech as crude and contemptible. He met this slander in chapter two. For from this contempt for the cross of Christ and for apostolic humility, the source of the divisions [ὁ διχοστασίων ἀφορμή] flowed as from a spring, since the false apostles insinuated themselves into the minds of the Corinthians under the name of wisdom and eloquence. Their aim was to draw disciples after themselves, having set aside the simple doctrine of the cross of Christ, and so to tear the Church of Christ apart. This also did much harm, because the Corinthians compared the teaching of the false apostles with the simplicity that they had first received from the Apostle as elementary. They admired the one as lofty and more perfect, and they despised the other as crude and humble. For this reason, thinking more highly of the false apostles than was right, they gloried in them and boasted that they were their disciples. So in this chapter he first sets out, by way of comparison with the hearers' condition, the reason why his teaching had been less advanced. Then he adds how no one ought to think or boast of the ministers of Christ beyond what is fitting, much less of those who swell up with the name of wisdom.

units.la: ET ego fratres nō potui loqui uobis ut spiritalibus.] Capite sequenti uidere est, quàm saturi fuerint Corinthij, & nomine eius doctrinæ quam pseudapostoli tradebant, ita inflati, ut quæ ab Apostolo acceperant, plane fastidirent, & in pseudapostolorum sapientia gloriantes dicerent: Talia tamque præclara & sublimia à Paulo antea non audiuimus. Quàm in sipida & rudia nobis tradita sunt hastenus istis collata, quæ nunc audimus? Hi sunt ueri doctores, qui uerà nobis adferunt doctrinam, qui nobis quæ hastenus latuerunt, in lucem proferunt. Paulus istis comparatus plane stultus, imbecillis & vilis est. Isti cogitationi oc-
units.tr: "And I, brethren, could not speak to you as to spiritual people." In the following chapter one can see how full the Corinthians were, and how inflated by the name of that teaching which the false apostles delivered. They so utterly despised what they had received from the Apostle that, boasting in the wisdom of the false apostles, they said: "We have never heard such fine and lofty things from Paul before. How insipid and crude is what we have been taught until now, when compared with what we now hear! These are the true teachers, who bring us real doctrine and bring into the light what has until now lain hidden from us. Paul, in comparison with them, is plainly foolish, weak and contemptible." This thought occurs to him by way of comparison. He does not say, "When I came to you, I taught you things loftier than what you now hear," but, "I could not speak to you as to spiritual people; I had to speak to you as to carnal people." As if he were saying: "It is true that I did not at first teach you what was higher and more perfect. But why was this so? Was it from my ignorance and poverty of speech? By no means! It was from your weakness, which I was bound to take into account. For I had to consider what you were able to grasp, not what I could teach. You could not grasp what was lofty and perfect, because you were carnal, as you still are; and so I had to speak to you not as to spiritual people but as to carnal people." Again, he calls them brethren, so that he may somewhat soften a word that otherwise would be unwelcome.

units.la: currit per translationem. Non dicit, Cū uenirem ad uos, sublimiora uobis tradidi, quàm quæ nunc auditis: sed, Non potui uobis loqui ut spiritalibus: sed loquendum fuit, ut carnalibus. Quasi dicat: Verum est non tradidi uobis initio sublimiora & perfectiora, sed qua ratione id factum est? An ex mea ignorantia & sermonis inopia? Nequaquam: sed ex uestra imbecillitate, cuius cogebar habere rationem. Vi dendum enim mihi erat, quid uos capere possetis, non quid ego tradere possem. Non poteratis autem sublimia & perfectiora capere, eo quod carnales essetis, quales etiamnum estis: ideoq; mihi loquendum ad uos fuit non uelut ad spirituales, sed uelut ad carnales. Rursus aūt uocat eos fratres, quo sermonem hūc alias ingratum nonnihil mitiget.
units.tr: runs through the translation. He does not say, "When I came to you, I delivered to you things more sublime than what you now hear," but rather, "I could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but I had to speak as to carnal ones." As if he were saying: It is true that I did not at first deliver to you the more sublime and perfect things; but for what reason was this done? Was it from my ignorance and poverty of speech? By no means; it was from your weakness, which I was bound to take into account. For I had to consider what you were able to grasp, not what I was able to deliver. Yet you could not grasp sublime and perfect things, because you were carnal, as you still are; therefore I had to speak to you not as to spiritual people, but as to carnal ones. Again, he calls them brothers, so that he may somewhat soften a discourse otherwise unwelcome.

units.la: V T infantibus in Christo. Lactis potu uos alui, & non cibo.] Similitudine declarat, cur nō potuerit illis initio sublimiora tradere. Facit se parentem, ut & infrà capite 4. dicit: Non multos habetis patres. Siquidem in Christo Iesu per Euangelium uos genui. Illos facit infantes in Christo & paruulos. Parentis est rationem habere ætatis & imbecillitatis liberorum suorum, illosq; ita alere, ut prouehat, non ut perdat. Hoc facit, ubi cibum accommodat illorum ætati & capacitati, infantibus lac & pulmentum, adultis solidum cibum porrigens. Ita Apostolus Corinthijs quos in Christo genuerat, primum ea quæ essent captui ipsorum accommoda tradidit, quæ hic lacti comparat, quæ perfectiora erant reseruās, donec in Christo uegetiores redderentur.
units.tr: AS TO INFANTS IN CHRIST. I fed you with milk to drink, and not with food.] By a comparison he declares why he could not at first deliver to them more sublime things. He makes himself a parent, as he also says below in chapter 4: "For you have not many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the Gospel." He makes them infants and little children in Christ. It is the part of a parent to take account of the age and weakness of his children, and to nourish them in such a way that he advances them, not destroys them. This he does when he adapts food to their age and capacity, offering milk and pap to infants, solid food to adults. So the Apostle, having begotten the Corinthians in Christ, first delivered to them those things which were suited to their capacity, which he here compares to milk, while keeping back the more perfect things until they should be made more vigorous in Christ.

units.la: QVAE SINT HIC obseruanda.
units.tr: What is to be observed here.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: NON potui loqui uobis.] Quærendū hic, quomodo nō potuerit Apostolus Corinthijs sublimiora ob id tradere, quod carnales adhuc essent, & infantes in Christo, cum tamen pseudapostoli potuerint illis sublimia proponere? Quis enim etiam stultissimus nō potest sublimia quæque proponere, licet non intelligantur? Respondeo. Elucet quidem hac in re Apostoli prudens dispensatio, qua quibusuis nouit competētem cibum subministrare, quæ & omnibus est imitanda Christi ministris, quà & Christus ipse seruauit, aliter instruens discipulos, & aliter populum: Vobis, inquit, datū est nosse mysterium regni Dei, cæteris autem in parabolis. Et inter ipsos discipulos quoq; hac in re discreuit, ubi Petrum, Iacobum & Iohannem seorsum in montem secum, & ad secessum precandi in hortum relictis aliis assum psit. Item cum dicebat Iohan. decimosexto: Adhuc multa habeo uobis dicere, sed non potestis portare modo. Verum præter hanc prudentiam spiritus obseruandum est, quàm fidelis fuerit Apostolus erga Corinthios in opere domini: in eo quod non quæ ad gloriam sibi, sed quæ ad illorū facerent utilitatem considerafiderauit & proposuit, qui affectus quaerendae salutis illorum cohibuit dispensationis apostolicę cursum, ut nequiuerit alia tradere, quàm quæ illis essent comprehensibilia, adeoque & utilia. Contrà uero pseudapostoli, longè aliter affecti, non Christianorū profectum, sed suam ipsorum spectantes gloriam, non expenderūt auditorum uires quid illis conducere posset, quid non, ut paulatim ad solidiora proficerentur, & in Christo crescerent: sed quid esset auditu magnificum, splendidum & plausibile, etiam si nunquam caperetur: uel si caperetur, nihil conferret, aut etiam obesset. idq; proposuerunt non patres, sed pædagogos agentes, ut infrà dicet: Et si multos habetis pædagogos, nō multos tamē habetis patres. Cōmeda tur itaq; nobis hoc loco prudentia pariter & fidelitas germanorum Christi ministrorum, quam sequamur, & uicissim infidelitas pseudapostolorum quam fugiamus. Qui malunt uideri uel insigniter docti, & seculares quoq; eruditionis haud expertes, uel singulariter eloquentes, aut solito sublimiora, & haętenus à nemine tradita adferentes, nihil hi minus q ædificationem imperitorum spectant: sed toti eo collimant, ut quam querunt inanem gloriā eleganter & erudite dicendo, & singularia quę dam docendo consequantur. Hoc genus concionatorum alienum est à Canone apostolico, quo à ministris Christi ac dispensatoribus mysteriorum Dei requiritur, ut fideles inueniantur. Qui sic docent, non modo inutiles sunt ad pascendum gregem domini, sed & instructi ad seducendum, præsertim si qualiscunq; accesserit hypocrisis.
units.tr: "I could not speak to you." Here one must ask why the Apostle could not deliver loftier teaching to the Corinthians on the ground that they were still carnal and infants in Christ, when the false apostles could set lofty things before them. For who, even the most foolish, cannot propound lofty things, even if they are not understood? I answer. The Apostle's prudent management shines forth in this matter, by which he knew how to supply suitable food to each kind of hearer. All ministers of Christ must imitate this, as Christ himself observed, teaching the disciples one way and the people another: "To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables." He also distinguished among the disciples themselves in this matter, when he took Peter, James and John apart with him onto the mountain and to a place of prayer in the garden, leaving the others behind. Likewise, when he said in John 16: "I have many more things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now." Yet beyond this prudence of the Spirit, we must observe how faithful the Apostle was toward the Corinthians in the work of the Lord. He considered and proposed not what would bring glory to himself, but what would benefit them. This concern for their salvation restrained the course of his apostolic teaching, so that he could deliver nothing but what they could grasp, and so what was useful to them. The false apostles, on the contrary, were moved quite otherwise. Looking not to the progress of Christians but to their own glory, they did not weigh what the hearers' powers could bear or not bear, so that they might gradually advance to firmer things and grow in Christ. They weighed only what would be magnificent, splendid and pleasing to hear, even if it were never grasped, or, if it were grasped, would contribute nothing or even do harm. And they offered these things not as fathers but as pedagogues, as he says below: "For if you have many pedagogues, yet you do not have many fathers." Let us therefore commend here the prudence and fidelity alike of the true ministers of Christ, which we should follow, and let us in turn flee the infidelity of the false apostles. Those who prefer to seem remarkably learned, or even secular men not without erudition, or singularly eloquent, or who bring forth things loftier than usual and taught by no one before, care least for the edification of the unlearned. They aim entirely at winning the empty glory they seek by speaking elegantly and learnedly and by teaching certain singular things. This kind of preacher is foreign to the apostolic rule, by which ministers of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries are required to be found faithful. Those who teach in this way are not only useless for feeding the Lord's flock, but are also equipped for leading it astray, especially if any hypocrisy is added.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: SED loquendū fuit, inquit, ut carnalibus.] Quærendum secundo loco, quomodo Corinthios uocet carnales, cum infrà cap.4. dicat: In Christo Iesu per Euangelium ego uos genui: Et hoc loco: Vt infantibus in Christo, lac potū dedi. Si erant Christo per Euangeliū nati, atq; ita infantes in Christo, certe habebant spiritū sanctum. Qui nanque spiritum Christi nō habet, hic non est eius, Rom.8. Et infrà hoc capite: An, inquit, nescitis quod templū Dei estis, & spiritus Dei habitat in uobis? Si spiritū sanctum habebant, quomodo erāt carnales? Aut quid aliud est esse carnalem, quàm non esse spiritalem & secundum carnem affici, ac uiuere? Respondemus carnalem bifariam uocari. Primum carnales uocantur qui prorsus secundū carnem uiuunt, & planè expertes sunt spiritus Christi ac gratiæ Dei, nondum regenerati, sed adhuc toti in uetustate carnis peccati constitu ti. De illis legere est Ro.8. Qui carnales sunt, quæ carnis sunt curant. Itē, Qui in carne sunt, Deo placere non possunt: uos autem in carne non estis, siquidem spiritus Dei habitat in uobis. Deinde carnales uocantur etiam illi, qui li cet sint in Christo regenerati: sunt tamen adhuc infirmi, & paruuli in Christo, cum quod cognitionem attinet, tum & affectuum carna-
units.tr: "But I had to speak, he says, to carnal people." Here, secondly, one must ask how he calls the Corinthians carnal, when in chapter 4 he says: "In Christ Jesus through the Gospel I begot you," and here: "As to infants in Christ I gave you milk to drink." If they were born in Christ through the Gospel, and so were infants in Christ, surely they had the Holy Spirit. For whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ is not his, Rom. 8. And later in this chapter: "Do you not know that you are God's temple, and that God's Spirit dwells in you?" If they had the Holy Spirit, how were they carnal? Or what else is it to be carnal than not to be spiritual, and to be affected and to live according to the flesh? We reply that "carnal" is used in two ways. First, those are called carnal who live entirely according to the flesh, are wholly without the Spirit of Christ and the grace of God, and are not yet regenerate, but are still wholly placed in the old nature of sinful flesh. Of these we read in Rom. 8: "Those who are carnal mind the things of the flesh." Also: "Those who are in the flesh cannot please God; but you are not in the flesh, since God's Spirit dwells in you." Second, those are also called carnal who, although regenerate in Christ, are still weak and little children in Christ, both in knowledge and in the mortification of the carnal affections. Such were the Corinthians here, who, by a name taken from what predominated in them, are called carnal. For in this respect they surpassed most others in those carnal affections on account of which they are called carnal. By the same manner of naming, those are usually called spiritual who are nevertheless not so spiritual as to be wholly freed from all fleshly affections, but are so called because spiritual knowledge and conduct are the stronger in them.

units.la: lium mortificationem, quales sunt hoc loco Corinthij, qui denominatione ab eo quod ex cellebat sumpta carnales uocantur. Siquidem superabant hac in re & plerisque alijs carnales in illis affectus, quorum gratia carnales dicuntur, iuxta quam denominandi rationem & spiritales uocari solent, qui tamen non ita spirituales sunt, ut prorsus uniuersis carnis sint affecti bus liberati: sed ita uocantur, ob id quod spiritalis in illis & cognitio & conuersatio potiores habeat.
units.tr: ...of the mortification of the affections, such as the Corinthians here were, who are called "carnal" from the name taken from the gift in which they excelled. For in this respect they surpassed in carnal affections many others, on account of which they are called carnal; and by the same manner of naming, those are usually called "spiritual," who nevertheless are not so spiritual as to be altogether freed from all the affections of the flesh; but they are so called because in them the spiritual knowledge and conduct have the upper hand.

units.la: Habet spiritalis natiuitas suos gradus, quibus paulatim adsurgit ad maiora, donec perfectionem attingat, & iuxta graduū istorū progressum plerunq; & denominatione sortiuntur qui ex spiritu regenerati sunt, ut carnales uocentur quatenus plus ex carne quàm ex spiritu uiuunt, infantes, cum adhuc rudes sunt ac teneri, nondum exercitatos habētes sensus in cognitione & uita Christi, infirmi, cū fide, spe & patientia nondum sunt corroborati, spiritales, fortes, perfecti, quando adulti in cognitione Christi, in fide, spe, charitate, patientia & uita Dei promouerunt. Ita etiam de seipso disputat Apostolus Rom.7. hac ratione se carnalem uocans, eo quod legi peccati in carne nihil esset obnoxius. Ita & comunis usus obtinuit ut insensatos, & stultos uocemus eos, qui tamen non prorsus sunt rationis expertes, ob id quod plus in uita ostendant stultitiæ quàm sapientiæ: sapiētes uocemus non eos, qui prin cipia quædam sapientiæ habent, sed eos qui nonnihil in sapientia progressi, ita uiuunt, ut indicia de se singularis sapientiæ præbeant.
units.tr: Spiritual birth has its degrees, by which it gradually rises to greater things until it reaches perfection; and according to the progress of these degrees, those who have been regenerated by the Spirit usually receive their names as well, so that they are called "carnal" insofar as they live more by the flesh than by the Spirit; "infants," while they are still raw and tender, not yet having their senses exercised in the knowledge and life of Christ; "weak," while they are not yet strengthened in faith, hope and patience; "spiritual," "strong," "perfect," when, grown up, they have advanced in the knowledge of Christ, in faith, hope, love, patience and the life of God. The Apostle himself disputes in this way about himself in Rom. 7, calling himself carnal on the ground that he was sold under sin and subject to the law of sin in the flesh. So too common usage has prevailed that we call "senseless" and "foolish" those who nevertheless are not altogether without reason, because they show more folly than wisdom in their life; and we call "wise" not those who have certain principles of wisdom, but those who, having advanced somewhat in wisdom, live in such a way as to give evidence of a singular wisdom in themselves.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: LACTIS potu uos alui, inquit, & non cibo.] Tertio, quærendū est, quà doctrinæ Christianæ partem intelligat per lactis potum, & quam per cibum. Quid illis primum dare potuit, nisi quod & acceperat à domino, & reficiendi uires haberet. Acceperat autem à domino Euangelium prædicandū, quemadmodum suprà dixit: Non enim misit me Christus baptizare, sed euāgelizare. Nec alia erat prædicatio quæ animā posset regenerare, quàm hæc ipsa, ut & infrà dicet, Per Euangelium ego uos in Christo genui: nulla itē alia facit ad recens regeneratæ mentis refectionem. Nam & suprà dixit: Visum est Deo per stultitiam prædicationis saluos facere credentes. Et Rom.1. Euangelium est uirtus Dei ad saluandū credentes: Quis ergo est solidus cibus, quem infantes in Christo Corinthij non poterant capere & ferre? An alia quædam doctrina præter Euangelium Christi, quemadmodum aliud adulto datur cibi genus, quàm infanti? Eiusdē enim generis non sunt, lac & panis.
units.tr: "I fed you with milk, he says, and not with food." Third, we must ask which part of Christian teaching he means by the drink of milk and which by food. What could he first give them but what he had himself received from the Lord, and what could restore their strength? He had received from the Lord the Gospel to preach, as he said above: "For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel." Nor was there any other preaching that could regenerate the soul than this very one, as he says below: "Through the gospel I begot you in Christ." Nothing else serves to refresh a newly regenerated mind. He also said above: "It pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe." And Romans 1: "The gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes." What then is the solid food which the infants in Christ at Corinth could not take in and bear? Or is there some teaching other than the Gospel of Christ, just as one kind of food is given to an adult and another to an infant? For milk and bread are not of the same kind.

units.la: Nequaquam alia, sed eadem Euangelij doctrina & lac est & panis. Lac infantib. in Christo, panis iá adultis. Quomodo? Ita uidelicet, ut gloria gratiæ, potētiæ ac regni Dei in Christo latius & clarius exponatur adultis quàm rudibus adhuc & recētibus. Velut lac est, quâ do docetur, unum esse Deum, hunc mundi mi-sertum misisse filium in carnem, illumque no-stre salutis gratia tradidisse in morte, ut quot-quot in illum credunt, habeant uitā æternam, resipiscendum esse à uitæ pristinæ erroribus & moribus corruptis, baptizandum esse in no-men Christi, in remissionem peccatorum, cre-dendum esse mortuorum resurrectionem, & uitam æternam: item iudicium futurum uiuo-rum & mortuorum. Ista & consimilia, qualia omnino habet initialis etiamnum fidelium in stitutio Symbolum illud fidei Christianæ, la-ctis similitudine intelligenda sunt, non quod in se sint modica, sed quod primum simpliciter credenda non exacte intelligenda proponantur. Quata uero sit amplitudo & maiestas dispensationis regni Christi, quanta gloria bonitatis & potentiæ Dei, quantaq; illius sapientia in Christo, de quibus admonet nonnulla Apostolus Eph.1.2.3. Coloss.1.si quis statim ue-lit proponere ijs, qui recès in Christo sunt nati: perinde faciet, atq; si quis panem uelit sta-tim proponere infantibus.
units.tr: By no means is it another teaching; the same doctrine of the Gospel is both milk and bread. It is milk for infants in Christ, bread for adults. How so? Plainly, the glory of the grace, power and kingdom of God in Christ is set out more broadly and clearly to adults than to those who are still raw and newly converted. Milk is what teaches that there is one God, that out of his mercy for the world he sent his Son in the flesh, and gave him up to death for the grace of our salvation, so that whoever believes in him may have eternal life; that one must repent of the errors and corrupt morals of the former life; that one must be baptized in the name of Christ for the remission of sins; that one must believe in the resurrection of the dead and eternal life; and likewise in the future judgment of the living and the dead. These things, and others of the same kind, which the initial teaching of the faithful still contains, that Creed of the Christian faith, are to be understood by the likeness of milk, not because they are slight in themselves, but because they are put forward to be believed simply at first, not yet understood exactly. But how great is the breadth and majesty of the dispensation of Christ's kingdom, how great the glory of God's goodness and power, and how great his wisdom in Christ, about which the Apostle reminds us in some measure in Ephesians 1, 2, 3 and Colossians 1: whoever wishes at once to set these before those who are newly born in Christ will do no differently than if he wished at once to set bread before infants.

units.la: Ad Ebr.cap.5.& 6.ista apertius ac fusius tra-duntur, unde loci huius declaratio petenda est.
units.tr: In Hebrews chapters 5 and 6 these things are set out more plainly and at greater length, and from there the explanation of this passage is to be sought.

units.la: Et id quod Iohan.16. Christus dixit: Adhuc multa habeo uobis dicere, quæ non potestis portare modo. Adhuc infantes erant apostoli, lac bibebant, non solidum cibum edebant car-nales & ipsi, non quæ Dei, sed quæ hominum sunt sapientes: deinde & de primatu inter se contendentes, unde non poterant solidiorem cibum adhuc ferre. Poenitendum esse, & credendum Euangelio, adesse regnum Dei, hunc Iesum esse filium Dei in quo uno sit salus, utique acceperant, & confessi quoq; iam fuerant. Mysterium uero mortis Christi, resurrectionis, ascensionis & glorificationis: deinde rationem regni illius & dispensationem per uirtutē spiritus, quæ omnia post acceptum spiritum demum cognouerunt, nondum ferre poterant, quæ uelut solidus cibus erant.
units.tr: And what Christ said in John 16: "I still have many things to say to you, which you cannot bear now." The apostles were still infants: they drank milk and did not yet eat solid food; they too were still carnal, wise not in the things of God but in the things of men; and they were also contending among themselves about primacy, so they could not yet bear more solid food. That repentance must be made and the Gospel believed, that the kingdom of God is at hand, that this Jesus is the Son of God in whom alone is salvation, these they had certainly received, and had already confessed. But the mystery of Christ's death, resurrection, ascension and glorification, and then the nature of that kingdom and its dispensation through the power of the Spirit, all these they came to know only after they had received the Spirit. They could not yet bear these, which were like solid food.

units.la: Proinde qui hunc locum exponunt de ceremonijs ac ritibus ecclesiæ quasi discipuli tum nondum potuerint intelligere talia, plane ridi-culi sunt. Quemadmodum & illud pontificia sublimitate dignum est, quod 35.quæst.3. Quæ-dam lex, ubi præsens Apostoli locus citatur, per lac intelliguntur illicita initio concedenda, per solidum cibum grandiora postea graua-mina imponenda.
units.tr: Therefore those who explain this passage of the ceremonies and rites of the Church, as if the disciples at that time could not yet understand such things, are plainly ridiculous. Equally worthy of papal loftiness is what is found in 35 qu. 3, the canon "Quaedam lex," where this passage of the Apostle is cited: there milk is understood as the unlawful things that were to be conceded at first, and solid food as the heavier burdens imposed afterwards.

units.la: Itaque non est aliud atque aliud doctrinæ genus per lactis potum & solidum cibum intelligendum, sed plane idem, non re: sed auctu & explicatu diuersum, perinde atq; fides ipsa in Christum & cognitio regni eius: non est alia in imperfectis & alia in perfectioribus, sed omnino eadem, licet auctior in istis quam in illis. Ita Basilius de sua fide scribit epistola 79.
units.tr: So the teaching is not one kind through the drink of milk and another through solid food, but altogether the same. It differs not in substance but in growth and explanation, just as faith itself in Christ and knowledge of his kingdom do. It is not one thing in the imperfect and another in the more perfect, but entirely the same, though fuller in the latter than in the former. So Basil writes of his own faith in Letter 79.

units.la: ὦ ἀ ὅτι γὰρ τὸ σπέρμα ἀνξανόμενον, μᾶλλον ἢ ἀπὸ μικροῦ γίνεται ταύτην ἡ ἀλλὰ ἱ ἐκ ἐκ ἡ κατὰ γὰρ μεταβαλλόμενον, ἀλλ' ἀλλ' ἐξ αὐξησιν τὴν ἐπ' ἐκ λογίζεται ἀνθρώπων ἀλλ' ἢ ἐκ ἀρχῆς ἔν-
units.tr: ὦ ἀ ὅτι γὰρ τὸ σπέρμα ἀνξανόμενον, μᾶλλον ἢ ἀπὸ μικροῦ γίνεται ταύτην ἡ ἀλλὰ ἱ ἐκ ἐκ ἡ κατὰ γὰρ μεταβαλλόμενον, ἀλλ' ἀλλ' ἐξ αὐξησιν τὴν ἐπ' ἐκ λογίζεται ἀνθρώπων ἀλλ' ἢ ἐκ ἀρχῆς ἔν- [For the seed, as it grows, becomes greater rather than arising from something small; it does not become another thing by change, but the same seed is increased, and men do not reckon it as something else but as the same from the beginning.]

units.la: Non alia lux in oculos caeci incurrebat, cum homines uidebat ut arbores, & alia cum omnia recte cernebat: sed utrobiq; eadem, licet clarior postea quam antea: nec alia uidebat postea quam antea, sed eadem, uerum clarius quam antea. Eadem lux est quam uident infirmi oculi, eiusdemque solis, quam & unde uident sani: nec quicquā interest, nisi quod isti solis splendorem plenius intuetur, illi uero minus ferre possunt. Ad hunc modum habet & captus doctrinæ Euangelicæ in credentibus pro ratione auditorum dispensandæ.
units.tr: No other light fell into the eyes of the blind man when he saw men as trees, and another when he saw everything rightly. In both cases it was the same light, though clearer afterwards than before. Nor did he see something different afterwards, but the same things, only more clearly. It is the same light that weak eyes see by, and the same sun that healthy eyes see by and from. Nothing differs except that the healthy eyes look on the sun's brightness more fully, while the weak eyes can bear it less. In the same way, the capacity of evangelical teaching in believers is to be dispensed according to the measure of the hearers.

units.la: Nondum enim poteratis, imo ne nunc quidem adhuc potestis. Nā adhuc carnales estis.
units.tr: For you were not yet able, nay, not even now are you able. For you are still carnal.

units.la: Rationem subiungit, quare nondum potuerit illis loqui uelut spiritalibus. Nondum enim inquit poteratis, uidelicet capere, uel ferre. Nam tale quid subintelligendum est. Non dicit, Nondum enim poteram: sed, Nondum poteratis.
units.tr: He gives the reason why he could not yet speak to them as to spiritual people. For, he says, you were not yet able, that is, to grasp or to bear it; for something of this kind must be understood. He does not say, "For I was not yet able," but, "For you were not yet able."

units.la: IMO ne nunc quidē adhuc potestis, inquit. Deijcit hic factū eorum. Putabat enim se plurimū excreuisse rerum spiritalium intellectu, ita ut simplicitatem doctrinæ Euangelicæ sper-nerent, quam tamen nondum rite intellexe-rant, atq; eam ob causam ad sublimiora adspi-rarent intempestiuius, perinde atque in disci-plinarum studio plerunq; fieri uidemus, ut an-tequam prima elementa rite cognoscantur, ad ulteriora plerique properent. Traducit simul & pseudapostolorum temeritatem & infide-litatem, qui rudes adhuc à lactis cibo auoca-bant ad sua ipsorum figmenta, culpabiles pla-ne, etiamsi illos ad uera spiritalia percipienda intempestiuius prouocassent.
units.tr: "Nay, not even now are you able," he says. Here he casts down their state. For they thought they had grown greatly in the understanding of spiritual things, so that they despised the simplicity of the Gospel teaching, which nonetheless they had not yet properly understood; and for that reason they aspired to higher things too early, just as we commonly see in the study of the disciplines, where many hasten on to advanced matters before the first elements are properly known. At the same time he rebukes the rashness and faithlessness of the false apostles, who, while the people were still infants fed on milk, called them away to their own inventions; these men were plainly to blame, even though they urged them to grasp true spiritual things too early.

units.la: NAM adhuc carnales estis, inquit. Ratio est, quare nondum illos posse dicat. Taxat au-tem illorum ignauiam, quod non dicit, Nam carnales estis: sed, Nam adhuc carnales estis. Quasi dicat: Tempus quidem esset, ut solidio-rem cibum caperetis, uerū uestra ignauia fit, ut necdum illum capere queatis, quandoqui-dem perpetuo carnales esse pergitis. Sic Ebr. 5.dicit: Etenim cū deberetis esse magistri pro-pter tempus rursum indigetis, ut uos docea-mini quæ sunt elementa exordij sermonum Dei, & facti estis quibus lacte opus sit, non so-lido cibo.
units.tr: "For you are still carnal," he says. This is the reason why he says they were not yet able. He censures their sloth, and does not say, "For you are carnal," but, "For you are still carnal." As if he said: There was indeed time for you to receive firmer food, but your sloth is such that you cannot yet take it, since you persist in being carnal all the time. So Hebrews 5 says: "For when by now you ought to be teachers, you again need someone to teach you the elementary principles of the oracles of God, and you have come to need milk, not solid food."

units.la: Síquidem cum inter uos sit æmula-tio & contentio, & factiones, nōne car-nales estis?
units.tr: For while there is jealousy and strife and divisions among you, are you not carnal?

units.la: Probat arborem ex fructibus. Quod adhuc carnales sint, probat ex operib.carnis, de qui-bus uide Gal.5. inter quæ connumerantur & æmulatio, & contentio, & sectæ.
units.tr: He proves the tree from its fruits. That they are still carnal he proves from the works of the flesh, on which see Galatians 5, among which jealousy, strife and factions are numbered.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Obseruandum autem est, quare non obij-ciat fornicationis immunditiam, deinde & co-messationes, & quæ huiusmodi & ipsa sunt
units.tr: It should be observed why he does not charge them with the uncleanness of fornication, and then with drunken revelries and such things, which are themselves

units.la: opera carnis, cum æquè istis essent Corinthij obnoxij, ut infrà uidebimus cap.5.&11. Quid est quod ad probandum quod adhuc carnales sint, producit æmulationem, côtentionem, & factiones? Primum quia coeperat hoc malum ante omnia corrigere, ideo ista inducit. Deinde coepit autem illud ob id ante omnia corrigere, quod esset perniciosissimum, & præterea generalius. Nam fornicationi unus, & comessationibus diuites tantum leguntur obnoxij fuisse. Ideo particularibus malis reseruatis, primum, quod totum Christi corpus occupabat, emendare instituit. Quemadmodū enim periti medici est, eum morbum cum primis curare qui & perniciosior est, & non unius tantū membri, sed totius corporis uires populatur: ita & hoc loco faciendum erat prudēti Apostolo in curandis morbis animorum.
units.tr: works of the flesh, since the Corinthians were equally liable to these, as we shall see below in chapters 5 and 11. Why does he bring forward jealousy, strife and factions to prove that they are still carnal? First, because he had begun to correct this evil before all others, therefore he introduces these. Next, he began to correct this before all others for this reason: it was the most pernicious, and moreover more general. For fornication is read of as belonging to one man, and drunken revelries only to the rich. So, leaving particular evils aside, he set about first amending that which occupied the whole body of Christ. For just as a skilled physician takes first in hand that disease which is both more dangerous and wastes the strength not of one member but of the whole body, so the prudent Apostle had to do in this place in curing the diseases of souls.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Deinde & hoc est notandum, quàm errent, qui per contentionem putant posse ad rerum spiritalium cognitionem pertingi, cum hic Apostolus aperte doceat, per æmulationē, contentionem, & factiones, impediri cognitionē rerum spiritalium. Quare? Quia animi carnales sunt, nec apti ad percipiendū ea quæ sunt spiritalia, ideo quod carnalibus affectibus sint excæcati. Deinde quicquid traditur, non ita acceptatur ut veritas cognoscatur, & pietas prouehatur, sed ut contentio & factio foueatur. Exigit enim captus spiritalis doctrinæ animum limpidum ac purum, qui non fit carnalibus affectibus perturbatus. Talis autē nō est, qui spiritu æmulationis & contentionis laborat. Vnde est illud: Nimium altercando amittitur veritas.
units.tr: Next, this too must be noted: how wrongly those err who think that by contention one can attain knowledge of spiritual things, when the Apostle here plainly teaches that the knowledge of spiritual things is hindered by jealousy, strife and factions. Why? Because carnal minds are not fit to perceive the things that are spiritual, being blinded by carnal affections. Further, whatever is taught is not received so that the truth may be known and piety advanced, but so that contention and faction may be fostered. For the capacity of spiritual teaching requires a clear and pure mind, which is not disturbed by carnal affections. Yet he who labours under the spirit of jealousy and contention is not such a one. Hence the saying: "By too much quarrelling truth is lost."

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Notandum est etiam hoc loco, unde sint factiones & sectæ in ecclesia. Primum quidē ex carne, ut qui sectarij sunt, licet uideantur esse spiritalissimi, reuera tamen carnales existant. Propius autem ex zelo uel æmulatione, quando alius pro alio zelo ducitur. Nam hinc oriuntur contentiones, dum quisq; eum in quo gloriatur, cupit ad cœlum usq; euehere, reliquos ad infernū deturbare. Et ubi ita contenditur, statim nascūtur sectę & factiones, ut scindatur unitas corporis Christi. Proinde in hoc est Apostolus, ut auferat primum istud æmulationis studiū, quod sciat illo sublato, cito Corinthios posse ad concordiam reuocari.
units.tr: It should also be noted here whence factions and sects arise in the Church. First indeed from the flesh: those who are sectarian, though they may seem most spiritual, are in fact carnal. More immediately, however, from zeal or rivalry, when one man is led by one zeal and another by another. For from this strife arises: each man wishes to raise to heaven him in whom he glories, and to hurl the rest down to hell. And where people contend in this way, sects and factions are at once born, so that the unity of the body of Christ is torn apart. Therefore the Apostle sets himself first to remove this zeal for rivalry, knowing that once it is removed the Corinthians can quickly be called back to concord.

units.la: ET secundum hominem ambulatis? Ergo carnalem esse, idem est atq; secundum hominem ambulare, id est, humanis duci affectibus. Nec carnē nec humanam naturam damnat Apostolus, sed illius corruptionem. Illam notabat & Christus in Petro Matth.16.cum dicebat, Abi retro me Satan. Nō enim sapis quæ Dei, sed quæ hominum.
units.tr: "And do you walk according to man?" To be carnal is the same as walking according to man, that is, being led by human affections. The Apostle condemns neither the flesh nor human nature, but its corruption. Christ too noted this in Peter, Matthew 16, when he said, "Get behind me, Satan. For you are not minding the things of God, but the things of men."

units.la: ETENIM cum dicat aliquis, Ego quidem sum Pauli, &c. Probat eos esse æmulatores contentiosos & sectarios, ideoque & carnales
units.tr: "For when someone says, 'I indeed am of Paul,' etc." He proves that they are rivals, contentious and sectarian, and therefore carnal,

units.la: ex ipso facto, quod negare non poterant. Atqui redit ad institutum, quod cap.1. coepit.
units.tr: from the very fact itself, which they could not deny. But he now returns to the subject he began in chapter 1.

units.la: Quis igitur est Paulus? Quis Apollos? nisi ministri, per quos credidistis?
units.tr: Who then is Paul? Who is Apollos? Only ministers, through whom you came to believe?

units.la: Posteaquam per translationem causam imperfectioris doctrinæ, quam contemnebant saturi Corinthij, imbecillo illorum captui deputauit, causatus eos ut carnales & infantes in Christo sublimiora capere non potuisse, neque dum etiam posse, ut qui adhuc carnales sint, greditur ad alteram huius capitis partem, nimiam & præposteram admirationem pseudapostolorum demoliturus, quæ plurimū faciebat ad studium sectarum, quo laborabant.
units.tr: Having shown, by way of a transition, that the cause of the less perfect teaching, which the satisfied Corinthians despised, lay in the weakness of their understanding, and having explained that they, as carnal and infants in Christ, could not yet grasp higher things, he now turns to the other part of this chapter, intending to overthrow the excessive and absurd admiration for the false apostles, which greatly fostered the factional spirit in which they were engaged.

units.la: Demolitur autem eam ratione cùm efficaci tum prudenti. Efficaci, per id, quod ostendit quo loco haberi & cuius æstimari debeant Christi ministri. Quicquid enim nimium est, nō potest melius restringi, quàm si ad iustum modum reuocetur. Est suus cuiq; æstimationis, honoris ac dignitatis modus, ad quem, si quid accesserit superflui, reformandū est. Prudenti ratione utitur in eo quod non aliorum, sed suam ipsius & Apollo personam inducit, in quibus declaret, quàm non debeat quisquam plus æquo de Christi sentire ministro: quod ob id facit, ne uideatur non tam ipsorum mederi malo, quàm suæ consulere gloriæ, & ut hanc causam alioqui periculosam, dexterè tractare queat. Et hoc est quod confideter dicit: Quis est Paulus? Quis est Apollos? quod cum minore suspicione facit q; si diceret, Qui sunt isti uestri apostoli, quos admiramini & tantū non adoratis? Vbi non putaretur dicturus unquam, Quis est Paulus?
units.tr: He overthrows it by a method that is both effective and prudent. It is effective because he shows what place Christ's ministers should be given and by whom they ought to be valued. Whatever is excessive cannot be restrained better than by being brought back to its proper measure. Every esteem, honour and dignity has its due limit, and if anything beyond it is added, it must be corrected. His method is prudent in that he does not bring in others as examples, but himself and Apollos, and in them he shows how no one ought to think more highly of a minister of Christ than is fitting. He does this so that he may not seem to be concerned more for his own glory than for the cure of their evil, and so that he may handle a matter otherwise dangerous with skill. This is why he says so confidently: Who is Paul? Who is Apollos? He does this with less suspicion than if he had said, "Who are these apostles of yours, whom you admire and almost worship?" In that case it would not have seemed that he would ever say, "Who is Paul?"

units.la: Illud autem, QVIS est Paulus? Quis est Apollos? Vetus sic habet: Quid est Paulus? Quid est Apollos? Verū Græca habent, τίς ἐστιν, Quis est: quod tamen ipso Apostoli sensu nihil aliud est, quàm quid est, id est, cuius momenti est, uidelicet, ut dignus sit, cui nomen det quisquam, uelut religionis authori. Innuit autem neminem apostolorum & ministrorum Christi tanti esse debere, ut ipsius se quisquá esse di cat, cum omnes simus Christi. Vrget itaq; rogādo, Quis est Paulus? Quis est Apollos? quē admodum solemus rogare de illis, quinā sint, quos uidemus plus æquo coli, & supra modū extolli.
units.tr: But the Latin Vulgate reads: "What is Paul? What is Apollos?" The Greek has "Who is" (τίς ἐστιν), which in the apostle's own sense means nothing other than "what is," that is, of what weight he is, namely, whether he is worthy that anyone should give him a name as the founder of a religion. He implies that no apostle or minister of Christ ought to be so great that anyone should call himself his, since we are all Christ's. So he presses the question: Who is Paul? Who is Apollos? as we are accustomed to ask about those whom we see honoured beyond measure and exalted above what is proper.

units.la: NISI ministri.] Hic est modus æstimandi apostolos. Ministri sunt, non domini. At ministrorum non est trahere post se discipulos, nec illis quisquam licite nomen dare potest, ut illorum esse se dicat, cum solius sit domini, qui caput est & princeps electorū omnium. Sic in frā cap.4. Sic nos existimet homo tanquā ministros Christi.
units.tr: BUT ministers. This is the measure for valuing the apostles: they are ministers, not lords. But it is not the business of ministers to draw disciples after themselves, nor may anyone rightly give them a name, so that he calls himself theirs, since that belongs to the Lord alone, who is the head and prince of all the elect. So below in chapter 4: "Let a man so regard us as ministers of Christ."

units.la: PER quos credidistis.] Non, In quos credidistis: nec, Qui uos ad fidē adduxerunt: sed, Per quorum ministerium uos Deus ad fidem filij sui adduxit. ὑπηρέτης, inquit Chrysostomus. {Greek} ἀλλ' ἡ παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ αὐτὰ καὶ Ἀπόλλων. At be neficij gloria, nō ministro, sed ipsi benefactori ac largitori debetur.
units.tr: THROUGH whom you believed. He does not say "in whom you believed," nor "who brought you to the faith," but "through whose ministry God brought you to the faith of his Son." "Servant" (ὑπηρέτης), says Chrysostom. [ὑπηρέτης] ... "But God gives the growth, and Apollos..." [ἀλλ' ἡ παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ αὐτὰ καὶ Ἀπόλλων]. But the glory of the benefit is owed not to the minister but to the benefactor and giver himself.

units.la: OBSER. I.
units.tr: OBSERVATION I.

units.la: QVIS est Paulus? Admonemur hoc loco q̄ liberè exi<bl>s</bl>timatione eorum eleuare debea-mus, qui supra quàm par est in ecclesia Christi extolluntur, etiamsi sint ueri Christi ministri, imò apostoli, per quos primum in Christum credere coeperimus. Audiant igitur qui Petri apostoli uolunt esse discipuli & successores, il-lumque sic constituunt ecclesiæ caput, ut pri-mum uniuersalis ecclesiæ in successores suos quasi hæreditario transmittere potuerit. Dicant nobis, quis sit Petrus. An non minister Christi? In hoc illum ordine relinquant. Quid uero de illis dicendum est, qui cum nō sint mi-nistri Christi, nec aliquè ad fidem Christi ad-ducant, nihilo tamen minus dominium sibij-psis uindicant in ecclesia, & quiduis mandan-di ac præcipiendi potestatem? Si recte dixit A-postolus: Quis est Paulus? Quis est Apollos? quanto iustius nos dicemus: Quis est iste pon-tifex? Qui sunt isti equestres Episcopi, nisi do-mini ecclesiarum, per quos non credidimus, sed perditi sumus?
units.tr: WHO is Paul? Here we are reminded that we must freely lower the esteem of those who are exalted in the Church of Christ beyond what is fitting, even if they are true ministers of Christ, indeed apostles, through whom we first began to believe in Christ. Let those hear this who want to be disciples and successors of the apostle Peter, and who set him up as the head of the Church in such a way that he could have handed on the primacy of the universal Church to his successors as though by hereditary right. Let them tell us who Peter is. Is he not a minister of Christ? In this rank let them leave him. But what must be said about those who, though they are not ministers of Christ and do not bring anyone to the faith of Christ, nevertheless claim lordship over the Church for themselves, and the power to command and order whatever they please? If the apostle rightly said, "Who is Paul? Who is Apollos?", how much more justly shall we say, "Who is this pontiff? Who are these equestrian bishops, except lords of the churches, through whom we did not believe but were lost?"

units.la: OBSER. II.
units.tr: OBSERVATION II.

units.la: Notandum est, quod dicit, Per quos credi-distis. Videtur extenuare ministerium uerbi: uerùm si recte reputes, illud pulchrè commen-dat ab effectu. Licet enim non sit primaria fi-dei causa, sed secundaria & instrumentalis, ma-gnum tamen uel hoc est esse instrumentum fi-dei ad salutē. Nam ita uisum est Deo per stulti-tiam prædicationis saluos facere credentes, ut ad Rom.10. merito prophetæ exclamatio-nem, Quàm pulchri sunt pedes annunciantiū pacem, annunciantium bona, ministris Euan-gelij applicet. Et hoc pacto, ubi uidetur se & Apollo deijcere, non parū sibi honoris contra contemptum quo laborare coeperat apud Co-rinthios uindicat, per id quod effectum prædi-cationis suæ commemorat, dicens, Per quos credidistis. Et ideo non dicit, Qui uobis annū ciarunt fidē Christi: sed, Per quos credidistis.
units.tr: It must be noted that he says, "through whom you believed." This seems to belittle the ministry of the word, but if you consider it rightly, he commends it finely from its effect. For although it is not the primary cause of faith but a secondary and instrumental one, it is nevertheless a great thing, even just to be an instrument of faith for salvation. For it has pleased God, through the foolishness of preaching, to save those who believe, so that the prophet's exclamation in Romans 10, "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring the good news of peace," rightly applies to the ministers of the gospel. In this way, where he seems to lower himself and Apollos, he claims for them no small honour against the contempt into which they had begun to fall among the Corinthians, by mentioning the effect of their preaching: "through whom you believed." So he does not say, "who announced to you the faith of Christ," but, "through whom you believed."

units.la: ET ut cuique dominus dedit.] Græce, {Greek} Et cuique sicut dominus dedit. Videtur aliquid desiderari, uel, ut Eras-mus reddidit, legendum esse, Et ut cuique do-minus dedit, {Greek}. Similis loquutio, ijsdemq; uerbis est Rom.12.
units.tr: AND as the Lord gave to each. The Greek reads: "And to each as the Lord gave." Something seems to be lacking, or, as Erasmus rendered it, it should be read, "And as the Lord gave to each," which is the Greek. A similar expression, in the same words, occurs in Romans 12.

units.la: Deinde ita posita est hæc particula, ut tam ad credentes Corinthios quàm ad ministros Christi apostolos Paulū & Apollo referri pos-sit, uel certe ad utrosque: ut intelligas Corin-thios tantū fidei adhibuisse prædicationi Apo-stolicæ, quantum gratiæd ominus largitus sit, & rursus apostolos tantum prædicando esse-cisse, quantum & ipsis à domino gratiæ & esse-ctus datum sit. Nam utrinque opus est uirtute Christi, apostolis, ut fructum adferant, sicut Io-han.15. dicit: Sine me nihil potestis facere, au-
units.tr: Then this particle is placed so that it can refer both to the believing Corinthians and to Paul and Apollos as ministers of Christ, or certainly to both together, so that you understand that the Corinthians gave to the apostolic preaching as much faith as the Lord had granted them grace for, and again that the apostles accomplished by preaching as much as was given to them by the Lord in grace and effect. For on both sides the power of Christ is needed: the apostles, to bear fruit, as John 15 says, "Without me you can do nothing";

units.la: ditoribus, ut credant. Nisi enim illis cor aperi-riat, ut est in exemplo Lyddæ purpurissæ Act. 16. frustra prædicauerit Apostolus.
units.tr: and the hearers, to believe. For unless the Lord opens their heart, as in the example of Lydia the seller of purple in Acts 16, the apostle will preach in vain.

units.la: Mihi uero uidetur simplicius, ut intelliga-mus eum loqui de suo & Apollo ministerio: & quia dixerat, Per quos credidistis, effectus illius gloriam dare Deo. Quasi dicat: Non so-lum ministri sumus, non domini, sed nec quic-quam præstare & efficere possumus: nisi quan-tum cuique dederit dominus, ut gloria sit non nostra, sed domini.
units.tr: But to me it seems simpler that we understand him to speak of his own and Apollos's ministry, and because he had said "through whom you believed," he gives the glory of its effect to God. As if he said: We are not only ministers, not lords, but we can accomplish and effect nothing except as much as the Lord has given to each, so that the glory may be not ours but the Lord's.

units.la: Ego plantaui, Apollos rigauit, Deus autem incrementum dedit.
units.tr: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase.

units.la: Explicat distributionem quam coepit in eo quod dixit, Sicut unicuique dedit dominus. Quasi dicat: Mihi dedit ut plantarem, Apollo ut rigaret, incrementum ipse, utriusque operi adiecit. Plátauerat ipse quia primus illic Chri-stum prædicauerat. Apollos postea eos qui cre-derant in fide Christi confirmauerat, ideo di-cit illum rigasse à se plantata. Est autem hæc simi-litudo plantandi & rigandi omnium pulcher-rima, & ad causæ declarationem accommodis-sima ac luculentissima, in qua, si recte reputes, hæc tria habentur.
units.tr: He explains the distribution he began when he said, "As the Lord gave to each." As if to say: the Lord gave me to plant and Apollos to water, but he himself added the increase to both labours. Paul had planted there because he was the first to preach Christ in that place. Apollos afterwards strengthened those who had believed in Christ, so Paul says that he watered what Paul had planted. This likeness of planting and watering is the most beautiful of all, and very well suited and very clear for explaining the matter. If you consider it rightly, three things are contained in it.

units.la: Primum declarat ratione ministerij uerbi, quod sit opus ministrorum Christi, dum illis tribuit plantationem & rigationem, faciês ex eis cultores hortorum & pomœrij regni cœle-stis, quorum geminum munus est. Aut enim plantant, hoc est, quod fyluestre est, uelut de oleastro sumptū, transferunt & in serūt oleæ: aut quod plantatum est, rigant, id est, fouent & prouehunt, ut fructum adferat in usum do-mini. Perinde omnino habet & uerbi minis-terium. Minister enim Christi, uel è regno Sata-næ translatas animas, ueluti surculos, inserit regno Christi, cum primum ad fidem illius præ-dicatione uerbi adducit incredulos, & per reli-pisicentiam ad innocentiam uitæ peccatores, uel eos quos Christo lucrifecit, aut ab alijs lu-crifacti sunt, uelut rigat, fouet ac prouehit, dū admonitionibus & exhortationibus in fide Christi, spe, dilectione, & patientia corrobo-rat, ne tentationibus uicti retrolabātur, & flac-cescentes pereant. In his duobus comprehen-ditur uniuersum ministrorum opus, quod per petuo uersandum est. Cogitemus autē, quan-tum exigat diligentiæ, studij ac sedulitatis in-defessæ, cultura illa hortorum & uinearum, ut inde colligamus, quàm fit officiosa & negocio sa plantandarū & rigandarū animarum cura.
units.tr: First, it sets out the nature of the ministry of the Word: it is the work of Christ's ministers, since he assigns to them planting and watering, making them tenders of the gardens and orchards of the heavenly kingdom, whose task is twofold. For either they plant, that is, they take what is wild, as it were from the wild olive, and transplant and graft it into the olive; or they water what has been planted, that is, they nourish and advance it, so that it bears fruit for the Lord's use. The ministry of the Word is wholly similar. For the minister of Christ either grafts souls, transferred from the kingdom of Satan like shoots, into the kingdom of Christ, when first by preaching the Word he brings unbelievers to faith in him and sinners by repentance to innocence of life; or he waters, nourishes and advances those whom he has won for Christ, or who have been won by others, when by admonitions and exhortations he strengthens them in faith in Christ, in hope, love and patience, so that they are not overcome by temptations and fall back and perish through weakness. In these two things the whole work of ministers is comprehended, and it must be carried on continually. Let us consider how much diligence, zeal and untiring care that cultivation of gardens and vineyards requires, and from this let us infer how laborious and demanding is the care of planting and watering souls.

units.la: Deinde, cauet hæc similitudo, ne nimium detur ministris, quod tum faciebat Corinthij, & post Corinthios pontificij. Quid enim facit, qui plantat: quid, qui rigat, nisi accedat incre-mentum à Deo? quod tamen nullo modo est in manu siue plantantis siue rigantis, sed om-nium liberrime & absolutissime in unius ma-nu & arbitrio Dei. Inanis labor scilicet est, si plantes & riges, nisi detur incrementū à Deo. Igitur ois gloria eius est qui dat incrementum. Tertio
units.tr: Next, this likeness guards against giving too much to ministers, which the Corinthians did, and after the Corinthians the Papists. For what does he who plants do, or he who waters, unless the increase comes from God? Yet this is in no way in the hand either of the planter or of the waterer, but in the hand and will of God alone, most freely and absolutely. It is plainly a vain labour if you plant and water, unless the increase is given by God. Therefore all the glory belongs to him who gives the increase. Third.

units.la: Tertiò, cauet & hoc, ne contemnatur è regione opus ministerij, dum ostendit, quàm sit ad salutem necessarium. Licet enim sine incremento, nec qui plantat, nec qui rigat, quicquâ efficiat, incrementum etiam non sit in manu plantantis neque rigantis, sed Dei: nihilominus ita diuinitus comparatum est, ut incrementum non detur, nisi plantetur & rigetur. Et huius gratia nemo sapiens plantandi & rigandi munus contemnit, si modo fructum quaerat.
units.tr: Thirdly, it also guards against the ministry of the Word being despised, while it shows how necessary it is for salvation. For although without the increase neither he who plants nor he who waters accomplishes anything, and the increase is not in the hand of the planter or the waterer but of God, nevertheless it has been so ordained by God that the increase is not given unless there is planting and watering. And for the sake of this, no wise person despises the office of planting and watering, if indeed he seeks fruit.

units.la: Igitur hac similitudine Apostolus prudentissime ita pseudapostolorum æstimationem præposteram deiecit, ut iuxta ministerium uerbi contemptui non reddiderit obnoxium: deinde ministerij rationem ita uindicauit, ut nihil gloriæ diuinæ derogarit.
units.tr: Therefore by this likeness the Apostle most wisely overthrew the absurd esteem of the false apostles, so as not to make the ministry of the Word liable to contempt; and then he so vindicated the nature of the ministry that he took nothing from the divine glory.

units.la: Itaque neque qui plantat, est aliquid, neque qui rigat, sed qui dat incrementum Deus.
units.tr: So then neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.

units.la: Collectio est ex præmissis, de ministerij ratione & effectu, ei respondens, quo supra dixit: Quis est Paulus? Quis est Apollos? Nam ibi inconsulte dixisset, Paulus nihil est, Apollos nihil est. Verum ubi declarauit utriusque opus & effectum in domino, quàm omnia pendeant à domini gratia & virtute, tum secure intulit, Ita que qui plantat nihil est, &c. Hoc est, non est, tanti momenti, ut ipsi adscribatur operis effectus. Si qui plantauit, & qui rigauit, nihil sunt, quid iam sunt pseudapostoli æstimandi?
units.tr: This is a conclusion drawn from what has gone before, concerning the nature and effect of the ministry, and it answers to what he said above: "Who is Paul? Who is Apollos?" For there he would have spoken carelessly if he had said, "Paul is nothing, Apollos is nothing." But once he has shown how both their work and its effect depend in the Lord, and how everything hangs on the grace and power of the Lord, then he confidently concludes, "So then he who plants is nothing," etc. That is, he is not of such importance that the effect of the work should be ascribed to him. If he who planted and he who watered are nothing, what then are the false apostles to be esteemed?

units.la: SED qui dat incrementum Deus, inquit.] Hic non est resumendum illud, est aliquid: sed est omnia, ut illi debeatur quod pseudapostolis dabatur.
units.tr: "But God who gives the increase," he says. Here that phrase "is something" is not to be taken up again, but "is everything," so that what was given to the false apostles may be owed to him.

units.la: Diligenter notandum est, quod non simpliciter dicit, sed Deus: neque, sed qui incrementum potest dare Deus: sed, qui dat incrementum Deus. Non solum potest dare incrementum plantatis à nobis & irrigatis, sed dat etiam sicuti reipsa uidemus, & sic dat, ut nō sinat nos frustra plantare & rigare. Itaq; si quem à studio plantandi & rigandi abstterret, quod dixit, Neque qui plantat est aliquid, neque qui rigat: hunc in officio retineat quod subijcit, Sed Deus qui dat incrementum. Sicut & illud, quod non dixit, neq; qui plantat efficit aliquid, neq; qui rigat: sed neq; qui plantat est aliquid, neq; qui rigat. Aliud est nihil efficere plantando & rigando, & aliud nihil esse. Minister Christi non plantat frustra, quia Deus dat incrementum. Frustra plantaret, si Deus incrementum non daret. Quamuis autem per incrementum à Deo datum utiliter plantet, nihil tamen est: hoc est, non is est, cui gloria debeatur incrementi, non est nisi minister operationis Dei. Hæc cogitet Christi minister, quo in officio suo constanter pergat.
units.tr: It must be carefully noted that he does not simply say "God," but "God who gives the increase"; not "God who can give the increase," but "God who gives the increase." God not only can give increase to what we have planted and watered, but he also gives it, as we indeed see in fact, and he gives it in such a way that he does not allow us to plant and water in vain. Therefore, if anyone is frightened away from the work of planting and watering by what he said, "Neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters," let him be kept in his duty by what he adds, "But God who gives the increase." Likewise, he did not say, "Neither he who plants effects anything, nor he who waters," but "Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters." It is one thing to accomplish nothing by planting and watering, and another thing to be nothing. The minister of Christ does not plant in vain, because God gives the increase. He would plant in vain if God did not give the increase. Yet although he plants usefully through the increase given by God, he is nevertheless nothing: that is, he is not the one to whom the glory of the increase is due; he is only a minister of God's working. The minister of Christ should consider this, so that he may persevere constantly in his office.

units.la: Cæterum is qui plantat, & is qui rigat, unum sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, he who plants and he who waters are one.

units.la: Quomodo unum sunt, cum dixerit iam, Neque qui plantat est aliquid, neque qui rigat? Si nihil sunt, quomodo unum aliquid sunt? Nihil sunt, id est nullius momenti, ob id quod per se nihil possunt, nec quicquam efficiunt, nisi incrementum detur à Deo. Vnum sunt, id est, diuersi non sunt, sed idem: Idem sunt primum, quod uterque minister Christi est: deinde & scopo idem sunt. Nam utetque ad eundem finem spectat, ad ædificationem ui delicet corporis Christi. Tertio & æstimatione idem sunt, ut neuter neutri sit præferendus. Quod si qui plantat & qui rigat unum sunt, ut nec qui plantauit, sit ei qui postea rigat præferendus: quomodo is qui rigat præferendus putabitur ei qui plantauit? Si præferendus non est alter alteri, quomodo ergo dicebant Corinthij, Ego sum Pauli, ego sum Apollo? Arguit ergo ab æqualitate ministrorum Christi, plurimum delinquere sectarios, qui præpostera admiratione ita de quibusdam ministris gloriantur, ut & nomina illis dent, & reliquos fastidiant.
units.tr: How are they one, when he has just said, "neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters"? If they are nothing, how are they one thing? They are nothing, that is, of no account, because by themselves they can do nothing and achieve nothing unless God gives the increase. They are one, that is, they are not different but the same. First, they are the same in that each is a minister of Christ. Second, they are the same in purpose, for each looks to the same end, namely the building up of the body of Christ. Third, they are the same in esteem, so that neither is to be preferred to the other. But if he who plants and he who waters are one, so that the one who planted is not to be preferred to the one who later waters, how will the one who waters be thought preferable to the one who planted? If one is not to be preferred to the other, how then could the Corinthians say, "I am of Paul," "I am of Apollos"? Therefore by appealing to the equality of Christ's ministers he shows that those factions greatly err, who, with a perverse admiration, so boast of certain ministers that they give them names and despise the rest.

units.la: Vnusquisq; tamen suam mercedem accipiet, iuxta suum laborem.
units.tr: Yet each one shall receive his own reward, according to his own labour.

units.la: Correctio est. Non enim per omnia idem sunt qui plantat & qui rigat. Nam licet ministerij, scopi, & æstimationis gratia pares sint, studio tamen & labore plerunque dispares sunt: ut & de seipso dixerit Paulus alicubi, Plus omnibus laboraui. Hoc est, quod dicit, Vnusquisque tamen suam mercedem accipiet, iuxta suum, nō iuxta alterius laborem: fidem, studium, ac diligentiam.
units.tr: This is a correction. For he who plants and he who waters are not the same in every respect. Although they are equal in respect of ministry, purpose and esteem, they are for the most part unequal in zeal and labour. So Paul also said of himself somewhere, "I have laboured more than all." That is what he means: "Yet each one shall receive his own reward, according to his own, not another's, labour, that is, his faith, zeal and diligence."

units.la: OBSER. I.
units.tr: OBSERVATION I.

units.la: Si quisque suam mercedem accipiet iuxta laborem suum, ergo qui minus laborat, licet sit unum ministerij, scopi, & æstimationis gratia cum eo qui multum laborat, coram Deo tamen illi par non est. Et rursus, qui plus laborat, plus etiam mercedis accipiet. Facit hoc ad intendendum studia & laborem ministrorum, ne quisquam putet esse laborem suum coram domino inanem.
units.tr: If each one shall receive his reward according to his own labour, then he who labours less, although he is equal to the one who labours much in ministry, purpose and esteem, is nevertheless not equal to him before God. And again, he who labours more will also receive a greater reward. This serves to spur on the zeal and labour of ministers, so that no one thinks his labour is empty before the Lord.

units.la: De mercede non est opus hic multis disputare. Neq; hinc potest colligi, quenquâ ex suis uiribus aliquid posse promereri, ut Deus iure cogatur aliquid illi dare mercedis.
units.tr: There is no need to dispute much here about reward. Nor can it be inferred from this that anyone can merit anything by his own strength, so that God is obliged by right to give him any reward.

units.la: Nemo enim quicquam habet, quod à Deo non acceperit, nemo quicquam potest, nisi Deus det & uelle & perficere. Vnde & hic Apostolus dixit, Vt cuique dominus dedit. Itaq; nihil aliud facit Deus quàm quod suaipsius dona & opera in nobis coronat. Vt recte dixerit Augustinus libro primo Confessionum, capite quarto: Reddis debita nemini quicquam debens.
units.tr: For no one has anything that he has not received from God; no one can do anything unless God grants both to will and to perform. Hence the Apostle also said here, "as the Lord has given to each." Thus God does nothing other than crown his own gifts and works in us. As Augustine rightly said in the first book of his Confessions, chapter four: "You repay debts, owing nothing to anyone."

units.la: Est igitur gratiæ Dei, quod mercedem daturus est, non nostri meriti, quod illam accepturi sumus. Neque hinc colligi debet, licet tum esse, ut quisquâ Deo mercedis gratia ser- {A}uiat. Nam id esset mercenarium agere, non filium, in domo Dei. Deinde esset admodum iniquum, si mercedem poscerct is, qui de suo nihil contulit, sed omnia ab eo accepit, à quo mercedem poscit. Sic Christus dicit: Si omnia fecerit as, dicite, inutiles serui sumus.
units.tr: It is therefore by the grace of God that he is going to give a reward, not by our merit that we are going to receive it. Nor should it be inferred from this, although it may be so, that anyone should serve God for the sake of reward. For that would be to act as a hireling, not as a son, in the house of God. Moreover, it would be extremely unjust if he who has contributed nothing of his own, but has received everything from him from whom he demands the reward, were to demand it. So Christ says: "When you have done all things, say: we are unprofitable servants."

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Obseruandum autem & hoc est, quod non dicit, unusquisque tamè propriam mercedem accipiet iuxta fructum suum quem adfert, sed iuxta laborem. Multum laborarunt prophetæ, & parum fructus attulerunt propter immensam populi malitiam. Merces igitur non fructus quantitati deputatur, sed laboris. Licet qui multum fructus adfert domino, suo sit potiturus honore, ut est in parabola de dispensatis talentis: hinc tamen non sequitur, in praeiudicium cessurum ac detrimentum operantis, si propter telluris malitiam fructus non respondeat labori. Incrementum est Dei, quod suæ libertati dispensandum reseruauit, ita & fructus. Nostrum est, ut diligenter laboremus in uinea domini, etsi datur multû adferre fructus, licebit de eo gaudere coram domino. Sin minus, nihilo secius operis nostri rationem habebit dominus.
units.tr: This also must be observed: he does not say that each shall receive his own reward according to the fruit he brings, but according to his labour. The prophets laboured much and brought forth little fruit because of the immense wickedness of the people. Reward is therefore assigned not to the quantity of fruit but to the labour. Although he who brings much fruit to the Lord will obtain his own honour, as in the parable of the talents entrusted to servants, it does not follow from this that the one who works will suffer prejudice or loss if, because of the wickedness of the soil, the fruit does not match the labour. The increase belongs to God, who has reserved its distribution to his own freedom, and so too the fruit. It is ours to labour diligently in the Lord's vineyard; if it is granted to bring forth much fruit, we may rejoice in it before the Lord. But if not, the Lord will nonetheless take account of our work.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Non debet populus discernere inter ministros Dei, & de illorum differentia iudicare. Neque enim ipsius, sed Dei est iudicare, quantû quisque fidei, studij, laboris ac diligentiæ impendat, qui & solus omnium pectora nouit, & scit quid cuique, & quantum dederit. Ergo qui discernit inter Christi ministros, alienum à se opus facit. Et haec de re infra cap. 4. admonebit, ubi col ligit: Proinde ne ante tempus quicquam iudicemus, antequam ueniat dominus.
units.tr: The people ought not to distinguish between the ministers of God or judge their difference. For it is not for them but for God to judge how much faith, zeal, labour and diligence each one expends; he alone knows the hearts of all, and knows what and how much he has given to each. Therefore he who distinguishes between Christ's ministers does work that is not his own. And he will admonish about this matter below in chapter 4, where he concludes: "Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes."

units.la: IIII.

Suggillat etiam studia pseudapostolorum qui non hoc curabant, ut opus suum approbarent domino, cuius solius est dare cuique competentem mercedem, sed gloriam ab hominibus quærebant, quibus sese approbabant, more pharisæorum, Matth. 6.
units.tr: He also rebukes the efforts of the false apostles, who did not care to have their work approved by the Lord, to whom alone it belongs to give each man his proper reward, but sought glory from men, by whom they wished to be approved, in the manner of the Pharisees (Matth. 6.).

units.la: Et enim Dei sumus cooperarij, Dei agricolatio, Dei ædificatio estis.
units.tr: For we are God's fellow workers; you are God's field, God's building.

units.la: Hoc referendum est ad id quod dixit: Qui plantat & qui rigat unum sunt, ut illud: Vnusquisque tamen sicut dominus dedit, sit uelut parenthesis uice adiectum. Declarat autem quomodo unum sint, qui plantat & qui rigat. Etenim, inquit, cooperarij Dei sumus utriq;, tam qui rigat, quàm qui plantat. Deinde & uos, in quibus ædificandis & colendis laboramus, Dei estis agricolatio & ædificatio. Quemadmodum itaque qui domino cuipiam ad agricolationem ministrant, licet alius alio studiosius id faciat, omnes tamen unum sunt: primum propter domini cui ministrant, unitatem, de-
units.tr: This must be referred to what he said: "He who plants and he who waters are one," while the words "yet each shall receive his own reward according to his own labour" are added as a kind of parenthesis. He explains how he who plants and he who waters are one. For, he says, we are both God's fellow-workers, both he who waters and he who plants. Next, you also, in whose building and cultivation we labour, are God's field and God's building. Just as those who serve some master in cultivating his field, although one does it more eagerly than another, are nevertheless all one: first, because of the unity of the master whom they serve; then, because of the end of the work; and thirdly, on this account too, that the field or building belongs to the master: so he joins the ministers of Christ as well, so that they are one, because they are ministers of one Lord, and all alike are his fellow-workers, because they are in the same ministry; and since they themselves are believers,

units.la: inde & operis finem, tertiò & hoc nomine quod ager seu ædificium domini est: ita coniungit ministros Christi quoque, ut unum sint, quia unius domini sunt ministri, æquè omnes illius cooperarij, quia in eodem sunt ministerio: & quoniam ipsi credentes, in quibus laboratur, sunt domini.
units.tr: inde also from the end of the work; thirdly, also on this account, that the field or building belongs to the Lord. So he joins the ministers of Christ together as well, so that they are one: because they are ministers of one Lord, all equally are his fellow workers, because they are in the same ministry, and because the believers themselves, among whom the labour is done, are the Lord's.

units.la: Vide ergo quàm absurdum fuerit, quod alius dicebat, ego sum Pauli: alius, ego sum Apollo, cum omnes essent Dei: nec essent unius ministri tantum, sed simul omnium opus, veluti si pars ædificij dicat, ego sum lapidicidæ: pars dicat, ego sum fabri lignarij: pars, ego sum fabri ferrarij, cum singulæ domus partes sint nec huius nec illius, sed ipsius domini, cui ædificantur. Tantudem ergo est, quod hac similitudine declarat, ac si dicat: Nos non sumus domini, sed ministri. Operamur non nobis, sed domino. Vos non estis nostri, sed domini. Cur ergo uos addicitis ministris, duplici nomine peccantes: primum, quod quæ domini sunt, ministris attribuitis: deinde, quod ministrorum unitatem & æqualitatem scinditis, imò & ipsum opus domini, quod estis uos, diuiditis.
units.tr: See then how absurd it was for one to say, "I am of Paul," and another, "I am of Apollos," when all of them belonged to God. They were not merely the servants of one man but together the work of all, just as if one part of a building were to say, "I am the stonemason's," another, "I am the carpenter's," and another, "I am the blacksmith's," when each part of the house belongs neither to this man nor to that, but to the lord for whom it is being built. So what he expresses by this comparison amounts to the same as saying: "We are not lords, but ministers. We work not for ourselves, but for the Lord. You are not ours, but the Lord's. Why then do you attach yourselves to ministers, sinning in two ways: first, because you assign to ministers what belongs to the Lord; then, because you divide the unity and equality of the ministers, and indeed divide the very work of the Lord, which you are."

units.la: Notandum autem quàm caute non dicat: Etenim Dei sumus incrementarij, sed operarij. Nihil enim amplius est ministri, quàm ut operetur. Deinde ne hoc quidem simpliciter dicit, sed, cooperarij, inquit, Dei sumus. Neque enim solum incrementum non est in nostra manu, sed ne ipsum opus quidem nostrarum est uirium: nisi habeamus cooperatorem Deum, nisi ille gratia & uirtute sua adsit, non solum incrementum & effectum largiendo, sed & uires operandi & perferendi dando.
units.tr: "For it is not you who speak," he says, "but the Spirit of your Father speaks in you" (Matt. 10.), and "I will give you a mouth and wisdom" (Luke 21.). Therefore the position of the ministers of Christ is not the same as that of craftsmen or workmen who hire out their labour to someone.
