Those men, even if the lord of the work is absent and contributes nothing, can by themselves supply the labour of working and complete the task. But ministers cannot do so; unless the Lord himself is present, both co-working with them and giving the outcome of the work, they will be able to do absolutely nothing in this work, let alone accomplish anything. For just as the tool of a craftsman fails in both respects, so that it can neither move itself nor accomplish anything unless it is moved and directed by the craftsman, so too the ministers of Christ fail in both respects. "For," he says elsewhere, "we are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as of ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God" (2 Cor. 3.).

units.la: Non enim uos estis, inquit, qui loquemini, sed spiritus patris uestri loquetur in uobis. Et, ego dabo uobis os & sapientiam. Igitur non est eadem ratio ministrorum Christi, quæ est artificum, uel operariorum, qui operas suas alicui locant. Illi etiamsi dominus operis non adsit, nec quicquam conferat, possunt per se operandi præstare laborem, & opus perficere. Isti uero non ita, qui, nisi adsit dominus ipse cum cooperando, tum effectum operis largiendo, nihil prorsus poterunt facere in hoc opere, nedum efficere. Quemadmodum enim instrumentum artificis in utroque deficit, ut nec per se possit moueri, nec aliquid perficere, nisi moueatur ac dirigatur ab artifice: ita & ministri Christi in utroque deficiunt. Non enim, inquit alibi, sufficientes sumus aliquid cogitare ex nobis, tanquam ex nobis, sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est.
units.tr: "For it is not you who speak," he says, "but the Spirit of your Father will speak in you." And, "I will give you a mouth and wisdom." Therefore the position of Christ's ministers is not the same as that of craftsmen or workmen who hire out their labour. Those men, even if the master of the work is absent and contributes nothing, can by their own strength perform the labour and complete the work. But this is not so for Christ's ministers. Unless the Lord himself is present, both working with them and giving the outcome of the work, they can do absolutely nothing in this work, much less bring it to completion. For just as an artisan's tool fails in both respects, since it cannot move by itself or accomplish anything unless it is moved and directed by the artisan, so Christ's ministers also fail in both respects. For elsewhere he says, "We are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as of ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God."

units.la: Imò si propius hanc causam inspexerimus, minus præstamus ad hanc ædificationem spiritalis ædificij, q; instrumentum præstet artifici. Est enim instrumenti usus artifici ita necessarius, ut sine illo nequeat destinatû opus perficere. Nô enim illo utitur ob id tantû, quod ita iubet, sed quod necessitate perficiendi operis illo cogitur uti. In hoc autem ædificio non ita habet. Nos non ita sumus cooperarij Dei instrumentales, quod sine nostra opera nequeat ædificare domum suam, cum absque ullis cooperarijs fecerit uniuersam cœli ac terræ machinam, idque solo uerbo. Dixit, inquit, & facta sunt. Sed quod ita singulari beneuolentia, qua erga nos est, infirmitatem nostram cognoscere, & mutuo cohonestandam proponere voluit, cum alioqui sine nobis omnia solus nihilo minus quam per nos aut nobiscum efficere queat.
units.tr: Indeed, if we look more closely at this matter, we contribute less to the building of this spiritual edifice than an instrument contributes to the craftsman. For the use of an instrument is so necessary to the craftsman that without it he cannot complete the work he has intended. He does not use it merely because he is commanded to, but because he is compelled by the necessity of finishing the work. In this building, however, it is not so. We are not God's instrumental co-workers in such a way that he cannot build his house without our labour, since without any co-workers he made the whole machine of heaven and earth, and that by the Word alone. "He spoke," it says, "and they were made." Rather, out of that singular goodwill which he bears towards us, he chose to acknowledge our weakness and to propose that we be honoured by mutual service, although otherwise he could accomplish all things alone, no less than through us or with us, out of nothing.

units.la: Secundum gratiam Dei, quæ data est mihi, ut sapiens architectus fundamentum posui, alius autem super illud ædificat.
units.tr: "According to the grace of God that was given to me, as a wise architect I laid the foundation, and another builds upon it."

units.la: Sensim labitur ad commendationem operis sui. Facit autem hoc per collationem. Confert enim opus suum operi eorum qui maximopere suspiciebantur à Corinthijs: id quod facit per similitudinem ædificij, quam commodum metaphoræ subijcit, qua dixit, Dei ædificatio eltis. Confidenter dicit, ut sapiens architectus fundamentum posui, alius autem super illud ædificat. Quasi dicat: Qualescunque sint isti apostoli uestri, quos supra modum admiramini, & quantumuis opus meum apud uos contemnatis, ego architectus sum, ego fundamentum posui: isti uero quid aliud faciunt, nisi quod labori meo superstruunt? Quod si tanti sunt, cur non ubi nondum facta est Christi mentio, ipsi fundamentum huius ædificij collocant in domino, quod certe maioris gloriæ materiam haberet, quandoquidem illam tantopere affectant, quàm quod in alieno labore sapientes uideri uolunt? Tale quid uidentur Apostoli uerba spirare. Omnino enim maioris gloriæ est esse architectum, & fundamentum ædificio ponere, quàm qualitercunq; iacto fundamento superstruere.
units.tr: He glides gently toward commending his own work. He does this by comparison. He sets his work beside the work of those whom the Corinthians held in the highest esteem, and he does so through the likeness of a building, which he fits to the metaphor he had used when he said, "You are God's building." He speaks with confidence: "like a wise master builder I laid the foundation, and another builds upon it." It is as if he said: Whatever those apostles of yours are, whom you admire beyond measure, and however much you despise my work among you, I am the architect, I laid the foundation. But what else do they do than build upon my labour? If they are so great, why do they not, where the name of Christ has not yet been preached, lay the foundation of this building themselves in the Lord? That would surely be a greater source of glory, since they strive so eagerly for glory, than to want to be seen as wise by building on another man's labour. The apostle's words seem to breathe something of this kind. For it is certainly of greater glory to be the architect and to lay the foundation of a building than to build upon a foundation laid in whatever way.

units.la: Ne uideatur autem sibi ipsi quicquam adscribere, præmittit confessionem gratiæ Dei, dicens: Secundum gratiam Dei, quæ data est mihi, quod & supra fecit, cum dixit, ut cuique dominus dedit. Vocat autem gratiam sibi datam, sapientiam illam & facultatem prædicandi Euangelij, maxime inter eos, quibus nondum innotuit Christus. Est autem omnino singularis quædam gratia Dei scite & efficaciter fundamentum hoc domus Dei ponere. Habet quidem & superstruendi labor, necessariam industriam, cuius admonebit infrà. Verum non statim cuiusuis est, ut scienter & docte fundamentum futuro ædificio collocet tale, quod sit solidum & firmum, id quod iusti fundamenti בדרשת est.
units.tr: So that he may not seem to claim anything for himself, he prefaces his words with an acknowledgement of the grace of God, saying: "According to the grace of God which has been given to me," as he also did above, when he said, "as the Lord has given to each." He calls the wisdom and the ability to preach the gospel that was given to him a grace, especially among those to whom Christ was not yet known. Indeed, it is altogether a singular grace of God to lay this foundation of the house of God skilfully and effectively. There is also the labour of building upon it, which requires its own diligence, and he will remind them of this below. But it is not immediately within anyone's power to lay, knowingly and learnedly, a foundation for the future building that is solid and firm, which is the mark of a sound foundation.

units.la: Porro quisque uideat quomodo superstruat.
units.tr: But let each one take care how he builds upon it.

units.la: Notat clanculum temeritatem falsorum apostolorum, qua præter iacti fundamenti rationem quiduis superstruebant. Videtur quidem simpliciter admonere, ne quisquam teme re supra fundamentum positum pro suo arbitrio quelibet struat, interea tamen reijcit temeritatem pseudapostolorum.
units.tr: He hints quietly at the rashness of the false apostles, by which, setting aside the principle of the foundation once laid, they would build up whatever they pleased. He seems indeed simply to warn that no one should rashly build on the foundation laid according to his own judgment whatever he likes, while at the same time he rejects the rashness of the false apostles.

units.la: Admonemur hoc loco, quanta solicitudine curandum sit, ut ubi fundamenta Christi iacta sunt, tale superstruatur ædificium, quod fundamento congruat. Et huius gratia nō est cuiuis committendum superstruendi officium. Exigit enim & illud suâ industriam & cautionem.
units.tr: We are warned here that great care must be taken that, where the foundations of Christ have been laid, such a building is erected as agrees with the foundation. For this reason the task of building must not be committed to just anyone; it demands diligence and caution of its own.

units.la: Nam fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere, præter hoc quod positū est, quod est Christus Iesus.
units.tr: For no one can lay any other foundation than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.

units.la: Vocula rationis γαρ innuit ista probandi gratia adiecta esse. Videntur autem mihi pertinere ad ea quibus dixit, se uelut sapientem architectum fundamentum posuisse: quod nihil aliud est quàm afferere fundamentū se posuisse iustum ac firmum. Huc itaq; respicit iam cum dicit: Fundamentum enim aliud nemo potest ponere, præter hoc quod positum est, quod est Christus Iesus. Non solum dicit, Christū enim pro fundamento firmo ac solido posui: sed tale posui fundamentum, quod ita necessarium est, ut nemo unquam aliud ponere queat.
units.tr: The little word for reason, γαρ [gar, "for"], indicates that these words were added to prove something. They seem to me to relate to what he had said, that he had laid the foundation like a wise architect. That is nothing other than asserting that he had laid a sound and firm foundation. He therefore looks back to this when he says: "For no one can lay any other foundation than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ." He is not merely saying that he laid Christ as a firm and solid foundation, but that he laid such a foundation that it is so necessary that no one could ever lay another.

units.la: Ergo duo habet hic locus. Vnum Christum esse fundamentum ecclesiæ. Vide Eph.2.1.Pet. 2.Esa. 28. Alterum: Non posse constitui aliud extra Christum fundamētum, quo nitatur ædificium hoc Dei. Non est enim aliud nomen sub cœlo datum hominibus in quo fit salus.
units.tr: So this passage has two points. The first is that Christ is the foundation of the Church; see Eph. 2; 1 Pet. 2; Isa. 28. The second is that no other foundation can be established outside Christ on which this building of God may rest. For there is no other name under heaven given to men by which salvation comes.

units.la: Emphasim habet, quod dicit: Quod positum est. Quasi dicat: Conentur uestri apostoli quantumuis uolunt Euangelij doctrinam obscurare, nūquam poterunt alium tradere Seruatorē, quàm eum ipsum, quē ego uobis tradidi, quem uobis iam posui fundamenti loco. Quid est igitur quod illos tantopere extollitis? Et forsan præter rationem non est; quod nō dicit, quod ego posui: sed quod positū est, ut innuat Christum iam à patre in fundamento collocatum esse, iuxta dictū Esaiæ cap.28. Atq; ideo neminī mortalium posse esse ut aliud fundamentū ponat, aut quod positū est, loco dimoueat.
units.tr: The word "laid" carries emphasis. It is as if he said: however much your apostles want to obscure the doctrine of the gospel, they will never be able to offer any other Saviour than the very one I have delivered to you, whom I have already laid before you in the place of the foundation. Why, then, do you exalt them so greatly? And perhaps this is not without reason: he does not say "which I laid," but "which has been laid," to suggest that Christ was already laid as the foundation by the Father, according to what Isaiah says in chapter 28. And so it is not possible for any mortal to lay another foundation or to move what has been laid from its place.

units.la: Quod si quis superstruit super fundamentum hoc, aurum, argentum, lapides preciosos, ligna, fœnum, stipulam, cuiusq; opus manifestū fiet. Dies enim declarabit, quod in igne revelatur: & cuiusq; opus quale sit, ignis probabit. Si cuius opus manserit quod superstruxit, mercedem accipiet, si cuius opus exustū fuerit, damnum patietur, ipse uero seruabitur, sed sic tanquam per ignem.
units.tr: But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw, the work of each will become manifest. For the day will declare it, because it is revealed in fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each has done. If anyone's work that he has built remains, he will receive a reward; if anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet as through fire.

units.la: Ista referenda sunt ad id quod dixit: Porro quisque uideat quomodo superstruat. Declarat enim q referat plurimū, quid quisq; super hoc fundamentū ædificet. Propterea qd' manifestū fit futurū, q uera quisq;, q solida & iacto fundamento digna ecclesiæ Christi tradat. Minatur natur enim adfore aliquando diem, id est,lucem,quę abscondita reuelet,discussis tenebris fore aliquando,ut probetur quid quisq; docuerit. Hic fi perstiterit tradita doctrina, dignam fore mercede:sin minus,digná quæ aboleatur, ut author illius lusurus fit omnem operam,ipfeq; una periturus, nisi solida in Christum fide ita fuerit præditus,ut examinis uim ferre queat.Ista uero parabolice trad t,non apertis uerbis, quandoquidem hanc causam per ædificij similitudinem ingressus est.
units.tr: These words refer to what he said: "But let each one take heed how he builds upon it." For he makes clear that it matters greatly what each builds upon this foundation. Because it will become manifest that each one has taught what is true, what is solid and worthy of the foundation laid for the Church of Christ. He threatens that a day will come, that is, a light, which will reveal what is hidden; once the darkness is dispelled it will at some time be shown what each has taught. If the doctrine handed down stands, its teacher will have a worthy reward; if not, it will be worthy of being destroyed, and its author will suffer loss, and he himself will perish, unless he has been endowed with solid faith in Christ so that he can bear the force of the test. He hands this down in parable, not in plain words, since he has entered upon this matter by way of the comparison with a building.

units.la: QVOD fi quis superstruit super fundamentum hoc.]Christus tum est ecclefię fundamentum,quando syncera & firma in illum fide creditur,tanquam filium Dei uiuentis,& unicum mundi Seruatorem.
units.tr: "But if anyone builds upon this foundation." Christ is the foundation of the Church when a sincere and firm faith is placed in him as the Son of the living God and the only Saviour of the world.

units.la: Super hoc fundamentum struitur,quicquid illi doctrinæ & fidei fundamentali,ecclesiæ fer uandum traditur.Id autem pro ædificantium, id est,doctorum opinionibus & affectibus ua rium est. Aliqui enim fynceriter in Christo docti,ueram & solidam pietatem,utpote indu bitatam fiduciam in unum Christum, certam salutis spem in eodem Christo, patientiam in ferendis aduersis pro eodem Christo, germanam per eiusdem Christi spiritum, & pristinæ uitæ immutationem, tanquam ædificium fundamento correspondens: alij uero cognitionem Christo non pure tenètes,uel erga Christum infynceriter affecti, fidei Christi adijciunt commenta philosophica, uel ob feruantiam legis, ut quidam ex Iudæis faciebant, uel traditiones quasdam humanitus inuentas. Illorum ædificium uocat hic Apostolus aurum,argentum,lapides preciofos (utpote marmoreos &consimiles)respiciens ad fundamenti dignitatem:istorum uero,lignum,fœnum,stipulam res uidelicet, tanto fundamento indignas,& parū respondentes,deinde non fatis firmas, quæ ignem probatorium ferre queant.
units.tr: Upon this foundation is built whatever is handed down to the Church as doctrine and faith that rests on the foundation. This varies according to the opinions and affections of those who build, that is, of the teachers. For some, taught sincerely in Christ, build a true and solid piety, namely an undoubting trust in Christ alone, a certain hope of salvation in the same Christ, patience in bearing adversity for the same Christ, genuine piety through the Spirit of that same Christ, and a change of former life; this corresponds to the foundation like a building. Others, however, not holding the knowledge of Christ purely, or affected toward Christ insincerely, add to the faith in Christ philosophical inventions, or, for the observance of the law, as some of the Jews did, or certain traditions devised by men. This Apostle calls gold, silver, and precious stones their building (namely marble and similar materials), looking to the worth of the foundation. But of the others he speaks of wood, hay, and straw, things clearly unworthy of so great a foundation and scarcely fitting it, and then not sufficiently firm to bear the testing fire.

units.la: CVIVS QVE opus manifeftū fiet.]Hęc est comminatio aduersum eos, qui propter ignorantiam rerum spiritalium,qua Corinthij labo rabant,humanæ sapientiæ nomine turgebant & illustres habebantur,tâquam apostoli Christi,cum effent pfeudapoftoli & difsipatores ec clefiæ Christi. Illis minatur futurū, ut manifeftū fiat qd ipse & qd illi docuerint, utri in hoc Christi ædificio pro fundamenti dignitate recta ac solida struxerint.
units.tr: "Each one's work will become manifest." This is a threat against those who, on account of ignorance of spiritual things, in which the Corinthians were labouring, swelled up in the name of human wisdom and were held in esteem as famous apostles of Christ, although they were false apostles and destroyers of the Church of Christ. He threatens them that it will come to pass that it will become manifest what he himself and what they taught, and which of them, in this building of Christ, has built rightly and solidly according to the worth of the foundation.

units.la: Habent autem ista comminatio bonæ conscientiæ fiduciam&securitatem,quę tam abest ut tenebras optet, & lucé fugiat, ut glorietur etiam de futura ueritatis reuelatione,illamq; operarijs subdolis comminetur. Et hanc securitatem infrà ca.4.aperte ponit,cum dicit:Mihi uero pro minimo est, ut à uobis dijudicer, aut ab humano die, imò nec meipfum iudico, &c.Cęterum qui me iudicat,dominus est. Pro inde ne ante tempus quicquam iudicetis donec uenerit dominus, qui & illustraturus est occulta tenebrarum, & patefaciet consilia cor dium,& tunc laus erit unicuique à Deo.
units.tr: These words give the good conscience confidence and security. It is so far from desiring darkness and shunning the light that it even glories in the future revelation of the truth, and threatens with it those deceitful workmen. And Paul plainly sets forth this security below in chapter 4, when he says: "But to me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by a human day; indeed I do not even judge myself. For he who judges me is the Lord. Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of the hearts; and then each one will have praise from God."

units.la: DIES enim declarabit, quod in igne reuelatur.]Rationem reddit qua fit manifestum futurum cuiusque opus.Quæ reuelantur per lucem reuelantur,ut quæ occuluntur, per tenebras occuluntur.Eph.5.Omnia quæ arguuntur, à lumine manifestantur. Intelligit autem per diem eam lucem qua quid manifestum redditur. Habet & ignis uirtutem examinandi, probandi, adeoq; & ualorem rerum manifestandi, utpote auri, argenti, &c. Vnde & scriptura per ignem tentantionem,examen& probationem intelligit.
units.tr: "For the day will declare it, because it is revealed in fire." He gives the reason why each one's work will become manifest. Things that are revealed are revealed by light, as things that are hidden are hidden by darkness; see Eph. 5: "All things that are reproved are made manifest by the light." By day he understands that light by which a thing is made manifest. Fire also has the power of examining and testing, and so of showing the worth of things, such as gold, silver, and so on. Hence Scripture also understands by fire temptation, trial, and proof.

units.la: Quid iam Apostolus exacte per diem,deinde & ignem, id est, quam lucem & probationem intelligat,per quam fit cuiufq; opus manifestum futurum,ambiguum est.
units.tr: It is uncertain exactly what the Apostle means by the day and then by the fire, that is, what light and what test he means by which each one's work will become manifest.

units.la: 1 Aut enim potest intelligi de reuelatione Christi cognitione, per quam olim futurum fit, ut manifesta reddatur qualitas doctrinæ cuiusque.
units.tr: (1) It can be understood of the revelation of the knowledge of Christ, through which it will in time come about that the quality of each one's doctrine is made manifest.

units.la: 2 Aut de probatione quæ est per tribulationes & crucem. Nam & ignis nomine tribulatio & afflictio significatur, & per afflictionem probari solet,quid quisq; de Christo & ueritate Dei sentiat,quamq; firme fundamento Christi nitatur.
units.tr: (2) Or it can be understood of the testing that comes through tribulations and the cross. For the name of fire also signifies tribulation and affliction, and through affliction it is customarily proved what each one thinks about Christ and the truth of God, and how firmly he rests on the foundation of Christ.

units.la: 3 Vel de die aduentus Christi intelligi potest, per quem sane omnia secreta reuelabuntur ut infrà capite quarto commemorabit. Huius diei iudicium, & omnium difcufsio, recte igni comparatur probatorio. Vt enim aurum per ignem iudicatur & manifestatur, ita & iudicio diei illius omnia probabuntur & manifesta reddentur.Mediam sententiam puto esse retinendam.
units.tr: (3) Or it can be understood of the day of the coming of Christ, by which indeed all secrets will be revealed, as he will mention in chapter 4. The judgment of that day and the examination of all things is rightly compared to a testing fire. For as gold is judged and made manifest by fire, so by the judgment of that day all things will be tested and made manifest. I think the middle opinion should be retained.

units.la: S I cuius opus manserit, quod superstruxit, mercedem accipiet. ] Opus manere dicitur, quod examinationem & explorationem ferre potest, quod examinatum perfiftit, & rectum deprehenditur. Vt ædificium,quod uetorum ac tempestatum uim sustinet, uelut examinatur,& rectum ac firmum deprehenditur: ita ea doctrina mansura est in Christo, quæ uel in lu ce plenæ cognitionis Christi,uel in quibusuis tétationib.uel in extremi diei iudicio recta ac solida,id est,ueritate suffulta,& fundamenti dignitati consona deprehendetur.
units.tr: "If anyone's work remains, which he has built, he will receive a reward." That is said to remain which can bear examination and testing, which, when examined, persists and is found to be right. Just as a building that withstands the force of storms and tempests is, as it were, examined and found to be right and firm, so that doctrine will remain in Christ which, whether in the light of the full knowledge of Christ, or in whatever temptations, or in the judgment of the last day, is found to be right and solid, that is, supported by truth and consonant with the worth of the foundation.

units.la: MERCEDEM accipiet.]Declaratio est eius quod supra dixit:Vnufquifq; suam mercedem accipiet,ut intelligas de illis, quorū opus in domino solidum est & firmum.
units.tr: "He will receive a reward." This is an explanation of what he said above: "Each one will receive his own reward." It should be understood of those whose work is solid and firm in the Lord.

units.la: S I cuius opus exustum fuerit. ] Hoc est,fi cuius doctrina deprehendetur inanis & friuola ad fundamentum ædificij nihil pertinens,ut in exploratione perfiftere nequeat. Loquitur enim ad similitudinem eorum quæ igne probantur.
units.tr: "If anyone's work is burned up." That is, if anyone's doctrine is found to be empty and frivolous, having nothing to do with the foundation of the building, so that it cannot persist under examination. For he speaks by way of likeness to things that are tested by fire.

units.la: Admonet autem ista similitudine,futurum, ut doctrina eorum, qui super fundamentum Christi humanæ sapientiæ confulta, aut legis obferuantiam, utpote de cibis, uestitu, cultu, ritibus externis, &c. uel humanas traditiones ædiædificant, sit aliquando comburenda, id est, an nihilanda & friuola deprehendenda. Omnis enim plantatio quæ ex Deo non est, eradicabitur.
units.tr: By this comparison he warns that the teaching of those who build upon the foundation of Christ things devised by human wisdom, or the observance of the law, such as about foods, clothing, worship, external rites, and so on, or human traditions, will at some time be burned, that is, will be found to be nothing and frivolous. For every plant that is not of God will be uprooted.

units.la: · DAMNVM patietur. ] Consumpti uideli-cet operis, ad cuius loquitur similitudinē. Vel certe mercedis apostolicæ damnum feret, quæ his tantum dabitur, quorum opus mansurum est. Laude, & gloria, & mercede, quæ manet fidos Christi ministros, priuabitur.
units.tr: It will suffer loss. This refers to the loss of the work that is consumed, to which the comparison alludes. Or at least it will bear the loss of apostolic reward, which will be given only to those whose work endures. He will be deprived of the praise, glory and reward that remain for faithful ministers of Christ.

units.la: IPSE uero seruabitur. ] Etiamsi opus fuerit exustum, non tamen mox ipse simul exuretur ædificator. Vt enim salus non est sita in ministerio Apostolico (alioqui soli Apostoli seruarentur) si id etiam rite administretur, sed in sola Christi fide per gratiam Dei: ita perditio ministri non est in eo sita, si inanem structurâ collocet super fundamentum Christum, id quod multi sancti patres per imprudentiam, zeloq; ignorantiæ fecisse deprehenduntur, sed in una incredulitate & impœnitentia, cui soli peccatorum negatur remissio. Hoc est scilicet quod dicit: Ipse uero seruabitur, sed quomodo? uelut per ignem. Quem ignem? Eum scilicet de quo iam meminit. Cuiusq; opus quale sit, ignis probabit. Per hunc probationis ignem structor in anis ædificij seruatur, si probatus fuerit in fide Christi uera & syncera deprehensus, utut opus inutile ignis ui absumatur.
units.tr: He himself will be saved. Even if the work is burned up, the builder himself is not at once burned up with it. For salvation does not lie in the apostolic ministry (otherwise the Apostles alone would be saved), even when that ministry is rightly administered, but in faith in Christ alone, through the grace of God. Likewise, the ruin of a minister does not lie in this, that he lays empty structure upon the foundation Christ, as many holy Fathers are found to have done through inexperience and zeal without knowledge. It lies in unbelief and impenitence alone, to which alone forgiveness of sins is denied. This is what he means: "He himself will be saved, but how? As through fire." What fire? That very fire of which he has already spoken. "Of what sort each man's work is, the fire will test." By this fire of testing the builder is saved, if he is found to have been tested as true and sincere in the faith of Christ, although his useless work is consumed by the force of the fire.

units.la: CONTRA OPINIONEM ignis purgatorij.
units.tr: AGAINST THE OPINION OF PURGATORIAL FIRE

units.la: Loci huius obscuritas male feritatis, uel certe imprudentibus in Christo hominibus, causam dedit opinionis eius, quæ passim de igne purgatorio obtinuit, quo peccata uenialia post mortem expurgentur, ut ex illo animæ mortuorum uelut aurum è camino ignis purificatæ ad cœlum euolent. Quàm autem ab isto commento alienus sit Apostoli sensus, satis patet uerba & statum causæ diligenter expendentibus.
units.tr: The obscurity of this passage, due to the ill-will of some or at least to the ignorance of men imprudent in Christ, has given cause to the opinion that has widely prevailed concerning purgatorial fire, in which venial sins are purged after death, so that souls of the dead, purified like gold from the furnace of fire, may fly up to heaven. How far the Apostle's meaning is from this fiction is sufficiently clear to anyone who carefully weighs the words and the circumstances of the case.

units.la: 1 Primum enim. Non loquitur de igne aliquo materiali, qualem isti dant purgatorio suo, sed de metaphorico, id est, probatione. Vt enim non loquitur de auro, argento, lapidibus preciosis, ligno, fœno, & stipula, sed de doctrina: ita non loquitur de igne aliquo materiali, sed de exploratione quæ instar est ignis, ut sicut aurum & cætera, ita & ignis dictionem parabolice posuisse intelligendus sit. Si isti urgent dictionem ignis, urgebimus nos dictiones auri, argenti, lapidum preciosorum, ligni, fœni, stipulæ, quibus si libet repleant, uel alant ignem suum purgatorium, si tamen saturari potest illius immensa ingluuies & auri sacra fames.
units.tr: (1) First, he does not speak of any material fire, such as they assign to their purgatory, but of a metaphorical one, that is, of testing. For just as he does not speak of gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay and straw, but of doctrine, so he does not speak of any material fire, but of an examination which is like fire. So, just as the gold and the rest are used figuratively, the word fire must also be understood as a figure of speech. If they press the word fire, we shall press the words gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay and straw, and let them fill or feed their purgatorial fire with these as they please, if indeed that immense gluttony of fire and that sacred hunger for gold can ever be satisfied.

units.la: 2 Deinde, nō loquitur de animalibus explorandis, neque negocium illi est cum operibus bonis uel malis, sed cum doctrina quam diuidit in synceram & adulteram: & illam permansuram cum laude, istam uero consumendam cum damno structoris prædicit. Quid hoc ad commentum peccatorum uenialium in igne purgatorio repurgandorum?
units.tr: (2) Next, he does not speak of souls to be tested, nor is his business with good or bad works, but with doctrine, which he divides into sincere and adulterated. He foretells that the former will remain with praise, but the latter will be consumed with loss to the builder. What has this to do with the fiction of venial sins to be purged away in purgatorial fire?

units.la: 3 Tertio. Quod omnium est potissimum & manifestissimum, non dicit, quorundam opus, sed cuiusque opus quale sit, ignis probabit. Ergo non solum pseudapostolorum, sed & Pauli & Petri opera isti igni obnoxia sunt. At isti non audent Apostolos igni suo purgatorio tradere, quem deputant solis peccatis uenialibus. Neque impiorum opera admittunt ad hunc ignem. Ignis uero Pauli omnia omnium probabit.
units.tr: (3) Thirdly, and this is the most important and most evident of all, he does not say "the work of certain men," but "of what sort each man's work is, the fire will test." Therefore the works not only of false apostles but also of Paul and Peter are subject to this fire. Yet they do not dare to hand over the Apostles to their purgatorial fire, which they assign only to venial sins. Nor do they admit the works of the impious to this fire. But the fire of Paul will test the works of all men.

units.la: 4 Quarto. Non dicit, purgabit, sed probabit. Quis non uidet aliud esse purgare, & aliud probare. Probabuntur omnia, non autem repurgabuntur omnia.
units.tr: (4) Fourthly, he does not say "it will purge" but "it will test." Who does not see that to purge is one thing and to test another? All things will be tested, but not all things will be purged.

units.la: 5 Quinto. Dat Apostolus igni suo uirtutem manifestandi & reuelandi, uidelicet ea quæ in hoc sæculo sunt abscondita. At quomodo hoc quadret igni purgatorio, ut possit dici reuelaturus peccata, ipsi uiderint.
units.tr: (5) Fifthly, the Apostle gives his fire the power of making manifest and revealing what is now hidden in this age. But how this agrees with purgatorial fire, so that it could be said to reveal sins, let them see for themselves.

units.la: 6 Sexto. Obijciunt patres. Quos quæso? An Hieronymum? Atqui ille locum hunc sic exponit: Magistros & doctores significat super fundamenrum quod Christus est, recte instituere homines uel praue, in quibus magistrorum doctrina in die iudicij in igne reuelabitur, ubi consumptis peccatoribus probati manebunt, doctores autem super his qui probati fuerint, mercedem retributionis accipient: in illis uero, quos ignis exuret, damno afficienter, quia inuacuum laborauerunt. Idem autem magistri in iudicium uenientes, salui fient, si tamen ipsi causa non fuerint perditorū. Item. Examinationem autem iudicij, igni uoluit comparare, iuxta consuetudinem scriptu-rarum. Hæc ille.
units.tr: (6) Sixthly, they object the Fathers. Which Fathers, I ask? Jerome? Yet he expounds this passage thus: "It signifies teachers and doctors who rightly or wrongly build men upon the foundation which is Christ, in whom the doctrine of the teachers will be revealed by fire on the day of judgment. There, when the sinners have been consumed, those who have been approved will remain; the teachers, however, will receive the reward of their recompense for those who have been approved, but those whom the fire burns will suffer loss, because they labored to no purpose. Moreover, the teachers who come to judgment will be saved, if indeed they were not the cause of the ruin of others." Again: "He wished to compare the examination of judgment to fire, according to the custom of the Scriptures." So he.

units.la: Ambrosium obijcerere non poterunt, qui manifeste de doctrina probanda locum hunc exponit.
units.tr: They cannot object Ambrose, who clearly expounds this passage as concerning the testing of doctrine.

units.la: Augustinus quoque cum illis non facit, qui in Enchiridio suo capite sexagesimo octauo sic scribit: Ignis enim de quo loquutus est Apostolus, talis debet intelligi, ut ambo per eum transeant, id est, & qui ædificat supra hoc fundamentum, aurum, argentum, lapides preciosos: & qui ædificat ligna, fœnum, stipulam. Cum enim hoc dixisset, adiunxit uniuscuiusque opus quale sit, ignis probabit. Si cuius opus permanserit, quod superædificauit, mercedem accipiet. Si cuius opus autem exustum fuerit, damnum patietur, &c. Non ergo unius eorum tantum, sed utriusq; opus ignis probabit. Est quidem ignis tentatio tribulationis, de quo aperte alio loco scriptum est: Vasa figuli probat fornax, & homines iustos tentatio tribulationis. Iste ignis in hac interim uita facit, quod Apostolus dixit, &c. Hæc iste.
units.tr: Nor does Augustine side with them, who in his Enchiridion, chapter 68, writes thus: "The fire of which the Apostle speaks must be understood in such a way that both pass through it: both he who builds upon this foundation gold, silver and precious stones, and he who builds wood, hay and straw. For when he had said this, he added: 'Of what sort each man's work is, the fire will test. If anyone's work remains which he has built upon it, he will receive a reward. If anyone's work is burned, he will suffer loss,' etc. Therefore the fire will test not the work of only one of them, but of both. Indeed, the fire is the trial of tribulation, concerning which it is plainly written elsewhere: 'The furnace tests the potter's vessels, and tribulation tests righteous men.' This fire, in the meantime in this life, does what the Apostle said," etc. So he.

units.la: Quin & ipse Chrysostomus, licet per fœnū, stipulam & ligna, intelligat opera mala, & per ignem supplicium malorū, nō tamen astipulatur cōmento ignis purgatorij: sed exponit de igne gehēnæ in quo mali ardebunt perpetuo. Id patet, ubi sic scribit: Detrimētum patietur. Ecce unum supplicium. Ipse autem saluus erit, sic tamen quasi per ignem. Ecce alterum. Hoc autem significat, quod ipse nō ita peribit, quemadmodum opera, in nihilum rediens, sed manebit in igne. Salutem igitur rem hanc appellat, sed nō simpliciter. Propterea addidit, Quasi per ignem. Etenim nobis consuetudo dicen di est, in igne salua esse quæ non comburuntur, neque in cinerem conuertuntur. Noli igitur cum ignem audis, in nihilum redire ardentes arbitrari. Quod si salutem tale supplicium appellat, noli admirari. Solet enim in male significantibus rebus bonis uti nominibus, & in bene malis. Vt exempli gratia, Captiuitatis nomen malæ significationis nomen uidetur. Sed in bona re Paulus eo utitur his uerbis: In captiuitatem redigentes omnem intellectum in obsequium Christi. Contrà in re mala, præclaro utitur uerbo, regnauit peccatum. Atqui regni nomē laudabilius est. Itidem hoc in loco cum inquit: Saluus erit, nihil aliud quàm supplicij incrementum significat. Quasi dicat: Ipse perpetuo in supplicio permanebit. Hæc ille. Imò contendit omnino ista nō de alio igne ignisq; supplicio intelligēda esse, quàm æterno. Cum isto facit, ut assolet, Theophylactus.
units.tr: Indeed, Chrysostom himself, although he understands by hay, straw and wood evil works, and by fire the punishment of the wicked, does not agree with the fiction of purgatorial fire. He expounds it of the fire of Gehenna in which the wicked will burn forever. This is clear where he writes thus: "He will suffer loss. Behold one punishment. But he himself will be saved, yet as through fire. Behold another. This means that he himself will not perish as the works do, returning to nothing, but will remain in the fire. He therefore calls this salvation, but not simply. For this reason he added, 'as through fire.' For it is our custom to say that those things are saved in fire which are not burned up nor turned to ash. Therefore, when you hear of fire, do not think that the burning ones return to nothing. But if he calls such punishment salvation, do not be surprised. For he is accustomed to use good names for bad things, and the reverse. For example, the name of captivity seems to be a name of bad meaning. Yet Paul uses it of a good thing in these words: 'Bringing every thought captive to the obedience of Christ.' On the other hand, of a bad thing he uses the fine word: 'sin reigned.' Yet the name of kingdom is more praiseworthy. Likewise here, when he says 'he will be saved,' he signifies nothing other than an increase of punishment. As if he said: 'He will remain in punishment forever.'" So he. Indeed, he maintains altogether that these things are not to be understood of any other fire or fire of punishment than the eternal one. Theophylact, as is his custom, agrees with him.

units.la: Vide iam quæ sit de hoc loco sententiarum uarietas, quàm male conueniant partibus istis.
units.tr: See now what a variety of opinions there is concerning this passage, and how badly they agree with those parties.

units.la: 1 Per superstructores Ieronymus intelligit magistros & doctores, cum quo facit Ambrosius: Augustinus & Chrysostomus quemcunque Christianum. Imo Chrysostomus secundo pernegat non posse intelligi de magistris & doctoribus.
units.tr: (1) Jerome understands by the builders on top teachers and doctors; Ambrose agrees with him. Augustine and Chrysostom understand any Christian whatever. Indeed, Chrysostom, in his second explanation, flatly denies that it can be understood of teachers and doctors.

units.la: 2 Per aurum, argentum, lapides preciosos, ligna, fœnum & stipulam, Ieronymus exponit auditores, discipulos, uel bonos uel malos. Ambrosius doctrinam aut bonam aut malam. Augustinus curam uel Dei uel mundi. Chrysostomus cum suo Theophylacto, opera uel bona uel mala.
units.tr: (2) Jerome expounds gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay and straw as hearers and disciples, whether good or bad. Ambrose expounds them as doctrine, either good or bad. Augustine expounds them as the care either of God or of the world. Chrysostom, with his Theophylact, expounds them as works, either good or bad.

units.la: 3 Per diem, Ieronymus, Chrysostomus, & Theophylactus, iudicij extremi diem. Augustinus præsentis sæculi tempus. Ex Ambrosio ægre colliges quid senserit.
units.tr: 3 By "day," Jerome, Chrysostom and Theophylact understand the day of the final judgment. Augustine understands the time of the present age. From Ambrose it is hard to gather what he thought.

units.la: 4 Per ignem, Ieronymus examinationem iudicij futuri. Augustinus tentationes præsentis temporis. Chrysostomus cum Theophylacto ignem æternum exponit, quod tamen Ambrosius aperte negat.
units.tr: 4 By "fire," Jerome understands the testing of the future judgment. Augustine understands the trials of the present time. Chrysostom, with Theophylact, explains it as eternal fire, though Ambrose clearly denies this.

units.la: Ecce isti sunt capita patrū, quibus adeo parum conuenit hoc loco ut & alter alterius sententiam reijciat. Vnde est ista sententiarum diuersitas. Ex loci scilicet obscuritate, unde posteriores commentum purgatorij ignis, quem tamen isti patres non uiderunt, corroborare uoluerunt.
units.tr: Here are the views of the Fathers, which agree so poorly with this passage that each one rejects the opinion of the other. Where does such a diversity of opinions come from? Evidently from the obscurity of the passage, and from this the later writers wanted to strengthen their invention of a purgatorial fire, which these Fathers nevertheless did not see.

units.la: An nescitis quod templum Dei estis, & spiritus Dei habitat in uobis? Si quis templum Dei prophanat, hunc perdet Deus. Nam templum Dei sanctum est, quod estis uos.
units.tr: Do you not know that you are God's temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone profanes God's temple, God will destroy him. For God's temple is holy, and that temple is you.

units.la: Dixit, Dei ædificatio estis. Ego fundamentum posui, alius superedificat. Iam declarat de quo ædificio loquatur. Videlicet de templo Dei, uel certe, quod magis placet, ab ædificij dignitate argumentum maioris comminationis aduersus pseudapostolos struit. Varia sunt ædificia, quorum omnium augustissimum & sanctissimum haberi debet ædificium templi Dei. Multum peccat, qui quoduis regni ædificium diruit, omniū uero maxime temerarius est, qui ipsam regiā demolitur. Hactenus quā periculosum fit quiduis superstruere super fundamentum ædificij Dei, quidque eos maneat, qui res illi friuolas superstruunt, admonuit: iā uero eos notat, qui non solum superstruunt quiduis, sed ipsum etiam Dei templum prophanant, minaturq; illis iudicium Dei admonum uehemens. Ratiocinatur autem ad hunc modum.
units.tr: He said, "You are God's building. I laid the foundation, and another builds upon it." Now he states what building he is speaking of: namely the temple of God. Or, what pleases me more, from the dignity of the building he builds an argument of greater threat against the false apostles. There are many kinds of buildings, and of all of them the most august and holy must be regarded as the building of God's temple. He who tears down any building of a kingdom sins greatly, but he who demolishes the royal palace itself is the most reckless of all. Up to this point he has warned how dangerous it is to build anything at all upon the foundation of God's building, and what awaits those who build worthless things upon it. Now he marks out those who not only build anything whatever, but even profane God's temple itself, and he threatens them with the very severe judgment of God. He reasons in this way.

units.la: 1 Quisquis templum Dei, ædificiū illud Dei sacrosanctum, prophanat & conspurcat, hunc iustissimo supplicio Deus destruet.
units.tr: 1 Whoever profanes and defiles God's temple, that holy building of God, God will destroy with the most just punishment.

units.la: 2 Qui uos autem destruit, templum Dei destruit. Vos, quos dixi ædificationem esse Dei, in quo ego fundamentum posui, quod est Christus, templum Dei estis sacrosanctum, in quo habitat spiritus Dei.
units.tr: 2 But whoever destroys you destroys God's temple. You, whom I have called God's building, on which I laid the foundation, which is Christ, are the holy temple of God, in which the Spirit of God dwells.

units.la: 3 Ergo quos prophanat & conspurcat, hunc Deus destruet.
units.tr: 3 Therefore, God will destroy those whom he profanes and defiles.

units.la: 2 AN nescitis quod templum Dei estis? Ad minorem pertinet hæc particula, quà hoc modo non solum tanquam uerā afferere, sed magis tanquam manifestam, ut quam ignorare non debebant, per interrogationem proferre uoluit. Ita enim de rebus manifestis, quæ sine pudore ignorari nequeunt, percontari solemus, dicentes, an ista ignoras? Videtur autem ignorare hoc ipsum quod est, qui conditioni suæ ex æquo pro dignitate non respondet, id quod Corinthij faciebant: unde Apostolus ad hunc modum percontatur: An nescitis, &c.
units.tr: 2 "Do you not know that you are God's temple?" This phrase belongs to the minor premise. By putting it as a question, he meant to present it not merely as a true statement but as a manifest one, something they ought not to be ignorant of. For we commonly ask about obvious things, which cannot be ignored without shame, saying, "Do you not know these things?" But a person seems to be ignorant of this very thing when he does not live up to his condition in proportion to its dignity, as the Corinthians were doing. Hence the Apostle asks in this way: "Do you not know," and so on.

units.la: 3 ET spiritus Dei habitat in uobis. Expositio est, quomodo credentes Christo templum sint Dei. Videlicet, propter inhabitantem spiritum Dei. Vocabulum templi numinis præsentiam significat, non simplicem & qualemcunq; (nam alioqui Deus ubiq; præsens est) sed singularem, quæ diuinam referat & paternam gratiam. Hoc exprimit Apostolus, cum dicit: Et spiritus Dei habitat in uobis, hoc est, gratia spiritus Dei in uobis est, quæ uos renouat & moderatur. Est itaq; templi Dei uera definitio, habitatio spiritus Dei.
units.tr: 3 "And the Spirit of God dwells in you." This explains how believers in Christ are God's temple: namely, because the Spirit of God dwells in them. The word "temple" signifies the presence of the divinity, not a simple or ordinary presence (for otherwise God is present everywhere), but a special presence, which expresses divine and fatherly grace. The Apostle expresses this when he says, "And the Spirit of God dwells in you," that is, the grace of the Spirit of God is in you, renewing and governing you. So the true definition of God's temple is the dwelling of the Spirit of God.

units.la: 4 SI quis templum Dei prophanat. Græce est, [Greek text]. Si quis templum Dei corrumpit, corrumpet illū Deus: quam allusionem forsan aliqua ratione interpres neglexit, uerbo prophanandi respiciens ad uiolatam templi consecrationem. Dicuntur enim res sacræ prophanari, quando uiolantur,
units.tr: 4 "If anyone profanes God's temple." The Greek is phtheirei [φθείρει]. "If anyone corrupts God's temple, God will corrupt him." Perhaps the translator neglected this wordplay for some reason, looking to the word "profane" and its reference to the violated consecration of the temple. For sacred things are said to be profaned when they are violated,

units.la: Hac Chrysostomi ex positione uulgata sunt Græci contra Latinos in Synodo Ferrariensi. iantur,& præter phano debitum honorem in abusum rapiuntur. Secundo uero loco, nō qua drabat reddere, hunc prophanabit Deus. Qui enim templum Dei prophanat, ut ipse propha nus est, ita à nemine prophanari potest. Et alio qui Deus neminem ex sacro prophanum red dit, prophanos uero perdit. Ideo recte uersum est, hunc perdet Deus. Licet enim φθείρειν fit cor rumpere, quoniam tamen quæ corrumpuntur perduntur, fit ut & perdere significet.
units.tr: Chrysostom's explanation was used by the Greeks against the Latins at the Synod of Ferrara. ...and, apart from the honor due to them, are seized for abuse. In the second place, it would not fit to render it, "God will profane him." For whoever profanes God's temple, being himself profane, cannot be profaned by anyone. Otherwise God makes no one holy from what is sacred, but destroys the profane. So it has been rightly translated, "God will destroy him." For although to corrupt [φθείρειν] means to corrupt, since things that are corrupted are also destroyed, it also comes to signify to destroy.

units.la: 5 Notandum est aut in uerbo φθάρα, qua in re sita sit templi Dei prophanatio. Corrumpendi enim uerbum ad ea pertinet, quæ in syncerita te & puritate subsistunt, quorum syncericas a dulterina mixtura corrumpitur & perditur. Ita templum Dei prophanatur, quando synce ritas animorum erga Christũ adulterino dog mate, contentione, disidio, sectarumq; studio corrumpitur: id quod faciebant tum pseuda postoli, quibus hic iudicium Dei minatur.
units.tr: 5 It must be noted in the word for corruption [φθορά] where the profanation of God's temple lies. For the word "corrupt" applies to things that subsist in sincerity and purity, and whose sincerity is corrupted and destroyed by an adulterous mixture. So God's temple is profaned when the sincerity of minds toward Christ is corrupted by adulterous doctrine, contention, division, and devotion to sects. This is what the false apostles were then doing, and God threatens them with judgment here.

units.la: 6 NAM templum Dei sanctũ est quod estis uos.] Hæc est ratio, cur graue Dei iudiciũ ma neat eos, qui templum Dei prophanant. Vide licet quia rem Deo consecratam prophanant.
units.tr: 6 "For God's temple is holy, and that temple is you." This is the reason why a grave judgment of God awaits those who profane God's temple: namely, because they profane a thing consecrated to God.

units.la: Videmus hoc loco, qua religione sit admi nistranda ecclesiæ ædificatio, quidq; expe ctan dum sit illis qui ecclesiæ Christi, fideiq; erga Christum syncericatem, adhæc & unitatem il lius labefactant. Perdet hunc, inquit, Deus. Nō optat, sed certo prædicit.
units.tr: Here we see with what reverence the building of the Church must be administered, and what must be expected by those who undermine the Church of Christ, and the sincerity and also the unity of faith toward Christ. "God will destroy him," he says. He does not wish it; he foretells it with certainty.

units.la: Ne quis se ipsum fallat. Si quis uide tur sibi inter uos sapiens esse, in sæculo hoc stultus fiat, ut reddatur sapiens.
units.tr: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, that he may become wise.

units.la: Parænesim cōminationi subiungit. Dehor tatur autē à duobus malis, quæ uelut radices sunt contentionum ac disidiorum, unde ple runq; studia sectarum oriuntur. Vnum est, phi lautiæ malum, quo fit, ut quis sibi ipsi sapiétiæ nomine placeat. Alterum est, quo quis sapien tiæ nomine in aliquo quem admiratur gloria tur. Contra primum est, quod dicit, Ne quis se ipsum fallat. Si quis sibi uidetur sapiés esse in ter uos, &c. Contra alterũ, quod ex præmissis colligit, Itaq; ne quis glorietur in hominibus.
units.tr: He adds an exhortation to the warning. He dissuades them from two evils, which are like the roots of contentions and dissensions, from which the party spirits of sects usually arise. One is the evil of conceit, by which a person takes pleasure in himself under the name of wisdom. The other is that by which a person boasts, under the name of wisdom, in someone he admires. Against the first he says: "Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you seems to be wise," and so on. Against the second, he draws the conclusion from what precedes: "So let no one boast in men."

units.la: 2 NB quis seipsum fallat.] Seipsum fallit, qui de seipso sentit, quod non est, qui sibi ipsi ap plaudit & assentitur, id quod fere omnes facil lime facimus. Loquitur autem contra opinio nem propriæ sapientiæ, qua qui præditi erant, super fundamentum Christũ ædificabant fœ nũ, stipulam, &c. Igitur fallax est persuasio pro prię sapientię, quam uix potest suspectam ma gis & fugiendam reddere, quàm quod illi falla ciam adscribit. Parum enim decorum est falli, turpe autem est, si quis seipsum fallat. Et ipsi sa pientiæ humanæ haud facile poterit quicquā turpius accidere, quàm qd fallaciæ arguitur. Quid enim minus potest cōpetere sapientiæ, quàm error & seductio.
units.tr: 2 Note well: "let no one deceive himself." A person deceives himself when he thinks of himself what is not so, when he applauds and agrees with himself, which almost all of us do very easily. He speaks against the opinion of one's own wisdom, by which those who were endowed with it built on the foundation of Christ hay, straw, and so on. So the persuasion of one's own wisdom is a deceitful one, and it could hardly make it more suspect and worth avoiding than by ascribing deception to it. For it is little becoming to be deceived, but it is shameful if someone deceives himself. And for human wisdom itself, nothing more disgraceful can easily happen than to be charged with deception. For what can be less fitting to wisdom than error and seduction?

units.la: 3 SI quis uidetur sibi.] Exponit quid admo neat. Non simpliciter dicit, Si quis uidetur, sed si quis sibi uidetur sapiens esse. Deinde ad-
units.tr: 3 "If anyone seems to himself." He explains what he is warning about. He does not simply say, "If anyone seems," but "If anyone seems to himself to be wise." Then he adds

units.la: dit, inter uos. hoc est, Si quis cum Christianus sit, putauerit se tanquam Christianũ inter Chri stianos esse sapientem. Tertio, non simpliciter dicit, stultus fiat, sed in seculo hoc stultus fiat, ut reddatur sapiens. Alioqui mirum uideri po teft quomodo stultitia per se posit reddere sa pientem, quę sententia plane paradoxon resi peret. Est autem prorsus inuersio quędam. Co rinthij putabant se tum esse sapientes, si iuxta morem sæculi sapientes essent. Admonentur autem hic per contrarium si sapientes fieri ue lint ut magis ea sectentur, quæ seculi iudicio stulta uidentur.
units.tr: "among you," that is, if anyone, being a Christian, has thought that he is wise as a Christian among Christians. Third, he does not simply say, "let him become foolish," but "let him become foolish in this age, that he may become wise." Otherwise it might seem strange how foolishness by itself could make someone wise, a statement that would plainly reverse the paradox. But it is in fact a kind of inversion. The Corinthians thought they were wise if they were wise according to the custom of the age. Yet here they are admonished, by the opposite, that if they wish to become wise they should rather pursue those things which seem foolish by the judgment of the age.

units.la: Stultum autem fieri quempiam in hoc sæcu lo bifariam dici potest. Primum, si nullo religi onis impulsu, sed mera temeritate faciat, aut p ignauiâ patiatur ea quæ noxia sunt, nec ulla ra tione probari possunt, ita ut sibijpsi non modo sit inutilis, sed & perniciosus. Stultitię huius in numera sunt exempla, quibus sic in seculo hoc declaratur stultus, ut interea tamen non posit haberi sapiens inter fideles. Deinde stultus fit in hoc seculo, qui cognita ueritate, quâ mŭdus hic intelligere non potest, totũ se, & omnia sua Christo seruatori addicit, cõtênit terrena hæc omnia, quę mundus impensissime admiratur, & propter Christum etiâ uitam suam non du bitat in quæuis conijcere descrimina, sic ut ex animo dicat: Mihi mŭdus crucifixus est, &ego mundo. Qui hoc pacto animatus est, à filijs hu ius seculi suauissime ridetur, ac p homine ha betur omnium stultissimo. Ac nisi tales stulti reddamur per spiritum Christi, sapientes coră Deo non erimus. De hoc genere stultitiæ lo quitur hic Apostolꝰ, cũ dicit: in seculo hoc stul tus fiat, ut reddatur sapiés. Tales stulti sunt ue ri Christiani, quos Roma ridet, cum uocat eos bon Christian, quod illic sonat fatuum.
units.tr: Now, to become foolish in this age can be understood in two ways. First, if someone acts not from any impulse of religion but from pure recklessness, or through laziness suffers those things that are harmful and cannot be justified by any reason, so that he becomes not only useless but also hurtful to himself. Examples of this foolishness are numerous, by which a man is so declared foolish in this age that he cannot, in the meantime, be regarded as wise among the faithful. Second, a person becomes foolish in this age who, having known the truth, which the world cannot understand, devotes himself and all his possessions wholly to Christ the Saviour, despises all these earthly things which the world admires most eagerly, and does not hesitate, for Christ's sake, to expose even his life to any dangers, so that he says from his heart: "The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world." A man so disposed is most delightfully laughed at by the children of this age, and is regarded as the most foolish of all men. And unless we are made such fools through the Spirit of Christ, we shall not be wise before God. It is of this kind of foolishness that the Apostle speaks here when he says: "let him become foolish in this age, that he may become wise." Such fools are the true Christians whom Rome laughs at, when it calls them "bon Christians," which in its language sounds like "simpletons."

units.la: ETENIM sapientia mundi huius stultitia est apud Deũ.] Per ... reddit rationem, qua re eum qui cupiat uideri sapiens, iubeat in hoc seculo stultum fieri. Quoniâ, inquit, sapientia mundi huius, quâ uos admiramini & affectatis, stultitia est apud Deum. Dicedum erat, E tenim stultitia mundi huius sapientia est apud Deũ. Verum mauult ita proferre tententiam, ut sapientiam mundi stultitiæ nomine iuxta propositum suum traducat, quàm ut mŭdi stul titiam sapientiæ nomine cohonestet.
units.tr: "For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God." He gives the reason why he bids one who wishes to seem wise to become foolish in this age. "For," he says, "the wisdom of this world, which you admire and aspire to, is foolishness with God." He ought to have said, "For the foolishness of this world is wisdom with God." But he prefers to put the sentence in such a way that, in accordance with his purpose, he calls the wisdom of the world by the name of foolishness, rather than to dignify the foolishness of the world with the name of wisdom.

units.la: 2 Non autem simpliciter sapientiam dicit ef se stultitiâ, sed eam quæ mundi huius est, qua uidelicet mundus de rebus diuinis, ad salutem pertinentibus, iudicare præsumit. Hanc scilicet ita prorsus deijcit, ut nō dicat, modici apud Deum momenti est: sed, qd gloriam sapientię pla ne in summâ disturbat ignominiâ, stultitia est apud Deũ. Quid enim ignominosius est opi nioni sapientiæ q quod eam uocat stulticiam, idq; apud Deum, ipsum sapientiæ fontê, nedũ exactum cognitorê. Similis est illa Christi sen tentia Luc. 16. Quod altum est coră hominib. abominatio est coră Deo. Omniũ rerũ perse ctum ac uerũ iudiciũ apud Deum est. Qualia ab illo æstimantur uniuersa, talia reuera sunt. Iudicia mortalium meræ sunt opiniones, plerunq; inanes.
units.tr: 2 Yet he does not simply say that wisdom itself is foolishness, but that wisdom which belongs to this world, by which, namely, the world presumes to judge the things of God that pertain to salvation. He casts it down so completely that he does not say it is of little weight with God, but, in a way that wholly overturns the glory of wisdom with the greatest disgrace, that it is foolishness with God. For what could be more disgraceful to the opinion of wisdom than to call it foolishness, and that before God, the very fountain of wisdom and its most exact judge? Similar is that saying of Christ in Luke 16: "What is high among men is an abomination before God." The complete and true judgment of all things is with God. Whatever things are valued by him are truly such. The judgments of mortals are mere opinions, mostly empty.

units.la: 3 Sententiam hanc non admodum curat qui gloriam sapientiæ apud homines, non uerâ sapientiam quærunt, quibus satis est, si habeatur pro sapientibus, qualescunq; iudicetur à Deo. Pij uero malunt ᵽ stultis haberi in hoc seculo, & uere interim coram Deo sapere q; diuersum. Huc igitur Corinthios Apostolus à pseudapo stolorum uanitate auocare conatur. Sciebat enim hac in replurimis esse situ, ad hoc, ut cessan te præpostera illorum admiratione, ad ecclesiasti cà unitate reiecto æmulationum studio pedem referrent. Perinde ac si animum uiri cuiusdã, formam mulieris alicuius misere suspicietis ac de pereuntis ad sanitatem reuocaturus dicas: Pulchritudo illa quâ in hac muliere deperis, omnium eorum iudicio, qui quasuis mulierum formas exacte æstimare norunt, tam non est pulchritudo, ut magis ipsissima sit turpitudo. Hoc quamprimum persuaseris, ad id certo faciet, ut sensim desinat amare, donec eo euadat, ut tandem & cóteminat. Tale quid molitur hic in Corinthijs Apostolus.
units.tr: 3 He who seeks the glory of wisdom among men, not true wisdom, does not much care about this sentence. For such people it is enough to be considered wise, whatever they may be judged to be by God. The godly, however, prefer to be regarded as fools in this age and in the meantime to be truly wise before God, which is the opposite. Here, then, the Apostle tries to turn the Corinthians away from the vanity of the pseudo-apostles. For he knew that this lay in very many of them, so that, once their absurd admiration ceased and the zeal for rivalries was rejected in favour of the unity of the Church, they would turn back. It is just as if you were to tell a man who was wretchedly smitten with the beauty of some woman, and whom you wished to bring back to health from his ruin: "That beauty with which you are infatuated in this woman is, by the judgment of all those who know how to weigh exactly the forms of women, so far from being beauty that it is rather the very essence of ugliness." As soon as you had persuaded him of this, he would surely gradually stop loving her, until at last he came to despise her too. Something of this sort the Apostle is aiming at among the Corinthians here.

units.la: 4 Expendenda hoc loco est mūdanæ sapientiæ peruersitas, & omnimoda cæcitas. Supra illi dedit, quod quę Dei sunt ᵽ stultitia reputet. Hic illi adscribit, quod q iudicio Dei stulta habentur, ipsa pro sapientia suspiciat & admiretur. An hoc non est esse peruersum prorsus cæcum, Deoq; repugnans ingenium?
units.tr: 4 Here we must weigh the perversity of worldly wisdom and its complete blindness. Above, the Apostle has said that it counts as foolishness what belongs to God. Here he adds that what is held to be foolish by the judgment of God, it itself admires and esteems as wisdom. Is this not to be a wholly perverse, blind disposition, opposed to God?

units.la: Scriptum est enim: Qui cōprehendit sapientes in astutia ipsorum. Et rursum, Dominus nouit cogitationes hominū, quod sint uanæ.
units.tr: For it is written: "He catches the wise in their own craftiness." And again: "The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain."

units.la: Duobus hisce scripturæ locis præmissa confirmat. Prior ex ca.5. Iob, posterior ex Psal.94. desumptus est. Videntur autem non referri ad idem probandum. Dixit: Sapientia enim mundi stultitia est apud Deum. Subijcit, Scriptum est enim, Qui cōprahendit sapientes in astutia ipsorum. Omnino hic locus aliud quid probat quàm habeat sententia proxime præmissa. Est enim aliud sapientiam mundi pro stultitia reputare, & aliud, sapientes in ipsorū astutia com prahendere. Proinde apparet priorem locum ad comminationem præmissam referendum esse, qua dixit: Si quis templū Dei prophanat, hunc perdit Deus. Notat enim non simplicem imperitorum hominum stulticiam, sed eorum qui sapientiæ nomine suspiciebātur, & astutia sua Corinthiorum simplicitatem & syncerita tem in Christo corrumpebāt. Illis minatus est iudicium Dei. Hoc iam scripturæ loco confirmat, quo minatur futurum, ut cōprehédantur in ea astutia, à domino, quatum ecclesiam Dei prophanabant: hoc est, ut hoc ipsum astutū cō silium, sit eos ad perditionē instar laquei intricaturū. ὁ ἀφαυσέμενος inquit, uerbum ἀφαυσάω significat aliquid non solū apprehedere, sed & ueluti pugno præhensum concludere & cohibere, ut elabi nequeat. ἀπάξ enim pugnū significat. Et πανουργία ea est astutia, quæ in omnes sese formas mutare potest. πανούργος est, qui in omnibus rebus uersatus est, ut habitum quēdam uersutiæ contraxerit, qualem poëtæ Proteum describunt.
units.tr: He confirms what precedes by two passages of Scripture. The first is taken from Job chapter 5, the second from Psalm 94. They do not seem, however, to be cited to prove the same thing. He said: "For the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God." He adds: "For it is written, He catches the wise in their craftiness." This passage proves something other than the sentence just laid down. It is one thing to count the wisdom of the world as foolishness, and another to catch the wise in their own craftiness. So it appears that the first passage refers to the warning given before, where he said: "If anyone profanes the temple of God, God will destroy him." For it denotes not the simple foolishness of unlearned men, but of those who were held in esteem for their wisdom and who, by their craftiness, were corrupting the simplicity and sincerity of the Corinthians in Christ. He threatened them with the judgment of God. Now he confirms this with the passage of Scripture, in which he threatens that they will be caught by the Lord in the very craftiness with which they were profaning the Church of God. That is, this crafty counsel itself will entangle them, like a snare, to their destruction. "The one who catches" [ὁ ἀφαυσέμενος], he says. The word ἀφαυσάω means not only to seize but also, as it were, to grip and hold shut with the fist, so that it cannot slip away; for ἀπάξ signifies a fist. And πανουργία is that craftiness which can change itself into every shape [πανουργία]. A πανούργος [panourgos] is one who has been versed in all things, so that he has acquired a certain habit of cunning, such as the poets describe in Proteus.

units.la: Igitur tam abest, ut uersutorum hominū cōsilia quod uolunt perficere queant, ut ea ipsa illis sint laquei loco futura. Exemplū esto ipsa Satanę πανουργία, deinde astutum sacerdotum & pharisæorum consilium contra Christum. Ne forte ueniant Romani, &c. Hinc illud: Malum consilium consultori pesimum.
units.tr: So far is it from being the case that the plans of crafty men can achieve what they want, that those very plans will become snares for them. Let the cunning of Satan himself be the example, and then the crafty counsel of the priests and Pharisees against Christ: "lest perhaps the Romans come," and so on. Hence that saying: "A bad counsel is most harmful to the one who takes it."

units.la: 2 Rursum. Dominus nōuit cogitationes hominum, quod uanæ sint. Posterior hic locus ad parænesim præmissam pertinet, qua dixit: Ne quis seipsum fallat, si quis sibi uidetur sapiens esse inter uos, stultus fiat in hoc seculo, ut sapiens reddatur. Etenim sapientia mundi huius stultitia est apud Deum. Huc referendum est quod Dauid dicit: Dominus nouit cogitationes hominum quod uanæ sint.
units.tr: 2 Again: "The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain." This latter passage pertains to the exhortation set down before, in which he said: "Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God." To this belongs what David says: "The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain."

units.la: Duo habet hic locus. Vnum quod cogitationes hominum Deo sint notæ. Alterum quod sint uanæ. Prius nemo facile negat, nisi expressè impius, simul Deum ipsum negans. Posterius non agnoscitur, nisi ab illis, qui spiritu Dei ducuntur, nempe, quod cogitationes hominū uanæ sint. Loquitur autem propheta non de quibusuis cogitationibus hominum, neque de quibusuis hominibus, sed de sapientibus sapientum cogitationibus. Vnde & Apostolus reddit ᵽ הבל ἐν σοφίᾳ. In Ebreo est ח״ב, id est, ingeniosæ & subtiles cogitationes. Id & Græci expresserunt, dum reddiderunt τὰς λογισμούς, id est, ratiocinationes. Igitur posterioris huius particulæ gratia, quod uanę sint, locum hunc adduxit Apostolus, ut probaret, sapientiam mundi stulticiam esse coram Deo.
units.tr: This passage has two points. One is that the thoughts of men are known to God. The other is that they are vain. No one readily denies the first, except one who is openly impious and at the same time denies God himself. The second is acknowledged only by those who are led by the Spirit of God, namely that the thoughts of men are vain. But the prophet speaks not of just any thoughts of men, nor of just any men, but of the thoughts of wise men who are wise. Hence the Apostle also renders the Hebrew word הבל [hevel] by the Greek phrase ἐν σοφίᾳ [en sophia]. In the Hebrew it is ח״ב, that is, ingenious and subtle thoughts. The Greeks also expressed this when they rendered it τὰς λογισμούς [tas logismous], that is, reasonings. Therefore, for the sake of this latter clause, that they are vain, the Apostle adduced this passage, to prove that the wisdom of the world is foolishness before God.

units.la: 3 Affirmat itaque Apostolus ista tria de mundi huius sapientia & uersutia. Primum, quod astutæ illius cogitationes, quibus innumera molitur, domino sint notæ. Secundum quod sint stultæ & uanæ, hoc est, inutiles, inanes & inefficaces, ut non sint assequuturæ quod uolunt. Tertium quod sint instar laqueorum, qui bus comprehendantur. Hæc omnia plurimum cedunt ad fidelium & simplicium consolationem, præterquam quod omnem humanæ sapientiæ admirationem & æmulationem ause runt apud credentes, in quem finem & ab Apostolo commemorantur. Cætera uide in Comment. nostris super hunc Psalmum.
units.tr: 3 The Apostle therefore affirms three things about the wisdom and craftiness of this world. First, that the crafty thoughts by which such men devise countless schemes are known to the Lord. Second, that they are foolish and vain, that is, useless, empty and ineffective, so that they will not attain what they want. Third, that they are like snares in which men are caught. All these things contribute greatly to the comfort of the faithful and the simple, and besides, they take away from believers all admiration and emulation of human wisdom, and it is to this end that the Apostle recalls them. See the rest in our commentaries on this Psalm.

units.la: IGITVR nequis glorietur in hominibus.] Alteram partem parænesis ponit, qua dehortatur Corinthios à præpostera admiratione pseudapostolorum, qua fiebat, ut sese illis adicerent, inque illis gloriarentur, atque ita in sectas diuiderentur. Colligit autem hanc particulam ex præmissis, ad quæ illationis nota, ὥστε, id est, itaque respicit. Quasi dicat: Cum itaque nihil sit qui plantat nihil qui rigat, nisi ministri tantum, cum ipsorum non sit incrementum, tum, sed Dei, cum non sit ipsorum ædificatio, quæ uos estis, sed Dei: cumq; omnis mundi sapientia, & quæuis humani cordis cogitatio, ut ut astuta, coram Deo stulta fit & uana, quid aliud sequitur, quàm quod admoneo, nepe, non esse gloriandum in hominibus. Igitur nemo uestrum glorietur in hominibus.
units.tr: "Therefore let no one glory in men." He sets down the second part of the exhortation, by which he dissuades the Corinthians from the preposterous admiration of the false apostles. From this admiration it came about that they attached themselves to them, gloried in them, and so were divided into sects. He draws this clause from what has gone before, to which the sign of inference, ὥστε [hoste], that is, "therefore," refers. As if he said: since neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but only the ministers, and the growth is not theirs but God's; since the building is not theirs, which you are, but God's; and since all the wisdom of the world, and every thought of the human heart, however crafty, is foolish and vain before God, what else follows than what I admonish, namely, that one must not glory in men? Therefore let none of you glory in men.

units.la: Loquitur autem nō de simplici quadam gloriatione, sed de tali, qua Corinthij alius aduersus aliū, in eo quisq; quē sectabatur, gloriabantur, sesēq; iactabant quasi præcipui aliquid nacti, & cuius nomine sibi belle placebant, ob id quod tanti uiri essent discipuli. Ita gloriari, nihil aliud est, quàm se authoris alicuius nomine gloriosum æstimare & iactare, ac reliquos præ se contenere, id qd̄ uidemus in Augustinianis, Benedictinis, Franciscanis & Dominicastris.
units.tr: He speaks not of simple glorying in general, but of that kind by which the Corinthians, one against another, gloried, each in the man he followed, boasting as if they had obtained something outstanding, and pleasing themselves greatly by the name of such a man, because they were his disciples. To glory in this way is nothing other than to esteem oneself glorious, and to boast, in the name of some author, and to look down on the rest in comparison. We see this among the Augustinians, Benedictines, Franciscans and Dominicans.

units.la: Quod uero non dicit, in apostolis Christi, ac ministris uerbi, in sapientibus ac doctis, cū tamen huc respiciat: sed in hominibus, ταπεινωσις est, per quam gloriam illam pseudapostolorū eleuat, qua propter sapientiæ splendorem, uel opinionem saltem, conspicui & in admiratione erant, quasi dicat: quales quales sint, homines sunt, nō dij. Sunt aut homines uani ac stulti. Quis igitur gloriabitur in uanis ac stultis? Vani sunt inquam ac stulti, quatenus homines fiunt. Quod si aliquid habent boni, ex Dei munere habent, ad quem etiam omnis cuiusq; boni gloria referenda est.
units.tr: That he does not say "in the apostles of Christ, and the ministers of the Word, in the wise and the learned," although he is looking to these, but says "in men," is a humbling, by which he lowers that glory of the false apostles. They were conspicuous and admired on account of the splendour of their wisdom, or at least the reputation of it. As if he said: whatever they are, they are men, not gods. But men are vain and foolish. Who then will glory in vain and foolish things? They are vain and foolish, I say, insofar as they are men. If they have anything good, they have it by God's gift, to whom the glory of every good must also be referred.

units.la: Notandum tamen est, quod non dicit, Itaq; nolite in pcio habere Christi ministros, id qd̄ alibi præcipit. Non hoc agit isto loco, ut admoneant auditores, quo debeant honore afficere uerbi ministros, sed magis auocat ab illorū præpostera & nimia admiratione. Est aut aliud gloriari in ministris, quod Corinthij faciebant in pseudapostolis: & aliud subdi præpositis & in precio habere uerbi ministros, quod medium quoddam est inter præposteram admirationem & hanc gloriationem quam uetat Corinthijs Apostolus: & inter contemptū illum ministrorum Christi, quo tum ab ijsdem Corinthijs Apostolus, & hodie fere omnes uerbi ministri sufq; deq; feruntur & annihilantur. Qui nimium extollunt Christi ministros, obliuiscuntur illos esse homines, nec cogitant eos nihil habere, qd̄ à Deo non acceperint: deinde & in multis deficere uelut homines non obseruāt, in id tantū respicientes quod plus æquo admiratur, utpote quod splendide ac sapienter loquūtur, aut si quod aliud singulare donum in illis elucescens, admiratione mouet. Rursus qui ministros cōtemnūt, nihil aliud in illis uidet, quàm quod homines sunt. Et si qua in re deprehendi possunt imbecilles & imperfecti, huc oculos habet obnixe intentos, idq; solū inspiciūt, uer sant atq; reuersant. Dona uero Dei, quib.pote rant bene uti, prorsus negligūt. Istis sane non est opus ut inculces ministros Christi esse homines, cū id abunde satis obseruent. Illis uero rursus nō pderit, si plurimū cōmendes dona Dei, quibus præditus sit Christi minister. Proinde
units.tr: It must be noted, however, that he does not say, "Therefore do not hold Christ's ministers in esteem," although he commands this elsewhere. In this place he is not doing this, so as to teach his hearers what honour they ought to show the ministers of the Word. Rather, he calls them away from the preposterous and excessive admiration of them. For it is one thing to glory in ministers, as the Corinthians did in the false apostles, and another to submit to those set over us and to hold the ministers of the Word in esteem. The latter is a kind of middle course between that preposterous admiration and the glorying which the Apostle forbids the Corinthians, and also between the contempt of Christ's ministers, by which the same Corinthians, and nearly all ministers of the Word today, are thrown aside and reduced to nothing. Those who extol Christ's ministers too much forget that they are men, nor do they consider that the ministers have nothing they have not received from God. Then, too, as men do, they fail to observe that the ministers fail in many things, looking only at what they admire beyond measure, namely that they speak splendidly and wisely, or some other singular gift shining in them that moves them to admiration. Again, those who despise ministers see in them nothing but that they are men. And if they can be detected in anything weak or imperfect, they keep their eyes fixed hard on this and look at nothing else, turning it over and over. But the gifts of God, by which the ministers could be well used, they utterly neglect. Such people certainly have no need to have it drummed into them that Christ's ministers are men, since they observe this quite enough. But for the others, again, it will not be useless if you commend greatly the gifts of God with which Christ's minister is endowed. Therefore

units.la: medium iter tenedū est, atq; itahonore afficiedi Christi ministri, ut meminerimus eos esse homines, iterumq; ita sciendū eos esse homines, ut simul sciamus esse Christi ministros.
units.tr: A middle course must be held: we must honour the ministers of Christ, remembering that they are men, and at the same time we must recognise that they are men in such a way that we also know they are ministers of Christ.

units.la: Omnia nanq; uestra sunt, siue Paulus siue Apollos, siue Cephas, siue mūdus, siue uita, siue mors, siue præsentia, siue futura, omnia uestra sunt, uos aut Christi, Christus uero Dei.
units.tr: For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come: all things are yours, and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's.
