units.la: Subijcit adhuc aliud argumentū de dignitate Christianorū sumptum, in quo duo uiden da sunt. Primum, quomodo dicat omnia esse Corinthiorum. Alterum, ad quid hoc dicat.
units.tr: He adds yet another argument drawn from the dignity of Christians, and in it two things must be considered. First, how he can say that all things belong to the Corinthians. Second, what he means to achieve by saying it.

units.la: Quare Corinthiorū sint omnia, ultro patet ex eo quod dicit, Vos aut Christi, Christus uero Dei. Vnde liquet eorū qui Christi sunt, esse hanc dignitatem, ut illorum sin omnia.
units.tr: Why all things belong to the Corinthians is plain enough from what he goes on to say: "you are Christ's, and Christ is God's." From this it is clear that those who belong to Christ have this dignity, that all things are theirs.

units.la: 1 Primo loco expendendū est, quomodo credentiū sint omnia. Multifariā enim aliquid alicuius esse dicitur. Nā omnino non ita sunt omnia nostra, quēadmodū nos Christi. Nec Christusita est Dei, quomodo nos Christi. Videndum itaq; quo modo nostra sunt omnia, nos uero Christi, Christus autem Dei.
units.tr: First, we must consider in what way all things belong to believers. Something is said to be someone's in many ways. For not all things are ours in the same way that we are Christ's, nor is Christ God's in the same way that we are Christ's. So we must consider in what sense all things are ours, we are Christ's, and Christ is God's.

units.la: 1 Fit aliquando ut meum dicatur, quod fidei meæ commissum est. Ita discipulus præceptoris dicitur: & ecclesiam cui in Domino præest, suā uocare potest minister. Hoc sensu Paulus Euangelium Christi suum esse dicit. 2. Tim. 2.
units.tr: 1 Sometimes something is called mine because it has been entrusted to my faith. Thus a disciple is called his teacher's, and a minister may call the congregation over which he presides in the Lord his own. In this sense Paul says that the gospel of Christ is his own. 2 Tim. 2.

units.la: 2 Alia ratione meum est, quod ex me natum est. Sic filius patris dicitur. Isto sensu dictū est hic, Christus uero Dei. Est enim primogenitus & unigenitus Dei, hæres omnium, Ebr. 1.
units.tr: 2 In another way something is mine because it has been born from me. So a son is called his father's. In this sense it is said here, "Christ is God's." For he is the firstborn and only-begotten of God, the heir of all things. Heb. 1.

units.la: 3 Rursus alio modo meū est, quod enim uel fide, uel amicitia, uel alia quadam ratione præcipue coniunctum est. Sic uxor mea dicitur, meus amicus, meus socius, meus collega, meus symmysta.
units.tr: 3 Again, in another way something is mine because it is especially joined to me by faith, friendship, or some other tie. So a wife is called my wife, a friend my friend, a partner my partner, a colleague my colleague, a fellow-initiate my fellow-initiate.

units.la: 4 Adhuc aliter meū dicitur, quod iuris mei est, & in proprietate ac peculiū mihi cesit. Et hoc uarie accidit.
units.tr: 4 Yet in another way something is called mine because it falls under my right and has come to me as my property and possession. And this happens in various ways.

units.la: 1 Aut enim est ex largitione gratuita. Sic omnia nobis cum Christo donantur. Ro. 8.
units.tr: 1 Either it is by free gift. Thus all things are given to us together with Christ. Rom. 8.

units.la: 2 Aut est ex opere meo. Nā opus proprie artificis dicitur. Ita Christi sunt omnia, tanquam per illum condita.
units.tr: 2 Or it is from my work, for a work is properly said to belong to the craftsman. So all things are Christ's, as having been made through him.

units.la: 3 Aut iuris mei est aliquid, eo quod ære meo comparatū fit. Ita Christi sumus, ab illo redempti. Empti estis, inquit Apostolus, precio magno, & non estis uestri.
units.tr: 3 Or something is under my right because it has been acquired with my money. Thus we are Christ's, redeemed by him. "You were bought," says the Apostle, "with a great price, and you are not your own."

units.la: 4 Aut ex hæreditate in ius meum aliquid cedit. Hac quoq; ratione Christi sunt omnia tāq; primogeniti Dei, & nostra etiā, quatenus filij Dei & heredes, cohæredes uero Christi sumus.
units.tr: 4 Or something passes into my right by inheritance. In this way too all things are Christ's, as the firstborn of God, and they are ours also, insofar as we are sons of God and heirs; and we are fellow-heirs with Christ.

units.la: Ex his puto satis liquet, quomodo nostra sit omnia, nos Christi, Christus Dei.
units.tr: From these points I think it is sufficiently clear how all things are ours, we are Christ's, and Christ is God's.

units.la: Nostra sunt omnia, primū ex dono gratuito, deinde hæreditario, quatenus per Christum facti sumus filj & hæredes Dei.
units.tr: All things are ours: first by free gift, then by inheritance, insofar as through Christ we have been made sons and heirs of God.

units.la: Nos sumus Christi, partim ut creatura creatoris, partim ut redempti redēptoris, item ut peculium domini omnium.
units.tr: We are Christ's, partly as creature of the Creator, partly as redeemed of the Redeemer, and likewise as the property of the Lord of all.

units.la: Rom. 8.
units.tr: Rom. 8.

units.la: Rom. 14. 2. Cor. 5. Christus uero Dei est neque ex largitione, neque ex redemptione, sed ex natiuitate, tanquam filius patris, siue diuinam siue humanam illius naturam respicias, licet alia sit diuinae & alia humanae generationis ratio & conditio.
units.tr: Rom. 14. 2 Cor. 5. Christ, however, is God's neither by free gift nor by redemption, but by birth, as the Son of the Father, whether you regard his divine or his human nature, although the manner and condition of divine generation and of human generation are different.

units.la: Secundo loco uidendum est ad quid ista scribat Corinthijs Apostol. Particula causalis γάρ indicat ea parænesi, qua dixit: Itaque nemo glorietur in hominibus, rationis vice esse subiecta, ut ostenderetur ob id Corinthios non debere gloriari in hominibus, quod ipsorum sint omnia. Quomodo autem haec ratio ad propositum faciat, non eodem modo traditur.
units.tr: Second, we must consider why the Apostle writes this to the Corinthians. The causal particle [γάρ] shows that this exhortation, in which he said "So let no one boast in men," is given as the reason, to show that the Corinthians ought not to boast in men on the ground that all things are theirs. How this reasoning bears on the point is not explained in the same way by everyone.

units.la: I Sunt qui ad hunc modum exponant: Cum ex aequo sint omnia uestra, siue Paulus siue Apollos, siue Cephas, &c. qua ratione alius gloriatur in alio, sibiq; peculiariter adscribit, quod commune est omnium. Si Paulus aliquid habet, certe non quibusdam tatum, sed omnibus ex aequo habet. Est enim omnium uestrum, non quorundam tatum.
units.tr: Some explain it like this: since all things are equally yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas, etc., by what reasoning does one man boast in another and claim for himself personally what is common to all? If Paul has something, surely he has it not for some only but equally for all; for he is of all of you, not of some only.

units.la: II Alij uero sic: Cum uos non estis alicuius hominis, sed Christi tantum, quae est ratio quod in hominibus gloriamini, & non magis in Christo? Rursus, cum non solum Christi sitis, & nullius alteri us, sed & isti, in quibus gloriamini, sint uestri (sut enim omnia uestra, siue Paulus, siue Apollos, &c. quare gloriamini in illis, quae uestri sunt? An non absurdum est, si is qui maior est glorietur in minore, dominus in seruo? Et hoc sensu notatur puerilitas pseudapostolorum, quod cum seruri essent ecclesiae, ex domina costituebat famulas, & ex seruis dominos. Rursus & stultitia Corinthiorum traducitur, quod cum domini essent ministrorum, in seruis gloriabatur. Et hic sensus uidetur esse retinendus. Non enim dicebant, Paulus meus est: sed, Ego sum Pauli, &c.
units.tr: Others explain it thus: since you belong not to some man but to Christ alone, what reason is there for you to boast in men rather than in Christ? Again, since you are not only Christ's and of no one else's, but also the men in whom you boast are yours (for all things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, etc.), why do you boast in those things which are your own? Is it not absurd if the greater boasts in the lesser, the lord in the servant? In this sense the childishness of the false apostles is noted: when they ought to have been servants of the church, they made the church, the mistress, into a maidservant, and the servants into lords. Again, the folly of the Corinthians is exposed, since, though they were lords over the ministers, they boasted in the servants. And this sense seems to be the one to keep here. For they did not say, "Paul is mine," but "I am of Paul," etc.

units.la: Chrysost. hic annotat, discipulos in Christo nullam debere gratiam magistris, sed magistros discipulis quorum gratia acceperunt a domino quae habent.
units.tr: Chrysostom notes here that disciples owe no thanks to their teachers for what they have, but teachers are indebted to their disciples, since through the disciples' grace they received from the Lord what they have.

units.la: SIVE Paulus, &c.] Enumeratio est propositio necessaria. Seipsum ponit primo loco, quia causam agit non inanis gloriae, sed humilitatis. Pseudapostolos non adnumerat nominatim, erat enim inuidiosum: sed tales sibi coniungit, quorum ut uerisimile est authoritate apud Corinthios abutebatur pseudapostoli, ad supprimendam Pauli aestimationem. Id enim quod apud Galatas sub nomine Petri factum est, credibile est, & apud Corinthios esse factum. Quasi dicat: Ipse ego, qui fundamentum apud uos posui, ueter sum: ipse Apollos qui me subsequutus est in opere domini, ueter est: ipse quoque Petrus, quem uestri isti Apostoli iactat, mihiq; opponunt, non est dominus ecclesiae, sed minister, & aliorum & uester: in quibus cum non liceat uobis gloriari, quanto minus istis uestris apostolis licet?
units.tr: Whether Paul, etc.] An enumeration is a necessary proposition. He places himself first, because he acts out of humility, not vainglory. He does not name the false apostles, for that would be invidious; instead he joins to himself men whose authority, as is likely, the false apostles were abusing among the Corinthians to suppress the esteem for Paul. For what was done among the Galatians under the name of Peter is credible to have been done among the Corinthians too. As if he said: I myself, who laid the foundation among you, am yours; Apollos himself, who followed me in the work of the Lord, is yours; Peter himself, whom your apostles boast of and set against me, is not the Lord of the church but a minister, both of others and of you. If you may not boast in these men, how much less may you boast in those apostles of yours?

units.la: Sed quaeredum est, quomodo dixerit se Apollo & Petrum esse Corinthiorum, cum & ipsi essent de numero eorum, quorum dicit esse omnia eo quod Christi sint? Videndum est, quatenus minister Christi sit ecclesiae. Hactenus non est quatenus & ipse credit in Christum. Sed quatenus ministrum agit. Vt credens enim est filius Dei, haeres omnium: ut minister est eorum, quibus seruire iussus est. Colligitur hinc maioris dignitatis esse, credere in Christum quam agere ministrum Christi. Nam hinc non est salus, illinc uero est.
units.tr: But it must be asked how he can say that Apollos and Peter belong to the Corinthians, since they too are among those of whom he says all things are theirs because they belong to Christ. We must see in what respect the minister is of the church. It is not insofar as he himself believes in Christ, but insofar as he acts as minister. For as a believer he is a son of God and heir of all; as minister he belongs to those whom he is commanded to serve. From this it is gathered that believing in Christ is of greater dignity than acting as minister of Christ, for there is no salvation in the latter, but there is in the former.

units.la: SIVE mundus.] Cur ista adjicit, cum uideantur propositio non esse necessaria? Neq; enim Corinthij gloriabatur de mundo, aut de uita, uel de morte, &c. sed de apostolis suis. Mihi uidentur per auxesim adiecta, qua non solum se-Apollo & Cepham dixit esse Corinthiorum, sed omnia, ut tolleret admirationem & insolentiam eius quod dixit praeceptores ac doctores esse discipulorum, & non discipulos praeceptorum. Vbi enim audimus omnia esse nostra, ipsum mundum, uitam, mortem, praesentia & futura: quomodo uideri poterit insolens, si homo quisquam noster esse dicatur? Quorum totum regnum & omni regni bona sunt, quid mirum fuerit, si regni quoq; ministri illorum esse dicantur?
units.tr: Whether the world, etc.] Why does he add these things, when they seem not to be a necessary part of the proposition? For the Corinthians did not boast of the world, or of life, or of death, etc., but of their apostles. These additions seem to me to be made by way of amplification, by which he says not only that Apollos and Cephas are the Corinthians', but all things, in order to remove the astonishment and offence at what he said: that teachers and doctors belong to the disciples, and not disciples to the teachers. For when we hear that all things are ours, the world itself, life, death, things present and things to come, how can it seem outrageous if any one man is said to be ours? Since the whole kingdom and all the goods of the kingdom are theirs, what wonder if the ministers of that kingdom are also said to be theirs?

units.la: SIVE uita, siue mors.] Hiero. de uita & morte Christi: Chrysost. de uita & morte ministrorum exponit. quasi dicat Apostolus: Siue uiuamus ad uestram utilitatem uiuimus, siue moriamur, ad confirmandos uos morimur. Ambr. intelligit de cuiusq; Christiani uita & morte. Simplicius est ut in uniuersum de omnium uita & morte siue Christi, siue ministrorum, siue aliorum quorumcunq;, siue etiam nostra intelligamus: ut idem sit ac si dicat, omnia uestra sunt, siue uiuat, siue moriantur, siue praesentia sint, siue futura.
units.tr: Whether life or death: Jerome explains this of Christ's life and death, and Chrysostom of the life and death of ministers. It is as if the Apostle said: whether we live, we live for your benefit; whether we die, we die to strengthen you. Ambrose understands it of the life and death of each Christian. It is simpler to understand it generally, of the life and death of all, whether of Christ, of ministers, or of anyone else, and even of ourselves. The sense is: all things are yours, whether they are alive or dead, whether they are present or future.

units.la: Videtur autem mirabilis esse possessio possidere mortem, illamq; reputari inter bona filiorum Dei. Verum si expendas illa esse Dei, a quo per Christum omnia accepimus, deinde cogites, quomodo omnia cogatur electis seruire in bonum, siue uiuedo siue moriedo: ia non admirabe ris, quid mors faciat inter electorum bona, quibus dispensante Deo mors quoq;, siue aliorum siue propria in bonum cedit.
units.tr: Yet it seems a remarkable possession to possess death and to count it among the good things of the sons of God. But if you consider that all things are God's, from whom we have received everything through Christ, and then think how all things are compelled to serve the elect for good, whether by living or by dying, you will not wonder what death does among the good things of the elect, since by God's providence death too, whether of others or our own, turns out for good.

units.la: SIVE praesentia, siue furura.] Per praesentia omnia ta corporalia quam spiritualia, ta aduersa quam amica: per futura, coelestia bona, credentibus promissa, quae per spem expectamus, ineffabilia & infinita intellige.
units.tr: Whether things present or things future: by "things present" understand all things, both bodily and spiritual, both adverse and friendly; by "things future" understand the heavenly goods promised to believers, which we await in hope, unspeakable and infinite.

units.la: OMNIA uestra sunt.] Ingeminatio est & asseueratio ad confirmandam istam electorum dignitatem posita.
units.tr: All things are yours: this is a repetition and an assertion, set down to confirm the dignity of the elect.

units.la: Ratio autem illius est, qua subiungit dicens: Vos autem Christi, Christus uero Dei. Nostra sunt omnia, quia Christi sunt omnia, cuius nos sumus. Christi uero sunt omnia, quia Dei sunt omnia, cuius ipse est. Sed dices: Quomodo consequitur ista argumentatio? Omnia uestra sunt, quia uos Christi. Recte ne dicetur ad seruum, omnia tua sunt, quia tu heri tui es? Nequaquam. Quia non est seruus haeres bonorum domini sui, sicuti filius est patris. Habet ergo argumentatio ista robur suum in illis, qui in Christo non sunt servi, sed filij & haeredes Dei.
units.tr: The reason for it follows, where he adds: "But you are Christ's, and Christ is God's." All things are ours because all things are Christ's, and we belong to him. All things are Christ's because all things are God's, and he is God's. But you will say: how does this argument follow? All things are yours because you are Christ's. Would it be correct to say to a slave, "All your things are yours, because you are your master's"? By no means. For a slave is not heir to his master's goods as a son is to his father's. This argument therefore has its force in those who in Christ are not slaves but sons and heirs of God.

units.la: Rursus dices: Cum Corinthij essent carnales & schismatici, quomodo tribuit illis praerogatiuam tiuam filiorum? Respondeo. Loquitur illis ut Christianis de prærogatiua uerorum Christia norum, ad quâ erant uocati & assumpti, ut declinantes in uiam reuocet.
units.tr: Again you will say: since the Corinthians were carnal and divided, how does he grant them the privilege of sons? I answer: he speaks to them as Christians, of the privilege of true Christians, to which they had been called and taken up, so that he might call back those who were straying from the way.

units.la: LOCI COMMVNES.
units.tr: Common Places

units.la: 1 Primus est: Ex Deo esse omnia, cuius est Christus, & quæcunq; sunt in cœlo & in terra.
units.tr: 1 The first is: that all things come from God, to whom Christ belongs, and whatever is in heaven and on earth.

units.la: 2 Alter est: In deum dirigëda esse omnia. Nâ ita sunt nostra omnia, ut nos simus Christi: & ita Christi sumus, ut simus Dei, & omnibus ad illius gloriâ utamur. Id colligitur ex ipsa enumerationis serie.
units.tr: 2 The second is: that all things are to be directed to God. For all things are ours in such a way that we are Christ's, and we are Christ's in such a way that we are God's, and we use all things for his glory. This is gathered from the very order of the enumeration.

units.la: 3 Tertiº est: Christũ esse dominũ omniũ. Nâ ideo nostra sunt omnia, quod Christi sumus.
units.tr: 3 The third is: that Christ is Lord of all. For all things are ours because we are Christ's.

units.la: 4 Quartus: Christum esse mediatorem nostrum, per quem omnia accepimus.
units.tr: 4 The fourth: that Christ is our Mediator, through whom we have received all things.

units.la: 5 Quintus: Omnia seruire electis, etiam quæ illis uidentur aduersa & inimica, ut sunt mundus & mors.
units.tr: 5 The fifth: that all things serve the elect, even those which seem to them adverse and hostile, such as the world and death.

units.la: 6 Sextº: Ministros uerbi, etiâ apostolos præcipuos, esse ecclesiæ non dominos, sed ministros.
units.tr: 6 The sixth: that the ministers of the Word, even the chief apostles, are not lords of the Church but its ministers.

units.la: 7 Postremus: Non esse gloriandum in quoq;, nisi in eo cuius sumus communiter omnes.
units.tr: 7 The last: that no one should glory in men, but only in him to whom we all belong in common.

units.la: CAPVT IIII.
units.tr: Chapter 4

units.la: Toto hoc capite Apostolus personæ suæ æstimatione contra eos vindicat, à quibus temerario iudicio & contemptu abijciebatur. Vt enim sectarij pseudapostolus supra modum admirabantur & extollebat, ita Paulum fastidiebant & contemnebant. Postquam igitur præposteram æstimationem pseudapostolorum animis Corinthiorum eximit, commodum & ministerij sui contemptum amolitur.
units.tr: Throughout this chapter the Apostle vindicates his own person against those by whom he was cast off with rash judgement and contempt. For just as the sectarian pseudo-apostles were admired and exalted beyond measure, so they despised and scorned Paul. Therefore, after he has removed the perverse estimation of the pseudo-apostles from the minds of the Corinthians, he now also removes the contempt for his own ministry.

units.la: Ic nos æstimet homo, ut ministros Christi, ac dispesato res mysteriorum Dei.
units.tr: Let a man so esteem us, as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.

units.la: Quid de se sentiri uelit, breui sententia declarat. Idq; necessario facit, posteaquâ ad deijciendas pseudapostolorũ glorias dixit: Itaq; nemo glorietur in homi-nib. Nô enim ita euelleda est animis fidelium peruersa pseudapostolorũ, aut etiâ ministrorũ Christi æstimatio, ut periclitetur ea, q illis debetur, & ministerio uerbi Ecclesiæq; ædificationi necessaria est. Hanc igitur ponit cũ dicit, Sic nos æstimet homo, &c. Quasi dicat: Quicquid de pseudapostolis uestris sentiatis, de nobis, utut cõceptis, hoc est sentiendũ, qd simus Christi ministri, dispensatoresq; mysteriorum Dei. Nec supra hoc quisquam, nec infrà de nobis sentiat. Nam utrũq; cedet ad ignominiam Christi. Ministri sumus ac dispensatores, igitur non adorandi uelut domini. At rursus Christi sumus ministri, & mysteriorum Dei dispensatores, & hoc nomine non abijciendi, sed propter Christum audiendi.
units.tr: He declares in a brief sentence what he wishes to be thought of himself. He does this necessarily, since after he had said, in order to cast down the glories of the pseudo-apostles, "Therefore let no one glory in men," it was not to be the case that the perverse esteem of the pseudo-apostles, or even the esteem of Christ's ministers, should be so uprooted from the minds of believers that what is owed to the ministry of the Word, and necessary for the building up of the Church, should be put in danger. He therefore sets down this estimation when he says, "Let a man so esteem us," etc. As if he said: whatever you think of your pseudo-apostles, you must think of us, whatever we are conceived to be, that we are Christ's ministers and stewards of the mysteries of God. Let no one think of us higher than this, nor lower. For either opinion would redound to the dishonour of Christ. We are ministers and stewards, therefore we are not to be worshipped as lords. But again, we are Christ's ministers and stewards of God's mysteries, and for this name we are not to be cast off, but heard for Christ's sake.

units.la: DISPENSATORES mysteriorũ Dei.] Hæc particula expositoria est, ad prioris decla-ratio-nem adiecta. Ministerium Christi, est dispensare mysteria Dei. Vocat autem mysteria Dei, gratiam noui testamenti, per sanguinem Christi partam, & fide apprehendendam, ad salutem & uitam æternã. Angustius est, si expo-namus de baptismate & cœna dominica, quam ut apostolicæ dispensationi conueniat. Loquitur de dispensatione omnium eorum quæ gratiæ regni Christi sunt annexa. Ea quoniâ nulla possunt humana ratione comprehendi, sed omnino reuelatione spiritus sancti opus habet, rectè mysteriorum nomine commendantur. Huius gratiæ dispensatio est prædicatio Euangelij. Per illam enim remisio peccatorum & uita æterna credentibus dispensatur. Sic supra dixit: Placuit Deo per stulticiam prædicationis saluos facere credentes. Ista dispensatio non est in potestate ministri, ut cuicunq; iubet, gratiam Dei largiatur: sed in uoluntate & uirtute eius, qui dat incrementum, & aperit corda audientiũ, ut est in exemplo Purpurissæ, Act.16.
units.tr: Stewards of the mysteries of God: this phrase is explanatory, added to clarify the former. To minister Christ is to dispense the mysteries of God. He calls the mysteries of God the grace of the New Testament, obtained through the blood of Christ and to be apprehended by faith, for salvation and eternal life. It is too narrow if we explain this of baptism and the Lord's Supper, as the apostolic stewardship would not fit that. He speaks of the stewardship of all those things which are attached to the grace of the kingdom of Christ. Since these cannot be comprehended by any human reason, but need altogether the revelation of the Holy Spirit, they are rightly commended by the name of mysteries. The dispensing of this grace is the preaching of the Gospel. For through it the forgiveness of sins and eternal life are dispensed to believers. So above he said: "It pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe." This dispensing is not in the power of the minister, so that he may bestow the grace of God on whomever he pleases; it lies in the will and power of him who gives the increase and opens the hearts of the hearers, as in the example of Lydia the seller of purple, Acts 16.

units.la: Pulcherrima metaphora ministrũ Christi cohonestat. enim nõ quiuis, sed domesticus est dispensator, cuius officium est uniuersæ familiæ, quæ cuiq; sunt necessaria distribuere. Sunt autem credentes, domestici Dei, Ephes.2.
units.tr: The most beautiful metaphor adorns the minister of Christ. For a steward is not just anyone, but a member of the household, whose duty is to distribute to the whole family what each one needs. Believers are indeed "the household of God," Eph. 2.

units.la: Res domestica, diuidenda familiæ, est, ut dixi, gratia noui testamenti quæ ad exteros non pertinet. Illius symbola quidë sunt baptismus & communicatio corporis & sanguinis domini, quæ & patres symbola gratiæ Dei uocarút, uerum plura sunt mysteria.
units.tr: The household matter, to be divided among the family, is, as I said, the grace of the New Testament, which does not pertain to outsiders. Its signs are indeed baptism and the communion of the body and blood of the Lord, which the Fathers also called signs of the grace of God; but the mysteries are more numerous.

units.la: 1 Notandum est itaq; hoc loco, quid sentiendum fit de Episcopis illis, qui in ecclesia Christi bona domini non dispensant, sed magis pessundant, & interim egregie saginantur in patrimonio quod uocant crucifixi, ut tyrannidë taceâ, qua Christi ouiculas misere opprimunt.
units.tr: 1 It must therefore be noted in this place what is to be thought of those bishops who do not dispense the goods of the Lord in the Church of Christ, but rather waste them, and meanwhile grow fat splendidly on the patrimony which they call "of the crucified," not to mention the tyranny by which they wretchedly oppress Christ's little sheep.

units.la: 2 Deinde & hoc obseruandũ est, quod cum mysteria illa dispensanda per Euangelium, Deo adscribat, ministros tamen illorum uocat ministros Christi. Ergo æqualem facit hic Christi & Dei potestatem & authoritatem. Ita & Rom.1. Euangelium in quo ministrabat, uocat Euangelium Dei: & dominum, cui ministrabat, facit Christum, uocans se seruum Christi. Cum ergo qui bona Dei administrat, seruus ac minister Christi uocatur, quid aliud innuitur, quàm Christum esse cum patre dominum omnium, adeoq; Deum salutis nostræ.
units.tr: 2 Next, this also must be observed: although he ascribes those mysteries, to be dispensed through the Gospel, to God, he nevertheless calls their ministers the ministers of Christ. Therefore here he makes the power and authority of Christ equal to that of God. So too in Rom. 1, he calls the Gospel in which he ministered the Gospel of God, and he makes Christ the Lord whom he served, calling himself the servant of Christ. Since, then, he who administers the goods of God is called the servant and minister of Christ, what else is implied than that Christ, together with the Father, is Lord of all, and thus God of our salvation.

units.la: Quod superest autem, illud requiritur in dispensatoribus, ut fidus aliquis reperiatur.
units.tr: What remains is this: that in stewards a man be found faithful.

units.la: 2 Ἀ λειτίν est, quod ordine sequitur quod secundo loco requiritur. Primarium enim est dispensare mysteria Dei. Post illud exigitur, ut bona fide dispensentur. Nihil autem refert sive fidelis, sive fidus legamus: fidelem esse tribuunt seruo, fidum amico. Cum autem dixerit Christus: Vos amici mei estis, si feceritis q ego præcepi uobis: existimo tales dispensatores esse & fideles seruos, & fidos amicos Chri-sti. Admonet igitur Corinthios, qd sit speƈtan-dum in Christi ministro, nempe quàm bona fi-de mysteria Dei dispéset. Is autem certe fidus domino non est, qui magis curat, ut sapientiæ nomine & splendore ab auditoribus suspici-atur & adoretur, quàm ut mysteria Dei fide-liter dispenset. Qui suam gloriam quærit in ec-clesia Christi, id qd' domini est sibi usurpat, cū si quid habet, domino debeat adscribere.
units.tr: 2 What follows in order is the second requirement. The primary duty is to dispense the mysteries of God; after that it is required that they be dispensed in good faith. It makes no difference whether we read "faithful" (fidelis) or "trustworthy" (fidus): faithfulness is ascribed to a servant, trustworthiness to a friend. Since Christ said, "You are my friends, if you do what I command you" (John 15:14), I think such dispensers are both faithful servants and trusted friends of Christ. Paul therefore admonishes the Corinthians what must be looked for in Christ's minister, namely how faithfully he dispenses the mysteries of God. Certainly he is not faithful to his Lord who cares more that he be admired and worshipped by his hearers for the name and splendour of wisdom than that he dispense the mysteries of God faithfully. He who seeks his own glory in the Church of Christ usurps what belongs to the Lord, when whatever he has he ought to ascribe to the Lord.

units.la: 2 Qui bonis domini in ecclesia pro suo arbi-trio utitur, iniurius est in dsm, nec agit fidum Christi ministrū. Fides in ministro requiritur, authoritas uerò domino relinquenda est.
units.tr: 2 He who uses the goods of the Lord in the Church at his own discretion wrongs the Lord, and does not act as a faithful minister of Christ. Faithfulness is required in the minister, but authority must be left to the Lord.

units.la: Duo sunt præclara boni ministri dona, pru-dentia, uidelicet, qua possit quæq; suis tempo-ribus, pro domesticorum conditione & cómo-dítate dispésare: deinde fides, qua nō qux sua, sed quæ domini sui sunt querat. Hęc si una fue-rint, plane cómendatissimum reddunt minis-trum. Quoniam uerò maior est in hoc seculo prudentiæ & sapientiæ quàm fidei gloria, ma-luerūt pseudapostoli sapiētiæ opinione apud Corinthios illustres esse quàm fidei probitate apud Deum commendari. Hoc uidetur Apo-stolus notare, cum dicit: In dispensatoribus re-quiritur, ut fidus quis inueniatur. Alioqui nō solum hoc requiritur in Christi ministro, ut fi-dus, sed simul ut & prudens sit, teste Christo Matth. 24. Quis putas, inquit, est fidelis seruus & prudens, quem cōstituit dominus super fa-miliam suam, ut det illis cibū in tempore? Nul-la habebatur fidei apostolicæ ratio, quam de-clarabat in ministerio suo Apostolus: sed una sapientiæ regnabat in pseudapostolis opinio, ideo non absq; ratione hic admonet, in dispen-satoribus requiri fidem.
units.tr: There are two excellent gifts of a good minister: prudence, namely, by which he can dispense each thing in its season, according to the condition and convenience of the household; and then faithfulness, by which he seeks not his own things but those of his lord. If these two are present, they make the minister entirely most commendable. But since in this age the glory of prudence and wisdom is greater than that of faithfulness, the false apostles preferred to be famous among the Corinthians for a reputation of wisdom rather than to be commended before God for the uprightness of faithfulness. The Apostle seems to note this when he says: "In stewards it is required that a man be found faithful." Otherwise, not only is faithfulness required in Christ's minister, but at the same time that he be prudent too, as Christ testifies in Matthew 24: "Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent servant whom the lord has set over his household, to give them food in due season?" No account was taken of apostolic faithfulness, which the Apostle displayed in his ministry; instead the opinion of wisdom alone reigned among the false apostles. Therefore it is with good reason that he here admonishes that faithfulness be required in stewards.

units.la: Potest hæc Apostoli sententia etiam hoc pa-ƈto exponi, quod fidem requiri dicat in dispen-satore mysteriorum Dei, ob id, quod licet & prudentia requiratur, maior tamen habeatur apud Deum fidei quàm prudentiæ ratio. Im-prudentiam enim, fidei probitas & synceritas facile excusat, perfidiam uero excusat pruden-tia nunquam.
units.tr: This saying of the Apostle can also be explained in this way: that he says faithfulness is required in a dispenser of the mysteries of God, because although prudence is required too, nevertheless a greater account is held before God of faithfulness than of prudence. For uprightness and sincerity of faithfulness easily excuse imprudence, but prudence never excuses faithlessness.

units.la: Obseruandum autem est, quod nō dicit, In dispensatoribus requiritur, ut fidus quis iudi-cetur: sed ut fidus inueniatur. Inuenias qui pu-tetur esse fidus: uerùm si exaƈte animi illius cā-dorem requiras, diuersum deprehendes. Erit autē olim tempus diuini iudicij, in quo quis-que qualis reuera fit inuenietur. Hic qui fidus inuentus fuerit audiet: Euge serue bone & fi-delis, &c.
units.tr: It must be observed that he does not say, "In stewards it is required that a man be judged faithful," but that he be found faithful. You may find someone who seems to be faithful; but if you examine the sincerity of that man's heart exactly, you will discover otherwise. There will be a time of divine judgment, however, in which each man will be found what he really is. He who is found faithful there will hear: "Well done, good and faithful servant," etc. (Matt. 25:21).

units.la: Non ingrediar hic mare illud magnum & spaciosum, infidelium ministrorum ac dispen-satorum, non eorum tantum qui in baptismo sub Babylone, Christi se mentiū̇tur esse, mini-stros: sed & eorum, proh dolor, qui Babylone reliquisse, & in ipsius Christi castra transisse & non mendacio, sed ueritati, seruire uideri uo-lunt. Rara auis in terris, nigroq; simillima cy-
units.tr: I shall not enter here upon that great and wide sea of unfaithful ministers and stewards, not only of those who in baptism under Babylon pretended to be ministers of Christ, but also of those who, alas, want it to seem that they have left Babylon and passed into the camp of Christ himself, and serve not a lie but the truth. A rare bird on earth, and very like a black swan, is a faithful minister of Christ,

units.la: gno fidelis Christo minister, præsertim hac no-stra ætate. Quod suo tépore Apostolus dixit, Omnes quærunt quæ sua sunt, non quæ Iesu Christi, nostro hoc decuplo magis potest uera-citer dici. Nec mirum est, catholicam ministro-rum ac dispensatorū obtinuisse in ecclesia per fidiam, cum fideles non ferantur, perfidi uero in precio habeantur: uel etiamsi propter ui-tæ leuitatem, correptionem, & impudentem immundiciam contemni cœperint: defendan-tur tamen, & ob id potissimum retineantur, quod se muntło huic pcruersissimo accommo-dare norunt.
units.tr: especially in this our age. What the Apostle said in his own time, "All seek their own things, not the things of Jesus Christ" (Phil. 2:21), can be said truthfully of our own age ten times more. Nor is it surprising that a universal faithlessness of ministers and stewards has taken hold in the Church, since the faithful are not put forward, while the faithless are held in high esteem. Or even if, because of the lightness of their life, they have begun to be despised for correction and shameless filth, yet they are defended, and kept chiefly for this reason: that they know how to accommodate themselves to this most perverse world.

units.la: Mihi uerò pro mínimo est, ut à uobis dijudícer, aut ab humano die.
units.tr: But it is a very small thing for me that I should be judged by you, or by man's day.

units.la: Notat pseudapostolos, quorum summum erat studium, ut hominum sese reputationi ap-probarent. Contrà ostendit se nihil huius cu-rare, ut uel probetur, uel improbetur humano iudicio: sed unum hoc quærere, ut iudicio Dei fidus inueniatur. Nō dicit, Pro iniquo est: sed, Pro minimo est. Moderate loquitur, ne nimi-um eos offendat. Satis iniquè inter ipsum & pseudapostolos iudicabant: uerum hoc non exprimit, contentus innocentia & confcien-tia sua, qua fretus non adeò magni faciebat, quomodo de se iudicarent, quos sciebat esse non homines tantum, sed & carnales, & existi-matione pseudapostolorum fascinatos. Potest illud ἐἰ ακηε̃ὶω in utranq; partem capi, ut non so-lum dicat de bona reputatione, sed & de con-temptu. Quasi dicat: Pro minimo mihi est, u-trum uos me iudicio uestro extollatis, quem-admodum extollitis uestros istos apostolos, aut explodatis, infraq; illos abijciatis? &c.
units.tr: He is referring to the false apostles, whose chief eagerness was to approve themselves before men's esteem. On the contrary, he shows that he cares nothing for being approved or disapproved by human judgment, but seeks this one thing: to be found faithful in the judgment of God. He does not say, "It is unjust for me" but "It is a very small thing for me" (for the least [εἰς ἐλάχιστον]). He speaks moderately, so as not to offend them too much. They judged him quite unjustly, between himself and the false apostles; but he does not express this, being content with his innocence and conscience, relying on which he did not greatly value how those judged him whom he knew to be not only men but also carnal, and bewitched by the esteem of the false apostles. That phrase can be taken in either sense, so that it means not only good reputation but also contempt. As if he said: "Is it a small matter to me whether you exalt me by your judgment, just as you exalt those apostles of yours, or whether you explode me, and cast me below them? etc."

units.la: AB humano die.] Declaratio est, cur mini-mi momenti faciat iudicium Corinthiorū, ne uideatur illos prorsus contemnere. Fit enim plerunque, ut licet non admodum curemus quid homines nihili de nobis sentiant, nolu-mus tamen à quibusuis contemni. Ideo pror-sus omne iudicium humanum à se contemni dicit, ne se putent Corinthij ab Apostolo pecu-liariter contemni. Nam alioqui probri loco ha-beri solet, si alicui dicatur in faciem, Non curo quid de me sentias. Vocat autem humanum diem, ad differentiam diei illius, quo Deus o-mnia iudicabit. Dies uerò hic nihil est aliud ⁊ iudicium: unde & Erasmus reddidit, Humanu iudicium.
units.tr: By man's day.] This explains why he makes the judgment of the Corinthians of very little moment, lest he seem to despise them utterly. For it commonly happens that, although we do not much care what men think of us as worthless, we nevertheless do not wish to be despised by anyone at all. So he says that all human judgment is utterly to be despised by him, lest the Corinthians think they are being despised by the Apostle in particular. For otherwise it is usually counted as an insult if someone is told to his face, "I do not care what you think of me." He calls it "man's day," to distinguish it from that day on which God will judge all things. This "day" here means nothing other than judgment; whence Erasmus also rendered it "human judgment."

units.la: OBSER. I.
units.tr: OBSERVATION I.

units.la: Admonemur itaq; hoc loco, quàm non de-beamus alicuius momenti facere humanum iudicium, quo alius in cœlum extollitur, alius in abyssum abijcitur. Traducitur enim hic ab Apostolo falsitatis. Alioqui immerito illud contempsisset. Non est autem hoc de seculari tantum foro intelligendum, sed & ecclesiasti-co, illis qui sibi non sunt alicuius mali con-scij. Cum enim dicit, ut à uobis dijudicer, om-nino nino ad ecclesiam Corinthiorum loquitur,non ad forense iudicium. Est quidem, ubi audienda,rursus est ubi non est audienda ecclesia.
units.tr: We are warned here how little weight we ought to give to human judgement, by which one man is lifted up to heaven and another cast down into the abyss. For the Apostol here calls it a judgement of falsehood, otherwise he would not have scorned it so justly. This must be understood not only of the secular court but also of the ecclesiastical one, for those who are not conscious of any evil in themselves. When he says, "that I may be judged by you," he is clearly speaking to the Church of the Corinthians, not to a court of law. Yet there are times when the Church is to be heard, and times when it is not to be heard.

units.la: Hinc autem nemo colliget,ita contemnendam esse sententiam de se mortalium,ut hoc liberius quæ mala sunt designet. Alibi docet ut omnibus studeamus placere,sed in bono. Hoc itaque curandum quidem est, sed non principaliter,quasi satis sit placuisse hominib. Quin magis curemus ante omnia,ut Deo placemur. Hoc facientes si fieri potest, ut simul placeamus hominibus, bene est:sin minus,non affligat nos sinistrum mortalium iudicium,contentos iudicio Dei.
units.tr: But no one should infer from this that the opinion of mortals about oneself is to be despised so freely that they may indulge in what is evil. Elsewhere he teaches that we should all strive to please others, but in what is good. So this matter must indeed be attended to, but not as the chief concern, as if it were enough to have pleased people. Rather we should be concerned above all that we please God. If, while doing this, it is possible also to please men, it is well; but if not, let the unfavourable judgement of mortals not trouble us, since we are content with the judgement of God.

units.la: Imò nec meipsum dijudico. Nullius enim rei mihi conscius sum, sed non per hoc iustificatus sum.
units.tr: Nay, I do not even judge myself. For I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not thereby justified.

units.la: Tam incertum esse ostendit humanum iudicium,ut neque de seipso nisi temerarius esse uelit, iudicare queat. Quid enim sit in homine,& qualis coram Deo æstimetur, tam no po test assequi humana cognitio, ut nemo seipsum satis agnoscere possit,quanto minus alios? Ideo seipsum quoque Apostolus nō dijudicat, nec condemnans,nec iustificans.
units.tr: He shows that human judgement is so uncertain that a man cannot judge even himself, unless he is rash. For what is in a man, and what he is worth before God, human knowledge cannot grasp so completely that anyone can know himself well enough, much less others. Therefore the Apostol does not judge himself either, neither condemning nor justifying himself.

units.la: NVLLIVS enim rei (malæ scilicet) mihi conscius sum.] In Græco simpliciter est, οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐμαυτῷ σύνοιδα: id est, Nullius enim mihi conscius sum. Multorum utique sibi conscius erat: uerùm loquitur de fide sua, qua Christo ministrabat, idq; secundum conscientiam suam inculpate.
units.tr: "For I am conscious of nothing against myself" (of evil, of course). In the Greek it is simply, οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐμαυτῷ σύνοιδα [ouden gar emautō synoida], that is, "For I am conscious of nothing to myself." Of course he was conscious of many things in himself, but he is speaking of his faith, by which he ministered to Christ, and he did so blamelessly according to his conscience.

units.la: Ratio est,cur non dijudicet seipsum. Primū condemnare se non potest,eo quod nullius sibi mali sit conscius. Deinde iustificare se non audet,eo quòd iustificatio ipsius non sit in eo, quod sibijpsi non sit alicuius mali conscius, cum possit esse,ut Deo pateat quod sibi sit igno tum.iuxta illud:Delicta quis intelligit, ab occultis meis munda me.
units.tr: This is the reason why he does not judge himself. First, he cannot condemn himself, because he is conscious of no evil in himself. Then, he does not dare to justify himself, because his justification does not lie in the fact that he is not conscious of any evil in himself, since it is possible that what is hidden from himself lies open to God, according to the words: "Who understands his errors? Cleanse me from my secret faults" (Ps. 19).

units.la: Dicet quisquam, cum infrà cap. undecimo dicat: Si nosipsi iudicaremus, non iudicaremur à domino:quomodo non modo non iudicat seipse, sed & hoc de se palam testatur, perinde atque si iuste faciat, seipse non iudicans? Respondeo. Distinguendum est inter causam & causam,eam de qua infrà,& hanc de qua agit in præsenti. Infrà reprehédit abusum cœnæ dominicæ,quem nec agnoscebant, nec iudicabant Corinthij,ut necesse esset iudicari eam à domino. Hic uero loquitur de fide & innocentia Apostolatus sui, cuius iudicium soli Deo tribuit, quod nec Corinthij de illa recte iudicare,nec per conscientiam ipse suam iudicare ac damnare se posset. Ideo cum dixisset, Lmò nec meipse iudico:subiecit, Nullius enim rei mihi conscius sum.
units.tr: Someone may object: since in chapter eleven he says, "If we judged ourselves, we should not be judged by the Lord" (1 Cor. 11), how can he not judge himself, and openly bear witness about himself as though he were acting rightly in not judging himself? I answer: a distinction must be made between one cause and another, namely the one he speaks of later and the one he is treating now. Later he rebukes the abuse of the Lord's Supper, which the Corinthians neither recognised nor judged, so that it was necessary for them to be judged by the Lord. Here, however, he speaks of the faith and innocence of his apostleship, whose judgement he assigns to God alone, since the Corinthians could not judge it rightly, nor could he himself judge and condemn himself by his conscience. Therefore, having said, "Nay, I do not even judge myself," he added, "For I am conscious of nothing against myself."

units.la: 1 Duo sunt hoc loco notanda. Primū quanta fuerit & quàm rara Apostoli innocétia, qua dicere potuit, nullius se mali conscium esse.
units.tr: 1 Two things are to be noted in this place. First, how great and how rare was the Apostol's innocence, by which he could say that he was conscious of no evil in himself.

units.la: Intelligendum autem est de administratione Euangelij.
units.tr: But this must be understood of the administration of the Gospel.

units.la: Magna emphasi non dicit, Nullius enim perfidiæ, aut flagitij:sed simpliciter,Nullius enim mihi conscius sum. Multa fiunt à ministro uerbi,quorum gratia reprehendi potest, etiamsi aliàs rectè doceat, nec ullius sceleris argui queat. Horum nihil agnoscit in se Apostolus.
units.tr: He does not say with great emphasis, "For I am conscious of no faithlessness or shameful deed," but simply, "For I am conscious of nothing against myself." Many things are done by a minister of the Word for which he may be blamed, even if otherwise he teaches rightly and cannot be charged with any wickedness. The Apostol recognises none of these in himself.

units.la: Cæterùm peccatis non caruit, unde alibi queritur de corpore peccati,& lege peccati,in membris suis agente.
units.tr: Yet he was not free from sins, whence he elsewhere complains of "the body of sin" and "the law of sin working in my members" (Rom. 7).

units.la: 2 Alterū, quàm non sit in conscientia nostræ innocentiæ sita,nostri iustificatio. Si non iustificátur, qui nullius sibi mali sunt conscij, quid sentiendum est de alijs qui conscientiam peccatorum excutere non possunt? Quis ausit autem dicere, Castum est cor meum? Reliquum igitur est,ut per fidem gratuito iustificemur.
units.tr: 2 The second thing is that our justification does not rest in the awareness of our innocence. If those who are conscious of no evil in themselves are not justified, what should we think of others who cannot search out the consciousness of their sins? Who would dare to say, "My heart is clean"? It remains, therefore, that we are justified freely through faith.

units.la: Dices:Ergo nec innocentia locum habet in iudicio Dei? Quæ est hæc iusticia, quæ nec innocenti parcit?
units.tr: You will say: then does innocence have no place in the judgement of God? What justice is this, which does not spare even the innocent?

units.la: Respondeo.Apostolus non dicit,Nihil peccaui,innocens sum: sed nec in hoc iustificatus sum. Sed, Nullius mali mihi sum conscius:ac tum subijcit,Sed nec in hoc iustificatus sum. Innocentia uera est, quæ non nostra, sed Dei conscientia comprobatur. Hac præditus est nemo per se. Interim nemo ueraciter innoces periclitatur coram Deo.Sed quis est hic,& laudabimus eum?
units.tr: I answer: the Apostol does not say, "I have sinned nothing, I am innocent," but, "Nor am I justified by this." He says, "I am conscious of no evil in myself," and then adds, "Yet I am not justified by this." True innocence is that which is approved not by our own consciousness but by the consciousness of God. No one is endowed with this of himself. Meanwhile no one who is truly innocent is in danger before God. But who is this, and shall we praise him?

units.la: Cæterum qui me iudicat,Dominus est.
units.tr: But he who judges me is the Lord.

units.la: Vni domino dat iudicium, ut ostédat se ob id non curare iudicia humani diei, quod uni domino placere gestiat, cui & intimæ cogitationes suæ pateant. Tantum enim est quod dicit,Dominus est qui me iudicat: atque,Domi nus nouit quis sum,quid animo geram,qua fide ipsi ministrem. Huius conscientia nitor, parum solicitus quid de me iudicent homines. Obsecro,unde securi comparebimus in cóspe ctu domini,cum non nostra ipsorum conscien tia, sed ipsius iudicio standum sit, uel cadendum? Dicamus igitur cum Dauide: Ne intres in iudicium cum seruo tuo domine.
units.tr: He gives the judgment to the one Lord, to show that he does not care about the judgments of the human day, because he longs to please the one Lord, to whom even his innermost thoughts lie open. For this is what he means: "The Lord is the one who judges me," and "The Lord knows who I am, what I intend in my heart, and with what faith I serve him." I rest on his conscience and am little concerned about what men judge of me. Tell me, how shall we appear before the sight of the Lord with confidence, if we must stand or fall not by our own conscience but by his judgment? So let us say with David: "Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord" [Ps. 143:2].

units.la: Proinde,ne ante tēpus quicquam iu dicetis,donec uenerit dominus, qui & illustraturus est occulta tenebrarum, & patefaciet consilia cordium, ac tūc laus erit unicuiq; à Deo.
units.tr: Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of the hearts; then each one's praise will come from God.

units.la: Colligit ex præmissis,abstinendū esse à iudicandi temeritate, eo quòd iudicium solius sit domini, qui solus nouit consilia cordium: quæ sunt à cogitatione mortalium abdita, & tenebris densissimis operta. Homo non potest aliter iudicare quàm secundum externam rerum faciem,Deus aùt intuetur corda. Nota est historia electionisDauidis,quàm erraverit Samuel in Eliab. Non uetat prosus iudicare.
units.tr: From what has been said he concludes that one must refrain from the rashness of judging, because judgment belongs to the Lord alone, who alone knows the counsels of hearts. These lie hidden from human thought and are covered in the thickest darkness. A man cannot judge otherwise than according to the outward appearance of things, but God looks upon the heart. The story of David's choosing is well known, how Samuel went wrong about Eliab. He does not forbid judging altogether.

units.la: Nequit enim iudicio carere, humanarum pari ter ac diuinarū rerum necesitas. Nam alioqui frustra dixisset: Omnia ˌpbate, qd̄ bonū est tene. & Spiritalis omnia dijudicat. Et 1. Tim. 5. Quorundam hominū peccata manifesta sunt præcedentia ad iudiciū. De illis non prohibet iudicare. Temeritate eam cohibet, qua Corinthij de ministris Christi iuxta faciem externa iudicantes, aliū in cœlum usq; euehebant, aliū prorsus abijciebant. Huius gratia dicit, Nolite ante tēpus, &c. itē, Donec uenerit dominus, qui illustraturus est occulta tenebrarū. Item, Tunc laus erit unicuiq; à Deo.
units.tr: For the necessity of judgment is no less present in human matters than in divine ones. Otherwise he would have spoken in vain: "Test all things; hold fast to what is good" [1 Thess. 5:21], and "The spiritual man judges all things" [1 Cor. 2:15]. And 1 Tim. 5: "The sins of some men are manifest beforehand, going before to judgment" [1 Tim. 5:24]. He does not forbid judging about these. He restrains the rashness with which the Corinthians, judging the ministers of Christ by outward appearance, lifted up one to heaven and cast another down altogether. For this reason he says, "Do not judge before the time," etc.; likewise, "until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness"; likewise, "then praise will come to each one from God."

units.la: Notantur iterum pseudapostoli, qui iudicij diuini nulla habita ratione laudē quērebāt apud homines in humano die. Minatur autē illis aduentū dñi, per quem olim sit lucis instar manifestū futurum, quod tum occulte ab illis gerebatur, cōscietiamq; mortalium fugiebat. Donec uenerit dominus, inquit, qui illustratu rus est occulta tenebrarū, & patefaciet cōsilia cordiū. Tum, inquit, diuersum apparebit. Qui nunc cōtēnuntur, si fideles fuerint inuenti coram Deo, gloriosi erunt & illustres: rursus qui nunc in precio sunt, si corā Deo fuerint deprehensi perfidi, prorsus abijciētur. Exemplo sint illi, de quibus Matth. 7. ad quos dicturus est Christus, Non noui uos, &c. Isti absq; dubio in humano die gloriosi fuerunt, prophetātes, uirtutes facientes, dæmonia eijcientes, &c.
units.tr: Again the false apostles are rebuked, who, with no regard for the divine judgment, sought praise from men in the human day. He threatens them with the coming of the Lord, through whom what was then secretly done by them, and hidden from the consciences of mortals, will one day be as manifest as the light. "Until the Lord comes," he says, "who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of the hearts. Then," he says, "the outcome will be different. Those who are now despised, if they are found faithful before God, will be glorious and illustrious; again, those who are now held in honor, if they are found faithless before God, will be utterly cast off." Let those of whom Matthew 7 speaks be examples, to whom Christ will say, "I never knew you," etc. Without doubt they were glorious in the human day: prophesying, doing mighty works, casting out demons, and so on.

units.la: Obserua uero, quod non simpliciter dicit, Cui nota sunt occulta tenebr. & consilia cord. sed, Qui illustraturus est, & patefaciet occulta teneb. & consi. cord. Nec simpliciter dicit, Cogitata: sed, Cōsilia cordiū. Acriter pūgit pseudapostolos, hactenus tamen parcens quod eos nō nominatim perstringit. Et parū forsan est, quod qui nunc in honore sunt, olim explodētur. Quis poterit exprimere cōfusionem eam, quam sustinebunt pseudapostolorum admiratores & adoratores, idq; duplici nomine. primum in illis quos suspexerunt: deinde in illis quos in hac uita contempserunt? Ista si fuerint probe ac sedulo expensa, absq; dubio coercebunt procliuitatē illam temere de Christi ministris iudicādi. Interea nō ˌphibet, quo minus iudicetur in ecclesia de reprobis tā ministris q; auditoribus. Iudicat ecclesia de manifestis, quæ iudiciū palā expofcūt: ipse uerò hic loquitur de occultis, de qbus nulli cōpetit ecclesiæ, ut iudicet, sed solius Dei est iudiciū. Quare nō simpliciter dicit, Proinde ne iudicetis quicq̄: sed, Proinde ne ante tēpus iudicetis quicq̄. Ante tēpus iudicat, qui de occultis sentētiā ˌpnūciat, priusq̄ manifestētur. Manifestatio aut occultorū, nō est horū temporū, nec cadit in cognitione & dijudicatione humani diei, sed reseruatur ultimo iudicio, secūdo Christi iudicis aduētui. Vnde subdit, Donec uenerit dñs qui & illustraturus est occulta tenebrarū, & patefaciet consilia cordium. Ad huius iudicij diem appellare nō est nisi eorū qui ueraciter dicere possunt, Nullius mihi mali cōscius sum. Cætero
units.tr: Observe, moreover, that he does not simply say, "To whom the hidden things of darkness and the counsels of the hearts are known," but, "Who will bring to light and reveal the hidden things of darkness and the counsels of the hearts." Nor does he simply say "thoughts" but "counsels of hearts." He stings the false apostles sharply, yet sparing them so far as not to name them. And perhaps it is a small thing that those who are now in honor will one day be hissed down. Who can express the confusion that the admirers and worshippers of the false apostles will endure, and that on two counts: first in regard to those whom they admired, and then in regard to those whom they despised in this life? If these things are duly and diligently weighed, they will without doubt restrain that proneness to judge rashly the ministers of Christ. Meanwhile he does not forbid that the reprobate, both ministers and hearers, be judged in the Church. The Church judges what is manifest, which openly calls for judgment; but he himself here speaks of hidden things, concerning which it does not belong to the Church to judge, but judgment belongs to God alone. Therefore he does not simply say, "Therefore judge nothing," but "Therefore do not judge anything before the time." He judges before the time who pronounces sentence on hidden things before they are made manifest. But the manifestation of hidden things does not belong to this age, nor falls within the knowledge and discernment of the human day; it is reserved for the last judgment, at the second coming of Christ the judge. Hence he adds, "until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of the hearts." Only those who can truly say, "I am conscious of no evil," can appeal to the day of this judgment. As for the sins of others that are already manifest, they are rightly judged, and they can no longer be judged before the time.

units.la: rorū peccata quæ manifesta iā sunt, rectè iudicātur, nec possūt amplius ante tēpus iudicari.
units.tr: Sins that are already manifest are rightly judged, and they can no longer be judged before the time.

units.la: Obserua uero q̄ elegāti similitudine cōparet aduentū Christi exortui solis, cū dicit: Donec uenerit dñs, q̄ & illuminabit occulta tenebrarū. Sol exortu suo illuminat ea quæ nocturnis fuerāt tenebris abdita & occulta, ut cunctorū oculis patefiāt. Sic Christus ubi uenerit ad iudiciū, dispellet oēs hasce tenebras, quibus nūc occulta cordiū nostrorum obteguntur, imò regni Satanæ quoq; regni tenebrarū neqtias quæ tūuis abditas & abstrusas patefaciet. In hisce tenebris multa occuluntur, præsertim in Antichristianismo, quæ dies dñi luce sua omnibus reddet manifesta. Multi iā habētur pro orthodoxis, quos cognoscem⁹ in illo die ipsissimos esse hæreticos. Rursus multi habētur ˌphæreticis, quos tū uidebimus à dño agnosci ˌp ueris fidelib. Ludit Satan in tenebris istis & cordibus incredulorū: uerum expectemus diem domini, & cōmittamus iudicium occultorum futuræ illius illustrationi.
units.tr: Observe further how elegantly he compares the coming of Christ to the rising of the sun, when he says: "Until the Lord comes, who will also illuminate the hidden things of darkness." The sun at its rising illuminates those things which were hidden and concealed by the darkness of night, so that they are laid open to the eyes of all. So Christ, when he comes to judgment, will disperse all those shadows by which the hidden things of our hearts are now covered; indeed, he will also lay open the wickednesses of Satan's kingdom, the kingdom of darkness, though they are now concealed and remote. Many things are hidden in these shadows, especially in Antichristianism, which the day of the Lord will make manifest to all by its light. Many are now held to be orthodox whom we shall know on that day to be the very heretics. Again, many are held to be heretics whom we shall then see acknowledged by the Lord as true believers. Satan plays in these shadows and in the hearts of unbelievers; but let us await the day of the Lord, and commit the judgment of hidden things to its future illumination.

units.la: Illud, Et tunc laus erit unicuiq; à Deo, non est nisi de ijs dictū, qui fideles in die iudicij inueniētur. Quare addēdū erat, quid hypocritis ac perfidis futurum sit. Verūm non eo spectabat, sed laudem duntaxat pseudapostolorum suggillare uolebat, qua tātopere à Corinthijs extollebātur, sibiq; præferebātur. Quasi dicat: Iam admodū uestros istos doctores laudatis, ac me respectu illorū fastiditis, uerū inconstās hæc est illorū laus. Laudis tēpus erit, ubi uenerit dominus. Ibi uere laudabuntur, qui synceri ac fideles à domino inuenientur.
units.tr: The words "and then praise will come to each one from God" are spoken only of those who are found faithful on the day of judgment. Hence it would have been necessary to add what awaits hypocrites and faithless men. But he did not have that in view; he meant only to strike at the praise of the false apostles, which the Corinthians extolled so greatly and set above his own. As if he said: "Now you praise your teachers so highly, and despise me in comparison with them; but this praise of theirs is inconstant. There will be a time of praise when the Lord comes. Then those will truly be praised who are found by the Lord to be sincere and faithful."

units.la: Hæc autē fratres per figurā trāstuli in meipsum & Apollo, propter uos, ut in nobis discereti, ne quis supra id quod dictū est sentiat, ut ne alius pro alio adueʀsus alium inflemini.
units.tr: These things, brothers, I have transferred by way of figure to myself and Apollos, for your sake, so that in us you may learn not to think beyond what is written, and that none of you may be puffed up for one against another.

units.la: 1 Exponit quomodo dixerit: Etenim cū dicat aliqs, Ego sum Pauli, &c. Et, Quis est Paulus? Quis est Apollos, &c. Et omnia uestra sunt, siue Paulus, siue Apollos, cū tamē nec sub sua, nec Apollo persona uiguerint Corinthiorū dissidia, quæ corrigere instituit: Hæc, inquit, fratres, per transfigurationē in me & Apollo transtuli, non quod nostra nomina dissidiorū dederint materiā, sed quod sub illis declarare uoluerim dissidiorum uestrorum absurditatē: ut admonerem uos, ne amplius alius pro alio aduersus alium inflemini.
units.tr: 1 He explains what he meant. For when someone says, "I am of Paul," etc., and "Who is Paul? Who is Apollos?" etc., and "All things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos," although the divisions of the Corinthians did not arise under his own name or Apollos's, which he set out to correct: "I have transferred these things, brothers," he says, "to myself and Apollos by a figure. I do not mean that our names gave rise to the divisions, but that under them I wished to show how absurd your divisions are, so that I might warn you not to be puffed up any further, one for another and against another."

units.la: 2 μεταχηματισμός, transfiguraui. Μετασχηματισμός est, quādo sub aliena persona, siue nostra siue aliorum, aut ficta, quorundam delicta incusamus. Eius generis etiā est, quando non solum persona aliena inducimus, sed & crime aliud sub alio cōfīcto, aut uero quoq;, cōsimili tamē, reprehendamus. Notū est exemplum prophetæ Nathan, qua transfiguratione, & persone & criminis in corrigendo Dauide fit usus.
units.tr: 2 "I have transferred" (μεταχηματισμός). A transfiguration (μετασχηματισμός) is when we accuse some people of their faults under the persona of another, whether real (ours or someone else's) or invented. This kind also includes the case where we introduce not only another person but also another, invented crime, or even a true one, though a similar one, and rebuke it. The example of the prophet Nathan is well known, who used this transfiguration of both person and crime in correcting David.

units.la: PROPTER uos.] Hoc est, ut uobis parcerẽ tanq̄ ægrotis & imbecillibus, ne uos scilicet offendeoffendere, si ex nomine quod suspicitis taxare. Relucet hic iterum Apostoli prudentia, omnibus Christi ministris observanda. Sectarij ingenio sunt animantium praediti, quibus durum est & intollerabile, si nominatim perstringantur, de quibus gloriatur & a quibus pendent, ita ut magis iritetur q curetur. Ideo prudeti consilio usus, re ipsam quidem q sit absurda ob oculos expositum, sed sub alienis psonis & nominibus, idq; non quibuslibet: sed ut tollerabilior esset admonitio cum primis sub sua, deinde & Apollo persona.
units.tr: "For your sake." That is, so that he might spare you as sick and weak people, lest he offend you if he criticised by name the person you admire. Here again the prudence of the Apostle shines out, to be observed by all ministers of Christ. Sectarians are men of a temperament like animals, to whom it is hard and intolerable to be attacked by name, the very people in whom they boast and on whom they depend, so that they are provoked rather than cured. So the Apostle, using wise counsel, set before their eyes the very absurdity itself, but under other persons and names, and not just any names: he chose his own name first, and then Apollos's, so that the admonition might be more bearable.

units.la: Prudentiam istam imitentur omnes uerbi ministri, castiganda sunt uitia, sed ita ut delinquentes curetur, no exasperetur: quod potissimum faciendum est, ubi studia partium inua lescant. Si ea est delinquetium imbecillitas, ut non sint laturi, si recta inuehamur in morbos, quibus laborat, aut taxemus ex nomine, a qui bus dependet: utendu est Apostoli exemplo, ut per obliquu & transfigurationem uel persona rum uel criminis, qd uolumus assequamur.
units.tr: All ministers of the Word should imitate this prudence. Vices must be rebuked, but in such a way that the offender is healed and not exasperated. This is especially to be done when the zeal of parties grows hot. If the weakness of the offenders is such that they will not bear it if we attack the diseases that afflict them directly, or name the men on whom they depend, we should follow the Apostle's example and achieve what we want obliquely, through a transfiguration of persons or of the crime.

units.la: Inest aut non solum prudentia in isto trasfi gurationis consilio, sed & affectus dilectionis, plane paternus, qui se in mille figuras uertit, ut laborati filio succurrat. No dicit, propter ue stros pseudapostolos, sed propter uos: ut intel ligas non metum esse, quod no ausus sit offendere tantos uiros, sed affectum charitatis, quo noluerit irritare imbecilles & aegrotos. Ingeniosa res est, & solliciti plena timotis amor. Qui isto praediti sunt affectu, no utcunq; inue hentur in delinquetes, sed magna id solicitudi ne, moderatione & cautione facient, unice spe stantes, quid ferre ualeant, quid non, quos emendare constituunt.
units.tr: In this counsel of transfiguration there is present not only prudence but also a feeling of love, plainly paternal, which turns itself into a thousand shapes so as to help its suffering child. He does not say "for the sake of your pseudo-apostles" but "for your sake," so that you may understand that it was not fear that stopped him from offending such great men, but a feeling of charity, by which he was unwilling to provoke the weak and sick. It is a clever thing, and love full of anxious care. Those who have this feeling do not attack offenders in just any way, but with great care, moderation and caution, looking only to what they can bear and what they cannot, in those whom they resolve to correct.

units.la: VT in nobis discerLetis. Duo dicit. Primu, quid toto hoc tractatu eos admonere voluerit, uidelicet, ut discerent no sentire supra eam regulam qua descripsit, de quoquā, nec inflari pro alio aduersus alium. Alteru, ut id disceret in se & Apollo, cum quod ipsi nihil huius unquam spectarint, nec unquam consilium disisidijs dederint, tum quod pro animi morbo no sustinuissent id in illis discere, quos plus equo extollebant. Ea nanq; amoris est caecitas, ut ui cium non uideatur uicium, in eo quē deperis: uideatur autem statim in alijs, quos no admodum curas. Quod ergo in pseudapostolis non didicissent, in se & Apollo spectandum ac discendum proposuit.
units.tr: "So that in us you may learn." He says two things. First, what he wished to teach them in this whole discussion: namely, that they should learn not to think about anyone beyond the rule he has described, and not to be puffed up for one against another. Second, that they should learn this in himself and Apollos, since neither of them had ever aimed at anything of this kind, nor ever given counsel for divisions; and also because, for the sake of healing their disease, they were unwilling to let those whom they were overpraising be the ones in whom they learned it. For love is so blind that a fault in the one it dotes on does not seem a fault, while it is seen at once in others whom we do not care for so much. So what they had not learned from the pseudo-apostles, he set before them to be observed and learned in himself and Apollos.

units.la: SVPRA id qd scriptū est. Chrysost. putat aliquē scripturae locum intelligi ab Apostolo, utpote: Quid uides festucā in oculo fratris tui, &c. uel, Nolite iudicare, ne iudicemini: uel, Qui se exaltat, humiliabitur: aut, Quicunq; uo luerit inter uos maior fieri, sit omniū minister. At ista domini licet uerba sint, non tamen ue risimiliter ab Apostolo per scripturam intelligi puto, eo quod cum ista scriberet, Euangelistarum scripta, aut nondum extabant, aut nondum Corinthijs innotuerant.
units.tr: "Beyond what is written." Chrysostom thinks the Apostle means some passage of Scripture, such as "Why do you see the mote in your brother's eye?" etc., or "Judge not, that you be not judged," or "He who exalts himself shall be humbled," or "Whoever among you wishes to be greater, let him be the servant of all." But although these are the Lord's words, I do not think the Apostle probably means them by "Scripture," because when he wrote this the Gospels of the evangelists either did not yet exist or were not yet known to the Corinthians.

units.la: Hieron. exponit, ne quisq; supra scripturae
units.tr: Jerome explains it: "that no one think beyond the discipline of Scripture."

units.la: disciplina sentiat. Ambrosius trāsit. Simplicius aut uidetur, ut intelligamus de eo quod supra scripsit. Sic nos existimet homo tanquam ministros Christi, &c.
units.tr: Ambrose passes it over. Simplicius, however, seems to refer it to what he wrote above: "Let a man so regard us as ministers of Christ," etc.

units.la: 6 [Greek].] Erasmus adiecit, De se, quasi nolit Apostolus quenq; de seipso supra mensura pscripta sentire. Verū, si addedu est aliqd, malim adijcere, de quoq. Alloquitur enim hic no uer bi ministros, de quibus plus aequo eximie sen tiebatur a Corinthijs: sed ipsos auditores ac di scipulos, quos a praepostera praeceptorū admi ratione auocat, quorū gratia trasfiguratione, cuius meminit, usum se esse dicit. Et huc facit etiā qd subiūgit, Vt ne alius p alio aduersus aliū inflemini. Nā id ex eo plerūq; sequitur, ut in flētur cōtra alios q de quibusdā ut eximijs ac praeclaris gloriātur. id qd inter sectarios usu uenire uidemus, dū Fracisani p suo Fracisco, aduersus Dominicastros inflātur, & illi uicif sim. Proinde praemisit illud, ne quisq; supra pre scripta regulā de quoq; sentiat. Qui enim de o mnibus uerbi praeconibus nihil aliud sentit q quod ministri sint Christi, ac dispensatores my steriorū Dei: is certe nullius gratia aduersum quenquam inflabitur, sed de uniuersis idē sen tiens, omnes ex aequo uenerabitur.
units.tr: 6 [μὴ ὑπὲρ ἃ γέγραπται φρονεῖν]. Erasmus added "concerning himself," as if the Apostle did not want anyone to think of himself beyond the measure prescribed. But if anything is to be added, I would rather add "concerning anyone." For here the Apostle is not speaking of ministers, about whom the Corinthians were thinking too highly, but of the hearers and disciples themselves, whom he calls away from a perverse admiration of the teachers; and he says that he used the transfiguration he mentioned for their sake. This also fits what follows: "that none of you may be puffed up for one against another." For this usually results from the fact that men are puffed up against others when they boast of certain people as outstanding and distinguished. We see this happen among the sectarians, when the Franciscans are puffed up for their Francis against the Dominicans, and the Dominicans in turn against them. Therefore he put first, "that no one think about anyone beyond the prescribed rule." For whoever thinks of all the heralds of the Word only that they are ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God will certainly not be puffed up on behalf of anyone against anyone else, but thinking the same of all, he will honour them all equally.

units.la: 7 [Greek], id est, inflemini. Metaphora est sumpta de membrorū inflatione, quae ex morbo, corruptis humoribus, aut spiritu malis humoribus pleno nascitur. Ad eum modū & animi superbia inflatio dicitur, propter spiritus perversi tumore. Quod si ista animorū inflatione idē cōcomitaretur dolorū sensus, qui in nodosa sentiuntur podagra, forsan citius curaretur.
units.tr: 7 [φυσιοῦσθε], that is, "be puffed up." It is a metaphor taken from the swelling of the limbs, which arises from disease, from corrupt humours, or from wind filled with bad humours. In this way pride of mind is also called inflation, because of the swelling of a perverse spirit. If the sense of pain that is felt in the knotted gout accompanied this swelling of minds, perhaps it would be cured more quickly.

units.la: Notatur aut a Chrysost. q sit stultū de aliena gloria inflari, quod perinde est, atq; si quis p pter alienas diuitias superbiat. Quid quaeso fa ciet in propria gloria constitutus, qui etiam alie na superbiendi sumit argumentum.
units.tr: Chrysostom also notes that it is foolish to be puffed up over another's glory, which is just as if someone were proud of other people's riches. What, I ask, will he do who is set up in his own glory, if he takes even another's glory as a ground for pride?

units.la: Quis enim te discernit? Quid autem habes quod no accepisti? Qd si etiā accepisti, quid gloriaris quasi no acceperis?
units.tr: Who makes you to differ? What do you have that you did not receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?

units.la: 1 Apostrophe est trina pcōtatione uehemēs & urgēs, deinde numero singulari uelut unū quēq; cōueniēs. exponitur aut no eodē modo. nā aliqui referūt ad ipsos doctores, q apud Corinthios difsidiorū authores erat, utpote Chrysost. & Hieron. Quidā uero ad auditores ac discipulos de praeceptoribus suis gloriātes, id qd Ambros. facit. Paraphrastes Eras. priore pcōtatione discipulis, reliquas doctoribus applicat.
units.tr: 1 This is an apostrophe, a threefold repetition, vehement and urgent, then addressed in the singular, as if to each person in turn. It is not explained in the same way by everyone. Some refer it to the teachers themselves, who were the authors of the divisions among the Corinthians, as Chrysostom and Jerome do. Others refer it to the hearers and disciples who boast about their teachers, as Ambrose does. Erasmus the paraphraser applies the first repetition to the disciples and the rest to the teachers.

units.la: 2 QVIS te discernit? [Greek] uariae significationis uerbū est. Nā & discernere significat, & extollere (quoniam selecta plerunq; discernuntur) & dijudicare: unde & Chrysostomus dijudicandi sensu particulam hanc exponit, quem sequutus est Erasmus, ita reddens: Quis enim te dijudicat? Si legerimus, Quis te discer nit? sensus est, Quis te reliquis praefert? quis te extollit? quis eximium reddit? Si, quis te dijudicat, idem est, ac si dicat, Cuius nam iudicio tibi places? quis te examinat, inquirit, probat,
units.tr: 2 "Who makes you to differ?" [διακρίνει] is a word of varied meaning. It signifies to distinguish, to exalt (since choice things are commonly set apart), and to judge. Hence Chrysostom takes this particle in the sense of judging, and Erasmus followed him in rendering it: "For who judges you?" If we read "Who distinguishes you?", the sense is: "Who prefers you to the rest? Who exalts you? Who makes you outstanding?" If we read "Who judges you?", it is the same as saying: "By whose judgment do you please yourself? Who examines, inquires into and approves you,"

units.la: bat, eximiumq; esse deprehendit? Cuius calcu lis usus extolleris? quasi dicat, Homines impe riti ac stulti, sua de te opinione decepti, eximi um te esse putant ac dijudicant, & inde super bis. Atqui non quem homo, sed quem Deus commendat ac dijudicat, ille demum probatus est. Hominum iudicium fallit. Videtur hoc sen su respicere ad ea quae initio capitis huius sub sua persona dixit, Mihi autem pro minimo est, ut a vobis dijudicer, aut ab humano die, &c. Caeterum qui me iudicat, dominus est, &c.
units.tr: and finds you outstanding? "By whose verdict are you exalted?" As if he said: "Foolish and unskilled men, deceived by their own opinion of you, think and judge you outstanding, and on that account you are puffed up. Yet it is not the one whom a man commends but the one whom God commends and judges who is at last approved. Human judgment deceives." This seems in this sense to refer to what at the beginning of this chapter he said in his own person: "But to me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you, or by man's day," and so on, "But he who judges me is the Lord," and so on.

units.la: Potest illud, Quis te discernit? ita exponi, ut ad Deum referatur. Quasi dicat, Si charismatis alicuius gratia superbis, quaeso quis est, qui te singulari dono a reliquis discreuit? An tu ipse? Certe nequaquam. Quid enim habes quod non acceperis? Atqui ita coueniet haec particula cum sequentibus.
units.tr: It is also possible to explain "Who makes you to differ?" as referring to God. As if he said: "If you are proud of some gift of grace, I ask, who is it who has set you apart from the rest by a singular gift? You yourself? Certainly not. For what have you that you have not received?" Explained this way, the particle fits well with what follows.

units.la: 3 QVID aut habes quod non acceperis? Co muniter exponunt, Quid habes quod non a Deo acceperis. Solus Ambrosius aliter. Is, ut dixi, arbitratur tota hac apostrophe ptinere ad eos, qui praeceptorum gratia aduersus alios inflabā tur, sefeq; a reliquis seiungebat, & exponit ad hunc modum: Quid iam habes, qui reliquos cōte nis, quod antea a me non acceperis? Quid cotulit tibi magister iste, de quo ita gloriaris, ut reli quos fastidias, quo hactenus carueris? Qua fi dem interea, & quae noua charismata per istū magistrū tuum consequutus es? Quod si quae audis, audisti & antea: quae habes, accepisti iam antea, ut nihil noui, nihil praecipui, quo carue ris hactenus, post abitū meum acceperis: quae so qua ratione usq; adeo de magistro hoc tuo, cui nomē das, gloriaris, ut a reliquis separeris?
units.tr: 3 "What have you that you have not received?" Commonly they explain this as: "What do you have that you have not received from God?" Only Ambrose reads it differently.
