As I said, he thinks that this whole apostrophe concerns those who were puffed up against others on account of their teachers and separated themselves from the rest. He explains it thus: "What do you now have, that you despise the others, which you did not receive from me before? What did that teacher of yours, of whom you boast so as to scorn the rest, bring you that you lacked until now? What new faith, and what new gifts, have you meanwhile obtained through this teacher of yours? But if you hear things, you heard them before as well. What you have, you received already before; nothing new, nothing special, which you lacked until now, did you receive after my departure. For what reason, I ask, do you so boast of this teacher of yours, whose name you take, that you separate yourself from the rest?"

units.la: Et isti sententiae duo uidentur in uerbis Apostoli fauere.
units.tr: Two things in the Apostle's words seem to favour this opinion.

units.la: Vnū est, quod non simpliciter dicit, Quis te discernit? Sed, Quis enim te discernit? ut quasi praemissae admonitioni rationis uice subiungatur istae percotationes, propter causalem γαρ. Dixit enim, ut in nobis disceretis: ne quis supra id quod scriptum est, de quoquā sentiat, ut ne alius p alio, contra aliū inflętur. Hic quasi ratio nē exiges, cur aliquis putet sibi contra reliquos alicuius nomine gloriādū esse, uel certe ostendes neminē tāti faciedū esse, ut illi gratia debeat quisq; a reliquo sese fideliū grege secerne re, subijcit: Quis enī te discernit? Quasi dicat, Quis enim tāti est, ut authoritate sua a reliquis Christianis te separare possit? Quisnā ille est, qui tāti facis, ut illi nomine infleris aduersus fratres? Si Christū spectas, at ille cōmunis est omniū credētiū dns. Si doctore aliquē, at quis qs ille & quātus quātus sit, nō dns est, sed mini ster, cuius non est officiū secernere, sed cōiun gere Christo credentes. Malus dux est, qui re giū exercitū authoritate sua disipat ac sepa rat, quē debebat seruare quām unitissimum.
units.tr: The first is that he does not simply say, "Who makes you to differ?" but "For who makes you to differ?" so that these interrogations are added as a kind of reason for the preceding admonition, by the causal "for" (γάρ). For he had said, "that in us you might learn" (1 Cor. 4:6): that no one should think of anyone beyond what is written, so that one is not puffed up for one man against another. Here, as if demanding a reason why anyone should think he ought to glory in another's name against the rest, or at least showing that no one is to be valued so highly that for his favour one should separate oneself from the flock of the faithful, he adds: "For who makes you to differ?" As if he said: "For who is of such account that by his authority he can separate you from the other Christians? Who is he whom you value so much that you are puffed up with his name against the brothers? If you look to Christ, he is the common Lord of all believers. If you look to some teacher, however great or small he may be, he is not Lord but minister, whose office is not to separate but to join believers to Christ. He is a bad leader who by his authority scatters and divides the king's army, which he ought to keep as united as possible."

units.la: Alterum est, quod nō dicit, Qd' si accepisti: sed, Quod si etiā accepisti, qd gloriaris? Quasi dicat: Qd' si id, cuius nomine gloriaris de no uo doctore, etiā a me iam antea accepisti, quid gloriaris quasi nō acceperis? Videntur aut̄ & sequētia huic sententiae astipulari, & uelut p dere affectum huc Apostoli, cum dicit: Iam sa turati estis, iam ditati estis, &c.
units.tr: The second is that he does not say, "But if you received," but "But if you also received, why do you glory?" As if he said: "But if that thing, on account of which you glory in the new teacher, you also received from me before, why do you glory as if you had not received it?" The words that follow also seem to support this opinion, and as it were to betray the Apostle's feeling here, when he says: "Already you are full, already you are rich," and so on.

units.la: Et sane ita plerūq; euenire uidemus, ut no uum doctorem adeptus populus, eum quem antea habuit fastidiat, deq; nouo insolescat & superbiat, etiam si is nihil adferat, quod antea non audierint.
units.tr: And indeed we see this happen often: a people who has obtained a new teacher despises the one it had before, and becomes proud and arrogant about the new one, even if he brings nothing that they had not heard before.

units.la: Quod si ista Ambrosij sententia cuiquam ar ridet, per me licet illa utatur. Alioqui cōmuni ter hęc Apostoli uerba cōtra arrogantes ac su perbos quosuis usurpātur. Quisquis enim glo riatur, alicuius nomine oportet glorietur, qd' sibi uel soli, uel cum paucissimis uindicet rarū & eximiū: ut sunt sapientia, eruditio, eloquen tia, opum splendor, corporis uenustas, opinio iusticiae, & quae alia sunt huiusmodi. Illis ogge ritur, Quid habes quod non acceperis? Quod si accepisti, quid gloriaris, quasi nō acceperis?
units.tr: But if Ambrose's opinion pleases anyone, let him use it by my leave. Otherwise these words of the Apostle are commonly applied against all arrogant and proud people. For whoever glories must glory in something, which he claims for himself alone, or with very few, as rare and remarkable: such as wisdom, learning, eloquence, splendour of wealth, beauty of body, a reputation for righteousness, and whatever else is of this kind. To these people it is said: "What have you that you have not received? But if you received it, why do you glory as if you had not received it?"

units.la: 4 Insunt autem his uerbis duo notanda.
units.tr: 4 Two points are to be noted in these words.

units.la: 1 Vnum est, Neminem habere quicquam, quod non acceperit a Deo, siue immediate, si ue per ministerium aliorum, uel angelorū, uel hominum uel bestiarum. Nam omne bonū de sursum est, &c.
units.tr: 1 The first is that no one has anything which he has not received from God, whether immediately or through the ministry of others: of angels, of men, or even of beasts. For every good gift is from above, and so on.

units.la: 2 Alterum est, illicitum esse gloriari de alieno bono. Nam omnis gloria illi debetur, cuius, & a quo sunt omnia. Ideo dicit: Si accepisti, quid gloriaris quasi non acceperis? Non dicit: Si accepisti, noli gloriari de alieno. Sed quid glo riaris? Notat enim impudentiā huiusmodi arrogantiae, quasi dicat: Quidnam rationis praetexere potes, ut merito uideare gloriari de eo quod non tuum est, sed aliunde habes? Ridicu lum plane est de alienis bonis superbire. Nota est Aesopica cornicula, quae alienis coloribus ornata, tandem pudefacta est. Iam uide, si stul tum est, ridiculum, absurdū, & si Deum respi cias, impium etiam gloriari de bonis, quę licet acceperis, habes tamē: quid sentiendū de illis, qui per hypocrisim ea simulant quę nō habēt, illorum opinione sese uenditant?
units.tr: 2 The second is that it is unlawful to glory in another's good. For all glory is owed to him of whom and by whom all things are. Therefore he says: "If you received it, why do you glory as if you had not received it?" He does not say: "If you received it, do not glory in what is another's." He says "why do you glory?" For he notes the shamelessness of such arrogance, as if he said: "What reasonable pretext can you offer, by which you could rightly seem to glory in what is not yours but you have from elsewhere? It is plainly ridiculous to be proud of another's goods. The Aesopic jackdaw is well known, who, decked out in others' colours, was at last put to shame. Now consider whether it is foolish, ridiculous and absurd, and if you look to God, even impious, to glory in goods which, though you received them, you nevertheless have. What then should we think of those who by hypocrisy pretend to have what they do not have, and put themselves on sale by that opinion of them?"

units.la: Iam saturati estis, iam ditati estis, absque nobis regnum adepti estis, atq; utinam sane adepti sitis, ut &nos simul uobiscum regnemus.
units.tr: Already you are full, already you are rich; without us you have obtained the kingdom. And would that you had indeed obtained it, so that we might reign together with you.

units.la: Haec & quae sequūtur admodum falsa sunt, & stomachū respiciunt. Primum autem notat Corinthiorum fastidium & cōtemptum, quo erga se & doctrinā ab ipso accepta alio a pseud apostolis abducti & inescati laborabant. Facit autem id non sine ironia, cum dicit: Iam satu rati estis, iam ditati estis, &c. Non enim iam e rant perfectam regni Christi cognitionē ade pti, neque dum aliquo usque in spiritu excre uerant. Siquidem, ut supra dixit, carnales ad huc erant. At uidebantur sibi iam abunde dita ti, & magnam coelestium rerum cognitionem adepti. Iuxta hanc ipsorum opinionem per iro niam loquitur, dicens: Iam saturati estis, iam ditati estis, &c.
units.tr: These words, and what follows, are quite false, and they smack of a disgusted stomach. First, he rebukes the Corinthians' disdain and contempt, by which, drawn away and enticed by the false apostles, they despised both him and the teaching they had received from him. He does this not without irony when he says, "Already you are full, already you are rich," and so on. For they had not yet attained a perfect knowledge of the kingdom of Christ, nor had they yet grown up in the Spirit; indeed, as he said above, they were still carnal. But they seemed to themselves already abundantly rich and to have attained a great knowledge of heavenly things. It is in accordance with this their own opinion that he speaks ironically, saying, "Already you are full, already you are rich," and so on.

units.la: Morbus hic omnino uulgaris est, & animū indicat imbecillem. Vt enim infirmi stomachi indicium est, si quisquam cito & modico cibo ita saturetur,ut fastidio edēdi afficiatur: ita & infirmi animi argumentū est & plane puerilis, si quisquam cum uix prima teneat rudimenta, putet se iam ad ipsum scietiæ rerum uerticem ascēdisse. Et ipsa saturitatis metaphora,qua utitur Apostolus,huc respicit,quemadmodū & reliquæ duæ,nēpe,iam ditati estis. itē, iam regnatis,cōsimilem morbum metaphoricas exprimunt. Nā quod in suo genere usuuenit stomacho infirmo,id & tenuioribus accidit, qui mox atq; aliquam adepti sunt facultatulā, iam arbitrantur se abunde diuites effectos esse ac prorsus regnare,cū adhuc multis egeant. Piorum itaq; est quod ad ueritatis cognitionē & solidæ pietatis studium attinet,insatiabilē habere ingluuiem & perpetuam auaritiam: nec unquā sibi persuadere quod aliquid sint perfectionis adepti.
units.tr: This sickness is wholly common and reveals a feeble mind. For just as it is a sign of a weak stomach if someone is quickly satisfied with a small amount of food, so that he is seized with a loathing of eating, so too it is a sign of a weak mind, and plainly a childish one, if someone who has scarcely learned the first rudiments thinks he has already climbed to the very summit of knowledge. The metaphor of fullness which the Apostle uses refers to this, and the two that follow, namely "already you are rich" and "already you reign," express a similar sickness in metaphorical terms. For what happens to a weak stomach in its own kind also happens to those of slender means, who, as soon as they have acquired some small ability, at once think they have become abundantly wealthy and altogether reigning, though they still lack many things. Therefore it is the duty of the godly, as far as the knowledge of truth and the pursuit of solid piety is concerned, to have an insatiable appetite and a perpetual greed, and never to persuade themselves that they have attained anything of perfection.

units.la: Quod secundo dicit,iam,iam,uidetur nō cama rere admiratione. quasi dicat: Tā cito saturati estis: Tā cito ditati estis: Et illud, ἐβασιλεύσατε, licet in forma præteriti sit positū,in præsenti tamē legendū est,ut & uetus reddidit. Nō enim actum notat præteritum,sed qui adhuc duret: ideo & Eras.reddidit,Non regnastis,sed regnū adepti estis. Potest accipi pro Ebraismo, quo præteritum positum sit pro præsenti.
units.tr: What he says secondly, "already, already," seems not to lack admiration, as if he were saying: "So quickly have you been filled! So quickly have you been made rich!" And as for the word [ἐβασιλεύσατε], although it is put in the past tense, it ought to be read in the present, as the Old translator rendered it. For the past tense does not denote a completed action but one that still lasts. Hence Erasmus too rendered it not as "you did not reign" but as "you have obtained the kingdom." It may be taken as a Hebraism, in which the past tense is used for the present.

units.la: Intelligit autem per uerbum regnādi nihil aliud quàm plena scientiæ facultate, ut nullius opem desiderent. Regnare enim hic idem est, atq; uicisse,enauigasse,eoq; euasisse,ut iam citra cuiusq; opitulationem cōsistere liceat. Regnum duo habet. Vnum, quod attinet rerū gerendarum facultatē: alterum,quod concernit imperādi potestatē. Iuxta primā regnandi rationem dicit,sine nobis regnatis. Hoc est, Eò promouistis iam opinione uestra, ut nulla in re putetis operam meā uobis esse necessariā, euasistis iam omnem rerum ignorantiam,omnem Christiani nominis ignominiam, omnē passionum Christi infirmitatem, in Christo regnatis, prudentes,ualidi & clari.
units.tr: By the verb "to reign" he understands nothing other than a full ability of knowledge, so that people no longer need anyone's help. For to reign here is the same as to have conquered, to have sailed through, and so to have got clear, so that it is now permitted to stand without anyone's assistance. Kingdom has two senses: one concerns the ability to carry out affairs, the other concerns the power of commanding. According to the first sense of reigning he says, "you reign without us." That is: by your own opinion you have advanced so far that you think my labour is necessary to you in no matter; you have now got clear of all ignorance of things, all disgrace of the Christian name, all the weakness of Christ's sufferings; you reign in Christ, prudent, strong and illustrious.

units.la: ATQVE utinā regnetis.] Pathos est,quo in dicat tā abesse,ut inuideat illis regnū in Christo, ut doleat sibi quòd magis opinioē regnet q ueritate,optetq; ipsis ex animo,ut regnet. Si mul tamē innuit eos nihil minus q regnū esse adeptos. Alioqui dicēdū erat, gratulor uobis, quòd hactenus ꝏmoueritis,ut iā regnetis. Cū uero optat ut regnent,indicat se diuersum uidere in illis ab eo regno,de quo superbiebant.
units.tr: "And would that you reigned." This is an expression of feeling, by which he says that he is so far from begrudging them the kingdom in Christ that he grieves that they reign more in opinion than in truth, and he wishes from his heart that they might truly reign. At the same time he hints that they have attained the kingdom in no way at all. Otherwise he ought to have said, "I congratulate you that you have so far advanced as now to reign." But when he wishes that they might reign, he shows that he sees in them something different from that kingdom of which they were boasting.

units.la: VT & nos simul uobiscū regnemus.] Hoc est,ut & nos in gloria simus uobiscū. Ergo gloria,pacē ac regnum sibi optat Apostolus: Nequaq. Sed hoc indicat, se merito debere participē esse gloriæ ipsorū,tanquā præceptorē, eo quòd à se acceperint,si quid habeant. Ita quip pe comparatum est in rerum æquitate, ut gloria discipulorum sit gloria præceptoris.
units.tr: "So that we might reign together with you." That is: so that we too might be with you in glory. So the Apostle does not wish for glory, peace and a kingdom for himself, by no means. But he indicates that, as their teacher, he deserves rightly to share in their glory, since they have received from him whatever they have. For it is so ordained by the equity of things that the glory of the disciples is the glory of the teacher.

units.la: Vel si ista expositio nō placet,intelligendus
units.tr: Or if this explanation does not please, one must understand that he speaks out of paternal affection,

units.la: A est ex affectu paterno loqui: quo fit,ut regnate filio,id est,cōmode & prosperè habeꝛe, regnet & pater,animi scilicet affectu, etiamsi foris nihil huius appareat. Et huius affectus infrà recordabitur. Et hic sensus magis arridet. Plus enim resipit Apostolici pectoris non seipsum, sed quæ aliorum sunt spectantis.
units.tr: by which it comes about that, when the son reigns, that is, is well and prosperously placed, the father also reigns, in his feelings at least, even if nothing of this appears outwardly. He will also recall this affection below. And this sense pleases me more. For it savours more of an apostolic heart which looks not to itself but to what belongs to others.

units.la: Arbitror em,quod Deus nos Apostolos nouissimos ostēderit tanquā morti destinatos. Quoniā spectaculū facti sumus mundo,& angelis & hominibus.
units.tr: For I think that God has displayed us apostles as last of all, as men destined to death, since we have been made a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men.

units.la: Declarat se nihil minꝰ q regnare: sed omniū esse abiectissimū,mirisq; modis iactari & affligi. Ostendit autē,licet occultius, nō ita destinatū esse à Deo,ut qui Christi sunt, in honore sint,& regnēt in hoc seculo: idq; cōiiciendum exhibet suo exēplo,qd opponit studio & fortunæ pseudapostolorū,quos admodū infyncē ritatis insimulat,qua nō quę Christi, sed q sua ipsorū quærentes,curabát & satagebant, ut in precio haberentur,nobiles & clari regnarent, cū ipse interea pro fide Christi ceu stultus, imbecillis & cōtemptus abijceretur. Tantū nō dicit,Non ambulatis recto pede ad Euangelium Christi,alioqui non regnaretis,sed mecū affligtaremini. Tanta náq; pro Christo patior quo tidie,ut appareat nos uelut morti destinatos esse à Deo,& ob eam causam missos,ut passim morti exponamur.
units.tr: He declares that he reigns in no way less, but is the most abject of all and is tossed and afflicted in marvellous ways. He shows, though more obscurely, that it is not God's intention that those who belong to Christ should be in honour and reign in this age; and he offers this as a conjecture from his own example, which he sets against the zeal and fortune of the false apostles, whom he accuses of great insincerity, in that they, seeking not the things of Christ but their own, took care and were busy that they might be held in esteem and, as nobles and illustrious men, reign, while meanwhile he himself, for the faith of Christ, was cast off as foolish, weak and despised. He does not quite say, "You are not walking with a straight foot to the Gospel of Christ; otherwise you would reign, but you would suffer with me." For I suffer so much daily for Christ that it appears that we have been destined to death by God, and for that reason sent so that we may be exposed to death on every side.

units.la: APOSTOLOS nouissimos.] Amphiboli ce dictū est,ut nescias,an dicat se nouissimum ostēsum esse Apostolū, uel se nouissimū apostolū ueluti morti destinatū ostēsum esse. Mihi placet posterior sensus, ut intelligamus affligtiones eas qbus premebatur quotidie, quasi declarasse Apostolū morti diuinitus esse destinatū,tā abfuisse,ut regnū in hoc seculo repere rit. Vocat autē se nouissimū Apostolū,non solū uocatione(scio qd Ambrosius de Enoc & Helias postremis apostolis,cū antichristo cōfligtantur scribat) sed & ꞓstimatione eo modo,quo infrà se uocat abortiuū & minimū inter apostolos. Vetus interpres uidetur priorem,Erasmus uero posteriorem sententiam secutus.
units.tr: "Last of all the apostles." The expression is ambiguous, so that you do not know whether he means that he has been shown to be the last of the apostles, or that he has been shown as the last apostle, as if destined to death. The latter sense pleases me, so that we understand those afflictions with which he was daily oppressed to have shown that the Apostle was destined to death by God, so far was he from having found a kingdom in this age. He calls himself the last apostle not only in calling (I know what Ambrose writes about Enoch and Elijah, the last apostles, who will fight with Antichrist) but also in estimation, in the same way as below he calls himself an abortive one and the least among the apostles. The Old translator seems to have followed the former opinion, Erasmus the latter.

units.la: QVONIAM spectaculū facti sumus.] Qua re dicat se uelut morti diuinitus destinatū, & quò,ostendit. Quia spectaculū,inquit,facti sumus mūdo, & angelis & hominib. Hoc est, tā nō regnam in hoc mūdo,ut nusq nō exploda mur,abijciamur,& ꝑ scelestissimo habeamur, adeoq; publico ꝑro afficiamur. Solebát tum nocentes publico spectaculo puniri,& omniū ꝑro puniēdi exponi. Et ꝑbri huius auxesim habet,quòd nō uni & alteri ciuitati,sed ipsi mūdo,& angelis & hoibus spectaculū se factū esse dicit. Mundum intelligo generaliter positum,angelos & homines distributiue.
units.tr: "For we have been made a spectacle." By this he shows in what way, and to what end, he is as it were destined to death by God. "Because," he says, "we have been made a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men." That is: we do not reign in this world so as to be cast out everywhere, rejected, and held as the most wicked, and so exposed to public shame. In those days the guilty used to be punished in public view, and were exposed to be punished by all. And he amplifies this disgrace by saying that he has been made a spectacle not to one or another city but to the world itself, to angels and to men. I take "world" as used generally, and "angels and men" distributively.

units.la: Per angelos alij bonos,alij malos spiritꝰ intelligunt. Chrysost. de bonis exponit ad hunc modū: Non solū cū mundo nobis,sed & cū spiritibus peruersis & potestatibus incorporeis certamē est,ideoq; nó solū mūdo & hominib; sed
units.tr: Some understand the angels to be good spirits, others evil spirits. Chrysostom explains it of the good in this way: "Our struggle is not only with the world but also with perverse spirits and incorporeal powers; therefore we have become a spectacle not only to the world and to men but

units.la: {A} Ita & nos in Christo olim regnabimus. sed ipsis quoq; angelis spectaculū facti sumus. A Tanta nanq; sunt nostra certamina, ut & angelorum digna sint spectaculo. Ambrosius uero mundo malos angelos coniungit, quibus spectaculum factus sit Apostolus. Intelligitur aūt dictione spectaculi publicum probrum & ludibrium, quo sensu certe bonis angelis Apostolus spectaculū nō fuit, qui magis, ut in psalmo est, castrametati sunt circa seruum Dei, illumq; ex afflictionibus eripuerunt.
units.tr: {A} So also we in Christ will one day reign, but also to the angels themselves we have been made a spectacle. For our contests are so great that they are worthy of the spectacle of angels." Ambrose, however, joins evil angels to the world, to whom the Apostle was made a spectacle. But by the word "spectacle" is understood a public shame and mockery; in this sense certainly the Apostle was not a spectacle to the good angels, who rather, as the psalm says, encamped around the servant of God and rescued him from afflictions.

units.la: Nos stulti propter Christum, uos autem prudentes in Christo: nos imbecilles, uos autem ualidi: uos clari, nos contempti. Ad hoc usq; tepus & esurimus & sitimus, & nudi sumus, & colaphis cædimur, & incertis uagamur sedibus, & laboramus operantes proprijs manibus, male audientes benedicimus, persequutionem patientes sustinemus, cuius affecti obsecramus, ueluti excrementa mundi facti sumus omnium reiectamentum ad hunc usq; diem.
units.tr: We are fools for Christ's sake, but you are prudent in Christ; we are weak, but you are strong; you are illustrious, we are despised. Up to this present hour we both hunger and thirst, and are naked, and are struck with fists, and wander about with no fixed dwelling, and labour working with our own hands; when reviled we bless, when persecuted we endure, when slandered we entreat; we have become as the refuse of the world, the offscouring of all things, up to this day.

units.la: Per collectionem amplificat disparitatē sortis suæ, quæ loge aliter habebat quàm ea quā pseudapostoli in Christo humanæ sapientię itu dio quærebant. Confert autē utrinq; quo ipse rerū statu cōsistat, imo magis iactetur, & quid ipsi per pseudapostolos inducti quærāt. Nos, inquit, Christū ita pdicamus, ut illius nomine stulti reputemur, ibecilles premamur, contemptui omniū exponamur, & ad hoc usq; tepus esuriamus, sitiam9, nudi simus, colaphis cædamur, incertis uagemur sedib9, laboremus proprijs operantes manibus, male audiamus, contuicijs afficiamur, & uelut excrementa mundi & omnium peripsema habeamur. In hunc usq; diem inquam nondum alia nobis conditio, alia sors obtigit in Christo, quàm ista omnium abiectissima, ac tot afflictionibus tantisq; probris obnoxia. Vos uerò longè aliter affecti, in Christo quæritis, ut prudentes, ualidi & clari sitis, ut non necesse sit esurire, sitire, nudari, colaphis cædi, incertis uagari sedibus, male audire, persequutionem ferre, conuicijs affici, & omnium peripsema, mundiq; uelut excrementa fieri. At mirum fuerit quomodo uos in Christo geratis, si ista in illo licet obtinere, cum mihi diuersissima illius nomine accidant.
units.tr: By this accumulation he magnifies the difference between his own lot and the one the false apostles sought in Christ by human wisdom, which was quite different. He compares on both sides what state he himself is in, or rather what he is tossed about in, and what the false apostles who have been brought in are seeking. He says: "We preach Christ in such a way that for his name we are counted fools, are pressed down by weakness, are exposed to the contempt of all, and to this very hour we hunger and thirst, are naked, are struck with fists, wander about without a fixed dwelling, labour working with our own hands, are ill spoken of, are subjected to reproaches, and are regarded as the scum of the world and the offscouring of all. Up to this day, I say, we have had no other condition or lot in Christ than this most abject one, exposed to so many afflictions and such great reproaches. But you, affected quite differently, seek in Christ to be wise, strong and illustrious, so that there is no need to hunger, thirst, go naked, be struck with fists, wander without a dwelling, be ill spoken of, bear persecution, be subjected to reproaches, or become the offscouring and scum of the world. Yet it would be astonishing how you conduct yourselves in Christ, if these things can be had in him, when for me the very opposite befalls me for his name."

units.la: Ad hūc modū Apostolus suo exēplo docet ⁊nō germanos Christi ministros habeat, cū quibus in Christo cupiant in hoc seculo pacē, gloriam & regnum obtinere, inter tot inimicos: à quibus certe, si regnum Christi cupiant exanimo promotum, eodem probro sint excipiēdi quo ipse. Quod si dux quidam Christianus exercitus contra Turcas impugnandos missus, ita se gerat cum Turcis, ut quietū ocium in ipsorū gremio agat: quis non suspicabitur illum non satis fideliter commissum administrare bellū, maximè cum alius quispiā, in pari munere co-
units.tr: In this way the Apostle, by his own example, teaches that those who are not true ministers of Christ, with whom they desire peace, glory and a kingdom in this age in Christ, amid so many enemies, must certainly, if they wish Christ's kingdom to be advanced sincerely, be received with the same reproach as he was. For if some Christian commander sent to fight against the Turks so conducted himself towards the Turks that he lived in quiet leisure in their bosom, who would not suspect that he was not faithfully administering the war entrusted to him, especially when another man, placed in the same office,

units.la: stitutus, crebris & indefinentibus Turcarum incursionibus & conflictationibus quotidie afflictetur. Solent huiusmodi duces proditionis argui. Tantundē ergo dicit Apostolus, doctores uestri non sunt fidi Christi ministri, nec regni illius promotores, sed proditores. Verū id aperte non dicit, sed per collationem disparis utrinq; suæ & illorū sortis ipsis intelligendum relinquit.
units.tr: is daily afflicted by frequent and unending incursions and conflicts with the Turks? Such commanders are usually accused of treachery. The Apostle therefore says just as much: your teachers are not faithful ministers of Christ, nor promoters of his kingdom, but traitors. Yet he does not say this openly; he leaves it to be understood by the comparison of his own lot and theirs, on both sides.

units.la: VOS prudētes, ualidi, clari in Christo. Nō quod essent tales, sed quod tales esse quærebant, nolētes propter Christum haberi stulti, esse imbecilles (id est omnium libidini exposi ti, ut sunt pauperes & inopes. Nam potētes nō facile infestantur) & contempti, sed ita sese gerebant, siue ita instituebantur à pseudapostolis ut probrum & calamitatem crucis Christi effugerent.
units.tr: "You, prudent, strong, illustrious in Christ." Not that they were such, but that they sought to be such, unwilling for Christ's sake to be considered fools, to be weak (that is, exposed to the lust of all, as the poor and needy are, for the powerful are not easily harassed), and contemptible; rather they conducted themselves, or were so trained by the false apostles, that they might escape the reproach and calamity of the cross of Christ.

units.la: AD hoc usq; tempus. Sic infrà, ad hūc usq; diem. Quasi dicat: Iam tot annos Christū prædito, nec unquam hactenus alia adeptus sum fortem, quàm istam calamitosissimam. Mihi nondum potuit obtingere quod uos in Christo quæritis ne hodie quidem.
units.tr: "Up to this present time." So below, "up to this very day." As if he said: For so many years now I have preached Christ, and until now I have never obtained any other lot than this most calamitous one. What you seek in Christ has not yet been able to fall to my share, not even today.

units.la: Clanculum autem animi fui cōstātiam spectandam proponit, quod in tot aduersis rebus tanquā diuturnis & irremisis nunquam à sco po deflexerit, cum ipsi reces Christo accensiti, iam pacē & gloriam in hoc mundo ambirent.
units.tr: He also sets before us, to be considered, the constancy of his mind, in that amid so many adversities, which were as it were lasting and unremitting, he never turned aside from his goal, while they, having cooled towards Christ, already sought peace and glory in this world.

units.la: ET esurimus & sitimus. Huiusmodi & apud ipsos Corinthios perpessus fuerat. Cum esset apud uos, inquit 2.Cor.11. & egerem, ne mini onerosus fui, &c. Et hodie esuriedum ac sitiedum esset Christi ministris, si libera essent contributione alendi.
units.tr: "And we hunger and thirst." He had suffered things of this kind even among the Corinthians themselves. "When I was among you," he says, "and in need, I was not a burden to anyone," etc. (2 Cor. 11). And today the ministers of Christ would have to hunger and thirst, if they were not supported by free contributions.

units.la: MALE audientes benedicimus. Hic nō solum quid patiatur, sed & quid ipse uicisim male affectus faciat: ad hoc commemorat, ut patientiæ & mansuetudinis suæ exemplo admoniti discant, quales habeant doctores, an Christi sint imitatores nec ne.
units.tr: "Being ill spoken of, we bless." Here he mentions not only what he suffers, but also how, in turn, he responds when ill treated; he recalls this so that, admonished by the example of his patience and gentleness, they may learn what sort of teachers they have, and whether they are imitators of Christ or not.

units.la: VELVTI excrementa mundi facti sumus. Quasi summatim uno uerbo completitur, q nō sit regnum adeptus in hoc mundo. Ipse inquit mundus ita nos pasim explodit, exibilat & abijcit, ut ceu excrementa illius habeamur, & omniū peripsema. sunt repurgamenta, quæ circumquaque ex omni domo congesta eijciuntur. Budæus dicit eos qui pro peste expianda dijs apud Gentes immolaban tur, dictos esse . Tale erat Ionas cum sedandæ tempestatis gratia abijcerentur in mare. Eiusdem mométi est qua dictione quicquid sordium uel à pedibus uel aliunde abstergitur, significatur , quod est abstergere.
units.tr: "We have become as the scum of the world." As if in a single word he sums up briefly that he has not obtained a kingdom in this world. He says that the world so widely spurns, hisses and casts us out, that we are regarded as its filth and the offscouring of all. [περίψημα] are the sweepings which are thrown out from every house, gathered from all around. Budaeus says that those who were sacrificed among the Gentiles to expiate a plague were so called. Such was Jonah, when he was thrown into the sea to calm the storm. Of the same meaning is the word by which whatever dirt is wiped off from the feet or elsewhere is signified, namely to wipe off.

units.la: OBSER. I.
units.tr: Observation I.

units.la: Quid ergo? Christi ministri germani & syn ceri esse non poterunt, qui non habentur pro stultis, qui non sunt contempti, qui non affliguntur, qui non esuriunt ac sitiunt, qui nō nudi sunt, qui non incertis sedibus circumuagantur.
units.tr: What then? Can those not be genuine and sincere ministers of Christ who are not regarded as fools, who are not despised, who are not afflicted, who do not hunger and thirst, who are not naked, who do not wander about without a fixed dwelling, who do not earn their food by working with their own hands?

units.la: Sic Christiani ubi pestis uel fames inquirebat, abijciebantur ad leones. uide Tertullianum. tur, qui nō proprijs manibus operando uictū quaerunt? Respondeo. In his rebus non est sista ministerij Christi, & fidei in Christum syncē ritas. Alioqui quotquot male haberent in hoc seculo probi habendi essent, cum inuenias sae-penumero pesimos nebulones hanc fortem perpeti, ut ubique male excipiātur. Quin hoc curandum est Christi ministris & fidelibus, primum ut ante omnia quaerant regnum Dei ex animo: deinde parati sint pro Christi nomine in omnem euentum. Quod si contigerit talibus esse in precio & pace, bene. Nam & Paulus nouit non solum esurire, sed & abundare & saturari: si uero crux, persequutio & cōtemptus acciderit pro Christo, ferendum & hoc est, in que fide & dilectione Christi perstiendū. De opere manuario, an ad ministerium Christi sit necessarium, infrā uidebimus cap.9.
units.tr: I answer: in these things lies not the sum of the ministry of Christ, nor the sincerity of faith in Christ. Otherwise all who fare badly in this age would have to be counted upright, since you will very often find most wicked scoundrels suffering this lot, that they are ill received everywhere. So Christians, when plague or famine raged, were thrown to the lions; see Tertullian. Rather, it must be the care of Christ's ministers and of the faithful, first, to seek above all the kingdom of God from the heart, and then to be ready for any outcome for the name of Christ. If it happens that such men are held in esteem and enjoy peace, well and good. For Paul knew not only how to suffer hunger, but also how to abound and be filled; but if the cross, persecution and contempt come upon them for Christ, this too must be borne, and in faith and love toward Christ they must persevere. Concerning manual labour, whether it is necessary for the ministry of Christ, we shall see below, in chapter 9.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Deinde notandum est hic omnibus Christi ministris, quanta debeant animi constantia praediti esse, ad hoc ut nihil non ferre possint pro Christo. Quis nostrum uel minimam partem eorum perpessus est pro Christo, quę Paulus hic connumerat?
units.tr: Next, it should be noted here that all ministers of Christ ought to be endowed with how great a constancy of mind, so that they can bear anything at all for Christ. Which of us has suffered even the smallest part of those things that Paul lists here for Christ?

units.la: Nō quo uos pudore suffundam, hęc scribo, sed ut filios meos dilectos admoneo. Nam etiamsi innumeros paedagogos habeatis in Christo, non multos tamen habetis patres. Siquidē in Christo Iesu per Euangelium ego uos genui.
units.tr: I do not write these things to make you blush, but I admonish you as my beloved sons. For even if you have countless pedagogues in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you.

units.la: Iam ad finem tendit huius causæ. Videri autem poterat, maxime hoc capite, animo parū amico, exprobrādi gratia, non solū dissidium, quo inter se, laborabant: sed & pessimum ingratitudinis uicium obijcere Corinthijs, quorum gratia tot labores, probra & pericula tulerit, pro quibus ipsi nihil reppenderint, nisi & nominis & doctrinæ ipsius cōtemptum, id quod certe merito illos pudore suffundere poterat. Curat ergo pro sua prudentia suspicione hanc mentibus ipsorū eximere, cum dicit: Non quo uos pudore suffundam, hæc scribo, &c. Admonedum enim urit beneficiorum improperatio, uehementerq; commouet ingenuos animos ingratitudinis imputatum uicium, praeterquā quod animum prodit nonnihil abalienatum, & haud facile reconciliabilem: deinde & suas glorias non aliorum utilitatem quaerentē. Vt igitur hęc omnia amoliatur, licet ipsi digni fuerint, qui pudefierent, commodum utitur ista animi sui declaratione, ostendens primum nō ea se ratione ista commemorare, quod cupiat eos aliquo pudore aspergere: deinde subiungens affectu se paterno eoq; adhuc constanti, admonendi gratia scribere.
units.tr: Now he comes to the end of this cause. It could seem, especially in this chapter, that he is reproaching them with a not very friendly spirit, not only for the dissension in which they were labouring among themselves, but also for charging the Corinthians with the worst vice of ingratitude, for whose sake he had borne so many labours, insults and dangers, and who in return had shown him nothing but contempt for his name and his teaching, which certainly could justly put them to shame. So, by his prudence, he takes care to remove this suspicion from their minds, when he says: "I do not write these things to make you blush," and so on. For the reproach of benefits stings, and it strongly moves generous minds when the vice of ingratitude is imputed to them; besides which, it betrays a mind somewhat estranged and not easily reconciled, and moreover one seeking its own glory rather than the benefit of others. Therefore, so that he may remove all of these things, although they deserved to be shamed, he suitably uses this declaration of his own mind, showing first that he does not recall these things for this reason, that he desires to cover them with some shame; then, adding that he writes to admonish them out of a paternal and still steadfast affection.

units.la: ΟΥΚ ὑπέρπων ὑμᾶς. Pulchre usurpatur à Graecis uerbum hoc ὑπέρπω, pro confundo, pudore suffundo. Licet enim proprie nō significeat pudefacere, sed inuertere: quia tamen, cui turpia quędam obijciuntur, per obiectionem probri sui in sese cum pudore redire, ac sententia mu
units.tr: "Οὐκ ὑπέρπων ὑμᾶς." The Greeks use this verb ὑπέρπω beautifully for "to confound" or "to bring shame upon." For although it does not properly mean "to put to shame" but "to turn upside down," nevertheless, since one to whom base things are objected is brought back to himself with shame through the objection of his own disgrace, the meaning is turned around.

units.la: Obseruandū est aūt quod dicit, Non cōfundens uos ista scribo: pro, Non ut pudore uos suffundā, hæc scribo. Hoc quisquā facere recte dicitur, qd' animo facere intendit, nō qd' ex ipso facto praeter faciētis sententiā accidit. Fieri potuit ut uehemēter sint hoc Apostoli scripto pudefacti Corinthij. At hoc ille nō spectauit, ideo se dicit illos scripto suo nō pudefacere, cū hoc animo nō scribat. Vt enim recte aliquem ignominia afficere dici potest, qui ignominiæ gratia aliquid facit, etiamsi ad ignominiam eius quem laedere conatur, nō cedat: ita uicisim recte dicitur non pudefacere quenq;, qui quod facit animo pudefaciendi non facit, etiāsi is quē reprehendit pudore suffundatur.
units.tr: It should be observed that he says: "I write these things not confounding you," that is, "I write these things not so that I may bring shame upon you." One is rightly said to do something when he intends it in his mind, not when something happens beyond the intention of the doer as a result of the deed itself. It could have happened that the Corinthians were greatly shamed by this writing of the Apostle. But he did not look to this, and therefore he says that he does not shame them by his writing, since he does not write with this intention. For just as one can rightly be said to inflict disgrace on someone who does something for the sake of disgrace, even if the disgrace does not come about for the one he tries to harm, so conversely one is rightly said not to shame anyone who does not do what he does with the intention of shaming, even if the person he rebukes is put to shame.

units.la: ὁ ἠκέν hoc loco est, ut studiose caueamus, ne quos arguimus ita arguamus, ut data opera pudefieri uideantur, maximè si reprehendantur eorum gratia, quę in nos immeritos commiserunt. Tum enim non illos corrigere, sed nos potius ulcisci uideri poterimus, id quod non poterit ad aedificationē errantiū cedere.
units.tr: The "ὁ ἠκέν" here means that we should carefully take care that we do not rebuke those whom we rebuke in such a way that they seem to be shamed on purpose, especially if they are rebuked for the sake of those things which they have committed against us though we did not deserve them. For then we may seem not to correct them, but rather to take vengeance on ourselves, which cannot contribute to the edification of those who err.

units.la: SED admoneo.] Non dicit, increpo, arguo uos, sed admoneo. νουθετῶ est aliquid menti cuiusquam suggerere, id quod fieri solet ab amicis ijs qui sui parumper obliuiscuntur, & quod delinquunt errando magis quam ex destinato delinquūt. Commendat igitur ista mitigatione scriptum suum, dum facit eam esse amicam admonitionem, ostenditq; se de illis quos admonet non id sentire quod malitiose, sed quod ex errore nonnihil delinquant.
units.tr: "But I admonish you." He does not say "I rebuke, I accuse you," but "I admonish." νουθετῶ means to suggest something to someone's mind, which is usually done by friends to those who somewhat forget themselves, and who do wrong by erring rather than by deliberate intention. He therefore commends his writing by this softening, while he makes it a friendly admonition, and he shows that he does not think of those whom he admonishes as acting maliciously, but as failing somewhat through error.

units.la: Et huc facit quod nō dicit, ut fratres, quod plerunq; solet: sed tanquā filios, idq; dilectos, quibus declarat se animo prorsus paterno illos admonere, nihilq; admonendo quaerere aliud quam quod pater quaerit, dum dilectos filios emendat, qui nullum alium habet corrigendi finem, quam unā filiorum salutē. Multum authoritatis est pareti in filios, & affectus ille paternus, omnia in filiorum profectum instituens, nullam non arguendi uehementiam & austeritatem excusat. Non potest ergo Apostolus fortiori argumento admonitione suam ab omni sinistra suspicione liberare, tolerabilemq;, imo acceptam reddere, quam hoc uno, quod Corinthios ponit in locum filiorum suorum sibi admodum dilectorum.
units.tr: And to this purpose is his not saying "brothers," as is customary, but "as sons," and beloved sons at that, by which he declares that he admonishes them with a wholly paternal spirit, and that in admonishing he seeks nothing other than what a father seeks when he corrects his beloved sons, who has no other end of correcting than the salvation of his sons alone. The father's authority over his sons is great, and that paternal affection, which orders everything for the advancement of the sons, excuses every vehemence and severity of rebuke. Therefore the Apostle could not free his admonition from every sinister suspicion, and make it tolerable, or rather acceptable, by a stronger argument than this one alone: that he places the Corinthians in the place of his own sons, very dear to him.

units.la: Nam etiāsi innumeros paedagogos habeatis in Christo, nō multos tamen habetis patres. Siquidē in Christo Iesu per Euangelium ego uos genui.
units.tr: For even if you have countless pedagogues in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you.

units.la: Quid iuris in eos habeat ut merito illos admoneat, ostendit per collationem, qua se cum doctoribus ipsorum confert, tanquam parentem cum paedagogis.
units.tr: He shows what right he has over them, so that he may rightly admonish them, by a comparison in which he sets himself against their teachers, as a parent against pedagogues.

units.la: 1 Multum discriminis est inter pędagogum & ipsum parentem. Potest esse ut puero prosit ad tępus paedagogus, & ius aliquod in ipsum obtineat: uerum non ita, ut parentis utilitatā & imperium puero adimat. At hoc moliebantur pseudoapostoli isti Corinthiorum in Chri sto pædagogi.
units.tr: 1 There is a great difference between a pedagogue and the parent himself. It may be that a pedagogue benefits a boy for a time and holds some right over him; but not in such a way as to take away from the boy the parent's care and authority. Yet these pseudo-apostles of the Corinthians, pedagogues in Christ, were striving to do exactly this.

units.la: 2 Deinde pædagogus paterni affectus fidē & suauitatem assequi non potest.
units.tr: 2 Further, a pedagogue cannot attain the fidelity and sweetness of a paternal affection.

units.la: 3 Tertio mutari potest, ut liceat per succes-sionem multiplicari pædagogorum numerū: parētis uero non item, qui perpetuo unus est. Hoc scilicet non expendebant Corinthij, atqz ideo satis imprudenter pædagogis ita sese ad-dicebant, ut quod infensati pueri solent, eius à quo fuerant in Christo geniti, fastidio iam & contemptu afficerentur. Hanc illis stultitiam obijcit, cum dicit: Nam etiamsi mille pædago-gos habeatis in Christo, non multos tamen ha betis patres.
units.tr: 3 Thirdly, the number of pedagogues can be multiplied by succession, as it is allowed; but this is not so for the parent, who is always one. The Corinthians evidently did not weigh this, and therefore, quite imprudently, they gave themselves over to pedagogues in such a way that, as boys who have become spoiled usually do, they came to feel disgust and contempt for him by whom they had been begotten in Christ. He charges them with this folly when he says: "For even if you have a thousand pedagogues in Christ, you do not have many fathers."

units.la: Emphasim collationis habet, quod non di-cit, Nam etiamsi multos habeatis pædagogos in Christo: sed, etiamsi mille vel innumeros ha-beatis pædagogos. Quasi dicat: Multum ex-tollitis, & plurimi facitis doctores vestros, ita ut putetis iam uos sine me regnare. Atqui in-sipienter hoc facitis, nō intelligentes, illos uo-bis nullo alio loco esse posse quàm pædago-gorum, me uero unum uobis esse in Christo parētem. Iam quæ potest esse pædagogi & pa-rentis comparatio? Esto habeatis innumeros huiusmodi doctores, quid aliud habetis q pæ-dagogos? Numerum parentis certe augere nō potestis, quem unum habetis. Quicquid sint vestri doctores, pædagogi sunt, non parentes: & licet innumeri sint, parentis tamen nec ius auferre, nec affectum adæquare poterunt.
units.tr: He has the emphasis of the comparison in that he does not say "For even if you have many pedagogues in Christ," but "even if you have a thousand or countless pedagogues." As if he said: You exalt yourselves greatly, and you esteem your teachers very highly, so that you think you already reign without me. Yet you do this foolishly, not understanding that those men can have no place among you other than that of pedagogues, while I am the one parent you have in Christ. Now what comparison can there be between a pedagogue and a parent? Grant that you have countless teachers of this kind: what else do you have than pedagogues? You certainly cannot increase the number of your parent, whom you have only one of. Whatever your teachers are, they are pedagogues, not parents; and although they may be countless, they can neither take away a parent's right nor equal a parent's affection.

units.la: Clanculum autem submonet Corinthios hac parētis & pædagogorum collatione, quid expectandum illis sit à doctoribus istis. Nēpe id quod puero à pædagogo, qui plerunq; arro-ganter sibi imperium sumit in alienum pue-rum, tyrannidi quàm commodæ institutioni similius. Noti sunt mores pædagogorū in pue-ros, qui se regnare putant, ubi quàm seuerifsi-me quiduis minarum plagarumq; illis infe-runt. Quod autem Corinthij huiusmodi sint pædagogorum suorum imperium experti, pa-tet in posteriore cap. II. ubi siclegitur: Suffertis enim si quis uos in seruitutem adigit, si quis exedit, si quis accipit, si quis attollit sese, si quis uos in facie cædit. quibus uerbis innuit, quid ab istis pædagogis perpessi sint Corinthij.
units.tr: Moreover, by this comparison of parent and pedagogues he quietly warns the Corinthians what they should expect from those teachers. Namely, what a boy receives from a pedagogue, who often arrogantly assumes authority over another's boy, something more like tyranny than sound instruction. The manners of pedagogues toward boys are well known, when they think they reign, and inflict whatever threats and blows they can with the utmost severity. That the Corinthians had experienced the rule of such pedagogues of theirs is clear from the later chapter 11, where it is read: "For you bear it if anyone brings you into bondage, if anyone devours you, if anyone takes from you, if anyone exalts himself, if anyone strikes you in the face" (2 Cor. 11:20). By these words he hints at what the Corinthians suffered from those pedagogues.

units.la: SIQVIDEM per Euang.] Declaratio est, quomodo se uocet ipsorum parētem, negetq; illos multos patres habere extra se posse. Si-quidem inquit non ipsi, sed ego uos genui in Christo. Hanc mihi gloriam præripere, quanti quanti sint non poterunt. Non dicit, Ego uos primus in Christo docui, non isti: sed ego uos genui in Christo per Euágelium. Quasi dicat: Quod Christiani estis in Christo renati, hoc mihi debetis, non uestris pædagogis. Proinde mei estis in Christo, non ipsorum filij.
units.tr: "For through the Gospel": this is a declaration of how he calls himself their parent, and denies that they can have many fathers apart from himself. "For," he says, "not they, but I begot you in Christ." They will not be able to snatch this glory from me, however great they may be. He does not say, "I first taught you in Christ, not they," but "I begot you in Christ through the Gospel." As if he said: That you are born again as Christians in Christ, you owe this to me, not to your pedagogues. Therefore you are mine in Christ, not their sons.

units.la: OBSER I.
units.tr: OBSERVATION I.

units.la: EGO.] Natiuitas in Christo, spiritussanƈti
units.tr: EGO.] The new birth in Christ is the work of the Holy Spirit, not of flesh and blood, nor of any human will. John 1.

units.la: opus est, non carnis & sanguinis, nec alicuius humanæ uoluntatis. Ioh. 1. Quomodo igitur sibi hic adscribit, quod ipse Corinthios in Chri-sto genuerit? An hic sibi sumit quod Dei est? Non supra dixit, Quid est Paulus? Ego plan-taui, qui plantat nihil est: sed Deus qui dat in-crementum? Reluctatur ne & gloriæ Dei, sibi sumens quod Dei est, & sibijpsi, impugnans quod supra fassus est? Respondeo.
units.tr: How then does he here ascribe to himself that he himself begot the Corinthians in Christ? Does he here take to himself what belongs to God? Did he not say above, "What is Paul? I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase; so neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase"? Is he not robbing God of his glory, taking to himself what is God's, and contradicting himself, opposing what he confessed above? I answer.

units.la: Nec sibi sumit quod Dei est, sed loquitur se-cundum gloriam dispensationis Euangelicæ, quam à Christo acceperat, non excludens uir tutem spiritussanƈti, cuius se ministrum pro-fessus est. Quoniam ipsius ministerio Corin-thij fuerant cooperante Christo, in Christo na-ti, hac ratione facit se ipsorum parētem. Alio-qui unus parens est omnium. Matth. 23. idque non solum in Christo, sed & in carnali natiui-tate, à quo est omnis paternitas quæ nomina-tur in cœlo & in terra. Carnalis etiam pater, magis ab usiue quàm proprie parens est. Ser-uit enim ministerio suo ad natiuitatem homi-nis, non ipse ut uerus pater suo arbitrio suaqı uirtute gignit.
units.tr: He does not take to himself what belongs to God, but speaks according to the glory of the Gospel dispensation, which he had received from Christ, without excluding the work of the Holy Spirit, whose minister he professed himself to be. For since the Corinthians had come to faith in Christ through his ministry, with Christ working alongside, they were born in Christ, and on this basis he makes himself their parent. Otherwise there is one parent of all, Matthew 23, and this is so not only in Christ but also in carnal birth, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named. Even a carnal father is a parent in a secondary sense rather than in the proper sense. For he serves by his ministry to the birth of a human being; he does not, as a true father, beget by his own will and his own power.

units.la: Rursus nec sibijpsi contrarius est. Nam su-prà, ubi deijcienda erat propostera admiratio pseudapostolorum, sopiendæque sectę Corin-thiorum, ex illa natæ: necessario retulit omnia ad Deum, ut nihil esset ministrorum, quo om-nis gloria uni daretur Deo, ac discerent Corin-thij modeste sentire de doctoribus suis, seque nō illis, sed uni Christo addicere. Hac ratione dixit: Quid est Paulus? Et, Qui plátat nihil est: sed, Deus, qui dat incrementum. Hic uero ubi authoritatem suam tueri proposuit aduersus pseudapostolos, idque ad Corinthiorum utili-tatem & salutem, non suam ipsius gloriam, fa-cit se in loco parentem ipsorum, conferens se-se non Deo, sed pseudapostolis: quorum certè respectu ipse parens erat Corinthiorum, quo-niam ipsius ministerio Christo crediderant.
units.tr: Again, he is not contrary to himself. For above, where the excessive admiration of the false apostles had to be cast down, and the faction of the Corinthians that arose from it had to be quieted, he necessarily referred all things to God, so that nothing would belong to the ministers, and all glory would be given to the one God; and so that the Corinthians would learn to think modestly of their teachers and to attach themselves not to them but to Christ alone. On this account he said, "What is Paul?" and "He who plants is nothing, but God who gives the increase." But here, where he has set out to defend his own authority against the false apostles, and that for the usefulness and salvation of the Corinthians, not for his own glory, he makes himself their parent in this place, referring himself not to God but to the false apostles; with respect to whom, certainly, he was the parent of the Corinthians, since they had believed in Christ through his ministry.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: GENVI.] Ergo credentes in Christū, sunt noua creatura: & credere Christo, est renasci. Hac similitudine depingitur omnimoda ue-teris natiuitatis, quæ ex Adam est, abolitio, & innouationis perfectio. Hac da re est Ioh. 3. Ni-si quis renatus fuerit, non potest uidere regnū Dei. Iam immutationem natiuitatis sequitur & ingenij, & affectuum, & morum immuta-tio. Hinc est, quod renatos in Christo hortan-tur apostoli ad depositionem uetustæ corru-ptionis & nouæ uitæ conuersationem.
units.tr: I BEGOT.] Therefore those who believe in Christ are a new creation, and to believe in Christ is to be born again. This likeness depicts the complete abolition of the old birth, which is from Adam, and the perfection of renewal. Hence John 3: "Unless a man is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." Moreover, the change of birth is followed by a change of mind, of affections, and of morals. Hence it is that the apostles exhort those reborn in Christ to put off the old corruption and to live a new life.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: PER Euangelium.] Vt minister commemorat organum regenerationis. Alioqui dicē-dum erat, Per spiritum Dei. Admonet autem eos ueluti seminis, ex quo erat in Christo nati. Videbātur enim illius modicam habere ratio-nem, seducti per pseudapostolorum præposte-ram admirationem. Certè magnum dat glo-riam Euangelicæ prædicationi, quod eam fa-cit. cit organum spiritalis natiuitatis. Per illam sci licet in Christo renascimur, per illam etiam ali mur in Christo.
units.tr: THROUGH THE GOSPEL.] The minister mentions the instrument of regeneration. Otherwise he ought to have said, "through the Spirit of God." But he reminds them of the seed, as it were, from which they were born in Christ. For they seemed to have little regard for it, led astray by the excessive admiration of the false apostles. Certainly he gives great glory to the preaching of the Gospel in that he makes it the instrument of spiritual birth. Through it, of course, we are born again in Christ, and through it we are also nourished in Christ.

units.la: Adhortor itaque uos, ut imitatores mei sitis. Hac de causa misi uobis Timotheum, qui est filius meus dilectus & fidelis in domino, qui uobis in memoriam reducet uias meas, quae sunt in Christo, quemadmodum ubique in omni ecclesia doceo.
units.tr: He has said "as my beloved sons I admonish you"; now he adds what he admonishes them to do: namely, to imitate him in Christ, and not the false apostles by whom they were being led astray.

units.la: Dixit, sed ut filios meos dilectos admoneo: iam subdit, quid eos admoneat. Nempe, ut se imitentur in Christo, non pseudapostolos iustos à quibus seducebantur.
units.tr: (1) To persuade them of this he does two things. First, he draws a conclusion from what has been premised, saying "therefore": that is, since I begat you in Christ and not they, you are mine and not theirs as sons; they are tutors, not fathers. It is only fair, then, that you imitate not them but me. It is the mark of a true son to imitate the nature and manners of his parent.

units.la: 1 Ad huius persuasionem facit, primum quod ex praemisso colligit dicens, igitur: hoc est, cum ego uos in Christo genuerim non illi, mei sitis non illorum filij, illi paedagogi sint non patres: aequum est, ut non illos, sed me imitemini. Germani filij est imitari paretis ingenium & mores.
units.tr: 1 To persuade them of this he first argues from what precedes, saying "therefore": that is, since I have begotten you in Christ and not they, you are my sons and not theirs, they are tutors and not fathers; it is only fair that you imitate not them but me. It is the mark of a true son to imitate the nature and manners of his parent.

units.la: 2 Deinde & illud, quod dicit, παρακαλῶ, lubet per obsecrantis affectum exponere. Ardet enim pectus Apostoli affectu erga Corinthios filios suos plane paterno. Et plus ponderis habet ad hoc quod agitur, ut legamus, obsecro, quàm hortor.
units.tr: 2 Next, the word he uses, παρακαλῶ ["I beseech"], should be explained by the feeling of one who entreats. For the Apostle's heart burns with a truly paternal affection towards the Corinthians, his sons. And "I beg," read as in our text, carries more weight for what is being done than "I exhort."

units.la: 3 Tertio, quoniam ad id instituti opus habebant praesenti aliquo instructore uel potius admonitore, nec dum integrum ipsi esset Apostolo uenire ad eos, misit ad eos Timotheum. Hoc est quod dicit: Hac de causa misi uobis Timotheum. Et hunc commendat illis primum à sui dilectione, quod sit sibi dilectus filius, utpote germanus ac syncerus, deinde quod sit fidelis in domino. Hoc est, talis qui uias ipsius, ut sedulus imitator, probe teneat, & syncera sit erga Christum fide, fidelis in illius opere, ideoque commodus ad id, ut in memoriam ipsis reuocet quibus uijs ingredi debeant.
units.tr: 3 Thirdly, since they needed for this purpose some instructor present, or rather a reminder, and since it was not yet possible for the Apostle himself to come to them, he sent Timothy to them. This is what he means: "For this cause I have sent you Timothy." And he commends him to them first from his own affection, in that he is his beloved son, being a true and sincere brother, and then in that he is faithful in the Lord. That is, one who as a diligent imitator thoroughly keeps to his ways, and is sincere in faith towards Christ, faithful in his work, and therefore fit to bring back to their memory the ways by which they ought to walk.

units.la: Qui uobis in memoriam reducet.] Caute non dicit, qui uos docebit uias meas: sed, Qui in memoriam reducet. Non enim erat illis nouì aliquid, quod antea nec uiderint nec audierint ab ipso Apostolo, allaturus: sed eorum tantum admonituras, quę primum ab Apostolo acceperant, sed postea per pseudapostolos seducti deseruerant.
units.tr: "My ways which are in Christ." This is a statement of the matter in which they ought to imitate their parent the Apostle: namely, in walking, teaching and living in Christ, that is, as they had seen him walking, teaching, and referring everything to the glory of Christ, and bearing and doing everything eagerly for its sake. For by the words "which are in Christ" he silently bites the false apostles, whose ways were not in Christ but in human wisdom and in the desire for empty glory.

units.la: VIAS meas quae sunt in Christo.] Declaratio est, qua in re debeant imitari parentem suum Apostolum. In ea uidelicet, ut ita ingrediantur, doceant, ac uiuant in Christo, quomodo ipsum uiderant ambulantem, docentem, & omnia ad Christi gloriam referentem, proque illa nihil non cupide ferentem ac facientem. Per illud enim quod dicit, quae sunt in Christo, tacite mordet pseudapostolos, quorum uiae non in Christo, sed in humana erant sapientia, & inanis gloriae studio.
units.tr: "As I teach everywhere in every church." He does not add this without reason. He indicates that he has handed on to them nothing that he had not at the same time handed on to the other churches. He does not say "as in many," but "everywhere in every church." A teacher of truth changes nothing. He constantly taught the same truth of Christ everywhere, though he was buffeted by countless dangers for the sake of that grace. At the same time he hints how absurd it is to fall away from that doctrine which all the churches of Christ had received.

units.la: QVEMADMODVM ubique in omni ecclesia doceo.] Non frustra hoc adijcit. Indicat enim se nihil illis tradidisse, quod non simul et aliis ecclesijs tradiderit. Nec dicit, quemadmodum in multis, sed ubique in omni ecclesia doceo. Nihil immutabat ueritatis doctor. Eandem ubique Christi ueritatem constanter docebat, licet illius gratia innumeris iactatus periculis. Et simul innuit quàm sit absurdum, ab ea doctrina degenerare, quam acceperant omnes ecclesiae Christi.
units.tr: AS I TEACH EVERYWHERE IN EVERY CHURCH.] He adds this not in vain. For he shows that he had handed on nothing to them that he had not at the same time handed on to the other churches. And he does not say "as in many," but "everywhere, in every church, I teach." A teacher of the truth changes nothing. He constantly taught the same truth of Christ everywhere, although he was tossed about by countless dangers for the sake of that grace. At the same time he hints how absurd it is to degenerate from that doctrine which all the churches of Christ had received.

units.la: DOCEO.] Verbo docedi admonemur, Apostolum si no in uniuersum, certe potissimum ad doctrinam respicere, cum dicit, Imitatores mei estote: &, qui uobis in memoriam reducet uias meas. Neque enim error Corinthiorum in quibusdam duntaxat ecclesiae ritibus situs erat, sed potissimum in ipsa doctrina crucis Christi, quam pseudapostoli philosophiae studio uiciauerant. Chrysost. uidetur non de doctrina, sed de traditionibus & statutis quibusdam, deinde & de aduersitatum tolerantia exponere, cum dicit, τατ' οψ, quod dicit, ἀλλὰ πάντα.
units.tr: I TEACH.] By the word "teach" we are reminded that the Apostle looks, not in general but chiefly, to doctrine, when he says, "Be imitators of me," and "who will remind you of my ways." For the error of the Corinthians lay not merely in certain rites of the Church, but chiefly in the very doctrine of the cross of Christ, which the false apostles had corrupted by their devotion to philosophy. Chrysostom seems to explain this not of doctrine but of certain traditions and statutes, and then of endurance of adversities, when he says, [τατ' οψ] ("therefore") and what he says, [ἀλλὰ πάντα] ("but all things").

units.la: OBSER. I.
units.tr: OBSERVATION I.

units.la: Notandum est hoc loco, quas uias ingredi debeamus in Christo, si uoluerimus sentire & facere cū ecclesia apostolica & catholica. Eas nempe quas Apostolus Christi ubique in omni ecclesia constanter docuit. Quas autem docuerit, testatur ipsi scripta. Hęc sint uice cuiuf dá Timothei, q nos in uijs Apostoli instruat.
units.tr: It should be noted here which ways we ought to walk in Christ if we wish to think and act together with the apostolic and catholic Church. These are certainly the ways which the Apostle taught constantly everywhere in every church. What he taught is attested by his own writings. Let these, as it were, be the guidance of Timothy, who instructs us in the ways of the Apostle.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Deinde in eo quod dicit: Qui uobis in memoriam reducet uias meas. Videmus quàm non sit insolens, quod querimur hodie ecclesias Christi à uijs apostolorum & Euangelij Christi degenerasse. Si enim ecclesia Corinthiorum adhuc supstite Apostolo, à quo fuerat in Christo genita, ita degenerauerat à doctrinę Christi puritate, ut illius, uelut oblita, admonenda fuerit per Timotheum, quale & ecclesiae Galatharum accidit: quaeso quid dubitatur fieri potuisse ut per tot saeculorum curricula puritas apostolicae doctrinae uiciaretur? Si admiratio pseudapostolorum nouis uijs ingredientium decepit ac seduxit filios Apostoli, ut iam fuerint obliti primariae suae institutionis, adhuc in uiuis agente Apostolo: quid non potuit accidere huiusmodi post apostolorum tempora, irrumpente undique in ecclesiam, uelut exercitu quodam, falsorum doctorum, humanae sapientiae & inanis gloriae studio turgentium impostura & seductione.
units.tr: Next, in what he says, "who will remind you of my ways," we see how little it is out of place for us to complain today that the churches of Christ have departed from the ways of the apostles and of the gospel of Christ. For if the church of the Corinthians, while the Apostle who had begotten them in Christ was still alive, had so degenerated from the purity of Christian doctrine that they had to be reminded of it through Timothy, as if they had forgotten it, as also happened to the churches of Galatia, then what doubt is there that over so many centuries the purity of apostolic doctrine could be corrupted? If the admiration of false apostles who entered upon new ways deceived and led astray the Apostle's sons, so that they had already forgotten their first instruction while the Apostle was still living, what could not happen of this kind after the time of the apostles, when false teachers, swollen with love of human wisdom and empty glory, burst into the Church from every side like an army, with their deceit and seduction?

units.la: Perinde quasi no sim ueturus ad uos, inflati sunt quidam. Sed uenia breui ad uos, si dominus uoluerit, & cognosca no sermonem istorum qui inflati sunt, sed uirtutem. Non enim in sermone est regnum Dei, sed in uirtute.
units.tr: "As if I were not going to come to you, some have become arrogant. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will know not the word of those who are arrogant, but their power. For the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power."

units.la: 1 Sciebat Apostolus Timotheum sua praesentia propter improborum fastum non tantum praestare posse, quantum mali corrigendi exigeexigebat necesitas, sed profuturum quidem ad hoc, ut saniores & corrigibiles ad uiâ Apostolicæ doctrinæ reducerentur: uerum non ita metuendum ipsis inflatis, ut cœpto se pateren tur per illius præsentiâ abduci, & ob eam causam aduentus suijpsius metum illis inculcat, quem non poterant ut absentem, ita præsentè quoque contemnere. Intelligebat enim illos propterea inflatos esse, quod securi essent de perpetua sui absentia. Igitur ut inflationis huius uelut radicem extirpet, adimit illis istam securitatem per metum aduentus sui, dicens: Perinde, quasi non sim uenturus ad uos, inflati sunt quidam. Sed ueniam breui ad uos, &c.
units.tr: 1 The Apostle knew that Timothy, because of the arrogance of the wicked, could not accomplish as much by his presence as the need to correct the evil demanded; yet his presence would indeed be useful for this, that the more sensible and correctable might be brought back to the way of apostolic doctrine. But it was not so much to be feared by the swollen-headed themselves that they would allow themselves to be drawn away from their undertaking by his presence. For this reason he instils into them the fear of his own coming, which they could not despise even when present, as they had despised him when absent. For he understood that they were arrogant because they were secure about his lasting absence. Therefore, in order to root out, as it were, the very source of this arrogance, he takes from them that security by the fear of his coming, saying: "As if I were not going to come to you, some have become arrogant. But I will come to you soon," and so on.

units.la: 2 Facit autem hoc prudenti consilio, ut infla tos doctores præsenti Timotheo reddat tra ctabiliores & contractiores, quos ille alioqui habituras erat insolentiores aduersarios, nisi obstitisset uenturi Apostoli metus. Et eò pertinet quod non simpliciter dicit, Veniam ad uos: sed addit, breui. Nec certum aliquod tempus prescribit, sed minatur cito se adfuturum, ut incerti de ipsius aduentu, modestius sese er ga Timotheum gererent, & opus illius in domino hoc minus impedire conarentur.
units.tr: 2 He does this with prudent counsel, so that he may make the arrogant teachers more manageable and more restrained toward Timothy when he is present; otherwise they would have been more insolent opponents, had not the fear of the Apostle's coming restrained them. To this belongs the fact that he does not simply say, "I will come to you," but adds "soon." He does not prescribe any fixed time, but threatens that he will be present quickly, so that, uncertain about his arrival, they might conduct themselves more modestly toward Timothy and try less to hinder his work in the Lord.

units.la: 1 QVASI non sim uenturus ad uos.] Pseudapostoli ergo ob id erant inflati quod nunc rediturum sperabat Apostolum, ideoq; ipsius absentia per arrogantiam abutebantur. Sed quibus coniecturis ducebantur, quod sperabant illum non uenturum amplius ad Corinthios? Verisimile est illos istam spe ex eo sum B pissè, quod sciebat illum persequutionis procellis è Corintho pulsum, atque ob id non facile ausurum regredi: nec si id tentaret, apud Corinthios, utpote quibus esset factus admodum inuisus hærere posse, & præterea propediem persequutionum fluctibus obruendum & interiturum. His spebus credibile est eos in istam inductos esse securitatem, ut sperarint nunquam uenturum ad Corinthios Paulum, & ob eam causam arrogantes esse cœperint.
units.tr: 1 "As if I were not going to come to you." The false apostles, then, were arrogant on this account, that they hoped the Apostle would now return, and so they abused his absence through pride. But on what conjectures were they led to hope that he would no longer come to the Corinthians? It is likely that they had this hope from the fact that they knew he had been driven out of Corinth by the storms of persecution, and therefore would hardly dare to return; and even if he tried it, he could not remain among the Corinthians, to whom he had become very hateful, and moreover he would soon be overwhelmed and destroyed by the waves of persecution. It is credible that they were led into this security by these hopes, so that they hoped Paul would never come to the Corinthians, and for this reason began to be arrogant.

units.la: 2 S I dominus uoluerit.] Et temeritatis no tam ita declinat, & simul ostendit quantum ad se pertineat, plane se uenturum, nisi impediat cõsilium domini. Hoc autem ideo facit ne putent se minari tantū aduentū suum, non autē proposuisse sibi ferio reditum ad Corinthios.
units.tr: 2 "If the Lord wills." He thus tempers rashness, and at the same time shows how far it lies with himself that he will certainly come, unless the counsel of the Lord hinders it. He does this so that they may not think he only threatens his coming, and that he had not firmly resolved to return to the Corinthians.

units.la: 3 ET cognoscam non sermonem istorum.] Quid facturus sit apud eos declarat. Sermone autem uocat, uerborum phaleras, & fucatam illam eloquentiam, cui studebant pseudapostoli, & cuius nomine sibijpsis & imprudentibus Corinthijs apprime placebant. Hanc dicit se non consideraturum sed longe aliud. Videlicet uirtutem. Hanc exponunt quidam facultatem edendi miracula, quibus confirmabatur tum doctrina Euangelij. Quidam uero intelligunt rectam uitæ conuersationem, qua quod uerbis docetur, ipso opere demonstretur, ut uirtus opponatur uerbis. Pulchre autē non dixit, Non cognoscam sapientiam & philosophiam eorum qui inflati sunt: sed, non co-
units.tr: 3 "And I will know not the word of those who are arrogant." He declares what he will do among them. By "word" he means the trappings of speech and that false eloquence which the false apostles pursued, and by whose name they pleased themselves and the unwise Corinthians very greatly. This he says he will not regard, but something quite different: namely, power. Some explain this as the capacity to work miracles, by which the doctrine of the gospel was then confirmed. Others understand it as a right manner of life, by which what is taught in words is demonstrated by the work itself, so that power is set against words. Notably, he did not say, "I will not know the wisdom and philosophy of those who are arrogant," but

units.la: gnoscam sermonem, λόγον eorum, ut intelligas doctrinam inflatorum hominum nihil fuisse aliud quàm inanes λόγος, omnium ueritatis ac pietatis uirtute destitutos.
units.tr: "I will not know the word [λόγον] of them," so that you may understand that the teaching of arrogant men was nothing other than empty words, destitute of all the power of truth and godliness.

units.la: 4 NON enim in sermone est regnum Dei.] Quare non sit sermonem inflatorum moratu rus forti & inuicta sententia declarat, qua tri bus quatuor uerbis & inanitatem logicam inflatorum hominum ex ecclesia, quasi uentila bro quodam, euentilat: & stultitiam Corinthio rū carpit, qui neglecta uirtute, qua regni Dei uis & efficacia quasi certo argumento declara tur, admirari cœperunt sermonis structuram, & uanæ scientiæ bullas, cum regnum Dei non sermone, sed uirtute constet.
units.tr: 4 "For the kingdom of God is not in word." Why the word of the arrogant is not to be admired he declares with a strong and unconquered sentence, by which, in three or four words, he winnows the empty logic of arrogant men out of the Church, as if with a winnowing fan, and rebukes the folly of the Corinthians, who, neglecting power, by which the force and efficacy of the kingdom of God are declared as by a sure proof, began to admire the construction of speech and the bubbles of vain learning, whereas the kingdom of God consists not in word but in power.

units.la: Ostendit autē hac sententia in ecclesia Christi non esse suspiciendas eas res, quibus regni Dei uis & efficacia non exprimitur, sed potius ad eas connitendum: quæ liquido declarant uirtutem regni Dei, quales sunt fidei in Christum syncerit as, spes, charitas, pax, gaudium, iusticia, malorum toleratia, spiritus modestia & quæ id genus sunt. Ita & Romanos confimi li ratione à dissidio cibario coercuit dicens: Nó est regnũ Dei esca & potus, sed, &c. ca. 14.
units.tr: By this sentence he shows that in the Church of Christ those things are not to be esteemed in which the force and efficacy of the kingdom of God is not expressed, but rather that we should strive for those things which clearly declare the power of the kingdom of God: such as sincerity of faith in Christ, hope, charity, peace, joy, righteousness, endurance of evils, gentleness of spirit, and things of that kind. So also he restrained the Romans by a similar reason from disputes about food, saying: "The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but," and so on, ch. 14.

units.la: Quid uultis? Cum uirga ueniam ad uos, an cũ charitate & spiritu lenitatis?
units.tr: What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?

units.la: 1 Comminationem & metum aduentus sui intendit, formidabilem illum reddens non solum inflatis spermologis, sed simul & alijs delinquentibus, adeoque transitum parat ad reli quorum uiciorum correctione, quorum iam deinceps primum est inauditum illud ftuprū, de quo mox cap. sequenti.
units.tr: 1 He sets before them the threat and the fear of his coming, making it dreadful not only to the puffed-up word-chatterers but also to the other offenders. He thus prepares the transition to the correction of the remaining vices, the first of which is the unheard-of fornication he takes up in the next chapter.

units.la: 2 Respiunt autem omnino paternum affectum hæc uerba. Patris nāq; est immorigeros filios disciplina uirgę ne pereant castigare, morigeros uero charitatis comitate ac lenitate có plecti. Ad utrunq; se paratu esse ostendit. Non est autem illud, an cum charitate, ita intelligendum, quasi uirga ad paternam charitatem non pertineat: cum ea ipsa fit, quæ uirga utatur erga filios dilectos, ut conseruentur ab interitu. Sed charitatis dictione usus est pro suauitate & comitate patris, quam ostendit erga morigeros filios. Videtur autē loqui iuxta sensum eorum qui corripiuntut & castigantur seueriter. Illi non sentiunt patris charitatē dum ua pulat, sed magis dū blāde ac suauiter tractatur.
units.tr: 2 These words certainly reflect a father's affection. It belongs to a father to correct disobedient sons with the rod, lest they perish, and to embrace obedient ones with the kindness and gentleness of love. He shows that he is ready for either. The phrase "or in love" should not be understood as if the rod did not belong to paternal love, since it is the very rod that a loving father uses toward his beloved sons so that they may be saved from destruction. Rather, he uses the word "love" for the kindness and courtesy of a father, which he shows toward obedient sons. He seems to speak according to the feeling of those who are rebuked and punished severely. They do not perceive a father's love while he beats them, but only when he treats them gently and kindly.

units.la: Non caret autem emphasi, quod non dicit, Cum autem uenero, in uirga ueniam ad uos, quod austerius fuisset: sed, Quid uultis? An cũ uirga ueniam ad uos, uel cum charitate, &c.
units.tr: Nor is the emphasis lacking in the fact that he does not say, "When I come, I will come to you with the rod," which would have been harsher, but rather, "What do you want? Shall I come to you with the rod, or with love," and so on.
