units.la: 1 Nam hoc pacto ostendit se, non sua sponte usurum uirga, sed ipsorum impœnitentia coactum, cum in ipsorum fit arbitrio aduentum suum uel seuerum uel mitiorem reddere.
units.tr: 1 For in this way he shows that he would not use the rod of his own accord, but would be compelled to it by their impenitence, since it is up to them whether his coming will be severe or milder.

units.la: 2 Et simul illos ad pœnitentiá inuitat. Quasi dicat: Vtrum uobis optabilius erit? An ut seuerus impœnitentium castigator aduenia, uel ut comiter uos ac suauiter pœnitétes complectar? An non & uobis & mihi iucundius erit, ut cum spiritu lenitatis ad uos q spiritu seueri tatis, uirga usurus adueniam? At qualis ueniā, in uobis est situm. Si mauultis mitem ac blandum quàm seuerum, bene, pœnitentiam agite, & ad uiam redite: sin uero pertinaciores facti comitatem meam despicitis, ideoq; pœnitentiam respuitis, ecce paratus sum ad ulcifcendū omnem uestram iniquitatem. Proinde etiam atq; etiam uidete utrū uelitis. Consimile auste ritate minatur & in posteriore, cap.10. & ult.
units.tr: 2 At the same time he invites them to repentance, as if to say: Which will be more welcome to you? Shall I come as a severe chastiser of the impenitent, or shall I embrace you kindly and gently when you repent? Would it not be more pleasing both to you and to me if I came to you with the spirit of gentleness rather than with the spirit of severity, to use the rod? But what kind of visit I make lies in your hands. If you prefer me gentle and kind rather than severe, well, repent and return to the right way. But if you become more stubborn and despise my kindness, and so reject repentance, behold, I am ready to punish all your iniquity. Therefore consider again and again which you want. He threatens with similar severity in the latter part, chapters 10 and at the end.

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Mnino auditur inter uos stuprum, & huiusmodi stuprū, quod nec inter Gentes nominatur, ut aliquis uxorem patris habeat. Et uos inflati estis, ac nō potius luxistis, ut tolleretur de medio uestrum, qui facinus hoc perpetrasset. Nam ego quidem, ut absens corpore, præsens autem spiritu, iam decreui tanquā præsens, utis qui sic hoc patrauit, in nomine domini nostri Iesu Christi, congregatis uobis & meo spiritu, unà cum potestate domini nostri Iesu Christi, tradatur Satanæ ad interitum carnis, quo spiritus saluus sit in die dni Iesu.
units.tr: It is actually reported among you that there is fornication, and such fornication as is not named even among the Gentiles, that someone has his father's wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who had done this deed might be removed from among you. For I indeed, though absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged, as if I were present, him who has done this, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are gathered together, and my spirit is with you, together with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.

units.la: Toto hoc capite Corinthios reprehendit propter commissum à quopiam ex ipsis stuprum, imo propter illius impunitatem: deinde urget, additis rationibus, ut eum qui deliquit tollant & eijciant ex ipsorum consortio, Satanæq; tradant. Et hac sectione tria facit. 1 Primum obijcit commissi facinoris enormitatem. 2 Deinde reprehendit eos, quod scortatorem non castigarant. 3 Tertio, præscribit suam sententiam, quid de illo in ipsorū conuentu statuere debeant.
units.tr: In this whole chapter he rebukes the Corinthians because of a fornication committed by one of them, or rather because of its going unpunished. Then he presses, adding reasons, that they should take away the one who has sinned and cast him out of their fellowship, and hand him over to Satan. In this section he does three things. 1. First, he sets before them the enormity of the deed committed. 2. Then he rebukes them because they did not punish the fornicator. 3. Third, he prescribes his own judgment on what they ought to decide about him in their assembly.

units.la: OMNINO auditur inter uos ftuprū. Exaggerat admodum scortatoris facinus, ut impudentiam non illius solum, sed & ipsorū Corinthiorum taxet. Nec conuenit eum qui deliquit, sed uniuersam ecclesiam, quod tam impudenter peccantem non castigassent.
units.tr: Actually it is reported among you that there is fornication. He greatly magnifies the crime of the fornicator, so as to censure not only his shamelessness but also that of the Corinthians themselves. He is speaking not to the one who sinned but to the whole Church, because they had not punished one who sinned so shamelessly.

units.la: AVDITVR. Non dicit, geritur, sed auditur. Tametsi enim multum in qualicunq; talis facinoris perpetratione aduersum Deū peccabatur, ei tamē peccato plurimū ex eo accedebat, quod absq; ullo pudore ita publice gereba tur, ut pesimo nomine religionem Christi cō spurcaret. Impudentiam ergo notat tum eius qui peccabat, tum eorum qui illius diffamia ni hil mouebantur.
units.tr: "It is reported." He does not say "it is done" but "it is reported." For although a great sin against God was committed in the very perpetration of such a deed, yet to that sin there was added especially this, that it was carried out so publicly and without any shame, that by its bad reputation it defiled the religion of Christ. He therefore marks the shamelessness both of the one who sinned and of those who were not moved by the report of it.

units.la: OMNINO. Nec simpliciter dicit, auditur inter uos ftuprū: sed, Omnino auditur, intendens impudentiam admisi facinoris quæ tan ta fit, ut indubitatū ac plenū circumquaq; rumorem sparserit: quē non quorundā tantum, sed omnium ora passim iactent. uel poterat ad stuprum referri, quasi dicat, auditur inter uos
units.tr: "Actually." He does not simply say, "it is reported among you that there is fornication," but "actually it is reported," intending to show that the shamelessness of the deed is so great that it has spread a certain and complete rumour on every side, which is tossed about everywhere on the lips of not just a few but of all. It could also be referred to the fornication, as if he said, "it is reported among you"

units.la: stuprum indubitatum.
units.tr: that the fornication is certain.

units.la: ET tale, quale nec inter Gētes. Diffamiā istam ostēdit non esse uanam ac temerariam, qualis plerunq; de modico aliquo lapsu spargi solet: sed esse talem, quæ merito plurimū inualescat, & maxima turpitudinis nota Christi ecclesiā apud Gētes infamem reddat. Stuprum enim inter uos tale, inquit, geritur, & geri narratur & auditur, quale Gentium, utut scelestarum, pudor non ferret. Et uerbum nominandi quod dicit, qualis nec inter Gētes nominatur, ad amplificandam flagitij huius turpitudinem facit, ut ostendat illam tātam esse, ut ne Gētes quidē illā admittant, imò ne nominare quidē sustineant. Sic Eph. 5. ne nominetur quidē inter uos inquit. Sceleris huius intentionem ex collatione struit, cōferens Gētes Christianis, qd alicubi & in alijs facit. Quantū enim Christianorū profesio pietate & uitæ sanctimonia Gētes cognitione Dei destitutas excellere debet, tāto turpius à Christianis peccatur, si peccando Gētibꝰ pares sint, nedū si illas superet.
units.tr: "And such as not even among the Gentiles." He shows that this report is not empty and rash, such as is usually spread about some small lapse, but is of such a kind that it deservedly gains great strength and, by the greatest mark of shame, makes the Church of Christ infamous among the Gentiles. For, he says, such fornication is committed among you, and is told and heard of, as the sense of decency, even among wicked Gentiles, would not tolerate. The word "not even named," which he uses, serves to magnify the shamefulness of this crime, so that he may show that it is so great that not even the Gentiles would admit it, indeed would not even bear to name it. So in Ephesians 5 he says, "let it not even be named among you." He builds up the seriousness of this wickedness by comparison, setting the Gentiles beside Christians, which he does elsewhere too. For the more the profession of Christians ought to excel the Gentiles, who lacked the knowledge of God, in piety and holiness of life, so much more shamefully do Christians sin if, by sinning, they are equal to the Gentiles, let alone if they fall below them.

units.la: Et hanc admisi stupri enormitatē diligenter obijcit, dū signanter illius qualitatē expendit. Nō enim dicit, Omnino auditur inter uos tale stuprū quale nec inter Gētes nominatur: sed postq; dixit, Omnino auditur inter uos stuprū, quali separatim illius qualitatē expendes subijcit, & tale stuprū, &c. Licet omnis scortatio cōtra Deū sit, est tamē alia alia grauior, maxime in qua iam non contra unū tantum Dei præceptū, sed plura delinquitur, & qua enormius honestas publica lęditur. Generaliter uetita est scortatio, singulariter uero turpiores illius speciēs adiectis minis sunt, phibitæ, qualis est, quæ hic reprehenditur.
units.tr: He rebukes this enormity of fornication diligently, while he weighs its quality particularly. For he does not say, "It is actually reported among you that there is fornication of such a kind as is not named among the Gentiles," but after he has said, "It is actually reported among you that there is fornication," he adds separately, weighing its quality, "and such fornication," and so on. Although all fornication is against God, yet one is more grave than another, especially where one sins not against a single commandment of God but against several, and where public decency is violated more grievously. Fornication is forbidden in general, but the more shameful kinds of it are singled out and prohibited with threats, such as the one here rebuked.

units.la: VT aliquis uxoré patris habeat. Non dicit, Vt aliquis nouercā suā habeat: sed per descriptionē nouercæ, turpitudinē sceleris exprimit, dū id ponit cuiꝰ gratia nō licet habere nouercā. Ob id uidelicet, qd uxor est patris. Sic Leui. 18. legimꝰ: Turpitudiné uxoris patris tui est. Naturæ repugnat, unā & eandē habere cū patre uxoré, & communis sensus, nō solū Dei præceptū, reclamat & abhorret. Ista turpitudo nō satis exprimitur dictione nouercę, licet in illa cōprehēdatur: exprimit aut si dicas, uxoré patris quenq; habere, ideo & Apostolus ad hūc modū loqui uoluit. Et Leuit. 20. cap. ubi pecca tū hoc morte puniri præcipitur, ea redditur ratio, qd patris turpitudiné reuelet, qui id ausit.
units.tr: "That someone has his father's wife." He does not say, "that someone has his stepmother," but by describing the stepmother he expresses the shamefulness of the sin, when he sets forth the reason why it is not lawful to have a stepmother: namely, because she is the father's wife. So we read in Leviticus 18: "It is the nakedness of your father's wife." To have one and the same wife as one's father is contrary to nature, and common sense, not only the command of God, cries out against it and abhors it. This shamefulness is not sufficiently expressed by the word "stepmother," although it is included in it. But it is expressed if you say that someone has his father's wife, and so the Apostle wished to speak in this way. And in Leviticus 20, where this sin is commanded to be punished by death, the reason is given: that he uncovers his father's nakedness who dares to do it.

units.la: HABEAT. Non dicit, cognouerit, sed habeat. Aliud est semel per insaniā delinquere, & postea abstinere per pœnitentiam, & aliud cō stanter peccato immorari: & hic, quod maius erat, etiā iure matrimonij publice cohabitantē habere patris uxoré. id quod iam nō solū est scortatiōe incesta in paterna delinquere reuerentiam, quale erat quod de Ruben legimus Gen. 35. sed & matrimonij sanctimoniā ad tāti sceleris obuelationem impie usurpare. Certe isto uerbo habendi plurimū taxat scortatoris huiꝰ pariter & reliquorū Corinthiorū impudē tiam. Expendendū hic uenit, quo abeat caro, {A}etiam sub Christianæ religionis operculo, ubi nemo est qui superiore potestate fultus, quiduis tentandi cohibeat licentiā. Quis dubitat istū incestuosam aliquo cōmento facinus suum palliasse? Qui quid nostris temporibus ab Anabaptistis tentatum sit, imò quid non sit, expenderit: nihil mirabitur &hoc stuprum inter eos, qui pseudapostolos præ Paulo admirari cœperant, nō stupri, sed coniugij esse loco habitum.
units.tr: "Has." He does not say "has known," but "has." It is one thing to sin once through madness and afterwards to abstain through repentance, and another to persist constantly in sin; and here, what was worse, he had his father's wife openly living with him under the right of marriage. This is not only to offend against the reverence due to a father by incestuous fornication, as Reuben did, of whom we read in Genesis 35, but also to abuse impiously the holiness of marriage to cover such a great crime. Certainly by this word "has" he greatly censures the shamelessness both of this fornicator and likewise of the other Corinthians. Here we must consider where the flesh goes, even under the cover of the Christian religion, where there is no one supported by higher authority to restrain the license to attempt anything. Who doubts that this incestuous man covered his deed with some pretext? Whoever considers what has been attempted by the Anabaptists in our own times, or rather what has not been attempted, will not be surprised that among those who had begun to admire false apostles above Paul, this fornication was regarded as a marriage rather than a fornication.

units.la: ET uos inflati estis.] Iam progreditur ad reprehensionē ecclesiæ Corinthiorum, q̄ obiurgat ob id quod facinus hoc nō prohibuerunt, sed impunitū abire permiserunt. Reprehensio nem autē hanc non simpliciter ponit dicens: Et uos illum non cohibuistis, non emendastis, nō è uestro consortio eiecistis: sed, Et uos inflati estis, ac non potius luxistis, ut tolleretur de me diouestrū, &c. quib. uerbis ipsas radices ponit. primū eius, quod faciebant: deinde eius quod facere debebát, & non faciebant. Tam enorme peccatū cōtemnebant, nec emēdabát. Vnde? Quia scilicet inflati erat. Ex inflatione quippe nascitur reliquorū neglectus. Ē contrario, ex luctu piorū, qui non dolere non possunt, ubi uident cōtra Deū ad diuini nominis ignominiā impudenter delinqui, sequitur conatus tollendæ offensæ Dei & conseruandæ puritatis ecclesiasticę. Hoc est q̄ dicit: Et uos inflati estis, & nō potius luctum habuistis, &c. Alij de pastoribus Corinthiorū istud exponunt: Et uos inflati estis, id q̄ facit Hier. Verū meo iudicio {B}quemadmodū per totā epistolam nō apparet q̄ doctorib. Corinthiorū scribat, sed uniuer sæ ecclesiæ, ita nec hic apparet. Nec causám uideo, cur ista necessario ad doctores referatur.
units.tr: "And you are puffed up" (1 Cor. 5:2). Now he moves on to rebuke the Corinthian church, which he reproaches for not having forbidden this crime but for having allowed it to go unpunished. He does not state the rebuke simply, as "And you did not restrain him, did not correct him, did not cast him out of your fellowship," but says, "And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, that he who did this might be removed from among you" (1 Cor. 5:2). In these words he sets out the roots of the two faults: first what they were doing, then what they ought to have done and did not do. They made light of so enormous a sin and did not amend it. Why? Clearly because they were puffed up. Neglect of others springs from such self-inflation. On the other hand, from the grief of the godly, who cannot fail to be sorry when they see God being offended and his name dishonoured by shameless sin, there follows an effort to remove the offence against God and to preserve the purity of the church. This is what he means by "And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned," and so on. Others explain this of the ministers of Corinth, as Jerome does: "And you are puffed up." But in my judgement, just as throughout the whole letter he does not appear to be writing to the teachers of Corinth but to the whole church, so he does not appear to be doing so here either. I see no reason why these words must be referred to the teachers.

units.la: Illud expendendū est, quomodo dicat Corinthios ita inflatos esse, ut propter inflationē tā insignis stupri emendationem neglexerint. Hiero. quoniā de doctorib. exponit, dicit eos uana scientia inflatos fuisse. Theophylactus uero Chrysost. ut assolet, sequutus istā Corinthiorū inflationē dicit fuisse super doctrina scortatoris: quasi is fuerit unus ex illorū doctoribus, ea præditus eloquentia, & inani philosophiæ scientia, ut pleriq; Corinthiorū in illo superbie rint. Mihi uero similius est Apostolum loqui de ea inflatione, cuius supra capite præcedenti meminit dicēs, ne hic illius, ille huius nomine, alius aduersus aliū inflemini. Vel simpliciter eā inflatione intelligit, qua ita sibi ipsi quisque placebat, ut nemini curæ esset, quid ab alijs gereretur: sed quisq; satis putaret, si ipse eo, quo alij, crimine nō teneretur, imò ex aliorū delictis occasionem sibi gloriandi ac superbiendi desumeret. id quod potissimum ab illis fieri solet, qui sectarum studio laborant.
units.tr: We must consider how he can say that the Corinthians were so puffed up that, because of this inflation, they neglected the correction of so notorious a fornication. Jerome, since he explains it of the teachers, says that they were puffed up with empty learning. Theophylact, following Chrysostom as is his habit, says that the Corinthians' inflation was over the teaching of the fornicator, as if he had been one of their teachers, endowed with such eloquence and empty philosophical learning that most of the Corinthians were proud of him. To me, however, it seems more likely that the Apostle is speaking of that inflation which he mentions in the preceding chapter, where he says, "Do not be puffed up, one man for another against another" (1 Cor. 4:6). Or he simply means that inflation by which each man so pleased himself that no one cared what was done by others, but each thought it enough if he himself was not bound by the same crime as the others, and indeed drew from the sins of others an occasion for boasting and pride. This is what is especially wont to happen among those who labour under the zeal of sects.

units.la: ET non potius luctū habuistis.] Hoc scilicet magis expressisset animos Christiana charitate, & spiritus synceritate præditos, q̄ inflatio illa uel propriæ uel alienæ scientiæ, aut etiā innocentiæ opinione contracta. Luctū poscit, & non irā: ut significet compatiendū membris esse omnibus, si unū ex illis patiatur, ac periclitetur. Nō loquitur aūt de priuato uniuscuiusuis, sed magis de publico luctu, qualis in ecclesia Israelis erat in usu, ubi quidpiā contra Deū esset gestū: ut cōgregato populo ieiunaretur, oraretur, quod delictū esset emendaretur, ac qui deliquisset ad placandā diuinæ maiestatis indignatione puniretur. Huius exemplū est euidens in facto Iesabel, 1. Reg. 21. Et hæc sententia magis conuenit ei quod agit Apostolus, q̄ quæ apud Chrysost. & Theophylactū legitur. Quod enim hic dicit, eos facere debuisse, id mox subijcit, præcipiens ut faciant.
units.tr: "And have not rather mourned." Clearly he would have wished this rather than that inflation, arising from one's own or another's learning, or from the reputation of innocence, to mark minds endowed with Christian love and sincerity of spirit. He asks for mourning and not anger, to signify that all the members should suffer with one who suffers and is in danger. He does not speak of the private grief of any individual, but rather of public mourning, such as was in use in the church of Israel when something had been done against God: the people were gathered together, fasted, and prayed; the offence was amended, and the one who had sinned was punished to appease the indignation of the divine majesty. A clear example of this is in the case of Jezebel, 1 Kings 21. This sense agrees better with what the Apostle is doing than the one read in Chrysostom and Theophylact. For what he says here, that they ought to have done this, he immediately adds by commanding them to do it.

units.la: VT tolleretur è medio uestrū.] Non dicit simpliciter, ut tolleretur è medio: sed addit, uestrū. Neq; enim hoc agit, ut prorsus extinguatur, eq; uiuis auferatur: sed ut ex ecclesiæ consortio ad tēpus eijciatur. Nec dicit, Vt pœnitētia ageret & resipisceret: sed, ut è medio uestrū tolleretur. Nam hoc erat in potestate ecclesiæ, alterū situm erat in animo eius qui deliquerat, uel potius in gratia Dei. Lugere potest ecclesia & deflere peccantes, eq; suo abijcere contubernio, & poenitentes cū gaudio recipere: animos uero illorum corrigere non potest, gratia domini potest. Augustinus hic annotat, quod non dicit, & nō luctum quia tollebatur: sed, ut tolleretur. Id est, ut lugentium dolor ad Deum ascenderet, & ipse tolleret hoc opus de medio eorū sicut ipse sciret, ne forte illi per humanam imperitiam eradicarent simul & triticum. Cōtra epistolam Parmeniani, lib. 3. cap. 1.
units.tr: "That he might be removed from among you." He does not simply say "that he might be removed," but adds "from among you." For he is not aiming at his complete destruction or removal from the living, but at his temporary expulsion from the fellowship of the church. Nor does he say, "that he might repent and return to his senses," but "that he might be removed from among you." For the second was in the power of the church, while the first lay in the mind of him who had sinned, or rather in the grace of God. The church can mourn and lament over sinners and cast them out of its company, and joyfully receive them back when they repent; but it cannot correct their minds, only the grace of the Lord can. Augustine here observes that he does not say "and not mourn because he was removed," but "that he might be removed," that is, that the sorrow of those mourning might rise up to God, and that he himself might remove this work from their midst as he himself knew, lest perhaps through human inexperience they should uproot the wheat along with the tares (Matt. 13:29). Against the letter of Parmenianus, book 3, chapter 1.

units.la: OBSER.
units.tr: OBSERVATION

units.la: Discimus ergo hoc loco, quā nō debeamus contenti esse nostra ipsorū innocentia, nisi & aliorum delicta primū deflere, deinde & charitatis studio emendare conemur. Vnius peccatum obijcitur toti ecclesiæ. Imò soli ecclesiæ. Neq; enim uerbo ipsum scortatorē alloquitur Apostolus, sed toto capite ecclesiam obiurgat, & uelut cōmisi criminis ream facit, hoc uno nomine, quod sua potestate ad castigandū delinquentem non fuerat usa. Et merito. Nihilo enim magis insons est eo qui deliquit, qui cū ex officio delinquente debeat emendare, uel contemptu uel negligentia, delinquendi illi impunitatem permittit.
units.tr: We learn therefore from this place that we ought not to be content with our own innocence, unless we also strive first to lament the sins of others, and then to amend them through the zeal of love. The sin of one man is laid to the charge of the whole church, indeed of the church alone. For the Apostle does not address the fornicator himself by name, but rebukes the church throughout the whole chapter, and makes it, as it were, guilty of the crime committed, on this single ground, that it had not used its power to punish the offender. And rightly so. For he who has sinned is no more guilty than the one who, when he ought to correct the offender by virtue of his office, through contempt or negligence permits him impunity in his sin.

units.la: NAM ego quidem, ut absens corpore, præsens autē spiritu.] Iam tertio loco, ut impellat eos ad eijciendū & castigandū impudentē illū scortatorē, sententiā suā iam latam præscribit: cuius prærudicio cohibeantur, ne uel con temnant amplius tam enorme facinus, uel secus de incestuoso statuat, q̄ ipse iam ex potestate dñi nostri Iesu Christi decreuerit. Nec differt hanc causam, donec ad eos ipse ueniat, sicut infrà cap. 11. quēdam disponenda sibi dicit, cum uenerit ad eos: sed magno serio iam sibi quid faciendū sit, decretū esse scribit, & ut hoc ipsi mox exequantur urget, uidelicet propter pestis huius cōtagionē, cuius infrà mentionē faciet, ubi dicit: Modicū fermenti totā cōsper. &c. Nec mandat hoc negocij Timotheo, sed suā authoritatē, spiritus sui præsentiam, & domini nostri Iesu Christi potestatē interponit,
units.tr: "For I indeed, as absent in body, but present in spirit." Now, thirdly, to urge them to cast out and punish that shameless fornicator, he sets out the sentence he has already passed, by whose prejudgement they should be restrained from either making light of so enormous a crime any further, or deciding about the incestuous man otherwise than he has already determined by the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ. Nor does he defer this matter until he himself comes to them, as in chapter 11 below, where he says that certain things are to be arranged when he has come to them; rather he writes that he has already, with great earnestness, decided what must be done, and he urges them to carry it out at once, namely because of the contagion of this plague, of which he will speak below, where he says, "A little leaven leavens the whole lump" (1 Cor. 5:6). Nor does he entrust this business to Timothy, but interposes his own authority, the presence of his spirit, and the power of our Lord Jesus Christ,

units.la: {ꝑ} nostri ne Timothei præsentiam apud Corinthios odiosam reddat.
units.tr: lest the presence of our Timothy make him odious among the Corinthians.

units.la: 1 NAM ego quidé ut absens corpore.] Quærendum hic, quamobrem corporalis absentiæ suæ mentionem faciat. Poterat simpliciter dicere: Nam ego quidem iam decreui, ut is qui sic hoc patrauit, &c. Verum, quoniam ut suprà meminit, uidebat absentiam suam multis causam dare pleraq; inepta & absurda per arrogantiam tentandi: ostendit se, licet corpore sit absens, nō tamen omnino absentem illis esse, sed spiritu coràm omnia illorum uidere & iudicare. qd̄ puto ad hoc scribit, ut in metu eos coti-neat, maxime qui ipsius absentia abutebatur: deinde ut & in futuro iudicio de scordatore se rendo diligentiores reddat.]
units.tr: "For I indeed, as absent in body." It must be asked here why he mentions his bodily absence. He could have simply said, "For I have already decided that he who has done this..." But since, as he mentioned above, he saw that his absence gave many people occasion to attempt many foolish and absurd things through arrogance, he shows that, although he is absent in body, he is nonetheless not wholly absent from them, but in spirit sees and judges all their affairs as if present. I think he writes this to hold them in fear, especially those who were abusing his absence, and then so that they may become more diligent in preparing for the future judgement concerning the fornicator.

units.la: Arbitor aut Apostolu loqui nō de tali spiritus præsentia, quæ uel in memoria, uel solicitudinis affectibus sita sit, qualis solet esse amicorū, quos cura & solicitudo per dilectionem extra corpus ad ea cogitanda rapit, quæ amicos cōcernunt: & qualis est ea de qua dicitur, quod amans magis sit ubi amat, quàm ubi animat, sed potius de miraculosa quadā & efficaci, quæ quid geratur, alibi uideat & cognoscat.
units.tr: I think the Apostle is not speaking of such a presence of spirit as lies in memory or in the affections of anxious care, such as is usual with friends whom care and concern for them, through love, carry away outside their bodies to think about those things which concern their friends; nor of that presence of which it is said that a lover is more where he loves than where he lives; but rather of a certain miraculous and effective presence, by which he sees and knows elsewhere what is being done.

units.la: Ita Col.2. dicit: Hoc aût dico, ut nemo uos decipiat in sublimitate sermonum. Nam etsi corpore absens sum, spiritu tamē uobiscum sum, gaudēs & uidens ordinē uestrū & firmamentum eius quæ in Christo est fidei uestræ. Nec mirū uideri debet singulari quadam diuinitus concessa uirtute, sanctos apostolos & prophetas spiritu ibi esse posse, ubi corpore non sunt: ita ut quid à procul dissitis geratur, quasi coràm cōstituti uideat, quod & de Elizeo 2.Reg.5. legimus, ubi ad Giezi dixit: Nonne cor meū in præsenti erat, quando reuersus est homo de curru suo in occursum tui? qñ legamus eos spiritus oculis etiā quæ posterioribus tēpori bus futura erant præuidisse. Et huic sententiæ astipulatur Hiero. maximè Colof.2. Ambr. uidetur exponere nō de spiritu Apostoli, sed de Spiritu Dei, qui nusquā nō adsit. Verū abfq; cōtrouersia de suo spiritu loquitur, idq; nominatim, cū dicit, congregatis uobis & meo spiritu.
units.tr: So in Col. 2 he says: "I say this, that no one may deceive you with persuasive speech. For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order and the steadfastness of your faith in Christ" (Col. 2:4–5). Nor should it seem strange that, by a certain singular power granted by God, holy apostles and prophets can be present in spirit where they are not in body, so that they see what is done at a distance as if they were standing before them. We read this also of Elisha, 2 Kings 5, where he said to Gehazi: "Did not my heart go with you, when the man turned from his chariot to meet you?" Likewise we read that those spirits foresaw by their eyes things that were to be in later times. Jerome agrees with this opinion, especially on Col. 2. Ambrose seems to explain it not of the Apostle's spirit but of the Spirit of God, who is everywhere present. But without controversy he speaks of his own spirit, and this by name, when he says, "when you are gathered together and my spirit is with you."

units.la: 2 IAM iudicaui tanquā præsens.] Ita sibi iam decretū esse ac fixū ostēdit, ut insignis ille fornicator Satanæ tradatur, ad hoc, ut sua illis sententia præiudicet: qua cohibeātur, ne secus istuāt, q̄ hic sibi præscribi uideant. Tanquā præsens, inquit. Spiritus sui præsentiā nō uult inferiore loco haberi, q̄ si omnino & corpore coram esset, id qd̄ & ipsum stimulandi gratia facit.
units.tr: 2 I have already judged, as if I were present.] He shows that he has already decided and settled that this notorious fornicator is to be handed over to Satan, so that his sentence may anticipate their judgment and restrain them from proceeding otherwise than they see prescribed here. "As if present," he says. He does not want his presence regarded as of lesser weight than it would be if he were wholly there in person, and he does this also to spur them on.

units.la: 3 VT is qui sic hoc patrauit.] Declarat quid & de quo statuerit. De eo scilicet qui sic hoc patrauit. Refricat facinus, idq; non simpliciter dicens, qui hoc patrauit: sed, qui sic hoc patrauit, ostēdens ad hoc se iudiciū impelli nō tam ipso facinore, q̄ illius impudētia, qua nō semel per insaniā constuprauerit patris uxorē exemplo Ruben, sed illam etiā uelut uxoris loco habeat. Et in hac particula propè deprehenditur Apostolus non usurus fuisse ista iudicij seueritate, nisi magis circūstātijs & enormitate deli-
units.tr: 3 Concerning the one who has done this.] He states what he has decided and about whom. Namely, about the one who has done this, and in this way. He reopens the crime, and he does not simply say "who has done this" but "who has done this in this way," showing that he is moved to this judgment not so much by the deed itself as by that man's shamelessness, by which he defiled his father's wife, not once but repeatedly in madness, after the example of Reuben, and even keeps her as if she were his wife. In this phrase the Apostle is seen to be nearly revealing that he would not have used such severity of judgment had he not been moved more by the circumstances and the enormity of the offence than by the bare fact of the sin.

units.la: A ēti quàm ipso delicto simpliciter admissio fuisset impulsus. Itaque admonemur hoc loco, ut delictorū discrimina non solum in se, sed & in modo & circūstantijs obseruemus, ut sciamus ubi opus sit seueriore castigatione, & ubi misericordia & condonatio locū habeat, ne ubiuis proni simus ad eijciendos ex ecclesia fratres.
units.tr: Therefore we are admonished here to observe the differences between offences not only in themselves but also in their manner and circumstances, so that we may know where stricter correction is needed and where mercy and forgiveness have their place, lest we be quick to cast brethren out of the Church at every turn.

units.la: 4 IN nomine domini nostri Iesu Christi.] Chrysost. indicat quosdā hanc particulā coniungere cum præcedēti, ut intelligamus scortatorē patris uxorē ita penes se habuisse, ut facinori suo Christi nomē prætexuerit, tanquam operculū flagitiosæ libertatis. Verū simplicius est ut referamus ad sequentia, intelligamusq; interponi ab Apostolo Christi authoritatē, in cuius nomine debeāt cōgregari Corinthij, deq; isto flagitioso homine castigando decernere.
units.tr: 4 In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.] Chrysostom notes that some join this phrase to what precedes, so that we understand the fornicator to have kept his father's wife in such a way that he used the name of Christ as a cover for his shameful licence. But it is simpler to refer it to what follows, and to understand that the Apostle interposes the authority of Christ, in whose name the Corinthians are to assemble and decide about punishing this shameful man.

units.la: 1 Est enim in nomine domini aliquid facere uelut loco & authoritate ipsius facere: quod si rite fiat, ita firmū & ratum est, ac si ab ipso domino personaliter geratur. Nō enim uult Apostolus in ecclesia quicq̄ geri, quod nō fulciatur potestate & authoritate Christi. 2 Præterea in nomine domini aliquid facere, aliquādo idē est atq; ad gloriā nominis dñi facere, ut Colos. 3.Quicquid egeritis, omnia in nomine dñi nostri Iesu Christi facite. Hoc est, ppter gloriā nominis Christi facite, ut & 1. Cor.10. admonet.
units.tr: 1 For to do something in the name of the Lord is to do it in his place and by his authority; and if it is done rightly, it is as firm and valid as if it were carried out by the Lord himself in person. For the Apostle does not want anything done in the Church that is not supported by the power and authority of Christ. 2 Moreover, to do something in the name of the Lord sometimes means the same as to do it for the glory of the Lord's name, as in Col. 3: "Whatever you do, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ." That is, do it for the sake of the glory of Christ's name, as 1 Cor. 10 also urges.

units.la: 3 Aliquando est in fiducia nominis domini aliquid facere, ut Psal.20. Nos autem in nomine domini Dei nostri uexilla erigemus. Et Dauid.1.Sam.17.ad Goliath dicebat: Tu uenis ad me cum gladio, & hasta & clypeo, ego autem uenio in nomine domini exercituum, &c.
units.tr: 3 Sometimes to do something in confidence in the name of the Lord is meant, as in Ps. 20: "But we will lift up our banners in the name of the Lord our God." And David in 1 Sam. 17 said to Goliath: "You come to me with sword, spear and shield, but I come in the name of the Lord of hosts," etc.

units.la: 5 CONGREGATIS uobis & meo spiritu.] Non uult suo solius iudicio eijci ex ipsorū cōfortio caelestū, sed cōmunib. totius ecclesiæ suffragijs. Hoc enim & ipsi ecclesiæ pderat,& emēdando peccatori, sicut & in posteriore dicit: Sufficit illi qui huiusmodi est obiurgatio ista, quæ fit à multis. Ecclesiæ haētenus cōducit, qd̄ dū de tā enormi facinore iudicat, quasi proprio præiudicio in posterum sibijpsi quisq; aditū ad cōsimilia pcludit. Et plurimū ad hoc facit, ut is qui cōmuni omniū iudicio cōdēna tur & eijcitur, pudefactus hoc citius resipiscat, quòd nusq̄ in ecclesia reperit, q palpet & locū subterfugij præbeat. Verū ius hoc ecclesiæ & institutū Apostolicū Rom.pont.prorsus irritū reddidit,& è medio sustulit, dū sibi soli & episcopis potestatē excommunicādi uindicauit.
units.tr: 5 Assembled together with you and my spirit.] He does not want the expulsion of such a person from the fellowship of the saints to rest on his own judgment alone, but on the common votes of the whole Church. For this both benefits the Church itself and serves to amend the sinner, as he also says later: "Sufficient for such a one is this rebuke, which is given by many." It is useful to the Church that when it judges so enormous a crime, each person, as it were, by his own prejudgment, closes off for himself in future the way to similar acts. And it contributes greatly to this that the man who is condemned and cast out by the common judgment of all, being shamed, repents the sooner, because he finds nowhere in the Church anyone who will flatter him and offer him a way of escape. But the Roman pontiff has entirely nullified this right of the Church and the apostolic institution, and has removed it from the midst, while claiming for himself and the bishops alone the power of excommunication.

units.la: Iterum autem inculcat illis spiritus sui præsentiam, ut appareat periculum fuisse, ne uel sententiam hanc non exequerentur, uel non unanimi consensu exequerentur, ut fieri solet, ubi sectarum studia obtinet, nisi impulsu fuissent spiritus Apostolici præsentia & metu.
units.tr: Again, he impresses upon them the presence of his spirit, so that it may appear that there was danger lest they either not carry out this sentence or carry it out without unanimous consent, as usually happens where the zeal of factions prevails, unless they were impelled by the presence and fear of the Apostle's spirit.

units.la: 6 CVM uirtute dñi nostri Iesu Christi.] Iá secundo dñi mentionē facit, ut inculcet illis oia hic dñi & potestate & uirtute geri. Græcè est σὺν τῇ δυνάμει, nō σὺν τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ: hoc est, cū uirtute, nō cū potestate. Nā illud suprà, in noie dñi nostri, idē est atq;, in potestate dñi nostri. Hic uero adiūgit & uirtutē Christi, miraculosam illā, quæ cooperabatur agétibus in nomine ipsius, nô solũ docendo & sanando,sed & ubi necesse erat, reprobos castigando. Eras.annotat, σὺν, nô semper cóiunctionis,sed aliquãdo & fauoris & aspirationis habere notã, ut cũ Deo geri dicatur,qd' propicio &fauëte Deo geritur. Ita sensus esset,cũ uirtute domini nostri Iesu Christi,id est,aspirante & fauëte uirtute dñi nostri Iesu Christi:qui quod decretũ in nomine ipsius fuerit,efficaciter sua uirtute exequitur.
units.tr: 6 With the virtue of our Lord Jesus Christ.] Now he mentions the Lord a second time, to impress on them that everything here is done by the Lord's will, power and virtue. The Greek is σὺν τῇ δυνάμει [σὺν τῇ δυνάμει], not σὺν τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ [σὺν τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ]: that is, with virtue, not with power. For the earlier phrase, in the name of our Lord, means the same as in the power of our Lord. Here, however, he adds also the virtue of Christ, that miraculous virtue which worked together with those acting in his name, not only in teaching and healing but also, where necessary, in punishing the wicked. Erasmus notes that σύν [σύν] does not always signify conjunction but sometimes also a sign of favour and assistance, as when something is said to be done with God, meaning it is done with God's favour and help. So the sense would be: with the virtue of our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, with that virtue breathing upon and favouring them, which efficaciously carries out by its own power whatever has been decided in his name.

units.la: 7 TON τωἰστεμ.] Videtur hoc uacare,qd' attinet ad orationis cõtextũ & plenitudinẽ. Nã supra satis expressit,quũ adiudicauerit Satanæ,nẽpe eũ qui sic hoc patrauerat. Verũ si spectes Apostoli mentẽ,nô est ociofe positũ. Nequit enim satis ingeminare culpã tã enormis flagitij. Et hac ratione nec supra nec hic dicit, iudicauì iã hũc hominẽ Satanæ tradendũ esse: sed,eũ qui sic hoc fecit & hic,eũ q est huiusmodi:ut ostẽdat huiusmodi flagitia in ecclesia nô esse seren da,sed cum seueritate cõpetenti extirpauda.
units.tr: 7 τὸν τοιοῦτον [such a one].] This seems superfluous as far as the context and fullness of the sentence go. For above he has sufficiently expressed that he had handed over to Satan the one who had done this. But if you consider the Apostle's mind, it is not placed idly. For he cannot repeat enough the guilt of so enormous a shame. And for this reason he says neither above nor here, "I have already judged that this man is to be handed over to Satan," but "the one who did this, and here, such a one," so as to show that crimes of this kind are not to be spared in the Church but uprooted with fitting severity.

units.la: 8 TRADATVR Satanæ,ad interitũ carnis, ut spiritus saluus fit in die dñi.] Hæc tandẽ est sententia Apostoli, qua quid de scortatore tam impudẽte fit statuẽdũ præscribitur.Et est bimẽ bris.Primũ enim indicat quid fit faciendũ,deinde ad quẽ finẽ dirigenda sit flagitiosi huius condenatio. Exponitur autuarie. Ambrosio Satanæ tradi ad interitũ carnis, est eijci ex ecclesia,& prorsus condenari.Carnis interitũ,in telligit carnalis hominis interitũ & condenatione.Et illud,Vt spiritus saluus fit in die dñi: exponit de spiritu sancto,nô de spiritû scortatoris.Spiritũ S.hic dicit ecclesiæ spiritũ intelligendũ esse,qui saluatur, cũ nô amittitur: quẽadmodum solemus rem nô amissam saluã, amissam uero perditã uocare,licet in se,ubi ubi fit,nô fit perdita,sed nobis. Vult ergo scortatoris huius interitum ad id institutũ esse ab Apostolo,ut ecclesiæ Corinthiorũ,spiritus sanctus uidelicet,in hominibus ecclesiæ, in die iudicij saluus reperiatur, eo quòd is soleat deferere cõtaminatos:periculũ aũt fuerit, ne per scortatoris huius exemplũ uniuersa inficiaretur ecclesia,adeoq; contristaretur & fugaretur spiritus sanctus.Hæc Ambrosij sententia nô uidetur exprimere mentẽ Apostoli, qui carnẽ & spiritum per antithesim hic posuit, non diuersorũ, sed eius qui corripiendus erat.
units.tr: 8 To be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.] This, finally, is the Apostle's sentence, by which it is prescribed what is to be decided about so shameless a fornicator. And it has two parts. First he indicates what is to be done, then to what end the condemnation of this shameful man is to be directed. It is explained variously. According to Ambrose, to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh is to be cast out of the Church and utterly condemned. By the destruction of the flesh he understands the destruction and condemnation of the carnal man. And the words, "so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord," he explains as referring to the Holy Spirit, not to the fornicator's spirit. Here he says the Holy Spirit is to be understood as the spirit of the Church, which is saved when it is not lost, just as we usually call a thing not lost "saved" and a thing lost "perished," although in itself, wherever it is, it is not lost, but only to us. Therefore he means that the destruction of this fornicator was appointed by the Apostle so that the Church of the Corinthians, that is, the Holy Spirit in the members of the Church, might be found safe in the day of judgment, since the Spirit is accustomed to forsake those who are defiled; and there was danger that through the example of this fornicator the whole Church would be infected, and the Holy Spirit would thus be grieved and driven away. This opinion of Ambrose does not seem to express the mind of the Apostle, who here set flesh and spirit against each other by antithesis, not of two different persons, but of the one who was to be corrected.

units.la: Chrysostomus exponit,scortatorẽ hũc Satanæ ita traditũ esse,ut morbo aliquo,uel malo uulnere,ad exemplum Iob:licet diuersa ratione,in carne percussus,euaderet in die domini æternas gehennæ pœnas.
units.tr: Chrysostom explains that this fornicator was handed over to Satan in such a way that, struck in the flesh by some disease or grievous wound, after the example of Job, though by a different means, he might escape on the day of the Lord from the eternal punishments of hell.

units.la: Augustinus nô eandem tantum, sed geminam expositionẽ ponit,contra Parmenianum lib.3.cap.1.ubi sic scribit:Quid ergo agebat Apostolus,nisi ut per interitũ carnis saluti consuleret,ut siue aliqua pœna uel morte corpora li,sicut Ananias & uxor eius ante pedes apostoli Petri ceciderũt,siue per pœnitentiã,quoniam Satanæ traditus erat, interimeret in se scelerãtam carnis concupiscentiam. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Augustine offers not only this explanation but a twofold one, against Parmenianus, book 3, chapter 1, where he writes thus: "What then was the Apostle doing, except to provide for salvation through the destruction of the flesh, so that either by some punishment or death the body should perish, as Ananias and his wife fell before the feet of the apostle Peter, or else, since he had been handed over to Satan, through repentance he might destroy in himself the sinful lust of the flesh." So far Augustine.

units.la: Ad consimilem modum & Hiero. exponit:
units.tr: In much the same way Jerome also explains it:

units.la: Certe in posteriore,ca 2. liquet Apostolũ scortatorẽ hunc nô eo consilio tradidisse Satanæ, ut prorsus in sempiternum periret, sed ut seruaretur.Nam ibi iubet illi impendi misericordiã,& quod deliquerat ab ecclesia condonari: hoc est,iterum absq; dubio,pœnitentem in ecclesiæ gremium recipi,ne abundantiori tristitia absorberetur,ne locus esset insidijs Satanæ, cuius notæ essent cogitationes, uidelicet ad perdendum pronæ & prorsus intentæ.
units.tr: Certainly in the second letter, chapter 2, it is clear that the Apostle did not hand this fornicator over to Satan with the intention that he should perish utterly forever, but that he should be saved. For there he orders that mercy be shown to him and that what he had done wrong be forgiven by the Church: that is, undoubtedly again, that he, having repented, be received back into the bosom of the Church, so that he might not be swallowed up by excessive sorrow, and so that there might be no opening for the snares of Satan, whose thoughts are known to be bent on destruction and wholly intent upon it.

units.la: OBSER. I.
units.tr: OBSERVATION I.

units.la: Videmus itaq; hic,Satanã etiam ecclefiç ministrum esse,idq; ad salutẽ eorum qui corripiuntur.Ita & 1.Tim.1.scribit Apostolus Hymenæum se & Alexandrũ tradidisse Satanæ, non ut perirent,sed ut discerent nô maledicere. Et certe liẽtor iste tum erat ecclesiæ necessarius, cũ carebat magistratu qui fontes puniret. Iam uerò ubi in ecclesia sunt principes & magistratus,quibus dici potest: Seruite domino in timore,qui potestate à Deo accepta, carnẽ delinquentẽ in interitum ducere possunt, ut spiritus seruetur in die Domini: merito cessauit miraculosa ista delinquentium castigatio, quæ tempore apostolorum ministerio facta est Satanæ,omnium periculosissimo, nisi adsit prudentia apostolica.
units.tr: We see here, then, that Satan is also a minister of the Church, and that for the salvation of those who are rebuked. So too in 1 Timothy 1 the Apostle writes that he had handed over Hymenaeus and Alexander to Satan, not that they should perish, but that they should learn not to blaspheme. And indeed that lictor was then necessary to the Church, when it lacked a magistrate who might punish offenders. But now, where there are princes and magistrates in the Church, to whom it can be said, "Serve the Lord in fear," and who, having received power from God, can bring the sinning flesh to destruction so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord, that miraculous punishment of offenders, which in the time of the apostles was carried out by the ministry of Satan, the most dangerous of all, has rightly ceased, unless apostolic prudence is present.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Sed quæri potest, quomodo per interitum carnis,spiritus seruetur in die domini. An per hoc tantũ,qd' caro punitur,spiritus saluari potest?Ergo quotquot in carne puniũtur, ppter delicta aliqua,spiritu seruantur? Et hoc est qd' infrà cap.11.dicit: Si nosipsos iudicaremus, à domino non iudicaremur:dum iudicamur autem à domino,corripimur,ne cum hoc mundo damnemur. De credentibus forsan potest hoc sentiri,ut in corpore puniti, spiritu ppter fidem in Christũ seruentur,de impijs uero nequaq.Minus habet periculi si intelligamus interitum carnis siue is fiat liētoris, siue Satanæ ministerio,tum facere ad salutẽ spiritus,quando per illum qui deliquit ad resipiscentiã ducitur,cuius interuétu spiritus gratiæ & peccatorum remissionis capax factus,seruatur. Ita solent parétes,dum liberorũ delicta emendant, dicere:Satius est ut per me uapules, q̃ ut liẽto ri plectendus tradare. At nô mox liētoris manum euadit,quisquis à patre iam antea castigatus est.Nisi enim paterna uirga cedat delinquẽti filio ad resipiscentiam,certe nihilominus traĥtabitur à liētore,imò durius,idq; merito.
units.tr: But it may be asked how the spirit is saved in the day of the Lord through the destruction of the flesh. Is it by this alone, that the flesh is punished, that the spirit can be saved? So then, as many as are punished in the flesh for some offences are saved in spirit? And this is what he says below in chapter 11: "If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord; but while we are judged by the Lord, we are chastened, so that we are not condemned with this world." Perhaps this may be understood of believers, that being punished in the body they are saved in spirit on account of their faith in Christ; but not of the impious at all. There is less danger if we understand the destruction of the flesh, whether it comes by the ministry of the lictor or of Satan, as serving the salvation of the spirit, when through the one who has sinned he is led to repentance, through whose intervention the spirit, made capable of grace and the remission of sins, is saved. So parents, while correcting the faults of their children, are accustomed to say: "It is better that you be whipped by me than that you be handed over to be punished by the lictor." But whoever has already been chastised by his father does not at once escape the lictor's hand. For unless the paternal rod brings the sinning son to repentance, he will nonetheless certainly be dealt with by the lictor, and more harshly, and deservedly so.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Deinde & hoc quæret aliquis forsan, an in die dñi solus spiritꝰ seruetur in illis, q in carne cum ageret in hac uita,sunt puniti? Vt spiritus inqt,seruetur in die dñii.Atqui in die dñii quot quot seruabũtur,nô spiritu solũ,sed & corporẽ seruabũtur.Quidã sic effugiũt,ut p carne expo nãt carnalẽ illũ hominẽ,p spiritũ uerò spiritalẽ & regeneratũ.Caro hoc sensu interit, dũ carnalis homo uirtute pœnitetiæ interit,mortificatis uidelicet carnis affectib.spiritus uerò seruatur, dum spiritalis homo, noua illa creatura in Christo, tota scilicet, cum corpore & anima in die domini seruatur. Verum meo iudicio simplicius est, ut de carne illa peccatrice intelligamus, quam in omnibus planè mortalibus interire necesse est & corrumpi: deinde & de spiritu hominis, id est, anima, quæ seruari potest sola, ne intereat nec temporaliter nec in futuro sempiterne. id quod carni nō potest, qualis nunc est, contingere, cui necesse est, ut intereat, id est, corrumpatur, ac in nouissimo demū die, uirtute Dei restituatur. Consilium itaque Apostoli erat, satius esse carnem illam alioqui propediem interituram, Satanæ affligendam tradere, quàm & carnem & spiritum perpetuę condemnationi permittere. Hic certe Apostolo in mentem non uenit solum spiritum saluū futurum neglecta carne, proinde neq; colligi debet ex ipsius uerbis.
units.tr: Again, someone may perhaps ask whether in the day of the Lord only the spirit is saved in those who were punished in the flesh while living in this life. "That the spirit," it says, "may be saved in the day of the Lord." And yet in the day of the Lord all who are saved will be saved not only in spirit but also in body. Some escape this by taking the flesh to mean the carnal man, and the spirit to mean the spiritual and regenerate man. In this sense the flesh perishes, while the carnal man perishes by the virtue of repentance, that is, with the affections of the flesh mortified; the spirit is saved, while the spiritual man, that new creature in Christ, is saved entire, with body and soul, in the day of the Lord. But in my judgment it is simpler to understand it of that sinful flesh, which in all mortals must necessarily perish and be corrupted, and of the spirit of man, that is, the soul, which can be saved alone, so that it perishes neither temporally nor eternally in the future. This cannot happen to the flesh as it now is, which must perish, that is, be corrupted, and be restored at the last day by the power of God. Therefore the counsel of the Apostle was that it was better to hand over that flesh, which in any case would soon perish, to be afflicted by Satan, than to permit both flesh and spirit to perpetual condemnation. Certainly the Apostle did not think only of the spirit being saved with the flesh neglected; therefore this should not be inferred from his words.

units.la: Nō est bona gloriatio uestra. An nescitis quod paululū fermenti totam cōspersionem fermentat? Expurgate itaq; uetus fermentum, ut sitis noua conspersio, sicut estis infermentati. Nam & pascha nostrum pro nobis immolatus est Christus. Itaq; festum celebremus, non in fermento ueteri, nec in fermento malitiæ & uersutiæ, sed in infermētatis syncerítatis & ueritatis.
units.tr: "Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Purge out therefore the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. For Christ our passover is sacrificed for us. Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth."

units.la: Post sententiæ suę præscriptum, adijcit ampliorem illius rationem, illustrationem & corroborationem. Et primum glorias illorum reijcit, & inconsiderantiæ cōdemnat, dicens: Nō est bona gloriatio uestra. An nescitis, &c.
units.tr: After stating his sentence, he adds a fuller reason for it, its illustration and confirmation. And first he rejects their boasting and condemns their thoughtlessness, saying: "Your boasting is not good. Do you not know," etc.

units.la: Exponit autem Chrysostomus de ea gloriatione, qua in scortatore ipso tanquam uiro singulariter sapiente & facundo (intelligit enim illū fuisse ex pseudapostolis doctoribus) sint gloriati: quam Apostolus ob id dicat non esse bonam, quod per illam impudentis hominis animum à resipiscentia impedierint, adeoque ædificationem ecclesiæ neglexerint: imò quātum in ipsis erat, corrumpendæ illius causam dederint. Mihi uerò cum alijs, ut & suprà monui, nec uerisimile est hunc scortatorem è numero doctorum fuisse: nec uidetur Apostolus de ista, sed magis de ea gloriatione loqui, qua quisq; de sua ipsius innocentia gloriantes malum hoc impunitum & inemendatum serpere relinquebát: quasi in ecclesia satis sit, per se esse innocentem, & non simul requiratur, ut quod male à quouis in illa geritur, corrigatur. Occurrit itaq; illorum cogitationi, in speciem bonæ, negatq; statim bonam esse, adiecta ratione, cur id faciat, cum dicit:
units.tr: Chrysostom explains this as the boasting by which they had exulted in the fornicator himself, as a man singularly wise and eloquent (for he takes him to have been one of the false-apostle teachers). The Apostle says it is not good because by it they had kept the impudent man's mind from repentance, and so neglected the building up of the Church; indeed, so far as they were concerned, they had given cause for its corruption. But to me, as I also warned above, along with others, it seems neither likely that this fornicator was among the teachers, nor does the Apostle seem to speak of that kind of boasting, but rather of that by which people, glorying in their own innocence, allowed this evil to creep on unpunished and uncorrected, as if in the Church it were enough to be innocent oneself, and it were not also required that whatever wrong is done by anyone in it be corrected. He therefore meets their thinking, which had the appearance of goodness, and at once denies that it is good, adding the reason why he does so, when he says:

units.la: AN nescitis quod paululum fermenti totá cōspersionem fermentat?] Ista ratio gnomen habet similitudinis luce illustratam, qua declarat quę sit uis mali exépli, in ecclesia impuniti. Est autem fermenti simile ita cóparatum, & ad malii exempli operatione declarandam appositū, ut multo sit efficacius quod dicit hoc pacto, q si proprie & absq; ullo simili dixisset: An nescitis, quod unius impudentis hominis exemplū uniuersam ecclesiā corrumpat? Vnde & præmittit inconsiderantiæ illorū reprehensionē, dicēs: An nescitis? Q.d. Tam estis inconsiderātes in hac causa, ut putetis uos apprimè excusatos uestra ipsorum innocentia: nec animaduertatis interea periculū esse, ne tota uestra ecclesia malo isto exeplo, uelut quodá fermento inficiatur. Quis adeo stupidus est, qui ignoret quid expectandū sit conspersioni alioqui puræ ac synceræ, si locus sit fermento? Et ne excusent negligentiá suam per delinquētis unitatē, quasi nō adeò periculosum sit unius hominis deliētū, cū adhuc reliquū ecclesiæ corpus sit saluū, nō dicit: An nescitis quod ex fermeto corrūpatur cōspersio, sed quod mo dicū fermeti: deinde nō aliquā tantū parte cōspersionis, sed totā cōspersioné. nec addit dubij euētus notā: sed asseueráter dicit, fermētat.
units.tr: "Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?" This reason takes the form of a comparison made clear by its own light, by which he shows what the force of an unpunished bad example is in the Church. The likeness of leaven is so framed, and so set forth to express the working of a bad example, that what he says in this way is far more effective than if he had said plainly and without any comparison: "Do you not know that the example of one impudent man corrupts the whole Church?" Whence he also prefaces it with a rebuke of their thoughtlessness, saying, "Do you not know?" As if to say: You are so thoughtless in this matter that you think yourselves wholly excused by your innocence; and meanwhile you do not notice the danger that your whole Church may be infected by this evil example, as by some leaven. Who is so stupid as not to know what is to be expected of a mass otherwise pure and sincere, if there is room for leaven? And lest they excuse their negligence by the unity of the offender, as if one man's offence were not so dangerous since the rest of the body of the Church is still safe, he does not say, "Do you not know that the mass is corrupted by leaven," but "that a little leaven"; then not some part of the mass, but "the whole lump." Nor does he add a note of uncertain outcome, but asserts flatly that it "leavens."

units.la: Ergo hæc altera ratio est quā assignat, cur uelit eiectū è cósortio ecclesiastico scortatoré. Supra dixit, ut tradatur Satanę ad interitū carnis, ut spiritus saluus sit in die dūi. quę ratio cōcernebat salutē eijciédi & corripiēdi. Hic talē causam adijcit, quę pertineat ad cóseruationé puritatis ecclesiasticæ, in qua nobis ob oculos ponitur, p similitudiné fermeti, quáta sit uis & pestis mali exempli, tāta uidelicet, ut unius hominis, uelut ouiculæ, scabies, totū grēgē inficiat, sicut modicū fermeti totā cōspersioné fermētat. Et huius contagionis causæ sunt istæ.
units.tr: This, then, is the second reason he gives why he wishes the fornicator cast out of ecclesiastical fellowship. Above he said that he is to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord; that reason concerned the salvation of the one cast out and rebuked. Here he adds a cause which pertains to the preservation of ecclesiastical purity, in which, through the likeness of leaven, the force and plague of a bad example is placed before our eyes: so great, namely, that the scab of one man, like that of a single little sheep, infects the whole flock, just as a little leaven leavens the whole mass. And the causes of this contagion are these.

units.la: 1 Prima, quod ingeniū mali ita sit efficax, ut facile & cito serpat, occupet & corrūpat, quod in bonis rebus nō fit, quæ nó adeò facile obtinent. In rebus amaris nó statim superat immixta dulcedo: & lanā tinctam albedinis puritas certe omniū egerrime uincit, si tamen uincere potest. Vicissim uerò absq; ullo negocio & q dulcia sunt acrore, & q alba nigrore corrūpun tur & inficiuntur. Ita sanè peccati cōtagio, qua uiciū uicio trahitur, & malū in ecclesiæ mēbra latissimè diffunditur, p suo ingenio: deinde & eorū quæ adhuc impolluta sunt teneritudine &capacitate, omniū facillime totū ecclesię cor pus corrūpit ae perdit, utut initio modica & exilis. Ex modica scintilla grande oritur incen diū, & integræ absumūtur ædes, imò & urbes. At uicissim grandia incēdia non ita facile una restinguūtur guttula. Hoc pacto nō eadem est conspersionis, quáuis magnæ operatio in modicū unius saltem pugilli fermentum, quæ est modici fermēti in magnā quoq; conspersionē.
units.tr: (1) The first is that the nature of evil is so powerful that it creeps in, seizes and corrupts easily and quickly, which does not happen with good things, which do not so readily take hold. In bitter things, a sweetness mixed in does not at once prevail; and the purity of whiteness most hardly overcomes a cloth dyed with colour of any kind, if indeed it can overcome it at all. Conversely, without any trouble, sweet things are spoiled and infected by sourness, and white things by blackness. Thus indeed the contagion of sin, by which vice is drawn from vice, spreads very widely into the members of the Church by its own nature; then also, by the tenderness and capacity of those things which are still unpolluted, it most easily of all corrupts and destroys the whole body of the Church, however small and slight it is at first. From a small spark a great fire arises, and whole houses, indeed whole cities, are consumed; but great fires are not easily put out by a single drop. In this way the working of a little leaven in the mass is not the same as the working of the mass, although a little leaven of a single handful leavens a great mass as well.

units.la: 2 Deinde accedit ui & efficaciæ peccati magnû adiumentū ex carnis nostrę corruptione: qua fit, ut alioqui ad mala recipienda & imbibenda proni simus, & plus æquo capaces. Vnde illud poëtæ est: Etenim dociles imitandis, Turpibus ac prauis omnes sumus, &c.
units.tr: 2 Next, a great help to the power and efficacy of sin comes from the corruption of our flesh, by which we are naturally prone to receive and soak up evil and more readily open to it than we should be. Hence the poet's line: "For we are all quick to imitate, and all of us are inclined to what is base and wicked," and so on.

units.la: 3 Tertia est, uicinitas, uelut administra cōtagionis. Nostra corruptione fit, ut etiá soli cósti tuti in uicia degeneremus: qd nō timendū est, ubi malorum uicinitas accesserit. Notum est illud: Vuaque contacta liuorem ducit ab uua. Conspersio farinæ alioqui plerunque acrorem, si negligatur, accersit: quod si accesserit fermentum, quomodo non infermetaretur per illius coniunctionem? Iam etiamsi essemus natura incorrupti, tamen ex conuersatione malorum mali mores contrahuntur: perinde atque balbutire discunt, qui cum balbis, & claudicare qui cum claudis conuersantur. Conuersationis enim tanta uis est, ut per illam imprudentes etiam uicia eorum quibuscum agimus imitemur, quemadmodum de Platonis & Aristotelis familiaribus legitur, quorum alij illius gibbu, alij istius exprimebant balbutiem.
units.tr: 3 The third is proximity, which serves as the agent of contagion. Because of our corruption, even those who are established in virtue degenerate into vices. This is not to be feared lightly where the proximity of evils has come near. The saying is well known: "A grape that touches another grape takes on its bruising." Flour that is mixed in, if neglected, generally brings on sourness; but if leaven is added, how could it not be leavened through their union? Even if we were naturally uncorrupted, evil morals would still be contracted from the company of evil people, just as those who live with stammerers learn to stammer, and those who live with lame people learn to limp. Such is the power of companionship that through it even the unwitting imitate the faults of those with whom we associate, as we read of the close companions of Plato and Aristotle, some of whom copied the hunched back of the one, others the stammering of the other.

units.la: Deploranda hic est ecclesiæ miserrima corruptio. Si tantum periculi est ecclesiæ ab unius delinquentis impunito exemplo, qualis qualis ille sit, modo in ecclesia constitutus: quantum quæso est, ubi non unus aut alter, sed tot milia impune delinquunt, idque non uulgares tantum, sed potissimum ij, quorum authoritas plurimum patrocinij omnis generis erratis ac sceleribus adfert? iuxta dictum poetæ: Maximè si subeat animos magnis authoribus. Loquitur autem de domesticis uiciorum exemplis. O rem difficilem ac raram, si datur paucissimis bonis in tanta ubique obtinente delinquendi licentia, fidei & innocentiæ synceritate illibatam custodire.
units.tr: Here the most wretched corruption of the Church must be lamented. If there is so much danger to the Church from the unpunished example of a single offender, whoever he may be, provided he is set in the Church, how much greater is it, I ask, where not one or two, but thousands offend with impunity, and not ordinary people only, but especially those whose authority lends the greatest support to every kind of error and crime? This is in line with the poet's saying: "Especially if it creeps into minds through great authors." He is speaking, moreover, of examples of vice within the household. O difficult and rare thing, if, amid such licence to sin prevailing everywhere, few good people are granted to keep their faith and innocence unstained and sincere!

units.la: EXPVRGATE itaque uetus fermentum.
units.tr: PURGE OUT therefore the old leaven.

units.la: Iam ex causa præmissa parænesim infert, adhortans ad id quod supra præscripsit, ut è medio ipsorum tam flagitiosorum scortatorem, ad conseruandam ecclesiæ puritate tollant. Hæc scilicet est capitis huius propositio, quam cohonestat, & mirum in modum illustrat per ueteris ac figuralis Paschatis declaratam in Christo ueritate. De institutione ac ritu typici Paschatis, esuque azymorum, & expurgatione fermenti, uidere est historiam Exo. 12 & 13.
units.tr: Now, from the cause set out above, he draws an exhortation, urging them to do what he prescribed above: to remove from their midst such scandalous fornicators, so as to preserve the purity of the Church. This is clearly the proposition of this chapter, which he supports and remarkably illustrates by the truth in Christ declared in the old and figurative Passover. Concerning the institution and rite of the typical Passover, the eating of unleavened bread, and the purging of leaven, one may consult the history in Exodus 12 and 13.

units.la: Paschatis festum duo habebat. Memoriam uidelicet liberationis ex Aegypto, & typu futuræ redemptionis, quæ per Christum contigit uerum agnum Dei, qui sanguine suo captiuos liberauit. Ad hoc festum adiectum est mandatum de reiectione fermenti, quod duplici nomine mysticum erat. Primum significans abijciendos esse redemptis, & ad terram promissam properantibus Aegyptios errores, inuedamque pectoris erga Deum synceram pietatem: deinde adumbrans illam in nouo testamento, immolato uero Paschate apud eos futura, qui non typice, sed cum ueritate Paschatis essent festum in Christo celebraturi. Huc respiciens Paulus Corinthios adhortatur, ut ueterem illam Gentilium errorum & affectuum impuritatem adhuc reliquam ex priscæ uitæ conuersatione expurgent dicens: Expurgate itaque, &c. Neque enim dicit: Cauete à ueteri fermento, sed expurgate: nec subdit, ut permanere positis nouaconspersio: sed, Vt sitis noua conspersio, exigens ut penitus cum summa di
units.tr: The feast of the Passover had two meanings. It was a memorial of the liberation from Egypt and a type of the future redemption accomplished through Christ, the true Lamb of God, who freed the captives by his blood. To this feast was added the command to put away leaven, which was mystical in two respects. First, it signified that the Egyptian errors must be cast off by those who had been redeemed and were hastening toward the promised land, and that sincere piety toward God must be found in the breast. Second, it foreshadowed what would take place in the New Testament, when the true Passover had been sacrificed, among those who were to celebrate the feast in Christ not typically but in the reality of the Passover. Looking to this, Paul exhorts the Corinthians to purge out that old impurity of Gentile errors and affections, which still remained from their former manner of life, saying: "Purge out therefore," and so on. For he does not say, "Beware of the old leaven," but "purge out"; nor does he add that the new leavening should remain as it is, but "that you may be a new lump," requiring that they thoroughly, with the greatest diligence,

units.la: ligentia ueteris uitæ reliquias (Augustinus, quicquid in eis superbiæ de ueteri homine remansisset) expurgent, ut prorsus puros ac syncros in conuersatione nouæ uitæ sese domino exhibeant. Arbitror tamen non esse periculum, si per uetus fermentum ipsum scortatores intelligamus.
units.tr: purge out the remnants of their old life (Augustine: whatever pride of the old man had remained in them), so that they may present themselves to the Lord in the conduct of a new life as wholly pure and sincere. I think, however, there is no danger if we understand the fornicators themselves by the "old leaven."

units.la: SICVT estis infermetati.
units.tr: AS you are unleavened.

units.la: Quomodo admonet ut fermentum expurgent, ut sint noua conspersio, si iam erat infermentati, id est, sine fermento. Arguit à gratia uocationis propter quâ illos dicit infermentatos, id est, synceros esse: admonens ut sint reuera quod esse debebant, & ad quod uocati erant. Sic infra 6. dicit, Sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis, cum tamen carpat in illis iam enormia uicia. Vide Commentarios nostros in Psal. 16. ibi, Sanctis qui sunt in terra eius.
units.tr: How does he urge them to purge out the leaven, so that they may be a new lump, if they were already unleavened, that is, without leaven? He argues from the grace of their calling, on account of which he says they are unleavened, that is, sincere, urging them to be in truth what they ought to be and to what they were called. So below in chapter 6 he says: "But you were washed, but you were sanctified," although he already rebukes them for enormous vices. See our commentaries on Psalm 16, there at "to the saints who are on the earth."

units.la: Augustinus contra epistolam Parmeniani lib. 3. ca. 2. sic annotat: Quid est, ut sitis, & quid est sicut estis? Nisi quia erant ibi tales, erant ibi non tales: quos ut tales essent, exemplo talium commonebat. Tamen omnes in uno tanquam eosdem admonet, ne illi quia tales erat, desperarent de his quia nondum tales erant, tanquam eosdem admonet, cum dicit: Vt sitis sicut estis, &c. Hæc ille: quæ argumento quod tractabat, accommodauit.
units.tr: Augustine, in his books against the letter of Parmenianus, book 3, chapter 2, comments thus: "What is the meaning of 'that you may be' and 'as you are'? Unless because there were there some who were such and some who were not such, he admonished them by the example of such people, that they might be such. Yet he admonishes all together as if they were the same, so that those who were such should not despair about those who were not yet such, and admonishes them as the same when he says: 'That you may be as you are,' and so on." Thus he; which he applied to the argument he was treating.

units.la: NAM & Pascha nostrum.
units.tr: For our Passover also...

units.la: Quare expurgare iusserit uetus fermentum, ut essent noua conspersio, iterum rationem addit, sumptam à perpetuo illo legis statuto, quo azyma Paschati sunt connexa, tantoque serio mandatum, ne à quoquam usurpetur fermentum, ut extirpationem minetur lex è populo Dei animæ fermentatum quid gustanti. Ne itaque Corinthiorum quisquam diceret, quid ad nos fermenti interdictum, qui non sumus Iudæi, nec usum Paschatis habemus: per occupationem dicit, Nam & nostrum Pascha immolatus est pro nobis Christus. Quasi dicat: Et nos habemus Pascha Christū: scilicet qui pro nobis immolatus est. Iudæi habent agnum typicū: nos uero non typicum, sed uerum illum habemus agnum Dei, qui pro nobis immolatus est.
units.tr: Having ordered them to purge out the old leaven so that they might be a new batch, he adds a further reason, taken from that perpetual statute of the law by which the unleavened bread is joined to the Passover. The law forbade any use of leaven with such seriousness that it threatened extirpation from the people of God for anyone who tasted anything leavened. Lest any of the Corinthians should say, "What has the prohibition of leaven to do with us? We are not Jews and have no Passover," he anticipates the objection and says, "For our Passover also, Christ, has been sacrificed for us." It is as if he said: we too have a Passover, namely Christ, who was sacrificed for us. The Jews have a typical lamb; but we have not a typical lamb, but that true Lamb of God, who was sacrificed for us.

units.la: ITAQVE festum agamus.
units.tr: Therefore let us keep the feast.

units.la: Iterum colligit, uel magis cœptam illationem resumit & absoluit, adiecta declaratione fermenti aeterris & conspersionis nouæ. Festū celebremus, inquit. Vetus habet, Itaque epulemur, quod in Græco est, ὥστε ἑορτάζωμεν. Itaque feriemur, uel festum celebremus. Ferias habebat Pascha Iudaicum totos septe continuos dies, per quos solennibus epulis operam dabant, abiecto fermento in azymis epulantes. Iam, inquit Apostolus, cum & nobis sit Pascha, quid aliud restat, quàm ut festum hoc celebremus.
units.tr: He draws the conclusion again, or rather resumes and completes the inference he had begun, adding an explanation of the leaven of wickedness and the new batch. "Let us keep the feast," he says. The old version has "Therefore let us feast," which in the Greek is [ὥστε ἑορτάζωμεν]. The phrase can be rendered "let us keep holiday" or "let us celebrate the feast." The Jewish Passover had holy days for the whole seven continuous days, during which they devoted themselves to solemn feasting, eating unleavened bread and having put away the leaven. Now, says the Apostle, since we too have a Passover, what remains but that we keep this feast.

units.la: 1 Habet autem mystica ista festi celebratio primum ferias ab operibus mortuis, ociu scilicet domino consecratum.
units.tr: 1 This mystical celebration of the feast has, first, a rest from dead works, that is, a leisure consecrated to the Lord.

units.la: 2 Deinde habet publicum gaudium. Est enim festum agere, publicæ lætitiæ symbolum. Et huius gratia, non dixit, Nam Christus occisus est: sed, Nam pascha nostrum Christus pro nobis immolatus est, ut transitus non typici, sed ueri, & agni immolati, non pro captiuis in Aegypto, sed ijs liberandis qui sub tyrannide Satanæ detinebantur, admoneat, quarū certe rerum memoria quam pijs mentibus adferat læticiam, in liberatione populi Israëlitici, liberationisq; solenni memoria adumbratum est.
units.tr: 2 Second, it has public joy. For to keep a feast is a sign of public gladness. And for this reason he did not say, "For Christ was slain," but "For our Passover, Christ has been sacrificed for us," so that he might remind us of a passing over that was not typical but true, and of a lamb sacrificed not for captives in Egypt but for the freeing of those who were held under the tyranny of Satan. The memory of these things certainly brings joy to pious minds; it was foreshadowed in the deliverance of the people of Israel and in the solemn remembrance of that deliverance.

units.la: 3 Tertio habet festum Paschatis etiam abiectionem ueteris fermenti, & epulas azymorū. Hanc particulam declarat Apostolus, cum dicit: Non in fermento ueteri, nec in fermento malicię & uersutię: sed in panibus fermento carentibus, synceritate scilicet & ueritate. Ergo per uetus fermetum intelligit maliciam & uersutiam: & per azyma, synceritatem & veritatem. Habet & regnum cœlorum fermentum suum, sed nouum, non uetus, Euangelij scilicet primordia, per quæ totus mundus infermentatus est. de quibus est parabola Christi Matth.13. Habent & pharisæi suum fermentū, sed uetus, non nouum, hypocrisim scilicet, Lucæ 12. & peruersam doctrinam, Matth.16. Habet & Iudæorum & Gentium caro suum fermentum: sed & hoc uetus est, non nouum, malicia scilicet & uersutia. Iudæi summo studio panis fermentum expurgant, ita ut & murium foramina & cauernulas expurgent, ne quid illius remaneat: deinde & diligenter azymis farinaceis uescuntur, maliciam uero interea & uersutiam, hoc est prauum & subdolum ingenium non abijciunt, ideoq; nec ueris azymis, synceritate & ueritate uesci possunt.
units.tr: 3 Third, the feast of the Passover also has the putting away of the old leaven and the feasting on unleavened bread. The Apostle explains this point when he says: "Not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." Therefore by the old leaven he understands malice and craftiness, and by the unleavened bread, sincerity and truth. The kingdom of heaven also has its leaven, but a new one, not an old one, namely the beginnings of the Gospel, by which the whole world has been leavened; this is the subject of Christ's parable in Matthew 13. The Pharisees also have their leaven, but an old one, not a new one: hypocrisy, namely, Luke 12, and perverse teaching, Matthew 16. The flesh of both Jews and Gentiles also has its leaven, but this too is old, not new: namely malice and craftiness. The Jews with the greatest zeal purge out the leaven of bread, so that they clean out even the holes of mice and the little crevices, lest any of it remain; then they carefully eat unleavened farinaceous bread. Meanwhile, however, they do not cast off malice and craftiness, that is, a perverse and deceitful disposition; and therefore they cannot feed on true unleavened bread, sincerity and truth.

units.la: Et uide quomodo non dicat, Neque in fermento scortationis: cum tamen contra hoc uiciū isto loco pugnet: sed, Neq; in fermeto maliciæ & uersutiæ. quibus uelut generalibus uicijs omnia reliqua complectitur. Ita neq; castitatem & continentiam ponit è contrario, sed synceritatem, quam opponit malicię: & ueritatem, quæ respondeat uersutiæ.
units.tr: And notice how he does not say, "Nor with the leaven of fornication," although in this passage he fights against that vice; but he says, "Nor with the leaven of malice and craftiness," under which general vices he embraces all the rest. So too he does not set against them, on the contrary, chastity and self-control, but sincerity, which he opposes to malice, and truth, which corresponds to craftiness.

units.la: Duo hæc habet uetus noster homo, maliciā scilicet & uersutiam. Malicia est ingenij corruptio, uicium, uel uiciositas, quemadmodum & Cicero magis ,p uicio cuiusq; rei, quàm malitia sumit.
