Et nos Germani dictione bœss plerunque hoc sensu utimur, ut intelligamus defectum & uicium magis quàm maliciam. Basilius de vita solitaria, cap.3. in fine: Malicia nihil est aliud quàm defectus uirtutis. Versutia est ingenij prauitas ad nocendum prona, coniunctam habens fraudem & simulationē. Vnde & Satan πανοῦργος dicitur, non simpliciter, sed uersute ac subdole malus, quamobrem illum Apostolus in angelum sese lucis mutare dicit. Ea ista uersutia perpetuo obtinet in prauis, omnia simulans, in quauis religione constituta. Hac enim cum simus praui & peruersi, nec Dei in animo, nec mortalium ratione habentes, egregie & metum Dei, & suauem erga proximos affectum simulamus. Hoc itaq; fermēti, id est, corrupti & acidi ingenij, genus expurgari uult à Christianis Apostolus, & Pa-
units.tr: Our old man has these two things, namely malice and craftiness. Malice is a corruption of the mind, a vice, or viciousness, just as Cicero also takes "malitia" more for the vice of any thing than for malice. We Germans too commonly use the word bœss in this sense, so that we understand a defect and vice rather than malice. Basil, in On the Solitary Life, chapter 3, near the end: "Malice is nothing other than a lack of virtue." Craftiness is a perversity of mind inclined to harm, having fraud and pretence joined with it. Hence Satan is also called [πανοῦργος], not simply evil but cunningly and craftily evil; for this reason the Apostle says he transforms himself into an angel of light. This craftiness persists continually among the wicked, pretending everything, in whatever religion they are established. For since we are wicked and perverse, having neither God in our mind nor regard for mortals, we splendidly simulate both the fear of God and a sweet affection toward our neighbours. The Apostle therefore wishes this kind of leaven, that is, of a corrupt and sour disposition, to be purged out by Christians,

units.la: schatis festum celebrari in synceritate & veritate: id est, animi puritate & integritate, cum erga Deum, tum erga proximum.
units.tr: and the feast of the Passover to be celebrated in sincerity and truth: that is, in purity and integrity of mind, both towards God and towards our neighbour.

units.la: 4 Quod autem Paschatis festum septem totos & continuos dies durabat, in quibus non licebat ullo fermento uti: admonemur, ne unquam ad uetus illud fermentum relictis azymis redeamus. Est enim numerus septenarius perfectionis symbolum, donec adueniat dies octauus, qui futurae quietis est. Quemadmodum itaq; continuum habemus & perpetuum hoc Paschatis festum, ita oportet ut & reliqua Paschati cohærentia continua sint & perpetua, ne cum Iudæis semel in anno duntaxat externo ocio festum hoc celebrare nos simulemus magis quàm celebremus, cum illius celebratio non typica, sed uera, sita sit non in ocio corporis, nonnunquam flagitioso, & quibusdam cæremonijs: sed in ocio spiritus ab operibus mortuis, & gaudio, synceritateq; ac veritate animi redemptionis suæ memoriam indefinen-ter celebrantis.
units.tr: 4 Moreover, since the feast of the Passover lasted seven whole and continuous days, during which it was not permitted to use any leaven, we are admonished never to return to that old leaven, leaving behind the unleavened bread. For the number seven is a symbol of perfection, until the eighth day comes, which belongs to the future rest. Just as we therefore have this feast of the Passover continuous and perpetual, so it is fitting that the other things connected with the Passover should also be continuous and perpetual; lest we pretend, together with the Jews, to keep this feast merely once a year by outward rest, rather than actually keep it. For its celebration is not typical but true, and rests not in rest of the body, which is sometimes shameful, and in certain ceremonies, but in rest of the spirit from dead works, and in joy, sincerity and truth of mind, always commemorating our redemption.

units.la: Scripsi uobis per epistolam, ne commisceremini cum scortatoribus, & non omnino cum scortatoribus mundi huius, aut cum auaris aut cum rapacibus, aut simulacrorum cultoribus. Alioquī debetis è mundo exire. Nunc autē scripsi uobis, ne commisceremini. Si quis frater nominatus, aut scortator fuerit, aut auarus, aut simulacrorū cultor, aut conuiciator, aut ebriosus, aut rapax, cū ciusmodi ne cibus quidē sumedus est. Quid enim ad me attinet, etiam de his qui foris sunt iudicare? Nonne de his qui intus sunt iudicatis? Eos uero qui foris sunt, Deus iudicat. Etiam auferte malum ex uobis ipsis.
units.tr: "I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with fornicators; not altogether with the fornicators of this world, or with the covetous and extortioners, or with idolaters; for then you would have to go out of the world. But now I have written to you not to keep company with anyone who is named a brother, if he is a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such a one, do not even eat. For what have I to do with judging those outside? Do you not judge those who are inside? But God judges those who are outside. Remove the evil from among yourselves."

units.la: Apparet hoc loco Apostolum iam antea epistola quadam, qua caremus, Corinthios admonuisse de uitandis & excommunicandis reprobis, id quod & Ambrosius sentit: quanquā Hieronymus & Theoph. intelligunt illum de hac ipsa epistola loqui, & ad id respicere, quod dixit, Expurgate uetus fermentum. Iam quicquid fit, scriptum hoc suum declarat & exponit Apostolus quid senserit, ne quo pacto hic errent Corinthij: putantes eam admonitionē etiā ad uitandos incredulos pertinere, & forsan ad Christianos non pertinere. uidebantur enim in isto scortatore ita se gerere, ut qui putarent non esse uitandum eum scortatore qui frater esset. Imò arbitror Apostolum non solum declarare scriptum suum, sed Corinthios simul reprehendere, quod admoniti quoque, idque peculiari scripto, tam insignem scortatorem in suo gremio tolerauerint. Quasi dicat: Ista iam antea uobis scripsi, ut nulla uobis esse posset excusatio. Scripsi enim per epistolam,
units.tr: It appears from this passage that the Apostle had already admonished the Corinthians, in an earlier letter that we do not have, about avoiding and excommunicating the reprobate; this is also the view of Ambrose. Although Jerome and Theophylact understand him to be speaking of this very letter, and to be referring to what he said, "Purge out the old leaven," whatever the case, the Apostle here explains and sets out what he had meant by his writing, so that the Corinthians should not go wrong on this point. They were thinking that that admonition applied to avoiding unbelievers, and perhaps did not apply to Christians. For they seemed to behave towards that fornicator in such a way that they thought one should not avoid a fornicator who was a brother. Indeed, I think the Apostle not only explains his writing but at the same time rebukes the Corinthians, because, although they had been admonished, and that by a special letter, they had tolerated so notorious a fornicator in their bosom. It is as if he said: I have already written these things to you, so that you could have no excuse. For I wrote to you in my letter

units.la: lam, ne commisceremini cum scortatoribus, &c. Verum nos,ut uideo, admonitione meam prorsus neglexistis. Quod si eam non intellexi stis,ecce iam illam uobis expono,&c.
units.tr: now, not to keep company with fornicators, and so on. But, as I see, you have utterly neglected my admonition. But if you did not understand it, here, now, I set it out for you again.

units.la: NB commisceremini cum scortatoribus.] Verbum commiscendi, maxime in scortationis scelere usurpatum, plerunque obscoenam habet significationem. Hic uero simpliciter ̨p conuersari, & commercium cum quoquam in rebus ac negocijs huius uitae habere sumitur. Quod autem no dicit συμμίγνυσθαι, sed συναναμίγνυσθαι: putat Erasmus ad hoc factum, ut admonerentur Corinthij pristinae uitae immunditiae, qua cum quibusuis reprobis absque ullo timore Domini commercium habuerint, eo quod συναναμίγνυσθαι fit idem atq; denuo cum aliquo commisceri.
units.tr: NB: "associate with fornicators." The verb to associate, used especially of the sin of fornication, usually carries an obscene sense. Here, however, it is taken simply to mean to live among others, and to have dealings with anyone in the affairs and business of this life. Paul does not write συμμίγνυσθαι [to mix with] but συναναμίγνυσθαι [to mix up together with]. Erasmus thinks this was done so that the Corinthians would be reminded of the uncleanness of their former life, when they had dealings with any reprobate whatever and without any fear of the Lord, since συναναμίγνυσθαι means to mix oneself again with someone.

units.la: AC non omnino cum scortatoribus mundi huius.] Particula haec non eodem sensu exponitur. 1 Quidá illud ὁ πνευτης, non omnino ad uerbum commiscendi referunt. Quasi dicat Apostolus: Scripsi uobis ne commiscere mini scortatoribus,idq; ita,ut omnino scortatoribus huius mundi, id est, infidelibus non commisceremini: alioqui, fi id facturi estis, optarim uos prorsus mundum hunc relinquere,uidelicet regionem illam Graeciae tot nomi nibus contaminatam. Nunc autem scripsi uobis,ne commiscereminii, uel ijs scortatoribus qui sunt in grege & numero fratrum,ut uel cum illis saltem nihil habeatis commercij,quandoquidem exigere non audeo,ut mundum hunc B relinquatis. Et huc uidetur respexisse Erafmus in uersione sua, quanquam in Paraphrasi aliu sensum fit fequutus.
units.tr: "And not altogether with the fornicators of this world." This clause is not explained in the same sense by everyone. Some do not refer the words "not altogether" to the verb to associate. Paul would then be saying: I wrote to you not to associate with fornicators, and I meant it in such a way that you should not associate with the fornicators of this world, that is, with unbelievers, at all. Otherwise, if you were going to do that, I would wish you to leave this world altogether, that is, that region of Greece so polluted by so many names. But now I have written to you not to associate with those fornicators who are in the flock and number of the brethren, so that you may at least have no dealings with them, since I do not dare to require you to leave this world. Erasmus in his translation seems to have had this sense in view, although in his Paraphrase he follows a different sense.

units.la: 2 Quidam uero ita exponunt, ut illud, non omnino,non ad uerbum commiscendi, sed ad sententiam Apostoli fit referendum. Quasi dicat: Scripsi uobis ne comifceremini cum scortatoribus,& id ita scripsi, ut omnino non hoc exegerim,ut nihil commercij habeatis cum scortatoribus auaris ac rapacibus huius mundi, quod scio fieri non posse. Nam alioqui debere tis mundum hunc plane relinquere. Nunc autem scripsi uobis ne comifceremini cum scortatoribus.quod intelligo de illis, qui inter fratres,in uestro gremio tales sunt. Et ad hac sententiam,quae comunior & fimplicior est,adiecta ratio pertinet. Quid enim mea refert etiam de his qui foris sunt iudicare?
units.tr: Others explain it in a different way: the words "not altogether" are to be referred not to the verb to associate but to the Apostle's meaning. The sense would be: I wrote to you not to associate with fornicators, and I wrote it in such a way that I did not altogether require you to have no dealings at all with the covetous and rapacious fornicators of this world, which I know cannot be done. Otherwise you would have to leave this world entirely. But now I have written to you not to associate with fornicators, which I understand of those who are such within the brotherhood, in your own bosom. To this sense, which is the more common and simpler one, the reason added belongs: "For what is it to me to judge even those who are outside?"

units.la: SI quis frater nominatus.] Illud, ἐννόμισι Graeci intelligunt eo sensu, quo nos Ger mani eos qui quod nomine dicuntur, reipfa non sunt, genant uocamus: quemadmodum sacerdotes,pontifices & monachos,quos uulgo spiritales uocát, genanten geiftlichen appellam. Respexerunt opinor Graeci ad id quod ij qui ueri fratres sunt in Christo,tales esse non possunt,quales hic ab Apostolo describuntur.
units.tr: "If anyone who is named a brother." The Greeks understand the word in the sense in which we Germans call those who are only so named, and are not really so, "so-called." Thus we call priests, bishops and monks, whom the common people call spiritual, "so-called spiritual." I think the Greeks had in mind that those who are true brothers in Christ cannot be such as the Apostle here describes.

units.la: Augustinus uero contra epistolam Parmeniani lib.3.cap.2.dictionem hanc sequentibus coniungit,ut intelligamus Apoftolu cum fratrem ita uelle uitari, ut nihil cum ipso comer-
units.tr: Augustine, however, in his book against the letter of Parmenian, book 3, chapter 2, joins this word to what follows, so that we understand the Apostle to want a brother so avoided that nothing is had in common with him,

units.la: cij habeatur,qui non solum fit scortator, auarus,rapax,&c.sed ita fit, ut iam infamis fit factus,nominatus, id est, diffamatus scortator, auarus & rapax. Na alioqui fieri potest, ut nescias fratrem, cum quo tibi necessario aliquid intercidit negocij,esse talem: deinde etiam fi scias,nő tamen statim ita uitandus est, ut redas eum infamem, cum occulto adhuc morbo laboret,quem alio queas pharmaco, quàm hoc praefenti,curare.quod illis duntaxat uide tur competere, qui publico offendiculo mali sunt,nec alia ratione fanari sustinet. Certe haec Augustini sententia multum habet rationis, li cet non statim necesse fit participium hoc,nominatus, ad sequentia coniungere. Videtur enim Apostolus loqui de his Christianis, q ̨p. sessioni Christianae nomen dederunt, & ab omnibus fratribus in ecclesia pro Christianis agnoscuntur. Vide apud Auguft.confeff.lib.8. cap.2.de Victorino quodam Romanorum rhetore. Erant enim tum quidam occulti discipuli ac fratres, qui metus gratia nomen Christo non aperte ac publice dabant,sicut & tempore Christi in Nicodemo & alijs ufuuenit:ut appareat Apostolum sententia hanc nō ita prae-scribere,ut occultos & imbecilles Christi discipulos hoc pacto declinari uelit,fi quid com miserint eorum peccatorum quae hic recefet, sed eos tantū qui ex professo sint Christiani.
units.tr: who is not only a fornicator, covetous, rapacious, and so on, but is one who has already been made infamous, that is, is publicly defamed as a fornicator, covetous and rapacious. For otherwise it can happen that you do not know that a brother with whom you must necessarily have some business is such a man; and even if you do know it, he is not to be shunned at once so that you make him infamous, since he may still be suffering from a hidden disease which you could cure with some other remedy than this present one. This, it seems, applies only to those who are a public stumbling block of evil and cannot be healed by any other means. Certainly this opinion of Augustine has much reason in it, although it is not necessarily the case that this participle, "named," must be joined to what follows. For the Apostle seems to be speaking of those Christians who have given their name to the Christian assembly and are acknowledged by all the brethren in the Church as Christians. See in Augustine's Confessions, book 8, chapter 2, about a certain Victorinus, a Roman rhetorician. For there were then some secret disciples and brethren who, for fear, did not openly and publicly give their name to Christ, as also happened in the time of Christ with Nicodemus and others. So it appears that the Apostle does not lay down this rule so as to want secret and weak disciples of Christ to be avoided in this way, if they have committed any of those sins which are mentioned here, but only those who are Christians by profession.

units.la: AVT simulacrorum cultor.] Putat Erafmus totum hunc sermonem perturbationem esse, & Delium aliquem natatorem desiderare, maxime huius particulae gratia: additq; rationem,eo quòd uerisimile fit tum inter Christianos nullum fuisse simulacrorum usum ac cultum. At meo iudicio nihil hic est obscuri. Quis enim dubitat Christianos fuisse, qui uel metus uel superstitionis gratia, philosophicis rationibus inducti, Gentium simulacra licet non uulgari sensu coluerint,inque illis uenera ti sint,non Iouem,aut Apollinem, aut Mercurium,sed uirtutes diuinas,quas philosophi deorum talium nomine & cultu uenerandas esse tradiderunt.de quorum sententia in Augustino alicubi,praesertim in libris de Ciuitate Dei legere est. Videmus hodie nonnullos ad quacunque religionem ita paratos esse, ut omnia praesumant commoda & tolerabili expositione mitigare, ufurpariaque praeter offensam Dei posse non solum fibijpfis,sed & alijs persuadere. Crediderim hoc hominum genus etiam apostolorum tempore, apud eos praefer tim fuisse,qui philosophiae studio celebres habiti sunt.
units.tr: "Or an idolater." Erasmus thinks the whole sentence is corrupt and calls for some Delian diver, especially because of this particle; and he adds the reason that it is likely that among Christians at that time there was no use or worship of images. In my judgement, however, there is nothing obscure here. For who doubts that there were Christians who, out of fear or superstition, led by philosophical reasons, worshipped the images of the Gentiles, though not in the common sense, and venerated in them not Jupiter, Apollo or Mercury, but divine powers, which the philosophers taught were to be venerated under the name and worship of such gods? One can read about their opinion in Augustine in various places, especially in the books on the City of God. We see today some men so ready for any religion that they think they can soften everything by a convenient and tolerable explanation, and can persuade not only themselves but others that they may practise such things without offence to God. I would believe that this kind of men existed also in the time of the Apostles, especially among those who were held in repute for devotion to philosophy.

units.la: CVM eiusmodi ne cibum quidem cap.] Non simpliciter dicit, Cum eiusmodi cibū nó esse fumendum,sed ne cibum quidem: innues omnem uitae consuetudinem illis denegandà esse,ita ut & id quod minus uidetur habere periculi,illis amputetur, nedum ea necessitudo & communio, quae est in religione Christi. Inuenias quid denegatum religionis ac mysteriorum Dei commercium facile ferant, dummodo modò reliquo uitę huius cõmercio nõ priuen tur.Igitur Apostolo delinquentiũ salutem spe stanti satis nõ est ecclesiasticam talibus ampu tasse consuetudinĕ, nisi & reliquam quę huius uitæ est,tollat,ut pudesiant & emendentur.
units.tr: "Not even to eat with such a one." He does not simply say that one should not take food with such people, but "not even to eat." He hints that all the customary intercourse of life must be denied to them, so that even what seems to carry less danger is cut off from them, let alone that fellowship and communion which exists in the religion of Christ. You will find that people readily tolerate the denial of fellowship in religion and in the mysteries of God, provided they are not deprived of the rest of the commerce of this life. Therefore, for the Apostle, who looks to the salvation of offenders, it is not enough to cut them off from ecclesiastical fellowship, unless he also takes away the rest of the intercourse of this life, so that they may be ashamed and amend themselves.

units.la: QVID enim ad me?) Hæc est altera ratio cur non mandauerit incredulorum declinare commercium, sed & eorũ qui cum fratres sint, uel scortantur, uel rapiunt, uel simulacra co-lunt. Videlicet quod increduli ad se non pertineat,iudicioq; suo subiecti non sint,eo quod foris sunt,& Dei tantum iudicio obnoxij. Neque enim locum habet in illis iudicium ecclesiæ,qui in ecclesia non sunt. Quemadmodum urbis iudicia in eos tantum ualent qui ciues & incolæ sunt,in exteros non item,& cuiusuis patrisfamiliâs censura in domesticis tantum locum habet,ita & iudicium ecclesiæ in ecclesiæ membris tantum ualet. Et præterea ipsa ratio ecclesiastici iudicij talis est, ut non com-petat exteris. Est enim instar medicinæ quam certè increduli non agnoscunt, qui non sepa-ratione,sed magis commercio & consuetudi-ne Christianorum, dummodo licita & casta, curari possunt.Quòd si per illam non curátur, diuino iudicio sunt relinquendi.
units.tr: "For what is it to me?" This is the second reason why he did not command that the commerce of unbelievers be avoided, but also that of those who, though brothers, are fornicators, robbers or worshippers of images. Namely, because unbelievers do not belong to him and are not subject to his judgement, since they are outside and liable only to the judgement of God. For the judgement of the Church has no place over those who are not in the Church. Just as the judgements of a city bind only those who are citizens and residents, and not foreigners, and as the censure of any head of a household has force only over his household, so the judgement of the Church has force only over the members of the Church. Moreover, the very nature of ecclesiastical judgement is such that it does not apply to outsiders. For it is like a medicine, which unbelievers certainly do not acknowledge; they are cured not by separation but rather by the company and fellowship of Christians, provided that it is lawful and chaste. But if they are not cured by that, they are to be left to the divine judgement.

units.la: ETIAM auferte malum ex uobis ipsis.) Ista est conclusio, & emphasim habet, quod dicit, ex uobis ipsis. Quasi dicat, Non iubeo ut ma-lum, id est, si quis malus est, auferatis ex illis qui foris sunt,quod fieri non potest, & ad uos non pertinet, sed solius Dei est. Ex uobisipsis auferte eum qui malus est. Nam ille demum uestro iudicio obnoxius est. Non est autem τὸν χαχὸν, sed τὸν πονηρὸν, ne putet quisquam quemcunq; malum auferendum esse ex eccle-sia, cum omnes simus mali, nemo bonus nisi unus Deus. πονηρὸς enim non simpliciter ma-lus est,sed uersutus ac peruerse malus. Videtur autem Apostolus hanc conclusionem sum psisse ex lege, ubi crebra est,uerùm non eo sen-su quo hic ab Apostolo ponitur. Lex enim ita loquitur, ubi iubet per mortis pœna tolli ma-lum è medio populi Dei,qua ecclesia non uti-tur,quæ excommunicatione contenta est. uide Aug.in quæst. Deuter.cap.39.
units.tr: "Put away the evil from among yourselves." This is the conclusion, and it has emphasis in the words "from among yourselves." It is as if he said: I do not command that the evil, that is, whoever is evil, be removed from those who are outside, which cannot be done and does not concern you but belongs to God alone. Remove from yourselves the one who is evil. For he alone is subject to your judgement. The word is not [τὸν κακὸν] the bad one, but [τὸν πονηρὸν] the wicked one, lest anyone think that whatever evil person must be removed from the Church, since we are all evil and no one is good but God alone. For πονηρός does not simply mean bad, but cunning and perversely wicked. The Apostle seems to have taken this conclusion from the Law, where it occurs often, but not in the sense in which the Apostle uses it here. For the Law speaks thus when it orders that the evil be removed from the midst of the people of God by the penalty of death, a practice the Church does not use, being content with excommunication. See Augustine, Questions on Deuteronomy, chapter 39.

units.la: DE EXCOMMV-nicatione.
units.tr: Concerning Excommunication.

units.la: Exigit capitis huius tractatus, ut quædam ad excommunicationem ecclesiasticam per-tinentia notentur.
units.tr: The subject of this chapter requires that certain matters pertaining to ecclesiastical excommunication be noted.

units.la: 1 Principio,quid illa fit,in eo uidere est,quod & cibi commercium ei qui excommunicádus est à fidelibus negari uult, multò magis com-munionem mysteriorum Dei. Est ergo talis se paratio, qua prorsus omnis uitæ consuetudo & communio negatur flagitioso. Scio quibus-dam excommunicationem esse, quæ non hu-manæ uitæ, sed religionis dùtaxat societatem amputet. Ego uero illam malo iuxta hanc A-postoli sententiam definire, maximè propter causam supra assignatam, quod uidelicet ple-risq; parû est religione separari à Christianis, modò reliqua uitæ societas non denegetur, in quibus certè inefficax est religionis separatio.
units.tr: 1. First, what it is may be seen from this: that he who is to be excommunicated is denied not only the fellowship of food, but much more the communion of the mysteries of God. It is therefore such a separation that all custom and communion of life is wholly denied to the wicked person. I know that some hold excommunication to cut off only the fellowship of religion, not of human life. But I prefer to define it according to this sentence of the Apostle, chiefly on account of the reason assigned above, namely that for most people it matters little to be separated from Christians in religion, provided the rest of life's fellowship is not denied them; in such cases, certainly, separation from religion is ineffective.

units.la: 2 Deinde uidemus hoc capite quorũ inter-fit potestas excommunicandi. Nempe non e-piscopi tantùm, neq; populi solius, sed simul & episcopi & populi, hoc est, totius ecclesiæ. Cógregatis uobis, inquit, & meo spiritu. Qui potestatem hanc transferunt in solos ecclesiæ præsides,non solùm iniuriam ecclesię faciunt, sed & inanem reddunt hanc medicinam.
units.tr: 2. Next, in this chapter we see whose power it is to excommunicate. Namely, not the bishops alone, nor the people alone, but both bishops and people together, that is, the whole Church. "When you are gathered together," he says, "and my spirit [is present]." Those who transfer this power to the presidents of the Church alone not only do wrong to the Church, but also render this remedy empty.

units.la: 3 Tertiò, admonemur & hic super qualibus delictis ferenda sit excommunicationis sen-tentia. Non quæuis hac uirga sunt castiganda in ecclesia,sed quepropter enormitatem suam regno Dei excludunt, de quibus etiam infrà cap.sequéti uidebimus. Reliqua sunt uel man-suetudine quadam corrigenda, uel patienter toleranda. At hodie quæ ferenda non sunt se-runtur, & quæ ferenda excommunicatione feriuntur.
units.tr: 3. Thirdly, we are admonished here also concerning what sorts of offences the sentence of excommunication should be pronounced. Not every fault is to be punished in the Church with this rod, but those which, on account of their enormity, shut people out of the kingdom of God; of these we shall also see more in the following chapter. The rest are either to be corrected with a certain gentleness, or patiently tolerated. But today those things which should be tolerated are pursued, and those which should be punished by excommunication are tolerated.

units.la: 4 Quartò,etiam de fide & usu excommuni-cationis hoc cap. perdocemur, qui triplex est. 1 Primus, ut infamiæ nota auferatur ab eccle-sia & nominis Christiani professione. Et hoc statim initio capitis innuitur,cum dicit: Om-nino auditur inter uos scortatio,&c. Ergo sub excommunicationis uirgam cadunt, quæ bo-num ecclesiæ odorem infamiæ fœtore abomi-nabilem reddunt exteris.
units.tr: 4. Fourthly, this chapter also teaches us thoroughly about the purpose and practice of excommunication, which is threefold. 1. The first is that the mark of infamy be removed from the Church and from the profession of the Christian name. This is hinted at at the very beginning of the chapter, where he says: "It is actually reported that there is fornication among you," etc. Therefore those who make the good odour of the Church a stench of infamy, abominable to outsiders, fall under the rod of excommunication.

units.la: 2 Alter est,ut qui perditè peccant, emenden-tur.Ut spiritus inquit saluus sit in die domini. Igitur excommunicandi sunt, qui perniciosè delinquunt, salutemq; suam prorsus pessun-dant,ut ad seipsos redeant & resipiscant.
units.tr: 2. The second is that those who sin destructively be amended, "so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord." Therefore those are to be excommunicated who offend to ruin and utterly wreck their own salvation, so that they may come back to themselves and repent.

units.la: 3 Tertius est,ut ecclesiæ puritas ab infectio-ne conseruetur, ne modicum fermenti totam conspersionem fermentet.
units.tr: 3. The third is that the purity of the Church be preserved from infection, lest "a little leaven leaven the whole lump."

units.la: Hi sunt excommunicationis fines ad quos excommunicando prospiciendum est. Quod si neuter horum apprehendi potest,iam inuti-lis est excommunicatio, imò magis pernicio-sa, adeoq; non usurpanda.
units.tr: These are the ends of excommunication, to which one must look when excommunicating. But if neither of these can be attained, then excommunication is already useless, indeed rather harmful, and so is not to be employed.

units.la: CAVTIO.
units.tr: CAUTION.

units.la: Ecclesiæ status raró talis est, ut isti excom-municationi sit locus. Vbi maior pars ita de-linquit, ut partem in regno Dei non habeat, fieri non potest,ut minor pars maiore excom-municare queat, nedum hos excommunica-tiones fines assequi. Nam aliòqui res abiret in schismata, & boni frumenti extirpationem, non in zizaniorum emendationem. Crimina nanq; quæ in uulgari sunt consuetudine & à multitudine committuntur, parua putantur. Quicquid enim sceleris & iniquitatis, ut Aug. annotauit, multitudine inebriat, amittit exa-minis ueritatem. Hic status est,corde & mori-bus separari à malis, & cum iustis ,de quibus est Ezech.9.lugere iniquitates populi Dei, ut lugentes ac gemètes per signum illud Ezech. reuelatum malorum uastatione euadere me-reamur.
units.tr: The state of the Church is seldom such that this kind of excommunication has any place. Where the greater part sins so far that it has no share in the kingdom of God, the lesser part cannot excommunicate the greater, much less attain the ends of excommunication. Otherwise the matter would end in schisms and the uprooting of the good wheat, not in the correction of the tares. For crimes that are common in custom and committed by the multitude are thought to be minor. Whatever wickedness and iniquity, as Augustine observed, intoxicates by its multitude, loses the clarity of judgment. This condition means being separated from the wicked in heart and morals and, with the just, of whom Ezekiel 9 speaks, lamenting the iniquities of the people of God, so that by lamenting and groaning, as the sign revealed in Ezekiel shows, we may deserve to escape the destruction of the wicked.

units.la: g reamur. Hic quippe cōsilia separationis & inia sunt, quia malos non corrigunt, & alioqui & nobis è mundo esset egrediendum, & simul perniciosa, quia plus perturbant infirmos bonos q; corrigant animosos malos, sed hic seuera disciplinę Dei misericordia necessaria est. Vbi uero pauci sunt qui delinquunt, & multitudo ab illis criminibus, quæ emēdanda sunt, libera est, ibi certè potest excōmunicationis usus esse iustus. Hic enim nullum est periculū schismatis, ubi qui castigatur, non habet multitudinis turbam in crimine sociam, uel talis nō est, qui possit authoritate sua schisma instituere. Et hic qui deliquit timore potest percuti & pudore sanari, cum ab uniuersa ecclesia anathematizatur, & salua pace fidelium non interfectorię punitur sed medicinaliter amputatur, ut hic locum habeat illud Apostoli, in posteriore ad Corint. Sufficit ei correptio quæ fit à multis: sed hac de re uide Aug.lib.3.cap.2.contra epistolā Parmen. unde ista desumpta sunt.
units.tr: Here, indeed, the counsels of separation are both unjust, because they do not correct the wicked, and otherwise we would have to leave the world, and they are at the same time pernicious, because they disturb the weak good more than they correct the bold wicked. Here the severe mercy of God's discipline is necessary. Where, however, few are sinning and the multitude is free from those crimes that must be amended, there the use of excommunication can indeed be just. For there is no danger of schism here, where the one who is rebuked does not have a crowd of the multitude as partners in the crime, or is not someone who could set up a schism by his own authority. And here the one who has sinned can be struck by fear and healed by shame, when he is cut off by the whole Church; and, with the peace of the faithful preserved, he is punished not by slaughter but cut off as a remedy. So here the saying of the Apostle in the second letter to the Corinthians applies: "Sufficient for such a man is this rebuke, which is given by many." But on this matter see Augustine, book 3, chapter 2, against the letter of Parmenian, from which these things are taken.

units.la: Et hæc tolerandorum malorum, cauendiq; schismatis ecclesiastici ratio, ibi ualet, ubi mali mores tantum non etiam falsi Dei cultus sunt in ecclesia ferendi. Alioqui magis Tobię exemplum sequēdum est ecclesiam Israelis falsi cultus perucrsæq; doctrinæ gratia relinquentis, quàm quod hic Augustino præscribitur.
units.tr: This reason for tolerating evil men and guarding against ecclesiastical schism holds only where wicked morals, though not false worship of God, must be borne in the Church. Otherwise the example of Tobit ought to be followed, rather than what is prescribed here by Augustine, since the Church of Israel left off because of false worship and perverse doctrine.

units.la: CAPVT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: AVdet aliquis uestrū, negocium habens aduersus alterum, iudicari sub iniustis, & non sub sanctis? An nescitis quod sanctì mundum iudicabunt? Etsi in uobis iudicatur mūdus, indigni estis minimis iudiciis? An nescitis quod angelos iudicabimus, nedum ea quæ ad uictū pertinent? Proinde iudicia siquidem habueritis de ijs quæ ad uictū pertinent, qui contempti sunt in ecclesia, eos constituite. Ad erubescentiam uestram dico. Adeo non est inter uos sapiens, ne unus quidem, qui possit diiudicare inter fratrē suum ac fratrem? Sed frater cum fratre litigat, idq; sub infidelibus? Itaq; iam quidē omnino delictū in uobis est, quod iudicia habetis inter uos inuicem. Cur non potius iniuriam patimini? Cur nō potius damnum accipitis? Imò potius iniuriam facitis & damno afficitis, idq; fratres. An nescitis quod iniusti regnū Dei nō possidebūt?
units.tr: Does any of you, having a dispute with another, dare to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints? Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? Do you not know that we shall judge angels, to say nothing of matters pertaining to this life? If then you have judgments concerning things pertaining to this life, appoint as judges those who are despised in the Church. I say this to your shame. Is it so that there is no wise man among you, not even one, who can decide between his brother and a brother? But brother goes to law with brother, and that before unbelievers! Indeed, it is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits against one another. Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather accept loss? But you yourselves do wrong and cause loss, and that to brothers. Do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God?

units.la: Delinquebant fideles Corinthij plurimum in eo quod inter se alter alteri lites iudiciarias mouebant, idq; sub iudicibus ethnicis, ad probrum Christiani nominis. Malum hoc obiter mediocri digressione carpit & emendat.
units.tr: The faithful Corinthians were greatly at fault in this, that they brought legal suits against one another, and that before heathen judges, to the disgrace of the Christian name. Paul touches on this evil in passing, in a short digression, and corrects it.

units.la: Deinde coeptam scortationis reprehensionē resumit, & ad finē usq; capitis prosequitur.
units.tr: Then he resumes the rebuke of fornication that he had begun, and carries it on to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Triplici nomine Corinthios Apostolus obiurgat in hac causa. Erat enim peccatum illorum, quod hic admittebant, non simplex, sed trimembre.
units.tr: The Apostle rebukes the Corinthians in this matter on three counts. For their sin, which they committed here, was not simple but threefold.

units.la: 1 Primùm admodum erat absurdum, quod Christianus Christianum ad ethnicorum tribunalia uocabat. Hoc primo loco uelut malæ radicis malum fructum amputat.
units.tr: (1) First, it was utterly absurd that a Christian should summon a Christian before the courts of the heathen. He cuts off this evil first, as if it were the bad fruit of a bad root.

units.la: 2 Deinde delictum erat, quod qui iniuria afficiebantur, illam non ferebant sicuti conuenie bat Christianis, sed lite iudiciaria ius suum persequebantur. Hoc carpit secundo loco.
units.tr: (2) Second, the fault was that those who were wronged did not bear the wrong as became Christians, but pursued their right by legal action. He censures this in the second place.

units.la: 3 Tertiò, quoniam qui ista faciebant cogi uebantur per eos à quibus lædebantur, adoriatur & illos, ostendens iniustis non esse locum in regno Dei.
units.tr: (3) Third, since those who did these things were compelled by those who harmed them, he attacks those also, showing that there is no place for the unrighteous in the kingdom of God.

units.la: Est autem ista obiurgatio admodum uehemens, crebrisq; interrogationibus referta, quibus non sine animi indignatione ita perstringit & urget delinquentes, ut planè sint inexcusabiles. Sed uideamus singula membra.
units.tr: This rebuke is very vehement, and full of rapid questions, by which he so strikes at and presses the offenders, not without indignation of mind, that they are plainly without excuse. But let us look at the individual parts.

units.la: AVDET aliquis uestrūm.) τολμᾷ τις ὑμῶν. Erasmus reddidit: Sustinet aliquis uestrū. Et uersionis suæ causam reddit in Annotationibus, ne temerè ita reddidisse uideatur. Intelligit Apostolum non temeritatem hac in re sine audaciam Corinthiorum tanquam rem periculosam audentium, sed impudentiam magis arguere, admirantem quod quisquam animū inducere possit, ut ob rem pecuniariam sub ethnicis iudicibus contendat, cum id esse debeat homini Christiano uehementer pudendum. Certè quamuis periculosum etiam fuerit Christianis, iudicio experiri cùm sub iniustis, tum sub impijs iudicibus Christiani nomi nis oforibus, quoniam tamen apparet Apostolum non tam quid periculi hac in re sit considerasse, quàm quantum turpitudinis ac dedecoris illa adferat professioni Christianę, uidetur ista Erasmi uersio nō esse præter rationem, ut legamus, Sustinet ne aliquis uestrum, &c. id est, Potestne quisquam hoc impudentiæ sibi permittere, tanquam nullam haberet nomis Christiani rationem, ut iudicio contendat cum fratre sub iudice ethnico & iniusto, & non magis sub sancto?
units.tr: DOES ANY OF YOU DARE. "τολμᾷ τις ὑμῶν" [τολμᾷ τις ὑμῶν]. Erasmus rendered it: "Does any of you endure?" and he gives the reason for his rendering in his Annotations, lest he seem to have rendered it rashly. He understands the Apostle to be censuring in this matter not rashness nor boldness of the Corinthians, as men who venture on a dangerous thing, but rather their impudence, marvelling that anyone could bring himself to contend for money before heathen judges, when this ought to be deeply shameful for a Christian man. Certainly, although it would also be dangerous for Christians to try a case before unrighteous judges, and before impious judges who were enemies of the Christian name, yet since it appears that the Apostle considered not so much what danger there was in this matter as how much baseness and dishonour it brought to the Christian profession, Erasmus's rendering does not seem unreasonable: let us read, "Does any of you endure to ...", that is, "Can anyone permit himself this impudence, as if he had no regard for the Christian name, to contend in a lawsuit with a brother before a heathen and unrighteous judge, and not rather before a holy one?"

units.la: Innuit autem Apostolus hac admiratione, ita comparatum esse debere animum Christiani hominis erga decorum Christianæ professionis, ut quæ illam dedeceant, uelut indigna, dura & intoleranda aspernetur, fugiat & abhorreat, nec ullo pacto quicquam illorum admittere sustineat. Non enim simpliciter dicit absq; admirationis & stuporis nota, sustinetis iudicio contendere sub iniustis, sed cum admiratione interrogādo, sustinēt ne quisquā uestrūm, &c. Quasi dicat, Satis admirari nequeo, posse uel aliquem ex uobis sub iniusto iudice litem intēdere fratri & non sub sancto. Vbi & illud τὶς ὑμῶν auxesim stuporis habet. Plus enim est, quàm si diceret, sustinetisne iudicio dicio contendere sub iniustis? Iudicat quippe rem hanc adeo esse absurdam,ut mirum fit aliquem esse posse inter Christianos, qui eam sibi admittere sustineat, nedum multos.
units.tr: The Apostle hints by this wonder that the mind of a Christian man ought to be so disposed towards the decorum of the Christian profession that he spurns, flees from and abhors whatever disgraces it, as unworthy, harsh and intolerable, and does not in any way endure to admit any of these things. For he does not simply say, without the mark of wonder or astonishment, "You endure to contend in a suit before unrighteous judges," but with wonder, asking, "Does any of you endure ...?" As if he were saying, "I cannot sufficiently marvel that even one of you could bring a suit against a brother before an unrighteous judge and not before a holy one." Here the phrase "τίς ὑμῶν" [τίς ὑμῶν] also has an amplification of astonishment. For it is more than if he had said, "Do you endure to contend in a suit before unrighteous judges?" He judges the matter to be so absurd that it is a wonder that anyone among Christians could endure to permit it to himself, let alone many.

units.la: NEGOCIVM habens aduersus alterum.) Græcè est πρὸς ἕτερον, quod Erafmus reddidit,cum aliquo. Verùm negocium habere cum aliquo,amphibolicum est.Potest enim & amicum comercium significare, & cótrouerfiam, ideo malo cum ueteri interprete legere,aduer sus alterum.Maxime cum & Græci hac præpo sitione aliquādo ad hunc modum utantur, ut μάχομαι πρός τινα pugno aduersum aliquem.
units.tr: HAVING A DISPUTE WITH ANOTHER. In Greek it is πρὸς ἕτερον [πρὸς ἕτερον], which Erasmus rendered "with someone." But "to have a dispute with someone" is ambiguous. For it can signify either friendly dealing or controversy. Therefore I prefer to read with the older translator, "against the other," especially since the Greeks also sometimes use this preposition in this way, as in μάχομαι πρός τινα [μάχομαι πρός τινα], "I fight against someone."

units.la: Est autē negocii uel causam habere aduersus aliquem, nihil aliud quàm læsum habere quod de aliquo querare, cuius gratia illum in ius uocare possis. Sic & Matth. 5. fi obtuleris munus tuum ad ara,& illic recordatus fueris, quod frater tuus habet aliquid aduersus te: Hocest,quòd iniuria aliqua illi affecisti,cuius gratia tibi fuccefet,&c.Cogita hic,quales christiani fimus,inter quos offensæ locū inuenīūt.
units.tr: To have a cause or a dispute against someone is nothing other than to have a grievance to complain of against someone, on account of which you can summon him to court. So also in Matt. 5: "If you bring your gift to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you": that is, that you have done him some wrong, on account of which he has a claim against you, and so on. Consider here what kind of Christians we are, among whom occasions of offence are found.

units.la: IVDICARI sub iniustis.) uerbum κείνομαι aliter atque aliter accipitur,licet simpliciter significat iudicari.Hic certè nō pro iudicari politum est,sed pro iudicio experiri, contendere & litigare. (sic κείνεσθαι ἀρτι est Marte decernere)ut pertineat nec ad reum nec ad iudicē,sed ad actorem, qui aliquem in ius uocat & accusat. Non enim de eo loquitur Apostolus, qui causam dicere cogitur,& de crimine aliquo ac cusatur qui & ipse κείνεται dicitur, sed de eo qui fratre apud iudicē accusat,& reum agere conatur.Infrà idem uerbum κείνεται significatione passiua pro condemnatur positum est.
units.tr: TO BE JUDGED BEFORE THE UNRIGHTEOUS. The verb κρίνομαι [κρίνομαι] is taken in different ways, although it simply means "to be judged." Here it is certainly not used in the sense of being judged, but in the sense of contending in a trial, disputing and litigating (so κρίνεσθαι ἄρτι [κρίνεσθαι ἄρτι] is "to decide by arms," that is, by war). Thus it pertains neither to the defendant nor to the judge, but to the plaintiff, who summons someone to court and accuses him. For the Apostle is not speaking of the one who is compelled to plead his case and is accused of some crime, who also is said κρίνεται [κρίνεται], but of the one who accuses his brother before a judge and tries to make him a defendant. Later the same verb κρίνεται [κρίνεται] is used in the passive sense of "is condemned."

units.la: SVB iniustis.) Infideles intelligit ethnicos, nominis & fidei Christi expertes. Infrà eos uocat infideles, ne putemus illū loqui de malis Christianis. Vocat autem eos iniustos fatis in loco.Iudicis enim est iustè decernere, reiectis sinistris affectibusuel odij uel fauoris. Ethnici uero non solum impietatis gratia coram Deo iniusti erant,sed & insigni maleuolentia contra nomē Christi excæcat,non poterant in caufaChriftianorum,quos immeritò exosos habebant, ex æquo quod iustum effet iudicare. Vnde certè periculosum quoq; erat Christianis illorum foro uti.
units.tr: BEFORE THE UNRIGHTEOUS. He means the heathen, unbelievers, who had no part in the name and faith of Christ. Later he calls them unbelievers, lest we think he is speaking of bad Christians. He does call them unrighteous in a suitable place. For it is the office of a judge to decide justly, setting aside perverse feelings of either hatred or favour. But the heathen were not only unrighteous before God on account of their impiety, but were also blinded by remarkable ill will against the name of Christ, and could not judge the cause of the Christians, whom they held in deserved hatred, on equal terms with what was just. Hence it was certainly dangerous for Christians also to make use of their tribunal.

units.la: ET non sub sanctis.) Admiratur Apostolus non solùm quomodo sustineat litigare sub iniustis,sed & quāfnobrem fanctorū iudicium fugiant uel contemnāt. Erat enim duplex ista uesania. Et hanc posteriorem parte ita urget, ut appareat illa plus offensum esse quàm prior e.Absurdum quidem est litigare sub iniustis, uerùm cum id fieri possit sub sanctis,nolle fan ctorum uti iudicio,id demum est, quod plurimum isti absurditati adfert augmenti,& admodum dedecori est existimationi sanctorum. Quemadmodum stultum est per fe,fodere cisternas ueteres,que aquas continere non ualent, ftultifsimum uero,fi id fiat non urgente necessitate,cū præstò fit fons aquæ uiuæ,&c.
units.tr: AND NOT BEFORE THE SAINTS. The Apostle wonders not only how they endure to go to law before the unrighteous, but also why they flee from or despise the judgment of the saints. For this madness was twofold. And he presses this second part so much that it appears to have offended him more than the first. It is indeed absurd to go to law before the unrighteous, but since this could be done before the saints, to be unwilling to use the judgment of the saints is the very thing that adds the greatest absurdity and is most disgraceful to the estimation of the saints. Just as it is foolish in itself to dig old cisterns, which cannot hold water, but most foolish if this is done when there is no pressing necessity, since a fountain of living water is at hand, and so on.

units.la: Obserua uero quòd dicit, & nó sub sanctis,
units.tr: Observe, moreover, that he says "and not before the saints,"

units.la: cum dicendum effet & non sub iustis , fecundum rationem oppositorum. Significat sanctos demū uere esse iustos,prophanos uerò in iustos.In iudicijs siquidem quæritur iustitia & æquitas,qua qui innocens est, à calumnia improborum liberetur.At ea iustitia plus loci habet apud sanctos ac diuinos homines, quàm apud prophanos & mundanos.
units.tr: whereas it should have been "and not before the just," according to the rule of opposites. He signifies that the saints are truly just, while the profane are unjust. For in judgments justice and equity are sought, by which the innocent is freed from the calumny of the wicked. But that justice has more place among holy and godly men than among the profane and worldly.

units.la: AN nescitis, quod sancti mundum iudicabunt?) Ob oculos illis exponit quanta contumelia afficiant ecclesiam sanctorum, dum illam indignam conftituūt, quæ iudicet de minutis membrorum suorum causis. Huc pertinet quod dicit, an nescitis quod sancti mundum iudicabunt?Et fi in uobis iudicatur minus, indigni estis minimis iudicijs. An nescitis,quod angelos iudicabimus? nedum uiētua lia ista?Primùm res ipsas de quibus sub ethnicis iudicibus litigabant, quàm sint uiles per collationem eorum, quæ per sanctos iudicabuntur expendit. Deinde enthymemate indignitate huius rei exprimit, cum dicit:Si mundus iudicabitur in uobis, indigni estis qui de minimis istis iudicetis. Ratio huius cófequentiæ est, quod indignus non fit minutarum rerum iudicio, qui de maximis iudicare potest. Sancti autem iudicabunt de maximis rebus: nā mundū & angelos quoq; iudicabunt.Ergo sancti indigni nō sunt rerū minutarū iudicio.
units.tr: DO YOU NOT KNOW THAT THE SAINTS WILL JUDGE THE WORLD? He sets before their eyes how great an insult they offer to the Church of the saints when they make her unworthy to judge the small matters of her own members. To this pertains what he says: "Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? Do you not know that we shall judge angels, to say nothing of these matters of this life?" First, by comparing the things themselves over which they were litigating before heathen judges with those that will be judged by the saints, he weighs how trivial they are. Then by an enthymeme he expresses the unworthiness of this matter, when he says: "If the world is to be judged by you, you are unworthy to judge these smallest things." The reason for this consequence is that one who is able to judge the greatest matters is not unworthy of the judgment of small things. But the saints will judge the greatest matters: for they will judge the world and the angels also. Therefore the saints are not unworthy of the judgment of small things.

units.la: Apparet itaq; Apostolum contemptum ecclesiæ uindicare hoc argumento. Nisi enim ij, qui fratres ad ethnicorū forum utiq; causas suas non transtulissent, sed arbitros ex fratrum gremio delegissent.Hoc intellexit Apostolus cum dixit,indigni ne estis. Ideoq; sanctorum honorem ista collatione uindicare uoluit.
units.tr: It seems, then, that the Apostle defends the honour of the Church with this argument. For if those who had not carried their causes to the heathen courts had chosen arbiters from among the brothers' own number, there would have been no such shame. The Apostle meant this when he said, "Are you not unworthy?" He therefore wished to defend the honour of the saints by this comparison.

units.la: Sed quæritur, quomodo credentes Christo mundum & angelos sint iudicaturi,cum pater omne iudicium dederit filio,isq; solus fit constitutus iudex uiuorum ac mortuorum. Ita uidelicet, quod exemplo fidei illorū mundi perfidia damnabitur. Ita exponit Ambrosius. Ita duodecim apostoli ex Israele sumpti, Israelis perfidiam condemnabunt. Sic Niniuitæ & regina Austri condemnabūt quamuis nationem incredulam.Matt.12.Terra fœcunda condemnat sua fertilitate terram sterilem, eodem cultu & imbre usam frustra. Qui eodem præceptore usus indoctus euasit, merito condemnatur à condiscipulo qui plurimum profecit. Ita uidelicet mundus ille recte condemnatur in credentibus,quod gratiam cœlestem in Christo exhibitam contempsit, quam isti sunt amplexi.Quidam tamen exponunt sic:Iudicabit sancti mundū, quia assessores erunt fuimmi iudicis,fecundum illud Matt.19. Cum sedent filius hominis in fede maiestatis suæ, sedebitis & uos super sedes duodecim,iudicantes duodecim tribus Israel. Nihil hic contradictionis est.Vterq; sensus habet,unde probetur.
units.tr: But it is asked how believers in Christ are going to judge the world and the angels, since the Father has given all judgement to the Son, and he alone has been appointed judge of the living and the dead. The answer is that the unbelief of the world will be condemned by the example of their faith. Ambrose explains it this way: the twelve apostles, taken from Israel, will condemn the unbelief of Israel. So the Ninevites and the queen of the South will condemn that unbelieving nation, Matt. 12. A fertile land condemns a barren land by its fertility, since the barren land has enjoyed the same cultivation and rain in vain. A man who has had the same teacher and turned out untaught is rightly condemned by a fellow pupil who has progressed much further. In the same way, that world is rightly condemned in the believers, because it has despised the heavenly grace shown in Christ, which these believers have embraced. Some, however, explain it differently: the saints will judge the world because they will be assessors of the supreme judge, according to that saying in Matt. 19., "When the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel." There is no contradiction here. Each sense has its own support.

units.la: Rursus de angelis non idem sentitur. Quidam intelligunt ministros ecclesiæ per eccle-fiam
units.tr: Opinions about the angels are likewise not the same. Some understand the ministers of the Church, through the Church,

units.la: Matth. 19.
units.tr: Matth. 19.

units.la: Matth. 11. {A}iam iudicados, quorum sententiam Chryfosto-mus reijcit. Alij de malis spiritibus exponunt, qui Matth.25.angeli Satanæ à Christo uocantur. Hos ideo dicit à sanctis damnari Hiero. quod cum in carne non sint, pietate superentur à sanctis qui in carne illa corrupta degunt.
units.tr: Matth. 11. Already to be judged, whose opinion Chrysostom rejects. Others explain it of evil spirits, whom Christ in Matt. 25. calls the angels of Satan. Jerome says that these are condemned by the saints for this reason: since they are not in the flesh, they are overcome in piety by the saints who live in that corrupt flesh.

units.la: Ergo fides ac uita Christianorū iudicat & condemnat mundum, id est, incredulos & impios. At uereor ne uiceuersa ad exemplū Israelitarum, per eos qui sub nomine Christi non sunt, iudicandi simus qui Christiani uocamur. Quod si uita uitam damnat, non uideo quomodo nostra fit Iudæorum, Turcorum, aliarumq; gētium damnatura, cum uiuatur à nobis usque adeo flagitiosè, ut nobis collati Turci & Iudæi sancti uideri posint. Cæterum solo nomine & ritibus quibusdam externis ab illis separamur. Sed uideamus singula.
units.tr: Therefore the faith and life of Christians judge and condemn the world, that is, the unbelieving and the impious. Yet I fear that, conversely, following the example of the Israelites, we who are called Christians may be judged by those who are not under the name of Christ. For if life condemns life, I do not see how our life will not condemn the Jews, the Turks, and other nations, since we live so disgracefully that the Turks and Jews may seem holy in comparison with us. Indeed, we are separated from them only by the name and by certain external rites. But let us look at the individual points.

units.la: An nescitis, inquit? Particulam hanc ingeminat. Colligimus inde, notissimum esse debere fidelibus, primum mundum & angelos, id est, malos spiritus, obnoxios esse iudicio & condemnationi. Deinde, iudicandos esse à sanctis. At iam uidentur sancti iudicari & condemnari à mundo & malis spiritibus. Verùm, ut sunt rerum uices, qui nunc iudicatur à mundo, olim iudices erunt mundi: & qui nunc sunt iudices sanctorum, olim iudicabūtur & condemnabuntur à sanctis. Consultò igitur non dicit, quod sancti iudicát, sed, quod iudicabūt mundum. Sic auocat fidelium mentes à ípectris rerum præsentium, ad considerationem futurorum, quibus nullæ subsequuturæ sunt uices & alterationes. Admodū uidetur esse miserum, iudicari & condemnari in hoc seculo, subiectumque esse non modò legitimis, sed & iniquis impiorum hominum iudicijs, quæ tunc, quemadmodum nunc quoq; ferre cogebātur sancti ac fideles. Appositissimè igitur admonet Corinthios non modò, quàm non conueniat ut sancti iudicentur à mūdo, sed & quàm non debeant animo esse deiecto si iudicentur à mūdo, quod futurū sit, ut ipsi iudicet mūdū.
units.tr: "Do you not know," he says? He repeats this particle. From it we gather that it ought to be well known to the faithful, first, that the world and the angels, that is, the evil spirits, are liable to judgement and condemnation; and second, that they are to be judged by the saints. Yet at present the saints seem to be judged and condemned by the world and by evil spirits. But as the wheel of fortune turns, those who are now judged by the world will one day be the judges of the world, and those who are now the judges of the saints will one day be judged and condemned by the saints. So he deliberately does not say that the saints judge, but that they will judge the world. In this way he draws the minds of the faithful away from the spectacle of present things to the consideration of future ones, in which no later changes and alterations will follow. It seems a very wretched thing to be judged and condemned in this age, and to be subject not only to lawful but also to unjust judgements of wicked men, which the saints and faithful were then, as now, compelled to endure. So he rightly warns the Corinthians, not only how unseemly it is that the saints should be judged by the world, but also that they ought not to be dispirited if they are judged by the world, since the time will come when they will judge the world itself.

units.la: QVOD sancti mundū, inquit, iudicabūt.) Quid est quod nō dicit: Quod sancti iniustos & prophanos iudicābunt? Admonet iniustos & prophanos pertinere ad hunc mundū, esseque mundum nihil aliud quàm iniustorū, impiorum ac prophanorū hominum colluuiem: ad quam potissimum pertineant, qui in illo cæteris dominantur.
units.tr: "That the saints shall judge the world," he says. Why does he not say, "that the saints shall judge the unrighteous and profane"? He reminds us that the unrighteous and profane belong to this world, and that the world is nothing other than a sewer of unrighteous, impious and profane men, to which especially belong those who rule over the rest in it.

units.la: ET si in uobis, inquit, iudicatur mundus.) Sic est in Græco. Erasmus uertit. Et si per uos Ebræum בכם nonnunquam sic capitur. Apparet tamen non esse frustra dictum ab Apostolo ἐν ὑμῖν, id est, in uobis. Iudicatur. i. damnatur in fidelibus mundus, primum, dum in illis crucifigitur & exterminatur quotidie: deinde, dum per spiritum ac uerbū regni Dei iudicantur increduli & arguūtur de peccato, iudicio & iusticia. Tertiò iudicabitur in illis in futuro seculo, dum respectu illorum condemnabitur. Atq; ita uidetur exponere quod dixit: An nescitis quod sancti mūdum iudicabunt?
units.tr: "And if the world is judged in you," he says. This is how it reads in the Greek. Erasmus translates it "by you." The Hebrew term [בכם] is sometimes taken in this way. Yet it does not seem that the Apostle said ἐν ὑμῖν [in you] without purpose. The world is judged, that is, condemned, in the faithful: first, while it is crucified and destroyed in them every day; second, while unbelievers are judged and convicted of sin, of judgement and of righteousness, through the Spirit and the word of the kingdom of God; third, it will be judged in them in the age to come, when it is condemned in regard to them. And this seems to be how he explains what he said: "Do you not know that the saints shall judge the world?"

units.la: INDIGNI estis, inquit, minimis iudicijs?) Sic citra interrogationē legerim us, uocātur iudicia prophanorum minima, respectu iudicio rum sanctorum. Si cum interrogatione, iudicia minima sunt quæ terrena cōcernunt. Et reuera sic sunt omnium minima cēsenda. Atho die habentur maximi momenti, suntq; iudicia de rebus salutis nostræ planè parerga.
units.tr: "Are you unworthy," he says, "of the smallest judgements?" If one reads this without a question mark, the judgements of the profane are called the smallest in comparison with the judgements of the saints. If one reads it with a question mark, the smallest judgements are those that concern earthly things. And indeed these must be counted the smallest of all. At Athens they were held to be of the greatest importance, yet judgements about the matters of our salvation are plainly the ornaments [parerga] of the rest.

units.la: AN nescitis quod angelos iudicabimus? inquit.) Assurgit amplificando dignitatem sanctorum: primum in eo, quod pro iniustis posuit mundum, deinde in eo, quod iam angelos quoq; iudicandos à nobis esse dicit.
units.tr: "Do you not know that we shall judge the angels?" he says. He rises higher, magnifying the dignity of the saints: first, in that he has put the world in place of the unrighteous; and second, in that he now says that the angels too are to be judged by us.

units.la: Obserua uerò, quomodo cum dixisset: An nescitis quod sancti mundū iudicabūt? Subiecit in secūda persona, Et si in uobis iudicatur mūdus, & hic in prima, An nescitis quod angelos iudicabimus? Ne uidelicet ad alios nescio quos sanctos ista referamus, & non ad fideles.
units.tr: Observe, however, how, having said, "Do you not know that the saints shall judge the world?", he added in the second person, "And if the world is judged in you," and here, in the first person, "Do you not know that we shall judge the angels?" This is so that we do not refer these things to some other saints, unknown to us, and not to the faithful.

units.la: PROINDE iudicia siquidē habueritis de uictualibus, contemptos, &c.) Argumento cō formem illationē subiungit. Quasi dicat, Cum itaq; tanta sit ecclesiæ dignitas, tam abest, ut indigna debeat haberi uictualium iudicio, ut uel ij qui sunt in illa propè nihil illorum iudices sint constituendi. Tanti uidelicet debebat uobis esse dignitas ecclesię, tamq; uiles uideri res istæ terrenæ, de quibus contenditis.
units.tr: "Therefore, if you have judgements about everyday matters, set them to judge those who are despised," and so on. He adds a conclusion that follows from the argument. As if he were saying: since the dignity of the Church is so great, it is far from fitting that it should be thought worthy of the judgement of everyday things; even those who are of little account in the Church should be appointed as judges of them. Surely the dignity of the Church ought to have been so precious to you, and these earthly things, over which you are contending, should have seemed so worthless.

units.la: DE uictualibus, inquit.) Græcè est βιωτικά, id est, uitam hanc sustentandam concernētia. Qua uoce iam secundò iudicia terrenarum rerū depreciat. At interim cogitet cordatus homo, quomo do extenuanda sint studia, & iudicia earum rerum, quæ ad superbiam, fastum, luxum, quæstum, uoluptates, & libidinem absque ulla necessitate usurpantur, si sic extenuantur uictualia, quibus in hac uita carere non possumus. Non discimus hinc contemnere dona Dei, quæ uitæ nostræ alendæ diuina largitate suppeditātur, absit: sed admonemur, ne illa sempiternis bonis præferamus, neue propter ipsa aliquid admittamus, quod fideles homines dedeceat.
units.tr: "About everyday matters," he says. The Greek is βιωτικά [βιωτικά], that is, things concerning the sustaining of this life. By this word he now belittles, for the second time, the judgements of earthly things. Yet at the same time let the sensible man consider how the pursuits and judgements of those things which are used without any necessity for pride, show, luxury, gain, pleasure and lust ought to be belittled, if everyday necessities, without which we cannot live in this life, are belittled in this way. We do not learn from this to despise the gifts of God, which are supplied by his divine bounty to nourish our life. Far from it! But we are warned not to prefer them to eternal goods, nor to commit anything on their account that would be unbecoming to faithful people.

units.la: CONTEMPTOS, inquit, qui sunt in ecclesia.) Ergo habet ecclesia quosdam contemnendos? Nequaquam. Quomodo nanq; contemnēdi sunt, propter quos mortuus est Christus? Qui ad dignitatem sunt filiorum Dei, & ad sempiternam felicitatem ac gloriā uocati? Intelligit ergo non de talibus quibusdam qui contemnendi sint in ecclesia, sed de pauperioribus, imperitiorib. & indoctis, qui à sectarijs & inflatis cum contemptu fastidiebātur. Perstringit igitur rursus sectariorum superbiam, quemadmodum & in præcedenti cum dixit, indigni estis minimis iudicijs?
units.tr: "Those who are despised," he says, "who are in the Church." Does the Church, then, have some despised members? By no means. For how can those be despised for whom Christ died, who are called to the dignity of the sons of God and to everlasting happiness and glory? He therefore means not that some such people should be despised in the Church, but that the poorer, the unlearned and the untaught, who were scorned with contempt by the sectarians and the puffed-up, are to be understood. So again he attacks the pride of the sectarians, just as he did in the preceding sentence when he said, "Are you unworthy of the smallest judgements?"

units.la: ILLOS constituite.) Græcè uox καθίζετε anceps est. Potest enim tam indicandi quàm imperandi modo legi. Vnde & quidā cōstituitis legunt. Vt Ambrosius, quę schola Vuittenbergen. sequuta est. Isti per contemptos intelligunt Gentes, quę sint in ecclesia contemptę, id est, quę ab ecclesia contemnantur. Alij uerò legunt constituite modo imperandi, è quibus est & Auguft. quorum sententia meo iudicio simplicior est & uero similior. Alioqui cum καθίζειν significet in sedem uelut iudicem collocare, quomodo dici possunt credentes Corinthij ethnicos collocasse in sedem iudiciariam, cum illi iam antea habuerint iudicandi potestatem, nec illam à Christianis accipere potuerint, etiamsi nó habuissent? Aliud certè est sub iudice ethnico litigare, & aliud ethnicum hominem in sedem iudiciariam collocare. Quare, quòd dicit: Contemptos in ecclesia, nó est ad gentes referendum, sed ad inferioris ordinis homines ac fideles, qui sunt in ecclesia.
units.tr: "Set them to judge," he says. The Greek word καθίζετε [καθίζετε] is ambiguous. For it can be read either in the indicative mood or in the imperative. Hence some read "you set," as Ambrose does, and the school of Wittenberg has followed him. These take the despised to be the Gentiles who are in the Church and are despised, that is, who are held in contempt by the Church. Others, however, read it in the imperative, "set," among whom is also Augustine; in my judgement their opinion is simpler and more probable. Otherwise, since to seat [καθίζειν] means to place in a seat, as it were, of a judge, how can it be said that the believing Corinthians had placed heathens in a judicial seat, when those men had already had the power of judging beforehand, and could not have received it from Christians even if they had not had it? It is certainly one thing to go to law under a heathen judge, and another to place a heathen man in the judicial seat. Therefore, when he says, "those who are despised in the Church," this is not to be referred to the Gentiles, but to men of lower rank and to the faithful who are in the Church.

units.la: AD erubesc.) Hanc particulam exponunt tanquâ correctionem praeteriti mandati, quasi Apostolus non serió uoluerit contemptos in ecclesia terrenarum rerum iudices constitui, malit tamen illud, quàm quod sub ethnicis litigabant. Et hoc quoq; ex sequenti particula colligunt. Meo tamè iudicio tam abest ut non serió id dixerit Apostolus, ut optandum illi fuerit, id ita fieri potuisse à Corinthijs. Faceret enim ad dignitatem ecclesiae Christi & contemptum rerum terrenarum.
units.tr: On "I say this to your shame." They explain this particle as a correction of the earlier command, as if the Apostle had not seriously wanted those despised in the Church to be made judges of worldly matters, but preferred this to their litigating before pagans. They also gather this from the following particle. In my judgement, however, the Apostle was far from not meaning it seriously, and it would have been desirable for the Corinthians to be able to do this, since it would serve both the dignity of the Church of Christ and the contempt of worldly things.

units.la: ADEO non est inter uos sapiens, ne unus quidem.) Q. d. Cum debeatis omnes intelligentes esse iustitiae & aequitatis, adeo ne omnes stupidi estis & insensati, ut ne unus quidè sit inter uos sapiês, qui possit discernere inter fratrē & fratrem. Omnia emphatice dicuntur. Innuit enim non opus esse magna iuris peritię subtilitate, ad hoc ut arbitrum quis agat inter Christianos, qui cum sint inter se fratres, facillimi sunt ad remittendum & componendum.
units.tr: "So there is not even one wise man among you." That is: "Since you ought all to be intelligent in justice and fairness, are you so utterly stupid and senseless that there is not even one wise man among you who can judge between brother and brother?" Everything is said emphatically. For he implies that no great subtlety of legal skill is needed for someone to act as arbiter among Christians, who, since they are brothers to one another, are most ready to forgive and settle.

units.la: At, bone Deus, quàta opus est hodie legum copia, cautioe & sinuositate, quàm omnia sunt referta aduocatorum, procuratorum & iurisperitorum turba? Vt taceam quod legum uolumina numerosa dicuntur, prae multitudine, quam uaria & multa iniquitas poscere uisa est. Ex hoc loco episcopi ansam sumpserunt implicandi sese negocijs uictualibus dijudicandis: qua de re uide August. de opere Monach. cap.29. Item annot. Erasmi.
units.tr: But, good God, how much need there is today of a abundance of laws, caution and intricacy, and how everything is crammed with a crowd of advocates, attorneys and lawyers! Not to mention that volumes of laws are said to be numerous because of the multitude of wrongs that various and many iniquities seem to demand. From this passage bishops have taken occasion to entangle themselves in the judging of everyday affairs; on this see Augustine, On the Work of Monks, ch. 29, and likewise Erasmus's notes.

units.la: SED frater cum fratre litigat, &c.) Vrget absurditatem huius mali. Debebant arbitrorū sententia componere causas, ad id tam nó facie bant, ut auderent litem intendere, idq; fratres fratribus, & hoc apud infideles. Haćtenus primum peccati huius mebrum declarauit, quod & ipsum ostedit non esse simplex, sed triplex. Primùm quod eligebant arbitros ex fratribus, id quod ex contemptu ecclesię faciebant. Deinde quod frater cum fratre litigabat contentione iudiciaria. Tertiò quod id etiá sub infidelibus iudicibus faciebant. Perinde ac si domestici causam nó sinerent ab alijs domesticis cóponi, sed in contentione iudiciariá, idq; sub exteris contra seipsos insurgerent. Obserua uerò, quod dicit, idq; sub infidelib. Supra uocauit ethnicos iudices iniustos. Hic uocat eos ἄπιστος, id est, infideles. Sunt aút duplici nomine ἄπιστοι, primū quod sunt increduli & infideles, alieni à fide Christi. Deinde quod sunt per fidi uel infidi, utroque nomine auersandi, nisi cogatur Christianus aliunde in ius uocatus in nocentiam suam sub illis defendere.
units.tr: "But brother goes to law with brother," etc. He presses the absurdity of this evil. They ought to have settled their cases by the judgement of arbiters, but they did not do so; instead they dared to bring a suit, and brothers against brothers, and this before unbelievers. Up to this point he has declared the first part of this sin, which he also shows is not simple but threefold. First, they chose arbiters from among the brothers, which they did out of contempt for the Church. Second, brother went to law with brother in a judicial contest. Third, they did this also before unbelieving judges, just as if members of one household would not let their affair be settled by other members of the household, but rose up against one another in a judicial contest, and that before outsiders. Observe what he says: "and this before unbelievers." Above he called the pagan judges unjust. Here he calls them unbelievers [ἄπιστος], that is, faithless. They are unbelievers [ἄπιστοι] in a twofold sense: first, because they are unbelieving and strangers to the faith of Christ; second, because they are faithless or untrustworthy. Both names are to be avoided, unless a Christian who has been summoned to court by someone else is compelled to defend his innocence before them.

units.la: ITAQVE iam quidé omnino delictum in uobis est, quod lites, &c.) Haćtenus Corinthios reprehendit Apostolus, quod apud infideles litigabant. Iam deinceps ne putent in eo solo se posse reprehendi, quod iudicio coram impijs contendebant, ad reliqua mali huius mébra trāfit, quę talia sunt, ut etiāsi in ecclesiae gremio litigaret, adhuc tamē defendi nó possent. Hoc est, quod dicit, ἤδη μὲν ἥττημα. Iá quidem igitur. Q. d. Etiámsi non apud impios litigaretis tamē culpabiles estis uel hoc nomine prorsus, quod lites habetis inter uos, cū sitis Christiani & filij pacis, &c. Illud ὅλως. Omnino, uel tandem est, atq; irrefragabiliter, absq; ulla contradictione, q certissimè, uel idè significat qd totaliter, eo quod utraq; litigantiū partes culpabiles sint, tam quae iniuriam iudicio uindicat, quàm quae illam intulit. Illa quod nihil iniuriarum patiêter sustinet, ista quod iniuriam intulit. Est ea nanq; litigandi cōditio & ratio, ut in ius congrediantur, & qui lęsus est, & qui laesit. Hinc enim lites sunt, quod alter laedit, alter laesus iniuriam non tolerat. Consideratis itaque litigiorum causis, utrasq; partes culpabiles esse ostēdit. Neutra nanq; illarū Christianis competit, à quibus tam abesse debet, ut iniuria quiquam afficiant, ut illatam etiam patienter ferant. Hoc scilicet est quod dicit: Iam quidem omnino deliĉtum in uobis est.
units.tr: "Now indeed there is altogether a fault among you, that you have lawsuits," etc. Up to now the Apostle has rebuked the Corinthians because they litigated before unbelievers. Now, lest they think they can be rebuked only for contending in court before the impious, he passes to the other parts of this evil, which are such that even if they were litigating within the bosom of the Church, they still could not be defended. This is what he means by now indeed a fault [ἤδη μὲν ἥττημα]: "Now indeed." That is: "Even if you were not litigating before the impious, you would still be altogether to blame on this ground alone, that you have lawsuits among yourselves, since you are Christians and sons of peace," etc. The word altogether [ὅλως] means entirely, or at last, and indeed without fail, without any contradiction, most certainly. Or it means wholly, because both parties to the litigation are to blame: the one who seeks redress in court for a wrong, and the one who inflicted it. The first does not patiently bear any wrong; the second has done the wrong. For this is the nature and condition of litigation, that both the injured party and the one who injured come into court. Lawsuits arise because one party injures and the other, having been injured, does not tolerate the wrong. So, having considered the causes of the lawsuits, he shows that both parties are to blame. Neither position suits Christians, from whom wrong ought to be so far removed that they neither inflict injury on anyone nor even bear patiently the injury done to them. This is certainly what he means by: "Now indeed there is altogether a fault among you."

units.la: DELICTVM.) Graecè est ἥττημα, quod defectum significat, ac diminutionē, Germanicè ein fehl oder mangel. Indicat enim hac dictione à Christianis exigi perfectionē innocentiae, patientiae & charitatis, quae certè apud eos non est, qui iudicio inter se contendunt. Erasmus dictione hanc à uerbo superandi ac uincendi, aut uictū esse deducit, ut intelligamus eos qui inter se litigant superatos esse uel ira, uel superbia, uel auaritia, uel impatientia, ἡττάομαι nanq; uinci significat. Et sanè uerum est, iam uictos esse aliqua tentatione, qui inter se litigant, etiā eos, q in iudicio superât & uictorcs abscedūt.
units.tr: "A fault." In Greek it is a defect [ἥττημα], which signifies a lack or diminution; in German, [ein fehl oder mangel]. By this word he indicates that Christians are required to show the perfection of innocence, patience and charity, which certainly is not found among those who contend with one another in court. Erasmus derives the word from the verb meaning to overcome or conquer, so that we understand that those who litigate with one another are overcome either by anger, pride, greed or impatience, for to be overcome [ἡττάομαι] means to be conquered. And indeed it is true that those who litigate with one another are already overcome by some temptation, even those who prevail in the court and leave as victors.

units.la: IN uobis.) Delicti huius immunes sunt iudices, sub quibus litigatur. Licet enim peccant qui inter se litigant, non tamē peccat, qui litigantes iuris sententia & potestatis suae authoritate dirimit, eumq; qui lęsus est uindicat, & iniustum punit. Huius enim officiū necessarium est, posteaquam ad lædendum omnes sumus proniores quàm ad illatam iniuriam patienter ferendum. Culpabiles tamen sunt qui isto officio uel utūtur ipsi, uel alios uti cogūt.
units.tr: "Among you." The judges under whom litigation takes place are free of this fault. For although those who litigate with one another sin, the one who settles the litigants by the sentence of law and by the authority of his office does not sin. He vindicates the one who was injured and punishes the unjust party. This office is necessary, since we are all more prone to injure others than to bear patiently the wrong done to us. Nevertheless, those are to blame who either use this office themselves or compel others to use it.

units.la: Cur nó potius iniuriá patiminī? Cur nó potius damnū accipitis?) Declarat qd dixit, eos omnino culpabiles esse in eo, quod iudicio inter se cōtenderēt. Et principio eos alloquitur q iniuste laesi, in ius uocabant aduersarios, ut ubi reliqui intellexerint nó licere Christiano illatā iniuriā iure uindicare, intelligant multò minus licere iniuriā cuiquā inferre. Nó aút dicit simpliciter, peccatis quod iniuriā nó fertis,
units.tr: "Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather accept loss?" He explains what he has said, that they are altogether to blame in contending with one another in court. First he addresses those who, unjustly injured, summoned their opponents to court. So, when the rest understand that it is not lawful for a Christian to avenge an injury through the courts, they may understand that it is much less lawful to inflict injury on anyone at all. He does not say simply, "you sin because you do not bear injury,"

units.la: quod damnum non accipitis, sed tacita quadam collatione rei huius delictū spectandum proponit, cum dicit: Cur non potius iniuriam patimini?
