Respicit enim ad aliud quod dā malum, quod plus debebant declinare ac fugere, quàm terrenæ cuiuspiam rei dispendium. Illud est, læsio charitatis & unitatis Christianæ. Vt enim Christiano potior esse debet charitas, quàm cōmodū aliquod terrenū, ita damnū lęsæ charitatis magis fugere debet quàm terrenæ facultatis. Nec emphasi caret, quod percontando instat ostendens sibi tam uideri absurdum quod faciebat, ut rationem illius nullam uidere queat, imò ab ipsis audire cupiat, qua nam ratione non magis ferant iniuriam, quàm quòd charitatem inter se lędunt. Et huc quoque facit illud Christi Matth.5. Ego autem dico uobis, nolite resistere malo, &c. Et qui uult iudicio tecum contendere, & tunicā tuam tollere, dimitte illi & pallium. Hoc certè lōgè consultius est quàm per impatientiæ malum mentis amittere tranquillitatem, charitatem fraternam uel lędere, uel læsam prorsus extinguere, mortificationem ueteris hominis praecludere, uindictam de manibus supremi iudicis eripere. Sed hac de re uide in annotationibus nostris super Matth.cap.5.
units.tr: "or because you do not accept loss," but sets this fault before them for consideration by a certain tacit comparison, when he says: "Why do you not rather suffer wrong?" For he looks to some other evil, which they ought to avoid and flee more than any loss of earthly property. That evil is the injury to charity and Christian unity. For as charity ought to be more valuable to a Christian than any earthly advantage, so the loss of charity ought to be shunned more than the loss of earthly wealth. Nor is it without emphasis that he presses the point with questions, showing that what they were doing seems to him so absurd that he cannot see any reason for it, and indeed wishes to hear from them why they do not bear injury more readily than they wound charity among themselves. This also agrees with that saying of Christ in Matthew 5: "But I say to you, do not resist evil," etc., "and whoever wants to contend with you at law and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well." This is certainly far more prudent than to lose tranquillity of mind through the evil of impatience, to injure fraternal charity or utterly extinguish it, to shut off the mortification of the old man, and to snatch vengeance from the hands of the supreme judge. But on this matter see our annotations on Matthew, chapter 5.

units.la: Est autem ista sententia tam rationabilis ut & Platoni multis fit tractata in Gorgia. Dicunt Græci βέλτιον ἐστὶ τὸ ἀδικεῖσθαι τῶ ἀδικεῖν.
units.tr: This opinion is so reasonable that Plato too treats it at length in the Gorgias. The Greeks say: it is better to suffer wrong than to do wrong [βέλτιον ἐστὶ τὸ ἀδικεῖσθαι τῶ ἀδικεῖν].

units.la: Contra hanc sententiam Christi & Apostoli non ueniunt, qui innocentiam suam paucis testatur, & aduersario quàm peccat significat. Non enim est boni hominis ad iniusta tacere, sed modestè corrigere, ita tamē, ut nihil aliud quæsat, quàm emendationem eius qui delinquit. Et Christus & Paulus innocētiam suam testati sunt, & improbo reprehenderunt, & nihilominus illatam iniuriam patienter tulerunt. Et Ieremias cap.37. ad regem Sedechiā dicebat: Quid peccaui tibi & seruis tuis & populo tuo, quia misisti me in domum carceris? Nunc ergo audi obsecro domine mi rex, ualeat deprecatio mea in conspectu tuo, & ne remittas me in domum Ionathae scribæ, ne moriar ibi. Ecce primum testatur innocentiam suam, peccatumq; regis in se insontem commissum reprehendit, deinde iniuriam etiam & uim deprecatur. Ista non sunt animi impatientis, nec doctrinæ isti repugnant.
units.tr: Christ's and the Apostle's teaching is not opposed to this opinion, for they briefly testify to their innocence and show the adversary how he sins. For it is not the mark of a good man to keep silent about wrongs, but to correct them modestly, yet in such a way as to seek nothing but the amendment of the one who offends. Both Christ and Paul testified to their innocence and rebuked the wicked, and nevertheless bore the wrong done to them patiently. Jeremiah too, in chapter 37, said to King Zedekiah: "What have I sinned against you, your servants, or your people, that you have put me in the house of the prison? Now therefore hear me, I beg you, my lord king: let my plea be acceptable in your sight, and do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the scribe, lest I die there." Here, first, he testifies to his innocence and rebukes the king for the sin committed against him, though he was innocent; then he begs for relief even from the wrong and the violence. These are not the words of an impatient mind, nor do they contradict this teaching.

units.la: IMO uos iniuriam facitis, & damno afficitis, idq; fratres.) Ista per auxesim delicti adiciuntur, ut ostendatur quàm absint adhuc à Christianæ professionis perfectione. In Christianismo delinquit, qui iniuriæ est impatiens. At quando ad eam perfectionē patientiæ peruenient, qui utqueadeo adhuc sunt iniusti, ut alios etiam per iniuriam lædant? Est enim omnino peius iniuria quenquam afficere, quàm illatam iniuriam iudiciaria lite repellere.
units.tr: Indeed you do wrong and inflict loss, and that on your brothers. These words are added by way of amplification of the offence, to show how far you still are from the perfection of the Christian profession. The one who cannot bear injury is at fault as a Christian. But how will those who are still so unjust that they wrong others by injury reach that perfection of patience? For it is altogether worse to inflict an injury on anyone than to repel an injury done to you by a lawsuit.

units.la: IDQVE fratres.) Et hic est delicti huius auxesis. Iniustum est quemcunq; per iniuriam lædere, etiā exterum & inimicum. Enormius autem peccatur, si id etiam fratri fiat. Quasi di-
units.tr: AND THIS TO BROTHERS. Here is the amplification of this offence. It is unjust to harm anyone by injury, even a stranger or an enemy. But the sin is more monstrous if it is done even to a brother. As if he said:

units.la: cat, Cum ne inimicos quidem lædere debeatis, tam estis iniqui, ut nec fratribus parcatis. Quales nam esse uos credendū est erga inimicos, cum tales sitis erga fratres?
units.tr: Since you ought not to harm even your enemies, you are so unjust that you do not spare your brothers. What sort of people must you be thought to be towards your enemies, since you are such towards your brothers?

units.la: Hoc itaque pacto Apostolus luce clarius exponit omnino delicto obnoxios esse Christianos, si iudiciarias inter se lites habeat. Primum enim indicium datur esse illos iniuriae impatientes, contra doctrinam Christi & omnium sanctorum mētem & ingenium. Deinde certum est factam esse aliquam iniuriam, aut saltem intendi. Tertiò exaggeratione criminis habet, quod frater fratri iniurius est, quem debebat non minus diligere quàm seipsum.
units.tr: In this way the Apostle explains, clearer than daylight, that Christians who carry on lawsuits among themselves are wholly liable to fault. First, this is a sign that they are impatient of injury, contrary to the teaching of Christ and the mind and character of all the saints. Second, it is certain that some injury has been done, or at least that one is intended. Third, he heightens the charge by pointing out that one brother wrongs another, whom he ought to love no less than himself.

units.la: AN nescitis quod iniusti regni Dei haereditate non consequētur?) Arguit eos hic sum mæ incogitantiæ, qua minuta quædā & inania persequētes regni Dei hæreditatē amittebāt. Quasi dicat, An adeo stupidi & incogitantes estis, ut propter res adeo viles & inanes negligatis summā illam regni Dei felicitatem, dum desiderijs uestris uanis obsequētes iniuste lædițis fratres? Certè nō potestis ignorare, iniustis nō esse locū in regno Dei. Vos aūt iniusti estis, cum dāno quenquam immerito afficitis. Quō igitur nō cogitatis q; sit insanū pro rebus terrenis amittere æternā regni Dei felicitatē?
units.tr: DO YOU NOT KNOW THAT THE UNJUST WILL NOT INHERIT THE KINGDOM OF GOD? Here he rebukes their thoughtlessness, by which, pursuing trifling and empty things, they were losing the inheritance of the kingdom of God. As if he said: Are you so dull and thoughtless that, for the sake of things so cheap and worthless, you neglect that supreme happiness of the kingdom of God, while, indulging your vain desires, you unjustly harm your brothers? Surely you cannot be ignorant that there is no place for the unjust in the kingdom of God. But you are unjust when you inflict loss on anyone who does not deserve it. Why, then, do you not consider how mad it is to lose the eternal happiness of the kingdom of God for earthly things?

units.la: Admonet nos hoc loco Apostolus commemoratione regni Dei, primarium hunc esse debere Christianorum in omni uita scopum, ne quid comittamus quod à cōsequutione regni Dei, hæreditario posidendi impediat. Ad illud enim uocati sumus per gratiā Christi. Ea uocatio nunquā debet mentibus nostris excidere, ne quo pacto per illius obliuionem immergamur rebus huius mūdi, inq; illis peccates, diui na nosipsos dignatione priuemus. Perinde mihi uidetur Apostolus facere, ac si quisquam bonarū literarū cādidatis, quorū scopus, est rerum cognitio, deq; rebus intellectis diserte ac di lucide posse loqui, si ocio uiderit plus æquo deditos dicat: An nescitis, quòd nemo ociosus & ignauus eruditus ac doctus euadere poterit? Hic nō solū denegaretur ocio rerū scientia, sed simul admoneretur adolescētes bonis literis consecrati, ad quē scopū spectare, sefeq; accōmodare, & quicquid ab illo consequedo impediat fugere debeat. Sed dicit quisquā: Si iniusti regno Dei excluduntur, ergo requiritur nostra iusticia ad hoc ut saluemur, & irrita est doctrina gratiæ. Respondeo: Ipsum uerbū hæreditandi nō admittit meritū proprię nostræ iustitiæ. Quare non consequitur, saluari nos pro pria iusticia, propterea quod iniusti hæreditate regni Dei priuantur. Per gratiā Dei sumus uocati & assumpti in adoptionem filiorū Dei. Hac dignitate retinere nō possunt, qui iniusti ciæ magis quàm iusticiæ post acceptā gratiam studēt. De illis iniustis intelligendū est qd' hic dicitur non de ijs qui nondū in hanc sunt gratiam assumpti & initiati. Alioqui nemo prorsus saluari posset. Verum in sequentibus patebit ista sententia, ubi dicet: Sed hæc eratis qui dā, uerū abluti estis, &c. Quod itaq; dicit, An nescitis, quod iniusti regnū Dei nō hæreditabūt, non est pro generali accipiendū sententia.
units.tr: Here the Apostle admonishes us, by recalling the kingdom of God, that this should be the chief aim of Christians throughout their whole life: that we commit nothing which might hinder us from attaining the kingdom of God and possessing it as an inheritance. For we have been called to that through the grace of Christ. That calling must never slip from our minds, lest by forgetting it we sink into the things of this world, and in them, by sinning, deprive ourselves of the divine favour. The Apostle seems to me to do the same as if someone were to say to candidates in the liberal arts, whose aim is knowledge of things and who want to speak clearly and eloquently about what they have understood, when he sees them too devoted to leisure: Do you not know that no one who is idle and lazy can become learned and wise? Here he would not only deny knowledge of things to idleness, but at the same time admonish the young, devoted to good letters, to what goal they should aim and apply themselves, and what they should flee if it hinders them from reaching it. But someone will say: If the unjust are excluded from the kingdom of God, then our righteousness is required for us to be saved, and the doctrine of grace is void. I answer: the very word "to inherit" does not admit the merit of our own righteousness. Therefore it does not follow that we are saved by our own righteousness, merely because the unjust are deprived of the inheritance of the kingdom of God. We have been called and adopted into the sonship of God through the grace of God. Those who strive more for injustice than for righteousness after receiving grace cannot keep this dignity. What is said here must be understood of those unjust people, not of those who have not yet been received and initiated into this grace. Otherwise no one at all could be saved. But this opinion will be made plain in what follows, where he says: "But such were some of you; but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified," and so on. Therefore what he says, "Do you not know that the unjust will not inherit the kingdom of God," is not to be taken as a general statement.

units.la: Ne erretis. Neque scortatores, neque cultores simulacrorum, neque adulteri, neque molles, neque qui concumbunt cum masculis, neque fures, neque auari, neque ebriosi, neque maledici, neque rapaces, regni dei hæreditatem accipient.
units.tr: Do not be deceived. Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor effeminate persons, nor men who lie with men, nor thieves, nor covetous people, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, will inherit the kingdom of God.

units.la: Intelligebat Apostolus vana quadam opinione ac securitate seduci Corinthios satis ad felicitatē esse putātes, quod Christo dedissent nomen, in illum baptizati essent, & qualicunq; illius fide præditi. Hoc vocat errorē cum dicit: Nolite errare. Q.d. Ne cogitetis, benignus est Deus, nō vlciscetur peccata nostra, Christiani sumus, gratia Dei acquisuimus, damnari nequimus, alia est nostra conditio quàm infidelium. Error est, putare Christianismum nihil esse aliud quā inanis tituli, pfessionē, & cultū quendam rituū externorū. Gentium est ista opinio, nō Christianorum, à quibus ad regni Dei possessione solida requiratur pietas & vera iustitia.
units.tr: The Apostle understood that the Corinthians were being led astray by a certain empty opinion and false security, thinking it enough for salvation that they had given their name to Christ, been baptized into him, and had some kind of faith in him. He calls this error when he says: "Do not be deceived." That is, as if he said: Do not think that God is kind and will not punish our sins; we are Christians, we have acquired the grace of God, we cannot be condemned, our condition is different from that of unbelievers. It is an error to think that Christianity is nothing but the profession of an empty title and a certain outward observance of rites. That opinion belongs to the Gentiles, not to Christians, from whom the solid possession of the kingdom of God requires godliness and true righteousness.

units.la: NEQVE scortatores.) Quos generaliter in iustos uocauit, consequenter per species expremit, haud quidem omnes iniusticiæ species recensens, sed eas salte, quibus sciebat obnoxios potissimum esse Corinthios, & reliquos Gentilismo assuetos, inter quos obtinebant scortationes, eidololatria, adulterium, mollicies, masculia venus, furtum, auaritia, ebrietas, maledicentia & rapacitas. Parat autem isto uiciorū ca talogo transitū ad pfequendā scortationis emendationē, atq; ideo priore illā loco ponit.
units.tr: NEITHER FORNICATORS. He first called them unjust in general, and then expresses them by particular kinds, not indeed listing every kind of injustice, but at least those to which he knew the Corinthians, and the rest who were accustomed to Gentile ways, were especially prone: among whom fornications, idolatry, adultery, effeminacy, male lust, theft, avarice, drunkenness, slander and rapacity were common. He prepares, moreover, by this catalogue of vices, a transition to pursue the correction of fornication, and therefore he puts that first.

units.la: Videtur hic locus quibusdā aliquato durior, quod ea vicia, quæ leuioris momēti videntur, cum grauioribus coniungit, eidemq; poenæ subijcit, nempe priuationi regni cælorū, cum tamē certū sit, vt gradꝰ sunt in peccatis, quorū aliud alio est grauius, ita & gradus esse pœnarū. Vtpote simplex scortatio nō est eadem grauitate qua est adulterium, mollicies, & masculorum concubitus: & ista rursus non tam sunt enormia, quā est cultus simulacrorū, quo in primā tabulā peccatur, deinde auaritia minus habet delicti quā furtū & rapacitas, siquidem illa iuxta vim Græcæ dictionis affectus quidam est plus habendi quā sit necesse. Aliud enim omnis non est plura appetere quā par sit, suaq; tenacis retinere, quā q aliorū sunt per furtū & rapinā auferre. Et peccatum ebrietatis plerisq; prorsus nullum videtur, certè ipsorum iudicio indignum, quod è regno Dei excludat.
units.tr: This passage may seem somewhat harsh to some, because he joins vices which seem of lesser weight with the graver ones and subjects them to the same punishment, namely exclusion from the kingdom of heaven. Yet it is certain that, as there are degrees in sins, one being graver than another, so there are also degrees of punishment. Thus simple fornication is not of the same gravity as adultery, effeminacy and intercourse with men; and these again are not so monstrous as the worship of images, by which the first table of the law is violated. Then avarice has less guilt than theft and rapacity, since avarice, according to the force of the Greek word, is a certain disposition to have more than is necessary. For it is one thing not to desire more than is fitting and to hold tightly to what one has, and another to take away from others by theft and robbery. And drunkenness seems to most people to be no sin at all, at least by their own judgment not worthy of excluding someone from the kingdom of God.

units.la: ἀσέλγεια
units.tr: lewdness [ἀσέλγεια]

units.la: Sciendū igitur, Apostolū nō hic quæ sint futurę peccatorū istorū pœnę describere, sed omnibus hoc dare, quod priuent regno Dei. Priuatos uero regno Dei, alia alios pœna manet. Vt enim venenū quodcunq; hoc in se habet, vt vita spoliet, licet aliud alio sit fortius, acerbioréq; morte adferat, ita iniusticia omnis regno Dei excludit, licet aliam alia grauitate sua excellat, maioresq; pœnas adferat. Non est autē vt flagitia quæ hic recensentur, singula explicemus. Sunt enim aliàs minus nota, & ab ipsis
units.tr: It must therefore be understood that the Apostle is not here describing what the future punishments of these sins will be, but is giving to all of them this result: that they deprive one of the kingdom of God. For those deprived of the kingdom of God, a different punishment awaits different people. Just as every poison has in itself the power to strip one of life, and although one is stronger than another and brings a more bitter death, so all injustice excludes from the kingdom of God, although one surpasses another in gravity and brings heavier punishments. It is not necessary for us to explain each of the crimes listed here one by one. For some are less known at other times, and are condemned by the Gentiles themselves, with the one exception of idolatry.

units.la: Simile.
units.tr: Similar.

units.la: gentibus damnata, vna dempta eidololatria.
units.tr: condemned by the Gentiles themselves, idolatry alone excepted.

units.la: Atq; hæc eratis quidā, sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis, sed iustificati estis p nomē domini Iesu, & p spiritū dei nostri.
units.tr: And some of you were such, but you have been washed, you have been sanctified, you have been justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God.

units.la: 1 Aut tacitę illorū cogitationi occurrit, quā poterant dicere: Quod si tales regnum Dei nō acquirent, neq; nos illud acquiremus. Tales enim fuimus. Cōcedit igitur, tales eos fuisse, sed declarat fuisse quondam talem, iam vero nō esse, sed per gratia Christi ab his vicijs emū datū, iusticiam accepisse, aliud esse q non solū fuisse, sed adhuc esse. Q.d. Scio quod olim tales fueritis. Id vero uos condemnare, regnoq; Dei excludere nō potest, posteaquam lauacro Christi abluti, purgati, sanctificati & iustificati estis, modò curetis, ne in pristinam immundicie relabamini. 2 Aut admonet eos acceptæ mūdationis, osteditq; quàm sit absurdū si post ablutione pristinę immundiciæ, post sanctificationē spiritus & fidei iustificationem, velint ad eafdē sordes recurrere, iterumq; fieri ppha ni, & iusticiā per fidē Christi acceptā prioris vitæ iniusticia cōmutare, atq; ita gratiæ Christi contumeliam inferre. Quæ est enim ratio abluendi, si licet sordibus pristinis iterūpolluiīque ratio sanctificandi, si vita prophana regno Dei non excludit? quæ iustificandi, si ad veram felicitatem nihil obest iniusticiæ studium?
units.tr: (1) Or the Apostle answers a thought they could have silently entertained: "If such people do not gain the kingdom of God, neither shall we gain it, for we were such." He grants, then, that they were such, but he points out that they were once such and are no longer, having been freed from these vices by the grace of Christ and having received righteousness. To have been something is one thing; to still be it is another. In effect he says: "I know that you were once like this. But that past cannot exclude you from the kingdom of God, now that you have been washed, cleansed, sanctified and justified by the laver of Christ, provided only that you take care not to fall back into your former filthiness." (2) Or he reminds them of the cleansing they have received, and shows how absurd it would be, after the washing away of their former uncleanness, after sanctification by the Spirit and justification by faith, to wish to return to the same filth, to become profane again, and to exchange the righteousness received through faith in Christ for the unrighteousness of their former life, and so to heap insult on the grace of Christ. For what is the point of washing if they may be polluted again by their old filth? What is the point of sanctifying if a profane life does not shut them out of the kingdom of God? What is the point of justifying if the pursuit of unrighteousness does nothing to hinder true happiness?

units.la: Obseruā vero, quod nō simpliciter dicit: Et hęc eratis, sed & hæc eratis quidam, ne omnes tam enormium flagitiorum maculis aspergat.
units.tr: I observe, however, that he does not simply say "and these you were," but "and these some of you were," so that he does not tar them all with the stains of such heinous crimes.

units.la: PER nomen domini Iesu, & per spiritum Dei nostri.) Trina maiestas Dei exprimitur hoc loco, cui in Christū credentiū ablutio, repurgatio, sanctificatio & iustificatio datur. Memint enim Dei nostri, deinde domini Iesu, tertiò & spiritussanti. Et hoc est, quod in nomen patris, ac filij & spiritussanti baptizamur. Obseruemus hic amplitudinem cœlestis gratiæ, p quam tam grauia flagitia abluuntur, & gratis remittuntur.
units.tr: "In the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God." Here the threefold majesty of God is set forth, by which washing, cleansing, sanctification and justification are given to those who believe in Christ. He mentions first "our God," then "the Lord Jesus," and thirdly "the Holy Spirit." This is what we are baptized into, the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Let us note here the greatness of heavenly grace, by which such grave crimes are washed away and freely forgiven.

units.la: Omnia mihi licent, at non omnia conducūt. Omnia mihi licent, at ego nō redigar sub ullius potestatem.
units.tr: All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient. All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anyone.

units.la: Locus hic non eodem modo exponitur, cū à veteribus tum recentioribus. Chryf. & Hier. intelligunt culpari ab Apostolo uentris ingluiem, idq; hoc loco non ob eā causam fieri, qd illa fomenta præstet scortationi, ad cuius reprehensionem transitus, vt suprà monui, paratur. Primùm omnino verum est, gulam ministram esse libidini, quod & ipsa iuxta sæculum doctorum virorum proverbia testatur, è quorum numero illud est: Sine Cerere & Baccho friget Venus, ad qd astipulatur etiam sacra scriptura, ut uidere est Ezec.16. de peccato Sodomorum. Deinde & hoc uerum est, quod Græci, præsertim Corinthij, utroq; & gulæ & libidinis nomine, ut fieri solet in emptorijs nobilibus, infames admodum fuerint, unde & Græcis κοεινθιαζεσθαι idem est atque pro genio & libidine intemperanter uiuere, si tamen id est
units.tr: This passage is not explained in the same way by the older and the more recent writers. Chrysostom and Jerome understand the Apostle to be rebuking gluttony of the belly, and they hold that this is not done here for the reason that such indulgence feeds fornication, to the rebuke of which the transition is being prepared, as I noted above. It is certainly true, first of all, that gluttony is the handmaid of lust, as the proverbs of learned men of the age also attest, among them the saying: "Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus grows cold." Holy Scripture too agrees with this, as may be seen in Ezekiel 16 concerning the sin of Sodom. Second, it is also true that the Greeks, and the Corinthians especially, were notoriously infamous for both gluttony and lust, as often happens in famous brothels; hence "to Corinthianize" [κορινθιάζεσθαι] means among the Greeks the same as to live intemperately for pleasure and lust, if indeed that is to live, and not rather to defile and extinguish life itself. But this interpretation, though plausible on these two grounds, has its difficulties.

units.la: viuere, & nō magis ipsam vitā cōspurcare & extinguere. Duabus hisce rationib. vero similis est istorū expositio. Quod si ea placet, erūt ista, omnia licent, & escæ vētri & vēter escis, uoces nō Apostoli, sed eorū qui intēperantiam gulæ & Christianę libertatis, & naturalis dispositio nis argumento defensabant, ab Apostolo p mi mesim in seipsum tráslatę, & præuia concessio ne ad correctionem adaptatæ, quā attexit, cū dicit, at non oía expediunt, at ego sub nullius potestatem redigar, at Deus & hunc & illas de struet. Quasi dicat. Gulæ uestræ prætexitis ciborū libertate quā agnosco quidē. Nam oía, fateor, mihi, quæ huiusmodi sunt, licent, at interea etiam atq; etiam uidendum est quid conducat, quid non. Nom enim oía conducunt. Deinde videndum etiā est, ne amissa, quā prętexitis libertate serui uentris reddamini, iam nihil mi nus quàm liberi. Ad hæc, prætexitis etiā ipsam dispositionē naturæ, qua escæ deputatæ sunt ventri, & uenter escis, quam & ipse agnosco: at considerandum est, quā illa sit trāsitoria, ne plus æquo ventri seruientes & escis indulgentes, quæ Deus olim abolebit, offendamus in rebus spiritalib. & ęternis. Ambr. hęc exposit de licito sumptu p dicandi Euágelij, à quo se Apostolus dicat abstinere, quod videat illū Euágelij cursui ppter pseudapostolos nō cōducere, deinde captiuū reddere quodámodo ministrū Christi in eorū seruitute, à quib. ille victus sustentatione accipit. At quomodo hæc sentētia vel præcedentib. uel subsequentib. adaptatur, nō ponit. Erafm⁹ in paraphrasi videtur fluctua re, incertus, quā sententiam ponat. Partim. n. hanc q Ambrosij est ponit, partim aliā quandā attingit, cū dicit: De cibis nihil veto uesscatur quisq; quib. velit, at fœdā libidinē dáno. Neq; .n. vt uenter escis dedicatus est, ita corpus dedicatum est spurcæ libidini. Ista videntur hoc velle, qd alia sit ratio escarū q scortationis. Escas deputari inter licita, quib. liberè sit vtendum, modò conducant, scortatione uero tanquam illicitam & noxiam esse fugiendam.
units.tr: If that view is accepted, then the words "All things are lawful for me; food is for the belly and the belly for food" are not the Apostle's own, but the words of those who defended the intemperance of gluttony by appeal to the liberty of Christians and the natural arrangement of things. The Apostle takes them up in a figure of speech, turning them against themselves, and by a preliminary concession he adapts them to the correction that follows, where he says: "but not all things are expedient," and: "but I will not be brought under anyone's power," and: "but God will destroy both this and those." As if he were saying: "You plead the liberty of foods, which I do acknowledge. For all such things, I admit, are lawful for me; yet in the meantime one must look again and again at what is expedient and what is not. For not all things are expedient. Further, one must also see to it that, by losing the liberty you plead, you do not become slaves of the belly, and so no more free than before. Moreover, you plead the very arrangement of nature, by which food is appointed for the belly and the belly for food, and this too I acknowledge. But it must be considered how transitory this arrangement is, lest in serving the belly beyond measure and indulging in food, which God will one day abolish, we offend in spiritual and eternal matters." Ambrose explains these words of the lawful expense of preaching the gospel, from which the Apostle says he abstains, because he sees that such maintenance does not help the course of the gospel on account of the false apostles, and because it would in a sense make him a minister of Christ captive to their service, from whom he would receive his livelihood. But he does not show how this sentence fits either what comes before or what follows. Erasmus, in his paraphrase, seems to waver, uncertain which view to adopt. For he partly gives this view, which is Ambrose's, and partly touches on another when he says: "Let no one forbid anything concerning foods, let him eat what he wishes, but I condemn foul lust. For just as the belly is devoted to food, the body is not devoted to filthy lust." These words seem to intend that foods are a different matter from fornication: foods are reckoned among lawful things, which may be freely used provided they are useful, whereas fornication, as unlawful and harmful, must be shunned.

units.la: Mea sententia est ista. Quā fugiēda uobis sit ô Corinthij, omnis scortatio, poteratis uel meo exéplo discere, qui etiam licitis abstineo, ubi intellexero illa non conducere, deinde stu diosè caueo, ne illorum seruituti subijciar. Et licet escæ & uenter res sint naturaliter coniun ctæ, non tamen utor illarum iure, ubi non conducit, considerans quàm sint olim destruendę ut indignæ sint, quarum gratia in res æternas peccem. Cum ergo à cibis, rebus licitis, ubi nō conducūt, abstineo, quàto magis cauendasunt illicita, è quorum numero est & scortatio.
units.tr: My own view is this. That all fornication must be shunned by you, O Corinthians, you could have learned even from my example, since I abstain even from lawful things when I understand that they are not expedient, and I carefully take care not to be made subject to their slavery. And although food and the belly are naturally joined, I do not use the right to them where it is not expedient, considering how they are to be destroyed in time, being unworthy things for whose sake I might sin against eternal things. Since, then, I abstain from foods, which are lawful things, where they are not expedient, how much more must unlawful things be avoided, among which is fornication.

units.la: OBSER.
units.tr: OBSERVATION.

units.la: OMNIA mihi licēt.) Loc⁹ hic nos docet q sint in usu rerū licitarū cosideranda. Licita uarijs circūstantijs aliquādo ita grauātur, vt Christiano homini iá nó sint licita. Quędam.n. licita quidem sunt, sed nō cōducunt. Talis est cibus per offendiculū proximi sumptus. Tale etiá est stipendiū propter Euangelij prædicatio nē datū, ubi id cedit in detrimentum Euágelij. Rursus qdam & licēt & coducunt. Talia erant q Paulus faciebat libero spiritu ad hoc ut aliquos lucrifaceret, cum Iudęis tanquá sub lege cōstitutᵒ, vetitis cibis abstinēs, cum Gentib.tā quá à legis iugo liber, quibuslibet uescens.
units.tr: "All things are lawful for me." This passage teaches us what must be considered in the use of lawful things. Lawful things are sometimes so burdened by various circumstances that they are no longer lawful for a Christian. Some things are indeed lawful but do not profit: food eaten to the stumbling of a neighbour is one such, and so is a stipend given for preaching the gospel when it turns to the gospel's harm. On the other hand, some things are both lawful and profitable. Such were the things Paul did in his free spirit, so that he might win some: among the Jews, as one under the law, he abstained from forbidden foods; among the Gentiles, as one free from the yoke of the law, he ate whatever was set before him.

units.la: Eorū uero q illicita sunt, ut sunt oía iniusta, legi Dei repugnātia, nihil cōducit. Sūt.n. ut iniusta oía, ita & noxia, unde damnatur uox illa impiorum, Faciamus mala vt eueniat bona. Quæ diuinitus disponuntur, aliam habet rationem. Illicitum est discipulo prodere pceptorem. At disponente Deo semel illicitum hoc facinus plurimum attulit utilitatis. Illicitū est crucifigere insonte, nedum filium Dei omniū saluato rem. Verūm hoc semel factum profuit toti orbi. At q huiusmodi sunt, nobis non sunt imitabilia, nisi expresso mandato Dei ad illa adigamur, queadmodū Abrahā iubebatur maċtare filium suū, & Israelitę per fraudē spoliare Ægyptios. Proinde impia erat sententia Rom.pon. qua subitum & improuisum Templariorū interitum decernebat, dicens: Etsi nō licet per viam iusticiæ, licet tamen per via expedientiæ, q vox plané erat digna Rom.pont. Quid aliud dicebat Caiphas: Expedit, aiebat, ut pereat unus homo, ne tota gēs pereat. Imo crudelior & iniquior erat Rom. Caiaphæ uox. Siquidem non vnius hominis, sed tot millium necem, eamq; non iudiciariam & legitimam, sed violentam administrandam decernebat.
units.tr: Things that are unlawful, however, such as all that is unjust and contrary to the law of God, bring no profit. For just as all unjust things are harmful, so the saying of the wicked, "Let us do evil that good may come," is condemned. Things that God arranges by his providence have a different account. It is unlawful for a disciple to betray his teacher, yet when God so ordered it, this once-unlawful deed brought great benefit. It is unlawful to crucify the innocent, much less the Son of God, the Saviour of all; yet this deed, once done, profited the whole world. But such things are not to be imitated by us, unless we are driven to them by an express command of God, as Abraham was commanded to slay his son, and the Israelites were ordered to despoil the Egyptians by deceit. Therefore the sentence of the Roman pontiff was impious, which decreed the sudden and unforeseen destruction of the Templars, saying: "Although it is not lawful by the way of justice, it is nevertheless lawful by the way of expediency." That word was plainly worthy of the Roman pontiff. What else did Caiaphas say? "It is expedient," he said, "that one man should die, lest the whole nation perish." Indeed, the words of the Roman pontiff were even crueler and more iniquitous than those of Caiaphas. For Caiaphas decreed the death of one man, whereas the pontiff decreed the death of many thousands, and that carried out not by judicial and lawful process but by violence.

units.la: At de istis non est hic locus. In reb. licitis qdam consideranda nobis ab Apostolo proponuntur. 1 Primùm, an conducant, hoc est, an vsus illorum nō cedat in dānum proximi. Qd si fuerit, iam ex licitis fiunt illicita pro loco videlicet & tempore. In se nanq; quæ licita sunt, non mutantur. 2 Deinde, an nō officiant nostræ libertati qua dfii sumus omnium. Iniustū enim est, ut prodita libertate, quaChristus nos donauit, serui reddamur elementorum, cū sub vnius dfii potestatem constituti simus¹, qui ab omnium nos seruitute redemit. Admonemur ergo ut inuersionem illam caueamus, qua fieri potest, ut dum in temerario rerum licitarum v su libertatem prætexímus, libertatem amittamus, iam non dfii, sed serui eorum de quorum libero usu frustra gloriamur.
units.tr: But these matters have no place here. Among lawful things the Apostle sets before us certain points to be considered. First, whether they are profitable, that is, whether their use does not turn to the harm of a neighbour. If it does, then lawful things become unlawful, according to place and time. For things that are lawful in themselves are not changed. Second, whether they do not hinder our liberty, by which we are made servants of all. For it is wrong that, having surrendered the liberty which Christ gave us, we should become slaves to the elements, since we have been placed under the power of one lord, who has redeemed us from the slavery of all. We are therefore warned to guard against that reversal by which, while we pretend liberty in the rash use of lawful things, we lose our liberty, and become no longer free men but slaves of those things whose free use we vainly boast of.

units.la: Escę uētri, & uēter escís, Deus aūt & hūc & illas abolebit. Corpus uero non scortationi, sed domino, & dominus corpori, Deus aūt & dominū suscitauit, & nos suscitabit per potentiam suam.
units.tr: "Foods are for the belly, and the belly for foods; but God will abolish both this and these." "The body is not for fornication, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body; and God has raised up the Lord and will raise us up by his power."

units.la: Ista lucē adferunt præcedentib. Nam primū declarant, de quib. rebus licitis loquatur Apostolus: videlicet de cibis, quorum usus liber est fidelibus, ne quisquam illud: Omnia mihi licent, uniuersaliter de quibuscūq; reb. intelligat, cū certū sit ex hoc loco Apostolū loq de escis, & alioqui nō oía sint licita, sed multa diuinitus prohibita & illicita. Huiusmodi sententiæ non sunt ultra authoris mentem diuexandæ, qualis est & illa qua alibi dicit: Omnibus omnia factus sum, & qua Christus Matt. 5. dicit: Ego autem dico vobis, nolite omnino iurare. Neq; enim in universum omne iusiurandum tanquam malum abijcit, cum tota scriptura, & ipsa iurisiurandi ratio reclamet, sed consuetudinem iurandi pravam illam & peruersam, qua Iudæi à scribis & pharisæis seducti peccabant, condemnat. Deinde uelut applicat, quod dixit, ad propositum. Q. d. Primùm naturaliter quidè cibus uentri, & uenter cibo adaptatus est, ut nihil sit illiciti, si cibus permittatur uentri, & uéter cibo. At cum res istæ sint perituræ, utpote quas dominus olim abolebit, non licet illarum gratia quæ potiora sunt turbare, sed maior est habeda regni Christi fraternæq; charitatis ac nostræ salutis ratio q̄ cibi ac uentris, utut naturaliter coniunctorum. Iam si id faciendum est in his naturalibus ac licitis, quàto magis in ijs quæ & illicita sunt, & contra naturæ dispositionem. Corpus etenim nō est ut cibo ita & scortationi deputatū, nec scortatio corpori.
units.tr: These words throw light on what precedes. For first they make clear which lawful things the Apostle is speaking of, namely foods, whose use is free for the faithful. So no one should take the saying "All things are lawful for me" as applying universally to all things whatever, since it is certain from this passage that the Apostle is speaking of foods; otherwise not all things are lawful, but many are forbidden and unlawful by God. Sayings of this kind must not be wrested beyond the author's meaning, such as that other one where he says, "I have become all things to all men," and that where Christ says in Matthew 5: "But I say to you, do not swear at all." For he does not reject every oath universally as evil, since the whole of Scripture and the very reason for oaths cry out against that, but he condemns the wicked and perverse custom of swearing, by which the Jews, seduced by the scribes and Pharisees, were sinning. Then he applies what he has said to his purpose, as if to say: First, indeed, food is by nature suited to the belly and the belly to food, so that there is nothing unlawful if food is allowed to the belly and the belly to food. But since these things are perishable, as the Lord will one day abolish them, it is not lawful to disturb for their sake the things that are more important. The consideration of the kingdom of Christ, of brotherly love and of our salvation is greater than that of food and belly, though these are naturally joined. Now if this must be done in these natural and lawful things, how much more in those things that are both unlawful and contrary to the disposition of nature? For the body is not destined for fornication any more than food is destined for the belly, nor fornication for the body.

units.la: ESCAE uētri.) Subintelligēdū est aliquid. Erasmus adiecit, destinatæ sunt, & commodè. Nihil enim uideo quod reclamet. Est nanque ista pars corporis diuinitus ad hoc destinata, ut alimenta accepta concoquat, & in reliqua corporis membra digerat. Et escæ ad hoc paratę sunt, ut uētri ad alendum corpus administrēt. In ea uerò particula, qua dicit, Corpus autem nō scortationi sed domino, & dominus corpori, non inuenio quo uerbo utrunq; membrū absoluam. Nam corpus quidem nostrū domino destinatū, uel cōsecratum esse, possum dicere: at uicissim dominū destinatū esse corpori nostro uel consecratū, non item. Est omnino quæ dā coniunctio corporū nostrorū ac domini, at què uno uerbo exprimi nequeat. Corpus enim nostrum ita coiunctum est domino ut illi subiit, dominus uerò corpori nostro coniunctus est, ut illi præsit. Notandum hic est, quod non dixit: Escæ corpori, & corpus escis, sed escæ uentri, & uenter escis. Nec dixit: Venter domino, & dominus uentri, sed corpus domino, & dominus corpori, ubi omnino honestius de corpore loquitur q̄ de uentre, ut intelligamus corpora nostra, licet uentris ac ciborū usu necesse habeant, escis tamen nō esse, sed domino deputata ac consecrata, ut non uentri & escis sed domino uiuamus. Et ista obseruatio etsi nō per omnia, nōnihil tamen astipulatur Chrysost.& Hiero.expositioni, qui hæc uerba contra gulæ uicium posita esse intelligunt. Licet enim de naturali uētre, & escis illius loquatur Apostolus, apparet tamē illū gulæ intēperantiam duplici argumēto ab illius organo & materia sumpto contemptā reddere. Primum est à uilitate & uentris & escarū. Ea nota est omnibus, uentris & escarū conditione sensate expendentibus, quos ipsa fallē uentris & escarū uocabula statim admonēt, quæ sit hic iminundicia quę molestia ac uilitas. Alterū est ab utroque corruptione & futuro interitu, cuius gratia certè minus nobis debet gulæ studium esse, cum sciamus illius & organum & mate-
units.tr: "Foods for the belly." Something must be understood here. Erasmus added "are destined for," and rightly so, for I see nothing that contradicts it. This part of the body has been divinely destined for this purpose, to digest the food received and to distribute it to the other members of the body. And foods are prepared for this purpose, that they may serve the belly in nourishing the body. But in the clause where he says, "The body is not for fornication but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body," I do not find a single word by which I can complete each member. For I can say that our body is destined or consecrated to the Lord; but conversely, that the Lord is destined or consecrated to our body, I cannot say. There is indeed a certain union of our bodies with the Lord, yet it cannot be expressed in one word. For our body is so joined to the Lord that it is subject to him, while the Lord is so joined to our body that he presides over it. It must be noted here that he did not say "Food for the body and the body for food," but "Food for the belly and the belly for food." Nor did he say "The belly for the Lord and the Lord for the belly," but "The body for the Lord and the Lord for the body," where he speaks of the body far more honourably than of the belly. Thus we understand that our bodies, although they need the use of the belly and of foods, are nevertheless not destined and consecrated to food but to the Lord, so that we live not for the belly and food but for the Lord. And this observation, though not in every respect, nevertheless somewhat agrees with the exposition of Chrysostom and Jerome, who understand these words to be spoken against the vice of gluttony. For although the Apostle speaks of the natural belly and its foods, it nonetheless appears that he renders the intemperance of gluttony contemptible by a twofold argument drawn from the organ and the matter of it. The first is from the baseness both of the belly and of foods. This is known to all who thoughtfully weigh the condition of the belly and of foods, whom the very words "belly" and "foods" at once remind of what filthiness, what annoyance and what baseness is here. The second is from the corruption and future destruction of both, for which reason surely the pursuit of gluttony ought to matter less to us, since we know that both its organ and its matter are fleeting things destined to perish soon.

units.la: riam res esse fluxas & breui interituras.
units.tr: Things that are fleeting and destined to perish soon.

units.la: DEVS abolebit.)
units.tr: GOD will abolish.)

units.la: Colos.2 dat escis Apostolus id imbecillitatis per extenuationē, quod ipso usu intereat & corrumpantur, notās eos, qui multum religionis in rebus hisce corrupti bilibus collocabāt. Hic uero Deum ipsum dicit & uentrem & escas pariter aboliturū. Hoc sanè licet uniuersaliter in fine mundi sit futurum, quotidie tamen per mortem fieri uidemus quidem, at parum consideramus. Ergo opus Dei est nō minus abolere ac destruere & uentrē & escas, q̄ condere. Et qd' de uentre & escis dicitur, idem & de reliquis uoluptatis generibus cogitandū est. Obserua uero quod nō dicit de corpore, esse illud abolendū à Deo sicut uentrem. Corpus enim manebit, ille uero uentris, usus qui huius est uitæ, abolebitur.
units.tr: In Colos.2 the Apostle diminishes meats by this mark of weakness: they perish through their very use and are corrupted. He rebukes those who placed much of religion in these corruptible things. Here, however, he says that God himself will abolish both the belly and meats alike. Certainly, although this will happen universally at the end of the world, we see it happening daily through death, yet we give it little thought. Therefore the work of God is no less to abolish and destroy both belly and meats than to create them. What is said of the belly and meats should also be understood of the other kinds of pleasure. Observe, however, that he does not say the body is to be abolished by God as the belly is. For the body will remain; what will be abolished is the belly, that is, the use of it which belongs to this life.

units.la: ABOLEBIT.)
units.tr: WILL ABOLISH.)

units.la: Hoc non ita intelligēdum est, ut putemus membrū hoc prorsus è corporibus nostris in die resurrectionis tollendum. Græcè est καταργεῖσθαι, i. ociosa reddet. Substantia mēbri huius non exterminabit de corporibus nostris, sed eo ministerio corruptionis quo nunc distinetur, per gloriam incorruptionis & immortalitatis futuræ liberabit quemadmodū & reliquas creaturas omnes, quā de re uidere est in Ro. ca.8. Nec est, uti dicat quisquā quę ergo erit illius necessitas, si hoc ministerio liberabitur? An habebimus mēbra, quorū nullus erit usus? Ipsum σῶμα corporum nostrorū, & ipsum decus exiget, ut nullū membrorū pereat, cū ne capillus quidē de capitib. nostris sit teste domino periturus. Nec manuū nec pedū, nec dentiū is certè, quē nunc habemus, tunc erit usus, nec tamen putandū est cor pora nostra iltis exptia iństat trucorū futura.
units.tr: This is not to be understood as if we thought this member will be altogether removed from our bodies on the day of resurrection. The Greek is καταργεῖσθαι [katargeisthai], that is, will make idle. The substance of this member will not be taken out of our bodies, but it will be freed from the service of corruption, in which it is now engaged, through the glory of future incorruption and immortality, just as all the other creatures will be; on this matter see Rom. 8. Nor should anyone ask what need there will be for it if it is freed from this service. Shall we have members with no use? The very form and beauty of our bodies will require that no member perish, since not even a hair of our heads will perish, as the Lord witnesses. Certainly there will be no use for hands, feet or teeth such as we now have, yet we must not think our bodies will be useless because they lack those things.

units.la: CORPVS aut nō scortationi.)
units.tr: CORPVS aut nō scortationi.)

units.la: Scortatio igitur hoc peccati habet, quod dispositioi diuinæ repugnat. Cuiusq; instrumenti peccatū est abusus. Abusus corporis est scortatio. Ergo scortatio peccatū est corporis, & malæ uoluntatis corpore abutētis. Sentētia ista reluctatur opinioni hominū carnaliū, qui non considera ta diuina dispositiōe, naturales corporis actus esse iudicāt, quibus affectuū libidini seruitur, cum reuera non sit naturale, quicquid naturę ut est à Deo condita, repugnat. Edere quidem naturale est, si legitimè ad corporis sustētatio nem edatur, si uero pro gulę intēperantia, iam naturale nō est. Ita & mulieri comisceri uirū, naturale est, si id iuxta ordinatione diuinā legitimē fiat, si secus, nō itē. Quare? Quia ut hic Apost.dicit: Corpus scortatiōi deputatū nō est.
units.tr: Fornication therefore has this character of sin: it runs against the divine ordering. The sin of every instrument is its abuse, and the abuse of the body is fornication. So fornication is a sin of the body, committed by a bad will that abuses the body. This sentence opposes the opinion of carnal men, who, not considering the divine ordering, judge the natural acts of the body to be those by which they serve the lust of the passions. But whatever runs against nature as God created it is not natural in fact. To eat is natural, if it is done lawfully for sustaining the body; but if it is done from intemperance of the palate, it is no longer natural. So too for a man to lie with a woman is natural if it is done lawfully according to the divine ordinance, but not otherwise. Why? Because, as the Apostle says here: the body is not destined for fornication.

units.la: SED dño, & dñs corpori.)
units.tr: SED dño, & dñs corpori.)

units.la: Quæ sit corporis & dñi coniunctio, infrà statim declarabit.
units.tr: He will show immediately below what the union of the body and the Lord is.

units.la: DEVS aūt & dñm suscitauit.)
units.tr: DEVS aūt & dñm suscitauit.)

units.la: Hoc opponit ei qd' de uentre & escis dixit, uidelicet, Deus aūt & hunc & illas destruet. Poterat enim dicere: Atqui tota nostra corpora nō modo uentres abolebūtur. Occurrit dicēs: Moriētur qui dē, uerum excitabūtur à Deo. Cōmendat autē corporū nostrorū dignitatē: primū à cōiunctiōe Christi, quod argumentū iam cōsequenter tractabit. Deinde à perēnitate & futura resurre. surrectiónis gloria, cū dicit: Deus autem & dñm suscitauit, & nos suscitabit, &c. Vt igitur à studio gulæ auocát argumēta à ueneris & escarū uilitate & corruptione supta ita à scortatioe p corporū nostrorū dignitate & futurā gloriā auocamur. Quod aūt futura corporū nostrorū resurrectione argumēto resurrectiónis Christi pteritę cōfirmat, pro suo more facit, vt fidei nostræ cōsulat, simulq; admoneat corporū nostrorū resurrectione ex Christi virtute & cōmunione cōtare. vnde & Christus dixit: Ego sum resurrectio & vita. Hac de re vide Rom. 8. At infrà in lam cap. 15. fusius ex proposito tractabit.
units.tr: This answers what he said about the belly and meats, namely, "But God will destroy both this and those." For he could have said: "Indeed, not only the bellies but our whole bodies will be abolished." He meets this by saying: they will indeed die, but they will be raised up by God. He commends the dignity of our bodies: first from their union with Christ, which he will treat in the following argument; then from their everlasting existence and the glory of the future resurrection, when he says: "But God both raised up the Lord and will raise us up," etc. So just as we are drawn away from devotion to the belly by arguments from the baseness, corruption and passing character of foods and of sexual pleasure, so we are drawn away from fornication by the dignity of our bodies and their future glory. That he confirms the future resurrection of our bodies by the argument of Christ's past resurrection is in keeping with his custom, so that he may provide for our faith and at the same time remind us that the resurrection of our bodies depends on the power and communion of Christ. Hence Christ also said: "I am the resurrection and the life." See Rom. 8 on this matter. But below, in chapter 15, he will treat it more fully and deliberately.

units.la: PER potentiā suam.) Vnica dictione omnium incredulorū ora obstruit, nisi per summam imprudentiā omniū oculis ac mentib. occurrēte Dei omnipotentiā negare velint. Solet resurrectionis articulo potentiam Dei adiungere, vt Rom. 1. & Eph. 1. vbi magnitudinem potentiæ Dei in resurrectione Christi declarata esse scribit. Vt ergo futuræ resurrectionis fidem nobis faciat, recte hæc duo coniungit, resurrectionem scilicet Christi, & potentiam Dei.
units.tr: PER potentiā suam.) By this single word he stops the mouths of all unbelievers, unless they are willing to deny, through the greatest folly, the omnipotence of God, which presents itself to the eyes and minds of all. He is accustomed to join the power of God to the article of the resurrection, as in Rom. 1 and Eph. 1, where he writes that the greatness of God's power was displayed in the resurrection of Christ. So, to give us faith in the future resurrection, he rightly joins these two things: the resurrection of Christ and the power of God.

units.la: 1 An nescitis, qd corpora uestra mēbra sunt Christi? Nū igitur tollens membra Christi faciā scorti mēbra? Absit. An nescitis qd qui adglutinatur scorto, unum corpus est? Redigentur enim, inquit, duo in carnem unam. At qui adglutinatur domino, unus spiritus est. Fugite fornicationē. Omne peccatū, qdcunq; fecerit homo extra corpus est, sed qui scortatur, in proprium corpus peccat. An nescitis quod corpus uestrum templū est habitātis in uobis spiritussancti quē habetis à Deo? Et non estis uestri iuris. Nam empti estis precio: glorificate igitur Deum in corpore uestro, & in spiritu uestro quæ sunt Dei.
units.tr: 1 Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a harlot? Far from it. Do you not know that he who is joined to a harlot is one body? For, it says, the two shall become one flesh. But he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit. Flee fornication. Every sin that a man commits is outside the body, but he who commits fornication sins against his own body. Do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, whom you have from God? And you are not your own. For you were bought with a price. Glorify God therefore in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.

units.la: Versatur Apost. diligēter in ijs argumētis q- bº scortatiōis peccatū & immunditiā Corinthijs adimere queat, ut appareat illos isti vicio vehementer obnoxios fuisse. In superioribus, tribus argumentis corpora nostra concernentibus usus est, vtpote quod ad scortandum nō sunt diuinitus deputata. Deinde quod cōsecrata sunt dño, ac cōiunctionis illius dignitate cohonestata. Tertiō, quod olim sunt excitāda p potentiam Dei, qua Christus excitatus est. Prēsenti vero loco primū argumentū illud cōiunctiōis Christi, quod suprà breuiter attigit, declarat & amplificat. Deinde alia tria adiungit. Primū, à singulari quadā scortationis cōditione, quā id peccati propriam habet. Secundum ab ea dignitate, qua corpora nostra tepla sunt spiritus sancti. Tertium à iure redemptionis, quod in nos habet qui nos redemit.
units.tr: The Apostle works diligently with these arguments by which he can take away from the Corinthians the sin and uncleanness of fornication, so that it appears they were greatly guilty of this vice. In the earlier passages he used three arguments concerning our bodies: first, that they have not been divinely appointed for fornication; second, that they have been consecrated to the Lord and honoured by the dignity of that union; third, that they will one day be raised by the power of God, by which Christ was raised. In the present passage he first declares and amplifies the argument of Christ's union, which he touched on briefly above. Then he adds three other arguments. The first is from a particular condition of fornication, which has a peculiar character of sin. The second is from the dignity by which our bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit. The third is from the right of redemption, which he has over us who redeemed us.

units.la: AN nescitis.) Etiā hic, quēadmodū & in superiori causa crebris interrogationib. instādo & vrgendo uehemens est & simul ostendit, q Corinthiorū incogitantiam satis admirari ne-
units.tr: DO you not know? Here too, as in the earlier argument, he is vehement, pressing and urging with frequent questions, and at the same time he shows that one can hardly wonder enough at the thoughtlessness of the Corinthians, how they could be ignorant

units.la: queat quomodo ignorare queant: qua sint dignitate prędita in Christo ipsorū corpora: q ex scortatione mēbra Christi fiāt mēbra scorti: q sit peccatis huiº peculiaris cōditio: quomodo sint corpora ipsorū tēplū spiritussancti, &c. unde facile possent colligere, q sit hoc peccatū de testandū ac fugiēdum homini Christiano. Hoc est qd' illud, ut ignoratis, tertiō repetit, quemadmodū & suprà hoc ipso cap. fecit.
units.tr: of the dignity which their bodies possess in Christ; that from fornication the members of Christ become members of a harlot; what the particular condition of this sin is; how their bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, and so on. From these things they could easily conclude what kind of sin this is, which a Christian man ought to detest and flee. This is why he repeats the phrase "Do you not know" a third time, just as he did earlier in this same chapter.

units.la: QVOD corpora vestra mēbra sunt Christi. Qd' s dixit, corpus non scortationi, sed dño, & dñs corpori, hic declarat. Ea est inter dñm & corpora nostra coniunctio, q est inter caput & mēbra. Tota Christi ecclesia, corpº Christi est, quē habet capitis loco. In hoc corpore membrū est qsq; Christianus. Hęc p similitudinē dicitur, de qua nonnulla habebimus infrà ca. 12. Nō est aūt frustra, qd' nō dicit: An nescitis, qd' mēbra Christi estis? id quod generaliꝰ erat, sed qd' corpora vestra mēbra sūt Christi? Nō hoc deo dicit, qd' ab hac dignitate aias credetiū ex cludat, quasi sola corpora nostra sint membra Christi, sed qd' ita quadrabat, ppositō. Lucatur. n. cōtra peccatū scortatiōis, quo potissimū corpora polluūtur. Ideo q illorū sit dignitas in mediū adducit, vt detestandam reddat scortationem, per quam illa cōspurcantur, & quā in Christo dignitatem acceperunt, amittunt.
units.tr: THAT your bodies are members of Christ. What he said before, "the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body," he explains here. The union between the Lord and our bodies is the same as that between the head and the members. The whole Church of Christ is the body of Christ, which he has in place of a head. Every Christian is a member in this body. This is said by way of likeness, and we shall have some things to say about it below in chapter 12. It is not without reason that he does not say, "Do you not know that you are members of Christ?", which would have been more general, but "that your bodies are members of Christ?" He does not say this as if he excluded the souls of believers from this dignity, as though only our bodies were members of Christ, but because it suited his purpose. For he is arguing against the sin of fornication, by which bodies above all are polluted. So he brings forward their dignity so that fornication, by which they are defiled and lose the dignity they received in Christ, may be made detestable.

units.la: NVM igitur tollēs mēbra Christi, faciā scorti mēbra? Lá quantā temeritatē, absurditatē, & q irreligiosā improbitate habeat in se scortatio ex eo quod dixit, corpora nostra esse membra Christi, ob oculos ponit. Nō dicit: Nū tollens corpus meū faciā illud mēbrum scorti? sed, Nū tollēs mēbra Christi, faciā illa membra scorti? Quod. n. corpus uiri scorto copulatur, nō vide tur tantū habere peccatū in oculis hominū carnaliū. Ideo causam hāc aliquato exactius & religiosius expēdens, id de corporib. nostris adducit, quod nō ex natura sunt, sed ex gratia & dignitate cōiūctiōis Christi, cū dicit: nū igitur tollēs mēbra Christi, faciā scorti mēbra? Deinde nō dicit, cōiungā illa scorto, sed id ponit qd' scortatio in coniunctione scorti facit. Facit aūt illa vt scortator cū scorto vnū fiat corpus. Hoc est quod dicit, faciā illa scorti mēbra? Quantū igitur di'criminis est inter Christū & scortū, in ter illius puritatē & huius immunditiā, tantū vtiq; temeritatis & absurditatis habet scortatio, q ex mēbris Christi facit mēbra scorti, qua prophanatione quid potest geri detestabilius?
units.tr: Now, then, if I take the members of Christ, shall I make them the members of a harlot? He sets before our eyes how great the rashness, absurdity and irreligious wickedness of fornication is, given what he has said, that our bodies are members of Christ. He does not say, "Shall I take my body and make it a member of a harlot?" but, "Shall I take the members of Christ and make them members of a harlot?" For the fact that a man's body is joined to a harlot does not seem to carry much sin in the eyes of carnal men. So, weighing the matter more exactly and religiously, he brings in the point that our bodies are members not by nature but by the grace and dignity of union with Christ, when he says: "Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a harlot?" Then he does not say, "I will join them to a harlot," but names what fornication does in the union with the harlot. It does so by making the fornicator and the harlot one body. This is what he means by "make them members of a harlot." So as great as the difference is between Christ and a harlot, between his purity and her filthiness, so great is the rashness and absurdity of fornication, which makes members of Christ into members of a harlot. What profanation could be more detestable?

units.la: Illud, Tollēs, ita exponitur à Hier. vt indicetur ea corpora q scorti mēbra fiunt, sublata esse & abscisa è corpore Christi. Tollit, inquit, mēbra Christi, i. abscindit se à corpore Christi, qui iunctus est meretrici. Idē ponit & Ambr. cum dicit: Ait, quia meretrici adhærentia membra desinunt esse membra Christi. Certē non potest fieri vt mēbrum scorti sit mēbrum Christi. Quæ enim esset coniunctio Christi & scorti? Duo sunt diuersissima corpora Christi & scorti. Impossibile est igitur ut quis simul vtriusq; possit esse membrum.
units.tr: The phrase "take" is explained by Jerome as meaning that those bodies which become members of a harlot are removed and cut off from the body of Christ. "He takes away," he says, "the members of Christ, that is, he cuts himself off from the body of Christ, since he is joined to a harlot." Ambrose also says: "He says that the members that cling to a harlot cease to be members of Christ." Certainly a member of a harlot cannot be a member of Christ. For what union could there be between Christ and a harlot? The bodies of Christ and of a harlot are most utterly different. It is impossible, therefore, that anyone should be a member of both at once.

units.la: Duo itaq; dat scortationi mala, quorum illa gra-
units.tr: Fornication therefore brings two evils, of which the first is grave...

units.la: {A} In margine: ## (Christi resurrectio) la gratia uehementer fit fugienda.
units.tr: In the margin: (The resurrection of Christ) Fornication must be fled vehemently.

units.la: 1 Vnum est, quod gratiâ Christi & dignitate corporum nostrorum, qua mébra Christi sunt perdit, & è corpore Christi abscindit.
units.tr: (1) The first is that by fornication they lose the grace of Christ and the dignity of our bodies, by which they are members of Christ, and cut themselves off from the body of Christ.

units.la: 2 Alterû, quod ex mébris Christi facit mem bra scorti. Multû est per scortatione abscindi è corpore Christi. Quàm vero absurdû est, coniunctione & incorporatione Christi cómutari coniunctione & incorporatióe uilissimi & impurissimi scorti. Quâ insana est ista commutatio. Quod si ad parē aliquem dignitate essel è corpore Christi trâsitus, haberet forsan talis p mutatio nõnihil rationis. Iâ à Christo abaliena tû incorporari scorto, quis non videt, quantæ sit impudentiæ, quâtus Christi contéptus. Tur pe est in se, corpus viri nō scortationi, se matri monio & legitimo cóiugio deputatum, facere mébrum scorti, ut istâ turpitudinem homo vel sæculari sapientia & honestate præditus, meri to fugere debeat. Iam non qualecunq; corpus sed membrum Christi è corpore Christi auul suum, mébrum scorti efficere, quantum quesore meritatis habet. Si rem indignam committit, qui cum nobili sit mulieri legitimæ coniúctus, turpissimo scorto conglutinatur, quid de illo sentiendum, qui corpus Christo coniunctum, membrum constituit scorti.
units.tr: (2) The second is that it makes members of Christ into members of a harlot. To be cut off from the body of Christ by fornication is a great evil. How absurd it is, however, that union and incorporation with Christ should be exchanged for union and incorporation with the most base and impure harlot. This exchange is insane. If someone were transferred from the body of Christ to a body of equal dignity, such a change might have some reason in it. But that one should be incorporated with a harlot, cut off from Christ, who does not see how great the shamelessness and how great the contempt of Christ is? It is shameful in itself to make a man's body, which was assigned not to fornication but to marriage and lawful wedlock, into a member of a harlot, so that a man endowed with even worldly wisdom and decency should rightly flee this foulness. Now, to make a member of Christ, cut off from the body of Christ, into a member of a harlot, how much rashness that involves! If a man commits an unworthy act who, being joined to a noble lawful wife, is glued to a most foul harlot, what should we think of the man who makes a body joined to Christ into a member of a harlot?

units.la: Et hoc notandum est quod nô dicit: Nû tol létes mébra Christi, facietis ex illis mébra scor ti. Sed, Nû tollés mébra Christi, facià membra scorti. Causam hâc in se transfert, & ostendit quomodo illâ expédat, q nunquâ fit cómiffur ut ré tot modis indignam designet, ut suo illos exèplo instruat, quâ à scortatione abhorrere debeat Christiani hois animus, quoq; loco ha bere tantâ dignitatemcorporis, qua Christo in corporati sumus, ne illam iuftineat ullo pacto cómaculare, nedum prorsus abijcere, & cû vili scorto cómutare. Obserua & illud: Non dicit: Facià membra vxoris, sed, facià mébra scorti. Quia coniugiû legitimû nô diuidit quéquâ à coiunctióe Christi, diuidit verò scortatio.
units.tr: And this must be noted: he does not say, "Shall you take the members of Christ and make members of a harlot out of them?" but, "Shall I take the members of Christ and make them members of a harlot?" He transfers the case to himself, and shows how he is affected by it, so that by his own example he may teach how the mind of a Christian man ought to shrink from fornication. He wishes us to hold the dignity of the body, by which we are embodied in Christ, so that we never stain it in any way, much less cast it off entirely and exchange it for a vile harlot. Observe also this: he does not say, "I will make members of a wife," but "members of a harlot." For lawful marriage does not separate anyone from union with Christ, but fornication does separate.

units.la: AN nescitis, quod qui adglutinatur scorto, vnû corpus est? &c.) Corpus scortatoris fieri mébrû scorti p carnalé illâ adglutinationé, pri mû pro indubitato asserit, tamq; manifestum, vt mirari se ostendat, si illud ignorent, deinde p scripturæ autoritate cófirmat. Quasi itaq; ne gates p scortatione, se ex mébris Christi facere mébra scorti, ac fecû dicêtes, absit, interrogat, an ignorêt quâta sit uis scortatiôis, & adglutinatiôis uiri cû scorto. Tanta videlicet ut p illâ ex duob. corporib. fiat vnum. Cum ergo certû fit corpora credentium Christo, esse membra Christi, deinde æquè certum sit, eum qui scorto adglutinatur, vnû corpus esse cû scorto, qd aliud colligi potest, quâ p scortationem membra Christi mutari in membra scorti.
units.tr: Do you not know that he who is joined to a harlot is one body? etc.) The author states first, as something beyond doubt and so plain that he would be astonished if anyone were ignorant of it, that the body of the fornicator becomes a member of the harlot through that carnal joining. He then confirms this by the authority of Scripture. It is as if he were anticipating objections: by fornication, he asks, do we make the members of Christ into members of a harlot? Do they not know how great is the power of fornication and of a man's joining himself to a harlot? It is so great that through it two bodies become one. Since it is certain that the bodies of believers are members of Christ, and equally certain that he who is joined to a harlot is one body with her, what else can be concluded but that by fornication the members of Christ are changed into members of a harlot?

units.la: REDIGENTVR enim, inquit, duo in car nê unâ.) Probatio est, sumpta ex cap. 2. Gene. vbi scriptû est, dixisse Adamum: Hoc tandê os est ex ossibus meis & caro de carne mea, prop pterea uocabitur Virago, quoniâ deuiro lúpta
units.tr: For the two, he says, shall become one flesh.) This is the proof, taken from Genesis 2, where it is written that Adam said: "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; therefore she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man."

units.la: A est. Propterea relinquet vir patrē suum, ac matrem suam, & adhærebit uxori suæ, & erunt in carnê unam. Postremam hanc particulâ, ריחיי לבשר אחר Et erunt in carnê unâ, probâdi gratia adducit hoc loco Apoft. Mirum aût videri potest, quomodo scortatorem & scortum unû esse corpus per hunc locum probet, cum Adâ ista non de scortatione, sed de legitima viri & mulieris coniunctione dixerit. Cum tanta sit inter scortatores & legitimos coniuges diuer sitas, quomodo eadé sentétia vtrifq; potest cô petere? Primû quod ad sexû vtrarûq; partiû attinet, nihil est discriminis. Vtrinq; est vir & mulier, tâ in scortatione quâ in coniugio. Deinde quod ipsam quoq; cómixtionem & copulâ carnalé cocernit, nihil est differentiæ. Vno discrimine discernuntur, liciti & illiciti. At in isto di scrimine non est sita coadunatio ista carnalis, vnde vnum utrinq; corpus ex uiro & muliere redditur, sed magis in carnali vtriusq; sexus copula & cómixtione. Proinde tam de scortatori bº dici potest quâ de legitimis cóiugib. erunt duo in carnê unâ. Benedictio illa Dei, Crescite & multiplicamini, & replete terrâ, certè nô est nisi ad legitimos coniuges dicta. At ipsa multi plicatio humani generis per cómixtionem uiri & mulieris non minus uim suâ exerit in illis qui illegitimè cômifcentur, quâ in veris & ordinatis coniugib. Quàm ergo ista uis multipli cationis nô pendet à licito uel|illicito uiri ac mulieris cógreffu, vtvt peccent qui illicitè cô iunguntur, sed simpliciter à carnali illorum cô mixtione, tâ & ista Adę sentêtia nô astringitur ad legitimû, sed quéuis utriufq; fexª cógreffû. Ita & qd in Pf. dicitur, Vinû lętificat cor hoís, & panis cor hoís confirmat, licet magna sit furis & iusti differentia, in vtroq; tñ uerum est.
units.tr: "Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they shall be one flesh." The Apostle brings forward this last clause, "and they shall be one flesh" [ולבשר אחד], in order to prove his point. It may seem strange how he proves by this passage that the fornicator and the harlot are one body, since Adam spoke these words not of fornication but of the lawful joining of man and woman. There is such a great difference between fornicators and lawful spouses; how can the same sentence apply to both? First, as far as the sex of both parties is concerned, there is no difference: in fornication as in marriage there is a man and a woman. Next, as to the mixing itself and the carnal copulation, there is no difference either. They are distinguished by one difference only, lawful and unlawful. But that difference does not lie in this carnal union, by which one body is made out of man and woman on both sides; it lies rather in the carnal copulation and mixing of the two sexes. Therefore it can be said of the fornicator no less than of lawful spouses that "they shall be two in one flesh." That blessing of God, "Increase and multiply, and fill the earth," was certainly spoken only to lawful spouses. Yet the multiplication of the human race through the mixing of man and woman exerts its force no less in those who unlawfully mingle than in true and ordained spouses. Just as this power of multiplication does not depend on whether the union of man and woman is lawful or unlawful, though those who join unlawfully do sin, but simply on their carnal mixing, so too this sentence of Adam is not restricted to the lawful, but applies to any coming together of the two sexes. So also what is said in the Psalm, "Wine gladdens the heart of man, and bread strengthens the heart of man," is true in both cases, although there is a great difference between the wicked and the just.

units.la: AT qui adglutinatur dño, unus spiritus est.) Videlicet cum dño: ut diuersimodè inter fe habent Christus & scortû, ita & diuersimodè de illis loquitur Apoft. id quod ineptè faceret, si i dè posset & scorto simul & Christo adglutina ri, & vnû corpus cum scorto, & vnus esse spiri tus cû Christo. Iâ cû ista inter se discreta sint & diuersa, liquet fieri nô posse, vt q scorto adhæ ret, pariter possit & Christo adhærere, & cû u nû fit corpª cû scorto, vnus esse spiritª cû Chri sto. Et uide quomodo utrobiq; uerbo κολλᾶσθαι adglutinâdi vtatur. Suprà nô dixit: Qui semel atq; iterum incidit in fcortû, vnum corpus est cû scorto, sed qui scorto adglutinatur. Nô enim ex vno & altero cógreffu quifquâ mox vnûcor pus cû scorto redditur, sed ad eâ rê opus est diu tina adhæsione & tenaci adglutinatione, cuiª & Adam mentinoê fecit Gen. 2. cû dixit: Pro pterea relinquet uir patrem suum ac matrem suam. ורבק באשתו והיו לבשר אחר & adglutina bitur, ual adhærebit uxori suæ, & erunt in car nê unâ. Et Græci illud דבק reddiderût ᾰᾱθῆσεται. i. uelut adglutinatus adhærebit.
units.tr: But he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit.) Clearly with the Lord: just as Christ and the harlot stand in different relations to one another, so the Apostle speaks of them in different ways. He would be speaking absurdly if it were possible to be joined both to a harlot and to Christ at once, and to be one body with the harlot and one spirit with Christ. Since these things are so separate and different from one another, it is plain that it is impossible for one who clings to a harlot to cling equally to Christ, and since he becomes one body with the harlot, he cannot be one spirit with Christ. And notice how he uses the word for joining, κολλᾶσθαι [kollāsthai], in both places. Above he did not say: "He who has fallen into fornication once or twice is one body with the harlot," but "he who is joined to a harlot." For no one becomes at once one body with a harlot through one or another act of intercourse; this requires lasting adhesion and tenacious joining. Moses also mentioned this in Genesis 2, when he said: "Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother," and "he shall cleave to his wife [וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ], and they shall be one flesh [וְהָיוּ לִבְשָׂר אֶחָד]." The Greeks rendered the Hebrew dabaq as προσκολληθήσεται [proskollēthēsetai], that is, he shall be joined as if glued fast and cling.

units.la: Ita & hic non dicit: Qui Christo nomen de dit, vel, Qui ad Christum uenit, sed, Qui domi nô adglutinatur, vnus spiritus est, ut indicet, ad
units.tr: So here too he does not say, "Whoever has given his name to Christ," or "Whoever comes to Christ," but "Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit," to show that for this unity of spirit a firm and constant cohesion is needed, Gen. 2. such as the members have in a body or the branches in trees.

units.la: Gen. 2. ad istam spiritus unitatem opus esse solida & constanti cohæsione, qualis est membrorum in corpore, & ramorum in arboribus, qua de re & Christus diligenter suos admonet Ioh.15. toties adhortâs, vt in se maneant. Manet autem in illo, qui syncera fide & charitate non ficta, constanter illi adhæret.
units.tr: Gen. 2. For this unity of the spirit a solid and constant cohesion is needed, such as that of the members in the body or the branches on the trees. This is why Christ also carefully admonishes his people in John 15, urging them so often to abide in him. But he abides in Christ who clings to him constantly with sincere faith and unfeigned love.

units.la: VNVS spiritus est.) Cur non dicit, unū corpus est: ut inter vtranq; diuersam inter se scorti & Christi coniunctionem discriminet, & ostendat eam quæ cum Christo est, non esse carnalem, qualis est viri cum muliere, sed spiritalem, quæ non corporum, sed spiritus coniunctione constat. Ideo & infrà cap.12. vsurpatâ dictione corporis adiungit unde ista incorporatio oriatur & subsistat, cum dicit: Etenim in vno spiritu oēs nos in vnum corpus baptizati sumus, vt ostendat istam coniunctionem esse non corporalem, sed spiritalem.
units.tr: ONE SPIRIT IS.) Why does he not say, "is one body"? So that he may distinguish the two different kinds of union, that of the harlot and that of Christ, and show that the union with Christ is not carnal, as that of a man with a woman is, but spiritual, consisting not in the joining of bodies but of spirits. For this reason also, later in chapter 12, using the word "body," he adds how this incorporation arises and is sustained, saying: "For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body," so as to show that this union is not bodily but spiritual.

units.la: Rursus, cur non dicit, vnum spiritum habet cum Christo, sed vnus spiritus est? An Christi spiritus est, & qui illi adhæret, spiritus est, & non caro? De Christo certè legimus etiam post resurrectionem quod dixerit: Palpate & videte, quia spiritus carnē & ossa non habet, sic vt me videtis habere. De Christianis, quod carnem & ossa habeant, nemo dubitat. Quid est ergo quod dicit: Qui domino adglutinatur, vnus spiritus est?
units.tr: Again, why does he not say that the one who is joined to Christ "has one spirit with Christ," but says "is one spirit"? Is the one who clings to the Lord a spirit and not flesh? We certainly read of Christ, even after his resurrection, that he said: "Handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have." That Christians have flesh and bones no one doubts. What then does it mean when he says, "He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit"?

units.la: Non hic expenditur ꝗd naturaliter & corporaliter fit qui Christo adglutinatur, sed quid fit per gratiam & operationem spiritus. Quod natum est ex carne, inquit Christus Ioh.3. caro est, & quod natū est ex spiritu, spiritus est, hoc est, spiritale est.
units.tr: Here the question is not what happens naturally and bodily to one who is joined to Christ, but what happens through grace and the working of the Spirit. "That which is born of the flesh," says Christ in John 3, "is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit," that is, spiritual.

units.la: Nec hic negatur vera Christi humanitas, qua sibi naturam nostram verbum Dei coniunxit, de qua loquitur hic ipse Apostolus Ephes. 5. cum dicit: Quia membra sumus corporis eius, de carne eius & de ossibus eius, sed quod in hac Christi coniunctione primarium est, excluditur.
