Non enim facilè diceret Apostolus: Qui carnem Christi non habet, hic non est eius: dicit autem: Qui spiritum Christi non habet, hic non est eius.
units.tr: Nor is the true humanity of Christ denied here, by which the Word of God united our nature to himself; of this the Apostle himself speaks in Ephesians 5, when he says, "For we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones." But what is primary in this union with Christ is excluded. For the Apostle would hardly have said, "Whoever does not have the flesh of Christ is not his." Rather he says, "Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ is not his."

units.la: Augustinus de Trinit. lib.6. cap.3. rationem reddit, quare non dicat Apostolus, qui adhæret meretrici, vnum sunt, & qui adhæret domino, unus est, uel, unum sunt: sed, qui adhæret meretrici, vnum corpus est, & qui adhæret domino, vnus spiritus est. Cum, inquit, sic dicitur vnum, ut non addatur, quid vnum, & plura vnum dicantur, eadem natura atque essentia non diffidens nec differentiens significatur. Cum uerò additur quid unum, potest aliquid significari ex pluribus unum factum, quamuis natura diuersis, sicut anima & corpus nō sunt vtrique vnum. Quid enim tam diuersum, nisi addatur aut subintelligatur quid vnum? id est unus homo, aut vnum animal. Inde Apostolus: Qui adhæret meretrici, inquit, vnum corpus est, non dixit, vnum sunt, aut vnum est, sed addidit corpus, tanquam ex duobus diuersis
units.tr: Augustine, in De Trinitate book 6, chapter 3, gives the reason why the Apostle does not say, "He who clings to a harlot is one, and he who clings to the Lord is one," or "they are one," but says, "He who clings to a harlot is one body, and he who clings to the Lord is one spirit." When it is said "one" without adding what the one is, and several things are called "one," the meaning is the same nature and essence, undivided and undifferentiated. But when "what one" is added, something can be signified as made one out of many, even though their natures are different, as soul and body are not each one thing. For what could be so different, unless "what one" is added or understood, that is, one man or one animal? Hence the Apostle: "He who clings to a harlot," he says, "is one body." He did not say "they are one" or "is one," but added "body," as one body composed by union out of two different sexes, male and female. And "he who clings to the Lord," he says, "is one spirit." He did not say, "he who clings to the Lord is one," or "they are one," but added "spirit." For the nature of the human spirit and the spirit of God is different, yet by cleaving it becomes one spirit out of two different things, and so on. So far Augustine. Certainly, although we are one spirit with God, we cannot be said to be one with him in the same way that the Father and the Son are one.

units.la: masculino & fœminino sexu vnum corpus ad iunctione compositum. Et qui adhæret domino, inquit, vnus spiritus est. non dixit: Qui adhæret domino, vnus est, aut vnum sunt, sed ad didit, spiritus. Diuersum enim est natura spiritus hominis & spiritus Dei, sed inhærendo fit vnus spiritus ex diuersis duobus, &c. Hæc ille. Sanè sic habet, licet vnus simus cum Deo spiritus, haud tamen sic vnum cum illo dici possumus, sicut pater & filius unum existunt.
units.tr: Augustine also in Epistle 174 draws the following argument from the present passage: "If it is said of the flesh of different sexes, 'He who clings to a harlot is one body,' and of the human spirit, which is not what the Lord is, it is consequently written, 'But he who clings to the Lord is one spirit,' how much more is God the Father in the Son, and God the Son in the Father, and the Spirit of Father and Son one God, where there is no different nature, when things that cohere with one another in a certain way are called either one spirit or one body? And since soul and body, cohering with one another, are called one man, why should not much more the Father and the Son, cohering inseparably with one another, be called one God, since they cohere inseparably with themselves, just as soul and body cohere? And since body and soul become one man, although body and soul are not one thing, why does not the Father and the Son become much more one God, since the Father and the Son are one, according to that voice of truth: 'I and the Father are one'?" So far there.

units.la: Et epistola 174. colligit ex præsenti loco ad hunc modum: Si de carne diuersi sexus dictū est: Qui adhæret meretrici, vnum corpus est, & de spiritu hominis, qui non est quod domi nus, consequenter scriptum est: Qui autem adhæret domino, vnus spiritus est, quanto magis Deus pater in filio, & Deus filius in patre, & Deus spiritus patris & filij vnus Deus est, vbi nulla est diuersa natura cum pro diuersis modo quo dam sibi cohærentibus dicatur vel spiritus vnus uel corpus vnum? Et cum & anima & corpore sibi cohærentib. dicatur vnus homo, cur non multo maximè pro patre & filio sibi cohærentibus dicatur vnus Deus, cum sibimet inse parabiliter cohæreant, quomodo non cohærēt corpus & anima? Et cum corpus & anima fit vnus homo, quamuis corpus & anima nō sint vnum, cur non multo magis fit pater & filius vnus Deus, cum pater & filius vnum sint, secū dum illam ueritatis uocem: Ego & pater vnū sumus. Hæc ibi.
units.tr: Also, in Epistle 174 he draws the following argument from the present passage: If it is said of the flesh of different sexes, "He who cleaves to a harlot is one body," and, consequently, it is written of the spirit of man, which is not what the Lord is, "But he who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit," how much more are God the Father in the Son, God the Son in the Father, and the Spirit of the Father and the Son one God? Where there is no different nature, when things that cling to one another in some way are called either one spirit or one body? And since the soul and the body, which cling to one another, are called one man, why is it not much more true that the Father and the Son, who cling to one another, are called one God, since they cohere inseparably with each other, in a way in which the body and soul do not cohere? And since the body and soul become one man, although the body and soul are not one thing, why does the Father and the Son not become one God much more, since the Father and the Son are one, according to that word of truth: "I and the Father are one." Thus far there.

units.la: Et in epistola 177. idem hoc argumentū rursus Pascentio obijcit, dicens: Tu autem digneris breuiter respondere, quomodo accipias quod ait Apostolus: Qui adhæret meretrici, vnū corpus est, qui autem adhæret domino, vnus spiritus est. Diuersi enim sexus corpora sibi adhærentia, vnum corpus dixit. Et cum spiritus humanus nullo modo possit dicere: Ego & domi nus unum sumus, tamen cum adhæret domino, unus spiritus est, quanto magis ille qui verissimè dixit: Ego & pater vnum sumus, quia inseparabiliter patri cohæret, ipse & pater vnᵒ Deus est. Hæc ibi.
units.tr: And in Epistle 177 he again raises this same argument against Pascentius, saying: "Please deign to reply briefly how you understand what the Apostle says: 'He who cleaves to a harlot is one body, but he who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit.' For he called the bodies of different sexes, which cling to one another, one body. And since the human spirit can in no way say, 'I and the Lord are one,' yet when it cleaves to the Lord it is one spirit, how much more is he who most truly said, 'I and the Father are one,' one God with the Father, because he cleaves to the Father inseparably?" Thus far there.

units.la: Fugite scortationem. Omne peccatum quodcunq; fecerit homo, extra corpus est, sed qui scortatur, in proprium corpus peccat.
units.tr: Flee fornication. Every sin that a man commits is outside the body, but he who fornicates sins against his own body.

units.la: FVGITE scortationem.) Πορνείαν admiscet qua non solum id agit, ne posthac amplius scortentur Corinthij, sed vt detestentur id peccati, & velut summam immunditiam fugiant. Non dicit, Ne scortemini, id quod & multi alijs de caus non faciunt pleriq; ob id quod pro uoto compotes illius euadere non possint, aut quod periculum vel diffamiam metuant, quibus competit illud:
units.tr: FLEE fornication.) He uses the word πορνεία [porneia], and by this he means not only that the Corinthians should stop fornicating from now on, but that they should detest this sin and shun it as the greatest uncleanness. He does not say "Do not fornicate." Many people refrain from it for other reasons: they cannot gratify their desire whenever they like, or they fear danger or disgrace. To them applies the saying:

units.la: Non audent peccare mali formidine poenæ Sed fugite, id est, abhorrete ab ista immunditia. Neque enim, meo iudicio, corporalem tantum fugam, sed eam potius quæ animi est horror & ror & criminis detestatio, præcipit, quæ locum habet: Vbi oderūt peccare boni uirtutis amore.
units.tr: "Bad men do not dare to sin for fear of punishment." But he says "flee," that is, shrink from this uncleanness with abhorrence. In my judgment he is commanding not merely a bodily flight but rather that horror of the mind and detestation of the crime which belongs to the place where "good men hate to sin for love of virtue."

units.la: Theophylactus putat notari ab Apostolo libidinis uiciū in eo quod carni nostræ insidietur, & nos indesinenter insectetur, cum dicit, fugite scortatione, quasi dicat: Infectatricem illam pestem studiosè fugite, ne uos apprehendat & perdat. Certè tot instructa illecebris est ista libido, ut magna opus sit cautione, ne per illa inescemur & illaqueemur, ut nō immeritò uelut impudes aliquod scortum & insidiosum pasim adolescentium oculis obuium, quàm diligentissime sit fugiendum. Vnde nemo miretur, cur hoc peccatū pasim obtineat, postea quam paucissimi sunt, qui nō etiam sponte in ulnas illius sese conijciant, cum ægrè cuadant, qui summa cautione insidias illius declinant.
units.tr: Theophylact thinks the Apostle is pointing to the vice of lust in that it lays snares for our flesh and pursues us without ceasing, when he says "flee fornication," as if he said: "Diligently flee that destructive pestilence, lest it seize you and destroy you." Certainly this lust is equipped with so many enticements that great caution is needed, lest we be lured and ensnared by them. Like some shameless harlot, offering herself everywhere to the eyes of young men, it must be avoided as diligently as possible. Hence no one should wonder why this sin prevails everywhere, since there are very few who do not even throw themselves willingly into its arms, when those who carefully avoid its snares hardly escape.

units.la: OMNE peccatū, &c.) Grauare uult & detestabile reddere scortationis peccatū. Videbat enim illud propter diuturnam & impunitatem consuetudinem ac licentiam, uel pro nullo, uel certè pro leui ac ueniali peccato reputari. Quoniam uero non potest ex gradibus peccatorū argumentum sumere, quasi maius hoc peccatum sit reliquis, cum sint pleraq; peiora, saltem ex illius dissimilitudine, qua singulari quadam conditione à reliquis omnibus differt, argumentatur. Odiosum enim est merito quicquid peculiarem quandam habet maliciam. Nam quodcunq; malum, communem cum aliis omnibus maliciam habet, hactenus nonnihil meretur veniæ, quatenus communi & generali malicia noxium est. Quod uero singulariter ac peculiariter malū est, singulari quoque ac peculiari odio dignū est. Hoc scilicet in scortatione spectat Apostolus, inducens peculiare quoddam illius malum, in quo cum nullo alio quocunq; peccato communicet. Non quod hoc solum peccatum tale sit, cum & pleraq; alia, si non omnia, si diligenter examines, aliquod in se peculiare malum habeat, ut exempli gratia, Auaritia hoc peculiariter habet, quod per etatem iam non decrescit, ut auctior etiam redda tur in senibus, cum reliqua peccata uel morbo, uel casu aliquo, uel tempore deficiant & extinguantur, nel saltem languescat, sed quod scortatio peculiari malo corpori scortatoris sit noxia, qua in re cum nullo alio peccato communicat.
units.tr: "Every sin," etc. He wants to make the sin of fornication serious and detestable. For, on account of its long-standing custom and impunity and licence, people saw it as either no sin at all or at least a light and venial one. But since he cannot argue from degrees of sin, as if this sin were greater than the others (since many are worse), he argues at least from its unlikeness, by which it differs from all the others in a certain singular condition. For whatever has a peculiar malice is rightly hateful. Every evil shares with all others a common malice, and so far deserves some pardon, in so far as it harms by a common and general malice. But what is singularly and peculiarly evil deserves a singular and peculiar hatred. This is what the Apostle has in view in fornication, pointing to a peculiar evil of its own, in which it shares with no other sin whatever. Not that this sin alone is of such a kind, since many others, if not all, if you examine carefully, have some peculiar evil in themselves. For example, avarice has this peculiar feature: it does not diminish with age but becomes even greater in old men, whereas other sins fail and are extinguished by sickness, some accident, or time, or at least grow weak. But fornication is harmful to the body of the fornicator with a peculiar evil, and in this respect it shares with no other sin.

units.la: Complectitur autem dissimilitudinem hac scortatiōis, qua à reliquis peccatis differt, duobus ueluti mēbris. Primum, dat omnibus peccatis, quæcunq; fecerit homo, quod extra corpus, proprium scilicet peccent. Deinde scortationi adscribit, quod illa sola in corpus proprium peccet. Hic opus est cognoscere, quid sit in corpus proprium peccare, & quid extra, ut dissimilitudinem istam intelligamus. Dicam quid mihi uideatur. In corpus proprium peccare, est illi iniuriā inferre, sanctimoniamque illius polluere. Honos enim corporis nostri est illius puritas & sanctimonia. Illa pol-
units.tr: Now this unlikeness of fornication, by which it differs from the other sins, is embraced by two members, as it were. First, he grants to all sins, whatever a man commits, that they sin outside the body, that is, not against one's own. Then he ascribes to fornication that it alone sins against one's own body. Here it is necessary to understand what it is to sin against one's own body and what it is to sin outside it, so that we may grasp this unlikeness. I shall say what seems to me. To sin against one's own body is to do it an injury and to defile its holiness. For the honour of our body is its purity and holiness. That is polluted

units.la: In corpus proprium peccare.
units.tr: To sin against one's own body.

units.la: luitur peccādo, ubi actus scilicet peccati in ipsum corpus transit. Peccatū ergo extra corpus est, cuius actus non ipsum delinquētis corpus polluit, sed in ea quæ foris sunt extenditur. Licet enim membrorum abusu peccemus furando, rapiendo, fallendo, falsum testimonium dicendo, occidendo, &c. Ipse tamen actus peccati, non totius corporis est, sed quorundam duntaxat membrorum, & in rebus extrarijs absoluitur, & alijs infert iniuriam. Peccatū uero in proprium corpus est, quo sanctimonia & honos illius actu aliquo immundo polluitur. Tale est autem scortatio. Ergo scortatio in hoc à reliquis peccatis differt, quod cum illa extra corpus, ista in proprium corpus peccet. Et hoc puto respicere Apostolum 1. Thessa. 4. ubi dicit: Hæc est enim voluntas Dei sanctificatio uestra, ut abstineatis à scortatione, & sciat unusquisq; uestrum uas suum possidere cum sanctificatione & honore, non cum affectu cupiscentiæ, quemadmodum & gentes quæ non nouerunt Deum. Videmus hic abstinere à scortatione, esse uas suum possidere, cum sanctificatione & honore. Loquitur autem de corporis uasculo. Ergo qui scortatur uasculi, id est, corporis sui honorem & sanctificationem polluit.
units.tr: by sinning, namely when the act of sin passes into the body itself. Sin is therefore outside the body when its act does not defile the body of the sinner himself, but extends to those things which are outside. For although we sin by misusing our limbs, when we steal, rob, deceive, bear false witness, kill, and so on, the act of sin itself belongs not to the whole body but only to certain members, is completed in external things, and does injury to others. But sin is against one's own body when the holiness and honour of the body are polluted by some unclean act. Such is fornication. Therefore fornication differs from the other sins in this, that while they sin outside the body, it sins against the body itself. I think the Apostle has this in view in 1 Thessalonians 4, where he says: "For this is the will of God, your sanctification, that you abstain from fornication, and that each one of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honour, not in the lust of desire, just as the Gentiles who do not know God." Here we see that to abstain from fornication is to possess one's own vessel in sanctification and honour. Now he speaks of the little vessel of the body. Therefore he who fornicates defiles the honour and sanctification of his vessel, that is, of his own body.

units.la: Chrysostomus & Theophilactus, istam corporum impurationem, quæ per scortationem est, adeo putāt esse notam omnibus, ut moris sit ab actu uenereo, tanquam purgandorum corporū gratia, balnea petere, quod post nullum aliud peccatum solebat fieri. Verum illi non cogitarunt Apostolum, non de eiusmodi corporali impuritate loqui, quæ per aquam ablui potest, nisi & coniuges legitimi in suaipsarum corpora peccent, qui & ipsi consimiliter balneis utuntur.
units.tr: Chrysostom and Theophylact think this pollution of the body that comes through fornication is so well known to everyone that it was customary, after the venereal act and as if for cleansing the body, to seek baths, which was done after no other sin. But they did not consider that the Apostle is not speaking of that kind of bodily impurity which can be washed away with water, since lawful spouses too, if they sin against their own bodies, also use baths in the same way.

units.la: Quidam huc locum exponunt de corpore mystico, quod est Christi & ecclesiæ, per alIusionem coniugij. Sed Ambrosius istam sententiam, quam Nouatiano adscribit, constater refellit, eo quod malus Christianus nequeat corpus Christi scortando polluere, cum illud non sit unus & alter Christianus, sed omnes Christiani, cuius singuli sint membra, adeoq; tam non possit corpus Christi polluere, quàm nequit omnes Christianos peccato suo contaminare.
units.tr: Some expound this passage of the mystical body, which is that of Christ and the Church, by an allusion to marriage. But Ambrose plainly refutes this opinion, which he ascribes to Novatian, on the ground that a wicked Christian cannot defile the body of Christ by fornication, since that body is not this or that Christian but all Christians together, of whom each is a member. Therefore he can no more pollute the body of Christ than he can contaminate all Christians by his sin.

units.la: Deinde res magnæ disputationis est, quomodo reliqua peccata omnia quæ à Christiano fiunt, dicantur fieri extra corpus Christi mysticum, ut sola scortatio in illud peccet.
units.tr: Next, there is a great matter of dispute as to how all the other sins that a Christian commits are said to be committed outside the mystical body of Christ, so that fornication alone sins against it.

units.la: Grauat ergo Apostolus scortationis peccatum magna inuidia, quod præter omnium aliorum peccatorum conditionem, ipsum solum peccet in propriū cuiusq; scortatoris corpus.
units.tr: The Apostle therefore lays heavy weight on the sin of fornication, because, unlike all other sins, it alone sins against the body of each fornicator.

units.la: 1 Finge tale quoddam esse peccatum domesticum, quod peculiari malicia ipsam domum commaculet, cum reliqua exteros tantum lædat. Nõne uidebitur illud singulari quodam odio dignum esse?
units.tr: (1) Imagine that there is some domestic sin which, by its peculiar malice, stains the household itself, while other sins harm only outsiders. Will it not seem worthy of a singular hatred?

units.la: 2 Aut finge ciuem quedam esse, qui singulari h quadam malicia, cum reliqui exteros tantum negocijs suis grauent, conciuibus uero parcant, rapina, fraude & usura conciues spoliet, an nō omnium ille communi & publico odio merito obnoxius essET.
units.tr: (2) Or imagine a citizen who, with a singular malice, while others burden outsiders with their business, spares his fellow citizens but robs and defrauds them by theft, fraud and usury. Would he not rightly be liable to the common and public hatred of all?

units.la: ʒ Omne belli genus malum est & fugiedum bono uiro. Omnibus autem detestabilius est, quod ipsum ciuium corpus, cum sit intestinum, perdit.
units.tr: (3) Every kind of war is evil and to be fled by a good man. But more detestable than all is that which destroys the very body of the citizens, since it is internal.

units.la: Ista non in hoc tendunt, ut putandū sit maius esse peccatum quod peccantem laedit, minus uero, quod alijs iniuriam infert, absit: sed quod communi sensu magis abhorreamus ea, quibus nosipsos quàm quibus alios lędimus. Haȼtenus isto argumeto utitur Apostolus, ut uel ista ratione, si superiora argumenta parum scortatores mouent, detestandam reddat scortationem.
units.tr: These examples do not aim to suggest that a sin which harms the sinner is greater, and one which injures others is less; by no means. Rather, they aim to show that by common feeling we shrink more from those things by which we harm ourselves than from those by which we harm others. So far the Apostle uses this argument, so that, even on this ground, if the earlier arguments move fornicators little, he may make fornication detestable.

units.la: Tale est etiam, quod istud peccatū non una tantum personam, sed duas inuoluit. Nequit enim à solo aliquo admitti, cum reliqua aut non inuoluant extra delinquentem alios aut non necessario inuoluant. Qui furatur, non perdit furto suo eum cuius bona furatur. Qui inuidus est sibi soli peccat. Qui mentitur, item & sic de singulis. Sola scortatio delicti socium exigit, ut & hoc nomine sit detestanda.
units.tr: It is also like this, that this sin involves not only one person but two. For it cannot be committed by one alone, whereas other sins either do not involve others outside the wrongdoer or do not necessarily involve them. The thief does not destroy by his theft the man whose goods he steals. The envious man sins against himself alone. The liar likewise, and so on for each. Fornication alone demands an accomplice in the offence, so that on this ground too it is to be detested.

units.la: An nescitis, quod corpus uestrum templū est spiritus sancti, qui in uobis est, quem habetis à Deo?
units.tr: Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God?

units.la: Iterum à dignitate corporum nostrorū arguit, deinde & à maiestate & sanctimonia spiritus sancti. Dignitas corporum nostrorū est, quod illa templum sunt spiritus sancti inhabitantis in nobis. Iam ea debetur maiestati illius reuerentia, ut nullo pacto uioletur ac profanetur templi illius sanctitas. Quod si enorme peccat, qui templum Dei sanctum, lapidibus structum, immundicia sua polluit, quomodo leue peccatū putatur, quo sancti spiritus templum, quod nō hominū sed Dei manibus structū est, conspurcatur, id quod scortationis immundicia facit, dum corpora credentium impurat. Et huc facit quod non habitaculi, sed templi dictione usus est, ut admoneat eam deberi corporibus nostris sanctimoniā quæ debetur templo Dei. Et ideo nō adiungit quàm scortationis impuritas templo Dei non conueniat, permittēs illud ipsorum consideratione. Quis enim ignorat, siue spiritus sancti naturam & puritatem, siue templo Dei debitam reuerentiam expendat, quàm indignum sit & inconueniens templo spiritus sancti peccatum hoc scortationis?
units.tr: Again he argues from the dignity of our bodies, and then from the majesty and holiness of the Holy Spirit. The dignity of our bodies is that they are temples of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us. Reverence is owed to that majesty, so that the holiness of this temple must in no way be violated or profaned. If he who pollutes with his own filth a holy temple of God, built of stones, commits a grave sin, how can it be thought a light sin to defile the temple of the Holy Spirit, which was built not by human hands but by God's, and this is what the uncleanness of fornication does when it stains the bodies of believers? Here also it matters that he uses the word temple rather than dwelling, so that he may remind us that our bodies should have the holiness that is owed to the temple of God. For this reason he does not add how far the impurity of fornication is unfitting for the temple of God, but leaves it to their own consideration. For who does not see, whether he weighs the nature and purity of the Holy Spirit or the reverence due to the temple of God, how unworthy and unbecoming to the temple of the Holy Spirit this sin of fornication is?

units.la: QVOMODO CORPORA NOSTRA templum sint spiritus sancti.
units.tr: HOW OUR BODIES are temples of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Sed quæritur hoc loco, quomodo corpora nostra crassa & corruptibilia templū esse possint spiritus sancti. Supra cap.3. dixit: An nescitis quod templum Dei estis, & spiritus Dei habitat in uobis? Hic dicit: An nescitis quod cor pus uestrum templum est spiritus sancti? An spiritus Dei habitat in corporibus nostris? Nunquid conueniētius corda nostra spiritus sancti habitationi assignarentur? Ita plane pu to. Ergo loquutio ista metaphorica est, ad similitudinem templi lapidei, quod habitationi Dei assignatur, propter sacrarium & sede propiciationis in templo, eo quod ibi Deus peculiariter gratiæ suæ dispensationem pollicitus est, cum alioqui nec cælo, nec terra capiatur. Ita uidelicet & corpora nostra templum sunt spiritus sancti, propter cordium uestrorum sanctificationem, quæ per spiritum Dei est, ut sacrarij locū obtineant, propterea quod in illis dona illa & uirtutes spiritus sancti peculiariter efficaciam suam exercet. Quis enim adeo absurdus est, ut putet spiritum Dei incomprehensibilem siue cordibus, siue corporibus nostris includi cum sit infinitus?
units.tr: But here it is asked how our bodies, which are gross and corruptible, can be temples of the Holy Spirit. Above, in chapter 3, he said: Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? Here he says: Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit? Does the Spirit of God dwell in our bodies? Would it not be more fitting for our hearts to be assigned as the dwelling of the Holy Spirit? Surely so I think. Therefore this way of speaking is metaphorical, in likeness to a stone temple, which is assigned as a dwelling of God because of the sanctuary and the mercy seat in the temple, since there God especially promised the dispensation of his grace, although otherwise he is contained neither by heaven nor by earth. So too our bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, because of the sanctification of your hearts, which is effected by the Spirit of God, so that they hold the place of the sanctuary, because in them the Spirit of God especially exercises his gifts and powers. For who is so absurd as to think that the Spirit of God, incomprehensible, is enclosed in our hearts or bodies, since he is infinite?

units.la: AVGVSTINVS.
units.tr: AUGUSTINE.

units.la: Colligit ex hoc loco Augustinus in libro contra sermone Arianorum cap.20. argumentum diuinitatis spiritus sancti contra Arianos qui illam negantes, minorem filio spiritum sanctum esse dicebant, id quod & Ambrosius alicubi facit. Medium autem argumenti huius est, quod templum nulli competit creaturæ, sed uni Deo. Hic uero tribuitur spiritui sancto templum. Ergo conuincitur esse Deus. Quod si de Salomone, inquit Augustinus, legeretur in scripturis, quod spiritui sancto templum iussu Dei struxisset, Deum esse spiritum sanctum non dubitarent, & eum deum esse negare audent, qui templum habet non ex lignis & lapidibus, sed ex membris Christi.
units.tr: Augustine, in his book against the sermon of the Arians, chapter 20, draws from this passage an argument for the deity of the Holy Spirit against the Arians, who denied it and said that the Holy Spirit was inferior to the Son, as Ambrose also does somewhere. The middle term of this argument is that a temple belongs to no creature but to God alone. Here, however, a temple is attributed to the Holy Spirit. Therefore he is proved to be God. And if it were read in the Scriptures, says Augustine, that Solomon had built a temple for the Holy Spirit by God's command, they would not doubt that the Holy Spirit is God, and yet they dare to deny that he is God, who has a temple not of wood and stones but of the members of Christ.

units.la: Notandum est & hoc, quod non dicit: An nescitis quod templum spiritus sancti fieri potestis, quem accepturi estis à Deo, si corpora uestra munda custodieritis, ut alliciat eos spe acquirendi spiritus Dei, sed, An nescitis quod corpora uestra templum sunt spiritus sancti, qui in uobis est, quem accepistis à Deo? Admonet igitur eos acceptæ gratiæ ad hoc, ut uideant ne illam per scortationis immunditiem amittant. Libenter hoc argumento utitur Apostolus, ubi ad uitæ sanctimoniam hortatur, unde credentes uocat sanctos, dilectos, ablutos, iustificatos, corpus & membra Christi, templum Dei & spiritus sancti. Erat enim manifestis argumentis ac signis uirtus & operatio spiritus sancti in credentibus declarata, ut illam negare nequiuerint, unde omnium sane fortissimo argumento ex illa sumpto, contra scortationis & omnis generis impuritatem pugnat.
units.tr: This too is to be noted: he does not say, Do you not know that you can become a temple of the Holy Spirit, whom you are about to receive from God if you keep your bodies clean, enticing them with the hope of obtaining the Spirit of God; but he says, Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have received from God? He therefore reminds them of the grace they have received, so that they may see to it that they do not lose it through the uncleanness of fornication. The Apostle gladly uses this argument when he urges holiness of life, whence he calls believers holy, beloved, washed, justified, the body and members of Christ, the temple of God and of the Holy Spirit. For the power and working of the Holy Spirit had been shown in believers by manifest proofs and signs, so that they could not deny it; and so, taking from it the strongest of all arguments, he fights against fornication and every kind of impurity.

units.la: Et non estis uestri. Nam empti estis precio.
units.tr: And you are not your own. For you were bought with a price.

units.la: Et Hieronymus & Ambrosius, Chrysostomus item & Theophylactus istam particulam à præcedenti diuulsam legunt & exponunt. Nam
units.tr: Both Jerome and Ambrose, and likewise Chrysostom and Theophylact, read and explain this clause as separated from what precedes. For

units.la: Esa.66.
units.tr: Isa. 66.

units.la: Nam separatum habet argumentum, à iure redemptionis sumptum, quod in nos habet dominus. Qui pecunia coemptus est, sui iuris nó est, sed eius à quo precio comparatus est. Non habet ergo proprij corporis arbitriū, nisi quantum permittit heri, cuius seruus est, uoluntas, contra quam in corpus proprium nihil habet potestatis. Cum ergo precio sanguinis Christi empti simus, non licet nobis permittere corporibus nostris, quicquid uoluntati domini nostri repugnat. Repugnat autē scortationis immunditia. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: For it contains a separate argument, taken from the right of redemption, which the Lord has over us. He who has been bought with money is not his own master, but belongs to the one by whose price he was acquired. He therefore has no right over his own body, except as far as the will of the master whose slave he is permits, and against which he has no power over his own body. Since therefore we have been bought with the price of Christ's blood, it is not lawful for us to allow our bodies to do whatever is contrary to the will of our Lord. Fornication's uncleanness is contrary to it. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Precij huius amplificationem ponit Apostolus Petrus, epist. 1. cap. 1. Scientes, inquit, quod non corruptibilibus, auro uel argento, redempti estis de uana uestra conuersatione paternę traditiōis, sed precioso sanguine quasi agni immaculati & incontaminati Christi, &c.
units.tr: The Apostle Peter amplifies this price in his first epistle, chapter 1: Knowing, he says, that you were redeemed not with corruptible things, gold or silver, from your vain conduct handed down from your fathers, but with the precious blood, as of a spotless and unblemished lamb, Christ, etc.

units.la: Igitur duplici nomine iniustum est & indignum facinus, si Christianus sanguine Christi redemptus corpus suum scortando polluat.
units.tr: Therefore it is doubly unjust and unworthy a deed if a Christian, redeemed by the blood of Christ, defiles his body by fornication.

units.la: 1 Primùm quod in alienam rem potestatem sibi sumit, contra ius & uoluntatem domini sui.
units.tr: (1) First, because he assumes power over a thing that belongs to another, against the right and will of his lord.

units.la: 2 Deinde quod ad pristinam immunditiam recurrit, ad uituperium tam inæstimabilis precij, cum ab illa sit redemptus & liberatus.
units.tr: (2) Second, because he returns to his former uncleanness, to the disgrace of a price so priceless, since he was redeemed and freed from it.

units.la: Quemadmodum si puellam quandam è domo & immunditia meretricia dato certo precio ob id redimas, ut ab ea miseria liberata tibi sit honesto coniugio coniuncta: illa uero tantæ oblita gratiæ, ad pristinam sese spurcitiam denuo recipiat, iniuria primum in potestatem tuam quam precio in illam acquisieras, deinde & in acceptam gratiam, qua fuerat à tanta immunditia liberata. Tale prorsus est, quod Christiani flagitiosi & scortatores admittunt.
units.tr: It is like this: if you were to redeem some girl from a house of harlotry and its uncleanness by paying a certain price, so that, freed from that misery, she might be joined to you in honourable marriage; but she, forgetting so great a kindness, were to return to her former filth again, this would be an injury, first against your power, which you had acquired over her with your price, and then against the grace you had shown, by which she had been freed from such uncleanness. This is exactly what wicked Christians and fornicators do.

units.la: Glorificate igitur Deum in corpore uestro, & in spiritu uestro, quæ sunt Dei.
units.tr: Therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.

units.la: Illatio est ex præcedenti propositione, qua enthymema construit, quod ad perfectum argumentum duci potest, si addatur maior propositio quæ desideratur, utpote ad hunc modum. Quicquid Dei est, ad gloriam Dei facere debet. Corpora uestra & spiritus uestri Dei sunt. Minorem hanc probauit ratione redemptionis, cum dixit: Empti enim estis precio. Ergo corpora uestra & spiritus uestri ad gloriam Dei facere debent. Iam ad gloriam Dei non facit immunditia scortationis, per quam cum in ius Dei quod in uos habet, tum in gratiam illius iniurij estis. Igitur ut Deum glorificetis in corpore uestro & in spiritu uestro, quę Dei sunt, fugite scortationem.
units.tr: This is an inference from the preceding proposition, by which he constructs an enthymeme, which can be brought to a complete argument if the major proposition that is wanting is added, namely in this way: Whatever belongs to God ought to serve the glory of God. Your bodies and your spirits belong to God. He proved this minor premise by the reason of redemption, when he said: "For you were bought with a price." Therefore your bodies and your spirits ought to serve the glory of God. Now the uncleanness of fornication does not serve the glory of God, by which you have offended both against the right that God has over you and against his grace toward you. Therefore, that you may glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God's, flee fornication.

units.la: ET in spiritu uestro.) Hanc particulam ob id adijcit, ut ostendat non corpusolum, sed & ipsum spiritum per scortationis impuritatem pollui, concupiscentijs uidelicet impuris. Alij id rationis assignant, quod puritas corporis sine ea quæ spiritus est, Deo nó admodum placeat, atque ideo non solum corpore, sed &
units.tr: "And in your spirit." He adds this particle for this reason, to show that not the body only but the spirit itself is polluted by the impurity of fornication, namely by impure desires. Others assign this reason: that the purity of the body, without that of the spirit, is not very pleasing to God, and therefore not only the body but also

units.la: CAPVT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 7.

units.la: IAm commodū Apostolus post reprehensam scortationis immunditiā coniugij causam subijcit, tanquam sanctorum hominum opinione uicinam, ne illam putetur unà cum scortatione damnasse, aut certè, ne non intellecta illa lapsus paretur ad scortationem. Apparet autem fuisse Corinthijs nonnihil contentionis de coniugio, ita ut quidam illo putauerint Christianæ religionis gratia abstinendum, quidam etiam coniuges iam sese propter religionem, maximè in impari coniugio constituti, separauerint, & hisce de rebus Apostolo scriptum esse per bonos & pios. unde & ait: De quibus autem scripsistis mihi, &c.
units.tr: Now the Apostle, after rebuking the uncleanness of fornication, adds a discussion of marriage, as a subject close to the holy men's opinion, lest it be thought that he had condemned marriage together with fornication, or at least lest, if that point were not understood, someone should be led into fornication. It is clear, however, that there was some dispute among the Corinthians about marriage. Some thought that it should be avoided for the sake of the Christian religion, and some married people, especially those in mixed marriages, had already separated from their spouses for the sake of religion. Good and pious men had reported these things to the Apostle. Hence he says: "Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me," and so on.

units.la: Agit itaq; hoc capite primum de coniugio, deinde de ἀγαμία, tertiò, de uirginitate, idq; omnia ita dilucide ac distincte, tantaq; cautione, ne cui laqueum ponat, ut mirum sit ueteres quosdam, alioqui doctos uiros, capitis huius lucem non uidisse. Verum implerí oportuit Apostoli propheriam, qua ille futurum prædixit, ut exurgat doctrina dæmoniorum, quā nuptiæ prohibeantur, uide 1. Tim. 4.
units.tr: In this chapter, then, he first deals with marriage, then with celibacy [ἀγαμία], and third with virginity. He does all this so clearly and distinctly, and with such caution, that he sets no snare for anyone. It is remarkable that some older writers, otherwise learned men, did not see the light of this chapter. But it was necessary for the Apostle's prophecy to be fulfilled, in which he foretold that the doctrine of demons would arise, forbidding marriage; see 1 Tim. 4.

units.la: Principio autem de coniugio docet, quod Christianis coniugibus esse liceat.
units.tr: At the start, he teaches that it is lawful for Christians to marry.

units.la: Deinde, quod quisq; coniugum compari suo debitum coniugij reddere debeat.
units.tr: Next, that each spouse ought to render to the other the debt of marriage.

units.la: Tertiò, quod non debeant separari coniuges.
units.tr: Third, that spouses ought not to be separated.

units.la: Quartò adijcitur consilium de coniugibus, quod ad religionem attinet, inter se diuersis.
units.tr: Fourthly, advice is added about spouses who differ from one another in religion.

units.la: DE quibus autem scripsistis mihi: Bonum est homini uxorem non attingere: attamen propter stupra uitanda suam quisq; uxorem habeat, & suum quæq; uirum habeat.
units.tr: "Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. Nevertheless, to avoid fornications, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband."

units.la: Quid Corinthij Paulo de causa coniugij scripserint non liquet penitus.
units.tr: What the Corinthians wrote to Paul about marriage is not entirely clear.

units.la: Chrysostomus arbitratur quod percontati sint an coniugium Christianis liceat, uel non liceat, uel, ut ipsa uerba illius assignem, εἰ δεῖ ἀπέχεσθαι γυναικὸς ἢ μή, id est, an abstinendum sit à muliere uel non.
units.tr: Chrysostom thinks that they asked whether it was lawful or unlawful for Christians to marry, or, to give his own words, whether it is necessary to abstain from a woman or not [εἰ δεῖ ἀπέχεσθαι γυναικὸς ἢ μή], that is, whether one should abstain from a woman or not.

units.la: Quidam uero illud, Bonum est homini uxorem non attingere, intelligunt hoc ipsum esse, quod Corinthij scripserunt, ut sit ista lectionis series. De quibus autem scripsistis mihi, uidelicet, Bonum esse homini, ut ab uxore abstineat, assentior quidem, uerumtamen propter stupra uitanda curandum est, ut quisque suam uxorem habeat, & suum quæque uirum. Et isti lectioni uidetur fauere, quod Græca habent καλὸν ἀνθρώπῳ, ut addi possit tam infinitiuus finitiuus ℨ, quàm indicatiuus ℨ, & legi, Bonum esse homini, æquè atque bonum est homini.
units.tr: Some, however, understand the words "It is good for a man not to touch a woman" to be the very thing the Corinthians wrote, so that the sequence of the reading is this: "Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me," namely, "It is good for a man to abstain from a woman." I agree with this, yet on account of avoiding fornications, each man must see to it that he has his own wife, and each woman her own husband. This reading seems to be supported by the fact that the Greek has καλὸν ἀνθρώπῳ, so that one may add either the infinitive "esse" or the indicative "est," and read either "It is good for a man to..." or "It is good for a man..."

units.la: Quidam autem legunt hanc particulam tanquam quæ non sit Corinthiorum, sed ipsius Pauli.
units.tr: Some, however, read this clause as not the Corinthians' words but Paul's own.

units.la: Credibile est autem Apostolo non solum de coniugibus, sed & de nuptis ac uiduis, item de imparibus coniugibus dirimendis, adhæc & de uirginibus, scriptum esse. Quid enim uetat ex ipso illius responso colligere, quid percontati sint Corinthij?
units.tr: It is credible that the Apostle wrote not only about married people but also about wives, widows, and the dissolving of mixed marriages, and also about virgins. For what prevents us from gathering from his answer what the Corinthians asked?

units.la: BONVM est.) De eo bono non loquitur, cuius oppositum est uicium, & tale malum quod iniustitiam coniunctam habeat. Si enim id uellet, non diceret hoc ipso capite, Quod si duxeris uxorem non peccasti, etsi nupserit uir go non peccauit. Proinde hoc bonum nihil aliud est quàm commodu & profuturum, cuius oppositum est malum quidem, sed quomodo dies mali, id est molesti dicuntur. Infrà declarabit seipsum, quomodo dicat bonum esse homini, ut uxorem non attingat.
units.tr: "It is good": he is not speaking of a good whose opposite is a vice, and an evil that involves injustice. For if he meant that, he would not say in this same chapter: "But if you take a wife, you have not sinned, and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned." Therefore this good is nothing other than what is convenient and advantageous, whose opposite is an evil, though only in the way that "evil days" are called, that is, troublesome days. Later he will explain himself, showing how it is good for a man not to touch a woman.

units.la: Quod si collectio Hieronymi aduersus Iouinianum hoc sensu posita est, firma perfiftit, si uero colligit coniugium esse ita malum ut sit illicitum, damnabilis expositio est.
units.tr: If Jerome's argument against Jovinian is put in this sense, it stands firm. But if it infers that marriage is so evil as to be unlawful, that interpretation is condemnable.

units.la: ATTAMEN propter stupra uitanda.) Quanquam propter præsentem necessitatem commodum esset abstinere à coiugio, non tamen hoc suadet, propter incontinentiam Corinthiorum, quos sciebat esse ad fornicationem procliues, ne daretur illis stuprorum occasio. Aliàs, quomodo conuenisset adimere illis coniugium, quos iam tanto serio fornicationis causa reprehenderat?
units.tr: "Nevertheless, to avoid fornications": although, because of the present necessity, it would be advantageous to abstain from marriage, he does not advise this, because of the Corinthians' incontinence. He knew they were prone to fornication, and he did not want them to be given occasions for fornication. Otherwise, how would it fit for him to take away marriage from those whom he had already rebuked so seriously for fornication?

units.la: Et uide quomodo non dicat, attamen propter stupra uitanda bonum est, ut quisque uxorem suam habeat, & quæque uirum suum, nec dicat, cōsulo, ut quisque suam habeat, ne polluatur ex aliena, sed ἐχέτω, habeat, idque non semel, sed iterum, id quod imperantis etiam est. Non quod simpliciter imperet quibusuis coniugiū quasi illicita sit ἀγαμία, sed quod sciat Corinthiorum incontinentiam illiq; uelit omnem adimere occasionem fornicandi. Ita & 1.Tim.5. ubi cognouit iuniores uiduas in Christo lasci uire, adeoque aduersario occasionem maledicendi dare, non dixit: Bonum est, & consulo, ut iuniores nubat, sed, uolo igitur iuniores nubere, quod certè est non iam consulentis tantum, sed magis præcipientis.
units.tr: And notice how he does not say, "Nevertheless, to avoid fornications, it is good that each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband," nor does he say, "I advise that each man have his own, so that he not be defiled by another's." Instead he says, "let him have" [ἐχέτω], and this not once but twice, which is also the language of one who commands. He does not simply command everyone to marry, as if celibacy were unlawful, but because he knows the Corinthians' incontinence, he wishes to remove every occasion for fornication. So also in 1 Tim. 5, when he learned that younger widows were wanton against Christ, and so gave the adversary an occasion for slander, he did not say, "It is good, and I advise, that the younger women marry," but "I will therefore that the younger women marry," which is certainly not the language of one merely advising, but rather of one commanding.

units.la: Quod si tempore Apostoli, ut fortiter colligit Erasmus, ubi pauci erant Christiani, & paucissimi Christi ministri, deinde persequutionis gratia malum erat nubere, propter stupra uitanda præcipit Apostolus, ut quisque suam, & queq; suum habeat, quanto magis ubi nunc tanta est credentium multitudo, tanta ociosorum pinguium ac libidinosorum sacerdotum copia, tantaq; pacis publicæ tranquillitas, curadum erat, ut omnis fornicatio tolleretur occasio, maximè cum uideamus iam olim omnis generis
units.tr: If, as Erasmus reasonably infers, marriage was to be avoided for fear of fornication in the Apostle's time, when there were few Christians and very few ministers of Christ, and when it was also a hardship because of persecution, then how much more should this be done now, when the number of believers is so great, there is such a supply of idle, fat, and lustful priests, and public peace is so secure? Now, when we see that every kind of impurity has long held sway and flourished openly among those who profess celibacy, to the irrecoverable loss of Christian honesty, every opportunity for fornication ought to be removed.

units.la: Aimmudiciam passim apud eos qui cœlibatum profitentur cum irrecuperabili Christianę honestatis detrimento obtinere & regnare.
units.tr: Impurity holds sway and reigns everywhere among those who profess celibacy, and this brings irreparable harm to Christian integrity.

units.la: SVAM quisq; uxorem, &c.) Non dicit mulierem quisque habeat. Nam & inter fornicatores reperias, qui mulierem penes se habeat, concubinam, qua fit contentus, cui & thori fidem feruet, è qua etiam liberos suscipiat, id quod de se scribit Augustinus in confessionibus libro 4.cap.2. qui & filium habuit ex concubina à Deo datum confess.lib.6. cap.15. Talis tamen copula illegitima est, quod & Augustinus fatetur. Coniugium uero docetur ab Apostolo, cum dicit, unusquisque suam habeat, & unaquæque suum. Quæ extra connubium legitimum uirum habet, non suum dicitur habere, sed alienum. Sic Iohan.4. Samaritanę dicebat Christus: Bene dixisti quod uirum non habeas. Quinq; enim uiros habuisti, & quem nunc habes non est tuus. Liquet itaque concubinatum istum, quem pontificij sacerdotes hodie libere sectantur, nihil esse aliud quàm fortationem, cum non sit coniugium legitimum, ad quod uitandæ fornicationis gratia quosuis adigit hic Apostolus iubens, ut quisque suam & quæque suum habeat. Proinde 17. canon Toletani concilij de concubinatu reprobus est.
units.tr: EVERY MAN HIS OWN WIFE, etc.) He does not say that each man should have a woman. For you will find among fornicators some who keep a woman with them as a concubine, one who satisfies them, to whom they also keep faith in their bed, and by whom they even have children. Augustine writes this about himself in the Confessions, book 4, chapter 2, and he also had a son by a concubine, given to him by God (Confessions, book 6, chapter 15). Yet such a union is unlawful, as Augustine himself admits. Marriage, however, is what the Apostle teaches when he says, "let every man have his own, and every woman her own." A woman who has a man outside lawful wedlock is not said to have her own, but another's. So Christ said to the Samaritan woman in John 4: "You have said well that you have no husband. For you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your own." It is clear, then, that the concubinage which the Papist priests today freely pursue is nothing other than fornication, since it is not lawful marriage. This is the very thing to which the Apostle, in order to prevent fornication, bids all people, when he says that each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband. Therefore the 17th canon of the Council of Toledo rightly condemns concubinage.

units.la: 1 Vitandâ esse fornicatione Christianis tam uiris q; mulieribus.
units.tr: 1. Fornication must be avoided by Christians, both men and women.

units.la: 2 Matrimonium huc conducere tam uiris quàm mulieribus.
units.tr: 2. Marriage is useful for men and women alike.

units.la: 3 Matrimonij fide esse non solum liberorum procreationem, sed & fornicationis uitationem.
units.tr: 3. The purpose of marriage is not only the procreation of children but also the avoiding of fornication.

units.la: OBSER. I.
units.tr: OBSERVATION I.

units.la: In eo quod dicit, propter uitandam fornicationem, habeat quisq; uxorem suam, satis indicatur coniugium legitimum remedium adferre contra fornicationem, ut possint cum uiri tum fœminæ licita copula illicitum uitare congressum. Et hoc uerum esse deprehenditur apud eos qui per coniugiū nihil aliud quærunt, quàm ut naturæ legi satisfaciant. Apud intem perantiores uero, qui libidini fræna absq; ullo Dei timore laxant secus habet. Nam illis quod licet non admodum placet, sed pane furtiuo delectantur. Audimus subinde coniugij irrisores, homines impuros, impuritate suam tam non tegentes, ut dicant, impossibile esse, ut una quis queat esse contentus. Et si quisquam hoc possit, illum eadem facultate & in uniuersum omnibus posse carere. Hi aperto ludibrio oraculū hoc spiritus sancti abijciunt, non alia ratione, quàm quod iuxta suam intemperantiam de aliorum uirorum natura & temperantiaiudicant.
units.tr: From the words "let each man have his own wife, because of the avoiding of fornication," it is sufficiently clear that lawful marriage is a remedy against fornication, so that by lawful union husband and wife can both avoid unlawful intercourse. This is found to be true among those who seek nothing from marriage but to satisfy the law of nature. It is otherwise with the more intemperate, who loosen the reins of lust with no fear of God at all. For such people, although lawful marriage does not greatly please them, they delight in stolen bread. We hear from time to time mockers of marriage, impure men who cover their impurity so little that they say it is impossible for anyone to be content with one partner, and that if anyone can manage it, he must by the same power be able to do without altogether. By this open mockery they cast aside this oracle of the Holy Spirit, for no other reason than that, measuring by their own intemperance, they judge the nature and self-control of other men.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Videmus etiam hoc loco coniugij finem non eum tantum esse, ut liberi crceantur, sed
units.tr: We see here also that the purpose of marriage is not only that children may be procreated,

units.la: hunc, ut uitetur scortandi occasio. Ergo plurimum errant, qui putát coniugium legitimum non esse nisi inter fœcundos, quasi in illis qui uel ætatis uel naturę defectu steriles sunt, nulla sit amplius coniugij ratio. Præscribitur hic ratio coniugij, ut uitetur scortatio. At illius peccatum timendum est & uitandum, non solum iunioribus & fœcundis, sed & ætate prouectioribus & infœcundis. Unde uiduam non agnoscit Apostolus quæ ali debeat in ecclesia, nisi quæ attigerit annum sexagesimum. Certum est igitur, quod & inter steriles & natu grandiores iusta sit coniugij ratio.
units.tr: but also that the occasion of fornication may be avoided. Therefore they greatly err who think that lawful marriage exists only among the fruitful, as if, for those who are sterile through age or nature, there were no longer any reason for marriage. Here the Apostle prescribes marriage as the means of avoiding fornication. But that sin must be feared and avoided not only by the young and fruitful, but also by those advanced in years and no longer fruitful. Hence the Apostle admits as a widow to be supported by the Church only one who has reached sixty years. It is certain, then, that a just reason for marriage exists both for the sterile and for those of greater age.

units.la: Et ne quis in uiris quidem senibus & grandæuis, si iuniores uxores habeant, ut de Abrahamo legitur, istam coniugij rationem concedat propter fœcunditatis posisibilitatem, in mulieribus autem negat, eo quod ex illis iam proiectioribus proles tolli nequeat, aduertendum est, quod ista coniugij ratio quá Apostolus hic assignat, non magis uiris copetit quàm mulieribus. De utrisque enim dicit, propter uitandam scortationé quisque uir uxorem suam, & quæque mulier uirum suum habeat. Tam enim mulieri quàm uiro uitanda præscribitur non solum scortatio, sed & scortationis occasio.
units.tr: And so no one should grant this reason for marriage to men, even aged and grave men, if they have younger wives, as we read of Abraham, on the ground that they are still able to beget children, and yet deny it to women on the ground that offspring cannot be brought forth by those already advanced in years. It must be noted that the reason for marriage which the Apostle assigns here belongs to husbands no less than to wives. For he says of both: let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband, because of the avoiding of fornication. For the avoiding not only of fornication but of the occasion of fornication is prescribed for the woman no less than for the man.

units.la: Vxori uir debitam beneuolentiam reddat, similiter autem & uxor uiro. Vxor proprij corporis ius non habet, sed maritus. Similiter & maritus proprij corporis ius non habet, sed uxor.
units.tr: The husband should render to his wife the due kindness, and likewise the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.

units.la: Ista coniugij legem ac ὀφειλὴν exprimút, & illud quod dixit, quisque suam, & quæque suú habeat, ad propositum coniugij finem applicat. Ad hoc enim, ut coniugibus stupra uitare liceat, opus est ut alter alteri coniugi debitam beneuolentiam reddat. Vocat autè debitā beneuolentiam, obsequium illud, quo naturæ legi utrinq; seruitur. Illam, ne putetur esse libera cuiquam coniugum, uocat debitam, & non dicit præstet, sed ἀποδιδότω reddat, ut debita reddi solent.
units.tr: These words express the law of marriage and the debt [ὀφειλὴν], and his saying, "each his own" and "each her own," applies this to the purpose of marriage. For in order that spouses may be able to avoid unchastity, it is necessary that each render to the other the due kindness. He calls it the due kindness, that compliance by which the law of nature is served on both sides. He calls it due, so that it may not be thought to be at the free disposal of either spouse; and he does not say "let him give" but "let him render" [ἀποδιδότω], as is the custom with things that are owed.

units.la: Rem parũ uerecundã, ut inquit Erasm. uerecundæ notat.
units.tr: "A matter somewhat immodest," as Erasmus says, the word of modesty marks it.

units.la: VXOR proprij corporis ius nõ habet.) Ve lut rationis uice subijcit, quare debitam uocet beneuolentiā hanc mutuam. Ob id uidelicet, quod neuter coniugũ proprij corporis ius habet, sed uiri uxor, & uxoris uir. Ea est lex coniugij, qua discernitur à concubinatu, in quo nec uiri corpus in potestate mulieris, nec mulieris in potestate uiri est, sed quisq; proprij corporis ius habet, ut relicto cócubinatu posit se legitimo addicere coniugio, nec peccatur, si altera ab altero discesserit. Et hoc ipsum est, cuius gratia plerique coniugio contempto liberam sectantur libidinem ne cogantur corporis libertatem amittere. Arbitrantur enim rem esse molestam & indignam uiro, corporis proprij potestate permittere mulieri, at uetita libidine polluere corpus non scortationi, sed domino destinatû, non putant rem esse indignam uiro.
units.tr: "The wife does not have authority over her own body." The Apostle adds this as if it were the reason why he calls this mutual kindness due: namely, because neither spouse has authority over his or her own body, but the wife belongs to the husband and the husband to the wife. This is the law of marriage, by which it is distinguished from concubinage, in which neither the man's body is in the power of the woman nor the woman's in the power of the man, but each has authority over his own body, so that, having left the concubinage, he may bind himself to lawful marriage, and no sin is committed if one separates from the other. And this very thing is the reason why many, scorning marriage, pursue unbridled lust, so that they will not be forced to lose the freedom of their bodies. For they think it a burden and unworthy of a man to yield the power over his own body to a woman, but to defile the body with forbidden lust, a body destined not for fornication but for the Lord, they do not think unworthy of a man.

units.la: Coniungit æqua lege utrosque & uirum & uxore Apostolus, parem utriq; in alterius cor-
units.tr: The Apostle joins husband and wife together under one equal law, giving each an equal power over the other's body,

units.la: A pus potestatem, & ius assignans quod ad mutuam istam beneuolentiam attinet & naturæ legem. Alioqui quod reliquam coniugij conditionem concernit, non est ea in uirum potestas mulieri, quæ est in mulierem uiro. Nam is caput est mulieris, cui à domino dictum est, sub potestate uiri eris, & ipse dominabitur tibi.
units.tr: and assigning a right in respect of this mutual kindness and the law of nature. Otherwise, as far as the remaining conditions of marriage are concerned, the husband does not have over the wife the same power that the wife has over the husband. For he is the head of the woman, to whom it was said by the Lord: you shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you.

units.la: Ne fraudetis uos inuicem, nisi si quid ex consensu, ad tempus, ut uacetis ieiunio & precationi, & rursum in unum conueniatis, ne tentet uos Satanas propter intemperantiam uestram.
units.tr: Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may be free for fasting and prayer, and then come together again, lest Satan tempt you because of your incontinence.

units.la: Hinc apparet uel tum fuisse qui religionis prætextu istam debitam beneuolentiam coniugibus negarint, uel Apostolum quod temporibus posterioribus futurū erat præuidisse, & antidotum parasse. Non dicit, ne alter alteri mutuam beneuolentiam deneget, sed ne fraudetis uos inuicem. Fraus enim est, quando quod debetur commenticio aliquo prætextu aufertur. Ita quippe uerbum ἀποστέρησις hoc loco capitur ut respondeat ei quod dixit, uxori uir debitam beneuolentiam reddat, similiter & uxor uiro.
units.tr: From this it appears either that even then there were some who, under the pretext of religion, refused this due kindness to their spouses, or that the Apostle foresaw what was to happen in later times and prepared a remedy. He does not say, "let not one deny the other mutual kindness," but "do not defraud one another." For it is a fraud when what is owed is taken away under some invented pretext. Indeed the word ἀποστέρησις [deprivation, withholding] is used here so as to match what he said before: let the husband render the due kindness to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband.

units.la: NISI si quid ex consensu.) Ista nec præceptum habent, nec consilium, sed permissionem ac dispensationem. Neque enim præcipit, nec consulit, ut precandi & ieiunandi gratia separentur coniuges, sed si id faciendum sit permittit quidem ac dispensat, iuxta uero normas præscribit, nec temere id & immodicè pariter & periculosè fiat. Ideo non dicit, ad ieiunandum & precandum separemini, sed nisi si quid tale faciendum est. Deinde addit limitationem ex consensu, ut ostendat repugnante altero id non licere, & summè periculosum esse. Nam ut Chrysostomus ait: Maioris est æstimanda concordia, quàm ieiunia & precandi studium. Et plurimum parit perturbationum, & periculi si id tentet quisquam coniugum altero reluctante. Item, ad tempus, ne perpetuo secubitu separentur, sed temporario dútaxat. Adhæc, non quauis de causa, sed ad ieiunandum & precandum. Hoc est, quando forte uel propter ecclesiasticam, uel ob domesticam necessitatem seriore ac feruentiore precatione ambienda est diuina misericordia. Vnde non dicit, ut ieiunetis & precemini, sed ut uacetis ieiunio & precationi. Ita & Chrysostomus exponit: Nam alioqui, inquit, si uetaret coniunctos precari, quomodo impleretur illud, Sine intermissione orate? Non enim precationem polluit ista cohabitatio, sed seriorem impedit. Præterea, ne ita deuotio mali det ansam, addit iubendo, & rursum in unum conueniatis, ne tentet uos Satanas propter intemperantiá uestram. Vide quanta solicitudine cauerit insidias Satanæ, sciens quàm essent intemperantes Corinthij, & tentationibus Satanæ facile expositi.
units.tr: "Unless perhaps by consent." These words carry neither a command nor a counsel, but a permission and an indulgence. For he does not command or counsel that spouses be separated for the sake of prayer and fasting; if such a thing is to be done, he permits and indulges it, but he prescribes rules for it, so that it is not done rashly, immoderately and dangerously. Therefore he does not say, "separate yourselves to fast and pray," but "unless something of that kind is to be done." Then he adds a limitation, "by consent," to show that it is not lawful if the other is unwilling, and that it is extremely dangerous. For, as Chrysostom says: concord is to be valued more highly than fasts and eagerness in prayer, and if one spouse resists and the other tries it anyway, it produces very many disturbances and dangers. Likewise, "for a time," so that they are not separated in perpetual abstinence from the marriage bed, but only for a limited period. Moreover, not for any cause whatever, but for fasting and prayer. That is, when perhaps, either because of the needs of the Church or because of a domestic necessity, the divine mercy must be sought with more earnest and fervent prayer. Hence he does not say, "that you may fast and pray," but "that you may be free for fasting and prayer." Chrysostom also explains it so: for otherwise, he says, if he forbade spouses to pray together, how would that saying, "Pray without ceasing," be fulfilled? For living together does not pollute prayer, but it hinders the more earnest kind. Further, lest such devotion give occasion for evil, he adds by way of command, "and come together again, lest Satan tempt you because of your incontinence." See with how much care he guarded against the snares of Satan, knowing how intemperate the Corinthians were and how easily exposed to Satan's temptations.

units.la: Abutitur hoc loco Papa Siritius contra
units.tr: Pope Siricius abuses this passage against

units.la: ipsam Apostoli mentem, in decretis suis ubi A de continentia sacerdotum ad hunc modum argutatur.
units.tr: the very mind of the Apostle, in his decretals, where he reasons about the continence of priests in this manner:

units.la: Præterea quod dignũ & pudicum & honestũ est suademus,ut Sacerdotes & Leuitæ cum uxoribus suis non coeant, quia in ministerio ministri quotidianis necessitatibus occupantur. Ad Corinthios nanq; Apostolus scribens, dicit: Abstinete,ut uacetis orationi. Si ergo lai cis abstinentia imperatur, ut possint deprecátes audiri, quantomagis Sacerdos utiq; omni momento paratus esse debet,mundiciæ purITATE securus,ne aut sacrificiũ offerat,aut baptizare cogatur: qui si contaminatus est carnali concupiscentia quid faciet? Excusabit? Quo pudore? Qua mente usurpabit? Qua conscientia, quo merito exaudiri se credet? cum dictũ sit,omnia munda mundis, coinquinatis autem & infidelibus nihil mundum. Qua de re hortor, moneo, rogo, tollatur hoc opprobriũ, quod potest iure etiá Gětilitas accusare. Forte licere creditur,quia scriptum est, unius uxoris uirum. Non permanentem in concupi scentia generandi, sed propter continentiam futuram,qui ait,uelle omnes homines sic esse, sicuti & ego. Et apertius declarat,dicës: Qui autem in carne sunt, Deo placere nō possunt, uos autem iam nō estis in carne, sed in spiritu.
units.tr: "Moreover, what is worthy, chaste and honourable, we urge: that priests and Levites should not have intercourse with their wives, since ministers are occupied with daily necessities in their ministry. For the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says: 'Abstain, that you may be free for prayer.' If therefore abstinence is commanded of laymen, so that their prayers may be heard, how much more should a priest, who ought to be ready at every moment and secure in the purity of chastity, so that he neither offers sacrifice nor is compelled to baptize? If he is defiled by carnal lust, what will he do? Will he excuse himself? With what shame? With what mind will he take up the office? With what conscience, and on what merit, will he believe he will be heard? since it has been said, 'To the clean all things are clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean.' Therefore I exhort, warn and beseech that this reproach be removed, which even the heathen may rightly accuse. Perhaps it is believed to be lawful because it is written, 'the husband of one wife.' He who said, 'I wish all men to be as I am,' spoke not of one remaining in the lust of begetting, but of future continence. And he declares it more plainly, saying: 'Those who are in the flesh cannot please God, but you are not now in the flesh, but in the Spirit.'"

units.la: Liquet hunc Papam & reliquos eiusdē fari næ coniugio immunditiá deputasse,cótra authoritatem sanctarum scripturarum, maximè Ebr.13.deinde & patrum ac ueterum concilio-rum,potissimum Niceni & Gangrensis. Atq; ideo passim uidemus commercium cõnubiale,obscœnam coniunctionem & libidinosam societatẽ ab istis impijs uocari. Verùm istam impietatem indelebili nota manifestæ acspurcissimæ immunditiæ iam olim ulcisci cœpit iudicium domini.
units.tr: It is clear that this Pope and the others of his kind have counted marital union as uncleanness, against the authority of the holy Scriptures, above all Hebrews 13, and also against the Fathers and the ancient councils, especially those of Nicaea and Gangra. And therefore everywhere we see the conjugal bond, the obscene conjunction and the lustful partnership, called by these impious men. But the judgment of the Lord has long since begun to avenge this impiety with the indelible mark of a manifest and most filthy uncleanness.

units.la: 1 Primùm iniuriam facit & menti & uerbis Apostoli. Neq; enim ille imperat laicis abstinentiam,neque causam istam assignat, ut possint deprecantes exaudiri, quasi coniuges,nisi separentur,à Deo non exaudiantur, cum non debita coniugum beneuolentia reddat iniustos Deo,sed peccatum.
units.tr: First, they do an injury both to the mind and to the words of the Apostle. For he does not command abstinence of laymen, nor does he give this reason, that they may be heard in their prayers, as if spouses, unless they were separated, were not heard by God, since the due kindness of spouses does not make them unjust before God, but sin does.

units.la: 2 Deinde quod ex isto fundaméto falso substruit æquè falsum est. Videlicet quod dicit Sacerdoti non licere ministrare sacris, nisi abneget commercium uxorium. Ista sententia dam nata est cum in Niceno concilio admonente Paphnutio congressum cõiugium legitimum castitatem esse non immunditiam,tum cap.4. concilij Gangrensis,ubi damnatur,qui coniugem Sacerdotem discernit, tanquam propter nuptias offerre non debeat.
units.tr: Second, what they build on this false foundation is equally false. Namely, that they say it is not lawful for a priest to minister in sacred things unless he renounces marital intercourse. This opinion was condemned at the Council of Nicaea, when, at the urging of Paphnutius, it was declared that lawful intercourse in marriage is chastity, not uncleanness; and in canon 4 of the Council of Gangra, where those are condemned who separate a priest from his wife as if he ought not to offer on account of the marriage.

units.la: 3 Vim facit & reliquis duobus locis Apostoli ex Tit.1.& Ro.8. Nam de ista corporali mundicia non loquitur Apost.sed de ea quæ mẽtis est, nec immúdus quisquá ex cógressu uxoris redditur:nec ita in carne sunt cóiuges,ut Deo non placeant, sed qui secundũ carnis concupiscentiam uetitam & immundam uiuunt.
units.tr: Third, they also do violence to the two other passages of the Apostle, from Titus 1 and Romans 8. For the Apostle is not speaking here of that bodily purity, but of that which belongs to the mind; nor is anyone made unclean by intercourse with his wife; nor are spouses "in the flesh" in such a way that they cannot please God, but those who live according to the forbidden and unclean lust of the flesh.

units.la: Sed reliĉtis istis nugis, expendamus istam Pauli admonitionem aliquanto exactius.
units.tr: But, leaving aside these trifles, let us weigh this admonition of Paul somewhat more exactly.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: NE fraudetis uos inuicem.) Saluberrima est ista, & ad propositum Apostoli, omniũ accômodissima admonitio. Debitor est consorti suo quisq; coniugũ. Vir ipse licet sit caput uxoris,illiq; dominetur, nihilominus debitor illi constitutus est,idq; non rei pecuniariæ tantum,sed proprij quoq; corporis. Non est itaq; cuiquá coniugũ cogitandũ, quid sibi arrideat, sed quid compari suo debeat :uidendumq; ne fraudem in coniugali debito cõmittat. Ista admonitio licet coniuges hoc loco concernat, talis tamen est, quæ omnib. sit mortalibus applicáda. Quis enim est, qui nõ aliquo usq; debitor sit illis, quibus cõuiuit? Et forsan,qui minores sunt, non ita opus habent hac admonitione, ne maiores suos defraudent. Nã illi cogi possunt,ut officium præstent:opus autẽ potissimũ habent,qui superiores sunt, & nec cogi possunt à minoribus, nec agnoscũt quid illis debeant,putantes esse sibi quicquid faciẽdi libertatem. Hoc quippe animo plerunque qui rerum potiuntur, ergo subditos sunt, ut alios arbitrentur sibi omnia, se uero nihil cuiquam debere. Illis itaq; crebrò inculcandũ est, quod capita sint,inferioribus suis ueluti mẽbris plurimũ debentia,ut curent non minus illis præstare quod debent,quàm exigere quod sibi ab illis debetur. Reditus annuos ac census & primitias & decimas,ut suis temporibus táquam debita exigant in cautiones referunt, uerùm quæ ipsi uicißim debent subditis , ne semel quidem inspiciunt.
units.tr: NE DEFRAUD ONE ANOTHER. This admonition is most wholesome and, for the Apostle's purpose, most fitting of all. Each spouse owes the other what is due. The husband, although he is the head of his wife and rules over her, is nonetheless made her debtor, and not only in money matters but also in respect of his own body. So neither spouse should consider what pleases himself, but what he owes to his partner, and each should take care not to defraud the other in the marital debt. Although this admonition concerns spouses in this place, it is of such a kind that it should be applied to all mortals. For who is not in some way a debtor to those with whom he lives? Perhaps those who are younger do not need this admonition so much, lest they defraud their elders. For the younger can be compelled to perform their duty; but the admonition is most needed by those who are superiors, who cannot be compelled by their inferiors and do not acknowledge what they owe them, thinking that whatever they do is their own freedom. Indeed, those who hold power are commonly of this mind, that others are there for them, while they owe nothing to anyone. Therefore it must often be pressed upon them that they are heads, owing much to their inferiors, as to their own limbs; so that they take care to render to them no less than what they owe, as they demand what is owed to themselves. They enter in their records the yearly rents and the census, the first fruits and the tithes, so that they may collect them at their due times as debts; but what they themselves owe in turn to their subjects, they do not so much as glance at, not even once.

units.la: Nec putandum est hac in re sitam esse Christianæ perfectionis metam. Non enim satis est Christianæ professioni,neminem defraudare, sed exigitur,ut de iure tuo concedas, & supra quàm debes proximo etiá inimico inseruias. Ab ista perfectione qui proximos defraudant tam absunt,ut ne Gentiũ quidé æquitatẽ dum teneát,nedum Christianorũ iusticiá. Inoleuit nostris temporibus impudētissima iniquitas, ut passim inuenias,qui pròptissimi sint ad hoc ut pecunias mutuò accipiát,cui nunquam in animum induxerunt, quod fidem reddendo quod debent,liberare uelint. Quando illi quæ suaipsorum sunt egenis impendent?
units.tr: Nor should it be thought that the goal of Christian perfection lies in this matter. For it is not enough for a Christian profession that no one be defrauded; rather it is required that you yield something of your right, and serve your neighbour, even your enemy, beyond what you owe. Those who defraud their neighbours are so far from this perfection that they do not even keep to the fairness of the Gentiles, much less the righteousness of Christians. In our times a most shameless iniquity has taken root, so that everywhere you will find men who are most eager to receive money on loan, yet who have never once thought of wishing, by repaying in good faith what they owe, to be released. When will they give what is their own to the needy?

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: NISI si quid ex cõsensu.) Hoc mediũ illud est,& uelut instrumentum , quo debiti retinaculum soluitur,ut iam non sit defraudatio,sic ubi non præstatur quod debetur. Consensu isto fit,ut quod alterius est iure, in alterius uel usum, uel dominium licitè cedat. Hinc illud est,uolenti non fit iniuria.
units.tr: UNLESS IT BE BY MUTUAL CONSENT. This is the means, as it were the instrument, by which the bond of debt is loosed, so that there is no longer defrauding when what is owed is not paid. By consent it happens that what belongs by right to one person may lawfully pass into the use or ownership of another. Hence the saying: no injury is done to one who consents.

units.la: Videndum tamen, ut consensus iste nõ repugnet diuinæ uoluntati. Nam non mox licebit cóiugibus status & copulæ suæ uinculum ex consensu prorsus dissoluere,ut alter ab alte ro in uniuersum perpetua separatione disiungatur. garur. Quod enim Deus coniunxit, homo, inquit Christus, non separet. Proinde nō simpliciter dicit, nisi ex consensu, sed nisi aliquid ex cōsensu, idq; ad tempus. Inuenias alioqui, qui mox vtrinq; coniugij pertæsi, vt status iste mo leftiarum plenus est, facili consensu à se inuicē dissiliret. Imò crediderim rarissima futura coniugia, quæ non hoc pacto dissoluerentur. Non est igitur in potestate coniugum, ut mutuam fidem inter se alter alteri relaxet. Nam id repugnat ordini Dei.
units.tr: Yet care must be taken that this consent does not conflict with the divine will. For spouses may not at once dissolve by consent altogether the bond of their state and union, so that one is separated from the other in perpetual and complete division. For, as Christ says, what God has joined together, let not man put asunder. Therefore he does not say simply "unless by consent," but "unless something by consent," and that for a time. Otherwise you would find people who, weary of marriage on both sides, as that state is full of troubles, would with easy consent leap apart from one another. Indeed I would think marriages would be very rare that were not dissolved in this way. It is not therefore within the power of spouses to release each other from mutual faith, for that is contrary to the order of God.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: V T vacetis ieiunio & precationi.) Serię precationi cōiungit ieiunium. Nota est consuetudo piorum, cùm veteris tũ apostolicæ ecclesię qua cum serio esset, propter calamitate aliquā vel præsentem uel futuram, ambienda diuina clementia ieiunij humiliationem & afflictionem precationibus coniunxerút. Et hoc genus instituti exigit vacationė ab alijs negocijs nō solum illicitis, quibus in vniuersum ac semper renunciandum est more Niniuitarum, sed & à licitis ut hic videmus.
units.tr: THAT YOU MAY GIVE YOURSELVES TO FASTING AND PRAYER. He joins fasting to earnest prayer. The custom of the godly is well known: both in the ancient and in the apostolic Church, when they were in earnest, because of some calamity present or future, they joined the humbling and affliction of fasting to prayers, seeking the divine mercy. And this kind of observance requires freedom from other business, not only unlawful business, from which one must always and altogether withdraw, after the manner of the Ninevites, but also from lawful business, as we see here.

units.la: Putat Erasmus uacationis dictione ad precationem tantum referēdam esse, eo quod illa ieiunio non perinde cōpetat, propterea quod hic non ita exigatur animus à mundanis curis abstractus atq; in absoluendis precationibus. Verum meo iudicio non sunt seperanda hoc loco, ieiuniū & precatio, ut non minus ieiunio isti quàm precationi cōpetat animus liber & ab alijs negocijs absolutus. Institutum hoc ieiunandi simul & precandi in desuetudine abijt magno ecclesiæ malo. Obserua uerò, nō minus esse coniugibus quàm continetibus accessum ad ecclesiastica ieiunia & ferias preces: at scortatoribus non item.
