units.tr: Erasmus thinks that the word "free time" (vacatio) should be referred only to prayer, because it does not belong to fasting in the same way, since here the mind is not so required to be withdrawn from worldly cares and fixed on the completion of prayers. But in my judgement fasting and prayer should not be separated in this place, so that a mind free and released from other business belongs no less to that fasting than to prayer. This custom of fasting and praying together has fallen into disuse, to the great harm of the Church. But observe that access to the Church's fasts and days of prayer belongs no less to married people than to the continent; but not so to fornicators.

units.la: IIII.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: E T rursum in vnum coeuntiatis.) Bona res ieiunij, bona precandi sedulitas. At est modus in rebus etiam bonis, ac talibus, quarum gratia res aliquando licitæ & honestæ seponedæ sunt. Notum est illud: Sunt certi deniq; fines. Item, Ne quid nimis. Istū modum si obseruaf- sent in ecclesia episcopi, minus loci fuisset insi dijs Satanæ & minus scădalorū. Regressus aut ītæ à ieiunio etiā ad hoc utilis est, ut paretur ad ista reditus, qui occluderetur si lapsus fieret ad stupra. Sicut per otium, quiete & refectione corporis, ad labores qui intercludūtur, per irremissum laborē vires corporis eneruantē.
units.tr: AND COME TOGETHER AGAIN. Fasting is a good thing, and zeal in prayer is good. Yet there is a measure even in good things, and in such things for whose sake lawful and honourable matters must sometimes be set aside. That saying is well known: there are certain limits after all. Likewise: nothing in excess. If the bishops in the Church had observed this measure, there would have been less room for the snares of Satan and fewer scandals. Moreover, returning thus from fasting is useful even for this, that one may be prepared for that return to those duties which would be closed off if a lapse into fornication occurred. Just as by leisure, rest and refreshment of the body, one is restored to labours, which are interrupted, lest through unremitting labour the strength of the body be weakened.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: N E tentet vos Satanas.) Vide quid ieiunātibus, precantibus, & licitis abstinentibus metuat. Ne tentet, inquit, vos Satanas. Nisi periculum esset etiam ieiunantibus & precantibus à tentationibus Satanæ, nihil huius admonuisset. Imò hic potissimum timēdæ sunt Satanæ insidiæ, vbi à licitis seceditur, idq; immoderate, vt ad illicita fiat lapsus. Rem hanc ipsa luce clariorem reddidit experientia. Igitur securio res sunt ne per Satanam tententur qui licitis vtuntur remedijs.
units.tr: That Satan may not tempt you. Note what the Apostle fears for those who fast, pray, and abstain from lawful things: "that Satan may not tempt you." Unless there were danger of temptations from Satan even for those who fast and pray, he would not have given this warning at all. Indeed, Satan's snares are to be feared most where people withdraw from lawful things, and do so immoderately, so that they fall into unlawful ones. Experience has made this plainer than daylight. So those who use the lawful remedies are safe from being tempted by Satan.

units.la: A Nec dicit: Ne perdat vos Satanas, aut, ne concijciat vos in stuprorū immunditiam, sed, ne tētet uos. Non vult igitur ne tentandi quidem occasionem relinqui Satanæ, nedum superādi ac perdēdi. Certè non mox victor euadit qui tētat, nec statim perditur qui tētatur. Imò multis tentatio Satanę occasionem præstitit nobilis victoriæ. At tētandi occasionē dare Satanę, non est hominis pij & cauti: vult nos fortes quidem esse in superandis aduersarij tentationib. at interea simul admonet cautionis, ne temerè illis causam demus. Ita & Christus orare docu it, ne inducamur intentationem maligni.
units.tr: He does not say, "that Satan may not destroy you," or "may not throw you into the filth of fornication," but "that he may not tempt you." He therefore does not want even an occasion of temptation to be left to Satan, let alone of overcoming and destroying. Certainly the one who tempts is not at once the victor, nor is the one who is tempted at once lost. Indeed, for many, Satan's temptation has furnished the occasion for a noble victory. But to give Satan an occasion for tempting is not the mark of a godly and careful person. The Apostle wants us to be strong in overcoming the adversary's temptations, and at the same time he warns us to be cautious, lest we rashly give him cause. So also Christ taught us to pray that we be not led into the temptation of the evil one.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: PROPTER intemperantiā uestram.) Nō dicit δια τὴν ἀκρασίαν ὑμῶν, propter vestram in frenē libidinē, sed δια τὴν ἀκρασίαν ὑμῶν, i. propter vestrā incōtinentiā, vel continēdi impotentiā. Licet aliquando ἀκρασία in vicio sumatur pro ἀκολασία, hoc tamen loco, vbi de coniugibus agitur, & de ea incontinētia, cui per coniugium licitè satisfit, non est posita aliter q̄ pro natura li lege, cui obnoxij sūt oēs mortales, nisi qd' q̄ dā dispēsatiōediuina ab illa liberatur. Et ista naturalis ἀκ ἀσία nō est peccatū. Alioq; peccaret oēs coniuges legi naturæ inseruientes, & malè iuberet Apost. coiuges in vnū redire, vt illi satisfacietes Satanæ tētationes effugiant. Quis quæso peccando insidias Satanæ declinat?
units.tr: Because of your incontinence. He does not say "δια τὴν ἀκρασίαν ὑμῶν" [dia tēn akrasian hymōn], because of your unbridled lust, but "δια τὴν ἀκρασίαν ὑμῶν" [dia tēn akrasian hymōn], that is, because of your incontinence, or inability to contain yourselves. Although ἀκρασία [akrasia] is sometimes taken in a bad sense for ἀκολασία [akolasia], licentiousness, in this passage, where he is speaking of married people and of that incontinence which is lawfully satisfied through marriage, it is used in no other sense than for the natural law to which all mortals are subject, unless someone is freed from it by some special dispensation of divine providence. And this natural incontinence is not sin. Otherwise all married people, who serve the law of nature, would sin, and the Apostle would be wrongly bidding married people to come together again, so that by satisfying it they might escape Satan's temptations. Who, I ask, avoids Satan's snares by sinning?

units.la: Imò audim dicere ἀκρασίαν istam, tanquā lege quandam naturæ esse à Deo, cùm in viris tū in mulieribus indita, ad hoc ut humani generis posteritas coseruetur, ita vt nemo seipsum queat ab illa eximere nisi diuinitȳ ac singulari ter eximatur. Ideo Christus dixit: Nō oēs capi unt verbū hoc, sed quibus datū est. Et infrà Apost. dicet: Sed quisq; propriū donū habet. Est itaq; ἀκρασία ista nō solū naturalis & sine peccato, nisi degeneret in libidinē infrenē, liberā, & vagam, sed & necessaria & vtilis coseruationi generis humani. Alioqui qs sustineret tantis subijci molestijs, siue quæ viros seu quę mulieres in cōiugio adobruunt, nisi vi sua vtrūq; sexum captiuum haberet ista ἀκρασία. Libido vs rō intemperans, & vaga scortationis impuritas, nec naturalis est, sed corruptæ naturæ vicium, nec vtilis, sed noxia & damnabilis. Et in coniugibus reprehensibilis est libido, si passionibus desiderij gentiliter inseruiatur, qua de re videre est 1. Thess. 4.
units.tr: Indeed, I hear it said that this incontinence is, as it were, a certain law of nature, implanted by God both in men and in women, so that the posterity of the human race may be preserved, so that no one can free himself from it unless he is set free by divine power and in a singular way. Therefore Christ said: "Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it is given." And below the Apostle will say: "But each has his own gift." This incontinence, then, is not only natural and without sin, unless it degenerates into unbridled, free and wandering lust, but it is also necessary and useful for the preservation of the human race. Otherwise who would endure being subjected to such great burdens, those which overwhelm both men and women in marriage, unless this incontinence by its own power held both sexes captive? Intemperate lust, and the wandering impurity of fornication, is neither natural, but a vice of corrupted nature, nor useful, but harmful and damnable. And lust is blameworthy even in married people if they serve the desires of passion like the heathen. On this matter one may see 1 Thessalonians 4.

units.la: Noui quid hac de re disputet Augustinus de ciuit. Dei, lib. 14. cap. 16. 17. 18. 19. 20. 21. 22. 23. & 24. facit eam pœnam peccati, ut est quidem, verum non sine diuinæ dispositionis prouidētia. Non mox peccatum est, quod pœna peccati est. dolor parturientium pœna peccati est, peccatum non est. Pane vesci in sudore vultus, pœna peccati est. At non est inobediens diuinæ voluntati quare peccatum non est. Mo leftiam habet adiunctam, propter carnis inobedientiam, at inde non redditur peccatū. Turpitudinē habet, vnde & pudenda uocātur mēbra illa quæ generationi subserviunt, pudorisq; gratia obteguntur. & actus ipse non solū vulgaris & illicitus, sed & coniugalis secretum amat & publicum fugit, & horum gratia pecca tum non habet. Sunt & alia quaedam incorpo-ribus nostris quae turpitudinem habent & o-culi gaudent. Malesuada est: At id & de fame dicitur. Seruit corruptioni, & originali malo, quod ex Adamo diffunditur in omne carnem. unde & Dauid dicit: Ecce in iniquitatibus co-ceptus sum, & in peccatis concepit me mater mea, attamen peccatū non est, nisi vel accedat vetita intemperantia, uel ordine coniugij re-spuat. Non eiusdem rationis sunt quae ex pec-cato sunt. Quaedam enim ex peccato sunt tanq; danabilis arboris damnabiles fructus, ut sunt inordinati affectus, irae, liuores, superbiae, pra-uae concupiscentiae, &c. cum suis prauis actib. homicidio, mendacio, adulterio, scortatione, &c. Quaedam vero sunt ex peccato, tanquam poena quaedam & calamitas, ut sunt vitae huius molestiae, carnis nostrae corruptio, & quae illa comitatur, fames, sitis, dolor & cruciatus, mor-bi, mors ipsa, per quam ad terram reuertimur. Inter ista connumeranda est & haec ἀνάγκη na-turalis necessitas & lex.
units.tr: I know what Augustine argues on this matter in De civitate Dei, book 14, chapters 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23 and 24. He makes it a punishment of sin, as indeed it is, but not without the providence of the divine disposition. A thing is not at once a sin because it is a punishment of sin: the pain of women in childbirth is a punishment of sin, but it is not a sin. To eat bread in the sweat of one's face is a punishment of sin, but it is not disobedience to the divine will, and so it is not a sin. Incontinence has annexed to it trouble, because of the disobedience of the flesh, yet it is not thereby made a sin. It has a shamefulness, whence those parts which serve generation are called "shameful" and are covered for the sake of modesty; and the act itself, not only when it is common and unlawful but also when it is marital, loves secrecy and flees publicity, and yet it has no sin on account of these things. There are also other things in our bodies which have a shamefulness and delight the eyes. It is "bad counsellor," but this is also said of hunger. It serves corruption and the original evil which spreads from Adam into all flesh; whence David also says: "Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me." Yet it is not sin, unless either forbidden intemperance is added or it departs from the order of marriage. Those things which come from sin are not of the same kind. For some things come from sin as the damnable fruits of a damnable tree, such as disordered affections, anger, envy, pride, wicked desires, etc., with their wicked acts: murder, lying, adultery, fornication, etc. But others come from sin as a certain punishment and calamity, such as the troubles of this life, the corruption of our flesh and what accompanies it: hunger, thirst, pain and torments, diseases, death itself, through which we return to the earth. Among these must also be counted this natural necessity and law [ἀνάγκη].

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Notandum est & hoc, quàm ex nobis tenta-tionis occasionem venetur Satan, nec quicquā tentando possit, nisi nostra incautione uel im-becillitate iuuetur. Ita Christum nō tentabat, nisi vbi animaduertit eum famem sustinere. Ita & Euam adorsus est, vbi illam solam repe-rit, idq; apud arborē pomi vetiti, illiusq; aspe-ctu nonihil oblectari animaduertit. Et hoc est, cur Iacobus cap.1. unumquenq; à sua ipsius co-cupiscentia abstractum & illectum tentari di-cat. Oportet enim Satanam principia quedam ex nobis uenari, quibusad tentandum, tanquā medijs quibusdam utatur, & ex quibus laque-os nobis struat. Sic Iudam tentauit posteaquā intellexit illum furem esse, & de quaestu solici-tum. Ita 1. Tim. 6. dicuntur incidere in tentatio-nem & laqueum, qui uolunt diuites fieri.
units.tr: This also must be noted: how eagerly Satan seeks an occasion for temptation from us, and he can accomplish nothing by tempting unless he is aided by our carelessness or weakness. So he did not tempt Christ except where he perceived that He was enduring hunger. So too he assailed Eve, where he found her alone, and that near the tree of the forbidden fruit, and perceived that she took some delight in the sight of it. And this is why James, in chapter 1, says that each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own lust. For Satan must seek out certain beginnings in us, which he uses as means for tempting and from which he builds snares for us. So he tempted Judas after he understood that he was a thief and anxious about gain. Thus in 1 Timothy 6 those who want to become rich are said to fall into temptation and a snare.

units.la: Hoc autem dico iuxta indulgentiam, non iuxta praeceptum. Nam uelim omnes homines esse, ut & ipse sum. Sed unus-quisq; proprium donū habet, alius qui-dem hic, alius autem sic.
units.tr: I say this by way of concession, not as a command. For I would wish all men to be as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that.

units.la: Per correctionem cauet, ne occasionem det futurae tentationi, quā cupit vitari. Ideo ostendit se ista dicere non praecipiendi, sed indulgēdi modo. Est autem συγγνώμη ea concessio, qua permittis & concedis non quod sit optimum tibiq; magis arrideat, sed quod aliorum captui & imbecillitati conuenire putaueris, quod alio vocabulo Graeci συγχωρεῖσθαι, id est, conde-scensum uocant. ἐπιτάγμα uero, praeceptum est, & alia habet rationem. Hic simpliciter absque ullo condescensu & indulgentia quod faciendum est, ita iniungitur, ut non sit in potestate subditi quicquam decidere de eo quod man-
units.tr: He guards by way of correction against giving occasion for the future temptation that he wishes to be avoided. Therefore he shows that he says these things not in the mode of commanding but of indulging. Now συγγνώμη [synggnōmē] is that concession by which you permit and allow not what is best and what pleases you most, but what you think suits the capacity and weakness of others; the Greeks call this συγχωρεῖσθαι [synchōreisthai], that is, to condescend. An ἐπιτάγμα [epitagma], however, is a command and has a different character. Here what must be done is enjoined plainly, without any condescension or indulgence, so that it is not within the subject's power to omit anything of what is commanded; whereas συγγνώμη does not compel, but leaves it free to do or omit what is conceded.

units.la: B
units.tr: B

units.la: datur, cum συγγνώμη non cogat, sed liberum permittat, an facias vel omittas quod conceditur. Cum ergo dicit se istud non praecipere, sed per indulgentiam & concessionem ponere, ad hoc facit, ne putent Corinthij, omnino necesse esse absq; vlla tergiuersatione aut differentia hoc singuli faciant, quod in verbis istis continetur.
units.tr: Therefore, when he says that he does not command this, but sets it down by indulgence and concession, he does so in order that the Corinthians not think it altogether necessary, without any exception or distinction, that each individual do what is contained in these words.

units.la: Videndum itaq; hoc loco, qua sobrietate & prudentia spiritus sint non solum patrum, sed & apostolorum scripta legenda & amplexanda. Nam aperte hoc loco Apostolus in suis ver-bis discrimen obseruandum ponit, admonens non omnia eiusdem esse rationis & conditionis. Quaedam facit consilia & concessionem, quibus nullius conscientia constringitur, quo-rum obseruantia pro cuiusq; captu libera per-mittitur. Quaedam vero non consulendi aut in dulgendi, sed praecipiēdi modo ponit, tanquā obseruatu necessaria, de quibus audiemus hoc capite, & nonnullis aliis sequentibus.
units.tr: Here we must consider with what sobriety and prudence the writings not only of the Fathers but also of the apostles are to be read and embraced. For in these words the Apostle clearly sets down a distinction to be observed, warning that not all things are of the same kind and condition. Some things he puts as counsels and concessions, by which no one's conscience is bound, and whose observance is left free according to each person's capacity. Other things, however, he states not in the mode of advising or indulging but of commanding, as things necessary to be observed; of these we shall hear in this chapter and in some that follow.

units.la: Notanda simul est Apostoli prudentia & vi-gilantia, qua diligenter cauet, ne de rebus peri-culosis ita disputet, ut rimam aperiat tentatio-nibus Satanae. Non spectat quid ipse, sed quid Corinthij possint. Nec adigit illos praeceptoria potestate ad res licet bonas, sed periculosas, ve-rum demittit se ad captum imbecillium, con-sideratq; quid humeri illorum ferre possint vel ferre recusent.
units.tr: At the same time we should note the Apostle's prudence and vigilance, by which he carefully guards against disputing about dangerous matters in such a way as to open a crack for the temptations of Satan. He considers not what he himself can do, but what the Corinthians can bear. Nor does he force them by the authority of a command to things that are indeed lawful but dangerous; rather he lowers himself to the capacity of the weak, considering what their shoulders can bear or refuse to bear.

units.la: Deinde non est contentus, quod non prae-cipit res liberas licet bonas & vtiles, sed admo-net eos etiam, quod ista non praecipiendi, sed concedendi modo scribat. Cur hoc facit? Me-tuit forsan ne ipsi id non intelligant? Omnino illos hoc scire vult. Alioqui tam diligenter hu-ius non admoneret. Ergo scribat operaepretiū esse, ut id intelligerent Corinthij. Quamobrē? Ne praeter rationē conscientiā peccati incurre-rent, vbi nihil esset peccati. Ista spiritus prudē-tiam, & paternam vigilantiam imitari debebāt ecclesię doctores ac pastores, nō solū ne de re-bus liberis praecepta statuerent, sed apostolica συγγνώμη uteretur, veruetiam ut diligēter rerū libertatem Christianis notā facerent, sefeq; ex plicaret, quid quatenus & qua ratione ppone-rent, quid necessario seruandum praeciperent, quid fidelium arbitrio & imbecillium captui liberum relinquerent.
units.tr: Furthermore, he is not content merely to not command things that are free, though good and useful; he also warns them that he writes these things by way of concession and not command. Why does he do this? Perhaps he fears they will not understand it? Certainly he wants them to know this, otherwise he would not warn them so carefully about it. Therefore he judges it worth the effort that the Corinthians understand this. Why? So that they would not, against reason, incur the guilt of sin where there is no sin. Teachers and ministers of the Church ought to imitate this prudence of the Spirit and this paternal vigilance: not only so that they do not lay down commands about free matters, but so that they use the apostolic συγγνώμη, and also diligently make the freedom of things known to Christians, explaining what they propose, how far and on what ground, what they command to be kept as necessary, and what they leave free to the judgment of the faithful and the capacity of the weak.

units.la: Sed quo referenda sit ista συγγνώμη omnino videndū est. Non enim eiusdem rationis sunt praecedentia, vt ad illa omnia indiscriminatim pertinere possint, sed plurimum interest, quo referas. Augustinus libro de bono coniugali, cap.6. ex hoc loco colligit concubitum coniu-galem, quem alter coniugum ex lege matrimo-nij tanquam debitum, negare non debet si nō fiat respectu prolis acquirēdę culpa nō carere. Vnde hoc colligit: Ex eo videlicet, quod istam συγγνωμίω refert ad id qd Apost. dixit. uxorivir debita beneuolentiam reddat, similiter aut & vxor viro. Hoc intelligit Apostolū non precpti uice, sed per ueniā posuisse & ignoscētiā, tanq; de re nonnihil quidem culpabili, sed propter maius malum concedenda. Et hoc indicant ipsius verba. Nam sic scribit.
units.tr: But we must consider altogether to what this συγγνώμη should be referred. For the preceding words are not of one kind, so that they can all be applied to them without distinction; it makes a great difference to what you refer it. Augustine, in his book On the Good of Marriage, chapter 6, from this passage gathers that conjugal intercourse, which one spouse under the law of marriage ought not refuse the other as a due, is not free of fault if it is not done with a view to offspring. He draws this from the fact that he refers this συγγνώμη to what the Apostle said: let the husband render to the wife her due benevolence, and likewise the wife to the husband. He understands the Apostle to have set this down not in the manner of a precept, but by pardon and indulgence, as a matter somewhat blameworthy, yet to be conceded on account of a greater evil. And his own words indicate this, for he writes thus.

units.la: Iam in ipsa quoq; immoderatione exactione debiti carnalis quam eis non secundum imperium praecepit, sed secundum veniam concedit Apostolus, vt etiam praeter causam procreandi sibi misceatur, etsi eos praui mores ad talem concubitum impellunt, nuptiae tamen ab adulterio seu fornicatione defendunt. Neque enim illud propter nuptias admittitur, sed propter nuptias ignoscitur. Et paulo post. Coniugalis enim concubitus generandi gratia non habet culpam, concupiscentiae vero satiandae, sed tamen cum coniuge propter fidem thori, venialem habet culpam.
units.tr: "Moreover, in the very immoderation and exacting of the carnal due, which the Apostle does not command them by authority but concedes by indulgence, so that a man may have intercourse even apart from the cause of procreation, although wicked habits drive them to such intercourse, marriage nevertheless defends them from adultery or fornication. For that is not admitted on account of marriage, but is pardoned on account of marriage." And a little after: "For conjugal intercourse for the sake of begetting has no fault; but for the sake of satisfying lust it has a venial fault, yet even so, with one's spouse, on account of the fidelity of the bed."

units.la: 1 At meo iudicio, primum non est necesse, vt intelligatur Apostolus hoc loco de debito coniugali, coniugibus inuicem reddendo, cum praecedentia alias aliquot habeant particulas, quo tutius referri possit ista συγγνώμη. Neque enim quadrat, vt intelligamus coniugale debitum ex Apostoli condonatione, etiam quatenus vitandae tantum fornicationi seruit, reddendum esse, cum id exigat lex ipsa coniugij, & fides thori legitimi, qua alter alteri obnoxius est. Potest referri vel ad id quod dixit. Propter vitandam fornicationem quisq; vxore suam & quaeq; maritum suum habeat, ne putetur omnibus praecipere coniugium, tanquam rem ita necessariam, vt sine peccati conscientia vitari nequeat, vel ad eam particulam qua dixit, nisi si quid ex consensu, ad tempus, vt vacetis ieiunio & precationi, &c. ne ista intelligantur necessaria praecipi, & non per concessionem dici.
units.tr: 1 But in my judgment, first, it is not necessary to understand the Apostle in this place as speaking of the conjugal debt, to be rendered by the spouses to one another, since the preceding words have several other parts, to which this συγγνώμη can more safely be referred. For it does not fit that we should understand the conjugal due to be rendered from the Apostle's pardon, even as far as it serves only to avoid fornication; since that is demanded by the very law of marriage and the fidelity of lawful wedlock, by which each is bound to the other. It can rather be referred either to what he said, "Because of the temptation to fornication, let each man have his own wife and each woman her own husband," so that it is not thought he commands marriage to everyone as something so necessary that it cannot be avoided without a sense of sin; or to that clause where he said, "unless perhaps by consent, for a time, that you may be free for fasting and prayer," etc., so that these things are not understood as commanded as necessary, but are said by concession.

units.la: 2 Deinde no statim συγγνώμην eam concessionem & indulgentiam perpetuo significat, qua quae culpa quidem habent, sed propter maioris culpae malum vitandum conceduntur, quale est quod repudij libellus Iudaeis per Mosen permissus est. Nam & tum aliquid recte per συγγνώμην fieri dicitur, quando relicto maiori bono certa ratione minus bonum suadetur & apprehenditur. Qui consulit, vt quisq; suam habeat vxorem vitandae fornicationis gratia, non consulit rem minus culpabilem, vt quae maioris est culpae vitetur, sed a re commodiore & vtiliore continentia videlicet & ἀγαμία ad eam quae & ipsa bona quidem est, sed minus commoda regno coelorum propter instantem necessitatem certa de causa auocat. Non enim, vt ipse testatur Augustinus, duo mala sunt coniugium & fornicatio, quorum alterum sit peius, sed duo bona sunt coniugium & ἀγαμία, quorum alterum est melius, quemadmodum duo mala sunt, fornicatio & adulterium, quorum alterum grauiorem culpam habet.
units.tr: 2 Next, συγγνώμη does not always signify that concession and indulgence by which things that do carry fault are permitted in order to avoid a greater fault, as is the case with the bill of divorce permitted to the Jews through Moses. For sometimes it is said that something is rightly done by συγγνώμη when, with a greater good set aside, a lesser good is advised and embraced for a certain reason. He who advises that each man have his own wife to avoid fornication does not advise a less blameworthy thing, as if a greater fault were being avoided; rather, from a more fitting and useful thing, namely continence and ἀγαμία [agamia, celibacy], he calls away to that which is indeed good, but less suitable to the kingdom of heaven, for a certain reason, on account of pressing necessity. For, as Augustine himself testifies, marriage and fornication are not two evils, one of which is worse; rather marriage and ἀγαμία are two goods, one of which is better, just as fornication and adultery are two evils, one of which carries the graver fault.

units.la: Proinde ex ista συγγνώμη qua Apostolus considerata Corinthiorum imbecilitate, ἀγαμίαν non ausus suadere, quae commodior erat, & vtilior regno Christi, admonet ut fornicationis vitandae gratia suam quisque vxorem, & quaeque maritum suum habeat, non euincit concubitum legitimum aliquid habere culpae
units.tr: Therefore, from that συγγνώμη by which the Apostle, considering the weakness of the Corinthians, did not dare to advise ἀγαμία, which was more fitting and more useful to the kingdom of Christ, he admonishes that each man have his own wife and each woman her own husband to avoid fornication; he does not thereby prove that lawful intercourse has any fault

units.la: etiam in illis, quibus nulla generandae sobolis spes esse potest.
units.tr: even in those for whom there can be no hope of begetting offspring.

units.la: Nā uelim omnes homines esse, vt & ipse sum. Sed unusquisq; proprium donum habet ex Deo, alius quidē sic, alius autem sic.
units.tr: For I would wish all men to be as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that.

units.la: Rationem reddit cur non praecipiat coniugium, sed suadeat. Non ideo videlicet, qd illo gaudeat ipse, vel beatos ducat coniuges, cum omnes homines continentiae dono praeditos esse sicut ipse erat, verum, quod sciat dona Dei esse varia, non eadem omnibus data, sed aliis aliud, atq; aliud, ob quam causam fieri nequeat, vt vulgaris sit continentia. Tantundem est quod his verbis dicit. Ideo illud θέλω γάρ commodè legendum est, videlicet, velim enim, non volo & addenda concessionis nota μέν, quidè propter sequentem correctionis particulam ἀλλά, sed id quod & mox initio capitis huius faciendum est.
units.tr: He gives the reason why he does not command marriage but advises it. Not, of course, because he himself rejoices in it, or counts married couples blessed, since he wished all men to be endowed with the gift of continence as he himself was; but because he knows that the gifts of God are various, not given equally to all, but one thing to one and another to another; for which reason continence cannot be made common. This is the same as what he says in these words. Hence the θέλω γάρ [thelō gar] should be read fittingly, namely "I would wish, for," not "I will," and the mark of concession μέν [men] should be added, because of the following correction particle ἀλλά [alla], as should be done also at the beginning of this chapter.

units.la: Habet itaq; ista διπλοῦν duas partes.
units.tr: This passage therefore has a double [διπλοῦν] structure, with two parts.

units.la: 1 Prima, qua ostendit quid cupiat, si quidem fieri posset, cum dicit, Nam velim quidem omnes homines esse sicut ipse sum.
units.tr: 1 The first part shows what he would desire, if it could be done, when he says: "For I would that all men were even as I myself am."

units.la: Contenditur hoc loco qualis fuerit Apostolus, quod ad coniugij, vel continentiae causam attinet. Non enim loquitur vel de Apostolatu suo, vel de gente & tribu Iudaica, e qua erat, vel de stimulo carnis, quem inuitus patiebatur, vel de peccatis suis, quorum remissionem & ipse cum omnibus sanctis precari cogebatur. Sed de hac causa in qua iam versatur. Hic quidam contendunt fuisse illum coniugem, eo quod sui mentionem facit in ipso coniugij & non virginitatis tractatu: cum istis sentit Eusebius & Erasmus. Alij vero contra, coniugij expertem fuisse volunt, eo quod dicat, velim omnes homines esse, sicut ipse sum, nec credendum sit illum optare, vt omnes homines non coelibes sint, sed coniuges, quae sententia est Ambrosij. Verum quid opus est inani ista contentione quasi coniugio quiddam addat coniunx vel demat coelebs Paulus?
units.tr: The question here is what sort of man the Apostle was, as far as marriage or the state of continence is concerned. He is not speaking of his apostleship, nor of his Jewish race and tribe, nor of the goad of the flesh which he suffered against his will, nor of his sins, whose forgiveness he, like all the saints, was bound to seek. He is speaking of the matter he is now dealing with. Some hold that he was married, because he mentions himself in the discussion of marriage and not in the discussion of virginity; Eusebius and Erasmus agree with them. Others, on the contrary, want him to have been unmarried, because he says, "I would that all men were even as I myself am," and it cannot be believed that he wished all men to be not unmarried but married; this is the view of Ambrose. But why bother with this empty dispute, as if Paul added something to marriage by being married, or took something from it by being single?

units.la: Non hoc agit isto loco, vt simpliciter optet omnium coelibatum, quasi ille per se quicquā faciat ad salutem, & singulari apud Deum prerogatiua sit commendabilis. Sed, ut infra dicet propter illius commoditatem, vt expeditius liceat regnum Dei & illius iusticiam confecta minusq; impediantur credentes persequuti onum procellis, optat omnibus hanc continentiam, qua ipse quamuis esset vxoratus vxore tamen carere poterat. Quis hoc nomine optet sibi continentiae donum?
units.tr: He is not concerned in this place to wish simply for the celibacy of everyone, as if celibacy in itself contributed anything to salvation or made a man especially commendable before God by a unique prerogative. Rather, as he will say later, on account of its convenience, so that the kingdom of God and his righteousness may be advanced more readily, and believers, when the storms of persecution have passed, may be less hindered, he wishes this continence for all, though he himself, although married, could still do without a wife. Who would wish for the gift of continence on his own account?

units.la: Deinde quaerunt quidam quale sit hoc uotum Pauli, quo, si fieri posset omnes mortales sibi similes, id est, cōtinentes esse vellet. Qd si coniugio abstineret vniuersus orbis, perire inquiunt, genus humanum. Augustinus simpliciter id velle putat votū Pauli, optatq; hoc ipse cum Paulo. Reddit rationem, quod ita supra citius compleretur ciuitas Dei, modò id fieret corde puro, & conscientia bona, ac fide non fĩcta, terminareturque mundus. Ego credo huc non prospexisse mentem Pauli, sed simpliciter considerasse commoditatem continentiæ, quatenus illa multis caret molestijs, & aptior est regno Dei, præsertim tempore persequutionum, idque optasse animo erga regni Christi profectum, & omnium mortalium salutem flagranti. Vbi notandum obiter est ingenium piorum, quibus hoc peculiare est, vt quàm à Deo gratiam acceperūt, cupiantomnibus mortalibus secum esse communem, rursus, si quid triste patiuntur, nolint id cum aliquo mortalium communicari. Tale quid & Act.26. in Paulo videre est. Contrarium est maleuolorum in genium, quibus gaudium est socios habere inpœnis, & gloriosum, si quid eximij soli habeant.
units.tr: Next, some ask what sort of wish this of Paul's was, by which he would want all mortals, if it were possible, to be like himself, that is, to be continent. If the whole world abstained from marriage, they say, the human race would perish. Augustine simply thinks that Paul's wish was this, and that he himself wishes it together with Paul. He gives the reason: the city of God would be completed the sooner, provided this happened with a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith, and the world would come to an end. I believe that Paul's mind did not look so far, but simply considered the advantage of continence, in that it is free from many troubles and is better suited to the kingdom of God, especially in a time of persecution; and that he wished this with a mind burning for the advance of Christ's kingdom and the salvation of all mortals. It is worth noting in passing the disposition of the godly, which is peculiar to them: when they have received grace from God, they want to share it with all mortals; but again, if they suffer anything bitter, they do not want it shared with any mortal. Something of this kind can be seen in Paul in Acts 26. The opposite is the disposition of the malicious, who delight in having companions in their sufferings, and take pride if they alone have something outstanding.

units.la: 2 Alteraadiecte rationis pars est, qua declaratur, quid ab eo voto impediat ne audeat omnium optare, quam vellet, continentiam, videlicet, quod quisq; suum donum habeat à Deo: alius quidem sic, alius verò sic. Habet autē ista particula, quam arbitror diligenter expendendam, quædam obseruanda.
units.tr: 2 The second part of the reasoning is the clause that explains what keeps him from daring to wish that all should have the continence he would want: namely, that each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that. This clause, which I think should be weighed carefully, contains some points to be observed.

units.la: OBSER. I.
units.tr: OBSERVATION I.

units.la: Primū est, quomodo impediatur à voto suo Apostolus, per id quod quisq; proprium donū habet ex Deo, alius quidem sic, alius verò sic. Ita videlicet, quod non audet sperare futurum salubriter, vtut præcipiatur, optetur, tentetur, exigatur, quod à Deo non est concessum. Non audet optare, nedum exigere, vt omnes mortales, ne Christiani quidem, continentiam profiteatur. Quare? Quia facultas continendi nō est omnibus à Deo concessa. Non enim omnibus eadem diuinitus, sed alijs alia data sunt. Quid est ergo, quod episcopi tanta imprudentia tot millibus hominum cōtinentiam imposuerūt? Et quæ est vouentium illam temeritas, cum & Christus dicat: Non omnes hoc capiunt, sed quibus datum est?
units.tr: First, consider how the Apostle is kept from his wish by the fact that each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that. The point is this: he does not dare to hope that something which God has not granted will turn out well, however much it is commanded, wished for, attempted, or demanded. He does not dare to wish, much less to require, that all mortals, not even Christians, should profess continence. Why not? Because the ability to be continent has not been granted by God to all. For God has not given the same to all, but different gifts to different people. Why then did the bishops so rashly impose continence on so many thousands of people? And what recklessness is it in those who take the vow, since Christ himself says: "Not all can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given"?

units.la: 1 Regerūt quidam. At promissum est à Christo, quod accepturi simus quicquid à Deo petierimus. Quod igitur nobis præstitu est impossibile, per gratiam largientis Dei redditur possibile. Verū est, si quid petatur nomine filij & petatur fide incōcussa, taleq; sit quod regno Christi sit vel gloriosum vel necessarium. At res ipsa declarat, qua ratione cœlibatus professionem imponant illi, isti apprehendant, deinde omnibus conspicuum est, quomodo petāt, & quid accipiant.
units.tr: 1 Some reply that Christ promised that we shall receive whatever we ask of God. What is impossible for us, therefore, is made possible by the grace of the bountiful God. This is true, if a thing is asked in the name of the Son, asked with unshaken faith, and is such that it is either glorious or necessary for the kingdom of Christ. But the thing itself shows by what reasoning some impose the profession of celibacy and others take it up; then it is plain to everyone how they ask, and what they receive.

units.la: 2 Alij dicunt, volenti nihil est difficile. Modò quis velit, facilè continentiam custodiet. Debebat ergo Christus dicere. Nō omnes hoc capiunt: quia non omnes volūt. Qui verò volue rint, accipient & poterunt. Iam cum dicit, sed quibus datum est, satis aperte innuit frustra tentaturos istam continentiam, quibus illa nō est à Deo concessa. Non est itaque & hoc loco,
units.tr: 2 Others say, "To one who is willing nothing is difficult." If someone is willing, he will easily keep continence. Christ ought therefore to have said: "Not all receive this saying, because not all are willing; but those who are willing will receive it and be able to." Now when he says "but those to whom it is given," he plainly hints that those to whom this continence has not been granted by God will attempt it in vain. So in this place too it is not the will of the man, but of the God who gives.

units.la: volentis, sed donantis Dei.
units.tr: It is not the willing of the man, but the giving of God.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Notanda est diuina bonitas & munificentia erga genus humanum, in eo quod non quibusdam tantum, sed omnibus mortalibus donafua largitus est. Non enim dicit, habent aliqui sua peculiaria dona, sed quisq; proprium donum habet ex Deo. Nemo ergo queri poterit, quod sit diuina beneficentia destitutus, sed quisq; habet, vnde Deum glorificet.
units.tr: The divine goodness and generosity toward the human race is to be noted, in that God has bestowed gifts not on some only but on all mortals. For he does not say, "Some have gifts of their own," but "each one has his own gift from God." No one therefore can complain that he has been left without God's kindness; each has something by which to glorify God.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Adhæc, quod non omnibus idem, sed alijs alia concessit, admonet nos sapientię & pruden tiæ Dei, qua omnia pro suo ineffabili consilio, certis quidem at nobis nec inuestigandis nec comprehensibilibus, sed magis à longinquo adorandis rationibus, omnium consonantissima varietate temperat & dispensat. Proinde omnium sunt ineptissimi, & parum reuerentes erga istam diuinæ dispensationis sapientiam, qui suis consilijs istam donorum Dei varietatem disturbant, aliud ex alio efficere tentātes, præterquam quod cuncta gubernans Dei pro uidentia in singulis instituit. Ego sapientiam mortalium hanc vnā & omnium maximā duxerim, si cum intelligentia versari in ista dono rum Dei varietate, cum in se quisquam, tum erga alios possit. Ista sapientia opus est potissimum illis, quorum est alios moderari, vt intelligant quo quenq; instituere, quidq;ex quouis exigere ac sperare possint.
units.tr: Moreover, that God has not granted the same thing to all, but different things to different people, reminds us of the wisdom and prudence of God, by which he orders and arranges all things according to his unspeakable counsel. He does this with the most harmonious variety, by reasons that are certain yet neither to be searched out nor comprehended by us, but rather to be adored from afar. Therefore those are most foolish, and show little reverence for this wisdom of the divine dispensation, who by their own plans disturb this variety of God's gifts, trying to make one thing out of another, since God's providence, which governs all things, has established each thing in its own place. I would count this the one and greatest wisdom of mortals: to understand how this variety of God's gifts may be dealt with, both in oneself and toward others. This wisdom is especially needed by those whose task it is to govern others, so that they may understand how each person should be instructed, and what each can be required and expected to do.

units.la: IIII.
units.tr: IIII.

units.la: Et hoc notandum est, quod non dicit, Sed aliqui tantum hoc donum habent, ne putemus continentiam tantum donum esse Dei, sed quisque proprium donum habet ex Deo: alius quidem sic, alius verò sic, vt intelligamus & coniugium reputari inter dona Dei, vt & ve rè donum Dei est. Hic cogitandum est quis illud, quibus, & ad quid, & qua benedictione in stituerit. Donum Dei est continentię facultas. Verùm & coniugalis castitas, & vidualis quoque, & ipsæ diuinitùs ad bonum concessę sunt mortalibus. Quod autem coniugium molestijs refertum est, nō est ex doni huius, sed mortalium vicio.
units.tr: And it should be noted that he does not say, "Only some have this gift," lest we think that continence alone is a gift of God. Rather, "each has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that way," so that we understand that marriage too is counted among the gifts of God, as it truly is a gift of God. Here we must consider who instituted it, for whom, for what purpose, and with what blessing he instituted it. The ability to be continent is a gift of God. Yet both conjugal chastity and widowed chastity, and marriage itself, have been given by God to mortals for their good. That marriage is burdened with troubles, however, is not the fault of this gift but of mortals.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Postremò videmus hoc loco, quàm nolit Apostolus cuiusquam vitam ad alterius, sed ad proprium donum institui. Quis non duxerit esse imprudentem eum, qui domum suam nō ad propriæ, sed ad alienæ facultatis mensuram instituat, aut qui pedibus æger non quantum ipse per se poterit per diem, sed quantum itine ris viderit eos qui sanis sunt pedibus confice re, sibi præsumat? Eadem stultitia sanctorum exempla multis præsumpta sunt ad imitationem, non expenso quid proprij humeri ferre possent, quid non possent.
units.tr: Finally, we see here how unwilling the Apostle is that anyone's life be ordered by another's gift rather than by his own. Who would not judge him imprudent who arranges his household not by his own means but by another's, or who, being lame in his feet, presumes to walk as far in a day not as much as he himself can manage, but as far as he sees those with sound feet walking? The same folly has led many to imitate the examples of the saints, without weighing what their own shoulders can bear and what they cannot.

units.la: Dico autem inconiugatis & uiduis, bonum eis est, si manserint, ut & ego. Quod si se non continent, contrahant matrimonium. Nam satius est matrimonium contrahere, quam uri.
units.tr: But I say to the unmarried and widows: it is good for them if they remain as I also am. But if they do not have self-control, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn.

units.la: Ista pertinent ad secundum capitis huius membrum, quo de viduis agitur. Quidam arbitrantur & ad digamiam pertinere, quam Apostolus licitam faciat uiduis, si se non continent. Illi digamiam esse putant, quando mortua priore coniuge, denuo nubitur. Talis certe licita est Christianis pسenti testimonio Pauli, licet ueteres quidam, e quorum numero Tertullianus est, illam fecerint illicitam. At verior digamia ea est, qua cum duabus coniugibus simul habetur matrimonium, ut monogamus est, qui unam duntaxat coniugem habet. De ista non agitur ab Apostolo hoc loco.
units.tr: These words belong to the second part of this chapter, which deals with widows. Some think that this also refers to digamy, which the Apostle permits to widows if they cannot contain themselves. Those who think of digamy as marrying again after the death of the first spouse. Such a marriage is certainly lawful for Christians by the present testimony of Paul, although some of the ancients, among whom is Tertullian, made it unlawful. But the truer sense of digamy is that in which a man has two wives at the same time, just as a monogamist is one who has only one wife. The Apostle is not speaking of that here.

units.la: DICO autem.) Ex sequenti moderatione patet, quomodo dicendi verbo utatur hic Apostolus. Non praecipit, nec iubet, sed consulit. Alio sensu dictum est a Christo Matth. 5. Dico uobis, diligite inimicos uestros, &c. Na ibi non consulendi, sed praecipiendi sensu, dicendi verbum positum est.
units.tr: "I say" (dico autem): the following moderation shows how the Apostle uses the word "say" here. He does not command or order, but advises. It was said in another sense by Christ in Matthew 5: "I say to you, love your enemies," and so on. There the word "say" is used in the sense of commanding, not advising.

units.la: INCONIVGATIS & uiduis. De viduis nihil est dubij, quod eas intelligat, quae viros suos morte amiserunt. De ἀγάμοις uero ambiguum uidetur, an eos intelligat, qui nunquam sunt experti coniugiū, vel eos, qui ab uxoribus per mortem liberati sunt, quos viduos uocamus. Nam ἄγαμος proprie est qui coniugatus non est. Unde & Erasmus reddidit inconiugatis, licet putet ἀγάμους dici non posse, qui semel sint experti nuptias. Non occurrit illi, quod infra de coniuge a viro discedente legitur: Si discesserit maneat ἄγαμος, ubi manifestum est, quod ea dictio etiam illis competere queat, qui nuptias sunt experti. Est itaque simplicius ut intelligamus agi hoc loco quid uiduos & uiduas facere deceat. De uirginibus enim infra in tertio capitis huius membro tractabitur.
units.tr: "To the unmarried and to widows." There is no doubt about widows, that the word refers to those who have lost their husbands by death. But it seems uncertain whether the word "unmarried" [ἀγάμοις] refers to those who have never experienced marriage, or to those who have been freed from their wives by death, whom we call widows. For ἄγαμος properly means one who is not married. Hence Erasmus also rendered it "unmarried," although he thinks that ἀγάμους cannot be said of those who have once experienced marriage. He did not notice what is read below about a wife who separates from her husband: "If she departs, let her remain ἄγαμος [unmarried]," where it is clear that this word can also apply to those who have been married. It is therefore simpler to understand that this passage is about what widowed men and women ought to do. For the virgins will be treated below, in the third part of this chapter.

units.la: BONVM illis est. Bonum hic non sumitur pro uirtute, sed pro commodo. Non hoc bonum intelligit, quod Deo placeat. (Nam coram Deo inter coniugem & cōtinentem nihil est discriminis.) Sed quod ad consequendam regni Dei iusticiam multum habet commoditatis. Unde non dicit ἀρεσκον τῷ Θεῷ. Gratum Deo, sed bonum illis est. At quare bonum sit, infra commemorabit.
units.tr: "It is good for them." Here "good" is taken not in the sense of virtue but of advantage. He does not mean what is pleasing to God, for before God there is no difference between a married person and a continent one. He means what greatly helps them toward attaining the righteousness of the kingdom of God. Hence he does not say "pleasing to God" [ἀρεσκον τῷ Θεῷ], but "it is good for them." Why it is good he will mention below.

units.la: SI manserint ut & ego.) Colligunt ex hoc loco Paulum fuisse viduum, eo quod se viduis collocet in exemplum. Certe non potest fortius vidualem suadere cōtinentiam, quam suo ipsius exemplo. Dicit bonum esse viduis, ut sic maneant. Et ne videatur alijs suadere aliud quam sibijpsi, proponit illis suum exemplum. Non potest quisquam maiore fide alijs consulere, quid sectandum, quid fugiendum, quam si quod alijs cōsulit, & ipse completi, & quod alijs dissuadet ipse auersari deprehendatur. Licet non mox alijs conducat, quod ipse conducturum putas, & reipsa sectaris, nemo tamen culpare poterit consulentis affectum. Non multum efficiunt, qui quod iniungunt alijs, ipsi ne digito quidem attingunt.
units.tr: "If they remain, as I also do." From this passage some infer that Paul was a widower, since he sets himself forward as an example to widows. Certainly nothing could urge widows to continence more strongly than his own example. He says it is good for widows to remain so. And lest he seem to urge on others something other than what he does himself, he sets his own example before them. No one can advise others with greater authority about what to pursue and what to avoid than by doing what he advises and by being seen to shun what he dissuades others from. Even if what you think will profit others is not immediately useful to them, and you yourself really pursue it, no one can blame the affection of the one who advises. Those who lay burdens on others and will not so much as touch them with a finger accomplish little.

units.la: QVOD si se non continent, nubant.) Moderatio consilij est, ne quod suadebatur in bonum, vergeret in damnum. Vt enim suprà dixit, unusquisque proprium donum habet, alius sic alius vero sic, atque ideo ut in se sit commodum regno caelorum, si abstineatur a coniugio, malum tamen redditur, si absit donum continentiae. Addit itaque vigilanter limitationem, ostendens quousque & quibus bonum sit absque coniugio manere.
units.tr: "But if they do not contain themselves, let them marry." This is the moderation of the advice, so that what was urged for good should not turn to harm. For as he said above, each has his own gift: one in this way, another in that way. Therefore, although it is good in itself for the kingdom of heaven to abstain from marriage, it becomes harmful if the gift of continence is lacking. So he carefully adds a limitation, showing how far, and for whom, it is good to remain without marriage.

units.la: Obseruandum autem est, quod non dicit, si se continere non possunt, sed, si se non continent. Non enim vlla hic proponitur continendi necessitas quasi teneantur Christiani ad continentiam, nisi continendi impotentia excusentur. Nemo cogitur. Quisquis non vult continere se, aequè liber est a continentia, atque is qui non potest. Iam quid de illis statuendum iam olim erat, qui quod se non contineant, manifesta immunditia declarant, de quibus certe disputandum non est, quod possint, aut non possint quid velint aut respuant. Quod enim cōtinere se nolint, deinde ne possint quidem, publica scortatione produnt. Quis credat illos praeter animi sententiam scortari? Aut poterit ne quisquam dicere, quod cotinentiae donum habeant, qui ita scortatur, ut prope ad nihil aliud nati esse videantur?
units.tr: We must observe that he does not say, "If they cannot contain themselves," but "if they do not contain themselves." For no necessity of continence is proposed here, as if Christians were bound to continence unless they were excused by an inability to contain themselves. No one is compelled. Whoever does not wish to contain himself is just as free from continence as one who cannot. Now what was to be decided long ago about those who, because they do not contain themselves, show their manifest impurity: about these certainly there is no need to argue whether they can or cannot, or whether they want or refuse. For that they are unwilling to restrain themselves, and then indeed are unable, is shown by their public whoring. Who would believe that they whore against their own intention? Or could anyone say that they have the gift of continence, when they whore in such a way that they seem born for almost nothing else?

units.la: Eximunt quidam isti sententiae Monachos & Nonnas, & Sacerdotes. Vtinā eadem opera illos & incontinentiae eximerent, & continentia donarent. Praetextitur votum. At ut in canonibus est, votum non debet seruire perditioni & iniquitati. Praeposterū est si ex voto nectatur laqueus perditiōis. Not⁹ est Cyp. locus ad Pomponiū: lib. 1. cap. 11. ubi hac de re sic scribit.
units.tr: Some exempt monks, nuns, and priests from this sentence. Would that they would at the same time exempt them from incontinence and grant them continence! A vow is put forward as a pretext. But, as the canons say, a vow ought not to serve destruction and iniquity. It is absurd if a snare of destruction is tied by means of a vow. The passage of Cyprian to Pomponius is worth noting: book 1, chapter 11, where he writes on this matter as follows.

units.la: Quod si se ex fide Christo dicauerūt (loquitur autem de virginibus Deo dicatis) sine vlla fabula perseuerēt, ita fortes & stabiles praemiū virginitatis expectent. Si autē perseuerare nolunt, vel non possunt, melius est vt nubāt, quā in ignem delicijs suis cadant. Certe nullū fratribus aut sororibus scandalum faciant cū scripsit. Si cibus scandalizat fratrem, non mādueat carnem in saeculum, &c. Et Aug. alicubi arguit eos inconsiderātię qui taliū coniugia pro veris coniugijs non agnoscunt, sed si potent, dirimunt proq; adulterio habent.
units.tr: If they have dedicated themselves to Christ in faith (he is speaking of virgins consecrated to God), let them persevere without any fable, and so, being strong and steadfast, let them look for the reward of virginity. But if they are unwilling or unable to persevere, it is better that they marry than fall into fire through their pleasures. Certainly let them not give offence to brothers or sisters, since it is written: "If food causes my brother to stumble, I will eat no meat for ever," and so on. Augustine also somewhere charges those with thoughtlessness who do not recognise such marriages as true marriages, but, if they can, dissolve them and call them adultery.

units.la: NVBANT.) Vbi cōtinentia manifesta obijcitur uotarijs, regerūt, orandum esse Deum, ut det donū continentiae. Atqui Apostolo poterat dicere: Quod si se nō continēt orēt ad Deū p dono cōtinentiae, vt quod melius est coiugio, seruare possint. Iam non ita dicit, sed nubant, inquit, si se non continent, uelut digito ostendens quid faciendum sit incontinentibus.
units.tr: MARRY.) Where clear continence is demanded of those who have taken vows, they reply that God must be prayed to give the gift of continence. Yet the Apostle could have said: "But if they do not contain themselves, let them pray to God for the gift of continence, so that they may keep what is better than marriage." He does not say that, but "let them marry," he says, "if they do not contain themselves," pointing, as it were, with his finger to what the incontinent must do.

units.la: NAM
units.tr: FOR

units.la: Cypr
units.tr: Cypr.

units.la: 27.q.1. Nuptiarum
units.tr: 27 q. 1, Nuptiarum

units.la: NAM satius est matrimonium contrahere quàm vri.) Hæc est ratio limitationis cur nubere debeant incontinentes. Quia melius est matrimonium cotrahere, quàm vri. Est autem perpetuo quod melius est, quo ad eius fieri poterit, amplectedum. Melius est continere quà nubere. Bene, qui potest capere capiat. Vbi autem deest cotinentia, melius est nubere quàm vri. Ergo continentiæ uel uoluntate uel facultate destitutis, melius est ut nubant, quàm ut concupiscentiæ flammas subeant. Melius esset prorsus abstinere ab omni cibo. Nam carere multis molestijs, ad quas cogimur cibi gratia, uerùm cum id fieri nequeat, melius est edere & bibere, quàm fame periclitari.
units.tr: FOR it is better to contract marriage than to burn.) This is the reason for the qualification why the incontinent ought to marry: because it is better to contract marriage than to burn. What is better, however, is always to be embraced, as far as it can be. It is better to be continent than to marry; "let him who can receive it, receive it." But where continence is lacking, it is better to marry than to burn. Therefore, for those who lack continence either by will or by ability, it is better that they marry than undergo the flames of lust. It would indeed be best to abstain entirely from all food; but since we cannot avoid the many troubles to which we are subjected for the sake of food, it is better to eat and drink than to be in danger of starving.

units.la: QVAM uri.) Vstione hanc quidà exposuerunt de incendio gehennæ, quos refutat Erasmus. Aliam sententiam habent Comment. Hieronymo attributi, in quib.sic legitur. Malo fornicatiõis melius est, quod igne punitur, sicut Iudas in Genesi de sua nuru pronunciat. Appa ret hunc intelligere uerba Apoft.de igne supplicij, quo puniri debeant scortantes, quasi dicat Apoft. Melius est ut matrimonium contrahant incontinentes, quà si se non continentes scortentur. ideoq; ignis supplicio tradantur. At nostro sæculo non quadrat hæc expositio. Nunc enim fcortatorib. nõ est metuendum ignis supplicium, sed fecerdotib. ac monachis coniugib.ut inuertenda sint Apostoli uerba, dicendum q;: Qui fe non continet, scortetur. Melius est enim scortari quàm uri.
units.tr: THAN to burn.) Some have explained this burning as the fire of Gehenna, and Erasmus refutes them. The commentaries attributed to Jerome have another opinion, in which it is read thus: "Evil fornication is better, since it is punished by fire, as Judah says in Genesis about his daughter-in-law." He seems to understand the Apostle's words as referring to the fire of punishment with which fornicators ought to be punished, as if the Apostle said: "It is better that the incontinent contract marriage than that, if they do not contain themselves, they fornicate and so be handed over to the punishment of fire." But this explanation does not fit our age. For now fornicators need not fear the punishment of fire, but priests and monks, and married men, so that the Apostle's words would have to be turned round and it would have to be said: "Let him who does not contain himself fornicate, for it is better to fornicate than to burn."

units.la: Apostolus nec de præsenti aliquo, nec gehennæ supplicio, sed de concupiscentiæ incendio loquitur, quod Chryfoftom.tyrannidem concupiscentiæ vocat. Nos Germani uocamus brunft des fleyfchs, aliàs, das heymlich leyde. Innuit enim Apoft. ubi donum continentiæ deest, ibi nihil aliud expectandum esse, quàm istas cocupiscentiæ flammas.
units.tr: The Apostle speaks neither of some present affliction nor of the punishment of Gehenna, but of the burning of lust, which Chrysostom calls the tyranny of concupiscence. We Germans call it Brunst des Fleisches, otherwise das heimliche Leid. For the Apostle implies that where the gift of continence is lacking, nothing else is to be expected than these flames of concupiscence.

units.la: Notandum autem est, quod non dicit: Melius enim est matrimonium contrahere, quàm scortari, sed, quàm uri. Non mox scortatur qui vritur, id est, qui libidinis æstu vexatur. Attamen etiàsi non publicè scorteris, ubi tamè incendium istud libidinis senseris, non est expectandum dū in fcortatione cadas, aliquòue alio immundiciæ opere cõtra deū pecces, sed u surpandum coiugij remediū, antequam tentatione uincaris. Hoc scilicet est, quod nõ dicit, melius est nubere quàm scortari, sed, quà vri. Nam ob id ipsum suadet matrimonium, ne infcortationem, imò in vstionem incidant incõtinentes, iuxta id quod initio capitis huius dixit. Propter fcortationem uitandâ, habeat quif que uxoré suam, & quæq; uirum suum. Quod fi ijs qui libidinis ustionem sentiunt, imò incõtinentib. antequam vrantur nubendum est, ne vrantur, ne dum scortentur, ne, ut Chryso. habet, continendi laborib. & fudorib. subuertantur, quid iubendum est illis, qui iam pleno impetu scortantur?
units.tr: It must be noted, however, that he does not say, "It is better to contract marriage than to fornicate," but "than to burn." The one who burns is not at once fornicating; that is, he is tormented by the heat of lust. Yet even if you do not fornicate openly, when you have felt that burning of lust, you must not wait until you fall into fornication or sin against God by some other unclean deed, but must seize the remedy of marriage before you are conquered by temptation. This is surely what he does not say: "It is better to marry than to fornicate," but "than to burn." For for this very reason he urges marriage, so that the incontinent may not fall into fornication, or rather into burning, as he said at the beginning of this chapter: "Because of the temptation to fornication, let each man have his own wife and each woman her own husband." But if those who feel the burning of lust, or rather the incontinent, must marry before they burn, so that they may not burn and then fornicate, and (as Chrysostom says) be overthrown by the labours and sweats of striving for continence, what must be commanded to those who already fornicate with full force?

units.la: Tres inuenio causas, propter quas nubendũ fit incontinentibus, & æstum hunc libidinis in carne sua sentientibus.
units.tr: I find three causes on account of which the incontinent must marry, those who feel this heat of lust in their flesh.

units.la: Prima est, de qua iam diximus, ad quam & Apoft. respicit periculũ videlicet fcortationis, & omnis generis impuritatis. Horrendum est cogitatu quid ista libidinis vstio monachis & Nonnis pepererit. Paucissimi nanq; sunt, qui illam vincant, nempe quib. id à Deo datum est. Reliqua turba quouis modo illius sese molestia quidem liberat ad tempus, uerũ incredibiles conscientiæ cruciatus incurrit.
units.tr: The first is the one we have already mentioned, and to it the Apostle looks: namely the danger of fornication and of every kind of impurity. It is horrible to think what this burning of lust has produced among monks and nuns. For very few indeed overcome it, namely those to whom it has been given by God. The rest of the crowd, in whatever way, is indeed freed for a time from its trouble, but incurs unbelievable torments of conscience.

units.la: 2 Altera est quod etiàsi opus libidinis non fe quatur, inutilis tamen, imò nulla est ista contnentia corporis ubi animus immundis quotidie cogitationib. conspurcatur. Neq; enim ita comparatus est Deus, ut non plus mentis quà corporis rationem habeat.
units.tr: 2. The second is that even if the act of lust does not follow, continence of the body is nevertheless useless, or rather is no continence at all, when the mind is defiled every day by unclean thoughts. For God is not so constituted that he takes less account of the mind than of the body.

units.la: 3 Tertia est, quod tales animi prorsus inepti sunt regno Dei, occupantur enim impuris cogitationib. ut sanctis meditationibus locus ul lus esse nequeat.
units.tr: 3. The third is that such minds are wholly unfit for the kingdom of God, for they are occupied with impure thoughts, so that there can be no room for holy meditations.

units.la: Satius itaq; est, ut & fcortationis uitetur periculum, & animi declinetur impuritas, matrimonium cotrahere, quàm libidinis perpeti incendium. Nisi enim coiugio veluti refrigerio quodam incontinentiæ sopiretur incendium, certè ridiculus effet Apoft. qui incontinentib. suadeat, ut nubant. Reipsa videmus eos qui coniugium abiurarunt, cum dono continetiæ careant, perpetuo quodam libidinis æstu occupàri, impurisq; & oculis & geftib. & verbis, vt reliqua taceam, quasi fumo quodam æstuatis pectoris malum prodere.
units.tr: It is therefore better, both that the danger of fornication be avoided and that the impurity of the mind be turned aside, to contract marriage than to endure the burning of lust. For unless the burning were quieted by marriage, as by a kind of cooling for the incontinent, the Apostle would certainly be ridiculous in urging the incontinent to marry. We see in fact that those who have renounced marriage, since they lack the gift of continence, are constantly occupied by a kind of heat of lust, and betray the evil, to say nothing of the rest, by impure eyes, gestures and words, as if by a smoke rising from a burning breast.

units.la: Quid aût dicemus de adolefcentib. quibus nec pmittitur, nec decorum est, neq; conducit etiam, ut ante iustæ maturitatis annos nubant & tamen libidinis malum sub ipsa pubertate vehementer insidiosum est & permolestum? An & hic locum habet Apostoli sententia: Melius est nubere quàm uri. Licet enim de viduis loquatur, res tamen ipsa quam vitari vult nõ solum uiduis, sed & illis qui ad nuptias adhuc sunt immaturi & inepti, timendum est.
units.tr: What then shall we say of young people, to whom it is neither permitted nor fitting, nor even expedient, to marry before the years of proper maturity? Yet the evil of lust, even at the very onset of puberty, is most insidious and very troublesome. Does the Apostle's saying, "It is better to marry than to burn," apply here too? For although he speaks of widows, the very thing he wishes to avoid must be feared not only in widows but also in those who are still too immature and unfit for marriage.

units.la: Consulendum est hic adolefcentib. quando quidem illis ad remedium coniugij nondum adspirare licet, multominus cũ Christiani sint ad scortandi exorbitare licentiam, qua & malum non restinguitur, sed magis incenditur, & ira Dei provocatur, vt hac in re cauti sint, ne malo recenti & insueto dum illud uel incautè admittunt, uel ferre nesciunt, subuertantur & pereant, antequam nubendi accesserit ætas.
units.tr: Advice must be given here to young people, since they are not yet permitted to aspire to the remedy of marriage, much less, being Christians, to rush into the licence of fornication, by which the evil is not quenched but rather kindled further, and the anger of God is provoked. Let them therefore be careful in this matter, lest, by admitting the fresh and unfamiliar evil carelessly, or by not knowing how to bear it, they be overthrown and perish before the age of marriage arrives.

units.la: Fons miraculofus in Epiro faces accensas extinguit quidem sicut alij fontes, uerùm extinctas redaccendit, quod cum alijs cõmune non habet. Tale quid habet & fcortatio, ut non tam extinguat quàm redaccendat libidinis incendium. Libido uero incensa instar est lapidis quam uocant Asbeston, eo quod extinguì nequeat. De vtroq; Augustin.de Ciuit.Dei, li.21. cap.5.
units.tr: A miraculous spring in Epirus indeed extinguishes torches that are lit, as other springs do, but it rekindles those that have been extinguished, which it does not share with others. Fornication has something of this kind: it does not so much extinguish the fire of lust as rekindle it. Lust, once kindled, is like the stone they call asbestos, because it cannot be put out. On both, see Augustine, De civitate Dei, book 21, chapter 5.

units.la: 1 Profuerit illis cum primis studium timoris domini, & exercitium eloquiorum Dei.
units.tr: 1. Above all, it will benefit them to cultivate the fear of the Lord and the practice of the words of God.

units.la: Bonum homini est,inquit ille,fi portauerit iugum domini ab adolescentia sua. Et Dauid: In quo corrigit adolescentior uiam suam? In custodiendo sermones tuos. Adijciendae & crebrae precationes ad dominū, quibus alitur timor domini, pij cordis propositum confirmatur, & sanctimonia quaedam ac mentis castitas imbibitur,qua fiet, ut immundae cogitationes, aut non facilè admittantur, aut si per imprudentiam admissae sint, omnium facillimè extinguantur.
units.tr: "It is good for a man," he says, "if he has borne the yoke of the Lord from his youth." And David: "Wherein shall a young man cleanse his way? By keeping thy words." Frequent prayers must be added to the Lord, by which the fear of the Lord is nourished, the purpose of a pious heart is strengthened, and a certain holiness and purity of mind is imbued; the result will be that impure thoughts are either not easily admitted, or, if they have been admitted through carelessness, are most easily extinguished.

units.la: 2 Deinde curandum illis est,ut temeritatem omnem,ac quiduis tentandi,audiendi,uidendi,loquendiue licentiam, deinde & eorū quibus deest timor domini, societatem fugiant. Cohibendus est uiisus, obseran-dæq; aures, ne quid uel uideatur,uel audiatur, unde occasio detur cogitationibus impuris: quae si fuerint semel atq; iterum receptae, & ad cordis ueluti focum instar scintillarum admissae,haud ita facilè poterunt extingui. Non frustra admonuit ille: Nil dictu foedum, uisuq; haec limina tangat, Intra quae puer est. Et alius:
units.tr: 2. Next, they must be careful to flee all rashness, and all licence to try, hear, see or speak anything whatever, and then the company of those who lack the fear of the Lord. The sight must be restrained and the ears closed, lest anything be seen or heard that gives occasion to impure thoughts; if these have once or twice been received and admitted, like sparks into the hearth of the heart, they will be very hard to extinguish. Not without reason did that poet warn: "Let nothing shameful to speak or to see touch these thresholds, within which the boy is." And another: [the line breaks off here in the text]

units.la: Adfluit incautis insidiosus amor.
units.tr: Insidious love flows in upon the unwary.

units.la: 3 Tertiò conducet & hoc plurimum,ut summo studio caueat ocium. Ocia si tollas,inquit ille, periere Cupidinis arcus. Contemptaeq; iacent & sine luce faces. Item: Queritur Ægistus quare sit factus adulter. In promptu causa est,desidiosus erat. Ocium literarium & honeste & salubriter negociosum est, quo si fuerit animus adolescentis occupatus, non admodum uacabit ut ad perniciosas cogitationes exorbitet. Domi parentibus debita obedientia satis exercebit morigeros adolescetes, nec locum ullum permittet uagae & uiciorum feraci libertati. Cum ocio uitandus est usus uini, quo sanguis accenditur, & in libidinem exaestuat.
units.tr: 3 Thirdly, this will greatly help: let them take the greatest care to avoid idleness. "If you take away idleness," says that poet, "the bows of Cupid are lost; his torches lie scorned and without light." Likewise: "Aegisthus complains why he became an adulterer. The cause is ready to hand: he was idle." Literary leisure is both honourable and wholesome, and it is a kind of busy occupation. If a young man's mind is occupied with it, he will have little leisure to wander off into harmful thoughts. At home, the duty of obedience owed to parents will keep dutiful young people sufficiently busy, and it will allow no room for the wandering freedom that breeds vices. Along with idleness, the use of wine must be avoided, since it heats the blood and sets it boiling with lust.

units.la: Quod si his medijs usi fuerint adolescētes, bona spes est, quod adolescentiam suam opę & gratia domini illibatam sint usque ad annos coniugio aptiores feraturi.
units.tr: If young people make use of these means, there is good hope that, by the help and grace of the Lord, they will carry their youth unstained into the years when they are fit for marriage.

units.la: At coniugatis praecipio, non ego, imò dominus, uxor à uiro ne separetur. Quod si separata fuerit maneat innupta,aut marito reconcilietur. Et maritus uxorem ne dimittat.
units.tr: But to those who are married I give this command, not I but the Lord: a wife is not to separate from her husband. But if she has separated, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. And a husband is not to divorce his wife.

units.la: Redit ad primum capitis huius membrum, alicuius adhuc admoniturus coiuges.In prioribus cauit ne coniunx coniugem iure suo defraudet,admonens ut uir uxori, & uxor uiro debitam reddat beneuolentiam, ne locus sit Satanae tentationibus.Hic adiungit de seruando coniugij uinculo infracto & illibato, domini praeceptum. Sunt enim haec duo propter astum Satanae tenenda coiugibus,ne praetextu religionis coiunx aut neget coniugi debitum, aut prorsus à coniuge discedat.Tametsi nanq; Corinthij de Iudaeis nō fuerint, sciebat tamen Apostolus quàm & inter Gentes ægrè seruaretur coniugij copula, & quanta temeritate dissilirent coniugia.Deinde sciebat astum Satanae,quàm iniquus sit legitimo connubio, & quanta uafriciè per religionis speciem carnalibus patrocinari soleat affectibus.Ad haec tenendum erat,ne ex eo quod ἁγνὸς ac uiduis continentiam suadebat, male feriati homines ac praepostere religiosi ansam sibi damnandi coniugia,& quos Deus coniunxit segregandi sumerent. Ideo causam coiugum posteaquam consilium suum de uiduis posuit, non absque ratione resumit.
units.tr: He returns to the first part of this chapter, because he is about to give further admonition to married people. Earlier he warned that a spouse should not cheat the other of his or her due right, urging that the husband render to the wife, and the wife to the husband, the goodwill that is owed, so that there be no room for the temptations of Satan. Here he adds the Lord's command that the bond of marriage be kept unbroken and undamaged. For these two points must be held fast by married couples, because of the cunning of Satan: that under the pretext of religion a wife should not either refuse her husband what is owed him or leave him altogether. Although the Corinthians were not Jews, the Apostle knew how hard it was to keep the marriage bond even among the Gentiles, and with what recklessness marriages were broken. Further, he knew how hostile Satan's cunning is to lawful wedlock, and with what craft it is accustomed to defend carnal desires under the appearance of religion. In addition, it had to be guarded against that people who were [ἁγνὸς] and urged continence on widows should not, through poorly instructed and perversely scrupulous piety, take it as an occasion to condemn marriages and to separate those whom God has joined. So after he has set out his advice about widows, he resumes the matter of married people, and not without reason.

units.la: NON ego,sed dominus.) Aperte distinguit Apostolus inter ea quae ab ipso domino sunt praecepta,& ea quae ipse abfq; peculiari domini mādato tradebat.Quod coniunx nō debeat separari à coniuge, nec uir dimittere uxorem à domino praeceptum est.Qua de re uidere est Matth.5.&19. Ideo dicit hoc praeceptum non esse suum ipsius sed domini,quod absq; dubio ob id commemorare uoluit,ut hoc plus reuerentiae erga coniugium legitimum rite seruandum incuteret coniugatis fidelibus.
units.tr: Not I, but the Lord. The Apostle clearly distinguishes between those commands that come from the Lord himself and those he gave without a special command from the Lord. That a wife should not be separated from her husband, and that a husband should not divorce his wife, was commanded by the Lord. On this see Matthew 5 and 19. So he says that this command is not his own but the Lord's. He doubtless wished to mention this so that it would instil greater reverence in believing married people for keeping the lawful marriage properly.

units.la: Obseruandum est igitur hoc loco duo esse praeceptorum Christi genera, /
units.tr: We must note, then, that there are two kinds of Christ's commands in this passage.

units.la: 1 Vnum quod per seipsum dedit,aut alias in scripturis expressum est. Tale est praesens hoc de coniugio non dirimendo,& quae alia sunt huiusmodi.
units.tr: 1 The first is what he gave by himself, or what is expressed elsewhere in Scripture. Of this kind is the present command that a marriage must not be dissolved, and others like it.

units.la: 2 Alterum eorum est quae non per seipsum, neque alicubi in scripturis, sed spiritu sancto per apostolos agente ac loquente dedit. Talia sunt pleraque Pauli, hoc ipso capite,ut audiemus infrà,& cap. II. de uelandis mulierū precantium capitibus, & quod de coena domini precipit,ut alius aliū expectet, & quae cap.14. de modo prophetandi & psallendi in ecclesia tradit, & quod mulieribus in ecclesia silētium praecipit,quae tamē,licet nusquam sint ab ipso domino praecepta, nec alicubi in scripturis sci licet expressa,asserit esse domini mādata, cum dicit: Si quis uidetur propheta esse aut spiritualis , agnoscat quae scribo uobis quòd domini sint mandata. Prioris generis praecepta uocantur γραφαι,posterioris uero ἀγραφα, quae certe & suam authoritatem merito habent in ecclesia Christi.
units.tr: 2 The second kind is what he gave not by himself, nor anywhere in Scripture, but through the apostles, the Holy Spirit acting and speaking in them. Many of Paul's are of this kind, as we shall hear below in this chapter, and in chapter 11 on women covering their heads when they pray, and what he commands about the Lord's Supper, that one should wait for another, and what he hands down in chapter 14 about the manner of prophesying and singing in the Church, and what he commands women about keeping silent in the Church. Yet although these were never commanded by the Lord himself, nor expressed anywhere in Scripture, he asserts that they are the commands of the Lord, when he says: "If anyone thinks himself a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge that what I write to you are the commands of the Lord." The first kind of command is called [γραφαι], written, and the second [ἀγραφα], unwritten; and certainly both rightly have their authority in the Church of Christ.

units.la: Nec firmum est tamen,quod hinc sibi tyranni ecclesiastici quiduis praecipiendi potestatem & authoritate uendicant. Non enim mox amplectendum est pro domini mādato , quod ab episcopis titularibus aut alio quopiā praecipitur,licet quae apostoli praeceperint authoritatem aflequuta sint. De illis nanq; certum est testimonio domini, quod non ipsi,sed spiritus sanctus ex ipsis fit loquutus, de istis uero non item. Proinde curandum est ut ea quae ἀγραφα in ecclesiam post apostolorum tempora sunt inducta, talia sint, quae liquidò fluant ex γραφοις.
units.tr: Yet it does not follow from this that the ecclesiastical tyrants may claim for themselves a power and authority to command whatever they like. For what is commanded by titular bishops or anyone else is not to be accepted at once as the command of the Lord, even though what the apostles commanded has the authority it does. For it is certain, by the testimony of the Lord, that the Holy Spirit spoke through the apostles and not they themselves; but the same cannot be said of the others.
