Therefore care must be taken that those [ἀγραφα] things introduced into the Church after the time of the apostles are such as clearly flow from the [γραφοις], the written things.

units.la: Deinde & iuxtà notandum est, quod licet loqueretur ex spiritu sancto, plus tamē authoritatis esse uoluit illis mandatis quae peculiariter domini sunt. Confidenter hic dicit: At coniugatis præcipio, non ego, sed dominus. Præcipere se dicit, & tamé ut id cũ authoritate irrefragabili faciat addit nõ ego, sed dominus. Ista fit hodie & episcopis præcipiendi modestia & confidentia quoq;, ut ubi præceptũ domini præcesit, confidenter præcipiant, sed ad dant nō ipsorum esse, sed domini præceptum.
units.tr: Furthermore, it must also be noted that although he spoke by the Holy Spirit, he nevertheless wished those commands that are specifically the Lord's to carry more authority. Here he speaks confidently: "To those who are married I give this command, not I but the Lord." He says he is giving a command, yet to make it carry irrefutable authority he adds "not I, but the Lord." Bishops today also show this modesty and confidence in commanding: where a command of the Lord has gone before, they command confidently, but they should add that the command is not theirs but the Lord's.

units.la: VXOR à uiro ne separetur. Item & maritus uxore ne dimittat.) 1 Locus hic Pauli, primũ pertinet ad eos qui legitimi sunt cõiuges. Alio qui si illegitimum fit cõiugium, non solum licebit uxori quę legitima non est separari à uiro, & uiro uicissim dimittere non suâ, sed peccabunt nisi quàmprimum separentur. Legitimis coniugibus non licet, ut à se inuicem separentur, nisi certis de causis, propterea quod se parádi non sunt quos Deus coniungit. Deus autem eos non coniungit, qui contra legem Dei, quę Leuit. 18. lata est, coniuncti sunt. Proinde propter peccati conscientiam separandi sunt, tam abest, ut separari nequeant.
units.tr: A wife is not to be separated from her husband. Likewise a husband is not to divorce his wife. This passage of Paul's first of all applies to those who are lawfully married. Otherwise, if the marriage is unlawful, it will not only be permissible for the wife who is not lawfully wed to separate from her husband, and for the husband in turn to put her away, but they will sin unless they separate as soon as possible. Lawful spouses may not separate from one another except for certain causes, because those whom God joins together must not be put asunder. But God does not join those who are united against the law of God, which is given in Leviticus 18. Therefore, because of their awareness of sin, such people must be separated, so far is it from being true that they cannot be separated.

units.la: 2 Deinde etiam in legitimis cõiugibus non erit uniuersale, quod nihil exceptionis admittat, quod dicit: Vxor à uiro non separetur, & maritus uxorem ne dimittat. Sunt enim casus quidã, in quib. licet fieri quod hic prohibetur.
units.tr: 2 Further, even among lawful spouses this will not be a universal rule admitting no exception, which says: "A wife is not to be separated from her husband, and a husband is not to divorce his wife." For there are certain cases in which what is forbidden here may be done.

units.la: 1 Vtpote, si intercesserit per adulterium coniugalis fidei violatio. Hic certè non solum licet insonti dimittere adulteram, sed & merito insipiens censetur, si illa apud se retineat. Unde Prouerb. 18. legimus. Qui tenet adulteram stultus est & insipiens. Et notum est exemplum {B}Ioseph Matt. 1. qui ob id quod iustus esset, non quidem prodendum esse coniugis delictum, ut putabat, attamen ab illa discedendum esse cogitabat.
units.tr: 1 For instance, if the breach of the marriage faith has come about through adultery. In this case it is not only permissible for an innocent party to put away an adulterous spouse, but he is judged foolish, if he keeps her with him. Hence we read in Proverbs 18: "He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and senseless." And the example of Joseph in Matthew 1 is well known: because he was a righteous man, he did not think the wife's offence should be made public, as he might have supposed, but he thought he ought to part from her.

units.la: 2 Item, si uir fit incurabiliter ex natiuitate impotens, ut nequeat prestare maritum, adeo que nec uti legibus matrimonij, certè licebit uxori ab illo diuertere.
units.tr: 2 Likewise, if a husband is from birth incurably impotent, so that he cannot provide a husband's service, and so cannot exercise the rights of marriage, then certainly the wife may turn away from him.

units.la: 3 Præterea & si uir uel ad eidololatriam cogat, uel indubitato uitæ uxoris insidietur, licebit utique fideli & insonti coniugi ab illo separari. & Apostolus ipse religionis causam subijciet, in quo liceat uxori discedere à uiro. Et Christus Matth. 5. & 19. adulterij casum excepit. Proinde non est aliter intelligēdum quod hic ponit Apostolus, quàm de tali separatione coniugum, quæ matrimonij vinculum soluat, & quos Deus coniũgit separet, quod in istis & similibus casibus quos recensui non fit. Vbi dimittitur adultera, per illius dimissionem non rumpitur coniugij vinculum, quod iam antea per adulterium dissolutum est. Et in casu impotentiæ non dissoluitur coniugiū, quod nun quam uerum fuit. Nec in religionis casu, eo quod ius coniugij improbo ademptum iam est uirtute potioris fidei quę Deo seruáda est. Et is qui uitę uxoris insidiatur, sibijpsi ius coniugij ademit, quod ipsius naturæ hostis in uxore effectus est.
units.tr: 3 Moreover, if a husband either compels his wife to idolatry, or lays an unmistakable plot against her life, then certainly a faithful and innocent spouse may be separated from him. The Apostle himself, in the matter of religion, will set out the case in which a wife may leave her husband. And Christ, in Matthew 5 and 19, excepted the case of adultery. Therefore what the Apostle says here must not be understood otherwise than of such a separation of spouses as dissolves the bond of marriage and separates those whom God has joined; and this does not happen in these and similar cases that I have listed. Where an adulteress is put away, the bond of marriage is not broken by her dismissal, for it was already dissolved by the adultery. In the case of impotence the marriage is not dissolved, because it never truly existed. Nor is it dissolved in the case of religion, because the right of marriage has already been taken away from the wicked person by the power of the higher faith that is to be kept for God. And the one who lays a plot against his wife's life has himself cancelled his right of marriage, since he has become an enemy of marriage's very nature towards his wife.

units.la: QVOD si separata fuerit, maneat innupta, aut marito reconcilietur.) 1 Hoc loco utûtur
units.tr: "But if she is separated, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband." 1 Some people use this passage,

units.la: A ij, qui prorsus illicitum esse cootendũt, ut prior uiua etiam licitè dimissa, nubatur alteri. Diuortium, inquiunt, approbat quidem in casu ecclesia, sed hactenus ut utriq; maneant coniugati, aut reconcilientur. Et huc applicat etiā uerba Christi Matth. 5. & 19. ubi adulterij damnatur, qui uxorem dimittit, & qui dimissam ducit. Respondemus hic, nec Christũ, nec Paulum loqui de tali diuortio, quod sit adulte rij gratia tentatum, sed de eo loqui Christum quod sit quauis de causa, iuxta consuetudinem Iudæorum quam ex lege Moysi traxerant, id quod ipsa quæstio indicat, qua dicebant, licet ne homini diuortium facere cum uxore sua qualibet ex causa? & de ea loqui Apostolum quod sit factum propter disidium aliquod & simultatem, quod patet ex eo quod dicit, aut marito reconcilietur.
units.tr: A ij, who maintain that it is utterly unlawful for a former wife, even one lawfully put away, to marry another. The Church, they say, does approve divorce in such a case, but only so far that both parties remain married or are reconciled. They also apply to this the words of Christ in Matthew 5 and 19, where he condemns as adulterers the man who puts away his wife and the one who marries her when she has been put away. We reply that neither Christ nor Paul is speaking here of a divorce undertaken on account of adultery. Christ speaks of the kind of divorce that was made for any cause whatever, according to the custom of the Jews which they had taken from the law of Moses. The question itself shows this, when they asked whether it is lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any cause. And the Apostle speaks of a divorce made because of some quarrel and enmity, as is clear from his words, "or be reconciled to her husband."

units.la: 1 Deinde, non loqui uel Christum uel Paulum de alio diuortij genere, quàm quod erat in usu cũm apud Gentes, tum apud Iudæos, quo ita separabantur coniuges, ut licuerint alterę nuptiæ. Et huius Christus quoque nomi natim meminit, taxans quidem illud & refutans, sed dempto casu adulterij commissi. Diuortium illud pontificium, nouum est inuentum, nec apud Gentes, nec apud Iudæos consuetum, quo ita separant in casu adulterij, ut neutri parti permittatur denuo nubendi libertas: quod genus diuortij nomine magis diuortium est quàm re.
units.tr: 1 Next, neither Christ nor Paul speaks of any other kind of divorce than the one in use both among the Gentiles and among the Jews, by which spouses were so separated that another marriage was permitted. Christ too mentions this kind by name, censuring and rejecting it, but excepting the case of adultery committed. That papist divorce is a new invention, unknown both among the Gentiles and among the Jews, by which they separate spouses in cases of adultery in such a way that neither party is granted the freedom to marry again. This kind of divorce is more a divorce in name than in fact.

units.la: Cum ergo nec Christus nec Paulus de alijs diuortij causis loquantur, quàm quibus utebantur Iudæi qualibet ex causa uxores dimittentes, & quæ oriātur ex domesticis disidijs, nec illorum tempore aliud fuerit diuortij genus, quàm quo transitus permissus fit ad alteras nuptias, non potest uel ex Christi uel Apostoli uerbis colligi, quod ubi licitum est diuortium, non etiam liceant alterę nuptiæ, saltem parti insonti. Excipit Christus casum adulterij. Quomodo? ut si ille fit, non committat adulterium, qui uxorem adulteram dimittit, & illa dimissa alteram ducit. Quare? Quia uidelicet licitum est eiusmodi diuortium, ratum & iustum. Alioqui nō liceret uiro alteri mulieri corporis sui potestatè permittere, nisi iam à prioris coniugij vinculo uerè liber esset.
units.tr: Since, then, neither Christ nor Paul speaks of any causes of divorce other than those the Jews used when they put away their wives for any reason, and which arise from domestic quarrels, and since in their time there was no other kind of divorce than one permitting a passage to another marriage, it cannot be inferred from the words of Christ or of the Apostle that where divorce is lawful, another marriage is not also lawful, at least for the innocent party. Christ makes an exception for adultery. How? In that if a man puts away an adulterous wife and marries another after she is put away, he does not commit adultery. Why? Clearly because such a divorce is lawful, valid and just. Otherwise a man would not be permitted to give the power over his body to another woman unless he were already truly free from the bond of the former marriage.

units.la: Dissentiūt hac in re etiam ueteres. Aug. & Hieronymus negant licere, etiam in casu adulterij, uerum quibus illi & quàm solidis argumentis ducantur, uidere est in disputatione Eras. Rot. omnium doctissima, quam annotationibus suis super hanc epistolam scriptis inseruit. Ambrosius apertè testatur licere. Nam ita in presenti loco annotauit. Et uirum uxorem, inquit, non dimittere. Subauditur autem excepta fornicationis causa. Et ideo non subiecit dicens sicut de muliere, quod si discesserit, manere sic. Quia uiro licet ducere uxorem, si dimiserit uxorem peccantem, quia non ita lege constringitur sicut mulier. Caput enim mulieris uir est. Hactenus ille, nisi quod mulieri
units.tr: The ancient writers also disagree on this point. Augustine and Jerome deny that it is lawful, even in the case of adultery. But what solid arguments they rely on may be seen in the discussion by Erasmus of Rotterdam, most learned of all men, which he included in his notes on this epistle. Ambrose plainly testifies that it is lawful. For he thus remarked in the present passage: "And a husband should not put away his wife," it is understood, "except in the case of fornication." And therefore he did not add, as he did for the woman, "if she departs, let her remain so," because a husband is permitted to take a wife if he has put away a wife who sins, since he is not bound by the law in the same way as a woman. "For the head of the woman is the man." Thus far Ambrose, except that he makes it unlawful for the wife what he permits the husband.

units.la: {B} Matth. 1. lieri illicitū facit quod permittit uiro. At qua de causa? Caput enim mulieris,inquit,uir est. Verum caput mulieris non est adulter. Nam ille ius suum in uxore uiolata thori fide amittit. Et hac in re idem potestatis utrique coniugum, alteri in alterius corpus facit quod & Augustinus asserit.
units.tr: {B} Matthew 1. He makes it unlawful for the wife what he permits the husband. But on what ground? "For the head of the woman," he says, "is the man." Yet the head of the woman is not an adulterer. For the adulterer loses his right over his wife by violating the fidelity of the marriage bed. And in this matter the power of each spouse is the same, so that each does with the body of the other what Augustine also asserts.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad Apostolū. Si separata fuerit,inquit,maneat innupta. Sunt qui hoc per concessionem & indulgentiam dictum esse putant, quasi permittat Apostolus separationem coniugibus male cohærentibus, quibus propter quotidiana dissidia & mores coniugio reluctantes male conuenit, ne placari aut componi inter se sustinent,quod satius sit talibus a se inuicem ad tempus salte dirimi,quàm cum animarum suarum iactura & animorum exacerbatione male conuiuere. At Apostolus non dicit:Si uero illi cum uiro male conuenerit separetur, modo non nubat alteri,quod sanè per concessionem cospicuè diceretur: sed,si uero separata fuerit, maneat innupta,&c. hoc est,si contra coniugis officium a uiro discesserit,si quod non debet,fecerit secedendo ab eo, cui debebat indiuulsè cohærere, maneat innupta. Non enim abijci debet hic quod premisit, uxor a uiro ne separetur. Quanquam non negauerim plerunque melius esse ut disiunctim quàm simul uiuât coniuges implacabiles, per petuis iurgijs conuictum suum sibijpsis perniciosum & intolerabiles reddentes. Non tamen uidetur Apostolus id agere hoc loco.
units.tr: But let us return to the Apostle. "If she is separated," he says, "let her remain unmarried." Some think this was said by way of concession and indulgence, as if the Apostle allowed separation to spouses who are ill-matched, who because of daily quarrels and conflicting characters cannot agree, who will not suffer themselves to be reconciled or brought together, and who it is better should at least for a time be parted from one another, rather than live miserably together to the loss of their souls and the exasperation of their minds. But the Apostle does not say, "But if she has not agreed with her husband, let her be separated, provided she does not marry another," which would plainly be said by way of concession. He says, "But if she is separated, let her remain unmarried," and so on. That is, if she has departed from her husband contrary to the duty of a wife, if she has done what she ought not to have done by withdrawing from him to whom she ought to have remained inseparably joined, let her remain unmarried. For what he had said before, that a wife should not separate from her husband, must not be set aside here. Yet I would not deny that it is often better for spouses who cannot be reconciled to live apart than together, when by perpetual wrangling they make their common life ruinous to themselves and intolerable. Still, the Apostle does not seem to be doing this in this place.

units.la: MANEAT innupta.) Non dicit, maneat separata, sed maneat innupta. Nō enim iubet, ut in separatione illa illicita, qua cōtra ius matrimonij a uiro discessit maneat, sed ne alteri iungatur, ut locus esse possit reconciliationi. Neque enim ex hoc colligi debet, quod uxor a uiro male separata non peccet, si ad illū non redeat, modo ita maneat, nec alteri nubat. In peccato uiuit ubi separata manet, nec reconciliari sustinet, adulterium uero committit si alteri iungatur. Nunquam diceret Apostolus maneat separata, qui ne orandi quidem gratia diutius uult separari coniuges, ne locus sit tentatori Satanæ.
units.tr: "Let her remain unmarried." He does not say, "let her remain separated," but "let her remain unmarried." For he does not command that she remain in that unlawful separation by which she departed from her husband contrary to the law of marriage, but that she not join herself to another, so that there may be room for reconciliation. Nor should it be inferred from this that a wife who has been wrongly separated from her husband does not sin if she does not return to him, provided she remains thus and does not marry another. She lives in sin where she remains separated and does not allow herself to be reconciled, but she commits adultery if she joins herself to another. The Apostle would never say "let her remain separated," he who does not want spouses to be separated even for a longer time for the sake of prayer, lest there be an opening for Satan the tempter.

units.la: Sed merito quæritur hic, quid uiro sit faciendum,si uxor separata nolit reconciliari, sed uel in separatione pertinaciter perdurauerit, uel alteri se iunxerit,siue scortatori,siue coniugi? Quid si prorsus cum nebulone aliquo aufugerit,ut spes resipiscentiæ esse nequeat? Continebit,inquis. Profectò bonum consilium,siquidé id poterit. At puto nō facile nupturum fuisse si id doni habuisset. Iam si continere nequiuerit,quid faciet? Scortabitur? Absit. Nubet igitur alteri. Idem & de uxore sentiedum, si a uiro fuerit præter culpam uel abacta, uel deserta,idq; sine ulla reconciliationis spe, maximè intercedente scortatione.
units.tr: But it is rightly asked here what the husband should do if a separated wife is unwilling to be reconciled, but either stubbornly persists in the separation, or has joined herself to another, whether to a fornicator or to another husband. What if she has fled altogether with some scoundrel, so that there is no hope of her repentance? "She will continue unmarried," you say. Certainly a good counsel, if she is able to do so. But I think she would not easily have remained unmarried had she had that gift. Now if she cannot contain herself, what will she do? Will she commit fornication? Far be it. Therefore she marries another. The same must be thought of a husband, if he has put away or deserted his wife, whether through her fault or not, and there is no hope of reconciliation, especially where fornication intervenes.

units.la: Plane mirabilis est astus Satanæ,ad excogitādum uias quibus scortationis impuritatem contra domini præceptum & publicam honéstatem inter Christianos prouehat. Primùm in eo quod ueluti continentiæ gratia,& propter diuini cultus sanctitatem sacerdotibus & monachis nuptijs interdici curauit,idque talibus qui dono continentiæ destituti sunt. Deinde in eo quod separatis coniugibus,&c ita separatis,ut reconciliari nequeant, alteras nuptias negari fecit. Ecce summam uersutissimi hostis peruersitatem. Cupiebat promoueri, idq; impune, scortationem etiam inter Christianos. Clamabat Paulus,Nolite errare,neq; scortatores,neque adulteri regnum Dei possidebunt. Videbat in admiratione esse continentiam, & in honore nuptias. Adinuenit rationes, quib: impunitâ introduceret scortatione. Primùm per speciem castitatis,deinde per speciem coniugij insolubilis. Excogitauit continentiæ uotum & coniugij legitimi interdictū. Nisi enim in sacerdotibus præcessissent ista, quis ferret illorum immunditiam,qua summum ecclesiæ probrū illatum est? Deinde nisi accessisset in eo causa diuortij interdictum denuò nubědi, certè non tolerarētur scortantes in separatione coniuges,sed redigeretur ad castitatē coniugij. Nunc uero condonatur utrisq; uaga libido,illis propter uotū continentiæ præmissum, istis uero propter ademptam denuo nubendi potestatem,ne coniugium dirimatur, cum iam olim sit diremptum. Ad hunc itaq; modū suis inuentis sub specie continetiæ, & coniugij non infringendi,contra utriusq; scortandi licentiā honestate pessimá in ecclesia Christi inuexit.
units.tr: Truly wonderful is the cunning of Satan in devising ways by which he advances the impurity of fornication among Christians, against the command of the Lord and public decency. First, in that for the sake of continence, and on account of the holiness of divine worship, he has arranged that marriage be forbidden to priests and monks, and that to those who lack the gift of continence. Next, in that for spouses who are separated, and so separated that they cannot be reconciled, he has caused another marriage to be denied them. See the great perversity of the most cunning enemy. He desired that fornication, and that with impunity, be promoted even among Christians. Paul cried out, "Do not be deceived: neither fornicators nor adulterers shall inherit the kingdom of God." Satan saw that continence was held in admiration and marriage in honour. He devised reasons by which he might introduce fornication unpunished: first under the appearance of chastity, then under the appearance of an indissoluble marriage. He devised the vow of continence and the prohibition of lawful marriage. For unless these things had first been established among the priests, who would have tolerated their uncleanness, which has brought the greatest disgrace upon the Church? Again, unless the prohibition of remarriage after divorce had been added, spouses who were separated and fornicating would certainly not be tolerated, but would be brought back to the chastity of marriage. As it is, a wandering lust is condoned for both: for the one because of the vow of continence put before them, for the other because the power to marry again has been taken from them, so that the marriage may not be dissolved, though it has long since been dissolved. In this way, by his inventions, under the guise of continence and of not breaking marriage, he has introduced into the Church of Christ, against the licence to fornicate of both, the worst dishonesty under the name of honour.

units.la: Reliquis autem ego dico,non dominus.Si quis frater uxorem habet infidelem,& ea assentitur ut habitet cum illo, ne dimittat eā.Et mulier quæ habet maritum infidelem,& ís assentitur ut habitet cum ea ne dimittat illum.
units.tr: "But to the rest I say, not the Lord: If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not put her away. And a woman who has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not leave him."

units.la: Coniugibus Christianis scribebat Apostolus. Illorum autem aliqui, pro temporis illius ratione,utraq; aliqui una tantum parte Christiani erant.Hactenus ijs,qui utraq; mādatum domini,nunc ijs qui una duntaxat parte ad fidem Christi uenerat, adeoq; impari coniugio cohærebant, quomodo se gerere debeant ex spiritus sancti instinctu præscribit.Erat autem huiusmodi coniugij duplex euentus. Vnde & sententiam suam iuxta euentuum rationem bipertita cōditione accommodat. Non enim eodem modo infideles coniuges erga fideles sese gerebant. Nam quidam eorum Christiani nominis professionem non usqueadeo in coniugibus fidelibus abhorrebant,ut illius nomine coniugij vinculum dissoluendum putaret: quidam uero contrà ita erant nomini Christiano infensi,ut fideles coniuges suas aut abigerent,aut ad pristinę superstitionis impietatem reclamante conscientia adigerent. Vt itaq; fidelis coniunx,siue maritus,siue uxor, quid utrobiq; faciedum sit cognosceret, causam hac tractare uoluit Apostolus, breuiter quidé, sed dilucidè.Erat enim periculū ne uel imprudēti zelo peccarent in legem coniugij, uel coniugij pretextu deficerent à fide ac professione Christianæ religionis, atque ita utrobiq; in Deum delinquerent.
units.tr: The Apostle was writing to Christian spouses. Some of these were Christians in both parts, while others, given the circumstances of that time, were Christian in only one part. Up to this point he has given instructions to those who were both believers. Now, to those who had come to faith in Christ through one party only, and so were joined in a mismatched marriage, he prescribes by the prompting of the Holy Spirit how they ought to conduct themselves. There were two possible outcomes of such a marriage, and so he adjusts his judgement to the two kinds of outcome, dividing his instruction in two. Unbelieving spouses did not all behave in the same way towards believing ones. Some of them did not so detest the profession of the Christian name in their believing spouses that they thought the marriage bond had to be dissolved because of that name. Others were so hostile to the Christian name that they either drove their believing spouses out or, against the protest of conscience, forced them back into the impiety of their former superstition. So that a believing spouse, whether husband or wife, might know what ought to be done in either case, the Apostle chose to treat the matter briefly, but clearly. For there was a danger that, either through an unwise zeal, they would sin against the law of marriage, or, under the pretext of marriage, would fall away from the faith and profession of the Christian religion, and so offend God in either case.

units.la: RELIQVIS autem.) Non intelligit alios quàm eos coniuges, quibus erat impar coniugium, quod sequent a declarant. Loquitur autem ad hunc modum, ut distinctim de utroq; coniugum genere tractet, separans impares coniuges à paribus, de quibus hactenus egit.
units.tr: "But to the rest": he does not mean anyone other than those spouses whose marriage was mismatched, as the following words show. He speaks in this way so that he may treat each kind of spouse separately, separating the mismatched spouses from the matched ones, of whom he has spoken so far.

units.la: EGO dico, non dominus.) An Apostoli est aliud loqui quàm uerbū domini? Qui loquitur inquit Petrus, loquatur tanquā sermones Dei. Et ipse Paulus: An experimentū quaeritis eius qui loquitur in me Christus? Quid est igitur quod hic dicit: Ego dico, nō dominus? Supra monui duplex esse præceptionum domini genus. Vnum quod per ipsum dominū, alterum quod per ministros domini apostolos ex instinctu spiritus domini traditum est. Ad posterius pertinet hic locus. Non intelligit hoc se non ex domini sententia dicere, sed distinguit hoc genus præcepti à superiore, quod peculiariter erat ab ipso domino positum. Non est autem hinc colligendū quod hoc præcepti genus liberè possit & impunè contēni ac transiliri, eo quod nō fit ab ipso domino, sed illius Apostolo datum. Licet enim merito plus moueat quod ab ipsius domini ore progressum est, ut tamen non est præter domini sententiam quod ab apostolis traditur, ita non debet contemni à fidelibus, & pro cuiusque arbitrio uel seruari uel negligi. Perinde atque in ædibus ac familijs bene institutis maximam quidem authoritatem habet quod ipse per se paterfamilias præcipit, ut liceat ἐμφαλικῶς illius œconomo dicere: Hoc non ego præcipio sed domi nus, interea tamen non est derogandum iussis œconomi cui paterfamilias gubernandæ domus potestatem concredidit, ut in ipsum patremfamilias peccare credatur, quisquis hoc temerè fecerit.
units.tr: "I say, not the Lord": Is it for an apostle to say anything other than the word of the Lord? "Whoever speaks," says Peter, "let him speak as the oracles of God." And Paul himself: "Do you seek proof of him who speaks in me, Christ?" What then does he mean here by saying "I say, not the Lord"? I have already pointed out that there are two kinds of precepts of the Lord: one given by the Lord himself, the other given through the ministers of the Lord, the apostles, by the impulse of the Spirit of the Lord. This passage belongs to the latter. He does not mean that he is speaking here not by the Lord's judgement, but he distinguishes this kind of precept from the earlier one, which was laid down particularly by the Lord himself. Nor should it be concluded from this that this kind of precept may be freely and with impunity despised and passed over, on the ground that it does not come from the Lord himself but was given by his apostle. For although what has issued from the Lord's own mouth rightly carries more weight, nevertheless, since what is handed down by the apostles is not contrary to the Lord's judgement, it ought not to be despised by the faithful, nor kept or neglected at each one's pleasure. Just as in well-ordered houses and households, what the householder himself commands has the greatest authority, so that his steward may say, in an emphatic way [ἐμφαλικῶς], "This I do not command, but the householder does", yet the orders of the steward to whom the householder has entrusted the management of the house must not be disparaged, so that whoever rashly does this is thought to sin against the householder himself.

units.la: SI quis frater) Notū est Apostolo fratris ac sororis dictione Christianū homine significari.
units.tr: "If anyone has a brother": It is well known to the Apostle that a Christian man is signified by the word "brother" or "sister".

units.la: ET mulier.) ut de marito loquitur qui frater fit, id est, fidelis, ita & de muliere non quauis, sed quę soror fit & fidelis intelligendus est hic, ubi dicit & mulier.
units.tr: "And a woman": just as he speaks of the husband who becomes a brother, that is, a believer, so here, where he says "and a woman", the woman meant must be understood not as any woman, but one who becomes a sister and a believer.

units.la: VXOREM habet infidelem. Et: Virum habet infidelem.) ἀπιστῷ etiam is dicitur, qui fidem datam non seruat, quem Latini perfidum uocamus. Sic Dido Æneam perfidum appellabat, dissimulare etiā aiebat, sperasti perfide tantū posse nefas? At hoc sensu non est posita ab Apostolo hæc dictio. Neq; enim præscribit quid faciendum sit in coniugio, si pars altera coniugalis fidei seruās non fuerit, sed quid Christianus facere debeat, si coniugem habeat non Christianā. Hoc sensu γυναῖκα ἀπιστον uxorem uocat infidelem, id est, extra Christianæ fidei professionem constitutā. Alioqui quis ita facilè certò cognoscet de uxore sua Christi fidem oretenus professa, reuera ne Christo fide-
units.tr: "Has a wife who is unbelieving", and "has a husband who is unbelieving": The word [ἀπιστῷ] is also applied to one who does not keep the faith he has given, whom the Latins call perfidious. So Dido called Aeneas perfidious, and even reproached him: "Did you hope, faithless one, that you could manage such a crime?" But the Apostle has not used the word in this sense. For he does not prescribe what must be done in marriage if one partner does not keep the faith of the marriage, but what a Christian ought to do if he has a wife who is not a Christian. In this sense he calls the wife "unbelieving" [γυναῖκα ἀπιστον], that is, one standing outside the profession of the Christian faith. Otherwise, who could easily and surely know whether a wife who has professed faith in Christ with her lips is really faithful to Christ, or pretends more faith in Christ than she has in her heart?

units.la: A' lis sit, an fidem Christi magis simulet quàm in corde habeat? Huius admoneo, ut id quod 2. Cor.6. de relinquēdis infidelibus ponitur, retinte intelligamus, ne cum anabaptistis separationē fidelium ab ijs qui putantur parum esse fideles, licet sub nomine Christi cōstituti, somniemus. Apostolo infideles non uocan ur, qui nominis ac fidei Christi religione, etiam falsò amplexi sunt, sed qui illam aperte respuunt, quos impios, incredulos, & gētiles uocamus.
units.tr: I warn that we should understand firmly what is set down in 2 Cor. 6 about leaving unbelievers, so that we do not dream, with the Anabaptists, of separating the faithful from those who are thought to be not very faithful, even though they are established under the name of Christ. Those are not called unbelievers by the Apostle who have embraced the religion of the name and faith of Christ, even falsely, but those who openly reject it; these we call impious, unbelieving, and heathen.

units.la: ET ipsa assentitur, ut habitet cū illo.) Non dicit, ἐχ αὐτὸς συνευδοκεῖ, & ille assentitur neq; ἐχ αὐτῇ εὐδοκεῖ, & ipsi placet, sed συνευδοκεῖ, assentitur, aut complacitū illi est, uidelicet infideli coniugi. Sunt itaq; duo notanda. Vnum, quod cohabitationem connubialem in arbitriū ponit non fidelis sed infidelis coiugis. Non dicit: Si quis frater uxorē habet infidelem, uolueritq; cum illa habitare, non dimittat eam, sed si illa assentitur ut habitet cum ipso, ne dimittat eam. Scribit enim non infideli sed fideli, nō quid ille facere posit aut non possit, sed quid in casu debeat, ostendens non licere etiam infidelē coniugē dimittere, nisi illa manere nolit. Alterū quod consensus iste debeat esse non mulieris infidelis tantū, sed cum primis & mariti fidelis. Præsumit enim ita comparatū esse fidelis uiri animū erga coiugē infidelē quoq;, ut illam cupidē, si fieri possit, apud se retineat. Ideo dicit: Et ipsa συνευδοκεῖ, id est, unà consentit, idē ipsi quod fideli marito placet. Ad hunc modum ubiq; affectos nos esse dicit: Vt primi quod iustum & æquū est probemus, paratiq; simus ad omnia, quæ uel Deo placent uel proximo sunt proficua, ut si cui infidelium quoq;, idem fit animus, possit nobis dici συνευδοκεῖν.
units.tr: "And she consents to dwell with him": He does not say "the husband consents with her" [ἐχ αὐτὸς συνευδοκεῖ], nor "the wife is pleased with him" [ἐχ αὐτῇ εὐδοκεῖ], but "consents" [συνευδοκεῖ], that is, the unbelieving spouse agrees or is pleased with it. There are therefore two things to note. The first is that the cohabitation of marriage is placed at the discretion not of the believing spouse but of the unbelieving one. He does not say, "If anyone has an unbelieving wife, and she wishes to live with him, let him not put her away," but "if she consents to live with him, let him not put her away." For he writes not to the unbeliever but to the believer, not about what the one may or may not do, but about what he ought to do in the case, showing that it is not lawful even to put away an unbelieving spouse unless she is unwilling to remain. The second is that this consent must come not only from the unbelieving wife but first of all from the believing husband. For he assumes that the mind of a believing husband is so disposed towards an unbelieving spouse that he would eagerly keep her with him, if that were possible. Therefore he says, "And she consents [συνευδοκεῖ]", that is, she agrees together with him, so that what pleases the believing husband also pleases her. In this way he says we ought to be disposed everywhere: that we should first approve what is just and fair, and be ready for all things that either please God or are profitable to our neighbour, so that if an unbeliever too has the same mind, he may be said to consent with us.

units.la: Obseruandum iuxtà est, quanta simplicitate fidelem coniugem instruat, ut retineat coniugem infidelem, si illa assentiatur ad cohabitandū, non expendens, quibus id caus is mota faciat, modò assentiatur. Potest enim iste infidelis coniugis assensus uarias habere causas. Vtpote, si fit ex tempore quodamergā propriam superstitionē, quod & inter nos uidemus multis accidere qui propter stupiditatē quandam & ἀδιαφορίαν erga Christianā religionem & utritatis causam, etiam cum Turcis usq; ad connubiale thorum, modo commodum esset, coniungerentur ac coherereret. Certe uerisimile est multos hac ratione fidelibus coniugibus cohæsisse. Aut si oriatur ex singulari quadam animi mansuetudine, aut ex carnali erga coniugē amore uel certē ex affectu propēsiore in communes liberos. Non curat ista Apostolus hoc in loco, nec exigit ut accedat fidei assensus, sed contentus est ut assentiatur infidelis ad cohabitandum iuxta leges coiugij. Proinde nec fidelis anxius esse debet, in perquirendis assensus huius causis, licet optare debeat, ut iustæ sint ac tales, quæ futuræ refipiscentiæ præludere queant. Videlicet, si assentiatur infidelis propter animi mansuetudinem, uel dilectionem connubialem, aut liberorum amorem, aut quod optimum esset, ex quadam animi ad fidem Christi inclinatione. In his omnibus posset aliquid spei esse, fore ut per mutuam cohabitationem sensim incipiat approbare Christi religionem. Et uero causa, quae ex stupore, tepore, & ἀδιαφορία erga propriam superstitionem est, ut motu facilis est, ita parum habet firmitudinis, ut metuendum sit, eundem fore talem coniugem in Christianismi qui est in Genilismi professione.
units.tr: It should also be noted how simply he instructs the believing spouse to keep an unbelieving spouse, if she agrees to live together, without weighing the causes that move her to do so, provided only that she consents. For this consent of an unbelieving spouse may have various causes: for instance, if it arises from a sudden inclination towards her own superstition, as we see happen to many among us, who, through a certain dullness and indifference [indifference (ἀδιαφορία)] towards the Christian religion, and for the sake of convenience, have joined themselves with Turks even in the marriage bed, provided it was useful, and remained so. Certainly it is likely that many have stayed with believing spouses for this reason. Or if it arises from a particular gentleness of mind, or from carnal love for the spouse, or certainly from a greater affection for the common children. The Apostle does not concern himself with these things in this place, nor does he require that a consent of faith be added; he is satisfied that the unbelieving spouse agrees to live together according to the laws of marriage. Therefore the believing spouse also ought not to be anxious in inquiring into the causes of this consent, although he ought to hope that they are just and such as may serve as a prelude to future repentance: namely, if the unbeliever consents because of gentleness of mind, or marital affection, or love of the children, or, what would be best, from some inclination of the mind towards faith in Christ. In all these cases there could be some hope that, through living together, she would gradually begin to approve the religion of Christ. But a cause that arises from torpor, lukewarmness, and indifference [indifference (ἀδιαφορία)] towards her own superstition is, as it is easily moved, so little firm that it must be feared that such a spouse will remain the same in the profession of heathenism as in that of Christianity.

units.la: Est autem non solum in isto praesenti casu observandum, quod de cohabitandi consensu scribit Apostolus, sed & in universis coniugijs, ut & nos illo contenti simus, nec curiose inquisitemus, quibus rationibus placeat uxoribus nostris, ut nobiscum iuxta coniugij legem cohabitent. Quis dubitat innumeros esse, qui pa rum honesta de causa legitimis maritis conuiuant? Quicquid illas moueat, modo ad cohabitationem legitimam consentiat, nō licebit maritis ultra illa aliquid ita exigere, ut nisi id assequatur diuortium affectent. Quanquam enim ut Chrysost. alicubi inquit, ἀπὸ τῆς γνώμης τὰ πράγματα κείνεται, iudicio tamen domini permittendū est, quid quamq; ad cōnubiale societatē permoueat, nisi quod optandum est, ut animo sint ad status huius sanctimoniam accomodo.
units.tr: This is to be observed not only in the present case, where the Apostle writes about the consent to live together, but in every marriage. We should be content with that and not pry too closely into the reasons why our wives are pleased to live with us under the law of marriage. Who doubts that there are countless men whose wives live with their lawful husbands for reasons that are not honourable? Whatever moves them, so long as they consent to lawful cohabitation, a husband may not demand anything more from them on pain of seeking divorce if he does not obtain it. For although Chrysostom says somewhere that "affairs depend on the intention" [ἀπὸ τῆς γνώμης τὰ πράγματα κεῖνται], it must still be left to the judgment of the Lord what moves each person to marital partnership. What we should wish is that their minds be suited to the holiness of this state.

units.la: NE dimittat eam.) Hoc est, bona & secura conscientia illam retineat. Non enim id tantum agit, ut infidelem coniugē si illa assentiatur ad cohabitandū, non dimittat frater, sed ut sciat se bona conscientia illius cōsuetudine pro ratione thori legitimi uti posse, & debere etiam, nō secus q; si & ipsa fidelis esset. Neq; enim tam consulit quieti domesticae, q; fideliū conscientijs, nec de noua quadam coniugum cohabitatione praescribit, quę expers sit legitimę statuts huius cōsuetudinis. Est quidē ista imparium coniugū cohabitatio quod ad religionis syncęritate attinet, satis periculosa, ut parū considerāti mirum videri possit, an non cogitauerit Apostolus fieri posse ut fidelis maritus per infidelis uxoris consuetudinē uel ad Gentilismum reducatur, uel certe ἀδιαφορίαν quādam erga Christi religionē imbibat. Quantum sanē hac in re sit periculi, ipsum mandatum Dei Iudaeis Deut.7. traditum satis exprimit: Non sociabis cum eis, inquit, id est, gentibus, coniugia. Filia tuam non dabis filio eius, nec filiā ilius accipies filio tuo. Quia seducet filiū tuū, ne sequatur me, &ut magis seruiat dijs alienis, irasceturq; furor domini, & delebit te citō. Deinde & exemplum Israelitarum apertā habet imparium coniugiorum dissolutionē, etiam eorum, in quibus coniuges procreatis liberis parentes euaserant, ut simul coniunx à coniuge, & parens à liberis separaretur. Quid ergo rationis fuit Apostolo, ut Christianis legem hanc periculosam praescripserit?
units.tr: "That he not put her away." That is, let him keep her with a good and secure conscience. The Apostle does not intend only that a believing brother should not put away his unbelieving wife if she consents to live with him, but also that he should know that with a good conscience he may, and indeed must, use her company in keeping with the legitimate bond of marriage, no differently than if she too were a believer. For he does not so much consult domestic peace as the consciences of the faithful, nor does he prescribe some new kind of cohabitation of spouses, one lacking the lawful character of this union. Admittedly, this cohabitation of unequal spouses is quite dangerous as far as the purity of religion is concerned, so that to someone who considers it carelessly it may seem strange whether the Apostle did not reflect that a believing husband might, through the company of an unbelieving wife, be drawn back to heathenism or at least take on some kind of indifference towards the religion of Christ. How great the danger in this matter is, the very commandment of God given to the Jews in Deut. 7 expresses well enough: "You shall not make marriages with them," he says, that is, with the nations. "You shall not give your daughter to their son, nor take their daughter for your son. For she will turn away your son, so that he will not follow me, and will serve other gods; and the anger of the Lord will burn, and will destroy you quickly." Then too the example of the Israelites clearly shows the dissolution of unequal marriages, even of those in which, after children had been born, the parents had become estranged, so that wife was separated from husband and parent from children. What reason, then, did the Apostle have for prescribing to Christians this dangerous law?

units.la: 1 Primū, spectandum hac in re fuit Apostolo nō quid plus, quid minus haberet periculi, sed quid esset ex ordine diuino iustum & seruandum. Seruandū autē est legitimi coniugij uin-
units.tr: 1. First, in this matter the Apostle had to consider not which course carried more or less danger, but what was just and to be kept according to the divine order. The bond of lawful marriage must be kept.

units.la: culū. Id legitimū & integrum est, donec fides illius, qua nititur salua perfistit. Illa uero non uiolatur aliqua superstitione, quia nō constat uerae religionis professione, quasi ij soli sint coiuges, qui pij sunt. Cum ergo in hoc casu integrū sit adhuc cuiq; coniugum matrimonij ius, nō potuit Apostolus aliud praescribere, quàm ut cauerent fideles, ne propter incredulitatem infidelis coniugis matrimonium dissolueret, utut esset ista cohabitatio periculosa. Non enim faciendum est malum, ut eueniant bona.
units.tr: That bond is lawful and whole for as long as the faith on which it rests remains safe. And it is not violated by some superstition, because it does not stand upon the profession of the true religion, as if only those who are godly were married. Since, then, in this case the right of marriage still remains whole for each spouse, the Apostle could not prescribe anything other than that believers take care not to dissolve the marriage because of the unbelief of an unbelieving spouse, however dangerous this cohabitation may be. For evil must not be done so that good may come of it.

units.la: 2 Deinde quod attinet ad praeceptum Dei Deut.7. aliud est praecipere fidelibus ne coiugium ineant cum infidelibus, cum liceat cuiq; de sua sibi gete & fide thori cōfortem sumere, & aliud uetare ne matrimoniū in Gentilismo ab infidelibus contractum, ubi fides alterutri parti accessit, religionis gratia dirimatur. Apostolus hic nō dicit: Si quis frater nupturus est cum muliere infideli, si illa assentitur ut habitet cum eo, nubat illi, sed si quis frater habet infidelem uxorem, & illa assentitur, &c. ne dimittat eam. Infrà uero dicit: Si uult nubat, tan tum in domino, quibus uerbis & ipse uetat fidelem nubere infideli.
units.tr: 2. Next, as regards God's command in Deut. 7: it is one thing to command believers not to enter into marriage with unbelievers, since it is allowed to each person to take a partner for their bed from their own nation and faith; and it is another thing to forbid that a marriage contracted in heathenism by unbelievers be dissolved for the sake of religion when faith has come to one of the parties. The Apostle here does not say: "If a brother is about to marry a woman who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, let him marry her." He says rather: "If a brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents, etc., let him not put her away." Later he says: "If she wishes to marry, let her marry only in the Lord," by which words he himself forbids a believer to marry an unbeliever.

units.la: 3 Tertiò, factū quoq; Israelitarū aliam habuit rationē. Qui alienigenas uxores duxerat, antequā illas duxissent erant fideles ex populo Dei, deinde contra expressum Dei mandatum, quod Esdras magno cum luctu queritur, illas duxerant. Itaq; merito separabantur huiusmodi coniugia. In hoc uero casu, quoniā nec fidelis infideli, nec contra aliquod Dei mandatū nupserat, nō potuit Apostouls talibus coniugibus aliud praescribere, quàm ne fidelis infidelem dimitteret, si assentiretur ad cōhabitandum.
units.tr: 3. Thirdly, the case of the Israelites had a different reason. Those who had taken foreign wives, before they took them had been believers from the people of God; then they had taken those wives contrary to the express command of God, over which Ezra laments with great grief. Such marriages were therefore rightly dissolved. In this case, however, since neither a believer had married an unbeliever nor had anyone married contrary to some command of God, the Apostle could not prescribe to such spouses anything other than that a believer should not put away an unbelieving spouse if she consented to live together.

units.la: Sanctificatus est enim maritus incredulus per uxorē, & sanctificata est uxor incredula per maritum. Alioqui filij uestri immūdi essent: nunc aūt sancti sunt.
units.tr: For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through the husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy.

units.la: Hæc est αἰτιολογία eius quod dixit, ne dimittat eam. Forsan putabant imperitiores Christiani talem cohabitationē esse immūdam & illicitam, metuebantq; ne unum corpus cum eidololatra coniuge fierent, quemadmodum qui scorto iungitur, unum corpus cum scorto redditur, atq; ita ex membris Christi facerent iam membra eidololatrae, quod plus haberet peccati, q; si illa facerēt membra scorti. Ob hāc causam dicit: Sanctificatus est enim maritus incredulus, &c. Hoc est, maritus enim incredulus in uxore, id est, in uxoris cōiunctione, quae per matrimonium est, iam olim uirtute nuptiarum mundatus est, ut illius coniunctio & copula nihil habeat impuri, ita uicisim & uxor incredula propter legitimum cōiugium quo uiro coniuncta est iam olim mūdata est, ut nō pulluatur fidelis, si illi cohabitet. Sumitur enim hic sanctitatis dictio pro mūdicia cōiugalis thori, quā ille habet ex traditione Dei. Ideo dicit: Alioqui filij uestri immundi essent, nunc autem sancti sunt. Debebat dicere, nūc autem mundi
units.tr: This is the reason [αἰτιολογία] for what he said: "let him not put her away." Perhaps less well-instructed Christians thought that such cohabitation was impure and unlawful, and feared that they would become one body with an idolatrous spouse, just as whoever is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with the prostitute, and so they would make the members of Christ into members of an idolater, which would be a greater sin than if they made them members of a prostitute. For this reason he says: "For the unbelieving husband is sanctified..." That is, the unbelieving husband has already long since been cleansed in the wife, that is, in the union of the wife, which exists through marriage, by the power of the marriage; so that his union and conjugal bond contain nothing impure. Conversely, the unbelieving wife, by reason of the lawful marriage to which she is joined to her husband, has likewise long since been cleansed, so that the believer is not defiled if he lives with her. The word "holy" is here taken to mean the purity of the marriage bed, which the spouse has from the institution of God. Therefore he says: "Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy." He ought to have said "now they are clean," were it not that here "holy" and "clean" mean the same thing.

units.la: {y} Vide hic Chrysost. mundi sunt, nisi idem hoc loco esset sanctum esse atq; mundū esse. Est itaq; simplicissimus huius loci intellectus primum in eo, ut sanctitatis dictionem non intelligamus de ea sanctitate quę est uel ex foedere Dei, uel ex spiritu fidei, quo credētes in populum Dei sanctificantur, sed de munditia coniugalis thori. Alioqui molestam pariet disputationē, quomodo uir infidelis sanctificatus dici possit. Deinde ut hanc sanctificationem, id est, mundiciam tribuamus non fidei coniugis fidelis, sed coniugio propter traditionem Dei, cum Hieronymo, qui dicit, quia ex traditione Dei sanctæ sunt nuptiæ, & Ambrosio, qui ita habet, sancti sunt liberi, quia ex legitimis coiugijs nati sunt. Proinde illud: ἐν τῇ γυναικὶ & ἐν τῷ ἀνδρὶ, i. in uxore, in marito, nō est ita legendū, ut addatur fideli, quod habet uetus interpres, sed simpliciter ut Græcus habet. Quod si addendum aliquid est, satius est ut addatur, legitimo, uel legitima, ut intelligamus uirū infidelem in coniuge legitima mundatum, id est, uirtute coniugij legitimi non esse impurum, sed purū quantū attinet ad legē & cohabitationem coniugij, licet impurus sit, quod attinet ad cōmercium religionis, de quo uox erat diaconorum in ecclesijs. Abscedant prophani, accedant sancti.
units.tr: {y} See here Chrysostom. They are clean, unless this place meant the same thing by being holy as by being clean. The simplest sense of this passage is therefore, first, that we should not understand the word "holiness" of that holiness which comes either from the covenant of God or from the Spirit of faith, by which believers are sanctified into the people of God, but of the purity of the marriage bed. Otherwise it would raise a troublesome dispute how an unbelieving husband can be called sanctified. Second, we should attribute this sanctification, that is, this cleanness, not to the faith of the believing spouse but to the marriage, on account of the institution of God; with Jerome, who says that marriages are holy because of the institution of God, and with Ambrose, who says that children are holy because they were born of lawful marriages. Accordingly, the phrase "in the wife, in the husband" [ἐν τῇ γυναικὶ ... ἐν τῷ ἀνδρὶ] is not to be read as if the word "believing" were added to it, as the old translator has it, but simply as the Greek has it. If anything must be added, it is better to add "lawful," or "legitimate," so that we understand that the unbelieving husband is cleansed in a lawful wife, that is, is not impure by the power of the lawful marriage, but is pure so far as the law and cohabitation of marriage are concerned, although he is impure as regards the fellowship of religion. On this point the deacons in the churches used to cry out: "Let the profane depart, let the holy draw near."

units.la: Notandus est hic locus, non solum in hoc casu dissimilis religionis, sed & in alijs consimilibus utpote si uxor maritum habeat sub signaculo quidem Christi constitutum, interea tamen nulla fide, nulloq; timore Dei præditū, sed nefarium & flagitiosum. Non fit anxia, ne polluatur admixtu mariti flagitiosi & improbi. Licet enim fit & uita, & animo & moribus impurus, purus tamen est illius congressus & conuictus, propter sanctitatē matrimonij. Purus est inquam piæ coniugi, licet ipsi impuro nihil sit purum. Spectandum est qua in re & quatenus coniugatur pius impio, fidelis infideli. Si mariti flagitijs non assentitur uxor pia, conuictu illius non potest pollui quemadmodum nec fidelis prophanatur per copulam infidelis, nisi illi in infidelitate coiungatur. Noui multas imbecilles conscientias hac in reflu-ctuare ac perplexas esse, quibus declaratione ista Apostolica succurrendum est, ne frustra turbentur, aut diuortium meditando contra legem coniugij in Deum peccent.
units.tr: This passage deserves note not only in this case of unlike religion but also in other similar cases, for example where a wife has a husband who is indeed marked with the seal of Christ, yet meanwhile is endowed with no faith and no fear of God, but is wicked and shameful. She is not anxious that she will be polluted by the company of a shameful and wicked husband. For although he is impure in life, spirit and morals, his company and fellowship are nonetheless pure, because of the holiness of marriage. I say that they are pure to the godly spouse, although nothing is pure to the impure husband himself. We must consider in what matter and how far a godly person is joined to an ungodly one, a believer to an unbeliever. If the godly wife does not assent to her husband's vices, she cannot be polluted by his company, just as a believer is not profaned through union with an unbeliever, unless she is joined to him in unbelief. I know that many weak consciences struggle and are perplexed on this point, and they must be helped by this Apostolic declaration, so that they are not troubled in vain or, by contemplating divorce, sin against God and against the law of marriage.

units.la: Qui opinionem septem sacramentorū ecclesiæ tuentur, & scripturis probare conantur, præsentem locum ad defendendum matrimonij sacramentū usurpant, rogates quamobrem maritus infidelis sanctificatus fit, & liberi talis coniugij sancti, nisi propter sacramentū coniugij? At isti debebat cogitare, statum quæstionis esse nō in genere de mysterijs, sed de sacramentis ecclesiæ & noui testamenti. Si noui testamenti sacramentum est matrimonium, fateantur aut illum non esse legitimum extra noui testamenti tempus, aut si hoc nequeunt, gentes & infideles nobiscum communicare in ecclesiæ sacramentis. Deinde respondeant,
units.tr: Those who defend the opinion of seven sacraments of the Church, and try to prove it from Scripture, use this passage to defend the sacrament of marriage, asking why an unbelieving husband is sanctified and the children of such a holy marriage are holy, unless it is because of the sacrament of marriage. But they ought to consider that the question here is not about mysteries in general, but about the sacraments of the Church and of the New Testament. If marriage is a sacrament of the New Testament, let them either admit that it is not lawful outside the time of the New Testament, or, if they cannot do that, admit that Gentiles and unbelievers share with us in the sacraments of the Church. Then let them answer

units.la: quomodo definitio sacramenti, quam tenent ex Augustino theologi, locum habeat n mat i monio. Dicit enim Augustinus: Accedat uerbum ad elementum & fit sacramentū. Per uerbum intelligit Christi promissionem & institutionem, ut in baptismate & Eucharistia, per elementum uero rem uisibi em, in qua fit simi litudo rei significatæ, quam queas uocare uisibile uerbum. Mysterium tribuit Apostolus coniugio, Ephesiorum quinto: At non mox sacramentum est ecclesiæ, quod mysterium in se habet. Alioqui tot habebimus sacramenta, quot mysteria.
units.tr: how the definition of a sacrament, which the theologians hold from Augustine, applies to marriage. For Augustine says: "The word comes to the element, and it becomes a sacrament." By the word he means Christ's promise and institution, as in baptism and the Eucharist; by the element he means the visible thing in which there is a likeness of the thing signified, which you may call a visible word. The Apostle does give marriage the name of mystery, in Ephesians 5. But not at once is a thing a sacrament of the Church just because it has a mystery in itself. Otherwise we would have as many sacraments as mysteries.

units.la: ALIOQVI
units.tr: Otherwise

units.la: filij uestri immundi essent, nūc autem sancti sunt.) Ambrosius hanc particulam ita exponit. Alioqui, id est, si uir fidelis coniugem infidelem dimitteres & aliam ducetes, essent filij uestri immundi, quia uos redde remini adulteri. Nunc autem, id est, si infidelem coniugem retineas, sancti sunt, quia de legitimo coniugio nati sunt. Simplicius uero est ut intelligamus Apostolum respicere ad coniugij sanctimoniam etiam eorum qui extra fidem Christi coniuges sunt. Quasi dicat, Nisi esset coniugium sanctum & mundum etiam inter infideles, quid aliud sequeretur quàm omnes infidelium liberos esse spurios & immundos? Sed absit. Sancti sunt, quia de legitimo coniugio nati sunt. Ambrosius respicit ad id quod dixit, ne dimittat eam. Altera expositio, ad id quod dixit, sanctificatus est uir infidelis in coniuge.
units.tr: your children would be unclean, but now they are holy.) Ambrose explains this clause thus: "Otherwise," that is, if a believing husband were to dismiss his unbelieving wife and take another, your children would be unclean, because you would be made adulterers. "But now," that is, if you keep the unbelieving wife, they are holy, because they were born of a lawful marriage. It is simpler, however, for us to understand that the Apostle looks to the holiness of marriage even of those who are married outside faith in Christ. As if he were saying: unless marriage were holy and clean even among unbelievers, what else would follow but that all the children of unbelievers are illegitimate and unclean? But far be it. They are holy, because they were born of a lawful marriage. Ambrose refers to what he said: "let him not dismiss her." The other explanation refers to what he said: "the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife."

units.la: Abusus sum aliquando præsenti loco contra errorem anabaptistarum, infantes Christianorum baptismo arcentiū, putans illud: Nunc autem sancti sunt, idem esse atque de populo Dei sunt propter fidelem parentem. Verum, licet in se firmum sit, quod credentium liberi & sancti ad populū Dei propter foederis participationem pertinentes, adeoque baptismatis, tanquam signi fœderis participes sunt, nihilominus ad hanc causam præsens locus nihil facit, in quo non de fœderis & populi Dei sanctimonia, sed de coniugij legitimi, etiam infidelium, puritate agitur. Nō enim liberis tantum, ad quos forsan poterit ita pertinere fidelis parētis sanctimonia, ut fœderis Dei sint propter illam participes, sed & maritis & uxoribus infidelibus sanctimonia adscribitur, ut fidei Christi repugnent. Nec de alia agitur sanctitate ac puritate liberorum, quàm quæ & infidelibus parentibus competit. Illi autem nō competit alia, quàm quę est ex coniugio legitimo. Aliàs satis testimonij habetur ex scripturis, un de erroris conuinci poterunt anabaptistæ, ut nihil opus sit hoc loco contra illos uti.
units.tr: I have sometimes used this passage against the error of the Anabaptists, who keep the children of Christians from baptism, thinking that "but now they are holy" means the same as "they belong to the people of God because of a believing parent." Yet, although it is firm in itself that the children of believers, being holy, belong to the people of God by participation in the covenant, and so, like baptism, are sharers in the sign of the covenant, nevertheless this passage does nothing for that cause, since it does not deal with the holiness of the covenant or of the people of God, but with the purity of a lawful marriage, even of unbelievers. For holiness is ascribed not only to the children, to whom the holiness of a believing parent may perhaps extend so that they share in God's covenant because of it, but also to unbelieving husbands and wives, so that they are not opposed to the faith of Christ. Nor is the holiness and purity of the children here meant in any other sense than that which belongs also to unbelieving parents. And that holiness belongs to them only by a lawful marriage. Otherwise there is enough testimony in the Scriptures by which the Anabaptists can be convicted of error, so that there is no need to use this passage against them.

units.la: Quod si incredulus discedit, discedat. Non est seruituti subiectus frater aut soror in huiusmodi, sed in pace uocauit nos Deus.
units.tr: But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not bound in such cases, but God has called us to peace.

units.la: Hactenus ostendit quid faciendum sit fideli, ii li, si coniunx infidelis ad cohabitandum con-senserit: nunc vero si accidat vt Christianæ religionis impatientior rupto coniugij vinculo discedat, quid tum facere debeat fidelis, quandoquidem id, vt verisimile est, crebrò vsuuenie bat, ex ordine docet, cum dicit: Quod si increduλus discedit, discedat. Quasi dicat, Si verò incredulus ad cohabitandum non assentitur, sed propter odium Christiani nominis diuortium instituit, atq; ita discedit, vt conuictum & consortium coniugij deneget, discedat, nihil est quod hic possis aut debeas, sed sine vt suopte vicio separetur, modo tamen illi non des iustam separationis causam.
units.tr: Up to this point he has shown what the believer must do if the unbelieving spouse consents to live together. Now, if it happens that the spouse, more impatient of the Christian religion, breaks the bond of marriage and departs, he teaches in order what the believer ought then to do, since this, as is likely, often happened, when he says: "But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart." As if he were saying: if, however, the unbeliever does not consent to live together, but on account of hatred of the Christian name sets up a divorce, and so departs that he refuses the life and fellowship of marriage, let him depart; there is nothing you can or ought to do here, but let him be separated by his own fault, provided only that you give him no just cause for separation.

units.la: Non hoc agit Apostolus, vt iubeat fidelem susque deq; ferre coniugis separationem, per id quod dicit: Quod si discedit, discedat neque vetat, si qua queat humanitate & comitate in officio retineri, quin hoc fiat, modo non obsit Christianæ professioni, sed consulit imbecillium conscientiæ, offendens per discessum in fidelis coniugis nihil peccati deriuari in fidelem, neque hoc exigi, vt discedentem vel vi vel iure detineat. Et huc etiam sequentia pertinent.
units.tr: The Apostle does not mean that the believer should take the separation of a spouse lightly. By saying "if he departs, let him depart," he neither forbids that, if the spouse can be kept in the duty by kindness and courtesy, this should be done, provided it does no harm to the Christian profession, and it serves the conscience of the weak; nor does he forbid the believer to keep the departing spouse by force or by law. The following words also belong here.

units.la: NON est seruituti subiectus frater aut soror in huiusmodi.) Ista expositionem habet eius quod dixit, discedat, si discesserit, vt indicet, per istum infidelis coniugis discessum liberari à lege coniugij fidelem. Quod enim dicit, non est seruituti subiectus frater in huiusmodi, quid aliud est, quàm liber est à lege ac seruitute coniugij. Et hinc est quod Ambrosius concludit, in huiusmodi casibus licere insonti denuo nubere. Nam sic scribit hoc loco: Non debetur reuerentia coniugij ei, qui horret authorem coniugij. Non enim ratum est matrimonium, quod sine Dei deuotione est, ac per hoc non est peccatum ei, qui dimittitur propter Deum, si alij se iunxerit. Cotumelia enim creatoris soluit ius matrimonij circa eum qui relinquitur, ne accusetur alij copulatus. Hæc ille. Est autem cautè legendus hoc loco Ambrosius in eo quod dicit: Non est ratum matrimonium quod sine Dei deuotione est. Apostolus non ita scribit. Libertatem nanque fidelis coniugis, à lege coniugij, non ponit in eo, si coniunx alter sine deuotione Dei, sed in discessu coniugis infidelis. Alioqui iubet, ne dimittatur si consentiat ad cohabitandum. Non dicit, si consenserit in Dei deuotione. Sequeretur ex verbis Ambrosij nec inter Gentes nec inter Iudæos, imò neque inter eos coniuges, qui etsi sub nomine Christi constituti, non vtrique pii essent, ratum censendum esse matrimonium, quasi fundamentum matrimonij sit in consensu deuotionis Dei constitutum, vt liceat pio coniugi absque vlla peccati conscientia discedere à coninge impio, nisi velit cohaerere in matrimonio non rato, quod nihil aliud esset quàm sub nomine ac specie matrimoni scortari. Verum est quod colligit, at nō ex causa quam assignat ipse, sed quam Apostolus ponit.
units.tr: A brother or a sister is not bound in such cases.) This clause explains what he said, "let him depart," if he has departed, so as to show that by this departure of the unbelieving spouse the believer is freed from the law of marriage. For when he says that a brother is not bound in such cases, what else is that than that he is free from the law and bondage of marriage? And hence Ambrose concludes that in such cases it is lawful for the innocent to marry again. For he writes thus in this place: "Reverence for marriage is not owed to one who abhors the author of marriage. For a marriage that is without devotion to God is not valid, and therefore it is no sin for one who is put away for God's sake, if he joins himself to another. For an insult to the Creator dissolves the right of marriage in regard to the one who is left, so that he is not accused of having joined himself to another." So far Ambrose. Yet Ambrose must be read with caution in what he says here: "a marriage that is without devotion to God is not valid." The Apostle does not write so. For he does not place the freedom of the believing spouse from the law of marriage in whether the other spouse lacks devotion to God, but in the departure of the unbelieving spouse. Otherwise he orders that the spouse is not to be dismissed if he consents to live together. He does not say, "if he has consented to devotion to God." It would follow from Ambrose's words that among the Gentiles and among the Jews, and indeed among those spouses who, though established under the name of Christ, are not both godly, the marriage must be counted as not valid, as if the foundation of marriage were laid in consent to devotion to God; so that a godly spouse may leave an ungodly spouse without any sense of sin, unless he wishes to remain in a marriage that is not valid, which would be nothing other than fornication under the name and appearance of marriage. It is true what he infers, but not from the cause he assigns, rather from the one the Apostle gives.

units.la: Non dicit quidem, non est seruituti subiectus frater in huiusmodi, sed alteri potest nubere. Satis est quod liberū facit fidelem, si coniunx infidelis discedat. Nam nihil aliud sequi potest, quàm si liber est fidelis, vt non peccet denuo nubendo. Si enim peccaret, non peccaret aliunde, quàm quod liber non esset à lege prioris coniugij. Ita Rom. 7. vbi dicit mortuo viro liberam esse vxorem à lege mariti, adiungit illam non esse adulteram, si iungatur alij viro. Quare? Quia per mortem liberata est àlege coniugij. Nisi hoc esset, non liceret aspirare ad alteras nuptias. Ita plane & hoc loco, vbi sua sententia liberum à seruitute coniugij pronunciat coniugem fidelem, si infidelis discedat, nemo rei huius intelligens aliud tenere potest quàm licitas esse derelicto fideli coniugi alteras nuptias. Nec opus erat illud adiungere, sed satis erat liberum cuiusuis conscientiæ & necessitati permittere. Alioqui debebat addere, quod in priore casu adiecit, videlicet, vt derelictus fidelis maneat innuptus, expectetq; separati reditum & conuersionem. Sed hoc fuisset periculosum.
units.tr: He does not indeed say, "a brother is not bound in such cases," but "he may marry another." It is enough that he makes the believer free if the unbelieving spouse departs. For nothing else can follow than that, if the believer is free, he does not sin by marrying again. For if he sinned, he would sin for no other reason than that he was not free from the law of the former marriage. So in Romans 7, where he says that the wife is free from the husband's law when the husband is dead, he adds that she is not an adulteress if she is joined to another man. Why? Because by death she is freed from the law of marriage. Unless this were so, it would not be lawful to aspire to another marriage. So too clearly in this place, where by his own judgment he declares the believing spouse free from the bondage of marriage if the unbelieving one departs, no one who understands this matter can hold anything other than that it is lawful for the deserted believing spouse to marry again. Nor was it necessary to add this, but it was enough to leave it free to the conscience and need of each. Otherwise he ought to have added what he added in the earlier case, namely, that the deserted believer should remain unmarried and wait for the return and conversion of the one who departed. But that would have been dangerous.

units.la: Simul aduerte, quod non viro tantum id libertatis assignat, sed pariter & vxori, quod repugnat sententiæ Ambrosij, cuius suprà alicubi memini, qua non id potestatis facit vxori quod viro, in huiusmodi casibus.
units.tr: Notice also that he grants this liberty not only to the husband but equally to the wife, which runs counter to the opinion of Ambrose, whom I mentioned somewhere above, who did not give the wife the same power as the husband in cases of this kind.

units.la: Sunt qui discessum infidelis coniugis latius extendant, quàm præsenti negocio conueniat videlicet, vt liceat denuò nubere derelicto, quacunque causa altera coniunx, siue propter iram, vel μοχθηείαν aliquam discesserit, eò quod illicitè deserere coniugē sit hominis nō Christiani, sed gentilis & infidelis. Temerarius discessus, si sit pertinax, videtur quidè à lege matrimonij eximere insontem ac derelictam. Verum meo iudicio plurimum refert, quibus causis discessus fiat. Nolim temerè in huiusmodi casibus pronūciare, nisi periculum certum sit scortationis, & nulla reconciliationis spes.
units.tr: There are some who extend the departure of an unbelieving spouse more broadly than the present matter requires, namely, that the one deserted may marry again whatever the cause for which the other spouse has left, whether because of anger or some wickedness (μοχθηρία). They argue that to desert a spouse unlawfully is the act not of a Christian but of a heathen and unbeliever. A rash departure, if it is obstinate, does indeed seem to release the innocent and deserted party from the law of marriage. But in my judgment it matters greatly for what causes the departure happens. I would not be quick to pronounce in such cases, unless there is a certain danger of fornication and no hope of reconciliation.

units.la: SED in pace vocauit nos Deus.) Græcè est ἐν δὲ εἰρήνῃ. In pace verò. Et sensus est: Nostri officij est vt cum omnibus pacifici simus, nemini dantes dissentiendi ac litigandi causam, nedū coniugibus. Non enim vocati sumus ad dissidia & iurgia, sed ad pacem.
units.tr: "But God has called us in peace." In Greek it is "ἐν δὲ εἰρήνῃ" [en de eirene], "but in peace." The sense is this: it is our duty to be peaceable with everyone, giving no one occasion to disagree or quarrel, and certainly not spouses. For we have not been called to strife and quarrels, but to peace.

units.la: 1 Quidam referunt ad id quod dixit: Si consenserit ad cohabitandum ne dimittat eam, vt intelligamus Christianæ fidei professionem non separare quæ bene coniuncta sunt, nec in dissidia constituere, quibus competit, vt pacem conseruent, vt illius gratia non debeat fidelis coniunx ab infideli separari, si assentiatur ad cohabitandum.
units.tr: 1. Some refer this to what he said: "If she is content to live with him, let him not put her away," so that we understand that the profession of the Christian faith does not separate those who are rightly joined, nor set them into discord, when they are bound to keep the peace. Thus, for its sake, a believing spouse ought not to be separated from an unbelieving one, if the latter agrees to live together.

units.la: 2 Alij applicant proximè præcedentibus, vbi dixit: Si discedit, discedat, ad hunc modū: Non exigit vocatio & professio Christianæ fidei, vt fidelis coniunx cum infideli iurgetur & contendat, coneturque illum vel vi vel iure in officio detinere, ne discedat, neque hoc exigit vt iurgantem & nomen Christi opprobrantem sustineat. Non enim ad dissidia, sed ad pa-cem vocati sumus. Proinde si non potest fide-lis consensum infidelis obtinere, vt in pace co-uiuat, sinet illum discedere. Ita ad vtrunq; sen-sum haud inepta est ista particula.
units.tr: 2. Others apply it to what immediately precedes, where he said: "If he departs, let him depart." In this sense: the calling and profession of the Christian faith does not require that a believing spouse quarrel and contend with an unbeliever, and strive to keep him in his duty by force or by law, so that he does not leave; nor does it require that she endure a quarrelsome man who reviles the name of Christ. For we have been called not to discord but to peace. Therefore, if the believer cannot obtain the unbeliever's consent to live together in peace, she shall let him depart. Thus this phrase fits either sense well enough.

units.la: Alibi dicit: Non est enim dissensionis Deus sed pacis. Admonemur igitur his verbis que ra-tionis vice adiecta sunt, vt in omnibus pacem sectemur, quantum in nobis est, vt neq; diffi-dijs nostris abigamus coniuges, neq; iurgates & discedentes contentiose retineamus. Vt e-nim pacis studio repugnat, si coniunx propter religionis diuersitatem dimittat coniugem, ita & pacis esse non potest, si diffidentem ac disce-dentem conetur vel violenta vel iuridica con-tentione retinere.
units.tr: Elsewhere he says: "For God is not a God of discord but of peace." We are admonished, therefore, by these words, which are added as a reason, to pursue peace in all things, as far as lies in us: neither to drive away our spouses by our distrust, nor to hold on to those who depart with contentious quarrelling. For just as it is contrary to the pursuit of peace if a spouse dismisses the other because of a difference of religion, so it cannot be peace if one tries to hold back the distrustful and departing spouse by violent or legal contention.

units.la: Sed quaeritur, quomodo dicat Apostolus in pace nos vocatos esse, quod cogimur intelli-gere hoc loco de domestica illa & coniugali tra-quillitate, cum tamen Christus dicat: Putatis quod pacem venerim mittere in terram? Non dico vobis, sed separationem. Erunt enim ex hoc quinq; in domo vna diuisi, tres contra du-os, & duo contra tres: diuidetur pater aduer-sus filium, & filius aduersus patrem, mater ad-uersus filiam, & filia aduersus matrem, socrus aduersus nurum suam, &nurus aduersus socrū suam. Et in Matthaeo additur: Et inimici homi-nis domestici eius. Si Christus istam separatio-nem venit in terram mittere, quomodo dicit Apostolus in pace nos esse vocatos? Quaestio nis huius duplex est solutio.
units.tr: But it is asked how the Apostle can say that we are called to peace, when we are compelled to understand this place of that domestic and marital tranquillity, since Christ says: "Do you suppose that I came to send peace on earth? I tell you, no, but rather division. For from now on there will be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three: the father will be divided against the son and the son against the father, the mother against the daughter and the daughter against the mother, the mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law." And in Matthew it is added: "and a man's enemies will be those of his own household." If Christ came to send this division on earth, how does the Apostle say that we are called to peace? There is a twofold solution to this question.

units.la: 1 Prima, vt dicamus separationem istam re-gni Dei praedicationem in terra consequutam esse, non à Christo studio quaesitam. Ita euenit vt per fidei praedicationem Euangelij contra-dicentibus incredulis oboriretur contentio i-sta & separatio domesticorum cognatorumq;, quae licet in se sit miserabilis, optabilior ta-men est, quam si in malo consitaret pax & concordia.
units.tr: 1. The first is that we say that this division followed upon the preaching of the kingdom of God on earth, and was not sought by Christ. It came about that through the preaching of the faith of the Gospel, this contention and separation of household members and kinsfolk arose from the contradiction of unbelievers. Although this is in itself wretched, it is nevertheless more to be wished for than if peace and concord were kept in evil.

units.la: 2 Altera, ut si omnino contenditur disidium hoc etiam quaesitum, & studiose à Christo mo-tum esse, dicamus intelligendum esse primùm non de alio quàm religionis. Neque enim credendum est, quod in se cupiuerit separata quae Deus coniunxit: deinde id etiam non ita, ut fideles dissidiorum sint authores, vt & reue-ra non sunt. Neque enim author dissidij est & separationis, qui veritatem ac pietatem am-plectitur, & ad hoc instruitur, vt quàm sanc-tissimè seruet quaecunque diuinitus sunt insti-tuta, vt sunt coniugia, & parentum maiorum-que obseruantia.
units.tr: 2. The second is that, if it is insisted that this discord was indeed sought, and deliberately brought about by Christ, we should say that it must be understood, first, not of anything other than religion.
