For it is not to be believed that he wished to separate those whom God has joined. Then, second, that the faithful are not the authors of the dissensions, as indeed they are not. For he who embraces truth and piety, and is trained to keep most holily whatever has been instituted by God, such as marriages and the observance of parents and elders, is not the author of discord and separation.

units.la: Proinde nihil diuersi est vtrinque in ver-bis Christi & Apostoli. Christus malam illam quae in errore erat concordiam, non eam quae coniugum & cognatorum est, disturbare ve-nit. Et fideles ab Apostolo non docentur, vt in errore ac superstitione consentiant infide-libus, sed vt seruata Christi fide, cupiant in of-ficio retinere coniuges, & caueant ne sua teme-ritate causam dent separationi. Si vero id fieri nequeat, reluctantibus incredulis, ac discedenti-bus, sinant illos absq; conscientiae scrupulo discedere, vt qui in huiusmodi non sint serui-tuti subiecti.
units.tr: Therefore there is no difference on either side between the words of Christ and of the Apostle. Christ came to disturb that wicked concord which rests on error, not the concord of spouses and kinsfolk. And the faithful are not taught by the Apostle to agree with unbelievers in error and superstition, but, keeping the faith of Christ, to desire to retain their spouses in duty, and to take care that they do not give cause for separation by their rashness. But if this cannot be done, and the unbelievers resist and depart, let them allow them to depart without a scruple of conscience, since such are not bound in servitude in such cases.

units.la: Qui nanq; scis mulier, an maritum sis seruatura? Aut qui scis vir, an uxorem sis seruaturus?
units.tr: For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?

units.la: Apostrophe est ad ipsos coniuges fideles percontatoria, rationemq; habens praemissorum, quod patet ex particula γὰρ. Exponitur au-tem bifariam.
units.tr: This is a questioning address to the believing spouses themselves, and it has a reason connected with what goes before, as the particle for [γὰρ] shows. It is explained in two ways.

units.la: 1 Quidam enim ad id referunt quod dixit, si discedit, discedat, quasi id nolentem fidelem, sed infidelem seruare cupientem percotetur, Vnde sciat se seruaturum, id est, ad fidem con-uersurum, infidelem ac discedentem coniuge, si conetur illam vel vi vel iure detinere? Appa-ret hoc sensu argumetum esse ex incerto & du-bio, cuius gratia nihil periculi certi sit subeun-dum. Periculosum enim est fideli coniugi habi-tare cum infideli contendete & iurgate, ut ma-gis sit illius timendus relapsus, quàm istius spe-randa conuersio. Quasi dicat: Cum incertum sit, an sis infidelem coniugem seruaturus, tan-topere reluctantem, vt cohabitare nolit, qua ra-tione conaberis illam tanto periculo retinere? Neq; enim aliquid spei apparet futurae conuer-sionis, posteaquam vsque adeò Christi religio-nem abhorret, vt illius gratia cohabitationem recuseт?
units.tr: 1. Some refer it to what he said, "If the unbeliever departs, let him depart." On this reading the question is put to the believer who does not want the separation but wants to keep an unbelieving spouse. "How do you know whether you will save the unbelieving spouse who is departing, that is, bring him or her to faith, if you try to hold him or her back either by force or by right?" On this sense the argument is drawn from what is uncertain and doubtful, so that no certain danger should be undertaken for its sake. It is dangerous for a believing spouse to live with an unbeliever, to quarrel and wrangle, so that the believer's relapse is more to be feared than the unbeliever's conversion is to be hoped for. It is as if he said: "Since it is uncertain whether you will save an unbelieving spouse who is so unwilling that he or she refuses to live with you, by what reasoning will you try to keep that spouse at such great risk? For no hope of future conversion appears, since the spouse so detests the religion of Christ that he or she refuses to live together for its sake."

units.la: 2 Alij ad id referunt, quod dixit: Si consen-rit ad cohabitandum, ne dimittat eum, quasi sit argumentum à spe meliori in rebus dubijs amplectenda sumptum, ad hoc faciens, vt per-suadeatur fidelis coniunx, ne infidelem, si ille consenserit ad conuiuendum, dimittat, quod non solum id fieri non liceat, sed & per hunc conuictum spes esse possit vt seruetur, & ad fi-dem conuertatur. Ita exponunt Chrysosto-mus, Hieronymus & Ambrosius. Vt ut intelli-gamus, certum est quod ista pendeant à praece-denti particula qua dixit: In pace vero uocauit nos Deus. Illa si probè intelligatur, adferet secum & huius adiectae rationis sensum. Non video quid periculi sit in vtroq; sensu. Nam v-trunq; verum est, videlicet quod spem conuer-sionis sibi concipere debeat fidelis de infideli, si cohabitare non detrectet, illiusq; gratia mul-ta facere, ad quod hortatur apostolus Petrus, rursus, quod non debeat contendere, & violen-ter ad cohabitandum cogere reluctantem ac discedentem, eò quod de huiusmodi haud fa-cile sperari possit, quod seruari queat. Proinde in hoc casu & consimilibus opus est prudentia spiritus, diligenterque videndum quid spera-ri possit, quid non, vt & proximi salutem, si illa sperari possit, non negligamus, & rursus cauea-mus, ne certa pericula subeamus, vbi nulla sunt argumenta respipiscentiae, nec aliquid spe-rari potest, cuius gratia quod periculosum est, subeatur. Vtcunq; fuerit, unusquisq; ut ipsi partitus est Deus, unusquisq; ut illum vocauit dominus, ita ambulet. Et sic in eccle sijs omnibus ordino. Circucisus aliquis vocatus est? ne accersat praeputium. In praeputio aliquis vocatus est? ne circuci datur. Circumcisio nihil est, & praeputiū nihil est, sed obseruatio mandatorū dei. Vnusquisq; in ea vocatione in qua vocatus fuit, maneat. Seruus vocatus es? ne sit tibi curae, quinetiam si potes liber fie ri, potius utere. Etenim qui in domino vocatus est seruus, libertus est domini. Similiter & qui liber vocatus fuit, seruus est Christi. Precio empti estis, nolite fieri serui hominum. Vnusquisq; in eo, in quo vocatus fuit, fratres, maneat apud Deum.
units.tr: 2. Others refer it to what he said: "If the unbeliever consents to live together, let him not leave." On this reading the argument is taken from a better hope to be embraced in doubtful matters, and it serves to persuade the believing spouse not to leave an unbeliever who has consented to live together. This is not only permitted, but through such living together there can be hope that the unbeliever will be saved and turned to the faith. This is how Chrysostom, Jerome and Ambrose explain it. However we understand it, it is certain that these things depend on the preceding particle, where he said, "But God has called us in peace." If that is rightly understood, it will also bring with it the sense of this added reason. I do not see what danger there is in either sense. For both are true: that the believer ought to conceive hope of conversion concerning the unbeliever, if he does not refuse to live together, and for his sake do many things, as the apostle Peter exhorts (1 Pet. 3); and again, that the believer ought not to quarrel or forcibly compel the unwilling and departing spouse to live together, because from such a person it cannot easily be hoped that he or she can be saved. Therefore in this case and in similar ones there is need of the prudence of the Spirit, and we must consider carefully what can be hoped for and what cannot. Thus we neither neglect the salvation of our neighbour, if it can be hoped for, nor on the other hand do we expose ourselves to certain dangers where there are no grounds for repentance and nothing can be hoped for, for whose sake a dangerous course should be undertaken. However it may be, "let each one walk as God has apportioned to him, as the Lord has called each one" (1 Cor. 7). And so I ordain in all the churches. "Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not seek to become uncircumcised. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of God's commandments. Let each one remain in the calling in which he was called. Were you called as a slave? Do not be concerned about it; but even if you can become free, rather make use of it. For he who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman. Likewise he who was called free is the slave of Christ. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men. Brothers, let each one remain before God in that state in which he was called."

units.la: Habet hoc Christiana religio, ut necessarios humanae vitae status tam non e medio tollat, damnet aut inuertat, ut si quid illis accesserit peruersi, magis corrigat, atque ita in integrum emendatos restituat, non iubens dirimi coniugia, sed illibata pro institutione Dei seruari, nec seruos adimens dominis, nec dominis excutiens ius in seruos, nec libertos conijciens in seruitutem, nec seruos extollens in externam illam saeculi huius libertatem, nec circumcisio iungens praeputium, nec praeputiato circumcisionem, sed omnes hoscé status intactos relinquens. Huius supra coeperat admonere vbi dixit: In pace vero vocauit nos Deus. Verum quoniam id erat & breuius & obscurius dictum, quàm ut ab imperitioribus satis intelligeretur, visum est ista declarandi gratia adijcere, & generaliter non de coniugio tantum, sed & de reliquis statibus instruere Corinthios. Credibile est multorum conscientias peruersa fuisse opinione turbatas, quasi nouitas religionis, non mentis & vitae solum, sed & pristini status immutationem exigat, maxime si cui relatio sit ad impios & incredulos, ut pote coniugis fidelis ad infidelem, serui fidelis ad infidelem dominum. Proinde ista declaratio, quamuis nihil aliud agat, quàm quod supra dixit: In pace nos esse vocatos, necessario tamen propter in considerantiores adiecta est, ne illorum conscientiae frustra vbi nihil est opus turbentur.
units.tr: The Christian religion has this characteristic: it does not remove, condemn or overturn the necessary conditions of human life, but rather corrects whatever perversity has attached itself to them, and so restores them to their wholeness and purity. It does not command marriages to be dissolved, but commands them to be kept unharmed, as God instituted them. It does not take slaves away from their masters, nor strip masters of their right over slaves, nor cast freedmen into slavery, nor lift slaves up into that outward liberty of this world; it does not join uncircumcision to circumcision, nor circumcision to the uncircumcised, but leaves all these conditions intact. He had begun to remind them of this above, when he said, "But God has called us in peace." But since that statement was both too brief and too obscure to be sufficiently understood by the less experienced, it seemed good to add these things for the sake of explaining it, and to instruct the Corinthians in general, not only about marriage, but also about the other conditions. It is credible that the consciences of many were troubled by a perverse opinion, as if the newness of the religion demanded a change not only of mind and life but also of their former condition, especially if someone had a relation to the impious and unbelieving, as a believing spouse to an unbelieving spouse, or a believing slave to an unbelieving master. Therefore this explanation, although it does nothing other than what he said above, that we are called to peace, has nevertheless been added necessarily, because of those who are more attentive, so that their consciences may not be troubled to no purpose where nothing needs to be done.

units.la: VTCVNQVE fuerit, vnusquisq;, &c.) Particula haec varie legitur, nec eodem modo exponitur. Sunt qui illam praecedentibus, sunt qui sequentibus connectát. Quidam illam etiam in seipsa conuellunt, & partem illius praece dentibus, partem vero sequentibus assignant. Graecè est εἰ μὴ, quod aliquando sonat, an non, aliquando, nisi.
units.tr: However it may be, "each one," etc. This particle is read in various ways and is not explained in the same manner. Some join it to what precedes, others to what follows. Some even split it apart, assigning one part to what precedes and the other part to what follows. In Greek it is εἰ μὴ [ei mē], which sometimes means "whether not," and sometimes "unless."

units.la: Qui legunt, an non, applicant praecedentibus ad hunc modum. Quis scis vir, an vxorem sis seruaturus, an non? Et istam distinctionem
units.tr: Those who read "whether not" attach it to what precedes in this way: "How do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife, or not?" And they make this division...

units.la: A Graeci quidam codices exigunt, qui pro εἰ μὴ habent ἐὰν μὴ, id est, aut non? Deinde quod sequitur: Vnicuiq; sicut diuisit dominus, faciunt initium sequentis contextus.
units.tr: Some Greek codices require the reading ἐὰν μὴ [ean mē], that is, "or not," instead of εἰ μὴ [ei mē]. Then what follows, "to each one as the Lord has apportioned," forms the beginning of the following context.

units.la: Qui vero legunt nisi, ita praecedentibus coniungunt: Qui sis vir an vxorem sis seruaturus? Nisi sicut vnicuiq; diuisit dominus, hoc est, nisi quatenusà domino vnicuique dispositum est, quando & per quos ad fidem veniat. Sic Ambrosius intelligit, cuius haec verba sunt: Diuisit vnicuique dominus quando saluetur, hoc est, scit quando possit credere, & sustinet illum. Sic & hic docet expectádos esse infideles, nec scandalū de his pati debere. Prior lectio & expositio mihi videtur & verior & simplicior esse.
units.tr: But those who read "unless" join it to what precedes in this way: "How do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife? Unless, as the Lord has apportioned to each one," that is, unless as far as it has been arranged by the Lord for each person, when and through whom he comes to faith. Ambrose understands it thus, and his words are: "The Lord has apportioned to each one when he is to be saved, that is, he knows when a person can believe, and he waits for him." In this way he also teaches here that unbelievers are to be waited for, and that no offence should be taken at them. The former reading and explanation seems to me both truer and simpler.

units.la: Erasmus aliter legit. Putat illud εἰ μὴ, seorsum esse legendum, vt nec praecedentibus, nec sequentibus conectatur, vt idem valeat atque in summa, vtcunq; fit, qua loquendi forma relictis incertis ac dubijs ad certa transfitur. Incertum est, infidelem ne fidelis seruaturus sit, aut non sit. Illo relicto ad id quod certum est, transfit, cum docet, vnicuiq; in eo statu manendum esse, in quo ad Christi fidem vocatus est. Ista loquendi forma Latinis quidem in vsu est, ignoro an Graeci illa per εἰ μὴ vtantur, alioqui haud inepta est haec lectio.
units.tr: Erasmus reads it differently. He thinks that εἰ μὴ [ei mē] should be read separately, so that it is connected neither with what precedes nor with what follows, and so that it has the same force as "in sum, however it may be," a form of speech by which, leaving aside uncertain and doubtful things, one passes to certain ones. It is uncertain whether the believer will save the unbeliever or not. Leaving that aside, he passes to what is certain, when he teaches that each person must remain in the state in which he was called to the faith of Christ. This form of speech is indeed in use among the Latins; I do not know whether the Greeks use εἰ μὴ [ei mē] in this way, but otherwise this reading is not unsuitable.

units.la: VNVSQVISQVE vt ipsi partitus est Deus.) Graeca lectio sic habet: ἕκαστος ὡς ἐμέρισεν ὁ Θεός. Id est, vnicuiq; sicut diuisit Deus. Et: ἕκαστον ὡς κέκληκεν ὁ κύριος, οὕτως περιπατείτω. Id est, vnumquenq; sicut vocauit dhs, ita ambulet. Atq; ita ad verbum reddidit vetus interpres. Verum Latinis aurib9 dura est ista versio. Proinde quod Apostolus suo more scribit, ἕκαστος ὡς, pro ὡς ἑκάστῳ & ἕκαστον ὡς, pro ὡς ἕκαστο, quemadmodum & Rom.12. legitur, commodius vertendum est, vt & Eras. reddidit, Videlicet, quisq; vt ipsi partitus est Deus, quisque vt illum vocauit dominus, ita ambulet.
units.tr: "Each one as God has apportioned to him." The Greek reading is: ἕκαστος ὡς ἐμέρισεν ὁ Θεός [hekastos hōs emerisen ho Theos], that is, "each one as God has apportioned." And: ἕκαστον ὡς κέκληκεν ὁ κύριος, οὕτως περιπατείτω [hekaston hōs kekleken ho kyrios, houtōs peripateitō], that is, "each one as the Lord has called, so let him walk." The old translator rendered it word for word in this way. But this version is harsh to Latin ears. Therefore, since the Apostle writes in his own manner, ἕκαστος ὡς [hekastos hōs] for ὡς ἑκάστῳ [hōs hekastō], and ἕκαστον ὡς [hekaston hōs] for ὡς ἕκαστον [hōs hekaston], as is also read in Rom. 12, it should be translated more suitably, as Erasmus also rendered it: "each one, as God has apportioned to him; each one, as the Lord has called him, so let him walk."

units.la: Summa loci huius est, vt quisq; maneat vt à domino vocatus est. At ista videtur bifariam exponi posse.
units.tr: The sum of this passage is that each person should remain as he was called by the Lord. But this can be explained in two ways.

units.la: 1 Primò, ut illa, vnusquisque vt ipsi partitus est deus, vnusquisq; vt illum vocauit dominus ita ambulet, idem sint, atque ad quemcunque vitae statum quisq; vocatus est diuinitus, in illo ambulet, vt vocandi verbum non ad fidei causam, sed ad ordines ac status humanae vitae pertineat. Et ista sententia primùm admonet status illos vitae nostrae, vtpote coniugum, viduarum, dominorum, seruorum, libertorum, & nationum varietatem, esse à Deo, ne quis putet tanquam saeculares & immundos hosce ordines vitandos esse Christiano. Deinde non solum illos à Deo esse, sed & illorum quoq; dispositionem ita diuinitus administrari, vt cuiq; sua conditio, ordinante Deo cedat. Id innuit diuidendi verbum, cum dicit: Vnusquisq; vt ipsi diuisit Deus, ne quem suae conditionis pudeat, sed quisq; sciat in eo sibi statu fideliter persistendum esse, in quem sit diuinitus constitutus. 2 Altero modo possunt ista exponi, vt vocan di verbum non ad status & ordines humanæ vitæ, sed ad Christi fidem sit referendum. Ita quod dicit: Quisq; vt illum vocauit dominus, ita ambulet, tantundem valebit, atq; in quocū que statu quisque constitutus, ad fidem Christi uocatus est, in illo ambulet. Sic illud: Circumcisus aliquis vocatus est, idem est atque in circumcisione constitutus aliquis ad Christum vocatus est,
units.tr: 1. First, the phrases "let each one walk as God has apportioned to him" and "let each one walk as the Lord has called him" may mean the same thing: that each person should walk in whatever state of life he has been divinely called to. On this reading the word "calling" refers not to the cause of faith but to the orders and conditions of human life. This interpretation first reminds us that these states of our life (of spouses, widows, masters, slaves, freemen, and the variety of nations) come from God, so that no one should think these orders are to be avoided by a Christian as worldly and unclean. Second, not only do they come from God, but their arrangement is also divinely governed so that each person's condition falls to him by God's ordering. The word "apportioned" implies this, when it says "as God has apportioned to each." So no one should be ashamed of his condition, but everyone should know that he must remain faithfully in the state into which he has been divinely placed. 2. The words may also be explained in a second way: the word "calling" refers not to the states and orders of human life but to faith in Christ. So when he says "let each one walk as the Lord has called him," it will have the same force as: in whatever state each person is placed, he has been called to faith in Christ, and in that let him walk. Likewise, "Someone was called while circumcised" means the same as "someone was called to Christ while placed in circumcision."

units.la: Quanquam illud quod in repetendo hanc summa dicet: Quisque in ea vocatione, in qua vocatus fuit maneat, videtur vtrique sententiæ competere. Habet enim duplicem vocationem. Primam status in quo quis positus ad Christum vocatur. De illa est, quod dicit: Quisque in ea vocatione, in qua &c. Alteram religionis Christi, ad quam vocatur quis, sive dominus, sive seruus, sive Iudæus, sive Græcus, sive coniunx, sive ἀγαμος. Hanc notat, cū dicit: Vocatus est, intellige ad Christianismū. Ista volui breuiter annotare, sed ita vt cuiq; liberum sit, quod magis germanum putat appre hendere.
units.tr: Although what he repeats in summarizing, "each should remain in the calling in which he was called," seems to fit either interpretation. For there is a twofold calling. The first is the state in which a person is placed when he is called to Christ; it is of this that he says "each in the calling in which he was called," and so on. The second is the calling to the religion of Christ, to which a person is called, whether master or slave, Jew or Greek, married or unmarried (ἄγαμος). He marks this when he says "was called," which you should understand as the calling to Christianity. I have wanted to note these points briefly, but so that each reader may take up whichever he thinks more genuine.

units.la: DE MONACHORVM statu.
units.tr: On the state of the monks.

units.la: Præsens hic Apostoli locus non potest aliter intelligi, quàm vel de ea vocatione quę statuū humanæ vitę est extra Christum, vel de ea qua ex statibus illis ad fidem Christi vocamur.
units.tr: This passage of the Apostle cannot be understood otherwise than either of the calling that belongs to the states of human life outside Christ, or of the calling by which we are called to the faith of Christ from those states.

units.la: Dicant autem monastici status defensores, quam ex hoc Apostoli loco uocationem assignare velint monachismo suo. Si priorem, ergo qui monachi sunt, in statu sæculari sunt, extra Christum posito, è quo ad Christi fidem vocandi sint, vt non sit melior huius vitæ statib9, & non plus quàm illi commercij habeat cum Christo. Si posteriorem, respondeant, quid fuerint ante monachismum, Christiani' ne vel incredulii? Incredulitatem negabūt, etiā ante monachismi professionem. Ergo Christiani, adeo que iam antea in vocatione Christi fuerunt, & permanerepotuerūt, etiamsi monachismū spre uissent. Non est igitur monachismus vocatio illa ad Christum, de qua hic loquitur Apostolus. Alioqui male iuberet quenque in suo statu manere, in quo fuit, cum ad Christum vocaretur, sed rectius quosuis vocaret ad monachatum.
units.tr: Let the defenders of the monastic state say which of these callings they wish to assign to their monasticism from this passage of the Apostle. If the first, then those who are monks are in a secular state, placed outside Christ, from which they must be called to the faith of Christ; so the monastic life is no better than the other states of life, and has no more fellowship with Christ than they do. If the second, let them answer: were they Christians or unbelievers before they became monks? They will deny that they were unbelievers, even before they professed monasticism. Therefore they were Christians, and already before this were in the calling of Christ, and could have remained in it even if they had rejected monasticism. So monasticism is not that calling to Christ of which the Apostle speaks here. Otherwise he would be ordering each person to remain in the state he was in when he was called to Christ, and would rather be calling everyone to monkhood.

units.la: Cum igitur monachismus non sit de his vocationibus, quæ hic ab Apostolo ponuntur, quæ est ista temeritas, quod hunc locum pro statu sui defensione citant? Quin iam rogent Apostolum an idem sit pronunciaturus de monachismi statu. Cum enim ista scriberet, ne sominiauit quidem de monachis.
units.tr: Since monasticism, then, is not among those callings which the Apostle sets out here, what is this recklessness, that they cite this passage in defence of their state? Let them rather ask the Apostle whether he would pronounce the same about the monastic state. For when he was writing these words, he did not even dream of monks.

units.la: Deinde certū est quidem, diuersitate quandam innui vocationis, de qua loquitur Apostolus, cum dicit: Vnusquisque vt vocauit dominus, ita ambulet. Verum ista diuersitas non est in eo ad quod vocat dominus, sed in eo vn de vocat, aut si mauis, nō in qualitate fidei, ad quam vocamur, sed in qualitate eorū qui vocantur. Nam fides ad quam uocamur, vna est & eadem, ad quam omnes pariter uocamur, ut nihil hic sit discriminis. At illi qui uocantur diuersi sunt, hoc est, in diuerso statu sunt. Nam alius seruus, alius libertus, alius coniunx, alius ἀγαμος uocatur, &c. Dicant nunc monachi quò suam uocationem referre velint. An ad eos status vnde vocat Christus, vel in eam vocationem ad quam vocat omnes absq; ullo discrimine. Puto quod nolunt ad status istos humanæ uitæ, vnde quidam ad Christum uocantur. Ergo ad eam vocationem, ad quam suos uocat Christus. Cur ergo diuersitatem habet monachismus à vocatione reliquorum Christianorum? Vocatio Christi, communis illa fidelium quæ ad salutem est, caret diuersitate. Ipsorum vero diuersa est. Ergo non est Christi vocatio, de qua Apostolus loquitur. Nihil igitur ad eos hic locus.
units.tr: Next, it is certain that some diversity is implied in the calling of which the Apostle speaks when he says "let each one walk as the Lord has called him." But this diversity is not in that to which the Lord calls, but in that from which he calls, or, if you prefer, not in the quality of the faith to which we are called, but in the quality of those who are called. For the faith to which we are called is one and the same, to which all alike are called, so that there is no distinction here. But those who are called are diverse, that is, they are in diverse states. For one is called a slave, another a freeman, another a spouse, another unmarried (ἄγαμος), and so on. Let the monks now say to which calling they wish to refer theirs: to those states of human life from which Christ calls, or to that calling to which Christ calls all without any distinction? I think they are unwilling to refer it to those states of human life from which some are called to Christ. Therefore it is to that calling to which Christ calls his own. Why then does monasticism have a diversity from the calling of the other Christians? The calling of Christ, that common calling of the faithful which is to salvation, admits of no diversity; but theirs is diverse. Therefore it is not the calling of Christ of which the Apostle speaks. So this passage has nothing to do with them.

units.la: V T illum vocauit dominus.) Vocationem fidelium tribuit ipsi domino, licet apostolorū fieret ministerio. Iste loquendi modus, quo do minus facere dicitur, quod per suorum ministerium fit, diligenter notandus est. Plurimum enim authoritatis Euangelico ministerio tribuit, & admodum consolatur conscientias eorum, qui ministerio Euangelico, per quod vocantur, obtemperant, vt sciant se non humanitus, sed diuinitus ad Christianæ fidei professione vocatos esse. Certè non est apostolorum, sed Christi vocatio, quæ non in apostolorum, sed Christi nomine prædicatur. Ministerium uocationis apostolorum quidem est, sed ipsa uocatio domini. Hinc illud Apostolo in vsu est: Qui vocauit uos. A' quo vocati estis. Et 2. Thessalonicensium 2. Qui vocauit uos per Euangelium nostrum.
units.tr: AS THE LORD HAS CALLED HIM. He attributes the calling of the faithful to the Lord himself, although it is made through the ministry of the apostles. This manner of speaking, in which the Lord is said to do what is done through the ministry of his servants, is to be carefully noted. For it gives great authority to the Gospel ministry, and greatly comforts the consciences of those who obey the Gospel ministry through which they are called, so that they may know that they have been called to the profession of the Christian faith not by man but by God. Surely the calling is not the apostles' but Christ's, since it is proclaimed not in the name of the apostles but in the name of Christ. The ministry of calling belongs to the apostles, but the calling itself is the Lord's. Hence the Apostle's words: "He who called you" and "by whom you were called." And in 2 Thessalonians 2: "He called you through our Gospel."

units.la: E T sic in ecclesijs omnibus ordino.) Non contentiosis plurimum valere debet, quod nō solum ab Apostolo instituitur, sed ab omnibus simul ecclesijs obtemperanter accipitur. Huiusmodi ordinationibus quisquis oblectatur, merito singularitatis & contentionis notā sustinet. Et hac puto ratione particulam istā adiectam esse, vt contentiosis minus esset occasionis reluctandi, vel certè imbecilliores conscientiæ hoc citius acquiescerent, quo videret sententiam hanc Apostoli in omnibus obtinere Christi ecclesijs. Talibus enim reliquorum fidelium consensus multum adfert persuasionis.
units.tr: AND SO I ORDAIN IN ALL THE CHURCHES. What is instituted not only by the Apostle but is received with obedience by all the churches together ought to carry great weight with the contentious. Anyone who takes pleasure in such ordinances rightly bears the mark of singularity and contentiousness. And I think this phrase was added for this reason: so that the contentious would have less occasion to resist, or certainly so that weaker consciences would more readily acquiesce, seeing that this judgment of the Apostle holds in all the churches of Christ. For agreement with the rest of the faithful brings much persuasion to such people.

units.la: Hinc tamen nemo me putet istorum patrocinari argumento, qui in religionis controuersia quiduis ex multarum ecclesiarum consensu stabilire conantur. Non enim mox pium est & Deo gratū, quod καθολικον est. Et multa sunt eiusmodi, quæ non possunt omnibus conuenire & prodesse ecclesijs. Et præterea non eandem meretur authoritatem cum eo quod ab Apostolo omnib. traditur ecclesijs, quod Pontifices & tyranni ecclesiarum fidelium multitudini obtrudunt, & vel errore vel metu admitmittitur.Locum habet catholicæ obseruantię authoritas in rebus licitis & vtilibus,& ad hoc vsurpanda est,vt ijs persuadeatur,qui res ipsas liquidò dijudicare non possunt,& vt simul irre quieti & contentiosi coerceantur.
units.tr: Yet let no one think that I am defending the argument of those who, in controversy over religion, try to establish anything by the consensus of many churches. For what is catholic is not at once pious and pleasing to God. Many such things cannot suit and benefit all the churches. Moreover, the authority of what the Apostle hands down to all the churches does not deserve the same weight as what the popes and tyrants of the churches impose on the multitude of the faithful, and what is admitted through error or fear. The authority of catholic observance has its place in matters that are lawful and useful, and it is to be invoked for this purpose: that it may persuade those who cannot judge the matters themselves clearly, and that at the same time the restless and contentious may be restrained.

units.la: Διατάσσομαι,inquit.) Ordino & constituo.Duplex est ordinationũ & constitutionũ genus.
units.tr: Διατάσσομαι [I ordain], he says. I order and I establish. There are two kinds of ordinance and establishment.

units.la: 1 Vnum,vt quę antea in vsu sunt, non diuel-lantur,sed ritè ac legitimè custodiantur.Sub isto cõprehėditur præsens ordinatio,in qua nō noui aliquid instituitur , sed status & ordines humanæ vitæ suo loco collocantur.
units.tr: One kind is that what was previously in use should not be uprooted, but should be duly and lawfully kept. Under this falls the present ordinance, in which nothing new is instituted, but the states and orders of human life are set in their proper place.

units.la: 2 Alterum,cum instituuntur noua quæ an-tea in vsu non fuerunt.Hoc genus traditionis vniuersam Christi ecclesiam occupauit.Est au-tem supra modum periculosum : licet enim in casu locũ habeat,si vera accedat,&solida spiri-tus sancti prudentia,& ecclesiæ regimen tene-ant viri vigilantes ac pij , qui sana doctrina li-bertatem conscientiarum in Christo fideli-ter tueantur,simul tamen magnam adfert ty-rannidi & omnis generis superstitioni, con-scientiarumque captiuitati occasionem , eam-dem sibi quiduis constituendi potestatem uin dicantibus ijs,qui non Christum,sed seipsos in ecclesia quærunt,quę veris Christi ministris & apostolis,omnia ductu spiritus moderantibus fuisse legitur.
units.tr: Second, when new things are introduced which were not previously in use. This kind of tradition has taken hold of the whole Church of Christ. It is, however, extremely dangerous. Although it has a place in cases of necessity, if the prudence of the Holy Spirit is true and sound, and if watchful and godly men hold the government of the Church and faithfully guard the freedom of conscience in Christ by sound doctrine, it nonetheless gives great opportunity to tyranny, to every kind of superstition, and to the captivity of consciences. Those who seek not Christ but themselves in the Church claim for themselves the same power of establishing whatever they please, whereas it is read that the true ministers of Christ and the apostles, guided by the Spirit, governed all things otherwise.

units.la: Est itaq; ista traditionum controuersia,quæ nostro sæculo viget,à pijs & in Christo prudė tibus viris,neq; pro veteri consuetudine,neq; carnalium hominum temeritate, sed pro ipsa veritatis & ędificandarum ecclesiarũ regula di metienda &dijudicanda.Videmus enim utrin-que non æquis oculis causam hanc intros-pici, dum illinc ecclesiastici quos vocant,magis re-gno suo quàm Christi ecclesijs consultum cu-piunt: hinc vero plebs dissoluta non spiritus, sed carnis libertatem amplectitur, & omnem vt vt piam & necessariam ecclesiæ disciplinam horret & auersatur.
units.tr: This controversy over traditions, which flourishes in our age, is therefore not one to be judged by old custom, nor by the rashness of carnal men, but by the rule of truth itself and of building up the churches; it must be measured and decided by that rule. For we see that this cause is not examined with even eyes on either side: on one side the so-called ecclesiastics desire that more care be taken of their own kingdom than of the churches of Christ; on the other, the dissolute common people embrace not the liberty of the Spirit but the liberty of the flesh, and shrink from and reject every kind of church discipline, however godly and necessary it is.

units.la: Circumcisus aliquis uocatus est? ne accersat præputium.In præputio aliquis uocatus est? ne circumcidatur.
units.tr: Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not seek to become uncircumcised. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised.

units.la: Ista exempli vice subijciuntur. Nec frustra. Erant enim qui cumaudirent finè venisse cir-cumcisioni,vel odio gentis suę,quod tanta per tinacia fidem Christi Iudæi persequerentur,& ipsum quoq; Christum occiderant,præputium sibi accersendum putabant,táquam in illo gra-tiores Christo futuri,eoq; pacto declaraturi se prorsus à Iudaica defecisse perfidia.
units.tr: These words are added as an example, and not without reason. For there were some who, hearing that they had come to Christ, thought that they ought to make themselves uncircumcised, either out of hatred for their own nation, because the Jews persisted so stubbornly in persecuting the faith of Christ, and had even put Christ himself to death, or because they supposed that they would be more acceptable to Christ if they were uncircumcised, and so would show plainly that they had wholly deserted Jewish unbelief.

units.la: Rursus erant qui propter Abrahæ præroga-tiuam putabant se meliores fore, si Christi fi-dei & circumcisionem coniungerent,maximè cum non deessent,qui illius etiam necessitate fidelibus ex Gentibus prædicarent:de quibus est in Act.cap.15.& in epist. ad Gal.
units.tr: Again, there were some who, on account of the prerogative of Abraham, thought they would be better if they joined circumcision to faith in Christ. This was especially so since there were not lacking those who preached its necessity even to believers from among the Gentiles. Of these there is mention in Acts chapter 15 and in the Epistle to the Galatians.

units.la: Vt igitur vtriusque consulat,illis dicit,ne ac cersant præputium, id est, ne putent se Chri-sto minus placere circumcisos,sed in ea condi-tione maneant,modo,syncera sint erga Chri-stum fidę;istis verò,ne circumcidantur,id est, ne arbitrentur se in præputio Deo placere nō posse,sed in illo fiducialiter & secura conscien-tia maneant.Hac de re vide in Galatis.
units.tr: So, to satisfy both, he says to the former: do not seek uncircumcision, that is, do not think you please Christ less because you are circumcised; remain in that condition, provided your faith in Christ is sincere. But to the latter he says: do not be circumcised, that is, do not think you cannot please God in uncircumcision; remain in it with trust and a secure conscience. On this matter see in Galatians.

units.la: NB accersat præputium.) Græcè est, μὴ ἐπι-ακάζω,id est,ne attrahat.Intelligit autem rele-ctam pelliculam.Sed quæritur quomodo præ-putium accersi queat à circucisio,& quod rese-ctum est restitui.
units.tr: "Let him not seek uncircumcision": in Greek it is μὴ ἐπισπάσθω [μὴ ἐπισπάσθω], that is, let him not draw it on. He means the foreskin that has been drawn back. But the question is how uncircumcision can be drawn on by one who has been circumcised, and how what has been cut away can be restored.

units.la: Scribunt quidam per pharmacum quoddã restitui posse præputium. Admonet huius & Theophylactus.Et Erasmus Cornelium Cel-sum hac de re citat lib.7.cap.25. Commenta-rij Hieronymo dati id pernegant, & particulă hanc exponunt nō de pelliculæ amputatæ re-stitutione, sed de abiectione cæremoniarum legis,& complexu vitæ gentilis:quasi dicat Apostolus , ne putet se peccare si non statim legis cæremonias abiiciat tanquam immũdas, cum in illis,modo fiduciam ac spem salutis in illas nõ collocet,nihil impediat,esse vere Christianum.
units.tr: Some write that the foreskin can be restored by a certain drug, and Theophylact also warns of this. Erasmus cites Cornelius Celsus on this matter, book 7, chapter 25. The commentary given under Jerome's name flatly denies this and explains the phrase not as the restoration of the cut-off skin but as the rejection of the ceremonies of the law and the embracing of the Gentile way of life. It is as if the Apostle said: let him not think he sins if he does not at once cast off the ceremonies of the law as unclean; provided he does not place his trust and hope of salvation in them, nothing hinders him from being a true Christian.

units.la: NE circumcidatur.) Hic quæritur, quare Timotheum circumciderit, si qui in præputio vocatus est,circumcidi nō debet?In promptu responsio est.Non ita dicit:Ne circumcidatur, quod peccatum sit circumcidi, sed quod non sit necesse, ut relicto præputio accersatur cir-cumcisio.Quemadmodum & illud: Ne accer-sat præputium,non habet vetandi vim,sed ne-cessitatis pernegationem.Neque enim peccă-bant, qui relictis legis cæremonijs Christianis mi libertatem amplectebantur,& cum præpu-tiatis absq; vllo discrimine quibusuis vescebã-tur.Hoc sensu & illa dicta sunt,ita ambulet, & infrà,in ea maneat.Non enim & ibi uetat, reli-cto eo statu in quo quis vocatus est.alium am-plecti, vt si quis agamos vocatus esset, aut ser-uus, non licuerit nubere, aut si per heri beni-gnitatem daretur,è seruo in liberti transfire có ditionem:sed vnum hoc agit, ut sciat quisque non peccare se, si in quo statu vocatus est, in eo persistat.
units.tr: Let him not be circumcised. Here it is asked why Timothy was circumcised, if one who was called in uncircumcision ought not to be circumcised. The answer is ready to hand. Paul does not say, "Let him not be circumcised" because it is a sin to be circumcised, but because it is not necessary to seek circumcision by giving up the foreskin. In the same way, "let him not seek to become uncircumcised" does not carry the force of a prohibition, but denies that it is a necessity. For those who, having abandoned the ceremonies of the law, embraced Christian liberty and ate indiscriminately with the uncircumcised, were not sinning. The same sense applies to the words "let him walk so" and below "let him remain in that," for there too he does not forbid a person, having left the condition in which he was called, to embrace another; as if a man were called while a slave, it would not be lawful for him to marry, or if by the kindness of his master he were given the chance to pass from slavery to freedom. Rather, he is doing only this: that each one should know that he does not sin if he persists in the state in which he was called.

units.la: Circumcisio nihil est, & præputiū ni-hil est,sed obseruatio mãdatorum Dei.
units.tr: Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God.

units.la: Hac sententia rationem reddit,quare nec præputiatus circumcisionem,nec circumcisus præputium accersere debeat. Quia circumci-sio nihil est,nihil est etiam præputium,sed ob-seruatio mandatorum Dei. Magna peruersi-tas est,anxium esse & solicitum in eo quod ni-hil est,id est,quo Deo non gratificatur, & ne-gligentem in eo quod vnum ab omnibus exi-gitur.Ecclesiastes vlt.Deum time,& mandata eius obserua,hoc est omnis homo.Et Act.10. In omni gente qui timet Deum & operatur iu-sticiam,acceptusest illi.Huc igitur Corinthios ista sententia dirigit, ut nihil de circumcisione vel præputio solicíti, seduli sint obseruatores mandatorum Dei.
units.tr: This statement gives the reason why neither the uncircumcised should seek circumcision nor the circumcised should seek uncircumcision. Because circumcision is nothing, uncircumcision is also nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God. It is a great perversity to be anxious and concerned about that which is nothing, that is, that which does not please God, and to be careless about that one thing which is demanded of all. Ecclesiastes at the end: "Fear God and keep his commandments; this is the whole duty of man." And Acts 10: "In every nation he who fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him." Therefore this sentence directs the Corinthians to this end: that, being in no way anxious or eager about circumcision or uncircumcision, they may be diligent keepers of the commandments of God.

units.la: SED obseruatio mandatorum Dei.) Am-brosius ita exponit,id est fidęs,quæ propitium
units.tr: "But the observance of God's commandments." Ambrose expounds it thus: that is, faith, which makes God propitious

units.la: facit Deum, si bonis operibus approbetur. Respicit autem ad locum in Galatis cap.5. ubi dicit: In Christo Iesu nec circumcisio aliquid valet nec praeputium, sed fides quae per dilectionem est efficax. Et cap.6. eandem sententiam ita ponit: In Christo enim Iesu nec circumcisio aliquid valet nec praeputium, sed nova creatura. Coniunguntur ergo ista, observatio mandatorum Dei, & fides per dilectionem efficax, & nova creatura, id est renovatio interni hominis. In his est veritas Christi.
units.tr: if it is approved by good works. He refers to the passage in Galatians chapter 5, where he says: "In Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything nor uncircumcision, but faith which works through love." And in chapter 6 he puts the same sentence thus: "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything nor uncircumcision, but a new creature." So these things are joined together: the observance of God's commandments, faith which is effective through love, and a new creature, that is, the renewal of the inner man. In these lies the truth of Christ.

units.la: At dicet quis, quomodo circumcisio nihil est, cum sit praecepta a Deo, si observatio praeceptorum Dei requiritur? Respondendum. In Christo nihil est, in quo evacuata est, velut umbra per corporis praesentiam. Finem accepit in Christo, quia non ad veritatem, sed ad umbras pertinebat.
units.tr: But someone will say: how is circumcision nothing, when it was commanded by God, if the observance of God's commandments is required? The answer is that in Christ it is nothing; in him it has been emptied, as a shadow vanishes at the presence of the body. It has come to an end in Christ, because it pertained not to the truth but to shadows.

units.la: Notanda est haec particula nostris potissimum temporibus, quibus pars ita de fidei iustitia contendit, ut prope nullam habeat seruandorum Dei mandatorum rationem, pars vero vsqueadeo operum studio omnia tribuit, ut ferre nequeat fidei dari iusticiam, quae tamen illi ab Apostolo tot testimonijs absque ulla controversia assignatur. Istis quod hic ab Apostolo ponitur, perinde est ac si dicat: Fides nihil est, sed observatio mandatorum Dei. Hi primum debent animaduertere Apostolum non de fide, sed circumcisione & praeputio dicere quod nihil sint. Possunt enim illa, ut sunt externa, ita seruari, ut nihil prorsus pietatis accedat vel circumcisorum vel praeputiatorum mentibus. Fides vero, modo vera sit, non potest inanis esse animi affectus, qui Deo non placeat, cum vsqueadeo placeat, ut sine illo impossibile sit Deo placere. Deinde observent, quod nō de quorumcunq; sed Dei mandatorum observantia loquitur. Alioqui per observantiam mandatorum hominum frustra Deo seruitur, etiam si quae Deus praecepit seruet quisquam. Opprobrat enim populo suo Deus, quod se mandato hominum, id est, ob id quod homo praecipiat, timeant. Ista quippe τυπος manda-torum Dei haec duo habet. Primum ut magis sit animi affectus & studium, quam externum aliquod opus. Deinde, ut obiectum habeat, non creaturam aliquam, sed vnum Deum, cui omnis debetur obedientia.
units.tr: This particle is especially to be noted in our own times, when one party so contends about the righteousness of faith that it has almost no regard for keeping God's commandments, while the other party attributes everything so much to the zeal for works that it cannot bear that righteousness should be given to faith, though the Apostle assigns it to faith with so many testimonies and without any controversy. For such people, what the Apostle sets down here is just as if he said: faith is nothing, but the observance of God's commandments. Let them first consider that the Apostle says circumcision and uncircumcision are nothing, not faith. For those things, as they are external, can be kept in such a way that nothing of piety is added to the minds either of the circumcised or of the uncircumcised. But faith, provided it is true, cannot be an empty affection of the mind that does not please God, since it pleases so much that without it it is impossible to please God. Next let them observe that he speaks not of the observance of any commandments whatever, but of God's commandments. Otherwise God is served in vain by the observance of the commandments of men, even if someone keeps what God has commanded. For God reproaches his people that they fear men's commandments, that is, that they fear because a man commands. For this character [τύπος] of God's commandments has two features. First, that it is more an affection and zeal of the mind than some external work. Second, that its object is not any creature but the one God, to whom all obedience is owed.

units.la: Hinc duo colliguntur. 1 Primum de ista mandatorum Dei observantia nihil sibi vendicare eos posse, qui plus homines quam Deum metuunt. 2 Alterum eorum infirmitatem, qui bonum quod volunt, praecarnis imbecillitate non faciunt, & malum quod detestantur faciunt boni a Deo consuli, propter sui reuerentiam quae certissimum est fidei opus. Ita nos Germani dicimus, Gott nimpt den willen fur das werck.
units.tr: From this two things are gathered. First, that those who fear men more than God can claim nothing for themselves from this observance of God's commandments. Second, the weakness of those who, because of the frailty of the flesh, do not do the good they wish, and yet do the evil they detest, are regarded favourably by God on account of their reverence, which is most certainly a work of faith. So we Germans say: "Gott nimmt den Willen für das Werk" [Gott nimpt den willen fur das werck], God takes the will for the deed.

units.la: SERVVS uocatus es? ne sit tibi curae.) De bebat dicere seruus maneas, quoniam in generali praeceptione dixerat, vnusquisque in qua vocatione uocatus est, in ea maneat. Verum quo niam non praecipiebat seruitutem, sed consu-lebat conscientijs fidelium, ne putarent se pec-care vbi nihil erat peccati, neue Christianismu in eas res collocarent, quibus Deo non seruitur, quasi per expositionem formam propositionis mutat, dicens: Ne sit tibi curae. Id est, ne sis anxius propter statu seruitutis, quasi Christianus esse nequeas, donec in illo fueris.
units.tr: "Were you called as a slave? Let it not be a concern to you." He had said that the slave should remain a slave, since in the general precept he had said that each should remain in the calling in which he was called. But since he did not command slavery, but rather advised the consciences of the faithful, lest they think they sin where there is no sin, and lest they place Christianity in matters in which God is not served, he changes the form of the proposition, as it were by way of explanation, saying: "Let it not be a concern to you." That is, do not be anxious about the state of slavery, as if you could not be a Christian while you remain in it.

units.la: QVINETIAM si potes liber fieri, potius vtere.) Ista per auxesim sunt adiecta. Tantundem enim dicit, Imo tam no esto anxius in seruitute, qui seruus vocatus es, ut etiamsi copia detur libertatis, malis in seruitute consistere, ut quod dicit, potius vtere, idem sit atque magis seruitutem exerce, illique conditioni in cumbe.
units.tr: Even if you can become free, make more use of your present condition. These words are added by way of amplification. The sense is: "Indeed, do not be anxious about your slavery, though you were called as a slave, so that even if the chance of freedom is offered, you would rather remain in slavery." So "make more use of it" means the same as "serve all the more, and embrace that condition."

units.la: Ergo praefert Apostolus seruitutem libertati? Atqui libertas multo commodior est regno Christi, maxime perfequutionis tempore, quam seruitus, dominorum plerunque infidelium, obnoxia voluntati. Respondeo. Apostolus non discernit hoc loco inter seruitutem & libertatem, sed in hoc vno est, ut doceat nihil habere seruitutem, cuius gratia quisquam a Christianismo possit impediri. Et vt hanc sententiam diligenter inculcet, & persuasissimam faciat, vtitur ista auxesi, dicens: Quinetiam si potes liber fieri, potius vtere. Tam enim liberum vult Christiani hominis animum in his rebus esse, ut etiam si seruus uocatus sit, nō affectet Christianismi nomine libertatem, nec tum quidem cum offertur.
units.tr: Does the Apostle then prefer slavery to freedom? Yet freedom is far more advantageous than slavery to unbelieving masters, which often subjects a person to their will, especially in a time of persecution, and so is more useful for the kingdom of Christ. I answer: the Apostle is not here distinguishing between slavery and freedom. His only point is to teach that slavery is no hindrance by which anyone could be prevented from being a Christian. To impress this opinion carefully and make it wholly persuasive, he uses this amplification, saying: "Even if you can become free, make more use of it." For he wants the mind of a Christian in these matters to be so free that even if he is called a slave, he does not aspire to freedom in the name of Christianity, not even when it is offered.

units.la: Vel certe, quod dicit: Si potes liber fieri, nō de oblata per herum libertate, sed de copia aufugiendi dicit, quod solenne erat seruis. Vt in Onesimo seruo Philemonis uisum est. Hoc sensu nihil aliud dicit, quam ne Christianus seruus ita horreat seruitutem, ut si copiam aufugiendi acquirat, in libertatem se uellit asserere, sed tam contentus ea sorte sit, ut nolit, etiasi periculo careat, iugum hoc abijcere, sed hoc maiore fide, postquam Christianus factus est, domino suo seruire.
units.tr: Or certainly, when he says "if you can become free," he speaks not of freedom offered by the master, but of the opportunity to run away, which was customary for slaves, as in the case of Onesimus, the slave of Philemon. In this sense he says nothing other than this: a Christian slave should not so dread slavery that, if he gets the chance to flee, he asserts himself into liberty. Rather he should be so content with his lot that he would not wish, even if it were free of danger, to cast off this yoke. Instead, after becoming a Christian, he should serve his master with greater faithfulness.

units.la: 1 Non tam metuendū erat Apostolo, ne putarent sibi Christiani non licere libertatem, ut monendi fuerint, quo illam, si copia detur, praeferuitute eligerent, quam ne putarent seruos Christo placere non posse.
units.tr: 1 The Apostle did not need to fear so much that Christians would think freedom was forbidden them, so that they had to be warned to prefer slavery to it if the chance were given. Rather he feared that they would think slaves could not please Christ.

units.la: 2 Deinde sciebat humani cordis superbiam, alioqui plus affectare libertatem, & horrere seruitutem.
units.tr: 2 Moreover, he knew the pride of the human heart, which otherwise would covet freedom more and shrink from slavery.

units.la: 3 Non ignorabat & seruorum ingenium ita corruptum, vt quasi ad seruitutem natum videatur, recte viuere non posse, nisi in seruitute eo quod hoc hominum genus plerunq; male educatum, seipsum regere nescat, ut si velis eos seruituti eximere, perinde facias, ac si velis pueros a paterna liberare obedientia, potestatemq; permittere suopte ingenio viuendi.
units.tr: 3 He was also not unaware that the nature of slaves is so corrupted that they seem born for slavery and cannot live rightly unless they are in slavery. This class of men, for the most part badly brought up, does not know how to govern itself. So if you wanted to free such people from slavery, you would be doing the same as if you wanted to release children from their father's obedience and give them the power to live by their own nature.

units.la: His quoq; rationibus adducor, ut magis arrideat eorum sententia qui illud μαλλον χρου. id est, magis vtere, idem esse volunt, atque magis seruias, & maiore fide ac sedulitate, absque que ullo conscientiæ scrupulo, seruitutis conditionem complectere.
units.tr: These reasons also lead me to favour the view of those who hold that the phrase [μᾶλλον χρῶ], that is, "make more use," means the same as "serve more," and that a slave should embrace his condition of slavery with greater faithfulness and diligence, without any scruple of conscience.

units.la: Sunt qui alium sensum adferant. Videlicet istum. Verùm si potes liber fieri, magis utere, id est, ea potestate oblatæ libertatis potius ute re, quàm seruitute. Sic paraphrastes Erasmus: Quin potius illud agendum, ut si detur occasio, libertatem arripiat ac mutet seruitutem. Verù meo iudicio ista sententia nec quadrat propo sito, nec subiectæ rationi. Et coniunctio ⸗ inserta, cum dicit: Quin etiam si potes liber fieri, satis indicat ista prioris particulæ, ne sit tibi curæ, auxesim habere. Proinde malo cum Ambrosio, Hieronymo, & Chrysostomo priorem sensum amplecti, quem Chrysostomus non solum ponit, sed & posteriorem hunc reijcit. Interea tamen non uetat Christianum oblatam libertatem, si iusta detur illius copia, abijcere. Quis enim non malit liber esse quàm seruus, si præter alicuius id fieri poterit iniuriam?
units.tr: Some offer another sense, namely: "But if you can become free, make more use of it," that is, use the power of the freedom offered rather than slavery. So the paraphrast Erasmus: "Rather, let this be done: if an opportunity is given, let him seize freedom and change his slavery." But in my judgment this opinion fits neither the proposition nor the reason that follows. And the conjunction inserted in "Nay, even if you can become free" sufficiently shows that the preceding clause, "let it not concern you," has an amplification. Therefore I prefer, with Ambrose, Jerome and Chrysostom, to embrace the former sense, which Chrysostom not only sets forth but also rejects the latter. Meanwhile, this does not forbid a Christian to cast off offered freedom if it can be lawfully obtained. For who would not prefer to be free rather than a slave, if it could happen without injury to anyone?

units.la: Etenim qui in domino uocatus est seruus, libertus domini est. Similiter & qui liber uocatus fuit, seruus est Christi.
units.tr: For he who in the Lord was called a slave is the Lord's freedman. Likewise he who was called free is Christ's slave.

units.la: 1 Rationem reddit, quare qui seruus uocatus est, anxius esse non debeat, ita ut ne appetat quidem Christi nomine libertatem, si illa poterit obtingere. Quare? Quia uidelicet iamme liorem libertate, quàm sit illa externa, in Christo adeptus est. Hoc est quod dicit: Etenim qui in domino uocatus est seruus, libertus domini est. Rursus, qui libertus in domino uocatus fuit, seruus est Christi. Vt non habeat, cur de carnis ingenuitate glorietur. Nö hic dixit libertus uocatus es: ne sit tibi curæ. Non enim ea erat libertis tentatio contèptus & abiectio nis, quæ erat seruis. Deinde non cogebantur infidelibus dominis obnoxium habere conui ctum, quod seruis usuueniebat. Conueniebat igitur magis ut seruos confirmaret quàm libe ros. Et huius gratia non liberos, sed seruos per apostrophen alloquutus est.
units.tr: 1 He gives the reason why one who was called a slave ought not be anxious, so that he should not even seek freedom in Christ's name, even if it could be obtained. Why? Because clearly he has already obtained in Christ a freedom greater than external freedom. This is what he says: "For he who in the Lord was called a slave is the Lord's freedman. Again, he who was called free in the Lord is Christ's slave." So he has no reason to glory in the freeborn status of the flesh. Here he did not say "you were called free, let it not concern you," for freedmen did not face the same temptation of contempt and abjection that slaves did. Further, they were not compelled to have dealings with unbelieving masters, as slaves were. It was fitting, therefore, that he should strengthen slaves rather than freedmen, and for this reason he addressed slaves, not freemen, by apostrophe.

units.la: Est itaque quisque Christianus, quacunque conditione sit, & seruus & libertus. Libertus ob id, quod à seruitute peccati liberatus & manumissus est per spiritum Christi. Sic Ioh. 8. Si uos filius liberauerit, uere liberi eritis. Seruus uero, propter obedientiam domino debitam, in quam omnes sanguine Christi redempti sumus. Neque enim ita facti sumus liberi à iugo peccati, ut nostri postea iuris simus, sed ut ei seruiamus, per quem sumus à tyrannide peccati liberati. Sic Rom. 6. Nunc uero manumissi à peccato, serui facti sumus Deo. Habent ista consolationem, ut nemo seruus molestè ferat carnalem seruitutem, cum sciat illam non nocere, nec impedire à uera nobilitate & libertate spiritus quæ est per Christum, sed eam demum fugiendam esse seruitute, quæ peccati, & apprehendendà libertate quæ spiritus est.
units.tr: Thus every Christian, whatever his condition, is both a slave and a freedman: a freedman because he has been freed and manumitted from the slavery of sin through the Spirit of Christ (so John 8: "If the Son shall make you free, you will be truly free"); a slave because of the obedience owed to the Lord, into which all of us were redeemed by the blood of Christ. For we have not been freed from the yoke of sin so that we would be our own masters afterwards, but so that we serve him through whom we were freed from the tyranny of sin (so Rom. 6: "But now, having been made free from sin, you have become slaves to God"). These words offer consolation, so that no slave should bear carnal slavery with resentment, since he knows it does not harm or hinder the true nobility and freedom of the spirit, which is through Christ. Rather, the slavery of sin is to be fled, and the freedom of the spirit is to be grasped.

units.la: 2 Video & hoc loco aliam à quibusdam adferri sententiam, talem uidelicet, quæ non loquatur de seruitute Christi, neque de libertate quæ per Christum est, sed de seculari utraque, hoc sensu. Etenim qui in domino uocatus est seruus, libertus domini est, id est, tantundem ualet apud dominum, ac si libertus esset. Et rursus qui liber uocatus fuit, seruus est Christi, hoc est, non maiori reputatione apud Christum est, quàm si seruus uocatus esset. Vt enim circumcisio nihil est, & præputium nihil est, ita certè nec seruitus quicquam est, nec libertas corà domino. Sic Gal. 3. dicit: Non est Iudæus neque Græcus, non est seruus neque liber, non est masculus aut fœmina. Omnes enim uos unus estis in Christo Iesu. Quomodo non sunt serui, non liberi, non Iudæi, non Græci, non mares, nec fœminæ in Christo, cum istæ conditiones per Christi fidem Christianis non sint adeptæ? Ita scilicet, quod nec impediunt quicquam nec promouent in Christo. Non hoc quæritur, ut uel seruus sit quisquam uel liber, uel masculus uel fœmina, ad hoc, ut Christianus sit, cum omnes isti eandem habeant apud Christum, quæ fidei est, prærogatiuam. Vt uerum fatear, ista sententia uidetur esse simplicior & germanior, licet prior tradaturferè ab omnibus. Verùm nihil est periculi, utram capiamus. Nam ambæ ueræ sunt & piæ.
units.tr: 2 I see also another view put forward by some, which speaks not of the slavery of Christ nor of the freedom that is through Christ, but of both in the worldly sense. The sense is this: "For he who in the Lord was called a slave is the Lord's freedman," that is, he counts for as much before the Lord as if he were a freedman. And again, "he who was called free is Christ's slave," that is, he is held in no greater esteem before Christ than if he had been called a slave. For as circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, so neither slavery nor freedom counts for anything before the Lord. So Gal. 3: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus." How can there be no slaves, no free, no Jews, no Greeks, no males or females in Christ, when these conditions have not been abolished for Christians by faith in Christ? Clearly, in this way: they neither hinder nor advance anything in Christ. The question is not whether someone is a slave or free, male or female, in order to be a Christian, since all of these have the same privilege before Christ that belongs to faith. To tell the truth, this view seems simpler and more genuine, although the former is handed down by almost everyone. Yet there is no danger in whichever we take, for both are true and pious.

units.la: PRECIO empti fuistis, nolite fieri serui hominum.) Cur hoc dicit, cum homini seruire nihil impediat à regno Christi? De qua nâq; alia seruitute loquutus est, cum dixit: Seruus uocatus es? ne sit tibi curæ, quàm de ea qua homo seruit homini, fideli uel infideli? Et quid aliud plerosq; mouebat, ut putarint indignum Christi sanguine redemptos, seruire homini, quàm quod Christianos credebát Christi sanguine redemptos non hominibus sed Christo seruire debere? Quid est igitur quod idem & eadem ratione hic ponit Apostolus, cum supra diuersa tradiderit? An forsan quæ supra dixit, ad illos qui in seruitute cöstituti ad Christum uocabanturdixit, hoc uerò quod nunc scribit, ad eos scribit qui liberi uocati erant, ne se permitterent humanæ seruituti, propterea quod non dicit: Nolite esse, sed: Nolite fieri serui hominum?
units.tr: "You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men." Why does he say this, since serving a man does not hinder one from the kingdom of Christ? For about what other slavery was he speaking when he said, "you were called a slave, let it not concern you," than that in which a man serves a man, whether faithful or unbelieving? And what else moved most people to think it unworthy for those redeemed by Christ's blood to serve a man, than the belief that Christians redeemed by Christ's blood ought to serve not men but Christ? What, then, is it that the Apostle here sets out in the same way and for the same reason, when he has taught different things above? Perhaps what he said above he addressed to those who, being in slavery, were called to Christ; but what he now writes he writes to those who were called free, lest they yield themselves to human slavery. For he does not say "do not be," but "do not become slaves of men."

units.la: Ratio quam præmittit, dicés: Precio empti estis, talis est, ut non solum competat liberis sed & seruis. Deinde nō potest intelligi, quod dicit: Nolite fieri serui hominū, de terrena illa & seculari seruitute, de qua loquutus est hacte nus, nisi uelimus Apostolum sibijpsi contrarium reddere. Quid igitur dicit? Videbat alia quandam hominum seruitutem longè pericu losiorem. Ea erat, qua alius dicebat: Ego sum Pauli, ego sum Apollo, ego sum Cephæ. Aduersus illam eodem argumento & supra usus est, cum dixit: Nunquid Paulus pro uobis cruci fixus est? Item: Omnia uestra sunt, uos autē Christi. Repugnat itaq; hic captiuitati cōscien tiarum, admonetq; Christianos, ut nisi uelint precio quo empti sunt iniurij esse, nullius hominis imperio, p sua libidine in ecclesia quidquis præcipientis, sese subdant, sed in libertate
units.tr: The reason he puts first, "you were bought with a price", applies not only to free people but also to slaves. Next, the words "do not become slaves of men" cannot be understood of that earthly and secular slavery he has been speaking of so far, unless we want the Apostle to contradict himself. What then does he mean? He saw another, far more dangerous slavery of men. This was the one by which one said, "I am of Paul, I am of Apollos, I am of Cephas." Against that he used the same argument above too, when he said, "Was Paul crucified for you?" Likewise: "All things are yours, but you are Christ's." So here he opposes the captivity of consciences and admonishes Christians that, unless they wish to be unfaithful to the price by which they were bought, they should not submit to the command of anyone in the Church who prescribes whatever he likes out of his own lust, but should remain in the liberty

units.la: {k} quam à Christo redemptore acceperunt, manent, & nullius imperium in rebus fidei, nisi unius redemptoris Christi, agnoscant. Metuebat illis iugum circumcisionis, metuebat magistros philosophiae. Nam utrunque Corinthijs periculum erat. Ita & Galatis scripsit, in libertate qua Christus nos liberauit state, & ne rursus iugo seruitutis implicemini. Astipulatur isti sententiae & Ambrosius. Nam is hominum seruos esse dicit, qui humanis se superstitionibus subijciunt.
units.tr: which they received from Christ the Redeemer, and acknowledge no one's authority in matters of faith except that of Christ the Redeemer alone. He feared for them the yoke of circumcision; he feared the teachers of philosophy, for both were a danger to the Corinthians. So too he wrote to the Galatians: "Stand in the liberty with which Christ has made us free, and do not be entangled again in the yoke of slavery." Ambrose agrees with this opinion, for he says that those are slaves of men who subject themselves to human superstitions.

units.la: Hinc tamen nemo putet authoritatem ministrorum Christi labefactari, de quibus dictum est. Qui vos audit, me audit. Nam licet illis obtemperemus, ubi non sua somnia, sed Christi verbum proponunt, non tamen illis, sed Christo obtemperamus. Vt enim illi non sunt magistri nostri, sed Christi discipuli dum non suam nobis sententiam, sed Christi praedicant, ita nos non sumus illorum serui sed Christi, dum non illorum sed Christi praeceptis obedimus.
units.tr: Yet let no one think from this that the authority of Christ's ministers is weakened, of whom it was said, "He who hears you hears me." For although we obey them when they set forth not their own dreams but Christ's word, we obey not them but Christ. Just as they are not our teachers but Christ's disciples while they preach not their own opinion but Christ's, so we are not their slaves but Christ's, while we obey not their commands but Christ's.

units.la: VNVS QVISQVE in eo in quo uocatus fuit, fratres, maneat apud Deum.) Iam tertio propositionem hac repetit absq; dubio, quod uideretur necessario propter turbatores inculcanda. Repetit autem eam no fine emphasi animi fideliter ista tanquam fratribus praecipientis cum fratres eos appellat. Deinde, & limitationem addit cum dicit, apud Deum: hoc est, quatenus cum Deo fieri licet, quatenus per fidem Deo debita fieri potest, maneat quisque in quo uocatus fuit. Et ista limitatio applicanda est omnibus in uniuersum statibus, ne putet sibi quisquam ita obediendum esse hominibus, ut voluntati Dei repugnet. Oportet Deo plus obedire quam hominibus. Per se contra Deum non est esse coniugem, esse seruum, esse circumcisum, esse praeputiatum, &c. ut in his statibus nihil impediat esse Christianum. Proinde non est necesse ut mutetur ac turbetur, modo salua permaneat fides in Christum, modo nihil praecipiatur quod sit contra Deum. Quod si casus accidat, ut aut relinquendus sit status in quo uocatus est quisquam, aut peccandum erga Christi fidem, ibi non manendum sed cedendum est, etiamsi sit a legitimo coniuge, nedum hero aliquo cedendum.
units.tr: LET EACH ONE remain in the condition in which he was called, brothers, before God. Now for the third time he repeats this proposition, undoubtedly because it seemed necessary to press it on account of the troublemakers. He repeats it not without earnest feeling, faithfully, as one giving instruction to brothers when he calls them brothers. Then he adds a qualification when he says "before God": that is, insofar as it can be done with God, insofar as it can be done consistently with the faith owed to God, let each remain in the condition in which he was called. This qualification must be applied to all states of life in general, lest anyone think he must obey men in a way that opposes the will of God. We ought to obey God rather than men. Being a wife, being a slave, being circumcised, being uncircumcised, and so on, is not in itself against God, so none of these states prevents a person from being a Christian. Therefore there is no need for anyone to be changed and disturbed, provided that faith in Christ remains intact and nothing is commanded that is contrary to God. But if a case arises in which either the state in which someone was called must be abandoned or faith in Christ must be violated, then one must not remain but must yield, even if it means leaving a lawful spouse, much less should one yield to any master.

units.la: De uirginibus autem praeceptum domini non habeo, consilium autem do, tanquam misericordiam consequutus a domino in hoc ut sim fidelis.
units.tr: Concerning virgins, however, I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful.

units.la: Hoc tertium membrum est praesentis capitis, quo de uirginitate quid sentiendum sit ponit. Dat autem illi in summa duo. Primum, esse liberam & nemini praeceptam. Deinde, esse utilem & commodam, certa de causa.
units.tr: This is the third part of the present chapter, in which he sets out what is to be thought about virginity. He gives two main points in summary. First, that it is free and not prescribed to anyone. Second, that it is useful and advantageous, for a certain reason.

units.la: DE uirginibus autem praeceptum domini non habeo.) Praeceptum domini non habere, aut idem est atq; dominum uirginitatem non praecepisse, uel Apostolo nihil de ea mandasse. Est autem utrunque uerum. Nam neq; legem de uirginitate ipse tulit dominus, neque Apostolo quicquam potestatis dedit, illam praecipiendi, id quod no frustra admoneo. Mihi plane uidetur Apostolus non solum hoc dicere quod ipse dominus nusquam de uirginitate praeceperit, sed quod & nihil a domino sibi de illa sit mandatum, unde a quoquam illam exigendi potestatem habeat.
units.tr: "Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord." To have no command of the Lord is either the same as saying that the Lord did not command virginity, or that he gave the Apostle no instruction about it. Both are true. For the Lord himself did not enact a law about virginity, nor did he give the Apostle any power to command it, which I note not without reason. It seems plain to me that the Apostle says not only that the Lord himself nowhere commanded virginity, but also that nothing was enjoined on him by the Lord about it, from which he might have the power of demanding it from anyone.

units.la: Quid est autem, quod non aeque de coniugio dixit, se non habere domini praeceptum, sicut de uirginitate? An illud praeceptum est? Nequaquam. Alioqui male consuleret uirginitatem, nec uirginitas esset libera. Liberam autem eam esse ostendit, cum se nullum de ea dicit habere praeceptum. Tantundem enim est, ac si dixisset: Virginitas libera est, ubi dicit: De uirginibus praeceptum domini non habeo. Id autem quod liberum est, ita liberum est, ut uel seruari uel omitti possit. Non est igitur coniugium praeceptu si libera est uirginitas. Cur iam de illo no hoc dicit, quod de uirginitate dicit? Quia uidelicet occurrendum erat hypocrisi quorundam, qui uirginitatis professione iam tum necessariam facere conabantur, & coniugium tanquam rem immundam explodebant. Ideo non erat opus dicere: De coniugio praeceptum domini non habeo, quia nemo illud necessarium faciebat, de uirginitate uero necessarium erat admonere, quod nihil esset a Deo de illa praeceptum. Ambrosius arbitratur, quod de hac quoq; Apostolo scripserint Corinthij. Videlicet cordatiores, qui fidelium conscientijs apostolica sententia consultum cupiebant.
units.tr: But why did he not say of marriage, as he did of virginity, that he has no command of the Lord? Is there a command about it? By no means. Otherwise he would be counselling virginity badly, and virginity would not be free. He shows that it is free when he says he has no command about it, for it is as if he had said, "Virginity is free," when he says, "Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord." What is free is so free that it can either be kept or omitted. So marriage is not commanded if virginity is free. Why then does he not say of marriage what he says of virginity? Evidently because he had to meet the hypocrisy of certain people who were already then trying to make virginity a necessity through profession, and who spurned marriage as an unclean thing. Therefore there was no need to say, "Concerning marriage I have no command of the Lord," since no one was making it necessary; but concerning virginity it was necessary to warn that nothing had been commanded about it by God. Ambrose thinks the Corinthians wrote about this to the Apostle too, clearly the more discerning ones, who wanted the consciences of the faithful to be guided by the apostolic opinion.

units.la: CONSILIVM autem do.) Graece est γνώμην δὲ δίδωμι. Id est, sententiam uero meam uidelicet do. Hoc est, quid mihi hac in re faciendum esse uideatur, oltendo. Consilium uero dare, nihil est aliud, quam quid sentias oltendere. Proinde recte γνώμη pro consilio ponitur. Est autem id discriminis inter praeceptum & consilium, ut in praecepto sit faciendi quod mandatur necessitas, nisi uelis contra Deum peccare, in consilio uero eius quod consulitur libertas, ut id absque ulla peccati conscientia libere possis uel facere uel omittere. Ista libertas merito seruatur in consilijs quae ab hominibus dantur, etiam apostolis. Quare? Quia non quod homo sanctus, sed quod Deus sentit, tale est, ut sine peccato omitti nequeat. Nō enim sumus serui hominum, sed Dei, nec ligat nos uoluntas sanctorum, sed domini.
units.tr: "But I give counsel." The Greek is γνώμην δὲ δίδωμι [gnōmēn de didōmi], that is, "but I give my opinion." That is, I show what seems to me must be done in this matter. To give counsel is nothing other than to show what you think, so γνώμη is rightly used for counsel. There is this difference between command and counsel: in a command there is the necessity of doing what is enjoined, unless you want to sin against God; in counsel there is the freedom of what is advised, so that you may freely either do or omit it without any consciousness of sin. This freedom is rightly kept in counsels given by men, even by apostles. Why? Because what a holy man thinks is not such that it cannot be omitted without sin, but what God thinks is. For we are not slaves of men but of God, nor does the will of the saints bind us, but the Lord's.

units.la: Notandum est hic, quae sit Apostoli modestia. Postquam dixit se non habere de uirginitate domini praeceptum, non audet subijcere, ego uero authoritate qua fungor, uobis mando, ut uirginitatem profiteamini, id quod Romani episcopi postea facere coeperunt, tametsi negent se uirginitatem praecepisse. Quid aliud autem faciunt, ubi ab illis qui ordinandi sunt in ministerium Christi, abiurationem matrimonij, & continentiae professionem exigunt? Virginitatem non extorquent nisi a clericis. Atqui Apostolus in toto isto tractatu nihil discriminat inter clericum & no clericum. Neque enim aliquid discriminis est inter ministros ecclesiæ & reliquos Christianos, quod ad uirginitatem uel matrimoniū attinet. Non enim iunt isti status de substantia uel Christianismi, uel ministerij ecclesiastici. Alioqui prorsus de hoc meminissFet Apostolus. Quomodo autem meminissFet, quū tam ministris quàm reliquis Christianis nihil præcepti de uirginitate datū sit diuinitus? Cur tantum consulit uulgo Christianorum uirginitatem, & nō præcipit? Quia non habet de ea aliquod domini præceptum. Si hic ualet ut non liceat Apostolo præcipere quod Deus non præcepit, cur non & in clericis ualet, cum neq; illis præcepta sit à Deo uirginitas? An Apostolus clericorum fuit dominus, & non Christianorum? Certè nec clerico rum. At quid opus hac de re uerba facere? Res ipsa declarat, Satanam non spectasse uirginitatem, sed sub specie uirginitatis quæsisse coniugij abiurationem & abominationem, ut locus esset omnis generis immundiciæ.
units.tr: Here one should note the modesty of the Apostle. After saying he has no command of the Lord about virginity, he does not dare to add, "But I, by the authority I exercise, command you to profess virginity." The Roman bishops later began to do this, although they deny that they have commanded virginity. What else do they do when they demand from those who are to be ordained to the ministry of Christ an abjuration of marriage and a profession of continence? They extort virginity only from clergy. Yet the Apostle, in this whole treatise, makes no distinction between cleric and non-cleric. For there is no difference between the ministers of the Church and the rest of Christians as far as virginity or marriage is concerned. These states belong neither to the substance of Christianity nor to the ecclesiastical ministry. Otherwise the Apostle would certainly have mentioned it. But how would he have mentioned it, since no command about virginity was given by God to ministers any more than to the rest of Christians?
