Why does he counsel the common run of Christians about virginity and not command it? Because he has no command of the Lord about it. If it holds that the Apostle may not command what God has not commanded, why would it not also hold for clerics, since virginity was not commanded by God to them either? Was the Apostle the lord of clerics and not of Christians? Certainly not of clerics either. But why make a fuss about this matter? The thing itself shows that Satan was not looking at virginity, but under its appearance sought the abjuration and abomination of marriage, so that there might be room for every kind of uncleanness.

units.la: Eccius in suis locis, de cœlibatu (egregius uidelicet cœlibatus commendator) hac Apostoli sententiam, tanquam uirginitatis laudem contra nos citat ad hunc modum. Cum in superiori puncto Christus laudauerit se castrantes (quod non est uerum sensu Eccij) propter regnum Dei, & Paulus uirgines, sequitur improbantes cœlibatum, Christum & Paulum conculcare. Hæc ille. Quis autè improbat uirginitatem? Necesitatem illius impugnamus, utilitatem commendamus, sequuti Apostolu. Paulus laudauit uirgines. Bene. Faciamus hoc utrinq;. Sed non ita, ut necessariam faciamus uirginitatem, non alio sensu, quàm quo Apostolus hoc fecit, nec ita ut cuiquá laqueu iniciamus, & coniugij remedium, si illo opus sit amputemus. Isti uirginitatis prædicatores, quod Deus non præcepit uerbis extollunt, & quod prohibuit opere faciunt. Nouū est prorsus religionis genus, ut quidā Saluianus Massiliensis episcopus scripsit, licita non faciunt & illicita committunt. Temperant à concubitu, (quamuis nec hoc faciant, nisi à licito) & non temperàt à rapina. Quid agis stulta persuasio? Peccata interdixit Deus, nō Matrimonia. Non conueniūt uestris studijs facta uestra. Non debetis esse amici criminum, qui dicitis uos esse effectores uirtutum. Præposterum est quod agitis, non est couuersio sed auersio, qui iampridem, ut fama est, opus honesti matrimonij reliquistis, tandem à scelere cessate. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Eck, in his places on celibacy (an outstanding commender of celibacy, to be sure), cites this sentence of the Apostle against us, as praise of virginity, in the following way. Since in the previous point Christ praised those who castrate themselves for the sake of the kingdom of God (which is not true in Eck's sense), and Paul praised virgins, it follows that those who disapprove of celibacy trample underfoot Christ and Paul. So he says. But who disapproves of virginity? We attack its necessity, we commend its usefulness, following the Apostle. Paul praised virgins. Good. Let us do this on both sides. But not in such a way as to make virginity necessary, not in any sense other than that in which the Apostle did it, nor so as to throw a noose around anyone and cut away the remedy of marriage, if there is need of it. These preachers of virginity extol in words what God did not command, and in deed they do what He forbade. It is a wholly new kind of religion, as Salvian, bishop of Marseilles, has written: they do not do what is permitted and they commit what is forbidden. They abstain from intercourse (although they do not even do this, except from what is lawful), and they do not abstain from robbery. What are you doing, foolish persuasion? God forbade sins, not marriages. Your deeds do not agree with your zeal. You ought not to be friends of crimes, you who say that you are the authors of virtues. What you do is perverse; it is not conversion but aversion. You who long ago, as rumour has it, abandoned the honourable estate of marriage, at last cease from your wickedness. So he says.

units.la: TANQVAM misericordiā consequutus à domino ut sim fidelis.) Particulā istam absq; dubio hoc nomine inseruit ut consilio suo fidem faceret. Solent enim eorū consilia plus mouere, qui fideliter consulunt. Et ideo illud, ut sim fidelis, intelligo cum Ambrosio de ea fidelitate, qua salubriter ubi opus est cōsulitur. Quanquam Hieronymus refert ad fidem, qua Christi seruitio fideliter incubebat, uidelicet hoc sensu. Consulo uirginitatem, tàquam per misericordiam Dei, donum illius consequu.
units.tr: AS ONE WHO HAS OBTAINED MERCY FROM THE LORD TO BE FAITHFUL. Without doubt he inserted this little phrase for this reason, that he might make his counsel credible. For the counsels of those who give advice faithfully usually carry more weight. And so I understand "that I might be faithful" with Ambrose, of that faithfulness by which advice is given wholesomely where it is needed. Although Jerome refers it to the faith by which he devoted himself faithfully to the service of Christ, namely in this sense: I counsel virginity, as one who has obtained its gift through the mercy of God, so that, freed from the burden of marriage, I may serve Christ faithfully in his ministry.

units.la: A tus, ad hoc, ut Christo in illius ministerio, coniugij molestia liberatus, fideliter seruiam. Itaq; quod dicit tanquam misericordiam consequutus, bifariam exponitur. Vno modo, ut per misericordiam, donū uirginitatis intelligamus, quasi suo exemplo Apostolus ad illā reliquos alliciat, & consilio suo fidem faciat. Altero, ut per misericordiam non uirginitatis sed fidelitatis, hoc est, animi fidelis & quibusuis beneuolētis donum exponamus. Et hæc posterior sententia mihi potior esse uidetur. Quanquam enim certum sit, donum uirginitatis magnum esse bonum, & misericordiæ Dei beneficium (attamen non ita, ut coniugij molestia irę Dei deputetur) illud tamen incertum est, quod Paulus suo exemplo hic uirginitatem suadeat cum uerosimilius sit coniugem illum fuisse, quàm uirginem.
units.tr: Therefore, that he says "as one who has obtained mercy" is explained in two ways. In one way, we understand the gift of virginity by "mercy," as if the Apostle, by his own example, were drawing the rest to it, and making his counsel credible. In the other way, we explain "mercy" not of virginity but of faithfulness, that is, of a faithful disposition of mind and of the gift of any kindly disposition. And this latter opinion seems to me the stronger. For although it is certain that the gift of virginity is a great good and a benefit of the mercy of God (yet not in such a way that the burden of marriage is reckoned as the anger of God), it is nevertheless uncertain that Paul here urges virginity by his own example, since it is more likely that he was a married man than a virgin.

units.la: Videtur autem Apostolus, quicquid misericordiæ diuinitus accepit, sentire ad hoc se accepisse, ut prosit fidelibus Christi. Hic animi fidelis affectus isto Pauli exemplo debebat omnibus Christi ministris summopere commendatus esse. Faceret enim plurimum ad hoc, ne putarent se fidelium cōstitutos esse dominos, sed potius ad ædificationem ministros & consiliarios. Deinde & fidelium animos huc permoueret, ut maiore promptitudine & alacritate, si quid illis consuleretur, obsequundarent. Nunc autem ubi malunt irę Dei quàm misericordiæ ministri esse, & quicquid possunt non ipsi solum, sed & auditores ac subditi, ad hoc unum referre, ut sint domini & magistri in ecclesia, ut non referunt spiritum Apostolicum, ita non inueniunt iustam ac spontaneam in ijs quæ statuunt obedientiam.
units.tr: Moreover, the Apostle seems to think that whatever mercy he received from God, he received for this purpose, that it might profit the faithful of Christ. This disposition of a faithful mind ought to have been most strongly commended to all ministers of Christ by this example of Paul. For it would greatly contribute to this, that they should not think themselves appointed lords of the faithful, but rather ministers and counsellors for their building up. Then, too, it would move the minds of the faithful to this, that they might obey with greater readiness and eagerness whatever is advised for them. But now, when they prefer to be ministers of the anger of God rather than of its mercy, and when they refer whatever they can do, not only themselves but also their hearers and subjects, to this one end, that they should be lords and masters in the Church, then, since they do not reflect the Apostolic spirit, they do not find a just and willing obedience in those things which they decree.

units.la: Simul quoq; notādum est, ubicunq; fuerint reperti fideles in domino ecclesiæ ministri, hoc est, qui syncero erga ecclesiam affectu, quæcunque fidelibus commoda sunt ac salutaria, consulunt, beneficium illos referre misericordiæ Dei erga ecclesiam. Et uicisim sicubi infideles fuerint ministri, apertū indicium esse iræ Dei aduersus ecclesiam. Reipsa nanq; fides ministri magis ob id à Deo datur, ut ædificetur ecclesia, quàm ut bene sit ministro. Et hinc est, quod suprà dixit: Omnia uestra sunt, siue Paulus, siue Apollo, &c.
units.tr: At the same time, it must also be noted that wherever faithful ministers of the Church in the Lord have been found, that is, men who with a sincere affection towards the Church advise whatever is convenient and wholesome for the faithful, this benefit is to be referred to the mercy of God towards the Church. And conversely, wherever ministers have been unfaithful, it is a plain sign of the anger of God against the Church. For indeed the faithfulness of a minister is given by God rather for the building up of the Church than for the good of the minister. And hence it is that he said above: All things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos, etc.

units.la: Vtitur Augustinus præsenti particula in disputatione aduersus Pelagianos, epistola 107. ad Vitalem Carthaginensem. Item Retractationū libro primo, capite 23. ad hoc ut doceat & euincat fidem esse donum miserentis Dei. Negabant enim hoc illi, afferentes in nostra situm esse potestate & uoluntatis arbitrio Euangelio credere uel non credere. Notat itaq; hoc loco, quod non dicit Apostolus, tanquam misericordiam cōsequutus, quia fidelis eram, sed ut fidelis essem, id est, ut relicta incredulitate eam fidem apprehenderem, quam antea impugnaueram. Et hinc colligit, misericordiam Dei etiam infideli impendi ad hoc, ut fidelis fiat. Verum est omnino & pium quod efficere conatur natur, attamen de hac fide, non loquitur hoc loco Apostolus.
units.tr: Augustine uses the present particle in his disputation against the Pelagians, in letter 107 to Vitalis of Carthage, and likewise in the first book of the Retractations, chapter 23, to teach and prove that faith is a gift of the God who shows mercy. For they denied this, asserting that it lies in our power and in the free choice of the will to believe or not to believe the Gospel. He therefore notes in this place that the Apostle does not say "as one who has obtained mercy, because I was faithful," but "that I might be faithful," that is, that, having abandoned unbelief, I might lay hold of that faith which I had previously assailed. And from this he gathers that the mercy of God is bestowed even on an unbeliever, so that he may become faithful. It is entirely true and pious what he tries to establish, but the Apostle does not here speak of this faith.

units.la: Arbitror igitur hoc bonum esse, propter praesentem necessitatem. Nam bonum est homini sic esse.
units.tr: I think, therefore, that this is good, on account of the present necessity. For it is good for a man to be so.

units.la: Verbum arbitrandi in literis apostolicis non est idem quod verbum opinandi, cui nihil incertitudinis inesse videtur. Certè bonum est quod consulit. Addit vero rationem. Nam alioqui videretur divinae repugnare sententiae qua Deus dixisse legitur: Non est bonum hominem esse solum, si simpliciter bonum esse diceret: Propter praesentem inquit necessitatem. Quae est ista necessitas? Fere omnes intelligunt molestias huius status, & curas huius vitae. Ambrosius nominatim ponit aerumnas partus, & orbitates liberorum. Sane innumera est coniugij incommoditas & multis molestijs semel liberatus est quisquis illo abstinet. At meo iudicio de huius generis molestijs, quae Christianis non sunt peculiares, sed cum omnibus infidelibus Iudaeis & Graecis in matrimonio constitutis communes, quas & Romanus ille Metellus vidit, non loquitur hic Apostolus, sed de tali quadam necessitate, quae Christianos & peculiariter premebat, & praesentum urgebat, cum dicit: Propter instantem necessitatem. Ea erat Christiani nominis persequutio qua coniuges separabantur, liberis & maritis spoliabantur, & ad defectionem à fide Christi propter coniugalem amorem & affectum erga liberos omnium fortissimum solicitabantur. Nisi enim maior esset molestia coniugū ubi calamitas persequutionis grassatur, nō dixisset Christus, uae prægnantibus in illa die.
units.tr: The verb "to think" (arbitror) in the apostolic writings does not mean the same as "to suppose" (opinor), which seems to carry no uncertainty. Certainly it is a good thing that he advises. But he adds a reason. Otherwise it would seem to contradict the divine sentence in which God is read to have said: "It is not good for man to be alone." If he were saying simply that it is good, he would not add "on account of the present necessity." What is that necessity? Nearly everyone understands the troubles of this state and the cares of this life. Ambrose names specifically the hardships of childbirth and the loss of children. Certainly the discomforts of marriage are countless, and whoever abstains from it is freed at once from many troubles. But in my judgement the Apostle is not speaking here of this kind of trouble, which is not peculiar to Christians but is common to all unbelieving Jews and Greeks who are married, and which that Roman Metellus also saw. He is speaking of a certain necessity that pressed particularly upon Christians and was at hand, when he says "on account of the impending necessity." This was the persecution of the Christian name, by which spouses were separated, children and husbands were taken away, and people were urged to fall away from the faith of Christ through their most powerful feelings, conjugal love and affection for their children. Indeed, unless the trouble of spouses were greater where the calamity of persecution rages, Christ would not have said, "Woe to those who are with child in those days."

units.la: Et huc etiam facit, quod repetendo dicit: Nam bonum est homini sic esse. Non dicit: Nam Deo placitum est, sic esse, sed bonum, id est, commodum est homini sic esse. Ostendit se non loqui de dignitate aliqua virginitatis, qua coniugium coram Deo excellat, sed de commodi tate & utilitate eius, quam in praesenti necessitate, persequutionis homini adferat, ut hoc minus ad defectionem à Christi fide permoveatur, sed liberior sit ad quaeuis pro nomine illius ferenda discrimina.
units.tr: This also agrees with what he says by repeating: "For it is good for a man to be so." He does not say, "It is pleasing to God that it be so," but that it is good, that is, expedient for a man to be so. He shows that he is not speaking of any dignity of virginity by which it surpasses marriage before God, but of its convenience and usefulness, which in the present necessity of persecution it brings to a man, so that he may be less moved to fall away from the faith of Christ and may be freer to endure whatever dangers for his name.

units.la: Haec observata prosunt contra eorum superstitionem qui nescio quantum meriti per se tribuerunt virginitati coram Deo. Deinde & contra eos, qui propter corporales illas & generales coniugij molestias, putarunt Apostolum virginitatem suasisse fidelibus, cum ipsa doceat experientia, extra procellas persequutionis, ubi tranquillus est rerumpublicarum & Christianismi status, periculosiore esse virginitatis professionem, & ruinae propiorem, quàm statum coniugij.
units.tr: These observations are useful against the superstition of those who ascribe to virginity, I know not how much, merit in itself before God. They are also useful against those who, on account of those bodily and general discomforts of marriage, have thought that the Apostle advised virginity to the faithful. Yet experience itself teaches that, apart from the storms of persecution, where the state of commonwealths and of Christianity is calm, the profession of virginity is more dangerous and closer to ruin than the married state.

units.la: Isti homines, admiratores videlicet & nimij depraedicatores virginitatis, non observarunt quantum discriminis sit inter ea bona, quae vitijs opponuntur, & quorū studium & exercitium omnibus competit, & inter ea quae tempora sunt, & pro ratione ac varietate temporum vel usurpanda vel ponenda, atque ideo mox ubi audiunt laudari virginitatem ab Apostolo, ibi non animadvertentes quo scopo id fiat, usurpandam esse putant. Quod si passim & semper bonum est virginitatis studium, cur quesito nec à Deo nec ab Apostolo praeceptum est? An nō Dei est, quicquid omnibus bonum est, praecipere? Vtique. Non praecipit autè virginitatem. Quare? Quia commodaquidem est sed in tempore, sed quibusdam, non omnibus, & illius conatus quàm est comodus & utilis ijs quib. abstinendi facultas diuinitùs concessa est, tam est noxius & periculosus diuersis.
units.tr: Those men, admirers and excessive extollers of virginity, did not observe how great is the difference between those goods which are opposed to vices, whose pursuit and practice suit everyone, and those things which belong to times and are to be taken up or set aside according to the reason and variety of the times. Therefore, as soon as they hear virginity praised by the Apostle, not noticing for what purpose this is done, they think it is to be taken up. But if the pursuit of virginity is good everywhere and always, why is it not commanded by God or by the Apostle, when it is asked for? Is it not God's business to command whatever is good for everyone? Certainly. But he does not command virginity. Why? Because it is convenient, indeed, but for a time, and for some, not for all; and the attempt at it is as harmful and dangerous to others as it is convenient and useful to those to whom the ability to abstain has been granted by God.

units.la: Alligatus es uxori? Ne quaere solutionem. Solutus es ab uxore? Ne quaeras uxorem. Quod si duxeris uxorem, non peccasti. Etsi nupserit virgo, non peccavit. Attamen afflictionem in carne habituri sunt huiusmodi. Ego vero vobis parco.
units.tr: Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek a release. Are you loosed from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you have taken a wife, you have not sinned. And if a virgin has married, she has not sinned. Yet such people will have affliction in the flesh. But I spare you.

units.la: Redit ad cautionem pro sua prudentia. Timedum enim erat ne virginitatis consilio male intellecto, causam coniugij grauaret, ansamque daret coniugibus matrimonij pertasis, instituendi diuortium, & ijs qui extra coniugium sunt, conscientiam peccati generaret, si matrimonium contraheret. Ideo non contentus eo quod de virginibus nullum se domini praeceptum habere, sed consilium dare dixit, simpliciter ac manifeste utriusque & coniugij & virginitatis libertatem repetit, & sententiae suae rationem ponit.
units.tr: He returns to caution, according to his prudence. For it had to be feared that virginity, if the counsel were misunderstood, would weigh down the cause of marriage, and would give occasion to spouses weary of marriage to institute divorce, and would produce in those outside marriage a conscience of sin if they should contract it. Therefore, not content with saying that he had no command of the Lord concerning virgins but gave counsel, he plainly and openly repeats the freedom of both marriage and virginity and sets out the reason for his opinion.

units.la: ALLIGATVS es uxori? Coiugio tribuit alligationem. Ea est fidei obligatio, unde constat matrimonium, quae virum alligat uxori, & uicissim uxorem viro, ut neuter sui sit arbitrij. Huius alligationis gratia, qui carnis sectantur libidines ac promiscuam venerem amplectuntur, coniugium vitant, & concubinatum uagū ac liberum eligūt, qua nequitia praesertim notabiles sunt qui sacris sunt, ut videri volunt, initiati. Hos sectantur & nonnulli alij Epicurei, qui de coniugio amplectendo ne verbo quidem admoneri sustinent. At fit interea, ut dum honesto coiugij vinculo stringi nolunt, implicentur non solum scortorum, sed & Satanae laqueis, quibus ad omnis generis immunditiam captiui detinentur.
units.tr: ARE you bound to a wife? He attributes binding to marriage. This is the obligation of faith, from which marriage is constituted, which binds the husband to the wife and in turn the wife to the husband, so that neither is master of himself. On account of this bond, those who pursue the lusts of the flesh and embrace promiscuous love avoid marriage and choose a wandering and free concubinage. Those are notably wicked especially who are initiated, as they wish to appear, into sacred rites. Several other Epicureans follow them, who cannot bear to be admonished even by a word to embrace marriage. Yet meanwhile it happens that, while they refuse to be bound by the honourable bond of marriage, they become entangled not only in the snares of harlots but also in those of Satan, by which they are held captive to every kind of uncleanness.

units.la: NE quaere solutionem. Item: Ne quaere uxorem.) Ista non eadem ratione prohibentur. Prius enim non consilij sed praecepti uigo rem habet. Posterius uero non praecepti, sed consilij. Neque enim qui solutus est ita à quaerenda uxore arcetur, sicut ligatus à repudianda. Coelibatus licitus quidem est, sed non ita, ut ad illum aspirare liceat coniugibus, rupto matrimonij vinculo, quemadmodum relicto coelibatu, licitus est ad coniugium transitus.
units.tr: Do not seek a release. Likewise: do not seek a wife. These are not forbidden on the same ground. For the first has the force of a precept, not of counsel; the second is of counsel, not of precept. For a man who is loosed is not kept from seeking a wife in the same way as a man who is bound is kept from putting away a wife. Celibacy is lawful indeed, but not so that spouses may lawfully aspire to it by breaking the bond of marriage; just as, having left celibacy, the passage to marriage is lawful.

units.la: Et ob id subiugit. Quod si duxeris uxorem non peccasti. Etsi nupserit uirgo, nō peccauit. Non autem addit: Quod si quæsieris solutionem, non peccasti. Vide hic quis sit spiritus ille, qui quod Apostolus tam luculenter absque ullo discrimine de uirginibus & inconiugatis dixit: Videlicet, quod non peccent si nupserint, inuentis uotorum impedimentis, & spiritali matrimonij, quod cum Christo instituut retinaculis, irritum reddiderit. Tale est quod Theophylactus eximit ab hac sententia uirginem Deo dicatam & Christo nuptā, eo quod illa, si nubat, adulterium contra Christum inducat. Belli homines non animaduerterunt Christianos omnes Christo desponsatos esse, attamen externum hoc & corporale coniugiū spiritali illo nihil impediri. Nos relictis iittis nugis, audiamus quid Apostolus Christi dicat, & firmiter teneamus, non esse peccatum si uirgo nupserit. Quod si stultum aliquod uotū intercesit, urgente ustionis necessitate proijcia tur, tanquam quod ex Deo non sit, & agatur pœnitentia de stultitia, id est, temeritate uouendi quæ stultissima est, licet uirginitas, si ex dono Dei ad iustum finem tendat, suam utilitatem ac laudem habeat.
units.tr: And for this reason he adds: "But if you have taken a wife, you have not sinned. And if a virgin has married, she has not sinned." He does not add: "If you have sought a release, you have not sinned." See here what spirit it is that, because the Apostle said so plainly and without any distinction about virgins and the unmarried, that they do not sin if they marry, has invented impediments of vows and a spiritual marriage which they have made with Christ, as bonds, and has made them void. Such is what Theophylact takes out of this sentence, a virgin dedicated to God and wedded to Christ, on the ground that if she marries she brings adultery against Christ. Fine fellows, who did not notice that all Christians are betrothed to Christ, yet that this external and bodily marriage is in no way hindered by that spiritual one. Let us, leaving these trifles, hear what the Apostle says under Christ's direction, and hold firmly that it is no sin if a virgin marries. If some foolish vow has come in between, it should be cast aside, as not being from God, when the urgent necessity of burning desire presses, and one should repent of the folly, that is, of the rashness of vowing, which is most foolish, although virginity, if it is from God's gift and aims at a just end, has its own usefulness and praise.

units.la: ATTAMEN afflictionem in carne habituri sunt huiusmodi. Ego uero uobis parco.) Hæc est sententiæ Apostolicæ declaratio quare dixerit: Consilium autem do, & bonum est homini sic esse. Non dicit: Deo non placebunt huiusmodi, nihil coram Deo prærogatiuæ singularis habebunt, sed afflictionem in carne habituri sunt. At carne affligi non est obnoxium peccato. Non loquitur autem de alia carnis afflictione, quam de qua iam supra memiuit, instanti uidelicet necessitate persequutionum. Non quod qui extra coniugium erant, persequutionis fuerint expertes, sed quod expeditiores fuerint ad quæuis aduersa propter Christum ferenda.
units.tr: "Yet such people will have affliction in the flesh. But I spare you." This is the declaration of the Apostolic sentence explaining why he said: "But I give counsel, and it is good for a man to be so." He does not say that such people will not please God and will have no singular pre-eminence before God, but that they will have affliction in the flesh. Yet to be afflicted in the flesh is not liable to sin. He is not speaking, however, of any other affliction of the flesh than that which he has already mentioned above, namely the impending necessity of persecutions. Not that those who were outside marriage were free from persecution, but that they were more unencumbered for enduring whatever adversities on account of Christ.

units.la: EGO uero uobis parco.) Nimirum tanquam imbecillibus. Quasi dicat, Non audeo tantum mihi roboris de uobis polliceri, ut necessitatem istam constanter feratis, atque ideo rationem habens uestræ infirmitatis, optarim uos esse cœlibes ut hoc minus feredum sit rerum aduersarum. Quid hic dicunt, qui uirginitatis ac cœlibatus professionem tāquam rem arduam, singularis cuiusdam apud Deum meriti esse contendunt, propter nescio quam uitæ austeritatem? Si recte sentiunt, quid est quod Apostolus se isto cōsilio uirginitatis pacere dicit Corinthijs? Quis non uidet, plus uirtutis exigi ab ijs qui coniuges sunt, ut syncere Christo adhæreant, q̄ à uirginibus? Quis igno rat mollius & tranquillius uiuere cœlibes quā coniuges? Imo innumera cœlibum multitudo, hoc nomine, quicquid foris simulet, cœlibatum apprehendit, ut coniugalis status curas & infinitas molestias declinet. Proinde si quid austeriori ac molestiori uitæ debetur sin gularis præmij, coniugio debetur non cœliba-
units.tr: "But I spare you." Surely as to the feeble. As if he were saying: "I do not dare to promise so much strength from you that you would bear this necessity steadfastly; therefore, having regard to your weakness, I wish you to be unmarried, so that the burden of adverse things may be less." What do those say here who contend that the profession of virginity and celibacy is, as a difficult thing, of a singular merit before God, on account of I know not what austerity of life? If they think rightly, why does the Apostle say that he spares the Corinthians by this counsel of virginity? Who does not see that more virtue is required of those who are married, that they may cling sincerely to Christ, than of virgins? Who does not know that the unmarried live more softly and calmly than the married? Indeed, a countless multitude of the unmarried, whatever they may pretend outwardly, take up celibacy for this very reason, to escape the cares and endless troubles of the married state. Therefore, if any singular reward is owed to a more austere and troublesome life, it is owed to the married state, and not to celibacy. But it is not owed, because the eyes of God do not look to this, but to the sincerity of souls; whatever the kind of life of this state may be, provided only that it is not unlawful.

units.la: tui. Non debetur autem. Quia non hūc est respectus oculorum Dei, sed ad animorum syn- ceritatem, qualis qualis sit uitæ huius status, modo non illicitus. Apostolo nunquam in mentem venit quod quidam de uirginitatis, uel cœlibatus singulari coram Deo præmio & prærogatiua dciosi homines nō ex spiritu Dei sed humani cordis somnijs tradiderunt, sed pro suo ergafideles charitatis affectu, & fide erga Christum de tali statu humani genere aliquo cogitauit, in quo Christiani tutius in fide Christi consisterent, & pro nomine Christi illata aduersa commodius ac leuius ferret. Expendebat enim carnis ingenium mobile & inconstans, uidebat quotidie causam regni Christi uersari non inter angelos sed homines infirmos & flexibiles, atqi ideo cōsilia sua huc referebat omnia, ut minus esset scandalorum. Hoc scilicet est, quod dixit: Bonum est homini sic esse propter instantem necessitatem. Et tribulationem carnis habebunt huiusmodi. Ego autem uobis parco.
units.tr: ...celibacy. But it is not owed. For the eyes of God do not look to this, but to the sincerity of the heart, whatever the condition of life may be, provided only that it is not unlawful. It never came into the Apostle's mind what some men have handed down, that virginity or celibacy carries a special reward and privilege before God. Such men spoke from the dreams of the human heart rather than from the Spirit of God. Rather, out of his own faithful and loving affection and his faith in Christ, he thought of such a condition for humankind, one in which Christians might stand more securely in the faith of Christ and bear adversities endured for Christ's name more readily and lightly. For he weighed the fickle and inconstant nature of the flesh, and saw every day that the cause of Christ's kingdom lies not among angels but among weak and changeable men; therefore he referred all his counsels to this, so that there might be less occasion for offence. This is plainly what he said: "It is good for a man to be so, because of the present necessity. And those who are such will have tribulation in the flesh. But I spare you" (1 Cor. 7.26-28).

units.la: Cæterum illud dico, fratres, tempus contractum est, superest, ut qui habent uxores, sint tanquam non habeant, & qui plorant, tanquam non plorent, & qui gaudent tanquam non gaudeat, & qui emunt tanquam non possideant, & qui utuntur mundo hoc, tanquam non utantur. Præterit enim habitus mūdi huius.
units.tr: But this I say, brethren: the time is short. It remains that those who have wives be as though they had none; and those who weep, as though they wept not; and those who rejoice, as though they rejoiced not; and those who buy, as though they possessed not; and those who use this world, as though they used it not. For the fashion of this world passes away (1 Cor. 7.29-31).

units.la: In rebus licitis, duo principaliter sunt cauēda. Vnum, ne cum peccati conscientia, illis tanquam illicitis uel utamur uel abstineamus. De illo hactenus. Alterum ne illis ita afficiamur, ut quæ seriora sunt & præcipuē curanda negligamus. De isto nunc agit.
units.tr: In lawful things there are chiefly two matters to be guarded against. The first is that we not use them, or abstain from them, as though they were unlawful, with a guilty conscience. Of that much has been said so far. The second is that we not become so attached to them that we neglect the things which are weightier and especially to be cared for. It is this second point that he now deals with.

units.la: CÆTERVM illud dico fratres.) Non admodum refert, quo quisque statu sit, uel cœlebs uel coniunx, uel seruus uel liber, unde ea de re nihil potuit generaliter præcipere, nisi quatenus propter instatem necessitatem pro cuiusque dono bonum & commodum esse iu dicauit, sed id uero plurimum refert & omnes concernit quod nunc traditurus est. Tantundem significare uidetur quod dicit: Illud autem dico fratres, atque: Illud uero ab omnibus communiter & indiscriminatim exigo, quicquid sit cum ijs de quibus hactenus loquutus sum.
units.tr: "But this I say, brethren." It matters little what state each man is in, whether unmarried or married, slave or free, so the Apostle could not prescribe anything in general on that matter, except insofar as, because of the present necessity, he judged it good and advantageous for each according to his gift. But what he is now about to deliver matters greatly and concerns everyone. The phrase seems to mean the same as "But I say this, brethren," that is: "I require this of all of you in common and without distinction, whatever the case may be with those of whom I have spoken so far."

units.la: In illis enim non tantum est periculi, quantum hic est. Proinde utut illa habeant, quod iam admonituros sum, omnibus promiscue curandum est. Indicat itaque ista loquutione Apostolus, licet fideliter consuluerit de ēōs libatu propter instantem necessitatem ample stendo, maioris tamen momenti esse quod iam præcepturus est, & maiore cura huc elaborandum, ut rebus licitis temperanter utamur, quàm ut illis prorsus abstineamus. Est enim illud regno Christi ita commodum, ut minus sit tentationibus & periculo obnoxiū;
units.tr: For in those others there is not so much danger as there is here. Therefore, whatever their situation, what I am about to admonish must be attended to by all alike. By this phrasing the Apostle indicates that, although he faithfully advised about freedom from marriage, showing it to be on account of present necessity, what he is about to command is of greater moment, and greater care must be spent on it, namely that we use lawful things temperately rather than abstain from them altogether. For this is so advantageous to the kingdom of Christ that it is less exposed to temptations and danger.

units.la: Periculosum consilium est prorsus abstinere à coniugio nisi adsit continentiæ donum, con iugio uero temperanter uti, & uxorem habere tanquam non habeas, & utile est & securum. Deinde illius oppositum coiugium uidelicet, non solum licitum est, sed & ad uitandam scortationem utile remedium, istius uero & illicitum est, & regno Christi incommodum. Et peccat enim & ineptus est regno Dei, quis-quis uxore & rebus huius sæculi intemperan-tius afficitur.
units.tr: It is a dangerous counsel to abstain entirely from marriage unless the gift of continence is present; but to use marriage temperately, and to have a wife as though you had none, is both useful and safe. Then the opposite of this, namely marriage, is not only lawful but also a useful remedy for avoiding fornication; but the opposite of temperate use, that is, immoderate use, is both unlawful and harmful to the kingdom of Christ. For whoever is too intemperately attached to a wife and to the things of this age both sins and is unfit for the kingdom of God.

units.la: TEMPVS contractum est.) ὁ χρόνος συν-σαλμένος. συνεσταλμένον dicitur, quicquid abie-cta amplificatione ac dilatatione in arctum & angustum cogitur, ut citò finiatur. Ita mundi huius tempus, utut in se longum & satis prolixũ, in nouo testamento contractũ dicitur, eo quod omnium rerum finem citò fit adductu-rum. Pulchrè autè de temporis angustia sump-tum argumentum præmittit, ut animos fidelium à rebus citò perituris hoc facilius auocet.
units.tr: "The time is shortened." Greek ὁ χρόνος συνεσταλμένος [ho chronos synestalmenos]. Whatever is compressed into a narrow and small compass, with its amplification and expansion laid aside, so that it may soon be finished, is said to be "shortened." So the time of this world, though in itself long and rather extended, is said in the New Testament to be shortened, because it is about to bring all things to an end soon. He rightly sets out an argument drawn from the brevity of time, so that he may more easily turn the minds of believers away from things that will soon perish.

units.la: Ambrosius putat Apostolum hoc loco tem poris breuitatem non ita inducere, quod re-uera contractum sit noui testamenti tempus, cum longum sit, sed quod pro sua prudentia ita uoluerit fidelium mentes terrore ultimi iu dicij ad meliorem uitam impellere. Verũ meo iudicio non solum pium est Apostoli propositum & utile, sed & uerum quod tempus contractum esse dicit. Nam licet in se sit longum, respectu tamen sæculorum quę prolapsa sunt, contractum est, ac simile tempori usipertino, quo dies ad noctem uergit.
units.tr: Ambrose thinks that the Apostle does not introduce the brevity of time here in the sense that the time of the New Testament is really shortened, since it is long, but that by his prudence he wished to drive the minds of the faithful toward a better life through the terror of the last judgment. But in my judgment the Apostle's purpose is not only pious and useful but also true, when he says that time is shortened. For although it is long in itself, with respect to the ages that have already passed it is shortened, and it is like the evening time when the day turns toward night.

units.la: SVPEREST.) Τὸ λοιπὸν ἔσχον. Reliquũ est. Particula ista bifariam legitur. Vno modo, ut præcedentibus coniungatur hoc sensu. Illud autem dico fratres, Tempus deinceps contractũ est, ut τὸ λοιπὸν fit idè atq; deinceps, & uer-bum substãtiuum ἔστιν ad participium συνεσταλ-μένον referatur. Altero modo, ut legatur seor-sum, & applicetur non præcedentibus sed se-quentibus, ac doceat quid iam deinceps à fi-delibus fit curãdum. Priorem lectionem Am-brosius, posteriorem uero & uetus interpres & Erasmus sequuti sunt. Ego non uideo quid referat, utram lectionem amplectamur. Nam ita est contextus uerborum, ut utrouis modo legi possit. Nec in sensu multum est discrimi-nis, nisi quod prior lectio ulterius ac dein-ceps iam noui testamenti tempus cõtractum, posterior uero, eo quod tempus contractum fit, hoc deinceps curandum esse dicit, quod sta-tim subiungitur.
units.tr: "It remains." Greek Τὸ λοιπὸν ἔσχον [to loipon eschon]. The phrase is read in two ways. In one way it is joined to what precedes, in this sense: "But I say this, brethren: henceforth the time is shortened," so that τὸ λοιπὸν means the same as "henceforth," and the substantive verb ἔστιν is referred to the participle συνεσταλμένον. In the other way it is read separately and applied not to what precedes but to what follows, teaching what the faithful must now henceforth attend to. Ambrose followed the former reading, but the old translator and Erasmus followed the latter. I do not see what difference it makes which reading we embrace, for the wording is so arranged that it can be read in either way. Nor is there much difference in sense, except that the former reading says that henceforth the time of the New Testament is shortened, whereas the latter, since the time is shortened, says that this is what must henceforth be attended to, which is immediately added.

units.la: VT qui habent uxores, sint tanquam non habentes.) Cauenda est hic Hieronymi ex-positio, qui dicit Apostolum hoc loco cum o-mni intentione coniuges quoque hortari ad continentiam ut hoc amplius persuadeat in-nuptis, ne matrimonium contrahant. Vxo-rem habere tanquã non habeas, illi continen-tiam seruare est, & uxore uti, incontinentem esse. Quod si Apostolus usum uxoris uetat, quid est, quod suprà dixit: Vxor uiro debitam beneuolentiam reddat? Ergo sibijpsi contra-rius est. Absit. Habere tanquam non habeas, est corde non nimium affici. Theophylactus dicit, esse non omne studium circa nuptias & uxores consumere. Et Ambrosius, non debere ad generandum esse solicitum, neque ad usum ipsum deditum. Non dicit, non debere gene-rare, & uxore uti, sed non debere solicitum ad generandum, & ad usum uxoris deditum, id est, plus æquo propensum esse. Ergo non abs-tinentiam, sed temperatum uxoris usum exigit.
units.tr: "That those who have wives be as though they had none." Here we must beware of the exposition of Jerome, who says that the Apostle, with all his effort, here exhorts even married people to continence, so that he may persuade the unmarried more strongly not to contract marriage. To have a wife as though one had none, on this view, is to keep continence, and to use a wife is to be incontinent. But if the Apostle forbids the use of a wife, what is it that he said above: "Let the wife render to her husband the affection due to him"? Therefore he would be contrary to himself. Far be it. To have as though not having is to be not excessively affected in heart. Theophylact says it is not to spend all one's zeal on marriage and wives. And Ambrose says one should not be anxious about begetting children, nor given over to the very use. He does not say that one should not beget children and use one's wife, but that one should not be anxious about begetting, nor devoted to the use of a wife, that is, inclined more than is fitting. Therefore he requires not abstinence but a temperate use of the wife.

units.la: 1 Apostolo uxorem habere, non est cum u-xore tantum habitare, sed illa simul pro ratio-ne & lege coniugij uti. Alias habere uidetur uxorem qui illa non utitur, reuera autem non habet. Omnino ista, qui habet uxores, qui plo-rant, qui gaudent, qui emunt, qui utuntur hoc mundo, non ita sunt ab Apostolo dicta, ut ex-ternam aliquam sui speciem significent, sed simpliciter ipsarum rerum ueritatem expri-munt. Vt quemadmodum de uere ploranti-bus, uerè gaudentibus, uere emetibus, & mun-do isto uere utentibus, ita & de ijs qui uere u-xores habent, non solum habere uidentur, in-telligenda sint.
units.tr: 1 For the Apostle, to have a wife is not merely to live with a wife, but also to use her at the same time according to the reason and law of marriage. Otherwise, one who does not use her seems to have a wife but in truth does not have her. Altogether, these expressions, "those who have wives, those who weep, those who rejoice, those who buy, those who use this world," are not spoken by the Apostle so as to signify some outward appearance, but simply express the truth of the things themselves. Just as concerning those who truly weep, truly rejoice, truly buy, and truly use this world, so too concerning those who truly have wives, they must be understood not merely as seeming to have them.

units.la: 2 Deinde sicut illa, sint tanquam non flentes, non gaudetes, non posidentes, non utentes, non idem sunt, atq; non fleant, non gaudeant, non posideant, non utantur hoc mundo, sic & hoc, sint tanquam non habentes, non idem est atq; non habeant, uel non utatur. Vt enim usum mundi huius utentibus illo non aufert quod dicit, sint tanquam non utantur, ita nec uxoris usum habenti uxorem aufert, quod di-cit, sint tanquam non habentes.
units.tr: 2 Then, just as "as though they did not weep, did not rejoice, did not possess, did not use" are not the same as "did not weep, did not rejoice, did not possess, did not use this world," so also "as though they did not have" is not the same as "did not have" or "did not use." For just as saying "as though they did not use" does not take away the use of the world from those who use it, so saying "as though they did not have" does not take away the use of a wife from one who has a wife.

units.la: 3 Tertiò, & ipse scopus Apostoli non hoc exigit ut è coniugibus reddatur cœlibes, qua-si cœlibatus apud Deum aliquid habeat præ-rogatiuæ, sed ut animi fidelium liberi sint à re-rum huius sæculi nexibus, quo cõstantes Chri-sto adhærere queant: cuius & infrà admone-bit. Ad hunc fiuem non minus pertingit con-iunx, si coniuge legitime & temperanter uta-tur, quàm si illa prorsus careat, sicut & ij, qui mundo utuntur tanquam non utantur, æquè constantes in fide Christi perseuerant, atque ij, qui illo non utuntur. Quapropter ista Hiero-nymi expositio prorsus aliena est à mente A-postoli, & studiosè cauenda.
units.tr: 3 Thirdly, the Apostle's own purpose does not require that married people be made celibate, as though celibacy carried some special prerogative before God. His aim is that the hearts of the faithful be free from the entanglements of the things of this age, so that they may cling constantly to Christ, as he will also urge further on. A wife reaches this goal no less if her husband uses her lawfully and moderately than if he lacks her altogether, just as those who use the world as if they did not use it persevere as steadfastly in the faith of Christ as those who do not use it at all. Therefore Jerome's exposition is wholly foreign to the mind of the Apostle and must be carefully avoided.

units.la: Sed esto, habere tanquam non habeas, sit idem atque non admodum delectari aut assi-ci uxore quam habes. Quid igitur est, quod hic ipse Apostolus Ephes. 5. iubet, ut mariti u-xores diligant sicut sua ipsorum corpora, imò quod arctius est, sicut Christus dilexit eccle-siam suam? Hic iubet habere tanquam non ha-beas, illic præcipit ut diligas plurimum. Docet ne hoc loco ut maritus frigido sit erga uxo-re affectu? Cur ergo illic tanta dilectione pro-sequi iubet? Certè nostro tempore satius est admonere, ut mariti uxores suas diligant, po-steaq tam pauci sunt, qui syncero amore erga cõiuges suas afficiãtur. Habenda est igitur ra-
units.tr: But grant that "to have as if you did not have" means the same as not delighting in or being overly attached to the wife you have. What then of the command in this very Apostle, Ephesians 5, that husbands love their wives as their own bodies, or rather, what is more demanding still, as Christ loved his Church? Here he bids us have wives as if we did not have them; there he commands us to love them greatly. Does he teach in this passage that a husband should be cold in his affection for his wife? Why then does he bid him there to show such great love? Surely in our own time it is more useful to exhort husbands to love their wives, since there are so few who are moved by sincere love for their spouses. The circumstances of the time must therefore be taken into account.

units.la: ratio. tio temporum, vt si nimius regnet amoris affectus in coniugibus, vt periculum sit defectionis à fide Christi, sicut persequutionis tempore accidere solet, locū habeat ista Apostoli admonitio: si vero tempore pacis refrixerit coniugalis dilectio, admoneantur mariti vt vxores suas sicut sua ipsorū corpora, & sicut Christus ecclesiam suam dilexit, diligant. Nō quod inconstans debeat esse dilectio mariti erga vxorē suam, sed quod admonitio Apostoli prudenter pro ratione temporum & personarū instituenda sit, & qd carnalis & corruptus amoris affectus à coniugibus fidelibus abesse debeat.
units.tr: Thus, if in married couples an excessive affection for love should reign, so that there is danger of falling away from the faith of Christ, as tends to happen in a time of persecution, then this admonition of the Apostle has its place. But if in a time of peace conjugal love has grown cold, let husbands be admonished to love their wives as their own bodies and as Christ loved his Church. This is not because the love of a husband for his wife ought to be inconstant, but because the Apostle's admonition must be applied prudently, according to the circumstances of time and persons, and because a carnal and corrupt affection ought to be absent from faithful spouses.

units.la: ET qui plorant, tanquam non ploret.) Plorare malum non est, fleuit enim & Christus, mo dum vero excedere malū est. Animū enim declarat tribulationis impatientem, adeoq; & regno Christi ineptū. Intelligit autē eos, qui in hoc sæculo affliguntur, quos docet, vt moderate lugeant. Non exigit ne prorsus fleant, sed iubet, vt in rebus tristibus non admodū animo deijciantur, & tā non illarū gratia à Christi veritate deficiant, quàm si prosperè habeant. Nō reddit igitur Apostolus Stoicos ex Christianis qui sapienti & iusto homini non permittunt, vt sensu rerum tristium non omnino tangatur. Sic & alibi non vetat contristari, sed immodestiā lugendi, quæ gentium est, vetat.
units.tr: "And those who weep, as if they did not weep." To weep is not an evil, for Christ also wept; it is excessive mourning that is evil. For such excess shows a mind impatient of affliction, and so unfit for the kingdom of Christ. He means those who are afflicted in this age, and he teaches them to mourn with moderation. He does not require that they not weep at all, but bids them not to be cast down too far in sad circumstances, nor to fall away from the truth of Christ on account of them any more than if they were prosperous. Therefore the Apostle does not make Christians into Stoics, who do not allow the wise and righteous man to be touched at all by the feeling of sad events. Likewise elsewhere he does not forbid sorrow but forbids immoderate mourning, which belongs to the Gentiles.

units.la: ET qui gaudent, tanquam non gaudeant.) Per gaudentes intelligit eos, qui rebus in hac vita fruuntur secundis, quibus terrena ista ex animi sententia succedunt, qui sanitate corporis, rerum opulentia, pace & honore huius sæculi potiuntur. Non enim de ijs loquitur, qui in domino gaudent. Illorum nanq; gaudium haudquaquam cohiberet, & ad temperantiam restringeret, illis nunquam diceret, vt sint tanquam non gaudentes.
units.tr: "And those who rejoice, as if they did not rejoice." By those who rejoice he means those who enjoy the pleasant things of this life, to whom these earthly matters turn out as they wish, who possess bodily health, abundance of goods, peace and honour in this age. For he is not speaking of those who rejoice in the Lord. For their joy would by no means need to be restrained or brought back to moderation, and he would never tell them to be as if they did not rejoice.

units.la: Itaque & inter Christianos malum non est, rerum prosperitate potiri, & gaudere in rebus secundis. Humanum est, & ita habet naturæ nostræ ingenium, vt miserè affecti lugeamus ac ploremus, rursus in rebus prosperis constituti gaudeamus. Istam naturæ nostræ conditionem tam non damnat Apostolus, vt Romanorum duodecimo iubeat gaudere cum gaudentibus, & flere cum flentibus. Non est itaque Christiani hominis Stoicorum ἀπάθεια sectari, quam nuper Anabaptistæ inducere conati sunt. Verùm vtrobique seruare modestiam, & nec rebus tristibus deiici, nec secundis extolli, id demum est Christianæ professionis, & plus habet virtutis, quàm si per Stoicorum ἀπάθειαν trunci ac stipites redderemur, omnibus humanis affectibus exuti.
units.tr: Therefore, even among Christians, it is no evil to possess the prosperity of things and to rejoice in good fortune. It is human, and it is the nature of our disposition, that when we are miserably affected we grieve and weep, and again, when placed in prosperous circumstances, we rejoice. The Apostle so little condemns this condition of our nature that in Romans 12 he bids us rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep. Therefore it is not the part of a Christian man to pursue the Stoics' apatheia, which the Anabaptists lately tried to introduce. Rather, to keep moderation on both sides, neither cast down by sad things nor lifted up by pleasant ones, this is the mark of Christian profession, and it has more virtue than if we were made stumps and logs, stripped of all human affections through the Stoics' apatheia.

units.la: ET qui emunt, tanquam non possideant.) Per ementes aut negociatores, intelligit aut eos qui domos, prata, agros, villas, vineta, & id genus bona coemunt. Alioqui quis mortalium est, qui non aliquando emat, quæ necessaria habet ad vitæ sustentationem, victum videlicet & amictum? De talibus emptoribus loquitur, quibus periculum est, ne ijs quæ coemunt, nimium afficiantur, qui videlicet emendo opulenti redduntur. Hos monet, ne opibus cor apponant, sed sint tanquam non possidentes. Quadruplex periculum est in opibus.
units.tr: "And those who buy, as if they did not possess." By buyers or merchants he means those who purchase houses, meadows, fields, estates, vineyards, and goods of that kind. Otherwise, who among mortals does not sometimes buy the things he needs for sustaining life, that is, food and clothing? He speaks of such buyers as are in danger of becoming too attached to what they buy, and who by buying become wealthy. He warns these not to set their heart on riches, but to be as if they did not possess them. There is a fourfold danger in riches.

units.la: 1 Vnum, ne animos possidentium se inflatos reddant. Sic nos Germani dicimus: Guot macht muot.
units.tr: 1. One is that they make the minds of those who possess them puffed up. So we Germans say: "Guot macht muot" (goods make the mind proud).

units.la: 2 Alterum, ne corda illorum sibi deuincant, & fiduciam in se generent. Hinc Dauid admonet: Diuitiæ si affluant, nolite cor apponere.
units.tr: 2. The second is that they bind hearts to themselves and generate confidence in themselves. Hence David warns: "If riches flow in, do not set your heart upon them."

units.la: 3 Tertium, ne luxui materiam suppeditent, & occasionem præstent. Id notatur in diuitè Euangelico.
units.tr: 3. The third is that they supply material for luxury and provide an occasion for it. This is noted in the rich man of the Gospel.

units.la: 4 Quartum, ne cupiditatem ac sitim plura habendi incendat. Vnde ille dicit: Crescit amor nummi, quantum ipsa pecunia crescit.
units.tr: 4. The fourth is that they kindle a desire and thirst for having more. Hence that saying: "The love of money grows as the money itself grows."

units.la: His omnibus liber est animus Christiani hominis, qui ita emit ac diues est, ac si non possideat. Is nec insolescet, nec fiduciā in opes collocabit, nec luxuriabitur, neque plura appetet, sed ita dives erit, vt nihilo sit minus modestus, corde libero, temperans, & præsentibus bene contentus.
units.tr: The mind of a Christian man is free from all these things; he buys and is rich as if he did not possess. He will not grow proud, nor place his confidence in riches, nor indulge in luxury, nor desire more; rather he will be rich in such a way that he is none the less modest, with a free heart, temperate, and well content with what he has.

units.la: Illud, ὡς μὴ καταχρώμενοι, tanquam non possidentes ad verbum est, tanquam non retinentes, quasi auellere ob id cupiat animos eméntium à bonis terrenis, quod ea retinere nequeant, sed nolint velint, amittere cogantur. Cerè qui id cogitat, haud facilè cor suum opibus terrenis addicet.
units.tr: The phrase ὡς μὴ καταχρώμενοι [hōs mē katachrōmenoi], "as if not possessing," is in the Greek literally "as not holding back," as though he wanted to tear the minds of buyers away from earthly goods, because those who cannot keep them, but who are forced to lose them against their will, will not... Surely whoever thinks on this will not easily give his heart over to earthly riches.

units.la: ET qui vtuntur hoc mundo, tanquam non vtantur. Græcè est, ὡς μὴ καταχρώμενοι, tanquam non abutentes. Theophylactus notandum putat inter vsum & abusum discriminis aliquid hoc loco. Erasmus arbitratur hic nihil esse discriminis. Videtur hæc particula ita posita, vt quasi summam habeat eorum quæ recensere coeperat Apostolus. Longum enim erat omnia adnumerare, in quibus licet licitis, seruandus est modus, ne vel deijciamur animis vel inflemur, atque ob eam causam compendiose adiecit: Et qui vtuntur hoc mundo, tanquam non vtantur. Per mundum autem intelligit ea quæ in mundo sunt, quæ vitam hanc præsentem concernunt. Illis vti licet, sed moderate, & corde non affixo. De his autem non intelligit, quæ in mundo Iohannes vidit & cauere docuit, cum dixit: Nolite diligere mundum, neque ea quæ in mundo sunt. Si quis diligit mundum, charitas patris in eo non est. Quoniam omne quod est in mundo, concupiscentia carnis est, & concupiscentia oculorum, & superbia vitæ. Istis certè non licet vti. Imò abusus mundi in istis est, quem vetat & Paulus.
units.tr: "And those who use this world, as if they did not use it." In Greek it is ὡς μὴ καταχρώμενοι [hōs mē katachrōmenoi], "as not abusing." Theophylact thinks there is some difference here between use and abuse. Erasmus holds that there is no difference here. This particle seems to be placed so as to contain, as it were, the sum of the things the Apostle had begun to enumerate. For it would be long to list everything, in which, although things are lawful, a measure must be kept, lest we be either cast down in mind or puffed up. For this reason he added briefly: "and those who use this world, as if they did not use it." By the world he means the things that are in the world, which concern this present life. It is permitted to use these, but with moderation, and with the heart not fixed upon them. He does not mean those things in the world that John saw and taught us to avoid when he said: "Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life." Certainly it is not permitted to use these. Indeed, that is the abuse of the world which Paul also forbids.

units.la: PRAETERIT enim habitus huius mūdi.) Rationem adijcit, sed talem, quæ commoda sit captui eorum quibus scribit. Nam alioqui dicendum erat: Nisi enim hoc feceritis, in fide Christi persistere non poteritis. Hoc quippe illis metuebat. Verū ea ratione paulo inferius vtetur. Nūc cōmodū, vbi mūdi metio incidit, ab illius fugacitate & inconstantia argumentū persuadendi sumit. Praeterit enim, inquit, habitus mundi huius, παράγει γὰρ ἐστι, quod & seducere & praeterire significat. Vnde Stapulensis quod nos legimus praeterit, vel transit, vertit seducit. Vide Erasm. Vtrunque vērum est, & causæ quam agit Apostolus, accommodum. Io annes in sua canonica verbo isto pro trāsire vtitur, cum dicit, παράγεται ὁ κόσμος. Notanter autem non de mundi substantia, sed figura & habitu quem nūc habet loquitur, cum σχῆμα ponit. Et satis contemptim, ea quæ mundi huius filij tantopere admirantur, figuram vocat, vmbra nanq; sunt, non solida veritas. Quæ itaque illo vel bona videntur vel mala, nec verè bona vel mala, nec diuturna sunt, sed vmbratilia & transitoria. Quid igitur causæ est vnde in tristibus anxij, & in prosperioribus elati esse debeamus, cum nec tristes nec secundæ res huius mundi veræ sint, aut constantes, sed non nisi vmbra quædam momentaria rerum tristium & secundarum, quas perpetuas & veras futurum sæculum habebit.
units.tr: "For the fashion of this world passes away." He adds a reason, but one suited to the understanding of those to whom he writes. Otherwise he ought to have said: "For unless you do this, you will not be able to persist in the faith of Christ." This was indeed what he feared for them. But he will use that reasoning a little further on. Now, since the mention of the world has come up, he takes an argument for persuading them from its transience and inconstancy. "For the fashion of this world passes away," he says, παράγει γὰρ [parágei gár], which signifies both to lead astray and to pass by. Hence Stapulensis translates the word we read as "passes away" or "goes by" as "leads astray." See Erasmus. Both meanings are true and suit the cause the Apostle is pursuing. John in his canonical letter uses this word in the sense of "pass by," when he says: ὁ κόσμος παράγεται [ho kósmos parágetai], "the world passes away." He notably speaks not of the substance of the world but of its form and the state it now has, when he uses σχῆμα [schēma]. And rather disdainfully he calls figure what the children of this world so greatly admire, for they are shadows, not solid truth. Therefore those things which seem either good or evil to them are neither truly good nor evil, nor lasting, but shadowy and transitory. What reason then is there for us to be anxious in sad times and elated in prosperous ones, since neither the sad nor the prosperous things of this world are true or lasting, but are only momentary shadows of sad and prosperous things, which the age to come will have as perpetual and true.

units.la: Velim autem uos sine solicitudine esse. Qui cœlebs est, curat ea quæ sunt domini, quomodo placiturus sit domino. At qui duxit uxorem, solicitus est de his quæ sunt mundi, quomodo placiturus sit uxori. Diuisa sunt hęc duo, mulier & virgo. Innupta curat ea quæ sunt domini, ut sit sancta & corpore & spiritu. Contra quę nupta est, curat ea quę suntmundi, quomodo placitura sit uiro. Hoc aūt ad id, quod uobis conducibile est, dico. Non uti laqueum uobis iniiciam, sed ut quod honestum ac decorum est, sequamini, & adhæreatis domino absque ulla distractione.
units.tr: Now I want you to be free from anxiety. The unmarried man is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife. The woman and the virgin are divided in this way. The unmarried woman is concerned with the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in both body and spirit. But the married woman is concerned with the things of the world, how she may please her husband. I say this for your advantage, not to throw a noose over you, but so that you may follow what is honourable and fitting, and cling to the Lord without any distraction.

units.la: Redit ad consilium quod supra de agamia dederat, asserens bonum esse cœlibatum propter instantem necessitatem, & quod tribulationem in carne sint habituri coniuges, quas declinari cupiat, eo quod illis parcat. Iam id consilij resumit, & adhuc aliam quandam illius rationem adijcit, vt doceat quantam commoditatem habeat cœlibatus in regno Christi præ matrimonio. Eam sumit à molestia coniugij, qua multis curis est obnoxium: cuius gratia fit, vt coniugatus minus sit appositus regno Christi quàm cœlebs, periculumq; sit, ne plus quæ sæculi quàm quæ Christi sunt curet.
units.tr: He returns to the advice he had given above about marriage, saying that celibacy is good because of the pressing necessity, and that married people will have tribulation in the flesh, which he wishes them to avoid, because he spares them. Now he takes up this advice again and adds another reason for it, to show how much greater an advantage celibacy has over marriage in the kingdom of Christ. He draws this from the trouble of marriage, which brings many cares with it. Because of this, a married person is less fitted for the kingdom of Christ than an unmarried one, and there is a danger that he will care more for the things of the world than for the things of Christ.

units.la: Θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς.) Volo autem vos. Non hoc dicit imperandi sed optandi modo, vt & Erasm. reddidit: Velim autem vos. Sic supra. Volo enim omnes esse sicut & ego sum, pro, velim enim omnes esse, &c.
units.tr: Θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς [Thelō de hymas].) "But I want you." He does not say this in the imperative but in the optative mood, as Erasmus also rendered it: "Velim autem vos" ("I would like you"). So above: "Volo enim omnes esse sicut et ego sum", for "velim enim omnes esse", etc.

units.la: SINE solicitudine esse.) Ἀμέριμνος ὑμῖν. Curarum multa sunt genera. Non exigit vt in vniuersum omnibus curis liberi sint. Est enim impossibile, deinde nec vtile est, animum habere prorsus solutum & otiosum, quod hominis est prorsus inepti ac leuiculi, & nullo rerum sensu præditi. Tales non optat esse Christianos, qui omnia susque deque ferant, & sint rerum cum diuinarum tum humanarum egregij contemptores. Rerum terrenarum curam ac solicitudinem abesse Christianis optat, quia sciat illorum ingenium esse, ut animum occupent, nec sui iuris esse permittat. Vnde & Christus Matthæi sexto dicit: Nolite soliciti esse quid manducetis, quid bibatis, quid induatis, &c. Sed primum quærite regnum Dei & iustitiam eius, & hæc omnia adijcientur vobis. Cur hoc præcepit? Ob id videlicet, vt liberiores essent ad quærendam regni Dei iustitiam, nullis huius vitæ curis impediti. Sic Matthæi decimotertio, curas huius vitæ spinis coparat, quibus verbi Dei fructus impeditur ac suffocatur. Et Lucæ vigesimoprimo dicit: Cauete ne corda vestra ingrauentur crapula & ebrietate, & curis huius vitæ. Ergo solicitudo rerum terrenarum his testimonijs conuincitur eo esse ingenio, vt animos mortalium captiuet, & à libera regni Dei consectatione impediat, quod etiam ipsa quotidie experientia declaratur.
units.tr: To be without anxiety.) [ἀμέριμνος ὑμῖν] There are many kinds of care. He does not require that they be free from all cares in general. For it is impossible, and moreover not useful, to have a mind wholly loose and idle; that belongs to a man who is utterly foolish and frivolous and endowed with no sense of things. He does not wish Christians to be such people, who take everything lightly and despise both divine and human matters of importance. He wishes Christians to be free of care and anxiety about earthly things, because he knows that such anxiety is of a nature to occupy the mind and not let it be its own master. Hence Christ also says in Matthew 6: "Do not be anxious what you shall eat, or what you shall drink, or what you shall put on," and so on. "But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you." Why did he command this? Evidently so that they might be freer to seek the righteousness of the kingdom of God, unimpeded by any cares of this life. So in Matthew 13 he compares the cares of this life to thorns, by which the fruit of the word of God is hindered and choked. And in Luke 21 he says: "Take heed that your hearts are not weighed down with carousing and drunkenness and the cares of this life." Therefore anxiety about earthly things is shown by these testimonies to be of a nature that captivates the minds of mortals and hinders their free pursuit of the kingdom of God, as daily experience itself also demonstrates.

units.la: QVI cœlebs est, curat ea quæ sunt domini.)
units.tr: He who is unmarried cares for the things of the Lord.

units.la: Declarat seipsum, quomodo cupiat eos sine solicitudine esse. Id autem facit per collationem vtriusque status, coniugij & cœlibatus, ostendens illius incommoditatem, & huius commoditatem. Quantum enim commoditatis habeat cœlibatus, non potest melius cognosci, quàm ex consideratione molestiarum coniugalium.
units.tr: He declares how he wishes them to be without anxiety. He does this by comparing the two states, marriage and celibacy, showing the inconvenience of the one and the advantage of the other. For how great the advantage of celibacy is cannot be better known than from considering the troubles of married life.

units.la: CVRAT ea quæ sunt domini.) Non mo̅ verum est, si assertiue legas. Reperias enim innumeros cœlibes & innuptos, qui nihil minus curent quàm quæ sunt domini, nec ob id cœlibatum amplexi sint, vt domino integrius ac plenius adhæreant, sed vt declinata coniugij seruitute, liberius liceat indulgere genio. Et nostri clerici cum omnes cogantur esse ἄγαμοι, quomodo quæso curant quæ sunt domini? Nisi velis per ea quæ domini sunt, bona ecclesiastica, id est, census ac reditus ecclesiasticos intelligere, quorum sanè iam olim magna quidem, sed prorsus infyncera cura tenentur. Quis enim non videt, quā non Christi, sed quę sua sunt curent?
units.tr: CVRAT ea quæ sunt domini.) This is true only if you read it as a statement. For you will find countless unmarried and celibate people who care for the things of the Lord least of all, and who have not embraced celibacy so that they might cling more fully and completely to the Lord, but so that, having escaped the bondage of marriage, they may indulge their inclinations more freely. And our clergy, since they are all compelled to be unmarried (ἄγαμοι), how, I ask, do they care for the things of the Lord? Unless you want to understand by "the things of the Lord" the church goods, that is, the ecclesiastical revenues and income, which indeed have long been held with great but utterly unsincere care. For who does not see how they care for their own things, not those of Christ?

units.la: Proinde quod dicit: Qui cœlebs est, curat ea quæ sunt domini, nō est aliter intelligendū, quàm vt eādem sit atq; aptus est & expeditus ad curandū ea quæ sunt domini. Hoc certè verum est, & summopere optandū fidelibus, maximè vbi tribulatio persequutionis sæuit.
units.tr: Therefore what he says, "He who is unmarried cares for the things of the Lord," is to be understood only in this sense: that he is equally fit and free to care for the things of the Lord. This is certainly true, and it is greatly to be wished for believers, especially when the tribulation of persecution rages. ## QVAE sunt dni.)

units.la: QVAE sunt dni.) Quę illa sunt? Nihil exprimit nominatim Apostolus. Nec opus erat. Simpliciter enim de perseuerantia fidei & confessio-
units.tr: The things of the Lord. What are those things? The Apostle names nothing specifically, and there was no need to. For he speaks simply of perseverance in faith and of the confession of

units.la: sessionis Christi loquitur, vt curare quæ Christi sunt, nihil aliud sit, quâ quærere regnū Dei & iusticiam eius, & non mundo, sed Christi esse voluntati addictum.
units.tr: Christ, so that to care for the things of Christ is nothing other than to seek the kingdom of God and its righteousness, and to be devoted to the will of Christ rather than to the world.

units.la: QVOMODO placeat domino.) Quasi expo-nit quid sit curare ea quæ sunt domini. Studio videlicet illi placendi teneri. Illud duo habet. Vnum, vt vitetur, quicquid illi displicet. Alterum, vt quæ placita illi sunt, fiant. Horum cognitio non est ex humanis cogitationibus, sed è verbo Dei petenda, ne quis hoc loco vitam monasticam somniet, cū nulla alia sit ineptior regno Christi. De ea loquor qualis nunc est, & quæ iam olim plus cœpit habere superstitionis quàm pietatis, nihilq; aliud est, quàm conscientiarum captiuitas, & liberæ charitatis impedimentum. Sedulitas audiendi verbū Dei, & precandi, bonum quidem habet ad pietatem exercitium, si ritè dispensetur, & accedat studium charitatis erga proximos. Omnē verò uitam vni isti exercitio addicere, abiectis reliquis pietatis officijs, qualia sunt, suscipere peregrinos, vestire nudos, solari mœstos, visitare captiuos & infirmos, id demum est, quod Christo placere nequit, nec ab Apostolo requiritur, nec tum temporis inter Christianos in vsu erat.
units.tr: How he may please the Lord. He explains, as it were, what it is to care for the things of the Lord: namely, to be held by the zeal of pleasing him. This has two parts. One is that whatever displeases him be avoided; the other is that whatever is pleasing to him be done. The knowledge of these things is not to be sought from human thoughts but from the word of God, lest anyone here dream of monastic life, since no other is more foreign to the kingdom of Christ. I speak of it as it now is, which long ago began to have more superstition than piety, and is nothing but captivity of consciences and an impediment to free charity. Diligence in hearing and praying over the word of God has a good exercise for piety, if it is rightly administered and the zeal of love towards neighbours is added. But to devote the whole of life to this one exercise, casting aside the other duties of piety, such as receiving strangers, clothing the naked, comforting the sorrowful, and visiting prisoners and the sick, this is indeed what cannot please Christ, nor is it required by the Apostle, nor was it in use among Christians at that time.

units.la: At qui duxit uxorem, solicitus est de his quæ sunt mundi.
units.tr: But he who has married is anxious about the things of the world.

units.la: Neq; hoc vbiq; verum est. Reperti nanque sunt multi qui licet coniuges essent, non tamē quæ mundi, sed quæ domini erant curarunt: quales erant Prisca & Aquila, qui coniuges vtique erant, & tamen non quæ huius sæculi, sed quæ Christi erant curasse legūtur, ita vt & ceruices suas pro Apostoli vita posuerint, Romanorum decimosexto. Proinde nec hoc per assertionem simpliciter intelligendum est sed vt idem sit atque, periculum est, ne tempore confitendi Christi, solicitus sit de his quæ sunt mundi, eò quod ipse status coniugalis talis sit, vt animum coniugis curis suis plerunq; adobruat, vt minus reddatur appositus regno Christi curando. Sic est in parabola Lucę decimoquarto: Vxorem duxi, & ideo non possum venire.
units.tr: This is not always true. For there have been many who, although they were married, cared not for the things of the world but for the things of the Lord. Such were Priscilla and Aquila, who were certainly married, and yet we read that they cared not for the things of this age but for the things of Christ, so much so that they laid down their own necks for the life of the Apostle (Romans 16). Therefore this statement must not be understood simply as an assertion, but as meaning that there is a danger that, at a time when Christ must be confessed, the married man may be anxious about the things of the world, because the married state itself is such that it often overwhelms the mind of the spouse with cares, so that he is made less fit to attend to the kingdom of Christ. So it is in the parable of Luke 14: "I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come."

units.la: DE his quæ sunt mundi.) Rem familiarem intelligit, cuius copiam status iste desiderare videtur, vt omnia affatim, quæ vxori, quæ liberis & domesticis necessaria sunt, ad manū sint, quæ res quantum adferat curarum ac solicitudinum, norunt experti.
units.tr: On "the things of the world": he means household property, the abundance of which this condition seems to call for, so that everything needed by a wife, children and servants is at hand in plenty. Those who have experienced it know how many cares and anxieties this brings.

units.la: QVOMODO placeat vxori.) Quid hoc est? An peccatum est, placere vxori? Nequaquam. Quemadmodum neque prouidere vxori, liberis, & reliquæ domui, peccatum est. Alioqui malè scriberet hic ipse Apostolus Timotheo, quod fidem abnegauerit, & infideli deterior sit, si qua suis, & maximè familiaribus non prouideat. Sed solicitum esse & anxium in his rebus quæ mundi sunt, & quomodo gratificeris vxori, præterquam quod
units.tr: "How he may please his wife": what is this? Is it a sin to please one's wife? By no means. Just as it is no sin to provide for wife, children and the rest of the household. Otherwise this same Apostle would have written badly to Timothy, that someone who fails to provide for his own, and especially for his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. But to be anxious and troubled about worldly things, and about how to gratify one's wife, is not only a sign of weak faith but also makes a person unfit for seeking the things of Christ with diligence.

units.la: infirmæ fidei indicium est, ineptum etiam reddit ad hoc, vt quæ Christi sunt, studiosè quærantur. Quoniam autem difficile est coniugatum harum rerū cura nó teneri, & molestissimū tempore persequutionis cum vxore habitare, quæ animo sit auerso, nec minus negociosum in omnibus illi gratificari & placere velle, eò quod multa sit mulierum intemperantia, propter varios & importunos illarum affectus, quibus facilè mouentur, difficilè vero imperant, arbitratur fidissimum Apostoli pectus in periculosis persequutionum procellis, multò commodius esse abstinere à coniugio, quàm istis molestijs obnoxium fieri, & sò adigi vt impediatur animus à studio placendi domino.
units.tr: Yet since it is hard for a married man not to be held by these cares, and since it is most burdensome in a time of persecution to live with a wife whose mind is turned away, and no less laborious to wish to please and gratify her in everything, because women are very intemperate and their various and importunate emotions move them easily but are hard to control, the Apostle's most faithful heart judged that in the dangerous storms of persecution it was much more advantageous to abstain from marriage than to become subject to these troubles and so be driven to let the mind be diverted from the zeal of pleasing the Lord.

units.la: DIVISA sunt hæc duo, coniunx & virgo.) Hactenus de viris, nunc idem & de mulieribus tradit. Est enim hac in re eadem vtrinque fortis & ingeniorum conditio. Vtrorunque est animo esse erga Christum syncero, & placiti illius studioso. Deinde & vtrique ita compatati sunt, vt terrenis curis occupati, minus quæ Christi sunt curent. Imò mulieres, quo mobiliores sunt, & intemperantiores, hoc periculosius terrenis curis & affectibus inuoluuntur.
units.tr: "The wife and the virgin are divided": so far he has spoken of men; now he gives the same account of women. In this matter the condition of the sexes is the same on both sides, both in strength and in disposition. Both ought to have a sincere mind toward Christ and be zealous to please him. And both are so constituted that, once occupied with earthly cares, they care less for the things of Christ. Indeed, women, the more changeable and intemperate they are, the more dangerously they are entangled in earthly cares and affections.

units.la: Μεμέρισται ἡ γυνὴ καὶ ἡ παρθένος.) Hæc particula bifariam legitur. Quidam illud μεμέρισται adiecta coniunctione καὶ, præcedentibus coniungūt & legunt. Qui autem vxorem duxit, solicitus est de his quæ sunt mundi, quomodo placeat vxori, & diuisus est. Deinde interiecto puncto, reliqua ita substruunt. Mulier & virgo innupta, cogitat quæ sunt domini. Ita legunt ac diuidunt vetus interpres & commentarij Hieronymo dati. Ambrosius quoque de viro coniugato ita legit, nisi quod verbum diuiden di de muliere & virgine repetit. Alij legunt ad hunc modum, quem sequimur, vt & Erasmus reddidit: Diuisa est vxor & virgo. Deinde subijcitur distributiua collatio vxoris ac virginis, qua declaratur quomodo diuisæ sint. Natura non sunt diuisæ, nec sexu, nec dignitate coram Deo, sed diuersitate affectuum & studi◦ dispari. Omnibus fidelibus cor debet esse vnum & anima vna, par erga Christum fidei syn ceritas & æquale studium illi placendi. Verūm pro conditione & varietate statuum sit, vt quod vnitum esse debebat, diuisum & in partes sectum reddatur, dum animi fiunt in Christi fidę ac studio impares.
units.tr: "The wife is divided, and the virgin" (Μεμέρισται ἡ γυνὴ καὶ ἡ παρθένος). This clause is read in two ways. Some join the word "is divided" (μεμέρισται), with the conjunction "and" added, to what precedes, and read: "He who has married is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and is divided." Then, after a full stop, they construct the rest thus: "The woman and the unmarried virgin think about the things of the Lord." This is how the old translator and the commentaries ascribed to Jerome read and divide it. Ambrose also reads of the married man in this way, except that he repeats the word "divided" for the woman and the virgin. Others read it as we follow it, as Erasmus also rendered it: "The wife is divided, and the virgin." Then comes a comparison distributing wife and virgin, by which it is shown how they are divided. They are not divided by nature, nor by sex, nor by dignity before God, but by a difference of affections and an unequal zeal. All believers ought to have one heart and one soul, an equal sincerity of faith toward Christ and an equal zeal to please him. But according to the condition and variety of states, it happens that what ought to be united is divided and cut into parts, while their minds become unequal in the faith and zeal toward Christ.

units.la: INNVPTA curat ea quæ sunt domini.) Id est, aptior est, vt curet.
units.tr: "The unmarried woman cares for the things of the Lord": that is, she is better suited to take care of them.

units.la: VT sit sancta & corpore ac spiritu,) Pro ratione collationis debebat dicere, quomodo placeat dño.
