Cum ergo huius loco dicit, vt sit sancta & corpore & spiritu, innuitur tantundem esse hoc loco, sanctam esse mulierem corpore & spiritu, atque placere domino. Ergo mulier si cupiat placere domino, innupta sit, vt possit sancta esse & corpore & spiritu. Quid igitur? Quæ nupta est, nec sancta est, nec domino mino placet? Quomodo ergo supra infidelem coniugem in marito sanctificatam esse dixit? Si de sanctitate loquitur, quae per fidem ac spiritum Christi est, quomodo adscribitur hic in nuptis, cum sit etiam nuptarum & fidelium omnium? Si de mundicia illic corporis & animi loquitur, quomodo illam hic dat virginibus, cum sit & coniugum? Coniunx nanque, si in fide coniugali maneat, nec corpore nec animo immunda est, quatenus coniunx est. Quid est igitur quod dicit: Ut sit sancta corpore & spiritu? Primum, non disputat quid sit virginitas, nec sanctitatis gratia inter illam & coniugium discriminat, sed simpliciter dicit quae sit illius commoditas ad hoc, ut Christo seruiatur. Deinde quoniam virginitas mundiam quandam habet corporis & animi, dicit fidelem virginem pro status sui commoditate hoc posse conari, ut vere sit sancta, non corpore tantum, sed & spiritu, id est animo, id quod tum est, quando curat quae Christi sunt, & quomodo illi placeat. Inde nemo recte colliget, quod coniunx immunda sit corpore & animo, & quod domino placere nequeat, nisi corpus impuris actibus, & animum immundis polluat affectibus, id quod & innuptae potest accidere.
units.tr: "That she may be holy in body and in spirit": according to the pattern of the comparison he should have said "how she may please the Lord." Since he says here instead "that she may be holy in body and spirit," it is implied that this means the same as the woman being holy in body and spirit, and pleasing the Lord. So if a woman desires to please the Lord, let her be unmarried, so that she can be holy in body and spirit. What then? Is a married woman neither holy nor pleasing to the Lord? How then did he say above that the unbelieving spouse is sanctified in the believing husband? If he is speaking of the holiness that comes through faith and the Spirit of Christ, why is it here ascribed to the unmarried, when it belongs to married women and to all believers too? If he is speaking of the purity of body and mind there, why does he give it here to virgins, when it belongs to married people as well? For a married person, so long as he or she remains in marital faith, is neither unclean in body nor in mind, insofar as they are married. What then does he mean by "that she may be holy in body and spirit"? First, he does not dispute what virginity is, nor does he distinguish between it and marriage in terms of holiness, but he simply says what its advantage is for serving Christ. Then, since virginity has a certain purity of body and mind, he says that the believing virgin, for the advantage of her state, can strive for this, so that she may truly be holy, not in body only but also in spirit, that is, in mind, which happens when she cares for the things of Christ and how to please him. From this no one can rightly conclude that a married person is unclean in body and mind, and cannot please the Lord, unless he pollutes his body with impure acts and his mind with unclean affections, which can also happen to the unmarried.

units.la: Colligimus ex hoc loco de virginitate.
units.tr: We gather from this passage concerning virginity:

units.la: 1 Primum illam non aestimandam alicuius esse momenti, si corporis tantum habeat mundiciam. Exigit enim hic Apostolus non corporis solum, sed & spiritus sanctimoniam.
units.tr: (1) First, that it is not to be valued as of any importance if it has only purity of body. For the Apostle here requires holiness not only of body but also of spirit.

units.la: 2 Deinde finem illius esse, ut curentur, non quae mundi, sed quae domini sunt, & expeditius regno Christi ministrari queat. Nihil ergo minus sunt quam virgines: quae etsi non corpore, animi tamen affectibus virile consortium appetunt. Nec Christo probantur otiosae illae etiamsi affectibus animi sint plane angelicis, quae nulla in re Christo seruiunt, sed suae tantum tranquillitati consulunt.
units.tr: (2) Second, that its purpose is that she may care not for the things of the world but for the things of the Lord, and may be more readily available for the service of Christ's kingdom. Therefore such virgins are by no means better than others: although they do not seek male company in body, they do seek it in the affections of their minds. Nor are those idle women approved by Christ, even if their minds' affections are altogether angelic, who serve Christ in nothing but seek only their own tranquillity.

units.la: Quae nupta est, curat quae sunt mundi quomodo placeat viro.
units.tr: She who is married cares for the things of the world, how she may please her husband.

units.la: 1 Non mox omnes. Maior tamen pars. Et hic status tempore persequutiois id secum adfert periculi.
units.tr: 1 Not all immediately, but the greater part. And this state, in a time of persecution, brings this danger with it.

units.la: 2 Nec peccat, si placeat viro, modo ita, ut potissimum Christo placeat. Si coniugis est, ut virum suum amet, prudens sit, casta, sobria domus curam habens, benigna & subdita, quomodo malum erit, si ista faciens (ut facere iubetur Titi secundo) viro placeat? Apostolus Petrus hortatur mulieres coniuges, ut dificiles & infideles maritos pia & honesta conuersatione ad dominum conuertant. Hoc certe fieri non potest, nisi viris placeant. Nihil ergo hic peccatur, si coniunx istis mediis pijs & honestis viro cupiat in bonum placere, deinde, si ante omnia cupiat placere Christo. Non vetat igitur Apostolus, coniugem placere viro, cum id sit & illi & marito necessarium, nec mali quicquam habeat, sed docet, quid periculi subsit, si id anxie fiat & praeter modum, quemadmodum plerunque solent, eo quod sexus iste viri sit appetentior, & id ingenij habeat, ut cupiat placere viris, atque huc luctetur nugis suis, crinibus tortis, ornatu vestium, auro, argento, serico, quae omnia abesse vult ab illis quae pietatem profitentur.
units.tr: 2 Nor does she sin if she pleases her husband, provided that she above all pleases Christ. If she is a wife, let her love her husband, be prudent, chaste, sober, caring for the household, kind and submissive. How can it be wrong, if in doing these things (as Titus 2 bids her to do) she pleases her husband? The Apostle Peter exhorts believing wives to turn difficult and unbelieving husbands to the Lord by a holy and honourable way of life. This certainly cannot happen unless they please their husbands. Nothing wrong is done here, then, if a wife, by these godly and honourable means, desires to please her husband for his good, and, above all, desires to please Christ. The Apostle therefore does not forbid a wife to please her husband, since this is necessary both for her and for her husband, and it contains nothing evil. But he teaches what danger lies in it if it is done anxiously and beyond measure, as women commonly do, because this sex is more eager for men, and has the disposition to want to please men, and so struggles toward this with its trifles: twisted hair, adornment of clothing, gold, silver, silk, all of which he wants to be absent from those who profess godliness.

units.la: HOC autem ad id quod vobis conducibile est dico.) Ista vel per insinuationem dicuntur, ut credant fideliter consulenti, nec aliud quicquam quam ipsorum utilitatem quaerenti, vel per cautionem adijciuntur hoc sensu. Quicquid id fit quod de commoditate caelibatus, & incommoditate coniugij dico, nonaliter dictum volo, nec a vobis aliter vsurpari, quam quatenus ad vestram ipsorum cessurum fit utilitate quam unam hic specto. Vos videte iam singuli quid vobis fit conducibile. Mihi visum est huius admonere, & ita arbitror causam hanc habere, sed, ut supra dixi, quisque proprium donum habet, alius sic, alius alio modo. Quod cui que conducibile est, sectetur.
units.tr: (But I say this for your advantage.) These things are said either by way of suggestion, so that they may trust one who advises them faithfully and seeks nothing but their own good, or they are added by way of caution, in this sense. Whatever it is that I say about the convenience of celibacy and the inconvenience of marriage, I want it said in no other way, nor used by you in any other way, than insofar as it will turn out to your own advantage, which alone I look to here. Let each of you now see what is advantageous for himself. It seemed right to me to admonish you of this, and I think this is the reason for the matter, but, as I said above, each has his own gift, one in this way, another in another. Let each follow what is advantageous for him.

units.la: NON vti laqueum vobis injiciam.) Quis non videt Apostolum id quod res erat vltro concederasse? Si consilium suum non tantope re declarasset, & causae istius libertatem monstrasset, videbat futurum, ut, quod suadebat imparitis & imbecillibus conscientijs in laqueu cederet. Quomodo? Si conarentur illo extra donum Dei uti. Hoc est, si caelibatui spreto coniugio sese addicerent, id quod non potest non male cedere, & perditioni seruire.
units.tr: (I will not cast a snare upon you.) Who does not see that the Apostle had freely conceded what the matter was? If he had not so clearly declared his counsel, and shown the freedom of this matter, he foresaw that what he urged would turn into a snare for unsteady and weak consciences. How? If they tried to use it outside the gift of God; that is, if, having despised celibacy, they devoted themselves to marriage. This cannot but turn out badly and serve destruction.

units.la: Vide admirabilem altum Satane. Data opera cauit Apostolus, idque nominatim expressit, quae de caelibatus commoditate disputabat non huc tendere, ut inde struatur laqueus conscientiarum, quasi res ista fit necessaria, sed cuiusque conscientiae liberum relinqui, quid sequatur, quid non. Et ausus est hinc impudentissimus Satan, contra expressam Apostoli mentem, curam & solicitudinem, tam innumeris animabus laqueos struere, in quibus miserè & corpore & spiritu pereant. Et quod crudelissimum est, eo tandem inualuit ista insania, ut malint ecclesiastici principes scienter ac prudenter perire tot animas, pro quibus Christus est mortuus, quam hunc laqueum, quem non Apostolus, sed Satanae altus struxit, per doctrinam Apostolicam solui.
units.tr: See the admirable depth of Satan! The Apostle took care deliberately, and expressly stated that what he argued about the advantage of celibacy did not aim at this, that a snare for consciences should be built from it, as if the thing were necessary, but that each conscience should be left free to follow or not to follow. And the most shameless Satan has dared, against the Apostle's clearly expressed mind, to build with such care and anxiety snares for so countless souls, in which they perish wretchedly in body and spirit. And what is most cruel, this madness has at last prevailed to such an extent that the leaders of the Church prefer that so many souls, for whom Christ died, should knowingly and deliberately perish, rather than that this snare, which was built not by the Apostle but by the cunning of Satan, be undone by the Apostolic teaching.

units.la: SED vt quod decorum est sequamini, &c.) Graece est, ἀλλὰ ... id est, sed ad id quod decorum est, & huc facit, vt indiuulsè dño adhæreatis intellige, hoc dico. Exponit mente cosilij sui, & illius vtilitate declarat, quâ decoro & constantiae circa Christi fidè & obseruantiam includit. Decorum hic non vocat ἁγιασμόν, sed status in quo quisque est honestatem, qua sic viuitur, ut nulli diffamiae Christiani hominis conuersatio reddatur obnoxia. Habet & Christianismi professio suum decorum. Id est, vt vita professioni respondeat. Professio spiritalis est & coelestis. Ergo decorum illius est, vt reiectis hu-ius ius vitæ cupiditatibus cœlesti conuersatione studeamus. Christo indiuulsé adhærere, est cō stanti & immota fide nō quę mundi, sed quæ Christi sunt curare, nec vllis tentationibus ab illius dilectione auelli. Liberum ergo permittit Apostolus cuiq; fideli pro suo dono vel cœlibatum vel coniugium amplecti, modò huc faciat, vt Christianæ professionis decorum seruetur, & in fide Christi immotè perseueretur. Quatenus cuiquam ad id seruire potest cœlibatus, hactenus illumconsulit. Sin secus, satius esse suprà dixit, nubere quàm vri.
units.tr: "BUT THAT WHICH IS COMELY, FOLLOW, etc." In Greek it is ἀλλὰ [but], that is, "but to that which is seemly", and this serves to mean that you should cling to the Lord without distraction; I say this. He explains the intent of his counsel and declares its usefulness, in which he includes seemliness and constancy in faith in Christ and in observance of him. Here he does not call sanctification [ἁγιασμόν] "seemliness", but the state in which each person is, the honour by which one so lives that the conduct of a Christian is not exposed to any disgrace. The profession of Christianity also has its own seemliness; that is, that life should correspond to the profession. The profession is spiritual and heavenly. Therefore it is seemly for us to reject the desires of this life and to strive after a heavenly way of living. To cling to Christ without distraction is to care, with constant and unshaken faith, not for the things of the world but for the things of Christ, and not to be torn from his love by any temptations. The Apostle therefore freely permits each faithful person to embrace, according to his gift, either celibacy or marriage, provided that he does so in such a way that the seemliness of the Christian profession is kept and one perseveres unshaken in the faith of Christ. Insofar as celibacy can serve a person for this, he counsels it. But if it is otherwise, he said above that it is better to marry than to burn.

units.la: Inepti plane sunt, qui Christiani status decorum putant esse virginitatem, & Christo indiuulsè adhærere idem esse atq; virginitatem constanter seruare, quasi coniugium & probrū habeat, & cōiuges Christo adhærere nequeàt, cum Apostolus cœlibatum hactenus suadeat, vt si ad decorum & perseuerantiā Christo adhærendi faciat, vsurpetur. Aliud est quod suadet, & aliud quod suadendo spectat. An Dauid virgo erat, cū diceret: Mihi autem adhærere Deo bonum est? Quomodo adhærebat Deo? Audi. Ponere in domino Deo spem meam. Ergo domino indiuulsè adhærere, est syncera fide, spe & dilectione constanter ab illo pendere, nec vllis tentationibus ab eo auelli. At id potuerunt per gratiam Dei, & possunt etiamnum pij homines in matrimonio constituti, non minus quàm virgines.
units.tr: Those are quite foolish who think that the seemliness of the Christian state is virginity, and that to cling to Christ without distraction is the same as to keep virginity constantly, as if marriage were a disgrace and married people could not cling to Christ, since the Apostle urges celibacy only insofar as it may be used for the seemliness and perseverance of clinging to Christ. What he urges is one thing, and what he aims at in urging it is another. Was David a virgin when he said: "But it is good for me to cling to God"? How did he cling to God? Hear: "to put my hope in the Lord God." Therefore to cling to the Lord without distraction is, with sincere faith, hope and love, to depend constantly on him, and not to be torn from him by any temptations. But this could be done, through the grace of God, and godly people established in marriage can still do it no less than virgins.

units.la: Quod si quis indecorum virgini suæ putat, si prætereat nubendi tempus, & sic oportet fieri, quod vult faciat, non peccat, iungantur matrimonio. Cæterum qui stat firmus in corde, non habens necessitatem, sed potestatè habet propriæ voluntatis, & hoc decreuit in corde suo vt seruet suā uirginem, bene facit. Itaq; qui elocat nuptum, bene facit. Attamen qui non elocat nuptum melius facit.
units.tr: But if anyone thinks it unseemly for his virgin if she passes the time for marriage, and it must be so done, let him do what he wishes; he does not sin, let them be joined in marriage. But he who stands firm in his heart, not under necessity but having power over his own will, and has decided in his heart to keep his virgin, does well. So he who gives her in marriage does well. But he who does not give her in marriage does better.

units.la: Adhuc ampliori declaratione cauet, ne cuiuspiam libertati cõsilio suo præiudicet. Nō satis est, quod dixit: Etsi nupserit virgo, non peccat. Deinde. Hoc ad id quod vobis coducibile est, dico, non vti laqueum vobis injicia, sed vt quæ decorum est, sequamini, sed adhuc opus esse putat pluribus rē eandem inculcare. Tantopere videlicet solicitus erat, ne cui suo consilio obtēperandi necessitatem obtrudere videretur. Descendit paululum ad species, licet hoc quod in specie dicit, antea generaliter dixerit.
units.tr: With still fuller explanation he takes care not to prejudice anyone's freedom by his counsel. It is not enough that he said: "Even if the virgin marries, she does not sin." Then: "I say this for your advantage, not to cast a snare upon you, but that you may follow what is seemly," but he still thinks it necessary to press the same point on many. He was evidently so anxious not to seem to impose on anyone the necessity of obeying his counsel. He descends a little to particular cases, although what he says in particular he had already stated in general terms.

units.la: QVOD si quis.) Non exigit, vt pater virginem suam domi seruet, contra vel suam vel illius voluntatem, sed totam hanc causam arbitrio & iudicio parentum committit. Vsuenit aliquando vt ignominiosum videatur virgini, si ultra nubendi tempus domi paternæ detinetur innupta. Argumentum enim habere videtur, esse ineptam & inutilem, aut malis moribus prædita, vel certè talibus orta parentibus, vt illorum gratia fastidiri mereatur. Et alioqui ridiculum est vetulam videre virginem. Hoc videtur dicere Apostolus, cum scribit: εἰ δέ τις ἀσχημονεῖν νομίζει, id est, si quis indecorū esse putat. Et ἐὰν ἦ ὑπέρακμος, id est, si sit supera dulta, si ætatem & maturitatem nubendi, pubertatem egressa, prætereat. Decorum hic de cuiusq; loci ordine & consuetudine intelligendum est. Potest quisquam apud eos populos habitare, vbi nihil indecori habeat, si superadultam virginem domi retineat. Rursus fieri potest, vt apud eos sit quibus id turpe videatur. Iam quicquid hac in re sit, cuiusq; iudicio permittit. Non enim dicit. Quod si indecorum fuerit, sed, si quis indecorum virgini suæ putat. Satis est, si pater putet indecorum virgini suæ, si ætatem nubendi supergrediatur, nec opus est, vt cuiquam ea sit de re ad reddendam rationem obnoxius.
units.tr: "BUT IF ANYONE..." He does not require that a father keep his virgin daughter at home, against either her will or his own, but he leaves the whole matter to the judgment and discretion of parents. It sometimes happens that it seems disgraceful for a virgin if she is kept unmarried in her father's house beyond the time for marriage. For it seems to suggest that she is unsuitable and useless, or endowed with bad morals, or at least born of such parents that she deserves to be despised on their account. And otherwise it is ridiculous to see an old virgin. This seems to be what the Apostle means when he writes: "But if anyone thinks himself unseemly" [εἰ δέ τις ἀσχημονεῖν νομίζει], that is, if anyone thinks it unseemly; and "if she be past her prime" [ἐὰν ἦ ὑπέρακμος], that is, if she has gone beyond the age and maturity for marriage, past the bloom of youth. Here "seemly" must be understood according to the order and custom of each place. Someone may live among peoples where there is nothing unseemly if he keeps an over-age virgin at home. Again, it may be that among those people it is thought shameful. Now whatever the case in this matter, he leaves it to each person's judgment. For he does not say: "If it be unseemly," but: "If anyone thinks it unseemly for his virgin." It is enough if the father thinks it unseemly for his virgin if she passes the age for marriage, and there is no need that he should be answerable to anyone for his reasons in this matter.

units.la: ET sic oportet fieri.) Alius articulus. Necessitatis videlicet. Vbi periculum est, ne incōtinentiæ tentationibus superata virgo, labatur in scortandi turpitudinem. Hoc est, si videatur viri appetentior, quàm vt tutum sit eam virginitati destinare. Non video aliam necessitatem contrahendi matrimonium in virgine præter istam. Et vtinam huius potiorem rationem haberent parentes, qui filias suas extra necessitatis huius experientiam in monasteria tuserunt immaturas, vt tum primum illius fiant expertę vbi voti vinculo ligatæ, ad nuptias amplius aspirare non permittuntur. Bene dicit. Et sic oportet fieri. Est enim reuera ineluctabilis necessitas nubendi, vbi continentiæ donum non habetur, nisi locum dare velint parentes omnis generis turpitudini. Istam necessitatem licet infanda libido hodie in monachis, nonnis ac sacerdotibus horrendis exemplis, & inexcusabili turpitudine proclamet, tanta tamen est episcoporum stupiditas, vt nullam dum illius habere rationem sustineant.
units.tr: And so it ought to be done.) Another point, namely of necessity. Where there is a danger that a virgin, overcome by the temptations of incontinence, may slip into the shame of fornication: that is, if she seems too eager for a husband for it to be safe to dedicate her to virginity. I see no other necessity for a virgin to contract marriage than this one. And would that parents took this more into account, those who have thrust their daughters into monasteries while still immature, outside the experience of this necessity, so that they first experience it only when, bound by the bond of a vow, they are no longer allowed to aspire to marriage. He speaks well: "And so it ought to be done." For there is indeed an unavoidable necessity to marry where the gift of continence is not present, unless parents are willing to give place to every kind of shame. Although unspeakable lust today cries out this necessity through monks, nuns and priests, with horrible examples and inexcusable shamefulness, the stupidity of the bishops is so great that they still tolerate it without taking any account of it.

units.la: QVOD vult faciat.) Quasi dicat, Nihil impeditur meo cōsilio. Non adimo illi quod vult faciendi hac in re libertatem. Per me licet facere, quod faciendum esse putauerit. Non dicit: Quod debet & necesse est faciat, ne prorsus hanc libertatem necessitati alligatam putemus, sed, quod vult faciat, vt agnoscamus omnimodam libertatem. Parenti pro excusatione satis est, si virginem suam nuptum elocat, quod ita faciendum putat, & sic facere placet, etiamsi non omnimoda vrgeat necessitas.
units.tr: "What he wills, let him do." As if he were saying: nothing is hindered by my counsel. I do not take from him the freedom to do what he wishes in this matter. As far as I am concerned, he may do what he thinks ought to be done. He does not say: "let him do what he ought and must do," lest we think this freedom is altogether bound by necessity; but "let him do what he wills," so that we may acknowledge complete freedom. For a parent, it is enough by way of excuse that he gives his virgin daughter in marriage, because he thinks this ought to be done and is pleased to do so, even if no absolute necessity presses.

units.la: NON peccat.) Idē suprà dixit. Repetit ob id, ne laqueum injiciat infidelium conscientijs. Sunt enim argutuli quidam, qui ad turbandas fidelium ac simplicium conscientias facile inferunt. Si hoc est consilium Apostoli, & Apostolus non ex seipso, sed ex spiritu sancto loquutus est, vt & infrà dicet: ergo qui consilio illius non obtemperat, spiritui sancto non obtemperat. Qui autem id facit, quomodo non quod malum est facit? Qui quod malum est fa cit,vtiq; delinquit. Ergo qui relicta virginitate vel se vel virginem suam matrimonio coniun-gĭt,peccat. Contra huiusmodi argutias opus fuit non semel,sed iterum inculcare, non peccari à quoquam si matrimonium contrahat.
units.tr: "He does not sin." He said the same above. He repeats it so as not to cast a snare upon the consciences of the unbelievers. For there are certain quibblers who readily bring in arguments to disturb the consciences of the faithful and the simple. If this is the counsel of the Apostle, and the Apostle spoke not from himself but from the Holy Spirit, as he will say below, then whoever does not obey his counsel does not obey the Holy Spirit. But whoever does this, how does he not do what is evil? Whoever does what is evil certainly offends. Therefore whoever, having abandoned virginity, joins either himself or his virgin to marriage, sins. Against arguments of this kind it was necessary to inculcate not once but again: that no one sins if he contracts marriage.

units.la: IVNGANTVR matrimonio.) Pluraliter loquitur,ad sponsum & sponsam respiciens. Copula nanq; ista singularitate non constat,sed in duobus consistit.
units.tr: "Let them be joined in marriage." He speaks in the plural, looking to the bridegroom and the bride. For that union does not consist in one person, but stands in two.

units.la: CAETERVM qui stat firmus.) Ista pertinet ad hoc vt sententia suam quam supra dederat,diserte declaret,ne putetur cuiuis sequenda,quod videbat esse periculosum. Proinde certis conditionibus illam limitat & circumscribit;videlicet istis:
units.tr: "But he who stands firm." This belongs to the point that he may clearly state the opinion he had given above, lest it be thought that it should be followed by anyone, since he saw that it was dangerous. Accordingly he limits and circumscribes it by certain conditions, namely these:

units.la: Prima, si firmus sit in corde. Hoc est,si non fluctuet in vtranq; partem. Non vult enim tale quid tentari animo non bene firmato.
units.tr: First, if he is firm in heart. That is, if he does not waver to either side. For he does not want such a thing to be attempted by a mind not well settled.

units.la: Altera,si nulla necessitas diuersum exigat. Nam etiamsi pater firmo sit proposito seruandi virginem suam,nunquam tamen id faciet secundum Apostoli consilium,si necessitas exigat matrimonium.
units.tr: Second, if no necessity demands the opposite. For even if the father has a firm purpose of keeping his virgin daughter, he will never do so in accordance with the Apostle's counsel if necessity requires marriage.

units.la: Tertia,si proprię voluntatis potestate habeat.Ea hac in re pendet à consensu filiæ. Citra illam non habet potestatem pater filiam vel nuptum dare,vel à nuptijs cohibere.
units.tr: Third, if he has the power of his own will. In this matter it depends on the consent of the daughter. Without her, the father has no power either to give his daughter in marriage or to restrain her from marriage.

units.la: Quod adijcit,& hoc decreuit in corde suo, nihil aliud est,quàm quod primo loco dixit: Qui stat firmus in corde.ἑδραῖος quippe aliquado significat non simpliciter iudicare, sed firmo & inconcussho propositio decernere & statuere. Ita in epistolis Plinij de quodam Corellio Russo legitur,quod cibum respuerit ægrotus,ob id, quod diutino morbi dolore victus, per ἀσιτίαν mori destinasset,atque ideo medico cibum admonenti respondērit,οὐκ ἐσθίω, id est i-ta decreui,& inconcusse statui. Ergo non vult temere quenquam consilio suo obtemperare, sed omnino exigit animum bene consultum, & firmatum,& vt nulla necessitas aliud suadeat,& virgo assensu suo patris voluntati aştipuletur. Hęc est mens & prudentia Apostoli, quà vtinam obseruassent præterita sæcula.
units.tr: What he adds, "and has decided this in his heart," is nothing other than what he said first: "who stands firm in heart." Indeed ἑδραῖος sometimes signifies not simply to judge, but to decide and resolve with a firm and unshaken purpose. Thus in the letters of Pliny it is read of a certain Corellius Rufus, that when sick he refused food, because, overcome by the long pain of his illness, he had resolved to die by abstinence from food; and so when the physician urged him to eat, he replied, "οὐκ ἐσθίω," that is, "I have so decided, and resolved without wavering." Therefore he does not wish anyone rashly to obey his counsel, but altogether requires a mind well advised and firmly settled, and that no necessity urges otherwise, and that the virgin agrees with her consent to her father's will. This is the mind and wisdom of the Apostle, which would that past ages had observed.

units.la: Istam expositionem malo,quàm eam quam adfert Theophylactus,qui scribit ista ad extolendum virginitatis meritum ab Apostolo dici, ita vt qui filiam suam virginem seruat, sit vir animo constanti,& sano iudicio præditus: rursus,qui filiam suam nuptum elocet,licet non peccet,sit tamen inconstans animo,& iudicio non bene sano. Non hic est animus Apostoli vt prædicet,sed vt requirat constantiam & rectum iudicium in eo qui filiam suam matrimonio non iungit,& vt , quemadmodum dixi, prohibeat, ne quisquam suæ sententiæ re non bene penšitata obtemperandum esse putet. Cautionem habent verba Apostoli,nō commendationem virginitatis. Alioqui si temerè quis nec animaduersa nubendi necessitate,nec consulta filiæ voluntate, virginitati illam consecrare voluerit,tam aberit, vt sit vir animo be ne constans,& iudicio recto præditus, vt magis temeritatis accusari queat,& verius contrà quàm iuxta Apostoli sententiam fecerit.
units.tr: I prefer this explanation to the one brought forward by Theophylact, who writes that these things are said by the Apostle to extol the merit of virginity, so that the man who keeps his virgin daughter is a man of constant mind and sound judgment; and again, that the man who gives his daughter in marriage, although he does not sin, is nonetheless inconstant in mind and not of sound judgment. The Apostle's intention here is not to proclaim, but to require constancy and right judgment in the one who does not join his daughter in marriage, and, as I have said, to forbid anyone to think that he should obey an opinion not well considered. The words of the Apostle contain a caution, not a commendation of virginity. Otherwise, if anyone rashly, without considering the necessity of marriage and without consulting the daughter's will, wishes to consecrate her to virginity, he will be so far from being a man of constant mind and right judgment that he may rather be accused of rashness, and will more truly have acted contrary to, rather than according to, the Apostle's opinion.

units.la: VT feruet suam virginem.) Domi videlicet,& in sua potestate. Ignorabatur enim illis temporibus captiuitas illa monastica,qua virginitatem professæ, sub potestatem alicuius monachi vel nonnæ ponuntur & ædibus ac potestati patris eximuntur. Domi seruabantur virgines sub custodia & obedientia parētum, idque multo tutius & castius quàm hodie sub tyrannide monastica. Deinde itaseruabantur, vt si postea necessitas aliqua exposceret,nemo prohiberet illas nuptum elocare. Peruersa obedientia est cui nonnæ subduntur hodie . Primùm ob id, quod non solum ius nubendi aufertur,etiam vbi necessitas perspicuè id exigit,sed & quod cassata paterna obedientia,vel inmulieris alicuius,vel impuri monachi potestatem veniunt . Consilium Pauli non hoc docet,sed relinquit virginem in domo & potestate patris,nec adimit vbi necesse est,ius nubendi.
units.tr: "That he may keep his virgin daughter." At home, of course, and in his own power. For in those times that monastic captivity was unknown, by which women who have professed virginity are placed under the power of some monk or nun and are removed from the house and authority of their father. Virgins were kept at home under the custody and obedience of their parents, and this far more safely and chastely than today under monastic tyranny. Moreover, they were kept in such a way that if afterwards some necessity demanded it, no one would prevent them from being given in marriage. Perverse is the obedience to which nuns are subjected today. First, because the right to marry is taken away not only where necessity plainly demands it, but also because, once paternal obedience is cancelled, they come under the power of some woman or some impure monk. The counsel of Paul does not teach this, but leaves the virgin in the house and power of her father, and does not take away the right to marry where it is necessary.

units.la: BENE facit.) Hoc est,prudenter facit. Ergo qui non obseruatis istis conditionibus id facere conatur,non bene,sed male, id est, stulte & imprudenter facit.
units.tr: "He does well." That is, he acts prudently. Therefore whoever tries to do this without observing these conditions does not act well, but badly, that is, foolishly and imprudently.

units.la: ITAQVE qui elocat nuptum,bene facit.) Summandi gratia dicit. Vide autem quàm nō sint duo contraria inter se elocare nuptum , & non elocare, vt ita bene faciat virginem suam feruans,vt qui suam nuptum elocat, malè faciat. Vt supra admonui,duo bona sunt,coniugium & virginitas,modò illis rectè vtamur.
units.tr: "So then he who gives his daughter in marriage does well." He says this for the sake of summing up. Note how far it is from being the case that giving in marriage and not giving in marriage are two contrary things, so that he who keeps his virgin does well, and he who gives his daughter in marriage does badly. As I admonished above, there are two goods, marriage and virginity, provided we use them rightly.

units.la: Potest enim fieri,vt qui filiam suam matrimonio iungit,melius faciat,quàm si illam virginę feruet. Proinde quod dicit, attamen qui nō elocat nuptum,melius facit, non nisi in eo sensu & illis conditionibus quas supra posuit verum est , aliàs ne bonum quidem est, nedum melius.
units.tr: For it can happen that he who joins his daughter in marriage does better than if he keeps her a virgin. Therefore what he says, "but he who does not give her in marriage does better," is true only in the sense and under the conditions which he set down above; otherwise it is not even good, much less better.

units.la: OBSER. I.
units.tr: Observation I.

units.la: In eo quod non solum liberum facit matrimoniū,sed & bonum cum dicit : Qui elocat nuptum,bene facit, admonentur parentes nō minus ad hoc,vt si opus & maturum sit, filias suas nuptum dent,quàm si necessitas nubendi non sit,virgines illas seruent. Huius æquè debebant habere rationem prędicatores cœlibatus,atq; continentię virginalis. Debebant docere non solum nubendi libertatem,sed &si cōtinentiæ donum desit, prudentiam & beneficentiam paternam ad elocandas filias.
units.tr: In that he says not only that marriage is lawful but also good, when he says: "He who gives her in marriage does well," parents are admonished no less to this, that if there is need and the daughter is of marriageable age, they should give their daughters in marriage, than if there is no necessity of marrying, they should keep those virgins. The preachers of celibacy and of virginal continence ought equally to have taken account of this. They ought to teach not only the freedom to marry, but also, if the gift of continence is lacking, the prudence and paternal kindness in giving daughters in marriage.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Deinde in eo, quod potestati & prudentiæ paternæ filiarum vel nuptias vel virginitatem subijcit,ita tamen,vt illarum accedat assensus, admonet primùm non esse in potestate filiæ, vt sine patris consensu matrimonio sese iungat, sed patris id esse officij . Id vocat elocare nuptum.Quid est igitur illa doctrina, quæ tradit dit iustum esse matrimonium ac plenum ex consensu sponsi & sponsæ, etiam si parentes contradicant, unde orta sunt clandestina matrimonia, quæ plerunq; intercedente uino, scortatione, & lenone aliquo, parum honeste, multo minus firme coeunt.
units.tr: Next, in that he makes the marriage or the virginity of daughters subject to the power and prudence of the father, yet in such a way that the consent of the daughters is also present, he first admonishes that it is not in the daughter's power to join herself in marriage without the father's consent, but that this is the father's duty. This he calls "giving in marriage." What then is that doctrine which teaches that a marriage is just and complete by the consent of the bridegroom and bride alone, even if the parents object? From this have arisen clandestine marriages, which, for the most part, through wine, debauchery and some pimp, are contracted dishonourably and much less firmly.

units.la: Inde & in decretis Euaristi papæ, qui post Linū ordine quintus fuisse legitur, ita habetur:
units.tr: Hence also in the decretals of Pope Evaristus, who is read to have been the fifth in order after Linus, it is thus stated:

units.la: Similiter custoditum & traditum habemus, ut uxor uiro legitime iungatur. Aliter enim legitimum, ut à patribus accepimus, & à sanctis apostolis, eorumq; successoribus traditum invenimus, non fit coniugium, nisi ab his qui super ipsam fœminam dominationem uidentur habere, & à quibus custoditur, uxor petatur, & à parentibus & propinquioribus sponsetur & legibus detur.
units.tr: "Similarly we have kept and handed down that a wife be lawfully joined to her husband. For we find that a marriage is not lawful, as we have received from the fathers and as has been handed down by the holy apostles and their successors, unless the wife is sought from those who seem to have authority over the woman herself, and by whom she is guarded, and is betrothed by the parents and nearer relatives and given according to the laws."

units.la: Hæc ille. Notum illud Euripidis.
units.tr: So he. The well-known saying of Euripides.

units.la: Respondeant hic decretarij illi doctores, qs isti decreto authoritatem suam ademerit.
units.tr: Let those decretalist teachers answer here, whose authority this decree has taken away from them.

units.la: 2 Deinde simul admonemur, in potestate patris non esse, noletem uirginem cogere, uel ad coniugium, (ut est etiam in historia Rebeccæ, ubi dicebant, Vocemus puellam, & quæramus ipsius uoluntatem.) uel ad uirginitatem. Vtra que in re plurimum peccatur subinde à parentibus, quod filias suas inuitas uel cogūt ad matrimonium, uel ab illo abstinent.
units.tr: 2 Next, we are at the same time admonished that it is not in the father's power to compel an unwilling virgin, either to marriage (as is also in the story of Rebekah, where they said: "Let us call the girl and ask her own will"), or to virginity. In both matters parents often sin greatly, in that they compel their daughters against their will to marriage, or keep them from it.

units.la: Vxor alligata est legi, quandiu uiuit maritus eius. Quod si dormierit maritus eius, libera est, ut cui uult nubat, modo in domino. Attamē beatior est, si sic manet, iuxta meam sententiā. Opinor autem quod & ipse spiritū Dei habeā.
units.tr: A wife is bound by law as long as her husband lives. But if her husband has died, she is free to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. Yet she is happier if she remains so, according to my judgement. And I suppose that I too have the Spirit of God.

units.la: Et hic locus solicitudinem Apostoli declarat. Nam fere nihil dicit, quod antea non dixerit. In summa autem tria dicit.
units.tr: And this passage declares the anxiety of the Apostle. For he says almost nothing that he had not said before. In sum, however, he says three things.

units.la: 1 Vxorem alligatam esse legi, quandiu uiuit maritus eius.
units.tr: 1 A wife is bound by law as long as her husband lives.

units.la: 2 Post uiri dormitionem liberam esse, ut nubat cui uelit.
units.tr: 2 After the husband has died, she is free to marry whom she wishes.

units.la: 3 Beatiorem tamē esse, si uidua maneat, iuxta suā sententiā. De istis omnib. suprà quoq; egit.
units.tr: 3 Yet she is happier if she remains a widow, according to his judgement. He treated all of these matters above as well.

units.la: VXOR alligata est legi. Huius meminit & Rom.7. sed alio respiciens. Hic uero non tam id agit, ut doceat uxorem legi obnoxiam esse quoad uir eius uixerit, qua in re forsan minus erat controuersię, quàm ut refricet mulieri ui duæ illicitū non esse, si mortuo priore uiro alteri se iunxerit. Nec putabit quisquā hac Apostoli solicitudinem præter rationem esse, si consideret, quid pleriq; doctores de secundis nuptijs tanquam illicitis respuendis tradiderint, é quorum numero est Tertullianus, qui in libro de Monogamia locum hunc Apostoli ita eneruat: ut dicat de his uiduis intelligendum qui priores maritos in fide Christi non habue-
units.tr: "A wife is bound by law." He mentions this also in Romans 7, but looking to something else. Here, however, he is not so much concerned to teach that a wife is subject to the law as long as her husband lives, a point in which there was perhaps less controversy, as to restore to the woman the sense that it is not unlawful for her, once her former husband has died, to join herself to another. Nor will anyone think that this anxiety of the Apostle is without reason, if he considers what many teachers have handed down about second marriages as things to be rejected as unlawful, among whom is Tertullian, who in his book on Monogamy so weakens this passage of the Apostle as to say that it must be understood of those widows who did not have their former husbands in the faith of Christ, and that second marriages are lawful when they are within the faith of the first.

units.la: rint, & secundas nuptias licitas esse, quæ in fide primæ sint. Verum nihil huius meminit Apostolus. Sunt hominis huius inanes cogitationes. Concilium postea Epaunense, cap.32. illicitas nuptias uocat, si relicta sacerdotis denuo nubat, iubetq; & maritum & uxorem à communione ecclesiastica arceri, donec separentur.
units.tr: But the Apostle makes no mention of any such thing. These are the empty imaginings of that man. Afterwards the Council of Epaone, canon 32, calls marriages unlawful if a woman, having been left by a priest, marries again, and orders both the husband and the wife to be kept from ecclesiastical communion until they are separated.

units.la: Quodam alio concilio mandatum est sacerdotibus, ut nec benedicat secundas nuptias, nec ad prandia illarum uocari se sinant. Prouidus est spiritus sanctus, atq; ideo opus fore putauit ut per os Apost. ea de re uel fidelibus consuleret, quid cōtētiosi & superstitiosi tentaturi essent. Arbitror aut multū hac in re tenebrarū offudisse abusum unius dictionis digamiæ. Digamia erat, quādo simul duę habebantur uxores, qd & hodie apud Turcos cōsuetudinis esse dicūt: polygamia, quādo plures: monogamia, quādo una tātū. Postea abusiue cœpit digam haberi, si quis mortua priore secundā ducat: & polygamus, qui sæpius priorib. uita defunctis matrimonium iterat: & monogamus, qui semel tantum in uita nubit. Hinc factum esse puto, ut horror prioris digamiæ per errorem sit in alienam hanc translatus. Veteres nolebant idq; ex præscripto Pauli, digamum ordinari in presbyterum aut diaconum, qui scilicet duas simul uxores habuerit. Postea translatum est & ad eos, qui duas non simul, sed morte intercedente habuerūt: ita scilicet factum est, ut uè re monogamus habitus sit & hodie habeatur pro digamo, cum nihil sit minus. Non potest Ecclesia dici duos habere episcopos, quę mor tuo priore alterius utitur successione: & quomodo potest mulier uocari digama, quæ priore uiro per mortem ablato, uni alteri iungitur.
units.tr: By another council it was commanded to priests that they should neither bless second marriages nor allow themselves to be invited to the feasts of such. The Holy Spirit is provident, and therefore thought it needful that through the mouth of the Apostle he should give counsel to the faithful on this matter, lest the contentious and superstitious should make trial of it. I suppose that the abuse of the single word "digamy" has spread much darkness in this matter. Digamy was when two wives were held at the same time, which they also say is customary among the Turks today; polygamy when several; monogamy when only one. Afterwards the term "digamist" began to be applied abusively to anyone who married again after the first wife had died, and "polygamist" to one who repeatedly remarried after former wives had died, and "monogamist" to one who married only once in his life. Hence I think it came about that the horror of the former digamy was transferred by mistake to this other case. The ancients did not want (and this was by Paul's prescription) a digamist to be ordained as elder or deacon, that is, one who had evidently had two wives at the same time. Afterwards this was extended also to those who had two not at the same time, but with one dying in between; and so it came about that one who is in fact a monogamist was and is still today held to be a digamist, although nothing is less so. The Church cannot be said to have two bishops when, after the death of the former, she makes use of another successor; and how can a woman be called a digamist, who, once her former husband has been taken away by death, is joined to one other man?

units.la: AD cui uelit nubendum. Hoc quadrat de uiduis, de uirginibus non item. Nam illæ sunt adhuc in potestate maiorū. Ambrosius eo refert, ut intelligamus coactas dānari nuptias.
units.tr: "To whom she wishes to marry." This fits widows; it does not fit virgins, for they are still in the power of their elders. Ambrose refers it to this, that we may understand that marriages forced upon them are condemned.

units.la: MODO in domino. hoc est, cum fideli mārito. Suprà uoluit dirimi impar coiugium, hic non uult, cum uitari possit, iniri. Ita & lex præcipit. Deut.5. Nemo det locum hic ineptis hominibus, qui illud modo in Domino, de spiritalibus nuptijs cum Domino ineundis exponere conantur, ut habeant quo superstitionē suam tueantur.
units.tr: "Only in the Lord": that is, with a believing husband. Above he wished an unequal marriage to be dissolved; here he does not wish it to be entered into, since it can be avoided. So also the law commands (Deut. 5). Let no room be given here to foolish men who attempt to expound that "only in the Lord" as concerning spiritual marriages to be entered into with the Lord, so that they may have something with which to defend their superstition.

units.la: ATTAMEN beatior est. Nō coram Deo, sed in hac uita. Non enim inter coniugium & uiduitatem discernit, ut habeant coram Deo, sed quomodo in hac uita statu alter altero commodior & pacatior sit admonet.
units.tr: "Yet she is happier." Not before God, but in this life. For he does not distinguish between marriage and widowhood as to standing before God, but reminds us how in this life one state is more convenient and more peaceful than the other.

units.la: ÓPINOR autem, quod & ipse spiritū Dei habeā. Respicit contentiosos & arrogantes pseudoapostolos, qui de spiritus Dei reuelatione multum gloriabantur. Vnde non dicit simpliciter, qud spiritum Dei habeā: sed quod & ego spiritum Dei habeam. quasi dicat, Non minus de spiritu Dei & forsan aliquanto uerius gloriari possum, quàm isti, quos tantopere suspicitis.
units.tr: "I suppose that I too have the Spirit of God." He has in view the contentious and arrogant false apostles, who boasted much of the revelation of the Spirit of God. Hence he does not say simply, "that I have the Spirit of God," but "that I too have the Spirit of God," as if to say: I can boast of the Spirit of God no less, and perhaps somewhat more truly, than those whom you so greatly admire.

units.la: CAPVT
units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Aeterum de his qui simulacris immolātur, scimus, quōd oēs scientiam habemus. Scientia inflat, charitas uero ædificat. Quod si quis uidetur aliquid scire, nondum quicquā nouit, quemadmodum scire oportet. At si quis diligit Deū, hic cognitus est ab illo.
units.tr: Now concerning those things which are sacrificed to idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone thinks he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, he is known by him.

units.la: Per libertatem quidlibet edēdi peccabatur. Inter Christianos plurimū ab ijs, qui reliquis uidebantur fide & scientia rerum potiores. Idq; dupliciter. Partim ita ut offenderetur, qui ex Iudaeis Christianismo accesserant, quorum conscientię adhuc imbecilles & legi nonnihil obnoxiæ interdictis à lege cibis abstinebant. De illo admonuit Ro. ca. 14. Partim ad offensionem eorū & lęsionē qui erat ex Gentib. Id fiebat per eos, qui absq; ulla fratrū imbecillū ratione simulacrorum sacrificijs sese admiscebant, etsi nō sacrificātes cū sacrificantib. Gentibus, cum uescentib. tū, & in epulo simulacrorū accūben tib. unà accumbentes, & ijs quæ simulacris oblata erant uescētes. Qua in re & Gentes in errore cōfirmabantur & imbecilles Christiani uel offendebantur, uel ad id exēpli impari scientia & fiducia, imò contra conscientiā allicebātur, unde haud parū de decoris & offensaculi Christianę professioni generabatur. Adoritur itaq; & istorum temeritatē Apost. ca. præsenti, admonetq; fortiores, ut magis ad ędificationem per charitatem, liberate Christiana, quā ad destructionem per scientiā, utantur. Tractat autē hāc causam conspicuis argumētis, nihil obscuri habentibus, & pleraq; sumpto de se exemplo, deinde & de casu ueterū, cautionis gratia immissum. Neq; enim hunc tractatum isto cap. absoluit, sed in decimū usq; protēdit, ut uidebimus.
units.tr: Through liberty to eat whatever they liked, they were sinning. This happened especially among Christians, by those who seemed to be superior to the rest in faith and knowledge. And this in two ways. Partly in such a way that offence was given to those who had come to Christianity from the Jews, whose consciences were still weak and somewhat bound to the law, and who abstained from foods forbidden by the law. Of this he admonished in Romans chapter 14. Partly the offence and harm were done to those who came from the Gentiles. This happened through those who, without any regard for the weakness of their brothers, mixed themselves with the sacrifices to idols, not indeed sacrificing with the sacrificing Gentiles, but eating with the eating Gentiles, reclining together with them at the feast of the idols, and eating the things that had been offered to idols. In this matter the Gentiles were confirmed in their error, and weak Christians were either offended or, through such an example, were enticed by a knowledge and confidence they lacked, indeed against their conscience; whence no small disgrace and stumbling-block arose for the profession of the Christian faith. The Apostle therefore attacks the rashness of these men in this chapter, and he admonishes the stronger to use Christian liberty more for building up through love than for destruction through knowledge. He treats this cause with clear arguments, having nothing obscure, and for the most part with an example taken from himself, and then also from the fall of the ancients, introduced for the sake of caution. For he does not finish this topic in this chapter, but extends it to the tenth, as we shall see.

units.la: CAETERVM de his, quę simulacris immolantur. Græcè est, περὶ τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων. Græ cę linguæ ignari arbitrantur discriminis aliqd esse inter ea quæ Græci εἴδωλα, & quę Latini simulacra uocant, atque ob eam rationem inter eidolatriā quoq; & simulacrorum cultū discriminant: ab eidolis & eidololatria quidē abstinendum putantes, à simulacrorū uero cultu & honore non item. Cum per omnia idem sint εἴδωλον & simulacrum, εἰδωλολατρία & simulacrorum cultus. Eidola intelligunt de dijs Gentiū, per simulacra uero & imagines putant nō nisi sanctorū pictūras & statuas significari. Belli homines mentem scripturæ, imo spiritussanƈti in scripturis non intelligunt, ubi prohibetur cultura eidolorum, putantq; eam tantū speciem impietatis phiberi, quę apud Gētes inualuit, atq; ideo secure in ipsissimā eidolatriā ruunt. εἰδωλόθυτα uocat Apost. ea quę in sacris & cultu eidolorum sacrificandi gratia mactabātur & offerebantur. Non quod Gētes eidolis tanquā eidolis cultū illū sacrificiorū exhibuerint (nō enim simulacris, sed dijs quorū uenerabantur simulacra, oblationes suas destinabat) sed qd in simulacris deorum deos coluerint. Ob eam rationē εἰδωλόθυτα uocat, quæ opinione Getium pro sacrificijs habebātur. Huius propterea admoneo, ut uideamus nullam esse excusationem eorum: qui, quem imaginibus sanctorū cultū impendunt, εἰδωλολατρίαν uocari nolint, eo quod in tētiō ipsorum non sit ad imagines, sed ad sanctos uel ad Deum ipsum, cuius uenerātur imaginem. Hac ratione & Iudei & Gentes negare potuissent, simulacris offerri, q offerebat dijs. Verū spiritussanctus in Apostolo nō mentitur, ubi dijs oblata εἰδωλόθυτα uocat. Quanquā ne sic quidem excusantur simulacrorum cultores. Neq; enim sacrificandū est nisi Deo soli, neq; id aliter quàm iuxta ipsius uerbū. Est autē uerbo Dei prohibitū, ne ad honorem ipsius & cultum fiant simulacra, contra quod mandatū ex presse delinquunt simulacrorum cultores.
units.tr: "Concerning those things which are sacrificed to idols." In Greek it is "peri tōn eidōlothytōn" [περὶ τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων]. Those ignorant of the Greek language suppose there is some difference between those things the Greeks call "eidōla" and those the Latins call "simulacra," and for this reason they distinguish between idolatry and the worship of images: they think that one should abstain from idols and idolatry, but not necessarily from the worship and honour of images. Yet "eidōlon" and "simulacrum" are in every respect the same, and "eidōlolatreia" and "the worship of images" are the same. They understand "eidola" to mean the gods of the Gentiles, but think that by "simulacra" and "images" only the paintings and statues of the saints are meant. Foolish men do not understand the mind of Scripture, or rather the mind of the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures, where the worship of idols is forbidden; they think that only that kind of impiety is forbidden which prevailed among the Gentiles, and so they rush headlong into the very idolatry without fear. The Apostle calls "eidōlothyta" [εἰδωλόθυτα] those things which were slaughtered and offered in the sacred rites and for the sake of the worship of idols. Not that the Gentiles offered that sacrificial worship to the idols as idols (for they directed their offerings not to the images but to the gods whom the images represented), but that in the images of the gods they worshipped the gods. For this reason he calls them "eidōlothyta," which by the opinion of the Gentiles were held to be sacrifices. Therefore I admonish that we should see there is no excuse for those who, while they pay worship to images of the saints, are unwilling to have it called idolatry, on the ground that their intention is not directed to the images but to the saints or to God himself, whose image they venerate. By this reasoning both the Jews and the Gentiles could have denied that things were offered to images, since they offered them to the gods. But the Holy Spirit does not lie in the Apostle, when he calls things offered to the gods "eidōlothyta." Yet even so the worshippers of images are not excused. For sacrifice is to be made to God alone, and not otherwise than according to his own Word. Now it is forbidden by the Word of God that images be made for his honour and worship, and against this command the worshippers of images plainly offend.

units.la: SCIMVS, quod oēs scientiā habemus. Hic locus potest exponi bifariā. Primū ut illud, scimus, intelligamus de scientia Apost. quę se dicat haud ignorare, scientiā de eidolorū uanitate passim obtinere inter Christianos. Deinde, ut generaliter pertineat ad oēs Christianos, illud scimus, quasi dicat: De eidolothytis, quæ illorū sit ratio & inanitas, satis habemus scientiæ, nō sumus ignari, sed scientes. Habemus enim oēs eā scientiā per ueritatis doctrinā instructi. Itaq; priore sensu, illud scimus expositorie per qd legendū est, ut ostēdat qd se dicat scire Apost. Altero uero rationaliter adiectū est pro Nam, uel, quoniā: ut reddatur ratio, quare Christianis tribuat eidolothytorū scientiā. Ob id uideli cet, qd Christianis passim per ueritatē reuelata uanitas eidolorū innotuerit. Prior tū expositio uidetur simplicior. Vt ut legam, Apost. in hoc est, ut scientię gloriatione arrogantib. & Christiana libertate abutentib. excutiat. Erat enim illa mali huius ueluti fons quidā. Arrogā tiam enim scientię, nō ipsam scientiā passim inter Corinthios obtinuisse satis indicatur infrā, ubi dicit: Sed nō in omnib. est scientia. Proinde illud, qd omnes scientiā habemus, ironice uidetur esse dictū, ad notandū studiū & ostētatione scientię. Sic illud, Scribimus indocti doctiq; poemata passim. Certe non oēs poemata scribebat. Verū quoniā studiū & ostētatio scribedorū poematū passim inualuerat, uisū est poetæ eam stultitiā hac loquutionis formula notare.
units.tr: "We know that we all have knowledge." This place can be explained in two ways. First, that we understand "we know" as referring to the knowledge of the Apostle, who says that he is not ignorant that the knowledge of the vanity of idols prevails everywhere among Christians. Second, that "we know" applies generally to all Christians, as if he said: concerning things sacrificed to idols, we have enough knowledge of their nature and emptiness; we are not ignorant but knowing. For all of us have this knowledge, having been instructed in the doctrine of the truth. So in the former sense "we know" must be read as an explanatory clause, to show what the Apostle says that he knows. In the latter sense it is added as a reason, in place of "for" or "since," so that a reason is given why he attributes to Christians the knowledge of things sacrificed to idols: namely, because the vanity of idols has become known to Christians everywhere through the revealed truth. Yet the former explanation seems simpler. Whichever reading we follow, the Apostle's purpose is to shake off those who boast arrogantly in knowledge and abuse Christian liberty. For that was, as it were, a kind of source of this evil. That the arrogance of knowledge, and not knowledge itself, prevailed everywhere among the Corinthians is sufficiently indicated below, where he says: "But not all have knowledge." Therefore the words "we all have knowledge" seem to be said ironically, to mark the zeal and ostentation for knowledge. So it is in the line: "We write poems, learned and unlearned, everywhere." Certainly not everyone wrote poems; but since the zeal and display of writing poems had prevailed everywhere, the poet seemed to mark that folly by this form of speech.

units.la: Nota qd nō dicit habetis, sed habemus, ne apertius mordeat. Ideo quasi seipsum quoq; immiscet, ut quod dicturus est, non Corinthijs solū, sed & sibijpsi dicere uideatur, quo tolerabilior sit correptio.
units.tr: Note that he does not say "you have," but "we have," so that he may not bite too openly. Therefore he mixes himself in as well, so that what he is about to say seems to be said not only to the Corinthians but also to himself, and the rebuke may be more tolerable.

units.la: SCIENTIA inflat, charitas uero ędificat. A præpostero scientię studio auocat ad id quod bonū est. A scientia nō auocat, sed à puerso illius studio. Alioq; scientia per se bona est, & donū Dei, quod multis modis ad gloriā Dei & mortalium salutem facere potest, si rectus usus accedat. Proinde pigri illi & ignaui homines, qui inuidentiæ stimulis agitati, bonas scientias literarum studium sugillant, nullâ liuoris fui ansam ex Apostoli uerbis habere possunt. Nā ut recte colligit Augustinus lib. aduersus Faustum Manichæum 15. cap. 8. si scientiā veritatis damnaret Apostolus, utiq; seipsum quoque damnaret. Nam & se inter scientes hoc loco connumerat, non solum in eo quod dicit quod omnes scientiam habemus, sed & quod ipsam ei dolo rum inaniū, & unius Dei ac domini cognitionem tā dilucide ponit. Et 2. Cor. 11. dicit. Nam etsi imperitus sum sermone, non tamen scientia. Imo non solum non damnat scientiā, sed illam etiam in Iudæorū zelo desiderat, cū dicit: Testimoniū illis perhibeo, quod zelum quidem Dei habent, sed nō secundum scientiam. Optabat igitur Iudæorū zelo scientiæ lumen accedere. uidebat enim illos ob id in veritate Dei delinquere, & propriæ saluti repugnare, quod scientia veritatis destituti essent. Et Ro. in eo commendat, quod repleti erant omni scientia. Et in hac ipsa Epistola gratias agit Deo propter Corinthios, quod in omni scientia diuites essent facti. Et alibi dicit scriptura: Quia tu repulisti scientiam, repellā & ego te. Et, Qui ignorat ignoret. Et infrà 14. Ftatres, nolite pueri effici sensibus, sed malicia paruuli estote, sensibus autem perfecti sitis. Itaq; non scientiam Apost. hoc loco dānat, sed peruersum illius studiū & usum.
units.tr: "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up." He calls them away from a perverted zeal for knowledge to what is good; he does not call them away from knowledge, but from the perverse zeal for it. Otherwise knowledge in itself is good, and a gift of God, which can serve in many ways for the glory of God and the salvation of mortals, if its right use is added. Therefore those lazy and idle men, who, driven by the goads of envy, disparage the study of good learning, can have no pretext for their spite from the words of the Apostle. For, as Augustine rightly infers in book 15, chapter 8, against Faustus the Manichaean, if the Apostle condemned the knowledge of the truth, he would certainly condemn himself also. For he counts himself among those who have knowledge in this place, not only in saying "we all have knowledge," but also in setting forth so clearly the knowledge of the vanity of idols and of the one God and Lord. And in 2 Corinthians 11 he says: "For though I am untrained in speech, yet I am not in knowledge." Indeed he not only does not condemn knowledge, but even desires it among the zeal of the Jews, when he says: "I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge." He therefore wished that the light of knowledge would be added to the zeal of the Jews; for he saw that they sinned against the truth of God and opposed their own salvation because they lacked the knowledge of the truth. And in Romans he commends them because they were filled with all knowledge. And in this same Epistle he gives thanks to God for the Corinthians, because they had become rich in all knowledge. And elsewhere Scripture says: "Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you." And: "Let him who does not know, not know." And below, in chapter 14: "Brethren, do not become children in understanding, but be infants in malice, and in understanding be mature." Therefore the Apostle in this place condemns not knowledge, but its perverse zeal and use.

units.la: DE PERVERSO SCIENTIÆ STUDIO.
units.tr: ON THE PERVERSE STUDY OF KNOWLEDGE.

units.la: Omnib. id mortalibus agnatum est, ut verā scientiam appetāt. Obseruauit illud in natura mortaliū Philosophus ex certis sensuū nostrorū indicijs, maxime ex uisu. Ita enim comparati sumus, ut oia uidere cupiamus ob id potissimū, quod hic sensus magnā nobis rerū cognitionē & multū discriminis adferre soleat. Verū unde sit in nobis ista scientiæ cupiditas, uidere nō potuit, quia veritatis p sanctā scripturā traditę expers fuit. Nos aut illā scimus nobis, ex primorū parentū transgressione, degustata arbore scientię boni & mali, per carnis successionē hęreditarie indita. Præuidebat spiritus Dei istam cupiditatē scientię boni & mali noxiā fore generi humano, atq; ob id gustū arboris illius uetu it. Hactenus tñ nobis seruit Philosophus, quod morbū hūc in mortalibus obseruat & prodit.
units.tr: All mortals have an innate desire to seek true knowledge. The philosopher observed this in human nature from the clear signs given by our senses, above all sight. We are so made that we want to see everything, chiefly because this sense usually brings us a great deal of knowledge and much power of discernment. But where this desire for knowledge in us comes from, he could not see, since he lacked the truth handed down in holy Scripture. We know, however, that it has been implanted in us by hereditary descent through the flesh, from the transgression of our first parents, who tasted the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The Spirit of God foresaw that this desire for the knowledge of good and evil would be harmful to the human race, and for that reason forbade the eating of that tree. So far the philosopher has served us, in that he observes and reveals this disease in mortals.

units.la: Deinde, ut omnia mortaliū corrupta sunt, ita & studium illud cognoscendarū rerum corruptum est & peruersum. Huius autē peruersitas uidetur esse duplex.
units.tr: Then, just as everything in mortals is corrupted, so too that zeal for knowing things has been corrupted and perverted. Its perversity appears to be twofold.

units.la: 1 Prima, Quod quæ ad nos nihil pertinēt, & quæ nihil utilitatis adferunt, aut certe nō mnl tum conferunt, magis affectamus cognoscere quàm quorum cognitio nos cōcernit, & multum habet momēti. Hoc curiositatis nomine à doctis quidē passim traducitur & carpitur, sed non ita facile deponitur.
units.tr: (1) First, we are more eager to know things that have nothing to do with us and bring no benefit, or at least contribute little, than things whose knowledge concerns us and matters greatly. The learned commonly censure and criticise this under the name of curiosity, but it is not so easily laid aside.

units.la: 2 Altera est. Quod etiā quę cognoscēda sunt, & quorū scientia glorię Dei & nostræ saluti seruire poterat, nō in eū fine discimus, ut illorum scientiā ipso opere bene collocemus, sed ut tā-
units.tr: (2) The second is this: even the things that ought to be known, and whose knowledge could serve the glory of God and our salvation, we learn not for this end, that we may put that knowledge to good use in our conduct, but only that we may know, and seem to be someone above others.

units.la: tū sciamus, & aliquid præ alijs esse uideamur. Pulchrum & gloriosum est, rerū diuinarum & humanarū haberi scientē. Habet enim ista scientia nonnihil diuinitatis. Eritis sicut dij, aiebat serpens, scientes bonū & malum. Ideo stupidi & rectè ignari bestiarū irrationaliū loco habeti solent. Hinc fit, ut sapientes penè deorum loco habeantur. Et qui aliquid in mundo uideri uolunt, non tam de ingenij malicia, & uitę corruptione, quâ de errorū obiectu uerecundantur, quod in nostri temporis sacrificis & episcopis apertum est. Vitæ prauitatē & uanitatē non diffitentur, errasse uideri nolunt.
units.tr: It is fine and glorious to be thought learned in divine and human matters. Such knowledge has something of divinity in it. "You will be like gods, knowing good and evil," said the serpent. Therefore the stupid and the wholly ignorant are commonly regarded as no better than irrational beasts, and the wise are almost regarded as gods. Those who want to seem to be something in the world are less ashamed of the malice of their wit and the corruption of their lives than of being shown to be in error. This is obvious in the sacrificing priests and bishops of our own time. They do not deny the depravity and vanity of their lives, but they do not want to seem to have erred.

units.la: Huc respicit Apostolus, cū dicit, Scientia inflat. Itellige primum, propter ingenij nostri corruptionem, non ex culpa scientiæ. Ita quip pe peruersi sumus, ut quod in se bonum est, & prodesse poterat, nostro uicio obsit. Et diuitiæ bonæ sunt. Attamen & ipsæ inflant. Sic Germani dicimus, Guot macht muot. Suo tamen uicio non hoc faciunt, sed nostro. Alioqui Deus qui omnium est ditisimus, omnium esset inflatisimus. Si scientia per se inflaret, quo quisque esset doctior, hoc esset etiam inflatior. Verum reperias innumeros indoctos sciolos, qui doctorib. multo sint inflatiores. Quare? Quia non scientia per se, sed magis opinio scientię in flat. 2. Cor. 3. dicit Apost. litera occidit. Loquitur aut de literali scientia legis. Quomodo illa occidit? Non suo, sed carnis nostræ uicio. Vtenim lex p carnē infirmatur, ita & per carnē ad mortē facit, quę data era t ad uitā. Tale scilicet est, quod & hoc loco dicit, Scientia inflat. Deinde intellige, si absit charitas: secus si illa accedat. Quemadmodū enim nec diuitiæ inflant, si adsit charitas, ne litera occidit, si accedat gratia spiritus, quæ uiuificat: ita certe nec scientia inflat, si charitas adsit. Libera potentia tyrannidem gignit. Verum, si desit amor erga populum. Is uero si accesserit, nō tyrannum reddit, sed patrē & populi iustissimum rectorem.
units.tr: The Apostle has this in view when he says, "Knowledge puffs up." Understand first that this is due to the corruption of our nature, not to any fault of knowledge. We are so perverse that what is good in itself and could benefit us is harmed by our vice. Riches are good, yet they too puff up. So we Germans say, Guot macht muot (wealth makes pride). Yet riches do not do this through their own fault, but through ours. Otherwise God, who is the richest of all, would be the most puffed up of all. If knowledge puffed up of itself, the more learned anyone was, the more puffed up he would be. Yet you will find countless half-learned smatterers who are far more puffed up than the teachers. Why? Because it is not knowledge in itself but the opinion of knowledge that puffs up. In 2 Corinthians 3 the Apostle says, "the letter kills." He speaks of the literal knowledge of the law. How does it kill? Not by its own fault, but by the fault of our flesh. For just as the law is weakened through the flesh, so through the flesh it brings about death, though it was given for life. This is the same kind of thing he says here: "Knowledge puffs up." Next, understand that this holds if love is absent, but not if love is present. For just as riches do not puff up when love is present, and the letter does not kill when the grace of the Spirit, which gives life, is added, so knowledge certainly does not puff up if love is present. Liberty without love begets tyranny; but if love for the people is present, it makes a ruler not a tyrant but a father and the most just governor of the people.

units.la: CHARITAS ædificat. Innuit Corinthios maiore scientię studio q; charitatis inflatos, parum curasse fratrū ædificationē. Ideo reiecta in flatione quę est per opinionē scientię, admonet eos charitatis. De illa nominatim infrà cap. 13. tractabit, quo loco ingeniū illius uidebimus.
units.tr: "Love builds up." He hints that the Corinthians, puffed up with a greater zeal for knowledge than for love, had little concern for the building up of their brothers. So, having rejected the puffing up that comes from the opinion of knowledge, he admonishes them about love. He will treat love by name below, in chapter 13, where we shall see its nature.

units.la: 1 Quantū præsens locus exigit, primū obser uandum est, quod nō dicit, Charitas uero non inflat: uel, charitas humiliat, ut inflatiōis uicio oppositā uirtute charitati tribuat: sed charitas ædificat. Quo uerbo metaphorico ostēdit, nō hoc se tantū requirere, ut abiecto fastu sint hu miles, sed ut alius aliū in Christo per charitatē quæ non quæ sua, sed quæ aliorū sunt, quærit, ꝑuehant & quotidie magis atq; magis confirmēt. Sumꝰ enim, ut supra dixit, Dei ædificatio.
units.tr: (1) As far as the present passage requires, it must first be observed that he does not say "love, however, does not puff up," or "love humbles," so as to assign to love a virtue opposed to the vice of puffing up. He says "love builds up." By this metaphorical word he shows that he is not asking only that, with pride laid aside, they be humble, but that each seek the good of the other in Christ through love, which does not seek its own but what belongs to others, so that they may be carried forward and strengthened more and more each day. For, as he said above, we are God's building.

units.la: 2 Deinde & hoc notandū est, quod ista ædificatio locum habere non potest, ubi regnat animorum inflatio. Nam ita charitati dat ædificationem, ut inflationi illam adimat. Imo illa no solū nō ædificat, sed magis, ut infrà patebit, destruit. Oppositā sunt, ædificare & destruere.
units.tr: (2) Next, this too is to be noted: this building cannot take place where the swelling of minds reigns. For he gives building to love in such a way that he takes it away from puffing up. Indeed puffing up not only does not build, but, as will become clear below, rather destroys. Building and destroying are opposites.

units.la: Et quoniam ista, scientia inflat, charitas uero aedificat, per modū oppositionis positafunt, nihil aliud potest colligi, q; ut scientiae inflatrici detur destructio, queadmodū charitati humili atrici ędificatio. Opposita non sunt, scientia & charitas, absit. Sed inflari scientia, & charitate humiliari, ea demū oppositiōis uí habēt. Certū igitur est ecclesiā Christi nulla ratiōe magis de strui, q; inflatiōe, siue illa sit ex opiniōe inanis glorię, siue ex potestate & authoritate supra re liquos, uel ex diuitijs: aut, uthic dicit, ex sciētia
units.tr: Since "knowledge puffs up" and "love builds up" are set in opposition, nothing else can be inferred than that destruction is to be assigned to puffing-up knowledge, just as building up is to be assigned to humbling love. Knowledge and love are not opposed, far from it. But knowledge that puffs up and love that humbles are the only things that have the force of opposition. It is certain, therefore, that the Church of Christ is by no means more destroyed than by puffing up, whether it comes from the opinion of empty glory, or from power and authority over others, or from riches, or, as here, from knowledge.

units.la: 3 Tertio, Cauendum tū hic est, ne ita demus charitati ędificatiōne ut scientiā excludamus. Vt enim scientia sine charitate inflat, ita charitas sine scientia humiliat quidē, & suauem reddit erga fratres affectū, ad ędificādi tū opus assurgere non potest. Imò magis nocebit ubi potissimum iuuare & ædificare conatur, nisi cognouerit, quid faciendum, quid non sit.
units.tr: (3) Thirdly, care must be taken here not to give love the building up in such a way that we exclude knowledge. Just as knowledge without love puffs up, so love without knowledge indeed humbles and makes our affection towards the brethren sweet, but it cannot rise to the work of building. Indeed it will do the most harm precisely where it most tries to help and build, unless it has learned what must be done and what must not.

units.la: Q V O D si quis uidetur aliquid scire.] Expo nit p mitam gnomen. Et primū eā parte, quadi xit, scientia inflat. Ad eā pertinet quod hic subijcit: Quod si quis uidetur aliquid scire, nōdū quicquā nouit, quemadmodū oporteat scire.
units.tr: "If anyone seems to know something." He explains himself in a brief sentence, and first in the part where he said, "knowledge puffs up." To this belongs what he adds here: "If anyone seems to know something, he does not yet know anything as he ought to know."

units.la: In eo, quod non dicit, Quod si quis aliquid scit: sed, Quod si quis uidetur aliquid scire, ostendit se non de scientia, sed magis scientię, opinione dicere illiq; dare quod inflet. Est autē illud ἀ τῆς ἐπιστήμης, si quis uidetur, non ita legendū, ut inte l gamus eum nihil dū scire, & inflatum esse, qui alijs sapiēs esse uidetur, sed qui sibi ipsi uidetur aliquid scire. Vnde & Erasmus de B suo adiecit: sibi, cum in Græco non sit. Potest etiam ita legi: Si quis aliquid se scire gloriatur, ut non nuda opinione, sed magis gloriatione intelligas. Nam ἀοκῶ nō solū opinari, sed & gloriosus esse, φυσιοῦσθαι significat, unde sunt ἀυξῶ & ἀ ἰξῶ per oppositū. Si iste sensus placet, nihil aliud erit illud ἀ ἐπιστήμης ἀξίως ἀξίωσιν, quā repetitio eius quod dixit, scientia inflat. Quasi dicat: Si uero quisquā alicuius scientię gloriatione inflatur, sibiq; ipsi illius nomine placet. Et ista repetitio ad id instituta est, ut inflatis scientiæ ueritatē adimat, ostendatq; omnino inanem esse illorum gloriatione & inflatione. Hoc est, quod addit, nihil dū nouit, id est, nondū ipsam scientiā de qua gloriatur, apprehendit. Imò amplius aliquid dicit, dū omnē prosus illi scientiā aufert. Et quoniam id uidebatur durius, interpretandi gratia subiungit, quē admodū oportet scire. Nam reuera nihil scit, qui non scit sicut scire oportet. Quid est autem scire, quemadmodū oportet? Est rectē scientia uti. Abusus scientię, nō est uera scientia. Est autem abusus scientię Dei, illius gratia inflari & reliquos contemnere. Hoc est quod dicit, Qui aut gloriatur se quicquā scire, nihil dū nouit, sicut scire oportet. Rectus uero scientiæ usus est, ut ad suum quæq; sciētia finē dirigatur. Est enim cuiq; arti finis suus. Vt scientię medendi finis est, ægroti corporis restitutio: scientię ædificādi, structura domus. Ita in regno Dei scientiæ Dei finis est, Deum diligere & illi per dile-
units.tr: In that he does not say, "If anyone knows something," but, "If anyone seems to know something," he shows that he is speaking not of knowledge but of the opinion of knowledge, and of what gives it its puffing up. The phrase "if anyone seems" [εἴ τις δοκεῖ] should not be read so as to mean that he who seems wise to others, and is puffed up, knows nothing yet; rather it means he who seems to himself to know something. Hence Erasmus also added "to himself" in his translation, though it is not in the Greek. It can also be read thus: "If anyone boasts that he knows something," so that you understand not mere opinion but rather boasting. For the verb [δοκεῖ] signifies not only to think but also to be puffed up [φυσιοῦσθαι], whence come the opposites [ἐπαίρεσθαι] and [ἐπαίρω]. If this sense pleases, then the phrase "if anyone seems to know anything" will be nothing other than a repetition of what he said, "knowledge puffs up," as if he were saying: "But if anyone is puffed up by the boasting of some knowledge, and is pleased with himself on account of it." This repetition is designed to take away from the puffed-up person the truth of his knowledge, and to show that their boasting and puffing up is wholly empty. This is what he adds: "he does not yet know," that is, he has not yet grasped the very knowledge of which he boasts. Indeed he says something more, since he takes all knowledge away from him altogether. And because this seemed too harsh, he adds, for the sake of explanation, "as he ought to know." For in truth he knows nothing who does not know as he ought to know. But what does it mean to know as one ought? It is to use knowledge rightly. The abuse of knowledge is not true knowledge. Now it is an abuse of the knowledge of God to be puffed up by it and to despise the rest. This is what he means: "But whoever boasts that he knows anything does not yet know as he ought to know." The right use of knowledge, however, is that each kind of knowledge is directed to its own end, for every art has its own end. The end of the science of healing is the restoration of the sick body; the end of the science of building is the structure of a house. So in the kingdom of God the end of the knowledge of God is to love God and to be united with him and saved through that love. Therefore, just as whoever does not use medicine for the health of the body does not know medicine as he ought, so certainly whoever does not yet use his knowledge of spiritual things

units.la: ctionē adunari & saluari.
