Vt igitur medicinam non nouit ut oportet, quisquis illa non ad corporum sanitatē utitur: ita certē nec scientiā rerum spiritualium rectā ac ueram habet, quisquis illa nō adhuc utitur, ut Deo seruiatur, & illius uoluntati studeatur, in quo uera salus est, & scientię Dei finis. Etenim si mundanæ istæ scientiæ non à nudis & ociosis opinionib. sed ab ipsarum finibus æstimantur, quanto magis hoc in scientia Dei spectandum est.
units.tr: through love to be united and saved. Therefore, as one does not know medicine as he ought if he does not use it for the health of the body, so surely one does not have a right and true knowledge of spiritual things if he does not yet use it to serve God and to seek his will, in which true salvation lies and the goal of the knowledge of God. For if these worldly sciences are judged not by bare and idle opinions but by their ends, how much more must this be considered in the knowledge of God.

units.la: A T si quis diligit Deum, hic cognitus est ab illo. ] Debebat dicere, At si quis Deum nouit, quemadmodū scire oportet, hic cognitus est ab illo. Ergo cum dicit, At si quis diligit Deū: innuit, Deum diligere, esse uerā Dei scientiam habere. Et rectē. Est enim finis diuinæ cognitionis, dilectio Dei. Itaq;, qui non diligit Deū, nec in Deo proximum, quicquid scire uideatur rerum diuinarū, etiā si omnē scientiam habeat, ut infrà ca. 13. dicturus est, planē nihil scit. Deum aut non diligit, qui opinione scientiæ inflatur. Nam arrogantia & fratrum contemtus non est scientiæ Dei finis.
units.tr: BUT if anyone loves God, this one is known by him. He ought to have said: "But if anyone knows God, as he ought to know him, this one is known by him." So when he says, "But if anyone loves God," he implies that to love God is to have true knowledge of him. And rightly so, for the love of God is the goal of divine knowledge. Therefore whoever does not love God, nor his neighbour in God, whatever he seems to know of divine things, even if he has all knowledge, as he is going to say below in chapter 13, knows plainly nothing. Indeed, whoever is puffed up with the opinion of knowledge does not love God, for arrogance and contempt of the brothers is not the goal of the knowledge of God.

units.la: Quid est autē, quod dicit, hic cognitus est ab illo? Particula ista uarie exponitur. Ex Ambrosio & Hieronymo, nihil potest elici, quod ad illius expositionem faciat.
units.tr: But what is meant by the words, "this one is known by him"? This phrase is explained in various ways. From Ambrose and Jerome nothing can be drawn that bears on its explanation.

units.la: 1 Erasmus in paraphrasi, Theophylactum se quutus uidetur, cui à Deo cognitū esse idē est, atq; notum illi & familiare esse factū: hoc est, Deo approbari diligentem se. Iam quoniam propositum Apostoli est dicere, quis sit, qui ue ram Dei scientiam habeat: non, qui à Deo cognoscatur uel probetur, uidetur debuisse dicere, hic nouit illum.
units.tr: (1) Erasmus in his paraphrase seems to have followed Theophylact, for whom "to be known by God" is the same as to be known to him and to have become familiar to him, that is, that the one who loves is approved by God. Now since the Apostle's purpose is to say who it is that has true knowledge of God, and not who is known or approved by God, he seems to have ought to have said, "this one knows him."

units.la: 2 Sunt qui putant idē esse atq;, hic instructus est ab illo ut ueram ipsius scientiā habeat. Atq; neq; hoc agit Apostolus ut doceat unde fit, sed quæ sit uera scientia Dei.
units.tr: (2) There are those who think it means the same as: "this one is instructed by him, so as to have true knowledge of him." But the Apostle is not doing this to teach where it comes from, but what true knowledge of God is.

units.la: 3 Philippus arbitratur Apostolum suo more mutata ratione grammatica dicere uoluisse, hic cognoscit Deum.
units.tr: (3) Philip thinks that the Apostle, changing the grammatical construction in his usual way, wanted to say, "this one knows God."

units.la: 4 Mihi uidetur ita legi posse: At si quis diligit Deū, ὑπ' αὐτοῦ γινώσκεται, i. ab eo cognitus est ille, id est Deus. Quod si ista lectionis copo sitio stare potest, simplex & ad προποsitū faciēs erit sententia. Staret aut meo iudiciō, confimi les loquendi formæ possent ostendi in literis Apostoli. Quanquā non multū est periculi, etiamsi cum Theophylacto intelligamus eū demū Deo probari, qui ipsum diligat. Atq; eo sensu nihil de scientia Dei cogitandū est, sed ad prę missæ gnomę posterioré parte respicendū, qua dixit, charitate ędificare: ut intelligamus illam duplici nomine cōmendari hoc loco. Vno, qui ad ędificationē fraternā faciat: altero, quod diligens Deo placeat, magis quam multiscius. Et ista charitatis commendatio non est extra argumenti huius προποsitum. Nam in eo est Apostolus, ut ab ostētatiōe scientię ad charitatē ędi ficante & Deo placetem Corinthios abducat.
units.tr: (4) It seems to me it can be read thus: "But if anyone loves God, he is known by him" [ὑπ' αὐτοῦ γινώσκεται], that is, he is known by him, namely God. If this combination of the reading can stand, the sense will be simple and suited to the proposition. In my judgment it would stand, since similar forms of speech could be shown in the Apostle's letters. Yet there is not much danger even if, with Theophylact, we understand that only the one who loves him is finally approved by God. And in that sense nothing is to be thought about the knowledge of God; rather, attention must be paid to the latter part of the preceding maxim, where he said "edification by love," so that we understand that love is commended in this place under a double title: first, because it serves the brotherly edification; second, because the one who loves pleases God more than the one who knows much. And this commendation of love is not outside the proposition of this argument. For the Apostle is concerned to lead the Corinthians away from the ostentation of knowledge to love, which edifies and pleases God.

units.la: Expedamus igitur hoc loco, qd de nostris tō porib. sentiendū fit, quibus scientia quide cum didiuinarū tum humanarū rerū in immēsum cre uit,charitas uero erga Deum & proximum ita refrixit, ut ne Gentium quidē humanitatem, & secularis amicitiæ officiositatem retinuerimus.Belle scilicet Deo placebimus multa scientes,cū id qd᷑ omniū est primariū negligamus.
units.tr: Let us therefore consider here what must be thought of our own times, in which knowledge, both of divine and of human things, has grown immensely, while love towards God and neighbour has so cooled that we have not even kept the humanity of the Gentiles and the courtesy of worldly friendship. Surely we will please God very well, knowing many things, while we neglect what is first of all.

units.la: De esu igit eorū quæ simulacris immolant, scimus, q̃ nihil est simulacrū in mundo, & quod nullus sit Deus alius, nisi unus.Nā etiāsi sunt q̃ dicātur dij, sive in cœlo siue in terra, quēadmodum sunt dij multi, & domini multi, nobis tñ est unus Deus, qui est pater ille, ex q̃ omnia, & nos in illū: & unus dns Iesus Christus, per quē omnia & nos per illū, sed non est in omnib.scientia. Nōnulli uero cū cōscientia simulacri, usq̃ ad hoc tempus tanq̃ simulacris immolatū edūt, et cōscientia illorū infirma cū sit polluitur.
units.tr: Concerning eating what is sacrificed to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no other God but one. For even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, as there are many gods and many lords, yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we unto him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him. But there is not knowledge in all. Some, however, with consciousness of the idol, even until now eat it as if it were sacrificed to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.

units.la: Hactenus Apostolus peruersam scientiæ gloriationē, quaCorinthiorū pleriq; insolescebāt, hoc nomine taxauit, quod sine charitate, quā negligebant, magis inflādo noceat q̃ prosit, cū charitas contrā & proximos ædificet & Deo gratos reddat.Nunc uero de qua scientia eidolothytorum loquatur declaraturus subijcit, τὴν τῶν βρωμάτων, &c. Suprā dixit, περὶ δὲ τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων οἴδαμεν ὅτι, hic repetēdo unica adiecta dictione τῶν βρωμάτων, ostendit Corinthios istos quos reprehendit, non in cultu eidolorum, sed in esu eorum, quæ eidolis immolabantur deliquisse.
units.tr: Hitherto the Apostle has censured by this name the perverse boasting in knowledge, in which many of the Corinthians were growing proud: that without love, which they neglected, it harms more by puffing up than it profits, whereas love, on the contrary, edifies neighbours and makes God favourable to us. Now, however, in order to explain what knowledge he is speaking of concerning things sacrificed to idols, he adds "[τὴν τῶν βρωμάτων]", etc. Above he said "[περὶ δὲ τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων οἴδαμεν ὅτι]"; here, repeating it with the single added word "of the foods" [τῶν βρωμάτων], he shows that these Corinthians whom he rebukes sinned not in the worship of idols but in eating those things which were sacrificed to idols.

units.la: S C I M V S, qd᷑ nihil est simulacrum in mundo.] Quomodo eidolothytorum esum scientiæ prætextu excusarint, ueluti ipsorū uerbis expri mit, & simul indicat, de qua scientia supra dixerit quam oēs habeant. Potest autē hęc particula bifariā legi & exponi. Aut, ut uet9 interpres habet: Quod nihil sit eidolū in mundo, uel ut Eraf.reddidit, qd᷑ nullū est simulacrū in mundo. Qd᷑ enim Græcè est εἴδωλον tā per nihil, quàm εἴδωλον ἀνυπαρκτον, id est, species quædam in qua nihil est ueritatis subsistentis, sed merū & inanē spectrum. Cum ergo nihil sit simulacrū, ex re certe nihili, ea quę simulacris offeruntur nihil possunt habere noxij. Si nihil habet noxij, cur illicitum esset illis uescī? Quo modo possent uescente polluere? Si uero legerimus: Scimus quod nullum est simulacrum in mundo, intelligendū nō ita est, quasi neget Apostolus in mundo esse & haberi simulacra, cū infinita fuerit & hodie sit illorum multitudo: sed quod nullum sit, quod ueri Dei sit simulacrum. Quam enim, inquit per prophetā Deus, similitudinem mihi ponetis? Ergo quæ simulacris offeruntur, meris figmentis offeruntur, quæ nihil habent ueri, nihil diuinitatis. Et hac
units.tr: WE KNOW that an idol is nothing in the world. Here he expresses, as it were in their own words, how they excused the eating of things sacrificed to idols under the pretext of knowledge, and at the same time he indicates which knowledge he meant above, the one that all have. This particle can be read and explained in two ways. Either, as the Vulgate translator has it, "that an idol is nothing in the world," or, as Erasmus rendered it, "that there is no image in the world." For the Greek word εἴδωλον means both "nothing" and "an unreal idol" [εἴδωλον ἀνυπαρκτον], that is, a kind of appearance in which there is nothing of subsisting truth, but a mere and empty phantom. Since therefore an image is nothing, and certainly comes from a thing of nothing, the things offered to images can have nothing harmful in them. If they have nothing harmful, why would it be unlawful to eat them? How could eating them pollute? If, however, we read, "We know that there is no image in the world," it is not to be understood as if the Apostle denied that images are in the world and are held there, since their multitude has been infinite and is still so today; rather, that there is none which is an image of the true God. For, says God through the prophet, "To what likeness will you liken me?" So the things offered to images are offered to mere fictions, which have nothing of truth and nothing of divinity. And by this

units.la: quoq; ratiōe nō possunt uescēte conspurcare.
units.tr: reasoning also they cannot defile by eating.

units.la: IN mundo.] Cauendū ne cœli distinctione positū esse putemus, quasi in cœlo sit simulacrū Dei. Habet magis uniuersitatis notā, ut intelligamus oia totius mundi simulacra uanitatis aut gui, idq; non eius tātum temporis, quo scribebat ista Apost.sed prīus omnium seculorū. Nihil sunt oia omnium tēporum, siue Iudaica, siue Gentilia, siue Christianorum simulacra.
units.tr: IN the world. We must take care not to think the words are placed with a contrast to heaven, as if there were an image of God in heaven. The phrase rather carries the mark of universality, so that we understand that all the images of the whole world are vanity or phantoms, and not only those of the time in which the Apostle was writing these things, but those of all the ages before. All images of all times, whether Jewish, Gentile or Christian, are nothing.

units.la: E T qd᷑ nullus sit Deus alius, nisi unus.] Hoc rationis uice adijcitur, quare nihil sit simulacrum quodcunq; in mundo. Quia unus est tantum Deus, nec est alius præter illū. Ergo Gētiū dij non sunt dij. Nullū igitur simulacrū diuinū aut Dei simulacrū est. Nā uero Deo nec licet, quia phibuit, nec possibile est aliqd᷑ ponere simulacrum. Quę aut dijs Gentium ponuntur, deorum simulacra esse non possunt, eo quod quorum simulacra sunt, dij non sint. Omnium itaq; potentissime simulacrorum cultum hoc loco prosternit, quod dicit nihil esse simulacrū in mundo, & rationem assignans addit, nō esse deum alium nisi unum.
units.tr: AND that there is no other God but one. This is added as a reason why there is no image whatever in the world. Because there is only one God, and there is none besides him, the gods of the Gentiles are not gods. Therefore no image is a divine image or an image of God. For it is neither permitted to make an image of God, since he has forbidden it, nor is it possible. But those things which are set up as the gods of the Gentiles cannot be images of gods, because those whose images they are are not gods. Thus in this place he most powerfully overthrows the worship of images when he says there is no image in the world, and, giving a reason, adds that there is no other God but one.

units.la: NAM etiam si sunt, qui dicantur dij.] Opinio multorum deorum passim obtinuerat. Illi re luctabatur hæc sententia, qua dixit, non esse ni si unū Deū. Ne ergo uideatur negare, quod omnibus erat notissimū, uidelicet multos habere deos, per distinctionē Christianorū fidem separat à Gentiū errore, & admonet aliud esse di ci multos deos, & aliud uere esse multos deos. Concedit quidem multos dici & haberi deos, sed per errorem, inter Gentes, reuera tū unum tantū esse uerū Deū affirmat, huiusq; cognitionem & fidē Christianis adscribit dicēs, nobis tamen unus est Deus. Notanter ergo dicit: Nā etiamsi sunt qui dicātur dij. Et quod sequitur, quemadmodū sunt dij multi, intelligēdum est iuxta præmissam particulam, multos dici & haberi deos, non autem esse.
units.tr: FOR even if there are those who are called gods. The opinion of many gods had prevailed everywhere, and this saying, in which he says there is only one God, struggles against it. So that he may not seem to deny what was known to all, namely that they have many gods, he separates the Christian faith from the error of the Gentiles by a distinction, and warns that it is one thing to be called many gods and another to be truly many gods. He does grant that many are called and held to be gods, but through error among the Gentiles; in reality he affirms that there is only one true God, and ascribes the knowledge and faith of him to Christians, saying, "yet for us there is one God." Notably, therefore, he says: "For even if there are those who are called gods." And what follows, "as there are many gods," is to be understood in accordance with the preceding particle: that they are called and held to be many gods, but are not.

units.la: S I V E in cœlo, siue in terra.] Duplex deorū genus à Gentib. cultum esse apparet. Cœlestium unum, terrestrium aliud. Per terrestres qui dam & inferos intelligunt, alioqui triplex erit Gentilium deorum genus. Illud, Siue in cœlo, Hieronymus intelligit de angelis, id est, cœlestibus spiritib. Chrysost. Theoph. Ambr. de sole & luna, & reliquis astris, quibus errore Gentili diuinitas quędam adscripta sit.
units.tr: "Or in heaven, or in earth." It appears that the Gentiles worshipped two kinds of gods, heavenly and earthly. Some understand the earthly gods to include the dead, since otherwise the Gentile gods would form a threefold kind. Jerome takes "in heaven" to mean the angels, that is, heavenly spirits. Chrysostom, Theophylact and Ambrose take it to mean the sun, the moon and the remaining stars, to which divinity was ascribed through Gentile error.

units.la: S I V E in terra.] Hierony. de sanctis in terra agentibus, de quibus dictum scribit illud: Ego dixi dij estis, & filij excelsi omnes. Ambrosius & Chrysost. de ijs, qui ex hominib. in deorū numerū relati sint, utpote Apolline, Aesculapio, Hercule, & Minerua. Mihi tamē uidetur, saluo aliorū iudicio: illud, in terra, non de mortuis q̃ diuino honore à Gentib. culti sunt, sed de uiuis intelligendū, huius mūdi, uidelicet principibus, qui omni in se mortaliū potestate transfata deorum loco uiui quoq; & habeantur & haberi uolebāt. Et ita puto sentiendū & de eo qd᷑ subijcit, quēadmodū sunt dij multi & domini multi: ut p dominos intelligamus rerum humanahumanarū potētes, omnib. oia præcipientes, & quiduis à quo q̄ pro arbitrio exigentes. Ita imperatores Rō. dñi uocati sunt. Quáquá de quibusdá legitur, qd̄ id nominis nō agnouerint, tá quá mortales, sed dijs adscripserint. Verū nō ,p hibeo, quin pro eodē sumātur hę duę particulæ, dij multi, & dñi multi, ut nihil sit aliud esse Deū quá esse dñm. Nā oīno diuinitatis potētiā exigit rerū potiri dominio. Vnde & nos Germani dicimꝰ, Go t ist ein herr, der apt ist ein munch.
units.tr: "Or in earth." Jerome takes this of the saints living on earth, about whom he writes that the saying applies: "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High." Ambrose and Chrysostom take it of those who were raised from among men into the number of the gods, such as Apollo, Aesculapius, Hercules and Minerva. It seems to me, saving the judgment of others, that "in earth" is to be understood not of the dead, who were worshipped with divine honour by the Gentiles, but of the living, namely the princes of this world, who, having transferred all mortal power to themselves, both were regarded as gods while still alive and wished to be so regarded. I think the same should be understood of what follows, "as there are many gods and many lords," so that by lords we understand those who hold power over human affairs, who command everyone in everything and demand whatever they like from each at their pleasure. Thus the Roman emperors were called lords. Although it is read of some that they did not acknowledge that title as mortals, but ascribed it to the gods. But I do not forbid these two phrases, many gods and many lords, to be taken as the same, so that to be God is nothing other than to be lord. For divinity above all requires possession of dominion over things. Whence we Germans also say: "God is a lord, the abbot is a monk."

units.la: NOBIS tñ unus est Deus. ] Ista distinctione qua Christianorū fidē à Gētiū errore seiungit, satis ostēdit, quod nō dicat uere multos esse deos ac dños: sed quod Gentib. multi habeantur. Nā si uere multi essent, iā nō Gētib. tātū, sed & nobis essent. Cū aūt nobis dicit non esse nisi unū Deū, indicat nō nobis, sed Gētib. multos esse deos. Potest aūt hęc particula intelligi uel de eo, quod nobis habeatur tantū unus Deus. i. quod nos unū tantū Deū credamus & colamus: sicut quod præmisit, quēadmodū sunt multi dij, idē est atq;, quēadmodū habetur, creduntur & colūtur à Gētib. multi dij: uel ita exponi, ut de gubernatione & prouidentia Dei erga nos intelligatur. quasi dicat: Nos uero relicto Gētib. multorū deorū fallaci patrocinio, uni ac ueri Dei protectione, moderatione & prouidētia fruimur: uerū simplicius est, ut priorē ex positione retineamus. Nō enim Christiani tātū punū ac uerū Deū gubernamur & sustētamur, sed oēs quoq; in uniuersum mortales. Nā omnes in illo uiuunt, mouentur & subsistunt. B Act. 17. Nisi uelimus de ea tantum intelligere gratia, quæ nobis per Christum contingit.
units.tr: By this distinction, by which he separates the faith of Christians from the error of the Gentiles, he sufficiently shows that he does not say there really are many gods and lords, but that many are held to be such by the Gentiles. For if they really were many, they would be gods not only to the Gentiles but to us as well. But since he says that for us there is only one God, he indicates that many gods exist not for us but for the Gentiles. This phrase can be understood either of what is held by us, namely that we believe and worship only one God, just as what he said before, "as there are many gods," means the same as "as many gods are held, believed and worshipped by the Gentiles"; or it may be explained as referring to God's governance and providence toward us, as if he said: "But we, having abandoned the deceitful patronage of the many gods of the Gentiles, enjoy the protection, direction and providence of the one true God." But it is simpler to keep the former explanation. For not only Christians are governed and sustained by the one true God, but all mortals in general. For "in him we live, move and have our being" (Act. 17.), unless we want to understand this only of that grace which comes to us through Christ.

units.la: QVI est pater ille, ex quo oia, & nos in illū. Et unus dñs Iesus Christus, per quē oia & nos per illū.] Primū generaliter ueri & unius Dei diuinitatē describit, deinde speciali-ter quantū illa erga credentes declarata est. Generalis descriptio est, qd̄ dicit: Qui est pater ille, ex quo oia. Dat enim illi, quod sit author & fons oīum cū ex eo dicit esse oia. Quod uero patrē uocat, potest quidē idē esse cū, eo quod omnia ex illo esse dicit: uerū meo iudicio, ad discretionē filij positū est, cuius statim mentio subijcit. Specialiter autē ad fideles pertinere uidetur, qd̄ dicit: Et nos in illū. Nos. i. in Christū credētes, quib. unus est Deus. In illū. i ad illū pertinem̄, populus illius sumus. Quanquā nō absurdū sit, si cū ueteri interprete legamus illud εἰς αὐτὸν in ipso, ut ad generalē Dei prouidentiā pertineat, qua fit, ut quemadmodū ex Deo sum̄, ita & in illo sustētemur, moueamur & uiuamus, ut est. Act. 17. Certe Ro. 11. generali prouidetię Dei tribuitur, non solū quod ex ipso & per ipsum, sed & εἰς αὐτὸν, in ipsum sint omnia. i. omnia ad illū tanquā ad suum principium sint referenda. Quan quam & ibi uetus interpres reddidit in ipso.
units.tr: "Yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we unto him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him." First he describes in general the divinity of the true and one God, then more specially how far it has been declared toward believers. The general description is what he says: "one God, the Father, from whom are all things." For he gives him this, that he is the author and fountain of all, since he says all things are from him. That he calls him Father may indeed be the same as saying that all things are from him; but in my judgment it is placed there to distinguish him from the Son, whose mention he immediately adds. The words "and we unto him" seem to pertain specially to the faithful: "we," that is, those believing in Christ, to whom there is one God; "unto him," that is, we belong to him, we are his people. Nevertheless, it is not absurd, if with the old translator we read εἰς αὐτὸν as "in him" [εἰς αὐτὸν], that it pertains to God's general providence, by which it comes about that, just as we are from God, so in him we are sustained, moved and live, as in Act. 17. Certainly Ro. 11. attributes to God's general providence not only that all things are from him and through him, but also that all things are εἰς αὐτὸν [unto him], that is, all things are to be referred to him as their beginning. Yet there too the old translator rendered it "in him."

units.la: ET unus dñs Iesus Christus per quem oia & nos per illū. ] More suo Deo patri coniūgit filiū dominū. Ita Ro. 1. & suprà 1. Et ut patri dat, quod ex ipso: ita isti, quod per ipsum sint oia.
units.tr: "And one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him." In his usual manner he joins the Lord the Son with God the Father. So in Ro. 1. and above, in 1. And as he gives to the Father that all things are from him, so he gives to these that all things are through him.

units.la: Et ista nō sunt eò rapiēda, quasi nō sit eiusdē diuinitatis cū patre filius, eo quod dñm illū uocat, & per ipsum dicit esse omnia: sed magis ad hoc usurpanda, ut declaretur filius eiusdē cum patre esse potētiæ ac diuinitatis. Quā enim, nō demit patri, ne fit etiā dñs omnium, quod filio dominatum adscribit, tā nec filio adimit diuinitatem, quod patrē Deū uocat: & ut non prohibet quo minꝰ per patrē quoq; sint oia, ut Ro. 11. est, p id quod de filio dicit, perquē sunt oia, ita certe nō uetat dicere, aliquo modo ex filio quoq; esse oia, in eo quod patri dat, quod ex illo sint omnia. Videtur aūt in eo quod Christū dñm appellat, ad id respicere, quod est unigenitus Dei, cuius omnia sunt quæ patris sunt, cui pater omnia in manus dedit. In eo uero quod dicit, per quē sunt oia, ad id quod uerbo Dei omnia sunt cōdita: iuxta illud, Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil. Illud, Et nos per illū, quidā ad singulare diuinę gratię dispensationē, per q̄ in Christo ante secula electi, postea uocati, iustificati & saluati sumus, referrūt, è quibus est Ambr. quidam uero idem esse uolunt quod id quo dixit per Christum esse omnia, nō solū cœlū & terram, sed & omnes in uniuersum mortales. Est autem probe notandum, quod filio hominis, quem uocat Iesum Christum, ista adscribit, quę tamen uerbo Dei competunt: ut sciamus nos non esse hominis alicuius adoratores, ubi Christum adoramus, sed eius qui est dominus omnium, per quem omnia sunt condita, qui eiusdem cum patre est diuinitatis, potentię & operationis.
units.tr: Yet these words are not to be snatched away as if the Son were not of the same divinity as the Father because he calls him Lord and says all things are through him. Rather they are to be used to show that the Son is of the same power and divinity as the Father. For just as in ascribing lordship to the Son he does not take it from the Father, so that he is also Lord of all, neither does he take divinity from the Son by calling the Father God. And just as he does not forbid that all things are also through the Father, as he says in Ro. 11., by what he says of the Son, through whom are all things, so certainly he does not forbid saying that in some way all things are also from the Son, since he gives to the Father that all things are from him. It seems that in calling Christ Lord he is looking at the fact that he is the only-begotten of God, to whom all the things of the Father belong, and to whom the Father has given all things into his hands. In saying "through whom are all things," he is looking at the fact that all things were created by the Word of God, according to that saying: "All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made." As for "and we through him," some refer it to the singular dispensation of divine grace, through which we were chosen in Christ before the ages, afterwards called, justified and saved; Ambrose is among these. Others, however, wish it to mean the same as what he said, that all things are through Christ: not only heaven and earth, but all mortals in general. It is also well to note that he ascribes to the Son of man, whom he calls Jesus Christ, things which nevertheless belong to the Word of God. This is so that we may know that when we worship Christ we are not adorers of some man, but of him who is the Lord of all, through whom all things were created, who is of the same divinity, power and working as the Father.

units.la: SED non in omnib. est scientia. ]Hactenus scientiā recitauit, qua se tuebātur & quā iactabāt ij qui eidolothytis temere uescebantur, illam q; tanquā uerā non improbauit, sed & suo calculo approbauit: iā uero deinceps quā non satis sit ista scire, sed cogitandū etiā sit, ne offen diculū ponatur infirmis admonet, & qd hac in re peccetur declarat. Et primū id ponit, quod erat illis primū quoq; cogitādū: nēpe, ista scien tiam de eidolis non esse in omnib. Ea cogitatio nonquā remittenda est perfectiorib. in ecclesia. Est enim ad id qd̄ sequitur oīno necessaria: uidelicet, ut nō cogitēt quid ipsi possint, sed magis expēdant quid non possint in eccle sia infirmi, qui nō sunt deferendi, multo minus perdendi. Malus est itineris comes, qui nō qd alij simul proficiscentes, sed hoc tantū spectat, quid ipse possit. Iacob expendebat imbecillitatem paruulorum fuorū, cū quib. proficiscendū erat, dicens: Noli domine mi, quod paruulos habeam teneros, & oues & boues fœtas me cū, quas si plus in ambulando fecero laborare, moriētur una die cuncti greges. Præcedat dñs meus seruum suum & ego sequar paulatim ue stigia eius, sicut uidero paruulos meos posse, donec ueniam ad dūm meū in Seir. Illi qui simul canunt, non expendunt quisq; quām ipse alte posit intēsa uoce assurgere, sed rationem habent eorū qui minus possunt. Sciunt enim alioqui cōcentū quē uolūt haud bene se posse obtinere, si cōcinentiū aliquis cantando deficiat.
units.tr: "But knowledge is not in all." Hitherto he has set out the knowledge by which those who rashly ate meat sacrificed to idols defended themselves and boasted, and he did not disapprove it as true but also approved it by his own judgment. Now, however, he warns that it is not enough to know these things, but one must also take thought, lest a stumbling block be placed before the weak, and he declares what is sinned in this matter. And first he sets down what was also to be considered first by them: namely, that this knowledge about idols is not in everyone. This consideration must sometimes be kept by the more mature in the Church. For it is wholly necessary for what follows: that they should not think about what they themselves can do, but rather weigh what the weak in the Church cannot do, who are not to be abandoned, much less destroyed. A bad companion on a journey is one who looks not at what the others setting out with him can do, but only at what he himself can do. Jacob weighed the weakness of his little children, with whom he had to travel, saying: "Do not, my lord, since I have tender little children, and sheep and cows with young with me, which if I make them labour too much in walking, all the flocks will die in one day. Let my lord go before his servant, and I will follow slowly in his footsteps, as far as I see my little ones can go, until I come to my lord in Seir." Those who sing together do not each weigh how high their own voice can rise, but take account of those who can do less. For otherwise they know that they cannot well keep up the harmony they want if any one of the singers falls short.

units.la: {A} Vide Aug. ad Placentiū Donatistam Epistola 174.
units.tr: See Augustine, to Placentius the Donatist, Epistle 174.

units.la: {B} Gen. 33. ciat. Talé animum cupit indere Corinthijs Apost.ut nemo quid ipse sciat,speẽtet,sed magis obseruet quid adhuc alijs desit, ne qui infirmi sunt ulla in re offendantur ac lædantur.
units.tr: Gen. 33. Such a spirit the Apostle wishes to instil in the Corinthians: that no one should look only to what he himself knows, but rather observe what is still lacking in others, so that the weak are not offended or harmed in any matter.

units.la: Et hoc erat etiam nostris temporibus faciendum, in plerisq;, maxime initio renouatæ doctrinæ ueritatis. Det dominus ut uel nunc tan dem isti admonitioni obsequamur.
units.tr: This also had to be done in our own times, in very many people, above all at the beginning of the renewed teaching of the truth. May the Lord grant that we now at last heed this admonition.

units.la: NON MVLLI uero,cũ cóscientia simulacri usq; ad hoc tépus,tanquá simulacris immo latum edút. Aegre dedicscitur qd̃ à pueris imbibitum est,maxime quod carni quoq; agnatũ est,ut est simulacrorũ cultus. Et hoc etiá Christianis plerisque ex Gentib.usuueniebat. Erat penitius infixum,nónihil numinis adesse simu lacris,adeoq; non poterát ea libertate uesci ijs quæ simulacris offerebantur, qua illi qui sciebant nihil esse simulacrũ:sed ubi illis uescebantur,cũ conscientia simulachri.i.tanquam sacro epulo,cũ religione simulacri uescebantur,non ut bonam Dei creaturam ad compescédam sa mem,sed ut rem sacrá magis animi quàm corporis gratia usurpantes.
units.tr: Not a few, indeed, with a conscience about idols, even up to this time, ate what was offered to idols as if it were truly the sacred food of the idols. It is hard to unlearn what has been soaked in from boyhood, especially what has grown into the flesh, as the worship of images has. This also happened to many Christians who came from the Gentiles. It was deeply fixed in them that some divine power was present in the idols, and so they could not eat with that freedom which those who knew that an idol was nothing enjoyed. When they ate with a conscience about the idol, that is, as a sacred feast, they ate with a religious regard for the idol, not using God's good creature to satisfy hunger, but taking up a sacred thing for the sake of the mind rather than the body.

units.la: VS QVE ad hoc tempus.] Apparet istá infirmitate aliquádiu durasse in Christianis plerisque. Nondum tũ uult illos Apost.cótemni. Et quid mirum est,si etiam hodie pleriq; in ecclesijs ubi ueritatis obtinet sciétia,per multũ tempori nonnihil de pristinis errorib. retineát,si id factũ est in illis ecclesijs, quas ipse instituit Apostolus: Discamus & nos consimilem uxnd erga huiusmodi infirmos ostendere.
units.tr: "Even up to this time." It appears that this weakness lasted for some time among many Christians. Yet the Apostle does not want them despised. And what wonder is it, if even today in many churches where the knowledge of the truth prevails, some people still retain something of their former errors for a long time, if this has happened in those churches which the Apostle himself founded? Let us also learn to show a like attitude toward such weak people.

units.la: ET coscietia illorû infirma cũ fit,polluitur.] Quid dãni sequitur istũ libertatis abusũ apud infirmos,cum cóscientia simulcari,& non libere eidolothytis uefcétes,exprimit. Quid illud: conscientiæ pollutio. Quid est aút pollui conscientiam: Ambr.dicit conscientiá pollui,si nó bene sentiat circa unum Deum. Ergo ignoratia Dei,est cóscientię poilutio: & rursus cognitio Dei,est mundatio conscientiæ.
units.tr: "And the conscience of those who are weak, when it is defiled." What harm follows from this abuse of freedom among the weak, when they eat what was offered to idols with a conscience about idols, and not freely? Consider that phrase, "defilement of the conscience." What is it to defile the conscience? Ambrose says that the conscience is defiled if it does not think rightly about the one God. So ignorance of God is the defilement of the conscience, and, conversely, knowledge of God is the cleansing of the conscience.

units.la: Notandũ aút est, qd̃ istá pollutionem non dat eidolothytis in se,sed conscientiæ infirmitati. Nam sanam conscientiam non polluút.Si cut infirmum stomachũ lędit bonus alioquibus,at non suo,sed stomachi ægrotantis uicio: ita & eidolothyta,cum sint bonę Dei creaturę, sanà conscientiá nó lędút, lædunt autẽ infirmá, culpa ægrotantis conscientiæ non propria.
units.tr: It should be noted that this defilement does not come to the food offered to idols in itself, but to the weakness of the conscience. For they do not defile a sound conscience. Just as good food harms a weak stomach, not because of its own fault but because of the fault of the sick stomach, so food offered to idols, since they are good creatures of God, do not harm a sound conscience, but they harm a weak one, through the fault of a sick conscience, not their own.

units.la: Habet aút mitigationis nónihil,qd̃ istorum hominum conscientiá,erroneam &superstitio sam,imo eidololatricam infirmá uocat: qd̃ ob id facit ut ad commiserationẽ perfectiores in fide,ac robustiores magis quàm ad cótemptû, aut condemnationem excitet.
units.tr: There is also some mitigation in the fact that the Apostle calls the conscience of these people erroneous, superstitious, and even idolatrous, yet weak. He does this so that they may be stirred to compassion by those who are more perfect in faith and stronger, rather than to contempt or condemnation.

units.la: I Primum qd̃ non fit detestandus,qui ex infirmitate peccat,aliud facturus si robustior esset. Nequit.n.præstare quod sani præstant.Mul tum exigebat roboris, tam diuturnam consue tudinem,deinde publica sacra abijcere & contemnere,quib.infirmi ueluti ponderibus quibusdam ne ad sciétiam ueritatis in liberiorem auráassurgeret premebátur & prohibebátur.
units.tr: First, the one who sins out of weakness is not to be detested, since he would do otherwise if he were stronger. For he cannot do what the strong do. It required great strength to cast off so long-standing a habit, and then to abandon and despise the public sacred rites, by which the weak were held down and hindered, as if by certain weights, so that they could not rise into the freer air of the knowledge of the truth.

units.la: A 2 Deinde,quod ista infirmitas olim omnib.cõ munis fuerit.Certe cómuni morbo laborátes, merito patienter toleratur & curantur,dum illis quisque sanus uidit,qualis & ipse fuerit.
units.tr: Second, this weakness was once common to all. Surely those who suffer from a common disease are rightly tolerated patiently and cared for, as long as each healthy person remembers what he himself once was.

units.la: Atq esca nos nõ cõmedat Deo. Neqʒ em si edamus aliquid,nobis superest:ne que si nõ edamus,quícquã nobis deest.
units.tr: Yet food does not commend us to God. For if we eat, we gain nothing; nor if we do not eat, do we lose anything.

units.la: Posteaquá infirmorũ admonuit robustiores,&quid illis timendum sit docuit,consequé ter arrogátiam sciolorum & temerariorum retundit.Et primo arguit ab inanitate huius rei. Ea est,quod neminem Deo commédat cibus.
units.tr: Having admonished the stronger about the weak and taught them what they should fear, he now restrains the arrogance of the half-learned and rash. And first he argues from the emptiness of this matter. It is this: food commends no one to God.

units.la: Et id argumenti plurimum faciebat ad deijciendum illorum fastum. Apparet enim sciolos istos nó simpliciter libera cóscíétia de eidolothytis manducasse,sed cũ ostétatione quadá singularis erga Deũ fidei,qua plurimum Deo, ueluti eidolorum uanitate profitétes ac declarantes,gratificarentur:rursus uero non uefcétes cum suo horrore nonnihil religionis eidolis adscriberent,atq; ita unius ac ueri Dei diui nitati detraherent.Isti arrogantiæ occurrit cũ dicit: Atqui esca nos non comendat Deo.Q.d. Quid arrogantes estis in re nihili, cuius Deo nulla cura est,qua nemo se Deo gratum uel in gratum reddere potest:Sic Rom.14.dicit, Nõ est regnum Dei esca & potus.
units.tr: This argument was very effective in casting down their pride. For it appears that these half-learned people did not eat food offered to idols simply with a free conscience, but with a certain show of their singular faith toward God, by which they thought they pleased God very much, declaring and proclaiming by their contempt the emptiness of the idols. On the other hand, when they did not eat, with their own scruple they ascribed some religious power to the idols, and so took away from the divinity of the one true God. The Apostle meets this arrogance when he says: "Yet food does not commend us to God." That is: why are you arrogant in a matter of nothing, in which God has no concern, and by which no one can make himself pleasing or displeasing to God? So Romans 14 says: "The kingdom of God is not food and drink."

units.la: Et ut rationem sententię suę reddat, subiungit:Neq;.n.si edam aliquid nobis superest,ne q; si nó edamus quicq nobis deest.Hoc est,nec potiores sumus reliqs Christianis apud Deũ, edétes,nec inferiores nõ edétes. Græce est ἀν ραφ ἀποφαγ.i.Neq;.n.abundamus. ἀν ὑστέρημα ἐστ.i.Neq;minus habemus. Nó exprimitur,qua in re non abúdent uefcétes, nec minus habeát non uescentes.Facile tũ intelligitur,ea de re lo qui Apost.quæ Deo gratos reddat.Ea est uera pietas.In hac certe nihil habemus præ cæteris, si uescamur quibuslibet:nec uefcentib.inferio res sumus,etiamsi non uescamur. Scio Hiero. & Ambrof.secus exponere.Verba Hierony sic habent: Cui enim dubium est,nullum neque manducando abundare,neq; non manducando egere,cum econtrariò illis magis formidáda sit inopia,qui gulam retinere non norunt:Ambrosius ad hunc modum exponit:Cótempta enim sacrificiorum esca, utiq; non deerit qd̃ edatur. Si aút sumpta fuerit,non abundabit,ita ut nihil requiratur,ac per hæc abijcienda,quia neq; sine illa non uiuitur, & scádalum fratrib.est.Ergo hi duo,nó de pietatis uel abúdátia uel defectu, sed de ipsa terrena alimonia intelligunt Apostoli uerba· quæ certe,ut Hier. habet,edendo non augeatur, nec non edendo minuatur,& secundũ Ambr.sententiá nó sit auctior uefcétib.nec destituat non uefcétes.Q.d. Apost. units.tr: And to give the reason for his statement, he adds: "For if we eat, we gain nothing; nor if we do not eat, do we lose anything." That is, we are not better before God than other Christians if we eat, nor worse if we do not eat. In Greek it is [ἀπερισσεύομεν], "we abound," and [ὑστέρημα ἐστίν], "it is a lack." It is not stated in what respect those who eat abound, nor what those who do not eat lack. Yet it is easily understood that the Apostle is speaking of that which makes people pleasing to God. This is true godliness. In this we have nothing above others if we eat whatever we like, nor are we inferior to those who eat if we do not eat. I know that Jerome and Ambrose explain it differently. Jerome's words are these: "For who doubts that no one abounds by eating, nor lacks by not eating, since on the contrary it is more to be feared lest want come upon those who do not know how to restrain their appetite?" Ambrose explains it in this way: "For if the food of sacrifices is despised, certainly nothing will be lacking to be eaten. But if it is taken, it will not abound, so that nothing is sought, and for this reason it is to be cast away, since one cannot live without it, and it is a stumbling block to the brothers." So these two understand the words of the Apostle not of piety, whether abundance or lack, but of earthly nourishment itself. Surely, as Jerome has it, it is not increased by eating, nor diminished by not eating, and according to Ambrose's sense, it does not make those who eat any richer, nor deprive those who do not eat. That is, the Apostle says: What profit comes to you from eating food offered to idols? Are you living more sumptuously because of it? What loss comes to those who do not eat? Are they forced to endure hunger? Have you been reduced to such poverty and scarcity of goods that you cannot do without eating idol-offerings? Far from it! Your sustenance does not depend on

units.la: stentatio
units.tr: sustenance

units.la: stětatio in hisce escis. Neq; enim abundam⁹ in uictu, si illis uescamur: neq; uictu destituimur, si non uescamur. Ergo hoc sensu duplex est hu ius rei uanitas. Prima, quod ex ea nemo Deo cōmendatur. Altera, quod neq; terrenæ quic quam utilitatis adfert. Prior tñ sententia, quam & Chrysost. sequitur, & imitator illius Theo phylactus, mihi magis placet. Apparet. n. hæc uerba declarandi gratia premissæ sententiæ ad ieεta esse, propter notâ causalem ῤ̈: quæ, licet ab Erasmo sit omissa, in Græco tamē habetur, &à ueteri interprete reddita est, nec ab ipsis patribus Hieron. & Ambros. neglecta.
units.tr: sustenance in these foods. For we do not abound in provisions if we eat them, nor are we deprived of provisions if we do not eat them. So in this sense the emptiness of this matter is twofold. The first is that no one is commended to God by it. The second is that it brings nothing of earthly usefulness. Yet the first sense, which Chrysostom also follows, and Theophylact, who imitates him, pleases me more. For these words appear to have been added to explain the preceding statement, on account of the causal particle, which, although Erasmus omitted it, is nevertheless found in the Greek, was rendered by the older translator, and was not neglected by the Fathers Jerome and Ambrose themselves.

units.la: Cur autem non dicit: Neq; enim si edamus, inferiores apud Deum sumus: neq; si non edamus, potiores? An nō & hoc uerū est? Certe negari non potest. Si esca Deo neminē cōmedat, & regnū Dei nō est cibus & potus, tā non cōmendari Deo qui non uescitur q̄ qui uescitur: nec minus abundare in pietate, qui edit, q̄ qui non edit. Si edamus, inquit, nihil nobis superest. Verum. Sed neq; quicquā nobis superest, si non edamus. Rursus. Si nō edamus, nihil nō bis deest. At ne tum quidē aliquid nobis deest, cum edimus. Cum ergo utrunque uerū sit, cur non utrunque posuit? Ratio est, quod ad propositum non faciebat. Propositum erat sciolo rum istorum qui uescendi libertate ad offendi culum infirmorum abutebantur, temeritatem & arrogantiam deijcere. Huc quadrabat admo nere, nihil potiorem esse apud Deū eidolothy this uescentem, nec inferiorem illis abstinēte. Alterum licet æque uerum, quia non temerita tem insolentium, sed magis superstitione igno rantium impugnat, proposito nō cōueniebat, imò magis obsuisset, & fastum temere uefcen tium confirmasset, atque ob eam rationem cō sulto omissum est. In Ro. propositum erat con ciliare dissidentes in hac causa & admonere, ne uescentes cōtemnerent non uefcētes, & uicif sim ne non uescentes iudicarent uescentes: i deo non ad unā tantū partē, sed ad utranq; cir cūspiciens, dicebat: Qui uescitur, dño uelcitur & gratias agit. Qui non uescitur, & ipse domi no non uescitur, & gratias agit. Ista conuenie bant proposito. Hic uero non hoc agit, sed in eo est, ut morbum arrogantium curet.
units.tr: But why does he not say: "For if we eat, we are not inferior before God; nor if we do not eat, are we superior"? Is this not also true? Surely it cannot be denied. If food commends no one to God, and the kingdom of God is not food and drink, then one who does not eat is no less commended to God than one who eats, and one who eats abounds in godliness no more than one who does not eat. "If we eat," he says, "we gain nothing." True. "But neither do we gain anything if we do not eat." Again: "If we do not eat, we lose nothing." But neither do we lose anything when we do eat. Since both are true, why did he not state both? The reason is that it did not serve his purpose. His purpose was to cast down the rashness and arrogance of those half-learned people who abused the freedom of eating to the offence of the weak. It was fitting to admonish that the one who eats idol-offerings is no better before God, nor the one who abstains any worse. The other point, though equally true, does not attack the rashness of the arrogant, but rather the superstition of the ignorant, and so it did not suit his purpose; indeed it would have been more harmful, and would have confirmed the pride of the rash eaters. For this reason it was deliberately omitted. In Romans, the Apostle's purpose was to reconcile those who disagreed on this question, and to admonish that those who eat should not despise those who do not, and conversely that those who do not eat should not judge those who eat. Therefore, looking to both sides rather than only one, he said: "He who eats, eats to the Lord, and gives thanks to God. He who does not eat, to the Lord he does not eat, and gives thanks." Those statements fitted his purpose. Here, however, he is not doing this, but is intent on curing the disease of the arrogant.

units.la: Cautionem aūt Apostolicam resipit, qd' nō dicit: Atqui esca uos nó cōmendat Deo. Neq; enim si edatis, abundatis, &c. sed: Esca nos nó cōmedat Deo, &c. ne putetur id singulari cui dam Corinthiorum defeētui, & nō ipsius cau sæ inanitati géeraliter ita deputare, ut oēs Chri stianos cōcernat. Neque. n. Corinthij soli tales sunt, ut escæ priuilegio nihil apud Deum asse quātur, sed ea est omniū fideliū conditio, ut ne cesse habeant nō escis, sed pietate Deo cōmen dari. Nec caret singulari artificio, quod istā ua nitatem escarum, in causa pietatis, futuræ re prehensioni præmittit. Habet. n. exaggeratio nem haud mediocrem commissæ stultitiæ, & eō tendit ut omnem illis excusatione adimat. Potest nōnihil excusari, qui in eo offendit ᴘxi
units.tr: The Apostle's caution recalls this point: he does not say, "But food does not commend us to God." For it is not that if you eat you abound, and so on, but: "Food does not commend us to God." He says this so that it will not be thought to apply only to a particular fault of certain Corinthians, and so that no one takes the emptiness of this cause as something that concerns only them rather than all Christians. The Corinthians are not the only ones who think that the privilege of food counts for nothing with God. Rather, this is the condition of all the faithful: they ought to be commended to God by piety, not by foods. Nor is his skill lacking here, in that before the coming refutation he states the emptiness of these foods, in a matter of piety. For he greatly exaggerates the folly committed, and aims to take away from them every excuse. Someone who gives offence in a matter from which some advantage can be hoped for, especially one necessary for salvation, may be somewhat excused.

units.la: mum, è quo emolumēti quicquā sperari potest, maxime tale, quod saluti necessarium sit. Absti nentia cultus simulacrorum habet suam utili tatem, eamq; ad salutē necessaria. Hic qui simu lacrorum cultores offendit, absq; culpa est. Ha bet quo excusetur. In hac uero causa nulla po test talis ratio pretexi. Nihil hic est utilitatis ue scēti, nihil damni non uefcēti. Vbi nec utilitas aliqua sperari potest uefcēdo, nec damni quic quā metui nō uefcēdo, ibi certe nulla est ratio offendēdi proximū. Plurimum detestamur ea flagitia, unde ad flagitiosos nihil redit emolu menti. Colligimus. n. ex illis, singularem quan dā eius generis reprobis hominib. inesse mali ciā: ita certe merito detestanda est ista arrogan tia, in re quidem inutili ac nihili, infirmis tamē noxia declarata. Subindicatur autē simul, qd' sit carnis in reb. fidei ingenium. Veram pietatē non amat, & tamen subinde maxime pia uide ri cupit. Pietatē aūt ostensura, uersatur in re bus ad pietatē facientib. in quibus uult religi osa uideri, utpote in escis, dierum obseruatio nib. indumentorū raritate, & aliis eius generis nugis. Ita isti scioli apud Corinth. apprime se Christianos esse declaraturi, Christianismum esu eidolothytorum metiebātur, inq; eo uehe menter insolescebant. Perinde faciūt & hodie, qui non Christi spiritu, sed carnis ingenio du cūtur. Qui de catholica & Apostolica fide glo riantur, maximam religionis partem collocāt in ciborum quorundam abstinentiam, pluri mum, ut opinantur Deo gratificaturi, si nō nisi piscium carnem certis diebus cōtingant. Qui uero de renouata Euangelij ueritate Christia naq; reddita libertate sese iactāt, supra modū Euangelici uideri uolunt, si erronea cōsuetudi ne abiecta, quibuslibet semper uescātur, surdi utriq; ad istā Apostoli uocē: Esca nos Deo nō cōmendat. Quid interea? Quæ curāda erat, & in quib. uera est pietas, strenue utrinque negli guntur, quod Apostolus haud obscure notat, cum dicit: Esca nos Deo non cōmendat. Quid enim aliud clamat, q̄, Quin ea curatis, quę Deo placent? Esca uos Deo non poteritis approba re, charitati studendū erat non escis, quæ nihil prosunt ambulantib. in eis. Sic Ro. 14. ubi di xit: Regnū Dei non est cibus & potus, subiun xit, sed iusticia & pax & gaudiū in spiritu san ēto. Qui in hoc seruit Christo, placet Deo, &c. Vnde igitur nūc, inquit hoc loco Erasmus, tot sunt inter Christianos præcepta de generib. ci borum, unde tanta in his obseruandis supersti tio, ut pene nulla ex re magis iudicemur?
units.tr: Abstinence from the worship of images has its usefulness, and that usefulness is necessary for salvation. Whoever gives offence to the worshippers of images is blameless; he has a ground of excuse. But in this matter no such pretext is possible. Here there is no advantage to the one who eats, and no loss to the one who does not eat. Where no advantage can be hoped for by eating, and no loss is to be feared by not eating, there is certainly no reason for offending a neighbour. We greatly detest those wicked deeds from which no gain returns to the wicked. For from them we gather that there is a peculiar wickedness in men of that kind who are reprobate. So this arrogance is rightly to be detested, since it is shown to be harmful to the weak, in a thing that is indeed useless and worth nothing. At the same time it is hinted what the nature of the flesh is in matters of faith. It does not love true piety, and yet it wants to seem most pious at every turn. Wishing to show piety, it busies itself with things that have to do with piety, in which it wants to appear religious, such as foods, the observance of days, the wearing of scanty clothing, and other trifles of this sort. So those smatterers among the Corinthians, eager to show that they were especially Christians, measured Christianity by eating food offered to idols, and grew very proud of it. People do the same today, who are led not by the Spirit of Christ but by the nature of the flesh. Those who boast of the Catholic and Apostolic faith place the greater part of religion in abstaining from certain foods, thinking they will please God very much if they touch only the flesh of fish on certain days. Those who boast of the restored truth of the Gospel and of Christian liberty restored want to seem more evangelical than others, if, having cast off an erroneous custom, they eat whatever they like at all times, deaf to both sides to that voice of the Apostle: "Food does not commend us to God." What in the meantime? What ought to have been cared for, and in which true piety consists, is vigorously neglected on both sides. The Apostle notes this quite plainly when he says: "Food does not commend us to God." For what else does he cry out, than: "Rather, take care of those things that please God"? You will not be able to win God's approval by food; one ought to strive for love, not for foods, which do nothing for those who walk in them. So in Romans 14, where he said, "The kingdom of God is not food and drink," he added, "but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. Whoever in this serves Christ pleases God," and so on. Why then, says Erasmus here, are there now so many precepts among Christians about kinds of food, and such great superstition in observing them, that we are judged by almost nothing more?

units.la: Sed uidete, ne quo modo facultas illa uestra offēdiculo sit iss, qui infirmi sunt. Etenim si quis cōspexerit te, qui habes scientiam, in epulo simulacrorū accūbē tem, nōne cōscientia eius qui infirmus est, edificabītur ad edēdū ea, quę sunt si mulacris oblata? Et peribit frater qui in firmus est, in tua scientia propter quem Christus fuit mortuus. Sic autem peccates A in fratres, & uulnerantes illorum conscientiam infirmam in Christum peccatis. Quapropter si esca offendit fratrem meum, haudquaquam uescar carnibus in æternum, ne fratri meo sim offendiculo.
units.tr: But see that this liberty of yours is in no way a stumbling-block to those who are weak. For if anyone sees you, who have knowledge, reclining at a feast in an idol's temple, will not the conscience of him who is weak be built up to eat the things offered to idols? And the weak brother will perish through your knowledge, for whose sake Christ died. Thus, too, sinning against the brethren and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. Therefore, if food gives offence to my brother, I will by no means eat meat for ever, lest I be a stumbling-block to my brother.

units.la: Posteaquam ad retundendam scioloru arrogantiam, rei de qua gloriabatur, & in qua plurimum delinquebat, uanitate illis obiecit dicens, Atqui esca nos nō commendat Deo: iam omniū cōmodissime subijcit, quid damni ex ea sequatur, qd tæetsi & supra attigerit, cum dixit: Nonnulli uero cū cōscientia simulacri usq; hodie tanquā simulacris immolatum edunt, & conscientia illorum infirma cum sit polluitur: nūc tamē ueluti suo loco fusius tractandum resumit, ut doceat eos, quā sit peruersum in re nihili & inani, quæ Deo non placeat, tantū nocumēti parere fratribus. Et ut appareat, quantū peccent, delictum ipsorum triplici nomine exaggerat. Primum, in eo quod admonet, in quem peccetur. Deinde, in eo qd offendit, quantum mali generent. Tertio, per quid id faciant.
units.tr: After he has, to blunt the arrogance of the smatterers, charged them with the emptiness of the thing in which they boasted and in which they sinned most, saying, "But food does not commend us to God," he now most conveniently adds what harm follows from it. Although he had touched on this above, when he said: "But some with the conscience of the idol still eat today as if it were sacrificed to idols, and their weak conscience is polluted," he now takes it up again, as if it had to be treated more fully in its own place, so that he may teach them how perverse it is that, in a thing of nothing and of emptiness, which does not please God, they should cause so much harm to their brothers. And so that it may appear how greatly they sin, he magnifies their offence in three respects. First, in that he admonishes against whom they sin. Next, in that he shows how much evil they cause by giving offence. Third, by what means they do it.

units.la: SED uidete, ne quo modo facultas illa uestra.] Admonitio est, ut caute scientia & potestate quā iactabant, utātur. Circūspectione opus esse, uerbo uidendi admonet. Quod cauere debeant, docet cū dicit, ne quo facultas illa uestra offendiculo sit ijs q infirmi sunt. Non simpliciter admonet, ut circumspecti sint, sed simul indicat quid metuere & cauere debeat.
units.tr: "But see that this liberty of yours..." This is an admonition that they use with care the knowledge and the power they were boasting of. By the word "see" he reminds them that caution is needed. What they ought to beware of he teaches when he says: "lest this liberty of yours be a stumbling-block to those who are weak." He does not simply admonish them to be cautious, but at the same time indicates what they ought to fear and guard against.

units.la: Et ut solicitam illis cautionem incutiat non dicit, uidete, ne facultas illa uestra offendiculo sit infirmis: sed addit, Quomodo. Indicat.n.nō simpliciter cauēdum offendiculum, sed ita, ut nullo modo generetur infirmis ruinæ occasio. Et merito. Maior enim erat infirmorum habeda ratio, ut ulla ratione in hac causa, qua Deo certe nemo gratificare poterit, offenderentur.
units.tr: And so that he may instil in them a careful caution, he does not say, "See that your liberty not be a stumbling-block to the weak," but adds, "how." For he shows that the stumbling-block is not simply to be avoided, but in such a way that no occasion of falling is produced at all for the weak. And rightly so. For a greater regard for the weak had to be had, so that in this matter, in which certainly no one can please God, they should not be offended in any way.

units.la: Ne ociosum est, quod non dicit, Facultas uestra, aut, facultas ista: sed facultas illa uestra. Videtur enim non quidem negare istā fidelium: uerum, quoniam ad offendiculum uergebat infirmorum, ita ea extenuat, ut nihil illi laudis relinquat utut eam iactēt scioli isti. Ideo uocat eam, ipsorum potestatem: deinde notan di gratia, illa, inquit, id est, in re ita nihili, in eis, quibus nemo seruire potest. Quasi dicat: Gloriamini multum de potestate hac uestra quidlibet edendi, quæ tamen uos Deo gratos non reddet. At etiam atq; etiam uidete ut non solū Deo uos illa non approbetis, sed infirmis quoq; conscientijs offendiculo sitis, ac graviter peccetis.
units.tr: It is not idle that he does not say "your liberty," or "this liberty," but "that liberty of yours." For he seems not indeed to deny that liberty of the faithful; but since it tends toward a stumbling-block for the weak, he so diminishes it that he leaves it no praise, however much these smatterers boast of it. So he calls it their power, and then, to mark it with a note, he says "that," that is, in a thing so worthless, in those things which no one can serve. As if he said: You boast much of this power of yours to eat whatever you like, which nevertheless will not make you pleasing to God. But see again and again, not only that you do not approve yourselves to God by it, but that you also become a stumbling-block to weak consciences, and sin grievously.

units.la: Offendiculo sit infirmis.] Græcè est προσκομμα. Est autem metaphorica dictio ἀπὸ τῆς προσκόπτειν, qd significat impingere ad lapidē, ut Matth. 4. μή ποτε προσκόψῃς πρὸς λίθον τὸν πόδα σου. Id est, Ne quando impingas in lapidem pedē tuum. Est igitur προσκομμα proprie impactio, qua quis inter eūdum ad terram sternitur, uel certe prope ad ruinam datur, cuius id occasio est, ad quod fit impactio. Hinc metaphorice ad spiritalem impactionē trāsfertur, qua quis in uia dei ad delinquendum impellitur. Quod enim corpori casus est, id animæ est peccatum.
units.tr: "A stumbling-block to the weak." In Greek it is προσκομμα [proskomma]. It is a metaphorical word, from προσκόπτειν [proskoptein], which means to strike against a stone, as in Matthew 4: μή ποτε προσκόψῃς πρὸς λίθον τὸν πόδα σου [mē pote proskopsēs pros lithon ton poda sou], that is, "Lest at any time you strike your foot against a stone." Proskomma therefore properly means a striking, by which someone while walking is thrown to the ground, or at least brought near to a fall, and the occasion of such a striking is the thing against which it happens. Hence it is transferred metaphorically to a spiritual striking, by which someone on the way of God is driven to sin. For what a fall is to the body, sin is to the soul.

units.la: Quam diligenter aut offendiculum istud cauendum sit, ex eo cōsiderandum proponit, qd addit, ijs qui infirmi sunt. Graue est quēcunq; ad ruinam impellere, etiam pedib. bene ualentem. Infirmum uero & plano quoque itinere ægre ingredientem iniecto offendiculo prosternere, quis non uidet esse grauissimum?
units.tr: How carefully this stumbling-block must be avoided, he sets out to consider from what he adds: "to those who are weak." It is a grave matter to push anyone into ruin, even someone who stands firm on his feet. But who does not see that it is most grievous to knock down a weak person, who walks with difficulty even on a level road, by placing an obstacle in his way?

units.la: ETENIM si quis conspexerit te.] Periculū quod caueri uult, declarat quō, nisi cauti sint, cōtingere ualeat, & iuxta q graue sit, latius ob oculos exponit. Conuenit aut uelut unūquen que separatim, cū singulariter & percōtatorie loquitur, dicens: Etenim si quis te in epulo simulacrorū accumbentem uiderit, nonne ædificabitur ad edendū ea, quę simulacris sunt immolata? Q.d. Teipsum couenio, qui eidolothytis uescerīs, inque ipso templo eidolorum una cum gentib. simulacrorum cultorib. in epulo simulacrorum accumbis, ut respondeas, quid futurum sit, si infirmus frater hoc te facere uiderit? An aliud expectandum est, quam ut & ipse, licet disimile fide, ad edendum eidolothyta tuo exēplo permoueatur? Q.d. Certe negare non potes hoc futurum. Hac.n.interrogatione fortius & confidentius Apost.id periculi futuratum asserit, quam si simpliciter dixisset: Etenim si quis te conspexerit in epulo simulacrorum accumbentem, ædificabitur illius conscientia ad edendum simulacris immolata.
units.tr: "For if anyone sees you," etc. He states how the danger he wants guarded against might come about, unless they are careful, and sets before our eyes at greater length how serious it is. He speaks to each one separately, singling him out and questioning him, saying: "For if anyone sees you reclining at a feast of idols, will not the conscience of the weak man be emboldened to eat things sacrificed to idols?" That is to say: I address you yourself, who eat food offered to idols and who recline at a feast of idols in the very temple of idols, together with the Gentiles and the worshippers of the images. Answer me: what will happen if a weak brother sees you doing this? What else can be expected than that he too, though unlike you in faith, will be moved by your example to eat food offered to idols? That is to say: surely you cannot deny that this will happen. By this question the Apostle asserts the coming danger more forcefully and confidently than if he had simply said: "For if anyone sees you reclining at a feast of idols, the conscience of that man will be emboldened to eat things sacrificed to idols."

units.la: Ergo hactenus malum est eidolothytis uesci, quatenus id fit cōspicientib. infirmis, & rui næ occasionem causatur. Quid igitur est, quod August. Epist. 154. ad quæstionem Publicolæ, qua quærebatur si uiator, famis necessitate pressus nihil uspiam cibi inuenerit, nisi in eidolio, ubi tamē nullus mortalium præsens sit, an satius illi sit fame emori quàm eidolothytum edere. breviter quidem, sed non iuxta sententiam Apost. respondet: Aut certum est esse, inquiens, eidolothytum, aut certum est non esse, aut ignoratur. Si ergo certū est esse, melius Christiani uirtute repuritur. Si aut uel non esse scitur, uel ignoratur, sine ullo conscientiæ scrupulo in usum necessitatis assumitur. Apost. plane aliud hic tradit: Non enim docet esse in se peccatum, uesci eidolothytis, si nemo infirmorum uideat, qui offendi possit. August. uero etiam si nemo mortalium præsens, & fame pereundum sit, satius esse putat fame emori quam eidolothyta edere. Erat. opinatur illum & hunc locū retractaturum fuisse, si quisquā admonuisset.
units.tr: So eating food offered to idols is an evil only to the extent that it is done in the sight of the weak and gives occasion for their fall. Why, then, does Augustine, in Letter 154, in answer to Publicola's question, whether a traveller pressed by hunger, who finds nothing to eat anywhere except in an idol's temple where no mortal is present, would do better to die of hunger than eat food offered to idols, answer briefly, but not in line with the Apostle's view: "Either it is certain," he says, "that the food is offered to idols, or it is certain that it is not, or it is unknown. If it is certain that it is, a Christian should be strengthened by his virtue to refrain. If it is known that it is not, or it is unknown, it may be taken for the sake of necessity without any scruple of conscience." The Apostle plainly teaches something else here: he does not teach that eating food offered to idols is in itself sin when no weak person is present who could be offended. Augustine, however, even if no mortal is present and one must perish of hunger, thinks it better to die of hunger than to eat food offered to idols. Erasmus thinks that Augustine would have retracted this passage too, had anyone warned him.

units.la: QVI habes scientiam] Non est frustra adiectum. Neque enim à quouis offendiculum est infirmis, sed ab ijs, qui rerum scientia reliquis præstantiores habeantur. Nam ita comparatum est ingenium imperitorum, ut non rerum cognitione, sed authoritate sapientum ducantur. Videmus hodie innumeram multitudinē exemplis doctorum & præstantium seduci.
units.tr: "Who have knowledge": this is not added in vain. For a stumbling-block is not offered to the weak by just anyone, but by those who are regarded as superior to the rest because of their knowledge. For the untrained mind is so constituted that it is led not by knowledge of things but by the authority of the wise. Today we see countless multitudes led astray by the examples of learned and eminent men.

units.la: Putes ne,inquiunt, tot doctores uiros errare posse? Quapropter ut periculosissime delinquunt,qui rerum scientia, uel saltem illius opinione pollent, ita summa illis cautione inter infirmam plebeculam uersandum est. Sed proh dolor,nemo est in ecclesia,qui licentius delinquat,&minus infirmos curet,quàm illijpsi qui scientiae nomine suspiciuntur.
units.tr: "Do you suppose," they say, "that so many learned men can err?" Therefore, just as those who excel in knowledge, or at least in the reputation of it, sin most dangerously, so they must move among the weak common people with the greatest caution. But alas, there is no one in the Church who sins more recklessly and cares less for the weak than those very men who are admired in the name of knowledge.

units.la: IN epulo simulachrorum accumbete.] Graece est, ψ ἀλωλεὶ κατακειμένων. Vetus no reddiditGreca uocé ἀλισκων. Eraf.uertit epulum simulachrorum. Significat uero téplum eidolorum, tametsi & mensam eidolorum significare putet Eraf.Notum est Gentes in téplis deorum peracto sacro coram simulacris epulatos esse ex his,quae dijs immolabatur. Et ad illas epulas abfq; dubio amicos uocarunt,&uicinos.Ex hac itaq; consuetudine euenicbat,ut & Christiani siue dolo, siue simpliciter ex more, ad eidolothyta uocarentur. Hic q de scietia gloriabantur, uocati nó quidè ad ipsum simulachrorum cultū,ad conuiuiū sacrum cóparebant, & unà cū Gentib.in deorum delubris epulabātur. Hoc cómemorat Apost. isto loco,ut doceat, quid inde mali sequatur.
units.tr: "Reclining at a feast of idols": in Greek it is "in an idol's temple reclining [ἐν εἰδωλείῳ κατακειμένων]". The old translator did not render the Greek word [ἀλισκων]. Erasmus translates "a feast of idols," though he thinks it may also mean the table of the idols. It is well known that the Gentiles, after performing sacred rites before the images in the temples of their gods, feasted on what was offered to those gods. And to those feasts they undoubtedly invited friends and neighbours. From this custom it came about that Christians, whether by trickery or simply out of habit, were invited to food offered to idols. Those who boasted of their knowledge came to the sacred banquet, not indeed for the worship of the images themselves, but they dined together with the Gentiles in the shrines of the gods. The Apostle recalls this in this passage, so that he may teach what evil follows from it.

units.la: NONNE cósciētia eius,qui infirmus est,ę-dificabitur ad edendū,&c. ] Aedificādi uerbo hoc loco,& Gal.2.abusiue in malo usurpat. Nā reipsa cósciētia infirmi per offendiculū magis destruitur q̄ ędificatur.Nihil igitur hic aliud significat,q infirmatur ac prouehitur,ut infirmi or reddatur,& uelut in ipsa infirmitate stabilitur. Ad quid ędificātur. Ad edēdū,inquit,ea q̄ B sunt simulachris immolata. Quid hoc periculi est:Si ille in se nihil mali facit, qui per scientiā uescitur,qui peccat infirmus,qui illius exemplo inductus & ipse uescitur? Externe quidem nihil apparet discriminis in utrisq; uelcentib. interne uero disimilitudo est. Nam ille ex fide quidem uescitur cum scientia unius ac ueri Dei,iste uero ex superstitione,atque ob eā causam in conscientia,ut suprà dixit,polluitur.
units.tr: "Will not the conscience of him who is weak be built up to eat," etc. In this passage the Apostle uses the word "build up" in an abusive sense for something bad, as he also does in Galatians 2. For in reality the conscience of the weak is destroyed rather than built up by a stumbling-block. So here it means nothing other than that the weak man is strengthened and advanced, so that he becomes still weaker and is established, as it were, in his very weakness. To what is he built up? "To eat," he says, "things sacrificed to idols." What danger is there in this, if he who eats with knowledge does no wrong himself, while the weak man who sins, being led by his example, eats as well? Outwardly, indeed, there appears to be no difference between the two who eat, but inwardly there is a dissimilarity. For the one eats from faith, with the knowledge of the one and true God, whereas the other eats from superstition, and for that reason, as said above, is defiled in conscience.

units.la: Obseruemus hoc genus offendiculi. Generalis in hoc cap.locus est,cauendū est ne perfortiores offendātur ac perdātur infirmiores. Verū cósiderandū est probe,qñ id fiat, quādo nō fiat,Sunt.n.hodie,qui &ipsi de scientia uerita tis gloriantes,qd simulacrū,nihil sit, cū simulachrorum cultorib.ubi sese offert occasio,nimis libere,cōmiscētur, & ubi reprehēduntur, mox regerūt ad hoc se id facere, ne offēdiculo sint infirmis,aut non intelligentes qñ infirmis sint offendiculo,aut maliciose id prętexentes. Nam hoc ipso,quòd in falso illo cultu Dei præsentes sunt, imperitos ad cultū simulacrorum ædificant. At hoc non est cauere, sed magis objicere infirmis offendiculum.Dicis: Nunquid & Paulus ipse factus est infirmis infirmus? Verū.Sed in alijs causis,in reb.uidelicet indifferētibus.ubi nō erat periculū, ne infirmi ad cultū simulacrorū ædificarentur.Aliud est nó uescit q-buslibet,idq; ad tępus,cum infirmis, ne offendantur in re media: uel certe ad hoc mouean-tur, ut & ipsi contra conscientiam uescantur
units.tr: Let us observe this kind of stumbling-block. The general teaching of this chapter is that care must be taken lest the stronger be offended and the weaker be destroyed. But it must be carefully considered when this happens and when it does not. For there are men today who, though they themselves boast of the truth of knowledge, that an image is nothing, mix far too freely with the worshippers of images whenever the opportunity presents itself. And when they are rebuked, they soon reply that they do it so as not to be a stumbling-block to the weak, either not understanding when they are a stumbling-block to the weak, or cunningly using this as a pretext. For by the very fact that they are present at that false worship of God, they build up the unlearned to worship images. But this is not guarding against offence; rather it is putting a stumbling-block before the weak. You say: "Did Paul himself not become weak to the weak?" True, but that was in other matters, namely in things indifferent, where there was no danger that the weak would be built up to worship images. It is one thing not to eat in the presence of anyone at all, and that only for a time, for the sake of the weak, lest they be offended by an indifferent thing; or at least to be moved to this, so that they too eat against their conscience. It is another thing, in unlawful matters and false worship, to build up the weak by one's own example, so that they are confirmed in their blindness.

units.la: quibuslibet:& aliud in reb.illicitis & falso cultu,proprio exèplo ędificare infirmos,ut in sua cęcitate confirmationes reddantur. Hactenus remittendum est de libertate Christiana, quatenus id facit ad ædificandum non in superstitione,sed pietate,eum qui infirmus est.Vbi uero nostro condescensu in peius ædificatur,ibi certe satius est non infirmitatem,sed firmitate uerae pietatis ac fidei ostendere.
units.tr: Christian liberty must be yielded so far as it does this to build up the weak man in piety, not in superstition. But where, by our condescension, he is built up for the worse, there it is certainly better to show not weakness but the firmness of true piety and faith.

units.la: ET peribit frater qui infirmus est,in tua scie tia,propter quem Christus fuit mortuus.] Ista ad exaggerandum offendiculi huius malum facit, ad quod singulae structae sunt particulae. Ostendit per declarationem,quo infirmis ponatur offendiculum.Iam consequenter explicat,quanto id malo fiat.
units.tr: "And the weak brother will perish in your knowledge, for whose sake Christ died." These words serve to magnify the evil of this stumbling-block, and each of the individual phrases is constructed for this purpose. He shows by explanation how a stumbling-block is placed before the weak. Now he goes on to explain by how great an evil this is done.

units.la: 1 Primū,Quod nō in cuiusuis mortalis laesio nem id cedat sed fratris,hoc est Christiani. Le uiculum quidem non est,cuiq; mortalium siue Indaeo siue Graeco,offendiculū dare. Vnde & alibi dicit,Sine offensione estote Iudeis & Graecis. Attamē multo grauius est fratri fideli occasionem generare ruinae.Quemadmodum iusti hominis esse non potest, quemuis mortalium iniuria afficere:at germanū fratrē lędere, nó solum iniusti, sed plane improbi hominis fuerit.
units.tr: First, this does not result in injury to any mortal, but to a brother, that is, a Christian. Certainly it is no great matter to give offence to any mortal, whether Jew or Greek. Hence he also says elsewhere: "Be without offence to Jews and Greeks." Nevertheless, it is much more grievous to give a faithful brother occasion for ruin. As it cannot be the mark of a just man to injure anyone at all, so to wound a true brother would be the mark not only of an unjust man but plainly of a wicked one.

units.la: 2 Deinde,qd non simpliciter lædatur frater, sed perdatur etiā.Et peribit,inquit, frater. Aedificari nanq; ad cultū simulacrorū,quid aliud est q perdi:Supra dixit,cap.6. Simulacrorum cultores regnum Dei posside nó posse.Siue enim talis frater, ad cultum simulacrorum ędificatus Christi profesionem retineat,siue hoc facilius ad negandum Christum & Gētilismū resumendum inducatur, salutem obtinere nó potest.Neque .n.saluari potest, qui Christo & templo Dei eidolorum cultum coniungit,de quo in posteriore cap.6.Quid couenit,inquit, templo Dei cum simulacris? neq; aliud quàm perire credi potest, qui per cultum simulacrorum ad negandum Christum inducitur.
units.tr: Second, the brother is not merely harmed but even destroyed. "And the brother will perish," he says. For to be built up to worship images is nothing other than to be lost. Above, in chapter 6, he said that worshippers of images will not possess the kingdom of God. For whether such a brother, built up to worship images, keeps his profession of Christ, or is more easily led to deny Christ and resume heathenism, he cannot obtain salvation. For he cannot be saved who joins the worship of idols to Christ and the temple of God, of which he speaks in the later part of chapter 6: "What agreement has the temple of God with images?" Nor can anyone who is led by the worship of images to deny Christ be believed to be anything but lost.

units.la: 3 Tertio,quod is frater perditur,qui infirmus est. Hoc certè crudelitatis quoq; notā habet, nō solum fratre quēcunq;, sed infirmum etiā, cuius singularis quædam erat habenda ratio, donec convalesceret, tāta temeritate perdere. Habet hoc in se vera charitas, ut infirmorū curam potissimum subeat.Mater omnesquidem liberos diligit,sed singulari quodam affectuad curandum infirmos rapitur,cum interea de sanis non admodū fit solicita.Ita & fraterna charitas,licet in sanis plerunq; nonnihil frigeat,in ægrotis tū curandis solicita redditur.Videtur enim periturum quod infirmum est.Ne pereat igitur,curare conatur anxia charitas.
units.tr: Third, that the brother who is weak is destroyed. This too bears the mark of cruelty, to destroy so recklessly not just any brother, but a weak one, whose case ought to receive special consideration until he recovers his strength. True love has this quality, that it especially takes on the care of the weak. A mother certainly loves all her children, but with a particular affection she is drawn to care for the sick, while meanwhile she is not very anxious about the healthy. So also brotherly love, though it is often somewhat cool towards the strong, becomes anxious to care for the sick.
