For what is weak seems likely to perish, so anxious love strives to care for it, so that it may not perish.

units.la: Nam ægre perire finit quod diligit. Est itaq; certissimum argumentum nihil esse illis fratrē dilectionis,qui ne infirmorum quidem fratrum,curat enentur. Qui uero perdunt etiam, quales illi tandem æstimandi sunt.
units.tr: Indeed, a person can hardly bear to let go of what he loves. So this is a very sure sign that those who do not even care for their weaker brothers have no real brotherly love at all. But what should we think of those who actually destroy them?

units.la: 4 Quartò.Et hoc finfiulari auxesi adiectum est,quod dicit Propter quem Christus mortuus est.
units.tr: 4 Fourthly. This is added with a special emphasis, in what he says: "for whom Christ died."

units.la: Primum enim nō is infirmus frater, qui è sa no sit factus infirmus, sed qui per Christum ex ipsa morte ereptus, ac uitę restitutus nondum plane conualuerat quidem, sed in sanitatis iam progressibus erat, perditur.
units.tr: For first, he is not a weak brother merely because he has become sick, but one who, having been snatched from death itself through Christ and restored to life, had not yet fully recovered but was already making progress toward health. Such a man is destroyed.

units.la: Deinde qui non quouis modo uitæ restitu tus erat, sed per Christi sanguine ac mortem. Quasi dicat: Tu ne perdis eum quem Christus sanguine suo redemptum saluum esse uoluit.
units.tr: Second, he was restored to life not in just any way, but through the blood and death of Christ. As if he were saying: "Do you destroy the one whom Christ wanted to be saved, having redeemed him with his own blood?"

units.la: 5 Quinto & hoc cum emphasi adiectum est, quod addit, In tua scientia. Per ignorantiā per dere fratrem, excusationis nonnihil habere po test. At rerum scientia hactenus abuti, ut quæ debebat ignorantibus & infirmis consulere, ce dat ad infirmorum & ignoratium perniciem, quid quæso excusationis admittere poterit? Me dicus q de arte medicandi gloriatur, si infirmū per scientiā suā occidat, certe maiore culpa hoc tacit, quàm si id fiat ab eius artis imperito.
units.tr: 5 Fifthly, this is also added with emphasis, in what he adds: "in your knowledge." To destroy a brother through ignorance may have some excuse. But to abuse knowledge in such a way that what ought to serve the ignorant and weak is turned to the ruin of the weak and ignorant: what excuse, I ask, could be admitted for that? If a physician boasts of his medical skill and kills a patient by that very skill, he certainly sins more gravely than if the same thing were done by someone unskilled in the art.

units.la: 6 Adiúge istis, quòd supra notatum est, nem pe, quòd ista infirmi fratris perditio sit in re pr sus inani, nempe in libertate quidlibet edendi, in qua tamen nemo Deo probatus redditur.
units.tr: 6 Add to these what was noted above, namely that this destruction of a weak brother is over a matter entirely empty, that is, over the liberty to eat anything, a liberty in which, however, no one is made acceptable to God.

units.la: Quó quæso excusari potest, qui cibi gratia eū perdit, quē Christus sanguine suo redemit? cu ius saluti Christus uitam suam posposuit. Qua lis tandem Christianus est, qui fratris gratia ne cibo quidem abstinere potest, cum Christus, p illo mori quoque non dubitauerit?
units.tr: What excuse, I ask, can be offered by the one who destroys for the sake of food a brother whom Christ redeemed with his own blood, and for whose salvation Christ did not hesitate to lay down his life? What sort of Christian is he who, for the sake of a brother, cannot even abstain from food, when Christ did not hesitate even to die for him?

units.la: SIC autem peccantes in fratres & conscie tiam illorum infirmam uulnerantes, in Christū peccatis. Cósulto eo deducit hoc peccatū, ut intelligatur iam non simpliciter in Christianū infirmū, sed in Christum ipsum peccari. Sentie bat enim arrogantib. istis parum uideri, quod in fratres infirmos peccabatur, maxime ea in re, qua Christi scientiā & libertate promouere se simulabant. Per inuersionem igitur conuin cit eos, tā non gratificari sua ista scientia Chri sto redēptori, ut magis in illum peccent, idque nō aliquo, sed omniū grauissimo peccato. Qd enim grauius peccatū in Christū cōmitti pote rit, q eū occidere, p quo ipse est mortuus. Ma ter impensissime diligit eum filium, quē partu doloris pleno peperit. Hunc si ui occidas, quō non grauiter in matrem peccaueris?
units.tr: Thus, those who sin against the brothers and wound their weak conscience, sin against Christ. He deliberately carries the sin to this point, so that it is understood that the sin is committed not simply against a weak Christian but against Christ himself. For he perceived that those arrogant men thought it a small matter that they sinned against weak brothers, especially in that very thing by which they pretended to advance Christ's knowledge and liberty. So by a reversal he rebukes them: their knowledge does not honour Christ their redeemer, rather they sin against him all the more, and not with just any sin but with the most grievous of all. For what more grievous sin could be committed against Christ than to kill the one for whom he himself died? A mother loves most tenderly the son whom she bore in full pain of labour. If you violently kill this son, how could you not sin grievously against the mother?

units.la: Et in hac particula nequit mali exaggeratio nem remittere. Non enim tantum dicit: Sic au tem peccantes in Christū peccatis. Sed sic pec cantes in fratres, & conscientiam illorum infir mam, non dicit, Offendentes: sed percutientes, in Christum peccatis.
units.tr: And in this clause he cannot lessen the exaggeration of the evil. For he does not merely say, "Thus sinning against the brothers you sin against Christ." He says: "sinning against the brothers and wounding their weak conscience." He does not say "offending," but "striking," and so "you sin against Christ."

units.la: Ambr. ut & uetus interpres illud ἁμαρτάνοντες le git in Christo, & putat aliud esse in Christo pec care, q in Christum peccare. In Christo pecca re, idem esse atq; sub Christo in eos qui Christi sunt peccare: in Christum uero, esse Christum negare. Verum apertum est, in Græco esse non in Christo sed in Christum.
units.tr: Ambrose, and the old translator as well, read the word ἁμαρτάνοντες [hamartanontes, sinning] as "in Christ," and think that to sin "in Christ" is something other than to sin "against Christ." To sin "in Christ" would mean the same as to sin under Christ's authority against those who belong to Christ; but to sin "against Christ" would mean to deny Christ. Yet it is plain that in the Greek it is not "in Christ" but "against Christ" [eis ton Christon].

units.la: QVAPROPTER, si esca offedit fratre meū haudquaquam uescar carnib. in æterū, ne fra tri meo sim offendiculo. ] Suo exēplo illos ad monet, quo loco haberi debeat salus fratrum,
units.tr: WHEREFORE, if food offends my brother, I will by no means eat flesh for ever, lest I be a stumbling block to my brother. He admonishes them by his own example what regard ought to be had for the salvation of brothers.

units.la: Nēpe eo ut licita etiam pro illicitis habeantur. Habet autem singularem uerborum diligen tiam, quod pro eidolothytis escam & carnes, & pro fratrum perditione, offensionem ponit. Nunquam enim sustinebit propter eidolothy ta fratrem infirmum perdere, qui quauis etiā carne, ne frater offendatur, abstinere paratus est.
units.tr: Namely, that lawful things should even be regarded as unlawful. He uses a special precision of words in putting "food" and "flesh" for meats offered to idols, and "offence" for the destruction of brothers. For he will never endure destroying a weak brother for the sake of meat offered to idols, when he is ready to abstain even from any flesh whatever, lest his brother be offended.

units.la: Quod autem addit, In æternum, contra illo rum querimonias positum est, quibus dicere poterant: Et quousque tandem ferendi sunt in firmi isti? Ego sane, inquit, in æternum quo que paratus sum ita infirmi fratris habere cu ram, ut nec quamuis carnem, si illius esu offen datur, cupiam attingere. Et ne propter pauci tatem contemnantur in ecclesia infirmi, unus & alter, notanter singulari numero utitur, di cens: Si esca offenderit fratrem, & ne offendi culo sim fratri meo.
units.tr: What he adds, "for ever," is directed against the complaints of those men, by which they could say: "And how long must these weak ones be put up with?" "I, indeed," he says, "am ready even for ever to have such care for a weak brother that, if he is offended by eating it, I would not desire to touch even any flesh at all." And lest the weak in the congregation be despised on account of their small number, he deliberately uses the singular, saying: "If food offends a brother, and lest I be a stumbling block to my brother."

units.la: CAPVT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: VIdetur hoc caput quibusdam aliam quandam à priore separatam habere causam, uerum ma nifestum est diligenter omnia expendentibus, quæ hic aguntur ad eundem pertinere tractatū qui capite præ cedenti contra temeritatem eidolothytophagorum cœ ptus est, & ut ibi memini, ad decimum usq; protendi tur. In calce præcedentis capitis suo illos exemplo pu defacere cœpit, in se ostendens, quanti fraterna salus fi eri debeat ueris Christianis, quàm non sit spectandum quid cuiq; liceat, sed quid infirmis prosit. Ad hoc illos amplificatione exempli sui toto hoc capite ualidissime inuitat, non contentus eo, quòd si cibus offendat fra trem, nunquam in sempiternum uelit edere carnes: sed adiungens factum suum, quo non simplicem aliquam libertatem, quæ communis sit Christianis omnibus, & talis, ut facile absq; ulla molestia contemni queat: sed ipsum Apostolici muneris ius, q o uictus sibi à fidelí bus in Euangelio Christi laboranti debebatur, ne cui ef set offendiculo, negligebat, non spectans quid sibi iure deberetur, & à Corinthijs petere posset: sed quid ipsis, quibus prædicabat, expediret, ut pudefaceret eos qui in re nihili quidem, periculosa tamen, & quæ facile po terat cauere, libertate sua ad perditionem infirmorum abutebantur.
units.tr: This chapter seems to some to have a separate cause from the previous one, but it is clear to anyone who carefully weighs what is being done here that it belongs to the same discussion which, in the preceding chapter, was begun against the rashness of those who eat meat offered to idols, and which, as I recalled there, extends to the tenth chapter. At the close of the previous chapter he began to shame them by his own example, showing in himself how great the salvation of a brother ought to be to true Christians, and that one must not look at what each is permitted, but at what benefits the weak. To this end he invites them most forcefully throughout this whole chapter by the amplification of his own example. He is not content with saying that if food gives offence to a brother he will never again eat meat for ever; he adds his own practice, in which he gave up not some simple liberty, common to all Christians and of such a kind that it could easily be set aside without any hardship, but the very right of the apostolic office, namely the sustenance owed to him by the faithful while he laboured in the Gospel of Christ. He did this so that he would be no stumbling block to anyone, not looking at what was rightly owed to him and what he could ask of the Corinthians, but at what was expedient for those to whom he preached, so that he might shame those who, in a matter of no account, yet dangerous and easily guarded against, abused their liberty to the ruin of the weak.

units.la: Non itaq; frustra quidā scripserunt toto hoc capite argumentum à maiori uersari. Quanquam illud intel lexerunt de authoritate ac dignitate Apostolatus sum ptum, atq; ob eam rationem amplificari Apostolici muneris dignitatem: ut appareat, si Apostolus libertà te sua non sit usus, multo minus Corinthios Apostoli di scipulos sua debuisse uti.
units.tr: It is therefore not without reason that some have written that throughout this chapter the argument proceeds from the greater. Although they understood this as concerning the authority and dignity of the apostleship, and on that ground the dignity of the apostolic office is magnified, so that it appears that if the Apostle did not use his liberty, the disciples of the Apostle, the Corinthians, ought much less to have used theirs.

units.la: Mihi uero non solum à dignitate Apostoli, sed simul ex ipsa causarum diuersitate argumentum ex maiori structum esse uidetur. Incst enim omnino magna diuer sitas inter eā causam, in qua Corinthios arguit, & eam in qua ipse iure suo se nō esse usum exēpli uice docet. In causa Corinthiorum, eidolothytis utscentium, liber tas eidolothyta edendi propter infirmos fratres erat negligēda: in causa & facto Apostoli nō simplex quædam libertas, sed ius debitum, non qualiscunq; almo- nia, sed necessaria, & laboranti Apostolo debita, ad ca- utendum offendiculum negligebatur. Quantulum erat, quod exigebat ab illis Apostolus, si conferas cum eo, quod ipse faciebat?
units.tr: To me, however, the argument from the greater seems to be built not only on the dignity of the Apostle but at the same time on the very difference of the causes. For there is indeed a great difference between the cause in which he rebukes the Corinthians, and the one in which he teaches by example that he did not use his own right. In the cause of the Corinthians, who ate meat offered to idols, the liberty of eating idol-meat had to be set aside for the sake of weak brothers; in the cause and practice of the Apostle, it was not some simple liberty but a right owed to him, not some casual almsgiving but a necessary and due support for an labouring apostle, that he set aside so as to avoid giving offence. How small was what he required of them, if you compare it with what he himself did?

units.la: Exempli gratia. Finge nos, qui Christum praedica- mus, excipere ab audioribus nostris, ut in gratiam & aedificationem infirmorum, libertatem carnes diebus uetitis edendi non usurpet, illosq; nostro exemplo Apostolum sequuti, ita ad hoc inuitare, ut nostro iure in ministerio uerbi non utamur, gratis Euangelium praedicantes & uictum labore manuum quaerentes. Quantum esset molestiae, feria 6. & sabbato non uesci carnibus, si conferas cum eo, si debitum & necessarium subsidium non inde, unde iure puterat, sed ex molesto manuum labore peteretur? Perinde omnino non tantum petit Apostolus a Corinthiis, quantum ipse faciebat. Plus enim erat de iure tantopere debito ac necessario remittere, quam eidolothytis infirmorum gratia abstinere. Sed uideamus textum.
units.tr: For example: suppose that we who preach Christ were to excuse ourselves from our hearers, so that for the sake of the edification of the weak we did not claim the liberty of eating meat on forbidden days, and, following the Apostle's example, invited them to this, by not using our right in the ministry of the Word, preaching the Gospel freely and seeking our living by the labour of our hands. How great a burden would it be, on Friday and Saturday, to abstain from meat, if you compare it with that? If the due and necessary support were sought not from where it could rightly be sought, but from the troublesome labour of the hands? In just the same way the Apostle asks of the Corinthians far less than he himself did. For it was a greater thing to give up so much of a right that was so greatly owed and necessary than to abstain from idol-meat for the sake of the weak. But let us look at the text.

units.la: N nō sum Apostolus? An non sum liber? An non Iesum Christum dominū nostrum uidi? An non opus meū uos estis in domino? Sí caeteris non sum Apostolus, at sane uobis sum. Siquidē signū Apostolatus mei uos estis in domino. Mea responsio apud eos qui me interrogāt haec est. An non habemus potestatem edendi ac bibendi? An nō habemus potestatem sororem mulierem circumducendi, quēadmodum & caeteri Apostoli, & fratres domini, & Cephas.
units.tr: Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord? If I am not an apostle to others, yet at least I am to you. For the seal of my apostleship is you in the Lord. My answer to those who question me is this: Have we not the power to eat and to drink? Have we not the power to lead about a sister, a wife, as also the other apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas do?

units.la: Vis exempli Apostolici in duobus sita est. Primum in eo, quod sumptus praedicationis non sumebat a Corinthiis. Deinde in eo, quod Apostolus cū esset, Apostolico iure illos a Corinthiis, quorum erat Apostolus, exigere potuisset. De priore non multis agit. Erat enim absque ulla contradictione manifestum, ut probationibus adductis fidem illius facere necesse non fuerit. Proinde tantum id semel atque iterum obiter commemorat, cum infrà dicit: Atqui non sumus usi ista potestate. Item: Ego tamen nullo horum usus fui. Igitur omne intentionem praesentis tractatus ad alteram partem probandam convertit, quae est de iure Apostolatus, quod multis argumentis amplificat. Et quoniam fieri potuit, ut ius quidem Apostolici muneris, in hac causa, nō negauerint pseudapostoli (nā & ipsi, ut in posteriore cap. 11. apparet, à Corinthiis sumptus accipiebant, licet uidere uellet Christi apostoli) negauerint autem ipsum Paulum esse Christi Apostolum, ut gloriam illius & existimationem eleuarent, necesse fuit Apostolo, hanc particulam ante o-
units.tr: The force of the apostolic example lies in two things. First, that he did not take payment for preaching from the Corinthians. Second, that although he was an apostle, he could by apostolic right have demanded maintenance from the Corinthians, of whom he was the apostle. He does not deal much with the first point. For it was clear without any dispute, so there was no need to make good its credibility by producing proofs. Accordingly he mentions it only once or twice in passing, when he says later: "But we have not used this power" and "Yet I have used none of these things." So he turns the whole intention of the present discussion to proving the other part, which concerns the right of the apostleship, and he amplifies it with many arguments. And since it could happen that the false apostles, in this matter, did not deny the right of the apostolic office (for they too, as appears in the later chapter 11, took payment from the Corinthians, although they would wish to be seen as apostles of Christ), but did deny that Paul himself was an apostle of Christ, in order to diminish his glory and reputation, it was necessary for the Apostle to assert this point above all: that he too is an apostle of Christ, so that the right to be paid for preaching is owed to him no less than to the other apostles. For this reason he begins in this way, with great confidence: "Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord? If I am not an apostle to others, yet at least I am to you. For the seal of my apostleship is you in the Lord."

units.la: mnia afferere, uidelicet, quod & ipse sit Christi Apostolus, ut & sibi non minus quàm reliquis Apostolis debeantur praedicandi sumptus. Et ea de causa, magna cum confidentia ad hunc modum orditur: An non sum Apostolus? An non sum liber? An non Iesum Christum, domi- num nostrum uidi? An nō opus meum uos estis in domino? Si caeteris non sum Apostolus, at sane uobis sum. Siquidem obsignatio Apostolatus mei uos estis in domino.
units.tr: Let me restate that opening, since it is the foundation of what follows: "Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord? If I am not an apostle to others, at least I am to you. For the seal of my apostleship is that you are in the Lord."

units.la: Apparet autem Apostolum crebris istis & uehementibus percontationibus ita quidem usum, ut iudicarit, prorsus impudentem esse, si quis neget se esse Apostolum Christi, ac liberum: simul tamen pseudapostolorum glorias notare uoluisse, qui, ut praedicationibus ueritatis omnem existimationem adimerent, seseque pro magnis uenditarent, Apostolatus dignitatem supra modum iactabant, se esse Christi apostolos, ab illis missos qui ueri sint Christi apostoli, qui Christum uiderint, & audierint, se esse liberos in omnibus. Vt igitur factū suum Apostolus Corinthiis exemplum imitandum contra seductores pseudapostolos asseveret, opponit se illorum gloriationibus, dicens, An non sum Apostolus? quasi dicat: Gloriantur se esse apostolos Christi, & liberos, & ab illis missos, qui Christum uiderunt, & hoc nomine nihil non apud uos possunt, animos uestros eo deducentes, ut ipsis magistris scientia & libertate uestra contra infirmos fratres abutamini. Qui fit quod non me potius sequimini? An ego non sum Apostolus? An nō sum liber? An ego Christum dominum non uidi? An nō opus meum uos estis in domino? Cur igitur ad me non respicitis, & conuersatio nis meae formam amplectiminí? Hoc uidetur agere Apostolus, sed tectius certis rationibus. Nam in posteriore euidentius pseudapostolos insectatur, & Apostolatum suū aduersum illos uindicat.
units.tr: It appears that the Apostle used these frequent and vehement questions because he judged it utterly shameless for anyone to deny that he is an apostle of Christ and free. At the same time he wished to mark the boasting of the false apostles, who, in order to strip the preaching of the truth of all its authority and to puff themselves up as great men, exaggerated beyond measure the dignity of the apostleship: they claimed to be apostles of Christ, sent by those who are the true apostles of Christ, who had seen and heard Christ, and that they were free in all things. So that the Apostle might assert his own conduct to the Corinthians as an example to be imitated against the seducing false apostles, he sets himself against their boasting, saying, "Am I not an apostle?" As if he said: "They boast that they are apostles of Christ, and free, and sent by those who saw Christ, and by this name they can do nothing but gain power over you, leading your minds so that, under these teachers, you use your knowledge and liberty against weak brothers. Why then do you not rather follow me? Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Christ the Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord? Why then do you not look to me and embrace the pattern of my way of life?" The Apostle seems to be doing this, but more covertly and by certain reasons. For in the later passage he attacks the false apostles more openly and defends his apostleship against them.

units.la: AN non sum liber? Hoc quidem nō addit, qua in re se afferat esse liberum. Infrà uero de libertate sua repetens, simulq; admonēs, quo- modo illa non utatur, dicit: Etenim cum liber sim ab omnibus, omnibus meipsum seruum feci, quo plures lucrifaciam. De qua libertate ibi dicemus.
units.tr: "Am I not free?" He does not add here in what respect he claims to be free. But later, returning to his liberty and at the same time admonishing them how he does not use it, he says: "For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might gain more." We shall speak about that liberty there.

units.la: AN Iesum Christum dominum nostrum non uidi? Non loquitur de uisione illa corporali, qua ante resurrectionem suā Christus non solum ab apostolis, uerumetiam ab innumeris Iudaeis, & absq; dubio ab ipso quoq;, cum Gamalielis esset discipulus, Ierosolymis uisus est, quae uisio nihil habebat praerogatiuę: sed de ea quę post resurrectionem suis quos elegerat ad hoc apparuit, ut certissimi testes essent resurrectionis suae, & omnium eorum quae per illā cōfirmata sunt. De praedicatione nanque, uita & morte Iesu, & ipsi Iudaei increduli testari potuissent. De hac uisione intelligit, non hoc solum loco, sed & infrà cap.15.
units.tr: "Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?" He is not speaking of that bodily sight by which Christ, before his resurrection, was seen not only by the apostles but also by countless Jews at Jerusalem, and without doubt by Paul himself too, who was a pupil of Gamaliel; that sight conferred no privilege. He means rather the sight which he granted after his resurrection to those whom he had chosen for this purpose, that they might be the most certain witnesses of his resurrection and of all the things confirmed by it. For the preaching, life and death of Jesus could even have been attested by unbelieving Jews. He understands this sight not only in this place but also in chapter 15 below.

units.la: Sed ubi uidit Paulus Christum post resurrectionem
units.tr: But when Paul saw Christ after his resurrection

units.la: ctionem illius: Actorum 22.ita legimus. Factū A est autem, cum essem reuersus Ierosolymam, & orarem in templo, ut raperer extra me, & uiderem eum dicentem mihi, festina & exi ue lociter Ierosolymis, quoniam non recipient testimonium tuum de me. Et ego dixi: Domine, ipsi sciunt, quod ego pertrahebam in carcerem, & cædebam in singulis synagogis eos qui credebant in te. Et cum funderetur sanguis Stephani testis tui, ego quoq; assistebam, & assentiebar morti illius, & custodiebam uestimenta interficientium illum. Et dixit ad me, uade, quoniam in nationes longè mittam te, &c. Ergo in mentis raptu & excessu uidit dominum. Vel si quis putat Apostolum non de ista uisione loqui, potest de apparitione ea intelligere, quæ in uia facta est, cum iret Damascum. Quanquam enim ibi non legatur sublimatis oculis dominum ipsum uidisse, sed uocem eius audisse, quia tamen Christus ipse dixit εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ ὤφθην σοι, id est, ad hoc enim uisus sum, uel apparui tibi. & paulò post, ipse Paulus ad regem Agrippam subiunxit: Unde rex Agrippa: Non fui inobediens cœlesti uisioni, &c. Visionem uocans eam apparitionem, utique non alterius cuiusquam, quàm ipsius domini: nihil puto impedire, quo minus de ista apparitione intelligamus, quod hic dicit: An Iesum Christum dominum nostrum nō uidi? maximè cum in ea uisione Apostolatus munus à domino acceperit, quod Christi uerba testantur.
units.tr: ...tion of that vision. Acts 22 reads thus: "It happened that, when I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I was caught up out of myself and saw him saying to me: 'Hurry and leave Jerusalem quickly, because they will not receive your testimony about me.' And I said: 'Lord, they know that I used to imprison and beat in every synagogue those who believed in you. And when the blood of Stephen, your witness, was being shed, I also stood by and approved of his death, and I guarded the garments of those who killed him.' And he said to me: 'Go, for I will send you far away to the nations,' etc." So he saw the Lord in a rapture and ecstasy of mind. Or if anyone thinks the Apostle is not speaking of this vision, he may understand it of the appearance that took place on the road when he was going to Damascus. For although it is not said there that he saw the Lord himself with raised eyes, but that he heard his voice, nevertheless Christ himself said εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ ὤφθην σοι [eis touto gar ōphthēn soi], that is, "for this purpose I have appeared to you." And a little later Paul himself added, speaking to King Agrippa: "Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision," etc. He calls that appearance a vision, certainly of no one other than the Lord himself. I think nothing prevents us from understanding in this sense the words here, "Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?", especially since in that vision he received the office of apostleship from the Lord, as the words of Christ attest.

units.la: AN non opus meum uos estis in domino?) Magna sanè gloriatio, quod rem tantam, omnes uires humanas superantem, & quę uni diuinę uirtuti reuera tribui potest, sibi adscribit. Sed magna fuerit necesse est pseudapostolorum impudentia & improbitas, quæ Apostolum ad hanc gloriandi necessitatem impulit, ut & in posteriore dicit: Vos me coegistis. Non est autem putādum, quod plus sibi tribuat, quàm Apostolo conueniat. Loquitur enim ut Christi Apostolus, & spiritus sancti minister. Proin de quod dicit, opus meum, idem est, atq; opus Apostolatus mei, uos estis in domino. Quasi dicat, Quicquid uos estis in domino, hoc estis per Apostolatū meū. Per me enim Christo credidistis. Theophylactus illudin domino, arbitratur idem esse, atq; per uirtutem domini, ne putetur opus hoc tam arduum suis adscribere uiribus. Verum prior sensus meo iudicio simplicior est. Quanq; posterior nō est abijciēdus; Luctatur Apostolus cōtra maliciam pseudapostolorum, atque illius gratia omnium euidentissimo testimonio probat se esse Christi Apostolū, ut constare posset, se Christiana prudentia & modestia cum sit Apostolus non tamen esse usum iure suo, ne occasionem daret maleuolis. Probat autem ex ipso opere, eoque non longè posito, sed præsenti, quod negari non poterat, quod ipsi scilicet erant. Quasi dicat, Si quispiam uestrum de Apostolatu meo dubitat, estis uos ipsi testes illius. Vos ipsi pro
units.tr: "Are you not my work in the Lord?" (This is a great boast, that he claims for himself a deed so great, surpassing all human powers, and which can truly be ascribed to divine power alone.) But the impudence and wickedness of the false apostles must have been great, for it drove the Apostle to this necessity of boasting, as he also says later: "You have compelled me." Yet we must not think he attributes more to himself than befits an Apostle. For he speaks as an apostle of Christ and a minister of the Holy Spirit. Therefore what he says, "my work," is the same as the work of my apostleship: "you are in the Lord." As if he said: whatever you are in the Lord, you are through my apostleship. For through me you believed in Christ. Theophylact, on the other hand, takes "in the Lord" to mean the same as "through the power of the Lord," so that the work is not thought to be ascribed to his own strength, since it is so arduous. But in my judgment the former sense is simpler, though the latter is not to be rejected. The Apostle struggles against the malice of the false apostles, and for their sake he proves by the most evident testimony of all that he is an apostle of Christ, so that it could be established that, although he is an apostle, he has not used his right out of Christian prudence and modesty, lest he give occasion to the ill-disposed. He proves this from the work itself, and not from a work far away but from one present, which could not be denied, namely they themselves. As if he said: If anyone of you doubts my apostleship, you yourselves are its witnesses. You yourselves prove

units.la: batis, quàm non sit inanis aduentus meus ad uos, per quem Christi insiti estis, qui in uobis non est infirmus sed potens. Sic in posteriore, uos ipsos, inquit, tentate, num sitis in fide, uos ipsos probate. An non cognoscitis uosmetipsos quod Iesus Christus in uobis est? Si ergo Christus in uobis est, quomodo ego non sum Christi Apostolus, per quem in Christum creditis? Non potest ullum esse euidentius testimonium quàm quod ipso opere datur. Sic Christus dicebat: Opera, quæ ego facio, testimonium perhibent de me. Vide igitur in quas angustias aduersarios suos peducat. Eas uidelicet, ut aut negare cogantur, Christianos esse, aut fateri, quod ipse sit Christi Apostolus. Quicquid enim erant in Christo hoc per ipsum erant.
units.tr: how far from empty my coming to you was, through which you have been implanted in Christ, who is not weak among you but powerful. So in the later passage he says: "Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?" If therefore Christ is in you, how am I not an apostle of Christ, through whom you believe in Christ? No testimony can be more evident than that which is given by the work itself. So Christ said: "The works that I do bear witness to me." See, then, into what straits he drives his adversaries: namely, that they must either be compelled to deny that the Corinthians are Christians, or confess that he himself is an apostle of Christ. For whatever they were in Christ, they were so through him.

units.la: Notandum est autem, quod ius Apostolo debitum, nō inani Apostolatus titulo, aut soli muneri commisso adscribit, sed operanti ac laboranti in domino, ne putemus ociosis illis & titulo tantum tenus episcopis episcopatus deberi sumptus. Probaturus sibi tanquam Christi Apostolo deberi prædicationis sumptus, nō nudam electionem Apostolatus, sed ipsum opus obijcit, quo se uerum esse Christi Apostolum probet. Faciant hoc & episcopi, qui hodie cœlum ac terram miscere conantur, moxatq; illis uel tantillum quid de iurisdictione episcopali aufertur. Dicant & ipsi cum Apostolo, opus nostrū uos estis in domino, si possunt.
units.tr: It must be noted, however, that he ascribes to himself the right due to an apostle not from the empty title of apostleship, nor from the office alone committed to him, but from working and laboring in the Lord. Lest we think that the bishops, who are idle and bishops only in name, are owed the expenses of preaching. In order to prove that the expenses of preaching are owed to him as an apostle of Christ, he does not set forth the bare election to apostleship, but the work itself, by which he proves that he is a true apostle of Christ. Let the bishops, who today try to stir heaven and earth, and who are angry if anything at all is taken away from their episcopal jurisdiction, do this too. Let them say with the Apostle, "You are our work in the Lord," if they can.

units.la: SI cæteris non sum Apostolus, at sanè uobis sum.) Hoc Hiero.ita exponit, quasi asserriuè dicat se non quidem Iudæis, Corinthijs tamen & alijs Gentibus esse Apostolum, respi ciens forte ad id quod Gal.2. dicit, sicut Petro circumcisionis Apostolatum, ita sibi præputij concreditum esse. At Apostolus non dicit: Licet nō sim cæteris Apostolus, sed: Si non sum cæteris Apostolus, at sanè uobis sum. Quod nihil est aliud, quàm, Si cæteris non habeor pro Apostolo, qui ministerium & opus meum in domino non agnoscunt, uos tamen negaré non potestis, me uestrum esse Apostolum.
units.tr: "If I am not an apostle to others, yet at least I am to you." Jerome explains this as if he were saying assertively that he is indeed not an apostle to the Jews, but is to the Corinthians and other Gentiles, perhaps looking to what he says in Gal. 2, that the apostleship of circumcision was entrusted to Peter, and so to himself the apostleship of the uncircumcised. But the Apostle does not say: "Although I am not an apostle to others," but: "If I am not an apostle to others, yet at least I am to you." This amounts to nothing other than: "If I am not regarded as an apostle by others, who do not recognize my ministry and work in the Lord, you nevertheless cannot deny that I am your apostle."

units.la: Respicit & Ambrosius ad Iudæos qui Christo legis obseruantiam, conniuentibus Petro, Iacobo & Ioanne, coniungebant, quibus Pauli Apostolatus in Christo non sit agnitus. Verum de Iudæis hoc loco non cogitat Apostolus, sed simpliciter opus suū apud Corinthios in domino ita extollit, ut etiamsi præterea nullis esset, ipsis tamē omnino sit Apostolus. Neque enim hic inter Iudæos & Gentes discriminat, sed quid Corinthijs sit præ aliis inculcat. Vnde & subdit:
units.tr: Ambrose also looks to the Jews who joined the observance of the law to Christ, Peter, James and John connivingly, and to whom the apostleship of Paul in Christ was not acknowledged. But the Apostle is not thinking here of Jews, but simply exalts his work among the Corinthians in the Lord so highly that, even if he were an apostle to no one else, he would still be wholly an apostle to them. For here he does not distinguish between Jews and Gentiles, but impresses on the Corinthians what is theirs in comparison with others. Hence he adds:

units.la: SIQVIDEM sigillū Apostolatus mei uos estis in domino.) Sigilli usus est, ut fidem faciat rei, de qua controuerti poterat. Ita da Apostolatu Pauli fidem facientes Corinthij, qui opus illius erant in domino, dicūtur esse Apostolatus ipsius sigillum. Est autem omnino auxesis quædam in his uerbis. Nam cum usq; adeò se Corinthiorum esse Apostolum dicit:
units.tr: "For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord." A seal is used to make certain a matter about which there could be dispute. So the Corinthians, who were his work in the Lord, bearing witness to Paul's apostleship, are called the seal of that apostleship. Now there is altogether a certain amplification in these words. For when he says that he is the apostle of the Corinthians to such an extent...

units.la: Vt illi contra maleuolos aduersarios pro figil lo sint Apostolatus fui, necesse est aliquid illis inesse propter quod præ alijs mereantur dici figillū Apostolatus ipsius. Quid hoc est quod ad fidem Christi per ipsum uenerút? Atqui id commune habent cum multis alijs ecclesijs. Mihi uidetur id commendari, quod singulari quadam gratia, studio, labore & patiétia illos ad Christum perduxerit, deinde & singulari quoq; effectu in illis diuina fe per spiritu sanctum uirtus in omni fcietia & gratia, ut signa, & prodigia taceam exeruerit. Sic supra cap.1. dixit: In omnibus diuites facti estis in Christo, in omni uerbo, & in omni scientia, sicut testimonium Christi confirmatum est in uobis, ita ut nihil uobis defit in ulla gratia. Et in posteriore cap.12. Tametsi nihil sum, signa tamen Apostoli perada sunt inter uos, cum omni patientia & signis & prodigijs, &potentib.factis. Hæsit apud illos annum & menses sex, quod de nulla alia ecclesia legitur, nisi quod Romæ integro biennio, sed captiuus, manere coactus est. Deinde accedit singularis quaedam corruptio Corinthiorum, ut plus fuerit Apostolo laboris insumendum hic quàm alibi. Et præterea singulari oraculo diuinitus est iussus in hac urbe fiducialiter & constanter agere, propterea quod multus erat in illa domino populus. Quemadmodum itaque fi Afer quisquam Scipionem Africanum neget esse imperatore, ille merito audiat, fi alijs non sum imperator, certe uobis Afris sum imperator, nam sigillum imperij mei uos estis: ita & Apostolus hoc loco, propter recensitas causas, omnium fortifi me aduersarijs ad probandum Apostolatum suum, Corinthiorum ecclesiam obijcit.
units.tr: ...that they serve as the seal of his apostleship against malicious adversaries, it is necessary that there be something in them on account of which they deserve to be called the seal of his apostleship more than others. What is this, that through him they came to faith in Christ? Yet this they have in common with many other churches. It seems to me that what is commended is that by a singular grace, zeal, labor and patience he led them to Christ, and then also by a singular effect the divine power itself was displayed in them through the Holy Spirit in all knowledge and grace, not to mention signs and wonders. So above in chapter 1 he said: "In everything you were enriched in Christ, in all speech and in all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed among you, so that you lack nothing in any grace." And in the later chapter 12: "Although I am nothing, the signs of an apostle were performed among you, with all patience, by signs and wonders and mighty deeds." He stayed among them a year and six months, which is not read of any other church, except that at Rome he was compelled to remain for two full years, but as a prisoner. Then there is also a particular corruption among the Corinthians, so that more labor had to be expended by the Apostle here than elsewhere. Besides, by a singular oracle he was divinely commanded to act boldly and steadfastly in this city, because the Lord had a large people in it. Therefore just as if some African were to deny that Scipio Africanus was a general, he would rightly be told: "If I am not a general to others, at least to you Africans I am a general, for you are the seal of my command," so also the Apostle here, for the reasons recounted, sets the church of the Corinthians against all his adversaries, to prove his apostleship.

units.la: Faciunt ista nō solum ad probandum quod fit Apostolus, sed huc potissimum quod cum effet præcipuè Corinthiorum Apostolus, iure tamen Apostolatus apud eos præcipuè nō fit usus, apud quos præcipuè poterat. Atque hoc ad propositum scopum facit, ad quem omnia collimantur, uidelicet, ut admoneantur hoc exemplo & ipsi non quod licet, sed quod expedit fratribus spectare & facere.
units.tr: These things serve not only to prove that he is an Apostle, but chiefly to show that although he was especially the Apostle of the Corinthians, he did not make use of his apostolic right among them, though among them above all he could have. This serves the purpose toward which everything is aimed, namely, that by this example they too may be admonished to seek and do not what is lawful but what is expedient for the brethren.

units.la: Videamus quæso de qua ecclesia Apostolus ista scribat, cuius fit præ alijs Apostolus, & quę sigillum fit Apostolatus ipsius. An de ea, quæ singulari fide, & pietate reliquas omnes excellat? Nequaquam. Quod fi enim quę hac epifto la scribuntur diligenter expendantur, conspicuum erit uix aliam esse, quæ pluribus uicijs laborauerit. Contentiones & schismata inter fe habebant, carnales erant, alius contra alium inflabatur, fcortationem inter fe habebant, qualis nec inter Getes reperiebatur. Illam nec corrigebant nec lugebant, sed inflabantur. Iudiciaria lite inter fe contendebant, atq; id coram impijs. Iniuriam inuicem alij alius fraudando faciebant. Eidolothytis temerè ad graue infirmorum offendiculum uescebatur, qui alijs præstantiores haberi uolebant. Mulieres non uelatæ ecclesiam abfq; ulla religione in-
units.tr: Let us see, I ask, of what church the Apostle is writing these things, the church of which he is the Apostle above others and which is the seal of his apostleship. Is it a church that surpasses all the rest in singular faith and piety? By no means. For if the things written in this epistle are carefully weighed, it will be plain that scarcely any other church labored under more vices. They had contentions and schisms among themselves, they were carnal, one was puffed up against another, they had fornication among themselves, such as was not found even among the Getae. They neither corrected it nor mourned it, but were puffed up. They contended with one another in lawsuits, and that before the impious. They wronged one another by defrauding. They ate idol-sacrifices rashly, to the grave stumbling of the weak, who wished to be held superior to others. Women entered the church unveiled, without any reverence whatever,

units.la: trabant, schismata etiam in ipsa dominica cœna habebant, seipsos non probabant, corpus domini à reliquo cibo non discernebant, alius ebrius erat, alius esuriebat, alius alium nó expectabat, sed quisque suam cœnam præsumebat. Qui singularia spiritus dona habebát con temnebant non habentes. Linguis insolescentes charitatem negligebant. Mulieres contra sexus rationem & ministerij decorum in ecclesia docebant. Ordinem prophetandi in ecclesia confundebant. Resurrectionem quidam ex eis negabant. Ignorantiam Dei plerique habebant.
units.tr: they also had schisms even at the Lord's Supper itself; they did not test themselves, and did not discern the body of the Lord from other food. One was drunk, another was hungry, one did not wait for another, but each presumed upon his own supper. Those who had the special gifts of the Spirit despised those who did not have them. Puffed up with tongues, they neglected love. Women taught in the church, contrary to the order of their sex and the decorum of the ministry. They confused the order of prophesying in the church. Some of them denied the resurrection. Most had no knowledge of God.

units.la: Ecce ista est ecclesia illa nō simpliciter apostolica, sed ita præ alijs apostolica, ut Paulo etiam sigillum fit Apostolatus. Cui igitur culpam dabimus tot uiciorum? Certè Apostolo nihil horum potest adscribi, cum singulari studio illa carpat, & emendata cupiat. Discamus igitur non mox eleuare ministerium feruorum Christi, ubi corruptas uidemus ecclesias. Deinde non speremus hodie ecclesiarum per sectam emendationem, cum iam infigniter apostolica uiuente adhuc Apostolo tam fuerit infigniter uiciofa.
units.tr: Behold, this is that church, not simply apostolic, but so apostolic above the others that even to Paul it is the seal of his apostleship. To whom, then, shall we ascribe the blame for so many vices? Certainly none of these can be attributed to the Apostle, since he rebukes them with singular zeal and desires them to be amended. Let us learn, therefore, not to be quick to disparage the ministry of the servants of Christ when we see churches corrupted. Nor let us hope today for the reformation of churches through a sect, since while the Apostle was still living, a church so eminently apostolic was so eminently vicious.

units.la: MEA refponfio apud eos.) Græcè est ἰμὶ ἀπολογία τοῖς ἐμὶ ἀναχρίνουσιν ἀυλὴ ὅδι. Hęc Eraf.red didit ad hunc modum: Mea refponfio apud eos qui me interrogant, hæc est. Mihi uero plane uidetur istam uersionem uim uerborum Apostoli non assequi.
units.tr: "My answer to those who question me is this." The Greek is ἡ ἐμὴ ἀπολογία τοῖς ἐμὲ ἀνακρίνουσιν αὕτη ἐστίν [ἡ ἐμὴ ἀπολογία τοῖς ἐμὲ ἀνακρίνουσιν αὕτη ἐστίν]. Erasmus rendered it in this way: "My answer to those who question me is this." But it seems to me that this version does not capture the force of the Apostle's words.

units.la: Primum enim ἀπολογία non est simplex refponfio, qua simplici interrogationi refponderatur, sed qua quis causam suam redditis rationibus aduersus accusationem maleuolorum tuetur ac defendit, unde magis erat uertendum mea defensio, ut & uetus habet, quàm mea refponfio.
units.tr: First, ἀπολογία [apologia] is not a simple answer, by which a plain question is replied to, but that by which someone defends and protects his cause, rendering reasons against the accusation of malicious men. Hence it ought rather to have been translated "my defence," as the old version also has, than "my answer."

units.la: Deinde, quod reddidit, qui me interrogant, non est positū per uerbum ἀνακρίνω, quod simpliciter interrogare significat, sed per uerbum ἀνακρίνω, quod significat aliquid dijudicare, examinare & in quæstione uocare. Sic Acto.25. Festus præses ad Agrippam de Paulo dicebat: Quapropter adduxi eum ad uos, & maxime ad te rex Agrippa, ὅπως τῆς ἀνακρίσεως γενομένης χῶ πρᾶξαι, id est, ut examinatione facta, habeam quod scribam.
units.tr: Then, the word rendered "who question me" is not the verb meaning simply to interrogate, but the word ἀνακρίνω [anakrinō], which means to judge, examine and call into question. So in Acts 25 Festus the governor said to Agrippa about Paul: "Therefore I have brought him before you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, once the examination has been made, I may have something to write," ὅπως τῆς ἀνακρίσεως γενομένης σχῶ τί γράψω [hopōs tēs anakriseōs genomenēs schō ti graspsō], that is, that, with the examination made, I may have what to write.

units.la: Tertiò, illud, apud eos, Græcè est in datiuo τοῖς, n equis putet Apostolum coràm interrogatū ista respondisse. Potest enim ita legi, Mea defensio aduersum eos qui me in quæstionem uocat hæc est. Palam nanq; est Apostolum hic de illis loqui, quos habebat aduersarios, de quibus credibile est, quod non in faciem sed seorsum authoritati ipsius detraxerint, aduersum quos fe his uerbis defenderit.
units.tr: Thirdly, the phrase "to those" is in the Greek dative, τοῖς [tois], so that no one should suppose the Apostle answered these things when questioned in person. For it may be read thus: "My defence against those who call me into question is this." It is plain that the Apostle is speaking here of those whom he had as adversaries, of whom it is credible that they detracted from his authority not to his face but in private, and against whom he defends himself with these words.

units.la: HAEC est.) Ambiguum est, an intelligat præcedentia uel sequentia, uel utraque. Chryfoftomus tam ad præcedentia quàm ad fequetia applicat. Ambrosius ad fequetia, Theophylactus ad præcedentia. Mihi uidetur ad præcedentia respici, ut intelligamus de Apostolatus stolatus defensione, cuius sigillum dixit esse Corinthios. Quasi dicat, Ijs qui Apostolatum meum in iudicium uocant, & in quæstionem rapiunt quasi non sim Apostolus, uos defensionis loco obijcio, qui estis opus meū in domino & sigillum Apostolatus mei.
units.tr: "This is": it is ambiguous whether he means what precedes or what follows, or both. Chrysostom applies it to both what precedes and what follows; Ambrose to what follows; Theophylact to what precedes. It seems to me that what precedes is meant, so that we understand it of the defence of his apostleship, whose seal he has said the Corinthians are. As if he said: To those who bring my apostleship into judgment and drag it into question as if I were not an Apostle, I offer you as my defence, you who are my work in the Lord and the seal of my apostleship.

units.la: Et hactenus, quod primo loco astruendum erat, uidelicet quod & ipse sit Christi Apostolus, contra pseudapostolos & pseudadelphos per asseuerationem, & conuersionem Corinthiorum absoluit.
units.tr: And thus far, what had to be established first, namely that he himself is also an Apostle of Christ, he has completed against the false apostles and false brethren, by asseveration and by the conversion of the Corinthians.

units.la: An non habemus potestatem edendi ac bibendi?
units.tr: Have we not the right to eat and drink?

units.la: Iam consequenter aggreditur iuris Apostolici amplificationem, ut doceat, quàm iuste potuerit sumptus sibi prædicationis Euangelicæ à Corinthijs sumere, quod tamen non fecerit, ut Corinthios suo exemplo admoneat, quàm non debeant contra infirmorum fratrum salutem libertate sua uti, sed magis spectare, quid faciat ad ædificationē quàm quid ipsis liceat.
units.tr: Next he goes on to enlarge on his apostolic right, to show how justly he could have taken support from the Corinthians for preaching the gospel, although he did not take it. By his own example he warns the Corinthians that they should not use their liberty to the harm of weaker brothers, but should consider what builds up rather than what is lawful for them.

units.la: A N non habemus potestatem edendi, &c.)
units.tr: Have we not the right to eat and drink, etc.?

units.la: Non loquitur de simplici esu ac potu à quo certè nec apud Corinthios abstinuerat, sed de tali, quo apud illos usus nō fuerat. Intelligendum igitur est de sumptibus propter Euangelij prædicationem debitis. Tantum enim dicit: Cum igitur Apostoli Christi sumus, quis prohibet quo minus sumptus à uobis quorū sumus Apostoli, sumamus? Non potestis autem negare, nos uestros esse Apostolos. Habemus igitur potestatem alimoniam à uobis exigendi ac sumendi tanquam Christi Apostoli.
units.tr: He is not speaking of ordinary eating and drinking, which he certainly did not give up among the Corinthians, but of that kind of thing which was not customary among them. So it must be understood of the support owed for the preaching of the gospel. He says only this: "Since we are Christ's apostles, who prevents us from taking support from you, whose apostles we are? You cannot deny that we are your apostles. Therefore we have the right to demand and receive sustenance from you as Christ's apostles."

units.la: An non habemus potestatem sororem mulierem circumducendi?
units.tr: Have we not the right to lead about a sister, a wife?

units.la: 1 Intellige, quæ alatur sumptibus fidelium. Prorsus enim ineptiunt, qui commentum hic adferunt de mulieribus opulentis, quæ apostolos sequutæ prædicationis sumptus administrarint. De Christo quidem tale quid legimus, de apostolis uero nō ita. Comminiscuntur istam euasionem, qui uirginitatem & continentiam ita defendunt, ut egrè audiant apostolos fuisse uxoratos. Verum satis clarum est quod hic ἀδελφὴν γυναῖκα uocet sororē uxorē, sororem uocans, fidelem in Christo. Quod autem γυνή & uxorem significet, capite septimo satis patuit. Alioqui, si de muliere tantum fideli, quæ uxor non esset, loqueretur, quid opus erat adiungere post sororem mulierem? Quæ enim soror esse poterat, quæ non sit mulier? Soror uero esse potest, quæ tamen non sit uxor. Cum ergo postquam sororem dixit, & γυναῖκα adiecit, puto plane stupidum esse si quis nolit animaduertere ob id adiectā esse τὴν γυναῖκα, ut declaret se non de quauis muliere fideli, sed de uxore fideli loqui. Quod si quis de muliere infideli dicat: Bona spes est, mulierem hanc Christo accessuram. Venit enim cum fratre ui ro in ecclesiam, quæso quis intelligit de alio uiro, quàm eo qui sit illius maritus? Nihil enim alioqui opus erat dictionem uiri adiungere, si de quouis fideli, qui non sit maritus, mentio fieret.
units.tr: 1 Understand: a woman who is supported by the gifts of the faithful. Those people are plainly talking nonsense who bring in here the fiction of wealthy women who followed the apostles and supplied the expenses of preaching. We read something of that sort about Christ, but not about the apostles. The people who defend virginity and continence so strongly that they can hardly bear to hear that the apostles were married invent this evasion. But it is quite clear that by "a sister, a wife" [ἀδελφὴν γυναῖκα] he means a sister who is a wife, calling her a sister because she is a believer in Christ. That [γυνή] also means wife has been made sufficiently plain in chapter seven. Otherwise, if he were speaking only of a believing woman who was not a wife, why add "woman" after "sister"? For what sister could there be who is not a woman? But a sister can be one who is not a wife. Since, then, after saying "sister" he added "woman," I think it is plainly foolish for anyone to refuse to notice that "the woman" was added so that he would show he is speaking not of any believing woman, but of a believing wife. And if someone says of an unbelieving woman, "There is good hope that this woman will come to Christ; for she comes into the church with her husband," who would understand "husband" to mean anyone other than her own husband? For there would have been no need to add the word "husband" otherwise, if mention were being made of any believer who was not a husband.

units.la: 2 Deinde, ipsum Apostoli argumentum ferre non potest, ut de talibus opulentis matronis, quæ Apostolis uictum administrarint, ista uerba intelligamus. Loquitur enim de sumptibus, quos Apostoli Christi iure poterant ab illis exigere, quibus Euangelium prædicabant, & non sibi tantum, sed & suorum necessitati impendere, quos secum ducebant. Hoc ostendit reliquos apostolos fecisse, se uero apud Corinthios non fecisse. Iam si intelligas de talibus matronis, unde Apostoli sumptus Euangelij prædicādi acceperint, quæro, an qui istas mulieres circumduxerunt, de fidelibus sumptus acceperint uel non acceperint. Si acceperunt, ad quid ergo mulieres istas circumduxerunt? Si non acceperunt, ergo idem fecerint quod de se hoc capite scribit Apostolus. Iam omnino inter se & reliquos apostolos ita discriminat, ut dicat se iure suo non esse usum, quo utebantur tum reliqui apostoli. Ergo necesse est reliquos apostolos uictum & necessariam sustentationem ab ecclesijs sibi ac suis sumpsisse. Si hoc fecerunt, ut planè hic scribitur, quid aliud restat, quàm no tales mulieres, quæ sumptus prædicandi Euangelij in se transtulerint, sed uxores quæ ab ecclesijs sustentatę sunt, circumductas esse ab apostolis?
units.tr: 2 Next, the apostle's own argument cannot bear the interpretation that these words refer to wealthy matrons of that kind who supplied the apostles with food. For he is speaking of the support which Christ's apostles could justly demand from those to whom they preached the gospel, and which they spent not only on themselves but on the needs of those whom they took with them. He shows that the other apostles did this, but that he did not do it among the Corinthians. Now if you take it to mean such matrons from whom the apostles received the support for preaching the gospel, I ask: did those who led these women about receive support from the faithful, or did they not? If they did receive it, why then did they lead these women about? If they did not receive it, then they did the same thing the apostle writes about himself in this chapter. Indeed he distinguishes himself from the other apostles in such a way that he says he did not use the right which the other apostles were then using. Therefore the other apostles must necessarily have taken food and necessary maintenance for themselves and their households from the churches. If they did this, as is plainly written here, what else remains but that the apostles led about not such women who had taken over the support of preaching the gospel, but wives who were supported by the churches?

units.la: Et si dicas, in hoc diuersum egisse Paulum à reliquis apostolis, quod sumptus labore manuum quæsiuerit, non ab opulentis matronis acceperit, sicut alij fecisse creduntur, adhuc tamen iniuriam facis argumento Apostoli. Nam non in eo est, ut doceat se non usum esse mulierculārum opulentarum subsidio cum reliquis apostolis, sed iuri suo apud Corinthios cesisse, nec quicquam ab illis alimoniæ sumpsisse. Atque in eo se non fecisse quod cæteri apostoli fecerint. Alioqui quid quæso refert, utrum à mulieribus fidelibus uictum sumpserit, uel reliquas ecclesias grauarit, ut licuerit sine sumptu Corinthijs tradere Christi Euangelium, id quod de se in posteriore his uerbis capite undecimo scribit: Quoniā gratis Euangelium Dei Euangelizaui uobis? Alias ecclesias expoliaui, accipiens stipendium ad ministerium uestrum. Si de eo hoc loco intelligamus, quod non circumduxerit diuites mulieres, à quibus uictum sumpserit, quum id æquè ac reliqui apostoli in potestate habuerit, quis non uidet omne argumentum Apostoli, & discrimen illud inter ipsum & reliquos apostolos prorsus irritum reddi, siquidem in eodem reperientur, & ij apostoli quos commemorat ipsi pares esse, ut qui nec ipsi sumptus ab ecclesijs quibus prædicabant, sed aliunde sumpserint sicuti & Paulus, ipsi à mulieribus opulentis, Paulus ab alijs ecclesijs, ut Corinthijs prædicaret. Ita expendenti arbitror clarum erit Paulum de coniugibus, non de opulentis matronis loqui.
units.tr: And if you say that Paul differed from the other apostles in this, that he sought support by the labour of his hands and did not accept it from wealthy matrons, as others are believed to have done, you still do injustice to the apostle's argument. For his point is not that he did not use the help of wealthy women as the other apostles did, but that he gave up his right among the Corinthians and received nothing from them for his support. In this he is saying that he did not do what the other apostles did. Otherwise, I ask, what does it matter whether he took his support from believing women or burdened the other churches, so that the gospel of Christ could be delivered to the Corinthians without expense? Yet in the later part of chapter eleven he writes about himself: "Did I preach the gospel of God to you for nothing? I robbed other churches, taking wages for your ministry." If we understand this passage to mean that he did not lead about rich women from whom he took his support, although he had the right to do so just as the other apostles did, who does not see that the whole argument of the apostle, and that distinction between himself and the other apostles, is made utterly pointless? For the same would be found in those apostles he mentions, who were his equals: they too did not take support from the churches to which they preached, but from elsewhere, just as Paul did. Some took it from wealthy women, and Paul took it from other churches so that he could preach to the Corinthians. Weighing this, I think it will be clear that Paul is speaking of wives, not of wealthy matrons.
2 Cor. 11

units.la: 3 Tertio accedit & hoc, quod cum certum sit apostolos habuisse uxores, inexcusabilis mali species fuisset, si relictis proprijs coniugibus mulierculas alias circumduxissent. Et maxime, cum loquatur hic in singulari de una tantum muliere. Quomodo suspicionem adulterij non mouisset Apostolus coniugatus, si relicta domi legitima coniuge, mulierculam quandam aliam circumduxisset? Notanter itaque cum de uxore, non alijs mulieribus loqueretur, non pluraliter sed in singulari de una, dixit: An non habemus (loquitur autem de sua tantum persona, ut coepit) potestatem sororem uxorem circumducendi?
units.tr: 3 A third point is this: since it is certain that the apostles had wives, it would have been an inexcusable appearance of evil if, leaving their own wives, they had led about other little women. And especially since he is speaking here in the singular, of only one woman. How would a married apostle not have aroused suspicion of adultery if, leaving his lawful wife at home, he had led about some other little woman? Therefore, since he was speaking of a wife and not of other women, he deliberately said not in the plural but in the singular, of one woman: "Have we not the right (for he speaks only of his own person, as he began) to lead about a sister, a wife?"

units.la: Argutatur Hiero. in uerbo circumducendi. Non dicit, inquit, mulieres ducedi, ne de uxoribus dicere putetur, sed circumducendi per prouincias, quę necessaria de suis facultatibus subministrarent. Verum est, non dicit ducendi. Non enim loquitur de potestate nubendi hoc loco, de qua egit cap.7. sed de potestate fumendi necessaria ab ecclesijs, ad sustentationem non Apostoli tantum sed & coniugis, si qua in illius sit tanquam legitimi mariti comitatu. Et hac potestate dicit se non usum, atque adeo nec sibi ipsi sumptus a Corinthijs accepisse, multo minus uxorem fidelem secum habuisse, quæ illorum facultatibus aleretur. Apparet enim ista de uxorum comitatu pertinere ad auxesim iuris apostolici, ut intelligamus non solum personæ Apostoli, sed & coniugi ipsius deberi ab ecclesia victum, & si qui alij ad ipsum pertineant. Eo uero se iure tam non esse usum, ut nec suæ personæ necessaria ab ipsis acceperit.
units.tr: Jerome makes a quibble over the word "to lead about." He says: "He does not say 'to lead', lest it be thought he is speaking of wives, but 'to lead about' through the provinces, so that they might supply necessities from their own means." It is true that he does not say "to lead." For here he is not speaking of the right to marry, which he treated in chapter seven, but of the right to receive what is necessary from the churches for the maintenance not only of the apostle but also of his wife, if she was in his company as his lawful husband. And he says he did not use this right, and so he did not receive support from the Corinthians even for himself, much less have a believing wife with him, who would be fed from their resources. For it appears that this talk about the companionship of wives belongs to the enlargement of the apostolic right, so that we understand that support is owed by the church not only to the apostle's person but also to his spouse, and to any others who belong to him. But he did not use that right so much that he did not even receive what was necessary for his own person from them.

units.la: 4 Addam & hoc. Nō dicit simpliciter se non circumducere sororem mulierem, sed rogat, an non habeat potestatem circumducendi sororem mulierem. Loquitur autem absque ulla contradictione de potestate quæ pertineat ad ius Apostoli, cuius usum nemo licite prohibere posset, modo ipse Apostolus hac uti uelit. Indicat potestatem hanc circumducendi sororem mulierem, esse sitam in uoluntate Apostoli. Iam rogo, an ad ius Apostoli pertineat, opulentas mulieres circumducere? An, si uelit Apostolus quasuis diuites mulieres circumducere, illę teneantur relictis sedibus & rebus domesticis circumerrantem, ac terras omnes peragrantem sequi, & in hoc alere, ut ubiuis Euangelii Christi prędicet? An fidelibus matronis nō sit liberum hoc facere uel detrectare? Certe arbitror neminem hoc asserturum, quod in uoluntate & potestate Apostoli sit, tales mulieres proprijs sedibus auocare, & pro suo iure ubilibet circumducere. Neque hoc quisquam dicet, quod Christiana mulier, etiam si id Christi minister exigat, teneatur obedire. Quod si id iuris habet in mulieres Christi Apostolus, absque ulla contradictione habet & in uiros opulentos. Cur ergo non uiros diuites secum sumeret, in id officij, cum non minus reperiantur diuitos uiri quam diuites mulieres, nec
units.tr: 4 I will add this too. He does not say simply that he does not lead about a sister, a wife, but he asks whether he does not have the power to lead about a sister, a wife. He speaks, without any contradiction, of a power that belongs to the apostle's right, whose use no one could lawfully forbid, provided the apostle himself wished to use it. He indicates that this power of leading about a sister, a wife, lies in the apostle's will. Now I ask: does it belong to the apostle's right to lead about wealthy women? If the apostle wished to lead about any wealthy women whatever, were they bound to leave their homes and domestic affairs, follow him as he wandered and travelled through all lands, and support him in this, so that he could preach the gospel of Christ everywhere? Or is it not free for believing matrons to do this or to refuse? Certainly I think no one will assert that it lies in the will and power of the apostle to call such women away from their own homes and lead them about wherever he pleases by his right. Nor will anyone say that a Christian woman is bound to obey, even if a minister of Christ demands it. But if Christ's apostle has this right over women, he has it without any contradiction over wealthy men as well. Why then would he not take wealthy men with him for that service, since wealthy men are found no less than wealthy women, nor...

units.la: APOSTOLOS FVISSE uxoratos.
units.tr: THAT THE APOSTLES WERE MARRIED.

units.la: Quod autem apostoli coniuges habuerint satis testimonij habemus ex illorum scriptis qui non solum contemporanei ipsorum sed & discipuli fuerunt. Ignatius in epistola ad Philadelphienses ad hunc modum scripsit: Non detraho autem cæteris beatis, qui nuptijs copulati fuerunt, quorum nunc memini. Opto enim Deo dignus ad uestigia eorum in regno ipsius inueniri, sicut Abraham, Isaac & Iacob, sicut Ioseph, & Esaias, & ceteri prophetę, sicut Petrus & Paulus, & reliqui Apostoli, qui nuptijs tuerunt sociati, qui non libidinis causa, sed posteritatis subrogandæ gratia coniuges habuerunt. Hæc Ignatius.
units.tr: That the apostles had wives we have sufficient testimony from the writings of men who were not only their contemporaries but also their disciples. Ignatius wrote in his letter to the Philadelphians in this manner: "I do not disparage the other blessed men who were joined in marriage, whom I now recall. For I hope to be found worthy of God and to follow in their footsteps in his kingdom, as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, as Joseph, and Isaiah, and the other prophets, as Peter and Paul, and the rest of the apostles, who were united in marriage, and who had wives not for the sake of lust, but for the sake of raising up offspring." Thus Ignatius.

units.la: QVOD APOSTOLVS HIC NON de opulentis mulieribus, sed de coniuge loquatur, testimonium Clementis.
units.tr: THAT THE APOSTLE IS HERE SPEAKING OF A WIFE, NOT OF WEALTHY WOMEN: THE TESTIMONY OF CLEMENT.

units.la: Eusebius in ecclesiastica hist. lib.3. ca.38. scribit. Clemens, inquit, sane hic cuius uoces annotauimus, scribens aduersum eos, qui nuptias spernunt, inter cætera etiam hæc dicit: An & apostolos improbant? Petrus enim ac Philippus & uxores habuerunt, & filias etiam uiris nuptum dederunt. Sed & Paulum Apostolum non tædet in quadam epistola sua mentionem uel salutationem facere comparis suę, quam se ideo negat circumducere, ut ad prædicationē Euangelij expediti-or hat. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Eusebius writes in his Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 38: "Clement, whose words we have noted, writing against those who despise marriage, says among other things: Do they condemn the apostles too? For Peter and Philip had wives, and gave their daughters in marriage. And the apostle Paul is not ashamed in a certain letter of his to mention or greet his wife, whom he says he does not take about with him, so that he might be freer for preaching the gospel." Thus he.

units.la: Quid igitur? An non æquius est in rebus gestismagis apostolorum discipulis & eis qui hos è uicino sequuti sunt, quam ijs habere fidem qui longe post tempora apostolorum uixerunt? Ignatius secundus post Petrum Antiochenæ ecclesiæ præfuisse scribitur. Clemens ante Origenem floruit. Prior apostolis Petro & Paulo cum reliquis non solum tribuit coniuges, sed & propositum ex coniugibus subrogandi posteritatem. Alter & apostolis coniugium attribuit, & ipsa quoq; Apostoli uerba non solum ista de quibus loquimur, sed & ea quæ in epistola ad Philippenses sunt, de legitima coniuge exponit. Quæso si opulentas matronas & non legitimas coniuges circumduxerunt apostoli, quomodo id ignorarunt apostolorum discipuli, & cognouerunt tam fere illos subsequuti Hiero: Chrisost. & alij posteri? Si coniuges non habuerunt apostoli, nec illas circumduxerunt, quare de illorum uxoribus ista scripserunt ipsorum discipuli? Clemens, citante Eusebio, loco & cap. prædicto, scribit apostolum Petrum cum uideret uxorem suam ad mortem duci post tergum illi inclamasse ac dixisse: O chara coniunx, memento domini. Obsecro, ubi putabimus hoc factum & quando? An non apparet tum esse factum, quando & ipsi Petro subeundum erat martyrium? uel putabimus nihil periculi fuisse Petro, cum uxorem ad martyrium constanter subeundum aperta inclamatione admoneret? Quis non uel hoc inde colligendum esse uidet, hunc Apostolum uxorem suam ad mortem usque secum circumduxisse?
units.tr: What then? Is it not more reasonable in matters of fact to trust the disciples of the apostles, and those who followed closely after them, than to trust those who lived long after the apostles' time? Ignatius is written to have been the second to preside over the church of Antioch after Peter. Clement flourished before Origen. The former attributes wives not only to the apostles Peter and Paul and the others, but also the purpose of raising up offspring from their wives. The latter also ascribes marriage to the apostles, and he himself explains not only these words we are discussing but also those in the letter to the Philippians as referring to a lawful wife. I ask: if the apostles took about wealthy matrons and not lawful wives, how could their disciples, who followed them so closely, be ignorant of it, and how could Jerome, Chrysostom and other later writers have come to know it? If the apostles had no wives, and did not take them about, why did their own disciples write these things about their wives? Clement, quoted by Eusebius in the passage and chapter mentioned above, writes that the apostle Peter, seeing his wife led to death, called out behind her and said: "O dear wife, remember the Lord." I ask, where and when do we suppose this happened? Does it not clearly seem to have happened at the time when Peter himself was to undergo martyrdom? Or shall we suppose there was no danger to Peter when he openly called out to his wife, urging her to undergo martyrdom steadfastly? Who does not see that this itself must be concluded, that this apostle took his wife about with him even unto death?

units.la: Constat itaq; cum ex ipsis apostoli uerbis, tum ex testimonio Ignatij & Clemetis, quibus hac in re haud temere credimus, primum apostolos, fratres domini, Petrum & Paulum, fuisse uxoratos, deinde uxores quoq; dempto Paulo, secum circumduxisse, tertio, id potestatis esse Christi ministro, ut non sibi tantum, sed & uxori ac suis sumptus necessarios ab ecclesiis quibus Euangelium administrat, exigat & sumat, inquit; ipsius uoluntate situm, an isto iure uti uelit uel nolit.
units.tr: It is therefore established, both from the apostle's own words and from the testimony of Ignatius and Clement, whom we rightly believe in this matter, first, that the apostles, the brothers of the Lord, Peter and Paul, were married; second, that they also took their wives about with them, except Paul; third, that it is a right of the minister of Christ that he may demand and receive necessary support not only for himself but also for his wife and children from the churches to which he administers the gospel. Whether he wishes to use this right or not, the apostle says, depends on his own will.

units.la: QVEMADMODVM & caeteri apostoli, & fratres domini, & Cephas.) Subintelligendum est, faciunt, uel circumducunt, aut potestate habent. Argum. est ab exemplo reliquorum apostolorum. Cum idem sit ius apostolorum, inquit, & ego non minus sim Apostolus quam reliqui apostoli fratres domini, & Cephas, quare non liceret mihi facere quod ipsi faciunt? Ideo no dicit: Quemadmodum apostoli, sed & caeteri apostoli, ut se reliquis apostolis connumeret.
units.tr: "As also the other apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas." It must be understood: "do," or "take about," or "have the power to." This is an argument from the example of the other apostles. Since, he says, the right of the apostles is the same, and I am no less an apostle than the other apostles, the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas, why should it not be lawful for me to do what they do? So he does not say, "As the apostles," but "and the other apostles," so that he counts himself among the rest of the apostles.

units.la: ET fratres domini.) Theophylactus numerat Iacobum Hierosolymorum episcopum, Ioannem, Simonem & Iudam, uerum Matt.13. & Marc.6. ponuntur ipsorum nomina, Iacobus, Ioseph, Simon & Iudas. Quomodo fuerint fratres domini non est eadem doctorum sententia. Theophyl. in prologo ante Euangelium Iohannis scribit Iosepho, Mariae sponso, antea fuisse uxorem ex qua suscepit filios quatuor & filias tres. Hieronymus refutat hoc, tanquam apocryphum, & dicit, fratres istos domini fuisse consobrinos Christi, ex sororibus Mariae matris. Sed quomodo horum mentionem facit Paulus? Chrysost. arbitratur medios inter apostolos insertos licet apostoli non fuerint. Certe de Iosepho non legimus, quod apostolis fuerit annumeratus. Apparet tamen ideo istos positos ab Apostolo, quod magnae aestimationis fuerint, atq; ita Petrum ultimo loco tanquam potiorem reliquis recensitum. Assurgit enim non solum minoris opinionis apostolis sese, sed & potioribus, fratribus domini, ipsi quoq; Petro, in iure Apostolatus adaequans. Sentiebat siquidem horum se authoritate per pseudapostolos improbe premi.
units.tr: "And the brothers of the Lord." Theophylact counts James, bishop of Jerusalem, John, Simon and Judas; but in Matthew 13 and Mark 6 their names are given as James, Joseph, Simon and Judas. Opinion among the learned is not uniform as to how they were brothers of the Lord. Theophylact, in the prologue before the Gospel of John, writes that Joseph, the husband of Mary, had previously had a wife, by whom he had four sons and three daughters. Jerome rejects this as apocryphal, and says these brothers of the Lord were cousins of Christ, from the sisters of Mary his mother. But why does Paul mention them? Chrysostom thinks they were inserted among the apostles even though they were not apostles. Certainly we do not read that Joseph was counted among the apostles. It seems nevertheless that the apostle placed them here because they were of great esteem, and so Peter is listed last, as one more important than the rest. For he does not only put himself on a level with apostles of lesser repute, but also with the more important ones, the brothers of the Lord, and even with Peter himself, in the right of apostleship. For he perceived that his authority was being wrongly undermined by false apostles.

units.la: Aut solus ego & Barnabas non habemus potestatem hoc faciendi?
units.tr: Or have not I and Barnabas power to do this?

units.la: In Graeco est ... non operadi, ut intelligas non de uxoribus circumducendis, sed de eo quod liceat Christi ministro absque manuum labore in ocio agere, & de labore Euangelij uiuere. Ita & Theophyl. exponit. Rogat
units.tr: In the Greek it reads [μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι], "not to work," so that you understand this is not about leading wives around with us, but about whether a minister of Christ may live in idleness without manual labour and live from the labour of the Gospel. Theophylact also explains it this way. He asks, therefore, whether it is not lawful for him and Barnabas alone to do what is lawful for all the other apostles of Christ, namely to live from the Gospel without manual work.

units.la: igitur, an solis sibi & Barnabe non liceat quod omnibus reliquis Christi apostolis liceat, uidelicet, ut & ipsi absque opere manuario de Euangelio uiuant. Indicat hic & Barnaba eadem molestia propter pseudapostolos coactu suo ipsius sumptu praedicare Euangelium, absq; dubio, quod eode ipiritu ac tenore cum Paulo ingrederetur, parum legali propitius observantiae, licet enim non legamus Barnabam cum Paulo uenisse Corinthum, fieri tamen potest, ut uel antea cum Pauli comes esset, antequam diuideretur pari ratione una cum Apostolo labore manuum uictum quaesierit, uel etiam tum, cum ista scriberentur, eadem alibi forte uixerit & praedicarit.
units.tr: Here he also indicates that Barnabas was under the same burden: because of the false apostles he was compelled to preach the Gospel at his own expense. No doubt this was because he went with Paul in the same spirit and purpose, not very favourable to legal observance. Although we do not read that Barnabas came with Paul to Corinth, it may be that he had been Paul's companion earlier, before they parted, and so had likewise earned his living by manual labour along with the Apostle. Or, while these things were being written, he may perhaps have been living and preaching in the same way somewhere else.

units.la: Obseruandum autem est, candidum Apostoli pectus, quam tueatur potestatem ac laude Barnabae, licet, ut in Actis uidere est cap.15. a se inuicem per contentionem propter Ioannem cognomine Marcum, discesserint, nec postea in unum redijsse legantur.
units.tr: It should be noted how the Apostle's upright heart defends both his own authority and Barnabas's good name. Although, as may be seen in Acts 15, they parted from each other in contention over John, called Mark, and are not read to have come together again afterwards.

units.la: Sed quaeri potest, quare no & reliqui apostoli ad istum modum neglecto suo iure gratis praedicarint Euangelium. Si enim hoc recte fecerunt Paulus & Barnabas, cur non & reliqui apostoli hac uia ingressi sunt? Primum, non culpat in apostolis, quod iure suo sint usi. Absit. Imo magis hanc Apostolatus potestatem tuetur ac defendit. Deinde, quod ipse apud Corinthios iure suo no est usus, certa ratione factum est. Hieron. dicit, quod reliqui apostoli fidelioribus praedicauerint, & potissimum Iudaeis, quibus non fuerit insolens religionis alere ministros. Hoc uero apud Gentes adhuc rudes sine offendiculo fieri non potuisse, atq; ob eam rationem Paulum gratis illis praedicasse Euangelium. Verum haec ratio mihi non admodum firma uidetur. Primum enim quis dubitat & Gentibus id moris fuisse ut sacrorum ministros aluerint. Deinde Apostolus non ubiq; apud Gentes sicut apud Corinthios gratis Euangelium praedicauit. Imo neq; hic prorsus suo ipsius sumptu fustetatus est, sed ab alijs ecclesijs accepit, unde sustentaretur apud Corinthios.
