Tertio ipse in posteriore cap. 11. ratione institui sui asignat, causam illius no in ruditatem Gentium sed in pseudapostolorum maliciam reijciens, qui tanquam subdoli operarij de eo quod ipsi faciebant, ac dissimulabat quaestum sectantes, Apostolo calumnia struere cupiebant. Ne itaque occasionem haberent praedicatione ipsius suspectam de quaestu reddendi, noluit quicquam a Corinthijs sumere, unde uiueret, sed cum labore manuum tum aliarum ecclesiarum Macedoniae sumptibus uiuere.
units.tr: But it may be asked why the other apostles did not likewise preach the Gospel freely, setting aside their right. For if Paul and Barnabas did this rightly, why did the other apostles not also take this course? First, he does not blame the apostles for using their right. Far from it. Rather, he upholds and defends this authority of the apostleship. Second, that he himself did not use his right among the Corinthians was done for a definite reason. Jerome says that the other apostles preached to more faithful hearers, and especially to the Jews, among whom it was not unusual to support the ministers of religion. But among the Gentiles, who were still untaught, this could not be done without causing offence, and for that reason Paul preached the Gospel to them free of charge. Yet this reason does not seem to me very sound. For first, who doubts that the Gentiles too had the custom of supporting the ministers of sacred things? Second, the Apostle did not everywhere preach the Gospel free of charge among the Gentiles, as he did among the Corinthians. Indeed, not even here did he live entirely at his own expense, but received support from other churches, from which he was maintained among the Corinthians. Third, in the later chapter 11 he himself gives the reason for his own practice, and he places the cause not in the rudeness of the Gentiles but in the malice of the false apostles, who, like crafty workmen, pursued gain while pretending otherwise, and were eager to bring slander against the Apostle. So, to avoid giving them an occasion to suspect his preaching of seeking gain, he was unwilling to take anything from the Corinthians on which to live, but lived by his manual labour and by the support of the churches of Macedonia.

units.la: Quis militat suis stipendiis unquam? Quis plantat uineam, & de fructu eius non edit? Aut quis pascit gregem, & de lacte gregis non edit?
units.tr: Who ever serves as a soldier at his own charges? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Or who feeds a flock and does not eat of the milk of the flock?

units.la: Postquam rogauit, an solus ipse & Barnabas non habeant potestatem non operandi, id est, no manuum labore sed accepto a fidelibus sumptu uiuendi, cum illis Christi administrêt Euâ gelium, consequenter probat Euangelij minî stro potestatē esse, ut de Euangelio uiuat. Probat autem id, primùm ex eo, quod iuxta natu ralem æquitatem, & communem omniû mor taliû sensum & usum, cibo dignus est, qui opera suam cuiquâ collocat. Hoc uero tribus exemplis ob oculos ponit, primo de milite, altero de plantatore uineæ, tertio de pastore. Videtur autem primum hoc argumentum emphasim quandam habere âminori ad maius, atque ita auxesim eius, quod probare instituit. Tantundem enim est quod dicit: Vel humanâ æquitatem & publicum sæculi usum, in rebus multo leuioribus inspicite, atq; inde colligite, quàm æquû fit, ut Euangelij minister de Euangelio uiuat. Qui militat non proprio sed alieno stipendio militat, si militet, non patriæ sed externo principi. Qui uineâ plantat, de uineæ fructu edit, & qui gregem pascit de lacte gregis uiuit. Quanto magis æquum est, ut qui domino militat, qui uineam domini plantat, qui gregem domini pascit, non suis, sed aliorum hoc sumptibus faciat? Si tantum est militare, uineam plâtare, gregem pascere, quanti quæso esse debet, Euangelium salutis administrare?
units.tr: Having asked whether he and Barnabas alone have no right not to work, that is, not to live by manual labour but by support received from the faithful, while they administer the Gospel of Christ among them, he goes on to prove that the minister of the Gospel has the right to live from the Gospel. He proves this first from the fact that, according to natural justice and the common sense and practice of all mortals, he who sets his labour at someone's service is worthy of food. He sets this before our eyes in three examples: first of a soldier, second of a planter of a vineyard, third of a shepherd. This first argument seems to have a kind of emphasis from the less to the greater, and so an amplification of what he undertakes to prove. For what he says amounts to this: look at human justice and the common custom of the world in matters far less weighty, and from them conclude how just it is that the minister of the Gospel should live from the Gospel. He who serves as a soldier does so at the pay of another, if he serves at all, and serves not his fatherland but a foreign prince. He who plants a vineyard eats of the vineyard's fruit, and he who feeds a flock lives on the milk of the flock. How much more just is it that he who serves the Lord, who plants the Lord's vineyard, who feeds the Lord's flock, should do this not at his own expense but at the expense of others! If to serve as a soldier, to plant a vineyard and to feed a flock is so much, what, I ask, ought the proclaiming of the Gospel of salvation to be worth?

units.la: 2 Quod percontatorie instando ista exempla adducit, inde est, quod nô solum æ- sed & ubiq; terrarum ita in usu est, ut qui militat, non suis stipendijs militet, qui plantat de fructu plantationis, & qui gregem pascit, de lacte gregis uiuat, ut impudens fuerit, si quis militi stipendium plantatori & pastori susten tatione necessariam deneget. Et huc facit particula percontatoria quis, toties repetita, cui necesse est, ut respondeatur, nemo. Item quod addit, unquam, quo extorquet, ius hoc, operario debitum, non solum ubique solenne esse & in usu, sed & perpetuum & constans.
units.tr: 2 That he presses these examples by asking questions shows that it is the practice not only in one place but everywhere on earth that the soldier serves at someone else's pay, that the planter eats of the fruit of his planting, and that the one who feeds a flock lives on the milk of the flock. So it would be shameless to deny the soldier his pay and the planter and shepherd their necessary support. The interrogative particle "who," repeated so often, fits here, since it must be answered: "No one." Likewise, when he adds "ever," by which he draws out the admission, he shows that this right owed to the labourer is not only universal and customary but also perpetual and constant.

units.la: Resolue nunc instantiam istam percontatoriam in simplicem asseuerationem. Si nemo unquam proprijs stipendijs militat, si nemo uineam unquam plantat qui de fructu uitis non edat, si nemo unquam gregem pascit, qui de lacte gregis nô uiuat, ergo uniuersale est & perpetuû hoc ius, communi omnium mortalium sensu & usu approbatum, ut qui operam suam alicui collocat, non suis id sumptibus faciat, sed eius cui famulatur ac seruit.
units.tr: Now reduce this questioning argument to a plain assertion. If no one ever serves as a soldier at his own pay, if no one ever plants a vineyard without eating of its fruit, if no one ever feeds a flock without living on its milk, then this right is universal and perpetual, approved by the common sense and practice of all mortals: that he who sets his labour at someone's service should do so not at his own charges but at the charges of him whom he serves.

units.la: 3 Pulchrè autem ista exempla ad propositû quadrât, si requiras cuius sit dare sumptus bel li militibus, plantandi plantatoribus, pascédi pastoribus, Euangelizandi Euágelij ministris, posteaquam constat æquisimum esse, ut non suis sumptibus ista faciant.
units.tr: 3 These examples fit the point very well if you ask whose duty it is to supply the soldiers with pay, the planters with food, the shepherds with sustenance, and the ministers of the Gospel with support for preaching the Gospel. Since it is agreed that it is most just that these men should not do such work at their own expense:

units.la: Quis debet stipendiû militibus? Princeps, cui militatur. Quis alimoniam uineatoři? Dominus uineæ. Quis pastori? Dominus ouium. Sed unde sumuntur stipendia militibus? Daa tur quidem nomine & iussu principis, sed sumuntur à subditis, quorum bono, ut liceat secure agere, bella geruntur. Vnde sumitur alimonia uineatori debita? Vnde pastori? Datur
units.tr: Who ought to pay the soldiers? The prince for whom they fight. Who gives food to the vinedresser? The owner of the vineyard. Who to the shepherd? The owner of the sheep. But whence is the soldiers' pay drawn? It is indeed given in the name and by the command of the prince, but it is drawn from the subjects, for whose good the wars are waged, so that they may live securely. Whence is the vinedresser's due food drawn? Whence the shepherd's? It is given indeed in the name of him who owns the vineyard and of him who owns the flock, but it is taken from the vineyard itself and from the milk of the flock.

units.la: illa quidem nomine eius, cuius est uinea, & ejus, cuius est grex, sumitur uero ab ipsa uinea & è lacte gregis. Ita & in hac causa. Constituit quidem dominus, ut qui Euangelio seruiunt, de Euangelio quoq;, sicut infra dicit, uiuant. Ergo sumptus ad prædicandum Euangelium Euangelizantibus nomine & iussu domini porrigendum est. Sed à quibus? Ab illis uidelicet, quorum bono celesti regi militatur, quorum bono uinea domini plantatur, quorum bono grex domini pascitur. Victum plantatori det uinea quæ plâtatur, pastori grex qui pascitur, militi populus cui militatur, Euangelistæ side les, quibus Euangelium prædicatur.
units.tr: So it is in this matter too. The Lord has indeed appointed that those who serve the Gospel should live from the Gospel, as he says below. Therefore the means for preaching the Gospel must be provided to those who proclaim it, in the name and by the command of the Lord. But from whom? From those, of course, for whose good we fight for the heavenly King, for whose good the Lord's vineyard is planted, for whose good the Lord's flock is fed. Let the vineyard being planted provide food for the planter, the flock being fed provide for the shepherd, the people for whom the soldier fights provide for the soldier, and the faithful to whom the Gospel is preached provide for the evangelist.

units.la: 4 Notandum & hoc est, quàm frugalem uistum ministro Christi deberi probet non solû exemplis istis militum, uineatorum, & pastorû, & infra aratoris, triturator is, ac bonis, sed & distionibus ὀψωνίς & edendi. Studiose cauetur, ne militi, uineatori, & pastori talis sumptus detur, unde materia luxus ac deliciarum peti possit, sed alitur hoc hominû genus sufficienti quidem sed iuxtà frugali alimonia. Negociatorum exemplo non est usus. Nam horum finis esse solet opulentia. Ita dictio opso nij Græcis tale significat stipendium, quod uentris necessitati seruiat. Est enim esculentû stipendium. Per se ὀψον significat omne esculentum, quod extra panem igne coquitur, unde pro delicatiore cibo sumi cœpit. Quidam in de dictum uolût, quod ueteres uesperi tandè opsonijs uti consueuerint, ὀψώνιον uero talis cibus tum uocatur quando precio comparatus est. Habet enim compositionem duarum dictionum ὀψον & ώνιον, ut intelligas cibû emptû. Ergo stipendium quod militibus datur ob id ὀψώνιον uocatur, quod in hoc datur, ut inde uiuant, ne cuiquâ cogantur esse oneri. Et hoc est quod Iohannes dicebat militibus, contenti estote stipendijs uestris. Et uerbum edendi, quo bis hic utitur, non est simpliciter accipiendum de esu, quasi uineator nihil debeat aliud edere quâ uuas, quæ magis potusquâ cibi gratia nascûtur, & pastor nulla re alia uésci quâ lacte, quod certè genus uiuendi esset in serrimû, sed de uniuerso uistu qui debeatur uineatori & pastori ex fructibus ac proueitibus laborum iplorû. Vnde idem hoc uerbum isto loco est, atq; si dixisset, & de fructu eius nô uiuit? Item & de lacte gregis nô uiuit? Iam iste uictus, qui ex fructibus uineæ, & lacte gregis prouenit & suppeditatur, certè nihil habet luxus, sed frugalis est. Ita & Euangelij ministro uictus debetur quidem, uerum ipse uideat ut non nisi necessarium ac frugalem petat.
units.tr: 4 It should also be noted how frugal a table he shows is owed to the minister of Christ, not only by these examples of soldiers, vinedressers and shepherds, and below of the ploughman, the thresher, and the good men, but also by the words ὀψώνια [opsōnia] and "to eat." Care is taken that no such provision be given to soldier, vinedresser or shepherd from which the matter of luxury and pleasures could be drawn, but such men are nourished with sufficient yet moderate sustenance. He did not use the example of merchants, because the aim of these is usually wealth. So the word ὀψώνιον [opsōnion] means among the Greeks such a stipend as serves the need of the belly, for it is a pay for food. Strictly, ὄψον [opson] means any food cooked over fire apart from bread, whence it came to be used for a more delicate fare. Some want it to be said that the ancients customarily used opsonia only in the evening, and that such food is called ὀψώνιον only when it has been bought for a price, for it is compounded of the two words ὄψον and ὤνιον, so that you understand bought food. Therefore the pay given to soldiers is called ὀψώνιον because it is given so that they may live on it and not be forced to be a burden to anyone. And this is what John said to the soldiers: "Be content with your wages." Also the verb "to eat," which he uses twice here, is not to be taken simply of eating, as if the vinedresser ought to eat nothing but grapes, which are grown more for drink than for food, and the shepherd should feed on nothing but milk, which would be a most wretched way of living. It refers rather to the whole sustenance owed to the vinedresser and shepherd from the fruits and produce of their own labours. Hence the same verb here is as if he had said, "and does not live from its fruit? Likewise does not live from the milk of the flock?" Now this sustenance, which comes from the fruits of the vineyard and the milk of the flock, certainly has nothing of luxury but is frugal. So too the minister of the Gospel is owed sustenance, yet he himself should see that he asks for nothing but what is necessary and frugal.

units.la: 5 Postremo & hoc notandum est, quod ius alimoniæ non ociofis adscribit, sed ijs, qui operam debitam impendunt. Quis militat inquit? Quis plantat uineam? Quis pascit gregé? Non dicit: Quis uocatur miles? Quis uocatur uineator? aut pastor? sed quis militat? quis plâtat? quis pascit?
units.tr: 5 Finally, it must also be noted that the right to sustenance is assigned not to the idle but to those who perform the work owed. "Who serves as a soldier?" he says. "Who plants a vineyard? Who feeds the flock?" He does not say, "Who is called a soldier? Who is called a vinedresser, or a shepherd?" but "who serves as a soldier? who plants? who feeds?"

units.la: Peccatur itaque hac in re in ecclesia Christi tripli-
units.tr: Sin is therefore committed in this matter in the Church of Christ in several ways.

units.la: tripliciter. 1. Primum ab illis, qui officium suum exequuntur quidem, sed sumptibus necessarijs non contenti, diuitias & luxum quæ-runt. 2. Deinde ab illis qui ociosi cum sint, nihilominus sumptu laborátibus debito gaudent. 3. Tertio, ab illis, qui non solum ociosi sunt, & sumptus laborantibus debitos ause-runt, sed ingentes quoq; diuitias colligunt, & sumptuosissime viuunt. 4. Quartum genus est omnium pessimum: eorum videlicet, qui tam abest vt militent, vt etiam vastent populum domini, tam abest vt plantét vineam domini, vt magis dissipent, & tam non pascunt gregem domini, vt verius mactent.
units.tr: (1) First, by those who indeed carry out their office, but, not content with necessary expenses, seek riches and luxury. (2) Second, by those who, though idle, nonetheless enjoy the support owed to labourers. (3) Third, by those who are not only idle and withhold the support owed to labourers, but also amass huge riches and live most sumptuously. (4) The fourth kind is by far the worst, namely of those who are so far from serving as soldiers that they even lay waste the people of the Lord, so far from planting the Lord's vineyard that they rather scatter it, and so far from feeding the Lord's flock that they rather slaughter it.

units.la: Non secundum hominem hæc dico: An non & lex eadem dicit? Etenim in Moisis lege scriptum est: Non obligabis os boui trituranti. Num boues curæ sunt Deo? An hoc propter nos omnino dicit? Propter nos enim hoc scriptum est, quod sub spe debeat is qui arat arare: & qui triturat sub spe, spei suæ particeps esse debeat.
units.tr: I do not say these things according to man. Does not the law itself say the same? For in the law of Moses it is written: "You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain." Are oxen a concern to God? Or does he say this altogether on our account? For this was written on our account: that he who ploughs should plough in hope, and he who threshes should be a partaker of his hope.

units.la: Hoc alterum argumentum est ab authoritate diuinæ legis sumptū. Quanquâ enim omnium æquissimum est quod agit, quia tamen non vt quâ ad repugnandū versipelle sit contentiosorum hominū ingenium, undecunque venás quod regeat, ne victū veritati locū dare cogatur, per occupationem occurrit obiectiōi, qua quis in speciem poterat obijcere. Atqui humanis tantū exéplis causam suā probat. An inox in religione locum habet, quod habet in rebus humanis? Addit itaq; authoritatem diuinam, ac docet, ista exépla licet humanæ, diuinæ quoque legi cōformia esse, dicés: Num secundum hominem hæc dico? Hoc est, num humano sensu ducor vbi ista dico? Num humana tantum authoritate & cōsuetudine motus istis vtor exéplis? An non & lex eadem dicit? Non ergo negat se humana dicere, cum omnino ista exempla sint humana, sed humano tamen sensu moueri se ac duci negat. Hoc est, causam hac adeo esse infirmam, vt humana tantū autoritate præter diuinā nitatur, hoc est, quod negat. Proinde subintelligendum est μόνον, id est, tantū, vt legamus: Num secundum hominem tātum hæc dico? Et hoc patet in sequenti particula, qua dicit: An non & lex eadem dicit? Cum enim non dicit: An non lex ista dicit? Sed: An non & lex eadem dicit? Satis clarum est, non negari humanum sensum, qui dictat, dignum esse opera ii in cibo suo, sed adiungi testimonium diuinæ legis, quo idem dicatur quod ista dictant exempla.
units.tr: This is the second argument, taken from the authority of the divine law. For although what he is doing is most fair in every respect, nevertheless, because the contentious nature of men is so crafty in resisting, and seeks from every quarter something to direct the argument, so that it is not forced to yield to the truth, he meets the objection by anticipating it, an objection which someone might bring forward in appearance. Yet he proves his case only by human examples. Does what holds good in human affairs hold good in religion too? Therefore he adds the divine authority and teaches that these examples, although human, are also in agreement with the divine law, saying: "Do I speak these things according to man?" That is, am I led by human feeling when I say these things? Am I moved and do I use these examples only by human authority and custom? "Does not the law itself say the same?" He therefore does not deny that he speaks human things, since these examples are altogether human, but he denies that he is moved and led by human feeling. That is, he denies that his cause is so weak that it rests on human authority alone apart from the divine. Accordingly, we must understand μόνον, that is "only", so that we read: "Do I speak these things according to man only?" And this is evident from the following clause, in which he says: "Does not the law itself say the same?" For since he does not say, "Does not this law say it?" but "Does not the law itself say the same?", it is clear enough that he does not deny the human sense which dictates that it is right for the worker to have his food, but he adds the testimony of the divine law, by which the same thing is said that these examples declare.

units.la: OBSER.
units.tr: OBSERVATION.

units.la: Est itaq; documento nobis præsens locus, q non debeant humanarum rerum exempla repudiari in causa religionis, sed quicquid in rebus humanis iustum est & æquum, commodum in tepore & loco vsurpari, modo propter contentiosos & maleuolos sacræ scripturæ authoritatem adijciámus, qua quod alioqui tanquam humanum & sæculare videri potest infirmū, testimonio verbi Dei corroboretur. Omne verum vero quidem, vt illeait, consonat. Verum Christi minister paratus esse debet, sacræ scripturæ locis ostendere, veri ex rebus humanis desumpti ad cœlestem veritatē consonantiam. Nec putandum est, quod ipse vsus humanorum exemplorū vilis sit ac superuacuus. Præterquâ enim qd' vsurpatū videmus ab Apostolo & Christo ipso, & prophetis, multum tamen roboris & magnam lucem cœlesti veritati adfert, vbi ostenditur hoc quod verbo Dei traditur, etiam in consuetudine & natura rerum humanarum locum & vsum habere. Proinde no parum exigitur à ministro verbi diligentig, ad hoc vt in rebus humanis non sit plane stupidus, sed audiat, videat, animaduertat & obseruet quicquid iustum, æquum, rectum, verum & vtile quouis modo in sæculo geritur, vt posit inde argumenta cœlestis veritatis, iustitiæ, æquitatis, & vtilitatis docendæ desumere. Ita quippe plerunq; peruersum est mortalium ingenium, vt quod in sæculo bonum agnoscit, & sepe numero vbi commodum est vsurpat, in causa Dei nolit agnoscere, nisi certis & irrefragabilibus argumentis conuictum.
units.tr: The present passage therefore teaches us that examples from human affairs ought not to be rejected in a matter of religion, but whatever in human affairs is just and fair may be used, where time and place allow, provided that, because of the contentious and ill-disposed, we add the authority of Holy Scripture, by which what might otherwise seem weak as merely human and worldly is strengthened by the testimony of the Word of God. Every truth agrees with truth, as the saying goes. Yet a minister of Christ ought to be ready to show from passages of Holy Scripture how the truths drawn from human affairs agree with heavenly truth. Nor should we think that the very use of human examples is cheap or superfluous. For apart from the fact that we see the Apostle, Christ himself, and the prophets employing them, they bring much strength and great light to heavenly truth when it is shown that what is delivered in the Word of God also has its place and use in the customs and nature of human affairs. Therefore a considerable diligence is required of the minister of the Word, so that he is not wholly dull in human affairs, but listens, looks, notices and observes whatever in the world is done in any way just, fair, right, true and useful, so that from it he may draw arguments for teaching the heavenly truth, justice, equity and usefulness. For human nature is so often perverse that what it recognises as good in the world, and frequently uses when it is convenient, it is unwilling to acknowledge in the cause of God, unless it is convinced by certain and irrefutable arguments.

units.la: ETENIM in Moisis lege scriptum est: Non obligabis os boui triturantis.) Locus hic habetur Deut.25. Consuetudo eius regionis est, vt fruges in area boum pedibus è paleis eruātur, ad quam rem apud nos agricolæ tribulis vtuntur. De isto triturandi more vide Eras.in Chil. pro. Bos lassus fortius figit pedem. Iniquum igitur fuerit boui trituranti os infrænare, vt in terea dum fruges circuēdo triturat, nihil ex illis decerpere possit, id quod ab illis fieri solet qui conductitijs bobus vtuntur.
units.tr: "For in the law of Moses it is written: 'You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain.'" This passage is found in Deut. 25. It is the custom of that region for the grain to be beaten out of the straw on the threshing floor by the feet of oxen, for which purpose our farmers use the threshing sledge. On this manner of threshing see Erasmus, in the Chiliades, under the proverb "A weary ox plants its foot more firmly." It would therefore be unjust to muzzle the ox treading out the grain, so that while it goes round treading out the grain it could pluck nothing from it, which is what those do who use hired oxen.

units.la: NVM boues curæ sunt Deo?) Ne quis dicat lex nō de hominibus, sed de bobus loqui, tur, negat boues Deo curæ esse ateq; ideo quod scriptum est, non boum, sed hominum gratia scriptum esse dicit.
units.tr: "Are oxen a concern to God?" Lest anyone say that the law speaks not of men but of oxen, he denies that oxen are a concern to God, and he says that what is written was written not for the sake of oxen but of men.

units.la: Huc tendunt quæ subijcit: Propter nos enim hoc scr ptum est, quod sub spe debeat arare qui arat, & qui triturat, spei suæ participes esse. Quæ verba bifariam exponuntur.
units.tr: What he adds points this way: "For this was written on our account: that he who ploughs should plough in hope, and he who threshes should be a partaker of his hope." These words are explained in two ways.

units.la: 1 Primum, vt illud propter nos referatur ad ministros Euangelij, quasi legis edictum paraboliçe referendum sit ad ministros Dei, qui p boues triturantes in area domini intelligatur. Ita intelligit & Augustinus de doctrina Christiana, lib.2.cap.10. Et eadem sententia dictum sit, quod connectitur, quod sub spe arare qui arat, & triturare qui triturat, debeat, non de agricolis ac triturat oribus terrenis, sed spiritualibus, Christi videlicet ministris.
units.tr: (1) First, that "on our account" is referred to the ministers of the Gospel, as if the command of the law were to be applied figuratively to the ministers of God, who are understood by the oxen treading out the grain in the Lord's threshing floor. Augustine also understands it so, in On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 10. And according to the same sense what follows is said, that he who ploughs ought to plough, and he who threshes to thresh, in hope, is to be understood not of earthly farmers and threshers but of spiritual ones, namely the ministers of Christ.

units.la: 2 Alio modo, vt non ad ministros, sed ad quosuis operarios arantes ac triturantes referatur, quod lex innuat tam iniquum esse laborantí negare sumptus necessarios, vt nec animanti irrationali id fieri debeat, nedum homi- ni. Et hoc sensu, quæ subiunguntur, simplicem habent huius legis expositionem, videlicet, quod homo arator ac triturator particeps esse debeat sperate frugis. Et ista expositio placet, propterea quod legem Mosi eadem dicere scri bit, quæ præmissa habent exempla. Nec timen dum est, ne non satis probet causam suam. Si enim & lex præcipit, aratori ac trituratori terrenarum frugum deberi victum, quanto magis debetur ministris Euangelij? Et 1. Timoth. 5. hanc legem eodem modo citare videtur, adiuncta Christi sententia, vulgari utique & generali, videlicet quod dignus sit operarius cibo suo.
units.tr: (2) In another way, the words are referred not to ministers but to any workers who plough and thresh, so that the law implies that it is as unjust to deny a labourer his necessary support as it ought not to be done even to an irrational animal, much less to a man. And in this sense the words that follow have a simple explanation of this law, namely that the man who ploughs and threshes ought to be a partaker of the hope of the crop. And this explanation pleases me, because it is the same as the examples set before. Nor is there any danger that he does not prove his case sufficiently. For if the law also commands that the plougher and thresher of earthly crops be given their sustenance, how much more is it owed to the ministers of the Gospel? And in 1 Timothy 5 he seems to cite this law in the same way, adding the saying of Christ, the common and general one, namely that the worker is worthy of his food.

units.la: Verba hæc, quod debeat qui arat, in spe arare, &c. in Græco nonnihil perturbatius posita sunt. Leguntur enim ad hunc modum: ὀφείλει ὁ ἀροτριῶν ἐπ' ἐλπίδι ... μετέχειν, i. Quoniam in spe debet qui arat arare, & qui triturat, spei suæ particeps esse in spe. Illud postremum in spe causam dedit quibusdam de duplici spe locum hunc exponendi. Vna præsentis ex labore solatij, mini stro verbi debiti à subditis, altera vitæ futuræ. Erasmus transpositione particularum lectioni consulendum putauit. Vnde de triturante ita legit, & qui triturat sub spe (ἐπ' ἐλπίδι) spei suæ particeps esse debeat. Vetus eam particulam ἐπ' ἐλπίδι non reddidit, nec legitur vel in Hieronym. vel Ambrosio.
units.tr: These words, "that he who ploughs ought to plough in hope," and so on, are put somewhat more confusedly in the Greek. For they read thus: ὀφείλει ὁ ἀροτριῶν ἐπ' ἐλπίδι ... μετέχειν [ought the ploughman in hope to plough, and the thresher to be a partaker in hope]. That last "in hope" has given some people cause to explain this passage in two senses of hope: one, the present comfort in labour, the due support from its subjects owed to the minister of the Word; the other, of future life. Erasmus thought that the reading should be helped by transposing the particles, and so he reads of the thresher thus: "and he who threshes, in hope (ἐπ' ἐλπίδι), ought to be a partaker of his hope." The old translator did not render that particle ἐπ' ἐλπίδι, nor is it found either in Jerome or in Ambrose.

units.la: Sed quæritur hoc loco, quomodo dicat, deo non esse curam de bobus, cum scriptum sit in Psalmo, Homines & iumenta seruas domine? Et in historia Niniue: Etiam animalium misereatur Deus. & in Euangelio: Pater non cadet super terram sine scitu patris nostri. Quomodo igitur boum curam non habet Deus? Commuiter ita soluitur hæc quæstio, vt dicatur hactenus boues non curare Deus, vt lege non illorum gratia condiderit, sed in ea magis respiciat homines, quam boues, qui hominum gratia conditi sunt, & finem legis huius esse, vt in animalibus discant homines, quid hominibus laborantibus debeant.
units.tr: But here it is asked how he can say that God has no care for oxen, since it is written in the Psalm, "Lord, you preserve man and beast," and in the story of Nineveh, "God has pity even on the animals," and in the Gospel, "Not a sparrow falls to the ground without the knowledge of our Father." How, then, does God have no care for oxen? This question is commonly resolved thus: God is said to have no care for oxen only in the sense that he did not frame the law for their sake, but in it he looks more to men than to oxen, who were created for the sake of men. The purpose of this law, they say, is that men may learn from animals what they owe to men who labour.

units.la: Si nos uobis spiritalia seminauimus, magnum est si nos uestra carnalia messuerimus?
units.tr: If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?

units.la: Tertium hoc argumentum est, sumptum à dignitate eorum quæ afferuntur mortalibus per ministerium Euangelij, quibus sumptus isti terreni ad sustentandam Apostoli necessitatem collati, certè parui & imparis deprehenduntur esse momenti. Vtitur collatione, perquè illam declarat, quàm non debeat videri molestum & sumptuosum, quod ministro Christi impenditur. Bona quæ per Christi ministrum adferuntur, sunt spiritualia in hac vita, spiritu hominis viuificantia, & ad veram felicitatem alentia: in futura verò, & corpori quoque sempiternam felicitatem pollicentia. Sumptus verò qui vicissim illi debetur, sunt carnales, hoc
units.tr: This is the third argument, taken from the worth of the things that are brought to mortals through the ministry of the gospel, against which those earthly expenses given to support the apostle's need are plainly found to be small and unequal in weight. He uses a comparison, and through it he shows how it ought not to seem burdensome and costly that is spent on Christ's minister. The goods brought through Christ's minister are spiritual in this life, giving life to the human spirit and nourishing it to true happiness; in the life to come they promise everlasting happiness to the body as well. The expenses owed in return are carnal, that is, (namely)

units.la: est, ad carnem hominis sustentanda pertinentes. Iam quantum carne hominis excellit spiritus, & quantum potior est cœlestis & vera vita quàm terrena ista & caduca, tantum vtiq; terrena & carnalia bona superantur à spiritalibus & æternis. Oportet itaq; singulariter ingratum esse cœlesti dono, quisquis grauatim terrena suppeditat ei, à quo ipse cœlestia accipit.
units.tr: that is, pertaining to sustaining the human flesh. Now, as the spirit surpasses the flesh of man, and as the heavenly and true life is more excellent than this earthly and fading one, so surely earthly and carnal goods are surpassed by spiritual and eternal ones. It is therefore right that whoever grudgingly supplies earthly things to him from whom he receives heavenly things should be singularly ungrateful for a heavenly gift.

units.la: Notandum est autem, quod non pronunciatiue dicit, parum est, si carnalia vestra messuerimus, sed percontando, magnùmne est, si carnalia vestra messuerimus? Quasi dicat: Magno putatis constare sustentationem ministri Christi, si is à vobis debeat quæ necessaria sunt accipere. Rogo, magnum vobis videtur, si pro spiritalibus impenderitis carnalia? Taxatur hic pesima mortalium ingratitudo, qui quicquid in seculi vanitatem insumant, parum, quantumuis verò parum Christi ministris impendant, multum & sumptuosum esse putant. Vnde quæso est ista ingratitudo? Ex eo videlicet, quod non agnoscunt vtilitatem ac precium ministerij Euangelici. Alioqui tam abest, vt multum putaretur, quod in sustentandos verbi ministros in sumendum est, vt etiam si omnia essent impendenda, haud granatim id fieret.
units.tr: It must be noted, however, that he does not say in a declarative way, "It is a small thing if we reap your carnal things," but by asking, "Is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?" As if he said: Do you think the support of Christ's minister costs much, if he must receive from you what is necessary? I ask, does it seem a great thing to you if you give carnal things in return for spiritual ones? Here the wicked ingratitude of mortals is rebuked: whatever they spend on the vanity of the world they count as little, but however little they give to Christ's ministers, they think it much and costly. Whence, I ask, comes this ingratitude? Clearly from this, that they do not recognise the usefulness and worth of the gospel ministry. Otherwise, far from being thought much, whatever must be spent on sustaining the ministers of the Word would not be given grudgingly, even if everything had to be spent.

units.la: Deinde & hoc obseruandum est, quod non simpliciter dicit: Si nos uobis adferimus vel exhibemus spiritalia, sed: Si nos vobis spiritalia seminauimus. Hac metaphora ad id respicit quod paulo ante dixit, quod sub spe debeat is qui arat arare, vbi ministrum Euangelij aratori comparauit. Nec frustra hac sationis metaphora vsus est. Spiritalia quippe bona illa, licet nobis per Euangelij prædicationem adferatur, ita tamen non adferuntur, vt ea in hac vita re ipsa possideamus, sed spe potius expectemus. Nam spe salui facti sumus. Suo tempore prodibit quod seminatum est, & quod nunc occultum & ab oculis mortalium abscondtum est, olim publicabitur, quodq; nunc per patientiam expectamus, vbi messis tempus aduenerit, possidebimus. Rectè itaque dixit: Si nos spiritalia uobis seminauimus. Alioqui ratio cogitat, vbi sunt spiritalia illa & cœlestia bona, quæ per fidem in Christum acquiri dicuntur, quum nemo sit Christianis in hac vita miserior & calamitosior?
units.tr: Next, this too is to be observed: he does not simply say, "If we bring or offer you spiritual things," but, "If we have sown spiritual things among you." This metaphor refers back to what he said a little earlier, that the one who ploughs ought to plough in hope, where he compared the minister of the gospel to the ploughman. Nor did he use this metaphor of sowing in vain. For those spiritual goods, although they are brought to us through the preaching of the gospel, are not brought in such a way that we possess them in fact in this life; rather we await them in hope. For we were saved by hope. In its time what has been sown will come forth, and what is now hidden and concealed from mortal eyes will one day be made public; what we now wait for with patience, when the time of harvest has come, we shall possess. Rightly, then, he said, "If we have sown spiritual things among you." Otherwise, reason asks, where are those spiritual and heavenly goods which are said to be acquired through faith in Christ, since no one in this life is more wretched and calamitous than Christians?

units.la: Si cæteri potestatis vestræ participes sunt, cur non potius nos?
units.tr: If others are partakers of your power, why not rather we?

units.la: Quarto, adhuc per collationem arguit ab eo quod Corinthij cum alijs hac in re alioqui faciebant. Conferebant enim pseudapostolis necessarios sumptus, & ferebant eos, qui acciebant ac devorabant, hoc nomine quod viderentur Christi apostoli. De illis loquitur, non de apostolis veris quorum supra memi-nit, vt & Chrysostomus annotat, cum dicit: Si alij potestatis vestræ participes sunt, cur non potius nos? Quasi dicat: Et vos ipsi testamini Christi ministro deberi prædicationis Euangelicæ sumptus. Sunt enim participes apud vos huius potestatis quos iam suspicitis tanq; præcipuos Christi ministros. Iam si illi participes sunt apud uos huius potestatis, cur nonpotius nos? Non addit, quare potius ad se pertineat ista potestas, quàm ad eos, qui illa vtebantur. Primùm enim relinquit hoc ipsorum conscientiæ. Deinde supra latis vrsit, se potissimum ipsorum esse Apostolum.
units.tr: Fourthly, he argues still by comparison, from what the Corinthians were otherwise doing in this matter with others. For they were supplying necessary expenses to false apostles, and were bearing with those who demanded and devoured, on the ground that they seemed to be Christ's apostles. He is speaking of those, not of the true apostles whom he mentioned above, as Chrysostom also notes when he says: "If others are partakers of your power, why not rather we?" As if he said: You yourselves bear witness that the expenses of gospel preaching are owed to Christ's minister. For those whom you now regard as the chief ministers of Christ are, among you, partakers of this power. Now if they are partakers among you of this power, why not rather we? He does not add why this power pertains rather to himself than to those who were using it. For first he leaves this to their own conscience; then, above, he has argued that he is especially their apostle.

units.la: Illud τῆς ἐξουσίας ὑμῶν μετέχουσιν. Id est, potestatis vestræ participes sunt, non est actiuè, sed passiuè intelligendum, de potestate non quam Corinthij habeant, sed quam habeant inter Corinthios Christi ministri. Unde & Erasmus reddidit, potestatis erga vos participes sunt. Chrysostomus exponit dominium & tyranni dem pseudapostolorum in Corinthios, motus eo, quod non dixit: Si alij potestatis huius participes sunt, sed: Si alij potestatis vestræ participes sunt, quod ipsi idem videtur, atque: si alij vos in potestate sua habent, vos possidènt, vobis dominantur, &c. Verùm meo iudicio non loquitur de alia potestate Apostol etiam: hoc loco, quàm de qua coepit. Neque enim alias adiunxisset, cur non potius nos? Quis nanque credet Apostolum dicturum fuisse, Si alij tyrannidem in vos exercent, cur nō potius nos? Deinde & statim addit: Atqui non sumus vsi ista potestate. Quod certè non potest de tyranni de intelligi. Non enim dicit se non vsum esse tyrannide erga Corinthios, sed iure suo, quo licitè vti potuisset, si quidem voluit, non esse vsum.
units.tr: The phrase "tēs exousias hymōn metechousin" [τῆς ἐξουσίας ὑμῶν μετέχουσιν], "are partakers of your power," is not to be understood actively but passively: it concerns not the power which the Corinthians have, but the power which Christ's ministers have among the Corinthians. Hence Erasmus also rendered it, "are partakers of power over you." Chrysostom explains it as the lordship and tyranny of the false apostles over the Corinthians, moved by the fact that he did not say, "If others are partakers of this power," but, "If others are partakers of your power," which seems to him the same as, "If others hold you in their power, possess you, lord it over you," and so on. But in my judgment he is not speaking here of a different power of the apostle from the one he began with. For otherwise he would not have added, "why not rather we?" Who indeed would believe the apostle would have said, "If others exercise tyranny over you, why not rather we?" Then he immediately adds, "Yet we have not used this power." This certainly cannot be understood of tyranny. For he does not say that he has not used tyranny towards the Corinthians, but that he has not used his right, which he could have used lawfully had he wished.

units.la: Veruntamen non sumus usi potestate ista, sed omnia sufferimus, ne quod offendiculum demus Euangelio Christi.
units.tr: But we have not used this power, but endure all things, so that we may not give any hindrance to the Gospel of Christ.

units.la: Posteaquam contendit se esse Christi Apostolum, & præcipuè Corinthijs. Deinde apostolis esse potestatem, qua & vterentur reliqui apostoli, fratres domini, & Petrus sumendi sumptus prædicandi Euangelium, à fidelibus, idque sibi licere non minus quàm ipsis, iam obiter interserit argumentis, quibus hanc potestatem confirmat, se non esse vsum iure suo, vt exemplum suum, quod proponere satagebat Corinthijs paulatim ad propositum accommodet.
units.tr: Having maintained that he is an apostle of Christ, and especially to the Corinthians, he now inserts in passing, among the arguments by which he confirms this power, that the apostles had the right both to be supported by the faithful and to take money for preaching the Gospel, and that this was no less lawful for him than for the other apostles, the brothers of the Lord, and Peter. He does so in order to adapt, little by little, his own example, which he was eager to set before the Corinthians, to the purpose he has in view. He had not used his lawful right.

units.la: VERVNTAMEN, inquit. Id est, neglectis argumentis istis omnibus, tametsi licitè potuissem sumptus à vobis sumere tanquam Christi Apostolus, non tamen isto iure usus sum.
units.tr: "But," he says. That is: setting aside all those arguments, although I could lawfully have taken money from you as an apostle of Christ, I have not made use of that right.

units.la: Nec dicit, veruntamen nihil à vobis accepimus, sed, nō sumus vsi hac potestate, vt maneat in proposito, videlicet, quod non simpliciter non acceperit aliquid; sed quod potestate sua non sit vsus. Et ideo non dicit: Non sumus aliqua potestate vsi in vos, sed hac, id est, licita & tot nominibus iusta, non sumus vsi. Alioqui ea vsus est in illos potestate, qua scortatorem Satanæ dedit, de qua 2. Cor.10. & 13.
units.tr: He does not say, "But we have received nothing from you," but "we have not used this power," so that the point stays the same: he did not simply receive nothing, but he did not use his power. Hence he does not say, "We have not used any power over you," but "this power," that is, the power that is lawful and justified by so many grounds. Otherwise, he did use a power over them: the power by which he delivered the fornicator to Satan, of which see 2 Cor. 10 and 13.

units.la: SED omnia sufferimus.) Non dicit abstinuimus ab illa, sed, Omnia sufferimus. Quo
units.tr: "But we endure all things." He does not say, "We have abstained from it," but "We endure all things."

units.la: A indicat se non sine magno incommodo famis, laboris, nuditatis, & aliarum molestiarum, qui bus carere potuisset, si iure suo vti voluisset hac potestate sua abstinuisse. Ne quis putet rem hac Apostolo fuisse facilem & nullius molestiæ.
units.tr: By this he indicates that he did not abstain from that power without great hardship of hunger, toil, nakedness and other troubles, which he could have avoided if he had wished to use his right. Let no one think that this was easy for the Apostle or free of any trouble.

units.la: Simul etiā quod non dicit, ista sufferimus, sed, omnia sufferimus, auxesim habet & intentionem propositi Apostoli, quo statuerat ita cauere, ne quod Euangelio Christi daret offendiculum, vt non solum nullos sumeret à Corinthijs sumptus ad prædicandum Euangelium, sed simul omnia incommoda ferret animo patienti vnius Euangelij gratia, ne qua in re offendiculum illi obiceretur.
units.tr: At the same time, the fact that he does not say "we endure these things" but "we endure all things" carries emphasis and expresses the Apostle's purpose: he had resolved to take such care that he would give no hindrance to the Gospel of Christ. Thus he would not only take no money from the Corinthians for preaching the Gospel, but would also bear with a patient mind all the inconveniences, for the sake of the Gospel alone, so that in no matter would any stumbling block be placed in its way.

units.la: Clanculù eos pudefacit, qui ne eidolothyto quidem Euangelij gratia abstinebat, quod tamen absq; vlla potuissent facere molestia.
units.tr: He secretly shames those who did not even abstain from idol meat for the sake of the Gospel, although they could have done so without any trouble.

units.la: NB quod offendiculum demus Euangelio Christi.) Hæc est ratio, propter quam dicit se non vsum esse potestate sua, & nihil non tulisse. Igitur profectus Euangelij, ipsa vita & omnibus commodis charior, & defectus omnibus molestijs, omnibus periculis, omnibus incommodis, nuditate, frigore, fame, molestiór fuit Apostolo.
units.tr: "Lest we give a hindrance to the Gospel of Christ." This is the reason why he says he has not used his power and has borne everything. Therefore the advance of the Gospel, dearer to him than life itself and all advantages, outweighed for the Apostle every trouble, every danger, every inconvenience, nakedness, cold and hunger.

units.la: Ad hunc scopum quemadmodum ipse collimauit, ita inducere conatur & Cotinthios, vt ad eundem & ipsi omnia dirigant.
units.tr: Just as he aimed at this goal himself, so he tries to lead the Corinthians to direct everything to the same goal.

units.la: Sed quomodo offendiculum dedisset Euangelio Christi si potestate sua fuisset vsus, cū id Euangelio non repugnasset?
units.tr: But how would he have given a hindrance to the Gospel of Christ if he had used his power, since that use would not have been opposed to the Gospel?

units.la: B Ambrosius intelligit inde diminutam fuisse authoritatem Apostoli, ita vt nequiuisset confidenter corripere delinquentes Corinthios, si quicquam ab illis accepisset. Pseudapostolos blanditos esse Corinthijs ad hoc, vt accipere mererentur, atq; ideo illos non reprehendisse. Hoc ne & Apostolo accideret, consilium fuisse, nihil ab illis accipere, vt saluo authoritatis Apostolicæ vigore liberè illos argueret.
units.tr: Ambrose understands from this that the authority of the Apostle would have been diminished, so that he could not have boldly rebuked the Corinthians for their faults if he had received anything from them. The false apostles, he says, flattered the Corinthians so that they might deserve to receive, and therefore they did not rebuke them. To prevent this from happening to the Apostle too, it was his plan to receive nothing from them, so that he could freely reprove them while the strength of his apostolic authority remained intact.

units.la: Veruntamen si hic fuisset finis Apostoli in hac causa, hoc est, si istam authoritatem Apostoli imminuisset vsus licitæ potestatis, debuissent idem consilium amplecti & reliqui Apostoli.
units.tr: However, if this had been the Apostle's aim in this matter, that is, if the use of a lawful power would have weakened his apostolic authority, the other apostles too ought to have embraced the same plan.

units.la: Chrysostomus aliam adfert loci huius expositionem videlicet, ne ab Euangelio abstereret Corinrhios, si quid ab illis acciperet. Verùm, vt supra annotaui, timendum erat Apostolo, ne partim suo exemplo abuteretur pseudapostoli, partim ne suspicionem illi moueret de quæstu, quasi quæstus gratia prædicaret Euangelium, quod sanè plurimam ἐγκοπὴν, id est, interruptionem & impactionem Euangelij cur sui dedisset.
units.tr: Chrysostom gives another explanation of this passage, namely that he did not want to turn the Corinthians away from the Gospel if he received anything from them. But, as I noted above, the Apostle had to fear that the false apostles would partly abuse his example and partly that he would arouse suspicion of gain, as if he preached the Gospel for the sake of profit. Such a suspicion would certainly have caused the greatest hindrance [ἐγκοπὴν], that is, an interruption and obstruction of the Gospel.

units.la: Interea tamen non negauerim id quod Ambrosius annotat, in multis verbi ministris habere locum, vt sint blandiores & in carpendis vicijs eorum, à quibus necessarios sumptus accipiunt, frigidiores, quia vident vitæ suæ sustentationem ab illis pendere. Reperias etiam talia collegia, quæ iureiurado ecclesiastas suos antequam ei muneri admittantur, obnoxios sibi certo præscripto reddant, ne quid contra se in suggestu dicant. Vnde hoc audent? Ex eo videlicet, quod in sua potestate habent admittendi, deinde rursus abigendi quem volunt: ad hæc & sumptus concionatoribus constituendi, quantos volunt. Hac licentia abutuntur ad hoc, vt linguam ecclesiastæ captiuam reddant, ne quid in ipsorum scelera possit, autcerte non diu possit.
units.tr: Meanwhile, I would not deny what Ambrose observes, that among many ministers of the Word it happens that they are more flattering, and more lukewarm in rebuking the vices of those from whom they receive their necessary support, because they see that the sustenance of their lives depends on them. You will also find such bodies that bind their own churchmen by oath, before they are admitted to that office, to certain prescribed terms, so that they say nothing against them from the pulpit. Where do they get the courage for this? Clearly from the fact that they have in their power the right to admit and then again to dismiss whomever they wish, and also to fix the stipends of the preachers as large as they like. They abuse this licence so as to make the tongue of the churchman a captive, so that nothing can be said against their crimes, or at least that it cannot be said for long.

units.la: Imbibendum & nobis omnibus est, quotquot Euangelij ministri sumus, propositum illud Apostoli, quo paratus fuit ad omnia ferenda, vtut molesta, ne quod daret offendiculum Euangelio Christi. Si enim dignus est, vt in profundum abijciatur, qui vnum tantum ex minimis offendit, quid quæso ille est, qui ipsi Euangelio, vnde mortalium salus constat, offendiculum ponit? Caute itaq; & circumspectè ambulandum est Christi ministris, ne per ipsos remoras accipiat cursus Euangelij. Offendiculo quidem non caret, si quando delinquunt Euangelij auditores. Verum tantum ab illis offendiculum Euangelio non datur, quantum datur, si ipsi Euangelij ministri delinquant. Maximum autem offendiculum est, si deprehendantur quæstum sectari. Imò etiamsi suspicionem tantum illius moueant ecclesiæ, quod non Christi gloriam, sed quæstum quærant.
units.tr: All of us who are ministers of the Gospel must soak ourselves in that purpose of the Apostle, by which he was ready to endure all things, however troublesome, so as not to give any hindrance to the Gospel of Christ. For if he is worthy to be cast into the depths of the sea who offends even one of the least, what, I ask, is he who places a stumbling block before the Gospel itself, from which the salvation of mortals comes? Christ's ministers must therefore walk carefully and circumspectly, lest through them the course of the Gospel receive obstacles. Indeed, a stumbling block is not absent when the hearers of the Gospel go astray. Yet a stumbling block is given to the Gospel not so much by them as it is when the ministers of the Gospel themselves go astray. The greatest stumbling block is if they are caught pursuing profit; indeed, even if they merely arouse in the Church the suspicion that they seek their own gain and not the glory of Christ.

units.la: An nescitis, quod ij qui in sacris operantur, ex sacrificio edunt? Qui altario assistunt, una cum altario partem accipiunt? Sic & dominus ordinauit, vt qui Euangelium annunciant, ex Euangelio viuant.
units.tr: Do you not know that those who serve in sacred things eat from the sacrifice? And that those who attend the altar share in what is on the altar? So also the Lord has ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel.

units.la: Redit ad propositum, quod probandum suscepperat, videlicet, quod ministro Christi debeatur victus. Vtitur autem argumento ad causam hanc viciniori & accommodatiori, sumpto à consuetudine populi legalis, apud quem ius erat diuinitùs traditum, licere sacerdotibus, sacris operantibus, victum sumere ex laboribus suis. Et quoniam illa consuetudo celebris erat & omnium notissima, quæ scilicet ignorari non potuit, cum admiratione dicit: An nescitis quod ij, &c.
units.tr: He returns to the point he had undertaken to prove, namely that the minister of Christ is owed his sustenance. He uses an argument closer to the matter and better suited to it, drawn from the custom of the people of the Law, among whom it was divinely ordained that priests who served at the sacred rites might take their food from their labours. Since that custom was well known and familiar to all, and could not have been unknown, he says with astonishment: Do you not know that those who...?

units.la: Q VI in sacris operantur.) Ambrosius, In sacrario legem Gentilium, in altari vero Iudæorum intelligit. Verum in ipsis Apostoli verbis nihil est, vnde possit ista sumi distinctio. Nam vtrunque & sacrarium & altare vtrisque tam Gentibus quàm Iudeis in vsu fuit. Non inquit quod Deus per Moysem Gentilium consuetudinem imitatus sit, sed quod ipsa naturalis ratio ita habeat, vt quisque ex labore suo viuat.
units.tr: Who serve in sacred things. Ambrose understands the Gentile law to be in the sanctuary and the law of the Jews at the altar. But there is nothing in the Apostle's words from which such a distinction could be drawn. For both the sanctuary and the altar were in use among Gentiles as well as Jews. He does not say that God imitated the custom of the Gentiles through Moses, but that natural reason itself has it so, that each person lives by his own labour.

units.la: EX sacrificio edunt.) Vide quomodo ista duo coniungat ἐργαζόμενοι & ἐσθίουσιν, inque eandem rem collocet vtraque, videlicet in operationem sacrorum, vt intelligamus in rebus sacris hæc duo ita esse coniuncta, vt iure alterum exigatur ab altero.
units.tr: Eat from the sacrifice. Notice how he joins these two things, working [ἐργαζόμενοι] and eating [ἐσθίουσιν], and places both on the same footing, namely the service of sacred things. So we understand that in sacred matters these two are so joined that by right the one may be demanded from the other.

units.la: Notandum censet hoc loco Chrysostomus & imitator, imò abbreuiator Chrysostomi Theophylactus, quod non dicit Apostolus: Qui in sacris operantur, ex bonis eorum qui offerunt, edunt, sed ex sacrificio edunt. Sicut & mox non dicit, qui altario assistunt, ex oblatio nibus eorum, qui victimas adferunt, sustentantur, sed, partem habent vna cum altari. Eò quod quæ offerebantur, oblata iam non erant amplius offerentium bona, sed sacrarij & altaris, hoc est, Deo consecrata. Certè diuino consilio, propter mortalium malignitatem ita ordinatum fuerat, vt victus sacerdotum esset ex oblationibus Deo factis, exegit sibi Deus certas oblationes. Et merito. Potuisset omnia exigere. Ex illis voluit alimoniam esse ministris suis, ne locus esset populo tergiuersandi, & victum sacerdotibus denegandi. Atq; hoc pacto admonebantur sacerdotes, vt cultui Dei fideliter inseruirent, scirètq; se magis esse Dei quàm populi ministros, ideoque victum verius à Deo quotidie sumere, quàm à populo, populus vero omni tergiuersatione priuabatur, quæ cùm ministris tum cultui Dei necessaria erant offerendi.
units.tr: Chrysostom, and Theophylact, who imitates and indeed abridges Chrysostom, think it worth noting here that the Apostle does not say: those who serve in sacred things eat from the goods of those who offer, but from the sacrifice they eat. Likewise, just after, he does not say that those who attend the altar are supported from the offerings of those who bring the victims, but that they have a share together with the altar. The reason is that what was offered was no longer the property of the offerers once it had been offered, but belonged to the sanctuary and the altar, that is, had been consecrated to God. Certainly by divine counsel, because of human malice, it was so ordained that the priests' sustenance should come from offerings made to God; God claimed certain offerings for himself. And rightly so. He could have claimed everything. From those offerings he wished there to be food for his ministers, so that the people would have no room for evasion and for denying the priests their livelihood. In this way the priests were reminded to serve the worship of God faithfully and to know that they were ministers of God rather than of the people, and so received their sustenance from God daily, more truly than from the people; while the people were deprived of every evasion, since what was offered was necessary both for the ministers and for the worship of God.

units.la: Per verbum ἐσθίειν, non solum cibus venit, sed & reliqua omnia vitæ necessaria. Sicut in oratione Dominica, cum dicimus, Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie, non de pane tantum intelligimus, sed simul de omnibus ad vitæ huius sustentationem necessarijs. Fit autem cibi ob id mentio præ cæteris, quod in illo potior sit constituta ad sustentandam vitam necessitas.
units.tr: By the verb to eat, not only food is meant, but all the other things necessary for life. Just as in the Lord's Prayer, when we say, Give us this day our daily bread, we understand not only bread but also all things necessary for sustaining this life. Food is mentioned in particular because necessity for sustaining life is chiefly placed in it.

units.la: Q VI altario assistunt.) Mihi videtur id quod de ijs qui sacris operantur, præmissum est, generaliter positum, & istam particulam specificandi, & exempli gratia esse subiectam. Etenim sacris operari generale est, multa & varia sacrorum ministeria complectens, vt non mox sit altaris minister quisquis sacris operatur.
units.tr: Who attend the altar. It seems to me that what was said before about those who serve in sacred things is put in general terms, and that this particle is added as a specification, by way of example. For serving in sacred things is a general term, embracing many and various sacred ministries, so that not everyone who serves in sacred things is at once a minister of the altar.

units.la: Obserua quod non dicit sacerdotes, sed qui altario assident, vt excludantur illi qui titulote nus tantum sacerdotes sunt, ociosi ventres, nihil commercij cum altaris ministerio habetes. At hodie vix alij sunt, qui plura titulo altaris tollant, & quæ altari debentur, immodestius à populo exigant.
units.tr: Observe that he does not say priests, but those who attend the altar, so that those are excluded who are priests only in name, idle bellies, having no dealings with the ministry of the altar. Yet today there are scarcely any others who take more in the name of the altar and demand more immodestly from the people what is owed to the altar.

units.la: VNA cum altario participant.) Bifariam ista particula exponitur. Quidam intelligunt ea quę ad altare offerebantur inter sacerdotes & leuitas esse diuisa. Alij verò ita exponunt, vt pars hostiæ cesserit altario, pars sacerdotib. Et ista sententia posterior videtur esse verisimilior. Nam & in lege determinatum est, quid Deo, & quid sacerdoti ex hostia debuerit offerri, & ipsa Apostoli verba hunc sensum afferunt. Non enim dicit, ἐν τῷ vel ἐκ τῶν, sed simpliciter τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ συμμετέχοντας, id est, vna cum altari participant, vt intelligamus partem altari, partem cessisse ministris.
units.tr: Share together with the altar. This phrase is explained in two ways. Some understand that what was offered at the altar was divided between the priests and the Levites. Others explain it so that part of the victim went to the altar and part to the priests. This second opinion seems the more probable. For the law also determined what from the victim was to be offered to God and what was due to the priest, and the Apostle's own words bear this sense. For he does not say ἐν τῷ or ἐκ τῶν, but simply τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ συμμετέχοντας [sharing with the altar], that is, share together with the altar, so that we understand that part went to the altar and part to the ministers.

units.la: SIC & dominus ordinauit.) Ne quis adhuc dicat, ista legis sunt, ad nos nihil pertinet, subijsubijcit etiam authoritatem domini, qui pari ratione constituerit, vt de Euágelio viuat, qui Euangelium annunciat. Tale quid legimus Matt.10. Dignus est operarius cibo suo. Et Lucæ decimo: Edentes & bibentes quæ apud eos sunt.
units.tr: So also the Lord has ordained. Lest anyone still say that these things belong to the law and have nothing to do with us, he adds the authority of the Lord, who by the same reasoning has ordained that the one who proclaims the Gospel should live from the Gospel. We read something like this in Matthew 10: The workman is worthy of his food. And in Luke 10: Eating and drinking what they have.

units.la: Οὕτως.) Sic. Nonquod legem fit imitatus do minus, vt propterea ministris Euangelij debea tur victus quod in lege altaris ministris id iuris fuerit, vel quod eo modo ex oblationibus & hostijs decimis & primitijs, vt in lege sancitum fuerat, victus debeatur Euangelij ministro. Sed ideo quod id æquum est & iustum, vt ex labore & ministerio suo quisque victum ac vitæ necessaria sumat, etiam suis ministris dominus hanc potestatem fecit. Quibus vero modis mi nistro Euangelij debeat subministrari victus, non præscripsit quicquam, sed ecclesiæ suæ liberum reliquit, vt non sit necesse id fieri per modos legales. Hactenus igitur ex lege sumen da sunt in his rebus exempla, quatenus æquita tem præferunt, & Euangelico cursui sunt accommoda.
units.tr: Thus [Οὕτως]. So. Not that the Lord imitated the law, so that the minister of the Gospel should be owed sustenance for the reason that the ministers of the altar had that right under the law, or because in that way sustenance is owed to the minister of the Gospel from offerings, tithes and firstfruits, as had been sanctioned in the law. But because it is fair and just that each person should take his sustenance and the necessities of life from his labour and ministry, the Lord has given this power also to his own ministers. As to the manner in which the minister of the Gospel ought to be supplied with sustenance, he has prescribed nothing, but has left it free to his Church, so that it is not necessary that this be done by legal means. Hence, so far as these matters go, examples are to be taken from the law only insofar as they carry equity and are adapted to the course of the Gospel.

units.la: Διάταξις, id est, constituit, ordinauit, præcepit. Ista domini constitutio subditos & auditores constringit, non ipsos verbi ministros. Verbi minister non peccat, si victum sibi ex Euangelio quod annunciat, non sumat. Alioqui peccasset hoc loco Paulus, si isti constitutioni dominicæ fuisset obnoxius. Tam abest autem vt peccarit, vt etiam plurimum in eo glorietur, quod hac constitutione domini non sit vsus. Auditor vero Euangelij, nisi obediat isti ordinationi, peccat in Dominum, cuius constitutionem contemnit.
units.tr: Ordinance [διάταξις], that is, he has established, ordained, commanded. This ordinance of the Lord binds the subjects and hearers, not the ministers of the Word themselves. A minister of the Word does not sin if he does not take sustenance for himself from the Gospel which he proclaims. Otherwise Paul would have sinned here, if he had been bound by this ordinance of the Lord. But so far is he from sinning that he glories greatly in the fact that he did not use this ordinance of the Lord. The hearer of the Gospel, however, unless he obeys this ordinance, sins against the Lord whose ordinance he despises.

units.la: VT qui Euangelium annunciant.) Duobus verbis & materiam & modum ministrandi domino exprimit. In dictione Euangelij materia est ministerij. Non in missis & cantionibus. In verbo annunciandi modus est quo debeat ministrari domino.
units.tr: That those who proclaim the Gospel. In two words he expresses both the matter and the manner of ministering to the Lord. In the word Gospel the matter of the ministry is stated, not in masses and chants. In the word proclaim is the manner in which the Lord ought to be served.

units.la: Et obserua quàm appositè Euangelio coniungat annunciationem, nó leges aut mandata. Euangelium est bonum nuncium de salute orbi parta per Christum, & fide in Christū apprehendenda. Hoc vult dominus in toto orbe vulgari & cum ingenti gaudio & tripudio annunciari, sicut solent res læte miseris & afflictis cum lætitiæ affectu prædicari. Qua de re vide Rom.10. Quàm speciosi pedes annunciantium pacem, &c.
units.tr: And observe how fittingly he joins proclamation to the Gospel, not laws or commands. The Gospel is the good news of salvation won for the world through Christ, to be grasped by faith in Christ. The Lord wills that this be published throughout the whole world with great joy and exultation, just as happy news is usually announced with a feeling of gladness to the wretched and afflicted. On this see Romans 10: How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, and so on.

units.la: EX Euangelio viuant.) Id est, ex Euangelij annunciatione, ex labore vel propter laborem suum, quem Euangelio annunciando impendunt, victum sumant à fidelibus. Alioqui ex Euangelio simpliciter non carnalis est cibus, sed spiritualis, & qui non minus auditorum animas pascat quàm Euangelizantium.
units.tr: Live from the Gospel. That is, from the proclamation of the Gospel, from their labour or on account of their labour, which they spend in proclaiming the Gospel, let them take their sustenance from the faithful. For food that comes from the Gospel simply is not carnal food but spiritual, and it feeds the souls of the hearers no less than of those who preach the Gospel.

units.la: VIVANT, inquit.) Victus necessitas viuendi verbo expressa est, vt intelligamus tantum victus deberi ex Euangelio Christi ministro, quantum ad necessariam vitæ sustentationem sufficere potest, non quantum delicię & luxus exigunt. Sic nos Germani quoq; hoc verbo vtimur, cū dicimus, Der arm man hat nit zu leben.
units.tr: Live, he says. The need for sustenance is expressed by the word live, so that we understand that the minister of Christ is owed from the Gospel only as much sustenance as can suffice for the necessary support of life, not as much as pleasure and luxury demand. So we Germans also use this word when we say, The poor man has not enough to live on.

units.la: Quærendum videtur hoc loco, quid opus fuerit Apostolo causam hanc omnium æquissimam, videlicet, quod ex Euangelio viuere liceat ei qui Euangelium annunciat, tot exemplis agricolæ, militis, pastoris, authoritate & consuetudine legis, collatione sementis & messis afferere, cum tamen tribus quatuor verbis potuisset dicere, dominus ita præcepit, vt qui Euangelium annunciat ex Euangelio viuat.
units.tr: Here it seems right to ask why the Apostle needed so many examples (the farmer, the soldier, the shepherd), the authority and custom of the law, and the comparison with sowing and reaping to establish this most just case, namely that the one who proclaims the gospel may live from the gospel. He could have said it in three or four words: the Lord has so commanded, that he who proclaims the gospel should live from the gospel.

units.la: Scilicet hoc vnum, quod omnium est æquissimum, quod tantum habet iuris, cum diuini tũ humani, tantũ æquitatis, tantũ consuetudinis, vix vnquam bene potuit persuaderi mundo. Nam perpetuò in alendis Euangelij ministris tenacissimus est, cũ sit ad reliqua vana & inepta profusissimus.
units.tr: Certainly this one thing, which is the most just of all and carries as much authority, divine and human, as much equity and custom, has scarcely ever been well persuaded upon the world. For the world is always most tight-fisted in supporting the ministers of the gospel, while it is most lavish with other vain and foolish things.

units.la: Pulchrè tamen hoc loco isto Apostoli studio consulitur ministrorum verbi conscientijs, partim ne hæsitent in sumendo victu pro labore suo, partim ne ægreferant ubi viderint otiosis ventribus affatim suppeditari ad luxū & delicias omnia, cum ipsi interea vix vitæ necessaria pro labore Euangelij accipiant, si cogitent ita constituisse dominum, vt qui Euangelio seruit, ex Euangelio non delicietur, sed viuat. Vix puto vnquam inuentus est Euangelij præco, candidus & syncerus, fidelis ac sedulus, cui quicquam vltra ea quæ necessaria sunt, ex Euangelij auditoribus cesserit. Luxus & delicię non laborantibus, sed ad mactationē destinatis pecoribus competunt. Laborantibus debetur victus necessarius, atq; ita constitutū est à domino. Illo itaque contenti sint Euangelij ministri.
units.tr: Yet here the Apostle's argument admirably serves the consciences of the ministers of the Word, partly so that they do not hesitate to take food in return for their labour, and partly so that they are not offended when they see everything supplied in abundance to idle bellies for luxury and pleasure, while they themselves scarcely receive the necessities of life for their labour in the gospel. If they reflect that the Lord has so ordained that he who serves the gospel should not live in delights from the gospel, but should live, they will be content. I think scarcely any herald of the gospel has been found who was sincere and upright, faithful and diligent, to whom anything beyond what was necessary has come from the hearers of the gospel. Luxury and delights befit not working animals but cattle destined for slaughter. Necessary sustenance is owed to those who labour, and this is how the Lord has ordained it. Let the ministers of the gospel therefore be content with that.

units.la: Ego tamen nullo horum usus fui.
units.tr: I, however, have used none of these.

units.la: Hactenus Apostolus ministri Euangelij ius quod ad victum attinet, exposuit, ac declarauit, quomodo illo non minus quàm reliqui apostoli vti potuerit, si quidem voluisset, atque ita propositi sui primam partem absoluit. Iam consequenter ad id, quod paulo ante cœperat, alteram videlicet partem progreditur, commemoraturus, quomodo hac potestate licita non sit vsus, & quare id fecerit, nec facturus etiam sit. Ego tamen, inquit, quanquam vt recensui, multis argumentis & rationibus hac vti potuissem potestate in vestra ecclesia, illorum tamē nullo sum vsus, nec quicquā quod ad hoc ius pertineat, vsurpaui.
units.tr: Hitherto the Apostle has set out and explained the right of the minister of the gospel as regards food, and how he could have used it no less than the other apostles, had he wished; and so he has completed the first part of his proposition. Now, following on from what he began a little earlier, he goes on to the second part, to relate how he did not use this lawful power, why he did not, and that he will not do so even in future. "Yet I," he says, "although, as I have reviewed, I could have used this power among your church on many grounds and reasons, have used none of them, nor have I claimed anything that pertains to this right."

units.la: Quanquam non scripsi hęc, vt ita fiat in me.
units.tr: Yet I have not written these things so that it might be done in my case.

units.la: Duo erant Apostolo propter præmissa curanda. Vnum, vt ostenderet, quod istam potestatem non sui gratia tam prolixè asseruerit, ac tot argumentis confirmauerit. Alterum, vt ad scopum collimaret, ostendens cur ista in duxerit. Postremum hoc non præstabit apertis verbis hoc capite, sed sequenti. Prius versabit ad finem vsque capitis præsentis. Est autē illius ratio, vt suspicionem amoueat, ne quis dicat ob id ista tam copiose praemissa, quod licet hactenus iure suo apud Corinthios non fit vsus, cupiat tamen vti in posterum, atque ob eā causam tot hac de re vsus sit argumentis, vt cō modo suo in futurum consulat. Proinde addit rationem cur nec in posterum vti velit ista potestate.
units.tr: The Apostle had two things to attend to on account of what he had said. One was to show that he had not asserted this power, and confirmed it with so many arguments, for his own sake. The other was to aim at his goal, showing why he had brought these matters forward. He will not state the latter in plain words in this chapter, but in the next. The former he deals with up to the end of the present chapter. Its purpose is to remove suspicion, lest someone say that these things were so copiously put forward because, although he has not so far used his right among the Corinthians, he wishes to use it in future, and has therefore marshalled so many arguments on this matter to provide for his own advantage later. So he adds the reason why he does not wish to use this power even in future.

units.la: Nota interea, quod caute nō dicit: Non scripsi hoc, vt ita fieri debeat in apostolis Christi, sed in me, inquit. Non vult alijs ipsorum ius adimere, licet ipse illo nolit vti apud Corinthios.
units.tr: Note meanwhile that he cautiously does not say, "I have not written this so that it should be done thus in the apostles of Christ," but, "in me," he says. He does not wish to take away their right from the others, although he himself is unwilling to use it among the Corinthians.

units.la: Nam bonum est mihi mori potius quam ut gloriationem meam aliquis inanem reddat.
units.tr: For it is better for me to die than that anyone should make my boasting empty.

units.la: His verbis ostendit tam abesse, vt cupiat temere vti sua potestate, vt malit mori, quàm amittere id, quod hoc proposito quaerit. Non dicit, melius est vt moriar, id est, fame peream, quàm vt hac potestate vtar: sed, melius est vt moriar, quàm vt hanc gloriationem meam aliquis inanem reddat, id est, quàm vt aliquis propositum hoc meum, in quo glorior, si vtar hac potestate, ex eo sibi occasionem sumat, gaudendi me suspicione quaestus, atque ita enervandi ac irritandi propositum meum, quod est, vt absque vlla suspicione liberè ac fideliter vobis praedicem Euangelium Christi, cuius gratia decreui non vti meo iure apud vos, vt amputem occasionem illis qui quaerunt occasionem.
units.tr: By these words he shows that he is so far from wishing to use his power rashly that he would rather die than lose what he seeks by this purpose. He does not say, "It is better that I die," that is, that I perish of hunger, rather than that I use this power. He says, "It is better that I die than that anyone make this boasting of mine empty," that is, than that anyone, if I use this power, should take from it an occasion of suspecting that I am seeking gain, and so weaken and frustrate my purpose. That purpose is to preach the gospel of Christ to you freely and faithfully, without any suspicion; for its sake I have resolved not to use my right among you, so as to cut off the occasion from those who seek an occasion.

units.la: Ista volui ob id annotare, ne quis cogitet, Deo gratius esse, si moriatur fame Apostolus, quàm si vtatur constitutione illa, quam ipse do minus ordinauit, atque inde colligat, satius fuisse futurum, si mortui fuissent reliqui apostoli, quā quod potestate sua in ecclesijs Christi usi sunt. Primum non loquitur de reliquis apostolis, sed de se tantum. Deinde non loquitur etiā de alia ecclesia, in qua id fieri necesse fuerit, praeter pseudapostolos, quàm de ecclesia Corinthiorum. Tertiò, non dicit, vt suprà monui, quàm vt potestate mea à domino concessa vtar: sed, quàm vt aliquis gloriationem hanc meam inanem reddat, id est, quàm vt ego vsu potestatis meae apud vos, occasionem dem pseudapostolis, gloriationem hanc meam, maligna suspicione reddendi inanem. Videtur Apostolus respicere ad dictum Christi Matth. 18. Vae qui offenderit vnum ex his pusillis, melius esset, si suspensa in collo eius mola asinaria, proijceretur in profundum maris.
units.tr: I wished to note this so that no one would think it more pleasing to God for the Apostle to die of hunger than for him to use that arrangement which the Lord himself ordained, and from this conclude that it would have been better if the other apostles had died than that they used their power in the churches of Christ. First, he does not speak of the other apostles, but of himself only. Second, he does not speak of another church in which it would have been necessary to do this, apart from the false apostles, but of the church of the Corinthians. Third, he does not say, as I noted above, "than that I use the power granted me by the Lord," but "than that anyone make this boasting of mine empty," that is, than that I, by using my power among you, give the false apostles an occasion of making my boasting empty through malicious suspicion. The Apostle seems to have in view the saying of Christ in Matthew 18: "Woe to him who offends one of these little ones! It would be better for him if a millstone were hung about his neck and he were cast into the depths of the sea."

units.la: Expendendum hic fuerit, quantum poenae maneat eos, qui cum Euangelium Christi non praedicent, nihilominus in ecclesiae bonis deliciantur, & vniuersam ecclesiam vitae turpitudine corrumpunt, si melius fuisset Apostolo facere mori, quàm licita potestate in ecclesia cum offendiculo Euangelij abuti.
units.tr: Here one should consider how great a punishment awaits those who, while they do not preach the gospel of Christ, nevertheless revel in the goods of the church and corrupt the whole church by the baseness of their lives. If it would have been better for the Apostle to die than to abuse a lawful power in the church to the stumbling of the gospel, how much worse for them.

units.la: QVAM vt gloriationem meam.) Annotat Chrysostomus, quod non dicit, quàm vt pro positum meum, aut molestiam hac meam, sed quàm vt gloriationem meam aliquis inanem reddat.
units.tr: "That my boasting": Chrysostom notes that he does not say "that my purpose or my hardship be made void," but "that anyone make my boasting void."

units.la: Videlicet, ostendit hac dictione, licet propositi huius nomine multum absque dubio tulerit molestiae, famis, frigoris, ac nuditatis, tā abesse tamen, vt molestè ista ferat, vt etiā gaudij & gloriationis loco ducat. Graecè est καύχησις gloriatio. Habet autem omnis gloriatio coniunctam animi laetitiam & exultationem: vnde & pleruque pro gaudio in scripturis sumitur, ut 2.Cor. 1. Gloriatio nostra est testimonium conscientiae nostrae.
