units.tr: Clearly, by this expression he shows that, although for the sake of this purpose he undoubtedly endured much hardship, hunger, cold and nakedness, he is so far from bearing these things grudgingly that he counts them as a cause of joy and boasting. In Greek it is καύχησις [kauchēsis], boasting. Every boasting, moreover, carries with it gladness and exultation of mind, and so it is very often taken in Scripture for joy, as in 2 Cor. 1: "Our boasting is the testimony of our conscience."

units.la: Quanquam non arbitror firmum esse satis gloriationem dicamus hoc loco pro gaudio cordis positam esse, nolim tamen primū assignari Apostolo eum gloriandi affectum, qui coniunctam habet animi elationem, & φιλαυτίαν, qua qui gloriatur, sibi ipsi placet in eo cuius nomine gloriatur, ac sese velut singulari laude & admiratione dignum iactat, vt solent hypocritae iusticiarij in sua propria iusticia, potentes ac robusti in suis viribus, diuites in sua opulentia, sapientes in sua sapientia, docti in sua eruditione gloriari, exultare, sefeq; iactare. Nam licet haec omnia sint dona Dei, in illis tamen non est gloriandum, sed in Deo. Scriptum est enim: Quid habes quod non accepisti? Si accepisti, quid gloriaris, quasi non acceperis? Et Apostolus certè hoc ipsum, de quo hic loquitur, non ex suis habebat viribus, sed ex dono Dei. Proinde distinguenda est sanctorum gloriatio à gloriatione impiorum. Illa habet adiunctam superbiam, ista humilitatem. Illa vires humanas, ista gratiam Dei commendat. Illa admirationem habet suijpsius, & contemptum aliorum, ista verò neminem contemnit. Sed ita de gratia Dei laetatur & gloriatur, vt cupiat illam omnibus esse communem. Illa propriam, ista Dei gloriam spectat.
units.tr: Although I do not think it is quite firm enough to say that boasting is here put for joy of heart, I would not wish first to ascribe to the Apostle that affection of boasting which carries with it an elation of mind and self-love [φιλαυτία], by which the one who boasts pleases himself in that in whose name he boasts, and vaunts himself as worthy of singular praise and admiration. This is how hypocrites who trust in their own righteousness, the powerful in their own strength, the rich in their wealth, the wise in their wisdom, and the learned in their learning, are wont to glory, exult and vaunt themselves. For although all these are gifts of God, one must not glory in them, but in God. For it is written: "What have you that you did not receive? If you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?" And the Apostle certainly had this very thing of which he speaks here not from his own strength, but from the gift of God. Therefore the boasting of the saints must be distinguished from the boasting of the impious. The former has pride joined with it, the latter humility. The former commends human powers, the latter the grace of God. The former has admiration for oneself and contempt for others, but the latter despises no one. Rather, it rejoices and glories in the grace of God in such a way as to desire that it be common to all. The former looks to its own glory, the latter to the glory of God.

units.la: 2 Deinde nō displicent, qui dicunt hoc loco Apostolum gloriari non in genere coram Deo de sua syncerit ate erga Euangelium, sed gloriari, magis contra pseudapostolos & illorum assectatores. Nam de Deo ipse suprà dixit: Nihil mihi conscius sum, sed nec in hoc iustificatus sum. At contra pseudapostolos verè potuit gloriari de ministerio suo, quod non solum irreprehensibile sit in se, sed & omnium sinistrae suspicionis occasione careat.
units.tr: 2 Nor do I object to those who say that the Apostle here is not boasting in general before God of his sincerity toward the Gospel, but is rather boasting against the false apostles and their followers. For about God he himself said above: "I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not thereby justified." But against the false apostles he could truly boast of his ministry, which is not only blameless in itself but also free from any occasion of ill suspicion.

units.la: Etenim si Euangelizem, nō est quod glorier. Necessitas enim mihi incumbit. Vae autem mihi est, nisi Euangelizem. Nam si uolens hoc faciam, premium habeo, sin minus, dispensatio mihi concredita est.
units.tr: For if I preach the Gospel, I have nothing to boast of. For necessity is laid upon me. Woe is me, unless I preach the Gospel. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been committed to me.

units.la: Exponit id quod dixit: Bonum est mihi mori potius, &c. Potest enim quisquam dicere: Quid opus est Paule, vt sine sumptu praedices, vt dicas tibi satius esse mori, quàm ut hanc tibi gloriam quisquam inanem reddat? An non satis est praedicare Euangelium, nisi gratis etiā praediprædices: Respondet. Mihi non est satis vt prædicem, ad illam gloriationem, qua opus habeo contra pseudapostolos in ista Corinthiorum ecclesia. Necesse quidem est ut prædicem; Nisi enim hoc fecero vę mihi est. Si volens prædico, habeo mercedem, sin inuitus, dispensatio mihi cōcredita est. Hæc sunt generalia omnes vbique Christi ministros concernentia. Mea ratio in hac ecclesia alia est. Mihi hic nō est ad gloriationem meam contra pseudapostolos satis vt prædicem, nisi sine sumptu collocem Euangelium Christi, ut amputem omnem occasionem malignis, sinistri quicquam de metuspi candi & obtendendi. Atq; hoc sensu puto subiectum illud.
units.tr: He explains what he said: "It is better for me to die," etc. For someone might say: "Why is it necessary, Paul, that you preach without expense, that you say it would be better for you to die than that someone should make this glory of yours empty? Is it not enough to preach the Gospel, unless you also preach it free of charge?" He answers: it is not enough for me to preach, for the sake of that boasting which I need against the false apostles in this church of the Corinthians. I must indeed preach; for unless I do this, woe is me. If I preach willingly, I have a reward; if unwillingly, a stewardship has been committed to me. These things are general and concern all the ministers of Christ everywhere. My case in this church is different. Here, for my boasting against the false apostles, it is not enough for me to preach, unless I also set forth the Gospel of Christ without expense, so that I cut off every occasion from those who are ill-disposed, who might seize on something to suspect and to object. I think that this is the sense of what follows.

units.la: Quod igitur mihi est præmium, vt cū Euangelizem, gratuitum efficiam Euangelium Christi, in hoc ne abutar potestate mea in Euangelio.
units.tr: Therefore what is my reward: that when I preach, I make the Gospel of Christ free of charge, so that I do not abuse my power in the Gospel.

units.la: Non dicit: Quod igitur est ministro Christi præmium? Sed quod mihi est præmium? Et mox, in hoc, inquit, ne abutar potestate mea in Euangelio, nō dicit, ne vtar potestate mea, sed ne abutar.
units.tr: He does not say, "What then is the reward of a minister of Christ?" but "What is my reward?" And soon after, when he says "so that I do not abuse," he does not say "so that I do not use my power," but "so that I do not abuse it."

units.la: In loco autem vti ista potestate, non est abuti. Vtendi illo nō erat locus apud Corinthios. Reliquis apostolis in alijs ecclesijs locus erat, ideoq; illi vtendo hac potestate nō sunt abusi, Paulus vero vtendo apud Corinthios abusus fuisset, Euangelioq; offendiculum dedisset.
units.tr: But to use this power in a place is not to abuse it. There was no place for using it among the Corinthians. The other apostles had a place for it in other churches, and therefore they did not abuse this power by using it; but Paul, using it among the Corinthians, would have abused it and given an offence to the Gospel.

units.la: Genuinus ergo ac simplex loci huius sensus est, vt discernamus inter ecclesias & ecclesias, non inter apostolos & apostolorum ministeria. In se quod officium erat Pauli erat & reliquorum apostolorum, quod ius erat reliquis erat & Paulo. Ecclesiarū vero varietas effecit, vt quod in genere satis fuisset Paulo apud alias ecclesias, apud Corinthios non fuerit satis ad eundendum culpam offendiculi, & obtinendā gloriam sedulo fidelis ac synceri Apostoli.
units.tr: The genuine and simple sense of this passage, then, is that we should distinguish church from church, not apostles from the ministries of the apostles. In itself the office of Paul was also that of the other apostles, and the right that the others had was also Paul's. But the variety of the churches brought it about that what was enough for Paul in general among other churches was not enough among the Corinthians to avoid the guilt of giving offence, and to win the glory of a diligent, faithful and sincere apostle.

units.la: Itaque præmium non omnia sunt plane generalia, nec passim locum habere in Christi ministris sed specialiter concernebant tū apostolum Paulum ratione ecclesiæ Corinthiorum, & hodie concernunt eos, quibus par est administrandæ ecclesiæ ratio. Nihil reliquis apostolis præscribit, sed rationem reddit, cur ipse nō sit vsus sua potestate apud Corinthios, nec vti velit, etiamsi fame moriendum sit. Sed expendamus singula.
units.tr: Therefore these things are not altogether general, nor do they apply everywhere to the ministers of Christ. They concerned the apostle Paul in particular, with regard to the church of the Corinthians, and today they concern those to whom the management of a church is rightly entrusted. He does not prescribe anything to the other apostles, but gives an account of why he himself has not used his power among the Corinthians, and does not wish to use it, even if he must die of hunger. But let us weigh the individual points.

units.la: ETENIM si euangelizem, non est quod glorier. Necessitas enim mihi incumbit.) Videmus hoc loco, non esse satis ad gloriam fidelis ac synceri ministri ut faciamus, quæ necessario facienda sunt ex præcepto, nisi ita illa faciamus, vt quantum in nobis est, nullum demus offendiculis occasionē. Euangelizare Christi ministro necesse est, necessitate præcepti, Matth. & Marci vltimo, & condenationis etiam de qua statim subijcit. Proinde non dum hanc gloriam fidelis ministri assequutus est, quisquis hoc tantum curat vt quouis modo prædicet, vtut Euangelio pariat interea offendiculā. Consimilis locus est Luce 17. Si omnia quæ mandata vobis sunt feceritis, dicete inutiles serui sumus, q facere debuimus fecimus.
units.tr: "For if I preach the Gospel, I have nothing to boast of; for necessity is laid upon me." We see here that it is not enough for the glory of a faithful and sincere minister to do what must necessarily be done by precept, unless he does it in such a way that, as far as lies in him, he gives no occasion for stumbling. A minister of Christ must preach the Gospel, by the necessity of precept (see the end of Matthew and of Mark) and of condemnation, which he mentions immediately after. Therefore whoever takes care only that he preach in any way at all, even if meanwhile he produces an offence to the Gospel, has not yet attained that glory of a faithful minister. A similar passage is Luke 17: "When you have done all the things that are commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done."

units.la: Sed quæri potest hoc loco, an maius aliquid sit non vti potestate concessa, quàm ipsa Euangelij prædicatio?
units.tr: But it may be asked here whether not using a power that has been granted is something greater than the preaching of the Gospel itself.

units.la: 1 Respondeo. Nequaquam in se, & ex ipsius rei natura. Nam alioqui reliqui apostoli, quod maius erat omisissent, & quod minus præstitisse sent. Vbi tamen ipse Euangelij profectus hoc postulat, vt iure suo cedat Christi ministér & nihilominus fideliter prædicet Euangelium Dei hic certè multò est amplius sine sumptu prædicare Euangelium, quàm simpliciter prædicare.
units.tr: 1 I answer: by no means in itself, and by the nature of the thing. For otherwise the other apostles would have omitted what was greater and performed only what was lesser. Yet where the progress of the Gospel itself requires that a minister of Christ yield his right and nonetheless faithfully preach the Gospel of God, here certainly it is far more to preach the Gospel without charge than simply to preach it.

units.la: 2 Deinde accedit & hoc, quod prædicatio cadit sub præcepto, ἀδιάφορον vero prædicatio non ita. Omissio prædicationis minas habet condenationis, vsus vero potestatis huius non ita. Quoniam autem qui facit quod necessario faciendum est, & nisi fiat, damnationem adiert omissum, nondum qua sit fide & synceritate ergo dominum ostendit, in eo quod quæ præcepta sunt facit, qui vero vitra hoc etiam id præstat, quod omissum non damnat, satis luculenter animi fidelis ac synceri affectum declarat, sit, ut maior sit gloria in eo, de quo gloriatur hic Apostolus, quàm in simplici Euangelij prædicatione. Et hoc videtur velle Apostolus, cum dicit: Etenim si Euangelizem, non est quod glorier. Necessitas enim mihi incumbit.
units.tr: 2 Furthermore, this too is added: preaching falls under precept, but it is not so with indifferent things [ἀδιάφορον]. The omission of preaching carries the threat of condemnation; the use of this power does not. Now, one who does what must necessarily be done, on pain of condemnation if it is left undone, has not yet shown by this what faith and sincerity he has toward the Lord, since he is only doing what is commanded. But one who goes beyond this and does what the omission of which would not condemn him declares quite plainly the disposition of a faithful and sincere mind. So it follows that there is greater glory in that in which this Apostle boasts than in the simple preaching of the Gospel. And this seems to be what the Apostle wants when he says: "For if I preach the Gospel, I have nothing to boast of; for necessity is laid upon me."

units.la: Væ autem mihi est, si non Euangelizem. Quasi dicat: Quod prædico Euangelium, nihil habet gloriæ Apostolicæ. Nam ipsa me vrget necessitas ut faciam, & prohibet condemnatione omittam. Liber hic non sum sed omnino captiuatus, in eo vero demum gloriatio mea est, quod id præsto, quod liberè poteram omittere, & omitto quod poteram facere, ad quod me nec vrget præceptum aliquod domini, nec invitam cogit condemnationis metus, sed ducit fidelis & synceros animi ad promouendum Euangelium Christi affectus.
units.tr: "But woe is me, if I do not preach the Gospel." As if he were saying: my preaching of the Gospel holds no apostolic glory; for necessity itself presses me to do it, and the threat of condemnation forbids me to omit it. I am not free but wholly captive. My boasting lies in this: that I offer what I could freely have omitted, and that I omit what I could have done, to which neither any command of the Lord urges me, nor fear of condemnation compels me against my will; rather, a faithful and sincere disposition of mind leads me to advance the Gospel of Christ.

units.la: Iltius Apostolicæ gloriationis imitatio pertinet ad omnes Christianos, si non hac specie, in genere tamen. Videlicet, vt sentiamus Christiani hominis gloriationem non esse in eo, vt quæ præcepta sunt faciamus & quæ vetita omittamus, legis adacti necessitate ac territi condenationis metu, sed vt quibus liberè vti possumus non vtamur, & quæ absq; metu pœnæ omittere possumus faciamus, si id exigat Euangelij & regni Christi profectus.
units.tr: The imitation of that apostolic boasting pertains to all Christians, if not in this particular form, yet in general. Namely, we Christians should understand that the boast of a Christian man lies not in doing what is commanded and omitting what is forbidden, driven by the necessity of the law and terrified by the fear of condemnation; rather, it lies in not using what we may use freely, and in doing what we may omit without fear of punishment, if this is required for the progress of the Gospel and the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: VAE autem mihi est, nisi Euangelizē.) Interiectio væ duplicem vsum habet in scriptu-ris. Aliquando notam habet temporariæ tantū calamitatis & miseriæ, ut Matth.24. Væ prægnantibus & lactantibus in illo die. Hic certè dominus prægnantes & lactantes non aliter miseras & calamitosas atque infœlices dicit, quàm quod in calamitate illa futura impediendæ sint à fuga & liberatione, propter graues vteros, & pueros ab ipsorum vberibus pendentpendentes. Aliquando notam habet æternæ condemnationis. Vt Luc.6. Væ vobis diuites, qui habetis hic consolationes vestras, & Matt. 23. Væ vobis scribæ & Pharisei, &c.
units.tr: "Woe is me, unless I preach the Gospel." The interjection "woe" has a twofold use in the Scriptures. Sometimes it marks only a temporary calamity and misery, as in Matthew 24: "Woe to those who are with child and to those who give suck in that day." Here indeed the Lord calls pregnant and nursing women miserable, calamitous and unhappy only in that, in that coming calamity, they will be hindered from flight and rescue by their heavy wombs and by the infants hanging from their breasts. Sometimes it marks eternal condemnation, as in Luke 6: "Woe to you rich, who have your consolation here," and Matthew 23: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees," etc.

units.la: Priore sensu non loquitur hic Apostolus. Nam sic quidem magis dicendum illi fuisset, væ mihi si Euangelizem, & bene mihi si non Euangelizem. Ita & Ieremias dicebat, væ mihi mater mea. Quare genuisti me virum rixæ, virum discordiæ in vniuersa terra. Non fœnerarui nec fœnerauit mihi quisquam, & tamen omnes maledicunt mihi. Et cap.20. Omnes subsannant me, quia iam olim loquor vociferans, &c. Et factum est mihi verbum domini in opprobrium & derisum tota die. Et: Maledicta dies in qua natus sum, &c. Hodie non est illis væ qui non Euangelizant cum id deberent ex officio facere. Vt sunt episcopi. Imò ne sit ipsis væ, studiosè cauent, ne Euangelizent. Posterio re verò sensu loquitur Apostolus ostendens æternam illis esse metuendam condemnationè & infelicitatem, qui quod à domino ipsis est iniuunctum, præstare neglexerint. Videmus hic quàm infelices sint nostri episcopi, imò quàm cæci, quod maledictionis huius æternæ nullo metu tenentur.
units.tr: The Apostle does not speak here in the former sense. For in that sense he would rather have said: woe is me if I preach the Gospel, and well for me if I do not. So also Jeremiah said: "Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife and a man of contention in the whole earth. I have neither lent nor has anyone lent to me, and yet all curse me." And in chapter 20: "All mock me, because I have long been speaking and crying out," etc. "And the word of the Lord has been made to me a reproach and a derision all day." And: "Cursed be the day on which I was born," etc. Today it is not woe to those who do not preach the Gospel, though they ought to do so by their office, as bishops are. Rather, to avoid any woe to themselves, they take care not to preach the Gospel. But the Apostle speaks in the latter sense, showing that eternal condemnation and unhappiness are to be feared by those who have neglected to perform what the Lord has enjoined on them. Here we see how unhappy our bishops are, or rather how blind, since no fear of this eternal curse holds them.

units.la: NAM si volens hoc facio, præmiū habeo.) Ambrosius assignat duas rationes. Vna est, quod dignus sit præmio, qui volens obtemperat præcepto domini, ob id, quod voluntati Dei consentiat. Altera, quod is multo melius ac diligentius iniunctum munus obeat. Vnde certè sequitur, quod & plus fructus adfertat, quàm si inuitus hoc faciat. Bobus etenim inui tis, vt ille ait, nunquam trahitur bene currus. Ita Apostolus Petrus exigit ab episcopis, vt munus suum in pascendo grege domini non coacte sed spontanee obeant, pollicés illis, vbi princeps pastorum venerit, immarcescibilem gloriæ coronam. Is autem volens facit, qui nec metu vindictæ, nec spe lucri prædicat, malens nō prædicare, si nulla vrgeret necessitas, sed amore domini & verbi ipsius iniunctum munus cum gaudio exequitur.
units.tr: "For if I do this willingly, I have a reward." Ambrose gives two reasons. The first is that he who obeys the Lord's command willingly deserves a reward, because he consents to the will of God. The second is that such a man performs the assigned task much better and more diligently. From this it certainly follows that he also produces more fruit than if he did it unwillingly. For, as Ambrose says, a cart is never drawn well by unwilling oxen. So the Apostle Peter requires bishops to fulfil their duty of feeding the Lord's flock not under compulsion but willingly, promising them the unfading crown of glory when the chief Shepherd appears. He preaches willingly who preaches neither from fear of punishment nor from hope of gain, preferring not to preach if no necessity pressed him, but out of love for the Lord and his Word carries out the assigned task with joy.

units.la: SIN inuitus, dispensatio mihi concredita est.) Hoc est, vrget tamen iniunctæ diuinitùs dispensationis necessitas. Tacet hic de præmio. Indignus etenim mercede est, qui quod facit inuitus, id est, animo repugnáte facit. De Mose legimus, quod munus suum inuitus susceperit. Nà aliquoties tergiuersabatur. Ita & Ieremias. Ah ah domine, inquit, puer sum. Et cap.20. Nō recordabor eius, inquit, nec loquar amplius in nomine illius. Et Ionas fugiebat etiam à facie domini, & tandem coactus prædicabat.
units.tr: "But if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship." That is, the necessity of the stewardship committed to him by God presses on him nonetheless. Here he says nothing about a reward. For he who does unwillingly what he does, that is, with a mind resisting, is unworthy of wages. We read of Moses that he received his task unwillingly, for he made excuses on several occasions. So too Jeremiah: "Ah, Lord God, I am a child," he says; and in chapter 20: "I will not remember him," he says, "nor speak any more in his name." And Jonah fled even from the face of the Lord, and at last, compelled, he preached.

units.la: Quid igitur? Amiserunt isti præmia sua? Vi dendum est, quid eos mouerit, quare officium detrectauerint, an hoc fecerint animo erga Deum sínistro & immorigero, vel fecerint partim consideratione vilitatis suæ & magnitudine in iuncti muneris. Moses certè & Ieremias hac ratione detrectabant aliquandiu suscipere man-
units.tr: What then? Did these men lose their rewards? We must consider what moved them, and why they shrank from the office: whether they did so from a perverse and unwilling disposition toward God, or partly from consideration of their own lowliness and the greatness of the task committed to them. Moses and Jeremiah, at any rate, for this reason shrank for a time from taking up the command,

units.la: datum, quod sibi ipsis viderentur causæ tam grandi impares futuri. Ionas etiam non hoc animo fugiebat à facie domini, quod ægrè ferret domino, sed quod metuebat notam subi re falsi prophetæ. Sciebat Deum esse miseri cordem, qui ignoturus esset pœnitentibus. Ob eam causam renuebat prædicationem iniunctam suscipere. Ita ipse fugæ suæ causam exponit.
units.tr: because they seemed to themselves unequal to so great a cause. Jonah too did not flee from the face of the Lord with the intention of displeasing the Lord, but because he feared to incur the reputation of a false prophet. He knew that God is merciful and would be ready to pardon the penitent. For this reason he refused to take up the preaching committed to him. Thus he himself explains the cause of his flight.

units.la: Colligimus ergo, non mox indignos esse præmio, qui munus aliquod inuiti subeunt, sed ex pendendas esse causas, cur id fiat.
units.tr: We gather therefore that those who undertake some task unwillingly are not at once unworthy of a reward, but that the causes why it is done must be weighed.

units.la: VT sine sumptu.) Græcè est ἀδάπανον, quod fit sine sumptu. Id autem amphibolum est, annotante Erasmo. Sine sumptu facit, qui nihil impendit. Sine sumptu etiam facit, cui nihil impeditur, quo sensu hic Apostolus loquitur.
units.tr: "Without charge." In Greek it is ἀδάπανον, that is, without expense. This word is ambiguous, as Erasmus notes. He acts without expense who spends nothing; but he also acts without expense to whom nothing is charged, and it is in this sense that the Apostle speaks here.

units.la: Queritur hic Erasmus, quod nunc in ecclesia nihil sit ἀδάπανον, sed omnia venalia, etiam sepulturæ tellus. Iustè hoc queritur, ego verò & hoc querimoniæ addiderim, quod vt tum vsuenit Apostolo, ita nunc quoque tanti momenti nō est ἀληθεια veritas, quàti est ἀψευδος mendacium. Gratis prædicabat Corinthiis Apostolus, & contemnebatur, pseudapostoli accipiebant, devorabant, in faciem cædebant, & suspiciebantur. Ista est perpetua mundi hu ius peruersitas.
units.tr: Erasmus complains that nothing in the Church now is ἀδάπανον, but everything is for sale, even burial in the ground. He complains justly; but I would add to this complaint that, as it happened then to the Apostle, so now too truth [ἀλήθεια] is not valued as highly as falsehood [ψεῦδος]. The Apostle preached to the Corinthians free of charge, and was despised, while false apostles took money, devoured their goods, struck them in the face, and were admired. This is the constant perversity of this world.

units.la: Videmus præterea hoc loco quatuor ministrorum Christi genera.
units.tr: Moreover, in this passage we see four kinds of ministers of Christ.

units.la: 1 Primum est eorum, qui Euangelium negle cto suo munere non annunciant, illis væ minatur Apostolus sub sua persona.
units.tr: (1) The first is of those who, neglecting their office, do not proclaim the Gospel; the Apostle threatens woe to them, speaking in his own person.

units.la: 2 Alterum est eorum qui Euangelizant quidem sed animo inuito. Hi adiguntur ex officij necessitate.
units.tr: (2) The second is of those who indeed preach the Gospel but with an unwilling mind. These are driven by the necessity of their office.

units.la: 3 Tertium est eorum qui volentes Euangeli zant. Horum est præmium.
units.tr: (3) The third is of those who preach the Gospel willingly. The reward belongs to them.

units.la: 4 Quartum eorum, qui non solum Euangelizant, idq; volentes, sed & sine sumptu collocant Euangelium Christi. Horum est præcipua fidelitatis gloria, sicubi id suo loco & tempore ad Euangelij profectum faciunt.
units.tr: (4) The fourth is of those who not only preach the Gospel, and do so willingly, but also set forth the Gospel of Christ without charge. The chief glory of their faithfulness belongs to them, provided they do this in its proper place and time for the advancement of the Gospel.

units.la: Etenim cū liber sim ab omnibus, omnibus me ipsum seruū feci, quo plures lucrifacia, & factus sum ludeis quasi lu deus, ut ludæos lucrifaciam, his qui sub lege sunt quasi sim sub lege, ut eos qui sub lege sunt lucrifacia. His qui sine lege sunt, tanquam sim sine lege, cum nō sim sine lege Deo, sed obnoxius legi Christi, ut lucri faciam eos qui sunt sine lege. Factus sum infirmis quasi infirmus, ut infirmos lucrifaciam. Omnibus factus sum omnia, ut omnino aliquos seruem. Hoc autem facio propter Euangelium, ut particeps illius fiam.
units.tr: For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might gain the more. And I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to those under the law as under the law, that I might gain those under the law; to those without law as without law, though I am not without the law of God but under the law of Christ, that I might gain those without law. I became weak to the weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I might by all means save some. And this I do for the sake of the Gospel, that I may share in it.

units.la: Declaratio est latior, eius quod dixit se cauere, ne potestate sua in Euangelio abutatur. GraGratis Euangelizabat Corinthijs, cum possit ab illis sumptus exigere prædicationis. Non enim erat illis ita obnoxius iure, vt cogeretur seruire gratis. Verùm ipse se vltrò ac sponte seruum illorum fecerat, vt aliquod ex illis Christo lucrifaceret. Atq; hoc affectu se & reliquis omnibus seruum faciebat, cum tamen liber ab omnibus, & Christi tantum seruus esset. Ad hunc charitatis affectum, & libertatis sponta-neam resignationem inuitat suo exemplo Corinthios, vt coeperat.
units.tr: This is a fuller explanation of what he had said, that he took care not to abuse his power in the Gospel. He preached the Gospel to the Corinthians free of charge, though he could have demanded payment for his preaching from them. For they were not so bound to him by right that they were compelled to serve him for nothing. But he of his own accord and willingly made himself their servant, so that he might gain some of them for Christ. And by this affection he made himself a servant to all the rest as well, though he was free from all and was the servant of Christ alone. By his own example he invites the Corinthians, as he had begun to do, to this affection of love and to a willing surrender of their liberty.

units.la: CVM liber sim ab omnibus.) Suprà dixit: An non sum Apostolus? An nō sum liber? Nec indicauit, qua in re se liberum esse dicat: Verù hoc loco seipsum nonnihil explicat. Licet enim non satis aperte tradat, quam intelligat libertatem, cum sit ciuica & terrena alia, alia spiritalis in Christo, ex genere tamen seruitutis, qua se dicit omnibus factum esse seruum, satis puto conspicuum est, quod de ea libertate loquatur, in quam erat per Christum assertus, vt & reliqui fideles omnes, vt nemini esset addictus seruiliter nisi vni domino, vt suprà cap. 7. monuit dicens: Precio empti estis, nolite fieri serui hominum.
units.tr: "Since I am free from all." Above he said: "Am I not an apostle? Am I not free?" Nor did he indicate in what respect he says he is free. Here, however, he explains himself somewhat. For although he does not state clearly enough what sort of liberty he means, since there is one civil and earthly, and another spiritual in Christ, yet I think it is sufficiently plain, from the kind of servitude by which he says he became a servant to all, that he is speaking of that liberty into which Christ had asserted him, as all the other faithful, so that he was enslaved to no one except the one Lord; as he warned above in chapter 7, saying: "You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men."

units.la: AB omnibus.) Tam ad homines quàm ad res alias referri potest. Verùm quoniam subdit quod omnium se seruum fecerit, quod sanè nō de rebus sed de hominibus, aut hominum generibus, Iudæis, Gentibus, infirmis, &c. intelligi potest: puto certius esse, ut & hanc particulam de ijsdem intelligamus, quod ab omnibus se liberum esse dicat.
units.tr: "From all." This may be referred to men as well as to other things. But since he adds that he made himself the servant of all, which can be understood not of things but of men, or of classes of men, Jews, Gentiles, the weak, and so on, I think it more certain that we should take this phrase also as referring to the same persons, so that he says he is free from all.

units.la: Ergo iure Christianisimi ac fidei, nemini mortalium erat obnoxius Paulus. Hoc enim est, quod dicit: Cum liber essem ab omnibus. Eodem certe iure & reliqui Christiani omnes ab omnibus mortalibus liberi sunt. Quæ est itaq; tyrannis illa, qua fideles episcoporum libidini in causa religionis subijciuntur?
units.tr: Therefore, by the right of Christian faith, Paul was bound to no mortal. For this is what he says: "Since I was free from all." By the same right all other Christians too are free from all mortals. What tyranny, then, is that by which the faithful are subjected to the lust of bishops in matters of religion?

units.la: OMNIBVS meipsum seruum feci.) Non dicit, quibusdam, uel uobis, sed omnibus. Nec dicit, prodesse statui, sed seruum feci. Neq; dicit, seruus factus sum, sed meipsum seruum feci. Magna charitas cùm erga Christum, tū mortales uniuersos. Contemptui solet esse omnis seruitus. Verùm ista seruitus, qua homo ab omnibus liber omnibus sese seruum facit, hoc est honorabilior, quo minus habet coactionis, & plus charitatis. Romanus pontifex, ut nusquam sit fallax &hypocrita, cum nihil aliud agat quàm ut dominus sit omnium, falso sese vocat seruum seruorum Dei.
units.tr: "I made myself a servant to all." He does not say "to some," or "to you," but "to all." Nor does he say "I was made to serve," but "I made myself a servant." Great is his love both toward Christ and toward all mortals. Every servitude is usually held in contempt. But that servitude by which a man, free from all, makes himself a servant to all is the more honourable, the less it has of compulsion and the more of love. The Roman pontiff, so that he may nowhere be false and hypocritical, while he does nothing but seek to be lord of all, falsely calls himself "servant of the servants of God."

units.la: QVO plures lucrifaciam.) Verbū lucrandi quinquies repetit, ut ardentem affectum lucrā di mortales declaret.
units.tr: "That I might gain the more." He repeats the verb "to gain" five times, to show his ardent desire to gain mortals.

units.la: Et hanc rationem reddit, quare seipsum cū liber sit ab omnibus omnium seruum fecerit, uidelicet, quod cupiat ita administrare Euangelium, & se quibusuis accommodare, ut hoc plures lucrifaciat.
units.tr: And he gives this reason why, though he is free from all, he has made himself a servant of all: namely, because he desires so to administer the Gospel and to accommodate himself to whatever sort of people, that he may gain more by this means.

units.la: Et hic uerbis haud obscurè innuit, non simpliciter prædicandum esse fideli Christi minis.
units.tr: And here he hints quite plainly in his words that the preaching of the faithful minister of Christ should not be simply unconditional.

units.la: I Ergo perditi sunt, quos Christo non lucrifacit Euangelij prædicatio. Hoc sciebat Apostolus, atq; ob eam rem cum summopere affectaret mortalium salutem, munus suum diligentissimè mortalium captui & rationi accommodauit, quo plures lucrifaceret.
units.tr: 1 Therefore they are lost whom the preaching of the Gospel does not win for Christ. The Apostle knew this, and because he earnestly desired the salvation of mortals, he adapted his office to the capacity and reasoning of mortals, so that he might win more of them.

units.la: 2 Lucrum in ecclesia est, non augere terrenas ditiones more Romanorum pontificum, sed lucrifacere Christo mortalium animas, id que per prædicationem Euangelij, qua constitutum est domino saluos facere credentes. Ac cessionibus fidelium animarum non terrenarum ditionum, gaudet Christi regnum, quod non de hoc mundo terrenum, sed in cordibus fidelium est cœleste ac spiritale. Huius lucri studium Apostoli, alterius uero Antichristi spiritum respipit.
units.tr: 2 Gain in the Church does not mean increasing earthly wealth and dominion in the manner of the Roman pontiffs, but winning souls for Christ. This is done through the preaching of the Gospel, by which it has been ordained that the Lord saves those who believe. The kingdom of Christ rejoices in the gain of believing souls, not of earthly dominions, for it is not an earthly kingdom of this world but is heavenly and spiritual in the hearts of believers. The Apostles pursued this kind of gain; the Antichrist's spirit is of the other kind, and they reject it.

units.la: ET factus sum Iudæis, quasi Iudæus.) Iudæos intelligit extra Christum constitutos. Illis factus est non Iudæus relicto Christianismo, sed quasi Iudæus, cum esset non Iudæus, sed Christi Apostolus, & tamen Iudæorum sacramenta ubi opportunum erat celebrat.
units.tr: And I became to the Jews as a Jew. He means the Jews who remained outside Christ. He became to them not a Jew, having abandoned Christianity, but as a Jew, although he was not a Jew but an Apostle of Christ; and yet, where it was fitting, he celebrated the sacraments of the Jews.

units.la: Ita circumcidit Timotheum Lystris, propter Iudæos, qui in illis locis erant, quod scirent omnes patre illum Gentili natum.
units.tr: So he circumcised Timothy at Lystra, on account of the Jews who were in those places, since they all knew that his father was a Gentile.

units.la: Ita purificatus more Iudaico ascendit in templum Hierosolymis.
units.tr: So, purified in the Jewish manner, he went up into the temple at Jerusalem.

units.la: Ita consuetudinem sabbatorum cum Iudæis seruauit. Et absq; dubio cibis quoq; in lege uetitis abstinuit, ubi cum Iudæis erat conuersandum, & si quæ aliæ sunt legales obseruationes, Iuæorum illas gratia ad tempus obseruauit.
units.tr: So he kept the custom of the Sabbaths with the Jews. And doubtless he also abstained from the foods forbidden by the law, wherever he had to live with Jews; and whatever other legal observances there are, he kept them for a time for the sake of the Jews.

units.la: Quæ uero mala habebant Iudei, utpote, qui propriam iusticiam statuentes iusticiæ Dei nō subijciebantur quod sacramenta legis adhuc ad salutem necessaria putabant, quod hostiliter prædicationi gratiæ aduersabantur, hæc Christianus factus reliquerat, nec amplius postea cuiusquam gratia resumpsit.
units.tr: But the evils that the Jews had, namely that, setting up their own righteousness, they did not submit themselves to the righteousness of God, that they thought the sacraments of the law were still necessary for salvation, and that they hostilely opposed the preaching of grace, these things he left behind when he became a Christian, and afterwards he never took up again for anyone's sake.

units.la: Admiranda planè fuit erga Iudeos Apostoli patientia, qua se acerrimis hostibus cum ab iis liber esset, seruum facere potuit. Infensiores quippe Iudeis hostes non habuit. Nemo enim illi pertinacius ac furiosius restitit.
units.tr: Truly admirable was the Apostle's patience towards the Jews. Although he was free from them, being their most bitter enemies, he was able to make himself their slave. For the Jews had no more hostile enemies than him, since no one resisted him more obstinately and furiously.

units.la: Amicorum gratia, & beneficium agnoscentium, sustineat forsan aliquis è libero mutari in seruum: at propter inimicos tam acerbos & irreconciliabiles lucrandos, seruitutem ultrò amplecti, quis non uidet, quantæ sit charitatis & patientiæ indicium. De isto affectu Apostoli in Iudæos uide Rom.9.
units.tr: One might perhaps endure being changed from free to slave for the sake of friends who acknowledge a kindness; but who does not see how great a proof of love and patience it is to embrace servitude willingly, for the sake of winning over enemies so bitter and irreconcilable? On this feeling of the Apostle towards the Jews, see Romans 9.

units.la: His qui sub lege sunt, quasi sim sub lege.
units.tr: To those who are under the law, as though I were under the law.

units.la: Ambrosius intelligit de Samaritanis, quod illi solam legem, id est, quinque libros Mosaicos agnouerint. Ita intelligi posse admonet & Hieronymus. Theophylactus vel de proselytis, vel de Christianis ex Iudæis ad Christum conuersis, & adhuc legis æmulationi obnoxiis intelligit, quæ sententia mihi videtur verosimilior.
units.tr: Ambrose understands this of the Samaritans, because they acknowledged only the law, that is, the five books of Moses. Jerome also reminds us that it can be understood this way. Theophylact understands it either of proselytes, or of Christians from among the Jews who had been converted to Christ and were still liable to zeal for the law; this opinion seems to me more probable.

units.la: Tales enim passim multi erant, & Hierosolymis aliquot millia, uide Act.21. Horum infirmitati consulebant & reliqui Apostoli, Iacobus, Petrus, Iohannes, tolerantes in illis legis æmulationem tantisper dum in Christo Iesu crescerent & corroborarentur.
units.tr: For many such people were everywhere, and at Jerusalem several thousand; see Acts 21. The remaining Apostles, James, Peter and John, also looked after the weakness of these people, tolerating in them zeal for the law for as long as they grew and were strengthened in Christ Jesus.

units.la: At dicet quisquam. Si de Christianis Iudeis intelligedus est hic locus, quid ergo est, quod dicit: Ut eos qui sub lege sunt lucrifaciam? Ergo adhuc erant extra salutem, licet Christiani? Puto huius gratia Hieronymum maluisse de Iudæis exponere hoc pacto, ut hic doceat Apostolus quomodo Iudæis sit, & in qua re factus quasi Iudæus: nempe, quasi & ipse sit sub lege. Et Chrysost. vocat exegesim prioris.
units.tr: But someone will say: if this passage is to be understood of Christian Jews, what then is the meaning of what he says, that I might win those who are under the law? Therefore they were still outside salvation, although they were Christians? I think that for this reason Jerome preferred to explain it of Jews in this way: that here the Apostle teaches how he became to the Jews, and in what respect he became as a Jew, namely, as one who himself too was under the law. And Chrysostom calls this an explanation of the former clause.

units.la: Verum nihil impedit hic scrupus, quo minus de Iudæis Christianis intelligamus. Erat enim illis admodum periculosa legis æmulatio, ne huius gratia vel Christum desererent, vel non satis in illum fiduciæ alerent, putantes sine legis operibus non posse salutem in Christo apprehendi, ita ut hac opinione liberati, recte dici potuerint, tum d.mum vere lucrifaciti domino. Ita & infra dicet, se infirmis quoque factum quasi infirmum, ut infirmos lucrifaceret.
units.tr: Yet this scruple does not prevent us from understanding it of Jewish Christians. For zeal for the law was very dangerous for them, lest on account of it they should either desert Christ or not nourish sufficient trust in him, thinking that salvation could not be apprehended in Christ without the works of the law. So, once freed from this opinion, they could rightly be said to have been won for the Lord at last and truly. So he also says below that he became to the weak as weak, in order to win the weak.

units.la: His qui sine lege sunt.) De gentibus loquitur. Sine lege erant Gentes, non naturali, nec ciuica, sed Mosaica, scripta illa, cuius æmulatione tenentur Iudæi.
units.tr: To those who are without law. He speaks of the Gentiles. The Gentiles were without law, not the natural or civil law, but the Mosaic written law, by zeal for which the Jews are bound.

units.la: Chrysostomus exponit de ijs qui nec Gentes, nec Iudæi, nec Christiani erant religione, qualis erat Cornelius & consimiles. Veritus opinor admittere, Paulum Gentibus immundis sese accommodasse.
units.tr: Chrysostom explains it of those who were neither Gentiles, nor Jews, nor Christians in religion, such as Cornelius and those like him. I think he was unwilling to admit that Paul accommodated himself to unclean Gentiles.

units.la: TANQVAM sim sine lege.) Libere cum illis agebat, præputium recipiebat, quibusuis cum illis vescebatur, legis scriptæ nullam habebat rationem, cuius summo odio & contemptu Gentes teneri sciebat.
units.tr: As though I were without law. He dealt freely with them: he received the uncircumcised, he ate with them whatever they offered, and he had no regard for the written law, which he knew the Gentiles held in the greatest hatred and contempt.

units.la: Cum non sim sine lege Deo, sed sim sub lege Christo.
units.tr: Not being without law toward God, but being under the law toward Christ.

units.la: Chrysostomus legit, μὴ ὢν ἄνομος θεῷ, ἀλλ' ἔννομος Χριστῷ. Quia dixit, tanquam sim sine lege necolligat quisquam, ergo & ipse Paulus sub lege Mosaica cum Iudæis erat. Non enim dicit se factum sine lege cum iis qui sine lege sunt, sed tanquam sit sine lege, ideo subijcit declarationem, quomodo revera non sit sine lege. Hoc est, non vtatur suo arbitrio, sed subditus sit imperio Dei, cuius voluntati morem gerat & obtemperet. Sic dicit, cum non sim sine lege Deo, id est, cum Deo seruiam no meo, sed ipsius arbitrio. Et vt planius exponat quia legem Dei intelligat, ne de Iudaica dicere videatur, subdit, sed sim sub lege Christi. Est autem lex Christi, lex dilectionis. Hoc est præceptum meum, inquit, ut diligatis vos inuicem. Chrysostomus legem Christi exponit per legem spiritus & gratiæ, Romanorum octauo: Lex spiritus vitæ. Et tertio meminit legis fidei: vel legem Christi intelligit, obedientiam Euangelij, obedientiam fidei, aut certe demandatum munus Euangelizandi. In summa, dicit se non esse sui iuris, licet sub Mose non sit, sed esse sub imperio domini.
units.tr: Chrysostom reads: "not being lawless toward God, but lawful toward Christ" [μὴ ὢν ἄνομος θεῷ, ἀλλ' ἔννομος Χριστῷ]. Because he said "as though I were without law," someone might infer that Paul himself was under the Mosaic law together with the Jews. But he does not say that he became without law together with those who are without law; he says "as though I were without law," and therefore he adds an explanation of how in truth he is not without law. That is, he does not use his own judgement but is subject to the command of God, and conforms to and obeys his will. So he says: not being without law toward God, that is, I serve God not by my own choice but by his will. And so that he may explain more plainly which law he means, lest he seem to speak of the Jewish law, he adds: but under the law of Christ. Now the law of Christ is the law of love. "This is my command," he says, "that you love one another." Chrysostom explains the law of Christ as the law of the Spirit and of grace, citing Romans 8: "the law of the Spirit of life." And in chapter three he mentions the law of faith. Or he understands by the law of Christ obedience to the Gospel, obedience of faith, or certainly the commission entrusted to him to preach the Gospel. In sum, he says that he is not his own master, although he is not under Moses, but is under the authority of the Lord.

units.la: Dixit, cum non sim sine lege Deo, & cum exponit de qua lege intelligat, adfert legem Christi. Ergo lex Christi est lex Dei, ut qui Christo obedit, Deo obediat. Sic dicit alibi: Qui me audit, non me audit, sed eum qui misit me.
units.tr: He said, "not being without law toward God," and when he explains which law he means, he brings forward the law of Christ. Therefore the law of Christ is the law of God, so that whoever obeys Christ obeys God. He says this elsewhere too: "He who hears me does not hear me, but him who sent me."

units.la: Videmus hic Christianos non esse ita sub Christo liberos, ut prorsus sine lege sint, & pro sua libidine viuere possint, sed subditos esse debere imperio Christi.
units.tr: Here we see that Christians are not so free under Christ that they are altogether without law and may live as they please, but that they ought to be subject to the authority of Christ.

units.la: FACTVS sum infirmis.) Propius accedit ad id quod volebat. Sic Chrysostomus: τῶν λοι ... Nam infirmorum gratia ista tam prolixè scribit, vt admoneat Corinthios, parcendum esse infirmis, ne illi abusu libertatis offendantur & perdantur. Neque enim satis est per Euangelij prædicationem, ex Iudæo vel Græco facere Christianum, nisi vbi factus fuerit, alatur etiam & sensim confirmetur compassione eorum qui robustiores sunt in fide: Vt enim ille inquit, Non minor est virtus quàm quærere, parta tueri.
units.tr: I became to the weak. He comes closer here to what he wanted to say. So Chrysostom: [τῶν λοι ...]. For he writes so extensively about the weak in order to admonish the Corinthians that the weak must be spared, lest they be offended and lost through the abuse of liberty. For it is not enough, through the preaching of the Gospel, to make a Christian out of a Jew or a Greek, unless, once he has been made, he is also nourished and gradually strengthened by the compassion of those who are stronger in faith. For, as someone says, "it is no less a virtue to keep what has been won than to seek it."

units.la: OMNIBVS factus sum omnia.) Quod coæquat particulariter dicere, tandem summatim complectitur. Quasi dicat. Quid multis? Nemini me non accommodaui, omnibus factus sum omnia. Nemini non seruio, neminem contemno, omnibus prodesse cupio, quousque id modo fieri liceat. Neque enim ita intelligendus est Apostolus, quasi vltra regulam liciti & iegis Christi sese quibusuis accommodauerit, id quod non esset Apostoli Christi, sed adulatoris, & non ad lucrandum sed perdendum faceret. Ita oportet istas vniuersales commode pro ratione materiæ, de qua agitur, intelligere. Hoc si obseruassent Anabaptistæ, non ita obstinate erassent in verbo Christi, vbi dicit, Vos autem nolite iurare omnino.
units.tr: To all things I became all things. What he has said particularly in the previous clauses he now sums up briefly, as if to say: why say more? I have accommodated myself to no one who was not there; I have become all things to all. I am a servant to no one, I despise no one; I desire to help all, as far as this can be done lawfully. For the Apostle is not to be understood as if he accommodated himself to anyone beyond the rule of what is lawful and of the law of Christ; that would not be the act of an Apostle of Christ but of a flatterer, and he would be doing it not for winning but for destroying. So these universal statements must be understood sensibly, according to the nature of the matter under discussion. If the Anabaptists had observed this, they would not have stubbornly stumbled over the word of Christ, where he says: "But you should not swear at all."

units.la: Quis non dicat Apostolum hominem fuisse omnium inconstantissimum ac versipellem, veluti Vertumnum quendam, in omnes sese formas vertentem, nisi scopum illius considerret. Hic erat, non vt ipse mutaretur à proposito, sed vt alios ad Christi cognitionem à sua sententia & errore mutaret ac lucrifaceret. ret. Proinde opus est ut cauti simus in iudi-candis Christi ministris, nec facile ambide-xtros uocemus, si quos uiderimus exemplo Pauli omnibus fieri omnia, nisi certo constet, quod non aliorum salutem, sed seipsos quærant.
units.tr: Who would not say that the Apostle was the most inconstant and shifty of men, like some Vertumnus who turned himself into every shape, if one did not consider his purpose? That purpose was not that he himself should be changed from his course, but that he should change others from their opinion and error, and win them to the knowledge of Christ. So we must be careful in judging the ministers of Christ, and we should not quickly call them double-dealers if we see them, after Paul's example, becoming all things to all men, unless it is clear that they seek not the salvation of others but their own.

units.la: VT omnino aliquos seruem.) Ergo Apostolus seruator est mortalium. Plane. Sicut est genitor & formator fidelium animarum. Seruat dum Christo seruandos ministerio suo lucrifacit, & è perditione eripit.
units.tr: THAT BY ALL MEANS I MIGHT SAVE SOME. So the Apostle is a saviour of mortals? Certainly, just as he is the begetter and former of believing souls. He saves when, by his ministry, he wins to Christ those who are to be saved by Him, and snatches them from destruction.

units.la: ALIQVOS.) Nec supra nec hic dicit omnes, licet omnibus factus sit omnia. Non quod non cupiat omnes saluare, uerum sciens hoc fieri non posse, uel aliquos lucrifacere conatur idq; tanto studio, ut eorum gratia omnibus se seruum constituat, utut non dubitet, multum de suo studio periturum, & debito fructu carituram.
units.tr: SOME. Neither above nor here does he say all, although he became all things to all men. Not that he does not desire to save all, but knowing that this cannot be done, he strives to win some, and with such zeal that for their sake he makes himself a servant to all, though he does not doubt that much of his effort will perish and will lack its proper fruit.

units.la: Chrysostomus: Ἀλλ' ὅτι τοῦτο ποιεῖ, πάντα τοῖς πᾶσιν γίνεται, οὐ δι' ἑαυτόν, ἀλλ' ὅτι ἐκεῖνο, ἑαυτὸν σώσῃ. Certe non est uerisimile eum qui ita affectus est, neminem prorsus seruare.
units.tr: Chrysostom: [Ἀλλ' ὅτι τοῦτο ποιεῖ, πάντα τοῖς πᾶσιν γίνεται, οὐ δι' ἑαυτόν, ἀλλ' ὅτι ἐκεῖνο, ἑαυτὸν σώσῃ.] Surely it is not likely that one so disposed would save no one at all.

units.la: Sit hoc non solum exempli, sed & consolationis gratia Christi propositum ministris, ne uelint animum despondere, si uiderint ministerium suum non quosuis adducere Christo. Electos seruare satis sit. Sic 2.Timoth. 2. dicit: Omnia sustinero propter electos, ut & ipsi salutem consequantur, quæ est in Christo Iesu cum gloria æterna.
units.tr: Let this be set before ministers of Christ not only as an example but also as a consolation, so that they may not lose heart if they see their ministry not bringing everyone to Christ. It is enough to save the elect. So in 2 Timothy 2 he says: "I endure all things for the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory."

units.la: HOC autem facio propter Euangelium.) Demonstratiua τοῦτο, ad præcedentia respicit, quibus dixit se omnibus omnia fieri, ut omnino aliquos seruet. Iam quoniam illas duas habent particulas: primam, qua dicit se omnibus omnia factum: alteram, qua huius rationem assignat, nempe, ut omnino aliquos seruet, fit ut incertum sit, ad quam referenda sit demonstratiua τοῦτο, priorem ne uel posteriorem particulam.
units.tr: "BUT I DO THIS FOR THE GOSPEL." The demonstrative "this" [τοῦτο] looks back to what precedes, where he said that he became all things to all men, so that he might by all means save some. Now since there are two parts: the first, in which he says that he has become all things to all men, and the second, in which he gives the reason for it, namely that he might by all means save some, it is uncertain to which of the two parts the demonstrative "this" should be referred.

units.la: 1 Si ad priorem, ut quod dicit, hoc facio, idem sit atque, omnibus me omnia facio: Videbitur nonnihil habere superstui, cum ei rei iam rationem suam assignarit sexies, nempe, quod cupiat alios lucrifacere, ac seruare, ut præter rationem uideatur, iam demum uelle ratio nem tradere, ob quam sit omnibus omnia factus. Nisi uelimus uni rei duas causas finales reddere, ut dicamus Apostolum omnibus omnia primum ob id esse factum, ut aliquos seruaret, deinde & ob id, ut ipse Euangelij particeps fieret.
units.tr: (1) If it refers to the first, so that "I do this" means the same as "I make myself all things to all men," it will seem somewhat superfluous, since he has already given his reason for this six times, namely that he desires to win and save others. It would then seem out of place that he should now at last wish to give the reason why he became all things to all men. Unless we want to assign two final causes to one thing, saying that the Apostle first became all things to all men so that he might save some, and then also so that he himself might become a partaker of the Gospel.

units.la: 5 Si ad posteriorem referamus, intelligendus erit Apostolus rationem uelle reddere non eius, quod omnibus omnia sit factus, sed eius, quod dixit, ut omnino aliquos seruem, id est, eius studij ac propositi, quod habebat in lucrandis ac seruandis per Euangelium mortalibus. Vt ostendat se non ideo cupere plures lucrifacere, ut terrenum aliquod ex illis emolumentum capiat, ut solebant pseudoapostoli, de quibus in Galatis dicit, circum-
units.tr: (2) If we refer it to the second part, the Apostle must be understood to wish to give the reason not for his becoming all things to all men, but for what he said, that he might by all means save some; that is, the reason for his zeal and purpose in winning and saving mortals through the Gospel. He wishes to show that he does not desire to win more people in order to gain some earthly advantage from them, as the false apostles did, of whom he says in Galatians:

units.la: cidi vos volunt, vt in carne vestra glorientur, sed vt Euangelij, hoc est, vt Ambrosius exponit, voluntatis ac finis Euangelij, salutis scilicet mortalium, particeps fiat, vel vt palmæ & coronæ, quæ promissa est fidelibus Euangelij ministris, particeps fiat; de qua alibi scribit: Bonum certamen certaui, cursum consummaui, fidem seruaui; de reliquo repositæ est mihi corona iustitiæ quam reddet mihi in illo die iustus iudex. Item secundæ Timothei primo: Scio cui credidi, & certus sum, quia potens est depositum meum seruare in illum diem.
units.tr: "They wish to circumcise you, so that they may boast in your flesh," but that he might become a partaker of the Gospel, that is, as Ambrose explains, of the will and end of the Gospel, namely the salvation of mortals, or that he might become a partaker of the palm and crown which is promised to the faithful ministers of the Gospel. Of this he writes elsewhere: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the righteous Judge will give me in that day." Likewise in 2 Timothy 1: "I know whom I have believed, and I am sure that he is able to keep what I have committed to him until that day."

units.la: Et certè facile est Apostolo Christi Euangelij gloriam, quæ fidos ministros manet, consideranti, nihil non illius gratia facere ac pati, vt ut molestum & arduum. Rursus, nisi illa ob oculos sit, arbitror difficillimum fore, vt hoc apostoli studium imitetur Euangelij minister. Nam vt metu crucis absterrebitur, aut fastidio languescet, aut affectatione terreni cuiusdam emolumenti prorsus auocabitur, vel cer tè corrumpetur. Opus igitur est, vt munquam non ad Euangelij gloriam prospiciat, certus olim fore, si syncerè ac fideliter Euangelio collaboraverit, vt Euangelij quoque particeps fiat. Quemadmodum si agricola benedictione sementis, in qua laborauit sedulò, ubi matura fuerit, potiatur. 2. Timoth.2. Agricolam qui laborauit, oportet primùm de fructibus accipere. Hac de re vide Matthæum vigesimoquarto, & vigesimoquinto.1.Pet.5.
units.tr: Certainly it is easy for the Apostle of Christ, when he considers the glory of the Gospel that remains for faithful ministers, to do and endure everything for its sake, however troublesome and hard. Again, unless that glory is before their eyes, I think it will be very difficult for a minister of the Gospel to imitate this zeal of the Apostle. For either he will be frightened off by fear of the cross, or he will grow weary through distaste, or he will be wholly diverted by the pursuit of some earthly advantage, or at least he will be corrupted. It is necessary, therefore, that he always look to the glory of the Gospel, being sure that if he labours sincerely and faithfully for the Gospel, he too will one day become a partaker of it, just as a farmer who has laboured diligently in sowing will, when the harvest is ripe, enjoy its blessing. 2 Timothy 2: "The farmer who has laboured ought first to receive a share of the fruits." On this matter see Matthew 24 and 25, and 1 Peter 5.

units.la: Quod ad hunc modum hanc particulam expono, de gloria futura quæ manet Euangelij præcones, si fideles permanserint, in munere & labore concredito, non hinc est quod præter verbi ministros neminem putem Euangelij fore participem, id est, consortem eius felicitatis, quæ per Euangelium mortalibus offertur, cum ad hanc felicitatem accessus sit non solum Euangelij prædicatoribus, sed & omnibus illi fidem habentibus, & ex animo obtemperantibus, unde & virtus Dei uocatur Euangelium, ad salutem non dicit omni prædicanti sed omni credenti: sed quod singularis sit parata corona Euangelij ministris, ad quam non dabitur aspirare, nisi ei qui in opere domini fidelis fuerit. Alioqui, si infidelis quisquam fuerit, adeoque piger & inutilis, proijcietur in tenebras exteriores, Matthæi vigesimoquinto.
units.tr: When I explain this phrase in this way, of the future glory that remains for the heralds of the Gospel if they remain faithful in the office and labour entrusted to them, I do not thereby think that no one except the ministers of the Word will be a partaker of the Gospel, that is, a sharer in that happiness which is offered to mortals through the Gospel. For access to this happiness is open not only to the preachers of the Gospel but to all who have faith in it and obey it from the heart; hence the Gospel is also called the power of God unto salvation, not for every preacher but for every believer. Rather, the particular crown prepared for the ministers of the Gospel is one to which no one will be allowed to aspire unless he has been faithful in the work of the Lord. Otherwise, if anyone is unfaithful, and therefore lazy and useless, he will be cast into outer darkness, Matthew 25.

units.la: Proinde, quod dicit, vt Euangelij, idem est, atque, ut Euangelici fructus, qui ex illius est prædicatione dum credentes saluantur, olim consors fiam ubi Christi ministris immarcescibilis dabitur gloria.
units.tr: Therefore, when he says "that I may be a partaker of the Gospel," it means the same as "that I may be a partaker of the fruits of the Gospel," which come from its preaching while believers are saved; that is, that I may one day share in the unfading glory that will be given to the ministers of Christ.

units.la: Quid ergo? mercedem tanquam mercenarius ita affectabat Apostolus, ut huius gratia ista faceret? Atqui alibi ita cupiebat ludæorum salutem, ut illorum gratia optarit ana thema esse à Christo. Quomodo hic dicit, se ideo omnibus omnia factum, quo aliquos feruet,vt huius gratia Euangelij particeps fiat {A} palmam adepturus olim & coronam fidis Christi ministris promissam? Chrysostomus diserte hic negat Apostolum alicuius ista mercedis gratia fecisse, sed ob id ita scripsisse, vt Corinthios alliceret, vt & ipsi caelesti hac spe inducti omnia fratrum gratia facerent. Alioqui, nisi hoc voluisset, quid opus erat ista scribere, cum nihil fauoris hoc sensu adferre potuerunt? Ita & Timotheo scribens, coronae meminit, quam sit olim accepturus a domino, absque dubio hoc illum pacto erigere & animare cupiés, vt & ipse in opere domini fortiter & alacriter pergeret.
units.tr: What then? Did the Apostle strive for reward like a hired man, so that he did these things for its sake? Yet elsewhere he so desired the salvation of the Jews that for their sake he wished to be accursed by Christ. How, then, does he say here that he became all things to all men so that he might save some, in order that for the sake of this he might become a partaker of the Gospel, about to obtain the palm and the crown promised to the faithful ministers of Christ? Chrysostom plainly denies here that the Apostle did these things for the sake of any such reward, but that he wrote thus in order to attract the Corinthians, so that they too, led by this heavenly hope, might do everything for the sake of their brothers. Otherwise, if he had not intended this, why did he write these things, since they could bring no favour in this sense? So also in writing to Timothy he mentions the crown which he is one day to receive from the Lord, undoubtedly wishing thereby to raise and encourage him, so that he too might press on bravely and eagerly in the work of the Lord.

units.la: Sed adhuc, inquis, manet quaestio. Non enim hoc quaeritur an Apostolo tantum liceat spe lucri & premij quae ad mortalium salutem & regni Christi profectum vtilia sunt facere, sed an Christi ministro cuicunque id competat. Iam si competit, cur non & ipsi Apostolo? Si Apostolo non licet, nec alijs licet. Quid ergo ista ad illectionem aliorum scribit?
units.tr: But, you say, the question still remains. For the question is not whether the Apostle alone may act out of hope of gain and reward, which are useful for the salvation of mortals and the advancement of the kingdom of Christ, but whether this is fitting for any minister of Christ whatever. If it is fitting, why not also for the Apostle himself? And if it is not lawful for the Apostle, it is not lawful for others either. Why, then, does he write these things in order to attract others?

units.la: Respondeo. In se quidem sinistri quid habet intuitu praemij seruire Christo. Verum quoniam infirmi sumus, vt homines, & humanis nonnunquam affectibus in rebus bonis vt cunque alimur & sustentamur, praesertim in tentationibus, non est praeter rationem, vbi adversa imminent Christi ministro, spe gloriae futurae animare imbecillem & tentatum animum. Huius multa sunt exempla non solum in apostolis literis sed & in Christi verbis, vt Matthaei {B}quinto: Merces vestra multa est in caelis. Et capite 19. Sedebitis super sedes, &c. Et Lucae. 12. Noli timere pusille grex, placuit patri meo dare vobis regnum. Hinc tamen non debet colligi, quod reprehensione careat, si quisquam velit nullo alio respectu seruire domino quam futuri praemij. Nec ita solent vere sancti, qui etiamsi nihil esset promissum praemij, ex amoris tamen affectu ad seruiendum domino sunt propensissimi.
units.tr: I answer: In itself, to serve Christ with an eye to reward has nothing wrong about it. But since we are weak as men, and are at times moved and sustained by human affections even in good things, especially in temptations, it is not beyond reason that, when adversity threatens a minister of Christ, his feeble and tempted mind should be encouraged by hope of future glory. There are many examples of this, not only in the letters of the Apostles but also in the words of Christ, as in Matthew 5: "Your reward is great in heaven"; and in chapter 19: "You shall sit upon thrones," etc.; and in Luke 12: "Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom." Yet it should not be concluded from this that it is free from blame if anyone wishes to serve the Lord with no other regard than future reward. Nor are truly holy people accustomed to this; even if nothing had been promised as reward, they are nonetheless most inclined to serve the Lord from the affection of love.

units.la: An nescitis, quod qui in stadio currūt omnes quidem currunt, sed vnus accipit praemium. Sic currite, vt comprehendatis. Omnes autem qui certat, per omnia temperans est: illi quidem igitur, vt perituram coronam accipiant, nos autem, vt aeternam. Ego itaque sic curro, vt non in incertum, sic pugilem ago, non velut aerem feriens, verum subijcio corpus meum, & in seruitutem redigo, ne quomodo fiat, vt cum alijs praedicauerim ipse reprobus efficiar.
units.tr: Do you not know that those who run in a stadium all indeed run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it. Everyone who competes exercises self-control in all things: they do it to receive a perishable crown, but we to receive an eternal one. I therefore run not aimlessly; I fight not like one beating the air, but I subdue my body and bring it into servitude, lest by any means, after preaching to others, I myself should become a castaway.

units.la: Quia dixit se propterea ad lucrandos mortales omnibus factum esse omnia, & cum liber esset ab omnibus, omnibus se constituisse seruum, vt Euangelij particeps fieret, id est, vt coronam Euangelij ministris, si fidelis fuerint, repositam acquireret, instituit adiectis similibus studium hoc suum declarare & illustrare, vt Corinthios suo exemplo ad idem propositum alliceret. Similia autem quibus vitur duo sunt, primum de illis iuniptum quiin stadio pro brabio currunt, alterum de pugillari certamine, vtrinq; non est satis currere, vel pugno caedere, nisi conatus in certum abeat & certanten voti reddat compotem, vt qui currit, praemium cuius gratia currit rite currendo apprehendat, & qui pugno certat, certado vincat. Ita innuere vult, non esse satis homini Christiano, si qualemcunque conatum ad hoc impendat, vt caeleste brabeion acquirat nisi tale impendat, vt victor euadat. Sed quomodo ista similia adaptet, in ipsa textus expositione videbimus.
units.tr: Since he had said that for the sake of winning mortals he had become all things to all people, and though free from all, he had made himself a servant to all, so that he might become a partaker of the Gospel, that is, so that he might acquire the crown of the Gospel laid up for ministers, if they are faithful, he added similes to declare and illustrate his zeal, so as to draw the Corinthians by his example to the same purpose. The two similes he uses are, first, that of those who run for the prize in the stadium, and second, that of the boxing contest. In both, it is not enough to run or to strike with the fist, unless the effort is directed to its goal and makes the competitor master of his desire: the runner, by running rightly, grasps the prize for which he runs, and the boxer, by fighting, wins the contest. He means to suggest that it is not enough for a Christian to expend any sort of effort to acquire the heavenly prize, unless he expends such effort that he comes out as victor. But how he applies these similes, we will see in the exposition of the text itself.

units.la: AN nescitis.) Quod Corinthios alloquitur ad hoc facit, vt intelligant haec omnia se ipsorum scribere gratia. Alioqui poterat post praemissa dicere, ciens quod qui in stadio currunt, omnes quidem currunt, &c. si simpliciter de studio & conatu suo dicere voluisset. Vt autem ostendat, vel certe moneat, quam contra communem sensum sit, brabium acquirere eu, qui non currat legitime, id est, Euangelij participem fieri eum qui in cursu Euangelij non rite se gerat, non solum vulgaribus similibus vtitur, sed rogat primum, an tam sint stupidi, vt ista non obseruent, cum debuerunt vel ex vulgari consuetudine & aequitate illorum, de quibus scribit, admoneri. Hoc est quod dicit, An nescitis, &c.
units.tr: Do you not know? In addressing the Corinthians in this way, he makes them understand that he writes all these things for their own sake. Otherwise, after what he had said before, he could have said, "Since those who run in a stadium all run," and so on, if he had wished to speak simply of his own zeal and effort. But in order to show, or at least to warn, how contrary to common sense it is that one who does not run lawfully, that is, who does not conduct himself rightly in the course of the Gospel, should acquire the prize, that is, become a partaker of the Gospel, he not only uses familiar comparisons but first asks whether they are so dull that they do not notice these things, when they ought to have been reminded by common custom and by the fairness of those about whom he writes. This is what he means by: Do you not know, and so on.

units.la: QVI in stadio currunt.) Pulchrè comparat Christiani nominis professionem non stationi ociosae, quae pigrorum est & inutilium hominum, sed stadio, in quo currendi & certandi studium exercetur, qui locus laborum & studiorum conatuum est, non torporis & negligentiae. In hoc stadio non est otiosè standum sed reliquis posterioribus semper ad anteriora tendendum, et tanta contentione properandum, vt tandem ad propositam metam pertingentes caeleste brabeion apprehendamus, vt recte alicubi dicat Nazanzenus, ὁ βάλλεται σε ὁ λόγ@ ποτε ἐν ταύτῳ μάνειν, ἀλλ' ἀεὶ κινητὸν ἔϊ). ἀὐ ἀμαρτάνεσθαι, εἰ κατοροῖς, ἐσιτέινοντα. Id est. Non vult te doctrina ista in eodem aliquando consistere sed semper moueri, vt si peccaueris, reuertare, si vero recte feceris, ad vlteriora progressum intendas. Vt igitur in stadio non plus in stando proficitur quàm retrogradiendo, ita & in Christianismo sine fidei & pietatis incrementis & quotidianis progressibus non magis ad praepositam metam peruenitur quàm si quis retrogrediatur & ad priora dilabatur.
units.tr: Who run in a stadium. He aptly compares the profession of the Christian name not to an idle station, which belongs to the lazy and useless, but to a stadium, where the zeal of running and contending is exercised. It is a place of labour and striving, not of sluggishness and negligence. In this stadium one must not stand idle, but must always press forward past those behind, and hasten with such effort that, reaching at last the appointed goal, we may grasp the heavenly prize. As the Nazianzen rightly says somewhere: [οὐ βούλεταί σε ὁ λόγος ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ ποτε μένειν, ἀλλ' ἀεὶ κινεῖσθαι· ἂν μὲν ἁμαρτάνῃς, ἐπιστρέφειν, ἂν δὲ καλῶς πράττῃς, ἐπὶ τὰ ὑψηλότερα προκόπτειν]. That is: this teaching does not want you ever to remain in the same place, but always to be moving; if you have sinned, to turn back; if you have done well, to press on to higher things. Just as in the stadium one makes no more progress by standing still than by going backwards, so too in Christianity, without increases of faith and piety and daily progress, one comes no nearer the appointed goal than if one went backwards and slipped into former things.

units.la: Omnes quidem currunt, sed unus accipit brabeon.
units.tr: All indeed run, but one receives the prize.

units.la: De dictione brabij vide annotationes Erasmi. Conditionem &cwoπ eorum qui in stadio currunt exprimit, & ad propositum suum adaptat. Ita solet fieri in stadio, vt non mox brabeon
units.tr: On the word for prize, see the annotations of Erasmus. He expresses the condition of those who run in the stadium and adapts it to his purpose. So it happens in the stadium that not at once the prize

units.la: beion apprehendant, quotquot in stadium descendunt, & vnâ cum aliis currunt, sed brabeio maneat eum qui currendo legitimè victor evasrit. Hoc est quod dicit: Omnes quidem currunt, sed vnus accipit brabeion. Id est. Quemadmodum in stadio nō est ad consequendum palmam satis simpliciter currere, nisi ita curras vt currendo vincas, ita & in Christianismo nō est satis fidei & pietatis cursum aggredi cum reliquis Christianis, nisi hunc ita teneas, disponas, intendasq; vt propositam coelestis gloriæ palmam victor apprehendas. Nisi enim hoc fiat, vt nemo putat iniquum esse si palma negetur ei, qui quidem cucurrit cum aliis, ad metâ autem legitime nō peruenit, & detur ei qui nō solum inter currentes fuit, sed & legitimè cucurrit, & currendo vicit, ita certè nemo sperare debet coelestè præmium his posse obtingere qui nominetenus tantum Christiani in stadio pietatis legitimum cursum non ad finem vsq; tenuerint. Itaq; omnes quidè Christiani vocamur, & videri volumus qui ad metam coelestis brabij currendo tendamus, verùm brabeion ipsum non apprehendent omnes. Quare? Quia non omnes legitimè ac serio, vt par erat, in hoc stadio currimus.
units.tr: ...[βραβεῖον] is seized by all who go down into the stadium and run along with others, but the prize remains for the one who, running lawfully, has emerged as victor. This is what he says: All indeed run, but one receives the prize. That is: just as in the stadium it is not enough, for winning the palm, simply to run, unless you so run that by running you win, so in Christianity it is not enough to take up the course of faith and piety along with other Christians, unless you so hold, arrange and direct this course that you grasp as victor the palm of heavenly glory set before you. For unless this is so, no one thinks it unfair that the palm be denied to one who indeed ran with the others but did not reach the goal lawfully, and be given to one who was not only among the runners but ran lawfully and won by running. Certainly, then, no one ought to hope that the heavenly reward can fall to those who, in the stadium of piety, have kept a lawful course only in name as Christians and not to the end. So indeed we are all called Christians, and we wish to seem to be running towards the goal of the heavenly prize; but not all grasp the prize itself. Why? Because not all of us run in this stadium lawfully and seriously, as was fitting.

units.la: His verbis Apostolus torporem excutit pigris ac negligentibus, vt cogitent sicut & alii dicit: Non coronandos esse, nisi eos, qui legitimè certauerint, atq; ita ad futuram palmam coelestis gloriæ prospicientes ad veru ac legitimum pietatis Euangelicæ cursum accingantur.
units.tr: By these words the Apostle shakes torpor off the lazy and negligent, so that they consider, as he says elsewhere, that only those are crowned who have competed lawfully, and so, looking forward to the future palm of heavenly glory, gird themselves for the true and lawful course of Gospel piety.

units.la: Notandum autem est quàm pulchrè simul hæc verba, si rite expendantur, contra desperationem faciat, & diffidentiam eorum, qui vbi audiunt paucos fore saluos, spe obtinendi brabijde stituuntur, currendiq; studiū remittunt. Isti sal tem conatus eorū imitentur qui in stadio currunt. Hi sciùt certo, non omnes fore victores. Sed vni tantū, qui reliquos vincat, competere palmam, & tamen omnes currunt. Vt quid hoc faciunt? Quoniam scilicet omnes spe potiūdæ victoriæ ducuntur. Quanto magis in hoc pietatis stadio diligentercurrendum est omnibus ita vt nemo sit qui de brabeio coelesti apprehendo desperet.
units.tr: It must be noted how beautifully these words, if weighed rightly, work against despair and the diffidence of those who, when they hear that few will be saved, are cast down in hope of obtaining the prize and give up their zeal for running. Let them at least imitate those who run in the stadium. These know for certain that not all will be victors, that the palm belongs to one alone who surpasses the rest; and yet all run. Why do they do this? Surely because all are led by the hope of gaining victory. How much more diligently, then, ought everyone to run in this stadium of piety, so that there is no one who despairs of grasping the heavenly prize.

units.la: SIC currite ut comprehendatis.) Non dicit: Sic currite, vt videamini currere, sed, vt comprehendatis. Alioqui nihil proderit currere, si non datur comprehendere. Complectitur autem similitudinis nota ὡς, sic, hæc omnia. Primum spem obtinendi brabeion, deinde animū ad currendum appositum. Tertio legitimum studium & constantem in perdurando tenorē. Ista si adfuerint, certè mediante gratia Dei poterit apprehendi palma. Mediante, inquam, & gubernante gratia Dei. Nam alioqui scriptum est: Non est currentis nec volentis, sed miserētis Dei, ne quis velit nostris conatibus dare, quod non est nisi gratiæ Dei.
units.tr: So run that you may obtain. He does not say, "So run that you may seem to run," but "that you may obtain." Otherwise running would profit nothing if obtaining were not granted. He includes all these things in the particle of comparison "so": first, the hope of obtaining the prize; then, a mind applied to running; and third, a lawful zeal and a steady perseverance in holding on. If these are present, surely the palm can be grasped through the mediation of God's grace. Through the mediation, I say, and by the governing grace of God. For otherwise it is written: "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy," lest anyone should wish to give to our efforts what belongs only to the grace of God.

units.la: Cautè autem non dicit: Sic currite, vt vnus vestrum apprehendat. Sed vt apprehendatis, indicàs hoc discriminis esse inter brabeion terrenum & coeleste, vt in cursu Christianismi nō vni tantum liceat palma potiri, sicut [in stadio corporalis cursus, sed copia sit & potestas omnibus apprehendendi brabeion, si rite currat. In stadio terreno certamen est inter ipsos currentes, ea conditione, vt nequeat quisquā eorum vincere, nisi reliquis deuictis & à consequutione palmæ reiectis. Deinde ita proponitur brabeion, vt ei tantum competat qui omnium victor currendo primus ad metam pertigerit.
