Hic verò in pietatis studio, nec tale est inter currentes certamē, vt nisi deuictis reliquis nō liceat potiri victoria, nec talis est brabij propositi conditio, vt vni tantum qui primus adcurret destinatum, sed summus est συντρεχόντων cō sensus, & licet cuiquā absq; aliorum incommodo vincere, imò & reliquos ad victoriam sine suo detrimento aut impedimento iuuare, vt nō cum minore gloria cum multis palma potiri liceat, quàm si solus quisquam vincat. Certamē enim in hoc cursu est non contra συντρεχόντας fratres, qui non vincendi, sed iuuandi sunt: Sed contra malignos spiritus, peccatum, carnem & sanguinem, omnis generis impietatem & mundum hunc peruersum. Hæc portenta sunt uincenda, non quod & ipsa una pro coelesti palma apprehendenda nobiscum currant, sed quod nos ab intentione cursus remorari ac perdere conantur.
units.tr: Carefully, moreover, he does not say, "So run that one of you may grasp it," but "that you may grasp it," indicating that there is this difference between the earthly and the heavenly prize: that in the course of Christianity it is not permitted for only one to take the palm, as in the bodily course of the stadium; rather, there is opportunity and power for all to grasp the prize, if they run rightly. In the earthly stadium there is a contest among the runners themselves, on the condition that none of them can win unless the rest are defeated and shut out from attaining the palm. Then the prize is set so that it belongs only to the one who, as victor over all by running, first reaches the goal. But here, in the study of piety, there is no such contest among the runners that victory cannot be seized unless the rest are defeated, nor is the condition of the proposed prize such that it is destined only for the one who arrives first. Rather, there is a supreme harmony among the fellow-runners, and anyone may win without harm to others; indeed, he may help the rest to victory without loss or hindrance to himself, so that the palm may be won by many no less gloriously than if one alone won. For the contest in this course is not against fellow-runners, who are to be helped, not defeated, but against wicked spirits, sin, flesh and blood, impiety of every kind, and this perverse world. These monsters are to be conquered, not because they run along with us to seize the heavenly palm, but because they try to hold us back from the intent of the course and to ruin us.

units.la: Et ipsum brabeion ita propositum non est, ut ad eum tantum pertineat qui primus ex currentibus ad metam pertingat. Absit. Omnes manent quotquot ab initio mundi ad finem usque in hoc pietatis studio cursum constantem ad propositam fidei metam tenuerint, ita ut posteriores nihil noceat quod sero adcurrunt, & prioribus nihil sit prærogatiuæ, quod posteriores in hoc cursu præuenerunt. Prioribus nanq;, ut in epistola ad Ebræos cap.11. scribitur, expectandum est, donec postremi adueniant, ut non detur illis accipere remissionem, Deo aliquid melius pro nobis prouidente, ne sine nobis consummentur.
units.tr: Nor is the prize itself set forth in such a way that it belongs only to the one who first among the runners reaches the goal. Far from it. All who, from the beginning of the world to its end, have held a steady course in this zeal for godliness, keeping to the goal of faith set before them, will all remain (in the prize): so that those who come later are not harmed by arriving late, and the earlier runners gain no privilege from having outrun the later ones in this race. For the earlier ones, as is written in the epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11, must wait until the latecomers arrive, so that they do not receive the remission apart from us, since God has provided something better for us, so that they might not be made perfect without us.

units.la: Omnis autem qui certat, per omnia temperans est.
units.tr: Every one who competes exercises self-control in all things.

units.la: Πάντα ἐγκρατεύεται, id est, χ̄ τὰ πάντα. In omnibus continens est. Vetus sic, ab omnibus se abstinet. Quæ videlicet certaturo sint noxia & impedimento futura. Nec abstinet solum à nocituris, sed & quæcunque profutura sunt adaptando & accommodando corpori, utut gravia & molesta, magna patientia perfert. Ista pertinent ad studium ac diligentiam animi, serio se ad certandum adaptantis. Hic multa tolerat molesta, à multis abstinet alioqui licitis & iucundis. Quare? Quia conditionem propositi fui talem scit esse, ut si velit nihil fer-
units.tr: He is self-restrained in all things [ἐγκρατεύεται, that is, the whole of it: ἐγκρατεύεται τὰ πάντα]. He is continent in all things. The old translator renders it thus: he abstains from all things. Namely, from those things that would be harmful and an obstacle to the one who is contending. Nor does he abstain only from things that would harm him, but he also bears with great patience whatever things are beneficial, though burdensome and troublesome, by adapting and accommodating them to the body. These things belong to the zeal and diligence of a mind that seriously prepares itself for the contest. Here he endures many troublesome things, and abstains from many things that are otherwise lawful and pleasant. Why? Because he knows that the condition of his purpose is such that, if he wishes to bear nothing

units.la: {A} Caute autem non dicit.
units.tr: Note that he does not say this carelessly.

units.la: reduri, sed magis quibuslibet pro libidine vti, frustra fit initurus certamé, corpore adhuc delicato & ad certandum prorsus inepto. Cogitat singulari opus esse studio in disponendo & exercendo corpore, vt reddatur vel ad currendum agile, vel ad certandum impigrum & commodum, ideo studiose curam illius gerit, spe victoriæ.
units.tr: but to use whatever he likes according to his desire, he would be entering the contest in vain, with a body still soft and altogether unfit for competing. He reflects that a special effort is needed in ordering and exercising the body, so that it may be made either nimble for running or vigorous and fit for fighting. Therefore he takes earnest care of it, in hope of victory.

units.la: Si hoc facit qui periturí brabij gratia certat, quomodo non magis nos, qui pro cœlesti & æterno certamus? Ita argumento à brabiorum cœlestis & terreni discrimine sumpto, pudefacit eos quod in studio certandi superarentur ab illis qui periturę coronæ gratia certantes, tantam ostendunt continentiam simul & patientiam, tanta possunt ferre incommoda, & à delicatis se continere, etiam licitis, vna vincendi spe inducti cum interea isti ne ab eidolothytis quidem se continere sustinuerint, Euangelij gratia.
units.tr: If he who competes for a perishable prize does this, how much more should we do so, who compete for a heavenly and eternal prize? Thus, by an argument drawn from the difference between the heavenly and the earthly prizes, he shames them, because in the zeal of competing they were surpassed by those who, competing for a perishing crown, show such self-control and such endurance, can bear such hardships, and keep themselves from delicate and even lawful things, led by the single hope of winning. Meanwhile these men could not bring themselves to refrain even from meat offered to idols, for the sake of the Gospel.

units.la: Adimitur nobis istis similibus omnis excusatio, vt non sit vllus locus cóquerendi de impossibilitate perferendi quæ dura & continendi à delicatioribus & propósito nostro nocitu ris, cum videamus tantum patientiæ & continentiæ in filijs huius sæculi, vel pro inani gloria vel vt terrenas opes acquirant, aut vt liberi us postea viuere liceat, studiose certantibus. Nam si illi tantum possunt spe rerum pereunti um & fluxarum, nos si spem haberemus æternorum bonorum quomodo non plura possemus?
units.tr: Every excuse is taken away from people like these, so that there is no room for complaint that it is impossible to endure hard things, or to abstain from delicate things that are harmful to our purpose, when we see so much endurance and self-control in the children of this age, who compete zealously either for empty glory, or to acquire earthly riches, or so that they may afterwards be allowed to live more freely. For if they can do so much for the sake of perishing and fleeting things, how much more could we do if we had hope of eternal goods?

units.la: EGO itaq; sic curro, vt non in incertum.) Redit ad suum exemplum, & in se declarat simul qua spe & quo studio cursui pietatis se accommodare debeant. Currere in incertum & aera pugno verberare, est omnem currendi & pugnandi operam ludere, vt fit ab illis qui nec de brabio apprehendendo persuasi, nec de scopo quem petere debeant instructi, temere currunt & verberant cum diffidentia, adeoq; remisse & frustra. Dicit itaq; se non in incertum currere, aut aera verberare, hoc est, non ex se incertum de brabio cœlesti, nec ignarum scopi qui sit petendus atque ideo cursum tenere certum constantem & recta ad metam properantem, id quod nihil est aliud, quàm quod supra dixit, omnibus se factum omnia vt vel aliquos seruet, idque propter Euangelium, vt illius particeps fiat. Hic erat rectus ac certus cursus, quem volebat imitari Corinthios. Cursus vero incertus, & aeris percussio erat, quod ipsi in libertatis ostentationem eidolothytis uescebantur, deque scientia, quod eidolum nihil esset & quod vnus sit Deus, plurimum gloriabatur, & non tam spectabant quid ad ædificationem faceret infirmorum quàm quod ipsis liceret.
units.tr: "I therefore run in such a way, not as uncertainly." He returns to his own example and at the same time declares in himself with what hope and what zeal they ought to adapt themselves to the course of godliness. To run uncertainly and to beat the air is to waste all the effort of running and fighting, as happens with those who, not convinced about winning the prize and not instructed about the goal they ought to aim at, run and strike at random, with doubt, and so carelessly and in vain. He therefore says that he does not run uncertainly or beat the air, that is, he does not run uncertain of the heavenly prize, nor ignorant of the goal that must be aimed at. Hence he keeps to a course that is sure, steady, and hastening straight to the mark. This is nothing other than what he said above: that he has become all things to all men, so that he might save some, and that for the sake of the Gospel, so that he might become a partner in it. This was the straight and certain course that he wished the Corinthians to imitate. But an uncertain course and beating the air was theirs, because they ate meat offered to idols to show off their liberty, and they boasted greatly of their knowledge that an idol is nothing and that there is one God, and they did not so much consider what would build up the weak as what was permitted them.

units.la: Opus est itaque in hoc cursu, vt adsit certa consequendi brabij spes, deinde, vt metæ propositæ non simus ignari, ad quam tendamus. Pestilens igitur est ea doctrina, quæ docet sa-
units.tr: In this course, therefore, there must be the sure hope of winning the prize, and then we must not be ignorant of the goal set before us, toward which we strive. Therefore that teaching is pernicious which teaches

units.la: lutis incertitudine, hominem scilicet scire non posse, an sit in gratia vel non sit. Qua certitudine & spe curret qui de gratia Dei dubitat?
units.tr: uncertainty of salvation, namely that a man cannot know whether he is in grace or not. With what certainty and hope will he run who doubts about the grace of God?

units.la: 2 Rursus & ea doctrina noxia est, qua docetur Deo placere quicquid bono animo fiat. Quasi nō sit præfixus certus scopus, quem petamus. Currendum est certa victoriæ spe, sed currendum est nō extra stadium. Viuendum est non secundum rationis nostrę regulam, sed secundum diuinæ voluntatis placita si uoluerimus legitimè currere.
units.tr: Again, that teaching is also harmful which teaches that whatever is done with a good intention pleases God, as if there were no fixed and certain goal that we ought to seek. We must run with the sure hope of victory, but we must run within the stadium, not outside it. We must live not according to the rule of our own reason, but according to the decrees of the divine will, if we wish to run lawfully.

units.la: VERVM subijcio corpus meum & in seruitutem redigo.) Ad certum cursum tenendum opus est vt supra dixi continuo formandi corporis studio. De hoc loquitur, & quod in simili propósuit, iam in suo exemplo aperit. Multa est corporum nostrorum corruptio, & ad ea quæ pietatis exercitium concernút ineptitudo, deinde multū inest in illis etiam inobedientiç aduersus moderamen spiritus. Itaq; nisi velimus periclitari, coercenda sunt & reprimenda, vt non dominetur per carnis desideria, cur fumq; hunc remorentur ac nos perdant, sedvt spiritui seruiat instar iumentorum. Hoc fit per continentiam, abstinentiam, & patientiam, labores, vigilias, ieiunia &id genus alia exercitia. Hoc scilicet est quod dicit se subijcere corpus suum & in seruitutem redigere.
units.tr: "But I subdue my body and bring it into bondage." To keep to a certain course, there is need, as I said above, of constant care in training the body. Of this he speaks, and what he proposed in the comparison he now makes plain in his own example. Our bodies are full of corruption, unfit for the exercise of godliness, and in them there is much disobedience against the government of the spirit. Therefore, unless we wish to be in danger, they must be restrained and held back, so that the desires of the flesh do not rule, delaying this course and destroying us, but so that they serve the spirit like beasts of burden. This is done through self-control, abstinence, and patience, through labours, watchings, fastings, and other exercises of this kind. This, of course, is what he means when he says that he subdues his body and brings it into bondage.

units.la: Pulchrè autem vtitur verbis ὑπωπιάζω & δὲ λαγωγεῖν, ὑπωπιάζω est plagis aliquem in facie liuidū & suggillatum reddere, sicut solet contingere contumacibus & immorigeris qui ad seruiendum plagis adiguntur. Vtitur hoc verbo sensu metaphorico, pro castigatione corporis, vt & vetusreddidit. Non enim faciem suam verberando liuidam reddidit Apostolus, sed diligenti abstinentia & competenti exercitio castigauit & macerauit, vt ad seruiendum spiritui redderetur aptum & morigerum. Seruus bene saginatus, ineptior est ad seruiendum, & contumacior quàm qui ritè obtemperet iussis heri. Vnde & nos Germani de talibus dicimus Das fuoter ligt inen zuo nach, causam contumaciæ & petulantiæ assignantes. Idem sentiendū est de corporibus nostris.
units.tr: He uses the words ὑπωπιάζω [I beat black and blue] and δουλαγωγῶ [I lead into slavery] beautifully. ὑπωπιάζω means to make someone's face livid and bruised with blows, as commonly happens to the stubborn and disobedient who are driven to obey by blows. He uses this verb in a metaphorical sense, for the chastening of the body, as the old translator also rendered it. For the Apostle did not make his face livid by beating it, but he chastened and wore down his body by careful abstinence and suitable exercise, so that it would be made fit and obedient to serve the spirit. A servant who is too well fed is less fit for service, and more stubborn than one who obeys his master's orders properly. Hence we Germans also say of such people Das fuoter ligt inen zuo nach [the fodder lies too close to them], assigning the cause of their stubbornness and wantonness. The same must be thought of our bodies.

units.la: Ne quomodo fiat, ut cum alijs prædi cauerim ipse reprobus efficiar.
units.tr: Lest somehow, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate.

units.la: Ratio est. 1 Ne reprobus fiat. Hoc est, ne inter eos sit, qui non rite currunt, adeoque nec brabio potiuntur.
units.tr: The reason is this: (1) lest I become reprobate, that is, lest I be among those who do not run properly and therefore do not win the prize.

units.la: 2 Idque cum singulari pudore ac turpitudine quod alijs cum prædicauerit, quomodo sit currendum & obtinendum brabium, ipse suam ipsius non sit sequutus doctrinam. Turpe enim est doctori cum culpa redargu-it ipsum.
units.tr: (2) And this would bring singular shame and disgrace: that, having preached to others how the race must be run and the prize won, I myself should not follow my own teaching. For it is shameful when a teacher is refuted by his own fault.

units.la: CAPVT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Olim autem uos ignorare fratres, quod partes nostri omnes sub nube fuerunt, & omnes per mare transierūt; & omnes in Mosen baptizati sunt in nu be & in mari, & omnes eandem escam spiritualem comederunt, & omnes eun dem potum spiritualem biberunt. Biberunt enim de spirituali, quæ sequuta est petra : Petra uero erat Christus. At plures illorum haud approbauit De us. Etenim prostrati sunt in deserto.
units.tr: Moreover, brethren, I would not have you ignorant that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea; and all were baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ. But God was not well pleased with most of them, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.

units.la: Totum hoc caput ad idem cum præcedenti bus duobus propositum facit. Proximè præ cedéti Apostolus suo Corinthios exemplo ad hoc inducere voluit, vt libertate quam in Chri sto prætexebant, & qua eidolothytis temerè vescendo grauiter abutebantur,non ad offen diculum infirmorum,sed magis ad ædificatio nem vterentur,nec spectarent quid sibijpsi li cere putarent,sed potius quid conduceret in firmis. Hoc vero præsenti capite fere ad calce vsque,alio argumento vtitur, admonens eos, vt si charitatis & ædificationis ratione suoque exemplo permoueri nolint, permoueantur sal tem iræ diuinæ & proprij exitij metu. Huc vsur pat veterum Israelitarum exempla, inque illis spectādum proponit,quid futurum sit ipsis si il lorum vestigijs ingredi velint.
units.tr: This whole chapter is directed to the same purpose as the two preceding ones. Immediately before, the Apostle wanted to lead the Corinthians by his own example to this: that they should use the liberty they claimed in Christ, and which they were recklessly abusing by eating freely of things sacrificed to idols, not to the offence of the weak but to their edification; and that they should not look to what they thought was lawful for themselves, but rather to what would benefit the weak. In this chapter, however, almost to the end, he uses another argument, admonishing them that if they will not be moved by the reason of charity and edification, or by his example, they should at least be moved by fear of divine wrath and of their own ruin. For this he uses the examples of the ancient Israelites, and sets before them what will befall themselves if they wish to walk in those footsteps.

units.la: NOLIM autem uos ignorare fratres.) Pau lo supra cum de re Gentibus & nota & vsitata loqueretur,non dixit Nolim vos ignorare fra tres,sed, An nescitis quod qui in stadio currit, omnes quidem currunt,sed vnus accipit præ mium? Hic vero non dicit: An nescitis? sed, nolim vos ignorare fratres, quod patres no stri omnes sub nube fuerunt,& omnes per ma re transierût, & omnes in Mose baptizati sunt in nube & in mari, &c. Nam quæ adducturus erat exépla Gentilia nó erant,sed ex sacris pri scorū Israelitarū historijs depropta,quarū Co rinthij ex Geutibus Christiani nullâ dum vel certè modicâ ac tenuem cognitionem habe bant.Cum autem essent illis ad doctrinā & admo nitionem vtiles,admonet eos vt harum sibi co gnitionem parent, in quibus quasi in speculo quodam videant,quid caueant , quid sequan tur.Haud modicæ prudentię est, ex alienis pe riculis reddi cautum. Et hoc consilio non di cit: Significo vobis quid patribus nostris acci derit,sed, Nolim vos harum esse rerum igno rantes . Monet eos,vt scripturas sacras inspi ciant,scientesque illarum esse curent.Vtinam sic animati sint erga populum Christi, qui se successores apostolorum esse gloriantur, vt & ipsi nolint fideles ignorantes esse sacrarū scri pturarum. Quàm autem diuersum agant, &
units.tr: I would not have you ignorant, brothers. A little above, when he was speaking of a matter familiar and common to the Gentiles, he did not say "I would not have you ignorant, brothers," but "Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize?" Here, however, he does not say "Do you not know?" but "I would not have you ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea," and so on. For the examples he was about to adduce were not Gentile ones, but were drawn from the sacred histories of the ancient Israelites, of which the Corinthians, Christians from the Gentiles, had as yet no knowledge, or at least a very slight and thin one. Since these examples were useful to them for teaching and admonition, he admonishes them to acquire knowledge of these things for themselves, so that in them, as in a mirror, they may see what to avoid and what to follow. It is no small prudence to be made wary by other people's dangers. And in giving this counsel he does not say, "I signify to you what happened to our fathers," but "I would not have you ignorant of these things." He urges them to examine the sacred Scriptures and to take care to know them. Would that those who boast that they are the successors of the apostles were so inspired towards the people of Christ that they too would not wish the faithful to be ignorant of the sacred Scriptures. But how differently they act, and

units.la: totis in id viribus incumbant,quo plebem sub iectam à lectione scripturarum arceat, adeoq; non cum Paulo dicant: Nolūmus vos ignoran tes esse,sed cum Antichristo,Nolumus vos sci entes esse scripturarum,quis est qui non vide at? Nouit Satan ignorantiá scripturarū esse ma trem omnium errorum. Sic Christus Saddu caeis dicebat:Erratis nescientes scripturas. Et Chrysost. Hinc omne malum est,inquit, quod scripturæ ignorantur.
units.tr: with all their strength apply themselves to keeping the subject people away from the reading of the Scriptures. And so, instead of saying with Paul, "We would not have you ignorant," they say with Antichrist, "We would not have you knowing the Scriptures." Who does not see this? Satan knows that ignorance of the Scriptures is the mother of all errors. So Christ said to the Sadducees: "You err, not knowing the Scriptures." And Chrysostom: "From this," he says, "comes every evil, that the Scriptures are ignored."

units.la: QVOD patres nostri omnes.) Maiores Is raelitarum intelligit , quos Deus ex Ægypto per Mosen eduxit. Hos ecclesiæ ex Gentibus colle&tas proponit, quatenus & ipsi populus Dei existêtes seueritatem iusti illius iudicij fue rant experti,eaq; in re exemplum cun&is po-steris facti,vnde admonerentur, non esse irri tandum dominum.
units.tr: THAT OUR FATHERS ALL. He means the forefathers of the Israelites, whom God led out of Egypt through Moses. He sets these before the churches gathered from the Gentiles, inasmuch as they themselves, being the people of God, had experienced the severity of that just judgment, and became an example in this matter to all posterity, from which they might be admonished not to provoke the Lord.

units.la: Non dicit autem simpliciter , quod patres nostri,sed,quod patres nostri omnes,nō quod omnes illorum maiores ex Ægypto edu&ti , & sub nube fuerint , perque mare transierint, & de manna cœlesti ederint,&c sed quod qui tū in viuis erant cum educerentur, edu&ti essent omnes,horumque participes facti. Et sic lo quendo omnem Israëlis ac populi Dei ecclesi am complectitur , inque illa considerandum proponit,cuius ecclesiam Noui testamenti ex Gentibus colle&tam admonendam esse duxit.
units.tr: He does not say simply "our fathers," but "all our fathers": not that all their ancestors were led out of Egypt, and were under the cloud, passed through the sea and ate the heavenly manna, and so on, but that all who were alive at the time they were led out were led out, and became sharers in these things. And so, speaking in this way, he embraces the whole of Israel and the church of God, and he sets it before us for consideration, since it was this church, whose New Testament counterpart gathered from the Gentiles, he thought should be admonished.

units.la: Id supra sic proposuit : Qui in stadio cur runt,omnes quidem currunt, sed vnus accipit præmium. Sic currite vt comprehendatis. Idé hic monet per exempla maiorum populi Israe litici,quibus hoc ipsum vsuenerat, vt omnes quidem currerent,pauci verò præmium appre henderent.
units.tr: He set this out above thus: "Those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize. So run that you may obtain it." Here too he gives warning, through the examples of the forefathers of the Israelite people, to whom this very thing had happened: that all indeed ran, but only a few obtained the prize.

units.la: Et hanc summâ diuidit in duas partes, qua tum prima vniuersalem gratiæ Dei communi eationem, altera abie&tionem ac reprobatio nem plurium habeat . Ad primam pertinet quod vniuersalem quinquies repetit dicens: Omnes sub nube fuerunt , omnes per mare transierunt,omnes baptizati fuerunt , omnes ederunt,omnes biberunt,quibus nihil vult a liud quàm quod supra dixit, omnes quidem currunt. Ad alteram verò,quod subiungit, sed plures illorum haud approbauit Deus,etenim prostrati sunt in deserto , quod ad id pertinet quod supra dixit,vnus accipit præmiū . Quasi dicat, Quæ in imagine currentium delineaui, ne putetis nobis qui in stadio Christianæ pie tatis currimus haud esse timenda, considerate exempla maiorum nostrorum, ac videte, an non illis ea acciderint.Ecquomodo nos poté rimus esse securi, ne idem patiamur , si confi mili præuaricatione patientiam Dei irritaue rimus?
units.tr: And he divides this summary into two parts, of which the first contains the universal communication of God's grace, and the second the rejection and reprobation of the many. To the first belongs his repetition five times of the word "all": all were under the cloud, all passed through the sea, all were baptized, all ate, all drank. By these he means nothing other than what he said above, that all indeed run. To the second belongs what he adds: "but God was not pleased with most of them, for they were overthrown in the desert," which corresponds to what he said above: "one receives the prize." As if he said: "What I have sketched in the image of runners, do not think that we who run in the stadium of Christian piety have nothing to fear. Consider the examples of our forefathers, and see whether these things did not befall them. How could we be secure that we would not suffer the same, if by a like transgression we provoke the patience of God?"

units.la: SVB nube fuerunt.) De columna nubis lo quitur,in qua Deus ante populum suum in de serto præcessit. De hac legimus Exod.13. in fi ne capitis ad hunc modum. Profectiq; de So chot , castrametati sunt in Ethan in extremis finibus solitudinis. Dominus autem præcede
units.tr: UNDER THE CLOUD. He speaks of the pillar of cloud, in which God went before his people in the desert. We read of it in Exodus 13, at the end of the chapter, in this way: "And they set out from Succoth and encamped at Etham, on the farthest edge of the wilderness. And the Lord went before

units.la: bat eos ad ostendendam viam per diem in co-lumna ignis, vt dux esset itineris vtroque tem-pore. Nunquâ defuit columna nubis per diē, neque columna ignis per noctem. Itaque nu-bes ista ad hoc erat populo Dei data, vt exter-no hoc inuolucro de praesentia Dei angelico ipsos ministerio ducentis ac simul protegen-tis admonerentur, imò certi redderentur. Vn-de & cap.14. de illa sic legimus: Tollensque se angelus domini, qui praecedebat castra Israel, abijt post eos, & cum eo pariter columna nu-bis, priora post tergum dimittens, stetit inter castra Ægyptiorum & castra Israelis. Et erat nubes tenebrosa & illuminans noctem, ita vt ad se inuicem toto noctis tempore accedere non valerent.
units.tr: them to show the way by day in a pillar of fire, so that he would be their guide on the journey at both times. The pillar of cloud never failed by day, nor the pillar of fire by night." Therefore that cloud was given to the people of God for this purpose: that by this outward covering they might be admonished, indeed made certain, of the presence of God, who led them by the ministry of an angel and at the same time protected them. Hence in chapter 14 we read of it thus: "And the angel of the Lord, who went before the camp of Israel, removed himself and went behind them; and with him the pillar of cloud, leaving behind the front, stood between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel. And there was a dark cloud that illuminated the night, so that they could not approach one another during the whole night."

units.la: Duplex itaq; erat columnae huius vsus. Vnus ducendi populum in itinere Solitudinis, alter protegendi illum cum ab aduersarijs tū ab æstu Solis, qui in Solitudinibus regionum illarum solet esse intensissimus. Accedebat & tertius, de quo est Exodi 16.19.24.33.34. & 40. quod per nubem, videlicet, apparere soleret dominus, & loqui cum Mose. Quoniam igitur in vniuersum omnes horum fuerant beneficio-rum participes, dicit hic Apostolus: Omnes sub nube fuerunt.
units.tr: The use of this pillar was therefore twofold. One was to lead the people on their journey through the wilderness; the other was to protect them both from enemies and from the heat of the sun, which is wont to be most intense in the deserts of those regions. There was also a third, of which we read in Exodus 16, 19, 24, 33, 34 and 40: that the Lord would appear through the cloud, that is, and speak with Moses. Since therefore in general all had been partakers of these benefits, the Apostle says here: "All were under the cloud."

units.la: Sub cœlo fumus omnes, & homines & be-stiæ. Quid igitur magni est, quod Israelitæ sub nube fuerunt? An cœlum non est maius, illu-strius, ac potius nube? Plane. Verùm Apostol non id intelligit quod vulgari modo simpliciter & sub qualicunq; nube fuerint, sed loquitur de communicatione gratiæ, præsentiæ, di-rectionis ac protectionis Dei per nubem mi-nisterio angelico administratæ, vt sub nube fuisse, idem sit, quod fuisse sub gratia diuinæ di-rectionis ac protectionis. Hanc gratiæ Dei co-munificationem in eo consideranda[m] propo-nit, quod vniuersalis fuit omnium. Aliàs pote-rat dicere: Quod patres nostri omnes in Ægy-pto fuerunt, Pharaoni seruierunt, defertû per-transierunt, &c. Vel: Quod Mosi loquutus est Deus per nubem.
units.tr: Under the sky we are all smoke, both men and beasts. What then is great about the Israelites being under the cloud? Is not the sky greater, more illustrious, and higher than a cloud? Certainly. But the Apostle does not mean that they were under some cloud in the ordinary sense, simply under any cloud whatever. He speaks of the communication of grace, presence, direction and protection of God, administered through the cloud by angelic ministry, so that to have been under the cloud is the same as to have been under the grace of God's direction and protection. He proposes that this communication of God's grace be considered in this respect, that it was universal to all. Otherwise he could have said: "That our fathers were all in Egypt, served Pharaoh, passed through the desert," and so on, or: "That God spoke to Moses through the cloud."

units.la: Sed quæ-rat hic forsan aliquis, quid sibi vo-luerit Deus quod per nubem populum suum in deserto duxit ac protexit, cum inuisibili sua prouidentia & potentia haud minus illi adesse posset, quàm per rem aliquam externam?
units.tr: But someone here might perhaps ask: what did God intend in leading and protecting his people through the desert by a cloud, since by his invisible providence and power he could be present with them no less than through some external thing?

units.la: Deinde, vbi placebat externæ ac visibilis alicu-ius rei ministerium, cur non lucidius aliquid & illustrius vsurpauerit quàm sit nubes, quæ vtut lucida fuerit, longè tamen infra eam erat claritatē quæ diuinæ naturæ ac maiestatis pos-set repræsentare splendorem?
units.tr: Next, if he was pleased to use the ministry of some external and visible thing, why did he not choose something brighter and more illustrious than a cloud? For however bright it was, it was still far below that brightness which could represent the splendour of the divine nature and majesty.

units.la: 1 Respondeo. Primùm propter ruditatem populi rebus spiritualibus & inuisibilibus mi-nus assueti, ne se omni putaret esse numine de-stitutum, opus erat visibili aliquo gratiæ hu-ius inuolucro, in quo fide præsentis Dei du-ctoris ac protectoris aleretur, & in ordine re-tineretur. Nam ita cōparata est humana infir-mitas, vt inuisibilis Dei gratiam ac præsentiā
units.tr: 1 I answer: first, because of the rudeness of the people, who were less accustomed to spiritual and invisible things, lest they should think they were abandoned by all divine power. There was need of some visible envelope of this grace, in which they might be nourished by faith in the present God as leader and protector, and be kept in order. For human weakness is so constituted that it

units.la: ægrè capiat, nisi sub externo aliquo signo & inuolucro exhibeatur. Nam aliàs sola fide ani-mi exercitatos sensus habētis capitur. Et hinc est quod Gentes absq; vsu imaginum nec nu-minis præsentiam, nec verum cultum Dei a-gnoscere potuerunt. Vnde ille Iudaicæ religio-nis irrisor dixit: Nil præter nubes & cœli nu-men adorant.
units.tr: grasps the grace and presence of the invisible God with difficulty, unless it is set before it under some external sign and covering. For otherwise it is grasped only by the faith of a mind exercised through the senses. And hence it is that the Gentiles, without the use of images, could recognise neither the presence of the deity nor the true worship of God. Whence that mocker of the Jewish religion said: "They worship nothing but clouds and the divinity of the sky."

units.la: 2 Deinde quoniam sub re aliqua visibili erat ei populo cœlestis gratiæ exhibenda præsen-tia, opus erat tali quæ cœlestis esset, & simul humanæ imbecillitati tolerabilis. Splendo-rem nanq; diuinæ maiestati competentem hu-manus conspectus ferre non poterat. Sic Exod. 33.cum dixisset ad dominum Moses: Ostende mihi faciem tuam. Item: Ostende mihi gloriā tuam. Responsum est illi: Non poteris videre faciem meam. Non enim videbit me ho-mo & viuet, &c. Imò ne Mosi quidem faciem inspicere potuit populus, & quomodo faciem id est, gloriam Dei videre posset humana infir-mitas?
units.tr: 2 Next, since the presence of heavenly grace was to be exhibited to that people under some visible thing, there was need of something that was heavenly and at the same time tolerable to human frailty. For human sight could not bear the splendour fitting to the divine majesty. Thus in Exodus 33, when Moses had said to the Lord, "Show me your face," and again, "Show me your glory," the answer was given to him: "You cannot see my face; for man shall not see me and live," and so on. Indeed the people could not even look upon the face of Moses, so how could human weakness see the face, that is, the glory of God?

units.la: Pulchre itaque hæc nubes eam dispensatio-nem Dei repræsentabat, qua suam ille nobis præsentiam ita attēperat, vt nostro sitcaptui tolerabilis, id quod mille modis facit, donec in hac carne viuimus. In futura verò vita præsen-tiam Dei haud obnubilatam, sed facie ad faciē contemplabimur. Sic dicit Apostolus infrà ca. 13. Cernimus nunc per speculum in ænigmate, tunc verò facie ad faciem. Nimirum nunc vi-get exercitium fidei, quod posteaquam hinc migrauerimus cessabit, nec opus vlliserit inuo lucris & obnubilationibus, vbi coràm omnia quæ nunc credimus & speramus, plena felici-tate contemplabimur.
units.tr: Beautifully, therefore, this cloud represented that dispensation of God by which he so tempers his presence to us that it is tolerable to our capacity, which he does in a thousand ways as long as we live in this flesh. In the future life, however, we shall contemplate the presence of God not veiled, but face to face. So the Apostle says below in chapter 13: "Now we see through a glass in a riddle, but then face to face." Clearly now the exercise of faith flourishes, which will cease once we have departed hence, and there will be no need of clouds and veils, where we shall contemplate in full happiness all the things we now believe and hope for.

units.la: OMNES per mare transierunt.) Hanc hi-storiam legimus Exo.14. Magnum sanè ac stu-pendum erat hoc diuinæ potentiæ opus, quo populus ex Ægypto liberatus, vt prorsus de manibus Ægyptiorum eriperetur, per maris est alueum traductus. Quare cum dicit, Om-nes per mare transierunt, idemest ac si diceret: Omnes plenam sunt liberationem ex Ægypto consecuti, omnes manum Pharaonis per trā-situm maris euaserunt. Sic è discrimine præ-senti cōmuniter erepti fuerūt omnes, quo gra-tia hæc liberationis ei populo prorsus esset vni-uersalis, & omnibus indiscriminatim commu-nis. At introitus terræ promissæ non omnib ⁊ est illis qui per mare transierunt cōcessus. Qua in re admonemur quantum malum sit nō con-stanter adhærere verbo & promissis Dei. Vbi legimus eos qui per hunc maris transitum rei-pla fuerant potentiam Dei experti, per diffidē-tiam & impatientiam retrocessisse, contraque dominum murmurasse, adeoque post tam lu-culenta illius beneficia ingressu terræ sanctæ indignos sese reddidisse, cogitemus quàm sit necessarium, ut summa cura in gratia Dei per-manere satagamus.
units.tr: ALL passed through the sea. We read this history in Exodus 14. It was a great and wonderful work of divine power, by which the people, freed from Egypt, were led through the channel of the sea so that they might be wholly snatched from the hands of the Egyptians. Therefore when he says, "All passed through the sea," it is the same as if he said: all obtained full liberation from Egypt, all escaped the hand of Pharaoh by the passage of the sea. Thus all were commonly rescued from the present danger, so that this grace of liberation was altogether universal to that people and shared indiscriminately by all. But entry into the promised land was not granted to all who had passed through the sea. In this matter we are warned how great an evil it is not to cling constantly to the Word and promises of God. For we read that those who had been the subjects of this passage through the sea and had experienced the power of God, went back through distrust and impatience, and murmured against the Lord; and so, after such clear benefits of his, they made themselves unworthy of entry into the holy land. Let us consider how necessary it is that we take the greatest care to remain in the grace of God.

units.la: OMNES in Mosen baptizati sunt, in nube & in mari. Si totam nubis huius & transitus historiam voluas ac reuoluas, ne verbo quidē A baptismi mentionem fieri inuenies. Quomodo ergo & quare dicit: Israelitarum patres omnes in nube fuisse & in mari baptizatos? Respondeo. Accommodat se proposito. Pleriq; Corinthiorum propter baptismum plurimum insolescebant, quemadmodum statim initio epistolæ huius vidimus, adhęc, sacramento quoque dominicæ cœnæ enormiter abutebantur, & interea horum mysteriorum fiducia cum de linquerent in multis salutem sibijpsi pollicebantur. Vt igitur admonerentur, quàm inanis esset hæc fiducia, tribuit Israelitis quoq; eorundem mysteriorum communicationem, idque generaliter omnibus, ne dicerent Corinthij nihil ad se pertinere illorum exempla. Sic dicit: & omnes baptizati sunt, nō minus quàm nos. Et quoniam interrogari poterat, in quem & quomodo baptizati essent, addit, in Mosen, in nube & in mari quibus verbis exponit, quomodo & in quem fuerint omnes baptizati, simulque aperit, ad quid dixerit: patres omnes fuisse sub nube, perq; mare transiuisse. Poterat dicere, & omnes circumcisi fuerunt in Mosen. Verùm non respiciens hic ad contentionem quæ de circumcisione à plerisq; mouebatur, sed pugnans cum illis qui propter baptismum insolescentes nihilo melius viuebant quàm oJim Iudæi in deserto, ad hunc modum loqui voluit: Et omnes in Mosen baptizati sunt, in nube & in mari. Quasi dicat: Ne putetis uos baptismatis & cœnæ dominicæ symbolis tutos esse ab exclusione regni cœlestis. Nisi enim post baptismum iter quod ingressi estis legitima fide, spe, dilectione, & patientia constanter tenueritis, tam non intrabitis in regnum cœlorum, quàm Israelitæ propter diffidentiam & impatientiam promissam terram non sunt ingressi, quamuis omnes essent in nube & mari baptizati, cœlestisque alimoniæ ac potus participes facti.
units.tr: ALL were baptized into Moses, in the cloud and in the sea. If you turn over and over the whole history of this cloud and passage, you will not find even a word about the mention of baptism. How then, and why, does he say that all the fathers of the Israelites were in the cloud and baptized in the sea? I answer: he accommodates himself to his purpose. Many of the Corinthians were growing very proud because of baptism, as we saw at the very beginning of this letter; moreover, they abused even the sacrament of the Lord's Supper excessively, and meanwhile, trusting in these mysteries, they promised themselves salvation even while they lived in many sins. So that they might be warned how empty this confidence was, he attributed a sharing in these same mysteries to the Israelites too, and to all of them in general, lest the Corinthians should say that the examples of those people did not concern them. So he says: "and all were baptized, no less than we." And since it could be asked into whom and how they were baptized, he adds: "into Moses, in the cloud and in the sea," by which words he explains how and into whom all were baptized, and at the same time makes clear what he meant by saying that all the fathers were under the cloud and passed through the sea. He could have said, "all were circumcised into Moses." But not looking here to the dispute which was raised by many about circumcision, and fighting against those who, puffed up on account of baptism, lived no better than the Jews once did in the desert, he wished to speak in this way: "And all were baptized into Moses, in the cloud and in the sea." As if he said: do not think yourselves safe from exclusion from the kingdom of heaven because of the symbols of baptism and the Lord's Supper. For unless after baptism you hold constantly to the way you have entered by true faith, hope, love and patience, you will no more enter the kingdom of heaven than the Israelites, because of their distrust and impatience, entered the promised land, although they were all baptized in the cloud and the sea and made partakers of heavenly food and drink.

units.la: Scriptura quidem non vocat nubem & mare baptismum, verùm Apostolus rem ipsam, vel si mavis, mysterium propius inspiciens, idem significat Israelitis fuisse nubem ac transitum maris, quod nobis in Novo testamento est baptismus, id quod paucis sic accipe. Populus Veteris testamenti sanguine agni ex Ægypto seruatus fuit, deinde cum eductus esset, p nubem est & transitum maris velut initiatus in Mosen, hoc est, in pædagogiam illam Mosai cæ legis, quæ postea est in monte Sinah lata. Sic nos sanguine agni immaculati è regno Satanæ liberati in Christum per baptismum initiamur. Deinde nubes separauit eos ab Ægyptijs ac protectioni diuinæ inclusit. Sic baptismo separamur ab infidelibus, & in gratiam cœlestè suscipimur & initiamur. Mare submersit Ægyptios, Israelitas verò, tanquam populum domini, velut ex morte viuos transmisit, & ad iter terræ promissæ sanctificauit. Sic baptismo quatenus sacramentum est remissionis peccatorum, peccata nostra submergit, & nos ad iter
units.tr: Scripture indeed does not call the cloud and the sea baptism, but the Apostle, looking more closely at the thing itself, or if you prefer, at the mystery, signifies that for the Israelites the cloud and the passage of the sea were what baptism is for us in the New Testament. Understand this in a few words. The people of the Old Testament were saved from Egypt by the blood of the lamb; then, when they had been led out, they were initiated into Moses through the cloud and the passage of the sea, that is, into that schoolmaster of the Mosaic law which was afterwards given on Mount Sinai. So we, freed from the kingdom of Satan by the blood of the spotless lamb, are initiated into Christ through baptism. Then the cloud separated them from the Egyptians and enclosed them in divine protection. So by baptism we are separated from unbelievers and received and initiated into heavenly grace. The sea drowned the Egyptians, but the Israelites, as the people of the Lord, it carried across as if living from death, and consecrated them for the journey to the promised land. So baptism, inasmuch as it is a sacrament of the remission of sins, drowns our sins, and consecrates us, rescued from eternal death, for the journey

units.la: cœlestis patriæ morti æternæ ereptos sanctificat. Nube suscepti & per mare sanctificati, paulo post doctrinam cœlestem per Mosen acceperunt, ad cuius præscriptum domino Deo suo bona fide ac religiosè adhærerent, omnemq; suam vitam dirigerent. Cosimili modo in Novo quoq; testamento initiatis ac baptizatis ponitur doctrina salutis, quam constanter sequantur. Vnde & Christus cum d iffet: apti zantes eos in nomen patris & filij & spiritussan cti, adiecit, docentes eos seruare mnia quæcunq; præcepi vobis. Propter consimilem huc cursum primordiorum vtriusq; testamenti, vocat Apostolus nubem ac transitum maris baptismū, hoc est, dicit Israelitis ea id fuisse quod nobis est baptismus.
units.tr: to the heavenly fatherland. Taken up under the cloud and consecrated through the sea, they shortly afterwards received the heavenly teaching through Moses, to whose prescription they were to cling to the Lord their God in good faith and devoutly, and to direct their whole life. In a similar way in the New Testament also, the teaching of salvation is set before those who have been initiated and baptized, which they are to follow constantly. Hence also Christ, when he said, "baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit," added, "teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you." On account of this similar course of the beginnings of both covenants, the Apostle calls the cloud and the passage of the sea baptism; that is, he says that for the Israelites these things were what baptism is for us.

units.la: Vbi & illa considerari possunt. In baptismate sunt tria. Gratia cœlestis, verbum, aqua. Gratia, in quam initiamur, verbum geminum, præcedens ac subsequens, præcedens, quo institutum est baptisma, subsequens, quo docemur baptizati. Aqua, qua externe sacramentaliter tingimur, initiamur ac sanctificamur. Hæc sunt pspicua. Deinde, aqua semel initiamur, gratia verò, in quam baptizamur initiamur ac suscipimur, donec sumus in hac vita perpetuò fruimur. Iam refer animum ad baptismum Israelis. Hic est nubes & verbum, & aqua maris. Nubes symbolum erat cœlestis gratiæ, in quâ populus ille suscipiebatur & initiabatur. Verbum erat mandatum Mosi datum à domino, de mari diuidendo. De nube non extat uerbum. Quia nihil erat in illa quod humano ministerio perficeretur. Quemadmodum in nostro quoq; baptismate non habemus. Verbum nisi instituens ac mandans quod faciat minister Euangelij, cum adiecta promissione, qua credenti ac baptizato salus promittitur. Aqua maris, qua populus transeundo ad iter terræ promissæ sanctificabatur, & initiabatur. Hæc sanctificatio per transitum maris semel est facta, nec vnquam repetitam legimus. Hanc volebant reddere irritam, qui de reditu in Ægyptum cogitabant. Consimiles illis sunt Anabaptistæ, quicquid prætexant. Nubes verò non semel tantum apparuit, sed præsto fuit indefinetter. Sic Exod.13. legimus. Nunquam defuit columna nubis per diem neque columna ignis per noctem coram populo. Innuebatur videlicet, sacramentum quidem gratiæ Dei semel tantum administrari, ipsam vero cœlestem gratiam esse perpetuam. Hisce cogitationibus existimo intelligi posse, quare & quomodo Israelitas omnes Apostolus in nube & in mari baptizatos esse dicat.
units.tr: Here these points too can be considered. In baptism there are three things: heavenly grace, the word, and water. The grace into which we are initiated has a twofold word, one preceding and one following. The preceding word is that by which baptism was instituted; the following word is that by which we are taught after we are baptized. Water is that by which we are externally and sacramentally washed, initiated and sanctified. These points are plain. Next, we are initiated by water only once, but the grace into which we are baptized, initiated and received, we enjoy continually for as long as we live in this life. Now turn your mind to the baptism of Israel. Here there are the cloud, the word, and the water of the sea. The cloud was a symbol of heavenly grace, in which that people was received and initiated. The word was the command given by the Lord to Moses about dividing the sea. There is no word about the cloud, because nothing in it was carried out by human ministry. Likewise in our baptism we have no word except that of the minister of the Gospel, who institutes and commands what he does, together with the added promise by which salvation is promised to the believer and the baptized. The water of the sea was that by which the people were sanctified and initiated as they passed over to the journey to the promised land. This sanctification through the crossing of the sea was done once, and we never read of it being repeated. Those who thought of returning to Egypt wanted to make it void. The Anabaptists are like them, whatever they pretend. But the cloud did not appear only once; it was present without end. So we read in Exodus 13: the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night never failed before the people. It was clearly signified that the sacrament of God's grace is administered only once, but heavenly grace itself is perpetual. By these considerations I think it can be understood why and how the Apostle says that all the Israelites were baptized in the cloud and in the sea.

units.la: Vbi consideret diligens Lector. Primùm, quid sit baptizari, deinde non baptizari simpliciter sed in aliquem. Baptismus est initiatio, obsignatio, & sanctificatio. Quæ initiantur, obsignantur & sanctificantur, omnino in alicuius nomen ac peculium initiantur, obsignantur & sanctificantur. Sic non simpliciter dicit Apostolus: & omnes baptizati sunt, sed ad-dit,
units.tr: Let the diligent reader consider this. First, what it is to be baptized; then, that one is not baptized simply but into someone. Baptism is initiation, sealing and sanctification. Those who are initiated, sealed and sanctified are necessarily initiated, sealed and sanctified into someone's name and possession. So the Apostle does not simply say, "and all were baptized," but adds

units.la: E-
units.tr: ad-

units.la: dit in Mosen. Dicet aliquis. Ecquid discrimi- nis est inter Apostolos & Mosen? In nomen Apostoli baptizari nō licet, & in nomē Mosis licuit? An nō suprà cap.1. dixit Apostolus. Nūquid Paulus crucifixus est pro vobis? Aut in nomen Pauli baptizati estis? Gratias ago Deo meo quod neminem vestrum baptizaui, nisi Crispum & Gaium, ne quis dicat, quod in nomé meum baptizauerim. Quid ergo est, quod hic Apostolus Israelitas in nomen Mosis baptizatos fuisse dicit? Respondeo. Multum discriminis fuit inter Mosen & apostolos. Tam ille quidem quàm isti non dominus sed minister domini fuit: verùm ille mediator fuit Veteris testamenti, cuius respectu Christus melioris testamenti mediator Ebr. 8 dicitur. unde & pro ipsa pædagogia lege ac dispensatione Veteris testament plerunque ponitur, id quod hoc loco factum esse constat, quale quid de apostolis dici non poterat. Præterea non dicit: & in nomen Mosis, sed, in Mosen baptizati fuerunt omnes. Aliud est in nomen Mosis, & aliud in Mosen, id est pædagogiam Mosis initiari. Tertiò illud quoque consyderandum est, quod in mysterio hoc baptismi nubem & transitum maris coniungit. Non dicit simpliciter, baptizati sunt in nube, sed addit, & in mari. Nec dicit: Baptizati sunt in mari, sed præmittit, in nube. & hæc duo, nubem & mare interposita copulationis uocula coniungit. Ergo ne gratiam cœlestem symbolo externo indiaulse connectit? Nequaquam. Nubem & mare connectit. At utraq; symbola erant non res ipsa. In symbolis gratiæ communicarunt omnes, in gratia ipsa non item. Neq; enim omnes placuerunt Deo. Nemo gratiæ cœlestis vere particeps Deo displicet. Nemo autem incredulus & immorigerus gratiæ est particeps cœlendus. Non est autem insolens, quod nubem & mare, res à se inuicem diuisas, in vnum sacramentū coniūgit. Nam & Christus ipse sub pane & vino rebus diuersis eiusdem nobis mysterij sacramentum propositum. Neq; excusantur hinc papistæ, qui falsum, oleum, sputum, & candeam accensam aquæ coniungunt in baptismo. Illic enim diuina est authoritas, apud ipsos uero humana temeritas.
units.tr: ds, "into Moses." Someone will say: is there any difference between the Apostles and Moses? Is it not lawful to be baptized into the name of an apostle, but lawful to be baptized into the name of Moses? Did not the Apostle say above, in chapter 1: "Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul? I thank God that I baptized none of you, except Crispus and Gaius, lest anyone say that I baptized in my own name." What then does this Apostle mean in saying that the Israelites were baptized into Moses? I answer: there was a great difference between Moses and the apostles. Both the one and the others were not the Lord but a minister of the Lord; yet Moses was the mediator of the Old Covenant, in respect of which Christ is called the mediator of the better covenant (Heb. 8). Hence the name Moses is also often put for the very pedagogy, the law and dispensation of the Old Covenant, as is evidently the case in this place, something that could not be said of the apostles. Moreover, he does not say "into the name of Moses," but "they were all baptized into Moses." It is one thing to be baptized into the name of Moses, and another to be baptized into Moses, that is, to be initiated into the pedagogy of Moses. Thirdly, this must also be considered: in this mystery of baptism he joins the cloud and the passage through the sea. He does not simply say "they were baptized in the cloud," but adds "and in the sea." Nor does he say "they were baptized in the sea," but puts "in the cloud" first, and he joins these two, the cloud and the sea, with the interposed little word of connection. Does he then join heavenly grace to an external sign? By no means. He joins the cloud and the sea. But both were symbols, not the reality itself. All shared in the symbols of grace, but not all in grace itself. For not all were pleasing to God. Nobody who is truly a partaker of heavenly grace is displeasing to God, but nobody who is unbelieving and disobedient is to be counted a partaker of grace. Nor is it unusual that he joins the cloud and the sea, things divided from one another, into one sacrament. For Christ himself also set before us, under bread and wine, different things as the sacrament of one and the same mystery. Nor are the Papists excused here, who join salt, oil, spittle and a lighted candle to water in baptism. For in the case of Christ there is divine authority, but with them it is human rashness.

units.la: ET omnes eandem escam spiritualem comederunt & omnes eundem potum spiritualem biberunt.) Vide quomodo se propositio accommodet etiam hoc loco. Non dicit, omnes manna comederunt, & aquam ex petra ,p-manantem biberunt, cum tamen de manna & aqua illa loquatur, sed quemadmodum in precedenti particula non simpliciter dixit: omnes sub nube fuerunt, & omnes mare transierunt, sed adiecit, omnes in Mosen baptizati sunt, in nube & in mari, ita hic quoq; vt mysterio cibi ac potus huius expresso argumento suo sese accommodaret, dixit, omnes eandem escam spiritualem commederunt, & omnes eundem potum spiritualem biberunt, ne quos exemplo hoc Israelitarum à vana fiducia externorum signorum reuocare conabatur, mox regeretur ecquid est quod manna comederunt & aquam biberunt? Nos spiritualem cibum ac potum edimus & bibimus, illi terrenum. Et illi, inquit, spiritualem cibum ac potum comederunt & biberunt, perinde atq; nos.
units.tr: And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. See how the sentence accommodates itself here too. He does not say "they all ate manna and drank water that flowed from the rock," though he is speaking of that manna and that water. Just as in the preceding clause he did not simply say "all were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea," but added "all were baptized into Moses, in the cloud and in the sea," so here too, in order to fit his argument to the mystery, he expressed the food and drink in this way: "all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink." He wanted to prevent those whom he was trying to call back from vain trust in external signs, by this example of the Israelites, from immediately asking: what then did they eat manna and drink water? We eat and drink spiritual food and drink, they earthly. He says that they ate and drank spiritual food and drink just as we do.

units.la: Deinde & illud argumento serviit, quod nō simpliciter dicit: omnes escam spiritualem comederunt & omnes potum spiritualem biberunt, sed vtrobiq; addit τὸ αὐτὸ, id est, eandem & eundem. Eandem, inquit, escam comederunt, & eundem potum biberunt omnes, id quod argumento huic duplici sensu accommodari potest.
units.tr: Next, this also serves his argument: he does not simply say "all ate spiritual food and all drank spiritual drink," but in both places adds the word τὸ αὐτὸ, that is, "the same." He says that all ate the same food and drank the same drink, which can be applied to this argument in two senses.

units.la: 1 Primò sic in tota illa multitudine eandem omnes inter se escam ederunt, & eundem potum biberunt. Non aliam escam pij, aliam reprobi sed omnes indiscriminatim eandem comederunt, ac consimili modo non alium atq; alium sed eundem omnes potum biberunt, & tamen non omnes Deo placuerunt, sed plures ex illis perierunt, quare videte ne idem contingat & vobis.
units.tr: (1) First, in that whole multitude all ate the same food among themselves and drank the same drink. The godly did not have one food and the reprobate another; all without distinction ate the same, and in the same way all drank not one drink and then another, but the same drink; and yet not all were pleasing to God, but many of them perished. Take care, therefore, lest the same thing happen to you.

units.la: 2 Deinde hoc pacto. Omnes eandem escam nobiscum comederunt, & eundem potum nobiscum biberunt, hoc est, eorundem nobiscum mysteriorum participes fuerunt, & tamen nō sunt propterea saluati omnes, & quomodo nos omnes obsecrabimus, ac potus huius communicatio seruaret, quæ illos non seruauit? Et hunc sensum sequutus Augustinus, quomodo eūdem quem nos, cibum & potum ederint ac biberint Israelitæ omnes, sic exponit, tractatu super Iohan. 45. Eundem, inquit, potum spiritualem biberunt, spiritualem eundem, corporalem non eundem. Quid enim illi bibebant? Bibebant de spirituali sequente petra, petra autem erat Christus. Videte ergo. Fide manente signa sunt variata. Ibi petra Christus, nobis Christus quod in altari Dei ponitur. Et illi pro magno sacramento eiusdem Christi, biberunt aquam profluentem de petra, nos quid bibamus, nostrum fideles. Si speciem visibilem intendas, aliud est, si intelligibilem significationem, eundem potum spiritualem biberunt. Hæc ille. Sanè vtroq; sensu populus ille eundem spiritualem cibum ac potum cum inter se tum nobiscum comedit & bibit.
units.tr: (2) Next, in this way: all ate the same food with us and drank the same drink with us; that is, they were partakers of the same mysteries as we are, and yet not all of them were saved on that account. And how shall we all be saved if the sharing of this food and drink preserved us, when it did not preserve them? Augustine, following this sense, explains how all the Israelites ate and drank the same food and drink as we do, in his tractate on John 45: "They drank the same spiritual drink; the same spiritually, not the same bodily. For what were they drinking? They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ. See then: the signs have varied, but the faith remains. There the rock was Christ; for us Christ is what is placed on the altar of God. And they, for the great sacrament of the same Christ, drank water flowing from the rock; what we drink is our own, the faithful. If you look to the visible appearance, it is different; if to the intelligible meaning, they drank the same spiritual drink." So far Augustine. Certainly in both senses that people ate and drank the same spiritual food and drink, both among themselves and with us.

units.la: Sed quæsierit hic quisquâ, quomodo Apostolus res corporeas & visibiles manna videlicet & aquam ex petra, quibus populi illius corpora alebantur in deserto, & unde ipsa quoque iumenta bibebant, Num. 20. spiritalem cibum ac potum vocet.
units.tr: But someone here may ask: how can the Apostle call spiritual food and drink things that are bodily and visible, namely the manna and the water from the rock, by which the bodies of that people were nourished in the desert, and from which the beasts themselves also drank (Num. 20)?

units.la: Respondeo. Si quod corporale est, visibile aut palpabile, nullo modo spirituale vocari potest nō video quomodo tueamur Apostolum hoc loco. Si vero aliquo respectu potest esse spirituale, quod substantia corporali constat, facilè intelligimus, non respicere illū ad substantiam vel Man vel aquę, sed vel ad originem illorum vel mysterium aliquod, vel vsum.
units.tr: I answer: if something is corporeal, visible, or tangible, it cannot in any way be called spiritual. I do not see how we can defend the Apostle on this point. But if something made of corporeal substance can be called spiritual in some respect, we easily understand that he is not looking at the substance of the manna or of the water, but at their origin, some mystery, or their use.

units.la: Ambrosius refert hanc loquutionem ad miraculosam. raculosam vtriusq; originem, qua citra consue tum naturæ cursum illud de cœlo, ista ex petra subministrabantur. Et Chrysost. quoq; hanc ra tionē adfert, verùm addit de vsu quoq; dicens. Εἰ γὰρ ᾧ αἰδηλα ὧν τὰ γινόμενα ἀλλὰ πνευματικῶς τὰ ῥεῖχετο κ᾿ χ᾿ φύσεως ἀκολυθίαν ἀλλὰ ἀπὸ δωρέας χαρίσματος, καὶ μετὰ τὸ σῶμα ὡς τὸ πνεῦμα ἴτησιν εἰς τὴν ναύρην ἡ ἐπιθυμία.
units.tr: Ambrose refers this expression to the miraculous origin of both: the one came down from heaven and the other was supplied from the rock, beyond the ordinary course of nature. Chrysostom also gives this explanation, but he adds the use as well, saying: "For if the things that happened were not invisible, but were poured out spiritually, and not according to the sequence of nature but from the gift of grace, and after the body the desire followed the Spirit into the wilderness." [Εἰ γὰρ ἀόρατα ἦν τὰ γινόμενα, ἀλλὰ πνευματικῶς τὰ ῥεῖθρα ἐχορηγεῖτο, καὶ οὐ φύσεως ἀκολουθίᾳ ἀλλὰ ἀπὸ δωρέας χαρίσματος, καὶ μετὰ τὸ σῶμα ὡς τὸ πνεῦμα ἔτι εἰς τὴν ἔρημον ἡ ἐπιθυμία.]

units.la: Sanè vsus vtriusq; huius cibi & potus gemi nus fuit. Dabantur enim ad alimoniam ac su stentationem corporum, & simul ad eum mo dum, miraculosum videlicet, ad alendam edē tium ac bibentium fidem subministrabantur. Etenim si corpora tantum pascere voluisset do minus, poterat hoc communi naturæ cursu absque miraculo facere. Et hic erat potissimus vsus cibi huius ac potus, faciens ad cibandum edentis ac bibentis spiritum, unde non immerito spiritualis hic cibus, & spiritualis potus ab Apostolo vocatur. Nec insolitum est denominare res à potiori illarum parte, vel respectu. Sicrectè panes illos ac pisces, quibus in deserto dominus populum se sequentem miraculosa virtute pauit, spiritualem escam vocabis.
units.tr: Indeed, the use of each of these food and drink was twofold. For they were given for the nourishment and sustenance of the bodies, and at the same time, in that miraculous manner, they were supplied to nourish the faith of those who ate and drank. For if the Lord had wished only to feed the bodies, he could have done so by the common course of nature without a miracle. And this was the chief use of this food and drink, serving to feed the spirit of the one who eats and drinks; hence this food and drink are not without reason called spiritual by the Apostle. Nor is it unusual to name things from their chief part or aspect. Thus you may call the loaves and fishes with which the Lord fed the people who followed him in the desert, by miraculous power, a spiritual food.

units.la: Licet enim populus & corporaliter illos edē ret, & corporaliter quoq; pasceretur, sic tamen virtute insolita exhibebantur, vt non corpora modo, sed & spiritus illorum, ad fidem, videli cet inducentes, alere possent.
units.tr: For although the people ate them bodily and were bodily fed, nevertheless they were provided by an unusual power, so that they could nourish not only the bodies but also the spirits of those who ate, namely by leading them to faith.

units.la: Et hic sensus satis quidè rationis habere vi detur, propter quam cibus ac potus Israelitarū in deserto spirituales ab Apostolo vocari po tuerint, meo tamen iudicio, quoniam non sim pliciter dicit, & omnes escam spiritualē, & po tum spiritualem, sed, & omnes eandem escam spiritualem comederunt, & omnes eūdem po tum spiritualem biberunt, quatenus non inter se modo, sed & nobiscum eodem quo nos cibo ac potu spirituali sunt vsi, respicientium hic ma gis est ad mysterium, in quo nos cum illis cō municamus, & cuius respectu nostr quoq; ci bus ac potus, quem vtrunque secundum Sen uatoris institutionem de mensa illius accipit fi delium ecclesia, spiritualis vocatur. Mysteri um autem nostræ communicationis est in Chri sto, panè vitæ, ac potu salutis. Ergo illic quoq; mysterium Man & aquæ in Christo fuit. Qua re & addit Apostolus, bibebant enim de spiri tuali quæ sequuta est petra, petra verò illa erat Christus. Igitur propter Christum, cibum no strum ac potum, cuius mysterium in Man & pe tra deserti adumbrabatur. Israelitas Apostolus cibum spiritualem comedisse, ac potum spiri tualem bibisse dicit. Rectè ergo Augustin fide manente signa variata esse, Israelitas q; pro ma gno eiusdem Christi sacramento aquam de pe tra profluentem bibisse dicit.
units.tr: And this sense seems to have considerable reason, on account of which the food and drink of the Israelites in the wilderness could be called spiritual by the Apostle. In my judgment, however, since he does not say simply "all ate spiritual food and drank spiritual drink," but "all ate the same spiritual food and all drank the same spiritual drink," the sense looks rather to the mystery in which we share with them, and in view of which our food and drink also, which the church of the faithful receives from his table according to the Savior's institution, are called spiritual. The mystery of our communion is in Christ, the bread of life and the drink of salvation. Therefore the mystery of manna and water was in Christ there also. Hence the Apostle adds: "for they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, and that rock was Christ." So, because of Christ, our food and drink, whose mystery was foreshadowed in the manna and the rock of the desert, the Apostle says that the Israelites ate spiritual food and drank spiritual drink. Augustine rightly says that while the faith remained the same, the signs were varied, and that the Israelites drank water flowing from the rock as a great sacrament of this same Christ.

units.la: Adhuc quæri poterit, quomodo Israelitæ in deserto eundem nobiscum spiritualem ci bum comedisse dicantur, cum Christus neget ipsis verum ac cœlestem panem datum esse à Mose, dicens Iohan. 6. Non Moses dedit vobis panem de cœlo, sed pater meus dat vobis panē
units.tr: It may still be asked how the Israelites in the wilderness are said to have eaten the same spiritual food as we do, since Christ denies that the true and heavenly bread was given to them by Moses, saying in John 6: "Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven."

units.la: de cœlo verum. Panis enim verus est, qui de cœ lo descendit, & dat vitam mundo. Et Patres ve stri manducauerunt manna in deserto, & mor tui sunt. Hic est panis de cœlo descendens, vt si quis ex ipsomanducauerit, non moriatur. Ego sum panis viuus qui de cœlo descendi, &c. qui bus vtique verbis & negat eos verum panem comedisse, & inter id quod illi ederunt & se pa nem verum quem nos edimus, discriminat. Quomodo ergo eundem nobiscum spiritualē cibum manducarunt?
units.tr: "For the bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world. Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness and died. This is the bread which comes down from heaven, that if anyone eat of it he may not die. I am the living bread which came down from heaven," etc. By these words he certainly denies that they ate the true bread, and he distinguishes between what they ate and the true bread which we eat. How then did they eat the same spiritual food as we do?

units.la: Respondeo. Manna quod manducarunt pa tres, non sic spiritualis cibus fuit, vt esset verus panis dans vitam mundo, sed vt esset illius sa cramentum. Christus igitur loquens Iudæis de hoc manna carnaliter & absq; scientia myste rij illius, ac simul de Mose contra ipsum gloriā tibus, vt manem ipsorum gloriationem refu tet, negat Mosen verum panem dedisse, sed da ri hunc à patre affirmat: deinde inter se panem vitæ & manna discriminat, vt illius infirmita tem perstringens ad se verum vitæ panē quod- uis inuitet. Hæc autem non eo sunt dicta vt negetur manna aliquo modo spiritualem suis se cibum, hoc est, veri cibi sacramentum, & ha ctenus patres eundem nobiscum cibum come disse. Christus loquutus est de manna sim pliciter, vt de cibo corporis contra carnales Iudæos ventris ac periturì cibi seruos, Paulus verò vt de cibo mystico & sacramentali, cōtra pseudochristianos sacramēto cœlestis cibi abu tentes, & interim de illo præsumentes. Sic a lio atque alio respectu diuersimodè de re eadē sunt loquuti.
units.tr: I answer: the manna which the fathers ate was not so spiritual food that it was the true bread giving life to the world, but that it was a sacrament of it. Christ, therefore, speaking to the Jews, who were boasting of this manna carnally and without knowledge of its mystery, and at the same time boasting of Moses against himself, in order to refute their boasting, denies that Moses gave the true bread, but affirms that it is given by the Father. Then he distinguishes between the bread of life and the manna, so that, censuring the weakness of the manna, he invites them to the true bread of life, which is himself. These things, however, were not said in order to deny that the manna in some way was spiritual food for them, that is, a sacrament of the true food, and that the fathers thus ate the same food as we do. Christ spoke of the manna simply, as of bodily food, against the carnal Jews, servants of the belly and of perishing food; but Paul speaks of it as mystical and sacramental food, against false Christians who abuse the sacrament of heavenly food and presume upon it. Thus the same thing was spoken of in different ways, from different and diverse points of view.

units.la: Rursus dicet quisquā. Si manna & aqua de petra cibus ac potus spiritualis, & sacramentū corporis ac sanguinis domini fuerūt, quare in deserto tantum & non etiam in ipsa terra Ca naan perseueranter tunt toto Veteris testamē ti decursu ad ipsum vsq; Christū exhibita, quē admodū nobis toto Noui testamenti tempore ad reditum vsq; Christi sacramentū corporis ac sanguinis illius subministratur?
units.tr: Again someone will say: if the manna and the water from the rock were spiritual food and drink and a sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord, why were they offered only in the wilderness and not also continually in the land of Canaan throughout the whole course of the Old Testament, up to Christ himself, as to us in the whole time of the New Testament until the return of Christ the sacrament of his body and blood is administered?

units.la: Respondeo. Duo sunt sacramentorum ge nera. Vnum eorū quæ mirabili & insolito mo do administrabantur. Alterum eorum quæ ci tra miraculum externum gerantur. In priori non est certa institutio, sed libera diuinæ pro uidentiæ dispensatio. In posteriori verò insti tutio est certo verbo expressa, ac toto testamē ti tempore durans. Ad prius genus pertinent nubes ac transitus maris, manna item & aqua de petra. Hæc sunt populo rudi modis insoli tis, cum miraculo attamperâter, partim semel tantum, vtpote transitus maris, partim toto de serti incolatu exhibita, urpote nubes, manna & aqua, quo non modo figuris, sed & manife stis miraculis in fide prouidentiæ Dei alere tur. Ad posterius pertinebant Circumcisio & agnus Paschatis, quorum administratio nihil ha bebat miraculi, habebat verò certam & expref sam institutionē toto illo Vet. testamenti tem pore durantem. Huc pertinent & nostra sacra-
units.tr: I answer: there are two kinds of sacraments. One kind is administered in a marvelous and unusual manner; the other is performed without an external miracle. In the first kind there is no fixed institution, but a free dispensation of divine providence. In the second, however, there is an institution expressed in a fixed word, and lasting through the whole time of the testament. To the first kind belong the clouds and the passage through the sea, likewise the manna and the water from the rock. These were offered to a rude people in unusual ways, attended by a miracle, partly only once, as the passage through the sea, partly throughout the whole sojourn in the wilderness, as the clouds, manna and water, by which the people were nourished in faith in God's providence not only by figures but also by manifest miracles. To the second kind belonged circumcision and the Passover lamb, whose administration had nothing miraculous, but had a fixed and express institution lasting through the whole time of the Old Testament. To this kind belong also our sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper, which are likewise dispensed without miracle and have an institution lasting to the end of the world. And because they are performed and administered by men, and are known to all, they can indeed be held in honor as religious rites, but cannot be held in amazement as miracles, to use the words of Augustine. That people therefore had two kinds of sacraments, even while constituted in the wilderness: one of which served for a time the rudeness of that people, while the other lasted through the whole time of the Old Testament until Christ.

units.la: Quaest. II.
units.tr: Question II.

units.la: Quaest. III.
units.tr: Question III.

units.la: Duo sacra mentorum genera. menta baptismus & cœna domini quæ & ipsa citra miraculum dispensantur, & institutione habent [?]ad finem vsq; mundi perseuerantem: & quia per homines fiunt & dispensantur, sunt que omnibus nota, honorem quidem tanquam religiosa habere possunt, stupore vero tanquam mira, vt verbis Augustini vtar, non possunt. Habuit igitur populus ille duo sacramentorum genera, etiam in deserto constitutum, quorum vnum ad tempus ruditati ipsius seruiebat alterum vero toto Veteris testamenti tempore ad Christum vsq; durauit.
units.tr: There are two kinds of sacraments: baptism and the Lord's Supper. These too are dispensed without miracle, and their institution remains in force until the end of the world. Because they are performed and dispensed by men, and are known to everyone, they can be held in honour as religious rites, but they cannot be held in wonder, to use Augustine's words. That people, then, though placed in the desert, had two kinds of sacraments. One of these served for a time to meet the crudeness of that people, while the other lasted through the whole period of the Old Testament, until Christ.

units.la: BIBERVNT enim de spirituali, quæ sequuta est petra.) Rationem reddit, quare patres potum spiritualem bibisse dicat, cum aquam terrenam biberint eandem vnà cum iumentis. De manna nihil rationis subiecit, ob quam ci-bum ipsum spiritualem vocauerit. Etenim illud & substantia sua inusitatum, & modo quo quæ mirabili cœlitus demissum fuerat, vt facile capi queat, quare illud spirituale cibum vocet. Biberunt inquit, de spirituali petra, quæ se quuta est, vel, quæ sequebatur. Ergo aquam illam propterea spiritualem vocat, quod ac petra spirituali promanauit. Cum dicit, biberunt de spirituali petra, auocat mentes legentium à petra corporali, ad Christum petram spiritua-lem: vnde & subdit, petra autem erat Christus. Potest & corporea petra spiritualis vocari, propterea quod figura fuit spiritualis petræ. Verum quoniam addit, quæ sequebatur, intelligendum esse puto de ipso Christo. Is enim consequebatur populum in deserto, & aquas illi miraculo sa scaturigine subministrabat. Quemadmodu hodie quoq; donec in transitu profectionis no-stræ sumus, ecclesiam suam consequitur, illiq; & panem & aquam vitæ suppeditat, vsq; dum ad coelestem patriam venerimus, vbi Deus erit omnia in omnibus. Sic promisit nobis dicens: Ecce ego vobiscum sum vsq; ad consummationem sæculi. Matthæi vltimo. Proponitur ergo nobis hoc sensu Christus non modo perpetuus in se durans inde ab initio ad finem vique, vt idem sit heri, & hodie, & in sæcula, sed & continuus populi Dei gubernator mediatorac Seruator.
units.tr: "They drank of that spiritual Rock which followed them." He gives the reason why he says the fathers drank a spiritual drink, when they drank the same earthly water along with their cattle. He added no reason why he calls the manna spiritual food. Indeed, its substance was unusual, and the way it was sent down from heaven made it easy to see why he calls it spiritual food. He says they drank of the spiritual Rock that followed them, or that was following them. So he calls that water spiritual because it flowed from a spiritual rock. When he says they drank of a spiritual rock, he turns the minds of his readers away from the physical rock to Christ, the spiritual Rock, and so he adds: "Now the Rock was Christ." The bodily rock could also be called spiritual, since it was a figure of the spiritual Rock. But since he adds "which followed them," I think this must be understood of Christ himself. For he followed the people in the wilderness and supplied them with water from the miraculous spring. In the same way today also, while we are on the journey of our pilgrimage, he follows his Church and gives it bread and the water of life, until we come to the heavenly fatherland, where God will be all in all. So he promised us, saying: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age" (Matthew, last chapter). In this sense, then, Christ is set before us not only as one who remains the same in himself from the beginning to the end of the world, so that he is "the same yesterday, today, and forever," but also as the continual governor, mediator, and Saviour of the people of God.

units.la: PETRA aut illa erat Christus.)
