Sic uisum est legere, quoniam in Græco est ἡ πέτρα, λῶ ὁ χριστός, quod idem esse videtur, ac si diceret ὡς ἡ πέτρα præsertim, cum de petra populum illū consequuta loquatur. Quasi dicat. Petra autem illa spiritualis, quæ populum consequebatur, & potū spiritualem subministrabat, erat Christus, idem ille qui nos quoq; consequitur, ac eibum nobis potumq; spiritualem dispensat. Augustinus intelligit de petra corporea, quia Moses baculo suo percussit, inq; fontem exundantium aquarum conuertit. Atq; ideo exponit, petra erat Christus, id est, significabat Christū. Significabat quidem Christum illa petra corporea & à Mose percussa, ac recte spiritualis vocari potest: verum quoniam prædicatum hoc consequutionis illi non potest commode tri-bui, existimo Apostolum loqui de Christo spirituali petra, populum consequuta, ideoq; qd dicit: Petra autem illa erat Christus, non esse exponendum, petra illa significabat Christum sed, quemadmodum verba sonant, petra illa, quæ sequebatur eos, erat Christus. Cum nemine tamen hac de re contendero. Si respexerimus ad petram corporalem, illa vtiq; Christus non erat, sed Christum figurabat ac significabat, si ad spiritualem, patres illos in deserto co sequutam, id est, ad Christum ipsum, non conueniet vt exponamus, petra illa significabat Christum. Neque enim seipsum significabat Christus, sed à petra corporea, à manna, à nube &c. significabatur.
units.tr: "Now that Rock was Christ." It seemed right to read it this way, because in the Greek it is "ἡ πέτρα δὲ ἦν ὁ Χριστός," which seems to be the same as if it said "ὡς ἡ πέτρα" especially since he is speaking of the rock that followed that people. It is as if he said: that spiritual Rock which followed the people and supplied them with spiritual drink was Christ, the same one who also follows us and dispenses to us spiritual food and drink. Augustine understands it of the bodily rock, because Moses struck it with his staff and turned it into a fountain of flowing waters. And so he explains "the Rock was Christ" as meaning "it signified Christ." That bodily rock, struck by Moses, did indeed signify Christ, and it can rightly be called spiritual. But since this attribute of following cannot fittingly be given to that rock, I think the Apostle is speaking of Christ, the spiritual Rock, who followed the fathers who were in the wilderness. So the words "that Rock was Christ" should not be explained as "that rock signified Christ," but, as the words sound, "that rock which followed them was Christ." Yet I will not contend with anyone about this matter. If we look to the bodily rock, it was not Christ, but it prefigured and signified Christ. If we look to the spiritual rock that followed those fathers in the wilderness, that is, to Christ himself, it will not fit to explain it as "the rock signified Christ." For Christ did not signify himself, but was signified by the bodily rock, by the manna, by the cloud, and so on.

units.la: SED plures illorum no approbauit Deus: prostrati sunt enim in deserto.) Hactenus vniuersalem gratiæ Dei communicatione absoluit, qua patres omnes baptismatis, spiritualisque cibi ac potus participes fuisse dixit, iam co sequeter quod supra ad alteram præsentis cau-sę partem pertinere dixi-mus, de plurium repro-batione subijcit, quo comprobet, non saluari quenquem externorum mysteriorum comunicatione, si fidesac veræ pietatis studium defuerit. Omnes, inquit, baptizati fuerunt, omnes cibum ac potum spiritualem ederunt & biberunt, eundem quem nos edimus ac bibimus, sed non omnes sunt saluati. Nam complures illorum non approbauit Deus. Quare videte ne quod illis accidit, vobis quoq; vsuueniat.
units.tr: "But God was not pleased with most of them, for they were overthrown in the wilderness." Up to this point he has finished his account of the common sharing of God's grace, by which he said that all the fathers were partakers of baptism and of spiritual food and drink. Now he follows on with what I said above belongs to the other part of the present argument, and adds the rejection of many, to show that no one is saved merely by sharing in the outward mysteries if faith and the zeal of true godliness are lacking. "All," he says, "were baptized, all ate and drank the same spiritual food and drink that we eat and drink, but not all were saved. For God was not pleased with many of them. So take care that what happened to them does not happen to you as well."

units.la: Illud, prostrati sunt enim in deserto, argumetum habet præcedentis, quo plures illorum à Deo reprobatos esse dixit. Nò dicit, mortui enim sunt, sed, prostrati sunt in deserto. In deserto mortui sunt & Moses & Aaró, & Maria, multiq; pij senes, priusquam populus ille in terram promissam intraret, de quibus dici non potest quod à Deo sint reprobati. Aliud est simpliciter mori, communi lege naturæ, & aliud singulari vltione diuina prosterni, & è medio tolli. Ex posteriori hoc colligit argumentū iræ Dei. Huc pertinent historiæ diuinæ vltionis, quas mox subijciet.
units.tr: The clause "for they were overthrown in the wilderness" supports the preceding statement, in which he said that many of them were rejected by God. He does not say "they died," but "they were overthrown in the wilderness." Moses and Aaron and Miriam died in the wilderness, and many godly old men too, before that people entered the promised land, and it cannot be said of them that God rejected them. It is one thing to die simply, by the common law of nature, and another to be struck down and removed from the midst by a singular vengeance of God. From this latter he draws the argument about the wrath of God. To this belong the histories of divine vengeance which he will set out shortly.

units.la: Obserua. SED plures illorum inquit.) Ergo non est sequenda multitudo, nec faciendū quod plures in populo faciunt. Neq; enim, inquit ille, tam bene cum rebus humanis genitur vt meliora pluribus placeant. Argumentum pessimi turba est. Quæramus quid optime factum sit non quid vsitatissimum, & quid nos in possessione felicitatis æternæ constituat, nō quid vulgo pessimo ueritatis interpreti proba-tum sit.
units.tr: Take note. "But God was not pleased with most of them." Therefore the multitude is not to be followed, nor should we do what most people in the people do. For, as someone says, human affairs are not so well ordered that better things please more people. The majority is an argument for the worst. Let us ask what has been done best, not what is most common, and what establishes us in possession of eternal happiness, not what has been approved by the worst crowd, the interpreter of the truth.

units.la: NON approbauit Deus, inquit.) Atqui mul-ta illis impendit beneficia, quæ vtiq; dilectionis erant indicia. Nemo ergo cum nostri tem-poris impostoribus secúritatem ex eo sibi pol-liceatur, quod in ecclesia suam dominus mul-ta beneficia contulit, quasi propterea maior il-lius multitudo errare ac præuaricari non pos-sit. Christus, inquiunt, diligit ecclesiam suam, quomodo ergo sineret illa tot sæculis errare? Diligit eam, sed plures ex illa nō approbat, & ab illis ipse non diligitur. Nisi acceptam gratiā bene collocemus placere illi non possumus.
units.tr: "God was not pleased," he says. Yet he bestowed many benefits upon them, which were certainly signs of his love. So no one among the impostors of our time should promise himself security from the fact that the Lord has bestowed many benefits on his Church, as if for that reason so great a multitude could not wander and fall away. "Christ," they say, "loves his Church; how then would he allow it to err for so many centuries?" He loves it, but he is not pleased with many who belong to it, and by them he is not loved. Unless we use the grace we have received well, we cannot please him.

units.la: PROSTRATI sunt, inquit, in deserto.) Sic pereundum est in itinere peregrinationis nostrę pluribus, propter diffidentiam & incredulitatem. Ergo pauci saluantur. Multi enim uocati, pauci electi.
units.tr: "They were overthrown," he says, "in the wilderness." So in the same way many will perish on the road of our pilgrimage, because of distrust and unbelief. Therefore few are saved. For "many are called, but few are chosen."

units.la: Hęc autem figurę nostri fuerunt, ne simus nos cōcupiscentes rerum malarū, quemadmodū & illi cōcupierunt. Neq; simulacrorū sitis cultores, sicut quidam illorū, quemadmodum scriptum est, sedit populus ut ederet ac biberet, & surrexerunt ut luderent. Neq; scortemur sicut quidam illorum scortati sunt, & cōciderunt uno die uigintitria millia. Neq; tentemus Christum, sicut & quidam illorum tentarunt, & a serpentibus extincti sunt. Neq; murmuretis, sicut & quidā illorū murmurauerūt, & interempti sunt ab exterminatore. Hęc autem omnia ęfigurę contigerunt illis, scripra uero sunt propter admonitionem nostri, in quos termini sęculorum inciderunt. Proinde qui sibi stare uidetur, uideat ne cadat.
units.tr: Now these things happened to them as figures for us, so that we should not crave evil things as they craved. Nor should we be worshippers of idols, as some of them were, as it is written: "The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play." Nor should we commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and in one day twenty-three thousand fell. Nor should we tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him, and were destroyed by serpents. Nor should we murmur, as some of them murmured, and were destroyed by the destroyer. Now all these things happened to them as figures, but they were written down for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall.

units.la: Applicat ea quæ de patribus Israelitarum in medium adduxit, ac declarat quomodo ad propositum faciant, proinde ac si Corinthij fideles dicat ... Hæc, inquit, nō sunt ut nuda & obsoleta facta sed ut typi inspicienda, deinde non sunt typi ad nos nihil sed potissimum ac peculiariter pertinentes. Ad primum pertinet, quod dicit: Hæc autem fuerunt figurę. In Græco est τύποι, quam uocem posuit pro ..., id est, exemplis, ut verti queat: Hæc autem exempla nostri fuerunt. Unde & Chrysost. inter cætera dicit, ... Ad alterum pertinet, quod non simpliciter dicit: Hæc autem exempla fuerunt, neq;: Hæc autem exempla fuerunt Israelitarum, sed, hæc autem exempla nostri fuerunt, Christianorum uidelicet. Sic occurrit illis qui poterant ista, tanquam Iudaica & a conditione Christianorū aliena respuere.
units.tr: He applies what he has brought forward about the fathers of Israel, and shows how it bears on his purpose, just as if he were speaking to the faithful Corinthians: these things, he says, are not to be seen as bare and outdated deeds, but as types to be looked into; and then, they are not types that have nothing to do with us, but especially and peculiarly pertain to us. To the first point belongs what he says: "Now these things were figures." In the Greek it is τύποι, a word he uses for examples, so that it may be rendered: "Now these things were examples for us." Hence Chrysostom also says, among other things... To the second point belongs the fact that he does not simply say, "These were examples," nor "These were examples of the Israelites," but "These things were examples for us," that is, of Christians. In this way he meets those who could reject these things as Jewish and foreign to the condition of Christians.

units.la: Non est autem hoc obiter, sed magna cum ratione dictum. Quę Israelitis tam mala quàm bona euenerunt, exempla fuerunt eorum qui illis in participatione eiusdem ecclesiæ, gratiæ ac salutis successerunt, nō illis, qui prorsus omnis cōsortij illorum exortes & ab ecclesia Dei alieni permanserunt. In eadē ecclesia duo sunt populi, Israelitarum & gentium, ex æquo quidem eiusdem fidei ac salutis consortes, uerum hoc ordine, ut Israelitæ præcesserint, gētes uero successerint. Quare ordinis huius lege cōsequitur, ut quæ Israelitis euenerunt exempla, fuerint fidelium ex gentibus. Ratio exempli est, ut cedat ad cautionem nō alia uia sed prorsus eadem insequentibus, nec possunt quæ cō-
units.tr: This is not said in passing, but with great reason. What happened to the Israelites, both evil and good, were examples for those who succeeded them in the participation of the same Church, grace, and salvation, not for those who remained wholly outside all fellowship with them and alien from the Church of God. In the same Church there are two peoples, that of the Israelites and that of the Gentiles, equal partners in the same faith and salvation, but in this order: the Israelites went before, and the Gentiles followed after. Therefore by the law of this order it follows that what happened to the Israelites were examples for the faithful from the Gentiles. The purpose of an example is that it serves as a warning, not by another way but by exactly the same way, for those who follow; and what happens cannot benefit those who went before, but only those who follow. Thus what befell the Israelites serves us, and for this reason the Apostle calls them our types. The chief reason is that we have the same God and Lord as they did, and the same

units.la: tingunt prodesse ijs qui præcesserunt, sed ijs tantum qui sequuntur. Ita seruiunt nobis quæ acciderunt Israelitis, & hanc ob causam typi nostri vocātur ab Apostolo. Ratio potissima est, quod idem nobis cum illis est Deus ac dominus, eademq; ab vtrisq; requiritur fidei ac pietatis synceritas, & quod mutatio iudicij & iustitiæ in Deum nō cādit. Admonemur igitur quomodo legendæ sint nobis sacræ Veteris testamenti scripturæ, haud videlicet, quasi à nostræ religionis sortis, ac salutis conditione alienæ sed tanquam exempla nos potissimum concernentia.
units.tr: They do not profit those who went before, but only those who come after. So the things that happened to the Israelites serve us in this way, and for this reason the Apostle calls them our types. The chief reason is that God and the Lord are the same for us as for them, that the same sincerity of faith and piety is required of both, and that a change of judgment and justice does not befall God. We are therefore taught how the sacred Scriptures of the Old Testament are to be read by us: not, of course, as though they were foreign to the condition of our religion and salvation, but as examples that chiefly concern us.

units.la: NE simus nos concupiscentes rerū malarū quemadmodum & illi concupierunt.) Duo sunt exemplorum genera, fugiedarum rerum unum, imitandarum alterū. Prius absterret ab imitatione, posterius allicit. Ad prius pertinere significans quæ attulit in medio Israelitarū exempla, dicit: Hæc autem figurę nostri fuerunt, ne simus concupiscentes rerum malarū, quemadmodum & illi concupierunt. Sunt autem duæ exempli partes. Factum uidelicet, & euentus uel fructus facti. Factum nec in priori exemplorum genere uim habet abstē rendi, nec in posteriori, alliciendi, sed adhibenda est utrobiq; euentuum consyderatio. Exempla uiciorum, præcipue si magnis subeant animos authoribus, ut ille canit, magnis inuitat q abstērēt, uirtutū uero, quis authoritate maiorum commendentur, prorsus infirma sunt ad alliciendum. Quare proponēdi sunt ante oculos euentus factorū; perditio uidelicet reproborum, & felicitas piorum studia consequuta. sic hoc quoq; loco non id tantum in exemplis est Israelitarū inspiciendū, quod mala cōcupiuerunt, sed adiungendum quod præmisit dicens, uerum plures illorum haud approbauit Deus, sed prostrati sunt in deserto. In eo nāque pars illa exempli est, quæ uim habet à malorum cōcupiscentia abstērrendi omnes eos, qui nec displicere Deo nec perire, sed potius placere illi, & ad salutem pertingere cupiunt.
units.tr: "Lest we be lusters after evil things, as they also lusted." There are two kinds of examples: one of things to be shunned, the other of things to be imitated. The former deters from imitation, the latter allures. To the former belongs what he sets out in the examples of the Israelites, saying: "Now these things were our figures, that we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted." An example has two parts: the deed itself, and the outcome or fruit of the deed. In the first kind of example the deed has no power to deter, nor in the second kind to allure; in both cases the outcome must be considered. Examples of vices, especially when they come upon minds with great authorities behind them, as that poet sings, invite and deter by their greatness; but virtues, when commended only by the authority of elders, are wholly weak at attracting. Hence the outcomes of deeds must be set before the eyes: namely, the destruction of the reprobate and the happiness of those who pursued piety. So in this place we must look at the examples of the Israelites not only in that they lusted after evil things, but also at what he added, saying: "But God was not pleased with most of them, for they were overthrown in the desert." In that is the part of the example that has the power to turn away from the lust for evil all those who desire not to displease God nor to perish, but rather to please him and attain salvation.

units.la: NE simus, inquit, concupiscentes rerū malarum.) Quid est quod non dicit: ne simus faciētes res malas? An nō peius est facere q cōcupiscere malum? Respondeo. Coram Deo concupiscentia pro facto est. Deinde & radix est facti. Vnusquisq;, inquit Iacobus, tentatur à concupiscentia sua abstractus & illectus. Deinde concupiscentia cum conceperit, parit peccatum, peccatum uero ubi consummatum est, generat mortem. Itaq; duplici nomine admonemur, ut fugiamus concupiscentiam rerum malarum: cum quod allicit ad opus peccati, tum quod etiāsi illud non sequatur, ipsa tamen corā Deo pro facto reputatur, iuxta illud Christi Seruatoris: Qui viderit mulierē ad cōcupiscēdū cā, iā adulteriū admisit cū ea i corde suo.
units.tr: "Lest we be," he says, "lusters after evil things." Why does he not say: lest we be doers of evil things? Is it not worse to do evil than to lust after it? I answer: before God, lust is counted as the deed. Moreover, it is the root of the deed. "Each one," says James, "is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own lust." Then lust, once conceived, bears sin, and sin, when it is complete, brings forth death. We are therefore admonished for two reasons to flee lust for evil things: first, because it entices to the work of sin; second, because even if the deed does not follow, lust itself is reckoned as a deed before God, according to that saying of Christ the Saviour: "Whoever looks on a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart."

units.la: QVEMADMODVM, inquit, & illi concupiuerūt.) Chrysost. visum hoc est generaliter dictum, sic ut quæ sequūtur, illius sint species, propterea quod unūquodq; peccatū ex mala nascatur
units.tr: "As, he says, they also lusted." Chrysostom: this seems said in general terms, so that what follows are its kinds, because every sin is born of evil lust.

units.la: Ratio exempli.
units.tr: The reason of the example.

units.la: Duo sunt exemplorum genera.
units.tr: There are two kinds of examples.

units.la: Duæ sunt partes exempli.
units.tr: An example has two parts.

units.la: Quæstio. i.
units.tr: Question 1.

units.la: Iacobi 1. nascatur concupiscētia. Verū, meo iudicio, ha bet hæc particula singulare malę concupiscē tiæ exemplum, &referenda est ad historiā quę Num. 11. legitur. Populus flagrabat desyderiò carnium, sedens flens, ac dicens: Quis dabit no bis ad vescendū carnes? Recordamur piscium, quos comedimus in Ægypto gratis: in mente veniunt nobis cucumeres & pepones porrio, & cepe & allia. Anima nostra arida est, oculi nostri nihil vident aliud q; Man. Hæc erat illo rum prauà cōcupiscentia. In hanc animaduer tit Deus graui vltione. Cum enim adhuc esset caro in ipsorū dentibus, cōcitatus est in eos su ror domini, percusíq; sunt plaga magna valde, ac vocatus est locus ille, sepulcra concupi scentiæ. Ibi nanq; sepelierunt populū, qui con cupierat carnes. Huius exēpli respectu dehor tatur Corinthios Apostolus à consimili praua concupiscentia, dicens: Ne simus concupiscē tes rerū malarū quēadmodū & illi cōcupierūt.
units.tr: ...is born of lust. (Compare James 1.) Yet, in my judgment, this clause contains a singular example of evil lust, and is to be referred to the history read in Num. 11. There the people burned with desire for meat, sitting down and weeping and saying: "Who will give us flesh to eat? We remember the fish which we ate freely in Egypt; the cucumbers and melons, the leeks, onions and garlic come to mind. Our soul is dry; our eyes see nothing but manna." This was their wicked lust, and God punished it with severe vengeance. For while the flesh was still between their teeth, the fury of the Lord was kindled against them, and they were struck with a very great plague; and that place was called the graves of lust, for there they buried the people who had lusted after meat. With respect to this example the Apostle warns the Corinthians against a similar wicked lust, saying: "Lest we be lusters after evil things, as they also lusted."

units.la: Sed nascitur hic quæstio, quōmodo dicat A postolus Israelitas concupiuisse res malas, vbi appetebát carnes, pisces, & pe&allia. Etenim si hæc mala in se erat, mala comederant in Æ gypto, quod tamē nusquā in illis reprehendi tur. Deinde, quomodo conueniat hæc admo nitio doctrinæ Euangelij, qua hic ipse Apostolus 1. Tim. 4. omnē creaturā Dei bonā esse, nec quicquā reijciendū dicit, vbi de interdictu ci borū loquitur, quē spiritus errorum in eccle siam Christi erant introducturi. Adhæc, si non sunt hæc mala sed bona quomodo reprehen sibilis sit concupiscentia rerum non malarum sed bonarum? Respondeo. Nec mala sunt caro, pisces, porri, cepe & allia, nec male docuit loco citato Apostolus, nec peccarunt Israelitæ talia comedēdo in Ægypto, nec in deserto talibus vescendo peccassent, nec malum est cibū bo num & necessariū concupiscere, sed ex circū stantijs mal . fuit ista Israelitarū concupiscen tia, quibus res in se bonæ malæ redduntur.
units.tr: But here a question arises: how does the Apostle say that the Israelites lusted after evil things, when they craved flesh, fish, leeks, onions and garlic? For if these were evil in themselves, they had eaten evil things in Egypt, which is nowhere blamed in them. Further, how does this admonition agree with the teaching of the Gospel, by which this same Apostle says in 1 Tim. 4. that every creature of God is good and nothing is to be rejected, where he speaks of the forbidding of foods which the spirits of error were going to introduce into the Church of Christ? Besides, if these things are not evil but good, how can lust for things not evil but good be blameworthy? I answer: neither flesh, fish, leeks, onions nor garlic are evil; nor did the Apostle teach falsely in the passage cited; nor did the Israelites sin by eating such things in Egypt, nor would they have sinned by feeding on such things in the desert. Nor is it evil to desire good and necessary food. But from the circumstances that Israelite lust became evil, by which things good in themselves are made bad.

units.la: Primum ipsi erat mali, increduli & immun di. Immundis aūt immunda sunt omnia. De inde fastidiebant cibū cœlestem & panem an gelicum. Tertio concupiscebant carnes nō ex fame sed ex libidine voluptuari & gulæ. Quar to concupiscendo murmurabát contra domi num ac serui eius Mosen. Huiusodi ergo cō cupiscentia merito displicebat domino, & re ete dicit Apostolus quod res malas cōcupiue rint. Nec est præter rationē, quod Corinthios monet, ne simili cōcupiscentiæ locū præbeat. Præterquā enim quod domino displicet, plu rimū habet efficaciæ ad synceritatē fidei labe factandum, dum procliuis est ad cōmercia in eunda cum infidelibus, & animum reddit de licatum, nulliusque laboris pro seruanda fide subeundi tolerantem.
units.tr: First, they themselves were evil, unbelieving and unclean; and to the unclean all things are unclean. Second, they loathed heavenly food and angelic bread. Third, they lusted for flesh not from hunger but from voluptuous desire and gluttony. Fourth, in their lusting they murmured against the Lord and against Moses, his servant. Lust of this kind therefore rightly displeased the Lord, and the Apostle rightly says that they lusted after evil things. Nor is it beside the point that he warns the Corinthians not to give place to similar lust. For besides displeasing the Lord, it has great power to stain the sincerity of faith, since it inclines a man to dealings with unbelievers, makes the mind delicate, and renders it unable to endure any labour in keeping the faith.

units.la: NEQVE simulacrorum fitis cultores, sicut quidā illorū, quemadmodū scriptū: sedit po pulus ut ederent & biberent, & surrrexerūt ut luderent. ) Quoniā periculum erat, ne praua concupiscētia seducti, qui cum infidelibus de
units.tr: "Nor become idolaters, as some of them did; as it is written: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play." Since there was a danger that men seduced by evil lust, who ate with unbelievers the things sacrificed to idols,

units.la: eidolothytis manducabant, paulatim ad cul tum eidolorum relaberentur, proponit illis a liud populi peccatoris exemplū, vnde moniti cultum simulacrorum fugerent. Ne simulacro rum, inquit, fitis cultores. Hoc peccati genus & supra cap 5. 6. & 8. perstrinxit. Plurimum e nim metuebat, ne recens à cultu simulacrorū per doctrinam Euangelij auocati, denuò ad il lum consortio infidelium pellicerentur. Capi te quinto recessuit eidolorum cultorem inter eos quos ab omni consortio fidelium tanquā malos excludere debebant. Postea sexto con numerauit eum illis quibus non est pars in re gno Dei. Octauo redarguit culturam simula crorum à vanitate eidoli, &⁠ ... In præsen ti abstterret ab ea inducto reproborum Israeli tarum exemplo, eoq; admodum ad causam quā agit accommodo. Sicut quidam illorum, in quit, sicut scriptum est, sedit populus vt ede rent, &c. Loquitur de historia vituli conflati lis, quem in absentia Mosis erexerunt & colue rūt, qua de re legere est Exodij 32. Notior aūt est historia sacrę scripturę studiosis, quā vt sit hic aduerbum recensendum. Quam vero per tinenter eam adducat, ex circumstantijs con syderari potest. Primum, hoc genus simulacro rum populus illepaulo ante adorauerat in Æ- gypto, à qua impietate recès erat magnis por tentis abstractus. Deinde, cito sunt ad eā quā plures relapsi, id quod & dominus ipse in illis reprehendit dicens, Vade desce nde, peccauit populus tuus quem eduxisti de terra Ægypti. Recesserunt cito de via quā oftēdisti eis. Ter tio relapsi sunt ad consuetam eidololatriā leui admodum occasione propter absentiā vide licet Mosis. Hæc ipsa consyderabat in isto exē plo Apostolus, metuebatque ne quoniam in ethnicisimo cultibus simulacrorum assueuerat Corinthij, cito ad illos idq; p occasione ab- sentiæ suæ, conuiuijs infidelium illecti relabe rentur. Quàm autem metus hic illius non fue rit vanus sequentia tempora declarant, quibus eidolomania mutatis nominibus & speciebus in ecclesijs eth̃ christianis denuo obtinuit.
units.tr: were gradually falling back into the worship of idols, he sets before them another example, of a sinful people, whereby warned they might flee the worship of images. "Nor become idolaters," he says. He also touched on this kind of sin in chapters 5, 6 and 8. For he feared greatly lest they, recently drawn away from idol worship by the teaching of the Gospel, would again be enticed back by association with unbelievers. In chapter 5 he counted the idolater among those whom they ought to exclude from all fellowship of believers as wicked. Afterwards, in chapter 6, he numbered him among those who have no part in the kingdom of God. In chapter 8 he rebuked the worship of images for the vanity of the idol, &c. Here he deters from it by the example of the reprobate Israelites, and adapts it very aptly to the cause he is pursuing. "As some of them," he says, "as it is written: the people sat down to eat," and so on. He speaks of the history of the molten calf, which they set up and worshipped in Moses' absence; on this one may read Exodus 32. The history is better known to students of Scripture than it needs recounting here. How fittingly he adduces it can be seen from the circumstances. First, this people had worshipped this kind of image in Egypt only shortly before, and had been drawn away from that impiety by great portents. Second, they quickly relapsed into it, which the Lord himself rebukes in them, saying: "Go down; your people has sinned, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt. They have quickly turned aside from the way you showed them." Third, they relapsed into their customary idolatry on very slight occasion, namely Moses' absence. The Apostle considered these very things in this example, and he feared lest, since the Corinthians had been accustomed to idol images in heathen cults, they would quickly fall back into them, and that on the occasion of his absence, enticed by the feasts of unbelievers. That this fear of his was not vain the following ages declare, when idolatry, with its names and forms changed, regained its hold in Christian churches.

units.la: Obserua vero quā caute hic à vocula vniuer sali abstineat. Supra dixit, omnes sub nube fue runt, omnes mare transierunt, omnes in Mo sen baptizati sunt, in nube & in mari, omnes eadem escam spiritualem comederūt, &c. hic vero non dicit, ne simus nos omnes cultores eidolorū sicut omnes illi fuerūt, sed, ne simus cultores eidolorum, sicut quidam illorum fue runt. Dat Israelitis gratiæ quidem vniuersale & catholicam communicationē, præuaricatio nis vero non item, cuius nō omnes sed quos- dam tantū accusat, ne videatur & tota Israelis ecclesiam damnare, & eam ad quam scribebat de catholica defectione habere suspectam.
units.tr: Observe, however, how carefully here he refrains from the little word "all." Above he said: all were under the cloud, all passed through the sea, all were baptized into Moses, in the cloud and in the sea; all ate the same spiritual food, etc. Here, however, he does not say, "let us not all be worshippers of idols, as all of them were," but, "let us not be worshippers of idols, as certain of them were." He grants to the Israelites a universal and catholic participation in grace, but not in transgression, of which he accuses not all but only certain ones, so that he may not seem to condemn the whole church of Israel, and so that he may not make the church to which he was writing appear suspect of general defection.

units.la: Quemadmodum scriptum est, inquit, sedit populus vt ederent & biberent, & surrexerūt vt luderent. Adijcit hanc particulam specifica tionis magis quā ꝓbationis gratia, ad declarā dum quam eidololatriā Israelitarum perstringat. Multoties enim in eam impietatem prefer tim in ipsa terra Canaan constituti inciderunt. Quod si voluisset testimonio scripturæ probare quod dixit, sicut quidam illorum, ea magis attulisset in medium, quæ particulam hanc in historia vituli præcedunt, vtpote, quod mane surgentes obtulerunt vitulo holocausta & hostias pacificas, vel quod sequitur, fecerunt sibi vitulum conflatilem, & adorauerunt, atq; immolantes illi hostias dixerunt: Isti sunt dij tui Israel, qui te eduxerunt de terra Ægypti, quàm quod populus ad manducandum & bibendum consedit, & ad ludendum surrexit. Verum qui dem est, hoc ipsum quod comederunt & biberunt, & ad ludendum surrexerunt, pars erat eidololatriæ, id quod ex circumstantijs patet.
units.tr: "As it is written," he says, "the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play." He adds this clause for the sake of specifying rather than of proving, to show what idolatry of the Israelites he is censuring. For they fell into that impiety many times, especially when they were settled in the land of Canaan itself. Had he wished to prove by the testimony of Scripture what he had said, "as some of them were," he would have brought forward those passages that precede this clause in the history of the calf, namely, that they rose early and offered to the calf burnt offerings and peace offerings, or what follows, "they made for themselves a molten calf, and worshipped it, and sacrificing to it they said: These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt." But it is true that this very eating and drinking, and rising up to play, was a part of idolatry, as is clear from the circumstances.

units.la: Etenim ante vitulum, in honorem vituli, inq; ipsa solennitate vituli, deniq; ex sacrificijs vitulo oblatis comederunt & biberunt, in ipso tamen comedere, bibere ac ludere nō est mox eidololatriam admittere. At quoniam illi quorum gratia scripta sunt hæc ab Apostolo, quàuis ederent & biberent cum infidelibus, nolebant tamen eam ob causam eidololatriæ videri, studio sic admonitionem hanc attemperauit, vt innueret esse illos facto Israelitarum admodum confines, & eodem cum illis laborare uentris studio, ideoq; timendum ipsis esse, ne cum eidololatris ex eidolothytis edentes ac bibentes paulatim ad ipsam eidolorum cultum pellicerentur. Astutissimus fulutis nostræ hostis diabolus, cultus ac dies festos eidolorum conuiuijs ventri iucundis sic insidiosos carnalibus hominibus reddidit, vt eos leui momento ad ipsam eidololatriam hoc quasi condimento pertrahat. Tolle ventris illecebras, & vide quàm sis antichristianismi cultus despicabiles ac desertos redditurus.
units.tr: For before the calf, in honour of the calf, and in the very festival of the calf, and finally from the sacrifices offered to the calf, they ate and drank; yet eating, drinking and playing in themselves do not at once amount to admitting idolatry. But since those for whose sake the Apostle wrote these things, although they ate and drank with unbelievers, were unwilling on that account to be seen as idolaters, he has so tempered this admonition with care, that he might intimate that they were very close to the deed of the Israelites, and labour under the same zeal for the belly, and that they must therefore fear, lest by eating and drinking meat offered to idols with idolaters they be gradually enticed to the very worship of idols. The most crafty enemy of our salvation, the devil, has made the cults and festival days of idols so insidiously attractive to carnal men by the feasts pleasing to the belly, that by this seasoning, as it were, he draws them in a moment into idolatry itself. Take away the allurements of the belly, and see how despicable and deserted you will make the cults of antichrist.

units.la: ET surrexerunt, inquit, vt luderent.) De quo genere ludi loquatur hic scriptura, ipsis quidem verbis non exprimitur, verùm ex circumstantijs ipsius causæ satis liquet fuisse ludum in honorem eidoli institutum, cuius diem festum agebant. Quare siue choro & cantico, siue alio quopiam modo ludum hunc luserint, pertinebat ad cultum vituli, de cuius sacrificijs comederant & biberant. Quare nonnulli exponunt, & surrexerunt ad ludendum, i. ad eidololatrandum. Etenim ad eum ludum à conuiuio eidololatrico, tanquâ ad laudes eidolo per agendas læti & hilares surgebant. Et quoniâ consimilis erat ethnicis consuetudo, vt de mensa eidolorum surgentes in honorem deorum suorum luderent, atq; ita periculum erat Christianis, ne post epulas quas cum illis in ipsorum sacrificijs comedebat, ad ludendum quoq; cum illis surgerent, omnium conuenientissimè præsenti admonitioni inseruit hæc verba: Sedit populus ut ederet ac biberet, ac surrexerut ut luderent. Quasi dicat: Videte ne vbi cum infidelibus editis & bibitis, pinde vobis accidat, atq; accidit Israelitis qui cum edissent ac bibissent, surrexerút ad ludendū coram eidolo.
units.tr: "And rose up," he says, "to play." What kind of play Scripture here means is not expressed in the words themselves, but from the circumstances of the matter it is clear enough that it was a game instituted in honour of the idol, whose festival they were celebrating. Therefore, whether they played this game with a dance and a song, or in some other way, it pertained to the worship of the calf, from whose sacrifices they had eaten and drunk. Hence some explain, "and rose up to play," that is, to worship idols. For they rose from the idolatrous banquet to that play, cheerful and merry, as if to perform praises to the idol. And since it was a custom similar to that of the heathen, to rise from the table of the idols and play in honour of their gods, and so there was danger for Christians, lest after the feasts which they ate with them at their sacrifices, they should also rise to play with them, the Apostle, most fittingly for the present admonition, added these words: "The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play." As if he said: See that, when you eat and drink with unbelievers, it does not happen to you as it happened to the Israelites, who, when they had eaten and drunk, rose up to play before the idol.

units.la: {A}NEQVE scortemur sicut quidâ illorû scortati sunt, & conciderût vno die viginti tria millia.) De scortatione cauenda supra quoq; monuit, cap.5. & 6.idq; fusius aliquanto. Hic de illa vno quidem & altero verbo repetit, verum haud sine singulari ratione. Etenim nō modo peccatū illius, sicuti suprà locis iam dictis, sed & illud in ea consideratqu od plurimum valet ad inducendum intemperantes ad peccatum eidololatriæ, perinde atq; studiû ventris. Carnalis scortatio non solum socia sed & proxena est spiritualis, id est, eidololatriæ. Et quoniâ in ter eidololatras impunè regnabat, periculumque erat, ne per illam carnaliores Christiani ad eidololatriam seducerentur, dehortatur eos ab exemplo Israelitarum, qui & ipsi scortatione carnali ad sacrificia eidolorum sunt perduti. Neq; scortemur, inquit, sicut quidam illorû scortati sunt, & conciderunt vno die viginti tria millia.Loquitur de historia filiarum Moab quæ vocauerunt Israelitas ad sacrificia deorû suorum, illiq; comederunt & adorauerunt Baalpeor, cuius mali illecta-mentum erat, quod cum illis scortarentur, quâ de re Num.25.sic legimus. Morabatur aûteo tempore Israel in Shittim, &coepit populus scortari cum filiabus Moab, & vocauerunt eos ad sacrificia deorum suorum & comedit populus & adorauit deos eorum, initiatusq; est Israel Baalpeor. Vides hæc tria in hoc quoq; exemplum cocurrisse, stu diû ventris, scortationem, & eidololatriam.
units.tr: "Nor let us commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and there fell in one day twenty-three thousand." He had also warned about fornication earlier, in chapters 5 and 6, and somewhat more fully. Here he repeats it in one or two words, but not without a special reason. For he considers in it not only the sin of that people, as in the passages already mentioned above, but also that which contributes most to leading the intemperate into the sin of idolatry, just as the zeal for the belly does. Carnal fornication is not only the companion but also the go-between of spiritual fornication, that is, of idolatry. And since fornication reigned unpunished among the idolaters, and there was danger that through it the more carnal Christians might be seduced into idolatry, he dissuades them by the example of the Israelites, who were themselves destroyed by carnal fornication into the sacrifices of the idols. "Nor let us commit fornication," he says, "as some of them committed fornication, and there fell twenty-three thousand in one day." He speaks of the history of the daughters of Moab, who invited the Israelites to the sacrifices of their gods, and they ate and worshipped Baal-peor; the enticement to this evil was that they committed fornication with them. Concerning this, we read thus in Numbers 25: "Israel abode in Shittim at that time, and the people began to commit fornication with the daughters of Moab; and they called them to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate and worshipped their gods, and Israel was joined to Baal-peor." You see that these three things met together in this example also: zeal for the belly, fornication, and idolatry.

units.la: ET conciderunt, inquit, vno die viginti tria millia.) Terret eos mentione plagę & vltionis qua perculsi fuerunt scortatores, & eidololatræ, qua de sic legitur, Et iratus dominus ait ad Mosen: Tolle cunctos principes populi, & suspende eos cōtra Solem in patibulis, vt auertatur furor meus ab Israele. Dixitq; Moses ad Iudices Israel. Occidat vnusquisq; proximos suos, qui initiati sunt Baalpeor, &c. & occisi sunt viginti quatuor millia. Numerum hunc voluit exprimere Apostolus, vt admoneret, q̃ cito malû crescat & obtineat in populo. Breui vsq; adeo inualuit ista in Israele præuaricatio, vt numerus peccantium tum ad multitudinem viginti quatuor millium excreuerit, periculumq; esset, ne si differretur vltio paulo post vniuersam multitudinem corriperet. Ab hoc igitur exemplo metuens Corinthijs, ne inter illos quoque modicum fermenti totam massam corrůperet, hac eos plaga admonet, q̃ debeant esse soliciti, ne simul & ipsi exitio perdantur.
units.tr: "And there fell," he says, "in one day twenty-three thousand." He frightens them with the mention of the plague and vengeance by which the fornicators and idolaters were struck down, concerning which it is thus read: "And the Lord, being angry, said to Moses: Take all the princes of the people, and hang them against the sun on gibbets, that my wrath may be turned away from Israel. And Moses said to the judges of Israel: Let each one slay his neighbours who have been joined to Baal-peor," etc. And there were slain twenty-four thousand. The Apostle wished to express this number so that he might warn how quickly evil grows and gains hold among a people. So swiftly did this transgression prevail in Israel that the number of sinners then grew to the multitude of twenty-four thousand, and there was danger that if the punishment were delayed, shortly afterwards it would seize the whole multitude. Fearing therefore from this example for the Corinthians, lest among them too a little leaven should corrupt the whole lump, he admonishes them by this plague, that they ought to be anxious lest they too be destroyed by the same ruin.

units.la: {B}Sed nascitur hic quæstio, quomodo Apostolus viginti tria millia hominum occisa esse dicat, cum in ipsa historia viginti quatuor millia tá in Ebræo, & Chaldæo, q̃ in versione Septuaginta legantur. Lyranus sic tuetur Apostolum Minor numerus, inquit, includitur in maiori, & ideo quod uerum est de maiori, verum etiâ est de minori. Hac ratione defendi posset, etiâ
units.tr: But here arises a question: how the Apostle says that twenty-three thousand men were slain, when in the history itself twenty-four thousand are read, both in the Hebrew and the Chaldee, and in the version of the Seventy. Lyra defends the Apostle thus: "The smaller number is included in the greater, and therefore what is true of the greater is true also of the smaller." By this reasoning it could be defended, even

units.la: si viginti tres homines occisos fuisse dixisset. Quare mihi solutio ista Lyrani non probatur. Meo iudicio, non scripsit Apostolus aliter q; veritas habet historiæ, quomodocunq; numerus iste vigintitrium pro vigintiquatuor irrepserit.
units.tr: if he had said that twenty-three men were slain. Therefore that solution of Lyra does not please me. In my judgment, the Apostle did not write otherwise than the truth of the history has it, however that number twenty-three for twenty-four may have crept in.

units.la: Suspicor per abbreuiationem, siue ab ipso Apostolo siue ab antiquario aliquo, scriptum fuisse εἰκοσιτρεῖς, pro εἰκοσιτέσσαρες, eamq; postea ab breuiatione per negligentiores mutatam esse in numerum istum εἰκοσιτρεῖς ac versum à Latino interprete, vigintitria. Nō affirmo, sed quod suspicor cum pace aliorum simpliciter annoto.
units.tr: I suspect that through an abbreviation, either by the Apostle himself or by some copyist, the word εἰκοσιτρεῖς was written for εἰκοσιτέσσαρες, and that afterwards, through abbreviation by more careless scribes, it was changed into that number εἰκοσιτρεῖς, and the Latin translator rendered it "twenty-three." I do not affirm this, but with the peace of others I simply note what I suspect.

units.la: Quòd si quis Apostolū omnino vigintitria millia scripsisse putat, referant hunc numerum ad eos tantum, qui gladio sunt occisi idq; forsan die post suspensionem principum sequenti, unde dicit, conciderunt uno die, reliquum vero millenarium ad principes in patibulis contra Solem suspensos, quos verosimile est non solos sed unà fuisse cum ministris suis ei supplicio traditos, sic ut numerus viginti quatuor millium, qui in historia habetur omnes complectatur tam suspensos quàm gladio occisos.
units.tr: But if anyone thinks the Apostle wrote twenty-three thousand at all, let them refer this number only to those who were slain by the sword, and perhaps to the day after the hanging of the chiefs, whence he says, "they fell in one day." The remaining thousand would then refer to the chiefs hanged on gibbets in the face of the sun, who were likely handed over to that punishment not alone but together with their attendants. In this way the number of twenty-four thousand in the history embraces all of them, both those hanged and those slain by the sword.

units.la: De hoc numero legitur in Iosepho ad hunc modum. Perierunt igitur ex eorum coetibus vi ri haud pauciores quatuordecim millibus, vbi decemmillia desiderantur. Mihi dubium non est scriptum fuisse à Iosepho ... i.haud pauciores viginti quatuor milibus, postea vero ... i. duab. myriadibus, quæ numerum viginti millium constituunt, corrupte esse positum μυρίων, quæ vox decem millia significat, & ex hoc defectu in hunc vsq; diem legi τεταρσιχιλίων μυρίων, ... De hac quæstione videantur & alij ex recentioribus, quid adferat in medium. Veteres nanq; Hiero. Ambr. & Chrysost. reliquerunt eam intactam.
units.tr: Concerning this number, Josephus is read to the following effect: "Thus there perished from their assemblies men not fewer than fourteen thousand, where ten thousand are missing." I have no doubt that Josephus wrote "not fewer than twenty-four thousand," but that later the "two myriads," which make twenty thousand, were corruptly put as the word for ten thousand, and that from this defect the reading has come down to the present day as fourteen thousand. Let others among the more recent writers be consulted on this question, to see what they bring forward. The ancients, Jerome, Ambrose and Chrysostom, left it untouched.

units.la: CONCIDERVNT, inquit, vigintitria millia vno die.)
units.tr: They fell, he says, twenty-three thousand in one day.

units.la: In historia non est temporis posita expressio, quo multitudo hæc conciderit. Posuit eam Apostolus, non simpliciter dicens conciderunt vigintitria millia, sed addens vno die. Facit autem hoc ad exaggerandum ira dei quo plus terroris Corinthijs tam grauis vltionis respectu incutiat.
units.tr: The history gives no time expression for when this multitude fell. The Apostle included it, not simply saying "twenty-three thousand fell," but adding "in one day." He does this to heighten the wrath of God, so that by the sight of so grave a vengeance he may strike greater terror into the Corinthians.

units.la: NEQVE tentemus Christum, sicut & quidam illorum tentarunt, & à serpentibus extincti sunt.) Hactenus dehortatus est eos à malo prauæ concupiscentiæ, ab eidololatria, studio quæ veritatis & scortatione, tanquam eidololatriæ appendicibus, iam consequentes metus il lis à malo diffidetiæ & impatientiæ, dehortatur eos à temeritate tentandi dominum, & murmurandi contra illius ministros. Neq; tetemus Christum inquit. Qui tales sunt vt periculum sit ne per comessationes & commercia infidelium ad eidololatriam & scortationem pellicea tur, omnino simul sunt proclives ad tentandum dominum, si quid incidat aduersi, propterea quod haud synceri sunt in fide, nec bonitati ac veritati domini fidunt. Dum itaque dicit, neq; tentemus Christu, satis innuit qua-
units.tr: "Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted, and were destroyed by serpents." Hitherto he has dissuaded them from the evil of depraved lust, from idolatry, and from fornication, which follows idolatry as its appendage. Now he dissuades them from the evil of distrust and impatience, from rashness in tempting the Lord, and from murmuring against his ministers. "Let us not tempt Christ," he says. Those who are such that there is danger they will be enticed to idolatry and fornication through feasting and dealings with unbelievers are altogether prone at the same time to tempt the Lord whenever anything adverse befalls them, because they are not sincere in faith and do not trust in the goodness and truth of the Lord. Therefore, when he says "let us not tempt Christ," he sufficiently hints at what sort

units.la: les eos esse velit in rebus aduersis, confidentes videlicet, & bona cum fiducia à Christo Seruatore pendentes. Qui sic animati sunt, Christum haud facile tentant, quantumuis rebus aduersis exerceantur. Quid autem sit tentare dominum alibi diximus, vt pote Matth. 4. & Psal. 95. Tentare dominum est Christum tentare, est non fidere illius verbo, sed vel de diuinitate illius vel potentia vel veritate, aut prouidentia & voluntate certum capture experimentum. Adhuc tetare Christum est patientiam illius irritare, & cotumaciter in malo pergere, quiduis ille reprobis minetur. Teu tant etiam Christū, qui fidelibus illius onerain ferenda imponunt, id quod illi faciebant, qui iugum legis cerucibus discipulorum imponere moliebantur, de quibus Actor. 15. videre licet, vt eos taceam qui Rom. tyrannum & animas, & fortunas & corpora fidelium diuexantem ecclesiæ Christi loco capitis imposuerunt. In summa, nullum non tentationis genus excludit, cum simpliciter dicit, neque tentemus Christum. Quod enim subiungit, sicut & quidam illorum tentarunt, non ad hoc facit, vt ab eo tantum genere Corinthios dehorretur, quo tentarunt illum olim Israelitæ in deserto, sed vt exemplo aliquo declaret, haud laturos impune, si Christum tentare velint, unde & subijcit, & à serpentibus extincti sunt.
units.tr: of people he wants them to be in adversity: confident, of course, and hanging on Christ the Saviour with a good trust. Those so encouraged do not easily tempt Christ, however much they are exercised by adversities. What it is to tempt the Lord we have explained elsewhere, as at Matthew 4 and Psalm 95. To tempt the Lord is to tempt Christ. It is not to trust his word, but to seize a certain experiment regarding his divinity, power, truth, providence or will. Again, to tempt Christ is to provoke his patience and to persist obstinately in evil, whatever he threatens to the reprobate. They also tempt Christ who impose unbearable burdens on his faithful, as those did who tried to place the yoke of the law on the necks of the disciples, as one may see in Acts 15; not to mention those who placed in the position of the head of the Church of Christ the Roman tyrant, who harasses the souls, goods and bodies of the faithful. In sum, he excludes no kind of temptation, since he simply says, "let us not tempt Christ." For what he adds, "as some of them tempted," does not serve to dissuade the Corinthians only from that kind by which the Israelites once tempted him in the desert, but to show by an example that they will not go unpunished if they wish to tempt Christ. Whence he adds, "and were destroyed by serpents."

units.la: Loquitur autem de historia quam Num. 21. legimus ad hunc modum: Et tædere cœpit populum itineris ac laboris, loquutusq; contra dominum & Mosen ait: Cur eduxisti nos de Ægypto, vt moriamur in solitudine? Deest panis non est aqua, anima nostra iam nauseat super cibo isto leuissimo. Quamobrem misit dominus in populum ignitos serpetes, &c. Quoniam omnino ad hanc historiam respicit Apostolus, quæredum est primo, quomodo murmur hoc Israelitarum vocet tentationem, deinde, quomodo dicit eos tentasse Christum. Etenim eti amsi nō legamus, sicut quidam illorum tentauerunt, satis tamen lecto ri haud cōtentioso patet, durius esse, si expona mus, sicut quidam illorum Deum tentarut, q; vt argumento Apostoli conueniat. Nec impedit quod in historia legitur, quod populus sit contra Deum & Mosen loquutus, quo minus tentatio hæc ad Christum possit referri. Sed videamus quid ad ista sit respondendum.
units.tr: He speaks of the history we read in Numbers 21, which runs thus: "And the people began to loathe the journey and the labour, and speaking against the Lord and against Moses they said: Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? There is no bread, there is no water, and our soul now loathes this very light food. Therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people," and so on. Since the Apostle certainly looks to this history, it must first be asked how he calls this murmuring of the Israelites temptation, and second, how he says they tempted Christ. For although we do not read "as some of them tempted," it is plain enough to any reader not contentious that it would be harsher if we expounded "as some of them tempted God," which does not fit the Apostle's argument. Nor does it hinder that the history says the people spoke against God and Moses, so that this temptation could not be referred to Christ. But let us see what answer may be given to these points.

units.la: Quare murmur populi, quo cum Mose iurgatus est dicens: Cur eduxisti nos de Ægypto, vt moriamur in solitudine? vocat tentationem non facit hoc præter rationem & exemplum scripturæ. Ratio est, quod hoc genus murmuris & iurgij, contra Mosen facti ex eo prouenerat, quod de præsentia Dei dubitabant, num ille vere apud ipsos esset, & an vere ab illo educi essent ex Ægypto, ideoq; cum Mose expostulabat, quod eduxisset ipsos ex Ægypto. Quasi dicat: Si non tu sed Deus nos eduxit ex Ægypto, nobiscum q; est in hac solitudine, quæadmodum uis vt tibi credamus, age, cur non dat panem suo populo? cur finit vt siti moriamur in hac
units.tr: Why the murmuring of the people, by which they quarrelled with Moses, saying "Why have you brought us out of Egypt to die in the wilderness?", he calls temptation: this he does not do beyond reason and the example of Scripture. The reason is that this kind of murmuring and quarrelling against Moses arose from their doubting God's presence, whether he truly was among them, and whether they had truly been led out of Egypt by him. Therefore they expostulated with Moses that he had brought them out of Egypt, as if to say: If it was not you but God who brought us out of Egypt, and if he is with us in this wilderness, as you wish us to believe, come, why does he not give bread to his people? Why does he allow us to die of thirst in this

units.la: A
units.tr: A

units.la: B in hac solitudine. Sic isto murmure & iurga bantur contra Mosen, & tentabat Deum. Ergo iurgium hoc respectu Mosis erat murmur, respectu Dei vero erat tentatio, vt recte dixerit Apostolus, sicut & quidam illorum tentarunt.
units.tr: wilderness? So they murmured and quarrelled against Moses, and in doing so tempted God. Therefore this quarrelling was murmuring with respect to Moses, but with respect to God it was temptation; so the Apostle rightly said, "as some of them tempted."

units.la: Exemplum autem scripturae cui se Apostolus conformasse videtur habemus Exo.17. vbi sic legimus: Castrametati sunt in Raphidim, vbi non erat aqua ad bibendum populo. Quo iurgatus contra Mosen ait: Da nobis aquam vt bibamus. Quibus respondet Moses: Quid sur gamini contra me? Quid tentatis dominum? Ite: Et vocauit Moses nomen loci illius, Tentatio, propter iurgium filiorum Israel, quo tentauerunt dominum, dicentes: Est ne Deus in nobis an non? Haec ibi, vbi satis patet, hoc genus murmuris coniunctum esse cum tentatione Dei, ideoque recte dici de illis, qui sic contra Mosen murmurarunt, quod dominum tentarint.
units.tr: The example of Scripture to which the Apostle seems to have conformed is in Exodus 17, where we read thus: "They pitched camp at Rephidim, where there was no water for the people to drink. Quarrelling with Moses, they said: Give us water that we may drink. Moses answered them: Why do you strive with me? Why do you tempt the Lord? And Moses called the name of that place Temptation, because of the quarrelling of the sons of Israel, by which they tempted the Lord, saying: Is God among us or not?" There, it is plain enough that this kind of murmuring is joined with the temptation of God, and so it is rightly said of those who murmured thus against Moses that they tempted the Lord.

units.la: Ad id vero quod illos Christum tentasse dicit facilis est responsio. Etenim si Christus, spiritualis petra, cosequut est eos in deserto, nec simpliciter consequutus est, sed & aquam illis ex petra, & Man de caelo suppeditauit, vtque omne hoc genus tentationis illorum recte ad illum refertur. Ipse nanque idem vtriusque testamenti Seruator, tam illum populum moderatus est & seruauit, quam praesentem hunc, qui Noui testamenti est, ad finem vsque mundi moderatur & seruat. Quare non immerito quidam nostrorum ex hoc loco diuinitatem Christi contra nouos Arrianos astruunt. Etenim quod populus ille iam Elohim, iam Iehouah tentasse memoratur, tam non impedit hunc sensum, vt illum magis coiungat Christum esse verum Deum & Iehouah.
units.tr: The answer to his claim that they tempted Christ is easy. For if Christ, the spiritual rock, followed them in the desert, and not merely followed them but supplied them with water from the rock and with manna from heaven, then all this kind of their temptation is rightly referred to him. For he is the same Saviour of both testaments: he governed and preserved that people just as he governs and preserves the present people of the New Testament to the end of the world. Therefore it is not without reason that some of our people, from this passage, assert the divinity of Christ against the new Arians. For that this people is recorded to have tempted now Elohim, now Jehovah, does not at all hinder this sense; rather it binds him more closely to us, showing Christ to be the true God and Jehovah.

units.la: De serpentibus illis, per quos extincti sunt tentatores, nolim curiosius inquiri, quales nam fuerint. Scriptura vocat eos שרפים, id est, ardentes, vel comburentes, quo nomine spiritus etiam caelestes stantes antethronum Dei, Esa. 6. vocantur. Inerat serpentibus illis ardor flatus, quo, si quos momordissent, necabant. Et hoc nomine a nonnullis praestetes, dipsades, & causones vocantur. Videmus hac vltione qd merentur, qui propter medicu & tolerabilem tribulationis ardorem per diffidentia dominum tentant, & contra seruos eius murmurant. Digni videlicet sunt, quibus modica & momentanea molestia vertatur in exitium. Sic nihil efficimus murmurando ac dominu tentando aliud q quod malum conduplicamus. populus ille ingratus erga beneficia Dei quibus fruebatur, non cogitabat vnde esset, quod illaesus in deserto draconibus ac serpetibus, alijsq; bestijs referto degeret, quare dignus erat, qui praesenti exitio experiretur, a quanto malo ad id vsq; temporis fuisset beneficio domini seruatus, & erga quantu bonu esset ingrat.
units.tr: I would not wish to inquire too curiously what sort of serpents they were by which the tempters were destroyed. Scripture calls them seraphim, that is, burning or fiery ones, the name by which the heavenly spirits standing before the throne of God are called in Isaiah 6. There was in those serpents a burning breath, by which, if they bit anyone, they killed him. By some they are also called prester, dipsades and causones. We see from this punishment what they deserve who, through distrust, tempt the Lord on account of the moderate and momentary burning of tribulation, and who murmur against his servants. Clearly they deserve to have a modest and momentary annoyance turned into destruction. Thus by murmuring and tempting the Lord we accomplish nothing but double our evil. That ungrateful people, unmindful of the benefits of God which they enjoyed, did not consider whence it was that they lived unharmed in the desert, full of dragons, serpents and other beasts. Therefore they deserved to learn by present destruction how great an evil they had been saved from until that time by the benefit of the Lord, and how ungrateful they were for so great a good.

units.la: Admonemur hoc exemplo, vt vbi aliquo exercemur incommodo, memores potius simus quam multis bonis per gratiam domini cumulemur, agamusque illi gratias, quam vt propter vnius aut alterius rei molestia benefi centiam illius turpissima in gratitudine negemus, & tot bonorum largitore tentando contra nos prouocemus.
units.tr: We are admonished by this example that when we suffer some hardship, we should rather remember how richly we are loaded with many blessings through the grace of the Lord, and give him thanks. We should not, on account of the annoyance of one thing or another, deny his most shameful ingratitude toward his kindness, and by testing the giver of so many good things, provoke him against us.

units.la: NEQVE murmuretis, sicut & quidam illorum murmurauerunt, & exterminati sunt ab exterminatore. Vel, vt in Graeco est, perierunt ab exterminatore. Quoniam plerunque tentatio Dei & murmur contra illius seruos concurrut, postquam dehortatus est, ne Christum tentaret, consequenter monet, ne sint murmuratores, propterea quod & talibus periculum sit, ne vltione diuina correpti pereant, cuius rei exemplu admodum tremendu in Israelitis praecesserit.
units.tr: NEITHER murmur, as some of them murmured, and were destroyed by the destroyer. Or, as it is in the Greek, they perished at the hands of the destroyer. Since testing God and murmuring against his servants often go together, after warning us not to tempt Christ, he next advises us not to be murmurers, because such people are also in danger of being seized by divine vengeance and perishing. An very dreadful example of this has already gone before in the Israelites.

units.la: NEQVE murmuretis, inquit.) Murmura re quid sit, notius est, quam vt diffinitionem requirat. Est autem genus duplex murmuris, Vnum inculpabile, alterum culpabile, & admodum viciosum.
units.tr: "Neither murmur," he says. What murmuring is, is too well known to need a definition. There are two kinds of murmuring: one blameless, the other culpable and very vicious.

units.la: Inculpabile est, quod alias musitationem vocamus, qua sermo de re aliqua in ore vulgi non palam, sed clanculum versatur. De hoc genere murmuris Ioan. 7. legimus ad huc modum: Iudaei ergo quaerebant eum in die festo, & dicebant, vbi est ille? Et murmur multis in turbis erat de eo. Quidam enim dicebant, bonus est, alij autem dicebant, non, sed seducit turbam. Nemo tamen palam loquebatur de illo propter metum Iudaeorum. Sic musitare de re aliqua, & non palam eloqui, quae sentiuntur propter metum potentiorum, infirmi quidem animi notam habet, mali vero non ita. De hoc murmure non loquitur Apostolus.
units.tr: The blameless kind is what we otherwise call muttering, when talk about some matter circulates among the common people not openly but in whispers. We read of this kind of murmuring in John 7, in this way: "The Jews therefore sought him at the feast, and said, Where is he? And there was much murmuring among the multitude concerning him. For some said, He is good; others said, No, but he deceives the people. Yet no one spoke openly of him for fear of the Jews." To mutter about some matter and not speak openly what people think, for fear of the more powerful, shows a weak spirit, but not an evil one. The Apostle does not speak of this murmuring here.

units.la: Culpabile murmur est, quo obloquuntur & conquerimur contra homines potentiores ac superiores, quasi inique aut absurde quid dicant vel faciant. Hic multum refert, quis, cui, & qua in re obmurmuret. Si is, qui subditus est, & cui benefactum est, si contra eum, cui multum debet, quem amare & laudare potius debebat, si in re leui ac tolerabili, nedum in ea obquam potius essent agendae gratiae, murmurauerit, admodum detestabile murmur est. Deinde haud parum refert, vnde hoc murmuran di vicium nascatur, an ex mera damni vel incommodi alicuius impatientia, vel ex superbia, contemptu, indignatione, inuidentia. Licet enim in se viciosum sit murmurare contra superiorem, minus tamen detestabile est, si id fiat propter acceptum aliquod incommodu per solam illius impatientiam, quam si fiat ex superbia & contemptu, vel ex spiritu inuidentiae, quale erat murmur Chore, Dathan, & Abiron, contra Mosen & Aaronem, & vt verosimile est, pseudapostolorum & sectariorum illorum qui inter Corinthios Apostolo obmurmurabant & obloquebantur. Murmurarunt & primi Christiani ex Gentibus contra eos, qui erant ex Ebraeis, Act. 6. propterea quod viduae eorum in ministerio quotidiano negligeretur, quod murmur concernebat ipsos Apostolos. Murmurarunt illi neq; ex superbia, neq; ex contemptu, neq; ex inuidetia, sed ex impatientia incommodi, quod viduis ipsorum eo neglectu obuenie-bat. bat. Nisi stipites fimus, facile inter id murmu-ris, & murmur quod cum superbia, cōtemptu & inuidentia coniunctum est, quale erat murmur Chore & sectatorū illi⁹, discriminabim⁹.
units.tr: The culpable murmuring is when people complain and grumble against men who are more powerful and superior, as if they said or did something unjust or absurd. Here it matters greatly who it is, against whom, and over what matter one murmurs. If someone who is subject, and who has received a kindness, murmurs against the one to whom he owes much, whom he ought rather to love and praise, and does so over a slight and bearable matter, indeed over one for which he ought rather to give thanks, it is an utterly detestable murmuring. Next, it matters not a little where this vice of murmuring arises from: whether from mere impatience at some loss or inconvenience, or from pride, contempt, indignation, or envy. For although murmuring against a superior is in itself vicious, it is less detestable if it happens because of some suffered inconvenience, through impatience alone, than if it arises from pride and contempt, or from a spirit of envy. Such was the murmuring of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram against Moses and Aaron; and, as is likely, that of the false apostles and sectarians who among the Corinthians murmured against and spoke evil of the Apostle. The first Christians from among the Gentiles also murmured against those who were Hebrews (Acts 6), because their widows were neglected in the daily ministry. This murmuring concerned the Apostles themselves. They murmured neither from pride, nor from contempt, nor from envy, but from impatience at the inconvenience which came to their widows through that neglect. Unless we were blockheads, we could easily distinguish between this kind of murmuring and that murmuring which is joined with pride, contempt and envy, such as the murmuring of Korah and his followers.

units.la: SICVT & quidem illorū murmurauerūt, inquit, & exterminati sunt ab extinctore.) Sę penumero murmurasse leguntur. Vtpote Exo di 15.16.&17.Nu.11.14.16.20.&21. Quare incertum videri posset, ad quam respiciat historiam Apostolus, nisi adiecefsit de vltione dicens: & exterminati sunt ab extinctore, quibus verbis satis admonemur, referenda hęc esse ad exem plum murmuris, quod mox est exterminationis vltio consequuta. In historijs, quæ in Exodo de murmurationibus huius populi legūtur, nulla fit exterminationis mentio. Quare ad illas nō respexit Apostolus hoc loco. Obiter obserua patientiā Dei, quā sit tardus ad irā. Tulit aliquoties populi huius impatientiā & obmurmurationes, tametsi dignus esset quē mox perderet. Num.11.&16. memoratur exterminatio murmurantium. Vndecimo sic legitur. Interea ortum est murmur populi dolētis præ labore, contra dominū, quod cum audisset iratus est, & accensus est in eos ignis domini, deuorauitque extremā castrorum partē. Cumque clamasset populus ad Mosen, orauit Moses ad dominū, & absorptus est ignis, vocauitq; nomen loci illius incensio. Num.16. murmurarunt Chore, Dathan & Abiron cum viris 250. Cōtra Mosen & Aaronem, & absum psit ignis 250. viros, reliquos terra cum omni ipsorum frequētia ab sorpsit. Sequēti dic omnis multitudo filiorū Israel murmurauit contra Mosen & Aaronē, dicens: Vos interfecistis populum domini. Atq; de his absumpsit ignis domini quatuordecim milia & septingentos.
units.tr: "As some of them indeed murmured," he says, "and were destroyed by the destroyer." They are read to have murmured often, as in Exodus 15, 16 and 17, and Numbers 11, 14, 16, 20 and 21. So it might seem uncertain which history the Apostle has in view, unless he had added the matter of vengeance, saying "and were destroyed by the destroyer." By these words we are sufficiently reminded that this should be referred to the example of murmuring, which was soon followed by the punishment of destruction. In the accounts in Exodus of the murmurings of this people, there is no mention of destruction. Therefore the Apostle did not look to those histories in this place. In passing, observe the patience of God, who is slow to anger. He bore many times the impatience and murmurings of this people, although they deserved to be destroyed at once. In Numbers 11 and 16 the destruction of the murmurers is recorded. In chapter 11 it is read thus: "Meanwhile the people, grieving from their labour, began to murmur against the Lord; and when he heard it he was angry, and the fire of the Lord was kindled against them, and devoured the outermost part of the camp. And when the people cried out to Moses, Moses prayed to the Lord, and the fire was quenched, and he called the name of that place Taberah (Burning)." In Numbers 16: "Korah, Dathan and Abiram murmured, with 250 men, against Moses and Aaron; and fire consumed the 250 men, and the rest the earth swallowed up, with all their households." The next day "all the multitude of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying: You have killed the people of the Lord. And of these the fire of the Lord consumed fourteen thousand and seven hundred."

units.la: Num.20. murmurarunt cōtra Mosen & Aaronē propter aquarum penuriā. Verum nulla illic memoratur plaga sequuta. Num 21. iterum murmurarunt, quapropter immisi sunt illis serpētes igniti. At eam historiā attigit particula præcedenti. Quare quod hic dicit, ad illam referri nō poterit. Refertur à nonnullis ad eaqua Num.14. legūtur. Verū quoniā nō est illic præsens & subita exterminatio sequuta, existimo restare, vt referamus vel ad eaquæ Num.11.legūtur, vel ad murmur quod cap.16. memoratur. Nā vtrobiq; habetur exterminatio murmurantiū facta per ignem cœlitus immissum. Nec impedit hanc expositione, quod nō dicit, & exterminati sunt ab incendio, sed ab extinctore, vel, ab exterminatore. Nam vltionis eius, quæ facta est per igne, dubio ꝓcul fuit angelus quispiam domini minister & exequutor, quem Apostolus hic vocat exterminatorē. Eodē nomine vocari potuit angelus per quē cædebātur Corinthij ꝓpter abusum cœnę dominicę, quo de ca.sequēti memorabitur.
units.tr: In Numbers 20 they murmured against Moses and Aaron because of lack of water; but no plague is recorded there as following. In Numbers 21 they murmured again, and therefore fiery serpents were sent among them. But the preceding clause touched upon that history, so what he says here cannot be referred to it. Some refer it to the things read in Numbers 14; but since no sudden and present destruction followed there, I think we must refer it either to what is read in Numbers 11, or to the murmuring recorded in chapter 16, for in both places there is a destruction of the murmurers by fire sent from heaven. Nor does it hinder this explanation that he does not say "destroyed by fire" but "by the destroyer," or "by the exterminator." For without doubt some angel of the Lord, a minister and executor, carried out that vengeance which was done by fire; and this the Apostle here calls the destroyer. The same name could be given to the angel by whom the Corinthians were struck down because of the abuse of the Lord's Supper, which will be mentioned in the following chapter.

units.la: Est autē obseruandum, quod particulā hac, sicut quidam illorum, toties repetit & inculcat. Tantum nō clamat ea quæ male fuerunt à Veteris testamenti populo admissa, grauiq; ul tione diuinitus punita, admitti posse & in ecclesia Christianorum. Imò admodum timet, ne admittantur. Quin futurum præuidet, vt admittantur. Et hic timor eius vanus nō fuit, nec vanum fuit mentis ipsius præsagium. Enim quæ admissa fuerunt ab Israelitis, vix um bram quandam eorum habuerunt, quæ post Apostolorum ac proxime illos sequentium tēpora palām admitti cœperunt, & hodie quoq; impudentissime geruntur.
units.tr: It should be noticed that he repeats and presses this particle "as some of them" so often. He almost cries out that the things which were wickedly committed by the people of the Old Testament, and divinely punished with severe vengeance, must not be admitted in the Church of Christians. Indeed he greatly fears lest they be admitted, and foresees that they will be admitted. And this fear of his was not vain, nor was the foreboding of his mind empty. For what was committed by the Israelites had only a kind of shadow of those things which, after the times of the Apostles and of those who came soon after them, began openly to be admitted, and which even today are carried on most shamelessly.

units.la: HAEC autem omnia figurę contigerunt illis.) Siue, quod magis placet, euenerunt illis: Est enim in Græco συνβαυον. Puto autē, quod dicit: Hæc omnia, non esse restringendum ad vltiones de scortantibus, Christum tentantibus, & murmurantibus sumptas, sed ad ipsas quoq; peccatorum species, quas recensuit, referendum, quod videlicet, mala concupiuerunt, eidola coluerunt, scortati sunt, Christum tentarunt & murmurarunt.
units.tr: "Now all these things happened to them as figures." Or, as I prefer, "happened to them." In the Greek it is συνέβαινον [sunebainon]. I think he means that these things, all of them, should not be restricted to the punishments taken for fornicating, tempting Christ, and murmuring, but should also be referred to the very kinds of sin which he has listed: namely, that they lusted after evil things, worshipped idols, committed fornication, tempted Christ and murmured.

units.la: Non est autem ociosum, quod iam secundo ista exemplaria fuisse dicit, iterum cauens, ne nihil ad Christianos pertinere putetur. Nec emphasi caret, quod nō simpliciter dicit: Hæc autē, sed addit, omnia, vt significet, nihil taliū delictorū & vltionū euenisse Israeli, quod non fuerit exemplar posteris inspiciendum & cauendum. Suspicor quod in Græco est ταύλα po situm esse pro πιαῦπα, vt sit sensus. Talia & quæ huiusmodi sunt omnia, figurę euenerunt illis, quo referatur non ad ea modo, quę recensuit, sed & ad omnia reliqua istis consimilia. Longum enim visum est cuncta talia, quæ Israeli euenerunt, enumerare.
units.tr: It is not idle that he now says for the second time that these were examples, again taking care lest it be thought that nothing of this concerns Christians. Nor is there lacking emphasis in his not simply saying "Now these things," but adding "all," to signify that no such sins and punishments befell Israel which were not to be looked at and guarded against as examples by posterity. I suspect that in the Greek the word ταῦτα [tauta] is put for πανταῦτα [pantauta], so that the sense is: "such things and all things like them happened to them as figures." This refers not only to the things he has enumerated, but also to all the other things like these. For it seemed too long to list all such things as befell Israel.

units.la: Priusquā hinc transeamus, admonēdus est lector, vt caueat expositione eorū, qui sic ista figuras Israeli fuisse sentiunt, vt veritas illorū in Novo testamento fuerit implenda, quēadmodū serpēs æneus figura fuit & vmbra Christi in cruce exaltandi. Multum discriminis est inter eiusmodi figuras, & ista exempla, quę hic cōmemorantur. Eadē veritas est in ijs quę euenerunt Israeli, & in nobis, qui facta illorum imitamur. Vere concupiuerunt mala, non figurate, vere simulacra coluerūt, vere scortati sunt, vere Christum tentarunt, vere murmurarunt. Adhæc vere percusi sunt, vere à serpentibus infecti perierunt, vereq; exterminati sunt ab exterminatore. Haud plus est veritatis in ijs quæ nobis talia euenīunt, quàm fuit in illis. Nisi quod in illis pręmonstratum est, quid expectandum sit ad quam eum modum contra Deum peccantibus, ob quam causam & typi ab Apostolo vocantur. Voluit enim Deus statim initio ædere exemplaria eiusmodi ad terrorē posteris incutiendum: perinde ac si rex quispiam initio regni sui sic animaduertat in reprobos ac perfidos, vt habeat posteri exempla quibus terreantur, ne & ipsi consimili perfidia digni fiant, qui exterminentur, vbi ineptum fuerit sic ea quæ populo regni initio euenerunt, vocare typos, vt veritas illorum tantummodo sit adimplenda in posteris.
units.tr: Before we move on, the reader should be warned to beware of the interpretation of those who think these things were figures for Israel in such a way that their truth was to be fulfilled in the New Testament, just as the bronze serpent was a figure and shadow of Christ being lifted up on the cross. There is a great difference between figures of that kind and the examples mentioned here. The same truth is present in what happened to Israel and in us, who imitate their deeds. They truly lusted after evil things, not in a figurative sense; they truly worshipped idols, truly committed fornication, truly tempted Christ, truly murmured. Moreover, they were truly struck down, truly perished from the serpents' bites, and truly were destroyed by the Destroyer. In what befalls us in such matters there is no more truth than there was in them. The only difference is that in them it was shown beforehand what awaits those who sin against God in this way, and for this reason they are also called types by the Apostle. For God willed from the very beginning to set forth such examples, to strike terror into posterity, just as if some king at the start of his reign should punish rebels and traitors in such a way that his descendants would have examples to frighten them, lest they too become worthy of the same faithlessness and be destroyed. It would be inappropriate to call the things that happened to the people at the start of the kingdom "types," so that only their truth would be fulfilled in later generations.

units.la: SCRIPTA vero sunt propter admonitionē ma sæcula sunt, vel, termini incidūt sæculorū. nostri.) Accommodat quæ attulit ad proposi- tum, sicuti cœpit. Facit autem hoc assignata ra- tione propter quam in scripturas relata sunt quæ olim Israeli euenerunt. Sensus est. Sit De us animaduertit in reprobum Israelis populū, vt essent exempla iusti iudicij, transmittenda ad posteros. Et ea propterea literis mandari vo luit, vt sit vnde admoneamur nos quoq;, etiam in quos sæculorum termini inciderunt. Locus hic valde vtilis est, rationem nobis & vsum sa- cræ scripturæ ostendens. Cessent igitur phanta- tici homines, qui Veteris testamenti scriptu- ras, quasi nihil ad nos pertineant, prorsus re- ijciunt. Quomodo ad nos non pertinēt, quæ ad hoc sunt scripta, vt animum illis opponā- mus? Scripta sunt, inquit, ... Quæ propter admonitione nostri scripta sunt, propter nos vtiq; sunt scripta, & quæ propter nos scripta sunt, ad nos vtiq;, imo ad nos potis- simum pertinent.
units.tr: "But these things were written for our admonition..." (the ends of the ages have come). He applies what he has said to his purpose, as he began to do. He does this by the stated reason for which the things that once happened to Israel were recorded in Scripture.
