The sense is this: God punished the rebellious people of Israel so that they would be examples of righteous judgment to be handed down to later generations. He therefore willed that these things be committed to writing, so that we also, on whom the ends of the ages have come, might have something by which to be admonished. This passage is very useful, showing us the purpose and use of Holy Scripture. Let those fanatical men, then, cease who reject the writings of the Old Testament altogether, as if they had nothing to do with us. How can they not pertain to us, when they were written so that we might set our minds upon them? They were written, he says... What was written for our admonition was surely written for us, and what was written for us pertains certainly to us, indeed pertains to us most of all.

units.la: Sed obsecro, quomodo animum ad illa ap- ponet plebs Christi, quæ malo pastorum stu- dio cogitur ignorare? Clamant aduersarij, non esse laicis lacram scripturam legendam. Hæc ipsissimi Satanæ vox est, semel ac breui compē- dio omnem scientiam Dei ex ecclesia auferens vt impleatur illud Christi: Erratis, nescientes scripturas. Et illud Chrysostomi: Hinc omnia mala, quod scripturæ ignorantur. Quis autem satis perpenderit, quanto bono priuetur ho- mo, qui cum sit ignorans, errans & peccans, o- mni admonitione destituitur, qua possit reuo- cari in viam?
units.tr: But I ask you, how will the people of Christ set their minds on those things, when the wicked diligence of their ministers forces them to remain ignorant? Our opponents cry out that Holy Scripture is not to be read by laymen. This is the very voice of Satan himself, which at a stroke and in a brief summary takes away all knowledge of God from the Church, so that Christ's words might be fulfilled: "You are wrong, not knowing the Scriptures" (Matt. 22). And that saying of Chrysostom: "All evils come from this, that the Scriptures are not known." But who could weigh sufficiently how great a good is taken from a man who, being ignorant, erring and sinning, is deprived of every admonition by which he might be called back to the right way?

units.la: IN quos termini sæculorum inciderunt.) Quæritur hoc loco, quomodo dicat Aposto- lus in eos qui tum viuebant, terminos incidi- se sæculorum, cum interea supra quindecim sæcula fluxerint, & nondum appareat sæculo- rum finis. Respondeo: Complectitur omnes Christianos, non eos tantum qui tum erant in viuis, sed & eos qui ad finem vsque mundi erat futuri, qui omnes vno corpore comprehendū tur, & eidem extremæ sunt dispensationi gra- tiæ Dei subiecti, quæ ad finem mundi vsque durans, extremorum sæculorum prædicatum sortitur.
units.tr: "On whom the ends of the ages have come." Here it is asked how the Apostle can say that the ends of the ages had come upon those who were living at that time, when more than fifteen centuries have since passed and no end of the ages is yet in sight. I answer: he embraces all Christians, not only those who were then alive but also those who were to be until the end of the world. All of them are comprehended in one body and are subject to the same final dispensation of God's grace, which lasts until the end of the world and therefore receives the title of the last ages.

units.la: Deinde, non dicit, in quos terminus mundi sed, in quos termini sæculorum inciderunt. Quemadmodum autem principia sæculorum non ea tantum censentur, quibus conditus est mundus, sed quibus priora conditi, recentisq; mundi sæcula ad diluuium vsque decurrerūt: ita rectè termini quoque sæculorum non sunt ad id temporis referendi, quo mundus termi- nabitur, sed ad postrema senescentis mundi sæ- cula, quæ à nato Christo ad finem vsque mūdi durant. Et hoc sensu tempus regni Christi, cō- paratione diei, quæ horarum decursu absoluī tur, nouissima hora vocatur, qua videlicet, no- tissima diurni temporis momenta absoluun- tur, vt quod illic est momentum, hic sit sæcu- lum, perinde ac si dixisset ille, filioli, nouissi-
units.tr: Next, he does not say "on whom the end of the world has come," but "on whom the ends of the ages have come." Just as the beginnings of the ages are reckoned not only by the creation of the world but also by the earlier ages of the world that were created, and the ages of the newer world ran on until the Flood, so too the ends of the ages are rightly referred not to the time when the world will end, but to the final ages of the aging world, which run from the birth of Christ until the end of the world. In this sense the time of Christ's kingdom is called the last hour, compared with the day which is completed by the course of its hours. That is, the most final moments of the daytime are completed, so that what is a moment there is an age here, just as if he had said, "Little children, it is the last hour..."

units.la: Quod si quis terminos sæculorum omnino accipit pro termino ac fine mundi, cogitet de verbo καταλήψεσθαι, id est, inciderūt, sic esse illud forsan, more Ebraico ab Apostolo natione E- bræo positum, vt præteritum sit loco futuri, le gendum q;, in quos termini sæculorum inci- dent, hoc est, qui sumus postremus ille populus Dei, post quem non ad finem vsque mundi expectandus alius. Verum prior expositio cer tior est ac firmior.
units.tr: But if anyone takes "the ends of the ages" entirely to mean the end and close of the world, let him consider the verb katalēpsesthai [καταλήψεσθαι], that is, "have come." Perhaps it is put, in the Hebrew manner, by the Apostle, who was a Hebrew by birth, so that the past tense stands in place of the future, and it should be read, "on whom the ends of the ages will come," that is, we who are that last people of God, after whom no other is to be expected before the end of the world. Yet the former explanation is more certain and more firm.

units.la: Non est autem hoc sic dictum ab Apostolo, quod quæ scripta sunt, non sint propter eos quòq; scripta, qui tum cum ea gererentur, sub Mose viuebant, & post Mosen ad Christum vs- que sequuturi erant, sed vt eam scripturam in vsus perpetuos eius quoque ecclesiæ, quæ po strema est in mundo, destinatam esse significa- ret, id quod potissimum inculcare voluit, tan- quam ad id quod agebat, cum primis cognitu necessarium.
units.tr: The Apostle did not say this in such a way as to mean that the things which were written were not also written for those who, at the time they were happening, lived under Moses, and were to follow after Moses until Christ. Rather, he means to show that this Scripture was destined for the constant use of that Church also which is the last in the world. This is what he especially wished to impress, as something most necessary to know for the matter he was treating.

units.la: PROINDE qui sibi stare videtur, videat ne cadat.) Applicat summariam admonitionē ex præcedentibus collectam, cum specificatio ne eorum ad quos illam potissimum pertinere iudicat. Neq; enim simpliciter dicit: Proinde videte ne cadatis, sed: Proinde qui sibi stare vi detur, videat ne cadat. Ad omnes quidem pertinet hæc cura, vt caueant ne ad exempla veteris populi in quæuis peccata prolapsi, ira in se Dei prouocent. Verum potissimum hoc illis est timendum, qui quoniam se stare putāt, securius agunt, eoque & facilius à Satana ten- tantur, & procliuiores sunt ad ruinam. Tales autem erant inter Corinthios, qui de scientia & fide præ aliis gloriantes, vnà cum ethnicis infidelibus & simulacrorum cultoribus securè de eidolothytis manducabant, & quæuis illo- rum commercia sectabantur, neque ruinam ti- mebant, quod se firmius stare putarent, quàm qui cadere possent. Horum securitatem pēt stringens dicit: Proinde qui sibi stare vide- tur, videat ne cadat. Quasi dicat: Quandoquī dem tot exemplis veterum humana est declara- rata infirmitas, thonstratumq;, leui momento fieri, vt qui participes sunt cœlestis gratiæ si- sti, vbi incautius agunt, in enormia peccata ,p- labantur, plane necessarium est illis, qui quoniam se stare putant, incunctanter commercia in fidelium sectantur, & conuiuijs eidololatricis miscentur, vt sibi timeant, ne dum incautius a- gunt, de gradu in quo se consistere putant, sa- dissimè cadant.
units.tr: "Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall." He applies the brief admonition gathered from what precedes, with a specification of those to whom he judges it especially pertains. For he does not simply say, "Therefore take heed lest you fall," but "Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall." This care pertains to all, that they take care lest, having lapsed into any sins like those of the ancient people, they provoke God's anger against themselves. Yet this is to be feared especially by those who, because they think they stand, act more securely, and are therefore more easily tempted by Satan and more prone to ruin. Such were some among the Corinthians, who, glorying in knowledge and faith above others, ate without concern of food sacrificed to idols together with heathen unbelievers and worshippers of images, and pursued all their business dealings, not fearing ruin, because they thought they stood more firmly than those who could fall. Touching their security, he says, "Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall." As if he said: since by so many examples from the ancients human weakness has been shown and proved, and it has been demonstrated that by a slight movement those who are partakers of heavenly grace may fall into enormous sins when they act carelessly, it is most necessary for those who think they stand, and who therefore pursue fellowship with the faithless without hesitation and mingle in idolatrous feasts, to fear for themselves, lest, while acting carelessly, they fall most grievously from the position in which they think they stand.

units.la: Admonetur hoc loco, quàm sit periculosa ac summopere vitanda securitas eorum qui se stare putant. Insidiosum malum est, & duplici nomine cauendum. Primò, quòd decipit, & ex non stantibus quasi stantes facit. Deinde quod securitas agentes ad quamuis ruinam ex positos reddit. Locus hic præcipuè notandus est illis, qui in religione recenti cæteris sunt præmaturiores. Hi sic sunt comparati, vt vbi aliquem veritatis gustū propere perceperūt, perinperinde animentur ac si iam ad ipsam usque per- sectionem ascenderint. Possemus nostro hoc saeculo plurima talium exempla in medium ad ferre. Hoc genus hominum ministrum uerbi fundamenta uerae religionis magno labore pa riter & discrimine ponentem plurimum initio exhilarat. Primi ueritatem amplectuntur, pro ueritate seruada ac propaganda decertant, mi nistro uerbi arctius iunguntur, & ad quaeuis di scrimina pro ueritate una cum illo subeunda paratissimi uidentur. Non dubito illos, quos hic perstringit Apostolus, fuisse tales initio, & paulo post illius discessum in hanc euasisse se curitatem, & quae a securis admitti solent ad misisse, ut opus habuerint admonitione hac tā feria ac diligenti.
units.tr: Here we are warned how dangerous is the security of those who think they stand, and how it must above all be avoided. It is an insidious evil and must be guarded against on two counts. First, because it deceives, and makes men who are not standing seem to be standing. Second, because security renders those who act in it open to any ruin. This passage is especially to be noted by those who, in a recently adopted religion, are more forward than others. Such people are so disposed that, when they have quickly tasted some sense of the truth, they are excited as if they had already reached perfection itself. We could in our own age bring forward very many examples of such people. This sort of person greatly cheers the minister of the Word at first, when he lays the foundations of true religion with great labour and danger alike. At first they embrace the truth, they contend for keeping and spreading the truth, they cling more closely to the minister of the Word, and they seem most ready to undergo any dangers with him for the sake of the truth. I do not doubt that those whom the Apostle here rebukes were such at the beginning, and that a little after his departure they fell into this security, and, admitting what is usually admitted by the careless, came to need this so severe and diligent admonition.

units.la: Deinde obserua, quam caute & moderate non dicat: Proinde qui uos stare putatis, uide te ne cadatis, ne palam eos & uelut in faciem perstringendo admonitionem hanc reddat sub acerbam, sed: Proinde qui sibi stare uidetur, id est, si quis est inter uos, qui se stare putat, uide at ille ne cadat, id quod aliquanto moderatius est, & tolerabiliorem reddit admonitionem: quam prudentiam Apostoli imitari debent, quorum studium est utiliter & cum fructu e mendare delinquentes.
units.tr: Next, notice how cautiously and moderately he speaks. He does not say, "Therefore let those who think they stand take heed lest they fall," which would rebuke them openly and to their faces and make the admonition harsh. He says instead, "Therefore let him who seems to himself to stand," that is, if anyone among you thinks he stands, let him take care lest he fall. This is somewhat gentler and makes the admonition more tolerable. Apostles ought to imitate this prudence, since their aim is to correct those who go wrong usefully and with profit.

units.la: Sed dices hic. Ergo, si audimus Apostolum, non erimus securi in gratia Dei, nec quisquam sibijpse certitudinem salutis pollicebitur, quā doquidem tam serio monet, ut qui se stare exi stimant, in fide uidelicet, uideant ne cadant. Quid ergo docemus de certitudine gratiae Dei contra eos, qui neminem de salute sua & gratia Dei certum esse posse contendunt? Et quid est, quod de seipse scribit Apostolus, dicens: Scio cui credidi, & certus sum, &c.
units.tr: But someone will say: "If we listen to the Apostle, we will not be secure in the grace of God, and no one will promise certainty of salvation to himself, since he warns so seriously that those who think they stand, namely in faith, should take heed lest they fall. What then do we teach about the certainty of God's grace against those who contend that no one can be certain of his salvation and the grace of God? And what of what the Apostle writes about himself: 'I know whom I have believed, and I am certain,' etc.?"

units.la: Respondeo. Sunt in hac causa duplices respectus: unus, quo gratiam Dei fide: alter, quo nos ipsos respicimus. Priori respectu certi sumus de gratia Dei, quae incerta & instabilis esse non potest. Hanc certitudinem salutis, quam fides respectu veritatis & gratiae Dei concipit, non impugnat Apostolus, nec de illa loquitur hoc loco. Quomodo enim reprobaret in aliis, quod de seipse tam diserte praedicat? Posteriori vero respectu, quo nos ipsos intuemur, non reddimur securi, sed solliciti ac timentes, ne de gradu gratiae Dei in quem recepti sumus, tentatione aliqua superati cadamus, propter carnis nostrae corruptionem & imbecillitatem. Et hunc timorem suadet Corinthiis, non dubitationem de gratia Dei. Neque enim loquitur illis, qui fide indubitata a gratia Dei pendebant, sed perstringit falsam eorum securitatem, qui seipsos infirmioribus comparatos stare putabant, & suarum virium respectu securi erant, quasi cadere non possent, & interea ea admittebant, quae securos facillime de gradu fidei praecipites dare poterant. Quare non dicit: Qui stat in gratia Dei, uel qui bene credit, beneque de gratiae Dei certitudine sperat, sed, qui se stare putat, uideat ne cadat.
units.tr: I answer: in this matter there are two points of view. One is that by which we regard the grace of God by faith; the other is that by which we look at ourselves. From the first point of view we are certain of the grace of God, which cannot be uncertain or unstable. This certainty of salvation, which faith conceives with respect to the truth and grace of God, the Apostle does not attack, nor does he speak of it in this place. For how would he condemn in others what he so plainly professes of himself? From the second point of view, by which we look upon ourselves, we are not made secure but anxious and fearful, lest, having been received into the state of God's grace, we fall through some temptation, on account of the corruption and weakness of our flesh. It is this fear, not doubt about the grace of God, that he urges on the Corinthians. For he does not speak to those who hung upon the grace of God with unwavering faith, but he rebukes the false security of those who thought themselves to stand, compared with weaker people, and were confident of their own strength, as if they could not fall, while meanwhile they admitted things which could very easily cast secure men headlong from the footing of faith. Therefore he does not say: "He who stands in the grace of God, or he who believes well and hopes well with regard to the certainty of God's grace," but: "He who thinks he stands, let him see to it that he does not fall."

units.la: Ad quem modum eos admonere solemus, qui uiribus & capitis & pedum suorum freti super glaciem securius incedunt, vel excelsa periculosius scandunt, ut videant ne cadant, non autem eos, qui nihil de firmitudine terrae a domino fundatae dubitantes, prout requirit necessitas, super illam ingrediuntur, nec incedunt locis vel modis cum periculo coniunctis, quibus nemo facile dicit: Videte ne cadatis, nec quisquam vicio vertit, quod nihil addubitant, terram super quam ingrediuntur, satis esse ad sustinendum ipsos stabilem & firmam. Et hac puto distinctione satis fieri manifestum haud quaquam patrocinari Apostolu pestilenti eorum doctrinae, qui Christianos magno studio de gratia Dei & propria salute reddunt incertos ac dubios.
units.tr: We usually admonish in this way those who, trusting in the strength of their hands and feet, walk more confidently upon ice or climb high places more dangerously: "Take heed lest you fall." We do not say it to those who, not doubting the firmness of the earth founded by the Lord, walk upon it as necessity requires, and do not go into places or ways attended with danger. To these no one easily says, "Take heed lest you fall," nor does anyone blame them for having no doubt that the ground they walk on is stable and firm enough to bear them. I think that by this distinction it is made sufficiently plain that the Apostle in no way favours the pestilent doctrine of those who make Christians anxious and doubtful about the grace of God and their own salvation.

units.la: Tentatio vos non cepit, nisi humana, fidelis autem est Deus, qui non sinet vos tentari, supra id quod potestis, sed faciet una cum tentatione exitum quoque, quo abunde sufferre possitis.
units.tr: Temptation has not seized you except such as is human; but God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but will also make with the temptation a way out, so that you may be able to endure it.

units.la: Occupatio est. Poterat ad ea quae dixit obij cere, magnam esse vim tentationum, per quam illa fieri, ut qui stant, nolint velint, victi cadant. Occurrit igitur dicens: Tentatio vos nulla dumce pit, quae non sit humana. Quasi dicat. Non est ut dicatis vos tentationum mole uinci. Nihil dum accidit uobis propter fidem in Christum, quod non accidat & aliis hominibus. Pauper tas, morbi, pestis, & alia huiusmodi incommoda, non sunt noua, non sunt insolentia, non sunt humanae miseriae forte excedentia. Sic intelligo per tentationes hoc loco tribulationes & afflictiones, & per humanam tentationem eam tribulationem quae ad communem mortalium miseriam pertineat, & accidat communiter omnibus. Significat non esse illis causam propter quam infidelibus usqueadeo miscean tur, ut & de eidolothytis illorum magno cum offendiculo & syncerae pietatis periculo una cum illis in eidolo uescantur.
units.tr: This is an occupatio. He could have replied to what he has said by pointing out the great force of temptations, by which it happens that those who stand, whether they wish it or not, are overcome and fall. So he meets this objection, saying, "No temptation has seized you that is not human." As if he said: "You cannot say that you are overcome by the mass of temptations. Nothing has yet happened to you on account of faith in Christ that does not also happen to other men. Poverty, sickness, plague, and other misfortures of this kind are not new, are not unusual, and do not go beyond human misery. So I understand by temptations here tribulations and afflictions, and by human temptation that tribulation which belongs to the common misery of mortals and happens to all in common." He means that there is no reason for them to mix so with unbelievers that, with great offence and danger to pure piety, they eat with them in an idol's temple the meat offered to idols.

units.la: Loquitur hic non omnibus fidelibus, qui tū erant in ecclesia Corinthiorum, sed illis tantum, qui cum nihil dum passi essent propter Christum, ad consortia infidelium sponte sua inclinabant. Dubio procul erant quidam, qui grauiter propter Christum afflictati, in statione fidei firmiter persistebant. Ad hos non pertinebat quod dicit: Tentatio uos non cepit nisi humana.
units.tr: He is speaking here not to all the faithful who were then in the church of the Corinthians, but only to those who, since they had not yet suffered anything for Christ, of their own accord leaned towards the company of unbelievers. Without doubt there were some who, severely afflicted for Christ, persisted firmly in the confession of faith. The words "Temptation has not seized you except such as is human" did not apply to these.

units.la: Chrysost. sic exponit: ἵνα μὴ λέγωσι. τί φοβῇ ὑ- μᾶς ἐκ ἐσμὲν τοῦτο ἀμελητὸν ἐν ταῖς ἐχθρῶν, ὅ γὰρ ἐλαβῆ- μεν ἐδὲ ἀρχῇ μεν ἡ πολλοὶς ἡ συνεχεῖς ἐπιμένει- ἐδ δύνεις, καταλλάω ἀντῶν παλιν τὸ φύσημα φησὶ, τί ῥασμὸς ὑμᾶς, &c. Deinde illud, nisi humana, exponit. μικρὸς, ἀρχὸς, σύμμετρος. Sentit ergo, uo luisse Apostolum superbiam spiritus illorum restringere, qua se sic in fide firmos esse gloriati sint, ut nulla esset ratio admonendi ipsos, ut qui se stare putarent, uiderent ne caderet. Sic sensi
units.tr: Chrysostom explains it thus: [ἵνα μὴ λέγωσι· τί φοβεῖτε ἡμᾶς; οὐκ ἐσμὲν τούτου ἀμελητέον ἐν ταῖς ἐχθραῖς· ὃ γὰρ ἐλάβομεν ἐν ἀρχῇ, μετὰ πολλοῦ καὶ συνεχοῦς ἐπιμελείας ἔχομεν] — that is, so that they may not say, "Why do you frighten us? This is not to be neglected among enemies..." Then he explains the words "except human" as "small, light, moderate." He thinks, therefore, that the Apostle wished to restrain the pride of their spirit, by which they boasted that they were so firm in faith that there was no reason to admonish them, as those who thought they stood, to take heed lest they fall. Thus I understood it.

units.la: esset: At sic estis securi, propter nescio quas te tationes quas uestro iudicio egregie sustinueritis, ut timendum uobis non esse iudicetis, ne cadatis unquam. Verum nondum estis graui ore rem aliquam tentationem experti. Quæ accid erunt uobis humana sunt, id est modica & momentanea. Nondum ad sanguinem usque certastis. Quare videte, ne dum uos stare putatis, ca datis. Recentiores aliud atq; aliud adferunt. Iudicet lector. Nos admonemur, minus excusationis esse illis, qui nondum graui aliqua tribulatione tentati, cum infidelibus miscentur, ne quid acerbius experiri cogantur, quàm qui post graues afflictiones stationem suam pau lisper deserunt, tametsi nec illi habent unde excusentur. Discernat pius homo inter afflictiones communes, & humanas, & eas, quæ instigante Satana, peculiari odio & crudelitate fidelibus propter Christum ac uerbum eius ab hoc impio mundo inferuntur, ac cogitet in cor de suo: Vel humana sunt quæ pateris, & ferenda sunt cum reliquis mortalibus communia, uel communem mortalium sorte excedunt. Si humana sunt, non est ut moleste feras. Si supra humana, magis est ut glorieris. Rom. 5. Ut animum desponedeas. Leuiter ferenda sunt, quæ humana sunt, quod tribulationes attinet, secus uero sentiendum est de erroribus & peccatis, quæ ex communi mortalium corruptione proueniunt. Hæc non sunt extenuanda hoc prætextu quod sint humana, sed magis deflede, vulgo dicitur, humanum est errare. Nimis quidem humanum est, uerum nihilo debet hoc malum ipsterea leuioris duci, quod humanum est, sed quato est humanius, hoc amplius deplorari.
units.tr: ...as if he were saying: "But you are so secure, because of I know not what temptations which, in your judgement, you have endured splendidly, that you think you need not fear ever falling. But you have not yet experienced any temptation of serious weight. What will happen to you is human, that is, moderate and momentary. You have not yet struggled even to the shedding of blood. Therefore take heed, lest, while you think you stand, you fall." Recent writers bring forward one thing after another; let the reader judge. We are reminded that those who have not yet been tested by any serious tribulation, and who mix with unbelievers, have less excuse than those who, after heavy afflictions, briefly desert their post, though neither group has any excuse. Let the pious man distinguish between common and human afflictions and those which, at the instigation of Satan, are inflicted on the faithful for Christ and his word by this impious world with peculiar hatred and cruelty. Let him think within his heart: either what you suffer is human, and is to be borne as common to mortals along with the rest, or it exceeds the common lot of mortals. If it is human, you need not bear it with resentment; if it is above the human, you have more reason to glory (Rom. 5.), so that you do not lose heart. Those things that are human are to be borne lightly, as far as tribulations go; but it is otherwise with errors and sins, which arise from the common corruption of mortals. These are not to be made light of under the pretext that they are human; rather, as the common saying goes, "to err is human." It is indeed very human, but this evil ought not on that account to be held lighter; the more human it is, the more it must be deplored.

units.la: FIDELIS autem est Deus, inquit, qui non sinet uos tentari supra id quod potestis, &c.) Inhæret cœptæ occupationi. Poterat dicere: Hactenus quidem nulla nos nisi humana tentatio cepit, uerum quis nos certos reddet de futuro, si uitanda in uniuersum sint infidelium consortia, & odia illorum exasperanda? Deinde, quod hactenus nulla graui sumus afflictione tentati, ex hoc ipso est quod tu prohibes, ex consortio uidelicet, quo illis, citra eidolola triam tamen, coniungimur. Nam hoc medio iram & odia illorum infringimus. Occurrit isti obiectioni dicens; Neq; uestro hoc consilio accepturum ferre debetis, quod hactenus non estis tentatione nō humana experti, neq; est, ut anxij sitis de futuro, sed fide uobis pendendu potius est à fideli Deo, q infirma uestra nec ignorat nec negligit, sed pro bonitate ac fide sua ea uebit, ne grauius tetemini, q sitis ferendo, cui etiá hoc ipsum debetis, quod hactenus leuius estis tetati. Quare nulla uobis excusatio relinquitur, nec ulla causa est, propter quá infidelib coniungi, & conuiuijs illorū miscerī debeatis.
units.tr: "But God is faithful," he says, "who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able," etc. He keeps to the line of argument he began. He could have said: "Hitherto indeed no temptation except a human one has seized us; but who will make us certain of the future, if we must altogether avoid the company of unbelievers and provoke their hatred and anger? Moreover, the fact that we have so far been tested by no grievous affliction is itself due to what you forbid, namely, to our association with them, without, however, the eating of idol sacrifices. For by this means we break their anger and hatred." He meets this objection, saying: "You must not bring this counsel to bear, because you have not so far been tested by temptation beyond the human, nor should you be anxious about the future. Rather you should depend on faithful God, who knows and does not neglect your weakness, but in his goodness and faithfulness will carry it so that you are not more severely tested than you can bear, and to whom you owe even this, that so far you have been tested more lightly. Therefore no excuse is left to you, and there is no cause for which you ought to join unbelievers and mix in their feasts."

units.la: FIDELIS autem est Deus, inquit.) Non simpliciter dicit: Non sinet uos tentari Deus, sed præmittit, fidelis autem est Deus. Prædicat de Deo, esse eum fidelem, quo & promissioni suæ fidem faciat, & omnem diffidetiæ solicitu dine tollat. Significat hinc potissimum esse cau sam præposteri metus, quod Deo nō satis fidimus, & simul monet, nullas esse nobis diffidendi illi causas, cum sit supreme fidelis. Vtinam autem tam credamus fidelem esse Deum, quàm quid sit esse fidelem nō ignoramus. Cum Deū fidelem esse dicit, non simpliciter de eo prædicat, quod sit fidelis, sicut de homine bono, ac ueraci dici potest, quod sit homo fidelis, sed quod sit fidelis Deus. Deum esse fidelem, est fidelem esse creatorem, ac conseruatorem seruandis nobis fideliter intentum, perinde ac si de rege prædices, quod sit fidelis rex, hoc est, quod officiū regis erga subditos fideliter obeat, & de pastore, quod sit fidelis pastor, gregem suum fideliter pascens & custodiens.
units.tr: "Faithful is God," he says. He does not simply say, "God will not allow you to be tempted," but first adds, "Faithful is God." He ascribes faithfulness to God, by which he both gives assurance of his promise and removes every anxious doubt. He thereby indicates that the chief cause of misplaced fear is that we do not trust God enough, and at the same time he warns us that we have no reason to distrust him, since he is supremely faithful. Would that we believed God to be faithful as surely as we know what faithfulness is! When he says God is faithful, he does not predicate of him merely that he is faithful, as one may say of a good and truthful man that he is a faithful man. He means that God is faithful. To say God is faithful is to say that the Creator and Preserver is intent on keeping us faithfully, just as if you were to say of a king that he is a faithful king, meaning that he faithfully discharges his duty towards his subjects, or of a minister that he is a faithful minister, faithfully feeding and guarding his flock.

units.la: Q V I non sinet vos tentari, inquit, supra id quod potestis.) Aperit, quid sibi de fideli Deo polliceri debeant. Timetis, inquit, graviores uobis euenturas esse tribulationes, quàm ut ferendo futuri sitis. Hæc est uestra diffidentia, uerum fidelior erga uos Deus est, q ut hoc fieri sinat. Esto, adoriatur uos mundus, & prorsus subuertere nitatur, nihil tamen in uos ipso non permittente poterit, & ipse non sinet ut possit. Novit enim quàm adhuc estis infirmi. Et huius infirmitatis uestræ rationem habens non permisit hactenus, ut supra humana uos tentatio capiat, nec permittet in posterum.
units.tr: "Who will not allow you to be tempted," he says, "beyond what you are able to bear." He explains what they ought to expect from the faithful God. You fear, he says, that the afflictions coming upon you will be heavier than you can endure. That is your distrust. But God is more faithful to you than to allow this to happen. Grant that the world assails you and strives utterly to overthrow you: it will be able to do nothing to you unless he permits it, and he will not allow it to have that power. For he knows how weak you still are. Taking account of this weakness of yours, he has not so far permitted that temptation should seize you beyond human strength, and he will not permit it in future either.

units.la: Est hic locus insignis, & omnib9 fidelibus, præsertim persequutionis tempore, memorimete ac fide firma fiducialiter vsurpadus. Primum, monet nos, nullâ esse tentatione, nullúq; tentatore, siue diabolo siue mundo, cui aliquid sit in nos potestatis, nisi ipsius fidelis Dei nostri permissu. Nō sinet uos tentari, inquit. Deo nō permittēte quis tabit electos Dei. Deinde nō simpliciter dicit, non sinet uos tentari. Non faceret hoc ad fidei nostræ exercitium & salutis profectū, si nunquā tentari nos sinet. Quate addit, supra id quod potestis. Immoderatâ tentatione, quâ tetati sternemur, & in exitium deiiceremur, haudquaquā admittit, moderatā uero fideliter ac prudēter despe-sat. In periculis itaq; & tribulationibus constituti, cogitemus nos tentari ac probari, idq́ue permissu Dei, nec ultra quā ferre queamus, progressuram esse tentationem. Nec est ut ipsi uires nostras metiamur, quæ ab ipso domino & cōfesuntur, & pro ipsius prudentia in ipsa lu cta augentur, ut possimus multa, qui nos statim defecturos existimabamus.
units.tr: This is a remarkable passage, and one which all the faithful should use with a firm and confident memory and faith, especially in time of persecution. First, it warns us that there is no temptation and no tempter, whether the devil or the world, who has any power over us except by the permission of our faithful God. "He will not allow you to be tempted," he says. Without God's permission no one can touch the elect of God. Next, he does not simply say, "He will not allow you to be tempted." That would not serve the exercise of our faith or the advancement of our salvation if he never allowed us to be tempted at all. Therefore he adds, "beyond what you are able to bear." He by no means permits temptation so immoderate that we are overthrown by it and cast down to destruction, but he faithfully and prudently moderates it. Therefore, when we are placed in dangers and afflictions, let us consider that we are being tested and proved, and that this happens by God's permission, and that the temptation will not proceed beyond what we are able to bear. Nor should we measure our own strength, which is granted by the Lord himself and, in accordance with his wisdom, is increased in the very struggle, so that we are able to endure many things which we thought would at once fail us.

units.la: SED faciet, inquit, unà cum tentatione exitum quoq; quo abūde sufferre possitis.) Duo sunt, quibus tentatio, id est tribulatio & afflictio gravatur & latu difficilior redditur. Magnitudo uidelicet, qua veluti mole quadā gravatur, & diuturna plixitas, qua sine fine durātura videtur. Contra prioris molestiam facit quod dicit: Nō sinet uos tentari supra id quod potestis, contra posterioris vero, quod subiungit, sed faciet unà cum tentatione exitu quoque. Recte sic leges: Quin exitum quoq; unà cum tentatione faciet. Non simpliciter dicit, sed faciet exitum, sed, vt significet curare dominum, non modo ne grauior sit tentatio, sed & ne sit prolixior & velut infinita, quin, inquit & exitum faciet. Vnà cum tentatione inquit, hoc est: Dum destinat vobis tentationem aliquam, simul hoc curat, vt breui terminetur, sitque illius modus aliquis & exitus, atq; ita tentationes attemperat, ut sint leues & momenta nex, quo sufferre possitis. Sic 2. Cor. 4. tribulationibus praesentis vitae & leuitatem & momentaneam breuitatem tribuit, dicens: Id enim quod in praesenti est momentaneum, & leue tribulationis nostrae, &c.
units.tr: "But he will make," he says, "together with the temptation, also the way out, so that you may be able to bear it fully." There are two things by which temptation, that is tribulation and affliction, is made heavier and harder to bear: its magnitude, by which it is weighed down as by a great mass, and its long duration, by which it seems to last without end. Against the first difficulty he sets what he says, "He will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear"; against the second, what he adds, "but he will make, together with the temptation, also the way out." You should read it thus: "Indeed he will also make the way out together with the temptation." He does not simply say "he will make a way out," but, to show that the Lord takes care not only that the temptation be not heavier but also that it be not longer and, as it were, endless, he says, "indeed he will make a way out too." "Together with the temptation," he says, that is: while he appoints some temptation for you, at the same time he takes care that it be brought to a speedy end, and that it have some measure and outcome; and so he tempers temptations so that they are light and momentary, so that you may be able to endure them. Thus in 2 Cor. 4 he ascribes to the tribulations of the present life both lightness and momentary brevity, saying: "For that which is momentary and light of our tribulation in the present, etc."

units.la: Nec illud ociosum est, quod non simpliciter dicit: τὸ δύνασθαι ὑμᾶς ἐνεγκεῖν, id est, quo possitis ferre, sed, τὸ δύνασθαι ὑμᾶς ὑπενεγκεῖν, id est, quo possitis esse ferendo supra & vltra quàm sit tentationis modus. Quare visum est vertere, quo abunde sufferre possitis. Metaphora est ab illis sumpta, quibus onera portanda imponuntur, vbi non est satis aliquousque quodimpositum est ferre, nisi ad terminum vsq; feratur quo est destinatum. Et qui robustis sunt lateribus, sic valent ferendo, vt si ita requiratur etiam vltra praescriptum terminum impositum onus ferre queant. Qui sic ferunt, dicuntur ὑπενεγκεῖν. Illis non est molestum onus, quod etiam vltra terminum destinatum ferre possunt. Sic visum est Apostolo animare fideles contra metum tentationum, quo fiebat, vt se mundo magis quàm Christo accommodantes cum infidelibus in conuiuijs immolaticijs accumberent, vnde eos auocare volebat, ne sic illecti ad cultum eidolorum relaberentur. Vnde & subdit:
units.tr: Nor is it idle that he does not simply say τὸ δύνασθαι ὑμᾶς ἐνεγκεῖν [to dynasthai hymas enenkein], that is, "that you may be able to bear," but τὸ δύνασθαι ὑμᾶς ὑπενεγκεῖν [to dynasthai hymas hypenenkein], that is, "that you may be able to bear up under and beyond the measure of the temptation." Hence I have judged it right to render it "that you may be able to bear it fully." The metaphor is taken from those who have burdens laid upon them. Where it is not enough to bear what has been laid on only up to a certain point, unless it is carried to the end appointed, and those who have strong backs bear so well that, if need be, they can carry the laid burden even beyond the prescribed limit: those who carry in this way are said ὑπενεγκεῖν [hypenenkein]. For them the burden is not troublesome, since they can carry it even beyond the appointed limit. So the Apostle thought fit to encourage the faithful against the fear of temptations, which was making them accommodate themselves more to the world than to Christ, so that they reclined at feasts with unbelievers at idol-sacrifices. From these he wished to call them away, lest, so enticed, they should slide back into the worship of idols. Hence he also adds:

units.la: Quapropter dilecti mei fugite à simulacrorum cultu.
units.tr: Therefore, my beloved, flee from the worship of idols.

units.la: Satis declarat hac particula, quorsum haec omnia dixerit, dum non velut ad alia transiens simpliciter dicit: Dilecti mei fugite à simulacrorum cultu, sed tanquam ex praemissis colligens & concludens: Quapropter dilecti mei. Quasi dicat. Cum igitur periculum sit ne cadatis à fide, dum eidolothyta cum infidelibus manducatis, nec sit vlla vobis causa ob quam metu tentationum gratificemini eidololatris, quaeso dilecti mei, fugite à cultu simulacrorum. Non dicit: ne colatis eidola, sed, fugite à cultu eidolorum. Non enim scribit eidola colentibus, sed ijs fidelibus, qui in eidolio cum eidololatris manducabant & bibebant, quod non fecissent, si à communicatione eidololatrarum abhorruissent, quem horrorem requirens dicit: Fugite à simulacrorum cultu. Poterat dicere abstinete, verùm quo significaret, quanto cum horrore communicationem eidolothytorum cauere deberent, fugite, inquit, à simulacrorum cultu. Potudus etiam habet, quod communicationem eidolothytorum vocat cultum simulacrorum. Plus vrget, quà si dicret, fugite ab immolaticijs, vel, fugite à mensis
units.tr: This particle sufficiently shows why he said all these things. He does not pass to a new subject with a plain statement, "My beloved, flee from the worship of idols," but draws his conclusion from what has gone before: "Therefore, my beloved." It is as if he said: Since there is danger that you fall from the faith while you eat idol-sacrificed food with unbelievers, and since you have no reason to gratify the idolaters out of fear of temptation, I beg you, my beloved, flee from the worship of idols. He does not say, "Do not worship idols," but "Flee from the worship of idols." He is not writing to those who worship idols, but to believers who ate and drank in the idol's temple with idolaters. They would not have done this had they shrunk from fellowship with idolaters. Seeking to rouse that shrinking, he says, "Flee from the worship of idols." He could have said "abstain," but to show with what horror they ought to guard against fellowship in idol-sacrificed food, he says, "Flee from the worship of idols." He could also call the communion in idol-sacrificed food the worship of idols. This presses harder than if he had said, "Flee from sacrificial meals," or "Flee from the tables."

units.la: Nos admonemur hoc loco, non esse satis si non colamus eidola, nisi etiam à cultu illorum abhorreamus, & abhorrentes fugiamus. Hic horror ferre non poterit, vt cultibus simulacrorum cum Papistis adstet homo vere pius. Quare viderint qui missis Papistarum adsunt, cù sciat illas ipsissimam esse eidololatriā, & inferendā abominationē. Accommodant se mudo, ne incidant in afflictiones veritatis gratia sufferendas, quasi non sit Deus tam fidelis vt velit, & tā potens vt possit, quicquid accidat tribulationum, sic moderari & attemperare, vt ferendo esse possint. Istis tandem eueniet, vt sua ipsorum conscientia condemnati vermem non morientem, & ignem inextinguibilem omnium infelicissimorum experiantur.
units.tr: We are reminded here that it is not enough not to worship idols, unless we also shrink from their worship and, shrinking, flee from it. A truly pious man cannot endure this horror of standing beside the Papists at the worship of idols. Let those who attend the Papists' masses see to it, since they know that these are the very idolatry and an abomination to be avoided. They accommodate themselves to the world so as not to fall into afflictions that must be endured for the truth's sake, as if God were not so faithful as to will, and so powerful as to be able, to temper and moderate whatever tribulations befall, so that they can be borne. In the end it will come to pass for these men that, condemned by their own conscience, they will experience the undying worm and the unquenchable fire, the most wretched of all.

units.la: Vt prudentibus loquor, iudicate vos quod dico. Poculum benedictionis cui benedicimus nonne communicatio sanguinis Christi est? Panis quem frangimus nonne communicatio corporis Christi est? Quoniam unus panis unum corpus multi sumus. Nam omnes ex uno pane participamus. Videte Israelem iuxta carnem. Nonne qui edunt victimas, cofor tes sunt altaris? Quid ergo dico? Quod simulacrum aliquid sit? Aut quod immolatum sacris immolatū aliquid sit? Non. sed illud dico, quod quae immolant gentes, daemonijs immolant, & non Deo. Nolim autem vos consortes daemoniorum fieri. Non poteritis poculum domini bibere, & poculum daemoniorum. Non poteritis mensae domini participes esse, & mensae daemoniorum. An prouocamus dominum? Num fortiores illo sumus?
units.tr: I speak as to the prudent; judge for yourselves what I say. Is not the cup of blessing, which we bless, a communion in the blood of Christ? Is not the bread which we break a communion in the body of Christ? Since we, being many, are one bread and one body, for we all partake of the one bread. Look at Israel according to the flesh: are not those who eat the sacrifices partners of the altar? What then do I say? That an idol is anything, or that what is sacrificed to idols is anything? No; but I say that the things the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I would not have you become partners of demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons. Or do we provoke the Lord? Are we stronger than he?

units.la: Cohaerent haec omnia, quare nolui lectionem eorum diuellere. Nam sensus priorum à posterioribus dependet, qui in summa talis est. Participes estis mensae domini, quare non conuenit ut participes sitis mensae eidolorum. Non debetis igitur comedere de mensa illorum, ne participes illius sitis, alias irā Dei in uos prouocabitis. Summam hac sic ordina. Particeps mensae domini non potest esse particeps mensae eidolorum. Vos participes estis mensae domini. Ergo non potestis participes esse mensae eidolorum. Maiorem non probat, tanquam per se notam. Minorem probat. Conclusionē simpliciter ponit, ex praecedentibus palàm resultantem.
units.tr: All these things hang together, so I did not want to tear their reading apart. For the sense of the earlier part depends on the later, and in summary it is this: You are partakers of the table of the Lord; therefore it is not fitting that you be partakers of the table of idols. You ought not, then, to eat from their table, lest you become partakers of it, otherwise you will provoke the wrath of God against you. I set out the argument thus: A partaker of the table of the Lord cannot be a partaker of the table of idols. You are partakers of the table of the Lord. Therefore you cannot be partakers of the table of idols. He does not prove the major premise, as being known in itself. He proves the minor. He states the conclusion plainly, as it results openly from what precedes.

units.la: VT prudentibus loquor, iudicate vos quod dico.) Priusquà certa argumentatione conuincat absurdū esse & cōtra Christi sacramentū quod faciebant, praefatiunculà hac reddit eos paulo attentiores, qua primùm illis hoc tribuit,
units.tr: "As I speak to the prudent, judge for yourselves what I say." Before he convicts by a firm argument that what they were doing was absurd and contrary to the sacrament of Christ, he makes them rather more attentive with this little preface, by which he first ascribes this to them:

units.la: quod sint φρόνιμοι, id est, uiri mente & intelligentia sic pręditi, ut facilè de ijs quæ dicuntur iudicare queant. Deinde permittit ipsis ut iudices sint eorum de quibus est dicturus. Quasi dicat, Scio me loqui non pueris, sed uiris prudentibus, quare quæ dicturus sum uestro ipsorū iudicio subijcere non uereor. Sic enim sunt manifesta & indubitata, ut modo quæ uera sunt probare uelitis, haudquaquam ea in quæstionem trahere positis.
units.tr: that they are φρόνιμοι [phronimoi], that is, men so endowed with mind and understanding that they can readily judge the things that are said. Then he allows them to be judges of the matters on which he is about to speak. It is as if he said: I know that I am speaking not to children but to prudent men; therefore I do not fear to submit to your own judgment what I am about to say. For these things are so plain and undoubted that you will not wish to call in question what is true, now that you are asked only to prove it.

units.la: Sed quæret hic quisquam, quomodo eos hic uiros prudētes uocet, cum suprà cap.3. uocarit carnales ac paruulos in Christo, quibus nondum queat solidum cibum sed lac submi-nistrare cogatur. Respondeo. Discernendum est primum inter fideles ecclesię Corinthiorū, deinde inter ipsas causas de quibus ad eos scri-bit. Puerile admodū erat, contendere de minis-tris, & secundum diuersam illorum qualitatem scindere ecclesiam in sectas. Huius mali causa erat rudis rudiū zelus. Quare eos qui illo laborabant carnales ac paruulos uocat. In præsenti uero causa à priori admodum diuer-sa, negocium illi erat cum prudentioribus, qui cęteris erant in causa fidei instructiores quidē sed non meliores. Plurimum iactabant scien-tiam & fidei nescio quam præstantiam. Deinde & iuxta sæculum erant reliquis prudentio-res. Hi se accommodabant sæculo quo crucis molestias effugerent, ideoq; cum infidelibus in conuiuijs immolaticijs miscebātur. Ipsa autem causa sic erat comparata, ut etiam iuxta sę-culum prudentibus facilis esset cognitu & iu-dicatu. Quid enim manifestius est & irrefraga-bilius, quàm nihil esse debere communicatio-nis Deo & dæmonibus, & eos qui participes sunt mensę Christi, non debere, imo nec posse participes esse mensæ dæmoniorum? Hacte-nus uocat eos prudentes, & constituit in causa tam manifesta argumenti huius iudices. Quæ uero suprà cap. 3. scribit, ad eos pertinent, qui in causa rudiori ipsi quoq; rudiores corrigendi erant. Quare nihil hic est contradictionis. Contradictio nanq; non est nisi in ijsdem. Pro sua prudentia Apostolus accommodat se & causæ de qua, & personis, cū quibus agit. Durum uidebatur, quod dixerat: Quapropter dilecti mei fugite à simulacrorum cultu, quibus uerbis accusationem exaggerauerat. Nihil enim illi minus quàm cultores simulacrorum uidebantur, nec ferre poterant, ut quod cum infidelibus de immolaticijs edebāt, tanquam confine cum cultu simulacrorum reprehenderetur. Vt hanc duriciem emolliat, & dicti sui æquitatem declaret, iudicium causæ quam agit defert ipsis, tanquam cęteris prudentiori-bus. At hi ipsi erant, quos redarguebat & accu-sabat. Sic igitur ut confidentiam suam in hac causa declaret, ipsos reos reprehensionis hu-ius iudices constituit.
units.tr: But someone here will ask how he can call them prudent men here, when above, in chapter 3, he called them carnal and infants in Christ, to whom he was forced to give milk rather than solid food. I answer: one must first distinguish between the believers of the Corinthian church, and then between the very matters about which he writes to them. It was utterly childish to quarrel about ministers and, according to the different quality of each, to split the church into sects. The cause of this evil was the untaught zeal of the untaught. That is why he calls those who were troubled by it carnal and infants. In the present matter, which is quite different from the earlier one, he had to deal with the prudent, who were indeed better instructed than the rest in the cause of faith, but not better men. They boasted greatly of their knowledge and of some kind of excellence in faith. Moreover, in worldly terms they were more prudent than the rest. These men accommodated themselves to the world so as to escape the troubles of the cross, and therefore mixed with unbelievers at idol-sacrificial feasts. The matter itself was so arranged that it was easy for the prudent, even by worldly standards, to recognise and judge. For what is more manifest and irrefutable than that communion with God and with demons can have nothing in common, and that those who partake of the table of Christ must not, nay cannot, be partakers of the table of demons? Thus far he calls them prudent, and in a matter so plain he makes them the judges of this argument. But what he writes above in chapter 3 applies to those who, in the more untaught matter, were themselves to be corrected as untaught. So there is no contradiction here. A contradiction exists only between the same things. According to his prudence, the Apostle adapts himself both to the matter he is treating and to the persons with whom he deals. What he had said seemed harsh: "Therefore, my beloved, flee from the worship of idols," words by which he had heightened the accusation. For nothing seemed further from them than being worshippers of idols, and they could not bear that what they ate with unbelievers from idol-sacrifices should be rebuked as though it were akin to the worship of idols. To soften this harshness and to show the fairness of what he says, he hands over to them the judgment of the matter he is pursuing, as to the more prudent among them. Yet these very men were the ones he was rebuking and accusing. So, to show his confidence in this cause, he makes the very men under accusation the judges of this rebuke.

units.la: Admonemur igitur hoc loco, non esse insolitum ac nouum, si uiris prudentibus accidat, ut ea faciant, quæ ipsorum iudicio, si ritè ad-
units.tr: We are reminded, then, that it is not unusual or new for prudent men to do things which, by their own judgment, if they were rightly admonished, could not be defended.

units.la: moneantur, defendi nequeant. Hoc enim genus hominum non peccat zelo rudi ac inerti, sed quod habet prudentiæ accōmodat ad declinandum odium mundi, & ad comminiscen-das excusationes eorum quæ astutè faciunt.
units.tr: For this kind of man does not sin from untaught and idle zeal, but uses his prudence to avoid the hatred of the world and to devise excuses for what they do craftily.

units.la: Deinde uidemus hic quàta sit essęq; debeat uis ueritatis in ecclesia Dei, in eo quod dicit: iudicate uos quod dico. Tanta uidelicet, ut etiam ab illis, qui reprehenduntur & accusan-tur, ad ipsorum condemnationem agnoscatur & approbetur. Prorsus impij sunt, qui contra suam ipsorum conscientiam quod falsum esse sciunt admoniti defendūt, & quod uerum esse norunt impugnant & negant, quibus minister uerbi Dei imprudenter dicturus est: Vt prudentibus loquor, iudicate uos quod dico. Nolim hoc patribus concilij papistici dicere, quia non sunt iudices constituendi eorum de quibus accusantur.
units.tr: Next we see here how great, and how great it ought to be, the power of truth in the church of God, in that he says: "Judge for yourselves what I say." It is so great that it is acknowledged and approved even by those who are rebuked and accused, to their own condemnation. Truly impious are those who, when admonished, defend against their own conscience what they know to be false, and who attack and deny what they know to be true. To such men a minister of the Word of God will speak imprudently if he says: "As I speak to the prudent, judge for yourselves what I say." I would not say this to the fathers of the Papist council, because they are not to be appointed as judges of the matters for which they are accused.

units.la: Poculum benedictionis cui benedici-mus, nonne communicatio sanguinis Christi est? panis quē frangimus, nonne communicatio corporis Christi est?
units.tr: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?

units.la: Pertinet ista ad probationem minoris, usq; ad illud: Quid ergo dico? Quod simulacrum aliquid sit? Minor aūt est in hac argumetatione: Vos estis participes corporis ac sanguinis domini. Probat hanc per expositionē ritus ec-clesiæ Christi, quo communiter quidem omnes panem domini de mensa illius edebant, & poculum bibebant, uerum non ita communiter omnes mysterio illius sese accōmodabāt, alioqui nemo ex illis de mensa eidolorū com-municasset. Ad ritum sacrū pertinet, quod dicit: Poculum benedictionis, cui benedicimus. Item, panis quem frangimus, ad expositionem uero illius, quod addit: nonne communicatio sanguinis Christi est? Et: Nonne communicatio corporis Christi est? Quasi dicat, Estis ergo uos participes corporis ac sanguinis domini, quotquot de poculo hoc bibitis, & de pane domini editis.
units.tr: This belongs to the proof of the minor premise, up to the words, "What do I say, then? That an idol is anything?" The minor premise in this argument is: "You are partakers of the body and blood of the Lord." He proves it by explaining the rite of Christ's Church, in which indeed all commonly ate the Lord's bread from his table and drank the cup, but not all alike devoted themselves to his mystery; otherwise none of them would have communicated at the table of idols. The words "the cup of blessing, which we bless" and "the bread which we break" belong to the sacred rite. The explanation of them, which he adds, is "is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?" and "is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" As if he were saying: "You therefore are partakers of the body and blood of the Lord, as many of you as drink of this cup and eat of the Lord's bread."

units.la: Poculum, inquit, benedictionis, cui benedi-cimus. Loquitur omnino de poculo & pane cœnæ dominicæ. Vocem ποτήριον, id est, poculū, ponit pro uino quod est in poculo, continens pro contento. Nisi ex uerbis Christi, quibus se non amplius de germine uitis bibiturū dixit, cum poculum hoc mysticum discipulis in ultima cœna porrigeret, expressa esset potus species, ut uinum eos in cœna bibisse constet, ex hac uoce ποτήριον nemo certo colligeret, quonam genere potus usus esset Christus, nisi què uti uoluisset. Sunt enim multa ac uaria genera liquidorū, quæ iuxta cuiusq; regionis ac gentis conditionem communiter bibuntur. Alij bibunt uinum, alij ceruisiam, alij melicraton, alij aquam tantū. Et tamen communiter, quicquid bibatur id unde bibitur ποτήριον uocatur etiam si aqua bibatur, quemadmodū & Christus Matth. 19. loquutus est, dicens: Quicunq; dederit ad bibendū uni ex pusillis istis poculū
units.tr: "The cup," he says, "of blessing, which we bless." He speaks altogether of the cup and bread of the Lord's Supper. He uses the word ποτήριον, that is, cup, for the wine which is in the cup, the container for the contents. Unless the kind of drink had been stated, from the words of Christ, in which he said he would no longer drink of the fruit of the vine when he handed this mystical cup to the disciples at the last supper, so that it is established that they drank wine at the supper, no one could reliably gather from this word ποτήριον what kind of drink Christ used, unless he had wished to say. For there are many and various kinds of liquids, which are commonly drunk according to the condition of each region and nation. Some drink wine, others beer, others mead, others only water. Yet commonly, whatever is drunk, the vessel from which it is drunk is called ποτήριον, even if the drink is water; just as Christ too spoke in Matth. 19., saying: "Whoever gives to drink to one of these little ones a cup of cold water," etc.

units.la: P aquæ frigidæ,&c. Hac consideratione defen- di possent aquarij, qui aqua tantum vsi sunt in cœna mystica, & alij, qui pro regionū suarum conditione ac more alio, quàm vini potu vtun tur, idq; nulla alia ratione faciunt, quàm quod vino destituuntur. Sic sentiens, eos excipio, q. superstitionis gratia ab eo deflectunt, quo dominum vsum esse constat.
units.tr: By this consideration the water-drinkers could be defended, who used only water in the mystical supper, and others who, according to the custom of their regions, use some other drink than wine, and do so for no other reason than that they lack wine. Thinking thus, I exclude those who depart from what the Lord is known to have used, for the sake of superstition.

units.la: Quod materialem poculi qualitatē attinet, nusquam expressum est, aureum ne, vel argenteum, vel vitreum, vel stanneum aut plumbeū vel ligneum fuerit, quo vsus est Dominus. Nec vspiam de eo constituerunt Apostoli. Sciebant illi quæ fuerit simplicitas & frugalitas mensæ Dominicæ, & quàm Sacramenta aurū non quærant, nec auro commendentur, quæ auro non emuntur. Quondam, inquit Bonifacius martyr & episcopus, nō aureis, sed ligneis calicibus vtebantur sacerdotes. Postea Vrbanus papa omnia fecit argentea. Concilium Triburiense decus ecclesiarum esse fuit in auro vel argento, ideoq; constituit, vt post simplicitatem & frugalitatem prioris ecclesiæ nullus sacerdos in ligneis vasculis mysteria sacra conficere præsumat, ne vnde placari debet inde irritetur Deus. Qua in re videmus quomodo papaliter pōtifices & episcopi à vero sensu mysteriorum & à simplicitate prioris ecclesiæ ad iplendorem sæculi defecerint. Sic factū est, vt ecclesia, quæ olim lignea pocula & ministros aureos habuit, nunc habeat aurea pocula & ministros ligneos.
units.tr: As for the material of the cup, it is nowhere stated whether the cup the Lord used was of gold, silver, glass, tin, lead or wood. Nor did the apostles lay down anything about it anywhere. They knew what the simplicity and frugality of the Lord's table were, and that the sacraments do not seek gold, nor are commended by gold, since they are not bought with gold. Formerly, says Boniface the martyr and bishop, priests used not golden but wooden chalices. Afterwards Pope Urban made everything silver. The Council of Tribur held that gold or silver was the ornament of the churches, and therefore decreed that, after the simplicity and frugality of the earlier church, no priest should presume to celebrate the sacred mysteries in wooden vessels, lest God be provoked by the very thing by which he ought to be appeased. In this matter we see how the papal pontiffs and bishops have fallen away from the true sense of the mysteries and from the simplicity of the earlier church, to the splendour of the world. So it has come about that the church, which once had wooden cups and golden ministers, now has golden cups and wooden ministers.

units.la: POCVLVM, inquit benedictiōis, cui benedicimus.) Non simpliciter dicit: Poculū quod B bibimus, & panis quē edimus, sed poculum benedictionis, cui benedicimus, & panis quē frangimus, quo se non de Epiphana, sed mystica dni mensa loqui significet: vocat autem poculū cœnæ dominicæ, poculū εὐλογίας, quod vertūt calicē vel poculū benedictionis. Saluo fano aliorū iudicio verti poterat poculū collectę, vel collationis, vel vt hāc vocem Erasmus 2. Co. 9 vertit, bonæ collationis, vbi de collectione agitur, qua contributio fidelium in vsus pauperū colligebatur, quā Apostolus illic omnino εὐλογίαν vocat dicens, vt præparēt ante promissam εὐλογίαν vestram. Quoniā autē constat primos Christianos in Synaxi sua, qua cœnam domini celebrabāt, nō modo comedisse vnā, sed & attulisse secū, quæ in vsus pauperum distribuerētur, eāq; contributionem vocatā esse collectā quę vox adhuc in vsu est papistice missantib», vt vocant, cum rem ipsam prorsus ignorent, existimo Apostolum hoc loco, mēsam dominicam vocare εὐλογίαν (quam postea vocarunt agapen, id est, dilectionem) præsertim cum ea vox nota esset inter Corinthios, ex frequēti collectiōis huius vsu. Hoc itaq; sensu poculū mensæ dominicæ vocat poculū Eulogiæ. Q.d. Poculū illud quod in cœtu sacro, dum eulogiam facimus, cū benedictione & gratiarū actiōe sumimus, &c. Verū quemadmodū dixi, sint hæc saluo aliorum iudicio annotata ne quis hic mihi litem moueat. Chrysost. εὐλογίαν retulit ad Deum, accepitq; pro ευεργεσία .i. beneficentia Dei. Sic enim expositus. Εὐλογίαν γὰρ ὅταν εἴπω, πάντα ἀναπτύσσων τὴν τῆς Ευεργεσίας ἢ ὅτι θησαυρὸν, ἡ τιμὴν ἡμῖν ἀναμιμνῆσκων δωρεῶν. Alij vel consecratione per εὐλογίαν, vel gratiarum actione intelligūt, vt quā sequitur ὁ εὐλογῶμεν, i. quod benedicimus, præcedentis τῆς εὐλογίας fit expositio, sitq; poculum eulogiæ nihil aliud quàm poculum consecrationis, vel poculū gratiarum actionis.
units.tr: "The cup," he says, "of blessing, which we bless." He does not simply say, "the cup which we drink, and the bread which we eat," but "the cup of blessing, which we bless, and the bread which we break," signifying that he speaks not of a feast of Epiphany but of the mystical table of the Lord. He calls it the cup of the Lord's Supper, the cup of εὐλογία, which they render "chalice" or "cup of blessing." Without prejudice to the judgment of others, it could have been rendered "cup of the collection," or "of the contribution," or, as Erasmus renders this word in 2 Cor. 9, "of good contribution," where the collection is discussed, by which the contribution of the faithful was gathered for the use of the poor, and which the Apostle there calls εὐλογία, saying, "that they may prepare beforehand your promised εὐλογία." But since it is established that the first Christians, in their synaxis in which they celebrated the Lord's Supper, not only ate together but also brought with them what would be distributed for the use of the poor, and that this contribution was called collecta, a word still in use among the Papists, as they call them, though they utterly ignore the thing itself, I think the Apostle in this passage calls the Lord's table εὐλογία (which they later called agape, that is, love), especially since that word was known among the Corinthians from the frequent practice of this collection. In this sense, then, he calls the cup of the Lord's table the cup of eulogia; that is: "that cup which, in the sacred assembly, while we make the eulogia, we take with blessing and thanksgiving," etc. But, as I said, let these things be noted without prejudice to the judgment of others, lest anyone stir up a quarrel with me here. Chrysostom referred εὐλογία to God and took it for εὐεργεσία, that is, the beneficence of God. For thus he expounds it: "For when I say εὐλογία, I unfold all the benefit..." Others understand it either of consecration through εὐλογία or of the action of thanksgiving, so that what follows, ὃ εὐλογοῦμεν, that is, "which we bless," is an exposition of the preceding "of blessing," and the cup of eulogia is nothing other than the cup of consecration or the cup of thanksgiving.

units.la: CVI benedicimus inquit.) Græcè est, ὃν εὐλογήμεν, id est, quod benedicimus. Vertit Erasm. cui benedicimus quasi sit posītū pro ὃ. Chrysostom. sic exponit: Nos enim postquam mefabilia beneficia Dei, & quibuscunq; potitisumus, super hoc poculo recensuimus, tum accedimus & cōmunicamus gratias agentes quod ab errore genus humanum liberauit, quod longe remotos reddidit propinquos, quod ipse destitutos & sine Deo existentes in mundo fratres suos & coharedes constituit, vbi pro his & talibus vniuersis gratias egimus, accedimus. Hæc ille, cui εὐλογήμεν idem est quod διὰ τὴν χάριν εὐχαριστίαν, id est, super quo gratias agimus. Et hūc sensum puto esse retinendū potius quā ea quæ nonnulli hic de consecratione calicis cōminiscuntur, quod Lyranus facit dicēs, cui benedicimus nos sacerdotes, quia licet consecratio ista fiat sola diuina virtute, tamen sacerdotes proferunt consecrationis verba & pro tato benedicere dicuntur, seu consecrare.
units.tr: "Which we bless," he says. In Greek it is ὃν εὐλογοῦμεν, that is, "which we bless." Erasmus translates "cui benedicimus" as if it were put for ὃ. Chrysostom explains it thus: "For we, after recounting over this cup the ineffable benefits of God and whatever good things we have obtained, then come forward and communicate, giving thanks that he has freed the human race from error, that he has brought near those who were far off, and that he himself has made his brothers and co-heirs those who were destitute and without God in the world; for these and all such things we give thanks, and we come forward." Thus he; for whom εὐλογοῦμεν is the same as διὰ τὴν χάριν εὐχαριστίαν, that is, "for which we give thanks." And I think this sense should be retained rather than those things which some here devise about the consecration of the cup, as Lyranus does, saying "which we bless, we priests," because although that consecration is effected by divine power alone, nevertheless priests utter the words of consecration and for this reason are said to bless, or consecrate.

units.la: Illud, quod poculi huius mentione præmittit, cū secundū ordinem institutiōis dominicę fractioni panis subijcienda videatur, puto non esse certa aliqua ratione factū, propter quā cō municatio poculi huius fractionem panis pro dere debeat. Simpliciter loquutus est Apostolus, abfq; solicita ratione seruādi ordinis, propterea quod non in eo erat, vt de celebriada cœna domini, vel de institutione dominica præscriberet, id quod facturus est capite sequenti, vbi ordinē institutionis seruabit, sed vt ex mystica corporis ac sanguinis domini communicatione argumentum sumeret, propositio suo accōmodum, vbi non referebat, vtriū metione panis vel poculi primo loco faceret. Alius aliud cōminiscitur, verū hoc pacto simplicius ad hanc quæstionē respōderi posse puto. Hieronymus dicit: Ideo primū calicē nominauit, vt posset de pane latius disputare. Verum in se quēntibus non erat de pane tantum, sed & de poculo mentionem argumentando facturus. Quare infirmior est hæc ratio, quām vt aliquid habeat momenti. Sunt qui dicant sanguinis hoc esse dignitati datum ab Apostolo, vt prior illius fieret mentio, propterea qu̇ sit loco animæ, quæ potior est corpore. Verum qui sic sentiunt, non vident Christum incogitantiæ damnari, quod non & ipse habita dignitatis huius ratione de poculo prius, deinde de pane cōstituerit. Nonnulli respiciunt ad morem Ebræorum, quibus exordia cœnæ à potu sumuntur.
units.tr: As for the fact that he mentions this cup before the bread, although according to the order of the Lord's institution the breaking of the bread seems to come first, I think it was not done for any definite reason on account of which the communion of this cup ought to precede the breaking of the bread. The Apostle spoke simply, without a careful reason for keeping the order, because it was not his purpose to prescribe the celebration of the Lord's Supper or the Lord's institution (which he will do in the following chapter, where he will keep the order of institution), but to draw an argument from the mystical communion of the body and blood of the Lord. So, arranging his proposition to suit his purpose, where it made no difference, he put mention of the cup or of the bread first as he pleased. Another invents something else, but I think this question can be answered more simply in this way. Jerome says: "He named the cup first so that he could discuss the bread more fully." But in what follows he was going to make mention of the cup as well as of the bread in his argument, so this reason is too weak to carry any weight. There are some who say that this priority was given by the Apostle to the blood out of regard for its dignity, so that it is mentioned first because it stands in the place of the soul, which is more excellent than the body. But those who think so do not see that Christ is not condemned for thoughtlessness because he did not, having considered this dignity, first set down the cup and then the bread. Some look to the custom of the Hebrews, among whom the beginnings of the supper are taken from the drink.

units.la: Et huc facere putant, quod in Luc. cap. 22. primus de poculo memoratur, quàm de pane. Verùm nec mos Ebræorum exemplo nobis in cœna domini esse debet, nec poculum illud Iudaici Paschatis, cuius prior fit mentio, ad mysterium pertinebat, quod erat post illud separatim instituendum à domino, sed ad ritum veteris Paschatis. In testamenti Noui institutione non poculum, sed fractio panis præcessit.
units.tr: They also think this supports the fact that in Luke 22 the cup is mentioned first, before the bread. But the custom of the Hebrews should not serve as an example for us in the Lord's Supper, nor did that cup of the Jewish Passover, which is mentioned first, belong to the mystery. It belonged to the rite of the old Passover, and it was not something the Lord instituted separately afterwards. In the institution of the New Testament, the breaking of bread came before the cup.

units.la: Quare neq; hæc ratio talis est, ut sit loco in medium adferenda, & Apostolo tribuenda. Puto itaq; satius esse, ut nullam rationem adferamus eius rei, quàm ab Apostolo nulla certa ratione factam esse apparet.
units.tr: So this reason is not of such a kind that it should be brought forward in the middle of the argument and ascribed to the Apostle. I think it better, therefore, that we give no reason for this matter, since it is clear that the Apostle made no certain reason for it.

units.la: NONNE communicatio sanguinis Christi est inquit?) Expositio est sacri ritus, quo de poculo domini participat ecclesia Christi. Est ea communicatio non prophana, sed mystica.
units.tr: "Is not the communion of the blood of Christ," he says? This is an explanation of the sacred rite by which the Church of Christ partakes of the Lord's cup. This communion is not profane but mystical.

units.la: Prophana non eget expositione. Est enim vini tantum, non spiritualis, sed corporalis, & omnibus manifesta, mystica verò quoniam aliud habet intellectu, & aliud externo aspectu, adeoq; non secundum id quod foris geritur, sed secundum id quod ab ipso authore sancitum & institutum est intelligendum venit, expositionem requirit, qua secretum ipsius exprimatur. Exponens igitur quid sit poculū illud Eulogiæ, in quo communicat ecclesia, dicit esse communicationem, non vini tantum, sed cum primis sanguinis Christi. Et de vino participamus, verùm quoniam communicatio ista non est propter vinum, sed propter mysterium sanguinis Christi redemptionisq; nostræ beneficium rememorandū ac fideli mente veluti ruminandum institutum à domino, conueniens est, ut expositio illius per prædicatum potioris fiat. propter quod significandum externa il la vini communicatio vsurpata est, quàm eius quod non propter se, sed illius gratia vsurpatur. In vino signum est, in sanguine verò signatum. Signum propter signatum est, non signatum propter signum. Quare in expositione signi non conuenit, ut dicamus: Poculum eulogiæ communicatio vini est, sed dicendum est: Poculum eulogiæ communicatio sanguinis, & panis quem frangimus, communicatio corporis Christi est. Et quoniam hæc sacramenti conditio nota erat fidelibus, non simpliciter dicit: Poculū eulogię communicatio sanguinis Christi est, sed, Poculum eulogiæ nonne communicatio sanguinis Christi est? &, Panis quem frangimus, nonne communicatio corporis Christi est? Dixerat enim: Vt prudentibus loquor. Iudicate vos quod dico. Quoniam ipsos constituerat causæ huius iudices, ut illam ipsorū iudicio censendam permitteret, dixit: nonne communicatio sanguinis Christi est? quasi dicat: De poculo eulogiæ pronunciate vos ipsi, an non sit illud communicatio sanguinis Christi. Vis argumenti erat in hoc articulo. Ideo vt indubitatam illius certitudinem contra ipsos exprimeret, hoc pacto loqui voluit.
units.tr: A profane communion needs no explanation. For it is only of wine, not spiritual but bodily, and it is plain to all. A mystical communion, however, has one meaning in the understanding and another in outward appearance. So it must be understood not according to what is done outwardly but according to what was sanctioned and instituted by the author himself, and it requires an explanation to express its hidden meaning. Explaining, then, what that cup of blessing is, in which the Church communes, he says it is a communion not only of wine but, above all, of the blood of Christ. We do partake of wine, but since this communion is not for the sake of the wine, but was instituted by the Lord so that the mystery of Christ's blood and the benefit of our redemption might be remembered and, as it were, chewed over in a faithful mind, it is fitting that the explanation of it be made through the more important element named. For this reason the outward communion of wine was used to signify it, since the thing that is used not for its own sake but for the sake of something else is used for that thing. The wine is the sign, but the blood is what is signified. The sign exists for the sake of what is signified, not what is signified for the sake of the sign. Therefore, in explaining the sign it is not fitting for us to say: "The cup of blessing is a communion of wine." Rather we must say: "The cup of blessing is a communion of the blood, and the bread which we break is a communion of the body of Christ." And since this condition of the sacrament was known to the faithful, he does not simply say: "The cup of blessing is the communion of the blood of Christ," but "Is not the cup of blessing the communion of the blood of Christ?" and "Is not the bread which we break the communion of the body of Christ?" For he had said: "I speak as to wise people; judge for yourselves what I say." Since he had made them the judges of this cause, so that he might allow it to be weighed by their own judgment, he said: "Is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?" as if to say: "Concerning the cup of blessing, judge for yourselves whether it is not the communion of the blood of Christ." The force of the argument lay in this point. So, in order to express its certainty beyond doubt against them, he wished to speak in this way.

units.la: Nec ociosum est, quod non dicit: Poculum eulogiæ quod benedicimus, nonne sanguis & panis quem frangimus, nonne corpus domini est? sed, Poculum eulogiæ quod benedicimus, nonne communicatio sanguinis Christi est? &, Panis quem frangimus, nonne communicatio corporis Christi est? Poterat de symbolis istis pronunciare secundum se uatoris ipsius verba ac dicere, Poculum est sanguis & panis est corpus Domini, verùm quoniam ad propositum ipsius faciebat, ut contra communicationem mensæ dæmoniorum communicationem mensæ Christi obijceret, noluit simpliciter hæc in se mysteria consideranda proponere, sed magis argumenti sui vim ex eo nectere, quod illa sunt sacramentaliter communicatibus. Sic argumentatur non ex rebus ipsis sed ex illarum communicatione, inq; illa considerandum proponit, quàm absurdum sit eos participes esse mensæ dæmoniorum, qui solenni sacramento de corpore ac sanguine Domini participant.
units.tr: Nor is it idle that he does not say: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the blood, and the bread which we break, is it not the body of the Lord?" but "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" He could have stated concerning these symbols in the Saviour's own words and said: "The cup is the blood, and the bread is the body of the Lord." But since it served his purpose to set the communion of the table of Christ against the communion of the table of demons, he did not wish to put these mysteries forward simply to be considered in themselves. Rather he wished to draw the force of his argument from the fact that they are shared sacramentally. So he argues not from the things themselves but from their communion, and he sets it before them to consider how absurd it is for those who partake of the solemn sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord to be partakers of the table of demons.

units.la: PANIS quem frangimus inquit.) Non est animus singula quæ ad materiam hanc pertinent accuratius persequi. Nam de illis volente domino videbimus in locis communibus, vbi de cœna Domini dicendum erit. Obiter hic admonendus est lector, vt obseruet quomodo Apost. loquatur. Panis, inqt, quę frágimus. Nō dicit, species vel accidens panis, sed panis quę frangimus. Nec dicit panis quę cōsecramus & transubstantiamus, sed, quem frangimus. Agnoscamus simplicitatem Apostolicam, ignaram commenticiæ transubstantiationis. Panem vocat, idq; in ipsa sacra fractione, id est, distributione, quem papistæ panem esse negant. Idem & de poculo sentiamus. Nam eadem est vtriusq; & panis & vini ratio. Quare si quod frangitur in cœna domini, panis est, vtiq; vinū est, quod è poculo bibitur.
units.tr: "The bread which we break," he says. It is not my purpose to pursue more precisely each of the points that belong to this matter. For we shall see these, God willing, in the common places, where we shall have to speak of the Lord's Supper. Here the reader should be warned in passing to notice how the Apostle speaks. He says "bread," not "the appearance or accident of bread," but "the bread which we break." He does not say "the bread which we consecrate and transubstantiate," but "which we break." Let us acknowledge the Apostolic simplicity, which knew nothing of the invented doctrine of transubstantiation. He calls it bread, and this in the very sacred breaking, that is, the distribution, which the Papists deny is bread. Let us think the same about the cup. For the reasoning is the same for both bread and wine. So if what is broken in the Lord's Supper is bread, then surely what is drunk from the cup is wine.
