units.la: COMMVNICATIO, inquit, est corporis domini.) Non dicit, fractio est corporis domini, sed communicatio. Panis frágitur, nō corpus dñi. Nulla rei fit scissura, signi tantū fit fractura, qua nec status nec statura signati inituitur. Fractuam signi communicatio sacramentalis requirit. Nō enim potest fieri, vt de pane non fracto communicent edentes, quem vt distribuatur nec cesse est frangi. Dominici verò corporis ea est cōditio, vt integrū possit communicari fidelibus. Nō diuiditur Christus, sed integer tot manet in cœlo, & in cordibus fidelium, cuius communicatio sacramentalis p fractione panis fit in sacramento. Nimis puerliter sentiut, qui corpus & sanguine Christi, nisi per diuisionē comunicāri nō posse putant, quasi rerum integrarum nulla possit esse communicatio. Sol integer in cœlo manens communis omnibus lux est, & Christus integer in cœlo non posset communicabilis esse fidelibus, nisi diuidatur. Num diuisus est Christus? inquit Apostolus, supra cap. 1.
units.tr: "The communion," he says, "is of the body of the Lord." He does not say "the breaking is of the body of the Lord," but "the communion." Bread is broken, not the body of the Lord. No rupture is made in the thing itself; only the sign is broken, and this breaking touches neither the state nor the stature of what is signified. The sacramental communion requires the breaking of the sign. For it cannot be that those who eat share in bread that has not been broken, since bread must be broken in order to be distributed. But the condition of the Lord's body is that it can be shared whole with the faithful. Christ is not divided, but remains whole in heaven and in the hearts of the faithful. His sacramental communion takes place in the sacrament through the breaking of the bread. Those are far too childish in their thinking who suppose that the body and blood of Christ cannot be shared unless they are divided, as if there could be no communion of things that are whole. The sun, remaining whole in heaven, is light common to all; and Christ, whole in heaven, could not be shareable with the faithful unless he were divided. "Is Christ divided?" says the Apostle, above in chapter 1.

units.la: Sed dicet rudis adhuc in fide. Cum in sacramento separarium sit corporis illius in pane, & sanguinis in vino instituta communicatio, quę-admo-
units.tr: But someone still unskilled in the faith will say: "Since in the sacrament the communion of his body in the bread and of his blood in the wine has been instituted as separate, how..."

units.la: {B} Sic argumentatur non ex rebus ipsis...
units.tr: Thus he argues not from the things themselves...

units.la: admodú hic Apostolus disertè dicit:Poculum eulogiæ quod benedicimus,nónne communi catio sanguinis Christi est:Et panis quá frangi mus,nónne cómunicatio corporis Christi est: quomodo nó est diuisus Christus? & quomodo de integro & non diuiso participamus? An nó ipsa corporis ac sanguinis eius cómunicatio manifestam habet diuisionem? Respódeo.
units.tr: ...in just this way the Apostle plainly says here: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" How then is Christ not divided? And how do we partake of him whole and undivided? Does not the very communion of his body and blood have a manifest division? I answer.

units.la: Quo rudiores huiusmodi instruantur,expli candú est, quotuplex sit corporis ac sanguinis Christi cómunicatio.Hanc inuenio quadrupli cem,naturalé videlicet,sacramentalé,spiritua-lé ac cœlestě.1 Naturalis est, qua eiusdé cū illo sumus naturæ,eiusdé carnis,& eiusdé sangui-nis,quatenus verus homo est, & filius Adæ, p omnia nobis similis & ὁμοίωσι dépto peccato Et de hac cómuniõe plurimú gloriantur fide-les.Licet enim sit vniuersalis,oēs homines cō-pleētens,illis tamé potissimū est,& bono &ho nori,qui incarnationis illius fructum fide per cipiunt,quos etiam ipse fratres suos vocare di gnatur,& quorum potissimú gratia homo fieri voluit,iuxtaillud Ebr.2.Quoniá pueri commu nicauerunt in carne & sanguine,& ipse simili-ter particeps factus est eorúdem,vt per morté aboleret eum,qui mortishabebat imperiú,hoc est,diabolú,&c. Et hinc est quod carnem nos de carne,& os de ossibus eius esse non more Iu dæorum,qui de carne tantum præsumunt,sed fide ad mysterium incarnationis respicientes gloriamur.
units.tr: So that the less skilled may be instructed in such matters, it must be explained how many kinds of communion of the body and blood of Christ there are. I find them to be fourfold: namely natural, sacramental, spiritual and heavenly. The natural communion is that by which we are of the same nature as he is, of the same flesh and the same blood, insofar as he is a true man and a son of Adam, like us in all things except sin, [ὁμοίωσις, likeness]. Believers greatly rejoice in this communion. For although it is universal, embracing all men, it belongs above all to those who receive the fruit of that incarnation by faith, to good and honourable people. Christ deigns to call these his brothers, and it was chiefly for their sake that he willed to become man, according to that passage in Heb. 2: "Since the children have shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same, that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil," and so on. And hence we rejoice that we are flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones, not in the manner of the Jews, who presume only on the flesh, but looking by faith to the mystery of the incarnation.

units.la: 2 Sacramétalis est,qua secundū institutionē dominicā,de sacramentalibus corporis ac san guinis illius symbolis,pane ac vino,in ecclesia cómuniter participamȳ. De hoc loquitur Apo stolus hoc loco, vocás eam communicationē corporis ac sanguns Christi, respiciens nó ad externa symbola panis ac vini,sed ad mentem institutionis dominicę,& rationem sacramen-talium signorū,qua signo nomé signati tribui-tur:qua de & supra paucis admonuimus.
units.tr: The sacramental communion is that by which, according to the Lord's institution, we commonly partake in the Church of the sacramental symbols of his body and blood, the bread and the wine. The Apostle speaks of this communion here, calling it the communion of the body and blood of Christ. He looks not to the outward symbols of bread and wine, but to the intention of the Lord's institution and to the nature of sacramental signs, by which the name of the thing signified is given to the sign. We have briefly reminded the reader of this above as well.

units.la: ȝ Spiritualis est,qua spiritu de fructu carnis ac sanguinis Christi,,p peccatis nostris crucifi xi,per fidem participamus,eiusdemq; gratię& redéptionis confortes sumus.Qui sic spiritua liter cómunicát,h nó in sacramēto, ut cū Au-gustino loquar.i.sacramétaliter tātū,sed & ve-re carnē Christi manducát,& sanguinē bibūt, hoc est, vere de merito & fructu mortis illius viuunt.In istis uere impletur, quod per sacra-mentalia signa,sacramétaliter in ecclesia exter na communicatione geritur.Et hęc spiritualis cómunicatio non est sic alligata sacramentali, ut nec extra illá locū habere , nec à quoquam sacramentaliter communicante abesse possit. Notum est quod ex Augustino de cófecratio-ne,dist.2 Can.Quia passus,legitur ad hunc mo dum:Nulli est aliquatenus dubitandū unum-quenq; fideliū corporis ac sanguinis dominici tunc esse participe,quádo in baptismate mem brū efficitur Christi,nec alienari ab illi⁹ panis calicisq; cófortio,etiási antequá pané illum co medat,calicemq; bibat de hoc sæculo migra-
units.tr: The third kind is spiritual: by the Spirit we partake, through faith, of the flesh and blood of Christ crucified for our sins, the fruit of that flesh and blood, and we become sharers in his grace and redemption. Those who communicate in this spiritual way do not do so only in the sacrament, as I may say with Augustine, that is, only sacramentally, but they truly eat the flesh of Christ and drink his blood; that is, they truly live by the merit and fruit of his death. In these people is truly fulfilled what is done in the external communion through the sacramental signs. And this spiritual communion is not so bound to the sacramental that it can neither exist outside it nor be absent from anyone who communicates sacramentally. It is well known that the following is read in Augustine, On the Consecration, distinction 2, canon "Quia passus", in this way: "No one should in any way doubt that each of the faithful becomes a partaker of the body and blood of the Lord when he is made a member of Christ in baptism, and that he is not cut off from the fellowship of that bread and cup, even if, having been established in the unity of the body of Christ, he departs from this world before he eats that bread and drinks the cup. For he is not deprived of the participation and benefit of that sacrament when what the sacrament signifies is found in him." These are the words there. Therefore what the sacrament signifies is found in the faithful man, as a member of the body of Christ, even outside the sacrament. Furthermore, it happens quite often that a person shares outwardly in the sacramental communion of the body and blood of Christ and yet is wholly without true and spiritual communion. So it is read in the same distinction 2 of the Consecration: "He who is at odds with Christ neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, although he receives the sacrament of so great a thing to his own judgment of perdition." Therefore it can happen that a man receives the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ and yet neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood. Sacramental communion, then, is common to all Christians, but spiritual communion belongs only to the faithful.

units.la: uerit,in vni tate corporis Christi constitutus. Sacraméti quippe illius ,participatione ac be-neficio nó priuatur,quádo in ipso hoc quod sa cramentū significat inuenitur. Hæc ibi.Ergo quod sacramentū significat in homine fideli tanquà membro corporis Christi, etiam extra sacramētum inuenitur.Deinde nimis frequen ter accidit,vt externe de sacramentali corpo-ris ac sanguinis Christi cómunicatioe partici-pet,qui tñ veræ ac spiritualis cómuniõis pror-sus est expers.Sic de cons.distin.2.legitur:Qui discordat àChristo nó máducatcarnẽ eius,nec bibit sanguiné eius,licet tátæ rei sacramentum ad iudiciū suæ perditionem accipiat. Ergo fieri potest,vt sacramentum corporis ac sanguinis Christi accipiat,q tamen nec máducet eius car nem,nec sanguinem bibat.Est itaq; sacramēta lis cómunicatio,cómunis omnium Christiano rum,spiritalis verò fidelium tantum.
units.tr: Furthermore, it happens quite often that a person shares outwardly in the sacramental communion of the body and blood of Christ and yet is wholly without true and spiritual communion. So it is read in the same distinction 2 of the Consecration: "He who is at odds with Christ neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, although he receives the sacrament of so great a thing to his own judgment of perdition." Therefore it can happen that a man receives the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ and yet neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood. Sacramental communion, then, is common to all Christians, but spiritual communion belongs only to the faithful.

units.la: 4. Cœlestis est cómunicatio,qua corpora no stra in futuro sæculo corporis Christi glorifica ti confortiū & cósiguratioṅe acquirent, cuius mentioné facit Apost.Phil.3.dicés:Nostra có-uersatio in cœlo est,ex quo & Seruatoré expe-ctamus dominū Iesum Christū,qui trásfigura-bit corpus nostrū humile,vt conforme reddat corpori suo glorioso,secundū efficaciā,qua po test etiá subijcere sibi omnia. Quadrupliccm hác corporis Christi cómunicatione in scriptu ris inuenio.Prima estmortalium omniū,secun da Christianorum ,pmiscuè,tertia & quarta e-leĉtorū ac fidelium tátum.Priores duæ sine ter tia nó saluant,p quartā salus & felicitas nostra absoluetur.Iam quod præsentem quæstionem attinet,nec prima corporis ac sanguinis Chri-sti cómunicatio,nec tertia,nec quarta requirit vt de diuiso Christo participemus. Sumus e-nim vt veri,ita & integri hominis Christi ὁμοί-ωσι.Deinde & totus nobis & integer simul est & cibus & couiuator.Quare cómunicatio spi-ritualis nullá illius diuisioné requirit.Nec po-stremæ cómunicationis ea est códitio,ut diui-sum Christũ poscat.Restat secúda quæ sacra-metalis est.In hac proponitur nobis diuisio & fractura,quia sub imagine externi cibi ac pot⁹ spiritualis cómunicatio sacramentaliter ꝓpo-nitur. Quod corporis alimoniá attinet,aliud est edere,& aliud bibere, aliud cibus & aliud potus,aliud panis,& aliud vinū. In gratia verò & spirituali alimonia nó habet locū huiusmo-di discrimen.Hic idem est edere ac bibere, ci-bus & potus.Sic Christum edimus ac bibim⁹, hoc est,per carnē ac sanguiné eius credēdo ue lut edēdo ac bibēdo ad vitá æterná resicimur. Huius refeĉtionis symbola, quoniam externa sunt,& ad terrenū cibádi ac potandi modum attéperata,diuisione habent , propter naturæ suæ imbecillitatem.Panis enim terrenus sic pa scit esurieté,vt nequeat simul potare sitiente. Et vinū sic potat sitiente,vt nequeat simul pa-scere esurientē.Cõstat autè plena corporis no stri alimonia haud cibo tātū,sed & potu, quia non esurie duntaxat,sed & siti labefactatur & perdi.
units.tr: 4. The heavenly communion is that by which our bodies in the future age will acquire the fellowship and conformity of the glorified body of Christ, of which the Apostle speaks in Philippians 3, saying: "Our conversation is in heaven, from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our humble body, that it may be made conformable to his glorious body, according to the working by which he is able even to subject all things to himself." I find this fourfold communion of the body of Christ in the Scriptures. The first is of all mortals, the second of Christians in common, the third and fourth of the elect and faithful only. The first two do not save without the third, and through the fourth our salvation and happiness will be completed. Now, as far as the present question is concerned, neither the first communion of the body and blood of Christ, nor the third, nor the fourth requires that we partake of a divided Christ. For he is both true and whole man, like us, in his likeness. Moreover, he is wholly and entirely present to us at once, both food and host. Therefore spiritual communion requires no division of him. Nor is it the condition of the last communion that it demands a divided Christ. There remains the second, which is sacramental. In this the division and breaking are set before us, because under the image of external food and drink the spiritual communion is set forth sacramentally. As regards the nourishment of the body, eating is one thing and drinking another, food is one thing and drink another, bread is one thing and wine another. But in grace and spiritual nourishment such a distinction has no place. Here eating and drinking are the same, food and drink are the same. Thus we eat and drink Christ, that is, by believing in his flesh and blood we are refreshed to eternal life, as if by eating and drinking. The symbols of this refreshment, since they are external and adapted to the earthly manner of eating and drinking, have division on account of the weakness of their nature. For earthly bread feeds the hungry in such a way that it cannot at the same time quench the thirsty; and wine quenches the thirsty in such a way that it cannot at the same time feed the hungry. Yet it is established that the full nourishment of our body consists not only of food but also of drink, because we are weakened and destroyed not only by hunger but also by thirst.

units.la: pditur. Vt admoneamur igitur plenā nobis & A pfectā in Christo parata esse refectione, gratia illi9 utriusq; & cibi &pot9 symbolis natura sua distinctis ac diuisis sacramentaliter ꝑponitur, cū tñ ipsanos, absq; diuisione integra & plena sic reficiat, ut ad ueram sempiternamq; uitam tam conseruandam quā conferedam sufficiat. Quare diuisionem hanc sacramenti non debe mus transferre ad ipsum Christū, quasi in partes diuisum, quarū alia edamus, & aliam bibamus. Diuisio ista, quæ in sacramento est, sacramentali est communicationi relinquenda, & non ad spiritualem trásfereda. Simul cauendū est, ne qua pars sacramenti auferatur, ne exple næ refectionis mysterio mutilum & imperfectū reddamus. Est enim integritas sacramenti huius, nō cibi tantū, sed & potus symbolo comprehensa, quia non dimidiatæ, sed plenæ refectionis gratiam fidelibus proponit. Quare sacrilegium admittunt, qui partem aliquā de illo auferunt, id quod in Papatu contentiosissime fieri uidemus.
units.tr: So that we may be reminded that a full and perfect refreshment is prepared for us in Christ, grace is set forth sacramentally under the symbols of both food and drink, each distinct and divided by its nature, although he himself refreshes us wholly and entire, without division, so that he suffices for both preserving and conferring true and everlasting life. Therefore we must not transfer this division of the sacrament to Christ himself, as if he were divided into parts, of which we eat one and drink another. That division which is in the sacrament is to be left to sacramental communion and not transferred to the spiritual. At the same time we must take care that no part of the sacrament be taken away, lest we make the mystery of the full refreshment mutilated and imperfect. For the integrity of this sacrament is comprehended not only in the symbol of food but also in that of drink, because it offers to the faithful the grace not of a halved but of a full refreshment. Therefore those commit sacrilege who take away some part of it, which we see being done most contentiously in the Papacy.

units.la: Quoniam unus panis, unum corpus multi sumus. Omnes enim de uno pane participamus.
units.tr: Since we, though many, are one bread, one body; for we all partake of one bread.

units.la: Habent ista ætiologiā ad declarationē præcedentiū subiectā, quā aliter atq; aliter exponi uideo. Dicam cū pace aliorū quid mihi videatur. Dixit panē quē in ecclesia frangimus, esse κοινωνίαν, id est, comunionem vel comunicatione corporis Christi, in cruce uidelicet ꝑnobis traditi, quod adhoc dixit, ut minorem argumenti sui probaret, esse scilicet eos cofortes corporis & sanguinis Christi. Sūt aūt dicte iā sententię duę partes. Vna subiecti, altera pdicati, quo de pane fracto prædicat, quod sit comunicatio corporis Christi. Quod panis iste sacramentū sit & mysterium corporis Christi, ex ipsi9 Christi uerbis patet, quibus dixit. Hoc est corpus meū, quod pro uobis traditur. Quod uerò fractio ac distributio illius nō modo participatio sed & communicatio sit corporis dñi, quoniā à Corinthijs nō satis obseruabatur, cōsequēter erat admonendū & exponendū. In comunione est unitas duplex. Comunicati uidelicet, & cōmunicantiū. Cōmunicantes uniuntur inter se uirtute cōmunicatioñis rei eiusdē, per quā ꝛedduntur communio. Sic incolas eiusdē ciui tatis, uocam9 cōmunionē, ein gemeind. Deinde uniūtur etiam cum re cōmunicata, cum illa in cōmunem usum conuertitur, præsertim si uel corpore uel spiritu communiter usurpetur. In cœna domini sunt cōmunicantes, & res cōmunicata. Communicantes uirtute communicationis rei eiusdem, de qua participant omnes, cōmunio redduntur, atq; ita inter se coadunātur, ut rectè unū corpus uocētur. Res ipsa quoque quæ in cōmunicatione omniū uenit, & in qua coadunantur quotquot de illa participāt, cum cōmunicantibus coadunatur. Est aūt hęc corpus & sanguis Christi, cuius communicationem supra sacramentalem & spiritalem esse
units.tr: These words have a causal clause that is attached to the preceding statements, and I see it explained in different ways. With due respect to others, I will say what seems right to me. He said that the bread which we break in the church is a [κοινωνία], that is, a communion or sharing in the body of Christ, namely the body delivered for us on the cross. He said this to prove the minor premise of his argument, namely that those who eat it are partners in the body and blood of Christ. Now the sentence has two parts: a subject and a predicate. The predicate says of the broken bread that it is a communion in the body of Christ. That this bread is the sacrament and mystery of the body of Christ is clear from Christ's own words, when he said: "This is my body, which is given for you." But because the Corinthians did not sufficiently notice that the breaking and distribution of the bread is not only a participation but also a communion in the body of the Lord, it had to be pointed out and explained. In a communion there is a twofold unity: that of the thing shared and that of those who share it. Those who share are united with one another by the power of sharing in one and the same thing, through which they become a communion. So we call the inhabitants of the same city a community, a gemeind. Then they are also united with the thing shared, when it is turned to common use, especially if it is used in common by body or by spirit. In the Lord's Supper there are those who share and the thing shared. Those who share, by the power of the sharing in the same thing, in which all participate, become a communion and are thus bound together, so that they are rightly called one body. The thing itself, too, which comes to all in the sharing, and in which all who partake of it are joined, is joined with those who share. This is the body and blood of Christ, whose communion is not only sacramental but also spiritual.

units.la: maximus. Qui spiritu nō in sacramento tantum communicant, verē cum eovniuntur, de cuius corpore ac sanguine participant. Quoniā verò argumentū suū Apost. à sacramētali cōmunicatione quæ in panis est fractiōe, & poculi distributione, ducere cœpit, quod illa tanꝫ commu nis omnium ad quos scribebat, ꝑpositio ipsius esset aptissima, panis vocabulum retinet, & hu ius vnitate simul & generalem omniū commu nicatione vrget, dicens: Quoniam vnus panis, intellige, est, de quo videlicet cōmunicamus, & nos multi unū corpus sumus. Vides urgeri unitate utranq; cū rei cōmunicatę, tum iplorū cōmunicantiū. Deinde uide quomodo probet quod dixit: Vnū corpus multi sumus. Omnes enim, inquit, de uno pane participamus. Non alius de alio, sed omnes de uno. Quasi dicat: Quāuis multi simus, unū tamen corpus sumus, quod patet per unitate panis, de qua participamus omnes. Panis aūt ille unus, de quo cunċti participamus, sacramentū est, & fractio illius, per quam ille nobis omnibus communi catur, communicatio est corporis Christi. Sumus igitur omnes consortes ac participes corporis Christi, quotquot de pane hoc eulogiæ participamus. Et uoshoc comuniter facitis. Ergo consortes & participes estis corporis Christi. Nō poteritis igitur cōfortes esse dæmoniorum, id qd paulo post est illaturus. Et hāc præsentis loci expositione puto germanam esse & facile, quam obscurat uetus uersio, quæ habet, quoniam unus panis & unū corpū multi sumus quasi dictio panis metaphoricè pōsita sit, & ad ecclesiam fidelium referri debeat. Videtur ex eo quoq; obscurari hic sensus, quod uerbū substantiuū, est, nō est expressē adiectū, ut legatur. Quoniā unus est panis. Verū nō debet hoc insolēs uideri in homine Ebraeo, si etiam Græcē scribēdo subinde Ebraismis utatur. Solent Ebrei sic loqui. i. Dns unꝰ, id est, Deus unus, pro, dominus unus est, Deꝰ unus est. Sic ipse quoq; Apost. loqtur, Eph. 4. unus dominus, una fides, unū baptisma, unus Deus & pater omniū, &c. Et 1. Tim. 2. Vnꝰ deꝰ, unus & mediator Dei & hominū, &c. ubi sanē uerbū hoc, est, nobis subaudiēdū uenit, ne qd aliud prædicatū desideretur, quod de uno deo uno domino, &c. prædicetur. Consimiliter & hoc loco, cū dicit: i. Quoniā panis unus, rectè subintelligimus uerbū, est, & referimus ad panē eulogię, de quo argumētari cœpit. Hāc sententia citra contentionem in medium adfero, interim haudquaquā aliter exponētibus præiudicare uolēs. Nec est ut dicat imperit9: Quō numerosa ecclesia in qua aliquot milia communicant, de uno pane participare poterit? Vnitas panis huius non est ad unitatē unius orbiculati panis, sed magis ad unitatem institutionis sacramenti, & communicationis referenda. Quemadmodum unius domus familia rectè unum & eundē panē mādūcare dicitur, etiā si plures orbes uno prādio absumat, sic in mensa Christi rectè omnes cōmunicātes
units.tr: Those who share in the Spirit, not only in the sacrament, are truly united with him, whose body and blood they partake of. But since the Apostle began to draw his argument from the sacramental communion, which consists in the breaking of the bread and the distribution of the cup, and since that communion, being common to all to whom he was writing, was most suitable for his purpose, he keeps the word bread and urges, by its unity, the general communion of all, saying: "Since there is one bread," that is, there is one bread, of which we share, "we, being many, are one body." You see that he insists on both unities, that of the thing shared and that of those who share it. Next, notice how he proves what he said: "we, being many, are one body." For, he says, "we all partake of one bread." Not one of one bread and another of another, but all of one. As if he were saying: although we are many, we are nonetheless one body, which is shown by the unity of the bread in which we all partake. That one bread, of which we all partake, is a sacrament, and its breaking, by which it is shared with us all, is the communion of the body of Christ. Therefore we are all partners and participants in the body of Christ, as many as partake of this bread of blessing. And you do this in common. Therefore you are partners and participants in the body of Christ. You will not then be able to be partners of demons, which he is going to bring up a little later. I think this is the true and easy explanation of this passage, which the old version obscures, the one that reads "since the bread is one and we, being many, are one body," as if the word bread were used metaphorically and ought to be referred to the church of the faithful. The sense is also obscured by the fact that the verb "is" is not expressly added, so that it reads: "since there is one bread." But this should not seem strange in a Hebrew writer, if he, while writing in Greek, sometimes uses Hebraisms. The Hebrews are accustomed to speak in this way, for example "The Lord one," that is, "God one," for "the Lord is one," "God is one." The Apostle himself also speaks so in Ephesians 4: "one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all," and in 1 Timothy 2: "one God, and one mediator between God and men." There the verb "is" must of course be understood, lest some other predicate be sought, such as that it is predicated of the one God or the one Lord. Likewise in this place, when he says "since the bread is one," we rightly supply the verb "is" and refer it to the bread of blessing, of which he has begun to argue. I offer this interpretation for discussion without contention, not wishing to prejudge those who explain it otherwise. Nor should an unskilled person object: how can a numerous church, in which several thousand communicate, partake of one bread? The unity of this bread is to be referred not to the unity of a single round loaf, but rather to the unity of the institution of the sacrament and of communion. Just as the family of one household is rightly said to eat one and the same bread, even if it consumes several loaves at one meal, so at the table of Christ all who communicate are rightly said to partake of one and the same bread, even though one loaf is not enough because of the multitude of those who communicate.

units.la: de uno & eodem pane participare dicuntur, licet propter cômunicantiû multitudinè vnus orbis nô sufficiat. Illud, Oés enim de vno pane participamus, in vulgata uersione absq; nota causali sic legitur, omnes qui de vno pane &de vno calice participam. Annotat Erafmus esse qui legât: omnesq; de vno pane participam. Quod si vocula, γάρ, abijci posset, meo iudicio rectè sic legeretur: vnum corpus multi sum, qui omnes de vno pane participamus. Cæterûm de metaphora & vnitate corporis ecclesiasticî dicemus infrà cap.12. vbi de illa maior erit dicendi occasio.
units.tr: The phrase "for we all partake of one bread" is read in the Vulgate without a causal particle, thus: "all who partake of one bread and of one cup." Erasmus notes that some read: "and we all partake of one bread." If the little word "for" [γάρ] could be dropped, in my judgment it would be rightly read thus: "we, being many, are one body, we who all partake of one bread." But I shall speak of the metaphor and the unity of the ecclesiastical body in chapter 12, where there will be a greater occasion for discussing it.

units.la: Videte Israelem iuxta carnem. Nõne qui edûtuictimas cõsortes sunt altaris?
units.tr: See Israel after the flesh. Are not those who eat the sacrifices partners of the altar?

units.la: Erafmus vertit sacrarij. Sed cum in Græco sit θυσιαστήριον, melius est, altaris, quèadmodû & vulgata versio habet. In eo est Apost. vt ostendat Corinthijs, esse ipsos cõsortes Christi. Et huc usus est argumento à cõmunicatione mystici panis & poculi sumpto, cuius vis in eo est, quod cõmunicatio signorû ad ipsa signata extenditur. Est enim hæc signorum cõditio, ut omnis illorû usus signatis seruiat, & ad illa referatur, perinde atq; verba ad sensum ac mentè loquêtis.
units.tr: Erasmus renders "of the sacred place," but since the Greek is θυσιαστήριον [thysiastērion], "of the altar" is better, as the Vulgate also has it. Here the Apostle aims to show the Corinthians that they themselves are partners of Christ. He uses the argument from the sharing of the mystical bread and cup, whose force lies in this: that the communion of the signs extends to the things signified. For this is the condition of signs: all their use serves the things signified and refers to them, just as words refer to the sense and mind of the speaker.

units.la: {B} Conditio signorum.
units.tr: {B} The condition of signs.

units.la: Videte Israelé, inquit, iuxta carnė.) Israelĩ iuxta carnė, carnalis est Israel, nô spiritualis. Et huic carnali Israeli dat victimas, sacrificia, altare, & altaris cõsortiû, hoc est, & sacerdotiû & religione, & cultus. Ergo externa hæc sacra, sacrorumq; cômunicatio nô faciebât ex carnali Israeli spiritualem.
units.tr: "See Israel," he says, "after the flesh." Israel after the flesh is carnal Israel, not spiritual Israel. To this carnal Israel he gave victims, sacrifices, the altar, and fellowship of the altar, that is, both the priesthood, religion and worship. Therefore these external sacred rites and the communion in sacred things did not make the spiritual out of the carnal Israel.

units.la: NONNE qui edût victimas, cõsortes sunt altaris?) Potest referri ad Sacerdotes & Leuitas, hoc sensu, Nõnne in lege esus victimarum ad eos tantû ptinet, q cõsortes sunt altaris. i. sacerdotij, vt qui altari seruit, de altari uiuat.
units.tr: "Do not those who eat the victims become partners of the altar?" This can be referred to the priests and Levites, in this sense: under the law, is not the eating of the victims a privilege only of those who are partners of the altar, that is, of the priesthood, since they serve the altar and live from the altar?

units.la: Vos aút non estis neq; esse vultis cõsortes eidolorû. Nô cõuenit igitur ut eidolis immolata comedatis. Vtrolibet sensu accipias, satis fortiter arguit illicitû esse quod reprehedit in Corinthijs.
units.tr: "But you are not, and do not wish to be, partners of idols. It is not fitting, therefore, that you eat what is sacrificed to idols." In whichever sense you take it, he argues quite forcefully that what he rebukes in the Corinthians is unlawful.

units.la: Priorexpositio nititur uirtute & vsu signorum externorumq; sacrorû. Posterior vero iure ordinis & sacri cõsortij, in quo nô cõuenit locû esse exteris.
units.tr: The former explanation rests on the power and use of external signs and sacred rites. The latter rests on the law of order and of sacred fellowship, in which there is no place for outsiders.

units.la: Hic quoque in Græco est uox κοινωνία, cõmunicationis significationem habes. Quæsierim igitur, quomodo hæc particula ad præcedetia faciat, quibus panem in cœna domini fractum, cõmunicatione corporis, & poculû cõmunicatione sanguinis Christi esse dixit. Qui corpus & sanguine dñi in cõmunicatione fideliũ, nisi corporaliter ac realiter in pane & vino constituta, vel nisi per transsiut. transsubstantiatione panis & vini, venire non posse docet, respondeat quomodo altare lapideū in communicatione edentiū victimas uenire possit. An dicturi sunt esse illud in vnaqua que portione victimarū corporaliter ac realiter? vel, victimas trāssubstātiari in altare lapideum? Sunt haec absurda. Sūt sane. Sed rogo quo sensu accipiendū est, quod Apost. dicit: Nonne qui edunt victimas, consortes sunt altaris? ne vel absurdū quid, vel alienū ab argumeto illius statuamus? An alio sensu accipiendū est, q̄ qui præcedentib. cōueniat? Sed quomodo stabit Apostoli argumentū? Si dicas: Qui edunt panē cœnæ mysticæ, cōsortes sunt corporis Christi, & qui bibunt poculū illius, consortes sunt sanguinis Christi, an nequit hoc alia esse ratioe verū, quā tali, quæ in hac præsenti particula constare nō poterit? Absit hoc ab Apostolo, vt instar ebrij argumentādo adferat nō coherentia. Viderint igitur qui cœlū terra miscētes vociferantur, auferri cōmunicatione corporis dñi ex ecclesia, nisi illud esse in pane corporaliter ac realiter, vel panem in illud trāssubstātiari credamus, dicamus & contendamus.
units.tr: Here too the Greek has the word κοινωνία [koinōnia], and you have the sense of communion. I would ask, therefore, how this particle relates to what precedes, where he said that the bread broken in the Lord's Supper is communion in the body, and the cup communion in the blood of Christ. Let whoever teaches that the body and blood of the Lord cannot come into the communion of the faithful unless they are present corporally and really in the bread and wine, or unless through the transubstantiation of bread and wine, explain how a stone altar can come into the communion of those who eat the victims. Will they say that the altar is in every portion of the victims corporally and really? Or that the victims are transubstantiated into the stone altar? These are absurd. Indeed they are. But I ask in what sense we are to take what the Apostle says: "Do not those who eat the victims become partners of the altar?" Lest we posit something absurd, or foreign to his argument? Or is it to be taken in another sense, one that agrees with what goes before? But how will the Apostle's argument stand? If you say: those who eat the bread of the mystical supper are partners of the body of Christ, and those who drink its cup are partners of the blood of Christ, can this not be true for some other reason than the kind that cannot hold in this present particle? Far be it from the Apostle that, like a drunken man arguing, he should bring forward things that do not cohere. Let those see to it who mix heaven and earth and cry out that communion in the Lord's body is removed from the Church unless we believe that it is in the bread corporally and really, or that the bread is transubstantiated into it: let them say, assert and contend this.

units.la: Quid ergo dico? Quod simulacrū aliquid sit? Aut quod simulacris immolatū aliquid sit? Non. Sed illud dico, &c.
units.tr: What then do I say? That an idol is something? Or that what is sacrificed to idols is something? No. But I say this, etc.

units.la: In Græco est: Quid ergo dico? Quod simulacrū sit aliquid? vel quod simulacris immolatū sit aliquid? Sed quod q̄ Gētes immolāt, dæmonijs immolāt, & non Deo. Vbi omnino negatiua subintelligenda est, & vel cū Chrys. legēdū: Quid ergo dico? i. Non qd simulacrum aliquid sit. Vel cū Eras. Non, sed quod quæ immolāt Gentes, &c. Minori iā explicatæ subiicienda erat cōclusio: ergo non potestis participes esse mensæ eidolorū. Verū quoniā videbatur idē de sacris eidolorum sentire, qd de sacris Iudæorū & Christianorū, illis q̄ tribuere altare sacrificiorū & mensam mysticā & religiosam, pterea quod primū de pane & poculo cœnæ dñi, deinde de altari ac victimis Iudæorū argumentū cōmunicationis inducebat, quo probaret, cōmedentes de externo sacro participes esse eius cui sacrificatur & immolatur, quasi tale qd sit eidolū cui possit immolari, & cuiꝰ participes esse queat, qui immolata ipsi comedūt, eiusmodi cogitationi occurrit priusquā conclusione subijciat. Quid ergo dico, inquit? Quod simulacrū aliquid sit? Quasi dicat: Ergo hæc dicens videor simulacris & sacrificijs illorū aliquid tribuere, cū supra nihil esse simulacrum in mundo dixerim. Verūnihil illis tribuo. Scio & ipse, esse ea vana & inania figmenta, quæ per se nec prodesse nec obesse queant, sed hoc specto, quod quę illis immolātur, nō Deo immolātur sed dæmonijs, atq; ita cōmunicatio eidolothytorū, cōmunicatio est dæmonū, nolim uero uos consortes fieri dæmoniorū. Sic cauet, ne simulacris numinis aliquid tribuere, & sibijpsi parū cōstare videatur, & simul conclusioni, quā subiecturus est, plurimū
units.tr: In the Greek it reads: "What then do I say? That an idol is something, or that what is sacrificed to idols is something? But that what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God." Here a negative must be understood. Either we should read with Chrysostom, "What then do I say? That is, not that an idol is something," or with Erasmus, "No, but that what the Gentiles sacrifice," and so on. A shorter conclusion, once this explanation was given, had to follow: "Therefore you cannot be partakers of the table of idols." But since it seemed that he held the same view of the rites of idols as of the rites of the Jews and Christians, ascribing to them an altar of sacrifices and a mystical and religious table, because he had first brought in the argument of communion from the bread and cup of the Lord's Supper, and then from the altar and victims of the Jews, by which he would prove that those who eat of an external sacred thing are partners of that to which it is sacrificed and offered, as if an idol were a thing to which something could be offered, and of which those who eat what is offered to it could be partners, the Apostle meets this kind of thought before he adds the conclusion. "What then do I say?" he asks. "That an idol is something?" As if he were saying: "In saying these things, do I seem to attribute something to images and their sacrifices, when above I said that an image is nothing in the world? But I attribute nothing to them. I know myself that these are vain and empty fictions, which can neither benefit nor harm of themselves. But this is my point: what is sacrificed to them is not sacrificed to God but to demons, and so the communion in idol-sacrifices is communion with demons. I would not want you to become partners of demons." Thus he guards against seeming to attribute anything to the images of the deity, and against seeming to contradict himself, and at the same time he prepares for the conclusion he is about to state with a great amplification.

units.la: auxesis parat, quo non simpliciter concludat: Ergo nō potestis mensæ eidolorū, sed: Ergo non potestis mensę dæmoniorū participes esse & mensę domini. Huc faciunt quæ dicit, quę Gentes immolant, dæmonijs immolant, & nō Deo. Nolim autem vos consortes fieri dæmoniorum. His dictis, concludit dicens: Non potestis poculum domini bibere, & poculū dæmoniorum. Nō potestis mēsæ domini participes esse, & mensæ dæmoniorum. Sed videamus ista singulatim.
units.tr: So he does not simply conclude, "Therefore you cannot be partakers of the table of idols," but "Therefore you cannot be partakers of the table of demons and the table of the Lord." To this point belong the words: what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God; "I would not want you to become partners of demons." With these things said, he concludes: "You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and the table of demons." But let us look at these things one by one.

units.la: Quid ergo dico, inquit? Videmus hic q̄ circūspectio competat ministro Christi in causa quantūuis bona argumentanti. Curandum illi est, vt cauté & circūspectéobseruet ne pgressu argumentationis abreptus sibijpsi excidat, & præcedentibus contraria dicat, & si quid tale, vel aliàs sinistrum, ex dictis in speciem saltem colligi possit, vt mox occurrat, priusquā ad sequentia progrediatur. Nihil horum præstare possumus, vbi calore disputatiōis & contētio-nis præcipites ferimur, id quod in multis nostrorū temporum scriptis videre licet. Parum fideliter, vel certè, parum prudenter docet, qui satis esse putant, si quę vera sunt dicant, & non simul obseruant, quid auditor ex dictis colligere possit, cum fructus & finis sermonis pertineat ad audientem, & inanis sit omnis sermo, nisi rite, imò noxius, si male intelligatur, quantum uis veraciter dicatur.
units.tr: "What then do I say?" he says. Here we see that circumspection befits a minister of Christ even when arguing in a very good cause. He must take care to observe cautiously and carefully, lest, carried away by the course of his argument, he fall into self-contradiction and say things contrary to what precedes, and if anything of this kind, or otherwise sinister, could be gathered from what he has said, at least in appearance, he should meet it at once, before he proceeds to what follows. We cannot achieve any of this when we are carried headlong by the heat of disputation and contention, as can be seen in many of the writings of our own times. He teaches unfaithfully, or at least imprudently, who think it enough to say what is true and do not at the same time observe what the hearer can gather from what is said. For the fruit and purpose of speech belong to the hearer, and all speech is empty unless it is rightly understood; indeed, if it is misunderstood it is harmful, however truly it is spoken.

units.la: QVOD simulacrum aliquid sit? Aut quod simulacris immolatum aliquid sit? Nō.) In eo quod negat aliquid esse tam simulacrū quàm si mulacris immolatum, admonemur quomodo sit de rebus sacris iudicandum, haud videlicet secundum externam illarum faciem, & corporalis substantiæ materiā, sed secundum id cuiꝰ gratia pro sacris habentur, & religiosè colūtur. Secundum hanc ipsorum qualitatem, aut aliquid sunt, aut nihil. Aliquid, si verè diuinarum rerum sunt signa. Nihil, si falsarum, in quibus nihil est eorum quæ putantur. Sic simulacrum nihil est, quia species est sine veritate eius rei, cuius gratia ponitur. Simulacrum Dei duplici nomine nihil est. Primum, quia figuratn & effigiem Deus non habet, & prorsus est inessigiabilis. Deinde quia falsa est opinio, qua cæci Deum in simulacro coli putant, cum in illo magis dehonestetur, propterea quod incorruptibilis Dei gloria in similitūdinem imaginis corruptibilis hominis, &c. mutatur. Roman. 1. Sic de simulacris tanquam simulacris iudicādum est. Aliud est esse aurum, argentum, ęs, lignum, ferrum, lapidem, &ç. & aliud, esse imaginem, vel haberi pro imagine alicuius rei. Secundū priorem essentiam, de simulacris canit Dauid: simulacra Gentium argentum & aurum, opera manuum hominum, &c. Secundum posteriorem dicit Apostolus, nihil esse simulacrum. Sic de eo quoq; dicendum est, quod subiungitur: Aut quod simulacris immolatum aliquid sit. Sacrificium pariformiter, aut aliquid est, aut nihil.
units.tr: Is an idol something? Or is what is sacrificed to idols something? No. In denying that an idol is anything, or that what is sacrificed to idols is anything, we are reminded how sacred things are to be judged: not, of course, according to their outward appearance and the matter of their bodily substance, but according to that for the sake of which they are held sacred and worshipped religiously. According to this quality of theirs, they are either something or nothing. Something, if they are truly signs of divine things; nothing, if they are signs of false things, in which there is nothing of what is thought. Thus an image is nothing, because it is a form without the truth of that thing for whose sake it is set up. An image of God is nothing for a twofold reason. First, because God has no figure or likeness and is altogether unimaginable. Second, because the opinion is false by which the blind think God is worshipped in an image; in that case he is rather dishonoured, since the glory of the incorruptible God is changed into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, etc. (Romans 1.) Thus images must be judged as images. It is one thing to be gold, silver, bronze, wood, iron, stone, etc., and another to be an image or to be held as the image of some thing. According to the former essence, David sings of the idols of the Gentiles: their silver and gold, the works of men's hands, etc. According to the latter, the Apostle says an idol is nothing. So it must also be said of what follows: "or that what is sacrificed to idols is something." A sacrifice likewise is either something or nothing.

units.la: Aliquid, si vero Deo legitimè. Nihil, si vel falso Deo, quocunq; modo, vel vero illegitimè fiat sacrificium falsum & illegitimum nihil est, quia non est quod putatur. Nihil est opinione, nihil effectu. Tale est sacrificium illud Missæ pa-pisticæ, quo se Christum Deo patri pro peccatis uiuorū & mortuorum offerre fingūt, & quod fingunt mundo seducto turpissimè vendunt.
units.tr: Something, if it is offered to the true God lawfully. Nothing, if the sacrifice is offered to a false god in any manner, or to the true God unlawfully: a false and unlawful sacrifice is nothing, because it is not what it is thought to be. It is nothing in opinion and nothing in effect. Such is that sacrifice of the Papistical Mass, in which they pretend that Christ is offered to God the Father for the sins of the living and the dead, and which they shamelessly sell to a deceived world as what they pretend it to be.

units.la: SED, inquit, quod quæ Gentes immolant, dæmonijs immolant, & nō Deo.) Atqui tā noua erant scienter impij vt dæmonijs, hoc est, malis spiritibus immolare vellet, & non Deo vero. Quid est ergo quod dicit: quę Gētes immolāt, immolāt non Deo, sed dæmonijs? In sacrificijs Gentiū sunt ista. Eidolū, sacrificiū, intentio sacrificantium, & mysteriū impietatis. Sacrificātes dū immolāt eidolo, destinant sacrificiū suū nec ligno & lapidi, auro & argento, sed Deo, quē esse, & cuius nomen in eidolo coli putant. Quare quod sacrificantiū intētione attinet, immolant nec simulacro, nec dæmonijs, sed Deo ad quē sacrificia sua destinant. Quod verò mysterium ab oculis illorū abscondītū attinet, immolant non Deo, sed dæmonijs, qui eiusmodi falsorū cultuū sunt authores, & in simulacris latitantes falsis miraculis & portentis seductas hominū mentes ad se pelliciunt, & hoc genere cultuū diuinitatis honorē ambiūt. Deoq; vero illudunt, cui p omnia aduersari studēt. Ergo non est de cultibus sacris secundū intentiones nostras, sed secundū veritatē ipsorū iudicādū, quam, quoniā abscōdita est à iudicio rationis humanæ, mysterium uoco, ex solo verbo Dei, tanquā diuinæ uoluntatis indicio cognoscendum. Loquitur igitur Apost. non secundū intētionē immolantiū ethnicorū, cū dicit, quæ Gētes immolant, immolāt nō Deo, sed dæmonijs, sed respectu mysterij huius, quo cultus simulacrorum, non ad Deum, sed ad dæmones tende-bat. Et hoc respectu Deut. 32. dicitur: Sacrificarunt לשדים i. dæmonijs, & non Deo, & Leuit. 17. Et non sacrificabunt ultra sacrificia sua שעירים i. dæmonijs, post quos scortantur. Secundum hanc regulam puto satis esse manifestum qd de oibus illis sacrificijs & cultib. sentiri debeat, quib. simulacra coluntur, quantumuis bona ptexant intentionē, & vel ad Deū vel sanctos sacrificia sua destinēt omnes illi, quorum mētes doctrinis ethelothrescię sunt fascinatę.
units.tr: "But," he says, "what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God." And yet no one was so knowingly impious as to wish to sacrifice to demons, that is, to evil spirits, and not to the true God. What then does he mean by saying that what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice not to God but to demons? In the sacrifices of the Gentiles there are these things: the idol, the sacrifice, the intention of those sacrificing, and the mystery of impiety. When those sacrificing offer to an idol, they direct their sacrifice not to wood and stone, gold and silver, but to God, whom they think exists and whose name they think is worshipped in the idol. So as far as the intention of the sacrificers is concerned, they sacrifice neither to the image nor to demons, but to God, to whom they direct their sacrifices. But as far as the mystery hidden from their eyes is concerned, they sacrifice not to God but to demons, who are the authors of such false worships, and who, lurking in images, by false miracles and portents entice into themselves the deluded minds of men, and by this kind of worship seek the honour of divinity. They mock the true God, against whom they strive in all things. Therefore worship is to be judged not according to our intentions but according to its truth, which, because it is hidden from the judgement of human reason, I call a mystery, to be known from the word of God alone as an indication of the divine will. The Apostle therefore speaks, not according to the intention of the heathen who sacrifice, when he says that what the Gentiles sacrifice they sacrifice not to God but to demons, but with respect to this mystery, by which the worship of images was directed not to God but to demons. In this sense it is said in Deut. 32, "They sacrificed to demons [לשדים], and not to God," and in Lev. 17, "They shall no more sacrifice their sacrifices to goat-demons [שעירים], after whom they play the harlot." According to this rule I think it is sufficiently clear what must be thought of all those sacrifices and worships in which images are honoured, however good the intention, and all those whose minds are bewitched by the doctrines of self-chosen worship [ἐθελοθρησκείας], even if they direct their sacrifices to God or to the saints.

units.la: NOLIM aūt uos confortes fieri dæmonio-rum.) Si sola immolatio qua dæmonijs sacrifi-catur, & non etiā communicatio rerum immolatarū confortes redderet dæmoniorū, dicendum fuisset: Quæ Gentes immolant, non Deo immolāt, sed dæmonijs, ideoq; confortes sunt dæmoniorum, & hoc nomine à uobis fugiēdæ, verūm quoniā ipsa quoq; immolaticiorū cibo-rū communicatio, perinde est dæmoniorum, q panis & poculū domini, corporis ac sangui-nis illius est communicatio, rectè dixit: Nolim uos confortes fieri dæmoniorum. Ne dicerēt, uidelicet: Esto, immolēt Gentes non Deo, sed dæmonijs, quid ad nos? Non immolamus cum
units.tr: "I would not have you become partakers with demons." If the mere immolation by which sacrifice is made to demons, and not also the sharing of the sacrificed things, made them partners of demons, he should have said: "What the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice not to God but to demons, and therefore they are partners of demons and are to be avoided by you on this account." But since the sharing of sacrificed food is itself just as much a sharing with demons as the bread and cup of the Lord is a sharing in the body and blood of that Lord, he rightly said: "I would not have you become partakers with demons." Lest they should say, namely: "Granted, the Gentiles sacrifice not to God but to demons; what is that to us? We do not sacrifice with them,

units.la: eis, sed ad mensam uocati accedimus, deq; im-molaticijs, non vt immolaticijs, sed vt cibo ac potu, bonis Dei creaturis, comedimus ac bibi-mus. Et hoc facientes, nō cōmunicamus cum dæmonijs, q nec colimus nec adoramus. Hoc illis effugium eripiēs, cōtendit externā illā im-molaticiæ mensæ cōmunicationē, communi-cationem esse dæmoniorū. Et quoniam horrē-dum est consortē esse dæmoniorū, id est, malo-rum & abominabilium spirituum, uide q pru-denter & moderatè nō dicat: Quę Gētes im-molant, immolāt nō Deo, sed dæmonijs, quare uos confortes estis dæmonum, immolaticijs il-lorum vescentes, id quod admodū fuissēt du-rum & acerbum, sed: Nolim vos fieri cōsortes dæmonum, quibus uerbis & affectum salutis ipsorū cupidum exprimit, & quod seuerè per asseueratione ac reprehēsionem pronunciare poterat, mitius exprimit, q ut offendi possent.
units.tr: but we come as guests to the table, and we eat and drink of the sacrificed food, not as sacrificed food but as food and drink, good creatures of God." In doing this, they say, they do not share with demons, since they neither worship nor adore them. Taking away this escape, he contends that that outward sharing at the table of sacrifices is a sharing with demons. And since it is dreadful to be a partner of demons, that is, of evil and abominable spirits, observe how prudently and moderately he does not say: "What the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice not to God but to demons; therefore you are partners of demons, eating their sacrificed food." That would have been harsh and bitter. He says instead: "I would not have you become partners of demons," words by which he also expresses a desire for their salvation; and what he could have pronounced severely with assertion and rebuke, he expresses more gently, so that they might not be offended.

units.la: De consortio autem dæmoniorum sic senti-endum esse puto. Naturali consortio non pos-sumus illis coniungi. Quare omne illorum cō-fortium est, uel sacramentale, vel spirituale, vel pœnale. Sacramentale voco, quod externorū cultuum ac sacrorum communicatione con-stat. Huc pertinent omnia sacra, quibus eidola coluntur, templa, delubra, sacella, arę, simula-cra, dies festi, sacrificia, mystica mensa, cum om-nibus ritibus, & cultibus. Qui in hisce commu-nicant, consortes sunt dæmoniorum, etiamsi non in omnibus, sed quibusdam tantum com-municent. De hoc consortij genere loquitur hic Apostolus. Spirituale est, quo spiritus ho-minis primùm erroribus tenebrarum, quod superstitiones & impietatem attinet, deinde & malicia cordis, cum malis spiritibus cōmu-nicat, vt non solum mācipium, sed & filius dia-boli rectè vocari possit. Sic consortes dæmo-num sunt omnes impij, superstitiosi, cæci, su-perbi, inuidi, blasphemi, homicidæ, perfidi, fla-gitiosi, hypocritæ, contemptores Dei, &c. Par-ticipant enim de spiritu diabolicæ malicię & nequitiæ. Tales autem consortes dæmonum in ecclesia seductorum hodie regnant.
units.tr: Now concerning the partnership of demons I think it should be understood thus. We cannot be joined to them by natural partnership. Therefore every partnership with them is either sacramental, or spiritual, or penal. I call sacramental that which consists in the sharing of outward worships and rites. To this belong all the sacred things by which idols are worshipped: temples, shrines, chapels, altars, images, festival days, sacrifices, the mystical table, with all their rites and cults. Those who share in these are partners of demons, even if they share not in all but only in some of them. It is of this kind of partnership that the Apostle speaks here. Spiritual partnership is that by which the spirit of man, first through the errors of darkness, as far as superstition and impiety are concerned, and then through the malice of the heart, shares with evil spirits, so that he may rightly be called not only a slave but a son of the devil. Thus all the impious, superstitious, blind, proud, envious, blasphemous, murderers, faithless, flagitious, hypocrites, and contemners of God are partners of demons. For they partake of the spirit of diabolical malice and wickedness. And such partners of demons, seduced in the Church, reign today.

units.la: Pœnale consortium est, consortium æternæ condemnationis, quod manet omnes eos, qui in hac uita uel sacramentaliter, uel spirituali-ter absque resipiscentia consortes sunt dæmo-num. De hoc consortio loquitur Christus Mat-thæi 25. dicens: Discedite à me maledicti in i-gnem æternum, qui paratus est diabolo & an-gelis eius. Ergo impij in igne æterno cum dæmonijs in sempiternum communicabunt, vt quorum maliciæ & impietatis fuere consor-tes, horum etiam condemnationis consortes efficiantur.
units.tr: Penal partnership is the partnership of eternal condemnation, which awaits all those who in this life are partners of demons, either sacramentally or spiritually, without repentance. Christ speaks of this partnership in Matthew 25, saying: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels." Therefore the impious will share with demons in eternal fire for ever, so that those whose partners they were in malice and impiety may also become partners in their condemnation.

units.la: Non potestis poculum domini bibere, & poculum dæmoniorum. Non potestis mensę domini participes esse, & mensæ dæmoniorum.
units.tr: You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons.

units.la: Hæc est conclusio, quëadmodū suprà dixi-mus.
units.tr: This is the conclusion, as I said above.

units.la: A Consortium dæmoniorum triplex.
units.tr: The fellowship of demons is threefold.

units.la: B Mysterium. mus. Hác simpliciter quidé, & ex pręcedentib. natâ, verû cũ auxesi ponit, quo plᵒ inferat terroris. Nó dicit: Nó potestis poculum dñi bibere, & immolare dæmonijs, sed quo argumento de cõmunicatione mensæ dominicæ sumpto inhęreat, nõ potestis, inquit, poculû domini bibere, & poculû dæmoniorû. Non potestis mesæ domini participes esse, & mêsę dæmoniorû. Neq; enim immolabant dæmonijs, sed interim de ijs quæ dæmonijs immolata erant, edebant & bibebant, & hoc se inculpate facere iudicabat. Neq; dicit: Nó potestis participes esse domini & dæmoniorû, sed: Nó potestis mêsæ domini participes esse, & mêsæ dæmoniorû, quo externa illâ cõmunicatione mêsæ eidolorû sic execrabilem esse admoneat, vt vera mêsę dominicæ cõmunionê prorsus excludat, & cõtra, hâc sic esse comparatam, vt illam iuxta se ferre nequeat. Quemadmodum enim summa est discrepantia inter Christû & Belial, ita nulla potest esse communicatio mêsæ Christi, & mensę Belial. Sed dices: Quomodo nó potuerût Corinthij facere, quod tamê fecisse cõuincuntur? Comederût ac biberût de vtraq; mêsa domini & dæmoniorû, atq; ita participes fuerunt vtriusq;, quantûuis inter se cõtrariæ, quomodo ergo dicit: Non potestis poculum dñi bibere & poculum dæmoniorû? Non potestis mêsę dñi participes esse, & mensæ dæmoniorû? Si diceret: Nó debetis poculû dæmoniorû bibere, qa poculû dñi bibitis, nó debetis mêsæ dæmonio rum participes esse, quia participes estis mêsæ dñi, nulla esset quęstio: verû cũ dicit: Nó potestis, quærendû videtur quomodo fit intelligendum, ne quod non modo facere poterant, sed & faciebant, falsò eos facere non posse dicat.
units.tr: B Mysterium. Paul states this simply, as a conclusion following from what precedes, but he adds it with an amplification, so as to strike greater terror. He does not say, "You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and sacrifice to demons," but he holds to the argument about communion at the Lord's table by saying: "You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons." For the Corinthians were not sacrificing to demons, but they were eating and drinking what had been offered to demons, and they judged that they did this without fault. Nor does he say, "You cannot be partakers of the Lord and of demons," but "You cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons." By this he warns that external communion in the table of idols is so detestable that it utterly excludes true communion in the Lord's table, and conversely that the two are so constituted that the one cannot bear the other alongside it. For just as there is the greatest disagreement between Christ and Belial, so there can be no communion between the table of Christ and the table of Belial. But you will say: how could the Corinthians not do what they are convicted of having done? They ate and drank from both the table of the Lord and the table of demons, and so were partakers of both, however mutually opposed. How then does he say, "You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons"? If he had said, "You ought not to drink the cup of demons, since you drink the cup of the Lord; you ought not to be partakers of the table of demons, since you are partakers of the table of the Lord," there would be no question. But since he says "You cannot," it seems we must ask how this is to be understood, lest he say falsely that they were unable to do what they not only could do but actually did.

units.la: Respôdeo. Poterât quidé facere quod faciebât, & facere nó debebant, verû mensę domini simul & mensæ dæmoniorû veraciter participes esse nó poterât. Sic poterant & nó poterât. Poterát externa cõmunicatione de vtraq; mêsa dñi & dæmoniorû edere ac bibere. Et hoc facientes reprehendebãtur. Veraciter vero participare de mensa dñi, & simul participare de mensa dæmoniorû nó poterât. Veraciter enim de mêsa dñi participant, qui nó externæ tantû de pane & vino edût & bibût, sed & fide ac spiritu de corpore & sanguine domini communicant, quæ communicatio eam q dæmoniorû est ferre nequit. Sic qui Mámonæ seruit, Deo seruire non potest, intellige veraciter, fideliter & legitimè. Alias innumeri sunt, qui simul & Deo & Mámonæ in specie seruiant. Si hæc vera sunt, quomodo cõtendimus hodie fieri posse, vt impij, & ipsissimi mystæ dæmoniorû partiçipes sint, nó modo sacramétalis signi, sed & ipsius signati quoties externè cũ fidelibus cõmunicant. Deinde, hâc quoq; ob causam non poterant simul mêsæ dñi, & mêsę dæmoniorû esse participes, quod eiusmodi Christianos nô esset dominus diutius toleraturus. Si dicas miliți, nõ solû à principe suo, sed & ab illius hoste stipendia accipiêti: Nó poteris miles esse prin cipis tui, & stipêdia accipere ab hoste, satis illi significas, fieri nó posse vt in vtráq; parte clau dicâs, in militia principis sui perduret, quod is talé militê in castris suis nô sit laturus. Consimili modo habet & conditio militiæ Christianæ. Christianus esse nó poterit, qui simul vult cósors esse dæmoniorû. Quare aut deserenda est communicatio mensæ dæmoniorû, & mensę domini adhęrendû, aut relinquêda mêsa domini, & adhęrêdû mêsę dæmoniorû. Vtriusq; cómunicatio retineri nõ poterit. Hoc sensu dicebat Iehosuah ad Israelé: Nó poteritis seruire dño. Deus enim sanctus & æmulator est. Quare nõ poterát seruire domino? Quia simul dijs solebât seruire alienis, quâ claudicatione dominus, tanquâ Deus æmulator, non potest ser re in suo populo. Perinde ac si dicat maritus vxori: Non poteris cósors esse mei thori, ac thori adulteri. Nó poteris participeps esse mêsę meę ac mensæ adulteri. Sic dicebat ad Israelê propheta Elias, 1. Reg. cap. 18. Vsquequo claudicatis in duas partes? Si dominus est Deus, sequimini eum. Si Baal uerò, sequimini illû. Poterat subiungere, Nõ poteritis populus esse domini, & colere deos alienos. Alterutrum eligite, vtrunq; esse & facere non poteritis. Hi duo præsentis loci sensus nihil habent diuersi: quare vtrique tanquam veri retineri possunt. Habent hic quod obseruent profæri illi, qui quâuis veritaté Dei cognoscát, illiq; nomen dederint, sic tamen sæculo se accómodât, vt & cum aduersa rijs poculum Babylônicæ meretricis; & cum si delibus poculum dominibibant. Dicimus illis cum Apostolo: Non potestis bibere poculû do mini, & poculum purpuratæ meretricis. Nofi potestis pattitipes esse sacrorum Christi & sacrorû Antichristi: Sed hac de re videatur Profcærus noster, quem anno millesimo quingentesimo quadragesimonono sub nomine Eutychij Myonis vulgauimus.
units.tr: I answer: they could do what they did, and yet they ought not to have done it; but they could not truly be partakers of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons at the same time. Thus they both could and could not. They could eat and drink from both the table of the Lord and the table of demons by external communion, and in doing so they were rebuked. But they could not truly partake of the table of the Lord and at the same time partake of the table of demons. For those truly partake of the table of the Lord who communicate not merely externally in the bread and wine, but also by faith and spirit in the body and blood of the Lord; and this communion cannot bear that of demons. So he who serves Mammon cannot serve God, understood truly, faithfully and lawfully. Otherwise there are countless people who serve both God and Mammon in appearance. If these things are true, how do we maintain today that it is possible for the wicked, and even the very initiates of demons, to be partakers not only of the sacramental sign but also of the thing signified, whenever they communicate outwardly with the faithful? Moreover, for this further reason they could not be partakers of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons at once, because the Lord would not long tolerate such Christians. If you say to a soldier who receives pay not only from his prince but also from his enemy, "You cannot be a soldier of your prince and receive pay from the enemy," you make it sufficiently clear that he cannot hold both sides and remain in his prince's service, since the prince will not keep such a soldier in his camp. The condition of Christian warfare is similar. He who wishes to be a partner of demons at the same time cannot be a Christian. Therefore either the communion of the table of demons must be abandoned and one must cling to the table of the Lord, or the table of the Lord must be left and one must cling to the table of demons. The communion of both cannot be kept. In this sense Joshua said to Israel: "You cannot serve the Lord, for he is a holy and jealous God" (Josh. 24.19). Why could they not serve the Lord? Because they were at the same time accustomed to serve alien gods, a double-dealing by which the Lord, as a jealous God, cannot be served among his people. It is just as if a husband said to his wife: "You cannot share my bed and the bed of an adulterer; you cannot be partaker of my table and of the table of an adulterer." So the prophet Elijah spoke to Israel, 1 Kings 18: "How long will you halt between two opinions? If the Lord is God, follow him; but if Baal, follow him." He could have added: "You cannot be the people of the Lord and worship foreign gods. Choose one; you cannot be and do both." The two senses of the present passage do not differ at all, so both can be held as true. Here there is something for those to notice who, though they know the truth of God and have given their name to it, nevertheless accommodate themselves to the world, so that they drink both the cup of the Babylonian harlot and the cup of the Lord with the adversaries. We say to them with the Apostle: "You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of the purple harlot. You cannot be partakers of the sacred things of Christ and of the sacred things of Antichrist." But on this matter let our Profcaerus be consulted, which we published in the year 1549 under the name of Eutychius Myonius.

units.la: An prouocatís dóminum? Num sor tiores illo sumus?
units.tr: Do we provoke the Lord? Are we stronger than he?

units.la: Qualitaté & enormitatem deliĉti, deinde & insaniâ delinquentiû cõsiderans velut exclamat, & in hæc verba prorúpit, quæ sanè utmo dica sunt, ita nõ sine singulari sunt ardore spiritus eiaculata. Nó dicit: An peccamus in dñm? sed: An prouocamus dñm? Aliud est, peccare in dñm, quod multis modis etiá à pijs fieri potest, & aliud, prouocare dñm. Prouocant dominû, qui in re illû omniû minimè ferenda cõtumaciter irritant, nec cœpto auocari sustinêt. Graue est aút prouocare & irritare dñm, quómodocunq; fiat. Gravius uerò est, si puocetur ad zelum & æmulationem per cultum fallorû deorum ab illis, quos in gratiam suam assumpsit, & in populum peculiarê, ac silios adoptauit. Potest à coniuge maritus uarijs modis irritari, ea uero irritatio quæ fit scortando & adulterádo, qua ad furore maritalis zeli prouocatur, cęteris multo est grauior. qua de Salam Prou. 6. dicit: Zelus & furor uiri non parcit.
units.tr: Considering the nature and enormity of the offence, and then the madness of those who commit it, he cries out as it were, and breaks forth into these words, which are indeed most apt and were uttered with no small ardour of spirit. He does not say, "Do we sin against the Lord?" but "Do we provoke the Lord?" It is one thing to sin against the Lord, which can be done in many ways even by the godly, and another thing to provoke the Lord. Those provoke the Lord who stubbornly irritate him in a matter that he by no means endures, and who will not suffer themselves to be called off from what they have begun. To provoke and irritate the Lord is grave, however it is done. It is graver still if he is provoked to jealousy and emulation by the worship of false gods on the part of those whom he has taken into his favour, made his peculiar people, and adopted as sons. A husband may be irritated by his wife in various ways, but that irritation which comes from whoring and adultery, by which the fury of marital jealousy is roused, is far graver than the rest. Of this Solomon says in Proverbs 6: "The jealousy and fury of a man will not spare."

units.la: Ad hoc genus prouocationis respiciés Apo stolus nó simpliciter dicit, ἢ παροργίζομεν, id est, an irritamus vel ad iram prouocamus, sed ἢ παραζηλῶμεν, id est, an ad zelū & æmulationē prouocamus dominum? Atq; ita admodū est hoc verbo pertinenter & in loco vsus. Quod enim Corinthij simul poculū domini cum fidelibus de mensa domini & poculum dæmoniorū cū eidololatris de mensa & sacrificijs dæmoniorū bibētes faciebant, quid aliud videri poterat q; scortatio spiritualis, qua dominum ad zelū & vltionem cótra se prouo cabant? In causa cósi mili vs⁹ est hoc verbo, & Moses Deu.32. vbi sic legim⁹ ..., id est, ad zelum prouocauerunt eum in dijs alienis, & abominationibus suis irritarunt eum. Immolauerunt dæmonijs & nō Deo. Et paulo pòst. Abscondā facie meā ab eis, & considerabo nouissima eorū. Generatio enim peruersa est, & infideles filij, ... quod Septuaginta verterunt, ... id est, ipsi ad zelum me prouocauerunt in eo qui non est Deus, &c. Quare Erasmus nō satis vim vocis huius expressit, cum vertit: An prouocamus dominum? Nec vulgata versio satisfacit, quamuis æmulationis sensum exprimere conatus est ille, quisquis fuit, interpres. Sic enim habet: An æmulamur dominum? Sumitur quidem aliquādo verbū æmulandi sensu odij & inuidiæ, verūm sæpius pro bono zelo reperitur in scripturis, quare mentem Apostoli hæc lectio non satis constanter exprimit.
units.tr: Having this kind of provocation in view, the Apostle does not simply say ἢ παροργίζομεν, that is, "do we irritate or provoke to anger," but ἢ παραζηλῶμεν, that is, "do we provoke the Lord to jealousy and emulation?" And the word is used so aptly and appropriately here. For since the Corinthians, while drinking the cup of the Lord with the faithful at the table of the Lord, also drank the cup of demons with idolaters at the table and sacrifices of demons, what else could this appear to be but a spiritual whoredom by which they provoked the Lord to jealousy and vengeance against themselves? In a similar case Moses uses this word in Deuteronomy 32, where we read thus: they provoked him to jealousy with strange gods, and angered him with their abominations; they sacrificed to demons and not to God. And shortly after: "I will hide my face from them, and I will consider their latter end; for they are a perverse generation, and faithless children." What the Seventy rendered, that is, "they provoked me to jealousy with what is not God," etc. Wherefore Erasmus did not sufficiently express the force of this word when he translated: "Do we provoke the Lord?" Nor does the Vulgate satisfy, although whoever the translator was he tried to express the sense of emulation. For it reads: "Do we emulate the Lord?" The verb "to emulate" is indeed sometimes taken in the sense of hatred and envy, but more often in Scripture it is found for good zeal; so this reading does not express the Apostle's meaning with sufficient consistency.

units.la: Nos hic obseruemus quā graue & enorme peccatum fit, si quid in populū, gratiam, & nomen Dei obsignati, & sacramento fidei despõsati sunt, cum eidolis scortantur, quanq; graui se ultioni Dei reddant obnoxios. Longè illi e normius peccant, q; eidololatræ ethnici, à nomine Dei alieni, magisq; Deum exacerbant. De ethnicis dici non potest, quod dominū ad zelum & æmulatione cultu eidolorum prouocant, quandoquidem à nomine illius & fide sunt alieni, rectè uerò hoc illis tribuitur, qui ad populum illius pertinent. Maritū non prouocat ad zelum cuiusuis mulierculæ scortatio prouocat uerò, si quę illi uxor est corpus suum communicet alienis. Quare quemadmodum olim Israelitarum, ita nunc & Christianorum eidololatria multo est in cõspectu domini gravior & enormior, quàm unquam fuerit Gentium. Nemo cordatus mirabitur, unde sit tam misera ecclesiarum Christi uastatio ac desolatio, si uel de sola eidololatria cogitet, quæ iam aliquot sæculis in illis obtinuit, & hodie quoque dominum ad zelū & ultionem prouocare non cessat.
units.tr: Here let us observe how grave and monstrous a sin it is, if those who are sealed with the name and grace of God and betrothed to him by the sacrament of faith whore after idols, and how greatly they render themselves liable to the severe vengeance of God. Far more monstrously do they sin than the heathen idolaters, who are alien from the name of God, and who rather exasperate God. Of the heathen it cannot be said that they provoke the Lord to jealousy and emulation by the worship of idols, since they are strangers to his name and faith; but this is rightly attributed to those who belong to his people. The whoring of any little woman does not provoke a husband to jealousy; but it does if his own wife shares her body with strangers. Wherefore, just as once with the Israelites, so now with Christians idolatry is far graver and more monstrous in the sight of the Lord than it ever was among the Gentiles. No sensible person will wonder whence comes so wretched a wasting and desolation of the churches of Christ, if he considers idolatry alone, which for some centuries has prevailed among them, and which even today does not cease to provoke the Lord to jealousy and vengeance.

units.la: Et hanc peccati istius enormitatem Apostolus non solū uerbo παραζηλῶμεν, sed & figura hac orationis expressit, qua nō simpliciter dehortando dixit: Ne prouocemus dominū, sed admirando & obstupescendo. An prouocamus dominum? Quasi dicat: Quid hoc uæsaniæ est? An adeo facti fumus deplorate insani, ut nó uereamur communicatione dæmoniorum zelū domini in nostrum exitium prouocare?
units.tr: And the Apostle expressed the enormity of this sin not only by the word παραζηλῶμεν but also by this figure of speech, by which he does not simply dissuade, saying, "Let us not provoke the Lord," but speaks with wonder and astonishment: "Do we provoke the Lord?" As if he said: What madness is this? Have we become so desperately insane that we do not fear to provoke the jealousy of the Lord to our own destruction by communion with demons?

units.la: Vide tamen quomodo vehementiam hanc sermonis Apostolica prudentia mitiget, nō di cens: An prouocatis dominum? Num fortiores illo estis? sed: An prouocamus dominum? Num fortiores illo fumus? Sic loquendo, delicti quidem grauitatem exaggerat, verūm exaggerationem hanc simul mitigat, dum quod à quibusdam speciali ter fiebat, in genere ad omnes transfert, ac se quoq; coniungit. Sapientis medici est, oleo miscere acetum, cuiusetiam in parabola Euangelica admonemur. Habent hic quod imitentur verbi ministri. Horum potissimum est inter corripiendum delinquetes, nec oleum sine aceto, nec acetum sine oleo curandis uulneribus, sed utrunq; coniunctim ac prudenter iuxta delinquentiū qualitatem attemperatum infundere.
units.tr: Yet see how the Apostolic prudence softens this vehemence of speech, not saying, "Do you provoke the Lord? Are you stronger than he?" but "Do we provoke the Lord? Are we stronger than he?" By speaking thus he magnifies indeed the gravity of the offence, yet at the same time tempers this exaggeration, while he transfers to all in general what was being done by certain persons in particular, and joins himself as well. It is the mark of a wise physician to mix vinegar with oil, a thing we are also admonished of in the Gospel parable. Ministers of the Word have here something to imitate. It is especially their task, when rebuking offenders, to pour in neither oil without vinegar nor vinegar without oil in curing wounds, but to apply both together and wisely, tempered to the nature of the offenders.

units.la: NVM fortiores illo fumus? inquit.) Prouocationis huius insaniam ab impossibili exprimit. Insanum est, si homo pusillus & infirmus ad pugnam prouocet gigantem & bellicosum uirum. Quanto insanius est, si homo prouocet Deum? Nemo sanus fortiorem se prouocat, ni si data opera exitiū sibijpse uelit accersere. Cū ergo dixisset: An prouocamus dominum? quo insaniam hanc exprimat, mox eadem sermonis figura subiungit: Num fortiores illo fumus? quasi dicat: Qua nam fiducia prouocamus dominum? Qui se fortiores esse cófidunt, prouocare solent impotentiores. Nos prouocamus dominū. Ergòne illo nos fortiores esse confidimus? Sin minus, quid aliud facimus quà quod more insanorum exitium nobis ipsi accersimus? Etenim impossibile est, ut irę illius resistamus ubi illam in nos prouocauerimus.
units.tr: "Are we stronger than he?" he says. He expresses the madness of this provocation by the impossible. It is mad if a small and weak man challenges a giant and warlike man to fight. How much madder is it if a man provokes God? No sane person provokes someone stronger than himself, unless he deliberately wishes to bring destruction upon himself. Therefore, having said, "Do we provoke the Lord?", in order to express this madness he immediately adds, by the same figure of speech: "Are we stronger than he?" as if he said: On what confidence do we provoke the Lord? Those who trust that they are stronger are wont to provoke the weaker. We provoke the Lord. Do we then trust that we are stronger than he? If not, what else do we do than, like madmen, bring destruction upon ourselves? For it is impossible that we should resist his wrath once we have provoked it against us.

units.la: Vtinam consimilis insaniæ nequeant argui, qui hodie incredibili pertinacia pariter & contumacia palàm contra se prouocát dominum, cuius uerbum blasphemant, pedibus concul cant, hæreseos condemnant, probris & contumelia proscindunt, Antichristum supra Christū extollunt, oues dominicas mactant, ecclesias opprimunt, in conspectu fidelium impudentissimè luxuriantur, scortantur, adulterantur, ut grauiora taceam, quæ hac nostra ætate publicis etiam scriptis defendere non erubescūt, & tantum non clamant: Linguam nostram magnificamus, labia nostra à nobis sunt, quis noster dominus est? Psal.11.
units.tr: Would that those who today, with incredible obstinacy and at the same time stubbornness, openly provoke the Lord against themselves could be convicted of a like madness!
