They blaspheme his Word, trample it underfoot, condemn as heresy, tear apart with reproaches and insults, exalt Antichrist above Christ, slaughter the Lord's sheep, oppress the churches, and in the sight of the faithful wantonly indulge in luxury, whoredom and adultery with the most shameless impudence. I pass over graver things, which in our own age they are not ashamed to defend even in published writings, and they all but cry out: "We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is lord over us?" Psalm 11.

units.la: Omnia mihi licent, at non omnia conducunt. Omnia mihi licent, sed non omnia edificant. Nemo quod suum est quæ rat, sed quisq; quod alterius.
units.tr: All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient. All things are lawful for me, but not all things edify. Let no one seek his own, but each the other's good.

units.la: Hactenus conatus est Corinthios cum infidelibus de mensa eidolorum edentes ac bibentes metu irę Dei ab ea communicatione auocare, iá consequenter redit ad argumētū charitatis fraternæ, quod duobus præcedentibus capitibus 8. & 9. tractauit, ac rursus inculcat, peccare eos in fratres infirmos & abuti libertate quid-libet edendi, contra charitatem, quę non tam quid liceat quàm quid cõducat spectare soleat
units.tr: Hitherto he has sought to call the Corinthians, who were eating and drinking the food of idols with unbelievers, away from that fellowship for fear of the wrath of God. Now he returns, as is fitting, to the subject of brotherly love, which he treated in the two preceding chapters, 8 and 9, and again impresses on them that they sin against weak brothers and abuse the liberty of eating whatever they like, against charity, which is accustomed to look not so much at what is permitted as at what is expedient.

units.la: Omnia mihi licet, inquit. Erat hoc illis in ore frequens. Vt dicerent, licere sibi quibuslibet vesci. Huc scilicet rapiebant: doctrinam libertatis per Christum partę, quam ipse prædicabat Apostolus contra pseudapostolos, qui cõ scientias fidelium obseruantia legalium escarum obstringere, & in seruitute Mosaicę litęrę nõ modo ex Israele, sed & ex Gentibus in Christū credentes abducere moliebatur. Sic illi nõ soļū escis in lege uetitis, sed & ijs vescebatur, quę dæmonijs erat ab idololatris immolatæ, atque ita fratres infirmos præpostera hac libertate non ædificabant, sed destruebant. Vt hunc illorum prætextum corrigat, ipsum verbum qd in ore habebant singuli, in medium adfert dicens: Omnia mihi licent, at non omnia condu cunt. Sic quisquis illorum dicebat: Licent mihi omnia, liber sum, non pecco, vsurpando quæ libet. Est itaque sensus.
units.tr: "All things are lawful for me," he says. This was a frequent saying on their lips, so that they claimed it was lawful for them to eat anything whatever. They were clearly twisting to this end the doctrine of the liberty obtained through Christ, which the Apostle himself preached against the false apostles, who tried to bind the consciences of the faithful to the observance of legal foods and to lead back into the slavery of the Mosaic letter not only those from Israel but also those from the Gentiles who believed in Christ. Thus they ate not only the foods forbidden in the law but also those things which had been sacrificed to demons by idolaters, and so by this perverse liberty they did not edify weak brothers but destroyed them. To correct this pretext of theirs, he brings into the open the very saying each of them had on his lips: "All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient." So whoever of them said: "All things are lawful for me, I am free, I do not sin," was claiming for himself whatever he pleased. This, then, is the sense.

units.la: Sed hæc omnia eludis frater, dices: Omnia mihi licent, omnia mihi sunt libera, quasi sic licent tibi omnia, vt simul de mensa domini & de mensa dæmoniorum communicando nihil peccęs. Sed audi: Licent quidem omnia, at tu hac libertate temere abuteris, teq; ipsum & proximum perdis. Neq; enim omnia tibi conducunt, sed pleraq; noxia sunt quæ facis, neq; omnia ædificant fratres infirmos, sed quæda magis destruunt. Quę vero noxia sunt & facieti & spectanti, quomodo licere poterant?
units.tr: But you will mock all this, brother, and say: "All things are lawful for me, all things are free for me," as if all things were lawful for you, so that by communicating at the table of the Lord and at the table of demons together you sin in nothing. But listen: indeed all things are lawful, yet you rashly abuse this liberty and destroy both yourself and your neighbour. For not all things are expedient for you, and many of the things you do are harmful; nor do all things edify the weak brothers, but some rather destroy them. But how could things that are harmful to the doer and to the onlooker be lawful?

units.la: Ad hunc modum puto Apostolum nõ de seloqui, cum dicit: Omnia mihi licent, sed Corinthiorum vetbum proferre & corrigere quod crebro in ore habebant. Quod autem secundo dicit: omnia mihi licent, propterea, puto, facit, quod ipsi verbum hoc subinde repetebat. Vel certe, vt geminum damnum, quod ex abusu libertatis huius nascebatur, hac repetitione perstringat. Primum enim dominū cõtra se provocabant, communicando de mensa dæmoniorum, id quod ipsis haud quaquam conducebat. Deinde conscientias infirmorum fratrū destruebant, & infideles in eidololatria sua cõfirmabant. Et hic sensus placuit Chrysostomo. Si quis tamen aliter exponens, utranq; particulam ad proximum referendam esse putauerit, per me licet hoc faciat.
units.tr: I think the Apostle does not speak in his own person when he says "All things are lawful for me," but rather repeats and corrects the saying of the Corinthians which they often had on their lips. And that he says a second time, "All things are lawful for me," he does, I think, because they kept repeating this saying; or at any rate, by this repetition he means to strike at the twofold harm which arose from the abuse of this liberty. For first they provoked the Lord against themselves by communicating at the table of demons, which was in no way expedient for them. Then they destroyed the consciences of weak brothers and confirmed unbelievers in their idolatry. This sense also pleased Chrysostom. If anyone, however, expounding it otherwise, thinks that both phrases are to be referred to the neighbour, let him do so; I do not object.

units.la: Dicet hic iinperitus aliquis: quomodo concedit Apostolus licere omnia, cum innumera sint, quæ prorsus sunt illicita & uetita? Etenim licet correctionem adiecerit dicens, at nõ omnia conducunt, ea tamen non negat licere omnia, sed abusum libertatis corrigens monet nõ conducere omnia quæ licent, id quod omnino est licere omnia concedentis. Respondeo: Communis regula est, uniuersales uoces non esse ultra terminos causæ de qua agitur extendendas. Sic hoc loco, quod dicit: omnia mihi licent, non est intelligendum nisi de escis, de quibus loquitur.
units.tr: Here some unskilled person will say: How does the Apostle concede that all things are lawful, when there are countless things that are altogether unlawful and forbidden? For although he has added the correction, "but not all things are expedient," he does not deny that these things are lawful; rather, in correcting the abuse of liberty, he advises that not all things which are lawful are expedient, which is entirely to concede that all things are lawful. I answer: it is a common rule that universal expressions are not to be extended beyond the limits of the matter under discussion. So in this place, what he says, "All things are lawful for me," is to be understood only of foods, which is the subject he is speaking of.

units.la: Consimilia dixit & suprà cap. 6. Omnia mihi licent, sed non omnia conducunt, Omnia mihi licent, at ego non redigar sub vllius potestatem, quæ verba causæ accommodauit, qua de illic egit. Vbi etiam annotauimus, quę hic quoque considerari possunt.
units.tr: He said similar things also above in chapter 6: "All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient," and "All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anyone." These words he fitted to the matter he was treating there, where we also noted what may be considered here too.

units.la: Nemo quod suum est quærat, inquit, sed quod alterius. Ne dicerent: Quid ad nos quod alij nostra libertate nõ ædificatur? Quod immolaticijs vescimur nostro commodo faciemus. Faciat quisq; quod sibi conducere putat. Nõ est vt aliorũ simus serui, &c. occurrit eiusmodi cogitationi dicens: Nemo quod suum est quærat, sed quisq; quod alterius. Quærere quod nostrum est, hoc loco, est nostris cõmoditatibus tantum esse addictos, quicquid accidat alijs. Quærere quod aliorum est, non est proprijs, sed aliorum commodis inseruire.
units.tr: "Let no one seek his own," he says, "but another's." Lest they should say: What is it to us if others are not edified by our liberty? We eat sacrificial meat for our own convenience. Let each do what he thinks expedient for himself; it is not right that we should be the servants of others, and so on. He meets such thinking by saying: "Let no one seek his own, but each the other's." To seek what is our own in this place means to be devoted only to our own conveniences, whatever happens to others. To seek what is another's means to serve not one's own interests but the interests of others.

units.la: Extra hunc sensum, sunt qui nimio studio quę rant quod alterius est, quo id ad se trahant, sicuti faciunt prelati Romani: rursu sunt qui re ēte res suas curantes ab alienis abstinent. In propsito quærere quod suum est, & negligere quod est aliorum, hominis est prorsus carnalis, quantumuis in cognitione veritatis probe instituti. Contrà, quærere quod est aliorũ magis, quàm quod est proprium, hominis est spiritu Christi, & veræ charitatis imbuti. Christus non quod suum sed quod nostrum erat, quæsiuit, ac semetipsum pro nobis tradidit, factus pauper, quo nos diuites redderet, & in sempiternum felices. Ad huius exemplum Corinthios componere studens dicit: Nemo nostrum quærat quod suum est, sed quisquę quod alterius.
units.tr: Apart from this sense, there are those who, with excessive zeal, seek what is another's in order to draw it to themselves, as the Roman prelates do; and again there are those who, while caring for their own affairs, keep their hands off what belongs to others. In the matter at hand, to seek what is one's own and to neglect what is another's belongs wholly to a carnal man, however well instructed he may be in the knowledge of the truth. On the contrary, to seek what is more another's than one's own belongs to a man imbued with the Spirit of Christ and with true charity. Christ did not seek what was his own but what was ours, and he gave himself up for us, becoming poor so that he might make us rich and happy for ever. Striving to conform the Corinthians to this example, he says: "Let none of us seek his own, but each the other's."

units.la: Cauendum autem est, ne admonitionem hanc extra normam veræ ac legitimæ charitatis trahamus, quæ non sic est comparata, vt reddat nos nostræ ipsorum salutis negligentes, sed ad hoc tendit, vt diuinæ dilectioni conformemur & coadunemur, id quod nos veræ reddit felicitatis participes. Dilectio proximi non excludit, sed requirit cum primis dilectionem Dei. Dilectio Dei reddit nos studiosos diuinæ voluntatis. Et hoc ante omnia nostrum debet esse studium, vt illi gratificemur in omnibus. Ergo quod suum est, id est, quod ad se pertinet, quærit quisquis diuinæ voluntati studet. Deinde non veræ, sed corruptæ & preposteræ dilectionis est, absque discrimine quærere quod est alterius, sic vt affectibus illius magis, quàm saluti seruiamus. Sic insanit seorstator, vt saorum oblitus ea tantum quærat quæ sunt scorti. Est itaque sic comparata præsens adhortatio, vt quemadmodum non vetat, ne nostram ipsorum salutem opereremur, ita non requirat, vt proximorum non saluti, sed affectibus studeamus. In rebus liberis & in differentibus ius ac libertatem nostram propter salutem proximi negligere debemus, ne hanc nostra licentia perdamus. Hoc facientes recte non quod nostrum, sed quod alterius est, quaerimus.
units.tr: Care must be taken, however, that we do not take this admonition outside the rule of true and lawful charity. That charity is not so framed as to make us negligent of our own salvation; it tends rather to this, that we be conformed and united to divine love, which makes us partakers of true happiness. Love of neighbour does not exclude but above all requires the love of God, and the love of God makes us zealous for the divine will. This must be before all else our concern, that we please him in all things. Therefore whoever is zealous for the divine will seeks what is his own, that is, what pertains to himself. Moreover, it is not true but corrupt and perverse love to seek indiscriminately what is another's, so that we serve his passions rather than his salvation. Thus the fornicator goes mad, forgetting his own salvation, and seeks only what belongs to the harlot. The present exhortation is therefore framed so that, just as it does not forbid us to work for our own salvation, so it does not require that we serve our neighbours' passions rather than their salvation. In things that are free and indifferent we ought to set aside our right and liberty for the sake of our neighbour's salvation, lest we lose this liberty through our licence. In doing this we rightly seek not what is our own but what is another's.

units.la: Cogitet hic minister Christi, quid sibi competat, & quid debeat ecclesiæ Dei. Si nullius Christiani est, quærere quæ sua sunt, sed ab omnibus requiritur, vt quæ aliorum sunt quærant, planè hoc duplici nomine competit illis qui in ecclesia Christi sunt, non modo fratres tanquam fideles, sed & patres tanquà doctores ac pastores, cuius rei exemplum in seipso proposuit Apostolus cap. præcedenti.
units.tr: Let the minister of Christ consider what befits him and what he owes to the Church of God. If it is the duty of no Christian to seek what is his own, but of all to seek what is of others, this applies in a twofold way to those who are in the Church of Christ: not only as brothers, being faithful, but also as fathers, being teachers and pastors. The Apostle set an example of this in himself in the preceding chapter.

units.la: Omne id quod in macello venditur, edite, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam. Domini enim est terra & plenitudo eius. Quod si quis vocat vos infidelium, & vultis ire, quicquid apponitur vobis edite, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam. Quod si quis vobis dixerit, hoc simulacris immolatum est, ne edatis propter illum qui indicauit, & propter conscientiam. Domini siquidem est terra & plenitudo eius. Porrò conscientiā dico non tuam, sed eam quæ est alterius. Cur enim libertas mea iudicatur ab alia conscientia? Quod si ego cum gratia participo, cur ob id mihi maledicitur, pro quo ego gratias ago?
units.tr: "Eat whatever is sold in the meat market, asking no question for conscience' sake. For the earth is the Lord's and its fullness. But if one of the unbelievers invites you and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no question for conscience' sake. But if someone says to you, 'This has been offered to idols,' do not eat it, for the sake of the one who pointed it out and for conscience' sake. For the earth is the Lord's and its fullness. But I mean conscience not your own, but that of the other. For why is my liberty judged by another's conscience? But if I partake with thanks, why am I reviled for that for which I give thanks?"

units.la: Sunt hæc instructionis gratia subiecta. Poterat videri scrupulosius exigere à fidelibus, vt ab eidolothytis, partim metu iræ Dei, partim studio charitatis in vniuersum abstinerēt, quasi illicitum sit illis quouis modo vesci. Instruit ergo eos luculento discrimine, docens quando immolaticia comedere licitè possint, & quando non possint. Omne, inquit, quod in macello venditur, edite, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam. Separat prophanas & vulgares occasiones edendi immolaticia à mensa sacrificiorum, qua in ipso eidolio eidololatræ immolaticia edebant & bibebant, quam communicationem hactenus reprehendit, & supra circa calcem capit. octauo nominatim perstrinxit. Aliud est commisceri mensis eidolorum, & aliud extra eidolium per occasionem vesci eidolothytis. Extra sacra est macellum & quicquid in macello venditur. Extra sacra sunt domestica conuiuia, quibus vel cognati vel amici vel vicini humanitatis studio accipiuntur. Ettamen vsuueniebat, vt in macello promiscuè venderentur carnes prophanæ & immolaticiæ. In domesticis quoq; infidelium conuiuijs nonnunquam prophanis esciis immolaticiæ miscebantur. Docet igitur fideles quomodo se gerant vtrobiq;. Primum, inquit, quicquid vēditur in macello securè comedite. Macellum enim non est eidolum, non est cultus, sed necessitatis gratia, ad alendam vitam nostram institutum. Et quoniam interrogari poterat: Quid si immolaticia vendantur in macello, & incidat Christianus in illa, siue prudenter siue ignoranter? addit, μυσλν ανακρινοντες, id est, nihil inquirentes aut interrogantes, hoc est, absque omni scrupulositate comedite ex oibus quæ in macello venduntur, nihil hæsitantes, etiāsi sint immolaticia, nec percontantes, immolaticia ne sint, vel secus. Et subijcit causam, quare inquirere & interrogare non debeant. Propter conscientiam inquit. Hanc autem particulam bifariam exponere possumus. Primo, vt intelligamus de conscientia emētis Christiani, hoc sensu. Omne quod in macello venditur, edite, nec conscientiæ vestræ gratia perquirite, immolaticia ne sint quę emitis, vel secus, quasi cō scientias vestras referat scire qualia sint quę in macello emitis. Non possunt illæ pollui per ea quæ in macello venduntur, etiamsi sciatis ea esse eidolothyta. Deinde, vt referamus ad conscientiam non ementis, sed magis vendentis, cuius rationem haberi volebat Apostolus. Consimili sensu infrà particulam hanc repetit. Chrysostomus sic exponit. Omne quod in macello venditur, edite, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiā, hoc est, ne conscij reddamini, eidolothyton esse quod editis, sed per ignorantiam excusemini. Etenim si ignorantes comederitis, impunè vobis erit. Verùm hæc sententia, meo iudicio, non satisfacit menti Apostoli. Aliàs infrà non debebat dicere: Quod si quis vobis dixerit, hoc simulacris immolatum est, ne edatis, propter illum qui indicauit. Sed simpliciter, propter conscientiam vestram, ne scienter immolaticia edatis. Neque hoc sensu bene consuluisset eorum scrupulositati, qui se peccati reos esse iudicabant, si quouis modo immolaticia gustassent.
units.tr: These things are added for the sake of instruction. It might have seemed that he should require of the faithful, more strictly, that they abstain altogether from things sacrificed to idols, partly from fear of God's wrath and partly from zeal for charity, as if it were unlawful for them to eat such food in any way. He therefore instructs them with a clear distinction, teaching when they may lawfully eat meat sacrificed to idols and when they may not. "Eat whatever is sold in the meat market," he says, "asking no questions for conscience' sake." He separates the profane and ordinary occasions for eating sacrificed meats from the tables of the sacrifices, where the idolaters ate and drank the sacrificed meats in the very idol temple. This fellowship he has condemned so far, and above, near the end of chapter 8, he attacked it by name. It is one thing to share in the tables of idols, and another to eat things sacrificed to idols on some occasion outside the idol temple. Outside the sacred precincts lies the meat market, and whatever is sold there. Outside the sacred precincts are also the domestic dinners to which relatives, friends or neighbours are invited out of kindness. Yet it happened that profane and sacrificed meats were sold together indiscriminately in the market, and in the domestic dinners of unbelievers, profane foods were sometimes mixed with sacrificed ones. He therefore teaches the faithful how to conduct themselves in both cases. First, he says, eat with a clear conscience whatever is sold in the market. For the market is not an idol, it is not worship, but is established for the sake of necessity, to sustain our life. And since it could be asked, "What if sacrificed meats are sold in the market and a Christian falls upon them, whether knowingly or unknowingly?", he adds μηδὲν ἀνακρίνοντες [mēdèn anakrinontes], that is, asking nothing or inquiring nothing; that is, eat without any scruple everything that is sold in the market, hesitating over nothing, even if it is sacrificed meat, and not inquiring whether it is sacrificed or not. And he adds the reason why they ought not to inquire or ask: "for conscience' sake," he says. We can explain this phrase in two ways. First, we may understand it of the conscience of the Christian buyer, in this sense: "Eat whatever is sold in the market, and do not inquire for the sake of your conscience whether the things you buy are sacrificed or not, as if your conscience depended on knowing what kind of things you buy in the market. Those things cannot be defiled by what is sold in the market, even if you know them to be things sacrificed to idols." Second, we may refer it to the conscience not of the buyer but rather of the seller, whose consideration the Apostle wished to be taken into account. He repeats this particle in a similar sense below. Chrysostom explains it thus: "Eat whatever is sold in the market, asking nothing for conscience' sake," that is, so that you may not be made aware that what you eat is sacrificed to idols, but may be excused on the ground of ignorance; for if you eat in ignorance, it will be without guilt for you. But this interpretation, in my judgment, does not satisfy the mind of the Apostle. Otherwise he ought not to have said below: "But if anyone says to you, 'This has been sacrificed to idols,' do not eat, for the sake of him who pointed it out." He should have said simply, "for the sake of your conscience, that you do not knowingly eat sacrificed meats." Nor would this sense have served well those scrupulous people who judged themselves guilty of sin if they had tasted sacrificed meats in any way.

units.la: DOMINI siquidem est terra & plenitudo eius.) Ex sacris scripturis, psalmo videlicet 24, confirmat suā doctrinā, qua dixit: Omne quod in macello venditur, edite, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam, quibus verbis significat nullo ciborum genere pollui conscientias fidelium, nec par esse, vt vllas nobis escas per se illicitas esse iudicemus. Quare? Quia domini est terra, inquit, & plenitudo eius. Mira videtur esse conscientia. Domini est terra & plenitudo eius, ergo licet vesci quibuslibet. Videamus igitur quale sit hoc argumentum. Eget enim explicatione propter rudiores. Quæ domini sunt munda sunt in se omnia, præsertim cum ab illo sint condita. Nihil enim fecit, quod sit immundum. Vidit cuncta quæ fecerat, & erant valde bona, Gen. 1. Domini autem est non modo terra hæc, sed & plenitudo eius, id est, omnis illa rerum omnium, frugum, fructuum & animalium copia, qua passim impleta est terra, vnde sumuntur à Gentibus, quæ eidolis immolantur. Ergo mundæ sunt escæ omnes, adeoq; per se haudquaquam illicitæ.
units.tr: "For the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof." He confirms his teaching from Scripture, namely Psalm 24, in which he said, "Eat whatever is sold in the market, asking no questions for conscience' sake." By these words he signifies that the consciences of the faithful are defiled by no kind of food, and that it is not right for us to judge any food unlawful in itself. Why? "Because the earth is the Lord's," he says, "and the fullness thereof." The argument seems remarkable: "The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof; therefore it is lawful to eat whatever we like." Let us consider, then, what sort of argument this is, for it needs explanation for the less learned. Things that belong to the Lord are in themselves all clean, especially since they were created by him. For he made nothing that is unclean. "He saw everything that he had made, and it was very good," Gen. 1. But the earth is the Lord's, and not only this earth, but also its fullness, that is, all that abundance of all things, of crops, fruits and animals, with which the earth is everywhere filled, from which the Gentiles take what they sacrifice to idols. Therefore all foods are clean, and so by nature in no way unlawful.

units.la: Quare non est, vt propter conscientiam abstineatis ab vlla esca, quasi sit impura, nec opus est vt interrogetis, immolaticia ne sit vel secus. Quòd enim eidolis immolata est à Gentibus, puritatem creationis non abstulit, quemadmodum nec essentiam illius, nec naturæ vires ademit, quo minus sit quæ creata est à Deo, & uires pascendi corporis à Deo acceptas per inde habeat, ac si nulli sit eidolo immolata. Quod autem mundum est, per se non polluit edentem. Munda est omnis creatura Dei. Ergo nulla creatura Dei polluit edentem. Sic 1. Tim. 4. Omnis creatura Dei bona est inquit, & nihil reijciendum quod cum gratiarū actione sumitur. Si qua creatura Dei impura est, nō est impura nisi impuris & infidelibus quorum inquinata est & mens & conscientia, mūdis ue ro nihil est immundū, sed munda omnia. Tit 1.
units.tr: Therefore there is no reason why you should abstain from any food on account of conscience, as if it were impure, nor is there any need to ask whether it is sacrificed or not. For the fact that it was sacrificed to idols by the Gentiles has not taken away its purity from creation, any more than it has taken away its essence or the powers of its nature, so that it is less what God created, or less the power to nourish the body that it has received from God, than if it had never been sacrificed to any idol. And what is clean in itself does not defile the one who eats it. Every creature of God is clean. Therefore no creature of God defiles the one who eats it. So 1 Tim. 4: "Every creature of God is good," he says, "and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving." If any creature of God is impure, it is impure only to the impure and unbelieving, whose mind and conscience are polluted; but to the clean nothing is unclean, but all things are clean, Titus 1.

units.la: Deinde potest & hic esse praesentis argumenti sensus. Quae domini sunt licite comeduntur à populo domini, qui estis vos, domini sunt autem quae in terra sunt omnia, etiam quae daemonijs immolantur à gentibus. Neque enim immolado in ius daemoniorum transeunt, sed in potestate & iure Dei permanent, unde nec à gentibus nec à daemonijs eximi possunt. Ergo licita sunt vobis ad cibum omnia, etiam immolaticia. Quare non est, ut haesitetis aut interrogetis, &c. Utroque sensu firmum est hoc argumentum. Domini est terra & plenitudo eius, ergo quicquid in macello venditur, edite. Sunt enim vobis munda & licita quae domini sunt omnia.
units.tr: Then, the sense of the present argument can also be this: what belongs to the Lord is lawfully eaten by the people of the Lord, who are you; and all things that are on the earth belong to the Lord, even those that the Gentiles sacrifice to demons. For things offered in sacrifice do not pass into the right of the demons, but remain in the power and right of God, whence they cannot be exempted either by the Gentiles or by the demons. Therefore all things, even sacrificed meats, are lawful for you to eat. Therefore there is no reason for you to hesitate or ask, etc. This argument is sound in either sense: "The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof; therefore eat whatever is sold in the market." For all things that belong to the Lord are clean and lawful for you.

units.la: Sed dicit quisquâ, An non sub Mose quoq; domini erat terra & plenitudo eius? An nõ tempore legis dictum est à Dauide? An non erat Iudaei populus domini? Utique ergo tum quoque erant munda omnia, & ad vescendum licita? Quid igitur impediuit, quo minus Iudaei licuerit vesci suilla, & nonnullis alijs esceis? à quibus tanquam immundis hodie quoque abstinent. Respondeo. Tum quoque nihil immundum erat per se, quod creatum esset à Deo, & erant Iudaei populus domini, verum quo minus licerent illis omnia, in causa erat non creaturae impuritas, quae nulla est, sed authoritas Dei quaedam paedagogiae gratia ei populo ad tempus uetantis; quae inhibitio ad Christum usque, & non ultra durare debebat. Propter hanc inhibitionem Dei fiebat, ut non esset Iudaeis licita omnia. Quod autem consimilem authoritatem & potestatem uetandi cibos in ecclesia Dei uendicauit sibi Romanae sedis temeritas, ex daemonibus est & spiritibus erroarum: unde non potest infringi quod hic Apostolus dicit: Omne quod in macello venditur edite, &c. Quam facile dicunt satellites filij perditionis: Domini quidem est terra & plenitudo eius, verum Rom. pontifex plenitudinem potestatis in omnia, tanquam vicarius Christi, habens, authoritate sua quaedam potest reddere illicita, quae in se non sunt immunda, ut non mox liceat iam edere quicquid in macello venditur, nisi ex ipsius indultu, imo non liceat quiduis in macello vedere, &c. quam facile inquam haec dicunt, tam facile nobis est agnoscere doctrinam daemoniorum, eamq; virtute uerbi Dei refellere & contemnere.
units.tr: But someone will say: Was not the earth and its fullness also the Lord's under Moses? Was this not said in the time of the law by David? Was not the people of the Jews the Lord's people? Therefore were not all things then also clean and lawful to eat? What then prevented the Jews from being permitted to eat pork and several other foods, from which, as unclean, they abstain even today? I answer: then too nothing created by God was unclean in itself, and the Jews were the Lord's people; but what prevented them from having everything permitted was not any impurity in the creature, for there is none, but a certain authority of God, which for a time forbade that people, by way of a schoolmaster's discipline. This prohibition was to last until Christ and no longer. Because of this prohibition of God it happened that not all things were lawful for the Jews. But as for the Roman see's rash claim to the same kind of authority and power to forbid foods in the Church of God, it comes from demons and spirits of error; therefore what the Apostle says here cannot be overturned: "Eat whatever is sold in the market," etc. How readily the henchmen of the son of perdition say: "Indeed the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof, but the Roman pontiff, having the fullness of power over all things, as the vicar of Christ, can by his authority make unlawful certain things that are not unclean in themselves, so that it is no longer permitted to eat at once whatever is sold in the market, except by his own indulgence; indeed it is not permitted to eat anything at all sold in the market," etc. As readily as they say these things, I say, so readily do we recognise this doctrine of demons, and refute and despise it by the power of the Word of God.

units.la: QVOD si quis vocat vos infidelium, & vult ire, &c.) Loquitur de conuiuijs non sacris & publicis quae in templis & delubris eidolorum fiebant, sed priuatis & prophanis. Quoniam subinde accidebat, ut Christiani ad eiusmodi infidelium conuiuia vocarentur, consequenter docet, quomodo se in hac causa gerere debeant. Alij iudicabant ne eundem quidem esse ad infidelium conuiuia, & euntes damnabant. Alij euntes curiosius ac superstitiosius immolaticia uitabant, alij illa edebant, etiam moniti, quod essent immolaticia, nullam habentes rationem unà comedentium, infidelium, Iudaeorum, & fidelium. Docet igitur uniuersos quo modo se hic gerant.
units.tr: "If any of those that believe not bid you to a feast, and you are disposed to go," etc. He is speaking of private and profane banquets, not the sacred and public feasts held in the temples and shrines of idols. Since it sometimes happened that Christians were invited to such banquets of unbelievers, he consequently teaches how they ought to conduct themselves in this matter. Some judged that one must not go to the banquets of unbelievers at all, and condemned those who went. Others, when they went, avoided meat offered to idols too scrupulously and superstitiously. Others ate it, even when warned that it had been offered to idols, having no regard for those eating alongside them, whether unbelievers, Jews, or believers. He therefore teaches all how they should behave here.

units.la: Quod si quis infidelium vos vocat inquit. Verbo vocandi separat eos qui ultro sese infidelium conuiuijs uel mensariae uoluptatis, uel celandae fidei suae gratia insinuabant, quibus correptio magis quam instructionis doctrina competebat.
units.tr: "If any of the unbelievers," he says, "invites you." By the word "invites" he distinguishes those who of their own accord pushed themselves into the feasts of unbelievers, either for the sake of pleasure at the table or to conceal their faith. For such people correction, rather than the teaching of instruction, was fitting.

units.la: Et vultis ire, inquit. Neque dicit, ite, neque, ne eatis, sed liberum permittit, ut eant, uel ne eant. Pro varietate circumstantiarum fieri poterat, ut irent cum fructu, rursus, ut satius esset non ire. Nihil igitur certi praescribit, sed quicquid hoc est totum uniuscuiusque permittit iudicio & arbitrio. Debebat aut praescribere, si non liceret Christiano conuiuari cum infidelibus & eidololatris. Hoc itaque pacto tollit eā scrupulositatem, qua nonnulli sentiebant nihil esse commercij ineundum cum infidelibus, ne in prophanis quidem & ciuilibus negocijs.
units.tr: "And if you are willing to go," he says. He does not say "go," nor "do not go," but leaves it free for them to go or not to go. Depending on the variety of circumstances, it could happen that going would be beneficial, and again that it would be better not to go. He therefore prescribes nothing definite, but leaves the whole matter to the judgment and discretion of each person. He would have had to prescribe something if it were not lawful for a Christian to dine with unbelievers and idolaters. In this way he removes that scruple by which some thought that no dealings whatever were to be entered into with unbelievers, not even in profane and civil affairs.

units.la: QVICQVID apponitur vobis edite, inqt.) Non impliciter dicit: ite & edite cum illo, sed ut omnem haesitationem & scrupulositatem eorum auferat, qui propter infirmitatem fidei haesitanter appositis vescebantur, metuentes ne escis infidelium inquinarentur, uniuersaliter loquitur dicens: Quicquid apponitur vobis edite. Quasi dicat, Indubitato credite nihil per se esse immundū, quale quale sit quicquid vobis apponitur, etiamsi sit immolatum eidolis, atque ita secura conscientia edite ex omnibus. Si haec doctrina mansisset in ecclesia, non videremus hodie in eadem mensa alios poscere carnes, alios pisces, idq; religionis uel potius superstitionis gratia. Apostolus dicit: Si quis infidelium uos uocat quicquid apponitur vobis edite. Qui successores apostolorum uideri uolut, in id seruitutis & superstitionis ecclesiam coniecerunt, ut in mensa Christiani non liceat Christiano uesci quibuslibet appositis. Recentes, teneros, ac rudes adhuc Christianos sic omnibus indiscriminatim vesci voluit Apostolus, ut ne ab ijs quidem propter conscientiam abstinerent, quae daemonijs essent ab infidelibus immolata, & ecclesia iam post aliquot saecula satis adulta, sic est incantationibus & mandatis pseudapostolorum dementata, ut putet sibi nō licere etiam ea quae nulla sunt eidololatria contaminata, existimetq; Deo se apprime gratificari, si certis diebus secundum doctrinam erroris & daemoniorum à quauis carne, caseo, ouis, & butyro abstineat.
units.tr: "Eat whatever is set before you," he says. He does not simply say, "Go and eat with him," but, in order to remove all hesitation and scruple from those who, because of the weakness of their faith, ate what was set before them with hesitation, fearing that they would be defiled by the food of unbelievers, he speaks in general terms: "Eat whatever is set before you." As if he said: Believe without doubt that nothing is unclean in itself, whatever sort of thing is set before you, even if it has been offered to idols; and so eat everything with a secure conscience. If this teaching had remained in the Church, we would not today see at the same table some asking for meat, others for fish, and that for the sake of religion, or rather superstition. The Apostle says: "If any of the unbelievers invites you, eat whatever is set before you." Those who wish to be regarded as the successors of the apostles have brought the Church into such slavery and superstition that a Christian at a Christian's table may not eat whatever is set before him. The Apostle wished the recent, tender, and still untaught Christians to eat indiscriminately of everything in such a way that they did not even abstain from those things which had been sacrificed by unbelievers to demons, on account of conscience. Yet the Church, now after several centuries grown quite mature, has been so bewitched by the incantations and commands of false apostles that it thinks it is not permitted to eat even things that are not in any way polluted by idolatry, and it believes it pleases God greatly if, on certain days, according to the doctrine of error and of demons, it abstains from every kind of meat, cheese, egg, and butter.

units.la: q
units.tr: q

units.la: Illud, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam, plane eodem sensu positum est quo particula praecedenti de ijs quae in macello uenduntur. Quemadmodum illicita hic quoque docet, absq; vlla conscientia peccati libere & secure quibuslibet esse appositis in ethnicorum quoq; conuiuijs vescendum, perinde atq; illis quae in macello uenduntur. Quicquid apponitur vobis edite, inquit, absque vlla peccati conscientia, nec conscientiae vestrae gratia quale sit, immolaticiu ne vel secus inquirite. Non prohibet quauis de causa interrogare de escis, prohibet vero ne propter conscientias suas interrogent, quasi peccaturi sint, & conscientias suas maculaturi si imprudenter de immolaticijs edant.
units.tr: The phrase "asking nothing for the sake of conscience" is clearly used in the same sense as the preceding clause about things sold in the meat market. Just as there he teaches that unlawful things are to be eaten freely and securely, with no consciousness of sin, so here too he teaches that whatever is set before you at the banquets of the Gentiles is to be eaten, just as those things sold in the market. "Eat whatever is set before you," he says, with no consciousness of sin, and do not inquire, for the sake of your conscience, what sort of thing it is, whether it was offered to idols or not. He does not forbid asking about foods for any reason at all; he forbids asking for the sake of their consciences, as if they would sin and stain their consciences if they unwittingly ate what had been offered to idols.

units.la: Sed dices. Ergo ne nulla fideli homini habenda est conscientiae ratio? Quid si quis adeo sit fide infirmus, vt citra conscientiam peccati nequeat vesci quibuslibet? Conuenit ne, vt propter dictum hoc Apostoli, quicquid apponitur vobis edite, contra conscientiam suam edat, quod illicitum esse sibi putat? Respondeo: Non hoc requirit Apostolus, vt contra conscien tiam suam quisquam edat quod edendum esse non putat, sed docet, nihil esse immundum ex omnibus escis, ideoq; liberè citra peccati conscientiam vescendum esse quibuslibet. Interea nonvrget infirmos, vt in conscientias suas peccent, donec sunt infirmi, sed proponit illis sanam doctrinam vt intelligant se frustra peccati conscientia teneri, vbi nihil est peccati, atq; ita ex infirmis firmi reddantur. Rom.14. dicit. Scio & persuasum habeo per dominum Iesum nihil esse commune, id est, immundum, per se, nisi ei qui existimat aliquid esse commune, illi commune est. Si taliter animato immundum est, quod putat esse immundum, ergo non conuenit ut conscientiam suam immunda edendo polluat. Quare non sunt eiusmodi infirmi & scrupulosi homines vrgendi nec fallendi etiam vt edant quod edendum non esse putant sed verbo domini, praesertim a pastoribus, sanandi, & ab ea scrupulositate liberandi, quare Timotheum suum monet Apostolus. 1. Timoth. 4.
units.tr: But you will say: "Then should no account at all be taken of the conscience of a believer? What if someone is so weak in faith that he cannot eat anything without a consciousness of sin? Is it fitting that, on account of this saying of the Apostle, 'Eat whatever is set before you,' he should eat against his own conscience what he thinks is unlawful for him?" I answer: The Apostle does not require that anyone eat against his own conscience what he does not think should be eaten; rather he teaches that nothing among all foods is unclean, and therefore that one may eat freely of anything without a consciousness of sin. Meanwhile he does not press the weak to sin against their consciences while they remain weak, but he sets before them sound teaching, so that they may understand that they are held by a consciousness of sin in vain where there is no sin; and so the weak may become strong. In Romans 14 he says: "I know, and am persuaded through the Lord Jesus, that nothing is common, that is, unclean, in itself; but to him who thinks anything to be common, it is common." If something is unclean for someone who thinks it unclean, then it is not fitting that he should defile his conscience by eating what he thinks unclean. Therefore such weak and scrupulous people are not to be pressed or deceived into eating what they think ought not to be eaten; rather they are to be healed and freed from that scrupulosity by the Word of the Lord, especially by the ministers, which is why the Apostle admonishes his Timothy (1 Tim. 4.).

units.la: QVOD si quis vobis dixerit, hoc simulacris immolatum est. ) Poterant dicere, mones ut edamus de omni quod vel in macello uéditur, vel in coùiuijs infidelium apponitur, nec quicquam interrogemus, quid si etiam non interrogantibus ultro dicat aliquis, immolaticium esse quod uenditur aut apponitur? An tum quoque edemus? Respondet igitur & docet quid hic fit faciendum. Quod si quis vobis dixerit, inquit, hoc simulacris immolatum est, ne edatis. Timendum erat ne ex praemissis colligeret: Si propterea quod domini est terra & plenitudo eius vescendum est quibuslibet, etiam immolaticijs, nec quicquam interrogandum, ergo etiamsi moneat quisquam, immolatum esse simulacris quod proponitur, edendum est. Etenim si ipsa, immolatio non reddit escam
units.tr: "But if anyone should say to you, 'This has been offered to idols,'" etc. They could have said: You advise us to eat of everything that is sold in the market or set before us at the banquets of unbelievers, and we ask nothing; but what if someone, even without our asking, volunteers that what is sold or set before us has been offered to idols? Shall we eat then too? The Apostle therefore answers and teaches what must be done here. "But if," he says, "someone says to you, 'This has been offered to idols,' do not eat." He had to fear lest someone should infer from what has gone before: since the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof, it may be eaten by anyone, even things offered to idols, and one should ask nothing; therefore, even if someone warns that what is set before you has been offered to idols, it must still be eaten. For if the offering itself does not make the food

units.la: impuram, multo minus ille qui indicat eam esse immolaticiam. Cum autem non sit impura, quid impedit, quo minus licitè edatur? Et reuera sic habet. Per se non est illicitum etiā scienter uesci immolaticijs, verum aliunde reddit illicitum, quia noxium. Sic dicit ne edatis, & addit rationem.
units.tr: impure, much less does the one who points out that it has been offered to idols. But since it is not impure, what prevents it from being eaten lawfully? And indeed it is so. Eating things offered to idols, even knowingly, is not in itself unlawful; but it is made unlawful by something else, because it is harmful. Thus he says, "do not eat," and adds the reason.

units.la: Propter illum, inquit, qui indicauit, & propter conscientiam. Nō dicit, ne polluaris, quia immundum est, propter immundiciam immolationis, sed, propter illum qui indicauit hoc est, ne uel offendas eum qui indicauit si sit frater infirmus, vel in errore exemplo tuo confirmes si sit infidelis. Etenim frater qui dicit, hoc simulacris immolatum est, cautionis hoc gratia dicit, ne de immolaticio edatur, putans id sine peccato fieri non posse, quare & scienter edentem iudicat & condemnat. Sic autem offendere fratrem infirmum, cum lege charitatis pugnat. Infidelis si dicit simulacris hoc immolatum est, uel tentat fidelem quid sit facturus, uel allicit, ut religiosius edat ex eo quod sacrū esse intelligit. Hic si ederit Christianus quiliud facit, quam quod errantem in errore confirmat, à quo illum potius exemplo suo auocare, uel saltem haesitabundum ac dubium reddere debebat.
units.tr: "For the sake of him," he says, "who pointed it out, and for the sake of conscience." He does not say, "lest you be defiled, because it is unclean on account of the uncleanness of the offering," but "for the sake of him who pointed it out," that is, lest you offend him who pointed it out, if he is a weak brother, or confirm him in error by your example, if he is an unbeliever. For a brother who says, "This has been offered to idols," says it as a caution, so that nothing may be eaten from what was offered to idols, thinking that this cannot be done without sin; and so he judges and condemns the one who eats knowingly. But to offend a weak brother in this way clashes with the law of love. If an unbeliever says, "This has been offered to idols," he either tests the believer to see what he will do, or he entices him to eat more scrupulously, as though it were something he understood to be holy. If a Christian eats here, what else does he do than confirm in his error the one who is in error? From whom he ought rather to have turned him away by his example, or at least made him hesitant and doubtful.

units.la: Illud, & propter conscientiam, non est referendum ad edentis sed ad indicantis conscientiam, sicut mox patebit. Apparet autem sic esse particulam hac adiectam, ut exponatur quod dixit: ne edatis propter illum qui indicauit, sit que sensus, ne edatis propter illum qui indicauit, ne uidelicet conscientia illius uel obfirmetur in errore, uel sine causa offendatur.
units.tr: The phrase "and for the sake of conscience" is not to be referred to the conscience of the one eating, but to the conscience of the one who points it out, as will soon become clear. It appears that this clause is added so as to explain what he said: "do not eat for the sake of him who pointed it out." The meaning is: do not eat for the sake of him who pointed it out, namely lest his conscience either be hardened in error or be offended without cause.

units.la: DOMINI siquidem est terra, inquit, & plenitudo eius.) De sententiae huius repetitione aliter atq; aliter sentitur. Existimant eam alij aliunde esse assutam, alij non suo loco positam, alij nec aliunde assutā, nec loco alieno sed suo posìtam. De repetitione illius nolim contendere, quamuis in uulgata uersione non repetatur neque ab Ambrosio, si non fallit illius aeditio, anno 1516. Basileae facta. Repetit eam, idq; hoc loco, Chrysostomo. & imitator illius Theophylactus. Apparet tamen eos non falli, qui existimant positam esse non suo loco. Meo iudicio sic est hic contextus legendus. Quod si quis in fidelium uos uocat, & uultis ire, quicquid apponitur uobis, edite, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam. Domini siquidem est terra & plenitudo eius. Quod si quis vobis dixerit, hoc simulacris immolatū est, ne edatis pro pter illum qui indicauit, & propter conscientiam. Conscientiam autem dico, non tuam, sed eam quae est alterius. Sic legentes, non laborabimus quomodo eandem scientiam diuersimodè positam competenter & sic exponamus ut supra confirmet affirmatiuam, edite, & hic negatiuam, ne edatis. Suspicor autem particulam illam, propter conscientiam, quae tertio repetitur, causam dedisse lapsui, non Apostolo sed aetiquarijs. Existimo illū eadem hac sententia
units.tr: "For the earth is the Lord's," he says, "and the fullness thereof." This sentence is understood in different ways as to its repetition. Some think it has been stitched in from elsewhere, others that it is not in its proper place, and others that it is neither inserted from elsewhere nor out of place but stands in its own position. I would not contend about its repetition, although it is not repeated in the Vulgate version, nor in Ambrose, if I am not mistaken about his edition made at Basel in 1516. Chrysostom repeats it, and in this place, and his imitator Theophylact too. Yet it appears that those are not wrong who think it stands out of its proper place. In my judgement the context should be read thus: "If anyone of the faithful invites you, and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking nothing for conscience' sake. For the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof. But if anyone says to you, 'This has been offered to idols,' do not eat, for the sake of him who informed you and for conscience' sake. I say conscience, not yours, but that of the other." Reading in this way, we shall not labour over how the same thought is placed in differing ways, and we shall explain it so that the affirmative "eat" above is confirmed, and the negative "do not eat" here. I suspect, however, that the phrase "for conscience' sake," which is repeated a third time, has given occasion for the slip, not to the Apostle but to the copyists. I think he wished to prove both points by this same sentence: that whatever is sold in the meat market, and whatever is set before one at the feasts of unbelievers, may be eaten with a secure conscience.

units.la: tentia {A}sentia vtrunq; probare voluisse,cū quod quic quid in macello venditur, tum quod quicquid in conuiuijs infidelium apponitur,securā conscientia edendum esse dixit. Qui referunt hanc sententiam ad id quod Apostolus dixit, ne edatis propter illum qui indicauit & propter cōscientiam, quasi hoc propterea fieri voluerit, quod domini sit terra & plenitudo eius, expo nendo laborant. Alius sic. Quemadmodum domini sunt escæ quæ eduntur, ita illius sunt etiam homines, ideoq; cauendū est, ne qsquá ex illis nostra libertate perdatur. Alius ad hūc modum. Ne edatis. Quare? quia domini est terra & plenitudo eius qui vos abundè potest alere, etiamsi ab immolaticijs abstinentes spreti ab infidelibus & eiecti fueritis. Verùm sentiat quisq; quod probabilibus esse putauerit.
units.tr: Those who refer this sentence to what the Apostle said, "do not eat for the sake of him who informed you and for conscience' sake," labour in explaining it, as if he wished this to happen because "the earth is the Lord's and its fullness." Another reads it thus: just as the foods that are eaten belong to the Lord, so too do human beings belong to him; therefore one must take care that none of them be lost to us through our liberty. Another in this manner: "Do not eat. Why? Because the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord, who is able to feed you abundantly, even if you abstain from things offered to idols and are despised and cast out by unbelievers." But let each one think what he judges to be more probable.

units.la: CONSCIENTIAM autē dico non tuam sed eam quæ est alterius.) Particulam hanc declarationis gratia adiecit. Quia dixit: ne edatis propter eum qui indicauit, & propter conscientiam, ne id de conscientia Christiani de omnibus appositis indiscriminatim edétis intelligeretur, quasi propter suam ipsius ille conscientia ab immolatis abstineret deberet, vbi quod simulacris immolata essent audisset, qui sens cum præcedentibus haud conueniret, declarationem hanc subijcit dicens: Conscientiam autem dico non tuam, sed eam quæ est alterius. Quasi dicat. Quod veto ne edas ex eo quod immolaticium esse indicatur, propter eum qui in dicauit & propter conscientiam, non ideo veto, quod tuam ex eo conscientiam pollui sentiam, sed quod parcendum sit conscientiæ eiꝰ qui quod immolaticium sit indicauit, ne vel offendatur tua libertate, si sit frater infirmus aut Iudæus, vel in errore eidololatriæ obsirmetur, si sit ethnicus infidelis.
units.tr: "But I say conscience, not your own, but that of the other." He added this phrase by way of explanation. Because he had said, "do not eat for the sake of him who informed you, and for conscience' sake," lest this be understood of the conscience of the Christian, as though he were to abstain from all things set before him without distinction, on his own conscience, because he had heard that they had been offered to idols, which sense does not agree with what goes before, he adds this explanation, saying: "But I say conscience, not your own, but that of the other." As if he were saying: "What I forbid you to eat, because it is indicated to be offered to idols, I forbid for the sake of him who informed you and for conscience' sake; not that I forbid it because I perceive your conscience defiled by it, but because the conscience of him who indicated that it was offered to idols must be spared, lest it be offended by your liberty, if he is a weak brother or a Jew, or be confirmed in the error of idolatry, if he is a heathen unbeliever."

units.la: Nos cogitemus hic, quà conueniat nos habere curam & rationem conscientiarum in ecclesia fidelium: primùm suæipsius quisq;, ne illam polluat, deinde & fratrum præsertim infirmorum, ne illos scandali obiectu vel offendat, vel ad ruinam solicitat, cum Apostolus tam diligenter moneat, ne Christianus libertate sua hominis ethnici & infidelis conscientiam quā tum in ipso est, perdat.
units.tr: Let us consider here how fitting it is that we should have care and regard for consciences in the Church of the faithful: first, each one for his own, that he not defile it; then also, and especially, for weak brethren, that he not offend them by putting a stumbling block before them, nor urge them to their ruin, since the Apostle so diligently warns that a Christian, by his liberty, should not destroy the conscience of a heathen or unbelieving man, so far as lies in him.

units.la: CVR enim libertas mea iudicatur ab alia cō scientia? Quod si ego cū gratia participo, &c.) Et ita aliter atq; aliter exponuntur.
units.tr: For why is my liberty judged by another conscience? "But if I partake with thanksgiving, etc." These words are explained in various ways.

units.la: 1 Existimant nonnulli obiectionem esse Corinthiorū, temerè & passim immolaticijs vescentium, qua factum suum prætextu libertatis contra doctrinam hanc Apostoli fuerint de sensuri, dicturiq;: Cur mea libertas iudicio alienæ conscientiæ subijcitur? Æquum ne est vt de eo quod ego pro mea lihertate & secura conscientia facio iudicet aliena conscientia? Ego cum gratia participo de mēsa eius q me uocauit, proq̈ue hac illius beneficentia gratias ago, æquum ne est. vt ob id mihi maledicatur, siue ab eo qui indicauit, siue ab ipso conuiatore? Et huic sententiæ putant conuenire se-
units.tr: 1 Some think that this is an objection of the Corinthians, who, rashly and everywhere, ate things offered to idols, and who, under the pretext of liberty, would speak against this teaching of the Apostle, saying: "Why is my liberty subjected to the judgement of another's conscience? Is it fair that another's conscience should judge what I do with my liberty and secure conscience? I partake with thanksgiving of the table of him who has invited me, and I give thanks for his kindness: is it fair that for this I should be cursed, whether by him who informed me or by the host himself?" And they think that the following words agree with this sense, as though added in the place of a reply, in this manner:

units.la: {B}quætia tanq̈ respósionis loco subiecta, ad hunc modum. Siue editis, siue bibitis, siue quid faciatis, omnia in gloriam Dei facite. Tales estote, vt nullum præbeatis offendiculū, &c. Quasi dicat: Non est vt omnia ad vestram libertatem metiamini. Habēda uobis est ratio gloriæ Dei. Hoc facientes, nemini scienter uoletis esse offendiculo, neq; Iudæo, neq; ethnico, neq; ecclæ siç Dei. Posset hic sensus probari, si sic legeretur. Cur libertas mea iudicatur ab alia conscientia, &c. Itē, siue editis siue bibitis, &c. Iam cum dicat, Cur enim libertas mea. Et, Siue igitur editis, &c. Impeditur hæc expositio duabus istis voculis, ENIM, & IGITVR, nisi dicturi sumus esse illas o ciosè adiectas.
units.tr: "Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. Be such that you give no offence, etc." As if he were saying: "It is not for you to measure everything by your liberty. You must have regard for the glory of God. In doing this, you will knowingly be willing to be an offence to no one, neither to the Jew, nor to the heathen, nor to the Church of God." This sense could be proved if it were read thus: "Why is my liberty judged by another conscience, etc." Likewise, "Whether therefore you eat or drink, etc." Since he says, "For why is my liberty," and, "Whether therefore you eat, etc.," this explanation is hindered by the two little words, FOR and THEREFORE, unless we are to say that these were added idly.

units.la: 2 Sūt qui referàt ista ad ea de quibus supra di xit: quicquid apponitur vobis edite, nihil inter rogantes propter conscientiā, quasi dicat quisquá, at hoc faciens fidelis iudicabitur ab aliis, quantumuis ipse secura conscientia comedat, & respondeat Apost. Cur libertas mea, qua liberè & cum gratiarum actione quicquid appositum fuerit comedo, ab alia coscientia iudicatur? Quid ad me, quod alij ob id mihi maledicunt, pro quo ego gratias ago?
units.tr: 2 There are those who refer these words to what he said above: "whatever is set before you, eat, asking nothing for conscience' sake," as if someone might say: "A faithful man who does this will be judged by others, however securely his own conscience eats." And the Apostle would answer: "Why is my liberty, by which I freely eat, with thanksgiving, whatever is set before me, judged by another conscience? What is it to me that others on that account curse me, for which I give thanks?"

units.la: 3 Alij referunt ad proximè præcedens, tanq̈ illi rationis vice subiecta ad hunc modum. Ne edatis propter illum qui indicauit, & propter conscientiam. Conscientiam autem dico non tuam sed eam quæ est alterius. Etenim quorsum attinet libertaiem nostrā alienæ conscientiæ iudicio reddere obnoxiam, & causam præbere, vt maledicatur nobis propter escam, pro qua nos gratias agimus? Et hæc mihi expositio magis probatur. Loquitur autem in sua ipsius persona. Quasi dicat, Etenim non video quare sic vti conueniat mea libertate, vt aliorum conscientiam offendam, efficiamq; vt iudicer, & blasphemijs impetar propter id, de quo cum gratia participo, & pro quo gratias ago. Transfert hæc in se, vt acceptabiliorem & probabiliorem reddat disti sui rationem. Si gnificat se non sic esse animatum, vt propter escam cuiuspiam velit conscientiam sua libertate offendere, & admittere, vt eam ob causam iudicetur, & maledictis exponatur. Qui temere immolaticijs vescebantur, & aliorum cōtra se iudicia & maledicta prouocabant, libertatē suam vbiq; iactabant, parum curantes, ædificarent ne vel destruerent aliorum conscientias, bene vel malè audirent. Vt hos perstringeret, dicendum erat: Conscientiam dico non tuam, sed eius quę est alterius, cuius habenda est ratio ne lædatur. Cur enim admittis unde libertas illa tua, qua abuteris, ab eius conscientia, quam offendis iudicetur & damnetur. & non magis vnde ędificetur? Participas de libertatis acceptæ gratia, & comedis cum gratiarum actione, cur hoc sic facis, vt pro eo tibi maledicatur, pro quo tu gratias agis? Iactas libertatē quidlibet edendi. At eo constat tibi ex gratia Dei, gratias agis Deo vbi comedis, atq; ita testaris, ex beneficio Dei esse, quæ comedis. Cur ergo gratiam hanc & libertatem aliorum redis iudicijs & blasphemijs citra necessitatem obnoxiam. Sic inq; dicendum erat, verù, vt dixi, mitigat hanc reprehensionem, quo fit acceptabilior, per id, quod hæc verba transfert in suam ipsius personam. Qua in re minister verbi rursus prudentiam obseruet Apostoli. Hac vt supra cap. 6. vsus est, vbi cum dicendum esset, Quare membra Christi facitis membra scorti? mutata sermonis figura dixit: Numtollens membra Christi faciam membra scorti?
units.tr: 3 Others refer it to what immediately precedes, as if it were added in the place of a reason, in this way: "Do not eat for the sake of him who informed you, and for conscience' sake. I say conscience, not yours, but that of the other. For what is the point of making our liberty liable to the judgement of another's conscience, and of giving occasion for us to be cursed on account of food for which we give thanks?" And this explanation seems to me more probable. He speaks in his own person. As if he were saying: "For I do not see why it is fitting to use my liberty in such a way that I offend the conscience of others, and bring it about that I am judged and assailed with reproaches on account of that for which I partake with thanksgiving and for which I give thanks. He transfers this to himself, so as to make his teaching more acceptable and more persuasive. He signifies that he is not so disposed as to wish, for the sake of anyone's food, to offend a conscience by his liberty, and to permit it, so that for that cause he should be judged and exposed to reproaches. Those who rashly ate things offered to idols, and provoked the judgements and reproaches of others against themselves, everywhere boasting of their liberty, caring little whether they built up or destroyed the consciences of others, and whether they were spoken of well or ill, were to be rebuked. To rebuke these, it had to be said: 'I say conscience, not yours, but that of him who is another's, whose conscience is to be regarded so that it is not harmed.' For why do you allow your liberty, which you abuse, to be judged and condemned by his conscience, which you offend, and not rather by which he is built up? You partake of the grace of liberty received, and you eat with thanksgiving; why do you do this so that you are cursed for that for which you give thanks? You boast of the liberty to eat anything. But since you are aware that it comes from the grace of God, you give thanks to God when you eat, and so you bear witness that what you eat is from God's kindness. Why then do you expose this grace and the liberty of others, without necessity, to judgements and blasphemies?" Thus, I say, it ought to have been put; but, as I said, he softens this rebuke, so that it becomes more acceptable, by the fact that these words transfer it to his own person. In this matter the minister of the Word should again observe the prudence of the Apostle, as he used above in chapter 6, where, when it had to be said, "Why do you make the members of Christ the members of a harlot?" he changed the form of speech and said: "Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them the members of a harlot?"

units.la: Admonet hic locus q; cauere debeat Christianus, ne quæ facit aliorum reddat probris & blasphemijs obnoxia, quatenus in ipso est, sed magis sic se gerat, vt occasione laudis ac beneplaciti offerat alijs, intellige, in reb. liberis, vbi non quid liceat sed quid conducat spectari debet.
units.tr: This passage also warns the Christian to take care that what he does does not, so far as it depends on him, expose him to the reproaches and slander of others. Instead he should so conduct himself that he gives others an occasion of praise and goodwill. This applies to matters that are free, where one must consider not what is permitted but what is expedient.

units.la: Si propter fidem nostram odio habemur & probris proscindimur, ferendum est, & domino comittendum, non cedendum & impijs gratificandum, secus vero, ubi rebus liberis & indifferentibus pro utilitate aliorum ex spiritu veræ charitatis laudabiliter uti poterimus. Non dicit hic Apostolus: Cur fides & religio mea, sed, cur libertas mea iudicatur ab alia conscientia? Magnum discrimen est inter fidem qua Deo obstringimur, & libertatem rerum indifferentium qua per gratiam illius in hoc mundo inter homines versamur. Illic in nullius hominis gratiam à verbo Dei cedendum est, hic vero per charitatem seruiendum est omnibus.
units.tr: If we are hated and abused for our faith, we must bear it and commit the matter to the Lord, and not give way to the ungodly or try to please them. It is otherwise in matters that are free and indifferent, where for the good of others, from the Spirit of true love, we may use them commendably. The Apostle does not say, "Why is my faith or my religion judged?" but, "Why is my liberty judged by another's conscience?" There is a great difference between the faith by which we are bound to God and the liberty in indifferent things by which, through his grace, we live among men in this world. In the former we must yield to no man's favour against the Word of God; in the latter we must serve all men through love.

units.la: Deinde obserua q; religiose & absq; omni temeritate vti debeamus beneficijs Dei, de quibus per gratiam illius participamus, & pro quibus illi gratias agimus. Non simpliciter dicit: Cur ob id mihi maledicitur, quod de creaturis Dei participo & comedo? sed: Si vero ego cum gratia participo, cur sic participabo, vt ob id mihi maledicatur pro quo ego gratias ago? Sic notat eorum temeritatem, qui beneficijs Dei temerè & irreligiose, atq; ita vtuntur, vt nocent alijs, efficiantq; vt iudicentur ac uituperentur ab alijs, à quib. si prudenter & vtiliter agerent laudari poterat, quæ res in probrum magis quã indecore nominis Dei uergit, illiq; uehementer displicet. Quomodo enim probaret eum, qui sibi quidem gratias agit, at proximum interea temerario donorum suorum usu perdit, ac nomini suo infamiam adurit? Hoc spectans Apostolus subiungit dicens:
units.tr: Next, notice that we ought to use the benefits of God, of which we partake by his grace and for which we give him thanks, both religiously and without any rashness. He does not simply say, "Why am I reviled for this, that I partake of and eat God's creatures?" but, "If I partake with thanks, why should I partake in such a way that I am reviled for that for which I give thanks?" Here he marks the recklessness of those who use God's benefits rashly and thoughtlessly, so that they harm others and cause themselves to be judged and censured by them. If they acted wisely and profitably they could be praised, but their conduct turns into disgrace rather than honour for the name of God, and this greatly displeases him. For how could he commend himself to God who gives thanks to God, yet meanwhile destroys his neighbour by a reckless use of his gifts and brings infamy upon his own name? With this in view the Apostle adds:

units.la: SIVE igitur editis, siue bibitis, siue quid facitis, omnia in gloria Dei facite.) Hanc generalem regulam, quasi summam quandam, præcedentia complectentem, præscribit fidelibus omnibus. Neque enim fieri poterat, vt omnes circumstantias & species eorum explicaret, quæ in hac causa contingere poterat. Quare quasi quendam generalem scopum præfigens, ad quem collimarent in omnibus dicit: Siue igitur editis, siue bibitis, siue quid facitis omnia in gloriam Dei facite. Quasi dicat. Innumera sunt quæ vobis accident, in medio infidelium tã Iudæorũ quàm Græcorum uersan-
units.tr: "Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God." He lays down this general rule, as a kind of summary embracing what has gone before, for all the faithful. For it was not possible to explain all the circumstances and kinds of cases that might arise in this matter. So, setting before them a certain general aim at which all their actions should be directed, he says: "Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God." As if to say: there are countless things that will happen to you, living in the midst of unbelievers, both Jews and Greeks,

units.la: tibus, de quibus singulatim præcipi nõ potest. Quarehoc sitis animo præditi, vt omnia in gloriam Dei & faciatis quæ faciëda, & feratis quæ sunt ferenda. Sic animatis non deerit spiritus domini, qui omnia vestra ad gloriam Dei dirigat. Hoc autem gloriæ Dei studium duplici nomine fidelibus competit. Primùm generaliter cum mortalibus omnibus, propterea quod sunt opus Dei ab illo creati & facti. Operis est, vt faciat ad gloriam opificis sui. Deinde specialiter, propter gratiam adoptionis, qua sunt in Christo Iesu in numerum filiorum Dei electi & assumpti. Filiorum est studere gloriæ patris. Hoc spectat Christus dicens: Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, vt videant opera vestra bona, & glorificent patrem vestrum qui est in cœlis. Matth. 5. Quemadmodum igitur omnis nostra vita tam creationis quàm regenerationis beneficio à Deo est, ita par est, vt vi ciffim gloriæ Dei seruiat.
units.tr: and these cannot be prescribed one by one. Therefore be so disposed in mind that you do all that is to be done, and bear all that is to be borne, to the glory of God. If you are so disposed, the Spirit of the Lord will not fail you, who will direct all your affairs to the glory of God. This zeal for the glory of God belongs to the faithful on two grounds. First, in general, in common with all mortals, because they are the work of God, created and made by him. It is the duty of a work to serve the glory of its maker. Second, specially, on account of the grace of adoption, by which in Christ Jesus they are chosen and taken into the number of the sons of God. It is the duty of sons to strive for the glory of their father. Christ has this in view when he says: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven" (Matt. 5). Therefore, just as our whole life, both by creation and by regeneration, is from God, so it is fitting that in turn it should serve the glory of God.

units.la: SIVE igitur editis, inquit, siue bibitis, siue quid facitis.) Vulgata versio habet, vel aliud quid facitis. At uocula aliud, in Græco non habetur, sed simpliciter, ἢ τι ποιεῖτε, id est, siue quid facitis. Edere & bibere non est aliquid operis facere, sed vitam & vires ad faciendum alere. Hactenus recte distincta sunt hæc ab Apostolo. Sic possumus distinguere inter ea quæ ad alimoniam noui hominis, & ea quæ ad illius vitam & opera pertinent. Ingredi ecclesiam, audire uerbum domini, & communicare de mensa domini, non est facere & operari, sed fidem alere, & ad operandum confirmare. Arbor facere dicitur, dum fructificat, non ita dum alimoniam & incrementa è terra accipit. Vtinam sic animati simus, ut quod edimus ac bibimus non habeamus operis, sed alimoniæ loco, quæ ad uiuendum & operandum corroboremur.
units.tr: "Whether therefore you eat or drink," he says, "or whatever you do." The Vulgate version reads, "or do anything else." But the word "else" is not found in the Greek, which has simply ἢ τι ποιεῖτε [e ti poieite], that is, "or whatever you do." To eat and drink is not to do some work, but to nourish life and strength for working. So far the Apostle rightly distinguishes these things. In this way we can distinguish between those things that pertain to the nourishment of the new man and those that pertain to his life and works. To enter the Church, to hear the Word of the Lord, and to communicate at the Lord's table is not to act and work, but to feed faith and strengthen it for working. A tree is said to make fruit when it bears fruit, but not while it takes nourishment and growth from the earth. Would that we were so disposed that what we eat and drink were not for us a work, but a nourishment by which we are strengthened to live and to work.

units.la: Ociosis hominibus qui non edunt ut viuant, sed viuunt ut edant & bibant, omne quod faciunt edendo & bibendo absoluitur. Præterea nanq; nihil operis faciunt. Tales sunt Christiani illi, qui præterquã quod ad ecclesiam veniunt, unaq; cum alijs verbum domini audiût & communicat, nihil Christianorum operum faciûnt. Illis opus est, quod uires operandi sufficere debebat. Hi similes sunt infrugiferis arboribus, quarum nullum aliud est opus, quà quod terrã occupant, & incrementũ ex illa cum alijs frustra accipiunt.
units.tr: For idle people, who do not eat in order to live, but live in order to eat and drink, everything they do in eating and drinking is wasted, since they accomplish no work at all. Such are those Christians who, apart from coming to the congregation and hearing and communicating together with others in the Word of the Lord, do none of the works of Christians. They need the work that the power of working ought to supply. They are like barren trees, whose only work is to occupy the ground, and who receive nourishment from it along with others to no purpose.

units.la: SIVE editis, inquit, siue bibitis, omnia in gloriam Dei facite.) Ergo non solum faciendo sed edendo ac bibendo gloriæ Dei studere possumus. Quomodo? Cauendo primum, ne nomen Dei edendo ac bibendo dehonestemus, sicuti faciebant Corinthij, edentes & bibentes in eidolio cum infidelibus, perinde ac si sacrificiorum illorum ac mensæ dæmoniorum participes esse vellent, & in priuatis infidelium conuiuijs de immolaticijs etiam præmoniti absque ulla uitandi scandali cura manducates, quod utrunque ad ignominiam nominis Dei uergebat. Quæso dum hodie Christianus uel simulacris lacris sanctorum oblata, vel superstitione aliqua polluta comedit, vel edendo & bibendo Antichristi mandatis serviit, vel intemperanter edendo ac bibendo suum ipsius corpus perdit, quid aliud facit, quàm quod nomen Dei cui ac censetur dehonestat? Sit ergo prima haec fidelis hominis cura ne quo pacto nomen Dei edendo ac bibendo dehonestet. Deinde eousque in hoc studio crescat, ut etiam ad gloriam Dei edat ac bibat. Hoc faciet, si cum gratiarum actione, si temperanter, si ad aedificationem una comedentiu adhibitis sermonibus pietatis edat & bibat, & membra Christi egena & esurientia mensae suae adhibeat. Sic enim edendo etiam infidelibus causam, quantum in ipso est, glorificandi nominis Dei objicit.
units.tr: "Whether you eat or drink," he says, "do all to the glory of God." Therefore we can strive for the glory of God not only by doing but also by eating and drinking. How? First, by taking care that we do not dishonour the name of God by eating and drinking, as the Corinthians did when they ate and drank in an idol's temple with unbelievers, as if they wished to be partakers of those sacrifices and of the table of demons; and when, at private feasts of unbelievers, they ate what had been offered to idols without any care to avoid scandal. Both of these tended to the dishonour of the name of God. I ask: when a Christian today eats what has been offered to sacred images of the saints, or what is polluted by some superstition, or by eating and drinking serves the commands of Antichrist, or by intemperate eating and drinking destroys his own body, what else is he doing than dishonouring the name of God by which he is named? Let this, then, be the first concern of the faithful man: that in no way he dishonour the name of God by eating and drinking. Then let him grow in this zeal so that he eats and drinks even for the glory of God. He will do this if he eats and drinks with thanksgiving, temperately, and for the edification of those who eat together with him, bringing in godly conversation; and if he shares his table with the needy and hungry members of Christ. For in this way, by eating, he presents to unbelievers, so far as lies in him, an occasion of glorifying the name of God.

units.la: TALES estote ut nullum praebeatis offendiculum neq; Iudaeis, neque Graecis, neq; ecclesiae Dei. In Graeco est ἀπρόσκοποι γίνεσθε, id est, absq; offendiculo fiatis. Hortatur ut quod nō erat fiant. Significat autem ἀπρόσκοπον eū qui sic se gerit, ut neminem offendat, vel certè nemini causam offendiculi praebeat. Dixit in summa, Siue editis siue bibitis siue quid facitis omnia ad gloriam Dei facite. Quoniam autem hoc non faciebant, qui temerè quosuis offendebant, ut intelligerent eam temeritatem non facere ad gloriam Dei, subijcit ista specificationis gratia, seruiens causae quam agit. Tales, inquit, estote, ut nullum praebeatis offendiculum, neque Iudaeis, neq; Graecis, neq; ecclesiae Dei. Quoniam Iudaei in orbem terrarum sparsi, ut inter alias gentes ita etiam inter Corinthios exulabant, metuebat ne temeritate eorum Christianorum, qui immolaticia cum in fidelibus in templis illorum edebant, offenderentur, & à religione Christiana auerterentur, monet fideles, ut cum primis caueant, ne quid offendiculi illis objiciant. Etenim simulacra & cultum simulacrorum unà cum illorum culto ribus summopere execrabantur, iuxta illud Roman.1. Abominaris simulacra, &c. Longè aliter animati sunt praelati ecclesiarum erga Iudaeos, pro quorum salute ne minimum quidè simulacrum è templis auferrent.
units.tr: "Be such that you give no offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Greeks, nor to the Church of God." In the Greek it is ἀπρόσκοποι γίνεσθε [aproskopoi ginesthe], that is, "be without offence." He urges them to become what they were not. Now ἀπρόσκοπος signifies one who so conducts himself that he offends no one, or at least gives no one cause of offence. In sum he has said: "Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God." Since those who rashly offended whomever they pleased did not do this, so that they might understand that such rashness does not serve the glory of God, he adds this specification, serving the cause he is pursuing: "Be such," he says, "that you give no offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Greeks, nor to the Church of God." Since the Jews, scattered throughout the world, lived as exiles among the Corinthians as among other nations, he feared that by the rashness of those Christians who ate what had been offered to idols in their temples, in the presence of the faithful, the Jews would be offended and turned away from the Christian religion. So he warns the faithful above all to take care not to put any stumbling block before them. For the Jews utterly abhorred images and the worship of images, together with their cult, in accordance with the saying of Romans 1: "You abhor idols," and so on. The prelates of the churches have been far otherwise disposed toward the Jews, for whose salvation they would not remove so much as the smallest image from the temples.

units.la: NEQVE Graecis inquit.) Graecos vocat non solum Corinthios, sed & omnes eos qui neque erant Iudaei neque Christiani, quosuis videlicet ethnicos. Facit autem hoc, meo iudicio, hac primùm ratione, quod Corinthij quibus scribebat, Graeci erant, & inter Graecos vivebant. Deinde, propterea quod Graeci & nominatiores erant caeteris gentibus, & ex illis primitiae gentium ad Christum venerant. Propter hanc etiam praerogatiuam Graecos proximè Iudaeis subijcere solet, sicuti videre est in Romanis cap.2.3.&10. Et Lucas in Actis cap.6. Graecos Ebraeis coniungit, ex quibus prima Christi ecclesia Hierosolymis constabat. Qua re si cui genti post Ebraeos aliquis primatus in ecclesia gentium deberetur, competeret ille, non Latinis sed Graecis. Si Euangelistae & Apostoli Latinè primùm non Graecè scripsissent,
