units.tr: "Neither to the Greeks," he says. He calls the Greeks not only the Corinthians but all those who were neither Jews nor Christians, that is, Gentiles of every kind. I think he does this first for this reason: the Corinthians to whom he was writing were Greeks and lived among the Greeks. Second, the Greeks were more distinguished than the other nations, and from them the first fruits of the Gentiles came to Christ. Because of this precedence he usually places the Greeks next after the Jews, as can be seen in Romans chapters 2, 3 and 10. Luke in Acts chapter 6 also joins the Greeks to the Hebrews, of whom the first church of Christ at Jerusalem consisted. So if any nation after the Hebrews were owed some primacy in the church of the Gentiles, it would belong to the Greeks rather than to the Latins. If the Evangelists and Apostles had written first in Latin and not in Greek,

units.la: obsecro quas non inde glorias efflaret Romp-ont. Quoniam ex Iudaeis & gentibus congregan-da erat ecclesia Christi, res ipsa postulabat, ut Christiani summo studio cauerent, ne vellu- deum aliquem vel ethnicum in rebus liberis & indifferentibus offenderent, & à fide Christi arcerent. Ea videlicet erat Apostolo solicitudo & cura propagandi regni Christi, quam & à reliquis fidelibus requirit.
units.tr: what glories would the Roman not have puffed himself up with, I beg you? Since the church of Christ was to be gathered from Jews and Gentiles, the matter itself demanded that Christians take the greatest care not to offend any Gentile by doing things that are free and indifferent, and not to keep him from the faith of Christ. This was clearly the Apostle's concern and care for spreading the kingdom of Christ, which he also requires of the rest of the faithful.

units.la: ET ecclesiae Dei inquit.) Per ecclesiam Dei intelligit fideles Christi, nō modo coniunctim omnes sed & singulos. Hanc offendit, quisquis vnum ex illis offendit, perinde atq; corpus vulnerat quisquis vnum duntaxat illius membrum vulnerat. Erant tum quoque, quemadmodu perpetuo, multi in ecclesia infirmi quorum conscientiae leui offendiculo offendebantur.
units.tr: "And to the church of God," he says. By the church of God he means the faithful of Christ, not only all of them together but each one singly. Whoever offends one of them offends the church, just as whoever wounds a single member wounds the body. There were then also, as always, many weak people in the church whose consciences were offended by a slight stumbling block.

units.la: Illis timens addit hic, & ecclesiae Dei. Sciebat haud minoris esse virtutis quàm quaerere parta tueri. Quare. Vt inhiabat lucrifaciendis adhuc infidelibus tam Graecis quàm Iudaeis, ita quos domino lucrifecerat faruare satagebat. Corpus, communionem, & populum fidelium vocat ecclesiam Dei, propterea quod fideles sunt à Deo ad gratiam & regnum ipsius vocati. Et hinc disce quid sit ecclesia. Corpus videlicet, communio, & populus ἐκκλησίαν χλητικὸν, id est, vocatorum fidelium Dei. Sonat ipsa vox ecclesia, euocationem, & pro euocatis plerunque accipitur, sicuti ciuitas pro ciuibus, communio pro communicantibus & societas pro socijs.
units.tr: Fearing for these, he adds here, "and to the church of God." He knew that to keep what has been won is no less a virtue than to seek what has not yet been won. Therefore, just as he longed to win unbelievers, both Greeks and Jews, so he took pains to preserve those whom he had won for the Lord. He calls the body, the fellowship and the people of the faithful the church of God, because the faithful have been called by God to his grace and kingdom. From this learn what the church is: namely a body, a fellowship and a people [ἐκκλησίαν κλητικὸν], that is, a called assembly of the faithful of God. The very word ecclesia means a calling out, and it is usually taken for those called out, just as a city is taken for its citizens, a fellowship for its members, and a society for its partners.

units.la: Non est autem ociosum, quod non simpliciter dicit, & Iudaeis & Graecis, & fidelibus, sed, & ecclesiae Dei. Plus enim ponderis habet elogium hoc fidelium, quo illos ecclesiam Dei vocat, quàm si simpliciter fideles vocaret. Proponit enim in illo considerandas duas res magni admodum momenti, quibus permoueri debeamus, ne quem fidelium offendamus. Gratiam videlicet coelestis vocationis & authoritatem Dei. Quos Deus per gratiam suam in peculiū suum è mundo euocauit, nemo sine grandi illius offensa offendere ac perdere poterit.
units.tr: It is not idle that he does not simply say "to Jews and Greeks and to the faithful," but "and to the church of God." For this title of the faithful, by which he calls them the church of God, carries more weight than if he had simply called them the faithful. For in it he sets before us two matters of very great importance, which ought to move us not to offend any of the faithful: namely the grace of heavenly calling and the authority of God. Whomever God has called out of the world to be his own people through his grace, no one can offend and destroy without great offence to God.

units.la: Qui offenderit vnum de pusillis istis, inquit Christus Matth.18.qui in me credunt, expedit ei, ut suspendatur mola asinaria in collum eius ac demergatur in profundum maris. Obsecro quid expedit illis, qui non modo offendunt sed & palàm seducunt, non vnum pusillum sed integras ecclesias, nec seducunt tantum impe-ritos, sed & omnes eo, qui seduci ab ipsis non sustinent, horribiliter condemnant, & huius saeculi principibus mactandos & perdendos obtrudunt.
units.tr: "Whoever offends one of these little ones," Christ says in Matthew 18, "who believe in me, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be drowned in the depths of the sea." I beg you, what good will it do those who not only offend but openly lead astray, not one little one but whole churches, and who not only lead astray the unskilled but also dreadfully condemn all who refuse to be led astray by them, and hand them over to be slaughtered and destroyed by the princes of this age?

units.la: Quemadmodū ego per omnia omnibus placeo, non quaerens meā ipsius utilitatem, sed multorum ut salui fiat. Imitatores mei estote, sicut & ego Christi.
units.tr: "Just as I too please all men in all things, not seeking my own advantage but that of many, that they may be saved. Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ."

units.la: Causam hanc terminaturus repetit vno & altero verbo exemplum suum, quod ipsis toto praecedenti capite imitandum proposuerat. Sciebat plus efficaciæ esse in factis quàm in uerbis doctorum. Parum efficaciter docet, qui ipse diuersum ab eo facit quod docet. Qui ipse turpitudine uitæ suæ ac morum depravatione quosuis offendit, etiamsi centies dicat alijs, Tales estote, ut nullum cuiquam præbeatis offendiculum, puto illum haud multis persuasurum, quod sibijpsi nondum persuasit. Sunt quidem audiendi etiam tales, & faciendum est quod rectè docent, licet quod docent ipsi non faciant, uerum quoniam auditores magis obseruant quid uiuat & faciat, quàm quid doceat ipsorum doctor, fit ut parum efficiat docendo, quisquis aliud loquitur & aliud uiuit, alios docet, seipsum non docet. Vbi uerò facta respondent uerbis, ut non habet audítor, quod præterexat, quominus obediat docenti itacum maiori efficacia docetur & pluribus persuadetur. Sciens hoc Apostolus, non modo irreprehensibiliter se gessit, sed & exemplum suum doctrinæ coniunctum fidelibus proposuit. Sic dicit:
units.tr: To bring this matter to a close, he repeats by one or two words his own example, which he had set before them to imitate throughout the preceding chapter. He knew that example has more power than the words of teachers. He teaches to little effect who himself does the opposite of what he teaches. A man who by the baseness of his life and the corruption of his morals offends everyone, even if he says a hundred times to others, "Be such that you give no stumbling block to anyone," I think will persuade few of what he has not yet persuaded himself. Such men are indeed to be heard, and what they teach rightly is to be done, even though they do not do what they teach. But since hearers watch more closely what their teacher lives and does than what he teaches, it comes about that whoever says one thing and lives another teaches others to little effect, and does not teach himself. Where deeds, however, match words, the hearer has no excuse for not obeying the teacher, and so he is taught with greater effect and persuaded by more people. Knowing this, the Apostle not only conducted himself blamelessly, but also set his own example, joined to his teaching, before the faithful. He says:

units.la: Estote absque offensione & Iudæis & Græcis, & ecclesiæ Dei, quemadmodum ego per omnia omnibus placeo. Corinthijs præscribit, ut neminem offendant, & subijciens, quemadmodum ego, pro eo quod dicendum erat, neminem offendo, dicit, per omnia omnibus placeo. Ergo neminé offendere, est omnibus per omnia placere. Per omnes autem intelligit Iudæos, Græcos & fideles. Sed nasciturhic gemina quæstio. Prima, quomodo se omnibus placere dicat, cum certò constet dispIicuisse ipsum Iudæis supra modum, nec dubium sit, innumeros fuisse Græcos, qui ipsum alij cò tempserint, ut Athenienses philosophi, alij summo odio prosequuti sint, ut Alexader ærarius, & eius farinæ alij. Altera, quomodo per omnia quibusuis placuerit, cum id fieri neque liceat neque possit. Vtrique huic quæstioni parata est solutio ex capite præcedenti, ubi sic dixit: Etenim cum liber sim ab omnibus, omnibus meipsum seruum feci, quo plures lucrifaciam, & factus sum Iudæis quasi Iudæus, ut Iudæos lucrifaciam, ijs qui sub lege sunt, quasi sim sub lege, ut eos qui sub lege sunt lucrifaciam, his qui sine lege sunt, quasi sim sine lege, cum non sim sine lege Deo, sed obnoxius legi Christi, ut lucrifaciam eos qui sunt sine lege. Factus sum infirmis, quasi infirmus, ut infirmos lucrifaciam.
units.tr: "Be without offence both to Jews and to Greeks and to the church of God, just as I too please all men in all things." He prescribes to the Corinthians that they offend no one, and by adding "just as I," in place of what he should have said, "I offend no one," he says, "I please all men in all things." Therefore not to offend anyone is to please all men in all things. By "all" he means Jews, Greeks and the faithful. But a twofold question arises here. First, how can he say that he pleases all, when it is certain that he displeased the Jews beyond measure, and there is no doubt that there were countless Greeks who despised him, as the Athenian philosophers did, and others who pursued him with the greatest hatred, such as Alexander the coppersmith and others of his kind? Second, how could he please everyone in all things, since this is neither permitted nor possible? A ready solution to both questions is found in the preceding chapter, where he said: "For although I am free from all, I have made myself a slave to all, that I might win more. I have become to the Jews as a Jew, that I might win the Jews; to those under the law as one under the law, that I might win those under the law; to those without law as one without law, though I am not without law toward God but under the law of Christ, that I might win those without law. I have become weak to the weak, that I might win the weak."

units.la: OMNIBVS factus sum omnia, ut omnino aliquos seruem, &c.) Ergo quod hic se omnibus placere dicit, intelligendum est de studio placedi omnibus. Placebat omnibus, hoc est, omnibus placere studebat, etiamsi interea quàm plurimis displiceret. Sic Christiano satis est, si neminem scienter offendere, sed omnibus placere studeat, etiamsi placeat paucis, & offendat contra animi sui sententiam multos. Deinde quod dicit per omnia, intelligendum est de rebus liberis, in quibus neglecta libertate sua seruum se fecit omnibus.
units.tr: "I have become all things to all men, that I might by all means save some," and so on. Therefore, when he says here that he pleases all men, it must be understood of his eagerness to please everyone. He pleased all, that is, he strove to please all, even though in the meantime he displeased very many. So for a Christian it is enough that he strive not knowingly to offend anyone, but to please all, even if he pleases few and, contrary to his own judgment, offends many. Next, when he says "in all things," this must be understood of things that are free, in which, setting aside his liberty, he made himself a slave to all.

units.la: Illud, non quærens meam utilitatem, sed multorum ut salui fiant, studium hoc placendi omnibus, & modum quoque exprimit. Studium in verbo quærendi exprimitur. Modus in eo cohæret, quod se non suam sed multorum utilitatem quæsisse dicit. Quemadmodum enim qui quæ sua ipsius sunt quærit, & quæ aliorum negligit, eiusmodi studio placet nemini offendit multos, faciens ea, quæ natura sua sic sunt comparata, ut multos offendant, ita, qui se omnium seruum facit, & omnibus gratificatur in rebus liberis, quoad eius salua conscientia poterit, placet multis, offendit paucos, faciens ea quæ multis placent, illorum bene uolentiam conciliant. Etenim obsequium natura sua mortalium animos reddit amicos.
units.tr: The words "not seeking my own advantage but that of many, that they may be saved" express both this eagerness to please all and the manner of it. The eagerness is expressed in the word "seeking." The manner is contained in the fact that he says he sought not his own advantage but that of many. For just as one who seeks what is his own and neglects what belongs to others, by such an eagerness pleases no one and offends many, doing things which by their nature are such that they offend many, so one who makes himself the servant of all and accommodates himself to all in things that are free, as far as his conscience allows, pleases many and offends few, doing what pleases many and winning their goodwill. For compliance by its nature makes the minds of mortals friendly.

units.la: Dicit quisquam, Quid si meam utilitatem pariter & aliorum quæsiero? An hoc nö licet? Licet sane, si sic fieri poterit. Quod si salus tua cum salute est aliorum coniuncta, ut utraq; simul quæri possit, nihil est quod prohibeat. Exèpli gratia. Communis omnium vtilitas est, ut per Christum saluemur. Eam potest minister quærere cùm pro se tum pro alijs. Sic fecit hic Apostolus, id quod declarat cum cap. præcedenti dicit: Hoc autem facio propter Euangelium, ut particeps illius fiam. Quid est participem fieri Euangelij aliud quàm participem fieri uitæ & æternæ salutis? Quid igitur est quod hic dicit: Non quærens meam utilitatem, sed multorum ut salui fiant? Loquitur de vtilitate diuersa, terrena videlicet & spirituali. Terrenam suam non quærebat, quo spirituali aliorum seruiret. Vocat autem vtilitatem suam, libertatem quam habebat in rebus indifferentibus, quam Corinthiorum quidam vsq; adeo sectabantur, vt citius aliorum salutem perderent q; quicq; amittere uellet. Illud Rom. 9. Optarim ego ipse anathema esse à Christo pro fratribus meis, &c. singulariorem & excellentiorem affectum habet, q; ut omnib. sit præscribendum.
units.tr: Someone may say: What if I seek my own advantage and that of others at the same time? Is this not permitted? It is indeed permitted, if it can be done in this way. If your salvation is so joined with the salvation of others that both can be sought together, there is nothing to forbid it. For example, the common advantage of all is that we are saved through Christ. A minister can seek this both for himself and for others. So this Apostle did, as he declares when, in the preceding chapter, he says: "I do all this for the sake of the Gospel, that I may become a partaker of it." What is it to become a partaker of the Gospel, other than to become a partaker of life and eternal salvation? What then does he mean here by: "Not seeking my own advantage, but the advantage of many, that they may be saved"? He speaks of a different kind of advantage, namely earthly and spiritual. He did not seek his earthly advantage, so that he might serve others in what is spiritual. He calls his "advantage" the liberty he had in things indifferent, which some of the Corinthians pursued so eagerly that they would sooner lose the salvation of others than give up anything at all. Compare Romans 9: "I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren," etc. That affection is more singular and excellent than that it should be prescribed to everyone.

units.la: IMITATORES mei estote, inquit, sicut & ego Christi.) Vulgata versio particulam hàc in principio habet capitis sequentis, quâ Græcus textus habet in calce præsentis, quemadmodum & Chrysostom. Et res ipsa declarat, pertinere eam non ad sequentia sed ad præcedentia. Quoniam suũ illis exemplum proposuit dicens: quemadmodum ego omnibus per omnia placeo, ne simpliciter hoc quærere uideatur, vt se sequantur in omnib. quemadmodum hoc quærere solent pseudapostoli & magistri sectarum, discipulos post se trahentes, exèplo suo Christi coniungit, imò præfigit exemplum, quo & authoritatem illi conciliet, & simul caueat, ne ecclesiam quibusuis doctorum factis imitandis subijciat, qui fideles hactenus sibi volunt esse obnoxios, vt quibusuis suis præceptis obediat, & quæuis sua studia imitetur. Itaq; nô simpliciter dicit: Imitatores mei estote, sed addit sicut & ego Christi. Sit hæc limitatio, quatenus auditores imitari debeant suos doctores. Quatenus videlicet illi imitatores sunt Christi. Sed dices: Ergo recte faciunt, qui A Christum imitantes abstinent à coiugio, quando quidem ipse fuit ἁγνὸς, & eam continentiá alijs quoq; imitandam proponunt. Deinde & xl. dies ieiunant, idq; ieiunij alijs praescribunt, propterea quod Christus totidē dies ieiunasse scribitur. Respondeo. Quod abstinentiá à coniugio attinet, si ea ad imitationē Christi pertinet, nō fuerūt apostoli imitatores Christi. Habuerunt enim cōiuges, sicuti supra cap.7. ostēdimus. Quod ieiuniū quadragesimale attinet, non est illud referendum ad exempla Christi fidelibus imitanda, id quod & Chrisostomus anno tauit, quemadmodū in Comment. nostris super Matth.cap.4. uidere licet. Id potius imitandum est, quod Christus & docuit & fecit. Docuit ea quae charitatis sunt, & opere quoque praestitit, dum semetipsum exinaniuit, accepta serui forma, & pro nobis in mortem tradidit, quaerens & saluum facies quod perierat. Hac in re sita est vera Christi imitatio. Et hac Chrysostomus recte perfectissimi dixit esse Christianismi canonem, ad quem si compares, prorsus nihil est omnis omnium monachorum disciplina, abstinentia, castigatio, &c. ... inquit Chrysostomus.
units.tr: "Be imitators of me," he says, "as I also am of Christ." The Vulgate places this particle at the beginning of the following chapter, whereas the Greek text has it at the end of the present one, as does Chrysostom; and the matter itself shows that it belongs to what precedes, not to what follows. For he had set before them his own example, saying: "as I also please all men in all things." Lest he seem to seek this simply, that they should follow him in everything, as the false apostles and the masters of sects usually seek, drawing disciples after themselves, he joins his own example to that of Christ, or rather places Christ's example first, so that he both wins authority for himself and at the same time takes care that the Church should not be made subject to the deeds of any teachers whatever to be imitated, which faithful people have hitherto wished to be bound to, so that they obey any of their precepts and imitate any of their pursuits. Therefore he does not simply say, "Be imitators of me," but adds, "as I also am of Christ." Let this be the limit: that hearers ought to imitate their teachers only so far as those teachers are imitators of Christ. But you will say: Then those do rightly who, imitating Christ, abstain from marriage, since he himself was holy and they propose that continence to others to be imitated as well. Then too they fast forty days and prescribe this fast to others, because Christ is written to have fasted as many days. I answer: as far as abstinence from marriage is concerned, if it pertains to the imitation of Christ, then the apostles were not imitators of Christ, for they had wives, as we have shown above in chapter 7. As for the Lenten fast of forty days, it is not to be referred to the examples of Christ to be imitated by the faithful, as Chrysostom also noted, as one may see in our Commentaries on Matthew chapter 4. Rather, that is to be imitated which Christ both taught and did. He taught what pertains to charity, and also made it good in deed, when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and delivered himself to death for us, seeking and saving what had perished. In this matter lies the true imitation of Christ. And Chrysostom rightly said this is the rule of the most perfect Christianity, against which, if you compare it, the whole discipline, abstinence and mortification of all monks is nothing at all, etc. ... says Chrysostom.

units.la: Nos admonemur hoc loco, quàm non sit omnium doctorū dicere: Imitatores mei estote, sicut & ego Christi. Non recte poscit ut se imitemur, qui in uia Dei non praecedit. Aliud est audire docentem, & aliud imitari praeeuntē. Ut multi sunt doctores, praeeuntes pauci, ita multi sunt auditores, imitatores uero pauci. B
units.tr: We are reminded here how it is not for every teacher to say: "Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ." He rightly asks to be imitated who does not go before in the way of God. It is one thing to hear a teacher, and another to imitate one who goes before. As there are many teachers but few who go before, so there are many hearers but few imitators.

units.la: CAPUT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Ollaudo autem uos fratres, quod omnia mea memoria tenetis, & quemadmodum tradidi uobis instituta, tenetis.
units.tr: I commend you, brothers, because you remember me in all things and hold fast to the traditions as I delivered them to you.

units.la: Apparet ecclesiam Corinthiorum improbitate quorundam non uno tantum, sed uarijs modis à synceritate apostolica abduci ac depravari in absentia Apostoli coepisse. Quare cum ea de re per fideliores esset admonitus, diligenti cura ingrueti corruptioni occurrit. Ha ctenus communicationem gentilium sacrorum tribus capitibus 8. 9. & 10. reprehendit, iam transit ad eos abusus corrigendos, qui in ecclesiasticum illorum coetum irrepserant, id quod quatuor sequentibus capitibus, 11. 12. 13. & 14. facit. Dum haec lego, mirari desino, quì factum sit, quod tam multis ac foedis corruptelis post apostolorum tempora deformatae sint ecclesiae. Etenim si tam modico tempore Apostolo absente quidem, uerum adhuc in viuis agente, tot modis ecclesia Corinthiorum defecdari potuit, quid mirum si tam prolixo tot saeculorum decursu partim superstitione, partim incuria, partim hypocrisi, partim dominatu pseudepiscoporum horrendis modis corrupta sunt in ecclesijs ferè omnia, maximè cum perpetuò pro haereticis & schismaticis habiti sint, quicunq; publicae corruptioni reclamandum esse censuerunt, quam ... in saniam hodie quoque experimur, qui adeo facti sunt impudentes, ut ausint contendere, non posse errare ecclesiam. Si ueri pastores essent, in id magis incumberent, ut ad exemplū Apostoli quicquid adulterinum obtinuit, in ecclesia diligenti cura corrigerent.
units.tr: It appears that the church of the Corinthians, through the wickedness of some, began in the Apostle's absence to be drawn away from apostolic sincerity and corrupted, and not in one way only but in many. So when he was informed of this by more faithful people, he met the spreading corruption with careful diligence. Up to this point he has rebuked the participation in pagan sacrifices in three chapters, 8, 9 and 10. Now he turns to correct the abuses that had crept into their ecclesiastical assembly, which he does in the four following chapters, 11, 12, 13 and 14. As I read these things, I stop wondering how it came about that the churches were deformed by so many foul corruptions after the time of the apostles. For if the church of the Corinthians, in so short a time, while the Apostle was absent yet still living, could be corrupted in so many ways, what wonder is it that over so long a course of centuries almost all the churches have been corrupted in horrible ways, partly by superstition, partly by negligence, partly by hypocrisy, and partly by the domination of pseudo-bishops? This is especially so since those who thought they must object to public corruption have always been held as heretics and schismatics. We experience this even today, to our loss, in those who have become so shameless that they dare to contend that the Church cannot err. If they were true ministers, they would labour all the more to correct, with diligent care and following the Apostle's example, whatever adulteration has taken hold in the church.

units.la: COLLAVDO autem uos fratres, inquit.) Orditur à laude eorum, qui cæteris saniores erant. Neque enim probandum est, quod Lyranus haec per ironiam dicta esse putat, ut, collaudo uos idem sit quod uitupero uos. Poterat ordiri à correptione reproborum, verum quoniam multum refert, quali exordio ad emendandum delinquentes utamur, praesertim vbi delictum non est catholicum, sed quorundam tantum, ne qui inculpabiles sunt, se quoque perstringi putent, adeoque frustra contristentur, consultius & circumspectius erat, vt mox initio laudaret saniores, eosque merita laude à delinquentibus segregaret. Exemplū hoc Apostolicae prudentiae imitentur pastores & doctores ecclesiae. Neq; enim tum tantum, sed hodie quoq; sic comparatae sunt ecclesiae, ut eiusmodi prudentiam requirant.
units.tr: "I commend you, brothers," he says. He begins with praise of those who were saner than the rest. For it is not to be accepted what Lyra thinks, that these words are spoken by irony, so that "I commend you" means the same as "I blame you." He could have begun with a rebuke of the wicked. But since it matters greatly with what kind of opening we approach the correction of offenders, especially where the fault is not general but belongs to some only, lest those who are blameless think themselves also struck and so grieve in vain, it was more prudent and more circumspect to praise the saner members at once, and to set them apart with due praise from the offenders. Let the pastors and teachers of the church imitate this example of apostolic prudence. For the churches are so constituted, not only then but today too, that they require such prudence.

units.la: Sic autem consilium Apostoli considerantes, liberamus eum à suspicione adulationis, à qua omnium fuit alienissimus. Quare non est ut hoc illius exemplum patrocinio sibi esse exi-stimet adulatores ecclesiastici, qui nec cum debito discrimine, nec sanctae prudentiae propositio, nec ea tantum quae iustae sunt laudis capacia, laudant in ecclesia, sed quo res suas agant magis quàm Christi laudant vituperanda, & abblandiuntur illis, quos magis corripere conueniebat. Alias non est inutile, necalienum, ut videmus, à sanctis laudare fratres recte agentes.
units.tr: Considering the Apostle's counsel in this way, we free him from the suspicion of flattery, to which he was most of all a stranger. Therefore let no church flatterers think that his example protects them, those who praise without due distinction and without holy prudence, and who praise in the church not only those things that are worthy of just praise, but also things that deserve blame, when they do so to advance their own affairs rather than Christ's. They flatter those whom it was rather fitting to rebuke. Otherwise, as we see, it is neither useless nor unbecoming for the saints to praise brothers who act rightly.

units.la: Potest autem hoc fieri bifariam. Primum coram alijs recte illorum facta praedicando & laudando. Sic infrà capite vltimo laudat Stephanam, Fortunatum, & Achaicum coram ecclesia Corinthiorum, praedicans de illis quod seipsos in ministerium sanctorum ordinarint, ac spiritum suum refocillarint. Et hoc plerunque in salutationibus, quas epistolis suis subiecit, facere consueuit. Hoc autem laudandi genus & plus habet candoris, & minus est suspectum. Deinde, in faciem aliquem, vel praesentem verbis vel absente literis laudando, quod hic facit; dicens: Collaudo autem vos fratres, quemadmodum & Philippenses & Thessalonicenses laudat. Vtroq; laudandi genere incitat fideles ad studium pietatis, siue ut eos quos laudat imitentur, siue ut in quo laudantur constanter pergant.
units.tr: This can be done in two ways. First, by praising and commending their good deeds in the presence of others. So in the last chapter he praises Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus before the Corinthian church, declaring that they have devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints and refreshed his spirit. He was accustomed to do this often in the greetings he added at the end of his letters. This kind of praise has more candour and is less open to suspicion. Second, by praising someone to his face, either present in words or absent in letters, as he does here when he says, "I commend you, brothers," just as he praises the Philippians and the Thessalonians. By both kinds of praise he stirs the faithful to zeal for godliness, either that they may imitate those he praises or that they may persevere constantly in the qualities for which they are praised.

Consimili modo dicimus nos dicit:Laudo quidē vos,quod omnia instituta de ritibus & traditionibus,qui diuersitate sua mea,quę uobis cū apud uos essem tradidi, me conuincūt,quod nihil minus sint quā vel apo- mori mēte seruatis:uerū iuxtā scire uos uolo,
units.tr: "That you remember me in all things," he says, "and hold fast to the traditions as I delivered them to you." In Greek it is "that you remember me in all things" [ὅτι πάντα μου μέμνησθε], which can be translated in two ways. First, as in the Vulgate, "that you are mindful of me in all things," where "in all things" is the same as [ταῦτα] "these things." Second, as Erasmus translated it, "that you remember all my teachings." By either reading he praises the Corinthians for something that is easy to do. He had instructed them not only in what to believe and how to live, but also in the order and decorum with which each thing was to be carried out in the assembly of the church. They faithfully kept in memory and retained what they had received. Observe how he first ascribes to them the memory of the traditions they received, and then their keeping of them. The memory of an accepted command serves that keeping, while forgetfulness prepares the way for transgression. Observe also how he does not simply say "what I [delivered]" but "all my things." This is the mark of a mind that remembers not one or another teaching but all of them together. Third, it is not idle that he does not simply say "what I delivered to you," but "as I delivered to you the instituted things, or traditions [παραδόσεις], you hold." They cite these words to confirm the authority of traditions and ecclesiastical rites, which today we reject as contrary to the word of God. "See," they say, "that the faithful keep not only those things that were written but also those that were handed down by word of mouth, because they were received from the apostles." First it had to be proved that all the rites we disapprove were handed down by the apostles, which will never be proved. Second, that they are not contrary to the word of God. Third, how they were handed down by the apostles and have been kept to this day. Unless these things are proved, what is the point of defending so many manifest abuses with these words of the Apostle, "as I delivered the instituted things to you, you hold," in vain? The Eucharist itself sufficiently shows that the Lord's and the apostolic institutions have not been kept as they were handed down, but have been greatly corrupted by additions, diminutions and alterations. Who is so mad as to want to believe that rites for which there is no authority in Scripture were instituted by the apostles, and kept uncorrupted in their first form, when even those things which are plainly circumscribed by the clear word have not been kept whole? Hence the passage in the end of this chapter, where he says, "The rest I will set in order when I come," should be noted. It is clear enough, I think, that he had not yet arranged in the Corinthian church all the things that were to be ordered by his own authority and prudence. The wiser members therefore kept all his institutions which he had commended to them in person. But meanwhile, as they were behaving not very decently among themselves while praying and prophesying, he corrects this, saying: "I praise you indeed, that you keep in mind all my instructions, which I gave you when I was with you; but I want you to know..." Here he is saying that they are to be corrected, not praised, by the cause of their error. Tertullian, in his book on the prescription of heretics, is also to be noted, where he says: "Their doctrine, because it differs and contradicts itself, will declare by its own diversity and contrariety that it is not of any apostle's authority, nor apostolic. For just as the apostles did not teach things that differ from one another, so they did not publish things contrary to the apostles, unless those who had departed from the apostles and preached otherwise had done so." Thus he wrote. In a similar way we say that the rites and traditions which convict us, by their diversity, of being in no way apostolic, are not to be defended against the word of God.

units.la: quàm sit inconueniens, quod uiri tecto, mulieres aperto capite in ecclesia oratis & prophetatis. Et sic Hieronymus intellexit, ad hunc modum exponens: Etiam in hoc uolo uos instruere, ut illud similiter teneatis, &c. Quod si quis existimat Apostolum iam antea hac de re praecepisse, & in presenti nihil facere aliud quàm ut traditam antea disciplinam rationibus confirmet, contra eos qui illam contentionibus suis diuexabant, nolim admodum reluctari.
units.tr: how unseemly it is that men pray and prophesy in the church with their heads covered, and women with their heads uncovered. Jerome understood it in this way, expounding: "In this too I want to instruct you, that you likewise hold to that," and so on. But if anyone thinks the Apostle had already laid down this matter earlier, and in the present passage does nothing more than confirm with reasons the discipline handed down before, against those who troubled it with their disputes, I am not at all inclined to resist.

units.la: Si nihil hac de re tradiderat antea, uidemus fieri potuisse, ut qui omnia apostolica instituta tenebant, nondum scirent caput mulieris esse uirum, uiri Christum, Christi Deum, nedum quid ex ea esset scientia colligendum. Si uero iam antea tradiderat, admonemur requiri scientiam ab illis, qui traditam disciplinam seruant, quod non sit satis externo facto quod traditum est seruare, nisi id iusta cum intelligentia fiat: quemadmodum decet populum non seruiliter, sed liberaliter & ad spontaneam disciplinam institutum. Laudanda igitur sic est iustae obedientiae diligentia, & traditae disciplinae custodia, ut simul etiam eorum quae seruanda sunt, intelligentia tradatur & requiratur. Etenim sine hac externum quidem corpus disciplina non intellecta exercetur, mens uero omni illius fructu destituitur, id quod à fidelibus omnium debebat esse alienissimum. Sic multa seruantur in ecclesijs Romanae dominationi subiectis, praesertim in monasterijs, de quibus si roges, nulla potest reddi certa ac praegnans ratio, quâ in ecclesia fidelium alicuius conueniat esse momenti. Nihil debet tradi in ecclesia, quod non uel scripturis canonicis, uel iustis rationibus fidelibus commendetur. Sic uidemus hic Apostolum non simpliciter statuere quid faciendum sit, quid non sit, sed traditionem suam rationibus & praemissis & subiectis communire. Seruilem subiectionem quaerunt in ecclesia Pontifices, qui solam personae, quam gerere uideri uolunt, dignitatem & authoritatem fidelibus obijciunt, dum quaelibet illis proprio arbitratu imponunt. Hoc quaeso, quid aliud est quàm in omes Christi exercere dominatum, ac dicere: Sic uolo, sic iubeo, sit pro ratione uolu tas: Et illud Pelagij, ubi est maioritas, ibi est mandandi potestas, caeteros manet obediendi necessitas.
units.tr: If he had delivered nothing on this matter before, we see that it could have happened that those who held all the apostolic institutions did not yet know that the husband is the head of the woman, Christ of the husband, God of Christ, much less what ought to be inferred from this. But if he had already delivered it before, we are reminded that knowledge is required of those who keep the delivered discipline: it is not enough to keep what has been handed down by outward action, unless it is done with right understanding, just as it befits a people to act not slavishly but freely, and to be instructed in a discipline freely embraced. Therefore the diligence of right obedience and the keeping of the delivered discipline are to be praised in such a way that, at the same time, understanding of what must be kept is both imparted and sought. For without this, the outward body is indeed exercised in a discipline not understood, but the mind is deprived of all its fruit, which ought to be most alien to all the faithful. Thus many things are kept in the churches subject to Roman domination, especially in the monasteries; if you ask about them, no certain and weighty reason can be given that would agree with the importance of a congregation of the faithful. Nothing ought to be handed down in the Church that is not commended to the faithful either by the canonical Scriptures or by sound reasons. So we see here that the Apostle does not simply lay down what must be done and what must not, but fortifies his tradition with reasons both preceding and following. The Pontiffs seek a slavish subjection in the Church, who impose upon the faithful only the dignity and authority of the person they wish to appear to hold, while they impose whatever they please at their own pleasure. I ask, what else is this than to exercise lordship over all of Christ's people, and to say: "Thus I will, thus I command, let my will stand for reason"? And to that saying of Pelagius: where there is the greater number, there is the power of commanding; for the rest there remains the necessity of obeying.

units.la: Quam autem traditionis huius primariam rationem praemittit:
units.tr: But the first reason which he sets forth for this tradition is this:

units.la: Sed scire uos uolo, inquit, quod omnis uiri caput Christus est, caput autem mulieris uir, caput uero Christi Deus.
units.tr: But I want you to know, he says, that the head of every man is Christ, the head of the woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God.

units.la: Sententiam hanc accommodat ipse ad causam de qua agit, ubi uidebimus, quomodo ex illa quod instituit, colligi uelit. In presenti ipsa haec est sententia inspicienda. Quadripartitò ordinem ponit, quo & distinctio pariter & coniunctio primum Dei & Christi, deinde Christi & uiri, tertiò uiri & mulieris explicatur. Maxi-
units.tr: He himself adapts this statement to the matter he is treating, and we shall see there how he wishes to draw from it what he sets down. In the present passage this is the statement to be examined. He sets out an order in four parts, by which both the distinction and the connection are explained: first of God and Christ, then of Christ and the man, and thirdly of the man and the woman. There is indeed a very great connection, namely such as that of the body and the head, between the woman and the man, the man and Christ, Christ and God; yet that connection does not remove the distinction of those joined, nor does it break the pre-eminence of the greater.

units.la: ma quidem est coniunctio, nimirum qualis est corporis & capitis, inter mulierem & uirum, uirum & Christum, Christum & Deum: Verum ea coniunctio non tollit distinctionem coniunctorum nec infringit potiorum praerogatiuam.
units.tr: The connection is indeed very close, namely such as that of the body and the head, between the woman and the man, the man and Christ, Christ and God. Yet that connection does not abolish the distinction of those joined, nor does it weaken the pre-eminence of the superior.

units.la: Ad coniunctionem arctissimam pertinet, quod non dicit: Quod omnis uiri dominus Christus est, dominus autem mulieris uir, dominus uero Christi Deus, sed: Quod omnis uiri caput Christus est, caput autem mulieris uir, caput uero Christi Deus. Coniunguntur & dominus & seruus, uerum ea coniunctio procul abest ab unitate capitis & corporis. Est quidem & Christus uiri, & uir mulieris dominus: uerum non ita quemadmodum sunt domini seruorum & mancipiorum, sed quemadmodum caput est sui corporis. Quare ad exprimendam uniuersissimam coniunctionem uocabulum posuit non domini, sed capitis.
units.tr: To the closest connection belongs the fact that he does not say: "The lord of every man is Christ, the lord of a woman is the man, and the lord of Christ is God," but: "The head of every man is Christ, the head of a woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God." Lord and servant are joined, but that connection is far from the unity of head and body. Christ is indeed the man's, and the man the woman's, lord; yet not as lords of servants and bondmen are, but as the head is of its own body. Therefore, to express the most complete connection, he has used the word head, not lord.

units.la: Ad distinctionem uero coniunctorum & praerogatiuam potiorum pertinet, quod non dicit Omnis uiri compar est Christus, compar autem mulieris uir; compar uero Christi Deus, sed, omnis uiri caput est Christus, caput autem mulieris uir, caput uero Christi Deus. In capite est excellentia moderationis & authoritatis, in corpore est subiecto & iustae obedientiae accommodatio. Praeest corpori caput, subest capiti corpus: Regit caput, regitur corpus. Ad hanc capitis & corporis metaphoram referendum est quod uirum mulieris, Christum uiri, Deum Christi caput esse dicit. Supereminet mulieri uir, Christus uiro, Deus Christo.
units.tr: Now to the distinction of those joined and the pre-eminence of the superior belongs the fact that he does not say: "Every man is equal to Christ, and the woman's equal is the man; and Christ's equal is God," but: "The head of every man is Christ, the head of a woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God." In the head is excellence of moderation and authority; in the body is accommodation to subjection and just obedience. The head presides over the body, the body is subject to the head; the head rules, the body is ruled. To this metaphor of head and body must be referred his saying that the man is the head of the woman, Christ of the man, God of Christ. The man excels over the woman, Christ over the man, God over Christ.

units.la: Sic omnis & summa supereminentia tribuitur Deo patri, quemadmodum etiam illius omnis est paternitas. Ex Deo patre per Christum sunt omnia. Ex illo est quod Christus caput est uiri, uir caput mulieris. Sic supra in calce capitis tertij retulit ad Deum patrem per Christum omnia, consimili gradatione dicens: Omnia uestra sunt, uos autem Christi, Christus uero Dei. Haec puto esse perspicua. Verum uidea- mus singula.
units.tr: So all and supreme pre-eminence is attributed to God the Father, just as all paternity is his. From God the Father through Christ are all things. From him it is that Christ is the head of the man, and the man the head of the woman. Thus above, at the end of the third chapter, he referred all things to God the Father through Christ, with a similar gradation, saying: "All things are yours, and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's." I think these things are clear. But let us see each point.

units.la: SED scire uos uolo, inquit, quod omnis uiri caput Christus est.) Potest hic quaeri, an in uniuersum omnis uiri, etiam increduli & genitilis, uel fidelis tantum & Christiani caput sit Christus. Chrysostomus negat Christum esse caput infidelium uirorum, sed fidelium tantum. Et addit hanc rationem: Nam si corpus Christi sumus & membra, & eius pars, & idcirco ipse nostrum caput, eorum qui in corpore non sunt, neque membra perficiunt, non utique erit caput. Itaq; haec particula, omnis, de uno quoque fideli intelligenda est. Et huic recentiores aliqui sequuntur. Verum si hunc sensum accepserimus, non uideo quomodo Christus uirorum fidelium magis quàm mulierum caput dici debeat, praesertim cum ecclesiae sue caput exeitat, in qua tam mulieres sunt quàm uiri, & Gal. 3. diserte legamus in Christo Iesu in quem baptizamur, nec uirum esse nec mulierem, hoc est, nihil esse discriminis inter uirum & & mulierem, quemadmodum nec inter Iudæũ & Græcũ, nec inter seruum & liberum. Et hoc Ambrosium mouisse puto, vt sic exponeret: Christus autem ideo caput viri est, quia per ipsum cum non esset, formatus est. At hęc ratio ad creationem masculini sexus pertinet, quæ non est ad fideles tantum, sed in vniuersum ad omnes viros referenda. Sic esset Christus omnis viri caput, propterea quod per illum est Adam & limo terrę formatus.
units.tr: BUT I want you to know, he says, that the head of every man is Christ. Here it may be asked whether, universally, Christ is the head of every man, even of the unbeliever and the Gentile, or only of the faithful and Christian man. Chrysostom denies that Christ is the head of unbelieving men, but only of the faithful. And he adds this reason: "For if we are the body of Christ and members, and his part, and therefore he is our head, he will not in any way be the head of those who are not in the body and do not complete its members." So this particle, every, is to be understood of each single faithful man. And some more recent writers follow this view. But if we accept this sense, I do not see how Christ ought to be called the head of faithful men rather than of faithful women, especially since he is the head of his church, in which there are women as much as men, and we read plainly in Galatians 3, "in Christ Jesus, into whom we are baptized, there is neither man nor woman," that is, there is no difference between man and woman, just as there is none between Jew and Greek, nor between slave and free. And I think Ambrose was moved by this to expound it thus: "Christ, however, is the head of man because through him, when he was not, man was formed." But this reason pertains to the creation of the male sex, and is to be referred not only to the faithful but universally to all men. So Christ would be the head of every man, because through him Adam was formed from the clay of the earth.

units.la: Nec insolés videri debet, verbum illud per quod facta sunt omnia, quod posterremis temporibus humani generis gratia incarnatũ est, vocari Christum.
units.tr: Nor should it seem strange that the Word, through whom all things were made, and who in the last times was made flesh for the sake of the human race, is called Christ.

units.la: Cogitandum tamen & illud est. Vir est ad imaginem Dei factus, cuius infrà quoq; mētio fiet. At in hac prerogatiua imaginis & gloriæ Dei inter viros omnes supereminet Christus, vt etiam hoc nomine rectè caput virilis sexus vocetur. Et hic sensus conueniens videtur tam coniunctioni quàm distinctioni capitis & corporis, & prærogatiuæ quoq;, qua caput membra sua singulari supereminentia excellit. Nec est vt hoc vel ad diuinam vel ad humanam naturam tantum referamus, sed ad totum Christum. Hic est caput omnis viri, non vxorati tantum, sed & vidui, adolescentis & iuuenis, hoc est totius masculini sexus, in quo perinde atq; caput in corpore principatum tenens excellit. Hanc meam cogitationem nō temerè affirmo, sed alijs iudicandam propono.
units.tr: Yet this too must be considered. Man was made in the image of God, of which mention will also be made below. But in this prerogative of the image and glory of God, Christ excels among all men, so that he is rightly called the head of the male sex also on this account. And this sense seems fitting both to the connection and to the distinction of head and body, and also to the prerogative by which the head excels its members with singular pre-eminence. Nor should we refer this only to the divine or only to the human nature, but to the whole Christ. He is the head of every man, not only of the married, but also of the widower, the young man and the youth; that is, of the whole male sex, in which, just as the head holding the principate in the body, he excels. I do not rashly assert this thought of mine, but I put it forward to be judged by others.

units.la: CAPVT autem mulieris uir, inquit.) Per virum & mulierem totum genus humanum in duos sexus includit. Quemadmodũ enim per virum masculinum, ita per mulierem muliebrem sexum, uirgines, maritatas & viduas intelligit. Duoru iftorū sexuum primus & potior est masculinus, ad imaginem Dei conditus, & muliebri præpositus, quem triplici præstantia excellit, ordine videlicet creationis, dignitate imaginis Dei, & viribus cùm metis, tum corporis, vt non frustra vir ab ipso conditore principatum super mulierem acceperit.
units.tr: "But the head of the woman is the man," he says. Through "man" and "woman" he divides the whole human race into the two sexes. Just as "man" means the male sex, so "woman" means the female sex, including virgins, married women and widows. Of these two sexes the male is the first and the more excellent. He was created in the image of God and set over the female, and he surpasses her in three ways: in the order of creation, in the dignity of the image of God, and in strength, both of mind and of body. It is therefore not without reason that the man received from the Creator himself the headship over the woman.

units.la: Duorum istorum sexuū vnitissima est carnis & naturę coniunctio, & simul ordinis dispositio, qua qui superior est capitis, qui inferior corporis vicem obtinet: vnde non tollitur eiusdem carnis & naturæ vnitas, sed magis imp letur & conseruatur. Quemadmodum enim in corpore humano non destruitur ex eo eiusdē naturæ & carnis vnitas, quod diuisum est in caput & membra, & caput præstantius est & excellentius reliquis membris, illaque gubernat & moderatur, ita inter virum quoq; & mulierem nō soluitur generis naturæ & carnis vnitas hac conditionis diuersitate, qua vir primatum tenet, mulier verò primatui illius subiacet.
units.tr: The union of these two sexes is the closest union of flesh and nature, and at the same time an arrangement of order, by which the one who is superior holds the place of the head and the one who is inferior holds the place of the body. The unity of the same flesh and nature is therefore not destroyed but rather made complete and preserved. For just as in the human body the unity of the same nature and flesh is not destroyed by the division into head and members, and the head is more excellent and superior to the other members and governs and directs them, so between man and woman the unity of kind, nature and flesh is not dissolved by this difference of condition, by which the man holds the first place and the woman is subject to his primacy.

units.la: Nec hinc aliquid est detrimenti muliebri sexui, quod virilis illi præfertur. Quicquid enim in viro est præstantię, mulieris est commodis destinatum, perinde atq; reliquo corpori seruiunt omnes illæ dotes, quæ capiti di-
units.tr: Nor does the female sex suffer any loss because the male is preferred to it. For whatever excellence there is in the man is destined for the benefit of the woman, just as all those gifts that have been granted by God to the head serve the rest of the body.

units.la: uinitùs sunt concessæ. Hinc multa cogitari diciq; possunt, quæ quoniam parerga sunt hoc loco, consultò transimus. Possunt illa bipartiri sic vt alia naturalem ordinem, coiunctionem, conuictum, & mispat vtriusq; generis humani sexus, quo alter est alteri obtrictus, & quæ hisce sunt annexa, alia mysterium Christi & ecclesiæ concernant, quo nobis ille vice capitis, ista vero corporis proponitur, vtpote Coloss. 1. vbi Apostolus dicit: Et ipse est caput corporis ecclesiæ, qui est principium primogenitus ex mortuis, vt fit in omnibus ipse primatum tenens, quia in ipso complacuit omnem plenitudinem diuinitatis inhabitare, & per eum reconciliari omnia, &c. Et Ephes. 5. Mulieres viris suis subditæ sint, sicut domino. Quoniam vir caput est mulieris, sicut Christus caput est ecclesiæ, ipse Saluator corporis ipsius, & quæ ibi plura sequuntur. Ex duobus illis locis videmus, quomodo metaphora capitis & corporis Christo competat & ecclesiæ, Christo inquam soli, & corpori ipsius, ecclesiæ videlicet electorum & fidelium.
units.tr: Many things can be thought and said about this, but since they are incidental to the present passage, I deliberately pass them over. They may be divided into two groups: some concern the natural order, the union, the living together and the mutual relation of the two sexes of the human race, by which each is bound to the other, and what is joined to these; others concern the mystery of Christ and the Church, in which he is set before us in the place of the head and they in the place of the body. So Colossians 1 says, where the Apostle writes: "And he is the head of the body, the Church, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence; for it pleased the Father that in him should all fulness dwell, and by him to reconcile all things," and so on. And Ephesians 5: "Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands, as unto the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the Church; and he is the Saviour of the body," and what follows there. From these two passages we see how the metaphor of head and body fits Christ and the Church: Christ alone as the head, and his body, namely the Church of the elect and faithful.

units.la: Contendunt hodie Romanum pontificem esse caput ecclesiæ. Quod me attinet, concedo hoc facile. Videmus illi ecclesiam esse subiectam, cui dominatur per omnia. Ecclesia autem est corpus quoddam multitudine credentium & vnitate religionis constans & compositum, quo sensu & Iudæi & Turci quoque suam habent ecclesiam. Deinde vnumquodq; caput sui corporis caput est, non alieni. Si caput est ecclesię Romanus pontifex, omnino suæ est caput, non alienę. Igitur eius quæ Christi est caput esse non potest, nisi facturi sumus ex ecclesia monstrum biceps. Imò quod adhuc absurdius est, nisi daturi sumus ecclesiæ electorum non simpliciciter duo capita, quæ sint æqualia & forma & conditione, & dignitate, & sensu, & spiritu, & facultate, sed in his omnibus omnium à se inuicem diuersissima, vnum terrenum, alterum cœleste, vnum mortale, alterum immortale, vnum in peccatis conceptū & natum, alterum à peccato alienissimum, vnum inconstans, & post mortem prioris alteri successione alterabile, alterum idem & perpetuum, vnum in cuius pectoris scrinio inhabitet, indeque promanet omnis plenitudo nō potestatis, non pietatis, non iustitiæ, non sanctæ intelligentię, sed fraudis, doli, malitiæ & nequitiæ, superbiæ, mendacij, auaricię, simoniæ, & omnis generis pessimarum cupiditatum ac libidinum, alterum in quo habitet omnis plenitudo diuinitatis, gratiæ, sapientiæ, iustitiæ, & spiritualium charismatum, quæ corpori suo largiter communicat, vnum quod sit pestis & perditio, alterum quod sit salus & vita, vnum quod disturbet & confundat omnia, cœlestia & terrestria, diuina & humana, alterum quod conciliet omnia tà terrena quàm cœlestia. Tam diuersis capitibus, obsecro, quomodo vnum & idem ecclesię corpus subijci poterit? Quid quod Romanum hoc caput nec ab Indię, Indiæ, nec Persiæ, nec Syrię, nec Asiæ, nec Aphricę, sed à paucis quibusdam, aliarum respectu, Europæ ecclesijs agnoscitur? An arctabimus ecclesiam Christi in solam Europam? Absit. Ergo nasçetur nobis aliud monstrum ecclesię, non modo bicipitis, sed & bicorporis, cuius unum corpus sit biceps, alterum acephalon. Neq; enim eius ecclesiæ quę Romanum caput non agnoscit, Christum esse caput concedunt, neq; in ea quæ Romano capiti subiecta est, Christum unà cum suo pontifice, capitis tenere eminentiam affirmare verentur. Ab sint hęc portenta à vera Christi ecclesia, de adulterina viderint qui illam pro vera amplectuntur. Sed pergamus:
units.tr: Today people contend that the Roman pontiff is the head of the Church. As far as I am concerned, I readily grant this, provided that the Church is subject to the one who rules over it in all things. But the Church is a body made up of a multitude of believers and held together by the unity of religion; in this sense the Jews and the Turks also have their own Church. Moreover, each head is the head of its own body, not of another's. If the Roman pontiff is the head of the Church, he is certainly the head of his own Church, not of another's. Therefore he cannot be the head of that Church which belongs to Christ, unless we are going to make from the Church a two-headed monster. Indeed, what is even more absurd, unless we are going to grant that the Church of the elect has not simply two heads, equal in form, condition, dignity, sense, spirit and power, but two that are utterly different from one another in all these respects: one earthly, the other heavenly; one mortal, the other immortal; one conceived and born in sins, the other most remote from sin; one inconstant and liable to be changed, after the death of the former, by succession to the other, the other the same and perpetual; one in whose breast there dwells, and from whom there flows forth, every fulness not of power, piety, justice or holy understanding, but of fraud, deceit, malice and wickedness, pride, lying, avarice, simony, and every kind of most wicked desire and lust; the other in whom dwells all the fulness of the Godhead, of grace, wisdom, justice and spiritual gifts, which he generously shares with his body; one who is a plague and destruction, the other who is salvation and life; one who disturbs and confounds all things, heavenly and earthly, divine and human, the other who reconciles all things, earthly as well as heavenly. With such different heads, I ask you, how can one and the same body of the Church be made subject? What is more, this Roman head is acknowledged not by India, nor by Persia, nor by Syria, nor by Asia, nor by Africa, but only by a few Churches of Europe, which are few in comparison with the others. Shall we confine the Church of Christ to Europe alone? Far from it. Therefore there would arise for us another monster of the Church, not only two-headed but also two-bodied, one body with a head and the other headless [ἀκέφαλον]. For those who do not acknowledge the Roman head do not concede that Christ is the head of that Church, and those who are subject to the Roman head do not hesitate to affirm that Christ, together with his pontiff, holds the eminence of the head. Let these portents be far from the true Church of Christ; let those who embrace that adulterous church as the true one see to it. But let us proceed.

units.la: CAPVT vero Christi Deus inquit.) Diximus per hanc capitis & corporis metaphoram summam eiusdem naturę & essentię vnitatem, & simul competentis discretionis ordinem ex primi. Vnitas inter Deum & Christum omnium est vnitissima, quod naturam & essentiam diuinitatis concernit. Quare non est hic locus Arrianis. Licet enim caput Christi sit Deus, id tamen vsqueadeo nô tollit diuinitatis à Christo naturam, vt eam magis requirat & confirmet. Etenim nisi eadem vtrobique sit natura, metaphora hæc capitis & corporis locum habere non poterit. Quod autem caput superius est corpore, non est hoc ad diuinam naturá qua filius æqualis est patri, sed ad humanam referendum, cuius ipse respectu dixit: Pater maior me est. Et, Vado ad Deum meum & Deum vestrum, & quæ alia sunt huiusmodi.
units.tr: "But the head of Christ is God," he says. Through this metaphor of head and body we have said that there is the highest unity of the same nature and essence, and at the same time the order of distinction that belongs to it, as shown above. The unity between God and Christ is the closest of all, so far as the nature and essence of the Godhead is concerned. So there is no place here for the Arians. For although the head of Christ is God, this does not so far take away from Christ the nature of the Godhead that it rather requires and confirms it. Indeed, unless the nature were the same on both sides, this metaphor of head and body could have no place. But that the head is superior to the body does not refer to the divine nature, by which the Son is equal to the Father, but must be referred to the human nature, in respect of which he said: "The Father is greater than I," and "I go to my God and your God," and other things of this kind.

units.la: Nos hic admonemur, primùm ex Deo esse omnia, tanquam ex fonte omnium. Deinde per Christum illi genus humanum coniungi, idque mediatione non vulgari, sed tali quæ vnitate eiusdem illi cum patre, & nobis cum illo naturę constet. Tertò in ipso genere nostro positam esse coniunctionis huius imaginem, copulatione maris & fœminę, quę tum esset perfectior ac felicior, si ad vnitatë Dei & Christi proprius accedens, non modo carne & natura eadem, sed eodem quoque cœlesti spiritu constaret. Verùm hunc defectum philanthropia Dei in Christo capite nostro sarcire dignatae est, in quo perfecta est non solum naturę & essentiæ diuinæ cum humana, sed & eiusdem spiritus coniunctio. Quare quod hic dicit: Caput vero Christi Deus, non sic est accipiendum à nobis, vt Christum separatim inspiciamus, sed ut nos in illo, tanquam capite comprehensos, supremo capiti Deo subiungi, atque ita illum hac intermediatione, omnia esse in omnibus sentiamus, donec ea plenitudo accepto à Christo regno in fine mundi consummatissima reddatur.
units.tr: Here we are reminded, first, that all things are from God, as from the fountain of all. Second, that the human race is joined to him through Christ, and this by a mediation that is not ordinary but one that rests on the unity of the same nature between him and the Father, and between him and us. Third, that the image of this union is set in our own kind, in the joining of male and female, which would be more perfect and happier if it came nearer to the unity of God and Christ, and consisted not only of the same flesh and nature but also of the same heavenly Spirit. But God in his philanthropy [φιλανθρωπία] has deigned to make good this defect in Christ our head, in whom is achieved a perfect union not only of the divine and human nature and essence, but also of the same Spirit. Therefore what he says here, "But the head of Christ is God," is not to be taken by us as if we were to look at Christ separately, but rather as meaning that we, comprehended in him as in our head, are subjected to God, the supreme head; and thus we understand that through this intermediary God may be all in all, until that fulness is brought to its complete end at the close of the world, when Christ has received the kingdom.

units.la: Hactenus sententiam hanc Apostoli utcunque & separatim inspeximus, qua omnis uiri caput Christum, mulieris uirû, Christi Deum esse dicit, iam uidendum est, quorsum eam in præsenti causa induxerit, quidq; & quomodo ex illa colligat.
units.tr: Up to now we have looked, in a general way and separately, at this sentiment of the Apostle, by which he says that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God. Now we must see to what end he has introduced it in the present matter, and what and how he draws from it.

units.la: Omnis uir orans aut prophetás quicquam habens in capite, probro afficitca put suum. Omnis uero mulier orans aut prophetans non velato capite, dehonestat caput suum.
units.tr: Every man who prays or prophesies with something on his head shames his head. But every woman who prays or prophesies with her head not covered dishonours her head.

units.la: Hoc est quod expremisso axiomate inferre voluit. Poterat dicere, Ergo omnis vir orans & prophetans, aperto, & omnis mulier oras, &c. tecto sit capite, verùm ut sententiam hanc præmisso axiomati accommodet, & simul id quod in illorum ecclesia fiebat, redarguat, dicit: Omnis vir orans aut prophetans quicquâ habens in capite, probro afficit caput suum. Omnis vero mulier orans aut prophetás non velato capite, dehonestat caput suum.
units.tr: This is what he wanted to draw from the stated axiom. He could have said, "Therefore every man who prays and prophesies with his head uncovered, and every woman who prays with her head covered, etc." But to fit this statement to the preceding axiom, and at the same time to rebuke what was happening in their congregation, he says: Every man who prays or prophesies with something on his head shames his head. But every woman who prays or prophesies with her head not covered dishonours her head.

units.la: Nihil hic est obscuri in sensu. Verùm de illo disputari potest, quomodo consequatur hoc ex præcedenti axiomate: Deus est caput Christi, Christus viri, vir mulieris, ergo caput suum dehonestat vir, si tecto. & mulier si aperto capite oret aut prophetet.
units.tr: There is nothing obscure in the meaning here. But one may ask how this follows from the preceding axiom: God is the head of Christ, Christ of the man, the man of the woman. Therefore the man dishonours his head if he is covered, and the woman if she prays or prophesies with her head uncovered.

units.la: Primum, si velamen capitis dedecorosum est in viro, quur non & in muliere? Rursus, si nuditas capitis inhonesta est in muliere, quomodo non & in viro, cum in Christo Iesu nihil sit discriminis inter virum & mulierem? Dein de quid iniuriæ accidit hinc vel Deo vel Christo, vel ipsis viris & mulieribus?
units.tr: First, if a covering on the head is disgraceful in a man, why is it not also in a woman? Again, if bareness of the head is dishonourable in a woman, how is it not also in a man, since in Christ Jesus there is no distinction between man and woman? Next, what harm comes from this either to God or to Christ, or to the men and women themselves?

units.la: Respondeo paucis. Quod gratiam regni Christi attinet, qua per fidem in sanguinem illius saluamur, nihil discriminis est inter virum & mulierem. Hic nulla est viro prærogatiua, nullum mulieri detrimentum. Verùm in externa politia non modo mundana, sed & ecclesiastica discriminis multum est inter duos sexus virilem & muliebrem, sic vt viro liceat, quod mulieri sit illicitum, & contrà mulierem deceat quod viro sit inconueniens. Habet quisque sexus suum decorum, cuius in sæculo quo quę publicæ honestatis gratia magna habetur ratio, tanto in ecclesia maior habenda, quanto illi plus est sapientiæ ac gratię diuinitus concessum, unde illud est Apostolo i: Quæcunque sunt vera, quæcunque honesta, quæcunque iusta, quęcunque pura, quęcunque accommoda, quęcunque boni nominis, &c. hęc cogitate. Ratio autem decori primaria & huc pertinens, in utroque uirili ac muliebri sexu ab ordine dependet, quo quæcunque infra Deum sunt, suis sunt capitibus subordinata; quibus etiam singulis hoc primarium ἀρχὴ est, ut suo unumquodque capiti competenter respondeat illiq; sese in omnibus accommodet. Mulieri caput uir est, uiro Christus, Christo Deus. Habet ergo mulier suum mi-spat, quo subest ui ro tanquam suo capiti, uir suum, quo præest mulieri tanquam corpori, & subest Christo tanquam capiti suo. Competit ergo mulieri subiectionis humilitas & pudor, uiro præeminentię prærogatiua. Et secundum hanc diuersitatem diuersum etiam est illorum prepon in habitu externo. Ita ut non est eadem illis uestiendi corcorporis, ita non est eadem tegendi capitis ratio. De capite meminit Apostolus, quia quod in eo membro peccabatur, corrigere statuit. Capiti muliebri competit velamen, symbolum subiectionis, virili vero aperta nuditas, symbolum praeminentiae. Mulier ergo, dum tecto capite apparet, & orat in ecclesia, seruat suum de corum, & cohonestat suum caput, virum videlicet, cui se manifesto subiectionis symbolo sub iectam esse profitetur. Vir contra, dum libero & aperto capite in ecclesia Dei orat & prophetat, suum & ipse decorum retinet, & suum caput Christum cohonestat, à quo virilis excellentiae gloriam accepit.
units.tr: I answer briefly. As far as the grace of Christ's kingdom is concerned, by which we are saved through faith in his blood, there is no distinction between man and woman. Here the man has no prerogative, and the woman suffers no disadvantage. But in external order, not only civil but also ecclesiastical, there is a great difference between the two sexes, male and female, so that some things are permitted to the man which are forbidden to the woman, and on the other hand some things are fitting for the woman which are unbecoming for the man. Each sex has its own decorum. In the world, where the claims of public decency are held in great regard, so much more must they be regarded in the Church, in proportion as God has given the one more wisdom and grace. Hence the Apostle's words: "Whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report," etc.; consider these things. The primary principle of decorum, which bears on this matter, in both the male and the female sex depends on order, by which whatever is beneath God is subordinated to its own head. For each one the first principle [ἀρχή] is that it should fittingly correspond to its own head and accommodate itself to him in all things. The head of the woman is the man, the head of the man is Christ, the head of Christ is God. Therefore the woman has her own station, by which she is subject to the man as to her head, and the man has his, by which he is over the woman as his body and is subject to Christ as his head. Humility and modesty therefore befit the woman, and the prerogative of pre-eminence befits the man. Corresponding to this difference, their outward dress also differs. Just as the way of clothing the body is not the same for both, so the way of covering the head is not the same. The Apostle speaks of the head because he has decided to correct what was done wrongly on that part of the body. A veil befits the female head, a symbol of subjection; open bareness befits the male head, a symbol of pre-eminence. Therefore the woman, when she appears with her head covered and prays in the Church, keeps her own decorum and honours her head, namely the man, to whom she declares by a clear sign of subjection that she is subject. The man, on the other hand, when he prays and prophesies in the Church of God with his head free and uncovered, also keeps his own decorum and honours his head Christ, from whom he has received the glory of male excellence.

units.la: Hoc igitur sensu ex praemisso axiomate colligit Apostolus, quoniam vir caput est mulieris, viri vero Christus, consequi, ut mulier dehonestet caput suum, si nudo, vir vero suum, si tecto capite oret aut prophetet, propterea quod hac inuersione decorum suum abijciant, & ordinis diuinitus instituti leges transgrediantur. Haec de viro & muliere infert ex ordine subordinatorum, quae praecedenti axiomate posuit, unde de Deo quoque & Christo multo poterat praestantiora inferre. Verum quia illa non faciebant ad propositum, ea tantum intulit, quae ad causam quam agebat, pertinere videbatur. Videamus nunc ipsa verba.
units.tr: In this sense, then, the Apostle draws from the stated axiom that, since the man is the head of the woman and Christ the head of the man, it follows that the woman dishonours her head if she prays or prophesies with her head bare, and the man dishonours his if he does so with his head covered; because by this reversal they cast off their own decorum and transgress the laws of the order divinely instituted. He draws these conclusions about man and woman from the order of subordinates which he set out in the preceding axiom; from it he could have drawn much more excellent conclusions about God and Christ too. But since those did not serve his purpose, he drew only those which seemed to pertain to the case he was dealing with. Let us now look at the words themselves.

units.la: OMNIS vir orans, inquit, aut prophetas.) Quemadmodum supra diximus, non loquitur Apostolus de uxoratis tantum, sed & adolescentibus, iuuenibus, senibus, agamis & viduis, hoc est, de toto virili sexu. Consimili modo B cum dicit, & omnis mulier, mulieris vocabulo virgines quoque & viduas, non maritatas tantum complectitur, si ut hac sententia etiam filias Philippi diaconi virgines, orantes ac prophetantes constringat.
units.tr: "Every man praying," he says, "or prophesying." As we said above, the Apostle does not speak only of married men but also of youths, young men, old men, the unmarried and widowers, that is, of the whole male sex. In the same way, when he says "every woman," the word "woman" embraces not only married women but also virgins and widows, so that by this statement he binds even the virgin daughters of Philip the deacon, who prayed and prophesied.

units.la: ORANS, inquit, & prophetans.) Orabant gratias agebant, psallebant, & prophetabant in coetu fidelium liberè & palam qui volebant pro abundantia spiritus, qui initio nascentis ecclesiae iuxta vaticinium Ioelis in corda fidelium caelitus infundebatur. Orationis vocabulo Psalmos quoque & gratiarum actionem comprehendit. Prophetia tum erat in ecclesia duplex. Vna, qua docendo praedicabant, altera, qua futura vaticinando praedicebant. Nihil vetat, quo minus Apostolum hic de utraque loqui sentiamus, quandoquidem utranque, in usu fuisse constat. Quanquam non repugno, si quis vel de priori, vel de posteriori tantum intellexerit.
units.tr: "Praying," he says, "and prophesying." They prayed, gave thanks, sang psalms, and prophesied freely and openly in the assembly of the faithful, those who wished, through the abundance of the Spirit, which at the beginning of the rising Church was poured from heaven into the hearts of the faithful, according to the prophecy of Joel. By the word "praying" he also includes psalms and thanksgiving. At that time there were two kinds of prophecy in the Church. One was preaching by teaching; the other was foretelling future things by prophesying. Nothing prevents us from thinking that the Apostle here speaks of both, since it is clear that both were in use. Still, I do not object if someone understands him to mean only the former or only the latter.

units.la: QVI CQVAM habes in capite, inquit.) In Graeco est, κατὰ κεφαλῆς ἔχων, id est, in capite habens. Et exponunt nonnulli non solum de uelte qua caput inuoluere, uel pileo, quo illud obtegere solebant, sed & de coma & capillo, qua si etiam qui comam habet, recte aliquid in capite habere dicatur, qui sane loquendi modus eum apud nos sensum non habet.
units.tr: "Having something on his head," he says. In Greek it is κατὰ κεφαλῆς ἔχων, that is, "having on the head." Some interpret it not only of a veil with which to cover the head, or a cap with which they were accustomed to cover it, but also of hair and locks; for one who has hair is rightly said to have something on his head. Yet this manner of speaking does not carry that sense among us.

units.la: PROBRO, inquit, afficit caput suum.) Ex posuimus no de capite naturali, sed metapho-
units.tr: "Shames his head," he says. We have explained this not of the natural head

units.la: rico, secundum praemissum axioma, quo Christus caput viri, & vir mulieris esse dicitur. Verum nolim admodum reluctari si quis exponat non de Christo, metaphorico viri capite, sed de eo quod inter orandum & prophetandum contra sexus sui decorum aliquo tegumento operit, & consimiliter de capite mulieris, quod illa denudat in coetu sacro. Etenim non solum Christum vir, & virum mulier, sed & sua ipsorum capita dehonestant, dum illa citra decorum sexus sui vel tegendo vel aperiendo in ecclesia fidelium non ornant, ut putant, sed deformant.
units.tr: but of the metaphorical head, according to the stated axiom, by which Christ is said to be the head of the man, and the man of the woman. Yet I would not strongly object if someone explained it not of Christ, the metaphorical head of the man, but of that which in praying and prophesying a man covers with some covering against the decorum of his sex, and similarly of the woman's head, which she bares in the sacred assembly. For not only does the man dishonour Christ and the woman her husband, but they also dishonour their own heads, when they do not adorn, as they think, but disfigure them, by covering or uncovering them in the assembly of the faithful contrary to the decorum of their sex.

units.la: Obseruandum autem est, quod haec sententia no damnat virum, si extra coetum sacrum vatur pileo pro suo commodo, aut mulierem, si domi suae capite sit aperto. Neque enim simpliciter dicit: Omnis vir quicquam habens in capite, neque: Omnis mulier capite existens non velato, deturpat caput suum, sed cum specificatione: Omnis vir orans aut prophetans, quicquam habens in capite, &, Omnis mulier orans & prophetans non velato capite, dehonestat caput suum.
units.tr: It must also be noted that this statement does not condemn a man who wears a cap outside the sacred assembly for his own convenience, nor a woman who goes with her head uncovered in her own house. For he does not simply say, "Every man having anything on his head," nor "Every woman existing with her head not covered dishonours her head," but with a specification: "Every man praying or prophesying, having something on his head," and "Every woman praying and prophesying with her head not covered dishonours her head."

units.la: Illud quoque admonuerunt nonnulli, non cogi hac sententia ministrum verbi, publicè in ecclesia docentem, quo minus si frigus sit, pileolo inter docendum utatur, modo initio ser monis capite sit libero ac nudo, cui moderationi facile assentiero, praesertim in senibus. Eos tamen excusare non possum, qui & aetate iuniores, & tempore efftiuo, pileati dicunt ad ecclesiam, haud secus, quàm si sententia haec A postoli ad ipsos nequaquam pertineat. Horum nonnulli caput suum dehonestant pileo, & digitos ornant auro.
units.tr: Some have also pointed out that this statement does not compel a minister of the Word, teaching publicly in the Church, to refrain from using a small cap while teaching if it is cold, provided that at the beginning of the sermon his head is free and bare. I can readily agree to this moderation, especially for the elderly. Yet I cannot excuse those who, being younger in age and in summer, come to the Church wearing caps, as though this statement of the Apostle did not in any way apply to them. Some of these dishonour their head with a cap, and adorn their fingers with gold.

units.la: OMNIS vero mulier orās aut prophetās.) Quaerunt hic, quomodo mulierem caput suum dehonestare dicat, si prophetet capite aperto, cum infrà circa calcem cap. 14. praecipiat illis ut in ecclesia taceant, eo quod turpe sit mulieri in ecclesia loqui. Et 1. Tim. 2. dicat: Ceterum mulieri docere non permitto. Quid opus est, inquiunt, praecipere ne capite aperto prophetet mulier, cum hoc illi nec tecto quidem facere liceat? Respondeo: Muliebrem temeritatem coercet, ne ut sunt plerunque loquaculae, ad docendum ac prophetandum sexus sui oblitae prosiliant, ubi vetat eas prorsus in ecclesia loqui.
