Verùm interea non extinguit spiritu, quo nonnullae inflatae futura praedicendo prophetabant, quales fuerunt filiae Philippi diaconi, & aliae multae, quae prophetarunt secundum vaticinium Ioelis cap. 2. ubi sic legimus: Et erit post ista, effundam spiritum meum super omnem carnem, & prophetabunt filij ueltri & filiae vestrae. Propter tales pronunciat, quod caput suum dehonestent, si nudo capite oret aut prophetent, de caeteris aliam laturus sententiam, si ad munus docendi etiam tectis capitibus prorupissent.
units.tr: "Every woman who prays or prophesies." Here people ask how a woman dishonours her head if she prophesies with her head uncovered, when near the end of chapter 14 he orders women to keep silent in the Church, because it is shameful for a woman to speak in the Church, and in 1 Timothy 2 he says: "But I do not permit a woman to teach." Why, they ask, should he need to forbid a woman to prophesy with her head uncovered, when she is not allowed to do it even with her head covered? I answer that he restrains female rashness, lest women, who are commonly talkative, rush forward to teach and prophesy and forget their sex, and so he forbids them altogether to speak in the Church. Yet meanwhile he does not extinguish the Spirit, by which some women, swollen with pride, used to prophesy by foretelling the future. Such were the daughters of Philip the deacon, and many others, who prophesied according to the prophecy of Joel chapter 2, where we read: "And it shall come to pass after these things that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy." It is of such women that he says they dishonour their head if they pray or prophesy with the head bare; about the others he would have given a different judgement, had they burst forth to the office of teaching even with their heads covered.

units.la: Alij aliter ad hanc quaestionem respondent, Apostolum uidelicet vnum improbando non probare alterum,sed improbatione illius differre in locum alium. Sane ita habet. Nó mox actum probat,qui modu illius speciali de causa improbat. Lyranus sic. Dicendum quod Apostolus intelligit ibi, 1.Tim.2. de sermocinationibus & doctrinationibus publicis, hic vero de orationibus & informationibus quas mulieres religiosæ in suis collegijs faciunt, quę fierent indicenter capite non velato. Hęc ille: defendens muliebrem& anilem Nonnarū temeritatem,qua sibi præeminentiam, & magisterium in alias fœminas eiusdem superstitionis consortes sumūt, inq; eorum collegijs sedendo præcipiunt ac statuunt, quasi Apostolo quicquam de illis venerit in mentem.
units.tr: Others answer this question differently, namely that the Apostle, by disapproving of one thing, does not approve of another, but defers the other to another place by disapproving of the first. Indeed it is so: he who disapproves of one practice for a special reason does not at once approve another. Lyra says this: "It must be said that the Apostle there, in 1 Timothy 2, is speaking of public speaking and teaching, but here of the prayers and instructions which religious women give in their own assemblies, which would be done improperly with the head not veiled." Thus he, defending the womanish and old-wifely rashness of some nuns, who claim for themselves precedence and mastery over other women who share the same superstition, and who sit in their assemblies and give orders and make rules, as if the Apostle had never thought of such things.

units.la: Vnum enim est & idem cum ea quæ rasa est. Quod si nō velatur mulier, tondeatur etiam. Si vero turpe mulieri est tonderi aut radi, obueletur.
units.tr: For it is one and the same as a woman who has been shaved. But if a woman is not veiled, let her also be shorn. But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her cover herself.

units.la: Apparet id quod in præcedenti dixit: deho nestat caput suū, de nudo mulieris capite, nō de viro esse intelligendum. Reddit enim hic illius rationem, eamq; talem,quæ nequeat ad virum referri, quem mulieris caput esse dixit: Omnis vero mulier, inquit, orās aut prophetans non velato capite dehonestat caput suū. Quomodo? Vnum enim est & idem, inquit, cum ea quæ rasa est. Hoc est. Quia sic in cœtu sacro nudo capite comparens nihil differt à rasa ac tonsa,sed perinde est ac si sit rasa.In Græco est, ἐν γὰρ καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ ἔστι τῇ ξυρημένῃ,quod legi potest etiam hoc pacto, vnū enim est & idem cum eo quod rasum est, vt referatur ad nudū mulieris caput, & subintelligatur post illud τῇ ξυρημένῃ, τῇ κεφαλῇ, id est, vnum enim & idē est cum raso capite. Nihil tamen refert vtram lectionem teneamus.Sensus enim idē manet.
units.tr: It is clear that what he said above, "dishonours her head," must be understood of the woman's bare head, not of the man. For he here gives the reason for it, and it is such a reason as cannot be referred to the man, whom he called the head of the woman. "Every woman," he says, "who prays or prophesies with her head not veiled dishonours her head." How so? "For it is one and the same," he says, "as the woman who is shaved." That is: because a woman who appears in the sacred assembly with a bare head differs in no way from one who is shaved and clipped, but is just as if she were shaved. In the Greek it is ἐν γὰρ καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ ἔστι τῇ ξυρημένῃ ["for it is one and the same as the shaven woman"]. This can also be read thus: "for it is one and the same as that which is shaved," so that it refers to the woman's bare head, and one understands after it τῇ ξυρημένῃ, τῇ κεφαλῇ ["the shaven one, the head"], that is, "for it is one and the same as a shaven head." Yet it makes no difference which reading we hold, since the sense remains the same.

units.la: Reddit igitur sententiæ suæ rationem sum ptam à turpitudine rasæ vel tonsæ mulieris. Sane ita habet. Communi sensu perturpe est fœmina rasa. Nec quicquam est,à quo mulier magis abhorreat quàm à turpitudine. Sic e-nim natura cōparata est, vt cupiat placere vi-ris. Et hoc studio multa est in ornādo suo cor-pore, capite præsertim, cuius capillos studio-sissime nutrit ac componit. Argumentatur i-gitur in hunc modum. Cum sexus hic mulie-bris natura à corporis sui,maxime capitis,tur pitudine abhorreat, quomodo sic desipit mu-lier, vt in cœtu sacro caput suum dehonestet? Dehonestat autem illud, dum inter orandum aut prophetandum apertum ac nudum osten-tat. Quare? Quia nuditas illa muliebris capi-tis nihil differt à tonsura. Norunt autem om-nes quam turpe sit mulier tonsa ac rasa. Con-sequens igitur est, vt veletur, si non vult tur-pis haberi.
units.tr: He therefore gives the reason for his statement, taken from the shamefulness of a shaved or shorn woman. Indeed it is so: by common sense a shaved woman is most shameful. Nor is there anything from which a woman shrinks more than from shame. For nature has so constituted her that she desires to please men, and for this reason she takes great pains in adorning her body, especially her head, whose hair she most carefully grows and arranges. The argument therefore runs thus: since the female sex by nature shrinks from shame in its body, above all in its head, how can a woman be so foolish as to dishonour her head in the sacred assembly? She dishonours it, however, when, while praying or prophesying, she shows it uncovered and bare. Why? Because that bareness of the female head differs in no way from shearing. Now everyone knows how shameful a shorn or shaved woman is. It follows, then, that she should veil herself, if she does not wish to be thought shameful.

units.la: Sunt hæc satis perspicua. Verum dicit hic quisquá: Atqui mulier ob id ipsum caput suū denudat, & capillos vel demissos vel studiose compositos ostētat, quod se putat hoc pacto posse placere viris, tam abest, vt nuditate hac
units.tr: These things are quite plain. But someone here may say: "Yet a woman bares her head for this very reason, and displays her hair, whether long or carefully arranged, because she thinks that in this way she can please men; so far is she from thinking that her head is disgraced by this bareness"

units.la: caput suū deturpari existimet. Et Apostolus ipse paulo infrà comam mulieri gloriæ esse fa-tetur. Quomodo ergo nudū illius caput, hoc est,à velo liberū,perinde est turbe ac si sit ra-sum? Rasum quidē communi sensu turpe est, apertum vero ad capillos vsq;,præsertim si illi sint insigniores non turpe sed spectabile ha-betur. Quare ratio hæc Apostoli cōmuni sen-su in eo cōstari non potest quod dicit: Vnum enim & idem est cum ea quæ est rasa.
units.tr: Yet the Apostle himself, a little below, admits that long hair is a glory to a woman. How, then, is her bare head, that is, free from a veil, just as shameful as if it were shaved? A shaved head is certainly shameful by common sense, but a head uncovered down to the hair, especially if the hair is rather fine, is not regarded as shameful but as becoming. Therefore this argument of the Apostle cannot rest on common sense in the point where he says: "For it is one and the same as the woman who is shaved."

units.la: Respondeo. Habet hæc ratio interpretatio-nem,cuius veritas non ex communi sensu, sed ab eo dependet, quod illos initio causæ huius scire voles dixit: Sed volo vos scire, quod o-mnis viri caput Christus est,caput autē mulie-ris vir,&caput Christi Deus. Hęc scientia nec tum erat,neq; nunc est communis omniū, sed pendet à cognitione ordinis à Deo dispositi. Quemadmodum igitur ex hoc ordine subor-dinatorum capitum consequitur turpe esse vi-ro, si tecto,& mulieri si aperto ac nudo capite oret,eaq; turpitudine dehonestari ipsorū ca-pita, ita & illud consequitur, quod hic vnum & idem esse dicit, si nudo capite oret mulier, ac si sit rasa vel tonsa. In oculis videlicet Dei, & secundum iudicium ordinis à Deo constitu-ti,secūdum quem viri decorum est nudo ora-re ac prophetare capite. Hoc cū facit mulier, decorum suū abijcit, & quod viri est vsurpat. Abiecto autem decoro ordinis Dei,non hone-statur capillis sed magis deturpatur, vt nihil iam in conspectu Dei differat à tonsa vel rasa. Sic quod naturæ ornamentum est vertitur in turpitudinem coram Deo, si decorum sexus diuinitus cōstitutum abijciatur. Tonsum esse viri est,nō mulieris. Mulier nudo capite orás, quatenus decorum suum abijcit, hactenus ad id quod viri est aspirat. Quare nihil differt ab eo quod omnino viri est, à tonsura videlicet vel rasura capitis,quādoquidem sexus sui πρὸς abiecit.
units.tr: I answer: this argument has an interpretation whose truth depends not on common sense but on what he wished them to know at the beginning of this matter, when he said: "But I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ, the head of the woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God." This knowledge was not then, nor is it now, common to all, but depends on knowledge of the order appointed by God. Therefore, just as from this order of subordinate heads it follows that it is shameful for a man to pray with his head covered, and for a woman with her head bare, and that by this shame their heads are dishonoured, so it also follows what he here says, that a woman who prays with her head bare is one and the same as a shaved or shorn woman: namely in the eyes of God, and according to the judgement of the order established by God, according to which it is fitting for a man to pray and prophesy with his head bare. When a woman does this, she casts off her proper decorum and assumes what belongs to the man. But once the decorum of God's order is cast off, the head is not honoured by its hair but rather disgraced, so that in the sight of God it differs in nothing from a shorn or shaved head. Thus what is an ornament of nature is turned into shame before God, if the decorum of the sex divinely appointed is cast off. To be shorn belongs to a man, not a woman. A woman praying with her head bare, insofar as she casts off her decorum, to that extent aspires to what belongs to the man. Therefore she differs in nothing from that which is wholly the man's, namely from the shearing or shaving of the head, since she has cast off in respect of her sex her own sex.

units.la: Cosimili modo poterat & de viro dicere: Omnis vir orans aut prophetans tecto capite dehonestat caput suum. Vnum enim & idem est ac si sit peplo muliebri obuolutus. Quod si non orat capite nudo,obueletur etiam peplo. Si vero turpe est viro,velari & obuolui peplo, denudetur. Quasi dicat: Quoniam obiectio vi-rilis sexus decoro ea quæ mulierum sunt asse-ctat,digno est,qui instar mulierū peplo obuol-uatur. Nam nihil differt ab eo quod est mulie-rum. Sic cogitabat,puto, abbatissa quædam, quæ anno millesimo quingentesimo vicesimo quinto oppressa rusticorum seditione suos ru-sticos in pœnam seditionis sic mulctauit, vt quotquot erat à cede superstites peplum mu-liebre non domi modo, sed & foris in agro, in foro,& in ecclesia gestare cogeret. Hac igno-minia muliebres illorum animos dignos esse cesuit.Verum Apostolus de viris hic tacet,sed mulieres vehementius, quemadmodum & in sequentibus, vrget,propterea quod maiore li-centia hac in re peccabant.
units.tr: In a similar way he could have said of the man: "Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonours his head. For it is one and the same as if he were wrapped in a woman's veil. But if he does not pray with his head bare, let him also be covered with a veil. And if it is shameful for a man to be veiled and wrapped in a veil, let him be uncovered." As if he were saying: since a man who imitates the things of women in a manner unbecoming to his sex is worthy to be wrapped in a veil like a woman, for he differs in nothing from what belongs to women. So I suppose thought a certain abbess who, in the year 1525, when a peasants' revolt had overwhelmed her, punished her peasants for the sedition by compelling every one of those who survived the slaughter to wear a woman's veil, not only at home but also outside in the fields, in the marketplace and in the church. By this disgrace she judged their manly spirits worthy of womanish ones. But the Apostle here says nothing about men, while he presses the women more vehemently, as he does also in what follows, because they sinned with greater licence in this matter.

units.la: QVOD si non velatur mulier, inquit,tódea tur.) in Græco est,ϰὶ γυνὴ καταϰαλύπτεται γυνή, id elt,si enim non obuelatur mulier. Rationale voculam hoc loco tanquam ociofam obmit timus,ne fit incómodo sensui. Et hanc ob cau sam in nonnullis Latinis exemplaribus non legitur.Conuenientius esset legere,ϰὶ ὑπ,id elt, si igitur,vt sit illatio ex præcedenti.
units.tr: "But if a woman is not veiled," he says, [καὶ γυνὴ καταϰαλύπτεται, "and let the woman be veiled"] in the Greek reads "and let the woman be veiled," that is, "for if a woman is not veiled." We pass over the little word "then" here as superfluous, lest it disturb the sense. For this reason it is not read in some Latin copies. It would be more suitable to read [καὶ ὑπ-], that is, "if therefore," so that the statement follows from what goes before.

units.la: SI vero turpe est mulieri tonderi aut radi, obueletur.) Turpe hoc esse notum est omni bus illis nationibus,quæ aliquo adhuc natu ræ sensu tenentur.Secus uero apud illas, qua rum mulieres vulgo, ut audio, tódentur, uiri vero comati incedunt. Debebant hinc nonnç & moniales admoneri, quàm sit alienum à de coro naturæ, quod tondentur. Obuelatur qui dem in publico,idq; non vulgari tantum mo do ied & singulari ac tinćto panniculo, religio nis indice, intus tamen sunt tonsæ. Quoisum tondentur, cum sint velatæ? Tonsuram Apo stolus tam nō requirit in Christiana fœmina, vt palàm etiam turpem esse dicat. Illæ vero sic dementantur,vt nisi tondeátur religiosas esse se non posse putent quasi Christiana religio re absurdam & naturæ contrariam poscat. Hoc videlicet spectabat concilium Gangrense, cū Can.17 sic statueret: Quęcunq; mulier religio ni iudicans conuenire,comam sibi amputaue- rit, quam Deus aduelamen eius & ad memo- riam ubiećtionis illi dedit, tanquam resolues ubiećtionis,anathema sit.Hæc ibi. Et de- mentatio ista eoufq; creuit, vt cõiugatę quoq; tonsuram monasticam religionis gratia acci- piant,quas hodie Tertianas vocát. Sub peplo gestant tófuram,qua se partim monachis par- tim maritis suis obstrićtas esse profitétur.De- teitandum plane maritorum genus, qui vxo- res suas cum monachis non modo occulta so- cietate sed & manifesta professione scienter communicant.
units.tr: "But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her be veiled." That this is shameful is known to all those nations that are still held by some sense of nature. But it is otherwise among those whose women, as I hear, are commonly shorn, while the men go about with long hair. Here some nuns too ought to be warned how far it is contrary to the dignity of nature that they are shorn. Indeed they are veiled in public, and not with an ordinary cloth only but with a single, dyed scrap that is the sign of their religious life; yet beneath it they are shorn. Why are they shorn if they are veiled? The Apostle does not require tonsure of a Christian woman, so that he would call it openly shameful. But they are so out of their minds that, unless they are shorn, they think they cannot be religious, as if the Christian religion demanded something absurd and contrary to nature. Clearly this is what the Council of Gangra had in view when it laid down in Canon 17: "Any woman who, judging it fitting for religion, cuts off the hair which God gave her as a covering and as a reminder of subjection, as one who dissolves subjection, let her be anathema." So far that council. And this madness has grown so far that married women too take up monastic tonsure for the sake of religion; today they call them Tertiaries. Beneath the veil they wear a tonsure by which they profess themselves bound partly to the monks and partly to their husbands. Plainly this is a kind of husband to be abhorred, who knowingly share their wives with monks, not only in secret fellowship but also in open profession.

units.la: Vir quidem non debet obuelare ca put, cum sit imago & gloria Dei, at mu- lier gloria viri est. Non enim est vir ex muliere,sed mulier ex viro. Neq; enim cōditus est vir propter mulierē,sed mu lier propter virum. Propter hoc debet mulier potestatē habere in capite, vel propter angelos. Alioqui neq; vír abs- que muliere,neq; mulier absq; viro in domino. Nam quemadmodū mulier ex viro est,ita & vir per mulierem,oma vero ex Deo.
units.tr: "For a man indeed ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of the man. For man is not from woman, but woman from man. Neither was man created for the sake of woman, but woman for the sake of man. For this reason the woman ought to have power on her head, because of the angels. Yet neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man, in the Lord. For as the woman is from the man, so also the man is through the woman; but all things are from God."

units.la: Postquam primariam sententiæ suæ ratio nem ad exprimendam denudati inter orandū muliebris capitis turpitudinem explicuit, re- dit ad discriminendum inter viri excellentiā & mulieris humilitatem a subiećtioné, quo alijs adhuc argumentis confirmet, orandum esse mulieri capite obuelato, viro vero nudo & aperto,Vir quidem,inquit, non debet obue lare caput,debet vero mulier.Quare? Quia vir est, inquit, imago & gloria Dei ,mulier vero gloria viri. Argumentatus est initio,ex eo qd vir caput est mulieris, Christus vero caput ui ri, & Deus caput Christi. In præsenti adducit argumentum ex prærogatiua viri,quam habet ex cöditione creationis qua factus est ad ima ginem Dei,telte scriptura Gen.1. Faciamus ho mihem ad imaginem & similitudinē nostram, &præsit piscibus maris,&c. Propter hacquo- que prærogatiuam competit viro,vt capite sit libero&aperto,quandoquidem obuelatio ca- pitis symbolum habet subiećtionis. Quomo- do autē imago Dei sit vir, in Genesi diximus. Propter principatū uidelicet totius orbis ,in quem est ab initio conditus. Et quoniam do- tibus suis ad eam est maiestatem à Deo instru- ćtus,vt cum gloria principatum suum gerere possit,dicit eum non imaginem modo sed & gloriá,hoc est, decus & ornamentū esse Dei, à quo hæc omnia accepit,quemadmodū prin- cipes regni gloria sunt regis.
units.tr: Having explained the chief reason for his opinion, namely the shamefulness of a woman's head uncovered in prayer, he turns to distinguish between the excellence of the man and the humility and subjection of the woman, so that by further arguments he may confirm that a woman must pray with her head covered, but a man with his head bare and open. "A man indeed," he says, "ought not to cover his head, but a woman ought." Why? Because the man, he says, is the image and glory of God, but the woman is the glory of the man. He argued at the start from the fact that the man is the head of the woman, Christ the head of the man, and God the head of Christ. Now he brings an argument from the pre-eminence of the man, which he has from the condition of creation, by which he was made in the image of God, as Scripture attests in Gen. 1: "Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let him rule over the fish of the sea," and so on. Because of this pre-eminence it also belongs to the man to have his head free and uncovered, since the covering of the head is a symbol of subjection. How the man is the image of God we have explained in Genesis: namely, because of his rule over the whole world, into which he was placed from the beginning. And since he is furnished by God with gifts that give him such majesty that he can bear his rule with glory, he says that he is not only the image but also the glory of God, that is, the adornment and ornament of God, from whom he has received all these things, just as the princes of a kingdom are the glory of the king.

units.la: AT mulier,inquit,gloria viri est.) Id est de- cus& ornamentum viri. Non quod ab illa sit condita, aut quæ habet ab illo acceper.t, sed quod ad illū pertinet, & ex illo ac propter il- lum est facta. Debet igitur illa uelare caput, vt eo symbolo sub.ećtionem, in quam est posita profiteatur.
units.tr: "But the woman," he says, "is the glory of the man." That is, she is the adornment and ornament of the man. Not because she was created by him, or because she has received from him what she has, but because she belongs to him and was made from him and for his sake. Therefore she ought to cover her head, so that by that symbol she may profess the subjection in which she has been placed.

units.la: Sed dicit quisquam. Atqui ad imaginē hác & gloriam Dei non vir tantum sed & mulier pertinere uidetur.Sic enim loco paulo ante ci tato dicit scriptura. Et creauit Deus homine ad imaginem & similitudinem: suam ,ad ima- ginem Dei creauit illū, masculū & fœminam creauit eos,benedixitq; illis Deus&ait:Cresci te & multiplicamini,&replete terram & subij- cite eam, & dominamini piscibus maris, &c. Non dicit: masculum creauit eum,sed mascu- lum& fœminá creauit eos.Nec dicit: benedi- xit illi Deus &ait: Crece & multiplicare, & reple terram & subijce eam, & dominare,&c. sed in plurali ad vtrumq; tam fœminam quàm virum,crescite, multiplicamini, replete terrā, & subijcite eam, & dominamini, &c. Quem- admodum igitur benedićtio hæc Dei crescē- di,multiplicandi ac terram implendi non ad virum tantum sed & ad mulierem pertinet:ita &dominatus terræ,in quo est imago Dei,non uiro tátum sed unà cum illo & mulieri est de- putatus.Quomodo igitur mulier ab hac digni tate separatur ab Apostolo,quasi vir solus ima go fit & gloria Dei?
units.tr: But someone will say: Yet it seems that not only the man but also the woman belongs to this image and glory of God. For Scripture says so in the passage cited a little above: "And God created man in his image and likeness; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. And God blessed them and said to them: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea," and so on. It does not say: "He created him male," but "he created them male and female." Nor does it say: "God blessed him and said: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion," and so on; but in the plural, to both the woman and the man alike: increase, multiply, fill the earth, subdue it, and have dominion, and so on. Therefore, just as this blessing of God to increase, multiply and fill the earth belongs not to the man only but also to the woman, so the dominion over the earth, in which the image of God lies, has been assigned not to the man alone but together with him to the woman as well. How then does the Apostle separate the woman from this dignity, as if the man alone were the image and glory of God?

units.la: Respondeo. Quatenus mascules&fœmi- na coniunćti unum hominem&carnem unam constituunt, hactenus nō uir tantum, quia nō solus,sed unà cum muliere imago est & gloria Dei.Quod uero ordinē concernit,quo discre- ti sunt inter se, sic vt vir sit caput mulieris,illi- que præsit,item quod attinet dotes viro prin- cipatus gratia diuinitùs traditas & adminis- stratione principatus,hactenus uir solus ima go est &gloria Dei. Hominem definimus ani- mal esse rationale. Prædicatū hoc carni quoq; compecompetit, quatenus illa ad plenitudinem hominis pertinet, quamuis dotes rationis nō insint illi sed menti, & rursus non competit, quatenus facultas rationis non illi sed menti est concessa, q̄ ppric rationalis vocari potest. Et Christus imago est & gloria Dei, solus, quod attinet prærogatiuam vnigeniti Dei, non solus, quod attinet coniunctionem carnis & spiritus, qua ecclesiæ suæ coniungi voluit, propter quam coniunctionem & nos in illo & cū illo regnamus. Hoc pacto sentiri posse puto & in hac causa. Imaginis & gloriæ Dei particeps est & mulier, quatenus caro viri est & ad plenitudinem illius pertinet, nō est particeps si separatim consideretur, quatenus viro est, tanquam capiti suo subiecta. Ad priorem sensum pertinent, quæ in Genesi leguntur, ad posteriorem vero, quæ hic ab Apostolo præsenti causæ conuenientia dicuntur.
units.tr: I answer: insofar as male and female, joined together, constitute one man and one flesh, so far the man is the image and glory of God not alone, because he is not alone, but together with the woman. But as regards the order by which they are distinguished from each other, so that the man is the head of the woman and rules over her, and likewise as regards the gifts divinely given to the man for the sake of his rule and the administration of that rule, so far the man alone is the image and glory of God. We define man as a rational animal. This predicate belongs also to the flesh, insofar as the flesh pertains to the completeness of man, although the powers of reason do not inhere in the flesh but in the mind; and again it does not belong to the flesh, insofar as the faculty of reason is granted not to the flesh but to the mind, which alone can be called rational. And Christ is the image and glory of God, alone as regards the pre-eminence of the only-begotten of God, not alone as regards the union of flesh and spirit, into which he willed to be joined to his Church, and through which union we also reign in him and with him. I think it can be understood in this case in the same way. The woman too shares in the image and glory of God insofar as she is the flesh of the man and belongs to the completeness of him; she does not share in it if she is considered separately, insofar as she is subject to the man as to her head. To the former sense belong the things read in Genesis; to the latter belong those which the Apostle here says are fitting to the present case.

units.la: Non est autem præter rationem, quod cum de viro dixerit, quod imago sit & gloria Dei, de muliere non subijcit, ac mulier imago & gloria viri sed, at mulier gloria viri est. Mulier enim sic est gloria, id est, decus & ornamētum viri, vt tamen nō sit illius imago, sicut ipse est imago Dei. Neq; enim instar viri est, sicut vir instar est Dei, ad cuius est imaginem constitutus. Potest tamen aliquo pacto imago viri dici. Hactenus videlicet, vt quemadmodum Luna imago Solis ob id recte vocari potest, quod noctu absentis illius uices sustinet, ita mulier absentis viri vicem gerēs imago viri dicatur. Sic videmus matresfamiliās in absentia maritorum suorum gubernationem sustinere domus, quemadmodū imago rem ipsam cuius est imago, repræsentat.
units.tr: Nor is it without reason that, having said of the man that he is the image and glory of God, he does not add of the woman that she is the image and glory of the man, but says only: "the woman is the glory of the man." For the woman is glory, that is, the adornment and ornament of the man, in such a way that nevertheless she is not his image, as he himself is the image of God. For she is not in the place of the man as the man is in the place of God, to whose image he was made. Yet in some respect she may be called the image of the man. So far, that is, as the moon may rightly be called an image of the sun because it sustains its place by night when the sun is absent; so the woman, standing in the place of the absent husband, may be called the image of the man. Thus we see wives, in the absence of their husbands, sustaining the management of the household, just as an image represents the very thing of which it is the image.

units.la: Habent hic vtriq; & vir & mulier vnde admoneantur officij sui. Si vir est imago & gloria Dei, competit illi ne dignitatis huius prærogatiuam in probrum nominis Dei perueretat, summo studio conniti, vt quod est ex diuina dignatione, id pietate & iustitia pro viribus exprimat. Deinde, quatenus gloria ipsius est mulier, hactenus illam honorifice non vt seruam sed vt sociam tractet. Mulier, quoniā gloria viri est, cogitabit cauendum sibi esse, ne in probrum viri degeneret, hoc est, ne sic se gerat vel verbis vel moribus, vel habitu indecenti, vt viro sit ignominia magis quàm gloria.
units.tr: Here both husband and wife are given cause to remember their duty. If the man is the image and glory of God, then he must take great care, lest he dishonour God's name by abusing the privilege of this dignity, and that he express by piety and justice, as far as he can, what he has received by God's gracious appointment. Next, since the woman is the glory of the man, he should treat her honourably, not as a slave but as a companion. And since the woman is the glory of the man, she should take care not to degenerate into the man's shame, that is, not to conduct herself by her words, her behaviour, or her indecent dress in such a way that she brings him disgrace rather than glory.

units.la: NON enim est vir ex muliere, inquit, sed mulier ex viro.) Ratione reddit eius quod mulierem gloriam viri esse dixit. Hanc adfert duplicem. Vna est, quod ex viro desumpta est mulier. Altera, quod propter virum est condita. Emphasim habet, quod non simpliciter dicit: Est enim mulier ex viro, & propter virum condita, sed, Non enim est vir ex muliere, neq; propter mulierem, sed mulier ex viro, & propter virum. Sic iterum luculenta discretione discernit inter virum & mulierem, & huic prærogatiuam suam vindicat, illam vero præeminentię ipsius subijcit. Etenim potius est id, un de & propter quod aliud, quàm quod ex illo
units.tr: "For the man is not from the woman," he says, "but the woman from the man." He gives the reason for what he said, that the woman is the glory of the man. He offers a twofold reason. The first is that the woman was taken from the man. The second is that she was created for the man's sake. There is emphasis here, since he does not simply say, "The woman is from the man and created for the man," but, "The man is not from the woman, nor for the woman's sake, but the woman is from the man and for the man." Thus again, with clear discrimination, he distinguishes between man and woman, claims the privilege for the man, and makes the woman subject to his pre-eminence. For indeed that from which and for which something else exists is more excellent than what is derived from it and for it.

units.la: & propter illud deducitur. Debetur enim illi gloria & originis & causæ. Virum dixit non debere obuelare caput suum, eo quod sit imago & gloria Dei. Hic illud etiā ex eo probat, quod vir neq; ex muliere est, neq; ppter mulierem conditus. Mulierem caput suum obuelare debere dixit, eo quod sit gloria viri. Hoc probat dicens: sed mulier est ex viro, item, sed mulier est propter virum. Contrarium vtriusq; præseferebant Corinthij, in eo quod mulier nudo & vir tecto capite orabant, quasi vir ex muliere & propter mulierem sit conditus. Quare constanter hoc negans dicit: Non enim est vir ex muliere, sed mulier ex viro, neq; conditus est vir propter muliere sed mulier propter virū.
units.tr: The man is owed glory both of origin and of cause. He said that the man ought not to cover his head because he is the image and glory of God. Here he proves this also from the fact that the man is neither from the woman nor created for her sake. He said that the woman ought to cover her head because she is the glory of the man. He proves this by saying: "But the woman is from the man," and again, "But the woman is for the man's sake." The Corinthians were putting forward the opposite of both, in that the woman prayed with her head uncovered and the man with his head covered, as if the man were from the woman and created for her sake. Therefore, firmly denying this, he says: "For the man is not from the woman, but the woman from the man; nor was the man created for the woman's sake, but the woman for the man's."

units.la: Rationem autem hanc vtranq; ex historia creationis vsurpat, quæ Gen. 2. legitur. Quod mulier sit ex viro, sic memoratur illic. Immisit dominus Deus soporem in Adam, cumq; obdormiuisset tulit vnam de costis eius, & replevit carne pro ea. Et ædificauit dominus Deus costam quam tulerat de Adam in mulierem, & adduxit eam ad Adam. Dixitq; Adam: Hoc tandem os est ex ossibus meis, & caro de carne mea. Hęc vocabitur ꞩɯn, id est Vira, si sic lo qui liceret, quoniā de viro sumpta est. Quod vero condita sit mulier non solum sed viro sed & propter uirum, ibidem sic legitur. Dixitque dominus Deus: Non est bonum hominē esse solum, faciamus ei adiutorium simili ipsi. Item: Adæ vero non inueniebatur adiutor similis ipsi. Immisitq;' dominus Deus soporem in Adam. &c. Hæc ibi. Ergo mulier facta est & propter virum & ex viro, vt sit illi adiutorium eiusdem cum illo consors & carnis & naturæ: qua de re pleraq; notari possunt, de quibus in Genesi nostra nonnulla attigimus.
units.tr: He draws this reasoning in both respects from the account of creation, which is read in Genesis 2. That the woman is from the man is recorded there thus: "The Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam, and while he slept, he took one of his ribs and filled up the place with flesh. And the Lord God built the rib, which he had taken from Adam, into a woman, and brought her to Adam. And Adam said: 'This at last is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. She shall be called [אשה] ishah, that is, Virago, if one may speak so, because she was taken out of man.'" That the woman was created not only for the man but also for his sake is read in the same place thus: "And the Lord God said: 'It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself.' Again: 'But for Adam no helper like himself was found. And the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam,' etc." Thus far the text there. Therefore the woman was made both for the man's sake and from the man, so that she might be his helper, a partner of the same flesh and nature as he. For this reason many things can be noted, some of which we touched upon in our commentary on Genesis.

units.la: Sed nascitur hic quæstio ex præsenti argumento Apostoli quo mulierem subijcit viro, tanquam ob id potiori quod ex illo & propter illum est condita. Dixerit enim quisquam: Si potior est vir muliere, propterea quod ex illo est & propter illū condita, consequitur & nos potioris esse Christo, eandē ob causam. quod ille ex carne nostra & propter nos homo est factus, atq; ita vel falsum erit Apostoli argumentum, quo illum nobis loco capitis præponit, & nos illi loco sponsæ & corporis subijcit Eph. 5. & Coloss. 1. vel non firmum est quod hic argumentatur, inferiorem esse mulierem viro, propterea quod ex illo & ppter illū est condita.
units.tr: But a question arises here from the Apostle's present argument, by which he subjects the woman to the man, as inferior because she was made from him and for him. For someone might say: "If the man is superior to the woman because he is from her and for him she was created, then it follows that we are superior to Christ for the same reason, since he was made man from our flesh and for our sake. Thus either the Apostle's argument, by which he places Christ before us in the place of the head and subjects us to him in the place of the bride and body (Eph. 5; Col. 1), will be false, or what he argues here is not sound, namely that the woman is inferior to the man because she was made from him and for him."

units.la: Respondeo. Inspiciantur hic & distinguantur circumstantiæ Christi & mulieris. Aliter est ex viro & propter virum mulier, & aliter est ex carne nostra & propter nos Christus. Mulier priusquam ex costa Adæ formaretur non erat in rerū natura. De Christo hoc dicere nō possumus quod non fuerit priusquam ex virgine nasceretur. Antequā Abraham esset ego eram inquit Iohan. 8. nedum, antequam esset Maria. Quare non debet nobis originem suā, sicut mulier debet viro. Deinde, mulier haud suopte consilio scienter ac prudenter originē suam ex viro defunctus sit, sed ignara eorum quae A diuinitus agebantur ex costa illius est formata. At Christus non inscius sed scienter & iuapte spote ex nobis dignatus est incarnari. Tertio, mulier nō sic est ex viro, & propter uirum condita, vt illum periclitante si ruet, & ne pereat in omnibus moderetur & gubernet. Sed vt adiumento quidem sit in propagatione generis, verum caetera ab illo tanquā capite suo regatur & alatur. Christus vero sic est ex nobis & propter nos natus, non vt à nobis regatur, alatur ac feruetur, sed vt noster ipse sit Seruator & gubernator. Quare non ob id est nobis inferior, quod ex nobis & propter nos est homo spōtanea & gratuita dignatione factus, inferior vero mulier est ob id viro, quod ex illo est ac propter illum priusquam esset condita, atque ita manet argumentum Apostoli ratum ac firmum.
units.tr: I answer: let the circumstances of Christ and of the woman be examined and distinguished here. The woman is from the man and for the man in one way, and Christ is from our flesh and for our sake in another. Before the woman was formed from Adam's rib, she did not exist in the nature of things. We cannot say this of Christ, that he did not exist before he was born of the Virgin. "Before Abraham was, I am," he says in John 8, let alone before Mary was. Therefore he does not owe his origin to us as the woman owes hers to the man. Next, the woman did not, by her own counsel, knowingly and prudently take her origin from the man, but was formed from his rib without knowing what was being done by divine action. But Christ was not unaware, but knowingly and of his own accord deigned to be incarnate for us. Thirdly, the woman is not so from the man and created for the man that she may guide and govern him when he is in danger of falling and in all things lest he perish; rather, she is a help to him in the propagation of the race, but in other respects she is ruled and nourished by him as her head. But Christ is so born from us and for us, not that he may be ruled, nourished and preserved by us, but that he himself may be our Saviour and governor. Therefore he is not inferior to us because he became man from us and for us by a voluntary and gratuitous act of grace; the woman, however, is inferior to the man because she was made from him and for him before she was created. And so the Apostle's argument stands valid and firm.

units.la: PROPTER hoc, inquit, debet mulier potestatem habere in capite.) Colligit. Quoniam mulier est ex viro & propter virum, conuenit illi tanq̄ subditę caput non apertum sed obuelatum. Quod vulgata versio habet, debet mulier velamē habere, in Graeco est, ἐξουσίαν ἔχειν, id est, debet mulier potestatē habere. Vtitur voce hic nō propria sed figurata Velamen capitis muliebris vocat potestatem, propterea quod signum est eius potestatis, virilis videlicet, cui ie hoc gestamine sub ecclam proferetur. Constituit rat one posset vocari sub iectio, tanquam subiectionis symbolū. Nō est aūt praeter rationem, quod figurata hac est loquutione vsus in re, quam Corinthij non satis intelligebant, quo illos admoneret, quae sit ratio muliebris pepli, quā nō simpliciter ad hoc faciat, vt caput contra frigus tegat, & honestati quoq; seruiat, sed & vt symbolum sit potestatis ac iuris virilis, cui se mulier gestamine hoc pepli subiecta esse fateri debet. In capite regimen est ac potestas in corpus subiectum. Et quoniam potestas haec viro data est à Deo non mulieri, conuenit, vt caput mulieris sit obuolutum ac tectum potestate viri, non liberū & apertum, quasi propriae sit potestatis ac nulli subiectum. Insertum esse debet potestati viri, ac circumscriptum, ne quid faciat suopte arbitratu, sed totum seruiat voluntati viri. Habet muliebre caput suas quoq; dotes, tam intelligetiq; quā naturalium sensuum, verum habet eas nō liberas sed potestati viri subiectas. Quapropter ne duo sint vnius corporis principalia ac libera capita, ipsa & ordinis & corporis & vnitatis necessitas hoc requirit, vt potestas cedat vni, & subiecto alteri, atq; ita libertum & apertum sit quod est superius, obuelatum vero & obstrictum quod est inferius. Vbi hic ordo diuinitus datus nuertitur, sic vt muliebre caput regat, & virile regatur, frustra est externa illa mulierum obuelatio. Nam signū est sine signato, externa subiectionis professio sine subiectione. Interea tamen ipso gestami ne pepli peruersionis huius arguitur mulier, & dominationis perfidiae, si alterius viri fit appetens. Quicquid enim sub peplo illius vel, vt Apostolus loquitur, sub potestate est, quam in capite gestat, id omne ac totum sub viri est iure ac potestate. PROPTER hoc, inquit, debet mulier potestatem habere in capite, propter angelos.) De sideratur vocula, vel, vt legatur, uel ppter angelos. Sensus enim est. Etsi non est pudor mulieri inter eiusdem moris homines nudo comparere capite, nec ratione habere sexus & decori sui, pudor sit saltem propter angelos, quos habet in ecclesia spectatores. Hic non est omnibus eadem sententia, de quibus angelis loquatur Apostolus, propterea quod uox haec, ἀγγέλων, uarie vsurpatur. Sonat nuncium & legatū. Et hic dubio procul loquitur de nūcijs Dei, quos ille quo vult mittit. Nuncius Dei est sacerdos in lege, sicut videmus Malachię 2. vbi sic legimus: Labia enim sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam & legē requirent ex ore eius, quia angelus domini exercituum est. Nūcius Dei est Apostolus. Sic apostoli, quos ante se Christus misisse legitur Lucae 9. angeli vocantur. Et discipuli Iohannis quoq; Lucę 7. Et coeletis spiritus communiter angeli propterea uocantur, quod à Deo ad obeunda ministeria sua mittuntur. Quod itaq; prae entem locū attinet, alius exponit de ministris uerb, alius de bonis, alius de malis spiritibus. Mihi arridet illorum expositio qui de bonis spiritibus intelliguntur à Deo ecclesiae deputatis, idq; non in co mune tantum, sed & singulis fidelibus. Hoc sensu poscit Apostolus, vt in ecclesia, imo & alias, vbi conscientia mortalium non uerentur, angelorum saltem aspectum reueriti abstineant ab omni eo quod vel tantum habet indecori. Quato quaeło latius esset, si populus fidelium ad id fuisset instructus, ut haud dubitaret ie agere in conspectu angelorum iustiū Dei praesentium, & omnia nostra spectantium, quam quod à turdis ac mutis simulacris impie pendet. ALIO QVIneq; vir, inqt, abiq; muliere, neque mulier abiq; viro, in domino.) In Graeco est vocula ἄλλω, quā hic recte vertes attame, quā alioq. Quoniam quod dixit, non elle viru ex muliere, sed mulierem ex viro, contra com munem propagandi generis nostri modū dictum esse videri poterat, quo secundum institutionem domini tam necessaria est viro mulier quā vir mulieri, particulā hanc correctionis gratia adiecit. Quasi dicat: Quod viru non ex muliere sed mulierem ex viro esse dico, ad primā illius originem pertinet, qua ex viro est facta, nō ad modum propagationis, ad quem nec uir solus abiq; muliere, nec mulier abiq; uiro quicquam praestare potest. Illud in domino, nonnuli ad religionē trahunt, verum simplicius ac rectius exponunt, qui referunt ad institutionē domini, secundum quam ad generis nostri propagationē necessaria est amborū, uiri & mulieris, coniunctio. In Satana vir viro, mulier mulieri miscetur (uae turpissiturpissimo cœlibatui) at in domino; neq; vir absq; muliere, neq; mulier absq; viro. Excludi tur hic omnis nefaria libido, & vtriusq; sexus coniunctio, quæ nō est in domino, ne fcortatio nes, & adulteria, & incestus probari videatur.
units.tr: "For this reason," he says, "the woman ought to have power on her head." He draws a conclusion here: since the woman is from the man and for the man, it is fitting that she have on her head a covering, not an open head but a veiled one, as a sign of subjection. The Vulgate has "the woman ought to have a veil," but the Greek has "to have power [ἐξουσίαν ἔχειν]," that is, "the woman ought to have power." Here he uses the word not in its proper sense but figuratively, calling the veil of the woman's head "power," because it is the sign of that power, namely the man's, under which she is to be placed by this covering. It could therefore be called subjection, as a symbol of subjection. Nor is it out of place that he uses a figurative expression in a matter the Corinthians did not sufficiently understand, to remind them what the purpose of the woman's veil is. It serves not merely to cover the head against the cold and to preserve decency, but also to be a symbol of the authority and right of the man, to which the woman by this covering ought to confess herself subject. In the head lies rule and authority over the subject body. And since this authority has been given to the man by God and not to the woman, it is fitting that the woman's head be covered and shielded by the man's authority, not free and open, as if it were of its own authority and subject to no one. It ought to be placed under the authority of the man and bounded by it, so that it does nothing at its own pleasure but wholly serves the man's will. The woman's head has its own gifts, both of understanding and of the natural senses, but it has them not free, rather subject to the man's authority. Therefore, lest there be two principal and free heads of one body, the very necessity of order, of the body, and of unity requires that authority yield to one and that the other be subject; so that what is superior be free and open, and what is inferior be veiled and restrained. Where this order given by God is overturned, so that the woman's head rules and the man is ruled, that external veiling of women is in vain. For it is a sign without the thing signified, an outward profession of subjection without subjection. Meanwhile, by the very covering of the veil the woman is convicted of this perversion and of the treachery of domination, if she is eager for another man. For whatever is under her veil, or, as the Apostle says, under the power which she wears on her head, all of that is under the right and authority of the man. "For this reason," he says, "the woman ought to have power on her head, because of the angels." The little word "because of" (propter) is debated, and it is read either "because of the angels" or "even because of the angels." The sense is this: although it is not shameful for a woman to appear bareheaded among men of the same custom, and though she does not take account of her sex and her dignity, let there be shame at least because of the angels, whom she has as spectators in the Church. Not all agree about which angels the Apostle means, since the word ἀγγέλων [angelōn] is used in various ways. It means messenger and envoy. Here he undoubtedly speaks of God's messengers, whom he sends wherever he wills. A priest under the law is God's messenger, as we see in Malachi 2, where we read: "For the lips of the priest keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth, for he is the angel of the Lord of hosts." An apostle is God's messenger; thus the apostles whom Christ is read to have sent before his face are called angels in Luke 9, and the disciples of John too in Luke 7. And the heavenly spirits are commonly called angels for the reason that they are sent by God to perform their ministries. As to the present passage, some explain it of ministers of the Word, others of good spirits, others of evil spirits. I am pleased with the view of those who understand good spirits, appointed by God to the Church, and that not only in common but also to each of the faithful. In this sense the Apostle requires that in the Church, and indeed elsewhere, where the conscience of mortals is not restrained, they at least, out of reverence for the sight of the angels, abstain from everything that has even the appearance of indecency. How much more widely would this apply if the people of the faithful had been instructed to this end, so that they would not hesitate to act in the sight of the holy angels of God who are present and who behold all our doings, rather than hang impiously upon deaf and dumb images! "Neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man, in the Lord." In the Greek there is the little word ἄλλω [allō], which the translator renders here correctly, though otherwise. Since he had said that the man is not from the woman but the woman from the man, this might seem to have been said contrary to the common manner of propagating our race, in which, according to the Lord's institution, woman is as necessary to man as man is to woman. So he added this particle by way of correction, as if to say: What I say, that the man is not from the woman but the woman from the man, pertains to the first origin of him, by which she was made from him, and not to the manner of propagation, in which neither the man alone without the woman, nor the woman without the man, can achieve anything. As for the words "in the Lord," some draw them to religion, but more simply and rightly those explain them who refer them to the Lord's institution, according to which the union of both man and woman is necessary for the propagation of our race. Outside the Lord (in Satan's realm) man is mixed with man, woman with woman (a most shameful and most foul celibacy); but in the Lord, neither man without woman nor woman without man. Here every unlawful lust is excluded, and every union of either sex that is not in the Lord, lest fornications, adulteries, and incest seem to be approved.

units.la: Potest & sic exponi. Attamen secundū institutione dni, neq; vir nascitur citra operā mulie ris, neq; mulier citra operā viri. Et sic sequitur.
units.tr: It can also be explained thus: nevertheless, according to the institution of the Lord, neither man is born apart from the work of woman, nor woman apart from the work of man. And so it follows.

units.la: NAM quemadmodū mulier ex viro est, ita &vir per mulierem.) Hoc est. Quemadmodū initio ex viro condita est mulier, sic postea vir per mulierē prouenit. Sic neq; infringit argu mentū virilis prærogatiuæ, quo ad propositum suū est vsus, neq; mulierem abijcit infra pedes viri, sed in consortio, & si non regiminis, propagationis tamen retinet, atq; ita princi patū viri separat à tyrānide, & mitigat quod mulieri durum esse videbatur, dum iuum illi honorem saluum relinquit, dicens eam perin de esse necessariā uiro atq; virū mulieri & per illam iam esse virū, sicut initio condita est illa ex viro. Admodum in eo se solantur mulierCU læ quod uident se necessarias esse viris, nec cō temni & abijci posse quasi inutiles. Deinde in eo quoq;, quod non sunt serue sed socie: item quod viri per mulieres sunt eque ac olim mu lier per virum. Hæc solatia non admit illis A postolus, sed testimonio suo confirmat modo præeminentiam regiminis uiro saluam relin quant, illiq; sese subiectas ipso habitu haud grauatim profiteantur.
units.tr: "For as the woman is of the man, so also is the man by the woman." That is: just as at the beginning the woman was made from the man, so afterwards the man comes forth through the woman. Thus he neither weakens the argument for the man's pre-eminence, for which he has used it for his purpose, nor casts the woman down beneath the man's feet; rather, in partnership, if not of rule, she keeps the status of propagation, and so he separates the man's primacy from tyranny and softens what seemed harsh to the woman, while leaving her his honour intact, saying that she is equally necessary to the man and the man to the woman, and that through her he now exists just as at the beginning she was made from him. Women find comfort in this, that they see they are necessary to men and cannot be despised and cast off as useless. Also in this, that they are not servants but companions; and likewise that men are through women just as women once were through men. The Apostle does not admit these consolations for their own sake, but confirms them with his own testimony, so that they may keep the pre-eminence of rule for the man, and willingly profess by their very dress that they are subject to him.

units.la: Adijcit: OMNIA uero ex Deo.) Hoc est, qd' uero initio conditus, quod ad imaginē & gloriā Dei factus, quod in caput mulieris posi tus, quod mulier primum ex viro, quod gloria uiri, illiq; subiecta. quod postea uir per mulie rem, quod neq; vir absq; muliere neq; mulier absq; viro, omnia hæc non sunt ex humana cō stitutione, neq; uiri alicuius neq; mulieris, sed ex Deo, qui vt masculum & fœminā condidit, ita inter illos ordinem hunc constituit. Quare nec uir habet, unde contra mulierē insolescat & feroeiat, nec mulier unde uiro tanq; capiti suo subiungi, eamq; submissionem capite obnelato profiteri grauetur. Est hęc particula di ligenter obseruanda omnibus quibufcūq; statibus, & cuiusquis ordinis hominibus, quod ex Deo sunt quæcunq; sunt ordinata, dispositione siue naturali, siue aliās ad vitæ huius sustentatione, generis nostri propagatione, pacis ac tranquillitatis conseruatione, & cum primis uerę pietatis religione necessaria. Vbi cōstat de ordine Dei secuti cōstat in coniugio legitimo, in magistratu, in ministerio verbi, & consimili bus aliis, ibi per conscientiam pij homines di uinæ se constitutioni ex animo accommoda bunt. Discretione tamen opus est, ne in hanc ordinationum Dei classem recipiamus quic quid humanitus est constitutū, & incidamus in illud Christi frustra colunt me docentes do ctrinas & mandata hominum.
units.tr: He adds: "But all things are of God." That is: that the man was created first, that he was made in the image and glory of God, that the woman was placed on the head, that the woman was first from the man, that she is the glory of the man and subject to him, that afterwards the man is through the woman, that neither the man is without the woman nor the woman without the man, all these things are not from human institution, neither of any man nor of any woman, but from God, who created male and female and so established this order between them. Therefore the man has no ground from which to grow insolent and rage against the woman, nor the woman ground to be burdened with subjection to the man as to her head and to profess that submission with a covered head. This particle is to be diligently observed by all states and by men of every rank: that whatever has been ordained is from God, whether by natural disposition or otherwise, necessary for the sustenance of this life, for the propagation of our race, for the preservation of peace and tranquillity, and above all for the religion of true piety. Where the order of God is evident, as in lawful marriage, in the magistracy, in the ministry of the Word, and in other similar things, there pious people will in their conscience accommodate themselves sincerely to the divine constitution. Yet discretion is needed, lest we admit into this class of divine ordinances whatever has been devised by human beings, and fall into that saying of Christ: "In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men."

units.la: Inter uos ipsos iudicate num decorū est mulierem non velatam Deū orare?
units.tr: Judge among yourselves: is it fitting that a woman should pray to God unveiled?

units.la: An ne ipsa quidē natura hoc uos docet quod uiro quidē si comatus fuerit pro bro sit: mulieri vero si comata fuerit glo rię sit, eo qd coma ,p uelamine data sit?
units.tr: Does not nature itself teach you this: that long hair on a man is a shame, but long hair on a woman is her glory, since the hair has been given to her as a covering?

units.la: Arguit eos summæ incogitantiæ, qua ne i- ipsius quidē naturæ documentū obseruabant, unde intelligere poterāt, quod nam sit mulie ris hac in re decorum. Inter uosipsos, inquit, iu dicate. Fiducia causæ prouocat ad ipsorū iudi cium. Res est, inquit, manifesta, & vestris ipso rum conscientijs nota, modo illas ad iudiciū adhibere volueritis. Quare depono illā ad ue- strū ipsorū iudiciū. Vosipsos cōstituo iudices.
units.tr: He charges them with the greatest thoughtlessness, since they did not observe even the evidence of nature itself, from which they could have understood what is fitting for a woman in this matter. "Judge among yourselves," he says. He appeals to their judgment with confidence in his cause. The matter is, he says, plain and known to your own consciences, provided you are willing to bring them to the judgment. Therefore I refer it to your own judgment. I make you yourselves the judges.

units.la: NVM decorū est mulierē nō velatā orare, inquit?) Exprimit qua de re iudicare debeat. Non dicit: num vsitatū est? num uenustū est? Erat plus æquo vsitatum, & habebatur pro ue nusto. Placebat carni. Sed, num decorū est in- quit? Quasi dicat num ita fieri conuenit? num decet? nū honestū est? Monet sensum decori & honesti, & præferendum esse tam publico usui, q; venustati carnis, & sic inditum esse mē tibus nostris, vt haud facile pronunciaturi si mus decorū esse quicquid vsitatum est & car ni adlubescit. Sic in corrupti sumus, vt oculis magis q; recto metis nostrę iudicio seruiamus.
units.tr: "Is it seemly for a woman to pray uncovered?" he asks. He sets out the point on which they ought to judge. He does not ask: Is it customary? Is it pleasing? It was customary beyond what was right, and it was regarded as pleasing. It pleased the flesh. But he asks, "Is it seemly?" As if to say: Is it fitting that it be done this way? Does it become us? Is it honourable? He reminds us of the sense of what is seemly and honourable, and that this must be preferred both to public custom and to the charm of the flesh. It is so implanted in our minds that we would not readily pronounce whatever is customary and pleases the flesh to be seemly. We are so corrupted that we serve our eyes rather than the right judgment of our minds.

units.la: NVM decorū est, inquit, mulierē non velatā orare Deum?) Poterat æque decere: num de eorum est uirum obuelatum orare? Verū ma gis vrget fœminas, quia malum hoc in illis & magis inualescebat, & plus habebat offendicu h. Hic enim non solum ordo & decorum sexus inuertebatur, sed & concupiscentiæ carnis ser uiebatur, oculi virorū sollicitabantur, & semi naria prauæ libidinis iaciebātur, atq; ita opus domini in cœtu sacro labefactabatur.
units.tr: "Is it seemly," he says, "for a woman to pray to God uncovered?" It could equally be asked: "Is it seemly for a man to pray covered?" But he presses harder on the women, because this evil was more rampant among them and gave more offence. Here not only the order and decorum of the sexes was overturned, but the lust of the flesh was served, the eyes of men were enticed, the seeds of wicked lust were sown, and so the work of the Lord was undermined in the sacred assembly.

units.la: Non est autem otiosum quod dicit: Deum orare. Quasi dicat. Audet ne mulier apparere in conspectu Dei, illuinq; orare tanta leuitate & irreuerentia, vt capite nudo, cōtra sexus sui decorū, uerba ad illum facere non dubitet? Si quis hoc ante regem constitutus faciat, an nō merito graues conteptus pœnas exigeretur? Magni nomenti censetur, verba facere ad ma iestatem regiam. Et certa hic reuerētia, certiq; submissionis gestus requiruntur. Quāto quę- so plus reuerentię competit maiestati diuinę? Quomodo non hic amplius de seruando con ditionis nostræ decoro cogitamus? Compo namus itaq; oraturi ad Deum, non modo in ternis hominis sensus, quo se humilient in cō spectu Dei, & ad maiestatē illius expauescant, sed & externi habitū & gestus, ne quid in illis sit quod & uos dedeceat & contemptū numi nis spiret. Non moratur Deus externa, at inte rim non amat euitatem neglecti decori.
units.tr: Nor is it idle that he says "to pray to God." As if to say: Does a woman dare to appear in the sight of God and pray to him with such levity and irreverence that, with head bare, contrary to the decorum of her sex, she does not hesitate to address words to him? If someone standing before a king did this, would he not rightly be punished with grave contempt? It is considered a matter of great weight to address words to royal majesty, and a definite reverence and a definite gesture of submission are required. How much more, I ask, is reverence due to the divine majesty? How is it that we do not think here more of keeping the decorum of our condition? Let us therefore compose ourselves when we are about to pray to God, not only in the inner sense of the man, by which we humble ourselves in the sight of God and are awed by his majesty, but also in outward bearing and gestures, lest there be anything in them that both disgraces you and breathes contempt for the divine majesty. God does not dwell on externals, yet he does not love the carelessness of neglected decorum.

units.la: AN ne ipsa quidem natura, inquit, hoc vos docet, &c.) Quasi dicat. Vsq; adeo ne stupidi estis & incogitantes, vt ne naturæ quidem du ctum obseruetis? Etiamsi Christiani non esse tis, an non vel ex ipso naturæ documento in telligeretis, q; sit indecorū viro, si tecto, & mulieri si nudo capite oret? Vocat autem natura, omnium eorum quae sunt naturalem, constantem, perpetuam, ultronea ac nullo artificio acquisitam seriem, uim, & operationem, quae non potest nisi opifici & conditori omnium adscribi, quem nonnulli philosophi naturam uocat efficientem, gubernatam ac <bl>ἀνωεργὸν</bl>. Natura hac sic est inter virum & mulierem discretum, ut uiro probrosum sit, si coma nutriat, mulieri vero decori deputetur, si sit comata. Et hinc est quod muliebris censeatur esse mollicies si comatus sit vir, ut non immerito dixerit ille: Sint procul a nobis iuuenes ut foeminacōpti. Ipsa natura quod mulieri ornatus gratia largiter subministrat, uiro grauatim & vtcunque, utut comam nutrienti, permittit, ut palam ne gare uideatur. Quod ueteres alij acrocomae, alij opisthocomae, alij simpliciter intonsi fuerunt, nihil incommodat argumento Apostoli, quemadmodum nec id quod aliquot regionum mulierculae vulgo tondetur, & in nonnullis Orientis populis uiri capitibus plusquam muliebri ter sunt obuelatis. Antiquum est in hoc mundo & nimis visitatum, multa ab hominibus usurpari ac geri aliter quam naturae ductus requirat. Et tamen quae naturaliter fiunt omnibus sunt in propatulo, nec incognitum est a conscientijs nostris quod nam sit naturae decorum. Quare quod hic dicit Apostolus: An ne ipsa quidem natura hoc uos docet, quod uiro si comatus fuerit probro fit? nō dicit secundum iudicium carnis affectibus corruptum, quo co ma viro haudquaqua turpis esse iudicabatur, sed secundum ipsius naturae documentum, quo etiam non obseruatibus coma viro probrosa esse monstratur. Docet hoc natura, etiasi pauci obseruent aut alicuius faciant.
units.tr: "Does not even nature itself teach you," he says, and so on. As if to say: Are you so stupid and thoughtless that you do not even observe the guidance of nature? Even if you were not Christians, would you not understand from the very evidence of nature that it is unseemly for a man to pray with covered head, and for a woman with bare head? Now nature denotes the whole constant, perpetual, spontaneous series, power and operation of those things that are natural and acquired by no artifice, which can be ascribed to none but the maker and creator of all. Some philosophers call this the efficient, governing nature, and [ἀνωεργόν]. Nature has so distinguished man and woman that it is disgraceful for a man to grow long hair, but seemly for a woman to have it. Hence long hair on a man is judged to be womanish softness, so that the poet rightly said: "Let young men who are like women keep far from us." Nature itself grants to a woman abundantly what serves for ornament, but to a man it grants it grudgingly and only in some measure, so that it seems openly forbidden to him, even if he grows his hair. That some of the ancients wore their hair long at the front, others at the back, and others simply went unshorn, does not weaken the Apostle's argument. Nor does the fact that the women of some regions are commonly shorn, or that among some peoples of the East men's heads are covered more than is womanly. It is an ancient and far too common thing in this world that men adopt and do many things otherwise than the guidance of nature requires. Yet what happens naturally lies open to all, and it is not unknown to our consciences what is natural decorum. Therefore when the Apostle says, "Does not nature itself teach you that for a man to wear long hair is a disgrace?", he does not speak according to the judgment of the flesh, corrupted by the passions, by which long hair was judged in no way shameful in a man. He speaks according to the evidence of nature itself, by which long hair is shown to be disgraceful in a man, even to those who do not observe it. Nature teaches this, even if few observe it or act on it.

units.la: MVLIERI uero, inquit, si comata fuerit gloriae sit.) Dicit hic quisquam. Quid ergo opus est mulieri, vt artificiosa pepli obuolutione tegatur in coetu sacro, si naturali tegumento capillorum cum gloria tegitur? Si coma illi est gloriae, ergo recte faciut, quae capillis demissis uel obortis sine peplo in coetum sacrum ueniunt.
units.tr: "But for a woman," he says, "if she has long hair, it is her glory." Someone may say: why then is there any need for a woman to be covered with the artificial wrapping of a veil in the sacred assembly, if with the natural covering of her hair she is already clothed in glory? If long hair is her glory, then those women do right who come into the sacred assembly with loose or curled hair and no veil.

units.la: Respondeo. Opus naturae commemorat, quo uiri ac mulieris capita sic discernuntur, ut huius sit aptissimum ad nutrendum comam, illius vero prorsus ineptum, huic coma sit gloriae, illi dedecori. In hoc autem non subsistit, sed monet quid ex eo sit colligendum, hoc est, quid natura hoc opere suo doceat. Non est hinc colligendum, nihil referre, si mulier comata absque peplo coetum sacrum ingrediatur, sed id potius non decere mulierem, si se inter orandum gerat in morem viri, capite apparens nudo & aperto, quasi nihil inter ipsam & illum sit discriminis in hac causa, cum ipsa quoque natura monstrante sit permultum. Aliud est opus naturae, & aliud documentum quod ex illo colligit Apostolus. Opus est, quod mulierem reddit comatam, virum non ita. Documetum hinc est, aliter mulieri comparendum esse in coetu sacro, & aliter uiro, illi capite tecto, isti aperto. Sic il-lud quod adijcit, eo quod coma pro velamine data sit, huc sensum habet. Coma mulieri gloriae est, propterea quod donum est naturae. Est enim illi non humanitus ascita sed diuinitus data. Data autem est pro velamine, ut innuat ipsa natura, obuelandum esse non aperiendum mulieris caput. Quod haec monstrat, ipsa obuelandi se studio sequatur.
units.tr: I answer: he recalls a work of nature by which the heads of man and woman are so distinguished that the one is most apt for growing long hair and the other wholly unsuited to it; for the one long hair is a glory, for the other a disgrace. But he does not rest there. He points out what is to be inferred from it, that is, what nature teaches by this work of hers. It is not to be inferred from this that it makes no difference if a woman enters the sacred assembly with long hair and without a veil. Rather, it is not becoming for a woman, if she conducts herself in prayer in the manner of a man, appearing with head bare and uncovered, as if there were no difference between her and him in this matter, when nature itself shows there is a great deal. The work of nature is one thing, and the lesson the Apostle draws from it is another. The work is that it makes a woman long-haired and a man not so. The lesson is that a woman must appear differently in the sacred assembly than a man: she with head covered, he with it uncovered. So too what he adds, "because the hair has been given for a covering," has this sense: long hair is a glory to a woman because it is a gift of nature. For it is not acquired by human effort but given by God, and it is given as a covering, so that nature may show that a woman's head must be covered, not uncovered. Let her whom nature thus instructs follow it, with zeal for covering herself.

units.la: Diligenter est hic locus obseruandus, quod attinet naturae documenta, ex quorum obseruatione multa possunt colligi ad vsus humanos, honestatem, commoditatem vitae, bonos mores, & pietatem quoque facientia. Est enim natura, quatenus incorrupta est, sapientissima diuinae prouidentiae dispositio, plena operibus & exemplis admirandis. Horum alia sunt abstrusa, alia in propatulo. Abstrusa vocant secretas naturae, & physicos appellant eos qui toti scrutandis illis sunt diti. Meo iudicio vtilius fuerit, ea diligenter obseruare quae sunt manifesta, obuia, & expo-sita omnibus, sic vt recte documenta & indicia vocari queant, ad quorum classem pertinet, quod hic Apostolus ducit. Talia possunt in nobis ipsis permulta obseruari. Vt exempli gratia. Natura sic est cor pus nostrum dispositum, vt sit coelum uersus erectum. An non admonet, quaerenda nobis esse coelestia magis quam terrena? Caput in illo supremum locum habet. Monstrat natura, quo loco habendi sint, qui alijs praesunt. Inest illi facultas rationis & iudicij. Videt, audit, & iudicat. Tales conuenit esse eos qui sunt capita populorum. Vnicum est in corpore uno. Sic unus est Deus in toto hoc coeli ac terrae vniuerso. Significatur pluralitatem esse malam. Si singulae corporis nostri patres considerentur, nulla est, quae non aliquid habeat documenti, indeinstruamur, in quibus multo nos vtilius exercebimus, quam si in cognoscendis causis illorum quae fieri uidemus per curiositatem oc cupemur.
units.tr: Here the passage concerning the evidences of nature must be carefully observed, since from the observation of them many things can be drawn for human use, things that promote honesty, convenience of life, good morals and piety too. For nature, insofar as it is uncorrupted, is the most wise disposition of divine providence, full of admirable works and examples. Some of these are hidden, others lie open. Those that are hidden they call the secrets of nature, and they call natural philosophers those who devote themselves wholly to searching them out. In my judgment it would be more useful to observe diligently those things which are manifest, obvious and set out for all, so that they may rightly be called evidences and indications, and to this class belongs what the Apostle here adduces. Very many such things can be observed in ourselves. For example: nature has so arranged our body that it stands upright, turned towards heaven. Does it not admonish us that we should seek heavenly things rather than earthly? The head has the highest place in it. Nature shows what place those should hold who preside over others. The head has the faculty of reason and judgment; it sees, hears and judges. Such should be those who are the heads of peoples. The body has one head. So there is one God over the whole universe of heaven and earth. It is signified that plurality is evil. If the individual parts of our body are considered, there is none that does not carry some lesson by which we may be instructed. In these we shall exercise ourselves far more profitably than if we busied ourselves with curiosity in learning the causes of the things we see done.

units.la: Simul tameu obseruandum est, quod non simpliciter dicit, An non natura, sed, an ne natura quidem uos docet? Christiani erat, & habebat doctrinam verbi Dei vnde satis instrui poterant. Ea est primaria, & peculiariter data electis. Documenta uero naturae secundo loco habent, & seruiunt rudioribus. Quare in causa pietatis non debent habere primas, nec conuenit vt sine verbo valeant. Sic uidemus hic Apostolum haud primo loco argumentum inducere a natura sed postremo, idq; ex abundanti, ad perstringendum Corinthiorum stupiditatem, qua ne naturae quidem ductu obseruabant.
units.tr: At the same time, it must be noted that he does not simply say, "Does not nature teach you?" but "Does not even nature teach you?" The Corinthians had Christianity and possessed the doctrine of God's Word, from which they could be sufficiently instructed. That doctrine is primary and is given in a special way to the elect. The lessons of nature, however, hold a secondary place and serve the less instructed. Therefore they should not have first place in the cause of piety, nor is it fitting that they should have force without the Word. So we see that the Apostle does not bring in the argument from nature first, but last, and that as a surplus, to rebuke the stupidity of the Corinthians, who did not even observe what nature leads them to.

units.la: Si quis vero contentiosus esse videtur, nos eiusmodi consuetudinem non habemus, neque ecclesiae Dei.
units.tr: But if anyone seems to be contentious, we do not have such a custom, nor do the churches of God.

units.la: Praeuidebat futurum, vt nonnulli in ecclesia nondum liberi a fastu saecularis literaturae, sed adhuc contendendi studio laborates, adducta iam argumenta minoris censerent esse momenti, quam quibus contenti esse deberet, non quod essent ad praesentem causam insuffi-cientia, sed quod illi morbo <bl>φιλονεικίας</bl> aborarent. Hoc ut reprimeret, particulam hac in calce adiecit, dicens: Si quis vero contentiosus esse videtur, nos eiusmodi consuetudinem non habemus, neq; ecclesiæ Dei. Quod Latinè legimus: Si quis contentiosus. in Græco est, <bl>εἰ δέ τις φιλόνεικος</bl>. Sonat autem <bl>φιλόνεικος</bl> non simpliciter contentiosum, sed amantem ac studiosum victoriæ. Qui autem sic est animatus, ut non veritatem sed victoriam quærat, is etiam non modicè & quantum satis est veritatis studioso, sed immoderatè & absq; fine pro victoria contendes altercatur, nec vllum argumentum sic recipit, ut veritati cedat, sed in omnes se formas mutat, quo saltem caveat, ne victus videatur, si certò vincere non poterit. Contendere pro re aliqua, per se nihil habet illicitum, imò si pro veritate fiat, laudem etiam meretur. Verùm si fiat pro re inhonesta & mala, vel studio inanis gloriæ, merito ethnicis quoque vicium censetur esse manifestæ superbiæ. Aliud est esse <bl>φιλόνεικον</bl>, & aliud <bl>φιλάληθες</bl>. Hoc est, aliud est contendere ut vel vincas tu, vel ut cum gloria, aut saltem non victus videaris, & aliud est contendere pro veritate, ut illa vincat, nec morari, utrum per te hoc fiat aut per alios, quemadmodum animati sunt homines non sui, sed veritatis unicæ amantes. Qui sunt <bl>φιλόνεικοι</bl>, ubi veritati semel repugnare coeperunt, nullis possint argumentis persuaderi ut cedant. Iudicat enim turpissimum esse, si videantur errasse. Non est, proh dolor, opus exemplis, quæ aliàs nimis multa & indefinentia nostro sæculo visuntur. Nisi esset hic <bl>φιλονεικίας</bl> morbus tam validus in ecclesia, facili negocio componerētur præsentium temporum dissidia.
units.tr: He foresaw that some in the Church, not yet free of the pride of secular learning but still labouring under the zeal for contention, would think that the arguments already adduced were of less weight than they ought to be content with. This was not because they were insufficient for the present case, but because those men were suffering from the disease of contentiousness [φιλονεικία]. To check this, he added this particle at the end, saying: "But if anyone seems to be contentious, we do not have such a custom, nor do the churches of God." In Latin we read "if anyone is contentious"; in the Greek it is "if anyone is φιλόνεικος [contentious]." Now φιλόνεικος means not simply contentious, but one who loves and is eager for victory. Someone so disposed does not seek truth but victory. He argues not moderately, as much as is enough for one who studies truth, but immoderately and without limit, contending for victory. He accepts no argument so as to yield to the truth, but changes himself into every shape, so that at least he may avoid appearing beaten, if he cannot surely win. To contend about some matter is in itself nothing unlawful; indeed, if it is done for the truth, it even deserves praise. But if it is done for a dishonourable and evil matter, or from a desire for empty glory, it is rightly judged by even the heathen to be a vice of manifest arrogance. Being φιλόνεικος [contentious] is one thing, and being φιλάληθες [a lover of truth] is another. That is, it is one thing to contend so that you yourself may win, or so that you may appear with glory, or at least not appear beaten; and it is another to contend for the truth, so that it may prevail, without troubling whether this is done by you or by others, as men are moved who love not themselves but the one truth. Those who are φιλόνεικοι [contentious], once they have begun to resist the truth, can be persuaded by no arguments to yield. For they judge it most shameful to seem to have been wrong. There is no need, alas, for examples, which in our age are seen too many and without end. Unless this disease of contentiousness [φιλονεικία] were so strong in the Church, the disputes of the present time could be settled with little trouble.

units.la: Observa vero, quod non dicit: Si quis vero contentiosus est, sed, si quis vero contentiosus esse videtur. Hoc est: Si quis est inter vos, qui nimio altercandi studio manifestum de se facit, quod sit homo contentiosus ac victoriæ cupidus. Non hoc agit, ut pro contentioso habeatur, quisquis solida veritatis argumenta quærit sed is potius, qui sic temerè contendit, ut palàm fit, quod morbo contendendi laboret. Quales sunt, qui vel de re nihili lites movet, vel in causa manifesta in contrarium tendunt, aut ob id tantum contendunt, ut cæteris contradicant, iuxta illud, Aiunt: nego. Negant: aio, quib. oppositi sunt assentatores, quorum vox est, aiunt: aio, negant: nego, aut absque vllo fine contendunt. Hisce notis proditur morbus <bl>φιλονεικίας</bl>. Talibus hominibus nemo satisfecerit. Quare relinquendos esse monens dicit: Si quis vero contentiosus esse videtur, nos eiusmodi consuetudinem non habemus, &c.
units.tr: Note, however, that he does not say, "If anyone is contentious," but "If anyone seems to be contentious."
