That is: "If there is anyone among you who by his excessive eagerness for arguing makes it plain of himself that he is a contentious man and eager for victory." He does not mean that whoever seeks solid arguments of truth is to be counted as contentious, but rather one who contends so rashly that it is evident he suffers from the disease of contending. Such are those who either stir up quarrels over a matter of nothing, or who, in a plain case, take the opposite side, or who contend only so that they may contradict the others, according to the saying: "They say, 'I affirm.' They deny, 'I affirm.'" Their opponents are flatterers, whose cry is "They say, 'I affirm,'" and "They deny, 'I deny,'" or who contend without any end. By these marks the disease of contentiousness [φιλονεικία] is revealed. No one will satisfy such men. Therefore, warning that they are to be left alone, he says: "But if anyone seems to be contentious, we do not have such a custom, etc."

units.la: Potest autem, quod dicit, nos eiusmodi consuetudinem non habemus, neq; ecclesiæ Dei, bifariam exponi, propterea quod minus expressum est, quam consuetudinem nec se nec ecclesias Dei habere dicat. Primò, ut intelligatur de consuetudine, qua viri obuelatis, mulieres vero tectis capitibus in ecclesiasticum coetum ingrediebantur. Deinde, ut referatur ad consuetudinem contendendi. Prior sensus sic habet: Si quis contentiosus esse videtur, sic ut argumentis nostris cedere nolit, sciat is in summa, quantumuis contendat, alienos esse & nos & ecclesias Dei ab hac consuetudine, qua ethnicorum mulieres nudis, viri vero tectis capitibus orant. Si nobis iungi voluerit, sequatur consuetudinem & nostrā & ecclesiarum Dei, nec adferat in nostrum coetum consuetudinem ethnicam. Sensum huc sequutus est Lyranus. Et Ambrosio quoque ad hunc modum exponere placuit. Post rationem redditam ut contentiosos vincat, autoritatem interponit, quia neq; Iudaismus hoc habuit. Unde dicit: Neq; nos neq; ecclesia Dei, ut neq; Moses neq; Salvator sic tradiderit. Posterior vero sensus talis est. Si quis contentiosus esse videtur, sit hoc si ne nobis. Alienum à nobis & ecclesijs Dei est muliebri more verbis contendere. Sic exponit Chrysostomus. Nos consuetudinem hanc nō habemus, ut contendamus, litigemus, accertemus. Et huc sensum recentiores fere sequuntur. Hieronymus utrunque ponit, dicens: Nos talem consuetudinem non habemus, sive contendendi, sive talia faciendi. Meo iudicio potest sic exponi, ut utrique sensus coniungatur. Omnino ab utraque consuetudine alienæ erant ecclesiæ Dei. Nec mulieres ipsarum nudis, nec viri tectis capitibus orabant, neque apostoli neque ecclesiæ Dei spiritu contentionis laborabant. Quare non incommodè exposuerimus ad hunc modum. Si quis eorum, qui ista faciunt, non corrigi, sed in contrarium contendere voluerit, sciat nec nos nec ecclesias Dei hoc habere in more, ut cum ipsis decorū sexuum peruertamus, & quod malefacimus, contentiosè defendamus. Nihil refert aut, an uocula nos, referamus vel ad ipsam Apostoli personam, vel ad cæteros quoq; apostolos. Ambrosius per illā intelligit Iudæos, ex quibus erat Paulus. Qui priorem sensum amplectuntur ex scholasticis, colligūt ex eo sequendā esse consuetudinem prælatorū & ecclesiarū, nec feredū ut quisquā illi cōtradicat. Vno verbo. Cōsentimus, ubi cōsuetudo nulla in re præiudicat veritati. Aliàs consuetudo sine veritate vetustas erroris est, nō sequēda, sed vitanda. Non placet libido nouādi recepta, in quibus nihil peccatur cōtra scripturas sacras. Rursus nō probamus eos, qui ubi veritatis calculis destituuntur, cōfessos abusus vetustate catholicæ cōsuetudinis tueri se posse confidunt. Non est quod ex præsenti loco patrocinium quærant. Placet & nobis consuetudo talis, quæ fuerit & apostolorum & ecclesiarum Dei.
units.tr: The words "we do not have such a custom, nor do the churches of God" can be explained in two ways, because it is less clearly stated what custom he says neither he nor the churches of God have. First, it may be understood of the custom by which men entered the ecclesiastical assembly with heads uncovered and women with heads covered. Second, it may be referred to the custom of contending. The first sense runs thus: "If anyone seems contentious, so that he is unwilling to yield to our arguments, let him know in short that, however much he contends, both we and the churches of God are alien to this custom, by which the women of the heathen pray with heads uncovered and the men with heads covered. If he wishes to join us, let him follow the custom of both us and the churches of God, and let him not bring the heathen custom into our assembly." Lyra followed this sense, and Ambrose also was pleased to explain it in this way. After giving the reason, in order to overcome the contentious, he adds an authority, because not even Judaism had this. Hence he says: "Neither we nor the church of God, just as neither Moses nor the Saviour handed down such a thing." The second sense is this: "If anyone seems contentious, let it be so, if it is on his own account. It is foreign to us and to the churches of God to contend in words in the manner of women." Chrysostom explains it thus: "We do not have this custom, of contending, litigating, or quarrelling." And most of the more recent writers follow this sense. Jerome gives both, saying: "We do not have such a custom, either of contending or of doing such things." In my judgment it can be explained so that both senses are joined. The churches of God were entirely alien to both customs. Neither their women prayed with uncovered heads, nor their men with covered heads; and neither the Apostles nor the churches of God laboured under the spirit of contention. Therefore we shall explain it not unsuitably in this way: "If anyone of those who do these things is unwilling to be corrected, but wishes to contend against it, let him know that neither we nor the churches of God have it as a custom to overturn the propriety of the sexes along with them, and to defend stubbornly what we do wrongly." It makes no difference whether we refer the little word "we" to the person of the Apostle himself or also to the other apostles. Ambrose understands by it the Jews, from whom Paul came. Those among the schoolmen who embrace the first sense conclude from it that the customs of prelates and churches must be followed, and that no one should be allowed to contradict them. In a word: we agree where custom in no way prejudices the truth. Otherwise custom without truth is the antiquity of error, not to be followed but to be avoided. We do not approve a lust for innovation in matters in which nothing is sinned against the holy Scriptures. Again, we do not approve of those who, when they are left without the support of truth, confidently believe they can defend admitted abuses by the antiquity of Catholic custom. There is no reason to seek patronage in this passage. We too approve of such a custom as was both of the apostles and of the churches of God.

units.la: In posteriori sensu doctrinam habemus potissimum nostro hoc sæculo necessariam, qua contra insaniam illam contendendi tranquillitatem conscientiarum nostrarum seruemus. Nihil intentatum relinquitur, quod non in contentionem rapiatur. Deinde quantumuis perspiperspicuè & diserte sententiam nostram expli cuerimus,nihil efficimus aliud,quàm quod o leum camino ardenti infundimus. Sciamus i gitur hoc & dicamus nos quoq; cum Aposto lo:Si qui videntur esse contentiosi, nos eiuf modi consuetudinem non habemus, neq; ec clesiæ Dei.Ministrorum Christi non est conté dere,sed simpliciter & fideliter docere.Eccle siæ quoq; non est contendere,sed credere & o bedire.Noli contendere verbis,inquit Aposto lus 2.Tim.2.Ad nihil enim est vtile, nisi ad sub uersionem audientium.Hanc quærens Satan seminat in ecclesia contentiones & rixas. Et habet organa sua, quibus quod quærit, conse quatur.
units.tr: In the second sense we have a teaching especially necessary in this age, by which we may preserve the calm of our consciences against that madness of contending. Nothing is left untried that is not dragged into contention. Moreover, however clearly and plainly we explain our opinion, we accomplish nothing else than pouring oil on a burning furnace. Let us therefore know this, and let us say with the Apostle: "If anyone seems to be contentious, we do not have such a custom, nor do the churches of God." It is not the business of the ministers of Christ to contend, but to teach simply and faithfully. Nor is it the business of the Church to contend, but to believe and to obey. "Do not strive about words," says the Apostle in 2 Tim. 2. "For it is good for nothing but the subverting of the hearers." Satan, seeking this, sows contentions and strifes in the Church, and he has his instruments, by which he may obtain what he seeks.

units.la: Illud autem præcipiens non laudo, quod nō in melius,sed in deterius con-uenitis.
units.tr: Now in giving this instruction I do not commend you, because you come together not for the better but for the worse.

units.la: Hactenus primumcapitis huius membrum absoluit,quo dissolutionem virilis pariter ac muliebris decori correxit, quam inuehere in ecclesiâ cœperant,qui ethnico & patrio more in cœtu sacro comparêtes, viri tectis,mulleres nudis capitibus orabant. Iam transit ad alia corrigenda.Et in præsenti eos abusus emenda re aggreditur,qui circa cœnam dominicâ ad-mittebantur.Et priusquam de illis dicat,transi tione vtitur tali,qua statim initio animos Co rinthiorum tanquam ad alterius & aliquanto grauioris mali correctionemexcitet. Sic dicit: Illud tamen præcipiens non laudo. Ita vertit B Erafmus. Vuulgata habet: Hoc autem præci-pio non laudans.In Græco est,τοῦτο δὲ παραγγέλ λων ὑκ ἐπαινῶ.Id est:Hoc autem denuncias , vel admonens,non laudo.Et Chrysostomus sic le git, quamuis interpres illius vulgatam versio-nem posuerit. Erafmus & nonnulli alij Chry sostomum sequuti , exponunt ad hunc mo-dum. Non laudo,quod hoc præcipere cogor vt quod dicit ,τοῦτο δὲ ἀπαγγέλλω, id est , hoc autem denuncians,idem sit quod,τοῦτο δὲ παραγ-γέλλω,id est: Hoc autem denunciare, parti-cipio pro infinito accepto . Sunt qui sic: Hoc autem quod iam denunciaturus , vel di-cturus sum,non laudo,nempe quod non inme lius, &c.
units.tr: Thus far he has completed the first part of this chapter, in which he corrected the disorder in both men's and women's dress and decorum. The Corinthians had begun to introduce this disorder, since men came to the sacred assembly with covered heads and women with bare heads, in the heathen and ancestral manner. Now he moves on to other matters to correct. At present he sets about correcting the abuses that had crept into the Lord's Supper. Before he speaks of them, he uses a transition by which, right at the start, he stirs the minds of the Corinthians as if towards the correction of another and rather more serious evil. He says: "Now in giving this instruction I do not praise you." So Erasmus translates it. The Vulgate has: "Now in giving this instruction I do not praise you." The Greek is τοῦτο δὲ παραγγέλλων οὐκ ἐπαινῶ [Now in giving this instruction I do not praise you]. That is: "Now in announcing or admonishing this, I do not praise you." Chrysostom reads it in this way, although the Vulgate translator gave the other version. Erasmus and several others who follow Chrysostom explain it thus: "I do not praise, because I am compelled to give this instruction." Read thus, the participle is taken for an infinitive, so that τοῦτο δὲ ἀπαγγέλλω, that is, "now in announcing this," means the same as τοῦτο δὲ παραγγέλλω, that is, "now to announce this." Some explain it thus: "I do not praise this, which I am now about to announce or say, namely that you come together not for the better, etc."

units.la: Addam & meam cogitationem . Apparet particulam hanc,ὑκ ἐπαινῶ,referendam esse nō ad præcedens,sed ad id quod sequitur,deinde illud, τοῦτο δὲ παραγγέλλω, idem esse quod ταῦτα δὲ παραγγέλλω,id est,de hoc autem denun cians & admonens , referendumq; ad præce-dentem correctionem,ac legendū:Vbi de hoc autem denunciaui & admonui,iam non lau-do quod non in melius,sed in deterius conue nitis.Notum est omnibus qui vel modice ver sati sunt in Græcis vsitatissimum esse in hac lingua,vt participia pro præteritis ponantur, præsertim in narrationibus, vt exempli gratia Galat.2.cum vellet Apostolus dicere , & tra-didit semetipsum pro me,dixit, ὃς παραδόντ᾽ ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἐμοῦ, quod si vertas in præsenti,& tra-
units.tr: I will add my own view too. It appears that this particle, οὐκ ἐπαινῶ [I do not praise], should be referred not to what precedes but to what follows. Then τοῦτο δὲ παραγγέλλω [now I announce this] is the same as ταῦτα δὲ παραγγέλλω [now I announce these things], that is, "now announcing and admonishing about this." It should be referred to the preceding correction, and the sentence should be read: "Where I have announced and admonished about this, I now do not praise you, because you come together not for the better but for the worse." It is known to everyone who has even a modest acquaintance with Greek that the participle is very commonly used in this language in place of past tenses, especially in narrative. For example, in Galatians 2, when the Apostle wanted to say "and delivered himself up for me," he wrote ὃς παραδόντ᾽ ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἐμοῦ [who delivered himself for me]. If you render this in the present, "who is delivering himself for me," you do not express the Apostle's meaning.

units.la: dentis seipsum pro me,non exprimis sensum Apostoli.Posuit enim participium παραδόντα non pro tradente,sed pro eo qui tradidit. Ta lia innumera occurrunt in scripturis.Sic cum hic per transitionem dicere vellet: Vbi autem de hoc denunciaui & admonui,iâ confequen-ter non laudo quod non in melius,sed in dete-rius conuenitis,dixit,Τοῦτο δὲ παραγγέλλω, ὑκ ἐπαι-νῶ ὅπ ὑκ ἑτέρ ς τὸ κρίτο, &c. Vulgatę versiôis au-tor non incommodè illud nō laudo, ad sequē tia retulit.Sic enim habet : Hoc autē præcipio, non laudans quod non in melius,sed in dete-rius conuenitis.Quod si quis illud: Hoc auté, non ad præcedentia,sed ad causam de qua di-cturus est,referendum esse putat,poterit expo nere ad hunc modum:Laudaui vos,quod om nia mea memoria tenetis,quod verò iam sum denunciaturus,nonhabet laudem,sed grauem reprehensionem vestri. Non enim laudo vos, quod non in melius,&c. Non enim laudo vos, quod non in melius, &c . Non est autem ociosum quod verbo denunciandi vtitur, si referas ad præsentem causam,de qua est dicturus , quod alios facere video.Sic enim ea de qbus dictu-rus est,plus habere poderis indicat q præcedē tia,seq; de illis nô simpliciter ecclesiæ cófuetu dinem & sexuû decorû proponere,sed denun ciare ac præcipere,propter authoritatē dñi vi delicet,cuius infrà mentionem faciet, dicés:E go enim accepi à dñio,qd & tradidi vobis,&c.
units.tr: For he put the participle παραδόντα not for "delivering" but for "he who delivered." Countless such constructions occur in Scripture. So here, when he wanted to say by way of transition, "Where I have announced and admonished about this, consequently I do not praise you, because you come together not for the better but for the worse," he wrote: τοῦτο δὲ παραγγέλλω, οὐκ ἐπαινῶ, ὅτι οὐκ εἰς τὸ κρεῖττον ἀλλὰ εἰς τὸ χεῖρον συνέρχεσθε [now I announce this; I do not praise you, because you come together not for the better but for the worse]. The author of the Vulgate version did not unsuitably refer "I do not praise" to what follows. For his text reads: "Now in giving this instruction, I do not praise you that you come together not for the better but for the worse." But if anyone thinks that "now in this" should be referred not to what precedes but to the matter he is about to speak of, he may explain it thus: "I have praised you because you keep in mind all that I have taught; but what I am now about to announce carries no praise, only a grave rebuke of you. For I do not praise you that you come together not for the better, etc." It is not idle that he uses the verb "to announce" if you refer it to the present matter he is about to discuss, as I see others doing. For this shows that what he is about to say carries more weight than what has gone before. He sets these matters forth not simply as church custom or as the proper decorum of the sexes, but announces and commands them, on the authority of the Lord himself, whom he mentions below, saying: "For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you," etc.

units.la: Q V O D non in melius,sed in deterius con uenitis,inquit.)In genere exprimit,quid non laudet inipsis.Verbo cöueniendi,συνίςχειν,si gnificat se dicturum de ipsorum conuentibus quod in illis inueniat quæ probare non possit, vnde fiat,vt non in melius,sed in deterius con ueniant.Non dicit,quod non conuenitis,aut, quod rarius ac tardius conuenitis, sed, quod non in melius conuenitis,sed potius in deteri us.Conueniebant quidem in cœtum sacrum, vt erant instituti,verùm non ad ædificationē conscientiarum,sed magis ad destructionem. Hanc ob causam frequentiâ conuentuû ipso-rum nô laudat. Quomodo enim laudaret,qd in destructionē corporis Christi cedebat.Mul to enim satius est non conuenire in cœtum, q ad deterius conuenire, quemadmodum meli-us est puero non ingredi ludũ, quâ sic ingredi vt quotidie redeat indoctior,& ægroto ,absti-nere à medico,q vti tali,p quê subinde morb⁹ incrudescat magis quâ curetur.Est enim cœt⁹ sacer ex numero eorû quæ nô propter se, sed propter finis alicuius cösequutioné fiút, tum bona tantum,quando ad destinatum finem tē dunt,in quibus non est satis, si opere vtcunq; fiant,sed multum refert quomodo gerantur.
units.tr: We are taught in this passage to think in this way about ecclesiastical assemblies. It is good to gather together one people of believers, and this institution is plainly according to the counsel of God. But if people come together for destruction rather than for edification, and so what could have been good, if rightly used, begins to be evil, then it is altogether better for a godly man to abstain from such an assembly than to appear in it to the destruction of his own conscience. For this reason, those assemblies in which no one is built up in true faith, but all are led into superstitions and idolatrous worship, should today be abandoned, not to mention the most defiled communion of whores and simoniacs.

units.la: Sic de conuentibus ecclesiasticis sentire ad monemur præsenti loco.Bonû est colligerein vnû populum fidelium, & institutû hoc plane est ex consilio Dei,verû si conueniatur ad de-structionem magis quàm ad ædificationem, atque ita quod bonum esse poterat , si rectè vsurparetur, incipit esse malum , omnino sa-tius est homini pio abstinere ab eiusmodi cœ-tu, tu, quàm comparere in illo ad conscientiæ suæ {A}destructionem. Et hanc ob causam deserendi sunt hodie conuentus illi, in quibus ad veram fidem ædificatur nemo, ad superstitiones vero, & cultus eidololatricos seducuntur omnes vt inquinatissimam illā scortatorū & simonia eorum communicationem taceam.
units.tr: Observe here that he does not simply say "not for the good," but "not for the better." Therefore the aim of the ecclesiastical assembly is not that we should be good in some measure, but that we should become better every day. And this progress must be sought by us for as long as we are in this flesh. For no one is so good today that he cannot become better tomorrow. Therefore, to this end we must attend the sacred assemblies for as long as we are in this life, so that we may be made better in faith, hope and love, and grow in the knowledge of Christ.

units.la: Obserua hic, quod nō simpliciter dicit, qd̄ non in bonū, sed, quod non in melius conueniatis. Ergo scopus ecclesiastici couentus est, nō vt qualitercunq; boni simus, sed vt quotidie meliores euadamus. Et hic profectus petendus nobis est, donec sumus in hac carne. Nemo enim sic bonus est hodie, vt cras melior fieri non possit. Quare in hunc finem frequentandi nobis sunt sacri conuentus donec in hac vita sumus, vt meliores fide, spe, & dilectione reddamur, & in cognitione Christi crescamus.
units.tr: "But you come together for the worse," he says. In this lay the increase of the evil. It is blameworthy enough to come together not for the better; how much more so if people come together even for the worse. Here think of the assemblies of believers as threefold. The first is one so instituted that by the grace of the Lord we may be made better in it. The second is one in which there is neither anything that makes us better nor anything that makes us worse.

units.la: SED in deterius, inquit, conuenitis.) In hoc erat mali huius auxesis. Satis culpabile est conuenire non in melius, quanto magis, si in deterius etiam conueniatur. Cogita hic triplices esse coeuentus fidelium. Primus, qui sic sit institutus, vt in illo meliores per gratiam domini fieri possimus. Secundus, in quo nec sit, vnde meliores, nec vnde deteriores reddamur.
units.tr: The third is one in which people come together not for the better but also for the worse. It is like schools, which are also of three kinds. In the first, a boy, even if he makes some progress, may nonetheless become more learned, and learn each day what he did not know before. In the second, he cannot advance beyond the first rudiments, and hears nothing in it that makes him more learned beyond those basics. In the third, he even unlearns what he knew before, and so becomes more ignorant.

units.la: Tertius, in quo nō in melius, sed in deteriorem quoq; coeuentur. Quemadmodum triplices sunt scholæ. Prima, in qua puer, etiamsi aliquouos proficit, doctior tamen fieri potest, & quotidie discere, quod antea nesciebat. Secunda, in qua nequeat vltra prima rudimenta accedere qd̄ praeter illa nihil in ea audiat, vnde doctior fiat. {B}Tertia, in qua etiam dedisçat ea quæ antea sciebat, atq; ita ndoctior euadat.
units.tr: The third kind is that in which they come together not for the better but also for the worse. Just as there are three kinds of schools. The first is that in which a boy, even if he makes some progress, can still become more learned and each day learn what he did not know before. The second is that in which he cannot advance beyond the first rudiments, and hears nothing in it by which he might become more learned. The third is that in which he even unlearns what he knew before, and so becomes more ignorant.

units.la: 1 Primum ecclesiæ couentum, in quo meliores reddi possimus, eum esse existimo, in quo pastores sunt docti ac fideles, verbum domini recte secantes, & sacramenta à Christo Seruatore accepta rite administrantes, in quo feruet oratio fidelium, leguntur palām sacræ scripturæ, & spiritus fidelium spiritualibus hymnis excitantur ac refocillantur, ac pterea subsidia Christianæ dilectionis in vsus pauperū contribuntur, quo fideles frugiferi esse discant.
units.tr: 1 I judge the first kind of church assembly, in which we can be made better, to be that in which the ministers are learned and faithful, rightly dividing the word of the Lord and rightly administering the sacraments received from Christ the Saviour. In it the prayer of the faithful is fervent, the holy Scriptures are read publicly, and the spirits of the faithful are stirred up and refreshed by spiritual hymns. Moreover, the aids of Christian love are contributed for the use of the poor, so that the faithful learn to be fruitful.

units.la: 2 Secundum eū esse sentio, in quo nihil falsi quidem nec in doctrina nec in ritibus geritur interea tamen doctores sic sunt vel negligentes, vel spiritualium rerum imperiti, vt verbū domini non satis dextre ac pertinenter secent & præterea quæ gerūtur, sic gerūtur frigidè ac perfunctorie, vt parum ad ædificationem faciant.
units.tr: 2 I think it is the kind of assembly in which nothing false is taught in doctrine or practised in the rites, yet the teachers are either so negligent or so inexperienced in spiritual matters that they do not divide the word of the Lord well or appropriately, and what is done is done so coldly and perfunctorily that it contributes little to edification.

units.la: 3 Tertius indubitato est, in quo & falsa dogmata verbo Dei contraria traduntur, & falsi cultus exercentur, & quæ à Christo sunt tradita, humano magisterio corrumpuntur, ac conscientiæ adulterina communicatione polluuntur. Hic non in melius sed omnino in deterius coeuenitur. Quare huiusmodi conuentus, quo cunq; nomine siue catholicæ siue Romanæ ecclesiæ vocentur, non minus fugiendi sunt quā ipsa gehenna.
units.tr: 3 The third kind is undoubtedly the one in which false doctrines contrary to the word of God are taught, false worship is practised, what Christ has handed down is corrupted by human teaching, and consciences are polluted by adulterous communion. Here people gather not for the better but altogether for the worse. Therefore such assemblies, whatever name they bear, whether Catholic or Roman, are to be shunned no less than hell itself.

units.la: Nam primū quidem, dum conuenitis in ecclesia, audio schismata inter uos esse, & aliqua ex parte credo. Oportet enim & hæreses inter uos esse, quo qui probi sunt, manifesti fiant inter uos.
units.tr: For first, when you come together in the Church, I hear that there are divisions among you, and I partly believe it. For there must also be heresies among you, so that those who are approved may be made manifest among you.

units.la: Quod in genere dixit, non laudare se, quod non in melius, sed in deterius conuenirent, id iam per specificationem declarat. Sic solet qui non ex affectu sinistro, sedcum iudicio aliquid improbant. Non est satis ad emendationem, si mille ies dicas, conuentus vestri fugiendi sunt, nisi declares quid insit illis mali. Quemadmodum doctrina sana opus habet declaratione, qua rite intelligatur, ita & correctioerrantium ac delinquentium adiecta est specificatione de claranda, quo quæ malè gerutur, agnosci emendariq; possint.
units.tr: Having said in general that they did not come together for the better but for the worse, he now declares this in detail. This is how someone speaks who disapproves of something not out of ill will but with judgment. It is not enough for correction if you say a thousand times that your assemblies are to be avoided, unless you state what evil is in them. Just as sound doctrine needs explanation so that it may be rightly understood, so the correction of those who err and offend is joined to a specific statement of the faults, so that what is done badly may be recognised and amended.

units.la: NAM primum quidem, inquit. ) Non vno abusuum genere delinquebant in coetu sacro, sed vario, quemadmodum in sequentibus patebit. Quare quod iam est in causa coenæ dominicæ reprehensurus, primum vocat, dicēs: Nam primùm quidem, dum conuenitis in ecclesia, audio schismata inter vos esse. Vulgata versio habet, audio scissuras esse inter vos. Erasmus, audio dissidia in vobis esse. Græcus habet σχίσματα, quam vocem retinui, tāquam vsitatam in ecclesia, quemadmodum & eam quæ sequitur, oportet enim & hæreses inter vos esse, vbi Erasmus vertit sectas. Sunt autē tres partes eorum quæ hoc loco de coena dominica scribit. Prima grauem habet abusus illius reprehensionem. Secunda, veri vsus expositionem. Tertia, seueram contra abutentes comminationem. Ad primam pertinet quod dicit:
units.tr: FOR FIRST, he says. Not in one kind of abuse were they going wrong in the sacred assembly, but in several, as will become clear in what follows. So when he is about to rebuke the matter of the Lord's Supper, he calls it first, saying: For first, when you come together in the Church, I hear that there are divisions among you. The Vulgate has: I hear that there are schisms among you. Erasmus: I hear that there are dissensions among you. The Greek has σχίσματα [schismata], which word I have kept, as customary in the Church, and likewise the next one: for there must also be heresies among you, where Erasmus translates sects. There are three parts to what he writes here about the Lord's Supper. The first contains a grave rebuke of this abuse. The second, an exposition of the true use. The third, a stern warning against those who abuse it. To the first belongs what he says:

units.la: DVM conuenitis in ecclesia.) Significat se loqui specialiter de ijs quę in coetu sacro delinquebant, quem hic vocat ecclesiam, quę dictio interpreteris euocationem sonat. Non omnis coeuentus statim est ecclesia vocandus, sed is tantum, in quo communiter vel à ciuibus, in causis ciuilibus, vel à fidelibus, religionis gratia conuenitur. Synodum ciuium ἐκκλησίαν Græci conuentum populi ex agro ἐκκλησιαν, cōsulum vero συγκλησιν vocarunt. Non loquitur ergo Apostolus de priuatis paucorum coitionibus, sed de ecclesiasticis conuentibus, in quibus multitudo fidelium conuenit.
units.tr: WHEN you come together in the Church. He means that he is speaking specifically of those things that went wrong in the sacred assembly, which he here calls the Church; the word means a calling out. Not every gathering is at once to be called a church, but only that in which people meet in common, either citizens for civil affairs, or the faithful for the sake of religion. The Greeks called an assembly of citizens ἐκκλησίαν [ekklesian], a gathering of the people called out from the countryside; but a gathering of consuls they called σύγκλησιν [synklēsin]. The Apostle therefore is not speaking of private meetings of a few people, but of ecclesiastical gatherings in which the multitude of the faithful comes together.

units.la: AVDIO, inquit, schismata inter vos esse.) Σχίσμα Græca uox est, & significat eorum quę integra sunt dissecationem ac scissuram. Sic solet ecclesiasticæ vnitatis dissecatio vocari schisma, quando corpus fidelium, quod vnitissimum esse conueniebat, in partes à se inuicem dissidentes scinditur. Ergo erat ecclesia Corinthiorum scissa in studia & partes, eáque ob causam fiebat, vt nō in melius, sed in deterius in ecclesiam conuenirent.
units.tr: I HEAR, he says, that there are divisions among you. Σχίσμα [schisma] is a Greek word and means the cutting apart or splitting of things that were whole. So the breaking of ecclesiastical unity is customarily called a schism, when the body of the faithful, which ought to have been most united, is torn into parts that are at odds with one another. So the Corinthian Church was split into factions and parties, and for this reason they were coming together not for the better but for the worse.

units.la: Quæ aut fuerint illorū schismata, nō exprimit hoc loco. Nā statim initio epistolæ post salutationē de illis meminit, dicēs: Obsecro autem vos fratres per nomen dūi nostri Iesu Christi, vt idem loquamini omnes, & non sint inter vos schismata,sed sitis integrũ corpus, eadem mente & eadem sententia. Significatum est enim mihi fratres mei de vobis, à familiaribus Chloæ,quod contentiones sint inter vos. Dico autem illud,quod vnusquisque vestrum dicit:Ego quidem sum Pauli, ego verò Apollo, ego vero Cephæ,ego verò Christi,&c.quibus verbis & schismata illorum expressit, & vnde de illis audierit,significauit.Quare hic simpliciter dicit:Nam primùm dum cōuenitis in ecclesiam,audio schismata inter vos esse.
units.tr: What these divisions were he does not express at this point. For at the very beginning of the letter, after the greeting, he mentions them, saying: Now I beg you, brothers, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be a whole body, of the same mind and the same judgment. For it has been reported to me, my brothers, about you, by the household of Chloe, that there are quarrels among you. I mean this, that each of you says: I am of Paul, I of Apollos, I of Cephas, I of Christ, and so on. In these words he has both expressed their divisions and indicated from whom he heard about them. Therefore here he simply says: For first, when you come together in the Church, I hear that there are divisions among you.

units.la: Qua verò de causa nequeant in melius, sed magis in deterius conuenire,qui à se inuicem factionib.sunt direpti,facilè cogitari potest.
units.tr: Why those who are torn apart from one another by factions cannot come together for the better, but rather for the worse, can easily be understood.

units.la: Primùm enim studia factionū in ipsos conuentus sacros inferuntur. Non conuenitur eodem,sed diuerso studio,& suam quisq; sectam palàm profitentur.
units.tr: For first, the spirit of faction is carried into the very sacred assemblies. People do not come together with one common purpose, but with divided zeal, and each openly professes his own sect.

units.la: Deinde, animi magis ac magis à se inuicem abalienantur.
units.tr: Second, their minds are more and more alienated from one another.

units.la: Tertiò,ipsæ factiones publica professione corroborantur.
units.tr: Third, the factions themselves are strengthened by open profession.

units.la: Quartò, omnes conciliandi rationes difficiliores redduntur.
units.tr: Fourth, all means of reconciliation become more difficult.

units.la: Quintò,ab eiusmodi conuentibus,vbi non corporis Christi ædificatio,sed sectarum amplificatio quæritur,operatio diuinę gratię excluditur. Non est enim Deus confusionis ac dissensionis,sed pacis & vnitatis. Quare mirũ non est,quod in talibus conuentibus malum non curatur,sed subinde peius ac peius reddi-tur.Cuius rei in synodis episcoporum euidentissima habemus experimenta,de quibus vide Nazanzenum in epistola ad Procopium , vbi propterea ad concilium episcoporum profici scì recusauit,quì nullo vnquā cōcilio mala cor rigi,sed magis corroborari vidisset,idq; propter episcoporum dissidia & contentiones.
units.tr: Fifth, from such assemblies, where the aim is not the building up of the body of Christ but the enlargement of sects, the working of divine grace is shut out. For God is not a God of confusion and dissension, but of peace and unity. So it is no wonder that in such assemblies the evil is not cured, but becomes worse and worse. We have the most evident experience of this in the synods of bishops, concerning which see Nazianzen in his letter to Procopius, where he refused for that reason to go to a council of bishops, since he had seen that evils were never corrected in any council but rather strengthened, and that because of the disagreements and contentions of the bishops.

units.la: Hinc tamen nemo colligat: ergo ubi nulla sunt schismata,ibi non in deterius,sed in melius conuenitur.Potest enim fieri, vt in falsa religione,idololatria,&adulterinis cultibus sit & episcoporum,& populi concordia,ingredi anturq; cœtum sacrum vnanimes & concordes , vbi tamen dici non potest, quod non in deterius,sed in melius qui eiusmodi sunt, conueniant. Sic conueniunt & Turci & reliqui in fideles,inter quos nulla sunt schismata.Et fide mus Papistis,quod alieni sint à schismatibus ac dissidijs,quod tamen verè illis dari non potest,alieni tamen non sunt ipsorum conuent9 à falsis dogmatibus & cultibus,ab impura communione,& à symonia omnium turpissima.
units.tr: Yet let no one conclude from this: therefore where there are no schisms, there people come together not for the worse but for the better. For it can happen that in false religion, idolatry and adulterous worship there is harmony among both bishops and people, and they enter the sacred assembly united and of one mind; yet it cannot be said that such people come together not for the worse but for the better. So the Turks and the other unbelievers come together, among whom there are no schisms. And we grant to the Papists that they are free from schisms and dissensions; this indeed cannot truly be granted to them. Yet their assemblies are not free from false doctrines and worship, from impure communion, and from simony, the most shameful of all.

units.la: ET aliqua,inquit,ex parte credo.)Moderationis est,quod non simpliciter dicit,& sic esse credo,sed,& aliqua ex parte credo. In Græco est,καὶ μέρ᾽ τί πιστεύω,id est,& partem aliquam credo pro καπὰ μέρος ἢ. Ergo non credidit per omnia verum esse,quod audierat à familiaribus Chloes,sed ex parte tantum. Considebat enim non omnes hoc esse schismatis morbo correptos,sed aliquâ tantum illorum partem. Et hoc propterea memorat, quo sanioribus parcat,eosq; in ordine retineat, vbi rursus Apostolicæ habemus prudentiæ exemplum.
units.tr: AND, he says, I partly believe it. This is moderation: he does not simply say, and so I believe it to be, but, and I partly believe it. In the Greek it is καὶ μέρ᾽ τί πιστεύω [kai mer' ti pisteuō], that is, and I believe some part, in place of κατὰ μέρος [kata meros], in part. Therefore he did not believe to be wholly true what he had heard from the household of Chloe, but only in part. For he considered that not all were infected with this disease of schism, but only some part of them. And he mentions this so as to spare the more sensible and keep them in their place, where again we have an example of apostolic prudence.

units.la: Potest tamen hæc particula sic quoq; expo ni,vt nō referatur ad partem Corinthiorũ,qui schismata induxerant in ecclesiam,sed ad ipsũ assensum Apostoli,quo ijs quæ de schismate il lorum audiebat,haud plene & omnino, sed aliqua tantum ex parte credebat,quemadmodum fieri solet,vbi per charitatem meliora sperantem ægrè credimus,quæ de fratrib. mala narrantur,& tamen vel fide narrantium vel circumstantijs quibusdam & coniecturis inducimur,vt haud possimus omnia quæ audimus,quasi vana in ventos abijcere. Sic quidem comparata est fama,vt plerunq; plura spargat,q̄ habeat veritas. Rursus tamen raro accidit,vt omnia vana sint,quę narrătur.Quę autē narrantur,aut certo scimus esse vera,aut credimus narrantibus,aut non plenè, sed ex parte credimus,aut de omnibus dubitamus, vel ꝑ sus nihil illorum verum esse credimus. Charitatis quidem est haud facilè fidem accommodare illis,quæ mala de fratrib.referuntur. Verum,vbi sic illa sunt comparata,vt vel ex parte a liqua credere vel dubitare cogamur, prudentiæ,imò charitatis Christianæ fuerit,& quæ p̄ sertim pastoribus & doctoribus competat, vt ad exemplū hoc Apostoli malo quantumuis nondum explorato, in tempore occurrere co nemur,nedum vbi per omnia credimus , aut quod adhuc amplius est,certo scimus.
units.tr: This particle, however, may also be explained in another way: not referring to the part of the Corinthians who had introduced the schisms into the Church, but to the Apostle's own assent, by which he believed what he heard of their schism not fully and completely, but only partly. This is what usually happens when, hoping for better things out of charity, we reluctantly believe the evil reports told of brothers, and yet we are moved by the reliability of those who tell them, or by certain circumstances and conjectures, so that we cannot simply cast away everything we hear as empty words to the winds. Rumour is so constituted that it often spreads more than the truth contains. Yet it rarely happens that everything reported is false. Of what is reported, we either know for certain that it is true, or we believe the informants, or we believe only in part, or we doubt all of it, or we believe that none of it is true at all. It is indeed a mark of charity not readily to give credence to the evil reported of brothers. But when things are of such a kind that we are compelled either to believe in part or to doubt, it would be a mark of prudence, and indeed of Christian charity, and especially fitting for ministers and teachers, to follow this example of the Apostle and to act in time against an evil, however unexplored it may still be, much less when we believe everything, or, what is even more, know it for certain.

units.la: OPORTET enim,inquit,&hæreses inter vos esse,quo q ꝑbi sunt,manifesti fiāt.)Ætiologia est.Dixit:Dū cōuenitis in ecclesiam,audio schismata inter vos esse,& aliqua ex parte credo,hoc,videlicet,quod audio esse verum. Iam rationem reddit,quare hoc non prorsus falsum,sed aliqua ex parte credat esse verum. Quia,inquit,oportet & hæreses esse inter vos. Non est necesse, vt hic vocula hæreses alio sen su accipiamus,q̄ quo accipimus schismata.Significat hæresis sectam,& in scripturis tribuitur Pharisæis, Nazaræis,Sadducæis,& Christianis quoq;,sicut i Act.ca.24.videre licet.Quare perinde est,ac si diceret:Oportet enim & schismata inter uos esse.Theologi discernũt inter schisma & hæresim, sic vt schisma sit, quando vel dogmatis alicuius gratia,vel aliam ob causam scinditur ecclesia,hæresis verò, quādo falsa dogmata contra cōmunem ecclesiæ sensum pertinaciter afferuntur ac retinentur, etiāsi id fiat sine schismate. Significat quidē αἵρεσις, electione quoq;,qua sibi quisquā singulare quidā eligit, vnde vox hæc ad hūc sensum à Theologis vsurpatur,verū in præsenti posita est ab Apostolo ꝑ secta & schismate.Alias infirma esset ipsi͏ᵍ ætiologia,p quā ratione reddere voluit,quare credat ex parte esse inter Corinthios schismata.Etenim non mox schisma est,vbi est hæresis,sensu Theologorum. Potest nanque esse,vt sine schismate sint in vna ecclesia multæ hætæ hæreses, hoc est, singulares opiniones, ac rursus, vt schisma fiat, quamuis nulla sint in doctrina ac fide diff dia. Hæresis est in animis, qua aliud atque aliud sentitur, & mordicus retinetur, etiamsi externa ecclesiasticæ communicationis societas haudquaquam discinditur. Schisma vero est, quando communicatio ecclesiæ in sectas dissecatur. Et hac dissecatione demum manifestatur qui probi sint, qui reprobi. Quare nisi hæresis hic accipiatur pro schismate, non modo infirma est æтiologia hęc Apostoli, sed nec illud stabit, quod sub jcit, quo qui probi sunt, manifesti fiant. Donec manent in ecclesia, qui non sunt vera illius membra, haud cognoscuntur ab omnibus, hoc est, non sunt manifesti. Verum vbi per schisma sese auellunt à reliquo corpore & exeunt, tum demum manifestatur quod non sint ex probis, sed ex reprobis, nec pertineant ad ecclesiæ corpus. Sic n.1. Ioha.2. legimus E nobis egressi sunt, sed non erant ex nobis. Nam si fuissent ex nobis, permansissent vtiq; nobiscum, sed vt manifesti fierent, quod non sint omnes ex nobis, &c. Si dicas hodie: Audio multa esse inter vos coniugum diuortia, & ex parte credo. Oportet enim & adulteria esse inter vos, quo qui probi sunt coniuges, manifesti fiant, non itabit hæc ratio. Neq; enim mox sunt diuortia, vbicunq; sunt adulteria, quod animiseit manifestum. Deinde, neq; mox manifesti fiùt probi coniuges, vbi sunt adulteria, sed diualsione ac diuortij, exoritur ita manifestatio. Quare sic potius dicendum est: Audio esse inter vos diuortia, & ex parte credo. Nam oportet esse diualiliones coniugum inter vos, quo qui probi sunt, manifesti fiant. Consimili modo & hoc loco accipiendum est quod Apostolus dicit: Audio esse inter vos schismata, & aliqua ex parte credo. Oportet enim & hæreses, id est, sectas & schismata esse inter vos, quo qui probi sunt, manifesti fiant. Hęc de sensu verborum vtorum sic annoto, vt tamen interea nemini secus sentienti præiudicem.
units.tr: For the Apostle says: "There must be heresies among you too, so that those who are approved may become manifest." This is an aetiology, a giving of the cause. He had said: "When you come together in the church, I hear that there are schisms among you, and I partly believe it, namely that what I hear is true." Now he gives the reason why he believes that this is not entirely false but partly true: "Because," he says, "there must be heresies among you too." We need not take the word "heresies" in a different sense from the one in which we take "schisms." "Heresy" signifies a sect, and in the Scriptures it is applied to the Pharisees, the Nazarenes, the Sadducees, and also to the Christians, as can be seen in Acts 24. So it is as if he said: "For there must also be schisms among you." Theologians distinguish between schism and heresy: a schism occurs when the church is torn apart for the sake of some doctrine or for some other cause; heresy occurs when false doctrines are stubbornly asserted and held against the common sense of the church, even if this happens without schism. αἵρεσις [haeresis] does indeed signify choice, by which someone picks out something peculiar for himself, and theologians use the word in this sense; but in the present passage the Apostle uses it for sect and schism. Otherwise his aetiology would be weak, by which he wished to give the reason why he believes that there are schisms among the Corinthians in part. For a schism does not immediately exist wherever there is heresy in the theologians' sense. There can be many sects, that is, individual opinions, in one church without schism; and conversely, a schism can arise even though there are no differences in doctrine and faith. Heresy is in the minds, when one thinks differently and holds to it obstinately, even if the external fellowship of ecclesiastical communion is not broken at all. Schism, however, is when the communion of the church is cut up into sects. And it is by this cutting apart that, at last, those who are good and those who are bad are made manifest. Therefore, unless "heresy" is taken here for schism, not only is this aetiology of the Apostle weak, but also what he adds will not stand: "so that those who are approved may become manifest." As long as those who are not true members of the church remain in it, they are not recognized by all; that is, they are not manifest. But when through schism they tear themselves away from the rest of the body and go out, then at last it becomes manifest that they are not of the approved but of the reprobate, and do not belong to the body of the church. Thus we read in 1 John 2: "They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us; but that it might be made manifest that not all are of us," and so on. If you were to say today: "I hear there are many divorces among you married people, and I partly believe it. For there must also be adulteries among you, so that the married couples who are approved may become manifest," this reasoning would not hold. For divorces do not immediately exist wherever there are adulteries, since adultery is in the mind; nor do approved married couples immediately become manifest wherever there are adulteries, but manifestation comes about through separation and divorce. Therefore it should rather be put thus: "I hear there are divorces among you, and I partly believe it. For there must be separations of spouses among you, so that those who are approved may become manifest." In the same way, in this place, what the Apostle says must be understood: "I hear there are schisms among you, and I partly believe it. For there must be heresies, that is, sects and schisms, among you, so that those who are approved may become manifest." I set down the sense of these words in this way, yet so that I prejudge no one who thinks otherwise.

units.la: OPORTET enim & hæreses, inquit, esse inter vos.) Non simpliciter dicit: Possibile enim est, sed, oportet enim, neq;, oportet enim hæreses esse, sed, oportet enim & hæreses esse, neq; hic quiescit, sed addit, inter vos: neque illa simpliciter pronunciat, sed subjicit causam dicens, quoquo probi sunt, manifesti fiant. Sūt hæc diligenter inspicienda.
units.tr: "For there must be heresies also among you," he says. He does not simply say "it is possible," but "for there must be"; nor does he say "for there must be heresies," but "for there must be also heresies"; nor does he stop there, but adds "among you." Nor does he pronounce these things simply, but adds the cause, saying "so that those who are approved may become manifest." These points must be examined carefully.

units.la: Principio, quod non dicit: possibile nanq; est, sed, oportet enim hæreses esse inter vos: admonet nos, non esse mox credenda quę de tribus narrantur mala, etiam si possibile sit, esse ea ab illis designata. Neque enim mox fiunt quæ sic sunt comparata, vt fieri possint. Quare non convenit vt dicas: audio in ciuitate esse factiones. Et aliqua ex parte credo. Possibile enim est, vt sint in illa factiones. Nimis proclivis est ad credendum, qui non alia ratione credit, quàm quod possibilia sunt quæ credit.
units.tr: First, he does not say "for it is possible," but "for there must be heresies among you." He admonishes us that what is reported of certain people's evils is not to be believed at once, even if it is possible that those things were done by them. For things that are of such a kind that they could happen do not at once happen. Therefore it is not fitting to say: "I hear there are factions in the city, and I partly believe it, for it is possible that there are factions in it." He who believes for no other reason than that what he believes is possible is far too ready to believe.

units.la: Longe graviorem ac magis vrgentem rationem
units.tr: The Apostle brings a much weightier and more pressing reason

units.la: adducit Apostolus, quare ex parte credat esse verum, quod in ecclesia Corinthiorum schismata esse audiebat. Ea est non probabilitatis, sed necessitatis. Oportet enim, inquit, & hæreses esse inter vos, quare ex parte credo, quod sint, vt audio, inter vos hæreses & schismata. Quod enim esse oportet, non modo facile, sed & necesse est vt fiat.
units.tr: why he partly believes that what he hears, that there are schisms in the church of the Corinthians, is true. This reason is not one of probability but of necessity. For, he says, "there must be heresies among you too," so I partly believe that, as I hear, there are heresies and schisms among you. For what must be, is not only easily but also necessarily brought about.

units.la: Sed nascitur hic quæstio, quæ fuerit illa necessitas propter quam schismata & sectas inter Corinthios esse oportuerit. Breuiter. Gemina erat eius rei necessitas. Vna, ex iudicio Dei prorsus immutabili. Altera, ex qualitate eorum, qui in illam ecclesiam conueniebant. Iudicium Dei ecclesiam suam disponentis erat, vt suo tempore qui in illa erant probi, separatione reproborum manifestarentur. Sic erat diuinitus constitutum, ideoq;, vt aliquando fieret, necessarium. Deinde qualitas eorum qui in ea erant ecclesia coniuncti, sic eratcomparata, vt in vnitate diu consistere non possent. Erant enim coniuncti reprobi cum probis, inter se longè diuersi. Coniunctio vero dissimilium ac diuersorum stabilis esse non potest.
units.tr: But here the question arises: what was that necessity on account of which schisms and sects had to exist among the Corinthians? Briefly: the necessity was twofold. One lay in the utterly unchangeable judgment of God; the other in the character of those who came together into that church. The judgment of God, who orders his church, was that at his appointed time those who were good among them should be made manifest by the separation of the reprobate. This had been divinely decreed, and therefore it was necessary that it should happen at some point. Then, the character of those who were joined together in that church was such that they could not remain in unity for long. For the reprobate were joined with the good, and they were very different from one another. But a union of unlike and diverse people cannot be stable.

units.la: Redeunt enim ad ingenium reprobi, & quales sunt, prodeunt, nec in vnitate cum probis permanere possunt, quia & spiritu ab illis διʼ διʼ πνευμα distant. Quare ad primam quamuis occasionem ab illis discedunt. Sciebat autem Apostolus haud omnes esse in ea ecclesia probos, sed probis immixtos reprobos: nec ignorabat, fieri non posse, vt diutius in vnitate ecclesiæ catam diuersa ingenia cohæreret, ac sumul de iudicio Dei cogitabat, electos suos haud perpetuo coniunctione reproborum obscuri tinentis. Horum itaque consideratione, cum audiret in ecclesia tali esse schismata, permouebatur, vt id aliqua ex parte crederet esse verum, eamque rationem hisce verbis expressit. Oportet enim hæreses esse, vt qui probi sunt, manifesti fiant. Tale est & illud Christi: Væ mundo ab offendiculis. Necesse nanq; est vt veniat offendicula, vel vt Lucas habet, ἀνάγκη, id est, nō capit, fieri non potest, impossibile est, vt non veniant offendicula. Hæ duæ necessitates sic sunt comparatæ, vt nō lic necesse dū vnā statuimus vt alterā reiciamus. Possunt enim ambæ in hac causa concurrere.
units.tr: For the reprobate return to their own nature and show what they are; they cannot remain in unity with the good, because they also differ from them in spirit [διὰ πνεῦμα]. Therefore, at the first opportunity, they depart from them. The Apostle knew that not all in that church were good, but that the reprobate were mixed in among the good; nor was he unaware that it was impossible for such diverse natures to cohere for long in the unity of the church. He also considered God's judgment, that his elect should not always be obscured by being joined with the reprobate. Having weighed these things, when he heard that there were schisms in such a church, he was moved to believe in part that this was true, and he expressed this reasoning in these words: "For there must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest." Christ's saying is of the same kind: "Woe to the world because of offences. For it is necessary that offences come," or, as Luke has it, ἀνάγκη [anankē], that is, "it is not possible that offences should not come." These two necessities are of such a kind that the one does not require us to reject the other. Both can concur in this matter.

units.la: Sic puto nihil hic loci esse disputationibus de necessitate fati, neque quærendum, quomodo malo tribuatur necessitas. Non enim loquitur Apostolus de necessitate malorum, sed potius de necessaria separatione malorum & bonorum, quæ fit per schismata. Non dicit, oportet enim reprobos esse, vel, oportet enim hæreticos esse, sed, oportet enim hæreses, id est sectas & schismata esse. Alia quæstio est, quare sint reprobi in ecclesia, & alia, quare sint in ecclesia schismata. Sed pergamus.
units.tr: So I think there is nothing here for disputes about the necessity of fate, nor should we ask how necessity can be attributed to evil. For the Apostle is not speaking of the necessity of evils, but rather of the necessary separation of the evil and the good, which comes about through schisms. He does not say, "for there must be reprobate people," or "for there must be heretics," but "for there must be heresies, that is, sects and schisms." Another question is why there are reprobate people in the church, and another is why there are schisms in the church. But let us go on.

units.la: OPORTET enim & hæreses esse, inquit.) Quoniam non simpliciter dicit, oportet hæreses esse, sed oportet & hæreses esse, existimant nonnulli per id significari & aliud, & amplius quiddam esse haeresim quàm schisma, quasi per intensionem dicat, oportet enim inter vos essenon modo schismata, sed etiam haereses. Illi schisma accipiunt pro dissidio animorum & ob scuram adhuc simultate, haeresim vero pro manifesto discessu ab ecclesia. Verum cum bona illorum pace, non est necesse ut exponamus ad hunc modum, oportet esse inter vos non solum schismata, sed & haereses, cum possit sic exponi: Audio inter vos esse schismata, & ex parte credo. Oportet enim esse inter vos etiam schismata, quandoquidem sunt inter vos reprobi & contentiosi. Perinde ac si de domo in qua mulier est morosa & rixosa, dicas, audio esse in illa quotidiana iurgia, & ex parte credo. Oportet enim esse in illa & rixas & iurgia, quandoquidem mulier in illa est tam morosa & rixosa.
units.tr: "Indeed there must be heresies also," he says. Since he does not simply say "there must be heresies," but "there must be heresies also," some think that this means something different, and that heresy is something more than schism, as if he meant by an intensifying phrase: "there must be among you not only schisms but also heresies." They take schism to mean a division of minds arising from a still unclear quarrel, and heresy to mean a plain departure from the Church. But with due respect to them, we need not explain it in this way, that "there must be among you not only schisms but also heresies." It can be explained thus: "I hear that there are schisms among you, and I partly believe it. For there must indeed be schisms among you, since there are reprobate and contentious people among you." It is like saying of a house where a woman is peevish and quarrelsome: "I hear there are daily brawls in it, and I partly believe it. For there must be both quarrels and brawls in it, since the woman there is so peevish and quarrelsome."

units.la: Nec otiosum est, quod non simpliciter dicit, oportet enim & haereses esse, sed addit, inter vos. Quasi dicat: Postquam inter vos tot contentiosi existunt, fieri non potest, quin unà cum reliquis malis etiam schismata inter vos oriantur. Admonemur huius particulae adiectione non esse hanc sententiam pro generali accipiendam, & cuiuis ecclesiae accommodandam. Loquitur enim de ecclesia Corinthiorum speciali ter, non in genere de omnibus. In talibus, quae lis erat illa, necesse est ut oriantur schismata. Sunt autem tales admodum multae, praesertim quae hominibus iuxta saeculum doctis, sapientibus & opulentis abundant.
units.tr: Nor is it idle that he does not simply say "there must be heresies also," but adds "among you." It is as if he said: "Since so many contentious people exist among you, it cannot be that, along with the other evils, schisms also arise among you." By the addition of this little phrase we are reminded that this sentence is not to be taken as a general rule and applied to every church. For he speaks of the church of the Corinthians specifically, not of all churches in general. In such situations, as the one at Corinth was, schisms must arise. Yet such situations are very many, especially where people who are learned, wise and wealthy by worldly standards abound.

units.la: QVO qui probi sunt, manifesti fiant inter uos, inquit.) Si diceret, unde qui probi sunt, manifesti fiunt inter uos, exprimeret effectum schismatis. Verùm cum dicit, ἵνα, id est, ut qui probi sunt, manifesti fiant inter vos, causam eius exprimit, quod dixit: oportet & haereses esse inter vos. Pertinet autem illa ad divinam providentiam, omnia ecclesiae suae, etiam mala & incommoda, ad bonum finem dirigentem & disponentem. Scio Chrysostomum particulà hanc accipere non pro causa schismatum, sed pro eventu. Verùm is sensu non satisfacit precedenti necessitati, quam posuit Apostolus dicens: Oportet enim & haereses esse inter vos. Non enim voluit simpliciter dicere, quid ex schismate sequatur & eveniat in ecclesia, sed ad quem finem oportet esse in tali ecclesia haereses & schismata. Ideo causam hanc finale expressurus dicit, ut qui probi sunt, manifesti fiant inter vos.
units.tr: "So that those who are approved may be made manifest among you," he says. If he had said, "Whence those who are approved are made manifest among you," he would be expressing the effect of the schism. But since he says "ἵνα," that is, "so that those who are approved may be made manifest among you," he expresses the cause of what he had said: "there must be heresies among you also." This belongs to the divine providence, which directs and orders all things, even the evils and inconveniences of his church, to a good end. I know that Chrysostom takes this particle not as the cause of schisms but as their outcome. But that sense does not agree with the preceding necessity which the Apostle laid down, saying: "For there must be heresies among you also." For he did not wish to say simply what follows from a schism and happens in the church, but for what end there must be heresies and schisms in such a church. Therefore, intending to express this final cause, he says: "so that those who are approved may be made manifest among you."

units.la: QVO qui probi sunt, inquit.) Sciebat non omnes esse reprobos, sed aliquos etiam probos in turba latitare malorum, & intelligebat illorum bono disponi schismata à reprobis ex citata. Istis nec multitudinem nec paucitatem tribuit, quamuis credibile est pauciores fuisse reprobis. Simpliciter dicit: quo qui probi sunt, manifesti fiant. Vocat autem probos non eos qui sint absque peccato, sed qui veri sint, nō re probi ac falsi Christiani. Oppositu probi est, infyncerum, falsum, & adulterinum. Quod discriminis est inter argentum & scoriam, inter fru mentum & paleas, inter oues & haedos, id est inter probos & reprobos Christianos.
units.tr: "So that those who are approved," he says. He knew that not all were reprobate, but that some approved people also lay hidden in the crowd of the wicked, and he understood that schisms were arranged by the reprobate for the good of these. He assigns to them neither a large nor a small number, although it is credible that there were fewer of them than of the reprobate. He simply says: "so that those who are approved may be made manifest." But he calls approved not those who are without sin, but those who are genuine, not reprobate and false Christians. The opposite of approved is insincere, false and adulterated. This is the difference between silver and dross, between wheat and chaff, between sheep and goats, that is, between approved and reprobate Christians.

units.la: MANIFESTI fiant inter uos, inquit.) Nō dicit: probi permaneant, vel, à reprobis liberè tur. Probi enim, etiamsi non discedant reprobi, in probitate sua perdurant, quemadmodum argentum etiam dum adhuc scoriâ habet adiunctam, probum argentum permanet, & frumentum etiam in medijs paleis, & oues in medio haedorum, in eo quod sunt, perdurant. Ne que sic liberantur probi discessu reproborum, ut nihil ab illis incommodi patiatur amplius, postquam communionem ecclesiasticam solverunt. Tum enim manifestis demum illorum odijs, probris, insidijs & insectationibus redduntur obnoxij, sic ut iam nō exteros tantum, sed & ipsos falsos fratres hostes habere incipiant.
units.tr: "May be made manifest among you," he says. He does not say: "those who are approved remain," or "they are freed from the reprobate." For the approved, even if the reprobate do not depart, persist in their approval, just as genuine silver remains genuine even while it still has dross attached to it, and as wheat remains in the midst of chaff, and sheep remain in the midst of goats, in what they are. Nor are the approved so freed by the departure of the reprobate that they suffer no further inconvenience from them after they have broken off ecclesiastical communion. For then, once the reprobate have made their hostility plain, they are exposed to their hatred, reproaches, plots and attacks, so that they begin to have as enemies not only outsiders but also false brothers themselves.

units.la: Quomodo ergo? Quo inquit, qui probi sunt, manifesti fiant. Manifestum fieri probum, est fieri probatum. Quare non est quaerendum, cum non probi modò, sed & reprobi per schismata manifesti fiant, quare non dicat, quo reprobi, sed, quo probi manifesti fiant. Non agitur causa reproborum per schismata, sed proborum, quemadmodum argentum probandum separatio fit per ignem. Quare recte non dixit, quo reprobi, sed quo probi manifesti, id est, probati fiant. Multa quidem sunt tentationum genera, quibus qui probi sunt in ecclesia, exercentur & probantur. Verùm inter illa haud minimum est, quod fidelibus per haereses & schismata obijcitur, ut merito manifestum fiat, probos eos esse, qui reprobis ab ecclesia discedentibus, ipsi constantes in illa perseverarunt.
units.tr: How then? He says, "so that those who are approved may be made manifest." For an approved person to be made manifest is to be proved. Hence there is no need to ask why, when schisms arise, it is not the approved only but also the reprobate who are made manifest; why he does not say "so that the reprobate," but "so that the approved may be made manifest." The matter at issue through schisms is not the reprobate but the approved, just as silver is separated for testing by fire. So he rightly did not say "so that the reprobate," but "so that the approved may be made manifest," that is, may be proved. There are indeed many kinds of temptation by which those who are approved in the church are exercised and tested. Yet among these is no small one: that faithful people are tested through heresies and schisms, so that it is rightly made plain that those are approved who, when the reprobate depart from the church, have themselves remained steadfast in it.

units.la: Obijciunt hic nobis adversarij. Ecce, inquunt, iam apparet qui sint probi, & qui reprobi, qui paleae & qui frumentum, qui oues & haedi, qui argentum & qui scoria. Discessio uestra & schisma quod excitastis, manifestat nos esse probos, qui manemus in ecclesia.
units.tr: Here our opponents object: "Look," they say, "it now appears who are approved and who reprobate, which are chaff and which wheat, which sheep and which goats, which silver and which dross. Your departure and the schism you have stirred up show that we who remain in the church are the approved."

units.la: Concedimus argumentum si ipsi in vera sunt ecclesia veri ac probri Christiani. Sed hic est quaestio, num sint in vera ecclesia, veri ac probi, & non magis in falsa non probi, sed pseudochristiani. Alias discessus ex falsa ecclesia & à falsis Christianis non eos à quibus discedituř, sed eos potius probatos reddit, qui iussu spiritus sancti è medio Babylonis exeunt, & communicationem reproborum, idololatrarum, superstitiosorum, symoniacorum, scortatorum, adulterorum, ac manus sanguine plenas habentium fugiunt.
units.tr: We grant the argument if they themselves are in the true church and are true and approved Christians. But the question here is whether they are in the true church, and are true and approved, and not rather in a false church, not approved but pseudo-Christian. Otherwise, a departure from a false church and from false Christians does not make approved those from whom people depart, but rather makes approved those who, by the command of the Holy Spirit, go out from the midst of Babylon and flee the fellowship of the reprobate, of idolaters, superstitious people, simoniacs, fornicators, adulterers, and men with hands full of blood.

units.la: Potest hic quaeri, unde sint in ecclesia reprobi, & quare oporteat probos discessu illorum manifestari. Item, quare non magis iusserit Apostolus, ut probi à reprobis discederent, vel ipsi illos excluderet, & quomodo praesens locus conueniat cum eo, quod Mat. 13. legitur: Sinite vtraque crescere, usque ad diem messis.
units.tr: Here it may be asked whence the reprobate are in the church, and why the approved ought to be made manifest by their departure. Likewise, why the Apostle did not rather order that the approved depart from the reprobate, or himself exclude them; and how this passage agrees with what is read in Matthew 13: "Let both grow together until the harvest."

units.la: Ad primum facilis est ex verbis domini responsio, quae Matth. 13. leguntur ad hunc modum: Domine, nonne bonum semen seminaras in
units.tr: To the first question the answer is easy from the words of the Lord, which are read in Matthew 13 in this way: "Lord, did you not sow good seed in

units.la: agro tuo. Vnde igitur habet zizania? Ille vero dicit: Inimicus homo hoc fecit. Et in expositione parabolæ. Zizania sunt filij illius mali. Inimicus autem qui seminat ea, est diabolus. Ergo ex diabolo est, quod reprobi in ecclesia permiscentur.
units.tr: your field? Whence then does it have tares?" But he said: "An enemy has done this." And in the explanation of the parable: "The tares are the sons of that evil one. The enemy who sows them is the devil." Therefore it is from the devil that the reprobate are mixed in the church.

units.la: Ad secundû respondeo, quo separetur plantatio Dei, à plantatione Satanæ, & fides electorum probata reddatur, sic esse consilium Dei, vt discessu reproborum probi manifestentur. Nemo quærit, quare agricola paleas separet a tritico, & aurifaber scoriam ab argento? Sic nö erat hic quærendum, quare oporteat per discessum reproborum manifestari probos.
units.tr: To the second I answer that it is God's purpose that the planting of God be separated from the planting of Satan, and that the faith of the elect be proved, and that the approved be made manifest by the departure of the reprobate. No one asks why the farmer separates the chaff from the wheat, or the goldsmith the dross from the silver. So here it was not to be asked why it is necessary for the approved to be made manifest by the departure of the reprobate.

units.la: Ad tertium respondeo. Nulli adhuc erat in ecclesia Corinthiorum falsi cultus, propter quos per conscientiam discedendum esset probis a reprobis, neq; opus erat exclusione illorum, cum ipsi sese vltro separarent. Vbi schisma-ta fiunt, ibi locum non habet excommunicatio.
units.tr: To the third I answer. There were as yet in the church of the Corinthians no false forms of worship on account of which the approved would have to separate from the reprobate in conscience, nor was there need of their exclusion, since they were separating themselves of their own accord. Where schisms occur, excommunication has no place.

units.la: Ad locum Mat. 13. Sinite vtraq; crescere ad diem messis, respondeo, nihil ibi praescribi consilio Dei quo ille suo tempore probos manifestare constituit, sed vetari, ne ministri verbi temere zizania ex agro domini euellere conentur, ne simul euellant & triticum. Interea nihil est incommodi probis, si reprobi sponte sua schisma faciant & discedant, quemadmodum nihil detrimenti accideret tritico, si zizania vltro discederet ex agro.
units.tr: As to the passage in Matthew 13, "Let both grow together until the harvest," I answer that nothing is prescribed there against the counsel of God, by which he has determined to make the approved manifest at his own time; rather, it is forbidden that the ministers of the Word should rashly try to uproot the tares from the Lord's field, lest they uproot the wheat along with them. Meanwhile there is no harm to the approved if the reprobate of their own accord make a schism and depart, just as no harm would come to the wheat if the tares went out of the field of their own accord.

units.la: Igitur cum convenitis in eundem locum, non est dominicam coenam manducare.
units.tr: Therefore when you come together in one place, it is not to eat the Lord's supper.

units.la: Nam unusquisq; propriam coenam edendo præsumit. Et hic quidem esurit, ille vero ebrius est. An domos nõ habetis ad edendum & bibendum? Aut, ecclesiam Dei contemnitis, & pudefacitis eos qui nõ habent? Quid vobis dicam? Laudabo vos? In hoc non laudo.
units.tr: For each one takes his own supper beforehand when eating. And one indeed is hungry, another is drunk. Do you not have houses for eating and drinking? Or do you despise the church of God and shame those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you.

units.la: Exponit quid mali ex schismate illorum in causa coenæ dominicæ eueniat. Sic intelligo, quod non simpliciter dicit: Dum convenitis, sed: Igitur cum convenitis. Illud in eundem locum, in Græco est, ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ, id est, in idem, quare interpres vocula locu, de suo adiecit. Vulgata versio habet, in vnu. Potest verti. Perinde in eundem coetum, atq; in eundem locum.
units.tr: He explains what evil results from their schism in the matter of the Lord's supper. I understand it thus: he does not simply say "when you come together" but "therefore when you come together." The phrase "in the same place" is, in Greek, ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ, that is, "into the same (place)", and so the translator added the little word "place" from his own. The Vulgate has "in one" (in unum). It may be rendered "into the same assembly" just as "into the same place."

units.la: Non est autem otiosum, quod non simpliciter dicit: Dū convenitis, sed addit, ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ. Submonet enim hac particula, quam non conueniant schismata illis, quorū est in eūdem conuenire coetum, imò quàm ab eiusmodi coùen tu procul abesse debeat schismata, in quo eiusdem fidei confortes pro more ecclesiæ conuenient. Ipsa vnius coetus in eundem locum congregatio a studio schismatum singulos auocare debebat.
units.tr: It is not idle, however, that he does not simply say "when you come together" but adds ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ. For this particle reminds them how schisms do not agree with those who are to assemble in the same gathering; indeed, how far schisms ought to be absent from such an assembly, in which the partakers of the same faith gather according to the custom of the church. The very gathering of a single assembly into one place ought to have drawn each person away from the pursuit of schisms.

units.la: IGITVR cum conuenitis in eundem locu, inquit, nó est dominicá coenam manducare.) Non est obscurû, vel ex Tertulliano, hûc fuisse morem Apostolicarum ecclesiarû, vt in vnû cogregati fideles non modo orationib. doctrinæ, caltigationi fraternę & Psalmis operâ derint, sed & secundum exemplum pariter & institutum Christi Seruatoris in ipso sacre Synaxeos loco vnà comederint ac biberint, in ea mesæ communicatione Eucharistiâ & memoriam dominicæ mortis per fractionem panis ac distributionem calicis celebrarint, eáq; potissimum ob causam coenam eam dominicá vocarint. Poterant hoc sacræ mense elogio ad moneri, non esse illam priuato ac proprio cuiusq; vsui, sed catholicę ac publicę fidelium communicationi destinatam. Quod enim domini cum est, & à domino ecclesiæ traditur, non debet à quoquâ priuato vsu præsumi, & in studia partium peruerti. Quoniam igitur Corinthij in schismata à se inuicem diuisi hoc facere coperant, diserte dominicam eos coenam edere negat, dicens: Igitur cum conuenitis in eundē locum, non est dominicam coenam edere, id est, quod editis & bibitis, non potest haberi coena dominica. Quare? Quia vnusquisq;, in quit, propriam coenâ edendo præsumit. Et hic quidē esurit, ille vero ebrius est. Sectarij, & diuites non expectabant, donec multitudo fidelium conueniret, quo communi mensa ederet ac biberent omnes, sed partim studio quique sectæ suæ, partim contemptu ecclesiæ edebât ac bibebát priuatim, priusquam collecta esset ecclesia. Et hoc perstringens nõ simpliciter dicit, Nam vnusquisq; propriam coenam edendo sumit, sed ... i. præsumit. Et hinc est, quod in cõclusione dicit: Itaq; fratres mei, cum conuenitis ad comedendum, alius alium expectate.
units.tr: "Therefore when you come together in one place," he says, "it is not to eat the Lord's supper." It is not unclear, even from Tertullian, that it was the custom of the apostolic churches for the faithful, gathered into one place, to devote themselves not only to prayers, teaching, brotherly admonition and psalms, but also, following the example and institution of Christ the Saviour, to eat and drink together in the very place of the sacred synaxis; in this communion of the table they celebrated the Eucharist and the memory of the Lord's death through the breaking of bread and the distribution of the cup, and chiefly for this reason they called that meal the Lord's supper. By this sacred title they could be reminded that it was not intended for the private and individual use of each, but for the universal and public communion of the faithful. For what belongs to the Lord, and is handed down by the Lord to the church, ought not to be presumed upon by any private use and perverted into the pursuits of factions. Since therefore the Corinthians, divided among themselves into schisms, had begun to do this, he plainly denies that they eat the Lord's supper, saying: "Therefore when you come together in one place, it is not to eat the Lord's supper." That is, what you eat and drink cannot be counted as the Lord's supper. Why? Because "each one," he says, "beforehand takes his own supper when eating. And one indeed is hungry, another is drunk." The sectarians and the rich did not wait until the multitude of the faithful had assembled, so that all might eat and drink together at a common table; instead, some from zeal for their own sect, others out of contempt for the church, ate and drank privately before the church had been gathered. In censuring this he does not simply say, "For each one takes his own supper when eating," but "beforehand" (praesumit). And hence it is that in his conclusion he says: "So, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another."

units.la: Et hæc Apostolica sententia diligenter notanda, qua diserte coenam negat esse dominicam, vbi catholica ecclesiæ communicatio nõ integra seruatur, sed priuata præsumptione scinditur. Colligimus ergo fortiter, quocunq; nomine Papistæ Missam suam vocent, non esse illam coenam dominicam. Si coena dominica nõ est, viderint ipsi quid respondeant domino, cuius institutione peruertunt. Quod me attinet, mihi parum refert vnam ne Missam sol lenniter, vt vocant, aut priuatas mille singulis diebus celebrent, quâdoquidem dominicum non est quod absque iusta communicatione sit deliuum in ecclesia faciût, sed humana præsumptio, ne quid durius dicam, reiecta dominicæ institutione, & Apostolica traditione in ecclesias Christi introducta. Ex ipso ordine, inquit Tertullianus, manifestatur id esse dominicum & verum, quod prius est traditum, id autem extraneum & falsum, quod posterius est immissum. Omnino quod ipsi faciunt non est institutum à domino, sed posterius immissum. Ergo non est dominicum & verum, sed extraneum & falsum, tanto magis ad iniuriam dominicæ institutionis faciens, quanto magis est catholicum.
units.tr: This apostolic judgment is to be carefully noted, by which he plainly denies that it is the Lord's supper where the catholic communion of the church is not kept whole, but is torn apart by private presumption. We therefore conclude confidently that, whatever name the Papists give their Mass, it is not the Lord's supper. If it is not the Lord's supper, let them see to what they will answer to the Lord, whose institution they pervert. As for me, it matters little whether they celebrate one Mass solemnly, as they call it, or a thousand private ones every day, since what they do without lawful communion is not the Lord's, but, to speak no more harshly, human presumption, rejecting the institution of the Lord and the apostolic tradition introduced into the churches of Christ. "From the very order," says Tertullian, "it is shown that what was handed down first is the Lord's and true, but what was sent in later is foreign and false." Indeed, what they do was not instituted by the Lord but sent in later. Therefore it is not the Lord's and true, but foreign and false, and it does all the more injury to the Lord's institution the more it claims to be catholic.

units.la: NAM vnusquisq; propriam coenam ededo præsumit.) Non est uocula, vnusquisque, refe-renda renda ad omnes qui erant in ecclesia Corin. thiorum, sed ad eos tantum, qui schismatici existentes, communicationem ecclesiae scindebant. Nam reliqua multitudo, quae ab istis contemnebatur hac reprehensione non perstringitur. Cogitet hic lector, quam sint illi ab Apostolica hac ratione diversi, qui sacrum Missaticum putant esse sibi inconspectu domini efficacius & utilius, si proprium sibi ac privatum data pecunia comparauerint, quam si publici tantum sint participes, cum omne bonum tanto sit diuinius quanto est communius. At istultam hanc opinionem plebs seducta sacerdotali debet nundinationi ac quaestui. Excogitatio Papistici sacerdotij omnis generis corruptelas in ecclesias inuexit, e quibus est & ista, qua sacrificulus sacerdotij sui op cuilibet emptori pro certa pecuniae summa priuatim vendit & applicat, miseroq; persuadet intomparabile bonum esse, quod propriam sibi Missam celebrari facit, cum hac dominicae coenae pphanatione diuinae Maiestatis magis exacerbetur quam placetur.
units.tr: "For each one beforehand takes his own supper when eating."
