Here he adds an exhortation to the threat, which is not yet complete, and tells us what a person ought to do before he communicates of this bread and the cup of the Lord, so that he does not make himself liable to so grave a condemnation. "But let a man examine himself," he says. The Greek is δοκιμαζέτω [dokimazetō]. This word means to make trial of something and to inquire into it in order to know what sort of thing it is, lest it be used either in vain or to one's loss through carelessness. Wise people do this in earthly matters, so that they do not undertake something in vain or suffer some loss; how much more ought it to be done in

units.la: A bus spiritualibus, vbi peccari non potest nisi cum maxima offensa Dei & graui condemnatione. Cū itaq; dicit, probet seipsum homo, monet ut in seipsum quisque inquirat, quid de pane hoc & poculo domini sentiat, quomodo erga sacramentum hoc corporis ac sanguinis domini animatus existat, quare & quo proposito ad communicationem illius accedere uelit, quo sciat, digne ne vel indigne sit accessurus.
units.tr: spiritual matters, where nothing can be sinned without the greatest offence to God and grave condemnation. When he therefore says, "let a man examine himself," he urges each one to inquire into himself: what he thinks of this bread and the cup of the Lord, what disposition he has towards this sacrament of the Lord's body and blood, and with what purpose he wishes to approach its communion, so that he may know whether he is coming worthily or unworthily.

units.la: Obserua autem, quod quemadmodū caute ac prudēter non dixit: Itaque manducatis panem hunc & bibitis de poculo hoc domini indigne, atque ita rei estis corporis ac sanguinis domini, id quod durius fuisset, quàm ut patienter tolerarent, sed in genere, quisquis ederit ac biberit de pane hoc & poculo domini indigne, reus erit corporis ac sanguinis dei, ita nō dicit, probate uos ipsi, sed absque ulla specificatione, in genere probet, inquit, seipsum homo, quo generalem faciat admonitionem, per tinentem ad omnes, eoq; tolerabilem omnibus. Quasi dicat: Nemo cibum hunc temere usurpet, quasi nihil referat quomodo usurpetur, sed quisquis de illo esurus est, seipsum prius examinet, &c.
units.tr: Notice also that he did not say, cautiously and prudently, "So then, you who eat this bread and drink of the cup of the Lord unworthily, and so are guilty of the body and blood of the Lord"; that would have been too harsh for them to bear patiently. Instead he speaks in general terms: "whoever eats or drinks of this bread and the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord." Nor does he say "you yourselves examine," but without any specification he says in general, "let a man examine himself," so that the admonition is general, applies to all, and is therefore bearable for all. As if to say: no one should take this food rashly, as though it made no difference how he takes it; rather, whoever is about to partake of it should first examine himself, and so on.

units.la: Nec dicit, abstinete igitur à pane hoc & poculo domini, ne rei fiatis corporis ac sanguinis domini, uel, qui hactenus indigne manducarunt ac biberunt, abstineant in posterū ab hac communione. Nam hoc pacto malum quod reprehendit non emendasset. Si medicus dicat ægroto, quoniā comedis ac bibis secus quàm valetudini tuæ restituendæ conducat, consulo ne posthac edas & bibas, hoc ipsum consilio non curat ac restitutit sed perdit. Etenim non restituitur ualetudo prorsus non edendo ac bibendo, sed cōpetenter pro qualitate morbi edendo ac bibendo. Consimili modo non correxisset Apostolus malum hoc Corinthiorum consulendo ne in posterum de pane domini ederent & de poculo illius biberet. Neque enim hoc pacto euasissent, quo minus culpabiles essent in conspectu domini, abstinentes à sacramento quod instituit ac ecclesiæ suæ commendauit. Quare consultius erat quod dicit: probet seipsum homo, & sic de pane illo edat, &c. Nam hoc pacto, nec auocat eos à communicatione mensæ dominicæ, nec finit ut de sacramento corporis ac sanguinis dominici indigne edentes ac bibentes rei fiant corporis ac sanguinis domini. Hoc Apostoli exemplū sequutus minister Christi, sicubi viderit esse quosdam qui cœna dominica abutantur, neque suspendat institutionis dominicæ usum, neq; iubeat ut illi ab eo abstineant, sed urgeat potius, ut in seipsos inquirant & gratiæ Dei sacramento sese competenter accommodent.
units.tr: Nor does he say, "Therefore abstain from this bread and the cup of the Lord, lest you become guilty of the body and blood of the Lord," or, "those who have hitherto eaten and drunk unworthily should abstain from this communion in future." For in that way the evil he rebukes would not have been corrected. If a physician said to a sick man, "Because you eat and drink in a way that is not good for restoring your health, I advise you not to eat or drink from now on," this advice would not cure or restore him but would destroy him. For health is not restored by not eating and drinking at all, but by eating and drinking in a manner suited to the nature of the illness. In the same way the Apostle would not have corrected this evil of the Corinthians by advising them not to eat the Lord's bread and drink of his cup in future. For in that way they would not have escaped being guilty in the sight of the Lord, by abstaining from the sacrament which he instituted and commended to his Church. Therefore it was more fitting to say, "let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread," and so on. For in this way he neither calls them away from partaking of the Lord's table, nor allows those who eat and drink of the sacrament of the Lord's body and blood unworthily to become guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. Following the Apostle's example, if a minister of Christ sees that some abuse the Lord's Supper, he should neither suspend the use of the Lord's institution nor order them to abstain from it, but should rather urge them to examine themselves and to prepare themselves fittingly for the sacrament of God's grace.

units.la: Nec hoc transeundum est, quod non dicit, probetur homo & sic de pane illo edat, sed probet seipsum homo. Apparet quidem necessarium & utile esse eorum studium, qui neminē ad cœnam domini admittunt, quem ipsi antea non probauerint, si modus & discretio adhibeatur, nec uelut uniuersali lege indiscrimina tim omnes, etiam qui inculpate se gerūt in ec clesia, ad huiusmodi examen constringantur, uerum iuxtā timendum est, ne institutum hoc quàm nunc magni æstimatur, tam olim in priscam seruitutem ecclesiam Christi reducat & noxium reddatur. Sane Apostolica admonitio nihil huius requirit, sed hortatur unumquenque, vt seipsum probet, quod genus inquisitionis ac probationis multo est certius. Quis enim conscientiæ suæ iudicium fallere potest. quemadmodum fallere potest conscientiam aliorum? Probate uosmetipsos, inquit, 2. Cor. ult. An non cognoscitis uosipsos?
units.tr: Nor should we pass over the fact that he does not say, "let a man be tested, and so let him eat of that bread," but "let a man examine himself." Indeed, the zeal of those who admit no one to the Lord's Supper whom they have not first tested seems necessary and useful, provided moderation and discretion are applied; yet all people without distinction, even those who conduct themselves blamelessly in the church, should not be bound to such an examination as though by a universal law. Rather, we must fear lest this institution, which is now esteemed so highly, should in time reduce the Church of Christ to its former servitude and become harmful. Certainly the apostolic admonition requires nothing of this kind, but exhorts each one to examine himself, a kind of inquiry and testing which is much more certain. For who can deceive the judgment of his own conscience, as he can deceive the conscience of others? "Test yourselves," he says, 2 Cor. last chapter. "Do you not know yourselves?"

units.la: Neq; dicit: Probet homo eos cum quibus est communicaturus. Forsan faciebat hoc Corinthij sectarij, cum ecclesiam Dei contemnerent, ac fratres pudefacerent, ut eos admodū pertinenter hortetur dicés: Probet homo seipsum. Quasi dicat. Non cōuenit, ut alius aliū probet, inq; aliorum uitam & qualitatem inquirat, qui de pane hoc est manducaturus. Quin, potius probet & inspiciat quisq; semetipsum. Pro se quisque, non pro alijs rationem est domino redditurus. Laborant hoc morbo plerique, ut seipsos negligētes in alios tātum inquirant, id quod Anabaptistæ facere solet.
units.tr: Nor does he say, "let a man examine those with whom he is going to communicate." Perhaps the Corinthian sectarians did this, when they despised the Church of God and shamed the brethren, so that he exhorts them very fittingly, saying, "let a man examine himself." As if to say: it is not fitting that one should test another, or inquire into the life and character of others, who is about to eat of this bread. Rather, let each one test and scrutinize himself. Each person will give account to the Lord for himself, not for others. Many suffer from this disease, neglecting themselves and inquiring only into others, which the Anabaptists are accustomed to do.

units.la: Chryso. sic annotat, ἑκ ἑαυτοῦ ἑαυτὸν ... ἀμαρτυρῶν τὸν ἔλεγχον.
units.tr: Chrysostom annotates thus: ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ ἑαυτὸν ... ἀμαρτυρῶν τὸν ἔλεγχον [ex heautou heauton ... amartyrōn ton elegchon].

units.la: ET sic de pane illo edat, inquit & de poculo illo bibat.) Ergo admittit Apostolus ad cœnam domini eos qui suæ ipsorum conscientiæ testimonio sic sunt animati, ut haud indigne accedere possunt, sed quid si minister ecclesiæ hac Apostoli sententia noluit esse contentus, nec admittat nisi eos quos ipse explorarit? Item, quid si fidelis ad panis tantum & non etiam poculi dominici communicationem admittatur, sicut in papatu fieri uidemus? Quid hic faciet fidelis? Respondeo. Vbi nec domini cainstitutio, nec apostolica doctrina seruatur ibi non est ut communicet fidelis. Sinat magistros illos regnare in ecclesia, donec uisum fuerit domino modū imponere illorum dominio.
units.tr: "And so let him eat of that bread," he says, "and drink of that cup." Therefore the Apostle admits to the Lord's Supper those who are so disposed, by the witness of their own conscience, that they can approach without unworthiness. But what if a minister of the Church is not content with this sentence of the Apostle, and admits only those whom he himself has examined? Likewise, what if the faithful are admitted to communion in the bread only and not also in the cup of the Lord, as we see done in the Papacy? What will the faithful man do here? I answer: where neither the institution of the Lord nor apostolic doctrine is observed, the faithful man should not communicate there. Let him allow those teachers to rule in the Church until it pleases the Lord to set a limit to their dominion.

units.la: NAM qui edit, in quit, ac bibit indigne, iudicium sibi ipsi edit ac bibit.) Rationem reddit eius quod dixit: Probet seipsum homo, & sic de pane illo edat. Dices: atqui poterat dicere. Nam qui hoc fecerit, quo digne edat & bibat, communicat de corpore ac sanguine domini. Verum, sed uoluit cœptam comminationem absoluere. Alias uerum est. Panis quem frangimus, communicatio corporis domini est, &c.
units.tr: "For he who eats and drinks unworthily," he says, "eats and drinks judgment to himself." He gives the reason for what he said: "let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread." You may object: but he could have said, "for whoever does this, so that he eats and drinks worthily, communicates in the body and blood of the Lord." But he wished to finish the threat he had begun. Otherwise it is true: "The bread which we break is the communion of the body of the Lord," and so on.

units.la: IVDICIVM, inquit, sibi ipsi edit ac bibit.) Dixit, qui indigne edit, reus erit corporis ac sanguinis domini. Id absoluens addit de iudicio, quod ei debetur, qui tam atroci peccato reum se corporis ac sanguinis domini constituit. Potuit autem κρίμα id est, iudicium, ἀντὶ τῆς κατακρίματος, id est, pro condemnatione. Iudicium aliās insonti est liberatio ac salus, sonti ue-
units.tr: "They eat and drink judgment to themselves," he says. He has said that whoever eats unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. In explaining this, he adds the word about judgment, which is owed to the one who has made himself guilty of the body and blood of the Lord by so atrocious a sin. He could have written krima [κρίμα], that is judgment, instead of katakrima [κατακρίματος], that is, condemnation. Elsewhere judgment means deliverance and salvation for the innocent, but for the guilty it means condemnation and destruction.

units.la: rō condemnatio ac perditio, quo sensu hoc loco positum est.
units.tr: In this sense it is used here.

units.la: Obserua uerò loquutionem. Non dicit: Iudicium incurrit, uel obnoxius est iudicio, sed, iudicium sibi ipsi edit ac bibit. Quomodo iudicium editur ac bibitur? Iudicium Dei sententia est, quæ nec edi nec bibi potest in se, ideoq; nec pāni nec uino includi, ut cum illo edatur ac bibatur. Panis hic neq; est iudicium, neque sacramentum iudicij. Et tamē qui de illo indigne manducat, iudicium manducat. Potest ergo in pane hoc māducari, quod in illo neq; naturaliter est, neq; sacramentaliter. Quomodo? Quemadmodum in cibo uetito primi parentes mortem comederunt, cum tamē in eo pomo non esset inclusa mors. Quoniam illicitè edendo mortis sese iudicio obnoxios reddiderunt, rectè mortem sibi ipsis comedisse dici possunt. Sic qui panem hunc indignè edēs reū se corporis domini constituit, iudicium edere id est, iudicio sese obnoxium reddere dicitur. Ipsum corpus domini, quod datum est in cruce pro uita mundi, nemini est ad iudicium, sed omnibus ad uitam, si fide sumatur. Panis uerò hic quem corporis sui sacramentum, ac mortis suæ ἀνάμνησιν esse uoluit, ut magna recreatione spiritus, si ritè ac digne, ita ad iudicium sumi potest, si indignè sumatur. Tantæ rei sacramentum, inquit Augustinus, ad iudicium sibi manducat & bibit, quia immūdus ad Christi sacramenta accedere præsumit.
units.tr: Now observe the manner of speaking. He does not say, "He incurs judgment," or "He is liable to judgment," but "He eats and drinks judgment to himself." How is judgment eaten and drunk? The judgment of God is a sentence, which cannot in itself be eaten or drunk, and so it cannot be contained in bread or wine, to be eaten and drunk along with them. This bread is neither judgment nor a sacrament of judgment, and yet whoever eats of it unworthily eats judgment. So something can be eaten in this bread which is in it neither naturally nor sacramentally. How so? Just as our first parents ate death from the forbidden food, though death was not enclosed in that fruit. Because by eating unlawfully they made themselves liable to the judgment of death, they can rightly be said to have eaten death for themselves. Likewise, whoever eats this bread unworthily and makes himself guilty of the body of the Lord is said to eat judgment, that is, to make himself liable to judgment. The body of the Lord itself, which was given on the cross for the life of the world, is for no one a judgment, but for all life, if it is received in faith. But this bread, which he willed to be the sacrament of his body and a memorial of his death, can bring great refreshment to the spirit if it is taken rightly and worthily, but it can bring judgment if it is taken unworthily. "He eats and drinks judgment to himself, because the unclean presume to approach the sacraments of Christ," says Augustine, speaking of so great a thing as a sacrament.

units.la: Non est autem ociosum, quod non simpliciter dicit: iudicium edit ac bibit: sed, iudicium sibi ipsi edit ac bibit. Videtur enim hac uocula culpam cūm ab institutione hac dominicę cœnæ, tum ab apostolatu suo amouere, & in ipsos indignè de hoc sacramento edentes ac bibentes reijcere. Quasi dicat: Seipsum perdit, idq; sua ipsius culpa, dum de eo quo utiliter uti potest, si modis cōpetentibus uteretur, indignè pro sua temeritate edit ac bibit.
units.tr: It is not idle, moreover, that he does not simply say "He eats and drinks judgment," but "He eats and drinks judgment to himself." For this little word seems to remove the blame both from the institution of this Lord's Supper and from his own apostleship, and to cast it back upon those who eat and drink unworthily of this sacrament. As if he were saying: "He destroys himself, and that by his own fault, since he eats and drinks unworthily, through his own rashness, something of which he could make useful use if he used it in the proper manner."

units.la: Seruit etiam hæc particula conscientijs infirmorum, qui se pollui putant, si cum illis communicent, qui indignè ad cœnam dominicam accedunt. Neminem polluit illorum communicatio, nisi unà cum illis & ipsi indignè communicemus. Seipsos iudicio Dei reddunt obnoxios, non alios. Erāt probi adhuc pleriq; in ecclesia Corinthiorum, quorum conscientijs Apostolus hac sententia consulit, ne propter reprobos de relinquenda ecclesiastica communione cogitent. Verūm magistris illis ac dominis ecclesiarum qui in causa sunt suis subditis, ut secus communicet q habet institutio Christi & doctrina apostolica, haud patrocinatur hic locus. Nam licet sibi ipsis iudicium edant & bibant, qui indignè communicant, cedit tamen id peccati ad culpam etiam ipsorum, qui indigne huius communionis imperitæ ac seductæ plebi sunt authores.
units.tr: This phrase also serves the consciences of the weak, who think they are defiled if they share in the Lord's Supper with those who come to it unworthily. The communion of those men defiles no one, unless we ourselves also communicate unworthily along with them. They make themselves liable to the judgment of God, not others. At that time many in the church of the Corinthians were still good people, and the Apostle with this sentence consults their consciences, so that they would not think of abandoning ecclesiastical communion because of the reprobate. But this passage does not support those teachers and lords of the churches who, being the cause for their subjects, would have them communicate otherwise than the institution of Christ and the apostolic doctrine require. For although those who communicate unworthily eat and drink judgment to themselves, that sin nevertheless also falls back upon the guilt of those who are the authors of this unworthy communion for the untaught and misled people.

units.la: NON dijudicans, inquit, corpus dñi.) Reddit rationem hac particula, quare Corinthij de pane domini indignè edentes iudicium sibi ipsis comecomederint. Quoniam uidelicet non dijudi-carunt corpus domini. Græcè est, μὴ διακρίνοντες. Significat autem διακρίνειν discernere πρᾶγμα ἐπ᾽ πράγματος. Hinc est discretio illa, qua pertinen ter de rebus secundum unusquisque qualitate sentimus, & ut sentimus competenter etiam singulis secundum illarum ἀξίαν utimur. Debe bat ergo uerti, nō discernens corpus domini, a cibo: uidelicet, pphano. Sic explicat Corin-thiorum peccatum, quo carnaliter ac prophanis modis cœnam domini quasi prophanū epulum edebant. Quod si quis participiū hoc, διακρίνων, non discernendi sed iudicandi sensu accipiendum esse putauerit, quasi in eo peccauerint Corinthij, quod non iudicauerint panē hunc dñi, esse corpus domini, atq; ita legerit, Non iudicans corpus domini, in speciem qui-dem errori papistarum patrocinabitur: uerum contra germanum dictionis huius sensum de-bemus quidem hunc panē uocare corpus domini, uerum sensu non proprio, sed sacramen-tali, & discernere eum à reliquis cibis, tanquā dominici corporis sacramentum, adeoq; habere pro pane non corporis, sed mentis: & ad esum illius parare non dentes ac uentrem, sed fidem ac spiritum. Respondeant hic missatores sacrificuli, quid ipsi de pane hoc domini sentiant, & quomodo corpus Domini dijudicet, dum illum quæstu omnium impijsimo ac manifestissimo quotidie pro certa pecuniæ summa uendunt, & in cultum uentris cōuertunt, dum illum priuatim extra ecclesiasticam communicationem tractant & edunt, dum & spiritu & corpore poluti in medio scortationum suarum ad missarum suarum celebrationē accedunt, & manibus adhuc calidis, ut prouerbio dicitur, mox ab hoc sacro ad spurcities suas recurrunt. Dum hæc faciunt, ipsi ne corpus domini dijudicant?
units.tr: "Not discerning," he says, "the body of the Lord." Here he gives the reason why the Corinthians, eating unworthily of the Lord's bread, ate judgment to themselves: namely, because they did not discern the body of the Lord. In Greek it is "mē diakrinontes" [μὴ διακρίνοντες]. Now diakrinein [διακρίνειν] means to distinguish one thing from another [πρᾶγμα ἐπ᾽ πράγματος]. Hence comes that discernment by which we judge things rightly according to their quality, and by which we use each thing appropriately according to its worth [ἀξίαν]. So it ought to be translated: "not discerning the body of the Lord from food," that is, treating it as profane. In this way he explains the sin of the Corinthians, by which they ate the Lord's Supper in a carnal and profane manner, as a common meal. But if anyone thinks that this participle, diakrinōn, is to be taken not in the sense of discerning but of judging, as if the Corinthians had sinned in not judging this bread to be the body of the Lord, and reads it thus, "not judging the body of the Lord," he will indeed seem to support the error of the Papists. But against the genuine sense of this word we ought to call this bread the body of the Lord, yet in a sense not proper but sacramental; and we ought to distinguish it from other foods, as the sacrament of the Lord's body, and so regard it as the bread not of the body but of the mind; and to prepare for eating it not our teeth and belly, but faith and spirit. Let the sending priests here answer what they themselves think of this bread of the Lord, and how they judge the body of the Lord, when every day they sell it for a sum of money, in the most impious and most manifest of all gains, and turn it into service of the belly; when they handle and eat it privately, outside ecclesiastical communion; when, defiled in spirit and body, they approach the celebration of their masses in the midst of their fornications, and with hands still warm, as the proverb says, they run straight from this holy rite back to their filth. While they do these things, do they not judge the body of the Lord?

units.la: PROPTER hoc inter uos multi sunt imbecilles & inualidi, & dormiunt multi. Quod in digne manducantem iudicium subijpsi manducare dixit à præsenti castigatione confirmat, qua tum flagellabatur diuinitus. Quasi dicat: Vnde est, quod tam multi iam inter uos sunt imbecilles & inualidi, & tā multi ex hac sunt uita abrepti, nisi ex eo quod panem hunc domini indigne edentes, ac de poculo illius indigne bibentes, iudicium sibijpsis manducarūt ac biberunt, & manum hanc diuinæ castigationis contra se prouocarunt. Ergo grassabatur in ecclesia Corinthiorum manus domini, flagellans peccantes siuepeste, ut apparet, siue alio quopiam genere morborū. Quorsum autē hoc factum sit mox memorabitur.
units.tr: "For this reason," he says, "many among you are weak and feeble, and many sleep." By the present punishment, by which they were then being scourged by God, he confirms what he said, that whoever eats unworthily eats judgment to himself. As if he said: "Where does it come from that so many among you are now weak and feeble, and so many have been snatched from this life, unless it is because, eating this bread of the Lord unworthily and drinking from its cup unworthily, they have eaten and drunk judgment to themselves, and have provoked against themselves the hand of divine chastisement?" Therefore the hand of the Lord was raging in the church of the Corinthians, scourging the sinners either with plague, as appears, or with some other kind of disease. How and why this came about will be recounted shortly.

units.la: Colligimus abusum illum cœnę dominicæ fuisse in ecclesia Corinthiorū haud paucorū, sed multorū. Non enim simpliciter dicit, Propter hoc inter uos quidam: sed, multi sunt imbecilles & inualidi, & dormiunt multi. Ergo, aut diu durauerat inter eos prophanatio cœnę dominicæ, aut si minus diu durauerat, breui temporis spacio multos corruperat. Si diu durauerat, agnosce patientiam Dei aliquādiu distulisse flagellum, quo resipiscerent, postquā uero malum non emendaretur, sed admodum crescerat, tum demum in peccantes animaduertere cœpisse. Si uero repete inualuit malū, cogita patientiam Dei magnitudine illi fuisse uictā, & ad flagellandum permotam, ne totam perderet ecclesiam. In eo uero quod causam illis malorum istorū exponit Apostolus, apparet eos neq; peccatū suum cum cœnā domini prophanarent, neq; cum prophanatiōis huius pœnas tam graues ac singulares darent, manum castigationis diuinæ intellexisse. Sic hodie quoq; maxima pars Christianorum nec intelligit prophanationem cœnæ dominicæ, nec agnoscit causas malorum, quibus castigamur & afferimur.
units.tr: We gather that this abuse of the Lord's Supper in the church of the Corinthians was found not in a few but in many. For he does not simply say, "For this reason some among you," but "many are weak and feeble, and many sleep." Therefore either the profanation of the Lord's Supper had lasted a long time among them, or, if it had not lasted long, it had corrupted many in a short space of time. If it had lasted long, recognize that the patience of God had for some time deferred the scourge by which they might come to their senses; but when the evil was not corrected, and had grown greatly, then at last God began to take notice of the sinners. But if the evil had prevailed suddenly, consider that the patience of God was overcome by its magnitude and was moved to scourge, lest he should destroy the whole church. Now in that the Apostle sets out the cause of these evils, it appears that they neither understood their sin, by which they profaned the Lord's Supper, nor understood the hand of divine chastisement, since the punishments for this profanation were so grievous and extraordinary. So today too the greater part of Christians neither understands the profanation of the Lord's Supper nor acknowledges the causes of the evils by which we are chastised and afflicted.

units.la: MVLTI sunt, inquit, imbecilles & inualidi, & dormiunt multi. ] Hoc est, multi decumbūt ægroti, multi sunt mortui. Ergo animaduertit in eos dominus inæqualiter, dum alios morti tradidit, alios infirmos ac languidos reddit.
units.tr: "Many," he says, "are weak and feeble, and many sleep." That is, many are laid low with sickness, many are dead. Therefore the Lord punished them unequally: some he delivered to death, others he made infirm and languid.

units.la: Huius rei non debemus quærere causas, etiāsi constaret æqualiter omnes peccasse. Sunt huiusmodi iudicia Dei occulta, & suspicienda, non inquireda. Interea probabile est alios alijs peccasse grauius, & minus fuisse emendabiles, adeoq; dignos qui & grauius punirentur. Crediderim etiam non fuisse hac plaga percussos omnes eos qui culpabiles inter illos erant. Solet diuina clementia nō modo pœnas quas infert mitigare, sed & nonnullos de numero peccantiū eximere, quibus sic parcat, ut pœnis aliorū q plectuntur, ad resipiscētiā perducātur.
units.tr: We ought not to seek the causes of this, even if it were certain that all had sinned equally. The judgments of God are hidden and to be revered, not to be pried into. Meanwhile it is probable that some sinned more gravely than others, and were less capable of amendment, and so were worthy to be punished more severely. I would also believe that not all who were guilty among them were struck with this plague. The divine clemency is accustomed not only to soften the punishments it inflicts, but also to exempt some from the number of sinners, sparing them in such a way that, by the punishments of others who are being smitten, they are led to repentance.

units.la: ET dormiunt multi, inquit. ] Non dicit, Et mortui sunt: sed, & dormiūt multi. Ergo & eorū mors, qui propter peccata sua singulari plaga percussi moriūtur, somnus est, propter futuram resurrectionem. Vnusquisq; enim cū causa sua dormit, & cū illa, siue bona sit siue mala resurget. Commodum aūt mortuos dormire dicit, scribens ad eos, inter quos erant, qui resurrectionem mortuorū negaret, quos singula ri erat tractatu correcturus, cui hac dormitionis metaphora præludit. Etenim si dormiunt mortui, resurrecturos esse consequitur. Tolle resurrectionē, nō erit ratio cur mortui dormire dicatur. Nō est aūt somnus iste transferendus ad spiritus mortuorū, qui capaces illius ef se non possunt: sed ad corpora quæ propterea dormire dicūtur, qd tandem sunt ad exortum diei futuræ surrectura, & in lucem è sepulchris uelut è cubiculis suis proditura. Apostolus cupiebat dissolui & esse cum Christo, spiritu uidelicet. In cœlestibus autem ubi Christus est, non est locus dormiendi, sed in uera felicitate uiuendi. Latro post mortem crucis translatus est cū Christo in paradisum, spiritu uidelicet, eoq; nō dormiente, sed gestiente & exultāte. Hodie, inquit Christus, mecum eris in paradiso. Et anima Lazari in sinu Abrahæ non dormit, sed consolationibus cœlestib. fruitur. Nō obdormit spiritus in corpore, sed egreditur ac deserit corpus morte obsoporatū, reditq; ad cum qui dederat ipsum. Quare consulto non spiritus,sed carnis nos resurrectione credere profitemur. Et Apostolus infra cap.15.ubi fuse de resurrectione mortuorum disserit, nusquā meminit resurrectionis spiritum, sed eā asserit, qua corpus corruptibile & mortale ad incorruptionem & immortalitatē trasferatur. Quemadmodum igitur nec corruptionis nec mortis capax est spiritus,ita nec resurrectionis huius capax esse potest, qua incorruptibilis & immortalis reddatur. Admodum igitur inconsiderate nonnulli fratres de dormitione spiritum & animarum disputant.
units.tr: "And many sleep," he says. He does not say "they are dead" but "many sleep." So the death of those who are struck down with a singular plague for their sins is also a sleep, with a resurrection to follow. For each person sleeps with his own cause, and rises with it, whether good or bad. He calls the dead sleepers because he is writing to those among whom some denied the resurrection of the dead, and he is about to correct them in a separate treatment, for which this metaphor of sleep serves as a preface. For if the dead sleep, it follows that they will rise. Take away the resurrection, and there is no reason why the dead should be said to sleep. But this sleep is not to be transferred to the spirits of the dead, which cannot be capable of it. It refers to the bodies, which are said to sleep because they are going to rise at the dawn of the coming day and come forth into the light from their graves, as from their bedchambers. The Apostle longed to be dissolved and to be with Christ, that is, in spirit. In heaven, where Christ is, there is no place for sleeping, but for living in true happiness. The thief, after his death on the cross, was carried with Christ into paradise, that is, in spirit, and that spirit was not asleep but rejoicing and exulting. "Today," said Christ, "you will be with me in paradise." And the soul of Lazarus in Abraham's bosom does not sleep, but enjoys heavenly comforts. The spirit does not fall asleep in the body; it departs and leaves the body, which has been put to sleep by death, and returns to him who gave it. Therefore we profess that we believe deliberately in the resurrection of the flesh, not of the spirit. And the Apostle, below in chapter 15, where he discusses at length the resurrection of the dead, nowhere mentions a resurrection of the spirit, but asserts that corruptible and mortal body is transferred to incorruption and immortality. Just as the spirit is therefore capable neither of corruption nor of death, so it cannot be capable of this resurrection, by which it is made incorruptible and immortal. Therefore some brethren argue very thoughtlessly about the sleep of the spirit and of souls.

units.la: Etenim si nosipsi dijudicaremus, haudquaquam iudicati fuissemus. At cum iudicamur, à Domino corripimur, ne cum mundo condemnemur.
units.tr: For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged. But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world.

units.la: Causam malorum reijcit in ipsorū socordiam & impœnitentiam. Quasi dicat: Non est autut propter hanc plagam accusetis dominum nimiæ seueritatis. Haud erat uos iudicaturus, si uosipsi peccatū uestrū damnates iudicassetis. Nunc quoniam illud nec agnouistis nec damnastis, iudicauit uos dominus, uestra uidelicet impœnitentia coactus. Quod autē non dicit, Etenim si uosipsi iudicassetis, sed in prima persona: Etenim si nosipsi dijudicassemus, haudquaquā iudicati fuissemus, leniendę sententię gratia facit. Ad hoc enim sic loquitur, ut communem faciēs hac causam minus pudoris incutiat ijs qui præ cæteris erant culpabiles, & minus contristet eos quorū amici, cognati, & fratres plaga domini erant percusi.
units.tr: He puts the cause of the evils on their own carelessness and impenitence, as if to say: "Therefore do not accuse the Lord of excessive severity on account of this plague. He would not have judged you if you had condemned your own sin and judged it yourselves. Now, since you have neither recognised nor condemned it, the Lord has judged you, being compelled by your own impenitence." That he does not say, "For if you had judged yourselves," but in the first person, "For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged," he does for the sake of softening the sentence. For he speaks in this way so that, by making the cause a common one, he may cause less shame to those who were more guilty than the rest, and may grieve less those whose friends, relatives and brothers were struck by the Lord's plague.

units.la: Puto autē nos à scopo Apostoli haud aberraturos, si quæ hic in præterito dicit, Si nosipsi dijudicassemus, haudquaquā iudicati fuissemus, per Ebraismum esse dicta sententiamus, quo pro præsenti positū sit præterito, legamusq; ad hunc modum: Etenim si nosipsi dijudicaremus, haud quaquā iudicaremur. cui lectioni quadrat quod sequitur, At cum iudicamur, à domino corripimur, ne cum mundo damnemur. Sic utraque particula generale habet sententiā, ne Corinthijs tantū sic fuisse domini propitiū futurum suspicemur, si seipsi dijudicassent. Hæc enim illius clementia omnib. est cōmuniter parata, qui ipsi se ultro dijudicant, priusquā ab ipso iudicentur. Præter rationem tamen non est, quod in forma præteri loqui uoluit. Sic enim sententiam hanc quāuis in seipsa generale, ad causam tamē Corinthiorū specialiter accomodauit.
units.tr: I think, however, that we shall not stray from the Apostle's aim if we say that what he says here in the past tense, "If we had judged ourselves, we would not have been judged at all," is put in Hebraism, by which the past is used for the present, and that we read it in this way: "For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged at all." To this reading the following words agree: "But when we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, so that we are not condemned with the world." Thus both clauses have a general sense, so that we do not suppose that the Corinthians alone would have found the Lord so gracious if they had judged themselves. For that clemency is commonly offered to all who judge themselves of their own accord before they are judged by him. Yet there is no reason why he did not wish to speak in the past form. For thus, although this sentence is general in itself, he has nevertheless adapted it specifically to the case of the Corinthians.

units.la: Si nosipsi dijudicassemus, inquit. In Græca est, ἀ γὰρ ἐαυτοὺς διεκρίνομεν. Suprà diximus verbum διακρίνειν discernendi habere significationē, unde & Ambrosius hic legit: Quod si nosipsos discernemus. Ea lectio exponi posset ad huc modum: Si nosipsos debita cum discretione iudicaremus, ac peccata nostra corrigeremus. Chrysost. non διακρίνωμεν, sed simpliciter διεκρίνωμεν, id est, iudicassemus legit. quæ lectio,
units.tr: "If we had judged ourselves," he says. In the Greek it is [εἰ γὰρ ἑαυτοὺς διεκρίνομεν]. We said above that the verb [διακρίνειν] has the meaning of discerning, whence Ambrose also reads here: "But if we discerned ourselves." That reading could be explained in this way: "If we had judged ourselves with due discrimination, and corrected our sins."

units.la: meo iudicio germanior est, & sequenti particulæ melius conuenit, qua dicit: ἀν ἐαυτοὺς ἐκρινόμεθα, id est, haud quaquam iudicati fuissemus.
units.tr: Chrysostom reads not [διακρίνωμεν] but simply [διεκρίνομεν], that is, "we had judged." In my judgment this reading is more genuine, and agrees better with the following clause, where he says: [ἄν ἑαυτοὺς ἐκρινόμεθα], that is, "we would by no means have been judged."

units.la: Obserua uero quod non dicit: Si nosipsi flagellassemus, haudquaquā flagellati fuissemus. Non hoc poscitur ut poenas nobis ipsi inferamus, sicuti faciunt flagellatores, sed ut nosipsi iudicemus & condemnemus. Iudicat autē seipsum, q se peccatorē esse & agnoscit & fatetur, atq; ita se in conspectu domini humiliat, & resipiscit. Non amat dominus sanguinem nostrum, sed resipiscentiam, emendatione & contritionem spiritus.
units.tr: Observe, however, that he does not say, "If we had scourged ourselves, we would by no means have been scourged." This is not what is asked of us, that we inflict punishments on ourselves, as scourgers do, but that we judge and condemn ourselves. He judges himself who both recognises and confesses that he is a sinner, and so humbles himself in the sight of the Lord and repents. The Lord does not love our blood, but our repentance, amendment and a contrite spirit.

units.la: HAVDQVAQVAM, inquit, iudicati fuissemus.] Si nō iudicati, nō etiā flagellati fuissēt. Neq; enim flagellat Deus quēquā sine iudicio. Non dicit dubitāter, forsan iudicati non fuissemus: sed asseueraêter, haudquaquā inqt, iudicati fuissemus. Insignis est hæc consolatio, tā certo ore Apostolico affirmata. Non est igitur ut dubitemus, esse rationē qua iudiciū Dei effugiat etiam fontes. Graue est incidere in iudicium Dei, impossibile autē est sic uiuere, ut illi non reddamur obnoxij. Vnica ergo salutis ratio est, ut nosipsi iudicates iudiciū Dei effugiamus.
units.tr: "By no means," he says, "would we have been judged." If they had not been judged, they would not have been scourged either. For God does not scourge anyone without judgment. He does not say doubtfully, "Perhaps we would not have been judged," but he affirms with assurance, "By no means would we have been judged." This consolation is remarkable, affirmed with such a certain Apostolic voice. Therefore we need not doubt that there is a way by which one may even escape the judgment of God. It is grave to fall into the judgment of God, but it is impossible to live so as not to be liable to it. The only way of salvation, therefore, is that by judging ourselves we escape the judgment of God.

units.la: Si quæras causam, quare non iudicentur à Deo qui seipsi iudicant, non post reddi alia, q liberæ bonitatis clementia, quæ locum habet in illis, qui libera præditi sunt potestate, uel ignoscendi uel pœnas inferendi delinquentibus. Iudex qui superioris potestatis uices sustinet, etiamsi seipse qui reus est iudicet, haud tamen dimittiteum impunitum, sed iudicat & punit ,p officio. At qui libera potestate præditus est, si clemens sit, nec quærat aliud quā emendationem mali: ubi uidet sontem iudicare ac cōdemnare seipsum, resipiscere, & corde esse humili ac contrito, clementer illi ignoscit, propter resipiscentiam & emendationem. Sic animatus est dominus. Cum seipsum iudicaret & humiliaret Achab, similiter impius, nolebat eum iudicare, 1.Reg.21. Nec iudicabat Niniuitas, cū illi seipsos iudicarēt ac resipiscerēt.
units.tr: If you ask why those who judge themselves are not judged by God, no other reason can be given than the clemency of free goodness, which holds place in those who have free power either to pardon or to inflict punishment on offenders. A judge who holds the place of a higher power, even if the guilty man judges himself, does not dismiss him unpunished, but judges and punishes by duty. But one who has free power, if he is merciful and seeks nothing but the amendment of the evil, when he sees the offender judging and condemning himself, repenting, and being humble and contrite in heart, pardons him kindly for the sake of his repentance and amendment. So the Lord was minded. When Ahab judged and humbled himself, though he was equally impious, the Lord was unwilling to judge him (1 Kings 21). Nor did he judge the Ninevites when they judged themselves and repented.

units.la: AT cum iudicamur, inquit, à domino, corripimur, ne cum mundo damnemur.] Per expositionem causæ finalis, ad quam spectabat dominus, cum delinquentes castigaret, mitigat priorem expositionem, qua causam illis propter quam flagellabantur exposuit. Dixerat: Qui indigne manducat, reus est corporis domini, & iudicium sibi ipsi manducat, propter quod multi sunt inter uos imbecilles & inualidi, & dormiunt multi. Nam si nosipsi iudicassemus, non iudicati essemus à domino. Hic cogitare poterant: ergo lues ista, quæ nos apprehendit, ex eo est, quod nos cōdemnauit domi nus, æternæq; morti adiudicauit. Ergo damnati sumus, qui iam decumbimus ægroti, & perierunt qui luc hac sunt interfecti.
units.tr: "But when we are judged," he says, "by the Lord, we are chastened, so that we are not condemned with the world." By the explanation of the final cause, toward which the Lord looked when he chastised offenders, he softens the earlier explanation, in which he set out the cause on account of which they were scourged. He had said: "Whoever eats unworthily is guilty of the body of the Lord, and eats judgment to himself; on account of this many among you are weak and infirm, and many sleep. For if we had judged ourselves, we would not have been judged by the Lord." Here they might think: "Therefore this plague which has seized us is because the Lord has condemned us and adjudged us to eternal death. Therefore we are damned, who now lie sick, and those who have been killed by this plague have perished."

units.la: Huic cogitationi occurrit, exponens consilium diuinæ clementiæ, quo suos flagellat nō ut perdat, sed ut seruet. At, inquit, adhuc bene habet, quod iudicamur à domino. Signum enim est, quod nondū abiecerit nos. Dum nos iudicat, non condemnat ut perdat, sed erudit ut seruet. Pater est, diligens suos filios. Quare flagellat nos, ne perdamur. Perderemur autē, si impune absq; ulla resipiscentia peccaremus. Melius igitur est, ut flagellemur à domino ad tempus, quàm ut cum mundo condemnemur in sempiternum.
units.tr: To this thought he replies, explaining the counsel of divine clemency, by which he scourges his people not to destroy them but to save them. "But," he says, "it is still well that we are judged by the Lord. For it is a sign that he has not yet cast us off. While he judges us, he does not condemn in order to destroy, but instructs in order to save. He is a Father, lovingly caring for his sons. Therefore he scourges us, lest we perish. But we would perish if we sinned with impunity and without any repentance. It is better, then, that we be scourged by the Lord for a time, than that we be condemned with the world for ever."

units.la: AT cum iudicamur, inquit, à domino corripimur. ] Illud, à domino sic est positum, ut referatur tam ad sequentia quàm ad praecedentia. Alias repetendum erat ad hunc modum: At cum iudicamur à domino, à domino corripimur. Vtrūq; enim est opus domini, tá quod flagellat, q̃ quod corripit suos ne pereant. cum dicit: Cum iudicamur à domino, intelligit immissas ab illo afflictiones & plagas, quib. peccantes flagellat. Cum addit, corripimur, mentem & consilium flagellantis nos Dei exponit. In Graeco est παιδεύεσθαι, quod verbum in morem pueri castigari & erudiri significat. Pertinet huc locus. Hebr. 12. Tam igitur abest ut perdere nos velit dominus, dū peccates vel morbis, vel morte immatura, vel fame, vel bellis, vel exilijs percuti & affligit, ut ob id ipsum hoc faciat, ne pereamus. Caro in afflictionib. constituta dicit: Odit me Deus, ac perditioni destinauit, ideo tot me modis affligit: uel, ex afflictionibus non liberat. Dicat igitur spiritus fidei: Diligit me Deus, & ideo flagellat, ne cū impijs peream. Nisi diligeret, non castigaret peccantem, sed in malo pergere sineret.
units.tr: "But when we are judged, he says, we are chastened by the Lord." The phrase "by the Lord" is placed so that it refers both to what follows and to what precedes. Otherwise it would have had to be repeated in this way: "But when we are judged by the Lord, we are chastened by the Lord." Both are the work of the Lord: that he scourges, and that he corrects his own so that they do not perish. When he says "when we are judged by the Lord," he means the afflictions and blows sent by him, with which he scourges those who sin. When he adds "we are chastened," he sets out the mind and purpose of God who scourges us. In Greek the word is παιδεύεσθαι [paideuesthai], which means to be disciplined and trained as a boy is. The passage relates to this: Heb. 12. So far is the Lord from wishing to destroy us, when he strikes and afflicts sinners with sickness, untimely death, famine, war, or exile, that he does this very thing so that we may not perish. The flesh, placed under afflictions, says: "God hates me and has destined me to destruction, therefore he afflicts me in so many ways," or "he does not free me from afflictions." Let the spirit of faith therefore say: "God loves me, and therefore scourges me, so that I may not perish with the wicked." Unless he loved, he would not chastise the sinner, but would let him persist in evil.

units.la: NE cum mundo, inquit, damnemur. ] Discernit inter fideles & infideles, filios regni Dei, & filios huius saeculi. Fideles quoniam salutI sunt destinati, corripiuntur peccantes, ne pereant. Infideles vero quoniam uasa sunt irae, parata ad interitum, ducūt in bonis dies suos, & post hanc vitam cum diuite epulone poenis aeternis cruciantur. Illos vocat hic mundum, homines carnales, mūdanos, impios, huic tantum saeculo absq; sensu Dei viuentes.
units.tr: "That we may not be condemned with the world, he says." He distinguishes between believers and unbelievers, the sons of the kingdom of God and the sons of this age. Believers, since they are destined for salvation, are corrected when they sin, so that they do not perish. Unbelievers, since they are vessels of wrath, made ready for destruction, spend their days in prosperity and after this life are tormented with eternal punishments, like the rich man who feasted. He here calls those people "the world": carnal men, worldly, impious, living only for this age, without any sense of God.

units.la: NE cum mundo damnemur, inquit. ] Videmus mundum hunc esse pessimum, & in hilto rijs inde ab initio in malo constitutum fuisse legimus, nec meliorem futurum sperare possumus, cum sacrae scripturae omnia illius circa finem pessima futura praedicant. Nemo ergo mi retur, dum illū condemnationi destinatū esse audit. Scimus iudicium & condemnationem prioris mundi, quem iustitia Dei aquis diluuij perdidit. Posterioris huius, qui igne perdetur, condemnationem fugientes, caueamus il lius consortium, & gratiam hanc qua erepti ac segregati sumus ad uitam, magnificentes benè collocemus, deq; illa admoneamur, quoties diuinitus castigamur. Qui & nominis & salutis suę rationem habet, haud facile consortia cum illis miscet, quos nouit esse homines deplorate malos, & cum publico dedecore periturosne ijsdem malis unà cum illis inuolutur. Sic nos de hoc mundo cogitare conuenit. Odit nos mundus: cogitemus illum esse con-
units.tr: "That we may not be condemned with the world, he says." We see that this world is very wicked, and we read in the histories that from the beginning it was set in evil, nor can we hope it will become better, since the holy Scriptures all foretell that its wickedness will be greatest toward the end. Let no one therefore be surprised when he hears that it is destined for condemnation. We know the judgment and condemnation of the former world, which the justice of God destroyed by the waters of the flood. Fleeing the condemnation of this latter world, which will perish by fire, let us beware of fellowship with it. Let us rightly employ the grace by which we have been snatched away and set apart to life, esteeming it highly, and let us be reminded of it whenever we are chastised by God. He who takes account both of his name and of his salvation does not readily mix in company with those whom he knows to be wretchedly wicked men, lest he be caught up in their evils and perish with them in public disgrace. So we ought to think about this world. The world hates us: let us consider it devoted to condemnation.

units.la: demnationi deuotum. Allicit nos ad consortium: cogitemus cauendum nobis esse, ne cum illo damnemur.
units.tr: It entices us into fellowship: let us consider that we must take care lest we be condemned with it.

units.la: CORRIPIMVR, inquit, ne cum mundo condemnemur. ] Ergo sufficiebat Corinthijs flagellum illud quo corripiebantur, ad hoc ut salvarentur, & condemnationem mundi effugerent: Si hoc dixerimus, consequetur posse satisfieri diuinę iusticiae si tribulationes à domino illatas perpetiamur, etiamsi nulla sequatur resipiscentia. Absit. Non sic sentit Apostolus cum dicit: Cum iudicamur, à domino corripimur, ne cum mundo damnemur. Significat potius correptionem & castigationem ad hoc immitti à domino, ut castigati resipiscamus, & resipiscentes seruemur. Sic pater castigat filium suum uirga, non quod satis sit, si percussus nō peccauerit impune: sed ut flagellatus in se redeat, & emendetur. Sunt flagella Dei non simpliciter supplicia, quibus puniatur delinquentes, ne impune peccent: sed magis παιδεύσεως, id est, eruditiones & castigationes, quibus corripiantur filij Dei, ut resipiscant, ne per impoenitentiam cum hoc mundo pereant.
units.tr: "We are corrected, he says, lest we be condemned with the world." So was the scourge by which the Corinthians were corrected enough for them to be saved and escape the condemnation of the world? If we say so, it would follow that divine justice can be satisfied if we endure tribulations inflicted by the Lord, even when no repentance follows. Far from it. The Apostle does not think this when he says: "When we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, lest we be condemned with the world." He rather means that correction and chastisement are sent by the Lord for this purpose: that the chastened may repent, and repenting may be saved. So a father chastises his son with the rod, not because the blow is enough in itself if the one struck has not sinned with impunity, but so that the one scourged may come to himself and be amended. God's scourges are not simply punishments by which offenders are penalised, so that they do not sin with impunity; they are rather of παιδεύσεως [paideuseōs], that is, instructions and corrections, by which the sons of God are corrected, so that they may repent and not perish with this world through impenitence.

units.la: Itaq; fratres mei cum conuenitis ad edendum, alius alium expectate. Quod si quis esurit, domi edat, ne ad iudicium conueniatis. Caetera vero cum uenero, disponam.
units.tr: Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you do not come together for judgment. The rest I will set in order when I come.

units.la: Tandem post redargutionem abusuū, quos in coenam domini inuexerant Corinthij, hanc conclusionem subijcit. Quoniam nonnulli ex illis non expectatis aliis, proprias coenas praesumebant, & priusquam multitudo conuenisset, iam alijs adhuc esurientibus inebriati erat, quam inaequalitatem reprehendit: ideo in conclusione iubet, ut in posterū, ubi ad edendum conueniendum sit, alius alium expectent: hoc est, ut nemo ex illis priuatam sibi coenam praesumat, sed omnes in communi secundum dominicā institutionē edant & bibant. Sic dicit:
units.tr: Finally, after rebuking the abuses which the Corinthians had introduced into the Lord's Supper, he adds this conclusion. Since some of them, not waiting for the others, presumed to eat their own suppers, and before the crowd had assembled were already drunk while others were still hungry, he rebukes this inequality. Therefore in his conclusion he orders that in future, when they assemble to eat, they should wait for one another: that is, that none of them presume on a private supper, but that all eat and drink together in common, according to the Lord's institution. So he says:

units.la: ITAQVE fratres mei cum conuenitis ad edendum alius alium expectate. ] Conclusionem hanc infert ex praecedenti tractatu, praesertim ex ijs quibus indigne edentes reos fieri corporis ac sanguinis domini, ac iudicium sibijpsis edere: idq; in eo coprobari dixit, quod multi inter ipsos sint infirmi & inualidi, dormiantq; multi. Hinc infert dicens: Itaq; fratres mei uel diuina castigatione admoniti, desistite in posterū à pprijs ac priuatis coenis. Quin potius, ubi conueniendum est ad coenam dominicam, quo illam haud ἀναξίως celebretis, alius alium expectate, donec collecta sit multitudo, ne peiora post hanc admonitionē meam & diuinam castigationem, si abusus hosce non emendaueritis, experiamini. Mitigat autem & conclusionem & praecedentia per id quod eos uocat fratres suos, ne uideatur cum illis agere pro imperio, sed magis pro cura ac solicitudine fraterna.
units.tr: "Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another." He draws this conclusion from the preceding discussion, especially from those points where he said that those who eat unworthily become guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, and eat and drink judgment to themselves; and he said this is proved by the fact that many among them are weak and feeble, and many sleep. From this he infers, saying: "Therefore, my brothers, now admonished even by divine chastisement, desist henceforth from your own private suppers. Rather, when you must come together for the Lord's Supper, so that you may not celebrate it unworthily, wait for one another until the multitude is gathered, lest you suffer worse things after this my admonition and divine chastisement, if you do not amend these abuses." He softens both the conclusion and what went before by calling them his brothers, so that he does not seem to deal with them by authority, but by fraternal care and concern.

units.la: {y} Hebr. 12.
units.tr: {y} Heb. 12.

units.la: CVM coluenitis, inquit, ad edendum.]Nó loquitur de alio q̃ de ecclesiastico cōuetu,quo ad edendū coenā duicam cōuenire solebat, de quo suprà initio materię huius dixit: Ná pri-mũ quidè cū conuenitis in ecclesiā. Et: Igitur cū conuenitis in eundē locū,non est dominicam cœnā edere,&c. Quare non placet quod nonnulli exponunt de conuiuio ecclesiastico quidem,uerum non cœnæ dominicæ.
units.tr: "When you come together, he says, to eat." He speaks of nothing other than the ecclesiastical assembly, to which they were accustomed to come together to eat the Lord's Supper, of which at the beginning of this subject he said: "For first, indeed, when you come together in the church..." and: "Therefore, when you come together in the same place, it is not to eat the Lord's Supper, etc." Hence it does not please me that some explain this of an ecclesiastical banquet, but not of the Lord's Supper.

units.la: Caute autem sine specificatione in genere dicit:alius aliū expectate. Poterat dicere,uos ditiores,potentiores, & sectarij,expectate do nec multitudo conueniat:uerum maluit gene raliter loq, quo facilius hoc malū corrigeret.
units.tr: He speaks cautiously, however, in general terms without naming anyone: "wait for one another." He could have said: "You who are richer and more powerful, and you sectarians, wait until the multitude gathers." But he preferred to speak generally, so that he might more easily correct this evil.

units.la: QVOD si quis esurit,inquit,domi edat.]Po terant tergiuersari qui culpabiles erant, & esu riem præextexere. Occurrit igitur,imo repetit quod suprà dixit: An domos non habetis ad edendum?' Non dicit: Etiamsi quis esurit,ex-pectet tamen,feruetq; ieiunij patientiam,quo cum multitudine communiter ac ieiunus e-dat.Non imponit ieiunij molestiam,quá con-uenit relinquere uel necesitati uel libertati. sed permittit, ut qui esuriem ferre non uult, domi suæ edat. Non est autem hoc sic intelli-gendum,quod esurientem uelit domi edendo negligere synaxim ecclesię,ac cœnam domini ca: sed potius, quod uelit eum domi suæ ali-quid cibi percipere, quo postea facilius in cō-uentu morā alios expectandi ferat. Quàm di-uersi sunt ab hac Apostoli sententia, qui à cœ-næ dominicæ cōmunione omnes eos exclu-dunt,qui uel per imprudentiam aliquid gusta-runt. Vsqueadeò ut de saliua disputent,an si glutiatur ante hoc sacrum,nō excludit à com-munione.
units.tr: "But if anyone is hungry, he says, let him eat at home." Those who were at fault could make excuses and put forward hunger as a pretext. So he meets this objection, indeed repeats what he said above: "Do you not have houses in which to eat?" He does not say: "Even if someone is hungry, let him nonetheless wait and endure the patience of fasting, so that he may eat in common with the multitude while fasting." He does not impose the burden of fasting, which ought to be left to necessity or to liberty; he permits whoever cannot bear hunger to eat at home. This is not to be understood as meaning that by eating at home he wants the hungry to neglect the synaxis of the church and the Lord's Supper; rather he wants him to take some food at home, so that afterwards he may more easily bear the delay of waiting for the others in the assembly. How different from this sentence of the Apostle are those who exclude from communion in the Lord's Supper all who have tasted anything through carelessness! To such a degree that they dispute whether, if someone swallows saliva before this sacred rite, he is not thereby excluded from communion.

units.la: præsumere cœnam, inebriari, ecclesiam Dei contemnere,&pudefacere non habentes,do-mi ille edat,non in ecclesia. Verum cum in eo fit,ut prætextum esuriei adimat,dicés:Si quis esurit,domi edat,non ut esurientes uel eccle-sia eijciat,uel necesitate esuriem ferendi pre-mat,ideoq; non dicat:Si quis esurit, non in ec clesia,sed domi edat,sed simpliciter: Si quis e-surit,domi edat,non possum Chrysostomi ex positionem probare, ne cogamur esurientes sacra communione priuare,&faturos tantum uel ad minus non esurientes admittere.
units.tr: But since the words in that form take away the pretext of hunger, by saying "If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home," and not in order to drive the hungry out of the church or to force them, by necessity, to bear their hunger, he would not have said "If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, not in the church," but simply, "If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home." I cannot prove Chrysostom's exposition, lest we be compelled to deprive the hungry of the holy communion and admit only those who are full, or at least those who are not hungry.

units.la: Peruersa religio est,curare quàm uacuo sto macho ad sacramenti huius cōmunicationem accedas,&interim fusq; deq; facere,si mente fatura & ebria communices.
units.tr: It is a perverse religion to take care with how empty a stomach you approach the communion of this sacrament, and meanwhile to be careless whether you communicate with a mind full and drunk.

units.la: NE ad iudicium,inquit,conueniatis.] E-rafmus quod in Græco est ᾿ἐ᾿ ἐρίμα,id est,iudiciū, condemnationem uertit. Eadem ratione & suprà,ubi dicit: ... uerterepoterat, condemnationem sibi ipsi momedit. Iterum abfteret ab indigna manducatione. Existimo autem præcedentem particulam occupatio-nis gratia per parenthesim sic esse positam,ut præsens ad eam connecti possit, qua dixit: I-taque cum conuenitis ad edendum, alius a-lium expectate. Legatur ergo ad hunc mo-dum:Itaque cum conuenitis ad edendum,a-lius alium expectate ( quod si quis esurit, do-mi edat) ne ad iudicium conueniatis. Intel-lige,si alijs non expectatis,priuatim comede-ritis,atque ita institutionem dominicam per-uerteritis.
units.tr: "Lest you come together for judgment," he says. Erasmus, where the Greek has [εἰς κρίμα], that is, judgment, translated it as condemnation; and by the same reasoning above, where he says that it could be rendered [...], he has bitten off his own condemnation. Again, the sense keeps away from unworthy eating. I think, however, that the preceding clause is placed in parenthesis for the sake of brevity, so that the present clause can be connected to it, where he said: "So when you come together to eat, wait for one another." Let it therefore be read in this way: "So when you come together to eat, wait for one another (if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home), lest you come together for judgment." Understand that if you do not wait for one another, but eat privately, you will pervert the Lord's institution.

units.la: CAETERA, inquit, cū uenero,disponā.] Non correxerat in præsenti omnia ad cōuen-tum illorum,ac cœnam dominicam pertinen-tia, sed ea tantum quæ minus erant ferenda. Reseruat igitur reliqua ad suum usq; ad illos ad uentum.Quæ illa sint,existimo non esse cu-riosius inquirendum.
units.tr: "The rest," he says, "I will set in order when I come." He had not yet corrected everything pertaining to their assembly and the Lord's Supper, but only those things which were least tolerable. He therefore reserves the remainder until his coming to them. I think it should not be inquired into too curiously what those things are.

units.la: Citant hunc locum nonnulli pro confir-matione omnis generis traditionum ac rituū Papisticorum,etiá eorū qui palàm uerbo Chri-fti & doctrinæ apostolicæ repugnant.Verū re- sponderūt illis ante me alij. Quod me attinet, nisi certiora adferant, quàm facilè quiduis cōminiscuntur, tam facilè huiusmodi illorū commenta respuero. Verbum disponēdi, quod est in Græco διατάξομαι nō significat perpetuo nō ua ponere statuta, sed & ea quæ antea fuerant constituta & postea confusa in ordinem redigere. De hoc uerbo diximus supra cap. 7. ibi, Et sic in omnibus ecclesijs ordino.
units.tr: Some cite this passage to confirm all kinds of Papist traditions and rites, even those which openly oppose the word of Christ and apostolic doctrine. But others have answered them before me. As for me, unless they bring forward more certain things than they easily invent, I will as easily reject these inventions of theirs. The word for setting in order, which in Greek is [διατάξομαι], does not always signify laying down new statutes, but also bringing into order things that were previously established and afterwards confused. We spoke of this word above, in chapter 7, where it says: "And so in all the churches I ordain."

units.la: CAPVT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Transit Apostolus ad dona spiritus, quæ plerisque baptizatis in nomen Christi manifesto miraculo ad ornandum, confirmandū & ædificandum ecclesiā conferebantur. Horum authorē & usum declarat, propter eos partim qui illis abutebantur, partim propter reliquos, qui quoniā illis se nō ut alios donatos esse uidebāt, perinde animo reddebātur pusillo, ac si ad ecclesiam Christi haud pertinerent. Ergo ut illorum insolentiam restringat, istorum uero delectu animum erigat, ingreditur materiæ huius tractatum disserens de donis spiritus tam primarijs quàm secundarijs idem; facit tribus capitibus, 12, 13, 14.
units.tr: The Apostle turns to the gifts of the Spirit, which were conferred on most of those baptized in the name of Christ by a manifest miracle, to adorn, confirm and build up the Church. He sets out the author and use of these gifts, partly on account of those who abused them, and partly on account of the rest, who, seeing that they had not been given such gifts as others had, were made faint-hearted, as though they did not belong to the Church of Christ at all. So, to restrain the insolence of the former and to raise up the spirits of the latter, he takes up the subject and discusses the gifts of the Spirit, both the principal and the secondary ones, in the same way. He does this in three chapters: 12, 13 and 14.

units.la: DE spiritualibus uero nolo uos ignorare.
units.tr: Now concerning spiritual gifts, I would not have you ignorant.

units.la: Statim initio exprimit, de quibus iam sit consequenter dicturus, uidelicet, de spiritualibus. {B}Quoniam uero uocem hanc absolutè absque specificatione posuit, fit ut aliter atque aliter exponatur. Alij accipiunt illam de gratijs sacramentorum, alij de miraculosis signis & charismatibus quæ fidelibus dabātur, alij de ipsis credentibus, qui per spiritū Christi uarijs linguis loquebantur, & res mirandas operabantur, quorum mihi sententia probatur. Poslet tamen communiter hæc uox accipi de omnibus illis qui alicuius spiritus siue mali siue boni afflatu moti miranda uel dicebant uel faciebāt. Omnino de fidelibus ac bono spiritu Dei afflatis intelligit cum infrà 14. dicit: Si quis uidetur esse propheta aut πνευματικός, id est, spiritualis. Et Galat. 6. Vos qui spirituales estis, instruite talē in spiritu mansuetudinis, &c. quibus locis perstringit eorum insolentiam, qui propter singularia charismata spiritus reliquos præ se fastidiebant. Apparet illos uel coepisse uocari spirituales, propter miraculosa charismata spiritus quæ acceperant per fidē in Christum, uel ab Apostolo sic uocari, quòd se tales esse gloriarentur, & quòd insolentiam illorum præsenti tractatu corrigere proponeret. Spirituale est, quod est à spiritu uel Dei, uel angelico, uel diabolico uel humano, uel quod pertinet ad spiritum uel Dei, uel angelicum uel diabolicum, uel humanum. Spiritualis homo est, qui aut natus est ex spiritu, uel agitur spiritu, siue bono siue malo, aut intelligit spiritualia, uel delectatur spiritualibus, uel consecratus ac
units.tr: At the outset he states what he is going to discuss next, namely, spiritual things. Since he uses this word absolutely, without specification, it is explained in different ways. Some take it of the graces of the sacraments, others of the miraculous signs and gifts (charismata) that were given to the faithful, others of the believers themselves, who through the Spirit of Christ spoke in various tongues and worked wonderful things. My own view is the one that is approved. Yet this word could in general be taken of all those who, moved by the inspiration of some spirit, whether evil or good, either said or did wonderful things. Certainly he means it of the faithful, inspired by the good Spirit of God, when below, in chapter 14, he says: "If anyone seems to be a prophet or a pneumatikos [πνευματικός], that is, spiritual." And in Galatians 6: "You who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness," etc. In these places he rebukes the insolence of those who, because of their singular gifts of the Spirit, looked down on the rest. It appears either that they had begun to be called spiritual because of the miraculous gifts of the Spirit that they had received through faith in Christ, or that the Apostle called them so, since they boasted of being such, and because he proposed in this treatise to correct their insolence. Something is spiritual if it comes from the Spirit, whether of God, of an angel, of the devil or of a human, or if it pertains to the Spirit, whether of God, of an angel, of the devil or of a human. A spiritual person is one who is either born of the Spirit, or driven by the Spirit, whether good or evil, or who understands spiritual things, or delights in spiritual things, or is consecrated and assigned to spiritual things. In this sense churchmen today are called spiritual, although in reality they are carnal and worldly.

units.la: deputatus est spiritualibus, quo sensu ecclesiastici hodie spirituales uocātur, cum reipsa sint carnales & mundani.
units.tr: In this sense churchmen today are called spiritual, although in reality they are carnal and worldly.

units.la: B spiritualib9 uero, inquit, nolo uos ignorare.) Id est, nolo uos esse ignorantes charismatum spiritus, quæ in spiritualibus uestris uisuntur & audiuntur. Significat ex illorum esse ignorātia, quod spirituales dōnis hisce abutentur, & reli ui, quasi minus essent Christiani doleret, & hanc ob causam instruit eos, ne sint amplius ignorantes.
units.tr: "Now concerning spiritual things," he says, "I would not have you ignorant." That is, I would not have you be ignorant of the gifts of the Spirit, which are seen and heard among you who are spiritual. By their ignorance he indicates that those who are spiritual abuse these gifts, and that he grieves over the rest, as though they were less Christian, and for this reason he instructs them that they should be ignorant no longer.

units.la: Plane Apostolica uox est: nolo uos fratres esse ignorantes. Studium antichristianorū nō apostolicorū est, tenebris ignorantiæ oppressam uelle ecclesiam, cui debemus omnem illā confusionem, superstitionem, impietatem, & corruptionem, quæ sæculis iamaliquot in ecclesijs obtinuit. Hinc sunt uoces illæ filiorum tenebrarum: Laici ne sint docti, ne legant sacras scripturas, Biblica scriptura facit hæreticos, qui simpliciter ambulat, bene ambulat; quasi simpliciter ambulare, fit ignoranter, & clausis oculis ambulare, & non magis syncerè absque fraude & dolo uiuere. Obsecro, quando sunt isti cum Apostolo dicturi: De spiritualibus fratres nolo uos esse ignorātes? Vtinam uniuersa ecclesia uel sero tandem gnara sit, & rerum & hominum uerè spiritualium, incipiat; inter uera & falsa discernere.
units.tr: Clearly this is an apostolic utterance: "I would not have you, brothers, be ignorant." It is the aim of the Antichristians, not of the Apostles, to want the Church kept oppressed in the darkness of ignorance. To this we owe all that confusion, superstition, impiety and corruption which has held sway in the churches for many centuries now. Hence come those words of the sons of darkness: "Let not the laity be learned, let them not read the Holy Scriptures; Bible-reading makes heretics; he who walks simply walks well," as though to walk simply meant to walk ignorantly, with eyes shut, and not rather to live sincerely, without fraud or deceit. I beg you, when will these men say with the Apostle: "Brothers, I would not have you ignorant concerning spiritual things"? Would that the whole Church might at last, however late, come to know both the things and the men that are truly spiritual, and begin to distinguish between the true and the false.

units.la: Scitis quod cum ethnici essetis, ad simulacra muta quomodocunque duceba mini, abducti fueritis,
units.tr: You know that when you were Gentiles, you were led away to dumb idols, however you were led.

units.la: Lectio huius loci sic est in Græco, ut sensum habeat imperfectū, nisi uel uoculam ὅτι, id est, cum, sustuleris & legeris: Scitis quod ethnici fueritis, ducti ad simulacra muta quomodocunque ducebamini, uel participium ἀπαγόμενοι, id est, abducti uel seducti, in uerbum mutaueris. Quædam exemplaria Græca nō habent ὅτι. Sic lectionis uarietas uariū sensum gignit. Scitis, inquit. Quid eos scire dicit? Aut, quòd fuerint ethnici eidololatræ, aut quòd cum ati tea essent ethnici, ad simulacra muta fuerint abducti. Posteriot & lectio & sensus magis probatur. Haud enim tam magni momenti erat in memoriam illis reuocare, quòd fuerint ethnici, priusquam Christiani fierent, quàm quòd cum ethnici essent, ad simulacra muta fuerint abducti.
units.tr: The reading of this passage in the Greek is such that the sense is incomplete, unless you either remove the little word hoti [ὅτι], that is, "that," and read: "You know that you were Gentiles, led to dumb idols however you were led," or change the participle apagomenoi [ἀπαγόμενοι], that is, "led away or seduced," into a verb. Some Greek copies do not have hoti. So variation in the reading produces various senses. "You know," he says. What does he say they know? Either that they were idolatrous Gentiles, or that, while they were Gentiles, they had been led away to dumb idols. The latter reading and sense is more approved. For it was not of such great importance to remind them that they had been Gentiles before they became Christians, as that, while they were Gentiles, they had been led away to dumb idols.

units.la: SCITIS, inquit, quòd cū ethnici essetis. Ah non tum quoque erant ἔθνη, id est, Gentes? Erant adhuc Gentes, sed natione, non religione. Alibi dicit: Israelitæ sunt, & ego. Et: Nam & ego Israelita sum. Quemadmodum ipse Israelita adhuc erat natione & carne, quamuis religione esset Christianus, ita & ij qui ex Gentibus in Christum credebant, Gentes adhuc erant carne, religione uero Christiani. Cum ergo dicit: Scitis quòd cum Gentes, uel ethnici essetis, respicit nō ad nationem, sed ad religionem ethnicam. Diuersitas nationum neq; impedit ueram religionem, neq; tollitur aut mutatus
units.tr: "You know," he says, "that when you were Gentiles..." Ah, were they not then also ethne [ἔθνη], that is, Gentiles? They were still Gentiles, but by nation, not by religion. Elsewhere he says: "They are Israelites, and so am I," and "For I too am an Israelite." Just as he himself was still an Israelite by nation and flesh, though a Christian by religion, so those who believed in Christ from among the Gentiles were still Gentiles in the flesh, but Christians in religion. So when he says, "You know that you were Gentiles or heathen," he looks not to nation but to heathen religion. A difference of nations neither hinders true religion nor is it taken away or changed by religion.

units.la: i.Cor.12.

Rom.11. tatur religione. Quare quod Ephes.2. legitur: A Quapropter memententote, quod vos quondam Gentes in carne, &c. non est vigilanter à vulgato, quisquis fuit, interprete versum: Propter quod memores estote, quod aliquando vos qui Gentes eratis in carne, quasi Christiani facti, non essent amplius Gentes in carne, cum verbum, eratis, non sit in Graeco. Ibi enim sic legitur: Διὸ μνημονεύετε, ὅτι ὑμεῖς ποτὲ τὰ ἔθνη ἐν σαρκὶ, οἱ λεγόμενοι ἀκροβυστία ὑπὸ τῆς λεγομένης περιτομῆς ἐν σαρκὶ χειροποιήτου, ὅτι ἦτε ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ χωρὶς Χριστοῦ, &c. Hoc est: Propterea memetote, quod vos quondam Gentes in carne, qui dicimini praeputium ab ea quae circumcisio dicitur in carne manufacta, quod fueritis in tempore illo sine Christo, &c. Ubi vocu ἐν σαρκί, id est, quondam non ad proximè subsequens referenda est, sed ad id quod dicit, ὅτι ἦτε ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ, sic ut ὅτι, i. quod, ociosè repetatur, sitque ordinanda lectio ad hunc modum: Propterea memententote, quod vos aliquando, qui Gentes estis in carne qui dicimini praeputium ab ea quae dicitur circumcisio in carne, fueritis in tempore illo sine Christo, &c. Et Erasmus quoque, quamvis alias vigilans interpres, inconsulto sic vertit: Quapropter memententote, quod vos quondam Gentes in carne vocabamini praeputium, &c. Quod in Graeco est οἱ λεγόμενοι, uertendumerat in praesenti, qui dicimini, non vocabamini. Etenim & tum quoque sic vocabantur, & Apostolus nô monet eos, ut recordentur se olim praeputium fuisse à Iudaeis vocatos, sed ut memores sint, se ante id temporis fuisse sine Christo, &c. Rectè tamen illud reddidit, quod inquam erat in tempore illo sine Christo, &c. Sed redeamus ad textum.
units.tr: Rom. 11. Therefore what is read in Ephesians 2, "Wherefore remember that you were once Gentiles in the flesh," etc., has not been carefully rendered by whoever the Vulgate translator was: "Wherefore remember that you who were once Gentiles in the flesh," as if, having become Christians, they were no longer Gentiles in the flesh, since the word "were" is not in the Greek. For there it reads thus: Dio mnemoneuete, hoti hymeis pote ta ethne en sarki, hoi legomenoi akrobystia hypo tēs legomenēs peritomēs en sarki cheiropoiētou, hoti ēte en tō kairō ekeinō chōris Christou, etc. [Διὸ μνημονεύετε, ὅτι ὑμεῖς ποτὲ τὰ ἔθνη ἐν σαρκὶ, οἱ λεγόμενοι ἀκροβυστία ὑπὸ τῆς λεγομένης περιτομῆς ἐν σαρκὶ χειροποιήτου, ὅτι ἦτε ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ χωρὶς Χριστοῦ, &c.] This means: "Therefore remember that you were once Gentiles in the flesh, who are called uncircumcision by that which is called circumcision made in the flesh by hand, and that you were at that time without Christ, etc." Here the phrase en sarki [ἐν σαρκί], "in the flesh," is not to be referred to what immediately follows, but to what he says next, hoti ēte en tō kairō ekeinō [ὅτι ἦτε ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ], so that hoti [ὅτι], that is, "that," is repeated needlessly, and the reading should be arranged in this way: "Therefore remember that you, who once were Gentiles in the flesh and are called uncircumcision by that which is called circumcision in the flesh, were at that time without Christ, etc." Erasmus too, although otherwise a careful translator, rendered it carelessly: "Wherefore remember that you were once Gentiles in the flesh and were called uncircumcision, etc." Where the Greek has hoi legomenoi [οἱ λεγόμενοι], it should have been rendered in the present, "who are called," not "were called." For they were called so at that time as well, and the Apostle does not warn them to remember that they had once been called uncircumcision by the Jews, but that they should remember that before that time they had been without Christ, etc. Nevertheless he rendered the phrase well: "that you were at that time without Christ, etc." But let us return to the text.

units.la: SCITIS, inquit, quod cum ethnici essetis, ad simulacra muta quomodocunque ducebamini, abducti fueritis.) Hoc videlicet est, quod eos scire dicit, quod in ethnicismo abducti fuerint ad simulacra muta, quomodocunque ducebantur, id est, absque ulla consideratione, bene ne vel male ducerentur. Non dicit simpliciter: Cum ethnici essetis, abducebamini ad simulacra muta, sed: Scitis, quod cum ethnici essetis, abducti fueritis ad simulacra muta. Tenetur ipsorum conscientiam. Loquitur enim de re omnibus ipsis manifesta. Quorsum autem hoc eos scire dicit? Probat ex praeterita caecitate, fuisse eos spiritualium rerum ignaros, cum enim dicit: Nolo vos ignorantes esse spiritualium, perinde est ac si dicat, quemadmodum fuistis hactenus. Quod enim ignorantes fueritis, vestra ipsorum conscientia testatur. Scitis nanque, quod ad muta simulacra passi fueritis vos abduci, id quod non erat recto iudicio ambulantium, sed per caecitatem aberrantium. Vtitur autem similitudine caecorum, qui quoniam destituti sunt proprij moderamine uisus, alienoductu reguntur, cui coguntur obsequi, quo modocunque bene vel male ducantur. Sic Gentes, cum spiritualium essent iudicio destitutae, abductae sunt ad simulacra muta, & interim
units.tr: "You know," he says, "that when you were Gentiles, you were led away to dumb idols, however you were led." This is clearly what he says they know: that in their heathenism they were led away to dumb idols, however they were led, that is, without any consideration of whether they were led well or badly. He does not say simply, "When you were Gentiles, you were led away to dumb idols," but, "You know that when you were Gentiles, you were led away to dumb idols." He appeals to their own conscience, for he speaks of a matter manifest to all of them. Why does he say they know this? He proves from their past blindness that they were ignorant of spiritual things.
