For when he says, "I would not have you ignorant concerning spiritual things," it is as if he were saying, "as you have been until now." That you were ignorant is attested by your own conscience. For you know that you allowed yourselves to be led away to dumb idols, which was not the judgment of those who walk rightly, but of those who wander through blindness. He uses the likeness of the blind, who, since they are deprived of the guidance of their own sight, are led by another's guidance, and must obey it, however they are led, well or badly. So the Gentiles, since they lacked judgment in spiritual things, were led away to dumb idols, and meanwhile thought they were being led to the true worship of God. He therefore puts the effect of blindness in place of the proof of ignorance of spiritual things. To be led away to dumb idols is a result of blindness of mind, and it has a clear sign of that blindness.

units.la: ad uerum fe cultum Dei duci putarunt. Ponit itaque effectum caecitatis pro argumento ignorantiae rerum spiritualium. Abduci ad simulacra muta, ex caecitate mentium est, habetque manifestum illius indicium.
units.tr: They thought they were being led to the true worship of God. He therefore puts the effect of blindness in place of the proof of ignorance of spiritual things. To be led away to dumb idols comes from blindness of mind, and it bears a clear sign of that blindness.

units.la: Ne autem uideatur hoc illis per exprobrationem obijcere, reijcit culpam in illorum ductores, vel potius seductores. Neque enim simpliciter dicit: Scitis quod cum Gentes essetis, coluericitis simulacra muta, sed, abducti fueritis ad simulacra muta quomodocunque ducebamini. Sic Euangelicis nostris dici potest: Scitis quod cum in Papatu essetis, ad simulacra muta quomodocunque ducebamini, abducti ac seducti fueritis. Misera planè conditio est caeci populi. Nulla est tam foeda superstitio, nulla tam abominabilis impietas, ad quam non possit abduci, ubi se semel ductoribus caecis ac perfidis permittere coepit.
units.tr: So that this may not seem to be a reproach he throws at them, he places the blame on their leaders, or rather their seducers. He does not simply say, "You know that when you were Gentiles you worshipped dumb idols," but "you were led away to dumb idols, however you were being guided." In the same way it can be said to our own people: "You know that when you were in Papistry, however you were being led, you were led away and seduced to dumb idols." The condition of a blind people is surely wretched. There is no superstition so foul, and no impiety so abominable, to which they cannot be led once they have begun to entrust themselves to blind and faithless guides.

units.la: AD simulacra muta, inquit.) Non est ociosum, quod non simpliciter dicit, ad simulacra, sed, ad simulacra muta. Non solum sugillat simulacra, sed & caecitatem eidololatrarum perstringit, quod illa colere voluerint, cum reipsa insensata esse cernerent, unde nihil illis esse numinis colligere poterant. Haec dicens stimulat eos & excitat ad excutiendum ignorantiam, & studendum spiritualium rerum intelligentiae. Unde & subiungit:
units.tr: "To dumb idols," he says. It is not idle that he does not simply say "to idols" but "to dumb idols." He does not merely mock the images; he also strikes at the blindness of the idolaters, who chose to worship things they could see were in fact senseless, from which they could gather that these things had no divinity. In saying this he stirs and rouses them to shake off ignorance and to strive for understanding of spiritual things. Hence he adds:

units.la: Quapropter notum vobis facio, quod nemo per spiritum Dei loquens dicit anathema Iesum, & quod nemo potest dicere dominum Iesum, nisi per spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking by the Spirit of God says "Jesus is accursed," and that no one can say "Jesus is Lord" except by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: QVAPROPTER, inquit.) Quare? Quia non convenit ut sitis ignorates spiritualium, sicut fuistis priusquam in Christum credere coepistis. Dixit: Nolo vos ignorare de spiritualibus. Quam caeci fueritis in ethnicismo nostis. Nunc tempus est ut veritatis, ita & intelligentiae. Nolo vos iniciar caecorum quovis abduci. Quapropter notum vobis facio, quid de spiritualibus sentire ac iudicare debeatis.
units.tr: "Therefore," he says. Why? Because it is not fitting that you should be ignorant of spiritual things, as you were before you began to believe in Christ. He said: "I do not want you to be ignorant concerning spiritual things." You know how blind you were in heathenism. Now is the time of truth, and so of understanding. I do not want you, as initiates, to be led away by any blind men whatever. Therefore I make known to you what you ought to think and judge concerning spiritual things.

units.la: QVOD nemo, inquit, per spiritum Dei loquens dicit anathema Iesum, & quod nemo potest dicere dominum Iesum, nisi per spiritum sanctum.) Incipit eos instruere de spiritualibus. Et primum ponit id quod generale est in omnibus fidelibus opus spiritus. Deinde subiicit de donis singularibus, quae non omnibus ex aequo, sed aliis alia conferebantur. Genera le opus spiritus est, fides illa, qua Iesum crucifixum uocamus dominum. Vultis, inquit, indicium loquentis in uobis spiritus Dei? Quod Iesum uocatis dominum, habetis ex spiritu Dei. Nisi ille in uobis sit, non poteritis Iesum uocare dominum. Si sit in uobis, non uocabitis eum anathema. Est enim spiritus Dei, quae accipiunt credentes, spiritus veritatis, testificans de Iesu, quod sit dominus. Quare fit, ut nemo per illum loquens, uocet Iesum anathema, nec quisquam possit Iesum uocare dominum, nisi per illum. Quid sit anathema, dixi-mus Rom.9. Hoc pacto erigit eos, quibus nō erat datum, ut linguis loquerentur, uel morbidos curarent, vel alia miranda facerent, dum asserit & ipsos loqui ex instinctu spiritus Dei, eiusq; indubitatum esse argumentum, quod Iesum uocet dominum, quem alij spiritu Dei destituti uocant anathema.
units.tr: "That no one," he says, "speaking by the Spirit of God says, 'Jesus is accursed,' and that no one can say, 'Jesus is Lord,' except by the Holy Spirit." He begins to instruct them about spiritual things. And first he sets out the work of the Spirit that is common to all the faithful. Then he adds about the particular gifts, which were not given equally to all, but some were given one thing and some another. The general work of the Spirit is that faith by which we call the crucified Jesus Lord. "Do you want," he says, "a sign of the Spirit of God speaking in you? That you call Jesus Lord, you have from the Spirit of God. Unless he is in you, you cannot call Jesus Lord. If he is in you, you will not call him accursed. For the Spirit of God is the Spirit of truth, which believers receive, testifying about Jesus that he is Lord." Therefore it comes about that no one speaking by him calls Jesus accursed, and no one can call Jesus Lord except by him. What "accursed" means, we explained at Rom. 9. In this way he lifts up those who had not been given the gift of speaking in tongues, or of healing the sick, or of doing other wonders, while he affirms that they too speak from the prompting of the Spirit of God, and that it is an undoubted proof of this that they call Jesus Lord, whom others, being destitute of the Spirit of God, call accursed.

units.la: Hanc puto praesentis loci expositione sim-plicem esse, & germanam. Nolim tamen con-tendere cum ijs qui Chrysostomi sententiam sequuntur. Ille sic exponit: De spiritualibus di-sturus, principio diuinationis & prophetię di-scrimen ponit, sic dicės: Scitis quod cum Gen-tes essetis, ad simulacra muta quomodocunq; ducebamini, abducti fueritis. Quod autem di-cit tale est. In cultu, inquit, eidolorum, si quan-do ab immundo quisquam spiritu detentus & occupatus est, & diuinat, quemadmodum agitur, sic trahitur a spiritu ligatus, nihil sciens eorum quae dicit. Hoc enim proprium est diui-natoris, mente motum esse, coactionem pati, impelli, rapi, & instar insani trahi. Propheta ue-rō non ad hunc modum, sed mente sobria, & dispositione sana ac sciens quae dicit, profert omnia, etiam priusquam illa eueniant. Et hinc agnoscę diuinatorem & prophetam. Et vide quomodo sermone a suspitione liberat. Ipsos citat testes, qui rei huius experientiam cepe-rant. Quod enim non mentiar, inquit, vos ipsi mihi testes eritis. Scitis enim, quomodo cum Gētes essetis, abducti fueritis ac tracti. Et pau-lo post: Et haec quidem prima est diuinatoris ac prophetę differentia, deinde & altera sub-ijcit, dicens: Quapropter notum uobis facio, quod nemo per spiritum Dei loquens, dicit anathema Iesum. Et nemo potest dicere do-minum Iesum nisi in spiritu sancto. Cum vi-detis, inquit, quendam non sonantem ipsius nomen, aut etiam anathemate damnantem, di-uinator est. Rursus vbi videris alium cuncta cum nomine ipsius sonantem, intellige illum esse spiritualem. Haec ille. Quae mihi uidentur in genere dicta. & ad omnes communiter cū in ethnicismo, tum in Christianismo constitu-tos pertinere, refert ille specialiter ad diui-tores ethnicos & prophetas veros, quasi ab-duci ad simulacra muta non sit nisi diuinato-rum, & non communiter omnium eidolola-trarum, & dicere Iesum dominum, prophēta-rum tantum sit, & non etiam quorumcun-que fidelium.
units.tr: I think that the exposition of this passage is simple and genuine, and I would not wish to contend with those who follow the opinion of Chrysostom. He explains thus: "Intending to speak about spiritual things, he first draws a distinction between divination and prophecy, saying: 'You know that when you were Gentiles, you were led away to dumb idols, however you were being led.' What he says next is this. In the worship of idols, if anyone is held and possessed by an unclean spirit and divines, he is driven as he is driven, and, bound by the spirit, he is dragged along, knowing nothing of what he says. For it is the mark of a diviner to be moved in mind, to suffer compulsion, to be impelled, carried off, and dragged like a madman. But the prophet is not like this; with a sober mind and a sound disposition, knowing what he says, he declares all things, even before they come to pass. And from this we recognise the diviner and the prophet. And see how he frees his speech from suspicion. He cites as witnesses the very people who had experienced this matter. For, so that I may not be lying, he says, you yourselves will be my witnesses. For you know how, when you were Gentiles, you were led away and dragged. And a little later: 'This is the first difference between the diviner and the prophet; then he adds a second, saying: "Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking by the Spirit of God says, 'Jesus is accursed.' And no one can say, 'Jesus is Lord,' except in the Holy Spirit." When you see someone who does not utter his name, or even condemns him with an anathema, he is a diviner. Again, when you see another uttering the name of Jesus in everything, understand that he is spiritual.'" So far Chrysostom. These words seem to me to be said in general, and to pertain to all who are established in heathenism and also in Christianity alike. But he refers them specially to the heathen diviners and to the true prophets, as if being led away to dumb idols belonged only to diviners and not commonly to all idolaters, and as if saying "Jesus is Lord" belonged only to prophets and not also to any of the faithful.

units.la: Nos admonemur hoc loco, vt obseruemus diligenter, quid de Christo Iesu sentiamus i-psi, & dicant alij. Probate spiritus, inquit Io-han.utrum sint ex Deo.probatio spirituum ne-cessaria nobis est, ne vel seducamur ab alijs, nel seducamus nosipsi. Ea uero certior esse nō potest, quàm si obseruemus tam nostram q a-liorum de Christo sententiam. Vt quo sim spi-ritu imbutus, intelligam, nō est mihi opus uer-bis. Possum enim ex eo periculum facere, si a-
units.tr: Here we are admonished to observe carefully what we ourselves think about Christ Jesus, and what others say. "Test the spirits," says John, "whether they are of God." The testing of spirits is necessary for us, lest we either be seduced by others or seduce ourselves. Yet this testing cannot be more certain than if we observe both our own opinion and that of others about Christ. That I am imbued with this Spirit, I need not learn from words. For I can make a trial of it from this,

units.la: nimaduertero, quid de Christo in corde meo sentiam. Si credo ac sentio firmiter esse illum dominum constitutum a Deo patre, argumen-tum habeo spiritus Dei, qui hanc in me fidem operatur. Vt aliorum vero spiritus probem, o-pus est vt audiam & cognoscam, quid de Chri-sto sentiant & loquantur. Si hunc confitentur esse dominum, agnosco in illis spiritum Dei. Nemo enim potest Iesum uocare dominum, nisi per spiritum sanctum. Ergo fidei huius con-sessio certum habet spiritus sancti argumentum. Quid igitur faciunt, qui veros hodie Christia-nos, Christum dominum ad sanguinis vsque effusionem confitentes, haereseos ob id dam-nant, & igni tradunt, quod non credunt insan-ctos, illos non inuocant. Rom. pontificem nō vocant dominum ecclesiarum, voces falsorū pastorum non audiunt, sed vni Christo domi-no adhaerent, illumq; in mediis flammis inuo-cant, ac cum Stephano dicunt: Domine Iesu ac cipe spiritum meum. Quare non cogitant de hac Apostoli sententia: Nemo potest dicere do-minum Iesum, nisi per spiritum sanctum?
units.tr: if I attend to what I think about Christ in my heart. If I firmly believe and feel that he has been appointed Lord by God the Father, I have a proof of the Spirit of God, who works this faith in me. But to test the spirits of others, it is necessary that I hear and learn what they think and say about Christ. If they confess that he is Lord, I recognise in them the Spirit of God. For no one can call Jesus Lord except by the Holy Spirit. Therefore the confession of this faith holds a sure sign of the Holy Spirit. What then do those do today who condemn as heretics the true Christians who confess Christ as Lord even to the shedding of blood, and deliver them to the fire, because they do not believe in the saints and do not invoke them? They do not call the Roman pontiff the Lord of the churches; they do not hear the voices of false ministers, but cling to the one Lord Christ, and call upon him in the midst of the flames, and say with Stephen: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." Why do they not consider this sentence of the Apostle: "No one can say Lord Jesus, except by the Holy Spirit"?

units.la: Dices: Atqui facile est Iesum vocare domi-num. An non dicturi sunt reprobi in illo die, Domine domine, nonne per nomē tuum pro-phetauimus, dicturusq; illis est dominus, non noui uos? An non diserte dixit Christus: Non quisquis mihi dicit domine domine introibit in regnum coelorum, sed qui fecerit voluntate patris mei qui in coelis est, Matt. 7. & Luc. 6. Quid me vocatis dominedomine, & no facitis &c. Quomodo ergo firmum esse potest, quod Apostolus hic dicit: Nemo potest dicere domi-num Iesum, nisi per spiritum sanctum? An nō est cognituraus eos Christus, qui per spiritū san-ctum moti vocant ipsum dominum? An tales non sunt ingressuri in regnum Dei?
units.tr: You will say: "But it is easy to call Jesus Lord. Will not the wicked say on that day, 'Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in your name?' And will not Christ say to them, 'I never knew you'? Did not Christ plainly say: 'Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter into the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven' (Matt. 7 and Luke 6)? 'Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say?' How then can what the Apostle says here stand firm: 'No one can say Lord Jesus, except by the Holy Spirit'? Will Christ not know those who, moved by the Holy Spirit, call him Lord? Will such people not enter the kingdom of God?"

units.la: Respondeo. Considerandum est quot mo-dis vocetur Iesus dominus, quandoquidem hac in re non sonitus oris, sed affectus cordis censendus venit.
units.tr: I answer: one must consider in how many ways Jesus is called Lord, since in this matter what counts is not the sound of the voice but the disposition of the heart.

units.la: 1 Principio, quemadmodum per spiritū Dei miraculorum patratorem prophetant, nonun quam homines reprobi sub nomine Christi, & res mirandas faciunt, ita & Iesum appellant dominum per idem donum spiritus. Et sicut non saluantur donis hisce faciendorum mira-culorum, & prophetandi, ita neq; appellatio-ne hac qua Iesum uocant dominum. Quod si sensus Chrysostomi placet, quo de mentione fecimus, ita ut Paulus hic de prophetis Chri-sti, non de cunctis fidelibus in genere loqua-tur, nulla est quaestio. Potest enim fieri, ut do-num prophetiae per spiritum Dei habeant e-tiam reprobi.
units.tr: (1) First, just as some wicked men sometimes prophesy through the Spirit of God, and do wonderful works in the name of Christ, so they also call Jesus Lord by the same gift of the Spirit. And just as they are not saved by these gifts of working miracles and prophesying, so neither are they saved by this confession by which they call Jesus Lord. If the view of Chrysostom, which we mentioned, is accepted, namely that Paul here speaks of Christ's prophets and not of all the faithful in general, there is no problem. For it can happen that even the reprobate have the gift of prophecy through the Spirit of God.

units.la: 2 Deinde, inuenias qui Iesum uocent domi-num eo sensu & affectu quo Papistæ beatam uirginem uocant nostram dominam, tanquā titulo honoris. De his dici non potest quod ex spiritu Dei loquantur.
units.tr: (2) Second, you will find people who call Jesus Lord in the sense and with the feeling with which the Papists call the blessed Virgin "our Lady", as a title of honour. Of these it cannot be said that they speak from the Spirit of God.

units.la: 3 Tertio, quoniam in ecclesia obtinuit, ut ca-tholica & inueterata consuetudine Iesum Chri-stum stum vocemus nostrum dominum dicentes: Credo in Iesum Christum filium eius vnicum dominum nostrum, &c. fit vt ijquoq; qui absque fide syncera viuunt, & zizania sunt in agro domini, non triticum, perinde Iesum dominū vocent atq; veri Christiani, cum tamen non colant ipsum vt dominum, nec vera ab ipso fide pendeant. Nec isti ex spiritu Dei loquuntur, cum Iesum vocant dominum, nec regnum coelorum ingredientur.
units.tr: (3) Third, since it has prevailed in the Church, by a Catholic and long-established custom, that we call Jesus Christ our Lord, saying: "I believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord," and so on, it happens that those too who live without sincere faith, and are tares in the Lord's field and not wheat, call Jesus Lord just as true Christians do, although they do not worship him as Lord, nor does their true faith depend on him. Such people do not speak from the Spirit of God when they call Jesus Lord, nor will they enter the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: 4 Quarto Iesum uocant dominum veri fideles, qui spiritu filiorum Dei praediti, agnoscunt eum esse vnigenitum Dei, dominum & haeredem omnium, suntq; erga illum tanquam erga vnicum suum dominium fideliter, obedienter, ac syncere affecti, & ab illo vnicè dependent. Hoc affectu Iesum vocare dominū potest nemo, nisi spiritu fidei & filiorum Dei imbutus. Cum ergo dicit Apostolus, neminem posse vocare Iesum dominum, nisi per spiritum sanctū, non loquitur, meo iudicio, nisi de iis, qui quod ore sonant, neq; ex consuetudine, neq; per superstitionē, sed corde syncero ac veraci loquūtur. Siue igitur Chrysostomo expositio probatur siue teneatur haec nostra, omnino verum est, quod Apostolus hic loquitur, licet aliis modis frequenter absq; vllo spiritus sancti instinctu vocetur Iesus dominus.
units.tr: (4) Fourth, true believers call Jesus Lord, who, endowed with the Spirit of the sons of God, acknowledge him to be the only-begotten of God, Lord and heir of all, and who are disposed towards him, as towards their only Lord, faithfully, obediently and sincerely, and depend on him alone. No one can call Jesus Lord with this disposition unless he is imbued with the Spirit of faith and of the sons of God. Therefore, when the Apostle says that no one can call Jesus Lord except by the Holy Spirit, in my judgement he speaks only of those who speak not merely with the mouth, nor from custom, nor through superstition, but from a sincere and true heart. So whether Chrysostom's exposition is approved or this one of ours is held, it is entirely true that the Apostle speaks here, although in other ways Jesus is often called Lord without any impulse of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Diuisiones vero donorum sunt, sed idem spiritus, & diuisiones ministeriorum sunt, & idem dominus, & diuisiones operationum sunt, idem vero est Deus, efficiens omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are differences of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God who works all things in all.

units.la: Postquam generale opus spiritus Dei posuit, quo cuncti fideles afflati Iesum vocāt dominum, pergit ad specialia, quae nō omnibus, sed aliis alia contingunt, propterea quod nō adeo sunt atq; generale illud ad salutem omnibus necessaria, quamuis vsus illorum saluti fideliū ministerialiter seruiat.
units.tr: After setting out the general work of the Spirit of God, by which all the faithful, inspired, call Jesus Lord, he goes on to the particular gifts, which do not fall to all, but to some one thing and to others another, because they are not so necessary for salvation as that general gift that all need, although the use of them serves the salvation of the faithful as ministry.

units.la: 1 Et haec primum generali vocabulo vocat χαρίσματα. Sunt autē χαρίσματα dona ac benefi cia gratuita, qua uoce mox initio gratiam ac liberalitatem Dei erga ecclesiam fidelium suorum commēdat, qua illam tot egregijs donis mox atque colligi coepit, ornare ac cumulare uoluit, ac simul fastum & insolentiam eorum reprobat, qui perinde ob haec dona spiritus insolescebant in ecclesia, ac si suapte illa uirtute parassent, & non per meram gratiam Dei in vsus aliorum accepissent. Eodem hodie quoq; uicio plerosque laborare uideas, q propter dona Dei aduersus alios superbiunt, & quosuis prae se fastidiunt, non cogitantes unde illa & in quos usus acceperint.
units.tr: (1) He first calls these by the general word "charismata". Now charismata are gifts and free benefits, and by this word at the very beginning he commends the grace and generosity of God towards his faithful Church, which he wished to adorn and enrich with so many outstanding gifts as soon as it began to be gathered together. At the same time he rebukes the pride and arrogance of those who, on account of these gifts of the Spirit, grew proud in the Church, as if they had obtained them by their own virtue and had not received them through the mere grace of God for the use of others. You may see that many today also suffer from this same vice: they grow proud on account of God's gifts against others, and despise all others, not considering whence and for what use they have received them.

units.la: 2 Secundo loco commendat donorum isto rum uarietatem dicens: Diuisiones uero charismatum sunt. Item, diuisiones uero sunt ministeriorum. Et, diuisiones sunt operationum, quam uarietatem infra explicabit. Tribuit autem illis diuisionem nō talem, qualis in eccle-
units.tr: (2) In the second place he commends the variety of these gifts, saying: "Now there are diversities of gifts." Likewise: "there are diversities of ministries." And: "there are diversities of operations", a variety he will explain further on. He attributes to them a division not of the kind that had begun to prevail in the Church of the Corinthians,

units.la: fia Corinthiorum inualescere coeperat, qua & mentes ipsorū & societas ecclesiastica, & Christiani nominis professio, quae vnitissimae esse debebant, studio erant sectariorum diuisae, sed qualem & ornatus & vtilitas ecclesiae poscebat, & per quam vnitas ecclesiae non scindeba tur, sed magis confirmabatur. Est autem eage mina. Primo nanque diuisa erant haec dona in seipsis, alia videlicet atque alia, hoc est, inter se varia. Deinde diuidebātur, dum alij aliud per spiritum Dei dabatur, quae distributio infrà diuisio vocatur, ubi dicit: & idem spiritus διαιρέσεις id est, diuidens peculiariter vnicuique sicut vult. Primam diuisionem recte uariationem alteram uero distributionem uocabis. Ad primam pertinet quod hic dicit: Diuisiones uero sunt charismatum, sed idem spiritus. De altera mox subiunget.
units.tr: by which both their minds and the fellowship of the Church and the profession of the Christian name, which ought to be most united, were divided by the zeal of sectarians; but of the kind which the adornment and usefulness of the Church required, and through which the unity of the Church was not torn apart but rather strengthened. Now there are two kinds of division here. For first, these gifts were diverse in themselves, one being other than another, that is, varied among themselves. Then they were divided, in that one was given to one and another to another through the Spirit of God; this distribution is called division later on, where he says: "and the same Spirit" [διαιρέσεις], that is, "dividing to each one individually as he wills." You may rightly call the first division variation and the second distribution. The first is what he means here: "Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit." He will add something about the second shortly.

units.la: 3 Tertiò partitur charismata in ministeria & operationes. Diuisiones sunt inquit, διακονιῶν. Ite: Diuisiones sunt ἐνεργημάτων. Existimo charismata esse genus, ministeria uero & operationes poni pro speciebus charismatum. Ministeria infrà circa calcem capitis recensetur, quemad modum & Eph. 4. operationes uero statim explicabit. Quod autem χαρίσματα generis loco accipio, ob id facio, quod Rom. 12. sic legimus. Habentes χαρίσματα iuxta gratiam datam nobis uaria, siue prophetiam iuxta portionem fidei, siue ministerium in administratione, &c. ubi omnino charismata partitur in prophetiā, ministeria, & quae alia ibi sequuntur. Chrysostomum eandem charisma, ministerium & operationem uocari putat. Mihi uidetur commodius, ut res distinctas generali uocabulo charismata uocari sentiamus. Ministerium charisma est, operatio charisma est. Sunt enim gratuita dona Dei. Et tamen per ministeria aliud intelligit, quàm per ἐνεργήματα, sicut in sequentibus uidebimus. Quod operationes uertim ἐνεργήματα, non satis exprimit uim uocis. Sonant enim ἐνεργήματα operationes non quasi bet, sed eas quas in nobis operatur Deus, quasi dicas, inoperationes.
units.tr: (3) Third, he divides the charismata into ministries and operations. "There are diversities," he says, "of ministries" [διακονιῶν]. Again: "there are diversities of operations" [ἐνεργημάτων]. I take charismata to be the genus, and ministries and operations to be set down as species of the charismata. Ministries are listed later, near the end of the chapter, just as in Eph. 4; operations he will explain immediately. The reason I take charismata as the genus is that in Rom. 12 we read: "Having gifts [charismata] differing according to the grace given to us, whether prophecy according to the proportion of faith, or ministry in administration," and so on, where he plainly divides the charismata into prophecy, ministries, and the others that follow there. Chrysostom thinks that charisma, ministry and operation are called by the same name. It seems more fitting to me that we understand distinct things to be called by the general word charismata. A ministry is a charisma; an operation is a charisma. For they are the free gifts of God. Yet by ministries he understands something other than by energemata [ἐνεργήματα], as we shall see in what follows. The word "operationes" does not fully express the force of the Greek word energemata. For energemata sounds not so much like operations we perform, but those which God works in us, as if you were to say "in-operations."

units.la: Quomodocunque capiamus haec uoces, satis pulchrè donorum Dei qualitatem & usum exprimunt. Quare charismata uocentur, supra diximus. Ministeriaob id uocātur, quod per illa seruitur ecclesiae ac ministratur Deo. Operationes dicuntur, quod non solum donat ea Deus, sed & operatur in nobis, & quod dedit, efficax reddit.
units.tr: However we take these words, they express very well the nature and use of God's gifts. Why they are called charismata we have said above. They are called ministries because through them the Church is served and ministered to God. They are called operations because God not only bestows them but also works them in us, and makes effective what he has given.

units.la: SED idem spiritus est, inquit. Et idem dominus, & idem Deus.) 4 Quartò. Donorum uarietatem etiam non moniti uidebant, unitatem uero largitoris non ita considerabant, quareillam inculcat propter eos, quibus dolebat, quod non eadem cum alijs, aut quod minorā quàm alij dona acceperant, quasi non ab eodem spiritu & magna & mediocria, & alia alijs dona darentur. Varietas charismatum, inquit, non est ex alio atque alio spiritu, sed prorsus eodem. Neque alterius atque alterius domini habet argumentum, quod uaria sunt ministeria in ecclesia. Est enim dominus idem, cui seruitur uario ministeriorum genere. Què admodum nō est alius atque alius ex eo statuē dus Deus quod diuisæ sunt operationes, sed unus & idem agnoscendus in omnib. In ethni cismo uariæ operationes dijs uarijs tribuebantur, aliæ Ioui, aliæ Neptuno, aliæ Saturno, aliæ Apollini, aliæ Mercurio, &c. quemadmodum in papatu uariæ uirtutes uarijs diuis asignantur. Alius præest nauigatibus in mari, alius bellige rantibus, alius agricolantibus, &c. Alius aliōs morbos curat. At Apostolus charismata ecclesiæ diuinitus collata refert nec ad diuos, nec ad angelicos spiritus, sed ad deum patrem, dominum Christum & spiritum sanctum. Sic enim placet ista de sancta diuinarum personarum Triade intelligere cum Chrysostomo & Ambrosio, cum nihil uideam quod hunc sensum impediat. Et ad Eph. 4. ubi de donis istis loquitur, cōsimiliter dicit: Vnus spiritus, unus dominus, unus Deus & pater omnium. Non est autem sentiendum quod charismata peculiariter asignat spiritui, ministeria dño Christo, & operationes Deo patri. Ex Deo patre p Christum in spiritu sancto sunt omnia dona Dei. Spiritu suo per Christum operatur in nobis sua dona Deus.
units.tr: "But it is the same Spirit," he says, "and the same Lord, and the same God." (4) Fourth: they did notice the variety of the gifts, but did not consider so carefully the unity of the giver. So he presses this point on account of those who were distressed that they did not have the same gifts as others, or that they had received smaller gifts than others, as if great and modest gifts, and different gifts to different people, were not given by the same Spirit. "The variety of charismata," he says, "does not come from one spirit different from another, but from altogether the same Spirit." Nor does the fact that there are various ministries in the Church imply a different and another Lord, for the Lord is the same, whom they serve by a varied kind of ministry. Just as God is not to be thought of as different and another because the operations are divided, but is to be acknowledged as one and the same in all. In paganism various operations were attributed to various gods: some to Jupiter, some to Neptune, some to Saturn, some to Apollo, some to Mercury, and so on; just as in papistry various virtues are assigned to various saints. One presides over sailing on the sea, another over warriors, another over farmers, and so on. One heals one disease, another another. But the Apostle refers the charismata conferred on the Church by God not to the deified or angelic spirits, but to God the Father, the Lord Christ and the Holy Spirit. For it pleases me to understand these things about the holy Trinity of the divine persons, with Chrysostom and Ambrose, since I see nothing that hinders this sense. And in Eph. 4, where he speaks of these same gifts, he says in like manner: "one Spirit, one Lord, one God and Father of all." Yet we must not think that he assigns the charismata particularly to the Spirit, the ministries to the Lord Christ, and the operations to God the Father. All the gifts of God come from God the Father through Christ in the Holy Spirit. God works his gifts in us through Christ by his own Spirit.

units.la: Et hisce uerbis fortiter perstringit eos, qui propter charismata & ministeria & energemata scindebant ecclesiam, quasi donorum uarie tas ad uarios esset referenda authores. Eiusdē spiritus, & eiusdem domini, eiusdemq; Dei ecclesia non debet scindi in partes, sed unitate in diuulsa uni suo adhærere domino spiritui ac Deo.
units.tr: And with these words he sharply rebukes those who, on account of the gifts, the ministries and the workings, were splitting the Church, as if the variety of the gifts had to be traced to various authors. The Church of the same Spirit, the same Lord and the same God must not be torn into parts; in its division it must cling to its one Spirit and God, who is also its one Lord.

units.la: IDEM Deus, inquit, efficiens omnia in omnibus.] Quāuis tres diuinitatis personas com memoret, haud tamen unitatis Dei obliuiscitur, cauens ne more ethnico tres deos constituant. Sic dicit: Idem Deus, non multi, operatur omnia in omnibus: intellige charismata, ministeria, & operationes. Neque enim loquitur de uniuersali operatione Dei, qua cœlum, terram, mare, & quę in illis sunt omnia diuina sua uirtute & efficacia conseruat, sed de ea qua operatur in electis ac fidelibus suis omnia ad salutem ipsorum facientia. Existimo Apostolū sententiam hanc accommodare causæ quam agit. Si cogitassent sectarij eundem Deum operari omnia in omnibus, haudquaquam alius se Pauli, alius Apollo, alius Cephæ esse dixissent: sed in omnibus eundem spiritum, eundem dominum, eundem Deum agnoscētes unitatem dominici corporis indiuulsam custodiuissent: Qui operabatur in Petro ad Apostolatum circumcisionis, idem operabatur, & in Paulo gentes, Gal. 2. Quorsum ergo pertinebat dicere: Ego sum Petri, ego sum Pauli, cum ambo eiusdem essent domini serui, eiusdem Dei Apostoli, & eiusdem uirtute spiritus loquerentur ac miranda facerent?
units.tr: "The same God," he says, "who works all things in all." Although he recalls the three persons of the Godhead, he does not forget the unity of God, taking care that they not set up three gods in the manner of the heathen. He says: "The same God, not many, works all things in all." Understand the gifts, the ministries and the workings. He is not speaking of God's general operation, by which he preserves heaven, earth, sea and all that is in them by his divine power and efficacy, but of that operation by which he works in his elect and faithful all things that serve their salvation. I think the Apostle adapts this statement to the case he is handling. If the sectarians had considered that the same God works all things in all, they would never have said, "I am of Paul," "I am of Apollos," "I am of Cephas." Recognising the same Spirit, the same Lord and the same God in all, they would have kept the unity of the Lord's body undivided. The one who worked in Peter for the apostleship to the circumcision worked also in Paul for the Gentiles (Gal. 2). To what purpose, then, was it to say, "I am of Peter, I am of Paul," when both were servants of the same Lord, apostles of the same God, and spoke and did wonderful things by the power of the same Spirit?

units.la: Quod si quis particulam hanc, Qui operatur omnia in omnibus generaliter de omnipotentia, uel ut sic dicam, omnificentia Dei dictum esse putat, qua omnia in omnibus suis creatis per uniuersam hanc cœli ac terræ machinam, in cœlo uidelicet, angelis, sole, luna, stellis, uentis, aere, turbine, pluuia, nubibus, niuibus, grandine, glacie, frigore, æstu, terra, plantis, arboribus, herbis, agris ac satis, mari tranquillo, mari moto, hominibus, bestijs tam marinis quā terrestribus omnipotentiæ suæ uirtutem siue insolitis, siue consuetis modis pro uoluntate sua operando declarat: caueat ne quicquam hinc colligat, quod & diuinā maiestatem dedeceat, & reliquis sacris scripturis aduersetur, quemadmodum solet homines impij, irreligiose huiusmodi sententias diuexantes, Deoq; tribuentes, quod uel Satanæ uel nostræ debetur malicię.
units.tr: But if anyone thinks that this phrase, "who works all things in all," is said generally of the omnipotence, or, if I may so put it, the all-creating power of God, by which he displays the power of his omnipotence in all his creatures throughout this whole machine of heaven and earth, that is, in the heavens, the angels, the sun, moon and stars, the winds, air, whirlwind, rain, clouds, snow, hail, ice, cold, heat, the earth, plants, trees, herbs, fields and crops, the calm sea and the stormy sea, men, and beasts both marine and terrestrial, acting at his will in unusual or customary ways, let him beware of drawing from this anything that would dishonour the divine majesty and contradict the other holy Scriptures. Impious men are accustomed to twist such statements irreligiously and to attribute them to God, when they ought to be attributed to Satan or to our own malice.

units.la: Quoniā de donis Dei loquitur Apostolus, quæ dedit & etiamnum dat ecclesiæ suæ tam generalia quam specialia, potest hęc nobis sententia ad doctrinam facere omniū utilissimā.
units.tr: Since the Apostle is speaking of the gifts of God, both general and special, which he has given and still gives to his Church, this statement can serve for teaching that is most useful to all.

units.la: Non dicit, qui magna operatur in magnis, ne mediocria in mediocribus ab operationib. Dei excludas & contemnas.
units.tr: He does not say, "He who works great things in great ones," so that you exclude and despise the ordinary things in the ordinary as not coming from God's operations.

units.la: 2 Neq; dicit, Qui insolita & miranda facit in prophetis & apostolis, ac reliquis miraculorū patratoribus, ne consueta dona non Deo, sed humanis uiribus ac studijs tribuas.
units.tr: 2 Nor does he say, "He who does unusual and wonderful things in prophets and apostles, and in the other workers of miracles," so that you do not attribute ordinary gifts to God but to human powers and efforts.

units.la: 3 Neq; dicit, Qui multa facit in multis, ne nō omnia bona ad Deum referas: sed, Qui omnia, inquit, operatur in omnibus. Ergo si quid uideris in fratribus, quod sit bonū & utile, agnosce opus Dei, siue magnum hoc sit siue modicum, siue rarum, siue usitatum, siue studio & exercitio acquisitum, siue naturaliter inditum, siue singulari spiritus sancti afflatu concessum. Nec discerne inter personas, sed in omnibus, etiam idiotis & abiectis, agnosce donum operantis omnia in omnib. Dei. Qui auro colligendo studēt, haud discernūt inter fodinas, & torrentes, & flumina, sed undecunq; offertur, agnoscunt & colligunt. Philargyris item haud refert qualis sit, à quo pecuniam accipiunt, doctus ne uel indoctus, superioris ne uel inferioris ordinis homo: sed oblatam cupide accipiūt ab omnib. & ne minutas quidem por tiunculas contemnunt. Sic cōuenit animatos nos esse erga dona Dei, quales quales sint in quibus illa operatur Deus, siue magna sint siue modica, siue consueta, siue rara.
units.tr: 3 Nor does he say, "He who does many things in many," so that you do not refer all good things to God. He says, "who works all things in all." Therefore, if you see anything in your brothers that is good and useful, recognise it as the work of God, whether it is great or small, rare or common, acquired by study and exercise, or naturally implanted, or granted by a singular breath of the Holy Spirit. Do not discriminate between persons, but in all, even the unlearned and the lowly, recognise the gift of God who works all things in all. Those who strive to gather gold do not distinguish between mines, streams and rivers, but gather wherever it is offered. Likewise the lovers of money do not care what sort of man they receive money from, whether learned or unlearned, of higher or lower rank; they eagerly accept what is offered by anyone and do not despise even the smallest coins. So we ought to be equally eager toward the gifts of God, of whatever sort they are in which God works them, whether great or small, customary or rare.

units.la: VNICVIQVE uero datur manifestatio spiritus ad utilitatem.] 5 Quinto monet etiā de ratione ac fine donorum Dei, dicens: Vnicuique uero datur manifestatio spiritus ad utilitatem. Græcè, ... id est, ad id quod cōducit. Q.d. Non ad inanem ostentationem, nō ad superbiam & insolentiam, non ad schismata & scindendum ecclesiam. Quoniam illi donis Dei ad ista abutebantur, abusus illorū uno hoc & altero uerbo notat, dum rationem ac finem eorum ponit. Vide autem quomodo hoc faciat.
units.tr: "But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good." 5 Fifthly, he also warns about the purpose and end of God's gifts, saying: "But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good." In Greek the word means that which is profitable, that is, what conduces to the good. As if he said: not for empty display, not for pride and arrogance, not for schisms or for splitting the Church. For they were abusing the gifts of God for these things, and by this one word and the next he marks their abuse, while he sets down the reason and end of the gifts. Now see how he does this.

units.la: u Primum, credunt, sed incredulis: prophetia uero A non incredulis, sed credentibus.
units.tr: First, [tongues are a sign] for believers, but for unbelievers; prophecy, however, [is a sign] not for unbelievers, but for believers.

units.la: Occurrit falsæ perfuasioni, qua multitudo persuasa erat, abunde sibi sufficere, si simpliciter crederent, etiamsi non omnia quæ in ecclesia dicebantur, intelligerent. Non est nostrum, aiebát, omnia intelligere ac scire, quod ad præpositos ac doctos ptinet: sed satis est, si simus instar puerorum, ambulemusq; simpliciter.
units.tr: He meets a false persuasion by which the multitude was convinced that it was quite sufficient for them simply to believe, even if they did not understand everything that was said in the Church. "It is not our business," they said, "to understand and know everything; that belongs to the leaders and the learned. It is enough for us to be like children and simply walk on."

units.la: Quare non est opus, ut intelligamus omnia quæ linguis in ecclesia dicuntur. Sufficit agno scere miraculosum spiritusanctí donū, illudq; cum admiratione uenerari. Ad quem modum planè in Papatu persuasum est plebeijs, scietiá rerū spiritualiū, & lectione intelligentiamq; sacrarum scripturarum cōpetere non ipsis, sed doctoribus, monachis, & sacerdotibus. Nos su mus, inquiunt, laici ac seculares, nostrum non est nisi simpliciter credere, quemadmodū crediderunt nostri maiores, ingredi ecclesiā, ibiq; orare, missam audire, & aliquid offerre.
units.tr: Therefore, they say, there is no need for us to understand everything that is spoken in tongues in the Church. It is enough to acknowledge the miraculous gift of the Holy Spirit and to revere it with wonder. In exactly this way, in the Papacy, the common people were persuaded that knowledge of spiritual things and the reading and understanding of the holy Scriptures belong not to them but to teachers, monks and priests. "We are laymen and secular people," they say; "it is not for us to do anything but believe simply, as our forefathers believed: to enter the church, pray there, hear Mass and make some offering."

units.la: Huiusmodi cogitationi occurrit Apostolus subacri correptiõe, dicēs: Fratres, ne sitis pueri sensibus, sed malitia pueri sitis. Quasi dicat: Quid hoc rei est? Dum patiēter auditis ea quæ nō intelligitis, nec ullam curam intelligentiæ, unde instituamini, impenditis: quid aliud esse uultis quàm pueri spiritualium rerum ignari? Instar puerorum ingredimini ecclesias, nec cu ratis quomodo ædificemini. Ad strepitum lin guarum incognitarum obstupescitis, & sic lo quētes admiramini: de prophetia uero, p quá intelligētes reddi possetis, nulla est cogitatio. An sic lubet ppetuo similes esse pueris? Quod si uultis esse pueri, sitis pueri, uerū malicia nō sensibus. Aliud est esse puerū sensibus, & aliud puerum esse malicia. In pueris sunt ignorantia rerum utilium, & innocentia nulla dum malitia imbuta. Quod ignorantiam attinet, non cōuenit Christiano, ut sit instar pueri, nescius eorum quæ cum primis scire debebat. Quod uero innocētis animi simplicitatem à maliciæ duplicitate alienā concernit: omnibus compe tit fidelibus, nō plebeijs modò, sed & doctoribus ac præpositis, ut similes sint pueris, alieni à malitia, nequitia, uersutia, iniquitate & iniustitia, arrogátia & superbia, &c. Magna itaque peruersitas est, puerorū uelle amplecti ac pfiteri insciitiam, in rebus salutem nostram cōcer nentibus: innocentiæ uero ac simplicitatis cā dorem auersari, & in malitia præstare adultos & exercitatos ueteratores. Sic faciebát Corin thij. Quod sensus rerū spiritualium attinebat, planè erant pueri: nec appetebant illarū scien tiā. In malitia interim nihil erant minus quàm pueri, carnales, contentiosi, uoluptuarij, arro gantes, iniurij in fratres, apud ethnicos iudi ces litigantes, scortantes, &c. Erat igitur tem pestiuum, ut hanc in illis peruersitatem correptione hac corrigeret, dicens: Fratres, ne sitis pueri sensibus, sed malitia pueri sitis, sensibus uerò perfecti sitis.
units.tr: The Apostle meets this kind of thinking with a sharp rebuke, saying: "Brothers, do not be children in your understanding, but be children in malice." As if he said: What is the meaning of this? While you patiently listen to things you do not understand, and spend no care on understanding, by which you might be instructed, what else do you wish to be but children ignorant of spiritual things? You enter the churches like children, and do not consider how you are built up. At the noise of unknown tongues you are astonished, and so speaking you wonder; but of prophecy, through which you could be made to understand, there is no thought at all. Do you wish to be always like children in this way? If you wish to be children, be children, but in malice, not in understanding. It is one thing to be a child in understanding, and another to be a child in malice. Children have ignorance of useful things, and an innocence not yet tainted by malice. As far as ignorance goes, it does not befit a Christian to be like a child, ignorant of those things which he above all ought to know. But as far as the simplicity of an innocent mind, free from the duplicity of malice, is concerned, it befits all the faithful, not only the common people but also the teachers and leaders, to be like children, far from malice, wickedness, craftiness, iniquity and injustice, arrogance and pride, and so on. Therefore it is a great perversity to wish to embrace and profess the ignorance of children in matters that concern our salvation, while shunning the candour of innocence and simplicity, and in malice to excel as adults and skilled cheats. This is what the Corinthians did. As far as the understanding of spiritual things went, they were plainly children and did not desire knowledge of them. Meanwhile in malice they were nothing less than children: fleshly, quarrelsome, given to pleasures, arrogant, wronging their brothers, going to heathen judges to litigate, committing fornication, and so on. It was therefore timely that he correct this perversity in them with this rebuke, saying: "Brothers, do not be children in understanding, but be children in malice; but in understanding be mature."

units.la: Chrysost. hanc particulā sic exposuit: Pueri sic sunt animati, ut res ludicras ac plerūq; nullius momenti admodum appetant, magníque faciant: eas uero quæ potiores sunt, ipsisq; uti liores esse possent, nec affectent, nec alicuius faciát. Consimili modo Corinthij, linguas unde nihil erat ædificationis, admirabantur, inq; precio habebát: at prophetiam interea, multo utiliore longe uilioris æstimabant. Hoc in illis reprehendens Apostolus monet, ne sensibus sint pueri, sed potius pfecti. Si respicias ea quę populariter in ecclesijs Papistarū magno serio exercentur, cum sint res nihili, planè deprehendes maximam in illis multitudinem admodū esse pueriliter animatam. Pueris facillime persuadetur, ut uera esse credant, quæ omniū sunt salsissima. Obsecro quid non puerili prorsus credulitate uulgo receptum est in Papatu? Nihil tam absurdū, nihil tam superstitiosum, nihil tam impium, nihil tam ludicrum ac ridiculum, nihil tam alienum à sanctis scripturis excogitari potuit, quod non sint maiores nostri pro uero & indubitato, proq; pio & Christiano amplexi. Pueri impensissime delectantur puppis, imagunculis qualicunq; ornatu splen didis. Sic illi nullis sumptibus pepercerút, quo omnia fierent imaginibus mortuorū sanctorū referta. Pueri quæ admirantur ac magnifaciunt, ipsis etiā parentibus suis magnifica uideri putant, eaq; illis deprædicant, ostentant, & offerunt. Planè consimili modo in Papatu fieri uidemus. Aurum, argentū, ueltes sericas, imagines, magnificas templorū structuras & quæ alia sunt eiusmodi magnifaciunt, quia arridét carni, ideoq; in illis cultū diuinum constituút, quod iudicát ea perinde atq; sibi apprime placere Deo. Pueriles omnino sunt hi sensus. Dicamus ergo illis: O fratres, ne sitis pueri sensibus, sed malitia pueri sitis: sensibus uero curate ut sitis perfecti.
units.tr: Chrysostom explained this phrase thus: children are so disposed that they desire and value playthings, which are usually of little importance at all, while they do not seek after or value the things that are more excellent and could be more useful to them. In the same way the Corinthians admired the tongues, in which there was nothing edifying, and held them in high esteem, but meanwhile they valued prophecy, which is far more useful, as something of much lower worth. The Apostle, rebuking this in them, warns them not to be children in their senses, but rather mature. If you look at the things that are carried on with great earnestness among the Papists in their churches, though they are worthless, you will plainly see that a very great multitude among them is childishly disposed. Children are most easily persuaded to believe that things are true which are the most absurd of all. Please, what has not been received among the common people in Papistry by a plainly childish credulity? Nothing so absurd, nothing so superstitious, nothing so impious, nothing so trifling and ridiculous, nothing so foreign to the holy Scriptures could be devised that our forebears did not embrace as true and beyond doubt, and as pious and Christian. Children take the greatest delight in dolls and little images, however adorned and splendid. So they spared no expense, so that everything was filled with images of dead saints. Children admire and magnify what they think splendid even to their own parents, and they proclaim these things to them, display them and offer them. We see exactly the same thing done in Papistry: they magnify gold, silver, silken garments, images, magnificent church buildings and other things of this kind, because they please the flesh, and so they establish divine worship in them, judging that these things are equally, indeed especially, pleasing to God. These feelings are wholly childish. Let us therefore say to them: "Brothers, do not be children in your senses, but be children in malice; yet in your senses take care that you are mature."

units.la: FRATRES, inquit, ne sitis pueri sensibus, sed, &c.] Quod igitur erant & esse uolebát Corinthij, reprehédit in illis Apostolus, ac dehortatur ne id esse uelint, dicens: Ne sitis pueri sensibus. Deinde quod nec erat nec esse curabát, ut id sint & esse curent, hortatur cum dicit: Sed malitia pueri sitis. Quod perinde est ac si populo Israelis stulto & insipiēti dixisset Deus, Ne sitis sapientes ad faciendum mala, sed ad benefaciendum sapientes sitis, ad mala uero facien dū sitis insipientes & inepti: ubi Hiere. 4. quæritur illos esse sapientes ad faciendū mala, bene uero facere prorsus nescire. SENSIBVS uero, inqt, perfecti sitis.] Dicēs hic, Quis nā est ex mortalib. omnibus, qui sensibus possit esse perfectus & cōsummatus? Quid enim est perfectū esse aliud, q; sic esse cōsummatum, ut nihil sit quod adhuc desiderari possit? At hoc solius est Dei. An non cap. præcedēti, ex parte nos cognoscere, & per speculū in ænigmate cernere dixit, donec ueniat tēpus illud perfectionis, in quo cognoscemus quē admodū iam cogniti sumus, & facie ad faciem cerut sapientiam ac sermonis facultatem coniun{A}gat, quo prosit ecclesiæ. Dat enim illa ad utilitatem. Non dicit simpliciter, Nam huic datur sermo: sed addit, Sapientiæ & scientiæ. Sic Christus Lucæ 21. dicit, Ego dabo vobis os & sapientiam. Est quidem sermonis facultas donū Dei humano generi peculiariter concessum, verū naturale, & studio humano excultum, ac sæculare, nisi singulari operatione spiritus ecclesiastici ac religiosi sermonis donum accesserit.
units.tr: "Brothers," he says, "do not be children in your senses, but, etc." The Apostle therefore rebukes in the Corinthians what they were and wished to be, and dissuades them from wishing to remain so, saying: "Do not be children in your senses." Then he exhorts them to become and to take care to be what they neither were nor cared to be: "But be children in malice." This is just as if God had said to the foolish and senseless people of Israel: "Do not be wise to do evil, but be wise to do good; and be foolish and unskilled to do evil," where in Jeremiah 4 it is complained that they are wise to do evil but altogether do not know how to do good. "But in your senses," he says, "be mature." Here one may ask: who among all mortals can be mature and complete in his senses? For what does being mature mean but being so completed that nothing remains which can still be desired? But this belongs to God alone. Did he not say in the preceding chapter that we know in part and see through a glass in a riddle, until that time of perfection comes, in which we shall know even as we have been known, and see face to face? Here the sense is therefore: be mature in understanding, not in the ability to speak. Yet he joins wisdom and the faculty of speech, by which it may profit the Church. For it is given for the benefit of the Church. He does not say simply, "For to this one is given speech," but adds, "of wisdom and knowledge." So Christ says in Luke 21: "I will give you a mouth and wisdom." The faculty of speech is indeed a gift of God granted especially to the human race, but it is natural, cultivated by human study, and secular, unless the gift of ecclesiastical and religious speech is added by a singular operation of the Spirit.

units.la: NAM huic quidem datur sermo sapientiæ inquit.] Supra cap.2. negauit se loqui uerbis sapientiæ, dicens: Et ego cum venirem ad uos fratres non veniebam cum eminentia sermonis aut sapientiæ, annuncians uobis testimonium Dei. Ergo ne Apostolus dono sermonis sapientiæ destituebatur, quod per spiritum Dei fidelibus ad utilitatem ecclesiæ dabatur? Nequaquam. Ponit eo loco duplicem sapientiam, humanam, & huius sæculi unam, diuinam ac cœlestem alteram. Humanam & sæcularem sibi non uindicat, uindicat uero diuinam ac cœlestem, cum dicit: Et sermo meus, & prædicatio mea non erat in persuasorijs humanæ sapientiæ uerbis, sed in manifestatione spiritus ac potentiæ, ut fides uestra non sit in sapientia hominum, sed in potentia Dei. Porro sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos, sapientiam autem non sæculi huius, neque principum sæculi huius qui abolentur: sed loquimur sapientiā Dei in mysterio, quæ est recondita, &c. De hac sapientia intelligit, cum hic dicit: Nam huic datur sermo sapientiæ. {B}
units.tr: "For to one indeed is given the word of wisdom," he says. In chapter 2 above he denied that he spoke in words of wisdom, saying: "And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come with excellence of speech or wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of God." Was the Apostle therefore deprived of the gift of the word of wisdom, which was given to the faithful through the Spirit of God for the benefit of the Church? By no means. In that place he sets out a twofold wisdom: one human and of this world, the other divine and heavenly. He does not claim for himself the human and secular wisdom, but he does claim the divine and heavenly, when he says: "And my word and my preaching were not in the persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith may not rest in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God." Moreover, we speak wisdom among the mature, but not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are brought to nothing; but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which is hidden, etc. It is of this wisdom that he speaks when here he says: "For to one is given the word of wisdom."

units.la: PER spiritum dicit.] Dixit Deum operari omnia in omnib. Operatur omnia per spiritū suum in cordibus credentium. Non est autem ut quoniam hic dicit: Nam huic datur per spiritum sermo sapientiæ, spiritum sanctum quasi organum Dei esse intelligamus, per quod operetur, quodque non eiusdē sit cum ipso ac uerbo eius diuinitatis. Etenim uocula hæc, Per, utriq; & Deo patri ac uerbo eius datur. De Deo patre, Rom.11. per illum, inquit, sunt omnia. De Christo supra 8. per quem omnia, inquit, & nos per ipsum, & Ebr.1. per quem fecit & sæcula. Cum Deus aliquid operatur per uerbum ac spiritum suum, operatur per seipsum.
units.tr: "Through the Spirit," he says. He said that God works all things in all. He works all things through his Spirit in the hearts of believers. Yet we must not take it, because he here says, "For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom," that the Holy Spirit is to be understood as an instrument of God through which he works, and that he is not of the same divinity as himself and his Word. For this little word "through" is applied both to God the Father and to his Word. Of God the Father, Romans 11: "from him," he says, "are all things." Of Christ, above in chapter 8: "through whom are all things, and we through him"; and Hebrews 1: "through whom he also made the ages." When God works something through his Word and Spirit, he works through himself.

units.la: ALII uero, inquit, sermo scientiæ.] Apparet hic separari scientiam à sapientia, quasi ab illa diuersam, cum distinctim loquitur Apostolus, dicens: Alij datur sermo sapientiæ, alij sermo scientiæ. Quæritur ergo quo sensu à se invicem distinguantur. Fere in hoc concordant, quod scientia minor fit, sapientia maior: quodq; inuenias scientem, qui tamen non fit sapiens, sapientem uero qui non fit sciens haud ita. Sane Iob 28. pro eodem ponuntur, ubi sic legimus, [Hebrew] licet Augustinus distinguat. Vbi tamen inspicio scripta huius Apostoli, inuenio illū duas hasce uoces sapientiam & scientiam aliquando eodem, nonnunquam discreto ponere sensu. Eodem, ut Rom.11. cum dicit: O profunditatem diuitiarum, & sapientiæ & scientiæ Dei. Et Col.1. In quo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ & scientiæ Dei, Eph.1. coniungit sapientiam & prudentiam. i. [Greek]. Et Col.1. [Greek]. i. sapientiam & intelligentiam spiritualem, & refert ad sapientiam & intelligentiam crucis Christi: discreto uero, hoc præsenti loco. Omnino uocem sapientiæ, Ephes.3. refert ad cognitionem mysterij Christi, quemad modum & Coloss. 1. Ab hac licet distinguere scientiam hoc pacto, ut referamus eam ad uariarum rerum spiritualium cognitionem, qualis ea est, de quæ supra cap.8. dixit: Ceterum de ijs quæ simulacris immolatur, scimus, quod omnes scientiam habemus, scientia inflat, charitas uero ædificat. Item, scimus nihil esse idolum in mundo, & quod nullus sit Deus alius nisi unus. Sic inuenias qui sciat unum esse Deum, sanctæ Triadis tamen mysterium nesciat: qui sciunt Christum esse crucifixum, mysterium crucis tamen ignorent. Scientiam illi habent, sapientiam uero Dei non habent, quæ intelligentia est mysterij Christi ab æterno abscondi ti. Hanc tñ duarum istarum uocum discretionē uideo haud constanter seruari ab Apostolo. Nam Philip.3. scientiam Iesu Christi uocat, quod alias uocat sapientiam, quemadmodum in uocibus fieri solet, quæ sensu nonnihil habet affinitatis. De discrimine sapientiæ, intelligentiæ, ac scientiæ nonnulla diximus in Coment. nostris super Esaiam cap.11. Non placet quod Lyranus sic diuidit, ut sapientia sit diuinarum, scientia humanarum rerum. Augustinum sequutus uidetur, cuius sententiam uide de Trinit.lib.12.cap.14.&15.
units.tr: "But to another," he says, "the word of knowledge." Here knowledge seems to be separated from wisdom, as if it were different from it, since the Apostle speaks distinctly, saying: "To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge." The question therefore is in what sense they are distinguished from each other. They generally agree in this, that knowledge is the lesser and wisdom the greater; and that you may find one who knows but is not wise, but a wise man who does not know, is not so. Indeed in Job 28 they are put for the same thing, where we read thus, [Hebrew], although Augustine distinguishes them. Yet when I examine the writings of this Apostle, I find that he sometimes puts these two words, wisdom and knowledge, in the same sense, and sometimes in a distinct sense. In the same sense, as in Romans 11, when he says: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God." And in Colossians 1: "In whom are all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God." Ephesians 1 joins wisdom and prudence, [Greek]. And Colossians 1 [Greek], that is, wisdom and spiritual understanding, and he refers them to the wisdom and understanding of the cross of Christ. In a distinct sense, in the present passage. Ephesians 3 refers the word wisdom altogether to the knowledge of the mystery of Christ, just as Colossians 1 does. From this one may distinguish knowledge in this way, by referring it to the knowledge of various spiritual things, such as he spoke of in chapter 8 above: "Now concerning things offered to idols, we know that we all have knowledge; knowledge puffs up, but love builds up." Likewise: "We know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no other God but one." So you may find someone who knows that God is one, yet is ignorant of the mystery of the holy Trinity; who knows that Christ was crucified, yet is ignorant of the mystery of the cross. They have knowledge, but do not have the wisdom of God, which is the understanding of the mystery of Christ hidden from eternity. Yet I see that this distinction between the two words is not consistently kept by the Apostle. For in Philippians 3 he calls it the knowledge of Jesus Christ, which elsewhere he calls wisdom, as is usual with words that have some affinity in meaning. I have said something about the distinction between wisdom, understanding and knowledge in my commentaries on Isaiah chapter 11. It does not please me that Lyra divides them so that wisdom is of divine things and knowledge of human things. He seems to follow Augustine, whose opinion see in On the Trinity, book 12, chapters 14 and 15.

units.la: SECVNDVM eundem spiritum, inquit.] Græcè est, [Greek]. Quoniam uocula, [Greek], nonnunquam à Græcis pro Dia. i. Per, ponì constat, meo iudicio, poterat hic uerti, Per eundem spiritum, ne rudis lector in uoce, secūdum, hæsitet. Quoniam uero omnes communiter reddunt, secundum eundem spiritum, ui sum est eam uersionem retinere. Subintelligedum autem est aliquid, utpote donum, secundum donum eiusdem spiritus. Cum dicimus: Euangelium secundum Matthæum, intelligimus Euangelium quod secundum historiam à Matthæo scriptam habemus. Sic datur non nullis sermo scientiæ secundum eundem spiritum, id est secundum donum ac gratiam eiusdem spiritus.
units.tr: "According to the same Spirit," he says. The Greek is [Greek]. Since the little word [Greek] is sometimes put by the Greeks for διά, that is, "through," I think it could have been rendered here as "Through the same Spirit," so that the unlearned reader would not stumble over the word "according to." But since everyone commonly renders it "according to the same Spirit," it is better to keep that translation. Something must be understood, namely "gift": according to the gift of the same Spirit. When we say "the Gospel according to Matthew," we mean the Gospel which we have as written by Matthew in the narrative. So the word of knowledge is given to some according to the same Spirit, that is, according to the gift and grace of the same Spirit.

units.la: ALII uero fides, inquit, per eundē spiritū.] Non loquitur de fide iustificāte, quæ communis est fidelib. omnib. sine qua Deo placere salua riq; non possumus, sed de fide signorum ac miraculorū, qd & Chrysost. & Hier. agnoscūt, quamuis Ambros. aliud sentit. Germanus interpres hoc scholion adiecit: Glauben beuuei-sen, die im offentlich bekennen mitt uuorten und mitt uuercken, uuie die marterer. Sequutus est Ambrosium. Ipsa distributio charismatum istorum ferre non potest, ut de fide iustificante intelligmus. Spiritus Dei in ecclesia electorum nō
units.tr: "But to another faith," he says, "through the same Spirit." He is not speaking of justifying faith, which is common to all believers and without which we cannot please God or be saved, but of the faith of signs and miracles. Chrysostom and Jerome recognise this, although Ambrose thinks otherwise. The German translator added this gloss: Glauben beweisen, die es öffentlich bekennen mit Worten und mit Werken, wie die Märtyrer. He followed Ambrose. The very distribution of these gifts cannot allow us to understand it of justifying faith. The Spirit of God is not fulfilled in the church of the elect in those things which are said: "Every good thing is the more divine the more it is shared." Since, therefore, those who received these gifts did not receive them so much for their own sake as for the sake of their brothers, and those to whom they were given made a use of them quite foreign to their purpose and end, they claimed them for themselves as if they were their own, displayed them vainly, did not value them at all, and split the church.

units.la: {A}impletur in illis quod dicitur: Omne bonum tanto diuinius, quanto communius. Cum ergo non tam sua quàm fratrum gratia charisma ta hæc acciperent, quibus ea dabantur, admodum alienum erat ab illorum usu, ratione ac fine, quod illa sibijpsis veluti propria uindicabát, inaniter ostentabant, non habentes flocci faciebant, & ecclesiam scindebant.
units.tr: For to one, indeed, is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith through the same Spirit; to another the gifts of healings through the same Spirit; to another the working of powers; to another prophecy; to another the discerning of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues. But all these things one and the same Spirit works, dividing to each one individually as he wills.

units.la: Nā huic quidem per spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ, alij uero sermo scientiæ secundum eundem spiritum, alij uero fides per eúdem spiritum, alij uero dona sanationum per eundem spiritum, alij uero efficaciæ potentiarũ, alij uero prophetia, alij uero discretiones spirituum, alij uero genera linguarum, alij uero interpretatio linguarum. Sed omnia hæc efficit unus ille, &idem spiritus diuidès peculiariter unicuiq; sicuti uult.
units.tr: For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another the gifts of healing by the same Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discerning of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. But all these things one and the same Spirit works, dividing to each one separately as he wills.

units.la: 6 Sexto. Declarat quod dixit: Vnicuique uero datur manifestatio spiritus, distributionem donorum Dei recensens. Recèfet autè non omnia, sed ea tantũ quæ nota erant Corinthijs, & quorum illi gratia scindebantur, utpote, sermonem sapientiæ, sermonem scientiæ, fidem, dona sanationum, efficaciá potentiarum, prophetiam, discretionem spirituum, genera linguarum, & interpretationem linguarum. {B}Per hæc manifestabatur uirtus spiritus Dei, quem accipiebant in Christum credentes.
units.tr: 6 Sixth. He explains what he said: "But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit," reciting the distribution of God's gifts. He does not recite all of them, but only those that were known to the Corinthians, and over which they were splitting into factions, namely the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, faith, the gifts of healing, the working of miracles, prophecy, the discerning of spirits, various kinds of tongues, and the interpretation of tongues. {B} Through these the power of the Spirit of God was made manifest, which those who believed in Christ received.

units.la: Nam huic quidem, inquit, per spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ, alij uero sermo scientiæ secundum eundem spiritum. Non dicit, Nam huic quidem datur sapientia, alij uero scientia: sed, nam huic quidem datur sermo sapientiæ, alij uero sermo scientiæ. Loquitur enim de dono sermonis qui talis fit, ut per illum spiritus Dei, spiritus sapientiæ & scientiæ manifestetur. Sapientia & scientia, nisi sermone & factis exprimantur, manifestatio spiritus uocari non possunt. At in eo est Apostolus, ut distributione hac declaret, quomodo unicuiq; detur manifestatio spiritus, idque ad utilitatem ecclesiæ. Quare nõ simpliciter dicit, Nam huic quidem datur sapietia, alij uero scientia: sed, Nam huic quidem datur sermo sapietiæ, alij uero sermo scientiæ. Inuenias sapientem & scientem, qui tamen dono sermonis destitutus nesciat proferre in lucem quæ sapit & cognouit. De hoc dici non potest, quod per dona sapietiæ & scientiæ manifestationem spiritus acceperit. Quare admodum inconsulto fieri uidemus, ut præficiantur ecclesijs homines, qui licet alius erudi ditionis, alius probitatis nomine commendari queant, sermonis tamè dono ad munus docendi necessario destituuntur. Nec consulitur ecclesijs, ubi loquaculi ac dicaculi nulla sapientia ac scientia prædití pastoratus munere funguntur, quibus multa quidem est uerborum facultas, nihil uero sapientiæ ac scientiæ. Quare spiritus sanctus hæc sua dona sic dispensat, ut sa-
units.tr: For to one, he says, is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit. He does not say, "For to one is given wisdom, to another knowledge," but "to one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge." For he speaks of the gift of speech, which is of such a kind that through it the Spirit of God, the Spirit of wisdom and knowledge, is made manifest. Wisdom and knowledge cannot be called a manifestation of the Spirit unless they are expressed in speech and deeds. Now the Apostle's aim in this distribution is to show how the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each one, and that for the benefit of the Church. Therefore he does not simply say, "For to one is given wisdom, to another knowledge," but "to one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge." You may find a man who is wise and learned, yet lacking the gift of speech, and unable to bring into the light what he knows and understands. Of such a man it cannot be said that he has received the manifestation of the Spirit through the gifts of wisdom and knowledge. Hence we see that it is very unwise that men be placed over churches who, although they may be commended for their learning or for their integrity, are nonetheless necessarily lacking the gift of speech needed for the office of teaching. Nor is the Church well served when chatterers and braggarts, endowed with no wisdom or knowledge, discharge the pastoral office, men who have much facility with words but nothing of wisdom and knowledge. Therefore the Holy Spirit so dispenses these his gifts that...

units.la: Primum, non dicit simpliciter, Datur autè: sed unicuiq; uero datur manifestatio spiritus ad utilitatem. Potest uocula hæc, Vnicuique, bifariam accipi. Vel uniuersaliter de omnibus ... Tertio. AD utilitatem inquit. Non addit, Ipsius, sed simpliciter dicit, ad utilitatem. Neque enim de priuata eorum utilitate loquitur, quibus dona hæc conferebantur, sed magis de ea quæ ex illis ad ædificationem ecclesiæ cedebat.
units.tr: First, he does not say simply, "But it is given," but "to each one, however, is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the benefit." This little word "each one" can be taken in two ways: either universally, of all... Third. "For the benefit," he says. He does not add "of himself" but simply says "for the benefit." For he is not speaking of the private advantage of those to whom these gifts were conferred, but rather of that which came from them to the building up of the Church.

units.la: uarijs linguis loquentes intelligebant, sed & ad utilitatem ecclesiæ quæ per illos dicebátur exponebant ac declarabant. Et donum hoc sic est necessarium, ut nolit Apostolus sine illo linguis quicquam dici in ecclesia.
units.tr: speaking in various tongues, they understood, and they also explained and made clear, for the benefit of the Church, what was being said through them. And this gift is so necessary that the Apostle would not have anything said in tongues in the Church without it.

units.la: SED omnia hęc, inquit, efficit unus ille & idem spiritus.] Supra dixit: Idem est Deus, qui efficit omnia in omnib. Hic eorundem operationem tribuit spiritui. Deinde postquàm aliquoties dixit per spiritum dari hæc charismata, iam dicit illum hęc omnia efficere. Sic idem illi quod Deo datur opus. Tertiò, qd' supra dixit: qui operatur omnia in omnib. hic dicit cū specificatione, sed omnia hæc efficit spiritus: unde admonemur illud supra quoq; de donis istis esse intelligendum. Quarto, non simpliciter dicit, Sed omnia hæc efficit spiritus: sed unus ille & idē spiritus: quèadmodum & illud, peúdem spiritum iam aliquoties inculcauit, & quod supra dixit: Diuisiones uero donorum sunt, sed idē spiritus, etiā atq; etiā considerandū esse monuit, quo studia sectarum in ecclesia Corinthiorū extingueret, & cōcordiā redaccederet.
units.tr: But all these things, he says, one and the same Spirit works. Above he said: "It is the same God who works all things in all." Here he attributes the same working to the Spirit. Then, after saying several times that these gifts are given through the Spirit, he now says that the Spirit works all of them. Thus the same work is ascribed to the Spirit that is ascribed to God. Thirdly, what he said above, "who works all things in all," he here says with a specification: "but all these things the Spirit works." Whence we are reminded that the earlier statement too is to be understood of these gifts. Fourthly, he does not simply say, "But all these things the Spirit works," but "one and the same Spirit," just as he has already repeatedly stressed "the same Spirit," and as he said above, "there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit." He warns us again and again that this must be considered, so as to extinguish the party spirit in the Corinthian Church and to bring back concord.

units.la: DIVIDENS, inquit, peculiariter unicuiq; sicuti uult. ] De diuisione diximus supra. Diui dens unicuiq;, inquit, peculiariter. Græcè est ἰδίως, quod uerti potest separata, propria, peculiaria: uel aduerbialiter, separatim, proprie, peculiariter. Quod toties uocibus istis ἰδίως & ἄλλῳ expressit, id hac quoq; uocula inculcat, uideli cet, sic diuidi charismata ista inter fideles, ut alij aliud quasi peculiare ac separatum detur, qd' B cæteris non detur. Hinc tñ non est colligendū, apostolis quoque nónisi unum & alterum donorum istorum fuisse concessum. Quo magis erat illis laborandum in opere Apostolatus, hoc pluribus donis spiritus opus habebant.
units.tr: "Dividing," he says, "to each one separately as he wills." We spoke of the division above. "Dividing to each one," he says, "separately." The Greek is [ἰδίως], which may be rendered separately, individually, peculiarly; or adverbially, apart, particularly, separately. What he expressed so often with the words [ἰδίως] and [ἄλλῳ], he here reinforces with this little word, namely that these gifts are so divided among the faithful that one receives one thing as a special and separate portion, which is not given to the others. Yet it must not be inferred from this that even the apostles received only one or two of these gifts. The more laborious the apostolic work was for them, the more of the gifts of the Spirit they needed.

units.la: Illud, Sicuti uult, tria complectitur, ad liberà hanc diuisionem charismatum spiritus pertinetia. Primum, cui secundum quod nam donum: tertium, quantum, uel cum qua mensura. Diui dit spiritus dona sua libera dispensatione, pro sua uoluntate, teneq; ꝓmiscue omnib. sed quibus ipse uoluerit: neq; singulis idem, sed alij aliud, sicuti uult: neq; eadem singulis mensura, sed alij plus, alij minus sicuti uult. Hæc tria una est uocula ὡς cōplexus Apostolus. Si dixeris, quare alijs diuidat, alijs non diuidat, quare aliud & alij, & quare alij plus & alij minus, in promptu respondetur: Diuidit libere & gratuito sua dona, non aliena, sicuti uult, ad proprij non ad alieni arbitrij sententiam. Consimili modo & Ebr.2. legimus: Quæ salus cum primum enarrari coepissset per ipsum dñm, ab ijs q audierat, in nos confirmata fuit, attestāte Deo & signis & prodigijs simul, uarijsq; potentijs & spiritussanĉti distributionib. iuxta ipsius uoluntatem. Sic aufert omnem contentionis occasionem, quæ propter donorum istorum diuisionem inter Corinthios orta fuerat, ne quis quam in posterum queritetur, quare non eodē cum alijs dono præditus sit, uel quare non tantum acceperit, quantum alius. Sic est, inquit,
units.tr: The phrase "as he wills" embraces three things pertaining to this free division of the Spirit's gifts. First, to whom; second, which gift; third, how much, or with what measure. The Spirit distributes his gifts by free dispensation, according to his own will, and does not give them indiscriminately to all, but to those whom he wishes; nor the same to each, but one thing to one and another to another, as he wills; nor the same measure to each, but more to one and less to another, as he wills. The Apostle has comprehended these three things in one little word, [ὡς]. If you ask why he divides to some and not to others, why one thing to one and another to another, and why more to some and less to others, the answer is ready: he divides his own gifts freely and graciously, as he wills, according to his own judgment and not another's. In a similar way we read in Hebrews 2: "Which salvation, when it had first begun to be spoken by the Lord himself, was confirmed to us by those who heard him, God also bearing witness with signs and wonders and various powers, and with distributions of the Holy Spirit, according to his own will." Thus he removes every occasion of strife which had arisen among the Corinthians on account of the division of these gifts, so that no one hereafter may complain why he does not have the same gift as another, or why he has not received as much as another. "So it is," he says,
