units.la: A uoluntas spiritus. Qui libere nemini debes donat, ut uult donat, nec est ob hác diuisionis suę libertatem à quoquam in ius uocandus. Obiter etiam obserua diuinitatis argumentum in eo quod spiritui dat Apostolus operationem in electis pro ipsius uoluntate liberam, q nulli potest competere creaturæ. Verum de diuinitate spiritussancti uide quæ Petrus Martyr hoc loco diligenter congesit.
units.tr: The will of the Spirit. He gives freely to no one who is in debt to him, distributing as he wills, and by reason of this freedom in dividing he is not to be summoned to account by anyone. Note in passing the argument for his divinity in the fact that the Apostle attributes to the Spirit an operation in the elect which is free and according to his own will, which cannot belong to any creature. On the divinity of the Holy Spirit, see what Peter Martyr has carefully gathered together at this point.

units.la: Quemadmodum enim corpus unū est, & membra habet multa, omnia uero membra corporis unius, multa cum sint, unum sunt corpus: sic & Christus. Etenim per unum spiritum nos omnes in unū corpus baptizati sumus, siue Iudæi siue Græci, siue serui siue liberi, & omnes unum spiritum hausimus.
units.tr: For as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the one body, though many, are one body: so also is Christ. For by one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free, and we have all drunk of one Spirit.

units.la: Similitudine declarat, qd' de diuisione uariorum charismatū, & unitate diuidētis ea spiritus dixit. Adducit aūt similitudinem omniū notisimam, qua gratiæ conditione ex ipsa natura constitutione, eaq; non ex reb. abstrusis, sed ex nobisipsis desumpta, declarat. Non inducit interni nostri hominis cum uarijs suis affectibus, sed externi corporis uidelicet, qualitatem ac constitutionem, quam nemo mortalium, nisi mente motus, ignorare potest. Quèadmodum enim corpus, inquit, sic & Christus intellige, comparatus est. Corpus quomodo? Multa sunt in humano corpore ad constitutionem illius pertinētia, utpote quod compositum est ex carne & spiritu, quod caro est é carne, spiritus de cœlo, caro alterius naturę quam spiritus. caro non uiuificat, sed spiritu uiuificatur: caro opus habet alimentis ac fomentis, & quæ alia sunt huiusmodi. Nihil horum adducit, quia ad propositum non faciebant', sed adducit hæc duo quod corpus uidelicet unū est in se, & quod multa habet ac uaria membra quibus constat. Hæc enim pulchre faciunt ad declarationem causæ in qua uersatur. Ad Rom. ca.12. eodem est corporis humani simili ad idē propositum usus, ubi tria de illo ponit. Primū, quod sit unum: secundum, quod habeat multa membra: tertium, quod non habeant eundem omnia membra actum in corpore, ubi pleraq; huc pertinentia diximus.
units.tr: By this similitude he illustrates what he has said about the division of the various gifts and about the unity of the Spirit who divides them. He brings in a very well-known comparison, drawn not from obscure matters but from ourselves, to explain the condition of grace from the constitution of nature itself. He does not introduce the inner man with his various affections, but the outer body, namely its quality and make-up, which no mortal, unless he is quite out of his mind, can fail to know. "Just as the body," he says, "so also understand Christ to be compared." The body in what way? Many things in the human body belong to its constitution: it is composed of flesh and spirit; the flesh is of the flesh, the spirit from heaven; the flesh is of a different nature from the spirit; the flesh does not give life, but is quickened by the spirit; the flesh needs food and nourishment, and other things of this kind. He brings in none of these, because they did not bear on his purpose, but he brings in these two: that the body is one in itself, and that it has many and various members of which it consists. For these serve admirably to illustrate the matter under discussion. In Romans 12 he uses the same likeness of the human body for the same purpose, where he makes three statements about it: first, that it is one; second, that it has many members; third, that not all the members have the same function in the body. On this, where most of the relevant points were discussed, we have said enough.

units.la: QVEMADMODVM enim corpus, inqt. ] Simpliciter quidem dicit, Quemadmodū corpus, sic & Christus: uerum ex tribus patet, & se quenti declaratione, loqui ipsum neq; de corpore quod una specie continetur, quale est lapis & lignum, &c. neq; de eo quod constat ἐκ ἀνθρώπων, id est, discretis & distantib. uni nomini subiectis, quale est, exercitus, ciuitas, classis: neq; de eo quod est ἐκ συνηλυμένων, id est, ex cō iunctis pluribus & inter se cohærentib. ut est domus, nauis, &c. sed de eo quod uocant ἁρμονία ἐν συμφύσει, id est, unitum & congenitū, qua le est corpus animale, siue hominum, siue bestiarum, quod est & animatum, & ex multis diuer sisq; dat alij fidem in Christum, alij spem, alij charitatem: sed dat omnibus ut credant in Christũ, sperent & expectent futuram vitā, ac diligant fratres. Licet ista det cum mensura, alij plus, alij minus, dat tū quantum necesse est singulis. At hanc fidem, quæ hic inter charismata ponitur, non dat omnib. sed quibusdam tātum. Neque enim ad salutem sic est necessaria, ut qui eam non habet, saluari nequeat. De hac fide, si cui lubet, Com. nostros in Mat. uideat cap.17.
units.tr: "For as the body..." He says simply, "as the body, so also Christ," but from three things, and from the explanation that follows, it is clear that he is speaking neither of a body held together by one kind of substance, such as a stone or a piece of wood, nor of that which is made up of separate and distinct parts subject to one name, such as an army, a city, or a fleet, nor of that which is made up of many things joined together and cohering, such as a house or a ship; but he speaks of that which the Greeks call [harmonia en symphysei], that is, united and innate, such as an animal body, whether of men or of beasts, which is both animated and made up of many diverse parts. To one he gives faith in Christ, to another hope, to another love; but he gives to all that they believe in Christ, hope and look for the life to come, and love the brethren. Although he gives these in measure, more to some and less to others, yet he gives to each as much as is necessary. But this faith, which is listed here among the gifts, he does not give to all but only to some. For it is not so necessary for salvation that one who does not have it cannot be saved. On this faith, if anyone wishes, let him look at our Commentaries on Matthew, chapter 17.

units.la: ALII uero dona sanationum, inquit, per eundem spiritum.] Loquitur de miraculosa curatione morborū, quam in se credetib. Christus promisit Marci ult. dicēs, Signa aut eos qui in me credunt, hæc sequetur, &c. super ægros manus imponent, & bene habebunt. Per hanc Apostoli plurimum ad propagandum fidem non minis Christi profecerunt, quod uidere est in historia claudi illius, quæ Petrus ante fores templi sedentem in pedes suos erexit ac sanitati restituit. Act.3. Quoniam autem multa sunt morborum genera, pluraliter loquitur, dicens: Alij uero dona sanationum. Comprehendit. n. curationes non modo lecto decumbentium paralyticorum & febricitantium: sed & cæcorū, surdorum, mutorum, claudorum, &c. usus isto rum charismatum eos potissimum concernebat, qui ad fidem Christi nondum accesserant, quo & potentiam Dei per miraculosam operationem, & beneficentiam diuinam in curationem sibijpsorum agnoscentes ad credendum Euangelio permouerentur, cuius confirmandi gratia signa huiusmodi ædebantur.
units.tr: "And to others the gifts of healings, by the same Spirit." He speaks of the miraculous curing of diseases, which Christ promised to those who believe in him, saying in the last chapter of Mark: "And these signs shall follow those who believe in me... they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover." Through this the Apostles greatly advanced the spreading of the faith of Christ, as can be seen in the story of that lame man whom Peter raised to his feet and restored to health as he sat before the gate of the temple, Acts 3. Since there are many kinds of diseases, he speaks in the plural, saying "to others the gifts of healings." For he includes the healing not only of paralytics and the feverish who lay in bed, but also of the blind, the deaf, the dumb, the lame, and so on. The use of these gifts chiefly concerned those who had not yet come to the faith of Christ, so that by recognizing the power of God in the miraculous operation, and the divine kindness in their own healing, they might be moved to believe the Gospel, for the confirmation of which such signs were performed.

units.la: ALII uero efficaciæ potentiarum, inquit.] Vulgata habet, alij operatio uirtutum. Græcè est pluraliter ἐνεργήματα, i. operationes. Et quoniam non habetur ἀρίστων, sed δυνάμεων, uertit Erasm. non uirtutum, sed potentiarum, ne quis imperitus de uirtutib. philosophicis intelligat. Euangelicæ literæ signa quæ Christus faciebat sanando ægrotos ac male habentes, expellendo dæmones, mortuos excitando, cæcos illuminādo, &c. communi uocabulo δυνάμεις, i. potentias ac uirtutes uocant. Quare laboratur à nonnullis, quomodo Apostolus hoc loco ἐνεργήματα δυνάμεων separet à donis sanationū, & ex genere speciem faciat. Alij exponunt de expulsionibus dæmonum, & excitatione mortuorū, quod ad hoc genus miraculosæ operationis plusculum requiratur, puto singularis potētię, qua & dæmonum & mortis uires reprimātur. Sic exponit Hiero. dicens: Opus uirtutis est, dæmoia eijcere, uel mortuos suscitare. Et Ambros. eiectionem dæmonum intelligit, cui tamen addit facultatem signa faciendi, atque ita speciem ad genus reducit. Chrysost. & Theophylactus referunt ad potentiam puniędi peccantes, quemadmodum Petrus Ananiam ac Sapphiram neci dedit, & Paulus Elymam magum excæcauit. Lyranus exponit de signis, quæ nihil aliud faciunt quàm quod diuinam potentiam ostendunt, ut si sol in cœlo sistatur, uel tale aliquid fiat. Et forsan hüc imitatus est Germanicus interpres, qui particulam hanc sic uertit, eynem anderen uuunder zuo thuon. i. miracula faciendi. Sane, ut quid mihi uideatur dicam, apparet Apostolum hac distinctione sanationum & potentiarum omnia signa mirabilium operum complecti uoluisse, quæ spiritus Dei per fideles tum operabatur: sic ut sanationes ad morbidorum restitutionem, potentias ue ro ad reliqua signa referat, quibus uel mortui excitabantur, uel dæmonia fugabantur, uel alia eiusmodi fiebant. Hinc tamen non sequitur, uocem δυνάμεων perpetuo esse ad has signorum species referendam, cum ut supra dixi, frequenter in genere omnibus signis, quæ à Christo fiebant, accommodetur, quale est illud Lucæ 6. Et δυνάμεως de illo exibat & sanabat omnes.
units.tr: "And to others the workings of powers," he says. The Vulgate has "to others the operation of virtues." In Greek the word is in the plural, [energēmata], that is, operations. And since the Greek does not read [ἀρίστων] but [δυνάμεων], Erasmus translated not "virtues" but "powers," lest some unlearned reader understand philosophical virtues. The Gospel writings call the signs which Christ did, in healing the sick and those who were ill, in casting out demons, raising the dead, giving sight to the blind, and so on, by the common name [dynameis], that is, powers and mighty works. Therefore some labour over how the Apostle here separates [energēmata dynameōn] from the gifts of healings and makes a species out of a genus. Others explain it of the casting out of demons and the raising of the dead, since this kind of miraculous operation requires something further, I think a singular power by which the powers of both demons and death are restrained. Jerome explains it thus: "It is a work of power to cast out demons or raise the dead." Ambrose understands it of the casting out of demons, to which however he adds the faculty of working signs, and so reduces the species to the genus. Chrysostom and Theophylact refer it to the power of punishing sinners, as Peter put Ananias and Sapphira to death, and Paul struck the sorcerer Elymas blind. Lyra explains it of signs which do nothing more than show the divine power, such as if the sun were stopped in the sky, or something of that sort. And perhaps the German translator followed this, who renders the phrase thus: "to do another miracle," that is, to work miracles. Indeed, to say what seems to me: it appears that by this distinction between healings and powers the Apostle meant to embrace all the signs of wonderful works which the Spirit of God then performed through the faithful, so that he refers the healings to the restoration of the sick, but the powers to the remaining signs, by which the dead were raised, or demons were driven out, or other things of this kind were done. Yet it does not follow from this that the word [dynameōn] must always be referred to these kinds of signs, since, as I said above, it is often applied in general to all the signs which Christ performed, as in Luke 6: "And power went out from him and healed all."

units.la: ALII uero prophetia, inquit.] Prophetiam cap. præcedenti diximus in ecclesia fuisse duplicem, unam generaliorem, qua plerique docendo prædicabant in cœtu fidelium: alteram specialiorem, qua pauci aliquot futura uaticinando prædicebant ecclesijs. De hoc charisma te cap.14. plura uidebimus, quare non est, ut hic plura de illo dicamus.
units.tr: "And to others prophecy," he says. In the preceding chapter we said that there were two kinds of prophecy in the Church: one more general, by which most men preached by teaching in the assembly of the faithful; the other more special, by which a few foretold future events by prophesying to the churches. We shall see more about this gift in chapter 14, so there is no need to say more about it here.

units.la: ALII uero discretiones spirituum, inquit.] Discernere spiritus, est homines spiritum uel reuelationem singularem profitētes dijudicare, acceptandi ne sint uel fugiendi. Et intelligendum est hoc donum de non generali quæ omnib. fidelibus Mat.7. proponitur: sed speciali ac miraculosa prudentia per spiritum Dei accepta, qua Apostoli Satanæ in Apostolos Christi conuersi dinoscuntur, & à ueris separantur. Sic spiritum Simonis Magi cognoscebat Petrus, & reprobabat: & spiritum puellę, quę Philippis post Apostolos ac discipulos Christi multis diebus clamabat: Isti homines sunt servi Dei excelsi, qui annunciant uobis uiam salutis, Paulus cognoscebat & expellebat. Donum hoc uehementer erat ecclesiæ necessarium, ad cognoscendum Satanam in angelum lucis transformatum, non modo apostolorum, sed & emergentis Antichristi temporibus, cuius signa & prodigia haudquaquam inualuissent, nisi charisma hoc discernendorum spirituum propter peccata nostra fuisset è medio sublatum.
units.tr: "And to others the discerning of spirits," he says. To discern spirits is to judge men who profess a spirit or a special revelation, whether they are to be accepted or avoided. And this gift must be understood not as the general one which is set before all the faithful in Matthew 7, but as a special and miraculous prudence received through the Spirit of God, by which the Apostles recognized those who had turned from Christ's Apostles to Satan and separated them from the true ones. Thus Peter recognized and rejected the spirit of Simon Magus; and Paul recognized and cast out the spirit of the slave girl at Philippi who for many days after the Apostles and disciples of Christ cried out: "These men are servants of the most high God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation." This gift was greatly necessary to the Church, for recognizing Satan transformed into an angel of light, not only in the times of the apostles but also in the times of the Antichrist who was to arise, whose signs and prodigies would by no means have prevailed, unless this gift of discerning spirits had been taken away from the midst of us on account of our sins.

units.la: ALII uero genera linguarum, inquit, alij uero interpretatio linguarum.] De linguis & interpretatione linguarū fusius dicturus est infrà ca.14. Donū linguarū mox initio in apostolos post Christi ascensionem per spiritum Dei infusum est, cum essent ad Apostolatum per totum orbem inter omnes gentes obeundum instrumendi. Postea uero in credentes quoq; transfundi cœpit, secundum illud Christi Marci ult. Signa eos qui in me credent hæc sequentur: Per nomen meum dæmonia eijcient, linguis loquentur nouis, &c. Et hoc genere charismatis Corinthij admodū insolescebant, ut infrà dicto iā capite patebit. Interpretatione uero linguarum eam fuisse intelligo, qua quidā nō modo uarijs
units.tr: "To another kinds of tongues," he says, "but to another the interpretation of tongues." I will speak more fully about tongues and the interpretation of tongues below, in chapter 14. The gift of tongues was first poured out on the apostles, through the Spirit of God, immediately after Christ's ascension, when they were being equipped to carry out their apostleship among all nations throughout the world. Afterwards it also began to be passed on to believers, according to the words of Christ in the last chapter of Mark: "These signs will follow those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons, they will speak with new tongues," and so on. The Corinthians were greatly puffed up by this kind of gift, as will become clear in the chapter already mentioned below. As for the interpretation of tongues, I understand it to be that by which certain people not only in various

units.la: sint, unum sunt corpus, sic & Moses. Etenim Israelitę omnes in unum corpus circucisi sunt, staret ne argumentatio? Respondeo, non staret. Quia Israelitæ neque sunt in Mosen carne, neq; per illius spiritum in cordibus circuncisi. Credentes uero in Christum, quoniam & sacramento in illum obsignantur, & in illius spiritu baptizantur & regenerantur, rectè unum cum illo corpus esse dicuntur, cui & sacramento & spiritu & fidei professione iunguntur. Quare quod hic Apostolus Christũ unum nobiscum esse corpus probaturus dicit: Etenim nos omnes per unum spiritum in unum corpus baptizati, & in unum spiritum potati sumus non est de alio quàm ipsius Christi spiritu intelligendum, per quem & in quo in unum cum illo corpus cooptamur. Hac cõiunctione fit Christus unum corpus constans ex multis membris, quod nec de Mose, nec de ullo uel prophetarum uel Apostolorum dici potest.
units.tr: ...are one body; so also with Moses. For all the Israelites were circumcised into one body. Would the argument then hold? I answer that it would not. For the Israelites are not in Moses in the flesh, nor are they circumcised in their hearts through his Spirit. But believers in Christ, since they are also sealed to him in the sacrament and are baptized and regenerated in his Spirit, are rightly said to be one body with him, to which they are joined by the sacrament, by the Spirit, and by the profession of faith. Therefore, when the Apostle here says, in order to prove that Christ is one body with us, "For we were all baptized into one body by one Spirit, and were all made to drink of one Spirit," this is to be understood of nothing other than the Spirit of Christ himself, through whom and in whom we are joined into one body with him. By this union Christ is one body made up of many members, which cannot be said of Moses, or of any prophet or apostle.

units.la: ETENIM per unum spiritum, inquit, nos omnes in unum corpus baptizati sumus.] In Græco est ἐν ἑνὶ πνεύματι, id est, in uno spiritu, quemadmodum & uulgata uersio habet. Nescio probandum ne fit quod Erasmus uertit, per unum spiritum. Mihi uidetur Apostolicam phrasim haud esse temere mutádam. Existimo Apostolum hic nõ dicere per quem, sed in quo baptizentur, & in quem potentur electi ac uiri fideles. Etenim, inquit, in uno spiritu baptizati sumus in unum corpus. Loquitur quidè de baptismate, quo erat baptizati Corinthij (non enim dicit, baptizamur: sed, baptizati sumus) Verum non dicit, in una aqua: sed, in uno spiritu baptizati sumus, ut significet se loqui de integro baptismi sacramento, in quo non aqua tantum, sed & spiritu Christi baptizantur ueri fideles, per quem haud sacramentaliter tātum, sed & ueraciter in corpus illius inseruntur. Et ne propositi sui obliuiscatur, non dicit simpliciter, Etenim baptizati sumus in illum: sed, Etenim in uno spiritu nos omnes in unum corpus baptizati, & in unum spiritum potati sumus. Quasi dicat: Quomodo scindimini in partes diuersas, & alij alios abijcitis? Si Christi estis, unum corpus & unus cum illo spiritus fitis necesse est. Vel baptisma ueštrum inspicite. In illo non estis diuerso, sed eodem spiritu non in sectas, sed in unum corpus baptizati, & in spiritum non alium atq; alium, sed eundē potati.
units.tr: "For by one Spirit," he says, "we were all baptized into one body." In the Greek it is ἐν ἑνὶ πνεύματι, that is, "in one Spirit," as the Vulgate also has it. I do not know whether Erasmus's rendering, "by one Spirit," can be defended. It seems to me that the apostolic phrasing should not be rashly altered. I think the Apostle here does not say by whom, but in whom, the elect and faithful are baptized and in whom they drink. For, he says, we were baptized into one body in one Spirit. He is indeed speaking of baptism, by which the Corinthians had been baptized (he does not say "we are baptized" but "we were baptized"). Yet he does not say "in one water," but "in one Spirit," to show that he is speaking of the whole sacrament of baptism, in which true believers are baptized not only with water but also with the Spirit of Christ, through whom they are inserted into his body not merely sacramentally but truly. And lest he forget his purpose, he does not simply say, "For we were baptized into him," but "For in one Spirit we all were baptized into one body, and were all made to drink of one Spirit." It is as if he were saying: "How are you torn into different parts, and how do you cast off one another? If you are Christ's, you must be one body and have one Spirit with him. Or look at your own baptism. In it you were not baptized into different things, but in the same Spirit, not into sects but into one body, and you were made to drink not one spirit after another, but the same one."

units.la: VNDE ergo sunt in uobis schismata?] Perinde est ac si ad redarguendum & tollendum dissidia fraterna dicat fratribus frater: Ex eodem sanguine in eandem sumus carnem nati, & eodem lacte potati, quare non modo conuenit, ut dissidijs & odijs mutuis scindamur. Quemadmodum eiusdem sanguinis & lactis & carnis argumento recte admonentur fratres, ut abiectis odijs & dissidijs ad philadelphiam conuertantur: ita Apostolus argumento eiusdem spiritus & corporis spirituales in Christo fratres reuocat à sectis ad unitatem ecclesię, & ueram concordiam seruandam.
units.tr: "Whence then are there divisions among you?" This is just as if a brother were to say to his brothers, to refute and remove their quarrels: "We were born of the same blood into the same flesh, and we were nourished on the same milk; therefore it is not fitting that we should be torn apart by mutual quarrels and hatreds." Just as brothers are rightly reminded, by the argument of the same blood, milk and flesh, to put aside hatreds and quarrels and turn to brotherly love, so the Apostle, by the argument of the same Spirit and body, calls spiritual brothers in Christ back from sects to the unity of the Church and to keeping true concord.

units.la: Illud, quod non dicit, in uno spiritu uos omnes: sed, nos omnes, in unum corpus baptizati sumus, obseruauit Chrysostomus diligens Apostolicæ doctrinæ lector. Singulari studio solet Apostolus in ijs se, quæ communem gratiam, & adhortationem quoque concernunt coniungere fidelibus, etiam illis, quorum delicta reprehendit. Sic hoc loco coiungit se Corinthijs in communicatione eiusdem spiritus ac sacramenti, quo se alienum ab illis esse declaret, qui propter baptismatis sacramentum unitatem ecclesiæ usque adeo scindebant, ut gratias ageret Deo quod non multos Corinthi baptizasset, ne quis diceret quod in ipsius esset nomine baptizatus. Nos omnes, inquit, baptizati sumus in uno spiritu in unum corpus, tã ego uester Apostolus, quàm uos. Quid ergo faciunt baptizatores illi, qui studio baptizandi non Christo, sed sibijpsis discipulos colligunt?
units.tr: Chrysostom, a careful reader of apostolic teaching, noticed that the Apostle does not say "you all in one Spirit," but "we all were baptized into one body." The Apostle is wont, with special care, to join himself to the faithful in those matters which concern common grace and exhortation, even to those whose faults he rebukes. So here he joins himself to the Corinthians in sharing the same Spirit and sacrament, thereby showing that he is estranged from those who, on account of the sacrament of baptism, so tore apart the unity of the Church that he had to thank God that he had baptized few at Corinth, lest anyone say that they had been baptized in his name. "We all," he says, "were baptized in one Spirit into one body, I, your apostle, no less than you." What then do those baptizers do, who in their zeal for baptizing gather disciples not for Christ but for themselves?

units.la: NOS omnes, inquit, siue Iudæi siue Græci, siue serui siue liberi.] Omnem differentiam à catholica totius ecclesiæ communione excludit. Huc facit primum, quod non simpliciter dicit I in uno spiritu baptizari nos sumus: sed, In uno spiritu nos omnes baptizati sumus. Deinde, quod uniuersitatis nota haud contentus specificationem quoque diuersarũ cũm nationum tum conditionum subijcit dicens, Siue Iudæi siue Græci, siue serui siue liberi. Duabus nationibus complectitur omnes reliquas, cum dicit, siue Iudæi siue Græci: duabus quoque conditionibus omnes diuersorũ statuum ordines comprehendit dicens, Siue serui siue liberi. Accommodat autem se dissidijs quæ tum in ecclesia uigebant. Primum enim quasi irreconciliabilis disceptatio erat inter Iudęos & Græcos, id est, ethnicos. Deinde cœperat diuitũ ac liberorum prærogatiua maior haberi in ecclesia quàm pauperum ac seruorum. Vt hæc igitur discrimina nihil debere loci habere in ecclesia moneat, specificatione hanc Iudæorum ac Græcorum, seruorumque ac liberorum expressit. Magna sane diuinę bonitatis dignatione eodem spiritu baptizatur ethnicus quo Iudæus, eodē seruus quo liber, pauper quo diues. Putidissima est humani cordis superbia, qua homo propter uel nationis, uel fortunę, uel conditionis qualecunq; diuersitate fastidit hominē quē nõ fastidit Deus, idque in causa non propria, sed ipsius Dei. Non discernit Deus inter Iudæum & Græcum, seruũ ac liberum: & homo corruptibilis puluis discernit in causa religionis gentem à gente, seruum à libero, pauperem à diuite, idiotam à docto, atque ita quos diuina dignatio in eadem uoluit esse gratia æquales & coniunctos, pro inæqualibus habet, & disiungit. Non loquor de statibus & ordinibus huius sæculi, quorum diuersitatem nõ tollit regni Christi gratia: sed de superbia qua homo hominem in religione ptopter externæ fortunæ humilitate non habet eo loco, quo dignata est illum D.maiestas.
units.tr: "We all," he says, "whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free." He excludes every difference from the catholic communion of the whole Church. This is shown first by the fact that he does not simply say, "we are baptized in one Spirit," but "we all were baptized in one Spirit." Secondly, because he is not content with the mark of universality alone, but adds a specification of the different nations and conditions, saying, "whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free." By two nations he embraces all the rest when he says "whether Jews or Greeks," and by two conditions he comprehends all the orders of different ranks when he says "whether slaves or free." He also accommodates himself to the divisions which then prevailed in the Church. For at first there was an apparently irreconcilable dispute between Jews and Greeks, that is, Gentiles. Then the privilege of the rich and free had begun to be held in greater esteem in the Church than that of the poor and of slaves. So, to warn that these distinctions should have no place in the Church, he expressed this specification of Jews and Greeks, slaves and free. Truly, by the great condescension of divine goodness, the Gentile is baptized in the same Spirit as the Jew, the slave in the same as the free man, the poor in the same as the rich. It is most foul human pride by which a man, on account of any difference of nation, fortune or condition, despises a man whom God does not despise, and this in a matter not his own but God's. God does not distinguish between Jew and Greek, slave and free, and yet man, a corruptible handful of dust, distinguishes in matters of religion nation from nation, slave from free, poor from rich, the unlearned from the learned; and so he regards as unequal, and separates, those whom the divine condescension willed to be equal and joined in the same grace. I am not speaking of the states and orders of this world, whose diversity the grace of Christ's kingdom does not abolish, but of the pride by which a man, on account of the lowliness of external fortune, does not hold a person in the place where the divine Majesty has deigned to put him.

units.la: ET omnes, inquit, unum spiritū haufim9. ] In Græco est, ἡ ϰάντ ἐς ἓν πνεῦμα ἐποτίσθημεν id est, & omnes in unum spiritum potati sumus. Vulgata uersio habet, & omnes eodem spiritu potati sumus. Referunt hanc particulam ad potum eucharistæ, & quærunt, quare non dixerit, Et omnes eodem sanguine: sed, & omnes eodé spiritu potati sumus, & quare potus tantum & non cibi quoq; mentionem fecerit, dicens: & omnes eadem carne pasti sumus. Meo iudicio non est opus hisce quæstionibus. Neque enim de sacramento eucharistiæ loquitur, quo frequenter utebantur, ut non esset dicendum, potati sumus, in præterito: sed potamur in præsenti, si de illo loqui uoluissēt. Loquitur de gratia spiritussauĉti, qua in Christum credentes baptizati, hoc est, renati fuerant & potati, & respicit ad similitudinem infantis, qui recens natus non cibo, sed materni lactis potu alitur, atque ita unde natus est, inde & nutritur. Sic eodem spiritu erant Corinthij fideles potati, quo erant & nati. Idem eos spiritus, quo erant in Christo renati, donis suis ueluti lacte quodam potauerat, quo crescerent in fide, & confirmarentur. Quod si placet metaphora plantationis, ut baptizari in eodem spiritu sit instar plantularum in eadem cœlestis gratiæ area plantari, conueniet uerbum porandi, sensu rigandi accipere. Verum infantis similitudo magis arridet. Ad hunc modum exponi potest hæc particula, si legerimus, Et omnes eodem spiritu potati sumus.
units.tr: "And all," he says, "were made to drink of one Spirit." In the Greek it is καὶ πάντες εἰς ἓν πνεῦμα ἐποτίσθημεν, that is, "and all were made to drink into one Spirit." The Vulgate has "and all were made to drink of the same Spirit." People refer this clause to the cup of the Eucharist, and ask why he did not say "and all of the same blood," but "and all were made to drink of the same Spirit," and why he mentioned only drink and not also food, saying "and all were fed on the same flesh." In my judgment there is no need for these questions. For he is not speaking of the sacrament of the Eucharist, which they used frequently; otherwise it would not have been necessary to say "were made to drink" in the past tense, but "are made to drink" in the present, if he had wished to speak of that. He is speaking of the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which believers in Christ were baptized, that is, reborn and made to drink, and he has regard to the likeness of a newborn infant, who is nourished not by food but by drinking its mother's milk, and so is nourished by the same from which he was born. Thus the faithful Corinthians had been made to drink of the same Spirit by whom they had been born. The same Spirit by whom they had been reborn in Christ had, with his gifts, given them to drink as it were of a kind of milk, so that they might grow in faith and be strengthened. But if the metaphor of planting pleases, so that to be baptized in the same Spirit is like being planted in the same plot of heavenly grace, the verb "to drink" may be taken in the sense of "to water." Yet the likeness of the infant pleases me more. In this way this clause can be explained, if we read, "and all were made to drink of the same Spirit."

units.la: Quod si secundum Græci exemplaris fidē legerimus, & omnes in eundem spiritum potati sumus, diligenter uidendum est, qui sensus ei lectioni conueniat: hoc est, quid sit fideles Christi in eodem spiritu baptizari, & in unum spiritum potari.
units.tr: But if we read, following the faith of the Greek copy, "and we have all been made to drink into one Spirit," we must carefully consider what meaning fits that reading: that is, what it is for the faithful of Christ to be baptized into the same Spirit and to be given to drink into the one Spirit.

units.la: Apostolus & minister Christi, quatenus est minister non literæ, sed spiritus, gignit, & potat recens genitos. In Christo Iesu, inquit, ego uos genui. Item: Lac uobis potum dedi. Regeneratos hic uocat in uno spiritu baptizatos. Ilos lacte doctrinæ eiusdem qua geniti fuerant, diligenter ac prudenter potauit. Apollos quoque post illius discessum. Hæc duo supra capite tertio per metaphoram plantationis & rigationis expresit, dicens: Ego plantaui. Apollo rigauit. Quemadmodum autem baptizati fuerant in unum corpus, ita potauit eos unà cū Apollo in unum spiritum. Hæc enim conditio est animati corporis, ut spiritum habeat nō uarium, sed unum & eundum. Sic unitati corporis ecclesiastici connectit etiam unitatem spiritus, quem alijs in locis uocat ἓν πνεῦμα, id est mentem & sententiam, ut supra capite primo dicens, Vt sitis integri eadem mente & sententia: & Philipp. 1. spiritum & animam, ubi dicit: Vt audiam de rebus uestris, quod stetis in uno spiritu, una anima. De hac unitate spiritus Eph. 4. sic dicit: Studentes seruare unitatem spiritus in uinculo pacis, unum corpus & unus spiritus (potest etiam legi in accu-
units.tr: The apostle, as minister not of the letter but of the Spirit, begets and gives drink to those newly born. He says, "In Christ Jesus I have begotten you" (1 Cor. 4.15). Likewise: "I have given you milk to drink" (1 Cor. 3.2). Here he calls them regenerate, baptized into one Spirit. He carefully and wisely gave them to drink the milk of the same teaching by which they had been begotten. Apollos did so too after his departure. In the third chapter above he expressed these two things by the metaphor of planting and watering, saying: "I planted, Apollos watered" (1 Cor. 3.6). Just as they had been baptized into one body, so he gave them to drink, together with Apollos, into one Spirit. For this is the condition of a living body, that it has not a varied but one and the same spirit. Thus he joins to the unity of the ecclesiastical body also the unity of the Spirit, which in other places he calls one Spirit [ἓν πνεῦμα], that is, one mind and one judgment, as above in the first chapter, where he says: "that you may be perfect in the same mind and in the same judgment" (1 Cor. 1.10). And in Philippians 1, speaking of the spirit and the soul, he says: "that I may hear of your affairs, that you stand in one spirit, with one soul" (Phil. 1.27). Of this unity of the Spirit he speaks thus in Ephesians 4: "Endeavoring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit" (the reading may also be taken in the accusative: "one body and one Spirit"), "just as you were called in one hope of your calling" (Eph. 4.3–4). In this sense, then, to be given to drink into one Spirit is for the minds of those born again, through the unity of the same teaching, to be nourished and strengthened into the unity of the same heart, soul and spirit. I state simply in what sense the Greek reading is to be taken; let others judge.

units.la: satiuo, unum corpus & unum spiritum) quem admodum & uocati estis in una spe uocationis uestræ. Hoc itaq; sensu potari in unum spiritum, est unitate doctrinæ regeneratorū mentes in unitatem eiusdem cordis, animæ, & spiritus ali & confirmari. Dico simpliciter, quo sensu accipienda sit Græca lectio, aliorum esto iudicium.
units.tr: "In the accusative, 'one body and one Spirit,' which also follows: 'as you were also called in one hope of your calling.' So to be made to drink [ἐποτίσθημεν] into one Spirit means, in this sense, that the minds of the regenerate are nourished and strengthened into unity of the same heart, soul and spirit through the unity of doctrine. I state simply in what sense the Greek reading should be taken; let others judge."

units.la: Et enim corpus non est unum membrum, sed multa. Si dicat pes, quia non sum manus, non sum de corpore, num idcirco nō est de corpore? Et si dicat auris, quoniā non sum oculus, nō sum de corpore, num ideo non est de corpore? Si totū corpus oculus, ubi auditus? Si totum auditus, ubi olfactus? Nunc autem Deus posuit membra, unumquodq; ipsorū singulatim in corpore, quemadmodum uoluit. Quod si essent omnia unū membrum, ubi esset corpus? Nūc autem multa quidē membra, unū uero corpus.
units.tr: For the body is not one member, but many. If the foot should say, "Because I am not a hand, I am not of the body," is it therefore not of the body? And if the ear should say, "Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body," is it therefore not of the body? If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the smell be? But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, as he willed. But if they were all one member, where would the body be? As it is, there are indeed many members, but one body.

units.la: Redit ad similitudinem corporis & membrorum, quam applicationis illius parte, ubi commodū uidebatur, interrupit, dicēs: Sic & Christus. Et enim in uno spiritu nos omnes in unū corpus baptizati sumus, &c. Dixerat, omnia membra corporis cum sint multa, unū esse corpus. Huic ueluti ratione annectit, dicens: Etenim corpus non est unum membrum, sed multa. Ratio sumpta est à conditione corporis. Quod etenim corpus nō sic est cōparatum, ut uno membro cōstet, sed multis. Multa membra nō multiplicant, sed cōplent & cōstituunt unum corpus. Quare? Quia corpus non est idē quod membrū, sed est connexio multorum membrorum. Ratio hęc ualet nō in quouis corporū genere, sed in eo, quod ex multis est mēbris compositum. Perinde est ac si dicas, ciuitas non est unus ciuis, sed multi. Dictū hoc locum habet, ubi in ciuitate, populo, uel ecclesia unius hominis existimatio eoufq; inualuit, ut unus oia esse & posse uideatur, pręq; illo omnes reliqui nihili ducantur. Hic comode dixeris: Ciuitas, non est unus homo, sed multi. Sic dicamus & nos: Ecclesia non est unus homo, sed multi, contra eos, qui Ro.pont. omnē eam potestatem tri buunt, quæ cōpetit ecclesiæ. Nec dubito quin Apostolus quorundam exīstimationē in eccle sia Corinthiorū hoc simili in ordinē redigere, & inferiorū animos, qui respectu illorū conte nebantur, erigere uoluerit. Ideo & subiunxit:
units.tr: He returns to the likeness of the body and its members, which he had interrupted at the point of application where it seemed fitting, saying: "So also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body," and so on. He had said that, although all the members of the body are many, the body is one. To this he attaches the reason, as it were, saying: "For the body is not one member, but many." The reason is taken from the nature of a body: a body is not constituted of one member but of many. Many members do not multiply the body; they complete and make up one body. Why? Because the body is not the same thing as a member, but is the connection of many members. This reasoning holds not for every kind of body, but for that which is composed of many members. It is just as if you said: a city is not one citizen, but many. This saying applies where, in a city, a people or a church, the esteem of one man has so prevailed that he seems to be everything and able to do everything, while all the others are counted as nothing in comparison with him. Here you may fittingly say: a city is not one man, but many. So let us also say: the Church is not one man, but many, against those who ascribe to the Roman pontiff all that power which belongs to the Church. I do not doubt that the Apostle wished, by this comparison, to bring to order the esteem of certain people in the Corinthian church, and to lift up the spirits of the inferior members, who were held down by comparison with them. Hence he added:

units.la: Si dicat pes, quia nō sum manus, non sum de corpore, num idcirco nō est de corpore? Et si dicat auris, quia non sum oculus, non sum de corpore, &c.] Succurrit pusillanimitati idiotarum ac rudium qui erant in ecclesia, quos comparat pedibus & auribus. Pedes inferiora sunt corporis membra, estq; illorum officium admodum seruile & humile. Aures quoque, etsi sunt in capite loco sublimi, seruile tamen habet audienaudiendi officium. Sic in ecclesia qui sunt inferiores & auditores, quasi pedum & aurium loco habentur. Hi ubi uident operationes potiorum, tam doctorum qui loco sunt oculorum, quàm eorum qui præclara opera, uel miranda facientes, initar manuum sunt in corpore, putant se respectu illorum nó esse eiusdem ecclesiæ consortes, propterea quod non sunt illis æquales. Quod perinde est, ac si dicat pes, quia non sum manus, non sum de corpore: & auris, quia non sum oculus, non sum de corpore. Num idcirco, inquit, non sunt pes & auris de corpore? Quasi dicat: Vtique sunt. Quis adeò desipit, ut sentiat pedes suos & aures nó pertinere ad reliqua corporis sui membra, propterea quod non sunt potiora? Hac parabola dilucide absurditatem cogitationis huiusmodi redarguit, potiorum arrogantiam restringit, & utrosque tam superiores quàm inferiores ad concordiam tanquam unius corporis membra reuocat, idq; facit absq; manifesta cuiusdã reprehensione.
units.tr: "Because I am not a hand, because I am not an eye," he says. He expresses the wishes of the lesser and unlearned who were then in the Corinthian church. They saw the gifts of the Spirit in the more eminent: some taught, some foresaw the future, some healed diseases, some spoke in tongues, some interpreted tongues. They thought themselves wretched and despised, because they were not equal to these, and so they wished to be in their place. But today the crowd of hearers in the church is disposed quite otherwise. You would find very few who so admire the higher offices of teachers and ministers that they desire to be equal to them; indeed, few who do not despise those by whom they ought to be built up in the knowledge of God and true piety. But the blame for this contempt must for the most part be imputed to the ministers and teachers themselves. The eyes in the church are dim, the hands are weak and crippled; therefore it is not for the foot to say, "Because I am not a hand," and the ear, "Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body." Rather, they ought to think that, unless the eyes see better and the hands labor more effectively, it will go badly for us and for the other members of our body; and they ought to pray the Lord both to free the eyes of the church from darkness and to make the crippled hands effective. These are today the wishes of the feet and ears in the ecclesiastical body.

units.la: QVIA non sum manus, quia non sum oculus, inquit] Exprimit uota inferiorum & idiotarum, qui tum erant in ecclesia Corinthiorum. Videbant charismata spiritus in potioribus, quorum alij docebant, alij futura præuidebát, alij morbos curabant, alij linguis loquebátur, alij linguas interpretabantur, ac se miseros esse arbitrabantur & contemptos, quod illis nó essent æquales. Optabant igitur illorum esse loco. At hodie longe aliter animata est multitudo auditorum in ecclesia. Paucissimos illorum inuenias, qui sic admirentur superiora doctorum & pastorum officia, ut se cupiant illis esse æquales, imò qui non contemnant eos, à quibus debebant in scientia Dei & uera pietate ædificari. At huius contemptus culpa maiori ex parte ipsis est pastoribus & doctoribus imputanda. Caligant in ecclesia oculi, languet & contractæ sunt manus, quare non est ut dicat pes, quia non sum manus: & auris, quia nó sum oculus, nó sum de corpore: sed est potius ut cogitent, nisi melius uideant oculi, & efficacius laborent manus, male consultū erit & nobis & reliquis corporis nostri membris: orentq; dominum, ut & oculos ecclesiæ à caligine liberet, & contractas manus efficaces reddat. Hæc sint hodie uota pedum & aurium in corpore ecclesiastico.
units.tr: "Because I am not a hand, because I am not an eye," he says. He expresses the wishes of the inferior and unlearned people who then existed in the Corinthian church. They saw the gifts of the Spirit in those who were more prominent: some taught, some foresaw the future, some healed diseases, some spoke in tongues, some interpreted tongues. They thought themselves wretched and despised because they were not equal to these, and so they wished to be in their place. But today the multitude of hearers in the church is disposed far differently. You will find very few who so admire the higher offices of teachers and ministers that they desire to be equal to them; indeed, there are few who do not despise those by whom they ought to be built up in the knowledge of God and true piety. Yet the blame for this contempt must for the most part be imputed to the ministers and teachers themselves. The eyes in the church grow dim, the hands grow weak and are cramped, so that the foot does not say, "Because I am not a hand," nor the ear, "Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body." Rather, they think that unless the eyes see better and the hands labour more effectively, it will go badly both for us and for the other members of our body. And they pray the Lord both to free the eyes of the church from darkness and to make the cramped hands effective. These are today the wishes of the feet and ears in the ecclesiastical body.

units.la: NON sum de corpore, inquit, num idcirco non est de corpore?] Obserua quod non dicit: non sum in corpore, num idcirco non est in corpore? sed, non sum de corpore, num idcirco nó est de corpore? Aliud est esse in corpore, & aliud esse de corpore. In corpore sunt & ulcera, & tubera, & pustulæ, sed non sunt de corpore: hoc est, ad constitutionem & cöplementum corporis nó pertinent, quia non sunt corporis membra: quemadmodū aliud est esse in ciuitate, & aliud esse de ciuitate. Sic aliud est esse in ecclesia, & aliud esse de ecclesia Christi. In ecclesia Christi sunt & reprobi, de ecclesia
units.tr: "I am not of the body," he says; "is it therefore not of the body?" Observe that he does not say: "I am not in the body; is it therefore not in the body?" but: "I am not of the body; is it therefore not of the body?" To be in the body is one thing, and to be of the body is another. Ulcers, swellings and pustules are in the body, but they are not of the body: that is, they do not belong to the constitution and completion of the body, because they are not members of the body. Just as it is one thing to be in a city and another to be of the city, so it is one thing to be in the Church and another to be of the Church of Christ. In the Church of Christ there are also reprobates; but those who are of the Church are not reprobates, but only the elect and faithful, who belong to the number of the members and constitute the true Church. "They went out from us," says John, "because they were not of us." How did they go out from the Church, if they were not of the Church? They had been in...

units.la: uero sunt non reprobi, sed electi ac fideles tantum, qui ad numerum membrorum pertinent, & ueram ecclesiā constituunt. Exierūt ex nobis, inquit Iohannes, quia nó erant ex nobis. Quo modo exierunt ex ecclesia, si nó fuerunt ex ecclesia? fuerant in ecclesia, sed nó erant de ecclesia. Sic & Corinthiacæ ecclesiæ idiotæ & rudes, satis uidebant esse se in ecclesia Christi: ueluti quoniam uidebant se destitutos donis spiritus, insignioribus illis quæ admirabantur, ut spicabantur se non esse de corpore ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Those, however, are not the reprobate but only the elect and faithful, who belong to the number of the members and constitute the true Church. "They went out from us," says John, "because they were not of us." How did they go out from the Church if they had not been of the Church? They were in the Church, but they were not of the Church. So too the unlearned and rude people of the Corinthian church thought they were quite sufficiently in the Church of Christ; yet, because they saw themselves lacking the gifts of the Spirit, those more outstanding ones that they admired, they supposed that they were not of the body of the Church.

units.la: SI totum corpus oculus, ubi auditus? Si totum auditus, inquit, ubi olfactus?] Quoniam inferiores potiorum charismata affectantes, humilis suæ sortis pudebat, ut indicet quanta absurditas, quanta confusio, quantaq; sequeretur totius ecclesiæ pernicies si quod affectabant, reipsa consequerentur: pergit in parabola membrorum corporis, quorum ea est conditio, ut non multitudine modo, sed & uarietate suacorpus compleant, & constitutionem illius conseruent, & argumentatur ad hùc modum: Si omnibus idem esset spiritus sancti charisma datum, ubi essent reliqua illius dona, sine quibus ecclesia consistere non poterit? Perinde esset, ac si totum corpus esset oculus, qua re quid corpori posset exitiosius euenire? Destitueretur enim necessarijs officijs pedū, manuum, aurium, oris, &c. esset q; deformis quidam truncus, etsi oculatus, prorsus tamen inutilis. Vel hinc igitur cogitate, quàm sint uota uestra noxia & absurda. Omnium ferè mortalium pectora occupat hic morbus, ut nemo sua sit sorte contentus, sed ad altiora quisq; si non conatibus, uotis saltem adspiret. Nemo inferiora, superiora affectant omnes. Stulta hæc & perniciosa uota ecclesias nunquam non turbarunt. Rarissimus omnino est, qui cum Dauidè plurimi faciat, quod in domum Dei receptus est, & aliquo saltem loco constitutus, dicatque ex animo: Elegi ad limè esse in domo Dei mei magis, quàm habitare in tabernaculis peccatorum. Per se tanti non est esse episcopum ac præ fidem, quanti est esse in ecclesia Christi. At ea gratia tam est inferioribus quàm superioribus concessa. Quemadmodum tanti non est esse oculum, quanti est esse membrum in corpore, ac frui communi corporis uita ac spiritu, id quod tam pedibus quàm oculis contingit.
units.tr: "If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the smell be?" Since the lesser members were coveting the greater gifts, they were ashamed of their humble lot. He shows how great an absurdity, how great a confusion, and how great a ruin of the whole Church would follow if they actually obtained what they were coveting. He goes on with the parable of the members of the body, whose condition is such that they fill the body not only by their number but by their variety, and preserve its constitution. And he argues in this way: If the same gift of the Holy Spirit were given to all, where would the remaining gifts be, without which the Church cannot stand? It would be just as if the whole body were an eye; what could happen more destructive to the body? For it would lack the necessary offices of the feet, hands, ears, mouth, and so on; and it would be a kind of deformed trunk, which, though it had eyes, would be wholly useless. Consider then from this alone how harmful and absurd your wishes are. This disease occupies the hearts of almost all mortals, so that no one is content with his own lot, but everyone aspires to higher things, if not by efforts, at least by wishes. No one covets lower things; all covet higher ones. These foolish and pernicious wishes have never failed to disturb churches. Very rare indeed is the man who, with David, values most highly that he has been received into the house of God and placed in some place, however small, and who says from his heart: "I have chosen rather to be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than to dwell in the tents of sinners." In itself, being a bishop or a deacon is not worth as much as being in the Church of Christ. Yet that grace is granted as much to the lower members as to the higher. Just as it is not worth as much to be the eye as to be a member in the body and to enjoy the common life and breath of the body, which is the case for feet as much as for eyes.

units.la: Qui hoc considerat, tam abest ut ad sublimiorem aliquem gradum aspirans fortis suæ pertæsus fiat, ut nesciat condignis modis diuinã erga se beneuolentā in eo deprædicare, quod in aliquam est ab illo sortem in ecclesia ipsius receptus. Quod autem omnes ad sublimiora aspiramus, ex eo est serpentis antiqui ueneno, quod prima nostra parés in ipso paradiso hau-sit, cum fore crederet, ut essent sicut dij, scientes bonum & malum, si de pomo uetito ederent. Diuinitas autē quædam esse uidetur, plura scire, pluraq; posse quàm sciant & posint alij: & si non amplius, saltē nó minus in precio haberi q habeātur alij. Hinc est qd in corpore eccleecclesiæ inferiorum loca non appetunt superiores, superiorum uero appetunt inferiores.
units.tr: One who considers this is so far from aspiring to some higher rank and becoming weary of his own lot that he does not know how, in fitting terms, to proclaim God's goodwill toward him, in that he has been received by Him into some lot in His Church. But that all of us aspire to higher things comes from the poison of the ancient serpent, which our first parents drank in paradise itself, when they believed they would be like gods, knowing good and evil, if they ate of the forbidden fruit. Now there seems to be a kind of divinity in knowing more and being able to do more than others know and can do; and if not more, at least to be held in no less esteem than others are. Hence it is that in the body of the Church the superior members do not seek the places of the inferior, but the inferior seek the places of the superior.

units.la: SI totum corpus, inquit, oculus est, ubi audit?&c.] Secus habet natura diuinitatis, quâ corporis humani constitutio. In corpore humano fieri non potest, ut ab uno aliquo membro totû comprehendatur. Et si posset, ut reliqua membra haud excludantur. Et enim si totum corpus esset oculus, nec auditui in illo, nec geltui, nec olfactui, nec manibus nec pedibus locus esse posset. In diuinitate uero non est ut dicas: Si totus Deus bonitas est, ubi iusticia? Si totus iusticia est, ubi sapientia? Si totus sapientia, ubi potentia? Etenim sic est comparatus, ut totus sit bonitas, totus iusticia, totus sapientia, totus potentia, quâuis diuersæ sint hæ uirtutes, & à se inuicem discretæ. Luceamur ergo ad eas potius uirtutes, q̃ sic sunt comparatæ, ut nullam nulla ab ecclesia excludat, si hanc totam occupet, q̃ ad officia, quorû nullû totam ecclesiâ sic occupat, ut cæteris locû in illa relinquat. Omnino etiâ diuinitus est, si uere de ecclesia dici possit, quod tota sit fides, tota sit spes, tota sit charitas, &c. Nihil impedit quo minus omnia illius membra prædita sint fide, & tñ simul sperêt omnia, & diligant oia, quæ tñ dona omnia charismata, ministeria, & energemata superant.
units.tr: "If the whole body," he says, "is an eye, where is the hearing?" etc. The nature of the divine is different from the constitution of the human body. In the human body it cannot happen that the whole is comprehended by any one member; and even if it could, the remaining members would not be excluded. For if the whole body were an eye, there could be no place in it for hearing, for taste, for smell, nor for hands or feet. In the divine nature, however, it is not as you might say: "If God is wholly goodness, where is justice? If He is wholly justice, where is wisdom? If He is wholly wisdom, where is power?" For He is so constituted that He is wholly goodness, wholly justice, wholly wisdom, wholly power, although these virtues are different and distinct from one another. Let us therefore look rather to those virtues which are so constituted that none excludes another, even if it occupies the whole Church; whereas the offices, none of which so occupies the whole Church as to leave room for the others in it. It is indeed divinely so, if it can truly be said of the Church that it is wholly faith, wholly hope, wholly love, and so on. Nothing prevents all its members from being endowed with faith, and yet all from hoping and loving together; and yet these gifts surpass all charismata, ministries, and energemata.

units.la: NVNC aût posuit Deus membra, inquit, unumquodq; ipsorû in corpore sicut uoluit.] Reddit rationê, quare fieri non posset, ut totû corpus sit unum aliquod membrû, & si sit, reliquis in illo membris locus esse posset. Núc autem, inquit, posuit Deus membra in corpore, unumquodq; ipsorum sicuti uult. Quasi dicat: Non placuit opifici corporû nostrorû Deo, ut côstet plenitudo corporis uno & eodê mébro. Voluit esse membra diuersa, singula à singulis secreta: & ut uoluit, sic unum quodq; illorû posuit. Quare diuinę illius dispositioni aduersaretur, si oia corporis membra in idê conuerterentur, & totû corpus in illo côplerent. Sic de ecclesiæ quoq; membris cogitandum, & in huius dispositione omnibus & singulis conquiescendum esse monet. Nam & hic Deus membra posuit unumquodq; ipsorum sicut uoluit. Qui pes igitur est in corpore ecclesiæ, cogitet sic uoluisse Deû, ut sit pes, & ab illo se in corpore ecclesiæ pedis esse loco positum. Et sic consequenter cogitent singula membra. Hoc uolens, nô simpliciter dicit: Nunc aût posita sunt: sed, núc aût posuit Deus membra in corpore. & notanter addit, unumquodq; ipsorû singulatim, ne quis aliunde se quâ ab ipso Deo positû esse in ecclesia cogitet, nec sic contentus an nectit illud, sicuti uoluit, ne quis ratione quærat, quare tanta sit in membris ecclesiæ diuersitas, & nô potius catholica æqualitas, uel doleat, qd inferiore sit & humiliore locû sortitus. Quoties admonemur facere Deû omnia quêadmodum uult, à curiositate ac temeritate carnis nostræ auocamur, ne operû illius rationes scrutemur. Homini pio uoluntas Dei summæ est & bonitatis, & iusticiæ, & sapientiæ, & po-
units.tr: "But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body as He willed." He gives the reason why it could not happen that the whole body should be one member, and, if it were, there could be no place in it for the other members. But now, he says, God has set the members in the body, each one of them as He wills. As if he said: It did not please God, the Maker of our bodies, that the fullness of the body should consist of one member alone. He willed that there should be different members, each separated from the others; and as He willed, so He set each one of them. Therefore it would be contrary to that divine disposition if all the members of the body were turned into the same thing and filled the whole body with themselves. So too we ought to think about the members of the Church, and he warns that in this arrangement all and each should be content. For here too God has set the members, each one of them as He willed. Therefore let whoever is a foot in the body of the Church think that God willed him to be a foot, and that he has been placed by Him in the body of the Church in the place of a foot. And in the same way let the individual members consider. In saying this he does not simply say, "Now they have been placed," but "Now God has set the members in the body," and he notably adds "each one of them singly," lest anyone think he was placed in the Church by some other agency than God Himself; and, not content with this, he adds "as He willed," lest anyone ask on what reasoning there is such great diversity among the members of the Church and not rather catholic equality, or lest he grieve that he has obtained a lower and humbler place. As often as we are reminded that God does all things as He wills, we are called away from the curiosity and rashness of our flesh, so that we do not search out the reasons of His works. To a godly man the will of God takes the place of supreme goodness, justice, wisdom, and power.

units.la: tentiæ loco. Non est autê hic transeundû, quod Deum dicit membra ponere in corpore. Licet enim de corpore humano loquitur, sub hac tamen parabola conditionem & constitutionê ueræ ecclesiæ Dei ob oculos exponit. Ergo uera membra ecclesiæ ponuntur à Deo, & quæ ab illo posita non sunt, inter membra censeri nô debent. Sunt enim ψευδομελη non à Deo, sed à Satana ueris ecclesiæ membris immixta.
units.tr: Nor is it to be passed over here that he says God sets the members in the body. For although he speaks of the human body, nevertheless under this parable he sets before our eyes the condition and constitution of the true Church of God. Therefore the true members of the Church are set by God, and those which have not been set by Him ought not to be counted among the members. For they are pseudomela, not from God but from Satan, mixed in with the true members of the Church.

units.la: QVOD si essent oia unû membrum, inquit, ubi corpus? ] Rursus colligit q̃ sit inconueniens & absurdum, si obtineat æqualitas in ecclesia, quam pleriq; Corinthiorum affectabât. Su prâ dixit: Etenim corpus non est unum membrum, sed multa. Item: Si totum corpus oculus, ubi auditus? Hic: Quod si essent omnia unum membrum, ubi corpus? Nunc autê multa quidem membra, unû uero corpus. Ergo duo incôuenientia colligit, unum quod membra, alterum quod corpus côcernit. Membra concernit quod dixit: Si totum corpus oculus, ubi auditus? Nam hoc pacto membra corporis tolerentur. Corpus attinet quod hic dicit: Quod si essent omnia unum membrum, ubi corpus? Sic enim & corpus ipsum aboleretur. Igitur uelut ob oculos exponit q̃ sit noxia affectatio æqualitatis, quam appetebant Corinthij. Sic uidelicet, ut & membra & corpus ecclesiæ perdi tura esset, si obtineret. Quare qui ἀταξίαν in ecclesiam inducunt, quantû in ipsis est, & membra & corpus illius perdunt. Ea nanq; est constitutio ecclesiæ ac membrorum illus, ut qui membrorum ordinem confundit, confundat & ecclesiam, quantumuis nomen ecclesiæ iactet, & ad cœlos usq; extollat.
units.tr: "But if all were one member," he says, "where would the body be?" Again he infers how unfitting and absurd it would be if that equality prevailed in the Church which many of the Corinthians were coveting. Above he said: "For the body is not one member but many." Likewise: "If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be?" Here: "But if all were one member, where would the body be? But now indeed there are many members, yet one body." Therefore he infers two inconveniences, one concerning the members, the other concerning the body. The first, the members, is what he said: "If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be?" For in this way the members of the body would be destroyed. The body is concerned in what he says here: "But if all were one member, where would the body be?" For thus the body itself would be abolished. Therefore he sets before their eyes, as it were, how harmful is the affectation of equality which the Corinthians were striving for. Namely, that if it prevailed, both the members and the body of the Church would perish. Wherefore those who introduce disorder into the Church, so far as in them lies, destroy both the members and the body of the Church. For this is the constitution of the Church and of its members: whoever confounds the order of the members confounds the Church as well, however much he boasts of the name of the Church and exalts it even to the heavens.

units.la: NVNC autem multa quidem membra, inquit, unum uero corpus. ] Absoluit & concludit sententiam, qua contendit, corpus nô constare uno membro, sed multis: & eam esse conditionem membrorû, ut multitudine sua non multa faciant corpora, sed unum dûtaxat. Sic multitudo fidelium non constituit natura sua sectas, sed unam ecclesiam.
units.tr: "But now there are many members, yet one body." He concludes and sums up the sentence in which he argues that the body does not consist of one member but of many, and that it is the nature of members that their multitude does not make many bodies, but only one. So the multitude of believers does not by its nature constitute sects, but one Church.

units.la: Non potest uero oculus dicere manui, non est mihi opus te: aut rursus caput pedibus, nô est mihi opus uobis, imo multo potius quę uidentur membra corporis imbecilliora esse, necessaria sunt, et quę putamus minus honesta esse corporis, his honorê uberiorê apponimus: et indecora nostri copiosiorê honorê habet, decora uero nostri nô indigent, sed Deus simul temperauit corpus, ei cui de crat copiosiorem addes honorem, ne sit dissidium in corpore, sed inuicem alia pro alijs eandem solicitudinem gerant membra. Et siue patitur unum membrû, simul patiûtur oia membra, siue glorificatur unum membrum, simul gaudent omnia membra.
units.tr: "The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you; or again the head to the feet, I have no need of you. Rather, those members of the body that seem to be weaker are necessary, and those we think less honourable we clothe with more abundant honour; and our unseemly parts have more abundant honour, while our seemly parts have no need of it. But God so tempered the body, giving more abundant honour to that part which lacked it, that there should be no division in the body, but that the members should have the same care for one another. And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honoured, all the members rejoice with it."

units.la: Pergit in cœpta corporis parabola. Hactenus de unitate illius, quomodo illa membrorum multitudine constat, disseruit, & humilium inferiorumq; in ecclesia fidelium animos erexit: iam superiorum arrogantiam aggreditur, illosque à contemptu inferiorum ad colendam eiusdem corporis unitatem & concordiam revocat. Non potest, inquit, oculus dicere manui, non est mihi opus te. Cum inferiores erigeret, & cogitationes illorum exprimere vellet, dixit: Si dicat pes, quia non sum manus, nō sum de corpore, &c. Hic ubi superiorum arrogantiam restringere, ac cogitationes eorū exprimere constituit, dicit: Non autem potest oculus dicere manui, non est mihi opus te. Per oculum & caput eos notat, qui id sunt in ecclesia, quod caput & oculi sunt in corpore, docto res uidelicet ac præsides. Habet ecclesia etiam num capita & oculos, uerum capita partim asinina, partim leonina, & oculos ad prædā plus quàm Lynceos, ad uidendum quæ rectā sunt acuera ipsis talpis magis cæcos. Per manus hic intellige idiotas & operarios manuarios.
units.tr: He goes on with the parable of the body. So far he has spoken of its unity, of how it consists of a multitude of members, and he has raised up the hearts of the lowly and inferior among the believers in the Church. Now he turns to the arrogance of the superiors, and calls them back from despising the inferiors to cultivating the unity and harmony of the same body. "The eye," he says, "cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you." When he was raising up the inferiors and wished to express their thoughts, he said: "If the foot should say, because I am not a hand, I am not of the body, etc." Here, where he decides to restrain the arrogance of the superiors and to express their thoughts, he says: "But the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you." By eye and head he marks those who in the Church are what the head and eyes are in the body, namely teachers and presidents. The Church still has heads and eyes, but its heads are partly asinine, partly leonine, and its eyes are more than lynx-like in looking out for prey, yet more blind than moles in seeing what is straight. By hands understand here the unlearned and manual workers.

units.la: NON potest, inquit, oculus dicere manui.] Oculus membrum illustre, preciosum, summopere toti corpori necessarium, in sublimi quasi specula constitutum est, ut lucem ac rerum omnium discretionem suppeditet. Oculus diuinum membrum, ac speculum naturæ uocatur. In oculo habitat hominis animus. Non potest tamen dicere manui, non est mihi opus te. Etiam si linguam haberet oculus, & loqui posset, ueraciter tamen manui dicere non possit, opera tua non indigeo. Aliena est ab hac arrogantia superiorum membrorum natura, ut inferiora cōtemnat. Oculus indesinenter manibus est intentus, & operantibus illis lucem fi deliter subministrat. Et homo, oculi munus in ecclesia sortitus, inferiora illius membra contemnere potest.
units.tr: "The eye cannot," he says, "say to the hand..." The eye is a distinguished, precious member, most necessary to the whole body, set as it were on a high watch-tower, so that it may supply light and the discernment of all things. The eye is called a divine member and the mirror of nature. The mind of man dwells in the eye. Yet the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you. Even if the eye had a tongue and could speak, it could not truly say to the hand, I have no need of your works. The nature of the superior members is alien to this arrogance, that they should despise the inferior. The eye is constantly intent on the hands, and faithfully supplies light while they work. And a man who has received the office of the eye in the Church can despise those members beneath him?

units.la: Quare autem non potest oculus dicere manui, non est mihi opus te? Quia cessante manu totum corpus periclitatur. Periclitante uero corpore, periclitatur & oculus, ut peculiaria ministeria taceam, quibus manus oculo subferuit. Quod hic accommodatur ecclesiæ, recte accōmodabitur & reipublicæ. In illa quomodo homines otiosi subsisterent, si operarum, id est, operariorum, tam in agris quàm reliquis necessarijs operantium destituerentur? Et tamen sic insolescunt hic quoq; oculi, ut operarios perinde susque deque faciant, ac si nulla illorum opera indigeant. Et esto, non sit otiosis illis ecclesiæ oculis opus idiotis & operarijs, quod tamen nunquam ueraciter cogitari, nedum dici potest, conuenit ne eam ob causam, ut eos contemnant, quorum opera nō indigeant? Bonorum meorū non eges, ad Deum canit Psalmista. An ideo contemnitur homo à Deo, quod nulla in re opus illo habet? Ne quaquam. Quomodo ergo conuenit homini, ut hominem contemnat, etiam eum, cuius opera non indiget?
units.tr: Why, then, can the eye not say to the hand, I have no need of you? Because when the hand ceases, the whole body is in danger. And when the body is in danger, the eye too is in danger, not to mention the particular services by which the hand serves the eye. What is applied here to the Church will rightly be applied also to the commonwealth. In that case, how would idle men survive if they were deprived of workmen, that is, of labourers, both in the fields and in the other necessary trades? And yet the eyes here grow so proud that they treat the workmen as if they were nothing, as though no work of theirs were needed. Grant that those idle eyes of the Church have no need of the unlearned and the workmen, which can never truly be thought, let alone said: is it fitting that they should therefore despise those whose work they do not need? "You have no need of my goods," the Psalmist sings to God. Is a man therefore despised by God because God has no need of him in any matter? By no means. How then is it fitting for a man to despise a man, even one whose work he does not need?

units.la: A AVT rursus caput inquit pedibus, non est mihi opus uobis. ] Duo prorsus extrema corporis membra coniungit, caput superne, & pedes inferne, inter quæ minus uidetur esse necessitudinis quàm inter manus & oculos. Et tamen horum quoque consimilem monet, ac talem esse conditionem, ut caput ministerio pedum carere non possit. Hic non est dictio capitis ad Christum referenda, sed pluraliter ad omnes ecclesiæ præsides. De Christo nanque sentire nos haud conuenit, quod opera quorumcunque membrorum suorum egeat. Potest ille ueracissime ad omnes suos fideles dicere, non est mihi opus uobis, uos uero sine me nihil poteritis facere.
units.tr: "Again, the head," he says, "to the feet, I have no need of you." He joins the two utterly extreme members of the body, the head above and the feet below, between which there seems to be less connection than between hands and eyes. And yet he warns that these also are similar, and that the condition is such that the head cannot do without the service of the feet. Here the word head is not to be referred to Christ, but in the plural to all the presidents of the Church. For we ought not to think of Christ that he needs the works of any of his members. He can most truly say to all his faithful: I have no need of you; but you can do nothing without me.

units.la: Admonentur præsides ecclesiæ summo gradu constituti, ne non media modò, sed ne infima quidem corporis ecclesiastici membra contemnant. Caput summum quidem, pedes uero prorsus infimum locum sortiti sunt. At unde subsisteret reliquo cum corpore caput, nisi pedibus sustentaretur, qui bases sunt ac fundamentum corporis. Vnde facultas esset quouis progrediendi, currendi, ascendendi, descendendi, inclinandi, sedendi, accumbendi, surgendi, nisi pedum adminiculo hæc omnia fierent? Prorsus inutile esset uniuersum capitis ἐγκεφαλον, si inferiorum membrorum officijs destituretur. Quare non potest dicere pedibus, non est mihi opus uobis. Cogitent igitur primores cū in ecclesijs tum in regnis ac rebuspublicis, nō posse se sine inferiorum obsequijs ac ministerijs subsistere, etiamsi sint omnium sapientissimi & illustrissimi: esse autem iniquissimum cōtemnere eos, quorum opera carere nequeant, cum ne illi quidem cōtemnendi sint, quorum nullus usus esse uidetur.
units.tr: The presidents of the Church, set in the highest rank, are admonished not to despise not only the middle members of the ecclesiastical body, but not even the lowest. The head has the highest place, the feet the lowest. But how could the head stand with the rest of the body, unless it were supported by the feet, which are the base and foundation of the body? How could there be any ability to go forward, run, ascend, descend, bend, sit, recline, or rise, unless all these were done with the aid of the feet? The whole brain [ἐγκέφαλον] would be utterly useless if it were deprived of the offices of the lower members. Therefore the head cannot say to the feet, I have no need of you. Let the leaders, then, both in the churches and in kingdoms and commonwealths, consider that they cannot stand without the service and ministry of the inferiors, even if they are the wisest and most distinguished of all; and that it is most unjust to despise those without whose work they cannot manage, since not even those are to be despised whose use seems to be nil.

units.la: IMO multo potius, inquit, quæ uidentur membra corporis imbecilliora esse necessaria sunt.] Totum quidem corpus humanum imbecile est, membris infirmis constans: sunt tamen illius membra alia aliis imbecilliora, per se firmum nullum: unde recte non dixit, quæ uidentur imbecilla, sed quæ uidentur imbecil liora esse. Imbecillum est, quod facile lædi potest, eo quod minus habeat uirium uel ad resistendum uel ad ferendum. In corpore humano robustiora sunt brachia & crura, quàm oculi & uenter, quia firmioribus sunt ossibus conso-lidata, tanquam ad ferendos labores destinata. Oculi uero & uenter, quamuis infirmiora, uehementer tamē sunt necessaria membra. Significat non esse in ecclesia, quæ inferiora sunt cōtemnenda à superioribus, quandoquidem nec imbecilliora contemni debeant à robustioribus. Vt enim inferiora superioribus, ita imbecilliora robustioribus admodum esse necessaria. Impiorum ac uiolentorum uox est illud Sap.2. Quod infirmum est, inutile inuenitur. Infirma erat Apostoli inter Corinthios præsentia, & tamen erat illis uehementer necessaria. Thesaurum uitæ portabant apostoli in uasis fictilibus. At quid potuit illis inueniri pre-
units.tr: "Rather," he says, "those members of the body that seem to be weaker are necessary." The whole human body is weak, consisting of feeble members; yet some of its members are weaker than others, and none is firm in itself. Hence he rightly did not say "those that seem weak," but "those that seem to be weaker." That is weak which can easily be harmed, because it has less strength either to resist or to bear. In the human body the arms and legs are stronger than the eyes and the belly, because they are consolidated with firmer bones, as if destined to bear labours. The eyes and the belly, however weak, are nevertheless exceedingly necessary members. He signifies that there is nothing in the Church which the superiors should despise among the inferiors, since the weaker should not be despised by the stronger. For just as the inferiors are necessary to the superiors, so the weaker are very necessary to the stronger. It is the voice of the impious and violent that is in Wisdom 2: "What is weak is found to be useless." The presence of the apostle was weak among the Corinthians, and yet it was exceedingly necessary to them. The apostles carried the treasure of life in earthen vessels. But what could be found among them more pre-

units.la: {A} ... ri preciosus? Videbantur esse imbecilles iudicio carnis, at erant summopere necessarij. Hoc uolens dicit: que uidentur imbecilliora esse. Ambrosius per imbecilliora intelligit subiectos: Chrysostomo idem est imbecille & minus honestum membrum.
units.tr: {A} ...more precious? They seemed weak by the judgement of the flesh, but they were exceedingly necessary. In saying this he means: "which seem to be weaker." Ambrose understands by the weaker the subjects; for Chrysostom the weaker and less honourable member is the same thing.

units.la: ET quae putamus, inquit, minus honestae corporis, his honorem uberiorem apponimus. Per minus honesta intelligit pudenda. Inhonosta sunt illa non per se, sed nostro iudicio. Nihil enim est inhonesti a Deo creatum. Quare non dicit, Et quae sunt: sed, & quae putamus minus esse honesta corporis. Sic de illis sentimus omnes ab eo tempore, quo nuditas corporum nostrorum propter diuini praecepti transgressionem, & innocentiae amissionem pudori coepit esse obnoxia. Haec inhonestacorporis nostri honoreuberiore amicimus: hoc est, diligentius fouemus & obtegimus. Etiam gentes illae quae nudis incedunt corporibus, sic sunt animatae, ut pudenda perizomate cingant & ornent.
units.tr: "And those we think less honourable of the body, upon these we bestow more abundant honour." By less honourable he means the shameful parts. They are unhonourable not in themselves but in our judgement, for nothing created by God is dishonourable. Therefore he does not say "those that are less honourable," but "those we think to be less honourable of the body." So all of us have thought of them from that time on, when the nakedness of our bodies, because of the transgression of the divine precept and the loss of innocence, began to be subject to shame. We clothe this dishonour of our body with more abundant honour: that is, we cherish and cover it more carefully. Even those peoples who go about with naked bodies are so animated that they gird and adorn their shameful parts with a loincloth.

units.la: ET indecora nostri, inquit, copiosiorem honorem habet. Eadem puto intelligit ἀσχήμονα quae ἀτιμότερα, uel est posterius hoc ad posterius rem corporis nostri partem referendum, qua excrementa illius eijcimus. Quod ecclesiae membra concernit, putat Ambrosius intelligendos esse eos fratres, qui egestate ac nuditate sua de spicabiles incedunt.
