Puto referri posse ad eos, qui officia minus honesta, siue in ecclesia, siue in republica obeunt. Hos monet Apostolus tā non esse contemnendos ut magis sint diligenter fouendi & decorandi, ne qua fiat ut commune corpus ecclesiae si negligantur, dehonestet. Non permittimus illis qui uagam libidine sub praetextu caelibatus sectantur, ut per minus honesta & indecora intelligant coniuges procreationi liberorum operam dantes, quorum statum censent esse impurum. Est enim coniugium honorabile inter omnes, & cubile impolutum. Ebr. 13. Nec est, ut concubinas suas uocent minus honesta & indecora ecclesiae membra. Primum enim non sunt scorta referenda inter membra ecclesiae. Deinde digna non sunt quae honorifice foueantur.
units.tr: "And our unseemly parts," he says, "have more abundant honour." I think he means by "unseemly" (ἀσχήμονα) the same as "less honourable" (ἀτιμότερα). Or the latter may refer to the lower part of our body, through which we expel its waste. As far as the members of the church are concerned, Ambrose thinks that the brethren are meant who go about despised in their poverty and nakedness. I think it can also apply to those who perform duties that are less honourable, whether in the church or in the commonwealth. The Apostle warns these that they are not to be despised, but rather are to be cherished and honoured all the more diligently, lest the common body of the church be dishonoured if they are neglected. We do not allow those who follow a wandering lust under the pretext of celibacy to understand by "less honourable and unseemly" the married people who devote themselves to raising children, whose state they judge to be impure. For marriage is honourable among all, and the bed undefiled (Heb. 13.). Nor should they call their concubines "less honourable and unseemly members of the church." In the first place, prostitutes are not to be counted among the members of the church; in the second place, they are not worthy of being honourably cherished.

units.la: DECORA uero nostri, inquit, non indigent. Qualia sunt caput, facies, oculi, aures, nares, os, manus, &c. Haec non indigent, ut aliunde ornentur, cum naturale sint ornatu conspicua. Consimili modo & in ecclesia non est ulla necessitas, qua singulari a nobis cura ornentur ac decoreturij, quos spiritus sanctus uario charismatum ornatu reddidit illustres. Sunt tamen uenerandi & in precio habendi, propter singularia dona. Non enim hoc agit Apostolus, ut quos Deus cohonestat, nos susque deq; faciamus: sed taxat praepositerum illud studium, quo qui caeteris sunt praestantiores, impense colantur, & interim infirmi & humiles inferioris ac posterioris ordinis homines prorsus negligantur: quod perinde est ac si honesta corporis no stri membra, caput, oculos, &c. sumptuosius te-
units.tr: "But our comely parts," he says, "have no need." Such are the head, face, eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth, hands, and so on. These have no need to be adorned from elsewhere, since they are conspicuous by their natural beauty. In the same way, in the church there is no necessity that those whom the Holy Spirit has made illustrious with the varied adornment of gifts be adorned and honoured by us with special care. Yet they are to be revered and held in esteem on account of their singular gifts. For the Apostle is not doing this, that we should make light of those whom God honours; rather, he censures that preposterous zeal by which those who are more outstanding than the rest are lavishly courted, while meanwhile the weak and humble, men of a lower and later rank, are utterly neglected. This is just as if we were to cover and adorn the honourable parts of our body, the head, eyes, and so on, more sumptuously, and expose the unseemly parts, and neglect the feet. We usually do so. We adorn where there is no need, and neglect where there is need. We give to those who are not needy, and take no account of the needy. Hence is that saying of Christ: "To everyone who has, more will be given; from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away."

units.la: gamus ac decoremus, & pudenda detegamus, pedesq; negligamus. Sic plerunq; solemus. Or namus ubi non est opus, ubi opus est negligimus. Damus non egentibus, egentium nullam rationem habemus. Hinc est illud dictum Christi: Omni habenti datur, non habenti etiam quod habet aufertur.
units.tr: Gegen? (see [2]) — [3] is the continuation: We cover and adorn the honourable parts, and expose the unseemly ones, and neglect the feet. We usually do so. We adorn where there is no need, and where there is need we neglect. We give to those who are not needy, and take no account of the needy. Hence is that saying of Christ: "To everyone who has, more will be given; from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away."

units.la: SED Deus simul temperauit corpus, inquit, ei cui deerat copiosiorem dans eorum. In Graeco est συνεκέρασεν τὸ σῶμα, id est, commiscuit corpus. Commiscuit corpus, dum membra illius commiscuit: hoc est, sic posuit, ut infirma & ignobilia immixta sint robustioribus ac nobilioribus, perinde atq; in rebus publicis commiscentur tenuiores & ditiores, senes & iuvenes, sapientes & idiotae. Supra dixit: Nunc autem Deus posuit membra unumquodque singulatim in corpore, quemadmodum uoluit.
units.tr: "But God," he says, "has tempered the body together, giving more abundant honour to the one who lacked it." In the Greek it is συνεκέρασεν τὸ σῶμα [synekerasen to sōma], that is, he mingled the body together. He mingled the body by mingling its members: that is, he so arranged them that the weak and ignoble are mixed in with the stronger and more noble, just as in public affairs the poorer and the richer, the old and the young, the wise and the untaught, are mingled together. Above he said: "But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he willed."

units.la: Idem hic repetit, & ad propositum suum accommodat, dicens: Sed Deus commiscuit corpus, ei cui deerat copiosiorem dans honorem. Inscrutabilem prouidentiam Dei adorandam nobis in uerbo commiscendi proponit, idque non in corpore nostro tantum, sed & in uniuersa coeli ac terrae machina, in qua summa prudentia sic commiscuit omnia, ut quod per se stare non posset, uel prorsus ferri nequiret, diuersarum mixtura & stabile sit & tolerabile. Sic corpus habemus carne & ossibus, neruis ac uenis, liquido & arido, frigido & calido, membris infirmis & ualidis, nobilibus & ignobilibus commixtum: cuius stabilimentum dura non potest, si mixturę huius temperamentum soluatur.
units.tr: Here he repeats the same thing and applies it to his purpose, saying: "But God has mingled the body, giving more abundant honour to the one who lacked it." By the word "mingling" he sets before us the inscrutable providence of God, which we ought to adore, and this not only in our body but in the whole machine of heaven and earth, in which with the highest wisdom he has so mingled all things that what could not stand by itself, or could not be borne at all, is stable and tolerable through the mixture of diverse things. Thus we have a body mixed of flesh and bones, sinews and veins, liquid and dry, cold and hot, weak and strong members, noble and ignoble; and its stability could not endure if the temperament of this mixture were dissolved.

units.la: EI, inquit, cui deerat, copiosiorem dans honorem. Potest haec particula bifariam exponi. Primo, ut intelligamus de membris infirmioribus quidem, uerum iuxta praestantioribus, qualia sunt, caput, facies, oculi, &c. Illa dici possunt ὑπερέχοντα, respectu robustiorum: uerum plus honoris acceperūt, propterea quod usus ipsorum praeclarior est. Deinde sic, ut respondeant ista praecedentibus, intelligamus per membrum ὑστέρῳ, pudenda, de quibus iam meminit. Significat haec uox non modo egens aliquid, sed & posterius, sicut proteron prius. Huic membro dedit Deus, id est, deputauit, copiosiorem honorem, quo à nobis tegatur ac foueatur. Vterque sensus conuenit ecclesiae. Nam & illam sic commiscuit Deus, ut & infirmiora membra reddiderit praestantiora per singularia dona, quibus illa illustrauit, & ignobiliora ac minus honesta nostrae curae singulari studio foueda, ornandaq; commiserit. Sane sic solet Deus, ut inferiorib. ac posteriores plus gratię largiatur, ne uidelicet habeat caro, quod glorietur in conspectu ipsius, & ut ipsius exemplo admonit inferiores diligentius foueamus.
units.tr: "To the one who lacked it, giving more abundant honour," he says. This phrase can be explained in two ways. First, we may understand it of members that are indeed weaker, yet are among the more outstanding, such as the head, face, eyes, and so on. These can be called ὑπερέχοντα [hyperechonta], superior, in comparison with the stronger members; yet they have received more honour because their use is more excellent. Second, so that these words may correspond to what precedes, we may understand by the member "later" (ὑστέρῳ), the unseemly parts, of which he has already spoken. This word signifies not only "lacking something" but also "later," as πρότερον [proteron] means "earlier." To this member God gave, that is, assigned, more abundant honour, by which it is covered and cherished by us. Both senses fit the church. For God has so mingled it that he has made the weaker members more excellent through the singular gifts with which he has adorned them, and has entrusted the more ignoble and less honourable members to be cherished and adorned by our special zeal. Indeed God is accustomed to act in this way, bestowing more grace on the lower and later members, so that flesh may have no ground for boasting in his sight, and, as the example of himself, that we may cherish the lower members more diligently.

units.la: NE fit disidiū, inquit, in corpore, sed inuicē alia pro alijs eandē solicitudinē gerāt membra. In Graeco est, ne fit schisma in corpore. Hoc est, ne membra à membris diuidātur, scin daturq; corporis unitas. Reddit ratione, quare
units.tr: "That there be no division," he says, "in the body, but that the members have the same care for one another." In the Greek it is "that there be no schism [σχίσμα] in the body." That is, that the members not be divided from the members, and that the unity of the body be preserved.

units.la: Deus corpus ad hunc modum commiscuerit, ad hoc uidelicet, ut in unitate & integritate sua perfiftat. Haud enim pfiftere posset, fi scinderentur à fe inuicem mebra: scinderentur uero, fi quæ inferiora sunt quasi prorsus inutilia à superioribus desererentur, atq; ita alia aliorû cura & συνεργάς destituerétur. Vnde & subdit, sed inuicem alia pro alijs eandem folicitudiné gerant: uel, ut in Græco est, idem aliud pro alio curent membra. Quomodo autem membra corporis nostri superiora inferiorum, inferiora superiorum curam gerant, non eget declaratione, cum nemo fit qui non in fuoipfius corpore irremiffam huius experientiam capiat.
units.tr: He gives the reason why God has mingled the body in this way, namely, so that it may persist in its unity and integrity. For it could not persist if the members were torn apart from one another; they would indeed be torn apart if the lower members were abandoned by the higher as if they were wholly useless, and so the members would be deprived of one another's care and cooperation. Hence he adds: "but that the members have the same care for one another"; or, as it is in the Greek, "that the members care for one another in the same way." How the members of our body, the higher for the lower and the lower for the higher, bear care, needs no explanation, since there is no one who does not experience this constant care in his own body.

units.la: Quà uero mutua hæc membrorû cura parum loci habeat in ecclesias, quæ Christi nomé pro fitentur: quorsum attinet meminisse, cum deplorandum magis fit, quàm exponendum. Si gnificat ipsissimum esse schisma ecclesiæ, quàdo membra illius ab hac sunt mutua folicitudine aliena, quicquid tandem uerbis ac ritibus profiteantur. Vnitas nanq; & integritas ecclesiæ, non modo externa religionis, ac rituû conformitate: sed & imo amplius, mentis ac spiritus consensu, concordia, & unitate constat. Detur autem è tot millibus una ecclesia, in qua mutua ista membrorum cura uigeat, & locum hoc genus schismatis non habeat, quo plane schismatici sunt ecclesiarum capita & præsides, quorum pectora nulla inferiorum membrorum cura tanguntur.
units.tr: But how little room this mutual care of the members has in those churches that profess the name of Christ is more a matter for lamentation than for exposition. It signifies that there is a very schism of the church whenever its members are estranged from this mutual solicitude, however much they profess it in words and rites. For the unity and integrity of the church consists not only in external conformity of religion and rites, but even more in agreement of mind and spirit, concord and unity. Yet let one church be found among so many thousands in which this mutual care of the members flourishes and which has no place for this kind of schism; by contrast, the heads and presidents of churches are plainly schismatic, whose hearts are not moved by any care for the lower members.

units.la: ET fiue patitur unum membrum, inquit, simul patiuntur omnia membra. ] Et hoc inest membris corporis nostri communiter omnibus, ut nullum ex illis fuijpfius tâtum doloris sensu tâgatur, quicquid interim accidat alijs, sed omnia uni ex ipsis dolenti codoleant. Nec refert quod nam illud fit, fiue ex superioribus fiue ex inferioribus. Vniufcuiufq; membri dolor totum corpus occupat & afficit. Hanc fym pathiam indit illis eiusdem spiritus & sanguinis connexio, unde est & illud quod sequitur.
units.tr: "And if one member suffers," he says, "all the members suffer together." This is common to all the members of our body, that no member is touched only by the feeling of its own pain, whatever happens meanwhile to the others, but all of them grieve together with the one that is in pain. It makes no difference which member it is, whether from the higher or from the lower. The pain of each single member occupies and affects the whole body. This sympathy is implanted in them by the connection of the same spirit and blood, whence comes also what follows.

units.la: SIVE glorificatur unum membrum, cogau dent illi omnia membra. ] Est in illis tam læ[…] quàm tristium rerû uiuacissima & prorsus miranda communicatio. Pedes non inuident capiti fupereminentiæ gloriâ. Caput non est expers laborum ac dolorum, quibus afficiuntur pedes. Nec interiorum & exteriorum hac in re ulla est diuisio. Corde ac spiritu contrito, lugete ac dolente poftrata reduntur omnia exteriora. Pedes labascunt, manus concidut, caput demittitur, oculi illachrymatur, lingua stupet, etiamsi externo corpori nihil accidat incommodi. Corde uero ac spiritu læto & exhilarato gestiunt & exultant exteriora, pedes subsiliunt, manus plaudunt, lingua cantat, frons to ta serenatur. Rursus externo corpore, uel mor bo, uel fame, uel plagis, aut alia quapiâ læsione afflicto, contristatur spiritus, & cor affligitur. Bene autem illo constituto & suauiter affecto, condelectantur illi & interiora.
units.tr: "And if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it." There is in them a most lively and altogether wonderful sharing of joys as well as of sorrows. The feet do not envy the head the glory of its pre-eminence. The head is not free from the labours and pains by which the feet are affected. Nor is there any division between the inner and outer parts in this matter. When the heart and spirit are crushed, and mourn and grieve, all the outer parts sink down prostrate: the feet give way, the hands fall, the head droops, the eyes weep, the tongue is struck dumb, even though nothing harmful has befallen the outer body. But when the heart and spirit are glad and cheerful, the outer parts rejoice and exult: the feet leap, the hands clap, the tongue sings, the whole forehead clears. Conversely, when the outer body is afflicted by sickness, hunger, blows, or some other injury, the spirit is saddened and the heart is afflicted. But when that outer body is well settled and sweetly disposed, the inner parts also rejoice together with it.

units.la: Sunt quidem hæc omnium notissima, & ta men haud frustra ab Apostolo ecclesiæ Corinthiorum proposita. Non potuit illis ullam ueræ cöcordiæ & unitatis imaginé aptiore proponere, ad quam sese omni schismate prorsus abiecto componerent, & ad uerá eiusdem corporis ac spiritus unitatem redirét, fine qua ecclesia illorum consistere non poterat. Vt enim corporis integritas in membrorum συνχαρίας, συνγύης, συμμιγεια, & συμπαθεια, sic consistit, ut fine istis omnino periclitetur: ita & ecclesiæ integritas, fine mutuæ fidelium indigentiæ, cooperationis, cure, & compassionis communicatio ne consistere non potest. Tollitur autem colligatio ista per schismata, quibus quasi compages membrorum soluuntur. Vbi hæc in ecclesia obtinent, ibi dicit caput pedibus, & oculus manibus, nõ est mihi opus uobis, ibi infirmiora & ignobiliora contemuuntur; ibi nulla est συμμιγεια, nulla συμπαθεια, ibi inferiora superioribus omnem quam habent gloriam, inuidet, & propter contemptû prorsus abiecta iacent. Quàm autem exitiosum fit toti ecclesiæ, fi membrum à membro deferatur, & quàm diaboli cum, fi membra membris omnem commoditatem & gloriam inuideant, cordatiores facile intelligunt. Non intelligebant hoc Corinthij, quare tam multis táq; diligenter huius ab Apostolo admonentur. Et utinam hodie intelligant, qui foli in ecclesia sapere uidentur.
units.tr: These things are indeed very well known to everyone, and yet the Apostle did not set them before the church of the Corinthians without good reason. He could not have offered them a more fitting image of true harmony and unity, by which they might compose themselves, utterly casting off every schism, and return to the true unity of the same body and spirit, without which their church could not stand. For just as the integrity of the body consists in the members' mutual rejoicing [συνχαρίας], joint service [συνγύης], mingling [συμμιγεια], and sympathy [συμπαθεια], so that without these it is altogether endangered, so the integrity of the church cannot exist without the sharing of mutual need, cooperation, care, and compassion among the faithful. But this bond is destroyed by schisms, which loosen the joints of the members as it were. Where these prevail in a church, the head says to the feet, "I have no need of you," and the eye to the hands; there the weaker and less honourable are despised; there is no mingling, no sympathy; there the inferiors envy the superiors all the glory they have, and lie cast down through contempt. How ruinous it is to the whole church if one member is torn from another, and how much more so if members envy one another every advantage and glory, the more discerning easily understand. The Corinthians did not understand this, which is why they are admonished by the Apostle so often and so carefully. And would that those who alone seem to be wise in the church today understood it.

units.la: Obserua uero, quod postquam dixit, Et fiue patitur unum membrum, simul patiuntur omnia membra: tum demum subijcit, fiue glorificatur unum membrû, congaudent omnia membra. Licet in corporibus nostris, non hinc congaudent inferiora superioribus, quod curam illorum, & compassionem sentiunt, sed faciût hoc naturali motu, & instinctu etiam fi superiora officium suum negligerent: in ecclesia ta men magnum est incitamentum inferioribus ad hoc, ut commoditati ac gloriæ superiorum ex animo congaudeant, fi senserint illos afflictionibus suis codolere, & curam necessitatis ipsorum fideliter gerere. Cum autê diuersum in illis hodie experiantur, mirû non est, quod honoribus illorum haudquaquam cógauder, sed usque adeo inuident, ut prouerbio apud Germanos, Laici odio doctos ac clericos prosequi dicantur.
units.tr: Notice, moreover, that after he said, "If one member suffers, all the members suffer together," only then does he add, "if one member is honoured, all the members rejoice together." In our bodies the lower parts do not rejoice with the higher because they feel their care and compassion; they do so by natural movement and instinct, even if the higher parts neglect their duty. In the church, however, there is a great incentive for the inferiors to rejoice from the heart in the advantage and glory of the superiors, if they have felt that the superiors grieve with their afflictions and faithfully attend to their needs. Since today they experience the opposite from them, it is no wonder that they do not rejoice at all in their honours, but envy them to such a degree that, as the proverb goes among the Germans, the laity are said to pursue the learned and the clergy with hatred.

units.la: Vos autem estis corpus Christi, & membra ex parte. Et alios quidem posuit Deus in ecclesia primum Apostolos, deinde prophetas, tertio doctores, deinde potestates, deinde dona sanationum, subsidia, gubernationes, genera linguarum.
units.tr: You, however, are the body of Christ, and members in part. And God has indeed set some in the church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, and kinds of tongues.

units.la: Imaginem ecclesiæ in corpore humano, ac membris illius spectandam proponens, ea in illa hactenus depinxit, quæ ad propositum facere iudicauit. Iam ut applicationem absoluat, quàm supra cœperat dices, sic & Christus, etenim in uno spiritu, nos omnes in unum corpus baptizati famus, &c. subijcit dicens: Vos autem estis corpus Christi,& membra ex par- te,&c Totius autem disputationis huius cum duae sint principales partes:una, quid sint fide les Corinthij,ad quos scribit:altera,quomodo inter se mutuo animati & affecti esse debeant, priorem tamen duntaxat in applicatione hac exprimit, qua dicit eos esse corpus Christi, & membra ex parte,& membra uaria,& à Deo in ecclesiam posita:posteriorem uero,quoniá ultro ex priori consequitur,& in imagine corporis,& membrorum diligenter expressa est, cogitandam ipsis relinquit.Dicit itaq;:
units.tr: Setting before us the image of the church in the human body and its members to be contemplated, he has so far portrayed in it those things which he judged to serve his purpose. Now, to complete the application, which he had begun above, saying, "so also Christ; for in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body," etc., he adds: "You, however, are the body of Christ, and members in part," etc. Of this whole discussion there are two main parts: one, what the Corinthians, to whom he writes, are; the other, how they ought to be mutually moved and disposed toward one another. In this application, however, he expresses only the former, saying that they are the body of Christ, and members in part, and various members, and set in the church by God; the latter, since it follows of its own accord from the former, and has been carefully expressed in the image of the body and its members, he leaves for them to think about. So he says:

units.la: VOS autem estis corpus Christi,] Quomodo facti sint corpus Christi, suprà expositum dicens:Etenim in uno spiritu nos omnes in unū corpus baptizati sumus. Quod illic in genere dixit,hic ad illos specificat.Cum aut dicit:Vos estis corpus Christi, simul eos omniū eorum admonet,que corpori ac membris tribuit. Quasi dicat:Ergo uehementer in eo peccatis, quod unitatem ecclesiae Christi scinditis, membrorum illius euertitis,qui superiores estis inferiores contemnitis, qui inferiores habemini superiorib. inuidetis.Poterat dicere,uos autem estis ecclesia Christi:uerum ut praemissorum eos admonet dicit:Vos autem estis corpus Christi.
units.tr: "You, however, are the body of Christ." How they became the body of Christ he has stated above, saying: "For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body." What he said there in general, he here applies specifically to them. When he says, "You are the body of Christ," he at the same time reminds them of all the things he ascribed to the body and its members. As if he said: "Therefore you sin greatly in this, that by dividing the unity of Christ's church you overthrow its members: you who are superiors despise the inferiors, and you who are considered inferiors envy the superiors." He could have said, "You, however, are the church of Christ"; but to remind them of what has gone before, he says, "You, however, are the body of Christ."

units.la: Eccius in locis suis citat haec uerba ad probandū ecclesiam Christi esse unam,ideoq; non scindendam,& extra hanc nemini constare salutem,quae si de uera Christi ecclesia intelligatur,nō negamus.Scimus illam esse unicā tanquā Christi corpus,fatemur non esse scinden- dam,nec diffitemur extra illā,quatenus Christi corpus est,non posse saluari quenquam, nō propter ipsorum membrorum,sed propter capitis Christi cohaesionem.Si uero referātur ad ecclesiam maligne agentium, ad defectricem & adulteram,sanguinariam, & cultibus eidolorū conspurcatam,diserte ad hanc ea pertinere negamus,quae non Christi corpus est,sed cō spiratio hominum seducentium & seductorū.
units.tr: Eck, in his places, cites these words to prove that the church of Christ is one, and therefore must not be divided, and that outside it no one can be saved. If this is understood of the true church of Christ, we do not deny it. We know that it is one, as the body of Christ; we confess that it must not be divided; and we do not deny that, insofar as it is the body of Christ, no one can be saved outside it, not because of the members themselves, but because of their cohesion with Christ the head. But if these words are referred to the church of those who act wickedly, to the apostate and adulterous, the bloodthirsty, and the one defiled by idolatrous worship, we expressly deny that these words pertain to that which is not the body of Christ but a conspiracy of men who seduce and are seduced.

units.la: ET membra,inquit,ex parte.]Vulgata editio habet,& membra de membro. Annotarunt & Valla & Erasmus interpretem hunc legisse, id est, membrū ex membro, pro id est,membrum ex parte. Dixit eos esse corpus Christi,quo de unitate cum capite Christo seruanda admonerentur.Addit eos esse membra quoque.Erant quidem corpus Christi,quia membra illius erant. Verum sepa ratim eos membra esse monet, quo de unitate quoq; inter ipsos,tanquā unius corporis membra haud scindenda commonefaciat. Vsitata est uox ecclesiae, & hodie quoque plurimum iactata, sed quotusquisq; est, qui se membrum cum alijs membris Christi esse serio cogitet,& quae membri sunt erga reliqua membra secundum leges membrorum praestet? Duo sunt membrorū respectus, ad caput unus, ad socia connexaque membra alter. Vtrosq; complexus est dicens:Vos autem estis corpus Christi & membra.
units.tr: "And members," he says, "in part." The Vulgate edition has "and members of a member." Valla and Erasmus have noted that this translator read it as "member out of member," in place of "member in part." He called them the body of Christ, so that they might be reminded to keep their unity with Christ the head. He adds that they are also members. They were indeed the body of Christ, because they were its members. But he reminds them separately that they are members, so that he may also remind them of unity among themselves, as members of one body which must not be divided. The language of the church is commonly used, and is still much bandied about today; but how few are there who seriously consider that they are a member along with the other members of Christ, and who render what belongs to members toward the remaining members according to the laws of the members? There are two respects of members: one to the head, the other to the companion and connected members. He embraces both in saying: "You, however, are the body of Christ and members."

units.la: Si legeris, Et membra de membro: sensus est, Et membra, quorum aliud ab alio pedet, aliud alij sic connexum est, ut uelut ex illo prouenisse uideatur. Sic sane in ecclesia membra corporis Christi inter se cohaerent, & connexu spiritus inuicem alligantur, ut recte membra ex membris uocari queant.Quare admodum crudelis est ea membrorum diuisio, quae in ecclesia fit per schismata.Quisnā patienti oculo humani posset corporis eam cernere direptione, qua membrum a membro discerperetur? At reuera multo crudelius est spectaculum, ubi hoc membris corporis Christi per schismata contingit.
units.tr: If you read, "and members of a member," the sense is: "and members, one of which hangs from another, and one is so connected to another that it seems to have proceeded from it as if from it." Thus indeed in the church the members of the body of Christ cohere with one another and are bound together by the bond of the Spirit, so that they may rightly be called members of members. Therefore that division of the members which occurs in the church through schisms is very cruel. Who could behold with a patient eye that tearing apart of the human body by which a member is torn from a member? Yet in truth a far more cruel spectacle is seen when this happens to the members of Christ's body through schisms.

units.la: Si uero placet,ut legas,& membra ex parte, aliter atq; aliter exponi potest.
units.tr: If, however, you prefer to read "and members in part," it can be explained in one way or another.

units.la: 1 Primo secundum sententiam Chrysostomi ad hunc modum: Quod dico uos esse corpus & membra Christi,non sic dico,quod in uobis totum Christi corpus compleatur.Nam illud non uestram tantum, sed omnes in uniuersum ecclesias coplectitur. Quare corpus & membra Christi estis ex parte.Hoc sensu connectit eos,non inter se modo,sed & cum reliquis omnibus Christi ecclesijs.
units.tr: (1) First, according to the opinion of Chrysostom, in this way: When I say that you are the body and members of Christ, I do not mean that the whole body of Christ is complete in you. For it embraces not only your church but all the churches together. Therefore you are the body and members of Christ in part. In this sense he connects them not only with one another but also with all the other churches of Christ.

units.la: 2 Deinde ad hunc modum uos corpus Christi estis,& membra ex parte,id est, ex aliqua parte, quodammodo, aliquatenus, qua parte uidelicet similes estis corpori ac membri illius, uel quatenus illi estis fide ac spiritu coniuncti.
units.tr: (2) Second, in this way: you are the body of Christ and members in part, that is, in some respect, in a certain way, to some extent; namely, in that respect in which you are indeed like the body and member of that body, or insofar as you are joined to him by faith and Spirit.

units.la: 3 Tertio sic.Vos corpus Christi estis & membra ex parte:hoc est,non omnes,sed aliqua uestri parte.Sic eximuntur ab hoc praedicato reprobi, de quibus praedicari non potest, quod membra sint corporis Christi, & includuntur fideles,ac probi tantum,de quibus suprà cap. praecedēti dixit:oportet hereses esse inter uos, ut qui probi sunt,manifesti fiant.
units.tr: (3) Third, thus: you are the body of Christ and members in part, that is, not all of you, but some part of you. In this way the reprobate, of whom it cannot be said that they are members of the body of Christ, are excluded from this predicate, and the faithful and upright alone are included, of whom he said in the preceding chapter: "There must be heresies among you, so that those who are upright may become manifest."

units.la: 4 Quarto sic,ut idem sit quod, id est, particulariter. Hoc est, non in genere modo corpus estis Christi,sed & singulatim & particulariter estis illius membra, unusquisque uestrum membrum est corporis illius, siue sit infirmus, siue fortis, siue superior, siue inferior, siue ignobilis,siue nobilis. Meo iudicio haud opus est accuratiore discretione in hisce expositionibus,quandoquidem nulla illorum sic est comparata,ut admodum a mente Apostoli abducat.
units.tr: (4) Fourth, thus, so that "in part" means the same as "particularly," that is, individually. That is: you are the body of Christ not only in general, but also singly and particularly you are its members; each one of you is a member of that body, whether he is weak or strong, superior or inferior, of humble or of noble birth. In my judgment there is no need for more exact distinction in these explanations, since none of them is framed in such a way as to lead far from the Apostle's mind.

units.la: Et alios posuit Deus in ecclesia, inquit, primum Apostolos,deinde prophetas,tertio doctores,&c.]Recensetaliquot officia,quibus ecclesiam suam Deus, tum temporis & ornabat & instructam reddebat. Dixit quidem:uos estis corpus Christi & membra ex parte,uel singulatim:uerum subijcit, non membrorum, ut membrorum, sed quorundam officiorum recensionem, quae Deus in usum membrorum omnium in ecclesia sua posuerat.Recensset autem ea cum distinctione ac uariationis specificatione non simpliciter dicés: Et posuit Deus
units.tr: "And God has set some in the Church," he says, "first apostles, secondly prophets, thirdly teachers, etc." He lists several offices by which God at that time both adorned his Church and furnished it. He had said indeed, "you are the body of Christ and members in part, or individually," but he now adds a listing not of members as members, but of certain offices, which God had appointed in his Church for the use of all the members.

units.la: in ecclesia sua, apostolos, prophetas, doctores, &c. sed: Et alios posuit Deus in ecclesia, primum apostolos, deinde prophetas, tertio doctores, &c. Vbi uocula discretiua Alios, quam praemisit, ad singulos est repetenda, quemadmodum illam ad Ephesios 4. singulis affixit, dicens: Et idem dedit alios quidem apostolos, alios uero prophetas, alios autem Euangelistas, alios autem pastores ac doctores. Et quoniam catalogum hunc ponit, non tanquam membrorum, sed tanquam officiorum, non dicit, Et alios posuit Deus in corpore Christi: sed, & alios posuit in ecclesia. Nec dicit, Et alios posuit inter uos: sed, in ecclesia generaliter. Neq; enim in ipsorum tantum ecclesiam haec erant a Deo posita officia.
units.tr: He lists them with a distinction and a specification of variety, not simply saying, "God has set in his Church apostles, prophets, teachers, etc.," but "God has set some in the Church: first apostles, secondly prophets, thirdly teachers, etc." The discriminating particle "some," which he has put first, is to be repeated for each one, just as he attached it to each one in Ephesians 4, saying: "And he gave some indeed as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, and some as ministers and teachers." And since he sets out this catalogue not as members but as offices, he does not say "God has set some in the body of Christ," but "has set some in the Church." Nor does he say "has set some among you," but "in the Church" in general. For these offices were appointed by God not only for their own congregation.

units.la: ET posuit Deus, inquit. Non igitur ecclesia apostolos, prophetas, &c. sed Deus in ecclesia posuit. Quae hic recensentur officia, sic sunt comparata, ut nullum eorum ab ecclesia, sed ab ipso Deo duntaxat poni possit. Ponit Deus huiusmodi ecclesiae suae officiales, non modo eligendo ac mittendo, sed & spiritu suo instruendo, quod in potestate ecclesiae esse non potest.
units.tr: "And God has set," he says. So it is not the Church that set apostles, prophets, etc., but God who set them in the Church. The offices listed here are of such a kind that none of them can be instituted by the Church, but only by God himself. God appoints such officers of his Church not only by choosing and sending them, but also by instructing them by his Spirit, which cannot be in the power of the Church.

units.la: ET posuit Deus. Solet uerbum ponendi usurpari pro firma eorum constitutione, qui muneri alicui praeficiuntur. Hic uero non sic usurpatur, ut officia quae recensentur, perpetua firmitudine in ecclesiam posita esse dicantur. Initio ad tempus aliquod posita fuerunt a Deo, donec doctrina Euangelij spargeretur & confirmaretur in orbe terrarum: postea uero defecerunt, cessantibus spiritualibus charismatis.
units.tr: "And God has set." The verb "to set" is commonly used of the firm installation of those who are placed over some office. Here, however, it is not used in such a way that the offices listed are said to have been placed in the Church with lasting firmness. At the beginning they were appointed by God for a certain time, until the teaching of the gospel was spread and confirmed in the world; afterwards, however, they ceased, when the spiritual gifts ceased.

units.la: PRIMVM, inquit, apostolos. Quando, quo modo, quo numero, & in quo usum positi sunt apostoli, notius est ex Euangelicis literis, quam ut sit hic memorandum.
units.tr: "First," he says, "apostles." When, how, in what number, and for what use the apostles were appointed is better known from the evangelical writings than it needs to be recalled here.

units.la: Obiter obserua, quod apostolos a Deo dicit esse positos, cum Christus ad illos dixerit, Ioannis.15. Non uos me elegistis, sed ego elegi uos, & posui uos, ut eatis & fructum afferatis, &c. Ergo quos Christus posuit, Deus posuit.
units.tr: Note in passing that he says the apostles were appointed by God, since Christ said to them (John 15): "You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit," etc. Therefore whom Christ appointed, God appointed.

units.la: Sonat autem Apostolus missum ac legatum, quod nominis specialiter ipsis propterea est a Christo ipso impositum, quod esset eos tanquam regni sui legatos, inde e Ierusalem totum missurus in orbem, ad Euangelizadum pacem tam Gentibus quam Iudaeis. Hos cum post resurrectionem in coelos ascensurus amadabat, sic dicebat: Ite in orbe universum, praedicate Euangelium omni creaturae.
units.tr: The word "apostle" means one sent or an envoy, and Christ himself gave them this name especially because they were to be his envoys of his kingdom, which he was going to send from Jerusalem into the whole world to proclaim the peace of the gospel to Gentiles as well as Jews. When he was about to ascend into heaven after the resurrection, he addressed them thus: "Go into all the world, preach the gospel to every creature."

units.la: Quare uel Petrus apostolus no satisfecit uocationi & apostolatui suo, si Romae sedit primus episcopus, annos uiginti quatuor, uel impudentissimum commentum est, quod hoc de illo tradunt. Deinde inedicibilis temeritas est, quapropter commetitium Petri episcopatum uniuersalem Christi ecclesiam, Romanae sedi subijciunt, atque ita quantum in ipsis est reliquorum apostolorum uocationem, apostolatum & ecclesias Christo lucrifactas repudiat, & a Christo excludunt, quasi solus Petrus positus fuerit in ecclesia apostolus. Sed audiant hic: Et posuit Deus, inquit, in ecclesia, non dicit, apostolum Petrum: sed in genere, apostolos. Qui posuit Petrum, posuit & Bartholomeum, & Andream, & Thomam, & Iacobum, & Ioannem, &c. Et posuit eos non minus in ecclesia, quam Petrum. An solus Petrus egressus est in orbem ad praedicandum Euangelium regni?
units.tr: Therefore either the apostle Peter did not fulfil his calling and apostolate if he sat as first bishop at Rome for twenty-four years, or the story they tell of this is a most shameless fiction. Then there is an unspeakable rashness in that they subject the universal Church of Christ to the Roman see by a pretended episcopate of Peter, and so, as far as they are concerned, they reject the calling and apostolate of the other apostles and the churches won for Christ, and exclude them from Christ, as if Peter alone had been set in the Church as apostle. But let them hear this: "And God has set," he says, "in the Church." He does not say "the apostle Peter," but in general "apostles." He who appointed Peter also appointed Bartholomew, and Andrew, and Thomas, and James, and John, etc. And he appointed them in the Church no less than Peter. Did Peter alone go out into the world to preach the gospel of the kingdom?

units.la: Absit: Illi autem, inquit Marcus, egressi praedicauerunt ubique, domino cooperante, & sermonem confirmante sequentibus signis. Cum dicit, praedicauerunt ubique, non intelligit tantum de Europa, & parte Asiae: sed & de Aphrica, Aegypto, Syria, Persia, & utraque India, cum aliis provinciis ac regnis. Ergo non est altera Romanae urbis ecclesia, inquit Hieronymus ad Euagrium, altera totius orbis exsisti manda. Et Galliae, & Britanniae, & Aphrica, & Persis, & Orien & India, & omnes barbarae nationes unum Christum adorant, unam observant regulam veritatis.
units.tr: Far from it. "But they," says Mark, "going out, preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word with the signs that followed." When he says "they preached everywhere," he does not mean only Europe and part of Asia, but also Africa, Egypt, Syria, Persia, both Indies, and other provinces and kingdoms. Therefore, says Jerome to Evagrius, there is not one church of the city of Rome and another of the whole world. Gaul, Britain, Africa, Persia, the East and India, and all barbarian nations adore one Christ and observe one rule of truth.

units.la: Si authoritas quaeritur, orbis maior est urbe. Haec ille palam contra Romanae ecclesiae primatum, cuius iam tum studia glisccebant. Notanter non dicit, Vnum apostolum adorant: uel, unum apostolum obseruant: sed, unum Christum adorant, & unam veritatis regulam obseruant.
units.tr: "If authority is sought, the world is greater than the city." Here he openly speaks against the primacy of the Roman Church, whose ambitions were already growing at that time. Notably he does not say "they adore one apostle" or "they observe one apostle," but "they adore one Christ and observe one rule of truth."

units.la: DEINDE prophetas, inquit. Quoniam secundo loco prophetas inter apostolos & doctores ponit, exiitimo hic intelligendum esse de prophetis, qui futura praedicebant. Alias prophetae uocantur & illi, qui loquuntur ad populum, uel exhortantes, uel corripientes, uel sacras scripturas exponentes, de quibus infra cap.14.
units.tr: "Then prophets," he says. Since in second place he puts prophets between apostles and teachers, I think here must be understood the prophets who foretold future things. Otherwise those are also called prophets who speak to the people, either exhorting, or rebuking, or expounding the sacred Scriptures, of whom more below, in chapter 14.

units.la: TERTIO, doctores. Non recenseт accurate omnia ministrorum Christi officia. Nam Ephes.4. Prophetis subijcit Euangelistas & pastores, ac tum ponit doctores. Apparet autem doctores eosdem esse, quos illic & pastores uocat. Manifesta uox est, ut intelligamus doctores esse qui docent in ecclesia. Hoc munus erat episcoporum et presbyterorum, qui & metaphorica uoce, pastores uocabantur, quos Apostoli ecclesijs a se plantatis praeficiebant, & tamen Act.20. hic Paulus a spiritu sancto, ad id positos esse dixit, ut ecclesiam Dei pasceret, quod non potest, nisi de doctrina uerbi intelligi. Sed hac de re in Locis nostris accuratius discemus, ubi de ministris uerbi dicendum erat. Meo iudicio angustius est, si referamus hac particulam ad catechistas & doctores scholarum ecclesiasticarum, qualis Origenes fuisse scribitur. Si generalis sensus placet, includi possunt & illi: si uero specialis tenendus est, intelligendos puto pastores, episcopos & presbyteros. Doctoribus illis titularibus, theologis, magistris nostris, Romano pontifici adiuratis, nihil hic loci est, quia de illis praedicari non potest, quod a Deo sint in ecclesia positi. Quare sae-penu-
units.tr: "Thirdly, teachers." He does not list accurately all the offices of Christ's ministers. For in Ephesians 4 he adds evangelists and pastors after the prophets, and then names teachers. It appears, however, that the teachers are the same as those he there calls pastors. The expression is plain, so that we understand teachers to be those who teach in the Church. This office belonged to bishops and elders, who were also called pastors by a metaphorical word, and whom the apostles set over the churches they had planted; and yet in Acts 20 Paul says that they were set by the Holy Spirit to feed the Church of God, which cannot be understood except of teaching the word. But we shall learn more precisely about this matter in our Loci, where we had to speak of the ministers of the Word. In my judgment it is narrower if we refer this particle to catechists and teachers of church schools, such as Origen is written to have been. If the general sense is preferred, they can be included too; but if the special sense is to be kept, I think pastors, bishops and elders are meant. Those titular teachers, theologians, our masters, sworn to the Roman pontiff, have no place here, because it cannot be said of them that they have been set in the Church by God. Wherefore I have often-

units.la: {A} Sed in Latino exemplari. Vide.
units.tr: {A} But in the Latin exemplar. See.

units.la: penumero admiratus sum, quid sibi nonnulli insignes Christi ministri uelint, quod de titulo Academici doctoratus, tantopere gloriantur, quasi aliquid authoritatis ex illo doctrinae ipsorum accedat.
units.tr: I have often wondered what some distinguished ministers of Christ want with the title of academic doctorate, about which they boast so much, as if some authority accrued to their teaching from it.

units.la: Collegia Canonicorum hoc plerunq; in consueto habent, ut muneri docendi in cathedralibus ecclesijs non praeficiant, nisi ab Academia aliqua titulo doctoratus insignitum.
units.tr: Colleges of canons commonly have this custom: they do not appoint to the duty of teaching in cathedral churches anyone who has not been honoured by some academy with the title of doctor.

units.la: Quàm autem illi diuersi sint à doctoribus ueris, & àDeo in ecclesia positis, nulla puto opus habere declaratione. Quid illi quaerant ignoro, qui cum sint in ecclesia Christi ueri doctores, ac recte doceant, sintq; ad id muneris legitime uocati, nihilo tamen secius titulum doctoratus in Academijs ambiunt, quasi sine illo doctores esse nequeant.
units.tr: How far those men differ from true teachers, and from those set in the Church by God, I think needs no explanation. I do not know what those men seek who, although they are true teachers in the Church of Christ, teach rightly, and are lawfully called to this office, nonetheless seek the title of doctor in the academies, as if they could not be teachers without it.

units.la: DEINDE potestates, inquit.] Graece est δυνάμεις, id est, potentias, quemadmodum eam uocem & supra uertit Erasmus, dum ἐνεργήματα δυνάμεων reddidit efficacias potentiarum. De il lis hic quoq; loquitur. Vide q; supra sint dicta.
units.tr: "Then powers," he says. In Greek it is δυνάμεις [dynameis], that is, powers, as Erasmus also translated this word above, when he rendered ἐνεργήματα δυνάμεων [energēmata dynameōn] as "efficacies of powers." He speaks here of these as well. See what has been said above.

units.la: DEINDE dona sanationum, inquit.] Et de his supra dictum est, ubi efficacijs potetiarum praemittuntur.
units.tr: "Then gifts of healings," he says. This too was said above, where it is put after "efficacies of powers."

units.la: SVB SIDIA inquit.] Vulgata aeditio habet opitulationes, Graece est ἀντιλήψεις. Significat autem ἀντιλαμβάνω, manu quempiam è regione porrecta in ferendo onere adiutare. Chrysost. exponit de illis, qui infirmis opitulantur. Lyranus sic: Opitulationes, quantum ad illos qui ferunt opem maioribus praelatis, cuiusmodi sunt decani, archidiaconi. Hodie cum sint magni illi praelati ociosi in ecclesia uentres, non uideo quomodo uicarij & officiales, & decani ipsorum ἀντιλήψεις uocari queant. Etenim ubi nō est ἀντίληψις, ubi locum non habet ἀντιλήψις, & qui non est ἀντιλήπτωρ, huic dari non potest ἀντιλήματων: quemadmodum ei qui non operatur, cooperarius esse nemo potest. Haud diffiteor quidé, intelligi posse de illis, qui Apostolis & presbyteris ecclesiarum in opere domini laborantib. opem tulerunt. Simul tamen haud displiceret Chrysostomi expositio, propter uerba Apostoli huius, quibus Act. 20. ad episcopos Ephesinae ecclesiae dixit: Omnia ostendi uobis quod sic laborantib. oportet ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι τῶν ἀσθενῶν, id est adiuuare: uel, ut uerterunt, suscipere infirmos, nisi hoc genus boni operis non esset peculiaris officij, aut charismatis, sed generaliter ad omnes pertineret Christianos, & hic specialia officia & charismata recenserentur. Sunt qui putent fuisse in ecclesia quosdam ad hoc specialiter deputatos, ut causas fratrum in se susciperent, & pro singulari prudentia ac dexteritate, qua dono spiritus pollebant, agerent & expedirent, quorum sententia probabilis esse uidetur. At hodie quale sit hoc hominum genus, quos procuratores uocant, nimis norunt qui experiuntur.
units.tr: "Helps," he says. The Vulgate edition has "assistances," the Greek is ἀντιλήψεις [antilēpseis]. The verb ἀντιλαμβάνω [antilambanō] means to help someone by stretching out a hand from the side in bearing a burden. Chrysostom explains it of those who help the weak. Lyranus thus: "Assistances, as far as concerns those who bring aid to greater prelates, such as deans and archdeacons." Today, since those great prelates are idle bellies in the Church, I do not see how their vicars and officials and deans can be called ἀντιλήψεις [antilēpseis]. For where there is no ἀντίληψις [antilēpsis], where ἀντίληψις has no place, and one who is not ἀντιλήπτωρ [antilēptōr] cannot be given ἀντιλήμψεως [antilēpseōs], just as no one can be a co-worker with one who does not work. I do not deny that it can be understood of those who gave aid to the apostles and elders of the churches labouring in the Lord's work. At the same time Chrysostom's exposition would not displease, on account of the words of this same apostle, in which in Acts 20 he said to the bishops of the Ephesian church: "I have shown you all things, that so labouring you ought to ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι τῶν ἀσθενῶν [antilambanesthai tōn asthenōn], that is, to help; or, as they have translated, to receive the weak." Unless this kind of good work were not a special office or gift, but pertained generally to all Christians, and here special offices and gifts were being listed. There are some who think that in the Church there were certain men specially appointed for this, to take upon themselves the causes of the brothers and to conduct and settle them by the singular prudence and skill which they possessed by a gift of the Spirit; their opinion seems probable. But what sort of men today those are whom they call procurators, those who have experience of them know all too well.

units.la: GVBERNATIONES, inquit.] Singulare donum est, instructum esse ad gubernandu ecclesiam Dei. Homines erant sapientia & intelligentia rerum praestantes, aetate matura ac graues aspectu, qui in senatum ecclesiae sublecti magno cum pondere inter fratrem & fratrem iudicabant, quorum mentionem Tertullianus in Apologetico suo facit dicens: Ibi sedent probati quinq; seniores, & iudicant magno cum pondere. Tales sunt hodie, quos consistorio, ut uocant, praefici uidemus, in quibus adhuc aliqua sunt ueteris ecclesiae, uel si mauis, ecclesiasticae gubernationis uestigia.
units.tr: GOVERNMENTS, he says. It is a special gift to be equipped to govern the Church of God. These were men who excelled in wisdom and understanding, mature in age and grave in appearance, who were raised into the senate of the Church and judged between brother and brother with great authority. Tertullian mentions them in his Apologeticus, saying: "There sit five approved elders, and they judge with great authority." Such are the men whom we see set over what they now call the consistory, and in these there are still some traces of the old Church, or, if you prefer, of ecclesiastical government.

units.la: Admonet nos hae uoces, ἀντιλήψεις καὶ ἀνθρώπων εστι, de conditione ecclesiae, qua fit ut propter imperitos, rudes, infirmos, & egenos opus habeat opitulatoribus, ac gubernatoribus. Gubernandi uox proprie competit illis, qui naui gantibus praesunt, quam Lucas in Actis capite 27. usurpauit dicens: Centurio autem gubernatori & nauclero magis credebat, quàm his quae à Paulo dicebantur. Et ecclesiae igitur suae dominus, uelut in pelago nauiganti subinde dedit gubernatores, quorum sapientia in medio gentium incredularum gubernaretur, & ipsius inter se membra componerentur ac dirigerentur.
units.tr: These words, "helps and governments" [ἀντιλήψεις καὶ κυβερνήσεις], remind us of the condition of the Church, namely that because of the unskilled, the weak, the needy and the ignorant it needs helpers and governors. The word "government" properly belongs to those who preside over a ship, and Luke used it in Acts chapter 27, saying: "The centurion, however, trusted the helmsman and the shipmaster more than what was said by Paul." So the Lord of his Church, as it were, has from time to time given governors to a Church sailing on the open sea, so that it might be steered amid the unbelieving nations, and so that its members might be arranged and directed among themselves.

units.la: Quemadmodum enim gubernator nauigij & nauem contra uim uentorum ac procellarum moderatur, & eorum qui in naui sunt curam gerit, illosq; in pace retinet: ita & gubernatores ecclesiae, cum erga exteros illam tuentur, tum membra illius regunt, ac sic moderantur, ut & honeste & pie in pace & concordia conuersentur. Hoc quidem praestare poterunt, qui à Deo in ecclesia ponuntur: uerum qui nō à Deo, sed aliunde constituuntur, ecclesiam illi magis subuertunt, quàm gubernant.
units.tr: For just as the helmsman of a ship steers the vessel against the force of winds and storms, takes care of those who are on board, and keeps them safe in calm, so the governors of the Church both defend it against outsiders and rule its members, guiding them so that they may live honourably and piously in peace and harmony. Those whom God places in the Church are able to do this. But those who are set up not by God but from some other source overturn the Church rather than govern it.

units.la: At haec est fors ecclesiae, ut imperitis gubernatoribus subijciatur. Quibus nauigàdum est in mari, diligentisime cauetur, ne cui nauis gubernatio credatur, quem non certo sciant ad id esse muneris idoneum, & sufficienter periti. At ecclesiae Christi gubernacula pueris etiā & ignauis committuntur. Interea admodum securi, nauiculam Petri submergi non posse ia ctant. Caeci non uident, & infensati non sentiunt, quantum immineat ei ecclesiae exitium, quam Petro assignant.
units.tr: Yet this is the misfortune of the Church, that it is placed under unskilled governors. When men must sail on the sea, the greatest care is taken that the steering of a ship is not entrusted to anyone whom they do not know for certain to be fit for the task and sufficiently experienced. But the rudders of Christ's Church are committed even to boys and to lazy men. Meanwhile, quite carefree, they boast that Peter's little boat cannot be sunk. The blind do not see, and the foolish do not perceive, how great a ruin hangs over that Church which they assign to Peter.

units.la: GENERA linguarum, inquit.] De hoc charismate dictum est supra, ubi dixit, Alij uero genera linguarum.
units.tr: KINDS OF TONGUES, he says. This gift was spoken of above, where he said: "to others, kinds of tongues."

units.la: An sunt omnes apostoli? an omnes prophetae? an omnes doctores? an omnes potestates? an omnes dona habent sanationum? an omnes linguis loquuntur? an omnes interpretantur?
units.tr: Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all having powers? Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?

units.la: Qd' dixit: Et alios quidé posuit Deo in ecclesia primū apostolos, deinde prophetas, &c. Id iá ex reipsa uerū esse contendit & comprobat dicens: An sunt omnes apostoli? an omnes prophetae, &c. Quasi dicat: An non reipsa distributionem donorum Dei, & officiorum talem esse uidetis, ut nemini omnia, sed alijs alia sint data? Inspicite apostolos. Súntne omnes apostoli? utique uidetis non omnes esse apostolos. Inspicite prophetas. An donum prophetiæ concessum est omnibus? Nequaquam omnibus, sed nonnullis paucis. Doctores uidete. An facultas docendi tradita est omnibus? Non esse traditam omnibus, reipfa uidetis. Transite ad reliqua charismata, potentiæ, fanationum, linguarum, & interpretationis. An horum aliquot omnibus factum est commune? Videtis non esse, sed alij aliud esse datum.
units.tr: What he said was: "And God has set some in the Church, first apostles, secondly prophets," and so on. Now he maintains and proves that this is true in fact, saying: "Are all apostles? Are all prophets?" as if to say: Do you not see for yourselves that the distribution of God's gifts and offices is such that not all have everything, but different people have been given different things? Look at the apostles. Are all apostles? Clearly you see that not all are apostles. Look at the prophets. Has the gift of prophecy been granted to everyone? By no means to all, but to a few. Look at the teachers. Has the ability to teach been given to all? You see for yourselves that it has not been given to all. Pass on to the remaining gifts: powers, healings, tongues and interpretation. Has any of these become common to all? You see that it has not, but to one person one thing has been given and to another something else.

units.la: Sed quorsum urget ista Apostolus? Vt cogitent non esse hæc dona & officia sic comparata, ut aliquod illorum sufficiat ad complementum corporis Christi, alioqui non fuisse,re liqua data ecclesiæ.
units.tr: But why does the Apostle press this? So that they may consider that these gifts and offices are not so arranged that any one of them suffices for the completing of the body of Christ. Otherwise the rest would not have been given to the Church.

units.la: Etenim fi fuffeciffet Apostolatus, omnes ad Christum pertinentes facti fuissent apostoli. Sic & de reliquis sentiendum. Deinde, ut nullum eorum tale fit, fine quo nemini salus constare possit. Aliàs sic quoque omnibus ad salutem uocatis effet datum. Cum ergo talia sint hæc dona & officia, præter rationem esse monet, quod quibus data erant tantopere insolescebant, & reliquos præ fe fastidiebant, quibus data non erant, animo sic erant deiecto, ac fi de corpore Christi nō effent. Præposteram hanc donorum istorum æmulationem reprehendens subiungit dicens:
units.tr: For if apostleship alone had been enough, all who belong to Christ would have become apostles. The same must be thought of the rest. Furthermore, since none of these is such that without it no one can have salvation, otherwise they too would have been given to all who are called to salvation. Since these gifts and offices are of this kind, he warns that it is contrary to reason that those to whom they were given grew so proud, and despised the rest, to whom they were not given, and were so cast down in spirit as if they were not members of the body of Christ. Rebuking this perverse rivalry over gifts, he adds, saying:

units.la: SECTEMINI uero dona potiora.
units.tr: But earnestly desire the greater gifts.

units.la: InGreco est, ζηλοῦτε τὰ χαρίσματα τὰ κρείττονα. Hoc est, zelate uero pro donis illis quæ sunt meliora. Quasi dicat: Sunt quidem ea pro quibus tanto zelo ardetis, charismata fpiritufanƈti, & sunt utilia ecclesiæ, ad ædificationem illius data: uerum non sunt tanti facienda, quanti facienda sunt meliora illa, quorum uos nulla cura teneri uideo. Quare inconsulto facitis æmulates ea quæ minoris sunt momenti, & interim quæ maioris sunt negligentes.
units.tr: In Greek it is: "zealously desire the greater gifts" [ζηλοῦτε τὰ χαρίσματα τὰ κρείττονα]. That is: be zealous, but for those gifts which are better. As if to say: those gifts for which you burn with such zeal are indeed gifts of the Holy Spirit, and they are useful, given for the building up of the Church; yet they are not to be valued as highly as those better ones, which I see you do not care about at all. Therefore you act without thought, when you are zealous for those things which are of lesser importance, and meanwhile neglect those of greater importance.

units.la: Quæ sunt autem potiora illa dona? Recentiores quidam referunt istam particulam ad præcedentia, & exponunt de bonis prophetiæ ac doctrinæ, quod utiliora sint ecclesiæ, quàm uel sanationum, uel linguarum, ideoque & potiora. Et Hieronymus exponit dicens: Hoc est, sectemini prophetias. Equidem fi conferatur prophetia cum dono linguarum, & charismatis fanationum, præstantior est multo, id quod infrà cap. decimoquarto fuse monstrabitur: uerum cum donum prophetiæ non effet omnibus, sed quibusdam duntaxat traditum, & iam dixerit, an omnes prophetæ? non puto conuenire proposito Apostoli, ut hortetur eos in genere ad studium prophetiæ.
units.tr: But which are those greater gifts? Some more recent writers refer this particle to what goes before, and explain it as the good gifts of prophecy and teaching, because they are more useful to the Church than gifts of tongues or of healing, and therefore greater. Jerome also explains it, saying: "That is, pursue prophecies." Indeed, if prophecy is compared with the gift of tongues and the gift of healing, it is far superior, as will be shown at length below in chapter fourteen. But since the gift of prophecy was not given to all, but only to some, and since he has already said, "are all prophets?", I do not think it fits the Apostle's purpose to exhort them in general to pursue prophecy.

units.la: Potest quidem dici, uel, quod non ad omnes hoc dicat in genere, sed ad eos tantum, qui propter donum linguarum inflabantur, uel quod non hortetur eos, ut omnes ad prophetandi munus adspirent: sed ut pluris illud faciant magisque admirentur & colant, quàm charismata linguarum, potentiarum, & fanationum. Verum meo iudicio simplicius esse puto, ut referamus ista cum Chryfoftomo & Ambrosio ad sequētia, intelligamusq; de fide, spe ac charitate, tanquam donis Dei ob id potioribus, quod fine ipsis salus nostra constare non potest, cum fine illis possit, quę Corinthij tantopere æmulabantur.
units.tr: It may indeed be said either that he does not say this to everyone in general, but only to those who were puffed up on account of the gift of tongues; or that he does not urge them all to aspire to the office of prophesying, but that they should value and honour it more than the gifts of tongues, powers and healings. But in my judgement it seems simpler to refer these words, with Chrysostom and Ambrose, to what follows, and to understand them of faith, hope and charity, as gifts of God that are greater for this reason, that our salvation cannot stand without them, whereas it can stand without those gifts which the Corinthians so greatly prized.

units.la: SECTEMINI, inquit, meliora charismata.] Obserua quod non dicit, Vtamini melioribus charismatis, ne uideatur usum eorum prohibere, quæ data erant ecclesiæ: sed, Æmulamini uero charismata meliora, ut auocet eos non ab usu cæterorum, sed præpostero zelo, ad zelum meliorum. Discriminat igitur inter usum ac zelum donorum Dei. Vsum relinquit minus necessarijs, zelum uero deputat potioribus.
units.tr: "Pursue," he says, "the better gifts." Observe that he does not say, "use the better gifts," lest he seem to forbid the use of those gifts which were given to the Church; but, "be zealous for the better gifts," so that he calls them away not from the use of the others, but from a perverse zeal to a zeal for the better ones. He therefore distinguishes between the use and the zeal of God's gifts. He leaves the use of the less necessary ones, but assigns zeal to the greater.

units.la: Bonis utendum est utiliter, meliora uero fe standa sunt ardenter. Bonus est cibus corporis, melior uero cibus mentis. Vtamur ergo cibo corporis utiliter, sectemur uero cibu mentis feruenter. Vtamur Magistratu obedienter, æmulemur uero Deum excellenter. Bonum est obedire magistratui, uerum fi præcipiat ille quod Deo displiceat, melius est obedire Deo, quàm Magistratui.
units.tr: Good things are to be used profitably, but better things are to be pursued eagerly. Food for the body is good, but food for the mind is better. So let us use bodily food profitably, but pursue spiritual food with fervour. Let us obey the magistrate dutifully, but let us be zealous for God above all. It is good to obey the magistrate, but if he commands what displeases God, it is better to obey God than the magistrate.

units.la: SECTEMINI, inquit, meliora. ] Si in donis Dei, quæ utique bona sunt omnia, sectanda sunt meliora: quanto magis ubi collatio est inutilium & utilium, uel malorum & bonorum, sectanda sunt utilia & bona? Vbi uero conferuntur inter fe bona disparia, res ipsa cum ratione monet, sectanda esse meliora.
units.tr: "Pursue," he says, "the better." If among the gifts of God, which are all certainly good, the better are to be pursued, how much more, where there is a comparison between the useless and the useful, or between the evil and the good, are the useful and the good to be pursued? But where goods of different kinds are compared with one another, reason itself declares that the better are to be pursued.

units.la: Si roget quisquam, sint ne meliora omnia omnibus, & semper abfq; discrimine sectanda? refpōdeo: Melius aliud est per fe aliud per accidens. Per fe melius est, quod melius est collatione malorum, uel deteriorum, utpote: melius est nubere, quàm scortari & adulterari: melius est cum uno tantum oculo seruari, quàm cum duobus mitti in gehennam. Quæ sic sunt meliora, utique & omnia, & omnibus, & semper sunt sectanda.
units.tr: If anyone asks, are all better things to all people, and always to be pursued without distinction? I answer: one thing is better in itself, another by accident. That is better in itself which is better when compared with evil or worse things; for example: it is better to marry than to play the whore and commit adultery; it is better to be saved with one eye than to be cast with two into hell. Things which are better in this way are certainly better for all, and always to be pursued.

units.la: Per accidens uero melius est, quod uel propter personam utentis, uel propter temporis qualitatem, aut alias circumstantias, aut excellit, aut melius esse definit: utpote quando quæritur, melius ne fit mulierem non tangere, quàm nubere, hic determinari non potest absque discrimine, uel personæ, uel temporis. Etenim ei, qui donum continentiæ non accepit, melius est nubere, quàm mulierem nolle tangere.
units.tr: But that is better by circumstance which either, on account of the person using it, or on account of the quality of the time, or other circumstances, either surpasses or determines what is better: as when it is asked whether it is better for a man not to touch a woman than to marry, this cannot be decided here without regard either to the person or to the time. For to one who has not received the gift of continence, it is better to marry than not to touch a woman.

units.la: Deinde ubi periculum est, ne propter uxorem & liberos cognitam ueritatem negemus, & nofipfi cœlesti gratia priuemus, utique melius est mulierem non tangere. Quare admodum imprudens fuit quorundam patrum zelus, quo cœlibatum illum tantopere urserunt, ut quasi per se sit melior coniugio, omnibus il- lum Christi ministris imponendum esse censuerint. Huius imprudentis zeli studiū quanta sequuta sint animarum discrimina, quis satis unquam perpendit?
units.tr: Again, where there is a danger that, on account of a wife and children, we deny the known truth and deprive ourselves of heavenly grace, then surely it is better not to touch a woman. Wherefore the zeal of certain Fathers was altogether imprudent, by which they urged celibacy so strongly that, as if it were better than marriage in itself, they judged that it must be imposed on all the ministers of Christ. Who has ever sufficiently weighed how great the dangers to souls have been that followed from this imprudent zeal?

units.la: Tenedum ergo est, ea quæ meliora sunt per se & generaliter, & semper, & omnibus, utique & omnibus & semper esse sectanda: quæ vero per accidens sunt meliora, illis tantum ac tunc esse sectanda, quibus sunt & quādiu sunt meliora, quandoquidem non mox mihi melius est, quod alteri cuipiam melius esse potest.
units.tr: It must therefore be held that those things which are better in themselves, and generally, and always, and for all, are to be pursued by all and always; but those which are better by circumstance are to be pursued only by those for whom, and for as long as, they are better, since what is better for me at once is not necessarily better for some other person.

units.la: Et adhuc excellentiorem uiam uobis ostendo.] Græce est, ἔτι καὶ ὑπερβολὴν ὁδὸν ὑμῖν δείκνυμι, quod uerti potest: Et adhuc ex abundanti uiam uobis ostendo, ut sit sensus: Quamuis manifesta sint quæ hactenus de donis Dei exposui, unde admoneri possitis, ea uobis esse sectada, quæ sunt potiora: adhuc tamen ex abundanti ostendam uobis uiam, id est, modum uelut gratia exempli, quo manifestissimū fiat quod dico. Verum quoniam cæteri communiter sic legunt: Et adhuc excellentiorem uiam uobis ostendo, quasi sit in Græco, ἔτι καὶ ὑπερβολὴν ὁδὸν, id est, & adhuc eam quæ excellens est uia, uobis ostendo: eam lectionem retineo, præsertim propterea quod charitatem, de qua dicturus est capite sequenti, in calce illius fide ac spe maiorem esse dicit, ut illam hic uideri possit uocare ὁδὸν καὶ ὑπερβολὴν, id est uiam secundum excellentiam.
units.tr: "And yet I show you a more excellent way." In Greek it is, ἔτι καὶ ὑπερβολὴν ὁδὸν ὑμῖν δείκνυμι, which may be rendered: "And yet, beyond measure, I show you a way" [ἔτι καὶ ὑπερβολὴν ὁδὸν ὑμῖν δείκνυμι], so that the sense is: although what I have so far set out concerning the gifts of God is plain, whereby you may be reminded that those things are to be pursued which are of greater worth, nevertheless I will show you, over and above, a way, that is, a manner, as an example, by which what I say may be made most evident. But since the others commonly read it thus: "And yet I show you a more excellent way," as if the Greek were ἔτι καὶ ὑπερβολὴν ὁδὸν, that is, "and yet I show you the way which is excellent," I retain that reading, especially because he says that charity, of which he is about to speak in the following chapter, is greater than faith and hope at the close of that chapter, so that it may be seen here to be called ὁδὸν καὶ ὑπερβολὴν, that is, a way according to excellence.

units.la: Cæterum negari non potest, particulă hanc pertinere ad sequentis capitis principium. In hac enim profitetur quid iam sit præcedentibus subiecturus, ut omnino ad principium eorum quæ dicturus est, pertineat: ad hoc illis præmissa, ut animos Corinthiorum excitet, qui maiore cum diligentia & attentius illa percipiant.
units.tr: Moreover, it cannot be denied that this particle pertains to the beginning of the following chapter. For in it he declares what he is about to subjoin to what precedes, so that it wholly pertains to the beginning of what he is about to say; it is placed before those things so as to stir up the minds of the Corinthians, that they may perceive them with greater diligence and attention.

units.la: CAPVT XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 13.

units.la: Si linguis hominum loquar, & angelorum, charitatem autem non habeam, factus sum æs resonans, aut cymbalum tinniens.
units.tr: If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I have become a sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal.

units.la: Et si habeam prophetiam, & nouerim mysteria omnia, omnemq; scientiam: & si habeam omnem fidem, adeo ut montes loco dimoueam, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil sum. Et si infumam in alimoniam omnes facultates meas, & si tradam corpus meum ut comburar, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil utilitatis capio.
units.tr: And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing. And if I give all my goods to feed others, and if I hand over my body to be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing.

units.la: Hæc est uia illa excellentior, quam se oftendrurum dixit. Videbat illam partim negligi, par tim etiam ignorari ab illis qui donis linguarum, & scientiæ, & sanationum abutebantur, quod charitatem non haberent. Hanc itaq; toto hoc capite commendat, & pro dignitate extollit: primo, affirmans sine illa nihil esse reliqua charismata, deinde ingenium illius explicans, tertio a perpetuitate quoq; illam communi dans, fideiq; & spei præferens.
units.tr: This is that more excellent way which he said he would show. He saw that it was partly neglected and partly even unknown to those who abused the gifts of tongues, knowledge and healings, because they did not have charity. So throughout this chapter he commends it and extols it according to its worth: first, by affirming that without it the other gifts are nothing; second, by explaining its nature; third, by granting it also the quality of permanence, and placing it above faith and hope.

units.la: Si linguis hominum loquar, & angelorum inquit. Quoniam propter donum linguarum plerique in ecclesia Corinthiorum insolescebant, & illo destitutos fastidiebant, denique sic in ecclesia linguis loquebantur, ut magis ostentationi seruirent, quam ecclesiam ædificarent: mox initio abusum doni huius perstringit, & eos qui sic linguis loquebantur æs resonans, & cymbalum tinniens esse pronunciat. Quo autem tolerabiliora sunt quæ dicturus est, non dicit: Qui linguis inter uos loquuntur, facti sunt æs resonans, aut cymbalum tinniens, quia sine charitate loquuntur: sed sermonem sic format, ut absq; offensione possit acceptari.
units.tr: "If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels," he says. Because on account of the gift of tongues many in the Corinthian church grew arrogant and despised those who lacked it, and finally they spoke in tongues in the church in such a way that they served display rather than building up the church, he censures at the very start the abuse of this gift, and declares that those who spoke in tongues in this way are a sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal. But he does not say, to soften what he is about to say, "Those of you who speak in tongues have become a sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal, because you speak without charity"; instead he shapes the sentence so that it can be received without offence.

units.la: Facit autem hoc duplici moderatione. Prima est per propositionem hypotheticam, qua nemo perinde atq; per categoricā diserte perstringitur. Deinde per accomodationem propriæ suæ persone, non dicens, Si quis uestrum linguis loquitur: sed, Si ego linguis loquar. Et hac moderatione cæptum sermonem primo capitis huius membro continuat.
units.tr: He does this by a twofold restraint. The first is the use of a hypothetical proposition, by which no one is openly rebuked as he would be by a categorical one. The second is that he applies it to his own person, not saying "If any of you speaks in tongues," but "If I speak in tongues." By this restraint he continues in the first clause of this chapter the sermon he had begun.

units.la: Si linguis loquar, inquit. Satis fuisset dicere: Si linguis loquar. (Etenim linguis loqui idem ipsi est, quod alijs atque alijs inusitatis & incognitis linguis loqui) nisi donum hoc linguarum intendere, & ad summum usque amplificare uoluisset. Amplificationis huius gratia adiecit, hominum & angelorum. Linguas hominum intelligit omnium Gentium & populorum.
units.tr: "If I speak in tongues," he says. It would have been enough to say "If I speak in tongues" (for to speak in tongues is the same as to speak in various and different unusual and unknown languages), except that he wished to magnify this gift of tongues and raise it to the highest degree. For the sake of this amplification he added "of men and of angels." By "tongues of men" he understands the languages of all nations and peoples.

units.la: Angelorum quoque per hyperbolen adiecit, quasi dicat: Si non modo unius & alterius gentis, sed simul mortalium omnium, imo & angelorum, quod adhuc esset multo excellentius, linguis loquar. Obliquè per hanc amplificationē perstringit eorum iactatiam, qui quod duplo uel triplo alieno idiomate loqui poterant, plurimum arrogantiæ spirabant.
units.tr: He also added "of angels" by hyperbole, as if to say: "If I speak in tongues not only of one or another nation, but of all mortals together, indeed even of angels, which would be far more excellent still." By this amplification he indirectly censures the boasting of those who, because they could speak two or three foreign languages, breathed great arrogance.

units.la: Illud, & angelorum, non sic est accipiendū, quasi angeli, id est, spiritus cœlestes linguis inter se loquantur, quomodo homo homini loquitur: sed quod uel simpliciter pro hyperbolica loquutione sit positum, uel de linguis intelligendum, quibus angeli cū in Veteri, tum in Nouo testamento loquuti sunt hominibus. quod genus loquutionis ipse hic Apostolus, haud semel fuerat expertus. Si linguis, inquit, omnibus non humanis tantum, sed & cœlestibus loquar. Hoc est, si nullo non linguarum genere loquar.
units.tr: The phrase "and of angels" is not to be taken as if angels, that is, heavenly spirits, speak with one another in tongues as man speaks to man. It is either put simply as a hyperbolic expression, or is to be understood of the tongues in which angels spoke to men both in the Old and in the New Testament. This kind of speech the Apostle himself had experienced more than once. "If I speak," he says, "in all tongues, not only human but also heavenly; that is, if I speak in every kind of tongue."

units.la: Quemadmodum P.om. 8. per hyperbolen intendere uolens quod dicebat: Nam mihi,
units.tr: As in Rom. 8, wishing by hyperbole to intensify what he was saying: "For I am persuaded," he says,

units.la: inquit,persuasum habeo, quod neque mors neque uita,neque angeli,&c.separare nos poterunt à dilectione Dei,quæ est in Christo Iesu.Et Galat.1.Et si angelus è cœlo prædicaue rit uobis Euangelium, præter id quod prædicauimus uobis,anathema sit: cum tamen impossibile sit,ut angelus è cœlo quenquam à dilectione Dei auocet,aut aliud à uero Euangelium prędicet,ita ut hoc loco intensionis gratia linguarum angelicarum per hyperbolé meminit,cum tamen nullæ sint angelorum linguę.
units.tr: "that neither death nor life, nor angels, etc., will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus." And in Gal. 1: "Even if an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel other than what we have preached to you, let him be accursed." Yet it is impossible that an angel from heaven should draw anyone away from the love of God, or preach a gospel other than the true one. So here, for the sake of intensity, he mentions by hyperbole the tongues of angels, although there are no languages of angels.

units.la: Est autem probabile,fecisse eum angelorum mentionem propter eos qui admodum de visionibus ac reuelationibus angelorum gloriabantur,illorumq; religionem introducebant, quos notat Coloss.2.dicés:Ne quis uobis pal-mam interuertat data opera per humilitatem & superstitionem angelorum.
units.tr: It is, however, probable that he mentioned angels because of those who boasted greatly of visions and revelations of angels, and introduced a cult of angels, whom he notes in Col. 2, saying: "Let no one rob you of the prize by deliberately delighting in humility and the worship of angels."
