units.la: SI linguis,inquit,loquar hominum & angelorum,charitatem autem non habeā,factus sum æs resonans,aut cymbalum tinniens.]In Græco est, ἀγάπην δὲ μὴ ἔχω, id est, dilectionem uero non habeam.quod ideo annoto, quoniā communiter hoc loco charitatem uertunt, ne quis anxie inter dilectionem & charitatem distinguat.Non nego aliquid inueniri discriminis inter amorem & charitatem, amorem itē & dilectionē,quo leuior fit dilectionis, uehementior amoris, familiarior & humanior charitatis affectus. Verū hoc loco simpliciter est, Dilectionem autem nō habeam. Quid autem sit diligere,norunt omnes.Et nos in Commentarijs nostris super Matth.cap.22. de dilectione Dei ac proximi pleraque annotauimus.Vtinam tam diligeremus Deum & proximum, quàm quid sit aliquē diligere non ignoramus. Diligimus omnes, nec est quisquam qui non aliquoufque dilectionis in se experiatur affectum.Verum ut corrupti ac depravati sumus, ita & dilectionis affectus corruptus in nobis est ac uiciatus:quo fit utinc onsulto diligamus plerunque non diligenda,& diligenda non diligimus,aut non ut competit diligamus ,imo sæpenumero odio prosequamur.Et hæc corruptio dilectionis non emendatur in nobis nisi per spiritum regenerationis, quo totus interior noster homo cum omnibus suis & metis & affectuum uiribus innouatur.
units.tr: "If I speak," he says, "in the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become a sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal." In Greek it is ἀγάπην δὲ μὴ ἔχω [agapēn de mē echō], that is, "but if I do not have love [dilectio]." I note this because in this place they commonly translate it "charity," and I do not want anyone to distinguish anxiously between dilectio and charitas. I do not deny that some difference can be found between amor and caritas, and between amor and dilectio: dilectio is a lighter affection, amor a more intense one, and caritas a more familiar and humane one. But here it is simply "but if I do not have dilectio." What it is to love, everyone knows. In our Commentaries on Matthew chapter 22 we have noted many things about the love of God and of neighbour. Would that we loved God and neighbour as well as we know what it is to love someone! We all love, and there is no one who does not experience in himself some degree of the affection of love. But as we are corrupted and depraved, so the affection of love in us is also corrupted and vitiated. Hence we often deliberately love what should not be loved, do not love what should be loved, or do not love as we ought, and very often pursue with hatred. And this corruption of love is not put right in us except by the Spirit of regeneration, by whom our whole inner man, with all its powers and affections, is renewed.

units.la: ET charitatem,inquit,non habeam.] Non ponit simplicem hypotheticam propositionē dicens:Si linguis loquar hominum & angelorum, factus sum æs resonans,&c.sed geminā, addens,Et dilectionem non habeam,quod in toto primo capitis huius membro tertio facit, ne charismata spiritus Dei, linguas, prophetiam,scientiam mysteriorum,fidem,alimoniá pauperum,& martyrium,nullius in se æstima re uideatur.
units.tr: "And if I do not have charity," he says. He does not state a simple hypothetical proposition, saying "If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, I have become a sounding brass," and so on, but a double one, adding "and if I do not have love." He does this a third time in the first clause of this chapter, so that the gifts of God's Spirit (tongues, prophecy, knowledge of mysteries, faith, feeding the poor, and martyrdom) may not seem to be valued at all in themselves.

units.la: Sine hac conditione nō debet accipi,quam pronunciat,sententia. Magna peruersitas est, in huiusmodi hypotheticis & conditionalibus sententijs, uel mandatis neglecta condi-tione apprehendere pronunciatum, aut usurpare mandatum. Sic Romani illud Petro dictum, Pasce oues meas, mordicus apprehendunt: conditionem uero præmissam, Simon diligis me plus his,fortiter negligunt ac dissimulant.Et illud iactant, Si quis episcopatum desiderat,bonum opus desiderat: Canonem uero subiectum,qualis debeat esse episcopus, ne semel quidem inspiciunt.
units.tr: This statement must not be taken without the condition attached to it. It is a great perversity, in such hypothetical and conditional sentences or commands, to seize on the assertion, or to claim the command, while neglecting the condition. So the Romanists grip firmly the saying to Peter, "Feed my sheep," but they strongly neglect and disregard the condition placed before it, "Simon, do you love me more than these?" And they boast of "If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work," but they never once look at the rule that follows about what sort of bishop he ought to be.

units.la: ET charitatem,inquit,non habeam.]Cum nemo sit qui prorsus sit omnis dilectionis expers,quærendum est quomodo dicat.Et dilectionem non habeam. Dubio procul non loquitur de dilectione simpliciter,sed de ea speciáliter, quæ non est omnium, sed regeneratorum tantum . Ea ut ordinata est,ita diligit cum primis Deum,omnis boni fontem,deinde & proximum. Hac qui destituitur, inter regeneratos ueraciter censeri non potest.
units.tr: "And if I do not have charity," he says. Since there is no one who is entirely without all dilectio, we must ask how he can say "and if I do not have dilectio." Undoubtedly he is not speaking of dilectio in general, but of that particular kind which belongs not to all, but only to the regenerate. This love, as it is ordered, loves first God, the fountain of every good, and then the neighbour too. Whoever lacks it cannot truly be counted among the regenerate.

units.la: Nec est, ut quæramus utrum de dilectione Dei uel proximi loquatur, cum dilectio proximi , sine dilectione Dei haberi nequeat.Apparet quidem de charitate intelligendum esse, qua proximus diligitur:uerum ab illa non est separanda dilectio Dei,per quam & proximū diligimus.
units.tr: Nor need we ask whether he speaks of love of God or of neighbour, since love of neighbour cannot be had without love of God. It is clear indeed that it must be understood of the charity by which the neighbour is loved; but the love of God is not to be separated from it, since through it we also love the neighbour.

units.la: Loquitur autem de dilectione,qua quæ facimus,uel ad gloriam Dei,uel ad commodum proximi dirigimus.
units.tr: He speaks, moreover, of the love by which we direct what we do either to the glory of God or to the benefit of the neighbour.

units.la: Quare cum dicit:Si linguis loquar, charitatem autem non habeam,non loquitur de otiosa charitate,neque de efficacia etiam, in aliis rebus sese declarante:sed de ea quæ donū linguarum ad utilitatem & ædificationem ecclesiæ moderetur . Sic linguis loqui & charitatem non habere,est citra affectum charitatis & studium ædificandi ecclesiam, ad ostentationem,uel ad quæstum,uel studio schisma tis,alijs atque alijs linguis loqui in ecclesia,id quod plerique Corinthiorum faciebant. Et quoniam qui spiritu charitatis ardet, ad hunc modum non loquitur in ecclesia,pro eo quod dicendum erat,Si linguis loquar, & ecclesiæ ędificationem non quæsiero:dicit, Si linguis loquar,& charitatem non habuero. Charitatē ergo non habet,qui in eo quod facit uel loquitur,nec ad gloriam Dei, nec ad utilitatē proximi spectat,sed suam ipsius gloriam & commoditatem quærit.
units.tr: Therefore, when he says, "If I speak in tongues, but do not have charity," he is not speaking of an idle charity, nor of an efficacy that shows itself in other matters, but of that love which governs the gift of tongues for the use and edification of the church. To speak in tongues and not have charity is to be without the affection of love and the zeal to build up the church: to speak in various and different tongues in the church for display, or for gain, or from a desire for schism, which many of the Corinthians did. And since one who burns with the Spirit of love does not speak in the church in this way, instead of saying "If I speak in tongues and do not seek the edification of the church," he says, "If I speak in tongues and have not charity." So he who does not have charity is one who, in what he does or says, looks neither to the glory of God nor to the benefit of the neighbour, but seeks his own glory and advantage.

units.la: Sic Ioannes dicit: Qui habuerit substantiam huius mundi,& uiderit fratrem suum egentem,& clauserit uiscera sua ab eo, quō charitas Dei manet in eo: Ecce uno argumento immisericordiæ colligit non esse charitatem Dei in eo, qui non miseretur fratris egentis. Quare? Quia ubi charitas est,ibi tali immisericordiæ locus esse non potest.
units.tr: Thus John says: "Whoever has the goods of this world and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him?" (1 John 3.17). From this single example of pitilessness he concludes that the love of God is not in the one who has no pity on his needy brother. Why? Because where love is, there can be no room for such pitilessness.

units.la: Censeo tamen hac de re caute esse pronunciandum,propter eos, qui nonnunquā tentatione aliqua uicti,alio quid quàm charitatis affectu dicunt uel faciunt: quamuis non sint prorsus uacui charitatis spiritu. Aliud est semel atque iterum præuaricari à regula charitatis per tentationem & occasionem, & aliud perpetuo carnis studio omnia citra charitatē dicere & facere.
units.tr: Yet I think we must state this matter with caution, on account of those who, overcome by some temptation, sometimes say or do something from another motive than love, although they are not entirely empty of the Spirit of love. It is one thing to stray once or twice from the rule of love through temptation and occasion; it is another to say and do everything without love, constantly following the desires of the flesh.

units.la: Illud nonnûquam & sanctis ufuuenit, hoc uero prorsus est impiorum. Sic potuit & nonnullis illorum ufuuenire, qui linguis inter Corinthios loquebantur, ut aliquando tentatione uictî citra charitatem in ecclesia loquerentur. Quibus hoc non singulari studio, sed per occasionem &tentatione accidebat, non mox prorsus sine charitate fuisse censeri debêt. Cû Dauid uxorem Uriæ pollueret, & insontem postea proditorię neci traderet, profecto ea faciebat, quæ omnino charitati repugnabant.
units.tr: The first sometimes happens even to the saints; the second belongs wholly to the wicked. So it could also happen to some of those who spoke in tongues among the Corinthians, that now and then, overcome by temptation, they spoke in the congregation without love. Such people did this not from settled purpose but through occasion and temptation, and they should not at once be judged to be wholly without love. When David defiled Uriah's wife and afterwards handed the innocent man over to be murdered treacherously, he surely did things that were utterly opposed to love.

units.la: Cû Petrus Christum negaret, charitatis puto modicam rationem habebat.
units.tr: When Peter denied Christ, I think he had little regard for love.

units.la: Verû nemo propterea ueraciter dicere poterit, uel hunc uel illum alienum fuisse à spiritu charitatis.
units.tr: Yet no one can therefore truly say that either this man or that was a stranger to the Spirit of love.

units.la: Quod autem non dicit, Si linguis loquar, & ædificationem ecclesiæ non quæram, sed & charitatē non habeam: ex eo est quod mauult causam defectus, quàm ipsum exprimere defectum. Charitas enim est causa eius studij, quo ædificatur ecclesia. Hinc alibi dicit: Scientia inflat, charitas uero ædificat. Vbi ergo illa deest, ibi deficit ædificandæ eccclesiæ studiū. Quare cum Petro dominus ouicularum suarum curam commendare uellet, primum illū de dilectione sui percontabatur, dicens: Simo B diligis me?
units.tr: As for the fact that Paul does not say, "If I speak with tongues and do not seek the edification of the Church, but also do not have love," the reason is that he prefers to name the cause of the defect rather than the defect itself. For love is the cause of that zeal by which the Church is built up. Hence he says elsewhere: "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up" (1 Cor. 8.1). Where love is lacking, therefore, zeal for building up the Church is also lacking. So when the Lord wished to commit his little sheep to Peter, he first asked him about his love for himself, saying: "Simon, do you love me?" (John 21.15).

units.la: Caute uero non dicit: Si linguis loquar, & ecclesia nô ædificatur. Potest enim fieri, ut ex charitate dicat in ecclesia minister, intendatq; illam ædificare in fide ac pietate: illa uero omnia frustra audiat, nonnunquam & sermonibus illius contradicat, id quod prophetis & Christo ipsi ufuuenit. Hic certe dici non potest, quod sic loquens charitatem non habeat. Satis est ministro, si fideliter & ex charitate agat omnia, etiam si ecclesia fidem ac dilectionem illius, omneque ædificationis studium respuat.
units.tr: But he carefully does not say, "If I speak with tongues and the Church is not built up." For it can happen that a minister speaks in the congregation out of love and intends to build it up in faith and godliness, yet the people hear all this in vain, and sometimes even contradict his words, as happened to the prophets and to Christ himself. Here it certainly cannot be said that one who speaks thus lacks love. It is enough for a minister if he acts faithfully and from love in all things, even if the Church rejects his faith and love and all zeal for edification.

units.la: S I linguis hominum loquar, inquit, & angelorum, charitatem autem non habeam, factus sum æs resonans, aut cymbalû tinniens. Ergo comparat sic linguis sine charitate loquentem æri sonanti, & cymbalo tinnienti. Sonat quidem æs, & tinnit cymbalum, uerum sonitu ac tinnitu inani. Sic qui linguis sine charitate loquitur, frustra & inaniter loquitur. Quare? Quia quę dicit, non intelliguntur, quandoquidem idiomate incognito loquitur, nec curat, ut sit qui interpretetur, quod faceret, si per charitatem ecclefię loqueretur. Sonitu & tinnitu uerborum uerberat quidem auares auditorum, uerum mentes illorum non ędificat.
units.tr: "If I speak," he says, "with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal" (1 Cor. 13.1). So he compares the one who speaks in tongues without love to sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal. Brass does sound and cymbals do clang, but with an empty sound and clatter. So one who speaks in tongues without love speaks in vain and to no purpose. Why? Because what he says is not understood, since he speaks in an unknown language and takes no care that there should be someone to interpret, as he would do if he spoke in the Church out of love. With the sound and clatter of words he indeed strikes the ears of the hearers, but he does not build up their minds.

units.la: Quare recte uocatur æs sonans, & cymbalû tinniens. Hoc simili pulchre perstringit illorû
units.tr: Therefore he is rightly called sounding brass and a clanging cymbal. By this comparison he admirably exposes the vanity of those

units.la: uanitatem, qui in ecclesia uerba incognita, magno sonitu frustra in aerem spargunt. Quid autem aliud faciunt Canonici, sacerdotes, clerici & monachi? An non & illos recte dixeris ęra esse sonantia, & cymbala inaniter tinnientia? Verum quis satis perpenderit, quantis ęra hæc & cymbala alantur sumptibus? Nisi sagi nata, nec sonant, nec tinniunt, & tamen frustra sonant, ac uanę tinniunt. Mirum quod non cogitant de hac Apostoli sententia, quoties nolas & cymbala in templis & sacris suis audiunt, quorum sonitus ac tinnitus plebs superstitiosa perinde intelligit, ac ea quę ab ipsis lingua ignota cantantur.
units.tr: who in the congregation scatter unknown words into the air with great noise and to no purpose. And what else do canons, priests, clerics and monks do? Would you not rightly call them sounding brass and cymbals clanging to no purpose? But who has considered how much these brasses and cymbals cost to maintain? Unless they were cast of bronze, they neither sound nor clang, and yet they sound in vain and clang to no end. It is strange that they do not consider this sentence of the Apostle, whenever they hear bells and cymbals in their temples and sacred rites, whose sound and clatter the superstitious common people understand no better than the things sung in an unknown tongue.

units.la: Aliud conuenit esse iudicium de illis, qui lingua cognita docent populum. Hi etiamsi charitatem non habeant, modo quæ uera sunt ecclesiæ proponant, æri tamen sonanti, & cymbalo tinnienti comparari non possunt, quandoquidem intelligibiliter loquentes, utiliter etiam audiri & intelligi possunt.
units.tr: A different judgment is to be made of those who teach the people in a language they know. Even if they lack love, provided they set before the Church what is true, they cannot be compared to sounding brass or a clanging cymbal, since, speaking intelligibly, they can also be heard and understood to profit.

units.la: E T si habeam prophetiam, inquit. ] A minori charismate exorsus assurgitad maiora. Maioris nanque momenti est donum prophetiæ, quàm linguarum. Sic assurgendo sententiam suam de charitatis excellentia ac prærogatiua magis ac magis intendit, quo dissidia & schismata ipsorum fortius redarguat. Etsi habeam prophetiam, inquit. Prophetiam habere, non est unam tantum prophetiam, sed donum prophetię habere. Loquitur aut de prophetia qua futura per spiritū reuelationis præscita prædicuntur. Donum hoc quanto humanæ scientiæ uires superat, tanto semper sublimius ac diuinius haberi confuenit, quo nomine etiamnū in magna sunt existimatione Veteris testamenti prophetæ.
units.tr: "And if I have prophecy," he says. Beginning from a lesser gift, he rises to greater ones. For the gift of prophecy is of greater importance than the gift of tongues. By thus rising, he presses his point about the excellence and pre-eminence of love more and more, so that he may the more forcefully refute their dissensions and schisms. "If I have prophecy," he says. To have prophecy is not merely to possess one prophecy, but to have the gift of prophecy. He speaks of the prophecy by which future things, foreknown through the Spirit of revelation, are foretold. The more this gift surpasses the powers of human knowledge, the more it is always rightly held to be lofty and divine; for this reason the prophets of the Old Testament are still held in great esteem.

units.la: E T nouerim mysteria omnia, omnemque scientiam. ] Chrysostomus existimat ista perinere ad auxesim prophetiæ, quo significet Apostolus loqui se non de mediocri aliquo prophetiæ dono: sed de summo ac tali, cui adiuncta fit omnium mysteriorum cognitio, rerumque omnium tam diuinarum, quàm humanarum scientia.
units.tr: "And I know all mysteries and all knowledge." Chrysostom thinks these words belong to an amplification of prophecy, by which the Apostle signifies that he is speaking not of some ordinary gift of prophecy, but of a supreme one, to which is joined the knowledge of all mysteries and of all things, both divine and human.

units.la: Puto eum motum esse ad hanc sententiam ex eo quod ista ueluti connexa prophetię sub iuncta uidentur. Sane magna est affinitas eorum cū prophetia. Nequit enim facultas prophetandi esse, ubi secretorum Dei nulla habetur sciëtia. Verum affinitas ista nihil impedit, quo minus sint hæc separata charismata, quęadmodum & nonnulli exponunt.
units.tr: I think he was moved to this view because these things appear to be closely joined to prophecy. Certainly their affinity with prophecy is great. For the power of prophesying cannot exist where there is no knowledge of God's secrets. Yet this affinity does not prevent these from being separate gifts, as some also explain.

units.la: Apparet autem, quod dicit, Et nouerim mysteria omnia: intelligendum esse de charismate sapientiæ, cuius capite præcedenti in catalogo charismatum mentionem fecit, cui etiam donum scientiæ subiecit, quemadmodum & hoc loco, ubi uide quæ annotauerimus.
units.tr: It appears, however, that when he says "And I know all mysteries," it must be understood of the gift of wisdom, which he mentioned in the preceding chapter in his catalogue of gifts, and to which he also added the gift of knowledge, as here; see what we have noted there.

units.la: Sed rogabit quisquâ, quomodo fieri possit, ut cognoscat quis omnia mysteria, omnemqʼ scientiam tám diuinarū, quàm humanarum re A Cum omni fiducia loqui uerbum tuum. Hu-rum habeat, cum fit utrunq; solius Dei. iufmodi loquutiones multæ leguntur in scri-pturis. Sic hoc quoque loco, cum Apostolus dicit, Et si habeam omni fid em: exponi potest per specificationé de tota illa fide, quâ miracu-lorum uocant, ut non sit necesse, in genere de quauis fidei specie exponere.
units.tr: But someone will ask how it can happen that a person knows all mysteries and all knowledge, both divine and human, since both belong to God alone. Many expressions of this kind are read in the Scriptures: "to speak your word with all confidence" [cum omni fiducia loqui verbum tuum]. So also in this place, when the Apostle says "And if I have all faith," it can be explained by specifying that it is that faith by which miracles are wrought, so that there is no need to explain in general every kind of faith.

units.la: Respondeo, usus est Apostolus hac hyperbola, non quod possibile sit ulli homini omnia nosse mysteria, omuemq; temere scientiā: sed ut hyperbolica hac fictione doceat, q; nihil sint omnia hæc charismata, etiamsi cui ad summum usq; gradū contingant, si desit charitas. Quare non est magis hinc argutandum, fieri posse ut acquirat quis omnium mysteriorum, omniumq; rerum scientiam, quàm ex eo quod dixit: Si linguis loquar hominum & angelorum, contingere alicui posse, ut nō hominum modo, sed & angelorum linguis loquatur. Cū Dauid dicit: Si ascendero in cœlum tu illic es, si descendero ad inferos, tu ades, si sumpsero pennas meas diluculo, & habitauero in extremis maris, illinc manus tua deducet me: an hinc colligendum est, posse hominem uel in cœlum uel ad inferos, uel ad extremos terminos maris sumptis pennis auolare? Et cum ad Iob à domino dicitur: Si habes brachium ut Deus, etsi uoce simili tonas, &c. Inferēdum ne est, ergo potest homo brachium habere ut Deus, &c. Et ex eo quod Hiere. 51. legimus: Si ascenderit Babylon in cœlum, &c. Colliget ne quisquam fieri potuisse, ut ascenderet Babylon in cœlum? Consimili modo non sunt præsentes istæ hyperbolæ eò rapiendæ, ut ex illis colligamus, posse alicui omnium secretorum cognitionem, & omnem rerum, omnium con tingere scientiam. Multa cognouit ex secretis B Dei, multaque sciuit hic Apostolus, eo tamen scientiæ non ascendit unquam, ut sciret omnia.
units.tr: I answer: the Apostle used this hyperbole not because it is possible for any man to know all mysteries and all knowledge, but so that by this hyperbolical fiction he might teach that all these gifts are nothing, even if someone should attain them to the highest degree, if love is lacking. Therefore one should not argue further from this that a person may acquire the knowledge of all mysteries and all things, any more than from his words, "If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels," one should conclude that someone may speak not only with the tongues of men but also of angels. When David says, "If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I make my bed in hell, behold, you are there; if I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there shall your hand lead me" (Ps. 139.8–10), are we to conclude that a man may, on taking wings, fly up to heaven or down to hell or to the farthest limits of the sea? And when the Lord says to Job, "Have you an arm like God? And can you thunder with a voice like his?" (Job 40.9), are we to infer that a man can have an arm like God? And from what we read in Jeremiah 51: "If Babylon should ascend into heaven" (Jer. 51.53), will anyone conclude that it was possible for Babylon to ascend into heaven? In the same way, these hyperboles are not to be pressed so far that we conclude from them that the knowledge of all secrets and of all things and every science can fall to anyone. This Apostle knew many things of God's secrets and understood much, yet he never rose to such knowledge that he knew all things.

units.la: ET si habeam omnem fidem, adeo ut montes loco dimoueam.] Transit ad fidem, non eam quæ communis est Christianorum omnium, qua Christiani reddimur, & in conspectu Dei iustificamur, ac corda nostra purificatur, & sine qua nemo Deo placere potest: sed ad eam quam capite præcedenti inter charismata spiritus recensuit, dicens: Alij uero fides per eundem spiritum. Ea fides miraculorum est, quæ non magis omnibus conferebatur, q; cætera charismata sapientiæ, scientiæ, prophetiæ, linguarum, sanationum, &c. De hac cap. præcedenti diximus.
units.tr: Even if I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains. He turns to faith, not the faith common to all Christians, by which we are made Christians, are justified in the sight of God, have our hearts purified, and without which no one can please God. He means the faith that in the preceding chapter he listed among the gifts of the Spirit, saying: "To another faith by the same Spirit." This is the faith of miracles, which was not given to everyone any more than the other gifts of wisdom, knowledge, prophecy, tongues, healings, and so on. We discussed this in the preceding chapter.

units.la: Nec est ut uoculam Omnem quisquam diuexet, quasi quod dicit, Et si habeam omnem fidem: idem sit quod, Et si habeam omnis generis fidem, indeque colligat, non solum de fide miraculorum, sed & iustificante loqui Apostolum, id quod sophistæ quidam faciunt.
units.tr: Nor should anyone twist the little word "all" so as to make the sense, "Even if I have all faith," the same as, "Even if I have every kind of faith," and then conclude from this that the Apostle speaks not only of the faith of miracles but also of justifying faith, as some sophists do.

units.la: Primum enim non est necesse, ut sic exponamus, cum uocula Omnis tam totum quid, quàm omne genus plerunque significet. Vt cū Mattæhi 18. legimus: Omne debitum remisi tibi. Et cap. 27. Respondit omnis populus. Et, Tenebræ factæ sunt super omnem terram. Et Lucæ 2. Vt describeretur omnis orbis. Et Ioannis 5. Pater, omne iudicium, id est, totamiudicandi potestatem, dedit filio. Et Actorum 4.
units.tr: For there is no need to explain it this way, since the little word "all" most often signifies either a whole thing or every kind. So we read in Matthew 18: "I forgave you all that debt." And in chapter 27: "All the people answered." And: "Darkness fell over all the land." And in Luke 2: "That all the world should be enrolled." And in John 5: "The Father has given all judgment, that is, the whole power of judging, to the Son." And in Acts 4.

units.la: CHARITATEM autem non habeam.
units.tr: But have not charity.

units.la: Quoniam prophetia & fides numerantur hic inter charismata spiritus, nascitur quæstio, quo possint haberi ab aliquo sine charitate. Quod prophetiam attinet, tractat hanc quæstionem Augustinus libro secundo ad Simplicium, quæstione prima: Potest quidem inueniri charitas in homine Christiano sine pphetia, & reliquis confimilib. charismatibus, pro phetiam uero sine charitate dicet forte quisquam inueniri non posse, quemadmodū non inuenitur qui corpus habeat, colore uero non habeat. Verum prophetia & charitas non sic iunguntur in nomine Christiano necessario, ut corpus & color. Christianus esse potest, qui prophetiam non habet, modo sit fide & charitate præditus: corpus uero sine colore aliquo potest habere nemo.
units.tr: Since prophecy and faith are here numbered among the gifts of the Spirit, the question arises how someone can have them without charity. As regards prophecy, Augustine treats this question in the second book to Simplicianus, the first question: "Charity can indeed be found in a Christian man without prophecy and the other similar gifts; but prophecy without charity perhaps someone will say cannot be found, just as there is no one who has a body and lacks colour. Yet prophecy and charity are not so necessarily joined in the Christian name as body and colour are. A person can be a Christian who does not have prophecy, provided he is endowed with faith and charity; but no one can have a body without some colour."

units.la: Quod autem possit haberi pphetia sine charitate, tate, nō modo in Bileam cōprobatur: qui cum propheta esset, contra charitatem tamen egisse conuincitur: sed & in Saule rege, qui in ipso proposito innocentem Dauidem occidēdi accepto spiritu Dei unà cum Samuele, ac reliquis prophetis prophetauit. 1. Samuel. 19. ubi usque adeò erat alienus à charitate, ut & genarum, & innoxium, imo benemeritum occidere conaretur. Nec est ut dicat quisquam & Bileam & Saulem non bono spiritu Dei, sed malo prophetasse: hic uero loqui Apostolum de prophetia, quæ charisma sit spiritussancti. Deinde exempla ista Bileam & Saulis pertinere ad Vetus testamentum, hic uero loqui Apostolum de donis spiritussancti, quæ in Christum credentibus initio Noui testamenti conferebantur, quare aliam esse rationem & conditionem huius prophetiæ, quàm fuerit eius quam Bileam & Saul prophetarũt. Etenim ex ipsa scriptura conuinci potest, bono non malo spiritu prophetasse utrunque, tam Saulem, quàm Bileam.
units.tr: That prophecy can be had without charity is shown not only in Balaam, who, though a prophet, is convicted of having acted against charity; but also in King Saul, who, while intending to kill the innocent David, prophesied together with Samuel and the other prophets after receiving the Spirit of God. 1 Samuel 19, where he was so far from charity that he tried to kill a man who was blameless and indeed deserving well of him. Nor can anyone say that Balaam and Saul prophesied not by a good spirit of God but by an evil one; and that the Apostle here speaks of prophecy as a gift of the Holy Spirit. Further, these examples of Balaam and Saul belong to the Old Testament, whereas here the Apostle speaks of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which were given at the beginning of the New Testament to those believing in Christ. Hence the reason and condition of this prophecy are different from those of the prophecy which Balaam and Saul uttered. For it can be proved from Scripture itself that both Saul and Balaam prophesied by a good, not an evil, spirit.

units.la: De Bileam manifestissimum est ex omni illius historia, præsertim ex uerbis angeli. De Saule quoque ex eo patet, quod eodem spiritu cum Samuele & reliquis prophetis in ipso conspectu Samuelis, unà cum ipso & cæteris prophetasse scribitur. Sic enim in Ebræo legitur: ויחי עליו רוח אלהים, id est, Et factus etiam super ipsum: uel, Et factus est super ipsum etiam ipse spiritus Dei. Vocula Etiam omnino indicat eodem ipsum prophetasse spiritu, quo Samuel & cæteri prophetæ prophetarunt. Quod uero hi duo in Veteri testamento prophetarunt, non impedit, quo minus firmum sit argumentum, unde probetur prophetiam habere posse sine charitate. Idē enim est prophetiæ spiritus, tam in Veteri quàm Nouo testamento.
units.tr: About Balaam this is most evident from his whole story, especially from the words of the angel. About Saul it is also clear from the fact that he is written to have prophesied, in the very sight of Samuel, together with him and the other prophets, by the same spirit. For so it is read in the Hebrew: "And the Spirit of God came upon him" [ויחי עליו רוח אלהים], that is, "And he was also come upon", or, "And the Spirit of God itself came upon him." The word "also" plainly indicates that he prophesied by the same spirit by which Samuel and the other prophets prophesied. That these two prophesied in the Old Testament does not weaken the argument by which it is shown that prophecy can be had without charity. For the spirit of prophecy is the same in the Old Testament as in the New.

units.la: Verum sententiæ huic & Christus ipse astipulatur, Matthæi 7. cum dicit: Multi dicent mihi in illo die: Domine, domine, nonne in nomine tuo prophetauimus, & in nomine tuo dæmonia eiecimus, & in nomine tuo uirtutes multas fecimus? Et tunc cōfiteborillis dicēs: quia nunquam noui uos. Discedite à me omnes qui operati estis iniquitatem. Puto eos quibus hęc in die iudicij dicturus est Christus, habuisse prophetiam ex dono spiritus Christi, & tamen non habuisse charitate. Alias non possent reijci à Christo, nedum uocari operarij iniqui. Cum ergo tam in Nouo quàm Veteri testamento inueniantur prophetæ sine charitate, omnino relinquitur, haberi posse prophetiam sine charitate. Quodenim factum est, fieri potuisse constat.
units.tr: Indeed, Christ himself supports this view in Matthew 7, when he says: "Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in your name, and cast out devils in your name, and done many mighty works in your name? And then I will profess to them: I never knew you. Depart from me, all you who work iniquity." I think those to whom Christ will speak these words on the day of judgment had prophecy from the gift of Christ's Spirit, and yet did not have charity. Otherwise they could not be rejected by Christ, much less called workers of iniquity. Since, then, prophets without charity are found in the New Testament as well as the Old, it follows entirely that prophecy can be had without charity. For what has been done, it is clear that it can be done.

units.la: Ad eam uero quæstionem, qua quærunt, num & fides possit haberi sine charitate, per diuisionem respondemus. Refert enim de qua specie fidei quæratur. Si de ea quam uocant historicam, palam est, esse illam in multis sine charitate, qua & dæmones sine charitate credunt. Nec moror, siue speciem hanc fidei fidē
units.tr: To the question whether faith too can be had without charity, we answer by making a distinction. For it matters which kind of faith is asked about. If it is about the kind they call historical, it is plain that this is in many people without charity, as devils too believe without charity. I do not mind whether you call this kind of faith a faith or an opinion.

units.la: uoces siue opinionem. Sic est comparata, ut haberi possit sine charitate.
units.tr: It is so constituted that it can be had without charity.

units.la: Quod si de ea quæritur, quam miraculorum uocant, & recte indubitatam de potentia Dei persuasionem dixeris, & illam constat haberi posse sine charitate, sicuti ex præcedentibus Christi uerbis patet. Porro si quæstio sit de fide iustificante, quam fiduciam esse misericordiæ Dei in Christo sentimus, hanc dicimus uerram esse non posse, si charitate destituatur. Tenetur hoc Apostolus, cum Galat. 5. dicit: Nam in Christo Iesu neq; circumcisio quicquam valet, neq; præputium, sed fides quæ per charitatem est efficax.
units.tr: But if the question is about the faith they call of miracles, and you rightly describe it as a firm persuasion of the power of God, it is agreed that this can be had without charity, as is clear from the preceding words of Christ. Further, if the question is about justifying faith, which we understand to be the trust in the mercy of God in Christ, we say that this cannot be true if it lacks charity. The Apostle holds this when he says in Galatians 5: "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith which works through charity."

units.la: Ergo uera in Christum fides, qua ueri Christiani reddimur, instar ignis est, q. ardore suo attacta comburit. Vt enim uerus ignis esse non potest, si non fit ardore præditus: ita & uera non est in Christum fides, quæ per charitatem non est efficax. Quare friuolum est, quod aduersarij nos inani, ac mortuæ fidei iustificationem adscribere dicunt. Sed hac de re in Locis nostris.
units.tr: Therefore true faith in Christ, by which we are made true Christians, is like a fire, which when touched by its heat burns. For just as there can be no true fire unless it is endowed with heat, so faith in Christ is not true if it is not effective through charity. Hence it is frivolous that our opponents ascribe justification to an empty and dead faith. But on this matter see in our Loci.

units.la: Quamuis igitur & hyperbolice & hypothetice loquatur Apostolus, ut inde colligi certo non possit, haberi nequeant prophetia, & mysteriorum omnium scientia, & omnis omnium miraculorum fides sine charitate: ad hunc tamen modum ad propositam possumus respondere quæstionem.
units.tr: Although, therefore, the Apostle speaks both hyperbolically and hypothetically, so that it cannot certainly be inferred from this that prophecy, knowledge of all mysteries, and all faith of all miracles cannot be had without charity, nevertheless we can answer the question proposed in this way.

units.la: NIHIL sum.] Sic pronunciat de omnibus illis, qui apud Corinthios propter dicta charismata insolescebant. Dicit eos nihil esse, idque sub suaipsius persona, quo tolerabilius loquatur. Non dicit autem, Nihil est, ne ipsa tam magna charismata floccifacere uideatur, sed nihil sum. Per se multum est habere prophetiam, mysteriorum Dei scientiam, & fidem ad faciendā miracula efficacem, idque dono spiritus sancti: uerum qui ea sine charitate habet, hoc est, citra charitatem prophetat, deque mysterijs Dei loquitur, & miracula ac portenta facit, non ad ædificationem ecclesiæ, sed ad inanem ostentationem, proprij nominis celebritatem, &, quod Corinthij nonnulli faciebant, ad scindendum ecclesiæ concordiam: is demum nihil est, intellige coram Domino, & in hac causa. Potest qui talis est, in alijs rebus, & coram mundo esse aliquid, etiamsi hic & coram Deo sit nihil, hoc est, nullius æstimandus.
units.tr: I am nothing. He pronounces this of all those who among the Corinthians were growing proud on account of the gifts mentioned. He says they are nothing, and this in his own person, so that he may speak more tolerably. But he does not say "it is nothing," lest he seem to make light of such great gifts, but "I am nothing." In itself it is much to have prophecy, knowledge of the mysteries of God, and faith effective for working miracles, and this by the gift of the Holy Spirit. But whoever has these without charity, that is, prophesies apart from charity, speaks of the mysteries of God, and does miracles and wonders, not for the building up of the Church but for empty show, the celebrity of his own name, and, as some Corinthians did, for tearing apart the concord of the Church, that person is finally nothing, understand before the Lord and in this cause. Such a person may be something in other matters and before the world, even if here and before God he is nothing, that is, of no account.

units.la: Augustinus de fide ad Petrum diaconum, cap. 37. locum hunc Apostoli citat ad hūc modum: Firmissime tene, & nullatenus dubita omnem extra ecclesiam catholicam baptizatum, participem fieri non posse uitæ æternæ, si ante finem uitæ huius catholicæ non fuerit redditus, atque incorporatus ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Augustine, in his letter on faith to Peter the deacon, chapter 37, cites this passage of the Apostle in this way: "Hold most firmly, and never doubt, that every person baptized outside the catholic Church cannot become a partaker of eternal life, unless before the end of this life he has been brought back and incorporated into the Church."

units.la: Quia si habeam, inquit Apostolus, omnem fidem, & nouerim omnia sacramenta (sic legit, quasi idem sit mysterium quod sacramentum) charitatem autem non habeā, nihil sum. Hæc ille.
units.tr: "For if I have," says the Apostle, "all faith, and know all the sacraments" (so he reads it, as if mystery and sacrament were the same thing), "but have not charity, I am nothing." So far Augustine.

units.la: Primum, magna cum ratione controuerti potest, quod salute illis negat, qui extra catholicam ecclesiam baptizantur, si hoc accipiatur eo sensu, quo hodie Romanam ecclesiam uocant catholicam, extra quam saluari possunt, quotquot syncera in Christum fide credunt, communionemq; illius propter horrendā defectionem & manifestas abominationes ex animo fugiunt.
units.tr: First, it can be argued with good reason against him that he denies salvation to those who are baptized outside the catholic Church, if this is taken in the sense in which the Papists today call the Roman Church "catholic," outside of which, they say, all who believe in Christ with sincere faith can be saved, yet who from their hearts shun its communion because of its horrible apostasy and manifest abominations.

units.la: Deinde, quod extra catholicam baptizatū esse pro eo accipit, quod Apostolus mysteria Dei sine charitate nosse dicit, & coactum est & infirmum.
units.tr: Next, he takes being baptized outside the catholic Church to mean what the Apostle describes as knowing the mysteries of God without charity; and this is a state that is both constrained and weak.

units.la: Etenim non mox charitate fraterna destitutus est, quisquis cum multitudine eius ecclesiæ, quæ se catholicam uocat, non communicat. Potest enim illa sic esse comparata ut magis sit corruptione, defectione, & adultera communicatione quàm uera ac syncera Christi fide catholica, id quod hodie notum est omnibus illis, qui ex uerbo domini de uera rectius possunt iudicare ecclesia. Quemadmodum igitur innumeri sunt in catholica sine charitate, ita & innumeri extra illam uera possunt esse & fide in Christum, & charitate præditi: nisi catholica uocetur ea ecclesia, quæ non multitudine, sed ueritate Dei & communione electorum omnium prophetarum, apostolorum, & fidelium constat.
units.tr: For whoever does not communicate with the multitude of that congregation which calls itself catholic is not at once deprived of brotherly charity. For that Church may be so constituted that it is more corrupt, apostate, and an adulterous communion than a true and sincere catholic Church in the faith of Christ. This is now known to all those who can judge more correctly from the Word of the Lord which Church is true. Therefore, just as there are countless people in the catholic Church without charity, so there can be countless people outside it who possess true faith in Christ and are endowed with charity; unless the Church that is catholic is taken to be the one which consists not in the multitude but in the truth of God and in the communion of all the elect, prophets, apostles, and believers.

units.la: ET si infumam in alimoniam omnes facultates meas.] Non dubito fuisse in ecclesia Corinthiorum inter schismaticos, qui distributio eleemosynarum, uel proprij nominis rumusculos, uel sectæ suæ celebritatem uenarentur, atque ita aliquam facultatum suarum partem in suæ sectæ consortes cæteris pauperiores insumerent. Sic enim primi Christiani instituebantur, ut qui ditiores essent, egenorum fratrum inopiæ facultatibus suis succurrerēt, cuius rei exempla in Actis Apostolicis legimus. Quare etiam ij, qui non erant uera philadelphia præditi, ne minus Christiani uiderentur: uel, quo nominis aliquid uenarentur, eleemosynas, perinde atque pij faciebāt, quale est quod de Anania & Sapphira in Actis habetur. Ex illis Satā dubio procul plerōsque sectarios subornauit inter Corinthios, qui studio eleemosynarum applausum cùm sibi tum sectę suę uenarentur.
units.tr: "And if I bestow all my goods to feed the poor." I do not doubt that in the Corinthian Church there were, among the schismatics, some who pursued the distribution of alms in order to win for themselves a little reputation, either for their own name or for the fame of their sect, and so spent some part of their wealth, more than the others, on the members of their sect. For the first Christians were taught in this way: those who were richer were to relieve the want of their needy brothers out of their means, and we read examples of this in the Acts of the Apostles. Hence those who had no true brotherly love, lest they seem less Christian, or in order to win some name for themselves, gave alms just as the godly did; this is what is recorded in Acts about Ananias and Sapphira. Undoubtedly Satan, by means of these people, stirred up many sectarians among the Corinthians who, through their zeal for almsgiving, sought applause both for themselves and for their sect.

units.la: Horum studia perstringēs, & inania esse docens: Etsi, inquit, infumam in alimoniam omnes faoultates meas, charitatem autem nō habeam, nihil utilitatis capio. Intésionem autem habet, quod non simpliciter dicit, Etsi cibauero pauperes: sed, etsi infumam omnes facultates meas, intellige, in cibos pauperum. Sic supremum eleemosynæ gradum exprimere uoluit. Etenim qui omnia sua erogat in pauperes, ut nō habet præterea quo altius in hoc studio ascendat, sic in illo perfectionis gradum adeptus uidetur.
units.tr: Rebuking their zeal and teaching that it is empty, he says: "Even if I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, but have not charity, I gain no advantage." There is an emphasis in the fact that he does not simply say, "Even if I feed the poor," but, "Even if I bestow all my goods," understood as "on the food of the poor." In this way he wished to express the highest degree of almsgiving. For he who spends all his possessions on the poor, having no further means by which he might rise higher in this zeal, seems thereby to have reached the highest degree of perfection.

units.la: Quod si ne talis quidem aliquid utilitatis
units.tr: But if not even such a person gains any advantage

units.la: coram Deo consequitur, si charitate destituatur: quanto minus sperandum est illis qui minus aliquid de superfluo absque charitate expendunt?
units.tr: before God, if he lacks charity, how much less should we hope for it from those who spend less of their surplus on alms without charity?

units.la: Locus hic est de eleemosyna, & de largitionibus, quib. maiores nostri facultates suas, cū moriēdum esset, in saginationem canonicorū & monachorum distribuerunt. Vtinam nostri hodie, uel uigesimam partem ex charitate in usus pauperum insumerent.
units.tr: This passage concerns almsgiving and the bequests by which our forebears, when they were about to die, distributed their goods for the feasting of canons and monks. Would that our people today devoted even a twentieth part of their wealth, out of charity, to the needs of the poor.

units.la: ET si tradam corpus meum ut comburar.] Non possumus lectionem eorum recipere, qui pro ναυδύεσθαι, id est, comburar, legunt ναυχέ-σεσθαι, id est, glorier ad hunc modum: Et si tradam corpus meum ut glorier. Sic enim præter rationem subijceretur, Et charitatem non habeam.
units.tr: "And if I give up my body to be burned." We cannot accept the reading of those who, instead of καυθήσωμαι, that is, "I be burned," read καυχήσωμαι, that is, "I glory," in this way: "And if I give up my body that I may glory." For that would introduce a sense inconsistent with what follows, "and have not charity."

units.la: Nō enim ex charitate dat corpus suum, qui eo dat animo, ut sit unde glorietur, ut necesse non fuerit eam conditionem exprimere dicendo, Et charitatem non habeam: siquidem dixisset, Et si tradam corpus meum ut glorier. Voluit magis intendere quod dixit: Et si tradam corpus meum. Ideo non adiecit, in periculum, uel in afflictiones, uel in mortem: sed, ut comburar. Est enim genus hoc mortis carni acerbissimum, quo homo uiuus flammis in cinerem redigendus, uel ut hodie solent catholici, carbonibus circumpositis crudeli & prolixo cruciatu torrendus & assandus traditur. Quoniam igitur sectarij martyria pro sua religione subire non dubitabant, indeq; gloriam quærebant, ut admoneat nihil hinc quoque esse illis emolumenti coram Deo, propter charitatis defectum, particulam hanc adiecit. quasi dicat: Etiamsi grauissimos corporum uestrorum dolores & cruciatus sustineatis, nihil tamen utilitatis ex eo capietis, donec contra charitatem ecclesiam Christi scideritis. Et ad eandem particulæ huius intentionem facit, quod non dicit: Et si tradatur: sed, Et si tradam corpus meum, ut comburar, ut etiam ea martyria inutilia esse moneat, quæ sponte subeuntur, si desit charitas.
units.tr: For he does not give his body out of charity who gives it with the intention that there may be something to glory in; so there would have been no need to express this condition by adding "and have not charity," if he had said, "And if I give up my body that I may glory." He preferred to press the point he made with the words "and if I give up my body." Therefore he did not add "to danger," or "to afflictions," or "to death," but "to be burned." This kind of death is the most bitter for the flesh, by which a living man is reduced to ashes in the flames, or, as the Papists are wont to do today, is handed over to be roasted and grilled with a cruel and lingering torment, with coals placed around him. Since, then, the sectarians did not hesitate to undergo martyrdom for their religion and sought glory from it, he added this clause to warn that even from this they gain nothing before God, because of their lack of charity; as if to say: "Even if you endure the most grievous pains and torments of your bodies, you will gain no advantage from it, so long as you rend the Church of Christ against charity." The fact that he does not say "and if it be handed over" but "and if I give up my body to be burned" also serves this same purpose, so that he may warn that even those martyrdoms are useless which are undertaken willingly, if charity is lacking.

units.la: CHARITATEM autem non habeam.]
units.tr: But if I do not have charity.

units.la: Hoc est, si non affectu charitatis, sed alio quopiam studio, sicut solent sectarij, facultates meas pauperibus alendis erogauero, imò si corpus meum, siue propter fidem meā, siue propter aliam quamlibet causam igni comburendum tradens alienus à charitate fraterna fuero.
units.tr: That is, if I distribute my goods to feed the poor, not from a feeling of love but from some other motive, as sectarians usually do; indeed, if I hand over my body to be burned, whether for my faith or for any other cause, and am estranged from brotherly love.

units.la: Non est autem ut quæramus quomodo possit quisquam siue charitate omnes facultates suas in pauperes alendos insumere, uel corpus suum ad comburēdum tradere. Sic enim comparatum est ingenium carnis, ut uel præpostero zelo, uel inanis gloriæ studio, nec facultatibus suis parcat, nec corpori. cuius rei non modo exempla permulta extant in historijs, sed & ipsa experientia quotidie in oculos eorum incurrit, qui obseruant.
units.tr: We need not ask how anyone could spend all his goods feeding the poor, or give his body to be burned, out of love. Human nature is so constituted that, through misguided zeal or a desire for empty glory, it spares neither its goods nor its body. Not only are there very many examples of this in histories, but experience itself meets the eyes of anyone who observes daily.

units.la: Vt quid
units.tr: Why

units.la: Vt quid parceret facultatibus illis caro, quę reparari possunt, quando uitæ suæ non parcit, quam semel amissam recuperare non poterit? Et eousque pertinax est, ubi insanire cœpit, ut non modo ferat omnis generis cruciatus aliùde uiolenter illatos, sed & suapte se sponte in il los proijciat. Nemo Mutij magù igni iniecit, sed ipse hoc ultro ostentationis gratia fecit. La cedæmoniensium Diamastigosis, flagellatio ui delicet, utiq; ex charitate, sed inanis gloriæ stu dio solenniter celebrabatur, adhortatibus pa rentibus suos adolescentes, ut strenue flagel lando perseuerarent: gloriæ sibi ducentes, si a nimam citius emitterent, quàm corpus flagel lo subducerent. Huiusmodi flagallatores per multi habentur etiamnum, qui usque adeo a lieni sunt ab affectu charitatis, ut citius sangui nem proprium, quàm obulum in usus paupe rum profundant. Sacerdotes & prophetę Baal cultris suaipsorum corpora ad sanguinē usque dilacerabant, quo adulteræ suæ religioni con sulerent. Peregrinus quidam temporibus Tra iani inanis gloriæ mancipium in rogum arden tem non iniectus est, sed ultro seipse iniecit. In ignes Aetneos insiliit sponte sua Empedo cles. Et Heraclitus quoq; cum se stercore bu balo obliuisset, igni uolens exustus est. Potue runt hæc fieri sine charitate, prępostero carnis studio, ut perspicuum sit pertinaciam proposi ti illius nullis posse doloribus & cruciatibus uinci, non in uiris tãtum, sed & fœminis. Cum Carthagine capta Scipioni supplex esset fact9 Asdrubal, uxor illius citius incendium corpo ris sui, quàm præsentem calamitatem ferens, in ardentis urbis flammas, sese unà cum filijs suis coniecit. Sit hoc priuatum & rarum. Quid quod in India nobiles fœminæ, præsertim ciui tatis Tarnasseræ, quintodecimo die post mor tem maritorum suorum, ijsdem locis ubi cor pora illorum exusta sunt, accenso rogo uiuas se comburendas, pro more patriæ tradunt? Quid ergo mirum si amor Dei & proximi in e lectis ac fidelib. hoc possit, ut nec facultates, nec propria corpora, si ita uisum sit Deo, impē dere dubitent?
units.tr: Why would the flesh spare those goods, which can be replaced, when it does not spare its life, which once lost it cannot recover? It is so stubborn, once it begins to rage, that it not only endures every kind of torment inflicted on it from outside but also throws itself into them of its own accord. No one threw Mucius into the fire; he did it himself, of his own will, for the sake of display. The Lacedaemonians' Diamastigosis, a ritual flogging, was solemnly celebrated, not indeed from love but from a desire for empty glory; parents urged their young men to persist bravely under the lash, counting it a matter of glory if they gave up their life sooner than they gave up their body to the whip. Many such flagellants are still found today, who are so estranged from love that they will sooner pour out their own blood than a penny for the needs of the poor. The priests and prophets of Baal lacerated their bodies with knives, even to the point of bleeding, to serve their adulterous religion. A certain pilgrim in the time of Trajan, a slave of empty glory, was not thrown onto the burning pyre but threw himself on it. Empedocles leapt into the fires of Etna of his own accord. Heraclitus too, when he had smeared himself with cow dung, was willingly burned by fire. These things could happen without love, through the perverse zeal of the flesh, so that it is clear that the obstinacy of such a purpose cannot be overcome by any pains or torments, not only in men but also in women. When Carthage was captured and Hasdrubal had become a suppliant to Scipio, his wife, unable to bear the present calamity, threw herself and her children into the flames of the burning city, preferring to be consumed by fire. Let this be considered a private and rare case. What of the fact that in India noble women, especially in the city of Tarnassera, on the fifteenth day after the death of their husbands, hand themselves over, according to their country's custom, to be burned alive on a lit pyre in the very place where their husbands' bodies were burned? Why then is it surprising if the love of God and neighbour can bring the elect and faithful to hesitate at nothing, not even their goods or their own bodies, if God should so will?

units.la: NIHIL utilitatis capio.] Dices, quomodo inutile est alere pauperes? Nā etiamsi fiat hoc alio, quàm charitatis studio, interim tamen be nefit miseris, & incitantur alij ad imitationem. Deinde quomodo non prodest corpus trade re in mortem, propter religionis confirmatio nem, cum hinc multi in fide cõfirmentur, etiā si fiat hoc citra charitatem?
units.tr: "I gain nothing." You will say: how is it useless to feed the poor? Even if this is done from some other motive than love, it still benefits the wretched, and others are stirred to imitate it. Again, how does it not profit to hand over one's body to death for the confirmation of religion, since many are thereby confirmed in the faith, even if this is done without love?

units.la: Respondeo: Non dicit impersonaliter, nihil prodest, nihil habet utilitatis: sed, ἀλλ᾽ ὠφελᾶσθαι, hoc est, nihil capio utilitatis, nihil mihi pdest. Quantumuis in se sit magnum & præclarum, profitę; quàm plurimis, facienti tamen utrun que prorsus est nihil &inutile coram domino, si desit charitas. Quare? Quia non tam factum spectatur à Deo, q animi affectus & facti ratio. Et quoniam ipse charitas est, amat eos qui eo dem sunt charitatis spiritu præditi. Sic, inquit ille, Deus est charitas: & qui manet in charita te, in Deo manet, & Deus in ipso. Et Christus seruator: In hoc, inquit, cognoscemini quod mei discipuli sitis, si charitatem inter uos mu tuã habueritis. Seductores itaq; sunt, qui mo rituris uitam æternam pollicētur, si facultates suas pro redimendis animabus suis, uel paupe ribus, uel ociofis uentribus tribuant. Nihil e nim illis prodest, quia quod faciūt, alieni à cha ritate fraterna faciunt, & interim hæredibus suis incommodant. Et si martyria quãtumuis acerba & insignia nihil prosunt sine charitate, consequitur per multos in ecclesijs Papisticis coli pro sanctis, quorum animæ cum hypocri tis sunt in gehenna. Non enim moratur Deus corporum cruciatus, sed animum spectat, fide ac dilectione præditum.
units.tr: I answer: he does not say impersonally that it profits nothing, or has no advantage; rather, ἀλλ᾽ ὠφελᾶσθαι [but I gain], that is, "I gain no advantage, nothing profits me." However great and admirable in itself, and however much it benefits many, it is nevertheless entirely nothing and useless before the Lord for the one who does it, if love is lacking. Why? Because God looks not so much at the deed as at the affection of the mind and the reason for the deed. And since God himself is love, he loves those who are endowed with the same spirit of love. So, says that writer, "God is love, and he who abides in love abides in God, and God in him." And Christ the Saviour: "By this," he says, "shall you be known to be my disciples, if you have love for one another." Therefore they are seducers who promise eternal life to those who are about to die, if they give their goods either to ransom their souls or to the poor, or to idle bellies. For this profits them nothing, because what they do they do estranged from brotherly love, and meanwhile they harm their heirs. And if martyrdoms, however bitter and remarkable, profit nothing without love, it follows that many in the Papist churches are worshipped as saints, whose souls are with hypocrites in hell. For God does not regard the torments of bodies, but looks at the mind, endowed with faith and affection.

units.la: Charitas patiens est, benigna est: charitas non inuidet, charitas non est pro cax, non inflatur, non est fastidiosa, non quærit quæ sua sunt, non irritatur, non cogitat malum, non gaudet super iniu stitia: sed congaudet veritati, omnia suf fert, omnia credit, omnia sperat, omnia sustinet.
units.tr: Love is patient, love is kind; love does not envy, love does not boast, it is not puffed up, it does not behave itself unseemly, it does not seek its own, it is not provoked, it does not think evil, it does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices in the truth; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

units.la: Hactenus primam capitis huius partem ab soluit, qua contendit charismata illa spiritus, quæ plus æquo magnifiebant in ecclesia Co rinthiorum, sine charitate nihil prodesse habe tibus: iam transit ad commendandum charita tem, quam celebrat & deprædicat hinc ad sinē usque capitis, primum ab ingenio plane diui no, deinde à perpetuitate. Commendationem ingenij illius quindecim elogijs admodū præ claris complectitur, quæ sic recenset, ut licet singula uno uerbo exprimat, nihil tamē obscu ritatis admisceat, imò cum luce ardorem quen dam animi erga charitatem coniungat, quem uerborum structura spirat.
units.tr: Thus far he has completed the first part of this chapter, in which he contends that those gifts of the Spirit, which in the Corinthian church were magnified beyond measure, profit nothing for those who lack love. Now he passes on to commend love, which he celebrates and proclaims from here to the end of the chapter, first from its wholly divine nature, then from its perpetuity. He embraces the praise of its nature in fifteen very notable epithets, which he recounts in such a way that, although he expresses each in a single word, he mixes in no obscurity, but rather joins to the light a certain ardour of mind towards love, which the very structure of his words breathes forth.

units.la: CHARITAS, inquit, patiens est. ] Græcè est, μακροθυμεῖ, quod sonat, longanimiter agit. In terpretib. magis placuit uertere, Patiēs est. Vo cula θυμὸς sumitur quidem pro animo: uerum significat animum nonnihil motum ac pertur batum, qualis est cum sanguis circa præcordia incipit ebullire, & in iram efferuescere. Sût qui id dicant esse in equo θυμὸν, quod ἀρχὴ est in ho mine. Hoc sensu μακροθυμῶ idé est Græcis qd Ebræis אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם, id est, procul ab ira. Siue ac cipiamus θυμὸν, pro animo simpliciter, siue μ animi commotione, μακροθυμία est uirtus, qua cohibemur, ne statim excandescamus ac præ cipites ad irafcēdum simus, ut recte uerterint, charitas patiens est. Hanc charitati uirtutem propterea adscribit, quod illa hominem patiē tem ac tardum ad iram reddit.
units.tr: "Love," he says, "is patient." In Greek it is μακροθυμεῖ [makrothymei], which means "acts with long-suffering." The translators preferred to render it "is patient." The word θυμὸς [thymos] indeed means mind, but it signifies a mind somewhat stirred and disturbed, such as when the blood begins to boil about the heart and to seethe into anger. Some say that θυμὸν [thymon] in a horse is what ἀρχὴ [archē] is in a man. In this sense μακροθυμῶ [makrothymō] among the Greeks is the same as the Hebrew אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם ['erekh 'appayim], that is, far from anger. Whether we take θυμὸν simply for the mind, or for the agitation of the mind, μακροθυμία [makrothymia] is a virtue by which we are restrained from flaring up at once and from being headlong to anger; so the translators rightly rendered it, "love is patient." He ascribes this virtue to love because love makes a man patient and slow to anger.

units.la: Tribuit scriptura Deo μακροθυμίαν erga pec catores. Vnde hanc habeat, admonemur hoc loco, cum dicit Apostolus, charitas patiēs est. Deus est charitas, ergo consequitur esse eum tardum ad iră ac patientem. Quàto autem no stro bono talis sit, quis satis cogitauerit, nedū explicuerit: Tolle patientiam à Deo, mox per eat mundus necesse est.
units.tr: Scripture ascribes μακροθυμία [long-suffering] to God towards sinners. Whence he has it we are reminded in this place, when the Apostle says, "love is patient." God is love; it follows that he is slow to anger and patient. But how greatly our good depends on such a nature, who could sufficiently consider, much less explain? Take away patience from God, and the world must immediately perish.

units.la: Sic cogitemus de unoquoque mortalium conuictu, contubernio, coetu, consortio, & ecclesia. Hic si desit charitas, deest patientia. Si desit patientia, omnis societas disturbatur, omnis unitas & concordia scinditur, omnis ordo confunditur: quandoquidem nemo parcit proximo, sed ad leuem offensam concitati animi cuncta subuertere moliuntur citius quàm ut condonent admissum, uel ferant quod uidetur esse molestum. Sapiens non feret stultitiam insipientis, qui docent non ferent tarditatem idiotæ, qui firmiores sunt infirmiorum defectus mox auersabuntur, &c. Quare haud præter rationem est, quod Apostolus elogium hoc patientiæ mox initio charitati tribuit, significans hinc potissimum esse schismata in ecclesia Corinthiorum, quod propter charitatis defectum hac essent mutua patientia destituti. Qui diligit, non facile consortium dissoluit eorum quos diligit, sed omnia tolerat & ir remisse satagit, quo cócordia seruetur, quoad eius citra offensam Dei fieri potest. Hoc signi ficans dicit, charitas patiens est. Hæc patiens [?] charitas præstat quod Basilius epistola 79. sic dicit, [?].
units.tr: Let us think in this way of every mortal in living together, in cohabitation, in assembly, in fellowship, and in the Church. Here, if love is lacking, patience is lacking. If patience is lacking, every society is thrown into disorder, every unity and concord is torn apart, every order is confounded; since no one spares his neighbour, but roused by a slight offence they strive to overturn everything, sooner than forgive what has been done or bear what seems troublesome. The wise man will not bear the folly of the foolish; those who teach will not bear the slowness of the unlearned; those who are stronger will at once turn away from the weaknesses of the weaker, and so on. Hence it is not without reason that the Apostle at the very beginning ascribes this commendation of patience to love, signifying chiefly that the schisms in the Corinthian church arose because, through lack of love, they were destitute of mutual patience. He who loves does not easily dissolve fellowship with those whom he loves, but bears all things and strives without rest that concord may be preserved, as far as it can be done without offence to God. Signifying this he says, "love is patient." This patient [?] love accomplishes what Basil says in his 79th letter, [?].

units.la: BENIGNA est, inquit] Græcè est, [?]. Sonat [?], placidum, humanum, comè, unde est uerbũ hoc [?], quo tribuit charitati Apostolus, quod sit ingenio placido, mi ti & humano: cuius oppositum est, esseasperũ, seuerum, ac morosum. Quod uero uerterunt, Benigna est, hoc est ad benefaciendum propè sa, ex eo est, quod [?] sonat etiam utilem, ut [?] idem sit quod aliorum utilitati studere. Sane parum refert utrouis modo legamus. Nam utrunq; præstat charitas, hominem reddens & humanum ac blandum & simul utilibus aliorum accommodum. Hanc itaq; charitatem desiderabat in Corinthijs qua reddereritur & [?] & [?], patientes & humani. Etenim si hac præditi fuissent, non ita proclives fuissent ad schismata. Qui [?] est, placidis, suauibus, & humanis moribus, neminé facile offendit aut fastidit: & qui [?] est, haud facile offenditur. Tales autem sunt, qui diligunt. Quare ubi charitas est, ibi non datur locus schismati. Quomodo enim scinderetur à se inuicem, qui spiritu charitatis præditi, patientes & humani, nec offenduntur quenquam, nec offenduntur facile?
units.tr: BENIGNA est, he says. In Greek it is [?]. The word means gentle, mild, humane, courteous, and from it comes [?], by which the Apostle ascribes to love a gentle, mild and humane disposition. Its opposite is to be harsh, severe and morose. The Latin rendering "benigna est," meaning "is kind, bent on doing good," comes from the fact that [?] also means useful, so that [?] is the same as to be eager for the usefulness of others. Indeed it matters little which way we read it, for love accomplishes both: it makes a man gentle, humane and pleasant, and at the same time accommodating to the usefulness of others. This is the love the Corinthians lacked, by which they would have been made [?] and [?], patient and humane. For had they been endowed with it, they would not have been so prone to schisms. One who is [?], of gentle, pleasant and humane manners, easily offends nobody or disdains anyone, and one who is [?] is not easily offended. Such are those who love. Therefore where there is love, there is no room for schism. For how could those be torn from one another who, endowed with the spirit of love, are patient and humane, neither giving offence to anyone nor taking offence easily?

units.la: Tales, inquam, reddit charitas fidissima unitatis & concordiæ custos. Ex oppostio, scientiæ, iusticiæ & sanctimoniæ opinio reddit homines inflatos, seueros, morosos, & omnium aliorum contemptores, qui & leui momento offendantur, & parú soliciti sint, ne quos mo-
units.tr: Such, I say, love makes us, being the most faithful guardian of unity and concord. The opinion of knowledge, righteousness and holiness, on the other hand, makes men puffed up, severe, morose and contemptuous of all others, who are offended by the slightest thing and are little concerned lest they offend anyone by their moroseness and harshness.

units.la: rositate & asperitate sua offendant. Vbi tales sunt in ecclesia, non potest firma esse concordia & unitas. Tales euaserant plerique Corinthiorum, defectu charitatis, ideoq; procliues erant ad schismata.
units.tr: Where such people are in the Church, firm concord and unity cannot exist. Many of the Corinthians had become such, through lack of love, and therefore they were prone to schisms.

units.la: Quod autem ordinem attinet, prior est [?] quàm [?]. Etenim quamuis utrãque uirtutes ex charitatis fonte promanant, est tamen [?], & non [?]. Et hoc ordine ad Rom. ca. 2. sic ponuntur: Aut diuitias [?] contenis, quo loco Deo, qui ipsisima charitas est, benignitas, uel ut Eras. & uulgatus interpres habent, bonitas, tolerantia, & lenitas tribuitur. Hunc tamen ordinem haud constanter seruat Apostolus. Nam Gal. 5. ubi fructus spiritus recenset, sic dicit: Fructus spiritus est charitas, gaudium, pax, [?], &c.
units.tr: As to order, [?] comes before [?]. For although both virtues flow from the fountain of love, [?] is nonetheless the first, and not the other way round. In this order they are set down in Romans chapter 2, where, after the words "Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness...", kindness (or, as Erasmus and the Vulgate translator have it, goodness), forbearance and gentleness are ascribed to God, who is love itself. The Apostle does not keep this order consistently, however. For in Galatians 5, where he lists the fruit of the Spirit, he says: "The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, [?]," and so on.

units.la: CHARITAS, inquit, non inuidet.] Vulgatus interpres uertit, non æmulatur. In Græco est: [?]. Significat autem zelus uehementis amoris studium, & inde transfertur ad æmulationem & inuidiam quoque, quę propter rè amatam nascitur in animo amantis. Quoniam autem uerbum æmulari aliquando pro zelo amoris quenquam prosequi, aliquando imitari amatum, nonnunquam pro inuidere cuipiam rem amatam accipitur: non satis expref sit uulgatus interpres sensum Apostoli per uerbum æmulandi. Etenim non rectè darentur charitati priores duæ significationes, quare tertia usurpanda erat, ac uertendum, charitas non inuidet. Quid est autem non inuidere aliud, quàm gratulari proximo quàuis rerum prosperitatè, etiam eorum bonorum, charissimatum, ac uirtutum communicationem, quibus uel potiti sumus nos uel potiri uellemus? Sic uero animatus esse poterit nemo, nisi per spiritum Dei affectu sit charitatis præditus. Etiamsi charissimata illa quæ supra recensuit, in unum aliquem hominem conferantur omnia, haud tamen poterant illum liberum reddere ab inuidia, quam sola excludit charitas. Vbi autè inuidiæ morbus obtinet, ibi non potest sana ecclesiastici corporis esse cōstitutio: id quod in ecclesia Corinthiorum patuit, ubi per schismata fuit diuulsa & instar dissolutæ scopæ facta.
units.tr: LOVE, he says, does not envy. The Vulgate translator renders it "does not emulate." In Greek it is [?]. Zelos signifies the eager pursuit of a passionate love, and from this it is transferred to rivalry and envy too, which arises in the mind of the lover on account of the thing loved. Since the verb "to emulate" is sometimes taken to mean to pursue someone out of zeal for love, sometimes to imitate the one loved, and sometimes to envy someone the thing loved, the Vulgate translator did not express the Apostle's meaning adequately by the verb "to emulate." The first two senses would not fit love rightly, so the third had to be used, and it should be rendered "love does not envy." What is it not to envy, but to rejoice with a neighbour in any prosperity, even in the sharing of those goods, gifts and virtues which we either possess or would wish to possess? Yet no one can be so disposed unless he is endowed with the affection of love through the Spirit of God. Even if all those gifts he listed above were conferred on one man, they could not free him from envy, which love alone excludes. Where the disease of envy prevails, the body of the Church cannot be in sound health. This became evident in the Corinthian church, where it was torn apart by schisms and made like a broken broom.

units.la: CHARITAS non est procax.] In Græco est, [?]. Chrysostomus exponit, [?]. Significat autem [?], id est, priusquam tempestiuum sit aliquid præripere & præsumere. Tractum est autem à pullis adhuc implumibus, uolare gestientibus, priusquam possint. Et addit Chrysostomus. Reddit enim charitas prudentem, grauem ac firmum. Ergo [?] idem est Chrysostomo, quod leuem & procliuem esse ad præsumendum quiduis intemperanter. Tales erant Corinthij, cum suam quisque cœnam alijs non expectatis præsumerent, quod utique non fecissent,si fratres dilexissent.Basilius ψ̈ ἐπὶ καὶ ἀ A ri ab hac inflatione. Vbi de gradibus,ordinibus,prærogatiuis,prælaturis ac titulis tanto pere coutenditur, putabimus ne omnia citra inflati animi arrogantiam geri.
units.tr: LOVE is not rash. In Greek it is [?]. Chrysostom explains it as [?], that is, before something is the right time to snatch it away and presume upon it. The word is drawn from young birds, still unfledged, eager to fly before they can. Chrysostom adds: "For love makes a man prudent, grave and firm." So for Chrysostom [?] means being light and prone to presume on anything intemperately. Such were the Corinthians, when each one anticipated the others and ate his own supper, which surely they would not have done had they loved their brothers. Basil... [?]... from this inflation. Where there is such great contention over degrees, orders, prerogatives, prelacies and titles, shall we think that everything is done without the arrogance of a puffed-up mind?

units.la: Hoc sensu perperàm agere, intemperanter est & oftentanter agere. Quid Erasmus senserit, dum uertit, Non est procax,in annotationib. illud uide.
units.tr: To act wrongly in this sense is to act intemperately and ostentatiously. As to what Erasmus thought when he rendered it "is not rash," see his annotations on that passage.

units.la: Meo iudicio, retinenda est Chrysostomi sententia,nisi placet eorum expositio, qui ψφρ. id est,cum iactantia elatum esse dicūt,aut eorum quibus perperàm agere,contumaciter & contumeliosè est agere. Generalius est quod nonnulli exponunt, Non agit perperàm,id est,peruerse, quàm ut huic loco conueniat. Germanicus interpres uertit,die liebe schalcket nit.
units.tr: In my judgement Chrysostom's opinion should be retained, unless we prefer the explanation of those who say [?], that is, that it means to be puffed up with boasting, or of those who take it to mean to act wrongly, that is, to act stubbornly and insultingly. The explanation of some, that it means "does not act wrongly," that is, perversely, is too general to suit this passage. The German translator renders it: die liebe schalcket nit ("love does not behave wickedly").

units.la: Tribuit igitur charitati,quod reddat homines non intemperanter præcipites,leues,inconstantes, & facile quod non deceat præsumentes,quales erant ex Corinthijs nonnulli: sed graues & constantes,qui non facile ad dif soluendam ecclesiæ unitatem & concordiam prorumpant,id quod assolent,qui procaci sūt ingenio præditi, quo uicio iuuenes plerùque laborant,& mulierculæ:illi propter ætatis,hę propter sexus leuitatem.
units.tr: Love therefore is credited with making men not intemperately headlong, light, inconstant, and readily presumptuous in what is unseemly, as some of the Corinthians were, but grave and steady, who do not easily break out into dissolving the unity and concord of the Church. Those of a bold disposition commonly do this, a fault to which young men for the most part are prone, and silly women too: the former because of the lightness of their age, the latter because of the lightness of their sex.

units.la: NON inflatur.] Græcè est, ψυσιοῦται. Sonat autem φύσω aliquando follem, aliquando flatum. Et Latinis uerbo infladi per metaphoram ad animi transfertur superbiam & arrogantiam, perinde atque Græcis uerbum φυσιοῦσθαι. Arrogans enim, qui perpetuo gloriàs suas & arrogantiam spirat,similis est tolli inflato, & uentos spiranti. Vnde & gloriosulos & arrogantes uenosos uocant. Inflationes huius metaphoram posuit hic Apostolus pro superbia animi inflati & arrogantis. Mater illius non est charitas,sed corruptæ ac uanæ mentis leuitas,quæ opinione propriæ,uel iusticię, uel sanctimoniæ,uel opulentiæ, uel scientiæ, aut terreni successus, uel qualitercunque acquisiti honoris,ueluti uento quodam inflata turgescit,insolescit,& arrogatiam spirat. Hinc illud est: Scientia inflat,charitas ædificat, supra capite octauo , ubi uide quæ sint annotata.Charitas omnes animi uirtutes ac dotes sic retinet & conseruat in ordine,ut singulæ possint esse ad ædificationem ecclesiæ utiles, dū animi inflationem & arrogantiam excludit: quæ ubi obtinuerit,omnia peruertit ac destru it.Hucputo respicere Apostolum,cum dicit: Non inflatur.
units.tr: NOT puffed up. In Greek it is [?]. Phusao sometimes means a bellows, sometimes a blast of wind. In Latin the verb "to be inflated" is transferred by metaphor to the pride and arrogance of the mind, just as the Greek verb [?] is. For the arrogant man, who constantly breathes out his boasting and arrogance, is like something puffed up by blowing and breathing winds. Hence they also call the vainglorious and arrogant "windy." The Apostle used this metaphor of inflation for the pride of a puffed-up and arrogant mind. Its mother is not love, but the levity of a corrupt and vain mind, which, swollen by the opinion of its own righteousness, holiness, wealth, knowledge, earthly success, or whatever honour it has acquired, swells and grows insolent and breathes arrogance as if inflated by some wind. Hence the saying: "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up" (1 Cor. 8), where see what has been noted. Love so holds and keeps all the virtues and gifts of the mind in order that each may be useful for building up the Church, while it excludes the inflation and arrogance of the mind. Where this inflation prevails, it perverts and destroys everything. I think the Apostle has this in view when he says: "Not puffed up."

units.la: Itaque ex hac Apostoli sententia, charitas non inflatur,firmisime colligitur,alienos esse à charitate omnes eos qui exîstimatione no minis qualicunque,uel aliàs undecunque erga fratres inflantur.Inspice nunc omnes ecclesias,omnia collegia,omnia monasteria, omnes episcoporum, cardinalium, prælatorum ac doctorum synodos,& uide quàm sint liberi ab hac inflatione. Vbi de gradibus,ordinibus,prærogatiuis,prælaturis ac titulis tanto pere coutenditur, putabimus ne omnia citra inflati animi arrogantiam geri.
units.tr: Therefore from this saying of the Apostle, "love is not puffed up," it is firmly concluded that all who are puffed up with a reputation for any kind of name, or otherwise puffed up towards their brothers from whatever source, are strangers to love. Look now at all the churches, all the colleges, all the monasteries, all the synods of bishops, cardinals, prelates and teachers, and see how free they are from this inflation. Where there is such great contention over degrees, orders, prerogatives, prelacies and titles, shall we think that everything is done without the arrogance of a puffed-up mind?

units.la: NON est fastidiosa.] Vulgatus] interpres habet,Nō est ambitiosa.In Græco est, ἀσχημονῶ:hoc est,non agit indecenter & inuerecundè, intellige contra proximum .
