Quatenus quicquid præter decorum & honestum inue recundius agitur,sub uerbo ἀσχημονῶ,comprehenditur:hactenus sub illo comprehendi potest & ambitio,ut ambitiosum esse, fit ἀσχημοσύνη:uerum non mox omnis ἀσχημοσύνη,pro ambitione est accipienda. Quare contractius est quod uulgata uersio habet,non est ambitiosa. Latius enim patet uerbum ἀσχημονῶ . Nec Erasmi uersio probatur. Sequutus ille uidetur expositionem Chrysostomi,cui ἐν ἀσχημοσύνῃ, idem est quod non uerecundari, non pudefieri,non indecorum iudicare,non fastidire rem ullam,quæ commodis proximi seruiat,quantumuis indecora uideatur.Sic sentiens Erasmus uertit,non est fastidiosa . Sane charitatis hoc quoque est ingenium, ut nulla de re uere cūdetur,quam nouit in usum eius cedere quę diligit:nec quicquam sit tam humile,quod nō illius nomine & gratia subeat. Non fastidit humilem,infirmum,contemptum, indoctum & idiotam,&ne peccatorem quidè , modò spes sit refipiscentiæ. Verū an ἐν ἀσχημοσύνῃ idem sit quod non pudefieri,non uerecūdari,non tur pe ducere,iudicent alij. Constat simplici sensu ἀσχημοσύνη idem esse quod haud indecèter, haud turpiter & haud inuerecunde agere, nihil agere quod uirum bonū, honestum & iustum dedeceat.σχῆμα sonat formam, figuram, externam personam,habitum,compositionē, colorem,ornatum uniuscuiusque rei. Est autem unicuique homini suum peculiare & competens σχῆμα,est σχῆμα etiam quouis modo usurpatum & effectum.Habet ecclesia,habet homo fidelis suum,habet hic muudus suum, habet suum secundum naturæ conditionem genus humanum. Cum Apostolus Philippensium secundo, Christum in forma & habitu ueri hominis inuentum esse dicere uellet, dixit,καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος.Et cum figuram,formam, exteruum habitum, aspectum, ac statum mundi huius perstringeret, instabilemque esse diceret,παράγει γὰρ, inquit, τὸ σχῆμα τοῦ κόσμου τούτου. Quod nos itaque Germanice uocamus,Eingestalt eines yeden dings, id Græci uocant σχῆμα. Et quod uocamus,ein ungestalt, id ipsi uocant ἀσχημονοῦν , qua uoce utuntur plerunque pro indecoro,quod fit præter morem & decorum publicum. Vt exempli gratia, inuenias ubi indecorum fit ,si filiam suam pater ultra iustam ætatem, uirginem domi suæ detineat. Hoc suprà capite septimo uocat ἀσχημονοῦν.Cum ergo cuiuis ætati,sexui,ordini,tempori,professioni,disciplinæ,suum fit σχῆμα: omnino ἀσχημονεῖ, quisquis præter decorum uel publicum,uel priuatum sui status, sexus,ordinis,professionis, &c. aliquid agit, {A}& is quoq; qui contra proximi sui σχῆμα quicquam præsumit.Et utrúque hoc carni nostræ facillimum est,quatenus non curat, quomodo & quàm indecenter agat cum fratribus,cu rat uero charitas. Germanicus interpres reddidit,sie stellet sich nitt unberdtig.Et explicádi gratia glossulam adiecit,Vuie die zornigen, stærrige, undultigen kœpffthuond.Sane fœda est ἀσχημόνων irascentium,ferocientium, & implacate indignantium,quo uicio plerunque laborant superbi & potentes.De talibns Germanice dice re solemus,sihe uuie er sich zerstellt, ὡς ἀσχημονᾶ:
units.tr: NOT unseemly. The Vulgate translator has "not ambitious." In Greek it is [?], that is, it does not act indecently or shamelessly, understood towards one's neighbour. Whatever is done more shamelessly than is proper and honourable is comprehended under the word [?]; so far ambition too can be comprehended under it, as being ambitious is [?]; but not every [?] is to be taken as ambition. Therefore the Vulgate reading "not ambitious" is narrower, for the word [?] has a wider range. Nor is Erasmus's rendering approved. He seems to have followed Chrysostom's explanation, for whom [?] means the same as not being ashamed, not blushing, not judging a thing unbecoming, not disdaining any matter that serves the advantage of a neighbour, however unbecoming it may seem. Thinking this way, Erasmus rendered it "not disdainful." Indeed this too is the nature of love: it is not ashamed of anything which it knows to be of use to those it loves, and nothing is so lowly that it does not undertake it for their sake and for their favour. It does not disdain the humble, the weak, the despised, the unlearned and the ignorant, nor even the sinner, provided there is hope of repentance. But whether [?] means not blushing, not being ashamed, or not behaving basely, let others judge. It is plain in its simple sense that [?] means to act neither indecently, nor basely, nor shamelessly, to do nothing that would be unbecoming to a good, honourable and just man. Schema signifies form, figure, outward appearance, bearing, composition, colour, the ornament of each thing. Each person has his own particular and fitting schema, and there is also a schema that is assumed and produced in any way. The Church has its own, the faithful man has his own, this world has its own, and humankind has its own according to the condition of nature. When the Apostle wished to say in Philippians 2 that Christ was found in the form and habit of a true man, he said [?]. And when he touched on the form, the outward habit, the appearance and state of this world, and said that it is unstable, he said: [?], "for the fashion of this world passeth away." What we therefore call in German Eingestalt eines yeden dings (the shape or form of every thing), the Greeks call schema. And what we call ein ungestalt (a misshapen thing), they call [?], a word they commonly use for what is unseemly, what happens contrary to custom and public decency. For example, you may find something unseemly if a father keeps his daughter at home as a virgin beyond a proper age. In chapter 7 above he calls this [?]. Since, then, each age, sex, order, time, profession and discipline has its own schema, whoever does anything contrary to the decency, public or private, of his own state, sex, order, or profession, does what is unseemly, and so does he who presumes anything against his neighbour's schema. Both of these come very easily to our flesh, insofar as it does not care how and how unseemly it acts towards its brothers, but love does care. The German translator rendered it: sie stellet sich nitt unberdtig ("does not behave unseemly"), and to explain it added a little gloss: Wie die zornigen, stærrige, undultigen kœpffthuond ("like angry, stubborn, intolerant men who act"). Indeed the unseemliness of those who are angry, fierce and implacably indignant is a foul thing, a fault to which the proud and powerful for the most part are prone. Of such people we commonly say in German: sihe wie er sich zerstellt ("see how he makes a fool of himself"), ὡς ἀσχημονᾶ.

units.la: NON quærit quæ sua sunt.] Suprà capite decimo communiter adhortatʼ est omnes, ut singuli quæ aliorum, nemo quę sua sint ipsius quærat.Et eius rei exemplum in seipso propo suit,dicens:Quemadmodum ergo per omnia omnibus placere studeo,non quærens meam utilitatem,sed multorum ut salui fiant.Hic idé inculcans unde fit eiusmodi affectus aperit, cum dicit: Charitas non quærit quæ sua sunt. Significat,quod Corinthij suæipsius quisquè utilitati studebant,ex eo fuisse,quod charitatis essent spiritu destituti.
units.tr: It does not seek its own. Above, in chapter ten, he generally exhorts everyone that each should seek the things of others and no one should seek his own. He set an example of this in himself when he said: "Just as I try to please everyone in everything, not seeking my own advantage but the salvation of many" (1 Cor. 10:33). Here, repeating the point, he shows where this kind of attitude comes from when he says: "Love does not seek its own." He means that the Corinthians each sought their own advantage because they lacked the Spirit of love.

units.la: Quid sit uero,non quæ sua, sed quæ aliorů sunt quærere,& cum qua sit hoc discretione faciédum,supradicto iam capite admonuimus. Dum facit hoc charitas,non negligit seipsam, sed rebus suis omnium consulit pulcherrime, dum communi est ecclesiastici corporis saluti procurandæ ac seruandæ dedita. Dum caput pro toto corpore solicitum est, ac cunctis illius membris rite moderandis intetum, hoc ipso sibijpsi melius consulit,quàm si neglectis reliquis membris quæ sua sunt,duntaxat quæ s. Et pedes non possunt sibijpsis prospice re melius,quàm si toti corpori seruiant. Optime consultum est singulis membris,dum omnia communi consensu corporis integritati ac saluti conseruandæ student.Sic habet & ecclesiæ conditio.Verum quoniam spiritu charitatis destituimur, & nemo quod aliorum, sed quæ sua quæ sunt singulí: quid aliud expe standum est, quàm ut tandem de summa rerum omnium periclitemur.' Etiam illi quorů officium poscit ut serui sint omnium,quærant que non quæ sua sint, sed quæ aliorum, neglectis rebuspublicis,toti subseruiunt propri is ac priuatis. Hodie sub Christianis nominis professione ita sunt luxata ac diuulsa omnia, ut nec regnum regno,nec principatus principatui, nec ciuitas ciuitati, nec ciuis ciui,nec ecclesia ecclesiæ,nec minister ministro, nec frater fratri ex animo cohæreat. An non reipsa impleri uidemus, quod Christus futurum prædixit,ut refrigescat charitas ? Frigus autem charitatis ardor est philautiæ, quo nō seruatur communis corporis incolumitas, sed consumitur ac perditur.Charitas naturalis est ac uitalis calor,unde uita corporis seruatur:philautia uero febrilis ardor est,omnes corporis uires depascens ac perdens. Cum i-
units.tr: What it means to seek not one's own but the things of others, and with what discretion this must be done, we explained already in the previous chapter. When love does this, it does not neglect itself. Rather, it best looks after its own interests by devoting itself to the common task of seeking and preserving the welfare of the ecclesiastical body. When the head is anxious for the whole body and busy in ordering all its members rightly, it thereby looks after itself better than it would if it neglected the other members and sought only its own things. Nor can the feet look after themselves better than by serving the whole body. Each member is best provided for when all, by common consent, labour to preserve the integrity and welfare of the body. So it is also with the condition of the Church. But since we are deprived of the Spirit of love, and each seeks his own things rather than the things of others, what else is to be expected than that in the end we should all be imperilled in the sum of all things? Even those whose office requires them to be the servants of all, and who ought to seek not their own but the things of others, neglect public affairs and serve only their private and personal interests. Today, under the name of Christian profession, everything is so dislocated and torn apart that no kingdom cleaves to a kingdom, no principality to a principality, no city to a city, no citizen to a citizen, no Church to a Church, no minister to a minister, no brother to a brother with a sincere heart. Do we not see with our own eyes what Christ foretold would happen, that love would grow cold? Now the coldness of love is the heat of self-love, which does not preserve the common soundness of the body but consumes and destroys it. Natural love is the vital warmth by which the life of the body is preserved; self-love, however, is a feverish heat that feeds upon and destroys all the strength of the body. Since, then, all the members now suffer from this pestilential fever,

units.la: gitur pestifera hac febri nunc omnia membra laborent,nemo cordatus non intelligit certũ nobis imminere exitium.
units.tr: no sensible person fails to see that destruction is hanging over us.

units.la: NON irritatur.]Græcè est,οὐ παροξύνεται.Si gnificat autem παροξύνεσθαι aliquando exacerbari,nonnunquam concitari. Nam uocula ὀξύς,unde componitur & uelocitatis & aceti significationem habet. A priore significatu est, quando παροξύνεσθαι concitari significat. Vnde est & ὀξύθυμος,id est,concitatus animus: cuius oppositum est μακροθυμος,id est,longanimis,le nis,patiens,procul ab ira,qualem paulò supra charitatem descripsit.A posteriore est, quando exacerbari sonat. Inuenias qui cito ac leui momento ad irascédum permoueatur, quem rectè uocabis ὀξύθυμον,irritabilem.Rursus inuó uias,qui tardior quidem sit ad iram, uerum irascendo nimium excàdescat & exacerbetur. Cum utrunque sit παροξύνεται, puto utrunque alienum esse ab ingenio charitatis,intelligendumque in eo quod Apostolus hic de illa dicit, ὁ παροξύνεται.
units.tr: IS NOT PROVOKED. The Greek is οὐ παροξύνεται. Now παροξύνεσθαι sometimes means to be exacerbated and sometimes to be stirred up. The little word ὀξύς, from which it is compounded, carries the sense both of quickness and of sharpness (of vinegar). In the first sense, παροξύνεσθαι means to be stirred up; hence also ὀξύθυμος, that is, a quick-tempered spirit, whose opposite is μακροθυμος, that is, long-suffering, gentle, patient, far from anger, the quality which he described a little above as love. In the second sense it means to be exacerbated. You may find someone who is moved to anger quickly and at the slightest provocation; him you may rightly call ὀξύθυμον, irritable. Conversely, you may find someone who is slower to anger but, once he is angry, flares up and becomes exasperated beyond measure. Since both are παροξύνεται, I think both are foreign to the nature of love, and in this passage the Apostle's words οὐ παροξύνεται must be understood accordingly.

units.la: Sed rogabit hic quisquam , quomodo tribuatur hic Apostolo Actor. decimoseptimo, quod spiritus ipsius παροξύνετο in ipso,ubi Erasmus uertit,incandescebat:uetus uero, incitabatur,si charitas neque incandescit,neque incitatur ad iram.Facilis hic est responsio. Paroxysmus ille spiritus Apostoli erat ex zelo Dei, hoc est, exardentis amoris Dei affectu, contra eidololatriam Atheniensium,cui tota erat dedita illorum ciuitas. Hunc zelum Dei charitas fraterna non extinguit. Quod uero propter Iohannem cognomento Marcum, interpres Paulum & Barnabam paroxysmus fuit, Act.decimoquinto (quem Erasmus acrem disceptationem, uetus interpres dissensionem uertit)ita ut à se inuicem seiungerentur:animi puto dandum esse impotentiæ.Etenim pij quoque nonnunquam tale quid admittunt, unde homines esse se experiantur . Interim habet& charitas suam iram, qua non fratribus delinquétibus,sed peccatis irascitur, nec tale quid irascendo admittit, quod incommodet fratribus: ad quem modum mater nonnunquam filio suo irascitur, quem tenere diligit.
units.tr: But someone will here ask how what is said of the Apostle in Acts 17 can be reconciled with this, that his spirit was παροξύνετο within him, where Erasmus renders it "was inflamed," and the old translator "was stirred up," if love is neither inflamed nor stirred up to anger. The answer is easy. That paroxysm of the Apostle's spirit arose from zeal for God, that is, from the affection of an ardent love of God, against the idolatry of the Athenians, to which their whole city was given over. Brotherly love does not extinguish this zeal for God. As for the paroxysm which arose on account of John, surnamed Mark, between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15; Erasmus renders it "sharp dispute," the old translator "dissension"), so that they were separated from one another, I think this must be ascribed to human weakness of mind. Indeed the godly too sometimes commit such things, by which they show that they are men. Meanwhile love too has its own anger, with which it is angry not at brothers who offend but at sins, and in its anger it does nothing that would harm the brothers. In this way a mother is sometimes angry with her son, whom nevertheless she loves tenderly.

units.la: NON cagitat malum.]Græcè est,ὁ λογίζεται. Significat autem uerbum λογίζομαι & imputo, & reputo,& cogito.Vt quando fidem imputari pro iusticia dicit, utitur hoc uerbo in passiuo, Credidit Abraham Deo, καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ, ad iusticiam. Cum uero commune non esse dicit, nisi ei qui reputat commune quid esse, inquit, ἀμὴ λογιζομένῳ τι κοινὸν εἶναι.Romanorum decimoquarto.Sensu autem cogitandi usurpauit Philippensium quarto,dicens: ταῦτα λογίζεσθε καὶ ἐμαθὸν.id est,Hæc cogitate, quæ & didicistis. Hoc triplici sensu usurpatur in scripturis uerbum hoc λογίζω & λογίζομαι. Sic malum,qui malus est, & proximum odit, tripliciter λογίζεται. Primum, omnia quæ dicit facit, imputat illi pro malo. Deinde reputat illum esse malum. Et quae ab illo fiunt, in specie uel etiam ueraciter mala reputat & exaggerat. Tertio cogitat etiam illi malum, hoc est, machinatur illius perniciem, & meditatur sedulo, quib. illum modis uel perdat uel laedat. Haec tria pertinent ad ingenium odij, & nota sunt nimium. Quemadmodum autem opposita est odio charitas, ita charitatis ingenium quoque oppositum est ingenio odij. Igitur charitas pro suo ingenio ne imputat fratri malum, nec reputat, nec cogitat. Quae fiunt a fratre, benigne interpretatur, & si quid ille mali fecerit, non reputat, sed extenuat: & cogitat illi non malum, sed bonum, paratus ad omnia, quae rebus illius commodare poterunt. Sicut itaque ingenium odij omnem unitatem & concordiam ecclesiae dissoluit, ita charitatis ingenium aedificat. Admodum ergo competenter Apostolus uerbum ἀνεχόμενοι usurpauit in hac causa, quo charitatis ingenium perfectius, qui praesentem particulam attinet, exprimeret, quemadmodum & in proxime praecedenti usus est uerbo ...
units.tr: DOES NOT TAKE INTO ACCOUNT EVIL. The Greek is ὁ λογίζεται. The verb λογίζομαι means to impute, to reckon, and to think. Thus, when he says that faith is imputed for righteousness, he uses this verb in the passive: "Abraham believed God, καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ, for righteousness" (Rom. 4). When he says that nothing is common except to one who reckons something to be common, he writes ἀμὴ λογιζομένῳ τι κοινὸν εἶναι (Rom. 14). In the sense of thinking he uses it in Philippians 4: ταῦτα λογίζεσθε καὶ ἐμαθὸν, that is, "think on these things which you have also learned." In this threefold sense the verb λογίζω and λογίζομαι is used in the Scriptures. So the one who is evil and hates his neighbour takes into account evil in three ways. First, he imputes to him as evil everything the neighbour says or does. Second, he reckons him to be evil, and what is done by him he regards and exaggerates as evil, either in appearance or even in truth. Third, he even thinks evil against him, that is, he plots his ruin and diligently devises by what means he may either destroy or harm him. These three belong to the nature of hatred and are only too well known. But just as love is opposed to hatred, so the nature of love is opposed to the nature of hatred. Therefore love, by its nature, does not impute evil to a brother, nor reckon it, nor think it. What is done by a brother it interprets kindly, and if he has done any wrong it does not reckon it but makes light of it; and it thinks not evil but good towards him, ready for everything that can serve his interests. Just as the nature of hatred dissolves all unity and concord in the Church, so the nature of love builds it up. Accordingly the Apostle rightly and fittingly used the word ἀνεχόμενοι in this matter, to express more perfectly the nature of love as far as the present clause is concerned, just as he used a word in the immediately preceding clause.

units.la: Chrysostomus haec duo, ... coniunctim exponit, idque per amplificationem uirtutis huius, quod charitas non modo uincat iram si obrepat, sed ne admittat quidem, & non modo malum non faciat, sed ne cogitet quidem. Sane magna est horum cognatio. Si cogitare malum accepetis pro intentare aliquid mali, potest quod dicit, ... id est, non irritatur, tanquam causa illius accipi. Vt enim irasci causa est maleficentiae, ita non irritari, causa potest esse, un de nihil mali machineris in proximum. Si uero legeris, Nō reputat, uel ... id est, non suspicatur malum potest illud, ... accipi pro effectu eius uirtutis, qua nihil mali de proximo suspicatur qui diligit. Omnino sic sunt haec duo, ... sic comparata, ut quocunque sensu accipiantur, aegerrime a se inuicem diuelli queant.
units.tr: Chrysostom expounds these two clauses together, and does so by amplifying the virtue, in that love not only overcomes anger if it creeps in but does not even admit it, and not only does not do evil but does not even think it. Certainly the two are closely related. If you take "to think evil" to mean "to threaten something evil," then what he says, ... that is, "is not provoked," can be taken as its cause. For as anger is the cause of doing harm, so not being provoked can be the cause of not plotting any harm against the neighbour. But if you read "does not reckon," or ..., that is, "does not suspect evil," then that ... can be taken as the effect of that virtue, by which he who loves suspects nothing evil of his neighbour. In short, these two are so related to each other that, in whatever sense they are taken, they can be separated from one another only with the greatest difficulty.

units.la: Quisquis irae locum praebet, procliuis est ad nocendum ei cui irascitur. Ira uiri iusticiam Dei non operatur. Rursus, qui pro malicia ingenij sui malum cito uel imputat, uel reputat, uel cogitat proximo, omnino procliuis est ad iram, & facili momento aduersus illū exacerbatur. Quare praeter rationem non est, quod ista a Chrysostomo coniunguntur, & coniunctim exponuntur.
units.tr: Whoever gives room to anger is inclined to harm the one he is angry with. "The anger of man does not work the righteousness of God" (James 1:20). Conversely, whoever, from the malice of his disposition, quickly imputes evil to his neighbour, or reckons it, or thinks it, is altogether inclined to anger and is easily exasperated against him at the slightest provocation. Therefore it is not without reason that Chrysostom joins these clauses and expounds them together.

units.la: Annotarunt alij prouenire, utraque ex duabus, ... uirtutibus, quas primo loco charitati tribuit.
units.tr: Others have noted that both arise from the two ... virtues which he attributes to love in the first place.

units.la: NON gaudet super iustitia, sed congaudet ueritati. ]Hoc est, non delectatur iniustitia, sed delectatur ueritate. Potest uarie exponi.
units.tr: DOES NOT REJOICE IN INIQUITY, BUT REJOICES WITH THE TRUTH. That is, it does not delight in injustice but delights in truth. This can be explained in various ways.

units.la: 1 Primo sic. Non est iniqua & maliciosa, ut laetetur si malefecerit, & exultet in rebus pessimis, sicut solet qui maligno sunt ingenio praediti: sed magis delectatur studio benefacien-di, & ex aequo ac ueraciter agendi cum proximo.
units.tr: 1 First, thus: love is not unjust and malicious, so as to rejoice if it has done wrong and exult in the worst things, as is the habit of those who are endowed with a malicious disposition; rather, it delights more in the zeal of doing good, and in dealing with its neighbour fairly and truly.

units.la: 2 Deinde si diceret, Sed gaudet ueritate, posset uideri sic dictum: Nō est hypocritica & fallax, ut gaudeat hypocrisi, sed uerax & syncera, ut gaudeat ueritate ac fide, quo sensu iniustitia pro hypocrisi & mendacio sic accipieretur, ut sit opposita ueritati.
units.tr: 2 Next, if he had said "but he rejoices in the truth," it might seem to have been said in this sense: he is not hypocritical and deceitful, so as to rejoice in hypocrisy, but truthful and sincere, so as to rejoice in truth and faithfulness. In that sense, injustice would be taken as the opposite of truth, in place of hypocrisy and lying.

units.la: 3 Tertio, quoniam non simpliciter dicit, sed gaudet ueritate: sed, ... id est, congaudet autem ueritati: existimo manifestum esse, quod non de ipsius diligetis, sed eorum quos diligit ueritate, id est, synceritate ac fide loquatur, cui charitas faueat & congaude at ex animo. Et apparet hunc esse senium. Fidelis homo, uera & Christiana charitate praeditus, non gaudet, si uiderit iniusticiam exerceri inter fratres, sic ut frater cum fratre iniique & improbe agat: sed super ea iniusticia magis contristatur ac dolet, delectatur uero si de ac syncéritate fratrum, & congaudet omnibus illis, cum quibus ueraciter, candide ac fideliter agitur, atque ita dolet cum dolentibus, & gaudet cum gaudentibus. Hoc genus doloris & gaudij locum non habet, ubi haereses & schismata obtinent in ecclesia. Sic enim sectariorum est ingenium, ut magis doleat ipsis, si qui non sunt de ipsorum secta, recte se gerant: uolupe uero sit si male, iniuste & flagitiose agant, id quod nostro seculo nimium experimur. Sic dubio procul fiebat in ecclesia Corinthiorum, propter studium sectarum. Quod pauperes contemnebantur in coena dominica, non dolebat ei sectae, in qua contemptores pauperum erant. Quod scortator ille rem habebat cum nouerca sua, non contristabat, sed magis reddebat inflatos. qua de re uide supra capite quinto. Huiusmodi ingenia aliena sunt a Christiana charitate, quae non gaudet, si exoriantur in ecclesia iniquitas, iniusticia, inuidia, scandala, schismata, falsa dogmata, falsi cultus, contentiones, &c. sed contristatur, dolet ac luget ex animo, ueritati uero congaudet, si illa uigeat in ecclesia, & regnet in omnium mente, affectu & concursatione.
units.tr: 3 Thirdly, since he does not say simply "he rejoices in the truth," but "he rejoices together with the truth," I think it is plain that he is speaking not of his own loves but of those whom he loves in truth, that is, in sincerity and faith, and that charity favours and rejoices in them from the heart. And this appears to be the sense. A faithful man, endowed with true and Christian charity, does not rejoice if he sees injustice practised among brothers, when one brother deals unfairly and wickedly with another. Rather, he is saddened and grieved by that injustice. But he is delighted when the brothers act sincerely, and he rejoices with all those with whom dealings are truthful, candid and faithful. So he grieves with those who grieve and rejoices with those who rejoice. This kind of grief and joy has no place where heresies and schisms hold sway in the Church. For it is the nature of sectarians to be more grieved if those who are not of their sect act rightly, and to be pleased if they act badly, unjustly and shamefully. We experience this too much in our own age. Without doubt this was happening in the Corinthian church, because of zeal for factions. That the poor were despised at the Lord's Supper did not grieve that faction, in which the despisers of the poor were numbered. That the fornicator had relations with his stepmother did not sadden them; rather, it made them more puffed up. On this matter, see above, chapter five. Such dispositions are foreign to Christian charity, which does not rejoice if iniquity, injustice, envy, scandals, schisms, false doctrines, false worship, contentions and the like arise in the Church. Rather, it is saddened, grieves and mourns from the heart. But it rejoices with the truth if the truth flourishes in the Church and reigns in the minds, affections and dealings of all.

units.la: OMNIA suffert. ]Graece est, ... Verbum ... significat aliquando obtegere, unde ... tectum sonat, sicuti Matthei 8. legimus: Vt intres ... & Marci secundo: ... aliquando ..., id est, abscondere: nonnunquam ..., & ..., id est, portare, tolerare & sufferre. Su prā capite nono dixit hoc sensu ..., id est, omnia sufferimus. Ad seruandam unitatem inter fratres summopere sunt haec duo ne cessaria. Vnum, ut delicta fratrum non manifestentur & exagitentur, sed obtegantur & abscondantur.
units.tr: ALL THINGS he endures. In Greek it is [...]. The verb sometimes means to cover, whence the word [...] means covered, as we read in Matthew 8, "that you should enter [under my roof]," and in Mark 2 [...]. Sometimes it means to hide, that is, to conceal; sometimes it means to bear, to tolerate and to endure. Above, in chapter nine, he used it in this sense, [...], that is, "we endure all things." For keeping unity among brothers, these two things are most necessary. First, that the faults of brothers are not made public and attacked, but are covered and hidden.

units.la: Alterum, ut alter alterius onera, infirmitatem, & iniurias quoque & offensas portet ac sufferat. At haec non praestat, nisi charitas quae pro suo ingenio peccata fratrum, quoad eius potest, perinde atque nuditatem corporis obtegit. tegit ac celat, & omnia citius tolerat, portat & suffert, quàm ut ullam unitatis rumpędæ occasionem præbeat. Quare rursus tale uerbum usurpauit Apostolus quod utrique sensui seruiret, dicens, <bl>πάντα στέγει</bl>: id est, omnia tegit ac suffert. Qui diligit, triplici nomine suffert omnia. Vt exempli gratia: Qui diligit amicam, pro illa, propter illam, & ab illa quæcunque inferuntur constantissime suffert. Quæ ad illius commoda facere poterunt, etiamsi molesta sint admodum, perfert. Quæ propter illam inferuntur ab aliis, probra & aduersa, & omnis generis discrimina, patienter tolerat omnia. Et ea quoque, quæ ab illa inferuntur & imponuntur, absque omni tergiuersatione suffinet omnia. Et hæc omnia leuia toleratu reddit amor. Consimili modo & charitas fraterna tales nos reddit qui sufferamus omnia pro fratribus, propter fratres, & à fratribus ipsis illata. Tolle hanc charitatem, non stabit unitas & concordia, dum nihil prorsus, neque pro fratribus, neque propter fratres, neque à fratribus ferre sustinemus. Cum ergo Corinthij charitate hac destituerētur, & nec aliquid uel à fratribus uel pro fratribus, uel propter fratres sufferre possent, nimis erat ad schisma ta procliues.
units.tr: Second, that one bears and endures the burdens, weakness, and also the injuries and offences of another. But this is achieved only by charity, which, by its nature, covers and conceals the sins of brothers as far as it can, just as one covers the nakedness of the body. It covers and hides them, and it tolerates, bears and endures everything, rather than give any occasion for breaking unity. Therefore, the Apostle again used a word that serves both senses, saying [πάντα στέγει]: that is, it covers and endures all things. He who loves endures all things in three ways. For example, he who loves a woman endures constantly everything that is inflicted on her, for her and because of her. Whatever can serve her advantage, he bears, even if it is very troublesome. What is brought against her by others, reproaches, adversities and every kind of danger, he patiently tolerates. And whatever is inflicted and imposed on him by her, he undergoes without any evasion. Love makes all these light to bear. In a similar way, brotherly charity makes us such that we endure all things for brothers, on account of brothers, and what is inflicted by the brothers themselves. Take away this charity, and unity and concord will not stand, since we bear absolutely nothing either for brothers, or on account of brothers, or from brothers. Therefore, since the Corinthians were destitute of this charity, and could bear nothing either from brothers, for brothers or on account of brothers, they were far too prone to schisms.

units.la: OMNIA credit.] Quemadmodum malum non suspicatur charitas, sed secundum seipsam de aliis sentit & iudicat: ita facilis est ad credendum quæ ab ijs quos diligit, narrantur & præteruntur omnia. Hac autem credendi facilitate fit ut frequenter fallatur, unde tamen non redditur ad credendum difficilis. Alioqui nō staret, quod hic ab Apostolo omnia credere dicitur. Qui semel atque iterum falsus, nemini postea credere sustinet, nec charitate prædituus, nec omnia credere dici potest.
units.tr: ALL THINGS he believes. Just as charity does not suspect evil, but judges others according to its own nature, so it is ready to believe everything that is related and reported by those whom it loves. Yet by this readiness to believe it is often deceived, and it is not thereby made difficult to believe. Otherwise it would not stand that the Apostle says here that it believes all things. He who, once or twice deceived, is no longer willing to believe anyone, is not endowed with charity, and cannot be said to believe all things.

units.la: Quæsierit autē quisquam, quomodo prædicetur hoc in charitate ab Apostolo quod omnia credat, cum omnia credere & stultum sit & periculosum? scriptuaque hoc tribuat, לְבַּחְרֵי, id est, paruulis & ætate & sensu, homi nibus simplicibus, Prouerbiorum decimoquarto dicens, יְהֵא יֹאמִין לְכָל דָּבָר, id est, simplex ac paruulus credit omni uerbo. Et propheta Michæas capite septimo dicat: Noli credere amico tuo. Et primę Iohannis quarto legatur. Nolite omni spiritui credere, moneatque Christus, ut simus simplices quidem sicut columbæ, iuxtà uero prudentes sicut serpentes: caueamusque à falsis prophetis, qui ueniunt ad nos in uestimentis ouium, quæ monita frustra sunt, si laudabile est credere omnia.
units.tr: But someone may ask how the Apostle can say of charity that it believes all things, since to believe all things is both foolish and dangerous. Scripture attributes this to the simple, [לְבַּחְרֵי], that is, to those simple in age and understanding, saying in Proverbs 14, "the simple believes every word" [יְהֵא יֹאמִין לְכָל דָּבָר]. And the prophet Micah in chapter seven says, "Do not trust your friend." And in 1 John 4 we read, "Do not believe every spirit." Christ also warns us to be simple indeed, like doves, yet prudent, like serpents, and to beware of false prophets who come to us in sheep's clothing. These warnings would be in vain if it were praiseworthy to believe everything.

units.la: Respondeo. Distinguendum est inter ea primum quæ fidem ac religionem nostram, & ea quæ res humanas ac terrenas concernunt: deinde & inter eam credendi procliuitatem, quæ est ex stulticia & leuitate cordis, & eam quæ ex spiritu charitatis proficiscitur. In causa religionis non habet locum hæc omnia credendi facilitas, sed requiritur summa cautio, ne cuiuis dogmati ac spiritui credamus, iuxta illud, Probate spiritus, utrum ex Deo sint: & illud, Omnia probate, quod bonum est tenete, & quæ alia sunt eiusmodi. In religione non recte dixeris, Charitas omnia credit. Neque enim fides erga Deum ex charitate est, sed charitas ex fide. At in rebus humanis fides ista, qua fratribus haud difficulter credimus, aut est ex simplicitate ac leuitate cordis, aut ex ingenio charitatis. Contra credulitatem, quæ ex leuitate cordis est, facit locus Prouerbiorum supra citatus, & quæ Ecclesiastici decimotertio & decimonono leguntur, utpote: Ne credas multis uerbis. Item, Ne omni uerbo credas. Et: Qui cito credit, leuis est corde. Hanc animi leuitatem scriptura utique & recte reprobat. Verum quis non uidet quàm sit illa longe diuersa à charitate fraterna, quamque aliud sit temere omnia credere leuitate cordis: & aliud, sic diligere fratrem, ut nescias male de illo sentire ac sinistri aliquid suspicari, ideoque facilem esse ad credendum ea quæ ab illo dicuntur ac prætexuntur.
units.tr: I answer: one must distinguish, first, between those matters which concern our faith and religion and those which concern human and earthly affairs; then, between that readiness to believe which comes from folly and lightness of heart, and that which proceeds from the spirit of charity. In matters of religion this whole readiness to believe has no place, but the greatest caution is required, lest we believe every doctrine and every spirit. This accords with the saying, "Test the spirits, whether they are of God," and that, "Test all things; hold fast what is good," and others of this kind. In religion one could not rightly say, "Charity believes all things." For faith towards God comes not from charity, but charity from faith. But in human affairs, that faith by which we readily believe brothers arises either from simplicity and lightness of heart, or from the disposition of charity. Against the credulity that comes from lightness of heart, the passage from Proverbs cited above speaks, and also what is read in Ecclesiasticus, chapters 13 and 19, namely: "Do not believe many words." Likewise: "Do not believe every word." And: "He who believes quickly is light of heart." Scripture certainly and rightly rejects this levity of mind. But who does not see how far this is from brotherly charity, and how different it is to believe everything rashly out of levity of heart, and, on the other hand, to love a brother in such a way that you know not to think ill of him or suspect anything sinister, and therefore to be ready to believe what is said and alleged by him?

units.la: Est autem duplex genus fidei. Vnum, quo quæ audimus uera esse credimus. Alterum, quo confidimus, quo sensu fidem fiduciamuo camus. Multum est utrunque discriminis. Nō mox fidit qui credit. Iacobi secundo legimus, <bl>καὶ τὰ δαιμόνια πιστεύουσιν</bl>: id est, Et dæmonia credunt, quod non potest uerti: Et dæmonia confidunt. Quemadmodum nec illud supra capite undecimo: Audio interuos esse schisinata, <bl>καὶ μέρος τι πιστεύω</bl>, id est, ex parte credo. Credebat, non considebat. Quod uero Marci quinto, & Lucæ octauo legimus, <bl>μὴ φοβοῦ, μόνον πίστευε</bl>: id est, Ne timeas, tantū crede, rectius uertitur, tantum confide, quemadmodum & <bl>πιστεύων εἰς τὸν θεὸν, καὶ χαρὰν, καὶ ἀσφάλειαν</bl>, omni no est fiduciam locare in Deum, in Christum & in nomen Christi. Cum ergo charitas & credat fratribus omnia, & in omnibus bona sit ergaillos fiducia, recte usus est Apostolus uerbo <bl>πιστεύει</bl>, quo illi utrunque & credendi & fidedi affectum tribueret. Ex opposito recte dixeris, <bl>ἀπιστία</bl>: i. Inimicitia nihil credit, nihil fidit. Etenim qui inimicus est, nihil credit, nihilque fidit, sed omnia habet suspecta, & diffidit in omnibus.
units.tr: There are two kinds of faith. One is that by which we believe that what we hear is true. The other is that by which we trust, and in this sense we speak of entrusting. The difference between them is great. He who believes does not at once trust. We read in James 2, [καὶ τὰ δαιμόνια πιστεύουσιν], that is, "the demons believe," which cannot be turned as "the demons trust." Nor does that passage above in chapter eleven, "I hear that there are schisms, and [καὶ μέρος τι πιστεύω]," mean anything but "I partly believe." He believed; he did not trust. But what we read in Mark 5 and Luke 8, [μὴ φοβοῦ, μόνον πίστευε], that is, "Do not fear, only believe," is more correctly rendered "only trust," just as [πιστεύων εἰς τὸν θεὸν, καὶ χαρὰν, καὶ ἀσφάλειαν] means entrusting oneself wholly to God, to Christ and to the name of Christ. Since, therefore, charity both believes all things of brothers and has good trust in them in all things, the Apostle rightly used the word [πιστεύει], by which he attributed to charity both the disposition to believe and the disposition to trust. On the contrary, one could rightly say [ἀπιστία]: the enemy believes nothing and trusts nothing. For he who is an enemy believes nothing and trusts nothing, but holds everything suspect and distrusts everything.

units.la: OMNIA sperat, omnia sustinet.] In Graeco est <bl>πάντα ὑπομένει</bl>, quod nonnunquam ferre ac pati, nonnunquam expectare ac perdurare significat, quo sensu usurpatum est hic ab Apostolo. Et uerbum sustinendi posuerunt interpretes sensu expectandi. Alias idem bis dicetur, si positum esset sensu perferendi uel sufferendi. Cohærent ista, Credere, sperare, & spe rando ad finem usque constanter perdurare. Exigit conuictus nostet, & societas non ecclesiastica tantum, sed & ciuilis & domestica, ut alia credamus inuicem in præsenti, alia speremus in futurum: & ne spes ista charitatis breuis sit & momentanea, qualis est quæ ex leuitate uitate cordis proficiscitur, expectando perseueremus. Nequit esse spes firma, nisi constanter sustinendo omnem impatientiam excludat: quæ si admittatur, non modo spem de fratre conceptam extinguit, sed & omnia reliqua ad charitatem pertinentia labefactat.
units.tr: ALL THINGS it hopes for, all things it endures. In the Greek it is πάντα ὑπομένει [panta hypomenei], which sometimes means to bear and suffer, and sometimes to wait for and persevere; the Apostle uses it here in the latter sense, and the translators have rendered it "endures" in the sense of "waits for." Otherwise the same thing would be said twice, if it were taken in the sense of enduring or suffering. These belong together: to believe, to hope, and by hoping to persevere constantly to the end. Our living together and our fellowship, not only ecclesiastical but civil and domestic, require that we believe one another in the present and hope for one another in the future; and lest this hope of charity be brief and momentary, such as arises from the fickleness of the heart, we persevere in waiting. Hope cannot be firm unless, by enduring constantly, it excludes all impatience. If impatience is admitted, it not only extinguishes the hope conceived of a brother but also weakens all the rest that pertains to charity.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem & alij monuerunt, nō sunt ista, charitas omnia suffert, omnia credit, omnia sperat, omnia sustinet, citra discretionem in uniuersum ad omnia referenda, sed adea tantum quæ homo pius ac syncerus non secundum carnem, sed secundum spiritum diligens sufferre, credere, sperare ac sustinere posse: potest autem omnia, quæ nec Deo displiceant, nec pietati repugnět, neque fratris quē diligit, saluti incommodent. Sine hac conditione prorsus uiciosa esset ea dilectio, quæ indiscriminatim ferret, crederet, speraret, & sustineret omnia, imò si urgeas uniuersaliter, propter impossibilis. Quare sicuti supra capite no no, illud: Omnibus factus sum omnia, ultra normam uerę pietatis & iustitiæ non extendimus, ne ex Apostolo uel mendacem, uel impium & inhonestum adulatorem faciam: ita hic quoque intra limites liciti, iusti, & honesti includendum est, quod charitatem omnia suffere, omnia credere, omnia sperare, & omnia sustinere dicit.
units.tr: As others have also observed, these words, "charity bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things," are not to be referred universally and without distinction to all things, but only to those things which a pious and sincere man, loving not according to the flesh but according to the spirit, can bear, believe, hope for and endure. He can do all those things which neither displease God, nor conflict with piety, nor harm the salvation of the brother he loves. Without this condition, that love would be utterly vicious which without discrimination bore, believed, hoped for and endured all things; indeed, if you press it universally, it would be impossible. Therefore, just as above in chapter 9, concerning "I have become all things to all men," we do not extend that beyond the norm of true piety and justice, lest we make Paul either a liar or an impious and dishonourable flatterer, so here too what he says, that charity endures all things, believes all things, hopes all things and bears all things, must be confined within the limits of what is lawful, just and honourable.

units.la: Charitas nunquam excidit, siue prophetiæ uero abolebuntur, siue linguæ cessabunt, siue scientia abolebitur. Ex parte enim cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus: ast ubi uenerit quod perfectum est, tunc quod ex parte est, abolebitur.
units.tr: Charity never fails. Whether prophecies, they will be abolished; whether tongues, they will cease; whether knowledge, it will be abolished. For we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect comes, then that which is in part will be abolished.

units.la: Hactenus charitatem commendauit, primum ab eo quod omnibus est charismatibus usqueadeo præstantior, ut sine ipsa nihil illa prosint habenti: deinde ab illius ingenio plane diuino, & ad concordiam, pacem & unitatem in ecclesia conseruandam appositissimo. Iam consequenter tertiam illius præstantiam subijcit, quam in eo considerādam proponit, quod perennis est, nūquam cessans, sed in sem piternum durans: cum tamen prophetiæ, linguarum & scientiæ charismata cessent & abolentur. Sic dicit:
units.tr: Thus far he has commended charity: first, because it is so much more excellent than all the gifts that without it those gifts profit the one who has them nothing; then, because of its entirely divine nature, most suited to preserving concord, peace and unity in the Church. Now he consequently sets forth a third excellence of charity, which he proposes to be considered in it, namely that it is perpetual, never ceasing but enduring forever, whereas the gifts of prophecy, of tongues and of knowledge cease and are abolished. So he says:

units.la: CHARITAS nunquam excidit.] Quod in Græco est, uariæ significationis uerbum est.
units.tr: CHARITY never fails. The Greek word is one of varied meaning.

units.la: 1 Primum, dicitur, qui in examine insufficiens deprehenditur & reprobatur, quo sensu Germanice dicimus, Er ist durch die reuter gefallen.
units.tr: First, it is said of one who is found insufficient and rejected in an examination; in which sense we say in German, "Er ist durch die Reuter gefallen" (he has failed the test).

units.la: 2 Deinde, qui ciuitate eijcitur & expellitur, & is dicitur. Sic qui excommunicatur ab ecclesia,.
units.tr: Second, it is said of one who is cast out and expelled from a city; so too one who is excommunicated from the Church.

units.la: 3 Tertio idem est quod emanare foras, & prorumpere. Aqua è fonte, & milites in præsidio constituti, dum erumpunt in hostem, Germanicè dicimus, sie sind her außgefallen.
units.tr: Third, it means the same as to flow out and burst forth: water from a spring, or soldiers posted on guard when they break out against the enemy; we say in German, "sie sind her außgefallen" (they have sallied out here).

units.la: 4 Quarto, est ab alio ad aliud degenerare: ut, .
units.tr: Fourth, it means to degenerate from one thing into another, as ...

units.la: 5 Quinto, deficere & cessare significat. Et hoc sensu positum hic est ab Apostolo. Quare uerti poterat: Charitas nunquam cessat: uel, nunquam deficit.
units.tr: Fifth, it means to fail and to cease, and in this sense the Apostle uses it here. Hence it could have been translated, "Charity never ceases," or "never fails."

units.la: Chrysostomus exponit de constantia charitatis, qua in hac uita nō deficit cuncta ferendo, credendo, sperando ac sustinendo: , inquit, . Est quidem insignis hæc charitatis uirtus, quod non est instabilis & fallax, qualis est amor carnis, sed constans ac firma. Verum si sequentem collationem inspiciamus, qua prophetijs, linguis, &c. confertur, puto perennitatem illius prædicari, qua sic est perpetua, ut post hanc quoque uitam in futuro seculo perduret. Et sic exponit Hieronymus dicens: Ipsa sola permanet in futuro. Et Ambrosius quoque: Et in æternum cum Deo manet.
units.tr: Chrysostom explains it of the constancy of charity, by which in this life it does not fail in bearing, believing, hoping and enduring all things. "It is indeed a remarkable virtue of charity that it is not unstable and deceitful, as the love of the flesh is, but constant and firm." But if we look at the following comparison, in which charity is set against prophecies, tongues and so on, I think its perpetuity is being proclaimed, by which it is so lasting that it endures in the future age after this life too. Jerome expounds it in this way, saying: "It alone remains in the future." And Ambrose too: "And it remains with God for eternity."

units.la: At hunc sensum arripiunt pro suo dogmate confirmando, qui mortuos sanctos ex hac uita ad cœlestem translatos, pro uiuentibus nobis in cœlis ad Deum orare & intercedere haud secus affirmant, quàm si præsentes hoc uiderint. Ecce, inquiunt, charitas sanctorum non terminatur hac præsenti uita, sed in futura quoque durat. At illa sic est comparata, ut oret pro miseris & afflictis. Fecerunt hoc sancti in præsenti uita ex charitate, faciunt igitur & in futura, quandoquidem ad huc eadem sunt charitate præditi. Nos uno uerbo respondemus: Charitas in se est eadem, uerum alij atque alij sunt illius effectus, juxta uarietatem status & rerum, in quibus uersatur. Ipsa per se perennis est, uerum non sunt mox perennes omnes illius effectus. Conspectu miseriæ mouetur ad misericordiam, & si nequit ipsa succurrere, orat pro miseris ad dominum. Cibat esurientes, potat sitientes, inuisit & consolatur infirmos ac captiuos, hospitio accipit peregrinos, uestit nudos, flet cum flentibus, &c. Hæc facit in eo rerum statu constituta, in quo & aspectu miserorum permouetur ad compassionem, & pro facultate quam habet, talia præstare potest. Is status autem præsentis est uitæ, non futuræ.
units.tr: But those who seize upon this sense to confirm their own doctrine, who affirm that the holy dead, translated from this life to heaven, pray and intercede to God for us who are living, no differently than if they were present and saw what we do, seize upon it. "Behold," they say, "the charity of the saints is not ended by this present life, but endures in the future too. But it is so constituted that it prays for the wretched and afflicted. The saints did this in the present life out of charity; therefore they do so also in the future, since they are still endowed with the same charity." We answer in a word: charity is the same in itself, but its effects are different, according to the variety of the state and of the things in which it is engaged. In itself it is perpetual, but not all its effects are perpetual at once. At the sight of misery it is moved to mercy, and if it cannot itself help, it prays to the Lord for the wretched. It feeds the hungry, gives drink to the thirsty, visits and comforts the sick and the captive, receives strangers in hospitality, clothes the naked, weeps with those who weep, and so on. It does these things while placed in that state of things in which, moved to compassion by the sight of the miserable, it can provide such help according to the ability it has. But that state belongs to the present life, not the future.

units.la: Quare fieri non potest ut quæ facit in hac uita, faciat etiam in futura. Non dicit Apostolus, Opera charitatis non excidunt: sed, Charitas non excidit. Et spiritus noster non excidit. At opera illa quæ facit in carne constitutus, non est facturus extra carnem in cœlo. Paralogismus igitur est, quo isti tribuunt accidentibus, quod solius est subiecti. Charitas sanctorum perennis est, oratio & intercessio non ita. Sed hac de re annotarunt & alij, & nos in Commentarijs nostris super Matthæum thæum capite sexto, nonnulla attigimus.
units.tr: Therefore it cannot be that what charity does in this life it will also do in the future. The Apostle does not say, "The works of charity do not fail," but, "Charity does not fail." And our spirit does not fail. But those works which it does while placed in the flesh, it will not do outside the flesh in heaven. It is therefore a paralogism, by which they attribute to the accidents what belongs only to the subject. The charity of the saints is perpetual; prayer and intercession are not so. Others have also noted this matter, and we touched on some points in our Commentaries on Matthew, chapter six.

units.la: SIVE prophetiæ, inquit, abolebuntur, &c.] Quoniam alij charismata prophetiæ, linguarum, scientiæ, &c. plus quàm charitatem suscipiebant, alij propter illa insolescebant: rursus illa infrà charitatem esse docet, idque facit per collationem, qua temporaria charismata & definentia confert charitati perenni, ac nunquam definenti. Ideo cum dixisset, Charitas nunquam excidit: subiecit, Sive prophetiæ autem abolebuntur, siue linguæ cessabunt, siue scientia abolebitur. Quasi dicat: Siue prophetiæ uero, siue linguæ, siue scientia (per hæc autem charismata & alia eius generis intelligit) charitati conferantur, longè sunt inferiora. Nam haud, ut illa, indesinenter perdurant, sed abolebuntur, desinent & cessabunt.
units.tr: "Whether prophecies, he says, shall be abolished," and so on. Since some were prizing the gifts of prophecy, tongues, knowledge and so on above charity, and some grew proud because of them, he teaches again that those gifts are below charity, and does so by comparison, setting temporary and ceasing gifts against perpetual charity, which never ceases. So, having said, "Charity never fails," he added, "But whether prophecies shall be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be abolished." As if to say: whether prophecies, or tongues, or knowledge (by these gifts and others of that kind he means) are set beside charity, they are far inferior. For they do not endure without ceasing as it does, but will be abolished, come to an end and cease.

units.la: Exiſtimant nonnulli fratres, particulam hanc sic esse legendam: Charitas nunquam destituit aut aberrat, etiamsi prophetiæ destituant. Vt sit sensus, etiamsi prophetiæ nos vel linguæ vel scientia destituant, charitas tamen tanquam fida comes & perpetua agendorum magistra, nunquam nos suo destituit moderamine. Verum, meo iudicio, quod in Græco est ἀπ' ἀ, non est idem quod etiamsi: sed sonat, siue uero. Nec temere est aduersatiua ἀλλ', id est, uero, vel autem, adiecta. Notam enim habet diuersi prædicati ab eo quod de charitate prædicatur. Deinde non dicit, destituant, cessent: sed in futuro, idque affirmando, abolebuntur, cessabunt, abolebit. Quemadmodum enim de charitate asserit, quod nunquam excidat, ita ex aduerso de prophetijs, linguis, & scientia affirmat, futurumq; prædicit, ut abolean tur ac cessent.
units.tr: Some brethren think the particle should be read thus: "Charity never fails or goes astray, even if prophecies fail." So that the sense is: even if prophecies, or tongues, or knowledge fail us, charity nevertheless, as a faithful companion and perpetual guide of our actions, never abandons us to its own direction. But in my judgment, what stands in the Greek is not the same as "even if"; it means "but whether." Nor is the adversative [ἀλλ'], that is, "but" or "however," added carelessly; it marks a predicate different from that which is said of charity. Next, he does not say "fail" or "cease" but speaks of the future, and affirmatively: "they will be abolished, will cease, will be done away." For as he asserts of charity that it never fails, so on the contrary he affirms and foretells of prophecies, tongues and knowledge that they will be abolished and cease.

units.la: Sanè iam olim charismata illa miraculosa prophetiæ, linguarum, curationum, &c. cessarunt in ecclesia, quia usus ac ratio illorum desijt, postquam Euangelium regni Dei prædicatum, confirmatum, ac receptum est in orbe. Verum de ea cessatione non loquitur Apostolus, sed de omnimoda illa quæ post hanc est uitam futura, sicuti patet in sequentibus. In hoc seculo locum habet prophetia, donum linguarum, & scientia, qualem hic peregrinationis nostræ status & conditio requirit, in futuro non ita.
units.tr: Indeed, those miraculous gifts of prophecy, tongues, healings, and so on, long ago ceased in the Church, because their use and purpose came to an end once the gospel of the kingdom of God had been preached, confirmed, and received throughout the world. But the Apostle is not speaking of that cessation. He is speaking of the complete cessation that will come after this life, as is clear from what follows. In this age prophecy, the gift of tongues, and knowledge have their place, of the kind that the condition of our present pilgrimage requires. In the future they will not be needed in this way.

units.la: SIVE linguæ, inquit.] Præbet hæc particula nonnullis occasionem curiosius de usu sermonis disputandi, qualis futurus nobis sit post hanc uitam in cœlis, an aliquis uel nullus: & si aliquis, an uarius sicut in hoc seculo post diluuium. Vt unaquæque gens suam retineat linguam, & tamen omnes intelligantur ab omnibus. Vel idem, sicut in priori mundo ante structuram turris Babel, & quo idiomate, Ebræo ne uel Græco, uel Latino, in honorem sanctæ Romanæ sedis, & sanctarum Missarum, quæ Latine leguntur, ac psalmodię quæ & ipsa in catholica ecclesia Latina habetur, quo regnans in cœlis ecclesia militandi in
units.tr: "Whether tongues," he says. This particle gives some people an occasion to dispute, rather too curiously, what kind of speech we shall have after this life in heaven, whether there will be any or none, and if there is any, whether it will be varied as it was in this age after the flood, so that each nation keeps its own tongue and yet all are understood by all; or whether it will be one language, as it was in the world before the building of the tower of Babel. And some ask which idiom it will be, Hebrew, Greek, or Latin: Latin, they suggest, in honour of the holy Roman see, of the holy Masses that are read in Latin, and of the psalmody that is also kept in the Latin of the catholic Church, so that the church reigning in heaven may be conformed to the church militant on earth.

units.la: terra conformetur. Curiosis istiusmodi quæstionibus occupantur homines otiosi. Qui pij sunt, magis curant ne cœlesti ac futura felicitate, per sanguinem Christi parta, male uiuendo priuentur, quàm quomodo cognoscant ea, quæ nec sacra scriptura prodit, nec ulla necessitate præscientiam sui requirunt.
units.tr: Idle men busy themselves with questions of this sort. Those who are godly are more concerned not to lose, by living badly, the heavenly and future happiness won by the blood of Christ, than to learn what those things are, which neither holy Scripture reveals nor any necessity requires us to foreknow.

units.la: SIVE scientia, inquit.] Non loquitur in uniuersum de omni scientia, sed de charismate scientiæ, quod initio regni Christi per spiritum sanctum credentibus miraculose dabatur, de quo supra, & capite præcedenti quoq; mentionem fecit: deinde & de scientia, studio & auditu percepta loquitur, quæ & ipsa post hanc uitam abolebitur.
units.tr: "Or knowledge," he says. He is not speaking of all knowledge in general, but of the gift of knowledge, which at the beginning of Christ's kingdom was miraculously given through the Holy Spirit to believers, and of which he made mention above and in the preceding chapter. Then he also speaks of knowledge gained by study and by hearing, and this too will be abolished after this life.

units.la: ABOLEBVNTVR, inquit, & cessabunt.] Quasi dicat. Quæ tum erit: uestra iactantia & inflatio, quando sine charitate prorsus eritis uacui & inanes, charismatibus hisce destituti, de quibus iam tantopere gloriamini? Quid habebitis præcipui? Nec prophetias, nec linguas, nec scientiam hanc retinebitis, & charitatem, quæ sola perennis est, non habebitis.
units.tr: "They will be abolished," he says, "and will cease." It is as if he said: what will your boasting and swelling be then, when without charity you will be utterly empty and void, deprived of these gifts of which you now glory so greatly? What will you have that is outstanding? You will keep neither prophecies, nor tongues, nor this knowledge, and you will not have charity, which alone is everlasting.

units.la: Admonemur, ne transitorijs bonis tantum incumbamus, neglectis perpetuis & æternis, ne in futuro seculo, dum illis priuabimur, prorsus nudi & inanes deprehendamur. Præclaræ sunt aliquot artes & disciplinæ, splendidæ sunt opes, illustres sunt honores, suspicienda est prudentia, reuerenda potentia, &c. Verum hæc omnia cessabunt, & in hac uita terminantur, relinquentque possessores suos prorsus egenos & inanes, nisi ueris ac sempiternis bonis potiantur.
units.tr: We are warned not to cling only to transitory goods, neglecting the perpetual and eternal ones, lest in the age to come, when we are deprived of the former, we be found utterly naked and empty. Some arts and disciplines are excellent, riches are splendid, honours are illustrious, prudence is to be admired, power is to be revered, and so on. But all these will cease and come to an end in this life, and they leave their possessors utterly destitute and empty, unless they obtain true and everlasting goods.

units.la: Ex parte enim cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus, &c.
units.tr: For we know in part, and we prophesy in part, etc.

units.la: Subijcit declarationem eius quod prophetias, linguas, & scientiam cessaturas esse dixit. Quoniam uarij sunt cessationis modi, ne quid hic erretur, uisum est declarare, quomodo charismata ista cessatura dixerit. Cessationis quatuor sunt modi. Cessant quæ ad tempus quiescunt, cessant quæ alterantur, cessant quæ annihilantur, cessant quæ complentur ac perficiuntur. Cessat operarius dum ab opere suo quiescit, cessat uinum dum in acetum alteratur, cessat ignis dum extinctus annihilatur, & fumus dum in aerem euanescit: cessat lux aurorae, dum exortu solis completur ac perficitur. Cum ergo dicit: Ex parte nanque cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus, at ubi uenerit quod perfectum est, tunc quod ex parte est, abolebitur: satis, opinor, patet, quod de quarto cessationis modo loquatur, quo imperfecta cessant, dum complentur ac perficiuntur. Tribuit autem charismatis istis imperfectionem, cum dicit: Ex parte enim cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus. Ex parte aliquid scire, est non ex toto, sed imperfecte scire. Ex parte prophetare, est non plenam & absolutam, sed imperfectam futuro
units.tr: He adds an explanation of what he said, that prophecies, tongues, and knowledge will cease. Since there are various modes of cessation, lest anything be misunderstood here, it seems right to explain how he means that these gifts will cease. There are four modes of cessation. Things cease when they rest for a time; things cease when they are altered; things cease when they are annihilated; things cease when they are completed and perfected. A workman ceases when he rests from his work; wine ceases when it is changed into vinegar; fire ceases when it is extinguished and annihilated, and smoke when it vanishes into the air; the light of dawn ceases when it is completed and perfected by the rising of the sun. So when he says, "For we know in part, and we prophesy in part, but when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be abolished," it is, I think, sufficiently clear that he is speaking of the fourth mode of cessation, by which imperfect things cease when they are completed and perfected. He ascribes imperfection to these gifts when he says, "For we know in part, and we prophesy in part." To know something in part is not to know it wholly, but to know it imperfectly. To prophesy in part is not to prophesy fully and completely, but imperfectly.

units.la: Cessatur quatuor modis. rum tenere cognitionem. Hæc dicendo non sic detrahit scientiæ fidelium, quam ex Deo habent in hac uita, ut damnet eam uanitatis uel incertitudinis. Non dicit, uanum est quod fecimus: neque ex incerto est, quod scimus: sed, ex parte cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus. Aliud est esse imperfectum, & aliud esse uel incertum uel uanum. Imperfecta nostra, quæ per gratiam diuinæ prouidentiæ secundum mensuram, non secundum plenitudinem accepimus, incerta & inania non sunt, sed uera ac certa bona, ideoque non contemnenda, sed cum gratiarum actione pie & utiliter collocandam. Neq; in hoc est Apostolus, ut doceat Corinthios, prophetias, linguas, & charisma scientiæ contemnere, dum tribuit illis imperfectionem: sed monet ne nimium illis tribuant, & sic illorum gratia alius aduersus alium inflentur, quasi in illis summam sint ueræ felicitatis adepti, atq; ita contra charitatem quæ multo est potior, peccent.
units.tr: Cessation happens in four ways. To hold knowledge imperfectly. By saying this he does not so detract from the knowledge of believers, which they have from God in this life, as to condemn it as vain or uncertain. He does not say, "What we have done is vain," nor, "What we know is uncertain," but, "We know in part, and we prophesy in part." To be imperfect is one thing; to be either uncertain or vain is another. Our imperfect gifts, which we have received through the grace of divine providence according to measure, not according to fullness, are not uncertain or empty, but true and certain goods, and therefore not to be despised, but to be held devoutly and usefully, with thanksgiving. Nor is it the Apostle's purpose here to teach the Corinthians to despise prophecies, tongues, and the gift of knowledge, when he ascribes imperfection to them. Rather, he warns them not to attribute too much to them, lest on account of these graces one should be puffed up against another, as if they had attained the highest true happiness, and so sin against charity, which is far greater.

units.la: Ast ubi uenerit quod perfectum est, tunc quod ex parte est, abolebitur.
units.tr: But when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be done away.

units.la: Hic est modus, quo cessabit imperfecta fides lium scientia. Promittit perfectionem suo tempore uenturam, cū dicit: Ast ubi uenerit quod perfectum est. Significat in futuro seculo fore perfectionem omnium eorum, quæ imperfecta tenemus in hac uita. Ideo quamuis de scientia loquatur in præsenti, non tamen dicit, Vbi uenerit perfecta scientia, tunc abolebitur quæ est ex parte: sed generaliter, ubi uenerit τὸ τέλειον, id est, perfectum & absolutum, tunc quod ex parte est abolebitur. Non solum scientia nobis imperfecta est in hac uita, sed & ipsa dilectio, laus & gratiarum actio, gaudium in domino, gloria filiorum Dei, salus etiam tam spirituum quam corporum nostrorum, quæ omnia in futuro tandem complebuntur. Nõdum sumus in statu perfectionis omnium, ad quem nobis inuicta est & irremissa patientia contendendum. Omnino nanque sic est comparatus dominus, qui nos condidit, & propter nos creauit omnia, ut quæ cœpit sub mensura, qua uoluit, & imperfecta adhuc per prouidentiam suam gubernat & conseruat, non relinquat imperfecta perpetuo, sed tempore ad id æterno constituto perfecta fit & absoluta reddituras.
units.tr: This is the way in which imperfect faith or knowledge will cease. He promises that perfection will come in its own time, when he says: "But when that which is perfect has come." He means that in the future age there will be perfection of all those things which we hold imperfectly in this life. So although he speaks of knowledge in the present tense, he does not say, "When perfect knowledge has come, then that which is in part will be done away," but in general terms: when the perfect [τὸ τέλειον], that is, what is complete and absolute, has come, then that which is in part will be done away. Not only is our knowledge imperfect in this life, but also love, praise and thanksgiving, joy in the Lord, the glory of the sons of God, and the salvation of our spirits and bodies alike, all of which will at last be completed in the future. We are not yet in the state of perfection in all things, and to reach it we must strive with unconquered and unrelenting patience. For the Lord who made us, and created all things for our sake, is so constituted that he does not leave imperfect what he has begun within the measure he willed, but, while still governing and preserving it by his providence, will in the appointed time, which is eternal, make it perfect and complete.

units.la: TVNC, inquit, quod ex parte est, abolebitur. Quod in Græco est, τὸ ἐκ μέρους: ηχει, τὸ τέλειον ... uerti poterat: Ast ubi uenerit esse perfectum, tunc abolebitur esse ex parte. Quemadmodum enim τὸ τέλειον per uerbum ... sic absoluitur, ut reddi possit, quod perfectum est: sic per infinitiuum ... absolui potest, ut reddendum sit, perfectum esse, sicut & τὸ ἐκ μέρους. Et præsens causa, de qua loquitur Apostolus, sic est comparata, ut legendum sit: Vbi uenerit esse perfectum, abolebitur esse ex parte. Non enim abolebuntur in se quæ habemus adhuc imperfecta in Christo, sed implebuntur per statum perfectionis: abolebitur uero illorum imperfectio, dum ad perfectionem peruenerint.
units.tr: "Then," he says, "that which is in part will be done away." In the Greek it is τὸ ἐκ μέρους [that which is in part], and τὸ τέλειον [the perfect] could have been rendered: "But when there shall come to be perfection, then there shall be an end to being in part." For just as τὸ τέλειον is rendered by a noun, so that it can be translated "that which is perfect," so by the infinitive it can be rendered "to be perfect," just as τὸ ἐκ μέρους can. And the matter of which the Apostle speaks is so framed that it may be read: "When there shall come to be perfection, there shall be an end to being in part." For the things we still have imperfectly in Christ will not be abolished in themselves, but will be fulfilled in the state of perfection; what will be abolished is their imperfection, once they have attained perfection.

units.la: Quare cum dicit: Vbi uenerit perfectum, non debemus cogitare de alijs quibusdam perfectis bonis, quibus in uniuersum destituamur in hac uita, simusque in futuro demum potituri: sed de illis ipsis, quæ per fidem in Christum in hac uita secundum mensuram donationis spiritus, alius plus, alius minus accepimus. Ea dem dona spiritus hic sunt ex parte, illic erunt perfecta.
units.tr: Therefore when he says, "When the perfect has come," we ought not to think of certain other perfect goods, of which we are altogether deprived in this life and which we shall at last obtain in the future; but of those very gifts which, through faith in Christ in this life, we have received according to the measure of the gift of the Spirit, one more and another less. These same gifts of the Spirit are here in part; there they will be perfect.

units.la: Cogitemus hic de singulari consilio Dei, quo cursum salutis nostræ sic disposuit, ut sit illius perfectio non principium, sed finem sortita, sitque nobis ab imperfectis ad perfecta uenien dum, non à perfectis ad imperfecta: deinde quod totam hanc nostram uitam, & uniuersum hunc mundum, in quo iam uiuimus, imperfectioni sic subiecit, ut impossibile sit ad perfectionem, siue iustitiæ, siue scientiæ, siue salutis, siue felicitatis peruenire, donec fumus in hac carne, priusquam tempus consummationis omnium uenerit.
units.tr: Let us consider here the singular counsel of God, by which he has so ordered the course of our salvation that its perfection is not the beginning but the end; so that we go from imperfect things to perfect ones, not from perfect to imperfect. Further, he has subjected this whole life of ours, and the whole world in which we now live, to imperfection in such a way that it is impossible to reach perfection, whether of righteousness, knowledge, salvation or happiness, while we are in this flesh, before the time of the consummation of all things comes.

units.la: Cum essem puer, ut puer loquebar, ut puer sentiebam, ut puer cogitabam: at ubi factus sum uir, abolevi puerilia.
units.tr: When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things.

units.la: Quod dixit: Ex parte enim cognoscimus, &c. Ast ubi uenerit esse perfectum, abolebitur esse ex parte, similitudine illustrat admodum accommoda & manifesta, de pueritia & uirili ætate sumpta. Comparat præsentem hanc uitam pueritiæ, futuram uero ætati uirili. Habet quidè animi ac mentis dotes pueritia, sed imperfectas: & facultatem quoq; loquendi, sed talem quæ magis sit garritus quidam, quàm ius sermo, cùm propter sensus immaturos, tū propter linguæ nondum satis exercitatæ balbutiem. Hæc imperfectio pueritiæ adhæret, donec per maturitatem uirilis ætatis abolea tur, qua & sensus & sermo perfectionem suam acquirant. Virilis enim ætas & sentit, ratiocinatur què perfectius, & loquitur dexterius, quam pueritia. Plane sic habet conditio præsentis uitæ, ut quæ dono Dei cognoscimus, affectamus, loquimur & facimus, imperfecta sint omnia ac ueluti puerilia, nec peruenïat ad iustam maturitatem ac perfectionem, antequā ad uirilem futuræ uitæ ætatem transferamur. Per hanc abolebitur sensuum, affectuū, sermonum & operum nostrorum pueritia. Sic dicit: Cum essem puer, uel paruulus, Græcè ... ut puer loquebar, ut puer sentiebam, ut puer cogitabā: uel, ratiocinabar, Græcè ... ut ubi factus sum uir, aboleui puerilia.
units.tr: When he says, "For we know in part, etc.," and "But when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be done away," he illustrates it with a very fitting and clear likeness, taken from childhood and manhood. He compares this present life to childhood and the future life to manhood. Childhood indeed has gifts of mind and understanding, but imperfect ones, and it also has the power of speech, but such that it is more a babbling than a true speech, both because its senses are immature and because its tongue is not yet sufficiently trained, so that it stammers. This imperfection clings to childhood until it is abolished by the maturity of manhood, by which both sense and speech acquire their perfection. For manhood both perceives and reasons more perfectly, and speaks more skilfully, than childhood does. Clearly the condition of the present life is such that all the things we know, desire, say and do by God's gift are imperfect, and as it were childish, and do not reach their due maturity and perfection before we are transferred to the manhood of the future life. By this childhood of our senses, affections, words and works will be abolished. So he says: "When I was a child, or a little one" (in Greek ...), "I spoke as a child, I felt as a child, I thought" (or, "reasoned," in Greek ...) "as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things."

units.la: Proponitur ergo nobis & præsentis uitæ immaturitas, & futuræ perfectio, sub hac pueritiæ & uirilis ætatis imagine ueluti ob oculos spectanda & considerandā. Quid igitur superbimus opinione uel sapientiæ uel opum uel potentiæ inflati, cum adhuc pueriliter sapiamus, pueriliter loquamur, puerilibus delectemur, & puerilia utcunque præstemus? Quis non rideat pueros, ineptias suas pro serijs habentes, seque multa scire ac posse iactantes? Et quid aliud facimus, dum opinione sapientiæ ac potentiæ inflamur? Quare qui aliquid sapientiæ ac scientiæ acceperunt, cogitent id adhuc esse puerile & imperfectum, & sectentur ea cum Apostolo, quæ nobis perfecta in cœlo sunt præfixa.
units.tr: Set before us, then, under this image of childhood and manhood, are both the immaturity of the present life and the perfection of the future life, which we should look at and consider as if before our eyes. Why then do we boast, puffed up with opinion of wisdom, or wealth, or power, when we still think like children, speak like children, delight in childish things, and perform childish deeds of whatever kind? Who would not laugh at children who count their silly things as serious matters and boast that they know and can do much? And what else do we do when we are inflated by the opinion of our wisdom and power? Therefore those who have received some wisdom and knowledge should consider that it is still childish and imperfect, and should pursue those things with the Apostle which are set before us as perfect in heaven.

units.la: Satis autem manifestum est in hoc simili, quo modo scientia diuinarum rerum, quam in hac vita acquirunt fideles, in futura sit abolenda. Quemadmodum uidelicet τὸ νήπιον illud quod habent pueri, in se non aboletur per uirilem ætatem, sed magis completur ac perfectius reditur, aboletur uero illius imperfectio: sic & ipsa scientia Dei in se manente abolebitur illius imperfectio, ubi perfectionis tempus aduenerit.
units.tr: It is clear enough from this comparison how the knowledge of divine things which the faithful acquire in this life is to be abolished in the future. Just as that childishness [τὸ νήπιον] which children have is not itself abolished by manhood, but rather is completed and made more perfect, while only its imperfection is abolished; so too the knowledge of God itself will remain, while its imperfection will be abolished when the time of perfection has come.

units.la: Illud obiter obseruet lector, quod tria hæc uerba, loqui, sentire & cogitare, id est, ratiocinari, ordine præpostero ponuntur. Primum enim est ratiocinari, deinde sentire aliquid ac ueluti concludere, tertio quod sentias proloqui. Ergo cum dixisset, Cum esset puer, loquebar ut puer: subijcit, sentiebam ut puer, ratiocinabar ut puer. Quasi dicat: Vt puer loquebar, quia sentiebam ut puer: sentiebā ut puer, quia ratiocinabar ut puer. Secundū qualitatem enim ratiocinationis, siue puerilis, siue uirilis ac maturæ colligitur sensus, & secundum qualitatem sensus prodit ex ore sermo cogitationū nostrarum index. Cum itaq; logicon illud quod est in mente hominis, unà cum ipsa ætate inde à puero ad uirilem usque maturitatem crescat, fit ut donec pueri sumus, pueriliter quoque cogitemus, sentiamus & loquamur. Vnde uulgo dicimus, Vuitz kompt nitt uor den taren. Quare puerilis illa & immaturior ætas instituenda est, fingenda & moderanda, ne incrementa τ. ἀ. λογικοῦ pro naturæ nostræ corruptione à bono & honesto ad omnis generis uicia exorbitent, & tandem habitum maliciæ acquirant, in malo obdurentur, & nec disciplinam nec correctionem amplius ferant. Stultitia est in corde pueri, inquit Sapiens, uirga disciplinæ effugat illam. Videmus hodie mirabilem ac stupendum instituendę iuuentutis neglectum, & incredibilem iuxtà nō dico stulticiam, sed maliciam & nequiciam inolescere, quæ ubi uires acceperit, monstra nobis omnis generis flagitiorum pariet, quibus domandis non sufficiet nostri magistratus, sed requiretur exoticus gladius inde ex Oriente, qui iudicia domini in reprobas nationes exerceat. Vtinam quod Paulus hic dicit, Cum puer essem, loquebar ut puer, sentiebam ut puer, & cogitabam ut puer: at ubi factus sum uir, aboleui puerilia, locū hodie in pueris nostris pariter ac uiris habeat. Aliud est pueriliter, & aliud impie, maliciose ac flagitiose cogitare, sentire & loqui. Aliud item est in uirili ætate abolere puerilia, & a-
units.tr: Let the reader observe in passing that these three words, to speak, to feel, and to think (that is, to reason), are set down in reverse order. For first there is reasoning, then feeling something and, as it were, concluding, and third, speaking what one feels. So after saying, "When I was a child, I spoke as a child," he adds: "I felt as a child, I reasoned as a child." It is as if he said: "I spoke as a child because I felt as a child; I felt as a child because I reasoned as a child." For according to the quality of reasoning, whether childish or manly and mature, the feeling is formed, and according to the quality of feeling, speech comes forth from the mouth as the indicator of our thoughts. Since, then, that rational faculty which is in the mind of man grows together with age itself from childhood up to mature manhood, it follows that as long as we are children we also think, feel and speak in a childish way. Hence we commonly say: "Wit does not come before the years" [Wuitz kompt nitt uor den taren]. Therefore that childish and more immature age must be instructed, shaped and governed, lest the growth of the rational faculty [τοῦ λογικοῦ], because of the corruption of our nature, swerve from good and honest things into every kind of vice, and at last acquire a habit of wickedness, harden in evil, and no longer bear discipline or correction. "Folly is bound up in the heart of a child," says the Wise Man; "the rod of discipline will drive it away." Today we see a remarkable and astonishing neglect of the instruction of youth, and an incredible growth, I do not say of folly, but of malice and wickedness, which, once it has gained strength, will bring forth monsters of every kind of crime, and to subdue which our magistrates will not suffice, but a foreign sword will be needed from the East to execute the judgments of the Lord upon reprobate nations. Would that what Paul says here, "When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I felt as a child, and I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things," had its place today among our children as well as our men! It is one thing to think, feel and speak childishly, and another to think, feel and speak impiously, maliciously and wickedly.
