It is also one thing, in manhood, to put away childish things, and another to let the malice of childhood, by the strength of manhood, become still greater and more firmly established.

units.la: liud pueritiæ maliciam uirilis ætatis robore ad huc reddere auctiorem & confirmatiorem.
units.tr: and another thing is to make the malice of childhood greater and stronger by the vigour of adult age.

units.la: Cernimus enim nunc per speculum in ænigmate, tunc autem facie ad faciē: nunc agnosco ex parte, tunc uero cognoscam, quemadmodum & cognitus sum.
units.tr: For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known. (1 Cor. 13.12)

units.la: Similitudinem puerilis & uirilis scientiæ applicat ad causam de qua agit, idq; hoc pacto: Cum puer essem, pueriliter loquebar, sentiebā & cogitabā, at ubi uir factus sum, aboleui puerilia: sic in causa pietatis & scientiæ Dei dum sumus in hac uita, pueriliter sentimus & cognoscimus, in futura ubi fuerimus, nō amplius puerili, sed uirili, id est, matura & perfecta cognitione præditi erimus. Nunc enim, id est, in præsenti seculo, cernimus non palàm & liquido, sed ueluti per speculum in ænigmate: tunc autem, id est, in futuro, ubi perfectio uenerit, cernemus facie ad faciem.
units.tr: He applies a comparison between childish and adult knowledge to the matter he is treating, in this way: "When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I felt and thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things." So in the matter of piety and the knowledge of God, while we are in this life we feel and know in a childish way; in the future, when we are there, we shall be endowed no longer with childish but with adult knowledge, that is, with mature and perfect knowledge. For "now," that is, in the present age, we see not plainly and clearly but as if through a glass, in a riddle; but "then," that is, in the future, when perfection has come, we shall see face to face.

units.la: CERNIMVS enim nunc, inquit.] Metaphoram uisus usurpat pro cognitione, quæ mentis est uisio. Non enim loquitur de uisu oculorum, sed de scientia & intelligentia rerum diuinarum, cum qua in præsenti uita utimur, tum qua potiemur in futura. Quæ de Deo, deque Christo filio eius, de gratia redemptionis, & tota salutis nostræ dispensatione sentimus ac credimus, licet imperfecte & ex parte, & in ænigmate: haud tamen imaginaria & incerta cogitatione opinamur, sed uera ac certa scientia cognoscimus, ut recte uerbum cernendi usurpatum hic fit, & ad fidei nostræ certitudinem translatum.
units.tr: "For now we see," he says. He takes the metaphor of sight for knowledge, which is the sight of the mind. For he is not speaking of the sight of the eyes, but of the understanding and knowledge of divine things, which we use in the present life and shall possess in the future. What we feel and believe about God, and about Christ his Son, about the grace of redemption and the whole dispensation of our salvation, we know, though imperfectly, in part, and in a riddle; yet we do not hold it by an imagined and uncertain thought, but know it by true and certain knowledge. So the verb "to see" is rightly used here and transferred to the certainty of our faith.

units.la: CERNIMVS enim nunc per speculum in quit.] Cum duo sint speculorum genera in usu, quorum alterum pellucidum, ideoq; διαύγης uocari posset: alterum uero haud διαφανής est, sed sic comparatum, ut recipiat ac spectandas præbeat obiectorum imagines: posset hic amphibolum esse, de quo genere loquatur Apostolus, nisi non diceret, Cernimus enim nunc ἐν αἰνίγματι, id est, in speculo sicuti Iacobus loquitur: sed, Cernimus enim nunc διʼ ἐσόπτρου, id est, per speculum. Quare puto eum loqui de priori speculorum genere, quo utuntur, qui infirma sunt oculorum acie, ideoq; minutiora obiecta sine speculo cernere ac dijudicare non possunt. Quemadmodum illi per speculū uel remotiora, uel minutiora utcunq; uident: ita nos præ imbecillitate mentis cœlestia & spiritualia haud possumus perspicue cernere, sed uti cogimur speculo uerbi Dei, per quod illa aliquo saltem usq; uideamus.
units.tr: "For now we see through a glass," he says. Since there are two kinds of mirror in use, one transparent, which could be called "clear" [διαύγης], and the other not transparent but made so as to receive and present the images of objects to be looked at, this phrase could be ambiguous, as to which kind the Apostle means, were it not that he does not say "Now we see in a riddle" [ἐν αἰνίγματι], that is, "in a mirror," as James puts it, but "Now we see through a mirror" [διʼ ἐσόπτρου], that is, "through a glass." Hence I think he speaks of the first kind of mirror, which is used by those whose eyesight is weak and who therefore cannot see or distinguish smaller objects without a mirror. Just as those people see things either more distant or smaller in some way through a mirror, so we, because of the weakness of our minds, cannot see heavenly and spiritual things clearly, but are forced to use the mirror of the Word of God, through which we may at least see them in some measure.

units.la: Nolim tamen admodum contendere cum illis qui locum hunc de posteriori speculorum genere exponunt, in quibus non res ipsæ, sed imagines rerum conspiciuntur. Et hic alij per speculū creaturas à Deo conditas intelligunt, in quibus diuinæ sapientiæ ac potentiæ imagines spectari possunt, secundum ea quę Apostolus Rom. 1. scribit: alij uero similitudinem spespeculi referunt ad uerbū & sacramenta, quod in illis imagines diuinæ gratiæ, consilij ac propositi Dei salutisq; nostræ uelut in speculo contemplandæ proponantur.
units.tr: Yet I would not wish to dispute at length with those who explain this passage of the second kind of mirror, in which not the things themselves but their images are seen. Some of these understand by the mirror the creatures made by God, in which images of divine wisdom and power may be seen, according to what the Apostle writes in Rom. 1. Others refer the likeness of the mirror to the Word and the sacraments, in which images of divine grace, of the counsel and purpose of God, and of our salvation are set before us to be contemplated as in a mirror.

units.la: Illud, in ænigmate, expositionis gratia adie ctum esse uidetur, ut idem sit, quod in obscuro. Est enim ænigma quoddam, quicquid obscurius esse apparet, quâ ut à quibuslibet perspicuô comprehendatur. Non est dictio hæc ænigmatis præter mentem Apostoli diuexâda, neque ipsi doctrinæ uerbi Dei, sed intellectus ac sensuum nostrorum imbecillitati tribuêda. Alias uerbum ueritatis non est ænigmatica cligo, sed lux quædam, qua mentes electorum illuminantur, quantumuis obscurum uideatur illis qui pereant. Respectu tamen perfectæ cognitionis, quæ in futuro seculo continget, dicit nos Apostolus in hac uita sic ex parte & im perfecte cognoscere, ut similes simus illis qui obscure & per speculum cernunt. Quod est obscurum primum rationi nostræ, deinde & imbecillitati nostræ fidei, ænigmaticum esse uidetur, cum sit lux omnium clarissima. Quare non seruit hic locus aduersarijs sacrarū scripturarum, qui quo neminem non à lectione illarum abterreant, & simul iniquissimam tyrannidem pontificiorum defendat, qua laicis illa, ut uocant Christi plebem, non competere contenditur: improbe clamant scripturā esse ænigmaticam, teste Paulo, adeoq; obscuram, ut intelligi non possit, nisi ab illuminatis patribus & ecclesiæ doctoribus: quibus, uolente domino, in Locis nostris, ubi de sacris scripturis dicemus, respondendum erit.
units.tr: The phrase "in a riddle" seems to have been added for explanation, so that it means the same as "in obscurity." For whatever appears rather obscure is a kind of riddle, so that it may be grasped by anyone who sees clearly. This word "riddle" is not to be wrested contrary to the Apostle's meaning, nor applied to the teaching of the Word of God itself, but ascribed to the weakness of our understanding and senses. Otherwise the word of truth is not an enigmatic obscurity, but a light by which the minds of the elect are illuminated, however obscure it may seem to those who perish. Yet with respect to the perfect knowledge that will come in the future age, the Apostle says that in this life we know only in part and imperfectly, so that we are like those who see dimly and through a mirror. What is obscure to our reason at first, and then to the weakness of our faith, seems enigmatic, although it is the clearest of all lights. Therefore this passage does not serve the adversaries of the holy Scriptures, who try to frighten everyone away from reading them, and at the same time to defend the most unjust tyranny of the Papists, by which the laity, whom they call the people of Christ, are said not to be fit for them. They shamelessly cry out that Scripture is enigmatic, as Paul bears witness, and so obscure that it cannot be understood unless by the enlightened Fathers and teachers of the Church. To this, God willing, we shall reply in our place, where we shall speak of the holy Scriptures.

units.la: TVNC autem facie ad faciem.] Abutuntur hoc loco anthropomorphitæ, & nonnulli alij sensu magis carnali quàm spirituali de rebus cœlestibus ac Deo ipso iudicantes. Ecce, inquiunt, palâ dicit Apostolus, uisuros nos Deum facie ad faciem, ubi tempus perfectionis aduenerit in futuro uidelicet seculo. Ergo faciem habet Deus ut homo, quæ uideri potest, inquiunt Anthrop. & uidebitur à nobis oculis hisce corporalibus, aiunt carnales. Verum Apostolus uerbo uidendi tam hic quàm in præcedenti membro in sensu cognoscendi usurpauit, qui non est faciei, sed mentis. Unde hic Deum uidemus, inde illum in futura quoque uita uidebimus, oculis uidelicet non corporis, sed mentis.
units.tr: "Then face to face." The anthropomorphites abuse this passage, and some others who judge heavenly things and God himself in a more carnal than spiritual sense. "Behold," they say, "the Apostle plainly says that we shall see God face to face when the time of perfection has come, that is, in the future age. Therefore God has a face as a man has, which can be seen, say the anthropomorphites, and will be seen by us with these bodily eyes, say the carnal." But the Apostle has used the verb "to see" here, as in the preceding clause, in the sense of knowing, which belongs not to the face but to the mind. Hence we see God here, and so we shall see him in the future life too, with the eyes not of the body but of the mind.

units.la: Deinde, utcunque urgeant, non dicit, Tunc Deum facie ad faciem uidebimus: sed simpliciter de rebus spiritualibus, quas hic uelut per speculum cernimus: Tunc, inquit, facie ad faciem cernemus.
units.tr: Furthermore, however hard they press it, he does not say, "Then we shall see God face to face"; he speaks simply of spiritual things, which we now see here as through a mirror. "Then," he says, "we shall see face to face."

units.la: Imo etiamsi ad Deum referatur, inde tamen non potest colligi sic esse illum uisibilē, ut corporis oculis ne in futura quidē uita cerni possit. Alias ex eo quod Deut. quinto legimus, facie ad faciem loquutus est nobis in monte de medio ignis. Et Num 12. ore ad os loquor ei, palam & non per ænigmata & figuras Deum uidet, consequeretur Deum non in futuro tan-
units.tr: Indeed, even if it is referred to God, it cannot be inferred from this that he is so visible that he cannot be seen even in the future life with bodily eyes. Otherwise, from what we read in Deuteronomy 5, "he spoke with us face to face out of the midst of the fire on the mountain," and from Numbers 12, "I speak with him mouth to mouth, plainly and not in enigmas and figures, and he sees God," it would follow that God is visible not only in the future but also in this present age, and can be seen with the eyes of the body; yet Exodus 33 expressly denies this from God himself, where he says: "You cannot see my face. For no man shall see me and live." And John 1...

units.la: tum, sed & in hoc præsenti seculo uisibile esse, & oculis corporis cerni posse, quod tamē Exodi 33. diserte ab ipso Deo negatur, ubi dicit: Non poteris uidere faciem meam. Non enim uidebit me homo, & uiuet. Et Iohan. 1. Deum, inquit, nemo uidit unquam. Quare si nec Moses Deum uidit, & tamen facie ad faciem & ore ad os cum eo loquutus memoratur: quid aliud restat, quàm hac loquutione pleniorem ac perfectiorem cognitionem illius exprimi. Sed hac de re si cui lubet uideat Augustinum epistola 6.111.112. & in quæst. super Deut. lib. 5.ca.9. Anthropologia est, quando facies Deo tribuitur in scripturis, qua humano more de illo sit sermo. Angeli eorum, inquit Christus, semper uident faciem patris mei qui in cœlis est. Matth 18. quod dictū est ad similitudinem eorum ministrorum, qui regi sunt proximi, & ante faciem illius præsto, & ad ministrandum parati. Eiusmodi ministri unà cum amicis secretiorib. solent stare ante faciem regis, sic scripturā tribuit angelis, & electis post hanc uitam quod uideant uiuriq; sunt Deum facie ad faciem: quod nihil est aliud, quam quod sint illi futuri electi omnium coniunctissimi, & omnia propius quàm nunc cognituri.
units.tr: ...so that he would be visible and perceptible to the eyes of the body not only in the future life but also in this present age. Yet God himself expressly denies this in Exod. 33, where he says: "You cannot see my face, for no man shall see me and live." And in John 1: "No one has ever seen God," he says. So if Moses did not see God, and yet is recorded as speaking with him face to face and mouth to mouth, what else remains but that this manner of speaking expresses a fuller and more perfect knowledge of him? On this matter, let anyone who wishes consult Augustine, Epistles 111 and 112, and his Questions on Deuteronomy, book 5, chapter 9. When a face is attributed to God in the Scriptures, speech about him is in human fashion; this is anthropomorphism. "Their angels," says Christ, "always see the face of my Father who is in heaven." Matt. 18. This was said by way of likeness to those servants who are near a king, stand before his face, and are ready to minister. Such attendants, together with the more intimate friends, are accustomed to stand before the king's face. In this way Scripture attributes to the angels, and to the elect after this life, that they see God and will see him face to face. This is nothing other than saying that they will be the most closely joined of all to him, and will come to know all things more nearly than they do now.

units.la: NVNC cognosco, inquit, ex parte.] Metaphorico uidendi uerbo relicto resumit uerbū cognoscendi: unde admonemur, quod in præcedenti particula dixit, Cernimus nūc per speculum, idē esse quod cognoscimus nunc subobscure. Haud dubie clarius ac penitius tunc uidebimus, quàm in hac iam mortali & imbecilli carne uideamus: uerum nō loquitur Apostolus de uisu oculorum in præsenti, neque eo quo uidebimus in futuro, neq; eo quo nunc uidemus, sed de uisu mentis.
units.tr: NOW I know in part, he says. Having left aside the metaphor of seeing, he takes up again the verb of knowing; whereby we are reminded that what he said in the preceding clause, "We see now through a mirror," means the same as "we know now somewhat obscurely." Undoubtedly we shall then see more clearly and thoroughly than we now see in this mortal and feeble flesh; but the Apostle is not speaking of the sight of the eyes, either of the present or of that which we shall have in the future, nor of that by which we now see, but of the sight of the mind.

units.la: Nec ociosum est, quod in singulari de sepe dixit: Nunc cognosco ex parte, tunc uero cognoscam, quemadmodū & cognitus sum. Quoniam enim in præcedentibus pluraliter dixit: Ex parte cognoscimus & ex parte prophetamus. Et: Cernimus nunc per speculum in ænigmate, ne hoc communiter quidem de aliis, non autem de se quoq; dicere uideatur, specialiter seipse quoque in istam cognitionis imperfectionem perinde atque alios includit. Non dicit, Cū iunior essem: aut, cum neophytus essem in Christo, cognoscebam ex parte: sed nunc cognosco ex parte, loquens non præcise de tempore, quo hæc scribebat, sed de tota hac præsenti uita. Ergo nec apostoli plenitudinem scientiæ Dei consequuti sunt in hac uita, sed expectarunt illam in futuro demum seculo apprehendendam.
units.tr: Nor is it idle that he says in the singular, "Now I know in part, but then I shall know, just as I also have been known." For in the preceding verses he had spoken in the plural, "We know in part and we prophesy in part," and "We now see through a glass, in a riddle." Lest it seem that he was saying this only generally of others and not of himself, he now includes himself specifically in this imperfection of knowledge, just as he does the others. He does not say, "When I was younger," or "When I was a novice in Christ, I knew in part," but "Now I know in part," speaking not strictly of the time when he was writing, but of this whole present life. Therefore the apostles did not attain the fullness of the knowledge of God in this life, but looked for it to be grasped in the age to come.

units.la: Deinde, omnes quidem nunc ex parte cognoscimus, nec datur ulli mortalium scientiæ Dei perfectio, quæ in futura demum uita dabitur: sunt tamen diuersæ mensuræ, quibus in hac uita alij plus, alij minus cognitionis Dei tribuitur. Hic Apostolus qui dicit, Nunc cognosco ex parte, in cœlum raptus arcana Dei cognouit, quæ non licet homini loqui.
units.tr: Next, while all of us now know in part, and no mortal is given the perfection of the knowledge of God, which will be given only in the life to come, nevertheless there are different measures in which, in this life, some are granted more knowledge of God and some less. The Apostle who says, "Now I know in part," had been caught up into heaven and had known the secrets of God, which it is not lawful for a man to utter.

units.la: TVNC uero cognoscam, inquit,sicut & cognitus sum.]Græce est, ἐπιγνώσομαι καὶ ὡς καὶ ἐπιγνωσθήν. Quemadmodum auxesis erit in futura cognitione, ita & uerbo ἐπεγνωσμένα auxesim expressit. Est enim ἀπὸ τῶν πρώτων γνώσεως ἡ μὲν ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς πραγματα ... κατὰ δύναμιν κατανόησις. Cum igitur dixisset, ἄρτι γινώσκω ἐκ μέρους, id est. Nunc cognosco ex parte, ut perfectius se in futuro cognituru m,imo agnituru m significaret non dixit, τότε δὲ γνώσομαι: sed, τότε δὲ ἐπιγνώσομαι καθὼς καὶ ἐπιγνωσθήν, id est, tunc amplius cognosca, sicut & amplius agnitus sum. Erit ergo cognitio futuri fe culi non simpliciter γνῶσις, sed ἐπίγνωσις, qua res antea in hac uita tenuiter & ex parte cognitas adhuc quidem agnoscemus in futuro, sed amplius & perfectius quàm nunc illas cognoscimus. Accidet nobis quod accidit reginæ Saba, quæ cum coràm omnem audiffet Salomonis sapientiam,uidiffetq; domum quam ædificauerat,ac cibos mensæ eius,& habitacula feruorū, & ordines ministrantium,ueftesq; eorū & pincernas,& holocausta quæ offerebat in domo domini,nō habebat ultra spiritū,ac dixit ad regem: Verus est sermo quē audiui in terra mea super sermonibus tuis &super sapientia tua,& non credebā narrantibus mihi donec ipsa ueni & uidi oculis meis, & experimento cognoui,quod dimidia pars nunciata mihi,non fuerit. Maior est sapientia & opera tua quàm fit rumor quem audiui, &c. Consimili modo nobis quoq; eueniet, ubi ad cœlestis patriæ gloriam translati fuerimus.Quę nunc de illa audimus, & uix per speculum ac transennam uel ut à longe uidentes obscure & ex parte cognoscimus, tunc adeo perspicue cognoscemus, ut non dimidiam tantum,sed ne millesimam quidem eorum partem nunciatam nobis non fuisse cogniturı ac fassuri fimus.
units.tr: "But then I shall know," he says, "even as I also have been known." In Greek it is ἐπιγνώσομαι καὶ ὡς καὶ ἐπιγνωσθήν [epignōsomai kai hōs kai epignōsthēn]. Just as there will be an increase in the knowledge of the future life, so he has also expressed this increase by the word ἐπεγνωσμένα [epegnōsmena]. For ἀπὸ τῶν πρώτων γνώσεως ἡ μὲν ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς πραγματα ... κατὰ δύναμιν κατανόησις [apo tōn prōtōn gnōseōs]. Since he had said ἄρτι γινώσκω ἐκ μέρους [arti ginōskō ek merous], that is, "Now I know in part," he did not, in order to signify that he would know more perfectly in the future, or rather recognise fully, write τότε δὲ γνώσομαι [tote de gnōsomai], but τότε δὲ ἐπιγνώσομαι καθὼς καὶ ἐπιγνωσθήν [tote de epignōsomai kathōs kai epignōsthēn], that is, "then I shall know more fully, just as I have been more fully known." The knowledge of the age to come will therefore be not simply γνῶσις [gnōsis] but ἐπίγνωσις [epignōsis], by which we shall recognise in the future those things which in this life we have known only dimly and in part, but more fully and perfectly than we now know them. It will happen to us as it happened to the queen of Sheba, who, when she had heard all the wisdom of Solomon and had seen the house he had built, and the food at his table, the dwellings of his servants, the order of his attendants, their clothing and cupbearers, and the burnt offerings which he offered in the house of the Lord, was no longer breathless, and said to the king: "The report which I heard in my own land about your words and your wisdom is true; yet I did not believe those who told me, until I came and saw with my own eyes and found by experience that the half had not been told me. Your wisdom and your works exceed the report which I heard," and so on. In the same way it will happen to us too, when we have been carried up to the glory of the heavenly homeland. What we now hear of that homeland, and know only dimly and in part, scarcely through a glass and a lattice, or as those who see from afar, then we shall know so clearly that we shall confess we were told not merely half, but not even the thousandth part of what there is.

units.la: SICVT & cognitus sum,inquit.]Vel lege, iuxta quod & agnitus sum. Sumus electi inde ab initio mundi. Vbi tempus uocationis uenit,agnoscit nos dominus, quos olim elegit. Quemadmodum igitur nos plenius agnoscemus in futuro quæ iam cognoscimus ex parte: ita iam agnoscit nos dominus,quos ante mundi constitutionem in peculium suum elegit. Sic hoc quoque loco, uerbo ἐπιγινώσκω admonedum est pertinenter usus Apostolus. Inde tamen non cofequitur,ea nos perfectione agnituros in cœlis & Deum & cœlestia omnia,qua ab illo in hac uita omnium agnoscimur perfectissime.Perfectio ista cognitionis, quæ continget nobis in futuro,fi ad cognitionem conferatur,qua nos Deo agnoscit in hac uita,prorsus est imperfectio: fi uero conferatur ad eam qua nos illum & cœlestia cognoscimus,dum peregrinamur in hoc seculo, tum demum erit perfectio.
units.tr: Or read, according to which also "I have been known" (agnitus sum). We were chosen from the beginning of the world. When the time of calling comes, the Lord acknowledges us, whom he chose long ago. Just as we shall know more fully in the future what we now know only in part, so the Lord now acknowledges us, whom he chose for his own possession before the foundation of the world. So in this place the Apostle aptly used the word epiginōskō [ἐπιγινώσκω], as should be noted. Yet it does not follow from this that in heaven we shall know God and all heavenly things with the same perfection with which we are most perfectly known by him in this life. That perfection of knowledge which will be given us in the future, if it is compared with the knowledge by which he knows us in this life, is altogether imperfection; but if it is compared with the knowledge by which we know him and heavenly things while we are pilgrims in this world, then indeed it will be perfection.

units.la: Magnæ fidei uerbum est,& magnæ quoque cófolationis,quod dicit,Tunc agnoscam,sicut & agnitus sum.Dicit fe non simpliciter cognitum esse Deo,fedagnitum. Cognoscit omnia Deus quæ in cœlo sunt & in terra: uerum non
units.tr: It is a word of great faith and also of great comfort, that he says, "Then I shall know, even as I also have been known." He says that he has not merely been known by God, but acknowledged. God knows all things that are in heaven and on earth, but not

units.la: agnoscit quoslibet pro suis,sed electos tantũ. Inter hos fe computat,cum fe agnitum esse dicit.Et hinc bona & certa cum fiducia colligit, fore ut & ipse agnoscat Deum suum & quę ob fcure hic cognouit, multo propius ac plenius quàm in hac uita. Agnitio ista,qua nos Deus pro suis agnoscit,prior est,& fundamentū salutis noftrę:nec impeditur imperfectione cognitionis noftrę,sed illā prouehit,donec in futuro perfectiorem reddat. Ne colligam9 igitur ad hunc modū:Agnoscet nos Deus in futuro, qa priores agnouimus eum in præfenti hac uita. Sed potius sic est colligēdū:Agnoscit nos Deus pro suis in hoc seculo, agnoscemus ergo eū in futuro,ubi fe nobis ac gloriam cœlestem,ad quā nos uocauit,non in obscuro,sed palā& clara luce manifestabit. Agnoscit hic nos ut saluet,illic fe nobis agnofcedū prębebit, ut glorificemur felicesq; fimus in sempiternum.
units.tr: acknowledge just anyone as his own, only the elect. Paul counts himself among these when he says that he has been acknowledged, and from this he draws the good and certain confidence that he himself will also know his God, and will know what he has here known obscurely, far more closely and fully than in this life. That acknowledgement by which God owns us as his own comes first, and it is the foundation of our salvation; it is not hindered by the imperfection of our knowledge, but advances it until in the future it makes it more perfect. Therefore we should not infer it in this way: God will acknowledge us in the future, because we first acknowledged him in this present life. Rather it should be inferred thus: God acknowledges us as his own in this age, so we shall acknowledge him in the future, when he will reveal himself to us and the heavenly glory to which he has called us, not in obscurity but openly and in clear light. He acknowledges us here so that he may save us; there he will offer himself to us to be acknowledged, so that we may be glorified and made happy for ever.

units.la: Nunc autem manent fides,spes, charitas, tria hæc, sed maior in his est charitas.
units.tr: Now, however, faith, hope, and love remain, these three; but the greatest of these is love.

units.la: Quod in Græco est μένει,pluraliter legendū est ac referēdum ad τὰ τρία ταῦτα, id est, tria hæc. Sic enim Græci neutris uocibus pluralis numeri,uerba singularia coniungunt. Nihil tamē refert etiamsi in singulari legamus:manet,ficu ti Vallæ placet.Concludit hac particula charitatis encomium,quo tribuit illi,quòd non excidat,sicuti charismata,quorum zelo ac studio inflabantur Corinthij,sed maneat etiam in futuro. Nunc,inquit.Id est,in hac uita. Neque enim alio sensu utitur hac uoce, quàm quo usus est illa iam fecundo.Manet, inquit, fides, spes, charitas,tria hæc. Quid est,quod fidei ac spei mentionem facit,illasque manere dicit,& non magis repetit de linguis, prophetia,&scientia, concludens: Nunc igitur cessabunt linguæ, prophetia, & scientia, charitas uero manet? quo pacto quæ hactenus dixit in speciem pertinenter conclusisset. Meo iudicio concludit per occupationem. Poterat iam dictis obijci:Esto cessent linguæ & prophetiæ,& reliqua charismata,maneatque charitas, an ideo præferenda est hoc nomine charitas,quod non excidit?An non fides quoq; & spes manent, perinde atq; charitas? Si charitas omnia credit & sperat,ergo fides & spes cum illa manent. Huiusmodi cogitationi respondens, primū concedit manere fidem,spem, unà cum charitate: deinde concessioni huic annectit expositionē ac limitationem, quousque fides ac spes cum charitate maneant. Tertio concludens pronūciat pro charitate esse illam etiá fide ac spe præstantiorem. Sic dicit: Nunc autem manent fides, spes, charitas, tria hæc, maior uero in his est charitas. Apparet autem legēdum esse adhunc modum,Νυνὶ δὲ μένει. Hoc est, Nunc quidem manent,&c. Nam aptissime sequitur adueršatiua uocula δέ, quæ hic non suo est loco posita.Concessio est in eo quod dicit:Manent quidē fides,spes,charitas. Ex hac concessione diuinare possumus,qd illi obijcere potuerint. Expositio est in uocula, Nunc, quæ omnino emphatice est posita. Quasi dicat: In hac quidē uita manent fides ac spes cum charitate, in futura uero non ita. Cóclusio in eo est quod subiúgit, maior uero in his est charitas. Quare maior. Propterea quod nunquam, neq; in hac neque in futura uita excidit, quod de fide ac spe pdicari nō potest. Hunc puto conclusionis hu ius esse sensum, iudicent fratres.
units.tr: What stands in the Greek as remains [μένει] must be read in the plural and referred to these three things [τὰ τρία ταῦτα], that is, these three. The Greeks join singular verbs to neuter plural subjects in this way. It makes no real difference, however, if we read the singular manet, as Valla prefers. Paul closes this with a eulogy of love, ascribing to it that it does not fall away, as the spiritual gifts did, through whose zeal and eagerness the Corinthians were puffed up, but that it remains even in the future. Now, he says, that is, in this life; for he uses the word in no other sense than the one in which he used it a little earlier. He says, faith, hope, and love remain, these three. Why does he mention faith and hope, and say that they remain, and not rather repeat what he said about tongues, prophecy, and knowledge, concluding, "Now therefore tongues, prophecy, and knowledge will cease, but love remains"? In that case his conclusion would have fitted what he had said so far. In my judgment he concludes by anticipating an objection. He could already have been challenged: granted that tongues and prophecies and the other gifts cease and love remains, is love to be preferred for the reason that it does not fall away? Do not faith and hope remain too, just as love does? If love believes and hopes all things, then faith and hope remain with it. Answering this kind of thought, he first concedes that faith and hope remain together with love; then he attaches to this concession an explanation and a limitation of how far faith and hope remain with love. Finally, drawing his conclusion, he declares that love is more excellent than even faith and hope. So he says: Now faith, hope, and love remain, these three; but the greatest of these is love. It appears that it should be read in this way: Now indeed remains [Νυνὶ δὲ μένει], etc. For the adversative particle de [δέ] follows most aptly, and here it is not placed in its proper position. The concession lies in what he says: faith, hope, and love indeed remain. From this concession we can guess what they might have objected. The explanation lies in the word now, which is placed quite emphatically, as if he said: in this life faith and hope remain together with love, but in the future life they do not. The conclusion lies in what he adds: but the greatest of these is love. Why is it greatest? Because it never falls away, neither in this life nor in the future, which cannot be said of faith and hope. I think this is the sense of this conclusion; let the brethren judge.

units.la: NVNC quidem manent fides, spes, charitas.] Admonemur præsens hoc tempus, quo uiuimus in carne, ac peregrinamur à domino, tempus esse fidei, spei & dilectionis, idq; comʼ muniter omnibus. Hæc tria omnis habent pie tatis & ueræ iusticiæ fundamentum, non in Nouo tantum, sed & in Veteri testamento. Sine his mortui sunt & inanes uniuersi ritus, omnes cæremoniæ, omnia sacramenta, quæ in uʼ riationem dispensationis pro conditione sua cadere potuerunt, cum hæc ad finem usq; maneant eadem. Eadem inde ab initio fides est, eadem spes, eadem charitas, quemadmodum & idem est Deus, in quē creditur & sper..atur: & idem spiritus, per quem charitas in corda electorum funditur. Loquitur autem non de fide miraculorū, cuius capite præcedenti mētionem facit, sed de fide iustificante, quę utráque habet adiunctam & spem & charitatem, & unà prædicatur, sicut & spes, Eph. 4. fides miraculorum nec communis est electorū, nec manet ad finem usq;, nec comites habet spem & charitatem.
units.tr: NOW indeed faith, hope, and love remain. We are reminded that this present time, in which we live in the flesh and are away from the Lord, is a time of faith, hope, and love, and that these belong to all alike. All these three are the foundation of godliness and true righteousness, not only in the New Testament but also in the Old. Without them all rites, all ceremonies, and all sacraments, however they could be varied according to the condition of each dispensation, are dead and empty, since these three remain the same to the end. From the beginning faith has been the same, hope the same, and love the same, just as God is the same, in whom we believe and hope, and the same Spirit, through whom love is poured into the hearts of the elect. He speaks, however, not of the faith of miracles, which he mentioned in the preceding chapter, but of justifying faith, which has both hope and love joined to it, and is proclaimed together with them, as also hope is (Eph. 4). The faith of miracles is neither common to the elect, nor does it remain to the end, nor does it have hope and love as its companions.

units.la: De eo uero non est ut multis disputemus, an aliquid loci fidei ac spei futurū sit post hac uitam. Si consideretur utriusq; cum præsentis seculi tum futuri status, puto satis liquere, ubi quæ nunc credimus & speramus reipsa implebuntur, ibi nullam fore adhuc amplius credendi ac sperandi rationem. Agricola dum arat, in spe arat, spēq; sustentatur ad id usq; temporis quo triticum colligit in horreū suum, ubi non est amplius ratio, ut mensurum se sperct, quod iam reipsa habet in horreo. Consimili modo eueniet & nobis. Vbi eorum quæ iam credimus & speramus compotes euaserimus, cessabit omnis fidei ac spei ratio. Tum quę iam absentia sunt & futura, ideoque fide ac spe expectanda, præsentia nobis erunt, & reipsa coram uidebuntur ac posside buntur. Nec est ut incœlesti patria nouas futurarum adhuc rerum pro missiones fore putemus quæ ulteriore sint fide credendæ & spe expectandæ. Nam ibi omnia perfectionem suam sortietur nec reliquus erit mundus aliquis expectandus, in quem adhuc amplior humanæ felicitatis perfectio differatur.
units.tr: Now there is no need for us to dispute at length whether there will be any place for faith and hope after this life. If we consider the state of both the present and the future age, I think it is sufficiently clear that where the things we now believe and hope for are actually fulfilled, there will be no further ground for believing and hoping. A farmer ploughs in hope, and is sustained by that hope until the time when he gathers the wheat into his barn; there is no longer any reason for him to hope for a measure of grain that he already actually has in the barn. It will be similar for us. When we have come into possession of what we now believe and hope for, all ground for faith and hope will cease. Then the things that are now absent and future, and therefore to be awaited by faith and hope, will be present to us, and will be seen and possessed in reality before our eyes. Nor should we think that in the heavenly fatherland there will be new promises of things still to come, which must be believed by further faith and awaited by hope. For there all things will attain their perfection, and there will be no further world to be awaited, in which a fuller perfection of human happiness would be deferred.

units.la: SED maior, inquit, in his est charitas.] Nō confert charitatem ad fidem ac spem per numeros omnes, sed hactenus tātum, quod illis cessantibus ipsa duratura est in sempiternum. Sic Chrysó. quoq; exponit dicens: ... Hinc nō consequitur,
units.tr: But the greatest, he says, of these is love. He does not compare love with faith and hope in every respect, but only in this: that when they cease, love alone will last for ever. Chrysostom also explains it this way, saying: ... It does not follow from this

units.la: quod nonnulli inferre conantur, non solam fidem iustificare, cum sit minor charitate, sed charitati hoc magis competere, tanquam maiori ac digniori. Minor est fides quā charitas nō uirtute & effectu, sed conditione, qua termina tur in hoc seculo. Quod iustificationem attinet, de illa nobis sentiendum est ac loquendū secundum scripturas, quæ fide nos, non charitate iustificari docet. Sed hac de re in Locis no stris uideri poterit.
units.tr: what some try to infer, that faith alone does not justify, since it is less than love, but that this belongs more to love, as to the greater and more worthy. Faith is less than love not in power and effect, but in its condition, by which it is limited to this age. As for justification, we must think and speak of it according to the Scriptures, which teach that we are justified by faith and not by love. But this matter may be seen in our Loci.

units.la: CAPVT XIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 14.

units.la: Ectemini charitatem, æmulemini spiritualia, magis tamen ut prophetetis.
units.tr: Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy.

units.la: Abusum linguarum redarguit hoc capite, simulq; uerum illarū usum docet, iuxta tamen præfert illi prophetiæ utilitatem, & ad huius studium hortatur, ac rectum prophetandi ordinem præscribit. Adiungit in calce de mulieribus, competere illis ut non doceāt, sed sileant in ecclesia, & huic suæ doctrinæ uindicat authoritatē diuini præcepti. Hæc fere summa est eorum quę toto hoc capite tractantur.
units.tr: In this chapter he rebukes the misuse of tongues, and at the same time teaches their proper use. He nonetheless places the usefulness of prophecy above them and urges the pursuit of it, and he prescribes the proper order for prophesying. At the end he adds that it is fitting for women not to teach but to be silent in the Church, and he supports this teaching by the authority of a divine command. This is more or less the sum of what is treated throughout the chapter.

units.la: SECTEMINI charitatem, inquit.] Ordi tur ab exhortatione, & simul transit, imò redit à præcedenti charitatis præconio ad charisma linguarum & prophetię disponenda. Quod dicit: Sectemini charitatem, & præcedentibus seruit, & sequentibus. Dixit, maior autē in his est charitas. Subiungit: Sectemini charitatem. Ad hoc enim elogia charitatis recensuit, illáq; omnibus charismatis prætulit, ut studiosius sectandam ac colendam esse admoneret.
units.tr: "Follow after charity," he says. He begins with an exhortation, and at the same time he passes over, or rather returns, from his previous praise of charity to the arrangement of the gift of tongues and of prophecy. The words "Follow after charity" serve both what precedes and what follows. He said "but the greatest of these is charity." He then adds, "Follow after charity." For he had recounted the praises of charity for this very purpose, and had placed it above all the gifts, so that he might warn them to pursue and cultivate it more eagerly.

units.la: Hoc sine laudantur & extolluntur uirtutes, ut cupidius illas amplectamur, eas præcipue, quæ cæteris præferuntur: quemadmodum au rū nobis in maiori est precio, propterea quod cæteris est metallis, argento quoq;, præstantius. Vtinam eo nobis loco esset charitas, quo est aurum.
units.tr: In this way virtues are praised and extolled, so that we may embrace them more eagerly, especially those that are preferred to the others. Just as gold is held in greater value by us because it is more precious than the other metals, and silver too. Would that charity had among us the place that gold has.

units.la: Deinde, haud inconsulto particula hæc: Sectemini chatitatem, præfixa est illis quæ præsenti sunt capite tractanda. Ad hanc enim collimantur omnia quæ de studio prophetandi præscribuntur, quatenus illa ædificat: hoc est, omnia dirigit ad ædificationem ecclesiæ. Varia quidem sunt studia & opera charitatis, uerum hoc omnium est potissimum, quod mentes fidelium ad ueram pietatem ac salutem stu diosissime ædificat. Quare de illo tam diligenter tamque multis agitur hoc capite, sicuti uidebimus.
units.tr: Next, this particle, "Follow after charity," has been placed before the matters to be treated in the present chapter, and not without reason. For everything that is prescribed about the pursuit of prophecy is aimed at this, insofar as prophecy builds up, that is, everything is directed to the building up of the Church. There are indeed various pursuits and works of charity, but this is the chief of all, that it most diligently builds up the minds of the faithful to true piety and salvation. Therefore this chapter treats of it so carefully and at such length, as we shall see.

units.la: Obseruandum autem est, quod non simpliciter dicit, Diligite, uel habete charitatem: sed ..., id est, Persequimini charitatē. Sunt autem duo persequutionis fines. Nā alia persequimur uel ira uel odio ad perdendum. Hinc expellere, fugare, & insectari signi ficat. Sic ad Paulū dicebat Christus: ... τὰ μὲν ἀνώτεροι: Alia uero persequimur amore uel ad fruendum uel ad feruandum. Et hinc est, quod διώκειν aliquoties accipitur pro cupide expetere & affectare. Sic Rom.14.dicit: τὰ δὲ ἀ- φῶν διώκωμεν. Et 1.Theff.5. διώκετε τὸ ἀγαθὸν διώκειν. Et hoc loco, διώκετε τὴν ἀγάπην. Hortatur ergo non simpliciter ad charitatem, sed ad ardens illius assequendæ & colendæ studium, quo pij faciunt ac ferunt omnia, quæ charitatis esse & ad illam fouendam retinendamq; inter fratres facere uidentur. Qui quod cupit persequitur, reliĉtis cæteris rebus totus in eo assequendo occupatur, quod persequitur. Verum nos charitatem corruptissimo hoc nostro seculo prioris modo persequimur, ad extinguendum uidelicet non ad retinendum & colendum. Quid enim aliud est odium illud intestinum, quod inter ecclesias & ecclesiæ ministros prorsus in reconciliabile obtinuit, quid aliud tam acerbæ fratrum insectationes, dilacerationes, contumicia, contentiones, proscriptiones, & carnificinæ, quàm grauissima quædam extinguendæ charitatis perfequutio: qua prorsus ex omniū cordibus fugatur, ex ecclesia eliminatur & extinguitur, atq; ita impletur: quod Christus futurum esse dixit, ut refrigescat charitas multorum. Matthæi 24.
units.tr: It must also be noted that he does not simply say "love" or "have charity," but "pursue charity" (διώκετε τὴν ἀγάπην), that is, press after it. Now there are two ends of pursuing. For we pursue some things out of anger or hatred, in order to destroy them. From this the word means to drive out, put to flight, and hunt down. Thus Christ said to Paul: [...]. But we pursue other things out of love, either to enjoy them or to keep them. And from this it is that διώκειν is sometimes taken for to desire eagerly and to aim at. Thus Romans 14 says: "let us pursue the things that build up one another" [τὰ δὲ ἀλλήλων διώκωμεν]. And 1 Thessalonians 5: "follow after that which is good" [διώκετε τὸ ἀγαθὸν]. And in this place, "pursue charity" [διώκετε τὴν ἀγάπην]. He therefore urges not merely charity but an ardent zeal for attaining and cultivating it, by which the godly do and endure all things that seem to belong to charity and to be done to foster and keep it among the brothers. He who pursues what he desires, leaving other things aside, is wholly occupied in attaining what he pursues. But we, in this most corrupt age of ours, pursue charity in the first manner, namely to destroy it, not to keep and cultivate it. For what else is that internal hatred which has taken hold between the churches and the ministers of the Church, a hatred that cannot be reconciled, what else are those so bitter attacks, tearings apart, rebellions, quarrels, proscriptions and butcheries among brothers, than a most grievous persecution aimed at extinguishing charity? By it charity is utterly driven from the hearts of all, eliminated from the Church and snuffed out, and so there is fulfilled what Christ said would come to pass, that the charity of many would grow cold (Matthew 24).

units.la: SECTEMINI charitatem, inquit.] Persequantur impij charitatem ad extinguendum, quantum illis permittitur: nos persequamur eam ad colendum. Debet autem hoc à nobis fieri bifariam.
units.tr: "Follow after charity," he says. Let the impious pursue charity in order to extinguish it, as far as is permitted them; let us pursue it in order to cultivate it. This ought to be done by us in two ways.

units.la: Primum, diligendo fratres, & ea quæ charitatis sunt in illos exercendo. Charitatis autem sunt omnis generis beneficia, tam spiritualia quàm corporalia. Hæc exercentes, charitatis affectum in cordibus nostris alimus, prouehimus, magisq; ac magis confirmamus.
units.tr: First, by loving the brothers and exercising toward them the things that belong to charity. Now the things that belong to charity are benefits of every kind, spiritual as well as bodily. By practising these, we nourish the affection of charity in our hearts, advance it, and confirm it more and more.

units.la: Deinde sic agere cum fratribus, ut prouocemus eos ad mutuam dilectionem, charitatemque in cordibus ipsorum accendamus, quo impleatur in nobis præceptum illud Christi: quo mandat, ut nos inuicem diligamus. Hoc est omnino dilectionis ingenium, ut qui diligit, uicissim diligi cupiat. Quare utroq; modo persequenda nobis est charitas, cùm ut fyncere diligamus fratres, tum ut ad mutuam illos dilectionem pro uiribus alliciamus.
units.tr: Second, we should so act with the brothers that we provoke them to mutual love and kindle charity in their hearts, so that the precept of Christ by which he commands us to love one another may be fulfilled in us. This is altogether the nature of love: whoever loves desires in turn to be loved. Therefore charity must be pursued by us in both ways, both that we love the brothers sincerely and that we draw them, as far as our strength allows, to mutual love.

units.la: AEMVLEMINI spiritualia, inquit.] Per spiritualia intelligit charismata spiritus, quorū capite duodecimo mentionem fecit. Horum zelo, studio & admiratione erant Corinthij usque adeo accensi, ut illorum gratia charitatem negligerent, imò cótra illam haud modice peccarent. Hoc in illis correcturus, cum dixisset: Sectamini charitatem, ne uideretur eos à zelo charismatum prorsus auocare, per concessionem subijcit, ζηλοῦτε, spiritualia. Qua fi dicat: Non prohibeo studium spiritualium charismatum, dum ad charitatem persequendam exhortor: absit, agnosco enim illa esse dona spiritus, & fi recte utamini uehementer utilia, quare æmulemini illa.
units.tr: "Desire spiritual gifts," he says. By spiritual things he means the gifts of the Spirit, of which he made mention in chapter twelve. The Corinthians were so inflamed with zeal, admiration and eagerness for these that they neglected charity for their sake, and indeed sinned not a little against it. Wishing to correct this in them, after saying "Follow after charity," lest he seem to draw them away altogether from zeal for the gifts, he adds by way of concession, "desire spiritual gifts" (ζηλοῦτε τὰ πνευματικά). As if he said: I do not forbid the pursuit of spiritual gifts while I exhort you to pursue charity; far be it, for I acknowledge them to be gifts of the Spirit, and very useful if used rightly; therefore desire them.

units.la: MAGIS tamen, inquit, ut prophetetis.] In Græco sic est, ζηλοῦτε δὲ τὰ πνευματικά, μᾶλλον δὲ ἵνα προφητεύητε. Hoc est, æmulamini autem spiritualia, magis autem ut prophetetis. Suspicor uoculam δὲ sic esse bis politam, ut prior fit idem quod ζηλοῦτε, posterior uero sensum suum retineat, legendumq; fit ad hunc modum: Æmulemini quidem spiritualia, magis uero ut prophetetis. Sic correctione subijcit concessioni. Requirit discretionem in æmulatione donorum Dei, propterea quod alia alijs sunt potiora, ideoq; maiori studio æmulanda. Quare uero prophetiam præferat alijs, infrà luculenter declarabit, ut non fit hic de ratione illius querendum.
units.tr: "But rather," he says, "that you may prophesy." In the Greek it is: ζηλοῦτε δὲ τὰ πνευματικά, μᾶλλον δὲ ἵνα προφητεύητε, that is, "desire spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy." I suspect that the little word δὲ has been placed twice in this way, so that the first has the same force as ζηλοῦτε, while the second keeps its own sense, and the sentence should be read thus: "Indeed desire spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy." Thus by way of correction he adds to the concession. He requires discernment in the zeal for God's gifts, because some are more excellent than others and so are to be desired with greater eagerness. Why he prefers prophecy to the others he will explain clearly below, so there is no need to inquire into the reason here.

units.la: De quo genere prophetiæ autem loquatur, cum monet Corinthios, ut singulari studio ad prophetandum ferantur, & ipsum in sequentibus patebit. προφητεύειν significat aliquando prædicere futura, nonnunquam quæuis occulta & abstrusa proloqui. Nam præpositio προ non semper ante, sed & pro significat, ut προάγειν, id est, pruducere, προβαίνειν, progredi, & innumera alia. Proloqui aút est, ut inquit Varro, quod in animo habemus loquendo proferre. Sic pro phetæ sunt interpretes diuinæ erga nos uoluntatis, fiue scripturas sacras interpretentur, fiue ex instinctu spiritus oracula Dei proferant, ac de futuris prænuncient. Quare ubicunq; uerbum prophetandi occurrit, etiam atq; etiam uidendum est, in qua materia usurpetur, ne à pro popofito dicentis aberretur.
units.tr: As to what kind of prophecy he is speaking of, when he urges the Corinthians to be carried on with a special eagerness toward prophesying, this too will become clear in what follows. The verb προφητεύειν sometimes means to foretell future things, and sometimes to utter any hidden and obscure matters. For the preposition προ does not always mean before, but also for, as in προάγειν, that is, to bring forth, προβαίνειν, to go forward, and countless others. To "proloqui," as Varro says, is to bring forth by speaking what we have in mind. Thus prophets are interpreters of the divine will toward us, whether they expound the holy Scriptures or, moved by the impulse of the Spirit, utter God's oracles and foretell future things. Therefore wherever the word for prophesying occurs, one must look again and again at what matter it is used in, lest one wander from the purpose of the speaker.

units.la: Et hic uehementer stupeo, quo nam spiritu ferantur, qui fe pro apostolis & orthodoxis uéditantes, sic Christi administrant ecclesias, imò ut uerius dicam, sic Christi dominantur ecclesijs, ut maximam partem zelo tribuant, non charismatum spiritus, sed ritu̅ acfacrorum humanitus excogitatorum: minimam uero prophetiæ, quam Apostolus charismatis spiritus sic præponit, ut potiffimam illi æmulationem deputet. Vnam missam præferunt omnib. prophetijs, cum unius horæ prophetia, germana ac legitima, omnibus fit missis ad ædificationem ecclesiæ utilior. Illi dicunt: Æmulemini spiritualia, magis tamen, ut missas uel celebretis uel audiatis. Apostolus uero longe aliter ec clefiæ præscribens, & non quæstum, sed ædificationem fidelium quærens: Æmulemini, inquit, spiritualia, magis tamen ut prophetetis.
units.tr: Here I am greatly astonished by what spirit those people are driven who, posing as apostles and orthodox, so administer Christ's churches, or rather, to speak more truly, so lord it over the churches of Christ, that they assign the greatest part of their zeal not to the spiritual gifts but to rites and sacred things devised by human invention, and the smallest part to prophecy, which the Apostle places before the gifts of the Spirit in such a way that he assigns to it the chief emulation. They prefer one Mass to all prophecies, whereas a single hour of genuine and lawful prophecy is more useful for the building up of the Church than all Masses. They say: "Desire spiritual gifts, but rather that you may celebrate or hear Masses." But the Apostle, prescribing quite differently for the Church, and seeking not gain but the building up of the faithful, says: "Desire spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy."

units.la: Nam qui loquitur lingua, non hominib. loquitur, sed Deo. nullus enim audit, spiritu uero loquitur mysteria. Cæterum qui prophetat, hominib. loquitur ædificationem, & exhortationem, & consolationem. Qui loquitur lingua, fe ipsum ædificat: at qui prophetat, ecclesiam ædificat. Volo autem omnes uos loqui linguis, magis tamen ut prophetetis. Maior em est qui prophetat, quàm qui loquitur linguis, nisi interpretetur, ut ecclesia ædificationem accipiat.
units.tr: For he who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men but to God; for no one understands him, but in the Spirit he speaks mysteries. But he who prophesies speaks to men, for building up, exhortation and consolation. He who speaks in a tongue builds up himself; but he who prophesies builds up the Church. "I would that you all spoke with tongues, but rather that you prophesied. For greater is he who prophesies than he who speaks with tongues, unless he interprets, so that the Church may receive building up."

units.la: Tanta debebat esse Apostoli authoritas, ut sufficeret dixisse, Æmulamini spiritualia, magis tamen ut prophetetis: uerum quoniam erant adhuc rudes Corinthij, adijcit sententiæ suæ declarandæ & confirmandæ certas & per spicuas rationes, unde intelligant quare potior sit prophetia, maiorique studio æmulanda. Nam, inquit, qui loquitur lingua, non hominibus loquitur, sed Deo. Dixerat in genere, æmulamini spiritualia, magis tamen ut prophetetis. Quare subijciendum uidetur: Nam qui æmulatur spiritualia, declarandumq; quomodo ille minoris momenti rem agat, quam si prophetiæ sit intentus: uerum quoniam propter studium ac zelum linguarum, quibus deditus erat Corinthij, spiritualia charismata in genere posuerat, mox mentem suam exprimit dicens: Nā qui loquitur lingua, ac simul declarat, quatenus ille inferior sit eo qui prophetat. Qua in re perinde facit, ac si quis hodie reprehensurus in papistis, quod certis diebus abstinent à carne, & non abstinent à peccatis, dicat: Ne æmulemini traditiones humanas, sed magis præcepta diuina. Nam qui à carne abstinet, hominibus seruit non Deo: qui uero præcepta diuina custodit, Deum veneratur & colit.
units.tr: Apostolic authority ought to have been so great that it was enough for him to say, "Be zealous for spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy." But since the Corinthians were still unskilled, he adds clear and evident reasons to explain and confirm his opinion, so that they may understand why prophecy is the greater gift and ought to be desired with greater eagerness. For, he says, "he who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men, but to God." He had said in general, "Be zealous for spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy." So it seems that the following should be added: "For he who is zealous for spiritual gifts..." and it needs to be shown how that person acts in a matter of lesser importance than if he were intent on prophecy. But since the Corinthians, through their zeal and eagerness for tongues, to which they were devoted, had put "spiritual gifts" in general terms, he now states his own meaning, saying: "For he who speaks in a tongue," and at the same time shows how far he is inferior to the one who prophesies. In this matter he acts just as if someone today, wishing to rebuke the Papists because on certain days they abstain from meat but do not abstain from sins, were to say: "Do not be zealous for human traditions, but rather for divine precepts. For he who abstains from meat serves men, not God; but he who keeps the divine precepts worships and honours God."

units.la: Confert autem utrunq; inter se & linguis loquentem & prophetantem, ac declarat, quo modo utilior sit qui prophetat quàm qui loquitur linguis. Nam, inquit, qui loquitur lingua. Quid est quod discernit lingua loquetem ab eo qui prophetat? An non & ille loquitur lingua? Quis enim sic loquitur ut non lingua loquatur?
units.tr: Paul then compares the two, the one speaking in tongues and the one prophesying, and shows in what way he who prophesies is more useful than he who speaks in tongues. "For," he says, "he who speaks in a tongue..." What is it that distinguishes the one speaking in a tongue from the one who prophesies? Does not the prophet also speak in a tongue? For who speaks in such a way that he does not speak in a language?

units.la: Lingua loqui, hoc loco, est ex dono linguarum alio atque alio idiomate uulgo incognito loqui. Quoniam charisma hoc ab eo tempore quo primum collatū fuit apostolis in die Pentecostes, sequens & usitatum erat in ecclesia, obtinuit consuetudo, ut linguis loqui diceren tur, qui alio atque alio peregrino idiomate ex dono linguarum in cœtu fidelium loquebantur. Hanc puto Paulinæ huius loquutionis esse rationem, qua lingua loqui pro eo ponitur quod est peregrino idiomate ex charismate linguarum loqui.
units.tr: To speak in a tongue, in this place, means to speak, by the gift of tongues, in another and different language that is unknown to the common people. Since this gift, from the time it was first bestowed on the apostles on the day of Pentecost, was both a sequel to that event and a common practice in the Church, custom prevailed that those were said to speak in tongues who, by the gift of tongues, spoke in the assembly of the faithful in some foreign language or other. I think this is the reason for Paul's way of speaking here, in which "to speak in a tongue" is used for speaking in a foreign language by the gift of tongues.

units.la: NON hominib. inquit, loquitur, sed Deo. Hæc est ratio propter quam loqui lingua minoris erat faciendum quàm prophetare, quod loquens lingua, Deo non hominib. prophetans uero hominibus loquitur.
units.tr: "He does not speak," he says, "to men, but to God." This is the reason why speaking in a tongue was to be valued less than prophesying: the one speaking in a tongue speaks to God, not to men, whereas the prophet speaks to men.

units.la: Sed dicet quisquam: Ergo ne pluris est loqui hominibus quam Deo? An nō dignior est homine Deus? Respondeo. Vtiq; dignior. At hoc magis convenit ut donis ipsius legitime, pro voluntate ipsius, & ad finem debitum utamur. Charisma linguarum ad Euangelij doctrinam in orbe inter uariarum linguarum Gentes propagandam dedit. Hæc erat illius ratio, hic scopus, hic usus & finis. Ergo abusus est sic loqui linguis, ut loquaris non hominibus, sed Deo, cui nihil refert qua lingua loquaris. Dedit nobis panem, uinum, uestitum, & omnia ad uitæ huius necessitatem pertinentia. Hæc autem non ideo dedit, ut inde quid à nobis accipiat, sed ut ad nostros illa & proximorum usus usurpemus. Quemadmodum igitur peruersa est eorum religio, qui dona huiusmodi Deo uel mortuis sanctis, quibus nullo sunt usui offerunt, & interea fratrum necessitates neglígunt, quibus succurrere debeant: ita & Corinthiorum peruersa erat religio, imo inanis ostentatio, qua linguis peregrinis sic utebantur in ecclesia, ut non hominibus, quibus erat destinatæ, sed Deo loquerentur, à quo nullo pacto requirebantur.
units.tr: But someone may say: "Then is it not more valuable to speak to men than to God? Is not God more worthy than man?" I reply: Certainly he is more worthy. But it is more fitting that we use his gifts lawfully, according to his will, and for their proper end. The gift of tongues was given for spreading the doctrine of the gospel in the world among the nations of various languages. This was its purpose, this its aim, this its use and end. Therefore it is an abuse to speak in tongues in such a way that you speak not to men but to God, to whom it makes no difference in what language you speak. He has given us bread, wine, clothing, and everything pertaining to the necessity of this life. Yet he did not give these so that he might receive anything from us in return, but so that we might use them for our own needs and those of our neighbours. Just as the religion of those is perverse who offer gifts of this kind to God or to dead saints, to whom they are of no use, while they neglect the needs of their brothers, whom they ought to help, so also the religion of the Corinthians was perverse, or rather an empty display, since they used foreign tongues in the Church in such a way that they spoke not to the men for whom they were intended, but to God, from whom in no way were they required.

units.la: NVLLVS enim audit, inquit.] Exponit utrunque quod dixit, non hominibus loquitur, sed Deo. Quomodo non loquitur hominibus, qui palam loquitur, aut orat, aut canit in ecclesia? Quoniam sic loquitur, inquit, ut nullus audiat. Hoc est, audiendo intelligat. Hoc enim demum uere est audire, audita intelligere. Audiebantur quidem linguis loquentium uoces, sed non intelligebatur. Et præterea sic animalis sum, ut ad sermones incognitę linguę haud auscultemus. Vt quid enim frustra auscultemus ad ea quæ intelligere non possumus? maxime in sermone, cuius usus sine intellectu, prius est inanis? Ergo non loquitur hominibus, qui sic loquitur, ut nullus audiat.
units.tr: "For no one hears," he says. He explains both parts of what he said: "he does not speak to men, but to God." How does he not speak to men, when he speaks openly, or prays, or sings in the Church? Because, he says, he so speaks that no one hears him, that is, understands by hearing. For this is truly to hear: to understand what is heard. Indeed the voices of those speaking in tongues were heard, but they were not understood. Moreover, we are so constituted by nature that we do not attend to speech in an unknown language. For why should we listen in vain to what we cannot understand, especially in speech whose use is empty without understanding? Therefore he does not speak to men who speaks in such a way that no one hears him.

units.la: Obserua tamen hic, quod non dicit, non enim omnes audiunt: sed, nullus enim audit. Potest fieri, ut Germanice inter Germanos sic loquaris, ut non audiaris ab omnibus, propter dialectorum uarietatem: utpote, si inferioris Germaniæ idiomate ad superioris populos loquaris. Hic etsi non ab omnibus, à plerisq; tamen audiri potes, ut haud omnino frustra loquaris. Verum si quis lingua prorsus aliena & populariter incognita loquatur in ecclesia, is quoniam audiri potest à nemine, non loquitur hominibus, sed Deo. Tale est, quod in ecclesijs Germanicis omnia Latino sermone loquuntur & canunt, qui sic alienus est à Germanico, ut nihil illius à Germanis tanquam Germanis possit intelligi. Et hoc faciunt homines Germani, & Germanice scientes melius quàm Latine. Verum hoc est Romanæ ecclesiæ institutum, quo Satan ex diametro doctrinæ huic Apostolicæ aduersari, & ecclesiarum Christi ædificationem impedire voluit.
units.tr: Notice here, however, that he does not say "not all hear," but "no one hears." It can happen that you speak German among Germans in such a way that you are not heard by all, because of the variety of dialects: for example, if you speak in the dialect of Lower Germany to people of Upper Germany. Here, although not by all, you can still be heard by most, so that your speaking is not altogether in vain. But if someone speaks in a language utterly foreign and unknown to the people in the Church, since he cannot be heard by anyone, he does not speak to men but to God. Such is the practice in German Churches where everything is sung and spoken in Latin, a language so foreign to German that none of it can be understood by Germans as Germans. And German men do this, though they know German better than Latin. But this is the custom of the Roman Church, by which Satan wished to oppose this apostolic doctrine directly and to hinder the building up of the Churches of Christ.

units.la: Deinde in eo quod Apostolus uerbo audiē di sic utitur, ut neget audiri quæ nō intelligun tur, habent quod obseruent auditores Papistarum missarum, qui subijpsi nescio quid salutis ex eo pollicentur, si quotidie unam saltem missam audiant, quam tamen intelligere non possunt. Hos Apostolus audire negat. Dicunt: Audiuimus missam. Si credendum est Apostolo, non audiunt quod nō intelligunt, & quod studio & instituto Apostolicæ ecclesiæ sic dicitur, ut uulgo intelligi nequeat. Non enim loquuntur hominibus, sed Deo.
units.tr: Further, in that the Apostle uses the word "hear" in such a way as to deny that things not understood are heard, the hearers of the Papists' masses have something to consider. They promise themselves I know not what salvation from them if they hear at least one mass every day, though they cannot understand it. The Apostle denies that such people hear. They say, "We have heard Mass." If we must believe the Apostle, they do not hear what they do not understand, and what is said, by the purpose and custom of the apostolic Church, in such a way that it cannot be understood by the common people. For they do not speak to men, but to God.

units.la: SPIRITV uero loquitur mysteria, inquit.] Exponit, quomodo Deo loquatur, qui lingua loqui-
units.tr: "But he who speaks in the Spirit," he says, "speaks mysteries." He explains how the one who speaks in a tongue speaks to God.

units.la: quitur. Trifariā fieri potest, ut Deo ꝗs loquatur.
units.tr: There are three ways in which someone can speak to God.

units.la: Primo, quando pro Deo, & ea quę Deū concernunt loquitur. Sic Deo loquitur, quemadmodum legatus suo regi. Hoc sensu nō loquun tur Deo, qui nec misi sunt à Deo, nec hoc agunt, ut illi loquendo seruiant.
units.tr: First, when he speaks on behalf of God and about those things that concern God. In this way he speaks to God as an envoy speaks to his king. In this sense those do not speak to God who have not been sent by God, nor do they act so as to serve him by speaking.

units.la: Deinde, quando ad Deum loquitur, sicuti solemus orantes & gratias agentes.
units.tr: Second, when he speaks to God, as we are accustomed to do when praying and giving thanks.

units.la: Tertio, quando sic loquitur ut non ab homi nibus, sed à Deo tantum intelligatur. Etiamsi non hoc intendat, ut Deo loquatur, hactenus tamen Deo loquitur, quatenus ab illo solo intelligitur. Perinde est ac si quis Ebraicē uel Græcē uel Latinē loquatur in cœtu fidelium, in quo unus tantum sit, qui intelligat. Huic ille loqui recte dicetur, etiamsi nesciat talem aliquem esse in concione. Huc pertinet & illud loquutionis genus, quo tacite submurmura mus, quæ ab alijs audiri nolumus. Sic loquentes nobisipsis & Deo loqui dicimur. Hoc sensu infrà dicit: Siue lingua quis loquitur fiat per binos, aut ad summum ternos, idq; uicissim, & unus interpretetur. Quod si non sit interpres, taceat in ecclesia, loquatur uero sibijpsi & Deo. Et hoc posteriore sensu dictum appareat hoc loco, quod qui lingua loquitur, Deo loquitur non hominibus. Hoc est, sic loquatur, ut non homines, sed Deus tantum intelligat. Sic exponit etiam Ambrosius. Et hoc uidetur exponere cum dicit: Spiritu uero loquitur mysteria. Hoc est, loquitur illis qui non intelligūt non manifesta & intelligibilia, sed mysteria, ab scondita uidelicet & abstrusa, soli Deo cognita. Mysteria uocare solemus, quæ non intelligi mus. Quod nos attinet, mysteria loquitur, qui idiomate nobis incognito loquitur, etiāsi res ipsę de quibus loquitur, satis in se sint intelligi biles, si uerbis intelligibilibus exprimerentur. Sic puto intelligendum esse simpliciter quod dicit: Spiritu uero loquitur mysteria.
units.tr: Third, when he speaks in such a way that he is understood not by men but by God alone. Even if he does not intend to speak to God, he nonetheless speaks to God insofar as he is understood by him alone. It is just as if someone were to speak in Hebrew or Greek or Latin in an assembly of the faithful in which only one person understood him. To that one it would rightly be said that he speaks, even if the speaker did not know that such a person was in the gathering. To this belongs also that kind of speech by which we mutter quietly what we do not want others to hear. Such speakers are said to speak to themselves and to God. In this sense Paul says below: "If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be by two, or at most three, and each in turn, and let one interpret. But if there is no interpreter, let him keep silent in the Church, and let him speak to himself and to God." And it appears that this later sense is what is meant in this place, that he who speaks in a tongue speaks to God, not to men. That is, he speaks in such a way that not men but God alone understands him. Ambrose also explains it this way, and this seems to be what he means when he says: "But he speaks mysteries in the Spirit." That is, he speaks to those who do not understand things that are not plain and intelligible, but mysteries, that is, hidden and obscure things known to God alone. We are accustomed to call mysteries those things which we do not understand. As far as we are concerned, he speaks mysteries who speaks in a language unknown to us, even though the matters about which he speaks might be sufficiently intelligible in themselves, if they were expressed in intelligible words. This, I think, is how we should simply understand what he says: "But he speaks mysteries in the Spirit."

units.la: Exponitur autem hæc particula aliter atq; aliter. Nam dictio spiritus sic indeterminate & obscure posita est, ut non liqueat certo quò sit referenda. Ponitur illa quinquies in hac materia. Hic dicit eū qui lingua loquitur, spiritu loqui mysteria. Et infrà: Nam si orē lingua, inqt, spiritus meus orat, at mens mea fructu uacat. Item: Orabo spiritu, orabo aūt & mente. Canam spiritu, sed canam & mente. Alioqui si benedixeris spiritu, is qui implet locum indocti, quomodo dicturus est amen ad tuam gratiarū actionem, quando quidem quid dicas nescit?
units.tr: This particle is explained in different ways. The word spiritus is placed so vaguely and obscurely that it is not clear to which thing it refers. It occurs five times in this context. Here he says that the one who speaks in a tongue speaks mysteries in the Spirit. And below: "For if I pray in a tongue," he says, "my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful." Likewise: "I will pray with the spirit, but I will also pray with the mind. I will sing with the spirit, but I will also sing with the mind. Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, how will he who fills the place of the unlearned say Amen to your thanksgiving, since he does not know what you are saying?"

units.la: 1 Per spiritum alij intelligunt ipsum charis ma linguarum, quod per spiritum dabatur credentibus. Sic Chrysostomus exponit: τὸ χάρισμα τὸ διδόμενον, καὶ κινοῦ τῶν γλωσσῶν. Et Ambrosius infrà exponit de spiritu qui datur in baptismo. Lyranus quoq;: Spiritu sanctus, inquit, loquitur mysteria, id est, sensus latentes per donum pro phetię reuelando, & ideo tale donum sequitur ædificatio ecclesię. Ideo subditur: Nam qui prophetat, &c. Hic particulam istam: Spiritu uero loquitur mysteria, auellit à præcedenti,
units.tr: 1. Some understand by "spirit" the gift of tongues itself, which was given through the Spirit to believers. So Chrysostom explains it: "the gift that is given and moves the tongues" [τὸ χάρισμα τὸ διδόμενον, καὶ κινοῦν τῶν γλωσσῶν]. Ambrose too, below, explains it of the Spirit who is given in baptism. Lyra likewise says: "The Holy Spirit speaks mysteries," that is, hidden meanings, by revealing them through the gift of prophecy; and therefore the building up of the Church follows such a gift. Hence it is added: "For he who prophesies, etc." Here they detach this phrase, "but in the Spirit he speaks mysteries," from what precedes,

units.la: & refert ad sequentem, intelligens de spiritu non lingua tantum loquete, sed & prophetan te. Motus uidetur uulgata lectione, quæ sic habet: Spiritus autem loquitur mysteria. Nam qui prophetat, hominibus loquitur ad ædifica tionem. Sentit mysteria loqui spiritum idē esse quod mysteria prophetando reuelare. Verum quoniam hæc lectio cum Græco textu nō con uenit, neq; hanc illius expositionem amplecti possumus.
units.tr: and refer it to what follows, understanding by "spirit" not only the one who speaks in a tongue but also the one who prophesies. They seem to be moved by the Vulgate reading, which runs: "But the Spirit speaks mysteries. For he who prophesies speaks to men for edification." They take it that the Spirit speaking mysteries means the same as revealing mysteries by prophesying. But since this reading does not agree with the Greek text, we cannot embrace this explanation either.

units.la: 2 Deinde, dictionem Spiritus exponunt alij & hic & infrà de halitu, flatu, ac sonitu uocis.
units.tr: 2. Next, others explain the word "spirit," both here and below, as breath, blast, and the sound of the voice.

units.la: 3 Tertio, sunt quibus spiritu loqui idem est quod in seipso loqui.
units.tr: 3. Third, there are those for whom to speak in the Spirit is the same as to speak within oneself.

units.la: 4 Quarto, nonnulli accipiunt uocem spiritus pro affectu.
units.tr: 4. Fourth, some take the word "spirit" to mean an affection.

units.la: 5 Quinto, placet quibusdam, ut quoniam in datiuo est πνεύματι, exponatur de Deo, qui spiritus est, ut idem sit cum eo quod dixit: non ho minibus loquitur, sed Deo. Verum non uideo, quomodo hęc expositio stare possit in sequen tibus.
units.tr: 5. Fifth, some are pleased to explain it of God, who is Spirit, since the Greek is in the dative (πνεύματι), so that it means the same as what he said: "he speaks not to men but to God." But I do not see how this explanation can stand in what follows.

units.la: In tanta uarietate quid sequendum putem, paucis commemorabo. Quoniam quemadmo dum tota hac disputatione inter linguam & prophetiam, ita & inter spiritum & mentem di scernit: puto conueniens esse, ut spiritu loqui, spiritu orare, spiritu canere, & spiritu gratias agere, idem esse sentiamus quod lingua loqui, lingua orare, canere & gratias agere. Etenim eodem sensu dicere potuisset: Lingua uero loquitur mysteria. Et: Nam si orem lingua, lingua mea orat, at mens mea fructu uacat. Orabo lin gua, orabo autem & mente. Canam lingua, sed canam & mete. Alioqui si benedixeris lingua, is qui implet locum indocti, quomodo dictu rus est amen ad tuam gratiarumactione, quan doquidem quid dicas nescit? Hieron. dicit: Ite rum linguam significat. Sed dices: Quomodo spiritus pro lingua potest accipi? Respondeo. Quemadmodum charisma illud linguarum, lingua ab Apostolo uocatur: ita hic afflatus il le numinis, unde plerique fideles alijs atque a lijs linguis loquebantur, recte spiritus uoca tur. Sic in scripturis sæpenumero uox רוּחַ, & πνεῦμα, & spiritus, pro afflatu numinis ponitur. Nec impedit hunc sensum, quod Apostolus di cit: Nam si orem lingua, spiritus meus orat. Vo cat afflatum hunc numinis suum spiritū, quod esset sibi datus à Deo. Quod si quis contendat uocem spiritus omnino accipiendam esse de spiritu hominis, de quo alibi dicit: Cui seruio in spiritu meo, existimo tamen ne sic quidem excludendum esse in hac causa afflatum numi nis, ut spiritus linguis loquens, linguis orās, ca nens, & gratias agens, sit spiritus hominis affla tu numinis ad hoc percitus, ut alienis linguis loquatur. Etenim unde alias esset spiritui ho minis facultas linguarū quas nūquā didicisset?
units.tr: Amid so great a variety, I will briefly state what I think should be followed. Since, just as throughout this whole discussion Paul distinguishes between tongue and prophecy, so too he distinguishes between spirit and mind, I think it fitting that we take to speak in the Spirit, to pray in the Spirit, to sing in the Spirit, and to give thanks in the Spirit to mean the same as to speak in a tongue, to pray in a tongue, to sing and to give thanks in a tongue. For in the same sense he could have said: "But in a tongue he speaks mysteries." And: "For if I pray in a tongue, my tongue prays, but my mind is unfruitful. I will pray in a tongue, but I will also pray with the mind. I will sing in a tongue, but I will also sing with the mind. Otherwise, if you bless in a tongue, how will he who fills the place of the unlearned say Amen to your thanksgiving, since he does not know what you are saying?" Jerome says: "again it signifies the tongue." But you will object: how can "spirit" be taken for "tongue"? I answer: just as the Apostle calls that gift of tongues "tongue," so this inspiration of the divine power, by which many believers spoke in various and different tongues, is rightly called "spirit." Thus in Scripture the word רוּחַ, and πνεῦμα, and spiritus, are often used for the inspiration of the divine power. Nor does it hinder this sense that the Apostle says: "For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays." He calls this inspiration of the divine power "my spirit," because it was given to him by God. But if someone contends that the word spirit must altogether be taken of the spirit of man, of which he says elsewhere, "whom I serve in my spirit," I still think that even so, in this matter, the inspiration of the divine power should not be excluded, so that the spirit speaking in tongues, praying in tongues, singing and giving thanks in tongues, is the spirit of man stirred by the inspiration of the divine power to speak in foreign tongues. For otherwise, whence would the human spirit have the ability of tongues which it had never learned?

units.la: CAETERVM qui prophetat, hominib. in quit, loquitur ædificationem, & exhortatione, & consolationem. Quoniam confert inter se lingua loquentem & prophetantem, postquā
units.tr: "But he who prophesies," he says, "speaks to men edification, and exhortation, and consolation." Since he compares the one who speaks in a tongue with the one who prophesies,

units.la: illius inutilitatem perstrinxit, iam de utilitate A prophetantis subiungit, quo doceat, quare praestantius sit prophetare, quam linguis loqui. Qui lingua loquitur, inquit, inutilis est hominibus. Non enim illis, sed Deo loquitur. At qui prophetat, utiliter loquitur. Loquitur enim hominibus. Hoc est: Sic loquitur ad homines, ut possit ab illis intelligi.
units.tr: after he has pointed out the uselessness of the former, he now adds the usefulness of the one who prophesies, to teach why it is more excellent to prophesy than to speak in tongues. "He who speaks in a tongue," he says, "is useless to men. For he speaks not to them but to God. But he who prophesies speaks usefully, for he speaks to men." That is: he speaks to men in such a way that he can be understood by them.

units.la: Satis ne utilitatis, inquies, in eo est, si loquetem intelligamus, ut no referat quid dicat? Refert admodum. Nam possent ea dici in ecclesia quae praestaret non intelligere prorsus, qualia sunt seductorum nugamenta, monachorum som nia, ad superstitionem & eidolatriam, deinde ad quaestum quoque facientia, quae Apostolus Petrus ficta verba vocat quibus impostores in ecclesia negociantur: deinde & traditio nes humanae ac mandata hominum, quibus conscientiae imperitae multitudinis in subiectionem domini Antichristi mancipantur & excruciantur. Quae huiusmodi sunt, utiliter no intelligerentur. At ea sic sunt praedicata in ecclesijs, ut conciones publicae fere nihil sonarint aliud. Quae vero utiliter audiri & intelligi poterant, aut alto sunt silentio pressa, aut lingua incognita sic in canticum versa, ut intelligi nequiuerint.
units.tr: "Is it enough of usefulness," you will ask, "if we understand the speaker, so that it does not matter what he says?" It matters greatly. For there could be said in the Church things which it would be better not to understand at all, such as the trifles of seducers, the dreams of monks, which tend to superstition and idolatry, and also to gain; these the Apostle Peter calls "feigned words" with which impostors trade in the Church; and also human traditions and the commandments of men, by which the consciences of the unlearned multitude are enslaved and tormented in subjection to the lord Antichrist.
