Such things would be useless if understood. But they have been so preached in the churches that public sermons have sounded almost nothing else. And those things which could have been usefully heard and understood have either been pressed into deep silence or turned into song in an unknown tongue, so that they could not be understood.

units.la: Haud itaque contentus Apostolus dixisse: Qui vero prophetat, loquitur hominib. mox subijcit qua utilitate loquatur hominib. quod uidelicet doctrinae genus proponat ecclesiae. Hominibus, inquit, loquitur aedificationem, exhortationem, & consolationem. Hoc est, ea loquitur hominibus, quae ad aedificationem, exhortationem, & consolationem facere possunt: & sic illa loquitur, ut intelligi, intellectaq; mentes audientium aedificare, exhortari, & consolari queant.
units.tr: Therefore the Apostle, not content to have said, "But he who prophesies speaks to men," immediately adds in what usefulness he speaks to men, namely what kind of teaching he sets before the Church. "He speaks to men," he says, "edification, exhortation, and consolation." That is, he speaks to men those things which can serve for edification, exhortation, and consolation; and he speaks them in such a way that they can be understood, and that, understood, they can build up, exhort, and console the minds of the hearers.

units.la: Hac autem sententia satis, opinor, declarat, de quo nam prophetiae genere loquatur. De eo uidelicet, quo docetur & instruitur ecclesia. Non dicit: Qui prophetat, quae futura sunt praenunciat. Haud enim de uaticinijs hic loquitur: sed, Qui prophetat, inquit, loquitur hominibus aedificationem, exhortationem, & consolationem. At hoc faciunt ecclesiae doctores, qui verbo doctrinae, exhortationis, & consolationis populum domini aedificant. Sunt ergo prophetae, qui docent in ecclesia, pluris faciendi quam si per miraculum linguis canerent & orarent. Obserua uero prophetici muneris breuem & luculentam descriptionem. Qui prophetat, inquit, hominibus loquitur aedificationem, exhortationem & consolationem. Ergo partes ecclesiasticI prophetae sunt aedificare, exhortari, & consolari.
units.tr: By this sentence, I think, he sufficiently makes clear what kind of prophecy he means. Namely that by which the Church is taught and instructed. He does not say, "He who prophesies foretells what is to come." For he is not speaking here of predictions, but "He who prophesies," he says, "speaks to men edification, exhortation, and consolation." But this is what the teachers of the Church do, who by the word of teaching, exhortation, and consolation build up the people of the Lord. There are therefore prophets who teach in the Church, to be valued more highly than if they sang and prayed in tongues by miracle. Note, moreover, the brief and clear description of the prophetic office: "He who prophesies," he says, "speaks to men edification, exhortation, and consolation." Therefore the duties of the church prophet are to build up, to exhort, and to console.

units.la: 1 Aedificatio metaphorica dictio est, pro doctrina posita. Qui docet ignorantes ac rudes, aedificat illos ad structuram domus Domini. Huc pertinent omnia quae fidem ac pietatem in cordibus electorum plantanda concernunt, quibus super fundamentum quod Christus est, in templo Dei tanqua uiui lapides construimur. Sed de hac aedificatione supra cap. 3. facta est
units.tr: 1. "Edification" is a metaphorical word, used for teaching. He who teaches the ignorant and rude builds them up into the structure of the house of the Lord. To this pertain all those things which concern the planting of faith and piety in the hearts of the elect, by which, upon the foundation which is Christ, we are built into the temple of God as living stones. But of this edification mention was made above, in chapter 3.

units.la: mentio. 2 Secunda pars est exhortatio, Graece παράκλησις. Hac propheta iam credentes ac religionem Christi profitentes ut in fide ac uera pietate constanter pergant sedulo exhortatur, ac veluti ex nomine inclamat, quemadmodum inclamari solent, qui in itinere constituti uel exorbitant, ueltardius promouet. Pars haec prophetiae summopere est omnibus illis necessaria, qui veritatem Christi & omnem pietatem cognouerunt quidem, uerum studio & conuersatione uitae non ita exprimunt, sicuti conueniebat. Hac parte diligenter functus est Apostolus, qui cum esset Ephesi per triennium, noctes ac dies non cessauit cum lachrymis unusquenq; fidelium monere & exhortari. Act. 20.
units.tr: 2. The second part is exhortation, in Greek παράκλησις. By this the prophet diligently exhorts those who already believe and profess the religion of Christ to persevere constantly in faith and true piety, and, as it were, calls to them by name, as people are usually called when they are on a journey and have strayed or are moving too slowly. This part of prophecy is most necessary for all those who have indeed come to know the truth of Christ and all piety, but do not express it with their study and manner of life as they ought. The Apostle discharged this part diligently; for when he was at Ephesus for three years, he did not cease night and day, with tears, to admonish and exhort each one of the faithful. Acts 20.

units.la: Tertia pars est consolatio. Graece παρακλησις. Est autem παρακαλεω amanter alloqui laborantes, afflictos, tristes, quales sunt pauperes, desolati, captiui, angustiati, praesertim propter Christum, illisq; talia proponere, unde consolationem accipiant, & in spiritu patientiae confirmentur. Pertinet studium hoc παρακαλεῖν ad omnes quidem Christianos, praesertim uero ad prophetas uerbi Dei ministros. Collectus populus Christi habet ignorantes, habet desides ac pigros, habet afflictos. Datur ergo ecclesiae domum prophetiq, quo doceantur ignorantes, ad moneantur desides, & consolationem accipiant afflicti. Quid quaeso censenda est lingua peregrina & incognita prophetiq tam multis modis utili collata?
units.tr: The third part is consolation. In Greek it is paraklēsis [παρακλησις]. The verb parakaleō [παρακαλεω] means to speak kindly to those who are labouring, afflicted, sad, such as the poor, the forsaken, the captive and the distressed, especially on account of Christ, and to set before them things by which they may receive consolation and be strengthened in a spirit of patience. This duty of exhorting [παρακαλεῖν] belongs to all Christians, but especially to the prophets, the ministers of the Word of God. The gathered people of Christ includes the ignorant, the lazy and sluggish, and the afflicted. So the church has prophets in its house, so that the ignorant may be taught, the idle may be admonished, and the afflicted may receive consolation. What, I ask, should we think of a foreign and unknown tongue compared with prophecy, which is so useful in so many ways?

units.la: QVI loquitur lingua, inquit, seipsum aedificat: at qui prophetat, ecclesiam aedificat. Dixit loquente lingua non hominibus loqui, sed Deo, propterea quod nemo sit qui loquentem intelligenter audiat. Eandem ob causam dicit illum aedificare seipsum. Hoc est, solum ipsum intelligere quae dicat, ideoq; solum per ea aedificare seipsum, no ecclesiam, si tame dicat, quae aliquid aedificationis habeant. Non habet haec particula locum in illis qui ne ipsi quidem intelligunt, quae Latina lingua orant & canunt, quales sunt indocti sacrificuli, monachi & nonnae quorum maxima multitudo, propter eiusmodi cantus & precum murmura ociosa & ignaua conniuentibus episcopis, ne obulo qui dem melioribus, alitur in ecclesia.
units.tr: "He who speaks in a tongue," he says, "edifies himself, but he who prophesies edifies the church." He said that one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God, because no one understands him when he speaks. For the same reason he says that such a person edifies himself. That is, he alone understands what he says, and so he edifies only himself, not the church, if indeed what he says has any edifying content. This clause does not apply to those who do not even understand what they pray and sing in Latin: the unlearned little priests, monks and nuns, of whom there is a very great multitude. Because of such chanting and idle, sluggish murmuring of prayers, the bishops look on and do not even pay them a penny for better things, yet they are maintained in the church.

units.la: AT qui prophetat, inquit, ecclesiam aedificat. Ille neminem nisi seipsum, at hic no modo seipsum, sed & alios aedificat. Et huc prouocat Timotheum suum dicens: Dum uenio attende lectioni, exhortationi & doctrinae. Noli negligere gratiam quae in te est, quae data est tibi per prophetiam cum impositione manuum presbyterij. Haec meditare, & in his esto, ut profectus tuus manifestus sit in omnibus. Attende tibi- ipsi & doctrinae. Nam id si feceris, teipsum seruabis, & eos qui te audierint. Itaq; quanto est melius sic aedificare seipsum ut & alij aedificetur, tanto melius est prophetare quam lingua loqui.
units.tr: "But he who prophesies," he says, "edifies the church." The one edifies no one but himself, but the other edifies not only himself but others too. He calls his Timothy to this when he says: "Until I come, attend to reading, exhortation and teaching. Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the eldership. Meditate on these things, and be in them, so that your progress may be evident to all. Take heed to yourself and to teaching. For if you do this, you will save both yourself and those who hear you" (1 Tim. 4). Therefore, the more it is better to edify oneself in such a way that others are also edified, so much the better is it to prophesy than to speak in a tongue.

units.la: Obserua uero, quod non simpliciter dicit: At qui prophetat, aedificat alios, sed aedificat ecclesiam. Loquitur autem non de alia quam Christi, adeoq; uera ecclesia. Est itaq; prophetia da taa ta à domino ad ædificationem ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Notice, however, that he does not simply say, "He who prophesies edifies others," but "edifies the church." He speaks, moreover, not of any other church but of Christ's, and so of the true church. Prophecy is therefore a gift given by the Lord for the building up of the church.

units.la: Consequitur hanc esse conditionem eccle-siæ, donec in terris uersatur, ut opus habeat mi-nisterio uerbi, quo ædificetur, quo non haberet opus, si perfectionem pietatis & iusticiæ hic in terris semel esset consequuta. Consequi-tur item, hinc potissimum esse uastationem ac desolationem ecclesiæ, quod ædificatores illius opus hoc domini partim omiserunt, patrim ui-ciarunt. Replerunt omnia templa missis & can-tionibus ecclesiæ incognitis, ritibus humanis, splendore auri & argeti, & eidolis surdis ac mu-tis, ac quæstu inexplebili: de doctrina uero, un-de erat ædificanda ecclesia, alibi prorsus nulla, alibi omnium minima est cogitatio.
units.tr: It follows that this is the condition of the church as long as it dwells on earth: it needs the ministry of the Word by which it may be built up, which it would not need if it had already attained perfection of piety and righteousness here on earth. It also follows that the chief cause of the church's devastation and desolation is that its builders have partly neglected this work of the Lord and partly corrupted it. They have filled all the temples with masses and chants unknown to the congregation, with human rites, with the splendour of gold and silver, with deaf and dumb idols, and with insatiable profit-seeking. But as for the teaching by which the church ought to be built up, in some places there is none at all, and in others it is the smallest of concerns.

units.la: VOLO autem omnes uos, inquit, loqui lin-guis, magis tamen ut prophetetis.] Quemad-modum supra mox initio capitis, priusquam elo-gia prophetiæ supra donum linguarum extol-leret, canens ne ad illius contemptum hæc lo-qui uideatur: dixit, æmulamini quidem spiri-tualia, magis tamen ut prophetetis, ita iam se-cundo eiusdé cautionis gratia postq; prophe-tiam linguis prætulit, subiicit dicens: Volo au-tem omnes uos loqui linguis, magis tamen ut prophetetis. Conuenit aut ut quoniam uocu-la ingeminatur, perinde atq; supra in parti-cula similí admonuimus, prior accipiatur pro id est, quidem, ac legetur. Volo quidem oēs uos loqui linguis, magis uero ut prophetetis.
units.tr: "I want you all," he says, "to speak in tongues, but rather that you may prophesy." Just as above, at the very beginning of the chapter, before he extolled prophecy above the gift of tongues, he added a caution lest he seem to speak in contempt of it, saying, "Earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy" (1 Cor. 14:1), so now, for the second time, for the sake of the same caution, after he has preferred prophecy to tongues, he adds, saying: "Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but rather that you may prophesy." The word "now" (autem) is repeated, and just as above in a similar particle we noted that the first (prior) should be taken as meaning "indeed," so it should be read here: "I indeed want you all to speak in tongues, but rather that you may prophesy."

units.la: Vide autem quomodo loquatur. Non dicit simpliciter: Non uero loqui linguis: aut, conce-do quidem loqui linguis, sed ut donum illud linguarum non modo ferre se in ecclesia, sed & magnificare ac diligere significet, uolo inquit uos loqui linguis. Imo, Volo omnes uos loqui linguis inquit. Quasi dicat: Non ideo extollo prophetię utilitate supra linguas ut nolim uos loqui linguis. Absit. Tam abest, ut cupiam ex uobis author esse uelim, ne posthac linguis lo-quatur, ut uelim potius non unum & alterum, sed omnes uos loqui linquis. Et hic, ne à scopo discedat, adijcit, quatenus hoc uelit. Hactenus uidelicet, ut & prophetent. Et ut hoc, se malle significet, non simpliciter dicit, sic tamen: sed, magis tamen, intellige, uolo, ut prophetetis. Sic cauet, ne uideatur illos auocare à dono lin-guarum, & tamen simul prophetiam constan-ter supra linguas extollit.
units.tr: Notice how he speaks. He does not simply say, "I do not want you to speak in tongues," or "I concede that you may speak in tongues"; rather, so that his words indicate that he not only tolerates the gift of tongues in the church but also values and loves it, he says, "I want you to speak in tongues." Indeed he says, "I want all of you to speak in tongues." As if he were saying: "I do not extol prophecy above tongues because of its usefulness in such a way that I do not wish you to speak in tongues. God forbid! So far am I from wishing to be the author of your ceasing to speak in tongues that I would rather have not just one or two but all of you speak in tongues." And here, lest he stray from his aim, he adds how far he wants this: "So far, of course, that you also prophesy." And so that he may signal that this is what he prefers, he does not say it simply, but "rather," understood as: "I want you, rather, to prophesy." Thus he guards against seeming to call them away from the gift of tongues, and yet at the same time he steadily extols prophecy above tongues.

units.la: Quæsierit quisquā, qua nam de causa nolue-rit Apostolus omnes tum temporis fideles in ecclesia Corinthiorum loqui linguis, cū Deo loquantur non hominibus qui linguis loquun-tur, nihilq; ex eo ædificationis ad ecclesiā pro-ueniat. Neq; enim existimandum est, quod si-mulando & non ueraciter dicat: Volo quidem omnes uos loqui linguis. Respondeo. Pri-mum, erat donum linguarum; nō humano stu-dio & exercitio acquisitum, sed insigni cū mi-raculo per spiritum Christi credentibus con-cessum, atq; ita arguebat rem eam geri diuini-tus, doctrinamq; ac fidem Christi plurimū con-firmabat in cordibus Gentiū. Deinde, etsi ec-clesiam non ædificabant linguis loquetes, se-
units.tr: Someone might ask why the Apostle at that time did not want all the faithful in the church of Corinth to speak in tongues, since they were speaking to God and not to men, and nothing of edification came from it to the church. For we must not suppose that he said, "I indeed want you all to speak in tongues," in pretence and not sincerely. I answer: first, this was a gift of tongues, not acquired by human zeal and practice but granted to believers by the Spirit of Christ with a remarkable miracle. It thus proved that the matter was carried out by divine power, and it greatly confirmed the teaching and faith of Christ in the hearts of the Gentiles. Next, although those who spoke in tongues did not edify the church,

units.la: A ipsos tamen ædificabant. Tertio, quoniam tan-tum inter eos erat æmulationis propter donū hoc linguarum, ut qui linguis loquebantur ad uersum non loquentes inflarentur, ac uicisim non loquentes uel liuore quodam aduersum loquentes afficerentur, uel præpostera illos ad miratione & nimia existimatione cæteris præ-ferrent: hac quoque ratione optabat, ut non ali qui tantum ex illis, sed omnes linguis loque-rentur. Nam tum nulla fuisset reliqua uel infla-tionis, uel liuoris, uel nimiæ admirationis & existimationis occasio. Hisce de causis dicit: Volo quidem omnes uos loqui linguis, & si-mul significat, usq; adeo se nō inuidere cuipiā illorum donum hoc linguarum, ut malit om-nes quā nullos loq linguis. Simile quid & Mo-si accidisse, Num.ii. legimus ad hunc modum: Descenditq; dominus per nubem & loquutus est ad eum, auferens de spiritu, qui erat in Mo-se, & dans septuaginta uiris. Cumq; requieuis-set in eis spiritus, prophetauerūt, nec ultra ces-sauerunt. Remanserant autem in castris duo uiri, quorum unus uocabatur Eldad, & alter Medad, super quos requieuit spiritus. nam & ipsi descripti fuerant, & non exierant ad taber-naculum. Cumq; prophetarent in castris, cu-currit puer, & nunciauit Mosi dicens: Eldad & Medad prophetant in castris. Statim Iosue fi-lius Nū, minister Mosi electus e pluribus ait: Domine mi Moses prohibe eos. At ille: Quid, inquit, æmularis pro me? Quis tribuat ut om-nis populus prophetet, ac det eis dominus suū spiritum? Hæc dicens, tam abesse significat, ut cupiam è populo donum spritus inuideat, pro-hiberēq; uelit, ne prophetet in illo quisquam ut optet ex animo hoc dari populo, ut omnes spiritu domini accepto prophetent.
units.tr: they nevertheless edified themselves. Third, since there was so much rivalry among them because of this gift of tongues, that those who spoke in tongues were puffed up against those who did not, and conversely those who did not speak were affected with a certain envy towards those who did, or else they placed those tongue-speakers above the others with an unseemly admiration and excessive esteem, for this reason too he wished that not just some of them, but all of them, would speak in tongues. For then there would have been no remaining occasion for puffing up, for envy, or for excessive admiration and esteem. For these reasons he says, "I indeed want you all to speak in tongues," and at the same time he signals that he does not begrudge anyone this gift of tongues to such an extent that he would rather have none of them speak in tongues than all. Something similar happened to Moses, as we read in Num. 11, in this way: "The LORD came down in a cloud and spoke to him, taking some of the Spirit that was on Moses and giving it to seventy men. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, and did not cease. But two men remained in the camp, one named Eldad and the other Medad, on whom the Spirit also rested; for they too had been enrolled, but had not gone out to the tabernacle. And when they prophesied in the camp, a boy ran and told Moses, saying: 'Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp.' At once Joshua, son of Nun, the minister of Moses, chosen from among many, said: 'My lord Moses, forbid them!' But he said: 'Why are you jealous on my behalf? Would that all the people prophesied, and that the LORD would give them his Spirit!'" By saying this, he signals that he is so far from envying the people this gift of the Spirit, or wishing to forbid it, that he earnestly desires that it be given to the people, so that all of them, having received the Spirit of the Lord, might prophesy.

units.la: MAGIS tamen ut prophetetis, inquit. ] Et-go uolebat ut omnes prophetarent. Dixit enim: Volo uos omnes linguis loqui. Quare quod annectit dicens, magis tamen ut prophetetis, accipiendum est secundum sensum præceden-tis uerbi uolo, ut legas, magis tamē uolo ut o-mnes prophetetis. Mira uidetur confusio, si o-mnes in ecclesia prophetēt. Verum ea de re in-frā uidebimus, ubi dicturas est: Potestis singu-latim omnes prophetare.
units.tr: "But rather that you may prophesy," he says. So he wanted all of them to prophesy. For he said, "I want you all to speak in tongues." Therefore the phrase he adds, "but rather that you may prophesy," must be understood according to the sense of the preceding words, "I want," so that you read, "but rather I want all of you to prophesy." There seems to be a strange confusion if all in the church were to prophesy. However, we shall see about this matter below, where he is going to say: "You can all prophesy, one by one."

units.la: MAIOR enim est, inquit, qui prophetat, q̄ qui loquitur linguis, nisi interpretetur, ut ec-clesia ædificationem accipiat.] Habent ista ra-tionem eius quod dixit: Magis tamen ut pro-phetetis. Quasi dicat: Quod malo ut prophete-tis omnes, in causa est, quod qui prophetat ma-ior est, quam qui linguis loquitur. Non adijcit rationem, quare dixerit: Volo quidem uos om-nes loqui linguis. Neq; enim hic illi aliquid ra-tionis requirebant, quod alio qui plus satis ma-gnifice de dono linguarum sentirent, de pro-phetia uero non ita. Quare cum mirum illis ui-deretur, quare prophetiam linguis præferret, malletq; omnes prophetare q̄ linguis loqui, cum ipsis diuersum uideretur, rationem hanc sententiæ suæ adijcit dicens: Maior enim est q̄ prophetat quam qui linguis loquitur. Sentiebant ipsi, maiorem esse qui linguis incognitis A simpliciter, sed sub suoipsius exemplo. loqueretur, quam qui uulgari idiomate prophetaret: id est doceret, exhortaretur, & consolaretur. Et sane in linguis plus apparebat diuinae operationis, & plus accedebat admirationis, quin in prophetia, at revera plus est utilitatis in prophetia quam in linguis, id qd ipsi praestupore linguarum fascinati non obseruabant. Quare cum utilitatem prophetiae ampliore quam sit linguarum, expositset, subjicit velut inde colligens ac dicens: Maior enim est qui prophetat, quam qui linguis loquitur.
units.tr: "For he who prophesies is greater," he says, "than he who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets, so that the church may receive edification." These words give the reason for what he said: "Yet rather that you should prophesy." As if he said: the reason I prefer that you all prophesy is that the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues. He does not add a reason for saying, "I indeed want you all to speak in tongues." For they did not ask for a reason here, since they thought very highly of the gift of tongues, but not so of prophecy. So when it seemed strange to them that he set prophecy above tongues, and preferred that all prophesy rather than speak in tongues, which seemed to them the opposite, he adds this reason for his judgment: "For he who prophesies is greater than he who speaks in tongues." They believed that the one who spoke in unknown tongues was greater than the one who prophesied in the common language, that is, taught, exhorted and comforted, simply, but by his own example. Certainly tongues showed more of divine working and drew more admiration, yet in fact prophecy is more useful than tongues. Dazzled by the amazement of the tongues, they did not notice this. So, having set out that the usefulness of prophecy is greater than that of tongues, he adds, as if drawing the conclusion: "For he who prophesies is greater than he who speaks in tongues."

units.la: Obseruemus hunc locum de maioritate, ut loquuntur, in ecclesia. Disceptarunt inter se discipuli Christi studio carnis non spiritus, quis inter ipsos futurus esset maior. Audierūt à domino, qui maior inter uos est, sit omnium seruus. Hoc est, sit talis, qui non sibi uiuat, sed seruiat ac prosit omnibus. Eodem spiritu Apostolus Corinthios inflatos, & maioritatis appetentes revocat ad studium prophetiae, pronuncians maiorem esse eum in ecclesia qui prophetat, hoc est, omnes aedificat, docet, exhortatur & consolatur. Audite ergo Romani pontifices, qui in maioritate caelum ac terram miscetis, maiore esse uobis qui prophetat, etiamsi alias infimus aliquis fraterculus esse uideatur. In ecclesia idem maioritas ex utilitate est aedificandae ecclesiae censenda, ut maior sit qui utilior. Sic maior Hieronymus, Damasus. Et maior Augustinus omnibus Romanis eidolis: & qui minor est in te eos doctores, quos uos haereseos damnatis, B maior est omnibus Romanis cardinalibus, episcopis ac praelatis, monachis ac Nonnis.
units.tr: Let us note this place about greatness, as they call it, in the church. The disciples of Christ, with the zeal of the flesh rather than of the Spirit, disputed among themselves who would be greatest. They heard from the Lord: "Whoever is greatest among you, let him be the servant of all." That is, let him be one who does not live for himself but serves and benefits everyone. In the same Spirit the Apostle calls back the Corinthians, puffed up and seeking greatness, to the zeal for prophecy, declaring that he is greater in the church who prophesies, that is, who builds up, teaches, exhorts and comforts everyone. Hear then, Roman pontiffs, who mix up heaven and earth in your pursuit of greatness: he who prophesies is greater to you, even if he seems otherwise to be some lowly little brother. In the church, greatness is to be judged by usefulness in building up the church, so that the one who is more useful is greater. Thus Jerome is greater, and Damasus. And Augustine is greater than all the Roman idols; and those teachers whom you condemn as heretics are greater than all the Roman cardinals, bishops and prelates, monks and nuns.

units.la: NISI interpretetur, inquit, ut ecclesia aedificatione accipiat. Exceptio est. Excipit eū qui sic lingua loquitur, ut simul ea quae loquitur, uulgari idiomate interpretetur, & ecclesiae intelligenda proponat. Non simpliciter dicit, Ni si interpretetur: sed addit, ut ecclesia aedificatio nem accipiat. Ad hunc finem astringit quae geruntur in ecclesia omnia. Non ita loquentem & interpretantem in ecclesia, ut nihil aedificationis proueniat ad ecclesiam. At eum qui ad aedificationem interpretatur, haud postponit, sed adaequat prophetanti, propter aequale aedificandae ecclesiae studium. Magna sane est interpretis utilitas. Licet ille de suo nihil adferat in medium, aperit tamē doctrinam sub lingua incognita propositā, redditq; illā intelligibilem & utilē. Quod perinde est ac si quis thesaurum in arcula ferrea clausum adhibita clave referat, illius copiam quibuslibet faciat.
units.tr: "Unless he interprets," he says, "so that the church may receive edification." This is an exception. He excludes the one who speaks in such a way that he interprets at the same time what he says into the common language and sets it before the church to be understood. He does not simply say, "Unless he interprets," but adds, "so that the church may receive edification." He binds everything done in the church to this end. He does not mean a speaker and interpreter in the church in such a way that nothing of edification comes to the church. But he does not put the one who interprets for edification behind the prophet; he places him on an equal footing, because of the equal zeal for building up the church. The usefulness of the interpreter is indeed great. Although he brings nothing of his own into the open, he unlocks the teaching set forth in an unknown tongue and makes it intelligible and useful. This is just as if someone, with a key at hand, should unlock a treasure shut in an iron chest and make its riches available to anyone.

units.la: Nūc autē fratres si uenia ad uos linguis loquēs, quid uobis prodero, nisi uobis loquar aut per revelationē, aut per scientiā, aut per prophetiā, aut p doctrinā.
units.tr: Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what will I profit you, unless I speak to you by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophecy, or by teaching?

units.la: Nullam esse utilitatem ecclesiae per eum qui linguis loquitur, ex eo quidem satis admoneri poterant, quod lingua loquentem Deo non hominibus loqui, nec a quopiam audiri dixit: verum quo illud penitius inculcet, expresse nihil hinc utilitatis ad ipsos uenire dicit, idq; nō
units.tr: That there is no benefit to the church from the one who speaks in tongues could be gathered well enough from the fact that he said the one speaking in a tongue speaks to God, not to men, and is heard by no one. But to press this more deeply, he states plainly that no benefit comes from this to them, and not

units.la: NVNC aut fratres, inquit, si ueniam ad uos linguis loquens, quid uobis prodero? Venerant ad eos quidam aliis atq; aliis linguis in ecclesia loquentes. Et hos admirabantur sine ullo profectu. Inutilem illorū aduētum perstringere uolēs, non dicit: Nunc autem fratres qui ad uos uenerunt linguis loquētes, quid uobis proderunt? ne mox animos fascinatorū auertat, ac suspicionem illis moueat, quod odio magis doctorum quos habebant, quā recto iudicio causam hanc tractet. Ideo suāipsius persona inducit, quo minus offendat, dicens: Nūc aut fratres, si ueniam ad uos linguis loquens, quid uobis prodero? Nec dicit, nihil uobis prodero, sed iplorum iudicium poscens, quid uobis prodero inquit? Quasi dicat: Iudicate uosipsi, num aliquid utilitatis ex eo poterit ad uos redire. Poterat dicere: Cum uenirem primum ad uos, si linguis loquens uenissem, quid uobis profuissem? Verum ne cogitarent, at hi doctores nostri linguis inter nos, iam Christianos sanctos non adhuc ethnicos loquuntur. Aliud est si quis hominibus nondū credentibus linguis loquatur, & aliud si hoc faciat in ecclesia iā credentium. Cum illi ad nos uenirent iam Christiani eramus. Cum Paulus primum ad nos uenire, gentes eramus, nihil de Christo scientes. Quare non conueniebat ut linguis inter nos loqueretur. At secus est, si quis iam in ecclesia nostra linguis loquatur. Ne sic inq; cogitarent, non dicit, Si primum ad uos uenissem: sed, Si ueniam ad uos linguis loquens, quid uobis prodero? Ergo non minus inutile est linguis loqui ac canere in ecclesia credendū, quā est, si quis hoc faciat inter eos qui ueritatem nōdum cognouerūt, necChristo dū nomina sua dederūt.
units.tr: "Now then, brothers," he says, "if I come to you speaking in tongues, what will I profit you?" Certain people had come to them speaking in various tongues in the church, and they admired them without any gain. Wishing to strike at the uselessness of their coming, he does not say, "Now, brothers, those who have come to you speaking in tongues, what will they profit you?" lest he at once turn their minds away from the speakers and stir in them the suspicion that he treats this matter out of hatred for the teachers they had, rather than with sound judgment. So he brings in his own person, so as to give less offence, saying: "Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what will I profit you?" He does not say, "I shall profit you nothing," but, asking for their own judgment, says, "what will I profit you?" As if to say: judge for yourselves whether any usefulness could come back to you from it. He could have said: when I first came to you, if I had come speaking in tongues, what would I have profited you? But lest they think that these teachers of ours speak in tongues among us, we who are already Christians, holy, and no longer heathens. It is one thing if someone speaks in tongues to men who do not yet believe, and another if he does it in a church of believers already. When they came to us we were already Christians. When Paul first came to us we were Gentiles, knowing nothing of Christ, so it was not fitting that he should speak in tongues among us. But it is otherwise if someone now speaks in tongues in our church. Lest they think in this way, he does not say, "If I had come to you first," but, "If I come to you speaking in tongues, what will I profit you?" Therefore speaking in tongues and singing in the church is no less useless to believers than if someone did this among those who have not yet known the truth, nor when they had given their names to Christ.

units.la: SI ueniam ad uos, inquit, linguis loquens, quid uobis prodero? Ergo requiritur à ministro, qui uenit ad ecclesiam ut ueniat utiliter, cum fructu, quo prosit illis ad quos uenit. Alio qui quorsum ,urtissēt hoc Apostolus dicens, Quid uobis prodero? At hodie non ueniūt ad episcopatus, ad parœcias, ad canonicatus, ad praelaturas, ut pfint ecclesiae: sed ueniunt tanquam ad dignitates & beneficia, quo pfint sibijpsis, hoc est, quo perdant & seipsos & ecclesiā. Vtinā dicat hodie quisq; sacrificulus: Si uo niam ad uos missas celebras, & nescio quas horas decantans, uel submurmurans, quid uobis prodero? Meo quidem uentri plurimum, salutī uero uestrae nihil.
units.tr: "If I come to you," he says, "speaking in tongues, what will I profit you?" Therefore a minister who comes to a church is required to come usefully, with fruit that benefits those to whom he comes. Otherwise the Apostle would not have said this to no purpose: "What will I profit you?" But today men do not come to bishoprics, parishes, canonries and prelacies so that they may benefit the church; they come as to dignities and benefices, so that they may benefit themselves, that is, so that they may ruin both themselves and the church. I wish some priest today would say: "If I come to you celebrating Mass, chanting or mumbling through I know not what hours, what will I profit you?" Certainly much to my belly, but nothing to your salvation.

units.la: NISI uobis loquar, inquit. Hoc est, nisi ad utilitatem uestrā lingua uobis intelligibili loquar. Supra dixit: Qui lingua loquitur, nō hominibus loquitur, sed Deo. Qui prophetat uero, hominibus loquitur. Eò respicit cum hic dicit: nisi uobis loquar, quod idem est, ac si dicat, nisi prophetem. Quare quemadmodum illic, qui prophetat, inquit, hominibus loquitur ad aedificationem, exhortationem & consolationem: ita hic quoq;, cum dixisset, nisi uobis loquar, addit, aut per reuelationem, aut per scientiam, aut per prophetiam, aut per doctrinam
units.tr: "Unless I speak to you," he says. That is, unless I speak to you in a tongue intelligible to you for your benefit. Above he said: "He who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men, but to God. But he who prophesies speaks to men." He looks back to that when he says here, "unless I speak to you," which is the same as saying, "unless I prophesy." Therefore, as there he says that he who prophesies speaks to men for building up, exhortation and comfort, so here too, having said "unless I speak to you," he adds, "by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophecy, or by teaching."

units.la: AVT per reuelatione, inquit.] Gemina est reuelatio, quæ per spiritum Christi contingit: generalis una, specialis altera. Generalis est, qua mysterium Christi filij Dei, unici nostri Seruatoris omnib. electis ac credentib. reuelatur. Sic Petrus cum dixisset: Tu es Christus filius Dei uiui, audiuit ab ipso domino: Beatus es Simon Barionah, quia caro & sanguis non reuelauit tibi, sed pater meus, qui est in cœlis. Et alibi dixit, Abscondi hæc à sapientib. ac prudentib. & reuelari paruulis, nec cognosci patrem ac filium, nisi per reuelationem. Specialis uero est, qua res uariæ, & singularia mysteria siue per uisionem, siue per initinctum spiritus, aut in præsens, aut in futurum respicientia reuelantur. Nec referre admodum puto, utrâ hic intelligamus. Nam utraq; ad ædificationē facit, & uius est Apostolus utraque.
units.tr: "Or by revelation," he says. Revelation is twofold, which comes through the Spirit of Christ: one general, the other special. The general is that by which the mystery of Christ, the Son of God, our only Saviour, is revealed to all the elect and believers. So Peter, when he had said, "You are Christ, the Son of the living God," heard from the Lord himself: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." And elsewhere he said: "I have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones, and no one knows the Father and the Son except by revelation." The special revelation is that by which various matters and singular mysteries, whether present or future, are revealed, either through a vision or through an inward impulse of the Spirit. I do not think it matters much which of these we understand here. For each serves for building up, and the Apostle uses both.

units.la: AVT per scientiam, inquit.] Supra cap.12. scientiæ meminit, ubi illam pro uariarum rerum spiritualium cognitione accipiendam esse diximus.
units.tr: "Or by knowledge," he says. Above, in chapter 12, he mentioned knowledge, where we said it should be understood as knowledge of various spiritual things.

units.la: AVT per prophetiam, inquit.] Intelligo de ea qua res futuræ prædicuntur. Ea de qua dixit hactenus, generalis est qua ministri uerbi ecclesiæ siue per reuelationem, siue per scientiam, siue per prophetiam, id est, uaticinium, siue per doctrinam loquuntur.
units.tr: "Or by prophecy," he says. I understand this of the kind by which future things are foretold. The kind he has been speaking of so far is general, the kind by which the ministers of the Word in the Church speak, whether by revelation, by knowledge, by prophecy (that is, prediction), or by teaching.

units.la: AVT per doctrinam, inquit.] Qui per reuelationem, aut per scientiam, aut per prophetiā loquitur, seruit fidei nostræ, & intelligentiæ rerum siue secretarum, siue futurarum in nobis formandæ. Qui uero per doctrinam loquitur, seruit uitæ nostræ componendæ, & moribus fingendis. Hactenus puto uocem hanc διδασκαλίας hoc loco, à generali doctrina, qua omnia quæ ex uerbo domini docentur, comprehedimus, haud incommode separari. Hiero. quoq; sic sensit. Exposuit enim hac paraphrali: Nisi uobis aut interpreter, aut plana faciam legis occulta quæ noui, aut prophetias exponā, aut uos moralibus doceam institutis.
units.tr: "Or by teaching," he says. He who speaks by revelation, by knowledge, or by prophecy serves our faith and the forming in us of understanding of things, whether hidden or future. But he who speaks by teaching serves the ordering of our life and the shaping of our morals. I think that the word here, διδασκαλίας [didaskalias], can reasonably be separated from general teaching, under which we include all that is taught from the Word of the Lord. Jerome also understood it this way. In his paraphrase he explains it thus: "Unless I either act as your interpreter and make plain the hidden things of the law that I know, or expound the prophecies, or teach you moral precepts."

units.la: Scio Ambrosium ista non diuidere, sed pro eodem accipere. Dicit enim: Hæc omnia unū significant. Docere enim nemo poterit, nisi intelligatur. Sane non possunt esse reuelatio, scientia, prophetia, & doctrina, nisi intelligatur. Quare loqui per reuelationem, per scientiam, per prophetiam, perq; doctrinam, omnino est intelligenter loqui. Et sic expoluit Chrysost. ἐ ἰλλα τὰ ἐντὸς, ..., ἀλλὰ μὴ τὰ ὡς ... Interea tamen nihil uetat, quo minus commoda & pertinenti diuisione inter ista distinguamus, ac singulis suum sensum tribuamus. Quemadmodum enim supra cum dixit: Qui prophetat, hominibus loquitur ad ædificationem, ad exhortationem, & ad consolationem, utilitatem generalis prophetiæ expressit: ita hic illius uelut pâr tes quasdam & organa: uel, si mauis, fontes posuit. Aliud enim est per quid, & aliud ad quid propheta loquitur in ecclesia.
units.tr: I know that Ambrose does not divide these, but takes them as the same thing. For he says: "All these mean one thing. For no one can teach unless he is understood. Certainly revelation, knowledge, prophecy and teaching cannot exist unless they are understood. So to speak by revelation, by knowledge, by prophecy, and by teaching is altogether to speak intelligibly." Chrysostom also explained it in this way: ἐ ἰλλα τὰ ἐντὸς, ..., ἀλλὰ μὴ τὰ ὡς ... [the Greek as printed, garbled in the scan]. Nevertheless, nothing prevents us from distinguishing these by a suitable and fitting division, and from giving each its own sense. For just as above, when he said, "He who prophesies speaks to men for building up, exhortation and consolation," he expressed the usefulness of prophecy in general, so here he sets down, as it were, certain parts and instruments of it, or, if you prefer, its sources. For it is one thing by what means a prophet speaks, and another thing for what purpose he speaks in the Church.

units.la: Quin & inanima uocem reddentia,
units.tr: Indeed, even things without life that give out a sound,

units.la: siue tibia, siue cithara, nisi distinctione sonis dederint, quo cognoscetur quod tibia canitur aut cithara. Etenim si incertam uocem tuba dederit, quis apparabitur ad bellum? Sic & uos nisi per linguam significantem sermonem dederitis, quo intelligetur quod dicitur? Eritis enim in aera loquentes. Tam multa, uerbi gratia, generâ uocum sunt in mundo, & nihil horum mutum. Itaq; si nescicro uim uocis, ero ei qui loquitur barbarus, & qui loquitur apud me barbarus.
units.tr: whether a flute or a harp, unless they give a distinction in their sounds, how will it be known what is played on the flute or the harp? For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? So also you, unless you utter by the tongue speech that is meaningful, how will what is said be understood? For you will be speaking into the air. There are, for example, so many kinds of sounds in the world, and none of them is mute. Therefore, if I do not know the force of a sound, I shall be a barbarian to him who speaks, and he who speaks will be a barbarian to me.

units.la: Ex abundanti adhuc clarius stulticiam Corinthiorum perstringit, qua tantopere linguis incognitis studebant. Dixit inutilem fore suū ad ipsos aduentum, si ueniens ad ipsos non prophetet, sed linguis loquatur: iam ut hoc illis adhuc amplius inculcet, proponit ipsis omnium earum conditionem uocum siue artificiū aliūm siue naturalium, quæ ad aures hominū diriguntur. Hanc esse dicit, ut sonos edant intelligibiliter discretos, alias esse confusas & inutiles. De artificialibus sic dicit: Quin & inanima uocem reddentia, siue tibia, siue cithara, nisi distinctionem sonis dederint, quomodo cognoscetur, quod tibia aut cithara canitur? Q.d. Vel inanima uocem reddentia confi derate, si in linguis hominum dijudicandis fascinati estis. Auditis subinde tibias & citharas & tubas. An non hic quæritis, ut quæ illæ sonant, distincte uobis sonent, aliàs non intelleturis quid sit quod per illas canitur? Si confusas uoces dederint, an non tanquam rem nō inutilem modo, sed & molestam auersaminí? Quid igitur in causa est, quod in uocibus rerum inanimarū distinctos sonos quæritis, unde cognoscatis quid canatur, & non quæritis in uocibus eorum hominum, qui in cœtu uestro peregrinis linguis loquuntur, cum tamen multo hic maiore ratione quæreda sit eorum quæ dicuntur intelligentia, quàm in cantu tibiæ, uel citharæ, uel tubæ? Hic uidetur esse spiritus uerborum istorum, quæ tũ nonnihil moderatius sunt posita, quo minus offendat.
units.tr: Further, and more clearly, he rebukes the folly of the Corinthians, who were so eager for unknown tongues. He said that his coming to them would be useless if, when he came, he did not prophesy but spoke in tongues. Now, so that he may press this home on them even more, he sets before them the condition of all those sounds, whether artificial or natural, which are directed to men's ears. He says that they must give out sounds that are intelligibly distinct, otherwise they are confused and useless. Concerning artificial sounds he says: "Indeed, even things without life that give out a sound, whether flute or harp, unless they give a distinction in their sounds, how will it be known what is played on the flute or the harp?" That is, as if he said: "Consider the inanimate things that give out a sound, if you are so captivated by the human tongues you must judge. You hear flutes, harps and trumpets from time to time. Do you not here seek that what those instruments sound should sound distinctly to you, otherwise you will not understand what is played on them? If they gave confused sounds, would you not turn away from them as a thing not only useless but also annoying? Why then is it that you seek distinct sounds from inanimate things, so that you may know what is played, and you do not seek them from the voices of those men who in your assembly speak in foreign tongues, when yet here the understanding of what is said ought to be sought with much greater reason than in the song of the flute, or the harp, or the trumpet?" The spirit of these words is here somewhat more moderate, so that it may give less offence.

units.la: QVIN & inanima, inquit.] Græcè est, ἐκτος τὰ ἄψυχα, quod uulgatus interpres uertit: Tamen quæ sine anima sunt. Si uocula, tamen eo sensu capiatur, quo reddidit Germanicus interpres, belt sichs doch auch also in denen dingen die da lautend und nitt lebend, retinēda est hæc uersio. Verum si legas: quin & inanima, sicut reddidit Erasmus, emphasim habebis argumenti à minori ad maius. Etenim si in uocibus inanimorum distincti & intelligibiles soni requiruntur: multo magis requirendi sunt in uocibus hominum, quib. non modo anima diuinitus est concessa, sed & mens ratione prædita.
units.tr: "INDEED, even things without life," he says. In Greek it is ἐκτος τὰ ἄψυχα [ektos ta apsycha, as printed], which the Vulgate translator renders "Yet those things which are without life." If the little word is taken in the sense in which the German translator rendered it, "so it is also in those things that sound and are not living," this version should be kept. But if you read "Indeed, even things without life," as Erasmus gave it, you will have an argument from the less to the greater. For if distinct and intelligible sounds are required in the voices of inanimate things, much more must they be required in the voices of men, to whom not only a soul has been given by God, but also a mind endowed with reason.

units.la: QVIN & inani.na, inquit, uocé reddétia.] Duo sunt ἄψυχα, id est, inanimatorum genera. Vnum eorum, quæ quondam animata fuerunt, nūc uero ademptis animabus facta sunt inanima, qualia sunt cadauera mortuorum tā hominum quàm bestiarum. Alterum eorum, quæ nec animata fuerunt, nec animæ capacia. Neutra sunt per se uocalia, nec uocem reddere possunt, cum spiritu careant, nisi illa per miraculosam diuinæ uirtutis operationem, ista per artificium humanæ industrię, uel impostu rę uoces aliquas reddant. Impostura, utpote quando imaginibus sanctorum prorsus inani mis ac mutis ad decipiendum nimis credulan plebem, & emungendum quæstum occulta in spiratione per calamum humanę uoces infun duntur, quæ ueluti ab ipso simulachro æditæ stolidas adstantium mentes in errorem abdu cant. Industrię uero, quando uidelicet organa musica uel flatu uel tactu percita, iuxta suum quælibet artificium sonos reddūt, arte moderandos ac distinguendos. De hoc τ ἀψύχων genere loquens hic Apostolus, cū dixisset, Quin & inanima uocem reddentia: subiunxit, siue tibia siue cithara, &c. Et, Si incertam uocem tuba dederit. Tibia & tuba inspiratione, cithara tactu, uocales redduntur.
units.tr: "INDEED, even things without life that give out a sound." There are two kinds of ἄψυχα [apsycha], that is, of inanimate things. One kind is those things which were once animate but, with their souls taken away, have become inanimate, such as the corpses of the dead, both of men and of beasts. The other kind is those things which were never animate and are not capable of a soul. Neither kind of thing is sounding in itself, nor can it give out a voice, since it lacks breath, unless, by the miraculous working of divine power, the former, or by the skill of human industry, or by deception, the latter give out some voices. Deception occurs when, by a hidden insufflation through a reed, human voices are poured into the images of the saints, which are altogether lifeless and dumb, so that the over-credulous common people may be deceived and their purses emptied; these voices, as though uttered by the statue itself, lead the foolish minds of the bystanders into error. Human industry, on the other hand, occurs when musical instruments, set in motion by breath or by touch, give out sounds according to the art of each, which must be regulated and distinguished by skill. In speaking of this kind of ἀψύχων [apsychōn, inanimate things], the Apostle, having said, "Indeed, even things without life that give out a sound," added, "whether flute or harp," etc., and, "If the trumpet gives an uncertain sound." The flute and the trumpet are made to sound by breath, the harp by touch.

units.la: SIVE tibia, inquit, siue cithara. Quo in usu tempore Pauli fuerint apud Corinthios tibia & cithara, non constat, ut opinor: notas tamen & usitatas uulgof uiffe, satis ex eo patet, quod ab illis argumentatur hoc loco Apostolus. Multas uero fuisse ueteribus tibiarum species ex historijs liquet. Alijs usi sunt Libyes, alijs Phryges, alijs Cares, alijs Lydi, alijs Aegyptij, alijs Phœnices, alijs Thebani, quos inter Græcos tibiæ artificio excelluisse ferunt. Et alia uocabatur Plagialos, alia Elymos, alia Hippophorbos, quod illa in pastu equorum utere tur Libyes Scenetæ, alia Monaulos, quæ potissimum nuptialis erat Aegyptijs, alia Parthenica, alia Pædica, alia Andria, alia Gingras quæ minutula existens flebilem sonum emittebat, alia Polyphthongos ex hordeaceis calamis compacta. Vsus illarum fuit uarius. Nam alijs Gentibus ad tristia, alijs ad lęta usurpabantur. Citharę uero usus multus apud Ebreos fuit, qd uel ex Psalmis patet. Apparet populariter tristas fuisse tibiam & citharā. Vnde & 1.Machab. 3. & Apoc. 18. alijsque locis perinde atq; hic iuguntur. Non est autut hoc Apostoli loco defendamus delicias organorum musicorum, tē plis Papistarum subintroductas, quas sane nū quā probassent, ne ethnici quidem, seueriores disciplinę studiosi, qui nec tibiam, nec citharā, nec ullum aliud artificiosum instrumetum ad miserunt, de tibia causantes, quod sit ἐψιγιστικός, & quod à sermone prohibeat eū qui illam inflat, quodque faciem illius deturpet, ob quam causam & Palladem tibiā abiecisse memorat.
units.tr: "WHETHER a flute," he says, "or a harp." It is not certain, I think, what use the flute and the harp had among the Corinthians in Paul's time; yet that they were known and in common use is sufficiently clear from the fact that the Apostle argues from them in this place. From histories it is evident that the ancients had many kinds of flutes. The Libyans used one kind, the Phrygians another, the Carians another, the Lydians another, the Egyptians another, the Phoenicians another, and the Thebans another, who are said to have excelled among the Greeks in the art of the flute. One was called the Plagiaulos, another the Elymos, another the Hippophorbos, because it was used in feeding horses; the Libyan Scenitae used one kind; the Monaulos, which was especially a wedding flute among the Egyptians; another was the Parthenica, another the Paedica, another the Andria, another the Gingras, which, being rather small, gave out a mournful sound; and another the Polyphthongos, put together from barley stalks. Their use was varied, for some were employed for sad occasions and others for joyful ones. The use of the harp was widespread among the Hebrews, as is clear even from the Psalms. It is apparent that the flute and the harp were commonly thought of as sad instruments, whence they are joined in 1 Maccabees 3 and in Revelation 18, and in other places just as here. Yet we should not defend, from this passage of the Apostle, the delights of musical instruments that were introduced into the temples by the Papists, which certainly even the heathen would never have approved, nor the stricter students of discipline, who rejected neither the flute, nor the harp, nor any other artificial instrument, complaining about the flute because it is ἐψιγιστικός [enthygistikos, as printed], because it hinders from speech the man who blows it, and because it disfigures his face; for which reason they also recount that Pallas threw the flute away.

units.la: NISI distinctione sonis dederint, inquit.] Hoc est, nisi distinctos sonos ex modulatione artis ediderint. In hac totum est artificiū musicēs, queadmodum literaturę in distinctione figurarum. Si una & eadē esset omniū literarū figura, haud cōstaret scribendi ac legendi artificiū, qd est ordinata, distincta, & intelligibilis uariarū literarū cōpositio. Consimili modo, si soni musici instrumenti ijdē essent, idēq; sonaret, irritū esset uniuersum musices artificium, qd nihil est aliud q distincta & cōcinna diuerfarū uocū modulatio, p quā aliquid qd intelligi posit, canatur. Tale quid est status politicus, ac domesticus quoq;. In utroq; sunt diuersi ordines, ac uaria uelut unius corporis membra, quasi quidam diuersi-soni. Horū moderatio cōpetētem poscit distinctionē, sine qua cō sistere nō possunt, sed necesse est turpi ac noxia cofusione quasi quadā desolatione pereat.
units.tr: "Unless they give distinct sounds," he says. That is, unless they produce distinct sounds through the modulation of art. The whole art of music lies in this, just as the art of letters lies in the distinction of their shapes. If all letters had one and the same shape, there would be no art of writing and reading, which is an orderly, distinct and intelligible arrangement of various letters. Likewise, if the sounds of a musical instrument were all the same, the whole art of music would be void, since it is nothing other than a distinct and harmonious modulation of different voices, by which something intelligible is sung. The political state and the household are of this kind too. In both there are different orders and various members, like the parts of one body, like different sounds. Their harmony needs a fitting distinction, without which they cannot stand, but must perish in a shameful and harmful confusion, a kind of desolation.

units.la: QVOMODO cognoscetur, inquit, qd tibia canitur aut cithara. ] In Græco est, τὸ ἀλλ... μένον ὁ τὸ κιθαριζόμενον, q. dicas, qd tibizatur, uel citharizatur, ne quis in uerbo canedi philosophetur, propter uulgatā uersionē, q sic habet, quo scietur id quod canitur, aut quod citharizatur? Nō sic distinguit Apostolus inter citha rā & tibiam, ut tibiæ det cantum, citharæ non det, cum recte possit utriq; dari, quáuis pneumatica sit tibia, cithara uero dactylica. Licet enim humano flatu inspirata sonet tibia, uocē tñ ædit perinde atq; cithara non humanā, sed artificiosam. Quare cōsulto sic uertit Erasmus, ut uerbum canendi competat utrique.
units.tr: "How will it be known," he says, "what is piped or played on the lyre?" The Greek is τὸ αὐλούμενον ἢ τὸ κιθαριζόμενον, that is, what is piped or what is played on the lyre. Lest anyone should make a philosophical point about the word "sung," I note that the common version reads: "how will it be known what is sung, or what is played on the lyre?" The Apostle does not distinguish between the lyre and the pipe in such a way as to give the pipe a melody but deny it to the lyre, since either may rightly be given one, although the pipe is wind-driven and the lyre is played with the fingers. For although the pipe is sounded by human breath, it gives forth a voice just as the lyre does, not a human voice but an artificial one. That is why Erasmus translates it deliberately so that the verb "to sing" fits both.

units.la: Obserua uero q sit Apostolus longē aliter animatus in audiendo musici instrumēti cantu, q sint ij qui sola cōsonantia, uel sonoro tinnitu uocū sic delectantur, ut de intellectu illarum non quærant, qualis delectatio in bestijs quoq; reperitur. Quo cognoscetur, inquit, qd tibia uel cithara canitur? Hoc nō quærit plebs imperita, dum in templis Papistarum organorum illecebras audiens uelut obstupefacta au ribus arrectis atque ore auscultat hianti.
units.tr: Notice that the Apostle is far differently moved in hearing the sound of instruments than those who take such delight in mere harmony or the resonant tinkling of voices that they do not ask what those voices mean, a delight found even in beasts. "How will it be known," he says, "what is piped or played on the lyre?" The untaught crowd does not ask this, but in the temples of the Papists, hearing the allurements of the organs, it stands as if stunned, ears pricked and mouth gaping open.

units.la: ETENIM si incertam uocem tuba dederit, inquit, quis apparabitur ad bellum? ] Bellicus est tubæ usus, non modò Romanis & alijs gentib. sed & Ebræis. Est aūt alia cornea, alia lignea, alia ductilis. Hac canitur classicum, quo milites ad pugnam, & receptui, quo à pugna uocantur. Omnino militaris tubæ clāgor plurimum habet efficaciæ ad exercitandam non militū modò, sed & equorū ferociā. Verum re quiritur, ut certa ędatur uocū distinctio, unde miles quid clangatur intelligat. Hoc uolens dicit Apostolus: Etenim si incertā uocem tuba dederit, quis apparabitur ad bellū? Sic de tēplarijs ocioforum aqualiculorum |boatibus recte dixeris: Cum incertam uocem templares emittant tubæ, quis apparabitur ad intelligendum, ad orandum, ad psallendum?
units.tr: "For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound," he says, "who will prepare himself for battle?" The trumpet has a military use, not only among the Romans and other peoples but also among the Hebrews. There are trumpets of horn, of wood, and of beaten metal. With the trumpet the signal to advance is sounded, by which soldiers are called to fight, and the signal to retreat, by which they are called back from the fight. Certainly the blare of the military trumpet has great power to rouse the ferocity not only of soldiers but also of horses. But it is required that a clear distinction of sounds be given, so that the soldier understands what is being signalled. The Apostle means this when he says: "For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle?" So too one could rightly say of the idle noise of the temple-mongers' empty bellows: "When the trumpets of the templars give an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself to understand, to pray, to sing psalms?"

units.la: SIC & uos per linguā, inquit, nisi significā te sermonem dederitis, quō intelligetur quod dicitur? ] Quę primū sub sua persona, deinde per similia tibiarum, citharārum ac tubarum consideranda proposuit, iam ad propositum accommodat. Facit autem hoc per apostrophā ad eos qui linguis in ecclesia Corinthio rum loquebantur. Non enim dicit, Sic & uos per linguam nisi significantem sonum audieritis, quo intelligetis quod dicitur? sed nisi significantem sonum dederitis, quomodo intelligetur quod dicitur? Exīstimo aūt quod dicit: cit:Sic & uos per linguâ,idem esse quod, sic & uos per linguâ loquentes. Alias conueniétius esset ad hunc modû: Sic & uos, [illegible, ~6 letters] i.Nisi per linguâ significantê sermonem deritis: sic legerem, si sic transponere uerba liceret. Vocat igitur linguis loquentes, [illegible, ~6 letters], & coparat eos tibijs, citharis ac tubis.
units.tr: "So also you," he says, "through the tongue, unless you give a clear word, how will what is said be understood?" Having first set out these points under his own persona, and then through the likenesses of pipes, lyres and trumpets, he now applies them to his purpose. He does this by turning directly to those who spoke in tongues in the church of the Corinthians. For he does not say, "So also you, if through the tongue you hear a sound that does not signify, how will you understand what is said?" but "unless you give a signifying sound, how will what is said be understood?" I take it that "so also you, through the tongue" means the same as "so also you, who speak through the tongue." Otherwise the sentence would fit better in this way: "So also you, unless you give a signifying word through the tongue." I would read it so, if it were permitted to rearrange the words. He therefore calls those who speak in tongues, and compares them to pipes, lyres and trumpets.

units.la: NISI significantem sermonê dederitis, inquit. Nullius linguae sermo est, qui non alicuius habeat sententiê significationé, siue gentis hominib. intelligibilem. Loquitur aut Apostolus de sermone Corinthijs uulgari & intelligibili. Eum uocat [illegible, ~3 letters] i.bene significantê, claro, perspicuo & manifesto. Quare nô male reddidit uulgatus interpres: nisi manifestum sermone dederitis. Vnicuiq; genti suae linguê sermo [illegible, ~3 letters] est. Sic nobis Germanis [illegible, ~3 letters] sunt, quê patria: [illegible, ~2 letters] uero, q peregrina lingua in ecclesia dicuntur & canûtur. At tenebrarû mystae malût [illegible, ~3 letters] populû lucis, quasi quadâ caligine inuoluere, quàm [illegible, ~3 letters] aedificare.
units.tr: "Unless you give a signifying speech," he says. No language's speech is without some meaning, intelligible to the people of a nation. The Apostle speaks of speech in the Corinthians' common and intelligible tongue. He calls it a well-signifying speech, that is, clear, perspicuous and manifest. So the Vulgate translator did not render it badly: "unless you give a manifest speech." Each nation has its own language, which is its own speech. Thus for us Germans our words are our native speech, but those words which are spoken and sung in church in a foreign tongue are not. Yet the initiates of darkness prefer to wrap the people of light in a kind of fog rather than build them up.

units.la: QVOMODO intelligetur inquit, qd dicitur? Suprà dixit: Quô cognoscetur quod tibia uel cithara canitur? Cõsimili modo urget hic dices: Quô cognoscetur qd dicitur? Quâ illic tam hic quoq; negat se uidere, quô posit intelligi quod idiomate non [illegible, ~3 letters] in ecclesia dicitur. Dicunt ecclesiastici: Quorsum opus est ut intelligantur quae Latino sermone in ecclesia oramus, consecramus & cantamus? Adoranda sunt cum stupore ac deuotione ab imperita multitudine, non intelligenda. Ignorabat hoc Apostolus. Alias non ita serio ursisset, dicens, Quô intelligetur quod dicitur? Si urgeatur Apostolica autoritate Romani: mox dicent, scripsisse apostolum nô Romanae, sed Corinthiorum ecclesiae, quae est in Graecia, & populari sermone utitur: Romana uero Latina lingua tanq patria, nô in urbe modo, sed & in omnib. prouincijs sibi subiectis uti, nec impediri hoc apostoli praescripto, quo minus sua lingua ubiuis gentium utatur, quod nûquam aliter consueuerit, sit uero consuetudo sua lege habenda. Sic animata est, quae se solam apostolica uenditat ecclesia.
units.tr: "How will it be understood," he says, "what is said?" Above he said, "How will it be known what is piped or played on the lyre?" In the same way he urges here: "How will it be known what is said?" In the same way, here too he declares that he cannot see how what is said in the church in a language not understood by the people can be understood. The churchmen say: "Why is it necessary that what we pray, consecrate and sing in Latin in church be understood? It is to be adored with wonder and devotion by the unlearned multitude, not understood." The Apostle did not know this, otherwise he would not have pressed so earnestly, saying, "How will what is said be understood?" If the Romanists press the authority of the Apostle, they will soon say that the Apostle wrote not to the Roman church but to the church of the Corinthians, which is in Greece and uses the vernacular; whereas the Roman church uses the Latin tongue as its native tongue, not only in the city but in all the provinces subject to it, and that this apostolic rule does not hinder it from using its own language everywhere in the world, since it has never done otherwise, and its custom is to be held as law. Such is the spirit of the church that boasts it alone is apostolic.

units.la: ERITIS enim, inquit, in aerem loquetes. Rationem reddit eius quod dixit: Quô intelligetur quod dicitur? quod idem est ac si dicat, nô potest intelligi quod dicitur. Quare? Quia, inquit, eritis in aerem loquentes. Ergo in aere loquitur, qui sic loqtur ut intelligi non possit. In aerem enim loqui, est in uanum loqui, sic ut nullus sermonis sensus ad intelligetiam audientiû perueniat. Quemadmodû in aerem uerberare, sic uerberare est in uanum, ut uerbera corpus aduersarij haudquaq feriat, qua simili tudine suprà est ca.9.usus, dices: Ego itaq; sic curro, ut non in incertum: sic pugilem ago, nô uelut aerem feriens. Germanice dicimus, Est ist eben als wenn einer in luft blast, qû significare uolumus, frustra dici, nec accipi, quae dicûtur. Ambr.exponit: Eritis nihil proficientes.
units.tr: "For you will be speaking into the air," he says. He gives the reason for what he said: "How will what is said be understood?" which is the same as saying: "what is said cannot be understood." Why? "Because," he says, "you will be speaking into the air." So he speaks into the air who speaks in such a way that he cannot be understood. For to speak into the air is to speak in vain, so that no sense of the speech reaches the understanding of the hearers. Just as to beat the air is to strike in vain, so that the blows do not at all hit the body of the opponent, so in a similar comparison the Apostle used the word earlier in chapter 9: "I therefore run in such a way, not uncertainly; I box in such a way, not beating the air." In German we say, "Es ist eben als wenn einer in Luft blast," which we mean as: the things said are spoken in vain and not received. Ambrose explains it: "You will accomplish nothing."

units.la: TAM multa, uerbi gratia, genera uocû sunt in mundo, & nih: horû mutû. Vulgata uersio habet: Tam multa genera linguarum sunt. Et sic Ambrosf.quoq; legit. Et Chrysostomus licet legat [illegible, ~4 letters] i. uocum, exponit tamen de linguis, dicens, [illegible, ~8 letters], [illegible, ~8 letters], &c. Omnino loquitur non de uocibus animalium, sed de linguarû quae sunt in mundo multitudine ac uarietate, siue legamus uoces, siue linguas, id quod ex sequê tibus patet. Tam sunt, inquit, in mundo multa linguarum genera, & nullum eorum est [illegible, ~4 letters] i.sine uoce, hoc est, sine certa uocum significatione. Ambros.sic: sed habet proprias uocum significationes, ut intelligantur. Germanicus interpres reddidit, Vnd ist doch ir keine untcudtlich, quasi [illegible, ~5 letters] ide fit qd [illegible, ~4 letters]. Vt uox speciës est soni, sic loquutio species est uocis, & omnis loquutio est uox. Sic potest [illegible, ~5 letters] ide esse quod sine loquutione, ut intelligamus nullam lingua esse, cui [illegible, ~5 letters] tribui possit. Si litera ur geas, sensus erit iste: Tâ multa sunt, uerbi gratia, genera uocum in mûdo, & nullum eorum sine uoce. Quorsum attinet praedicare de uocib.quod non sint sine uoce? Ridiculus es, si dicas: tam multa sunt genera linguarum in mundo, & nullum eorum est sine lingua. Tâ multa sunt genera metallorum in mundo, & nullum eorum est sine metallo. Quare apparet lectionem uulgatam plus habere rationis, q habeat Graeca, quae nunc est in manib. Si uero legendû uidetur, [illegible, ~5 letters] i.nocum, suspicor qd sequitur, & nullum eorum [illegible, ~5 letters] i.sine uoce, scriptum fuisse ab Apostolo [illegible, ~5 letters] i.& nullum eorum sine sensu existit, & sine mente: postea uero per incuriam antiquariorum [illegible, ~4 letters] positum pro [illegible, ~5 letters]. Verum magis placet, ut legamus: Tam multa sunt genera linguarum in mûdo, & nullum eorum est sine uoce. Nam sequitur: Si igitur nesciero uim uocis, ero ei qui loquitur barbarus, &c. unde satis apparet, non loqui Apostolum de uocib.quorumcunq; animalium, sed de linguis gentium in mundo, quarû nulla est [illegible, ~5 letters] sine uoce, q frustra audias, nisi uim uocis intelligas. Et est sensus: Vel ipsam multitudinem linguarum quae sunt in mundo, considerate, & quae sit illarum conditio perpedite. Nulla illarû est, quae non utatur uocib.aliquid significantibus, quae si non intelligantur, frustra audiuntur, perinde ac si audias hominem barbarum, hoc est perigrinum & lingua incognita loquentem. Sic dicit:
units.tr: "So many, for example, are the kinds of voices in the world, and none of them is mute." The Vulgate version reads: "So many kinds of tongues are in the world." And Ambrose reads it so too. And Chrysostom, although he reads the word for voices, nevertheless explains it of tongues, saying... Altogether the Apostle speaks not of the voices of animals but of the multitude and variety of tongues that are in the world, whether we read voices or tongues, as is clear from what follows. So many kinds of tongues, he says, are in the world, and none of them is without voice, that is, without a definite signification of voices. Ambrose says: "but each has its own meanings of voices, so that they may be understood." The German translator rendered it: "And yet there is none without meaning," as if it were the same thing. As voice is a species of sound, so speech is a species of voice, and every speech is a voice. Thus there can be nothing which is the same as without speech, so that we understand there is no language to which such a thing could be ascribed. If you read the word differently, the sense will be this: "So many kinds of voices, for example, are in the world, and none of them is without voice." What is the point of saying of voices that they are not without voice? You would be ridiculous if you said: "So many kinds of tongues are in the world, and none of them is without tongue. So many kinds of metals are in the world, and none of them is without metal." Hence it appears that the common reading has more reason than the Greek that is now in the hands of readers. But if it seems that the word should be read otherwise, I suspect that what follows, "and none of them is without voice," was written by the Apostle in another form, and that later, through the carelessness of copyists, it was put in place of another word. But it pleases me more to read: "So many kinds of tongues are in the world, and none of them is without voice." For it follows: "If therefore I do not know the force of the voice, I shall be a barbarian to him who speaks, and so on." From this it is clear enough that the Apostle is not speaking of the voices of any animals, but of the tongues of the nations in the world, none of which is without voice, so that you hear it in vain unless you understand the force of the voice. And the sense is: consider the very multitude of tongues that are in the world, and weigh carefully what their condition is. There is none of them that does not use voices signifying something, which, if they are not understood, are heard in vain, just as if you heard a barbarian, that is, a foreigner speaking an unknown language. Thus he says:

units.la: ITAQVE si nesciero uim uocis, ero ei qui loquitur barbarus, & qui loquitur apud me barbarus. Secundum coeptam apostropham dicendum erat: Itaque si nesciatur uis uocum, quib.loquimini, erùt uobis qui audiût barbari, & uos loquentes eritis illis barbari. Verum quo sermonem mitiget, rursus suamipsius per sonam inducit, dices: Itaq; si nesciero uim uocis, ero ei qui loquitur barbarus, & qui loquitur apud me barbarus. Significat non esse sic comparatam Christi ecclesiam, ut amet barbariem, aut debeat in illam religionis loco intro duci inutilis & obscura barbaries.
units.tr: THEREFORE, if I do not know the force of a voice, I shall be a barbarian to the one who speaks, and the one who speaks will be a barbarian to me. Following the address he had begun, he should have said: "Therefore, if the force of the voices in which you speak is not known, those who hear will be barbarians to you, and you who speak will be barbarians to them." But to soften the speech, he again brings in his own person and says: "Therefore, if I do not know the force of a voice, I shall be a barbarian to the one who speaks, and the one who speaks will be a barbarian to me." He signifies that the Church of Christ is not so constituted that it should love barbarism, or that a useless and obscure barbarism should be introduced into its religion in place of worship.

units.la: Satis aute in loco, licet modeste, obijcit illis barbabarbariem, eamq; tă audientium q loquentiū. A Græci nanq; præ cæteris sic erant Gentib.animati, ut omnes peregrinas Gentes pro barbaris haberent, & præ se uehementer fastidirent. Itaq; uelut exprobras dicit: Qui fit ut tato studio linguis incognitis delectemini, cum aliàs omnes peregrinas linguas tanq; barbaras præ uestra summopere exuffletis & fastidiatis? An non barbaries est, quando incognitis linguis in ecclesia loquentes, haud melius intelligimi ni, q fi loquantur inter uos homines barbari?
units.tr: In this passage, though modestly, he indeed rebukes them for barbarism, and for the barbarism of hearers as much as of speakers. For the Greeks, above all other peoples, were so spirited that they regarded all foreign nations as barbarians and held them in great contempt. So, as if reproaching them, he says: "How is it that you delight so eagerly in unknown tongues, when at other times you so greatly sneer at and despise all foreign languages as barbarous? Is it not barbarism, when those who speak in the Church in unknown tongues are understood no better than if men of barbarous speech were talking among you?"

units.la: Obserua uero, quod non simpliciter dicit, Ero ei qui loquitur barbarus: sed addit, & qui loquitur apud me barbarus erit. Qui linguis in ecclesia Corinthiorũ loquebantur, facile cò cessissent, barbaros esse idiotas illos, à quibus loquetes non intelligebātur, dixiffentq;, quid ad nos imperitia ac ruditas barbarorũ? Verũ quod addit: Et qui loquitur, apud me ιψ ιμοι, i. in me, meo iudicio, barbarus erit, magis aliquâ to habebat acrimoniæ, ad perstringendum illorum ftulticiam & inflatione. Quàm.n.facile ferebant idiotas uocari barbaros, tam ægre audebant se illis uicisim esse barbaros. Romani quoque cæteras, præsertim Germanorum, nationes pro barbaris iam olim habere cõsue uerunt. Qui lingna illorum in ecclesijs Germanorum utuntur, haud grauatim admittent, si dicas omnes eos esse barbaros, à quib. Latinè murmurantes ac boantes non intelliguntur. Quid.n.hic grauarentur, cum nõ dubitent eos uocare bestias? At si dixeris oês eos, qui in ecclesia lingua utuntur incognita, esse populo Christianorum barbaros, id demũ prorsus inferendum esse clamabũt. Piaculum quippe du cet latina lingua, Romana illâ uocari barbarâ.
units.tr: Observe that he does not simply say, "I shall be a barbarian to the one who speaks," but adds, "and the one who speaks to me will be a barbarian." Those who spoke in tongues in the Church of the Corinthians could easily have conceded that those ignorant men, by whom they were not understood, were barbarians, and could have said, "What concern is the inexperience and roughness of barbarians to us?" But what he adds, "and the one who speaks, [ἐν ἐμοί], that is, in me, in my judgment, will be a barbarian," has more sharpness, to strike at their folly and conceit. For as easily as they bore being called barbarians by the uneducated, so reluctantly would they dare to be called barbarians in turn by them. The Romans too had long been accustomed to regard the other nations, especially the Germans, as barbarians. Those who use their tongue in the churches of the Germans will not be at all offended if you say that all of them are barbarians, by whom those who mutter and bellow in Latin are not understood. For why should they be offended here, since they do not hesitate to call them beasts? But if you say that all who speak in the Church in an unknown tongue are barbarians to the Christian people, they will cry out that this must be the very conclusion drawn. For they consider it a sacrilege to call the Latin tongue, the Roman tongue, barbarous.

units.la: Ita & uos, quandoquidem sectatores estis spiritus, ad ædificatione ecclesiæ, quærite ut excellatis. Quapropter qui loquitur lingua, oret ut interpretetur.
units.tr: Thus also you, since you are zealots of the Spirit, seek to excel for the edification of the Church. Wherefore, let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret.

units.la: Eraf.uertit.Itaq; & uos: quasi sit in Græco, καὶ ὑμεῖς ἐν. Vulgata uero habet: Sic & uos. Atq; sic est in Græco, ὅτως καὶ ὑμεῖς. Quèadmodū pau lò suprà, cũ similitudine tibiæ, citharæ, ac tubæ induxisset, ut illam accomodaret, subiecit: Sic & uos per linguâ loquentes. Q.d. Similes estis tibijs, citharis ac tubis, nisi significatem sermonem dederitis, &c. consimili modo & hic, ubi dixit, Si nesciero uim uocis, ero ei qui loquitur barbarus, & qui loquitur apud me barbarus, ut id illis applicet, subiungit: Ita & uos, subaudi, si nescieritis uim uocis, barbari estis illis qui loquuntur: & qui loquùtur apud uos, sunt barbari. Ista quidem non expressit, nisi sub sua persona, ne morosiores illorũ offenderet, interim tñ cogitanda esse significauit, dicens, ὅτως καὶ ὑμεῖς: Sic & uos. Scio alios aliter exponere, uerum hæc expositio, mea sententia, apparet esse simplicior.
units.tr: Erasmus translates "Itaque & uos" [καὶ ὑμεῖς ἐν] as though the Greek had this reading, whereas the Vulgate has "Sic & uos" [ὅτως καὶ ὑμεῖς]. Just above, when he had introduced the comparison of the flute, the lyre and the trumpet, in order to apply it he added: "So also you, speaking in tongues." That is to say: you are like flutes, lyres and trumpets, unless you give a meaningful sound, and so on. In the same way here, where he said, "If I do not know the force of a voice, I shall be a barbarian to the one who speaks, and the one who speaks to me is a barbarian," in order to apply this to them he adds: "So also you," supply: if you do not know the force of a voice, you are barbarians to those who speak, and those who speak among you are barbarians. He did not express this in his own person except to avoid offending the more peevish among them, yet he signified that it must be considered, saying [ὅτως καὶ ὑμεῖς]: "So also you." I know that others explain it differently, but this explanation, in my view, appears to be the simpler.

units.la: Q VANDO Q VIDEM sectatores estis spiritũ, inquit, ad ædificatione ecclesiæ quærite ut excellatis.] Subijcit argumentatroni parænesim, adhortans eos, ut linguis utilitate inter
units.tr: "SINCE YOU ARE indeed zealots of the Spirit," he says, "seek to excel for the edification of the Church." He adds to his argument an exhortation, urging them that, with the usefulness of tongues among

units.la: ptationis adiungât. Huius rei studiũ poscit, dices: Quærite ut excellatis. Ité, oret ut interpretetur. Cũ dicit, Quærite ut excellatis, intelligit de prophetia & interpretatione, quibus excellentiá supra linguas hactenus tribuit. Supràdixit: Aemulemini spiritualia, magis tñ ut ppheletis. Idé hic alijs uerbis inculcans, dicit: Quàdoquidem æmulatores estis spiritũ, quærite ut excellatis. Aemulabantur spiritualia. i. charismata spiritus, quare eos appellat æmulatores spiritũ, donorum uidelicet spiritus. Et ex hac illorum æmulatione occasione sumit, hortandi eos ad studium prophetiæ & interpretationis, per quas excellenter spirituales reddererentur.
