Perinde facit Apostolus, ac si quis eos qui umbratili doctrina ad ostentatione tantũ acquisita impèse delectantur, hortaturus ut so lidiore qrant dicat: Quandoquidé sectatores estis bonarum literarũ, quærite ut excellatis: hoc est, ei uos doctrinæ tradite, in qua singularem eminentiam inueniatis.
units.tr: ...interpretation be joined to them. He demands zeal for this matter, saying: "Seek to excel." Likewise: "Let him pray that he may interpret." When he says, "Seek to excel," he means prophecy and interpretation, by which he has hitherto ascribed excellence above tongues. Above he said: "Be zealous for spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy." Here, inculcating the same thing in other words, he says: "Since you are emulators of the Spirit, seek to excel." They were zealous for spiritual things, that is, the charismata of the Spirit, and therefore he calls them emulators of the Spirit, namely of the gifts of the Spirit. And from this emulation of theirs he takes occasion to exhort them to the study of prophecy and interpretation, through which they might be made eminently spiritual. The Apostle does the same as if someone, wishing to exhort those who take great delight in a shadowy learning acquired only for display, to seek something more solid, were to say: "Since you are zealots of good letters, seek to excel; that is, devote yourselves to that teaching in which you may find a singular eminence."

units.la: Ne uero simpliciter eos ad studiũ excellentiæ ac supereminentiæ prouocare uideatur, cũ dicit, quærite ut excellatis: prærnittit scopum ac finem, ad quê eo studio collimare debeant, nempe ad ædificationem ecclesiæ. Hic scòpus alienisimus est à studio carnis, quæ non hoc fine excellere cupit, ut prosit alijs, sed ut golri osa appareat. Ad gloriam eminentiæ aspirabat alioqui, quos tota hac disputatiõe perstringit. Et hoc illorum studium obliquè perstringens dicit, ad ædificationem ecclesiæ quærite ut excellatis. Q.d. Non ad inanem oftetationem & gloriam, cuius facti estis auidi.
units.tr: But lest he seem simply to provoke them to a zeal for excellence and superiority when he says, "seek to excel," he sets before them the aim and end to which they ought to direct that zeal, namely the edification of the Church. This aim is most alien to the zeal of the flesh, which desires to excel not for this end, that it may profit others, but that it may appear glorious. Otherwise, those whom he censures in this whole disputation aspired to the glory of eminence. And, touching this zeal of theirs obliquely, he says: "Seek to excel for the edification of the Church." That is: not for empty ostentation and glory, for which you are eager.

units.la: Est ergo studiũ excellentiæ in ijs rebus, quæ uel prodesse possunt alijs, uel religionis ac pietatis nostræ professione concernunt, tam non uituperabile, ut apostolica quoq; dignũ sit ad hortatione, modo absit affectatio inanis gloriæ, adsit uerò propositũ iuuandi alios, & facie di quod Christianæ fidei professione deceat. Tale est qd' 1.Tim.3.dicit: Qui episcopatũ desiderat, bonũ opus desiderat. Sed refert admodũ quo proposito, & ad quê finê desideretur, ne episcopalis illa ambitio quę obtinuit, proh dolor, in ecclesia probanda uideatur. Luctandũ nobis est, ut excellamus in uera iustitia, in spe, in opere dñi, in quouis opere bono, in charitate fraterna, &c. Huc uocat nos dñs, Matth. 5.dicens, nisi abundauerit: uel, excelluerit iustitia uestra plus quàm Scribarum & Pharisęorum, non intrabitis in regnum cœlorum. Et Apostolus Rom.15 Vt excellatis in spe. Et infrà ca.15.Excellètes in opere dñi semper. Et 2. Cor.9.Excellite ad omne opus bonũ. Et Phil. 1.Vt charitas uestra magis ac magis excellat.
units.tr: Therefore the zeal for excellence is in those matters which either can profit others or concern the profession of our religion and piety, and it is so far from blameworthy that it is even worthy of apostolic exhortation, provided that empty vainglory be absent and there be present a purpose of helping others and of doing what befits the profession of the Christian faith. Such is what he says in 1 Tim. 3: "He who desires the episcopate desires a good work." But it matters greatly with what purpose, and to what end, it is desired, lest that episcopal ambition which, alas, has prevailed in the Church, seem to be approved. We must strive to excel in true righteousness, in hope, in the work of the Lord, in every good work, in brotherly love, and so on. The Lord calls us to this in Matt. 5, saying: "Unless your righteousness abounds, or excels, more than that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven." And the Apostle, Rom. 15: "That you may excel in hope." And below, ch. 15: "Always excelling in the work of the Lord." And 2 Cor. 9: "Excel in every good work." And Phil. 1: "That your love may excel more and more."

units.la: Q VA P R O P T E R, inquit, qui loquitur lingua, oret ut interpretetur.] Illatio est pareneti ca pariter & expositoria. Quod nõ simpliciter dicit: Qui loquitur lingua: sed, Quapropter q loqtur lingua, oret ut interpretetur, illatione habet qua ex præmisis infert adhortationem ad studiũ interpretationis. Q.d. Quapropter cũ hæc sint linguarum & uocum conditio, ut nisi intelligantur, inanes sint ac barbarae, qui loquitur lingua, oret ut interpretetur.
units.tr: "WHEREFORE," HE says, "let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret." This is an inference both exhortatory and explanatory. He does not simply say, "The one who speaks in a tongue," but, "Wherefore, let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret." By this inference he draws from what precedes an exhortation to the study of interpretation. That is: therefore, since this is the condition of tongues and voices, that unless they are understood they are empty and barbarous, let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret.

units.la: Deinde quod dicit, qui loquitur lingua, oret ut interpretetur, trina habet expositione. Primum eius quod in praecedenti generaliter dixit, quadoquidè sectatores estis spiritu um: deinde eius quoq; qd' adiecit, quaerite: tertio & eius qd' sequitur, ut excellatis. Quid voluerit dicens, Quandoquidè sectatores estis spiritu um, in eo exprimit quod hic dicit: qui loquitur lingua. Ad hoc studiu linguis loquendi respexerat, cum uocaret eos sectatores spiritu. Deinde quo uelit eos quaerere ut excellant, aperit dicens, oret. Tertio, qua in re uelit eos excellere, exponit cum dicit, ut interpretetur.
units.tr: Next, what he says, "let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret," has a threefold explanation. First, of what he said generally above, "Since you are zealots of the Spirit"; then of what he added, "seek"; and third, of what follows, "that you may excel." What he meant in saying, "Since you are zealots of the Spirit," he expresses in what he says here: "the one who speaks in a tongue." He had regard to this zeal for speaking in tongues when he called them zealots of the Spirit. Then, in what respect he wishes them to seek to excel, he makes clear by saying "let him pray." Third, in what matter he wishes them to excel, he explains when he says, "that he may interpret."

units.la: Quod no simpliciter dicit, qui loquitur lingua, interpretetur: sed, oret ut interpretetur, a dimit illis tergiuersatione, ne dicat, quo interpretabimur, nisi sciamus? Oret, inquit, ut interpretari sciat, hoc est, nt donu interpretandi accipiat: qui lingua loquitur, postulet a domino, qui no negabit. Cum enim ultro dederit donum linguarum, quo petentibus negaret donum interpretationis, tam ad ecclesiae edificationem necessarium? Efficaciam orationis huius promisit ipse dominus, dicens: Petite, & dabitur uobis, quaerite & inuenietis, pulsate & aperietur uobis. Omnis enim qui petit accipit, & qui quaerit inuenit, & pulsanti aperietur. Matt. 7. Et Iacobi 1. sic legimus: Quod si cui uestrum deest sapientia, postulet ab eo qui dat, nempe Deo qui dat omnibus simpliciter, nec exprobrat, ac dabitur ei. Verum postulet cum fiducia, nihil haesitans. Hinc tamen non est ut ocio sis ac ignauis uentrib. patrocinium permittamus, qui neglectis sacrae scripturae studijs exercitijs ac disciplinis, uotis, nescio quibus, cum Deo agendu esse putant, ut doctieuadat. Cum Apostolus ista scriberet, uigebant in ecclesia miraculosa illa spirituum sanctiharismata, doec sparsum esset in orbe, & confirmatu Euangelii, quae postea cessarunt, studijsq; disciplinis & exercitijs legendi ac discedi scripturas locu dederunt. Haud quidè excludeda est orationis sedulitas, uerum coiungenda illi sunt necessaria studia, & ignauum excludendum ocium.
units.tr: He does not simply say, "He who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret," but "let him pray that he may interpret." Why does he put it this way, so as to avoid evasion? Otherwise someone might say, "How can we interpret unless we know how?" He says, "Let him pray that he may be able to interpret, that is, that he may receive the gift of interpreting. Let him who speaks in a tongue ask the Lord, who will not refuse." For when God has freely given the gift of tongues, would he refuse the gift of interpretation to those who ask, when it is just as necessary for the building up of the Church? The Lord himself promised the efficacy of this prayer when he said: "Ask, and it will be given you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened" (Matt. 7). And in James 1 we read: "If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of him who gives, namely God, who gives to all generously and without reproach, and it will be given him. But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing." Yet from this we should not grant a defence to lazy and idle bellies, who, neglecting the studies, exercises and disciplines of Holy Scripture, think that they must deal with God by vows, I know not what, so that they may be taught. When the Apostle wrote these things, those miraculous gifts of the Holy Spirit were flourishing in the Church, until the Gospel had been spread through the world and established; afterwards these gifts ceased, and gave place to study, discipline and exercise in reading and examining the Scriptures. Certainly the diligence of prayer is not to be excluded, but those necessary studies are to be joined to it, and idle leisure is to be excluded.

units.la: Nam si ore lingua, spiritus meus orat, at mens mea fructu uacat. Quid igitur est? Orabo spiritu, sed orabo & mente. Canã spiritu, sed cana & mente. Alioqui si benedixeris spiritu, is qui implet locu idiotae, quo dicturus est Ame, ad ad tua gratiarua ctione? Quandoquidè quid dicas nescit. Nam tu quidè bene gratias agis, uerum alius non aedificatur.
units.tr: "For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful. What then is to be done? I will pray with the spirit, but I will pray with the mind also. I will sing with the spirit, but I will sing with the mind also. Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, how will he who fills the place of the untrained person say 'Amen' to your thanksgiving? For he does not know what you are saying. For you indeed give thanks well, but the other is not built up."

units.la: Dixit: Quapropter qui loquitur lingua, oret ut interpretetur. Hic subiungendum erat: nam qui loquitur lingua, spiritus quidè eius loquitur, at mens eius fructu uacat. Verum quoniam illi non modo mysteria Dei linguis in ecclesia loquebantur, sed & linguis orabát, cane
units.tr: He had said: "Therefore let him who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret." Here he had to add: "For he who speaks in a tongue, his spirit indeed speaks, but his mind is unfruitful." But since those men not only spoke the mysteries of God in tongues in the Church, but also prayed, sang

units.la: bát et gratias agebát, ut eis quoq; rei inutilitate pstringat, mutata psona seipsum inducit, dices: Nā si oré lingua, spiritus meus orat, &c. Quid sit aut orare, canere ac bene dicere spiritu, supra dictu est, ibi: Spiritu uero loquitur mysteria.
units.tr: and gave thanks in tongues, he sets forth, by changing the person, the uselessness of this even for them, saying: "For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays," and so on. What it is to pray, sing and bless in the spirit has been said above, where he says: "But in the spirit he speaks mysteries."

units.la: NAM si ore lingua, inquit. Per occasionē eius quod dixit, Qui loquitur lingua, oret ut interpretetur: abusum illu corrigit, quo lingua incognita in ecclesia orabát. Et cōcedit quidè orare eu, qui sic orat, uerum annectit, quid in hoc orationis genere desideretur. Spiritus quidem meus orat, inquit, uerum mens mea fructu caret. Q.d. Concedo quidem si lingua ore, orare me spiritu, hoc est, spiritus afflatu, per quē linguis loquor. Verū quoniā hoc orationis genus intellectu audientiū destituitur, fit ut mens mea, id est sensus mentis meae, qui est in ui uerborū, nihil adferat fructus. Quo.n. fructum non intellecta cuiq; adferret? Chrysost. sic exponit: Ostendit non modo alijs eum qui lingua orat, sed & sibijpsi esse inutile, quod nec ipse intelligat ea quę orat. Sic exponunt istam particulam, At mens mea fructu uacat, & Hiero. & Ambr. de fructu non aliorū audientium, sed eius qui lingua orans, nō intelligit sensum uerborum quae orando loquitur: ad quē modum orant Nonnae, & ij qui dominica oratioæem Latine exprimūt, cum sint idiotae, nihil Latine scientes. Priori tū expositioni sequentia magis fauent. Quicquid sit, improbatur hactenus qui lingua incognita orat, quatenus sine intellectu uerborū orat. Obsecro an nō omnium uerissime orationes illas Papisticas, quas Latino sermone profundunt in templis, ἀκάρπους. i. infrugiferas & inanes uocabimus? qd' ueros uerae pietatis fructus attinet, quantumuis sint simoniacis uentriculis admodum quaestuosae? quorū pars maxima sine mete orat, reliqua multitudo plebis prorsus nihil ex illis intelligit, pro quib. tū nunquam non numerare cogitur. Quid quod superstitio eidololatrica accedit, qua aures Dei irritantur magis quam placatur. Quàm est parum, qd' dicit hic Apostolus, mente incognita lingua orātis uacare fructu, si respicias quantum hodie accedat impostura, quaestus & impietatis?
units.tr: "For if I pray in a tongue," he says. On the occasion of what he said, "Let him who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret," he corrects the abuse by which people prayed in an unknown tongue in the Church. He does indeed concede that he who prays in this way does pray, but he adds what is lacking in this kind of prayer. "My spirit indeed prays," he says, "but my mind is without fruit." That is: I grant indeed that if I pray in a tongue, I pray in the spirit, that is, by the inspiration of the Spirit through which I speak in tongues. But since this kind of prayer is deprived of the understanding of the hearers, it comes about that my mind, that is, the sense of my mind which lies in the power of the words, brings forth no fruit at all. For how could it bring fruit to anyone who does not understand it? Chrysostom explains it thus: "He shows that the one who prays in a tongue is useless not only to others, but also to himself, since he does not himself understand the things he prays." Jerome and Ambrose also explain this clause, "but my mind is unfruitful," as referring to the fruit not of the other hearers, but of him who prays in a tongue and does not understand the sense of the words he utters in prayer. In this way pray the nuns, and those who render the Lord's Prayer in Latin, though they are unlearned and know no Latin. Nevertheless the following words favour the former explanation more. Whatever the case, what is condemned so far is the one who prays in an unknown tongue, insofar as he prays without understanding the words. I ask, shall we not most truly call those Papist prayers, which they pour out in Latin in their temples, unfruitful [ἀκάρπους], that is, barren and empty? As for the true fruits of genuine piety, how profitable they are even to the simoniacal bellies! The greater part of them pray without mind, and the rest of the crowd of common people understand nothing of them, for which they are nonetheless always forced to pay. Add to this that idolatrous superstition is joined, by which God's ears are provoked rather than appeased. How little is it, then, that the Apostle says here, that those who pray in a tongue unknown to the mind are deprived of fruit, if you consider how much imposture, profit-making and impiety is added today!

units.la: QVID igitur est, inquit. Intellige faciedu? Hoc est: Quo igitur orabo, ne mens mea fructu uacet? Sic animati sunt pij, ut ubi admonētur inania & infrugifera esse q faciunt, praesertim in operib. religione ac pietatem concernētibus, confestim de emendatione consultent, ac dicant: Quid igitur faciendum? Non delectantur uanis & inutilibus, nedum noxijs & abominandis. Clamat Christus: Fruštra colūt me docentes doctrinas & mādata hominum, at quotusquisq; eorum est, qui partim haec imponunt humeris fidelium, partim imposita su perstitiose portant, qui dicat: Quid igitur faciendum? Tam multis disputat hoc loco Apostolus contra eos qui linguis incognitis in ecclesia Christi utuntur, at quis ex illis est, qui dicit: Quid igitur faciendum?
units.tr: "What then is to be done?" he says. Understand what is to be done. That is: "Then how shall I pray, so that my mind is not unfruitful?" The godly are so disposed that, when they are warned that what they do is vain and unfruitful, especially in works that concern religion and piety, they immediately seek correction and say: "What then is to be done?" They do not delight in vain and useless things, much less in harmful and abominable ones. Christ cries out: "They worship me in vain, teaching doctrines and commandments of men" (Matt. 15). But how few of them are there who, partly laying these burdens on the shoulders of the faithful, and partly superstitiously carrying the burdens laid on them, say: "What then is to be done?" The Apostle argues at such length in this place against those who use unknown tongues in the Church of Christ; but who among them is there who says: "What then is to be done?"

units.la: ORABO, inquit, spiritu, sed orabo & mente. Canam spiritu, sed canam & mente.] Sic docet quid sit faciendum. Quoniam donum linguarum uigebat in ecclesia, ne illi propter quorundam glorias iniquus esse uideatur, dicit: Orabo & canam spiritu, hoc est, utar linguis & orando & canendo: uerum sic illud faciam, ut & mens accedat, hoc est, quae linguis orauero ac cecinero, intelligeter etiam orabo ac cana, lingua uidelicet communi & usitata.
units.tr: "I will pray with the spirit," he says, "but I will pray with the mind also. I will sing with the spirit, but I will sing with the mind also." Thus he teaches what is to be done. Since the gift of tongues was flourishing in the Church, lest he seem unfair to some on account of the glory of certain people, he says: "I will pray and sing in the spirit," that is, I will use tongues both in praying and in singing; but I will do it in such a way that the mind also comes in, that is, I will pray and sing so that what I have prayed and sung in tongues is also understood, namely in the common and customary tongue.

units.la: ORABO spiritu, inquit, sed orabo & mente.] Dices: Cum oratio fiat ad Deum, idq; secreto, quorsum attinet lingua uulgari orare, quasi non intelligat Deus aliam? An non satis intelligenter orat, qui ipse quid dicat & petat intelligit? An qui Latine sciens Latine orat, etiamsi patriam linguam non ignorat, non orat sufficienter, nisi quae Latine dicit, dicat & lingua uulgari?
units.tr: "I will pray in the spirit," he says, "but I will pray with the mind also." You will say: since prayer is made to God, and that in secret, what is the point of praying in the common tongue, as if God did not understand another? Does not he pray intelligently enough who himself understands what he says and asks? Or does not he who knows Latin and prays in Latin pray sufficiently, unless he also says in the vernacular tongue what he says in Latin, even though he is not ignorant of his native language?

units.la: Respondeo. In oratione priuata & secreta satis est mentis, si orans suaipsius uerba intelligit, quacunque tandem lingua ad omnia intelligentem Deum utatur. Verum non loquitur hic Apostolus de priuatis orationibus, sed de Ecclesiasticis, quae in coetu fidelium linguis incognitis absque omni fructu fiebant. Hic poscit, ut qui palam orat in ecclesia, oret non lingua tantum, sed & mente, quo cum fructu oret.
units.tr: I answer. In private and secret prayer it is enough for the mind if the one praying understands his own words, in whatever tongue he uses toward God, who understands all things. But the Apostle is not speaking here of private prayers, but of ecclesiastical ones, which in the assembly of the faithful were made in unknown tongues without any fruit. Here he requires that he who prays openly in the Church should pray not only with the tongue but also with the mind, so that he prays with fruit.

units.la: CANAM spiritu, inquit, sed canam & mente.] In Greco est ψαλῶ, id est, Psallam. Credibile est, nonnullos in ecclesia Corinthiorum Psalmos Dauidis Hebraico idiomate cecinisse. Illos sub sua persona monet, ut Psalmos suos lingua canant, quae intelligi possit ab ecclesia. Si ue Psalmos Dauidis, siue alia quaedam cecinerint, puto satis constare morem fuisse in ecclesia, ut Deo canerent. Non est autem ut uerbum psallendi ad ea cantica restringamus, quibus ad instrumenta musica, siue citharam, siue psalterium, siue lyram cantare nonnulli solent. Licet enim psallere proprie sit ad tale instrumentum canere, nihil tamen impedit, quo minus, praesertim in ecclesia, de quouis cantico accipiatur. Nec uerosimile est primos Christianos musicis instrumentis usos esse in ecclesia.
units.tr: "I will sing with the spirit," he says, "but I will sing with the mind also." In the Greek it is ψαλῶ [psalō], that is, "I will psalm" (Psallam). It is credible that some in the Corinthian Church sang the Psalms of David in the Hebrew idiom. He admonishes them, in his own person, to sing their psalms in a tongue that can be understood by the Church. Whether they sang the Psalms of David or certain other songs, I think it is sufficiently clear that it was the custom in the Church to sing to God. Nor are we to restrict the word "to psalm" to those songs which some are accustomed to sing to musical instruments, whether the cithara, the psaltery or the lyre. For although to psallein properly means to sing to such an instrument, nothing prevents it, especially in the Church, from being taken of any song whatever. Nor is it likely that the first Christians used musical instruments in the Church.

units.la: Alioqui si benedixeris spiritu, inquit, is qui implet locum idiotae, quomodo dicturus est, Amen, ad tuam gratiarum actionem?
units.tr: Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, he says, how will the one who fills the place of the layman say Amen to your thanksgiving?

units.la: Vulgata uersio habet: Caeterum si benedixeris spiritu. In Greco est, εὐλογῆς, quod sane sonat alioqui: uerum uulgatus interpres legisse uidetur ἐπεί, id est, praeterea, deinde, ceterum, quae lectio haud uidetur inconueniens. Et sic Ambrosius quoque legit. Quod si omnino legendum uidetur, Alioqui, referenda sic est haec particula ad praecedentia, ut rationem illorum adferat. Solenne est ecclesiae, ut publicis precibus ac psalmis gratias agat Deo, offeratque illi sacrificium laudis. Plebs rudis & indocta uotis astipulabatur, & ad finem orationis aut Psalmi
units.tr: The Vulgate version reads: "Caeterum si benedixeris spiritu." The Greek has εὐλογῆς [eulogēs], which indeed means "otherwise," but the Vulgate translator seems to have read ἐπεί [epei], that is, "moreover, then, besides," and that reading is not unsuitable. Ambrose also reads it this way. If it must be read "Otherwise" (alioqui), the particle is to be referred to what precedes, so that it gives the reason for those things. It is the custom of the Church to give thanks to God in public prayers and psalms and to offer him the sacrifice of praise. The uneducated common people added their assent with their prayers, and at the end of a prayer or psalm they sang back that word Amen, whose great use is still found in the Church today.

units.la: mi succinebat illud, Amen, cuius hodie quoque magnus est usus in ecclesia. Cum ergo admonuisset, & orandum & psallendum esse non spiritu tantum, sed & mente: subiecit hanc rationem dicens, Alioqui si benedixeris, id est, gratias egeris spiritu, intellige, tantum, & sine mente, quid consequetur? Hoc uidelicet, ut plebs imperita, cuius uos nullam rationem habetis, quamuis adstet, & sonitum uocis strepitumq; labiorum audiat, nesciat tamen animo & ore consentire in ea quae dicis. Hoc intelligit cum dicit: quomodo dicturus est, Amen, ad tuam gratiarum actionem? Est enim Amen uox Hebraea, idem quod ueraciter ac certo. Hac consentiens & adstipulans ecclesiae populus confirmabat publicas preces, psalmos & gratiarum actiones. Sic Hieronymus in prologo secundi libri in epistolam ad Galatas de populo Romano dicit: Vbi sic ad similitudinem coelestis tonitrui Amen reboat. Vnde facile conijcitur non clerum duntaxat, sed totam ecclesiam ad finem orationum succiuuisse illud Amen, idq; tantae multitudinis reboatu, ut instar coelestis esset tonitrui.
units.tr: Having admonished that one must pray and sing not only with the spirit but also with the mind, he added this reason: "Otherwise, if you bless, that is, give thanks, in spirit (understand: only) and without the mind, what will follow?" Namely this: the unskilled common people, whom you take no account of, though they stand by and hear the sound of your voice and the noise of your lips, do not know how to agree in heart and mouth to what you say. This is what he means when he says: "how will he say Amen to your thanksgiving?" For Amen is a Hebrew word, meaning the same as "truly and certainly." Agreeing and assenting with it, the people of the Church confirmed the public prayers, psalms and thanksgivings. So Jerome, in the prologue to his second book on the Epistle to the Galatians, says of the Roman people: "where Amen resounds like heavenly thunder." Hence it is easily conjectured that not the clergy alone but the whole Church joined in that Amen at the end of the prayers, with such a roar from so great a multitude that it was like heavenly thunder.

units.la: IS qui implet locum idiotae, inquit.] Sic est in Greco. Erasmus uertit, is qui implet locum indocti. Idiota, uox Graeca, sonat hominem priuatum, nullo fungentem publico officio: unde uulgares ac plebeij idiotae uocantur. Et quia plebeij homines plerunque sunt indocti, fit ut nonnunquam idiota pro indocto accipiatur. Meo iudicio idiotas uocat Apostolus plebem ecclesiae, quae in coetum uenit, ut audiat, discat, & in fide aedificetur. Et huius potissima est a doctoribus habenda ratio: perinde atque in scholis habenda est maior ratio rudiu, eorumque qui tardo sunt ingenio, & in domibus parvulorum, & in grege omnium imbecillorum. Ideo non simpliciter hic dicit, is qui audit: sed, is qui implet locum idiotae, quomodo dicturus est Amen, ad tuam gratiarum actionem?
units.tr: "Who fills the place of the layman," he says. So it is in the Greek. Erasmus translates "who fills the place of the unlearned." Idiota, a Greek word, means a private person who holds no public office; hence common and plebeian people are called idiotae. And because plebeian people are mostly unlearned, idiota is sometimes taken to mean unlearned. In my judgment the Apostle calls the common people of the Church idiotae: those who come into the assembly to hear, learn and be built up in faith. Teachers ought chiefly to take account of these, just as in schools greater account is to be taken of the beginners and the slow of wit, in the households of little children, and in the flock of all the weak. So he does not simply say "he who hears," but "he who fills the place of the layman: how will he say Amen to your thanksgiving?"

units.la: Quid est autem quod non simpliciter dicit, is qui idiota est: sed is qui implet locum idiotae? Primum, non est philosophandum in verbo implendi uel supplendi. Quemadmodum supplere locum ministri in ecclesia, est esse ministrum ecclesiae, locum implere magistratus, est esse magistratum: ita implere locum idiotae, est esse idiotam. Vtitur autem singulari pro plurali, ut sit sensus, Qui idiotae sunt in ecclesia. Deinde innuitur alium esse locum, id est, condition em, ordinem & gradum ministrorum & alium idiotarum, id est, plebis. Qui hic idiotae uocantur, aliàs auditores appellari solent. Locus ministrorum, est locus pastorum: plebis uero, locus est gregis. Templa communiter in duas separatas stationes diuiserunt, quarum superiorem, quae fit in conspectu populi, sacerdotibus ac clero, inferiorem uero plebi doputarunt. De huiusmodi locis non intelligit Apostolus. Potest fieri ut in statione chori sit minister, qui tamen locum suum non impleat,
units.tr: But why does he not simply say "he who is a layman," but "he who fills the place of the layman"? First, one should not philosophize about the verb "to fill" or "to supply." Just as to supply the place of a minister in the Church is to be a minister of the Church, and to fill the place of a magistrate is to be a magistrate, so to fill the place of the layman is to be a layman. He uses the singular for the plural, so that the sense is: those who are laymen in the Church. Next, it is hinted that there is one place, that is, one condition, order and rank, of ministers, and another of laymen, that is, of the people. Those who are here called laymen are otherwise commonly called hearers. The place of the ministers is the place of the pastors; the place of the people is the place of the flock. Churches have commonly been divided into two separate stations: the upper, which is in view of the people, they assigned to priests and clergy, and the lower they assigned to the people. The Apostle does not mean places of this kind. It can happen that a minister is in the choir's station and yet does not fill his place,

units.la: A
units.tr: A

units.la: B pleat, hoc est, officium suū non faciat, & in statione idiotarum sit idiota: qui tamen idiotę locum non impleat, hoc est, non cogitet, in quę finem appareat in cœtu, dum nō est animo ad audiendum ac discendum intentus ad ea quæ dicuntur & geruntur.
units.tr: that is, does not do his office; and one who is a layman in the laymen's station may still not fill the layman's place, that is, he does not think about what is said and done, and so he appears in the assembly while his mind is not intent on hearing and learning from what is said and done.

units.la: QVOMODO dicturus est, Amē, inquit.] Omnino requiritur, ut concordia sint, & consentientia fideliū uota, dum oratio ad Deū dirigitur. Haud est inusitatū ecclesiæ, ut publicè oret unus pro omnibus. Et multa sunt quæ omnes communiter concernentia rectè unius ore petuntur à domino. Verūm admonet nos hic præsens Apostoli locus, eiusmodi preces claudendas esse & cōfirmandas idiotarum, id est, auditorum succlamatione, qua se hæc ipsa in uotis habere testentur, quæ unus ipsorum nomine ad Deū orauit. At hodie, nec qui orat, nec qui audiunt admodum in uotis habēt quę uerbis inter orandum proferuntur. Dum oratur in ecclesia unius ore ministri, & per pueros ad mensam, quotusquisq; est, qui respondeat, Amen, cum id ex animo fieri cōueniat ab omnibus. Clerus Papistarū satis fortiter clamat, Amen. At interim non facit hoc ex cōsensu ac uoto cordiū, sed pro more recepto, magis gaudens de fine orationum, quàm de principio, ideoq; inuenias qui pro Amen, dicant, Amend: præterquam quod plerunq; non animaduertunt, quibus nam petitionibus Amen hoc sucinant. Quid igitur mirū, quod tot seculis iam maiori ex parte frustra oramus ad Deum?
units.tr: "How will he say Amen," he says. It is altogether required that the prayers of the faithful agree and consent while the prayer is directed to God. It is not unusual in the Church for one person to pray publicly for all, and many things that concern everyone in common are rightly asked of the Lord by one mouth. But this passage of the Apostle admonishes us that such prayers should be closed and confirmed by the acclamation of the laymen, that is, the hearers, by which they bear witness that they hold in their desires the things which one of them prayed to God in their name. But today neither he who prays nor those who hear have much in their desires what is spoken in words during prayer. While prayer is made in the Church by the mouth of one minister, and through boys at the altar, how few there are who answer Amen, although it ought to be done from the heart by everyone. The clergy of the Papists shout Amen fairly loudly, yet they do not do this from the consent and desire of their hearts, but from received custom, rejoicing more at the end of the prayers than at the beginning. Hence you will find some who say "Amend" instead of Amen; besides, they mostly do not notice which petitions they are endorsing with Amen. What wonder, then, that for so many centuries now we have for the most part prayed to God in vain?

units.la: AD tuam gratiarum actionē, inquit.] Quare non dicit, Ad tuam benedictionem, cum periodum hanc sic coeperit: Alioqui si benedixeris spiritu, is qui implet locum idiotæ, quomodo dicturus est Amen: ubi sane subiūgendum uidetur, Ad tuam benedictionem?
units.tr: "To your thanksgiving," he says. Why does he not say "to your blessing," since he began the sentence thus: "Otherwise, if you bless in spirit, how will he who fills the place of the layman say Amen"? Surely "to your blessing" seems to be what should be added there?

units.la: Respōdeo. Si de alio quopiam benedictionis genere loqueretur, quàm quod idē est cū gratiarum actione, utiq; benedictionis uerbū retinuisset. Iam uerò, quoniam de publica benedictione ecclesiæ loquitur: quæ nihil est aliud quàm laus & gratiarum actio, ut seipsum declaret, mauult dicere ad tuam gratiarum actionem, quàm ad tuam benedictionem. Sunt & alia quædam loca scripturæ, in quibus uerbum εὐλογεῖν, id est benedicere, pro gratias agere ponitur, de quibus alibi diximus.
units.tr: I answer: if he were speaking of some other kind of blessing, different from thanksgiving, he would certainly have kept the word blessing. But since he is speaking of the public blessing of the Church, which is nothing other than praise and thanksgiving, he prefers to say "to your thanksgiving" rather than "to your blessing," so that he may make his meaning plain. There are also other passages of Scripture in which the verb εὐλογεῖν [eulogein], that is, to bless, is used for to give thanks, which we have discussed elsewhere.

units.la: QVANDOQVIDEM, inquit, quid dicas nescit.] Ratio est, quare idiotæ nequeāt ad eiusmodi gratiarum actionem dicere, Amen, quæ lingua peregrina profertur in ecclesia. Quomodo, inquit, qui implet locum idiotæ, dicturus est, Amen, ad tuam gratiarum actionem? Quid impedit, quo minus uno uerbo dicat Amen? Quia, inquit, quod dicas nescit. Ergo qui non intelligit uerba orantis, & gratias agētis, nō potest ad illius orationem & gratiarum actionem respondere Amen. At qui hodie satis est intelligere sonum, quo oratio uel gratiarū actio clauditur, quo respondeas Amen: ut nō fit opus totius orationis uerba, ac sensus intelligere. Verū Apostolo nō est satis, si sciat plebs exusu quo fine consueto terminetur oratio, qualis est apud Græcos in oratione dominica, illud ἀλλ᾽ ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ, & in Missa Papistica, Per omnia secula seculorum: & illud per Iesum Christum, sed requirit ut intelligat ea quę dicuntur, & ex corde consentiat, eodemq; illa uoto confirmans dicat Amen.
units.tr: "Since," he says, "he does not know what you say." This is the reason why laymen cannot say Amen to such a thanksgiving, which is uttered in a foreign tongue in the Church. "How," he says, "will he who fills the place of the layman say Amen to your thanksgiving?" What prevents him from saying Amen in one word? "Because," he says, "he does not know what you say." Therefore one who does not understand the words of the one praying and giving thanks cannot answer Amen to his prayer and thanksgiving. Today, however, it is thought enough to understand the sound by which the prayer or thanksgiving is closed, so that you may answer Amen; there is no need, it is said, to understand the words and sense of the whole prayer. But it is not enough for the Apostle that the people know from custom at what customary point a prayer ends, as among the Greeks in the Lord's Prayer the words ἀλλ᾽ ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ [all' apo tou ponērou], or in the Papist Mass "for ever and ever," or "through Jesus Christ." He requires that they understand what is said, consent from the heart, confirm it with their desire, and then say Amen.

units.la: Quare admodum alienū est à doctrina Apostoli, & prioris ecclesiæ consuetudine, quod Lyranus hic adfert dicēs: Quid proficit populus simplex & non intelligens? quasi dicat: Nihil, aut modicum, quia nescit se conformare tibi, qui es minister ecclesiæ, respondendo Amen. Propter qd in primitiua ecclesia benedictiones & cætera communia fiebāt in uulgari. Sed postquam populus multiplicatus fuit, & consueuit se conformare ministris ecclesiæ, utpote, stando, quando dicitur Euangelium, depositō caputio, adorando Eucharistiam, & consimilibus, fiunt in Latino in Ecclesia Latina, & sufficit, quod clerus respondeat pro toto populo. Expeditius enim fit hoc modo quàm in uulgari. Hæc ille. Non hoc quærit Apostolus ut expeditius, sed ut ad ædificationem populi utilius oretur in ecclesia: nec sufficit illi ut clerus pro populo, sed ut quilibet idiota pro sui cordis uoto exprimendo dicat Amen: nec requirit à populo, ut religionem suam stando ad Euangeliū depositō caputio & adorando Eucharistiā profiteatur, sed ut audiat, intelligatq; quæ in ecclesia dicuntur, & ex animo consentiat, quo in fide Christi ædificetur. Verum sic coguntur exponere scripturas, qui omnes ecclesiæ abusus religionis loco defendunt.
units.tr: Therefore what Lyranus brings in here is quite foreign to the teaching of the Apostle and to the custom of the earlier Church, when he says: "What does the simple and unknowing people profit?" as if to say: nothing, or very little, because it does not know how to conform itself to you, who are a minister of the Church, by answering Amen. For this reason, in the primitive Church, blessings and other common parts of the service were done in the vernacular. But after the people multiplied and became accustomed to conform themselves to the ministers of the Church, as by standing when the Gospel is read, uncovering the head, adoring the Eucharist, and things like these, they are done in Latin in the Latin Church, and it is enough that the clergy answer on behalf of the whole people, since this is done more expeditiously than in the vernacular. Thus he. The Apostle does not seek this, that it be more expeditious, but that prayer be made in the Church more usefully for the building up of the people. Nor is it enough for him that the clergy answer for the people; he wants any layman, by expressing the desire of his heart, to say Amen. Nor does he require of the people that they profess their religion by standing at the Gospel, uncovering the head and adoring the Eucharist, but that they hear and understand what is said in the Church and consent from the heart, so that they may be built up in the faith of Christ. But those are forced to expound the Scriptures in this way who defend all the abuses of the Church in place of religion.

units.la: NAM tu quidē bene gratias agis, inquit, ut rum alius non ædificatur.] Rationi rationem subijcit. Dixit fieri nō posse, ut idiota dicat, Amen, ad gratiarum actionem lingua peregrina prolatam. Et huius rationem hac posuit, quod quæ dicuntur non intelligat. Iam quasi quæratur, quare ignorantia eorum quę dicuntur, impediat idiotam, quo minus ad gratiarum actionem non intellectam quidem, uerum bene, platam uno uerbo, Amen, respondere nequeat, subijcit: Nam tu quidem bene gratias agis, ut rum alius non ædificatur. Quibus uerbis significat in ecclesia non quæri quid utcunque dici ac fieri, sed quid ad ædificationem dici fieri què possit. Non potest idiota ad orationem non intellectam dicere Amen: intellige, ad ædificationem. Quid ad me, aiebant, quod idiota non intelligit quæ dico? Ego interim gratias ago domino. Respondet. Tu quidem bene gratias agis, uerum alius non ædificatur. Refert igitur non quàm bene loquaris & ores in ecclesia, sed quàm ad ædificationē aliorum. Non loquitur, ut id iterum admoneam, de priuata gratiarum actione, quę tacitè fieri potest, sed de publica. In priuata satis bene gratias agit, qui hoc ex animo facit, quacunque lingua utatur, modo ipse illam intelligat: in publica uero non quæritur quàm bene, sed quàm utiliter liter, & ad ædificationem hoc fiat. Ideo ut admoneat inanem esse eiusmodi obiectionē, dicit: Nam tu quidem bene gratias agis, uerum alius non ædificatur. Admonemur ergo friuolum esse omnem illum bonæ intētionis, & nescio cuius deuotionis prætextum, quo Latina rum cantionum & orationum strepitū defendūt, qui in ecclesia Christi negociantur. Quātumuis illas in precio haberi uolunt, interim plebs fidelium per eas non ædificatur.
units.tr: "For you indeed give thanks well, but the other is not edified." He answers reason with reason. He had said that an unlearned person cannot say "Amen" to a thanksgiving offered in a foreign tongue, and he gave this reason: the person does not understand what is said. Then, as if someone asked why not understanding what is said should keep the unlearned person from answering "Amen" to a thanksgiving he does not understand, though he can grasp at least one word, "Amen," he adds: "For you indeed give thanks well, but the other is not edified." By these words he indicates that in the church the question is not what may be said or done in any way, but what can be said or done for edification. The unlearned person cannot say "Amen" to a prayer he does not understand; understand, for edification. "What does it matter to me," they would say, "if the unlearned person does not understand what I say? Meanwhile I give thanks to the Lord." He replies: "You indeed give thanks well, but the other is not edified." It matters, then, not how well you speak and pray in the church, but how much it serves the edification of others. He is not speaking, let me remind you again, of private thanksgiving, which can be made silently, but of public. In private, a person gives thanks well enough if he does it from the heart, in whatever tongue he uses, provided he himself understands it. In public, however, the question is not how well, but how usefully, and whether it is done for edification. So to show that such an objection is empty, he says: "For you indeed give thanks well, but the other is not edified." We are warned, therefore, that all that pretext of good intention and I know not what devotion is frivolous, by which they defend the racket of Latin chants and prayers that are carried on in the church of Christ. However much they want these to be held in high esteem, the people of the faithful is meanwhile not edified by them.

units.la: Gratías ago Deo meo quod magís omnes uos línguís loquor. At ín ecclesia uolo quínque uerba mēte mea loquí, ut & alios ínstituam potius quām decē millia uerborum língua.
units.tr: "I thank my God that I speak with tongues more than all of you; yet in the church I would rather speak five words with my mind, so that I may instruct others also, than ten thousand words in a tongue."

units.la: Vulgata lectio habet: Gratias ago Deo meo, quod omnium uestrum lingua loquor. At in Græco est, πλεόντων ὑμῶν μᾶλλον γλώσσαις λαλῶ, id est, magis q; omnes uos linguis loquens. Vocu lam μᾶλλον, id est magis, interpres ille neglexit: & perinde uertit, ac si esset πάντων ὑμῶν γλώσσαις λαλῶ. Et uerosimile est, sic illum legisse in exemplari Græco, unde uertit. Nam & Ambrosius ad hunc modum legit. Meo tamen iudicio nō conuenit ea lectio menti Apostoli. Is enim nō Corinthiorum dūtaxat, sed omnium aliarum quoque Gentium linguis loquebatur, quibus Euangelium regni prædicabat. Neque conue nit ut de linguis intelligamus, quibus nonnul li in ecclesia Corinthiorum ad ostentationem magis quām ædificationem loquebātur. Neq; enim illis tantū, sed adhuc pluribus alijs loqui poterat, sicubi necesitas postulasset. Hoc siquidem linguarum dono non modò Corinthios, sed & reliquos omnes excellebat. Quare existimo hanc esse germanam lectionē: Gratias ago Deo meo, quod magis quàm omnes uos linguis loquor. Hoc est, loqui possum, ubi id aliqua ratio postulat.
units.tr: The Vulgate reading has: "I thank my God that I speak with the tongue of all of you." But in the Greek it is, "πλεόντων ὑμῶν μᾶλλον γλώσσαις λαλῶ" [πλεόντων ὑμῶν μᾶλλον γλώσσαις λαλῶ], that is, "speaking with tongues more than all of you." The translator neglected the word μᾶλλον, that is "more," and translated as if it were "πάντων ὑμῶν γλώσσαις λαλῶ" [πάντων ὑμῶν γλώσσαις λαλῶ]. It is likely that he read it this way in the Greek copy from which he translated, for Ambrose also reads it in this manner. Yet in my judgement that reading does not agree with the mind of the Apostle. For he spoke with the tongues not only of the Corinthians but of all other nations also, to whom he preached the gospel of the kingdom. Nor does it fit that we understand it of the tongues by which some in the church of Corinth spoke for display rather than for edification. For he was able to speak not only in those tongues but in many others as well, wherever necessity demanded. Indeed, in this gift of tongues he excelled not only the Corinthians but all the rest. Therefore I hold this to be the genuine reading: "I thank my God that I speak with tongues more than all of you." That is, I am able to speak them, where some reason requires it.

units.la: Dices: Quorsum hoc iactat, cū in ceteris ab omni sit ostentatione alienus? Non habet ista inanem gloriationem, sed necessariā doni Dei professionem, ad retundendā & corrigendam uanam quorundam inutiliter linguis loquentium ostentationem. Quoniam tantopere urget, inutile studiū esse, quo in ecclesia linguis incognitis coram multitudine loquebātur, orabant, psallebant, ac benedicebant, ne id uel odio charismatis huius, uel inuidia linguis loquentium ob id facere uideatur, quod ipse do no hoc destituatur, in hæc uerba prorumpit dicens: Gratias ago Deo meo, quod usqueadeò non destituor dono hoc linguarum, quod nō nulli apud uos tantopere ostentant, ut magis etiam quàm omnes uos linguis loqui possim, ne me quisquam illud propter ignorātiam insectari putet.
units.tr: You will say: why does he boast of this, when in other matters he is free from all show? This is not empty boasting but a necessary acknowledgement of God's gift, to check and correct the vain display of some who speak in tongues to no purpose. Since he urges so strongly that it is a useless practice to speak, pray, sing psalms and give blessings in the church before the crowd in unknown tongues, lest he seem to do this out of hatred of this gift or envy of those who speak in tongues, or because he himself lacks it, he breaks out into these words: "I give thanks to my God that I am so far from lacking this gift of tongues, which some among you display so ostentatiously, that I can speak with tongues more than all of you, so that no one may think I am attacking them out of ignorance."

units.la: GRATIAS ago Deo meo, inqt. Agnoscit donū Dei, ne quid suæ uideatur tribuere indu striæ. Et facit illud plurimi, ne quæ dicit, ad illius dicere contemptum existimetur. Magna quippe erat illius utilitas, ubi in tepore ac pertineter usurpabatur. Simul illos suo exemplo monet, ut gratias potius agant doni huius largitori Deo, illoq; bene utantur, quàm ut de illo pueriliter glorientur. Sane quisquis gratus agnoscit dona Dei, magna ratione cohibetur, ne de illis inaniter glorietur: quæ non de suo habet, sed ex largitate diuina gratuitò accepit. Poterat simpliciter dicere, Linguis loquor & ipse, idque magis quàm uos omnes: uerum ut ista innuat de quibus iam diximus, maluit dicere: Gratias ago Deo meo, quod magis q; uos linguis loquor.
units.tr: "I give thanks to my God," he says. He acknowledges God's gift, so that he may not seem to ascribe anything to his own diligence. He does this for the sake of many, so that what he says may not be taken as contempt for that gift. For its usefulness was great when it was used with reverence and properly. At the same time, by his own example he advises them to give thanks rather to God, the giver of this gift, and to make good use of it, rather than to boast of it childishly. Indeed, whoever gratefully acknowledges God's gifts is held back by a strong reason from boasting of them vainly, since he does not have them from himself but has received them freely from divine bounty. He could have simply said, "I too speak with tongues, and more than all of you." But in order to hint at the things we have already mentioned, he preferred to say: "I give thanks to my God that I speak with tongues more than you all."

units.la: Nec ociosum est, quod nō simpliciter dicit, Gratias ago Deo: sed, Gratias ago Deo meo. Solem9 suaui affectu agnoscere eos p nostris, quorū in nos singularia beneficia experimur. Et hic affectus peculiaris est omnibus illis qui ex animo benefactori suo Deo gratias agunt, ut uocent eum suum Deum. Sic dicit: Gratias ago Deo meo. quasi dicat, Qui me singulari sua gratia sic reddidit etiam hoc linguarū dono instructum, ut non minus, sed magis etiam quàm uos omnes linguis loquar: ne dum eos corrigo, qui tam insigni charismate ad ostentationem abutuntur, ex ignorantia ac penuria ii lius, adeoq; & liuore id facere uidear.
units.tr: Nor is it idle that he does not simply say, "I give thanks to God," but "I give thanks to my God." He acknowledges with a sweet affection those whom we experience as bringing us singular benefits. This affection is peculiar to all those who give thanks from the heart to God their benefactor, so that they call him "their God". So he says: "I give thanks to my God," as if to say: he who has so made me, by his singular grace, endowed with this gift of tongues, that I speak not less, but even more, than you all, has done so that I may correct those who abuse so distinguished a gift for display; and I may appear to do this not from ignorance and lack of it, nor from envy.

units.la: QVOD magis, inquit, quàm omnes uos linguis loquor. Cōsideremus hic primum prouidentiam Dei, quæ quos ad singularia ministeria obeunda eligit ac destinat, singulari etiā necessariæ gratiæ eminentia sic reddit instructos, ut obeūdis ministerijs pares esse possint. Cum uellet Apostolatu Pauli uti, nō ad unam aliquam, sed ad multas, uarias ac remotas Gentes ad fidem in Christum conuertendas, quèadmodū illi quoq; Act.22.cap. dixisse legitur: Vade, quoniam ego in nationes longe mittam te, ideoq; necessarium esset, ut omnium illarū linguis loqueretur, quibus erat prædicaturus: hoc illum charismate multo uberius instructū reddidit, quàm reliquos.
units.tr: "That I speak with tongues more than all of you," he says. Let us consider here first the providence of God, who chooses and appoints some for particular ministries, and by singular grace, which is necessary, equips them so that they are fit for the ministries they must perform. When he wished to use Paul's apostleship not for one nation but for many, various and distant nations, to be converted to faith in Christ, as is also read where he is told: "Go, for I will send you far away to the nations" (Acts 22), he therefore needed to speak the tongues of all those nations to which he was to preach. God equipped him with this gift far more richly than the rest.

units.la: Deinde obseruandum etiam est, quàm non fit alienum à sanctis agnoscere, pfiteri, ac gloriari palam de donis à Deo acceptis, ubi id certa ac necessaria ratio poscit, sicuti in hac & sequenti, & in ea quæ ad Galatas est epistola po scebatur. Sic dicit hic: Magis quàm omnes uos linguis loquor. Et supra, Per Euangelium ego uos genui. Et cap. sequenti, Gratia Dei, inqt, in me uacua non fuit, sed plus omnibus illis laborau. Et 2. Corint. 11. & 12. de ijs quæ propter Christum pertulit, deq; singularibus reuelatio nibus gloriatur. Et illic dicit: Nihil minus feci quàm illi qui sunt uehementer apostoli. Et Galat.2. gloriatur se nihil accepisse ab hominib. ne apostolis quidem, imò Petro restitisse in faciem, quod non recte ambularet ad ueritatem Euangelij. Nihil horum non coactus dixit, pter pseudapostolos, quo Apostolatus sui authoritatem tueretur.
units.tr: Next, it must also be observed how far it is from alien to the saints to acknowledge, profess and openly boast of the gifts received from God, when a sure and necessary reason demands it. This is so both in this passage and in the following one, and in the epistle to the Galatians, where such a thing was needed. Here he says: "I speak with tongues more than all of you." And above: "I begat you through the gospel." And in the next chapter: "The grace of God," he says, "in me was not in vain, but I laboured more than all of them." And in 2 Cor. 11 and 12 he boasts of what he suffered for Christ, and of singular revelations. There he says: "I was not at all behind those who are the very great apostles." And in Gal. 2 he boasts that he received nothing from men, not even from the apostles, and indeed that he withstood Peter to his face, because he was not walking straight according to the truth of the gospel. He said none of these things without compulsion, on account of the false apostles, so that he might defend the authority of his apostleship.

units.la: AT in ecclesia, inquit, uolo quinque uerba mente mea loqui. Postquā meminit, qua sit lingualinguarum facultate prę ipsis omnibus prædi tus,iá subijcit de illarū usu.Loquor & ipse linguis,inquit,magis q uos omnes: uerū nó in ecclesia ad ostentatione,sed ubi necesitas postulat.In ecclesia qppe nó requirutur linguæ, sed pphetia,p quá qui audiunt ædificetur. Quare in ecclesia malo quinq; uerbis mentē meā intelligibiliter exprimere, quo alios instituá, q decē milla uerborū lingua incognita inutiliter pfundere. Sic discernit inter ecclesiasticū cœtū,& alias extraordinarias loquendi, docendi,orādi & psallendi occasiones.Qui hic uerbi sunt ministri,ubi per eos cōueniūtur qui Germanice nesciunt,Latine uero sciunt, loquūtur illis nō Germanice,sed Latine:uel Gallis Gallice,si Gallice loqui poterunt.In ecclesia uero, ubi loquēdū est populo, lingua utūtur patria, non exotica & ignota. Cōsimili modo Paulus cū loquēdū esseт Ebreis,Ebraice, Græcis,Græce, Syris, Syriace, Romanis, Romane,Persis, Persice loquebatur.In ecclesia uerò nó alia lingua utebatur, q quæ illi esset patria & usitata. Iam Papistæ cū extra ecclesiā uulgari loquantur idiomate:in ecclesia, ubi potissimum erat intelligentiæ studendum, malunt decē millia uerborum exotica lingua loqui, quàm unū sal tem uerbulum patria & usitata.
units.tr: "But in the Church," he says, "I want to speak five words with my mind." After he has mentioned the gift of tongues, in which he surpassed all of them, he now goes on to its use. "I too speak in tongues," he says, "more than all of you. But not in the Church for show, but where necessity demands it. For in the Church it is not tongues that are required but prophecy, by which those who hear are built up. So in the Church I would rather express my mind intelligibly in five words, so as to instruct others, than pour out ten thousand words uselessly in an unknown tongue." In this way he distinguishes the ecclesiastical assembly from other occasions for speaking, teaching, praying and singing. Where ministers of the Word meet with people who do not know German but do know Latin, they speak to them not in German but in Latin, or to the French in French, if they are able to speak French. But in the Church, where one must speak to the people, they use their native language, not a foreign and unknown one. Likewise Paul, when he had to speak to the Hebrews, spoke Hebrew; to the Greeks, Greek; to the Syrians, Syriac; to the Romans, Latin; to the Persians, Persian. In the Church he used no other language than the one that was native and customary for them. But the Papists, though they speak the vernacular outside the Church, in the Church, where understanding above all should be sought, prefer to speak ten thousand words in a foreign tongue rather than one little word in the native and familiar language.

units.la: AT in ecclesia,inqt uolo quinq; uerba mēte mea loqui.] Ambr.pro Διὰ νοῦς μου, id est,per mentē meā,legit Διὰ νοὸς μου,id est,per legē. Supra dictum est quid sit loqui mente, & quid loqui lingua,ut nó fit denuo explicādū.Poterat simpliciter dicere,In ecclesia malo loqui mente,q lingua:uerū ut declararet,quáto sit prophetia præstantior & utilior linguis,maluit per collationē dicere, Volo quinq; uerba mente mea loqui, quā decē millia uerborū lingua:quod per inde est ac si aurum supra plumbum extollere uolens dicas,Malo quinq; pondo auri q decē millia plumbi.Nihil autem refert utrū quinq; uerba,& decē millia uerborum:uel quinq; sermones,& decem millia sermonū legas. Quod enim in Græco est χίλιοι λόγοι, & μυρίοι λόγοι,utro que sensu accipi potest. Deinde manifestū est non esse philosophandum in numero quinario,ne & in eo qui sequitur philosophari cogimur.Quinq; uerba simpliciter pro paucis posuit.quasi dicat: Volo uno & altero uerbo, tribus,quatuor uerbis, &c mentē meā explicare potius q innumeris frustra & inutiliter garrire.Et Ambr.sic exponit:utili dicit paucis uerbis in apertione sermonis loqui, quod oēs intelligant q prolixam orationem habere in obscuro.Nec Hiero.nec Chrysost.nec hic Ambr. uiderunt hoc loco quod uidit Aquinas, q per quinq; uerba perfecta orationem expositi: in qua sint subiectū,prædicatū, copula uerbalis, determinatio subiecti,& determinatio prædicati:uel si id nó placeat,significari iudicauit perfectā doctrinā,cuius quinq; sint partes , prima prędicare credēda,secunda docere agēda,tertia mōstrare uitāda,quarta indicare spērāda,quinta comminari timēda.Posterior hæc sententia
units.tr: "But in the Church," he says, "I want to speak five words with my mind." Ambrose reads "through my mind" [Διὰ νοῦς μου], that is, "through my mind," whereas he reads "through the law" [Διὰ νοὸς μου], that is, "through the law." It has been said above what it is to speak with the mind and what to speak with the tongue, so it need not be explained again. He could simply have said, "In the Church I would rather speak with the mind than with the tongue." But to show how much prophecy surpasses and is more useful than tongues, he preferred to put it by way of comparison: "I want to speak five words with my mind rather than ten thousand words in a tongue." This is just as if, wanting to raise gold above lead, you were to say, "I prefer five pounds of gold to ten thousand pounds of lead." It makes no difference whether you read "five words and ten thousand words" or "five speeches and ten thousand speeches," for the Greek "a thousand words" [χίλιοι λόγοι] and "ten thousand words" [μυρίοι λόγοι] can be taken in either sense. Further, it is clear that one should not philosophise about the number five, lest we be compelled to philosophise also about the number that follows. He simply put "five words" for "a few." It is as if he said: "I would rather explain my mind in one or two words, three or four words, than chatter on uselessly and to no purpose in countless words." Ambrose also explains it this way: he says it is useful to speak in a few words when opening a discourse, because everyone understands it, whereas a long speech is obscure. Neither Jerome, nor Chrysostom, nor Ambrose here saw what Aquinas saw: that by "five words" he means a complete sentence, in which there are a subject, a predicate, a verbal copula, a determination of the subject and a determination of the predicate. Or, if that does not please, he judged that it signifies a complete doctrine, whose five parts are: first, to proclaim what is to be believed; second, to teach what is to be done; third, to show what is to be avoided; fourth, to indicate what is to be hoped for; fifth, to threaten what is to be feared.

units.la: placuit Lyrano. Huiusmodi cōmēta uisa sunt monachis tantū nó Canone digna.Mirū quod non sunt in numero decē millium quoq; philosophati: in quo de inani tēplariorū boatuū strepitu facillimè admoneri poterant, quem quomodo insectetur Erasmus hoc loco,in annotationibus illius uidere licet.
units.tr: This latter opinion pleased Lyra. Such commentaries seemed worthy only of monks and not of the canon. It is remarkable that they did not also philosophise about the number ten thousand, in which one could easily have been warned about the empty noise of the Templars' bellowing. How Erasmus attacks this in his annotations on this passage may be seen there.

units.la: VT & alios instituá,inquit.] Inhæret ,ppositio,urgens institutione & ædificationē fideliū, quod id sit primariū fidelis Apostoli opus,& unicus scopus,ad quē collimādi sunt ecclesiastici cōuentus.Est autem in Græco uerbū κατὰ χώραν,quod uoce aliquē instituere significat: ad quam rem opus est sermone intelligibili, eoq; nó uerbosō & cōfuso,sed succinēto ac methodico.Qui sic in ecclesia instituebát rudes, catechistę,& id genus institutiones catechismi uocabátur,quorū nullus usus in Papatu remāsit.
units.tr: "And so that I may instruct others," he says. What is stressed is the proposition that urges the instruction and edification of the faithful, because this is the primary work of the faithful Apostle and the one aim at which the ecclesiastical assemblies must be directed. In the Greek there is the word "to instruct" [κατὰ χώραν], which means to instruct someone by word. For this a comprehensible speech is needed, not a wordy and confused one, but a concise and orderly one. Those who thus instructed the unlearned in the Church were called catechists, and such instructions were called catechisms; none of this practice has remained in the Papacy.

units.la: Quod autem nó simpliciter dicit, Vt alios: sed,Vt & alios instituam: eo sensu accipiendū est,quo suprà dixit: Qui loquitur lingua, seipsū ædificat:qui prophetat,ecclesiam ædificat.Sic dicit:Volo quinq; uerba mēte mea loqui,ut & alios,hoc est,ut non me duntaxat, sicuti faciūt qui linguis loquuntur, sed & alios qui me audiunt,instituā.At hodie qui Latine inter Germanos, Gallos, Hispanos, Britannos, Bohemos,Danos,Suedos,Hungaros, &c.in ecclesijs loquuntur & cantillant: maxima ex parte, nec seipsos nec alios instituunt.
units.tr: As for why he does not simply say, "that I may instruct others," but "that I may also instruct others," this must be understood in the sense he gave above: "He who speaks in a tongue edifies himself; he who prophesies edifies the Church." So he says: "I want to speak five words with my mind, so that I may also instruct others," that is, so that I may instruct not only myself, as those who speak in tongues do, but also the others who hear me. But today those who speak and chant in Latin in the churches among the Germans, French, Spanish, English, Bohemians, Danes, Swedes, Hungarians, and so on, for the most part instruct neither themselves nor others.

units.la: POTIVS,inquit,quàm decē millia uerborū lingua.]Solet numerus myriadis, quis decem millia comprehendat,pro innumera plerunq; & infinita multitudine in scripturis poni,quo sensu omnino positus est hoc loco. Nō est autem illo Apostolus ociosè usus. Si simpliciter prophetiā lignis aliquoufq; præferre uoluisset,poterat dicere,potius quàm decē uerba lingua.Verùm maluit dicere,potius q decē millia uerborū lingua,quo primū uanissimam illorū ostentatione perstringeret,qui nec modum ullum seruabant,nec finē faciebant, cum linguarum donū in ecclesia ostentaret:deinde & eiusmodi loquacitatis & exoticarū orationum uanitate carperet, admoneretq; hoc esse illas uaniores quo sunt uerbosiores.Quicquid enim uanum est & inutile,quo magis multiplicatur,operosiusq; ac sumptuosius geritur,hoc uanius & auersandum magis redditur, tam ab est,ut multiplicando commendari possit. Nō est numerus,non est modus,non est finis,intolerabilis est sumptus cantionum, orationum, missarum,cæremoniarum Papisticarum, quæ in cōfpectu domini hoc sunt abominabiliores,quo plures ac sumptuosiores.
units.tr: "Rather," he says, "than ten thousand words in a tongue." The number of the myriad, which comprises ten thousand, is commonly used in the Scriptures for an innumerable and often infinite multitude, and it is used in exactly this sense here. The Apostle has not used this figure idly. If he had wished simply to prefer prophecy to tongues, he could have said, "rather than ten words in a tongue." But he preferred to say "rather than ten thousand words in a tongue," first to lash the empty show of those who observed no measure and made no end when displaying the gift of tongues in the Church; and then to rebuke the vanity of such loquacity and foreign speech, warning that these are the more vain the more verbose they are. For whatever is empty and useless, the more it is multiplied and the more laboriously and expensively it is carried out, the emptier and more to be shunned it becomes. Far from being commended by multiplication, it is rendered more detestable. There is no number, no measure, no end; the cost of the Papist chants, prayers, masses and ceremonies is intolerable, and these are all the more abominable in the sight of the Lord the more numerous and costly they are.

units.la: Fratres,ne sitis pueri sensibus,sed malicia pueri sitis,sensibus uero perfecti sitis. In lege scriptum est: Varijs linguis & labijs uarijs loquar populo huic: & nec sic quidē audiēt me, dicit dominus. Itaq; linguæ signi uice sunt,non ijs qui crecredunt, sed incredulis: prophetia vero A non incredulis, sed credentibus.
units.tr: "Brothers, do not be children in your understanding, but be children in malice; but in understanding be mature. It is written in the law: 'With other tongues and with other lips will I speak to this people, and even so they will not hear me, says the Lord.' Therefore tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, but prophecy is not for unbelievers but for believers."

units.la: Occurrit falsæ persuasioni, qua multitudo persuasa erat, abunde sibi sufficere, si simpliciter crederent, etiamsi non omnia quæ in ecclesia dicebantur, intelligerent. Non est nostrum, aiebát, omnia intelligere ac scire, quod ad præpositos ac doctos pinet: sed satis est, si simus instar puerorum, ambulemusq; simpliciter.
units.tr: He meets the false persuasion by which the multitude was convinced that it was quite enough to believe simply, even if they did not understand everything that was said in the Church. "It is not our business," they said, "to understand and know everything; that pertains to the leaders and the learned. It is enough for us to be like children and to walk simply."

units.la: Quare non est opus, ut intelligamus omnia quæ linguis in ecclesia dicuntur. Sufficit agno scere miraculosum spiritussanEti donũ, illudq; cum admiratione venerari. Ad quem modum planè in Papatu persuasum est plebeijs, scientiá rerũ spiritualiũ, & lectione intelligentiamq; sacrarum scripturarum copetere non ipsis, sed doctoribus, monachis, & sacerdotibus. Nos sumus, inquiunt, laici ac seculares, nostrum non est nisi simpliciter credere, quemadmodũ crediderunt nostri maiores, ingredi ecclesiá, ibiq; orare, missam audire, & aliquid offerre.
units.tr: Therefore, they said, there is no need for us to understand everything that is said in tongues in the Church. It suffices to acknowledge the miraculous gift of the Holy Spirit and to venerate it with wonder. In exactly this way it has been persuaded among the common people in the Papacy that knowledge of spiritual things, and the reading and understanding of the Holy Scriptures, belong not to them but to the teachers, monks and priests. "We," they say, "are laymen and secular people; it is our part only to believe simply, as our forebears believed: to enter the church, pray there, hear the mass and offer something."

units.la: Huiusmodi cogitationi occurrit Apostolus subacri correptioe, dicēs: Fratres, ne sitis pueri sensibus, sed malitia pueri sitis. Quasi dicat: Quid hoc rei est? Dum patiēter auditis ea quæ nō intelligitis, nec ullam curam intelligentiæ, unde instituamini, impenditis: quid aliud esse vultis quàm pueri spiritualium rerum ignari? Instar puerorum ingredimini ecclesias, nec curatis quomodo ædificemini. Ad strepitum linguarum incognitarum obstupescitis, & sic loquētes admiramini: de prophetia vero, p quâ intelligētes reddi possetis, nulla est cogitatio. An sic lubet ppetuo similes esse pueris? Quod si vultis esse pueri, sitis pueri, verũ malicia nō sensibus. Aliud est esse puerũ sensibus, & aliud puerum esse malicia. In pueris sunt ignorantia rerum utilium, & innocentia nulla dum malitia imbuta. Quod ignorantiam attinet, non cõuenit Christiano, ut sit instar pueri, nescius eorum quæ cum primis scire debebat. Quod vero innocētis animi simplicitatem à maliciæ duplicitate alienā concernit: omnibus compe tit fidelibus, nō plebeijs modò, sed & doctoribus ac præpositis, ut similes sint pueris, alieni à malitia, nequitia, veršutia, iniquitate & iniustitia, arrogátia & superbia, &c. Magna itaque peruersitas est, puerorũ uelle ampleċti ac ₚpfiteri inscitiam, in rebus salutem nostram cõcer nentibus: innocentiæ uero ac simplicitatis cădorem auersari, & in malitia præstare adultos & exercitatos ueteratores. Sic faciebát Corinthij. Quod sensus rerũ spiritualium attinebat, planè erant pueri: nec appetebant illarũ scientiá. In malitia interim nihil erant minus quàm pueri, carnales, contentiosi, uoluptuarij, arrogantes, iniurij in fratres, apud ethnicos iudices litigantes, scortantes, &c. Erat igitur tempestiuum, ut hanc in illis peruersitatem correptione hac corrigeret, dicens: Fratres, ne sitis pueri sensibus, sed malitia pueri sitis, sensibus uero perfecti sitis.
units.tr: The Apostle meets this kind of thinking with a sharp rebuke, saying: "Brothers, do not be children in your understanding, but be children in malice." As if to say: "What is the point of this? While you patiently listen to things you do not understand, and devote no care to understanding, by which you might be instructed, what else do you wish to be than children ignorant of spiritual things? You enter the churches like children, and you do not care how you are to be built up. You are struck dumb by the noise of unknown tongues and marvel at those who speak them, but about prophecy, by which you could be made to understand, there is no thought at all. Is it your wish to be forever like children? If you want to be children, then be children, but in malice, not in understanding. It is one thing to be a child in understanding and another to be a child in malice. Children have ignorance of useful things, and an innocence not yet imbued with malice. As far as ignorance goes, it is not fitting for a Christian to be like a child, ignorant of those things he ought above all to know. But as for the simplicity of an innocent mind, far removed from the duplicity of malice, this belongs to all the faithful, not only to the common people but also to the teachers and leaders, so that they may be like children, free from malice, wickedness, deceit, iniquity and injustice, arrogance and pride, and so on. Therefore it is a great perversity to want to embrace and profess the ignorance of children in matters that concern our salvation, while shunning the innocence and simplicity of children, and to excel in malice as adults and practised tricksters." This is what the Corinthians did. As far as the understanding of spiritual things went, they were plainly children and did not desire knowledge of them. Meanwhile in malice they were nothing less than children: carnal, contentious, given to pleasure, arrogant, wronging their brothers, going to law before heathen judges, consorting with prostitutes, and so on. It was therefore timely that he correct this perversity in them with this rebuke, saying: "Brothers, do not be children in your understanding, but be children in malice; but in understanding be mature."

units.la: Chrysost. hanc particulā sic exposuit: Pueri sic sunt animati, ut res ludicras ac plerũq; nullius momenti admodum appetant, magniq́ue faciant: eas uero quæ potiores sunt, ipsisq; uti liores esse possent, nec affectent, nec alicuius faciát. Consimili modo Corinthij, linguas unde nihil erat ædificationis, admirabantur, inq; precio habebát: at prophetiam interea, multo utiliore longe uilioris æstimabant. Hoc in illis reprehendens Apostolus monet, ne sensibus sint pueri, sed potius pfecti. Si respicias ea quę populariter in ecclesijs Papistarũ magno serio exercentur, cum sint res nihili, planè deprehedes maximam in illis multitudinem admodũ esse pueriliter animatam. Pueris facillime persuadetur, ut uera esse credant, quæ omniũ sunt salsissima. Obsecro quid non puerili prorsus credulitate uulgo receptum est in Papatu? Nihil tam absurdũ, nihil tam superstitiosum, nihil tam impium, nihil tam ludicrum ac ridiculum, nihil tam alienum à sanctis scripturis excogitari potuit, quod non sint maiores nostri pro uero & indubitato, proq; pio & Christiano amplexi. Pueri impensissime delectantur puppis, imagunculis qualicunq; ornatu splendidis. Sic illi nullis sumptibus pepercerũt, quo omnia fierent imaginibus mortuorũ sanctorũ referta. Pueri quæ admirantur ac magnificant, ipsis etiá parentibus suis magnifica uideri putant, eaq; illis deprædicant, ostentant, & offerunt. Planè consimili modo in Papatu fieri uidemus. Aurum, argentũ, ueltes sericas, imagines, magnificas templorũ structuras & quæ alia sunt eiusmodi magnifaciunt, quia arridet carni, ideoq; in illis cultũ diuinum constituút, quod iudicát ea perinde atq; sibi apprime placere Deo. Pueriles omnino sunt hi sensus. Dicamus ergo illis: O fratres, ne sitis pueri sensibus, sed malitia pueri sitis: sensibus uero curate ut sitis perfecti.
units.tr: Chrysostom explains this phrase thus: children are so minded that they desire and greatly value playthings, and things of little real importance, but they neither seek nor esteem the things that are more excellent and might be more useful to them. In the same way the Corinthians admired tongues, though they brought no edification, and held them in high regard, while they valued prophecy, which is far more useful, as something much less worthy. The Apostle rebukes this in them and warns them not to be children in their understanding but rather mature. If you consider the things that are commonly practised with great seriousness in the churches of the Papists, though they are worth nothing, you will plainly see that a very great multitude there is minded in a thoroughly childish way. Children are very easily persuaded to believe as true what is utterly false. I ask you, what has not been accepted in the Papacy with a wholly childish credulity? Nothing so absurd, nothing so superstitious, nothing so impious, nothing so silly and ridiculous, nothing so foreign to the holy Scriptures could be devised, which our forebears have not embraced as true and beyond doubt, and as pious and Christian. Children take the greatest delight in dolls and little images of any sort of splendid decoration. So they spared no expense, so that everything might be filled with images of dead saints. Children think that what they admire and magnify must also seem magnificent to their own parents, and they proclaim, display and offer these things to them. In exactly the same way we see things done in the Papacy. They magnify gold, silver, silken garments, images, magnificent church buildings and other things of this kind, because they please the flesh; and therefore they set up divine worship in them, judging that these things are just as pleasing to God. These attitudes are altogether childish. Let us therefore say to them: O brethren, be not children in understanding, but be children in malice; yet in understanding take care that you are mature.

units.la: FRATRES, inquit, ne sitis pueri sensibus, sed, &c.
units.tr: Brethren, he says, be not children in understanding, but, etc.

units.la: Quod igitur erant & esse uolebát Corinthij, reprehédit in illis Apostolus, ac dehortatur ne id esse uelint, dicens: Ne sitis pueri sensibus. Deinde quod nec erat nec esse curabát, ut id sint & esse curent, hortatur cum dicit: Sed malitia pueri sitis. Quod perinde est ac si populo Israelis stulto & insipiēti dixisset Deus, Ne sitis sapiētes ad faciendum mala, sed ad benefaciendum sapientes sitis, ad mala uero facien dũ sitis insipientes & inepti: ubi Hiere. 4. queritur illos esse sapientes ad faciendũ mala, bene uero facere prorsus nescire.
units.tr: The Apostle therefore rebukes the Corinthians for what they were and wished to remain, and dissuades them from wishing to remain so, saying: Be not children in understanding. Then he exhorts them to become and to take care to be what they neither were nor cared to be, when he says: But be children in malice. This is just as if God had said to the foolish and senseless people of Israel: Do not be wise in doing evil, but be wise in doing good; and for doing evil be foolish and unskilful. There, in Jeremiah 4, God complains that they were wise in doing evil, but utterly did not know how to do good.

units.la: SENSIBVS uero, inqt, perfecti sitis.
units.tr: But in understanding, he says, be mature.

units.la: Dices hic, Quis nā est ex mortalib. omnibus, qui sensibus posit esse perfectus & cōsummatus? Quid enim est perfectũ esse aliud, q̃ sic esse cōsummatum, ut nihil sit quod adhuc desiderari posit? At hoc solius est Dei. An non cap. præcedēti, ex parte nos cognoscere, & per speculũ in ænigmate cernere dixit, donec ueniat tēpus illud perfectionis, in quo cognoscemus quē admodũ iam cogniti sumus, & facie ad faciem cer-
units.tr: Here you will say: who then among all mortals can be mature and complete in understanding? For what is it to be perfect other than to be so completed that nothing remains which can still be desired? But this belongs to God alone. Did he not say in the preceding chapter that we know in part, and see through a mirror in an enigma, until that time of perfection comes, in which we shall know even as we are known, and see face to face?

units.la: cernemus? Quomodo igitur hortatur Corinthios, ut sensibus sint perfecti, cum nondum adesset perfectionis tempus? Respondeo. Non loquitur de omnimoda sensuum perfectione, quae in futura demum vita continget, sed de ea quae virilis est aetatis, cui respectu pueritiae perfectio tribuitur. Quare quod dicit, Ne sitis pueri sensibus, sed perfecti: perinde est, ac si dicat, Ne sitis pueri, sed viri sensibus. Vtitur enim similitudine pueritiae & virilis aetatis, qua usus est & cap. praecedenti dices: Cum essem puer, loquebar ut puer, sentiebam ut puer, cogitabam ut puer. At ubi factus sum vir, aboleui puerilia. Vt ruditas & imperfectio adhaeret pueritiae, ita perfectio ad virile pertinet aetate: intellige, qualis in hac vita contingere potest. Sic etiam Eph. 4. similitudine hac puerilis ac virilis aetatis utitur dices: Donec perueniamus omnes in unitatem fidei & agnitionis filij Dei in virum perfectum in mensuram aetatis plenae adultae Christi, ut non amplius simus pueri qui fluctuemus & circumferamur omni vento doctrinae per versutiam hominum.
