Et ad hanc virilem perfectionem consequendam dicit a Deo datos esse apostolos, euangelistas, prophetas & doctores. Consimili modo urget etiam Corinthios, ut prophetiae ac doctrinae det operam potius quam linguis, quo possint institui & aedificari in cognitione Christi, ne perpetuo sint pueri sensibus, sed aliquando ad virile perfectionem promoueant, Chrysost. exponens dicit: Ἰσάντο ἀνδρες ... Ambros. exponit ad hunc modum: Perfectos illos vult esse, ut sciat quid ad instructionem ecclesiae sit necessarium: ut recedentes a malitia & erroribus his studeat, quae proficiant ad utilitatem fratrum. Hic est enim sensu perfectus, qui agit ut prosit alicui, maxime fratri. Haec ille: qui aliter etiam particulam hanc legit, quam & Graecus contextus & aedictio vulgata habeat. Sic nam legit: Sed malitia paruuli estote, ut sensibus perfecti sitis. Quasi fieri non possit, ut perfectus sit sensibus, qui non est malitia paruulus. Sane licet inuenias nimis multos, qui in virili aetate & sensibus ualeat & malitia: in causa tamen uerae pietatis fieri non potest, ut ualeat sensibus, qui non est malitia paruulus: qua de re uide Chrysostomum hoc loco. Sed pergamus.
units.tr: How then does he exhort the Corinthians to be mature in understanding, when the time of perfection had not yet arrived? I answer: he is not speaking of the complete perfection of understanding, which will be attained only in the future life, but of that which belongs to the age of manhood, to which perfection is attributed in comparison with childhood. Hence when he says, Do not be children in understanding but mature, it is just as if he said: Do not be children, but men, in understanding. For he uses the likeness of childhood and manhood, which he also used in the preceding chapter, where he says: When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things. As roughness and imperfection cling to childhood, so perfection belongs to the age of manhood, understood as it can be attained in this life. So also in Ephesians 4 he uses this likeness of childhood and manhood, saying: Until we all come to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the full stature of Christ, so that we are no longer children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine, by the cunning of men. And he says that apostles, evangelists, prophets and teachers were given by God to attain this manly perfection. In the same way he also urges the Corinthians to devote their effort to prophecy and teaching rather than to tongues, so that they may be instructed and built up in the knowledge of Christ, and not remain children in understanding forever, but at last advance to manly perfection. Chrysostom, explaining this, says: Be men [Γίνεσθε ἄνδρες]. Ambrose explains it in this way: he wants them to be mature, so that they know what is necessary for the instruction of the church; that, turning away from malice and errors, they may apply themselves to those things which profit the brethren. For he is mature in understanding who acts so as to benefit someone, especially a brother. So far Ambrose, who reads this phrase differently from what the Greek text and the common edition have. For he reads it thus: But be little children in malice, that you may be mature in understanding. As if it could not happen that one should be mature in understanding who is not a little child in malice. Indeed, although you may find many who are strong in understanding in manhood and yet strong in malice, yet in the cause of true piety it cannot happen that one is strong in understanding who is not a little child in malice. On this matter see Chrysostom at this place. But let us proceed.

units.la: IN lege, inquit, scriptum est: Varijs linguis & labijs uarijs loquar populo huic, &c.] Accidere illis significat, quod olim Deus Israeli euenire coqueftus est: uel, si mauis, euenturu praedixit. Quod uidelicet uerbu suu missum per prophetas, haud secus absq; iusto intellectu audirent, q; si quis lingua incognita & barbara loquente audiat. In lege, inquit, scriptum est. Nusquam in libris Mosaicis reperies ea quae citat. Imo si uerba exacte spectes, non inuenies ullu in omni scriptura locum, in quo scriptum sit: Varijs linguis & labijs uarijs loquar populo huic, & ne sic quidem audiet me. Et tamen necesse est, ut alicunde sint ista ex lege desumpta, nisi daturi sumus Apostolo, quod e lege citet, quae nusquam
units.tr: In the law, he says, it is written: With other tongues and with other lips will I speak to this people, etc. He means that what God once threatened to bring upon Israel happens to them, or, if you prefer, he foretold that it would happen. Namely, when his word was sent through the prophets, they heard it without right understanding, just as if someone were to hear a language unknown and barbarous. In the law, he says, it is written. You will nowhere find in the books of Moses what he quotes. Indeed, if you look at the words exactly, you will not find anywhere in all Scripture a passage in which it is written: With other tongues and with other lips will I speak to this people, and even so they will not hear me. And yet these words must have been taken from somewhere in the law, unless we are to grant that the Apostle is quoting from the law something that is written nowhere

units.la: sint in lege scripta. Non inuenio autem locum aliquem, unde uerosimilius haec uideatur desumpta, praeter eum qui est Esa.28. Non debet uero insolens uideri, quod scripta prophetarum uocat legem: & quae in illis sunt, in lege scripta esse dicit. Etenim dictione legis nonnunquam in genere utitur de ijs quae ad uetus pertinent testamentum, siue sint pentateuchon, siue libri Iudicum, siue Samuel, siue libri Regum, siue Psalmi, siue prophetae, &c.
units.tr: in the law. Now I find no passage from which these words seem more likely to have been taken than Isaiah 28. Nor should it seem strange that he calls the writings of the prophets the law, and says that what is in them is written in the law. For he sometimes uses the word law in a general sense of all that belongs to the Old Testament, whether it be the Pentateuch, or the book of Judges, or Samuel, or the books of Kings, or the Psalms, or the prophets, and so on.

units.la: Habet autem locus Esaiae in Ebraeo ad huc modum: Et illi quoq; praeuino errant, & praeficera errat, sacerdos & propheta errant, sicera absorpti sunt: praeuino errat, praeficera errant, in uisione errant, in iudicio impingunt. Nam omnes mensae repletae sunt uomitu, ut non sit locus. Quem docebit scientiam? & quae intelligere faciet auditu? ablactatos ne a lacte? auulsos ne ab uberibus? Quoniam praeceptum ad praeceptum, praeceptum ad praeceptum, regula ad regulam, regula ad regulam, modicum hic, modicum hic. Quoniam balbutietibus labijs, & lingua alia loquitur ad hunc populum, qui dicit ad eos, Haec requies est, refocillate lassum, & haec refocillatio, & noluntaudire. Et est eis uerbum domini, praeceptum ad praeceptum, praeceptum ad praeceptum, regula ad regulam, regula ad regulam, modicum hic, modicum hic: propterea uadent & cadent retrorsum, & coeteren tur, & illaqueabitur & capietur. Propter hoc audite uerbum domini uiri illusores, dominato res populi huius, qui estis in Hierusalem, &c.
units.tr: Now the passage of Isaiah in the Hebrew reads thus: "Yea, these also reel with wine, and stagger with strong drink; the priest and the prophet reel with strong drink, they are swallowed up of wine, they stagger with strong drink; they err in vision, they stumble in judgement. For all tables are full of vomit, so that there is no place. Whom will he teach knowledge? and whom will he make to understand the message? those who are weaned from the milk, those who are drawn from the breasts? For precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little. For with stammering lips and with another tongue will he speak to this people, to whom he said, This is rest; give rest to the weary, and this is refreshment; yet they would not hear. So the word of the LORD is to them: precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little; that they may go and fall backward, and be broken, and be snared and taken. Therefore hear the word of the LORD, you scoffing men, who rule this people that is in Jerusalem," etc.

units.la: Haec omnia cohaerent: nec facile germanus pphetae sensus patebit, nisi totus hic cotextus inspiciatur: qua de re tamen non est, ut hic dicamus. Inspiciantur ea quae in Commentarijs nostris super hunc prophetam diximus: in quibus praesente locum qua potuimus diligentia explicuimus. Apostolus quaedam ex illo truncatim excerpsit, & propposito suo accommodauit: quae uidelicet ad summam propheticae reprehensionis facere, & causae qua agebat conformia esse iudicauit. Summa autem est, Israelitis praesertim sacerdotib. & pseudoprophetis una cum maioribus erat uerbum domini, quod prophetae praedicabat, usq; adeo obscurum & barbarum, ac si lingua aliena & labijs balbutietibus proponeretur. Non quod prophetae peregrina lingua uaticinando & corripiendo uterentur, sed quod animi illorum essent alio auersi, & plane a uerbo domini abhorretes, ac studio scientia Dei fugietes. Hactenus ide accidit Corinthijs, in eo quod malebant audire linguis loquentes, quas non intelligebant, q; prophetantes, quos intelligere, & unde edificari potuissent. Et hoc sensu prophetae locu citat, dicens: In lege scriptu est, Varijs linguis, & labijs uarijs: uel, ut in Graeco est, alijs linguis, & labijs alijs, sicut & uulgata habet, Loquar populo huic, & ne sic quidem audient me. Non inhaeret uerbis, sed liberè citat, quatenus ppositio accommodare iudicat. Primu, in Ebraeo non est in prima persona, Loquar populo huic: sed in tertia, Loqtur ad huc quar populo huic: sed in tertia, Loqtur ad huc popu-
units.tr: All these things cohere, and the true sense of the prophet will not readily become plain unless this whole context is examined. Yet this is not the place to say so. Let those things be consulted that we set out in our Commentaries on this prophet, where we explained the passage with all the care we could. The Apostle excerpted certain words from it in a truncated form and adapted them to his purpose, namely those which he judged to serve the sum of the prophetic rebuke and to agree with the cause he was pleading. The sum is this: for the Israelites, especially the priests and false prophets together with the leaders, the word of the Lord which the prophet preached was so obscure and barbarous, as if it were set forth in a foreign tongue and with stammering lips. Not that the prophets used a foreign language when prophesying and rebuking, but that their minds were turned away and utterly averse from the word of the Lord, and fled from the study of knowing God. The same thing happened to the Corinthians, in that they preferred to hear those speaking in tongues, which they did not understand, rather than prophesying, which they could understand and by which they could have been edified. In this sense the prophet cites the passage, saying: "In the law it is written, By other tongues and by other lips," or, as it is in the Greek, "by other tongues and other lips," as the Vulgate also has: "I will speak to this people, and not even so will they hear me." He does not cling to the words but cites them freely, as far as his purpose judges fit. First, in the Hebrew it is not in the first person, "I will speak to this people," but in the third person: "He will speak to this peo-

units.la: {A} Ioan. 3.
units.tr: {A} Ioan. 3.

units.la: populum: deinde nō uarijs, uel alijs labijs, sed balbutiētibus labijs: tertio, illud, & ne sic quidem audiet me: in Ebraeo est, Et nolūt audire: & ponitur demū post ista qui dicit ad eos, Hęc reqes est, refocillate lapsum, & haec refocillatio: quarto, quod addit, Dicit Dns, in Ebraeo nō est. Adiecit hoc, ut significaret uerba ista di ēta esse sub persona domini. Admonemur hac cōsideratione q̄ sint ea scripturae loca, quae citantur ab apostolis & euangelistis uigilanter ex ponenda, ne omnia uidelicet illorū ad causas, quibus adaptantur, cōtorqueantur: sed ea tantum applicentur, quae ad propositum faciunt, ne uis inferatur scripturis. Ambrosius exponit hunc locum bifariam. Primo ad hunc modū: Hoc dominus de his dixit quos praesciuit, nec Saluatori credituros. In alijs enim linguis & in alijs labijs loqui, Nouū test. est prędicare, &c. hoc est, immutata ratione aliter loqui q̄ legis ueteris uerba habeant, dum audiūt sabbatum solui, neomenias euacuari, circucisionem cessare, sacrificia immutari, &c. hoc est, alijs linguis & alijs labijs loqui. Et nec sic perfidi Deū audire uoluerūt. Deinde, putat etiam id fuisse alijs linguis loqui, quādo Euangelium Iudaeis est per parabolas praedicatum, Matth. 13.
units.tr: ple." Then, it does not say "by other or different lips" but "by stammering lips." Third, "and not even so will they hear me" is in the Hebrew "and they would not hear," and it is placed finally after those words in which he says to them, "This is rest; refresh the weary; and this is refreshment." Fourth, the words "says the Lord" are not in the Hebrew. He added them to signify that these words were spoken under the person of the Lord. From this consideration we are reminded which passages of Scripture are cited by the apostles and evangelists, and we must take care in expounding them, lest all of their words be twisted to the causes to which they are applied; rather, only those should be applied which bear on the purpose, lest violence be done to the Scriptures. Ambrose expounds this passage in two ways. First, in this manner: "The Lord said this of those whom he foreknew would not believe the Saviour. For to speak in other tongues and with other lips is to preach the New Testament," and so on; that is, to speak in a manner changed from what the words of the old law have, while they hear that the sabbath is loosed, the new moons are emptied, circumcision ceases, sacrifices are changed, and so on. This is to speak in other tongues and with other lips. And even so the faithless were unwilling to hear God. Then he thinks that it was also to speak in other tongues when the gospel was preached to the Jews through parables, Matt. 13.

units.la: Lyranus existimat hunc locū fuisse impletū Hierosolymis in die Pentecostes, cū discipuli omnis generis linguis loquerētur. Et sane nō est incōueniens illius sententia, si quae ex propheta citantur, uaticinium habēt de re futura, quemadmodum nonnulli sentiunt. Nos expo B suimus ea tanquam Iudaicae obstinationis reprehensione, qua tēpore prophetae uerbū Dei sic auersati fuerint: ut perinde nō intellexerint audiendo, ac si lingua prorsus aliena audirent. Quod si magis placet, ut per modum uaticinij ab Apostolo accepta sentiamus, nō est imperti nens, ut de Iudaeis intelligamus quibus dominus per discipulos in die Pētecoltes, alijs atq; alijs est linguis loquutus, qui tamē ne sic quidem ad fidem sunt conuersi. Quicquid statuamus de sensu prophetae, haud grauatim adducor, ut sentia Apostolum uerbis istis respexisse ad miraculum linguarū, eoq; illa per catachresim deflexisse. quasi dicat: Quid accidit Iudeis? An nō illis quoq; alijs atq; alijs linguis loquutus est Deus, ita ut stuperent? Quid inde utilitatis consequuti sunt? Non audierunt Deum, neq; Euangelio crediderunt: ut impletum sit in illis quod in lege scriptum est: Varijs linguis ac uarijs labijs loquar populo huic, & ne sic quidem audient me.
units.tr: Lyra thinks this passage was fulfilled at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost, when the disciples spoke in all kinds of tongues. And indeed his opinion is not unsuitable, if the things cited from the prophet contain a prophecy of a future matter, as some think. We have expounded them as a rebuke of Jewish obstinacy, by which, in the time of the prophet, they so turned away from the word of God that they did not understand when they heard it, as if they were hearing a wholly foreign language. But if it pleases more to understand what the Apostle took from the prophet by way of prophecy, it is not inappropriate to understand it of the Jews, to whom the Lord spoke through the disciples on the day of Pentecost in one tongue after another, and who nevertheless were not converted to faith even so. Whatever we decide about the sense of the prophet, I am not reluctant to hold that the Apostle in these words looked to the miracle of tongues, and by catachresis turned those words to it, as if he were saying: What happened to the Jews? Did not God also speak to them in one tongue after another, so that they were astonished? What advantage did they gain from it? They did not hear God, nor believe the gospel; so that what is written in the law was fulfilled in them: "By other tongues and by other lips will I speak to this people, and not even so will they hear me."

units.la: ITAQVE linguae signi uice sunt, inquit, nō ijs qui credūt, sed incredulis, &c.] Aperit quid ex loco pphetae colligat. Nō enim simpliciter dicit, Linguae signi uice sunt, sed per notā illationis. Itaque linguae signi uice sunt: uel, ut in Graeco est, εἰς σημεῖον εἰσὶν i. in signū sunt: ut intelligas colligi hoc ex praemisso pphetę loco, uel ex historia linguarum, cui illū accōmodat. Quoniā autē dictio signi iā pro indicio, iā pro sacramento, ut uidere est Ro. 4. iā pro miraculo in
units.tr: THEREFORE tongues are for a sign, he says, not to those who believe, but to unbelievers, etc. He states what he gathers from the passage of the prophet. For he does not simply say "tongues are a sign," but marks the conclusion with "therefore": "therefore tongues are for a sign," or, as it is in the Greek, "they are for a sign" [εἰς σημεῖον εἰσίν], that is, they are for a sign, so that you understand this is gathered either from the prophet's passage put before it, or from the history of the tongues to which he applies it. Since the word "sign" is used in Scripture sometimes for an indication, sometimes for a sacrament, as may be seen in Rom. 4, and sometimes for a miracle,

units.la: scripturis sumitur: dubitari potest, quo sit hic sensu dictū ab Apost. qd' linguae sint in signū. Verū expeditius est, ut intelligamus eas fuisse uice miraculi: uel, ad miraculū datas, ut essent argumento, q̄ gerebatur geri diuinitus, quo mētes audiētiū obstupesceret, & ad credēdū permouerētur, sicuti in historia diei Pētec. patet.
units.tr: it may be doubted in what sense the Apostle said here that tongues are for a sign. Yet it is more straightforward to understand that they were in place of a miracle, or given for a miracle, so that they would be evidence that what was being done was done by divine power, by which the minds of the hearers would be astonished and moved to believe, as is clear from the history of the day of Pentecost.

units.la: NON ijs qui credūt, inquit, sed incredulis, pphetia uero nō incredulis, sed credentibus.] Arguit ex ratioe linguarū & pphetiae quo cōpbet peruersum esse ipsorū studiū: quo negle cta pphetia linguis tātopere inhiabant. Ratio linguarū erat ratio signorū. Quēadmodū signa ædebātur diuinitus propter eos qui nō facile credebat uerbo: quo manifesto diuinae operationis argumento permoti uerbum audirent & crederent, ita & linguae propter eosdem & in eundem finē erant datę. Hoc est quod dicit: Linguae in signū sunt, nō ijs qui credūt, sed incredulis. Hoc est, nō ijs qui uerbo Euangelij iā credunt (illis quippe nō est opus, ut miraculo quopiā ad credēdū inducātur) sed ἀπίστοις, id est nō credentibus ad prędicatione uerbi: sed alij quo ueritatis argumēto certificari uolētibus, quale erat quod Thomę accidebat, cū diceret: Nisi uidero in manib. eius uestigiū clauorū, & mittā digitū meum in uestigium clauorum, & mittā manū meā in latus eius, nō credā: cui dictū est à Dño, Infer digitū tuū huc, & uide manus meas, & admoue manum tuā, & immitte in latus meū, & noli esse ἄπιστος ἀλλὰ πιστός, i. non credēs, sed credēs. Propter eiusmodi homines facta sunt signa & portēta, & datū omniū linguarū charisma, quo ad fidem perducerentur. Non est igitur quod Apost. linguas in signum incredulis esse dicit: de ijs intelligendum, qui neq; uerbo neq; signis ad fidem unquam perducuntur, sed prorsus manent increduli, quales erant obstinati Iudęi: sed de ijs tantum, qui uerbo sine signis non credunt.
units.tr: NOT for those who believe, he says, but for unbelievers; prophecy, however, not for unbelievers but for believers. He argues from the nature of tongues and of prophecy, by which he shows that their zeal was perverse: prophecy being neglected, they were so eager for tongues. The nature of tongues was the nature of signs. Just as signs were given by God on account of those who did not readily believe the word, so that, moved by the clear proof of divine working, they would hear the word and believe it, so tongues too were given for the same people and to the same end. This is what he says: tongues are for a sign, not to those who believe, but to unbelievers. That is, not to those who already believe the word of the gospel (for these have no need to be brought to faith by any miracle), but to unbelievers [ἀπίστοις], that is, to those not believing the preaching of the word, but wishing to be certified by some argument of truth. Such was the case with Thomas, when he said: Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe. To him the Lord said: Put your finger here, and see my hands, and bring your hand and put it into my side, and do not be unbelieving [ἄπιστος] but believing [πιστός]. On account of men of this kind signs and wonders were made, and the gift of all tongues was given, by which they might be led to faith. It is not therefore the case that the Apostle says tongues are for a sign to unbelievers in the sense that this must be understood of those who are never brought to faith either by the word or by signs, but remain wholly unbelieving, like the obstinate Jews; it applies only to those who will not believe the word without signs.

units.la: PROPHETIA uero non incredulis, inqt, sed credētibus.] Pertinēt hęc ad rationē pphe tiæ, q̄ hactenus diuersa est à ratione linguarū, quod data est nō incredulis, sed credētibus. Hi nanq; uerbo, cui credūt institutuntur & ædifi cātur: illi uero nequaquam, quia nō credūt. Et hactenus rationē linguarū ac pphetię exprefit, in eo diuersam, quod illę incredulis, ista uero credētibus cōpetit. Iam addendū erat, Vos autē non estis incredulì, sed credētes. Pertinet igitur ad uos prophetia, potius q̄ linguę. Verū nō erat necessariū, ut minorē & conclusionem subijceret, quod hæ ultro ex maiori paterēt & cōsequerētur. Neq; enim timēdū erat, ne seipsi p incredulis potius q̄ p credentibus haberēt. Quare abunde satis erat rationem explicuisse linguarū & prophetiæ, ac monuisse, illas non ad credentes pertinere, sed ad incredulos: hāc uero in usum & ædificationem esse datam nō incredulis, sed credentibus.
units.tr: PROPHECY, however, he says, is not for unbelievers but for believers. These things pertain to the nature of prophecy, which up to this point differs from the nature of tongues, in that it is given not to unbelievers but to believers. For these are instructed and built up by the word in which they believe, whereas the others are not, because they do not believe. And so far he has expressed the nature of tongues and of prophecy, differing in this, that the former befits unbelievers and the latter believers. He should now have added: But you are not unbelievers, but believers. Therefore prophecy pertains to you rather than tongues. But it was not necessary for him to add the minor premise and the conclusion, since these would of themselves follow from the major. For there was no need to fear that they would count themselves unbelievers rather than believers. Wherefore it was enough to have explained the nature of tongues and of prophecy, and to have warned that the former do not pertain to believers but to unbelievers, while the latter was given for use and edification not to unbelievers but to believers.

units.la: Ergo si cōuenerit ecclesia tota simul, & oēs linguis loquātur, ingrediantur aūt idiotæ idiotę aut incredulí, an nō dícēt uos ín-fanire? Sí uero omnes prophetetís, in-grediatur autem íncredulus aut ídiota, coarguitur ab omnibus, díjudicatur ab omnibus, & sic occulta cordis eíus ma-nífesta fiunt, atque ita procídens ín fa-ciem adorabit Deū, pronuncians quod Deus reuera sit ín uobís.
units.tr: Therefore if the whole church comes together at one place and all speak with tongues, and uninstructed people or unbelievers come in, will they not say that you are out of your minds? But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or an uninstructed person comes in, he is convicted by all, he is judged by all, and so the secrets of his heart are made manifest; and so, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you.

units.la: Arguit ab euētu, iuxta diuersam linguarum & prophetię ratione diuerso, indeq; adhuc am-plius urget, ut magis prophetiæ quàm linguis operā impendát. Vtitur autē argumēto hypo-thetico ponēs cōditionalē, unde colligat euen-tū. Cōditionalis particula gemina est. Prior sic habet: Ergo si cōuenerit ecclesia tota simul, & oēs linguis loquátur, ingrediantur aūt idiotæ aut increduli. Altera est: Si uero oēs prophete-tis, ingrediatur autē incredulus aut idiota. Et hinc geminum colligit ac diuersum euentum. Prior est: an nō dicent uos insanire? Posterior est, coarguitur ab omnibus, iudicatur ab omni-bus, & sic occulta cordis eius manifesta fiunt, atq; ita procides in facie adorabit Deū, pronū-ciás quod Deus reuera sit in uobis. Hinc infe-rendū erat: An nō igitur satius est & utilius, ut prophetetis, q; ut linguis in ecclesia uestra lo-quamini? Nisi dicturi estis, melius esse, ut pro insanis habeamini, q; ut incredulos & idiotas lucrifaciatis dño: At erat adeo manifestū, utrū esset utilius, & malle cōtrariū illius adeo absur-dū, ut nō esset necesse huiꝰ expresse meminisse.
units.tr: He argues from the outcome, which differs according to the different manner of tongues and of prophecy, and from this he urges still more that they should devote their effort to prophecy rather than to tongues. He uses a hypothetical argument, setting out a conditional, from which he draws the outcome. The conditional clause is double. The first runs: "Therefore if the whole church comes together at one place and all speak with tongues, and uninstructed people or unbelievers come in." The second is: "But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or an uninstructed person comes in." And from these he draws two different outcomes. The first is: "will they not say that you are out of your minds?" The second is: "he is convicted by all, he is judged by all, and so the secrets of his heart are made manifest; and so, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you." From this it must be inferred: "Is it not therefore better and more useful that you prophesy rather than speak in tongues in your church? Unless you are going to say that it is better for you to be thought mad than to win unbelievers and uninstructed people for the Lord." But it was so plain which of these was more useful, and the opposite so absurd, that there was no need to mention this expressly.

units.la: ERGO, inquit, si cōuenerit ecclesia tota si-mul.] In Græco est ἐαν συνέλθῃ, quod uulgata ha-bet, in unum. Et Eras. supra cap. ii. transtulit, in eundem locum. Significat se loqui nō de qui-busuis sermonibus, quibus Christianus homi-ni peregrino & nódum fideli, peregrino illius uidelicet, idiomate lnquatur: sed de illis qui in cōuētibus ecclesiasticis exoticis linguis inter Corinthios ostētationis gratia fiebāt. Ideo po-nit nó quoduis colloquiū, quod inter paucos fiat, sed plenū ac iustū totius ecclesię cōuentū, dicens: Ergo si conuenerit ecclesia tota simul.
units.tr: "Therefore," he says, "if the whole church comes together at one place." In the Greek it is ἐὰν συνέλθῃ, which the Vulgate renders "into one place," and Erasmus, above in chapter 2, translated "into the same place." He means that he is not speaking of any chance conversations, such as a Christian might hold with a foreign and not yet faithful man in that man's own language, but of those who in the ecclesiastical assemblies among the Corinthians spoke in foreign tongues for the sake of display. Therefore he sets down not any conversation that takes place among a few, but a full and proper assembly of the whole church, saying: "Therefore if the whole church comes together at one place."

units.la: ET omnes, inquit, linguis loquantur.] Hoc est, & quotquot in ecclesia loquuntur, linguis incognitis loquātur oēs, ut nemo sit ex omni-bus qui prophetet. Posset in genere de omni-bus fidelibus in ecclesiā uenientibus exponi: uerūm satius esse uidetur, ut id sentiamus per-stringi quod in ecclesia Corinthiorum fiebat, in qua non omnes, sed ij qui loquebantur, lin-guis incognitis utebantur. Quanquam nō ad-modū repugnarim, si quis de omnibus in uni-uersum exponat, atq; ita maiore eiusmodi ec-clesiæ confusionem exprimi sentiat. Q.d Apo-stolus: Quid si quemadmodū omnes estis cha-rismatis linguarum æmulatores & admirato-res, ita omnes linguis in ecclesia loquamini? Quid inde consequetur.
units.tr: "And all," he says, "speak with tongues." That is, all who speak in the church speak in unknown tongues, so that no one among them prophesies. This could be explained generally of all the faithful coming into the church; but it seems better that we understand him to be censuring what was happening in the church of the Corinthians, in which not all, but those who spoke, used unknown tongues. Yet I would not greatly object if someone explains it of everyone in general, and so understands a greater confusion of this kind of church to be expressed. The Apostle is saying: "What if, just as you all are zealous and admirers of the gift of tongues, so you all speak with tongues in the church? What would follow from that?"

units.la: INGREDIANTVR aut idiotæ, inqt, aut increduli.] Hoc Apostolus nisi euenire cōsue-uisset, frustra posuisset. Solebant dubio procul in cœtum ecclesiæ, non modò fideles quidé ac rudes adhuc idiotę, sed &infideles ingredi: illi pro more ecclefię, isti ut uiderent & audirent, deq; fide ac religione Christianorum cogno-scerent. Vnde obtinuit in ecclesia, ut cum my-steriorum instaret communio, per diaconū iu-berentur discedere prophani, & accedere san-cti, id est fideles.
units.tr: "Or uninstructed people," he says, "or unbelievers, come in." The Apostle would have been wasting words if this had not been customary. Without doubt, not only the faithful, and the uninstructed who were still raw, but also unbelievers used to enter the assembly of the church: the former according to the custom of the church, the latter in order to see and hear, and to learn about the faith and religion of Christians. Hence it became established in the church that when the communion of the mysteries was about to take place, the profane were ordered by the deacon to withdraw, and the holy, that is the faithful, to approach.

units.la: AN non dicent uos insanire, inquit?] Ponit euentum qui sequutus esset ex cōsufione prę-missa. Q.d. Age, si omnes linguis in ecclesia lo-quamini, quid utilitatis inde uel ad uos, uel ad rudes idiotas, uel ad infideles, qui subinde cœ-tum uestrum ingrediútur, prouenire poterit? Iudicate uosipsi, an non magis pro insanis ha-bebimini? Etenim sani hominis non est in cœ-tu hominum ea dicere quæ à nemine possunt intelligi, sed magis mête moti. Et hæc insania quo plures simul corripuerit, hoc plus stupo-ris incutit spectantibus.
units.tr: "Will they not say that you are out of your minds?" he says. He sets out the outcome that would follow from the confusion just mentioned. He means: "Come now, if you all speak with tongues in the church, what benefit can arise from this either for you, or for the rude and uninstructed, or for the unbelievers, who from time to time enter your assembly? Judge for yourselves: will you not rather be considered mad? For it is not the mark of a sane man to say in a gathering of men things which no one can understand, but rather of one out of his mind. And the more people this madness seizes at once, the more astonishment it stirs in the onlookers."

units.la: Ergo cauendum est ecclesię fidelių, ne quid admittat quod specie aliquam stulticiæ & infa-niæ, uel rudibus uel infidelibus obiciat. Ipsa quidem fides in Christum, ipsa spes, ipsa patie-tia crucis ac tribulationum, ipsa mundi & car-nis nostræ abnegatio, stultitiæ damnátur à fi-lijs huius seculi, id quod patienter est & fortiter ferendum: uerùm in rebus alijs, quæ pos-sunt cū ratione, cum decoro & utiliter agi: ca-uendum est, ne infensate, inutiliter, & sic agan-tur, ut risum magis & contemptum, quàm lau-dem & commendationem mereantur. Huc re-fer ineptos ac portentosos monachorū in me-dio seculo, ac frequentia populorū passim ob-ambulantium cucullos, & barbaros templario-rum boatus, ac ridiculas missantium gesticula-tiones, & quæ alia sunt eiusmodi.
units.tr: Therefore the faithful church must take care not to admit anything that, in some appearance of folly or madness, would expose it to the rude or to unbelievers. Indeed, faith in Christ itself, hope itself, patience in the cross and in tribulations, the denial of the world and of our own flesh, are condemned as foolishness by the sons of this age; and that must be borne patiently and bravely. But in other matters, which can be done with reason, with decorum and usefully, care must be taken that they are not done in a disorderly, useless way, so that they earn mockery and contempt rather than praise and commendation. To this belong the absurd and monstrous hoods of the monks in the midst of the world, wandering about everywhere among the crowds of people, and the barbarous bellowing of the templars, and the ridiculous gestures of those who say mass, and other things of this sort.

units.la: Nec est ut per impudentiam, ut sunt magna ex parte perfrictæ frontis, dicát: Quid ad nos, quod ridemur ac pro insanis habemur? An nó hoc ipsi quoque Paulo accidit? cum diceretur ipsi: Insanis Paule. Nemo nos pro insanis ha-bet: præter eos, qui irrisores sunt religionis. Quod Paulo accidit, in re accidit necessaria, i-psam nostrá salutem fidemq; ac religioné Chri-sti concernente. Quare & immerito pro infa-no habebatur. At quæ isti faciunt, nulla neces-sitate, nec religionis, nec salutis nostræ faciút: & in se sic sunt comparata, ut si superstitionem illam inueteratam spectantibus abstuleris, ne-queant non ridicula & insana uideri.
units.tr: Nor is it right, as many with brazen foreheads do, to say shamelessly: "What is it to us that we are laughed at and held to be mad? Did this not also happen to Paul himself, when it was said to him: 'You are mad, Paul'?" No one holds us to be mad except those who are mockers of religion. What happened to Paul happened in a necessary matter, concerning our very salvation, faith and the religion of Christ. Therefore he was held to be mad unjustly. But what these men do they do from no necessity, either of religion or of our salvation; and they are so constituted in themselves that, if you take away from the onlookers that long-established superstition, they cannot but appear ridiculous and mad.

units.la: Deinde non est Christiani hominis in eius-modi rebus dicere, quid est quod rideor, & in-sanire uideor? Nam etiamsi hoc faciant homi-nes parum sobrij ac religiosi: melius tamē est, ne illis quidem occasionem ridendi & oblo-quendi obijcere, quando Apostolus ne infide-les quidem offendendos esse censeat. Non e-nim dicit, Ingrediantur autem sapientes, ac pij homines: sed, Ingrediantur autem idiotæ aut increduli, an non dicent uos insanire?
units.tr: Furthermore, it is not the part of a Christian man in such matters to say: "What is it that I am laughed at, and seem to be mad?" For even if men who are not very sober or religious do this, it is still better not to offer them even an occasion for laughing and speaking against us, since the Apostle thinks that not even unbelievers are to be offended. For he does not say, "But if wise and pious men come in," but "But if uninstructed people or unbelievers come in, will they not say that you are out of your minds?"

units.la: An nó potuissent hic regerere Corinthij: age dicát nos insanire infideles & idiotæ, quid ad nos?Infideles sunt & idiotę. Si saperent, non ri derent donum Dei.
units.tr: Could not the Corinthians have replied here: "Well then, let the unbelievers and the uninstructed say that we are mad; what is that to us? They are unbelievers and uninstructed. If they were wise, they would not laugh at the gift of God."

units.la: Puto illos aliquanto maiore potuisse cū ratione hoc pacto studiū linguarū, cui nimium dediti erant, defendere, quàm isti qui res in se ridiculas hodie defendunt. Et tamen statim & recte audissent ab Apostolo: Ergo ne uos idio tarum putatis & infideliū nullam esse in ecclesia Christi habendam rationem, cum id sine detrimento doni Dei fieri possit? Quid putas illum hisce nostris barbaris, morionibus, & gesticulatoribus dicturum?
units.tr: I think they could have defended the study of tongues, to which they were too much devoted, with somewhat greater reason in this way than those who today defend things that are in themselves ridiculous. And yet they would at once and rightly have heard from the Apostle: "Do you therefore think that no account is to be taken of the uninstructed and unbelievers in the church of Christ, since this can be done without loss to the gift of God?" What do you think he would say to these barbarous fools, buffoons and mountebanks of ours?

units.la: SI uero omnes prophetetis, inquit.]Intelligeper uices, & ordine, sicuti mox docebit. Alioqui grandis & absurda prorsus esset confusio, non minus insaniæ damnanda, si oēs absq; ordine ac simul in conuentu ecclesiæ prophetent, quàm si omnes linguis loquantur.
units.tr: "But if all prophesy," he says. Understand this by turns and in order, as he will teach presently. Otherwise there would be a great and utterly absurd confusion, to be condemned no less as madness if all prophesied together in the assembly of the church without order, than if all spoke with tongues.

units.la: INGREDIATVR autem incredulus, aut idiota.]Iam secundo idiotas & incredulos coniungit. Nam illi potissimum sunt qui & facile offendantur, si quid absurdi in ecclesia uiderint, & in quibus maxime locū habeat studiū ædificationis, si pphetia recte administretur. Löge alia ratio est sapientium ac prudentiū eorumq; qui exercitatos sensus habet in rebus spiritualibus. Hic nec leui momento offenduntur, nec multa opus habent institutione, qua ædificentur. Cæterū hoc loco non est incōmodū, si cum Erasmo per idiotam intelligamus indoctum, eum uidelicet qui scientię respectu parūdiffert ab eo qui adhuc est infidelis, nisi quod in rudimentis Christianæ fidei institutus & sacro baptismate initiatus est ecclesiæq; incorporatus.
units.tr: "But if an unbeliever or an uninstructed person comes in." Now he couples uninstructed people and unbelievers a second time. For these are especially the ones who are easily offended if they see anything absurd in the church, and in whom the zeal for edification has the greatest place, if prophecy is rightly administered. The case of the wise and prudent, and of those who have trained senses in spiritual things, is different. These are not offended by a slight matter, nor do they need much instruction by which to be edified. Yet in this place it is not inconvenient, with Erasmus, to understand by "uninstructed" the unlearned, namely one who, in respect of knowledge, differs little from one who is still an unbeliever, except that he has been instructed in the rudiments of the Christian faith and initiated by holy baptism and incorporated into the church.

units.la: COARGVITVR ab omnib. dijudicatur ab omnibus, inquit.] Euentum à priori diuersum ponit, qui sequuturus sit ex studio prophetandi in idiotis aut infidelibus, ecclesiæ cōuentum ingresis. Recensent autem triplicem euentum. Primus ipsum idiotam aut infidelem, secundus Deum, tertius ecclesiam concernit.
units.tr: "He is convicted by all, he is judged by all," he says. Here he sets out an outcome different from the earlier one, which will follow from the practice of prophesying for the unlearned or unbelievers who enter the assembly of the Church. He names a threefold outcome. The first concerns the unlearned or unbelieving person himself, the second God, and the third the Church.

units.la: 1 De primo sic dicit: coarguitur ab omnibus, dijudicatur ab omnibus, & sic occulta cordis eius manifesta fiunt. De secundo, atq; ita proci dens in faciem, inquit, adorabit Deum. De tertio, pronuncians, inquit, quod Deus reuera sit in uobis. Prima itaque utilitas, quæ ex pphetia contingit idiotæ & infideli, in eo est qd arguitur & iudicatur: hoc est, qd de errore deq; peccatis in conscientia sua per doctrinam ueritatis & iustitiæ conuincitur, idq; non ab uno tantum & altero, sed ab omnibus, intellige prophetantibus.
units.tr: 1. Of the first he says: "He is convicted by all, he is judged by all, and so the secrets of his heart are made manifest." Of the second, and so "falling on his face, he will worship God." Of the third, declaring "that God is truly among you." The first benefit, then, which comes to the unlearned and unbelieving person from prophecy, lies in this: that he is convicted and judged. That is, he is shown, in his own conscience, to be in error and in sin, through the teaching of truth and righteousness. And this happens not by one person alone, but by all, that is, by all who prophesy.

units.la: Argui & iudicari, deprehendi est conuinci, perinde ac si quis in iudicio deprehendatur & conuincatur esse reus.
units.tr: To be convicted and judged is to be caught out, just as when a man in a court is caught and found guilty.

units.la: Non est autem præter rationem, quod hæc particula priore loco ponitur. Est enim prima in opere conuersionis, nec fieri potest, ut sine illa quisquam ad dominum cōuertatur. Et hinc est principium resipiscentiæ. Nisi conscientia primum de errore ac peccatis conuincatur, ut quàm erret ac deliquerit intelligat, non habet locum resipiscentia, sine qua salutari potest nemo. Nihil autem huius euenit illis qui nihil audiunt in ecclesia, nisi boatum quendam, & missas, unde nihil intelligunt, nec in conscientijs suis arguuntur & iudicantur.
units.tr: It is not without reason that this phrase is placed first. It is the first step in the work of conversion, and no one can be turned to the Lord without it. From this comes the beginning of repentance. Unless the conscience is first convicted of error and sin, so that it understands how far it has strayed and offended, there is no place for repentance, and without repentance no one can be saved. But none of this happens to those who hear nothing in the Church except a certain bellowing and the Masses, from which they understand nothing, and so are not convicted or judged in their consciences.

units.la: Et hanc ob causam tantopere uidemus hodie defendi Latinas illas cātiones & missas ab illis potissimum, qui in superstitionib. & peccatis sunt immersi, quod per illas nec arguuntur, nec iudicantur, & interim secure in peccatis pergunt, falso persuasi, nihil fore periculi in causa salutis, si seduli sint missarum auditores. Vtinā hanc pestem intelligant principes, quibus in una missa omnis est posita salutis ancora: prophetia uero ob id est exosa, quod conscientias de peccatis & erroribus conuincit, inquietas q; reddit. Quare malunt centum missas, quàm una audire iustam ac necessariā prophetiam, & centum alere missatores sacrificulos, quàm unum uerbi Dei ministrum ueraciter & legitime prophetantem.
units.tr: For this reason we see today how eagerly those Latin chants and Masses are defended, chiefly by those who are sunk in superstitions and sins. Through them they are not convicted or judged, and meanwhile they continue securely in their sins, falsely persuaded that there is no danger to their salvation provided they are diligent hearers of Masses. Would that the princes understood this plague, they in whom the whole anchor of salvation is placed in a single Mass! Prophecy, however, is hated for this very reason, that it convicts consciences of sins and errors and makes them restless. Therefore they prefer a hundred Masses to one hearing of a just and necessary prophecy, and they prefer to support a hundred Mass-mongering little priests rather than one minister of the Word who truly and lawfully prophesies.

units.la: COARGVITVR, inquit, ab omnibus, dijudicatur ab omnib. ]Obseruandum est, quod non simpliciter dicit: arguitur & dijudicatur, sed utrobiq; addit ab omnibus. Tantus uidelicet est uerę ac legitimæ prophetiæ consensus, ut à quocunq; administretur, cōscientias erran tium ac delinquentium arguat & dijudicet.
units.tr: "He is convicted," he says, "by all, he is judged by all." It must be noted that he does not simply say, "he is convicted and judged," but adds "by all" to both. Such is the agreement of true and lawful prophecy that, whoever administers it, it convicts and judges the consciences of those who err and do wrong.

units.la: Quare falsarios eos esse prophetiæ oportet, qui sic prædicant, ut neminem peccati conuincant, accommodantes se foro quo placeat magnatibus, & odia populi quoq; uitent. Quemadmodum enim luminarium quamuis multorum, ex ipsa lucis natura idem est splendor, & eadem uis illuminandi: ita in ministris uerbi, ueris ac fidelibus quamuis multis, tatus est ex ipsa natura pphetiæ consensus, ut omnes prophetando conscientias auditorum de peccato conuincant ac diiudicent.
units.tr: Therefore those must be false prophets who preach in such a way that they convict no one of sin, accommodating themselves to the court and to the magnates as they please, and avoiding the hatred of the people. For just as many lights, by the very nature of light, have the same brightness and the same power to illuminate, so in the ministers of the Word, however many they are, if they are true and faithful, there is by the very nature of prophecy such an agreement that all, in prophesying, convict and judge the consciences of their hearers of sin.

units.la: ET sic occulta cordis eius, inquit, manifesta fiunt.]Exponit, quomodo arguatur idiota aut infidelis, si audiat in ecclesia prophetantes. Sic uidelicet, ut occulta cordis eius manifesta fiant. Intelligit autem per occulta cordis, errores superstitiones, & omnis generis impietatem & iniusticiam, quæ ab illo non intelliguntur, donec per prophetiam, quasi quandam lucem, illuminetur, ac conscius propriæ miseriæ reddatur. Infideles enim, priusquam ad lucem ueritatis peruenerit, ignorat se esse impiū, tenebras cordis sui non uidet, quæ in illo sunt prorsus sunt à conscientia ipsius occulta. Et in hac cæcitate errat, impingit, & in omnis generis delicta labitur, perituris omnino, nisi luce ueritatis à tenebris hisce conscientię suæ liberetur. Ecclesiā igitur ingressus, auditu pphetiæ arguitur & dijudicatur, & manifesta ipsi reddūtur q antea fuerat in corde illi occulta.
units.tr: "And so the secrets of his heart," he says, "are made manifest." He explains how the unlearned or unbelieving person is convicted when he hears prophets in the Church: namely, in such a way that the secrets of his heart are made manifest. By the secrets of the heart he means errors, superstitions, and every kind of impiety and injustice, which are not understood by him until he is illuminated through prophecy, as by a certain light, and is made aware of his own wretchedness. For the unbeliever, before he comes to the light of truth, does not know that he is impious, and does not see the darkness of his heart, which is wholly hidden from his conscience. In this blindness he wanders, stumbles, and slips into every kind of sin, certainly destined to perish unless he is freed from these shadows of his conscience by the light of truth. Therefore, when he enters the Church, he is convicted and judged by hearing prophecy, and what had been hidden in his heart is made manifest to him.

units.la: Hæc uidelicet est uis & operatio lucis propheticæ. Quæ manifeste sunt mala in moribus infidelium, utpote adulteria, homicidia, odia, superbia, luxus, furta, rapinæ, &c. ab ipsis philosophis, ac naturæ quoque lege reprehendun-tur. tur. At occulta illa impietatis, superstitionum, errorum, & corruptæ naturæ mala, quæ iudicium humanum effugiunt, non reuelantur, nō arguuntur ac dijudicantur, nisi luce Euangelicæ ueritatis, quæ sic est accensa & candelabro imposita, ut luceat omnib. qui ecclesiam uerorum Christianorum ingrediuntur, ac prophetias audiunt.
units.tr: This, certainly, is the power and working of prophetic light. Those evils that are plain in the conduct of unbelievers, such as adulteries, murders, hatreds, pride, luxury, thefts, robberies, and so on, are rebuked even by the philosophers and by the law of nature. But those hidden evils of impiety, superstition, error, and corrupt nature, which escape human judgment, are not revealed, convicted, or judged except by the light of the Gospel truth, which is so kindled and set upon the lampstand that it shines for all who enter the Church of true Christians and hear the prophecies.

units.la: Tria sunt manifestarum rerum genera. Primum earum quæ Deo soli, secundū earū quæ Deo & conscientijs nostris, tertium uero earū quæ & Deo, & nobis, & alijs quoq; sunt manifestæ. Occultarum uero sunt duo genera tantum. Vnum earum quę ab aliorum, alterū earū quæ à nostris quoq; sunt conscientijs absconditæ. Cum igitur Apostolus dicit, & sic occulta cordis eius manifestantur: non est intelligēdū de ijs quę manifestentur coram Deo. Huic enim ut nihil est occultum, ita nihil potest per prophetiam manifestari. Restat igitur, ut de ijs intelligamus, quæ uel nostris uel aliorum conscientijs, per lucem prophetię manifestari possunt. Priorem sensum exponendo sequuti sumus, q plus uidetur habere simplicitatis: & nō illorū tantū, sed nostrorum quoq;, imò omniū temporū prophetis conuenit. Posteriorem sequitur Chrysoft. quemadmodum & nonnulli recétiores. Exponūt de reuelatiōe occultorū, qualis erat qua factū Ananię ac Sapphirę ab apostolo Petro in cœtu fideliū manifestatū est, & qua Daniel regi Nebucad Nezar, & somniū quod habuerat, & sensum illius manifestauit, & Christus Samaritanæ mulierculę secreta ad fontem exposuit. Sic sentiunt occultainfideliū & idiotarum, ubi ecclesiam ingresi sunt miraculo spiritus instinctu coră omnibus fuisse manifestata. Verum an hoc recte tribuatur prophetiæ, quatenus illa præfertur linguis, & an generale & perpetuum sit opus hoc prophetię, & an fecerit ad ædificationē idiotarum & conuersionem infidelium, & an mox omnes prophetátes hoc reuelationis genere, quorūlibet idiotarum & infidelium occulta coră ecclesia manifestare potuerint, uiderint q hūc sensum sequuntur. Si diceret, arguitur à nonnullis, diiudicatur à nonnullis, à quibus occulta cordis eius manifestantur ecclesiæ: facilis esset intelle ctus, quem isti perhibent: uerum cum dicat, arguitur ab omnibus, dijudicatur ab omnib. & sic occulta cordis eius manifesta fiunt, nec uero simile sit, omnibus fuisse pphetantib. miraculosum illud reuelandorum secretorū donū concessum diuinitus: puto & simplicius, & securius, mentiq; Apostoli uicinius, & usui prophetiæ, de quo disputat conuenientius esse, ut priorem sensum tenentes, exponamus de manifestatione occultorum, quæ ante prophetiæ auditum conscientias idiotarum & infidelium lateant, postea uero ipsis per lucem prophetiæ reuelantur.
units.tr: There are three kinds of manifest things: the first are those manifest to God alone; the second are those manifest to God and to our consciences; the third are those manifest to God, to us, and to others as well. Of hidden things there are only two kinds: one of those hidden from others, and the other of those hidden even from our own consciences. When the Apostle therefore says, "and so the secrets of his heart are made manifest," this is not to be understood of things made manifest before God. For nothing is hidden from him, and so nothing can be made manifest to him through prophecy. It remains, then, that we understand it of those things which can be made manifest, through the light of prophecy, to our own consciences or to those of others. We have followed the former sense, which seems to have more simplicity, and which fits not only those prophets of that time but ours as well, indeed the prophets of every age. Chrysostom follows the latter, as do some more recent writers. They explain it of the revelation of hidden things, such as that by which the deed of Ananias and Sapphira was made manifest by the apostle Peter in the assembly of the faithful, and by which Daniel revealed to King Nebuchadnezzar both the dream he had had and its meaning, and by which Christ laid bare the secrets of the Samaritan woman at the well. They hold that the hidden things of unbelievers and of the unlearned, when they enter the Church, were made manifest before all by a miracle and by the impulse of the Spirit. But whether this can rightly be attributed to prophecy, insofar as prophecy is preferred to tongues; whether this work of prophecy is general and perpetual; whether it served for the edification of the unlearned and the conversion of unbelievers; and whether all who prophesied could at once reveal, by this kind of revelation, the hidden things of any unlearned or unbelieving person before the Church, let those who follow this sense consider. If he were saying, "he is convicted by some, he is judged by some, by whom the secrets of his heart are made manifest to the Church," the meaning they propose would be easy to grasp. But since he says, "he is convicted by all, he is judged by all, and so the secrets of his heart are made manifest," and since it is not likely that all the prophets were given that miraculous gift of revealing secrets by divine grant, I think it is both simpler and safer, and closer to the Apostle's meaning and to the use of prophecy of which he is arguing, to keep the former sense and to explain it of the manifestation of those hidden things which, before the hearing of prophecy, lie concealed in the consciences of the unlearned and unbelievers, and which are afterwards revealed to them through the light of prophecy.

units.la: ATQVE ita procidens in faciem, inqt, adorabit Deum. ] Postquā exposuit quid accidat idiotæ aut infideli ex auditu prophetiæ eccle-
units.tr: "And so, falling on his face," he says, "he will worship God." After he has explained what happens to the unlearned or unbeliever from hearing ecclesiastical prophecy,

units.la: siastice, subiungit de secundo euentu qui Deū concernit, exponens, quo affectu idiota aut in fidelis de impietate, iniusticia, & erroribus suis admonitus ad Deum rapiatur: uel si mauis, quo pudore uelut ad tribunal Dei constitutus percellatur. Sic est comuniter coparata quęuis conscientia de peccatis suis couicta, ut mox ue lut in conspectu Dei cōstituta, uel metu uel pu dore corripiatur, cū antea fuerit admodū secura. Hoc est quod dicit: atq; ita procidens in faciem adorabit Deum. Per externū gestum exprimit internū perculsi animi affectum, pudorem & humiliationem. Procidere nō modo in genua, sed & in faciem, gestus est conscientiæ in conspectu Dei prostratæ ac confusæ.
units.tr: he adds the second outcome, which concerns God, explaining with what feeling the unlearned or unbelieving person, admonished about his impiety, injustice, and errors, is drawn to God. Or, if you prefer, with what shame he is struck, as if he were standing before the judgment seat of God. Any conscience convicted of its sins is commonly so disposed that, once it is set, as it were, in the sight of God, it is struck with fear or shame, although before it had been quite secure. This is what he means: "and so, falling on his face, he will worship God." By an outward gesture he expresses the inward feeling of a soul struck with alarm, shame and humiliation. To fall not only on the knees but on the face is the gesture of a conscience prostrated and confounded in the sight of God.

units.la: Illud, adorabat Deum, in Græco est, προσκυνῶ i. humiliabit se suppliciter ac subijciet Deo, perinde atque solent catelli, ubi ab heris suis increpantur. Est enim uox ista à more canum desumpta, quo se pedibus dominorū suorum humiliter aduoluūt. Et quoniā hic gestus inclusam habet supplicationē, solet προσκυνεῖν, & Ebræum illud השתחוה per uerbum adoran di transferri. Huiusmodi aut conuictæ conscientiæ confusio, humiliatio, submissio, ac supplicatio acceptior est in cōspectu Dei q̃ sit omnis iusticiariorum iusticia, &omnis sapientum sapientia, qua securi nec humiliantur coram diui na Maiestate, nec agnoscunt sua delicta, quib. illam quotidie offendunt. Sic plus reuerentiæ & gloriæ accedit ad Deum ab idiotis & infidelibus conscientia peccatorum perculsis, quàm à pharisæis, iusticarijs, & hypocritis.
units.tr: "He will worship God" is, in Greek, προσκυνῶ [proskynō], that is, he will humble himself suppliantly and submit to God, just as little dogs do when their masters scold them. The word is taken from the custom of dogs, which humbly fawn at the feet of their masters. Since this gesture contains supplication within it, προσκυνεῖν is customarily rendered by the verb "to adore," and the Hebrew השתחוה [hishtachawah] is rendered the same way. Such confusion, humiliation, submission and supplication of a convicted conscience is more acceptable in the sight of God than all the righteousness of the self-righteous and all the wisdom of the wise, who, being secure, neither humble themselves before the divine Majesty nor acknowledge the sins by which they offend it every day. Thus more reverence and glory comes to God from the simple and the unbelieving, struck by the consciousness of their sins, than from the Pharisees, the self-righteous and the hypocrites.

units.la: PRONVNCIANS, inqt, quod Deus reuerafit in uobis. ] Hoc tertium habet euentū ac fructum prophetiæ, qui redit ad ecclesiā, dum per prophetiam illuminati, ac de peccatis suis conuicti agnoscunt, & testatur esse in illa Deū. In Græco est ἀπαγγέλλων. Significat ea uox renū ciare ac recitare uisa & audita, quæadmodū solent legati ad heros suos reuersi. Et hoc sensu dixit Seruator ad discipulos Ioannis ad se missos, Euntes ἀπαγγείλατε: idest, renunciate Ioannī quæ auditis & uidetis. Sic dicit hic Apostolus idiotam aut infidelem ad Deū p prophetiam conuersum renunciaturū suis, & alijs quoque esse Deū reuera in ecclesia Christianorū. Quare pertinenter reddidit Eras. renuncians quod Deus reuera in uobis sit: quod & uerti potest, inter uos sit. Dices: Atqui cum sit ubiq; Deus, repleatq; cœlum, terrā & omnia, & recte dictū sit illud, Est Deus in nobis, agitāte calescimus illo, & ab hoc ipso Apost. quod nō absit longe ab unoquoq; mortalium, & quod per ipsum uiuamus & moueamur: quomodo singulariter in ecclesia fideliū esse prædicatur, aut quid magni etiam est, esse in Christianis Deum, qui esse conuincitur ubiq; & in omnibus? Respondeo. Quod diuinam potentiam & generalē quoq; prouidentiam attinet, ubique est Deus moderans, gubernans & conseruans ea quę cōdidit omnia. Et hoc pacto est in mortalib. omnibus. Quod uero singularem illius gratiā, dignationem nem ac beneuolentiam concernit, per quam non sæculariter tantum,sed & spiritualiter ad ueram ac sempiternam salutem sanctificamur ac dirigimur, singulariter est per uirtutem & operationes spiritussanĉti in medio sui populi & in cordibus fidelium. Et hæc illius præsentia uarijs modis in ecclesia fidelium manifesta tur:utpote,per signa & portenta, quibus olim Euangelij doctrinam confirmauit:per lucem ueritatis, quæ est euangelica prophetia, qua corda fidelium conuertuntur, & rudes idiotæ in fide Christi instituuntur:per omnis generis pietatem,iusticiam,uitæ innocentiam, beneficentiam, mansuetudinem spiritus, fraternam charitatem,& infractam quantumuis tribulationum tolerantiam. Arguunt enim hæc omnia diuinam & cœlestem uirtutem in hominibus ea operantem,quæ à communi sunt naturæ nostræ consuetudine,& cursu aliena.
units.tr: "Declaring," it says, "that God is truly among you." This is the third effect and fruit of prophecy, which returns to the Church: when those who have been enlightened by prophecy and convicted of their sins acknowledge and bear witness that God is present in it. In Greek it is ἀπαγγέλλων [apangellōn]. That word means to report back and relate what has been seen and heard, as envoys do when they return to their masters. In this sense the Saviour said to the disciples of John who had been sent to him: "Go and report [ἀπαγγείλατε] to John what you hear and see." So the Apostle here says that the simple or unbelieving man, converted to God through prophecy, will report to his own people, and to others too, that God is truly in the Christian congregation. Therefore Erasmus fittingly rendered it "declaring that God really is among you"; it may also be rendered "is among you." You will say: since God is everywhere, fills heaven, earth and all things, and it is rightly said that we live, move and have our being in him, and that he is not far from any mortal (Acts 17), how is he said to be present in the assembly of the faithful in a special way? Or what great thing is it that God is among Christians, when he is shown to be everywhere and in all? I answer: as regards his divine power and general providence, God is everywhere, governing, guiding and preserving the things he has made; and in this way he is present in all mortals. But as regards his special grace, favour and goodwill, through which we are sanctified and directed not merely in worldly matters but spiritually, to true and everlasting salvation, he is present in a special way, by the power and operations of the Holy Spirit, in the midst of his people and in the hearts of the faithful. This presence is made manifest in the Church of the faithful in various ways: namely, through signs and wonders, by which he formerly confirmed the doctrine of the Gospel; through the light of truth, which is evangelical prophecy, by which the hearts of the faithful are turned and simple folk are instructed in the faith of Christ; and through every kind of piety, righteousness, innocence of life, beneficence, gentleness of spirit, brotherly love, and unbroken endurance of whatever tribulations. For all these things bear witness to a divine and heavenly power working in men, a power foreign to the common course and custom of our nature.

units.la: Cum igitur conuersus infidelis, Deum esse in ecclesia Christianorum renunciat ac deprædicat,agnoscit & testatur doctrinam, fidem, ac religionem illorum esse diuinam, esse ueracē, & nihil minus quàm erroneam & hæreticam, quo quid maius & augustius de illa prædicari poterit? Interea hostes ueritatis,iusticiarij, hypocritæ, sapientes huius mundi, damnant illá hæreseos,uocant erroneam ac seductricē,quia opus gratiæ Dei nō agnoscunt. Offenduntur simplicitate illius & humilitate, deinde & diuersitate illa,qua dissidet à splendore ac super stitione falsorum cultuum,& aliena est ab opi- nione & fiducia proprię iusticię,& à gloria mū danæ sapientiæ.
units.tr: Therefore, when a converted unbeliever declares and proclaims that God is in the Christian congregation, he acknowledges and testifies that their doctrine, faith and religion are divine, true, and by no means erroneous or heretical. What greater and more honourable thing could be said of it? Meanwhile the enemies of the truth, the self-righteous, the hypocrites, and the wise of this world condemn it as a heresy, calling it erroneous and seductive, because they do not recognise the work of God's grace in it. They are offended by its simplicity and humility, and then also by that difference which separates it from the splendour and superstition of false worship, and which is alien to the opinion and confidence in one's own righteousness, and to the glory of worldly wisdom.

units.la: Hactenus ergo ,pphetia utilior est linguis, quod cum illę ecclesiam reddant ridiculam, & nec fidelibus,nec infidelibus intempestiue usurpatę prosint:ipsa utilis est omnibus,feruit gloriæ Dei,& cœlestis gratiæ testimonium confert ecclesiæ Christi. Contemnunt ista,qui malunt exclusa ,pphetia,quotidianis & barbaris boatibus,ac missarum gesticulationibus,oculos& aures fascinare rudium & imperitorum.
units.tr: So prophecy is more useful than tongues. For while tongues make the Church ridiculous, and, when used out of season, benefit neither believers nor unbelievers, prophecy is useful to all: it serves the glory of God and bears witness to heavenly grace for the Church of Christ. Those who prefer, with prophecy shut out, to dazzle the eyes and ears of the unlearned and ignorant with daily barbarous bellowings and the gesticulations of the Mass, despise these things.

units.la: Priusquam progrediamur ad sequentia,respondendum est ad quæstiones quę hoc loco moueri possunt, & à Chrysostomo attingun- tur. Dixit Apostolus,linguas esse vice signi nō ijs qui credunt,sed incredulis:prophetiam uero non incredulis,sed credentibus. Et hinc colligens subiungit:Ergo si cōuenerit ecclesia tota simul,& omnes linguis loquantur, ingrediantur autem idiotę, uel increduli, an non dicent uos insanire? Quæritur hic quomodo linguę sint in signum, unde moueantur ad credendū increduli,si auditis illis dicturi sunt increduli insanire eos qui linguis loquuntur? Deinde pergens:Si uero omnes prophetetis,inquit,in grediatur autē incredulus uel idiota,coarguitur ab omnibus,dijudicatur ab omnibus,& sic occulta cordis eius manifesta fiunt, atq; ita ,p- cidens in faciem adorabit Deum, renuncians quod Deus in uobis sit. Quæritur ergo quomodo prophetiam dixerit competere non incre-
units.tr: Before we go on to what follows, we must answer the questions that can be raised at this point, and which Chrysostom touches upon. The Apostle said that tongues are a sign not for those who believe but for unbelievers, and that prophecy is not for unbelievers but for believers. Drawing a conclusion from this, he adds: "If therefore the whole church comes together and all speak with tongues, and simple people or unbelievers come in, will they not say that you are mad?" The question is raised here: how are tongues a sign, by which unbelievers are moved to believe, if, on hearing them, the unbelievers are going to say that those who speak in tongues are mad? Then he goes on: "But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or a simple person comes in, he is convicted by all and judged by all, and so the secrets of his heart are made manifest; and so, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you." The question therefore is how he could say that prophecy is suited not to unbelievers but to believers,

units.la: dulis,sed credentibus, si per illam non modo credentes ędificantur,sed & increduli illumi- nantur,& ad Deum conuertuntur.
units.tr: when through it not only believers are built up but unbelievers too are enlightened and converted to God.

units.la: Respondeo. Nihil hic contradictionis est,si quę dicuntur recte considerentur.Linguæ in- signum sunt incredulis,intellige, datę a domino,ut dum Græcus uirū Ebræum Græce,Romanus Romane,&c. loquente audiret, sicut ac cidit in die Pētecoftes,obstupefactus intelligeret illū ex instinctu spiritus Dei,lingua quā nō didicerit, expedite loqui,eoq; facilius ad credendū permoueretur. Huic non repugnat quod dicit:Si cōuenerit ecclesia tota simul,& oēs lin- guis loquantur,ingrediantur aut idiotę aut in creduli,an nō dicent uos insanire? Primum e- nim qui linguis in ecclesia Corinthiorū loque bantur,nō loquebātur illis quę possent ab idio- tis & incredulis qui illic erat intelligi, sicuti fecerat apostoli Hierosolymis,quos oēs aduenæ illic sua quisq; lingua loquentes audiebat & in telligebat. Deinde,nō dicit:Si quidā inter uos, sed si oēs linguis loquantur.id quod non potest rat fieri sine graui confusione. Tertio nō loqui tur de quibusuis incredulis,sed de illis q eccle siam fidelium in dno collectā ad hoc ingredie- bantur,ut de ueritate Christianæ religionis co gnoscerent.Hi si audissent omnes alienis & in- cognitis linguis loquentes, sic ut nec ipsi nec reliqua multitudo collecta quicquam intelli- gerent, utiq; recte eos insanire dixissent. Nec mirum,cū Apostoli à nonnullis habiti sint pro ebrijs in die Pentecostes,quàuis uarijs linguis loquētes,à uarijs nationib.intelligeretur. Hęc puto ad priorē posse responderi quæstionem. Ad posteriore quoq; facilis est responsio. Prophetiam dixit non esse data incredulis,sed credentibus:hic uero tribuit illi, quod increduli quoq; prosit ad illuminatione &cōuersionem. Distinguendū est inter eos incredulos qui nō sunt crediturī uerbo nisi per signa & portenta moueantur, & eos infideles qui iā cœperunt de cognoscenda ueritate cogitare,eāq; ob cā fam conuentus fidelium ultro & cupide ingre diuntur, ut in illis audiant, quēnā fit & qualis Christianorū doctrina,fides & religio. Prioribus non est destinata ,pphetia,à quib.non reci pitur.Hic uerum est quod dixit, ,pphetia uero non credulis,sed credentibus.Posteriorib.uero admodū est utile,si ,pphetiam audiāt.In illis enim cōpletur quod hic dicit: Coarguūtur e- nim,dijudicātur,&in cognitione occultorū su orū tā errorū quàm deliĉtorum perducuntur. Nihil igitur hic quoq; cōtradictionis est, fi in- ter incredulos & infideles distinguatur.
units.tr: I answer: there is no contradiction here, if what is said is rightly considered. Tongues are a sign for unbelievers, that is, they were given by the Lord so that when a Greek heard a Hebrew speaking in Greek, or a Roman speaking in Latin, and so on, as happened on the day of Pentecost, he would be astonished and understand that by the impulse of God's Spirit the man was speaking fluently in a language he had never learned, and so would be more easily moved to believe. What he says does not conflict with this: "If the whole church comes together and all speak with tongues, and simple people or unbelievers come in, will they not say that you are mad?" For first, those who spoke in tongues in the church of the Corinthians did not speak in such a way as could be understood by the simple and unbelievers who were there, as the apostles had done at Jerusalem, where all the foreigners heard them and understood each speaking in his own tongue. Second, he does not say "if some among you," but "if all speak in tongues," which could not happen without great confusion. Third, he is not speaking of any unbelievers whatever, but of those who came into the assembly of the faithful gathered in the Lord for this purpose, to learn about the truth of the Christian religion. If these had heard everyone speaking in foreign and unknown tongues, so that neither they nor the rest of the gathered crowd understood anything, they would rightly have said that the speakers were mad. Nor is it surprising, since the Apostles were taken by some for drunkards on the day of Pentecost, although, speaking in various tongues, they were understood by people of various nations. I think this can serve as the answer to the first question. The answer to the second is also easy. He said that prophecy is not given to unbelievers but to believers; here, however, he attributes to it that it also benefits unbelievers for their enlightenment and conversion. One must distinguish between those unbelievers who will not be moved by the word unless they are stirred by signs and wonders, and those infidels who have already begun to think about coming to know the truth, and for that reason gladly and eagerly enter the assemblies of the faithful, so that they may hear there what the doctrine, faith and religion of the Christians are and what they are like. Prophecy is not intended for the former, by whom it is not received. What he said here is true: prophecy is not for unbelievers but for believers. But for the latter it is very useful, if they hear prophecy. For in them is fulfilled what he says here: "They are convicted, they are judged, and they are led to the knowledge of the secrets of their hearts, both of their errors and of their sins." Therefore there is no contradiction here either, if a distinction is drawn between unbelievers and infidels.

units.la: Tria sunt genera ἀπιστων. Primū est eorum, qui sic sunt obstinati, ut nullis nec signis, nec prophetijs ad fidem perduci queant.
units.tr: There are three kinds of ἀπιστοι [unbelievers]. The first is of those who are so obstinate that they can be brought to faith neither by signs nor by prophecies.

units.la: Secundum eorum qui uerbo non credunt, nisi signis & portentis ad credendum inducantur. Ad illos pertinet quod linguas incredulis signi uice datas esse dixit.
units.tr: The second is of those who do not believe the word unless they are led to belief by signs and portents. To these belongs what he said, that tongues were given to unbelievers as a sign.

units.la: Tertium eorum qui iam de ueritate cognoscenda facti sunt soliciti, ideoque in ecclesiam fidelium ingrediuntur, ut audiant & intelligant. In istis uera sunt quæ hic ab Apostolo dicuntur.
units.tr: The third is of those who have now become anxious to know the truth, and therefore enter the assembly of the faithful, so that they may hear and understand. What the Apostle says here is true of these.

units.la: Quid igitur est fratres? Quoties conuenitis, unusquisque uestrum psalmum habet, doctrinam habet, linguâ habet, reuelationem habet, interpretationem habet, omnia ad ædificationem fiant. Siue lingua quis loquitur, fiat per binos, aut ad summum ternos, idq; uicissim, & unus interpretetur: quod si non est interpres, taceat in ecclesia, loquatur uero sibi ipsi & Deo.
units.tr: What then is it, brethren? Whenever you come together, each one of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a tongue, has a revelation, has an interpretation. Let all things be done for edification. If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be done by two, or at most three, and each in turn, and let one interpret. But if there is no interpreter, let him keep silent in the church, and let him speak to himself and to God.

units.la: Hactenus argumentatus est contra abusum linguarum, discreuitq; inter illas & prophetiâ, & hortatus est, ut prophetiæ, quoniam præstantior est atq; utilior, maiori studio incumbant quàm linguis. iam uela cótracturus subijcit ordinem, quo debeant donis Dei uti in ecclesia, & define præscribit, ad quem dirigenda sint omnia. Quid igitur est fratres, inquit? quasi dicat: Cum itaque tam sint dispares linguarum & prophetiæ euentus, ut plurimum referat, quo modo & ordine usurpentur charismata hęc in ecclesia, quid conuenit, ut faciatis? Hæc uidelicet.
units.tr: Up to this point he has argued against the abuse of tongues, distinguished them from prophecy, and urged that, since prophecy is the more excellent and useful gift, people should give themselves to it with greater zeal than to tongues. Now, about to remove the veils, he sets out the order in which the gifts of God ought to be used in the church, and he prescribes the end to which everything must be directed. "What then is it, brethren?" he says, as if to say: since the results of tongues and of prophecy differ so greatly, and it matters much how and in what order these gifts are employed in the church, what is fitting for you to do? Namely this.

units.la: QVOTIES conuenitis, unusquisq; uestrum psalmum habet, &c.] Omnia ad ædificationem fiant. Pertinent hæc ad finem omnium eorum quæ in conuentu ecclesiæ geruntur. Is est, ut omnia fiant ad ædificationem fidelium, uidelicet, qui sunt in ecclesia. Hoc est, ut omnes in fide & cognitione Christi, ueraq; pietate & iustitia crescant, magisq; ac magis confirmetur. Hæc est uera ædificatio templi domini. Qui sunt autem illius ædificatores? Vnusquisq; uestrum inquit. Ergo omnes tum temporis qui membra erant ecclesiæ, simul erant illius ædificatores. Sic infrà dicit: Potestis omnes prophetare. Mirabilis sane structura in qua lapides & struebant & struebantur. Poterat hoc tum fieri propter ubertatem donorum Dei, quæ per spiritum Christi lagiter in eos qui credebant effundebantur. Ea erant instar organorum, quæ ad hoc erant accommodata, ut structuræ huic & ædificationi seruirent. De his admonens nō simpliciter, Quoties conuenitis, omnia ad ædificationem facite, inquit: sed, Quoties conuenitis, unusquisq; uestrum psalmum habet, doctrinam habet, linguam habet, reuelationem habet, interpretationem habet. Ergo ædificationis huius organa sunt, psalmi, doctrina, linguæ, reuelationes, & interpretationes. Hisce sic erat instructa prima illa ecclesia, ut in cœtu conuenientes fideles haberent & cóportarét alium psalmum, alius doctrinam, alius linguas, alius reuelationem, alius interpretationem uel sacræ scripturæ, uel eorum quæ linguis dicebantur. Sic intelligendum est quod dicit, Vnusquisq; uestrum psalmum habet, &c. Hoc est, unusquisque uestrum aliquid adfert, alius psalmum, alius
units.tr: "Whenever you come together, each one of you has a psalm," and so on. "Let all things be done for edification." These words pertain to the end of all that is done in the assembly of the church. That end is that all things be done for the edification of the faithful, that is, of those who are in the church: that all may grow in the faith and knowledge of Christ, in true piety and righteousness, and be ever more and more confirmed. This is the true building of the temple of the Lord. But who are its builders? "Each one of you," he says. Therefore all who were then members of the church were at the same time its builders. So below he says: "You can all prophesy." Certainly a wonderful structure, in which the stones both built and were built. This could happen then because of the abundance of God's gifts, which were poured out richly through the Spirit of Christ upon those who believed. These gifts were like instruments fitted for this purpose, that they might serve this structure and this building. Admonishing them about these things, he does not simply say, "Whenever you come together, do all things for edification," but "Whenever you come together, each one of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a tongue, has a revelation, has an interpretation." So these are the instruments of this edification: psalms, teaching, tongues, revelations and interpretations. The first church was thus equipped with these, so that the faithful, when they came together in assembly, each brought and contributed something: one a psalm, another a teaching, another a tongue, another a revelation, another an interpretation, whether of Holy Scripture or of what was said in tongues. This is how we must understand what he says, "Each one of you has a psalm," and so on. That is, each one of you brings something: one a psalm, another

units.la: lius doctrinam, &c. uel, unusquisque uestrum uel psalmum habet, uel doctrinam, uel linguâ &c. Non tribuit singulis omnia, quia nec spiritus sanctus hæc dona sic distribuit, ut singulis conferret omnia, sed alij aliud, quèadmodum & suprà cap. 12. commemoratum est. Neq; recenset omnia dona spiritus, sed ecclesiastica tantum quæ in conuentibus ecclesiæ usurpari poterant. Itaq; sic donis spiritus alij alijs instructi fideles, & in cœtum congregati, perinde sese mutuo poterát in unum illis ueluti sym bolis collatis ædificare, atq; membra corporis dum corpori sustentádo & alendo singula suas uires, suaq; officia impendunt, sese mutuo sustentant & alunt.
