Nunc uero postquam cessanti bus donis illis in ecclesia facta sunt omnia con tractiora, redijt ædificatio ecclesiæ ad paucos ministros, pastores & doctores, qui utinâ nusquam non sint domino fideles, & necessarijs or ganis ad structuram templi domini instructi.
units.tr: another a teaching, and so on. Or: each of you has either a psalm, or a teaching, or a tongue, and so on. He does not assign everything to each individual, because the Holy Spirit did not distribute these gifts so that each individual received everything, but one this and another that, as was also mentioned above in chapter 12. Nor does he list all the gifts of the Spirit, but only those ecclesiastical gifts which could be exercised in the assemblies of the church. And so the faithful, each equipped with the gifts of the Spirit and gathered into one body, could build one another up in the same way, as if their gifts were brought together like symbols, just as the members of the body, while each contributes its own strength and function to sustaining and nourishing the body, also sustain and nourish one another. But now that those gifts have ceased in the church, all things have become more restricted, and the building up of the church has returned to a few ministers, pastors and teachers, who would that they were faithful to the Lord everywhere and equipped with the necessary instruments for the building of the Lord's temple.

units.la: VNVSQVISQVE uestrum, inquit, psalmum habet.] Erasmus uertit canticū. Nos notam & usitatâ in ecclesia uocem retinemus. Habebant aliqui psalmos, id est, dono & instinctu spiritus componebant cantica spiritualia, quibus magnalia ac laudes Dei decantabant. Poterant illa facere ad ædificationem ecclesiæ, si idiomate patrio & uulgo intelligibili decantarentur. Valent enim plurimum ad excitandos audientium spiritus, præsertim si communiter à plebe fidelium decantetur, quemadmodum in reformatis ecclesijs fieri uidemus.
units.tr: "Each one of you," he says, "has a psalm." Erasmus renders this as "a canticle." We retain the word that is familiar and in common use in the church. Some had psalms, that is, by the gift and inspiration of the Spirit they composed spiritual songs, in which they sang the great works and praises of God. They could make these for the edification of the church, if they were sung in the native tongue and in a language the common people understood. For they are very effective in stirring the spirits of the hearers, especially when sung together by the common body of the faithful, as we see done in the reformed churches.

units.la: DOCTRINAM habet, inquit.] Dupliciter exponi potest. Primũ in genere, ut doctrinâ habere, idem sit quod præditum esse facultate docendi, quæsane non est omnium. Reperias qui intelligentia rerū docendarū destituti, quod ipsi nesciunt alios docere nequeant. Rursus inuenias qui etsi apprime sint scietia rerū instructi, dicendi tamen facultate destituti, quæ sciunt exprimere non ualent. Quare singulari dono opus est, ut & scias & eloqui ualeas, si munere docendi functurus sis in ecclesia. Deinde specialiter, de parte aliqua doctrinæ, quæ utilis sit & necessaria ecclesiæ, ut doctrinâ habere, aliquid sit habere, quod speciali de causa proponendum sit ecclesiæ. Hoc sensu legendū esset, Dum conuenitis, unusquisque uestrum uel psalmum aliquem, uel doctrinam aliquam habet. Vterq; sensus probabilis est, at mihi posterior germanior esse uidetur.
units.tr: "Has a teaching," he says. This can be explained in two ways. First, in general: to have teaching may be the same as to be endowed with the ability to teach, which is certainly not given to everyone. You will find people who lack understanding of the things to be taught, so that they cannot teach others what they themselves do not know. Again, you will find people who, though thoroughly versed in the subject matter, lack the ability to speak, and so cannot express what they know. Therefore a special gift is needed, so that one may both know and be able to speak, if one is to perform the office of teaching in the church. Second, more particularly: to have teaching may mean to have some part of doctrine that is useful and necessary to the church, something which for a special reason is to be set before the church. In this sense it would be read: "When you come together, each of you has either some psalm or some teaching." Both senses are plausible, but to me the latter seems more genuine.

units.la: REVELATIONEM habet, inqt.] Id est, rem aliquam ecclesiæ reuelandam habet. Est autem reuelatio, secreti alicuius manifestatio. Et sunt duo secretorum genera. Præsentium unum, futurorum alterum. Posterius ad uaticinia pertinet sensu communi, prius uero ad præsentium secretorū manifestatione. Quan quam reperias ubi futurorū quoq; prædictio, reuelatio uocatur, quemadmodum uidere est in libro Apocalypseos.
units.tr: "Has a revelation," he says. That is, he has some matter to reveal to the church. A revelation is the manifestation of some secret, and there are two kinds of secrets: one of present things, the other of future things. The latter pertains in common sense to prophecies, the former to the disclosure of present secrets. Yet you will find cases where the prediction of future things too is called a revelation, as can be seen in the book of the Apocalypse.

units.la: LINGVAM habet.] Id est, donum linguarum habet, siue unius aut plurium. INTERPRETATIONEM habet, inqt.] Puto hoc intelligendum esse non de re quapiā speciāliter interpretāda, sed de dono interpretationis. Est autem gemina interpretatio. Vna qua sacræ scripturę, altera qua linguę, id est, ea quæ peregrinis linguis in ecclesia, uel psallūtur, uel orantur, uel dicuntur, uulgari idiomate exprimuntur. de quo genere interpretationis supra est cap.12. facta mentio.
units.tr: "Has a tongue," that is, has the gift of tongues, of one or of several. "Has an interpretation," he says. I think this should be understood not of some particular matter to be interpreted, but of the gift of interpretation. Interpretation is twofold: one of Holy Scripture, the other of tongues, that is, what is sung, prayed or said in foreign tongues in the church is expressed in the vernacular. Of this kind of interpretation mention was made above in chapter 12.

units.la: OMNIA ad ædificationem fiant, inquit.] Id est, omnia hæc sic geratur in ecclesia, ut possint facere ad ædificationem fidelium. Duo requirit ab ijs qui aliquid in ecclesia, uel dicunt uel faciunt. Vnum est, ut quod agunt, ex proposito ædificationis agant. Alterum, ut eo modo agant, quo ad ædificationem facere possit. Hic refert qualia in se sint, quæ geruntur in ecclesia. Etenim si natura sic sint comparata, ut ad ueram ædificationem facere non possint, inane erit propositum, & intentio frustranea, nec utilis erit ullus agendi modus. Cauendum ergo est ne particulam hanc sic intelligamus esse generalem, quasi decernat omnia posse geri in ecclesia, modo ad ædificationem. Loquitur Apostolus non de omnibus omnium adinuentionibus, somnijs, ritibus ac cæremonijs, quæ à superstitiosis hominibus in ecclesiá post Apostolorum tempora induci cœperunt: sed de psalmis, linguis, doctrina, reuelatione & interpretatione. Post horum catalogum subiecit: omnia ad ædificationem fiant. Quare non cōuenit, ut quod dicit, extra limites materiæ de qua loquitur extēdatur. Cum igitur fiunt in ecclesia, quæ diuinitus sunt ad ædificationem fidelium tradita, fiuntq; & propositio ædificationis & modo legitimo ac utili, secundum qualitatem ecclesiæ: inculpabiles erunt ministri ecclesiæ, siue ædificentur per illa fideles, siue minus. Est enim incrementum, non in manu ministri, sed in manu Dei.
units.tr: "Let all things be done for edification," he says. That is, let all these things be so conducted in the church that they can serve the edification of the faithful. He requires two things of those who either say or do anything in the church. One is that they act from the purpose of edification; the other, that they act in such a way that it can contribute to edification. Here he states what kind of things are done in the church. For if by their nature they were such that they could not contribute to true edification, the purpose would be empty, the intention vain, and no manner of acting would be useful. We must therefore take care not to understand this particle as so general, as if he decreed that all things could be done in the church, provided it was for edification. The Apostle speaks not of all the inventions of all men, dreams, rites and ceremonies, which superstitious men began to introduce into the church after the times of the Apostles, but of psalms, tongues, teaching, revelation and interpretation. After this catalogue he added: let all things be done for edification. Therefore it is not fitting that what he says be extended beyond the limits of the matter he is discussing. When, then, those things are done in the church which were divinely handed down for the edification of the faithful, and are done with edification as their purpose and in a lawful and useful manner, suited to the character of the church, the ministers of the church will be blameless, whether the faithful are edified through them or not. For the increase is not in the minister's hand, but in the hand of God.

units.la: SIVE lingua quis loquitur, inquit.] Post præscriptum scopi ac finis, ad quem sunt colli manda omnia, iam subiungit expositione modi & ordinis, quo geri debeant, quæ geruntur in ecclesia.
units.tr: WHETHER anyone speaks in a tongue, he says. Having set out the aim and end to which all these things are to be directed, he now explains the manner and order in which the things done in the Church ought to be carried out.

units.la: 1 Et primum præscribit illis qui linguis loquebantur. Non dicit: Ne quis linguis loquatur. Neq; enim prohibet loqui linguis. Nec iubet linguis loqui, sed liberum hoc illis permittens, de modo & ordine præscribit dicens: Si lingua quis loquitur, fiat p binos, aut ad summum (in Græco est τὸ πλεῖστον, id est, ut plurimū) per ternos, idq; uicissim, ut unus interpretetur. Tria præcipit.
units.tr: First he gives instructions to those who spoke in tongues. He does not say, "Let no one speak in tongues," for he does not forbid speaking in tongues. Nor does he command it. He leaves it free to them, and prescribes the manner and order, saying: "If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be by two, or at most (in Greek [τὸ πλεῖστον], that is, as a rule) by three, and that in turn, so that one may interpret." He lays down three things.

units.la: Primum est, ne ultra ternos linguis loquantur. Non uetat, ne unus tantum, sed ne plures tribus ad loquendum linguis admittantur. Sic cauere uoluit, ne si plures loquantur, omne tempus, quo congregata est ecclesia, sic linguis detur, ut non uacet audire prophetias. Hac restrictione numeri innuitur, quàm non fuerit modus ullus linguis in ecclesia Corinthiorum loquentium, usque adeò inualuerat inanis ostentatio quemadmodum in Papatu quæstus Missaticus: per quem fit, ut cum ueteres uno tantū Eucharistiæ sacro cōtenti fuerint, iam omnes templorum angulos multitudine Missarū impleri uideamus.
units.tr: The first is that they should not speak in tongues more than three at a time. He does not forbid that only one speak, but that more than three not be admitted to speak in tongues. He wished to guard against the danger that, if many spoke, the whole time during which the church was assembled would be given over to tongues, so that there would be no leisure to hear prophecies. By this limit on number it is hinted that there was no restraint at all on speaking in tongues in the church of the Corinthians, so far had empty display prevailed. It is like the Mass-trade in the Papacy, through which it happens that, while the ancients were content with the one sacred Eucharist, we now see every corner of the temples filled with a multitude of Masses.

units.la: 2 Deinde præcipit, ut uicissim loquantur, ad uitandum uidelicet confusionem. Ergo illi sic inhiabant ostentationi quisq; suæ, ut omnis morę impatientes, haud expectarent tanti spatium, dum prior loqui desineret: sed simul alius alia loquerentur, atque ita speciem quandam insaniæ spectantibus objicerent. Etenim quis non dicat meram esse insaniam, si in eodem conuētu plures simul ad populū diuersa diuersis linguis alius Latine, alius Gallice, alius Germanice concionentur? Sic Missatores papistę plures eadem hora diuersis locis palā in templis, sub unius conuentus spacio, alius de spiritusanōto, alius de beata uirgine, alius pro defunctis, alius de nescio quo diuo, alius de tempore missant.
units.tr: The second thing he orders is that they speak in turn, namely to avoid confusion. Those men were so eager for their own display, and so impatient of any restraint, that they would not wait for the previous speaker to finish. Instead several spoke at once, each in a different tongue, and so presented to the onlookers a kind of madness. For who would not call it sheer madness if, in the same assembly, several men at once preached to the people in different tongues, one in Latin, another in French, another in German? So the Papist Mass-mongers, at the same hour, openly in different places in their temples, within the space of one congregation, one says Mass about the Holy Spirit, another about the blessed Virgin, another for the dead, another about some unknown saint, another about the season.

units.la: 3 Tertio, constituit, ut unus interpretetur ecclesiæ quæ linguis dicuntur, ne donum spiritus maneat inutile, & citra ædificationem ecclesiæ euanescat in auram. Ideo addit dicens, quod si non est interpres, taceat in ecclesia. Igitur illi sine interprete, alijs atq; alijs linguis multi ac simul magna cum confusione ad populum fidelium loquebantur, magis insaniam admirationem ac stuporem, quàm utilem ædificationem quærentes. Ecquid aliud faciūt in templis Papistarum, ubi omnibus illis Missis & boatibus, ne unus quidem interpres adhibetur, & tamen nemo est, qui sic insanientes tacere iubeat in ecclesia. Neq; sic sunt Apostolici, ut constitutionem hanc Apostoli alicuius faciant, quantumuis nomina & imagines apostolorum iactent & ostentent.
units.tr: The third thing he establishes is that someone should interpret for the church what is said in tongues, so that the gift of the Spirit does not remain useless and vanish into the air without edifying the church. Therefore he adds that, if there is no interpreter, the speaker should keep silent in the church. Those who spoke without an interpreter, in various and different tongues, many at once, addressed the faithful people with great confusion. They sought astonishment and amazement rather than useful edification. What else do they do in the temples of the Papists, where with all those Masses and bellowings not even one interpreter is employed, and yet no one bids such madmen keep silent in the church? Nor are they so apostolic that they make this regulation the work of some apostle, however much they boast of and display the names and images of the apostles.

units.la: LOQVATVR uero sibi ipsi & Deo, inqt.] Hoc est loquatur intra se tacite, sic ut ipse tantum audiat & Deus, cui secreta patent omnia. Refert omnino cui loquaris. Est enim sermo personæ accomodandus, ad quam dirigitur. Quisquis loquitur, aut Deo loquitur, aut hominibus, aut bestijs, aut sibi ipsi. Qui Deo loquitur, nullis expresis uerbis, ac nullius linguæ idiomate opus habet. In auribus illius cogitatio cordis manifestus est sermo. Ad homines loquenti curandum est, ut idiomate illis noto utatur, quo possit intelligi. Alias frustra loquitur. Ad bestias loquenti nonnunquam necessarium est, ut notis illis uocibus utatur. Qui sibi ipsi loquitur, sola cogitatione quod uult expedire potest. Cum ergo inutilis sit alienæ linguæ sermo ad homines factus, recte constituit Apostolus, ut qui nec ipse potest intelligibiliter loqui in ecclesia, nec aliquem habet interprete, taceat in ecclesia, & uel Deo, uel sibi ipsi loquatur: ubi nō refert quibus uerbis, aut quo idiomate, modo ipse intelligat, loquatur.
units.tr: "But let him speak to himself and to God," he says. That is, let him speak silently within himself, so that only he and God, to whom all secrets lie open, hear it. It matters entirely to whom you speak, for speech must be adapted to the person it is addressed to. Whoever speaks, speaks either to God, or to men, or to beasts, or to himself. One who speaks to God needs no express words nor the idiom of any tongue; to his ears the thought of the heart is a plain speech. One who speaks to men must take care to use an idiom known to them, by which he can be understood; otherwise he speaks in vain. One who speaks to beasts sometimes needs to use those familiar cries. One who speaks to himself can accomplish what he wishes by thought alone. Since, then, speech in a foreign tongue addressed to men is useless, the Apostle rightly lays down that whoever cannot speak intelligibly in the church himself, and has no interpreter, should keep silent in the church and speak to God or to himself. In that case it does not matter in what words or idiom he speaks, so long as he himself understands.

units.la: Prophetæ uero duo aut tres loquantur, & ceteri dijudicent. Porro si alij fuerit rit reuelatum assidenti prior taceat.Potestis enim singulatim omnes propheta re, ut omnes discant, & omnes consolationem accípiant. Et spíritus prophetarum prophetis subijciuntur. Non enim est confusionis author Deus, sed pacis, ut in omnib. congregationib. sanctorū.
units.tr: "But let the prophets speak, two or three, and let the others judge. But if anything is revealed to another who is sitting by, let the first keep silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may be comforted. And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. For God is not the author of confusion but of peace, as in all the assemblies of the saints."

units.la: Post linguas transit ad prophetiam, deque illa quoq; præscribit, ne uel modus excedatur, uel iustus ordo confundatur in re omnium utilissima. Licet enim præstantisimum sit illius donum, poterit tamen sic administrari, ut reddatur inutile, si citra modum & ordinem usurpetur. Nihil nanq; tam est in se bonum ac diuinum, quod non inter ipsas nostras manus corrumpatur. quod si agnoscerent qui prelati sunt ecclesiarum, facile cófuleretur ecclesijs, & corrigerentur innumeri errores & abusus.
units.tr: After tongues he passes to prophecy, and prescribes for it too, so that either the measure is not exceeded or the proper order is not confounded in a matter most useful of all. For although this gift is most excellent, it can nevertheless be so administered that it becomes useless if it is used without measure and order. Nothing is so good and divine in itself that it cannot be corrupted in our very hands. If those who are set over the churches recognized this, the churches would easily be helped, and countless errors and abuses would be corrected.

units.la: PROPHETAE uero duo aut tres loquantur inquit.]Præscribit illis hic quoq; modū, ordinem, & finem administrandę prophetię. Ad modum & ordinem pertinet quod dicit: Prophetæ uero duo aut tres loquantur, & cæteri dijudicent. Non addit hic τὸ ἀλλᾶτον, id est, ut plurimum, quod de linguis præscribens adiecit. Non enim in eo est, ut numerū prophetātium in ecclesia Corinthiorum restringat, sicuti linguis loquentium restrinxit. Etenim maluisset omnes esse prophetæ deditos, quemadmodū mox dicet: Potestis omnes prophetare. Nec ita erant animati Corinthij erga prophetiam, ut metuendum esset ne modum in illa excederent, sicut excedebant in linguis. Quod igitur dicit, Prophetæ duo uel tres loquantur, non sic dicit, quod nolit plures: sed quod totidem prophetis uelit esse cótentus, quot illis linguis loquentes permisit. Neq; enim ob eam rationem numerum eundem utrobiq; posuit, quod par esset linguis loquentium & prophetantium ratio & utilitas, sed quod sic animatis sic conueniret.
units.tr: "Let the prophets, two or three, speak," he says. Here too he prescribes the measure, order and end of the administration of prophecy. To the measure and order belongs what he says: "Let the prophets, two or three, speak, and let the others judge." He does not add here the words "as a rule" (in Greek [τὸ πλεῖστον]), which he added when prescribing about tongues. For it is not his purpose to restrict the number of those prophesying in the church of the Corinthians, as he restricted the number of those speaking in tongues. Indeed he would rather have all of them devoted to prophecy, as he will say soon: "You can all prophesy." Nor were the Corinthians so eager for prophecy that there was any fear they would exceed the measure in it, as they exceeded it in tongues. So when he says, "Let two or three prophets speak," he does not mean that he is unwilling to have more. He means that he wants to be content with as many prophets as he allowed speakers in tongues. He did not set the same number in both cases because the reason and usefulness of speaking in tongues and of prophesying are the same, but because that number suited such men as they were.

units.la: Cum anno millesimo quingentesimo trice simo primo Augustam uocatus uenissem, accidit in ecclesia quam sancti Vdalrici uocant, ut dominica quadā die tres Anabaptistæ ad prophetandum propria temeritate surgentes ab hora duodecima ad tertiam usq; per uices ad populum loquerentur, è quibus postea duo recantarunt, tertius è carcere aufugit. Illi putabant se numero hoc ternario pulchre satisfacere constitutioni Apostolicæ. Sic ad scindendum ecclesiam pro se rapiebant quod ab Apostolo ad tollenda erat schismata secundum statum ecclesiæ Corinthiorum præscriptum. Deinde sumpserant sibi tres horas, quo quisq; ipsorum ad spacium unius horæ ad populum diceret, ne minus ad dicendum instructi uiderentur, quàm essent ij qui ex officio & pro consuetudine ad horam in ecclesia loquuntur. At Apostolus conuentum ecclesiæ non astrinxit ad certum temporis spacium, nec ideo binos
units.tr: When I had been called to Augsburg in the year 1531, it happened in the church they call St Ulrich's that on a certain Sunday three Anabaptists, rising to prophesy by their own rashness, spoke to the people in turn from the twelfth hour until the third. Afterwards two of them recanted, and the third fled from prison. They thought they satisfied the apostolic rule nicely by the number three. Thus they were seizing for the splitting of the church what the Apostle had prescribed to remove schisms, according to the state of the Corinthian church. Then they had taken three hours for themselves, so that each of them would speak to the people for the space of one hour, lest they seem less prepared to speak than those who, by office and custom, speak in the church for an hour. But the Apostle did not bind the assembly of the church to a fixed length of time, nor did he therefore appoint two or three

units.la: uel ternos ad prophetandum constituit, quod nequeat unus satisfacere concioni, uel piaculum fit si plures tribus loquantur, & quisque tantisper dicat, dū quod uolebat sermone breui ac perspicuo expresserit.
units.tr: to prophesy because one could not satisfy the sermon alone, or because it would be a sin if more than three spoke, and each spoke only as long as it took to express in a brief and clear speech what he wanted to say.

units.la: PROPHETAE uero duo, inquit, aut tres loquantur.]Quæruntʼhic, an liberum illis hac sententia fecerit, ut absq; certa uocatione quolibet ecclesiæ conuentu ad dicendum duo uel tres surgerent: uel, an fuerint duo uel tres è numero fidelium eligendi, qui singulis conuenti bus prophetarent. Meo iudicio, quoniam Apostolus hic amans erat ordinis, uerosimilius est præscripsisse illum hoc ecclesiæ Corinthiorū, ut è numero fidelium duos uel tres deligeret, qui dono prophetiæ præditi in conuentibus ipsorum prophetarent ex ordine, quos etiam ob id prophetas uocat, non simpliciter dicés, duo uel tres prophetent: sed, prophetæ uero duo uel tres loquantur. Etenim non mox propheta uocari meretur, qui semel atq; iterum in ecclesia loquitur, sed cui munus est prophetandi iusta uocatione commissum.
units.tr: Here it is asked whether by this sentence he left it free to them that, without any certain calling, two or three might rise to speak at any assembly of the church, or whether two or three were to be chosen from the number of the faithful to prophesy at the individual assemblies. In my judgment, since the Apostle here loved order, it is more likely that he prescribed to the church of the Corinthians that he should choose two or three from the faithful who, endowed with the gift of prophecy, would prophesy in their assemblies in turn. He calls these men prophets for that reason, not simply saying "let two or three prophesy," but "let the prophets, two or three, speak." For a person does not deserve to be called a prophet at once merely because he has spoken in the church once or twice; rather, he is one to whom the office of prophesying has been committed by lawful calling.

units.la: CAETERI, inquit, dijudicent.] Per cæteros, intelligit omnem eam multitudinem ecclesiastici conuentus, quæ prophetātes audit. Diuidit ecclesiam in loquentes & auditores: & ne sint auditores instar stipitū, tribuit illis iudicium eorum quæ dicuntur. Non dicit, cæteri audiant, nec dicit cæteri essentiantur, aut cæteri applaudant: sed, cæteri dijudicent. Requirit igitur ab auditoribus, ut attente audiant prophetantes, & quæ dicuntur sano cum intellectu probent, uera ne sint & ex spiritu Dei, uel falsa & humanitus in medium allata, atq; ita quæ uera sunt amplectantur, quæ falsa reprobent. Et utinam eiusmodi iudicij discretio libera fuisset auditoribus in ecclesia relicta. Hac enim per episcoporum dominationem sublata, summa est prophetantibus facta securitas quæuis somnia & commenta ad quæstum facientia oppresse multitudini proponédi. Quid enim metuerent nemine non modo reclamante, sed cōtrà ne hiscere quidem audente? Hinc sunt in ecclesia falsa dogmata, hinc eidoloma nia, cum omnis generis falsis cultib. hinc quæ stuofissimus ille non Petrus, sed Simon, hinc dominatus episcoporum, hinc plebis stupiditas & sacrarum scripturarum ignorantia, omnium errorum mater. Reddatur liberum ecclesiæ iudicium, prouocentur auditores ad intelligentiam sacrarum scripturarum, unde sensus acquirant exercitatos, & ad iudicandum instructos, & uidebimus breui omnia hæc quæ per oppressionem liberi iudicij in ecclesiam irrepserunt, prorsus concidere. Plurimum refert quem audias in ecclesia loquentem, fratrene, cum quo libere de rebus fidei conferre liceat, uel eum qui sit uel dominus ipse ad opprimendum contradicentes paratus, uel à tali domino ad dicendum constitutus & certo iuramento astrictus, cui nemo impune cōtradixerit. Non est ecclesiasticum, si non loquatur frater ter in medio fratrum, propheta in medio libere dijudicantium, Christi minister in medio membrorum Christi: sed magnus dominus in medio seruorum, lupus in medio ouium, uafer & uersutus sophista in medio infipientiū. Tyrannicum est nolle libera ferre populi iudicia. Omnis tyrannus osor est legitimæ libertatis. Omnis male agens, amans est tenebrarum, & osor lucis. Halce notas utinam possint excutere episcopi, ecclesiarum domini.
units.tr: "The others," he says, "should judge." By "the others" he means the whole multitude of the church assembly who hear those who prophesy. He divides the church into speakers and hearers, and so that the hearers are not like blocks of wood, he gives them the judgment of what is said. He does not say "let the others listen," nor "let the others hiss," nor "let the others applaud," but "let the others judge." He therefore requires the hearers to listen attentively to those who prophesy, and with sound understanding to test what is said: whether it is true and from the Spirit of God, or false and brought forward from human wit; and so to embrace what is true and reject what is false. Would that this freedom of judgment had been left to the hearers in the church! For once it was suppressed by the domination of the bishops, it became completely safe for prophets to put forward any dreams and inventions that served their gain before a crowd kept under. For who would fear, when no one objected, and no one dared even to open his mouth against them? Hence come false doctrines in the church, hence idolatries, with every kind of false worship; hence that most mercenary man, not Peter but Simon; hence the domination of the bishops; hence the stupidity of the people and ignorance of the Holy Scriptures, the mother of all errors. Let the church's free judgment be restored, let the hearers be called to an understanding of the Holy Scriptures, from which they may acquire trained senses and be equipped for judging, and we shall soon see all these things that crept into the church through the suppression of free judgment utterly collapse. It matters greatly whom you hear speaking in the church: a brother with whom it is lawful to confer freely about matters of faith, or one who is himself a lord, ready to crush those who contradict him, or one appointed by such a lord to speak and bound by a sworn oath, against whom no one may speak without punishment. It is not in keeping with the church if a brother does not speak in the midst of brothers, a prophet in the midst of those who judge freely, a minister of Christ in the midst of the members of Christ; but rather a great lord in the midst of slaves, a wolf in the midst of sheep, a crafty and wily sophist in the midst of the ignorant. It is tyrannical to be unwilling to bear the free judgments of the people. Every tyrant is an enemy of lawful liberty. Everyone who does evil loves darkness and hates the light. Would that the bishops, lords of the churches, might shake off these marks!

units.la: Hinc tamen non est ut patrocinium sibi petant homines contentioti, ad diuexandum omnia & ad turbandas ecclesias parati. Non dicit, caeteri diuexent, altercentur, & temere contendant: sed, & caeteri dijudicent. Aliud est ad intelligendum ac dijudicandum audire docente in ecclesia, & aliud spiritu contentionis omnia quantumuis bene dicta in quæstionem rapere. Hoc ad lites & disturbationem, illud uero ad ædificationem facit. Ad dijudicandum non est opus ut in ipso coetu contradicat auditor docenti: sed satis est si dijudicet in corde suo de ijs quæ audit, & post conuentum si quid desiderat, seorsum de illo quærat. Nisi hæc moderatio custodiatur, nihil expectandum est aliud quàm inanis imo noxia, altercatio coetui Christiano dedecorosa.
units.tr: Yet from this one should not conclude that contentious men may claim for themselves a license to harass everything and to disturb the churches, being ready for it. He does not say "let the others harass, quarrel and contend rashly," but "let the others also judge." It is one thing to listen to a teacher in the church in order to understand and judge, and quite another, by a spirit of contention, to drag into question everything, however well said. The former serves for building up; the latter serves for strife and disturbance. For judging, there is no need for the hearer to contradict the teacher in the very assembly; it is enough if he judges in his own heart concerning what he hears, and afterwards, if he wants anything more, asks about it privately. Unless this restraint is observed, nothing can be expected but a vain, indeed harmful, quarrelling, a thing disgraceful to a Christian assembly.

units.la: PORRO si alij fuerit reuelatu assidenti, prior taceat, inquit. Quod in Græco est καθημένῳ, Erasmus uertit assidenti: cum simpliciter uertendum sit, sedenti, quemadmodum & uulgata habet. Sedentes autem uocat auditores, ne quis per assidentem intelligat eum qui sit ex ordine prophetarum. Hieronymus tamen diuersum exponit. Ille per sedetes, intelligit prophetas: & per auditores, stantes. At Ambrosius sedentem refert ad inferiores in ecclesia, id est, ad auditores. Probabilius est sedentes uocare Apostolum eos qui in ecclesia quiescunt, & ad audiendum sedendo se composuerunt. Sic Paulus sedet ad pedes Gamalielis, & Maria ad pedes Christi docentis. Sic erat consuetudo synagogæ, ut auditores sederent. Ideo ad eum qui manum habebat aridam dicebat in synagoga dominus, Surge & sta in medio. Et ipse cum inter auditores in synagoga sederet, ac legere uellet, surrexit ad sedendum, Lucæ 4. Quæ consuetudo in prima quoq; ecclesia fuit, sicuti uidere est in epistola Iacobi. Et admodum conuenit, ut sedeant in ecclesia, qui ad audiendum ac discendum ueniunt, ubi audiuntur prophetiæ, adhortationes & consolationes. Secus uero fieri uidemus in templis eidolorum, in quibus non sonant prophetiæ, sed prostant ad cultum eidola diuorum: muti libri ut uocat laicorum, ad quorum aras plebs cæca cum oblationibus discurrit, & adorandi gratia in genua prouolui tur. Sic ipsa facies, ipsi gestus, ipsi mores ecclesiam quæ nunc est prorsus à priore mutatam esse demonstrant.
units.tr: Moreover, "if a revelation is made to another who sits by, let the first keep silent," he says. In the Greek it is "to the one sitting" [καθημένῳ]; Erasmus renders it "sitting by," whereas it should simply be rendered "sitting," as the Vulgate also has it. Now he calls the hearers "those sitting," lest anyone understand by "one sitting by" a man who is of the order of the prophets. Jerome, however, explains it differently: by "those sitting" he understands the prophets, and by the hearers, "those standing." But Ambrose refers "sitting" to those lower in the church, that is, to the hearers. It is more probable that the Apostle calls "sitting" those who rest in the church and have settled themselves by sitting to listen. So Paul sat at the feet of Gamaliel, and Mary at the feet of the teaching Christ. Such was the custom of the synagogue, that the hearers sat; so the Lord said to the man who had the withered hand in the synagogue, "Rise and stand in the midst," and when he himself was sitting among the hearers in the synagogue and wished to read, he rose to read (Luke 4). This custom also existed in the first church, as can be seen in the Epistle of James. And it is fitting that those who come to hear and learn sit in the church, where prophecies, exhortations and consolations are heard. We see things done otherwise in the temples of idols, where prophecies do not resound, but idols of the gods stand ready for worship: "dumb books," as the laity call them, at whose altars the blind people run about with offerings and fall on their knees to worship. Thus the very face, the very gestures, the very manners show that the church as it now is has been completely changed from the earlier one.

units.la: PORRO, inquit, si alij fuerit reuelatu sedenti.] Constituit de casu contingenti nonnunq, propter quem certo ordini ac numero prophe tantium stari non possit. Præscripsit quidem, ut prophetæ duo uel tres loquantur, caeteri audiant ac dijudicent. Verum quoniam libera erat reuelatio spiritus nulli nec ordini nec per sonæ alligata, ideoq; subinde eueniebat, ut in terea dum ordinarij prophetæ loquerentur, uni ex sedentibus per spiritum ea reuelaretur, unde uel corrigerentur, uel magis elucidarentur iam dicta: constituendū erat, quid in eiusmodi casu fieri conueniret, & utile esset ecclesiæ. Sic dicit igitur: Porro si alij fuerit reuelatu sedeti, prior taceat. Non dicit, significet loqueti, ut ille hoc ecclesiæ proponat: nec dicit, surgat & ipse & loquatur: neq; dicit, feruet sibi psi: sed, prior taceat, ne uidelicet illicitū putetur ei loqui in ecclesia qui nō sit in ordine prophetarum, sed de numero sedentium & auditorum: uel ne simul ambo loquantur, & sit confusio: uel, ne ecclesia reuelatione spiritus priue tur. Hisce rationibus permittit cuiuis sedenti, si quid reuelationis acceperit, ut in medio fratrum, surgat & reuelata sibi ecclesiæ proponat: sed ea moderatione ut prior, qui tum loquitur taceat quo omnium animi & aures haud distrahantur, sed uni sint loquenti audiedo addicti.
units.tr: "Moreover," he says, "if a revelation is made to another who sits by..." He makes provision for a case that sometimes happens, on account of which the fixed order and number of prophets cannot be kept. He had indeed prescribed that two or three prophets should speak while the others listen and judge. But since the revelation of the Spirit was free and bound to no order or person, it followed from time to time that, while the regular prophets were speaking, a revelation came through the Spirit to one of those sitting, by which what had been said might be corrected or made clearer. It had to be determined what ought to be done in such a case, and what would be useful to the church. So he says: "Moreover, if a revelation is made to another sitting, let the first keep silent." He does not say "let him signify it to the speaker, so that he may propose it to the church," nor "let him stand up and speak himself," nor "let him be fervent in himself," but "let the first keep silent," lest it be thought unlawful for a man who is not in the order of the prophets, but in the number of those sitting and listening, to speak in the church; or lest both speak together and there be confusion; or lest the church be deprived of the revelation of the Spirit. For these reasons he permits anyone sitting, if he has received some revelation, to stand up in the midst of the brothers and set before the church what has been revealed to him; but with this restraint, that the first, who is then speaking, keep silent, so that the minds and ears of all are not drawn apart, but are devoted to the one who is speaking and listening.

units.la: PRIOR, inquit, taceat.] Quisquis loquitur, aliquando est finito sermone taciturus. Quod si hoc sensu capiedum est, quod hic dicitur, ut qui prior dixit tum demū taceat, quàdo quod uolebat ad finem usq; est eloquutus, ut tantisper exspectandum sit ei, qui nouam reuelationem accepit, dum ille sermonem suum finiat: uidetur hoc clarius fuisse exprimendum dicedumq;, expectet, donec prior taceat. Alioqui non erat ratio constituendi, ut prior taceat. Si uero sic tacere iubetur prior, ut mox atq; alius accepta reuelatione ad dicendum in ecclesia surrexerit, ipse abrupto sermone taceat, illiq; dicendi locum & copiam faciat: non immerito quæritur, quur id fieri cœueniat. Quod si nō aliud aliquid, sed idem quod prior: uel si aliud quidé, uerum nō melius: aut si tale quid quod non lateat ecclesiam, utpote iam antea ab alijs dictum allaturus est in medium, qui reuelationem accepit: nulla uidetur esse ratio, propter quam sermone suum propheta qui ex officio loquitur, illius gratia abrumpere ac tacere debeat. At nihil inane adfert reuelatio spiritus. Quare necesse est, ut quod audienti per spiritu reuelatur, cuius gratia tacendum sit loquenti prophetæ, tale quid sit, quod nec sit ociosum, nec inane, nec antea ecclesiæ cognitum, ut uere posit esse reuelatio. Non simpliciter dicit, Si alius quicquam cogitauerit, aut, dicendnm sibi putauerit: sed, Si alij reuelatum fuerit sedeti, prior taceat. Quare uerbo reuelandi satis significat Apostolus, non esse leue causam, propter quam iubeat tacere priorem, si ex auditoribus quisquam reuelationem spiritus accepe rit. Et simul excludituir omnis audacuorum, contentiosorum dicaculorum & phanaticorum hominum temeritas, cui nō est ut cedat, pheta.
units.tr: "Let the first keep silent," he says. Whoever is speaking will at some point be silent when he has finished his discourse. But if what is said here is to be taken in this sense, that the one who spoke first should then keep silent when he has uttered to the end what he wished to say, so that the one who has received the new revelation must wait until the first finishes his speech, then it seems this should have been expressed and said more clearly: "let him wait until the first has fallen silent." Otherwise there would have been no reason to order that the first keep silent. But if the first is commanded to be silent in such a way that, as soon as another, having received a revelation, has risen to speak in the church, he himself should break off his discourse and be silent, giving that other place and opportunity to speak, then it is not unreasonably asked why this should be done. For if the revelation is not something other than what the first said, or if it is something different but no better, or if it is something of such a kind that it is not hidden from the church, since it is something already said by others which the one who received the revelation is going to bring forward, then there seems to be no reason why the prophet who speaks in virtue of his office should break off and be silent on that man's account. But the revelation of the Spirit brings nothing empty. Therefore it is necessary that what is revealed by the Spirit to the hearer, on whose account the prophet who is speaking must be silent, be something that is neither idle, nor empty, nor previously known to the church, so that it can truly be a revelation. The Apostle does not simply say, "If another has thought something, or has judged that he ought to say something," but "If a revelation is made to another sitting, let the first keep silent." Thus by the word "revelation" the Apostle sufficiently signifies that it is no slight cause on account of which he orders the first to be silent, if any of the hearers has received a revelation of the Spirit. And at the same time the rashness of bold, contentious and talkative fanatics is shut out, for whom it is not right to give way.

units.la: POTESTIS enim, inquit, singulatim omnes prophetare. ] Rationem reddit eius quod iam dixit.Poteat dicere: Licet enim ei qui reuelationem accepit,surgere ac prophetare. Verum ut afferat hanc communem omnibus libertatem, maluit dicere: Potestis enim omnes prophetare.Et alioqui sic poterat colligere ex praecedenti constitutione: Si licet uni sedenti accepta reuelatione surgere in ecclesia & prophetare,licet & reliquis:fi reliquis, ergo & omnibus. Recte ergo uelut occupans dicit: Potestis enim omnes prophetare. Sane quod licet omnibus,licet & singulis,in causa consimili,omnes & singulos concernente.
units.tr: "For you can all prophesy one by one," he says. He gives the reason for what he has just said. He could have said: "It is permitted for the one who has received a revelation to stand up and prophesy." But to make this freedom common to all, he preferred to say: "For you can all prophesy." He could also have inferred it from the preceding rule: if it is allowed for one seated person, having received a revelation, to stand up in the Church and prophesy, it is allowed for the rest too; and if for the rest, then for all. So he rightly puts it summarily: "For you can all prophesy." Certainly what is permitted to all is permitted to each, in a similar case that concerns all and each.

units.la: Non possum autem eorum probare sententiam,qui haec referunt non ad auditores, sed ad ordinem prophetarum,doctorum,ac pastorum. Videtur illis inconueniens,fi laicis,ut uocant, libertas detur in ecclesia loquendi. Et interim ne clericis quidem concedunt quod hic constituitur ab Apostolo, atq; ita doctrina spiritus sancti prorsus reddunt inanem. Belli homines existimant gratiam ac sapientiam spiritus alligatam esse oleo ac rasurae, & negari plebi sanguine Christi redemptae.Illud autem tenendum est,non loqui Apostolum simpliciter de omnibus,sed cum conditione reuelationis, qua praemisit dicens: Quod si sedenti reuelatum fuerit, prior taceat.Quod uero addit καθ' ἕνα,id est, secundum unum, quod reddunt singulatim, per singulos:non est ad ius ac libertatem singulorum fidelium,sed ad ordinem referendum, quo constituitur, ne duo uel tres uel plures simul prophetent,sed alius post alium, si adsit reuelatio spiritus.
units.tr: I cannot, however, approve the opinion of those who refer this not to the hearers but to the order of prophets, teachers and ministers. It seems improper to them that liberty to speak in the Church should be granted to the laity, as they call them. And meanwhile they do not even grant to the clergy what is laid down here by the Apostle, and so they make the teaching of the Holy Spirit altogether empty. These fine fellows think that the grace and wisdom of the Spirit are bound to oil and the tonsure, and that they are denied to the common people redeemed by the blood of Christ. But we must hold that the Apostle is not speaking simply of all, but under the condition of revelation, which he set down beforehand when he said: "But if a revelation is made to one who sits, let the first be silent." As for what he adds, by one [καθ' ἕνα], that is, "one by one," which they render "singly, through individuals," this does not refer to the right and liberty of the individual faithful, but to the order by which it is arranged that two or three or more should not prophesy at the same time, but one after another, if a revelation of the Spirit is present.

units.la: Locus hic palam adstipulatur ei doctrinae, qua initio renouatae religionis nostrae doceri coepit, Christianos omnes esse sacerdotes,etsi non ordine ministerij, dignitate tamen caelestis uocationis, quemadmodum 1. Pet. legimus: Vos autem genus electum, regale sacerdocium,gens sancta,populus acquisitionis, ut uirtutes annuncietis eius qui uos de tenebris uocauit in admirabile lumen suum. Propter hanc dignitatem potestas est fidelibus omnibus,annunciare uirtutes Dei ac prophetare in medio ecclesiae, quantumuis pseudoepiscopi reclament. Omnino quod Corinthijs est ab Apostolo dictum, Potestis omnes prophetare,ad omnes Christianos pertinent.
units.tr: This passage plainly supports that doctrine which, at the beginning of our renewed religion, began to be taught: that all Christians are priests, though not by the order of ministry, yet by the dignity of their heavenly calling, as we read in 1 Peter: "But you are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his marvellous light." On account of this dignity all the faithful have the power to proclaim the virtues of God and to prophesy in the midst of the Church, however much the pseudo-bishops cry out. Certainly what the Apostle said to the Corinthians, "You can all prophesy," pertains to all Christians.

units.la: Interea tamen no infringitur ordo ministeriorum, quibus carere non potest ecclesia: quia communis haec omniu potestas non debet usurpari a quoquam nisi in casu necessitatis,ubi officium non faciunt uel contrarium magis faciunt episcopi, pastores ac doctores, & ubi certa fuerit facta reuelatio spiritus,que casum hic ponit Apostolus: In eiusmodi casibus prophetare possunt, quorum ad id animi per spiritu Dei excitantur. Quod si prophetare possunt omnes, possunt utiq; & reliqua facere in ecclesia quae minoris sunt momenti, utpote administrare utraq; baptismatis & coenae dominicae sacramenta, psallere, orare, & gratias
units.tr: Meanwhile, the order of ministries, without which the Church cannot exist, is not thereby overturned. For this common power of all must not be assumed by anyone except in a case of necessity, where the bishops, pastors and teachers do not perform their office, or do the opposite; and where a revelation of the Spirit has been clearly made, which is the case the Apostle posits here: "In such cases they can prophesy, whose minds are stirred up to this by the Spirit of God." But if all can prophesy, they can certainly also do the other things in the Church which are of lesser importance, namely administer both sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper, sing psalms, pray, and give thanks

units.la: agere in ecclesia,uisitare ac cosolari infirmos, catechisare rudes,&c. Nec est,ut quaeratur uocatio titularium episcoporum ac malorum seruorum, ubi diuina uocatione necessitati succurritur ecclesiae, & impletur quod hic dicit Apostolus: Potestis enim omnes prophetare. Huius no frustra admoneo hoc loco, propter infirmos fratres, quorum conscientiae in eiusmodi casibus haesitant,putantes no licere prophetare in ecclesia,nisi ordinaria electione ad id muneris uocatis. Vbi officium non facit oeconomus,munus eius recte obit in domo quis quis hero suo ac familiae fidelis inueniri cupit, etiamsi oeconomus reclamet. Vbi uero no deest ille suo officio,non conuenit cuipia ex domesticis in id se muneris ingerere, nisi speciali ter ab ipso sit patrefamilias iussus. Consimilis est in ecclesia Christi seruanda ratio.Vbi ministri domino sunt fideles,ac mynisteria regni Dei rite dispensant, non est ut extra ordinem quisquam se fidelium in munus prophetandi ingerat, nisi singulari aliqua spiritus reuelatio ne accepta,quam debeat proponere ecclesiae: ubi uero uel nulli sunt ministri,uel sunt quide, uerum officium aut non faciunt, aut perfide faciunt,populum domini non rite docentes,sed seducentes:in eiusmodi casu potestas est fidelibus omnibus prophetare,& reliqua necessaria officia obire in ecclesia. Quod si plebs ipsa no est corrupta,sed fida adhuc & pietate sana, potest sibi deligere pastores ac ministros, qui domino fideliter seruiant.Agnouit hoc & Cyprianus,q libro primo epistola quarta sic scribit:Propter quod plebs obsequens praeceptis dominicis,&Deum metuens a peccatore praepositto separare se debet, nec se ad sacrilegi sacerdotis sacrificia miscere, cum ipsa maxime habeat potestatem uel eligendi dignos sacerdotes,uel indignos recusandi.Haec ille. Sed reddeamus ad Apostolum.
units.tr: in the Church, visit and comfort the sick, catechise the ignorant, and so on. Nor is there any need to inquire about the calling of titular bishops and bad servants, where, by a divine calling, the need of the Church is met and what the Apostle says here is fulfilled: "For you can all prophesy." I give this warning here, not without reason, on account of weak brothers, whose consciences hesitate in such cases, thinking that it is not lawful to prophesy in the Church unless they have been called to this office by ordinary election. Where the steward does not perform his office, the one who wishes to be found faithful to his master and household rightly discharges his duty in the house, even if the steward protests. But where that man is not lacking in his office, it is not fitting for any of the household to thrust himself into that duty, unless he has been specially ordered to do so by the head of the household himself. The same rule must be observed in the Church of Christ. Where the ministers are faithful to the Lord and dispense the ministries of the kingdom of God rightly, no one of the faithful should thrust himself into the task of prophesying outside the order, unless he has received some singular revelation of the Spirit, which he ought to set before the Church. But where either there are no ministers, or there are some but they either do not perform their office or perform it faithlessly, not teaching the Lord's people rightly but leading them astray, in such a case all the faithful have the power to prophesy and to discharge the other necessary offices in the Church. But if the people themselves are not corrupted, but still faithful and sound in piety, they can choose for themselves pastors and ministers who will serve the Lord faithfully. Cyprian also acknowledged this, who in the fourth letter of his first book writes thus: "Therefore the people, obedient to the Lord's precepts and fearing God, ought to separate themselves from a sinful prelate, nor mix themselves into the sacrifices of a sacrilegious priest, since they especially have the power either of choosing worthy priests or of refusing unworthy ones." So he. But let us return to the Apostle.

units.la: VT omnes discant,inquit, & omnes consolationem accipiant. ] Hic est finis ad quae diriuenda sunt omnia in ecclesia. Eundem paulo supra una uoce expressit dices:Quoties coueniti s, unusquisq; uestrum psalmum habet,'doctrinam habet, linguam habet, reuelationem habet,interpretationem habet, omnia ad aedificationem fiant.Ergo doctrina & consolatione aedificatur ecclesia.Duas hic ponit aedificationis partes cum dicit: Vt omnes discant, & omnes consolationem accipiant.Discendo ad cognitionem ueritatis ac uoluntatis Dei peruenimus.Per consolationem confirmamur,ne ullis modis, tentationibus ac tribulationibus a cognitione accepta,& sancto propósito auel li nos patiamur.
units.tr: "That all may learn," he says, "and all may receive comfort." Here is the end to which everything in the Church must be directed. He expressed the same thing a little above in one sentence, saying: "Whenever you come together, each of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a tongue, has a revelation, has an interpretation; let all things be done for edification." Therefore the Church is built up by teaching and by consolation. Here he sets down two parts of edification when he says: "That all may learn, and all may receive comfort." By learning we come to the knowledge of the truth and the will of God. Through consolation we are strengthened, so that by no means should we allow ourselves to be torn away from the knowledge we have received and from our holy purpose by temptations and tribulations.

units.la: Obserua uero,quod non dicit, Vt imperiti discant,& infirmi cosolationem accipiat: sed, Vt omnes discant & omnes consolatione accipiant.Ergo discendum est omnibus in ecclesia,& cosolationibus opus habent omnes.Nemo hic excipitur,ne illi quidem quorum est alios docere & cosolari, siue sint episcopi, siue presbypresbyteri siue pastores & doctores. Sic om-{A}nes perpetuo sumus discipuli spiritus sancti, semper opus habentes doctrina & consolatione. Mirabilis sane fidelium conditio. Potestas docendi & consolandi est omnibus, & tamen simul incumbit omnibus discédi & consolandi necessitas. Potestis, inquit, omnes prophetare, ut omnes discant & omnes consolationem accipiant. Quod perinde est ac si membris corporis dicas: Potestis omnia sustentare corpus, ut omnia sustétemini ac seruemini. Idem propheta qui docet in ecclesia, opus habet ut discat: qui consolatur alios, opus habet, ut & ipse consolatione mutua confirmetur. Qui iam relationem spiritus sancti accepit, & per hanc alios docet & consolatur, non ideo mox est omnem scientiæ ac fortitudinis perfectionem consequutus: sed opus habet & ipse, qui discat ab alijs, & confirmetur. Nemini quippe simul omnia per spiritum sanctum reuelatur. Neq; mox perpetuo firmus est in aduersis tolerandis, qui hodie consolatione per ministerium prophetiæ consequitur: sed ut sumus in bono instabiles, ita fit, ut cras denuo opus habeat consolatione, perinde atque cibo cras opus habet, qui hodie comedit ac bibit.
units.tr: Observe, however, that he does not say, "That the unskilled may learn, and the weak may receive comfort," but, "That all may learn and all may receive comfort." Therefore everyone in the Church must learn, and all have need of consolations. No one is excepted here, not even those whose task it is to teach and comfort others, whether they be bishops, presbyters, pastors or teachers. Thus we are all perpetually disciples of the Holy Spirit, always in need of teaching and consolation. A wonderful condition for the faithful indeed! The power to teach and to comfort belongs to all, and yet at the same time the necessity of learning and being comforted presses upon all. "You can all prophesy," he says, "so that all may learn and all may receive comfort." This is just as if you were to say to the members of the body: "You can all sustain the body, so that all may be sustained and preserved." The prophet who teaches in the Church himself needs to learn; he who comforts others needs to be confirmed by mutual consolation himself. He who has now received a revelation of the Holy Spirit, and through it teaches and comforts others, has not therefore at once attained the full perfection of knowledge and strength; he too needs to learn from others and be confirmed. For no one receives all things by revelation of the Holy Spirit at once. Nor is he who today obtains consolation through the ministry of prophecy at once constantly firm in bearing adversities; rather, just as we are unstable in good things, so it happens that he needs consolation again tomorrow, just as he who eats and drinks today needs food tomorrow.

units.la: VT omnes discant, inquit.] Quid est quod non dicit: Vt omnes credant? Est quidem potiſsimus scopus uerbi Dei, quod in mūdo prædicatur, ut ad fidem perducatur increduli, nec fieri potest, ut citra fidem saluemur. Verum Apostolus loquitur de prophetia, quę proponitur non ad fidem perducedis, sed illis qui iam antea facti sunt fideles, ut in fide Christi crescat & confirmentur: ad quod opus est, ut quoti die discat, hoc est, in scientia Dei magis ac magis instituantur. Sic puto duas esse prophetæ partes. Vnam, ut incredulos ad fidem conuertat, qua de paulo supra meminit. Alteram, ut credentes in scientia Dei instituat, qua de hic loquitur. Illam plantationi, istam rigationi suprà cap. 3. assimilauit. Et posterior hæc non est priore inferior. Neque enim minor est uirtus quàm quærere parta tueri.
units.tr: "That all may learn," he says. Why does he not say, "That all may believe"? The chief aim of the word of God, which is preached in the world, is indeed that unbelievers may be brought to faith, and we cannot be saved without faith. But the Apostle is speaking of prophecy, which is set forth not to bring people to faith, but for those who have already become believers, so that they may grow and be established in the faith of Christ; for this work it is necessary that they learn daily, that is, that they be instructed more and more in the knowledge of God. So I think there are two parts of prophecy. One, to convert unbelievers to the faith, which he mentioned a little above. The other, to instruct believers in the knowledge of God, which he speaks of here. He likened the former to planting and the latter to watering, above in chapter 3. And this latter is not inferior to the former. For it is no less a virtue to keep what has been gained than to seek it.

units.la: ET omnes consolationem accipiát, inquit.] Ergo homo hominem & docet & consolatur? Atqui Iohan. 6. dictū est à Christo: Scriptū esse in prophetis, futuros omnes doctos à Deo, uel discipulos Dei, & omnem eum qui à patre audiuit ac didicit ad se uenturum. Et 2. Cor. 1. uocat Apostolus Deum, patre Domini nostri Iesu Christi, Deum totius consolationis, qui consoletur nos in omni tribulatione nostra.
units.tr: "And let all receive comfort," he says. Does a man then both teach and comfort a man? Yet in John 6 Christ said that it is written in the prophets that all shall be taught by God, or be disciples of God, and everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to him. And in 2 Cor. 1 the Apostle calls God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our tribulation.

units.la: Respondeo. Vtrunq; uerum est. Deus solus docet, solus consolatur. Docet & consolatur per suum spiritum. Verum homines interim ministros spiritus sui & cooperatores suos constituit. Admonemur hinc, ut cogitemus quàta sit philanthropia Dei, qua hominem in id dignitatis assumit, ut cooperetur sibi in opere omnium clarissimo, cum omnia sine illius ope ra suapte possit uirtute perficere. Docet homi nem doctrina qua possit ille docere & alios,
units.tr: I answer: both are true. God alone teaches, and God alone comforts. He teaches and comforts through his Spirit. Yet in the meantime he appoints men as ministers of his Spirit and as his co-workers. We are reminded here to consider how great is the kindness of God, who raises man to such a dignity that he cooperates with him in the most illustrious of all works, although he could accomplish everything by his own power without anyone's help. He teaches man with a teaching by which that man can in turn teach others.

units.la: consolatur homine consolatione spiritus, qua ille consoletur & alios. Sic Apostolus cum dixisset, Benedictus Deus & pater domini nostri Iesu Christi, pater misericordiarū, & Deus totius consolationis, qui consolatur nōs in omni tribulatione nostra: subiecit, ut possimus & ipsi consolari eos qui in omni pressura sunt, per consolationem, qua nosipsos consolatur Deus. Deo sic docente & consolante, uere docent & consolantur, ac uere discunt, & consolationem accipiunt homines. Deo neq; docente neq; consolante frustra docet & consolatur homo hominem. Quare nemo propheta docere ac consolari præsumat, nisi prius dominum ipsum inuocauerit, si modo efficaciter ac cum fructu ministerio suum obire uoluerit. Et hac ratione solennis est & laudabilis ecclesiæ consuetudo, ut doctrinæ & exhortationi precatio non modo præmittatur, sed & subijciatur.
units.tr: He comforts man with the comfort of the Spirit, by which the man in turn comforts others. So the Apostle, having said, "Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our tribulation," added that we too may be able to comfort those who are in every distress, through the comfort by which God comforts us. When God teaches and comforts in this way, men truly teach and comfort, and truly learn and receive comfort. When God neither teaches nor comforts, a man teaches and comforts another man in vain. Therefore let no prophet presume to teach or comfort unless he has first called upon the Lord himself, if indeed he wishes to discharge his ministry effectively and with fruit. And for this reason the custom of the Church is solemn and praiseworthy, that prayer is not only placed before teaching and exhortation but also added after it.

units.la: ET spiritus prophetarum prophetis subijciuntur, inquit.] Vulgatus interpres uertit in singulari, Et spiritus prophetarum prophetis subiectus est: uerum in Græco non est, πνεῦμα, sed in plurali πνεύματα. Quod autem non est ὑποτάσσεται, sed ὑποτάσσονται, Græca est constructio, qua uerba singularia nominibus neutrius generis in plurali positis iunguntur.
units.tr: "And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets," he says. The Vulgate translator renders it in the singular, "And the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets," but in the Greek it is not [πνεῦμα] but in the plural [πνεύματα]. And the reading is not [ὑποτάσσεται] but [ὑποτάσσονται]; this is a Greek construction, by which a singular verb is joined to a neuter noun placed in the plural.

units.la: Locus hic uarijs modis exponitur. Alij referunt ista ad proxime præcedens: potestis enim omnes prophetare. Quasi dicat, Nam spiritus sanctus donis suis subleruit ecclesiæ, atq; ita subditus est & obsequens prophetantibus, nec inuidet sua dona cuiquâ fidelium. Alij referunt ad id quod dixit: Quod si cui sedenti reuelatum fuerit, prior taceat, sed alio atque alio sensu. Primò, sunt qui sic. Spiritus prophetarum, id est, charismata spiritus, prophetis concessa, prophetis alijs subiecti sunt, ut de illis cognoscat ac censeant. Quare non debet quisquâ propheta sic insolescere, ut tacere nolit, si alius ad dicendum surrexerit, quasi nullius sit censurae subiectus. Deinde quidam ad hunc modum. Spiritus prophetarum prophetis subijciuntur, hoc est, ueri prophetæ non sit loquuntur, ut tacere non possint, si id postulet certa ratio. Neq; enim mente sunt moti, arreptitij, ac lymphatici, sicut diuinatores, prophetæ Satanæ, qui more infanorū uaticinantur quæ non intelligunt: & nolint uelint loquuntur secundum uim spiritus mali à quo rapiuntur & agitatur, sic ut neq; principium, neq; cursum, neq; sensum, neque finem sermonis habeant in sua potestate. Veri prophetæ tacere possunt, ubi uolūt. Non enim cogūtur, sed in potestate sua habet donum spiritus. Sic quod dicit, Spiritus prophetarum prophetis subijciuntur: idem esset, quod, dona prophetarum ipsis subijciun tur. id est, sunt in ipsorum potestate.
units.tr: This passage is explained in various ways. Some refer these words to what immediately precedes, "for you can all prophesy." As if he said: for the Holy Spirit has made his gifts subservient to the Church, and so is submissive and obedient to those who prophesy, and does not begrudge his gifts to any of the faithful. Others refer it to what he said, "If something is revealed to one who is sitting, let the first be silent," but in different senses. First, there are those who take it thus: the spirits of the prophets, that is, the charismata of the Spirit granted to the prophets, are subject to other prophets, so that these may examine and judge them. Therefore no prophet should become so proud as to be unwilling to keep silent if another rises to speak, as though he were subject to no judgment. Second, some take it in this way: the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets, that is, the true prophets do not speak in such a way that they cannot keep silent when sound reason requires it. For they are not moved in mind, seized, or frenzied, like the diviners, the prophets of Satan, who prophesy like madmen what they do not understand; and who, whether they wish it or not, speak according to the power of the evil spirit by which they are seized and driven, so that they have no control over the beginning, course, meaning, or end of their speech. True prophets can keep silent whenever they wish. For they are not compelled; the gift of the Spirit is in their power. So what he says, "The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets," would amount to the same as saying, "The gifts of the prophets are subject to them," that is, they are in their power.

units.la: Tertiò, nonnulli sic exponunt, Spiritus, id est, animi ac mentes prophetarum, subijciuntur alijs prophetis, ut illis ad ecclesiam dicturis haud grauatim cedant: non sunt præfracti, sed submissi, agnoscetes in alijs quoq; ac uenerá-testes dona spiritus. Quare non erit molestũ ulli prophetæ, si surgat ex sedentibus aliquis, reue lationem spiritus propositurus ecclesiæ, ut taceat, & cum alijs audiat. Et hæc sententia simplicior mihi præq; alijs retinenda uidetur. Reprimit igitur Apostolus factum eorum qui in ecclesijs Corinthiorũ spiritus arrogãtię inflati quosuis præ se fastidiebant, & haud facile cuiq; cedebant: & simul admonet, q; sint alieni, qui eiusmodi sunt, ab ingenio & modestia uerorũ prophetarum, quibus hoc unũ in uotis est, ut ædificetur ecclesia, per quoscunq; tádem hoc fiat: ideoq; parati sunt omnibus cedere, & tacere, modo sint qui uerbum domini rite administret. Sic olim spiritus episcoporũ episcopis subijciebantur, & alius alij cedebat, ubi maior erat futuræ ædificationis expectatio. Hodie citius sol lunæ cedet, q; episcopus episcopo.
units.tr: Third, some explain it thus: the spirits, that is, the minds and souls of the prophets, are subject to other prophets, so that they readily yield to them when these are about to speak to the Church. They are not stubborn but submissive, recognising and honouring the gifts of the Spirit also in others. Therefore it will be no trouble for any prophet if someone among those seated rises to set before the Church a revelation of the Spirit, and that he keep silent and listen with the others. This interpretation seems to me simpler and to be preferred above the rest. Therefore the Apostle rebukes the conduct of those in the churches of the Corinthians who, puffed up with the spirit of arrogance, looked down on everyone else and scarcely yielded to anyone; and at the same time he admonishes that those who are of this kind are unlike the character and modesty of true prophets, whose only desire is that the Church be built up, by whomever it is finally accomplished. Therefore they are ready to yield to all and to be silent, provided there is someone who rightly administers the word of the Lord. Thus formerly the spirits of the bishops were subject to the bishops, and one yielded to another when the expectation of future edification was greater. Today the sun will sooner yield to the moon than a bishop to a bishop.

units.la: Et obserua quale sit hoc genus subiectionis. Spiritus prophetarum prophetis, inquit, subijciũtur. Ergo ne propheta dominiũ habet in prophetă tanq; superior in eũ qui ipsi subijcitur? Absit. In sæculo sic fieri uidemus, ut ubi subiectio est, ibi sit & superior aliquis cui qui inferiores sunt subijciantur & obediant. Inter prophetas, episcopos, & reliquos ecclesiæ ministros, non habet locum pontificiũ illud, Vbi maioritas, ibi mandandi est potestas, reliquos manet obediendi necesitas. Hic frater fratri, propheta prophetæ, Apostolus Apostolo, minister ministro subijcitur, sic ut neq; sit minor q se fratri subijcit, nec maior cui ille subijcitur. Est enim subiectio ista non coacta, sed spontanea: nõ externa tantũ, sed & spiritualis, & præterea mutua, sic ut cui hodie propheta subijcitur, cras ipse eidẽ uicissim subijciatur. Quare non potest hic inferri: Ergo spiritus prophetarum prophetis dominantur. Nihil hic est domini, ubi donis spiritus inseruitur, & pari ab omnibus studio ecclesiæ ædificatio quæritur. Nihil, inquam, dominij est, ubi nemo quæ sua sint quærit, sed fratres fratribus spiritu charitatis uicissim subijciunt.
units.tr: And observe what kind of subjection this is. "The spirits of the prophets," he says, "are subject to the prophets." Therefore does the prophet have dominion over the prophet, as a superior over one who is subject to him? Far from it. In the world we see that where there is subjection, there is also some superior to whom those who are inferior are subject and obey. Among prophets, bishops, and the other ministers of the Church, that Papist saying has no place: "Where there is greater authority, there is the power to command; the rest remain under the necessity of obeying." Here brother is subject to brother, prophet to prophet, apostle to apostle, minister to minister, so that he is neither less than one who subjects himself to his brother, nor greater than the one to whom he is subject. For this subjection is not compelled but voluntary; it is not merely external but spiritual, and moreover mutual, so that the one to whom a prophet is subject today will in turn be subject to him tomorrow. Therefore it cannot be inferred here: "Therefore the spirits of the prophets lord it over the prophets." There is nothing of lordship where the gifts of the Spirit serve, and the edification of the Church is sought with equal zeal by all. There is nothing of lordship, I say, where no one seeks his own, but brothers in the spirit of charity yield to one another.

units.la: NON enim est cofusionis author Deus, inquit, sed pacis.] Ratio est, unde fiat quod spiritus prophetarum subiecti sunt prophetis. Est aut ratio hæc gemina. Prior tribuit hoc Deo, per cuius spiritũ spiritus prophetarum sic diriguntur, ut prophetis ultro subijciatur. Cum dicendum uideatur, Non enim sunt arrogantes & præfracti, sed humiles & submisi: reijciens causam subiectionis huius in ipsum Deum dicit, Nõ enim est Deus author confusionis, sed pacis. Hoc est, non reddit spiritus Dei prophetas contentiosos, qui omnia in ecclesia cófundant, & pacem turbent, sed placidos & pacis amates: fieret aut confusio, & disidium in ecclesia, si non cederet alter alteri, sed uel prohiberentur alij dicere, quibus reuelatum est, uel simul omnes prophetarent. Deus aut non potest esse cofusionis author. Hinc uidelicet est, quod spiritus uerorum prophetarũ prophetis subijciuntur. Tales non reddit sapientia, eruditio, potentia & opulentia carnis. Quare non
units.tr: "For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace." This is the reason why the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. There is a twofold reason. The first ascribes this to God, through whose Spirit the spirits of the prophets are so directed that they willingly submit to the prophets. Since it seems that it should be said, "For they are not arrogant and stubborn, but humble and submissive," he rejects the cause of this subjection and attributes it to God himself, saying: "For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace." That is, the Spirit of God does not make prophets contentious, who throw everything in the Church into confusion and disturb the peace, but calm and lovers of peace. Confusion and discord would arise in the Church if one did not yield to another, but either others who have received a revelation were forbidden to speak, or all prophesied at once. But God cannot be the author of confusion. Hence it is clearly the case that the spirits of true prophets are subject to the prophets. Wisdom, learning, power, and the wealth of the flesh do not produce such people. Therefore it cannot truly be said

units.la: posseт ueraciter dici: Spiritus sapientũ sapientibus, eruditorum eruditis, potentium potentibus, opulentorũ opuletis subijciuntur. Etenim spiritus carnis & mundi huius non est amás pacis & subiectionis, sed contentionis & inanis glorię. Et reuera magna pars doctorum hominum nostra hac ætate nimis palàm declarant, quo spiritu ferantur, dum omnia contentionibus admodum acerbis turbant, ac turpe sibi fore putant, si alijs subijciantur ac cedant.
units.tr: that "the spirits of the wise are subject to the wise, of the learned to the learned, of the powerful to the powerful, of the rich to the rich." For the spirit of the flesh and of this world does not love peace and subjection, but contention and empty glory. And indeed a great part of learned men in our own age declare all too plainly by what spirit they are carried, while they throw everything into turmoil with very bitter disputes, and think it shameful for themselves to be subject to others or to yield.

units.la: Posterior ratio declarat, quare Deus tales spiritu suo prophetas reddat, q prophetis subijciantur. Propterea, uidelicet quod ut non est amás contétionum, ita suis ministris ac fideli-bus nõ est author cofusionis, sed pacis & concordiæ. Et hanc ob causam, qui spiritu Dei diriguntur, non sunt amantes confusionũ ac disturbationum, sed pacis seruandę gratia fratribus facile cedũt. Prophetæ spiritus subijcitur prophetæ, quia sic à Deo dirigitur, interea uero nõ subijcitur cuipiam ueritatis hosti, quantumuis potenti: nec tacet, etiási uitę discrimen loquendo incurrat. Est hæc sententia generalis, ideoq; non ad præsentem duntaxat causam, sed & ad reliquas consimiles accommodanda. Confusionem hic uocat Apostolus ἀκα-ταταξίαν. Sonat κατάταξιν rectam rerũ dispositionem, statum & ordinem: & hinc est, ἀκαταστασία, statũs & ordinis dissolutio & confusio. Vulgatus interpres uertit dissensionẽ. Ex dissensione nascitur ista ordinis ac status dissolutio ac cófusio. Quàm magnum autẽ est recti ordinis bonum, tam magnum est confusionis malum. ordine recti status seruátur omnia, dissolutio ne ac confusione dissipantur. Cum ergo Deus sit cõditor ac seruator omnium, condideritq; omnia in pondere, numero & mensura omniũ sapientissime, consequitur nihil ab illo magis esse alienum, quàm rerum confusionem.
units.tr: The second reason shows why God makes those whom he fills with his Spirit into prophets who must be subject to other prophets. It is because, just as he is not a lover of contentions, so he is not the author of confusion to his ministers and faithful people, but of peace and concord. For this reason, those who are guided by the Spirit of God are not lovers of confusion and disturbance, but for the sake of keeping peace they readily yield to their brothers. The spirit of a prophet is subject to a prophet because it is so directed by God. But it is not subject to any enemy of the truth, however powerful he may be, nor does it keep silent, even if speaking puts its life in danger. This statement is a general one, and so it is to be applied not only to the present case but also to the other like cases. The Apostle calls confusion here ἀκαταταξίαν [akatataxian]. Κατάταξιν [katataxin] means the right arrangement of things, their state and order, and hence ἀκαταστασία [akatastasia] is the dissolution and confusion of state and order. The Vulgate translator renders it dissension. From dissension arises this dissolution and confusion of order and state. As great as the good of right order is, so great is the evil of confusion. By the order of a right state all things are preserved, while by dissolution and confusion they are scattered. Since God is the creator and preserver of all things, and created all things most wisely in weight, number and measure, it follows that nothing is further from him than the confusion of things.

units.la: Sunt uero uaria genera cófusionis, secundũ uarietate rerum, quæ certo sunt ordine dispositæ, & certo quodam statu firmatæ. Habent cœlestia & terrena, habent ecclesiastica, politica & domestica suam catastasim, ut priuata taceam. Author huius est Deus, & per hũc in ordine ac statu suo seruantur omnia. Satan uero tanq aduersarius Dei, totus in eo est, ut dissoluat opera Dei. Quare perpetuo huc incumbit, ut κατάστασιν rerum quæ à Deo sunt subuertat, & ἀκαταστασίαν inducat, potissimũ in ecclesiam, gloriæ Dei & salutis humanæ officinam. Nos igitur, ubi rerum confusionem uidemus, agnoscamus opus nõ Dei, sed satanæ. Nisi eueniat, ut quæ male sunt iuncta, uel male gerũtur, confundantur. Eiusmodi cófusio nõ est à Satana, sed ab ipso Deo, qualis erat confusio linguarũ, ædificátium turrim Babel. Hanc imprecemur omnes Antichristianæ Babyloni, quæ se in cœlum usq; erexit, Deoq; & ecclesiæ iam olim repugnare cœpit. Illud obseruet pius lector, quod pacem opponit cófusioni. Cum enim dicendum esset: Non est Deus author confusionis, sed ordinis: dixit, Non est Deus author cõfusionis, sed pacis. Ergo per disidia, cõtentio nes & rixas confunditur ecclesia, dum pax & tráquillitas illius subuertitur: per pacem uero seruatur ordo, quo omnia competéter geruntur, & opus Dei feliciter promouet, hoc est, ecclesia salubriter ædificatur. Hæc pax, Deū habens authorem, qua cuncta legitime ac recto ordine geruntur, spiritus prophetarū prophetis subijciuntur, & ecclesia per doctrinam & consolationē in uera fide ædificatur, non convenit ecclesiæ Antichristianæ, dignæ quæ confundatur, sed ecclesiæ Christi. Et hanc quærimus ex animo: eam uero, qua fideles Antichristo quasi mancipia tyranno subijciantur, auersamur ac detestamur.
units.tr: There are indeed various kinds of confusion, according to the variety of things, which are set in a fixed order and established in a certain state. Heavenly and earthly things have their state; so do the ecclesiastical, political and domestic spheres, not to mention private ones. The author of this is God, and through him all things are kept in their order and state. Satan, however, as the adversary of God, is wholly intent on overturning the works of God. Therefore he constantly labours to subvert the κατάστασιν [katastasin] of things that come from God and to bring in ἀκαταστασίαν [akatastasian], above all into the Church, the workshop of God's glory and of human salvation. Therefore we, when we see confusion of things, should recognise the work not of God but of Satan. Unless it happens that things badly joined or badly managed are thrown into confusion. Confusion of this kind is not from Satan but from God himself, such as the confusion of tongues when the tower of Babel was built. Let us all pray for the confusion of that Antichristian Babylon, which has raised itself up even to heaven and has long since begun to resist God and the Church. Let the pious reader observe that the Apostle opposes peace to confusion. For when one would have expected him to say, "God is not the author of confusion but of order," he said, "God is not the author of confusion but of peace."
