Therefore the Church is thrown into confusion through dissensions, contentions and quarrels, while its peace and tranquillity are overturned; but through peace the order is preserved by which all things are rightly done, and the work of God is happily advanced, that is, the Church is healthily built up. This peace, which has God as its author, by which all things are carried on lawfully and in right order, so that the spirits of prophets are subject to the prophets and the Church is built up in true faith through teaching and consolation, does not suit the Antichristian Church, which deserves to be confounded, but the Church of Christ. This is what we seek from our heart. That other state, in which the faithful are subjected like slaves to a tyrant Antichrist, we shun and detest.

units.la: VT in omnibus, inquit, congregationibus sanctorū.] Desideratur uerbum aliquod, quo sensus perficiatur. Vulgata uersio habet, sicut & in omnibus ecclesijs sanctorum doceo. Sic legit & exponit Ambrosius & Chrysostomus quoq; addidit ἰδιάσκω: id est, doceo, quemadmodū exemplar habet, quod mihi est ad manum. Et sic Theophylacti quoq; uersio habet. Sunt qui legendū esse putát, sicuti fit in omnibus ecclesijs sanctorum. Interest quò referas hāc particulā. Si ad ea quæ præscripsit Corinthijs, dicens: Prophetæ uero duo aut tres loquantur, & cæteri dijudicent. Si uero alij fuerit sedenti reuelatum, prior taceat. Potestis enim omnes singulatim prophetare, ut omnes discant, & omnes consolationē accipiant, & spiritus prophetarū prophetis subijciuntur, sensus erit: Hæc uobis præscribens nihil noui præscribo. Nam sic doceo, & sic fit in omnibus ecclesijs sanctorum, à quibus non est quur uos in hac causa segregetis. Quod si hic sensus placet, illud, Non est enim confusionis author Deus, sed pacis: includendum est parethesi, ac sic legēdum, Potestis enim singulatim omnes prophetare, ut omnes discat & omnes consolationem accipiat, & spiritus prophetarum prophetis subijciuntur (non enim est confusionis author Deus, sed pacis) sicut in omnib. ecclesijs sanctorum fit, uel doceo. Si uero referas ad proxime precedens, Non enim cōfusionis author est Deus, sed pacis: sensus erit, quèadmodum id comprobatur, uel uidere est in omnibus sanctorū ecclesijs, in quibus paci studetur ab omnibus sanctis, nec locus datur disidijs & confusioni. Quare si sancti estis & ipsi, operam dabitis, ne in uobis solis confusionis author uideatur esse spiritus Dei, cuius donis ab utimini. Dubio procul erant & in alijs ecclesijs sanctorū disidia, quibus maleuolorum ac reproborum improbitate exercebantur: uerum hoc genus confusionis, quod ex donis Dei in abusum raptis nascebatur, peculiare erat ecclesiæ Corinthiorum, ac speciem quandā imperitis obijciebat, quasi author illius esset spiritus Dei, qd charismata linguarū & prophetiæ in homines cōtentiosos effudisset. Cum ergo dicit, Non enim cōfusionis author est Deus: sed pacis, sicuti patet in omnibus ecclesijs sancto rum: hoc sensu perinde est ac si dicat, quod ecclesia uestra tantopere cōfunditur, nō est dum spiritui Dei, sed uestris studijs quibus alij charismata hæc imprudenter æmulantur, alij inutiliter iactant & ostentāt. Neq; enim sic est comparatus Deus, ut eiusmodi uelit esse confusionis author, id quod abunde patet in reliquis omnibus sanctorum ecclesijs, quarū nulla hac confusione turbatur: turbaretur autem illa omnes, si Deus cōfusionis esset author per id, quod charismata linguarum & prophetiæ credentibus uobis elargitus est. Nam effudit hunc suum spiritum non in uos solos, sed & in cæteros fideles, qui tamen ordini, ac paci, & ædificationi charismata ista accommodant.
units.tr: "As in all the congregations of the saints," he says. Some word is lacking by which the sense may be completed. The Vulgate version has, "as I also teach in all the churches of the saints." So Ambrose reads and explains it, and Chrysostom too added διδάσκω [didaskō], that is, "I teach," as the copy I have at hand has it. The version of Theophylact also reads so. Some think it should be read, "as is done in all the churches of the saints." It matters to which earlier words this clause is referred. If it refers to what he has prescribed to the Corinthians, saying, "Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge; but if something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may receive consolation, and the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets," then the sense will be: "In prescribing these things to you I prescribe nothing new. For I teach thus, and it is done thus in all the churches of the saints, from whom there is no reason why you should separate yourselves in this matter." But if this sense pleases, the words "For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace" must be enclosed in a parenthesis, and read thus: "For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may receive consolation, and the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets (for God is not the author of confusion, but of peace), as is done, or as I teach, in all the churches of the saints." But if you refer it to the immediately preceding words, "For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace," the sense will be: "As this is proved, or as may be seen, in all the churches of the saints, where all the saints strive for peace, and no place is given to dissensions and confusion." Therefore, if you too are saints, you will take care that the Spirit of God does not seem to be the author of confusion among you alone, whose gifts you use. Without doubt there were also dissensions in the other churches of the saints, with which they were troubled by the wickedness of the malicious and the reprobate. But this kind of confusion, which arose from the gifts of God seized for abuse, was peculiar to the church of the Corinthians, and it presented to the inexperienced a certain appearance, as if the Spirit of God were its author, since he had poured the gifts of tongues and prophecy into contentious men. Therefore when he says, "For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as is evident in all the churches of the saints," in this sense it is as if he said: "That your church is so greatly confused is not owing to the Spirit of God, but to your zeal, by which some imprudently emulate these gifts and others vainly boast of and display them. For God is not so constituted as to wish to be the author of such confusion, as is abundantly clear from all the other churches of the saints, none of which is troubled by this confusion. But all of them would be troubled if God were the author of confusion through the fact that he has bestowed the gifts of tongues and prophecy on you who believe. For he poured out this his Spirit not only on you, but also on the other faithful, who nevertheless adapt these gifts to order, peace and edification."

units.la: Vtro hæc sensu accipiamus, omnino impro perat illis reprehensibilem hanc singularitatē, qua se ab omnibus alijs ecclesijs sanctorū separabant, & ordinem donorum Dei inuertebat, quo utebantur alij omnes. Quantum autem dedecoris habeat eiuismodi singularitas, haud opus est ut admoneā. Sed obsecro, quid aliud facere iā olim cœpit ecclesia Romana, ubi ab hoc cōmuni præscripto Apostoli deficiēs, omnium aliarum ecclesiarū sanctarum & apostolicarum consuetudinē contempsit, inq; ea singularitate etiamnū perdurat: imò, quod peius est, eos qui ad consuetudinē priorum ecclesiarum redire cupiunt, hæreseos dānat. Percurre lector omnia pontificum decreta, canones ac cōstitutiones, & uide num in illis inuenias aliquid ex tota hac materia sumptum, quā Apostolus singulari diligentia tam multis tractat & inculcat. In ecclesijs sanctorū omnibus, ab Apostolis uidelicet institutis, pluris fiebant quinq; uerba lingua intelligibili & uulgari, qd decē millia idiomate incognito prolata. Si in hisce ecclesijs, cū scriberet ista Apostolus, Romana quoq; fuit: quę est illa temeritas qua contra catholicā ecclesiarū consuetudinē, cōtraq; catholicam Apostoli doctrinā, peregrinam & ignotam linguam, Latinam uidelicet ecclesijs Occidentalibus obtruserūt? Quomodo hodie hæresis est, quod Apostolus tāto ferio docuit, quod ratio ædificandæ ecclesiæ posćit, quod communis sensus requirit, quodq; catholica sanctarum ecclesiarum consuetudo in tam uarijs Orientalium nationibus seruauit?
units.tr: Whichever sense we accept, he utterly condemns that blameworthy singularity by which the Corinthians separated themselves from all the other churches of the saints and reversed the order of God's gifts that all the others used. How much shame such singularity carries, there is no need for me to remind you. But I ask, what else did the Roman Church begin long ago to do, when, departing from this common prescription of the Apostle, it despised the custom of all the other holy and apostolic churches, and still persists in that singularity? Indeed, what is worse, it condemns as heresy those who wish to return to the custom of the earlier churches. Let the reader run through all the decrees, canons and constitutions of the pontiffs, and see whether he can find in them anything drawn from this whole matter, which the Apostle treats and impresses with such singular diligence and in so many places. In all the churches of the saints, instituted by the Apostles, five words spoken in an intelligible and common tongue were worth more than ten thousand spoken in an unknown language. If the Roman church too was among these churches when the Apostle wrote this, what is that rashness by which, against the catholic custom of the churches and against the catholic teaching of the Apostle, they have forced a foreign and unknown language, namely Latin, upon the Western churches? How is it heresy today to do what the Apostle taught so earnestly, what the reason of building up the church demands, what common sense requires, and what the catholic custom of the holy churches has kept among so many diverse nations of the East?

units.la: Respondeant ad ista, qui nobis uicium singularitatis, hæreses matris, obijciunt, propterea quod à cultibus ac ritibus aliarū ecclesiarū defecimus, & Romanæ sedis dominatum respuimus. Comprobét ea quorū gratia cum Romanis ecclesijs haud cōmunicamus, ecclesijs esse sanctorū ab apostolis tradita, & usu catholico seruata, sicuti nos comprobare possumus, quæ ipsi contra uerbum Dei sectantur adulterina esse, & à doctrina Apostolica, ufuq; ecclesiæ catholicæ aliena. Magnum sane præiudicium est in catholica ecclesiarū consuetudine. Et utinam illa sic sit hodie comparata, ut recedentes ab ea merito hæreticæ queant singularitatis argui. Verum non habet locū hoc præiudiciū nisi in ecclesijs ritè institutis. Ab illis citra necesitate studio singularitatis dissentire, omnino dignum est reprehensione. Quàm autem tem uelim ab hoc singularitatis uicio omnes eas alienas esse ecclesias, quæ in Romana Babylone discesserunt. Laudabilis est ab illa dissessus: uerum non posse in rebus licitis & utilibus conuenire cum ecclesijs reformatis: nemo,puto,cordatus probauerit. Priusq; ad sequentia transeamus, respondendum est Eccio, qui in Locis suis uerba hęc Apostoli sic citat,ut ex illis comprobet,intelligentiá scripturæ magis quærendam esse apud Romanã ecclesiam, concordé & unitá,q; apud Lutherů,uel Zuinglium,uel Osiandrum,eo quòd non sit dissensionis author Deus,sed pacis: isti uero inter se dissentiant. Non cogitauit ille, neminem esse fidelium,qui S.scripturæ intelligentiá quærat apud ecclesiam uel homine aliquem quantùuis doctũ,& non magis apud eum, qui clauêm habet scientiæ,& mentes fidelium aperit, ut scripturas intelligant. Quod uero attinet dissidia nostrorum temporum,nó est nouum quod in ecclesia oriuntur schismata. Vetus hoc est,etiá temporibus apostolorũ cognitum, præsertim in ecclesia Corinthiorũ: quá nihilo secius uocat Apostolus ecclesiam Dei,& membra illius uocatos sanctos,ablutos,sanctificatos & iustificatos. Quàm autem unita sit Rom.ecclesia,& qualis sit,quaq; in re ipsius unitas,quid attinet meminisse.
units.tr: Let those who charge us with the fault of singularity, the mother of heresies, answer this. They object that we have departed from the rites and ceremonies of the other churches and rejected the dominion of the Roman see. Let them prove that those things for which we do not share with the Roman churches are handed down from the apostles and kept by the universal custom of the Church, as we can prove that what they defend against the word of God is adulterous and alien to apostolic doctrine and to the practice of the catholic Church. Certainly the custom of the churches carries great weight. I wish it were so constituted today that those who depart from it could rightly be charged with heretical singularity. But this presumption holds only in churches that have been rightly established. To dissent from them without necessity, out of a love of singularity, deserves reproof in every way. Yet how much I would wish that all those churches which have withdrawn from Roman Babylon were free from this fault of singularity. Their departure from that city is praiseworthy; but that they cannot agree with the reformed churches in lawful and useful matters, I think no sensible person will approve. Before we pass on to what follows, we must answer Eck, who in his Loci quotes these words of the Apostle in such a way as to prove from them that the understanding of Scripture is to be sought more in the Roman Church, which is harmonious and one, than with Luther, Zwingli or Osiander, because God is not the author of dissension but of peace, whereas those men disagree among themselves. He did not consider that there is no believer who seeks the understanding of Holy Scripture from the Church or from any man, however learned, rather than from him who has the key of knowledge and opens the minds of the faithful so that they understand the Scriptures. As for the dissensions of our own times, it is no novelty that schisms arise in the Church. This is an old evil, known even in the times of the apostles, especially in the church of the Corinthians; yet the Apostle nonetheless calls it the Church of God, and calls its members saints, washed, sanctified and justified. How united the Roman Church is, and of what sort, and in what respect its unity lies, there is no need to recall.

units.la: Mulieres uestræ ín ecclesijs sileant: neq; enim permissum est illis ut loquan tur,sed ut subdítę sint,quemadmodum & lex dicit: Quod si quid discere uo- lunt,domi suos uíros ínterroget. Nam turpe est mulieribus ín ecclesia loquí.
units.tr: Let your women keep silence in the churches, for it is not permitted to them to speak, but they are commanded to be subject, as also the law says. And if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home. For it is a shameful thing for women to speak in the church.

units.la: Supererat adhuc corrigenda muliebris temeritas,qua mulieres Corinthiorũ in ecclesijs haud secus atq; uiris prophetandum sibi esse censebant,alias poterat iam præsentem materiam claudere. Quoniam autem dixerat,Potestis enim omnes prophetare per uices, ut omnes discant & consolationem accipiát:ne hoc sic generaliter acciperetur,ut ad mulieres quoque pertinere putaretur, consulto de illis subiecit ac temeritate illarũ hoc canone coercuit.
units.tr: There still remained the rashness of women to be corrected, by which the women of the Corinthians thought that they ought to prophesy in the churches no less than men. Otherwise he could already have closed the present matter. But since he had said, "For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and receive comfort," lest this be taken so generally that it would be thought to pertain to women also, he deliberately added a word about them and restrained their rashness with this rule.

units.la: MVLIERES uestrę in ecclesijs sileant inquit.] Poterat uerti, uxores uestræ in ecclesijs sileant. Quod enim de uxoribus præcipuè loquatur,ex eo satis patet, quod dicit, Sed ut subditæ sint,quemadmodum lex dicit: Quod si quid discere uolunt,domi uiros suos interrogent. Etenim licet ad uirgines quoq; & ad uiduas pertinet hoc præscriptum: quia tamen uxoratæ plus sibi licentiæ ut domi erga maritos & domesticos: ita in ecclesia quoq; in cœtu publico uindicabant, q uirgines & uiduæ: quarũ illæ uirginali pudore,istæ uiduali solitudine affectæ submisius agere solent,haud præter rationé præcipuè illarum licentiam restringit.Prudenter autè facit,quod non dicit, pauca,uel moderate,uel submisse ac uerecunde,in ecclesijs loquantur: sed, Ne quid quouis modo ausint,in uniuersum eas compescit,dicens, Sileant. Vno uelut ictu omnem muliebre garrulitate amputat,unde plurimũ fuisset altercationum & rixarum exortum in ecclesijs.
units.tr: "Let your women keep silence in the churches," he says. It could have been translated "let your wives keep silence in the churches." That he speaks chiefly of wives is clear enough from what follows: "but they are commanded to be subject, as also the law says. And if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home." For although this precept also applies to virgins and widows, nevertheless married women claim more freedom, both at home toward their husbands and in the household, and also in the church, in public assembly, than virgins and widows do. Virgins, moved by virginal modesty, and widows, by the loneliness of widowhood, are accustomed to behave more humbly. So it is not without reason that he chiefly restrains the freedom of the married women. He acts prudently in not saying "let them speak few words, or speak moderately, or humbly and modestly in the churches," but he restrains them altogether, so that they dare nothing in any way, saying "let them keep silence." With one blow, as it were, he cuts off all female chatter, from which there would have arisen very many quarrels and brawls in the churches.

units.la: NEQVE enim permissum est illis ut loquâ tur,inquit.]Reddit rationem huius constitutionis:non quod id poscat res ipsa,quâ cômunis ubique sensus approbat: sed quod Corinthiorũ esset leuitati ac uanitati occurrendum. Reddit aũt geminá ratione:illiciti unam,turpitudinis alterá.Illicitũ esse mulierib. loqui monet,dicens:Neq; enim permissum est illis ut loquatur.Non licet illis quod nó est permissum. Dupliciter aút nó est illis permissum ut loquátur.Primũ,dum contrariũ ipsis est diuina lege præceptum.Hoc exprimit dicens,sed ut subdi tæ sint,quêadmodũ lex dicit. Deinde, quatenus in omnibus gentibus,ubi aliquis est honestatis publicæ sensus,& utriusq; humani sexus decorum seruatur, à publicis actionibus muliebris sexus remouetur. Scio quid hac de re apud nonnullos philosophos legatur: uerũ nihil hinc est præiudicij contra communes gentium ac populorum mores.Cum ergo mulieri nec diuina lege,nec catholica omnium sit populorum consuetudine ac publica honestate permissum ut loquatur,restat illicitum illi esse ut loquatur. Non est autē uerbum loquendi simpliciter hic positum ab Apostolo,quasi mutieri nihil omnino loqui liceat:sed de eo loquê di genere,quo publicæ actiones uel causæ ex officio proponuntur ac tractantur in conuentibus uirorum in ecclesijs,& in foro, quod uiris competit,non mulieribus. Quemadmodũ & uerbũ currêdi nô est de quolibet cursu usus patũ,in eo quod pseudoprophetis exprobrat dominus dicês:Cucurrerunt, & ego non misi eos:sed de cursu legationis, qui non competit nisi delectis ac missis.
units.tr: "For it is not permitted to them to speak," he says. He gives the reason for this ordinance, not because the matter itself demands it, which common sense everywhere approves, but because the levity and vanity of the Corinthians had to be met. He gives a twofold reason: one of unlawfulness, the other of indecency. He warns that it is unlawful for women to speak, saying: "For it is not permitted to them to speak." What is not permitted is not lawful for them. It is not permitted to them to speak in two ways. First, when the divine law prescribes the contrary. He expresses this in saying, "but they are commanded to be subject, as also the law says." Then, in all nations where there is a sense of public decency and the proper bearing of both human sexes is preserved, the female sex is kept back from public activities. I know what is written on this matter by some philosophers, but it carries no prejudice against the common customs of nations and peoples. Since, then, it is permitted to a woman to speak neither by divine law nor by the universal custom of peoples and public decency, it remains unlawful for her to speak. The word "to speak" is not here used by the Apostle simply, as if women were allowed to say nothing at all; but it refers to that kind of speaking by which public affairs or causes are proposed and handled by office in the assemblies of men in the churches and in the forum, which belongs to men and not to women. Just as the word "to run" in the Lord's rebuke of the false prophets, "They ran, and I did not send them," is not used of any kind of running at will, but of the running of an embassy, which belongs only to the chosen and sent.

units.la: SED ut subditæ sint,inquit.] Subintelligêdum est,præceptũ:ac legendũ,neq; enim permissum est illis ut loquantur, sed præceptũ ut sint subditæ. Non enim rectè dixeris, permissum esse mulieribus ut sint subditæ, cum ea sit illis subiectio non sic permissa,ut non peccent obediendo:sed sic præceptũ, ut peccêt nisi subdantur & obediant suis uiris. Ergo non esse permissum mulieribus ut loquatur, ex eo probat,quod præceptum ipsis est, ut sint subditæ. Valeret argumentũ,si præceptũ esset illis ut sileant. Cui præceptũ est silentium, utiq; nõ est permissum ut loquatur, quemadmodũ cũ præceptũ esset Apostolo ut euãgelizaret, permissum illi non erat ut sileret. Quare dicebat: Væ mihi si non euangelizauero. Iam cum pro eo quod dicendum erat,sed ut sileat, dicit, sed ut subditæ sint: uidendũ est quomodo ex eo qd' subditę sunt uiris mulieres, cõsequatur nõ licere illis ut loquátus,cũ tamẽ spiritus prophetarũ haud ideo loqui uetentur, quod prophetis subijciũtur. Sciendũ hic est, aliter subdità esse mulierem uiro,& aliter spiritus prophetarum prophetis. Mulier subdita est uiro, propter illius eminentiam, qua primum est ad imaginem Dei conditus : deinde iudicio & facultate mentis, corporis quoque uiribus præstan. stantior caput mulieris constitutus: ipsa uero, tanquam in hisce omnibus inferior, non est apta ad regendum, sed opus habens ut regatur. Prophetæ uero prophetis non sic subijciûtur, quod alij alijs sint præstâtiores ac superiores: sed quod hoc postulat ratio feruandæ pacis, ui tandæq; confusionis, & ædificandi ecclesiam. Quare Apostolus recte colligit ex subiectione mulieris nö esse illi pmissum, ut loquatur, qd' tamē ex subiectione spirituū propheticorum non colligit. Respicit enim illic non tam subiectionem, q subiectionis causas, propter quas mulieri negatur: uiro autē datur, ut publicas actiones & causas loquendo & agendo obeat. Quanquam & prophetarum subiectionem loco silentij ac cessionis posuit. Tantisper enim propheta prophetæ subijcitur, dum loquens loquuturo ad tempus cedit ac tacet.
units.tr: "But that they be subject," he says. A precept must be understood, and it should be read: "It is not permitted to them to speak, but it is commanded that they be subject." For one would not rightly say that it is permitted to women to be subject, since that subjection is not permitted in such a way that they do not sin by obeying, but is commanded in such a way that they sin unless they submit and obey their husbands. Therefore he proves from the fact that women are commanded to be subject that it is not permitted to them to speak. The argument would hold if they were commanded to keep silence. For when silence is commanded to someone, it is certainly not permitted to speak, just as when the Apostle was commanded to preach the gospel, it was not permitted to him to keep silent. Hence he said: "Woe is me if I do not preach the gospel." Now since, in place of what should have been said, "but let her keep silent," he says, "but let them be subject," we must see how from the fact that women are subject to their husbands it follows that it is not lawful for them to speak, when yet the spirits of the prophets are not forbidden to speak for this reason, that they are subject to the prophets. Here we must note that a woman is subject to her husband in one way, and the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets in another. A woman is subject to her husband on account of his pre-eminence, by which he was first made in the image of God, and then, being superior in judgment and mental ability and in bodily strength too, was set as head of the woman; while she herself, as inferior in all these respects, is not fit to rule but needs to be ruled. But the prophets are not subjected to the prophets in such a way that some are more excellent and superior to others, but because the keeping of peace, the avoiding of confusion and the building up of the Church require it. Therefore the Apostle rightly infers from the subjection of the woman that it is not permitted to her to speak, which he does not infer from the subjection of the prophetic spirits. For he looks there not so much at the subjection as at the causes of subjection, on account of which speaking is denied to the woman, while it is given to the husband to discharge public duties and causes by speaking and acting. Yet he also put the subjection of the prophets in place of silence and yielding. For a prophet is subject to a prophet only so long as, while he speaks, he yields and is silent for a time to the one who is about to speak.

units.la: QVEMADMODVM, inqt, & lex dicit.] Non modò lege naturæ & conditionis, sed & lege Dei singulariter post præuaricationē lata, subiecta est uiro mulier. Lex ista legitur Gen. 3. ad hunc modum: Ad uirum tuum, hoc est, in potestate uiri tui erit desiderium tuum, & ipse dominabitur tibi. De hac lege loquitur, nö de tota lege Mosis, cum dicit: Quemadmodum & lex dicit. Non simpliciter, inquit, queadmodū lex: sed, Quemadmodū etiā lex dicit. Q.d. Præter alia quæ mulieris subiectionē comprobât, præcipitur illa etiam lege diuina. De lege autē hac non est ut hic annotemus. Diximus de illa in Comment. nostris super Genesim.
units.tr: "As also the law says," he says. Woman is subject to man not only by the law of nature and of creation but also by a special law of God, given after the transgression. That law is read in Genesis 3 in this manner: "Your desire shall be for your husband, that is, your desire shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you." He speaks of this law, not of the whole law of Moses, when he says "as also the law says." He does not say simply "as the law," but "as also the law says," that is: besides other things which confirm the subjection of the woman, it is also commanded by the divine law. We need not annotate here on this law. We have spoken of it in our Commentaries on Genesis.

units.la: Illud considerandum est, quod legem Dei citat Apostolus in causa omnibus non modò Christianis, sed & reliquis populis ac gētibus cognita & indubitata. Quæ est enim natio, in qua non subsit mulier uiro, ut uideri possit otiosum ac superfluum: quod causam omnibus notam, in qua nulla est controuersia, lege Dei comprobandam putauit. Verùm non est hoc citra rationem factum. Homini Christiano fatis nō est, ppterea facere quæ recta sunt, quòd communi usu ac sensu comprobentur, sed facienda sunt illi ex fide ac conscientia Dei. Mulier Christiana non ob id tantum subdit se uiro, quod ea sit omnium gentium consuetudo, sed quod sciat ita placere Deo: eaq; sit fide erga illum & obedientia prædita, ut quod facit, ex animo faciat. Huc autem feruit scientia diuinæ legis, unde uoluntas ac placitum Dei cognoscitur. Quare magna illam ratione Apostolus hoc loco citauit.
units.tr: We must consider that the Apostle cites the law of God in a matter known and undisputed not only to Christians but also to the other peoples and nations. For what nation is there in which the wife is not subject to the husband, so that it might seem an idle and superfluous thing? Even so, he thought a matter known to everyone, about which there is no controversy, ought to be confirmed by the law of God. Yet this was not done without reason. It is not enough for a Christian man to do what is right simply because it is approved by common custom and common sense; things must be done from faith and from awareness of God. The Christian wife does not submit herself to her husband only because this is the custom of all nations, but because she knows it pleases God. She is endowed with such faith and obedience towards him that she does what she does from the heart. Now the knowledge of the divine law serves this purpose, since from it the will and pleasure of God are known. Therefore the Apostle rightly cited it in this place.

units.la: QVOD si quid discere uolunt, inquit.] Occupatio est. Poterat enim obijci: Ergo mulier sedebit in cœtu ecclesiastico instar stipitis, nec discet ea, quæ ignorat, nec quæret sicubi hæsi tauerit? Quomodo enim quæret ac discet, nisi interroget? Quomodo interrogabit, nisi loquatur? Respondet: Non prohibeo, ne discat. Potest audiendo ac tacendo discere in ecclesia. Quod si ecclesiastica illi doctrina non satisfecerit, sed est in quo hæsitet, uirum suum domi interroget. Hoc dicens, non uetat mulieres discere in ecclesia, quę perinde atq; uiri ædificant
units.tr: "If they wish to learn anything," he says. This is a figure called occupatio. For it could be objected: "So then the woman will sit in the ecclesiastical assembly like a log, and will not learn what she does not know, nor ask if she has stuck anywhere? For how will she seek and learn unless she asks? How will she ask unless she speaks?" He answers: I do not forbid her to learn. She can learn in the Church by listening and by keeping silent. But if the church teaching does not satisfy her, and there is something about which she hesitates, let her ask her husband at home. In saying this he does not forbid women to learn in the Church, women who, no less than men, are built up in the knowledge of God and in the zeal of true piety. He rather takes care that under the pretext of learning they do not overstep the modesty proper to women, and cast off the shame of their sex by wrangling.

units.la: dæ sunt in cognitione Dei ac ueræ pietatis studio: sed cauet ne prætextu discendi decorum muliebre excedant, & pudorem sexus altercando abijciát. Sic uerbo discendi usus est hoc loco sensu interrogandi, quod ex eo patet quod adijcit, dicens: Domi uiros suos interrogent. Q.d. Si quid interrogare uolunt, interrogent non in ecclesia prophetas, sed domi suos ipsarum maritos. Præextextum interrogandi ac loquendi tollit, quo ipsam publicam interrogationem tollat. Poterant enim studium discendi præextexere, eoq; præextextu licéter quiduis in terrogare. Hoc quippe ingenio curioso pleræque sunt ex illis, præsertim ditiores, quales erant de quibus 2. Tim. 3. meminit, dicēs: Ex his enim sunt qui subeunt in familias, & captiuas ducunt mulierculas oneratas peccatis, quę du cuntur concupiscentijs uarijs semper discentes: hoc est, semper interrogantes, nec unquā ad cognitionem ueritatis uenire ualētes. Nec alienum est à phrasi Græcorum, si discere pro interrogare sumpserimus hoc loco. Nam & illis ματὼμα idem nonnunquam est, quod sαπα, id est, quæro & interrogo.
units.tr: Thus he uses the verb "to learn" in this passage in the sense of "to ask," as is clear from what he adds: "let them ask their own husbands at home." That is: "If they wish to ask anything, let them ask not the prophets in the Church, but their own husbands at home." He removes the pretext of asking and speaking, so that he may take away public questioning itself. For they could have used the pretext of eagerness to learn, and under that pretext ask whatever they liked. Indeed, most women of this curious disposition are of that kind, especially the wealthier ones, such as those of whom he speaks in 2 Tim. 3, saying: "For of this sort are those who creep into households and lead captive silly women laden with sins, who are led away by various lusts, always learning, that is, always asking, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth." Nor is it foreign to Greek idiom if we take "to learn" here as "to ask." For the Greek verb for learning [μανθάνω] sometimes means the same as the verb for seeking and asking [ζητῶ], that is, to inquire and to ask.

units.la: DOMI, inquit, suos uiros interrogent.] Nō dicit, extra ecclesiam prophetas accedát & interrogent, ne det illis occasione prophetas curiosis quæstionibus diuexandi: uel tandē successu tèporis minus honesta sub præextu con stitutionis Apostolicæ tentandi, qualia in Papatu sub specie cöfessionis, aut cösilij quæren di innumera fieri cöstat. Domi, inquit, ̨pprios uiros interroget. Hic nihil sinistræ suspicionis oriri potest. Deinde facile poterit maritus curiositati uxoris authoritate sua imponere modū, & inutiles illius quęstiones graui & matura reprehensione multo abscindere melius, q quisq̄ alius, quis accurate illis & subtiliter respondens. Puto autnon dare illis Apostolū occasione maritos suos de quibuslibet inutili bus rebus interrogandi, cū dicit: Si quid disce re uolunt, domi uiros suos interrogent. Quomodo enim permitteret illis, quod nemo poterit probare cordatus? Loquitur de ijs rebus de quibus dictum est à prophetis in ecclesia. Hic, inquit, si quid discere uolunt, non interroget in ecclesia, sed quæràt domi à suis maritis. Nec est quòd dicas: Quò poterit uxoratus laicus & idiota docere suā uxoré domi? Nō enim intelligit de quibuslibet abstrusis rebus, sed de ijs quas oēs audierūt in ecclesia: de quibus facile fuerit uiro pio & auditori haud ofcitati respōdere uxori interrogāti. Verū in Papatu, ubi multa idola habētur loco librorū ac doctorū, qd respodebit uxori suę laicus? imō de qb. illa domū è tēplo eidoloru regressa interroga bit, cū nihil quod discēdū sit in tēplo audierit?
units.tr: "At home," he says, "let them ask their own husbands." He does not say that they should go outside the Church to the prophets and ask them, lest he give the prophets an occasion to harass them with inquisitive questions, or in time, under the pretext of testing an apostolic ordinance, some less honourable practice should develop, of the kind that is known to be done in numberless ways under the Papacy, under the guise of confession or of seeking counsel. "Let her ask her own husband," he says. Here no sinister suspicion can arise. Further, a husband can easily set a limit on his wife's curiosity by his authority, and by serious and mature rebuke can cut off her useless questions far better than anyone else, answering her carefully and wisely. I think the Apostle does not give women an occasion to ask their husbands about any useless matters when he says: "If they wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home." For how would he permit what no sensible person could approve? He is speaking of those matters that have been set forth by the prophets in the Church. "Here," he says, "if they wish to learn anything, let them not ask in the Church, but seek it at home from their husbands." Nor should you say: "But how can a married layman, an unlearned man, teach his wife at home?" For he does not mean any abstruse matters, but those which all have heard in the Church, about which it will be easy for a godly man, and one who is not a poor listener, to answer his wife when she asks. But under the Papacy, where many idols are held in place of books and teachers, what will a layman answer his wife? Indeed, what will she ask him when she has come home from the temple of idols, having heard nothing in the temple that needs to be learned?

units.la: NAM turpe est, inquit, mulieribus loqui in ecclesia.] Reddit adhuc aliam rationē, quá su pra diximus esse alteram, quare nó debeat mu lier loqui in ecclesia, sed domi, si quid interrogare uelit, interrogare suum maritum. Hanc sumit à turpitudine, dicens: Nam turpe est mulieribus loqui in ecclesia. Turpitudo est, quanquando quid præter decorum uel personæ, uel officij, uel naturę, uel sexus, uel loci, uel tempora admittitur. Oppositum huius est honestas, quando omnium istorum seruatur decorum. Decorum autem muliebris sexus est submissio & silentium in publico. Turpitudo igitur illius est, si sit mulier audacula in publico, sic ut abiecto pudore prosiliat ad dicendum in medio uirorum.
units.tr: "For it is shameful," he says, "for women to speak in the Church." He gives yet another reason, which we said above is the second, why a woman ought not to speak in the Church but, if she wishes to ask something, should ask her husband at home. He draws this from shamefulness, saying: "For it is shameful for women to speak in the Church." That is shameful which is permitted contrary to what is fitting for a person, or an office, or nature, or sex, or place, or time. The opposite of this is honour, when all these fittings are observed. What is fitting for the female sex, however, is submission and silence in public. So it is shameful for a woman to be a bold little thing in public, so that, casting off modesty, she rushes forward to speak in the midst of men.

units.la: Turpitudo hæc merito reprehenditur ab Apostolo. Sed obsecro, si reprehensibilis est turpitudo, quæ dedecorosa est mulierculæ in cœtu ecclesiastico quid interroganti: quanto est ea reprehensibilior, qua ad dedecus uirilis sexus ac dignitatis uiri, imò integra nonnunquam regna reguntur à mulierculis? Iurisdictiones datæ sunt monialibus, & nonnullis illarum titulus est principalium abbatissarum. Sit hoc leuiculum: an non illud dedecus est ecclesiæ Christi omnium maximum, quod mulier scortum non modò loquuta est, sed & dominata uniuersali ecclesiæ sub titulo & persona pontificalis eminentiæ? imò tot iam seculis meretrix purpurata tyrannidem exercet in ecclesia?
units.tr: The Apostle rightly rebukes this shamefulness. But I ask you: if shameful conduct is reprehensible, and it is disgraceful for a little woman to ask something in the ecclesiastical assembly, how much more reprehensible is that which brings disgrace on the male sex and on the dignity of men, and indeed sometimes whole kingdoms are ruled by little women! Jurisdictions have been given to nuns, and some of them hold the title of principal abbesses. But let that be a small matter. Is it not the greatest disgrace of the Church of Christ that a woman, a harlot, has not only spoken but has even ruled over the universal Church under the title and person of pontifical eminence? Indeed, for so many centuries now the purple harlot has exercised tyranny in the Church!

units.la: Sed ualeant ista, donec corrigantur iudicio domini. Nos interim qui uiri sumus, maxime dignitate, iudicio & potestate præstantiores, colligamus ad hunc modum: Si turpe mulieri est loqui in ecclesia, quomodo non est turpius uiris episcopis non loqui in ecclesia, cum loquendum sit ipsis ex officio? quomodo nō est turpius uiris doctoribus nugari in ecclesia, & fictis uerbis negociari? Si turpe est mulieri aliquo pacto sexus ac personæ suæ decorum excedere: quid censendum de uiris est, nullam sui sexus suæque personæ rationem habentibus? Turpe mulieri est obire uelle in ecclesia, quæ non nisi uiros concernunt: & non est turpe episcopis, prælatis, pastoribus ac doctoribus muliebrem sectari molliciem, leuitate ac uanitatem? Natura mulier rixatrix. Quomodo nō turpe est doctoribus, quauis leui de causa muliebriter cōtendere ac rixari in ecclesia? Vicia mulierum quàm sint turpia, uidemus: uerum non ita diligenter cauemus, ne in turpiora incidamus.
units.tr: But let these things go, until they are corrected by the judgment of the Lord. Meanwhile, we who are men, and more excellent in dignity, judgment and power, let us reason in this way: If it is shameful for a woman to speak in the Church, how is it not more shameful for men who are bishops not to speak in the Church, when it is their duty to speak? How is it not more shameful for men who are teachers to trifle in the Church and trade in empty words? If it is shameful for a woman in any way to exceed the fitness of her sex and person, what should be thought of men who have no regard for their sex or their person? It is shameful for a woman to wish to meddle in the Church, in matters that concern only men; and is it not shameful for bishops, prelates, ministers and teachers to pursue womanish softness, lightness and vanity? By nature woman is quarrelsome. How is it not shameful for teachers to contend and wrangle in the Church like women over any trifling cause? We see how shameful the vices of women are; but we are not so careful to avoid falling into more shameful ones.

units.la: An à uobis sermo Dei profectus est, aut in uos solos incidit?
units.tr: Has the word of God gone out from you, or has it fallen upon you alone?

units.la: Ambrosius ista & quæ ad finem usque capitis sequuntur, immediatè subiungit præcedentibus hisce uerbis: Non est enim confusionis author Deus, sed pacis, ut in omnibus congregationibus sanctorum: & quæ de silentio mulierum immixta sunt, in calcem capitis locat. Cur id faciat, facile cogitari potest. At, meo iudicio, nō erat opus serie contextus diuellere.
units.tr: Ambrose immediately joins these words and what follows up to the end of the chapter to the preceding sentence, namely: "For God is not the author of confusion but of peace, as in all the congregations of the saints." He places the material about the silence of women, which has been inserted here, at the end of the chapter. Why he does so can easily be guessed. In my judgment, however, there was no need to tear it apart from the order of the text.

units.la: AN à uobis, inquit, sermo Dei profectus est? Stomachum nonnihil resipiunt ista aduersum arrogantes: qui, ut apparet, cum philosophia essent turgidi, fideles ex Iudæis, & ipsos quoque apostolos, quod Iudæi essent, contemnebant, eoque confidentius abusus, qui in ecclesiam Corinthiorum irrepserant, tuebantur. Hi perinde insolescebant, ac si uel primi uel soli essent Christiani. Cū ergo doctrina regni Dei, quam hic uocat sermonem Dei, profecta esset non ex Gentibus ad Iudæos, sed ex Iudæis ad Gentes, quemadmodum & Christus salutem ex Iudæis esse dixit: & Iesaias uerbum Dei è Zyon & Hierusalem egressurum uaticinatus est: deinde non ad solos Corinthios, sed & ad reliquos populos uenisset, atque ecclesias constituisset, à quibus ipsi dissidebant: insultat illis, & exprobrat utrunque, quod neque primi neque soli essent Christiani, non quod ob eam essent causam culpandi, sed quod cæteras ecclesias præ se haud secus fastidiebant, quàm si ipsi uel primi uel soli essent Christiani, cum tamen neutrum sibi uendicare possent. Dicit itaque: Vnde uobis tantum est supercilij, ut cæteras ecclesias omnes contemnatis, dum ordinem quem illæ sibi traditum religiose seruant, soli respuitis, & uestro arbitratu cuncta in ecclesia uestra geritis, illamque non ædificatis, sed confunditis? An putatis sermonem Dei à uobis egressum uenisse ad alias ecclesias? Sic sane putatis uestra exempla imitanda esse alijs ecclesijs: haud secus, quàm si quod habent, à uobis acceperint, ideoque à uestris debeat pendere placitis. Verùm non est sermo Dei à uobis ad alios, sed à Iudæis ad uos quemadmodum & ad alios profectus. Vel, putatis uos solos esse Christianos, quasi non & aliæ sint ecclesiæ ad Christum pertinentes, in quibus spiritus sanctus charismata sua, non minus quàm in uos, in eos effudit qui crediderunt, quę tamen omnes acceptum à nobis ordinem seruant. Sic perstringit singularitatis ipsorum superbiam & arrogantiam.
units.tr: "Has the word of God gone out from you?" he says. These words have a somewhat sharp edge against the arrogant, who, as is apparent, were puffed up with philosophy and despised the faithful from among the Jews, and the apostles themselves because they were Jews. Trusting in this, they defended the abuses that had crept into the church of the Corinthians. They grew proud as if they were the first or the only Christians. Since the teaching of the kingdom of God, which he here calls the word of God, went forth not from the Gentiles to the Jews, but from the Jews to the Gentiles (just as Christ said that salvation is from the Jews, and Isaiah prophesied that the word of God would go out from Zion and Jerusalem), and since it came not only to the Corinthians but also to the other peoples and established churches from which these men held themselves apart, he mocks them and reproaches them on both counts: that they were neither the first nor the only Christians. He does not blame them for this in itself, but because they looked down on the other churches as if they were the first or only Christians, though they could claim neither distinction. So he says: "How is it that you have such pride that you despise all the other churches, while you alone reject the order that they faithfully keep as it was handed down to them, and you do everything in your church by your own judgment, and you do not build up the church but throw it into confusion? Or do you think that the word of God went out from you to other churches? Indeed you think so, that your examples must be imitated by other churches, as if they had received from you what they have and must therefore depend on your decisions. But the word of God did not go from you to others; it went from the Jews to you, as also to others. Or do you think you alone are Christians, as if there were no other churches belonging to Christ, on whom the Holy Spirit has poured out his gifts no less than on you, and who nevertheless all keep the order received from us?" In this way he strikes at their pride and arrogance of singularity.

units.la: Interea cogitemus quàm ista Apostolus, uel quiuis Christianus, multò iustius exprobret Romanis, quàm tum exprobrauit Corinthijs. Hi nanque perinde primatum sibi uendicant in omnes Christi ecclesias, ac si principium Christianæ fidei & ecclesiæ sit ab ipsis, nec possit esse ecclesia Christi, quæ nō sit ipsis incorporata: hoc est, ab ingluuie ipsorum absorpta, cum nec primi sint Christiani, nec soli. Quid non auderent, si scriptum legeretur: Salus ex Romanis est: &, E Roma exibit lex & uerbum domini?
units.tr: Meanwhile let us consider how much more justly the Apostle, or any Christian, could reproach the Romans with these words than he then reproached the Corinthians. For they claim primacy over all the churches of Christ as if the beginning of the Christian faith and of the church were from them, and as if no church could be a church of Christ unless it were incorporated into them, that is, swallowed up by their gluttony, although they are neither the first Christians nor the only ones. What would they not dare if the words were read: "Salvation is from the Romans," and "From Rome shall go forth the law and the word of the Lord"?

units.la: Præter Romanos sunt & alij nostra hac ætate, qui propterea quod apud ipsos primum Papistici abusus reuelari taxariqué cœperunt: conuenire sibi putant, ut sint magistri reformandarum ecclesiarum, nec aliunde posse rectius normam instituendæ reformationis petiti iudicant quàm ab ipsis. Ab his, nisi ad omnia ipsorum consentias, mox audies: Quid habes, quod nō à nobis acceperis? Quare & istis recte obiceris: An à uobis profectus est sermo Dei? uel in uos solos incidit? Fatendū quidem est, aliquid deberi honoris illis ecclesijs, quæ ueluti primitiæ fuerunt renascentis ueritatis: uerum probari non potest, si sibi superciliū linm primatus in reliquas ecclesias hoc nomi-ne uindicent. Licet enim primus uideas auroram sequuturi solis prænunciam: non conuenit tamen ut eam ob causam sic insolescas, ac si totus ille sol uelut ex oculis tuis progressus reliquo orbi illucescere cœperit. Non fert Apostolus, ut Iudæi contra Gentes superbiant: licet primum ad illos, deinde ex illis sermo Dei prouenerit ad Gentes. Thessalonicensibus hoc laudis adscribit, quod ab ipsis sermo domini personuerit in Macedonia & Achaia: imò fides ipsorum in omnem locum dimanauerit, ita ut exemplo fuerint omnibus credentibus in Macedonia & Achaia. Hinc tamen nec ipsi sese supra cæteras ecclesias extulerunt, nec tu liffet Apostolus si id fecissent. Et quomodo nō summæ damnandum est impudentiæ, quod supra cæteras ecclesias primatum ac dominiū ambiunt, qui nec authores sunt Christianæ fidei, nec soli illam profitentur?
units.tr: Besides the Romans there are others in our own age who, because the abuses of the Papists were first revealed and censured among them, think it fitting that they should be the masters of reforming the churches, and they judge that the rule for establishing reformation can be sought more rightly from themselves than from anywhere else. From these men, unless you agree with everything they say, you will soon hear: "What have you that you did not receive from us?" So they too may rightly be confronted with the question: "Has the word of God gone out from you, or has it fallen upon you alone?" It must indeed be admitted that some honour is owed to those churches which were, as it were, the first fruits of the revived truth. But it cannot be granted if on that account they claim a proud primacy over the other churches. For although you may be the first to see the dawn that announces the coming sun, it does not befit you to be so puffed up as if that whole sun had risen from your eyes and begun to shine on the rest of the world. The Apostle did not tolerate the Jews boasting against the Gentiles, although the word of God came first to them and then from them to the Gentiles. He ascribes this praise to the Thessalonians, that from them the word of the Lord sounded out in Macedonia and Achaia; indeed their faith spread abroad in every place, so that they became an example to all believers in Macedonia and Achaia. Yet they did not exalt themselves above the other churches, and the Apostle would not have approved had they done so. How can it not be judged the height of impudence for those to claim primacy and lordship over the other churches, when they are neither the authors of the Christian faith nor alone in professing it?

units.la: Si quis uidetur propheta esse, aut spiritualis, agnoscat quæ scribo uobis, quæ domini sint præcepta.
units.tr: "If anyone seems to be a prophet, or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things I write to you are the Lord's commandments."

units.la: Priusquam materiam hanc concludat, uindicat ijs quæ dixit authoritatem præceptorum dominicorum, ne quis ea sufq; deq; facienda esse putet. Non dicit autē simpliciter, quæ scribo uobis, domini sunt præcepta: sed, ut notet eos, quorum potissimum gratia motus fuit, ut hæc scriberet: Si quis, inquit, uidetur propheta esse aut spiritualis, agnoscat quæ scribo uobis, quod domini sint præcepta. hoc est, quantumuis propheta aut spiritualis esse uideatur: haud tamen eam ob causam contemnat quæ scribo, nisi domini uelit cōtemnere præcepta. Si quod charisma accepit, nō debet propterea eximere se ab obedientia dominicorum præceptorum: sed quo plus accepit donorū Dei, hoc magis dominicis obedire præceptis, & ita diose cauere, ne confusionem inducat in ecclesiam.
units.tr: Before he brings this subject to a close, he vindicates the authority of the Lord's commandments for what he has said, so that no one thinks these things may be disregarded at will. He does not simply say, "the things I write to you are the Lord's commandments," but he points to the people for whose sake he was chiefly moved to write. "If anyone," he says, "seems to be a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things I write to you are the Lord's commandments." That is, however much he seems to be a prophet or spiritual, he should not on that account despise what I write, unless he wants to despise the Lord's commandments. If he has received some gift of grace, he must not for that reason exempt himself from obedience to the Lord's commandments. Rather, the more gifts of God he has received, the more he should obey the Lord's commandments, and so take care diligently that he does not bring confusion into the Church.

units.la: Nec ociosum est, quod non dicit, Si quis propheta est, aut spiritualis: sed, Si quis uidetur propheta esse aut spiritualis, quo perstringat illorum ostentationem, qui charismata spiritus in ecclesia ostentabant, & opinione illorum inflati minus erant erga Apostolicam doctrinam morigeri. Erat autem uertendum, Si quis sibijpsi uidetur esse propheta: hoc est, si quis sibijpsi donum uindicat prophetiæ, & hac opinione sibijpsi belle placet. Nō enim loquitur de illis qui aliorum opinione habebantur pro spiritualibus & prophetis: sed de inflatis illis, qui seipsi pro talibus uenditabant. Et hoc pacto Germanicus interpres uertit: So sich yemands lasst duncken. Atq; ita supra cap.3. eandē phrasim. Vertit Erasmus: Si quis sibi uidetur esse sapiens. Et cap.8. reddidit: Quod si quis sibi uidetur aliquid scire: ubi & uulgata uersio habet, Si quis autem se existimat scire aliquid. Et Gal.6.
units.tr: It is also not idle that he does not say, "If anyone is a prophet or spiritual," but, "If anyone seems to be a prophet or spiritual." By this he strikes at the showing off of those who displayed the gifts of the Spirit in the Church, and who, puffed up by their own opinion, were less compliant with apostolic teaching. It ought, however, to be rendered, "If anyone thinks himself to be a prophet," that is, if anyone claims for himself the gift of prophecy and is pleased with himself on this account. He is not speaking of those who were regarded as spiritual and prophets by the opinion of others, but of those puffed up men who put themselves forward as such. In this way the German translator renders it: So sich yemands lasst duncken ("If anyone lets himself think"). So too, above in chapter 3, he uses the same phrase. Erasmus renders it, "If anyone thinks himself to be wise." And in chapter 8 he gives, "But if anyone thinks he knows anything," where the Vulgate also has, "But if anyone thinks he knows something." And in Galatians 6, the Greek is rendered by Erasmus, "If anyone thinks himself to be something," while the Vulgate translator has, "If anyone thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceives his own mind." That phrase cannot apply to one who is thought great by others, but must be referred to the one who considers himself to be something. There is no need for me to remind you how much it matters whether someone regards himself as spiritual and a prophet, or is thought to be such by others. Augustine says that the Apostle, by these words, restrains and recalls to order restless men, who were all the more prone to sedition because they thought they excelled in the Spirit, and who by their pride threw everything into confusion. As for what he understands by "spiritual," there is no need for me to remind you, since when we discussed this word at the beginning of chapter 12 we judged that we had said enough.

units.la: kατὰ ... transtulit: Si quis sibi uidetur aliquid esse: & uulgatus interpres, Si quis existimat se aliquid esse: ubi additur, Cum nihil sit: suum ipse fallit animum: quod in eo nō poterit habere locum, qui ab alijs magni quid esse putatur: sed ad eum est referendum, qui seipse ali quid esse censet. Haud opus est, ut admoneam quantum referat, an seipse quisquam habeat spirituali ac propheta, uel ab alijs talis esse putetur. Augustinus dicit Apostolum hisce uerbis coercere, & in ordinem reuocare inquietos tanto ad seditionem faciliores, quanto sibi uidebātur spiritu excellere, cum superbiendo cuncta turbaret. Qualem autem intelligat per spiritualem: nō est ut admoneam, cum de hac uoce supra initio cap.12. quantum sufficere iudicauimus, dixerimus.
units.tr: We are reminded at this point what kind of people, above all others, oppose apostolic teaching and corrupt the Church: namely, those who think themselves superior to others, and want to be regarded as prelates, lords, learned men, wise men, spiritual men, religious men, and so on. While they do not arrange everything in the Church according to right order, but throw it into confusion by their own judgment, they are so far from feeling that they have transgressed, that they judge what they do to be their duty and want it to be accepted as authoritative. The Apostle struggled against this kind of man, but to this day in vain. They have corrupted all the churches, and this gout has never yielded to a healing hand. But let us see what he sets before them that they ought to respect.

units.la: Nos admonemur hoc loco, quodnā genus hominum Apostolicæ doctrinæ præ cæteris aduersetur, & ecclesiam corrumpat: ... uidelicet, id est eorum, qui sibi uidentur esse cę teris præstantiores: haberiq; uolunt pro præ-latis, pro dominis, pro doctis, pro sapientibus, pro spiritualibus, pro religiosis, &c. Hi dum omnia proprio arbitratu in ecclesia non constituunt, sed confundunt: tam abest, ut præuarirari se sentiant, ut magis quæ faciunt, pro officio se facere iudicent, & pro authenticis haberi uelint. Cum hoc hominum genere luctatur Apostolus, sed in hunc usq; diem frustra. Omnes ecclesias corruperunt, nec unquam tulit medicam ista podagra manum. Sed uideamus quid illis obijciat, quod reuereri debeant.
units.tr: "Let him acknowledge," he says, "that the things I write to you are the Lord's commandments." Why does he not say, "Let him acknowledge that I am an apostle of Christ, through whom you believed, and let him reverence apostolic authority"? Instead he veils his own authority and points to the authority of the Lord himself, saying, "Let him acknowledge that the things I write to you are the Lord's commandments." Because he understood that his own person was despised by those great prophets and spiritual men, he does not put forward his apostleship, but the authority of the Lord's commandments. For a pious and faithful layman it is enough to be reminded of apostolic authority and teaching. But it is not so for those who want to be held in the place of prophets, apostles and spiritual men. Today even the authority of the Lord's own commandments does not satisfy them. If he had been speaking of the common and unlearned faithful and said, "You who are considered unlearned," he would have added something useful: let him acknowledge his apostle, through whom you began to believe, and obey what I write. But the evil he was correcting did not lie among those people, but among those who judged themselves to be prophets and spiritual, and who therefore dared everything in the Church by their own rashness. So he sets against them, not the others, the claim that what he writes are the Lord's commandments.

units.la: AGNOSCAT, inquit, quæ scribo uobis, quod domini sint mandata.] Quid est quod nō dicit, Agnoscat me esse apostolum Christi, per quem credidistis, & reuereatur apostolicā authoritatem: sed ipsius domini authoritatē præ texit, dicēs: Agnoscat quæ scribo uobis, quod domini sint mandata? Quoniam intelligebat personam suam sordere magnis illis prophetis ac spiritualibus: non obijcit suum Apostolatum, sed authoritatem dominicorum præceptorum. Pio ac fideli laico satis est, si de apostolica authoritate & doctrina admoneamur. Verum illis qui se prophetarum, apostolorum & spiritualium loco haberi uolunt, non ita. Illis hodie nec ipsa dominicorum præceptorū authoritas satisfacit. Si de plebeijs & idiotis fidelibus loquens dixisset: Qui inter uos idiotę habentur, satis utiliter adiecisset: agnoscat suum Apostolum, per quem credere cœperunt, & ijs quæ scribo obtemperent. Verum malū quod corrigebat, non erat ex illis, sed ex ijs qui se prophetas & spirituales esse iudicabant, ideoq; omnia in ecclesia propria temeritate audebant. Quare non illis, sed istis obijcit, dominica esse præcepta quæ scribit.
units.tr: And observe that he does not simply say, "Let him think or consider, or believe," but, "Let him acknowledge that what I write are the Lord's commandments." As if he said: if they are prophets or spiritual, as they wish to appear, they do not need to be taught much in this matter, but without any difficulty they will recognise that what I write is not my own invention, but the commandment of the Lord himself. Let them therefore prove that they are prophets, and truly spiritual, by acknowledging these to be the Lord's commandments. This is just as if you were to say of the Roman "apostles": "If anyone seems to be a vicar and apostle of Christ, let him acknowledge that what we bring forward to purge religion is the teaching of Christ and the apostles." Let us then test true prophets and spiritual men by this mark which the Apostle sets forth. If they acknowledge the teaching and ordinances of the Lord, and not only acknowledge them but faithfully set them before the Church, then let us acknowledge them to be true prophets and spiritual men of the Lord. But if they do not even acknowledge them, nay, if they reject and condemn them, then they are so far from being acknowledged as spiritual men and prophets of the Lord that they should rather be held as ministers, prophets and instruments of Satan.

units.la: Et obserua, quod non simpliciter dicit, Cogitet aut reputet, uel credat: sed, Agnoscat quę scribo, quod domini sint præcepta. Quasi dicat: Si sunt prophetę, aut spirituales, quemadmodū uideri uolunt, non sunt multis instruendi in di in hac causa: sed absque ullo negocio agnoscent, quæ scribo non mea esse commenta, sed ipsius Domini præcepta. Declarent ergo esse se prophetas, & uere spirituales, & agnoscant hæc esse præcepta domini. Quod perinde est ac si dicas de Romanis apostolis: Si quis uideTur esse uicarius & apostolus Christi, agnoscat quæ in medium ad repurgandam religionem adferimus, esse doctrinam Christi & apostolorum. Probemus ergo ueros prophetas & spirituales hac nota quam proponit Apostolus. Si agnoscunt doctrinam & constituta domini: nec agnoscunt tantum, sed & fideliter ecclesiæ ponunt: agnoscamus eos esse ueros domini prophetas, & spirituales. Si uero ne agnoscunt quidem, imo reijciunt & damnant: tam abest, ut agnoscendi sint pro spiritualibus & prophetis domini, ut magis habendi sint pro ministris, phetis & organis Satanæ.
units.tr: You will say: what are those commandments of the Lord about which he says he is writing here? I answer: those he wrote concerning the proper order of speaking in tongues in the Church, concerning interpretation, concerning prophecy, concerning the edification of the Church, concerning the silence of women, and so on. These he calls the commandments of the Lord, although they are nowhere expressly read as commanded by the Lord himself, because he wrote them under the evident prompting of the Holy Spirit, as matters necessary for establishing the Church of the Lord. For just as the gifts which the faithful received through the apostolic ministry were not the Apostle's own but the Lord's, so the commandments by which he prescribed the use, manner, order and usefulness of those gifts were not his own but the Lord's commandments. No less so than the word of grace and faith which he preached to them was not his own but the Lord's. There were two parts of the apostolic office. One was to gain and gather the Church for the Lord through the preaching of the Gospel; the other was to establish and build up the gathered Church by precepts and ordinances. As the work of the former, so the work of the latter was not that of a man teaching and commanding, but of the Lord himself, by whose Spirit and command both were done. Therefore it was most justly his wish that this kind of commandment, belonging to the second part of the apostolic stewardship, should be acknowledged not as his own but as the commandments of the Lord himself.

units.la: Dices: Quæ sunt illa Domini præcepta, de quibus hic se scribere dicit? Respondeo. Quæ de recto ordine linguis in ecclesia loquendi, de interpretatione, de prophetia, de ædificatione ecclesiæ, de mulierum silentio, &c. scripsit. Hæc uocat præcepta Domini: quamuis nusquam ab ipso domino expresse præcepta legantur, propterea quod ea ex euidenti spiritus sancti instinctu tanquam necessitatem instituendi ecclesiam domini concernentia scripsit. Quemadmodum enim charismata illa quæ fideles ministerium apostolicum acceperant, non ipsius erant Apostoli, sed domini: ita & præcepta, quibus de usu, modo, ordine, & utilitate charismatum præscribebat, non erant ipsius, sed domini præcepta, non minus quàm uerbum gratiæ ac fidei quod ipsis prædicauerat, non ipsius erat, sed domini. Duæ erant Apostolici muneris partes. Vna, per Euangelij prædicationem acquirere & congregare Domino ecclesiam: altera, acquisitam ecclesiam præceptis & constitutionibus instituere & ædificare. Quemadmodum prioris opus, ita & posterioris non erat hominis docentis ac præcipientis, sed ipsius domini, cuius spiritu & mandato fiebat utrunque. Quare omnium iustissime hoc genus præcepta, ad alteram Apostolicæ dispensationis partem pertinentia, agnosci uoluit non pro suis, sed pro ipsius domini præceptis.
units.tr: You will ask: what are those precepts of the Lord that he says he is writing about here? I answer: those he wrote concerning the proper order of speaking in tongues in the church, concerning interpretation, concerning prophecy, concerning the building up of the church, concerning the silence of women, and so on. He calls these the precepts of the Lord, although they are nowhere expressly read as commands from the Lord himself, because he wrote them under the clear prompting of the Holy Spirit, as matters bearing on the necessity of establishing the Lord's church. For just as the gifts that the faithful had received through the apostolic ministry were not the Apostle's own but the Lord's, so also the precepts by which he prescribed the use, manner, order and benefit of those gifts were not his own but the Lord's precepts, no less than the word of grace and faith that he had preached to them was not his own but the Lord's. The apostolic office had two parts. One was to gain and gather the church for the Lord through the preaching of the gospel; the other was to establish and build up the church once gained by precepts and ordinances. The work of the latter was no more the work of a man teaching and commanding than the work of the former was; both were done by the Lord's own Spirit and command. Therefore he rightly wished this kind of precept, which pertains to the second part of the apostolic dispensation, to be acknowledged not as his own but as the precepts of the Lord himself.

units.la: Hinc tamen non est ut patrocinium domino suo quærant ecclesiarum principes, qui sibi quiduis præcipiendi potestatem sic uindicant, ut conscientias fidelium præceptis suis constringant, perinde ac si domini sint præcepta. Apostolus non est ea quę de uirginibus sua prædicat cap. 7. & de imparibus coniugijs in medium attulit, ausus referre in classem præceptorum Domini, sed expresse illic dixit: De uirginibus præceptum Domini non habeo, consilium tamen do: hic uero, Reliquis, inquit, ego dico, non dominus, si quis frater uxorem habet infidelem, & hęc assentitur ut habitet cum illo, ne dimittat eam, &c. Et isti ecclesiarum domini, omnia sua uolunt esse authentica, quorum e-
units.tr: Yet from this it does not follow that the rulers of the churches should seek patronage for their own pronouncements under the name of their Lord, those who claim for themselves such power of commanding anything whatever that they bind the consciences of the faithful with their precepts, as if they were the Lord's precepts. The Apostle did not dare to count among the precepts of the Lord those things he taught on his own about virgins in chapter 7, and about unequal marriages, but he expressly said there: "Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, yet I give counsel." Here, however, he says: "To the rest I speak, not the Lord: if any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not put her away," and so on. Yet these lords of the churches want all their own decrees to be regarded as authoritative, and they demand the observance of them with even greater seriousness than that of the Lord's precepts, whose

units.la: tiam obseruantiam maiori serio requirunt, q præceptorum domini. Tantam uidelicet uindicant sibi mandandi authoritatem in ecclesia.
units.tr: ...they insist on the observance of their own rules with far greater earnestness than on the commands of the Lord. Clearly they claim for themselves so great an authority to command in the Church.

units.la: S I uero quis ignorat, ignoret.] Sic est in Græco, ἀλί τις ἀγνοεῖ, ἀγνοείτω. Vulgata uersio habet: Si quis autem ignorat, ignorabitur. Sic legunt & Ambrosius & Augustinus. Ambrosius exponit ad hunc modum: Recte, quia qui nescit domini esse quæ loquitur Apostolus, & ipse à domino ignorabitur in die iudicij, dicente domino: Amen dico uobis quia nescio uos. Augustinus epistola 102. Si quis, inquit, ignorat, ignorabitur, id est, improbabitur. Non enim Deus, si ad scientiam referas, ignorat eos quibus dicturus est, Non noui uos: sed eorum improbatio hoc uerbo insinuata est. Consimili modo exponit & Hieronymus. Verum non conuenit hæc ut lectio, ita & expositio cū uerbis Pauli, quæ Chrysostomus rectius legit & exponit, quemadmodum & Theophylactus. Dixit: Si quis uidetur propheta esse aut spiritualis, agnoscat quæ scribo uobis, quod domini sint præcepta. Iam quoniam considerabat, non defore ex illis quos perstringebat, qui nō essent ea pro præceptis domini agnituri, sed magis reclamaturi, quo significaret se suo functum esse officio, nec quenquam reluctantem contentiosius in ordinem coacturum: subiunxit, dicens: Si quis autē ignorat, ignoret. quod idem est ac si dicat, ἀλί τις ἂν ἐπιγινώσκει ἀν ἐπιγινώ-σκειν: id est, si quis autem non agnoscit, non agnoscat. Quasi dicat: Per me licet non agnoscat, qui hæc domini esse præcepta non uult agnoscere. Puto enim ἀγνοεῖν idé hic esse quod ἀν ἐπιγινώσκειν, quo uerbo in præcedenti est particula usus. Quare nō est ut multis hic de ignorantia disputemus, cum Apostolus de illa non loquatur: nec respiciat ad auditores simplices ac rudes, multa adhuc ignorantes, sed ad eos qui prophetæ ac spirituales uideri uolentes, magis suum ipsorum magisterium in ecclesia introducere, quàm Apostolicæ doctrinæ acquiescere studebant.
units.tr: "But if anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant." The Greek reads: "εἰ δέ τις ἀγνοεῖ, ἀγνοείτω." The Vulgate version has: "But if anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored." Ambrose and Augustine also read it this way. Ambrose explains it thus: "Rightly so, because whoever does not know that the things the Apostle says are the Lord's will himself be ignored by the Lord on the day of judgment, the Lord saying: 'Truly I tell you, I do not know you.'" Augustine, in letter 102, says: "'If anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored,' that is, he will be disapproved. For God, if you refer it to knowledge, does not ignore those to whom he is going to say, 'I do not know you'; but their disapproval is suggested by this word." Jerome explains it in a similar way. But this reading and this explanation do not fit the words of Paul as well as the reading and explanation of Chrysostom, which are more accurate, and so also of Theophylact. Paul had said: "If anyone seems to be a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge what I write to you, that they are the Lord's commands." Since he foresaw that there would be some among those he was rebuking who would not acknowledge these things as the Lord's commands, but would rather object, he wished to show that he had done his duty, and that he would not contentiously force into line anyone who resisted. So he added: "But if anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant." This is the same as saying: "εἰ δέ τις ἀγνοεῖ, ἀγνοείτω" [if anyone does not acknowledge, let him not acknowledge]. As if he said: "So far as I am concerned, let him not acknowledge, since he does not want to recognise that these are the Lord's commands." For I think that ἀγνοεῖν here means the same as ἐπιγινώσκειν, a word which he used in the preceding clause. Therefore we need not debate here at length about ignorance, since the Apostle is not speaking of that. Nor is he looking at simple and rude hearers, who still know many things poorly, but at those who wished to seem prophets and spiritual, and who were more eager to introduce their own teaching into the Church than to submit to apostolic doctrine.

units.la: Pertinet hic locus ad eos Christi ministros, qui officium suum fideliter obeuntes in ecclesia, quosfuis delinquentes admonent, ut resipiscant, & præceptis dominicis obediant. Illi, quoniam neminem cogūt, sed quosfuis ad uoluntariam emendationem uocāt, ubi reluctantes inueniant, bona possunt cum conscientia dicere, Qui obedire detrectat, detrectet: qui peritatem respuit, respuat: qui perire mauult q seruari, pereat: qui sordet, sordeat: ego quod meum erat feci, uiderint qui præceptis domini obedire detrectant. Horum uero uox ista non debet esse, qui officium suum nō rite obeunt. Non cōuenit ut qui non docet, non hortatur, non reuocat errantes ac delinquentes in uiam, dicat, Qui ignorat, ignoret: qui perit, pereat. Sic animatus proprij oris indicio perfidus esse cōuincitur. Si pastor, neglectis ouibus res alias agat, & interim errantibus ac pereuntibus illis dicat: Quæ errat, errent: quę pereunt, pereant,nō facto modò,sed & proprio ore infi A delem se ac talem declarat, qui nulla prorsus cōmissarum ouium curam gerat,sed sufq; deq; faciat,quicquid illis acciderit.
units.tr: This passage applies to those ministers of Christ who discharge their office faithfully in the Church, admonishing those who sin, that they may repent and obey the Lord's commands. Since they compel no one, but call each person to voluntary amendment, when they meet with resistance they can say with a good conscience: "Let him who refuses to obey refuse. Let him who spurns salvation spurn it. Let him who prefers to perish rather than be saved perish. Let him who scorns it scorn. I have done what was mine to do; let those who refuse to obey the Lord's commands see to it." But this language should not be used by those who do not discharge their office properly. It is not fitting that one who does not teach, does not exhort, and does not call back erring and sinning people to the right way should say, "Let him who is ignorant remain ignorant; let him who perishes perish." Such a man is convicted of being faithless by his own mouth. If a pastor, neglecting the sheep, busies himself with other things, and meanwhile, while they go astray and perish, says, "Let the one that strays stray, and the ones that perish perish," he declares himself not only by deed but by his own mouth to be faithless and of that kind, one who cares nothing for the sheep committed to him, but lets whatever happens to them happen.

units.la: Proinde fratres ad id enitamini, ut prophetetis,&loqui linguis ne uetue-ritis.
units.tr: Therefore, brothers, strive to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.

units.la: Concludit omnia ea quæ hactenus de lin-guis & prophetia disputauit.Collectionis no-ta est in uocula ἅστι, id est,proinde,itaq;. Quasi dicat:Quandoquidem sic est comparata pro-phetia,ut multo sit linguis præstantior, & uti-lior illius usus: ζηλοῦτε, id est, æmulamini ac stu-diosè contendite,ut prophetetis. Et quoniam linguarum aliquis potest esse usus in ecclesia: si interpretatio accesserit,neminem linguis lo-qui prohibueritis.Sic propositio inhærens,hor-tatur quidem eos,ut primas tribuant prophe-tiæ,illiq; studiosè incumbant: interea tamen a-liquid loci permittit linguis,ne charisma spiri-tus reprobare uideatur.
units.tr: He concludes all that he has so far argued about tongues and prophecy. The mark of inference is in the little word "therefore" (ἄστε, that is, proinde, itaque). It is as if he said: since prophecy is so constituted that it is far superior to tongues, and its use is more useful, "strive" (ζηλοῦτε, that is, emulate and eagerly contend) "to prophesy." And since some use of tongues can be in the Church if there is interpretation, do not forbid anyone to speak in tongues. Thus the proposition that follows urges them indeed to give first place to prophecy and to devote themselves eagerly to it, yet meanwhile allows some room for tongues, lest it seem to reject the gift of the Spirit.

units.la: PROINDE fratres, inquit.] Rursus miti-gat animos eorum,quos semel atq; iterū non-nihil acrius perstrinxerat,dum eos fratres ap-pellat.Aliena est omnis adhortatio à suspicio-ne dominationis, quæ non domini ac præce-ptoris,sed fratris animum spirat.Quare iam a-liquoties fraternam hanc appellationē studio se adhortationibus suis immiscet.
units.tr: "Therefore, brothers," he says. Again he softens the minds of those whom he had once and again rebuked rather sharply, by calling them "brothers." Every exhortation is far from any suspicion of domination; it breathes not the spirit of a lord and teacher but of a brother. Therefore he now several times mixes this fraternal address into his exhortations.

units.la: AD id enitamini, inquit, ut prophetetis.] Nō simpliciter dicit,Prophetate:sed,Ad id eni B tamini ut prophetetis.Studio linguis loquen-di tenebantur:monet igitur, ut id ad prophe-tandi facultatem conuertant. Sic quod initio cœpit,in fine conclusionis uice repetit. Dixit enim initio: Æmulamini spiritualia, magis ta-men ut prophetetis.Et:Volo autē omnes uos loqui linguis,magis tamē ut prophetetis. Iam concludens idem inculcat,dicēs:Proinde fra-tres æmulamini ut ppphetetis, & loqui linguis ne uetueritis.
units.tr: "Strive," he says, "to prophesy." He does not simply say, "Prophesy," but "Strive to prophesy." They were devoted to eagerness in speaking in tongues; he therefore advises them to turn that eagerness to the ability to prophesy. So what he began at the outset he repeats at the end, in the manner of a conclusion. For at the beginning he said: "Desire spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy." And: "I want you all to speak in tongues, but rather that you may prophesy." Now, concluding, he presses the same point again, saying: "Therefore, brothers, strive to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues."

units.la: ET loqui linguis,inquit,ne uetueritis.] Quor sum istud? An non aliàs plus æquo dediti erat linguis? Timebat uidelicet, ne sic acciperent quæ scripsit,ut putaret in uniuersum abstinen-dum esse à linguis. Sane sic comparati sumus, ut de corrigēdis rerum abusibus admoniti,ci-tius res ipsas abijciamus, quàm rectum illarū usum amplectamur.
units.tr: "And do not forbid speaking in tongues," he says. Why is this? Was it not that at other times they had been devoted to tongues more than was right? He was evidently afraid that they would take what he had written in such a way as to think they must entirely abstain from tongues. Indeed we are so constituted that, when warned about correcting abuses of things, we cast away the things themselves more quickly than we embrace their right use.

units.la: 1 Abusus sanè magnus est in Papatu,quod peregrina & exotica lingua psallunt in eccle-sia.Hunc nonnulli sic abstulerunt, ut iam nul-lum prorsus habeant in ecclesijs suis psallendi usum,cū utiliter possent fideles lingua patria secundū Apostolicam institutionem psallere.
units.tr: 1. There is certainly a great abuse in Papistry, in that they sing psalms in the Church in a foreign and strange tongue. Some have removed this abuse so completely that they now have no use at all of singing psalms in their churches, although the faithful could usefully sing psalms in their native tongue according to the apostolic instruction.
