They also hold that the two days during which Christ lay in the tomb signify two thousand years of the New Testament, and that the beginning of the third day, on which he rose, signifies the time of the future resurrection and the beginning of the age to come. Thus they think that after the end of the sixth millenary, at the beginning of the seventh, Christ will again appear to the world and begin a new age. But since it is not for us to inquire into the times and seasons of the future resurrection, it is better to leave them to the Lord and to watch unceasingly, lest we be overtaken unprepared, dozing, by the coming of the righteous judge.

units.la: SECVNDVM scripturas, inquit.] Existimo hoc non solum ad resurrectionem, sed & ad sepulturam esse referendum, ut coiunctim legamus, & quod sepultus fuerit, & quod resurrexerit tertio die secundum scripturas. Scriptura autem de resurrectione habetur Psalmo 16. & in figura Ionæ prophetæ, cuius Christus ipse meminit Matthæi 12. dicens: Sicut Ionas fuit in uetre ceti tribus diebus & tribus noctibus, ita erit filius hominis in corde terræ tribus diebus & tribus noctibus.
units.tr: "According to the Scriptures," he says. I think this must be referred not only to the resurrection but also to the burial, so that we read together, "that he was buried, and that he rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures." The Scripture concerning the resurrection is found in Psalm 16, and in the figure of the prophet Jonah, which Christ himself mentions in Matthew 12, saying: "As Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights."

units.la: ET quod uisus sit Cephæ, inquit.] Alia ratio est comprobādæ resurrectionis quàm mortis & sepulturæ Christi, quæ non modo scripturis, sed & ipso manifesto facto comprobantur. Mors & sepultura illius non egent testificatione, qua mortuus & sepultus comprobetur: sed satis testimonij habent ex scripturis propheticis, quod sic Christum mori ac sepeliri oportuerit. Resurrectionis uero comprobatio non pendet à solis scripturis, quibus prædictum sit, resurrecturum à mortuis Christū, sed requiritur, ut resurrexisse comprobetur. Neque enim manifesta fuit omnibus illius resurrectio, sed paucis tantum quos habuit discipulos ac fideles. Quare de morte ac sepultura illius non adduxit testes, quibus sit in cruce mori, ac postea sepeliri uisus, adduxit uero qui bus post resurrectionem rediuiuus apparuerit. Poterat enim obijci, etsi scripturæ de Christo prædixerint, quod sit à mortuis resurrectu rus: haud tamen constare, quod Iesus ille à mortuis resurrexerit, ut inde Christum eum esse, ac scripturas ad ipsum pertinere comprobetur. Citat itaque testes resurrectionis eius, dicens:
units.tr: "And that he appeared to Cephas," he says. The proof of the resurrection is a different matter from the proof of Christ's death and burial. These are confirmed not only by the Scriptures but also by the plain fact itself. His death and burial need no testimony to show that he died and was buried; they have sufficient witness in the prophetic Scriptures, which foretold that Christ had to die and be buried in this way. But the proof of the resurrection does not depend on the Scriptures alone, which foretold that Christ would rise from the dead; it must also be shown that he did rise. For his resurrection was not manifest to everyone, but only to the few disciples and believers he had. Therefore, concerning his death and burial he did not bring forward witnesses who saw him die on the cross and afterwards buried; but he brings forward those to whom he appeared alive after the resurrection. For it could be objected that, although the Scriptures foretold that Christ would rise from the dead, it is not certain that this Jesus rose from the dead, so that it might be proved from this that he is the Christ and that the Scriptures pertain to him. He therefore cites witnesses of his resurrection, saying:

units.la: ET quod uisus sit Cephæ, &c.] Sexuisiones rediuiui ex mortuis Christi recitat, non quòd nō sit sepius post resurrectione uisus, sed quod hæ ad faciendam resurrectionis fidem sufficiant. Cum primis uisus erat Mariæ Magdalenæ ac reliquis mulierculis, eas tamè apparitiones non citat, ne testimonio mulierculařum in causa tam magna niti uideatur. Quare non dicit: & quod nunciatum sit Cephæ à mulieribus, quod resurrexerit, sicuti mandatum fuerat ab angelo: Ite & dicite Petro, &c. neque memorat uacuum esse sepulcrum à Petro uisum, sed quod certius est, quod ipse dominus uisus sit Petro. In historijs quatuor Euangelistarum septem apparitiones domini, quibus post resurrectionem fidelibus suis apparuit, recitantur, quarum prima facta est mulieribus à uisitatione sepulcri in urbe redeuntibus: secunda Mariæ Magdalenæ separatim in ipso loco sepulcri: tertia Petro, qua de Lucæ ultimo, cuius hic ab Apostolo sit mentio: quarta duobus discipulis euntibus in Emaus: quinta decem apostolis; Thoma absente. Et hæ apparitiones factę sunt in ipso resurrectionis die. Sexta undecim apostolis, Thoma uidelicet præsente: septima ad lacum Tiberiadis piscantibus Petro, Thomæ, Nathanaeli, filijs Zebedæi, & duobus alijs discipulis. His apparitionibus potest adijci octaua, quæ in ipso est ascensionis die facta, qua de Act.1.legitur. Non quod illa sit numero octaua, cum quædam hic à Paulo recitatæ, & multæ aliæ nō scriptæ, præcesserint, quibus suis dominus per dies quadraginta loquens de regno Dei, cum in Iudæa tum in Galilæa frequenter apparuit: sed quod ex ijs quæ ab Euangelistis conscriptæ sunt, octaua reperiatur.
units.tr: "And that he appeared to Cephas," etc. He recounts six appearances of Christ alive from the dead, not because he did not appear more often after the resurrection, but because these are enough to produce faith in the resurrection. He had first appeared to Mary Magdalene and the other women, yet he does not cite those appearances, so that the matter should not seem to rest on the testimony of women in so great a cause. Therefore he does not say, "and that it was announced to Cephas by the women that he had risen, as the angel had commanded: Go and tell Peter, etc."; nor does he mention that Peter saw the empty tomb, but what is more certain: that the Lord himself appeared to Peter. In the histories of the four Evangelists, seven appearances of the Lord, by which he appeared to his faithful after the resurrection, are recounted. The first was to the women returning to the city from visiting the tomb; the second was to Mary Magdalene alone at the very place of the tomb; the third was to Peter, which is recorded in the last chapter of Luke, and of which the apostle here makes mention; the fourth was to two disciples going to Emmaus; the fifth was to the ten apostles, Thomas being absent. These appearances took place on the very day of the resurrection. The sixth was to the eleven apostles, with Thomas present; the seventh was to them fishing at the lake of Tiberias, with Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee and two other disciples. To these appearances an eighth may be added, which took place on the very day of the ascension, of which we read in Acts 1. Not that it is the eighth in number, since several recounted here by Paul, and many others not written down, came earlier, when the Lord, speaking for forty days about the kingdom of God, appeared often both in Judea and in Galilee; but that among those written down by the Evangelists it is found to be the eighth.

units.la: Quod autem Apostolus eam quę Petro contigit, primo loco recitat, propterea factum est; quod illa ex ijs quæ post mulieres factæ sunt, uiris discipulis & apostolis prima fuit, quod nō caret ratione. Volebat enim hoc pacto dominus tristisimum Apostoli sui animum singulari studio erigere, ne se propter trinam negationem neglectum iri iudicaret.
units.tr: Why the Apostle mentions the appearance to Peter first has a reason: it was the first of those that took place after the women, to the men, the disciples and apostles, and this is not without reason. For in this way the Lord wished to raise the deeply saddened spirit of his Apostle with particular care, so that Peter would not judge himself neglected because of his threefold denial.

units.la: Cogitet autem hic pius lector, quantus sit Apostolici pectoris candor. Quamuis uidisset Petrum cum nonnullis alijs haud recto pede ingredi ad ueritatem Euangelij, ideoq; illum coram omnibus reprehendisset. Gal.2.deinde nomine & existimatione illius nonnullos contra syncerum Euangelij doctrinam, & contrà se abuti cerneret: haud tamendisimulauit hac illius gloriam, sed candide primo loco memorauit, quod uisus sit illi dominus. Faciebat enim hoc ad gloriam Christi, & resurrectionis illius confirmationem.
units.tr: Let the pious reader consider here how great the candour of the Apostle's heart is. Although Paul had seen Peter, with some others, not walking straight toward the truth of the Gospel, and had therefore rebuked him before everyone (Gal. 2), and although he saw that some were using Peter's name and reputation against the pure doctrine of the Gospel and against Paul himself, he nevertheless did not conceal Peter's honour, but openly mentioned first that the Lord had appeared to him. For this served the glory of Christ and the confirmation of his resurrection.

units.la: DEINDE, inquit, duodecim illis.] Vulgata habet, & post hoc undecim. Sic legit & Ambros. & sic habet Comentarij Hiero. adscripti. Verū Græca cōstāter habet duodecim. Sed ibi quæritur, quomodo uisus sit duodecim, cū Iudah è medio sublato, esset dūtaxat undecim, donec accederet Matthias, qui autē post ascen​sionem demum in locū Iudæ electus numerū duodenariū denuo cōpleuit. Chrysost. sentit hanc uisionem demum esse post ascensionem factā, idq; in gratiam Matthiæ duodecimi apostoli. Mihi uero non apparet necessarium esse, ut sic sentiamus. Primū enim Matthias ille iam antea uiderat dominum rediuiuum ex mortuis, ut non esset illi opus separata post ascensionem uisione. Sic enim habent uerba Petri Act 1. Oportet igitur ut ex ijs uiris qui nobiscum uersati sunt toto tempore, quo dominus Iesus perpetuam uitę consuetudinem egit nobiscū, exorsus à baptismo Ioannis ad eum usq; diem, quo receptus est à nobis, unus quispiam constituatur, qui sit unà nobiscum testis resurrectionis eius. Et statuerūt duos, Iosephū, qui uocatur Barsabas, q cognominatus est iustus, & Mathiam, &c. Ob eam itaq; causam electus fuit Mathias, quod asiduus fuerat sectator Christi, & in comitatu illius persistens uiderat ipsum etiam post resurrectionem cum alijs discipulis & apostolis, usq; ad diem ascensionis, quo cum ipsis esset testis resurrectionis eius. Quare non erat ratio ut singulari uisione post ascensionem demum de resurrectione domini instrueretur. Deinde, non est præter morem receptum, ut uel undecim apostoli, uel decem uel nouem propter numerū duodenariū, quo fuerant initio electi à domino, duodecim uocentur. Cum Romæ olim, & hodie quoque in nonnullis Imp. ciuitatibus, tredecemuiri con-uenirent, nemo ita ineptus erat, ut cum dicere tur, cōuenisse tredecemuiros, recte id dici negaret, si unus & alter defuisset. Sunt hæc minuta quidem, uerum ad hoc facientia, ut Ieftio Græca non ita facile reprobanda uideatur.
units.tr: "Then," he says, "to the twelve." The Vulgate has "and after this to the eleven," as Ambrose also read, and as the commentary of Jerome attached to it has it. But the Greek consistently has "twelve." Here, however, the question is how he appeared to the twelve when, Judas having been removed, there were only eleven until Matthias came, who was chosen only after the ascension to complete the number of twelve. Chrysostom thinks this appearance took place after the ascension, for the sake of Matthias, the twelfth apostle. But it does not seem necessary to me that we should think so. First, Matthias had already seen the Lord risen from the dead, so there was no need for a separate appearance after the ascension. For this is what Peter's words in Acts 1 say: "It is necessary, therefore, that of those men who have been with us all the time the Lord Jesus lived his life among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day on which he was taken up from us, one should be chosen who, together with us, is a witness of his resurrection. And they put forward two, Joseph, who is called Barsabas and was surnamed Justus, and Matthias, etc." Matthias was therefore chosen for this reason: he had been a constant follower of Christ, and, remaining in his company, had also seen him after the resurrection, together with the other disciples and apostles, up to the day of the ascension, when he was with them as a witness of his resurrection. So there was no reason for him to be instructed about the Lord's resurrection by a special appearance after the ascension. Next, it is not contrary to accepted usage that the eleven apostles, or ten, or nine, should be called "the twelve," on account of the number twelve to which they had originally been chosen by the Lord. In Rome formerly, and today also in some free cities, the thirteen-men (tredecemviri) used to assemble, and no one was so foolish as to deny that it was correctly said that the thirteen-men had assembled even if one or two were absent. These are small points indeed, but they serve to show that the Greek reading should not be easily rejected.

units.la: POSTEA, inquit, uisus sit plus q quingentis fratribus simul. Voces istæ ἐφάπαξ, ἐπὶ ... quas repetit, &c. non sic sunt accipiedæ, quasi ordinem apparitionum Christi constáter exprimant: sed simpliciter illis usus est Apostolus, memorans uisiones quasdam dñi, quem admodum scribenti occurrebant. Apparet autem uisionem hac factam esse in Galilæa. Nam illo discipulos & fideles suos colligi post resurrectionem uoluit. Sic dicebant angeli: Præcedet uos in Galilæam, ibi eum uidebitis. Chrysostomus aliorum sententias adfert. Quidam, inquit, illud ... idem esse uolunt, quod ... id est, superne ex cœlis, quasi non in terra ingrediens illis, sed in aëre supra capita ipsorum apparuerit, ut non modo resurrectioni suæ, sed & ascésioni fidem faceret. Quidam uero idem esse uolunt, quod pluribus quàm quingétis fratribus. Et hic posterior sensus recte est ab interpretibus reddi-tus. De hac uisione nulla est mentio in reliquis scripturis. Quare Ambrosius hic annotat, dicere hoc Apostolum sua fide.
units.tr: "Afterwards," he says, "he appeared to more than five hundred brethren at once." The words "at once" [ἐφάπαξ] and the others he repeats should not be taken as if they exactly set out the order of Christ's appearances. The Apostle simply used them, recalling certain appearances of the Lord as they came to his mind while he wrote. It appears that this vision took place in Galilee, for the Lord wished his disciples and faithful to be gathered there after the resurrection. So the angels said: "He will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him." Chrysostom brings forward the opinions of others. Some, he says, want the phrase to mean "from above," that is, from heaven, as if he appeared to them not walking on the ground but in the air above their heads, so as to give confirmation not only of his resurrection but also of his ascension. Others want it to mean the same as "to more than five hundred brethren," and this latter sense has been rightly rendered by the translators. Nothing about this vision is mentioned in the other Scriptures. Hence Ambrose here notes that the Apostle says this on his own faith.

units.la: Puto autem uisionem hac factam esse cum in unum esset multitudo illa quingentorum fidelium congregata. Nō enim simpliciter di-
units.tr: I think, however, that this vision took place when that multitude of five hundred faithful had been gathered together into one place. For he does not simply say

units.la: cit: postea uisus est plus quàm quingentis fratribus, sed addit ἐφάπαξ, id est, simul, uel semel, Germanicè, Vff ein mal, una uidelicet uisione. Sic animatus est dominus, ut procliuis sit ad inuisendum eos qui suo nomine congregātur.
units.tr: "he was seen by more than five hundred brethren," but adds "at once" [ἐφάπαξ], that is, all together, or once; in German, "uff ein mal," namely in one vision. Thus the Lord is so inclined to appear to those who gather in his name.

units.la: EX quibus plures, inquit, manent ad hunc usque diem.] Memorat hoc, quo plus fidei distis suis conciliet. Apparet autem epistolam hanc diu esse post dominicam resurrectionem scriptam. Alioqui non fuisset ratio commemorandi, quod ad eum usque diem quo hæc scribebat, plures adhuc de quingentis illis fratribus superessent. Poterat dicere, ex quibus multi sunt qui hac de re testari possunt. Verū quoniam multum temporis effluxerit, utitur uerbo manendi, dicēs: Ex quibus plures manent ad hunc usque diem. Non est autem sine singulari consilio Dei factum, quod plures ex testibus resurrectioīs Christi in multos annos perdurarunt in hac uita, quo uidelicet ad confirmationem credentium diutius de apparitionibus Christi testarentur.
units.tr: "Of whom," he says, "many remain until this day." He mentions this to lend more faith to his account. It appears that this letter was written long after the Lord's resurrection. Otherwise there would have been no reason to mention that many of those five hundred brethren were still alive up to the day on which he was writing. He could have said: "of whom there are many who can testify about this matter." But since much time has passed, he uses the word "remain": "of whom many remain until this day." Nor was it without the singular counsel of God that many witnesses of Christ's resurrection lived on for many years in this life, so that they might testify for longer about Christ's appearances, for the confirmation of believers.

units.la: QVIDAM autē & obdormierunt, inquit.] Quoniam non poterat dicere quingentos illos adhuc superesse omnes, posseq; de apparitione domini testari: ideoq; dixit, ex quibus plures manent ad hunc usq; diem, consequens erat nonnullos ex illis uel à fide Christi defecisse, uel in domino obdormiuisse.
units.tr: "But some have also fallen asleep," he says. Since he could not say that all those five hundred were still alive and able to testify about the Lord's appearance, he said "of whom many remain until this day." It follows that some of them had either fallen away from faith in Christ or had fallen asleep in the Lord.

units.la: Vide autem q competenter usurparit uerbum obdormiscendi, in materia hac qua de re surrectione mortuorum est disputaturus. Significat enim mortem corporis non esse mortem, sed obdormitionem, propter futuram si licet resurrectionem. Sic usus est conuenienter hoc uerbo & Matthæus cap. 27. dicēs: Multa corpora eorum sanctorū qui obdormierant surrexerūt. Quemadmodum & Christus Ioan. 11. de Lazaro mortuo, quē die quarto excitaturus erat: Lazarus, inqt, amicus noster dormit.
units.tr: Notice how fittingly he uses the word "fall asleep" in a matter about which he is going to argue the resurrection of the dead. For it signifies that the death of the body is not death but a falling asleep, on account of the resurrection that is to come. Matthew too uses the word suitably in chapter 27: "Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose." So too Christ, in John 11, about Lazarus dead, whom he was about to raise on the fourth day: "Our friend Lazarus sleeps," he says.

units.la: DEINDE, uisus sit, inquit, Iacobo.] Cum duo fuerint Iacobi inter apostolos, Zebedæi unus, frater Ioannis, & Alphæi alter, & præterea adijciant tertium, cognomento Iustum, quem uocant fratrem domini, eò quod sit filius Mariæ, sororis matris domini, & constituunt episcopum Hierosolymorum: incertum est quem ex his intelligat hic Apostolus. Chrysostomus exponit de tertio. Nec de hac uisione quicquam habent Euangelistæ, quare & illam fide posuit.
units.tr: "Then," he says, "he appeared to James." There were two Jameses among the apostles, one the son of Zebedee, brother of John, and the other the son of Alphaeus. Besides these they add a third, surnamed the Just, whom they call the brother of the Lord, because he was the son of Mary, the sister of the Lord's mother, and they make him bishop of Jerusalem. It is uncertain which of these the Apostle means here. Chrysostom explains it of the third. The Evangelists say nothing about this appearance, so Paul also set it down on trust.

units.la: POST, inquit, apostolis omnibus.] Cum supra dixerit, dominum uisum esse duodecim, utiq; apostolis: consequens est, ut cum hic dicit, post apostolis omnibus, non esse de duodecim tantū intelligēdum. Ergo præter illos & alij fuerunt apostoli. Apparet intelligēdum esse de septuaginta discipulis, quos dominus elegisse, binosq; ac binos ante faciē suam misisse legitur, ob quam causam recte & ipsi uocari possunt apostoli, id est, missi.
units.tr: "After," he says, "all the apostles." Since above he said the Lord was seen by the twelve, who were of course apostles, it follows that when he says here "after all the apostles," it must not be understood of the twelve alone. So there were other apostles besides them. It appears this must be understood of the seventy disciples, whom the Lord is read to have chosen and sent before his face, two by two. For this reason they too can rightly be called apostles, that is, those sent.

units.la: Non est aūt præter rationē factum à domino, quod se post resurrectionem manifestauit haud
units.tr: It was not without reason, however, that the Lord showed himself after the resurrection not only to the twelve chosen apostles

units.la: LUC. 10. haud solũ duodecim sele& tioribus apostolis: sed & reliquis, quos ad hoc delegerat, ut & ipsi de se testificarentur in mundo & Euangelium regni prædicaret. Horum omnium fidem non uoluit constare aliorum relatu sed certitudine uisus, quo possent ueraciter dicere, quod uidimus testamur.
units.tr: (Luc. 10.) but also to the rest whom he had appointed for this purpose, so that they too might bear witness to him in the world and preach the Gospel of the kingdom. He did not want the faith of all of these to rest on the report of others, but on the certainty of sight, so that they could truly say: "What we have seen, we testify."

units.la: Alia est certitudo fidei, quæ est ex auditu, per operationem spiritus sancti, & alia quæ est ex ipso rerum gestarum ac prædicedarum uisu. Prior satisfacit simpliciter credentibus, posterior requiritur in illis, qui ad hoc erant destinati, ut de morte, sepultura, resurrectione, & reliquis gestis domini testificarentur in mundo. Quare conueniebat, ut nõ duodecim tantum, sed & reliqui discipuli testes domini futuri de resurrectione illius non crederet alijs; sed ipso domino uiso certam illius caperent experientiam. possentq; dicere, quod uidimus oculis nostris, quod perspeximus, quod manus nostræ contrectauerũt, annũciamus uobis.
units.tr: There is one certainty of faith, which comes from hearing through the working of the Holy Spirit, and another which comes from seeing the things done and foretold themselves. The first is enough for those who simply believe. The second is required of those who were appointed to bear witness in the world to the death, burial, resurrection and the other deeds of the Lord. So it was fitting that the other disciples, who were to be witnesses of the Lord, should not believe about his resurrection on the word of others, but should gain sure experience of it by seeing the Lord himself. Thus they could say: "What we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked upon, what our hands have handled, we proclaim to you."

units.la: POSTREMO uero omnium, inquit, uelut abortiuo, uisus sit & mihi.] Ne dicat quisquã, Citas alios, qui domin̄ post resurrectionem uiderint, deq; illa testari queant. Quid hoc ad te, qui perinde te atque illos uis haberi Apostolum, cum dominum nõ uideris? tandem se quoq; illis cõnumerat, qui non ex aliorum relatu resurrectionem Christi prædicent, sed ex certitudine uisus de illa testificentur. Prædicaui uobis, inquit, resurrexisse Christum ex mortuis, citauiq; huius rei testes, eos uidelicet qui ἀυλοπται fuerunt, non alios tantum, sed & meipsum, qui ipse quoq; dominum uidi. Quando autem uiderit illum, suprà annotauimus initio capitis noni, ubi dicit: An non sum Apostolus? An non sum liber? An nõ Iesum Christum dominum nostrum uidi?
units.tr: "Last of all, as to one born out of due time, he appeared to me also." Lest anyone say: "Others saw the Lord after the resurrection and can bear witness to it, what is that to you, who wish to be regarded as an apostle just as they are, when you have not seen the Lord?" Paul counts himself among those who bear witness to the resurrection of Christ not from the report of others but from the certainty of sight. "I have preached to you," he says, "that Christ rose from the dead, and I have cited as witnesses of this thing those who were eyewitnesses [αὐτόπται], not only others but also myself, who also saw the Lord himself." When he saw him, we noted above at the beginning of chapter nine, where he says: "Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?"

units.la: POSTREMO uero omnium, inquit, uisus est & mihi.] Intellige post eos omnes, quos recensuit, quibus uisus est dominus post resurrectionē, ut de illa certo testificari possent. Nam ipse dominũ haud cum illis ante, sed aliquanto post ascensionem uidit. Alias, dubio procul, etiam post Paulum nonnullis alijs apparuit dominus.
units.tr: "Last of all, he appeared to me also." Understand: after all those whom he has enumerated, to whom the Lord appeared after the resurrection, so that they could testify to it with certainty. For Paul did not see the Lord with them before, but some time after the ascension. Otherwise, beyond doubt, the Lord also appeared to some others after Paul.

units.la: Magnæ autem modestiæ & humilitatis est, quod non simpliciter dicit, tandem uisus est & mihi: sed, Postremo omnium uelut abortiuo, uisus est & mihi. Vocat se non abortiuum, sed uelut abortiuum, id est, abortiuo aliqua ratione similem. Abortiuus fœtus est, qui non iusto ac maturo partu nascitur, sed nondum maturus, nondum ad consuetum usq; tempus rite fotus, & iustis incrementis auctus modis insolitis ac uiolentis utero materno eijcitur. Græci uocant abortiuum ἐκτρωμα quasi uulnere accepto læsum ἀπὸ τὰ ἐκτιτρώσκω, id est, uulnerando ac lædendo eijcio. Significat eiusmodi se fuisse abortiuo similem, propterea quod post aliorũ apostolorum omnium partum, quos gratia diuinæ prouidetiæ in Christo conceperat, iustis diuinæ institutionis incrementis uelut in ute-
units.tr: It is a sign of great modesty and humility that he does not simply say, "At last he appeared to me also," but, "Last of all, as to one born out of due time, he appeared to me also." He calls himself not an untimely birth but as it were an untimely birth, that is, one in some way like an untimely birth. An abortion [abortivus fœtus] is a child that is born not by a full and mature delivery, but is not yet mature, not yet duly nourished up to the usual time, and, not having been brought to proper growth, is expelled from the mother's womb by unusual and violent means. The Greeks call the abortion [ἐκτρωμα], as if wounded, from [ἐκ τιτρώσκω], that is, I cast out by wounding and injuring. He signifies that he was like such an abortion, because, after the birth of all the other apostles, whom the grace of divine providence had conceived in Christ, he had, as it were, nurtured them in the womb through the proper stages of the divine institution, and had brought them to a due birth.

units.la: ro finxerat & ad iustum partum prouexerat, ipse quasi simul conceptus & utero eiectus in itinere Damasceno cœlitus prostratus, uocatus, & in Apostolatũ emissus fuit. Solent eiusmodi abortiones accidere postremis fœtibus. Huc alludit, cum sibi dominum postremo omnium uelut abortiuo fuisse uisum dicit.
units.tr: He himself, as it were conceived at the same time and cast out of the womb, was thrown down from heaven on the road to Damascus, called, and sent out into the apostolate. Such abortions tend to happen to the last offspring. He alludes to this when he says that the Lord appeared to him last of all, as to one born out of due time.

units.la: Interea tamen cum se similé facit abortiuo respectu præcedentium apostolorũ, unà cum illis eiusdem se uteri, id est, gratiæ Dei unde nati sunt apostoli fœtum esse significat, quemadmodũ abortiuus & immaturus infans eodem patre utero & sanguine prouenit, unde præcedentes ipsum pueri sunt prognati. Sic omnino hic Apostolus licet postremus sit, ac subito insolitoq; modo productus à Christo: eundem tamen habet conuersionis suæ & Apostolatus authorem, quem habent Petrus, Iacobus, Ioannes, & cæteri omnes.
units.tr: Yet at the same time, in making himself like an untimely birth with respect to the earlier apostles, he signifies that, together with them, he is an offspring of the same womb, that is, of the grace of God from which the apostles were born, just as an abortion or immature infant comes forth from the same father, womb and blood, and the earlier children were begotten before it. So in every way this apostle, although he is last and was brought forth suddenly and in an unusual manner by Christ, has nevertheless the same author of his conversion and his apostleship as Peter, James, John and all the rest.

units.la: Sunt qui synagogam Israelis uterum constituant unde nati sunt apostoli, & Paulus hic uelut abortiuus eiectus. Verum hanc illorum sententiam amplectatur qui uelit. Nec apostolorum matura natiuitas, nec Pauli abortio ex synagoga est, sed utraque ex singulari dispensatione gratiæ Christi, per quam illi primũ mox initio Euangelij ad fidem uocati, deinde à uocatione ad tempus usq; Apostolatus obeundi copetentibus sunt instructionibus per ea quæ uiderunt & audierunt foti ac confirmati: ipse uero sero tandem post omnes, subito conuersus, obiter per Ananiam instructus ac baptizatus, ac confestim non expectatis iuste parturitionis mensibus ad Apostolatum est expulsus.
units.tr: There are some who take the synagogue of Israel to be the womb from which the apostles were born, and Paul here cast out as an untimely birth. Let whoever wishes embrace that opinion. Neither the mature birth of the apostles nor Paul's abortion came from the synagogue, but both came from the singular dispensation of the grace of Christ. By this grace the others were called to faith at once at the beginning of the gospel, and then, from their calling until the time of undertaking the apostolate, were nourished and confirmed by the instructions appropriate to them through what they saw and heard. But he himself, late at last after all of them, was suddenly converted, briefly instructed and baptized through Ananias, and immediately, before the months of due labour had been awaited, was driven out into the apostolate.

units.la: Ego enim sum minimus apostolorũ, qui non sum idoneus ut dicar Apostolus, propterea quod persequutus sum ecclesiam Dei, sed gratia Dei sum id quod sum. Et gratia eius quæ profecta est in me non fuit inanis, sed copiosius quàm illi omnes laborauì: non ego tamen, sed gratia Dei, quæ mihi adest.
units.tr: "For I am the least of the apostles, who am not fit to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God; but by the grace of God I am what I am. And his grace which was bestowed on me was not in vain, but I laboured more abundantly than they all; yet not I, but the grace of God which is with me."

units.la: Pertinent ista ad secundum capitis huius membrum, quo Apostolatum suum commendat. Postremi fœtus & abortiui minores præcedentibus esse solent. Cum ergo dixisset, postremo omniũ uelut abortiuo uisus est & mihi, cur se abortiuo similem faciat, exponit, dicens: Ego enim sum minimus apostolorum, id quod non de duodecim tantum, ad quorum numerum referri non potest: sed de omnibus apostolis in genere, quibus dominum uisum esse dixit, intelligendum esse puto. Neque enim ponit se medium inter duodecim apostolos & septuaginta discipulos, ut minorem quidem se duodecim illis, maiorem uero cæteris esse sentiat, sed postponit se apostolis omnibus tam secundarijs quàm primarijs. Nec puto hoc illum dicere tanquam non suo, sed pseudapostolorum sensu, quasi non de seipse, sed illi
units.tr: These words pertain to the second part of this chapter, in which he commends his apostleship. Later and abortive offspring are usually smaller than those before them. Having said, "Last of all, as to one born out of due time, he appeared to me also," he explains why he makes himself like an untimely birth, saying: "For I am the least of the apostles." This cannot be understood of the twelve only, since he cannot be counted among their number, but I think it must be understood of all the apostles in general, to whom he said the Lord appeared. For he does not place himself midway between the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples, so that he would think himself less than the twelve but greater than the rest; rather he places himself after all the apostles, both those of the second rank and those of the first. Nor do I think he says this in his own sense, but in the sense of the false apostles, as if it were not of himself but of them

units.la: sic senserint, eumque contemptum sui repri- mere uelit. Longè diuersus est Apostoli spiri- tus ab illis, qui se omnium minimos ac seruos seruorum Dei uocant, quoniam Christus di- xit: Si quis uult primus esse, erit omnium no- uissimus & omnium minister. &: Qui minor est inter uos omnes, hic maior est. &: Qui ma- ior est in uobis, fiat sicut minor, & qui prin- ceps est, sicut qui ministrat, ut hoc praetextu priores obtineant in ecclesia. Verum consu- luerim fidelibus omnibus, ut sibi non ab humi- litate, sed ab humilitatis specie, hypocrisi ui- delicet fratrum minorum, minimorum, mini- strorum, ac seruorum seruorum Dei uigilan- ter caueant.
units.tr: that they thought so, and he wished to suppress their contempt for himself. The spirit of the apostle is far different from that of those who call themselves the least of all and the servants of the servants of God, since Christ said: "Whoever wishes to be first will be the last of all and the minister of all"; and: "He who is least among you all, he is greatest"; and: "He who is greater among you, let him become as the least, and he who is the leader, as he who serves," so that under this pretext they might not obtain the first places in the Church. Yet I would advise all the faithful to watch carefully against this, not that they be humble, but that they keep away from the appearance of humility, namely the hypocrisy of the lesser brethren, the least, the ministers, and the servants of the servants of God.

units.la: QVI non sum idoneus, inquit, ut dicar Apo- stolus.] Non solum dicit se esse minimum apo- stolorum, sed & indignum, inidoneum, insuf- ficientem, qui dicatur Apostolus. Qui minimus est in manu digitus, recte digitus uo- catur: & satis est suo loco, quem habet postremum in manu. Sic qui minimus est in ordine apostolorum, non est ob id indignus, qui uocetur Apostolus, nisi sit prorsus ad id muneris inidoneus. Quare cum dixisset, ego enim sum minimus apostolorum, quasi non- dum satis expresserit, quàm se infra alios abij- ciat: addit, qui non sum idoneus, ut dicar Apo- stolus. Non dicit, ut sim Apostolus: sed, ut di- car Apostolus, quod minus tamen est, quàm esse apostolū. Etenim q nomine apostoli indi- gnus est, magis est ipso apostolatu indignus.
units.tr: "Who am not fit," he says, "to be called an apostle." He not only says that he is the least of the apostles, but also that he is unworthy, unfit, insufficient to be called an apostle. The least finger on the hand is rightly called a finger, and it is enough that it holds its place as the last on the hand. So he who is least in the order of the apostles is not on that account unworthy to be called an apostle, unless he is altogether unfit for that office. Therefore, having said, "For I am the least of the apostles," as if he had not yet expressed sufficiently how far he casts himself below the others, he adds, "who am not fit to be called an apostle." He does not say, "that I may be an apostle," but "that I may be called an apostle," which is a lesser thing than to be an apostle. For he who is unworthy of the name of apostle is all the more unworthy of the apostleship itself.

units.la: PROPTEREA quod persequutus sum, inquit, ecclesiā Dei.] Exponit quare se inido- neum esse iudicet, qui dicatur Apostolus. Po- test enim dicere quisquam: Ecquid magni est, quod se nomine Apostoli dicit esse indignum, hoc est, inidoneum & insufficientem, cum ne- mo sit piorum, qui se dignum & idoneum ad munus tam arduum esse glorietur, & ipse epi- stola sequeti cap.2. dicat, ἐχει ἀρὸς ταῦτα τὶς ἱκανός; Sciendum igitur est posse hoc, nō sum dignus, trifariam, hoc est, triplici respectu dici. Primū, personae, secundum quam dicebat Saul: Nun- quid non filius Iemini ego sum de minima tribu, &c. Deinde mali meriti, quo respicit hic Apostolus, dicens: non sum dignus qui dicar Apostolus, propterea quod persequutus sum ecclesiam Dei. tertio facultatis insufficientis ad exequutionem muneris suscepti, ad quem respectum pertinet quod dicit: Et ad ista quis idoneus? Et 2. Cor. 3. Non sumus idonei à no- bismipsis ad cogitandum aliquid tanquam ex nobis. Nec priori igitur nec posteriori, sed me- dio respectu dicit se inidoneum & indignum esse, qui uocetur Apostolus, propterea uideli- cet, quod persequutus sit ecclesiā Dei: id quod non potest competere cæteris apostolis, sed singulariter àPaulo dicitur, quo se singulariter præ cæteris omnibus indignum esse fateatur, qui Apostolus dicatur. Omnino autem indi- gnus est persequutor ecclesiæ, qui constitua- tur Apostolus. Quis lupū, hostem ouium, di-
units.tr: "Because," he says, "I persecuted the Church of God." He explains why he judges himself unfit to be called an apostle. For someone may say: "What great thing is it that he says he is unworthy of the name of apostle, that is, unfit and insufficient, when none of the godly boasts that he is worthy and fit for so arduous an office? And in the following epistle, chapter 2, he says, 'Who is sufficient for these things?' [τίς ἱκανὸς πρὸς ταῦτα]." We must therefore recognise that this statement, "I am not worthy," can be made in three respects, that is, with a threefold reference. First, with respect to the person, in which sense Saul said: "Am I not a son of Benjamin, of the least tribe, and so on?" Second, with respect to bad merit, to which this apostle refers when he says: "I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God." Third, with respect to the insufficiency of ability to carry out the office undertaken, to which belongs what he says: "And who is sufficient for these things?" and in 2 Corinthians 3: "We are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves." Therefore he says he is unfit and unworthy to be called an apostle neither in the first nor in the last respect, but in the middle one, namely because he persecuted the Church of God. This cannot apply to the other apostles, but is said of Paul alone, by which he confesses that he alone, above all others, is unworthy to be called an apostle. Indeed, a persecutor of the Church is altogether unworthy to be appointed an apostle. Who would think that a wolf, an enemy of the sheep, is worthy to become the shepherd of the sheep, or an enemy of the kingdom worthy to be made the king's envoy?

units.la: gnum censuerit, qui fiat ouium pastor? & ho- stem regni dignū qui efficiatur regis legatus?
units.tr: Who would think fit to make a wolf, an enemy of the sheep, into the shepherd of the sheep? Or who would think fit to make an enemy of the kingdom into the king's ambassador?

units.la: Obserua uero persequutionis huius genus, qua Saulus persequutus est ecclesiam Dei. Erat Israel adhuc ecclesia Dei, cum ille fideles Christi persequeretur, & erat catholica eccle- sia, & habebat templum, sacerdotium, cultus, ac legem à Deo, habebat patres, habebat pro- missiones, habebat temporis, multorum ui- delicet sæculorum præscriptionem. Eius ec- clesiæ membrum erat Saulus, enutritus in le- ge Dei, & paternarum traditionum uehemens æmulator, magis quàm ipsius coætanei. In- terea Christiani ex Israele nihil uidebantur a- liud moliri quàm schisma ecclesiæ, & sapere nouam hæresim, dignam quæ modis omni- bus extirparetur. Hoc respectu primores ec- clesiæ catholicæ persequebantur omnes eos qui se nouæ sectæ addixerant, & iudicabant se causam habere omniū iustissimā, Deoq; præ- stare obsequium. Huiusmodi zelo perseque- batur Christianos & Saulus, ignorans perse- qui se ecclesiam Dei, quod postea cognouit, & palàm est fassus frequenter. Ergo qui potiores erant in ecclesia catholica persequuti sunt schi smaticam quidem & nouā, at interim Dei ec- clesiam. Videmus itaq; in hac imagine quàm nec nouum sit nec rarum, quod hodie eccle- siam Christi persequuntur ij qui catholicę ec- clesiæ capita uideri uolunt, iactantes nomen ecclesiæ, patres præscriptionem temporis, ca- tholicam consuetudinem, & alia consimilia, quę ecclesia Israelis fratribus suis in Christum credentibus æquè probabiliter obijcere po- tuit ac dicere, Existis ex nobis, quia non estis ex nobis, scinditis ecclesiam Dei, inducitis no- uam doctrinam, contemnitis ordine sacerdo- tij, deficitis à lege & cultu Dei, irritam reddi- tis circumcisionem, fœderis Dei symbolum, uiolatis sabbata: in summa, præuaricamini à Deo, à fide maiorum nostrorum, & ab ecclesia Dei, quare uos merito tanquam schismaticos, defectores, hæreticos & impios persequimur. Quid autē contra hæc omnia habebant Chri- stiani à fratrib. suis catholicis exagitati, quàm unam ueritatem Christi, oraculis ac testimo- nijs scripturarum, multisq; miraculis & por- tentis tanquam diuinæ operationis argumen- tis comprobatam? Hac nitentes in fide Christi perseuerabat, ac propter illam aduersa & pro- bra à carnali ecclesia illata fortiter tolerabant. Hoc se exemplo solentur, quotquot hodie à catholicis propter Euangelicā ueritatem pro- scribuntur, damnantur & neci traduntur.
units.tr: Now observe the kind of persecution by which Saul persecuted the Church of God. Israel was still the Church of God when he persecuted the faithful of Christ. It was the catholic Church, and it had the temple, the priesthood, the worship, and the law from God. It had the fathers, it had the promises, and it had the prescription of time, that is, of many centuries. Saul was a member of this Church, brought up in the law of God and a zealous defender of his fathers' traditions, more so than his contemporaries. Meanwhile the Christians from Israel seemed to be attempting nothing but a schism in the Church and to be spreading a new heresy, one worthy of being rooted out by every means. For this reason the leaders of the catholic Church persecuted all who had attached themselves to the new sect, and they judged that they had the most just of causes and were rendering service to God. Saul too persecuted the Christians with this kind of zeal, not knowing that he was persecuting the Church of God, which he later came to know and often openly confessed. So those who were the most powerful in the catholic Church persecuted a schismatic and new sect, yet in fact the Church of God. We see then from this picture how neither new nor rare it is that today those who wish to be seen as the heads of the catholic Church persecute the Church of Christ, boasting of the name of the Church, of the fathers, of the prescription of time, of catholic custom, and other such things. The Church of Israel could have brought these same charges against its brothers who believed in Christ, with equal plausibility, and could have said: "You have gone out from us, because you were not of us. You split the Church of God, you introduce a new doctrine, you despise the order of the priesthood, you depart from the law and worship of God, you make circumcision void, the sign of God's covenant, you violate the sabbaths. In sum, you transgress against God, against the faith of our ancestors, and against the Church of God. Therefore we rightly persecute you as schismatics, defectors, heretics and impious men." But what did the Christians, harassed by their catholic brothers, have to set against all these things, other than the one truth of Christ, confirmed by the oracles and testimonies of the Scriptures and by many miracles and portents as proofs of divine working? Relying on this, they persevered in the faith of Christ, and on account of it they bravely endured the adversities and reproaches inflicted by the carnal Church. Whoever is today proscribed, condemned and handed over to death by the Catholics on account of the Gospel truth may be comforted by this example.

units.la: Deinde & illud consideremus. Plerunque fit, ut secundum dictum huius Apostoli carna- lis persequatur spiritualem, Cain Habelem, Ismael Isaacum, Esau Iacobum, filij Iacob Iose- phum, &c. & non uiceuerfa spiritualis carna- lem. At hic uidemus persequutorem ecclesiæ de quo nō possumus dicere, quod perinde at- que Cain fuerit ex maligno. Erat enim ex ele- ctis Dei, atq; ex utero matris electus in organum Dei omnium seleētissimum. Ergo admonemur ne mox de quoquam desperemus, ne illis quidem, qui ecclesiam Christi persequuntur: quandoquidem fieri potest, ut faciant hoc electi, donec veritatem Dei ignorates zelo ecclesiæ catholicæ citra scientiā accēsi feruntur.
units.tr: Next let us also consider this. It often happens, according to the saying of this Apostle, that the carnal persecutes the spiritual: Cain persecuted Abel, Ishmael Isaac, Esau Jacob, the sons of Jacob Joseph, and so on; and not the reverse, the spiritual persecuting the carnal. But here we see a persecutor of the Church of whom we cannot say, as we could of Cain, that he was of the evil one. For he was among the elect of God, chosen from his mother's womb as the most select instrument of God. Therefore we are warned not to despair at once of anyone, not even of those who persecute the Church of Christ, since it can happen that the elect do this, while being carried away by zeal for the catholic Church without knowledge, ignorant of the truth of God.

units.la: PROPTEREA, inquit, quod persequuutus sum ecclesiam Dei.] Christianos persequebatur, quos inueniebat, uiros & mulieres, & hic dicit se persequutum esse ecclesiā Dei, quemadmodum & Gal.1. Audistis enim, inquit, conuersationem quondā meam in Iudaismo, quomodo supra modum persequebar ecclesiam Dei, ac depopulabar illam. Ergo qui fideles persequitur, ecclesiam Dei persequitur. Perin de atque corpus persequitur, qui membra corporis, ciuitatem qui ciues, regnum qui filios regni persequitur.
units.tr: "FOR THIS REASON," he says, "because I persecuted the Church of God." He persecuted the Christians whom he found, men and women, and here he says that he persecuted the Church of God, just as in Gal. 1. "You have heard," he says, "of my former conduct in Judaism, how I persecuted the Church of God beyond measure and laid it waste." Therefore whoever persecutes the faithful persecutes the Church of God. Just as one who persecutes the body persecutes its members, and one who persecutes a city persecutes its citizens, and one who persecutes a kingdom persecutes the sons of the kingdom.

units.la: Refert tamē quam ob causam Christianum quis persequatur. Si ob priuatam aliquam iniuriam qua est ab illo læsus, uel ex officio iudicis ac magistratus tāquam fontem ac noxium persequitur, non potest dici persequutor ecclesiæ Dei. Si uero propter fidem ac religionem, quam ille habet cum ecclesia Dei cōmunem, tum rectè persequutor ecclesiæ cēsebitur, quā totam in membris ipsius si posset extinguueret.
units.tr: It makes a difference, however, on what ground someone persecutes a Christian. If he does so on account of some private injury by which he was wronged, or if, in the office of judge or magistrate, he pursues him as a criminal and an offender, he cannot be called a persecutor of the Church of God. But if he does so on account of the faith and religion which the Christian holds in common with the Church of God, then he will rightly be counted a persecutor of the Church, and he would destroy it entirely in its members if he could.

units.la: SED gratia Dei sum, id quod sum.] Humilitati & indignitati suæ subijcit cōmendationem gratiæ Dei, ne quid hinc detrimenti Apostolatui ipsius nascatur. Quàm sese deijcit & humiliat, tam gratiam Dei sibi collatam extollit & amplificat. Sed gratia Dei sum id quod sum, inquit. Quasi dicat: At quamuis sum apostolorum postremus, minimus, uelut abortiuus, & indignus qui dicar Apostolus, sum tamen id quod sum per gratiam Dei in me collatam. Quid erat autem per gratiam Dei? Non modo Apostolus, sed & insignis Apostolus, nullis aliis inferior. Modeste adhuc, non dicit, sed gratia Dei sum Apostolus Christi, nulla in re cæteris minor: sed, gratia Dei sum id quod sum. Ergo quod dignitati suæ tribuere nō potest, tribuit gratiæ Dei, & agnoscit se aliū esse persone ac meriti sui indignitate, & alium per gratiam Dei. Sit nobis omnibus hæc regula, secundum quam discernamus inter id quod sumus naturæ nostræ indignitate & malicia, & quod sumus per Dei gratiā. Natura sumus uani, multis modis corrupti, infirmi, peccatores & filij iræ: gratia uero Dei Christiani, alijs atq; alijs donis Dei ornati, filij Dei, & hæredes uitæ æternæ. Augustin. libro de Ecclesiast. dogmatib. cap.43. locū hunc Apostoli sic contra Pelagianos citat: Si quis sine gratia Dei credentibus, uolentibus, desiderantibus, conantibus, studentibus, petentibus, quærentibus, pulsantibus nobis misericordiam dicit cōferri diuinitus, nō autem ut credamus, uelimus, uel hæc omnia sicut oportet agere ualeamus per infusionē & inspirationē sancti spiritus in nobis fieri cōfitetur, & aut humilitati, aut obedientiæ humanæ subiungit gratiæ adiutorium, nec
units.tr: "But by the grace of God I am what I am." He subjects his own humility and unworthiness to the commendation of God's grace, so that no loss to his apostleship may arise from it. The more he abases and humbles himself, the more he exalts and magnifies the grace of God bestowed on him. "But by the grace of God I am what I am," he says, as if to say: although I am the last and least of the apostles, like a premature birth, and unworthy to be called an apostle, yet I am what I am through the grace of God given to me. But what was it, through the grace of God, that he was? Not only an apostle, but a distinguished apostle, inferior to none. He does not yet say, modestly, "By the grace of God I am an apostle of Christ, in no respect less than the others," but "By the grace of God I am what I am." So what he cannot ascribe to his own dignity, he ascribes to the grace of God, and acknowledges that by the unworthiness of his person and merit he is one thing, and by the grace of God another. Let this be the rule for all of us, by which we distinguish what we are by the unworthiness and wickedness of our nature, and what we are by the grace of God. By nature we are vain, corrupted in many ways, weak, sinners and children of wrath; but by the grace of God we are Christians, adorned with various and diverse gifts of God, sons of God and heirs of eternal life. Augustine, in his book On the Dogmas of the Church, chapter 43, cites this passage of the apostle against the Pelagians thus: "If anyone says that mercy is conferred divinely on those who believe, will, desire, strive, study, ask, seek and knock, without grace, and does not confess that it is brought about in us by the infusion and inspiration of the Holy Spirit, that we may believe, will, and be able to do all these things as we ought, but subjoins the help of grace to humility or to human obedience, [he is wrong]...

units.la: ut obedientes & humiles simus ipsius gratiæ donū esse consentit, resistit Apostolo dicenti: Quid enim habes quod nō accepisti? Et gratia Dei sum id quod sum. Hæc ille. Sane Apostolus gratiā hanc & fidei & Apostolatus nec quę sierat, nec uoluerat, nec desiderauerat, nec petierat. Quare omnino nihil illius libero debetur arbitrio, aut uiribus ac meritis humanis.
units.tr: ...and does not agree that it is a gift of grace itself that we are obedient and humble, he resists the apostle who says, 'For what have you that you did not receive?' and 'By the grace of God I am what I am.' Thus he. Indeed the apostle did not seek, will, desire, or ask for this grace, either of faith or of apostleship. Therefore nothing at all is owed to free will, or to human strength and merits.

units.la: Solenne est episcopis Romanis & alijs illis adhæretibus, ut in bullis suis ac rescriptis gloriētur se esse per gratiā Dei episcopos, archiepiscopos, patriarchas & cardinales, cum uerius sint quod sunt per indignationem Dei, quàm per gratiam. Qui per gratiā Dei constituuntur apostoli, episcopi, & pastores ecclesiarū, donis etiam ad apostolatum, episcopatum & pastoratum necessarijs per eandem gratiam instruuntur, quo posint prodesse ecclesijs. Quibus isti sint modis instructi, & prosint ne ecclesijs uel obsint, me tacente res ipsa clamat.
units.tr: It is customary for the Roman bishops and their adherents to boast in their bulls and rescripts that they are bishops, archbishops, patriarchs and cardinals by the grace of God, when they are more truly what they are through the indignation of God than through his grace. Those who are appointed apostles, bishops and ministers of the churches by the grace of God are also, through the same grace, furnished with the gifts necessary for the apostolate, the episcopate and the ministry, so that they may profit the churches. In what manner these men are equipped, and whether they profit or hinder the churches, the thing itself cries out, though I say nothing.

units.la: ET gratia eius quæ profecta est in me, inquit, nō fuit inanis.] Græcè est, & gratia eius, id est, quæ in me, & subintelligendum est, uel collata est, uel data est: aut ut Erasmus uertit, profecta est. Cōmendat Apostolatū suū ab effectu gratię Dei, quā sibi collatā dicit non fuisse inane, id est sterile & infrugifera. Ego, inquit dñs, elegi uos, ut eatis & fructum adferatis. Fructū adferre, est domino lucrifacere populum, & multos conuertere ad cognitionem ueritatis, quo salui fiant. Significat igitur Paulus prædicationem suam fuisse frugiferam ac plurimos ad fidem conuertisse, cum gratiam à Deo acceptam haud inanem fuisse dicit.
units.tr: "AND HIS GRACE WHICH WAS BESTOWED ON ME," he says, "WAS NOT IN VAIN." In Greek it is "and his grace [καὶ ἡ χάρις αὐτοῦ]", that is, the grace which is in me; and one must understand either "was bestowed" or "was given", or, as Erasmus translates it, "came forth". He commends his apostleship from the effect of God's grace, saying that the grace bestowed on him was not empty, that is, barren and unfruitful. "I have chosen you," says the Lord, "that you should go and bear fruit" (John 15). To bear fruit is to win people for the Lord and to convert many to the knowledge of the truth, so that they may be saved. Paul therefore signifies that his preaching was fruitful and had converted very many to the faith, since he says that the grace he received from God was not in vain.

units.la: Vt id obiter annotem, tres sunt Apostolicæ gratiæ partes. Voco autem Apostolicam gratiam non quā conferat cuiquā Apostolus, sed quam à Deo accipiat. Prima est, qua eligitur, uocatur, & cōstituitur Apostolus. De hac Rom.1. dicit: per quē accepimus gratiā, & Apostolici muneris functione. Et Gal.1. At ubi Deo placuit, qui segregauerat me ab utero matris meæ, & uocauit per gratiam suā, ut reuelaret filiū suū per me, &c. Secunda est, qua donis spiritus instruitur & ornatur, ut munus Apostolicū obire posset. Hanc cōmendat 2. Cor.3. dicens: Sed si ad aliquid idonei sumus, id ex Deo est, qui & idoneos fecit nos ministros Noui testamenti. Vtranq; innuit, cum dicit: Gratia Dei sum id quod sum. Tertia est, qua datur prædicanti ac laboranti Apostolo efficacia incrementi quo multum fructus adferat. Hanc intelligit, cum hic dicit: Et gratia eius quæ in me collata est, inanis non fuit. Et suprà cap.3. Ego plantaui, Apollo rigauit, sed Deus incrementum dedit. Commendat igitur Apostolatum suum in hisce tribus, primum quod sit ex gratia Dei, deinde quod sit donis Apostolicis ornatus, tertiò quod sit non inanis, sed efficax ac uerax Apostolici fructus. Eant Romani apostoli, & apostolicas suas eminentias cum hisce ueri Apostoli notis conferant.
units.tr: To note this in passing, there are three parts to Apostolic grace. I call it Apostolic grace not because an apostle confers it on anyone, but because he receives it from God. The first is that by which a man is chosen, called and appointed an apostle. Paul speaks of this in Rom. 1: "through whom we have received grace and apostleship." And in Gal. 1: "But when it pleased God, who set me apart from my mother's womb and called me by his grace, to reveal his Son in me," and so on. The second is that by which he is furnished and adorned with the gifts of the Spirit, so that he can discharge the apostolic office. He commends this in 2 Cor. 3: "But if we are sufficient for anything, that sufficiency is from God, who also made us sufficient as ministers of the New Testament." He indicates both when he says: "By the grace of God I am what I am." The third is that which is given to an apostle who preaches and labours, so that his work has the power of increase and bears much fruit. He means this when he says here: "And his grace bestowed on me was not in vain." And above, in chapter 3: "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase." He therefore commends his apostleship under these three heads: first, that it comes from the grace of God; second, that it is adorned with apostolic gifts; third, that it is not in vain, but yields effective and true apostolic fruit. Let the Roman apostles go and compare their pre-eminence as apostles with these marks of a true apostle.

units.la: SED copiosius, inquit, q; illi omnes laborauì. raui.] Poterat simpliciter dicere, & gratia eius quæ in me collata est, non fuit inanis, sed effi-cax: nisi abundante ac singulare efficacia gratiæ Dei in Apostolatu suo declarata extollere uo-luisset. Sic dicit: Sed copiosius q; illi omnes la-boraui. Non simpliciter περιστοτερως, id est, abun-dantius: sed, abundantius q; illi omnes. Neque enim abundantius q; coueniebat Apostolatui suo, sed q; cæteri omnes laborauit. Nemo po-test simpliciter abundantius diligere dominū, quantumuis enim diligas illum, supra q; coue-nit diligere non poteris: abundantius uero q; multi alij poteris, quemadmodum Petro non simpliciter dicebat dns: Simon tu me plus di-ligis, sed: Simò, diligis me plus q; hi? Consimili modo nō potuit Paulus abundantius q; coue-niebat in Apostolatu suo laborare, potuit uero per gratiam Dei abundantius quàm cæteri.
units.tr: "But I laboured more abundantly than they all." He could have simply said, "and his grace bestowed on me was not in vain, but effective," unless he wished to extol the abundant and singular efficacy of God's grace declared in his apostleship. So he says: "But I laboured more abundantly than they all." Not simply περισσοτέρως [perissotérōs], that is, "more abundantly," but "more abundantly than they all." For he did not labour more abundantly than was fitting for his apostleship, but more than all the others. No one can simply love the Lord more abundantly; however much you love him, you cannot love him beyond what is fitting. But you can love him more abundantly than many others, just as the Lord did not simply say to Peter, "Simon, you love me more," but "Simon, do you love me more than these?" In the same way Paul could not labour more abundantly than was fitting for his apostleship, but he could labour more abundantly than the others through the grace of God.

units.la: SED copiosius, inquit, quàm illi omnes la-boraui.] Dicendum fuisse uidetur, sed copio-siore fructu attuli, quàm illi omnes. Siquidem non laborando tantum, sed multū fructifican-do declarabatur, quàm non esset in Apostola-tu ipsius gratia Dei inanis. Quare uerbum la-borandi non simpliciter de laboribus suis, sed simul & de fructibus illorum posuit.
units.tr: "But I laboured more abundantly than they all." It seems it should have been said: "but I brought forth more abundant fruit than they all." For it was shown not only by labouring but by bearing much fruit that the grace of God was not vain in his apostleship. Hence he put the verb "to labour" not simply of his labours, but of their fruits as well.

units.la: QVAM illi omnes, inquit.] Quoniam non simpliciter dicit, quàm omnes: sed, quàm illi omnes, ut certos quosdā intelligat, existimant nonnulli intelligēdū esse de pseudapostolis Co-rinthiorum, quasi illorum iactantiā reprimere uoluerit, qua se supra ipsum extollebant, & A-postolatum suum floccifaciebant. Vt sit sen-sus: Glorientur contra me uestri illi sapientes ac doctores, & Apostolatum meum contem-nant quantum uolunt, ego licet postremus & minimus Apostolorum, & olim ecclesiæ Dei perseguutor, ideoq; indignus qui dicar Apo-stolus, in Apostolatu meo per gratiam Dei in me collatam, plus laboraui quàm ipsi omnes, idque apud uos, ubi fundamentum structuræ Dei posui. Quantulum est, quod illi omnes præstät apud uos, si laboribus meis coferatur?
units.tr: "Than they all," he says. Since he does not simply say "than all," but "than they all," some think it must be understood of certain people, namely the false apostles of the Corinthians. As if he wished to check their boasting, by which they exalted themselves above him and held his apostleship in low esteem. The sense would be: "Let your wise men and teachers boast against me and despise my apostleship as much as they like. I, though the least and last of the apostles, and formerly a persecutor of the Church of God, and therefore unworthy to be called an apostle, have through the grace of God bestowed on me laboured more than all of them in my apostleship, and this among you, where I laid the foundation of God's building. How little is what all those men have done among you, if it is compared with my labours?"

units.la: Licet hic sensus nihil habeat incommodi, existimo tamen coueniētius esse, ut quod di-cit, quàm illi omnes, referamus ad apostolos, nō duodecim tantum, sed & reliquos omnes, quorum se minimum esse dixit: ut quorum se dixit esse minimum propter meriti indignita-tem, & postremam uocationem, supra horum omnium labores Apostolatum suum extollat, propter fructuum copiam ac præstātiam. Nec debet arrogantię tribui, quod non dicit, quàm nonnulli, uel, quàm multi ex illis: sed, quàm illi omnes. Etenim reuera sic habet. Cursus A-postolatus Pauli tam est amplus, tantorumq; successuum, ut inde à Hierosolymis & regioni-bus circumiacentibus ad Illyricum usque im-pleuerit Euangelium Christi (qua de re si cui iubet, inspiciat peregrinationem Pauli ab E-rasmo congestam) ideoq; merito præferatur cæteris omnibus. Quod sane non facit con-tendens contra ipsos apostolos, sed impro-
units.tr: Although this sense has no inconvenience, I think it more fitting to refer "than they all" to the apostles, not only the twelve but all the rest, of whom he said he was the least. Thus, since he calls himself the least of all of them on account of his unworthiness and his late calling, he exalts his apostleship above the labours of all of them, on account of the abundance and excellence of his fruits. Nor should it be ascribed to arrogance that he does not say "than some" or "than many of them," but "than they all." For indeed it is so. Paul's course of apostleship was so wide, and so great in its successes, that from Jerusalem and the surrounding regions as far as Illyricum he filled the world with the gospel of Christ (on which matter, if anyone wishes, let him look at the journeys of Paul gathered by Erasmus). Therefore he is rightly preferred to all the others. He does not do this in order to contend against the apostles themselves, but to repel the malice of those who tried to make his apostleship cheap and contemptible by pretending to disparage the other apostles, especially Peter, James and John.

units.la: bitatem eorum retundens, qui Apostolatum ipsius prætextu cæterorum apostolorū, præ-cipue Petri, Iacobi & Ioannis, uilem & abie-ctum reddere moliebantur. Non erat propositum ipsius apostolos reliquos reddere con-temptibiles, sed huc adigebatur per maleuo-lentiam pseudapostolorum, ut quod uerum erat pro Apostolatus sui defensione obijce-ret. Sane constat Petrum, Iacobū & Ioannem diu, hoc est, annos plus minus decé ac septem post conuersionem Pauli manssisse Hierosoly-mis, cum interea circumiacentes ille regiones Arabiam, Syriam & Ciliciam Euangelio Dei impleret. Et cum post annos decem ac septem Hierosolymam denuo uenisset, sic inter ipsos conuenit, ut ipse cum Barnaba in Gentes, ipsi uero in circumcisionem Apostolatu fungeren-tur. Vnde facile colligitur, tā esse labores Pau-li copiosiores laboribus istorū apostolorum, quàm tam multæ Gentium regiones, quibus ille Christū prædicauit, unam Iudæorū Gen-tem superant. Et præterea, sic illi sese in apostolatu suo gesserunt, ut reprehensibiles essent, quod non recto pede incederent ad ueritatem Euangelij. Quare & Petrum coram omnibus reprehendit, dicens: Si tu cum sis Iudæus, gen-tiliter uiuis, & non Iudaice, cur Gentes cogis Iudaissare? Igitur hac quoque ratione merito labores Pauli, laboribus reliquorum apostolo-rum præferūtur, quod dexterius Euangelium Christi quàm ipsi propagauit.
units.tr: It was not his purpose to make the other apostles contemptible, but he was driven to this by the malice of the false apostles, so that he might bring forward what was true in defence of his own apostleship. It is certain that Peter, James and John remained in Jerusalem for a long time, that is, about seventeen years after Paul's conversion, while in the meantime he was filling the surrounding regions, Arabia, Syria and Cilicia, with the gospel of God. And when, after seventeen years, he came again to Jerusalem, they agreed among themselves that he and Barnabas should labour among the Gentiles, but they among the circumcision. From this it is easily gathered that Paul's labours were as much more abundant than the labours of those apostles as the many regions of the Gentiles, to which he preached Christ, surpass the one nation of the Jews. Moreover, those men so conducted themselves in their apostleship that they were blameworthy, because they were not walking straight towards the truth of the gospel. Therefore he also rebuked Peter before everyone, saying: "If you, though a Jew, live as the Gentiles do and not as the Jews, why do you compel the Gentiles to live as Jews?" So for this reason too Paul's labours are rightly preferred to the labours of the other apostles, because he spread the gospel of Christ more effectively than they did.

units.la: De reliquis apostolis, Andrea, Philippo, Bartholomæo, Thoma, Matthæo, Iuda fratre Iacobi, & Simone Zelota, denique de septua-ginta discipulis, illorumq; omnium labori-bus, quid sentiendum sit certo, non uideo. Quamuis credibile est, non fuisse eos ociosos, sed prædicasse alios in Perfia, alios in India, a-lios in Mesopotamia, alios in Ægypto, alios in Aphrica: probabile tamen est tantū lucis, tan-tum successus, tantumq; dexteritatis non suis-se in illorum omnium, quantum in unius Pau-li apostolatu. Sane quicquid sit de regionibus illis, quibus cæteri apostoli Christū prædica-rūt, totus ille tractatus à Hierosolymis in Oc-cidentem usq; laboribus Pauli debet, quod ad cognitionem & fidem Christi peruenit.
units.tr: Concerning the other apostles, Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, Matthew, Jude the brother of James, and Simon the Zealot, and finally the seventy disciples, and what should be thought of all their labours, I cannot see with certainty. Although it is credible that they were not idle, but that some preached in Persia, some in India, some in Mesopotamia, some in Egypt, and some in Africa, yet it is probable that there was not as much light, as much success, and as much effectiveness in all of theirs as in the apostleship of Paul alone. Certainly, whatever may be said of those regions in which the other apostles preached Christ, that whole course from Jerusalem westward to the West owes to the labours of Paul that it came to the knowledge and faith of Christ.

units.la: NON ego tamē, sed gratia Dei, inquit, quæ mihi adest.] Quoniam nō dixit: Et gratia eius quæ collata est in me, non fuit inanis, sed co-piosius per me quàm per illos omnes labora-uit: sed, copiosius quàm illi omnes laboraui, ne sibi hoc tribuere uideatur, particulam hanc correctionis loco adijcit, dicens: Non ego ta-mē, sed gratia Dei quæ mihi adest, quibus om-nino uerbis totius Apostolatus sui labores ac fructus uni gratiæ Dei tribuit, quam idcirco tertio nominat, ne quid sibi arrogare uidea-tur. Quare friuolum est & præter mentem A-poftoli, quod Eccius in Locis suis, de libero arbitrio, ex his uerbis probare molitur, libe-rum hominis arbitrium, & gratiam Dei ope-rari simul, propterea quod in uulgata uersio-ne est, ne est: non ego autem, sed gratia Dei mecum. Nó est in Græco, & ego, & gratia Dei: sed, Nõ ego, sed gratia Dei: neq; ἐκ ἰγὼ ἀ̓ ἰ̔, id est, nó ego uero solus, sed simpliciter, ἐκ ἰγὼ ἀ̓, id est, non ego autem, sed gratia Dei. Sic loquendo non facit se socium, sed organum gratiæ Dei, cui uni tribuit omnia. Quemadmodum & Christus cum dicit, Nõ uos estis qui loquimini, sed spiritus patris uestri loquetur in uobis: nó coniungit liberum arbitrum & spiritum sanctum, sed omnem sapiétiam ad respondendū pro Euangelio tribuit spiritu sancto. Deinde, non est in Græco, gratiæ Dei mecum: sed, gratia Dei ἐ̔ ἰ̔, id est, gratia Dei quæ mecum est.
units.tr: "Not I, however, but the grace of God that is with me." Since he did not say: "and his grace bestowed on me was not in vain, but he laboured through me more than through all of them," but, "I laboured more than all of them," lest he seem to ascribe this to himself, he adds this little particle by way of correction, saying: "Not I, however, but the grace of God which is with me." By these words he attributes all the labours and fruits of his whole apostleship to the grace of God alone, and he names it third for this reason, lest he seem to claim anything for himself. Therefore it is trivial, and contrary to the mind of the apostle, that Eck in his Loci, on free will, labours to prove from these words that the free will of man and the grace of God work together, because in the Vulgate version it reads: "not I, but the grace of God with me." It is not in the Greek: "and I, and the grace of God," but "Not I, but the grace of God." Neither is it "οὐκ ἐγὼ μόνος" [ouk egō monos], that is, "not I alone," but simply "οὐκ ἐγώ δέ" [ouk egō de], that is, "not I, but the grace of God." Speaking thus, he does not make himself a partner, but an instrument of the grace of God, to which alone he attributes everything. Just as Christ, when he says, "It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father will speak in you," does not join free will and the Holy Spirit, but ascribes all wisdom for answering on behalf of the gospel to the Holy Spirit. Further, it is not in the Greek "the grace of God with me," but "the grace of God ἡ σὺν ἐμοί" [hē syn emoi], that is, "the grace of God which is with me."

units.la: Aliud est, si dicas, non ego laboraui, sed gratia Dei quæ mecum est: & aliud, si dicas non ego tantum laboraui, sed gratia Dei mecum. Sic enim illud σὺν ἰ̔, id est, mecum referretur ad uerbum laboraui, & tribueretur pars laboris Paulo & pars gratiæ. Verum Paulus nõ dicit de gratia quod secū laboraverit, sed quod secum existens ipsa laboraverit ac perfecerit omnia. Ipsam gratiam Dei specificat dicens, quæ est mecum, uel quæ mihi adest, non labores inter se, & ipsam diuidit. Videmus hic quid faciat interpretis uel scribarum neglectus. Vnius enim articuli, ἐ, omisso ansam præbet sophistis, ut mentem uerborum Apostoli ad patrocinium falsi dogmatis statuendum pertuertant.
units.tr: It makes a difference whether you say, "I did not labour, but the grace of God which is with me," or say, "I did not labour only, but the grace of God with me." For in the second form the phrase "with me" [σὺν ἐμοί], that is, "with me," would refer to the verb "I laboured," and a share of the labour would be assigned to Paul and a share to grace. But Paul does not say that he laboured together with grace. He says that grace, being present with him, itself laboured and accomplished all things. He specifies the grace of God by saying "which is with me," or "which is present to me," and does not set the labours of the two side by side, and so he does not divide them. Here we see what the carelessness of translators or copyists can do. By the omission of a single article, [ἡ], they give the sophists an opening to twist the meaning of the apostle's words so as to establish support for a false doctrine.

units.la: SIVE igitur ego, siue illi sic prædicamus, & sic credidistis.] Quomodo? Quod, uidelicet mortuus sit Christus, secundum scripturas, quodq; sepultus sit & resurrexerit secundum scripturas, & quod suis sit apostolis & discipulis post resurrectionem uisus. Sic, inquit, prædicamus, & sic credidistis. Quid est autem quod non dicit: Sic igitur euangelizaui uobis, & sic credidistis, ut ingressum sermonis huius seruet. Neq; enim in principio dixit, Notū uobis facio Euangelium, quod siue ego, siue cæteri apostoli euangelizamus: sed, quod euangeliza ui uobis. Quoniam incidit in mentionem reliquorum apostolorum, quorum existimatione pseudapostoli contra Apostolatum ipsius abutebatur, sic loqui uoluit: Siue igitur ego, siue illi sic prædicamus, ut conatus illorum reprimat, alleratque doctrinæ huius de morte, sepultura & resurrectione Christi conformitatem, quæ seruetur tam in sua quàm cæterorum apostolorum prædicatione. Vt sit sensus: Itaq; siue ego prædicem, siue illi, quos nonnulli tantopere iactant, sic cöcorditer prædicamus, nihil hic est discrepantiæ. Quare qui meam doctrinam reijcit, simul & reliquorum apostolorum omnium eadem opera reijcit. Seruit hoc dicens argumento quod est contra negatores resurrectionis illaturus.
units.tr: "Whether therefore I or they, so we preach, and so you believed." In what way? That Christ died according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried and rose again according to the Scriptures, and that after his resurrection he appeared to his apostles and disciples. "So we preach," he says, "and so you believed." But why does he not say, "So I preached the gospel to you, and so you believed," as would keep the opening of his discourse consistent? For at the beginning he did not say, "I make known to you the gospel which both I and the other apostles preach," but "which I preached to you." Since he has come to mention the rest of the apostles, whose standing the false apostles were using against his own apostleship, he wished to speak in this way: "Whether therefore I or they, so we preach." By this he checks their attempts and points out that the teaching about the death, burial and resurrection of Christ agrees, and that this agreement is kept in his own preaching and in that of the other apostles. The sense is this: whether I preach, or they, whom some boast of so much, we preach in the same way, and there is no disagreement here. So whoever rejects my teaching at the same time rejects the teaching of all the other apostles. He uses this statement as an argument he is about to bring against those who deny the resurrection.

units.la: Cogitemus hic de consensu doctrinæ Apostolicæ, quàm sit ille ualidus ad destruenda pseudapostolorum dogmata, dum nõ permittit illis ullum patrocinium ex cuiusquam apostoli authoritate. Siue Petrus, siue Paulus, siue Ioannes, eundem Christum, & eandem salutis uiam prædicarunt.
units.tr: Let us consider here the agreement of apostolic teaching, how strong it is for overthrowing the doctrines of the false apostles, since it allows them no support from the authority of any single apostle. Whether Peter, or Paul, or John, they all preached the same Christ and the same way of salvation.

units.la: Addit: ET sic credidistis.] Quemadmodum supra dixit, quod & accepistis: sic hic, & sic credidistis, inquit. Nisi quod hic admonet quod quemadmodum non prædicauerit ipsis aliud Euangelium, quàm quod ab alijs quoq; sit apostolis omnibus prædicatū, ita fidem ipsorum, qua prædicationi suæ crediderunt, haud esse aliam ac diuersam à fide reliquorum Christianorum omnium. Sic parat argumentatum ad futuram disputationem, tam à concordi apostolorum omnium prædicatione, quàm à catholica Christianorum omnium fide.
units.tr: He adds: "And so you believed." As he said above, "which also you received," so here he says, "and so you believed." Except that here he reminds them that just as he did not preach to them any other gospel than that which was preached by all the other apostles, so their faith, by which they believed the preaching, is not other or different from the faith of all the other Christians. In this way he prepares an argument for the coming dispute, drawing on both the harmonious preaching of all the apostles and the catholic faith of all Christians.

units.la: Obiter obserua, quod dicit: Sic prædicamus, & sic credidistis. Chrysostomus rationes annotauit, quare non dicat in præsenti, sic creditis: sed in præterito, sic credidistis: nec in preterito, sic prædicauimus, sed in præsenti, sic prædicamus. Ex qualitate prædicationis quidem qualitas est fidei, ut quemadmodum prædicatur sic credatur: uerum uidemus hoc Corinthiorum exemplo, ut nonnunquam fides auditorum mutetur, dum interea doctrina Apostolica in se non mutatur, sed eadem constanter permanet. Sic possumus hodie dicere: Sic prædicant apostoli, & sic initio maiores nostri crediderunt. Eadem etiamnum est apostolorum prædicatio, qua etsi non uoce, literis tamen Euangelicâ ueritatem concorditer docent. Verum utinam usque adeo nihil præuaricationis in fidem Christianam irrepserit, ut ueraciter dicere possimus omnes: Sic prædicant apostoli, & sic credimus.
units.tr: Observe in passing that he says, "So we preach, and so you believed." Chrysostom has noted the reasons why he does not say in the present tense, "so you believe," but in the past, "so you believed"; and why he says not "so we preached" in the past but "so we preach" in the present. The quality of faith does indeed follow the quality of the preaching, so that as a thing is preached, so it is believed. But the example of the Corinthians shows us that sometimes the faith of the hearers changes, while the apostolic teaching in itself does not change, but remains constantly the same. So today we can say: "So the apostles preach, and so at the beginning our forebears believed." The preaching of the apostles is still the same, and although not by voice, yet by their writings they teach the truth of the gospel in harmony. Would that there had crept into the Christian faith so little of prevarication that we could all truly say: "So the apostles preach, and so we believe."

units.la: Quod si Christus prædicatur à mortuis resurrexisse, quomodo dicunt quidam inter uos non esse resurrectionem mortuorum? Si resurrectio mortuorum nõ est, neq; Christus resurrexit. Si uero Christus nõ resurrexit, inanis igitur est prædicatio nostra, inanis est & fides uestra. Reperimur autem & falsi testes Dei, quoniam testificati sumus de Deo, quod excitauerit Christum, quem non excitauit, si uidelicet mortui non resurgunt. Etenim si mortui non resurgunt, neque Christus resurrexit. Quod si Christus non resurrexit, superuacanea est fides uestra, adhuc estis in peccatis uestris.
