For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive; but each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ's, at his coming.

units.la: Refutauit errorem eorum, qui resurrectionem mortuorum negabant inter Corinthios: fecitque hoc argumentis, non apud Gentes, sed apud Christianos authenticis. Horum autem primum & potissimum est, quod de resurrectione Christi attulit, ex quo reliqua deducuntur: & unde resurrectio mortuorum constat, quam in fine mūdi futuram expectamus. Consequenter igitur quarto capitis huius membro docet resurrectionem Christi causam esse nostræ resurrectionis. Et facit hoc simili & exemplo. Simile habet, quod dicit: Primitiæ eorum qui dormierant, fuit. Notum est, quis usus primitiarum fuerit in lege. Offerebantur illæ & consecrabantur domino: ad hoc, ut in illis omnia reliqua quoque, unde erant desumpta, sanctificarentur.
units.tr: He refuted the error of those among the Corinthians who denied the resurrection of the dead, and he did this by arguments drawn not from the Gentiles but from sources authentic to Christians. The first and chief of these is what he brings forward concerning the resurrection of Christ, from which the rest are deduced, and on which the resurrection of the dead rests, which we await at the end of the world. Consequently, in the fourth part of this chapter he teaches that the resurrection of Christ is the cause of our resurrection, and he does this by a likeness and an example. The likeness lies in what he says: He was the firstfruits of those who had fallen asleep. It is well known what use firstfruits had under the law. They were offered and consecrated to the Lord, so that by them all the rest from which they had been taken might be sanctified.

units.la: Sic primitiæ frumenti, uini & olei, sanctificatio erat reliquorum fructuum omniū, quos de manu Domini acceperant. Consimili modo resurrectio Christi instar primitiarum fuit, per quam corpora nostra ad futuram sunt resurrectionem sanctificata.
units.tr: So the first-fruits of wheat, wine and oil were the sanctification of all the other fruits that they had received from the hand of the Lord. In a similar way, the resurrection of Christ was like the first-fruits, through which our bodies are sanctified for the future resurrection.

units.la: Etiam hoc nomine primitiæ resurrectionis Christo dantur, quod is ex omni dormientiū numero primus resurrexit: intellige, resurrectione plena ac perfecta, quam nō est mors ulla sequutura, qua ante ipsum nemo surrexit unquam. Hoc sensu Coloss.1.& Apoc.1. Vocatur primogenitus ex mortuis. Non est tamen primogenitura hæc ex mortuis excitati Christi ad ordinem tātum simpliciter referendu, quo primus omnium ex mortuis resurrexit, quem admodum primogenitus primus de numero sequuturorum fratrum ex utero matris sic nascitur: ut tamen non sit illis causa nascendi, sed simul ad dignitatem capitis, quod sic primum in partu uterum egreditur, ut & omnia corporis sui membra post se trahat: sicut illis nō modo exemplum, sed & causa nascendi. Sic Christus primitiæ dormientiū, & primogenitus ex mortuis fuit. Hoc sensu collimat Apostolus ad resurrectionem nostram communem, facitq; causam, principium, spem ac fiduciam illius ex resurrectione Christi.
units.tr: Christ is also given the name "first-fruits of the resurrection" for this reason: he rose first from the whole number of those who had died, that is, to a full and perfect resurrection, which no death would follow, and which no one had ever attained before him. In this sense Colossians 1 and Revelation 1 call him "the firstborn from the dead." Yet this firstborn status of Christ, raised from the dead, is not to be referred simply to order, as if he rose first of all from the dead. The firstborn of brothers is the first of those who follow, born from his mother's womb in such a way that he is not the cause of their birth, but at the same time, by the dignity of the head, he comes out first in the birth and drags all the members of his body after him. So for them he is not only an example but also the cause of their birth. Thus Christ is the first-fruits of those who have died, and the firstborn from the dead. In this sense the Apostle aims at our common resurrection, and he makes Christ's resurrection its cause, beginning, pledge and ground of confidence.

units.la: Quid est autem quod in præterito dicit, primitiæ, quod Erasmus uertit, Eorū qui dormierant. An eorum tantum primitias habet Christi resurrectio, qui tum cum ipse resurgeret, mortui fuerant, & non omniū etiā ad finem usque mundi sequentium? Si non omnium, sed illorum tantū, ergo non omnes mortui, sed illi tantum resurgent. Si uero resurecturi sunt omnes, ergo non illorum tantū, sed & futurorum omnium primitiæ in Christi resurrectione præcesserūt. Quid igitur est, quod non simpliciter dicit, Primitiæ dormientium: sed in præterito, Primitiæ eorum qui obdormierant.
units.tr: But what does he mean by saying in the past tense "first-fruits," which Erasmus translates "of those who had fallen asleep"? Does Christ's resurrection have the first-fruits only of those who had died at the time when he himself rose, and not of all who will follow until the end of the world? If only of those, then not all who have died will rise, but only those. But if all are going to rise, then the first-fruits of not only those but of all future people came before in Christ's resurrection. Why then does he not simply say "first-fruits of those who sleep," but in the past tense, "first-fruits of those who had fallen asleep"?

units.la: Potest bifariam responderi. Primum illud idem esse, quod, somno sopitorū, obsoporatorum, adeoq; & dormientiū, quem admodum & uulgata habet uersio: ut non sit referendum ad eos specialiter, qui ante mortem Christi inde ab initio mundi mortui fuerant, sed in genere ad omnes etiam ad finē usque mundi morituros. Deinde, si omnino sensus præteriti, & Erasmi uersio retinenda uidetur: exi-stimo sic loquutum esse Apostolum, ut significet ante Christum, neminem mortalium, ne patriarcharum quidem, necMosen, nec prophetarum quempiam plena & perfecta resurrectione resurrexisse, quo gloriam primitiarū ac primogenituræ ex mortuis soli Christo destinatam fuisse intelligamus: ut ipse primus omnium ad cœlestem gloriam & immortalitatem resurgens omnibus esset futuræ resurrectionis princeps & author. Et hoc sensu nihil demitur nobis, qui post resurrectionem Christi obdormimus. Etenim si illorum potuit esse mortuorum primogenitus, qui ante ipsum mortui erant: multo magis eorum esse potest,
units.tr: This can be answered in two ways. First, the phrase means the same as "of those who were lulled to sleep" or "fallen asleep," and so of "those who sleep," as the Vulgate also has it. So it is not to be referred specially to those who had died from the beginning of the world before Christ's death, but generally to all who would die even until the end of the world. Second, if the sense of the past tense is to be kept entirely, and Erasmus's version seems to be retained, I think the Apostle spoke so as to signify that before Christ no mortal, not even the patriarchs, nor Moses, nor any of the prophets, rose again with a full and perfect resurrection. So we understand that the glory of the first-fruits and of the firstborn from the dead was destined for Christ alone, so that he, rising first of all to heavenly glory and immortality, would be the prince and author of the future resurrection for all. In this sense nothing is taken from us, who fall asleep after Christ's resurrection. For if he could be the firstborn of those who died before him, much more can he be the firstborn of those

units.la: qui post illum mortui sunt, & ad finē usq; mundi moriuntur.
units.tr: who died after him and will die until the end of the world.

units.la: Postquam enim per hominē mors, etiam per hominē resurrectio mortuorum. Quemadmodum enim per Adam omnes moriuntur, ita & per Christum omnes uiuificabuntur.
units.tr: Since death came through a man, so also the resurrection of the dead comes through a man. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.

units.la: Reddit rationē, quare & quomodo sit Christus primitiæ dormientium resurgēdo factus. Et facit hoc per contrarium exemplum inductæ per hominem mortis. Mors occupauit uniuersum genus humanum, inducta per hominem. Sic igitur constitutum est diuinæ bonitatis consilio: ut quoniam per hominem mors est, sit etiam per hominem resurrectio mortuorum. Hoc est quod dicit: Postquam enim: uel, Quoniam enim. Græcè ἐπειδὴ γάρ, per hominem mors, etiam per hominem resurrectio mortuorum. Nō dicit, Quoniam inter homines mors obtinet: uoluit Deus ut sit etiam inter homines resurrectio mortuorum: sed, Quoniā per hominem mors, etiam per hominem resurrectio mortuorum. Confert utriusque & mortis & uitæ originem: & refert illam ad duos homines: quorum primum mortis, alterum uitæ authorem.
units.tr: He gives the reason why and how Christ became the first-fruits of those who sleep by rising. He does this by the contrasting example of death brought in through a man. Death, brought in through a man, took hold of the whole human race. So by the counsel of divine goodness it has been ordained that, since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead should also come through a man. This is what he says: "For since" (or "For"). The Greek is since then [ἐπειδὴ γάρ], "death through a man, resurrection of the dead also through a man." He does not say, "Since death prevails among men, God willed that there should also be resurrection of the dead among men." He says, "Since death through a man, resurrection of the dead also through a man." He sets the origin of both death and life side by side, and refers each to two men: the first is the author of death, the other of life.

units.la: PER hominē mors, inquit.] Rom.5. locus hic fusius explicatur. Ibi morte nō simpliciter per hominē, sed per unum hominē esse dicit. Deinde quomodo id factū fit, explicat, dicēs: Propterea quemadmodum per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introijt, ac per peccatū mors, & sic in omnes homines mors peruasit. Ergo mors est per unum hominē & per peccatum. Necesse igitur est per unum hominem peccatorē uenerit mors in mundum. Sed ea de re fusius diximus in ea quę est ad Romanos. Modum hic Apostolus non explicat, quia nō agit de peccato & iustificatione, sed de morte & resurrectione, idq; non in uniuersum, sed quatenus concernebat propositum afferendę resurrectionis mortuorum, quæ est per uirtutem ex mortuis resuscitati Christi.
units.tr: "Death through a man," he says. Romans 5 explains this place more fully. There he says death came not simply through a man, but through one man. Then he explains how this happened, saying: "Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, so death spread to all men." So death is through one man and through sin. Therefore death must have come into the world through one sinful man. But we have spoken more fully on this matter in our commentary on Romans. Here the Apostle does not explain the manner, because he is not dealing with sin and justification, but with death and resurrection, and not in general, but only as far as it bears on his purpose of asserting the resurrection of the dead, which is through the power of Christ raised from the dead.

units.la: ETIAM per hominem resurrectio mortuo rum, inquit ]Vt homo per peccatum mortuus à peccato & morte liberaretur ac seruaretur, cum id diuina constitueret clementia, potuit ne aliter fieri quàm per hominem? Si homine condidit solo uerbo: quem uerbo condidit, nō potuit solo uerbo uitę quā amiserat restituere? Quid necesse erat, ut hoc faceret per hominē?
units.tr: "And through a man the resurrection of the dead," he says. Since man had died through sin, and God's clemency had determined that he be freed and saved from sin and death, could this have happened in any other way than through a man? If God made man by a word alone, could he not restore by a word alone the life that man had lost? Why was it necessary that he do this through a man?

units.la: Respondeo. Arcanum consilij Dei nō est temere scrutandum, sed religiose adorandū. Satis sit, quæ salutis nostræ sunt scire, redemptos uidelicet nos esse per gratiā: & quemadmodū mors per unum hominem introijt in mundū, ita uitam nobis per unum hominem contigisse. Quare per hominem contigerit, & num aliter contingere nequiuerit: nec scrutari debemus, nec etiam si scrutemur, capere poterimus.
units.tr: I answer: the hidden counsel of God is not to be rashly searched into, but to be worshipped with reverence. It is enough to know what belongs to our salvation: that we are indeed redeemed by grace, and that as death came into the world through one man, so life has come to us through one man. Why it came through a man, and whether it could not have come in another way, we ought neither to search into, nor, even if we search, will we be able to grasp.

units.la: Est enim abyssus quædā consilij huius quo
units.tr: For there is a certain abyss in this counsel, by which

units.la: Deus hominem ad imaginem suam condere, A & post lapsum restituere, ac philanthropiam suam non solùm restituendo, sed & ipso resti-tutionis modo declarare voluit. Lapsus est an-gelus: verùm usqueadeò φιλάνϑρωπον non est, ut angeli assumpta natura prolapsos restitueret angelos. Lapsus est homo, & morti per pecca-tum factus obnoxius. Hic quo declararetur quàm esset Deus φιλάνϑρωπος, non modò resti-tuit prolapsum ac mortuum, sed & communi-catione hoc utriusque naturæ divinæ & hu-manæ per hominem communicationis huius mediatorem faeere voluit. Hic ne ego quæ-ram, quare ad hunc modum voluerit: & num aliter fieri nequiuerit, & non magis obstupe-scam erga tantam divinæ Maiestatis digna-tionem?
units.tr: God willed to make man in his own image, and after the fall to restore him, and to declare his love for mankind not only by restoring him, but by the very manner of restoration. The angel fell, but God is not so loving toward mankind that he restored the fallen angels by assuming the angelic nature. Man fell, and by sin became subject to death. Here, to show how loving God is toward man, he willed not only to restore the fallen and dead man, but also, by the communion of both the divine and human natures, to make a man the mediator of this communion. Shall I here inquire why he willed it in this way, and whether it could not have been otherwise, and shall I not rather be amazed at so great a condescension of divine Majesty?

units.la: Si quæras, quare non angelum, sed homine ad imaginem suam condere voluerit: quid re-sponderi poterit aliud, quàm quod sic dilexe-rit hominem magis quàm angelum.
units.tr: If you ask why he willed to make man, and not an angel, in his own image, what answer can be given other than that he so loved man more than the angel?

units.la: Rursus, si quæras, quare hominem peccato rem morti eripere voluerit, cū angelum pro-lapsum non restituat: iterum rectè responde-bitur, Quia hominem diligit magis quàm an-gelum.
units.tr: Again, if you ask why he willed to snatch man from sin and death, when he does not restore the fallen angel, the answer again will rightly be: because he loves man more than the angel.

units.la: Tertio, si quæras, quare ut hominē redime-ret, humanam in se naturā suscipere voluerit, cum angeli naturam non suscepcerit: etiam hic non potest responderi melius, quàm quia ma-gis diligit hominem, quàm angelum.
units.tr: Third, if you ask why, in order to redeem man, he willed to take upon himself human nature, when he did not take the nature of angels, not even here can a better answer be given than that he loves man more than the angel.

units.la: Si verò pergens tantæ philanthropiæ cau-sam quæsieris, quare hominem magis diligat Deus quàm angelum: hic non habemus quod respondeatur aliud quàm tantæ philanthropiæ mysterium adorandum esse religiosissime, nō scrutandum curiosè.
units.tr: But if, pressing on, you ask the cause of such love, why God loves man more than the angel, then we have no other answer than that the mystery of such love must be adored with the utmost reverence, and not searched into with idle curiosity.

units.la: PER hominem, mors, inquit, & per homi-nem resurrectio mortuorum.] Mors per homi-nem peccatorem propter peccatum. Resurre-ctio igitur per hominem iustum, propter illius iustitiam. Ergo quàm diuersa sunt à se inuicè peccatū & iustitia, mors & resurrectio ex mor-tuis: tam diuersos hos duos à se inuicem opor-tet esse homines, & tamen uere homines. Ete-nim peccatorem esse, uel iustum esse: nec de-mit quicq̄, nec addit humanæ naturæ. Quàm uerum est quod dicit, Per hominem mors: tā-uerum est quod addit, Et per hominem resur-rectio mortuorum. Erat Adam uerus homo, tam ante, quàm post peccatum. Sic Christus propterea non est non uerus homo, quod non est nobiscum peccato obnoxius. Et nos ubi à peccato erimus prorsus liberi, ueri utiq; homi-nes adhuc erimus.
units.tr: "Through a man, death," he says, "and through a man, the resurrection of the dead." Death is through a sinful man, on account of sin. The resurrection therefore is through a righteous man, on account of his righteousness. So as sin and righteousness, death and resurrection from the dead, are mutually different, so these two men must be different from each other, and yet truly men. For to be a sinner, or to be righteous, takes nothing from human nature nor adds anything to it. As true as it is that he says "through a man, death," so true is what he adds, "and through a man, the resurrection of the dead." Adam was a true man, both before and after sin. So Christ is not less a true man because he is not, like us, subject to sin. And when we are wholly free from sin, we will still be true men.

units.la: PER hominem mors, inquit, &c.] Sic est mors per hominem, ut non in alios tantum sit ab illo propagata, sed ipsum quoque corripue-rit ac mortuum reddiderit. Sic nanque par e-rat, ut malo suo ipse conficeretur illius author. Iam si resurrectio mortuorum perinde est per hominem, atque per hominem mors est, con-sequitur, illum non alijs tantum debuisse fieri
units.tr: THROUGH MAN, he says, death, etc. Death is through man in such a way that it not only spread from him to others but also seized him himself and made him mortal. For it was fitting that the author of it should be undone by his own evil. Now if the resurrection of the dead is through man just as death is through man, it follows that he ought to have become the author of resurrection not only for others, but that he himself should also rise from the dead. But one cannot rise from the dead unless one has first died. Thus in a few words great mysteries are comprehended.

units.la: resurrectionis authorem, sed ipsum quoque à mortuis resurgere. Resurgere autē à mortuis non potest, nisi antea mortuus. Sic paucis uer-bis mysteria magna comprehenduntur.
units.tr: For AS IN ADAM ALL DIE, he says, SO IN CHRIST ALL SHALL BE MADE ALIVE. He expresses more specifically what he said: through man death, and through man the resurrection of the dead.

units.la: QVEMADMODVM enim per Adam omnes moriuntur, inquit, ita & per Christum om-nes uiuificabuntur.] Specificantius exprimit quod dixit: Per hominem mors, & per hominē resurrectio mortuorum.
units.tr: For first he specifies those two men: calling one Adam, the other Christ. How death comes through Adam, since the first woman sinned, we have explained in Romans.

units.la: Primū enim specificat duos illos homines: unum uocans Adamū, alterum Christū. Quo-modo per Adamum sit mors, cum mulier pri-ma peccarit, diximus in Romanis.
units.tr: First he specifies the two men, calling one Adam and the other Christ. How death comes through Adam, since the first woman sinned, we have discussed in Romans.

units.la: Deinde explicat collationem utriusq;, non simpliciter dicens, Per Adam morimur, & per Christum uiuificamur: sed, Quemadmodum enim per Adam omnes moriuntur, ita & per Christum omnes uiuificabuntur.
units.tr: Then he explains the comparison between them. He does not simply say, "Through Adam we die, and through Christ we are made alive," but, "For as through Adam all die, so also through Christ all will be made alive."

units.la: Quod omnes moriamur, manifestū est per quotidianam experientiam.
units.tr: That we all die is plain from everyday experience.

units.la: Deinde quod omnes mortales ab Adamo primo homine generis propagatione descen-damus, nihil habet controuersiæ.
units.tr: That all mortals descend from Adam, the first man, by generation is not disputed.

units.la: Tertiò, quod communem mortalitatem ex illo hæreditaria lue nascendo cōtrahamus om-nes, sacris literis docetur, & aliàs facili ratione comprehenditur. Cui nanq; tam commune, tā- perpetuum, tamq; hæreditarium malum depu-tabimus, quàm primo parēti, à quo omnes de-scendimus. Ergo consimili modo non pauci aliquot: sed omnes per Christum uiuificabun-tur, sicut omnes per Adam moriuntur.
units.tr: Thirdly, that we all contract common mortality from him by being born with a hereditary plague is taught in Holy Scripture, and is also easily grasped by other reasoning. For to what would we assign an evil so common, so perpetual and so hereditary, if not to the first parent from whom we all descend? Therefore, in like manner, not a few but all will be made alive through Christ, just as all die through Adam.

units.la: Est hic locus admodum insignis. In eo nan-que maximè, sicut & Augustinus annotauit, fi-des Christiana consistit. Primam illius partē de communi omnium mortalitate per Ada-mum contracta, humana ratio facile agnoscit: alteram uerò de uiuificatione quę est per Chri-stum, non ratio sapientium, sed fides creden-tium capit & agnoscit: quam qui negat, nullo modo ad gratiam hanc pertinet, quæ per Chri-stum communicatur credentibus. Quod uiui-ficabimur, quod omnes, quod per Christū nul-la humana ratione capitur. Quare propter fi-dem hanc in Christū à sapientibus huius mun-di ridemur.
units.tr: This is a very notable passage. In it, as Augustine also observed, the Christian faith chiefly consists. Human reason readily acknowledges the first part, concerning the common mortality contracted through Adam. The second part, concerning the making alive that is through Christ, is grasped and acknowledged not by the reason of the wise but by the faith of believers. Whoever denies it has no share in this grace, which is communicated through Christ to believers. That we shall be made alive, that all, that through Christ: no human reasoning comprehends this. Therefore, on account of this faith in Christ, we are laughed at by the wise of this world.

units.la: Sed quæritur hic, quomodo dicatur ab Apo-stolo, omnes esse uiuificandos per Christum, perinde atq; omnes moriuntur per Adamū? Cum constet ex alijs sacræ scripturę locis non omnes per Christum: sed electos tantū & cre-dētes uiuificari, ac saluari. Malum enim quod est per Adamum, uniuersale est non potentia tantum, sed & actu omnes in uniuersum mor-tificans. At gratia quæ est per Christum, licet potentia sit uniuersalis, ut posset saluare om-nes: actu tamen non est nisi fidelium, ideoque ad latitudinem uniuersalis mali non perueni-ens. Quare uidetur nō fuisse dicendum, Ita & per Christum omnes: sed, Ita & per Christum multi uiuificabuntur.
units.tr: But here it is asked how the Apostle can say that all are to be made alive through Christ, just as all die through Adam. For it is established from other passages of Scripture that not all are made alive and saved through Christ, but only the elect and believers. The evil that comes through Adam is universal, killing all people not only in power but also in act. But the grace that comes through Christ, although in power it is universal, so that it could save all, is in act only that of the faithful, and so does not reach the full extent of the universal evil. Therefore it seems he should not have said, "So also through Christ all," but, "So also through Christ many will be made alive."

units.la: Respondeo: Non hoc agit Apost. ut omnes in uniuersum saluos fore dicat: sed quoniā in præ-
units.tr: I answer: The Apostle does not do this in order to say that all will in general be saved, but because in the present

units.la: Quæstio. præsenti disputatione, fidé resurrectionis mortuorum per Christi resurrectionē astruit, ut hanc illustret, utitur hac collatione Adæ & Christi, docens Christum esse uitę authorem, quemadmodum Adam est mortis: ut sicut extra Adamum nemo hominum moritur, in Adamo nemo constitutus non moritur, ita extra Christū nemo uiuificetur, & in illo nemo non uiuificetur. Hic non conueniebat ut diceret, Ita & in Christo aliqui, pauci, multi uiuificabuntur. Mox enim inferri posset, Ergo nō est ille communis omnium uiuificator: sed fieri potest, ut aliunde etiam uiuificemur, qui sensus plenitudinem collationis huius infringeret. Recte ergo non dixit, Ita per Christum multi: sed, Ita & per Christum omnes uiuificabuntur. Siue enim uiuificationem hæc de ea quæ electorum & fidelium est tantum, siue de communi omnium mortuorum resurrectione intellexerimus: uerisimū est, quod dicit: nec potuit melius particulam hanc exprimere. De resurrectione communi omnium intelligi posse non abnuit Ambrosius, dicens: Quamuis & generalem tribuet resurrectionem, ut sicut in Adā omnes siue iusti siue iniusti moriuntur, ita & in Christo omnes, tam credentes quam diffidentes resurgant, licet ad pœnam increduli: ui uificari tamen uidentur, quia corpora sua recipient, iam non morituri, sed passuri pœnam in eis sine fine, quod credere noluerunt. Hæc ille. Et Chrysost. hac de re annotans, dicit: Quid autem, dic quæso, num omnes in Christo uiuificabuntur? Et ubi erunt, qui in gehennam abducentur? Quod si de corpore fuerit hoc dictum, perstat sermo: si de iustitia uero & peccato, non item. Hæc ille. Sane uerbo uiuificandi usus uidetur Apostolus, pro uerbo resurgendi. Cum enim dixisset, Posteaquam per hominē mors: per hominem & resurrectio mortuorum, subiecit explicandi gratia. Quemadmodum enim per Adam omnes moriuntur, ita & per Christum omnes uiuificabuntur, cum dicendum esset, resurgent. Deinde non dixit, Viuificantur, in præsenti, sed, Viuificabuntur, in futuro. Ea autem uiuificatio quæ electorum est per spiritum Christi: non demum erit in futuro, sed in hac uita incipit per fidem. At hic non de illa, sed de resurrectione mortuorum loquitur: quam quidam ex Corinthijs negabat, corporum utique non animorum uiuificationem negantes. Transit quidem peccatum Adæ in omnes: non autem iustitia Christi consimiliter omnibus est concessa: uerum hinc non est argutandum hoc loco, sed permanendum in propositio, quo Apostolus causam resurrectionis mortuorum tueri uoluit. Quod si hūc sensum acceperimus, non debuit dicere Apostolus, Ita & per Christum multi: sed, Omnes uiuificabuntur. Nam omnino ut omnes in Adam moriuntur, sic in Christo omnes in die iudicij boni & mali, electi ac reprobi resurgent, idq; non nisi Christi uirtute, quem pater ad hoc est missurus, ut iudicium ferat in omnes.
units.tr: Question. In the present discussion he establishes faith in the resurrection of the dead through the resurrection of Christ. To illustrate this, he uses the comparison of Adam and Christ, teaching that Christ is the author of life just as Adam is the author of death: so that, just as no man dies outside Adam, and no one who is constituted in Adam fails to die, so no one is made alive outside Christ, and no one in him fails to be made alive. Here it was not fitting for him to say, "So also in Christ some, a few, many will be made alive." For it could soon be inferred, "Therefore he is not the common life-giver of all, but it may be that we are made alive also by other means," and this sense would break the fullness of the comparison. Rightly, then, he did not say, "So through Christ many," but, "So also through Christ all will be made alive." For whether we understand this making alive as that which belongs only to the elect and faithful, or as the common resurrection of all the dead, what he says is true, and he could not have expressed this particle better. Ambrose does not deny that it can be understood of the common resurrection, saying: "Although he will also grant a general resurrection, so that just as in Adam all die, both just and unjust, so in Christ all rise, both believers and unbelievers, though the unbelievers rise to punishment; yet they seem to be made alive, because they receive their bodies, no longer to die, but to suffer punishment in them without end, which they were unwilling to believe." Thus he. Chrysostom, annotating on this matter, says: "But tell me, I ask, will all be made alive in Christ? And where will those be who are led away into Gehenna? If this was said of the body, the saying stands; if of righteousness and sin, it does not." Thus he. Surely the Apostle uses the verb "to make alive" in place of the verb "to rise." For when he had said, "Since through a man came death, through a man also comes the resurrection of the dead," he added by way of explanation, "For as through Adam all die, so also through Christ all will be made alive," where he ought to have said "will rise." Then he did not say "are made alive" in the present, but "will be made alive" in the future. That making alive which belongs to the elect is through the Spirit of Christ. It does not come only in the future, but in this life it begins through faith. Here, however, he speaks not of that but of the resurrection of the dead, which some of the Corinthians denied, denying, of course, the making alive of bodies, not of souls. The sin of Adam indeed passes into all; but the righteousness of Christ is not similarly granted to all. Yet we should not quibble over this point here, but remain with the proposition by which the Apostle wished to defend the cause of the resurrection of the dead. If we take this sense, the Apostle ought not to have said, "So also through Christ many," but, "All will be made alive." For just as in Adam all die, so in Christ all, good and bad, elect and reprobate, will rise on the day of judgment, and this only by the power of Christ, whom the Father is to send for this purpose, that he may pass judgment on all.

units.la: Quod si nō de communi resurrectione, sed de electorum ac fidelium uiuificatione intelle xerimus, quod dicit: Ita & per Christum omnes uiuificabuntur: retinēda est Græca lectio, quemadmodum in Adam omnes, id est, quot-quot communicatione carnis sunt in Adam, moriuntur: ita & in Christo omnes, id est, quot-quot sunt in Christo, in communicatione uiuificantis spiritus, uiuificabuntur. Illic omnes, & hic omnes. Illic omnes homines, hic omnes electi & credentes. Adam suis omnibus author est mortis, Christus uicissim suis omnibus qui sibi sunt incorporati, author est uitæ.
units.tr: But if we understand it not of the common resurrection but of the making alive of the elect and faithful, then the reading of the Greek must be retained: as in Adam all, that is, all who are in Adam by communion of flesh, die, so in Christ all, that is, all who are in Christ, by communion of the life-giving Spirit, will be made alive. There, all; and here, all. There all men; here all the elect and believers. Adam is the author of death to all his own; Christ in turn is the author of life to all his own, who are incorporated into him.

units.la: Hanc sententiam Augustinus sequutus est, illamque sic exposuit Epistola uigesimaoctaua. Per hanc enim Apostolicam diuinam clara mque sententiam, satis euidenter elucet, neminem ire in mortem nisi per Adam: neminē ire in uitam æternam, nisi per Christum. Hoc est quippe, omnes & omnes: quia sicut omnes homines per primam, hoc est, per carnalem generationem pertinent ad Adam: sic omnes homines ad secundam, id est, spiritualem regenerationem ueniunt, quicunque ad Christū perueniant. Ideo ergo dictum est, Et hic omnes, & ibi omnes. Quia sicut omnes qui moriuntur, non nisi in Adam moriuntur: ita omnes qui uiuificabuntur, non nisi in Christo uiuificabuntur. Hæc ille. Sane sic habet electorum uiuificatio. Atq; ita ne hoc quidem sensu conueniebat ut diceret, ita per Christum multi uiuificabuntur.
units.tr: Augustine followed this opinion and expounded it thus in Epistle 28: "Through this divine and apostolic sentence it shines forth quite plainly that no one goes to death except through Adam, and no one goes to eternal life except through Christ. For this is 'all' and 'all': because just as all men belong to Adam through the first, that is carnal, generation, so all men who attain to the second, that is spiritual, regeneration come to Christ. Therefore it is said, 'and here all, and there all.' Because just as all who die die only in Adam, so all who are made alive will be made alive only in Christ." Thus he. Surely this is how the making alive of the elect stands. And so not even in this sense was it fitting for him to say, "So through Christ many will be made alive."

units.la: Annotationes quæ Hieronymo dantur, sic habent: Omnes quidem resurgent, sed soli hi uiuificabuntur in Christo, qui Christi merebūtur copulari corpori. Item, de communi morte, & de communi resurrectione dicit. Hæc ibi leguntur, quibus utranq; sententiam posuit.
units.tr: The annotations that are attributed to Jerome say this: "All indeed will rise again, but only those will be made alive in Christ who deserve to be joined to the body of Christ." He also speaks there of the common death and the common resurrection. These are the words found there, in which he sets out both opinions.

units.la: Augustinus loco supra citato, hæc de paruulis adijcit: Quisquis dixerit quod in Christo uiuificabuntur etiam paruuli, qui sine sacramē ti eius participatione de uita exeunt: hic profecto & contra Apostolicam prædicatione uenit, & totam condemnat ecclesiam, ubi propterea cum baptizandis paruulis festinatur & currit, quia sine dubio creditur, aliter eos in Christo uiuificari omnino nō posse. Qui autē non uiuificatur in Christo, restat ut in eadem damnatione maneat, de qua Rom. 5. Per unius delictum in omnes homines ad condemnationem. Hæc ibi, quibus gratiam salutis quæ per Christum est, sic alligat sacramento, ut priuationem illius, etiam eam quæ necessitate fit, non uoluntate, ad condemnationem facere, uel certe in condemnatione paruulos fidelium retinere afferat, cum non priuatio, sed contemptus baptismi damnet. Eadem incogitantia de Eucharistia scripsit, faciens eam necessariā usqueadeo, ut si qui de illa non communicent, ui tam habere nequeant.
units.tr: Augustine, in the passage cited above, adds this about infants: "Whoever says that even infants who depart this life without participating in his sacrament will be made alive in Christ certainly contradicts the apostolic preaching and condemns the whole Church, which hastens and runs to baptize infants for the very reason that it is firmly believed they cannot in any other way be made alive in Christ. Whoever is not made alive in Christ remains in the same condemnation of which Romans 5 speaks: 'Through the offence of one, judgment came upon all men to condemnation.'" These are his words, by which he ties the grace of salvation that is through Christ so closely to the sacrament that he asserts that the deprivation of it, even the deprivation that comes by necessity and not by will, brings condemnation, or at least holds the infants of believers in condemnation, since it is not the deprivation but the contempt of baptism that condemns. He wrote with the same lack of thought about the Eucharist, making it so necessary that those who do not communicate in it cannot have life.

units.la: Sane uerum est, nemo prorsus uiuificatur, nisi in Christo constitutus. At in Christo esse cum non sacramentaliter tantum cōtingat, sed alijs etiam modis, ijsq; uerioribus & effica cioribus puto incogitanter asseri, paruulos in Christo nisi per baptismum esse non posse. In Christo sunt electi, quos illi pater dedit ab æterno, & ad salutem prædestinauit. In Christo sunt credentes, in Christo sunt credentium liberi, uirtute fœderis, secundum illud: Ego sum Deus tuus, & Deus seminis tui. Vnde & Christus ipse dixit: Sinite paruulos uenire ad me, talium enim est regnum cœlorum. Hos omnes propter baptismi priuationem tanquâ à Christo alienos habendos esse pro damnatis, nō ui deo quomodo firmis argumentis possit probari. Quod ecclesia cū infantibus hanc ob causam ad baptismum festinat & currit, quod credat eos alia nō posse ratione uiuificari in Christo: non magis est probandum, quàm quod olim eadem ratione cū paruulis suis ad Eucharistiæ communicationem festinandum & currendum esse credidit: quam tamē opinionem & consuetudinem tanquam erroneam, postea abiecit.
units.tr: It is indeed true that no one at all is made alive unless he is established in Christ. But to be in Christ does not happen only sacramentally, but also in other ways, which are truer and more effective. I think it is asserted without thought that infants cannot be in Christ except through baptism. Those whom the Father gave to Christ from eternity and predestined to salvation are in Christ. Believers are in Christ, and the children of believers are in Christ by virtue of the covenant, according to that word: "I am your God, and the God of your seed." Hence Christ himself said: "Suffer the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven." All these, on account of being deprived of baptism, are not to be counted as condemned and as aliens from Christ. By what strong arguments this could be proved against God, I do not see. That the Church hastens and runs with infants to baptism for this reason, because it believes they cannot otherwise be made alive in Christ, is no more to be proved than that once, for the same reason, it believed that its little children must hasten and run to the communion of the Eucharist. That opinion and custom, however, it later rejected as erroneous.

units.la: Quod uerò Apostolicam prædicationem citat, si de præsenti loco intelligit, non probat quod ex eo colligit. Neq; enim aliud Apostolus docet, quàm ut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita in Christo omnes esse uiuificados. Dogma autem hoc, quod fidelium paruuli in Christo esse ac saluari nisi per baptismum non possunt, nemo Apostolus unquam tradidit. Paruulos fidelium scimus in Adam morti esse obnoxios propter originale peccatum, in quo concipiuntur & nascuntur: atq; ita nisi per Christum saluari non posse, id quod Pelagiani non agnoscentes, merito sunt reprobati. Iuxtà tamen scimus illos esse in fœdere Dei, pertinere ad regnum cœlorum & esse in Christo, ideoque illi adferendos & per baptismum, tanquam initiationis ac regenerationis sacramentum corporis illius etiam sacramentaliter inferendos, si id nulla necessitate impediatur. Sacramentale signum non facit, ut sint in Christo: sed quoniam ad illum pertinent, inq; illo sunt uirtute electionis ac fœderis Dei, ideo sunt ecclesiæ Dei sacramento baptismatis incorporandi. Quod si id fieri non poterit, solentur se fideles parentes certitudine diuinæ electionis ac fœderis Dei: nec dubitent omnium esse certissimum quod dictum est à domino: Ego sum Deus tuus, & Deus seminis tui: & quod Christus regnû cœlorum talium dixit esse paruulorum, quæ duo oracula sic sunt firma & fideli homini indubitata, ut etiâ si mille Augustini diuersum disputent, ne unum quidem ex illis apicem irritum reddere possint.
units.tr: As for his citing the apostolic preaching: if he understands it of the present passage, it does not prove what he gathers from it. For the Apostle teaches nothing other than that as all die in Adam, so all are to be made alive in Christ. But this doctrine, that the infants of believers cannot be in Christ and be saved except through baptism, no apostle ever handed down. We know that the infants of believers are liable to death in Adam on account of original sin, in which they are conceived and born, and so they cannot be saved except through Christ; the Pelagians, who did not acknowledge this, were rightly rejected. Yet we know that they are in the covenant of God, belong to the kingdom of heaven, and are in Christ. Therefore they are to be brought to baptism, and are to be introduced sacramentally into the body of Christ through baptism, as the sacrament of initiation and regeneration, if no necessity prevents it. The sacramental sign does not make them to be in Christ; rather, because they belong to him and are in him by virtue of God's election and covenant, therefore they are to be incorporated into the Church of God by the sacrament of baptism. But if this cannot be done, let believing parents be comforted by the certainty of God's divine election and covenant. Let them not doubt that most certain of all is what the Lord said: "I am your God, and the God of your seed," and what Christ said, that the kingdom of heaven belongs to such little ones. These two oracles are so firm and beyond doubt to the faithful man that even if a thousand disputations by Augustine argued otherwise, they could not render void even one iota of them.

units.la: VNVSQVISQVE autʼ in proprio ordine, primitiæ Christus, deinde ij qui sunt Christi, in aduētu ipsius. ]Ne confusam fore resurrectionem putemus, cum dixisset, Ita & in Christo omnes uiuificabuntur: hoc est, è mortuis resurgent, particulam hanc adiecit, dicens: Vnusquisque autem in proprio ordine. Quibus uerbis admonet, causam resurrectionis esse à Deo certo quodam ordine dispositam. Non quo sit alius aliter, & alijs alij temporibus resurrecturi: sed quo inter communem & eam quæ Christi est, resurrectionem discrimen sit constitutum. Quare quod dicit: Vnusquisque autem in proprio ordine, non est præter sensum Apostoli diuexandum, quasi ea quisque ætate qua est mortuus: uel ea conditione qua erat cum in uiuis ageret, sit resurrecturus. Et enim mox exponit de quo ordine loquatur, cū subijcit, dicēs: Primitiæ Christus, deinde qui sunt Christi, in aduētu ipsius. Resurrexit Christus triduo post mortem suam primus omnium, quo primitiæ esset resurrectionis & primogenitus ex mortuis, id quod supra expositum.
units.tr: "But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ's at his coming." Lest we think the resurrection would be confused, when he had said, "So also in Christ shall all be made alive," that is, they will rise from the dead, he added this phrase, saying, "But each in his own order." By these words he reminds us that the cause of the resurrection has been arranged by God in a certain fixed order. Not that one will rise in one way and another in another way, or at different times, but that a distinction has been established between the common resurrection and that which belongs to Christ. Therefore, what he says, "But each in his own order," is not to be twisted contrary to the meaning of the Apostle, as if each would rise in the age in which he died, or in the condition in which he was while living. For he immediately explains what order he is speaking of, when he adds, saying: "Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ's, at his coming." Christ rose on the third day after his death, first of all, that he might be the firstfruits of the resurrection and the firstborn from the dead, as has been explained above.

units.la: Hic erat illi ordo dispositus à patre. Cætero rum resurrectio in alium est ordinem destinata, etiam eorū qui sunt Christi membra. Is est, ut in aduentu ipsius demum è mortuis excitetur, quod fiet in fine mundi. Sic dicit: Deinde ij qui sunt Christi in aduentu ipsius. Non soli resurgent qui sunt Christi. Resurgent omnes. Sed ij primi. Sic 1. Thess. 4. dicit: Et mortui in Christo resurgent primum, post illos surgent & reliqui. At horum mentionem nō facit, quia quæ scribit, ad fidem ac spem Christianorū cō firmandam scribit.
units.tr: This was the order appointed for him by the Father. The resurrection of the rest is destined for another order, including those who are members of Christ. It is that they will be raised from the dead only at his coming, which will happen at the end of the world. So he says: "Then those who are Christ's at his coming." Not only those who are Christ's will rise; all will rise. But these first. So in 1 Thessalonians 4 he says: "And the dead in Christ will rise first; afterwards the rest will rise too." But he makes no mention of these here, because what he writes, he writes to strengthen the faith and hope of Christians.

units.la: Illud, In aduentu ipsius: in uulgata uersione est, Qui in aduentu eius crediderunt. At uerbum, Crediderunt, in Græco non est, nec legitur ab Ambrosio, nec à Chrysostomo. Ambrosius refert ad utrunq; Christi aduentum, quod in secundo resurrecturi sint sancti communiter, & in primo nonnulli resurrexerint speciali-ter. Verùm rectius ad secundum dùtaxat refertur, sicut & Chrysostomus facit. Loquitur enim nō de speciali paucorum resurrectione, sed de ordine quo communiter in aduentu domini resurgemus.
units.tr: As for "at his coming": in the Vulgate translation it reads, "who believed at his coming." But the word "believed" is not in the Greek, nor is it read by Ambrose or by Chrysostom. Ambrose refers it to both comings of Christ, so that the saints will rise in common at the second coming, and some have risen specially at the first. But it is more rightly referred to the second alone, as Chrysostom also does. For he speaks not of a special resurrection of a few, but of the order in which we all in common shall rise at the coming of the Lord.

units.la: Non est autem præter rationem, quod ordinis huius meminit & temporis, quo futura est mortuorum resurrectio. Quoniam enim magna ea est humani ingenij curiositas & impatientia, periculum erat, ne propter tot seculorum moras diceremus: Si Christus primitiæ fuit resurrectionis mortuorum: qui fit quod non statim resurgunt, qui ad illum pertinent? Occupans igitur, primus quidem resurrexit, inquit, Christus tanquam primitiæ dormientium: nec mox resurgent qui ad illum pertinet, sed constitutus est illis certus certi temporis ordo, quem præuenire non poterunt. Is autem erit in illius aduentu.
units.tr: Nor is it beside the point that he mentions this order and this time at which the resurrection of the dead is to take place. For since the curiosity and impatience of the human mind is great, there was a danger that, because of so many delays of ages, we would say: "If Christ is the firstfruits of the resurrection of the dead, how is it that those who belong to him do not rise at once?" Therefore, anticipating this, he says: Christ indeed rose first, as the firstfruits of those who sleep. Nor will those who belong to him rise immediately, but a fixed order of a fixed time has been appointed for them, which they cannot anticipate. That time will be at his coming.

units.la: Quare uerò differatur communis resurrectio fidelium in aduentum Christi secundum, qui futurus est in fine mundi, facilè cogitari potest. Tunc enim præsentis mundi status terminabitur, & completus erit electorum numerus. Deinde ea erit resurgentium conditio, & corporum qualitas, quę non præsentis mundi corruptioni, sed futuri claritati & incorruptioni cōueniat. Possunt & aliæ esse causæ, sed hæ sunt manifestæ.
units.tr: Why the common resurrection of believers is deferred to the second coming of Christ, which is to happen at the end of the world, can easily be understood. For then the state of the present world will come to an end, and the number of the elect will be complete. Then the condition of those rising and the quality of their bodies will be fitting, not to the corruption of the present world, but to the brightness and incorruption of the world to come. There may be other causes too, but these are plain.

units.la: Quomodo per aduentū Christi excitandi sunt mortui, Matth.24. memoratur ad hūc modum: Et uidebunt filium hominis ueniente in nubibus cœli cum uirtute & gloria multa. Et mittet angelos suos cum magna uoce tubæ, & congregabunt electos eius à quatuor uentis, à terminis cœlorum usq; ad terminos eorum. Et Iohan.5. Veniet hora, in qua omnes qui in monumentis sunt, audient uocē eius (filij hominis) & prodibunt qui bona fecerunt in resurrectionem uitæ: qui uero mala egerunt, in resurrectionem iudicij. Et 1.Thess.4. ipse dominus cum hortatu & uoce archangeli, ac tuba Dei descendet de cœlo, & mortui in Christo resurgent primum.
units.tr: How the dead are to be raised at the coming of Christ is recorded in Matthew 24 in this way: "And they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. And he shall send out his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other." And John 5: "The hour is coming, in which all who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of man, and those who have done good shall come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgement." And 1 Thess. 4: "The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel and the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ shall rise first."

units.la: Mox finis, cū tradiderit regnū Deo ac patri, cum abolueriт omnem principatū, & omnem potestatem ac uirtutē. Nam oportet eum regnare, donec posuerit omnes inimicos sub pedes suos. Nouissimus hostis aboletur mors. Nā omnia subiecit sub pedes illius. Atqui cum dicit, quod omnia subiecta sint, palam est excipiendum eum qui subiecit illi omnia. Cum autem subiecta fuerint illi omnia, tunc & ipse filius subijcietur ei, qui illi subiecit omnia, ut sit Deus omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: "Then comes the end, when he shall have handed over the kingdom to God and the Father, when he shall have abolished all rule and all authority and power. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be abolished is death. For he has put all things under his feet. But when he says that all things are made subject, it is plain that he who subjected all things to him is excepted. And when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all."

units.la: Habent ista occupationē qua respondetur illis, qui dicturi erant: Si futura est mortuorū resurrectio, quis erit pōt illam rerū status in hoc mundo? Necesse est turbentur & confundantur omnia. Vbi redierint maiores, conabūtur occupare suas sedes, suas facultates, suas dignitates, quas olim possederunt. Volunt usurpare rerum gubernacula, & subijcere sibi eos, quos uiuos in mundo reperient. Illi contradicent, uolentq; retinere omnia, ut necesse sit ista tum rerum omnium maximam esse incursurū confusionem ac perturbationē. Deinde, si reuersurus est Christus in hunc mundum, resurrecturiq; omnes qui ad illum pertinent, quomodo in tanta rerum confusione excipiētur? Minus loci habebunt quàm antea. Sic exagitabuntur, ut satius fuerit haudquaquam resurre xisse. Huiusmodi cogitationes necessariò occurrunt illis qui uirtutem Dei, finem præsentis mundi, & qualitatem futuri seculi non intelligūt. Hac illis igitur occupatione occurrit, qua finem mundi ac mutatione præsentis status in longe alium tore dicit.
units.tr: These words contain an answer to an objection, given to those who were about to say: "If there is to be a resurrection of the dead, what will become of the state of things in this world? Everything must be thrown into turmoil and confusion. When the elders return, they will try to occupy their seats, their property and their dignities which they once held. They will want to seize the reins of affairs and subject to themselves those whom they find alive in the world. Those others will resist and want to keep everything, so that it is bound to come about that the greatest confusion and disorder of all things will ensue. Again, if Christ is to return to this world and all who belong to him are to rise, how will they be received amid such great confusion? They will have less room than before. They will be so harassed that it would have been better not to have risen at all." Thoughts of this kind necessarily occur to those who do not understand the power of God, the end of the present world, and the nature of the age to come. The Apostle therefore meets this objection by the occupation (the business at hand) in which he speaks of the end of the world and the change of the present state into a very different one.

units.la: MOX finis, inquit.] In Græco est, ἔπειτα τὸ τέλος, id est, postea finis erit. Erasmus magis suū sensum, quàm uerbum Apostoli hoc loco expressit. Quasi interrogatus, quid sit post resurrectionem futurum, uno uerbo respondet, Finis erit. Dixit: Per Christum omnes uiuificabūtur: unusquisq; autem in proprio ordine, primitiæ Christus: deinde ij qui sunt Christi, in aduentu ipsius. Poterat cogitari Christum propterea denuo aduenturum, ut suos è mortuis excitaret, cum dicit, Postea finis erit. Hoc est, postea terminabitur & consumabitur hic mundus, præsens hic rerum omnium status auferetur è medio.
units.tr: "Then the end," he says. In the Greek it is "then the end" [ἔπειτα τὸ τέλος], that is, "afterwards there will be the end." Erasmus expressed his own sense here rather than the Apostle's words. It is as if he had been asked what will happen after the resurrection, and answers in one word: "The end." He had said: "By Christ all will be made alive; but each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ's, at his coming." It could be thought that Christ will come again for this reason, to raise his own from the dead, when he says "Afterwards the end will come." That is, afterwards this world will be brought to an end and finished, and this present state of all things will be taken out of the way.

units.la: tet, & unà cum illis in hoc mundo regnet. rum non esse tale quid expectandum ignis cat, cum dicit, Postea finis erit. Hoc est, postea terminabitur & consumabitur hic mundus, præsens hic rerum omnium status auferetur è medio. De hoc fine loquitur apostolus Petrus dicens: Omnium finis appropinquabit. Quā- lis autem futurus sit hic mundi finis, aliis scripturæ locis memoratur. Terminabitur mundus non temere, sed cum iudicio, quo separabuntur boni à malis, & in utrosq; finalis sententia pronunciabitur, sic ut illi uitæ æternæ, isti igni sempiterno adiudicētur: deinde totus hic orbis, & quicquid in illo est, igne concremabitur, quæ de re uide 2.Pet.ult. Hæc erit præsentis mundi catastrophe, mox resurrectionem mortuorum subsequutura. Hanc uidebimus omnes, pars cum horrore ac tremore incredibili, pars cum gaudio inedicibili: quandoquidem resurrectionem non præcedet, sed subsequetur. Qui hæc fore credunt, haudquaquam accommodabunt se perituro mundo, cuius finem appropinquare sciunt: sed ei potius, qui aduetu ac iudicio suo hæc omnia terminabit. Si scias domum, quam inhabitas, totam igne conflagraturam, & nescias quando id sit futurum, poteris ne secure in illa morari? poteris illam magnificare? poteris illi quos habes thesauros tuto concredere? poteris eam operosius ac sumptuosius construere & ornare? Si sapias nihil horum poteris, sed cogitabis potius de alia in qua securius agas. Atqui sic habitamus nos in hoc mundo, de quo usq; adeo certum est, quod sit igne concremandus, ut ea de re non modo sacræ, sed & ethnicorum literæ ante Christi natum prædixerint, unde est illud Ouidij Metamorph.i. Esse quoq; in fatis reminiscitur, affore tempus Quo mare, quo tellus, correptaq; regia cœli Ardeat, & mundi moles operosa laboret.
units.tr: ...and together with them reign in this world. That nothing of this kind is to be expected from fire... when he says, "Afterwards there will be the end." That is, afterwards this world will be brought to an end and finished, and this present state of all things will be taken out of the way. The apostle Peter speaks of this end when he says: "The end of all things will draw near." What this end of the world will be is recorded in other passages of Scripture. The world will not end by chance but with judgement, in which the good will be separated from the evil, and a final sentence will be pronounced on both, so that the one is adjudged to eternal life and the other to everlasting fire. Then this whole globe, and whatever is in it, will be burned up with fire; on this matter see 2 Pet. 3 at the end. This will be the catastrophe of the present world, which will follow soon after the resurrection of the dead. We shall all see it, some with horror and incredible trembling, others with unspeakable joy, since it will not precede the resurrection but follow it. Those who believe these things will by no means accommodate themselves to a world that is perishing, whose end they know to be near, but rather to him who will bring all these things to an end by his coming and judgement. If you knew that the house in which you live was going to be totally burned with fire, and did not know when this would happen, could you dwell in it securely? Could you adorn it? Could you safely entrust to it the treasures you have? Could you build and decorate it more laboriously and expensively? If you were wise you could do none of these things, but would think rather of another house in which you might live more securely. Yet we live in this world, about which it is so certain that it is to be burned with fire, that the Scriptures, and also the writings of the heathen before Christ's birth, have foretold this matter. Hence that line of Ovid's Metamorphoses, book 1: "He also remembers that in the fates there is a time coming when the sea, the earth, and the royal vault of heaven, caught up, will burn, and the laborious frame of the world will suffer."

units.la: Obseruet uero pius lector, quomodo Apostolus hæc duo tribuat futuro Christi aduētui. Primum quod sit fideles suos ad uitam excitaturus: alterum, quod post illorum excitationē finem sit huic mundo impositurus. Vnde pulchre admonemur, quod mundus hic etiamnum durat, deberi electis ac pijs, propter quorū nu merum complendum protrahitur Christi aduentus, ad quem usque præsentem mundi statum durare oportet. Habentur fideles in hoc mundo uelut expurgamenta quædam. Verū nisi essent hæc expurgamenta, mox terminaretur omnis huius seculi impietas, malitia, superbia, & contumacia. Donec adhuc est triticum, in agro tolerantur zizania: quæ tum demum colliguntur, & in ignem iniiciuntur, quando triticum maturitate accepta, in horreū est collectum. Vt ager aratur ac seritur non propter zizania, sed propter triticum: ita zizania tolerantur in agro usq; ad messem, non propter se, sed propter absoluendam tritici maturitatem. Consimili modo conditus est hic mundus nō propter impios illius filios, sed propter electos: E & & tandiu per tolerantiâ Dei durat, donec nu-merus electorum compleatur, quorum complementum finem adferet mundo.
units.tr: The pious reader should observe how the Apostle assigns these two things to the future coming of Christ: first, that he will raise his faithful to life; second, that after their raising he will put an end to this world. From this we are finely reminded that this world still endures for the sake of the elect and the godly, on whose account the coming of Christ is delayed, and until which the present state of the world must endure. The faithful are in this world like a kind of refuse. But if these were not like refuse, all the impiety, wickedness, pride and obstinacy of this age would soon be brought to an end. While the wheat is still in the field, the tares are tolerated; these are gathered up and cast into the fire only when the wheat, having reached ripeness, has been collected into the barn. As the field is ploughed and sown not for the sake of the tares but for the sake of the wheat, so the tares are tolerated in the field until the harvest, not for their own sake but for the sake of bringing the wheat to full ripeness. In a similar way this world was made not on account of its ungodly sons but on account of the elect, and it endures by the forbearance of God only until the number of the elect is complete, and that completion will bring an end to the world.

units.la: CVM tradiderit, inquit, regnum Deo ac patri.]Dixerit quisquam: Si post resurrectionem fidelium finis erit mundi, quid fiat cum illis & Christo? quorsum excitabūtur? Cogitationis huius gratia docet iâ de mutatione regni Christi, ad quam sequentia pertinent: imò de illius complemento, ad quod est destinatum. Post resurrectionem fidelium, inquit, finis erit mūdi: sed ita, ut primum Christus, qui 1am sedens à dextris Dei regnū suū habet in electis, in hoc mŭdo, inq; illis per spiritū suū, fidem ac spem regnat: regnū hoc suū, regnū spiritus fidei ac spei Deo ac patri tradat: hoc est, remotis oībus impedimentis corruptæ naturæ, imperfectio nis, mortalitatis, Satanę, mundi, tribulationū, & quicquid horum est, Deo ac patri plenum ac perfectum sistat, ut nō amplius sit in electis suis ac filijs regni tanq̄ mediator & sacerdos per uerbum ac spiritum suum in fide ac spe regnaturus: sed illos ad perfectam uisionem, cognitionem, præsentiā, fruitione & claritatem Dei perducturus. Vsq; ad tempus consummationis omnium regnat Christus rex noster sacerdos ac mediator in suo populo, docens ac regenerans nos uerbo ac spiritu suo: & nos in illū credentes recōciliamurDeo, accedimusq; ad ipsum fide tanquam ad thronum gratiæ, ut misericordiam inueniamus: tandem per illū à mortuis excitamur, & ad ueram æternæ uitæ felicitatem trásferimur. Hoc regnum Christi regnum est gratiæ, quod post resurrectionem in regnum glorię mutabitur, in quo glorificati ac præsentes, coram, absq; ullis inuolucris faciem Dei patris nostri, perfectè felices cōtemplabimur. De hac mutatione regni Christi intelligit Apostolus, cum dicit: Cū tradiderit regnum Deo ac patri.
units.tr: "When he shall have handed over the kingdom to God and the Father." Someone might ask: if the end of the world is to come after the resurrection of the faithful, what will happen to them and to Christ? Why will they be raised? For the sake of this question, he teaches about the change of Christ's kingdom, to which what follows pertains; indeed about its completion, for which it was destined. After the resurrection of the faithful, he says, the end of the world will come; but first Christ, who now sits at the right hand of God and has his kingdom in the elect, reigns in this world, and in them through his Spirit, in faith and hope, should hand over this his kingdom, the kingdom of the Spirit of faith and hope, to God and the Father. That is, once all the hindrances of corrupt nature are removed (imperfection, mortality, Satan, the world, tribulations, and whatever of these there is), he will present it to God and the Father full and perfect, so that he will no longer reign in his elect and the sons of the kingdom as mediator and priest, through his Word and Spirit, in faith and hope; but he will lead them to the perfect vision, knowledge, presence, enjoyment and glory of God. Until the time of the consummation of all things, Christ our king, priest and mediator reigns in his people, teaching and regenerating us by his Word and Spirit; and we, believing in him, are reconciled to God, and approach him by faith as to the throne of grace, that we may find mercy; at last through him we are raised from the dead and transferred to the true blessedness of eternal life. This kingdom of Christ is a kingdom of grace, which after the resurrection will be changed into the kingdom of glory, in which, glorified and present, we shall contemplate the face of our Father God, perfectly blessed, openly and without any veils. It is of this change in Christ's kingdom that the Apostle speaks when he says: "When he shall have handed over the kingdom to God and the Father."

units.la: Sunt autē hic duo absurda cauenda. Vnū, ne dum audimus Christum regnū Deo ac patri traditurū, sentiamus illū postea non regnaturum amplius. Alterū, ne cogitemus iam non regnare Deum patrem: sed tum demū regnaturum, ubi regnum à Christo filio suo accepe-rit. Non separantur pater & filius. Regnat pater in filio, regnabit filius in patre. Qualitas tantum regni Dei mutabitur. Quemadmodū Moses dispensationem suam tradidit Christo, dū à litera facta est ad spiritum Christi œconomię Dei translatio: ita Christus regnū suum tradet Deo ac patri, cum nos à moderatione spiritus & conuersatione fidei ad manifestam cœlestis patris uisionem ac fruitionem transferet. Tūc fulgebunt iusti sicut sol, inquit Christus, Matthæi 13. in regno patris eorum. Et Lucæ 22. tamen idem illud regnum gloriæ uocat suū regnum, dicens: Disponō uobis sicut disposuit mihi pater meus regnum, ut edatis & bibatis super mensam meā in regno meo. Iohan. 14. dicit: In domo patris mei māsiones multæ sunt. Si quo minus, dixissem uobis, quia uado parare uobis locū. Et si abiero & præparauero uobis locū, iterum ueniam, & accipiā uos ad me ipsum, ut ubi sum ego, & uos sitis. Ergo sic tradet Christus Deo ac patri regnum, ut nos inducat in domū patris sui, sinusq; ibi cum ipso in uera uita ac felicitate sempiterna. Domus patris ipsum cœlū est. Huc nos trásferet Christus, ut cum ipso simus, uideamusq; claritatē ipsius, quam à patre ante mundi constitutione accepit. Iohan. 17.
units.tr: Two absurd ideas must be guarded against here. The first is that, when we hear that Christ will hand the kingdom over to God and the Father, we might think he will no longer reign at all afterwards. The second is that we might think God the Father does not reign now, but will begin to reign only when he has received the kingdom from his Son Christ. The Father and the Son are not separated. The Father reigns in the Son, and the Son will reign in the Father. Only the manner of God's reign will change. Just as Moses handed over his administration to Christ, when the transition was made from the letter to the spirit, from the economy of the law to the economy of Christ, so Christ will hand his kingdom over to God and the Father when he transfers us from the governance of the Spirit and the life of faith to the manifest vision and enjoyment of the heavenly Father. Then, Christ says, the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matthew 13). And in Luke 22 he nevertheless calls that same kingdom of glory his own, saying: I appoint for you a kingdom, as my Father has appointed one for me, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom. In John 14 he says: In my Father's house there are many dwelling places. If it were not so, I would have told you, for I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, that where I am, you may be also. Therefore Christ will hand the kingdom over to God and the Father in such a way that he brings us into his Father's house and bosom, to be with him there in true life and everlasting blessedness. The Father's house is heaven itself. Christ will bring us there, that we may be with him and see his glory, which he received from the Father before the foundation of the world (John 17).

units.la: Non est inconueniens sensus, quo nonnulli regnum hoc loco exponunt populum regni, electos uidelicet & fideles ut tradere regnum Deo ac patri sit illi tradere populum electorū. Et sic August. lib. 1. de Tri. cap. 7. accipisse uidetur, cum dicit: Quid ergo est: Cū tradiderit regnū Deo ac patri, quasi modo nō habeat regnū Deus & pater? Sed quia omnes iustos, in quibus nunc regnat ex fide uiuentibus mediator Dei & hominum homo Christus Iesus perducturus est ad speciem, quā uisione dicit idem Apostolus facie ad facie, ita dictū est: Cum tradiderit regnum Deo ac patri. ac si diceret, Cū perduxerit credentes ad contemplatione Dei & patris. Et aliquanto post: Cōtemplabimur enim, inquit, Deū patrē, & filium & spiritū sanctum, cum mediator Dei & hominum homo Christus Iesus, tradiderit regnū Deo ac patri, ut iā nō interpellet pro nobis mediator & sacerdos noster filius Dei & filius hominis, &c. Hæc ille. Ambros. sic exponit: Traditio hęc est regni, ut cum omnia filio fuerint subiecta, & adorauerint illum ut Deum, destructa morte, tunc filius ostendet illis se non esse ex quo omnia, sed per quem sunt omnia. Et hoc erit tradere regnum Deo ac patri, ostendere ipsum esse ex quo omnis paternitas in cœlis & in terra nominatur. Hæc ille.
units.tr: The sense which some give to the word kingdom in this passage is not unsuitable: that the kingdom means the people of the kingdom, namely the elect and the faithful, so that to hand the kingdom over to God and the Father is to hand over the people of the elect. Augustine seems to have understood it this way in book 1 of On the Trinity, chapter 7, when he says: What then is the meaning of "when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father," as though God and the Father did not now have a kingdom? But because the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, is going to bring to the sight of God all the righteous, in whom he now reigns over those who live by faith, that sight which the same Apostle calls "face to face," it is said: "When he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father," as though he were saying: "When he has brought believers to the contemplation of God and the Father." And a little later: "For we shall contemplate," he says, "God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, when the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, has delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father, so that the mediator and our priest, the Son of God and the Son of man, no longer intercedes for us," and so on. Thus he. Ambrose explains it thus: This handing over of the kingdom is such that, when all things have been subjected to the Son and have worshipped him as God, death being destroyed, the Son will then show them that he is not the one from whom all things are, but the one through whom all things are. And this will be to hand the kingdom over to God and the Father: to show that he himself is the one from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named. Thus he.

units.la: Chrysost. exponit: Cum tradiderit regnum Deo ac patri: id est, cum regnū Dei uelut è ma nu Satanæ, mundi & aduersariorum omnium uindicauerit, illisq; deletis omnibus plenū ac integrū Deo & patri restituerit. Satan sane per inductionē peccati regnū Dei inuasit, deq; illo usq; adeo magnam sibi partē uindicauit, ut à Christo princeps mundi & ab hoc Apostolo Deus huius mundi sit dictus. Huic seruit ipsa nostra caro, per peccatū illi mancipata: seruit illi quicquid sublime est in hoc mundo, sapientes, principatus, potestates ac uirtutes, ac totus reliquus mundus in maligno positus. Seruit illi mors per peccatum inducta, unā cū omnis generis calamitatibus & corruptione. Cū sic regnaret in genere humano hostis antiquus suis satellitibus, missus est filius Dei in mundum, factusq; carnis nostræ particeps, p peccatis nostris moritur, quo per mortem debellaret eum qui mortis habebat imperiū: resurgit, ut esset primitiæ mortuorū: cœlos ascēdit sedetq; ad dexteram patris, quo & suos in mundo uirtute spiritus ac uerbi sui regat, & inimicos regni sui uelut scabellū pedibus suis subijciat: id quod & facit, nec facere desinet, donec omni aduersaria potestate Satanæ, peccati, mortis, mundi, &c. sublata regnum Deo ac patri in integrũ, quale fuit ab initio: imò multo adhuc augustius ac perfectius, restituat. Futurum hoc est per ipsius aduetum, ubi mortuos excitauerit, mundum iudicauerit ac terminauerit, electos sibi coniunxerit, &in cœleste gloriam ac felicitatem transtulerit, Satanam uero cum omni suo satellitio, impiorumq; multitudine ignibus sempiternis adiudicauerit, & omnem hanc cœli ac terræ machinam, rebellione malorum spirituum, & hominum inde ab initio præuaricationis prophanatam ac pollutã immisso cœlitus igne repurgauerit, cœlumq; nouũ ac terram nouam, in qua iustitia in sempiternum habitet, reddiderit. Hæc utiq; pertinent omnia ad regni Dei plenam ac perfectã restitutionē: qua fiat, ut Deus sit omnia in omnibus, cuius pars magna per primum Christi aduentum cœpit, perfectio uerò in secundum est reseruata. Ad hanc certè regni Dei plenitudinem, propter quam filius Dei uenit in hunc mundum: iam in cœlis regnat, ac tandem in fine est rediturus: extendi debent cordium nostrorum uota, cum in oratione dominica dicimus: Pater noster qui es in cœlis, sanctificetur nomen tuum, ueniat regnum tuum, fiat uoluntas tua sicut in cœlo & in terra.
units.tr: Chrysostom explains: "When he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father" means: when he has rescued the kingdom of God, as it were, from the hand of Satan, of the world and of all adversaries, and, with all of these destroyed, has restored it whole and complete to God and the Father. Satan, to be sure, by inducing sin, invaded the kingdom of God, and claimed for himself so large a part of it that by Christ he is called the prince of this world, and by this Apostle the god of this world. Our very flesh serves him, having been sold to him through sin. Whatever is lofty in this world serves him: the wise, the principalities, the powers and the virtues, and the whole rest of the world which lies in evil. Death, brought in through sin, serves him, together with every kind of calamity and corruption. When the ancient enemy, with his henchmen, reigned thus over the human race, the Son of God was sent into the world, and, having become a sharer in our flesh, died for our sins, so that by his death he might overthrow him who held the power of death. He rose again, that he might be the firstfruits of those who have died. He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father, where he rules his own in the world by the power of his Spirit and his word, and places his enemies under his feet as a footstool. This he does, and does not cease to do, until, with every adverse power of Satan, of sin, of death, of the world, and so on, removed, he restores the kingdom of God to the Father entire, as it was from the beginning, indeed even more glorious and more perfect than before. This will come about through his coming, when he raises the dead, judges the world and brings it to an end, joins his elect to himself, and transfers them to heavenly glory and blessedness; and when he has condemned Satan with all his henchmen, and the multitude of the wicked, to everlasting fires, he will cleanse this whole machinery of heaven and earth, profaned and polluted by the rebellion of evil spirits and of men from the beginning of the transgression, with fire sent from heaven, and will render a new heaven and a new earth, in which righteousness will dwell forever. All these things pertain to the full and perfect restoration of the kingdom of God, by which it comes about that God may be all in all. A great part of this began with the first coming of Christ; its perfection is reserved for the second. Toward this fullness of the kingdom of God, for which the Son of God came into this world, and who now reigns in heaven and will at last return at the end, our hearts' desires ought to be stretched out, when in the Lord's Prayer we say: "Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven."

units.la: C V M aboleuerit, inquit, omnem principatum, & omnem potestatem & uirtutem.] Exponit quomodo & quando sit Christus Deo ac patri regnum traditurus. Cum aboleuerit, inquit, omnem principatũ, potestatem, & uirtutem. Hoc est, cum effecerit ut nō sit amplius ullus princeps, ulla potestas, ulla uirtus, nec in cœlo nec in terra, nisi Deus unus, omnia existens in omnibus. Alij de ordinibus archangelorum & angelorum: alij de principatu, dominio, ac uirtute malorum spirituũ, alij de principatibus, potestatibus, ac uirtutibus huius mundi exponunt. Quid de omnibus istis futurum sit in fine mundi, satis patet credentibus. Manebunt quidem angeli, uerum non erit illorum usus is qui in hac est uita. Mali spiritus pœnis æternis dabuntur. Principes ac potentatus huius mundi alij sunt regno Dei inimici & aduersarij, alij seruant usum magistratus à domino constitutum. In fine mundi nec iusti nec iniusti principes & magistratus manebūt, sed abolebuntur omnes. Iustorũ non erit amplius ullus. Quia non erūt mali qui puniātur, nec ea erit conditio bonorum, ut opus habeat defensione magistratus. Iniusti cum principe suo Satana exterminabuntur. Ergo in uniuersum abolebitur omnis principatus, omnis potestas & uirtus. Verum, meo iudicio, loquitur hic Apostolus de principibus, potestatibus, & uirtutibus regno Dei aduersarijs & inimicis, qualis est principatus malorum spirituum, & impiorum tyrannorum, Deo ac Christo eius aduersantiũ, de quorũ rebellione finaliq; exterminio Psalmus 2. canit ac uaticinatur.
units.tr: "When he shall have abolished," he says, "all principality and all power and might." Here he explains how and when Christ will hand the kingdom over to God and the Father. "When he shall have abolished," he says, "all principality, power and might"; that is, when he has brought it about that there is no longer any prince, any power, any might, either in heaven or on earth, except God alone, who is all in all. Others explain these as the orders of archangels and angels; others as the principality, dominion and power of evil spirits; others as the principalities, powers and virtues of this world. What will become of all these at the end of the world is sufficiently clear to believers. The angels will indeed remain, but their use will not be that which it is in this life. Evil spirits will be given over to eternal punishments. Some princes and potentates of this world are enemies and adversaries of the kingdom of God, while others maintain the function of magistrate instituted by the Lord. At the end of the world neither the righteous nor the unrighteous princes and magistrates will remain, but all will be abolished. There will be no more of the righteous, since there will be no wicked to be punished, and the condition of the good will not be such as to need the defence of the magistrate. The unrighteous will be destroyed together with their prince Satan. Therefore every principality, every power and might will be abolished altogether. But in my judgment, the Apostle here speaks of the princes, powers and might which are adversaries and enemies of the kingdom of God, such as the principality of evil spirits and of wicked tyrants who oppose God and his Christ; concerning whose rebellion and final destruction the second Psalm sings and prophesies.

units.la: Non est autem ut anxiè quæramus, quomo do principatum, potestatem, & uirtutem distinguamus. Qui referunt ista ad magistratus seculares, sic diuidunt ut ἀρχὰ, id est, principatus sit eorum, qui merum habent imperium: ἐξουσία uero, id est, potestas, eorum qui quam habent potestatē, à principe aliquo acceperunt: quales sunt præsides, præfecti, iudices, œconomi, &c. ἀνάμεις uero, id est, uirtus, ministrorum, satellitum, militum, lictorum, &c. Verum hæ uoces nonnunquam accipiũtur de cœlestibus ac bonis spiritibus, ut Eph. 3. aliquando de malis spiritibus, ut Eph. 6. & Coloss. 2. aliquando de magistratibus huius seculi, ut Tit. 3. Quare simplicius esse puto, ut sentiamus per eas significari quicquid potens & sublime est, siue inter spiritus aduersarios, siue inter impios huius seculi tyrannos.
units.tr: There is no need to fret over how exactly we should distinguish principality, power and virtue. Those who refer these terms to secular magistrates divide them thus: ἀρχὰ [archē], that is, principality, belongs to those who hold full authority (merum imperium); ἐξουσία [exousia], that is, power, belongs to those who hold a power they have received from some prince, such as governors, prefects, judges, stewards, and so on; and ἀνάμεις [dynameis], that is, virtue, belongs to ministers, attendants, soldiers, lictors, and so on.
