But these words are sometimes used of heavenly and good spirits, as in Eph. 3; sometimes of evil spirits, as in Eph. 6 and Col. 2; and sometimes of the magistrates of this age, as in Tit. 3. So I think it is simpler to understand by them whatever is mighty and exalted, whether among the hostile spirits or among the impious tyrants of this world.

units.la: NAM oportet eũ regnare, donec posuerit omnes inimicos sub pedes suos.] Reddit rationem præcedentis: quare tum demum tradeturus sit Deo ac patri regnum, ubi aboleuerit omnem principatum, potestatem ac uirtutē, & non magis quod in fine mundi facturus est, mox à mortuis excitatus fecerit. Quia sic, inquit, constitutum est, ut ipse filius regno potiatur, donec omnem aduersariam potestatem & potentiā, omnes regni Dei inimicos pedibus suis subijciat: hoc est prorsus opprimat, ac tum demum perfectum Deo ac patri regnum tradat. Omnimoda autem inimicorum obolitio ante finem præsentis mundi futura non est: Quare nec regnum Deo ac patri tradet, donec durat hic mundus.
units.tr: "For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet." He gives the reason for the preceding statement: why the Son will only then hand the kingdom over to God the Father, once he has abolished every principality, power and virtue, and not merely when, having been raised from the dead, he does at the end of the world what he is about to do. For, he says, it has been so decreed that the Son himself should hold the kingdom until he subjects to his feet every hostile power and might, every enemy of the kingdom of God; that is, until he utterly crushes them, and then at last delivers to God the Father a perfected kingdom. But the complete destruction of the enemies will not happen before the end of the present world. Therefore he will not hand the kingdom over to God the Father as long as this world endures.

units.la: Respicit autem ad id quod de regno Christi Psalmo 110. prædictum est ad hunc modum: Dixit dominus domino meo sede à dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorū: propter quam irrefragabilē diuini consilij constitutionem dicit Christū oportere regnare, donec posuerit omnes inimicos sub pedes suos. De oraculo autem Psalmi huius diximus in Commentarijs nostris super Psalmos Dauidis.
units.tr: He is, however, looking back to what was foretold in Psalm 110 about the kingdom of Christ, in this way: "The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." On account of this unshakeable constitution of the divine counsel, he says that Christ must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. I have discussed the oracle of this Psalm in our commentaries on the Psalms of David.

units.la: DONEC posuerit, inquit, omnes inimicos sub pedes suos.) Nam oportet eum, inquit, regnare. Quandiu? Donec, inquit, posuerit omnes inimicos sub pedes suos. Ergo ubi posuerit inimicos omnes sub pede suos, non opor tebit Christū regnare amplius? Sic sonant uerba. Nec est sensus incommodus, si ad qualitatem regni, & rationem hic adiectam respicias. Non enim erit necesse, ut postquam posuerit inimicos omnes sub pedes suos, Satanam cū membris suis æternis pœnis mancipauerit, fideles suos à mortuis excitauerit, mundum iudicauerit ac terminauerit, atq; ita restitutis omnibus Deo ac patri regnum integrū ac perfectum tradiderit, adhuc eo modo quo nūc, & ad eum finem ad quem nunc, posthæc omnia regnet. Hinc non sequitur, fore illum postea regni hæreditate & gloria exclusum. Regnabit cum patre in sempiternum, uerum alio regnandi modo, quàm quo nunc in medio inimicorum regnat. Quare quod Apostolus dicit: Nā oportet eum regnare, donec posuerit omnes inimicos sub pedes suos, non sic est accipiendum, quasi propter uoculam, donec, concludedum sit, ergo postea omni regno destituetur. Sed hac de re in Commentarijs nostris super Psal. 110. nonnulla diximus.
units.tr: "UNTIL he has put," he says, "all his enemies under his feet." "For he must," he says, "reign." How long? "Until," he says, "he has put all his enemies under his feet." Therefore, when he has put all his enemies under his feet, will Christ no longer have to reign? That is what the words sound like. Nor is the sense awkward, if you consider the nature of the kingdom and the reason added here. For it will not be necessary that, after he has put all his enemies under his feet, has consigned Satan with his members to eternal punishments, has raised his faithful from the dead, has judged and ended the world, and so, all things having been restored, has handed over to God the Father a full and perfect kingdom, he should still reign afterwards in the same way and to the same end as now. From this it does not follow that he will afterwards be excluded from the inheritance and glory of the kingdom. He will reign with the Father for ever, but in a different manner from that in which he now reigns in the midst of his enemies. So what the Apostle says, "For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet," is not to be taken as if, because of the little word "until," it must be concluded that he will afterwards be deprived of all kingdom. We have said some things about this matter in our commentaries on Psalm 110.

units.la: DONEC posuerit, inquit.] In Psalmo est עַד אֲשֶׁר, id est, donec ponam. Sic loquitur pater filio: Sede ad dextram meā (quod Apostolus hic regnare uocat) donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Apostolus uero: Nam oportet eū regnare, inquit, donec posuerit omnes inimicos sub pedes suos. quibus uerbis ipsi Christo opus subijciendi inimicos tribuit, quod Dauid tribuit patri. Et tamē nihil est diuersi. Pater enim in regno filij sui operatur, & simul operatur ipse filius. Pater meus usque modo, inquit, operatur, & ego operor. Regnat pater, regnat cū patre filio. Subijcit inimicos pater filij sui pedib. subijcit cum patre filio.
units.tr: "UNTIL he has put," he says. In the Psalm the Hebrew is עַד אֲשֶׁר [ad asher], that is, "until I put." So the Father speaks to the Son: "Sit at my right hand" (which the Apostle here calls reigning), "until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." But the Apostle says: "For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet." By these words he attributes to Christ himself the work of subduing the enemies, which David attributes to the Father. And yet there is no difference. For the Father works in the kingdom of his Son, and at the same time the Son himself works. "My Father," he says, "works until now, and I work." The Father reigns; the Father and the Son reign together. The Father puts his Son's enemies under his Son's feet; he subdues them together with the Son.

units.la: OMNES inimicos, inquit.] Quoniā partia cula hæc rationis uice subiecta est præcedenti, qua dixit, cū aboleuerit omnè principatū, potestatem & uirtutem, cōsequens est, ut potisimū de illis inimicis Christi loquatur, qui sunt potentes, utpote principes, potestates & uirtutes. Subijciet sibi quidem omnes inimicos, at istos potisimū, qui & plus regno illius aduersantur, & quorum subiectio plus habet argumenti de diuina regnantis Christi uirtute. Ex minutorum hostium oppressione parum est cœlesti regi laudis & glorię. Ipsum Satanam & ipsos principes & potentatus huius mundi ui cisse, ac pedibus substrauisse, id demum cœlestis habet uirtutis argumentum.
units.tr: "ALL his enemies," he says. Since this clause is added as a reason for what precedes, where he said that when he has abolished every principality, power and virtue, it follows that he speaks chiefly of those enemies of Christ who are mighty, namely principalities, powers and virtues. Indeed he will subdue all his enemies, but chiefly those who oppose his kingdom most, and whose subjection gives the greatest proof of the divine power of the reigning Christ. The overthrow of lesser foes brings little praise and glory to the heavenly King. That he has conquered Satan himself and the princes and potentates of this world, and placed them beneath his feet, that is the true proof of heavenly power.

units.la: Non debemus autem in classem inimicorum Christi eos tantum reijcere qui sunt illius hostes ex professo, qualis est ipse Satan, & mundi huius tyranni, Nero, Maximinus, Diocletian, Iulianus, Iudæi, Turci & consimiles alij: sed & apostolos Satanæ transfigurantes se in apostolos Christi, falsos pastores, falsos doctores, falsos episcopos, & cum primis Antichristū, qui cum se pro vicario Christi venditet, ex diametro Christo aduersatur, cuius veritate & eccle siam olim hypocrisi, nunc quæstu & tyrannide opprimit. Si diligis me, inquit ad Petrum dominus, pasce oues meas. Ergo amicus Christi esse declaratur, qui oues illius fideliter pascit. E contrario igitur inimicus Christi comprobatur, qui oues illius uorat & perdit. Nocentissimum hoc est inimicorum genus, quod sub specie amicitiæ gerit ea quæ sunt inimici, ac nomine Christi contra Christum abutitur. Merito infra alios Christi inimicos ad ima inferorū detrudentur, cuius supplicij uates iam olim in ecclesia coeperunt esse pictores, qui in pictura extremi iudicij Papas, cardinales, episcopos, prælatos, abbates, &c. in ipso fundo inferorū ipectandos omnibus proposuerunt.
units.tr: We ought not, however, to count among the enemies of Christ only those who are his avowed foes, such as Satan himself and the tyrants of this world, Nero, Maximinus, Diocletian, Julian, the Jews, the Turks and other like ones; but also the apostles of Satan who transform themselves into apostles of Christ, false ministers, false teachers, false bishops, and above all Antichrist, who, while he puts himself forward as the vicar of Christ, is diametrically opposed to Christ, and who oppresses the Church with his falsehood, first with hypocrisy and now with profit and tyranny. "If you love me," the Lord said to Peter, "feed my sheep." Therefore he is shown to be a friend of Christ who faithfully feeds his sheep. On the contrary, then, he is proved to be an enemy of Christ who devours and destroys his sheep. This is the most harmful kind of enemy, who under the appearance of friendship does the things that belong to enemies and abuses the name of Christ against Christ. Deservedly, among the other enemies of Christ, they will be thrust down to the depths of the underworld; and the prophets of this punishment have long since begun to be painters in the Church, who in their pictures of the last judgment have set before everyone, to be looked upon in the very bottom of hell, popes, cardinals, bishops, prelates, abbots, and so on.

units.la: SVB pedes suos, inquit.] Non dicit simpliciter, donec uicerit: sed, donec sub pedes suos posuerit inimicos suos omnes. Ergo non simpliciter reprimentur inimici Christi, ut nō pos sint efficere quę uolunt, sed & in ipsam Christi potestatem tradetur, imò sub pedes illius abijcientur ac proculcabūtur, unde in sempiternū consurgere nō poterunt. His enim uerbis omnimodam suppressionē notat Apostolus. Cogitet ergo pius lector, q pacatus sit ac tranquillus futurus post resurrectionem electorū ac fidelium status. Ibi nemo erit qui noceat in monte sancto Dei, propterea quod deleti erūt omnes impij, reprobi & inimici, qui nūc non terra modo, sed & ipsū cœlū subuersuri uidentur.
units.tr: "Under his feet," he says. He does not simply say "until he has conquered," but "until he has put all his enemies under his feet." So Christ's enemies will not merely be restrained so that they cannot carry out their wishes. They will be handed over into Christ's own power, or rather cast down beneath his feet and trampled, so that they can never rise again for eternity. By these words the Apostle marks a complete suppression. Let the godly reader consider how peaceful and tranquil the state of the elect and faithful will be after the resurrection. There will be no one there who harms "in my holy mountain," because all the ungodly, reprobate and enemies will be destroyed, those who now seem ready to overturn not only the earth but heaven itself.

units.la: NOVISSIMVS aūt hostis aboletur mors.] Non loquitur de morte æterna, quæ uitę est æternæ opposita; sed de morte corporis, quæ post resurrectionē non habebit locū amplius. Dixit Christum aboliturū omnè principatum, potestatem, & uirtutem. Illis adiungit & mortem, cōnumerans eam inimicis Christi.
units.tr: "The last enemy to be abolished is death." He is not speaking of eternal death, which is opposed to eternal life, but of bodily death, which will no longer have any place after the resurrection. He had said that Christ will abolish every principality, power and virtue. To these he adds death, counting it among Christ's enemies.

units.la: Sed quæri poterit, quomodo eam uocet hostē Christi, cum sit à Deo tanq poena ac stipendium diu peccati iustissimo iudicio imposita. Quis nam adeo desipit, ut lictorem & supplicia sceleratorum inter hostes regis iudicium & iustitiam exercentis connumeret? Respondeo. Est quidem a Deo mors homini peccatori iusto iudicio imposita: uerum haud ab illo facta, secundum illud Sap.1. Deus mortem non fecit. Nec delectatur illa Deus. Dicit enim: Nolo morte peccatoris, Ezec.18. Et: Nec delectatur perditione filiorum hominum, Sap.1. Quare nihil hinc est impedimenti, quo minus certis de causis habenda sit inter hostes Christi. Primum, si originem illius inspicias, per inuidiam diaboli introducta est in mundum, Sap.2. & per peccatum, Rom.5. Igitur ipsa illius origo ea quae hostis sunt spirat. Deinde si consideres illius naturam & opus, aduersatur operi conditoris. Destruit enim eos, quos Deus ad gloriam nominis sui condidit. Qua ob causam filius Dei missus est in mundum, ut & causam & opus illius, una cum ipsa aboleret. Quare & hactenus recte hostis Christi censetur. Tertio, accedit & iniquitas, qua seruit imperio diaboli, hostis & aduersarij Dei, dum interimit innocentes & iustos. Unde & Apostolus Ebraeorum 2. Christum carnis nostrae participem esse factum dicit, ut per mortem destrueret diabolum, qui mortis habebat imperium. Sic diabolo seruiuit mox initio in parricidio Cain, cum ille fratre suum Habelem iustum ac pium occideret. Sic seruiuit illi interimendo prophetas, Christum, apostolos, martyres, & innumeros alios iustos & innocentes. Itaque propter originem suam, naturam, & iniquitatem hostis Christi est. Ergo uicissim Christus illius quoque est inimicus.
units.tr: But someone may ask how the Apostle can call death an enemy of Christ, since it was imposed by God as the punishment and wages of sin, by the most just judgment. Who is so foolish as to count the executioner and the punishments of criminals among the enemies of a king who exercises judgment and justice? I answer: death is indeed imposed on sinful man by God through a just judgment, but it was not made by him, according to that saying in Wisdom 1: "God did not make death; nor does he take pleasure in it." For he says, "I do not desire the death of the sinner" (Ezek. 18), and, "nor does he delight in the destruction of the sons of men" (Wisd. 1). Therefore nothing prevents death from being rightly reckoned among the enemies of Christ, for certain reasons. First, if you look at its origin, it was brought into the world through the envy of the devil (Wisd. 2) and through sin (Rom. 5). So its very origin breathes what is hostile. Second, if you consider its nature and work, it opposes the work of the Creator, for it destroys those whom God created for the glory of his name. For this reason the Son of God was sent into the world, to abolish both its cause and its work together with itself. Therefore death is rightly regarded as an enemy of Christ up to this point. Third, there is also its wickedness, by which it serves the rule of the devil, the enemy and adversary of God, while it kills the innocent and the just. Hence the Apostle in Hebrews 2 says that Christ became a partaker of our flesh, so that through death he might destroy the devil, who held the power of death. So death served the devil from the very beginning, in the murder of Abel by Cain, when that one killed his brother Abel, who was just and godly. So it served him by killing the prophets, Christ, the apostles, the martyrs, and countless other just and innocent people. Therefore, because of its origin, its nature and its wickedness, death is an enemy of Christ. Conversely, then, Christ is also its enemy.

units.la: Deinde quaerendum est, quomodo uocet eam Apostolus nouissimum hostem. Vulgata habet aduerbialiter: Nouissime autem inimica destruetur mors, quasi in Graeco sit ἔσχατος, id est, nouissime: postremo, cum sit nominaliter ἔσχατος, id est, nouissimus hostis aboletur mors. Esse autem mortem nouissimum hostem, a Christo abolendum, bifariam exponitur.
units.tr: Next we must ask why the Apostle calls it the last enemy. The Vulgate has it as an adverb: "But last of all the enemy death will be destroyed," as if the Greek were [ἔσχατος], that is, "lastly, at last." But here the word is used as a noun, [ἔσχατος], that is, "the last enemy, death, is abolished." Now that death is the last enemy to be abolished by Christ is explained in two ways.

units.la: Primum, propterea quod sit post diabolum & peccatum, omnisque generis srumnas postremo loco inducta. Deinde, propterea quod cesante peccato, carnis nostrae malicia, Satana, mundo, mors sola omnes nos sub clausTris suis ad ipsum usque resurrectionis diem captiuos tenet. Sane dum morimur qui sumus in Christo, liberi sumus ab omnibus infestationibus Satanae, peccati, carnis nostrae, & mundi, ut nihil in nos possint amplius. Verum nondum sumus liberi ab ultimo hoste, morte uidelicet, quos tenet captiuos usque ad ultimum diem, qui resurrectionis est & iudicij. Utroque sensu mors est ultimus hostis. Ultimus exortu, ultimus post alios perdurando. Potest de eo quoque cogitari, quod omnium eorum quae homini contingunt in hoc mundo ultimum locum sortita mors est. Unde ille recte dixit: Mors ultima linea rerum est. Et philosophus, ultimum terribilium mors est. Si ultimum terribilium, igitur
units.tr: First, because it comes after the devil and sin, and is introduced last of all the troubles of every kind. Second, because when sin has ceased, death alone holds all of us captive under its bars until the very day of resurrection, namely, the flesh of our nature, Satan, and the world. Indeed, while we who are in Christ die, we are freed from all the assaults of Satan, sin, our flesh and the world, so that they can have no further power over us. But we are not yet free from the final enemy, death, which holds us captive until the last day, the day of resurrection and judgment. In either sense death is the last enemy: last in its arising, and last in enduring after the others. We may also consider that, of all the things that happen to man in this world, death holds the last place. Hence someone rightly said: "Death is the final boundary of things." And the philosopher: "The last of terrible things is death." If it is the last of terrible things, then [it is] also the last enemy.

units.la: & ultimus hostis. Tertio, nec illud transeundum est, quod cum dicendum uideretur, abolebitur mors: dicit in praesenti, aboletur mors. Est enim in Graeco καταργεῖται, id est, aboletur: uulgata habet in futuro, destruetur. In posteriore ad Timotheum cap.1. legimus in praeterito, qui mortem quidem aboleuit, uitam autem in lucem produxit. Et infra hoc praesenti capite: Cum corruptibile hoc induerit incorruptibilitatem, & mortale hoc induerit immortalitate, tunc fiet sermo qui scriptus est, Absorpta est mors in uictoria. Ergo morte Christus, ultimum hostem, & aboleuit, & abolet, & abolebit. Aboleuit in cruce pro peccatis nostris moriedo, non ut amplius non esset, sed ne posthac fideles perderet: abolet quotidie, dum suos per mortem traducit in uitam, & abolebit in uniuersum in fine mundi. Quae abolitio bifariam fiet. Primum mortuos omnes ex ipsis mortis claustris ac penetralibus eruedo & excitado quod per mortuorum resurrectione fiet.
units.tr: Third, we must not pass over the fact that where one would expect "death will be abolished," the Apostle says in the present tense, "death is abolished." In Greek it is [καταργεῖται], that is, "is abolished"; the Vulgate has the future, "will be destroyed." In the letter to Timothy, chapter 1, we read in the past tense: "who indeed abolished death, but brought life to light." And later in this same chapter: "When this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory." Therefore Christ has abolished, is abolishing, and will abolish death, the last enemy. He abolished it on the cross by dying for our sins, not so that it would no longer exist, but so that it would not destroy the faithful from then on. He abolishes it daily, as he leads his own from death into life, and he will abolish it completely at the end of the world. This abolition will happen in two ways: first, by raising all the dead from the very barriers and innermost chambers of death, which will happen through the resurrection of the dead.

units.la: Deinde, excitatos ad uitam immortalitatis gloria induendo, ut in sempiternum uiuentes mortem nunquam sint gustaturi amplius, impleaturque illud Apoc. 21. Mors ultra non erit. Neutrum possibile est ulli humanae potentiae, imo ne angelicae quidem. Nemo mortuus ad uitam redire, & si redeat per impossibile, efficere potest ne denuo moriatur. Omnia haec, quae ad abolitionem mortis pertinent unius Christi uiribus facta sunt, fiunt quotidie, & perficetur prorsus in fine mundi. Haec est fides Christiana qua a cunctis totius orbis nationibus diuidimur, quae nec Christum, nec uirtutem eius agnoscentes resurrectionem mortuorum & mortis abolitionem irridet. Quare quod illis merum uidetur esse nugamentum, nobis credentib.in omni humanae uitae miseria contra omnis generis afflictiones, contra Satanam, peccatum morte ac mundu, summum est & unicum solatium.
units.tr: Second, by clothing those raised to life with the glory of immortality, so that living forever they will never again taste death, and the saying of Revelation 21 will be fulfilled: "Death will be no more." Neither of these is possible for any human power, nor even for an angelic one. No dead man can return to life, and even if he returns, by an impossibility, he cannot make sure that he will not die again. All these things that pertain to the abolition of death were done by the power of Christ alone, are done daily, and will be fully completed at the end of the world. This is the Christian faith, by which we are divided from all the nations of the whole world; they neither acknowledge Christ nor his power, and they mock the resurrection of the dead and the abolition of death. So what seems to them sheer nonsense is, for us who believe, the highest and only comfort in every misery of human life, against every kind of affliction, against Satan, sin, death and the world.

units.la: NAM omnia subiecit sub pedes illius. Supra usus est oraculo Dei, qd habetur Psal.110. quo comprobaret futurum, ut omnem principatum, potestate & uirtute aboleret Christus. Hic eiusdem argumenti gratia, cum dixisset, Nouissimus hostis aboletur mors: inducit sententiam hac generale ex Psalmo octauo, Nam omnia subiecit sub pedes illius, quae quomodo Christo competat, cum Psal. ille de dignitate primi hominis a Deo concessa canat, in Comment. nostris super Psal. annotauimus. Si uerba Psalmi sequentia & praecedentia inspicias, & ad argumentum quod tractat Apostolus coferas, uidebitur haec particula uel per catachresim adducta, uel non esse ex dicto Psal. desumpta, sed libero spiritu ab Apostolo prolata, id quod nonnullis recentioribus sentiendum esse uidetur. Habent enim uerba Psal.ad hunc modum: Constituisti eum dominatorem super opera manuum tuarum, omnia subiecisti sub pedes eius oues & boues omnes, & pecudes agri, uolucres caeli, & pisces maris, qui perambulant semitas maris. Haec Psal. quae si
units.tr: "For he has put all things under his feet." Above, the Apostle used the oracle of God found in Psalm 110, by which he proved that Christ would abolish every principality, power and virtue. Now, for the same purpose, after saying "the last enemy, death, is abolished," he introduces a general statement from Psalm 8: "For he has put all things under his feet." How this applies to Christ, since that psalm sings of the dignity granted by God to the first man, we noted in our commentaries on the Psalms. If you look at the words of the psalm that come before and after, and compare them with the subject the Apostle is treating, this clause will seem either to be brought in by catachresis, or not to be taken from the psalm, but uttered by the Apostle under the free impulse of the Spirit, which some more recent writers seem to think. The words of the psalm read as follows: "You have made him ruler over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet: sheep and oxen, all of them, and the beasts of the field, the birds of the heavens, and the fish of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea." This psalm, if

units.la: sola uelis Christo tribuere, haud faciét ad plenitudinem potestatis à patre acceptę exprimédam. Apostolus uero disserit hic de potestate Christi in cœlo regnantis, & ad iudicandum ui uos & mortuos in fine mundi rediturì, qua fit omnem principatum, potestatem & uirtutem, aboliturus, & omnes inimicos pedib. suis subiecturus, quibus & mortem táquam ultimum hostem connumerat. Huc uidetur impertinen ter adduci subiectio operum Dei, ouium, boū, pecudum agri, uolucrum cœli, ac piscium maris quæ in uius sunt humanæ sustentationis dinatione primo homini subiecta. Inimici Christi, quos pater illius pedibus proterendos & abolendos subijcit, non pertinet in clas sem operum manuum Dei, sed ad opera Satanæ. Quare, quemadmodum diximus, aut per catachresim Apostolus generalem hanc particulam relictis praecedentibus & sequentibus ex memorato Psal. aut de suo attulit. De suo autem attulisse haud apparet, propter sequentia, quibus dicit: Atqui quum dicit, quod omnia subiecta sint, palam est excipiendum esse eum, qui subiecit illi omnia: unde puto, satis liquet quod locum scripturæ adduxerit. Quomodo autem in ea quæ ad Hebræos est cap. 2. locum hunc Psal. iam dicti Christo accommodet, diximus in ipsius Psal. Commentariis.
units.tr: you wish to attribute it to Christ alone, will not serve to express the fullness of power received from the Father. But the Apostle here discusses the power of Christ reigning in heaven, and about to return to judge the living and the dead at the end of the world, by which he will abolish every principality, power and virtue, and subject all enemies under his feet, among which he also counts death as the last enemy. The subjection of the works of God, of sheep, oxen, beasts of the field, birds of the heavens and fish of the sea, which were subjected to the first man in the ordering of human sustenance, seems to be brought in here without relevance. The enemies of Christ, whom the Father subjects under his feet to be trampled and abolished, do not belong to the class of the works of God's hands, but to the works of Satan. Therefore, as we said, the Apostle either by catachresis took this general clause from the aforementioned psalm, leaving aside what precedes and follows, or he added it of his own. That he added it of his own does not appear, because of what follows, where he says: "But when he says that all things are subjected, it is plain that the one who subjected all things to him must be excepted." So I think it is quite clear that he cited a passage of Scripture. How he applies this psalm, already mentioned, to Christ in the second chapter of Hebrews, we have explained in our commentaries on that psalm itself.

units.la: Obseruet autem prius lector, quàm pertinen ter accommodetur præsenti causæ generalis hæc particula: omnia subiecit sub pedes eius. Data est Christo omnis potestas in cœlo & in terra & tradita sunt ei à patre omnia. Verum diuersimode, alio uidelicet atq; alio fine. Quædam tradita accepit ut tanquâ redemptor, mediator, ac seruator seruet. Sic oues habet accepltas à patre, quas nemo, inquit, de manu mea, non dicit de pedibus meis, rapiet. Ioh. 10. Quædam accepit, quę prorsus supprimat, & aboleat. Hæc recte pedibus illius subiecta dicuntur, tanquam hostilia ac proterenda. Verum ubi generaliter de potestate Christi fit mētio, quæ competat Seruatori, dicuntur illi omnia esse tradita, uel simpliciter absque specificatione, uel, in manus. Vt Iohan. 3. Pater diligit filium, & omnia dedit ei in manus. Et cap. 13. Sciens, quod omnia dederit sibi pater in manus, &c. Habet ergo Christus ouiculas suas, electos & fideles, uitamq; & salutem illorū in manu sua, ad seruandum & contra omnem uim aduersariam asserendum: inimicos uero suos Satanā, peccatum, mundum, tyrannos, & mortem pedibus suis subijcit, & tádem prorsus abolebit.
units.tr: The reader should first notice, before this general phrase is fittingly applied to the present question, that "he has put all things under his feet." All power in heaven and on earth has been given to Christ, and all things have been delivered to him by the Father, but in different ways and for different ends. He received some things as redeemer, mediator and saviour, to keep and preserve. Thus he has the sheep given to him by the Father, whom, he says, no one will snatch out of my hand, John 10. He received other things which he is wholly to suppress and abolish. These are rightly said to be placed under his feet, as hostile things to be trampled down. But where general mention is made of Christ's power as it belongs to the Saviour, all things are said to have been delivered to him either simply, without specification, or "into his hands," as in John 3: The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hands; and ch. 13: knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, etc. Christ therefore holds his little sheep, the elect and faithful, and their life and salvation, in his hand, to keep them and defend them against every hostile force. But his enemies, Satan, sin, the world, tyrants and death, he puts under his feet and will at last utterly abolish.

units.la: Deinde & illud obseruandum est, quod patrem hic omnia pedibus filij subiecisse dicit, in telligendo de illius inimicis, cum dixerit: Nā oportet eum regnare donec posuerit omnes inimicos sub pedes suos, id quod sane de re adhuc futura est dictum. Ergo pater subiecit iam olim inimicos regni sui sub pedes Christi, & Christus in fine mundi demum illos est pedibus suis omnino subiecturus. Subiecit pater omnem filio potestatem destinando ac tra-
units.tr: Next, it must also be observed that here he says the Father has put all things under the feet of the Son, and this is to be understood of his enemies, since he said: For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. This was indeed said of something still future. Therefore the Father had already long ago put the enemies of his kingdom under the feet of Christ, and Christ at the end of the world will finally put them wholly under his feet. The Father subjected all power to the Son by appointing and handing it over; the Son will subject it by carrying out the power received from the Father and bringing it to effect.

units.la: dendo: subijciet filius potestatem à patre acceptam exequendo & in effectum perducendo. Consimili modo, quemadmodum Ephe. 2. legimus, conuiuificauit nos pater unà cū Christo, simulq; cum eo resuscitauit, & simul cum eo sedere fecit inter cœlestes. Et tamen in fine mundi demum uiuificabimur per filium, uiuificati resurgemus, & ad cœlestia unà cum illo collocabimur. Pater hæc fecit, dum Christum mediatorem nostrum è mortuis uiuificauit, ex citauit, & in cœlos ad dexteram suam euexit, quia hæc omnia nostra sunt gratia facta. Filius uero in fine mundi facturus est ista, dum opus redemptionis nostræ in cruce cœptum, & à patre ante sæcula destinatum, ad suam est perfectionem perducturus.
units.tr: In a similar way, as we read in Eph. 2, the Father made us alive together with Christ, raised us up together with him, and made us sit together with him among the heavenly beings. Yet at the end of the world we shall be made alive through the Son; made alive, we shall rise again and be placed with him in the heavenly places. The Father did these things when he made our mediator Christ alive from the dead, raised him up, and lifted him into heaven to his right hand, because all these things were done for us by grace. But the Son is going to do these things at the end of the world, when he brings to completion the work of our redemption, begun on the cross and destined by the Father before the ages.

units.la: AT cum dicat quod omnia subiecta sint, palam est eum esse excipiendum, qui subiecit illi omnia. Redit ad propositum, quod erat mutationem præsentis rerum status in longe alium desituri exprimere, de quo dicere cœperat, post resurrectionem fore finé mundi, & Christum regnum iam perfectum & integrū Deo patri traditurum, quem sermonem parenthesi de regno Christi ad omnium usq; inimicorum subiectionem & abolitionem regnaturi interruperat. Cum ergo ex Psalmo octauo generalem hanc sententiam, Nam omnia subiecit sub pedes illius, Christo regnáti accommodasset: ex illa occasionem sumit ad propositum reuertendi, colligens ad hunc modum: At cum dicat, intellige, propheta Dauid, quod omnia subiecta sint, filio uidelicet: manifeste consequitur, intelligēdum hoc sic esse de omnibus, ut excipiatur ipse pater, qui subiecit illi omnia. Neq; enim conueniebat, ut paterin classem se conjiceret eorū quæ filio inter se & homines mediaturo, & genus humanum sibi reconciliaturo subijciebat. Subiecit illi omnia quę in cœlo sunt & in terra, quo illa reconciliaret & pacificaret: Coloss. 1. In ordinem autem reconciliandorum ac pacificandorum non est reponendus pater, cui erant omnia per filium mediatorem reconcilianda. Seruāda erat ipsi suprema diuinæ maiestatis & paternę authoritatis prerogatiua, ex qua sunt omnia, & ad quam omnia tendere necesse est. Imago huius rei præcessit in Pharaone rege Aegypti, qui Iosepho omnem & domus & regni sui potestatē subijciens dicebat: Tu eris super domum meam, & ad os tuum cibabitur omnis populus meus, tātum hoc solio maior te ero. Vide, pono te super omnem terram Aegypti, &c. Gen. 41. Sic igitur Iosepho subijciebantur omnia, ut integrim exciperetur Pharao, q subijciebat illi oia.
units.tr: But since he says that all things are subjected, it is plain that he who subjected all things to him must be excepted. He returns to his point, which was to express the change of the present state of things into a very different one. He had begun to say that after the resurrection there will be the end of the world, and that Christ will hand over to God the Father the kingdom now perfect and complete. He had interrupted this statement with a parenthesis about the reign of Christ, who is to reign until all enemies are subjected and abolished. Therefore, having applied this general saying from Psalm 8, For he has put all things under his feet, to Christ's reign, he takes from it an occasion to return to his point, concluding in this way: But since he says, understand, the prophet David, that all things are subjected, namely to the Son, it clearly follows that this must be understood of all things, so that the Father himself is excepted, who subjected all things to him. For it was not fitting that the Father should place himself in the class of those things which were subjected to the Son, who was to mediate between God and men and reconcile the human race to himself. He subjected to him all things in heaven and on earth, so that he might reconcile and pacify them, Col. 1. But the Father is not to be placed in the order of those things to be reconciled and pacified, since all things were to be reconciled to him through the mediating Son. The supreme prerogative of the divine majesty and paternal authority, from which all things are and to which all things must tend, had to be preserved for him. An image of this matter went before in Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who, subjecting the whole power of his house and kingdom to Joseph, said: You shall be over my house, and all my people shall be fed at your word; only in the throne will I be greater than you. See, I set you over all the land of Egypt, etc., Gen. 41. Thus all things were subjected to Joseph, except that Pharaoh, who had subjected all things to him, was wholly excepted.

units.la: Quorsum autem hæc patris exceptio ponitur ab Apostolo? Ne uidelicet diuinitatis unitas, cuius origo & caput est pater (quatenus ex illo est filius) per id quod filio subiecta sunt omnia, uel diminuta, uel mutationem passa uideatur. Subiecit pater filio suo omnia, non ut ipsius authoritas & regnū detrimenti aliquid pateretur: sed magis ut opere diaboli destru-ēto, {A}sto, & restitutis omnibus, secundum ea quæ lo quutus est Deus per os sanctorum suorum à se culo prophetarum, regnum ipsi integrum ac perfectum restitueretur, ac veræ diuinitatis unitas in sempiternum illibata redderetur. Cauendum scilicet erat Apostolo, tanquam doctori gentium, ne sic de materia ista scriberet, ut aliquid ethnico errori confine tradere uideretur, & totam Israëlis gentem quasi fidem unius Dei labefactaret, offenderet. Poterat enim ex ijs quæ de subiectione omnium qua pater filio cuncta subiecit, in medium attulit, colligi & inferri. Ergo interea dum regnat Christus in cœlo, & subiectis sibi omnibus, omnem habet potestatem in cœlo & in terra, exauthoratus est pater, & otiosus in omnibus regnanti filio subiectus. Absit inquit. Qui filio subiecit omnia, authoritatem diuinitatis suæ non imminuit, nec se illi cum creatis omnibus subiecit, sed paternam suam ac diuinam maiestatem & ante incarnatum filium, & illo iam regnante integram seruat, integramq; post perfectum susceptæ à filio dispensationis opus in sempiternum omnia existens in omnibus seruabit.
units.tr: But why does the Apostle place this exception of the Father? Clearly so that the unity of the Godhead, whose origin and head is the Father (inasmuch as the Son is from him), should not seem diminished or changed by the fact that all things have been subjected to the Son. The Father subjected all things to his Son, not so that his authority and kingdom should suffer any loss, but rather so that, the work of the devil having been destroyed, and all things restored, the kingdom might be restored to him whole and perfect, according to what God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from the beginning of the world, and the unity of true divinity might be rendered unimpaired for ever. The Apostle, as teacher of the Gentiles, had to take care lest he write about this matter in such a way that he seemed to hand something over to ethnic error, and offended and weakened the faith in the one God in the whole Israelite nation. For from what he set forth about the subjection of all things, by which the Father subjected everything to the Son, something could be gathered and inferred. Therefore, while Christ reigns in heaven, having all things subject to him and all power in heaven and on earth, the Father would seem to be deprived of authority and idle, subject in all things to the reigning Son. Far be it, he says. He who subjected all things to the Son did not diminish the authority of his divinity, nor did he subject himself with all created things to him. Both before the incarnate Son and while the Son now reigns, he keeps his paternal and divine majesty entire, and after the Son has completed the work of the dispensation he received, he will keep it entire for ever, existing over all things and in all things.

units.la: De filo quidem dici potest, quod cum in forma Dei esset, Deoq; æqualis, semetipsum exinaniuerit, forma serui sumpta, inq; similitudine hominum constitutus, ac figura ut homo repertus, humilem se præbuerit ipsum, obediensque factus sit patri usque ad mortem, eamque ob causam pater illum extulerit in summam celsitudinem, & ad gloriam suam collocarit. Verum de patre nihil tale cogitandum est, cuius diuinitas & paterna authoritas nullam est unquam intercapedinem regnandi passa, aut interpollationis alicuius capax facta. Quin ipse filius tanquam mediator noster, interea dum omni potestate in cœlo & in terra potitur, ad hoc in cœlos ascedit, ut appareat uultui patris sui, & interpellet pro nobis. Ebr.7.9. Agatque nostrum aduocatum. 1.Iohan.2. Vsq; adeo scilicet, non est pater filio subiectus, per hoc quod illi subiecit omnia.
units.tr: Of the Son indeed it can be said that, though he was in the form of God and equal to God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself and became obedient to the Father even unto death. For this reason the Father exalted him to the highest height and set him in his own glory. But nothing of this kind is to be thought of the Father, whose divinity and paternal authority has suffered no interruption in its reign and has never been capable of any interpolation. Indeed the Son himself, as our mediator, while he holds all power in heaven and on earth, ascends into heaven for this purpose: that he may appear before the face of his Father and intercede for us, Heb. 7.9, and be our advocate, 1 John 2. So far, certainly, is the Father not made subject to the Son by the fact that all things have been subjected to him.

units.la: Cum autem subiecta fuerint illi omnia, tunc & ipse filius subijcietur ei qui illi subiecit omnia, ut sit deus omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: When all things shall have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also shall be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all.

units.la: Quemadmodum timendum erat Apostolo, ne ex eo quod patrem omnia sub pedes Christi filij sui subiecisse dixit inferretur, ergo & se ipsum illi pater subiecit, cui cogitationi particula præcedenti occurrit: ita timendum erat, ne ex eo quod patri suam paternæ diuinitatis authoritatem saluam uindicans, negat illum filio regnanti, & omnem potestatem habenti, factum esse subiectum: inferat aliquis, ergo regnabit pater, & simul regnabit filius, ubi subiecerit sibi omnia, atque ita futuri seculi status duobus erit ueluti capitibus hinc patri, illinc filio, partita inter ipsos rerum summa, regnantibus subiectus. Futurû hoc negans dicit: Cum autem subiecta fuerint illi omnia, tunc & ipse filius subijcietur ei qui illi subiecit omnia. Q:d. Vbi in fine mundi omnibus inimicis, omni principatu, potestate, & uirtute abolitis, ipsa quoq; morte deleta, subiecta erunt Christo filio Dei omnia: non seruabit sibi eam regni gloriam, quo ueluti diuiso imperio cum patre regnet, sed tradito patri regno pleno ac perfecto erit illi subiectus, quo fit ille Deus omnia in omnibus. Non sic Iupiter, qui cum Saturno patri suo deuictis illius hostibus regnum restituisset, nihilo secius ipse regnauit, imò postea patrem regno pulsum profligauit, tam aberat ut illi subijceretur.
units.tr: Just as the Apostle had to fear that, from his having said that the Father had put all things under the feet of his Son Christ, it might be inferred that the Father had also subjected himself to him (a thought which occurred to him in the preceding clause), so he had to fear that, while he preserved for the Father the authority of his paternal deity, and denied that the Father had been made subject to the Son who reigns and holds all power, someone might infer: therefore the Father will reign, and the Son will reign at the same time, when he has subjected all things to himself; and so the state of the future age would be, as it were, with two heads, the Father on one side and the Son on the other, the sum of things divided between them, both reigning and both subject. Denying this, he says: "When all things shall have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also shall be subjected to him who subjected all things to him." That is: when at the end of the world all enemies, every principality, power and virtue having been abolished, and death itself destroyed, all things shall have been subjected to Christ the Son of God, he will not keep for himself that glory of reigning, by which, as with a divided empire, he would reign together with the Father; but, having handed the kingdom over to the Father, he will be subject to him in a full and perfect way, so that God may be all in all. It is not so with Jupiter, who, after he had defeated the enemies of his father Saturn and restored the kingdom to him, nonetheless reigned himself, and indeed afterwards drove his father from the kingdom and overthrew him; so far was he from being subject to him.

units.la: Sed dices: Atqui suprà dixisti, cauendum esse, ne dum Christum Apostolus regnum Deo ac patri suo traditurum dicit, inde non esse illum amplius postea regnaturum colligamus. Si postea quoq; regnaturus est cum patre, quomodo hic dicit Apostolus, quod subijciendus sit illi, postquam ipsi subiecta fuerint omnia? Etenim regnare cum patre, & subiectum esse patri, haud uidentur eidem posse competere tempori ac personæ. Basilius hac de re sic annotauit: ... Hoc est: Si secundum diuinitatem filius patri subijcietur, subiectus illi fuit inde à principio, ex quo & Deus erat. Si uero non fuit illi subiectus, sed postremo subijcietur, subijcietur illi secundum humanitatem pro nobis, non secundum diuinitatem pro seipso. Hæc ille. Recte quidem inter diuinitatem & humanitatem Christi distinguit. Verum secundum humanitatem non in futura tantum uita, sed & hic in carne constitutus subditus fuit nō modo Deo patri in omnibus, sed & parentibus secundum carnem. Sic enim illum Lucæ 2. dixisse legimus: Quid est, quod me quærebatis? Nesciebatis, quod in his quæ patris mei sunt, oportet me esse? Et ipsi non intellexerunt uerbum quod loquutus est ad eos. Et descendit cum eis, & uenit Nazareth, & erat subditus illis. Si loquitur Apostolus simpliciter de subiectione hominis Christi, ille certe ab ipsa incarnatione subditus fuit, & etiamnum est Deo ac patri. Verum cum dicat: Cum autem subiecta fuerint illi omnia, tunc & ipse filius subijcietur ei, qui subiecit illi omnia: puto manifestum esse, loqui ipsum non simpliciter de subiectione humanitatis, sed de tali, quæ sit in futura demum uita post mundi huius finem, & inimicorum omnium abolitionem futura. Existimo nihil aliud hac particula ab Apostolo dici, quàm quod suprà dixit: Cum tradiderit regnum Deo ac patri. Si recte intellexerimus, quomodo sit post finem mundi filius regnum Deo ac patri traditurus, haud erit intellectu difficile, quod hic illum subijcendum ei dicit, qui ipsi subiecit omnia, ut sit Deus omnia in omnibus. Inspiciendū est regnum Christi, quale ad dispensandā nostrā redemptionē ac salutē, pacificedāq; omniū restitutione, à patre mediator, redemredemptor, seruator, sacerdos & rex constitutus accepit: cuius regni dispensatio non sic est comparata, ut sit in futuro seculo post horum omnium adimpletionem locum habitura. Dixit adhuc illud: Postula a me, & dabo tibi gentes hæreditatem tuam & possessionem tuam terminos terræ. Reges eos in virga ferrea, & tanquam vas figuli confringes eos. Et nunc reges intelligite, erudimini qui iudicatis terram. Servite domino in timore, & exultate ei cum tremore. Obsculamini filium, ne pereatis de via, &c. Et illud: Virga virtutis tuæ emittet dominus ex Sion, dominare in medio inimicorum tuorum. Adhuc regnat in cœlis, dans spiritu suo electis, regenerans ac seruans eos in hac vita. Adhuc purgat & seruat ecclesiam suam in terris constitutam. Adhuc est aduocatus & sacerdos noster, interpellans pro nobis in cœlis. Ad hunc uenturus est cum gloria & potentia in fine mundi ad excitandum mortuos, ad iudicandum totum mundum, ad colligendum ad se electos, ad abolendum & perdendum Satanam & omnes reprobos. Hoc genere regni regnat adhuc Christus. Vbi hæc omnia perfecta erunt, mutabitur huius regni forma, in eam quæ propria est futuro seculo reseruata, cuius qualitatem uelle exprimere admodum temerarium esse iudico. Terminans hoc genus regni in fine mundi, tradet Deo patri regnum plenum ac perfectum. Et hactenus illi subiectus erit & ipse, non regnans amplius sicut regnauerat antea, & tamen tanquam unigenitus Dei, uerus Deus, ac patri æqualis æterni cum illo regni particeps erit, potieturque uera ac sempiterna eiusdem diuinitatis gloria, qua habuit ante constitutionem mundi, habet toto seculorum omnium decursu, habiturusque est post finem mundi in sempiternum.
units.tr: But you will say: Yet above you said that we must take care, lest, when the Apostle says that Christ will hand over the kingdom to God and his Father, we infer from this that he will not afterwards reign any more. If he is also going to reign afterwards with the Father, how does the Apostle here say that he is to be subjected to him, after all things have been subjected to him? For to reign with the Father and to be subject to the Father do not seem able to belong to the same time and person. Basil has noted on this matter as follows: ... That is: If the Son will be subject to the Father according to his deity, he was subject to him from the beginning, since he was also God. But if he was not subject to him, but will be subjected at the last, he will be subjected to him according to his humanity for us, not according to his deity for himself. So he. He rightly distinguishes between the deity and the humanity of Christ. But according to his humanity, not only in the future life but also here, while he was constituted in the flesh, he was subject not only to God the Father in all things, but also to his parents according to the flesh. For we read that he said so in Luke 2: "Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things of my Father?" And they did not understand the word which he spoke to them. And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them. If the Apostle speaks simply of the subjection of the man Christ, then certainly he was subject from the very incarnation, and is still subject to God and the Father. But since he says: "When all things shall have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also shall be subjected to him who subjected all things to him," I think it is clear that he is speaking not simply of the subjection of the humanity, but of that subjection which is to come in the future life after the end of this world and the abolition of all enemies. I think the Apostle says nothing else by this clause than what he said above: "When he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father." If we rightly understand how the Son is to hand over the kingdom to God and the Father after the end of the world, it will not be difficult to understand why here he says that he is to be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all. We must consider the kingdom of Christ, such as he received from the Father, constituted as mediator, redeemer, saviour, priest and king, for the dispensing of our redemption and salvation and the restoration of all things into peace; the dispensation of this kingdom is not so arranged that it is to have its place in the future age after all these things have been fulfilled. He also said this: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession. You shall break them with a rod of iron, and dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel. And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you that judge the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice in him with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest you perish from the way," etc. And that: "The Lord shall send forth the rod of your strength out of Zion; rule in the midst of your enemies." Even now he reigns in the heavens, giving his Spirit to the elect, regenerating and preserving them in this life. Even now he cleanses and preserves his Church established on earth. Even now he is our advocate and priest, interceding for us in heaven. He is to come to this end with glory and power at the end of the world, to raise the dead, to judge the whole world, to gather the elect to himself, and to abolish and destroy Satan and all the reprobate. In this kind of kingdom Christ still reigns. When all these things shall have been completed, the form of this kingdom will be changed into that which is proper to the future age and reserved for it, the quality of which I judge it to be very rash to wish to express. Bringing this kind of kingdom to an end at the end of the world, he will hand over to God the Father the kingdom full and perfect. And up to that point he himself will be subject to him, no longer reigning as he reigned before; yet as the only-begotten of God, true God, and equal to the Father eternally, he will share the kingdom with him, and will possess the true and everlasting glory of the same deity, which he had before the foundation of the world, has throughout the whole course of all ages, and will have forever after the end of the world.

units.la: Augustinus de Trinit. lib. 1. cap. 10. sic exponit: Cum mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus, tradiderit regnum Deo & patri, ut iam non interpellet pro nobis mediator & sacerdos noster filius Dei & filius hominis: sed & ipse, in quantum sacerdos est, assumpta propter nos serui forma, subiectus sit ei qui illi subiecit omnia, ut in quantum Deus est, cum illo nos subiectos habeat: in quantum sacerdos, nobiscum illi subiectus sit. Hæc ille. Et hic sensus nihil demit ei quod angelus Lucæ 1. de Christo dixit: Dabit illi dominus Deus sedem Dauid patris sui, & regnabit in domo Iacob in æternum, & regni eius non erit finis. Licet enim finita dispensatione propter nos suscepta traditurus sit Deo patri regnum, seque illi, modo quo diximus subiecturus, secundum diuinitatem tamen regnum habebit cum patre sempiternum & infinitum.
units.tr: Augustine, in On the Trinity, book 1, chapter 10, explains it thus: When the Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, shall have handed over the kingdom to God and the Father, so that the Mediator and our priest, the Son of God and Son of man, no longer intercedes for us; but he himself also, insofar as he is priest, having taken on the form of a servant for our sake, will be subject to him who subjected all things to him, so that, insofar as he is God, he may have us subject to himself together with him; insofar as he is priest, he will be subject to him together with us. So he. And this sense takes nothing away from what the angel said of Christ in Luke 1: "The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign in the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end." For although, the dispensation undertaken for our sake having been completed, he will hand over the kingdom to God the Father, and will himself be subject to him in the way we have said, nevertheless according to his deity he will have an everlasting and infinite kingdom together with the Father.

units.la: VT sit Deus omnia in omnibus, inquit. Potest hæc particula multifariam exponi.
units.tr: That God may be all in all, he says. This phrase can be explained in many ways.

units.la: 1 Aut ut sit idem quod, Vt omnes omnia habeant ex Deo solo. Quasi dicat: Vt det Deus omnibus omnia solus. Sic nonnulli exponunt: ut commoda quæ nunc per creaturas nobis a Deo subministrantur, tunc ab ipso Deo immediate accipiamus. In hac vita sustentamur cibo & potu, mutua operatione uicissim iuuamur, per magistratum protegimur, verbo & sacramentis in fide & cognitione Christi instituimur, fide ac spe futuræ vitæ ambulamus. Verum in futuro seculo pro his omnibus erit omnibus unus Deus summa sufficientia.
units.tr: 1 Or it may mean the same as: that all may have all things from God alone. As if he said: that God alone may give all things to all. Some explain it thus: the benefits that God now supplies to us through creatures we will then receive immediately from God himself. In this life we are sustained by food and drink, helped by one another's mutual service, protected by the magistrate, instructed in faith and the knowledge of Christ by the Word and the sacraments, and we walk by faith and by hope of the life to come. But in the future age, in place of all these things, God alone will be the all-sufficient good for everyone.

units.la: 2 Aut ut idem sit quod, Vt faciat Deus omnia in omnibus. Qui sensus cum priore coincidit.
units.tr: 2 Or it may mean the same as: that God may do all things in all. This sense coincides with the former.

units.la: 3 Vel ut habeatur Deus ab omnibus pro omnibus. Hoc est, ut nihil extra Deum appetatur a quoquam. Sunt quidem hæc uera, & sic post resurrectionem futura: uerum quoniam Apostolus non simpliciter dicit, Et erit Deus omnia in omnibus, sed, ut sit Deus omnia in omnibus: puto particulam hac eo sensu exponendam esse, qui ex præcedentibus rite sequatur. Dixit Christum in fine mundi traditurum Deo ac patri regnum, postquam abluerit omnes inimicos, omnem principatum, potestatem & uirtute, fibiq; subiecerit omnia, & concludens adijcit: Tunc & ipse filius subijcietur ei qui illi subiecit omnia, ut sit Deus omnia in omnibus. Ergo ad hunc finem tradet Christus Deo ac patri regnum, seq; illi subijciet, ut sit in futura vita Deus omnia in omnibus. Quod idem est atque, ut regnet Deus solus unice ac perfecte in omnibus, plenum & perfectum habeat in omnibus imperium, una illius voluntas locum habeat in omnibus, ab ipso pendeant omnes, nemo alio respiciat nedum declinet, nemo sit amplius qui aduersetur, &c. Hieron. ad hunc sensum accedit. Sic enim exponit: Cum morte & omni malicia deuicta, omniq; errore sublato, solus regnabit in omnibus. Omnino loquitur de regno Dei, quale futurum sit post hanc vitam, quàm scilicet plenum & perfectum. Sic de eo dicimus, in cuius potestate sunt omnia, quem omnes obseruant, & qui unus agit omnia, esse illum totum in toto. Sic Deus erit in omnibus omnia, quando unus ac solus omnia pro voluntate sua faciet in omnibus, adeoque regnum habebit prorsus absolutum ac perfectum id quod non habet, donec sumus in hac vita, donec Satan cum suis membris nondum est prorsus pedibus Christi subiectus, donec mundus hic in maligno positus est, donec caro nostra concupiscit aduersus spiritum, donec bonum quod uolumus non facimus, facimus uero malum, quod odimus, donec spiritus noster a corpore per mortem separatur, corpus uero mortalitati & corruptioni est obnoxium, donec locum in nobis habent fames, egestas, morbi, & omnis generis afflictiones, donec cognoscimus ex parte, per speculum & in ænigmate, donec peregrini sumus in hoc mundo, donec carnalis spiritualem, malicia innocentiam, iniusticia iusticiam, impietas pietatem, & mendacium ueritatem persequitur, donec omnis adhuc creatura uanitati subiecta ingemiscit ac parturit: in summa, donec nondum prorsus extinctum est regnum Satanæ, peccati, mortis & mundi. Donec, inquam, hæc omnia durant, sicuti durabunt. bunt ad finem usq; mundi, nondum est Deus omnia in omnibus, quia nondum regnum habet plenum & absolutum. Habat quidem, sed potentia, non actu, habiturus post finem mundi & potentia & actu. Potest semper omnia esse inomnibus absoluta sua potentia, verum inscrutabili sua sapientia cursum regni sui sic disponit, ut perfectio illius ad futurum saeculum seruetur, sequaturq; praecedentis noctis tenebras splendor solis diurni.
units.tr: 3 Or it may mean that God is held by all to be all things for all; that is, that nothing outside God is sought by anyone. These things are indeed true, and they will be so after the resurrection. But since the Apostle does not simply say "And God will be all in all," but "that God may be all in all," I think the phrase should be explained in the sense that follows properly from what goes before. He said that Christ, at the end of the world, will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father, after he has brought to nothing all enemies, every principality, power and virtue, and has subjected all things to himself; and concluding, he adds: "Then the Son himself will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all." Therefore to this end Christ will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father, and will subject himself to him, so that in the future life God may be all in all. This is the same as saying: that God alone may reign uniquely and perfectly in all things, that he may have full and perfect dominion over all, that his will alone may hold sway in all, that all may depend on him, that no one may look to anything else, let alone turn aside, and that no one remains who opposes him, and so on. Jerome comes close to this sense. For he explains it thus: "With death and all malice overcome, and all error removed, he alone will reign over all." He is speaking altogether of the kingdom of God as it will be after this life, namely how full and perfect it will be. We say of someone in whose power all things lie, whom all obey, and who alone does everything, that he is wholly in the whole. So God will be all in all when he alone, by his own will, does all things in all, and so holds a kingdom altogether absolute and perfect, which he does not yet have while we are in this life: while Satan with his members is not yet fully subjected under the feet of Christ; while this world lies in the power of the evil one; while our flesh lusts against the spirit; while we do not do the good we want, but do the evil we hate; while our spirit is separated from the body by death, and the body is subject to mortality and corruption; while hunger, want, sickness and every kind of affliction have a place among us; while we know in part, through a glass and in a riddle; while we are strangers in this world; while the carnal pursues the spiritual, malice pursues innocence, injustice pursues justice, impiety pursues piety, and falsehood pursues truth; while the whole creation still groans and travails in bondage to vanity. In sum, while the kingdom of Satan, of sin, of death and of the world is not yet utterly destroyed. As long as, I say, all these things endure, as they will endure until the end of the world, God is not yet all in all, because he does not yet have a full and absolute kingdom. He has it indeed, but in power, not in act; he will have it both in power and in act after the end of the world. By his absolute power he is always able to be all in all; but by his inscrutable wisdom he so orders the course of his kingdom that its perfection is reserved for the future age, and the brightness of the day sun follows the darkness of the preceding night.

units.la: Vbi haec omnia, quae recensuimus, erunt è medio sublata, tunc erit Deus omnia in omnibus, regnum habens omnium perfectissimum. Ad perfectionem enim regni Dei requiritur, non modo perfectu ius, & absoluta potestas: sed & perfecta iuris & potestatis exequutio, perfecta iustitia, perfecta filiorum regni obedientia, & perfecta felicitas.
units.tr: When all the things we have listed are removed from the midst, then God will be all in all, having the most perfect of kingdoms. For the perfection of the kingdom of God requires not only full right and absolute power, but also the perfect exercise of that right and power, perfect righteousness, perfect obedience of the sons of the kingdom, and perfect blessedness.

units.la: Hunc sensum puto esse germanum. Nec est ut quaeramus, quae omnia, & in quibus omnibus futurus sit Deus. Est enim omnia esse in omnibus, plenam omnium habere potestatem. Quare frustra laborant, qui de eo disputant, quaenam sint illa omnia in futuro saeculo, quae Deus erit in omnibus. Etenim, si futurae vitae bona intelligunt, non sunt illa nobis scrutabilia. Nec oculus ea uidit, nec auris audiuit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt, quae diligentibus se praeparauit Deus. Et illi frustra contendunt, qui ex hoc loco generalem omnium, etiam Satanae, salutem post finem mundi futuram colligunt. Neque enim illud In omnibus, ad homines siue bonos siue malos referendum est: sed ad universitatem eorum, quae in regno Dei erunt gerenda & perficienda.
units.tr: I think this is the genuine sense, and we need not ask what all things are, or in what all things God will be. To be all in all is to have full power over all things. So those labour in vain who dispute what those "all things" will be in the future age in which God will be all in all. For if they understand the good things of the future life, these are not knowable to us: "Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him." And those contend in vain who from this passage infer a general salvation of all, even of Satan, after the end of the world. For the words "in all" are not to be referred to men, whether good or bad, but to the totality of those things which are to be done and completed in the kingdom of God.

units.la: Hinc igitur accidit, quod nemo in hac uita perfectam potest uel iusticiam, uel sapientiā, uel felicitatem acquirere, propterea quod nondum est Deus omnia in omnibus. Ea nanque vera demum erit felicitas, quando solus Deus omnia erit in omnibus.
units.tr: Hence it happens that no one in this life can acquire perfect righteousness, or wisdom, or blessedness, because God is not yet all in all. For that will be true blessedness only when God alone is all in all.

units.la: Alioqui quid facient ij, qui baptizantur pro mortuis, si omnino mortui non resurgunt? Cur & baptizātur pro illis?
units.tr: Otherwise, what will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all? Why are they even baptized for them?

units.la: Ab eo loco quo dixit, Postea finis, cum tradiderit regnum Deo ac patri, argumentatione de resurrectione mortuorum digressiuncula de fine mundi, & statu futuri saeculi inserta interruperat. Ad hanc igitur reuertens, aliud adhuc absurdum post praecedentia ijs obijcit qui resurrectionem mortuorum negabant. Supra dixerat: Quemadmodū in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita et in Christo omnes uiuificabūtur. Huc respiciens dicit: Alioqui, quid facient ij, qui baptizantur pro mortuis, si omnino mortui non resurgunt? Quasi dicat: Dixi fore ut omnes uiuificentur in Christo: nisi hoc sit, omnium uidentur esse stultissimi, qui baptizantur pro mortuis. Quid enim faciunt, nisi rem prorsus inanem, si, quemadmodum nonnulli ex uobis dicunt, mortui non resurgunt? Et ad
units.tr: From the point where he said, "Then the end, when he shall have delivered the kingdom to God and the Father," he had interrupted the argument about the resurrection of the dead with a short digression on the end of the world and the state of the age to come. Now returning to this argument, he adds another absurdity against those who denied the resurrection of the dead, after the points already made. He had said above: "As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive." Looking back to this, he says: "Otherwise, what will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all?" As if he were saying: I have said that all will be made alive in Christ. Unless this is so, those who are baptized for the dead seem to be the most foolish of all. For what do they accomplish, if, as some of you say, the dead do not rise? And to expose the great folly and absurdity that would follow from their error, he adds, pressing the point: "Why are they even baptized for them?" As if he were saying: If the dead do not rise, what is the point of baptism for them? Since they have departed from this life, and if what those men say is true, no other life follows it in which the dead might rise. What benefit could come from the administration of baptism to the dead, who are capable neither of the present life nor of the future one? Every benefit belongs either to the present life or to the future life. None reaches the dead unless they are restored to life. But if there is some benefit of baptism which could reach the dead, it is necessary that they rise to life at some time. Those, then, who are baptized for the dead bear witness about themselves that they hope for the future resurrection of the dead, and so become capable of the benefit that comes from baptism in the future life. Let those who deny the resurrection of the dead at least look to the deed of these people.

units.la: tantam stulticiam & absurditatē perstringendam, quae ex errore illorum consequeretur, adijcit inculcans: Cur & baptizantur pro illis? Quasi dicat: Si mortui nō resurgunt, quorsum illis baptismus? Quoniam ex hac uita migrarunt, &, si uerum est quod illi dicunt, nulla post hanc consequitur alia, ad quam mortui resurgant: quae potest utilitas ex baptismi communicatione redire ad mortuos, nec praesentis amplius nec futurae uitae capaces? Omnis utilitas aut praesentis est, aut futurae uitae. Ad mortuos nulla pertingit, nisi uitae restituantur. Quod si aliqua baptismi utilitas est, quae possit redire ad mortuos, necesse est ut aliquando ad uitam resurgant. Testantur ergo de se, qui pro mortuis baptizantur, quod futurum sperent, ut resurgant mortui, fiantq; utilitatis quae ex baptismo est in futura uita capaces. Saltem igitur istorum factum inspiciant, qui resurrectionem mortuorum negant.
units.tr: Such, it appears, is the Apostle's argument, if we follow the opinion of those who think that some people had the custom of having themselves baptized for dead friends, relatives, brothers and children, if these had departed without baptism. Chrysostom attributes this custom to the Marcionites, reporting how they hide a living man beneath a dead one's bed, who answers for the dead man and asks for baptism, and they baptize him in place of the dead man. Whether that practice of theirs derived from such a custom among certain Corinthians, I cannot affirm. For it is uncertain whether the Apostle is speaking of that practice at all; some deny it, others affirm it, as usually happens in an uncertain matter. Those who deny it have their reasons, which are not to be scorned, and they follow them. Those who affirm it cling to the words, which seem to support them. And since it is not enough to reject the opinion of others unless you bring forward what you think is true, those who deny the accepted explanation each bring forward another, which they also offer as the genuine one. For although they agree that the Apostle is not speaking of certain people who had themselves baptized on behalf of dead friends, they are nevertheless divided in setting out the explanation that is true and genuine.

units.la: Huiusmodi apparet esse argumentationem Apostoli, si sequamur sententiam eorum, qui existimant fuisse nonnullis in usu, ut pro mortuis amicis, cognatis, fratribus, & liberis baptizari se facerent, si illi sine baptismate discessissent. Quam consuetudinem Chrysostomus tribuit Marcionitis, recitans, quomodo sublectum mortui hominem uiuum abdant, quipro mortuo respondeat, ac baptismum petat, illumq; loco mortui baptizent. Quod illorum factum, an ex eiusmodi consuetudine Corinthiorum quorundam originem duxerit, affirmare non possum. Est enim incertum, an Apostolus de illa loquatur, quod alij negant, alij asserūt, sicut in re incerta fieri solet. Qui negant, habent suas rationes haud aspernandas, quas sequuntur. Qui asserunt, inhaerent uerbis, quae pro ipsis facere uidentur. Et quoniam non est satis aliorum reijcere sententiam, nisi quam uerum putes in medium adferas, qui negant receptam expositionem: alij aliam, suam quoque pro germana adferunt. Quamuis enim in eo consentiunt, quod non loquatur Apostolus de quibusdam, qui se pro mortuis amicis baptizari fecerint: in assignanda tamen expositione, quae uera sit & germanda diuiduntur.
units.tr: 2 Some indeed explain it of the bed-ridden, that is, catechumens, who were near death and therefore regarded as dead, because their recovery was despaired of; these, so that they would not depart from this life without baptism, had themselves baptized as if they were already in the very jaws of death. Certainly it is well known that this kind of baptism of the bed-ridden was in use in the Church, although I cannot prove whether it was in use at the time of Paul. Nor does it seem very firm, that to be baptized for the dead is the same as to be baptized when about to die.

units.la: 2 Alij siquidem de clinicis exponūt, hoc est, catechumenis, mortiiam uicinis, ideoq; pro mortuis habitis, quod de uita illorum desperaretur: qui se, ne sine baptismate ex hac uita discederent, uelut in ipsis mortis faucibus constitutos baptizari fecerint. Sane notum est, usi tatum fuisse in ecclesia hoc genus clinicorum baptismum, quamuis an tempore Pauli fuerit in usu, nescio ,pbari ne posit. Nec admodum firmum uidetur, quod baptizari pro mortuis, idem esse dicūt quod baptizari iam moriturū.
units.tr: 2 Others, however, explain it of the sick (clinici), that is, catechumens who were near death, and who were therefore counted as dead because their lives were despaired of. They had themselves baptized, so that they would not leave this life unbaptized, as though they were placed at the very jaws of death. It is certainly known that this kind of sickbed baptism was in use in the Church, though I cannot tell whether it can be shown to have been practised in Paul's time. Nor does it seem very firm to say that being baptized for the dead is the same as being baptized about to die.

units.la: 3 Alij exponunt de ijs, qui se super uel ad sepulcra mortuorum propterea baptizari fecerint, ut hoc facto fidem futurae resurrectionis profiterentur. Illis quod in Graeco est ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν, id est, pro mortuis, idem quod ὑπὲρ τοὺς νεκρούς, id est, super mortuos. Ebraicē על המתים supra
units.tr: 3 Others explain it of those who had themselves baptized over or beside the graves of the dead, so that by this act they might profess their faith in the future resurrection. The Greek hyper tōn nekrōn, that is, "for the dead," is the same as hyper tous nekrous, that is, "over the dead." In Hebrew, al ha-metim [על המתים] means "over" or "beside" the dead.

units.la: A tantam stulticiam
units.tr: A Such folly.

units.la: B supra uel iuxta mortuos, hoc est, mortuorum sepulchra. Hic quoque nec de historia constat, quod ego sciam, nec de mente Apostoli, quod de eiusmodi baptismate hoc scripserit.
units.tr: B Over or beside the dead, that is, the graves of the dead. Here too, as far as I know, there is no support in history, nor in the Apostle's meaning, for his having written about baptism of this kind.

units.la: 4 Chrysostomus & Theophylactus aliud adferunt. Quoniam in consueto apud ipsos erat, ut baptizandi symbolum fidei palàm pronunciarent, & ubi se resurrectionem mortuorum credere in calce symboli professi essent, mox baptizarentur: sentiunt idem esse baptizari pro mortuis, quod in fidem resurrectionis mortuorum baptizari, & existimant hunc esse sensum Apostoli. Alioqui, quid facient, qui dum baptizantur, mortuorum se resurrectionem credere profitentur, si mortui non resurgunt?
units.tr: 4 Chrysostom and Theophylact offer another explanation. Since it was customary among them to recite the creed publicly before baptism, and to profess at the end of the creed that they believed in the resurrection of the dead, and then to be baptized straightaway, they hold that being baptized for the dead is the same as being baptized in faith in the resurrection of the dead, and they think this is the Apostle's sense. Otherwise, what will those do who, while being baptized, profess that they believe in the resurrection of the dead, if the dead do not rise?

units.la: Verum unde constat morem hunc de resurrectione mortuorum postremo loco interrogandi, & ad illius fidem mox baptizandi, tempore Pauli fuisse in usu, ut in illum hic respexisse credi possit?
units.tr: But how is it established that this custom of asking about the resurrection of the dead last, and then baptizing immediately upon belief in it, was in use in Paul's time, so that it could be believed that he had this in view here?

units.la: Deinde si ad communem eiusmodi baptismum, quo non aliqui tantum, sed omnes baptizari consueuerint respexisset, non dixisset: Alioqui quid faciunt, qui pro mortuis baptizantur? sed magis ad hunc modum: Alioqui quid facimus, qui pro mortuis, id est, propter fidem resurrectionis mortuorum baptizamur?
units.tr: Further, if he had been referring to a common kind of baptism, in which not some only but all were accustomed to be baptized, he would not have said, "Otherwise what will those do who are baptized for the dead?" He would have said rather in this manner: "Otherwise what shall we do, who are baptized for the dead, that is, on account of faith in the resurrection of the dead?"

units.la: 5 Commentarij Hieronymo assignati sic exponunt: Quicunque baptizati sumus in Christo, in mortem ipsius baptizati, id est, cum illo iam quasi commortui sumus. Huc respiciens carnem nostram mortuam uocat, ideoq; increpando dicit: Alioqui quid facient, qui baptizantur pro mortuis, si omnino mortui non resurgunt: id est, quid baptizari opus est carnem, si non resurgat? Ad hanc expositionem respondemus idem quod ad praecedentem. Baptizamur omnes in mortem Christi. Debebat igitur dicere, Quid facimus dum pro mortuis baptizamur? potius quàm, quid faciut, qui pro mortuis baptizantur? Ad hoc, non est idem baptizari mortuum peccatis & mundo, quod baptizari pro mortuis.
units.tr: 5 The commentaries attributed to Jerome explain it thus: "As many of us as were baptized into Christ were baptized into his death," that is, we have already died together with him. Looking to this, he calls our flesh dead, and so he reproves with the words, "Otherwise what will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all?" That is, why is it necessary for the flesh to be baptized, if it does not rise? To this explanation we answer the same as to the previous one. We are all baptized into the death of Christ. He ought therefore to have said, "What do we do when we are baptized for the dead?" rather than "what will those do who are baptized for the dead?" Besides, to be baptized as one dead to sins and to the world is not the same as being baptized for the dead.

units.la: 6 Lyranus sic: Pro mortuis, id est, pro peccatis mortalibus, quae sunt opera mortua, pro quibus abluendis accipitur baptismus. At sic baptizari non est quorundam tatum, sed communiter omnium. Loquitur autem Apostolus de baptismate quodam, quo non omnes, sed aliqui tantum utebantur. Deinde hoc sensu non stabit argumentum Apostoli. Etenim si per mortuos, pro quibus nonnulli baptizabantur, intelligenda sunt peccata mortalia, quod sequitur si mortui non resurgunt: uel idem erit, quod, si peccata mortalia non resurgunt, quod est absurdum: uel si de mortuis hominibus accipiatur, uis argumenti Apostolici enervatur. Poterat enim responderi: Etiam si mortui non resurgunt, utile tamen est, & ad praesentem hanc uitam conducibile, peccata mortalia per baptismum abluere, quo conscientias saltem quietiores habeamus, & praesentis uitae bonis digniores reddamur.
units.tr: 6 Nicholas of Lyra says: "For the dead, that is, for mortal sins, which are dead works, for whose washing away baptism is received." But being baptized in this way is not the practice of some only, but of all in common. Yet the Apostle is speaking of a certain baptism which not all, but only some, used. Further, on this sense the Apostle's argument will not stand. For if by "the dead," for whom some were baptized, mortal sins are to be understood, then what follows, "if the dead do not rise," either means "if mortal sins do not rise," which is absurd, or, if it is taken of dead men, the force of the Apostle's argument is weakened.
