For it could be answered: "Even if the dead do not rise, it is nonetheless useful, and conducive to this present life, to wash away mortal sins through baptism, so that at least we may have quieter consciences and be made more worthy of the good things of the present life."

units.la: 7 Ambrosius sic exponit: In tantum ratam & stabilem uult ostendere resurrectionem mortuorum, ut exemplum inducat de eorum facto, qui tam erant de resurrectione mortuorum securi, ut etiam p mortuis baptizarentur, si quis forte mors praeueniisset, timentes ne aut male, aut non resurgeret, qui baptizatus non fuerat, atque ita uiuus nomine mortui tingebatur. Unde subiecit: Quid & baptizantur pro illis? Exemplo autem hoc non factum illorum probat, sed fixam fidem in resurrectionem ostendit. Haec ille. Vbi has omnes expositiones pro mea mediocritate inspicio, ad primam, quae & Ambrosij est, magis inclino. Nec impedit me, quod exemplum hoc eorum qui pro mortuis baptizatur, reprehensibile factum habet, quando & Christus oeconomum iniquum fidelibus suis non iniquitatis, sed prudentiae respectu proposuit & laudauit. Et huic sententiae fauere uidetur, quod non simpliciter dicit, Cur baptizantur: sed, cur & baptizantur pro illis? Hoc est, cur non sepeliunt eos simpliciter, & auferunt e me dio tanquam mortuos, & nunquam reuicturos, si mortui non resurgunt, sed baptismum etiam illis impendunt. De sententia Tertulliani, quae eadem est, annotarunt alij.
units.tr: 7 Ambrose explains it thus: "He wishes to show the resurrection of the dead to be so certain and firm that he brings in an example from the deeds of those who were so confident of the resurrection of the dead that they even were baptized for the dead, if death by chance had anticipated someone, fearing lest he should either rise badly or not rise at all, and so a living man who had not been baptized was dipped in the name of the dead. Hence he adds: 'Why are they also baptized for them?' By this example, however, he does not approve their deed, but shows their fixed faith in the resurrection." Thus far Ambrose. When I survey all these explanations to the best of my modest ability, I incline more to the first, which is also Ambrose's. Nor am I hindered by the fact that this example of those who are baptized for the dead has a blameworthy deed, since Christ also set forth and commended the unjust steward to his faithful followers, not in respect of his injustice but of his prudence. And this opinion seems to be favoured by the fact that he does not simply say "Why are they baptized?" but "Why are they also baptized for them?" That is, why do they not simply bury them and remove them from sight as dead, never to live again, if the dead do not rise, but also bestow baptism upon them? Others have noted that Tertullian's opinion, which is the same, is of this kind.

units.la: Quicquid fit de hoc sensu, omnino constat superstitionem illam, qua uiui, nescio quibus caeremonijs saluti mortuorum consuli posse in Papatu putant, non esse recentem, sed antiquam, & tam inter Christianos, quàm Iudaeos & Gentes usitatam. Qualis est quod aqua lustrali sepulcra mortuorum in Papatu aspergut, quem morem ex Gentium superstitionibus superstitem esse crediderim: & qualis est, quod Graeci mortuos suos oleo inungunt, & quod sacrificulus Papista Eucharistiam pro mortuis comedit. Sic Satan mox ab initio usum sacramentorum baptismi & Eucharistiae uarijs superstitionibus consPurcare & peruertere coepit. Quid autem interest inter eos qui pro mortuis baptizabantur, & eos qui Eucharistia pro illis comedunt? Quàm non procul ab eorum sunt superstitione, qui aquam lustralem sepulcris mortuorum inspersam ad ablutionem peccatorum illorum facere putant?
units.tr: Whatever the sense of that passage, it is quite certain that the superstition by which the living think they can help the salvation of the dead through certain ceremonies, as the Papists imagine, is not recent but ancient, and was practised among Christians, Jews and Gentiles alike. An example is the Papists' sprinkling of graves with holy water, a custom I believe survives from the superstitions of the Gentiles. Another example is the Greeks anointing their dead with oil, and the Papist priest eating the Eucharist on behalf of the dead. In this way Satan, from the very beginning, began to defile and pervert the use of the sacraments of baptism and the Eucharist with various superstitions. What difference is there between those who were baptized on behalf of the dead and those who eat the Eucharist for them? How close are they to the superstition of those who think that holy water sprinkled on graves washes away the sins of the dead?

units.la: Quid & nos periclitamur omni tempore? Indies morior, per nostram gloriationem, quam habeo in Christo Iesu domino nostro.
units.tr: Why are we also in danger every hour? I die daily, by the boasting I have in Christ Jesus our Lord.

units.la: Si secundum hominem cum bestijs depugnaui Ephesi, quae mihi utilitas, si mortui non resurgunt? Edamus & bibamus, cras enim moriemur. Ne decipiamini. Mores bonos corrumpunt colloquia praua. Expergiscimini iuste, & ne peccetis. Nam ignorationem Dei nonnulli habent. Ad pudorem uobis loquor.
units.tr: If, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what good is it to me if the dead do not rise? Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. Do not be deceived: evil company corrupts good morals. Awake righteously, and do not sin; for some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.

units.la: Instat, obijciens adhuc aliud absurdum, qd sibi cum primis nascatur, si mortui non resurgant. gant. Hinc enim sequebatur frustra ipsum tot discrimina propter Euangelium subeundo quo tidie periclitari. Quidá & apostolos reliquos Paulo hic coniungunt, quoniam pluraliter loquitur: Quid & nos periclitamur, inquit, omni tempore: intellige, si mortui non resurgant. Non dicit simpliciter, quid & nos afflictamur: sed, quid & nos periclitamur? Periclitari non est simpliciter affligi, sed periculum amittendę uitæ subire. Nec simpliciter dicit: Quid & nos periclitati sumus aliquoties? sed, quid & nos periclitamur omni tempore? Quasi dicat: An non prorsus insani essemus, tam crebra & inde finentia discrimina mortis subeundo, & præsentis huius uitæ usurâ nobis ipsis citra rationem frustra amputando, si mortui non resurgant? Quàm autē crebris fuerit periculis obnoxius, in posteriore epistola ad Corinth. cap. 11. luculentius exponit, ubi sic legitur: Ministri Christi sunt? Desipiens loquor, excellentius sum ego, in laboribus copiosius, in verberibus supra modum, in carceribus abundantius, in mortibus frequenter. A Iudæis quinquies quadragenas plagas una minus accepi. Ter uirgis cæsus fui, semel fui lapidatus, ter naufragium feci, noctem ac diem in profundo egi, in itineribus, sæpe in periculis fluminum, periculis latronum, periculis ex genere, periculis ex Gentibus, periculis in ciuitate, periculis in deserto, periculis in mari, periculis inter falsos fratres, in labore & molestia, in uigiliis sæpe, in fame & siti, in ieiunijs sæpe, in frigore & nuditate, &c. Tot modis, tamque frequenter uitam in discrimen propter Euangelium, fide ac spe resurrectionis frustra ponere, si nulla sit mortuorum resurrectio, ipsissimæ fuerit dementiæ.
units.tr: He presses on, raising yet another absurdity that would arise first of all for himself if the dead do not rise. For it would follow that he was in vain exposing himself to so many dangers for the sake of the Gospel every day. He here also joins the other apostles with Paul, since he speaks in the plural: "Why are we also in danger every hour?" Understand: if the dead do not rise. He does not simply say, "Why are we also afflicted?" but "Why are we also in danger?" To be in danger is not simply to be afflicted, but to undergo the risk of losing life. Nor does he simply say, "Why have we also been in danger at times?" but "Why are we also in danger every hour?" As if he were saying: Would we not be utterly mad, if the dead do not rise, to undergo such frequent and never-ending perils of death, and to throw away, without reason and in vain, the use of this present life? How greatly he was exposed to dangers he sets out more fully in the second letter to the Corinthians, chapter 11, where it is read as follows: "Are they ministers of Christ? I speak foolishly: I am more so: in labours more abundant, in stripes above measure, in prisons more frequent, in deaths often. Of the Jews five times I received forty stripes save one. Thrice I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep; in journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren; in weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness, etc." To expose life to danger in so many ways and so often for the sake of the Gospel, if there is no resurrection of the dead, and to do so in faith and hope of the resurrection, would be sheer madness.

units.la: Sed dices, quid hoc magni est? An non passim in historijs occurrunt eorum exempla, qui sine spe resurrectionis uel amore patriæ ac suę gentis, uel studio inanis gloriæ, uitâ suam certissima morte scienter commutarunt? Vnde nemo certo poterit colligere, nihil eos horum fuisse subituros, nisi futurum crederent, ut è mortuis aliquando ad futurâ gloriâ resurgant.
units.tr: But you will say: what is so great about this? Do not examples of those who, without hope of resurrection, or from love of their country and nation, or from zeal for empty glory, knowingly exchanged their lives for certain death, occur everywhere in histories? From this no one can conclude with certainty that they would not have undertaken these things unless they believed that they would one day rise from the dead to future glory.

units.la: Respondeo. Longè alia erat Apostoli, quàm illorum & causa & conditio. Etenim qui rebus patriæ suæ periclitando consulebant, & sibi gloriam, & patriæ salutem conciliabant, ideoque non frustra periclitabantur. Qui gloriæ studio uitam suam periculo exponebant, habebant & ipsi quo respicerent, sequuturam uidelicet nominis celebritatem. At Apostolus nec profuisset cuiquam periclitando, si nulla esset mortuorum resurrectio, imò innumeros frustra secum perdidisset: nec poterat aliquid sibi gloriæ polliceri, in causa toto terrarum orbe omnis generis ignominiæ, probris, & odijs obnoxia, cuius uniuersa commoda à futura uita pendent. Quare nō sine ratione dicit: Quid & nos periclitamur omni tempore, si mortui non resurgunt?
units.tr: I reply: the case and condition of the Apostle was very different from theirs. For those who exposed themselves to danger in order to serve the interests of their country both gained glory for themselves and secured the safety of their country, and so their danger was not in vain. Those who exposed their lives to peril from a desire for glory also had something to look to, namely the celebrity of a name that would follow. But the Apostle would not have profited anyone by exposing himself to danger if there were no resurrection of the dead; indeed, he would have brought countless others to ruin with himself in vain. Nor could he promise himself any glory, in a cause that throughout the whole world was liable to every kind of disgrace, reproach and hatred, and whose every benefit depends on the future life. Therefore he rightly says: "Why are we also in danger every hour, if the dead do not rise?"

units.la: Et hinc non probat contentiosis resurrectionem mortuorum. Poterat enim ab illis audire: Sane nisi motæ mentis esses, nec teipsum nec alios uana resurrectionis spe in discrimina uitæ conijceres. Verum interim Christianis hominibus cogitandū relinquit, quàm oporteat ipsum firma fide ac spe, ab indubitata mortuorum resurrectione tot ac tam indefinentia uitæ pericula propter Euangelium subeundo pendere. Et reuera uix potest fortius comprobari ab Apostolo doctrinam suam de futura uita per Christum, haud esse uanam, quàm si illa non uerbis tantum proponat & asserat: sed & propter illam, quoties opus est, uitâ suam periculo incunctâter exponat. Facile quippe est, uerbis afferere uitam post finem mundi futuram: uerum illius fide ac spe præsentem hanc susq; deq; facere, & in discrimè propter Euangelium Christi adducere, non est quorumuis, sed eorum tantum qui de certitudine futurae felicitatis in cordibus suis persuasi, quod certo futurum sciùt, cupidissime appetunt. Quis credat prælatos ecclesiarum, episcopos, canonicos, presbyteros, abbates, &c. ulla esse futuræ resurrectiónis fide ac spe præditos, cum sole clarius puppim ac proram ad præsentis uitæ commoda, gloriam ac delicias totis uiribus conuertant ac dirigant? proq; illis mordicus retinendis cœlum ac terrā miscere parati sint, citius quàm latum unguem de possessione illorum cedere sustineant.
units.tr: And from this he does not prove the resurrection of the dead to the contentious. For they could have replied: Surely, unless you were out of your mind, you would not throw yourself and others into dangers of life on the strength of a vain hope of resurrection. Yet meanwhile he leaves it for Christian men to consider how much it behoves him to depend, with firm faith and hope in the indubitable resurrection of the dead, on undergoing for the Gospel so many and such unceasing perils of life. And indeed the Apostle's teaching about the future life through Christ can hardly be more strongly confirmed as not being empty than by his not merely proposing and asserting it in words, but also, whenever necessary, exposing his life to danger without hesitation for its sake. For it is easy to assert in words that life will come after the end of the world; but to hold this present life of little account through faith and hope in it, and to bring it into danger for the sake of the Gospel of Christ, is not the work of just anyone, but only of those who, persuaded in their hearts of the certainty of future happiness, most eagerly seek what they know will certainly come. Who would believe that the prelates of the churches, bishops, canons, presbyters, abbots, and so on, have any faith or hope in future resurrection, when they turn and direct their whole strength, clearer than the sun, to the comforts, glory and pleasures of this present life, and are ready to mix heaven and earth to hold on to them with their teeth, rather than yield a finger's breadth of their possessions?

units.la: <bl>INDIES</bl> morior, inquit.] Idem dicit quod in præcedenti particula. Nihil enim hic aliud est, quotidie mori, quàm omni tempore de uita periclitari. Quanquam sunt qui exponant non de externis uitæ periculis, quorum suprà catalogum ex undecimo capite posterioris ad Corinthios epistolę adduxi: sed de lucta quotidiana, quam in animo sustinuerit, certâtibus inter se uita & morte, peccato & iustitia, gaudio & tristitia, spe ac desperationis tentatione, fiducia ac diffidentia, &c. Nemini dubium sit, eiusmodi internas in animo suo pugnas frequenter esse Apostolum hunc expertum. Nec inconueniens est, si quis eas mortem uocet.
units.tr: "DAILY I die," he says. He says the same thing as in the preceding clause. For to die daily here means nothing other than to be in danger of life at all times. Yet there are some who explain it not of the external dangers to life, whose catalogue I have cited above from the eleventh chapter of the second letter to the Corinthians, but of the daily struggle he endured in his mind, the conflicts between life and death, sin and righteousness, joy and sorrow, the temptation of hope and despair, trust and distrust, and so on. There is no doubt that this Apostle frequently experienced such inner battles in his mind. Nor is it inappropriate to call these a kind of death.

units.la: Mors quædam erat, quod bonum non faciebat, ut uolebat: malum uero faciebat, quod odio magno prosequebatur. Mors item erat, quæ omnes quæ sua erat, non quæ Iesu Christi quę rere cernebat. Mors erat, quod ecclesias, quarum solicitudine tantum non enecabatur, per subintroeúntes fratres ac pseudapostolos post discessum suum inspersis falsorum dogmatū zizanijs corrumpi uidebat. Mille huiusmodi mortis genera expertum esse hunc Apostolum ex scriptis illius abunde patet, si quis diligenter illa inspiciat. Attamen quoniam in causa hac resurrectionis mortuorum de eo mortis genere loquitur, quo uita corporis in discrimè inducitur, existimo simplicius, ac conuenientius esse, ut de illo intelligamus. Non morieba tur quotidie, uerùm quotidie mortis reddeba tur periculis obnoxius. Etenim quo plus cæteris in opere domini laborabat, hoc pluribus sese periculis inuoluebat. Haud enim indesi- nentem ipsius zelum princeps huius mundi ferre poterat.
units.tr: It was a kind of death for him when he saw that the good he wished to do was not done, and the evil he greatly hated was done. It was likewise a death when he saw that the things which were his own, not those of Jesus Christ, were being sought. It was a death when he saw the churches, for whose care he was almost killed, being corrupted after his departure by the tares of false doctrines sown by intruding brethren and false apostles. That this Apostle experienced a thousand kinds of death of this sort is abundantly clear from his writings, if anyone examines them carefully. Nevertheless, since in this argument about the resurrection of the dead he speaks of that kind of death by which the life of the body is brought into danger, I think it is simpler and more fitting to understand it in that sense. He was not dying daily, but was daily exposed to the dangers of death. For the more he laboured in the Lord's work beyond others, the more he involved himself in dangers. For the prince of this world could not bear his zeal, which never ceased.

units.la: PER nostram gloriationem, quam habeo in Christo Iesu domino nostro.] Græcè est, τὴν ὑμετέραν καύχησιν, quibus uerbis iuramento quod dicit confirmat. Iurat autem per gloriationem suam, eamq; non quamuis, sed quam habebat in Christo Iesu, cuius se gloriabatur esse Apostolū, & propter quem omnia illa discrimina ferebat, sciens eum esse dominū uitæ & mortis, regnare ad dexteram patris, reditu- rumq; ad abolendos omnes inimicos, ipsam quoq; mortem, & ad excitandum suos è mortuis, &c. Huiusmodi puto gloriationem intelligit, quæ ipsi adeo erat certa & firma, ut non dubitet per illam iurare. Quid non pateretur animus eiusmodi pro Christo? Quenam discrimina pro ueritate illius subire detrectaret?
units.tr: THROUGH MY GLORYING, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord. In Greek it is your glorying [τὴν ὑμετέραν καύχησιν], and by these words he confirms with an oath what he says. He swears by his own glorying, and not by just any glorying but by the one he had in Christ Jesus, whose apostle he gloried in being, and for whose sake he bore all those dangers, knowing that Christ is the Lord of life and death, reigns at the right hand of the Father, and will return to abolish all enemies, death itself included, and to raise his own from the dead. I take it that he means a glorying so certain and firm to him that he did not hesitate to swear by it. What would such a mind not endure for Christ? What dangers would it shrink from undergoing for the truth of Christ?

units.la: Chrysostomus legit, τὴν ὑμετέραν καύχησιν, id est, per uestram gloriationem. Existimo tamen eam lectionem non esse germanam. Primò nanq;, non est uerosimile, uoluisse Apostolum iurare per eam gloriationem, quam de Corinthijs habebat in Christo, cuius meminit in epistola sequenti cap. 7. dicens: Multa mihi fiducia erga uos, multa mihi gloriatio de uobis. Erat enim illa incerta. Deinde, non dicit, quam habetis: sed, quam habeo in Christo Iesu domino nostro. Quare neq; de ipsorum gloriatione loquitur, quam habuerint in Christo Iesu. Neque enim per illam, utpote incertam sibi, rectè iurasset. Cum ergo necesse sit ut per suâ gloriationem iuret, quam in Christo habebat, puto manifestum esse, lectione Chrysostomi non conuenire menti Apostoli.
units.tr: Chrysostom reads your glorying [τὴν ὑμετέραν καύχησιν], that is, by your glorying. I think, however, that this reading is not the genuine one. First, it is not likely that the Apostle meant to swear by the glorying he had concerning the Corinthians in Christ, which he mentions in the next letter, chapter 7, where he says: "I have great confidence in you, great glorying on your behalf." For that was uncertain. Second, he does not say "which you have," but "which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord." So he is not speaking of the glorying they themselves had in Christ Jesus. For he would not rightly have sworn by something uncertain to him. Since, then, he must be swearing by his own glorying, which he had in Christ, I think it is clear that Chrysostom's reading does not agree with the Apostle's mind.

units.la: Colligunt ex hoc loco, non esse iuramentū Christiano illicitum per se, modò non accedat illicitæ circumstantiæ: quandoquidem Apostolus Christi non hic tantum, sed alijs locis il lo uti non dubitauerit. Verùm de iuramento si quis pleraq; cognoscere uoluerit, uideat tractatum, quem de illo Commentarijs nostris in Psalmos appendicis uice adiecimus.
units.tr: From this passage some gather that an oath is not in itself unlawful for a Christian, provided no unlawful circumstances attach to it, since the Apostle did not hesitate to use it here and in other places as well. But if anyone wishes to learn more about oaths, let him see the treatise on the subject that we appended, by way of an appendix, to our Commentaries on the Psalms.

units.la: Vulgata editio aliter habet, uidelicet ad hunc modum: Quotidie morior propter uestrā gloriam fratres, quam habeo in Christo Iesu domino nostro: quasi sit in Græco non, νὴ, quæ iurātis est uocula, sed ἀλλὰ id est, propter: neq; καύχησις, id est, gloriatio: sed δόξα, id est, gloria. Et sic Ambrosius quoq; legit & exponit. Ad hoc festinabat, inquit Apostolus, semper solicitus, ut gloria illi accrescceret apud Deum acquisitę salutis multorum. Verùm si hoc uoluisset Paulus, non dixisset, Propter uestram gloriā, quam habeo: sed simpliciter, Propter gloriam quam in Christo Iesu habere cupio.
units.tr: The Vulgate edition has a different reading, namely this: "I die daily, brethren, by your glory, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord," as if the Greek had not nē [νὴ], which is the little word of swearing, but alla [ἀλλὰ], that is, by; and not kauchēsis [καύχησις], that is, glorying, but doxa [δόξα], that is, glory. Ambrose also reads and expounds it this way: "To this end," says the Apostle, "he always hurried, anxious that glory might increase for him before God from the salvation won for many." But if Paul had meant this, he would not have said "by your glory, which I have," but simply, "by the glory which I desire to have in Christ Jesus."

units.la: Augustinus tamen de doctrina Christiana lib. 3. cap. 4. sic annotat. Ait quidam interpres: Quotidie morior, per uestram iuro gloriam: quia in Græco uox iurantis manifesta est sine ambiguo sono.
units.tr: Yet Augustine, in On Christian Doctrine, book 3, chapter 4, notes thus: "A certain interpreter says: 'I die daily; I swear by your glory,' because in the Greek the word of swearing is clear, without any ambiguity of sound."

units.la: Et Epistola 89. ad Hilarium, paulo ante cal-
units.tr: And in Letter 89 to Hilary, a little before the end, he says:

units.la: cem sic dicit: Sed etiam illa ibi contra eos inuenta est, quam confitentur esse iurationem, ubi ait Apostolus: Quotidie morior per uestram gloriam fratres, quam habeo in Christo Iesu domino nostro. In Græcis enim codicibus reperitur omnino esse hanc iurationem, ne quis in Latina lingua hoc sic intelligat dictum, Per uestram gloriam, quomodo dictum est, per meum aduentum iterum aduos, & multa similia, ubi dicitur per aliquid, & non est iuratio. Hæc ibi.
units.tr: "But that passage too, which they confess to be an oath, is found there against them, where the Apostle says: 'I die daily, by your glory, brethren, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord.' For in the Greek manuscripts it is found to be altogether an oath. Lest anyone in Latin understand it as said in the sense of 'by your glory,' just as it is said 'by my coming again to you,' and many similar phrases where 'by' is used of something and it is not an oath." Thus far there.

units.la: Et lib. 1. de Sermone domini in monte: Nisi forte quis dicat, inquit, tunc cauendam esse iurationem, cum per aliquid dicitur quod iuratur, ut non iurauerit Apostolus, quia non dixit, per Deum: sed dixit, testis est mihi Deus. Ridiculum est hoc putare: tamè propter contetiosos ac tardiores, ne aliquid interesse quis putet, sciat etiam hoc modo iurasse Apostolū, dicentem: Quotidie morior per uestram gloriam, quod ne quis existimet ita dictum, tanquam si diceretur: Vestra gloria me facit quotidie mori, &c. Græca exemplaria dijudicant, in quibus scriptum est, τὴν ὑμετέραν καύχησιν, quod non nisi à iurante dicitur. Hæc ibi. Volui ista lectionis gratia annotare.
units.tr: And in book 1 of On the Sermon on the Mount: "Unless perhaps someone says," he writes, "that an oath must be avoided only when something is named by which one swears, and that therefore the Apostle did not swear, since he did not say 'by God' but said 'God is my witness.' This is ridiculous to think. Nevertheless, on account of the contentious and slower-witted, lest anyone suppose there is any difference, let him know that the Apostle also swore in this way, saying: 'I die daily by your glory.' Lest anyone think it was said as if it meant 'your glory makes me die daily,' etc., the Greek copies decide the matter, in which it is written your glorying [τὴν ὑμετέραν καύχησιν], which is said only by one who swears." Thus far there. I wanted to note these things for the sake of the reading.

units.la: Apparet hic, meo iudicio, quemadmodum & multis alijs locis, in Commentarijs qui Hieronymo adscribuntur, Hieronymi desiderari eruditionem, ideoque illos nihil esse minus q Hieronymi. Sic enim, quisquis illorum author est, annotauit. Per gloriā uestram fratres. Per, non semper significatio iuramenti est. Nam si dicam, Per puerum misi, non statim per puerū iurasse recte putabor. Hæc ille, quasi Apostolus non Græcè τὴν ὑμετέραν καύχησιν, sed Latinè per uestram gloriationem, scripserit. Quis credat Hieronymum tam pueriliter fuisse hallucinaturum?
units.tr: It is clear here, in my judgement, as in many other places in the Commentaries ascribed to Jerome, that the learning of Jerome is lacking, and therefore that these works are anything but Jerome's. For whoever their author is, he has noted thus: "By your glory, brethren. 'By' does not always signify an oath. For if I say, 'I sent it by a boy,' I shall not be rightly thought to have sworn by a boy." Thus he, as if the Apostle had written not your glorying [τὴν ὑμετέραν καύχησιν] in Greek but by your glorying in Latin. Who could believe that Jerome would have gone astray so childishly?

units.la: Si secundum hominem cum bestijs depugnauì Ephesi, quæ mihi utilitas, si mortui non resurgunt?
units.tr: If I fought with beasts at Ephesus as a mere man, what good is it to me, if the dead do not rise?

units.la: In genere dixerat, Periclitamur omni tempore, & in dies morior. Iam ex tam multis suis periculis, unum exempli uice memorat: ut in illo considerandum proponat, quàm oporteat se omnino esse demetem tam horrenda discrimina subeundo, cum illa uitare posset, & præsenti se uitæ accommodare, nisi certo esset de futura mortuorum resurrectione persuasus, ac sciret cui nam crederet, quamq; ille potens sit ad reddendum in illo die, quicquid ipsius fidei deponeret & concrederet.
units.tr: In general terms he had said, "We are in danger every hour, and I die daily." Now, out of so many dangers of his own, he mentions one as an example, so that the Corinthians may consider in it how entirely resolute a man must be who faces such dreadful perils when he could avoid them and accommodate himself to present life. Unless he were certain of the future resurrection of the dead, and knew in whom he trusted, and how powerful that person is to repay on that day whatever he has committed and entrusted to him in faith, he could not do so.

units.la: SI secundum hominem cum bestijs depugnaui Ephesi, inquit.] Hoc est, si cum essem Ephesi, ibiq; Christum prædicarem, depugnaui cum bestijs, neque Dei spiritu & uirtute adiutus, neque fide ueritatis impulsus: sed humano aliquo consilio, temeritate ac præsumptione motus, quid utilitatis ex tam horrendo periculo expectare potui, in quo non certa modò, sed & infamis & horrendissima mors ipso primo bestiarum aspectu in oculos incur{A}tium ne conspectum quidem uenit, nisi quod rere solet, siquidem mortui non resurgunt? Etiáfi eo facto integrum regnū sperasset, quorsum regnum, imo totus hic mundus, homini à bestijs discerpto ac consumpto? siquidem nō est post hanc uitam expectanda alia.
units.tr: "If I fought with beasts at Ephesus as a mere man," he says. That is: if, while I was at Ephesus and preaching Christ there, I fought with beasts, not aided by the Spirit and power of God, nor driven by faith in the truth, but moved by some human plan, rashness and presumption, what advantage could I expect from so dreadful a danger? In it death was not only certain but also infamous and most horrible, for at the first sight of the beasts it would come before the eyes of those who attacked him. Would it even be a question of profit, unless the dead rise, as is commonly supposed? Even if by that deed he had hoped for an entire kingdom, what would the kingdom be to him, or indeed this whole world, once he had been torn apart and consumed by beasts? For after this life nothing else is to be expected.

units.la: Quod Christiani ad bestias damnari cōsueuerint, ex Tertulliano patet. Si qua cōmunis calamitas poenas de impio mundo sumpsisset, tribuebatur id Christianis, & clamabatur, Christianos ad leonem. Vide in illius Apologetico cap.39. De eo cum nemine disceptarim, armati ne ad pugnandum, uel nudi ad hoc ut mox discerperentur, bestijs fuerint obiecti fideles. De cæteris, præsertim gladiatoribus, non est dubium, quin armati in arena cum bestijs spectante populo pugnaturi descenderint. Verum quod Paulum attinet, controuertitur cum bestijs ne, leonibus, leopardis, ursis, &c. uere depugnasse se, uel cum impijs hominibus quauis bestia ferocioribus pro veritate Christi decertasse dicat. Postremū sensum Theophylactus sequitur, exponens de Iudæis incredulis, & Demetrio aurifabro, qui sane leonum instar Paulum discerpere ac prorsus deuorare satagebant. Qui sic sentiunt, ex eo mouentur, quod nusquam fit in Actis mentio, quod Ephesi fuerit Paulus bestijs obiectus. Qui uero priorem sensum tenent, existimant non esse temere ex propria loquutione faciendā metaphoricam, nisi cogat uel aliqua propriæ loquutionis absurditas, uel impossibilitas, uel manifesta veritas. Quod Lucas nihil de bestijs meminit, tam non impedit simplicem sensum, quàm non impedit illum in epistola sequenti, ubi cap.unde cimo grauissimorum periculorum catalogus ponitur, quod nullam illorum mentionem in Actis factam legimus. Quare in cōfesso est, nō omnia esse in Acta relata q uel gessit uel passus est Apostolus. Si Lucas Apostolum Ephesi cum bestijs depugnasse narraret, crederemus id ita fuisse factum, etiamsi Paulus de illo tacuisset. Iam cum ipse Paulus hoc de se scribat, cur non credam sic esse factum, quantumuis nihil huius à Luca scribatur? Sic puto non esse satis pregnates causas, quare à simplici ac proprio uerborum sensu hoc loco discedamus.
units.tr: That Christians were commonly condemned to the beasts is clear from Tertullian. If some common calamity had exacted punishment from the wicked world, it was attributed to the Christians, and the cry went up, "The Christians to the lion!" See his Apologeticus, chapter 39. Nobody has disputed that the faithful were thrown to beasts, whether armed to fight or naked so that they might be torn to pieces at once. As for others, especially gladiators, there is no doubt that they went down armed into the arena to fight beasts while the people watched. But as for Paul, it is debated whether he means that he truly fought with beasts, with lions, leopards, bears and the like, or that he contended for the truth of Christ against wicked men, who are fiercer than any beast. Theophylact follows the last sense, explaining it of the unbelieving Jews and of Demetrius the silversmith, who were eager to tear Paul apart like lions and devour him entirely. Those who hold this view are moved by the fact that nowhere in the Acts is there any mention that Paul was thrown to beasts at Ephesus. Those who hold the former sense think that a figurative meaning should not be rashly drawn from ordinary speech, unless some absurdity, impossibility or manifest truth of the ordinary wording compels it. That Luke says nothing about beasts does not hinder the plain sense any more than it hinders the sense in the following epistle, where in chapter 11 a catalogue of very grave dangers is given, none of which we read was mentioned in the Acts. Therefore it is agreed that not everything the Apostle did or suffered is related in the Acts. If Luke were narrating that the Apostle fought with beasts at Ephesus, we would believe it had so happened, even if Paul had said nothing about it. Now, since Paul himself writes this about himself, why should I not believe it happened so, although Luke writes nothing of it? So I think there are not sufficiently weighty reasons for departing here from the plain and proper sense of the words.

units.la: Quod si quis historiam Demetrij & artificum quos ille aduersus Paulum cōcitauit, dili genter inspiciat, non inueniet Apostolū cum illis ne uerbo quidem depugnasse, imò in ipso rum seditione ne cōparuisse quidem. Sic enim Act.19. legimus. His auditis, repleti sunt ira & exclamauerunt dicentes: Magna Diana Ephesiorum. Et impleta est ciuitas tota cōfusione, & impetum fecerunt uno animo in theatrum, correpto Gaio & Aristarcho Macedonibus, comitibus Pauli. Paulo autem uolēte intrare ad populum, nō permiserunt discipuli. Quidam autem & ex Asiæ primoribus qui erant amici eius, miserunt ad eum, rogantes, ne se daret in theatrum, &c. Ergo non pugnauit cum bestijs illis Demetrio ac socijs eius, in quorum furentium ne conspectum quidem uenit, nisi quod accidit illius comitibus in ea seditione, ipsi de putetur. Verū quorsum attinuisset in hac causa aliena citare pericula, cum de suis haberet abunde multa, quæ commorarētur?
units.tr: If anyone carefully examines the story of Demetrius and of the craftsmen whom he stirred up against Paul, he will not find that the Apostle fought with them even in words, but that he did not even appear in their uproar. For so we read in Acts 19: "When they heard these things, they were filled with anger and cried out, saying, 'Great is Diana of the Ephesians.' And the whole city was filled with confusion, and they rushed with one accord into the theatre, having seized Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians, companions of Paul. But when Paul wished to go in among the people, the disciples did not allow it. Some of the Asiarchs also, who were his friends, sent to him, begging him not to venture into the theatre," and so on. So he did not fight with those beasts, Demetrius and his companions, and he did not even come into the sight of those raging men, except that what happened to his companions in that uproar befell him as well, as might be thought. But why would it have been useful in this case to cite the dangers of others, when he had many of his own enough to dwell on?

units.la: QVAE mihi utilitas, inquit, si mortui nō resurgant? Quid hic illi, qui etsi resurrectionem corporum negant, animarum tamen immortalitatem sic concedunt, ut per hanc omnia quæ Christianismi sunt saluari posse putent. Si nulla utilitas est ei qui propter Deum mori non dubitat, nisi corpora mortuorum resurgant, ergo omnis illa pietas, quę in scripturis traditur, prorsus à resurrectione mortuorum omnem suā expectat utilitatē? Desinant ergo esse Christiani, uel fidem resurrectionis amplectantur.
units.tr: "What good is it to me," he says, "if the dead do not rise?" What do those say here who, although they deny the resurrection of bodies, yet concede the immortality of souls in such a way that they think all the things of Christianity can be saved through it? If there is no advantage for one who does not hesitate to die for God, unless the bodies of the dead rise, then is all that piety which is handed down in the Scriptures wholly without any expected advantage apart from the resurrection of the dead? Let them therefore cease to be Christians, or else embrace the faith of the resurrection.

units.la: QVAE mihi utilitas, si mortui non resurgāt? Nulla. Ergo quoniam resurgent mortui, proderit Paulus ad bestias depugnasse pro veritate Christi in hac vita. Firma est hæc consequentia. Habebitur igitur ratio in futuro sæculo eorum quæ iam gerimus in præsenti: & quisquē seminat in hoc mortali corpore, metet in immortali, à mortuis excitato.
units.tr: "What good is it to me, if the dead do not rise?" None. Therefore, since the dead will rise, it will profit Paul that he fought with beasts for the truth of Christ in this life. This inference is sound. Thus account will be taken, in the future age, of what we now do in the present; and whoever sows in this mortal body will reap in the immortal body raised from the dead.

units.la: Ex oppositō possumus colligere ad hunc modum: Si secundum hominem, pro ingenio meo, uixero in hac vita, & nullam prorsus pietatis & iustitiæ rationem habuero, quid inde erit detrimenti ac damni, si mortui non resurgant? Nihil. Et sic sensus hæret in multorum animis, id quod ipsa vita proclamat. Ergo, si tollas resurrectionē mortuorum, Paulo nihil proderit, ad bestias depugnasse propter Euangelium Christi, & innumera alia illius gratia felicisse ac pertulisse, & Neroni nihil obesse Paulū, nec Iudęis incredulis Christum ipsum occidisse. Tanti uidelicet momenti est in articulo hoc resurrectionis mortuorum. Quare haud præterrationem tantopere Apostolus in asserendo illo laborat.
units.tr: From the opposite we can conclude in this way: If I live in this life according to my own wit, and have no regard at all for piety and righteousness, what loss or harm will follow from it if the dead do not rise? None. And so this sense sticks in the minds of many, as life itself proclaims. Therefore, if you take away the resurrection of the dead, it will profit Paul nothing to have fought with beasts for the sake of the gospel of Christ, to have endured and suffered countless other things for his grace; and Paul would be harmed in nothing by Nero, nor the unbelieving Jews by having killed Christ himself. So weighty, of course, is this article of the resurrection of the dead. Therefore the Apostle labours so much in asserting it, and not without reason.

units.la: EDAMVS & bibamus, cras enim morimur. Chrysostomus sic legit: Si secundum hominem cum bestijs depugnaui Ephesi, quæ mihi utilitas? Si mortui non resurgūt, edamus & bibamus, cras enim morimur. Verum nihil refert, siue præsenti particulæ siue sequenti coniungamus illud, Si mortui nō resurgunt, unde omnia hæc absurda colliguntur. Si mortui nō resurgūt, cogitat uoluptuarius, Ergo post mortem mihi non erit ulla uoluptas. Et breuis hæc vita est, mors ultima linea rerum, Cras aderit, cur non igitur præsentibus utor Delitijs? cur non edo? cur non suauia queuis, Vina bibo? in genio cur non indulgeo totus? Hæ sunt cogitationes uoluptuariorum, ubi audiunt non resurgere mortuos, quas hic Apostolus duobus tribus uerbis expressit, sub ipsorum persona dicens: Edamus & bibamus, cras enim morimur.
units.tr: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." Chrysostom reads it thus: "If I fought with beasts at Ephesus as a mere man, what good is it to me? If the dead do not rise, let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." But it makes no difference whether we join that clause to the preceding part or to the following, "If the dead do not rise," from which all these absurdities are drawn. "If the dead do not rise," thinks the pleasure-seeker, "then after death I shall have no pleasure. And this life is brief, death is the final boundary of things. Tomorrow it will be here; why then do I not use the present delights? Why do I not eat? Why do I not drink sweet wines of every kind? Why do I not wholly indulge my spirit?" These are the thoughts of pleasure-seekers when they hear that the dead do not rise, and the Apostle here has expressed them in two or three words, speaking in their own person: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die."

units.la: Quo autem significet se metuere ne Corinthijs fidelib. id accidat, quod olim accidit Hierosolymitanis, uerba hæc uoluptuariorum, Edamus & bibamus, cras enim morimur, haud
units.tr: But in order to show that he fears the faithful Corinthians may suffer what once befell the Jerusalemites, he presents these words of the pleasure-seekers, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die," not from his own invention,

units.la: F de suo, sed ex uicesimo secundo capite Ieshaię desumpta ponit, ubi post grauem futuræ uastationis ac cladis comminationem subijcitur ad hunc modum: Et uocabit Dominus Deus exercituum in die illa ad fletum & plầctum ad caluicium & ad cincturam sacci, & eccekæticia & gaudium, cædendo boues, mactando oues, edendo carnes & bibendo uinum, אכל ושתה, id est, edendo ac bibendo, cras enim (dicetis) moriemur. Hæc ibi.de quibus, si cui lubet, uideat Commentarios nostros in Ieshaiam.
units.tr: but taken from the twenty-second chapter of Isaiah, where, after a grave threat of coming devastation and slaughter, it is added in this way: "And the Lord God of hosts will call in that day to weeping and mourning, to baldness and to girding with sackcloth; and behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen, killing sheep, eating flesh and drinking wine, [אכל ושתה] that is, eating and drinking, for tomorrow (you say) we die." So far there. Whoever wishes may consult our commentaries on Isaiah concerning these matters.

units.la: Erant Hierosolymitani, præsertim primores, non solum carnales & impij, sed & diuinarum admonitionum & comminationum irrisores. Cum exitium & uastationem minaretur illis per prophetam dominus, nisi resipiscerēt, illi usquę adeo nullam ne cogitationem quidem resipiscentiæ animo concipiebant, ut magis quàm antea uoluptatibus operam darent commessationibus & compotationibus indulgentes, & alius alium ad irridendum prophetam prouocantes, ac dicētes: Edamus & bibamus, cras enim morimur, cras Hierushalē tota corruet: sic enim futurum propheta noster minatur. Et hæc irrisio usque adeo displicuit domino, ut iureiurando affirmauerit, huic se illorum iniquitati haud ignoturum, nec quieturum donec morte absumerentur. Cum igitur acciderit hoc in populo Dei, nō immerito metuit Apostolus, ne idem & Corinthijs fidelibus accideret, præsertim cum adhuc uiuerent inter impios, & in ipsa ecclesia sua multos haberet carnales.
units.tr: The people of Jerusalem, especially their leading men, were not only carnal and wicked but also mockers of the divine warnings and threats. When the Lord, through the prophet, threatened them with destruction and devastation unless they repented, they did not so much as entertain a thought of repentance. Instead they gave themselves all the more to pleasures, indulging in drinking parties and carousing, and urging one another on to mock the prophet, saying: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die; tomorrow all Jerusalem will fall, for this is what our prophet threatens." This mockery so displeased the Lord that he swore an oath that he would not overlook their iniquity, nor rest until they were consumed by death. Since this happened among the people of God, the Apostle had good reason to fear that the same might happen to the faithful at Corinth, especially since they still lived among the impious and his own congregation still had many carnal members.

units.la: Nos hic obseruemus, quò euadat caro, fide resurrectionis destituta, & quàm infensate scientia mortalitatis suæ abutatur. Edamus, inquiunt, & bibamus. Edere ac bibere per se nihil habet reprehensibile, quandoquidem natura sic est ut utrunque requirat. Sed refert quo fine edas ac bibas. Edamus & bibamus. Quare? Cras enim morimur, inquiunt. Ergo ne dictat hoc ratio, ut quoniam cras moituri sumus, hodie edamus & bibamus: & non magis ob id comedamus & bibamus, ne si cibum necessarium naturę nostrę negemus, cras moriamur? Quod si cras moriendum est, quorsum hodie comedes ac bibes? Cum finis cibi ac potus sit non mors, sed uitæ huius sustentatio. Etiamsi non sit futura resurrectio, conuenit ne homini hæc stultitia, ut comedat & bibat, non ut uiuat: sed quia moritur ne non satis ebrius, & bene curata cute distentoque aqualiculo moriatur? Quæ bestia sic est animata, ut quo citius moritura est, hoc plus edat ac bibat? Animalis homo, quàtumuis futuræ resurrectionis ignarus, non dicit, Edam & bibam, cras enim moriar: sed, Edā & bibam ne moriar. At caro, crassis istis Bacchi & Veneris uoluptatib. immersa, & ad hoc tantum uiuens, ut edat & bibat, non edens & bibens ut uiuat: ubi de mortalitate sua admonetur, in hanc uocem erumpit, Age edam ac bibam, cras enim moriar. Inde
units.tr: Here we should note how far the flesh goes when it is cut off from faith in the resurrection, and how it abuses the knowledge of its own mortality. "Let us eat and drink," they say. Eating and drinking in themselves contain nothing blameworthy, since nature itself requires both. But what matters is the purpose for which you eat and drink. "Let us eat and drink. Why? For tomorrow we die," they say. Does reason really dictate that, since we must die tomorrow, we should eat and drink today? Should we not rather eat and drink so that, by denying our nature the food it needs, we do not die tomorrow? And if we must die tomorrow, why do you eat and drink today, since the purpose of food and drink is not death but the sustaining of this life? Even if there were no resurrection to come, would it be reasonable for a man to be so foolish as to eat and drink not in order to live, but so that he may die not sober enough, with his skin well tended and his belly stretched? What beast is so constituted that the sooner it is going to die, the more it eats and drinks? Animal man, however ignorant of the resurrection to come, does not say, "I will eat and drink, for tomorrow I die," but "I will eat and drink so that I do not die." But the flesh, immersed in the gross pleasures of Bacchus and Venus, living only so as to eat and drink, not eating and drinking so as to live, when it is reminded of its mortality, bursts out into this cry: "Come, let me eat and drink, for tomorrow I die." Thus

units.la: sumit causam uoluptuādi, unde debebat causam sumere à uoluptatibus abstinendi. Sic refert in quem hominem scientia & cogitatio mortalitatis incidat. Si in uoluptuarium, dicit: Edam & bibam, cras enim moriar. Si in animalem ac qualicunque humanæ rationis sensu præditum: dicit, Quorsum uoluptatib. operā dabo? Cras enim moriar. Quorsum opes collegam potētiamque & honores appetam? Cras enim moriar. Si in Christianum ac fidelem, caueb, inquit, ne peccem, cras enim ex hac uita migrabo ad dominū. Odit ac persequitur me mundus? Non faciet hoc diu. Cras enim obdormiam in domino: & de manibus omnium inimicorum meorū liberabor. Caro mea relūctatur spiritui? An non faciet hoc in sempiternum. Cras enim morietur, & mortua non relūctabitur amplius. Premunt me omnis generis ærumnæ, paupertas, fames, morbi? Bene habet. Non modo mortalis sum, sed & breui moriar, & beneficio mortis ex hisce miseriis omnibus liberatus mortalitatem istam immortalitate commutabo. Hæc & consimilia multa proferet homo fidelis de morte sua breui uentura admonitus. Quare bonū quidem est, nun quam obliuisci, quàm cito pede mors ultima rerum linea immineat. Verum multum refert, in quem hæc cogitatio incidat. Inspice Germaniam nostram, & uide an non hæc illi uox copetat: Edamus & bibamus, cras enim morimur. Siue pestis grassatur siue gladius hostilis fœuit: editur ac bibitur, imò non amplius gulę indulgetur, quo magis intentant omnia mortem. Quid hoc aliud est: quàm, edamus & bibamus, cras enim morimur? Vide Sap.2. quomodo cogitationes carnalium & uoluptuariorum exprimantur. Adeste, inquiunt, bonis præsentibus fruamur, uino preciosò & unguentis nos repleamus, nullum pratum sit expers nostræ luxuriæ, &c. Quare? Quia breuis est uita nostra & umbræ transeunti similis. Nemo est qui non moriatur, nemo qui ex morte reuertatur. Vnde hęc cogitat? Quia excæcati sunt, & neque mysteria Dei norūt, neque futuram hominis immortalitatem credunt.
units.tr: it takes as the reason for indulging in pleasure what it ought to have taken as the reason for abstaining from pleasure. So it matters into what kind of man the knowledge and thought of mortality falls. If it falls on a voluptuary, he says: "I will eat and drink, for tomorrow I die." If it falls on a merely natural man, endowed with some sense of human reason, he says: "Why should I devote myself to pleasures? For tomorrow I die. Why should I seek wealth, power and honours? For tomorrow I die." If it falls on a Christian and a believer, he says: "I will take care not to sin, for tomorrow I shall depart from this life to the Lord. The world hates and persecutes me? It will not do so for long; for tomorrow I shall fall asleep in the Lord and be freed from the hands of all my enemies. My flesh struggles against the spirit? It will not do so for ever; for tomorrow it will die, and being dead it will struggle no more. Every kind of distress presses upon me, poverty, hunger, sickness? Good! I am not only mortal, but I shall soon die, and by the benefit of death, freed from all these miseries, I shall exchange this mortality for immortality." A faithful man, reminded that his death is near, will utter these and many similar things. It is good, therefore, never to forget how quickly the final line of all things is at hand, as it were, on foot. Yet it matters greatly into whom this thought falls. Look at our Germany, and see whether this cry does not fit it: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." Whether plague is raging or the enemy's sword is raging, people eat and drink; indeed, they no longer even indulge their appetite the more all things threaten death. What is this other than "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die"? See Wisdom 2, how the thoughts of carnal and voluptuous men are expressed: "Come," they say, "let us enjoy the good things at hand; let us fill ourselves with costly wine and ointments; let no meadow be free from our luxury," and so on. Why? Because our life is short and like a passing shadow. No one returns from death, and no one escapes it. Whence do they think thus? Because they are blinded, and neither know the mysteries of God nor believe in the future immortality of man.

units.la: NE decipiamini. Mores bonos corrumpūt colloquia mala.] Immiscet succinctam admonitionem propter imperitiores & minus cautos. Ne decipiamini, inquit. Græcè est μὴ πλανᾶσθε, quod supra capite sexto uertit: Ne erretis. Verum quoniam de errore loquitur Apostolus, qui ex prauis impiorum colloquijs cōcipi potest, recte uertit hoc loco: Ne decipiamini. Et uulgata habet: Nolite seduci. Hoc est, ne credite seductoribus illis, qui resurrectionē mortuorū negantes, præsentis uitę delicias sectantur, & quosuis à studio pietatis abducere conantur, ne soli in barathrum perditionis descendant. Et quod nam est seductionis huius periculum? Mores bonos, inquit, colloquia corrumpunt mala. Colloquium prauum est, uenite edamus & bibamus, cras enim morimur. Post mortē nulla uoluptas. Non enim resurresurgunt mortui. Quorsum attinet frustra stu sunt, ut iam nihil illis timendum esse uideatur, dere rebus, in quibus nihil est ueri, nihil utilita tis, & interim nec præsenti uita frui, nec post mortem ulla alia potiri? Hoc genus parui col loquij omnium est perniciosissimum. Corrû pit enim bonos mores, mores uidelicet pieta tis, iusticiæ, religionis, honestatis, probitatis, modestiæ, temperantiæ, & humanitatis. Hoc est, reddit ex pijs impios, ex iustis iniustos, ex religiosis ac timentibus Dei irreligiosos & cô temptores Dei, ex honestis inhonestos, ex pro bis improbos, ex modestis & temperantibus immodestos & intemperantes, ex humanis in humanos, &c. Etenim ubi sermonibus impio rum seducti, nullam nobis post mortem reli quam fore uitam, sed esse homine similem be stijs & iumentis, ac morte consummari illius omnia & transire in nihilum, credimus ac sen timus: qui aliud consequi potest, quàm ut & i psam hanc uitam nostram bestialem & impiâ reddamus, & omnibus carnis nostræ affectib. indulgeamus?
units.tr: "Do not be deceived: bad company corrupts good morals." He adds a brief warning for the less experienced and less cautious. "Do not be deceived," he says. The Greek is μὴ πλανᾶσθε [do not be led astray], which above, in chapter six, he rendered "Do not err." But since the Apostle is speaking of an error that can arise from the wicked talk of the impious, it is right to translate it here "Do not be deceived." The Vulgate has "Do not be seduced." That is, do not believe those seducers who deny the resurrection of the dead, pursue the delights of the present life, and try to draw anyone at all away from the pursuit of godliness, so that they alone may not go down into the pit of destruction. And what is the danger of this seduction? "Bad company," he says, "corrupts good morals." Bad company says: "Come, let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. After death there is no pleasure; the dead do not rise." What is the use of being busy with things in which there is no truth and no profit, and meanwhile neither to enjoy the present life nor to obtain any other life after death? This kind of little conversation is the most pernicious of all. For it corrupts good morals, namely the morals of piety, justice, religion, honesty, uprightness, modesty, temperance and humanity. That is, it makes the godly impious, the just unjust, the religious and God-fearing irreligious and despisers of God, the honest dishonest, the upright wicked, the modest and temperate immodest and intemperate, and the humane inhumane, and so on. For when, led astray by the talk of the impious, we believe and feel that no life remains for us after death, but that we are like beasts and cattle, and that everything ends in death and passes into nothing, what else can follow except that we make this very life of ours bestial and impious, and indulge all the affections of the flesh?

units.la: CORRVMPVNT bonos mores collo quia mala, inquit. Est hæc sententia generalis ac latissime patens, ita ut species eius omnes adnumerari nequeant. Accommodauit illam Apostolus causæ quam agebat. Vir prudens, præsertim minister uerbi, usurpabit eam cótra omnis generis corruptelas. Sermo delatoris malum est colloquium. Corrumpit amicorum concordiam, & inflammat animos eorum ad inimicitias & odia mutua. Sermo eius qui pa tiétiam iniuriarum dissuadet, & ad uindictam incitat, malum est colloquium, suaues ac placi dos patientis animi mores corrumpens, & in sæuos hostiles sq; peruertens. Assentatoris adu latio, & illud aulicum EVGE, malum est col loquium, modestiam animi corrumpens, & in pessimam superbiæ inflationem mutans. Im pudicorum hominum sermo malum est collo quium, pudicos adolescentum mores corrum pens. Sermo dehortans à studio sapientiæ, scie tiæ, & bonarum artium, à laboribus & seduli tate disciplinæ, malum est colloquium. Reddit enim ignauos, desides & inertes. Sunt eius ge neris corruptelæ innumeræ.
units.tr: "Bad company corrupts good morals," he says. This is a general saying of very wide application, so that its kinds cannot all be enumerated. The Apostle adapted it to the matter he was handling. A prudent man, and especially a minister of the Word, will use it against every kind of corruption. The talk of an informer is bad company. It corrupts the concord of friends and inflames their minds to enmity and mutual hatred. The speech of one who dissuades a man from patience under injuries and urges him to revenge is bad company, corrupting the gentle and placid manners of a patient mind and turning them into savage hostility. The flattery of a sycophant, and that courtly "Bravo!", is bad company, corrupting modesty of mind and changing it into the worst swelling of pride. The talk of immodest men is bad company, corrupting the chaste manners of young people. Speech that dissuades from the pursuit of wisdom, knowledge and the liberal arts, from labour and diligence in learning, is bad company, for it makes men lazy, idle and sluggish. The kinds of such corruption are countless.

units.la: Sed unde est ista uis mali colloquij, cum uer bis tantum, ijsq; non Dei, sed hominis cõstet? An uox humana eius est efficaciæ, ut animum hominis mutet ac transformet? Nisi esset, ma lum colloquium bonos mores non corrumpe ret. Corrumpit autè. Est igitur efficax. Hæc il lius efficacia tam est certa, indubitata ut & e thnicis hominibus per quotidianam fit expe riétiam cognita, unde sententiâ hâc senário uer siculo comprehésam Menander poeta comi cus tanquam omnibus notam affirmanter po suit, dicês: ... Si quæ ras causam, cur inter homines ab homine pro latum malum colloquium tantum habeat effi caciæ, ut non modo bonas cogitationes piaq; & honesta proposita, sed & bonos mores, qui propter consuetudinem uelut in habitû dueti
units.tr: But where does the power of bad conversation come from, since it consists only of words, and those human rather than divine? Does the human voice have such efficacy that it can change and transform a person's mind? If it did not, bad conversation would not corrupt good morals. But it does corrupt them. So it is effective. This efficacy is so certain and undoubted that even the heathen know it from daily experience. That is why Menander, the comic poet, stated this idea in a verse of six feet, as if it were known to all, saying: ... If you ask why bad conversation, spoken by one person to another, has such power among men that it not only overturns good thoughts, pious purposes and honourable intentions, but also good morals, which by long habit have been brought almost into a settled disposition,

units.la: Quod autem Apostolus senarium hunc ex Menandri Comœdia Corinthijs consideran dum proponit, documento nobis esse debet, quàm conueniat ministro Christi, ut undequa que sit non è sacris tantum, sed & ethnicorum scriptis munitus, quo se accommodet illis, quos uel emendare, uel ad ueram pietatem æ dificare debet. Gentilium poetarum, præser tim comicorum scripta Corinthijs erant uul go nota. Cum ergo scriberet illis de uitándis malis colloquijs, possetque ex sacris scripturis adferre, quæ huc facerent, maluit illis comicâ sententiam omnibus notissimam & celeberri mam obijcere, quo citius ex antea cognitis & tritis ad cauendum praua colloquia permoue rentur. Possunt igitur in religionis quoque causa Gentilium scripta citari, uerum non ad stabilienda fidei nostræ dogmata, sed ad mo res uel bonos commendandos, uel malos re prehendendos, præsertim si sint indubitato ac communi sensu uera, & uulgo trita, qualis est hic Menandri senarius.
units.tr: The Apostle's citing this iambic line from Menander's comedy to the Corinthians should teach us how fitting it is for a minister of Christ to be equipped not only with the sacred writings but also with the writings of the heathen, so that he can adapt himself to those whom he ought either to correct or to build up in true godliness. The writings of the heathen poets, especially the comic poets, were commonly known to the Corinthians. So when he was writing to them about avoiding bad conversation, and could have brought forward passages of Scripture that bore on the matter, he preferred to set before them a saying of the comic poet, known to everyone and very famous, so that they would be more quickly moved to beware of wicked company by means of something already known and familiar. Therefore the writings of the Gentiles may also be cited in matters of religion, not to establish the dogmas of our faith, but to commend good morals or to rebuke bad ones, especially when they are true by undoubted and common judgement and are a commonplace, as this verse of Menander is.

units.la: Non est autem hic locus inani eorum ofien tationi, qui non aliam ob causam Gentilium poetarum, comicorum, historicorum & phi losophorum scripta lucubrationibus suis e tiam sacris frequenter inspergunt, quàm ut multa legisse, ac seculariter quoque eruditi uideant.
units.tr: Nor is this the place for the empty display of those who fill their writings, even their sacred ones, with the works of heathen poets, comic writers, historians and philosophers for no other reason than to make it look as if they have read widely and are learned in secular matters too.

units.la: Simile. uideantur. Probanda quidem est multijuga bonorum authorum lectio, uerum ostentatio nem illius nemo cordatus probauerit, maxi me in causa religionis.
units.tr: Like... let them look. Certainly a wide reading of good authors is to be commended, but no sensible person would approve a display of it, especially in matters of religion.

units.la: EXPERGISCIMINI iuste, & ne pecce tis.] Coeptæ admonitioni immiscuit metû pe riculi, quod est ex malis colloquijs. Iam illam resumit & absoluit. Dixit: Ne decipiamini, mo res bonos colloquia corrumpunt mala. Ne id Corinthijs eueniat, inter quos erat nugatores resurrectionis, excitat eos uelut e somno in quo negligetiæ & nimię securitatis uicio ine briati iacebant: dicens, Expergiscemini iuste. Vox Græca ἐκνήψατε ad sobrietatem euigilare significat. Ratio humana inebriat, doctrina ue ritatis sobrios reddit in causa fidei. Quoniam calicem rationis humanæ, quem negatores resurrectionis biberat ipsi & alijs porrigebat, securi & incauti gustauerant, excitat eos ad so brietatem, hoc est, ad cautionem ac studiû per manendi in doctrina sanæ fidei, quam per Euá gelium acceperant. Ex qualitate admonitio nis, quasi medicinæ, de qualitate morbi iudica re possumus.
units.tr: AWAKE, as you ought to, and do not sin. To the admonition just begun he has added a fear of the danger that comes from bad company. Now he takes up that thought again and completes it. He has said: Do not be deceived; bad company corrupts good morals. So that this may not happen to the Corinthians, among whom there were those who denied the resurrection, he rouses them, as if from a sleep in which they lay drunk with negligence and the vice of excessive security, saying: Awake as you ought [ἐκνήψατε]. The Greek word means to become sober, to wake up to soundness. Human reason makes men drunk; the teaching of truth makes them sober in the matter of faith. Since they had tasted, carelessly and incautiously, the cup of human reason, which the deniers of the resurrection had drunk themselves and were handing to others, he rouses them to sobriety, that is, to caution and diligence in remaining in the teaching of sound faith, which they had received through the Gospel. From the kind of admonition, as from a remedy, we can judge the kind of disease.

units.la: EXPERGISCIMINI iuste, inquit. In Græco est ἐκνήψατε, quod Græcis aliquando idé est quod ἐξύπνωσον, id est, digne ac competenter. Et hoc sensu capiêdum existimo in præsenti. Ad monet enim eos conditionis ac professionis Christianæ, quæ homines requirit in hoc secu lo non ebrios ac dormiantes, sed uigiles ac so brios. Et utinam prælati ecclesiarum pastores ouium Christi è tam graui uterno tandem ἀνανήψωσιν expergiscantur, quo uigiles & sobrij pa scendo gregi dominico incumbant. Verû sic sunt inebriati & obsoporati, ut citius sint in die domini è claustris mortis resurrecturi, �], ab hoc lethargo ad sobriâ mętem euigilaturi.
units.tr: AWAKE as you ought, he says. In Greek it is [ἐκνήψατε], which the Greeks sometimes use in the same sense as [ἐξύπνωσον], that is, worthily and fittingly. I think this sense should be adopted here. For he reminds them of the condition and profession of the Christian, which in this world requires men not to be drunk and sleeping, but watchful and sober. And would that the prelates and ministers of the churches might at last wake up [ἀνανήψωσιν] from so heavy a drowsiness, so that, watchful and sober, they might apply themselves to feeding the Lord's flock. But they are so drunk and stupefied with sleep that they will sooner rise from the chambers of death on the day of the Lord than wake to a sober mind from this lethargy.

units.la: ET ne peccetis, inquit. Vocula ἐκνήψατε, id est, &, pro ut est posita, ut sit idem quod ἵνα μὴ ἁμαρτάνητε, id est, ut nô peccetis. Significat quor sum expergefieri debeant, ad hoc uidelicet, ut sibi prospiciant ne dormitantes ad peccandû abducantur. Qui uoces Syrenarum audiunt, nisi sint oculis ἀναιμάκτως, facile soluuntur in so mnum, ut pereant. Consimili modo ubi sonât mala colloquia quibus resurrectio mortuorû, futura uita, & iudicium mundi in dubium uo cantur, periculû est ne qui incauti sunt obdor miscant & in omnis generis peccata pellicia tur. Quod si ex peccatorum multitudine, enor mitate ac securitate certum de cuiusq; fide ac spe argumentû colligi potest, uidetur prorsus impleri illud Christi, tardante uero spôso dor mitauerunt omnes ac dormierût. Quid est tar dante spôso dormitare aliud, quàm partim re iecta dominici aduetus expectatione in quod uis peccati genus ueluti grauem somnum sol ui, partim tædio superatum negligentius sese in causa pietatis gerere? Hic somnus occupat prope omnes tam prudentes quàm fatuas uir gines, sicut est in parabola.
units.tr: AND do not sin, he says. The small word [ἐκνήψατε], that is, "and", as it is placed here, means the same as [ἵνα μὴ ἁμαρτάνητε], that is, so that you do not sin. It shows the purpose for which they ought to be roused: namely, that they may take care not to be led into sin while they are asleep. Those who hear the voices of the Sirens, unless their eyes are [ἀναιμάκτως] closed, are easily lulled into sleep and perish. In the same way, where bad conversation sounds out, in which the resurrection of the dead, the future life and the judgement of the world are called into doubt, there is danger that those who are careless will fall asleep and be enticed into every kind of sin. And if from the multitude, enormity and security of sins a sure proof of each man's faith and hope can be gathered, then that saying of Christ seems fully fulfilled: "While the bridegroom delays, they all slumbered and slept." And what is it to slumber while the bridegroom delays, but to cast off, in part, the expectation of the Lord's coming and to sink into every kind of sin as into a heavy sleep, and, in part, to be overcome by weariness and to behave more carelessly in the cause of piety? This sleep seizes almost all, the wise virgins as well as the foolish, as in the parable.

units.la: NAM ignorationem Dei nonnulli habet.
units.tr: FOR some have ignorance of God.

units.la: Reddit rationem, quare ad id eos excitet, ne peccent. Quia sunt inter uos, inquit, nonnulli, qui quoniam uirtutem Dei non cognoscunt, resurrectionem mortuorum quasi prorsus fit impossibilis, negare non uerentur. Sic reijcit illorum incredulitatem in ignorantiam Dei, perinde atq; Christus ad Sadduceos dicebat: Erratis, neq; scripturas, neq; uirtutem Dei scie tes. Ab illis erat periculum incautis, quemad modum apud Iudęos ita & apud Christianos. Ergo articulus hic de resurrectione mortuorû incomprehensibilis est illis, qui Deum igno rant. Non enim capitur humana ratione, quæ prorsus impossibile cesset, ut mortui resurgât, contraq; eam fidem multum disputat. Qui ue ro nec potentiam Dei nec uirtutē uerbi eius ignorât, illis habetur mortuorum resurrectio & facillima & certo futura. Cum credât illum ex nihilo condidisse cœlum & terram, & quæ in illis sunt omnia, sciantq; hominem ab illo initio esse ex puluere terræ conditum, & spira culo uitæ animatû: quomodo dubitarent esse illi facillimum, ut corpora nostra in puluerem terræ soluta, unde primum sunt desumpta, ubi uoluerit excitet, ac denuo uiuificet? Nisi puta re debemus accidisse hoc illi præ senio, ut pristi nas uires amiserit, scientiamq; creandi ac uiui ficandi obliuioni tradiderit: deinde sic esse có paratam Christi doctrinam, ut quo antiquior est, hoc minus mereatur fidei. Abiit. Diuina po tentia ac ueritas ut sunt sempiternæ, ita nullo quis multorû seculorû decursu labefactantur.
units.tr: He gives the reason why he rouses them, so that they may not sin. Because, he says, there are some among you who, since they do not know the power of God, do not hesitate to deny the resurrection of the dead, as if it were altogether impossible. So he traces their unbelief to ignorance of God, just as Christ said to the Sadducees: "You are wrong, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God." This was a danger to the incautious among the Jews, and in the same way among Christians. Therefore this article about the resurrection of the dead is incomprehensible to those who do not know God. For it is not grasped by human reason, which thinks it entirely impossible that the dead should rise, and it argues much against this faith. But for those who know neither the power of God nor the power of his word, the resurrection of the dead seems both very easy and certain to come. Since they believe that he created heaven and earth from nothing, with all that is in them, and know that man was at the beginning formed from the dust of the earth and animated with the breath of life, how could they doubt that it is very easy for him to raise our bodies, dissolved into the dust of the earth from which they were first taken, whenever he wills, and to quicken them again? Unless we must suppose that this has happened to him, as it were, through old age, so that he has lost his former strength and forgotten his skill in creating and giving life; and that the teaching of Christ is so constituted that the older it is, the less it deserves faith. Far from it! The divine power and truth are everlasting, and so they are not weakened by the passage of any number of ages.

units.la: AD pudorem uobis loquor. Comuniter exponunt de pudore quem hęc scribendo Co rinthijs ad hoc uoluerit incutere, ut ad se re uersi minus auscultarent mala incredulorum colloquia. Hoc genus pudoris non ad ignomi niam, sed ad resipiscentiam inducens, recte uo catur ἐντρέπω, à uerbo ἐντρέπεσθαι, quod reuereor ac solicitus fio significat. Verum quoniâ nô di cit, πρὸς ἐντροπὴν ὑμῶν. i. ad pudorem uestrû: sed, πρὸς ἐντροπὴν ὑμῖν λέγω, id est, ad pudorem uobis loquor, posset exponi de pudore quem ipse Apostolus hęc dicendo in seipso senserit. Q.d. Confundor in uobis hæc dicendo, pudorem mihijpsi gigno, dum hæc ad uos loquor, quæ tamen necessitate salutis uestræ compulsus scribo. Pudefaciebat Apostolum, quod igno rationem Dei nonnullis obijcere cogebatur, cum esset illorum Apostolus, quod perinde e rat, ac si præceptor discipulis suis, quos iâ spe rauerit admodum profecisse, ignorationę pri morum elementorum opprobrare cogatur. Et enim fides omnipotentiæ Dei, & resurrectiôis mortuorum, & resipiscentia ab operibus mor tuis, ad prima pertinent doctrinæ Christi ru dimenta, sicuti uidere est Ebr. 6. Meo iudicio, quoniam supra cap. 4. diserte dixit, non ut pu dore uos suffundam hæc scribo, haud inconu eniēs est, si de suoipsius q; illorum pudore lo qui intelligatur. Quanquam cum nemine con tenderim. Simpliciter quid hic cogitari possit admoneo, liberum sit alijs iudicium.
units.tr: I SPEAK to you to your shame. Commentators generally explain this of the shame which by writing this he wished to bring upon the Corinthians, so that, turned back upon themselves, they would listen less to the bad talk of unbelievers. This kind of shame, which leads not to disgrace but to repentance, is rightly called [ἐντρέπω], from the verb [ἐντρέπεσθαι], which means to feel reverence and become anxious. But since he does not say [πρὸς ἐντροπὴν ὑμῶν], that is, "to your shame", but [πρὸς ἐντροπὴν ὑμῖν λέγω], that is, "I speak to you to your shame", it could be explained as the shame that the Apostle himself felt in himself while saying these things. As if he said: "I am ashamed in your case to say these things; I beget shame in myself while I speak these things to you, which yet I write under the compulsion of your salvation." The Apostle was put to shame because he was forced to charge some with ignorance of God, since he was their Apostle; it was much as if a teacher, having hoped that his pupils had made great progress, were forced to reproach them for not knowing the first elements. For faith in the omnipotence of God, the resurrection of the dead, and repentance from dead works belong to the first rudiments of Christ's teaching, as may be seen in Hebrews 6. In my judgement, since he had clearly said above, in chapter 4, "I do not write these things to shame you," it is not unlikely that the meaning is that he speaks of his own shame and theirs. Yet I contend with no one. I am simply pointing out what may be meant here; let others judge freely.

units.la: {A} Matth. 22.
units.tr: {A} Matth. 22.

units.la: {B} Matth. 25.
units.tr: {B} Matth. 25.

units.la: AT dicet aliquis: Quomodo resurgét mortui? Quali uero corpore ueniēt? Hactenus resurrectionem mortuorum sic futurā affirmauit, ut nisi illa sit, uniuersa Christianæ religionis doctrina, fides, & patientia tribulationum prorsus inanis existat, simusq; adhuc in peccatis nostris perditioni obnoxij, & omniū mortalium miserrimi, quotquot fidē in Christum profitemur. Iam per occupationem respondet illis, qui quoniam impossibile iudicabant ut resurgant aliquando mortui, hæc incredulitatis uerba frequēter in ore habebāt: Quomodo resurgent mortui? Et: Quali cum corpore ueniēnt? Hoc est: Quomodo fieri poterit, ut qui inde ab initio mundi mortui, & ad finem usq; adhuc morituri sunt resurgant, cum corpora mortuorum alia igne in cinerem sunt redacta, qui mos multarum est nationū, præsertim Orientalium, alia à piscibus in mari, alia à bestijs absumpta, alia putredine corrupta. Quomodo quod absumptum & uel in cinerē uel puluerem redactum, uel in carnem ac sanguinem bestiarum conuersum est, uitæ restitutum resurget? Iam esto, resurgant mortui quali nam cum corpore prodibūt? cum alijs atq; alijs mo dis mortuorum corpora defœdentur, ac præsenti uitæ prorsus non modo inutilia, sed & abominanda reddantur. Sane cum tali uenire non poterūt, quali iam utimur. Nam eam corporum qualitatem mors & corruptio prorsus auferunt. Cum igitur eò deueniant mortuorū corpora, ut nec qualia fuerūt ante mortē, nec qualia facta sunt post mortem redire queant, qd restat aliud q; impossibile esse ut resurgāt? Hunc apparet esse sensum obiectionum istarum. Nolim tamen admodū repugnare, si quis tribuat eas nō negatoribus resurrectionis, sed fidelibus imperitioribus quidem, ipsam tamē resurrectionem non negantibus, ut sit sensus: At forsan aliquis resurrectionem quidem mortuorum non negans, at interim modum illius, & futuram corporum qualitatem intelligere cupiens dicet: Quomodo resurgent mortui? Et quali cum corpore uenient? Vtra sententia probabilior sit, lectoris esto iudicium.
units.tr: But someone will say: How will the dead rise? And with what kind of body will they come? Up to this point he has affirmed the resurrection of the dead so firmly that, if there were no such resurrection, the whole doctrine of the Christian religion, our faith and our patience under tribulation would be utterly empty, and we who profess faith in Christ would still be subject to destruction in our sins and would be the most wretched of all mortals. Now he anticipates those who, because they judged it impossible that the dead should ever rise, often had these words of unbelief on their lips: How will the dead rise? And: With what kind of body will they come? That is: how can it be that those who have been dead since the beginning of the world, and who are still destined to die until the end, should rise, when the bodies of the dead have been reduced to ash by fire, as is the custom of many nations, especially the Eastern ones, others have been consumed by fish in the sea, others by beasts, and others corrupted by putrefaction? How can what has been consumed, or reduced to ash or dust, or converted into the flesh and blood of beasts, rise restored to life? Suppose the dead do rise: with what kind of body will they come forth, when their corpses have been defiled in various ways and made not only useless but even loathsome for the present life? Certainly they cannot come with the body we now use, for death and corruption utterly take away that quality of body. Since, then, the bodies of the dead come to such a state that they can return neither as they were before death nor as they have become after death, what remains but that their resurrection is impossible? This seems to be the sense of these objections. Yet I would not greatly object if someone should attribute them not to deniers of the resurrection, but to rather unskilled believers who do not deny the resurrection itself, so that the sense would be: Someone, not denying the resurrection of the dead but wishing to understand its manner and the future quality of bodies, will say: How will the dead rise? And with what kind of body will they come? Which opinion is more probable, let the reader judge.

units.la: Stulte, tu quod feminas non uiuificatur nisi mortuum fuerit. Et hoc quod feminas, non corpus quod nascetur feminas, sed nudum granum, utputa, tritici aut alicuius ex cæteris: sed Deus illi dat corpus, ut uoluit, & unicuiq; feminum suum corpus.
units.tr: Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies. And as for what you sow, you sow not the body that is to come up, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind. But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each seed its own body.

units.la: Si respondet impijs & incredulis, fidem resurrectionis non simpliciter negātibus, sed & irridentibus, dicendū magis erat: Impie quàm stulte. Etenim non est stultus simpliciter, sed impius qui rationis suæ calculis magis q; uerbo Dei acquiescens, quod nō credit irridet etiam ac diuexerat. Accidit hæc stulticia subinde & fidelib. ut modum earum rerum quas futuras credunt, scire cupiant & inquirant. Ma-
units.tr: If he is answering the impious and unbelieving, who not merely deny faith in the resurrection but even mock it, he ought rather to have said: Impious rather than foolish. For a person is not merely foolish, but impious, when, trusting the reckonings of his own reason more than the Word of God, he mocks what he does not believe and even reviles it. This kind of folly sometimes also afflicts believers, who desire to know and inquire into the manner of those things which they believe will come to pass. Ma-

units.la: ria dicebat: Quomodo fient ista, quoniam uirum non cognosco? Quare apparet respondere Apostolum non impijs negatoribus resurrectionis, sed rudioribus & minus exercitatis fidelibus. Quod si non istis, sed incredulis & impijs respondet, moderatur responsum, ne magis offendat quàm ædificet.
units.tr: ry said: How shall these things be, since I do not know a man? Hence it is clear that the Apostle is answering not impious deniers of the resurrection, but rather rougher and less trained believers. But if he answers not these but the unbelieving and impious, the answer is tempered so that it may not offend more than it edifies.

units.la: Græca uox est ἄφρον, quæ amentē significat.
