Innuit huiusmodi quæstiones eorum esse, qui quantumuis sapientes uideri uolunt: hinc tamen errant, quod mente sunt excæcati, non uidentes & intelligentes ea unde de ueritate cognoscenda instrui poterant, sicuti patet hoc loco ex subiectis similibus.
units.tr: The Greek word is ἄφρον [ἄφρον], which signifies senseless. He hints that such questions belong to those who wish to seem very wise, yet go astray in this, that their minds are blinded, not seeing and understanding those things from which they could be instructed in knowing the truth, as is plain here from the similar examples that follow.

units.la: TV quod feminas non uiuificatur, inquit, nisi mortuum fuerit. Vt & comprobet esse eum, qui sic quærat, dementē, & simul id quod quæritur declaret, inducit simile de re nō modo nota, sed & ipsi ad hunc modum quærenti usitata, unde nisi demens sit facile intelligere poterit, quid ad hæc quæsita possit respondere. Inducit autem simile sationis & communis eorum quæ seminantur conditionis. Tu, inquit, quod feminas. Non dicit simpliciter, Quod seminatur: sed, quod tu feminas, ut irrefragabile reddat dementiæ huius redargutionem, qua ne ea quidem intelligimus & obseruamus quę ipsis nostris manibus non semel atque iterum, sed frequenter perficimus. Quasi d. Quid quaeris quomodo resurrecturi sint mortui? Inspice femina tua quæ feminas. Dic primū qua spe seminas? An nó ut quod feminas, multo cum fœnore surgat & fructificet? Vtique. Deinde dic quomodo surgat & fructificet? An non ita ut primum putrescat emortuum sub terra, postea uero uiuificetur. Plane sic habet. Ergo qd feminas non uiuificatur, ut uotis tuis respondeat, nisi prius fuerit emortuum, tam abest ut mortuum esse uiuificationem illius impediat. Cuius autem potentiæ est mortuum semen uiuificare ac frugiferum reddere? An non Dei, q solus potest omnia? Qui igitur mortuum semē uiuificat, quomodo non uiuificabit emortua nostra corpora?
units.tr: You, he says, sowing what you sow, is not made alive unless it dies. To show both that the one who asks in this way is foolish and to declare at the same time what is being asked, he introduces a comparison drawn from a matter not only well known but also familiar to those who ask in this way, so that unless one is foolish one can easily see what answer can be given to these questions. He introduces the comparison of sowing and the common condition of what is sown. You, he says, sowing what you sow. He does not say simply, What is sown; but, what you sow, so that his refutation of this folly may be irrefutable, for it is a matter we do not understand and observe, though we perform it with our own hands not once or twice but frequently. As if he said: Why do you ask how the dead are to rise? Look at what you sow. First tell me, in what hope do you sow? Is it not that what you sow may rise and bear fruit with much increase? Surely. Then tell me, how does it rise and bear fruit? Is it not that it first rots, dead under the earth, and afterwards is brought to life? Plainly so. Therefore, that what you sow is not made alive, so as to answer your wishes, unless it has first died, is so far from hindering its quickening by being dead, that it is the very means of it. But whose power is it to make dead seed alive and fruitful? Is it not God's, who alone can do all things? He who makes dead seed alive, how will he not make our dead bodies alive?

units.la: Sic igitur respondet Apostolus ad primam quæstionem: quomodo fieri possit, ut quod mortuum est, resurgat: ut non modo possibile hoc esse doceat, sed & quod amplius est, euincat: fieri non posse, ut uiuificetur quod nō prius est mortuum. Ergo mors corporū nostrorum tam non impedit illorū resurrectionem, ut magis futuræ illorum uiuificationi seruiat, quem admodum seminis mortificatio ad frugiferam illius uiuificationem facit. Seminantur corpora nostra, dum mortua sepeliuntur, ut locus sepulturæ illorum omnium iustissime agri loco habeatur à fidelibus, quemadmodū Augustæ Vindelicorum, quam Deus in ueritate sua ad finem usq; custodiat, uulgo ager Dei, der Gottes acker, uocatur. Iudicio ratiōis probabilius est, ut ex uiuo corpore quàm ex mortuo proueniat uita. Respicit illa non uirtutem & consilium Dei, qui uitam è morte producit, seu qualitate creatucreaturarum. Verum reipsa innumeris exem- plis gloriam omnipotentiæ Dei in eo declara ri uidemus, quod è morte uitam producit, è quibus Apostolus unum hic de semine in ter-ram proiecto adfert in medium. Mirabile con silium Dei. Præsens hæc uita nostra nullo nisi mortis & corruptionis cibo coseruatur. Mor-tua sint & corrumpantur oportet,quęcunque ad sustentandam uitam nostram faciűt. Dum uiuunt,aut corruptionis sunt expertia, cibare non possunt. Nec Christus ipse cibus esset ani-marū nostrarū,nisi pro nobis in cruce mortu⁹ esset.Ex morte illius pascimur ad uitam.
units.tr: So the Apostle answers the first question in this way: how it can be that what is dead should rise. He teaches not only that this is possible, but, what is more, proves that it cannot be otherwise than that what has not first died should be made alive. Therefore the death of our bodies does not so hinder their resurrection that it rather serves their future quickening, just as the dying of the seed produces its fruitful quickening. Our bodies are sown while, dead, they are buried, so that the place of their burial may most justly be regarded by the faithful as a field, as Augsburg, which God in his truth keeps until the end, is commonly called God's field, der Gottes acker. By the judgment of reason it is more probable that life should come from a living body than from a dead one. Reason regards not the power and counsel of God, who brings life out of death, nor the quality of the creatures created. But in fact, by countless examples we see the glory of God's omnipotence displayed in this, that he produces life from death; of these the Apostle brings forward here one, that of seed cast into the earth. The wonderful counsel of God. This present life of ours is sustained by no food but that of death and corruption. Whatever serves to sustain our life must be dead and corrupted. While things are alive, or free from corruption, they cannot nourish us. Nor would Christ himself be the food of our souls, unless he had been dead for us on the cross. By his death we are fed unto life.

units.la: E T hoc quod feminas, inquit, non corpus quod nascetur feminas,sed nudū granū, &c.] Respondet ad alteram quæstionem, quali cor pore furreƈturi sint mortui.Est autem respon-sio bimembris,de eodem,unde prior, sationis simili sumpta.Primum negat mortuos corpo-re quali moriuntur furreƈturos: deinde indicat illos nouo corpore secundū uoluntatem Dei uenturos.Et hoc,inquit,quod feminas,nō cor pus quod nascetur feminas,sed nudū granum. Res ipsa manifesta est non egens expositione. Scimus quid seminetur, & quid ex eo quod fatum est nascatur. Granū nudum seminatur, & ex illo nascitur uel arbor caudice, ramis,fo-lijs & fructibus ornata & copleta, uel culmus cum spica sua & arista, uel aliud quoddam cor pus secundum feminis sui naturam ad speciē. Quod ex grano fato nascitur nō est diuersum ab illo secundum naturam ac substantiam,sed prorsus idem . Quare quod dicit,Non corpus quod nascetur feminas , sed nudū granum: nō est intelligendū de substátia & natura utriusq; & feminis quod seminatur,& corporis qũ ex illo nascitur,sed de qualitatis diuersitate. Tale corpus non seminatur, quale ex fato semine nascitur,si circunstantias utriusque inspicias. Quod seminatur granum est,unicū &nudum. Quod ex illo nascitur,nō est nudum granum, sed corpus competenti uestitu ornatū:nec est unicū granum,sed pro natura speciei suæ mul tiplicatum.quo simili usus est & Christus, di-cens:Nisi granum frumenti cadens in terram mortuū fuerit ipsum solū manet: si uero mor-tuum fuerit,multū fructum adfert.Erat ipse in star grani frumentarij,cum pro nobis morere-tur.Vbi surrexit prodijt non unicum & nudū granum,sed corpus multorum granorum,quę cum ipso surrexerunt. Confuscitauit enim cū illo nos Deus,Eph.2.Sed ad propositum.
units.tr: AND that which you sow, he says, is not the body that is to come up, but a bare grain, etc.] He answers the second question, with what kind of body the dead will rise. The answer has two parts, drawn from the same comparison of sowing; the first part, as we have seen. First he denies that the dead will rise with the body in which they die; then he shows that they will come with a new body according to God's will. And that which you sow, he says, is not the body that is to come up, but a bare grain. The matter itself is plain and needs no explanation. We know what is sown and what springs from what is sown. A bare grain is sown, and from it springs either a tree adorned and complete with trunk, branches, leaves and fruit, or a stalk with its ear and awn, or some other body according to the species of its seed. What springs from the grain that is sown is not different from it in nature and substance, but altogether the same. Therefore when he says, Not the body that is to come up, but a bare grain, this is not to be understood of the substance and nature of either the seed that is sown or the body that springs from it, but of a difference of quality. The body is not sown in the form in which it springs from the seed, if you consider the circumstances of each. What is sown is a grain, single and bare. What springs from it is not a bare grain, but a body clothed in its fitting garment; nor is it a single grain, but multiplied according to the nature of its kind. Christ also used this comparison, saying: Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it brings forth much fruit. He himself was like a grain of wheat when he died for us. When he rose, there came forth not a single bare grain, but the body of many grains, which rose with him. For God has quickened us together with him, Eph. 2. But let us return to our purpose.

units.la: Cum morimur,seminantur corpora nostra tanquam unica & nuda grana at ex illis per re surrectionem nascetur non amplius nuda gra na,quæ denuo possint seminari, sed corpora plena,& cœlesti ornatu immortalitate ac clari tate cumulata.Et hoc discriminis est inter re-surrectionem Lazari & consimilium , & eam quæ Christi fuit,& futura est nostra in fine mū di.Quale corpus Lazari mortuum fuit, ac se-pulchro traditum,tale postea & surrexit, ite-rum uidelicet mortalo, corruptibile & omni-
units.tr: When we die, our bodies are sown like single bare grains. But from them, through the resurrection, there will spring up no longer bare grains that could be sown again, but full bodies, endowed with heavenly adornment and heaped with immortality and brightness. This is the difference between the resurrection of Lazarus and others like it, and the resurrection that Christ had and ours will be at the end of the world. The body of Lazarus, once dead and laid in the sepulchre, rose again in the same state, that is, mortal, corruptible, and subject to all the miseries it had before.

units.la: bus,ut antea,miserijs obnoxium. Hic locū nō habuit,quod Apostolus dicit:non corpus quę nascetur feminas,sed nudum granum : habuit uero in corpore Christi,& habituru est in no-stris.Duo sunt igitur resurrectionis genera,q-bus mortui aliter atque aliter resurgunt. Vnū expressum est in Lazaro,alterum in Christo. Vtriusque imagines in muscis & bombycibus uisuntur.Muscæ omni hyeme cauernis abdite moriuntur, & tamen ad initium æstatis uiuæ prodeút corpori non modo eodem quo mor-tuæ fuerant,sed & nullis uel accessionibus uel detrimentis in diuersum mutato. Bombyces uero noti uermes sepulchris suis quæ cótexūt immoriuntur,& è carne corrupta refurgūt nō amplius uermes,quales fuerant antea,sed can didæ auiculæ,cute pristina,uermis speciem re tinente,in sepulchris relićta. Sic in illis quoq; nō resurgit corpus quod, id est, quale mortuū fuit,sed multo agilius ac præstantius, dum ex mortuo & corrupto uerme surgit albicans aui sula.Quid magis terrenū uerme? Cōtrà,quid conformius cœlestibus quàm candida auicu-la? Qui hæc oculis suis uidet, poterit ne adeo esse stupidus, ut nō admoneatur de qualitate corporum nostrorū,qua in fine mundi ad ima ginem clarificati capitis nostri Christi resurge mus? Vermiculum Deus mortuum & corru-ptum suscitat,uiuificat,& in candidam auicu-lum transmutat: & hominem quem ad imagi-nem suam condidit,uel non potest, uel dedi-gnabitur à mortuis excitare,& ex terreno cœ-lestem reddere?
units.tr: The Apostle's words, "not the body that is to be born, but a bare grain," had no place in the case of Lazarus, but they do hold in the body of Christ, and will hold in ours. There are therefore two kinds of resurrection, by which the dead rise in different ways. One is expressed in Lazarus, the other in Christ. Images of both are seen in flies and silkworms. Flies die every winter, hidden away in caves, and yet at the beginning of summer they come forth alive, in a body not only the same as that in which they died, but changed into something different, with no additions or losses. Silkworms, well-known worms, die in the tombs they spin for themselves, and from the corrupt flesh they rise no longer worms as they were before, but white little birds, leaving their old skin behind in the tombs while keeping the appearance of the worm. So in those cases too the body does not rise as it was, that is, in the state in which it died, but far more nimbly and excellently, since from the dead and corrupt worm there rises a white butterfly. What is more earthly than a worm? On the contrary, what is more like the heavenly than a white little bird? Can anyone who sees these things with his own eyes be so dull that he is not reminded of the quality of our bodies, with which at the end of the world we shall rise, made bright after the image of our glorified head, Christ? God raises up and quickens a dead and corrupt little worm and transforms it into a white little bird; and the man whom he made in his own image, can he not raise from the dead, or will he not deign to, and make him heavenly from earthly?

units.la: S E D nudum granum, inquit.] Dum uiui-mus in hoc seculo uestiti,opibus cumulati, & alius alio personę genere ornati conspicimur. Verum ubi exeundum est è mundi huius fa-bula,omnem illius personā, & ornatum exuti quales huc uenimus,tales hinc recedimus, & instar nudi grani telluri committimur. Quid igitur in hac mundi fabula tantopere persona ti insolescimus, quæ breui finietur, & nudos nos omni dedecore spoliatos dimittet? Regē esse,principé,comitem, baronem, equite aura tum,nobilem ac ducem esse,magistratum,có-sulem,senatorem, iudicem, præfeƈtum , ciuè, patremfamiliás,episcopum, pastorem ac do-ƈtorem esse,ad figuram huius mundi pertiner, quam ueluti scenicam personam ubi uisum est dño ponere oportet, uno hoc cōmuniter ma-nente,quod sumus initio nati,singulariter ue-ro quod sumus per gratiam Christi regenera-ti.Grana sumus, telluri, ubi sationis tépus est, nuda committęda. Quod homines sumus,id manet in omnibus:quod Christiani, in electis ac fidelibus, cætera accessoria destituent nos ac nudos relinquent.
units.tr: "But a bare grain," he says. While we live in this world we are seen clothed, heaped with wealth, and each adorned with some rank or other. But when we must leave the stage of this world, we shed all its masks and trappings, and as we came here naked, so we depart, and are committed to the earth like a bare grain. Why, then, do we swell with such pride in this worldly drama, which will soon end and send us away naked, stripped of all dishonour? To be a king, prince, count, baron, knight, noble, duke, magistrate, consul, senator, judge, prefect, citizen, head of a household, bishop, minister, or teacher: these belong to the figure of this world, which the Lord puts on as a stage role whenever he sees fit. The only thing that remains common to all is that we were born; what is singular is that we have been regenerated through the grace of Christ. We are grains, to be committed bare to the earth when the time for sowing comes. That we are men remains in all; that we are Christians remains in the elect and the faithful; the other accessories will desert us and leave us naked.

units.la: Bene tamen habet,quod quamuis nudi,spo liati ac mortui sepelimur,grana tamen sumus, idque non spiritu,qui morti nō est obnoxius: nec in terram reconditur, sed corpore, quod prorsus in oculis mundi in nihilum abire ui-detur,& testimonio diuinæ sententiæ in pul-uerem uerem terræ conuertitur. Nemo agricola, nemo hortulanus, grana sua telluri cunctanter concredit, communi experientia edoctus, non perite illa dum seminantur, sed magno esse cũ fœnore suo tempore progerminatura. Hac cogitatione animos nostros contra mortis tentionem obfirmemus, horumque memores simus, quoties uel bello uel pestę grassante, magnam hominum multitudinem in terram proijci uiderimus. Cogitemus cœlestem agricolam Deum egressum esse ad seminandum, suaque grana plena manu spargere in terrā, quæ postea tempore suo magno cum lucro prose- rat in lucem.
units.tr: Yet it is good that, although we are buried naked, stripped and dead, we are nonetheless grains; and this is so not in spirit, which is not subject to death, nor is that buried in the earth, but in body, which in the eyes of the world seems wholly to pass into nothing, and by the testimony of the divine sentence is turned into the dust of the earth. No farmer, no gardener, taught by common experience, entrusts his grains to the earth hesitantly, without knowing well that while they are being sown they will sprout in due time with great increase. Let us fortify our minds with this thought against the dread of death, and let us remember these things whenever, with war or plague raging, we see a great multitude of men cast into the earth. Let us consider that God, the heavenly farmer, has gone out to sow, and scatters his grains with a full hand into the earth, which afterwards, in its time, will spring forth into the light with great gain.

units.la: VTPOTE tritici, aut alicuius ex cæteris, inquit.] Non in uno, sed quocunque genere granorum, quæ seminantur, imaginem nobis futurę resurrectionis proponit. In omnibus quippe diuinæ uirtutis operatio declaratur. Diuersa est & multifaria forma, conditio, qualitas, natura, quantitas, & utilitas feminum in terra, funtq; alia alijs uel potiora uel minoris momenti, uel rariora uel uulgatiora. Et tamen nullum est inter omnia, quod dedignetur Deus interuetu mortis renouare, multiplicare, & ab interitu uindicare. Vnde & subdit:
units.tr: "Just as of wheat, or of some other of the rest," he says. He sets before us the image of the future resurrection not in one kind of grain only, but in any kind that is sown. For in all of them the working of divine power is displayed. The form, condition, quality, nature, quantity and usefulness of seeds in the earth are diverse and manifold; some are more or less important, some rarer or more common. Yet among them all there is nothing that God disdains to renew, multiply, and rescue from destruction through death. Whence he adds:

units.la: Sed Deus illi dat corpus, ut uoluit, & unicuiq; feminum suum corpus.
units.tr: But God gives it a body as he has pleased, and to each seed its own body.

units.la: Quid ergo de corporibus nostris dubitamus? Sunt illa quidem & magnitudine, & sexu & ætate, & existimatione quoque diuersa. In eo tamen conuenit omnibus, quod sunt instar feminum, per mortem à perpetuitate mortis diuina uirtute uindicanda, & in præstantioris uitæ gloriam asserenda.
units.tr: Why then do we doubt about our bodies? They indeed differ in size, sex, age, and also in esteem. Yet they agree in this, that they are like seeds, which through death are to be rescued by divine power from the perpetuity of death and secured to the glory of a better life.

units.la: SED Deus illi dat corpus, inquit, ut uoluit.] Non dicit, sed natura, aut terra, uel ætas: sed quæ illos diuinæ uirtutis admoneat, per quam corpora nostra uiuificabūtur ac surget, sed Deus, inquit. Qui semen in terra emortuū uiuificat, idem & corpora nostra uitæ restituet. Quare non debemus uel corporum nostrorum qualitatem, uel naturæ uires, sed uirtute Dei, cui nihil est impossibile, in hac causa considerare.
units.tr: "But God gives it a body," he says, "as he has pleased." He does not say nature, or earth, or age; he points us to the divine power by which our bodies will be quickened and raised. "But God," he says. He who quickens the dead seed in the earth will also restore our bodies to life. Therefore in this matter we ought to consider not the quality of our bodies or the powers of nature, but the power of God, to whom nothing is impossible.

units.la: Deinde non simpliciter dicit, Deus dat corpus: sed, Deus dat illi corpus. Si aliud, prorsus ab eo quod seminatur alienū, dat corpus, quomodo dat illi corpus? Ergo corpus quod ex grano seminato nascitur, ipsius grani corpus est, eiusdem cum illo naturæ & substantię. Sic corpus nostrum, quod olim resurget, corpus erit eius quod mortuū in terra sepelitur. Quid autem aliud est corpus dare grano seminato, & corpori sepulto, quàm aliam quàm habuerat antea dare qualitatem & conditionem?
units.tr: Next, he does not simply say "God gives a body," but "God gives it a body." If the body given were something quite foreign to what is sown, how would he give it a body? So the body that springs from the sown grain is the body of that same grain, of the same nature and substance as it. Likewise our body, which will one day rise, will be the body of that which is buried dead in the earth. And what else is it to give a body to the sown grain and the buried body than to give it a quality and condition other than what it had before?

units.la: Tertio, non dicit, Deus creat aut facit: sed, Deus dat illi corpus. Verbo dandi & facilitatem resurrectionis, & donum Dei expressit. Donum Dei est omnis illa quorumcunq; feminum annua conseruatio & multiplicatio, usibus nostris seruiens. Et futura corporum no-
units.tr: Thirdly, he does not say "God creates or makes," but "God gives it a body." By the word "give" he expresses both the ease of the resurrection and the gift of God. The yearly preservation and multiplication of all seeds, serving our uses, is the gift of God. And the future resurrection of our

units.la: strorum resurrectio donum Dei erit infirmis nostris & mortalib. corporibus concessum. Labora t agricola arando ac seminando, uerū corpus frugiferum ei quod satum est, non est nisi ex dono Dei. Sic & de corporibus nostris sentire debemus.
units.tr: bodies will be a gift of God, granted to our weak and mortal bodies. The farmer labours in ploughing and sowing, yet the fruitful body of what is sown comes only from the gift of God. So we too should think about our bodies.

units.la: VT uoluit, inquit.] Restringit curiositatem eorum qui obnixe de qualitate corporum nostrorum, qua resurrecturi sumus, quæ runt. Cogimur uoluntati illius permittere, qualia det corpora seminibus in terram proiectis. Licet enim unicuique speciei suam proprietatem conseruet, potest tamen singulis annis plus uel minus liberaliter donum fructificationis dispensare. Hoc quidem sensu uidetur intelligendum quod dicit. Verum quoniam non dicit, ut uult, sed in præterito, id est, quemadmodum uoluit: apparet accipiendum esse de prima creationis uoluntate, qua initio mundi unicuiq; speciei ex terrenascentibus suum corpus destinauit ac tradidit. Vnde & subiicit uelut exponens;
units.tr: "As he has pleased," he says. He restrains the curiosity of those who eagerly ask about the quality of the bodies with which we are to rise. We are bound to leave to his will what bodies he gives to seeds cast into the earth. For although he preserves to each kind its own property, he may yet dispense the gift of fruitfulness more or less generously each year. Indeed this seems to be the sense in which it should be understood. But since he does not say "as he wills" and instead uses the past tense, "as he has pleased," it seems to be understood of the first will of creation, by which at the beginning of the world he assigned and handed to each kind of things that spring from the earth its own body. Whence he adds, as if explaining:

units.la: ET unicuiq; feminum suum corpus. ]Non dicit, & unicuique semini corpus: sed, & unicuique semini id est, suum proprium corpus. Quemadmodum igitur nō datur grano tritici corpus auenę, aut alterius cuiuspiam speciei, sed proprium ipsius corpus, tritici uidè licet: ita dabuntur nobis, ubi resurgendū erit, non aliena quædam, sed suū unicuiq; proprium corpus, quod cum ipso uel gloria filiorum Dei fruatur, uel pro meritis impietatis pœnas luat æternas. Si compassi fuerimus, dicit alibi Apostolus, unà etiam regnabimus. Non potest hoc accidere corporibus nostris, quæ propter Christum tristia quæuis patiuntur, si sic sunt moritura, ut non ipsa resurgant, sed aliena substituantur. Et alio in loco: Omnes nos manifestari oportet ante tribunal Christi, ut recipiat unusquisque ea quæ siunt per corpus, iuxta id quod fecit siue bonum siue malum. Quomodo poterit iusto hoc iudicio fieri, ut peccatorum pœnę inferantur non corpori, in quo sunt admissa, sed alieno ac nouo, in quo nihil est peccatum? Et alibi: Qui transfigurabit, inquit, corpus nostrum humile, ut conforme reddat corpori suo glorioso. Surrexit Christus, ac clarificatus est in eodem suo corpore, in quo fuerat crucifixus ac mortuus, cuius rei argumenta præbeant stigmata manuum ac pedū. Huic suo corpori quomodo humilia nostra corpora cōformia reddet, si non ea ipsa, sed aliena ab ipsis in resurrectione sumus accepturi? Quare uigilanter Apostolus, ne errori huic locum per id daret, quod dixit, Et hoc quod feminas non corpus quod nascetur feminas, sed nudum granum, Deus uero illi dat corpus ut uoluit: subiecit, Et unicuique feminum proprium suum corpus.
units.tr: "And to each seed its own body." He does not say "and to each seed a body," but "and to each seed," that is, its own proper body. Just as the grain of wheat is not given the body of oats, or of any other kind, but its own body, that of wheat, so when we are to rise we shall be given not some foreign body but each his own proper body, which, with that same body, either enjoys the glory of the sons of God or, for the merits of impiety, bears eternal punishments. "If we suffer with him," says the Apostle elsewhere, "we shall also reign together." This cannot happen to our bodies, which for Christ's sake endure whatever afflictions, if they are to perish in such a way that they themselves do not rise, but other bodies are substituted. And in another place: "We must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, that each may receive the things done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad." How could this just judgment be carried out, if the punishments of sins were inflicted not on the body in which they were committed, but on another, new body, in which there is no sin? And elsewhere: "He will transform," he says, "our lowly body, so that it may be made conformable to his glorious body." Christ rose and was made bright in the same body in which he had been crucified and dead, as the marks of the hands and feet prove. How will he make our lowly bodies conformable to this, his body, if in the resurrection we are to receive not those same bodies but others foreign to them? Therefore the Apostle, watchfully, lest he give room to this error through what he said ("And that which you sow is not the body that shall be, but a bare grain; but God gives it a body as he has pleased"), added: "And to each seed its own proper body."

units.la: Nō omnis caro, inquit, eadem caro, sed alía quidem caro hominum, alía uero caro pecorum, alía uero piscium, alía uero uolucrium. Et sunt corpora cœle- stia, & sunt corpora terrestria. Verum alia quidem cœlestium gloria, alia uero terrestrium. Alia gloria solis, & alia gloria lunæ, & alia gloria stellarum. Stella siquidem à stella differt in gloria. Sic & resurrectio mortuorum.
units.tr: "Not all flesh is the same flesh," he says, "but there is one flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fish, and another of birds. There are also celestial bodies and terrestrial bodies. But the glory of the celestial is one thing, and that of the terrestrial another. There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars. For star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead."

units.la: Exponitur hic locus aliter atque aliter. Alij referunt duo hæc carnis & corporum similia, ad differentiam gloriæ quæ futura sit post resurrectionem in corporibus resuscitatis, qua alij alijs sint illustriores secundum meritorum præstantiam futuri. Vt sit sensus: Non modo alia erit in resurrectione corporis nostri qualitas ab ea quam habet mortuum ac sepultum, sed & ubi resurrexerimus, erit magna inter resuscitatos differentia, quod gloriam attinet clarificatorum corporum. Quemadmodum enim in hac vita alia est qualitas humanæ, alia pecudinæ, alia piscinæ, alia volatilis carnis: quamuis, quod substantiam attinet, eadem sit omnis caro: & sicut differunt inter se corpora, quorum alia sunt cœlestia, & alia terrestria, licet in eo conueniat omnibus quod sunt corpora: & ut alia est atque alia gloria cœlestium, sic ut stella differat à stella in gloria, & luna præstantior sit stellis, lunam uero sol splendore suo excellat, quamuis substantia sint eadem: ita erit in resurrectione mortuorum. Ibi alia erit gloria Christi tanquam solis, alia gloria patriarcharum, alia prophetarum, alia apostolorum, alia patrum, ac doctorum, alia martyrum, alia reliquorum fidelium, licet eadem sit omnibus futura resurrectionis, felicitatis, & immortalitatis communicatio.
units.tr: This passage is explained in different ways. Some refer these two comparisons of flesh and bodies to the difference of glory that will exist after the resurrection in the raised bodies, by which some will be more illustrious than others according to the excellence of their merits. The sense is this: not only will the quality of our body in the resurrection be other than that which it has when dead and buried, but once we have risen there will also be a great difference among the raised, as regards the glory of their glorified bodies. For just as in this life the quality of human flesh is one thing, that of cattle another, that of fish another, and that of birds another, although as to substance all flesh is the same; and just as celestial and terrestrial bodies differ from one another, though they agree in this, that they are all bodies; and just as the glory of celestial things is one thing and another, so that star differs from star in glory, and the moon is more excellent than the stars, while the sun surpasses the moon in its brightness, although they are the same in substance: so it will be in the resurrection of the dead. There the glory of Christ will be one thing, like that of the sun; the glory of the patriarchs another, that of the prophets another, that of the apostles another, that of the fathers and teachers another, that of the martyrs another, and that of the rest of the faithful another; although the communion of resurrection, happiness and immortality will be the same for all.

units.la: Et hunc sensum sequuti sunt patres, Chrysostomus, Ambrosius & Augustinus. Chrysostomus quippe sic exponit: ἐπὶ μὲν γὰρ τὰ σώματα αὐτὰ ...
units.tr: The Fathers Chrysostom, Ambrose and Augustine followed this sense. Chrysostom, indeed, expounds it thus: For in the case of the bodies themselves ... [ἐπὶ μὲν γὰρ τὰ σώματα αὐτὰ ...]

units.la: Ambrosius sic: Quemadmodum ergo ex una impensa diuersa animantium caro est, ita & unius carnis homines diuersi erunt dignitate in resurrectione, ut talis unusquisque appareat, qualis fuerit meriti.
units.tr: Ambrose says: "Just as, therefore, from one material the flesh of living creatures is various, so also men of one flesh will be of different dignity in the resurrection, so that each will appear such as his merit was."

units.la: Augustinus epistola centesima quadragesimasexta, exponit ad hunc modum: Iam uero quod adiungit, ad differentiam pertinet resurgentium, propter diuersas glorias fidelium atque sanctorum. Non omnis, inquit, caro eadem caro. Alia quippe hominum, alia autem caro pecorum, alia uolucrium, alia piscium: & corpora cœlestia & corpora terrestria, sed alia est cœlestium gloria, & alia terrestrium, & alia gloria solis, & alia gloria lunæ, & alia gloria stellarum. Stella enim à stella differt in gloria. Sic & resurrectio mortuorum. In his omnibus iste sensus est: Si genera carnis cum sint
units.tr: Augustine, in letter one hundred and forty-six, expounds it in this way: "Now as to what he adds, it pertains to the difference among those who rise, on account of the diverse glories of the faithful and the saints. Not all flesh, he says, is the same flesh. For there is one flesh of men, another of beasts, another of birds, and another of fish; and there are celestial bodies and terrestrial bodies, but the glory of the celestial is one thing and that of the terrestrial another, and one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars. For star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead. In all these things the sense is this:"

units.la: cuncta mortalia, differunt tamen inter se prodiuersitatibus animantium, & corpora cum sint omnia visibilia, differunt tamen pro diuersitatibus locorum, unde alia est cœlestium gloria, alia terrestrium, & in locis sublimibus cum sint cuncta cœlestia, differunt etiam ipsa claritatibus luminum: non mirum est quod in resurrectione mortuorum distabit gloria meritorum. Hæc ille.
units.tr: "Although all kinds of flesh are mortal, they nonetheless differ among themselves according to the diversity of living creatures; and although all bodies are visible, they nonetheless differ according to the diversity of places, whence the glory of celestial things is one thing and that of terrestrial things another. And since in the lofty places all things are celestial, they also differ in the brightness of their lights. It is no wonder, then, that in the resurrection of the dead the glory of merits will differ." Thus he.

units.la: His astipulatur & Theophylactus, qui sic exponit, Non omnis caro eadem caro. Hoc est: Nequaquam omnes pari honore resurgent, sed iustorum corpora tantum different a corporibus impiorum, quantum a terrenis hisce cœlestia. Erit præterea & inter iustos ipsos haud paruum graduum discrimen, sicut in sequentibus dicturus est. Quinetiam uel inter improbos ipsos distabit plurimum. Inquit enim, quemadmodum caro humana a pecorum & reliquorum brutorum est longe diuersa: sic erit peccantibus & damnatis, uel in ipsis supplicijs magna diuersitas. Quæ autem dicta in præsentia sunt, peccatorum duntaxat exprimunt differentiam. Est nanque de iustis paulo post dicturus, cum de cœlestibus ipsis faciet corporibus mentionem. Hæc iste. Et horum patrum expositionem maior etiam pars recentiorum sequitur.
units.tr: Theophylact agrees with these, and he expounds it thus: "Not all flesh is the same flesh. That is: by no means will all rise with equal honour, but the bodies of the just differ from the bodies of the impious as much as heavenly things differ from these earthly ones. Moreover, there will also be no small difference of degrees among the just themselves, as he is going to say in what follows. Indeed, even among the wicked there will be a great difference. For he says: just as human flesh is far different from that of cattle and other brutes, so there will be great diversity among sinners and the damned, even in their punishments. But what has been said at present expresses only the difference of the sinners. For he is going to speak of the just shortly afterwards, when he makes mention of the celestial bodies themselves." Thus he. And the greater part of more recent writers also follows the exposition of these Fathers.

units.la: Alij referunt ista non ad differentiam resuscitatorum corporum, qua uel electi à reprobis, uel etiam electi inter se dispari claritate discriminentur: sed ad eandem, de qua in præcedenti simili corpus quod nascitur à suo grano, unde nascitur qualitate differre significauit. quæ expositio mihi quoque probatur. Et Lyranus eam ponit, usque ad eum locum, ubi Apostolus dicit: Alia gloria solis, alia gloria lunæ, & alia gloria stellarum, &c. quæ uerba refert ad differentem electorum gloriam, qua illi secundum diuersa merita uarie sint de lumine gloriæ post resurrectionem par ticipaturi.
units.tr: Others refer these words not to the difference of the raised bodies, by which the elect are distinguished from the reprobate, or the elect among themselves by unequal brightness, but to that same difference of quality which in the preceding comparison he signified between the body that is born and the grain from which it is born. This exposition also seems acceptable to me. Lyra adopts it as far as the place where the Apostle says: "One glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars," and so on; and he refers these words to the differing glory of the elect, by which they, according to their diverse merits, will variously share in the light of glory after the resurrection.

units.la: NON omnis caro, inquit, eadem caro, sed alia quidem caro hominum, &c.] Quoniam dixit, Nō hoc corpus quod nascetur seminas, sed nudum granum, Deus uero dat illi corpus ut uoluit: significans corpora nostra in futura resurrectione, licet substantia manente, qua litate tamen à mortuis ac sepultis fore diuersa, ne quis dicat: Si diuersa erunt, non erunt uera corpora, subiungit dicens: Non omnis caro eadem caro. Et ut id declaret, Sed alia, inquit, caro hominum, alia pecorum, alia piscium, alia uolucrium. Quasi dicat: Nec mirum uideri debet, quod corpora nostra diuersa ab ijs quæ nunc habemus, in resurrectione fore significo. Neque enim illa diuersitas substantiæ erit, sed qualitatis: unde non consequitur, haud fore illa uera & uere nostra corpora.
units.tr: "Not all flesh," he says, "is the same flesh, but there is one flesh of men," and so on. Since he had said, "That which you sow is not the body that will be, but a bare grain; but God gives it a body as he wills," he signifies that our bodies in the future resurrection, though their substance remains, will nevertheless be different in quality from the dead and buried. Lest anyone should say: "If they are different, they will not be true bodies," he adds: "Not all flesh is the same flesh." And to make this clear: "But," he says, "there is one flesh of men, another of beasts, another of fish, another of birds." As if he said: It ought not to seem strange that I say our bodies will be in the resurrection different from those we now have. For that difference will not be of substance but of quality; hence it does not follow that they will not be true and truly our own bodies.

units.la: An non uidemus magnam esse diuersitatem in carne, quam Deus condidit? Alia nanque est non eadem caro hominum, & alia caro pecorum, & alia caro piscium, & alia caro uoro uolucrium, fi qualitatem illius admodum diuersam in diuersis istis speciebus inspicias. Et tamen diuersitas ista non facit,quo minus caro hominum fit uera caro, propterea quod non est pecorum:uel pecorum, quia nô est homo minum. Cum ergo diuersitas qualitatis in diuersarum specierum carne ueritatem & unitatem substantiæ carnis non auferat,quomodo auferet illam in una & eadem generis nostri specie,faceretque, ne corpora nostra in resurrectione futura sint eadem substantia, propterea quod à qualitate illorum, quam habent in hac uita, diuersa erunt? Lyranus sic exponit: Ex hoc conclufiditur,quod cum hoc fiat uirtute naturæ, uirtute Dei fieri poterit, quod caro morientis ac resurgentis erit eadem identitate naturæ,sed alterius gloriæ.
units.tr: Do we not see the great diversity in the flesh which God created? For there is one flesh of men, not the same as the flesh of beasts, and another flesh of fish, and another flesh of birds, if you look at how very diverse its quality is in these different kinds. And yet this diversity does not prevent the flesh of men from being true flesh, because it is not that of beasts, or the flesh of beasts because it is not that of men. Since, then, diversity of quality in the flesh of different kinds does not take away the truth and unity of the substance of flesh, how will it take it away in the one and same kind of our race, so as to make our bodies in the resurrection not of the same substance, because they will differ from the quality they have in this life? Lyra expounds it thus: "From this it is concluded that, since this happens by the power of nature, it can happen by the power of God, that the flesh of one who dies and of one who rises will be the same in identity of nature, but of another glory."

units.la: Notâter ergo non dicit Apostolus, Non omnis caro, caro est(haberet enim hæc loquutio contradictionem) sed,non omnis caro eadem caro. Cum negat eandem esse omnē carnem, non negat substantiam, quia est caro:sed qualitatem diuersam constituit, per quâ alia est hominum, alia pecorum, alia piscium,alia uolucrium caro. Sic possumus dicere,alia est caro moriens, & alia resurgens: moriens corruptibilis, ignobilis, infirma & animalis, resurgens uero incorruptibilis, gloriosa, fortis ac spiritualis,cuius mentionem paulò infrà faciet. Et tamen sub utriufq; cõditionis quamuis diuersa qualitate non est diuersa,sed eadem caro.
units.tr: Therefore the Apostle carefully does not say, "Not all flesh is flesh" (for such a statement would contain a contradiction), but "not all flesh is the same flesh." When he denies that all flesh is the same, he does not deny the substance, since it is flesh; rather he sets up a diversity of quality, by which the flesh of men is one thing, that of beasts another, that of fish another, and that of birds another. So we may say: the flesh that dies is one thing, and the flesh that rises is another; the flesh that dies is corruptible, ignoble, weak and natural, but the flesh that rises is incorruptible, glorious, strong and spiritual, which he will mention a little further on. And yet under either condition, though the quality differs, it is not a different flesh but the same flesh.

units.la: Non fuit igitur infinira illa potentia Dei cõditoris omnium uni tantum qualitati carnis al ligata,ut nequiuerit aliam dare homini, aliam pecori,aliam pisci,aliam uolucri: quemadmodum non est uni feminum qualitati obstrictus, ut nequeat aliud corpus dare tritico, aliud hor deo,aliud auenæ,&c. Sed pro incomprehensibili sua uirtute singulis tam animalium quàm feminum speciebus suum proprium corpus de dit ut uoluit. Eadem sua uirtute dabit etiam nobis in die resurrectionis uerum quidem & unicuiq; proprium corpus,diuersum tamen & præstantius multo,quâ fit quod in hac uita circumferimus.Dat unicuiq; feminum suum corpus.Non dat tritico corpus auenæ. Est enim il lud à natura tritici diuersum. Non dat homini carnem pecoris, aut piscis, uel uolucris. Est enim alia caro pecoris quàm fit hominis: sed dat homini carnem hominis, quæ illi est propria, pecori carnem pecoris, &c. sic dabit nobis in resurrectione corpora non aliena, sed propria:non pecorum uel angelorum, sed hominum.Obsecro,fi in carne nô hominum tantum,sed & pecorum,piscium ac uolucriû, eaq; mortali, corruptibili, infirma & ignobili tantas uirtutis suæ diuitias in præsenti hoc & tran situro sæculo declarare dignatus est:quomodo non est illas multo præstantius in corpori bus nostris ad æternæ uitæ felicitatem ac gloriam excitatis declaraturus?
units.tr: Therefore the infinite power of God, the creator of all, was not bound to one quality of flesh alone, so that it could not give one kind to man, another to beast, another to fish, and another to bird; just as it is not bound to one quality of seeds, so that it cannot give one body to wheat, another to barley, another to oats, and so on. Rather, by its incomprehensible power, it gives to each species of living creatures and of seeds its own proper body as it wills. By that same power he will also give us, on the day of resurrection, a true and proper body for each of us, yet different and far more excellent than what we bear about in this life. He gives to each seed its own body: he does not give wheat the body of oats, for that is different from the nature of wheat; he does not give man the flesh of beast, fish or bird, for the flesh of a beast is other than that of a man; but he gives man the flesh of man, which is proper to him, and beast the flesh of beast, and so on. So he will give us in the resurrection bodies not alien but our own, not those of beasts or angels, but those of men. I ask: if he has deigned to display such riches of his power in flesh not only of men but also of beasts, fish and birds, and that mortal, corruptible, weak and ignoble, in this present age that is passing away, how will he not display them far more excellently in our bodies raised to the happiness and glory of eternal life?

units.la: E T sunt corpora cœlestia,inquit,& sunt corpora terrestria:uerum alia quidem est cœleftiû
units.tr: And there are heavenly bodies, he says, and there are earthly bodies; but the glory of the heavenly is one, and the glory of the earthly another.

units.la: gloria, alia uero terrestrium.] Ad idem argumentum pertinet & hoc simile. Corpora nostra sunt adhuc terrestria. In resurrectione uero erunt nô amplius terrestria,sed cœlestia, ut ra quidem corpora,sed interim à qualitate pristina quam nunc habent diuersa. Quare alia erit illorum post resurrectionē gloria,quâ nunc fit.Est enim in hoc præfenti quoq; sæculo omnium oculis expofitū, quàm fit alia gloria terrestrium corporum, & alia cœlestium. Non est ullius terrestris corporis gloria tanta, ut cœlestium fplēdorem adæquare possit. Siue argentum,fiue aurum, fiue lapides preciofos prose res,longè sunt infra cœlestium corporum gloriam.Sic quamuis magnam corporum nostro rum gloriam, quæ illis in præfenti est sæculo concessa,inspicias,prorsus euanida est,& nihili ad eam collata quam habebunt post resurrectionem,ubi non erunt amplius terrestria, sed cœlestia. Et nihilo secius erût adhuc corpora. Veritatem enim corporum nô adimet illis muta conditio,& cœlestis gloriæ præstantia.
units.tr: To the same point belongs this comparison as well. Our bodies are still earthly. In the resurrection, however, they will no longer be earthly but heavenly, though they will still be bodies, yet differing from their former condition in quality, which they now have. Therefore the glory of those bodies after the resurrection will be other than the glory they now have. For even in this present age it is plain to everyone's eyes how different the glory of earthly bodies is from that of heavenly ones. No glory of any earthly body is so great that it can equal the splendour of the heavenly bodies. Whether one sets silver, gold, or precious stones before them, they fall far short of the glory of heavenly bodies. Thus, however much you look at the great glory of our bodies which has been granted to them in the present age, it is utterly faded and nothing when compared with the glory they will have after the resurrection, when they will no longer be earthly but heavenly. And nonetheless they will still be bodies. For their lowly condition does not take away the reality of their bodies, nor does the excellence of heavenly glory.

units.la: Et huc facit quod dicit: Alia est gloria solis, & alia gloria lunæ, & alia gloria ftellarū. Stella siquidem à stella differt in gloria. Quasi dicat:Quid confero inter fe corpora terrestria & cœlestia?Ipsa cœlestia quoq; & uera sunt corpora,& tamen aliud alio præstantiore est gloriam sortitum,quod in sole,luna & stellis cernere licet. Potuit Deus stellam stella, deinde lunam stellis, tertio solem & stellis & luna illustriorem reddere,tantumque differentiæ in corporibus cœlestibus ostendere: quomodo non multò potest facilius corpora nostra post resurrectionē sic reddere cœlestia,ut illustriori gloria decorentur,quàm habeant in præfenti,& tamen uera & nostra corpora maneant? An ideo sol non habet uerum corpus, quod iu bare suo reliqua corpora cœlestia excellit? An ideo minores stellæ non sunt uera corpora, quod præstantioribus non sunt in gloria pares?Ergo nec humilitas,nec singularis præftătia ueritatem corporum tollit. Sic puto Apostolum respondere illis, qui dicere poterant: Si mortui in resurrectione non sunt uenturi tali corpore,quale habuerunt in hac uita,ergo non habebunt uerum corpus,ideoq; nec uere resurgent.
units.tr: And to this point is what he says: "The glory of the sun is one, and the glory of the moon another, and the glory of the stars another; for star differs from star in glory." As if he were saying: Why do I compare earthly and heavenly bodies with one another? The heavenly bodies themselves are also true bodies, and yet one has obtained a glory more excellent than another, as can be seen in the sun, the moon and the stars. God could make one star differ from another star, then the moon from the stars, and thirdly the sun brighter than both stars and moon, thus showing so great a difference among the heavenly bodies. How much more easily, then, can he make our bodies after the resurrection heavenly in such a way that they are adorned with a more brilliant glory than they have at present, and yet remain true bodies and our own? Does the sun then not have a true body because it surpasses the other heavenly bodies in its brightness? Are the lesser stars not true bodies because they are not equal in glory to the more excellent ones? Therefore neither lowliness nor singular excellence removes the reality of bodies. I think the Apostle answers in this way those who might say: If the dead in the resurrection are not going to come with such a body as they had in this life, then they will not have a true body, and therefore will not truly rise again.

units.la: S I C & resurrectio mortuorū,inquit.] Parti cula hæc referenda est ad similitudinem seminati grani,& corporis ex illo nati,in qua dixit:Nô corpus quod nascetur feminas,sed nudum granum, Deus uero illi dat corpus ut uoluit,& unicuiq; femini suum corpus. Huc pertinet quod hic dicit: Sic & resurrectio mortuorum. Etenim quæ de carne in diuersis speciebus diuersa,&de differenti corporum terrestrium & cœlestium gloria subiecta sunt, ad illuftrationem materiæ huius faciunt,& cogitationi quæ hic nasci poterat occurrunt. Post illa redit ad simile sationis, illudq; applicat ad propositum,dicens: Sic & resurrectio mortuorum. Quasi dicat: Quemadmodum non corpus pus quod nascetur seminas,sed nudu granum: Deus vero dat illi corpus ut voluit,&unicuiq; semini suum corpus, ita non moritur ac sepelitur corpus illud quod resurget, sed caro infirma,mortalis & corruptibilis, Deus vero dabit illi corpus ut volet.Et sic continuans applicationem adijcit: Seminatur in corruptione,resurgit in incorruptibilitate,&c. Quare particula ista: Sic & resurrectio mortuorum, magis ad sequentia,tanquam praemissae similitudinis applicatione, quam ad praecedentia de carne & corporibus,diuersaq; illorum gloria pertinet.
units.tr: "So also is the resurrection of the dead." This phrase is to be referred to the likeness of the sown grain and the body born from it, in which he said: "Not the body that is to be born, but a bare grain... but God gives it a body as he wills, and to each seed its own body." To this belongs what he says here: "So also is the resurrection of the dead." For the things that have been set out concerning flesh, which differs in various kinds, and concerning the different glory of earthly and heavenly bodies, serve to illustrate the matter at hand and meet the thought that could arise here. After those things he returns to the likeness of sowing and applies it to his purpose, saying: "So also is the resurrection of the dead." As if he were saying: Just as it is not the body that is to be born that is sown, but a bare grain, and God gives it a body as he wills, and to each seed its own body, so that body which will rise is not what dies and is buried, but the weak, mortal and corruptible flesh; and God will give it a body as he wills. And continuing the application he adds: "It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption," and so on. Wherefore this phrase, "So also is the resurrection of the dead," pertains more to what follows, as an application of the likeness just set forth, than to what precedes concerning flesh and bodies and their different glory.

units.la: Patres tamen, quoniam futurę vitę gloriam secundum diuersa iustorum merita diuersam fore sentiunt,exponunt ad hunc modum:Alia est gloria solis,alia gloria lunae, alia gloria stellarum:stella siquidem a stella differt in gloria, sic & in resurrectione mortuorum erit. Alia erit gloria solis, id est Christi: alia gloria lunae, id est beatae uirginis (sic Lyranus) alia gloria stellarum,id est sanctorum:&stella differt a stella in gloria,id est sancti alij alijs erunt illustriores propter praestantiora merita. Quae sententia plus habet disputationis, quam certitudinis & utilitatis,praesertim in eo quod differentiam futurae gloriae filiorum Dei secundum praesentis vitae merita metiuntur, id quod nescio qua gloriae gratiae Dei conueniat.Si secundum praecedentia merita distribuetur gloria futurę vitae,non debebat Apostolus in simili praemisso dicere: Deus vero dat illi corpus ut voluit: sed,ut debuit. Nisi sic est uita aeterna ab illius gloria separanda, ut donum Dei sit uita aeterna, hominis vero meritum vitae aeternae gloria:quod quomodo sacris scripturis confirmari posit,uiderint alij. Et si omnino concedendum est, alios alij fore in futura uita clariores,periculosum tamen dogma est, dare id nostris meritis. Petrus Martyr, uir in sacris scripturis apprime exercitatus, materiam hanc in praesenti loco fusius tractauit, ad quem lectorem mitto.
units.tr: The Fathers, however, since they judge that the glory of future life will be different according to the different merits of the righteous, expound it in this manner: "There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory; so also will it be in the resurrection of the dead." One glory of the sun will be, that is, of Christ; another glory of the moon, that is, of the blessed virgin (so Lyranus); another glory of the stars, that is, of the saints; and star differs from star in glory, that is, some saints will be more illustrious than others because of their more excellent merits. This opinion has more of dispute than of certainty and usefulness, especially in that it measures the difference of the future glory of the sons of God by the merits of the present life, which I do not know how to reconcile with the grace of God. If the glory of future life were distributed according to preceding merits, the Apostle ought not to have said in the parallel he put forward: "God gives it a body as he wills," but "as it is due." Unless eternal life is so separated from his glory that eternal life is the gift of God, and the merit of eternal life belongs to man, which the holy Scriptures could not confirm in any way; let others see to that. And even if it must be altogether conceded that some will be brighter than others in the future life, it is nevertheless a dangerous doctrine to ascribe this to our merits. Peter Martyr, a man most thoroughly trained in the holy Scriptures, treated this matter more fully in the present passage, to whom I send the reader.

units.la: Seminatur in corruptione, resurgit in incorruptibilitate: seminatur in ignominia,resurgit in gloria:seminatur in infirmitate,resurgit in potetia: seminatur corpus animale, resurgit corpus spirituale.
units.tr: It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption; it is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power; it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body.

units.la: Coepit applicationem praemisso sationis simili subijcere dices: Sic erit & resurrectio mortuorum.Eam prosequitur istis uerbis,quibus exponit quod in simili dixit,Non hoc corpus quod nascetur seminas, sed nudum granum, Deus vero dat illi corpus ut voluit. Quod dixit,Sed nudum granum seminas, explicat dicens:Seminatur in corruptione,in ignominia, in infirmitate:hoc est,sepelimur corpus corruptibile, ignominosum, infirmum & animale. Quod vero dixit, Sed Deus dat illi corpus ut voluit, & unicuique semini suum corpus: sic applicat,Resurget in incorruptibilitate, in gloria, & in potentia: hoc est, resurget corpus incorruptibile, gloriosum, potens, & spirituale. Sic inculcat longe aliam fore corporum nostrorum qualitatem post resurrectione, quam sit ea in qua moriuntur ac sepeliuntur. Quantum enim discriminis est inter corruptionem & incorruptionem, inter ignominiam & gloriam, inter infirmitatem & potentiam, inter animale & spirituale: tantum erit differentiae inter corpora nostra,qualia iam sunt, moriuntur ac sepeliuntur, & qualia in fine mundi resurgent.
units.tr: He begins to apply the simile of sowing, saying: "So also is the resurrection of the dead." He pursues this with the words in which he explains what he said in the simile: "That which you sow is not the body that shall be, but a bare grain, but God gives it a body as he has pleased." When he said "a bare grain, which you sow," he explains it by saying: "It is sown in corruption, in dishonour, in weakness"; that is, we are buried as a corruptible, dishonoured, weak and natural body. When he said "But God gives it a body as he has pleased, and to each seed its own body," he applies it thus: "It is raised in incorruption, in glory, and in power"; that is, the body will rise incorruptible, glorious, powerful and spiritual. In this way he impresses that the quality of our bodies after the resurrection will be quite different from that in which they die and are buried. For as great as the difference is between corruption and incorruption, between dishonour and glory, between weakness and power, between natural and spiritual, so great will be the difference between our bodies, as they now are when they die and are buried, and as they will rise at the end of the world.

units.la: SEMINATUR,inquit.]Dicendum erat proprie,Sepelitur:uerum metaphoricum seminadi uerbum studio retinuit, nec semel tantum, sed quarto hic ponit, ut appareat esse illo impense delectatum. Voluit uidelicet inculcare fidelibus, sepulturam mortuorum nostrorum corporum magis esse seminationem, unde futura sit resurrectionis mesis speranda, q; sepulturam,unde timendus sit perpetuus interitus.
units.tr: "It is sown," he says. He ought properly to have said "it is buried," but he deliberately kept the metaphorical word "sown," and he uses it here not once only but four times, so that it is evident he took great delight in it. He wished, of course, to impress on the faithful that the burial of our dead bodies is more a sowing, from which the harvest of the resurrection is to be hoped for, than a burial, from which perpetual destruction is to be feared.

units.la: SEMINATUR, inquit, in corruptione.] Corruptionis uocabulum Graece φθορα, hoc loco deStructionis est sensu positum. Est autem gemina in corpore nostro corruptio. Vna, qua corpus nostrum coseruatur:altera,qua destrui tur.Prior cibi est & potus, qui in corpore nostro ab integritate sua corrumpuntur, ideoq; perire a Christo dicuntur, Ioh. 6.nosque nisi corrumperetur alere non possent, quorum pars necessaria in carnem ac sanguinem conuertitur,pars superflua in secessum abit. De hac corruptione non loquitur hoc loco Apostolus. Posterior est ipsius corporis, quod morte interuenientecorrumpitur ac destruitur.Destructionis huius duae sunt partes. Prior est καταλυσις, id est,dissolutio illa, qua spiritus a corpore separatur,quam Paulus optabat dicens:Cupio dissolui & esse cum Christo.Hanc mortem uocamus. Posterior est corporis putrefactio, qua illius omnia corrumpuntur, destruuntur, & secundum conditoris sententiam in terram unde sumpti sumus, conuertuntur. Posterioris huius prior causa est, uel, si mauis principium.Philosophantur nonnulli de hac corruptione sic: Quatuor, inquiunt, elementa sunt, philosophis quoque nota & medicis, de quibus omnes res & corpora humana compacta sunt,terra,aqua,aer,ignis.Terram in carnibus, aerem in halitu,aquam in humore,ignem in calore intelligi. Cum ergo anima caducum hoc frigidumq; corpusculum Dei iusione dimiserit, paulatim omnia redire ad matrices suas substantias,carnes in terram relabi, halitum in aera misceri, humorem reuerti ad abyssos,calorem ad aethera subuolare. Sic philosophantur illi,qui licet corporum nostrorum resurrectionem confiteantur,carnis tamen negant,at que ita & corporum destruunt. Nos simpliciter corpora nostra per corruptionē in terram unde sumpta sunt, redire dicimus, nec distribuimus illius partes in coelum, terram,aerem & abyssos.
units.tr: "It is sown," he says, "in corruption." The word corruption, in Greek [φθορα], is here used in the sense of destruction. Now there is a twofold corruption in our body. One by which our body is preserved, the other by which it is destroyed. The first is that of food and drink, which in our body are corrupted from their original wholeness, and for this reason are said to perish, as Christ says (John 6), and unless they were corrupted we could not be nourished, since a necessary part of them is turned into flesh and blood, and the superfluous part passes out into waste. The Apostle does not speak of this corruption here. The second is that of the body itself, which by the intervention of death is corrupted and destroyed. This destruction has two parts. The first is [καταλυσις], that is, the dissolution by which the spirit is separated from the body, which Paul desired when he said: "I desire to depart and be with Christ." We call this death. The second is the putrefaction of the body, by which all its parts are corrupted and destroyed, and, according to the Creator's sentence, are turned back into the earth from which we were taken. Of this second, there is a first cause, or, if you prefer, a principle. Some philosophize about this corruption as follows: there are four elements, known also to philosophers and physicians, of which all things and human bodies are composed: earth, water, air, and fire. By earth they understand the flesh, by air the breath, by water the moisture, and by fire the warmth. Therefore, when the soul has dismissed this frail and cold little body at God's command, all things gradually return to their own matrices: the flesh slips back into the earth, the breath mingles with the air, the moisture returns to the deep, and the warmth flies up to the heavens. So those philosophize who, although they confess the resurrection of our bodies, nevertheless deny the flesh, and in this way also destroy our bodies. We simply say that our bodies, by corruption, return to the earth from which they were taken, and we do not distribute their parts among heaven, earth, air and the deep.

units.la: SEMINATVR, inquit, in corruptione.] Obserua diligentiam Apostoli. In re eadem, sepultura uidelicet emortui corporis, seminationem & corruptionem coniungit, quarum altera communi omnium mortalium experientia omnibus est notissima, altera fidei tantum sensu capitur. Quod corpora nostra in corruptione sepeliantur, notum est omnibus, fidelibus &infidelibus, qui posteriores usqueadeo non sunt corruptionis huius ignorantes, ut ex illa argumenta colligant negandae resurrectionis. Etenim quo illam magis inspiciunt, hoc magis fieri posse negant, ut corpus corruptum uiuificetur ac resurgat. Quod uero sepultura corporum nostrorum sit illorum non interitus, sed seminatio, non est probabile infidelibus sed certum & indubitatum fidelibus. Qua re omnium consultissime, sic non dissimulauit corporum nostrorum corruptionem omnibus manifestam, ut iuxta non dubitauerit sepulturam illorum uocare seminationem, quo certitudinem fidei nostrae de futura resurrectione, manifestae corruptionis experientiae coniungeret.
units.tr: "It is sown," he says, "in corruption." Observe the diligence of the Apostle. In the same matter, namely the burial of the dead body, he joins sowing and corruption, of which the one is most well known to all from the common experience of all mortals, while the other is grasped only by the sense of faith. That our bodies are buried in corruption is known to all, faithful and unfaithful alike; and the unfaithful are so far from ignorant of this corruption that they draw from it arguments for denying the resurrection. For the more they look at it, the more they deny that a corrupted body can be made alive and rise again. But that the burial of our bodies is not their destruction but a sowing is not probable to the unfaithful, but is certain and indubitable to the faithful. For this reason, most wisely of all, he did not dissemble the corruption of our bodies, which is manifest to all, but he did not hesitate to call their burial a sowing, so that he might join the certainty of our faith concerning the future resurrection with the manifest experience of corruption.

units.la: Imo, nisi caecitas infidelium corda in causa salutis nostrae occuparet, non esset adeo difficile cognitu, tam non impedire corruptionem corporum nostrorum, quo minus suo tempore resurgant, ut hinc magis sperari debeat, fore ut resurgant, quod in terra corrumpuntur. Ipsorum quippe philosophi, unius corruptionem, alterius generationem esse dicunt. Non nitimur illorum dicto, ne naturae uiribus futuram corporum nostrorum resurrectionem tribuere uideamur, sed aliquo hic pacto mentes infidelium quoq; ad fidem resurrectionis induci posse sentimus.
units.tr: Indeed, unless the blindness of unbelievers occupied their hearts in the matter of our salvation, it would not be so difficult to recognise that the corruption of our bodies does not prevent them from rising in their time; so that one should rather hope that they will rise because they decay in the earth. For the philosophers themselves say that the one is the corruption of another and the other its generation. We do not rest on their saying, lest we seem to attribute the future resurrection of our bodies to the powers of nature; but we perceive that in this way the minds of unbelievers too can be led to faith in the resurrection.

units.la: SEMINATVR, inquit, in corruptione.] Cogita hic de singulari prouidentia Dei, qua corruptionem corporum nostrorum ante morte fieri uoluit: sed tum demum inchoari illam facit, quando per mortem facta spiritus & corporis dissolutione nullo illius uel alterius incommodi sensu tangimur. Quantum molestiae cum ipsis aegrotantibus, tum aliis adstantibus accidat, ubi singulari genere morbi uel externa aliqua uel interna membra in corpore adhuc uiuo corrumpuntur, putredinisque foetorem emittunt, saepenumero experimur. Quod si uniuersae corruptionis foetor & aspectus abominabilis, qualis est post mortem, ad finem usque ferendus sit, quis nam tam est firma corporis ualetudine ac patientia, ut ferendo esse posset? Quem habemus usqueadeo charum in hac uita, cuius demortui corruptione ad quartum aut quintum diem usque aspicere & olfacere possimus? Hanc ob causam charissimos quosq;, ubi mortui sunt, sepulturae properanter damus. Et sic parcit infirmitati nostrae cum aegrotantium, tum aegrotantibus ministrantium diuina prouidentia, ut priusquam intolerabilis ille corruptionis foetor e corpore nostro prodeat, morte dissoluamur, & corpus
units.tr: "It is sown," he says, "in corruption." Consider here the singular providence of God, by which he willed that the corruption of our bodies should take place after death; but he makes it begin only when, by death, the separation of spirit and body has been effected, and we are no longer touched by any sense of its discomfort or of any other harm. How much trouble arises, both for the sick themselves and for those standing by, when, through some particular kind of disease, external or internal members in a living body decay and give off the stench of putrefaction, we have often experienced. But if the stench and the abominable sight of universal corruption, such as there is after death, were to be borne to the end, who would be so firm in bodily health and patience that he could bear it? Whom do we have in this life so dear that we could look upon and smell his corruption after death for the fourth or fifth day? For this reason we quickly give all the dearest ones to burial when they are dead. And so divine providence spares our weakness, both of the sick and of those who minister to the sick: before that intolerable stench of corruption comes forth from our body, we are dissolved by death, and the body

units.la: A mortuum sepeliatur, & ad futuram messem, in qua cum gloria resurgat, seminetur.
units.tr: (dead) is buried, and is sown for the future harvest, in which it will rise in glory.

units.la: RESVRGIT, inqt, in incorruptibilitate.] Resurgit, inquit. Secundum metaphoram seminandi dicendum erat, nascitur, ut metaphora satiationis ac messis integra poneretur. Verū maluit uerbum resurgendi ponere, quoniā de illo erat contentio inter Corinthios. Resurgit. Quidnam resurgit? Quod seminatur in corruptione, corpus uidelicet mortuum, & propter corruptionem sepulturae traditū. Si aliud corpus non qualitate tantum, sed & substantia diuersum resurget, non stabit quod Apostolus hic dicit: Seminatur in corruptione, resurgit in incorruptibilitate. Ergo hoc ipsum corpus quod seminatur, resurget.
units.tr: "It is raised," he says, "in incorruption." "It is raised," he says. According to the metaphor of sowing, he ought to have said "it is born," so that the metaphor of sowing and harvest would be kept whole. But he preferred to use the word "rise," because there was a dispute about this among the Corinthians. It is raised. What is raised? That which is sown in corruption, namely the dead body, and which is committed to the grave because of its corruption. If another body, different not only in quality but also in substance, were to rise, what the Apostle says here would not hold: "It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption." Therefore this same body which is sown will rise.

units.la: Quale corpus resurget? Resurgit, inquit, in incorruptibilitate. Resurget ergo corpus incorruptibile, quod seminatur in corruptione. De semine non potest hoc dici. Quod ex grano tritici mortuo & corrupto nascitur, quantumuis multiplicatum & ornatum nascitur, perinde tamen corruptibile est, atque granum erat unde nascitur. Nondum enim liberata est creatura a seruitute corruptionis. Rom. 8. Et hoc usibus ac necessitatibus nostris attemperatum est. Alioqui nisi corruptibile esset quod ex grano uel tritici uelhordei, &c. nascitur, nec cibo nostro conduceret, nec ad conseruationem speciei suae seminari posset. Verum longe alia est ratio corporum nostrorum. Resurgent illa ad uitam omnis corruptionis expertem. Quare necesse est ut & ipsa fiant incorruptibilia. Vetus interpres non satis expressit Apostoli metem, dum uertit, Surget in incorruptione. Non modo sic surgent corpora nostra, ut sint incorrupta, sed magis ut sint incorruptibilia. Rectius ergo legitur, Resurgit in incorruptibilitate, hoc est, tale resurget corpus, quod amplius corrumpi nequeat. Si autem incorruptibiles erimus post resurrectionem, consequitur fore nos & immortales, & inuulnerabiles, & nullarum passionum, siue famis, siue sitis, siue morborum capaces. Sic erunt corpora nostra, ut nullis passionibus laedi, nedum destrui possint. Potientur ergo non solum uita, sed & incolumitate & integritate sempiterna. Possent hinc multa disputari, uerum satius est ut otiosis illa hominibus relinquamus, & magis hac fide corruptionis nostrae molestiam solemur, qua futurum credimus, ut superata illius seruitute ad ueram sempiternae felicitatis uitam ac gloriam incorruptibiles resurgamus. Multum nobis erit solatij, si fuerit spes ista reposita in sinu nostro.
units.tr: What kind of body will rise? "It is raised," he says, "in incorruption." Therefore an incorruptible body will rise, which is sown in corruption. This cannot be said of the seed. What is born from a grain of wheat that has died and decayed, however much it is multiplied and adorned when it springs up, is nevertheless as corruptible as the grain from which it arises. For creation has not yet been freed from the bondage of corruption (Rom. 8). And this is fitted to our uses and needs. Otherwise, if what springs from a grain of wheat or barley, etc., were not corruptible, it would neither serve our food nor could it be sown for the preservation of its kind. But the case of our bodies is far different. They will rise to a life free of all corruption. Therefore it is necessary that they too become incorruptible. The old translator did not express the Apostle's meaning well when he rendered it: "It will rise in incorruption." Our bodies will rise not only so that they are uncorrupted, but rather so that they are incorruptible. So it is more rightly read: "It is raised in incorruptibility," that is, the body will rise such that it can no longer be corrupted. And if we shall be incorruptible after the resurrection, it follows that we shall also be immortal, invulnerable, and capable of no sufferings, whether of hunger, thirst, or diseases. Our bodies will be such that they cannot be harmed by any sufferings, much less destroyed. They will therefore enjoy not only life but also everlasting soundness and integrity. Many things could be debated here, but it is better to leave these to idle men, and rather to console ourselves in the trouble of our corruption by this faith, by which we believe that, the bondage of corruption being overcome, we shall rise incorruptible to the true life and glory of everlasting happiness. It will be a great consolation to us if this hope is laid up in our bosom.

units.la: SEMINATVR in ignominia, resurgit in gloria.] Quod dixit, seminatur in corruptione, resurgit in incorruptibilitate: commune erit omnibus, tam impijs & iniustis, quàm pijs & iustis. Nam non soli pij incorruptibiles resurgent, sed & impij, quo in ipsis poenis sic perdu rent, ut tamen haud absumantur. Si corrumpi possent, in sempiternum puniri non possent. PunienPunientur autem in sempiternum. Ergo, &c. Quod uero hic subiungit, dicens: Seminatur in ignominia, resurget in gloria, piorum ac iustorum tantum est, qui soli resurgent in gloria, cum impij interim resurgent in maxima & indelebili confusione.
units.tr: IT IS SOWN IN DISHONOUR, IT IS RAISED IN GLORY. What he said, that it is sown in corruption and raised in incorruptibility, will be common to all, to the wicked and unjust as well as to the godly and just. For not only the godly will rise incorruptible, but the wicked too, so that in their punishments they may endure in such a way that they are yet not consumed. If they could be corrupted, they could not be punished forever. But they will be punished forever. Therefore, etc. Yet what he adds here, "It is sown in dishonour, it will be raised in glory," belongs only to the godly and the just, who alone will rise in glory, whereas the wicked will rise in the greatest and indelible shame.

units.la: SEMINATVR, inquit, in ignominia.
units.tr: It is sown, he says, in dishonour.

units.la: Graece est, ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ, quae uox neglectum & contemptum, uel si mauis honoris priuationem significat. Ignominia, nominis est nota & infamia, quae non mox quosuis mortuos comitatur. Inuenies enim multos, quorum nomen post mortem magis adhuc gloriosum reddatur. Verum in sepultura corpus emortuum eam gloriam non retinet, qua potitum fuerat dum uiueret, & in precio haberetur. Excluditur a conuictu & commercio pristino, ab aspectu & a contactu uiuentium, uestitu consueto spoliatur, uili panniculo obuoluitur, non conclaui modo, sed & ipsis prorsus aedibus exportatur, & ne foetore suo abominationi sit transeuntibus, terrae infoditur, quae omnia si uiuo homini fierent, quis non grauissimam uocet contumeliam & abiectionem? Quamuis autem ista faciant mortuis suis etiam charissimi amici, faciantq; non ex contemptu, sed necessario: ipsa tamen sic est cadaueris conditio, & sic sunt haec comparata, ut alienissima sint a pristino honore, quo paulo ante cum uiuerent, fuerant potiti. Quare non immerito dictum est ab Apostolo: Seminatur in ἀτιμίᾳ, id est, absque honore. Ipsa corporis nostri uita, cum omnis generis dotibus, quibus cohonestatur, diuinum quiddam spirat. Verum ubi instar iumenti moritur, & per mortem uita cunctisq; suis dotibus priuatum, inutile, immo abominabile ac foedum cadauer redditur, & in corruptione sepelitur, utiq; ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ sepelitur. Etenim honore suo spoliatum per mortem & corruptione simile redditur bestijs & iumentis. Unde est illud Ecclesiast. 3. Dixi in corde meo de filijs hominum, ut probaret eos Deus, & ostenderet similes esse bestijs, idcirco unus interitus est hominis & iumenti, & aequa utriusq; conditio. Sicut moritur homo, sic & illa moriuntur, &c. Et hanc ἀτιμίαν non euadunt ulli mortales, ne reges quidem ac principes. Imo hanc illi plus caeteris in currunt. Quanto enim plus gloriae consecuti sunt in hac uita, tanto plus moriendo amittunt, ideoq; maiore cum ἀτιμίᾳ sepeliuntur, etiamsi auro ac lapidibus preciosis onusti sepeliantur. In summa communis haec sors est mortalium omnium, ut quamuis in honore uiuant in hoc seculo, hinc tamen exeant & sepeliantur in ἀτιμίᾳ. Quod uero alibi legitur: Preciosa in conspectu domini mors sanctorum eius, non communis nostrae mortalitatis, sed singularis gratiae Dei respectu dicitur, qua & uita & mortem תמירה, id est eorum quibus beneuult, prosequitur.
units.tr: In Greek it is [ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ], a word which signifies neglect and contempt, or, if you prefer, the loss of honour. Dishonour is a mark and infamy of name, which does not immediately accompany every dead person. For you will find many whose name becomes even more glorious after death. But in the grave the dead body does not keep that glory which it had enjoyed while alive and held in esteem. It is shut out from the company and dealings it had before, from the sight and touch of the living; it is stripped of its customary clothing and wrapped in a cheap rag; it is carried out not only from the room but from the house itself; and so that its stench may not be an abomination to passers-by, it is buried in the earth. If all these things were done to a living man, who would not call them the gravest insult and humiliation? Although even the dearest friends do these things to their dead, and do them not from contempt but of necessity, yet the condition of a corpse is such, and these things are so ordered, that they are utterly alien to the former honour which the person enjoyed while alive a little before. Therefore the Apostle rightly said: it is sown in [ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ], that is, without honour. The very life of our body, with all the gifts by which it is adorned, breathes something divine. But when it dies like a beast of burden, and by death is deprived of life and all its gifts, it becomes a useless, indeed abominable and foul carcass, and is buried in corruption, and certainly is buried in [ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ]. For stripped of its honour by death and corruption, it is made like beasts and cattle. Hence that saying in Ecclesiastes 3: "I said in my heart concerning the sons of men, that God might prove them and show that they are like beasts; therefore there is one death of man and beast, and the condition of both is alike. As man dies, so do they die," etc. No mortal escapes this dishonour, not even kings and princes. Indeed they fall into it more than others.
