For the more glory they have obtained in this life, the more they lose by dying, and therefore they are buried with greater [ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ], even if they are buried laden with gold and precious stones. In sum, this is the common lot of all mortals: though they live in honour in this age, they nevertheless depart from here and are buried in [ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ]. But what is read elsewhere, "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints," is said with respect not to our common mortality but to the singular grace of God, by which he cares for both the life and the death of those whom he favours, tamirah [תמירה], that is, of those whom he wishes well.

units.la: RESVRGET, inquit, in gloria. Simpliciter quidem dicit, In gloria: uerum non loquitur simpliciter de gloria per mortem amissa, quasi illam tantum pet resurrectionem recuperaturi simus: sed de gloria caelestis claritatis, qua fulgebunt corpora nostra ad imaginem corporis Christi clarificata, quo sensu pau lo supra claritatem solis, lunae, ac stellarum, gloriam uocauit. Hic tamen non excludimus gloriam illa, quae ex eo nobis futura est, quod coram toto mundo reuelabitur ac declarabitur, quod sumus filij Dei. De utroque caelestis gloriae genere competenter intelligi potest, quod dicit: Resurget in gloria. Ante resurrectionem sumus adhuc inglorij, quia nondum apparet illa filiorum Dei gloria, quae in nobis a resurrectione reuelabitur, & corpora nostra non minus quam aliorum mortis sunt & corruptioni obnoxia: a qua ἀτιμίᾳ tum demum uindicabuntur, quando caelestis claritatis splendorem a mortuis excitata sortientur, cuius imago quaedam in Christo capite nostro in monte monstrata est, ubi facies eius instar solis splenduit, ac uestimenta eius candida facta sunt sicut lumen, Matth. 17.
units.tr: "It will be raised," he says, "in glory." He says simply "in glory," but he does not speak simply of the glory lost through death, as if we were to recover only that by the resurrection. He speaks of the glory of heavenly brightness, in which our bodies, made like the glorified body of Christ, will shine; in this sense, a little above, he called it the glory of the sun, moon and stars. Yet here we do not exclude that glory which will come to us from the fact that it will be revealed and declared before the whole world that we are sons of God. The phrase "it will be raised in glory" can fittingly be understood of both kinds of heavenly glory. Before the resurrection we are still without glory, because that glory of the sons of God, which will be revealed in us at the resurrection, does not yet appear; and our bodies are no less subject to death and corruption than those of others. From this [ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ] they will finally be freed when they receive the splendour of heavenly brightness, raised from the dead; a certain image of which was shown on the mount in Christ, our head, when his face shone like the sun and his garments became white as light, Matthew 17.

units.la: SEMINATVR in infirmitate, resurgit in potentia.
units.tr: It is sown in weakness, it is raised in power.

units.la: Infirmitatem corporis nostri uocat non eam qua communiter ante mortem aegrotamus, in qua quidem morimur, uerum non sepelimur: sed eam quae naturae est nostrae, per quam fit, ut nec morbis, nec passionibus, nec morti, nec corruptioni resistere queamus. Eam & Christus in se transtulit, unde & 2. Corinthiorum decimotertio legimus: Nam quamuis crucifixus fuit ex infirmitate, uiuit tamen ex uirtute Dei. Infirmitatem utique uocat susceptae nostrae carnis imbecillitatem, qua esurimus, sitimus, algemus, calescimus, fatigamur, dormimus, aegrotamus, morimur, &c or rumpimur. Et propter hanc comparatur caro nostra gramini & flori leui momento flaccescenti ac decidenti, etiam ubi in flore est ac robusta uidetur, infirma est adeo ut leui febricula tacta languescat ac procidat: quanto magis ubi mortua sepelitur, & putredini ac uermibus exponitur. Bene tamen habet, quod infirmitas illius non impedit, quominus aliquando resurrectura seminetur.
units.tr: By "weakness" he does not mean that weakness by which we commonly sicken before death, in which we indeed die but are not buried. He means the weakness that belongs to our nature, through which we cannot resist diseases, sufferings, death or corruption. Christ also took this weakness upon himself, and so we read in 2 Corinthians 13: "For though he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives by the power of God." He calls it weakness, namely the feebleness of the flesh we have assumed, by which we hunger, thirst, grow cold, grow warm, grow weary, sleep, sicken, die, or are broken, and so on. Because of this our flesh is compared to grass and to a flower that wilts and falls in a moment. Even when it is in bloom and seems strong, it is so frail that a slight fever makes it languish and collapse. How much more so when it is dead, buried, and given over to rot and worms. Yet it is good that this weakness does not prevent the body from being sown with the hope that it will one day rise.

units.la: RESVRGIT, inquit, in potentia.
units.tr: It is raised, he says, in power.

units.la: Potest hoc bifariam exponi. Primo, de potentia Dei qua corpora nostra e puluere terrae excitabuntur, ut sit sensus: Seminatur in infirmitate propria, resurget in potentia Dei. Huic potentiae Dei omnis omnium etiam Christi resurrectio tribuitur, qua de ad Ephesios capite primo sic legimus: Et quae sit superueniens magnitudo potentiae eius in nos qui credimus, secundum operationem roboris fortitudinis eius, quam exercuit in Christo, cum suscitaret eum ex mortuis, &c.
units.tr: This can be explained in two ways. First, of the power of God by which our bodies will be raised from the dust of the earth, so that the sense is: it is sown in its own weakness, and it rises in the power of God. All resurrection, even Christ's own, is ascribed to this power of God, as we read in Ephesians 1: "And what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his mighty strength, which he exerted in Christ when he raised him from the dead," and so on.

units.la: Deinde, de potentia qua corpora nostra in resurrectione donabuntur, ut simus non amplius infirmi sicuti fueramus antea, sed potentes. Potentia haec erit, non esse amplius necessitatibus edendi, bibendi, dormiendi, quiescendi, ac uestiendi, & passionibus morborum, mormortalitatis & corruptionis obnoxium. Erit enim opposita infirmitati qua circūdamur in hac uita, ne quis nescio quam potentiam hic somniet. Quemadmodū infirmitatis est quod esurimus,sitimus,lassamur,dormimus, quiescimus, uestimur, edimus ac bibimus, algemus, sudamus,ægrotamus, morimur ac corrumpimur:ita potentiæ erit nullius horum amplius esse necessitati obstrictum.In hac potentia nemo surrexit ante Christum, qui resurrectionis huiusmodi primitias habet. Quamuis autē uterq; sensus uerus est, in loco tamen posterior magis probatur, propterea quod ad propositum Apostoli propius accedit, quo non simpliciter resurrectionem astruit, sed illis respondens,qui quærunt,quali nam cum corpore uéturi sint mortui postquam resurrexerunt: futuram corporum nostrorum qualitatem sic describit,ut doceat,haud fore illa amplius corruptibilia,ingloria,infirma & animalia,sed in corruptibilia, gloriosa, potentia ac spiritualia, ad quod propositum conuenientius est, ut intelligamus, resurgere in potentia idem hic esse, quod resurgere corpus potens, quod seminatum fuerat infirmum.
units.tr: Second, of the power by which our bodies will be endowed in the resurrection, so that we are no longer weak as we were before, but powerful. This power will consist in no longer being subject to the necessities of eating, drinking, sleeping, resting and clothing, nor to the sufferings of disease, death and corruption. For it will be opposed to the weakness that surrounds us in this life, so that no one dreams of some unknown power here. Just as it is a weakness that we hunger, thirst, grow weary, sleep, rest, are clothed, eat and drink, grow cold, sweat, sicken, die and decay, so it will be power to be bound by none of these necessities any longer. No one rose in this power before Christ, who has the firstfruits of such a resurrection. Although both senses are true, the latter is the better one in this place, because it comes closer to the Apostle's purpose. He does not simply assert the resurrection, but answers those who ask with what kind of body the dead will come after they have risen. He describes the future quality of our bodies so as to teach that they will no longer be corruptible, inglorious, weak and natural, but incorruptible, glorious, powerful and spiritual. For this purpose it fits better that we understand "raised in power" to mean the same as "a powerful body is raised, which was sown weak."

units.la: SEMINATVR corpus animale, resurgit corpus spirituale. ] Quæ de discrimine corporis emortui,&c mortuis excitati dixit,uelut in summa complectitur dicens: Seminatur corpus animale, resurgit corpus spirituale. quasi dicat: In summa, corpus hoc nostrum,quod moritur & sepelitur, animale est: ubi uero resurget, non erit amplius animale, sed spirituale. Animale corpus corruptibile est,inglorium &infirmum:spirituale uero incorruptibile,gloriosum & potens.
units.tr: "It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body." Here he sums up what he has said about the difference between the body that is buried and the body that is raised, as if to say: in short, this body of ours, which dies and is buried, is natural; but where it rises, it will no longer be natural but spiritual. A natural body is corruptible, inglorious and weak; a spiritual body is incorruptible, glorious and powerful.

units.la: Vocat autem corpus nostrum ψυχικὸν, id est animale, propterea quod perinde atq; bestiæ ratione destitutæ,uitam habet per infusionem animæ,illaq; adempta moritur & corrūpitur, ut recte corpus animatum dicatur. Et hanc ob causam Ebræi nonnunquam uocem ψυχη quæ animam significat,pro corpore animato usurpant.Huiusmodi autem animalis corporis conditio est, ut opus habeat alimonia & protectio ne,qua & sustentur & conseruetur. Est enim infirmum,ut facile lædatur,& habet in se igneam quandam consumendi uim, quæ nisi cibo &potu alatur ipsum corpus conficit, unaque cum illo perit & ipsa,ac morti corruptionique locum permittit.
units.tr: He calls our body psychikon [ψυχικὸν], that is, natural (animale), because, just as beasts lacking reason have life through the infusion of a soul, and die and decay when it is taken away, so the body is rightly called animated. For this reason the Hebrews sometimes use the word psyche [ψυχή], which means soul, for an animated body. The condition of such a natural body is that it needs nourishment and protection, by which it is sustained and preserved. For it is weak, so that it is easily harmed, and it has within it a kind of fiery force of consuming. Unless it is fed with food and drink, this force wastes the body itself, and together with the body it perishes too, giving place to death and corruption.

units.la: RESVRGIT, inquit, corpus spirituale.] Quemadmodum corpus nostrum quatenus uitā habet ex anima, animale uocatur:ita post resurrectionem quatenus spiritu cœlesti uiui-ficabitur, non erit amplius animale, sed spirituale. Iam anima corpus nostrum sic firmū & immortale reddere non potest, ut nullis opus habeat alimentis, nullisq; sit passionibus obnoxium: qua in re æquá habet cum iumentis conditionem,quæ & ipsa corpora habent animata,in resurrectione uero sic firmabitur ac ui uet cœlesti spiritu,ut sit immortale & incorru-
units.tr: "It is raised," he says, "a spiritual body." Just as our body, insofar as it has life from the soul, is called natural, so after the resurrection, insofar as it will be quickened by the heavenly Spirit, it will no longer be natural but spiritual. The soul cannot make our body so firm and immortal that it needs no food and is subject to no sufferings. In this it has the same condition as beasts, which also have animated bodies. But in the resurrection the body will be so strengthened and quickened by the heavenly Spirit that it will be immortal and incorruptible.

units.la: ptibile.Obserua uero, quod non dicit,Seminatur corpus,resurget spiritus:sed,seminatur corpus animale,resurget corpus spirituale. Tam illic resurget corpus,quàm hic seminatur corpus. Illic quidem spirituale, attamen corpus. Qualitas spiritualis tam non exinguet corporis nostri ueritatem, quàm animalis qualitas non facit in nobis, ut corpus nostrum non sit corpus,sed anima. Corpus nostrum in resurrectione nec mutabitur in spiritum,ut spiritus iungatur spiritui, nec in nihilum redigetur, ut nonnisi spiritus futuri simus:sed ueritatem sub stantiæ suæ retinebit,ut conueniat illi quoque quod de suo corpore Christus post resurrectionem ad discipulos dixit, cum illis spiritus esse uideretur,Palpate & uidete,quoniam spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicuti me habere uidetis.Luc.24.Augustinus epistola 146. sic exponit corpus spirituale: Quoniâ, inquit, spiritui in separabiliter copulatū est. Et libr.13. de ciuitate Dei cap.22.Spiritualia erūt, inquit, non quia corpora esse desistent, sed quia spiritu uiuificante subsistent.Et libro eodem ca.20. Sicut spiritus carni seruiens,inquit,non incongrue carnalis,ita caro spiritui seruiens recte appellatur spiritualis,non quod in spiritum conuertetur,sicut nonnulli putant ex eo quod scriptum est: Seminatur corpus animale, surget corpus spirituale, sed quia spiritui summa & mirabili obtemperandi facilitate subdetur, usque ad implendam immortalitatis indissolubilis securisimam uoluntatem, omni molestiæ sensu, omni corruptibilitate & tarditate detracta.
units.tr: Note, moreover, that he does not say "the body is sown, the spirit is raised," but "a natural body is sown, a spiritual body is raised." There the body will rise just as here the body is sown; there it will be spiritual, yet still a body. The spiritual quality will no more extinguish the reality of our body than the natural quality makes our body not a body but a soul. In the resurrection our body will be changed neither into spirit, so that spirit is joined to spirit, nor reduced to nothing, so that we would be nothing but spirits. Rather, it will keep the truth of its substance, as Christ also said of his own body after the resurrection to the disciples, who thought they saw a spirit: "Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have." Luke 24. Augustine, in Epistle 146, explains "spiritual body" thus: "because," he says, "it is inseparably joined to the spirit." And in book 13 of The City of God, chapter 22: "They will be spiritual," he says, "not because they will cease to be bodies, but because they will subsist by the quickening Spirit." And in the same book, chapter 20: "Just as flesh serving the spirit is not unfittingly called fleshly, so flesh serving the spirit is rightly called spiritual. This is not because it will be turned into spirit, as some think from what is written, 'It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body,' but because it is made subject to the spirit with the greatest and most wonderful ease of obedience, until it fulfils the most secure will of indissoluble immortality, all sense of trouble, all corruptibility and sluggishness having been removed."

units.la: Hæc ibi. Ergo tria ponit Augustinus, quorum gratia corpus nostrum,quale post resurrectionem habituri sumus, nō amplius futurum sit animale,sed spirituale. Primum est, quod spiritui inseparabiliter copulabitur. Secudum quod illo uiuificante subsistet.Tertium, quod illi mirabili quadam obediendi facilitate subdetur. Possent & aliæ rationes assignari, uerū quod me attinet,hæ sufficiant.
units.tr: So far Augustine. He therefore sets down three things by which our body, as it will be after the resurrection, will no longer be natural but spiritual. The first is that it will be inseparably joined to the spirit. The second is that it will subsist through the spirit's quickening. The third is that it will be subject to the spirit with a wonderful ease of obedience. Other reasons could be given, but as far as I am concerned these are enough.

units.la: Posset etiam quæri de spiritu, quo uniuscuiusque corpus spirituale reddetur. (Necesse nanq; est,ut propter spiritum spirituale sit futurum)quis nam sit ille spiritus,idemne quem quisq; in corpore suo mortali habuit, uel alius quisquam,uel spiritus Dei. Erit quidem Deus omnia in omnibus, uerum quoniam de spiritu nostro, scriptum est, quod reuertatur ad eū qui dedit illum:nec cogitandum est, quod uel extinguatur in cœlestibus, uel in locum illius alius substituatur,in quo corpus nostrū resurgat,puto indubitatum esse, eodem nos spiritu spirituales futuros,qui corpus nostrum in hac præsenti uita inhabitat, & morte ab illo separatur,inq; cœlestia ad Deum reuertitur. Hic non est quærendum quomodo ille tantæ futurus sit potentiæ post resurrectionem,ut corpus nostrum reddat spirituale, immortale, incorruptibile,potens & gloriosum, cū nihil horum præstet in hac uita. Omnis enim illa potentia, tentia, qua corpora nostra è mortuis excitabũ-tur, spiritualiaq; immortalia, incorruptibilia& gloriosa reddentur, non erit alicuius creati spiritus, sed ipsius Dei. Per hunc habebit omnem spiritualem efficaciam spiritus noster, ea præstandi in nobis, quæ in corpore animali præsta re iam non poterit. Huius efficaciam nō debemus omnipotētem futurā credere. Quare moderate de illa disputandum censeo. Satius est ad ueram illam felicitatem spiritualem corporū fide syncera, & spe infracta aspirare, quā de facultatibus illorum temere disputare.
units.tr: One could also ask about the spirit by which each person's body will be made spiritual. (For it must be that it will be spiritual because of the spirit.) Who is that spirit: the same one each person had in his mortal body, some other spirit, or the Spirit of God? God will indeed be all in all. But since it is written of our spirit that it returns to God who gave it, and we should not think that it is extinguished in heaven or that another is substituted in its place in which our body rises, I judge it beyond doubt that we shall be spiritual by the same Spirit who dwells in our body in this present life, is separated from it by death, and returns to God in heaven. Here we should not ask how that Spirit will be of such power after the resurrection as to make our body spiritual, immortal, incorruptible, powerful and glorious, since it accomplishes none of these things in this life. For all that power by which our bodies are raised from the dead and made spiritual, immortal, incorruptible and glorious will not belong to any created spirit, but to God himself. Through him our spirit will have all its spiritual efficacy, to accomplish in us those things which it can no longer accomplish in the natural body. We ought not to believe that its efficacy will be omnipotent. Therefore I think we should discuss it with moderation. It is better to aspire with sincere faith and unbroken hope to that true spiritual felicity of the body than to dispute rashly about its faculties.

units.la: Est corpus animale, & est corpus spirituale, quemadmodum & scriptū est: Factus est primus homo Adam in animam uiuentē, extremus Adam in spiritum uiuificantem.
units.tr: There is an animal body, and there is a spiritual body, just as it is written: "The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit."

units.la: Erat Corinthijs inusitata loquutio, qua dixit: Seminatur corpus animale, resurgit corpus spirituale. Imò ne hodie quidē admodum est trita in ecclesia, & perspicua etiam magnis doctoribus. Quare ad illius declarationem resumit eam explicandam.
units.tr: The way of speaking was unfamiliar to the Corinthians when he said: "It is sown an animal body; it is raised a spiritual body." Indeed, even today it is not very common in the Church, and it is not clear even to great teachers. Therefore, to explain it, he takes it up again for explanation.

units.la: EST corpus, inquit, animale, & est corpus spirituale. Non dicit, Sicut corpus animale, est etiam corpus spirituale, quemadmodum habet uulgata uersio. Non enim propterea est corpus spirituale, quod est corpus animale, quasi unumquodq; corpus animale ob id sit & spirituale, quod est animale, sed simpliciter tanquā de duabus diuersis corporum qualitatibus: Est corpus animale, inquit, & est corpus spirituale. Non dicit, & erit: sed, & est corpus spirituale. Erit quidem corpus nostrum spirituale in futura uita, quod animale est in præsenti: uerum non de illo iam loquitur, sed collimat ad illius exemplar, quod in glorificato Christi corpore per resurrectionem ex mortuis esse coepit.
units.tr: "There is an animal body," he says, "and there is a spiritual body." He does not say, "As there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual body," as the Vulgate version has. For the body is not spiritual because it is an animal body, as if every animal body were for that reason also spiritual, because it is animal. He speaks simply, as of two different qualities of bodies: there is an animal body, he says, and there is a spiritual body. He does not say "there will be" but "there is a spiritual body." Our body will indeed be spiritual in the future life, which is animal now; but he is not speaking of that now. He aims at its pattern, which began to exist in the glorified body of Christ through resurrection from the dead.

units.la: QVEMADMODVM, inquit, scriptū est. Ne nouæ loquutionis author esse uideatur, præsertim in eo quod homini animale corpus tribuit, scripturæ testimonium adducit, idq; ex ipsa creati primi hominis historia, quæ Genesis secundo iisdem uerbis repetitur: Et formauit Dominus Deus Adamum puluerem de humo, & inspirauit in nares eius, flatum uitæ, & factus est Adam in animam uiuam. Huc respiciens dicit: Quemadmodum scriptum est: factus est primus homo Adam in animam uiuentem. Illud, primus homo, non est in uerbis scripturæ quam adducit, quæ simpliciter habet & factus est Adam in animam uiuā. Adiecit hoc de suo, primum gratia specificationis, de quo Adamo loquatur scriptura: deinde propter collationem duorum principalium capitum, Adç uidelicet & Christi, quorum alterum extremū, alterum primum Adamum uocat. Extremus Adam, inquit, in spiritum uiuificantem. De primo quidem Adamo loquitur citata scriptura, de extremo uero, id est Christo, non loquitur. Quare ergo de primo scripturam inducit, de al
units.tr: "As it is written," he says. Lest he seem to be the author of a new way of speaking, especially in attributing an animal body to man, he adduces the testimony of Scripture, and this from the very history of the creation of the first man, which is repeated in Genesis 2 in the same words: "And the Lord God formed Adam dust from the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and Adam became a living soul." Looking to this, he says: "As it is written: the first man Adam was made a living soul." The words "first man" are not in the words of Scripture he cites, which simply has "and Adam became a living soul." He added this on his own account: first, to specify of which Adam Scripture speaks; then because of the comparison of the two principal heads, Adam and Christ, one of whom he calls the last Adam, the other the first. "The last Adam," he says, "into a life-giving spirit." The cited Scripture speaks of the first Adam, but it does not speak of the last, that is Christ. Why then does he bring in Scripture about the one, but not about the other, that is Christ?

units.la: tero, id est Christo, non inducit? Meo iudicio, quoniam auribus illorum Christianorum, qui philosophicis loquutionibus assueuerant, insolēs uideri poterat, quod homini corpus animale tribuebat, quasi similis sit bestijs: eius loquutionis authoritatem assignat ex ipsa sacra scriptura, quod de Christo extremo Adamo non facit, quoniam non erat insolens, quod illi corpus spirituale tribuebat.
units.tr: In my judgment, it is because to the ears of those Christians who were accustomed to philosophical expressions it could seem strange that he attributed an animal body to man, as if he were like the beasts. So he gives the authority for this expression from Holy Scripture itself. He does not do this for Christ, the last Adam, because it was not strange that he attributed a spiritual body to him.

units.la: FACTVS est primus homo Adam, inquit, in animam uiuentem. ] Qualis est primus homo Adam, tales sumus & nos omnes illius posteri. Quare illius creationem & factura inducit, unde probet, quod plerique in nobis ipsis nō agnoscimus dū pro semidijs haberi uolumus, deq; acumine & præstantia intelligentiæ & sapientiæ humanæ, & de libero nostro arbitrio, ac nescio quib. uirtutibus admodū gloriamur.
units.tr: "The first man Adam was made," he says, "a living soul." Such as the first man Adam was, such are we, all his posterity. Therefore he adduces his creation and making, from which he proves what most of us do not recognise in ourselves, while we want to be regarded as demigods, and boast greatly of the keenness and excellence of human understanding and wisdom, of our free will, and I know not what other virtues.

units.la: Vocat autem Adamum primum hominem non modo tempore & ordine, quo primus est à Deo conditus, quemadmodum primus dies in septimana, uel primus regni alicuius annus uocari solet: sed originali potiŷ principio, quo factus est totius humanæ posteritatis caput & fons. Prima est arbor in horto, quæ prima in illo plátatur. Ea uero duplici nomine prima est, quæ & tempore est & propagatione prima, sic ut ex ipsa cæterę omnes propagentur. Hoc duplici pacto primus homo est Adá. Sic uero uocatur ab Apostolo, non prioris, sed posterioris gratia, tanquam omnium mortalium ex ipso descendentium exemplar.
units.tr: He calls Adam the first man not only in time and order, in which he was first created by God, just as the first day of the week or the first year of some reign is usually called first; but rather by original principle, by which he was made the head and fountain of the whole human posterity. The first tree in the garden is the one first planted there. Now a thing is first in a twofold sense when it is both first in time and first in propagation, so that all others are propagated from it. In this twofold way Adam is the first man. He is so called by the Apostle not for the sake of his priority, but of his posterity, as the pattern of all mortals descending from him.

units.la: Et quid factus est ille primus homo Adam? In animam, inquit, uiuentem. Ebr. לנפש חיה. Germanicus interpres uertit in Genesi cap.2. Ein lebendige seel: hic uero in Paulo, ins naturlich leben. Gen. cap.1, ubi de creatione piscium legitur habetur prorsus idem: Et dixit Deus: Producant aquæ reptile נפש חיה, id est animam uiuē. Et: Creauit Deus cete grādia & omnē נפש, id est, anima uiuēte. Deinde ubi creatio bestiarū ac pecorum memoratur. Et dixit Deus inquit: Producat terra נפש חיה id est, animam uiuentem in genere suo, iumentum, & reptile, & bestias terræ, &c. Et ubi de cibo hominū & bestiarū fit mentio. Et dixit Deus, inquit, Ecce dedi uobis omnem herbā, &c. & omni bestiæ terræ, & omni uolucri cœli, & omni reptili terræ in quo est נפש חיה id est, anima uiuens. Et cap.9. ubi memoratur pactum quod cōstituit Deus post diluuium inter se & Noah & cuncta animantia terræ, non semel, sed quarto tribuitur bestijs נפש חיה anima uiuens. Et cap.7. pro anima uiuente ponitur רוח חיים id est, spiritus uitæ datur quæ bestijs, & additur uox נשמה id est, flatus, ad huc modū: Et expirauit omnis caro repens super terram, &c. omne in cuius naribus erat נשמת רוח חיים id est flatus spiritus uitæ. Vnde apparet idem esse נפש חיה quod נשמת חיים & רוח חיים quod נשמה id est, flatus uitę, qui & homini à Deo inflatus, ideoque ille in נפש חיה factus legitur hoc loco quę Apostolus citat. Vbi sermo est de bestijs, reddit GerditGermanicus interpres, Ein lebendigs thier. Est ergo primus homo Adam, per id quod inflauit in ipsum Deus flatum uitę factus לנפש חיה id est, in animam uiuentem: uel, si mauis, in animal uiuum. Poterit hic quæri, quare Apost. non potius dixerit, Et factus est primus homo Adam ad imaginem ac similitudinem Dei, cū & illud habeat sacra scriptura: quàm, Et factus est primus homo Adam in animā uiuente, præsertim cum sciret prædicatum hoc, נפש חיה toties in scripturis tribui bestijs terræ, ideoq; nihil habere, in quo homo pisces maris & bestias terræ excellat. Responsio facilis est. Non faciebat ad propositum prærogatiua imaginis Dei homini in scripturis tributa. Loquitur enim de homine, quatenus est instar iumenti, infirmus, mortalis & corruptibilis, non quatenus singulari est honore præ bestijs à Deo ornatus. Quare conuenientius erat ut hoc prædicatū, נפש חיה quod homini commune est cū bestijs, ex scriptu ris adferret in medium, indeq; authoritate faceret suæ sententiæ, qua dixit: Seminatur corpus animale. Non est autem præter rationem, quod scriptura idem prædicat de homine quàm de bestijs. Facit enim plurimum ad reprimendū humani ingenij typhum. Et hàc ob causam pro bari non debet, quod Thargum Onkelos prædicatum hoc primi hominis Adę: Et factus est Adam רוח חיה באדם לרוח חיה sic transtulit hoc est, & factus est (intellige flatus illè uitæ, quem Deus formato à se Adæ inflauit) in Adamo in spiritum loquentem. Neq; enim נפש חיה idem est quod spiritus loquens, nisi & bestias terræ in spiritum loquentem factas esse dicturi sumus.
units.tr: And what did that first man Adam become? "Into a living soul," he says. Hebrew: לנפש חיה. The German translator renders it in Genesis chapter 2 as "ein lebendige Seel"; here in Paul, "ins natürlich Leben" (into natural life). Genesis chapter 1, where the creation of fishes is read, has exactly the same: "And God said: let the waters bring forth the creeping thing נפש חיה," that is, a living soul. And: "God created the great whales and every נפש," that is, living soul. Then where the creation of beasts and cattle is mentioned: "And God said," he says, "let the earth bring forth נפש חיה," that is, a living soul according to its kind, cattle, creeping thing and beasts of the earth, etc. And where mention is made of the food of men and beasts: "And God said," he says, "Behold, I have given you every herb," etc., "and to every beast of the earth, and to every fowl of the heaven, and to everything that creeps upon the earth, in which is נפש חיה," that is, a living soul. And in chapter 9, where the covenant which God made after the flood between himself and Noah and all living creatures of the earth is recorded, the beasts are given נפש חיה, living soul, not once but four times. And in chapter 7, instead of living soul, רוח חיים, that is, breath of life, is given to the beasts, and the word נשמה, that is, breath, is added in this way: "And every creeping flesh upon the earth expired ... everything in whose nostrils was the נשמת רוח חיים," that is, the breath of the spirit of life. Whence it appears that נפש חיה is the same as נשמת חיים, and רוח חיים is the same as נשמה, that is, breath of life, which was also breathed into man by God; and therefore he is read here to have become לנפש חיה, which the Apostle cites. Where the discourse is about beasts, the German translator renders it A living creature. Therefore the first man Adam, through the breath of life which God breathed into him, became לנפש חיה, that is, a living soul; or, if you prefer, a living animal. Here it may be asked why the Apostle did not rather say, "And the first man Adam was made in the image and likeness of God," since Holy Scripture also has that, rather than, "and the first man Adam was made into a living soul," especially since he knew that this predicate, נפש חיה, is so often attributed to the beasts of the earth in the Scriptures, and so there is nothing in it by which man excels the fishes of the sea and the beasts of the earth. The answer is easy. The prerogative of the image of God attributed to man in Scripture did not serve his purpose. For he speaks of man as he is like a beast, weak, mortal and corruptible, not as he is adorned by God with singular honour above the beasts. Therefore it was more fitting that he bring forward from the Scriptures this predicate, נפש חיה, which is common to man with the beasts, and so make it an authority for his opinion, by which he said: "It is sown an animal body." Nor is it beyond reason that Scripture predicates the same of man as of beasts; for it greatly serves to restrain the pride of human ingenuity. And for this reason it should not be held against Onkelos, the Chaldee paraphrast, that he translated this predicate of the first man Adam thus: "and Adam became a living spirit in Adam, into a speaking spirit" (ruach chaya be-adam le-ruach memallela). That is, it became (understand the breath of life which God breathed into Adam formed by himself) in Adam a speaking spirit. For נפש חיה is not the same as a speaking spirit, unless we are going to say that the beasts of the earth were made into a speaking spirit.

units.la: EXTREMVS Adam, inquit, in spiritum uiuificantem. Hactenus de eo, quod corpus animale seminari dixit, ad cuius declarationē exemplum Adæ primi hominis induxit, iā ad declarationē eius quod dixit: resurget corpus spirituale, illius quoq; exempla proponit dicēs: Extremus Adam in spiritum uiuificante. Quis ille sit extremus Adam, August. dubitáter exponit dicens: Nouissimus Adam in spiritū uiuificatem, siue intelligatur primus Adā, qui de puluere antè formatus est, nouissimus autem Adā qui de uirgine procreatus est, siue in unoquoque homine utrunq; cōpleatur, ut primus Adā sit in corpore mortali, nouissimus Adam idē ipse in corpore immortali. Hęc ille. Verum posterior sententia nō cōuenit sequentib. præsertim ei quod dicturus est Apost. Primus homo de terra terrenus, secundus homo ipse dominus de cœlo. Seduxit Augustus, uulgata lectio quę sic habet, secūdus homo de cœlo cœlestis. Ambrosius, quáuis & ipse legit, secūdus homo de cœlo cœlestis, de Christo tamen constanter exponit. Quàquam quę in Ambrosio à præsenti loco ad finem usq; Epistolæ leguntur, ad uerbum habentur in Cōmētarijs, quę Hieronymo tribuuntur. Sic parum certitudinis habēt, qui scripta patrum prope canonicis scripturis adæquant. Vocat autem Christum Adā, eo sensu quo uox אדם hominem significat. Extremum appellat, nō qd omniū sit mortaliū extremus, sed quod inter duo principalia humani generis capita, alterum ipse locū habet post Adamū. Sic uocat eum mox infrà secundū homine. Parum honorificum uidetur, quod Christū uocat non modo Adamum, sed & extremū Adamū, nisi quo hoc sensu faciat diligenter cōsideres. Communi sensu diminutionis notā habet esse nouissimum. Sic Saul, cum se coram Samuele humiliaret, indignumq; esse honore regio diceret: An non filius Iemini ego sum, inquit, de minima tribu Israël, & cognatio mea nouissima inter omnes familias de tribu Beniamin? 1. Sam. 9. & de Hieroboam legitur qd fecerit sibi sacerdotes de extremis populi, Et 2. Reg. 17. Fecerunt aut sibi, inquit, de nouissimis sacerdotes excelsorum, quod de uilissimis est intelligendum, quales hodie quoq; cum inter Papistas tum inter σαρκικωγγελικος ministerijs ecclesiasticis præfici uidemus. Verum non hoc sensu uocat Apost. Christum extremū Apā, sed lõge alio, tali uidelicet, quo plus est prærogatiuæ posterius esse quàm esse primū. Neq; enim mox præstantius est quod primū, neq; statim deterius quod postremum est. Prior pars naturalis diei, uespera est cum nocte, posterior subsequens dies. Priore locum diei habent luna & stellę, posteriorem sol. Dum homo in utero matris cōcipitur, prior est caro, posterior spiritus. Cum Adam formaretur, priorem locum habebat puluis, posteriorem spiritus. In uita nostra prior est infantilis ætas, posterior ea quæ usu rationis est instructa. Prius est esse discipulum, posterius esse doctore. Priores sunt huius uitę passiones, posteriores futuri sęculi gloriæ. Innumera sunt exempla, in quibus uidere est, nō mox potius esse, quod primum: neq; statim deterius, quod postremum existit. Quare nec hic quicquam gloriæ Christi incōmodat, quod extremus Adam: nec ad prærogatiuā Adæ facit, quod primus Adam uocatur. Imo præstantius hic est, postremum esse quàm primū. In primo siquidem ruditas est, infirmitas & imperfectio: in postremo maturitas, firmitudo & perfectio. In primo peccatum, perditio, mors & corruptio: in postremo iusticia, salus, uita & incorruptio. Hanc præstantiam extremi Adæ exprimens dicit: Extremus Adam in spiritum uiuificātem. August. Epistola paulo suprà citata sic exponit: Inter animā uiuente & spiritū uiuificantem hoc interesse uoluit, ut illic sit corpus animale, hic spirituale. Anima quippe in corpore animali uiuit qdem, sed nō uiuificat usq; ad auferēdā corruptionē. In corpore uero spirituali, quoniā pfecte adhęres domino, unus spiritus est, sic uiuificat ut spiritale corpus efficiat absumēs omne corruptione, nullā metuēs separationē. Hęc ille, quibus extremum Adamū in spiritū uiuificate factū corpus nostrū spirituale intelligit, quale in resurrectione acquiremus. Verum, quemadmodum diximus, duo nobis exemplaria proponit: unū animalis corporis, quod
units.tr: The last Adam, he says, became a life-giving spirit. So far he has spoken of what he said about the animal body being sown, and to explain that he brought in the example of Adam, the first man. Now, to explain what he said next, that the body is raised a spiritual body, he sets out a parallel example, saying: The last Adam became a life-giving spirit. Augustine hesitantly explains who this last Adam is, saying: The last Adam became a life-giving spirit. This may be understood as the first Adam, who was formed earlier from dust, and the last Adam, who was born of the virgin; or both may be fulfilled in each man, so that the first Adam is in the mortal body and the last Adam is the same man in the immortal body. So far Augustine. But the latter view does not agree with what follows, especially with what the Apostle is about to say: The first man is of the earth, earthly; the second man, the Lord himself, is from heaven. Augustine was misled by the Vulgate reading, which runs: the second man from heaven is heavenly. Ambrose, although he too reads the second man from heaven, is consistent in interpreting it of Christ. Yet the comments attributed to Jerome, which cover this passage down to the end of the Epistle, are word for word the same as those under Ambrose's name. So those who put the writings of the Fathers almost on a level with the canonical Scriptures have little certainty. Paul calls Christ Adam in the sense in which the Hebrew word אדם means man. He calls him the last, not because he is the last of all mortals, but because, of the two principal heads of the human race, he himself holds the second place after Adam. In the same way he calls him the second man shortly below. It seems not very honourable that Christ is called not only Adam but the last Adam, unless you consider carefully the sense in which he does this. In common usage, to be last carries a mark of lowliness. So Saul, when he humbled himself before Samuel and said he was unworthy of royal honour, said: "Am I not a son of Jemini, of the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my family the lowest of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin?" (1 Sam. 9.) And we read of Jeroboam that he made priests for himself from the lowest of the people (1 Kings 12); and in 2 Kings 17 it says: "they made for themselves priests of the high places from the lowest," which must be understood of the most worthless sort, such as we see today appointed to ecclesiastical ministries both among the Papists and among the carnal gospellers [σαρκικοῖς εὐαγγελικοῖς]. But the Apostle does not call Christ the last Adam in this sense; he means something quite different, namely that being later carries more pre-eminence than being first. For what is first is not at once more excellent, nor is what is last at once inferior. The first part of a natural day is evening with night, the later part is the day that follows; the moon and stars hold the first place in the day, the sun the later. While a man is conceived in his mother's womb, the flesh is first and the spirit later. When Adam was being formed, dust had the first place and spirit the later. In our life, infancy comes first and the age furnished with the use of reason comes later. To be a pupil comes first, to be a teacher later. The sufferings of this life come first, the glories of the age to come later. There are countless examples in which it is plain that what is first is not at once better, nor what is last at once worse. So the fact that Christ is the last Adam does not diminish his glory, and the fact that Adam is called the first Adam does not add to Adam's pre-eminence. Indeed, here it is more excellent to be last than first. In the first there is rawness, weakness and imperfection; in the last, maturity, firmness and perfection. In the first there is sin, ruin, death and corruption; in the last, righteousness, salvation, life and incorruption. Expressing this pre-eminence of the last Adam, he says: The last Adam became a life-giving spirit. Augustine, in the letter cited a little above, explains it thus: he meant there to be this difference between a living soul and a life-giving spirit: that there is an animal body in the one case, a spiritual body in the other. For the soul indeed lives in an animal body, but does not give life so as to remove corruption. But in a spiritual body, since it adheres perfectly to the Lord, it is one spirit with him, and so gives life that it makes the body spiritual, consuming all corruption and fearing no separation. So far Augustine, by whom the last Adam made a life-giving spirit is understood to be our spiritual body, such as we shall acquire in the resurrection. But, as we have said, he sets before us two examples: one of the animal body, which

units.la: A Vide ad Gen. 2.
units.tr: A See on Gen. 2.

units.la: B Gen. 2. quod morti est & corruptioni obnoxiū, alterū spiritualis,qd immortale erit & incorruptibi le. Primum facit Adamū, alterum Christū. Vt Adam exemplar est animalis, ita Christus spiri rualis,quem in spiritum uiuificantem factū di cit,propterea quod non modo ad immortali tatem & incorruptibilitatem pro sua persona resurrexit, sed & omnia sua membra uiuificat & immortalia reddit. Quare non dicit,in spiri tum uiuentem:sed,in spiritum uiuificantem.
units.tr: B Gen. 2. is subject to death and corruption; the other of the spiritual body, which will be immortal and incorruptible. The first makes Adam, the second makes Christ. As Adam is the pattern of the animal body, so Christ is of the spiritual body, and he is said to have become a life-giving spirit because he rose not only to immortality and incorruptibility in his own person, but also gives life to all his members and makes them immortal. Therefore Paul does not say "a living spirit" but "a life-giving spirit."

units.la: Dices,an non ipse quoq; Christus factus est in animam uiuente,perinde atq; nos.Respon deo. Quatenus ex Adam est, anima uiuentem accepit,quemadmodū & nos : quatenus uero dominus de cœlo est,factus est in spiritū uiuifi cantem.Cauendum est,ne cum Apollinaristis spiritū illi uiuificantem pro anima demus, uel cum Manichæis sic in spiritū uiuificante factū esse dicamus,ut veritatem corporis illi aufera mus.Quemadmodum non ideo corpus nō ha bebat Adam, quod factus esset in animam ui uentem: ita non ideo spiritus est sine corpore Christus,quod in spiritū uiuificante est factus.
units.tr: You may say: did not Christ himself also become a living soul, just as we are? I answer: insofar as he is from Adam, he received a living soul, as we do; but insofar as he is the Lord from heaven, he became a life-giving spirit. We must take care not to say, with the Apollinarians, that by a life-giving spirit we mean a soul, nor, with the Manichaeans, to say that he became a life-giving spirit in such a way that we take away the reality of his body. Just as Adam did not therefore lack a body because he was made a living soul, so Christ is not without a body because he was made a life-giving spirit.

units.la: At non primum quod spirituale, sed quod animale, deinde quod spirituale. Primus homo de terra terrenus, secundus homo ipse dominus de cœlo. Qualis terrenus ille, tales & hi qui terreni sunt. Et qualis ille cœlestis, tales & hi qui cœlestes sunt. Et quemadmodū gestauimus imaginem terreni, gestabimus & imaginem cœlestis.
units.tr: But the spiritual is not first, but the animal, then the spiritual. The first man is of the earth, earthly; the second man, the Lord himself, is from heaven. As the earthly one was, such are also those who are earthly; and as the heavenly one is, such are also those who are heavenly. And as we have borne the image of the earthly, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.

units.la: Pergit declarando diuersitatem corporum nostrorum qua post resurrectione præsentem illorum qualitate superabūt. Declaratione illo rum in duobus originalibus hominibus Adamo & Christo propositam prosequitur. Dixit, Est corpus animale, & est corpus spirituale. Huic adiecerat scriptura. Ut ut ordinem incul cet,quo Deus nec simul illa esse,nec aliter ordi nari uoluit,quàm ut præcedat animale, subse quatur uero spirituale,dicit:
units.tr: He goes on, explaining the difference between our bodies, by which they will surpass the present condition of those bodies after the resurrection. He pursues the explanation proposed in the two original men, Adam and Christ. He had said: there is an animal body, and there is a spiritual body. To this Scripture adds, to press home the order in which God willed that these not be together, nor be arranged otherwise than that the animal comes first and the spiritual follows. He says:

units.la: AT non primum quod spirituale,sed quod animale,deinde quod spirituale. ]Dices:Qui bus nam rationib. sic constitutum est, ut non simul sit animale & spirituale corpus, sed ani male prius,spirituale posterius. Respondeo. Pio homini satis est, si intelligat sic esse cōsiliū prouidentiæ Dei.Possunt tamen certę aliquot causæ assignari.Prima est,quod animalis & spi ritualis qualitas non prædicatur ab Apostolo de corporibus natura & substantia diuersis,alijs atq; alijs,sed ,prʃus eodem. Idē corpus utrius que qualitatis capax inducitur.At nō potest u tranq; simul capere ut sit & animale & spiritua le,mortale & immortale,corruptibile & incor ruptibile,ingloriū & gloriosum,infirmū & for te,terrenū & cœleste:sed necesse est ut compe tenti mutatione,ab una qualitate trāseat ad al terā:& quale fuit antea,tale non sit amplius.In corporib.natura & substantia diuersis diuersę
units.tr: But the spiritual is not first, but the animal, then the spiritual. Someone may ask on what grounds it has been established that the animal and spiritual body are not simultaneous, but the animal first and the spiritual later. I answer: it is enough for a godly man to understand that this is the counsel of God's providence. Yet some certain causes can be assigned. (1) The first is that the animal and spiritual quality are not predicated by the Apostle of bodies differing in nature and substance, one from another, but of one and the same body. The same body is introduced as capable of either quality. But it cannot receive both at once, so as to be both animal and spiritual, mortal and immortal, corruptible and incorruptible, inglorious and glorious, weak and strong, earthly and heavenly. It must rather, by a fitting change, pass from one quality to the other, and what it was before, it is no longer. In bodies differing in nature and substance, different qualities can exist at the same time.

units.la: simul possunt esse qualitates. Eodem momen to terreni terrena,cœlestis cœlestis potest esse qualitas.In corpore nostro id fieri non potest. Quare necesse est ut per mutationem alio tem pore fit animale,alio fiat spirituale.Secunda ra tio est, quod sapientiæ Dei conuenientius est ac multis modis melius,ut quoniā mutationi destinatum est corpus nostrum, primū sit ani male,ac postea mutetur in spirituale, q; ut præ cedat spiritualis qualitas, quæ postea mutetur in animale.Indignū opus diuina maiestate est, spiritualem præstantiā mutare in animale humi litatem & infirmitatē. Ea demū spectabilis est mutationis ratio,qua deterius mutatur in me lius,non qua melius in deterius. Imo sic copa ratum erit corpus spirituale,ut quoniā immor tale erit & incorruptibile, in animale mutari non possit.Animale uero nihil habet,unde ne queat mutari in spirituale, cū sit natura sua mu tationi & alterationi obnoxium. Tertia ratio est ista:Ordo sęculorum,præsentis & futuri,se riem hac requirit, ut prius sit corpus nostrum animale,deinde fiat spirituale.Est enim sic cō ditū àDeo,ut utriusq; fieret sæculi particeps. At præsens hoc,in quo iam uiuimus,& ordine præcedit(quod nos attinet)& iuxta est terre num ac transitorium non cœleste, & sempiter nū.Futurū uero transitorium non est,sed sem piternum:nec terrenū,sed cœleste.Qouenit i gitur,ut in transitorio ac terreno corpus habe amus animale, in sempiterno uero ac cœlesti corpus accipiamus spirituale.Hasce ob causas non primum est spirituale,sed animale, dein de quod spirituale. Cum igitur cōsilio Dei o mnium sapientissimo sit cōstitutum, & simul utilissimū sit,ut primū animale sit corpus no strum,postea spirituale,imò diuersum fieri ne queat:cogitandum nobis est,q; sint inconsulta carnis nostræ uota, quib. ordinē hunc inuer sum iri uellemus,sic ut ea quæ futuri sunt secu li,& ad uerā felicitatē pertinēt, in hac uita con stitutis contingant,nascamurq; primum, non animales,sed spirituales,ne uidelicet subeun dę sint animalis hominis infirmitas, miserię et ærumnę,mortalitas & corruptio. Corrigenda sunt in nobis huiusmodi stulta uota, dicéduq; cum Apostolo, Non primum quod spirituale est, sed quod animale:deinde quod spirituale, ac feredum patienter, quicquid ad animalem hanc nostram uitam necessario pertinet.
units.tr: At the same moment the earthly can have earthly qualities and the heavenly heavenly qualities. This cannot happen in our body. Therefore it is necessary that by change it become animal at one time and become spiritual at another. (2) The second reason is that it is more fitting to the wisdom of God, and in many ways better, that since our body is destined for change, it should first be animal and afterwards be changed into the spiritual, rather than that the spiritual quality should come first and be changed afterwards into the animal. It would be an unworthy work for the divine majesty to change spiritual excellence into animal lowliness and weakness. The only praiseworthy kind of change is that by which the worse is changed into the better, not the better into the worse. Indeed the spiritual body will be so constituted that, since it will be immortal and incorruptible, it cannot be changed into the animal. But the animal has nothing in it by which it could not be changed into the spiritual, since by its nature it is subject to change and alteration. (3) The third reason is this: the order of the ages, present and future, requires this sequence, that our body should first be animal and then become spiritual. For it has been so ordained by God that it should share in each age. The present age, in which we now live, precedes in order (so far as we are concerned), and is near at hand, and is earthly and transitory, not heavenly and everlasting. But the future age is not transitory, but everlasting, and not earthly, but heavenly. It is fitting, therefore, that in the transitory and earthly age we should have an animal body, and in the everlasting and heavenly age we should receive a spiritual body. For these reasons the spiritual is not first, but the animal, then the spiritual. Since, then, it has been established by the counsel of God, most wise, and at the same time most useful, that our body should first be animal and afterwards spiritual, and indeed cannot become otherwise, we must consider how unwise are the desires of our flesh, by which we would wish this order reversed, so that the things belonging to the age to come and to true happiness should fall to us while we are in this life, and that we should be born first not animal but spiritual, so that, of course, the weakness, misery and distress, mortality and corruption of the animal man would not have to be undergone. Such foolish desires must be corrected in us, and we must say with the Apostle: The spiritual is not first, but the animal, then the spiritual; and we must bear patiently whatever necessarily belongs to this animal life of ours.

units.la: PRIMVS homo de terra terrenus, inquit, secundus homo ipse dominus de cœlo.]Con tinuat cœptā collationē Adę & Christi,tanquā duorum diuersæ conditionis capitū,ut in illis declaret quod dixit:Seminatur corpus anima le resurget corpus spirituale. Erat aūt nonihil obscurius,quod initio collationis huius dixe rat:Primus homo Adam factus est in animam uiuentē,extremus Adá in spiritū uiuificatem. Quare adiungit ista,quibus collationem hanc & absoluat & intelligibiliorem reddat.
units.tr: "The first man is of the earth, earthly; the second man is the Lord himself, from heaven." He continues the comparison begun between Adam and Christ as the two heads of different conditions, so that in them he may explain what he said: "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." Something he had said at the start of this comparison was rather obscure: "The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit." So he adds these words, by which he both completes the comparison and makes it clearer.

units.la: PRIMVS homo,inquit,de terra terrenus.] Vocat Adamum primum hominem terrenū, propter originem illius quę est de terra, quade A quod sit secundus homo, nouū quid humanō legere est, Gen. 2. Formauit Deus, inquit, homi-nem puluerē de terra. Et ca. 3. donec reuertaris in terram, de qua suptus es. Quia puluis es, & in puluerem reuerteris. Huc respiciens Apost. dicit: Primus homo de terra terrenus. Expri-mit illius & originē & cōditionē. Origo de ter-ra & cōditio terrena sibi inuicē correspōdent. Sic Io. 3. Qui de terra est, de terra est. i. terrenus est, & de terra. i. terrena loquitur. Terrenus igi-tur est primus homo Adā, & origine & cōditio-ne. Vt ē terra est, ita & in terra uiuit, terrenis a-litur, terrena sapit, terrenis afficitur, terrenis est pasionibus mutationibus & corruptioni-bus in corpore terreno obnoxius. Cū dicit eū in animam uiuentē esse factum, respicit ad con-ditionē animæ, quā inflauit illi Deus cōditor. & eam ob causam uocat eum animalem. Cum hic eum terrenum uocat, respicit ad originem corporis ē puluere terræ formati. Atq; ita tam in anima quàm in corpore illius inuenit, unde inter ipsum & Christum dominū discriminet.
units.tr: "The first man, he says, is of the earth, earthly." He calls Adam the first man earthly on account of his origin, which is from the earth. Scripture says this in Genesis 2: God formed man, dust of the earth. And in chapter 3: until you return to the earth from which you were taken, for you are dust and you will return to dust. Looking to this, the Apostle says: "The first man is of the earth, earthly." He expresses both his origin and his condition. Origin from the earth and earthly condition correspond to each other. So in John 3: "He who is of the earth is of the earth," that is, he is earthly and speaks of the earthly. The first man Adam, therefore, is earthly in both origin and condition. As he is of the earth, so he lives on the earth; he is nourished by earthly things, has earthly thoughts, is affected by earthly things, and in his earthly body is subject to earthly passions, changes and corruptions. When he says that Adam was made a living soul, he looks to the condition of the soul, which God the Creator breathed into him; and for this reason he calls him animal. When here he calls him earthly, he looks to the origin of the body, formed from the dust of the earth. So in both his soul and his body he finds grounds for distinguishing him from Christ the Lord.

units.la: SECVNDVS homo, inq;, ipse dominus de cœlo. ] Poterat dicere, Secūd⁹ homo Christus, uerū utitur hac periphrasi, ut alterā collationis parte priori cōformiter exprimat, & cœlū ter-ræ, cœlestē hominem terreno opponat, quo de clarat, quantū discriminis sit inter corpus ani-male, quali nunc circūdamur, & spirituale, qua li ad futurā uitā resurgemus. Suprà monui ali-ter habere lectionē uulgatā, uidelicet, secundus homo de cœlo cœlestis. Verum Græca habent, B ἐ κύ ρ ιο ς ὁ ἄ νθ ρ ω π ο ς, id est, dominus de cœlo. Suspi-cor tamen ἐ κύ ρ ι ο ς, corruptum esse per antiqua-rios, & ab Apostolo scriptum fuisse ὁ ἄ ν θ ρ ω π ο ς. Facile negligentia ἄ ν θ ρ ω π ο ς mutari potuit in ἐ κύ ρ ι ο ς. Et praeterea magis respondet praecedenti collationis parti, si legas, secundus homo de cœlo cœlestis. Sic quidem suspicamur, uerum non est tutum recedere à lectione Græca, nul-la causa necessario urgente.
units.tr: "The second man, he says, is the Lord himself, from heaven." He could have said, "The second man is Christ," but he uses this periphrasis so that he may express the second part of the comparison in agreement with the first, and set heaven against earth and the heavenly man against the earthly. By this he shows how great the difference is between the animal body with which we are now surrounded and the spiritual body with which we shall rise to the future life. I noted above that the Vulgate reading is different, namely "the second man from heaven, heavenly." But the Greek has ὁ κύριος ὁ ἄνθρωπος [ἐ κύ ρ ιο ς ὁ ἄ νθ ρ ω π ο ς], that is, "the Lord from heaven." Yet I suspect that ἐκύριος has been corrupted by copyists, and that the Apostle wrote ὁ ἄνθρωπος. Through carelessness ἄνθρωπος could easily have been changed into ἐκύριος. Moreover, it agrees better with the preceding part of the comparison if you read "the second man from heaven, heavenly." So indeed we suspect, but it is not safe to depart from the Greek reading without some compelling reason.

units.la: SECVNDVS homo, inquit. ] Quod Christū paulo antè Adā, & hic hominē uocat, fidem nostrā cōfirmat, qua uerū illū hominē, perinde atq; nos, ꝑ nobis factū esse credimus. Nec est, ut quisquam in eo philosophetur, quod uocat eum secundum hominem, quasi sentiat eum al-terius esse generis hominē, q̄ simus quotquot ab Adamo descendimus. Ex eodē quippe ge-neris nostri fonte originem carnis suæ ducit, ex quo uniuersum genus humanū descendit. Hoc uolebat Lucas, cum generatione illius ad Adamū usq; deduceret. Secundū eum hominē uocat, propter dispensationem redimendi ge-neris humani, ac restitutionem omnium, quæ per ipsum erat perficienda, & propter opus re-generationis nostræ, qua ut in Adamo uetus, ita in ipso noua creatura reddimur. Hanc ob causam rectè secundus & nouus homo uoca-tur, licet in humana nobiscum natura ueraci-ter communicet.
units.tr: "The second man, he says." That he calls Christ a man, a little before Adam and here, confirms our faith, by which we believe that this true man was made for us just as we were. Nor should anyone philosophize about the fact that he calls him the second man, as though he thought him to be a man of a different kind from all of us who descend from Adam. For he derives the origin of his flesh from the same source of our kind from which the whole human race descends. This is what Luke meant when he traced Christ's genealogy back to Adam. He calls him the second man on account of the plan for redeeming the human race and restoring all things, which was to be accomplished through him, and on account of the work of our regeneration, by which we are made a new creature in him just as we were old in Adam. For this reason he is rightly called the second and new man, although he truly shares our human nature.

units.la: IPSE dñs de cœlo, inquit. ] Tria de Christo prædicat, ad causam hanc facientia. Primū est
units.tr: "The Lord himself, from heaven, he says." He predicates three things of Christ that bear on this matter. The first is

units.la: quod sit secundus homo, nouū quid humanō generi post primum Adamum auferes. Dein, de qd' sit dñs, tertio quod sit de cœlo. Nō sim-pliciter dominȳ, seddominʳ de cœlo. Sūt aliàs domini multi, uerū unus est uerus ac cœlestis dominus, unigenitus ille Dei, cui pater omnē potestatē dedit in cœlo & in terra. Neq; simpli citer, de cœlo, sed ipse dominus, inq̄t, de cœlo. De cœlo ac cœlestes sunt & angeli, uerum non sunt domini de cœlo, sed administratorij spiri-tus. Neq; sunt humanæ naturæ nobiscū partici-pes, ideoq̄ nequeunt nos ex terrenis reddere cœlestes. Homines quidē sunt Adā, patriar-chę & ꝑphetę, at neq; sunt de cœlo, sed de ter-ra perinde atq; Adam, sicuti ipse Baptista de se prædicare non dubitat. Ioā. 3. neq; sunt domini, sed serui. Quare nec per illos ad cœlestē corpo-rum nostrorum qualitatem & gloriam perue-nire possumus. Vnus igitur est Christus, uerus nobiscum homo, uerus omnium dominus, & de cœlo cœlestis. In homine cōmunicatio est naturæ nostræ, quę non est in angelis. In domi-no, potestas est & authoritas omniū, per quam in eo quod de cœlo est, cœlestis est conditio & gloria, ad quam terrenam nostram originē, na-turam & conditionem in resurrectione sua in seipso transtulit: in nobis uero ingenerali mor-tuorū resurrectiōe, quod in se cœpit absoluet.
units.tr: that he is the second man, something new given to the human race after the first Adam. Next, that he is Lord; third, that he is from heaven. Not simply "lord," but "the Lord from heaven." There are many lords elsewhere, but there is one true and heavenly Lord, that only-begotten Son of God to whom the Father gave all power in heaven and on earth. And not simply "from heaven," but "the Lord himself, he says, from heaven." Angels too are from heaven and heavenly, but they are not lords from heaven; they are ministering spirits. Nor do they share our human nature, and so they cannot make us heavenly out of earthly things. Adam, the patriarchs and the prophets were indeed men, but they are not from heaven; they are from the earth just as Adam was, as John the Baptist himself does not hesitate to say of himself (John 3), and they are not lords but servants. Hence we cannot, through them, attain to the heavenly quality and glory of our bodies. Christ is therefore one, a true man with us, a true Lord of all, and heavenly from heaven. In the man there is a sharing of our nature, which is not in the angels. In the Lord there is power and authority over all, by which, in that which is from heaven, he has a heavenly condition and glory. By his resurrection he transferred to himself, in himself, our earthly origin, nature and condition, to which he will bring to completion in us at the general resurrection of the dead what he has begun in himself.

units.la: Non est autem ut locum hic quærat, qui car-nem Christi cœlitus allatam, non ex uirgine ac femine Abrahę desumptam dogmatizant. Cū Apost. Christum hic dominum de cœlo uocat, non de origine carnis, sed de gloria ac prærō-gatiua cœlesti loquitur, quam habet unigeni-tus Dei, à patre in hunc mundum missus. Si car-nis origo quæritur, notatur illa in eo quod A-dam & homo uocatur: si excellentia & prærō-gatiua unigeniti Dei, exprimitur illa in eo qd' dominus de cœlo uocatur. Tertullianus in li-bro de resurrectione carnis, in hunc locum sic annotat: Primus homo de terra choicus, id est limatius, hoc est Adā. Secūdus homo de cœlo, id est sermo Dei. i. Christus, nō aliter tamen ho-mo licet de cœlo, nisi quia & ipse caro atq; ani-ma, quod homo quod Adam. Itē: At substantia nullo modo separātur choici & cœlestes semel ab Apostolo homines dicti. Hæc ille. Cęci non uident, quid agat Apost. ideoq; uerba illius in eum sensum detorquent, qui propósito illius incommodat. Etenim quæ nobis spes carnis nostræ ē mortuis excitandæ, & in cœlestē glo-riam transmutandæ reliqua erit, si Christi car-nem ē communione nostræ naturæ excluseri-mus? Non uidet, quo consilio Christum uocet extremum Adamum, & secundum hominem. Nec animaduertunt tam nō negari ueritatem carnis Christi, ē carne Adæ & Abrahæ desum-ptę, per id quod dominus de cœlo prædicatur, quàm non negatur cœlestis animæ in Adamo origo, per id quod de terra terrenus uocatur. Quomodo Adam de terra? Non anima, sed cor-pore. Animæ origo non est de terra, sed de cœ-lo. Et tamen de terra ac terrenus uocatur.
units.tr: Yet there is no need to seek here a place for those who teach that the flesh of Christ was brought down from heaven and not taken from the Virgin and the seed of Abraham. When the Apostle calls Christ here "the Lord from heaven," he is not speaking of the origin of his flesh, but of the heavenly glory and prerogative which the only-begotten Son of God has, sent by the Father into this world. If the origin of the flesh is in question, it is indicated by the word "man," which he is called, Adam; if the excellence and prerogative of the only-begotten Son of God is in question, it is expressed by the fact that he is called "the Lord from heaven." Tertullian, in his book on the resurrection of the flesh, comments on this passage as follows: "The first man is of the earth, earthly, that is, made of clay, that is, Adam. The second man is from heaven, that is, the Word of God, that is, Christ; yet he is a man in no other way than that, though from heaven, he too is flesh and soul, just as man is, just as Adam is." Again: "But substance is in no way separated from the earthly and the heavenly, once the Apostle has called them men." So far Tertullian. Blind men do not see what the Apostle is doing, and so they twist his words into a sense that suits their own purpose. For what hope of our flesh being raised from the dead and transformed into heavenly glory will remain, if we exclude Christ's flesh from communion with our nature? They do not see for what purpose he calls Christ the last Adam and the second man. Nor do they notice that the truth of Christ's flesh, taken from the flesh of Adam and Abraham, is no more denied by the fact that he is proclaimed as the Lord from heaven than the heavenly origin of the soul in Adam is denied by the fact that he is called earthly, of the earth. How is Adam "of the earth"? Not in his soul, but in his body. The origin of the soul is not from the earth but from heaven. Yet he is called of the earth and earthly.

units.la: Distingue inter animam & corpus, ne res diuersas confundas. Quomodo Christus de cœlo? Non carne corporis sed diuinitate & conditione unigeniti Dei. Origo carnis illius non è cœlo, sed ex Adamo, unde est caro uniuersi generis humani. Sëtiamus igitur, sic esse Christũ dñm de cœlo, ut simul sit homo de terra: & sic esse hominē de terra ut simul sit dñs de cœlo.
units.tr: Distinguish between soul and body, so that you do not confuse different things. How is Christ from heaven? Not in the flesh of his body, but in the divinity and condition of the only-begotten God. The origin of that flesh is not from heaven but from Adam, from whom is the flesh of the whole human race. Let us therefore understand that Christ the Lord is from heaven in such a way that he is at the same time man from earth, and that man is from earth in such a way that at the same time he is the Lord from heaven.

units.la: QVALIS terrenus ille, tales & hi qui terre ni sunt: & qualis ille cœlestis, tales & hi qui cœ lestes erunt. ] Hactenus duos principales homines Adamum & Christum proposuit, tanq; duo exemplaria animalis: unū spiritualis, corporis alterū: præsentis uitæ unum, futuræ alte rū. Iam aptat utrunq; ad propositū, ne quis dicat, quid ad nos cōditio Christi domini de cœlo? Id nanq; in quæstionem uenire poterat. De Adami posteris, quod illi respondeant origini unde descendunt, nulla erat quæstio. Ipsa nâq; uniuersalis in omnibus experientia omne quę stionem excludit. Facit tamen & primæ huius partis, quæ Adamum cōcernit, mentione, quo integra sit collatio, & facilis paretur ad fidem posterioris inductio. Qualis terrenus ille, inqt, id est Adam primus homo, de terra terrenus, tales & hi qui terreni sunt: hoc est, omnes ab illo descēdentes. Qualis autem terrenus ille Adam? Suprà hoc est memoratum. Terrenus erat & origine & conditione, tā corporis quàm uitæ. E terra factus, terrena sapiebat, in terra uiuebat, terrenis afficiebatur, terrenis erat mutationibus & corruptionib. obnoxius. Tales sunt & hi qui terreni sunt. Qui sunt autem terreni? An soli reprobi? Nequaquam, sed mortales omnes, etiâ pij, donec in carne hac uiuunt. Circumferunt enim pij quoq; terrestrem domum, corpus uidelicet terrenū: infirmū, mortale & corruptibile, suntq; necessitatib. illius & molestijs obnoxij, quamuis animo conuersentur in cœlis, ubi Christus est ad dexterā patris. Terrenam illis originem & terrenæ uitæ conditionem non adimit innouatio mētis, regeneratio è supernis, & studium pietatis. Regeneratione quidem de cœlo sunt, & ex Deo spirituales & cœlestes, quod nouum in illis & internū hominem attinet, carnis uero origine, & externi corporis cōditione, de terra sunt, & terreni, perinde atq; reprobi esuriunt, sitiunt, edunt, bibunt, dormiunt, uestiuntur, fatigan tur, morbis corripiuntur: moriuntur, & corrū puntur, nec alieni sunt à reliquis terrenę huius uitæ circūstantijs ac necessitatibus. Laborant, uxores ducunt, prolem gignunt & alunt, legi bus & magistratibus subbūtur, &c. Sic sunt ter reni & ipsi, qualis fuit Adam terrenus.
units.tr: "As is the earthly man, so also are those who are earthly; and as is the heavenly man, so also are those who will be heavenly." Up to this point the Apostle has set forth two principal men, Adam and Christ, as two patterns of the living being: one of the natural body, the other of the spiritual; one of the present life, the other of the future. Now he applies both to his purpose, lest someone say, "What does the condition of Christ the Lord from heaven have to do with us?" For that could indeed have been called in question. About the posterity of Adam, that they correspond to the origin from which they descend, there was no question at all, since universal experience in all men rules out every doubt. Yet he does mention the first part, which concerns Adam, so that the comparison may be complete and the induction to the second part may be easily accepted. "As the earthly man was," he says, that is, Adam the first man, earthly from the earth, "so also are those who are earthly," that is, all who descend from him. But what sort of earthly man was Adam? This has been noted above. He was earthly both in origin and in condition, as much in body as in life. Made from the earth, he savoured of earthly things, lived on the earth, was affected by earthly things, and was subject to earthly changes and corruptions. Such also are those who are earthly. But who are the earthly? Are they only the reprobate? By no means; all mortals are, even the godly, for as long as they live in this flesh. For the godly too carry about an earthly house, that is, an earthly body: weak, mortal and corruptible, and subject to its needs and troubles, although in spirit they live in the heavens, where Christ is at the right hand of the Father. The renewal of the mind, regeneration from above, and the pursuit of godliness do not take away from them their earthly origin and the earthly condition of their life. By regeneration they are indeed from heaven, and spiritual and heavenly from God, as far as the new and inner man is concerned; but as to the origin of the flesh and the condition of the outward body, they are from the earth and earthly, just as the reprobate are. They hunger, thirst, eat, drink, sleep, are clothed, grow weary, are struck down by diseases, die and decay; nor are they strangers to the other circumstances and necessities of this earthly life. They labour, take wives, beget and rear children, are subject to laws and magistrates, and so on. Thus they too are earthly, just as Adam was earthly.

units.la: Reprobi uero duplici nomine terreni sunt. Terreni sunt eo modo quo pij carne uidelicet, cùm quod originem, tum quod conditionem illius attinet. Terreni sunt & mente & uniuer sæ uitæ suæ studio. Nonnisi terrena sapiunt, ter renis tantum delectantur & student, uoluptatibus immerguntur, uentri seruiunt: uel certe, si quo pacto crassas illas carnis uoluptates con temnunt, terrenæ tamen sunt gloriæ mācipia. Reperis eiusmodi terrenos Apost. inter Chri stianos quoque, deq́ue illis flens conqueritur, Philip.3.dicens: Multi ambulant, de quibus sæ pe dicebam uobis, nunc autem & slens dico, ut inimici crucis Christi quorum finis interitus, quorum deus uenter est, & gloria in confusio ne ipsorum, qui terrena sapiūt. Nostra aūt con uersatio in cœlis est, &c. Verum de hoc terre norum hominum genere, quo pij terreni non sunt, in prsenti no loquitur Apostolus, sed de eo tantū, quod commune est mortalibus om nibus, in carne hac mortali uiuentibus. Quare cum dicit: Qualis terrenus ille, tales & hi qui terreni sunt, non discriminat inter præsentis seculi homines, sed inter præsentem corporū nostrorum, & eam quæ post resurrectionem su tura est qualitatem: & hanc in Adamo, illam in Christo declarat. Non confert inter se præsen tis uitæ homines, quatenus alij terreni sunt, a lij spirituales ac cœlestes: sed confert eos om nes pios & impios, quatenus terreni sunt ex terreno cum omnibus qui in futura uita omni terrena conditione exuti corpus habebunt spi rituale & cœleste.
units.tr: The reprobate, however, are earthly in a twofold sense. They are earthly in the same way as the godly, that is, in their flesh, both as to its origin and as to its condition. They are also earthly in mind and in the whole pursuit of their life. They savour of nothing but earthly things, delight and labour only in earthly things, are sunk in pleasures, and serve the belly; or at least, if in some way they despise the coarse pleasures of the flesh, they are still slaves of earthly glory. You find such earthly men even among Christians, and the Apostle weeps and laments over them, saying in Philippians 3: "Many walk, of whom I have often told you, and now I tell you even weeping, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction, whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who savour of earthly things. But our conversation is in heaven," and so on. Yet the Apostle is not speaking here of this kind of earthly man, in which the godly are not earthly, but only of that which is common to all mortals who live in this mortal flesh. Therefore when he says, "As the earthly man was, so also are those who are earthly," he does not distinguish between men of the present age, some earthly and others spiritual and heavenly; rather, he sets the godly and the ungodly alike together, as far as they are earthly, along with the earthly state of our bodies at present, and the quality that will belong to them after the resurrection. He shows this quality in Adam, and that in Christ. He does not compare men of the present life with one another, as if some were earthly and others spiritual and heavenly; he compares all of them, godly and ungodly, insofar as they are earthly, with the earthly, and with all those who in the future life, stripped of every earthly condition, will have a spiritual and heavenly body.

units.la: E T qualis ille cœlestis, inquit, tales & hi qui cœlestes erunt. ] In Græco simpliciter est: tales & cœlestes. Quoniam uero nondum tales su mus, sed in futuro demū erimus, existimo con uenientius esse, ut legamus, tales & hi qui cœ lestes erūt: quàm, tales & hi qui cœlestes sunt.
units.tr: "And as is the heavenly man, so also are those who are heavenly," he says. In the Greek it simply reads, "such also are the heavenly." But since we are not yet such, and will be only in the future, I think it is more fitting to read, "such also are those who will be heavenly," rather than "such also are those who are heavenly."

units.la: Nam mox dicturus est: quemadmodum ge stauimus imaginem terreni, gestabimus & ima ginem cœlestis.
units.tr: For he is about to say shortly: "just as we have borne the image of the earthly, so we shall also bear the image of the heavenly."

units.la: QVALIS ille cœlestis, inquit. ] Christus ui delicet. Loquitur autē de illo, non quatenus ui xit in carne nostra, infirma & mortali, edit, bi bit, esurijt, sitijt, fatigatus est, dormiuit, cõtrista tus fleuit, & tandē mortis dolores unà cū mor te expertus est, neq; quatenus uerbum est pa tris ac uerus Deus. ( Neq; enim erimus hacte nus illi similes) sed quatenus tertia die glorio sus, & corpore clarificato ac cœlesti surrexit, in cœlos ascendit, inq; cœlestibus ad sine usque mundi manet. Tales uidelicet erimus, & nos post resurrectionem, nō iam amplius terreni, sed cœlestes. Corpus nostrū uerum quidē erit & proprium nostrū corpus, quemadmodum & supra monuimus, iuxtà tamen liberum erit & repurgatum ab omni terrena sece: purum, cla rum, firmum, immortale & incorruptibile, & reliquis cœlestibus dotibus ornatum, & hacte nus non terrenum, sed cœleste.
units.tr: "As is the heavenly man," he says: that is, Christ. He speaks of him not insofar as he lived in our flesh, weak and mortal, ate, drank, hungered, thirsted, grew weary, slept, was sorrowful and wept, and at last experienced the pains of death together with death itself; nor insofar as he is the Word of the Father and true God. (For we shall not be like him in these respects until now.) Rather, he speaks of him insofar as on the third day he rose glorious, with a glorified and heavenly body, ascended into heaven, and remains in heavenly things until the end of the world. Such we too shall be after the resurrection, no longer earthly but heavenly. Our body will indeed be true and our own body, just as we have said above; yet it will be free and purged of all earthly dregs: pure, bright, strong, immortal and incorruptible, adorned with the other heavenly gifts, and not earthly up to now, but heavenly.

units.la: Obseruet uero diligens lector, q̃ inconside rantes sint, qui quoniâ Apostolus Christū hic uocat dominum de cœlo & cœleste, colligunt ex eo, carnè illius nõ esse ex uirgine matre de sumptam, sed cœlitus delatā. Si recte colligūt, ergo nec nostra caro de terra est, sed originem habet de cœlo. Sic enim erimus cœlestes, què admodum dominus ipse cœlestis existit. Si cœ lestem esse post resurrectionem terrenam car nis originem tollit in Christo, tollit & in illis qui &c. qui & ipsi cœlestes erunt, ac cœlesti corpore præditi. Si uero in illis non tollit, quę necessitas est, ut tollat in Christo? An terrenū nostrū corpus per resurrectionis gloriam cœleste fieri potest, ut iam nō amplius terreni simus, sed cœlestes: Christi uero non potest, nisi sit initio cœlitus delatum?
units.tr: Let the diligent reader observe how thoughtless those are who, because the Apostle here calls Christ the Lord from heaven and heavenly, conclude from this that his flesh was not taken from the Virgin Mother, but was brought down from heaven. If they conclude rightly, then our flesh too is not from the earth, but has its origin from heaven. For we shall be heavenly in the same way as the Lord himself is heavenly. If the earthly origin of the flesh is removed in Christ, because after the resurrection he is heavenly, it is removed also in those who, being heavenly, will themselves be endowed with a heavenly body. But if it is not removed in them, what necessity is there that it be removed in Christ? Can our earthly body become heavenly through the glory of the resurrection, so that we are no longer earthly but heavenly; and yet Christ's body cannot become heavenly unless it was brought down from heaven at the beginning?

units.la: ET quemadmodum gestauimus imaginē terreni, gestabimus & imaginem cœlestis.] Ni hil aliud dicit à præcedenti.
