Idem est gestare imaginem terreni, quod esse quali est terrenus: & gestare imaginem cœlestis, quod esse qualis est cœlestis, ne quid in dictione imaginis philosophandum putet. In Græco εἰκόνα, quæ uox usurpata est ab Apostolo pro ὁμοιότητα. Imago aliàs rei non præsentis repræsentatio est, qui sensus in prima similitudinis huius parte constat. Etenim quotquot ex Adamo sumus, terre ni hominis, iam olim non præsentis imaginem gestamus, & exprimimus: uerum post resurrectionē cœlestis hominis, Christi uidelicet, nō ita absentis, sed prorsus præsentis, non imaginem, sed similitudinē gestabimus. Quare uox φορέσωμεν in posteriore parte, non ita locum habet, sicut in priore, nisi pro similitudine accipiatur, ut idem sit gestare imaginem cœlestis aut terreni, qd' similem esse cœlesti uel terreno.
units.tr: "And as we have borne the image of the earthly, so we shall also bear the image of the heavenly." He says nothing other than what precedes. To bear the image of the earthly is the same as to be such as the earthly is; and to bear the image of the heavenly is to be such as the heavenly is. Let no one think there is some philosophy to be made of the word "image." In the Greek it is εἰκόνα [eikona], a word which the Apostle uses in place of ὁμοιότητα [homoiotēta], likeness. An image is generally a representation of a thing not present, a meaning which lies in the first part of the comparison. For all of us who are from Adam, earthly men, have long borne and expressed the image of one who is not present. But after the resurrection, we shall bear not an image but a likeness of the heavenly man, Christ, who is not absent but wholly present. Therefore the verb φορέσωμεν [phoresōmen], "we shall bear," in the latter part does not fit as it does in the former, unless it is taken to mean likeness, so that to bear the image of the heavenly or of the earthly means the same as to be like the heavenly or the earthly.

units.la: QVEMADMODVM gestauimus, inquit.] Quid est, inquies, quod in præterito dicit, Gestauimus, cū etiamnū gestemus terreni hominis imaginem, simusq; gestaturi illam ad eum usq; diem, quo ex mortuis resurgemus. Neq; enim ab illa liberabimur, nisi per eam quæ erit cœlestis hominis Christi. Ná & ipsa corruptio corpourm nostrorum ad imaginē terreni hominis pertinet, quæ durabit usq; ad tempus resurrectionis, quo incorruptibiles reddemur. Respondeo. Si sententiam hanc sic ordinaueris: Gestabimus olim ubi resurrexerimus, cœlestis hominis imaginem, quemadmodum antea gestauimus imaginem terreni, nihil erit in commodi. Sap. 5. sic legimus: Tunc stabunt iusti in magna constantia aduersus eos, qui se angustiauerunt. Atqui etiamnum angustiantur iusti à reprobis. Verum in fine mundi locū habebit præteritum hoc uerbū, angustiauerunt. Tum enim non amplius angustiabūtur. Sic est cogitatio nostra extendenda ad diem resurrectionis, in quo non poterit dici, gestamus: sed gestauimus imaginem terreni hominis. Quādo cœlestes erimus, qualis & cœlestis dominus nosterde cœlo: tunc quemadmodum antea gestauimus imaginem terreni hominis, gestabimus & imaginem cœlestis.
units.tr: "As we have borne," he says. You may ask why he speaks in the past tense, "we have borne," when we still bear the image of the earthly man and will go on bearing it until that day when we rise from the dead. For we shall not be freed from it except through the image of the heavenly man, Christ. Indeed, the corruption of our bodies also belongs to the image of the earthly man, and it will last until the time of the resurrection, when we shall be made incorruptible. I answer: if you arrange the sentence thus, "We shall bear the image of the heavenly man once we have risen, just as we formerly bore the image of the earthly man," nothing is gained. We read in Wisdom 5: "Then the righteous will stand in great confidence against those who have afflicted them." Yet the righteous are still afflicted by the reprobate. But the past tense "have afflicted" will apply at the end of the world, for then they will no longer be afflicted. So our thought must be extended to the day of resurrection, on which it cannot be said, "we bear," but "we have borne the image of the earthly man." When we shall be heavenly, as the heavenly Lord himself is from heaven, then, just as we formerly bore the image of the earthly man, we shall bear the image of the heavenly one as well.

units.la: GESTABIMVS & imaginem cœlestis, inquit.] Vulgata lectio habet per modum hortādi, portemus. Et Chrysostomus legit φερέσωμεν, id est, portemus. Verum cum Græca exempla ria habeant φερέσωμεν in futuro, portabimus, & non φερέσωμεν portemus, sitq; præter scopum Apostoli, loqui hic per adhortationem, ubi de futura resurrectione loquēs adhuc in eo est, ut ad propositam quæstionē, quali corpore resur recturi sint mortui, respondeat, doceatq; quā sit diuersa futura in resurrectione corporum qualitas ab ea quā habemus in hac uita: existimo lectionem hanc, portemus imaginem cœlestis cum expositione Chrysost. sicut mala fecimus, sic bona faciamus, alienam esse à mente Apostoli. Non enim loquitur hic de innoua tione mentis nostræ, qua ad imaginem eius qui creauit ipsum nouo homo in nobis formatur, Coloss. 3. sed de qualitate corporis nostri, qua in hac uita terreni Adæ imaginem portamus: in futura uero cœlestis, Christi uidelicet, portabimus.
units.tr: "We shall bear also the image of the heavenly man," he says. The Vulgate reading has the hortatory form, "let us bear." Chrysostom too reads "let us bear" [φερέσωμεν]. But since the Greek copies have, in the future, "we shall bear" [φορέσομεν], and not "let us bear" [φερέσωμεν], and since it is beside the Apostle's purpose to speak here by way of exhortation, when he is still discussing the future resurrection and answering the question with what kind of body the dead will rise, and teaching how different the quality of the bodies in the future resurrection will be from the one we have in this life, I hold that this reading, "let us bear the image of the heavenly man," together with Chrysostom's explanation, "as we have done evil, so let us do good," is foreign to the mind of the Apostle. For he is not speaking here of the renewal of our mind, by which the new man is formed in us according to the image of him who created him (Col. 3), but of the quality of our body. In this life we bear the image of the earthly Adam, but in the future life we shall bear that of the heavenly one, namely Christ.

units.la: Sumus diuersarū imaginum capaces, secundum diuersitatem duorum nostrorū principū & capitum, unius à quo carnis origine descendimus, alterius ad cuius imaginem reformamur. Carne terreni Adæ, spiritu uero eiusdem peccatoris imaginem gestamus. Loquor autē de spiritu nodum regenerato. Spiritu regenerato, uel si mauis innouato, Christi innocentis ac iusti, in hac uita portamus imaginem, quotquot in illum ueraciter credimus, corpore uero eiusdem cœlestis ac glorificati imaginem in futura uita portabimus. Sic quadruplices imagines inuenio, quarum primam communiter portamus omnes: secundam non portare, sed pgratiam regenerationis abijcere debemus, tertiam quotidie magis ac magis assumere iubemur, postremam per resurrectionem corporū nostrorū acquiremus, & in futura uita in sempiternū portabimus. De prima & postrema loquitur hic Apostolus, nō de secunda ac tertia. Prima & secunda abolentur, tertia & quartaim Christo perfectæ sunt, in nobis uero mox à resurrectione perficientur.
units.tr: We are capable of different images, according to the difference between our two principles and heads: one, from whom we descend by the origin of the flesh, and the other, to whose image we are reformed. In the flesh we bear the image of the earthly Adam, and in the spirit the image of the same sinner. But I speak of the spirit of the regenerate man. In this life we bear, by the regenerate, or if you prefer, renewed spirit, the image of Christ, innocent and just, as many as truly believe in him; and in the future life we shall bear in our body the image of that same heavenly and glorified one. Thus I find four kinds of images. We all commonly bear the first. The second we ought not to bear but to cast off, namely the grace of regeneration. The third we are commanded to take on more and more each day. The fourth we shall acquire through the resurrection of our bodies, and shall bear forever in the future life. The Apostle speaks here of the first and the last, not of the second and third. The first and second are abolished; the third and fourth are perfected in Christ, but in us they will be perfected immediately after the resurrection.

units.la: Hoc eutem dico fratres, quod caro ac sanguis regni Dei hæreditatem consequi nō possunt: neq; corruptio incorruptibilitatis hæreditatem accipit.
units.tr: But this I say, brethren: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, and corruption does not inherit incorruption.

units.la: Ne aberremus à scopo Apostoli, curandum est ut in sensu simplici constanter maneamus. Exponunt nonnulli ad hunc modum.
units.tr: Lest we stray from the Apostle's purpose, we must take care to remain constantly in the plain sense. Some explain it in the following way.

units.la: 1 Caro & sanguis. i. animalis homo cum omni sua sapientia, regni Dei hæreditatem consequi. i. intelligere & cognoscere non possunt. Quare cauete, ne audiatis pseudapostolos carnis resurrectionem negantes. Sunt homines carnales, non possunt ea quæ Dei sunt intelligere. Et huc citant illud Christi, Matth. 16. Caro & sanguis non reuelauit tibi. Et illud supra cap. 2. Animalis homo non percipit ea quę sūt spiritus Dei. Verum aliud est non posse κληρονομῆσαι, i. hæreditario possidere, & aliud non posse intelligere regnum Dei. De hæreditaria acquisitione ac possessione, non de intellectu regni Dei loquitur Apostolus.
units.tr: (1) "Flesh and blood," that is, the natural man with all his wisdom, cannot obtain [κληρονομῆσαι] the inheritance of the kingdom of God, that is, cannot understand and know it. Therefore beware of hearing the false apostles who deny the resurrection of the flesh. They are carnal men and cannot understand the things of God. And they cite here that saying of Christ, "Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you" (Matt. 16), and that above in chapter 2, "The natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God." But it is one thing not to be able to inherit, that is, to possess by inheritance, and another not to be able to understand the kingdom of God. The Apostle is speaking of hereditary acquisition and possession, not of the understanding of the kingdom of God.

units.la: 2 Alij per carnem & sanguinem intelligūt corpus peccati, ueneno peccati infectū & uitiarū, sceleratā peccatorū ac uitiorū coeuersatione, & p regnū Dei futuræ uitæ felicitate ut sit sensus: Caro & sanguis, id est homines dediti uitijs delicijs,regnū Dei possideri non possunt, quia A ad illud nō intrabūt. Vterq; sensus nihil habet in se falsi,uerū neuter facit ad Apost. ,ppositū.
units.tr: (2) Others understand by flesh and blood the body of sin, infected with the poison of sin and of vices, and by the wicked association of sins and vices; and by the kingdom of God, the happiness of the future life. So the sense is: flesh and blood, that is, men given over to vices and pleasures, cannot possess the kingdom of God, because they will not enter into it. Both interpretations contain nothing false in themselves, but neither bears on the Apostle's purpose.

units.la: 3 Alij non modo abludunt à scopo Apostoli, sed & sensum prorsus cōtrariū & falsum adfe- runt. Colligunt enim,Si caro & sanguis regnū Dei posidere nō possunt, ergo spiritualis erit resurrectio,qua nō resurget caro nostra,sedspi ritus. 1 Quicquid enim regnum Dei posi- dere non potest,non resurget. 2 Caro regnū Dei nō possidebit. 3 Ergo caro nō resurget. Quorsum enim,inquiunt,resurget caro,regnū Dei possidere non ualens? Referunt hæc uer- ba ad substantiam carnis, quæ ad qualitatem illius pertinent,non ad substantiam.
units.tr: (3) Others not only stray from the Apostle's purpose but also bring forward a sense entirely contrary and false. For they infer: If flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, then the resurrection will be spiritual, and our flesh will not rise, but only the spirit. (1) For whatever cannot possess the kingdom of God will not rise. (2) The flesh will not possess the kingdom of God. (3) Therefore the flesh will not rise. For why, they say, will the flesh rise if it is unable to possess the kingdom of God? They apply these words to the substance of the flesh, when they pertain to its quality, not to its substance.

units.la: Verum relictis illis partim impertinētibus, partim falsis expositionib. germanā ac simpli- cem retineamus,quę sic habet: Dixit gestatu- ros nos imaginē cœlestis hominis Christi,quē admodū gestauimus imaginē terreni Adę: di- xit fore cœlestes, qualis est cœlestis dns de cœ lo:seminari corpus animale,resurrecturū cor- pus spirituale. Iā ratione reddit quare alia futu ra sit corporis nostri qualitas, q nūc sit, cœle- stis uidelicet &spiritualis. Sic dicit: Hoc aūt di co fratres,qd scilicet futuri sum⁹ cœlestes,cœ lesti dño similes. Quare ... i.quia, caro & san- guis regnū Dei hereditario possidere nō pos- sunt. Hoc est,quia impossibile est,ut in tali cor pore quale nūc habemus,regnū Dei, statū ui- delicet & felicitatē regni Dei cœlestē ac spiri- tualē possideamus. Nō cōueniet corp⁹ morta le,infirmū,mutabile,& corruptibile, carne ac sanguine corruptibili cōstás, ei statui qui pror sus est cœlestis,spiritualis,ac sēpiternus. Qua- re necesse est,ut caro &sanguis mutētur in aliā, non substantiā,sed qualitatē. In nouissimo die furreturus sum,inquit Iob,de terra,&rursum circūdabor pelle mea, & in carne mea uidebo Deū:ca.19. Intellige,nō qualis nūc est, sed qua lis est p resurrectione futura. Atq; ita cōueniet utriq; sententiæ Iob & Apost. Caro & sanguis regnū Dei non possidebunt, & tñ pelle nostra rursum circundabimur,& in carne nostraDeū seruatore nostrū uidebimus. Christus carnē & ossa,quę post resurrectione discipulis in ar- gumentū uerę resurrectiōis palpāda dedit, cœ lo secū intulit,& tñ non modo possidet regnū Dei,sed & à dextris patris sedēs regnat. Haud igitur caro nostra regno Dei excluditur per id qd Apostolus dicit: Caro & sanguis regnum Dei non possidebunt,sed terrena illius quali- tas in cœlestem mutanda significatur.
units.tr: But setting aside those explanations, partly irrelevant and partly false, let us keep the genuine and simple one, which runs thus. He has said that we shall bear the image of the heavenly man, Christ, just as we have borne the image of the earthly Adam. He has said that we shall be heavenly, such as the heavenly Lord is from heaven; that the animal body is sown and that a spiritual body will rise. Now he gives the reason why the quality of our body will be different in the future from what it is now, namely heavenly and spiritual. He says: "But this I say, brethren," namely that we shall be heavenly, like the heavenly Lord. "Therefore..." that is, because "flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God by inheritance." That is, it is impossible that we should possess the kingdom of God, that is, the heavenly and spiritual state and happiness of the kingdom of God, in such a body as we now have. A mortal, weak, mutable and corruptible body, consisting of corruptible flesh and blood, would not suit that state, which is wholly heavenly, spiritual and eternal. Therefore it is necessary that flesh and blood be changed into another, not in substance but in quality. "In the last day I shall rise from the earth," says Job, "and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God" (ch. 19). Understand this not as it is now, but as it will be after the future resurrection. And so the saying of Job and that of the Apostle agree: "Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God," and yet "we shall again be clothed with our skin, and in our flesh we shall see God our Saviour." Christ carried into heaven with him the flesh and bones that he gave to his disciples to be touched as proof of the true resurrection; and yet he not only possesses the kingdom of God, but also reigns seated at the right hand of the Father. Therefore our flesh is not excluded from the kingdom of God by what the Apostle says, "Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God," but what is signified is that its earthly quality is to be changed into a heavenly one.

units.la: NEQVE corruptio,inquit,incorruptibili- tatis hæreditatē accipit.]Adhuc clarius expri- mit qd dixit. Exponit enim,quare caro & san guis regnū Dei posidere nō possint, dū carni ac sanguini corruptionē,regno Dei uero inco ruptibilitatem assignat.Significat fieri nō pos se,ut caro nostra,donec corruptioni est obno xia hæreditatē regniDei cōsequatur,in quo lo cū corruptio habere nō potest,sed necesse est, ut corruptibile mutetur in incorruptibile. Ad
units.tr: "Nor does corruption," he says, "inherit incorruption." He expresses what he said even more clearly. For he explains why flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, while assigning corruption to flesh and blood and incorruption to the kingdom of God. He means that it cannot happen that our flesh, as long as it is subject to corruption, should inherit the kingdom of God, in which corruption cannot have any place; rather, what is corruptible must be changed into what is incorruptible. To

units.la: Iob. ca.19.
units.tr: Job 19.

units.la: modum caute loquitur. Nō dicit,Neq; corru- ptibile incorruptibilitatis hæreditate accipit. Futurum.n.est, ut corpus nostrum corruptibi le hæreditate illam incorruptibilitatis accipi- at,sic tamen ut incorruptibile reddatur. Ipsa uero corruptio nihil illic loci habere poterit, sed prorsus excludetur.Rectę ergo dicit: neq; corruptio incorruptibilitatis hæreditatem ac cipit.Verū infrà exprimit hoc clarius. 1 Si per carnē ac sanguinē sensus animalis homi- nis intelligendus esset, dicendum potius suis- set Apostolo neq; stultitia sapiētię Dei profua ditatem capit,quàm, neq; corruptio incorru- ptibilitatis hæreditatem accipit. 2 Sic de ea quoq; expositione sentimus, qua per carnē & sanguinē alij malicia & peccatū carnis ac san- guinis intelligunt.Ei sensui conuenientius di xisset Apostolus:Neq; iniusticia iusticiæ,q ne q; corruptio incorruptibilitatis hæreditatem accipit. 3 Et illi quoque qui sentētia hac A- postoli,caro ac sanguis regnum Dei non pos- sidebunt,ad negandam carnis nostræ resurre- ctioné abutuntur:de errore suo satis poterant particulę huius adiectione admoneri,ut intel ligeretur,à resurrectione futura,non substantiā, sed corruptionem carnis nostræ excludi.
units.tr: speaks cautiously here. He does not say, "Neither the corruptible inherits incorruptibility," but rather, "Corruption does not inherit incorruptibility." For our body will indeed be corruptible when it receives that inheritance of incorruptibility, but it will be rendered incorruptible. Corruption itself will have no place there but will be utterly excluded. So he rightly says, "Neither does corruption inherit incorruptibility." Yet below he expresses this more clearly. (1) If "flesh and blood" were to be understood as the animal sense of man, the Apostle should rather have said, "Neither does foolishness take hold of the wisdom of God," than "neither does corruption inherit incorruptibility." (2) We think the same of that interpretation by which others understand "flesh and blood" as malice and the sin of the flesh and blood. For that sense the Apostle would have spoken more fittingly: "Neither does injustice inherit justice." (3) And those who abuse this saying of the Apostle, that flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God, to deny the resurrection of our flesh, could have been sufficiently warned of their error by the addition of this little word, so that it would be understood that the future resurrection excludes not the substance but the corruption of our flesh.

units.la: Ecce mysterium uobis dico: Nō om nes quidem dormiemus, omnes tamē immutabimur,in pūcto tēporis,in mo- mēto oculi,per extremam tubā. Canet enim,& mortui resurgent incorruptibi les,& nos immutabimur. Oportet cū corruptibile hoc induere incorruptibi litatem,& mortale hoc induere immor talitatem.
units.tr: Behold, I tell you a mystery: We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump. For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.

units.la: Priusquam materiam hanc de resurrectiõe mortuorum absoluat ac terminet,appēdicem hanc adiecit precedentibus,qua modum futu ræ corporum nostrorū mutationis paulo cla- rius cum distinctione exprimat. Ecce,inquit, mysterium uobis dico. Mysterium abscondi- tum quid ac secretum est, quod sub intelligen tiam communem non cadat, ne fidelium qui- dem,sed selectis duntaxat per reuelationē pa- tefiat.Sunt autem duplicis generis mysteria. 1 Primum est eorum quorū intelligentia & fi des ad salutem est omnibus necessaria. Horū dispensatores sunt Apostoli.Huc pertinent o- mnia Christianę fidei capita,quę mysteria sūt, ,ppterea qd rationi humanę suntincomprehē sibilia.De his extát testimonia & oracula in sa cris scripturis. 2 Alterum eorū est, quę citra salutis dispēdiū à fidelib.quoq; ignorantur,& de quib.nihil est maiseste in scripturis traditū. Ad primū genus pertinet ipsa mortuorū resur rectio,cuius fides necessaria est omnibus, & testimoniū habet ex scripturis. Ad posterius uero pertinet præsens hoc mysterium,de mo- do futuræ resurrectionis & immutationis cu- ius nulla fit mentio in scripturis,& cuius scien tia sine detrimento salutis ignorari potest.
units.tr: Before he finishes and concludes this subject of the resurrection of the dead, he has added this appendix to what precedes, so as to set out a little more clearly, and with distinctions, the manner of the future change of our bodies. "Behold," he says, "I tell you a mystery." A mystery is something hidden and secret, which does not fall under common understanding, not even among the faithful, but is revealed only to the chosen through revelation. There are, however, two kinds of mysteries. (1) The first is of those things whose understanding and faith are necessary to salvation for all. The Apostles are the dispensers of these. To this belong all the articles of the Christian faith, which are mysteries because they cannot be comprehended by human reason. Testimonies and oracles of these exist in the sacred Scriptures. (2) The other kind is of those things which, without loss to salvation, are unknown even to the faithful, and about which nothing is handed down plainly in the Scriptures. To the first kind belongs the resurrection of the dead itself, whose faith is necessary for all, and which has testimony from the Scriptures. To the latter belongs the present mystery, concerning the manner of the future resurrection and change, of which there is no mention in the Scriptures, and whose knowledge may be lacking without detriment to salvation.

units.la: Mysterium
units.tr: Mystery.

units.la: Quemadmodū enim satis est, si credā Deū omnipotētem, cœlum, terram, mare, & omnia uirtute uerbi sui condidisse, etiamsi nesciā modum creationis huius, & reliquas circunstantias, si credam verbū illud incarnatū esse propter nostram salutē, & natum ex uirgine, uerū Deū esse, & uerum homine, licet ignorem omnes eius rei circūstātias, &c. sic satis est, si credam futuram esse corporum nostrorum resurrectionem, & uitam nos habituros æteroam & cœlestē, etiamsi modos & circūstantias, tā resurrectionis q̄ perennis uitæ ignoremus. Sed dices: Quorsum igitur attinebat mysterium hoc patefacere fidelib. Corinthiorū, idq; non secreto selectis aliquot, sed comuniter omnib. scriptā ad omnes Epistolā, quæ coram omnib. erat legenda, & ad posteros quoq; trāsmittenda, si cognitio illius nō est ad salutē necessaria? Respondeo. Non fecit hoc Apost. temere aut iactāter, sed fideliter & utiliter. Quoniam de fide resurrectionis periclitabātur, propter sermones eorū qui illam negabant, uel saltē in dubium uocabant: deinde & propter quæstionem eorū, qui quali nā simus corpore surrecturi quærebāt: uoluit appendicem hanc adijcere de modo alterandorum nostrorum corporum, non q̄d̄ per se sit necessaria illius cognitio, sed q̄d̄ illis esset utilis qui de ipsa resurrectione dubij reddebantur à reprobis, quo in fide illius confirmatiores redderentur. Consimili modo & Rom.ii. cum eos qui ex Gentibus crediderant de non contemnendo Israelitarū populo multis admonuisset, tantum mysterium cæcitatis & futuræ conuersionis illius subiecit, dicēs: Nō uolo uos ignorare fratres mysterium hoc, ne sitis apud uosmetipsos elati animo, q̄d̄ excæca tio ex parte Israel accidit, donec plenitudo Gentium aduenerit, & sic totus Israel saluus erit. Mysterium hoc poterat à fidelibus ignorari citra salutis dispendium quemadmodum eiusmodi adhuc multa ignoramus, nisi perigno rantiam illius Israelem contemnendo, ac prorsus abijciendo contra dominum peccassent.
units.tr: For just as it is enough if I believe that God omnipotent created heaven, earth, sea, and all things by the power of his Word, even if I do not know the mode of this creation and the remaining circumstances; and if I believe that that Word was made flesh for our salvation, born of a virgin, true God and true man, even though I am ignorant of all the circumstances of that matter, and so on; so it is enough if I believe that there will be a resurrection of our bodies, and that we shall have eternal and heavenly life, even though we do not know the manner and circumstances both of the resurrection and of perpetual life. But you will say: Why then was it necessary to disclose this mystery to the faithful of Corinth, and to disclose it not secretly to a few chosen, but commonly, in a letter written to all, which was to be read before everyone and handed down also to posterity, if the knowledge of it is not necessary to salvation? I answer: The Apostle did not do this rashly or idly, but faithfully and usefully. Since the faith of the resurrection was in danger, on account of the talk of those who denied it, or at least called it into doubt; and then also on account of the question of those who asked in what kind of body we shall rise; he wished to add this appendix about the manner of the changing of our bodies, not because the knowledge of it is in itself necessary, but because it would be useful to those who were made doubtful about the resurrection itself by the wicked, so that they might be made more firm in faith concerning it. In a similar way also, in Romans 11, when he had admonished those who were of the Gentiles and had believed not to despise the people of Israel with many arguments, he added the mystery of the blindness and future conversion of that people, saying: "I would not have you ignorant, brethren, of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own conceits, that blindness in part has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and so all Israel shall be saved." This mystery could have been unknown to the faithful without loss to salvation, just as we are still ignorant of many things of this kind; but they would have sinned against the Lord, had they despised Israel and utterly cast away the expectation of it.

units.la: Vt autem animos Corinthiorum attētiores ad percipiendum mysteriū hoc reddat, nō sim pliciter rem ipsam ponit, dicēs: Haud quidem dormiemus oēs, &c. sed cū præfatiuncula, ad excitandum illorum animos accōmoda: Ecce inquit, mysterium uobis dico. Vocula, Ecce, uim habet excitādi aliàs negligētius auscultatores. Deinde auidi sumus ad percipiendum mysteria hactenus abscondita. Ea est nostracu riositas, qua utitur Apost. ad suum propositū. Accedit & illud, quod amicitiæ argumentum habet, secretorum cōmunicatio. Sic Christus, Vos, inquit, dixi amicos, quia omnia quæcūq; audiui à patre meo, nota feci uobis. Ioan.15.
units.tr: But so that he might make the minds of the Corinthians more attentive to perceiving this mystery, he does not state the thing simply, saying, "We shall not all indeed sleep," etc., but with a little preface suited to arousing their minds: "Behold," he says, "I tell you a mystery." The little word "Behold" has the power of rousing listeners who are otherwise rather careless. Moreover, we are eager to learn mysteries hitherto hidden. This is our curiosity, which the Apostle uses for his purpose. There is also this, which is a sign of friendship: the communication of secrets. So Christ says: "I have called you friends, because all things that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you." John 15.

units.la: NON omnes quidem dormiemus, omnes tamen, inquit, immutabimur.] Exponit secretum. Legitur autem hæc particula bifariam.
units.tr: "We shall not all indeed sleep, but we shall all be changed," he says. He explains the secret. This clause is read in two ways.

units.la: 1 Primo, quemadmodū est in Græco, Haud quidē oēs dormiemus, omnes tamen immutabimur, quā lectionē retinendā esse iudicamus.
units.tr: (1) First, as it is in the Greek: "Indeed we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed," which reading we judge is to be retained.

units.la: 2 Deinde, sicut uulgata habet æditio, Oēs q̄dē resurgemus, sed nō omnes immutabimur.
units.tr: (2) Second, as the common edition has it: "We shall indeed all rise, but we shall not all be changed."

units.la: 3 Tertio. Omnes quidē dormiemus, sed non oēs immutabimur. Prima quidem & tertia lectio in Græcis codicibus inuēta est, quarū prima hodie quoq; in illis inuenitur ac legitur: sed cundā uero Latini tantū habēt, Græci nequaq̄, q̄d̄ & Hieron. in calce Epistolæ ad Minerium & Alexandrū annotauit. Sensu tamen illa cum tertia coincidit, dū oēs resurrecturos esse affirmat, immutādos negat. Quomodocunq; acciderit hæc uarietas, qua alij legūt: haud oēs dormiemus, sed omnes immutabimur: alij, oēs q̄dē dormiemus, sed non oēs immutabimur, unius uocula ꝛ.i.nō, trāspositione accidit. Verū de lectione hac inspiciatur Eras. cuius annotationibus non est quod quicquam addam.
units.tr: 3 Thirdly. All indeed will sleep, but not all will be changed. The first and third readings are found in the Greek manuscripts, and the first is still found and read in them today; but the second is held only by the Latins, and not at all by the Greeks, as Jerome noted at the end of his letter to Minerius and Alexander. Nevertheless, in sense it coincides with the third, since it affirms that all will rise and denies that all will be changed. However this variation arose, by which some read "not all indeed will sleep, but all will be changed" and others "all indeed will sleep, but not all will be changed," it came about through the transposition of one little word, non. But on this reading let Erasmus be consulted; there is nothing I need add to his annotations.

units.la: NON omnes quidem dormiemus, inquit.] Intellige, in aduētu dñi, tempore futuræ resurrectionis. Vtitur aūt uerbo dormiendi in significatu mortis. Ergo ubi dñs aduenerit in die iudicij, ad excitādum mortuos, neq; erimus oēs mortui ac dormiētes in sepulchris, sed inuenie mur quàmplurimi adhuc superstites ac uiui: neq; qui uiui inueniemur obdormiemus moriendo, quemadmodū hodie morimur, ac dormimus. 1 De priori abūde satis est testimoniorum. In priore ad Thess.4. sic scribit Apostolus: Hoc enim dicimus in uerbo dñi, quod nos qui uiuemus & reliqui erimus in aduentu dñi, nequaq̄ præueniemus eos qui dormiunt: Ergo, non dormiemus omnes, si adhuc Christiani aliquot in uiuis erimus. De illis nanq; lo quitur, tametsi innumera futura sit in toto terrarum orbe uiuentium hominum multitudo.
units.tr: "Not all indeed will sleep," he says. Understand: at the coming of the Lord, at the time of the future resurrection. He uses the word "sleep" in the sense of death. Therefore, when the Lord comes on the day of judgement to raise the dead, we shall not all be dead and sleeping in the graves; rather we shall find very many still surviving and alive. Nor will those who are found alive fall asleep by dying, as we die and sleep today. Of the former, there is ample enough testimony. In the first letter to the Thessalonians, chapter 4, the Apostle writes thus: "For this we say to you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive and remain until the coming of the Lord will by no means precede those who sleep." Therefore, we shall not all sleep, if some Christians are still alive. For he is speaking of them, although in the whole world there will be an innumerable multitude of living men.

units.la: Deinde, cū dñs diē illū sic inexpectatū & ex improuiso edētib. bibētibus, nubētib. ædificātib. & plantātibus hominib. ad futurū dicit, ut similis sit futurus furi clāculum, ubi minus putatur subintroeunti, an non satis innuit, non dormituros omnes? Tertio cum dicit: Tunc duo erunt in agro, unus assumetur, alter relinquetur. Duæ molētes in mola, una assumetur, altera relinqtur. Vigilate ergo, &c. manifeste significat, multos adhuc fore in uiuis. Nō cōuenit itaq; hoc sensu, ut legamus: Omnes quidē dormiemus: sed legendū est, Haud quidē oēs dormiemus. Nec impedit illud parabolicum, Matth.25. Tardante uero sponso dormitauerūt oēs ac dormierūt. Haud enim de morte corporis dictum est, sed de omnimoda securitate, q̄ mentes omniū sic est tēpore aduentus dñi occupatura, ut similes sint dormientib. nihiloq; plus indicia præcurrentia, q̄ qui dormiunt aurorā aduentātis diei prænunciam obseruent.
units.tr: Next, when the Lord says that the day will come upon men so unexpectedly and suddenly, while they are eating, drinking, marrying, building and planting, so that it will be like a thief coming secretly, when he is least expected, does he not sufficiently hint that not all will sleep? Thirdly, when he says: "Then two will be in the field: one will be taken, the other left. Two women will be grinding at the mill: one will be taken, the other left. Watch therefore," and so on, he clearly signifies that many will still be alive. So it does not agree in this sense that we read "all indeed will sleep"; rather it must be read "not all indeed will sleep." Nor does that parable, Matth. 25, stand in the way: "While the bridegroom delayed, they all slumbered and slept." For this was not said of bodily death, but of complete security, which will seize the minds of all at the time of the Lord's coming, so that they are like sleepers, and the signs that go before them are observed no more than sleepers observe the dawn announcing the day.

units.la: Alterum illud eos uidelicet, qui uiui in aduentu domini inuenientur, non esse dormituros, id est morituros, negatur è nonnullis, præterea quod Eb.9 legitur: Quatenus illud manet omnes homines, ut semel moriantur, post hoc autem iudicium. Et suprà: Quemadmodū in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita in Christo omnes uiuificabuntur.
units.tr: The other point, that those who are found alive at the Lord's coming will not sleep, that is, will not die, is denied by some, and also because of what is read in Heb. 9: "Inasmuch as it is appointed for all men to die once, and after this the judgment." And above: "As in Adam all die, so in Christ all shall be made alive."

units.la: Ideo legunt illi, Omnes quidē dormiemus. Verū non satis firmo nituntur argumento. Et enim communis quidem lex est ut moriamur omnes: uerum illa non infringitur paucorum exceptione, nec diutius locū habet, q; constitu tū est à dño: nec sic illi alligata est potentia & prouidentia Dei, ut nequeat aliter agere cum illis quos iudicij dies uiuos reperiet, quàm cū reliqua multitudine, quę inde ab initio ad finē usque fuit, & etiamnum est in mundo.
units.tr: Therefore they read, "Indeed we shall all sleep." But they rest on an argument that is not very firm. For dying is indeed the common law for us all, but that law is not broken by the exception of a few, nor does it hold any longer than the Lord has established it. Nor is the power and providence of God so bound to that law that it cannot deal differently with those whom the day of judgment finds alive than with the rest of the multitude, which has existed from the beginning to the end and still exists in the world.

units.la: Duo hęc omniū sunt certissima. Vnū, quod aduētus dñi inexpectatus ac subitus uiuos inueniet eos omnes qui tū erunt in mūdo super stites, id quod suprà satis cōprobatum. Alterū, quod fideles qui in uiuis erunt, quicquid de reliquis futurum sit, in puncto temporis, in ictu oculis immutabuntur, quemadmodum hic te statur Apostolus, & simul cum illis qui è mortuis surrexerunt, rapiētur in nubibus, in occursum domini in aera. An in ista subita immutatione & raptu uirorū fidelium, mors corporis, quali reliqua iam multitudo moritur, habitura sit locum, non uideo quō possit certo docere. August. quidem sit sensit, ut uidere est li. de ciuit. Dei 20. cap. 20. Verum nō solide probat. Quod enim lectionem illam, Omnes quidem dormiemus: sequitur, infirmū est, quandoquidem ueteres Græci eam sequuti sunt, quę iā in Græco legitur, è quibus est & Chrysostomus.
units.tr: Two things are the most certain of all. One is that the Lord's coming, unexpected and sudden, will find alive all those who are then left over in the world, as has already been sufficiently proved above. The other is that the faithful who are alive, whatever becomes of the rest, will be changed in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, as the Apostle here states, and together with those who have risen from the dead they will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. But whether bodily death, by which the rest of the multitude now dies, will have a place in this sudden change and rapture of the faithful, I do not see how it can be taught with certainty. Augustine indeed thought so, as may be seen in De civitate Dei, book 20, chapter 20. But he does not prove it solidly. For that the reading "Indeed we shall all sleep" is followed is a weak argument, since the early Greeks, among whom is also Chrysostom, followed it, and it is already read in the Greek text.

units.la: Quicquid sit, dormiendi uerbū nō cōuenit illis quos dies dñi uiuos, & puncto temporis, in ictu oculi immutandos inueniet: etiamsi secundum opinionē Augustini mutatio illorum qualicunq; sit morte intercedēte futura. Haud enim rectè eiusmodi mors, quæ subito terminatur, & in uitam æternam mutatur, dormitio uocari poterit. De mortuis qui sepeliuntur, sic loquitur scriptura, quod in terræ puluere dormiant. Quis eum dormire dicet, qui in ictu oculi ex alio mutatur in alium? An oculi ictum somnū esse dicemus? Quare, meo iudicio, simplicius est ac certius, ut legamus: Haud quidē omnes dormiemus, quàm, omnes quidem dormiemus: uel, omnes quidem resurgemus. Resurgent quidem omnes, uerum intellige de illis quos dies domini non uiuos, sed mortuos inueniet. De uiuis non potest dici quod resurgant, dicitur autem quod immutantur. Differte nanque inter mortuos ac uiuos discriminat Apostolus, 1. Thessa. 4. cum dicit: Et mortui in Christo resurgent primum: deinde nos qui uiuemus, qui reliqui erimus simul cū illis rapiemur in nubibus in occursum domini in aera.
units.tr: Whatever the case, the word "sleep" does not suit those whom the day of the Lord will find alive and who are to be changed in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, even if, according to Augustine's opinion, their change is to take place with some death intervening. For such a death, which ends suddenly and is changed into eternal life, can rightly not be called a sleep. Scripture speaks of the dead who are buried as sleeping in the dust of the earth. Who would say that someone sleeps who in the twinkling of an eye is changed from one state into another? Shall we say that the twinkling of an eye is a sleep? Therefore, in my judgment, it is simpler and more certain to read "Indeed not all of us shall sleep" than "Indeed we shall all sleep," or "Indeed we shall all rise again." All will indeed rise again, but understand this of those whom the day of the Lord will find not alive but dead. It cannot be said of the living that they rise again; it is said that they are changed. For the Apostle distinguishes between the dead and the living in 1 Thess. 4, when he says: "And the dead in Christ shall rise first; then we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air."

units.la: NON omnes quidem dormiemus, inquit.] Verum hoc erit non in pijs modo & fidelibus, sed & in reliquis omnibus, quos aduentus domini in toto mundo inueniet. Verū apparet Apostolum loqui de fidelibus, & per occupationem occurrere cogitationi, quæ ex eo nasci poterat, quod suprà dixit: Quemadmodum in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita in Christo omnes uiuificabuntur. Et, Stulte, tu quod seminas, non uiuificatur nisi fuerit mortuū. Ne cogitaret fideles, Ergo in aduentu domini ac tempore resurrectiōis nemo erit amplius in uiuis, sed dormient omnes, quo possint è mortuis excitari oēs.
units.tr: "We shall not all indeed sleep," he says. But this will be true not only of the pious and faithful but also of all the rest whom the coming of the Lord will find in the whole world. Yet it appears that the Apostle is speaking of the faithful, and by anticipation he meets a thought that could arise from what he had said above: "As in Adam all die, so in Christ all shall be made alive," and "Foolish man, what you sow is not made alive unless it has died." Lest the faithful should think: therefore at the coming of the Lord and the time of the resurrection no one will any longer be among the living, but all will sleep, so that all may be raised up from the dead.

units.la: Non dormiemus, inquit, oēs, sed multi erimus adhuc in uiuis, ubi dominus aduenerit. Nos hinc rectè colligimus ecclesiā Christi duraturam in terris usq; ad finē mundi. Vbi dñs ad iudicium uenerit, inueniet adhuc fideles suos uiuos ac superstites, toto terrarum orbe dispersos. Quare fieri nō potest, ut prorsus deleantur de terra uiuentium, quantumuis sæuiat in illos, & mundus & mundi princeps.
units.tr: "We shall not all sleep," he says, "but many of us will still be among the living when the Lord comes." From this we rightly gather that the Church of Christ will endure on earth until the end of the world. When the Lord comes to judgment he will find his faithful still alive and surviving, scattered throughout the whole orb of the earth. Therefore it cannot happen that they are utterly wiped from the land of the living, however much both the world and the prince of the world rage against them.

units.la: OMNES tñ immutabimur, inquit.] Rursus colligi poterat: ergo non resurgemus omnes, si non dormiemus omnes, sed multi adhuc uiui ac superstites erimus. Si non resurgemus, quum uiui erimus, ergo glorię illius, immortalitatis, incorruptibilitatis & felicitatis, quam ac quirent, qui à mortuis resurgēt, atque ita & regni Dei, participes nō erimus.
units.tr: "Yet we shall all be changed," he says. Again one could infer: therefore we shall not all rise again, if we shall not all sleep, but many will still be alive and surviving. If we shall not rise again when we are alive, then we shall not share in that glory, immortality, incorruptibility and blessedness which those who rise from the dead will obtain, and so we shall not share in the kingdom of God.

units.la: Dicis enim carnem & sanguinem regni Dei hæreditatem, & corruptionem incorruptionis gloriam possidere non posse. Quid ergo de nobis tum uiuentibus fiet? Respondet. Ita quidē habet. Non resurgemus oēs, quia non dormiemus oēs: uerū est & illud, quod carnem & sanguinem regnū Dei possidere non posse dixi.
units.tr: For you say that flesh and blood cannot possess the inheritance of the kingdom of God, nor corruption possess the glory of incorruption. What then will become of us who will then be living? He answers: indeed it is so. We shall not all rise again, because we shall not all sleep; but it is also true what I said, that flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God.

units.la: Hinc tamen nō consequitur, fore nos, qui tum uiuemus, à futurę gloriæ, immortalitatis, incorruptibilitatis, adeoq; & regni Dei cōsortio exclusos. Nō enim qualitatē hanc animalis, mortalis, & corruptibilis corporis retinebimus, quā nunc circumferimus, sed immutabimur & ipsi, nō minus q; qui ex mortuis resurgent, reddemur q; ex animalibus, mortalibus & corruptibilibus, spirituales, immortales, incorruptibiles, & in summa cœlestes.
units.tr: From this, however, it does not follow that we who will then be living will be excluded from fellowship in the future glory, immortality and incorruptibility, and so also from the kingdom of God. For we shall not keep this quality of an animal, mortal and corruptible body which we now carry about; but we ourselves shall be changed, and no less than those who rise from the dead we shall be made from animal, mortal and corruptible into spiritual, immortal, incorruptible and, in short, heavenly.

units.la: Et hoc est mysterium illud quod se dicturum meminit. De uiuis loquitur, non de dormientibus. Illos subita metamorphosi immutandos esse, res erat occulta, mysterium fidelib. tū adhuc incognitū. Quod oēs morimur ac dormimus, nihil habet obscuri. Quare lectio illa, Omnes dormiemus, non modo aliena est à uero, sed & inconueniens ei qd præmisit, dicēs: Ecce mysteriū uobis dico.
units.tr: And this is that mystery which he recalled he would speak of. He speaks of the living, not of those who sleep. That they are to be changed by a sudden metamorphosis was a hidden thing, a mystery still unknown to the faithful. That we all die and sleep contains nothing obscure. Therefore that reading, "We shall all sleep," is not only foreign to the truth but also inconsistent with what he had premised, saying: "Behold, I tell you a mystery."

units.la: OMNES tñ immutabimur, inquit.] Quęrūt quò referēda sit uniuersalis hæc, Omnes? De eo quidē cōstat, qd tā ad mortuos acresurgentes, q ad uiuos ptineat. Omnes enim immutari oportet, sicuti mox est dicturus. Immutatio corporum nostrorum communis erit omnib. mortuis ac uiuis: resurrectio uerò non ita, sed dormientib. tantum. Quoniam uero & mortuorum & uiuorum pars maxima exre pbis erit & impijs, quæritur an perinde sint immutādi impij, atq; pij, ideoq; quod Apost. hic dicit, Omnes tamē immutabimur, eque ad impios atque ad pios pertineat. Qui negant pertinere ad impios, legūt hic, sed non oēs immutabimur. Iudicat enim Apostolū cōmuniter de omnib. loqui mortalib. tā impijs q; pijs, & sentiūt nō impios, sed pios tātū esse immutādos.
units.tr: "Yet we shall all be changed," he says. They ask to what this universal "all" should be referred? Of this much is certain: it applies both to the dead who rise and to the living. For all must be changed, as he is about to say. The change of our bodies will be common to all, to the dead and the living; but the resurrection is not so, but only for those who sleep. Since, however, the greater part both of the dead and of the living will be reprobates and impious, it is asked whether the impious are to be changed in the same way as the pious, and so whether what the Apostle says here, "Yet we shall all be changed," applies equally to the impious and to the pious. Those who deny that it applies to the impious read here, "but we shall not all be changed." For they judge that the Apostle speaks commonly of all mortals, both impious and pious, and they think that only the pious, and not the impious, are to be changed.

units.la: Verum de fidelibus illum loqui ipsa uerba satis conuincunt. Cum autem illi absq; contro uersia sint immutandi omnes, patet nō esse legendum, Non omnes immutabimur. Interea tamen quod quæstionem hanc de impijs attinet, licet de illis nō loquatur Apostolus: nō uideo tamen quō non sint, uel cum mortuis resurgentes, uel uiui in aduentu dni, ab ea corporum qualitate, quam in hac uita cōmuniter gestamus, in eam mutandi, quę capax sit incorruptionis & immortalitatis, nō ad id ut gloria & felicitate regni Dei cū copijs potiantur: sed ut pœnas sempiternas cum diabolo & angelis eius patiantur. Quemadmodum enim caro & sangis regnum Dei non possidebunt, donec mortalitati & corruptioni subiacet: ita nec indefinentes inferorum pœnas sine fine pati poterunt, si eandem mortalitatis & corruptionis qualitatem quam in hac uita habent, in futuro seculo retinebunt. Non est præter rationem igitur quod Valla magna corporum immutationem fore dicit, qua fiet ut non possint ullis ignib. cremari, neq; ullis supplicijs ab anima se iungi. Et Theodorus Heracleotes, citante Hieron. Canet enim tuba, inquit, & mortui resurgent incorrupti, & nos immutabimur. Oportet enim corruptibile istud induere incorruptionem, & mortale hoc induere immortalitatem, ut possit in utramque partem, uel in pœnis, uel in cœlorum regno manere perpetuo. Hæc ille. Nō est itaque ut impios simpliciter immutandos esse negemus. Licet enim non mutabūtur in claritatem & gloriam filiorum Dei, cum pijs & iustis: hactenus tamen mutabuntur, ut ex mortalib. immortales, & ex corruptibilib. incorruptibiles reddantur, id quod sine mutatione fieri non potest. Si angelus ex immortali mortalis, & ex incorruptibili corruptibilis in die indicij fieret, quis adeo stupidus est, qui mutare illum neget? Iam cum constet impios ex mortalib. futuros immortales & incorruptibiles, admodum inconsulte faciunt, qui mutādos eos esse negant.
units.tr: But the very words sufficiently prove that he is speaking of the faithful. Since, however, all are without controversy to be changed, it is plain that it should not be read, "We shall not all be changed." Meanwhile, as far as this question about the impious is concerned, although the Apostle does not speak of them, I do not see how they will not be changed, whether rising with the dead or alive at the Lord's coming, from that bodily quality which we commonly bear in this life into one capable of incorruption and immortality. This is not so that they may obtain the glory and happiness of the kingdom of God with its resources, but so that they may suffer everlasting punishments with the devil and his angels. For just as flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God as long as they are subject to mortality and corruption, so neither will the impious be able to endure the unending punishments of hell without end if in the future age they retain the same quality of mortality and corruption which they have in this life. It is not therefore beyond reason that Valla says there will be a great change of bodies, by which it will come about that they cannot be burned by any fires, nor be joined by the soul to any punishments. And Theodore of Heraclea, as cited by Jerome: "The trumpet will sound," he says, "and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality, so that it may remain forever in either condition, either in punishments or in the kingdom of heaven." So he. It is not, therefore, that we should simply deny that the impious are to be changed. For although they will not be changed into the brightness and glory of the sons of God with the pious and just, yet they will be changed so far that from mortal they become immortal and from corruptible incorruptible, which cannot happen without change. If an angel were made from immortal mortal, and from incorruptible corruptible, on the day of judgment, who is so stupid as to deny that he would be changed? Since it is agreed that the impious will become immortal and incorruptible from mortal, those who deny that they are to be changed act very unwisely.

units.la: IN puncto temporis, inquit, in momento oculi. Græce est ἐν ἀτόμῳ, ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ. Atomos est punctus indiuisibilis. Ponitur hic pro momento, tempore sic subito, ut in partes diuidi nequeat. Et quoniam non ab omnibus statim capitur quid sit punctus indiuisibilis, adiecit in ictu oculi, qui omnib. est notissimus. Significat igitur immutationem corporum nostrorum fore subitā, ne quis illam per gradus temporū perficiedam esse putet. Nec est ut per hyperbolam dictum hoc putemus ab Apostolo, quasi impossibile sit omnipotenti Deo carnē à se sola uerbi uirtute condita eadem potentia in momento temporis in eam mutare qualitatem, ad quam illam ab æterno destinauit. Qui dicit, & fit quod dicit, nō habet opus mora temporis, qua per gradus quod dicit fiat: sed ut iubet, ita mox est quod fieri iubet. Multa quidē in oculis nostris facit non subito, sed per gradus & spacia temporum, quod in æstate singulis annis cernimus: uerum facit hoc nō ex defectu potentiæ, sed certo cōsilio prouidentiæ, quo se se captui nostro sic attemperat, ut nō solum facta iam, sed & fieri uideamus: dumque principia, media & fines rerum ipsis nostris oculis cernimus, in potentiæ, sapientiæ ac prouidentiæ ipsius cognitionem, ueluti manu ducamur. Alia erat ratio creandi initio omnia ex nihilo, quemadmodum & futura est alia creaturam hactenus uanitati subiectam in fine mundi reformādi. Sicut illic subito condidit omnia uirtute uerbi sui, ita tum corpora nostra eiusdē uerbi sui uirtute subito excitabit mortua, & immutabit uiua.
units.tr: "In a point of time," he says, "in the moment of an eye." The Greek is ἐν ἀτόμῳ, ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ [en atomō, en rhipē ophthalmou]. An atom is an indivisible point. Here it stands for a moment of time so sudden that it cannot be divided into parts. Since not everyone immediately grasps what an indivisible point is, he adds "in the twinkling of an eye," which is known to everyone. He therefore means that the change of our bodies will be sudden, so that no one should think it will be accomplished by stages over a period of time. Nor should we suppose the Apostle is speaking hyperbolically, as if it were impossible for almighty God, by the sole power of his word, to change a body he created, in a moment of time, into the quality for which he destined it from eternity. He who speaks, and what he speaks comes to pass, has no need of an interval of time in which his command is fulfilled step by step; as he commands, so at once is what he orders done. Indeed, in our sight he often works not suddenly but through stages and spans of time, as we see every year in summer. Yet he does this not from any lack of power but from a settled plan of providence, by which he so adapts himself to our capacity that we see things not only already done but also being done, and while we watch beginnings, middles and ends of things with our own eyes, we are led, as it were by the hand, to the knowledge of his power, wisdom and providence. The manner of creating all things out of nothing at the beginning was different, just as the manner of reforming the creation, hitherto subjected to vanity, at the end of the world will be different. As there he created all things suddenly by the power of his word, so then by the power of the same word he will suddenly raise our dead bodies and change the living.

units.la: PER extremam tubam, inquit. Modū exprimit, per quem immutabimur. De illo dominus ipse, Matt. 24. sic loquitur: Et tunc apparebit signum filij hominis in cœlo, & tunc plangent omnes tribus terræ, & uidebūt filiū hominis uenientem in nubibus cœli, cū uirtute multa & maiestate, & mittet angelos suos cū tuba, & uoce magna, & congregabunt electos eius, &c. Et Apost. 1. Thess. 4. Quoniā ipse dns, inquit, cū iussu & uoce archangeli, & cum tuba Dei descendet de cœlo. Ergo non erit aduētus dni placidus ac mansuetus, qualis fuit prior: sed uehementer terribilis, qualis esse solet aduentus potētissimi regis, instructissimo cū exercitu aduersum hostes suos ac rebelles motetis, ubi etiam bellicarum tubarum sonitus, nedum Maiestatis ipsius excellentia, & uis exercitus terrorem incutit rebellibus.
units.tr: "At the last trumpet," he says. He sets out the manner by which we shall be changed. The Lord himself speaks of this in Matt. 24: "And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty, and he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and they will gather his elect," etc. And in 1 Thess. 4: "For the Lord himself, with a command and the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven." Therefore the Lord's coming will not be calm and gentle, as his first coming was, but dreadfully terrible, as the coming of a most powerful king is wont to be, who advances with a fully equipped army against his enemies and rebels. There, the sound of war trumpets, and still more the excellence of his majesty and the might of his army, strikes terror into the rebels.

units.la: Tubam aut hanc alij aliter accipiunt. Mihi simpliciter ac rectius sentire uidetur, qui iudicant omnino soniturum horribile clangorem ueluti tubæ regiæ ac bellicæ, cū quo fit dns de scefurus de cœlo, ac mortuos excitaturus. Huius exemplum olim præcessit in monte Sina, cum in illum descenderet dns lege populo suo laturus. qua de re Exo. 19 legimus: Et ecce cœperunt audire tonitrua, ac micare fulgura, & nubes densissima operire montem, clangorq; tubæ uehementius perstrepebat, & timuit populus qui erat in castris. Item: Eratq; omnis mons terribilis, & sonitus tubæ paulatim crescebat in maius & prolixius tædebatur. Qualis autē futura sit uox archangeli, & uox filij Dei, qua de Ioh. 5. meminit ipse dns, dicens: Venit hora, in qua omnes qui in monumētis sunt, audient uocem filij Dei, & procedent, &c. nō est temere statuendum. Verosimile tamen est, ut quemadmodum uox præconis, uox est regis: ita uox archangeli mortuos è sepulchris iussu domini euocantis uocetur uox filij Dei.
units.tr: Others understand this trumpet in other ways. To me it seems more simple and more correct to think, as those do who judge that a dreadful blast will sound, like a royal and warlike trumpet, with which the Lord will come down from heaven and raise the dead. An example of this went before long ago on Mount Sinai, when the Lord came down upon it to give the law to his people. On this matter we read in Exod. 19: "And behold, they began to hear thunders and lightnings to flash, and a very thick cloud to cover the mountain, and the sound of the trumpet grew louder, and the people who were in the camp trembled." Likewise: "And the whole mountain was terrible, and the sound of the trumpet gradually increased and grew longer." But what the voice of the archangel and the voice of the Son of God will be like, of which the Lord himself speaks in John 5, saying, "The hour comes in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and will come forth," etc., is not to be rashly determined. Yet it is probable that, just as the voice of a herald is the voice of the king, so the voice of the archangel calling the dead from their graves at the command of the Lord is called the voice of the Son of God.

units.la: Non est uero ociosum, quod nō simpliciter dicit, Per tubam: sed, per extremā tubā. Ergo præcessurae sunt aliæ quædā, quas extrema sit subsequutura, ad quam cogantur ad iudicium omnes, & uiui & mortui. Quales autem futuræ sint præcedentes, nō est ut pnunciemus. Siuo futuræ sunt angelicæ cœlitus clagentes, & aduentum dni prænunciantes, siue humanæ per ministerium selectorū quorūdam prophetarū aduentum dni instar tubæ prænunciantium, admiadministrandæ,id cõstat ad extremam tubam resurgituros esse mortuos,& uiuos immutan pos,quemadmodum subiungitur.
units.tr: It is not idle, moreover, that he does not simply say "by the trumpet" but "by the last trumpet." Therefore there will be other trumpets preceding it, which the last one will follow, and by which all, both living and dead, will be summoned to judgement. As to what the preceding trumpets will be, we should not pronounce. Whether they will be angelic sounds proclaiming from heaven the coming of the Lord, or human ones through the ministry of certain chosen prophets, announcing the Lord's coming like a trumpet, it is certain that the dead will rise at the last trumpet and the living will be changed, as follows.

units.la: C A N E T enim,inquit,& mortui resurgent incorruptibiles,& nos immutabimur.]In Græ co est, σαλπίσει γάρ: quod recte uerteris,Clanget enim.Vulgata habet: Canet enim tuba.At tu ba non est in Græco.Satis tamen expressa est in uerbo,Clanget.Angelos suos emittet cum tuba dñs.Illi sic clangent tuba cœlesti, ut in to to sint terrarum orbe audiendi At hunc clan gorem enim mortui,inquit,resurgent incorru ptibiles,& nos immutabimur. Sic rationem reddit,quare tubæ mentionem fecerit. Pro pterea uideli et, quod ad clangorem illius o mnium penetrantissimum excitabuntur mor tui. Nō erit uis excitandi mortuos in externo clangore:uerum adiuncta erit illi potentia spi ritus Dei,per quam uiuificabuntur mortui.
units.tr: "For the trumpet will sound," he says, "and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed." In the Greek it is σαλπίσει γάρ [salpisei gar], which you rightly translate "for it will sound." The Vulgate has "for the trumpet will sound," but "trumpet" is not in the Greek; it is nonetheless sufficiently expressed in the verb "will sound." The Lord will send forth his angels with a trumpet. They will sound with a heavenly trumpet so that it can be heard throughout the whole orb of the earth. But this sound, he says, the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. In this way he gives the reason why he made mention of the trumpet. For it seems that the dead will be raised by the most piercing sound of it, which reaches all. The power of raising the dead will not lie in the outward sound, but the power of God's Spirit will be joined to it, by which the dead will be made alive.

units.la: Obserua uero quantum sit discriminis in ter tubam bellicam terrenorum regum,& hæc cœlestis regis Christi .Illa , ubi clasicū sonat, occidit uiuos:ista uero,ubi clanxerit,uiuifica bit mortuos.
units.tr: Observe, moreover, how great a difference there is between the warlike trumpet of earthly kings and this heavenly trumpet of Christ, the King. That one, when the signal sounds, kills the living; but this one, when it sounds, makes the dead alive.

units.la: Nō dicit autem simpliciter,Et mortui resur gent:sed addit,Incorruptibiles:& nos,intelli ge,q uiui erimus,adeoq;cũ mortuis resurgere haudpoterimus,immutabimur:hoc est,ex cor ruptibilibus,& mortalibus incorruptibiles,& immortales diuina uirtute reddemur. Sic di- stinguit inter mortuos & uiuos, illisq; resurre ctionem,istis immutationem, utrisq; uero in- corruptibilitatem promittit. Per hæc enim u triq; regni Dei , & sempiternæ fœlicitatis ac gloriæ simul poterunt esse capaces.
units.tr: He does not, however, simply say, "And the dead will rise," but adds "incorruptible." And "we," understand, who shall be alive, since we cannot rise with the dead, shall be changed: that is, we shall be made incorruptible and immortal from corruptible and mortal by divine power. Thus he distinguishes between the dead and the living, promising resurrection to the former and change to the latter, but incorruptibility to both. For by these means both will be able to be capable of the kingdom of God and of everlasting happiness and glory alike.

units.la: Obseruandum uero est,quod rursus in pri ma persona loquens: cum dicit,& nos immu tabimur,de fidelibus se loqui significat. Nã ho rum gratia mysterium hoc exponit, quemad modum & in ea facit quæ prior est ad Thessalo nicenses.Nec facit hoc præter rationem. Ipse siquidem resurrectionis ordo,quem illic expri mit,satis innuit,singulari cura discriminatur ũ dominum inter pios & impios,sic ut pios pri mum uelut à sece impiorum separaturus sit,& in gloriam suam asserturus. Horum igitur ra tionem habens Apostolus, ne semel quidè de impiorum resurrectione meminit, non quod non illi quoq; sint resurrecturi : sed quod satis esse censuit,si mysterium hoc probe teneat fi- deles,quomodo mortui qui in Christo sunt,re surrecturi sint primum : deinde fideles adhuc uiui immutandi subito,& unà cum illis in oc- cursum domini in aera rapiendi. Quare nimis curiosi sunt, qui de reprobis anxie quærunt, qualibus nam illi resurrecturi sint corporibus, similes illis qui,ubi in ædificationem fidelium rectus est & germanus cœnę Dominicæ usus tradendus, contentiosè disputant de impijs, quid illi de mensa Domini accipiant & man- ducent.Sciat triticum quę sit fors tritici,finem palearum permittat agricolę.Sciat fidelis quę sit uocatio & spes fidelium,iudicium reprobo rum permittat iusto iudici.
units.tr: It must further be observed that, again speaking in the first person, when he says "and we shall be changed," he signifies that he speaks of the faithful. For he expounds this mystery for their sake, as he also does in the earlier letter to the Thessalonians. Nor does he do this without reason. Indeed, the order of resurrection which he sets out there sufficiently suggests that the Lord distinguishes with particular care between the godly and the ungodly, so that he will first separate the godly, as it were, from the ungodly, and will bring them to his glory. The Apostol, therefore, taking account of these matters, makes mention of the resurrection of the ungodly only once and not at length, not because they too will not rise, but because he thought it enough if the faithful understand this mystery well: how those who are dead in Christ will rise first, and then the faithful who are still alive will be suddenly changed and caught up with them to meet the Lord in the air. Hence they are overly curious who anxiously inquire about the reprobate, with what kind of bodies they will rise; and, when the right and genuine use of the Lord's Supper is to be handed down for the building up of the faithful, they contentiously dispute about the impious, what they receive and eat at the Lord's table. Let the one who knows what the wheat is know what the chaff is, and let the farmer leave the end of the chaff to himself. Let the faithful know what their calling and hope is, and leave the judgement of the reprobate to the just Judge.

units.la: O P O R T E T enim corruptibile hoc, inq;, inducere incorruptibilitate,& mortale hoc in- duere immortalitate.] Pro ratioue eius quod nõ simpliciter dixit,Canet tuba,& mortui re- surgent:sed,& mortui resurgent incorruptibi les,& nos immutabimur,necessitatem ponit, dicens:Oportet enim corruptibile hoc induere incorruptibilitatem,&c. Quæ est autem il la necessitas,propter quam hoc fieri oportet? Hanc suptà posuit dicens,Caro & sanguis re- gni Dei hæreditatem consequi non possunt, neque corruptio incorruptibilitatis hæredita tem accipit. Quod illic carnem & sanguinem, hic corruptibile & mortale uocat,notans car- nis nostræ qualitatem,qua mortalis est, & cor ruptibilis:ideoque regni Dei hæreditati pror sus,nisi mutetur,inconueniens. Cum ergo ad illam electi,prædestinati & uocati simus, om- nino necesse est,ut quicquid in nobis est, qd capax illius esse non potest,auferatur.Mortali tas autem,& corruptibilitas carnem nostram occupant,quæ utræque regni Dei felicitatem ac perpetuitatem recipere non possunt.Necef se est igitur,ut à carne nostra auferantur. Ause rentur autem non ablatione, qua caro nostra redigatur in nihilum,sed mutatione,qua præ- stantiorem & regno Dei conuenientem quali tatem sortiatur.Ea est,qua ex mortali immor- talis,& ex corruptibili incorruptibilis euadat. Quemadmodum enim corruptibilitas & mor talitas excludunt è regno Dei,ita incorrupti- bilitas & immortalitas aptos reddunt regno Dei,si non impediat ira Dei, & merita conde- mnatio.Nam alioqui & mali spiritus immorta les sunt & incorruptibiles,& tamen regni Dei participes esse non possunt,propterea qd sub condemnatione sunt,quæ nunquam est habi- tura finem.
units.tr: "For this corruptible," he says, "must put on incorruptibility, and this mortal must put on immortality." As the reason for what he did not say simply, "The trumpet will sound and the dead will rise," but "and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed," he sets out a necessity, saying: "For this corruptible must put on incorruptibility," etc. But what is that necessity, on account of which this must happen? He has set it out just before, saying: "Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruptibility." That which he here calls corruptible and mortal, he there calls flesh and blood, noting the quality of our flesh, by which it is mortal and corruptible; and therefore it is wholly unfitting for the inheritance of the kingdom of God unless it is changed. Since, then, we are elect, predestinated and called to that kingdom, it is altogether necessary that whatever in us cannot be capable of it be taken away. Mortality and corruptibility, however, occupy our flesh, and neither of these can receive the happiness and perpetuity of the kingdom of God. It is necessary, therefore, that they be taken away from our flesh. They are taken away, however, not by an abolition by which our flesh would be reduced to nothing, but by a change by which it obtains a more excellent quality suited to the kingdom of God. This is the change by which what is mortal becomes immortal, and what is corruptible becomes incorruptible. For just as corruptibility and mortality exclude from the kingdom of God, so incorruptibility and immortality make one fit for the kingdom of God, provided the wrath of God and the condemnation deserved do not hinder. For otherwise evil spirits too are immortal and incorruptible, and yet cannot be partakers of the kingdom of God, because they are under a condemnation which will never have an end.

units.la: Quod ita dicit Apostolus: Oportet enim corruptibile hoc induere incorruptibilitate, & mortale hoc induere immortalitatem ,ne- cessitatem habet geminam. Prima est æternæ electionis & prædestinationis, quæ irrita fieri non potest,propter quam necesse est, ut caro nostra consors fiat regni Dei. Altera est causa, quam uocant sine qua non.Sine immortalita- te & incorruptibilitate fieri non potest, ut ca- ro nostra regnum Dei possideat,quamuis im- mortalem & incorruptibilem esse per se non reddat illius hæredem ac possessorem. Oportet reddi non modo immortalem,quo sempi- ternæ:sed & cœlestem,quo cœlestis uitæ cum angelis Dei consortio frui possit.Nō possum cum uolucribus cœli circumuolitare in aere, propter terrenam corporis nostri molé, pror- sus ab auium leuitate & agilitate alienam: & quomodo in cœlestibus cũ angelis Dei uiue- mus,nisi quod terrenum,mortale,corruptibi- le,ac póderosum est in corpore nostro in qua- litatem cœlo,angelis Dei, & perpetuæ felici- tati conuenientem mutetur.
units.tr: The Apostle says this: "For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality." This necessity has two grounds. The first is eternal election and predestination, which cannot be annulled, and on account of which our flesh must necessarily become a partner in the kingdom of God. The second is what they call the sine qua non: without immortality and incorruption our flesh cannot possess the kingdom of God, although immortality and incorruption do not in themselves make it an heir and possessor of that kingdom. It must be made not only immortal, so that it may be everlasting, but also heavenly, so that it may enjoy the heavenly life in fellowship with the angels of God. I cannot fly about in the air with the birds of heaven, because the earthly bulk of my body is wholly alien to the lightness and agility of birds. And how shall we live among the angels of God in heaven, unless what is earthly, mortal, corruptible and heavy in our body is changed into a quality suited to heaven, to the angels of God, and to perpetual happiness?

units.la: Obseruandum autem est,quod non simpliciter dicit: Oportet autem accipere incorruptibilitatem: sed, Oportet autem corruptibile hoc induere incorruptibilitatem. Cum connotatione dicit: corruptibile hoc, tantum non digito carnem hanc nostram commonstrans. Deinde aptissime utitur metaphora induendi, in qua duo sunt: unum, quod induit: alterum, quod induitur. Induens hic est corpus nostrum corruptibilem habens qualitatem veluti vestem. Induendum est ipsa in corruptibilitas. Mutatio haec, qua corruptibile induet incorruptibilitatem, contingiet non substantiae corporis, sed vestis. Ponet utique remac laceram vestem, et induet novam nunquam corrumpendam. Ipsum corpus non est instar veteris indumenti ponendum, ac novo mutandum, sed novo ac caelesti incorruptibilitatis veste induendum ac ornandum. Quare non est, ut alia nos corpora, in die resurrectionis sumpturos putemus. Ipsum non strum corpus mortale hoc et incorruptibile, immortalitate ac incorruptibilitate vestietur.
units.tr: We must observe that he does not simply say, "It is necessary to receive incorruption," but "This corruptible must put on incorruption." With the word "this" he points, as it were, to this very flesh of ours with his finger. Then he uses the metaphor of putting on clothing very aptly, in which there are two things: one that puts on, and one that is put on. Here the one who puts on is our body, which has a corruptible quality as if it were a garment; what is put on is incorruption itself. This change, by which the corruptible puts on incorruption, will affect not the substance of the body but its garment. Surely one puts off a worn and torn garment and puts on a new one that will never decay. The body itself is not to be discarded like an old garment and exchanged for a new one, but is to be clothed and adorned with the new, heavenly garment of incorruption. Therefore we should not think that in the day of resurrection we shall take on other bodies. This same mortal and corruptible body of ours will be clothed with immortality and incorruption.

units.la: Deinde et illud obiter observa. Dixit, Et nos immutabimur. Ut autem immutationis huius necessitatem exprimat, subijcit: Oportet enim corruptibile hoc induere incorruptibilitatem, et mortale hoc induere immortalitatem. Ergo immutari in hac causa, est ex mortali et corruptibili fieri immortalem et incorruptibilem. Utrumque autem sunt spiritus illi mali et condemnationi sempiternae obnoxij. Quare non video, quare reproborum corpora post resurrectionem ab hac debeam immutatione excludere, qua tam abest ut felices reddantur, ut quo magis erunt immortales et incorruptibiles, hoc futuri sint magis sempiterni supplicij capaces, et malorum spirituum consortes.
units.tr: Next, observe this in passing. He said, "We shall be changed." To express the necessity of this change he adds: "For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality." So to be changed in this respect is to become immortal and incorruptible instead of mortal and corruptible. Yet those evil spirits are both of these things, and are liable to everlasting condemnation. Therefore I do not see why I should exclude the bodies of the reprobate from this change after the resurrection, a change which is so far from making them happy that the more immortal and incorruptible they are, the more capable they will be of everlasting punishment, and the more they will be partners with evil spirits.

units.la: Cum autem corruptibile hoc induerit incorruptibilitatem, et mortale hoc inducerit immortalitatem, tunc fiet sermo qui scriptus est: Absorpta est mors in victoriam. Vbi tuus mors aculeus? Vbi tua inferne victoria? Aculeus autem mortis peccatum, potentia vero peccati lex. Sed Deo gratia, qui dedit nobis victoriam, per dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.
units.tr: When this corruptible has put on incorruption and this mortal has put on immortality, then will come to pass the saying that is written: "Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is your sting? O grave, where is your victory? The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ."

units.la: Hactenus revelavit Corinthijs mysterium de corporum nostrorum immutatione, quam sic necessariam esse dixit, ut oporteat per illam quod mortale et corruptibile in nobis est, induere immortalitatem et incorruptibilitatem. Ne hoc sine scripturis dicere videatur, subiungit testimonium ex vaticinijs prophetarum dicens: Cum autem corruptibile hoc induerit incorruptibilitatem, et mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem (Sic utraque particula habetur in Graeco) tunc fiet sermo qui scriptus est. Quasi dicat: Tunc scriptura, quae quod hic dicimus futurum esse praedixit, quando corporum nostrorum mortalitas et corruptibilitas in immortalitatem et incorruptibilitatem mutabuntur, vteraciter et prorsus implebitur, atque itatum erit factum, quod iam est sermo scriptus.
units.tr: Thus far the Apostle has revealed to the Corinthians the mystery of the change of our bodies, which he has said is so necessary that through it what is mortal and corruptible in us must put on immortality and incorruption. Lest he seem to say this without the Scriptures, he adds a testimony from the prophecies of the prophets, saying: "When this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality" (both clauses are so given in the Greek), "then will come to pass the saying that is written." As if he said: then the Scripture, which foretold that what we are speaking of would happen, will be fully and completely fulfilled, when the mortality and corruptibility of our bodies are changed into immortality and incorruption; and then what has already been written as a saying will have been done.

units.la: Quemadmodum enim impleri oportet scripturam, ita quod futurum esse dico, in corporibus nostris fieri oportet. Consimili modo et Rom.11. cum mysterium de futura Israelis conversione expositurum, testimonium propheticae scripturae, quam impleri oportet, subiecit, dicens: Sicut scriptum est, Veniet ex Sion qui eripiat, et auertat impietatem a Iacob. Et hoc illis a me testamentum, cum abstulero peccata eorum. Sic prudens et fidelis Apostolus, non contentus authoritate Apostolica, adiungit illi prophetias scripturas, ne quid temere de suo ecclesiae Dei proponere videatur. Et qui se apostolorum gloriantur esse successores, sine scripturis loquentibus omnia sibi credi volunt.
units.tr: For just as Scripture must be fulfilled, so what I say will happen must come to pass in our bodies. In a similar way, in Romans 11, when he was about to set out the mystery of the future conversion of Israel, he added a testimony of prophetic Scripture, which must be fulfilled, saying: "As it is written, There shall come out of Zion the deliverer, and he shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob. And this is my covenant with them, when I shall take away their sins." So the wise and faithful Apostle, not content with Apostolic authority, adds to it the prophetic Scriptures, lest he seem to propose anything rashly of his own to the Church of God. And those who boast that they are successors of the apostles want everything to be believed on their word, without Scriptures speaking.

units.la: Quis est autem sermo ille scriptus, in futura corporum nostrorum immutatione implendus? Absorpta est mors, inquit, in victoriam. Vbi tu mors aculeus? Vbi tua inferne victoria? Si verba haec praecise et expresse quaesieris, non invenies ea, ut posita sunt ab Apostolo, uspiam in scripturis uno et eodem loco. Prior illius pars vaticinium habens de morte absorbenda Esaiae cap.25. sic habetur, בלע המות לנצח, quae si cum functis legas, ut habentur in Hebraeo, sensum hunc habent: Deuorauit mortem in sempiternum, vel in victoria. Verbum בלע quod devorare et absorbere significat, legitur in Hebraeo in Piel, בלע, in qua forma sonat actiue, devoravit, absorpsit. Apostolus vero legit non בלע, absorpsit, sed בלע, i.
