Absorpta est, devorata est. Sic et Germanicus interpres vertit, nisi quod praeteritum mutavit in futurum. dann der todt uniert gar uerschlungen werden. Illud ἐς νίκος, i. In victoriam, in Hebraeo est לנצח. Significat autem נצח aliquando aeternum, aliquando victoriam et triumphum. Posteriorem sensum amplexus est Apostolus, ideoque legit: Absorpta est mors in victoriam. Quanquam aeque convenienter poterat legere, in sempiternum. Sic puto constare particulam hanc desumptam ex dicto Esaiae loco. Quis autem sit in illa prophetae sensus, expositum in Commentarijs nostris super hunc prophetam. Apostoli sensus planus est: Vbi quod mortale et corruptibile est in corporibus nostris, immortalitate et incorruptibilitate mutabimur, utique tum prorsus erit absorpta mors, sic ut nihil de illa superfuturum sit amplius. Donec mortales sumus et corruptibiles, obtinet adhuc illa in corporibus nostris. Vbi uero coeperimus esse immortales et incorruptibiles, absorbebitur prorsus in victoriam. Victoriam mortis intelligit, non quod illa vincat, sed qua vincitur et absorbeatur mortalitas a vita, 2.Cor.5. idque virtute vivificantis nos Christi. Victoria haec immortalitas est. Perinde enim atque nocturnae tenebrae per solis exortum, ita mors per donum immortalitatis absorbebitur ac vincetur.
units.tr: What then is that written saying which is to be fulfilled in the future change of our bodies? "Death is swallowed up in victory," he says. "O death, where is your sting? O grave, where is your victory?" If you seek these words precisely and exactly, you will not find them anywhere in the Scriptures in one and the same place as the Apostle has put them. The first part of it, which is a prophecy about death being swallowed up, is in Isaiah 25 and reads, in the Hebrew, bl' hmwt lnsh [בלע המות לנצח]. If you read this with the points as they stand in the Hebrew, it has this sense: "He has swallowed up death for ever, or in victory." The verb bl' [בלע], which means to devour or swallow up, is read in the Hebrew in the Piel form, bl' [בלע], in which form it has an active sense: he devoured, he swallowed up. But the Apostle does not read bl' [בלע] "he swallowed up," but bl' [בלע], that is, "is swallowed up," "is devoured." The German translator also renders it so, except that he changed the past into the future: dann der todt uniert gar uerschlungen werden. The phrase eis nikos, that is "into victory," is in the Hebrew lnsh [לנצח]. But nsh [נצח] sometimes means "for ever" and sometimes "victory and triumph." The Apostle embraced the latter sense, and therefore reads: "Death is swallowed up in victory." Yet he could just as suitably have read "for ever." So I think it is established that this particle is taken from the words of Isaiah. What the prophet's sense is in that passage has been set out in our Commentaries on this prophet. The Apostle's sense is plain: when what is mortal and corruptible in our bodies is changed into immortality and incorruption, then death will be utterly swallowed up, so that nothing of it will remain any more. As long as we are mortal and corruptible, death still holds sway in our bodies. But once we have begun to be immortal and incorruptible, it will be wholly swallowed up in victory. By "victory" he means the victory of death, not that death conquers, but that mortality is conquered and swallowed up by life, 2 Corinthians 5, and this by the power of Christ who quickens us. This victory is immortality. For just as the darkness of night is dispelled at the rising of the sun, so death will be swallowed up and conquered by the gift of immortality.

units.la: Obserua uero, quam nihil loci relinquatur illis qui carnis resurrectionem negantes, scriptura
units.tr: Observe, moreover, how no room is left to those who deny the resurrection of the flesh, the Scripture...

units.la: {A} Aduersus Antiochum mortem.
units.tr: {A} Against Antiochus's death.

units.la: {B} Mors.
units.tr: {B} Death.

units.la: Esa.25. pturas huiusmodi de morte spirituali exponunt. Mortem sentiunt absorptam esse, quatenus spiritus credentis ab æterna morte & condemnatione per mortem Christi liberatus est. Pars hæc est redemptionis nostrę non totum. Non modo spiritus nostri, sed & carnis redemptor est Christus. Non dicit, Cum iniusticia induit iusticiam: sed, Cum corruptibile hoc induerit incorruptibilitatem, &c. tûc fiet sermo qui scriptus est: Absorpta est mors in victoriâ. Manifestum est non loqui Apostolum de morte spirituali, sed corporali, quæ dono immortalitatis & incorruptibilitatis absorbebitur.
units.tr: Esa.25. They expound such Scriptures of spiritual death. They hold that death is swallowed up insofar as the spirit of the believer has been freed from eternal death and condemnation through the death of Christ. But this is only one part of our redemption, not the whole of it. Christ is the redeemer not only of our spirit but also of our flesh. The Apostle does not say, "When unrighteousness has put on righteousness," but "When this corruptible has put on incorruption, etc., then will come to pass the saying that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory." It is clear that the Apostle is not speaking of spiritual death, but of bodily death, which will be swallowed up by the gift of immortality and incorruption.

units.la: Hæc de prima scripturæ huius particula, Absorpta est mors in victoriam, uideamus iam de reliqua. Vbi tuus mors aculeus, inquit? Vbi tua inferne victoria? Leguntur hæc in Hoseah cap.13. ubi sic habetur [Hebrew]. De manu inferni (sepulchri) liberabo eos, de morte redimam eos. Ero pestis tua mors, ero exterminium tuum inferne. Illud, De manu inferni liberabo eos, de morte redimam eos, omisit Apostolus. Deinde uoculâ [Hebrew], accepit pro [Hebrew]: Sonat autem [Hebrew], alias [Hebrew], ero, [Hebrew] uero ubi. Nec fecit hoc præter rationem, & mentem prophetæ. Nam ille paulò suprà uoculam hac [Hebrew], posuit pro, [Hebrew], id est, ubi. Sic enim dicit: [Hebrew], quod & Septuaginta verterunt. Et vulgatus interpres, ubi. Vbi, inquit est rex tuus nunc. Litera n, in [Hebrew], est accessoria. Alias [Hebrew], significat ubi. Hoc autem loco posita quidem est in medio, uerum nihil aliud facit, quàm in uoce [Hebrew]. Quare præter rationem non est, quod Apostolus legit, Non ero, sed Vbi. Tertio illud [Hebrew], accepit pro aculeo, & [Hebrew], pro victoria: significat autem [Hebrew], causam, [Hebrew], uero cum sex punctis, pestem. Septuaginta verterunt, id est, Vbi plaga tua mors? Vbi stimulus uel aculeus tuus inferne? At uox [Hebrew], exterminium sonat. Quod [Hebrew], uertit, aculeus tuus, respexit ad oculeos uenenatorum animalculorum, qui uim habent mortiferæ pestis.
units.tr: Let us now consider the first part of this Scripture, "Death is swallowed up in victory," and then the rest. "O death, where is your sting?" he says. "O grave, where is your victory?" These words are read in Hosea 13, where the text reads thus (in the Hebrew): "I will ransom them from the hand of the grave (the sepulchre); I will redeem them from death. I will be your plague, O death; I will be your destruction, O grave." The Apostle omitted the words "I will ransom them from the hand of the grave, I will redeem them from death." Then he took the little word which in the Hebrew means "I will be" as if it meant "where," and the Hebrew word that means "where" he read as if it meant "I will be." The word that normally means "I will be" is one thing, and the word for "where" is another. Nor did he do this against the sense and intention of the prophet. For a little earlier the prophet used the same word in the sense of "where" (the Hebrew for "where"), as he says: "where is now your king," which the Seventy also translated so, and the Vulgate translator "where." The letter n in the Hebrew word for "I will be" is an added one; elsewhere the word means "where." In this passage, indeed, it is placed in the middle, but it does nothing other than what the same letter does in the word for "where." So it is not against reason that the Apostle reads "where" and not "I will be." Thirdly, the Apostle took the Hebrew word that means "destruction" as "sting," and the word meaning "destruction" as "victory." The word for "destruction" means cause, while the word for "destruction" with a particular vowel point means plague. The Seventy translated it as "your plague, O death; your sting or goad, O grave?" But the word for "destruction" means extermination. The Greek word which he rendered "your sting" looked to the stings of poisonous little creatures, which have the power of deadly plague. The Greek word which he rendered "victory" follows from the preceding clause, in which death is said to be swallowed up in victory. And besides, the extermination which death brings is in place of victory. I think these things about the present testimony of Scripture, taken from Isaiah and Hosea, are certain, so that not...

units.la: Quod [Hebrew] reddidit victoriam, factum est propter præcedentem particulam, qua mors absorpta dicitur in victoriam. Et alioqui exterminium quod mors infert, est illi loco victoriæ. Hæc de præsenti testimonio scripturæ ex Esaiah & Hoseah desumptæ puto esse certa, ut non sit causa, propter quâ anxie inquiramus, unde nam sit ab Apostolo desumptum. Laborant citra necessitatem, qui totum ex Hoseah desumptum esse censent.
units.tr: The Hebrew word that the translator rendered as "victory" is so rendered because of the preceding particle, by which death is said to be swallowed up in victory. Otherwise, the destruction that death brings takes the place of victory here. I think these points about the present testimony of Scripture, taken from Isaiah and Hosea, are certain, so there is no reason for us to inquire anxiously where the Apostle took it from. Those who think the whole passage is taken from Hosea labour without any need.

units.la: VBI tuus mors, inquit, aculeus? Vbi tua inferne victoria? Habet hæc particula propheti cam insultationem, qua morti tanquam prorsus deuicto & exterminato hosti insultatur. Nondum illa penitus est deuicta. Quare insultatio ista fidei est in id quod certissime futurû est prospicientis, deq; illo haud secus quàm si iam sit factum gloriantis & exultâtis. Citat ille Apostolus ad causam quam agit omnium appositissime. Etenim si futurum est, ut mors & corruptio funditus extirpentur, ita ut insultatio hæc locum habere queat, necesse est, ut quod mortale & corruptibile in nobis est, immortalitate & corruptibilitate mutetur.
units.tr: "Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O hell, is your victory?" This verse of the prophet contains a taunt, by which death is mocked as if it were already completely defeated and destroyed. It is not yet wholly overcome. So this taunting belongs to faith, which looks forward to what is most certainly going to happen, and rejoices and exults about it just as if it had already happened. The Apostle cites this passage most aptly for the cause he is pleading. For if death and corruption are to be utterly rooted out, so that this taunt can stand, then whatever in us is mortal and corruptible must be changed into immortality and incorruption.

units.la: Vtitur autem propheta prosopopœia, persona tubuens morti, dum illi tanquam deuictæ insultans dicit: Vbi est mors aculeus tuus? quæ admodum & inferno. Est ista personæ fictio prophetis solennis, pulchre conueniens illis qui singulari futurarum rerum fide ac certitudine sic mouentur, ut de illis haud secus quàm si iam præsentes sint exultent. Monet nos Apostolus qua debeamus fide corporum nostrorum resurrectionem & immutationem expectare, imò de exterminio mortis quantumuis adhuc regnantis gloriari. Tam abest scilicet, ut ulla re surrectionis nostrę dubitatio locum in animis nostris habere debeat.
units.tr: The prophet uses a personification, speaking to death as if it were a person, and mocking it as already conquered when he says: "Where is your sting, O death?" and likewise to hell. This fiction of a person is customary among the prophets, and fits well with those who are so moved by a singular faith and certainty about future things that they rejoice about them as if they were already present. The Apostle warns us with what faith we ought to await the resurrection of our bodies and their transformation, and indeed to glory over the destruction of death, even though it still reigns. Clearly, then, there ought to be no room in our minds for any doubt about our resurrection.

units.la: VBI tua inferne victoria, inquit. In Ebreo est [Hebrew], quæ uox foueam ac sepulchrû significat, ne quis de infernali gehenna intelligat, quæ nunquam est habitura finem. Accipit hac nocem Apostolus in præsenti de corruptione corporum nostrorum, quæ perinde atqi mors absorbebitur, & amissa victoria, qua adhuc de corporib. nostris triumphat, prorsus deuicta iacebit. Et ipsa quidem gehenna debellata est per Christum, uerum nö in uniuersum, sed qd electos ac fideles attinet tantum, impijs uero ac reprobis durabit in sempiternum. At mors & corruptio corporum nostrorum penitus tâ ab electis quàm à reprobis auferentur, & in nihilum redigentur.
units.tr: "Where, O hell, is your victory?" says the Apostle. In the Hebrew the word means a pit or a sepulchre, so no one should take it to mean the infernal Gehenna, which will never have an end. In the present passage the Apostle takes the word to mean the corruption of our bodies, which will be swallowed up just as death will be, and, its victory lost, by which it still triumphs over our bodies, will lie wholly defeated. Gehenna itself has indeed been overcome through Christ, but not altogether: as far as the elect and faithful are concerned only, while for the impious and reprobate it will endure forever. But the death and corruption of our bodies will be removed entirely, both from the elect and from the reprobate, and reduced to nothing.

units.la: ACVLEVS autem mortis peccatum, inquit, potentia uero peccati lex. Exponit uerba prophetę, qui sit per aculeum mortis intelligendum. Comparat Satanam bestiæ uenenatæ, cuius aculeus est lethalis. Satan inflixit humano generi uirus suum per peccatum, quasi quendam aculeum, atque ita intulit illi morte. Sic aculeum mortis, id est, mortiferum aculeum dicit esse peccatum. Mors non habet aculeum, sed infertur per aculeum. Per mortem non est peccatum, sed per peccatum est mors. Sic Augustinus lib. 3. de peccat. meritis & remissione cap.11. Aculeum, inquit, quo mors facta est, nö quem mors fecit. Peccato enim morimur, non morte peccamus. Sic itaq; dictum est, aculeus mortis quomodo lignum uitæ, non quod hominis uita faceret, sed quo hominis uita fieret: & quomodo lignum scientiæ, per quod scientia fieret hominis, non quod per suam scientiâ fecerit homo. Sic ergo & aculeus mortis, quo mors facta est, nö quem mors fecerit. Sic enim dicemus & poculum mortis, quo aliquis mortuus sit uel mori posit, non quod moriés mortuus ue confecerit. Hæc ille: Ergo per peccatum est mors.
units.tr: "But the sting of death is sin," he says, "and the power of sin is the law." He explains the words of the prophet, showing what is to be understood by the sting of death. He compares Satan to a poisonous beast whose sting is deadly. Satan inflicted his venom on the human race through sin, as if it were a kind of sting, and so brought death upon it. Thus he says that sin is the sting of death, that is, a deadly sting. Death does not have a sting; rather, it is inflicted through a sting. We do not die through sin because of death, but death comes through sin. So Augustine, in book 3 of On the Merits and Remission of Sins, chapter 11: "The sting by which death was made, not the sting which death made. For we die by sin; we do not sin by death. So it is said that the sting of death is like the tree of life, not because it made human life, but by which human life came about; and like the tree of knowledge, through which knowledge came to be in man, not because man made knowledge by his own knowledge. So also the sting of death is that by which death was made, not that which death made. For we will also say the cup of death, by which someone has died or can die, not because the one dying or dead has made it." Thus far Augustine. Therefore death comes through sin.

units.la: Cum itaque morti deuictæ insultat porphe ta, dicens: Vbi est mors aculeus tuus, & morte & peccatum exterminio subijcit, significans deleto primum peccato, tanquam mortifero aculeo, ipsam quoq; morte interituram. Quomodo autem mors per peccatum peruenerit in omnes homines, uidere est Rom. 5. unde & mortem uocat finem peccatorum, & peccatū stipendium, cap. 6. Hanc mortis causam ignorant philosophi. Mortalitatem uident obtinere in omnibus, causam illius non uident.
units.tr: So when the prophet mocks death as already conquered, saying, "Where is your sting, O death?", he subjects both death and sin to destruction, signifying that once sin, the deadly sting, is removed, death too will perish. How death came upon all men through sin may be seen in Romans 5, where he also calls death the wages of sin and sin the end of sinners, in chapter 6. The philosophers do not know this cause of death. They see that mortality prevails in all men, but they do not see its cause.

units.la: Illud admonent & alij, loqui hic Apostolū, non de peccato (ut uocant) actuali, sed originali, quod latet in carne nostra, & regnat in membris nostris, in quo concepti sumus & nati, & lethaliter infecti. Vnde & infantes priusquam aliquid peccati actualis admiserunt, mori uidemus, quod non fieret nisi mortifero essent peccati aculeo in ipso conceptu.
units.tr: Others also point out that the Apostle is speaking here not of actual sin, as it is called, but of original sin, which lies hidden in our flesh and reigns in our members, in which we were conceived and born, and fatally infected. Hence we see infants die even before they have committed any actual sin, which would not happen unless they had been struck by the deadly sting of sin at the very moment of conception.

units.la: POTENTIA uero peccati lex, inquit. ]Expònit unde peccato tantum sit potētiæ, ut instar uenenati aculei pungendo occidat. Vno uerbo tribuit hoc legi, dicens: Potentia uero peccati lex. Primum, quod peccatum illud primorum generis nostri parentum attinet, unde sumus omnes facti mortales, potētia illius ad occidendum fuit lex in paradiso de non edendo ligno scientiæ boni & mali lata. Eius enim illius per se nec peccatum fuisset, nec mortem intulisset, quod utrunque debetur legi ac legis transgressioni. Non legi simpliciter, sed legi per inobedientiam uiolatæ. Deinde quod peccatum attinet in carne nostra latēs, factum est illud adhuc fortius per legem, primum naturę, quæ naturaliter conscientijs nostris est indita: deinde & literæ, qua de Apostolus Rom. 7. copiose disputat. Hac in præsenti intelligit, cum dicit, Potentia uero peccati lex. Est autē hæc potentia, quam peccatum sumit ex lege, impropria. Primum, ubi non est lex, ibi nō est transgressio. Deinde, ubi non est lex, ibi peccatum est mortuum: ubi uero lex est, ibi peccatū reuiuisset, & fortius insurgit. Sic de lege loquitur loco iam citato. At neutrum proprium est legis opus, sed per accidens & impropriū. Neque enim per se gignit transgressionem, neque peccatum corroborat, sed magis prodit, uetat & damnat. Ipsum uero peccatum pro ingenij sui malitia, unde debebat corrigi inde magis occasionem maioris sibi potentiæ accipit. At ea de re, si cui lubet, Coment. nostros in Epist. ad Romanos consulat.
units.tr: "But the power of sin is the law," he says. He explains how sin has such power that, striking like a poisoned sting, it kills. He attributes this to the law in a single phrase: "But the power of sin is the law." First, as far as that sin of our first parents is concerned, from which we have all become mortal, its power to kill lay in the law given in Paradise not to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For by itself that eating would neither have been sin nor brought death, both of which are owed to the law and to its transgression: not to the law simply, but to the law violated by disobedience. Next, as far as the sin lying hidden in our flesh is concerned, it has been made even stronger through the law, first the law of nature, which is naturally implanted in our consciences, and then the written law, about which the Apostle argues at length in Romans 7. It is this that he means in the present passage when he says, "the power of sin is the law." But this power, which sin takes from the law, is improper. First, where there is no law, there is no transgression. Next, where there is no law, sin is dead; but where there is law, sin revives and rises up more strongly. So he speaks of the law in the passage already cited. Yet neither of these is the proper work of the law, but incidental and improper. For the law does not by itself beget transgression, nor does it strengthen sin; rather, it reveals, forbids and condemns. But sin itself, by the malice of its nature, which ought to have been corrected by the law, takes from the law an occasion for greater power. On this matter, let whoever wishes consult our commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans.

units.la: Videtur autem Apostolus legis metionem fecisse, illiq; peccati potentiam tribuisse propter Iudæos Mosaicæ legis æmulatores, quorum etiam inter Christianos multi erant, præsertim Hierosolymis ac reliqua Iudæa, sub apostolatu Iacobi ac Petri, sicuti uidere est in Actis cap. 21. ubi Iacobus ad Paulum dixit: Vides frater quot millia sunt in Iudæis, qui crediderūt, & omnes æmulatores sunt legis. Obiter igitur uno uerbo admonet, tam abesse ut lex aculeum mortis auferat, hoc est, peccatum e carne nostra tollat, ut magis illi ad ampliorem potentiam seruiat. Quare necesse esse, ut uictoria contra peccatum & mortem aliunde acquiratur. Atq; ita mox unde illa sit subiungit, dicēs:
units.tr: The Apostle seems to have mentioned the law and attributed power to sin on account of the Jews, zealots for the Mosaic law, of whom there were many even among the Christians, especially at Jerusalem and in the rest of Judaea, under the apostleship of James and Peter, as may be seen in Acts 21, where James said to Paul: "You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and all of them are zealots for the law." Thus in passing he warns, in a single word, that the law is so far from removing the sting of death, that is, from taking sin out of our flesh, that it rather serves sin to gain greater power. Therefore it is necessary that victory over sin and death be gained from elsewhere. And so he immediately adds where that victory comes from, saying:

units.la: SED Deo gratia, qui dedit nobis uictoriā per dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. ] Sic quod per legem fieri non potuit, tribuit Christo. Nō autem simpliciter dicit, At uictoria per Christum: sed quoniam omnis illa salutis nostræ & futuræ immortalitatis gratia in hac est uictoria sita, cū affectu gratitudinis: Sed Deo, inquit, gratia, qui dedit nobis uictoriā per dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Primum, dicit Deū nobis dedisse uictoriam. Non 'simpliciter dicit illum uicisse peccatū, mortem & infernum, sed nobis dedisse uictoriam. In uerbo Dandi, agnoscit uictoriam hanc esse donum Dei. Loquitur autem in præterito de re nondum in nobis in uniuersum impleta, sed in futuro demum implenda. Qui dedit nobis, inqt, uictoriam. Ergo deuicta sunt peccatum, mors & infernus. Atqui peccamus adhuc, & morimur, & corrumpimur. Verum, sed omne peccati dominium, & ius quo nos æternæ reddebat condemnationi obnoxios, extinctum est, ut nihil superfit, nisi reliquiæ quædam quæ tamen nos, nec in morte, nec in corruptione retinere possunt. Plena uictoria erit, ubi prorsus absorpta erit mors cum suo aculeo. Et ea tam est certa, ut iam nobis illam à Deo datam esse dicat.
units.tr: "But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." So he attributes to Christ what could not be done by the law. He does not simply say, "But the victory through Christ," but because all that grace of our salvation and future immortality rests in this victory, he speaks with a feeling of gratitude: "But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." First, he says that God has given us the victory. He does not simply say that God conquered sin, death and hell, but that he has given us the victory. In the word "given," he acknowledges that this victory is a gift of God. He speaks of it in the past tense, of a thing not yet fully accomplished in us, but to be accomplished in the future. "Who has given us," he says, "the victory." So sin, death and hell have been defeated. Yet we still sin, die and are corrupted. True, but all the dominion of sin, and the right by which it made us liable to eternal condemnation, has been extinguished, so that nothing remains except certain remnants, which nevertheless cannot hold us either in death or in corruption. The victory will be complete when death has been utterly swallowed up with its sting. And that victory is so certain that he already says it has been given us by God.

units.la: Deinde non dicit, qui dedit ut uictores eua deremus: sed, Qui dedit nobis uictoriam per dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Ergo ille uicit Satanam, peccatum, mortem, & infernū, atq; per hunc nobis hæc est uictoria perta. Vicit autem in cruce ubi chirographum decreti quod contrarium nobis erat de medio sustulit, deleuit ac cruci affixit, deque potestatibus inferorum triumphauit, & mortem destruxit. Sic uicit mediator noster, uicitque nō sibi, sed nobis. Ad hunc modum totum uictoriæ huius opus, soli gratię Dei, quæ est per Christum assignatur. Quare ex animo & merito dicit, Deo sit gratia, qui dedit nobis uictoriam per dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Hæc gratiarū actio nō potest reddi ex animo, nisi ab illis, qui & agnoscunt, & fatentur, donum esse Dei prorsus gratuitum, quod à peccato sunt, & morte liberati: nec esse hic quicquam, quod propriæ suæ iusticiæ meritis possint adscribere, agnoscunt, inquam, mortem deberi peccato, uitam uero, & uictoriam mortis solius esse gratię Dei per Christum. Hæc est sana & Christiana doctrina, quam nec Iudæi, nec Turci, nec pseudo christiani, sed ueri tantum fideles recipiunt, & gratias agunt Deo, & domino Iesu Christo, unico mediatori ac redemptori.
units.tr: Then he does not say, "who gave us victory" in the sense that we should be made victors; rather, "who gave us victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." Therefore he conquered Satan, sin, death and hell, and through him this victory has been obtained for us. He conquered on the cross, where he removed the handwriting of the decree that was against us, nailed it to the cross, blotted it out, triumphed over the powers of the underworld and destroyed death. Thus our mediator conquered, and he conquered not for himself but for us. In this way the whole work of this victory is ascribed to the grace of God alone, which is through Christ. Therefore he rightly and sincerely says, "Thanks be to God, who gave us victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." This thanksgiving cannot be offered sincerely except by those who acknowledge and confess that the gift of God is wholly free, by which they have been freed from sin and death, and who recognise that there is nothing here that they can ascribe to the merits of their own righteousness; they acknowledge, I say, that death is owed to sin, but life and victory over death belong solely to the grace of God through Christ. This is sound and Christian doctrine, which is received not by the Jews, nor the Turks, nor pseudo-Christians, but only by true believers, who give thanks to God and to the Lord Jesus Christ, the only mediator and redeemer.

units.la: Itaq; fratres mei dilecti, stabiles sitis, immobiles, abundantes in opere domini semper, scientes quod labor uesterno est inanis in domino.
units.tr: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.

units.la: Hac paraenesi omnem hanc de resurrectione disputationem sic concludit, ut simul exprimat, quid Corinthijs à prauo eorū colloquio timuerit, qui resurrectionem mortuorum alij prorsus negabant, alij in dubium uocabát. Timebat uidelicet, ne si illis aures pręberent, red derentur in fide Christi instabiles, & in opere domini remisi ac desides, propterea quod cogitarent, ergo uanum est quicquid propter Christum uel fecerimus uel passi fuerimus, quandoquidem mortui non resurgent. Vt igitur ei periculo occurreret, finalem hanc parænesim attemperauit ad hunc modum, Itaq; fratres mei dilecti stabiles sitis, &c. Quasi dicat: Cum itaq; certo sit futurum, ut resurgant mortui in die domini, nosq; qui tum superstites erimus immutemur, hoc est, immortales & incorruptibiles & peccato & morte deuictis reddamur, sitq; ea nobis uictoria per Christum iam parta, & à Deo patre dono gratuito omnium certissime data: etiam atq; etiá cauete, ne praui sermonibus eorum, qui resurrectione mortuorum negant, seducti, tam insigni hac gratia uosipsi priuetis: quod facturi estis, si de illa dubitantes instabiles, immobiles ac desertores operis domini facti fueritis. Quare curate potius, ut sitis stabiles, immobiles, abundantes in opere domini semper, &c.
units.tr: With this exhortation he concludes the whole of this discussion about the resurrection, and at the same time expresses what he feared for the Corinthians from the perverse talk of those who either altogether denied the resurrection of the dead or called it into doubt. He was evidently afraid that if they lent them their ears, they would become unstable in the faith of Christ and slack and idle in the work of the Lord, because they would reason: "It is therefore vain whatever we have done or suffered for Christ, since the dead will not rise." So, to meet this danger, he tempered this final exhortation in this way: "Therefore, my beloved brethren, be steadfast," and so on. As if he were saying: since it is certain that the dead will rise in the day of the Lord, and we who then remain alive will be changed, that is, made immortal and incorruptible, conquerors over sin and death, and since this victory has already been won for us through Christ and given by God the Father as a free gift most surely of all; take even more and more care not to be led astray by the words of those who deny the resurrection of the dead, and not to deprive yourselves of so remarkable a grace. You will do so if, doubting it, you become unstable, unmovable, and deserters of the work of the Lord. Therefore take care rather to be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, and so on.

units.la: ITAQVE fratres mei dilecti, inquit.
units.tr: Therefore, my beloved brethren, he says.

units.la: Observa affectum fraternæ charitatis, cuius emphasis est nō modo in persona Apostoli, sed & in qualitate eorū quibus scribit. Carnales adhuc erant, ac multis nominibus culpabiles. Et tamen haud dedignatur eos diligere & habere pro fratribus, qui uix idonei erant, ut essent discipuli.
units.tr: Notice the affection of brotherly love, whose emphasis lies not only in the person of the Apostle but also in the character of those to whom he writes. They were still carnal and blameworthy in many respects. Yet he does not disdain to love them and to regard them as brethren, though they were scarcely fit to be disciples.

units.la: STABILES, inquit, fitis, immobiles.
units.tr: "Be steadfast," he says, "immovable."

units.la: Cogitemus hic, quàm non sit satis ab errore uenire ad cognitionem ueritatis, participemq; fieri cœlestis gratię, nisi in ueritate & gratia Dei firmi perfistamus. Natura sumus instabiles, præsertim in bono. Quare crebris est adhortationibus opus, ut in bono ad finem usq; perseueremus. Nisi enim perseuerauerimus, salui fieri non poterimus. Imò, si defecerimus, peiora erunt posteriora prioribus. Multo nanq; melius est nō cognoscere uiam iustitiæ quàm post illius cognitionem retro à sancto propositio auerti. Quare Apostolus non minore cura ad perseuerantiam hortatus est fideles, quàm ad gratiam Christi uocauit infideles.
units.tr: Let us consider here how it is not enough to come from error to the knowledge of the truth and to become partakers of heavenly grace, unless we persevere firmly in the truth and grace of God. By nature we are unstable, especially in what is good. Therefore frequent exhortations are needed, that we may persevere in good to the end. For unless we persevere, we cannot be saved. Indeed, if we fall away, the latter things will be worse than the former. For it is much better not to know the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment proposed to us. Therefore the Apostle exhorted the faithful to perseverance with no less care than he called the unbelievers to the grace of Christ.

units.la: STABILES, inquit, estote.
units.tr: "Be steadfast," he says.

units.la: In Græco est, ἑδραῖοι γίνεσθε. Sonat autem ἕδρα Græcis firmam basim ac fundamētū, unde est ἑδραῖος fundatus. Requirit ergo non simplicem ac uulgarem stabilitatem, sed qualem habent bases ac fundamenta. Nec immerito. Est enim ueritas Christianæ fidei omnium in se firmissima, instar petræ, contra quā ne portę inferorum quidē quicquam poterunt. In illa firmi esse possunt fideles, quod in mendacio fieri non potest.
units.tr: In Greek it is ἑδραῖοι γίνεσθε. The word ἕδρα in Greek signifies a firm base or foundation, whence ἑδραῖος means founded. He therefore requires not a simple and common stability, but such as bases and foundations have. Nor without reason. For the truth of the Christian faith is of all things the most firm in itself, like a rock, against which not even the gates of hell can prevail. In that truth the faithful can be firm, which cannot be done in a lie.

units.la: IMMOBILES, inquit.
units.tr: "Immovable," he says.

units.la: Græce est, ἀμετακίνητοι. Est autem ἀμετακίνητος non simpliciter immobilis, sed is, qui de loco in quo est in alium, uel de sententia quam tenet in aliam transmutari non potest. Tales autem sunt ἱδρᾶιοι, homi-
units.tr: In Greek it is ἀμετακίνητοι. ἀμετακίνητος means not simply immovable, but one who cannot be transferred from the place where he is to another, or from the opinion he holds to another. Such are the ἑδραῖοι, men

units.la: nes in sententia sua firmiter fundati. Et in hûc finem hortatur eos ut sint in fide fundati ac firmi, ne uidelicet instar harúdinis in aliam atq; aliam sententiam ad quemuis seductionis uentum transmoueri se sinant. Quicquid leue est, ac superficiei tantū inhæret, ἀμετακίνητον esse nō potest. Quæ fundo innituntur, haud facile cuiuis uento cedunt. Vtinam eiusmodi stabilitas ostendant in fide ac ueritate Dei, qui de uerbo & Euangelio Dei gloriantur.
units.tr: firmly founded in their opinion. And to this end he exhorts them to be founded and firm in the faith, lest, that is, they allow themselves to be moved like a reed into one opinion after another at every gust of seduction. Whatever is light and clings only to the surface cannot be ἀμετακίνητον. Those things that rest on a foundation do not easily yield to every wind. Would that those who boast of the word and Gospel of God would show such stability in the faith and truth of God.

units.la: ABVNDANTES, inquit, in opere domini semper.] Ergo non hoc tantum requirit, ut sint in fide stabiles & immobiles, sed & ut in opere domini semper sint abundantes. Vocat autem opus domini, non quod ipse dominus per uerbum & spiritum suum in ipsis coeperat, & ministerio Apostolico pficiebat, de quo capite sequenti loquitur, cum dicit: Quod si uenerit Timotheus, uidete ut absq; metu sit apud uos: opus enim domini operatur, quēadmodū & ego. Laborabat enim & ipse in Euangelio Dei, quē labore uocat opus domini: sed uocat hic opus domini, opus charitatis mutuæ, quo frater fratri ac fideli & tribuēdo quæ necessaria erant, & consolando adhortandoq; seruiebat. Idem epistola sequenti capite nono sic exprimit: Vt abundetis in omne opus bonum. Loquitur autem ibi de eleemosyna, quæ facienda erat in pauperes.
units.tr: "ABOUNDING," he says, "in the work of the Lord always." Therefore he requires not only that they be steadfast and immovable in the faith, but also that they always abound in the work of the Lord. He calls it the work of the Lord not because the Lord himself had begun it in them through his word and Spirit and it was being carried on by the Apostolic ministry, of which he speaks in the following chapter when he says: "But if Timothy comes, see that he is without fear among you; for he works the work of the Lord, as I also do." For he too laboured in the Gospel of God, and this labour he calls the work of the Lord. But here he calls the work of the Lord the work of mutual charity, by which one brother served another and fellow believer, both by giving what was needful and by comforting and exhorting. The same thing he expresses in the ninth chapter of the following epistle: "that you may abound in every good work." There he speaks of almsgiving, which was to be done for the poor.

units.la: Non est uero ociosum, quod opus Christianæ charitatis uocat opus domini. Præterquā enim quod fit ex spiritu domini, etiam hoc non mine recte uocatur opus domini, qd' in mem bra domini confertur, adeoq; ipsi domino impenditur. Sic enim dicturus est in nouissimo die: Quicquid fecistis uni ex minimis meis, mihi fecistis, Matthęi 25. Sic cohonestat opera pietatis & misericordiæ, uocans ea, opera domini. Quemadmodum enim si uolens abstterrere fideles ab odio fratrum & malefaciendi studio, uoces illud opus diaboli: sic Apostolus fraternam charitatem & studium beneficentiæ mutuæ opus domini ad hoc uocat, ut animos nostros respectu domini ad quæuis bona opera plus aliquanto accendat.
units.tr: It is not idle that he calls the work of Christian charity the work of the Lord. For besides the fact that it is done by the Spirit of the Lord, it is also rightly called the work of the Lord because it is contributed to the members of the Lord and so is bestowed upon the Lord himself. For so he will say on the last day: "What you did to one of the least of these my brethren, you did to me," Matthew 25. Thus he honours works of piety and mercy by calling them works of the Lord. For just as, if one wished to frighten the faithful away from hatred of brethren and from the zeal of doing harm, he would call that the work of the devil; so the Apostle calls brotherly charity and the zeal of mutual kindness the work of the Lord, in order that, with regard to the Lord, he may kindle our minds somewhat more to every good work.

units.la: Vide autem quid à fidelibus in hoc opere domini requirat. Nō simpliciter dicit, operantes opus domini: sed, abundantes in opere domini semper. Vulgata habet, in omni, hoc est, in quouis, opere domini. Requirit ergo non simpliciter, ut quod bonum est, qualitercunq; & semel atq; iterum operemur, sed ut in opere domini copiose ac largiter deinde indesinenter laboremus. Qui non ex fide, sed ne non religiosi ac pij uideantur, aliquid boni operis faciunt, faciunt hoc primum non larga manu & abundanter, sed parce ac tenuiter, utcunq; & perfunctorie: deinde nonsemper ac indesinenter, sed semel atq; iterū, & postea cessant. Duabus hisce notis iudicare poteris de bonis illorum operibus, qui nō ex fide & corde integro quod bonum est faciunt, sed uel ad ostentatio nem, uel ad cauendum ne habeantur pro minus nus Christianis. Quarecum timeret Apostolus ne Corinthij de futura resurrectione dubitantes parcius ac rarius quod bonum est facerent, quemadmodum eos hortatur, ut in fide sint stabiles & immobiles: ita hortatur etiam, ut abundantes sint in opere domini semper, significans eos qui nihil prorsus de futura resurrectione ac vita dubitant, haud parce & inconstanter, sed abundanter ac iugiter in opere domini versari.
units.tr: But notice what he requires of the faithful in this work of the Lord. He does not simply say "working the work of the Lord," but "abounding in the work of the Lord always." The Vulgate has "in every," that is, "in whatever," work of the Lord. He requires, therefore, not merely that we do what is good in whatever manner and once or twice, but that we labour in the work of the Lord copiously and generously, and then without ceasing. Those who do some good work not from faith, but lest they should not seem religious and pious, first do it not with an open hand and abundantly, but sparingly and meagrely, in whatever way and perfunctorily; then not always and without ceasing, but once or twice, and afterwards they stop. By these two marks you may judge the good works of those who do what is good not from faith and a sincere heart, but either for display or to avoid being thought less than Christian. Therefore, since the Apostle feared that the Corinthians, doubting the future resurrection, would do what is good more sparingly and rarely, he exhorts them to be steadfast and immovable in the faith; so he also exhorts them to be always abounding in the work of the Lord, signifying that those who entertain no doubt at all about the future resurrection and life are not sparing and inconstant, but abundant and continual in working in the work of the Lord.

units.la: Non est autem eo rapiendum, quod dicit, abundantes, quasi requirat, ut fideles plura faciant in opere domini quàm debeant, sitq; locus supererogationi, quam doctores meritorum & mundinatores indulgentiarum comminiscuntur. Simpliciter requirit, ut copiose non parce laborent in opere domini, sicut in epistola sequenti cap.9. hortatur. Abundare in opere domini, est uel respectu aliorum qui minus operantur exuberare, quo sensu usus est hac uoce Christus Matth.5. dicens: Nisi abundauerit iusticia uestra plus quàm scribarū & pharisęorum: uel de die in diem crescere in studio benefaciendi, quemadmodum fideles numero indies abundasse Act.16. legitur: uel simpliciter, non tenuiter & parce, sed copiose ac largiter, sicuti solent q quod faciunt, faciūt ex animo, bonis operibus studere. Abundantia quæ iustum ac debitum beneficentię modum excedat, in Christiana pietate locum non habet, in qua synceritas cordis totum sese in usus proximi effundentis, & dilectionis perfectio requiritur, qua & inimicos diligamus, & animas nostras pro fratribus, si ita necesse sit, tradere non dubitemus.
units.tr: It should not, however, be taken in this way, that he says "abounding," as if he required that the faithful do more in the work of the Lord than they ought, and so leave room for that supererogation which the teachers of merits and the hawkers of indulgences invent. He simply requires that they labour in the work of the Lord copiously and not sparingly, as he exhorts in the following epistle, chapter 9. To abound in the work of the Lord means either to excel in comparison with others who do less, in which sense Christ used this word in Matthew 5, saying: "Unless your righteousness abound more than that of the scribes and Pharisees"; or to grow from day to day in zeal for doing good, as it is read in Acts 16 that the faithful abounded in number daily; or simply not to be meagre and sparing, but copious and generous, as those who do what they do from the heart are accustomed to be zealous in good works. An abundance that exceeds the just and due measure of beneficence has no place in Christian piety, in which sincerity of heart, pouring itself wholly out for the use of one's neighbour, and perfection of love are required, by which we love even our enemies and do not hesitate to lay down our lives for the brethren, if so it should be necessary.

units.la: SCIENTES, inquit, quod labor uester non est inanis in domino.] Magnæ emphasis est hæ particula. Triplex est labor fidelium in domino. Primus ministrorum Euangelij. Secundus ac tertius fidelibus omnibus & ministris communis. Primus in prædicatione Euágelij, secundus in charitate fraterna. Tertius in servanda fidei integritate & Christianæ uitæ sanctimonia. Nec primus, nec secundus nec tertius est inanis. Inanis est labor, ubi frustra laboratur. Frustra laborare, est laboris finem non assequi, uel in eo laborare, unde nullus potest provenire laboris fructus. Labor ministrorum & fidelium in domino, inanis esse non potest, non laborantium merito, aut laboris respectu, sed propter bonitatem ac veritatem domini, qui labores suorum contemnere ac frustrare non potest. Quare locū hic non habent, qui fiduciā operum ac laborū docent in ecclesia. Quod labor noster inanis non est, domino adscribit Apostolus, non nobis. Ideo non simpliciter dicit, quod labor uester non est inanis: sed addit, in domino. Nec cuilibet labori, sed labori, qui sit in domino, hoc est, in causa veritate ac spiritu dei factus: nec in nobis, sed in domino, hoc est, in gratia & virtute domini, hoc tribuitur, quod non sit inanis. Nihil igitur tribuitur ab Apostolo laboribus nostris, quod non totum
units.tr: "KNOWING," he says, "that your labour is not in vain in the Lord." This particle carries great emphasis. The labour of the faithful in the Lord is threefold. The first is that of the ministers of the Gospel. The second and third are common to all the faithful and to the ministers. The first is in the preaching of the Gospel, the second in brotherly love, the third in keeping the integrity of the faith and the holiness of Christian life. None of the first, second or third is in vain. Labour is in vain when it is laboured to no purpose, that is, when one does not attain the goal of the labour, or labours at something from which no fruit of labour can come. The labour of ministers and of the faithful in the Lord cannot be in vain, not because of the merit of those who labour, nor by reason of the labour itself, but on account of the goodness and truth of the Lord, who cannot despise or frustrate the labours of his own. Therefore those who teach confidence in works and labours in the Church have no place here. That our labour is not in vain the Apostle ascribes to the Lord, not to us. Hence he does not simply say that your labour is not in vain, but adds, "in the Lord." And it is not to any labour whatever, but to labour which is done in the Lord, that is, performed in the cause of truth and by the Spirit of God, and not in us but in the Lord, that is, by the grace and power of the Lord, that this is granted, that it is not in vain. Nothing therefore is attributed by the Apostle to our labours which does not wholly

units.la: pendeat à gratia & uirtute domini. Quod nos attinet, inania sunt quę molimur omnia. Quid enim aliud præstiterit homo qui uanitas uanitatum uocatur à propheta? Quod uero bonitatem, gratiam, & uirtutem domini attinet, non est labor noster in ipso inanis.
units.tr: depend on the grace and power of the Lord. As far as we are concerned, all the things we undertake are empty. For what else has man accomplished, whom the prophet calls "vanity of vanities"? But as far as the goodness, grace and power of the Lord are concerned, our labour in him is not in vain.

units.la: Obserua uero quod non simpliciter dicit, quoniam fieri potest, ut nó sit labor uester inanis in domino: sed, scientes quod nó sit labor uester inanis in domino. Verbum sciendi opponit diffidentiæ ac dubitationi. Qui hæsitat, fluctuat inconstans, nec firmo gradu in opere bono pergit. Qui uero scit se non in uanũ operari, constanter in bono opere perseuerat.
units.tr: Observe, moreover, that he does not simply say, "It may happen that your labour is not in vain in the Lord," but "knowing that your labour is not in vain in the Lord." He sets the word "knowing" against diffidence and doubt. The one who hesitates wavers unsteadily and does not press on in good work with a firm step. But the one who knows that he does not labour in vain perseveres constantly in good work.

units.la: Ergóne Apostolus respectu fructus, ex bonis operibus prouenturi, animos Corinthiorum ad bene operandum incitat? Cum dicit: scientes quod non sit labor uester inanis in domino. Respondeo. Generalis hic est laborantium omnium scopus, ut sperent se non laborare inaniter. ut quid enim facias, quod scias esse inane? Verum alius atq; alius est laborum nostrorum fructus. Alius laboranti, alius illis propter quos laboratur cedit. Si sciam laborē meum in usus uel gloriæ Dei, uel proximi, uel meæ ipsius salutis cedere posse, cur non inde reddar in illo alacrior, quàm si dubitem ac fluctuem? Quis seruus, imò quis filius, non pluri mam inde ad iustam obedientiam permouetur, si sciat se hero uel patri uoluntati ipsius obtemperando, posse gratificari? Cū diceret hic Apostolus: Scio cui credidi & certus sum, quod potens sit depositum meum seruare in illum diem, 2. Timot. 1. Et illud capite ultimo eiusdem epistolæ: Bonum certamen certaui, cursum cōsummaui, fidem seruaui, quod reliquum est, repositia est mihi corona iusticię, quam reddet mihi dominus in illa die iustus iudex, non est ut iusticiarius ac mercenarius Apostolus solquutus: sed non modo laborum suorum solatium exprimere, sed & Timotheum suum & alios Christi ministros in opere domini sicut hic Corinthios, animare uoluit.
units.tr: Does the Apostle therefore stir the minds of the Corinthians to do good works by regard to the fruit that will come from good works, when he says, "knowing that your labour is not in vain in the Lord"? I answer: this is the general aim of all labourers, that they may hope they are not labouring in vain; for why would you do what you know to be empty? Yet the fruit of our labours is one thing for the labourer and another for those for whose sake the labour is undertaken. If I know that my labour can result in the use of God's glory, or of my neighbour, or of my own salvation, why should I not be more eager in it than if I doubted and wavered? What servant, nay, what son, is not much more moved to just obedience if he knows that by obeying his master or father's will he can give him pleasure? When this Apostle said, "I know whom I have believed, and I am sure that he is able to keep what I have committed to him until that day" (2 Tim. 1), and in the last chapter of the same epistle, "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me in that day" (2 Tim. 4), he did not speak as a Apostle who was a mere hireling seeking reward; but he wished not only to express the solace of his labours, but also to encourage his Timothy and other ministers of Christ in the work of the Lord, as here he encourages the Corinthians.

units.la: CAPVT XVI.
units.tr: Chapter 16

units.la: Aeterum de collatione in sanctos, quemadmodū ordinaui ecclesijs Galatię, ita & uos facite. In una sabbatorum unusquisq; uestrum apud se seponat, recondens quicquid commodum fuerit, ne cum uenero, tunc collationes fiant.
units.tr: Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do. On the first day of the week let each of you set something aside at home, storing up whatever he has been able to spare, so that no collections need to be made when I come.

units.la: Haætenus Apostolus mala in ecclesia Corinthiorum in moribus uitæ, in ritibus sacris, in donis spiritus, & fide resurrectionis mortuorum pullulantia diligenti correctione amolitus: iam cōsequenter ad opus fraternę charitatis dirigendum progreditur dicens, Cęterum de collatione in sanctos quemadmodum ordinaui ecclesijs Galatię. dinaui ecclesijs Galatię,ita & uos facite.Quáuis multis ecclesia illa uicijs laborabat,nō contentus tamen illorum reprehensione & correctione adhortationem annectit,qua fideles illius ad opera Christianæ dilectionis rite prosequenda dirigat.
units.tr: Up to this point the Apostle has, with careful correction, removed the evils that had sprung up in the Corinthian church: in their conduct of life, in their sacred rites, in the gifts of the Spirit, and in their faith in the resurrection of the dead. Now he goes on, in sequence, to direct the work of brotherly love, saying: "Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also do." Although that church was troubled by many faults, he does not rest content with rebuking and correcting them, but adds an exhortation by which he rightly directs his faithful people to carry out the works of Christian love.

units.la: Loquitur autem de sanctis ecclesiæ Christi quæ erat in Iudæah. Hi potissimum opus habebant subsidio ecclesiarum,quæ erant inter Gentes,partim propter insignem illam famé, quam propheta Agabus futuram prædixerat, quæ & sub Claudio imperatore euenit, sicut Actorum undecimo legimus: partim propter grauissimas persequutiones,quibus à sua gente afflictabantur, quarum meminit hic Apostolus,1.Thess.2.dicens: Vos enim imitatores facti estis fratres ecclesiarum Dei quæ sunt in Iudæa in Christo Iesu,quia eadem passi estis & uos à contribulibus uestris sicut & ipsi à Iudæis,&c. Quare & apostoli Iacobus, Cephas & Iohannes,Paulo & Barnabæ,cum cõstituerent,ut illi inter Gentes Christum annunciarent,iniunxerũt ut memores essent pauperũ, quod etiam diligenter fecerunt, sicut ipse Paulus Gal.2.meminit,& hoc præsenti loco uidere licet, quemadmodum & in ea quæ ad Romanos est capite 15.
units.tr: He speaks of the saints of the church of Christ which was in Judaea. These above all needed the help of the churches that were among the Gentiles, partly because of that severe famine which the prophet Agabus had foretold would come, and which did happen under the emperor Claudius, as we read in Acts 11; and partly because of the very grievous persecutions by which they were afflicted by their own nation, which this Apostle mentions in 1 Thess. 2, saying: "For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God that are in Judaea in Christ Jesus, for you also suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews," etc. Therefore also the apostles James, Cephas and John, when they agreed that Paul and Barnabas should proclaim Christ among the Gentiles, enjoined that they remember the poor, which they also did diligently, as Paul himself records in Gal. 2. And in the present place we can see this, as also in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 15.

units.la: CAETERVM,inquit,de collatione.] Græcè est, ... posuit pro ... uocem simplicem pro composita. Sonat collectionem,quam aliàs uocát collectam: quippe colligere significat. Vsus est Apostolus hac uoce tantum hoc loco. Ad Romanos cap.15. ..., id est,cómunicationem uocat, quâ hic uocat collectionem. Colligebantur tributa fidelium, quæ communicarentur fratribus egenis in Iudæah. Quare illa hic collectam,illic communicationem uocauit. Colligunt & sacrificuli in missis suis,retinétq; ipsum adhuc collectæ nomen,uerum collecta ipsorum non poterit uocari cômunicatio,quia in priuatos ipsorum non in communes egentium fratrum usus conuertitur.Quemadmodũ igitur factio nem panis habent in missis suis fine cômunicatione,ita & collectas habent à cômunicatio ne alienas.In epist.sequenti cap.9.ubi de eadẽ hac causa fecundo scribit,quam hic uocat ..., uocat ..., ubi Eraf.uertit,bonam collationem,cum aliàs sonet benedictionem: uerũ de ea uoce illic,uolente domino dicemus.
units.tr: "Concerning the collection," he says. In Greek it is ... The Apostle has used the simple word in place of the compound. It means a collection, which elsewhere he calls a gathering, for it signifies bringing together. The Apostle uses this word only in this place. In Romans 15 he calls it ..., that is, communication, which here he calls collection. The contributions of the faithful were gathered, to be shared with the needy brothers in Judaea. Hence he calls it a collection here and a communication there. The little priests also collect in their masses and still keep the very name of collect, but their collects cannot be called communication, because they are turned not to the use of needy brothers but to their own private use. Just as they have a distribution of bread in their masses without any communication, so they have collects that are foreign to communication. In the following epistle, chapter 9, where he writes a second time about this same matter, which he here calls ..., and where Erasmus translates it "a good collection", although elsewhere the word means blessing, we shall speak of that word there, the Lord willing.

units.la: Ergo subsidium quo leuatur inopia egetiũ fratrũ,uocat Apostolus ..., & ..., collectionem uidelicet, benedictionē & communicationem. Collectionis uoce etiam Germani utimur,dũ eleemosynā in usus pauperum collectam uocamus,famlung.Quemadmodum enim fructus feracis agri tépore messis colliguntur.ita in ecclesia, ueluti feracium arborum agro, colligitur à fidelibus eleemosyna,qua sustententur egeni.
units.tr: So the help by which the want of needy brothers is relieved the Apostle calls ... and ..., namely collection, blessing and communication. We Germans also use the word collection when we call alms gathered for the use of the poor "famlung". For just as the fruits of a fertile field are gathered at harvest time, so in the church, as in an orchard of fruitful trees, alms are gathered from the faithful by which the needy are sustained.

units.la: Agrũ hunc ecclesiasticorũ fructuũ ingressi sunt collectores monachorum mendicantiũ, hominum ociosorum,subsidia uerorum pau-
units.tr: Into this field of ecclesiastical fruits have entered the collectors of the mendicant monks, idle men, who divert to themselves the support meant for the true poor,

units.la: perum interuertentium,deinde & stationarij, & quæstionarij, & indulgentiarij, &c.qui omnes deuotione,ut uocant,simplicium Christianorum in quæstum suum ad saginandos ocio sos uentres hactenus sunt abusi:utinā uel nūc tandem uere Christianæ collectæ per fraternæ charitatis spiritū post tot impositas luce uer bi Dei proditas in ecclesijs obtineant. Habeát ueri pauperes suos collectores,homines pios ac fideles,qui sciant se seruiendo pauperibus Christi,ipsi seruire Christo.Ad hanc collectionem requiritur à Christianis, ut dent largiter cũ benedictione,ut quod quisq; dat,uere positi uocari benedictio.qua de re in epist. sequẽti diligenter admonemur. A collectoribus uero requiritur,ut quod ex liberali fidelium charitate collegerunt,fideliter & competenter egenis fratribus secundum cuiusq; necessitate distribuant,ut sit non solum larga fidelium benedictio, & sedula collectio,sed & fidelis distributio,& fraterna communicatio.
units.tr: and then the stationers, the questors and the indulgence-sellers, and so on, who all, up to now, have abused the devotion, as they call it, of simple Christians to make profit for themselves, in order to fatten their idle bellies. Would that now at last truly Christian collections might prevail in the churches, through the spirit of brotherly love, after so many lights of the Word of God have been brought forth and published. Let the true poor have their own collectors, pious and faithful men, who know that in serving Christ's poor they serve Christ himself. For this collection, Christians are required to give generously and with blessing, so that whatever each person gives may rightly be called a blessing; on this matter we are carefully admonished in the following epistle. From the collectors, however, it is required that what they have gathered from the generous love of the faithful they distribute faithfully and suitably to the needy brothers, according to each one's need. Thus there will be not only a generous blessing and a diligent collection from the faithful, but also a faithful distribution and a brotherly communication.

units.la: DE collatione, inquit,in sanctos.]Colligit in sanctos &diabolus,uerum non subsidia,sed uim aduersariam,ecclesiam uidelicet malignatium.Colligimus in hostem copias militum. At hoc loco colligere in sanctos, est colligere subsidium in usus sanctorum, qd' perinde est ac si te dicas æstate colligere in hyemem, & pa rentes colligere in liberos.
units.tr: "Concerning the collection," he says, "for the saints." The devil also collects for the saints, but not for aid; rather for hostile force, namely the church of the wicked. We gather troops of soldiers against an enemy. But in this place, to collect for the saints is to collect aid for the use of the saints, just as if you were to say that you collect in summer for winter, or that parents collect for their children.

units.la: Obserua uero, quales habeat ecclesia sanctos. Tales uidelicet,in quos possint, imò necesse sit,corporalia uitæ huius colligi subsidia. Hoc genus sanctorum, pauperum esurientiũ, sitientium,nudorum, infirmorum, exulum & captiuorum non agnoscit papatus, in quo nō habentur sancti, nisi canonizati diui, quibus nullus est collectæ subsidiariæ usus. At ueris sanctis neglectis, in diuos colligunt opes regias.Et interim accusant nos quod contemna mus sanctos,propterea quod Deum colimus non diuos,& in ueros sanctos non diuos colli gimus.Quod autem pauperes uocat sanctos, cum posset dicere, De collectione in pauperes:ad hoc facit, ut commendet illis pauperũ fidelium necessitates,reddatq; illos ad conferendum propensiores,dum admonet, nō esse contemnendos pauperes Christi, qui licet iuxta seculum egestate premantur,& propter egestatem,quæ ridiculos solet homines reddere in hoc seculo,cótemptibiles appareant: pter gratiam tamen cœlestis uocationis sint uere sancti & in precio habendi.Paupertas nō reddit sanctum.Inuenias passim pauperes im pios & prophanos. Verum si fideles sint pauperes,Christianæ fuerit mentis respicere in illis non quid appareant in seculo sed quid sint in regno Dei,ideoq; uocare eos non pauperes cum seculo,sed sanctos cum Apostolo.
units.tr: Observe, however, what kind of saints the church has: namely, such as bodily aids for this life can be, and indeed must be, collected for. The papacy does not recognise this kind of saint, the hungry, thirsty, naked, sick, exiles and captives. In the papacy no one is counted a saint except the canonized divine ones, to whom there is no use for a collection of aid. But while the true saints are neglected, they collect royal wealth for the divine ones. And meanwhile they accuse us of despising the saints, because we worship God and not the divine ones, and because we do not collect for the true saints, who are not divine ones. Now the reason he calls the poor "saints", when he could have said "a collection for the poor", is to commend to them the needs of the faithful poor and to make them more ready to contribute, while he admonishes that the poor of Christ are not to be despised. For although they are oppressed by want according to the world, and because of that poverty, which is wont to make men ridiculous in this world, they appear contemptible; yet by reason of the grace of the heavenly calling they are truly saints and to be held in honour. Poverty does not make a man holy. You will find poor men everywhere who are impious and profane. But if the poor are faithful, it is the mark of a Christian mind to regard in them not what they appear to be in the world but what they are in the kingdom of God; and therefore to call them not "the poor" according to the world, but "saints", with the Apostle.

units.la: QVEMADMODVM ordinaui,inquit, ecclesijs Galatiæ,ita & uos facite. ] Non solum docuit quid sit faciendum fidelibus in operibus charitatis,sed & ordinem faciendorũ præscripsit.Non dicit, Collectas in sanctos facite: sed, de collectione aut in sanctos, quèadmodum ordinaui ecclesijs Galatię, ita & uos facite. Est igitur apostolici uiri nō solū facienda docere, sed & modos & ordinem faciendorū cōstitue re, quo quę facienda sunt, rite, cōpetenter & utiliter fiant. Ipsius quidem domini est leges statuere faciendorum, quas ministri & interpretes ipsius pponant ecclesię. Verū ut illę decēter & ordine seruentur, ministrorū est ordinare, sicut hic in Apostolo uidemus. Præceptum domini est, nō Apostoli, ut nos inuicem diligamus, & hoc faciētes inuenimur discipuli nō Apostoli, sed ipsius domini: ut uero charitas ista in certis casibus competenter exerceatur, ad officium pertinet Apostoli ac ministri Christi ut plebi fideliū uias & modos faciendorum ordinet ac disponat. Neq; enim satis est homini Christiano, si bonis operib. studeat, nisi quod faciendum est rite & utiliter, secūdū circūstantias tēporum, locorū, personarū & causarū faciat, ad quam rem prudens Christi minister ecclesiæ disponendo & ordinando subseruiet.
units.tr: "Just as I ordered," he says, "the churches of Galatia, so you also do." He has not only taught what the faithful must do in works of love, but has also prescribed the order of doing them. He does not say "Make collections for the saints", but "Concerning the collection for the saints, just as I ordered the churches of Galatia, so you also do." It is therefore the task of an apostolic man not only to teach what is to be done, but also to establish the methods and order of doing it, so that what must be done is done duly, suitably and usefully. It is indeed the Lord's own prerogative to lay down laws for what is to be done, which his ministers and interpreters set before the church. But that these laws are observed becomingly and in good order is the task of ministers, as we see in the Apostle here. It is the Lord's precept, not the Apostle's, that we love one another, and in doing this we are found to be disciples not of the Apostle but of the Lord himself. But that this love is exercised suitably in certain cases belongs to the office of the Apostle and of Christ's minister, who arranges and disposes the ways and methods of doing for the people of the faithful. For it is not enough for a Christian to be eager for good works unless he does what must be done duly and usefully, according to the circumstances of times, places, persons and causes. To this end the prudent minister of Christ in the church will serve by arranging and ordaining.

units.la: QVEMADMODVM ordinaui, inqt, ecclesijs Galatiæ. ] De Galatia si quid dicendum est, uidebitur in epistola q̃ ad Galatas scripsit, si per gratiā dei ad explicationē illius peruenerimus.
units.tr: "Just as I ordered the churches of Galatia." If anything is to be said about Galatia, it will appear in the epistle he wrote to the Galatians, if by the grace of God we come to explain it.

units.la: ITA & uos facite, inquit. ] Duo sunt hic quę rēda. Primum, quare ecclesiarū Galatię mentionem facere, & non simpliciter rem ipsam, de qua mox subiuncturus est, proponere uoluerit. Alterum, quare non hac de re disposuerit, cum esset præsens apud Corinthios.
units.tr: "And so you also do," he says. Two things are to be considered here. First, why he chose to mention the churches of Galatia, rather than simply to set out the matter itself, which he is about to add. Second, why he did not arrange this matter while he was present among the Corinthians.

units.la: 1 Ad primum facilis est responsio. Galatarū mētionem facere uoluit, ne ipsis noui aliquid ordinare uideretur, & ut simul exemplo illorū quasi quodam stimulo, ad obtemperandū inducerentur. 2 Ad alterum existimamus respondendum esse ad hunc modū. Apparet in dubio esse, an cum apud Corinthios esset, collectam hanc in ecclesia illorum instituerit, de cuius hic modo & ordine præscribit. Si non instituit præsens, parcebat illis, tanquam adhuc infide recentibus, & simul cauebat ne suspicione quæstus incurreret, & maleuolis causam obtrectandi obijceret. Si uero instituerat, simpliciter ut occasio tulerat, nullo dum certo ordine præscripto, quæ dabātur collegerat. Postea uero, cum iā essent paulò in fide maturiores, communem ecclesiæ ordinem præscripsit, cuius initio non ita fuissent tolerantes. Vtrum fecerit, dubio procul singulari & uere Apostolica prudentia fecit.
units.tr: To the first the answer is easy. He wished to mention the Galatians so that it would not seem he was ordaining something new for them, and so that at the same time, by their example as a kind of spur, the Corinthians might be led to obey. To the second, we think the answer should be given in this way. It is doubtful whether, while he was with the Corinthians, he set up this collection in their church, the manner and order of which he now prescribes. If he did not set it up while present, he was sparing them, as still too recent in the faith, and at the same time took care lest he incur suspicion of seeking profit and give malicious people cause for disparagement. But if he had set it up, he had simply gathered what was given as occasion offered, with no fixed order yet prescribed. Afterwards, however, when they were now somewhat more mature in the faith, he prescribed the common order of the church, to which at the beginning they would not have been so tolerant. Whichever he did, without doubt he did it with a singular and truly apostolic prudence.

units.la: IN una sabbatorum, inquit, unusquisq; uestrum apud se seponat, &c. ] Hoc erat scilicet, quod ecclesijs Galatię ordinauerat, & ab ea quoq; quę Corinthi erat fieri uolebat. Summa est: Nolebat collationem in suum usq; aduentum differri, sed expediri priusquam ad ipsos ueniret. Deinde modum tradit, quomodo id commode fieri possit.
units.tr: "On the first day of the week," he says, "let each of you set something aside at home," and so on. This was evidently what he had ordered for the churches of Galatia, and he wanted it done also by the church at Corinth. The sense is this: he did not want the collection postponed until his own arrival, but wanted it arranged before he came to them. He then explains how this can conveniently be done.

units.la: Principio, quibus ordine hunc præscribat, in eo exprimit, quod dicit: Vnusquisq; uestrū. Vestrū, inquit, id est, qui Christiani estis, & fidē in Christum profitentes ad ecclesiā illius pertinetis: uestrū, inquit, unusquisq;. Ergo in genere Christianis omnibus qui erant in ecclesia Corinthiorum præscribit quæ hic ordinat.
units.tr: First, the words in which he prescribes this order show to whom it applies. He says, "Let each one of you." "Of you," he says, that is, you who are Christians and, professing faith in Christ, belong to his church: "each one of you," he says. Therefore he prescribes what he orders here to all Christians generally who were in the church of the Corinthians.

units.la: At eleemosyna cum sit libera, uidetur non esse communis cuiusdam præscripti capax, sed uniuscuiusq; relinquenda uoluntati. Hilarem enim datorem diligit Deus, qui det non ex cōstituto, sed ex libera beneuolentia.
units.tr: But since almsgiving is voluntary, it seems not to be open to any common rule, but should be left to each person's own will. For God loves a cheerful giver, who gives not by appointment but from free goodwill.

units.la: Respondeo. Christianæ charitatis sunt, quę ordinat hic Apostolus. Lex aūt charitatis Christianos constringit cōmuniter omnes. Quare præter rationem non est, quod de illa cōmuniter omnibus ac singulis præscribit. Hoc enim faciens accommodat se legi Christi. Et tamen neminem cogit inuitum, nec cuiquam onus impossibile imponit, licet à singulis fructum ueræ & Christianæ charitatis requirat.
units.tr: I answer: the things Paul orders here belong to Christian love. The law of love binds all Christians together in common. It is therefore not unreasonable that he prescribes for everyone and for each one what belongs to that love. In doing so he conforms himself to the law of Christ. Yet he compels no one against his will, nor lays on anyone an impossible burden, although he requires from each the fruit of true Christian love.

units.la: Duo sunt aūt genera subsidiorum, quibus pauperum in ecclesia necessitatibus subuenitur. Vnū est ecclesiasticū, alterū cuiusq; priuatū. De ecclesiastico loquitur hoc loco. Hoc cōmune omnium & singulorū cōtributione requirit, & opus habet cōmuni præscripto & ordine. Alterū arbitrariū est, & in cuiusq; uoluntate sitū, quid, quantū, cui, quomodo & quādo dare uoluerit. Quare cum 1. Tim. 6. de diuitibus monet, dicens: His qui diuites sunt in præsenti seculo præcipe, &c. nullum certū contributionis ordinem præscripsit: sed in genere dixit, ut benefaciāt, ut diuites sint operib. bonis, ut faciles sint ad impartiendū, libenter cōmunicantes, &c. Cum igitur ecclesiastica & publica collecta in omnib. debeat ecclesijs fieri, quo pauperum fidelium sustentatio nō à priuata pauperum cōtributiōe pendeat: haud probare quarundā possumus ecclesiarū negligentiam, in quib. & nulla est ecclesiastica collecta, & pauci simi sunt qui priuata beneficentia pauperibus succurrant. Etsi de stipendijs mortuorum certis temporibus aliquid in turbam pauperū erogatur, non potest hoc tamē uiuētium liberalitati adscribi. Deniq;, etiamsi de publico aliquid subinde datur, nequit tamen eiusmodi eleemosyna pro fructu charitatis haberi, qui à singulis in ecclesia feratur. Nō tā requirit hoc loco Apostolus publicam aliquam summam, quàm singulorum fidelium collectionem, notanter dicens: Vnusquisq; uestrum. Inuenias in nonnullis Euangelicis ecclesijs quàm pluri mos, qui totius anni decursu ne obolum quidem in usus pauperum Christi expendant, quibus magnopere necessarius esset hic cordo, quę Apostolus præscribit. Sane sic conueniebat in stitutas esse ecclesias, ut discerēt omnes ac singuli fideles bonis operibus præesse ad necessarios usus, ne essent infrugiferi. Tit. 3. In Papatu dandum est singulis, uerum quæ dantur, non cedunt necessitatibus pauperum, sed libidini uoluptuariorum.
units.tr: There are two kinds of help by which the needs of the poor are relieved in the church. One is ecclesiastical, the other is private to each person. He speaks here of the ecclesiastical kind. This requires the contribution of all and of each, and needs a common rule and order. The other kind is left to choice, and depends on each person's will as to what, how much, to whom, how and when he wishes to give. Therefore when in 1 Timothy 6 he admonishes the rich, saying, "Charge those who are rich in this present age," and so on, he prescribed no fixed order of contribution, but said in general that they should do good, be rich in good works, be ready to share, willing to give, and so on. Since, then, the ecclesiastical and public collection ought to be made in all churches, so that the support of the faithful poor does not depend on private giving to the poor, we cannot excuse the negligence of some churches, in which there is no ecclesiastical collection at all and very few people help the poor by private kindness. Even if something is distributed to the crowd of poor from the endowments of the dead at certain times, this cannot be credited to the generosity of the living. Finally, even if something is given now and then from public funds, such alms cannot be regarded as the fruit of charity which is brought in by each member of the church. The Apostle here does not so much require some public sum as the collection of each of the faithful, pointedly saying, "each one of you." You will find in some evangelical churches how many people, in the whole course of a year, do not spend even a penny on the needs of Christ's poor, though this kind of contribution, which the Apostle prescribes, would be greatly needed. Certainly the churches ought to have been so established that all and each of the faithful learned to give priority to good works for necessary uses, lest they be unfruitful. Titus 3. Under the Papacy something is given to each, but what is given does not go to the needs of the poor, but to the lusts of the self-indulgent.

units.la: VNVSQVISQVE uestrū, inquit, apud se seponat recōdens quicquid cōmodū fuerit. ] Duo dicit. Primū, quid quisq; facere: alterum, quanquantū seponere debeat. Ad primū pertinet, quod dicit, apud se seponat. Nō dicit, apud pastorem, doctorē, diaconū, hunc uel illum: sed apud se reponat. Reponere apud se, est aliquid à reliquo usu priuato & domestico eximere, & in usus sanctorum conferēdum seorsim reponere & asseruare. Unde quod in Graeco simpliciter est παρ' ἑαυτῷ τιθέναι, id est, apud se ponat. Erasmus uertit, apud se seponat. Sic ordinasse uidetur ad hoc, ut & omnis defraudationis ac subtractionis suspicio uitaretur, & simul pudori tenuiorum consuleretur, ne modica conferentes erubescerent, si illa singulis cogerentur septimanis in manus aliorum reponere.
units.tr: "Let each one of you," he says, "set aside at home, storing up whatever is convenient." He says two things: first, what each one should do; second, how much he ought to set aside. To the first belongs what he says, "let him set aside at home." He does not say "with the minister, the teacher, the deacon, this one or that one," but "let him set aside at home." To set aside at home is to take something out of one's remaining private and household use, and to store it apart and keep it, to be given to the uses of the saints. So the Greek words, which are simply παρ' ἑαυτῷ τιθέναι [parʼ heautō tithenai], that is, "to put aside with oneself," Erasmus translates "to set aside at home." In this way he seems to have ordered things so that any suspicion of fraud or embezzlement was avoided, and at the same time the shame of the poorer folk was spared, so that those giving small amounts would not blush if they were forced to hand them over to others every week.

units.la: Ad alterum referendum est quod addit, recondens quicquid commodum fuerit. In Graeco est, θησαυρίζων. Significat autem θησαυρίζειν non simpliciter colligere ac recōdere, sed copiam quandā in futuros usus ac tēpus longinquum accumulare. Quod sic accumulatur, thesaurus uocatur. Mira aūt est Apostoli philosophia, cui pprijs bonis adimere, & in alienos usus reponere, thesaurum est colligere. Sane cōmuni sensu non thesaurizat, qui de bonis suis tollit quod suis usibus adimat, & alienis deputet: sed qui undecunq; acquisita sibi ac suis in futurum recondit. At Apostolo erogare in sanctos, est thesaurizare. Hoc genus thesaurizandi depauperationi putatur esse confine. Verū non est aliud quod sit ad ueram opulentiā cōparandam cōpendiosius ac certius. Sic usurpauit hanc thesaurizandi uocem, & Christus Lucæ 12 & 18. ubi de bonorū in pauperes erogatione loquitur. Et Apostolus 1. Tim. 6. cū dixisset, Ut faciles sint ad impartiendū, libenter cōmunicantes: adiecit ἀποθησαυρίζοντας sibi ipsis fundamentum bonū in posterū, ut apprehendant uitā æternam. Vbi appositissime usus est hac uoce ἀποθησαυρίζοντας: significat enim ἀποθησαυρίζειν de ijs quę quotidiano usu absumimus subinde aliqd seponere, & in futuros usus thesauri loco recōdere. Multa insumunt huius sæculi diuites, quæ ipso usu, imò sæpius abusu intereunt: & ea deniq;, quæ post mortē relinquunt hæredibus, saluti ipsorum nihil cōmodant. Monet igitur Apostolus ut studio impartiendi & cōmunicandi pauperibus indesinenter de bonis suis alioqui perituris aliquid seruent, & in thesaurū colligant, quo post hāc uitā fruantur. Hoc idem & in præsenti monens dicit: Vnusquisq; uestrū apud se seponat thesaurizans. Cum autem addit, quicquid cōmodum fuerit, cauet ne cuiquā præscribat, quantum in usus sanctorum reponere debeat. Hic enim nihil certi potest statui. Quare consultissime hoc uniuscuiusq; & facultati & cōmoditati permittit dicens, Quicquid cōmodum fuerit. Est autē in Graeco, ὅτι ἂν εὐοδῶται. Valla uertēdum putat, quod facile fit: uel, quod leue fit: aut, quod bene cedat. Erasmus uertit: quicqd cōmodum fuerit. Vulgata editio habet, quod ei bene placuerit, quasi fit εὐοδῶται. Germanicus interpres reddidit, Vuas im leidlich ist. Sunt
units.tr: To the second point belongs what he adds, "storing up whatever is convenient." In the Greek it is θησαυρίζων [thēsaurizōn]. But θησαυρίζειν [thēsaurizein] does not mean simply to gather and lay up, but to accumulate a store for future use and a distant time. What is so accumulated is called a treasure.
