The philosophy of the Apostle is remarkable: to take from one's own goods and set them aside for the use of others is, for him, to gather a treasure. Certainly in ordinary sense a person does not store treasure who takes from his goods what he might use for himself and assigns it to others; rather, he stores up for himself and his own in the future what he has acquired from wherever. But for the Apostle, to spend on the saints is to store up treasure. This kind of storing up is thought to border on impoverishment. Yet there is nothing else that gets true wealth more quickly and more surely. Christ also used this word "to store up treasure" in Luke 12 and 18, where he speaks of giving goods to the poor. And the Apostle in 1 Timothy 6, after saying "ready to share, willing to give," added "storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that they may lay hold on eternal life" [ἀποθησαυρίζοντας]. There he used the word ἀποθησαυρίζοντας [apothēsaurizontas] very aptly: for ἀποθησαυρίζειν [apothēsaurizein] means, of the things we consume in daily use, to set some aside from time to time and store it away in the manner of a treasure for future use. The rich of this age spend much that perishes through use, or rather more often through misuse; and what they finally leave to their heirs contributes nothing to their own salvation. The Apostle therefore warns that, out of zeal to give and share with the poor, they should without ceasing keep back something from their goods, which would otherwise perish, and gather it into a treasure, to enjoy after this life. Warning of this same thing in the present passage, he says, "Let each of you set aside at home, storing up." When he adds "whatever is convenient," he takes care not to prescribe to anyone how much he ought to lay aside for the uses of the saints. For nothing certain can be fixed here. So very wisely he leaves this to the means and convenience of each person, saying, "whatever is convenient." In the Greek it is ὅτι ἂν εὐοδῶται [hoti an euodōtai]. Valla thinks it should be rendered "what is easily done," or "what is light," or "what turns out well." Erasmus translates it "whatever is convenient." The Vulgate edition has "what has pleased him well," as if reading εὐαρεστῶται. The German translator rendered it, "what is tolerable for you."

units.la: nulli qui uertendū censeant, quod successerit. Sane εὐοδῶσθαι prospere succedere significat. Verum non est in Graeco, ὡς ἂν εὐοδῶται, id est, quatenus successerit, prout cuiq; benedixerit Deus secundū facultatum uel copiā uel tenuitatē: sed ὅτι ἂν εὐοδῶται, i. quicquid successerit. Germanice melius reddi potest ad hūc modū: uuas im nit ybel Kompt. i. qcqd nō fuerit molestū, sed cōmodū, ut idē sit cū eo quod Erasmus uertit.
units.tr: Some think it should be rendered "whatever has prospered." Indeed εὐοδῶσθαι [euodōsthai] means to succeed well. But the Greek is not ὡς ἂν εὐοδῶται [hōs an euodōtai], that is, "as far as he has prospered, as God has blessed each one in means, either in abundance or in poverty"; it is ὅτι ἂν εὐοδῶται [hoti an euodōtai], that is, "whatever has prospered." It can be rendered better in German in this way: "was ihm nit übel kompt," that is, whatever does not come to him as a burden, but is convenient, so that it comes to the same thing as what Erasmus translated.

units.la: Quomodocunq; legamus, manifestū est ca uere Apostolum, ne dum ab omnibus ac singulis requirit, ut apud seipsos reponant aliquid in usus sanctorū, quenq; ex illis uel nimia uel coacta cōtributione grauare uideatur. Sicut igitur in epist. sequenti cap. 8. dicit, non ut alijs sit relaxatio, uobis aūt angustia: ita & hoc loco non imponit illis tantā cōtributionem, unde quisquā grauetur, sed permittit unicuiq; liberū, ut tantum det quantū sine suo cōmodo dare poterit. Vtinam hæc duo mansissent in ecclesia: unum, ut quisq; fidelium aliquid reponeret in usus pauperū: alterū, ut contributionis huius quantitas unicuiusq; fuisset facultati & cōmoditati libere permissa. Nihil prorsus in pauperum conferre subsidia, sterilis est & infrugiferi Christiani. Quare satagendum est singulis, ut contribuendo tanquam fructificādo declarēt se arbores esse in domo domini non steriles, sed frugiferas. Quantum quisq; conferat, nulla lege præscribitur. Neq; arborum fructiferarum eadem est fertilitatis copia. Satis est unicuiq;, ad euadendum sterilitatis culpā, si non sit prorsus ἀναρπος. Consimili modo in ecclesia nemo de quanto censetur, sed ij tantū steriles habentur, qui prorsus nihil ad alimoniam pauperum conferunt.
units.tr: However we read it, it is clear that the Apostle is careful not to require from all and each that they set aside something for the uses of the saints in such a way that anyone seems to be burdened by excessive or forced contribution. Therefore, just as in the following chapter, 2 Corinthians 8, he says, "not that others should be eased, but you burdened," so here too he does not impose on them such a contribution that anyone is weighed down, but leaves it free to each to give as much as he can give without loss to himself. Would that these two things had remained in the church: first, that each of the faithful set something aside for the uses of the poor; second, that the amount of this contribution was left freely to the means and convenience of each person. To contribute nothing at all to the support of the poor is the mark of a barren and unfruitful Christian. Therefore each person must take care that by contributing, as by bearing fruit, they show themselves to be trees in the house of the Lord that are not barren but fruitful. No law prescribes how much each one should give. Nor is the abundance of fertility the same in all fruit trees. It is enough for each, to escape the blame of barrenness, not to be altogether unfruitful [ἄκαρπος]. In the same way in the church no one is rated by how much he gives; only those are counted barren who contribute absolutely nothing to the support of the poor.

units.la: Adhunc collectionis ordinem pertinet & illud, quod dicit: in una sabbati, sicut habet uulgata æditio. Sic tēpus quoq; præscribit, in quo debeat quisque penes se aliquid in usus sanctorū reponere. Grecè est κατὰ μίαν σαββάτων, i. per unā sabbatorū. Chrysost. habet in singulari σαββάτου, idest, sabbati. In historia resurrectionis dominicæ nota est hæc loquutio, in qua una sabbati more Ebræo pro prima est sabbati posita. Vocula nanq; אחד Ebræis sæpenumero יום primo accipitur. qua de re in Genesi annotauimus ca. 1. ibi. Et factū est uespere & mane dies unus. Sic una sabbati, prima est post sabbatum dies in septimana, quæ nobis est dominica, pterea quod in ea dominy à mortuis surrexit.
units.tr: To this order of collection also belongs what he says, "in una sabbati," as the Vulgate edition has it. In the same way he also prescribes the time at which each person should set something aside at home for the use of the saints. The Greek is [κατὰ μίαν σαββάτων], that is, "on one of the sabbaths." Chrysostom has the singular [σαββάτου], that is, "of the sabbath." This phrase is familiar from the account of the Lord's resurrection, where, after the Hebrew manner, "one of the sabbaths" stands for "the first of the sabbaths." The little Hebrew word [אחד] is often taken by the Hebrews to mean "first," as [יום] does. We noted this on Genesis 1, where it says, "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." So "one of the sabbaths" means the first day after the sabbath in the week, which for us is the Lord's Day, because on it the Lord rose from the dead.

units.la: Si hūc sensum hoc quoq; loco acceperimus, querendū uidetur, quare uoluerit Apostolus, ut die dominicaquisq; seponeret aliquid apud semetipsum in usus sanctorū. Chrysost. dicit hoc esse propterea factū, quod is dies plurimū habeat incitamēti ad cōtribuendū egenis fratribus cum propter dñicę resurrectionis memoriam, tum propter mysteria Christi, quæ in cœtu sacro dominicis diebus dispensantur, de niq; propter quietem, qua in illis fideles à laboribus suis feriantes, aptiores redduntur ad ueræ pietatis & charitatis exercitia.
units.tr: If we take this meaning here too, it seems right to ask why the Apostle wanted each person to set something aside at home for the use of the saints on the Lord's Day. Chrysostom says this was done because that day especially encourages contributions to needy brothers, both because of the memory of the Lord's resurrection and because of the mysteries of Christ, which are dispensed on the Lord's Days in the sacred assembly; and finally because of the rest in which the faithful, ceasing from their labours, become more fit for the exercises of true piety and love.

units.la: Sunt
units.tr: There are some

units.la: A nulli qui uertendū censeant ... (marginal letter A)
units.tr: Others who think it should be translated ... (marginal letter A)

units.la: Sunt qui respectu forsan eius quod legitur uelut in plurali, in una sabbatorum, exponant ad hunc modum: Quisque uestrum per aliquā diem ex sabbatis, quam ipse uoluerit, aliquid apud se reponat, &c. quasi κατὰ μίαν σαββάτων idem sit quod per unum ex sabbatis, &non positum sit pro prima sabbati. Verū utut accipiamus, manet hæc quæstio, quare ad hoc ut quisque apud se reponeret aliquid in usus sanctorum, uel unum ex sabbatis uel diem dominicū deputare uoluerit Apostolus, cum posset id quo uis die fieri. Si requirere uoluisset, ut quisque in cœtum sacrum eleemosynam suam adferret, ibique illam fidei diaconorum concrederet, sane ad id institutí cōmodior cæteris fuisset dies dominicus propter conuentus sacros. At cum dixerit, unusquisque uestrum apud se reponat recondens quicquid commodum fuerit, apparet nulla ratione hunc esse ab illo die ad id institutí designatum. Hocuero sentire de Apostolo admodum censemus esse temerarium. Quare, ut quid mihi hic cogitari posse uideatur, aliis proponam, puto illud in Græco, παρ' ἑαυτῷ τιθέτω, non esse positum pro, apud se reponat: sed hoc sensu, In una sabbatorum quisque uestrum suapte sponte ponat: intellige, in cœto sacro, thesaurizans, hoc est, in thesaurum qui colligendus est, conferens, quicquid commodum fuerit. Huic sensui pulchre conuenit dominicę diei deputatio, deinde &illud quod sequitur, ne cum uenero tunc collationes fiát. Etenim hoc dicens satis indicat uelle se, ut diebus dominicis in cœtu sacro fiant collectę, priusquam ad ipsos ueniat, cui propósito non satisfecisset, si quisq; apud se domi aliquid in futurā contributione repositum fuisset. Eiusmodi nam que repósita tum demū colligenda fuissent, cū ipse ad eos uenisset id quod uitari uolebat. Hæc cogitari possunt hoc loco, uerū an firma sint, aliorum esto iudicium.
units.tr: Some, perhaps looking at the plural form that is read, "in una sabbatorum," explain it thus: "Let each of you, on some day of the sabbaths that he himself chooses, lay something up with himself," etc., as though [κατὰ μίαν σαββάτων] meant the same as "on one of the sabbaths," and were not used for "the first of the sabbath." However we take it, the question remains: why did the Apostle want the Lord's Day, or one of the sabbaths, to be assigned for each person to set something aside at home for the use of the saints, when he could have said any day he liked? If he had wanted each person to bring his alms to the sacred assembly and there entrust them to the faith of the deacons, the Lord's Day, because of the sacred gatherings, would certainly have been more suitable for this purpose than the others. But since he said, "let each of you lay up at home whatever he has gained," it appears that for no reason was that day designated by him for this purpose. To think this of the Apostle we judge to be altogether rash. So, to set before others what seems to me possible here, I suppose that in the Greek [παρ' ἑαυτῷ τιθέτω] does not mean "let him lay up with himself," but rather in this sense: "On one of the sabbaths let each of you of his own accord put aside," that is, in the sacred assembly, storing up, that is, contributing into the treasury to be gathered, whatever he has gained. The assignment of the Lord's Day agrees well with this sense, and so does what follows, "that collections be not made when I come." For in saying this he sufficiently indicates that he wants the collections to be made in the sacred assembly on the Lord's Days before he comes to them; he would not have achieved this purpose if each person had kept at home something set aside for a future contribution. For such sums would then have been collected only when he himself came to them, which is what he wished to avoid. These things may be thought of at this point; whether they are sound, let others judge.

units.la: NE cum uenero, inquit, tunc collectiones fiant.] Quare collectiones tum demum cum ad eos uenisset fieri noluerit, in epistola sequēti uidere licet, ubi cap. 9. sic scribit: Misi tamen hos fratres, ne gloria nostra, qua glorior de uobis, inanis fiat in hac parte, ut quemadmodum dicebam, parati sitis, ne quo pacto fiat, ut si me cum uenerint Macedones, & offenderint uos imparatos, nos pudore suffundamur, ut ne dicam uos in hoc argumento gloriationis. Hæc ibi. Ergo metuebat, ne negligentius agerent in hac causa, atq; ita imparati in aduentu suo deprehensi, gloriationem suam de ipsis redderent inanem, & non se tantum, sed & seipsos pudori & confusioni exponerent. Sic in posteriore epistola expressius ponit, quare collectionem hanc in aduentum suum differri noluerit, quàm in hac priore. Erat autem & hoc metuendum, quamuis illud non attingit, ne si tūdemū collectæ fierent, cum ad ipsos uenisset, uideretur ob id tantū uenisse, ut pecuniā sub prætextu eleemosynę corraderet, qua ipsum suspicioē maleuoli uehementer grauare poterat.
units.tr: "That collections be not made when I come," he says. Why he was unwilling for collections to be made only when he came to them can be seen in the following letter, where in chapter 9 he writes thus: "Yet I have sent these brothers, lest our boasting, which I make concerning you, should be vain in this respect, so that, as I said, you may be ready; lest by any means, if the Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we should be ashamed, not to say you, in this matter of boasting." Thus far there. So he feared that they would act more carelessly in this matter, and so, found unprepared on his arrival, would make his boasting about them vain, and would expose not only himself but also themselves to shame and confusion. So in the later letter he states more clearly why he did not want this collection deferred until his coming than he does in this earlier one. Yet there was also another thing to fear, though he does not touch on it: that if the collections were made only when he came to them, he might seem to have come for no other reason than to gather money under the pretext of alms, a thing which could greatly burden him with the suspicion of ill-wishers.

units.la: Admonemur hoc exemplo, quàm deceat nos non modo benefacere fratribus, sed & sic studere beneficentiæ, ut quod bene facimus, nulli reddatur uel negligentiæ uel tergiuersationis, hoc est, animi non satis ad beneficiendum prompti & alacris, culpæ ac pudori obnoxium: quo pudore non modo ecclesia negligens ac tergiuersatrix, sed & ipse minister suffunditur, qui si fidelis sit domino, & amans salutis eorum, quibus est in uerbo præpositus, non minus de illorum dedecore, quàm suoipsius contristatur, quemadmodum nō minus de illorum gloria quàm suaipsius lætatur.
units.tr: This example teaches us how fitting it is for us not only to do good to the brothers, but also to take such care in doing good that what we do well is not rendered liable to blame and shame on account of negligence or evasion, that is, a mind not sufficiently ready and eager to do good. By this shame not only a negligent and evasive congregation is covered with confusion, but also the minister himself. If he is faithful to the Lord and loves the salvation of those over whom he is set in the Word, he grieves no less over their disgrace than over his own, just as he rejoices no less in their glory than in his own.

units.la: Vbi uenero autem, inquit, quoscunque probaueritis, per epistolas hos mittam, ut perferant munificentiam uestrā Hierosolymā. Quod si fuerit operæprecium ut & ipse proficiscar, mecum proficiscentur.
units.tr: When I come, he says, I will send by letter whomever you approve, to carry your bounty to Jerusalem. And if it is worth while for me to go too, they will travel with me.

units.la: Hactenus de modo collationis in sanctos colligendæ præscripsit, iam subiungit de modo quo sit illa Hierosolymam mittenda. Vbi uenero autem, inquit, quoscunq; probaueritis, per epistolas hos mittā. Nolebat eam mitti nec ante suum ad illos aduentū, nec per quoslibet, neq; suopte arbitratu absq; illorum calculis. Ad prius pertinet quod dicit, ubi uenero aut: ad posterius, quod subijcit, quoscunq; probaueritis, &c. Vtrobiq; admonemur, quàti fecerit Apostolus curam egentiū sanctorum & quàm fideliter, quantaq; cum diligentia uoluerit nō modo colligi illorum subsidia, sed & collecta dispensari.
units.tr: So far he has prescribed the manner of gathering the collection for the saints; now he adds the manner in which it is to be sent to Jerusalem. "When I come," he says, "I will send by letter whomever you approve." He did not want it sent either before his own arrival, or through just anyone, or on his own authority without their approval. The words "when I come" relate to the first point, and "whomever you approve" to the second. In both we are reminded how greatly the Apostle cared for the needy saints, and how faithfully and with what diligence he wanted not only their relief to be gathered but also the collected funds to be distributed.

units.la: VBI uenero autem, inquit. ]Vide prudentiam Apostoli. Duæ patres erant collationis, de qua scribit. Vna colligendæ illius, altera dispensandæ. Priorem noluit in suū aduentum differri. Posteriorem uoluit differri, dū Corinthum uenisset. Prioris ratione paulo ante assignauimus. Posterioris licet nulla exprimatur ratio, res ipsa tamen admonet, quibus de causis illam in suum usque aduentum differri uoluerit. Primum haud parum referebat scire ipsum quàm liberaliter contribuissent fideles, & quomodo essent erga fratrum suorum necessitates affecti. Erat enim in eo magna pars efficaciæ uerbi ac laboris Apostolici uelut in fructu spectanda. Prudēter igitur nolebat collectam hanc Hierosolymam mitti, priusquam ad ipsos uenisset. Deinde hoc consilio simulca uebat, ne parcius ac illiberalius contribuerēt. Voluit igitur ut stimularet eos expectatio aduentus sui. Si quæ nanque collecta essent absque Apostoli conscientia Hyerosolymam mittere licuisset, dubio procul multo pauciora contribuissent, quàm hac aduētus ipsius expectatione moti contribuerunt. Nolebant enim in præsentia illius pudefieri, sed magis approbari tanquam liberales in sanctos. Tertio cauendum erat, ne quo pacto, siue per negligētiam, si quibuslibet absq; delectu collecta hæc Hierosolym. rosolymam deportanda concrederetur,siue si nistro studio à nonnullis cura hęc præsumere tur, dispensatio ista non satis diligenter ac fi- deliter expediretur. Præterea, non erat com- mittēdum,ut causam hanc singulari cura à cæ teris apostolis commendatam,susq; deq; face re uideretur,si neq; collectionis illius,neq; di- spensationis curam præsentia sua adornasset. Hisce rationibus,& alijs forsan uel consimili- bus uel grauioribus uel secretioribus apparet Apostolum hanc dispensandæ collectæ partē in suum distulisse aduentum. Nos eas indica- mus quæ uidentur esse probabiles, nihil inte- rim de mente illius affirmantes, sed quid hic cogitari, & Apostolo in tali causa competere possit admonentes.
units.tr: "WHEN I COME," he says. See the Apostle's prudence. There were two stages to the collection he is writing about: gathering it and distributing it. He did not want the first postponed until his arrival; the second he wanted postponed until he had come to Corinth. The reason for the first we have already suggested. For the second, although no reason is stated, the matter itself suggests why he wished it deferred until his own coming. (1) First, it mattered greatly to him to know how generously the faithful had contributed and how they felt toward their brothers' needs, for much of the fruit of his preaching and apostolic labour was to be seen in this. Prudently, then, he did not want this collection sent to Jerusalem before he came to them. (2) Second, by this plan he was also aiming to prevent them from giving more sparingly and less generously. He therefore wished the expectation of his coming to spur them on. For if the collection could have been sent to Jerusalem without the Apostle's knowledge, there is no doubt they would have given far less than they did, moved as they were by the expectation of his arrival. They did not want to be shamed in his presence, but rather to be commended as generous toward the saints. (3) Third, care had to be taken that the collection, if it were entrusted to be carried to Jerusalem by negligence or chance and without proper selection, should not be handled carelessly, or that, through the ill will of some who presumed to take up the task, the distribution should not be carried out with sufficient diligence and fidelity. Moreover, it was not to be allowed that a cause commended with special care by the other apostles should seem to be held in contempt, if he did not himself oversee the gathering and distribution of it. For these reasons, and perhaps others, similar or weightier or more hidden, it appears that the Apostle put off to his own coming the part of the collection concerned with its distribution. We point out those reasons which seem probable, affirming nothing about his mind, but reminding us what may be thought here and what the Apostle could properly do in such a case.

units.la: QVOSCVNQVE probaueritis,inquit, p epistolas hos mittam. ]Ambiguum est quod dicit,per epistolas. Potest enim tam ad sequēs quàm ad præcedens referri. Ad præcedens re ferūt utriq; interpretes, uulgatus & Erafmus, quemadmodum apparet in distinctione lecti onis. Sic enim habent,Quoscunq; probaueri- tis per epistolas,hos mittam. Sic coniungunt illud,per epistolas,uerbo probandi, & intelli- gunt de epistolas non Pauli, sed Corinthiorū ad Paulum. Ad sequens refert Chrysost. Non enim modo sic distinguit,... sed & exponit ad hunc modū, ... Sic ille de epistolis nō Corin thiorum ad Paulum sed Pauli, non ad Corin- thios, ut Lyranus exponit: sed ad Hierosoly- mitanos scriptis intelligit,quibus operā suam quoque pollicitus fit illis,quos ipsi essent Hic rosolymam mittēdos probaturi & electuri.Et hæc mihi sententia uerofimilior & causæ ac- commodatior uidetur.Etenim quorsum atti- nuisset per epistolas probare absenti Aposto- lo quos Hierosolymam mitti uellent cum ad ipsos uenturum se significaret,possetq; hęc probatio breui momento in ipsius fieri præsentia, idq; aliquanto melius quàm in absentia.
units.tr: "WHOMEVER YOU APPROVE," he says, "I will send by letter." The phrase "by letter" is ambiguous, for it can be referred either to what follows or to what precedes. Both the Vulgate translator and Erasmus refer it to what precedes, as the punctuation of the reading shows. For they read: "Whomever you approve by letter, these I will send," and so they join "by letter" to the verb "approve", understanding the letters not of Paul but of the Corinthians to Paul. Chrysostom refers it to what follows; for he does not punctuate in this way only, but also explains it in this manner. Thus he understands the letters not as letters of the Corinthians to Paul, nor as letters of Paul to the Corinthians, as Lyra explains, but as letters written to the Jerusalemites, in which he also promised them that he would send men whom they themselves should approve and choose for the task of carrying the collection to Jerusalem. This view seems to me more probable and better suited to the matter. For to what purpose would it have served to approve, by letter, those whom they wished sent to Jerusalem, when he was signifying that he would come to them himself? And this approval could be made in a brief moment in his presence, and rather better than in his absence.

units.la: QVOSCVNQVE probaueritis, inquit.] Quoniam collecta illa Hierosolymam mitten da ipsorum erat,ex communi omnium libera litate contributa, permisit ipsorum potestati, per quos illam mittere uellent. Non dicit, Quoscqūue probauero: sed, quoscunque pro baueritis. Sic cauet omnibus modis, ne quam sinistram de se suspicionem concipiant, quasi in hac causa res agat nō sanctorum egentium, sed suas. Dispensationem communis collectę permittit ipsis, at nostri episcopi quàm ege- rint in hac causa fideliter, nemini non est om- nium notissimum.
units.tr: "WHOMEVER YOU APPROVE," he says. Since that collection was to be sent to Jerusalem by their own decision, having been contributed from the free generosity of all, he left the choice of those through whom they wished it sent to their own power. He does not say, "Whomever I approve," but "whomever you approve." In this way he guards against every suspicion of himself, lest they should conceive that he was pursuing the matter for his own advantage rather than for the needy saints. He leaves the distribution of the common collection to them. As for how faithfully our bishops have acted in this matter, it is well known to nearly everyone.

units.la: Obserua uero quàm prudenter non dicat, Quoscunq; uoluerit is,aut quicunq; inter uos uolent,hos mittam:sed,quoscunq; probaueri tis.In Græco est ..., quod uerbum cer- tis experimentis aliquid quale nam sit proba- re & cognoscere significat. Quasi dicat: Quos- cunq; uiros probatę fidei & huic negocio ob- eundo accommodos certo cognoueritis ac iū dicaueritis,hos mittam. Igitur sic illorum po- testati electionem eorum permittit, quos Hie rosolymam sit missurus, ut simul prudentiam ac diligentiam requirat, qua nō quoslibet ad id instituti usurpent, sed cum iudicio eligant probatos.Sane requirebat res ipsa uiros & fi- deles & gnauos.Fideles qui pecuniā fidei suæ concreditam,nulla perfidia interueniret, sed pro uoluntate eorum qui illam contribuerāt, sanctis egentibus, fideliter subministrarent: gnauos,qui in peregrinatione & longinqua & periculosa, quæ subeunda erat, prudenter se- se gererent, ne per imprudentiam & sibijpsis periculum accerserent, & necessitatibus san- ctorum incommodarent.Sic Act.6. cum uide retur apostolis eligendos esse uiros aliquot, qui eleemosynæ dispensandæ præficerentur, iusserunt circumspicere multitudinem disci- pulorum, & eligere uiros septem ei negocio idoneos, ... uidelicet, id est,qui bonū haberent probitatis testimonium,essentq; ple ni spiritu sancto,& sapientia præditi.Tanta sci licet cura uoluerunt apostoli prouinciā hanc concredi non quibusuis temere, sed selectis probatę fidei ac prudentiæ hominibus.
units.tr: Observe how prudently he does not say, "Whomever he wishes, or whomever among you wish, these I will send," but "whomever you approve." In the Greek it is δοκιμάσητε, a word which means to prove something by sure tests and to know what sort of thing it is. As if he were saying: "Whatever men you have certainly known to be of tested faith and suited to carrying out this business, and have judged them so, these I will send." Thus he leaves the choice of those whom he was to send to Jerusalem to their power, so that at the same time he requires prudence and diligence, by which they should not take up just anyone for the task, but choose men who have been tested, with judgement. Indeed the matter itself demanded men both faithful and diligent. Faithful, who would administer the money entrusted to their good faith, without any treachery, to the needy saints according to the will of those who had contributed it. Diligent, who would conduct themselves prudently on the long and dangerous journey that had to be undertaken, so that by imprudence they would not bring danger upon themselves and burden the needs of the saints. So in Acts 6, when it seemed that some men had to be chosen to be placed over the distribution of alms, the apostles ordered them to look round among the multitude of disciples and choose seven men fit for the task, that is, men who had a good testimony of uprightness, and who were full of the Holy Spirit and endowed with wisdom. With such great care, clearly, the apostles wished this charge to be entrusted not rashly to just anyone, but to chosen men of tested faith and prudence.

units.la: PER epistolas, inquit, hos mittam. ] Pro- bationem mittendorum tribuit ecclesiæ, mis- sionem uindicat sibi, quod non facit tuendæ authoritatis suæ gratia,sed ad hoc ut missa col lecta sanctis Hierosolymitanis competentius assignetur & exhibeatur.Erat scribendum ad apostolos, uel eos saltem qui eleemosynæ e- rant in ecclesia Hierosolymitana præfecti. At hoc à nemine poterat melius ac magis authen tice fieri quàm ab ipso Apostolo.Hoc innuens non simpliciter dicit,Hos mittam:sed, per epi stolas hos mittam.Quod autem non singula- riter, per epistolam, sed pluraliter, per episto- las,dicit:intelligi potest de literis quarū erant aliæ scribendæ ad apostolos domini, Petrum, Iacobum & Ioannem : aliæ ad diacanos, aliæ ad ipsam multitudinem egentiū sanctorum, quibus collectam Corinthiorum erat missu- rus.Hæ sunt uerę Apostolicæ epistolæ, nō pe taces & imperiosæ,sed,uel sanctę doctrinę uel benedictionis, cósolationis ac refocillationis feraces.
units.tr: "BY LETTERS," he says, "I will send these." He assigns the approval of those to be sent to the church, but claims the sending for himself. He does this not for the sake of preserving his own authority, but so that the sent collection might be more fittingly assigned and delivered to the Jerusalem saints. It would have been necessary to write to the apostles, or at least to those who were set over the alms in the Jerusalem church. But this could be done better and more authentically by no one than by the Apostle himself. Implying this, he does not simply say, "These I will send," but "by letters these I will send." That he says "letters" in the plural rather than "a letter" in the singular can be understood as meaning that some letters were to be written to the lords apostles, Peter, James and John, others to the deacons, and others to the multitude of needy saints themselves, to whom he was going to send the Corinthian collection. These are true apostolic letters, not petitionary and imperious, but fruitful of holy doctrine, of blessing, of consolation and of refreshment.

units.la: VT perferant, inquit, munificentiam ue- stram Hierosolymam.] Poterat Apostolus sic ordinare hanc causam, ut aliqui ex fratribus Hierosolymitanis circuiret per ecclesias Chri sti inter gentes, & subsidia in usus sanctorum peterent,colligerent, & Hierosolymā perfer- rent.Verum ea ratio circueundi ac colligendi eleemosynam tam fuisset dedecorosa Christi ecclesijs,quàm ad speciem mendicitatis accef sisset.Quare honestius & Christianæ charita- ti conformius erat mittere ex ecclesia Corin- rhiorum uiros probos, honestos & gnauos, qui gratiam hanc Hierosolymam perferret,& sanctis ἁγίοις redderent. Obseruandum autem est, quod non dicit: Vt perferant collectā, uel collationem, aut pecuniam: sed, ut perferant munificentiam uestram Hierosolymam. In Græco est τὴν χάριν ὑμῶν, id est, gratiā uestrā. Sic reddidit & uulgatus interpres. Vsurpat autem dictionem gratiæ pro beneficio gratuito & liberali, quem sensum Erasmus expressurus uertit, munificentiam uestram. Iterum eos hac quoque uoce prouocat ad liberalem collationem, quæ possit singularis munificentiæ loco haberi, ac simul cauet, ne quam erant Hierosolymam missuri pecuniam debiti loco habere-tur, quo loco habentur quæ ex omni Europa seculis iam aliquot non Hierosolymam, sed Hierosylimam, Romam illam omnis generis sacrilegiorum uoraginem mittuntur.
units.tr: "THAT THEY MAY CARRY," he says, "YOUR BOUNTY TO JERUSALEM." The Apostle could have arranged this matter so that some of the Jerusalem brethren should go round the churches of Christ among the Gentiles, seek and gather help for the use of the saints, and carry it to Jerusalem. But such a method of going round and gathering alms would have been as disgraceful to the churches of Christ as it would have had the appearance of begging. Therefore it was more honourable and more in keeping with Christian charity that upright, honest and diligent men should be sent from the Corinthian church to carry this grace to Jerusalem and deliver it to the saints [ἁγίοις]. It must be observed, moreover, that he does not say, "that they may carry the collection," or "the contribution," or "the money," but "that they may carry your bounty to Jerusalem." In the Greek it is τὴν χάριν ὑμῶν [tēn charin hymōn], that is, your grace. So the Vulgate translator also rendered it. He uses the word "grace" for a free and generous benefit, a sense which Erasmus, wishing to express it, translates as "your bounty." Again he challenges them by this word to a generous contribution, which could be regarded as a singular act of munificence; and at the same time he guards against the money they were to send to Jerusalem being regarded as a debt. This is how those things are regarded which for some centuries now have been sent from all over Europe, not to Jerusalem but to Rome, that whirlpool of every kind of sacrilege.

units.la: Obiter obserua, qualia Noui testamenti sacrificia Hierosolymam Apostolico missa sint instituto. In lege adferebantur undiq; hostiæ, uictimæ, oblationes, & holocaustā, quibus Deo in templo illius sacrificaretur. Hoc genus Veteris testamenti sacrificia uidemus hoc in philadelphiæ gratiam esse mutata, qua non pecudes Deo, sed collectæ in usus sanctorū egentium distribuuntur. Et hanc gratiam reposcit dominus pro sua, quam nobis Apostolicæ literæ non satis possunt commendare. Per gratiam domini saluamur credentes, per nostram refocillantur esurientes ac sitientes. Si huic dominicæ gratiæ in nos, & nostræ in fratres egenos uicissitudini sacrificium laudis adiunxeris, compendium habes & nostræ salutis, & ueri cultus Dei.
units.tr: Note in passing what kind of sacrifices of the New Testament were sent to Jerusalem by apostolic direction. Under the Law, victims, sacrifices and offerings, and burnt offerings were brought in from every side to be offered to God in the Temple there. We see that these sacrifices of the Old Testament have been changed, by the grace of brotherly love, into a kind of offering in which gifts are not slaughtered animals for God but are collected and distributed for the needs of the poor saints. The Lord asks for this grace in return for his own, which the apostolic letters cannot commend to us sufficiently: we are saved by the grace of the Lord through faith, and the hungry and thirsty are refreshed by our giving. If you add to this exchange of the Lord's grace toward us and ours toward needy brothers the sacrifice of praise, you have the sum of both our salvation and the true worship of God.

units.la: QVOD si fuerit operæprecium, inquit, ut & ipse proficiscar, mecū proficiscentur. ] Tria agit hisce uerbis. Primum, ut significet Corinthijs, quam sit sibi causa hæc cordi. Vsqueadeo uidelicet, ut quamuis sit Apostolus Christi missus ad Gentes, sitq; omnium occupatissimus, partim prædicando illis Euangelium, quibus Christus nondum innotuit, partim eos qui crediderunt in fide Christi confirmando: paratus tamen sit inde Corintho Hierosolymam usq; proficisci, ac sanctis fratribus gratiam hanc ipsorum perferre. Secundum, ut rursus eos ad liberaliorem contributionem prouocet, dicit: Quod si fuerit operæprecium, ut & ipse proficiscar. Græcè est, ἐὰν ἄξιον ᾖ, id est, si uero dignum fuerit: hoc est, si tam largiter ac liberaliter contuleritis, si tanta fuerit collectæ uestræ gratia & copia, si ecclesiam sanctorum quæ Hierosolymis est, collatione uestra tam eltis refocillaturi, ut dignū fuerit hac uestram gratiam per meipsum Hierosolymam perferri, non grauabor ipse proficisci. Hoc dicens ad modum excitat eos ad liberaliorem collationem, dum significat, si largiter contulerint, seipsum collectam ipsorum Hierosolymā perlaturum: sin minus, per alios missurum.
units.tr: "IF IT BE MEET," he says, "that I also go, they shall go with me." He accomplishes three things with these words. First, he shows the Corinthians how close this cause lies to his heart. So much so that, although he is the apostle sent by Christ to the Gentiles and is the most burdened of all men, partly preaching the gospel to those to whom Christ is not yet known and partly confirming in the faith of Christ those who have believed, he is still ready to travel from Corinth all the way to Jerusalem and to carry this gift of theirs to the holy brothers. Second, he again urges them to a more generous contribution, saying: "If it be meet that I also go." The Greek is ἐὰν ἄξιον ᾖ [ean axion ē], that is, "if indeed it be worthy": that is, if you give so largely and so generously, if your collection is of such grace and abundance, and if you are going to refresh by your contribution the church of the saints that is at Jerusalem so fully that it is worthy for your gift to be carried to Jerusalem by myself, I will not hesitate to go myself. In saying this he stirs them, in a manner, to a more generous contribution, since he signifies that if they give liberally he will himself carry their collection to Jerusalem, but if not, he will send others.

units.la: Tertium est, ut iterum caueat, ne quid mali de studio suo erga hanc causam suspicetur ma leuoli, ex eo quod seipsum, si dignum fuerit,
units.tr: The third thing is that he again guards against the ill-disposed suspecting any wrong in his zeal for this cause, arising from the fact that he says he himself will go to Jerusalem with their collection, if it be worthy.

units.la: Hierosolymam cum ipsorum collecta profecturum dicit. Ideo non simpliciter dicit, Si dignum fuerit ipse proficiscar: sed, si dignum fuerit, ut ipse proficiscar, mecum proficiscentur, ij uidelicet quos probaueritis. Sic magno studio cauet ubiq;, ne quam sinistram in hac causa suspicionem incurrat. Non solum à malo, sed & à specie mali cauet sibi uir pius & probus: quanto magis faciendum hoc est Christi apostolis & ministris: præsertim in eiusmodi causa, in qua caro perfidiam suam studio quæstum exercere potest.
units.tr: Therefore he does not simply say, "If it be worthy, I will go myself," but "if it be worthy that I also go, they will go with me, namely those whom you approve." Thus he takes great care everywhere that he should incur no unfavourable suspicion in this matter. A pious and upright man guards himself not only from evil but also from the appearance of evil. How much more must this be done by the apostles and ministers of Christ, especially in a cause of this kind, in which the flesh can practise its faithlessness under the pretext of zeal for gain.

units.la: MBCVM proficiscentur, inquit. ] Non dicit, Quod si dignū fuerit, ut & ipse proficiscar, proficiscar cum ipsis: sed, proficiscētur mecū. Seruat decorum eius, qui quod agendum est, in suam curam suscipit. Huic si qui adduntur, adduntur uel tanquam adiutores, uel tanquam testes. Hi cum illo, non ille cum ipsis proficisci dicitur. Hic ubi nihil est periculi à sinistra suspicione, seruat officij & personę suę decorum. Poterat dicere, Si dignum fuerit ut ipse proficiscar, non erit opus ut proficiscantur ipsi. Potero nanq; omnia sine ipsorum expedire præsentia. Verum ea res facile dedisset prauæ suspicioni occasionem. Ideo finit, imò cōstituit, ut probati ab ecclesia & ipsi proficiscantur: uerū seruat interim personæ suæ decorum, dicens, Proficiscentur mecum.
units.tr: "THEY SHALL GO WITH ME," he says. He does not say, "If it be worthy that I also go, I shall go with them," but "they shall go with me." He keeps the dignity of one who takes upon himself the care of what must be done. If others are added to him, they are added either as helpers or as witnesses. They are said to go with him, not he with them. Here, where there is no danger from unfavourable suspicion, he keeps the dignity of his office and person. He could have said, "If it be worthy that I go myself, there will be no need for them to go too, for I can manage everything without their presence." But that would easily have given occasion for a wicked suspicion. Therefore he allows, indeed he appoints, that those approved by the church should also go; yet meanwhile he preserves the dignity of his own person, saying, "They shall go with me."

units.la: Ad id quoq; consilium hoc conducebat plurimum, ut fratres ex Gentibus & per hos ipsæ ecclesiæ Gentium ecclesiæ Israelis in domino arctius & familiarius per occasionem istā con glutinarentur. Magna difficultate Gentes in consortium Israelis admitrebantur, sicuti patet in Actis apost. Quare prudenti consilio Apostolus, doctor gentium, per occasionē hanc collectarum Gentes ecclesiæ Israelis magis ac magis commendare satagebat. Magnifiquidem est beneficentiæ & gratiæ efficacia, præsertim ubi egestati & penuriæ rerum necessariarum in rebus afflictis succurritur.
units.tr: This plan also contributed greatly to this end: that through this occasion the brothers from the Gentiles, and through them the churches of the Gentiles, might be more closely and familiarly bound together in the Lord with the churches of Israel. The Gentiles were admitted into fellowship with Israel only with great difficulty, as is clear in the Acts of the Apostles. Therefore the Apostle, the teacher of the Gentiles, by his prudent counsel, sought more and more to commend the Gentiles to the churches of Israel by means of this collection. Indeed, the power of beneficence and grace is great, especially where help is given to those who are afflicted and lack the necessities of life.

units.la: Veniam autem ad uos cum Macedoniam transiero. Macedoniam enim per transiturus sum. Apud uos autem forte permanebo, aut etiāhybernabo, ut uos me deducatis, quocūqʒ proficiscar. Non enim uos nunc in transcursu uidere, sed spero me tempus aliquantum mansurū apud uos, si dominus permiserit.
units.tr: "But I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia; for I am going to pass through Macedonia. But perhaps I will stay with you, or even winter, so that you may send me on whatever way I go. For I do not wish to see you now in passing, but I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits."

units.la: De aduentu suo ad ipsos iam aliquoties meminit. Supra cap. 4. Perinde, inquit, quasi non sim uenturus ad uos, inflati sunt quidam. Sed ueniam breui ad uos, si dominus uoluerit: & cognoscam non sermonem istorum qui inflati sunt, sed uirtutem. Non enim in sermone regnum est Dei, sed in uirtute. Quid uultis? cum uirga uenio ad uos, an cum charitate & spiritu lenitatis? Et cap. 11. Cætera, inquit, cum uenero disponam. Et capite hoc præsenti, ne cum uenero, inquit, tunc collationes fiant: ubi uenero autem, quoscunq; probaueritis, per epistolas hos mittam. Ipse Corinthiorum ecclesiæ stat us admodum depravatus & corruptus aduen tum Apostoli magnopere flagitabat, quo ut in absentia illius mala multa inualuerant, ita per præsentiam quæ corrigenda erant corrigeren tur. Ideo toties se uenturum ad eos non in hac tantum, sed & sequenti epistola scribit, ut & male inter eos agentes in ordinem reuocet, & synceros in ordine retineat.
units.tr: He has already mentioned more than once his coming to them. Above, in chapter 4, he says: "As though I were not going to come to you, some are puffed up. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will know not the speech of those who are puffed up but their power. For the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power. What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?" And in chapter 11: "The rest I will arrange when I come." And in this present chapter: "that when I come, collections are not made then; but when I come, I will send those whom you approve, with letters." The state of the Corinthian church was very depraved and corrupt, and it greatly required the Apostle's coming. As in his absence many evils had grown strong, so by his presence what was to be corrected would be corrected. Therefore he writes so often that he will come to them, not only in this letter but also in the following one, so that he may both call back to order those who behave badly among them and keep the sincere in order.

units.la: VENIAM autem ad uos, inquit, cum Mace doniam transiero. Macedoniam enim petran siturus sum. ] De hoc Macedoniæ transitu me minit Lucas in Actis cap. 20. Non dicit se pro secturum in Macedoniam, sed Macedoniam pertransiturum. Ecclesiæ nanq; Macedonum præsentiam ipsius non requirebant, quando quidem adhuc in fide Christi immote perstabant. Quare pertransire tantum Macedoniam constituerat.
units.tr: "I WILL COME to you," he says, "when I have passed through Macedonia; for I am going to pass through Macedonia." Luke mentions this passage through Macedonia in the Acts, chapter 20. He does not say that he will go to Macedonia, but that he will pass through Macedonia. For the churches of the Macedonians did not require his presence, since they were still standing firm in the faith of Christ. Therefore he had decided merely to pass through Macedonia.

units.la: APVD uos autem forte permanebo, aut etiam hybernabo, inquit. ] Ne cogitarent, etsi uenerit, haud tamen hærebit apud nos, sed ut per Macedones, ita & per nos transibit, nosq; in transcursu tantum est uisurus: cum dixisset, Macedoniam enim pertransiturus sum, subiecit: apud uos autem forte permanebo, aut etiá hybernabo. Sic erigit pios, & solicitos reddit eos: qui quoniam male agebant, malebát eum uel nunquam redire ad ipsos, uel si rediret, nō hærere, sed quàm citissime transire.
units.tr: "BUT PERHAPS I will stay with you, or even winter," he says. So that they might not think that, even if he came, he would not stay with them but would pass through them as he passes through the Macedonians, and would see them only in passing: having said, "for I am going to pass through Macedonia," he adds, "but perhaps I will stay with you, or even winter." Thus he raises up the godly and makes them anxious; for since they were behaving badly, they would have preferred that he never return to them, or if he did return, that he not stay but pass through as quickly as possible.

units.la: Quid est autem quod non simpliciter dicit, Apud uos permanebo: sed, apud uos forte per manebo? An scribebat hoc uoluntate non certa, sed dubia? Etenim uocula, id est forte, non est animi certo persuasi, sed dubitantis, qualis esse solet eorum, qui res incertas propo nunt ac tentant, & secundum carnem pleraq; præsumunt, id quod est hominum uanorum ac leuium. At talem fuisse hanc suam cogitatio nem negat, capite primo epistolæ sequentis.
units.tr: But why does he not simply say, "I will remain with you," but "perhaps I will remain with you"? Was he writing with a will not fixed but doubtful? For the little word "perhaps" does not belong to a mind firmly persuaded but to one that doubts, such as is usual with those who propose and attempt uncertain things, and who presume much according to the flesh, which is the mark of vain and light men. Yet he denies in the first chapter of the following letter that his intention was of this kind.

units.la: Respondeo. Certitudo uoluntatis humanæ duplicem habet considerationem. Vnam, qua secundum constans uolentis propositum: al teram, qua secundum sequuturi effectus certi tudinem censetur. Priore modo ipsa uoluntas in se, propter certam & firmam deliberationē, certa uocatur. Sic dicimus, certum nobis est excutere iugum Antichristi: id est, deliberatū ac certo decretum, etiamsi non omnino hoc ex animi sententia succedat. Posteriore modo, id quod uolumus ac proponimus, certo futu rum significatur. Sic ex oppositio, uoluntas du bia dupliciter est consideranda. Primo, in seipsa, quando uidelicet quæ uolumus, non con stanter deliberamus ac proponimus, sed de illis hæsitando ac fluctuando cogitamus: uel etiamsi in præsenti certo ea uelle uidemur, mox tamen sententiam in diuersum mutamus. Deinde in effectu non certo sequuturo. Secundū priorem consideration em non erat dubia Apostoli uoluntas, quam significabat dicens: Apud uos autem forte permanebo, sed certa ac deliberata, quò pertinent ea quæ cap. 1. sequen tis epistolæ hac de causa leguntur. Relinquitur ergo dubiam fuisse secundum posteriorem consideratione m. Non enim certus erat de cô filio Dei, à quo omnium propositorum nostro rum effectus dependet, iuxta illud: Homo pro ponit, Deus uero disponit. Sciebat omnem Apostolatus sui cursum pendere ab immutabili dispositione diuinæ uoluntatis. Quare cū hac in re nihil haberet de illa certi, non simpliciter dixit, Permanebo: sed, Forte permanebo. Secus habet in rebus quæ uerbo Dei nituntur, de quibus si dixeris, forte sic erit, omnino animi non fidelis, sed increduli notam expresseris.
units.tr: I answer: the certainty of human will has a twofold consideration. One is according to the steadfast purpose of the one willing; the other is according to the certainty of the effect that will follow. In the former way the will itself, on account of a certain and firm deliberation, is called certain. Thus we say, "It is certain to us to shake off the yoke of Antichrist," that is, it is deliberately and firmly decided, even if this does not in every way turn out according to our own mind. In the latter way, what we wish and propose is signified as certain to come about. So, conversely, a doubtful will must be considered in two ways. First, in itself, when we do not steadily deliberate and propose what we wish, but think about it hesitating and wavering; or even if we seem to wish something with certainty at present, we soon change our mind to the opposite. Second, in regard to the effect, which is not certain to follow. According to the former consideration, the Apostle's will was not doubtful, which he signified by saying, "But perhaps I will remain with you"; it was certain and deliberate, to which pertain the things read in chapter 1 of the following letter concerning this matter. It remains, then, that it was doubtful according to the latter consideration. For he was not certain about the will of God, on which the effect of all our purposes depends, according to that saying: "Man proposes, but God disposes." He knew that the whole course of his apostleship depended on the unchangeable disposition of the divine will. Therefore, since in this matter he had nothing certain, he did not simply say, "I will remain," but "perhaps I will remain." It is otherwise with matters that rest on the Word of God; if of these you were to say, "perhaps it will be so," you would display the mark not of a faithful mind but of an unbelieving one.

units.la: Ergo ne Apostoli quidem in omnibus quæ uolunt, certi possunt esse de euentu. Sciunt quid uelint, at non ita sciūt futurū ne fit quod uolunt uel secus, quare & ipsi ad euitandam sal sitatis temeritatem, in multis illud usur pare coguntur.
units.tr: Therefore not even the Apostles can be certain of the outcome in all that they wish. They know what they want, but they do not know for certain whether what they want will or will not happen. So, to avoid the rashness of presumption, they too are forced to use this kind of qualification in many cases.

units.la: AVT etiam hybernabo, inquit. ] Dubio pro culadiecta est hæc particula ad intendendum futuræ apud ipsos mansionis moram. Quasi di eat: Imo tota etiá hyeme manebo forsan apud uos. Ergo quod dixit, Apud uos forte perma nebo, non est de perpetua manstione intelligē dum, qualis est episcoporum, ab ecclesiis uus haud discedentium: sed de mora quam apud il los aliquousq; necter e ad hoc constituerat, ut quæ delinquebant corrigeret.
units.tr: "Or even I will winter," he says. This phrase is added with a note of doubt, to indicate the length of his future stay with them, as if he said: indeed, I may even stay with you through the whole winter. So when he said, "Perhaps I will remain with you," this is not to be understood of a perpetual stay, such as that of bishops who never leave their churches, but of a stay which he had determined for some time with them, so that he might correct those who were offending.

units.la: AVT etiá hybernabo, inquit. ] Molesta est & incommoda hyems itinerantibus, nauigan tibus & militantibus, propter frigora, niues ac pluuias. Quare in consueto illis est, ut hyber nent, donec sublata hyemis incommoditate cœ ptum possint absoluere cursum. Ergo & Apo stoli ut molestias hyemales declinent, hyber nis stationibus utuntur. Vtuntur sane, uerum sic, ut nihil ex eo decedat propagando Euan gelio. Etenim si nō minor est uirtus quàm quę rere parta tueri, non est minor Euangelij in ri gando quàm plantando profectus. Hyberna Apostoli statio non erat Euangelij apud Co rinthios hyematio, sed sedula propagatio. Quę admodum capto Apostolo non erat captum Euangelium, ita hybernante Apostolo non hy bernabat Euangelium. Hybernantibus militi bus & nauigantibus, hybernat militia & naui gatio: at hybernantibus Apostolis non hyber nat ministerium Apostolicum, sed tam hyeme quàm æstate fructificat, ac perpetuo ad propo situm scopum collimat. Sic sunt Apostolicæ stationes, quas imitari debebant, qui se succes fores apostolorum esse gloriantur. At horum tam est hodie plus quàm mundanus fastus ac luxus, ut uni Romani pseudoepiscopi hyber nam stationem uix ferat ciuitas, quamuis am pla, si sumptus illius sustinere debeat.
units.tr: Winter is troublesome and inconvenient for travellers, sailors and soldiers, because of the cold, snow and rain. It is therefore customary for them to winter, until the discomfort of winter is over and they can complete the journey they have begun. So the Apostles too, to avoid the troubles of winter, make use of winter quarters. They do use them, certainly, but in such a way that nothing is lost to the spread of the Gospel. For if it is no less a virtue to keep what has been won than to win it, then the progress of the Gospel in watering is no less than in planting. The Apostle's winter stay was not a wintering of the Gospel among the Corinthians, but a diligent propagation of it. Just as when the Apostle was taken captive the Gospel was not taken captive, so when the Apostle wintered, the Gospel did not winter. When soldiers and sailors winter, military service and navigation winter with them; but when the Apostles winter, the apostolic ministry does not winter. It bears fruit in winter as in summer, and always aims at the goal set before it. Such were the apostolic stations, which those who boast that they are the successors of the apostles ought to imitate. But today there is so much worldly pride and luxury among these men that a city, however large, can scarcely bear the winter residence of the one Roman pseudo-bishop, if it must support his expense.

units.la: VT uos me deducatis, inquit. ] Officium co mitandi ac deducendi proficiscentes aliquot nobis scripturæ locis commendatur. Deduci mus autem amicos, uiros honorabiles, & hospites.Amicos,quo significemus nos ægre à di scedentibus auelli,paratosque esse,si ita res fe rat,unà cum illis proficisci. Sic fideles olim de ducebant discedentes à se ministros Christi & apostolos,ut uidere est Actorū 15.20.& 21. Vi ros honorabiles, quo cum honore à nobis di scedant.Sic olim Laconum iuuentus,senes do mum,è foro redeuntes honoris gratia deduce bat,& à tergo prosequebatur. Sic comitatum suum habent principes ac magnates.Hospites & peregrinos tanquam uiarum ignaros dedu cimus,& ne quid illis aduersi contingat in iti nere comitando cauemus. Habet hoc quoque deductionis genus officium humanitatis &ho noris.Sic Abraham suos hospites angelos de ducebat.Gen.18.
units.tr: "That you may bring me on my way," he says. The duty of accompanying and escorting those who set out is commended in several places of Scripture. We escort friends, honourable men and guests. We escort friends to show that we are reluctantly torn away from those who depart, and are ready, if circumstances require, to set out together with them. So the faithful formerly escorted from among themselves the ministers of Christ and the apostles when they departed, as can be seen in Acts 15.20 and 21. We escort honourable men so that they may leave us with honour. So formerly the youth of Sparta, on returning from the forum, escorted their elderly men home as a mark of honour and followed behind them. So princes and great men have their retinues. We escort guests and strangers, as ignorant of the roads, and take care that nothing adverse happens to them on the journey. This kind of escort also belongs to the duty of kindness and honour. So Abraham escorted his guests, the angels. Gen. 18.

units.la: Cum ergo hic dicit Apostolus, Vt uos me deducatis,significat qua sit erga eos singulari fiducia,promittes sibi ipsi omne de illis, & cha ritatis & honoris obsequiū. Et hoc pacto mi tigat ea quæ supra cap.4.de aduentu suo non nihil asperius dixisse uideri poterat. Qua in re Apostolicæ nobis prudentiæ proponitur exe plum,quo cum Samaritano oleum beneuole tiæ correptionis uino immiscea mus.
units.tr: Therefore when the Apostle here says, "That you may bring me on my way," he signifies the singular trust he places in them, promising himself everything from them, both of charity and of respectful service. In this way he softens what he had said above, in chapter 4, about his coming, which might have seemed somewhat harsh. In this matter an example of apostolic prudence is set before us, by which we may mix the oil of kindly correction with the wine, as the Samaritan did.

units.la: QVOCVNQVE proficiscar,inquit.]Cogi tabat quidem Iudæam,sicuti patet capite pri mo epistolæ sequentis. Verum quemadmodū incertus erat, māsurus ne apud ipsos esset uel secus,ita incertus erat,quo nam ab ipsis discedens esset profecturus. Quare ut illic incerti tudinem euentus expresit,dicens:Apud uos forte permanebo,ita hoc quoq; loco indefini te dicit,Quocunq; proficiscar.Quod non alio sensu dicit q; isto:Vt uos me deduc tis,quocū que me proficisci uolet dominus. Etenim sic erat omnino animatus,ut in quemcunq; locū diuina ipsum esset prouidentia uocaturus,illo incunctanter proficisceretur.Reuera autē qui sic sunt animati,digni sunt ut à fidelibus & a mantèr &honorifice deducantur,quocunque proficiscantur.
units.tr: "Wherever I go," he says. He was indeed bound for Judea, as is clear from the first chapter of the following epistle. But just as he was uncertain whether he would remain with them or not, so he was uncertain where he would go when he left them. Therefore, as he expressed uncertainty about the outcome there, saying, "Perhaps I will remain with you," so here too he speaks indefinitely: "Wherever I go." He means nothing other than this: "That you may bring me on my way," wherever God wishes to send me. For he was so disposed that wherever divine providence should call him, he would set out there without hesitation. Indeed, those who are so disposed deserve to be lovingly and honourably escorted by the faithful, wherever they go.

units.la: NOLO enim uos nunc in transcursu uide re,inquit.]Rationem uidetur reddere eiusqd dixit:Veniam autem ad uos cum Macedonia pertransiero.Macedonia enim pertransituru sum.Poterat uidere eos obiter, cum Macedo niam transeundam peteret:uerum id nolebat, propterea quod quæ apud eos erant corrigen da,in transcursu corrigi non poterant,sed diu turnas aliquas moras requirebant, unde & subdit:Sed spero me tempus aliquātum man surum apud uos.Et hoc ipsum quidem amico rum est uidere amicos & salutare in transcursu, si diuturna non conceditur mansio, quemad modum uisurus erat Macedones:uerum aliud poscebat corrigendæ illius ecclesiæ necessi tas. Quare si quis rationem poscat, quorsum non magis inuiseret Corinthios priusquā Ma cedoniā peteret,cum id etiam situs regionum poscerit,exprimitur ratio,cur id facere nolu erit, cum dicit: Nolo enim uos nunc in trans cursu uidere,&c.Scribit autem hoc eā,ut existimo,ob causam,ne Corinthij,ubi audituri e rat,transfire Apostolum Macedoniam, sinistri aliquid ex eo colligerent, quod in transcursu illo ad ipsos non uenisset,atq; ita pij contemni se ab illo suspicarentur,repro bi uero magis ad huc pro ingenio suo peruerse agendi occasio nem sumerent. Sic inquam uidentur hæc esse exponenda.Verum,meo iudicio,non erraue ris,si non de transitu Macedonico,sed alia qua piam occasione exponas,quę tum fuerit illi in manibus, per quam ad eos in transitu uenire potuerit. Nam in sequenti epistola dicerte significat,quod uoluerit per eos transfire in Ma cedoniam,& inde redire ad ipsos.
units.tr: "For I do not wish to see you now in passing," he says. He seems to give the reason for what he said before: "But I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia." For he was going to pass through Macedonia. He could have seen them on the way, when he went through Macedonia, but he did not want to, because the matters that had to be corrected among them could not be corrected in passing; they needed some lengthy delay. Whence he adds: "But I hope to remain with you for some time." It is indeed characteristic of friends to see friends and greet them in passing, if a long stay is not allowed, as he was going to see the Macedonians. But the need to correct that church demanded something else. So if someone asks why he did not visit the Corinthians before going to Macedonia, since the layout of the regions also seemed to call for it, the reason is given for his unwillingness to do so when he says: "For I do not wish to see you now in passing," and so on. I think he writes this for the following reason: so that the Corinthians, among whom he was to be heard, should not gather something sinister from it, namely that the Apostle had passed through Macedonia without coming to them even in passing. They might then suspect that the pious were despised by him, while the wicked would take greater occasion, according to their perverse disposition, to act wrongly. These, I say, seem to be the right explanations. But in my judgment you will not be wrong if you understand it not of the passage through Macedonia but of some other opportunity which was then open to him, by which he could come to them on the way. For in the following epistle he clearly indicates that he wished to pass through them into Macedonia, and to return from there to them.

units.la: Nec ociosum est, quod non simpliciter di cit,Nolo uos in transcursu uidere:sed,nolo uos nunc in transcursu uidere. Vocula Nunc,tale præsentem esse ecclesiæ ipsorum statum signi ficat,qui non transcursum,sed mansionem ali quam requirat. Sic non discriminat inter Ma cedones & Corinthios fideles, dum illos in transcursu uidere : istos non in transcursu ui dere,sed tempus aliquantum apud eos mora ri constituit,quasi illos minus, istos plus dili gat,sed prudenter circunstantias status utro rumq; considerat,& quid salus Corinthiorum in præsenti poscat perpendit,cum dicit:Nolo uos nūc in traiscursu uidere,quasi dicat, quē admodum Macedones:sed aliquantum me tē pus apud uos mansurum spero. Diligebat u trosq; ex æquo,tanquam eos quos per Euan gelium Christo genuerat:uerum ut mater ma iore cura ægrotantem filium quam incolumē prosequitur, licet utrunq; tenere diligat:ita & Apostolus magis est de Corinthiorum quàm Macedonum salute solicitus, quamuis utro que pari dilectione prosequatur. Sic in uno & eodem pectore par est charitas erga fideles omnes,cura uero ac solicitudo dispar.
units.tr: Nor is it idle that he does not simply say, "I do not wish to see you in passing," but "I do not wish to see you now in passing." The little word "now" signifies that the present state of their church is such that it needs not a passing visit but some stay. Thus he does not distinguish between the Macedonian and the Corinthian faithful, as if he wished to see the one in passing and not the other, staying longer with the latter as if he loved them less and these more. Rather, he prudently considers the circumstances of each and weighs what the salvation of the Corinthians requires at present, when he says: "I do not wish to see you now in passing," as if to say: not as I would the Macedonians; but I hope to remain with you for some time. He loved both equally, as those whom he had begotten to Christ through the Gospel. But just as a mother follows a sick son with greater care than a healthy one, although she loves both, so the Apostle is more anxious for the salvation of the Corinthians than of the Macedonians, though he attends to both with equal love. So in one and the same breast charity towards all the faithful is equal, but care and solicitude are unequal.

units.la: SED spero me,inquit,tempus aliquantum mansurū apud uos.] Quid est quod non sim pliciter dicit:sed tempus aliquātum apud uos manebo,cum hoc esset ipsius consilium & có cepta uoluntas.Si certo dicere potuit: Nolo uos nunc in trásitu uidere, quomodo nō ēque certo dixit,sed manebo apud uos. Si certum non erat māsurūs ne esset apud eos uel secus, utique ne id quidem certū erat, quod nō esset eos in transcursu uisurus. Quomodo ergo di cit,se nolle eos uidere in transcursu, quod mā surum se aliquandiu apud eos speret, & non magis ad huuc modum:Spero me non uisurū uos in transcursu tātum,sed mansurum apud uos aliquandiu:præsertim cum utrunq; ex ę quo penderet non ab ipsius uoluntate & pro posito,sed à permisione diuina, de qua subiū git,dicens:Si Deus permiserit.
units.tr: "But I hope," he says, "to remain with you for some time." Why does he not simply say, "But I will remain with you for some time," since this was his plan and settled intention? If he could say with certainty, "I do not wish to see you now in passing," why did he not say just as certainly, "but I will remain with you"? If he was not certain whether he would remain with them or not, then surely it was not certain either that he would not see them in passing. How then does he say that he does not wish to see them in passing, because he hopes to remain with them for some time, rather than saying: "I hope not merely to see you in passing, but to remain with you for some time"? This is especially so since both depended not on his own will and purpose but on divine permission, which he adds, saying: "If God permits."

units.la: Respondeo.Aliud est uelle,& aliud perfice re quod uolumus.Qui uellet ac nollet,sciebat Apostolus,& expresit etiam in eo quod di xit:Nolo uos nunc in transcursu uidere, quid uero futurū esset non ita sciebat,sed spe à diui na permissione pendebat, in cuius potestate situm erat utrunq;, cùm uisurus ne esset ipsos in transcursu uel secus, tum mansurus ne esset apud eos aliquádiu, sicuti sperabat, uel minus. Quare ut non dicit, Sed manebo apud uos: ita non præmisit, Non sum enim nunc uisurus uos: sed, nolo enim nunc uidere uos in tráscur su. quibus uerbis non præiudicat permissioni diuinę: sed uoluntatis suæ cõsilium exprimit, cuius tamen effectum mox se nõ scire, sed sperare, dicens, permissioni Dei subijcit.
units.tr: Answer: to will something and to bring about what we want are two different things. The Apostle knew what he wished and what he did not wish, and he expressed it in what he said: "I do not want to see you now in passing." But what would happen he did not know. He depended on hope, on divine permission, in whose power it lay both whether he would see them in passing or otherwise, and whether he would remain with them for some time, as he hoped, or for less. So just as he does not say "But I will remain with you," he did not put it as "For I am not now going to see you," but as "For I do not want to see you now in passing." By these words he does not prejudge divine permission. He states the purpose of his will, and immediately subjects its outcome, which he does not know but hopes for, to the permission of God, saying "if the Lord permits."

units.la: Obseruet uero diligens lector, duo hęc uerba, Nolo & spero, quomodo hic cõiungantur & usurpentur. Duæ diuersæ res sunt, transitus & aliquanti temporis mansio, quarum altera alteram excludit. Qui aliquandiu manet, non potest obiter transire: rursus qui obiter trásit, non potest aliquandiu mansisse dici. Diutur-nam ergo mansionem sperans Apostolus, nolebat Corinthios uidere in transcursu. Quod si mâsionem hanc non sperasset, uidere eos in transcursu non recusasset, imò statuisset. Quis enim amicos nolit uidere uel in transcursu, apud quos se aliquandiu mansurum sperare nõ potest? Quod igitur nolebat eos uidere in trás cursu, ex eo erat, quod se tempus aliquantum mansurum apud eos ut necessarium ipsis iudi-cabat, ita & sperabat. Sic maioris boni spes mi-noris uoluntatem excludit.
units.tr: A diligent reader should notice how these two words, "I do not want" and "I hope", are joined and used here. Passing through and remaining for some time are two different things, and each excludes the other. One who stays for a while cannot pass by quickly, and one who passes by quickly cannot be said to have stayed for a while. So the Apostol, hoping for a lengthy stay, did not want to see the Corinthians in passing. If he had not hoped for that stay, he would not have refused to see them in passing; he would even have intended it. For who would not want to see friends, even in passing, when he cannot hope to stay with them for some time? That he did not want to see them in passing therefore came from the fact that he judged, and hoped, that a stay of some length with them was necessary for their good. So the hope of a greater good excludes the wish for a lesser one.

units.la: Consimili modo & electis ac fidelibus acci-dit. Nolunt oblectari transitorijs ac perituris huius mundi bonis. Quare? Quia sperant se mansionem habere paratam in cœlis, ubi om-nia sunt perpetua & infinita. Hac spe freti non inhiant terrenis ac transitorijs præsentis uitæ bonis. Reprobi uero, quia spem hanc non ha-bent, transitoria bona sectantur, cogitantes in cordibus suis, Fruamur bonis quæ sunt, de su-turis enim nihil nobis est certi. Quid igitur quisq; speret uel nõ speret, ex eo quod impen-se sectatur uidere licet.
units.tr: It is much the same with the elect and the faithful. They do not want to delight in the fleeting and perishing goods of this world. Why? Because they hope to have a dwelling prepared for them in heaven, where all things are everlasting and infinite. Trusting in this hope, they do not crave the earthly and transitory goods of this present life. The reprobate, however, because they do not have this hope, pursue transitory goods, thinking in their hearts: "Let us enjoy the goods that exist, for we have no certainty about the future." So one can see what a person hopes or does not hope for from what he eagerly pursues.

units.la: Deinde obseruandum est, qualis sit hæc Apostoli spes, de qua dicit: Spero me mâsurum apud uos, si dominus permiserit. Videtur esse incerta prorsus. Alioqui diceret: Quoniam do-minus permittet. Spes autem incerta quid a-liud est, quàm ut Basilius alicubi scite dicit, ui-gilantis hominis somnium? At talis spes uide-tur non competere fidelibus, multo minus a-postolis. Non enim est Christiani hominis & ministri Christi, ut dicat, Spero me mansurum in cœlis, si dominus permiserit: sed potius ad hunc modum, Spero me mansurum in cœlis, quoniam dominus id credentibus in se pro-misit. Cogitandum est, cuius admonendum esse puto propter rudiores, duo esse spei gene-ra: certæ unum, incertæ alterum. Prius ex cer-titudine fidei uerbo Dei innitétis nascitur, ad quod pertinet quod alibi dicit: Spes non con-fundit. Hoc spei genere dicit Christianus: Spe-ro me mansurum in cœlis, quia hoc in se credē-tibus promisit dominus. De spe eiusmodi nõ loquitur hic Apostolus. Posterius ex consilio & proposito est cordis nostri. Et quoniam uer-
units.tr: Next we must observe what kind of hope this Apostolic hope is, of which he says: "I hope to remain with you, if the Lord permits." It seems to be altogether uncertain. Otherwise he would have said: "Since the Lord will permit." But what is an uncertain hope, except, as Basil wisely says somewhere, the dream of a waking man? Yet such a hope does not seem fitting for the faithful, much less for the apostles. For it is not the mark of a Christian man and minister of Christ to say: "I hope to remain in heaven, if the Lord permits." He should rather say: "I hope to remain in heaven, since the Lord has promised this to those who believe in him." I think I must remind the less experienced of this point: there are two kinds of hope, one certain and the other uncertain. The first arises from the certainty of faith, resting on the Word of God, to which belongs what he says elsewhere: "Hope does not disappoint." It is in this kind of hope that the Christian says: "I hope to remain in heaven, because the Lord has promised this to those who believe in him." The Apostle is not speaking here of this kind of hope. The second kind arises from the counsel and purpose of our heart. And since it cannot rest on the Word of God, clear and certain,

units.la: bo Dei certo & expresso niti non potest, certũ esse nequit quod speratur. Huius generis est spes ista, qua se Apostolus sperare dicit fo-re ut aliquandiu apud Corinthios maneat. Id quoniam erat incertum, non dicit, Quoniam dominus permittet: sed, Si dominus permise-rit. Ergo, inquis, ferebatur Apostolus in Apo-stolatu suo spebus incertis, non ex uerbo Dei, sed consilio humano conceptis? Respondeo. Ipse Apostolatus Pauli ad Gêtes, certo uerbo Dei nitebatur, quod dictũ ipsi erat à domino: Vade, quoniam ego in nationes lõge mittam te. Quò uero & quando iret, & quandiu singu-lis in locis hæreret, non erat uerbo Dei singu-lariter expressum, sed à libera dispositione ac ductu spiritus Dei pédebat. Quare quáuis cer-to fungebatur Apostolatu, certo tamen de o-mnib. illius circunstantijs statuere non pote-rat, sed necessariũ erat ut se ductui spirit᷒ totũ permitteret. Sic sperabat multa sub hac con-ditione, si dominus permitteret. Ergo utrunq; spei genus locum habet in sanctis, qui ut fide-les fide uerbi Dei sperant ea quę omnium sunt certissima, & ut homines multa sperât sub hac conditione, si dominus permittat. sciunt enim omnia pendere à diuinæ prouidentiæ consi-lio & permissione. Prius spei genus non est ni-si fidelium. Alterum commune est fidelibus et infidelibus, sic tamen, ut infideles spem suam non subijciant permissioni diuinæ, sed uel sa-pientiæ, uel uiribus carnis.
units.tr: what is hoped for cannot be certain. Of this kind is the hope by which the Apostle says he hopes that he will stay for some time with the Corinthians. Since this was uncertain, he does not say "Since the Lord will permit," but "If the Lord permits." "Therefore," you say, "the Apostle in his apostleship was carried along by uncertain hopes, conceived not from the Word of God but from human counsel?" I answer: Paul's apostleship to the Gentiles itself rested on the certain Word of God, which the Lord had spoken to him: "Go, for I will send you far away to the nations" (Acts 22). But where and when he would go, and how long he would remain in each place, was not expressed individually in the Word of God; it depended on the free disposition and guidance of the Spirit of God. Therefore, although he certainly discharged his apostleship, he could not decide with certainty about all its circumstances, and it was necessary for him to submit himself entirely to the guidance of the Spirit. So he hoped for many things under this condition: "if the Lord permits." Thus both kinds of hope have their place among the saints: as believers they hope, by faith in the Word of God, for those things that are most certain of all, and as men they hope for many things under this condition, "if the Lord permits," for they know that all things depend on the counsel and permission of divine providence. The first kind of hope belongs only to the faithful. The second is common to the faithful and the unbelieving, except that the unbelieving do not subject their hope to divine permission, but to their own wisdom or the strength of the flesh.

units.la: S I dominus permiserit, inquit. ] Conditio-nem hanc spei suę adijcit, significans inane es-se etiam sanctorum hominum propositum, si dominus illud permittere noluerit. Verũ exi-stimo considerandum esse hoc loco, quomo-do uerbum permittendi diuinæ possit tribui prouidentiæ. Etenim aut mala sunt aut bona, uel indifferentia, quæ proponimus. Si mala, quomodo conuenit Deo, ut mala quæ uolu-mus permittat? Permittere nanq; malũ quod prohibendum est, & prohiberi potest, ei non uidetur conuenire iusticię, quæ culpa est libe-ra ab omni. Si bona, uidetur non esse satis per-mittere, quod præcipiendum etiam est, & cum singulari numinis auxilio perficiendum. Si in differentia, quorsum attinet impedire ea quæ propterea quod sunt indifferentia, liberasunt, ut absq; culpa uel omitti possint uel fieri?
units.tr: "If the Lord permits," he says. He adds this condition to his hope, signifying that even the purposes of holy men are empty if the Lord is unwilling to permit them. But I think we must consider here how the word "permit" can be attributed to divine providence. For the things we propose are either evil, or good, or indifferent. If they are evil, how does it suit God to permit the evils we wish? For to permit an evil that ought to be forbidden and could be forbidden does not seem to agree with justice, which is free from all fault. If they are good, it seems not enough to permit what must even be commanded and carried out with the singular help of the divine power. If they are indifferent, what is the point of hindering things which, because they are indifferent, are free, so that they may either be omitted or done without fault?

units.la: Considerationẽ hanc uideo esse geminam. Primum enim inspicienda est præsentis loci lectio: deinde transeundum ad id quod in ge-nere de permissione Dei quæritur. Quod le-ctionem hanc, si dominus permiserit, attinet, in Græco est, ἐὰν ὁ κύριος ἐπιτρέψῃ. Verbũ ἐπιτρέπειν non modo permittere, sed & committere non nunquam significat, quo sensu & Salustius uer-bo permittendi subinde usus est. Quod si illũ hoc loco reperimus, ut legamus, Si dominus commiserit, nulla remanet quæstio. Si uerò le-gerimus, si dominus permiserit, cogitandum est triplex esse permissionis genus. Primum, quo uoluntarij permittimus ea quæ impedire poterapoteramus, nisi potetium uotis assentiremus Sic legitur dominus permisisse spiritibus immundis, ut sicuti petebant, demigraret in gregem porcorum Matth.8. Secundum, quo coacti & inuiti permittimus ea potetioribus, quæ impedire non possumus. Sic & nos & omnes nostras fortunas hosti permittimus, ubi resistendi uiribus destituimur. Tertium, quo neq; probātes, neq; coacti, sed certas ob causas per mittimus ea fieri, quæ aliàs impedieda, aut impedimus que permittenda fuisse uidetur. Iam quod primum permissionis genus attinet, copetere illud Deo nemo cordatus inficias ibit. Quis enim adeo stupidus est, ut neget Deum precibus suorum permittere innumera, quæ omnium possit & iustissime & liberrime negare? Cosimiliter quod attinet tertium genus, existimo sine omni controuersia recte tribui Deo, quod non modo permittat, id est, fieri sinat mala, quæ certis de causis impedire: sed & impediat bona, quæ in speciem recte permittere poterat. Quod mala fieri sinat, manifesto testimonio ex uerbis Apostoli comprobatur, quæ Actorum 14. leguntur ad hunc modū: qui in præteritis ætatibus sinebat omnes Gentes ingredi uijs suis. Poterat hoc utiq; prohibere, & à uita humana auertere: uerum erant causæ quur omnes sub incredulitatem concludens ea fieri permitteret, quæ absq; ullo poterat impedire negocio.
