Quod bona in speciem non-nunquam certas ob causas impediat, uel in eo manifestum est, quod aliquando prohibitus est Apostolus loqui sermonem Euangelij, sicut uidere est Actorum 16. In se utiq; bonum est loqui sermonem uitæ, in quo uirtus est ad seruandam credentes. Erant tamen causæ propter quas tum temporis nolebat illum prædicari spiritus Christi in Asia. Secundū uero per misiionis genus, quod est impotentiæ & coactionis, nemo sanæ mentis tribuerit Deo inuincibili & omnipotenti. Ergo quod hic Apostolus dicit, Sperare permansurū se apud Corinthios, si dominus permiserit: recte, ut iudico, ad primū genus referetur. Erat enim hoc illi in uotis, ideoq; petebat à domino, ut permissione ipsius quod sperabat perficere posset. Recte igitur tribuit scriptura Deo non modo bonorum & indifferentium, sed & malorū permissionem. Vbi uel mala permittit, uel bona impedit, cogitandum nobis est, esse illi causas & iustas & sufficientes, cur hoc faciat. Vbi permittit bona, de bonitatis illius ingenio: ubi indifferentia permittit, de libera illius uoluntate, potestate, & prudentia cogitemus. Haec enim libera sunt indifferentia, quatenus nullis redduntur circumstantijs illicita. Hæc obiter de permissione diuina in gratiam imperitorum annotare uoluimus. Neque enim propositi nostri est operosam disputatione ultra ea instituere, quæ homini pio tanquam uera & simplicia satisfacere possunt.
units.tr: I see that this consideration is twofold. First, we must examine the reading of the present passage; then we must turn to what is asked in general about the permission of God. As to this reading, "if the Lord permits," the Greek is "ἐὰν ὁ κύριος ἐπιτρέψῃ" [if the Lord permits]. The verb ἐπιτρέπειν sometimes means not only "to permit" but also "to entrust," and in this sense Sallust too has now and then used the word "permit". If we find it in this sense here, so that we read "if the Lord entrusts," no question remains. But if we read "if the Lord permits," we must consider that there are three kinds of permission. The first is that by which we willingly permit what we could have prevented, unless we agreed to the wishes of the powerful. Thus we read that the Lord permitted the unclean spirits, as they asked, to pass into a herd of swine (Matt. 8). The second is that by which we, compelled and unwilling, permit what the stronger do, which we cannot prevent. Thus we and all our fortunes are handed over to the enemy when we are deprived of the strength to resist. The third is that by which, neither approving nor compelled, but for certain reasons, we permit things to happen which seem to have been either to be prevented or not to be permitted. Now as to the first kind of permission, no one of sound mind will deny that it belongs to God. For who is so foolish as to deny that God, at the prayers of his people, permits countless things which he could most justly and most freely refuse? Likewise as to the third kind, I think it is beyond all controversy rightly attributed to God that he not only permits, that is, lets evils happen for certain reasons which he could prevent, but also prevents goods which he seemed able to permit. That he lets evils happen is clearly proved by the words of the Apostle, which are read in Acts 14 in this way: "who in past generations allowed all nations to walk in their own ways." He could certainly have forbidden this and turned human life aside from it, but there were reasons why he permitted, while shutting all under unbelief, things that could be prevented without any trouble. That he sometimes hinders what is good in appearance, for certain reasons, is clear from the fact that the Apostle was at one time forbidden to preach the word of the gospel, as we see in Acts 16. In itself it is certainly good to speak the word of life, in which there is power to save believers. Yet there were reasons why at that time the Spirit of Christ did not want it preached in Asia. The second kind of permission, however, which belongs to impotence and compulsion, no one of sound mind would attribute to the invincible and omnipotent God. Therefore what the Apostle says here, that he hopes to remain with the Corinthians, if the Lord permits, is rightly referred, as I judge, to the first kind. For this was among his prayers, and therefore he asked the Lord that by his permission he might be able to accomplish what he hoped for. Rightly, then, Scripture attributes to God the permission not only of good and indifferent things but also of evil ones. Where he either permits evils or hinders goods, we must think that he has causes both just and sufficient for doing so. Where he permits good things, let us think of the goodness of his nature; where he permits indifferent things, let us think of his free will, power and prudence. For these are free indifferent things, insofar as no circumstances make them unlawful. We have wished to note these points in passing about divine permission for the benefit of the unlearned. For it is not our purpose to pursue a laboured disputation beyond what can satisfy a pious man as true and plain.

units.la: Commorabor autem Ephesi usq; ad
units.tr: But I will remain at Ephesus until

units.la: Pentecosten. Ostium enim mihi apertum est magnum & efficax, & sunt aduersarij multi.
units.tr: Pentecost. For a great and effective door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries.

units.la: Ambiguum est, Ephesi ne fuerit cum hæc scriberet, uel alio quodam loco constitutus Ephesum proficisci, ibiq; ad Pentecosten usque commorari constituerit. Sunt qui priore sententiam sequantur. Ad calcem tamen epistolæ subiecerunt Græci, scriptam eam fuisse Philippis, perq; Stephanam, Fortunatum, Achaicum, & Thimotheū missam. Ephesi fuisse scriptam, non uideo quàm certo ex hoc statui possit, quod illic se ad Pentecosten usque commoraturum dicit. Si diceret: commorabor autē hic uel nunc Ephesi usq; ad Pentecosten, nulla superesset ambiguitas. Iam cum simpliciter dicat: Commorabor autem Ephesi, quèadmodum & cap. præcedenti non dixit: Si secundum hominem cum bestijs hic Ephesi depugnaui, sed simpliciter: Si secundum hominem cum bestijs Ephesi depugnaui, existimo non posse hinc certo statui, quod epistolam hác Ephesi constitutus scripserit. Hæc dicens, illic scriptam non esse nego. Nolim temere contra dicere illorum sententiæ, qui sic sentiunt, non solum recentiores, sed ex ueteribus Græcis nonnulli, è quorum numero est & Chrysostomus, qui sic dicit: ... Et qui ex Græcis præfatus est, consimili modo, inquit, ... Vt non puto firmum esse ex præsentibus Apostoli uerbis quod sentiút, ita nō affero esse falsum, sed lectoris relinquo iudicio. Quid autem sequuti sint, qui è Philippis missam esse scripserunt, ne Erasmus quidem coiectare potuit.
units.tr: It is uncertain whether he was at Ephesus when he wrote this, or whether he was elsewhere and intended to set out for Ephesus and stay there until Pentecost. Some follow the former opinion. Yet at the end of the epistle the Greeks added that it was written from Philippi and sent by Stephanas, Fortunatus, Achaicus and Timothy. I do not see how it can be firmly concluded from this that it was written at Ephesus, merely because he says he will remain there until Pentecost. If he had said, "I will remain here, or now, at Ephesus until Pentecost," there would be no ambiguity. But since he simply says, "I will remain at Ephesus," just as in the previous chapter he did not say, "If I have fought with beasts here at Ephesus after the manner of men," but simply, "If I have fought with beasts at Ephesus after the manner of men," I think it cannot be certainly established from this that he wrote the letter while staying at Ephesus. In saying this I do not deny that it was written there. I am unwilling to rashly oppose the opinion of those who think so, not only more recent writers but also some of the ancient Greeks, among whom is Chrysostom, who says: ... And he who among the Greeks was mentioned earlier, says in a similar way: ... Just as I do not think what they hold is firm from the present words of the Apostle, so I do not assert that it is false, but I leave the judgment to the reader. As for those who wrote that it was sent from Philippi, even Erasmus could not guess what they followed.

units.la: COMMORABOR autem Ephesi, inquit, usque ad Pentecosten. Quoniam Macedoniam transiturum se, ac postea ad ipsos uenturum, ibiq; mansurum aliquandiu dixit, ne putarent ad id se itineris mox accinctūrum, particulam hanc adiecit dicens: Commorabor autem Ephesi usq; ad Pentecosten. Sic cauit ne futura mora, quam Ephesi facere constituerat, inanis propositi suspicionem gignens omnem aduersus sui expectationem utrisq; & pijs & reprobis extinguueret.
units.tr: "I will remain at Ephesus," he says, "until Pentecost." Since he had said that he would pass through Macedonia and afterwards come to them and stay with them for some time, lest they think he would soon set out on that journey, he added this clause, saying: "But I will remain at Ephesus until Pentecost." Thus he took care that the delay he had determined to make at Ephesus should not give rise to a suspicion of an empty purpose, and so he removed all doubt about his expectation, both for the godly and for the reprobate.

units.la: Chrysostomus particulam hanc amicitię indicium habere dicit, cuius hoc est proprium, ut consilia rerum gerendarum amicis reuelet. Mihi uero cautionis potius ac circumspectionis diligentiam spirare uidetur.
units.tr: Chrysostom says that this clause shows friendship, which is characteristic of one who discloses to his friends the plans of his undertakings. But to me it seems rather to breathe the diligence of caution and circumspection.

units.la: Illud, Vsque ad Pentecosten, Erasmus uertit, Vsq; ad diem quinquagesimum: quasi significarit se Apostolus quinquaginta dierum spacio Ephesi hæsurum. Meo tamen iudicio magis expresit anni tempus, quo relicta Epheso Macedoniam transfire constituerit, quàm morę spacium, quo Ephesi mansurus fuerit, præsertim cum in Græco per articulum eius sit temporis expressa specificatio. Non enim simpliciter dicit: ... sed, ... quæ simpliciter de die Pentecostes intelligendum est, nota & populo legali propter annuam solennitatem, & ecclesiæ Christi propter missionem spiritussanêti.
units.tr: Erasmus translates "until Pentecost" as "until the fiftieth day," as if the Apostle meant that he would stay at Ephesus for a space of fifty days. In my judgment, however, it expresses rather the time of year at which he resolved to leave Ephesus and cross over into Macedonia, than the length of the delay during which he would stay at Ephesus, especially since in the Greek the specification of that time is expressed by the article. For he does not simply say ... but ..., which must be understood simply of the day of Pentecost, known both to the people under the law because of the yearly solemnity, and to the Church of Christ because of the sending of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Quam uero ob causam ad Pentecosten usq; Ephesi manere, ac tum demum proficisci constituerit, quoniam expressum non est, non est ut curiosius inquiramus: sed indubitato sentiamus, fuisse illi certas eius propositi causas, è quibus unam subiungit, qua tamen non tam singularem eius solennitatis, quàm propositæ moræ rationem reddit dicens: Ostium enim mihi apertum est magnum & efficax.
units.tr: As to why he resolved to remain at Ephesus until Pentecost and only then to depart, since this is not expressed, we need not inquire too curiously. Let us rather hold without doubt that he had definite reasons for his purpose, one of which he adds, though in giving the reason for the delay he does not so much explain that particular festival as he gives the reason for the stay he proposed, saying: "For a great and effective door has been opened to me."

units.la: Quod autem Pentecostes diem attinet, puto illum tum temporis non Christianis, sed iis fuisse Iudæis legaliter solennem ac festum.
units.tr: As for the day of Pentecost, I think that at that time it was a legal solemnity and feast for the Jews, not for Christians.

units.la: Quare si rationem illius aliquam habebat Apostolus, habebat illam aut propter temporis illius qualitatem proficientibus accommodam, aut propter Iudæos, qui legali diei illius observantia celeberrimos solebant habere conventus, quorum ipse occasionem ad regni Christi propagationem captare consueuit, id quod & Actorum 20. apparet, ubi memoratur, quàm cupide properarit ut diem Pentecostes ageret Hierosolymis. Potest & illud cogitari. Erat natione Iudæus, inter Iudæos natus & educatus, atq; ita moribus illorum à puero assuetus. Iudæis autem in more erat, ut anni partes dividerent secundum spacia & interstitia dierum solennium, Paschatis, Pentecostes, & festi tabernaculorum, & hac divisione in rebus suis gerendis quoq; uterentur: ad quem modum in Papatu quoque fieri uidemus, in quo uel actiones suas uel propositæ, aut compromissa certis solennium dierum festis utpote Natalis domini, Paschatis, Pentecostes, diuorum quoq; beatæ uirginis, Georgij, Ioannis, Iacobi, Michaelis, Galli, Martini, &c. terminare solent. Cum ergo educatus in hac esset Iudæorum consuetudine Apostolus, uerosimile est Christianum quoq; factum esse illa usum, atq; ita hic simpliciter Pentecostes sibi diem propositum, ad quem usq; Ephesi in opere domini commoraretur, non quod dierum esset observantiæ ritu Iudaico obstrictus, sed quod eam sibi moram ad opus domini prouehendum necessariâ fore iudicaret. Consimile est quod à nostris quoq; fieri uidemus, qui licet Papisticis superstitionibus ualedixerint, adhuc tamen anni spacia in rebus gerendis secundum diuorum festa metiuntur ac terminant. Quid cogitari possit hoc loco simpliciter admoneo. Iudicet lector.
units.tr: Therefore, if the Apostle had some regard for it, he had regard to it either because of the nature of that time, which suited those who were making progress, or because of the Jews, who were accustomed to hold very crowded assemblies on the legal observance of that day, and the Apostle was accustomed to seize on these as an opportunity for spreading the kingdom of Christ. This is also apparent in Acts 20, where it is recorded how eagerly he hurried to keep the day of Pentecost at Jerusalem. One may also think of this: he was by birth a Jew, born and brought up among the Jews, and so accustomed from boyhood to their customs. Now it was the custom of the Jews to divide the parts of the year according to the spans and intervals of the solemn days, of Passover, Pentecost and the feast of tabernacles, and to use this division also in managing their affairs. We see this same practice in the Papacy, where they are accustomed to end their actions, or their appointed or agreed matters, by the fixed feasts of the solemn days, such as the Lord's Nativity, Easter, Pentecost, and also the days of the blessed Virgin, of George, John, James, Michael, Gall, Martin, and so on. Since therefore the Apostle had been brought up in this Jewish custom, it is likely that he too, as a Christian, used it, and so here he simply set Pentecost before himself as the day up to which he would remain at Ephesus in the work of the Lord. He did this not because he was bound to observe days according to the Jewish rite, but because he judged that this delay would be necessary for advancing the work of the Lord. Something similar we see done by our own people, who, though they have renounced Papist superstitions, still measure and end the spans of the year in their affairs by the feasts of the saints. What might be thought in this place I simply point out. Let the reader judge.

units.la: OSTIVM enim mihi, inquit, apertu est magnum & efficax.] Rationem reddit, quare non sit statim Macedoniam transfuturus, & Corinthum uenturus, sed ad Pentecosten usq; Ephesi hæsurus. Cauet ne segniter ac negligenter in opere domini uersari, aut aliàs leuibus de causis tandiu Ephesi hærere uideatur. Neq; enim Apostolici muneris erat diutius eodem in loco sine causa moras nectere ac tempus inaniter perdere. Assignat ergo propositæ sibi morae causam satis grauem ac prægnatem, eamq;
units.tr: "For a door," he says, "has been opened to me, great and effective." He gives the reason why he will not immediately pass over into Macedonia and come to Corinth, but remain at Ephesus until Pentecost. He guards against appearing to be idle and negligent in the work of the Lord, or to linger at Ephesus for so long for slight reasons. For it was not the duty of the apostolic office to make long delays without cause in the same place and to waste time to no purpose. He therefore assigns a cause for the delay that is sufficiently weighty and significant,

units.la: talem, quæ digna sit Apostolica diligentia & cura, cum dicit: Ostium enim mihi apertum est magnum & efficax, & sunt aduersarij multi. Causa hæc erat gemina. Prior cancer nebat aditu & accessum lucrifaciedi domino quamplurimos morales. Posterior nascebatur ex im proba impiorum hominum contradictione & reluctatione, quibus erat fortiter ac dextre resistendum. Vtraq; præsentiam Apostoli diuturniorem requirebat.
units.tr: and one such as is worthy of apostolic diligence and care, when he says: "For a great and effective door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries." This cause was twofold. The first was that it offered access and an opening for winning very many men to the Lord. The second arose from the wicked opposition and resistance of ungodly men, against whom it was necessary to resist strongly and skilfully. Both required the Apostle's longer presence.

units.la: Vtitur autem metaphorica dictione, cum si bi ostium apertum esse dicit. Significat nō modo rimam aliquam introducendi ad Ephesios salutis doctrinam, sed & ostium, id est, uiam & accessum esse factum, idq; non angustum, sed amplum & magnum. Videbat multorum animos paratos esse ad audiendum sermonem Euangelij, & non paucos illum iam fide acceptasse, atq; ita magno successu propagari illic regnum Christi.
units.tr: He uses a metaphorical expression when he says that a door has been opened to him. He means not only that a chink has been made for introducing the teaching of salvation to the Ephesians, but also that a door, that is, a way and access, has been made, and not a narrow one but a wide and great one. He saw that the minds of many were ready to hear the word of the Gospel, and that not a few had already received it by faith, and so the kingdom of Christ was spreading there with great success.

units.la: Obserua uero, quod non dicit, Ostium mihi aperui: sed, ostium mihi apertum est. Non aperiebat ipse ostium sermoni Dei, cuius erat minister & Apostolus: sed aperiebat ille, qui & clauem habet cordium humanorum, & omnia obstacula potentiæ aduersariæ nutu suo amouere potest & tollere. unde & ad Colossenses 4. hortatur fideles ad orandum pro se, ut Deus aperiat sibi ostium sermonis. Quasi quodam ostio occlusa erant mortalium corda cæcitate & obstinatione, sic ut nullus pateret ad illa scientiæ Dei aditus. Cum autem aperiret illa spiritus Dei afflatus, quid fiebat aliud, quàm qd aperiebatur Apostolo Dei ostium introducen di regni Dei, & excludendi regni Satanæ. Nec impedit hunc sensum, quod non dicit, ostium apertum est regno Dei: sed, ostium aperti est mihi. Non erat ipse princeps, sed dux principis Christi, cui Apostolica functione militabat. Cum ostium aperitur duci, aperitur non duci, sed principi. Sic cum ostium aperitur Apostolo, aperitur non Apostolo, sed principi apostolorum ipsi Christo.
units.tr: Observe, moreover, that he does not say, "I have opened a door," but "a door has been opened to me." He did not open the door to the word of God, though he was its minister and Apostle. It was opened by him who holds the key of human hearts and who by his nod can remove and take away all the obstacles of the adverse power. Hence also in Colossians 4 he exhorts the faithful to pray for him, that God may open to him a door for the word. As if the hearts of mortals were shut by a kind of door through blindness and obstinacy, so that no access to the knowledge of God lay open to them. When the breath of the Spirit opened these hearts, what else happened than that a door was opened to the Apostle of God for introducing the kingdom of God and for shutting out the kingdom of Satan? Nor does it hinder this sense that he does not say, "A door has been opened to the kingdom of God," but "a door has been opened to me." He was not the prince himself, but the leader of the Prince, Christ, whom he served in the apostolic office. When a door is opened to a leader, it is opened not to a leader but to the prince. So when a door is opened to the Apostle, it is opened not to the Apostle but to the Prince of the apostles, Christ himself.

units.la: MAGNVM, inquit, &c. efficax.] Magno ostio aperto magna datur introeundi copia. Quo maius aperitur ostium, hoc maiori datur multitudini ingrediendi facultas. Cũ ergo significare uellet Apostolus per singularem Dei gratiã esse factũ, ut multorum essent animi ad recipiendũ Euangelium patefacti, non simpliciter dixit, ostium enim mihi apertum est: sed adiecit, magnum & efficax.
units.tr: "Great," he says, "and effective." A great door, once opened, gives a great opportunity of entering. The larger the door opened, the greater the freedom given to a crowd to enter. Since the Apostle wished to indicate that, by the singular grace of God, the minds of many had been opened to receive the gospel, he did not simply say, "For a door has been opened to me," but added, "great and effective."

units.la: ET efficax, inquit.] Quorsum hoc adiecit: est ne magnum aliquod ostium quod non sit efficax? Plane licet inuenire magnam oblatam gerendæ rei copiam, cui tamen desit perficiendi efficacia. Significans igitur non modo magnum & patentem dari sibi accessum ad propagandum ueritatis doctrinam, sed simul dari & efficaciam, qua mentes multorum illuminentur, & magna lucrifiat domino credentium multitudo: addit, & efficax. Magnum ueluti ostium apertum est, quàdo ueritatis doctrinam audiunt passim multi. Efficax uero tum demum est, quando non solum audiunt multi, sed & quod audiunt auidè & bono corde recipiunt, atque ita ad cognitionem veritatis perducti recipiscunt & conuertunrur. Cum hoc Ephesi ad initium Euangelicæ prædicationis fieret, magna erat Apostolo ratio, tam præclara propagandi regni Dei occasionem non negligendi, sed magno diuturnioris præsentiæ suæ studio prosequendi.
units.tr: "And effective," he says. Why did he add this? Is there any great door that is not effective? Plainly one may find a great opportunity offered for doing a work, yet lacking the power to bring it to completion. So by adding "and effective," he signifies that he has been given not only a great and open access to spreading the teaching of the truth, but also the efficacy by which the minds of many are enlightened and a great multitude of believers is gained for the Lord. A door is, as it were, great and open when many everywhere hear the teaching of the truth. It is truly effective, however, only when many not only hear, but also receive eagerly and with a good heart what they hear, and so, led to knowledge of the truth, they repent and are converted. Since this was happening at Ephesus at the beginning of the gospel preaching, it was of great concern to the Apostle not to neglect so splendid an occasion for spreading the kingdom of God, but to pursue it with great zeal by staying longer.

units.la: Quod lectioem attinet, habet uulgata æditio, non efficax, sed euidens. Apparet interpretè legisse ιναργὲς pro ἐνεργὲς. Sonat enim ιναργὲς euidentem, ἐνεργὴς uero efficacem. Sed hac de re annotauit & Erasmus. Si cum uulgata legerimus, euidens, sensus erit: Quoniam ostium mihi apertum est non angustum, sed amplum: non obscurum, sed luculentum & manifestum, manebo Ephesi usque ad Pentecosté, ut tam insigni gratiæ Dei, tamq; luculenter declaratæ diutius subseruiam. Est hic quoque sensus haud incommodus. Nec priorem excludit, imò necessario requirit. Prius enim est gratiam Dei esse efficacem in ministerio Euanglij, deinde efficatiam hanc sequitur ut fiat illustris, euidens & luculenta, dum uirtus illius manifestissimis diuinæ operationis argumentis declaratur.
units.tr: As for the reading, the Vulgate edition has not "effective" but "evident." The translator seems to have read ιναργὲς [inarges] for ἐνεργὲς [energes]. For ιναργὲς means evident, while ἐνεργὴς means effective. Erasmus also noted this matter. If we read with the Vulgate, "evident," the sense will be: Since a door has been opened to me that is not narrow but wide, not obscure but bright and manifest, I shall remain at Ephesus until Pentecost, so that I may serve longer such a remarkable grace of God, so brightly displayed. This sense is also not unsuitable. Nor does it exclude the former; rather it necessarily requires it. For it is first that the grace of God is effective in the ministry of the gospel, and then this efficacy follows, so that it becomes illustrious, evident and bright, while its power is declared by the most manifest proofs of divine working.

units.la: ET sunt, inquit, aduersarij multi.] Hæc erat illi altera diutius manendi causa. Quo enim plures ostium illud regno Dei apertum denuo conabantur occludere, hoc magis Apostoli tanquam ducis præsistentia ac dexteritas requirebatur.
units.tr: "And there are many adversaries," he says. This was his second reason for staying longer. For the more numerous were those who tried again to close that door opened to the kingdom of God, the more the presence and skill of the Apostle, as of a leader, was required.

units.la: 1 Sunt autem hic duo notanda. Vnum, quæ sit fors Euangelij. Ea uidelicet, ut hoc plures sortiatur aduersarios, quo maius illi & efficacius aperitur ostium. Huius rei exemplum hoc loco proponitur. Quemadmodum enim non simpliciter dicit, Ostium enim apertum est mihi, sed, ostium apertum est mihi magnum & efficax: ita non simpliciter subijcit, & sunt aduersarij nonnulli, sed, & sunt aduersarij multi. Sic princeps huius mundi quo magis inualescit Euangelij cursus, hoc plures illi obijcit aduersarios. Horum igitur multitudo haud mediocre, sed magnum ueritati ostium apertum esse innuit. Quare tam abest, ut terreri debeamus, si plures aduersarij contra doctrinam ueritatis insurgant, ut magis id nobis conueniat esse solatio, propter certum inualescentis regni Dei argumentum. Si non agnoscimus illius successum in seipso, agnoscamus saltem in multitudine aduersariorum. Augescens quippe furor Satanæ tantum non uociferatur, augeri illi metum breui destruendi ipsius regni, quod uideat regni Dei uires quotidie magis ac magis inualescere.
units.tr: 1 Two things here are to be noted. The first is what the lot of the gospel is: namely, that the more wide and effective the door opened to it, the more adversaries it obtains. An example of this is set before us in this place. For just as he does not simply say, "For a door has been opened to me," but "a door has been opened to me, great and effective," so he does not simply add "and there are some adversaries," but "and there are many adversaries." So the prince of this world sets more adversaries against the gospel the more its course prevails. The great number of them therefore signifies that a door, and no small one, has been opened to the truth. Hence we ought by no means to be terrified if many adversaries rise up against the teaching of the truth; rather this should be a consolation to us, since it is a sure sign that the kingdom of God is prevailing. If we do not recognise its success in itself, let us at least recognise it in the multitude of adversaries. For the raging of Satan, growing ever greater, all but cries out that his fear of the destruction of his own kingdom grows, because he sees the powers of the kingdom of God gaining strength more and more each day.

units.la: 2 Alterum est obseruandum hoc loco, quod multitudo aduersariorum causam dedit Apostolo non discendi, sed potius diutius manendi. Carnalis homo cogitasset, frustra se man surum eo loco, ubi tam multi aduersarij contra se insurgant, quod unus tam multis retundendis sufficere non posse uideatur. At Apostolus, quoniam non solum multitudinem considerabat aduersariorum, sed simul, imò magis tam luculetam cælestis gratiæ efficatiam, imperterrito spiritu uim aduersariorum sustinebat, & hoc sibi manendum ac pugnandum diutius statuebat, quo plures Euangelio Christi contradicebant. Exemplum hoc fidelibus Christi ministris proponitur, ut & ipsi hoc minus à grege commisso discedant, quo pluribus ille hostibus obiectus esse uidetur.
units.tr: 2 The second thing to be observed here is that the multitude of adversaries gave the Apostle a reason not for leaving but rather for staying longer. A carnal man would have thought that he would be wasting his time in a place where so many adversaries rose up against him, since one man seemed unable to repel so many. But the Apostle, considering not only the multitude of adversaries but at the same time, and even more, the so much brighter efficacy of heavenly grace, endured the force of his opponents with an undaunted spirit, and decided that he must stay and fight there longer, the more people contradicted the gospel of Christ. This example is set before the faithful ministers of Christ, that they too may not depart from the flock committed to them the more it seems exposed to enemies.

units.la: Dicet mihi quisquam: quur ergo tu ecclesiam Augustanam in eo discrimine deseruisti, quo pluribus erat & ualentioribus aduersarijs quàm unquam antea obiecta? Respondeo. Abegit me ab ea ecclesia nō terror aduersariorum, sed horror accepti Interim, cuius præuaricatio nis ne in minimo quidem consors esse uolebam. Vbi lupus in ouile recipitur, & uoces illius pro uocibus pastoris sectandas esse decernitur, hic discedens pastor non deserit gregè, sed à grege destertus melioribus sese usibus, si domino uideatur, asseruat.
units.tr: Someone will say to me: Why then did you abandon the Church of Augsburg in that crisis, when it was exposed to more and stronger adversaries than ever before? I answer: It was not the terror of the adversaries that drove me from that church, but the horror of the things that had been accepted there, in whose prevarication I was unwilling to share even in the least degree. When a wolf is received into the sheepfold, and its voices are decreed to be followed in place of the voice of the shepherd, the pastor who departs does not desert the flock; rather, driven away by the flock, he preserves himself for better uses, if it seems good to the Lord.

units.la: Qui uero fuerint aduersarij illi multi, qui doctrinæ Apostoli resistere moliebātur, Actorum 19. uidere licet. Alij erant ex iudæis, qui indurati non credebant, sed male de uia domini coram multitudine loquebantur: alij erant ex Gentibus, quorum uelut antesignanus erat Demetrius faber argentarius, quæstū in cultu Dianæ, perinde atq; Papistarum sacrifices in cultu diuorum, sequens. Huius improbitate non modo eiusdem quæstus complices, sed & tota ciuitas aduersus Apostolum in furore seditionis concitabatur. Quare non immerito multorum hic facit aduersariorū mentionem.
units.tr: Who the many adversaries were who tried to resist the Apostle's teaching may be seen in Acts 19. Some were from the Jews, who, hardened, did not believe, but spoke evil of the way of the Lord before the multitude. Others were from the Gentiles, of whom Demetrius the silversmith was as it were the standard-bearer, pursuing his gain from the worship of Diana, just as the Papists do from the worship of the saints. Through the wickedness of this man, not only his fellow-workers in the same trade but the whole city was stirred up in a rage of sedition against the Apostle. So it is not without reason that he here makes mention of many adversaries.

units.la: De eo uero, quod ostium sibi magnum & efficax apertum dicit, eodem capite legitur ad hunc modum: Ingressus autem synagogam libere loquebatur, ad tres menses disputans & suadens de regno Dei. Cum autem quidam indurarentur, nec crederent male loquētes de uia domini coram multitudine, digressus ab illis segregauit discipulos, quotidie disputans in schola Tyrâni cuiusdam. Hoc autem factū est per biennium, ita ut omnes qui habitabant in Asia audirent sermonem domini Iesu, Iudæi simul & Græci. Sic magnum erat illi apertum ostium. Quàm uero fuerit illud efficax, memoratur hoc pacto: Virtutesque non uulgares æ… debebat Deus per manus Pauli, ita ut etiam super infirmos deferrentur à corpore eius sudaria & semicinæta, & recederent ab eis morbi & spiritus mali egrederētur. Item: Hoc autem innotuit omnibus Iudæis simul & Græcis qui habitabant Ephesi, & incidit timor in omnes illos, & magnificabatur nomen domini Iesu. Multique credentium ueniebant confitentes & annunciantes facta sua. Multi autem ex eis, qui curiosas artes executerant conportatos libros exusserunt coram omnibus, & supputatis precijs illorum repererunt pecuniæ cuniæ quinquaginta millia. Ita fortiter crescebat sermo Dei & confirmabatur, &c. Hæc ibi quib. satis perspicue exponitur, quod hic Paulus ad Corinthios scribit.
units.tr: As for his saying that a great and effective door was opened to him, the same chapter reads as follows: "And he went into the synagogue and spoke boldly, for three months disputing and persuading concerning the kingdom of God. But when some were hardened and did not believe, speaking evil of the way of the Lord before the multitude, he withdrew from them and separated the disciples, disputing daily in the school of a certain Tyrannus. This was done for two years, so that all who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks." So a great door was open to him. How effective it was is recorded in this way: "And God worked no ordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs and aprons were carried from his body to the sick, and diseases departed from them and evil spirits went out." Likewise: "And this became known to all the Jews and Greeks who lived at Ephesus, and fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified. And many of those who believed came, confessing and declaring their deeds. And many of those who had practised curious arts brought their books together and burned them before all, and when they reckoned up the price of them, they found fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of God grew strongly and was confirmed, etc." These passages there explain quite clearly what Paul here writes to the Corinthians.

units.la: Quod si uenerit Timotheus, uidete ut absque metu sit apud uos. Opus enim domini operatur, quemadmodum & ego. Ne quis igitur eum spernat, sed pro sequamini eum cum pace, ut ueniat ad me. Expecto enim illum cum fratribus.
units.tr: But if Timothy comes, see that he is without fear among you. For he works the work of the Lord, as I also do. Let no one therefore despise him, but send him on his way in peace, that he may come to me. For I am expecting him with the brothers.

units.la: Timotheum ecclesiæ Corinthiorum commendat. Hunc enim ad illos miserat priusquam epistolam hanc scriberet. Qua de re supra capite quarto sic legimus: Hac de causa misi uobis Timotheum, qui est filius meus dilectus, & fidelis in domino, qui uobis in memoriam reducet uias meas quæ sunt in Christo, quemadmodum ubiq; in omni ecclesia doceo. Quando autem, & unde & cum quo hunc miserit, existimo Actorum decimonono memorari, ubi sic legitur: His autem expletis proposuit Paulus in spiritu transita Macedonia & Achaia ire Hierosolymam: dicens, postquam fuero ibi, oportet me & Romam uidere. Misisis autem in Macedoniam duobus ex ijs qui ministrabant sibi, Timotheo uidelicet & Erasto, ipse remansit ad tempus in Asia. Misit ergo Timotheum non solum, sed una cum Erasto. Et Christo hoc in more erat ut binos discipulos mitteret ante faciem suam. Præterquam autem quod eiusmodi duorum missio exemplo Christi sanctificata est, commendatur etiam suaipsius commoditate. Quod uero & hic & supra capite quarto solius facit Timothei mentionem, non ob id facit, quod hunc solum miserit: sed quod legationis onus in illum præcipue, tanquam singulari fide & dono spiritus præditum incumberet. Qua in re rursus obseruanda est prudentia Apostoli, non in eo modo quod binos sed & quod impares misit, de quo non est hic dicendi locus. Deinde apparet misisse eum ex Epheso, quandoquidem Asiæ fit mentio. Tertio misit eum, cum Macedoniam & Achaiam transire constituisset, priusquam Hierosolymam proficisceretur. Vbi hæc circumstantiæ considerantur, uerosimile apparet loqui illum hoc loco & supra capite quarto de eadem missione Timothei qua una cum illo Erastum transituro sibi Macedoniam ad hoc præmisit, ut quæ in ecclesijs cum Macedoniæ tum Achaiæ gerentur cognosceret, priusquam iter illud ingrederetur. Neque enim consultum erat, ut nesciushorum ad illas ueniret.
units.tr: He commends Timothy to the congregation of the Corinthians. Paul had sent him to them before writing this letter. Concerning this, we read above in chapter four: "For this reason I have sent you Timothy, who is my beloved son and faithful in the Lord, who will remind you of my ways which are in Christ, just as I teach everywhere in every church." When, whence and with whom he sent him, I think is recorded in Acts chapter nineteen, where we read: "When these things were completed, Paul resolved in the Spirit, after passing through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying, 'After I have been there, I must also see Rome.' And he sent into Macedonia two of those who ministered to him, namely Timothy and Erastus, but he himself remained in Asia for a time." So he sent Timothy, and not only him but together with Erastus. It was also Christ's custom to send disciples in pairs before his face. Apart from the fact that such a sending of two has been sanctified by the example of Christ, it is also recommended by its own usefulness. That both here and above in chapter four he mentions only Timothy does not mean that he sent only him, but that the burden of the mission lay chiefly upon him, as one endowed with singular faith and the gift of the Spirit. In this matter again the Apostle's prudence is to be observed, not only in that he sent them in pairs but in that he sent them unequal, about which there is no place to speak here. Next, it appears that he sent him from Ephesus, since mention is made of Asia. Third, he sent him when he had decided to pass through Macedonia and Achaia, before he set out for Jerusalem. When these circumstances are considered, it appears probable that in this place and above in chapter four he speaks of the same mission of Timothy, in which Erastus was to go through Macedonia with him, which he had sent ahead for this purpose, so that he might learn what was happening in the churches both of Macedonia and of Achaia before he entered upon that journey. For it was not advisable that he should come to them without knowing these things.

units.la: QVOD SI uenerit, inquit, Timotheus. Rursus non affirmanter, sed cum conditione loquitur, non dicens, Venturus est ad uos: sed, Si uenerit ad uos Timotheus. Multa poterant illi in itinere impedimenta obijci, quibus impeditus non esset Corinthum uenturus. Erat enim iter illud nihilo facturus securius, quàm si agno uersandum sit in medio luporum. Qua re consulto dicit: Si uenerit ad uos Timotheus. Quasi dicat: Si uoluntas domini fuerit, ut quemadmodum proposui, in hac ad uos profectione ueniat.
units.tr: "But if Timothy comes," he says. Again he speaks not affirmatively but conditionally, not saying, "He will come to you," but "If Timothy comes to you." Many hindrances could be thrown in his way on the journey, by which he might be prevented from coming to Corinth. For that journey was no safer than if one were to live as a lamb in the midst of wolves. Therefore he deliberately says, "If Timothy comes to you," as if to say: "If it is the will of the Lord that he come to you in this journey, as I have proposed."

units.la: Quod autem non in præterito dicit, Si uenit, sed in futuro, si uenerit: ex eo est, quod tamen misericoriter eum priusquam literas illas scriberet, haud tamen sic misit, ut recta Corinthiā abiret, sed ut primum Macedoniam transiret, & ecclesias inuisseret, ac tum demum Achaiam & Corinthum peteret. Quare qui literas hasce perferendas acceperunt, priusquam ille tanquam recta absque ambagibus proficiscentes Corinthum appellere potuerunt.
units.tr: That he does not say in the past tense, "If he has come," but in the future, "if he comes," arises from the fact that although he had sent him ahead before writing that letter, he did not send him in such a way that he would go straight to Corinth, but that he would first pass through Macedonia and visit the churches, and only then seek Achaia and Corinth. Hence those who received these letters to carry could not reach Corinth by going straight there without delay.

units.la: VIDETE ut absque metu, inquit, sit apud uos.] Tria petit ab ecclesia Corinthiorum in hac commendatione Timothei. Vnum est, quod hic exprimitur: ut uidelicet sit apud eos, si uenerit absque metu. Poterit autem hic quæri, quomodo petat hoc à Corinthijs fidelibus, cum ne ipsi quidem contingere potuerit uspiam, ut sine metu secure Christum prædicaret. An non supra capite secundo dixit: Et ego per infirmitatem & cum timore ac tremore multo apud uos uersatus sum? Deinde, quomodo potuerunt curare fideles, ut absque timore agerent apud ipsos Christi ministrer, cum & ipsi in medio impiorum agerent, nec furias illorum compescere possent?
units.tr: "See that he is without fear among you," he says. In this commendation of Timothy he asks three things of the church of the Corinthians. One is what is expressed here: that he may be among them, if he comes, without fear. But here one may ask how he asks this of the faithful Corinthians, since not even they themselves could anywhere preach Christ securely without fear. Did he not say above in chapter two: "And I was among you in weakness, and with much fear and trembling"? Furthermore, how could the faithful take care that the ministers of Christ should act among them without fear, when they themselves were acting in the midst of the impious and could not restrain their rage?

units.la: Respondeo. Rem petit Apostolus à Corinthijs nec iniquam, nec inutilem, nec impossibilem. Duplex autem timoris genus poterat euenire Timotheo apud Corinthios constituto, ab infidelibus uidelicet unum, à falsis fratribus alterum. Vtrunque sæpius expertus fuerat ipse apostolus. De priori autem non præscribit hic fidelibus, cui & ipsi erant obnoxij, nec resistere poterant. Alias perinde fecisset, ac si quis præscribat ouibus, quomodo curare debeant, ut pastor ipsarum absque timore sit luporum, leonum, & ursorum, quam securitatem ipsæ nec sibijpsis nec illi præstare possunt. Reliquum est ergo ut de posteriori loquatur, petens ut Timotheo apud ipsos secure sine metu falsorum fratrum agere liceat. Id erat & æquum & utile, & ipsis præstitu possibile.
units.tr: I answer: the Apostle asks of the Corinthians a thing that is neither unjust, nor useless, nor impossible. Now there could be two kinds of fear befalling Timothy while he was stationed among the Corinthians: one from unbelievers, the other from false brothers. The Apostle himself had often experienced both. Concerning the former, however, he does not here prescribe anything to the faithful, since they too were exposed to it and could not resist it. Otherwise he would have acted as if someone were to prescribe to sheep how they ought to take care that their shepherd be without fear of wolves, lions and bears, a security which they could neither provide for themselves nor for him. It remains, therefore, that he speaks of the latter, asking that Timothy be permitted to act among them securely and without fear of false brothers. This was both just and useful, and possible for them to provide.

units.la: Non est autem otiose transeundum, quod hoc Timotheo suo procurare studet, ut apud Corinthios absque timore degat. Considerat animum illius imbecilliorem adhuc quàm qui falsorum fratrum insidias dextrè & intrepidè sufferre ualeat. Et reuera magnæ sit fortitudinis oportet, quisquis illas animo infracto sustinere potest. Multo omnino facilius est, homini pio contemnere furorem infidelium quàm insidias eorum qui se fidelibus Christi annumerari, & pro fratribus haberi uolunt. Dici non potest quàm cruciat animum fidelis ministri, & omnem illius alacritatem in obeundo ministerio deijciat, si se falsorum fratrum insidijs obnoxium esse uiderit, nisi singulari
units.tr: Nor should we pass over lightly the fact that he takes care for his Timothy that he should live among the Corinthians without fear. He considers that Timothy's spirit is still too weak to bear the snares of false brothers skilfully and fearlessly. And indeed, whoever can bear them with an unbroken spirit must have great fortitude. It is far easier for a godly man to scorn the fury of unbelievers than the snares of those who wish to be counted among the faithful of Christ and to be regarded as brothers. It cannot be said how greatly it torments the heart of a faithful minister, and how much it deflates all his eagerness in performing the ministry, if he sees himself exposed to the snares of false brothers, unless he is sustained by God with a singular strength of the Spirit

units.la: gulari spiritus robore diuinitus suffulciatur. Non est animus ministri in ecclesia contentio nibus, contradictionibus, obloquijs, contemptu, & insidijs deijciendus: sed obsequijs potius, consensu, obseruantia & officijs dilectionis erigendus, quo ministerium suum alacri spiritu obire & indefesso studio ecclesiam aedificare possit. Abiectus enim animus nec est ad ferendos infidelium insultus, nec ad corrigenda ecclesiae uicia, satis idoneus.
units.tr: of the Spirit. The mind of a minister in the church must not be cast down by quarrels, contradictions, slanders, contempt and snares; rather it must be raised up by obedience, agreement, respect and the duties of love, so that he may discharge his ministry with a cheerful spirit and build up the church with tireless zeal. For a downcast spirit is not sufficiently fit either to bear the insults of unbelievers or to correct the vices of the church.

units.la: OPVS enim domini operatur, inquit, quemadmodum ego. ] Reddit rationem, quare uelit eum secure agere apud Corinthios. Quo uidelicet liberius aberrantes a uia Apostolica in ordinem reuocet, dum non est quod sibi ab ullis fratribus metuat. Et hoc uocat opus domini operari. Opus enim domini operatur non ille modo, qui fundamenta illius iacit, sed & qui praeuaricationes aedificij illius rite corrigit. Non dicit autem, opus domini nouit: sed opus domini operatur. Necessarium quidem est ministro, ut sciat opus domini: uerum sufficiens non est ad hoc ut sit fidelis, nisi quod nouit operetur etiam. Nec dicit, operabitur, in futuro, sed operatur. Hoc est, sic fidelis est in ministerio, ut quocunq; uenerit, operi domini rite perficiundo sit sedulo intentus. Quid tale de nostris hodie potest episcopis ac presbyteris dici? Opimas praelaturas ac dignitates sectantur, quicquid fiat de opere domini. Imo tam abest ut opus domini operentur ipsi, ut nec ab alijs hoc fieri sinant. Et quod adhuc detestabilius est, condemnent etiam & horrendis poenis obijciant, si quis opera domini fideliter incumbat.
units.tr: "For he works the work of the Lord," he says, "as I do." He gives the reason why he wishes him to act securely among the Corinthians: namely, so that he may more freely call back to order those who wander from the Apostolic way, since there is nothing for him to fear from any brothers. And this he calls working the work of the Lord. For not only he who lays the foundations of it works the work of the Lord, but also he who duly corrects the faults of its building. He does not say, however, "he knows the work of the Lord," but "he works the work of the Lord." It is indeed necessary for a minister to know the work of the Lord; yet knowledge is not enough to make him faithful unless he also works what he knows. Nor does he say, "he will work," in the future, but "he works," in the present. That is, he is so faithful in the ministry that, wherever he comes, he is diligently intent on duly completing the work of the Lord. What of this kind can be said today of our bishops and presbyters? They pursue rich prelacies and dignities, whatever becomes of the work of the Lord. Indeed, they are so far from working the work of the Lord themselves that they do not even allow others to do it. And what is still more detestable, they even condemn and subject to dreadful punishments anyone who faithfully applies himself to the works of the Lord.

units.la: Quid est autem opus domini a fideli ministro obeundum? An mitram gestare bicornem, anulis uincire digitos, pedum ostentare pastorale, pallio ueluti contra pluuias amiciri, lumbos in morem pascentium oues praecingere, semel atque iterum in anni spacio scenicam ludere fabulam, parietes ecclesiae, calices, aras & campanas inungere? Haec nugae non sunt opus domini. Opus domini est, ministerium praedicandi Euangelij, plantandi & rigandi ecclesias, & sedula cura saluti fidelium incumbere. Opus domini est, quod non humanitus est excogitatum, sed ab ipso domino apostolis & apostolorum successoribus impositum, quod & apostoli fideliter sunt operati. Operentur hoc opus episcopi, uel si ipsi hoc facere nesciunt, permittant idoneis hominibus, & sublata erit omnis nostrorum temporum controuersia.
units.tr: But what is the work of the Lord to be undertaken by a faithful minister? Is it to wear a two-horned mitre, to bind the fingers with rings, to display the pastoral staff, to clothe oneself in a cloak as if against the rain, to gird the loins in the manner of shepherds tending sheep, to play a theatrical farce once or twice in the course of a year, to anoint the walls of the church, the chalices, the altars and the bells? These are trifles, not the work of the Lord. The work of the Lord is the ministry of preaching the Gospel, of planting and watering churches, and of devoting careful attention to the salvation of the faithful. The work of the Lord is that which was not devised by human beings, but imposed by the Lord himself upon the apostles and the successors of the apostles, and which the apostles faithfully performed. Let the bishops perform this work, or if they do not know how to do it themselves, let them permit suitable men to do it, and all the controversy of our times will be ended.

units.la: QVEMADMODVM & ego, inquit. ] Ergo ne Timotheus par erat Paulo in opere domini perficiundo, cum ille plus omnibus laborauerit? Non hoc dicit. Commendauit illum in eo, quod in opere domini non declinaret uel ad dexteram uel ad sinistram, sed eadem secum, regia uidelicet, uia ingrederetur. Quod igitur dicit, Opus enim domini operatur, quemadmodum & ego: idem est ac si dicat, Non praeuaricatur in opere ministerij sui, sed operatur opus domini fideliter, idque secundum meas uias, de quibus uos admonebit. Clanculum hoc dicens pseudapostolos & pseudapostolorum discipulos perstringit, qui non recto pede ad Euangelium Christi accedebant, sed ecclesiam Corinthiorum a uijs Apostolicis, quibus erat plantata, seducere molieban tur. Sic igitur commendat Timotheum tanquam fidelem operarium domini, ac germanum suum discipulum, ut & morigeros illi reddat Corinthios, & simul pseudapostolorum studia retundat.
units.tr: "Even as I also do," he says. Was Timothy therefore equal to Paul in carrying out the Lord's work, since Paul labored more than all of them? He does not say that. He commends Timothy for this: in the Lord's work he does not turn aside to the right or to the left, but walks the same royal road that Paul himself walks. So when he says, "For he works the work of the Lord, as I also do," it amounts to saying: he does not go astray in the work of his ministry, but faithfully does the Lord's work, and does it according to my ways, which he will remind you of. In saying this covertly, he strikes at the false apostles and their disciples, who did not approach the Gospel of Christ with a straight foot, but were striving to lead the Corinthian church away from the apostolic ways in which it had been planted. Thus he commends Timothy as a faithful worker of the Lord and his own true disciple, both so that he may make the Corinthians compliant towards him and so that he may check the zeal of the false apostles.

units.la: Obiter obseruandum est bonae conscientiae ingenium, in eo quod tam confidenter non solum de Timotheo, sed & de seipso praedicat, quod opus domini operetur. Sciebat ad illud neminem esse per se idoneum, quemadmodum & epistola sequenti capite tertio scribit: uerum quoniam bona cum conscientia in opere domini uersabatur, non dubitauit hoc de se contra pseudapostolos praedicare, interim ab omni inani iactantia alienus.
units.tr: In passing we should notice the character of a good conscience, in that he preaches so confidently not only about Timothy but also about himself, that he works the Lord's work. He knew that no one is fit for that task of himself, as he also writes in the third chapter of the following epistle. But since he was engaged in the Lord's work with a good conscience, he did not hesitate to proclaim this about himself against the false apostles, while yet remaining free of all empty boasting.

units.la: NE quis igitur eum spernat, inquit. ] Secundum hoc est, quod Timotheo suo apud Corinthios conciliare satagit, codignam uidelicet existimationem & authoritatem, tanquam ei, qui perinde atque ipse opus domini operetur. Vnde & non simpliciter dicit, ne quis eum spernat: sed, ne quis igitur eum spernat. Quasi dicat: Quoniam opus domini operatur perinde atque ego, dignus est quem in precio habeatis, & a nemine uestrum contemni sinatis.
units.tr: "Let no one therefore despise him," he says. This is in line with what he is eager to win for his Timothy among the Corinthians, namely a worthy esteem and authority, as for one who works the Lord's work just as he does. Hence he does not simply say, "let no one despise him," but "let no one therefore despise him." As if he were saying: since he works the Lord's work just as I do, he is worthy to be held in honor, and you must not allow him to be scorned by any of you.

units.la: Obserua hic, quos nam ministros & quam ob causam, in precio habere debeat ecclesia. Eos uidelicet qui similes sunt Timotheo, propterea quod opus domini operantur, sicut operati sunt apostoli. Sic alibi dicit eos qui bene praesunt in uerbo, duplici esse honore dignos. Dubio procul non erat hic Timotheus iuxta seculum spectabilis. Verum quoniam opus domini rite operabatur, dignus erat & Apostolica commendatione & honore fidelium in ecclesia Christi. Qui huic sunt dissimiles, etiamsi mille canones praetexant, & huius seculi principes adaequent, ut non commendantur nobis commendatione Apostolica: ita indigni sunt, qui habeantur in precio, dignissimi uero qui non modo contemnantur, sed & fugiantur.
units.tr: Observe here which ministers, and for what reason, the church ought to hold in honor: namely those who are like Timothy, because they do the Lord's work as the apostles did. So elsewhere he says that those who rule well in the Word are worthy of double honor. Without doubt this Timothy was not, by the standards of this age, a man of distinction. But since he carried out the Lord's work properly, he was worthy both of apostolic commendation and of the honor of the faithful in the church of Christ. Those who are unlike him, even if they bring forward a thousand canons and match the princes of this age, since they are not commended to us by apostolic commendation, are unworthy of being held in honor; and they are most worthy not merely of being despised, but of being shunned.

units.la: Quid autem causae erat, quur hoc peteret a Corinthijs, ne Timotheum suum quisquam ipsorum sperneret, cum essent Christiani, quibus scribebat, & ad quos illum mittebat? Vt hoc ab illis proscereet in causa erant reprobi ac praeuaricatores in ecclesia Corinthiorum, a quibus ipse quoque contemnebatur. Sciebat illis non placiturum discipulum fidum ac syncerum in causa, in qua ipse ante illum displicebat & contemnebatur. Neque scribebat hoc propter illos, sed propter imbecilliores, qui sermonibus illorum facile poterant ad contemnen
units.tr: But what was the reason he asked the Corinthians that none of them should despise his Timothy, since they were Christians, to whom he was writing, and to whom he was sending him? He wanted them to grant this, because among the Corinthians there were reprobates and transgressors in the church, by whom he himself too was despised. He knew that a faithful and sincere disciple, in a cause in which he himself had been displeasing and despised before him, would not please them. Nor was he writing this on account of those people, but on account of the weaker ones, who could easily be led by their speeches to despise Timothy.

units.la: A ... B ... temnendum Timotheum induci. Admone- mur hoc loco, quid expectandum sit ueris ac fynceris uerbi Dei ministris, ab illis qui nec Christū ipsum nec apostolos alicuius faciunt. Quomodo uenerabuntur discipulum, qui præceptorem contemnunt?
units.tr: We are reminded at this point what should be expected by the true and sincere ministers of God's Word from those who make nothing of Christ himself or of the apostles. How will they respect a disciple who despise his teacher?

units.la: SED prosequamini eum cum pace, inquit, ut ueniat ad me.] Vulgata habet, deducite au tem illum in pace. quæ lectio recte conuenit cum Græco uerbo προπέμψατε. Tertium hoc est, quod à Corinthijs Timotheo suo præstandum possit. De ratione & usu deductionis dixi- mus suprà, unde facile uidere est, quur officiū illius Timotheo impendi uelit. Hoc uero di- cens, significat eum non ad hoc esse missum, ut apud ipsos maneat, sed ut in transitu quæ in ecclesia ipsorum geratur uideat, & quæ cor- rigenda sint moneat, ac postea deductus ab i- psis cum pace, ad se properet.
units.tr: "But send him on his way in peace," he says, "that he may come to me." The Vulgate has, "Bring him on his way in peace," a reading that agrees well with the Greek word [προπέμψατε]. This is the third thing that the Corinthians could render to their Timothy. I have spoken above about the manner and use of such escorting, so it is easy to see why he wishes this service to be rendered to Timothy. But in saying this, he signifies that Timothy has not been sent to stay with them, but so that in passing through he may see what is going on in their church and advise what needs correcting; and afterwards, once he has been escorted from them in peace, he may hasten to himself.

units.la: Dictione pacis monet eos charitatis & con cordiæ, auocans à studio sectarum quo labo- rabant inter illos plerique. Vbi nanque obti- nent studia sectarum, ibi contentiones & dif- sidia uigere necesse est. Vbi hæc uigent, peri- clitatur charitas, concordia & pax. Cum igi- tur deductionem Timothei ab illis poscit quæ fiat cum pace, cum pace inquam non aliquo- rum tantum, sed omnium simul fidelium: simul monet ut relictis disiidijs & contentionibus studeant charitati, paci & concordiæ, sintque unum in domino.
units.tr: By the word "peace" he admonishes them to charity and concord, calling them away from the zeal for factions in which many among them were labouring. For where the pursuit of factions prevails, quarrels and dissension must necessarily flourish. Where these flourish, charity, concord and peace are in danger. Therefore, when he asks that Timothy be escorted from them with peace, and with peace I mean not of some only but of all the faithful together, he at the same time admonishes them that, having set aside divisions and contentions, they should aim at charity, peace and concord, and be one in the Lord.

units.la: VT ueniat ad me, inquit.] Etiam hac illos particula solicitat, ut amanter ac reuerenter Timotheum ab ipsis discedentem deducant, ut quem sciant recta ad se properare, & quæ acciderint sibi indicaturum. Sic legatos regū honorifice non solum accipimus ob id quod à regibus suis ad nos missi ueniūt, sed & ideo potissimum honorifice tractamus ac dimitti- mus, quod à nobis ad reges suos omnia quæ cognouerunt exposituri discedunt. Sic Corin- thios suos Apostolus in hac causa animatos esse uolebat.
units.tr: "That he may come to me," he says. By this little phrase too he urges them to escort Timothy lovingly and respectfully as he departs from them, since they know that he is hastening straight to him and will report what has happened to himself. Thus we receive the envoys of kings with honour, not only because they come to us sent by their own kings, but chiefly because we treat them honourably and let them go precisely because they depart from us to expound to their own kings everything that they have learned. So the Apostle wanted his Corinthians to be encouraged in this matter.

units.la: EXPECTO enim illum, inquit, cum fratri bus.] Verbo expectandi desiderium expri- mit absentis discipuli, quem ut filium dilige- bat, & in omnibus fidelem ac syncerum expe- riebatur. Et hoc quoque dicens monet eos q debeant illum amanter & honorifice accipe- re, tractare & à se dimittere tanquam sibi us- queadeo charum, ut ab sentiam illius, si diutur nior futura sit, ægre sit laturus.
units.tr: "For I look for him," he says, "with the brethren." By the word "look for" he expresses the longing for an absent disciple, whom he loved as a son and had found to be faithful and sincere in all things. And in saying this too he admonishes them that they ought to receive, treat and dismiss him lovingly and honourably, since he is so dear to the Apostle that, if his absence should be prolonged, he would bear it with difficulty.

units.la: Omnino significat se reditum illius auidè expectare, siue expectationis huius desideriü ad personam Timothei, siue ad cognitionem eorum quæ in ecclesijs Macedoniæ & Achaiæ gerebantur, propter quam Timotheum hunc à se miserat, uel ad utranque referamus. Nota est solicitudo ecclesiarum, quæ pectus Apo- stoli noctes ac dies occupabat, per quam fie- bat, ut quam solicite mittebat à se discipulos, per quos de statu ecclesiarū cognosceret, tam auidè reditum illorum expectaret, id quod illi dubio procul in hac quoque causa accidit.
units.tr: Clearly he means that he eagerly awaits his return, whether this longing of expectation is directed to Timothy's person, or to knowledge of what was going on in the churches of Macedonia and Achaia, for which reason he had sent this Timothy from himself; or we may refer it to both. The concern of the churches, which occupied the Apostle's heart night and day, is well known; through it it came about that, just as anxiously as he sent out disciples from himself to learn the condition of the churches, so eagerly did he await their return. Without doubt this happened to him in this matter too.

units.la: Illud, cum fratribus, amphibole ac sic posi- tum est, ut tam ad eos possit referri fratres, qui cum Timotheo essent, uel ab ecclesia Corin- thiorum, aut alijs missi uenturi, uel cum ipso in eam legationem amandati rediturí, quàm ad eos qui unà cum Paulo reditum Timothei cupide ac solicite expectarint. Si priore sensu dictum est, significatur quo affectu fuerit Apo ftolus non modo erga discipulū cl risimum, sed & erga reliquos fratres syncere in Christo affectos. Si posteriore, innuitur quàm charus fuerit Timotheus non Apostolo tantum, sed & fratrib. reliquis, id est, toti ecclesiæ, in qua tum morabatur Apostolus.
units.tr: The phrase "with the brethren" is ambiguous and so placed that it can refer either to the brethren who were with Timothy, whether they were to come sent from the Corinthian church or from others, or who had been commissioned to that embassy along with him and were to return with him; or to those who eagerly and anxiously awaited Timothy's return together with Paul. If the former sense is intended, it signifies with what affection the Apostle regarded not only his most beloved disciple but also the other brethren sincerely devoted to Christ. If the latter, it implies how dear Timothy was not only to the Apostle but also to the other brethren, that is, to the whole church in which the Apostle then dwelt.

units.la: Ergo hæc tria poscit Apostolus à Corin- thijs: primum, ut Timotheum suum quem mi- serat, absque metu secure apud ipsos agere fa- ciant: secundum, ut eum in honore ac precio babeant: tertium, ut in pace deducant, quo ad se ueniat, eo quòd ipsum auide unà cum fratri bus expectet. An nō Romanus quoque ponti- sex hæc ipsa Carnalibus suis, quos à latere suo legatos ad reges ac principes mittit, præstari poscit? Securitatem uidelicet, honorem & pa- cificam deductionem. Poscit utique, idq; non simpliciter, sed cum imperio, & comminatio- nib. grauissimæ maledictionis, nisi obtineat. Verum an suos legatos quæstuarios illos, de, auratos ac purpuratos sic commendare uera- citer possit, quod opus domini operentur, ui- derit ipse. Potecтquidem, uerum si addat, Sicut & ego, ut enim ipse, sic & illi opus domini ope rantur. Nam qualis ipse Apostolus est, tales à se discipulos mittit.
units.tr: So the Apostle asks three things of the Corinthians: first, that they make sure that Timothy, whom he has sent, may act among them securely and without fear; second, that they hold him in honour and esteem; third, that they escort him in peace so that he may come to him, since he eagerly awaits him together with the brethren. Does not the Roman pontiff too demand that these very things be rendered to his own worldly men, whom he sends from his side as legates to kings and princes? Namely security, honour and a peaceful escort. He demands them, certainly, and not simply but with authority and with threats of the gravest curse, unless they are obtained. But whether he can truthfully commend those profit-seeking, gilded and purple-clad legates of his in this way, that they do the work of the Lord, he himself will see. He could indeed, if he were to add, "as I also do," for just as he himself is, so also do those men do the work of the Lord. For the Apostle sends out disciples such as he himself is.

units.la: Porro de Apollo fratre multum hor tatus sum illum, ut iret ad uos cum fra- tribus, & omnino non erat uoluntas nunc eundi. Venturus est autem, cum opportunitatem erit nactus.
units.tr: Moreover, concerning our brother Apollos, I have strongly urged him to go to you with the brothers, but he was altogether unwilling to go now. He will come, however, when he has found an opportunity.

units.la: Particulam hanc non sine ratione adijcit. Est enim excusatoria. Apollos, de quo suprà capite 1 & 3. ecclesiam Corinthiorum à Paulo plantatam laboribus suis diligenter post illius abitum rigauerat: quare non modo notus erat Corinthijs, sed & in precio habitus, idque ma- gis quàm Timotheus. Ne igitur indigne fer- rent, quod hunc non misisset, sed illius loco mi sisset hominem iuuenem, cuius nec eruditio- nem nec zelum pro domino per experientiam perinde atq; Apollos cognouissent, deinde si- multates inter se & ipsum obortas esse suspi- carentur, atq; ita erga præsentiam Timothei animo parum æquo afficeretur: excusationem hanc ponit, qua non se modo, sed & ipsum A- pollo excusat, & simul spe aduetus illius facit. Sic oiauigilàter ac prudèter agès cauet ne qua sinistræ suspicionis occasio fidelib. obijciatur.
units.tr: He adds this clause not without reason, for it is an excuse. Apollos, of whom Paul speaks above in chapters 1 and 3, had watered with his labours the Corinthian church that Paul had planted, after Paul's departure. So he was not only known to the Corinthians but also held in high esteem, more so even than Timothy. Lest they should take it badly that Paul had not sent him, but had sent instead a young man whose learning and zeal for the Lord they did not know from experience as they knew Apollos, and lest they should suspect that rivalry had arisen between Apollos and Paul, and so be less well disposed towards Timothy's presence, Paul gives this excuse. It excuses not only himself but Apollos as well, and at the same time it holds out hope of Apollos's coming. In this way, acting with great care and prudence, he guards against giving the faithful any occasion for an unfavourable suspicion.

units.la: Porro de Apollo fratre, inquit, intellige, sic accipite, uocat eum fratrē, significàs se illū cō- plecti amanter, non ut discipulū, sed ut fratrē.
units.tr: Now concerning our brother Apollos, he says: understand it, take it thus. He calls him brother, signifying that he embraces him affectionately, not as a disciple but as a brother.

units.la: MVLTVM inquit, hortatus sum illum, ut iret ad uos cum fratribus.] Significat usquea- deo se non impediuisse, quo minus ad ipsos uenire tur Apollos, ut conatus quoq; sit author illi esse, ut cum fratribus ad ipsos proficiscere- tur. Quasi dicat: Scio hunc uobis esse non im- merito acceptum, idque sic probo, ut conatus sim persuadere ipsi, non modice & obiter, sed plurimum, ut una cum fratribus quos misi, uos inuiseret.
units.tr: "I have urged him greatly," he says, "to go to you with the brothers." He means that he had not hindered Apollos at all from coming to them, and that he had even tried to be the one who encouraged him to set out to them with the brothers. As if he were saying: I know that this man is deservedly dear to you, and I show it by trying to persuade him, not casually and in passing, but earnestly, that he should visit you together with the brothers whom I have sent.

units.la: Quid est autem quod dicit: multum hortatus sum illum? Quare illi non ut Timotheo le- gationem hanc Apostolica authoritate iniun- xit? Erat συνεργὸς? Erat & Timotheus. Erat fra- ter? Erat & Timotheus. Rigauerat ecclesiam Corinthiorum? Quid aliud faciebat Timo- theus? Quur ergo illum hortatur multum ut faciat, ad quod Timotheum non horatur, sed cum mandato mittit? Videmus hoc exemplo quàm inter sanctos quoque seruanda sit per- sonarum differētia. Erat Timotheus iuuenis, Apollos uir aetate maturus. Erat Timotheus à Paulo genitus in Christo, hoc de Apollo non potuit dicere Paulus. Quare ut nec discipu- lus, nec filius illius erat in Christo, ita alia erat ratione tractandus quàm Timotheus. Ideo hortatu obnixo cum illo egit, non mandato. Pontifex Romanus mádasset illi sub α na ex- communicationis latae sententiae.
units.tr: But what does he mean by saying, "I have urged him greatly"? Why did he not impose this mission on Apollos by apostolic authority, as he did with Timothy? Was Apollos a fellow worker? Timothy was too. Was he a brother? Timothy was too. Had he watered the Corinthian church? What else was Timothy doing? Why then does he urge Apollos so strongly to do what he does not urge Timothy to do, but sends Timothy with a command? We see from this example how the difference of persons must be observed even among the saints. Timothy was a young man, Apollos a man mature in years. Timothy had been begotten in Christ by Paul; Paul could not say this of Apollos. Since Apollos was neither Paul's disciple nor his son in Christ, he had to be treated in a different way from Timothy. So Paul dealt with him by earnest exhortation, not by command. The Roman pontiff would have sent him under a sentence of excommunication latae sententiae.

units.la: Nec transeundum est, quod non simpliciter dicit, Hortatus sum illum: sed multum hor- tatus sum illum. Graece est, πολλὰ παρακαλέσα αὐτόν. Significat autem πολλὰ nonnunquam idem quod πολλάκις, id est, saepenumero & frequen- ter. Deinde uerbum παρακαλέω, non hortari tan- tum, sed & obsecrare significat: ut aeque uerti potuerit, multum obsecraui illum, atque mul- tum hortatus sum illum. Haec annotamus, ut cogitet lector, quàm fuerit ardens pectus Apo- stoli, in procurando opere domini: quàm non facile molestè tulerit repulsam, sed patienter hortando & obsecrando animos recusantium flectere sategerit.
units.tr: Nor should we pass over the fact that he does not simply say, "I urged him," but "I urged him greatly." In Greek it is: polla parakalesa auton [πολλὰ παρακαλέσα αὐτόν]. The word polla sometimes means the same as pollakis, that is, often and frequently. Moreover, the verb parakaleo means not only to exhort but also to entreat. So it could equally well be translated, "I entreated him greatly," as "I urged him greatly." We note this so that the reader may consider how ardent the heart of the Apostle was in promoting the work of the Lord, and how little he took it amiss to be refused, but patiently strove by exhorting and entreating to bend the minds of those who refused.

units.la: VT iret ad uos, inquit, cum fratribus.] Non simpliciter dicit, Vt iret ad uos: sed addit, cum fratribus. Existimo autem loqui ipsum de fra- tribus, quos una cum Timotheo miserat. Et apparet hic quod supra expectare se Timo- theum cum fratribus dixit, intelligendum esse de ijsdem. Sicut Timotheum misit cum fratri- bus, ita uolebat mittere cum fratribus Apollo, si ille acquieuisset, quos sperabat acceptiores fore Corinthijs, si cum illo coniuncti Corin- thum uenissent.
units.tr: "That he might go to you," he says, "with the brothers." He does not simply say, "that he might go to you," but adds, "with the brothers." I think he is speaking of the brothers whom he had sent together with Timothy. And it appears here that what he said above, that he was expecting Timothy with the brothers, must be understood of the same men. Just as he sent Timothy with the brothers, so Apollos too was willing to send them with himself, if Apollos had agreed; he hoped the brothers would be more acceptable to the Corinthians if they came to Corinth joined with Apollos.

units.la: ET omnino, inquit, non erat uoluntas nunc eundi.] Hoc est, uerum quamuis multum hortarer & obsecrarem, nihil tamen efficere potui, propterea quod nulla illi erat nunc ad uos eundi uoluntas. Non simpliciter dicit, & non erat uoluntas: sed, & omnino non erat uoluntas nunc eundi. Sic intendit utrinque ut suam hortandi instantiam, ita & illius recusa- tionem.
units.tr: "And he was altogether unwilling," he says, "to go now." That is: although I urged and entreated him greatly, I could achieve nothing, because he had no will at that time to go to you. He does not simply say, "and he was not willing," but "and he was altogether unwilling to go now." In this way he stresses both his own insistence in urging and Apollos's refusal.

units.la: Videmus autem hoc duorum sanctissimo- rum uirorum exemplo, quàm etiam sanctis non fit eadem in omnibus uoluntas. Pauli uo- luntas erat, ut Apollos una cum fratribus ec- clesiam Corinthiorum inuiseret. Et hoc illum impense ac multum ut faceret hortabatur. Vo- luntatis huius nihil prorsus erat in Apollo.
units.tr: We see from the example of these two most holy men that even among the saints the will is not the same in all. Paul's will was that Apollos should visit the Corinthian church together with the brothers, and he urged him earnestly and strongly to do this. Of this will there was nothing at all in Apollos.

units.la: Deinde uidemus quàm nonnunquam & sancti non modo difficiles sint, sed & imper- suasibiles ad obsequendum uoluntati fratrum etiam in rebus nihil illiciti habentibus, idque haud aliam ob causam, quàm quod nolunt. Non dicit hic, Et non erat illi facultas: sed, & omnino non erat illi uoluntas eundi nunc. Si recte Paulus & motu spiritus sancti impulsus tam hortabatur obnixe Apollon, ut iret cum fratribus Corinthum, consequitur tam obsti- natam huius recusationem non fuisse exspi- ritu Christi. Contra, si hic ex spiritu Christi recusabat, non erat ex spiritu Christi quod hortabatur Paulus. Atque ita alteruter spi- ritu Christi in hac causa destituebatur, & hu- mani quid patiebatur. Sic non sunt omnia sanctorum ex spiritu Christi, nec eadem sem- per sunt uoluntate praediti, nec in omnibus alij aliorum uoluntati obsequuntur. Nec est ut haec in sanctis excusemus, ne excusemus & in nobis: rursus, non est ut propterea san- ctos damnemus, ne consimili de causa dam- nemus & hodie fratres in ecclesia Christi. Per- sectionem quaeramus & speremus in coelis, & sic persequamur in terris, ut imperfectionem nec in nobis excusemus, nec in fratribus dam- nemus.
units.tr: Next we see how sometimes the saints are not only difficult but also hard to persuade to obey the wishes of the brothers, even in matters that contain nothing unlawful, and for no other reason than that they are unwilling. He does not say here, "And he had no opportunity," but, "and he was altogether unwilling to go now." If Paul, rightly and moved by the Holy Spirit, so earnestly urged Apollos to go with the brothers to Corinth, it follows that Apollos's so obstinate refusal did not come from the Spirit of Christ. On the other hand, if Apollos refused from the Spirit of Christ, then what Paul urged did not come from the Spirit of Christ. And so one of them was lacking the Spirit of Christ in this matter, and suffered something human. Thus not everything in the saints comes from the Spirit of Christ, nor are they always endowed with the same will, nor do all obey the wills of others in everything. Nor is it right to excuse these faults in the saints, lest we excuse them in ourselves; nor again is it right to condemn the saints for this, lest for the same reason we condemn the brothers in the church of Christ today. Let us seek and hope for perfection in heaven, and so pursue it on earth, that we neither excuse imperfection in ourselves nor condemn it in our brothers.

units.la: Vide autem quàm caute non dicat simpli- citer, & omnino non erat uoluntas eundi: sed, & omnino non erat uoluntas eundi nunc: id est, hac anni tempestate, qua Timotheum mi- si. Significat hoc factum esse ab Apollo non i- psorum fastidio, quasi ipsos contemnat, sed su- isse illi causas alias propter quas induci nequi- uerit, ut tum iret. Sic non modo seipsum, sed & Apollon excusat, ne quod de illo scribit, ac- cusandi studio scribere uideatur. Huc pertinet quod subijcit.
units.tr: Note also how carefully he does not say simply, "and he was altogether unwilling to go," but, "and he was altogether unwilling to go now," that is, in this season of the year, in which I sent Timothy. This signifies that Apollos did this not out of disdain for them, as if he despised them, but that he had other reasons which prevented him from being persuaded to go then. In this way Paul excuses not only himself but also Apollos, so that what he writes about him does not seem to be written from a desire to accuse him. To this belongs what he adds next.

units.la: VENTVRVS est autem, cum opportunita tem erit nactus.] Non simpliciter dicit, Ven- turus est autem ubi uolet tempore alio: sed, Venturus est autem, cum opportunitatem fue- rit nactus. Ergo significat non fuisse illi tum opportunum ut iret, alias non fuisse detrecta- turum quo minus iret. Vides candorem ani- mi synceri. Obstinata Apollos recusatione tā non fert molestè, ut etiā cōmode & candide in- terpretetur. Exemplū hoc singulare summo- pere necessarium est reb. humanis. Incidis in consimilem recusandi obstinationem sic, ut e- tiamsi multum horteris & obsecrādo obsecres fratrem, nihil tamē impetres: absit ut irriteris, & contemptum tui interpreteris. Quin ma- gis exemplo huic Apostolico conformeris di- cens: Nunc recusat frater. Est illi forsan nunc quod peto, incommodum & importunum.
units.tr: "He will come, however, when he has found an opportunity." He does not simply say, "He will come, however, whenever he wishes, at another time," but, "He will come, however, when he has found an opportunity."
