So he means that it was not opportune for him to go then, and that otherwise he would not have refused to go. You see the candour of a sincere mind. Paul does not take Apollos's obstinate refusal so badly that he does not also interpret it kindly and frankly. This singular example is very necessary for human affairs. You may meet with a similar obstinacy of refusal, so that although you greatly urge a brother and entreat him with entreaties, you obtain nothing. Far be it from you to be provoked and to interpret it as contempt for yourself. Rather, conform yourself to this apostolic example and say: "My brother refuses now. Perhaps what I ask is inconvenient and unseasonable for him at present."

units.la: Consen. Cōsentiet ubi opportunitatem fuerit nactus, ac tum faciet ex animo, quod nunc facere detrectat.
units.tr: Consen. He will consent when he has got the opportunity, and then he will do from his heart what he now refuses to do.

units.la: Deinde uide quàm prudenter Corinthiorū quoq; rationem habeat in hac causa. Poterat dicere: Et omnino non erat illi uoluntas eundi nunc, quod esset illi importunum. Sic dixisset, si se & Apollon duntaxat excusare uoluisset. Verum quoniam curandum simul erat, ne spem Corinthiorum, qua Apollon aliquando ad se uenturum expectabant, extingueret: sed potius lactaret, uisum est aduentum illius promittere, sic tamen ut hac conditione adiecta, cum opportunitatem fuerit nactus, quod promittebat non tenere, sed circumspecte promitteret. Promittit autem hoc non ex certitudine futuri euentus, sed ex bona qua erat erga Apollon fiducia. Considebat illum sic esse erga Corinthios affectum, ut si aliquando opportunitatem esset nactus eundi ad ipsos, non esset id officij detrectaturus amplius.
units.tr: Consider also how prudently Paul takes the Corinthians' situation into account in this matter. He could have said simply: Apollos did not at all want to go now, because it would be inconvenient for him. He would have said that if he wished only to excuse Apollos. But since he had to take care at the same time not to extinguish the Corinthians' hope, by which they expected Apollos to come to them sometime, and rather to keep it alive, he judged it best to promise his coming, yet with this condition added: when he has got the opportunity. So he did not promise what he could not keep, but made the promise with care. He promised this not from certainty about the future outcome, but from the good confidence he had in Apollos. He believed Apollos was so disposed towards the Corinthians that, if he ever got the chance to go to them, he would no longer refuse that duty.

units.la: Ergo opportunitatis rationem in rebus gerendis habent & sancti, idque ut in exemplo praesenti patet non in prophanis modo, sed & ecclesiasticis ac religionis negotijs. Etenim qd Paulus Apollon tantopere hortabatur, ut iret cum fratribus Corinthum, non erat prophanum negocium, sed pertinebat ad confirmandum ac moderandum Christi, quę illic erat, ecclesiam. Et hoc ille facere nolebat, propterea quod non esset sibi tum temporis opportunū. Et id Paulus usqueadeò non damnat, ut etiam ad excusandum eum Corinthijs pro sufficienti causa adducat. Sane non est susque deque facienda gerendarum rerum opportunitas. Quicquid enim, dempta necessitate, uel tempore, uel loco, uel modo importuno geritur, parum utiliter, nonnunquam etiam cum damno geritur. τὸ γὰρ καλὸν μὴ ὑχάρως γινόμενον ἐὸ καλόν.
units.tr: Therefore the saints also take account of opportunity in their affairs, and as this example makes plain, not only in secular matters but also in ecclesiastical and religious business. For the matter to which Paul urged Apollos so strongly, namely to go with the brothers to Corinth, was no secular business, but pertained to strengthening and guiding the church of Christ that was there. Apollos was unwilling to do this at that time because it was not the right opportunity for him. Paul does not condemn this at all; indeed, he offers it as a sufficient reason to excuse him to the Corinthians. Yet the timing of affairs is not to be treated lightly. Whatever is done at an inconvenient time, place or manner, apart from necessity, is done to little profit and sometimes even to loss. "For a good thing not done graciously is not good" [τὸ γὰρ καλὸν μὴ χάριτι γινόμενον οὐ καλόν].

units.la: Videndum tamen etiam atque etiam, ut opportunitati recte studeamus. Opportunitas gerendae rei alia est temporis, alia loci, alia ipsius rei, alia nostrae ipsorum personae, aut sententiae. Respectu commodi temporis uocatur Graecis καιρός. Loci uero, Latinis uocatur Opportunitas, cuius uocis metaphora sumpta est à commoditate portus, in quem tam nauigaturi commode quae uehenda sunt inferunt, quàm qui nauigarunt naues suas ex alto mari deducunt: ad quod utrunque magna est portus commoditas, ut recte quae commode geruntur, opportune geri dicantur. Accidit saepenumero ut res ipsa talis offeratur in se, ut sit apta ad gerendum, modo respondeat temporis uel loci commoditas. Sed haec sunt permittenda iudicio prudenti ac gnauo. Id ue ro probandum non est, quod saepenumero gerendae rei opportunitatem secundum nostram molliciem ac socordiam tum esse iudicamus, quando uel nullo potest, uel admodum modico geri negocio. Sic enim animatis importunum est & incommodum, quicquid cum la bore aliquo gerendnm esse apparet, quemadmodum pigris ac desidibus nullum est opportuniter, quàm quod uel naui, uel uehiculo confici potest. Haec obiter per occasionē praesentis loci de opportunitate annotada esse diximus. Nolle obire in praesenti, quod incommodum & importunum esse uidetur, non damnatur, sed probatur sanctorum exemplis, modo absit sinistrae mentis pigricies ac socordia.
units.tr: We must nevertheless look again and again to pursue opportunity rightly. The opportunity for doing a thing is one thing with respect to time, another with respect to place, another with respect to the thing itself, and another with respect to ourselves or our judgement. With regard to a suitable time the Greeks call it καιρός [kairos]. The Latins call the opportunity with regard to place "opportunitas", a word taken from the metaphor of a harbour's convenience: those who are about to sail bring what is to be carried conveniently into the harbour, and those who have sailed bring their ships in from the deep sea. For both, the harbour's convenience is great, so that things done conveniently are said to be done opportunely. It often happens that the thing itself is offered in such a way that it is fit to be done, provided the convenience of time or place is also present. But such matters are to be left to prudent and diligent judgement. What must not be approved is this: people often judge that the opportunity for doing a thing has not yet come, according to their own softness and sloth, when the thing can be done with no effort or only a very little. For to lazy people whatever appears to have to be done with some labour is inopportune and inconvenient, just as for the idle nothing is opportune except what can be done by ship or carriage. We have said these things in passing, on the occasion of this place, concerning opportunity. To be unwilling to undertake in the present case what seems inconvenient and inopportune is not condemned but is approved by the examples of the saints, provided that the sluggishness and sloth of a perverse mind is absent.

units.la: Vigilate, state in fide, uiriliter agite, estote fortes, omnia uestra cum charitate fiant.
units.tr: Watch, stand fast in the faith, act like men, be strong, let all your things be done in love.

units.la: Epistolam terminaturus, priusquam commendationem quorundam selectorum fidelium ac salutationis officia subiungat, succinctà hac & summaria paraenesi ferè omnia complectitur, quae ecclesiae illi cum primis erant necessaria. Principio, uigilate, inquit. Hoc est, cauete somnolentiam animi, estote in causam salutis uestrae uigiles, intenti ac circumspecti. Si uigilassent, tatum seductionis in ecclesiam ipsorum haud quaquam irrepsisset. Si uigilassent unquam locum sectis ac pseudoapostolis haud permisissent. Unde est quod in ecclesijs Christi passim obtinuerunt errorum, superstitionum, Simoniae, falsorumque cultuum magistri, una cum toto Antichristianismo, quàm ex eo quod dormitare coeperunt omnes, seque ductoribus caecis totos permittere. Quę nam mala in ea domo locum habere non possunt, in qua uigilat nemo, dormitant omnes? Quare Christus quoq; tam diligenter suos hortatur, ut uigilent. Cum dux exercitus milites suos monet ut uigilent, an non satis significat immi nere ipsis periculum ab hostibus? Sic Apostolus Corinthios hoc loco ad uigilandum hortatur, cum uideret eos per incuriam obnoxios pseudapostolorum esse insidijs factos.
units.tr: Concluding the letter, before he adds the commendation of certain chosen faithful people and the greetings, Paul sums up in this brief and compact exhortation nearly everything that that church especially needed. First, he says, "Watch." That is, beware of drowsiness of mind; be watchful, attentive and careful in the cause of your own salvation. If they had been watchful, the plague of seduction would never have crept into their church; if they had been watchful, they would never have allowed the sects and false apostles a place. Indeed, why have the teachers of error, superstition, simony and false worship, together with the whole of Antichristianism, taken hold almost everywhere in the churches of Christ, except that all began to doze and handed themselves wholly over to blind guides? What evils cannot have a place in that house where no one keeps watch and all are asleep? For this reason Christ too exhorts his people so diligently to watch. When the commander of an army warns his soldiers to keep watch, does he not sufficiently signal that danger from the enemy is upon them? So the Apostle here exhorts the Corinthians to watch, since he saw that through carelessness they had been made open to the snares of false apostles.

units.la: Deinde ut in coepta metaphora pergat, addit, State in fide. Excubantium est neque iacere humi prostratos, neque ociose sedere, sed stare paratos ad obseruandum & excipiedum insidias hostis: neque esse muliebriter perterritos, sed agere uiriliter, & esse fortes: neque disidere inter se odijs & simultatibus, sed esse inuicem alius in alium amanter & concorditer affectos. Sic coeptam excubandi metaphoram prosequens, dicit: State in fide, uiriliter agite, estote fortes, omnia uestra cum charitate fiant.
units.tr: Then, to carry on the metaphor he has begun, he adds, "Stand fast in the faith." It belongs to those who keep watch neither to lie prostrate on the ground nor to sit idly, but to stand ready to observe and to meet the snares of the enemy; not to be frightened like women, but to act manfully and be strong; and not to be at odds with one another through hatreds and quarrels, but to be lovingly and harmoniously disposed towards one another. Thus, pursuing the metaphor of watching that he has begun, he says: "Stand fast in the faith, act like men, be strong, let all your things be done in love."

units.la: STATE in fide, inquit. In fide parum firmi stabant, cum resurrectionem mortuorum negarent. Hoc in illis perstringens, in genere hortatur, ut stent in fide. Stare in fide, est in nulla partem, nec à dexteram nec ad sinistram à uera ac syncera Christi fide uacillare, sed immote contra quosuis Satanae ac ministrorum illius insultus perfistere. Quàm steterint ecclesiae post Apostolorum tempora in uera Euangelij Dei fide, non est ut examinemus. Clamat res ipsa. Quàm difficile sit in illa stare, etiam tiam adhuc uiuentium apostolorum tempora docuerunt.
units.tr: "Stand fast in the faith," he says. Those who denied the resurrection of the dead stood weakly in the faith. Touching on this among them, he exhorts them in general to stand fast in the faith. To stand in the faith is to waver in no direction, neither to the right nor to the left, from the true and pure faith of Christ, but to persevere unmoved against all the assaults of Satan and his ministers. How firmly the churches stood in the true faith of God's Gospel after the time of the Apostles we need not examine; the thing itself cries out. How difficult it is to stand in it, the time of the apostles while they were still living has taught.

units.la: VIRILITER agite.] Græcè est ἀνδρίζεσθε, id est, Viros præstate. Viri est animo esse non pusillo, sed hosti uiriliter resistere, ac dextre pugnare. Sic in religione Christi Christiani homines est, siue uir sit siue mulier, uirili, id est, maturo & infracto præditum esse animo. Et tales reddit uiua & efficax fides, nó modo uiros, sed & fœminas: non iuuenes modo, sed & puellas, cuius rei innumera sunt exépla ædita in Christianismo, & nostra quoque ætate æduntur quotidie.
units.tr: "Act like men." In Greek it is ἀνδρίζεσθε [andrizesthe], that is, "show yourselves men." To be a man is to have a mind that is not timid, but to resist the enemy manfully and fight vigorously. So in the religion of Christ a Christian person, whether man or woman, must possess a manly mind, that is, a mind mature and unbroken. A living and effective faith makes such people, not only men but also women, not only young men but also girls. Countless examples of this have been brought forth in Christianity, and every day they are still brought forth in our own age.

units.la: ESTOTE, inquit, fortes.] Vt uiriliter agatur, fortitudo requiritur, sine cuius dono nemo uiriliter agere poterit. Hanc requirit à fidelib. dicés: Estote fortes. Atq; ita uelut exponit, quid uelit cum dicit, ἀνδρίζεσθε. i. Viri estote, id uidelicet, ut sint fortes. Loquitur autem non de robore corporis quo destituuntur senes, parvuli, ægroti, & sexus muliebris: sed de fortitudine spiritus, quæ sit in fide Christi, apta & instructa non modo ad operandum opera fidei, sed & ad quæuis aduersa propter Christum fortiter ferenda, & ad resistendum Satanæ circueunti, ac quem deuoret quærenti.
units.tr: "Be strong," he says. For acting manfully, strength is required, and without the gift of it no one can act manfully. He requires this of the faithful when he says, "Be strong." And so he explains, as it were, what he means by "act like men" [ἀνδρίζεσθε], that is, "be men," namely so that they may be strong. He speaks not of bodily strength, which the old, the little children, the sick and the female sex lack, but of the strength of spirit that is in the faith of Christ, fitted and equipped not only to do the works of faith, but also to bear bravely all adversities for Christ's sake, and to resist Satan, who goes about seeking whom he may devour.

units.la: Sed dices: Vnde carni nostræ hæc poterit esse fortitudo, quæ ipsius quoque Christi testimonio admodum infirma est & imbecillis? Respódeo. Scribit Apostolus Christianis, in Christum credentibus, ac spiritu Christi regeneratis, & poscit ab illis non quod carnalium est & animalium hominum, sed quod est Christiano rum ac regeneratorum: quod habet non ex nativitate carnis, sed ex dono & regeneratione spiritus. Si fortitudinem hanc requiras à prima natiuitatis carne, perinde feceris ac si aquà requiras à pumice, & robur eundi, operandi, edendiq; & bibendi ab ægroto. A spiritu uero è supernis regenerato si requiras, requiris non quod habeat ex seipso, sed quod accepit, & quotidie accipere potest dono Dei, modo ex fide petat. Et Paulus homo erat, & tamen dicebat: Omnia possum per eum qui me confortat. dicebat autem non ut animalis homo, sed ut spiritualis, per spiritū Christi regeneratus. Nihil possumus, inquis, uerum est, sed adde, ex nobis ipsis. Omnis autem nostra sufficientia ex Deo est. Discipulis suis dicebat dominus, inquis: Nihil potestis facere. Dixit quidē, sed præmisit, Sine me. At Christiani non sunt sine Christo. Deus est, inquis, teste Apostolo hoc ipso, qui operatur & uelle & perficere.
units.tr: But you will say: how can this strength come to our flesh, which by Christ's own testimony is very weak and feeble? I answer: the Apostle is writing to Christians, who believe in Christ and are regenerated by the Spirit of Christ, and he asks of them not what belongs to carnal and natural men, but what belongs to Christians and the regenerate. This they have not from the birth of the flesh, but from the gift and regeneration of the Spirit. If you were to ask this strength of the flesh from the first birth, you would act just as if you asked water from a pumice stone, or the power to walk, work, eat and drink from a sick man. But if you ask it of the spirit regenerated from above, you ask not for what it has of itself, but for what it has received and can daily receive by the gift of God, provided it asks for it in faith. Paul was a man, and yet he said: "I can do all things through him who strengthens me." He said this not as a natural man, but as a spiritual man, regenerated by the Spirit of Christ. "We can do nothing," you say; that is true, but add: of ourselves. "Our sufficiency, however, is from God." The Lord said to his disciples, you say: "You can do nothing." He said it, but he prefaced it with: "Without me." But Christians are not without Christ. God, you say, as the Apostle himself testifies in this very place, is the one who works both to will and to perform.

units.la: Quid ergo nos poterimus? Verū est, operatur in nobis Deus, ut & uelimus & perficiamus: at hinc non sequitur, Christianos homines nec uelle nec perficere posse quod bonum est, sed magis sequitur contrariū. Quis.n. non uolet & perficiet, quod Deus in ipso operatur ut uelit & perficiat? Si Deus operatur in nobis, & uelle & perficere, utiq; poterimus & uelle & perficere, etiam si ex nobis nihil horum poterimus. An non possumus, quod etsi non ex no bis, ex Deo tamen in nobis operâte possumus? Num recte dicet corpus animatum: caro sum, nihil possum, spiritus enim est qui uiuificat. qui sapit, intelligit, iudicat, uidet, audit, sentit & operatur omnia. Verum quidem, facit hæc omnia spiritus, at interim facit hæc partim in corpore, partim per organa corporis, ut corpus harum operationum spiritus expers dici non possit. Vt ergo recte dixerit corpus animatum, Ex meipso quidem nihil horum potero quæ facio: uerum est in me spiritus, per quē uidere, audire, sentire, stare, sedere, ire, edere, bibere, operari, intelligere, uelle, nolle, amare, odisse, gaudere, tristari, timere, sperare, &c. secundum mensuram operationum illius ualeo: ita & Christianus per spiritum Christi regenerat ratus, ut gloriam det gratiæ Dei, recte quidem negabit boni se quicquam ex seipso posse operari, at simul recte fatebitur se quod per seipsum non potest posse per operationem habitantis in se spiritus Christi, idq; etsi non perfecte, secundum mensuram tamen donationis Christi. Sic itaque Christiani infirmi sumus & fortes: infirmi per carnem, fortes per spiritū Christi. Quoniam autem spiritus Christi non operatur in nobis ea serie & continuatione naturali, qua spiritus noster operatur in corpore nostro, sed ut uult & quando uult: orandum nobis est, ut sufficientiam nobis operationum suarum, quoties illam & gloria redemptoris nostri & salutis nostræ ratio & fratrum necessitas poposcerit. Cum igitur hortatur Apostolus, ut fidamus, sperēmus, diligamus, uigilemus, stemus in fide, uiriliter agamus, fortesq; simus: non requirit hæc à nobis quasi ex nobis, sed monet ut ad dominum conuersi, quæ deesse nobis sentimus, suppliciter & instanter ab illo petamus, & acceptis fideliter & constanter utamur.
units.tr: What then shall we be able to do? It is true that God works in us, so that we both will and accomplish. But it does not follow from this that Christians are unable to will or to accomplish what is good. On the contrary, the opposite follows. For who would not will and accomplish what God works in him to will and accomplish? If God works in us both to will and to accomplish, then surely we shall be able both to will and to accomplish, even though we can do none of these things from ourselves. Or can we not do what we can do, not from ourselves, but by God working in us? Would an animated body rightly say: "I am flesh, I can do nothing, for it is the spirit that gives life"? It is the spirit that understands, judges, sees, hears, feels and works all things. True, the spirit does all these things, but it does them partly in the body and partly through the organs of the body, so that the body cannot be called wholly without share in these operations. So the animated body may rightly say: "Of myself I can do none of these things that I do. Yet the spirit is truly in me, through whom I see, hear, feel, stand, sit, walk, eat, drink, work, understand, will, refuse, love, hate, rejoice, grieve, fear, hope, and so on, and I am able to do these things according to the measure of the spirit's operations." So too the Christian, regenerated by the Spirit of Christ, who gives glory to the grace of God, will rightly deny that he can work any good from himself. At the same time he will rightly confess that he can do through the operation of the Spirit of Christ dwelling in him what he cannot do through himself, and this though not perfectly, yet according to the measure of Christ's gift. Thus we Christians are both weak and strong: weak through the flesh, strong through the Spirit of Christ. But since the Spirit of Christ does not work in us in that natural order and continuity by which our spirit works in our body, but as it wills and when it wills, we must pray that it supply us with the sufficiency of its operations whenever the glory of our Redeemer, the reason of our salvation and the need of our brothers demand it. Therefore, when the Apostle urges us to trust, hope, love, watch, stand fast in the faith, act manfully and be strong, he does not require these things of us as though from ourselves. Rather he advises us, turning to the Lord, to ask of him earnestly and persistently the things we feel are lacking in us, and to use them faithfully and steadfastly once received.

units.la: OMNIA uestra, inquit, cum charitate fiat.] Græcè est πάντα ὑμῶν, non πάντα ὑμῖν. Quare cū uulgata malo legere omnia uestra, quàm cum Erasmo, omnia uobis: præsertim ob id, quod amphibolum est, si legamus: omnia uobis cū charitate fiant. Nam æque id sonat, omnia uobis fiant ab alijs cum charitate, atq; omnia fiant à uobis cum charitate. At in uulgata lectione nihil est amphiboli.
units.tr: "Let all your things," he says, "be done in love." In Greek it is [πάντα ὑμῶν], "all your things," not [πάντα ὑμῖν], "all to you." Therefore I prefer to read with the Vulgate "all your things" rather than with Erasmus "all to you," especially because the latter is ambiguous. If we read "let all things be done to you in love," it sounds equally like "all things are done to you by others in love" and "all things are done by you in love." But in the Vulgate reading there is no ambiguity.

units.la: OMNIA uestra, inquit.] Quæ omnia? In summa, omnia quæ cogitatis, constituitis, dicitis & facitis. Sic omnem nostrā uitā duab. distionib. cōpleētitur, dicés: Omnia uestra. Docet igitur, quomodo omnis uita nostra instituti debeat, cum dicit: Omnia uestra cum charitate fiant. Quid est autem omnia facere cum charitate? Obsecro, ignoramus ne quid sit omnia facere cum liuore & odio? uel, cum inanis gloriæ studio? uel, cum auaricia? Qui odit proximum, quicquid agendum cum illo est, agit ex odio, animo iniquo, iudicio sinistro, studio malo, hoc unum spectans, ut rebus illius quoad eius poterit incommodet. Econtrario, qui diligit proximum, agit cum illo omnia ex charitate, ritate, animo benevolo, iudicio syncero, studio bono, nihil quærens aliud, quàm ut rebus illius commodet pro viribus. Sic est comparata charitas, & hoc est illius ingenium. Non inuidet, non est procax, non inflatur, non fastidit, non quærit proprium commodum, nó irritatur, non cogitat malum, non gaudet de iniustitia: sed congaudet veritati, patiens est, benigna est, suffert, credit, sperat & sustinet omnia. Sed de hoc charitatis ingenio uidimus supra cap. 13.
units.tr: "All your things," he says. What are all these things? In sum, everything you think, decide, say and do. Thus he embraces our whole life in two words when he says "all your things." He teaches, therefore, how our whole life ought to be ordered when he says: "Let all your things be done in love." But what is it to do all things in love? I ask, do we not know what it is to do all things with envy and hatred, or with a desire for empty glory, or with greed? He who hates his neighbour acts, in whatever he has to do with him, from hatred, with an unfriendly mind, a sinister judgement and an evil purpose, looking only to this: that he may harm his neighbour's property as far as he can. On the contrary, he who loves his neighbour acts with him in everything from love, with a benevolent mind, a sincere judgement and a good purpose, seeking nothing else than to benefit his neighbour's property as far as his powers allow. Such is the nature of love, and this is its character. It does not envy, it is not boastful, it is not puffed up, it does not act unbecomingly, it does not seek its own advantage, it is not provoked, it does not think evil, it does not rejoice in injustice, but rejoices with the truth; it is patient, it is kind, it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things and endures all things. But we have seen this character of love above, in chapter 13.

units.la: OMNIA uestra, inquit, cū charitate fiant.] Quare non dicit: Omnia uestra cum fide, cum timore dni, cum iusticia fiant? Quid est quod charitatem poscit in omnibus? Respondeo. Accommodat se ecclesiæ cui scribit. Illa quantum deficeret ab ingenio charitatis, plus satis declarabat studio sectarum, contentionum ac disidiorum, & reliquis carnis operibus. Quare illam præcipue reuocat ad studium charitatis, quemadmodum & supra cap. 13. fecit. Quod ergo dicit: Omnia uestra cum charitate fiant, non est sic in uniuersum ad omnia referendū, quæ nobis sunt agenda, partim cum Deo, partim cum hominibus, siue hi sint impij siue pij, siue superiores nobis, siue pares, siue inferiores, siue cognati & coniuncti, siue alieni, partim cum uobisipsis, ut fidem, spem, iustitiam, iudicium, timorem Dei. &c, excludamus: sed simpliciter hoc loco secundum mentem Apostoli de ijs intelligendum, quæ agenda sunt cum proximo. Diligendus est Deus, idq; cum primis, ac præ omnib. Verum de hac parte cogitationum, studiorum, uerborum & operum uitæ nostræ quæ Deum concernit, meo iudicio non loquitur hoc loco Apostolus, sed respicit ad morbum quo Corinthij laborabant, & plurimum à fraterna charitate deficiebat, illique hoc ueluti remedium apponit, ut curetur. Vbi nanq; charitati fraternæ studetur in omnib. ibi sane disidia, contentiones ac sectæ, si obtinuerunt antea, cessabunt & euanescent, ut pax & concordia restituatur, si non obtinuerunt, ne obtineant in posterum, impedientur & arcebuntur, ne pax & concordia labefactetur.
units.tr: "Let all your things," he says, "be done in love." Why does he not say: "Let all your things be done with faith, with the fear of the Lord, with righteousness"? Why does he demand love in all things? I answer: he adapts himself to the church to which he writes. How far that church fell short of the character of love, it declared more than enough by its zeal for factions, contentions and dissensions, and by the other works of the flesh. Therefore he especially recalls it to the pursuit of love, as he also did above in chapter 13. So when he says "let all your things be done in love," this is not to be referred in general to everything we must do, partly with God and partly with men, whether these be ungodly or godly, whether they be superiors, equals or inferiors, whether kin and close or strangers. Nor should we exclude from it, partly with ourselves, such things as faith, hope, righteousness, judgement, the fear of God and so on. Rather, in this passage, according to the mind of the Apostle, it must simply be understood of those things that have to be done with our neighbour. God must be loved, and that above all and before all. But concerning this part of our thoughts, pursuits, words and deeds, which concerns God, in my judgement the Apostle is not speaking in this place. He is looking rather at the disease with which the Corinthians were afflicted, who were far from brotherly love, and he applies this as a kind of remedy so that it may be cured. For where zeal for brotherly love prevails in all things, there surely dissensions, contentions and sects, if they have already taken hold, will cease and vanish, so that peace and concord may be restored; and if they have not taken hold, they will be hindered and kept away in future, lest peace and concord be shaken.

units.la: Et utinam beneficio Christi detur hoc nostræ ætatis ecclesijs, ut uel inter fratres, eiusdē fidei & doctrinæ consortes, fiant omnia cū charitate: uel si minus sperandum hoc est, ea saltē cum charitate fiant, quæ cum primis singulare charitatis studium poscunt, è quibus est mysteriorum Christi communicatio, qua unum nos corpus esse in dno declarari conueniebat.
units.tr: And would that by the benefit of Christ this might be granted to the churches of our age: that among brothers, partakers of the same faith and doctrine, all things be done in love; or, if this is too much to hope for, at least that those things be done in love which above all demand a singular zeal for love. Among these is the communion of the mysteries of Christ, by which it was fitting that we should be declared to be one body in the Lord.

units.la: Obsecro autem uos fratres, nostis familiā Stephanæ esse primitias Achaiæ, & quod in ministerium sanctis ordinarunt seipsos, ut & uos subditi sitis talibus, & omni adiuuati & laborati. Gaudeo uero de aduentu Stephanæ, & Fortunati & Achaici, quoniam id quod mihi deerat uestri hi suppleuerunt. Refo-
units.tr: I beg you, brothers, you know that the household of Stephanas is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints. Be subject to such people, and to everyone who helps and labours with them. I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus, since these men have supplied what was lacking on your part.

units.la: cillauerunt enim spiritum meum ac uestrum. Agnoscite itaq; eiusmodi.
units.tr: For they have refreshed my spirit and yours. Acknowledge such men, therefore.

units.la: Habent ista singularem commendationem trium selectarum personarum de ecclesia Corinthiorum existentium, Stephanæ uidelicet & Fortunati & Achaici. Obsecro, inquit, uos fratres. Quamuis æque uerti poterat: Hortor autem uos fratres, placet tamen legere: obsecro uos fratres, propter Apostolici pectoris affectum, ad obsecrandum magis quàm ad hortandum propensum. Licet nihil inde emolumenti ad ipsum, multum uero ad illos esset redituru: perinde tamen obsecrat, ac si ipsius essent bono obsecranti sibi obtéperaturi. Qua in re ipsissimum exprimitur uerae charitatis ingenium.
units.tr: These words contain a special commendation of three chosen persons who were in the church of the Corinthians, namely Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus. "I beg you, brothers," he says. Although it could equally well be translated "I exhort you, brothers," it is nevertheless better to read "I beg you, brothers," on account of the Apostle's feeling, which was inclined to beseech rather than to exhort. Although nothing of advantage would come from this to himself, but much to them, he nonetheless begs as if those whom he begs were going to obey him for their own good. In this matter the very nature of true love is expressed.

units.la: NOSTIS familiam Stephanæ, inquit, esse primitias Achaiæ.] Commendaturus hac meminit singularis gratiæ Dei, qua præ alijs erat Achaiæ fidelibus ornata. Hanc exprimit dum uocat eam primitias Achaiæ, propterea uidelicet quod ex omni Achaia cum primis crediderat Euangelio Dei, atque ita dno instar primitiarum oblata & consecrata fuerat. Quod salutem quidem attinet, nihil decedit illis qui non primi, sed postremi credunt, nec Deo illi minus sunt accepti: cuius rei admonemur in Paulo, qui postremus inter apostolos ad fidem est Christi conuersus, & in parabola dominica, ubi dicit: Volo autem huic nouissimo dare sicut & tibi, Matth. 20. Singularem tamen meritò sortiuntur prærogatiuam, qui ex omni regione uel ciuitate, uel gente primi honorem hunc Deo tribuunt, ut uerbo eius credant, & uocanti obediant, simuiq; alijs ad eandem gratiam quoad eius possunt uel operam suam uel occasionem, saltem exemplo suo offerūt. Quare quemadmodum communi omnium sensu admodum est execrabilis, qui publici alicuius mali primus ex omnibus est uel author, uel propagator: ita communi conuenit omnium sensu, singulariter in precio habere eos, qui publici boni primitiæ constituti sunt à dno, modo in ea gratia perseuerent. Alias ex primis fiunt nouissimi. Hoc nomine commendat Apostolus ecclesiæ Corinthiorum familiam Stephanæ, dicens: Obsecro autem uos fratres, nostis familiam Stephanæ esse primitias Achaiæ.
units.tr: "You know the household of Stephanas," he says, "to be the firstfruits of Achaia." Intending to commend them, he recalls the singular grace of God by which they were adorned beyond the other believers of Achaia. He expresses this when he calls them the firstfruits of Achaia, obviously because out of all Achaia they were the first to believe the gospel of God, and so had been offered and consecrated to the Lord like firstfruits. As for salvation, nothing is lost to those who believe not first but last, and they are not less acceptable to God. We are reminded of this in Paul, who was the last of the apostles to be converted to the faith of Christ, and in the Lord's parable, where he says: "I wish to give to this last one just as to you" (Matth. 20.). Yet those who are first, from any region, city or nation, to give this honour to God, by believing his word and obeying his call, rightly obtain a singular prerogative. At the same time, as far as they can, they offer to others the same grace, either by their own labour or by an opportunity, or at least by their example. Just as, by the common feeling of all, he who is first of all to be the author or spreader of some public evil is utterly detestable, so by the common feeling of all it is fitting to hold in singular esteem those who have been constituted by the Lord as the firstfruits of a public good, provided they persevere in that grace. Otherwise the first become the last. On this ground the Apostle commends to the church of the Corinthians the household of Stephanas, saying: "I beg you, brothers, you know the household of Stephanas to be the firstfruits of Achaia."

units.la: Vulgata autē lectio cōjungit in hac prærogatiua familiæ Stephanæ, Fortunatū & Achaicum. Sic enim habet: Nostis domum Stephanæ, Fortunati & Achaici, quoniam sunt primitiæ Achaiæ. Verum de duobus hisce posterioribus non fit mentio in Græcis exemplaribus hoc loco, & nec à Chrysostomo quoq;.
units.tr: The Vulgate reading, however, joins Fortunatus and Achaicus with Stephanas in this distinction of the household. For it reads: "You know the house of Stephanas, of Fortunatus and of Achaicus, because they are the firstfruits of Achaia." But there is no mention of these last two in the Greek copies in this place, nor in Chrysostom either.

units.la: Obseruandum est hoc loco, quod non simpliciter dicit, Nostis Stephanam: sed, nostis familiam Stephanę esse primitias Achaię. Patrifamiliās domesticam suam adiungit familiam. ηλω ελαίαν, inquit, στεφανᾶ. Verosimile est Stephanam hunc credidisse primum, & ubi credere coepit familiæ suæ fuisse authorem, ut & ipsa ad fidem induceretur. Et tamen non solum ipsum nominat, sed simul & ipsum, & domesticos eius complectitur, dicens: Nostis familiam Stephanæ esse primitias Achaiæ. Facit hoc nō ut patremfamiliās gloria sua priuet, quasi credente familia non crediderit ipse, sed magis ut singularem gratiam Dei prædicet, quia concessum illi erat, ut concordem haberet in uera religione amplestenda non unam & alteram domesticorum personam, sed totam familiam. Quare obsecro quid nam poterit homini pio accidere iucundius? Annon hic implebatur il lud Psalmistæ: Ecce quàm bonum & quàm iucundum habitare fratres in unum? Contrà q; triste est molestum, si fidelis paterfamiliàs dissentientem habeat familiam, uxorem pietati reluctantem, filios ueritatem Dei blasphemátes, familiam & honori & saluti suæ perfide in fidiantem: ut impleatur illud Christi: Erunt quinque in una domo diuisi, &c. Triste hoc est per comparationem, respectu eius felicitatis, qua & paterfamiliàs, & familia unanimes dono Dei ueritatis doctrinam amplestuntur. In se uero si consideres, multo iucundius est domesticum hoc dissidium propter regnum Dei exortum, quàm pax domestica tenebris ignorantiæ inuoluta.
units.tr: It should be observed here that he does not simply say, "You know Stephanas," but, "You know that the household of Stephanas is the firstfruits of Achaia." He joins his household to the head of the family. "The house of Stephanas," he says, "[ηλω ελαίαν]." It is likely that Stephanas was the first to believe, and that when he began to believe he was the author of faith for his household, so that they too were brought to faith. Yet he does not name only himself, but at the same time embraces both himself and his household, saying: "You know the household of Stephanas is the firstfruits of Achaia." He does this not to deprive the head of the family of his glory, as though the household believed and he himself did not, but rather to proclaim the singular grace of God, because it was granted to him that he had in agreement in embracing the true religion not one or another member of his household, but the whole family. Therefore, I ask, what could be more pleasing to a godly man? Was not that saying of the Psalmist fulfilled here: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity"? On the other hand, it is sad and troublesome when a faithful head of the family has a dissenting household: a wife who resists godliness, sons who blaspheme the truth of God, a household faithlessly opposed to his honour and salvation, so that the saying of Christ is fulfilled: "There shall be five in one house divided, etc." This is sad by comparison with that happiness in which the head of the family and the family alike, in unity, embrace through God's gift the doctrine of truth. But if you consider it in itself, this domestic division arising for the sake of the kingdom of God is much more pleasant than a domestic peace wrapped in the darkness of ignorance.

units.la: Non est autem ociosum, quod non simpliciter dicit, Familia Stephanæ primitiæ sunt Achaiæ: sed, Nostis familiā Stephanæ primitias esse Achaiæ. Quod in Græco est οἰκίας, uerti quidem potest: uel, Scitote, uel scitis ac nostis: uerum ubi consideramus non hoc agere Apostolum, ut hortetur Corinthios, ut familiā Stephanæ primitias esse Achaiæ sciant aut agnoscant, cum hoc illi non ignorarent: sed conscietiam ipsorum appellare de re omnib. ipsis nota, quod uidelicet familia Stephanæ primitiæ sint Achaiæ, atq; hinc illos admonere, ut subditi sint talibus: existimamus conuenientius esse, ut legamus, nostis, quàm noueritis uel scitote. Sic cauet, ne prƽter rationem familiā hàc illis commendare, & magis suos in illam affectus, quàm iustam aliquam causam sequi uidea-tur, præsertim cum ea familia amanter ac reuerenter in se esset affecta, idq; multis modis declaret. Vos ipsi, inquit, nostis familiam Stephanæ primitias esse Achaiæ. Non est ut mihi hac in re gratificemini. Testimonio conscientiæ uestræ conuicti æquisimum esse fatebiini ni, ut quod moneo faciatis.
units.tr: It is not idle, moreover, that he does not simply say, "The household of Stephanas is the firstfruits of Achaia," but, "You know the household of Stephanas to be the firstfruits of Achaia." In the Greek it is οἰκίας, which may indeed be rendered "Be aware," or "You know," or "You know and recognise." But when we consider that the Apostle does not intend to exhort the Corinthians to know or acknowledge that the household of Stephanas is the firstfruits of Achaia, since they were not ignorant of this, but rather to appeal to their conscience concerning a matter well known to them all, namely that the household of Stephanas is the firstfruits of Achaia, and from this to admonish them to be subject to such people, we judge it more fitting to read "you know" rather than "you have come to know" or "be aware." So he guards against seeming to commend this household to them without reason, and to urge them towards it out of mere affection rather than from some just cause, especially since that household had shown them love and reverence, and declared this in many ways. "You yourselves," he says, "know that the household of Stephanas is the firstfruits of Achaia." There is no need for you to favour me in this matter. Convinced by the testimony of your own conscience, you will confess it to be most just that you do what I advise.

units.la: Considerandū hic est Christi ministris, quæ sit uis earum admonitionum, quarum argumenta sumuntur ex rebus cognitis, de quibus ipse possunt eorum appellari conscientiæ, qui admonendi ueniunt. Siue doceant, siue corripiant, siue hortentur & admoneant, curandum est, ut conscientiæ auditorum conuincantur, quarum συμμαρτυρία, uel urget fortiter ad obediendum ueritati, uel adimit omnem excusationem immorigeris.
units.tr: Here the ministers of Christ must consider what force there is in admonitions whose arguments are drawn from things known, which the consciences of those to whom they come to admonish can themselves be appealed to about. Whether they teach, rebuke, exhort or admonish, care must be taken that the consciences of the hearers are convicted; their joint witness either urges them strongly to obey the truth, or takes away every excuse from the disobedient.

units.la: ET quod in ministerium sanctis, inquit, ordinarunt seipsos.] Non solum id in illis com-
units.tr: "And who have devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints," he says.

units.la: mendat, quod cum primis crediderunt Euangelio Dei, sed & hoc considerandum propo-nit, quod posteaquà credere cœperant, omnē suam quam poterant operam credentibus fratribus pio ac diligenti studio impenderunt. Eos qui Christo credebant, pauperes, exules, & afflictos, uocat iam secundo sanctos, simul admonens, quo loco habuerit eos, & quo respectu ministrarit illis familia hæc Stephanæ. Reputabat & agnoscebat eos esse sanctos Domini, & hoc illos respectu suscipiebat hospicio, alebat, uestiebat, & omnis generis quibus poterat refocillationibus & consolationibus afficiebat, inq; fide Christi corroborabat. Hæc omnia dictione ministerij, complectitur Apostolus, ne quis aliud ad hanc causam non pertinens cogitet. Discant hic cultores diuorum, quos in Papatu sanctos uocat, quibus sanctis, & quo ministerij genere, ministrare nos doceat Apostolica doctrina. Colite Deum, ô fratres, persidem ac seruite illi soli, sanctis ue-ro, hoc est Christi fidelibus, multis in hoc sæculo modis afflictis per charitatem quæ necessaria sunt ministrate. Hoc facientes legitimi eritis cultores ac serui Dei, & uerorum sanctorum ministri.
units.tr: He commends them not only because they were among the first to believe the Gospel of God, but he also sets before us for consideration that, after they had begun to believe, they devoted all the effort they could, with godly and diligent zeal, to the brothers who believed. Those who believed in Christ, poor, exiles and afflicted, he now calls saints a second time, at the same time reminding us in what regard he held them and in what respect this household of Stephanas ministered to them. He regarded and acknowledged them as the saints of the Lord, and in this respect received them into hospitality, nourished them, clothed them, and refreshed and comforted them in every kind of way open to them, strengthening them in the faith of Christ. The Apostle embraces all these things in the word "ministry," so that no one thinks of anything else not pertaining to this cause. Let those who worship the so-called saints in the Papacy learn here which saints, and by what kind of ministry, apostolic doctrine teaches us to minister. Worship God, O brothers, and serve him alone in faith; but to the saints, that is, to the faithful of Christ, afflicted in many ways in this age, supply by love what is necessary. Doing this, you will be the lawful worshippers and servants of God, and true ministers of the saints.

units.la: Obserua uero quod non simpliciter dicit, Et quod ministrarunt sanctis: sed, & quod in ministerium sanctorum ordinarunt seipsos. A liud est ministrare, & aliud in ministerium ordinare seipsum. Prius sine uoluntatis propositi to per occasionem fieri potest, posterius uero propenso ac beneuolo corde perficitur. Sic Christus non simpliciter ministrauit nobis redimendis ac saluádis, sed seipsum ad ministrádum nobis ordinauit, & hac uoluntate carne nostra assumpta uenit in hunc mundum. Hoc igitur Apostolus in familia Stephanæ cömendat, quod non modo cum primis crediderūt: sed & singularem erga fratres egenos charitatis zelum non simpliciter ministrando illorū necessitatibus, sed & seipsos ex animo totos in id misterij ordinando declararunt. quasi dicat: Sic ministrant sanctis ardéti ac sedulo studio, ut manifestum sit, ad hoc se ministerium totos ordinasse.
units.tr: Observe, moreover, that he does not simply say, "And they ministered to the saints," but, "And they have devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints." It is one thing to minister, and another to devote oneself to ministry. The former can happen by chance, without a purpose of the will; the latter is accomplished with an inclined and benevolent heart. So Christ did not merely minister to us in redeeming and saving us, but ordained himself to minister to us, and by this will, having taken on our flesh, he came into this world. The Apostle therefore commends in the household of Stephanas that they not only believed first, but also declared a singular zeal of love for needy brothers, not simply by ministering to their necessities, but by devoting themselves wholly from the heart to this ministry. As if he were saying: they minister to the saints with such burning and diligent zeal that it is evident they have wholly devoted themselves to this ministry.

units.la: Exemplum hoc in Papatu nonnulli ex monachis ac Nonnis imitari se uelle simulant, atque hac specie irrepserunt in Xenodochia & Ptochodochia, præsertim ea, quibus abunde annuis est reditibus prospectum. Horum pro positum si penitius inspiciatur, imò si manifesta ipsorum studia spectentur, deprehenditur ordinasse quidem se in ministerium, uerū non sanctis fidelibus, sed saginandis suis uentrib. Non reprehēdo, absit, sed laudo, si quid hoc si bi uitæ genus deligant, ut nihil agant aliud, q; ut ministrent sanctis, ad quod institutum nō-nullis in locis habentur cōstituta διακονοτροφία, in quib. huiusmodi propositi homines in hūc usum aluntur, ut ad ministrandum, præsertim ægrotis, sicubi necessitas poposcerit, usurpari possint. Non reprehendo, inquam, sed laudo, si quod faciunt, faciant animo & studio nō se- standi ociū: sed ministrandi sanctis, ut sanctis, sintq; non minus prompti ad ministrádū, si in humilia pauperum tuguria, q; si in splendidas diuitū ædes ministraturi uocentur. Qui sic sūt animati, horum ego propositum, omnium dixerim esse sanctissimum ac plane diuinum, di gnumq; quod inter Christianos magno habea tur in precio, ac templarijs illis cultibus lógis- sime præferatur.
units.tr: Many monks and nuns in the Papacy pretend that they wish to imitate this example, and in this guise have crept into hospices and almshouses, especially those which are abundantly provided with annual revenues. If the purpose of these people is examined more closely, indeed if their manifest pursuits are observed, it will be found that they have indeed devoted themselves to ministry, but not to the faithful saints; rather to fattening their own bellies. I do not reprehend, far from it, but I praise it, if they choose this kind of life so as to do nothing else but minister to the saints; for which purpose in some places institutions called dispensaries are maintained, in which men of such purpose are fed for this use, so that they may be employed in ministering, especially to the sick, wherever need requires. I do not reprehend, I say, but praise it, if what they do they do with a mind and zeal not for standing idle, but for ministering to the saints, as saints, and are no less ready to minister if they are called to serve in the humble hovels of the poor than in the splendid mansions of the rich. Those so disposed, I would say, have a purpose most holy and plainly divine among all, and worthy to be held in great esteem among Christians, and far to be preferred above those temple-cults.

units.la: Magnū est, si quis suis sumptibus alat eos, q seipsos in ministerium sanctis ordinarunt. Et utinam sint hodie multi diuites in ecclesijs Euangelicis, qui hoc faciant. In tenebris super- stitionum Papisticarū multi fuerunt, qui partim zelo bono, partim spe meritorum facultatibus suis ἀπλοῦς ἐπιλογὴ profpexerút: at in ecclesijs nostrorum citius inueniās, qui qđ datū est à maioribus in suos prophanos usus auferre, q il lorum exéplum sequi cupiant. Id uero multo est præclarius, si quis nō modo facultates suas, sed & seipsum & in ministerià sanctis ordinet.
units.tr: It is a great thing if someone supports at his own expense those who have devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints. And would that there were today many rich men in the Evangelical churches who would do this. In the darkness of Papistical superstitions there were many who, partly from good zeal and partly from hope of merit, provided for them with their resources, out of simple choice; but in the churches of our people you will more quickly find those who desire to take away from profane uses what was given by their forebears, than to follow their example. Indeed it is much more excellent if someone devotes not only his resources, but also himself, to the ministry of the saints.

units.la: VT & uos, inquit, subditi sitis talibus. Quo niā non simpliciter dicit, & uos : sed, ut & uos subditi sitis talibus: apparet quidē illud, ὀιδάσκ hortandi modo esse dictum, ac legendum, no- ueritis, ut hic finis eius agnitionis subijciatur, qui sit, ut talibus sint subditi & ipsi. uerum hæc particula non est ad uerbum, ὀιδαν sed ad uer- bum παρακαλῶ referendum, & lectio ordinada ad hunc modum: Nostis fratres familiam Ste- phanæ, esse primitias Achaiæ, & quod in mini- sterium sanctis ordinarunt seipsos, obsecro, ut sitis & uos subditi talibus.
units.tr: "Ye also, he says, be subject to such": he does not simply say "and ye," but "that ye also be subject to such." This makes it clear that the word "ye know" [οἴδατε] is to be read as an exhortation, and that the purpose of this knowledge is stated: that you too be subject to such people. This particle, however, does not belong with the verb "know," but with the verb "I beseech" [παρακαλῶ]. The sentence should be read like this: "You know, brothers, that the household of Stephanas are the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints. I beseech you that you also be subject to such people."

units.la: Quid igitur? Poscitne à Corinthiorū ecclesia Apostolus, ut subiecta sit familiæ Stephanę, pa tiatur q; illius magisterij ac dñium cū dicit: Vt subditi sitis talibus? Respondeo. Nō hoc agit, ut reddat ecclesiam Christi alicui quátumuis sanctæ familiæ subiectam ac seruā: sed ut admo neat Corinth. fideles, ut quemadmodū familia Stephanę ordinauit seipsam in ministerium san ctis, ita ipsi uicissim subordinet se, & ipsi in mi nisterium illis qui sunt tales. Est enim in Græco idem utrobiq; uerbum, tam in eo quod poscit à Corinthijs, q in eo quod fecit familia Stepha næ, nisi quod hic simplici ὑπῆξαν, illic uero com posito, ὑποτάσσεσθε usus est, quod uerti poterat, subordinemini. Huc pertinet & illud qđ non simpliciter dicit, ut subditi sitis: sed, ut & uos subditi sitis talibus. quasi dicat: Vicissim, sicut illi subordinarūt se in ministerium uobis & aliis sanctis. Caute autē non dicit, Vt & uos subditi sitis ipsis: sed, ut & uos subditi sitis talib. ut significet se non gratificari illorū personis, sed comendare pietate & charitatis studiū non in illis modo, sed & in omnibus alijs cōsimili stu dio prædititis. Poterat uideri propésus ob id ef se in hanc Stephanæ familiā, qđ illa cum pri- mis doctrinæ suæ crediderat, sibiq; cōstanter adhærebat: uerū ut significet se in illa nō ea cō- mędare quę se cócernant, sed ipsam pietatem & charitatem, quá non in illa tantum, sed & in
units.tr: What then? Does the Apostle demand of the Corinthian church that it be subject to the household of Stephanas, and allow that household its teaching and lordship when he says, "that ye also be subject to such"? I answer: he does not intend to make the church of Christ subject and servile to any household, however holy. Rather he exhorts the faithful at Corinth that, just as the household of Stephanas has devoted itself to the ministry of the saints, so they in turn should subordinate themselves and place themselves at the service of such people. The same Greek verb is used both in what he asks of the Corinthians and in what the household of Stephanas did, except that here the simple form [ὑπῆξαν] is used, and there the compound form [ὑποτάσσεσθε], which could be rendered "be subordinated." To this belongs also the fact that he does not simply say "that ye be subject," but "that ye also be subject to such." It is as if he said: "In return, just as they have subordinated themselves to the ministry for you and for other saints." Notice, too, that he carefully does not say "that ye be subject to them," but "to such." He means that he is not pleasing their persons, but commending piety and a zeal for charity, which he wants to be shown not only toward them but toward all others with the same zeal. It might seem that this household was preferred because it had first believed his teaching and clung steadfastly to him. But by saying "to such," he signifies that in them he commends not what concerns themselves, but piety and charity, which he wants them to regard in all, not only in these. He does not say "subject to them," but "subject to such," to show that they should look to this quality, wherever they find it.

units.la: omnib. alijs respiciat, respiciendamq; esse mo- neat, non dicit, ut subditi sitis illis, sed ut subdi ti sitis talib. Quod amat ac suspicit in pijs hoc in illis cōmendat, non personas, sed uirtutē, & hanc in precio habendam esse monet in omni bus. Qui bonos amat propterea quod sunt ta les, amat non personas, sed bonitatem, & liber est ab omni personarum acceptione. Doctri- na hæc facilis est cognitu, usu uero difficilis.
units.tr: What he loves and admires in the godly, he commends in these people: not their persons but their virtue, and he warns that this virtue must be prized in everyone. He who loves good people because they are such loves not persons but goodness, and is free from all respect of persons. This teaching is easy to know, but difficult to practise.

units.la: ET omni adiuuati, inquit & laborati. Græ ce est ⲭⲩⲱⲁⲣⲧⲓ ... i. & omni cooperan- ti. Sic quod sequitur, ... i. & laboranti, positum est pro ... i. collaboranti. Per cooperarios aut & collaborantes intelligit e- os qui Apostolis erant in ministerio uerbi ad- iumento, siue prædicando, siue alia nec essaria obeundo, quales erant Apollos, Titus, Timo- theus, &c. Tales erant etiam Stephanas cū suæ familia, & Fortunatus, & Achaicus, quorū hic meminit. Vult ergo, ut in precio habeátur, nō modo qui primores sunt operarij ac laborato res in opere dñi, quales erant Apostoli, sed & omnes illorum cooperarij & collaboratores.
units.tr: "And helped by all, he says, and labouring." In Greek it is "cooperating [συνεργοῦντι]," that is, "and to everyone cooperating." Likewise what follows, "and labouring" [κοπιῶντι], is put for "collaborating." By "co-workers" and "collaborators" he means those who assisted the Apostles in the ministry of the Word, whether by preaching or by performing other necessary tasks, such as Apollos, Titus, Timothy, and so on. Stephanas with his household, Fortunatus and Achaicus, whom he mentions here, were also of this kind. He wants them to be held in high regard, not only those who are the chief workers and labourers in the Lord's work, such as the Apostles, but also all their co-workers and collaborators.

units.la: Vide autem quid in illis cōmendet. Non di cit, & omni pręlato ac pręposito: sed, & omni cooperanti & collaboranti. Operis uult ac la- boris nō dignitatū haberi ratione. Nec quod- cunq; operis ac laboris genus: sed id commen dat, qđ adiumento erat Apostolis operantib. ac laborantibus in Euangelio Christi. Opera- bantur ac laborabát apostoli in opere dñi, qui code cum illis opere laborabant, erant illorū cooperarij & collaboratores. Apparet autem rursus cōmendare illis Timotheum, & fratres quos cum illo miserat, tăquam cooperarios ac collaboratores suos in opere dñi. Habent ho- die episc ɔpi suos coadiutores, & pareci suos collaboratores, cum nec episcopi, nec pareci operentur ac laborent in opere dñi. Ridiculū plane est, quód homini ociofo & nihil operáti datur coadiutor & collaborator, cū nemo pos- sit nisi operantis esse cooperator, & laboran- tis collaborator. At sic fieri solenne est inter e- os, qui solis inanib. titulis cōspicui sunt in ec- clesia, & non ueritati seruiunt, sed nugaci fabu la ecclesiam Christi ludificant.
units.tr: Note what he commends in them. He does not say "every prelate and superior," but "every co-worker and collaborator." He wants account to be taken of work and labour, not of dignities. He commends not any kind of work or labour, but that which helped the Apostles as they worked and laboured in the Gospel of Christ. The Apostles worked and laboured in the Lord's work, and those who worked with them in that labour were their co-workers and collaborators. It appears again that he commends Timothy, and the brothers whom he had sent with him, as his co-workers and collaborators in the Lord's work. Today bishops have their assistants, and parish priests their collaborators, though neither bishops nor parish priests work or labour in the Lord's work. It is plainly ridiculous that a man who is idle and does nothing should be given an assistant and collaborator, since no one can be a co-worker except of one who works, or a collaborator except of one who labours. Yet it is customary among those who are conspicuous in the church only by empty titles, who serve not the truth but a trifling fable, and mock the church of Christ in this way.

units.la: GAVDEO uero de aduētu, inquit Stepha næ & Fortunati & Achaici. Venerant illi ad i- pisum, an suapte sponte, uel missi à Corinthijs puto esse incertū. Quicquid sit, significat se ad uentu illorum fuisse exhilaratū. Sunt quialiter exponant. Quoniā uulgata æditio habet: Gau deo in præsentia Stephanę, Fortunati & Acha ici, exponunt de prękentia, non qua illi fuerint cū Apostolo, sed qua fnerint præsentes eccle- siæ Corinthiorum. quasi dicat: Gaudeo quod apud uos sunt Stephanas, Fortunatus & Acha icus. Hi nanq; quæ uobis desunt præsentia & cura sua adimplent. Huic lectioni & expositio ni causam dedit, quod in Græco est uox ... quasi illa nihil sonet aliud quàm præsentiā. Et Ambrosius quamuis ambigue exponit, & utrunque sensum assignat, hunc tamen prorei
units.tr: "I rejoice, however, at the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus." Did they come to him of their own accord, or were they sent by the Corinthians? I think it is uncertain. Whatever the case, he signifies that he was gladdened by their arrival. Some explain it differently. The Vulgate has, "I rejoice at the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus," and they explain "presence" not as their being with the Apostle, but as their being present with the church of the Corinthians, as if he said: "I rejoice that Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus are with you. For they supply by their presence and care what you lack." What gave occasion to this reading and explanation is that the Greek word [παρουσίᾳ] seems to mean nothing other than "presence." Ambrose, although he explains it ambiguously and gives both senses, nevertheless puts this one first,

units.la: loco ponit, dicens: Quia præsentes sunt apud uos, & in illis magnum potestis habere profectum, quèadmodum & in Commentarijs, qui Hieronymo tribuuntur, nō modo eadem ambigua expositio, sed & eadem uerba ponétur, quę in Ambrosio leguntur, unde lector diligēs facile olfacere potest, quid de illis sentire debeat. Chrysostomus tñ, cui dubio procul uox ϖα ρωσίχ notior aliquanto fuit quàm Latinis scriptoribus, non de præsentia trium istorum uirorum, qua ecclesiæ Corinthiorum præsentes fuerint: sed de aduentu illorum ad Paulum expönit, quam lectionem & expositionem retinendam esse iudicamus.
units.tr: saying: "Because they are present with you, and you can gain great profit from them." Likewise in the Commentaries attributed to Jerome, not only the same ambiguous explanation but the same words are given as those read in Ambrose, so that a diligent reader can easily perceive what he ought to think of them. Chrysostom, however, for whom the word [παρουσίᾳ] was undoubtedly somewhat better known than to Latin writers, explains it not of the presence of these three men with the church of the Corinthians, but of their coming to Paul. We judge this reading and explanation should be retained.

units.la: Quam autem ob causam tres hi uiri ex ecclesia Cotinthiorum ad Paulum proficisci uoluerint, non exprimitur. Erant causæ satis multæ, ob quas qui synceriores erant, ad Apostolum proficiscerentur, & quæ in ecclesia ipsorū gererētur ad illum deferrent. Deinde etsi nullæ tales fuissent, ipsum Apostoli desiderium potuit animos illorum excitare, ut quamuis magno ad illum uidendum, audiendū & alloquēdum itinere proficiscerētur. Hoc sane peregrinationis genus, quo uiuorum apostolorum facies & colloquium expetitur, multo est cōsultius & utilius, quàm quo à superstitiosis hodie ad limina apostolorum, ut aiunt Petri & Pauli Romam usq; excurritur, ubi inueniuntur non Apostoli, sed Apostatæ: nō Petrus piscator hominum, sed Simon uterq; & uēditor Christi & nundinator gratię spiritus sancti: non Paulus doctor Gentium, sed Saulus persequutor & matator fidelium animarum: ubi inuenitur inquam, nō apostolica Roma, sed apostatica Babylon, & flagitiosissima Sodoma, in quasi quisquá adhuc uere pius uiuit, hunc dñs, oro quèadmodum olim Lothum suum, clementer eripiat, nec cum illa breui interitura pereat.
units.tr: The reason why these three men wished to set out from the church of the Corinthians to Paul is not stated. There were quite enough reasons why those who were more sincere should go to the Apostle and report to him what was happening in their church. Moreover, even if no such reasons had existed, the Apostle's own desire could have stirred their minds, so that they set out on a long journey to see, hear and speak with him. Indeed this kind of pilgrimage, which seeks the face and conversation of living apostles, is far more advisable and useful than the one which superstitious people today rush to, as they say, to the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul, all the way to Rome. There they find not apostles but apostates; not Peter, the fisher of men, but Simon, each one a seller of Christ and a trader in the grace of the Holy Spirit; not Paul the teacher of the Gentiles, but Saul, the persecutor and butcher of faithful souls. There, I say, one finds not apostolic Rome but apostate Babylon, and the most shameful Sodom. I pray the Lord that, as he once mercifully rescued his Lot, he may snatch from it any who still live truly godly, and that they may not perish with that city, which is soon to perish.

units.la: QVONIAM, inquit, id quod mihi deerat uestri, hi suppleuerunt.
units.tr: Because, he says, these men have supplied what was lacking in you.

units.la: In Græco est, ὅτι τὸ ὑμῶν ὑστέρημα αὐτοι ἀνεπλήρωσαν: hoc est, quoniam uestri defectū hi suppleuerūt: uulgata habet, quoniā id quod uobis deerat, &c. Rationem reddit, quare de aduentu sit Stephanæ, Fortunati, & Achaici gauisus. Desiderabat præsentiā & cōuictum fidelium, quos per Euangelium Corinthi genuerat, perinde atque pater præsentiā desiderat filiorum, quos domi suæ peregre profectus reliquit. Cum ergo uenissent ad se tres hi uiri gaudebat impense, amplexus eos, haud aliter quàm si tota in ipsis Corinthiorum ad se uenisset ecclesia. Hoc igitur desiderium suum, uel si mauis, absentiam fidelium Corinthiorū, uocat illorum ὑστέρημα. i. defectum, quem non illi, sed ipse patiebatur, dicitq; hunc suppletum esse per aduentum Stephanæ, Fortunati & Achaici, seq; per illorum præsentiā, perinde exhilaratum, ac si ipsi uenissent ad se omnes.
units.tr: In Greek it is [ὅτι τὸ ὑμῶν ὑστέρημα αὐτοι ἀνεπλήρωσαν], that is, "because these men have supplied the lack of you." The Vulgate has "because what was lacking to you, etc." He gives the reason why he rejoiced at the arrival of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus. He longed for the presence and company of the faithful whom he had begotten at Corinth through the gospel, just as a father longs for the presence of the children he has left at home when he goes abroad. So when these three men came to him, he rejoiced greatly and embraced them, just as if the whole Corinthian church had come to him. This longing of his, or if you prefer, the absence of the Corinthian faithful, he calls their ὑστέρημα, that is, their lack. It was not they who suffered it, but he himself. He says that this lack was made good by the coming of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, and that he himself was cheered by their presence just as if they had all come to him.

units.la: Quos suprà præsentem locum, de præsentia trium istorum uirorū exponere diximus, qua non Paulo, sed Corinthiorum ecclesiæ præsentes fuerint, ad hunc illi modum uerba hæc ex-
units.tr: Earlier, when we discussed this passage, we said that the presence of these three men should be explained as a presence to the Corinthian church, not to Paulus. Those who take this view explain the words in this way:

units.la: ponunt. Quoniam id quod uobis deerat ad profectionem boni, ipsi suppleuerunt, & quia de hoc profectu gaudebat, Apostolus subdit: refecerunt enim & meum spiritum gaudio spiritu ali, & uestrum ex profectu boni. Hi intelligūt per ὑστέρημα non desiderium Apostoli, quo præsentiam Corinthiorum, qua destituebatur, deriderat: sed defectum Corinthiorum, quo in causa pietatis deficiebant: uel absentiam Apostoli, cuius præsentiam ecclesia Corinthiorum poscebat, quá tres hi uiri sua præsentia supplerent. Verū si hoc uoluisset Apost. rectius dixisset non in præterito, hi suppleuerunt: sed in præsenti, hi suppleant. Cum enim hęc scriberet, nōdum sic impletus fuit Corinthiorum iste defectus, per præsentiam Stephanæ, Fortunati, & Achaici, ut præsentiam Apostolicam statūs ecclesiæ illic non requireret amplius.
units.tr: Since what was lacking to you for the progress of good, they themselves have supplied, and because he rejoiced at this progress, the Apostle adds: "for they have refreshed my spirit, and yours, by the gain of good." These interpreters understand ὑστέρημα not as the Apostle's longing, by which he missed the presence of the Corinthians, but as the Corinthians' deficiency, in which they fell short in the cause of piety; or else as the Apostle's absence, whose presence the Corinthian church needed, and which these three men supplied by their presence. But if the Apostle had meant this, he would have spoken more correctly not in the past tense, "have supplied," but in the present, "may supply." For when he was writing this, that deficiency of the Corinthians had not yet been so fully made good by the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus that he no longer required the Apostle's presence there for the state of the church.

units.la: QVONIAM, inquit, id quod mihi deerat uestri hi suppleuerunt.
units.tr: Because, he says, what was lacking to me in you, these men have supplied.

units.la: Obseruemus hic uere charitatis ingeniū, nō in eo tātū, qd præsentiā ecclesiæ Apost. quá in Christo genuerat, tàtopere desiderauit: sed in eo quoq;, qd in tribus uiris, qui ex illa ad se uenerant; totam complectitur, illorumq; aduentū perinde exhilaratur, ac si cū istis uenissent reliqui oēs. Locū habet hic charitatis affectus, ubi regnat idē spiritus, & cor est unum & anima una. Ibi in uno ecclesiæ membro, tota ecclesia suscipitur ac repræsentatur, præsertim cum ab illa sit missum.
units.tr: Let us notice here the true nature of charity: he not only longed greatly for the presence of the church which he had begotten in Christ, but he also embraced in these three men, who had come to him from that church, the whole of it, and was cheered by their arrival just as if all the rest had come with them. Here the affection of charity has its place, where the same Spirit reigns, and there is one heart and one soul. There, in one member of the church, the whole church is received and represented, especially since that member has been sent by it.

units.la: REFOCILLAVERVNT enim meū spiritum, inquit, ac uestrū. Rursus nō erat in præterito, Refocillauerūt: sed in præsenti dicēdum, Refocillant enim meū spiritū ac uestrū, si quo sensu uolunt alij, esset hęc dicta. Dixit se gaudere super aduentu Stephanæ, & Fortunati, & Achaici, ppterea quod illi defectū Corinthiorum præsentia sua suppleuerint. Iā huius quoque ratione reddens, dicit, Refocillauerunt. n. meum spiritum ac uestrum. Sic exponit, quō illi defectum ipsorum suppleuerint, refocillādo uidelicet utrunq; & suum & ipsorum spiritum. Fatigatus fuerat ipsius spiritus desiderio fidelium ecclesiæ Corinthiacæ. Consimili modo fatigatus fuerat spiritus illorū desiderio ipsius tanquam Apostoli ac parentis ipsorum, cuius præsentia ægre carebat. Hac utrorumq; fatigatione tres hi uiri aduētu & præsentia sua sustulerunt, atq; ita spiritus ipsorum refocillarunt. Sicut. n. spiritum Pauli cum ad ipsum uenissent, & ecclesiam Corinthiorū repræsentarent: ita illorum spiritum cum à Paulo ad ipsos essent reuersi, refocillarūt. Nam ut ipsi quodāmodo in tribus hisce uiris ad Paulum, ita Paulus uicisim in illis ad ipsos uenit, atq; ita est utrorunq; spiritus uirorum istorum legatione uel ultronea profectione refocillatus.
units.tr: "For they have refreshed my spirit," he says, "and yours." Again, it is not written in the past tense, "they refreshed," but should be said in the present, "they refresh my spirit and yours," if the words are to be taken in the sense that others want. He said that he rejoiced at the arrival of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because by their presence they had supplied the Corinthians' lack. Now, giving the reason for this too, he says, "for they have refreshed my spirit and yours." So he explains how they supplied the lack of the Corinthians: by refreshing both his spirit and theirs. His spirit had been worn out by longing for the faithful of the Corinthian church, and in a similar way their spirit had been worn out by longing for him, as their apostle and father, whose presence they sorely lacked. These three men relieved the weariness of both sides by their coming and their presence, and so refreshed their spirits. Just as, when they came to Paul, they represented the Corinthian church to him, so, when they returned from Paul to them, they refreshed their spirit. For just as they came to Paul in these three men, so Paul in turn came to them through these men, and so each spirit was refreshed by the mission, or the voluntary journey, of these men.

units.la: REFOCILLAVERVNT enim, inquit, spiritum meū. In Græco est ἀνέπαυσαν γάρ. i. denuo quiescere fecerunt. Vbi animo fatigato datur quietis insterstitiū, per laboris uel ablationē, uel alleuationē, ἀνάπαυσις dicitur. Hoc genere quietis refocillabatur spiritus Pauli p aduentum Stephanę, Fortunati & Achaici. Nā illorum presentia etsi nō in uniuersum auferebatur desideriū ecclesię Corinthiorū, quo spiritū ipsius fatigabatur, nonihil tamē reuelabatur. Sic refocillatur in hac uita spiritus piorū, à quib. etsi non auferuntur labores quib. diuina dispositione exercetur: datis tn subinde interstitijs reuelatur, ne prsus concidant, donec tepus adueniat, quo plena & indefineti quiete potiatur, requiescantq; à laborib. suis in sempiternum. Sustinebat spiritus Apostoli solicitudine omniū ecclesiarū. Huius molestia non auferebatur in uniuersum per aduentū trium istorū uirorū, sed ex parte & ad tepus releuabatur. Et tn dicit illos refocillasse suū spiritum. Intellige, ex parte. Sic sunt coparatę refocillatio nes piorum, quibus in hac uita recreantur.
units.tr: "For they have refreshed," he says, "my spirit." In Greek it is ἀνέπαυσαν γάρ, that is, "they caused it to rest again." Where a wearied mind is given a pause from toil, either by the lifting of the burden or by its easing, it is called ἀνάπαυσις. By this kind of rest the spirit of Paul was refreshed through the coming of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus. For although their presence did not wholly remove the longing of the Corinthian church, by which his spirit was worn down, it did in some measure lighten it. So in this life the spirit of the godly is refreshed: although the labours by which they are exercised under divine providence are not taken away, yet from time to time pauses are granted, so that they do not utterly collapse, until the time comes when they will possess full and unending rest, and will rest from their labours for ever. The spirit of the Apostle bore the anxiety of all the churches. The distress of this was not removed altogether by the coming of these three men, but was lightened in part and for a time. And yet he says that they refreshed his spirit. Understand: in part. Such are the refreshments of the godly by which they are revived in this life.

units.la: AGNOSCITE itaq; huiusmodi, inquit. Hic non est ἐπιγινώσκειν in Græco, sed γινώσκειν, qd nō simpliciter nosse, sed agnoscere significat, quēadmodum filius à patre, frater à fratre, herus à seruo, &c. agnoscitur. Hortatur igitur Corinthios, ut agnoscāt tales fratres pro suis, habeantq; illos in precio. Rursus uero cauēs, ne priuato erga illos affectu ob id motus qd ad se uenerāt hæc scribat, nō dicit, Agnoscite illos: sed agnoscite igitur eos qui sūt eiusmodi. Hoc est, qui seipsos ordinarunt ad ministrandū sanctis, atq; ita cooperantur, & collaborant in opere dni, syncere cum erga Christū ipsum, tn erga illius fideles & ministros affecti.
units.tr: "Acknowledge, therefore, such men," he says. Here the Greek is not ἐπιγινώσκειν but γινώσκειν, which means not simply to know but to acknowledge, just as a son is acknowledged by his father, a brother by a brother, a master by a servant, and so on. He therefore urges the Corinthians to acknowledge such brothers as their own and to hold them in honour. But being careful, lest he seem to write these things out of private affection because they had come to him, he does not say "acknowledge them," but "acknowledge therefore those who are of this kind." That is, those who have devoted themselves to serving the saints, and so cooperate and labour in the work of the Lord, being sincerely disposed both towards Christ himself and towards his faithful and ministers.

units.la: Quid ergo faciendum erga eos qui nō sunt eiusmodi? Si ecclesia habeat pastores & doctores insynceros, & nec Christo, nec fidelibus ipsius fideles: agnoscetne eos pro ueris pastoribus ac doctoribus? Absit. Quis petat ab ouib. ut agnoscant lupum pro pastore? Quis à pio, ut impium agnoscat pro fratre?
units.tr: What then should be done with those who are not of this kind? If a church has ministers and teachers who are insincere, and who are faithful neither to Christ nor to his faithful, will it acknowledge them as true ministers and teachers? Far from it. Who would ask sheep to acknowledge a wolf as their shepherd? Who would ask a godly man to acknowledge an ungodly one as a brother?

units.la: Salutant uos ecclesiæ Asiæ. Salutant uos in dno multū Aquila &Priscilla, cū ea quæ in dno est ipsorum ecclesia. Salutant uos fratres oēs. Salutate inuicē osculo sācto. Salutatio mea mau Pauli.
units.tr: The churches of Asia salute you. Aquila and Priscilla salute you much in the Lord, together with the church that is in their house. All the brothers salute you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. The salutation of me, Paul, with my own hand.

units.la: Claudit Epistolā salutationib. p more, quo scribimus amicis. Est enim officiū salutandi amicitiæ symbolū. Qui nanq; salutat amicum, quid illi apprecatur aliud q salute & oīs generis felicitate, cupiens eū semp esse saluum & felicem? At id demum ueri est amici affectus.
units.tr: He closes the letter with greetings, as is the custom when we write to friends. For the duty of greeting is a token of friendship. For who greets a friend without wishing him nothing but health and every kind of happiness, desiring that he always be safe and happy? That is truly the feeling of a friend.

units.la: SALVTANT uos, inquit, ecclesię Asię. Videntur hæc uerba habere argumetum eius sententiæ, qua iudicatur hāc esse ab Apostolo Epistolā scriptam Ephesi, quæ metropolis erat Asiæ. Quò potest accōmodari & illud quod sequitur: Salutant uos in dño multum Aquila & Priscilla, cum ea quæ in domo est ipsorum ecclesia. Illi nāq; cum Corinthi antea habitarent, Paulum hospitio acceperant, & postea cū illo Ephesum usq; migrauerāt, ibiq; manserāt, sicuti uidere est Act. 18. Iam cum hic dicit, Salutant uos in dño multum Aquila & Priscilla, cū ea quæ in domo est ipsorum ecclesia: innue-
units.tr: "The churches of Asia salute you," he says. These words seem to support the opinion that this letter was written by the Apostle at Ephesus, which was the metropolis of Asia. The following also fits this view: "Aquila and Priscilla salute you much in the Lord, together with the church that is in their house." For they had earlier lived at Corinth, had received Paul into their home, and afterwards had migrated with him as far as Ephesus, and had stayed there, as may be seen in Acts 18. Now when he says here, "Aquila and Priscilla salute you much in the Lord, together with the church that is in their house," he hints that

units.la: reuidetur, ibi hanc se scripsisse Epistolam, ubi Aquila & Priscilla morabantur. Et hoc sentiens uulgatus interpres, adiecit, apud quos & hospitor. Et Chrysostomus licet hoc in textu non legat, nec in Græcis exemplaribus habeatur, idem tamen sentiēs dicit, apud eos enim manebat.
units.tr: it is evident that he wrote this letter there, where Aquila and Priscilla were staying. The Vulgate translator, perceiving this too, added "with whom I also lodge." And Chrysostom, although he does not read this in the text, nor is it found in the Greek copies, nevertheless holding the same view, says, "for he was staying with them."

units.la: SALVTANT uos inquit, ecclesiæ Asiæ. Generaliorem salutationem, ut quæ potioris erat momenti, præmisit. Magnum est, si frater fratrem salutet ex animo, ac uera charitate ,psequatur in dño. Maius tamen est, si sic amanter complectentur ecclesiæ ecclesias, idq; non unius tantum & eiusdem nationis, quod forsan eiusdē poterit fieri amore patriæ ac linguę: sed & aliarum atque aliarum regionum ac nationum, ut si ecclesiæ Germanicæ diligant ex animo Gallicas, Italicas, Anglicanas, Hispanicas, propter Christum, & hæ mutuo diligunt aliæ alias.
