Hanc communem & generalem ἐκκλησίαν unius & eiusdem fidei in Christū pro fesio, eadem sacramenti obsignato, eadem sub capite Christo incorporatio, & quæ per eundem est spiritum regeneratio ac moderatio requirit. Qualis qualis illa tn temporis fuerit, id certum est, propterea generalem hāc ecclesiarum salutationem poni ab Apostolo, ut admoneat ecclesias omnes, q debeāt amanter inter se affici & coniungi, siquidem non in speciem tantum, & solo titulo, sed ueraciter pro Christi uolunt haberi ecclesijs. Hoc agebat ac molie batur diligētissime Apostolus Christi, doctor Gentium, pro solicitudine, quam erga omnes Christi ecclesias gerebat in pectore, ut illas in ter se mutuę charitatis & concordię spiritu cō glutinaret.
units.tr: "Salute you," he says, "the churches of Asia." He put the more general greeting first, since it was of greater importance. It is a great thing when a brother greets a brother from the heart and follows him with true love in the Lord. It is greater still when churches embrace churches so lovingly, and not only those of one and the same nation, which may happen through a shared love of country and language, but also those of other and yet other regions and nations: as when German churches sincerely love the French, Italian, English and Spanish churches for Christ's sake, and these in turn love one another. This common and general church [ἐκκλησίαν] of one faith in Christ's confession, one sealed sacrament, one incorporation under Christ the head, and the one regeneration and governance through the same Spirit requires such love. Whatever the state of the times was, this much is certain: the Apostle placed this general greeting to the churches so as to admonish all churches that they ought to be lovingly disposed and joined to one another, since they wish to be held churches of Christ not in appearance only and by title alone, but truly. This the Apostle of Christ, the teacher of the Gentiles, was doing and striving to do most diligently, out of the concern he bore in his heart for all the churches of Christ, so that he might bind them together in the spirit of mutual love and concord.

units.la: Nec impediri ab hoc studio uolebat ecclesias Asiæ, per ea quę in ecclesia Corinthiorum tam multa culpabiliter fiebant, quo minus illā salutarent in dno. Hodie uidemus quarūdam ecclesiarum magistros usq; adeo alienos esse ab hoc Apostoli studio, ut in colloquijs, ad cociliatione ecclesiarum institutis, primā actionem condemnandis ecclesijs dari uelint, & ut detur improbe contendant, quas tn nec uiderunt, nec uel à limine salutarunt unquam, idq; propter unius dogmatis in sensu uariatione. Si hoscē magistros habuisset Apostolus in ecclesijs Asiæ, nunquam illos inducere, ut ecclesiam Corinthiorum salutarent in domino, & cohibere potuisset, ne diris eam deuoueret ac Satanæ traderent.
units.tr: Nor did he want the churches of Asia to be hindered from this zeal by the many faults committed in the Corinthian church, so that they would not greet it in the Lord. Today we see teachers of some churches so alien to this zeal of the Apostle that at conferences held to reconcile churches they want the first business to be the condemnation of churches, and they stubbornly contend that this should be done against churches which they have neither seen nor ever greeted, even from the threshold, and all on account of a difference in the sense of a single doctrine. If the Apostle had had such teachers in the churches of Asia, he would never have brought them to greet the Corinthian church in the Lord, and he could not have restrained them from cursing it and handing it over to Satan.

units.la: SALVTANT uos in dño multū Aquila & Priscilla, inquit, cū ea quæ in domo est ipsorum ecclesia. Erat hic Aquila ex Ebræis Christianus, genere Pōticus. Roma cū uxore sua inter alios Iudæos à Claudio eiectę uenerat Corinthum. In hunc inciderat Paulus cum uenisset Corinthū, & quoniam eiusdē erat artificij, mā ferat apud eū. Artificium aūt illius erat, texere tabernacula. Postea cū Corintho discederet, habuit illū & uxorem eius Priscillā in comitatu, Ephesum usq;, ubi substiterūt hi duo, ac pedem dem fixerunt. Reuersus aliquanto post Ephesum, ut probabile est, denuo factus est illorum hospes, causamq; praesentia sua dedit, ut in illorum domo subinde colligeretur ecclesia fidelium Christi. Iam cum esset apud illos, & Epistolà hác scriberet, utiq; uolentib. ac petentibus ipsis, salvere ipsorum nomine iubet ecclesiam Corinthi, cuius aliquado pars fuerant, cum Corinthi morarentur. Et ut singulare illorum erga eà ecclesiam exprimat dilectionis affectu, nó simpliciter dicit, Salutát uos Aquila & Priscilla: sed, Salutát uos in dño multú Aquila & Priscilla. Quauis essent illi ex Iudeis credentes, usq; adeo tñ non auersabantur ecclesiá ex Gentib. congregatá, sicuti faciebant quàmplurimi fideles ex Iudaeis, praesertim qui adhuc erant in Iudaea, ut illá in domino non leuiter, sed multum amarent, & ex animo saluam esse cuperent, atq; ita multum illi salutis apprecarentur. Sic erant uidelicet à Paulo gentium Apostolo instituti.
units.tr: "Aquila and Priscilla greet you much in the Lord," he says, "with the church that is in their house." This Aquila was a Christian of the Hebrews, a Pontic by birth. He had come to Corinth from Rome with his wife, among other Jews expelled by Claudius. Paul fell in with him when he came to Corinth, and since they were of the same trade, he stayed with him. Their craft was making tents. Afterward, when Paul left Corinth, he took Aquila and his wife Priscilla with him as far as Ephesus, where these two settled and made their home. Paul returned to Ephesus some time later, as is likely, and again became their guest, and by his presence he gave occasion for the faithful of Christ to gather from time to time in their house. Now, while he was with them and writing this letter, at their own wish and request, he bids the church of Corinth be greeted in their name, since they had once been part of it while they lived at Corinth. To express their singular affection of love toward that church, he does not simply say, "Aquila and Priscilla greet you," but "Aquila and Priscilla greet you much in the Lord." Although they were believers from the Jews, they were nonetheless not so averse to the church gathered from the Gentiles as very many believers from the Jews were, especially those still in Judea. Rather, they loved it not lightly but greatly in the Lord, and wished from their hearts that it be safe, and so prayed for it much salvation. Thus had they been instructed by Paul, the apostle of the Gentiles.

units.la: CVM ea, inqt, quae est in domo ipsorum ecclesia. Siue intelligas de domesticis, siue de peregrinis & hospitib. siue de indigenis fidelib. qui in domo illorum cóuentus sacros facere consueuerint, egregiá illorum commendatione hac particula exprimit, quod & Ro. 16. fecit dicés: Itē salutate quae in domo est illorum ecclesiam. Ergo ecclesia nó debem9 amplitudine ac splendore templorum, ac multitudine fidelium metiri, quádoquidé unus domus familia Christo credes, uel hospites ppter Christū domo accepti, uel talis credentiū paucitas, q priuatis aedib. accipi posit, ecclesiá constituát. Sed hac de re in Locis nostris annotauimus, titulo de ecclesia.
units.tr: "With the church that is in their house," he says. Whether you understand by this their household members, or guests and strangers, or native believers who had been accustomed to hold sacred assemblies in their house, he expresses their outstanding commendation by this phrase, as he also did in Rom. 16., saying: "Likewise greet the church that is in their house." Therefore the church must not be measured by the size and splendour of buildings, or by the multitude of the faithful. One household family believing in Christ, or guests received into a house for Christ's sake, or such a small number of believers as can be received in a private dwelling, constitutes a church. But we have noted this matter in our Loci, under the title on the church.

units.la: SALVTANT uos fratres omnes. Q.d. Nó ij tantum qui sunt in domo Aquilæ & Priscillæ, quos cognouistis: sed & caeteri fratres oës, facie uobis & nominibus ignoti, salutē uobis in dño apprecátur. Nemo ex omnib. est, qui non optime uobis uelit in domino. Cláculú inuitat eos ad studiū concordię, dū à fratrib. omnibus absq; discrimine salutari eos scribit, ut & ipsi interse tanquam fratres unanimes sint in Christo, & fraternæ dilectionis mutuo affectu praediti, quo possint erga reliquos etiá fideles amãter amplectedos & in domino salutandos esse concordes. Etenim qui secū disidet ipsi, quomodo unanimi spiritu cæteros in domino fratres cóplecti poterūt. Hoc innuens subiungit:
units.tr: "All the brothers greet you." That is: not only those who are in the house of Aquila and Priscilla, whom you know, but all the other brothers, unknown to you by face and name, pray salvation for you in the Lord. There is no one among them all who does not wish you well in the Lord. By this he invites them to a zeal for concord, since he writes that they are greeted by all the brothers without distinction, so that they too among themselves may be brothers of one mind in Christ, endowed with the mutual affection of brotherly love, by which they may also embrace the other faithful lovingly and agree in greeting them in the Lord. For how can someone who is at odds with himself embrace others as brothers in the Lord with a united spirit? Signifying this, he adds:

units.la: SALVTATE uos inuicé, inquit, osculo sancto. Nó precipit simpliciter, ut alij alios osculetur, cum hoc aliàs ex more facere soleret: sed ut quod faciebant, facerent sancte. Sanctū osculum est, quod fit nec prophano affectu, nec externa simulatione absq; dilectiónis ueritate, sed religiose & ueraciter propter concordiá fidei quæ sit in Christo. Hoc uti non possunt discordes & contentiosi sectarij, sed ij tantum qui unanimes sunt in domino. Cum ergo dicit: Salutate uos inuicem osculo sancto, omnino requirit mutuam inter ipsos dilectionem & concordiam. Hac enim obtinēte, necesse est ut studium sectarum languescat, & tandem è medio
units.tr: "Greet one another," he says, "with a holy kiss." He does not simply command that some kiss others, since they were in the habit of doing this anyway by custom, but that they do sincerely what they were doing. It is a holy kiss which is given neither with a profane affection nor with outward pretence and without the truth of love, but devoutly and truly, for the sake of the concord of faith which is in Christ. Quarrelsome and contentious sectarians cannot use it; only those who are of one mind in the Lord can. Therefore, when he says, "Greet one another with a holy kiss," he wholly requires mutual love and concord among them. For when this holds, the zeal of the sects must necessarily wane and at last be taken out of the way.

units.la: tollatur. Pro osculo, quod Graecis est φίλημα, dilectionis uidelicet & amicitiae symbolum, pro consuetudine nostrarum nationum coniunctione dexterarum inter salutandum táquam societatis signo, utimur. Verū multo redimendū esset, plus esse in hoc signo ueritatis, quàm simulationis.
units.tr: In place of the kiss, which in Greek is the philema [φίλημα], the symbol of love and friendship, we use, according to the custom of our nations, the joining of right hands in greeting as a sign of fellowship. But it would be well worth the effort that there be more truth than pretence in this sign.

units.la: SALVTATIO mea manu Pauli, inquit. Duo facit. Primum salutat éos & ipse. Deinde salutatione hanc, non ponit per amanuensem, quo utebatur, sed suapte manu, quo & certi de illa ac simul de tota Epistola essent, & omnis occasio impostoribus adimeretur, nequid in il la mutarent & suppositititam aliquam falsam & corruptam sub nomine Pauli ecclesijs obtruderent. Et hac cautione usus est non in hac modo, sed & in omnibus alijs Epistolis suis, sicuti in posteriore ad Thessalonicenses uidere licet; ubi sic dicit: Salutatio mea manu Pauli, quod est signum in omni Epistola. Sic scribo:
units.tr: "My greeting with the hand of Paul," he says. He does two things. First, he greets them himself. Then he does not have this greeting written by the amanuensis he used, but writes it in his own hand, so that they might be certain both of it and of the whole letter, and every opportunity be taken from impostors, lest they alter something in it and foist on the churches some false and corrupt supposititious writing under Paul's name. He used this caution not only in this letter but in all his other letters as well, as can be seen in the later letter to the Thessalonians, where he says: "My greeting with the hand of Paul, which is the sign in every letter. So I write:"

units.la: Sí quis non diligít domínū Iesum, sit anathema maranatha.
units.tr: If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema maranatha.

units.la: Cum hæc manu sua scriberet, & impostoribus occasionem impostura adimeret, cogitare cœpit de mala illa radice, unde omnis in ecclesia Corinthiorum hypocrisis, impostura, syncericitatis corruptio, pacisq; & unitatis dissolutio nascebatur. Eam sentiebat esse cor non rectum ac syncerum erga dominum Iesum, quale erat pseudapostolorum, qui cum essent Apostoli non Christi, sed Satanæ transfigurabant se in Apostolos Christi, quae sua erat ipsorum, non quae Christi quaerentes. Horum itaq; maliciam & perfidiam perstringens, imò condemnans dicit:
units.tr: When he was writing these things with his own hand, and was taking away from the impostors the occasion for their imposture, he began to think about that evil root from which all hypocrisy, deceit, corruption of sincerity, and dissolution of peace and unity in the Church of the Corinthians sprang. He judged it to be a heart not right and sincere toward the Lord Jesus, such as was that of the false apostles, who, though they were apostles not of Christ but of Satan, transformed themselves into apostles of Christ, seeking what was their own and not what was Christ's. Therefore, censuring and indeed condemning their malice and treachery, he says:

units.la: SI quis non diligit dominum Iesum, sit anathema.] Quasi dicat: Si quis corde est adeo perverso ac malicioso, ut alienus cum sit à dilectione domini Iesu, nihilo tamen minus fingat ac simulet se illum impense diligere, illiusq; discipulus & Apostolus haberi uelit, sit ille uobis anathema, potius quàm Christi uel discipulus uel Apostolus.
units.tr: "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema." As if he were saying: If anyone is so perverse and malicious in heart that, though he is a stranger to love for the Lord Jesus, he nonetheless pretends and feigns to love him intensely, and wishes to be regarded as his disciple and apostle, let him be anathema to you, rather than a disciple or apostle of Christ.

units.la: Vide autem quàm moderate & caute nó exprimat eorū nomina, quos tamen dubio, pcul tales esse sciebat, sed per sententiā hypotheticā dicit: Si quis nō diligit dominū Iesū, sit anathema. Moderationis huius erat ratio, ut parceret non ipsis pseudapostolis ac seductoribus, sed ijs qui ab illis seducti pedebant, ac nominibus eorum usq; adeo erat addicti, ut execratione illorum tā graué & horrendam ferre nequirent, ac citius à toto Christianismo relapsuri, q illá patienter laturi uiderētur. Horū rationem habes abstinet quidé à specificatione impostorū, uerū ea moderatione, ut interim radicé mali considerandā illis & animaduertédā exponat, ut in quocunq; illā deprehenderint, sua ipsorū conscientia impulsi damnet illū, & pro anathemate habeant & ipsi. Hac prudentia & moderatione Apostolici spiritus utēdum est in illis ecclesijs præcipue, in quib. obtinent studia sectarū, quo plebs seducta ipsum malum agnoscat prius, q̃ ad damnandum impostores cogatur, quos ad huc ipsissimos putat esse Christi apostolos.
units.tr: Note how moderately and cautiously he does not name those whom he nevertheless knew without doubt to be such, but speaks by a hypothetical sentence: "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema." The reason for this moderation was that he spared not the false apostles and seducers themselves, but those who were led astray by them and were so attached to their names that they could not bear such a grave and dreadful execration of them, and would sooner seem likely to fall away from all Christianity than patiently endure it. You have the reason: he refrains indeed from specifying the impostors, but with such moderation that he sets out the root of the evil for them to consider and notice, so that, wherever they detect it, being moved by their own conscience they may condemn it and hold it as anathema themselves. This prudence and moderation of the apostolic spirit is to be used especially in those churches in which the zeal of sects prevails, so that the misled common people may first recognise the evil itself, before they are compelled to condemn the impostors, whom they still think to be the very apostles of Christ.

units.la: Hoc sensu puto, intelligendum esse quod dicit: Si quis non diligit dominum Iesum, sit anathema. Neq; enim loquitur de Iudeis aut Gentibus incredulis, & à professione Christiani no minis alienis, quorum nemo dominum Iesum diligit, & tamen hac anathematis sententia feriendi non sunt ab Apostolo, qui de illis qui foris sunt, iudicium sibi non sumit.
units.tr: In this sense, I think, what he says must be understood: "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema." For he is not speaking of Jews or unbelieving Gentiles, who are strangers to the profession of the Christian name and none of whom loves the Lord Jesus; yet these are not to be struck with this sentence of anathema by the Apostle, who does not take to himself judgment over those who are outside.

units.la: SI quis non diligit dominũ Iesum, inquit. Considerandũ hic est, quæ sit nota dilectionis Christi, unde cognoscantur veri illius amici, fideles, discipuli, & ministri. Ea nõ est quærenda in verbis, aut specie pietatis externa & fallaci, sed in vera verborũ Christi obseruantia. Hæc enim ipse nobis proponit dicês: Si quis diligit me, sermonẽ meũ seruabit. Itẽ: Si diligitis me, præcepta mea seruata. Et: Vos amici mei estis, si feceritis quæ ego præcepi uobis. Ergo obseruatia uerborũ Christi, arguit animũ illius amãtem. Contrà, neglectus & cõtemptus illorum hominem arguit à dilectione Christi alienum. Quod si accesserit hypocrysis, quæstus & nũdi natio sub nomine Christi præsumpta, plane dignus est anathemate, tanquam subdolus, impius, & maliciosus impostor.
units.tr: "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus," he says. Here we must consider what the mark of love for Christ is, by which his true friends, faithful ones, disciples and ministers are recognised. It is not to be sought in words, or in an outward and deceptive show of piety, but in the true observance of Christ's words. For he himself sets this before us, saying: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word." Likewise: "If you love me, keep my commandments." And: "You are my friends, if you do what I command you." Therefore observance of Christ's words shows the soul that loves him. On the contrary, neglect and contempt of them show a man to be a stranger to the love of Christ. But if hypocrisy is added, and gain and display are pursued under the name of Christ, he is plainly worthy of anathema, as a crafty, impious and malicious impostor.

units.la: Quid est autẽ quod nõ dicit, Si qs non diligit Deũ: sed, Si quis nõ dilifiit dñm Iesum? An non refert, Deũ ne diligamus uel secus, modo diligamus dñm Iesum? Respondeo. Dñm Iesum B nemo diligit sine dilectione Dei patris. Filium enim quomodo diligemus ut filiũ ac dominũ, nisi in illo diligam̃ & patrẽ, à quo datus est nobis filius? Apost. aut quoniã singulare malicia & impostura pseudapostolorũ pstringere & execrari uoluit, q se in apostolos Christi diaboli ca impostura trãsfigurabant, cũ corde essent ergo illũ nõ recto: notater dilectione dñi Iesu adduxit in medium, in qua deprehenderetur ueri ministri Christi, & secũdũ q iudicaretur de falsis. Nõ enim hic tã impietatis erga Deum in genere, q impostura pseudapostolorũ sub nomine Christi præsumptæ notam exprimere uoluit.
units.tr: But why does he not say, "If anyone does not love God," but "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus"? Does it not matter whether we love God or not, provided we love the Lord Jesus? I answer: no one loves the Lord Jesus without the love of God the Father. For how shall we love the Son as Son and Lord, unless in him we love also the Father, from whom the Son was given to us? The Apostle, moreover, since he wished to strike at and curse the singular malice and imposture of the false apostles, who with a diabolical imposture transformed themselves into the apostles of Christ while their heart was not right, expressly brought forward the love of the Lord Jesus, in which the true ministers of Christ are discerned, and by which the false are judged. For he did not here wish to express a mark of impiety toward God in general, but the imposture of the false apostles presumed under the name of Christ.

units.la: SIT anathema, inquit. De uoce anathema non est ut hic dicamus. Diximus enim de illa, Ro.9. Et est aliàs admodũ nota in ecclesijs, & plus æquo usitata in concilijs ac decretis Pontificum. Laborat enim illi singulari quadam anathematizandi procliuitate, qua mox execrantur, & ab alijs pro execratis haberi uolunt omnes eos, qui non ad omnia ipsorum statua subeunda ceruices suas submittunt.
units.tr: "Let him be anathema," he says. We need not discuss the word anathema here, for we spoke of it at Romans 9. It is otherwise quite well known in the churches, and used more than enough in the councils and decrees of the Popes. For they suffer from a peculiar readiness to anathematise, by which they at once curse, and want all those who do not submit their necks to all their decrees to be held as cursed by others.

units.la: MARANATHA. De hac uoce nõ est eadẽ omniũ sentètia. Si Chaldæa est uel Syra, sonat dñs noster uenit. מרן siquidẽ. i. maran, idẽ est, quod dñs noster. Sic illud Dauidis, Non nobis dñe non nobis, in Chaldæo est, La lan marana la lan. i. non nobis domine noster non nobis, Et אתא uel אתא. i. atha: sonat, uenit. Sic Hieron. quoq; in Epistola ad Marcellam expo suit. Et hunc sequuti sunt nonnulli alij.
units.tr: MARANATHA. On this word opinions are not all the same. If it is Chaldean or Syriac, it means "our Lord comes." For מרן [maran] means "our Lord." So too that line of David, "Not to us, O Lord, not to us," is in Chaldean "La lan marana la lan," that is, "not to us, our Lord, not to us." And אתא [atha] means "comes." Jerome also explained it thus in his letter to Marcella, and several others have followed him.

units.la: Burgensis aliud sentit. Existimat accommodasse se Apostolum hoc loco mori Iudæorum, quo rebellių & cõtẽptorũ legis cõdemnationẽ trifariã exercuernnt. Primo p exclusione ecclesiæ sortio populi Dei quá nostri, excommunicationẽ uocat. Deinde p destructione ac dissipationẽ bonorũ, quá uocat חרם. Tertio p extremam maledictionẽ, cui soleni tubarum clagore denuebantur. Ad primã condenationis partẽ p tinere dicit, quod Apost. uocat anathema, ad iecundam, quod subiũgit: maran, quasi idem sit quod maheram. i. dissipatio, à uoce חרם, ad tertiam, q̃ addit, atha quá uocẽ idẽ esse uult, q̃ est שמרמתח. i. mortificatio. Et hac Burgesis opinionem sequuntur nonnulli ex recentioribus, quam ꝑbare non possum, propterea quod longius à structura uerbi huius discedit. Augustin altercatione quá habuit cũ Pascentio Arriano præsentis loci meminit ad hunc modũ: Simul utitur Græco & Syro uerbo. Si quis, inquit, nõ amat dominũ Iesum, sit anathema maranatha. Anathema Græco sermone dixit condemnatus: maranatha, donec dominus redeat.
units.tr: Burgensis thinks otherwise. He judges that the Apostle here accommodated himself to the custom of the Jews, by which they exercised a threefold condemnation of rebels and despisers of the law. First, by exclusion from the lot of the people of God, which they call excommunication, as ours do. Then, by destruction and dissipation of goods, which they call חרם [herem]. Thirdly, by the extreme curse, to which they were devoted with the solemn clamour of trumpets. He says that the word anathema which the Apostle uses pertains to the first part of the condemnation, the second part is what he adds, maran, as if it were the same as maherah, that is dissipation, from the word חרם [herem]; and to the third, which he adds, atha, he wills the same word to be what is שמרמתח [mortification]. Several of the more recent writers follow Burgensis in this opinion, which I cannot approve, because it departs too far from the structure of the word. Augustine, in the disputation he had with Pascentius the Arian, mentions the present passage in this way: "He uses at once a Greek and a Syriac word. 'If anyone,' he says, 'does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema maranatha.' He said anathema, condemned, in the Greek language; maranatha, until the Lord returns."

units.la: Placet quibusdam, מרנאתא. i. maranatha, positum esse pro מהרמתא. i. maheramatha, ut sit deductũ à uoce חרם, acidè sonet, quod dictio præcedens ἀνάθεμα. Si constaret, Chaldæis חרן per nõ idè esse quod Ebreis חרם per mem, posset probabile uideri, legendum esse, מהרגנאתא. i. maherenatha, ut sonet, perditio quæ uentura est: aut, perditio ueniens. Verum nihil hic certi inuenio, nec conuenit ut quod incertum est pro mere affirmemus. Si uspiam in scripturis מחרם pro חרם positum inueniré, ut Chaldæis מהרן esse possit idem quod Ebreis חרם, facile in hac sententiam inclinare, ut sentirem Apostolum post Græcam uocẽ anathema subiecisse Chaldæam uel Syram idem significantem, propter eos potissimum, qui ex Ebræis in Christũ credentes, imò uerius credere se simulantes, non Christum sed seipsos quærebant, & Christum uidisse se, esseq; uerorum Apostolorũ discipulos, ad hoc iactabant, ut ecclesiã scinderent ac discipulos post se traherent. Verum nusquam inuenio מחרם positum pro חרם. Ebræis sonat חרך, irá. Si מחרךuspiã poneretur in scripturis pro חרך, posset uideri maranatha positũ esse, מהרגנאתא. i. maheronatha: ut sensus sit, Si quis nõ dliligit dominũ Iesum sit anathemia irę, uel ad irá, quę uenit. Quicqd huiusmodi cogitam nihil habet certi. Quare simplicius est, ut retineamus eá expositionẽ, quę de uoce hac, ut posita est, ne litera quidẽ uel mutat uel desiderat, quá primo loco posuimus. Quid uero uoluerit sibi Apostolus, quod cum dixisset, Qui nõ diligit dominũ Iesum, sit anathema: subiecit, Dominus noster uenit. deinde quod id sermone Syriaco magis, q̃ Græco expressit, nõ adeo facile est explicare. Si legerimus. Si qs non diligit dominũ Iesum, sit anathema domini nostri qui uenit: uel, Si qs non diligit dominũ Iesum, Dominũ inquam nostrũ qui uenit, sit anathema: sensus erit, meo iudicio, nõ incommodus.
units.tr: Some are pleased that מרנאתא [maranatha] stands for מהרמתא [maheramatha], so that it is derived from the word חרם [herem], and the sense is harsh, matching the preceding word ἀνάθεμα [anathema]. If it were established that for the Chaldeans the letter ן stands for the same as ם does for the Hebrews, it might seem probable that we should read מהרגנאתא [maherenatha], so that it means destruction that is to come, or coming destruction. But I find nothing certain here, nor is it fitting that we affirm as plain fact what is uncertain. If I found anywhere in Scripture מחרם [mecherem] used for חרם [herem], so that for the Chaldeans מהרן could mean the same as the Hebrew חרם, I would easily incline to this view: that the Apostle, after the Greek word anathema, added a Chaldean or Syriac word with the same meaning, chiefly on account of those who, being Hebrews believing in Christ, or rather pretending to believe, sought not Christ but themselves, and boasted that they had seen Christ and were disciples of the true apostles, in order that they might split the church and draw disciples after themselves. But I nowhere find מחרם used for חרם. In Hebrew it means חרך [charak], burning anger. If מחרך were anywhere used in Scripture for חרך, maranatha might seem to be מהרגנאתא [maheronatha], so that the sense would be: "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema to the anger that is coming, or to anger that comes." Whatever is of this kind has nothing certain. Therefore it is simpler to retain the explanation which we placed first, which neither changes nor needs to alter a letter of the word as it stands. But what the Apostle meant in adding, after "does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema," the words "our Lord comes," and why he expressed it in Syriac rather than Greek, is not so easy to explain. If we read: "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema of our Lord who comes"; or, "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, our Lord, I say, who comes, let him be anathema," the sense will be, in my judgment, not unsuitable.

units.la: Quod si omnino exponendū est in nomina A catur, & dilectionem suam in Christo denunciat & offert dicens:
units.tr: But if it must be explained entirely as being in the nominative case, and he declares and offers his love in Christ, saying:

units.la: tiuo, id quod tamen nulla necessitas cogit, melius esse puto ut in futuro legamus, dominus noster ueniet, quàm in præterito: Dominus noster uenit. Quin etiā si legamus, Dominus noster uenit, nihil uetat, quo minus idem esse intelligamus, quod dominus noster in procinctu est, prope est, non tardat, sed ueniendo uenit: ut habeat sensum comminationis de aduentu domini breui futuro, quo retribuetur unicuiq; secundum quod gesisit in hac uita, dicetur; reprobis illis & hypocritis; Discedite à me operarij iniqui, non noui uos.
units.tr: I think it better, though no necessity compels it, to read the verb in the future, "our Lord will come," rather than in the past, "our Lord has come." Indeed, even if we read "our Lord has come," nothing prevents us from understanding it to mean that our Lord is at hand, near, not delayed, but coming by coming. It then carries a warning about the Lord's soon-future coming, when each will be repaid according to what he has done in this life, addressed to those reprobate hypocrites: "Depart from me, you workers of iniquity; I never knew you."

units.la: Quare uero Syro sit usus sermone, nō inuenio probabiliorem causam, quàm quod, ut supra dixi, clanculū hoc pacto eos pseudapostolos perstringere uoluerit, qui sub nomine Christi Euangelio regni Dei plurimum incommodabant, & quoniam Ebraei erant de Christo & apostolis, contra Apostolatum Pauli admodū gloriabantur, cum quærerent non Christum, sed seipsos. Hæc de uoce maranatha. Si cui datum est aliquid certius, adferat in medium.
units.tr: As to why he used the Syriac language, I find no more probable reason than that, as I said above, he wished to strike at those false apostles secretly in this way. Under the name of Christ, they greatly hindered the gospel of the kingdom of God, and since they were Hebrews, they boasted greatly against the apostleship of Paul concerning Christ and the apostles, seeking not Christ but themselves. So much for the word maranatha. If anyone has been given anything more certain, let him bring it forward.

units.la: Quærūt hic, liceat ne Apostolo anathemati devouere quempiā. Neq; enim dicit, erit anathema: sed ϑʹ*, id est sit anathema. Sed hac de re annotauit Petrus Martyr clarissimus in domino fraterl. Duo sunt hic consideranda. Vnū est, singularis zelus pectoris Apostolici in gloriam Christi incomparabili amore ardentis. Alterum muneris apostolici officium. Neutrum commune est fidelibus omnibus. Quare quod hic Apostolus dicit, Si quis non diligit dominum Iesum, sit anathema maranatha: siue ad Apostolici pectoris zelum, siue ad munus Apostolicum referatur, nihil habet illiciti, & tamen non est cuilibet fideli temere usurpandū. Si ex zelo Christi dictum est, deuotionem habet & execrationem: si uero ex Apostolici muneris officio, admonitionem habet ad ecclesiam fidelium de eo factam, quo debeat eos habere loco, qui cum Christum non diligant, nomen tamen illius iactant, & sub illo impostores agūt ad seducendum imperitos. Qui dominū Iesum, inquit, non diligit, qualis qualis foris apparet, & quicquid tandem iactet, sit uobis anathema. Quo sensu dictum est illud Christi: Si ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi tanquam ethnicus & publicanus.
units.tr: Here they ask whether the Apostle may devote anyone to anathema. For he does not say "he will be anathema," but ἔστω ἀνάθεμα, that is, "let him be anathema." On this matter the most distinguished Peter Martyr, in the Lord our brother, has made a note. Two things are to be considered here. One is the singular zeal of the apostolic heart, burning with incomparable love for the glory of Christ. The other is the duty of the apostolic office. Neither is common to all the faithful. Therefore, whether what the Apostle says here, "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema, maranatha," is referred to the zeal of the apostolic heart or to the apostolic office, there is nothing unlawful in it, yet it is not to be rashly claimed by any believer. If it was said from zeal for Christ, it expresses devotion and execration. If it was said from the duty of the apostolic office, it is a warning to the Church of the faithful, so that they should regard as such those who, though they do not love Christ, still boast of his name and act as impostors under it to deceive the unskilled. "Whoever does not love the Lord Jesus," he says, "whatever he may outwardly appear to be, and whatever he may boast of, let him be anathema to you." In this sense is that saying of Christ: "If he refuse to hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector."

units.la: Gratia domini Iesu Christi uobiscū. Dilectio mea cū omnib. uobis in Christo Iesu. Amen.
units.tr: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.

units.la: Separauit ab ecclesia uerorū fidelium, à gratia Christi, & à sua dilectione reprobos & impostores, qui Christum non diligebant, sed res suas sub nomine illius agebant, cum dixit: Si quis non diligit dominum Iesum, sit anathema maranatha. Post eam sententiā synceris ac ueris fidelibus ualedictionis loco & gratiam appre-
units.tr: By the words "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema, maranatha," he separated from the Church of true believers, from the grace of Christ, and from his love, the reprobate and impostors who did not love Christ but pursued their own affairs under his name. After that sentence, he offers the grace of farewell to sincere and true believers.

units.la: GRATIA domini Iesu Christi sit uobiscū; dilectio mea cum omnibus uobis in Christo Iesu.] Quod si legerimus ut est in Græco & æditione uulgata: Gratia domini Iesu Christi uobiscum, ut intelligatur uerbum substantiuum est, non habebit apprecationis, sed magis Apostolicæ annunciationis sensum. quasi dicat: Vt anathema est à Christo qui illum nō diligit, ita uos in illius estis gratia, qui & creditis in eū, & credetes diligitis. Quod Erasmus uertit: sit uobiscum, suo sensu fecit, quæ habet cum Chrysostomo commune; qui & ipse hoc apprecandi modo dictum esse sensit.
units.tr: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you; my love be with all of you in Christ Jesus." If we read it as it is in the Greek and in the common edition, "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you," so that the verb is understood as a substantive verb, it will carry not the sense of a prayer but rather of an apostolic declaration, as if he said: As he who does not love Christ is anathema, so you are in the grace of him who both believes in him and, believing, loves him. Erasmus translated it "be with you," and in doing so followed his own sense, which agrees with Chrysostom, who also thought the phrase was meant as a form of prayer.

units.la: DILECTIO mea, inquit, cū omnibus uobis. Amen.] Vide quomodo dilectionem suam gratiæ Christi cōiungat ut significet se impense diligere eos, qui sic sunt Christiani, ut non solum externæ sint professionis, sed & gratiæ illius participes:
units.tr: "My love," he says, "be with all of you." Notice how he joins his love to the grace of Christ, to signify that he loves intensely those who are Christians not only in outward profession but also as partakers of that grace.

units.la: Non est autem ociosum quod post tot ac tā graues correptiones, quibus plerosq; illorum per hanc Epistolam corripuit, hanc dilectionis suæ denunciationem in calce conclusionis uice posuit, ut intelligerent nihil esse à se sinistro affectu, sed omnia dilectionis impulsu scripta:
units.tr: It is not idle that, after so many and such grave rebukes, with which he corrected most of them throughout this Epistle, he placed this declaration of his love at the end of the conclusion, so that they might understand that nothing in it was written from ill will, but everything from the impulse of love.

units.la: Et ne uideatur aliquos tantum ex illis diligere, segregatis illis, quos alias atque alias ob causas corripuit, non dicit simpliciter, dilectio mea uobiscum: sed uniuersaliter, dilectio mea cum omnibus uobis. Sic neminem illorum excludit, & interim admonet eos retinendę unitatis, ut quemadmodum ipse omnes absq; discrimine dilectionis suæ uinculo cōplectitur, ita & ipsi omni sectarum studio abiecto unum esse uelint in domino, sesetq; mutua dilectione concorditer amplecti.
units.tr: And lest it seem that he loved only some of them, setting apart those whom he rebuked for various reasons, he does not say simply "my love be with you," but universally, "my love be with all of you." Thus he excludes none of them, and at the same time he urges them to keep unity, so that, as he embraces all of them without distinction in the bond of his love, so they too, having cast aside all party zeal, may wish to be one in the Lord and mutually embrace one another in harmony through mutual love.

units.la: Addit, in Christo: hoc est, propter Christū; quatenus estis in Christo, illiq; fideliter adhæretis. Iactat dilectionem fidelium & Pontifex Rom. ut simulet se apostolico affectum esse spiritu. At ex fructibus cognoscitur arbor. Diligit quidem, uerū ut lupus diligit oues. Et lupi ad oues uox esse potest: Dilectio mea cum omnibus uobis. At hæc dilectio non est erogatrix, sed magis deuoratrix. Apostolica dilectio impendit omnia in usus fidelium: lupina uero omnia omnium deuorat. Dicat igitur catholicus hic pastor: Dilectio mea cum omnibus uobis, omnis at è contra sit uestra pecunia mecum.
units.tr: He adds "in Christ," that is, for Christ's sake, insofar as you are in Christ and cling faithfully to him. The Roman Pontiff also boasts of the love of the faithful, pretending that he is animated by an apostolic spirit. But a tree is known by its fruits. He indeed loves, but as a wolf loves sheep. And the words "my love be with all of you" could be the voice of a wolf to the sheep. Yet this love does not dispense, but rather devours. Apostolic love spends everything for the uses of the faithful; wolfish love devours everything belonging to everyone. Let this Catholic pastor, then, say: "My love be with all of you, but on the other hand let all your money be with me."

units.la: Sit procul à nobis dilectio falsa luporum, Seruet nos potius gratia Christe tua.
units.tr: Far from us be the false love of wolves; may your grace, O Christ, rather keep us safe.

units.tr: Argument of the Second Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians.

units.la: QVAM non in prophanis modo sed & religionis ac fidei negocijs res sit solliciti plena timo-ris amorisque in aliis Apostoli literis tum in his potissimum apparet, quas alteras ad Co-rinthiorum ecclesiam impense sibi dilectam scripsit, in qua singularem quandam & uere Apostolicam solicitudinem spirant omnia, ut ubique paternum pectus deprehendere lice-at non modo ubi mitis ac blandus, quos priore epistola contristauerat uersus uelis consola-tur & erigit, sed & ubi seuerus & grauis Apostolicae potestatis experimentum impoenitë-tibus & contemptoribus comminatur. Et hinc est uarietas illa τῶν παθῶν, quae ab initio e-pistolae ad calcem usq; occurrit.
units.tr: That the Apostle was anxious, full of fear and love, not only in worldly affairs but also in matters of religion and faith, appears in his other letters, and above all in these, which he wrote a second time to the Corinthian church, dear to him in the highest degree. Everything in it breathes a singular and truly apostolic solicitude, so that a fatherly heart can be discerned everywhere: not only where he gently and kindly consoles and raises up those whom he had saddened in the earlier letter, but also where, severely and gravely, he threatens with a proof of apostolic authority those who are impenitent and despise him. And hence comes that variety of feelings (τῶν παθῶν) which appears from the beginning of the letter to its end.

units.la: Causae uero, quur denuo ad illos scriberet, praeter generalem ecclesiarum solicitudinem speciales erant ista.
units.tr: The reasons why he wrote to them again, apart from the general concern for the churches, were these particular ones.

units.la: 1 Prima, quod Apostolatum suum propter crebras & prope extremas afflictiones, praesertim in Asia studijs impiorum suscitatas, despicabilem fieri sentiret, quod malum mox initio epistolae amoliendum iudicauit, quod et capite quarto & quinto facit.
units.tr: 1. The first was that he perceived his apostleship to be held in contempt on account of the frequent and almost deadly afflictions stirred up by the schemes of the impious, especially in Asia. He judged this evil to be removed at once at the beginning of the letter, which he does in chapters four and five.

units.la: 2 Secunda ex eo nascebatur, quod in priore epistola uenturum se ad illos pollicitus fuerat, & tamen alijs impeditus promissa non praestiterat. Hic leuitatis erat occurrendum suspicioni, quod facit in calce capitis primi, et initio secundi.
units.tr: 2. The second arose from the fact that in the earlier letter he had promised to come to them, yet, hindered by other matters, he had not kept his promise. Here it was necessary to meet the suspicion of fickleness, which he does at the end of the first chapter and the beginning of the second.

units.la: 3 Tertiam pepererat cura seruandi peccatoris, quem propter scortationem e communione fidelium eiectum Satanae ad interitam carnis Epistola praecedente tradiderat. Hunc igitur resipiscentem recipit, ne pereat, quem antea peccantem damnauerat.
units.tr: 3. The third was prompted by his care for saving a sinner whom, because of fornication, he had cast out of the fellowship of the faithful and delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh in the previous letter. Therefore he receives him back now that he has repented, so that he may not perish, whom he had earlier condemned for sinning.

units.la: 4 Quarta erat ex eo quod obseruantiam legis nonnulli contra Noui testamenti gratiam inducere moliebantur. Ad reprimendam hanc pestem Noui testamenti gratiam & ministerium, supra obseruantiam & ministerium legis extollit capite 3. & 4.
units.tr: 4. The fourth was that some were striving to introduce the observance of the law against the grace of the New Testament. To suppress this plague, he exalts the grace and ministry of the New Testament above the observance and ministry of the law, in chapters three and four.

units.la: 5 Quinta generalior ex eo erat, quod nonnulli sibijpsis gratiam Noui testamenti studijs carnis inanem reddebant. Hos ad uerae pietatis studia obsecrando hortatur, ne tam insignem gratiam in uacuum recepisse deprehendantur, simulq; auocat a consortio impiorum & infidelium. Facit hoc cap. 6.
units.tr: 5. The fifth, of a more general kind, was that some were rendering the grace of the New Testament empty for themselves by pursuing the works of the flesh. He exhorts these, by entreaty, to the pursuit of true godliness, so that they may not be found to have received so great a grace in vain; at the same time he calls them away from fellowship with the impious and unbelieving. He does this in chapter six.

units.la: 6 Sextam ex eo uidebat esse, quod priore illos Epistola admodum contristauerat. Quare ut hunc illorum mo-rorem leniat ac mitiget, utilitatem illius exponit. quod facit cap. 7.
units.tr: 6. The sixth he saw arose from the fact that by the earlier letter he had greatly saddened them. Therefore, in order to soothe and mitigate their grief, he sets out the usefulness of that letter. This he does in chapter seven.

units.la: 7 Septima erat collationis in usus sanctorum faciendae, qua de in Epistola priore monuerat. De hac denuo mo-niturus usurpat & proponit illis exemplum ecclesiarum Macedoniae. Facit hoc cap. 8. & 9.
units.tr: 7. The seventh was the making of a collection for the use of the saints, about which he had advised them in the earlier letter. Now, about to advise them again on this, he uses and sets before them the example of the churches of Macedonia. He does this in chapters eight and nine.

units.la: 8 Octava erat ex contemptu potestatis Apostolicae, quam ut asserat, obsecrat eos ne velint authoritatem ac po-testatem praesentis sui, quam habeat in Christo, per contemptum experiri. cap. 10.
units.tr: 8. The eighth arose from contempt for his apostolic authority. Since he asserts it, he entreats them not to wish to test, through contempt, the authority and power which he, present among them, has in Christ. Chapter ten.

units.la: 9 Nonam obtrudebant pseudapostoli. Contra illos luctatur, Apostolatum suum asserens, & afflictiones pro Christo toleratas, ac singulares reuelationes commemorans. Facit hoc cap. 11. & 12.
units.tr: 9. The ninth was thrust upon him by the false apostles. He struggles against them, asserting his apostleship, and recalling the afflictions endured for Christ and his singular revelations. He does this in chapters eleven and twelve.

units.la: 10 Vltimam offerebant impoenitentes, quos nec prior Epistola, nec aduentus Timothei ac Titi correxerant. His se ubi uenerit ad eos, haudquaquam parsurum minatur. cap. ult.
units.tr: 10. The last was presented by the impenitent, whom neither the earlier letter nor the coming of Timothy and Titus had corrected. He threatens that when he comes to them he will by no means spare them. Last chapter.

units.la: His itaq; de causis motus Epistolam hanc paternorum affectuum plenam ad Corinthios scribit. Oro dominum ut per gratiam spiritus sui expositionem illius largiatur, & ger-manam & ecclesijs aedificandis utilem.
units.tr: Moved therefore by these causes, he writes this letter, full of fatherly affections, to the Corinthians. I pray the Lord that, through the grace of his Spirit, he may grant an exposition of it that is both sincere and useful for building up the churches.

units.la: COMMENTARII VVOLFGANGI MVSCVLI DVSANI, IN POSTERIOREM EPISTOLAM PAVLI AD CORINTHIOS.
units.tr: THE COMMENTARIES OF WOLFGANG MUSCULUS OF DIEPPE ON THE SECOND EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: VErilitatem afflictionum cùm suarum tum cæterorum Christi fidelium expo nit, & amplitudinem consolationum Christi deprædicat, deinde quod ad ipsos sicuti promiserat, non venerit, excusat, causamq; huius assignat.
units.tr: He sets out the reality of his own afflictions and those of the other faithful followers of Christ, and proclaims the abundance of the consolations of Christ. Then he excuses himself for not having come to them, as he had promised, and states the cause of this.

units.la: CAPVT PRIMVM.
units.tr: CHAPTER 1.

units.la: AVLVS Apostolus Iesu Christi, per voluntatem Dei, ac Timotheus frater, ecclesiæ Dei quæ est Corinthi, unà cū sanctis omnib. qui sunt in tota Achaia. Gratia vobis & pax à Deo patre nostro, & domino Iesu Christo.
units.tr: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the church of God which is at Corinth, together with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Sunt hæc ferè initiò præcedentis epistolæ declarata. Habent inscriptionem epistolæ, salutationem, & subscriptionem. Inscriptio est, vbi dicit: Ecclesiæ Dei quæ est Corinthi, vnà cum sanctis omnib. qui sunt in tota Achaia. Salutatione ponit dicés: Gratia vobis & pax à Deo patre nostro & domino Iesu Christo. Subscriptio est: Paulus Apostolus Iesu Christi, per voluntatem Dei, ac Timotheus frater.
units.tr: These things were mostly explained at the beginning of the previous epistle. They comprise the address, the greeting and the signature. The address is where he says: to the church of God which is at Corinth, together with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia. The greeting is where he says: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The signature is: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Timothy our brother.

units.la: PAVLVS Apostolus Iesu Christi, inquit.) Quod subscriptionem mox initiò ponit, Apostolicæ authoritati dandû esse puto. Facit hoc in omnibus suis epistolis. Faciút & Iacobus & Petrus. Humilitatis esse volunt, vt qui priuatus ad superiores scribit, inscriptioni subscriptionem nominis sui subijciat.
units.tr: "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ," he says. That he places the signature at the very beginning, I think, should be credited to his apostolic authority. He does this in all his epistles, and James and Peter do the same. They wish to show humility: one who writes privately to his superiors places the name of the writer in the signature below the address.

units.la: Apostolatum autem suû nusquam non inculcat, vocàs se Apostolum Iesu Christi, quod non est temerè ab eo iactantiæ spiritu, sed magna necessitate factum. Etenim sciebat Apostolatum suum à multis non agnosci, propterea quod ex illis non essent Apostolis, qui cum domino in carne fuerant conuersati, & numero duodenario in apostolos electi. Quare quâ pseudapostoli Apostolatui ipsius detrahebant vbiq;, ita ipse illum inculcat ubiq; , non quærens aliquid hinc gloriæ, sed vnum hoc agens, ut Christo domino suo fideliter simul & utiliter seruiat.
units.tr: Yet he nowhere fails to stress his apostleship, calling himself an apostle of Jesus Christ. He did not do this rashly, out of a spirit of boasting, but out of great necessity. For he knew that his apostleship was not recognised by many, because they were not apostles who had lived with the Lord in the flesh and had been chosen as apostles among the number of the twelve. Therefore, just as the false apostles everywhere detracted from his apostleship, so he everywhere insists upon it, not seeking any glory from it, but doing this one thing: that he may serve Christ his Lord faithfully and at the same time usefully.

units.la: Habent quod imitentur veri ac fideles Christi ministri. Hi non modò officium suum fideliter administrare debent, sed & ministerij sui authoritatem & existimationem contra reprobos & sectarios fortiter tueri, ne sua negligentia & incuria locum præbeant Satanæ, qui summo hoc studio molitur, vt ministerij fructus dispereat, inq; hunc finem ministrorû existimationem quoad eius poterit, per suos impostores subuertit. Titulos dignitatum ac prælaturarum suarum interim extollunt falsi apostoli, falsi doctores, & pseudepiscopi, quo authoritate sua falsò præsumpta plebem imperitam sub iugo dominationis suæ detineant. Quanto iustius est, vt legitimos ministeriorum suorû titulos veri Christi ministri contra veritatis aduersarios tueantur, quo ministerijs suis in ecclesia Dei efficacius fungi possint.
units.tr: True and faithful ministers of Christ have an example to imitate. They must not only administer their office faithfully, but also defend with courage the authority and reputation of their ministry against the reprobate and the sectarians, lest by their negligence and carelessness they give place to Satan, who with the utmost zeal labours to destroy the fruit of the ministry, and to this end, as far as he can, overthrows the reputation of the ministers through his impostors. Meanwhile false apostles, false teachers and pseudo-bishops extol the titles of their own dignities and prelacies, so that by an authority falsely presumed they may keep the ignorant common people under the yoke of their domination. How much more right it is that true ministers of Christ should defend the lawful titles of their ministries against the adversaries of the truth, so that they may be able to discharge their ministries more effectively in the church of God.

units.la: PER voluntatem Dei, inquit.) In hoc est authenticus Apostolatus, quod non est propria temeritate præsumptus, sed diuina voluntate mandatus & impositus. Hæc voluntas Dei cœlitùs illi declarata fuit, & multis virtutibus ac singulari prædicationis efficacia comprobata.
units.tr: "Through the will of God," he says. The genuineness of his apostleship lies in this: that it was not presumed by his own rashness, but was enjoined and imposed by the divine will. This will of God was declared to him from heaven, and was confirmed by many powers and by the singular effectiveness of his preaching.

units.la: Obseruà uerò, quod cũ dixisset: Paulus Apostolus Iesu Christi, non subiecit: secundû illius voluntatem, sed secundum voluntatem Dei. Ab ipso erat Christo in Apostolum delectus. Quare poterat dicere, secundû illius voluntatem. Verùm voluntatis authoritatë tribuit Deo quod & Christus ipse aliquot locis fecisse legitur. Ab hac enim tota suscepte dispensationis summa & origo pendebat. Præterea, quoniam nomen Iesu Christinon nisi fideles recipiebât, Dei verò agnoscebant etiam infideles, maluit dicere per Dei quàm per illius voluntatē, quo significaret fungisse Apostolatu nulla humana, sed prorsus diuina authoritate suffultum. Non quòd in nomine Christi non sit satis diuinę authoritatis, sed quòd sit fidelibus tantum, infidelibus nequaquam.
units.tr: Observe, however, that when he had said "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ," he did not add "according to his will," but "according to the will of God." He had been chosen as apostle by Christ himself, so he could have said "according to his will." But he attributes the authority of the will to God, as Christ himself is also read to have done in several places. For the whole sum and origin of the office he had undertaken depended on this. Moreover, since only the faithful received the name of Jesus Christ, while even unbelievers acknowledged God, he preferred to say "through the will of God" rather than "through his will," to signify that he exercised the apostleship supported by no human but by entirely divine authority. Not that the name of Christ lacks sufficient divine authority, but that it is recognised only by the faithful and not at all by unbelievers.

units.la: AC Timotheus frater, inquit.) Sic discipulos suos & cooperarios cohonestat, dũ eos in subscriptionib. epistolarũ nomini suo quasi æquales coniungit. Poterat dicere: Et Timotheus discipulus, verum maluit eū vocare fratrê, quo plus apud Corinthios authoritatis haberet ipsius ministerium.
units.tr: "And Timothy our brother," he says. In this way he honours his disciples and fellow workers, while in the subscriptions of his letters he joins them with his own name as though they were equals. He could have said "and Timothy his disciple," but he preferred to call him brother, so that his ministry might carry more authority with the Corinthians.

units.la: ECCLESIÆ Dei, inquit, quæ est Corinthi.) In priore epistola vide, quare non separatim quibusdam, sed toti Corinthiorum scripserit ecclesiæ. Scribit ecclesiæ fidelium Christi ipse Apostolus Christi, & vocat hanc ecclesiam Dei. Sic perpetuò ac vigilanter Christum & Deum connectit, vt voluntas Christi, sit voluntas luntas Dei, Apostolus Christi, seruus Dei, ecclesia Christi, ecclesia Dei. Quantū ergo Christi in nobis est, tantum est Dei in nobis. Et quâ procul sumus à Christo, tam sumus procul à Deo.
units.tr: "To the church of God," he says, "which is at Corinth." In the earlier epistle, see why he wrote to the church of the Corinthians as a whole and not to certain individuals separately. The apostle of Christ himself writes to the church of the faithful in Christ, and calls this church the church of God. So constantly and watchfully does he link Christ and God, that the will of Christ is the will of God, the apostle of Christ is the servant of God, the church of Christ is the church of God. Therefore, as much as there is of Christ in us, so much is there of God in us; and as far as we are distant from Christ, so far are we distant from God.

units.la: Reuera autem obseruabilis est exempli qd ecclesiam, quæ tum erat Corinthi, uocat ecclesiam Dei, cum tot ac tantis uicijs laboraret, quot & quanta epistola precedente in illa redarguit ac reprehendit. Consimile est, quod Christus regnum cœlorū Mat.13. agro in quo sunt zizania comparat. Qua in re quid obseruandum ueniat, vide in Comment. nostris super Matth.
units.tr: Indeed, there is a notable example here: he calls the church which then existed at Corinth the church of God, although it was labouring under so many and such great faults, which in the preceding epistle he rebukes and reproves. Similar is what Christ says in Matthew 13, comparing the kingdom of heaven to a field in which there are tares. As to what must be observed in this matter, see our Commentaries on Matthew.

units.la: VNA cum sanctis omnib9, inquit, qui sunt in tota Achaia.) Credētes in Christū uocat sanctos, quod sanctificati sint Deo, & à mundo in populum peculiarem segregati. Vt autem significet hanc se epistolam scribere non ecclesiæ tantum quæ erat Corinthi, sed & omnibus reliquis Christianis, qui in tota erant Achaia, postquam dixit, & ecclesiæ Dei quæ est Corinthi, adiecit, unà cum omnibus sanctis, qui sunt in tota Achaia. Hoc faciens, uelut in unū corpus totius Achaiæ fideles conglutinati, ne quę Corinthi erat ecclesia, propter Metropolitanā eminentiam supra cæteros extra vrbem in agro sparsos fideles sese extolleret, illosq; quasi ad ipsorum ecclesiam non pertinentes fastidiret. Et hāc quoq; ob causam uocat eos sanctos, ne qua in re minoris faciendi uideantur, quàm ij qui erant in ipsa vrbe. Necuult aliquid esse in illis dissidij ac separationis. Ideo non simpliciter dicit, unà cum sanctis, sed, unà cum sanctis omnibus, neq; qui sunt in Achaia, sed, qui sunt in tota Achaia.
units.tr: "Together with all the saints," he says, "who are in the whole of Achaia." He calls believers in Christ saints, because they have been sanctified to God and set apart from the world as a peculiar people. In order to signify that he is writing this epistle not only to the church which was at Corinth, but also to all the other Christians who were throughout Achaia, after saying "to the church of God which is at Corinth," he added "together with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia." In doing this, he binds the faithful of the whole of Achaia together as into one body, so that the church at Corinth should not exalt itself above the other faithful scattered in the countryside outside the city, because of its metropolitan eminence, and despise them as not belonging to its own church. For this reason too he calls them saints, so that they should not seem to be held of less account in any respect than those who were in the city itself. Nor does he wish there to be any division or separation among them. Therefore he does not simply say "together with the saints," but "together with all the saints," and not "who are in Achaia" but "who are in the whole of Achaia."

units.la: Sic igitur & inter se omnes totius Achaiæ fideles, & cum ecclesia quæ erat in ipsa metropoli, connectit. Qua in re studium conciliandi in vnum verè Apostolicum uidemus, quod vtinam imitentur qui successores apostolorū videri volunt.
units.tr: In this way he binds together all the faithful of the whole of Achaia both with one another and with the church which was in the metropolis itself. In this we see a truly apostolic zeal for uniting into one, and would that those who wish to be seen as successors of the apostles would imitate it.

units.la: Sed dicet aliquis. Atqui hoc ipsum agūt omnes vbiq; Christiani coadunentur, & schismata fugiant. Et in hunc finem damnant schismaticos, & quosuis ad concordiam & vnitatem ecclesiæ catholicę partim vocant, partim etiam cogunt.
units.tr: But someone will say: Yet all Christians everywhere do this very thing; they strive to be gathered together and to flee schisms. To this end they condemn schismatics, and some they call, and some even compel, to concord and to the unity of the catholic church.

units.la: Respondeo. Verum est, damnant schismata metropolitani nostri episcopi, & Romanus cum primis, ac prædicant pacem & vnitatem. Et faciunt hoc magno studio, violento ac sanguinario quoque. At etiam atq; etiam considerandum est, quod genus pacis & vnitatis in ecclesia Christi spectent. Tale videlicet, in quo ipsi dominentur omnibus, non quo omnes in Christo sint coniuncti. Dominationis studiū pacis & vnitatis prætextu palliant. Vt quid dominationem vocant pacem & subiectionem plus quàm seruilem, concordiam & vnitatem? Pacem & vnitatem volumus & appetimus nos quoque, sed eam quæ sit in Christo, quæ sit non falsa, sed uera, quæ nos non vt seruos dominis subijciat, sed vt fratres fratribus in domino & uera pietate coniungat. Hodie impensè à multis quæritur ecclesiarum vnitas. Vtinam vniat nos spiritus & veritas domini. Verum metuo, ne quod Hieronymus alicubi de suis temporibus quęstus est, sub nomine vnitatis & fidei infidelitas uel inueterata stabiliatur, uel noua aliqua scribatur. Etenim plerisque iam nihil tam videtur pium, nihil tam conueniens seruis Dei, quàm vnitatem sequi, & à catholica totius mundi communione non auelli, præsertim vbi sic omnia quæ in controuersia sunt, finguntur ac refinguntur, vt superficies expositionis nihil impium & auersandum præferre videatur. Quæramus vnitatem, ô fratres, quæramus autem non simulatam & superficialem, sed veram & intimam, quæ sit non in catholica consuetudine, sed in Christi spiritu & veritate, vt simul possit esse in vera sanctorum consensione ac charitate.
units.tr: I reply: It is true that our metropolitan bishops condemn schisms, and the Roman bishop above all, and they proclaim peace and unity. And they do this with great zeal, and even with violence and bloodshed. But we must consider again and again what kind of peace and unity they are aiming at in the church of Christ. Clearly it is that kind in which they themselves rule over all, not that in which all are joined in Christ. They cloak their desire for domination under the pretext of peace and unity. Why do they call domination "peace," and a subjection more than servile "concord and unity"? We too want and seek peace and unity, but that which is in Christ, which is not false but true, which does not subject us as slaves to masters, but joins us as brothers to brothers in the Lord and in true piety. Today the unity of the churches is earnestly sought by many. Would that the Spirit and truth of the Lord might unite us. But I fear that what Jerome somewhere complains of in his own times may come to pass: under the name of unity and faith, unbelief is either established in its inveterate form or some new one is written. For to many people nothing now seems so pious, nothing so fitting for the servants of God, as to follow unity and not to tear themselves away from the catholic communion of the whole world, especially when all matters in controversy are so feigned and refeigned that the surface of the exposition seems to present nothing impious or to be shunned. Let us seek unity, brothers, but let us seek it not feigned and superficial, but true and heartfelt, which lies not in catholic custom but in the spirit and truth of Christ, so that it may at the same time exist in the true agreement and charity of the saints.

units.la: GRATIA vobis & pax, inquit, à Deo patre nostro, ac dño Iesu Christo.) Eadē vsus est salutatione ad verbum, tam in ea quam ad Romanos scripsit, quàm in precedente ad Corinthios. Vtrobiq; aut illam exposuimus, & quæ ob seruanda sint annotauimus. Quare non est ut hic vel eadem repetamus, vel alia illis addam nisi hoc vnū, vt qui Christiani sumus, felicitatē nostram in hac Apostolica salutatione agnoscamus, & agnitam bene cum gratiarum actione collocemus.
units.tr: GRACE to you and peace, he says, from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. He used the same greeting word for word here as in the letter to the Romans, and also in the earlier letter to the Corinthians. We have explained it in both places and noted what is to be kept in mind. So there is no need to repeat those points here, nor to add anything new to them, except this one thing: that we who are Christians should recognise our happiness in this apostolic greeting, and, having recognised it, rightly give thanks for it.

units.la: 1 Ea autem est, quod non sumus populus sine Deo in hoc mūdo, quales sunt, qui alieni sunt à Christo, vide Eph.2. Non est vt dicatur nobis ab impijs huius sæculi filijs: Vbi est Deus uester? Deus noster in cœlo est. Dicant ipsi, vbi & quę Deum habeant.
units.tr: 1. This is our first happiness: we are not a people without God in this world, as those are who are strangers to Christ; see Eph. 2. Let the sons of this age, who are ungodly, not say to us: "Where is your God?" Our God is in heaven. Let them say where and what gods they have.

units.la: 2 Deinde, quod idem nobis est & Deus & pater. Qui Deus est & omnipotēs, & solus, in manu sua habens omnia pater noster est. Quid poterit stupendum magis dici? Quis enumerauerit omnes uerę felicitatis species, & veras in uictasq; consolationes, quæ ex vno hoc proue niunt, quod eundem habemus patrem quem & Deum?
units.tr: 2. Second, the God who is ours is also our Father. He who is God and almighty, who alone holds all things in his hand, is our Father. What could be said that is more amazing? Who could count all the kinds of true happiness, and the true and unconquerable consolations, that come from this one fact, that we have as our Father the same one who is God?

units.la: 3 Tertiò, ad cumulū hunc felicitatis nostræ accedit, quod vnigenitus Dei, homo ex carne nostra factus, datus est nobis à patre in dominum, non vt illi plus honoris quàm habuerit antea accedat, sed vt sit nobis redemptor, Seruator & gubernator, ac possideat quidem nos iure regni à patre accepti: uerum ut fratres ac filios, ad seruandum, non ad coartandum.
units.tr: 3. Third, to crown our happiness, the only-begotten Son of God, made man from our flesh, has been given to us by the Father as Lord. Not that he gains more honour than he had before, but that he may be our redeemer, saviour and governor, and may indeed hold us by the right of the kingdom received from the Father; but as brothers and sons, to save us, not to confine us.

units.la: 4 Quartò, quod ab vtroque, & Deo patre nostro & domino Iesu Christo, gratia & pace cœlesti beamur. Quod enim salutando Apostolus gratiam & pacem Corinthijs à Deo patre nostro, ac domino Iesu Christo apprecatus est, non sic est accipiendum, quasi non vtraque in Christo fruamur, quotquot in illum credimus, sed quod hac salutatione & paternam nam suam erga eos beneuolentiam declarare, & iuxta de felicitate eos per fidem in Christū accepta admonere uoluit, quo illā & bene collocarent, & per omnis generis afflictiones, quibus propter fidem in Christū obnoxij erant, saluam & integram ad finem vsq; retinere sata gerent. Si quis ista diligenter in hac salutatione perpenderit, puto abūde habiturum, unde & consolationem petat, & in fide Christi aedificetur.
units.tr: 4. Fourth, we are blessed with grace and heavenly peace from both God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. When the Apostle, in greeting the Corinthians, wished them grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, this must not be taken to mean that we enjoy only one of these in Christ, as many as believe in him. Rather, by this greeting he wished to declare his fatherly goodwill towards them, and to remind them of the happiness they had received through faith in Christ, so that they would both make good use of it and take care to keep it safe and whole to the end, despite all kinds of affliction to which they were exposed for the sake of faith in Christ. If anyone weighs these things carefully in this greeting, I think he will have enough, both to draw consolation from it and to be built up in the faith of Christ.

units.la: Benedictus Deus & pater domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui est pater misericordiarum, & Deus omnis consolationis, consolas nos in omni afflictione nostra, in hoc ut possimus consolari eos, qui sunt in quavis afflictione, per consolationē qua consolatur nosipsos Deus. Quoniam sicut abundant afflictiones Christi in nobis, ita per Christū abūdat & consolatio nostra.
units.tr: Blessed be God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which God himself comforts us. For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds. (2 Cor. 1:3–5)

units.la: In oculis carnis nullum poterat maius contra Euangelium Christi oriri scandalum, quàm quòd Apostolo Christi vbique contradicebatur, & omnis generis afflictiones ac discrimina vitae passim excitabantur. Hinc impij in erroribus suis obstinatiores reddebantur, & pseudapostoli argumenta Apostolatui Pauli obloquendi ac detrahendi, & infirmiores in fide ab Apostolica doctrina auocandi ac seducendi sumebant. Scandalum hoc amoliturus Apostolus tam abesse docet, ut multitudo afflictionum, quibus exercebatur, cuiquam debeat esse offendiculo, ut pijs hominibus & opus Dei intelligentibus materiam magis offerat doxologiae Dei, cuius in seipso exemplum mox in ipso epistolae exordio ponit dicens: Benedictus Deus, & pater domini nostri Iesu Christi, pater misericordiarum & Deus omnis consolationis, consolans nos in omni afflictione nostra, &c. Quasi dicat: Multis tribulationibus & afflictionibus vbique exerceor. Verum est, sed non est ut hoc quenquam vestrū vel offendat, vel pusillanimem reddat. Quod me attinet, tam abest ut super afflictionibus hisce meis per impatientiam conquerar, aut animo in causa Christi deijciar, ut magis hinc luculentissimo diuinarum consolationum argumento ad glorificandum ac laudandum Deū exciter, quod is me in omni afflictione, quantumuis graui, sic cōsolatur, ut & alios afflictos ea possim consolatione, qua me consolatur, cōsolari.
units.tr: In the eyes of the flesh, no greater scandal could arise against the gospel of Christ than that the Apostle of Christ was everywhere opposed, and all kinds of afflictions and dangers to life were stirred up on every side. From this the ungodly became more stubborn in their errors, and false apostles took up arguments to disparage and belittle Paul's apostleship, and to lead astray and seduce those weaker in the faith away from apostolic teaching. The Apostle, wishing to remove this scandal, teaches that the great number of afflictions with which he was troubled ought not to be a stumbling block to anyone. Rather, they should offer material for praising God to godly people who understand the work of God. He sets an example of this himself at the very beginning of the letter, saying: Blessed be God, and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who comforts us in all our affliction, etc. It is as if he said: "I am troubled on every side by many tribulations and afflictions. It is true, but this should not offend or discourage any of you. As for me, far from complaining of my afflictions out of impatience, or being cast down in spirit for the cause of Christ, I am rather stirred up by them to glorify and praise God, all the more because he so comforts me in every affliction, however grievous, that I am able to comfort others who are afflicted with the same comfort with which he comforts me."

units.la: Hunc existimo exordij huius esse sensum. Chrysostomus tamen aliud cogitat. Causam exordij huius fuisse Apostolo censet, ut rationem redderet, quur Corinthum non venerit, cum precedente epistola venturum se scripsisset. Quasi dicat, Scio me uobis aduentum meū ad uos esse pollicitum. Verum benedictus sit Deus, qui me in tam grauibus afflictionibus non deseruit, quibus interea temporis adob-
units.tr: I think this is the sense of the opening. Chrysostom, however, thinks otherwise. He believes the Apostle wrote this opening to give the reason why he had not come to Corinth, although in the previous letter he had written that he would come. It is as if he said: "I know that I promised you a visit. But blessed be God, who did not forsake me in such grievous afflictions, by which in the meantime I was beset

units.la: rutus & impeditus fui, quo minus qd̄ promiseram, praestare potuerim: quare non est, ut hasce moras uel leuitatem vel socordiam interpretemini. Ex recentioribus nonnulli utranque causam, tam eam quam posui, quàm hac Chrysostomi connectunt. Sanè non est insolens, ut vnius rei plures sint causae. Prior tamen mihi probabilior apparet.
units.tr: and hindered, so that I could not carry out what I had promised. So you must not interpret this delay as lightness or carelessness." Some of the more recent writers join both reasons together, the one I have given and this one of Chrysostom's. Certainly it is not unusual for one thing to have several causes. Still, the former seems to me the more probable.

units.la: BENEDICTVS Deus, inquit.) Doxologiae vox est, ut Ebraeis בָּרוּךְ, ita Graecis εὐλογητός. Possumus Latine vertere hoc loco, laudatum, vel, celebratum. Benedictum vertunt communiter. Nec male, si recte intelligatur. Vt enim εὐλογεῖν Graecis, & benedicere Latinis, bene est de aliquo loqui, laudibus aliquem extollere, ita & εὐλογητός, ac benedictus is recte dicitur, qui velcelebratur laudibus, de quo omnes bene ac praeclarè loquuntur, vel sic se gerit, ut sit laudabilis, debeatque suo merito laudari ab omnibus. Iam quod praesentem locum attinet, quod doxologiam Dei Apostolus cum exclamatione exprimit, dicens: Benedictus Deus, accipi potest pro grati animi & in laudē Dei ac censi voto, ut idem sit quod: Benedictus, lauda tus ac glorificatus sit Deus. Hoc est, benedicatur, laudetur & glorificetur ab omnibus. Qualem ipse Deum sentiebat in corde suo, talem cupiebat ab omnibus agnosci, praedicari ac laudari.
units.tr: BLESSED be God, he says. This is a word of praise, as the Hebrews say בָּרוּךְ [barukh], and the Greeks say εὐλογητός [eulogētos]. In this place we could render it in Latin as "praised" or "celebrated." Commonly it is rendered "blessed," and not wrongly, if it is rightly understood. For as the Greeks say εὐλογεῖν and the Latins benedicere to mean to speak well of someone, to extol someone with praises, so εὐλογητός, or benedictus, is rightly said of one who is celebrated with praises, of whom all speak well and gladly, or who so conducts himself that he is worthy of praise, and deserves by his merit to be praised by all. Now as regards the present passage, where the Apostle expresses his praise of God with an exclamation, saying "Blessed be God," it can be taken as an expression of a grateful mind and a wish for God's praise, so that it means: "Let God be blessed, praised and glorified." That is, let him be blessed, praised and glorified by all. Just as he felt God in his heart, so he wished him to be acknowledged, proclaimed and praised by all.

units.la: Quod si quis ad hunc modum intelligendū esse putat: O vere benedictū, celebrem ac laudatū Deum. Vel: O laudabilem Deum, ac dignum cui benedicatur ab omnib. non erit ineptus sensus. Huiusmodi abruptae exclamationes vt exuberantium cordiū spirant affectus, ita varijs modis possunt exponi, modò expositiones ab ipsa causa quę geritur haud abludāt, ac longius discedant.
units.tr: If anyone thinks that it should be understood in this way, "O truly blessed, celebrated and praised God!" or "O God worthy of praise, and worthy to be blessed by all," the sense will not be absurd. Exclamations of this broken kind breathe out the feelings of overflowing hearts, and so they can be explained in various ways, provided the explanations do not stray far or depart from the subject in hand.

units.la: ET pater domini nostri Iesu Christi, inquit.) Quoniā propter Christū affligebātur fideles, videbanturq; ob crebras afflictiones singulari quadā ira Dei exagitari, quasi Christianū esse idem sit quod impium esse, ac Deum habere infensum. Cōsultò vocat hic Deū patrē dni nostri Iesu Christi, vt significet afflictiones fidelium Christi non esse ex eo quod iratum habeat: Deum, quasi extra verum Deum colant alienum dum Christum colunt. Quomodo enim irascetur Deus illis qui filium ipsius vnigenitum ac dilectum Salutis nostrae gratia in mundum hunc missum suncera fide amplectuntur ac colunt? Imò potissima hinc est consolatio fidelibus, quod dum affliguntur in mundo, affliguntur propter filium Dei.
units.tr: AND the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, he says. Since the faithful were suffering for Christ's sake, and seemed because of their frequent afflictions to be harassed by a particular anger of God, as if to be a Christian were the same as to be ungodly, and to have God as an enemy. He deliberately calls God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, to show that the afflictions of Christ's faithful do not come from God being angry with them, as if they worshipped a strange god, outside the true God, while they worshipped Christ. For how would God be angry with those who sincerely embrace and worship his only-begotten and beloved Son, sent into this world for the sake of our salvation? Indeed, the chief consolation for the faithful is this: that while they are afflicted in the world, they are afflicted for the sake of the Son of God.

units.la: Vide autem quàm competenter particulam hanc elogijs illis Dei praemittat, quibus eum vocaturus est patrem misericordiarum, ac Deum omnis consolationis. In eo siquidē quod pater est domini nostri Iesu Christi, fons & origo est omnium misericordiarum ac consolationū quibus ij qui in Christo sunt, recreantur & sustentantur.
units.tr: Notice also how fittingly he puts this clause before those praises of God by which he is going to call him the Father of mercies and God of all consolation. For in that he is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, he is the fountain and origin of all the mercies and consolations by which those who are in Christ are refreshed and sustained.

units.la: Deinde nec illud transeundum est, quod cū antea Deũ nostrũ patrem uocarit,iamuocat e- um patrẽ dñi nostri Iesu Christi. Ergo idẽ Deꝰ & noster ac dñi nostri Iesu Christi pater. Sic ad Mariam Ioh.20.ipse Christus post resurrectio- nem dicebat: Vade ad fratres meos & dic eis: Ascendo ad patrẽ meũ & patrem vestrũ, Deũ meũ & Deũ uestrũ. Sic itaq; fumus filij Dei,vt simus & fratres vnigeniti Dei Christi Iesu, & eundem cuius fratres sumus ,habeamus dñm.
units.tr: Next we must not pass over the fact that, after calling God our Father, he now calls him the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. So the same God is both our Father and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Thus Christ himself, after the resurrection, said to Mary: "Go to my brothers and say to them: I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God" (John 20).
