So we are the sons of God in such a way that we are also brothers of the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, and have the same Lord whose brothers we are.

units.la: QVI est pater misericordiarum inquit, & Deus omnis consolationis.) Qui sine ratione quempiam laudat,quoniam affectibus suis ma gis quàm veritati indulget , magis eum quem laudat, sinistra suspicione grauat,quàm vera laude ornat. At Apostolus noster,quamuis ar- denti zelo propensus fuerit ad laudandum De um,sic tamen eum laudat ut talia de illo prose rat in medium quæ nulla vnquam laude satis extolli poterunt. Sic cum dixisset,Benedictus Deus & pater domini nostri Iesu Christi,mox quare eum benedictum uocet,exprimit dicēs: Qui est pater misericordiarum,& Deus omnis consolationis. Multa facta sunt à Deo,& fi- unt quotidie magnifica & miranda, quorum gratia celebrandus est in cœlo & in terra ab angelis, hominibus,& omnis generis bestijs, neicio tamen an vlla sit amplior & illustrior di uinæ laudis materia quàm qua bonitas clemē tia & misericordia Dei, cuius nec modus est, nec numerus, nec finis, passim celebranda oc currit . Ad hanc pertinet præsens elogium, quo Deum Apostolus patrem misericordiarũ ✝ & Deum omnis consolationis uocat. Etenim reuera,quemadmodũ Dauid Psal.145.canit: Miserationes eius super omnia sunt opera eiꝰ, excelluntq; gloriam potentiæ,sapientiæ & iu sticiæ eius,& magis quàm illæ naturam diuini tatis exprimunt.
units.tr: "Who is the Father of mercies," he says, "and the God of all consolation." Someone who praises another without good reason, indulging his own feelings more than the truth, burdens the one he praises with a suspicion of ill will rather than adorning him with true praise. But our Apostle, although he was eager with burning zeal to praise God, nevertheless praises him in such a way that he brings forward things about him that no praise could ever extol enough. So, having said, "Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ," he at once explains why he calls him blessed, saying: "who is the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation." God has done many great and wonderful works, and does them every day, for which he ought to be praised in heaven and on earth by angels, men and beasts of every kind. Yet I do not know whether there is any broader or more illustrious matter for praising God than his goodness, clemency and mercy, which have no measure, number or end, and which are to be celebrated everywhere. To this belongs the present eulogy, by which the Apostle calls God the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation. Indeed, as David sings in Psalm 145: "His mercies are over all his works," and they surpass the glory of his power, wisdom and justice, and express the nature of the divinity more than these do.

units.la: PATER,inquit,misericordiarum.) Patrem hic accipiût pro fonte & origine,quasi hoc de Deo præd cet Apostolus,quòd sit fons & ori- go misericordiarũ,nõ modo quas ipse cœlitùs declarat,sed & omniũ earũ quę contingũt no bis vndecunq;,medijsq; ac modis qbuscunq;, qui sensus nihil habet incõmodi. Nam ita ha bet: Omne bonum desursum est. Si qua nobis misericordia cõtingit,cœleste bonũ est, ab eo proueniens,qui omnis est boni fons & origo. Verũ an hoc in præsenti dicere voluerit Apo- stolus,meo iudicio,cõtrouerti potest. Dicam quid mihi videatur. Quoniam singularem illã gratiam commendaturus,qua filiũ suum Deꝰ nostra gratia in mũdum hunc misit,eumq; no- bis redemptorem dedit ac dominum , nõ sim- pliciter dixit:Benedictus Deus,sed adiecit, & pater domini nostri Iesu Christi, hac occasiõe uocem istam pater,repetit,ut qualis pater sit, exprimat,dicens,pater misericordiarum,Ebr. אב רחמים,quod sonat Ebraico more,patrẽ mi sericordem , propensissimum ad omnis gene- ris miserationes,qua in re omnino paterna in nos,imò & in omnia quę condidit,uiscera de- clarat,id quo d propriũ est ueri ac germani pa-
units.tr: "The Father of mercies," he says. Here "Father" is taken for the fountain and origin, as if the Apostle were saying of God that he is the fountain and origin of mercies, not only those which he himself declares from heaven, but also of all those which happen to us from whatever source and by whatever means. This sense has no difficulty. For it is said: "Every good gift is from above" (James 1). If any mercy comes to us, it is a heavenly good, coming from him who is the fountain and origin of every good. But whether the Apostle meant this in the present passage, in my judgment can be disputed. I will say what seems to me. Since he was about to commend that singular grace by which God, in his grace, sent his Son into this world and gave him to us as Redeemer and Lord, he did not simply say, "Blessed be God," but added, "and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." On this occasion he repeats the word "Father" in order to express what kind of Father he is, saying "Father of mercies" [אב רחמים], which in Hebrew idiom means a father merciful, most inclined to every kind of compassion. In this he wholly reveals the paternal bowels toward us, and indeed toward all that he has made, which is proper to a true and genuine father toward his own children.

units.la: tris erga sua pignora,quo respicit propheta di ces:Quemadmodum miseretur pater filiorũ, ita miseretur Deus timentium se . Hoc sentiês dicit:pater misericordiarum. Quasi dicat,Qui verè pater est,paternis viscerib. ad omnis ge- neris miserationes propensus . Sic duas hæce voces,pater,& miserationum,Græcè οἰκτιρμῶν Ebraice רחמים,omnium aptissimè coniunxit.
units.tr: Hence the prophet, perceiving this, says: "As a father has compassion on his children, so God has compassion on those who fear him" (Psalm 103). Meaning this, he says: "Father of mercies." As if he were saying: he who is truly a Father, with paternal bowels, is inclined to every kind of compassion. So he joined these two words most aptly, "Father" and "of mercies," which in Greek are οἰκτιρμῶν and in Hebrew רחמים.

units.la: Quid est aũt quod non in singulari dicit, pa ter misericordiæ,sed in plurali,pater misericor diarum?An non vt vna in se bonitas , qua bo- num,ita & misericordia vna est qua misericor dem Deum esse sentimus?Respondeo.Side i- psa virtute misericordiæ quæritur,qua miseri- cordes reddimur,ea plane in se est vna,quem- admodũ & duricies cordis vna est quæ nos in humanos & immisericordes reddit.Verum v- bi non simpliciter de affectu misericordiæ,sed de illius operibus ac specieb.fit mentio, ibi re ẽte de misericordijs ac miserationibus loqui- mur.Licet enim vna sit in se misericordiæ vir- tus,plures tamen sunt , imò innumeræ operũ illius species,præsertim in Deo,in quo solo in- finita est & inexhausta illi plenitudo.Quèad- modum igitur humanæ nostræ miseriæ innu- merœ sunt ac varię species,quarũ omnium mi sericors Deus miseretur , cuius proprium est semper misereri ac parcere,ita omnium conue nientissimè proponuntur nobis in Deo omnis generis misericordiarũ species, ut quàm , imò supra quàm sumus miseri , misericordem nos patrem in cœlis habere sciamus.
units.tr: But why does he not say in the singular "the Father of mercy," but in the plural "the Father of mercies"? Is it not that, just as goodness is one in itself and so good is one, so mercy is also one, by which we perceive God to be merciful? I answer: if we are speaking of the very virtue of mercy, by which we are made merciful, it is indeed one in itself, just as hardness of heart is one, which makes us inhuman and unmerciful. But where mention is made not simply of the affection of mercy, but of its works and kinds, there we rightly speak of mercies and compassions. For although the virtue of mercy is one in itself, its works have many kinds, indeed innumerable species, especially in God, in whom alone its fullness is infinite and inexhaustible. Just as our human miseries are innumerable and of various kinds, and the merciful God has compassion on all of them, and it is his property always to show mercy and to spare, so in God are set before us most fittingly all kinds of mercies, so that we may know that we have a merciful Father in heaven, who is far more, indeed beyond measure, than we are wretched.

units.la: Nec ociofum est,quod misericordię species & opera misericordias vocat. In Deo veritas est,non inanis ac fallax rerum species. Opera illius,quib.benefacit humano generi,neq; per occasionem aliquam,neq; per hypocrisim aut diuerso aliquo studio , sed per misericordiam veraciter fiunt:ideoq; omnium rectissimè mi- misericordiæ vocantur,vt ex ipso nobis fonte vnde promanant,commendentur.A nobis ve- rò multa fiunt,speciem quidem misericordiæ præferentia,verùm à veritate illius prorsus a- liena,ideoq; indigna,quæ misericordiæ voce- tur.Qui nudum vestit,esurientem cibat,exulã tem hospicio accipit , infirmum visitat, &c.si hæc affectu misericordiæ motus facit, rectè q facit misericordiæ uocabuntur,si uero non ex misericordia,sed ex simulatione pietatis facit, non est ut misericordiæ vocentur, sed rectius hypocrises uocabuntur. Veritas operis non est secundum externam illius qualitatem, sed secundum operantis affectum ac studium cen senda,ut rectè dixerit ex patribus quidam : χ? τῶν γνωμῶν τὰ ἀφ' ἡμῶν κείνη τω. Dum cibat nos Deus,dum sanat,dum feruat acliberat,aut alio quopiam beneficio afficit, non inuenio unde faciat, nisi ex sola sua bonitate & misericordia. Quare non video quid eiusmodi illius opera rectius quàm misericordiæ uocentur . Sed pergamus.
units.tr: Nor is it idle that he calls the kinds and works of mercy "mercies." In God there is truth, not an empty and deceptive appearance of things. His works, by which he does good to the human race, are done truly out of mercy, not by some chance occasion, nor through hypocrisy or any different motive. Therefore they are rightly called mercies, most rightly of all, so that they may be commended by the very source from which they flow. But many things are done by us which bear the appearance of mercy, yet are wholly alien to its truth and therefore unworthy of being called mercy. If someone clothes the naked, feeds the hungry, receives the exile into his house, visits the sick, and so on, and does these things moved by the affection of mercy, he does rightly, and they will rightly be called mercies. But if he does them not out of mercy but out of pretence of piety, they should not be called mercies, but more correctly hypocrisies. The truth of a work is judged not by its outward quality but by the affection and purpose of the one who does it, so that one of the Fathers rightly said: [οὐ τῶν ἔξωθεν, ἀλλὰ τῶν γνωμῶν]. When God feeds us, heals us, preserves and frees us, or bestows some other benefit upon us, I find nothing from which he acts except his own goodness and mercy alone. Wherefore I do not see why works of this kind should be called mercies more rightly than mercies. But let us go on.

units.la: ET Deus omnis consolationis, inquit.)Vul gata æditio habet:& Deus totius consolatio- nis, his, quasi integram & perfectam in Deo consolationem nobis commendet Apostolus. At in Graeco non est ὅλης, id est, totius, sed παντὸς, id est, omnis, quod idem est, atque omnis generis consolationis. Etenim pro varietate tribulationum, quibus exercemur & corpore & spiritu, parata nobis est in Deo varia omnis uideli cet generis consolatio, ob quam illum causam uocat hic omnis consolationis Deum, hoc est, Deum qui nos in omnis generis tribulationibus consoletur. Est hoc elogium Dei abscondITUM à carnalibus hominibus, in quorum oculis Deus magis est omnis tribulationis, quàm omnis consolationis Deus, praesertim ubi afflictiones sanctorum aspiciunt, quibus in hoc saeculo exercentur, uidentque multas esse tribulationes iustorum. Verum Apostolus scribit ista non carnalibus, sed fidelibus Christi, qui uera fide elogia diuinae bonitatis amplectuntur.
units.tr: "And the God of all consolation," he says. The Vulgate edition has "and the God of the whole consolation," as if the Apostle were commending to us a complete and perfect consolation in God. But in the Greek there is not ὅλης, that is "of the whole," but παντὸς, that is "of all," which is the same as "of every kind." For according to the variety of tribulations by which we are exercised both in body and in spirit, there is prepared for us in God a varied consolation of every kind, which is why he here calls God the God of all consolation, that is, the God who consoles us in tribulations of every kind. This eulogy of God is hidden from carnal men, in whose eyes God is more the God of all tribulation than of all consolation, especially when they look upon the afflictions of the saints, with which they are exercised in this world, and see that the righteous have many tribulations. But the Apostle writes these things not to carnal men but to the faithful in Christ, who with true faith embrace the eulogies of divine goodness.

units.la: Vide autem quàm competeter particulam hanc praecedenti subiecerit. Generalius est quod dixit: & pater misericordiarum. Complectitur enim hoc elogium omnia beneficiorum Dei genera. Quare ut ad propositum suum collimet, quo de consolationibus diuinis quas in seipso in omni tribulatione experiebatur, dicere constituerat, generaliori elogio id subiicit quod erat & specialius (nam consolatio species quaedam est misericordiae Dei) & propius ad propositum accedebat. Sic dicit, Et Deus omnis consolationis, cui conuenientissimè subiicit, consolans nos in omni afflictione nostra.
units.tr: See how fittingly he has added this phrase after the preceding one. What he said before, "and the Father of mercies," is more general, for this eulogy embraces all the kinds of God's benefits. Therefore, aiming at his purpose, in which he had resolved to speak of the divine consolations which he himself experienced in every tribulation, he adds to the more general eulogy one that is both more specific (for consolation is a certain kind of God's mercy) and closer to his purpose. So he says, "and the God of all consolation," to which he most fittingly adds: "who consoles us in all our affliction."

units.la: Priusquam ad sequentia transeamus, admonendus est lector, ne putet hic locum esse Manichaeis, qui duos deos ponentes, Veteris testamenti unum, Noui alterum, eum qui Veteris fuerit, durum, seuerum, immitem ac malum, alterum qui Noui, misericordem, mitem ac bonum, eumque patre domini nostri Iesu Christi esse dixerunt. Apostolus cum hic Deum patrem domini nostri Iesu Christi, patrem misericordiarum & omnis consolationis Deum uocat, non hoc agit, ut alium Noui quàm Veteris testamenti Deum praedicet, absit, sed ut immensam unius ac eiusdem, tam Veteris quàm Noui testamenti Dei bonitatem, non simpliciter & qualitercunque, sed ut Apostolus Christi, & ad Christi fidelium fidem confirmandam, ac mentes ad quarumcunque tribulationum patientiâ erigendas commendet. Alibi nanque ut cap.8. praecedentis epistolae de Deo praedicat, quod sit & unus, & pater, ex quo omnia.
units.tr: Before we move on, the reader should be warned not to think that this passage gives any support to the Manichaeans. They posited two gods, one of the Old Testament and another of the New. The god of the Old Testament they called hard, severe, merciless and evil, while the god of the New Testament they called merciful, gentle and good, and they said he was the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. When the Apostle here calls God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort, he is not doing so to proclaim a God of the New Testament different from the God of the Old. Far from it. He is commending the immense goodness of one and the same God, of the Old Testament and of the New, not in a casual or general way, but as an apostle of Christ, to confirm the faith of Christ's faithful and to raise their minds to patient endurance of whatever tribulations come. Elsewhere, as in chapter 8 of the previous epistle, he likewise declares of God that he is both one and the Father, from whom all things come.

units.la: CONSOLANS nos, inquit, in omni afflictione nostra.) Huc ibat, cum Deum ut patrem misericordiarum, & Deum omnis consolationis praedicaret. Talem enim experiebatur erga se, quoties affligebatur ab impiis. De se nanque loquitur, licet pluraliter dicat: Consolans nos in omni afflictione nostra.
units.tr: "Comforting us," he says, "in all our affliction." He was heading there when he called God the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort. For this is the comfort he experienced from God whenever he was afflicted by the impious. He speaks of himself, although he uses the plural: "comforting us in all our affliction."

units.la: Vide autem quomodo hoc interpretetur, quod in omni tribulatione consolantem se Deum experiebatur. Non dicit: Benedictus Deus & pater domini nostri Iesu Christi, pater iustorum, & Deus omnis ultionis, qui causam nostram uindicat, & nos è manibus impiorum liberat. Sunt quidem haec uera, & locum habuerunt in ipso Apostolo, quem dominus saepenumero uelut ex ore luporum eripuit, ac causam eius iustam utique asseruit. Verum huc ille non respexit in praesenti, sed omnem hanc causam, omnemque in quacunque tribulatione consolationem Deo non ut iusto iudici, sed ut patri misericordiarum tribuit, agnoscens opus illius in se, opus esse misericordiae, & huius consideratione in hanc doxologiam illius rapitur, ut exclamando celebret ac praedicet eum patrem misericordiarum, & Deum omnis consolationis. Non dicit, quia sic nobis in scripturis praedicatur, sed, qui nos consolatur, inquit, in omni afflictione nostra. Viuo sensu misericordiarum Dei motus, praedicat eum esse patrem misericordiarum. Vbi uidemus unde uerus nascatur laudandi Dei affectus. Qui ex scripturis tantum de bonitate Dei praedicat, uera quidem dicit: uerum ex mortua litera, non ex uiuo sensu spiritus.
units.tr: Notice, however, how he interprets the fact that he experienced God as comforting him in every tribulation. He does not say: "Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of the just, and the God of all vengeance, who defends our cause and delivers us from the hands of the impious." These things are true, and they applied to the Apostle himself, whom the Lord often snatched as if from the mouths of wolves, and whose just cause he certainly vindicated. But he did not have these things in view at the moment. He ascribes this whole cause, and all the comfort in any tribulation, to God not as a just judge but as the Father of mercies. Recognising that God's work in him is a work of mercy, he is carried away by this consideration into that doxology, so that by exclaiming he may celebrate and proclaim him the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort. He does not say, "because this is how he is proclaimed to us in the Scriptures," but "who comforts us in all our affliction." Moved by the living sense of God's mercies, he declares him to be the Father of mercies. Here we see where the true affection for praising God is born. Whoever proclaims God's goodness only from the Scriptures speaks true things, but from the dead letter, not from the living sense of the Spirit.

units.la: QVI consolatur nos, inquit.) Nō dicit, qui potest nos consolari, sed, qui consolatur nos. Magna quidem ex eo quoque est tribulatorum consolatio, quod Deum se habere credunt & cogitat, qui ipsos in omni potest qua detinentur afflictione consolari. Verum id demum multo est amplius, sic dicere poterimus, qui consolatur nos, ut praedicemus de Deo non modo quid possit, sed & quid faciat, atque ita cum Paulo uersemur in argumento laudandae non solum potentiae eius, sed bonitatis quoque & misericordiae. In opere quippe consolationis iunguntur & potentia in facto, & misericordia in causa facti.
units.tr: "Who comforts us," he says. He does not say "who is able to comfort us," but "who comforts us." Great indeed is the comfort of the afflicted in this also, that they believe and think that they have a God who is able to comfort them in every affliction by which they are held. But the fact that he actually comforts us is much more than this. We can therefore say, "who comforts us," so that we proclaim of God not only what he can do but what he does. In this way we engage with Paul in praising not only his power but also his goodness and mercy. For in the work of comfort, power in the deed is joined with mercy in the cause of the deed.

units.la: Praeterea obserua quod nō in praeterito dicit, qui nos consolatus est in praeteritis nostris afflictionibus, sed in praesenti qui nos consolatur in omni afflictione nostra. Sic dices non tam de opere consolationis, quod antea expertus aliquoties fuerat, quàm de iugi & indefinenti erga se misericordia Dei gaudet, quam se antea quidem expertum sciebat: uerum simul in posterum quoq; & ad finem usq; expertum esse credebat ac sperabat. Quod enim dicit: Qui consolatur nos in omni tribulatione nostra, idem est quod qui nos pro sua infinita misericordia in nullis unquam tribulationibus deserit, sed consolatur in omnibus. Hoc dicens, & praeteritas consolationes cum gratia rumactione praedicat, & indubitata fide de futuris sperat.
units.tr: Notice also that he does not say in the past tense, "who comforted us in our past afflictions," but in the present, "who comforts us in every affliction of ours." He says this rejoicing not so much in a work of comfort he had experienced several times before, as in the continual and unending mercy of God towards himself, which he knew he had experienced before, and which he also believed and hoped he would experience in future, right up to the end. For when he says, "who comforts us in every tribulation of ours," this means: who, in his infinite mercy, never abandons us in any tribulation, but comforts us in all of them. In saying this he proclaims both past comforts with thanksgiving, and with unwavering faith hopes for future ones.

units.la: IN omni afflictione nostra, inquit.) Non dicit simpliciter, in tribulatione nostra, sed, in omni tribulatione nostra. Qui sic loquitur, significat se non modicis tribulationibus semel atq; iterum, sed frequenter multis ac grauibus affligi. At de his audiemus in sequentibus, capite uidelicet II. Forte suum athletâ dominus multis certaminibus exercere, & gloriam iuam in illo illustrare voluit.
units.tr: "In all our affliction," he says. He does not simply say "in our tribulation," but "in every tribulation of ours." By speaking in this way he signifies that he is afflicted not by slight tribulations, once or twice, but frequently and by many grievous ones. We shall hear more about these in what follows, namely in chapter 2. Perhaps the Lord wished to exercise his athlete with many contests and to make his own glory shine forth in him.

units.la: Et illud obserua. Qui consolatur nos inquit. Vbi in omni afflictione nostra. Ergo locum habent diuinae consolationes, non in quietis, securis, prosperè habentibus, ac dies suos in pace transigentibus, sed in tribulatis & afflictis.
units.tr: Notice this too. "Who comforts us," he says, "in all our affliction." Thus divine consolations have their place not among those who are quiet, secure and prospering, and who spend their days in peace, but among those who are troubled and afflicted.

units.la: Quid est autem quod non dicit, Qui consolatur nos post omnem tribulationem, nostrâ, sed, in omni tribulatione nostra? Duplex est consolationis genus. Vnum, quo afflicti in medijs tribulationibus quasi coelesti rore consolationibus spiritus in seipsis erigūtur & refocillantur. Alterum, quo post fine afflictionum pace, quiete, & coelesti gaudeo beantur, quale est quod de Lazaro dicebat Abrahā. Lazarus pertulit mala in uita sua, nunc consolatur. De priori genere loquens Apostolus non dicit: qui consolatur nos post omnē afflictionem, sed, in omni afflictione nostra. Licet enim subinde praesens terminaretur afflictio, mox tamen ingruebat alia, ut uix aliqua intermedia daretur respiratio: quemadmodum in tempestatibus marinis procella procellam sic excipit, ut nauis crebris reciprocantiū procellarum ictibus feriatur. In omnibus tamen recurrētibus illis afflictionibus non deserebat coelestis pater Apostolum suum, sed quoties noua irruebat tribulatio, toties noua illum consolatione spiritus sui erigebat, & in ipsa afflictione infractum seruabat. Hoc praedicans dicit: qui consolatur nos in omni afflictione nostra.
units.tr: But why does he not say, "who comforts us after every tribulation of ours," but "in every tribulation of ours"? There are two kinds of comfort. One is that by which the afflicted, in the midst of their tribulations, are raised up and refreshed in their spirits, as if by heavenly dew. The other is that by which, after the end of their afflictions, they are blessed with peace, rest and heavenly joy, as Abraham said of Lazarus: "Lazarus suffered evils in his life; now he is comforted." Speaking of the first kind, the Apostle does not say "who comforts us after every affliction," but "in every affliction of ours." For although the present affliction sometimes came to an end, another soon pressed in, so that there was hardly any breathing space in between. Just as in sea storms one gust follows another, so that the ship is battered by the repeated blows of returning squalls. Yet in all these recurring afflictions the heavenly Father did not abandon his Apostle. As often as a new tribulation rushed in, so often did he raise him up with a fresh comfort of his Spirit, and kept him unbroken in the very affliction. Declaring this, he says: "who comforts us in every affliction of ours."

units.la: IN hoc, inquit, ut possimus consolari eos, qui sunt in quauis afflictione, per consolationem qua consolatur nos ipsos Deus.) Vbi dixit: Benedictus Deus, &c. qui nos consolatur in omni afflictione nostra, ne suijpsius amore motus hoc in Deo laudare, quod se subinde in afflictionibus consolaretur, quo affectu & impij Deum laudant, cum benefacit ipsis, uel aliquid hinc sibi laudis uenari uideretur, quod tanti sit Deo, ut nusquam ab illo deferatur, rationem & usum gratiae huius assignans, & ad alios transferens subiungit: in hoc, ut possimus consolari eos, qui sunt in quauis afflictione, &c.
units.tr: "So that we may be able," he says, "to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God." Having said, "Blessed be God, etc., who comforts us in every affliction of ours," lest he should be moved by love of himself to praise God for this, that he is comforted from time to time in his afflictions (a feeling with which even the impious praise God when he does them good, or when some praise for themselves seems to be gained from it, as if it were so great a thing for God that it is never withdrawn from him), he assigns the reason and use of this grace and turns it to others, adding: "so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, etc."

units.la: Q. d. Et hoc facit misericordissimus pater, non tam mea quàm aliorum gratia ad hoc me in afflictionibus erigens, ut per me consoletur & alios suos filios, qui & ipsi, perinde atque ego, omnis generis afflictionibus exercentur, & opus habent crebris consolationibus, ne molē tribulationum supra uires oppresi cocidant.
units.tr: That is to say: the most merciful Father does this, raising me up in afflictions not so much for my own sake as for the sake of others, so that through me he may also comfort his other sons, who, just like me, are exercised by afflictions of every kind and need frequent consolations, lest they, oppressed by a weight of tribulations beyond their strength, collapse.

units.la: Est hic locus insignis. Proponitur nobis diuinae misericordiae prouidētia, qua nostrae infirmitatis corroborādae studio insigniora gratiae suae organa benignissimus pater sic reddit singulari fide, fortitudine, & patientia instructa, ut tota nobis seruandis constanter & animo infracto seruire possint. Huius rei exēpla praecesserunt in prophetis & apostolis. Quicquid diuinitus accepere prophetae in Veteri quicquid apostoli in Nouo testamēto, siue sin-gularem diuinae uoluntatis cognitionem, siue fidem, siue sermonis gratiam, siue alia charismata spiritus, siue tolerantiam afflictionum, accepere ut prophetae, ut doctores, ut apostoli, ut ministri, in usus fidelium, quorum gratia mittebantur, ut non modo tales essent ipsi, sed & donis acceptis populo Dei seruiret. Sic Apostolus diuinas consolationes interpretatur, quibus in omni afflictione sustentabatur, ut dicat eas ad hoc, sibi fuisse datas, ut erectus ipse erigeret per eas & alios, qui similiter affligebantur. Et hic est perpetuus singularium donorum Dei usus. Qui donum scientiae accepit, sciat se accepisse non tam propter se quàm propter alios instruendos ac docendos. Vnde illud tritum est. Scire tuum nihil est nisi quod scis sciat & alter. Qui diuitias accepit, cogitet eas sibi concessas esse ad succurrēdum egenis.
units.tr: This is a remarkable passage. We are shown the providence of divine mercy, by which the most kind Father, for the sake of strengthening our weakness, so equips the more outstanding instruments of his grace with singular faith, fortitude and patience that they can serve constantly and with unbroken spirit for the preservation of all of us. Examples of this went before in the prophets and apostles. Whatever the prophets received from God in the Old Testament, and whatever the apostles received in the New, whether a singular knowledge of the divine will, or faith, or gift of speech, or other gifts of the Spirit, or endurance of afflictions, they received as prophets, as teachers, as apostles, as ministers, for the use of the faithful, for whose sake they were sent, so that they should not only be such themselves but should also serve the people of God with the gifts they had received. So the Apostle interprets the divine comforts by which he was sustained in every affliction: he says that they were given to him for this purpose, that he, having been raised up, might by them raise up others too, who were suffering in the same way. This is the constant use of God's particular gifts. Whoever has received the gift of knowledge should recognise that he has received it not so much for himself as for instructing and teaching others. Hence the familiar saying: "Your knowledge is nothing unless the other person knows what you know." Whoever has received riches should consider that they have been granted to him to help the needy.

units.la: Qui dono est sapientiae praeditus, omnino sentiat se propterea alijs esse factum sapientiorem, ut sanis consilijs succurrat imperitis. Et quid aliud in ipsis corporum nostrorum membris quàm hęc eadem diuina prouidentia relucet? Quod oculi uidendi sunt facultatem consequuti, aures audiendi, caput intelligendi ac iudicandi, manus operandi, lingua loquendi, nares olfaciendi, pedes ambulandi, &c. an nō magis pro toto corpore facultates istas, quàm pro seipsis acceperunt? Quod Sol in coelo tam splēdidus & illustris, tanquam feruidus appa-ret, utique non suo ipsius, sed nostro bono talis est à Deo conditus, & in superiora coeli cōuexa locatus. Eadem est & Lunae & stellarum ratio, imò omnium eorum quae sunt condita.
units.tr: Whoever is endowed with the gift of wisdom should certainly recognise that he has therefore been made wiser than others, so that by sound counsel he may help the unskilled. And what else shines forth in the very members of our bodies but this same divine providence? The eyes have received the power of seeing, the ears of hearing, the head of understanding and judging, the hands of working, the tongue of speaking, the nostrils of smelling, the feet of walking, and so on. Have they not received these faculties for the good of the whole body rather than for themselves? The sun in heaven is so splendid and bright, and seems so fiery, that it has surely been made by God and placed in the highest part of the heavenly vault not for its own good but for ours. The same is true of the moon and the stars, indeed of everything that has been created.

units.la: Quin & angelorum conditio haec ipsa est, ut electis Dei seruiant. Sic omnia sunt nostra, siue Paulus, siue Apollo, siue Cephas, siue mundus, siue uita, siue mors, siue praesentia, siue futura. 1. Cor. 3. Cum itaq; tot modis diuina prouidentia rebus nostris, & uniuscuiusque egestati prospexerit, quis nam adeo est excors, ut desertū se & necessarijs bonis destitutū queri posit? Haec annotare uisum est ex eo quod non simpliciter dicit: qui nos consolatur in omni afflictione nostra, sic ut consolari possimus, &c. uel ut uulgatus interpres uertit, ut possimus & ipsi consolari, sed diserte, id est, ad hoc, ut possimus nos consolari eos, &c. Non enim tam abundati se consolatione recreari dicit, ut si uelit & alios consolari possit, sed agnoscit propte rea se tam iugi consolatione potiri diuinitus, ut per illam consolari possit & alios, & hac se diuina gratia debitore constitui omnibus illis qui & ipsi propter Christum affligebātur. Reperias facilè diuitem, qui sic se facultatibus huius saeculi instructum esse fateatur ut ex abundantia sua multorum pauperum necessi-tatibus succurrere possit modo uelit. At qui se propterea quas habet facultates accepisse sentiat & fateatur, ut illas magis pauperum quàm suijpsius rebus impendat, non ita facilè reperias.
units.tr: Indeed, the very condition of the angels is this, that they serve the elect of God. So all things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come (1 Cor. 3). Since, then, divine providence has looked after our needs and the needs of each one of us in so many ways, who is so foolish that he can complain of being forsaken and deprived of the goods he needs? I have thought it worth noting this from the fact that Paul does not simply say, "who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort," etc., or as the Vulgate translator renders it, "so that we may ourselves be able to comfort." He says it explicitly, that is, "for this purpose, that we may be able to comfort those," etc. For he does not say that he is so abundantly refreshed by consolation that, if he wishes, he can also console others. Rather, he acknowledges that he has been granted by God such a constant consolation that through it he can console others too, and that by this divine grace he is made a debtor to all those who also suffer for Christ. It is easy to find a rich man who admits that he is so equipped with the goods of this age that from his abundance he can relieve the needs of many poor, if only he is willing. But it is not so easy to find one who feels and admits that he has received the wealth he has in order to spend it on the needs of the poor rather than on his own.

units.la: VT possimus,inquit,consolari.) Ergo con solari alios non potuisset, nisi prius ipse cœle-sti fuisset consolatione suffultus. Quid enim infirma nostra caro in afflictionibus aliorum præstare poterit,nisi in proprijs diuina conso-latione firmetur: Diuinum quiddam est,con-solari afflictos. Non poterit hoc præstare,neq; qui nunquam tribulatus fuit ipse, inq; tribula-tione diuinam consolationem expertus, neq; qui quamuis sit afflictus, aliquid cõsolationis in seipso experitur. Loquimur autem non de consolationibus illis quæ solis uerbis ineffica-cibus, quibus nos qui ualemus facilè consilia damus ægrotis,sed de talibus, quæ uiuo spiri-tu efficaciter,tanquam per organa spiritus pa-racleti fiunt. Nam de hoc consolationum ge-nere loquitur hic Apostolus.
units.tr: "That we may be able to comfort," he says. So he could not have comforted others unless he had first beenupheld by heavenly consolation himself. For what can our weak flesh accomplish in the afflictions of others, unless it is first strengthened in its own by divine consolation? Comforting the afflicted is something divine. Neither one who has never himself been troubled, nor one who, though afflicted, has never experienced divine consolation in tribulation, will be able to do this. We are speaking not of those consolations which are ineffective in mere words, the kind we who are well easily give to the sick as advice, but of those which are effective through the living Spirit, as it were through the instruments of the Paraclete Spirit. For it is of this kind of consolation that the Apostle speaks here.

units.la: VT possimus,inquit, cõsolari eos qui sunt in quauis afflictione.) Loquitur de fidelibus, quos mundi huius princeps Satan per organa sua,homines impios ac sanguinarios, propter Christum omnibus quibus permittitur mo-dis affligit &exagitat. Horum rationem habet Deus plane singularem & paternam. Et quo-niá iuxta carnè sunt infirmi, ordinat ipsis spiri-tus sui paracleses,cùm per internum illius in-stinctum, tum per externa prophetarum & a-postolorum suorum ministeria. Talibus hic & Paulus destinatas suas scribit afflictiones pari-ter & consolationes. Admirabile est omnino consilium hoc Dei, quo sic disponit infirma ec-clesiæ suæ membra, ut afflictus unus quamplu-rimis sit afflictis solatio & cõfirmationi.Posset ad consolados afflictos mittere cœlitùs ange-los nullis afflictionibus obnoxios.Verum pla-cet ipsi,sic declarare suâ in infirma nostra car-ne uirtutem, ut quod infirmũ est per se ad con-solandum cæterorum infirmorum imbecilli-tatem paternæ suæ curæ seruiat. Nihil hic loci est magnis illis ecclesiarum dominis ac præ-latis, qui magis ad hoc sunt per irâ Dei accom-modi,ut secundum morem falsorû pastorum, lac ouium comedant, lanis operiantur, quod crassum est macten t,quod infirmum non cor-roborent, quod ægrotum non sanent, quod contritum non alligent, quod abieƈtum non reducant,quod perijt non requirant,quàm ut afflictos in tribulationibus consolètur,quam-uis successores apostolorum uideri uelint.
units.tr: "That we may be able," he says, "to comfort those who are in any affliction." He speaks of the faithful, whom Satan, the prince of this world, afflicts and harasses in every possible way on account of Christ, through his instruments, impious and bloodthirsty men. God has a plainly singular and fatherly regard for them. And since they are weak according to the flesh, he appoints for them the comforts of his Spirit, both through the inner prompting of that Spirit and through the external ministries of his prophets and apostles. It is to such people that Paul here writes that his afflictions and consolations are equally destined. This counsel of God is altogether admirable, by which he so arranges the weak members of his Church that one afflicted person becomes a solace and strengthening to very many who are afflicted. He could have sent angels from heaven, who are subject to no afflictions, to console the afflicted. But he is pleased rather to display his power in our weak flesh, so that what is weak in itself serves, by his fatherly care, to console the weakness of other weak people. Those great lords and prelates of the churches have no part in this. They are more fitted, by the wrath of God, to do as false ministers do, eat the milk of the sheep, cover themselves with the wool, slaughter the fat, not strengthen the weak, not heal the sick, not bind up the broken, not bring back the straying, not seek the lost, than to console the afflicted in their tribulations, although they wish to be seen as successors of the apostles.

units.la: PER consolationem, inquit, qua nosipsos consolatur Deus.) Potest hæc particula bifa-riam exponi. Primò sic,ut referatur ad præce-dens uerbum posimus,doceatq; unde potue-rit Apostolus alios consolari afflictos,hoc est, unde fuerit in eam rem animo factus erecto & apposito. Ex consolatione,inquit,qua nos cõ-solatur Deus. Diuina illâ consolatio instructû & idoneû reddidit ad hoc, ut alios quoque in tribulationibus consolaretur.Deinde,ut refe-ratur ad uerbum consolari, quasi dicat se afflì-ctos eadem qua ipse sit refocillatus, consolatio-ne erigere & cõfirmare. Aliud est,unde possis, & aliud quomodo quod potes facias. Conso-
units.tr: "Through the consolation," he says, "with which God himself comforts us." This phrase can be explained in two ways. First, it may be referred to the preceding word "that we may be able," and show from where the Apostle was able to console the afflicted, that is, from what he had been made ready and disposed in mind for this task. "From the consolation," he says, "with which God comforts us." That divine consolation made him equipped and fit to console others too in their tribulations. Second, it may be referred to the verb "to console," as if he means that he raises up and strengthens the afflicted by the same consolation with which he himself has been revived. One thing is to know whence you may do something, and another is how you do what you can do.

units.la: lationes illę, quibus ipse per spiritum sanctum in tribulationibus erigebatur, non erant in ipsius potestate, ut uteretur illis ad consolan-dum alios:sed sic per eas cõfirmabatur,ut ani-mo esset ad consolandum afflictos apposito, idq; consolationibus quas ad id instituti sin-gulariter,& ad uniuscuiusque conditionẽ con-formiter subministrabat spiritus.
units.tr: Those consolations by which he himself was raised up in tribulations through the Holy Spirit were not in his own power, so that he could use them to console others. Rather, through them he was so strengthened that he was disposed in mind to console the afflicted, and this by consolations which the Spirit supplied, singularly appointed for this purpose and suited to the condition of each person.

units.la: Lyranus tamen posteriorem sensum sequi-tur. Exponit enim ad hunc modũ:Proponen-do eis præmium æteruũ sicut à Deo nobis est propositũ,& exponendo eis scripturas indu-centes ad tolerantiam passionum,si ut à Deo reuelatæ sunt nobis. Staret hæc expositio, si Apostolum suum Deus proponendo ei præ-mium æternum, & exponendo scripturas, & non magis interno spiritus sui afflatu in omni esset afflictione consolatus.
units.tr: Lyra, however, follows the second sense. He explains it in this way: "By setting before them the eternal reward, as it has been set before us by God, and by expounding to them the Scriptures which lead them to endure sufferings, as they have been revealed to us by God." This explanation would stand if God had comforted his Apostle in every affliction only by setting before him the eternal reward and by expounding the Scriptures, and not rather by the inward breath of his Spirit.

units.la: Sunt qui exponât de efficacia exẽpli, quasi Apostolus quoties in aduersis diuina esset cõ-solatione confirmatus ac seruatus,exẽplo suo alios afflictos erexerit. Si diceret,qui nos con-solatur in omni afflictione nostra ut & eos qui in omni sunt afflictione consoletur per conso-lationem qua nos consolatur,esset hæc exposi-tio haud impertinens. Iam,quoniam dicit, ad hoc,ut possimus consolari eos qui sunt in om-ni afflictione,per consolationem qua nosipsos consolatur Deus,puto illam non sufficientem habere sensum. Multæ quidem efficaciæ sunt exempla sanctorum, quos Deus in omni est tribulatione cõsolatus, uerum Apostolus hoc loco magis deprædicat diuinam in se opera-ratione, qua reddebatur ad consoládum alios instructus,quàm exempli sui efficaciam.
units.tr: There are those who explain it of the efficacy of example, as if the Apostle, whenever he was strengthened and kept in adversity by divine consolation, raised up the afflicted by his own example. If he had said, "who comforts us in every affliction of ours, so that he may also comfort those who are in every affliction, by the consolation with which we ourselves are comforted," this explanation would not be irrelevant. But since he says, "so that we may be able to comfort those who are in every affliction, through the consolation with which God himself comforts us," I think that explanation does not have sufficient sense. There are indeed many examples of the efficacy of saints whom God has comforted in every tribulation. But here the Apostle emphasises more the divine work in himself, by which he was made equipped to console others, than the efficacy of his own example.

units.la: Concedimus f. c. lé. etiam mortuos sanƈtos per eam nos consolationem in afflictionibus posse consolari, qua ipsos Deus dum in uiuis essent in afflictione bu. est consolatus,si inteĺi-gas de uirtute exempli. Huc facit illud Chri-sti Matth.5.Beati estis cum probra iecerint in uos,& insectati fuerint,& dixerint omne ma-lum uerbũ aduersum uos mentientes propter me. Gaudete & exultate, quoniá merces ue-stra multa est in cœlis. Sic enim persequuti fuerunt prophetas,qui fuerũt ante uos. Ecce prophetæ mortui consolantur uiuos, uerum nonnili exempli ipsorum respeƈtu. Verum si uelis illis id genus cõsolationis tribuere, quo-dum in uiuis essent diuinis consolationibus suffulti alios consolari potuerunt,planè fuerit hoc falsum ac superstitiosum.
units.tr: We grant that even dead saints can console us in afflictions by that consolation with which God comforted them while they were living in their afflictions, if you understand it of the power of example. To this belongs that saying of Christ in Matthew 5: "Blessed are you when men revile you, and persecute you, and say all manner of evil against you falsely for my sake. Rejoice and be exceedingly glad, for your reward is great in heaven. For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you." Behold, the dead prophets console the living, but only by the regard for their example. But if you wish to attribute to them that kind of consolation by which, while they were alive, they were upheld by divine consolations and were able to console others, that would clearly be false and superstitious.

units.la: QVONIAM,inquit, sicut abundát afflictio-nes Christi in nobis, ita per Christum abúdat & consolatio nostra.) Rationem reddit eius quod Deũ & patrem domini nostri Iesu Chri-sti consolari se in omni afflictione dixit. Hanc transfert in ipsum Christum, ac taliter ponit, ut prorsus reddat, in gratiam infirmorũ pro-babilem. Poterat simpliciter dicere:quoniam per Christum abundat in nobis consolatio no stra,uerum ut æquitatem quandam eius gra-tiæ exprimeret,qua illam probabilẽ redderet, quoquoniam, inquit, sicut abundant afflictiones Christi in nobis, ita per Christum abundat & consolatio nostra. Etenim communi sensu censetur æquum, ut qui propter dominum suum abundanter affligitur, per dominum suum vicissim abundanti consolatione refocilletur.
units.tr: "Since," he says, "as the afflictions of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds." He gives the reason for what he said, that God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ comforts him in every affliction. He transfers this reason to Christ himself, and so puts it that he makes it entirely probable in the eyes of the weak. He could simply have said, "since through Christ our consolation abounds in us." But in order to express a certain fairness of that grace, by which he makes it plausible, he says, "since, as the afflictions of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds." For by common sense it is judged fair that one who is abundantly afflicted for the sake of his Lord should in turn be abundantly refreshed by consolation through his Lord.

units.la: QVONIAM, inquit, sicut abundant afflictiones Christi in nobis.) Non dicit simpliciter, quoniam sicut abundant afflictiones in nobis, sed sicut abundant afflictiones Christi in nobis: ut quemadmodum consolationes relaturus est ad Christum, ita referat ad illum & afflictiones. Vocat autem afflictiones Christi neq; quas ille pertulerit, neq; quas alijs inferat, sed quas ipse propter Christum à mundo illatas tolerabat. Lyranus sic. Id est, tribulationes quæ in capite Christo inceperunt. Hieron. tamen, quemadmodum & in Comment. quæ Ambrosio tribuuntur legitur, id est, pro nomine Christi inquit. Et Chrysost. quoq; de afflictionibus intelligit, quas propter Christum ferebat.
units.tr: WHEREAS, he says, as the afflictions of Christ abound in us.) He does not say simply, "since as afflictions abound in us," but "as the afflictions of Christ abound in us," so that just as he will refer the consolations to Christ, so he refers the afflictions to him as well. He calls them the afflictions of Christ, not those that he himself endured, nor those he inflicts on others, but those which he bore from the world on account of Christ. Lyra explains it thus: that is, the tribulations which began in Christ the Head. Jerome, however, as is read also in the commentaries attributed to Ambrose, says: that is, for the name of Christ. Chrysostom too understands it of the afflictions which he suffered on account of Christ.

units.la: Loquutionem hanc diligenter observemus, qua quæ propter Christum nobis inferuntur afflictiones, Christi afflictiones vocantur. Proprie non sunt Christi, nisi quas ipse olim in carne sua propter peccata nostra pertulit. Et tamen hæ quoq; quas propter ipsum patiuntur fideles, ipsius esse dicuntur. Huius duæ sunt rationes. Prima est ex eo quod ipse harum est causa. Ipsum siquidem in nobis mundus hic persequitur. Si de mundo essemus, & non ad Christum pertineremus, non persequeretur sed diligeret nos mundus. Verum quoniam ipse nos è mundo hoc elegit, & à colluvie impiorum seperauit, odit nos mundus non ut homines peccatores sed ut Christianos. Altera hinc est, quod ipse est caput nostrum, & nos ipsius membra, atq; ita hoc quoq; nomine afflictiones nostræ ipsius sunt, cuius sumus membra. Hæ duæ rationes locum habent non modo in afflictionibus propter Christum illatis, sed & in omnibus studijs & operibus, quæ propter Christum ab ijs qui Christi sunt fiunt. Sic omnia fraternæ charitatis opera, quibus alij aliorum fratrum necessitatibus seruimus, Christi sunt opera, quia propter Christū & Christi membris impenduntur. Hinc illud est, Esuriui & cibastis me. Et, quod uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis. Et illud, Saule, Saule, quid me persequeris? Dici non potest, quàm hæc cogitatio si perpetua mentibus nostris insederit, efficax fit cum ad faciendum, tum ad patiendum omnia, quæ pro Christi nomine vel facienda sunt vel perferenda. Etiamsi nihil emolumenti speran dum esset ex afflictionibus pro Christo toleratis, id tamen unū abundè refocillare posseт Christi amantes quod pro Christi nomine affliguntur. Sic apostoli Christi gaudebant, quod digni habiti essent qui pro nomine Christi contumelijs à concilio sacerdotum afficerentur.
units.tr: Let us carefully note this way of speaking, by which the afflictions brought upon us on account of Christ are called the afflictions of Christ. Strictly speaking, they are not Christ's, except those which he himself once suffered in his flesh for our sins. Yet these also, which the faithful suffer for his sake, are said to be his. There are two reasons for this. The first is that he himself is their cause. For the world persecutes us in him. If we were of the world and did not belong to Christ, the world would not persecute us but would love us. But since he has chosen us out of this world and set us apart from the filth of the wicked, the world hates us not as sinful men but as Christians. The second is that he is our head and we are his members, and so on this account too our afflictions are his, since we are the members of him. These two reasons apply not only to afflictions suffered on account of Christ but also to all the zeal and works which those who belong to Christ perform on account of Christ. Thus all the works of brotherly love, by which we serve one another in the needs of our brethren, are the works of Christ, because they are bestowed on account of Christ and on the members of Christ. Hence that saying: "I was hungry and you gave me food"; and "What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me"; and that: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" It cannot be said how efficacious this thought becomes, if it has settled perpetually in our minds, both for doing and for suffering all things which must be done or endured for the name of Christ. Even if no advantage were to be hoped for from afflictions endured for Christ, this one thing alone would abundantly refresh those who love Christ, that they are afflicted for the name of Christ. Thus the apostles of Christ rejoiced that they were counted worthy to be treated with contempt by the council of priests for the name of Christ.

units.la: Quid autem de eo dicendum est afflictionum genere, quo neq; ab infidelibus sed à Christianis, ecclesiarum Christi magistris, dominis, præulatis, pontificibus, principibus ac regibus catholicissimis & Christianissimis, neque sic propter Christum quod hunc ipsi persequantur, sed quòd illi se putet præstare obsequium persequendo hæreticos & ecclesiæ ipsius inimicos, affliguntur nostra hac ætate omnium atrocissime, quotquot Papatui Romano valedicentes ad puram Euangelij Christi doctrinam aspirant. Si persequutorum intentionem respicias, sunt hę afflictiones afflictiones Christi utpote propter Christum hæreticis illatæ. Sed hinc afflictis nihil esse potest consolationis plurimum uero condemnationis. Si uero patientium consideres causam & intentionem, sustinet illi afflictiones non ut aduersarij Christi & ecclesiæ hostes, sed ut uerbi illius sectato res, ac ueræ & primæ ecclesiæ illius confortes, atq; ita propter Christū afflicti Christi patiuntur afflictiones, quàtumuis aliter interpretentur illorum persequutores. Hoc sensu plurimū consolationis est afflictis & horribilis condemnatio Cainis illis fratrum suorum persequutoribus & parricidis. Non refert hic, neq; à quib. affligatur uerus Christianus, siue ab extraneis & infidelibus ex professo Christi hostibus, siue à falsis Christianis nomen Christi profitentibus, neque quid prætendat persequutor, sed ueritas causæ inspicitur, propter quam odio habetur & affligi sustinet qui affligitur. Secundum hæc iudicatur etiam Augustino teste, qui non passionem sed causam martyrem facere dicit. Immo præstantius est martyrij genus, si quis uerus Christianus à pseudochristianis propterea affligatur, quod mauult uerbo Christi obedire, quàm conspirationi illorum & manifestis superstitionibus cōsentire, quàm si à manifestis Christi hostibus propter nomen Christi affligeretur. Quemadmodum illustrior est patientia Abel, quòd à fratre propter religionis puritatem Deo acceptā occisus est, quàm si occisus esset ab alienis. Et martyria prophetarum hoc nomine sunt clariora, quòd ab ipsis populi Dei primoribus propter impositū pro phetandi munus sunt occisi, quā si interempti essent ab ethnicis, ab ecclesia Israelis alienis.
units.tr: But what must be said of that kind of affliction, in which men suffer most atrociously of all in our age, not from unbelievers but from Christians, the teachers, lords, prelates, pontiffs, princes and kings of the Churches of Christ, the most Catholic and most Christian, and not in such a way that they persecute him on account of Christ, but because they think they render obedience by persecuting heretics and enemies of the Church itself? All who, bidding farewell to the Roman Papacy, aspire to the pure doctrine of the Gospel of Christ. If you look to the intention of the persecutors, these afflictions are afflictions of Christ, as being inflicted on heretics on account of Christ. But from this the afflicted can have no consolation, but very great condemnation. If, however, you consider the cause and intention of those who suffer, they endure these afflictions not as adversaries of Christ and enemies of the Church, but as followers of that Word and as true partakers of that first Church, and so those who are afflicted on account of Christ suffer the afflictions of Christ, however their persecutors may interpret it otherwise. In this sense there is much consolation for the afflicted, and a dreadful condemnation for those Cains, the persecutors and murderers of their brothers. It makes no difference here, either by whom the true Christian is afflicted, whether by strangers and unbelievers who are openly enemies of Christ, or by false Christians who profess the name of Christ, nor what the persecutor pretends; but the truth of the cause is examined, on account of which he who is afflicted is hated and suffers affliction. By this judgment, too, according to the witness of Augustine, who says that it is not the suffering but the cause that makes a martyr. Indeed, a kind of martyrdom is more excellent if a true Christian is afflicted by pseudo-Christians because he prefers to obey the word of Christ rather than consent to their conspiracy and manifest superstitions, than if he were afflicted for the name of Christ by open enemies of Christ. Just as the patience of Abel is more illustrious, because he was killed by his brother for the purity of his religion acceptable to God, than if he had been killed by strangers. And the martyrdoms of the prophets are more famous on this account, because they were killed by the chief men of the people of God themselves on account of the office of prophesying laid upon them, than if they had been slain by the heathen, aliens from the Church of Israel.

units.la: QVONIAM, inquit, sicut abundát afflictio nes Christi in nobis.) Quoniam non simpliciter dicit: sicut multæ uel magnæ sunt, sed, sicut abundant, quæri potest quo respectu afflictiones Christi abundare in se dicat. Etenim omnis abundantia aliquo dici respectu uidetur eius uidelicet rei supra quam abundando excellit. Chrysost. respicit ad ea quæ Christus in carne sua passus est, quasi afflictiones fidelium tum temporis abúdauerint supra afflictiones Christi. Verū, meo iudicio, loquitur hic Apostolus non ipsius Christi, sed cæterorum fidelium, etiam apostolorum respectu, cum in se Christi dicit abundare afflictiones. Quemadmodum enim plus cæteris in opere Christi laborauit, ita & pluribus est afflictionibus quàm cæteri exercitatus.
units.tr: WHEREAS, he says, as the afflictions of Christ abound in us.) He does not simply say, "as they are many or great," but "as they abound"; one may ask in what respect he says the afflictions of Christ abound in himself. For every abundance seems to be in respect of something, namely that thing beyond which it excels by abounding. Chrysostom refers to what Christ himself suffered in his flesh, as if the afflictions of the faithful at that time abounded beyond the afflictions of Christ. But, in my judgment, the Apostle here speaks not with respect to Christ himself but to the other faithful, even the apostles, when he says that the afflictions of Christ abound in himself. For just as he labored more than the others in the work of Christ, so he was exercised with more afflictions than the others.

units.la: ITA per Christum, inquit, abundat & consolatio solatio nostra.) Quoniam ad hoc destinatus erat singulari consilio Dei, ut non modò doce ret errantes ac Christo lucrifaceret plurimos, sed & ut afflictos in omni tribulatione conso laretur, res ipsa poscebat, ut abundanti cosola tione per gratiam Christi potiretur ipse, & in hunc usum instructus redderetur. Huc tende bant abundantes illius afflictiones, quas tamè pseudapostoli magis ad detrimentum Aposto latus ipsius quàm ad ornamentum sinistrè in terpretabantur. Ipse uero hanc illarum utilita tem esse docet, quòd per Christum hoc sit in structior ad consolandum afflictos factus, quo abundantius ipse cæteris sit afflictatus.
units.tr: SO through Christ, he says, our consolation also abounds.) Because by the singular counsel of God he was destined for this, that he should not only teach those who erred and win very many to Christ, but also comfort the afflicted in every tribulation, the matter itself required that he should obtain abundant consolation through the grace of Christ, and be made fit for this use. To this end his abundant afflictions tended, which, however, the false apostles interpreted perversely, more to the detriment of his apostleship than to its ornament. But he himself teaches that the usefulness of those afflictions is this: that through Christ he has been made more fitted to console the afflicted, the more abundantly he himself has been afflicted beyond the others.

units.la: ITA per Christum, inquit.) Quid est quod non dicit, ita & consolatio Christi abundat in nobis, sed, ita per Christum abundat & conso latio nostra? Si consolatio ipsius perinde atq; afflictio Christi fuisset, recte dixisset, ita & con solatio Christi abundat in nobis. Verùm aliter Christi erant afflictiones quas ferebat, & aliter Christi erat consolatio de qua loquitur. Illæ nanque Christi erát, propterea quod propter Christum inferebantur, hæc uero propterea quod per Christum cóferebatur. Quare ne ui deatur consolatio fidelium non esse Christi ali ter quàm quomodo illius sunt illorū afflictio nes, diligenter & cautè non dixit, ita & conso latio Christi, sed, ita per Christum abundat & consolatio nostra. Aliud est, si consoletur nos pater misericordiarû propter Christū, quem admodum affligit nos mundus propter Chri- stum, & aliud, si hoc faciat per Christum, quod facit etiam, dum corda nostra per spiritū Chri sti fidelium omnium paracletum, id est, conso latorem consolatur & erigit.
units.tr: SO through Christ, he says.) Why does he not say, "so also the consolation of Christ abounds in us," but "so through Christ our consolation also abounds"? If his consolation had been in the same way as the affliction of Christ, he would have rightly said, "so also the consolation of Christ abounds in us." But the afflictions which he bore were Christ's in one way, and the consolation of which he speaks was Christ's in another. For the former were Christ's because they were inflicted on account of Christ, but the latter because it was conferred through Christ. Therefore, lest the consolation of the faithful seem not to be Christ's in the same way that their afflictions are his, he carefully and cautiously did not say, "so also the consolation of Christ," but "so through Christ our consolation also abounds." It is one thing if the Father of mercies comforts us on account of Christ, just as the world afflicts us on account of Christ; and another thing if he does this through Christ, which he also does, while through the Spirit of Christ he comforts and raises up our hearts, that is, the Comforter of all the faithful.

units.la: ABVNDAT & consolatio nostra, inquit.) Amphibolum est an de ea loquatur cósolatio ne, qua in afflictionibus suis ipse confirmaba tur per Christum, uel de ea, qua alios ipse in o mni afflictione consolabatur.
units.tr: "And our consolation abounds," he says. It is ambiguous whether he means the consolation by which he himself was strengthened through Christ in his own afflictions, or the consolation by which he comforted others in every affliction.

units.la: Prior sententia magis placet. Ea autem re stius exprimitur si legamus, abundat & conso latio nostri, quàm, abúdat & cósolatio nostra.
units.tr: The former opinion pleases more. It is expressed more precisely if we read "and the consolation of us abounds" rather than "and our consolation abounds."

units.la: Siue autem affligimur, pro uestri consolatione ac salute, quæ operatur in tolerantia earundem afflictionum, quas & nos patimur, siue consolationem accipimus, pro uestri consolatione ac salute. Spes enim nostra firma est pro uobis, cū sciamus, qd sicut participes estis afflictionum sic futuri sitis & consolationis.
units.tr: "Whether we are afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation, which works through the endurance of the same afflictions that we also suffer; or whether we receive consolation, it is for your consolation and salvation. For our hope for you is firm, since we know that as you are partakers of the afflictions, so you will also be of the consolation."

units.la: Vulgata æditio aliter habet hoc loco. Ad hunc uidelicet modum. Siue autē tribulamur pro uestra exhortatione & salute, siue consola mur, pro uestra cōsolatione, siue exhortamur, pro uestra exhortatiōe & salute. Quod in Græ co est ΕΙΤΕ ΤΗΣ ΥΜΩΝ ΠΑΡΑΚΛΗΣΕΩΣ. i. pro uestri con solatione, uertit interpres, pro uestra exhorta tione. Ἰτὲ ΕΙΤΕ ΠΑΡΑΚΑΛΟΥΜΕΘΑ ΥΠΕΡ ΤΗΣ ΥΜΩΝ ΠΑΡΑΚΛΗΣΕΩΣ, id est, siue consolationem accipimus, uel,
units.tr: The Vulgate edition reads differently here, in this way: "Whether we are troubled, it is for your exhortation and salvation; whether we are consoled, it is for your consolation; whether we exhort, it is for your exhortation and salvation." In the Greek it is "for your consolation" [εἴτε τῆς ὑμῶν παρακλήσεως], which the translator rendered "for your exhortation." That is, "whether we receive consolation, or" [εἴτε παρακαλούμεθα ὑπὲρ τῆς ὑμῶν παρακλήσεως].

units.la: ΖΙVE autem affligimur, inquit, pro uestri consolatione ac salute.) Intellige affligimur, sit uel disponitur, aut tale quid aliud. Nam om nino uerbum eiusmodi aliquod desideratur in utroq; mébro, quo sensus impleatur. Eras. reddidit, id fit pro uestri cófolatione ac salute. Præcedentia, quibus ista cohærent, duobus membris, de afflictionibus Christi uno, de co solatione afflictorū quæ per Christum est alte ro contexta sunt. Illis rationem & usum affli ctionum & consolationum suarum adiecit, di cens, ut possimus consolari eos qui in quauis sunt afflictione. Rationem hanc declaraturus duo illa membra repetit, & eam unicuiq; illo rum accommodat & amplificat. De afflictio nibus sic dicit: Siue autè affligimur, id fit pro uestri consolatione ac salute. De consolationi bus ad hunc modum subijcit: Siue consolatio nem accipimus, id fit pro uestri consolatione ac salute.
units.tr: "But whether we are afflicted," he says, "it is for your consolation and salvation." Understand "we are afflicted" as "is brought about" or "is disposed," or something of that kind, for some such verb is indeed lacking in both members to complete the sense. Erasmus rendered it: "this happens for your consolation and salvation." The preceding clauses to which these are joined were framed in two members: one about the afflictions of Christ, the other about the consolation of the afflicted, which is through Christ. To these he added the reason and use of his afflictions and consolations, saying that we are able to console those who are in any affliction. Intending to explain this reason, he repeats the two members and applies and amplifies it to each. About afflictions he says: "Whether we are afflicted, this happens for your consolation and salvation." About consolations he adds in this way: "Whether we receive consolation, this happens for your consolation and salvation."

units.la: SIVE autem affligimur, inquit, siue con solationem accipimus.) Non est ociosum quod de afflictionibus & consolationibus sic distinctim loquitur. Afflictiones Christi sic cómendat, ut etiá citra consolationem consi deratas utiles esse doceat. De utilitate conso lationū declaranda minus erat negocij, & ta men de illa quoq; subijcit. Siue autem affligi mur, inquit. Magna ratio est, quod de afflictio nibus seorsim loquitur. Neq; enim mox adest illis consolatio talis, quæ spectantium oculos incurrat, & in seipsis admodum sunt horribi les. Propositum igitur est sic eas commendare ut seorsim consideratæ, admodum utiles de prehendantur. Quasi dicat, Siue affligimur, nō est ut uos afflictionum nostrarum inamœ nus aspectus à ueritate Euangelij in hoc mun do sectâda absterreat. Etenim afflictiones hæ Christi quas patimur quâtumuis carni uidean tur acerbe, suauisimū tamē fructum gignunt, dum cōsolationi ac saluti uestræ seruiūt. Qua re ne audiatis eos, qui ex illis colligunt, displi cere domino Apostolatum nostrum, quasi ar gumentum habeant irati nobis Dei, cum argu mento potius sint diuinæ erga uos prouiden tiæ, qua sic disponuntur, ut consolationi ac sa luti uestræ seruiant.
units.tr: "Whether we are afflicted," he says, "or receive consolation." It is not idle that he speaks of afflictions and consolations separately in this way. He commends the afflictions of Christ so as to teach that they are useful even when considered apart from consolation. Explaining the usefulness of consolations was less of a task, yet he adds that too. "Whether, however, we are afflicted," he says. There is a good reason why he speaks of afflictions separately. For that consolation which catches the eyes of onlookers is not immediately present to them, and in themselves they are very dreadful. His purpose, therefore, is to commend them so that, considered separately, they may be seen to be very useful. As if he said: "Whether we are afflicted, the unattractive look of our afflictions should not frighten you away from following the truth of the gospel in this world. For these afflictions of Christ which we suffer, however bitter they may seem to the flesh, nevertheless bring forth a very sweet fruit while they serve your consolation and salvation. So do not listen to those who gather from them that God is displeased with our apostleship, as if they had an argument that God is angry with us; whereas they are rather an argument of divine providence toward you, by which they are so arranged that they serve your consolation and salvation."

units.la: QVÆ operatur, inquit, in tolerantia earun dem afflictionum quas & nos patimur.) Ex
units.tr: "Which works," he says, "in the endurance of the same afflictions that we also suffer."

units.la: positio est eius quod afflictiones suas ad ipsorum consolationem ac salute facere dixit. Docet enim quomodo id fiat. Dum enim affligimur, inquit, nostrarũ afflictionũ exemplo corroborantur & incitantur animi uestri ad eorundē malorũ toleratiam: ut quemadmodum uidetis nos pro Christi nomine fortiter quauis ferendo cōtra mundum hūc & principem illius decertare, ita ad eadem certamina sustinenda armemini & uos. Et cum hoc facitis afflictionum mearum exemplo moti, utiq; salus uestra exeritur, & quodammodo perficitur, atq; ita fit, ut dum affligimur pro consolatione ac salute uestra affligamur. Si quod in Græco est τῆς ἐνεργουμένης haud illibeter ad dictionem salutis quæ praecedit referimus, & sensu passiuo accipimus, quod & Chrysostomus facit, dum annotat, nō legi ἐνεργοῦσης, quod actiuum esset, sed ἐνεργουμένης quod passiuā habet significationem. & exponit idem esse, quod, declaratur, augescit, & intenditur dum patientiam sibi coniunctam habet, dum patitur, dum omnia fortiter tolerat. Germanicus interpres uertit ad hunc modum, Vuölches heil bevueyset sich, so ist leidet mit gedult dermassen vnte vuir leiden. Potest tamen non incommode uerti, quæ efficax redditur in toleratia earundē afflictionū, hoc est, ad tolerandū easdem afflictiones quas & nos patimur. Quod si cui illud, in toleratia, idem esse uidetur, quod per tolerantiā earundem afflictionum, non admodū reclamauero.
units.tr: This is an explanation of what he said, that his afflictions make for their consolation and salvation, for he teaches how this comes about. For while we are afflicted, he says, your minds are strengthened and stirred up by the example of our afflictions to endure the same evils, so that just as you see us bravely contending for the name of Christ, bearing whatever comes against this world and its prince, so you too may arm yourselves to sustain the same struggles. And when you do this, moved by the example of my afflictions, your salvation is surely brought forth and in some way completed, and so it comes about that while we are afflicted, we are afflicted for your consolation and salvation. If what is in the Greek is "effective" [τῆς ἐνεργουμένης], we refer it not unwillingly to the salvation that precedes, and take it in a passive sense, as Chrysostom also does, when he notes that it is not read "ἐνεργούσης" [active], but "ἐνεργουμένης" [passive in meaning]; and he explains it as the same as "is declared, grows and is intensified," while it has patience joined to it, while it suffers, while it bears everything bravely. The German translator renders it thus: "whose salvation shows itself effective, so that it suffers patiently just as we suffer." It can nevertheless fairly be rendered: "which is made effective in the endurance of the same afflictions," that is, "for enduring the same afflictions that we also suffer." But if anyone thinks that "in endurance" is the same as "through endurance of the same afflictions," I shall not greatly object.

units.la: Non est autem, ut insoles putemus, si detur afflictionibus Christi, quas fideles in hac carne pro nomine ipsius, & ueritatis confessione patiuntur, quod salutem ipsorum uel operentur, uel efficacem ac certiorem reddant. Nam infrà cap. 4. sic diserte dicit: Etenim momenta nea leuitas afflictionis nostræ supra modum æternum pondus gloriæ parit nobis. Et Christus beatos uocat, qui persequutionem patiū tur propter iusticiam. Matth. 5. Et ad Rom. 5. datur afflictionibus quod pariant patientiam, patientiæ, quod gignat probationem, probationi, quod operetur spem tam certam, ut non pudefaciat sperantem. Interea tamen propriè loquendo non operantur nostræ afflictiones salutem, quę opus est diuinæ misericordiæ per redemptorem Christum, cuius fide reddimur participes. Verū sic recte loquimur, quod per gratiam Dei fides nostra per quam seruamur tribulationibus exercetur, comprobatur, crescit, & corrobatur, atq; ita ipsa quoq; salus nostra magis ac magis perficitur & confirmatur.
units.tr: Nor should we think it absurd if it is granted that the afflictions of Christ, which the faithful suffer in this flesh for his name and the confession of the truth, either work their salvation or make it more effective and certain. For below, in chapter 4, he says plainly: "For our momentary and light affliction produces for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure." And Christ calls blessed those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake (Matth. 5). And in Rom. 5 it is said that afflictions produce patience, patience produces proof, and proof produces a hope so sure that it does not disappoint the one who hopes. Meanwhile, however, properly speaking our afflictions do not work salvation, which is the work of divine mercy through the Redeemer Christ, of whose faith we are made partakers. But we speak rightly in this way: that through the grace of God our faith, by which we are kept, is exercised, tested, grows and is strengthened by tribulations, and thus our salvation too is more and more perfected and confirmed.

units.la: Illud interim obseruet diligēs lector, quod suas afflictiones Apostolus fidelibus Corinthiorum ad hoc ualuisse dicit, ut ad cōsimilem malorum tolerantiam animarentur & ipsi. Sic fiebat, ut quo plus sæuiret Satan in religionis Christianę professores, hoc plures ad eandem fidei constantiam excitarētur. Hinc illud Tertulliani est, quo sanguinem Christianorum semen esse scribit. Videbat hoc Iulianus Aposta ta, ideoq; clementior erga Christianos in spe- ciem apparens, abstinebat à sæuitia, qua ante ipsum hostes Christi usi fuerat: non quod illis parceret, sed ne Christianismus pristino suo more quo magis afflictionib. premeretur, hoc magis inualesceret. Vide hac de re Sozomenum lib. 5. cap. 4. Et hoc ipsum hodie quoque uidere licet in illis regionibus ac regnis, quorū principes persequutionibus, vinculis, proscriptionibus, bonorum confiscationibus, gladio, laqueis & igne propter ueritatem Euāgelij Dei ac defectionem ab Antichristianismo in Christianos sæuiunt. Quo nanque sequitiam hanc magis ac magis intendunt, hoc numerus fidelium magis ac magis crescit, sic ut iam multi tudo illorum ipsis tyrannis pertimescenda uideri possit. Sic uidelicet constatia eorum, qui pro ueritate Christi quæuis mala fortiter tolerant, aliorum quoq; consolationi ac saluti conducit, infatuatq; consilia impiorū, quibus dum ueritatem Dei in sanguine fidelium sæuiendo subuerti posse putant, occasionem præbent, qua magis illa inualescat quàm subuertatur.
units.tr: Meanwhile let the diligent reader observe that the Apostle says his afflictions were of value to the faithful Corinthians for this purpose: that they too might be encouraged to endure similar evils. Thus it happened that the more Satan raged against the professors of the Christian religion, the more were stirred up to the same constancy of faith. Hence is that saying of Tertullian, in which he writes that the blood of Christians is seed. Julian the Apostate saw this, and therefore, appearing milder toward Christians in outward show, he refrained from the cruelty which the enemies of Christ had used before him: not because he spared them, but lest Christianity, as in its former manner, should grow the stronger the more it was pressed by afflictions. See Sozomen, book 5, chapter 4, on this matter. And this very thing can be seen today too in those regions and kingdoms whose princes rage against Christians with persecutions, chains, proscriptions, confiscations of goods, the sword, snares and fire, on account of the truth of God's gospel and their defection from Antichristianism. For the more they intensify this cruelty, the more the number of the faithful grows, so that now their multitude may seem to be feared by the tyrants themselves. Thus the constancy of those who bravely endure any evils for the truth of Christ serves also the consolation and salvation of others, and frustrates the plans of the impious, who, while they think they can overthrow God's truth by raging against the blood of the faithful, provide an occasion by which it grows stronger rather than being overthrown.

units.la: IN tolerantia, inquit, earundē afflictionum quas & nos patimur.) Obseruemus hic quibus nam sanctorum apostolorum ac martyrū passiones ad consolationem & salutem facere queant. Illis nimirum, qui perinde atq; illi pro ueritate Euāgelij Dei affliguntur, non ijs, qui in pace ac securitate uiuentes, ecclesiæ maligñatium sese accommodant, adeoq; nullis afflictionibus exercentur. At hi legendas, ut uocant, sanctorum martyrum magnificiunt, quorum tamen afflictionum socij esse nollet. Non prosunt ille ociofis, ignauis, mollibus, securis, nullo sectandę ueritatis zelo præditis, sed fide libus, quos Antichristiani omnis generis afflictionibus persequuntur.
units.tr: In the endurance of the same afflictions which we also suffer.) Let us observe here for whom the sufferings of the holy apostles and martyrs can serve as consolation and salvation. Surely for those who, just as they did, are afflicted for the truth of God's Gospel, not for those who live in peace and security and accommodate themselves to the malice of the Church and so are exercised by no afflictions. Yet these men magnify the so-called legends of the holy martyrs, whose companions in affliction they themselves would not wish to be. Such things do not benefit the idle, the cowardly, the soft, the secure, and those with no zeal for pursuing the truth, but the faithful, whom the Antichristians persecute with afflictions of every kind.

units.la: SIVE consolatione accipimus, inquit, pro uestri consolatione ac salute.) Chrysostomus istis verbis particulam quæ sequitur præmittit, sic legēs, Et spes nostra firma est pro uobis. Siue consolationem accipimus pro uestri consolatione ac salute. Et hanc lectionis serie exponēdo quoq; sequitur. Quin & Hispanicum Græcum exēplar nonnulli sic habere tradunt. Mihi placet eam retinere lectionē quę in Græcis codicibus, quos habemus in manu, reperitur. Siue consolationem accipimus, inquit, pro uestri consolatione ac salute, intellige, accipimus. Hoc est: Siue dum nos in mediis afflictionibus consolatur Deus, in eo quoq; non tam nostri quàm uestri rationem habens consolationi ac saluti uestræ consulit. Quomodo hoc fiat, facile intelligi potest. Quemadmodum enim afflictionibus suis ad consimilem illos afflictionum tolerantiam prouocabat: ita dum diuinis consolationibus suffultiebatur ac seruabatur, ad spem eos consimilium consolatio num erigebat. Hoc sentiens, dicit: Siue consolationem accipimus, pro uestri consolatione ac salute accipimus.
