units.tr: Or if we take it for your consolation and salvation.) Chrysostom places before these words the particle that follows, reading thus: "And our hope is firm for you. Or if we take consolation for your consolation and salvation." In expounding the passage in its order he follows this reading too. Indeed, some report that the Greek copy from Spain has it this way. I prefer to keep the reading found in the Greek manuscripts we have in hand: "Or if we take it, for your consolation and salvation," understanding "we take." That is: whether God comforts us in the midst of afflictions, in this too he considers not so much our interest as yours, and provides for your consolation and salvation. How this happens is easy to understand. For just as he encouraged them by his own afflictions to a similar endurance of suffering, so, while he was sustained and preserved by divine consolations, he raised them to hope through the consolation of like things. Feeling this, he says: "Whether we receive consolation, we receive it for your consolation and salvation."

units.la: Admonemur hoc loco, quo nobis facere debeant exempla beneficiorum Dei, quę sanctis
units.tr: Here we are reminded for what purpose the examples of God's benefits to the saints ought to serve us, which

units.la: ētis suis prophetis & apostolis, dum in carne uiuerent,& postea quoque diuina liberalitate concesit. Ad consolationem uidelicet ac salutem nostram. In hunc enim usum quæ cum illis egit Deus propositá nobis sunt, ut reipsa uideamus, non deserere illum sperantes in se. Et hanc ob causam conscripta sunt & memoriæ mandata, ut per consolationem scripturarum spem habeamus. Sic quæ Deus egit cum suis sanctis non debent referri ad ipsorum merita, sed ad consilium Dei, quo eos nobis exemplarium loco, non tam ipsorum iusticiæ quàm suæ gratiæ proponere voluit.
units.tr: he granted to his prophets and apostles while they lived in the flesh, and afterwards also by divine generosity. Namely, for our consolation and salvation. For what God did with them has been set before us for this very use, so that we may see in fact that he does not forsake those who hope in him. And for this reason they have been written down and committed to memory, so that through the consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope. So what God did with his saints ought not to be referred to their merits, but to God's counsel, by which he willed to set them before us as examples, not so much of their righteousness as of his grace.

units.la: SPES enim nostra, inquit, firma est pro uobis.) Rationem assignat, quare consolationes suas, ad illorum consolationem & salutem facere scribat. Dicit se spem hanc de illis concepisse, eamque non dubiam sed certam ac firmam. Hac spe fretus tam diligenter illis utilitatem afflictionum ac consolationum suarum exponit, quod non faceret, si spe hac de illis destitueretur. Spes nanq; mater est conatuum ac studiorum, gignens non modo uoluntatem, sed & conatum ac studium operandi, & quod coeptum est prosequendi, si non sit dubia, sed constans & firma.
units.tr: "For our hope," he says, "is firm for you." He gives the reason why he writes that his own consolations are for the consolation and salvation of the Corinthians. He says that he has conceived this hope about them, and it is not doubtful but certain and firm. Relying on this hope, he so diligently sets out for them the usefulness of his afflictions and consolations, which he would not do if he were deprived of this hope about them. For hope is the mother of efforts and endeavours, giving rise not only to willingness but also to the effort and zeal of acting, and of pursuing what has been begun, provided it is not doubtful but constant and firm.

units.la: Adiecit autem particulam hanc de spei suæ firmitudine admodum prudenter. Cum enim dicit: Nam spes nostra firma est pro uobis, mirum in modum erigit & accendit illorum animos, redditque ad omnis generis afflictionum tolerantiam uehementer alacres. Quemad- modum enim si ægroto dicat medicus, esse sibi de salute illius ac sanitate recuperanda spem firmam, hoc dices animum illius reddit ad recipiendas quasuis ab ipso oblatas potiones, & quæuis alia iuxta consilium ipsius uel facienda uel patienda paratum, desyderio uidelicet sanitatis ac spe medici sui accensum: consimili modo, qui pij erant in ecclesia Corinthiorum, hac spe apostoli sui animabantur & accendebantur, ad ferendum pro fide Christi quæuis aduersa.
units.tr: Moreover, he added this remark about the firmness of his hope most prudently. For when he says, "For our hope is firm for you," he wonderfully raises and kindles their minds and makes them vigorously ready to endure afflictions of every kind. Just as, if a physician told a sick man that he had firm hope of his recovery, this would make the patient ready to take whatever drinks were offered, and to do or suffer whatever else was according to the physician's counsel, kindled by desire for health and by trust in his doctor, so too those who were godly in the church of the Corinthians were encouraged and kindled by the hope of their apostle to bear whatever adversities for the faith of Christ.

units.la: Simul nota discrimen inter uteros ac falsos apostolos. Spe dispari discernuntur. Verus spe- rat ea quæ salutis sunt fidelium, & hac spe fretus omnia illorum gratia quæ poterit facit ac to lerat. Sic erat animatus erga Corinthiorum & aliorum fidelium ecclesias Paulus. Falsus sperat uel numos, uel eminentiam alicuius in ecclesia dominij, aut aliud aliquid, quod sibi putat fore commodum, parum de salute fidelium solicitus. Hoc discrimine admodum luculento discerni possunt hodie quoque synceri Christi ministri à reprobis.
units.tr: At the same time, note the difference between true and false apostles. They are distinguished by their different hopes. The true apostle hopes for what belongs to the salvation of the faithful, and relying on this hope he does and endures everything he can for their good. Thus Paul was disposed toward the churches of the Corinthians and the other faithful. The false apostle hopes for money, or for some prominence of lordship in the church, or for something else which he thinks will be advantageous to himself, being little concerned for the salvation of the faithful. By this very clear distinction, sincere ministers of Christ can be told apart from the reprobate even today.

units.la: CVM sciamus, inquit, quod sicut participes estis afflictionum, sic futuri sitis & consolationis.) Vnde firmam de illis spem conceperit hisce uerbis exprimit. Non dicit: Putamus enim, sed, cum sciamus, quod futuri sitis participes consolationis, sicut estis afflictionum. Spes alia nascitur ex opinione, alia ex scientia, alia ex fide uerbi Dei. Prima incerta est ac sal-
units.tr: "Since we know," he says, "that as you are partakers of the afflictions, so you will also be of the consolation." By these words he expresses whence he conceived his firm hope about them. He does not say, "For we think," but "since we know that you will be partakers of consolation, as you are of afflictions." One hope arises from opinion, another from knowledge, another from faith in the word of God. The first is uncertain and deceptive.

units.la: lax. Secunda ac tertia non item sed certa ac firma. Secundam exprimit cum dicit: Cum sciamus, sed unde sciebat? Ex uiua uidelicet ac suaipsius experientia. Quæ illa? Quemadmodum abundabant in ipso afflictiones Christi, sic abundabat uicisim in ipso & consolatio. Id non contigerat ipsi semel atque iterum, sed quoties affligebatur, toties consolationes diuinas experiebatur. Hac experientia certus erat factus non deesse Deum, patrem miseri-cordiarum, fidelium suorum afflictionibus.
units.tr: The second and third are not like this, but certain and firm. He expresses the second when he says, "Since we know." But whence did he know? Surely from living and personal experience. What was it? Just as the afflictions of Christ abounded in him, so in turn consolation abounded in him too. This had not happened to him once or twice, but as often as he was afflicted, so often did he experience divine consolations. By this experience he had been made certain that God, the Father of mercies, does not fail his faithful ones in their afflictions.

units.la: Igitur in eandem fortem, quæ contigerat ipsi, collocat & cæteros fideles: Collocat hac te nus, quatenus omnibus in Christum uere credentibus parata est communiter & pariformiter incomparabilis diuinæ prouidentiæ & misericordiæ gratia, quæ non distinguit inter Apostolum & discipulum, sed ex æquo & indiscriminatim adest omnibus, syncere erga veritatem Dei affectis, ac propter illa afflictis. Hoc innuens non dicit, cum sciamus quod sicuti nos sic & uos cœlesti consolatione potiemini, sed, quod sicut participes estis afflictionum, sic futuri sitis & consolationum. Consortes afflictionum Christi, digni habentur coram Deo ut sint & consolationis consortes quantumuis dispares alias sint conditione & donis spiritus, sic ut alius sit apostolus, & excellentioribus Spiritus sancti charismatibus præditus, alius uero priuatus, & minus donorum spiritus consequutus.
units.tr: Therefore he places the other faithful in the same lot that had fallen to him. He places them there insofar as the incomparable grace of divine providence and mercy is ready, in common and alike, for all who truly believe in Christ. This grace does not distinguish between apostle and disciple, but is present equally and without distinction to all who are sincerely devoted to God's truth and are afflicted on its account. Hinting at this, he does not say, "Since we know that as we, so you will obtain heavenly consolation," but "that as you are partakers of afflictions, so you will be of consolations too." Partners in the afflictions of Christ are deemed worthy before God to be partners in consolation as well, however much they otherwise differ in condition and in the gifts of the Spirit, so that one is an apostle endowed with more excellent charisms of the Holy Spirit, while another is a private person who has obtained fewer gifts of the Spirit.

units.la: Negandum tamen non est, quemadmodum excellebant in Apostolo afflictiones Christi, quibus plus cæteris impetebatur, ita excelluisse in eo & consolationes spiritus, idque haud præter rationem, cum esset positus à Deo in exemplar gratiæ ipsius, quo cæteri fideles ad fidei constantiam animarentur. Quare quod dicit: Cum sciamus quod sicut participes estis afflictionum, sic futuri sitis & consolationis, non est trahendum eo, ut sentiamus non fuisse consolationes Apostoli excellentiores ijs, quibus cæteri fideles recreabantur: quemadmodum nec illud ex hisce uerbis sequitur, quod afflictiones illius non fuerint graviores quàm cæterorum fidelium. Sicut socius esse potest afflictionum, qui licet non tam grauiter affligatur quàm afflicti fuerunt apostoli, propter eandem tamen Christi ac veritatis ipsius causam affligitur, propter quam illi affligebantur, sic socij possunt esse consolationis quoque, qui etsi non pari mensura cum apostolis consolatione spiritus potiantur, eiusdem tamen sunt consolationis participes. In bello milites socij laborum sunt ac periculorum cum ducibus, licet non æqua mensura, etsi principem habent æquum & suorum ex æquo amante, præmiorum quoque & solatiorum sunt socij, tametsi maior hic quoque habeatur ducis ratio. Plane idem est in hac causa cogitandum.
units.tr: Yet it must not be denied that just as the afflictions of Christ excelled in the Apostle, since he was assailed more than others, so the consolations of the Spirit excelled in him too, and not without reason, since he had been set by God as an example of his grace, by which the other faithful might be encouraged to constancy of faith. Therefore what he says, "Since we know that as you are partakers of afflictions, so you will be of consolation," is not to be taken to mean that we should think the apostle's consolations were no greater than those by which the other faithful were refreshed; nor does it follow from these words that his afflictions were no heavier than those of the other faithful. One can be a partner in affliction though he is not afflicted as heavily as the apostles were, yet is afflicted for the same cause of Christ and of truth for which they were afflicted. So too, partners can be in consolation who, although they do not obtain the consolation of the Spirit in equal measure with the apostles, are nevertheless sharers in the same consolation. In war, soldiers are companions with their leaders in labours and dangers, though not in equal measure; and if they have a fair prince who loves his men equally, they are also companions in rewards and comforts, although the leader's rank is still held to be greater. Exactly the same must be thought in this matter.

units.la: Illud: sic futuri sitis & consolationis, Græcè est, συλλως καὶ ἡ παρακλήσεως, id est, sic & consolationis. Quare quod Erasmus uertit: sic futuri fitis,in Græco non est, quod & ipse annotat. Nec ulla necesitas est,ut de futuræ uitæ consolationibus intelligamus,cum loquatur Apostolus de consolationibus quibus afflicti in ipsis afflictionibus eriguntur. Interim tamen in futuro quoq; uera erit hæc sententia.
units.tr: The phrase "so you may be of the consolation too" reads in Greek [οὕτως καὶ τῆς παρακλήσεως], that is, "so also of the consolation." So Erasmus's rendering "so you may be" has nothing in the Greek to match, as he himself notes. There is no necessity to take this as referring to the consolations of the life to come, since the Apostle is speaking of the consolations by which those who are afflicted are raised up in their very afflictions. Nevertheless, this sentiment will also hold true of the future.

units.la: Non enim uolumus uos ignorare fratres,de afflictione nostra,quę nobis accidit in Asia,quoniâ supra modū grauati fuimus, supra uires,adeò ut desperauerimus etiâ de uita. Quin ipsi in nobis sententiâ mortis acceperamus, ne cõsiderem us in nobisipsis, sed in Deo, qui ad uitâ suscitat mortuos,qui ex tâta mor te eripuit nos & eripit,in quo spem fixâ habemus,quod etiam posthac ereptu-rus sit,simul adiuuantibus & uobis per deprecationem pro nobis,ut ex multis personis,pro dono in nos collato , per multos gratiæ agantur pro nobis.
units.tr: "For we would not have you ignorant, brethren, of our trouble which came to us in Asia, that we were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life. Yea, we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God who raiseth the dead; who delivered us from so great a death, and doth deliver: in whom we trust that he will yet deliver us; ye also helping together by prayer for us, that for the gift bestowed upon us by means of many persons, thanks may be given by many on our behalf."

units.la: Referunt ista nonnulli non ad præcedentia, sed ad sequentia,quibus rationem reddet,quur Corinthum nondum uenerit, cum uenturum se promiserit. Secundum illorum sententiam, non debebat dicere:Non enim,sed,Non autem uolumus uos ignorare fratres,&c.Iam cum dicit:Non enim,puto manifestum esse,quod subijciat hæc præcedentibus , quæ de afflictionibus suis scripsit , præsertim quibus afflictiones Christi abundare in se dixit, ut abundantiam illarum exemplo recenti, quod paulò antequam hæc scriberet expertus fuerat, comprobaret, inque illo quæ de consolatione per Christum accepta adiecerat declararet. Sic dicit: Non enim uolumus uos ignorare fratres, de afflictione nostra quæ nobis accidit in Asia. Quasi dicat : Quæ de afflictionum nostrarum abundantia scribimus data opera scribimus,ad hoc, ut sciatis quid nobiscum agatur. Neque enim pudet nos afflictionum Christi . Imò uos cum primis scire illas uolumus, ut simul ex grauitate illarum opus diuinæ in nobis consolationis ad uestri consolationem ac salutem cognoscatis.
units.tr: Some refer these words not to what precedes but to what follows, where he gives the reason why he has not yet come to Corinth, though he had promised to come. On their view, he should not have said "For" but "Now, we would not have you ignorant, brethren," and so on. But since he says "For," it is plain, I think, that he is attaching this to what precedes, namely what he had written about his afflictions, especially where he said that the sufferings of Christ abound in him, so that he might confirm their abundance by a recent example, which he had experienced shortly before writing this, and in it declare what he had added about the consolation received through Christ. He says: "For we would not have you ignorant, brethren, of our affliction which came to us in Asia." As if he were saying: "We write about the abundance of our afflictions deliberately, so that you may know what is happening with us. For we are not ashamed of the afflictions of Christ. Indeed, we especially want you to know them, so that from the weight of those afflictions you may also recognise the work of divine consolation in us, for your consolation and salvation."

units.la: QVARE nolumus uos ignorantes esse afflictionis quæ contigit nobis in Asia,&c.) Ergo tam aberat , ut occultari uellet afflictiones suas, propter pseudapostolos, à quibus hoc nomine pro seditioso ac turbulento Apostolo habebatur,quod ubique turbas aduersariorum in se excitaret,ut ipse ad ecclesiam Corinthiorum de illis scribere maluerit potius, quàm ferre ut esset illa harum ignara.
units.tr: "Wherefore we would not have you ignorant of the affliction which befell us in Asia," and so on. So he was far from wishing to hide his afflictions because of the false apostles, by whom he was held, on this account, to be a seditious and troublesome apostle, because he everywhere stirred up the uproar of his opponents. Rather, he preferred to write to the Church of the Corinthians about them, rather than allow them to be ignorant of them.

units.la: Prudenti tamen consilio non mox initio epistolæ absque præfatione afflictionis Asiaticæ meminit, sed præmisit illi doxologiam Dei, celebrans ac laudans Deum ac patrem domini nostri Iesu Christi, patrem misericordiarum ac Deum omnis consolationis, propter conso-lationes illius quibus in omni afflictione corroborabatur, & simul utilitatem afflictionum Christi exposuit , quo animos Corinthiorum præpararet,ne per expositionē Asiaticæ tribulationis uel offenderentur uel turbarentur, si de illa statim in exordio meminisset.
units.tr: Yet with prudent judgement he did not mention the Asian affliction straight away at the opening of the letter without preface, but first placed before it a doxology to God, praising and blessing God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, for the consolations by which he was strengthened in every affliction. At the same time he set out the usefulness of Christ's afflictions, so as to prepare the minds of the Corinthians, lest they should be offended or disturbed by the exposition of the Asian tribulation, had he mentioned it immediately at the beginning.

units.la: NOLVMVS enim uos ignorare fratres, inquit, de afflictione nostra,quæ nobis accidit in Asia. ) Verbum accidendi non est in Græco , sed ibi legitur ad hunc modum τῆς ... id est,quæ facta est nobis, quemadmodum habet & uulgata quod ob id admoneo, ne quis hic in uerbo accidedi philosophetur, quasi afflictiones sanctorum inter fortuito contingentia & accidentia numerari possint, cum uix sit in rebus humanis aliquid quod minus accidentaliter geratur,& maiori certiorique consilio diuinæ prouidentiæ disponatur.
units.tr: "For we would not have you ignorant, brethren," he says, "of our affliction which came to us in Asia." The word "came" is not in the Greek; there it reads in this manner [τῆς ... ] , that is, "which was made to us," as the Vulgate also has. For this reason I warn that no one should philosophise here over the word "came," as if the afflictions of the saints could be counted among things that happen by chance and accident, when there is hardly anything in human affairs that is carried on less by accident and is arranged by the greater and surer counsel of divine providence.

units.la: De qua uerò afflictione loquatur, non est ut operosius inquiratur. Capite ultimo præcedentis epistolæ , dixit esse sibi aduersarios Ephesi multos. Vbi multi sunt aduersarij, ibi facilè multæ excitantur afflictiones. Nec dissimile à uero est, quod nonnulli hæc referunt ad tumultum quem Demetrius faber argentarius Ephesi sic excitauit contra Paulum,ut tota ciuitas repleta sit confusione, post quàm seditioné relicta Epheso profectus est in Macedoniam, ex quo itinere epistolam hanc Corinthijs scripsisse iudicatur.
units.tr: What affliction he means need not be investigated at length. At the end of the preceding letter he said that there were many adversaries for him at Ephesus. Where there are many adversaries, many afflictions are easily stirred up. Nor is it far from the truth what some refer these words to: the uproar which Demetrius, the silversmith, stirred up against Paul at Ephesus, so that the whole city was filled with confusion, after which he left Ephesus for Macedonia. It is judged that he wrote this letter to the Corinthians from that journey.

units.la: QVONIAM supra modum,inquit, grauati fuimus supra uires,adeò ut desperauerimus etiam de uita, quin ipsi in nobisipsis sententiâ mortis acceperamus.) Poterat quod in Græco est ὅτι ... uerri, quod supra modum grauati fuerimus . Nam hoc est, quod Corinthios de Asiatica sua afflictione scire uolebat, quod ea u delicet non fuerit leuis sed uehementer grauis , supra quàm ferre potuerit. Si legerimus: quoniam supra modum grauati fuimus,sensus erit: Volo, ut nota sit uobis afflictio, quæ facta est mihi in Asia, propterea quod nos supra modum grauauit, & uires nostras superauit.Sic solemus ea, quæ singularis momenti mala nos premunt,nolle ignota ef se amicis.
units.tr: "For we were pressed out of measure," he says, "above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life; yea, we had the sentence of death in ourselves." The Greek [ὅτι] could have been translated "that we were pressed beyond measure." For this is what he wanted the Corinthians to know about his affliction in Asia: that it was not slight but very heavy, more than he could bear. If we read "since we were pressed beyond measure," the sense will be: "I want you to know the affliction which befell me in Asia, because it weighed us down beyond measure and overcame our strength." In this way we are accustomed not to want our friends to be ignorant of those evils of singular weight which press upon us.

units.la: Significat his uerbis , quàm fuerit hæc sibi afflictio grauis . Grauitatem eius exaggerat amplificatione quadruplici.
units.tr: By these words he signifies how grave this affliction was for him. He magnifies its gravity by a fourfold amplification.

units.la: 1 Non simpliciter dicit:quoniam grauati fuimus,sed primum addit, id est, excellenter.Verterunt supra modum. Sunt graua mina alia alijs grauiora. Quæ supra reliqua graʋitate sua excellunt, grauant ac premunt.
units.tr: (1) He does not simply say "since we were burdened," but first adds "beyond measure," that is, exceedingly. Some translate it "beyond measure." Some burdens are heavier than others. Those which surpass the rest in their weight burden and crush.

units.la: 2 Deinde,adijcit ὑπὲρ δύναμιν, id est, supra uires.Non mox etiam ea quæ excellenter grauia sunt,cuiuslibet athletæ uires superant.
units.tr: (2) Then he adds [ὑπὲρ δύναμιν], that is, "above strength." Things that are exceedingly heavy are not at once beyond the strength of every athlete.

units.la: Quare ut significet tam fuisse afflictionem hanc excellenter grauem ac molestam , ut etiam uires suas superauerit , postquam dixit: quoniam excellenter grauati fuimus, adiecit, supra uires. Sic non est idem, ὑπὲρ ὑπερβολὴν, &c ἀπὸ δύναμιν, sicuti uidetur,ubi legimus,supra modum grauati fuimus,supra uires.
units.tr: So, to signify that this affliction was so exceedingly grave and burdensome that it overcame even his own strength, after saying "since we were exceedingly burdened," he added "above strength." Thus it is not the same to say [ὑπὲρ ὑπερβολήν] and [ἀπὸ δύναμιν], as it seems where we read "pressed beyond measure, above strength."

units.la: 3 Tertio amplificat & hoc dicens,adeò ut desperauerimus etiam de uita. Vulgata habet, ita ut tæderet nos etiam uiuere. In Græco est ἐξαπορηθῆναι ἡμᾶς καὶ τῆς ζωῆς. Significat ἐξαπορεῖσθαι inopem fieri consilij & rationis rei gerendæ,& per omnia perplexum, ut nec uiam nec rationem uideas ullam, qua imminens discrimen euadas. Sic eueniebat Apostolo in tam graui & abundanti afflictione,qua sic supra uires premebatur,ut omni esset ratione,consilio & facultate seruandæ uitæ destitutus. Hunc sensum uulgatus interpres non expressit, expressit uero Erasmus melius,dum uertit:adeò ut desperauerimus etiam de uita.
units.tr: (3) He amplifies this a third time, saying "insomuch that we despaired even of life." The Vulgate has "so that it wearied us even to live." In the Greek it is [ἐξαπορηθῆναι ἡμᾶς καὶ τῆς ζωῆς]. [ἐξαπορεῖσθαι] signifies to be left without counsel or plan for managing a matter, and to be perplexed in every way, so that you see neither a way nor a method by which to escape the impending peril. So it happened to the Apostle in so grave and overwhelming an affliction, by which he was so pressed beyond his strength that he was deprived of every means, counsel and resource for preserving his life. The Vulgate translator did not express this sense, but Erasmus expressed it better when he rendered it "insomuch that we despaired even of life."

units.la: 4 Quarto,addit quod erat extremum. Quin ipsi in nobis ipsis, inquit, sententiam mortis ἐσχήκαμεν, id est, habebamus. Quasi dicat. Non modo perplexi hæsitabamus de uita seruanda, uerùm adeò uidebantur omnia certam intentare mortem,ut in nobisipsis decretū iam esset, omnino nobis esse in eo discrimine morien-dum. Significat igitur quadruplici hac exagneratione afflictionem illam Asiaticam supremum obtinuisse discriminis gradum,sic ut suo ipsius iudicio mortem tam esset certò illatura, ac si mortis iam esset sententia condemnatus & lictori necandus traditus.Et hoc erat quod Corinthios suos ignorare nolebat.
units.tr: (4) Fourthly, he adds what was the extreme. "Yea, we had," he says, "the sentence of death in ourselves" [ἐσχήκαμεν], that is, "we had." As if he were saying: not only were we perplexed and hesitated about preserving our life, but all things seemed so to threaten certain death that it was already decided in ourselves that we must in every way die in that peril. He therefore signifies by this fourfold amplification that the Asian affliction reached the highest degree of peril, so that in his own judgement death would certainly come, just as if he had already been condemned to death and handed over to the executioner to be killed. And this was what he did not want his Corinthians to be ignorant of.

units.la: QVONIAM supra modum,inquit,grauati sumus. ) Non erat Apostolus hic alienus ab eo quod de cæteris apostolis legitur, quod gaudentes abierint à conspectu concilij,propterea quod digni habiti essent,qui pro nomine Iesu contumelijs afficerentur. Et ipsa causa propter quam tam grauiter affligebatur,non erat alia ab ea, propter quam contumelijs fuerant cæteri apostoli affecti,sed prorsus eadem, & tamen significat hoc loco fuisse se grauatum, idque excellenter. Qui se grauari queritur, utique non gaudet de eo quo se grauari queritur. Sensit igitur in carne sua afflictionis gravitatem & molestiam, idque sicut patet in ijs quæ subijcit non gaudens sed anxius & perplexus deque ipsa uita desperans. Quomodo conueniebat illi hac in re cum cæteris apostolis? Imò cum eo quod infrà capite quarto tribulationi suæ non grauitatem sed leuitatem eamque non mediocrem aliquam sed momentaneam tribuit dicens: Nam mirè momentanea leuitas afflictionis nostræ supra modum æternum pondus gloriæ parit nobis? Quomodo ergo excellenter ac supra uires hic se grauatum fuisse dicit, si afflictio ipsius leuis fuit ac momentanea?
units.tr: "Since we were pressed beyond measure," he says. The Apostle here is not foreign to what is read of the other apostles, that they departed from the presence of the council rejoicing, because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus. Nor was the cause for which he was so grievously afflicted any different from that for which the other apostles were dishonoured, but altogether the same; yet here he signifies that he was burdened, and that exceedingly. One who complains that he is burdened certainly does not rejoice at that by which he complains of being burdened. So he felt in his flesh the gravity and burden of the affliction, as is clear from what he adds, being not joyful but anxious and perplexed, and despairing even of life. How did this agree with the other apostles in this matter? Indeed, how does it agree with what he says later in chapter four, where he ascribes to his tribulation not gravity but lightness, and that not a moderate lightness but a momentary one: "For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory"? How, then, can he say that he was burdened exceedingly and beyond his strength here, if his affliction was light and momentary?

units.la: Respondeo. Sensus afflictionum alius est atque alius. Alius dum caro præsentibus afflictionibus premitur,alius post afflictiones cõsolatione diuinitus accepta. In ipsa afflictione grauis est ac molestus, post afflictionem uero non ita,sed leuis ac momẽtaneus. Quare quod Ebr.12.de castigationibus legitur: Omnis ca-
units.tr: I answer: the sense of afflictions is one thing and another. One sense comes while the flesh is pressed by present afflictions; another comes after the afflictions, when consolation has been received from God. In the affliction itself it is heavy and burdensome, but after the affliction it is not so, but light and momentary. Hence what is read in Hebrews 12 about chastisements:

units.la: stigatio in præsens quidem non uidetur esse gaudij sed molestiæ,at postea fructum tranquillum iusticiæ reddit ijs qui per illam fuerint exercitati,omnium cõuenientissimè de afflictionibus quoque sanctorum dici potest. Iam quod præsentem quæstionem attinet, quod se Apostolus supra modum grauatum fuisse dicit, referèdum est ad ipsum præsentis afflictionis tempus, in quo quæ hic scribit in carne sua fuerat expertus, quæ uero infra capite quarto scribit,referenda sunt ad sensum non præsentis sed præteritæ afflictionis,& ad collationem æternæ gloriæ,quę transitoriam afflictionem cõsequitur.
units.tr: "Every chastening for the present seems not to be joyous but grievous; yet afterwards it yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness to those who have been exercised by it." This can most fittingly be said of the afflictions of the saints too. As for the present question, when the Apostle says he was burdened beyond measure, this must be referred to the time of the present affliction, in which he had experienced in his flesh what he writes here. But what he writes below in chapter four must be referred to the feeling of the past affliction, and to its comparison with the eternal glory that follows the transitory affliction.

units.la: Admonemur hoc Apostoli exemplo, quàm non sit illud Stoicum, non sentio, non dolet, ad præsentes sanctorum afflictiones referendum,sed ad præteritas.Et ipsi apostoli,non leguntur inter ipsa fuisse uerbera gauisi, sed postea demum,cum cæsi essent dimisi. Sic enim habet textus.Et cum aduocassent apostolos,cę-sis præceperunt ne loquerentur in nomine domini Iesu,& dimiserunt eos. Et illi quidem ibant gaudentes à conspectu concilij, quod digni habiti essent,ut pro nomine eius contumeliam paterentur.
units.tr: This example of the Apostle admonishes us that the Stoic saying, "I do not feel it, it does not hurt," is not to be applied to the present afflictions of the saints, but to past ones. Nor are the apostles themselves read to have rejoiced during the very beatings, but only afterwards, when they had been let go after being scourged. For the text says: "And when they had called the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of the Lord Jesus, and let them go. And indeed they went out from the presence of the council rejoicing, because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for his name" (Acts 5).

units.la: SVPRA uires,inquit.) Nascitur & hic quæstio, quomodo conueniat hæc particula cum eo quod in præcedenti epistola capite decimo dixit ad hunc modum? Tentatio uos non cœpit nisi humana, sed fidelis est Deus, qui non sinet uos tentari supra id quod potestis, imò faciet unà cum tentatione euentum, quo possitis sufferre. Si sic fidelis est Deus,ut non sinat fideles suos tentari supra quàm ferre pos-sunt, quomodo permisit Apostolum suum grauari supra uires? Respondeo. Quod Apostolus supra uires grauatus fuit, non impedit quo minus uerè fidelis sit Deus qui sic fideli-um suorum in ecclesia Corinthiorum infirmitati pepercit,ut non sineret eos tentari supra uires. Quæ uerba non sic sunt prolata,ut generalem habeant sententiam, quasi fidelis Deus prorsus neminem suorum supra uires tentari sinat, sed ut in eo fidelem esse Deum prædicent,quod infirmos non sinat tam grauiter tentari quàm eos qui sunt robustiores, & ad hoc positi ut in ipsis diuinæ uirtutis gloria illustretur.Idem Deus tam erga firmiores quàm erga infirmiores fidelis, firmum suum Apostolum tentari sinebat supra uires, infirmos uero Corinthios non ita, utrorumque salutem procurans ex æquo etiamsi diuersimodè,iuxta quod mensura donorum suorum poscebat ac ferebat.
units.tr: "Beyond their strength," he says. Here too a question arises: how does this phrase agree with what he said in the earlier letter, chapter ten, in this manner? "No temptation has taken you except what is human; but God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear, but will even make with the temptation the outcome by which you may be able to endure it." If God is so faithful that he does not allow his faithful ones to be tempted beyond what they can bear, how did he permit his Apostle to be burdened beyond his strength? I answer: that the Apostle was burdened beyond his strength does not prevent God from being truly faithful, who so spared the weakness of his faithful ones in the church of the Corinthians that he did not allow them to be tempted beyond their strength. These words are not spoken so as to have a general sense, as if the faithful God would allow absolutely none of his people to be tempted beyond their strength; rather they declare God to be faithful in this, that he does not allow the weak to be tempted as severely as those who are stronger, and who are appointed so that the glory of divine power may be displayed in them. The same God, faithful towards the stronger and towards the weaker alike, allowed his firm Apostle to be tempted beyond his strength, but did not so treat the weak Corinthians, providing equally for the salvation of both, though in different ways, according to the measure of gifts he had given and that each could bear.

units.la: ADEO,inquit, ut desperauerimus etiam de uita. ) Ergo erat anxius pro seruanda uita, & quoniam afflictio mole sua grauior erat quàm ipse ferendo esset,desperabat fieri posse, ut uitam retineret. Sic uidemus etiam Apostolos in afflictionibus solicitos esse de sua uita, & rationes seruandæ illius metiri secundum uirium suarum facultatem,sic ut ubi illæ pro-
units.tr: "So that," he says, "we despaired even of life." Therefore he was anxious to preserve his life; and since the affliction, by its weight, was heavier than he himself could bear, he despaired that it would be possible for him to keep his life. Thus we see that the Apostles too, in afflictions, are anxious about their life, and measure the reasons for preserving it by the measure of their own strength, so that when those strengths lie prostrate, they become perplexed and destitute of counsel about preserving it.

units.la: Act. 5. stratæ iacent, de seruanda ea perplexi & inopes consilij reddantur. Sunt hæc humana & naturalia, quibus Deus nō irritatur, quare nec aliena sunt ab afflictionibus sanctorum, uerū Apostolus, qui cupiebat dissolui & esse cum Christo, non tam hic uitæ suę desyderio, quàm cura ecclesiarum afficiebatur. uide Philippensium primo. Quomodo autem ista diuina prouidentia dirigantur, in consequentibus uidebi mus.
units.tr: "Acts 5." These are human and natural feelings, by which God is not provoked; so they are not foreign to the afflictions of the saints. But the Apostle, who desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ, was affected not so much by a longing for this life as by care for the churches; see Philippians 1. How these things are directed by divine providence we shall see in what follows.

units.la: QVIN ipsi in nobisipsis, inquit, sententiam mortis habebamus.) Vulgata editio habet, responsum mortis. In Græco est, ἀπόκριμα, quæ uox & responsum, & sententiam, & condemnationem significat. Cuius ergo sententiam habebat in seipso? Dei non habebat, aliàs moriendum ipsi fuisset. Nec à magistratu lata erat in ipsum sententia mortis. Quod igitur dicit, nihil est aliud, quàm quod in tam graui afflictione perinde se morti adiudicatum esse putabat, ac si mortis iam sententiam uel à Deo uel à magistratu accepisset. Tanta inualuerat in ipso desperatio uitæ. Ergo & sancti in discrimine constituti falluntur in seipsis, dum ignari diuinæ sententię, secundum externæ afflictionis sensum, morti se adiudicatos esse existimant. Huius rei multa testimonia occurrunt in Psalmis Dauidis, qui quod hic Paulo accidit, non semel est expertus. Tale erat, quod primo Samuelis uigesimotertio legitur, ubi à Saule in modum coronæ sic cinctus fuisse memoratur, ut iamiam capiendus uideretur. Hinc illa: Circūndederant me funes mortis, & torrentes Belial conturbauerant me. Funes sepulcri circundederant me, occupauerant me la quei mortis.
units.tr: "Indeed we ourselves had the sentence of death within ourselves." The Vulgate edition has "the answer of death." In the Greek it is [ἀπόκριμα], a word that signifies both answer and sentence, and also condemnation. Whose sentence, then, did he have within himself? He did not have God's sentence, for otherwise he would have had to die. Nor had a sentence of death been pronounced against him by the magistrate. What he says therefore is nothing other than this: in such a grave affliction he thought himself as good as condemned to death, as if he had already received a sentence of death either from God or from the magistrate. So great a despair in life had taken hold of him. Thus even the saints, when placed in peril, are deceived about themselves, while ignorant of the divine sentence, and according to the feeling of external affliction they suppose they have been condemned to death. Many testimonies to this occur in the Psalms of David, who experienced once what happened here to Paul. Of this kind was what is read first in 1 Samuel 23, where he is recorded as having been so surrounded by Saul, as in a ring, that he seemed about to be taken at any moment. Hence that: "The cords of death surrounded me, and the torrents of Belial troubled me. The cords of the grave surrounded me; the snares of death overtook me" (Psalm 18).

units.la: NE consideremus, inquit, in nobisipsis sed in Deo.) Reddit hic rationem, quare uoluerit Deus afflictionem suam eosque inualescere, ut in ipsa iam mortis sententia constitutus uideretur, & quæ sit tam grauis afflictionis utilitas. Totum, inquit, hoc non est humano aliquo sed diuino consilio factum, quo adimeretur nobis nostri ipsorum fiducia, ne post unquam confidentes simus in nobisipsis, sed in Deo cum iam reipsa deprehenderimus, nihil ualuisse in tam graui discrimine omnes nostras tam mentis, ac proprię iusticię & innocentiæ quàm corporis uires, sed moriendum fuisse prorsus, nisi nos Deus ueluti manu prehæ sos è laqueis mortis extraxisset.
units.tr: "Let us not trust in ourselves," he says, "but in God." Here he gives the reason why God willed that his affliction and his peril should grow so severe that he seemed already condemned to death, and what the usefulness of so grievous an affliction was. All of this, he says, was done not by any human counsel but by the divine plan, so that our confidence in ourselves might be taken away, and that we might not afterwards trust in ourselves but in God. For when we have actually found out that in so grave a danger all our powers, both of mind and of body, and our own righteousness and innocence, were of no avail, and that we would have been utterly lost unless God had drawn us out of the snares of death, as if by the hand.

units.la: Locus hic de fiducia notandus est. Confidere quid sit notum est omnibus. Est sic animo alicui rei inniti, in qua uel subsistere, uel uoti compotes cuadere possimus, ut illius fiducia nihil non faciamus ac feramus. Hæc fiducia argumentum habet humanæ nostræ infirmitatis. Quorsum enim opus esset alicui ueluti sustentaculo confidendo inniti, si sic essemus firmi, ut nulla esset ratio timendæ ruinæ? Iam quoniam tales non sumus, natura sic comparati sumus, ut sine fiducia nemo mortalium uiuat, nisi in quo omnimoda obtinue-
units.tr: This passage on confidence deserves notice. What it is to trust is known to everyone. It is to lean the mind on some thing on which we can either stand firm or reach the object of our wish, so that, relying on it, we do and endure anything. This confidence is evidence of our human weakness. For why would there be any need to lean on something as a prop to trust in, if we were so firm that there was no reason to fear a fall? Since, however, we are not such, we are so constituted by nature that no mortal lives without confidence, except one in whom complete despair has taken hold.

units.la: rit desperatio. Nec sancti ulli fiduciæ possunt esse expertes. Nec requirit hoc à nobis diuina maiestas, ut ab omni prorsus sinus fiducia alie ni. Nec dicit hic Apostolus simpliciter, ne cō fidamus, sed addit, in nobisipsis. Imo ut signi ficet placere Deo, ut in se confidamus, mox sub ijcit, sed in Deo. Qui uult ut sibi fidendo innitamur, utique non uult nos omnis esse fiduciæ expertes. Quæ insunt nobis naturaliter, naturæ nostræ cōditioni cōformia, utpote, amor, odium, timor, spes, gaudium, tristitia, fiducia, &c. in se non sunt damnabilia, nec ulla nobis pietate auferuntur sed corriguntur, & ad iustum finem perducuntur. Sic damnatur hic non affectus fiduciæ in se, sed corruptio illius, qua caro confidit in eo quod est uanum, uel in seipsa uel in alio.
units.tr: Nor can any saints be free of confidence. Nor does the divine majesty require this of us, that we be altogether strangers to all confidence. Nor does the Apostle here say simply, "let us not trust," but he adds, "in ourselves." Indeed, to show that it pleases God that we trust in him, he immediately adds, "but in God." He who wills that we lean on him in trust does not will that we be void of all confidence. The affections that are naturally in us, conformable to the condition of our nature, such as love, hatred, fear, hope, joy, sadness, confidence, and so on, are not in themselves blameworthy, nor are they removed by any piety, but they are corrected and brought to their just end. So what is condemned here is not the affection of confidence in itself, but its corruption, by which the flesh trusts in what is vain, either in itself or in another.

units.la: NE consideremus, inquit, in nobisipsis.) Qui confidit in seipso, facit hoc respectu uel propriæ sapientiæ, uel potentiæ, uel opulentiæ, uel fortitudinis, uel iusticiæ, uel alterius cuiuspiam uirtutis aut doni Dei. Paulus cum Euangelium Christi prædicaret, non potuit confidere in propria potentia, quia non erat potens iuxta sæculum, neque in opulentia, qua nulla potiebatur, uictum labore manuū quærens, nec in robore corporis, quo tot periculis suffcere non poterat, quare non erat periculum ut tribus hisce respectibus consideret in seipso. Est igitur reliquum, periculū fuisse in alijs, qualia erant, propriæ iusticiæ, sapientiæ, fortitudinis, & singularium reuelationū. In nullo fuisse dicere non possumus, nisi placet ut dicamus frustra fuisse illum tam excellenti afflictione grauatum, & quæ hic dicit, uerba esse inania ad iudificādum Corinthios. Sed absit ut hoc dicamus.
units.tr: "Let us not trust in ourselves," he says. He who trusts in himself does so with respect either to his own wisdom, power, wealth, strength, righteousness, or some other virtue or gift of God. When Paul preached the gospel of Christ, he could not trust in his own power, since he was not powerful according to the world; nor in wealth, of which he possessed none, earning his living by the labour of his hands; nor in the strength of his body, by which he could not endure so many dangers. Therefore there was no danger that he would trust in himself on any of these three grounds. What remains is that the danger lay in other things, such as his own righteousness, wisdom, fortitude, and his singular revelations. We cannot say that he was in no danger in these respects, unless we are willing to say that he was in vain burdened with so excellent an affliction, and that the words he speaks here are empty, meant only to deceive the Corinthians. But far be it from us to say this.

units.la: Cum tot tanque præclaris donis spiritus, ut magnitudinem reuelationum taceam, præditus esset Apostolus, periculum erat ne respectu illorum consideret in seipso. Infra capite duodecimo dicit: ne magnitudo reuelationum extollat me, datus est mihi stimulus, &c. Sanè sic comparatum est hoc uicium, ut insidiosum sit non uulgaribus hominibus sed selectioribus, ut quo quisque pluribus ac maioribus est præditus uirtutibus, procliuior ad hoc sit ut confidat in seipso. Quare opus illis est cum primis ut subinde humilientur, & in propriæ infirmitatis sensum & cognitionem in ducantur.
units.tr: Since the Apostle was endowed with so many and such outstanding gifts of the Spirit, not to mention the greatness of his revelations, there was a danger that he might look to himself because of them. In the twelfth chapter below he says: "Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn was given to me," and so on. This vice is truly so constituted that it lays its snares not for ordinary people but for the more select, because the more virtues and greater gifts a person has, the more inclined he is to trust in himself. Therefore such people above all need to be humbled from time to time and led into a sense and knowledge of their own weakness.

units.la: Malum autem, quo noxia est & auersanda hæc confidentia qua in nobisipsis confidimus, admodum est multiplex, sic ut uanitatis ac maliciæ illius species numerari nequeant. Excæcat mentes nostras, ut uidere nequeamus quàm simus in nobisipsis uani ac prorsus nihili. Quod Dei solius est dat creaturis. Idolum facit ex donis à Deo acceptis. Reddit nos securos, ubi nulla est securitas, & egregios diuinæ uoluntatis contemptores, ac tandem in barathrum perditionis præcipites impellit. Haud igitur præter rationem est, quod pro-
units.tr: The evil by which this confidence in ourselves is harmful and must be shunned is very manifold, so that its kinds of vanity and malice cannot be counted. It blinds our minds, so that we cannot see how vain and utterly worthless we are in ourselves. It gives to creatures what belongs to God alone. It makes an idol out of the gifts received from God. It makes us secure where there is no security, and outstanding despisers of the divine will, and at last it hurls us headlong into the abyss of perdition. It is therefore not without reason that the prophet says:

units.la: pheta dicit: Maledictus qui confidit in homine,& ponit carnem brachium suum.
units.tr: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm."

units.la: SED in Deo, inquit.) Sic relinquitur quidem nobis fiducia, qua pendeamus aliunde, ab eo uidelicet,unde sustentari ac seruari posumus,uerum talis,qua innitamur non uano & rudineo alicui baculo,sed ei tantum,in quo solo ueram licet inuenire salutem,Deo uidelicet, omnium ut conditore ita & Seruatore.
units.tr: "BUT in God," he says. Thus a trust is indeed left to us by which we depend on something else, namely on him from whom we can be sustained and preserved. It is a trust, however, not resting on some empty and reedy staff, but only on him in whom alone true salvation can be found, namely God, the creator and also the Saviour of all things.

units.la: Significatur autem hoc loco diserte,hanc esse uoluntatem Dei ut confidamus in ipso. Dum enim cauet ac uetat, ne confidamus in nobisipsis, aut ullis alijs creaturis, quid aliud quaerit, quàm ut nos trahat ad se & omni auxilio destitutos cogat etiam, ut ad se solum confugiamus. Agnouit hoc rex Iosaphat, cum secundo Paralipomenon vigesimo ad Deum oraret ac diceret: In nobis quidem non est tanta fortitudo, ut possimus huic multitudini resistere, quae irruit super nos. Verum cum ignoramus quid facere debeamus, hoc solum habemus residuum, ut oculos nostros dirigamus ad te.
units.tr: Moreover, the will of God that we should trust in him is plainly indicated in this passage. For when he guards against and forbids us to trust in ourselves or in any other creatures, what else does he seek than to draw us to himself and, indeed, to compel us, when we are deprived of all help, to flee to him alone? King Jehoshaphat recognised this when, in the twentieth chapter of Second Chronicles, he prayed to God and said: "In us indeed there is not such strength that we can withstand this multitude that comes upon us. But since we do not know what we ought to do, we have this one remaining resource: to direct our eyes to you."

units.la: Sunt autem rationes diuinę huius erga nos uoluntatis tres iste prae caeteris admodum graues.
units.tr: There are three reasons for this divine will towards us, which are especially weighty above the rest.

units.la: 1 Prima est, ut nominis ipsius gloria uindicetur, quae nulla in re magis obscuratur, quàm si salus eorum quae condidit non ab ipso solo sed aliunde sperC​etur & quaeratur, ex quo fonte omnis generis eidololatria promanat, unde innumera eidola tam externa quàm interna in cordibus mortalium eriguntur. Quod si nulla esset alia ratio, praeter hanc unam quae requiritur, ut in solo Deo confidamus, nec ulli uspiam nec terrenae nec coelesti creaturae innitamur, ne per nos quae nomini ipsius debetur gloria inexcusabili impietate interuertatur, & ad creaturas transferatur, debebat una haec abunde sufficere, si uel tantillum in nobis esset famae mentis ac cordis.
units.tr: (1) The first is that the glory of his name be vindicated, which is nowhere more obscured than when the salvation of the things he has made is hoped for and sought not from him alone but from elsewhere. From this source every kind of idolatry springs, and from it innumerable idols, external as well as internal, are raised up in the hearts of mortals. Yet even if there were no other reason besides this one, namely that we should trust in God alone and lean on no creature anywhere, neither earthly nor heavenly, lest through us the glory due to his name be overturned by inexcusable impiety and transferred to creatures, this one reason should suffice abundantly, if there were even a little soundness of mind and heart in us.

units.la: 2 Secunda est immensa illa bonitas ac philanthropia Dei, cuius hoc est ingenium, ut nihil possit minus ferre quàm si ipsi non innitamur, nec poscat à nobis tam impense quicquam, atque synceram erga se fiduciam. Hac uf queadeo delectatur, ut nequeat sperantes ac confidentes in se deserere. Quàm autem grue fit, alienum ab eo fieri, quo diuina bonitas pro naturae suae ingenio cum primis delectatur, & admittere quod modis omnibus detestatur, & in quod grauibus ultionibus animaduertit, cordatis hominibus per se satis est manifestum.
units.tr: (2) The second is the immense goodness and love of man of God, whose nature is such that he can bear nothing less than that we should not rely on him, and he does not ask anything of us so earnestly as a sincere trust in himself. He so delights in this that he cannot abandon those who hope in him and trust in him. How grievous it is for a person to turn away from him, in whom the divine goodness above all takes delight according to the nature of its character, and to admit what it detests in every way and punishes with severe vengeance, is clear enough to thoughtful people in themselves.

units.la: 3 Tertia est salutis nostrae ratio, quae sic est comparata ut non nisi gratia ac bonitate Dei constare possit, cuius autem participes fieri nequimus, nisi credendo, sperando ac fidendo ex animo ab ea sola pendeamus. Sine hac cordis fiducia impossibile est placere Deo. Non saluamur autem si illi displicuerimus, quare consequitur ad salutem nostram necessariam esse hanc fiduciam, qua illi pro bonitatis ipsius
units.tr: (3) The third is the reason for our salvation, which is so constituted that it can consist in nothing but the grace and goodness of God, and of which we cannot become partakers unless, by believing, hoping and trusting, we depend on it alone from the heart. Without this trust of the heart it is impossible to please God. But we are not saved if we have displeased him. Hence it follows that this trust is necessary for our salvation, by which we please him according to the nature of his goodness.

units.la: ingenio placeamus. Haec rationes nihil habent dubij, nihil obscuri, sed & certę sunt & manifestae, ut facile constet, quare nolit Deus, ut confidamus in creaturis siue illae sint intra siue extra nos, & sint uel terrenae uel coelestes, uelit autem & poscat, ut confidamus in se uno ac solo Deo conditore nostro & Seruatore.
units.tr: These reasons contain nothing doubtful and nothing obscure, but they are both sure and manifest, so that it is easily established why God does not want us to trust in creatures, whether they are within us or outside us, and whether they are earthly or heavenly, but wants and requires us to trust in himself alone, our Creator and Saviour.

units.la: Priusquam ad sequentia progrediamur, admonendus est pius lector, ut duo haec, quod praesentem causam concernit, diligenter ac mente retineat. Vnum: Omnium nostrarum afflictionum hunc esse finem, ne confidamus in nobisipsis sed in Deo. Alterum, confidere nos Deo non posse, nisi desinamus confidere in nobisipsis.
units.tr: Before we proceed to what follows, the godly reader is to be reminded that, as far as the present matter concerns, he should carefully keep these two things in mind. The first: the end of all our afflictions is this, that we should trust not in ourselves but in God. The second: we cannot trust in God unless we cease to trust in ourselves.

units.la: QVI ad uitam suscitat mortuos, inquit.) Accommodat hoc ad causam afflictionum suarum. Multa sunt in Deo argumenta, quorum gratia monemur, ne in nobisipsis sed in illo confidamus. Praesens tamen propterea commodius uisum est caeteris, quod de afflictionibus extremis loquitur, in quibus carni desperata uidentur omnia, haud secus quam si quis in ipsis claustris mortis & inferorum detineatur, unde eripi ueluti mortuum est suscitari. Est haec generalis sententia, qua de Deo tantam praedicat potentiam, ut & mortuos suscitet ad uitam. Praedicat autem illam duplici de causa. Primo ob id, ut stimulet eos, qui inter Corinthios resurrectionem mortuorum negabant. Deinde ut admoneat omnes, quàm magna sit ratio confidendi Deo in afflictionibus quibuscunque, ex eo, quod & mortuos suscitat ad uitam, nedum afflictos uiuos in uita conseruat. Qui posterius hoc, quod multo est minus, non credit, quomodo credet prius, quod longe est maius? Rursus qui credit Deum ad uitā suscitare mortuos, quomodo dubitabit illum in uita seruare afflictos? Qui mortuorum itaque resurrectionem negabat, magnam fiduciae erga Deum partem amiserant, & procul erant ab eo, ut non in seipsis sed in Deo sicubi in afflictiones incidisent, considerent.
units.tr: "WHO RAISES THE DEAD TO LIFE," he says. He applies this to the cause of his afflictions. There are many arguments in God by which we are admonished not to trust in ourselves but in him. Yet this one seemed more fitting than the others, because he speaks of extreme afflictions, in which all things seem hopeless to the flesh, just as if someone were held within the very prison-house of death and of the underworld, from which to be rescued is like being raised from the dead. This is a general statement by which he proclaims God's power so great that he raises the dead to life. He proclaims it for a twofold reason. First, so that he might stir up those among the Corinthians who denied the resurrection of the dead. Then, so that he might admonish everyone how great a reason there is to trust in God in whatever afflictions, from the fact that he raises the dead to life, not to mention that he preserves in life the living who are afflicted. Whoever does not believe the latter, which is much less, how will he believe the former, which is far greater? Again, whoever believes that God raises the dead to life, how will he doubt that God preserves the afflicted in life? Therefore those who denied the resurrection of the dead had lost a great part of their trust in God, and were far from considering, when they fell into afflictions, not themselves but God.

units.la: QVI extanta morte, inquit, eripuit nos, & eripit, in quo spem fixam habemus, quod etiam posthac erepturus sit.) Magnitudinem afflictionum suarum in praecedentibus expressit, iam illud explicat, quod dixit: qui consolatur nos in omni afflictione nostra. Duabus hisce partibus afflictionum & consolationum erudiebatur ad confidendum non in seipso sed in Deo, qui suscitat mortuos. Et ut consolationis magnitudinem exprimat, non dicit simpliciter qui ex afflictione, sed, qui ex morte, neque sic simpliciter, sed, qui ex tanta, inquit, morte eripuit nos. Afflictiones suas quas erat perpessus uocat mortem eamque magnam, ut simul & potentiam Dei in se declaratam amplificet, qua erat ex illa liberatus. Sic non minoris censet eam liberationem, quàm si e media morte fuisset ereptus. Quod enim morte non fuerat absorptus, non erat aliunde, quàm ex eo quod diuina ipsum potentia pariter & miseri-cordia cordia ex ipsis quasi faucibus mortis eripuerat, A cuius iam in seipso, sicuti paulo ante meminit, sententiam acceperat.
units.tr: "WHO DELIVERED US FROM SO GREAT A DEATH," he says, "AND DELIVERS US, IN WHOM WE HAVE A FIXED HOPE THAT HE WILL ALSO DELIVER US HEREAFTER." In the preceding words he has expressed the magnitude of his afflictions; now he explains what he said: "who comforts us in all our affliction." By these two parts, of afflictions and of consolations, he was taught to trust not in himself but in God, who raises the dead. And to express the greatness of the consolation, he does not say simply "who delivers from affliction," but "who delivers from death," and not even simply that, but "who delivered us from so great a death," he says. He calls the afflictions he had suffered death, and a great death, so that at the same time he might magnify the power of God displayed in himself, by which he was set free from it. Thus he counts that deliverance no less than if he had been snatched out of the midst of death. For the fact that he had not been swallowed up by death was owing to nothing else than that the divine power and mercy alike had snatched him from the very jaws of death, as he had already received the sentence of this in himself, as he mentioned a little earlier.

units.la: Hoc pacto glorificat Deum, & gratiam ab illo praestitam amplificat, quo exemplo monemur, quae nos decet gratitudo, quoties beneficio Dei ex aduersis ac tribulationibus liberamur. Talis uidelicet, qua gratiam Dei pleno ore deprædicemus, ut impleamus illud: Invoca me in die tribulationis & eripiam te & glorificabis.
units.tr: Thus he glorifies God and magnifies the grace bestowed by him. By this example we are reminded what gratitude becomes us whenever we are delivered from adversities and tribulations by the benefit of God: namely, that we proclaim the grace of God with full mouth, so that we fulfil that word: "Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me."

units.la: ET eripit, inquit.) Intellige, quoties in afflictiones incidero porrigit manum, & ne pereat. Idem dicit quod supra, qui consolatur nos in omni afflictione nostra. Non modo eam liberationem tribuit Deo, qua ex portis mortis fuerat ereptus, sed & caeteras omnes, nihil sui ipsius relinquens diligentiae ac curae, non in minimo quidem ullo discrimine.
units.tr: "And he delivers," he says. Understand: as often as I fall into afflictions, he stretches out his hand so that I do not perish. He says the same as above, "who comforts us in all our affliction." He ascribes to God not only that deliverance by which he had been rescued from the gates of death, but all the others as well, leaving nothing to his own diligence and care, even in the smallest danger.

units.la: IN quo spem fixam habemus, inquit, quod etiam posthac sit ereptu rus.) Vide quomodo Deum nobis proponat, qui suis non semel atque iterum sed constanter & ad finem usque benefaciat. Qui misero propterea benefacit ac succurrit, quod ferre non potest, ut sit miser, is utiq; succurrit illi non semel atque iterum, sed quoties miserum esse factum uidit. Qui eripit periclitatem ne pereat, toties eripit quoties uidet esse periculum ne pereat, quandoquidem hic illi scopus est seruare periclitatem ne pereat. Sic comparatus est erga suos pater il le misericordiarum & Deus omnis consolationis. Propterea eripit suos ne pereant, quos uidelicet in sempiternum seruare constituit. Eripit igitur non semel tantum sed quoties periculum est ne pereant. Sic paulum eripiebat quoties periclitabatur. Nolebat enim ut secundum impiorum uota periret. Et hanc illi protectionem Actorum decimo octauo cum esset Corinthi promiserat dicens: Noli timere sed loquere, & ne taceas. Nam ego sum tecum, & nemo apponet tibi ut noceat te.
units.tr: "In whom we have a fixed hope, he says, that he will also deliver us henceforth." See how he sets God before us, who does good to his own not once or twice but constantly and to the end. He who helps and succours the wretched because he cannot bear that they should be wretched helps them surely not once or twice, but as often as he sees them made wretched. He who delivers the endangered from perishing delivers them as often as he sees there is danger of their perishing, since his aim is to preserve the endangered from perishing. So that Father of mercies and God of all comfort is disposed toward his own. He therefore delivers his people from perishing, whom he has determined to preserve forever. He delivers them, then, not merely once, but as often as there is danger of their perishing. Thus he delivered Paul as often as he was in peril, for he did not want him to perish according to the wishes of the ungodly. He had promised this protection in Acts 18, when Paul was at Corinth, saying: "Do not fear, but speak and do not be silent. For I am with you, and no one will lay a hand on you to harm you."

units.la: Deinde uide quid ex eo colligat, quod ereptus erat & eripiebatur a domino, e quauis tribulatione. Postquam dixit: qui ex tanta morte eripuit nos & eripit, subijcit: in quo spem fixam habemus, quod etiam posthac sit ereptu rus. Ex eo quod constantem illius opem in tribulationibus experiebatur de futuro quoque spem capit, quod & in posterum declaraturus sit eandem erga se curam & fidem. Sic praeteritorum ac praesentium beneficiorum experientia spem gignit de futuris, in animis hominum non reprobatorum. Reprobi perpetuo haesitant, quantumuis multis ac crebris beneficijs a Deo cumulati.
units.tr: Next, see what he infers from the fact that he had been rescued, and was being rescued by the Lord, from every tribulation. After saying "who delivered us from so great a death and does deliver us," he adds: "in whom we have a fixed hope that he will also deliver us henceforth." From experiencing his constant help in tribulations, he gains hope also for the future, that in time to come he will show the same care and faithfulness toward him. Thus the experience of past and present benefits begets hope about future ones in the minds of men who are not reprobate. The reprobate waver perpetually, however greatly and frequently they are loaded with benefits by God.

units.la: Quod autem interpres Erasmus non simpliciter uertit: In quo spe habemus, sed in quo spem fixam habemus, ad hoc facit, ut Apostolicae spei certitudo omni haesitatione reiecta exprimatur. Est spes alia mobilis, alia fixa. Mobilis & inconstans est, quae uel carnalis animi inconstantia, uel uanitate eorum unde concepta est, prorsus est imbecillis & euanida. Qui inconstans est animo, etiamsi de rebus certis ac firmis aliquid spei concepit, sperat tamen non constanter, sed ad primam tentationem spem omnem abijcit. De rebus uanis si quid etiam a bonis speratur, non potest spes eiusmodi esse fixa. Spes fixa est hominis fidelis, in fiducia diuinae ueritatis ac bonitatis constantis, de rebus concepta non uanis sed ueris & indubitatis. Spei huius duo sunt fundamenta. Veritas uidelicet & bonitas Dei. Veritas uerbo illius expressa per fidem, bonitas reipsa declarata per experientiam capitur. Spes Pauli merito fixa erat quia & uerbum habebat & experientiam. Ve nostrae caecitati ac stupiditati, qua fit ut nec ueritate uerbi Dei, nec bonitatis illius ulla experientia ad fidendum ac sperandum permoueamur.
units.tr: That the translator Erasmus did not simply render "in whom we have hope" but "in whom we have a fixed hope" serves to express the certainty of apostolic hope, with all wavering rejected. There is one hope that is changeable and another that is fixed. The changeable and inconstant hope, which arises either from the inconstancy of a carnal mind or from the vanity of that from which it was conceived, is altogether weak and vanishing. A man inconstant in mind, even if he has conceived some hope regarding certain and firm things, hopes nonetheless inconstantly, and at the first temptation casts off all hope. If anything is hoped for from vain things, even from good ones, such hope cannot be fixed. A fixed hope belongs to a faithful man, conceived in trust in the divine truth and constant goodness, concerning things that are not vain but true and indubitable. This hope has two foundations, namely the truth and goodness of God. The truth is grasped by faith through his word; the goodness, declared in fact, is grasped through experience. Paul's hope was rightly fixed because he had both the word and the experience. Woe to our blindness and dullness, by which it happens that we are moved neither by the truth of God's word nor by any experience of his goodness to trust and hope.

units.la: SIMVL adiuuantibus & uobis, inquit, per deprecationem pro nobis.) Quam extol lit opem Dei, qua eripiebatur ex omni afflictione, ta seipsum humiliat, ne quid illius meritis suis tribuere uideatur. Sic supra Deum patrem misericordiarum uocauit, cum de hac causa epistolam ordiretur. Sic in praesenti, postquam dixit, qui ex tanta morte eripuit nos, & eripit, in quo spem fixam habemus, magno humilitatis affectu subijcit: simul adiuuantibus & uobis per deprecationem pro nobis. Quamuis esset Apostolus, & tam grauibus ac crebris afflictionibus pro nomine Christi grauaretur, simulque plus omnibus laboraret in opere domini, nihilo tamen minus magnifacit precationes fidelium pro se factas ad dominum, illisque ex parte fert acceptum, quod ope domini ex afflictionibus ereptus esset, eriperetur, & in posterum se eripiendum consideret. Hoc affectu uocat eos qui pro se orabant συνυπεργούντες, hoc est, una cum alijs precando pro se sublaborantes & operam suam quantum in ipsis erat subministrantes.
units.tr: "Helping together also you, he says, by prayer for us." Paul extols the help of God by which he was delivered from every affliction, yet humbles himself so that nothing might seem to be ascribed to his own merits. So above, when he began the epistle on this subject, he called God the Father of mercies. So here, after saying "who delivered us from so great a death, and does deliver us, in whom we have a fixed hope," he adds with great humility: "helping together also you by prayer for us." Although he was an apostle, and burdened by such grave and frequent afflictions for the name of Christ, and at the same time laboured more than all in the work of the Lord, he nonetheless esteems highly the prayers of the faithful made for him to the Lord. He acknowledges in part that they received from them that by the Lord's help he had been delivered from afflictions, was being delivered, and reckons that he will be delivered in future. In this spirit he calls those who prayed for him "fellow workers" [συνυπεργούντες], that is, labouring along with others in prayer on his behalf and supplying their effort as far as lay in them.

units.la: Accommodissima hac uoce tria significat.
units.tr: This very apt word signifies three things.

units.la: 1 Primum, huc fuisse morem ecclesijs, ut pro apostolis & ministris, propter opus domini afflictis & periclitantibus, preces suas funderent ad dominum. Sic pro Petro quoque, cum in vinculis esset, precationes ad Deum fiebant ab ecclesia.
units.tr: (1) First, it was the custom of the churches to pour out their prayers to the Lord for apostles and ministers who were afflicted and in peril for the work of the Lord. So also for Peter, when he was in chains, prayers were made to God by the church.

units.la: 2 Deinde non solum Corinthiorum ecclesiae sed & alias fuisse prosecratas. Quare no simpliciter dicit, συνυπεργοῦντες sed συνυπεργῶν, hoc est una cum alijs sublaborantibus.
units.tr: (2) Next, this was practised not only by the church of the Corinthians but by others as well. Wherefore he does not simply say [συνυπεργοῦντες] but [συνυπεργῶν], that is, labouring along with others.

units.la: 3 Tertium, eiusmodi preces non esse frustraneas coram domino. Licet enim principalis causa, quur eripuerit Apostolum suum Deus, fuerit ipsius misericordia, placebat tamen illi studium hoc fidelium, & concors uotum, pro Apostolo ipsorum supplicitur ac sedulo ad se precantium. Quare & ex parte fert illis acceptum, quod tam constanter in omni afflictione diuinitus eripiebatur. Annotat hic Chrysostomus, etiamsi constituerit dominus succurrere afflictis, plurimum tamen ea in re habere momenti preces fidelium, praesertim si concorditer diter fundantur. Misericors est, bonus ac fide-lis, & haëтenus ipse sibi prima est omnis boni-tatis, misericordię ac beneficentiæ causa. Iuxtà tamen amans est syncerę fidei ex animo ad se precantium, amans item est fraternę charitatis qua concorditer alij pro alijs ad se precantur. Quare conuenit, ut Ecclesiæ studiosissime ad huiusmodi preces in conspectu Domini fundendas prouocentur.
units.tr: (3) Third, such prayers are not in vain before the Lord. For although the principal cause why God delivered his apostle was his own mercy, yet this zeal of the faithful and their united vow, supplicating for their apostle and earnestly praying to him, pleased him. Wherefore he also, in part, ascribes to them that he was so constantly delivered by God from every affliction. Chrysostom observes here that, even if the Lord has determined to succour the afflicted, the prayers of the faithful carry great weight in this matter, especially if they are offered in harmony. He is merciful, good and faithful, and is himself the first cause of all goodness, mercy and beneficence. Yet he also loves those who pray to him from a sincere faith of heart, and he likewise loves the fraternal charity by which believers pray for one another in harmony. Therefore it is fitting that the churches be most diligently stirred up to pour out such prayers in the sight of the Lord.

units.la: VT ex multis personis pro dono in nos collato, inquit, per multos gratiæ agantur pro nobis. Locus hic satis quidem manifestus est, quod sensum attinet, in uerbis uero non ita. Nam illa aliquid uel superflui habere uel desiderare uidentur, unde lectio in Græco reddatur expedita. Græca exemplaria quib. utimur sic habet ἵνα ἐκ πολλῶν πρόσωπον τὸ εἰς ἡμᾶς χάρισμα διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαριστηθῇ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν. i. ut ex multis personis, uel faciebus, donū quod in nos (collatum est) per multos cum gratiarum actione pro nobis depredicetur. Hic quoniā ista duo, ex multis personis, & per multos, unum & idem esse uidentur, quærunt alij aliud, quo commodior lectio adferatur, in qua nihil sit superflui.
units.tr: "That for the gift bestowed upon us through many persons, thanks may be given by many on our behalf," he says. This passage is quite plain as to sense, but not so as to words, for the words seem to contain something superfluous or to lack something, so the reading in the Greek needs to be made smoother. The Greek copies we use read thus: [ἵνα ἐκ πολλῶν πρόσωπον τὸ εἰς ἡμᾶς χάρισμα διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαριστηθῇ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν], that is, that the gift bestowed upon us may be made known with thanksgiving by many, from many persons or faces, on our behalf. Since "from many persons" and "by many" seem to be one and the same, others seek another reading, in which nothing is superfluous, and bring forward a more convenient one.

units.la: Chrysostomus legit: ἵνα ἐκ πολλῶν πρόσωπον ubi nostra exemplaria habent ἵνα ἐκ πολλῶν πρόσωπων. Et exponit ad hunc modū: τὸ δὲ εἰς ἡμᾶς χάρισμα ... Hoc est. Donum enim quod in nos (collatum est) id est, salutem nostram omnibus uobis largiri uoluit, ut multæ sibi personæ gratias agant, quandoquidem & multæ gratiam hanc acceperunt.
units.tr: Chrysostom reads [ἵνα ἐκ πολλῶν πρόσωπον], where our copies have [ἵνα ἐκ πολλῶν πρόσωπων]. He explains it in this way: [τὸ δὲ εἰς ἡμᾶς χάρισμα ...]. That is: the gift bestowed upon us, that is, he wished to bestow our salvation on all of you, so that many persons might give thanks, since many also have received this grace.

units.la: Valla sic uertendum putauit. Vt de gratia in me ex multis personis, siue respectu multorum collocata p multos gratiæ agatur propter uos. Legit enim ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν, ubi noshabemus ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν.
units.tr: Valla thought it should be translated thus: "That thanks may be given for me by many persons, or, placed with respect to many, by many on your account." He reads ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν [on your behalf], where we have ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν [on our behalf].

units.la: Erasmus in annotationibus suis sic reddidit. Vt ex multis personis de dono in nos collato multis modis gratiæ agantur pro nobis. Sic illud, διὰ πολλῶν, quod in uersione sua reddidit, p multos, uertit hic, multis modis, atq; ita no retulit ad personas, sed neutraliter accepit.
units.tr: Erasmus, in his annotations, rendered it thus: "That, from many persons, thanks may be given in many ways for us for the gift conferred upon us." So he rendered διὰ πολλῶν [through many], which in his own version he translated "by many," here as "in many ways," and thus did not refer it to persons but took it as neuter.

units.la: Germanicus interpres sic habet: auff das uber vns, fur die gab die vns gegeben ist durch vil personen vil dancks geschehe. Hic illud, διὰ πολλῶν, ad multitudinem gratiarum actionis retulit, quasi διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαριστήσαδαι, idem sit quod multis agi gratias.
units.tr: The German translator has it thus: "auff das uber vns, fur die gab die vns gegeben ist durch vil personen vil dancks geschehe," that is, "so that much thanks may be given through many persons for us, for the gift that has been given to us." Here he referred διὰ πολλῶν [through many] to the multitude of thanksgivings, as if διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαριστήσαι [to give thanks through many] meant the same as "to be thanked by many."

units.la: Quando quisque quod verosimile putat in medium adfert, dicam & ego quid mihi videatur. Potest uideri admissum esse errorem in dictione προσώπων, ut posita sit per somnolentiā antiquariorum pro προσευχῶν. Nam apparet scripsisse Apostolum ad hunc modum. ἵνα ἐκ πολλῶν προσευχῶν τὸ εἰς ἡμᾶς χάρισμα διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαριστηθῇ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν. Hoc est, ut donū quod multorum in nos est precibus (collatum) per multorum gratiarum actiones pro nobis factas depredicetur. Quod si dictio πρόσωπον ab ipso Apostolo
units.tr: Since each person brings forward what he thinks probable, I too will say what seems right to me. It may be seen that an error has crept into the word "persons" [προσώπων], placed there through the drowsiness of the copyists in place of "prayers" [προσευχῶν]. For it appears that the Apostle wrote in this way: "that from many prayers [ἐκ πολλῶν προσευχῶν] the gift toward us [τὸ εἰς ἡμᾶς χάρισμα] may be given thanks through many on our behalf [διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαριστηθῇ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν]." That is, that the gift conferred upon us by the prayers of many may be proclaimed through the thanksgivings of many made on our behalf. But if the word "persons" [πρόσωπον] seems to have been placed by the Apostle himself,

units.la: lo posita uidetur, potest ordinari lectio ad hunc modum. Vt quod ex multis est personis (intellige, pro nobis ad Deum precantibus) in nos collatum donum, per multos etiam gratias pro nobis agentes deprædicetur. Quod in Græco est, εὐχαριστηθῇ in passiuo Germanicè melius possumus reddere, bedancket wuerden, q; Latinè. Si periodum hanc sic diuidas ut primū illius membrum sit, ut ex multis personis in nos collatum donum, alterum uero quod sequitur, per multos cum gratiarum actione deprædicetur, puto nihil remanere incommodi.
units.tr: the reading can be arranged in this way: that the gift conferred upon us from many persons (understand, praying to God for us) may also be proclaimed through many giving thanks for us. In the Greek, εὐχαριστηθῇ [may be thanked] is in the passive, which we can render better in German, "bedancket wuerden," than in Latin. If you divide this period so that its first member is "that the gift conferred upon us from many persons," and the following part is "may be proclaimed through many with thanksgiving," I think no inconvenience remains.

units.la: Sensus autem Apostoli est. Qui ex tāta mor te eripuit nos, & eripit, in quo spem fixam habemus, quod etiam posthac erepturus sit, non modo pro incomparabili sua misericordia, sed & ob id, ut quemadmodum propter multarum personarum preces pro nobis factas ex omni nos liberat afflictione, ita per multas etiam personas gratię ipsi pro nobis propter tam insigne beneficium agantur.
units.tr: The meaning of the Apostle is this: he who has snatched us from so great a death, and snatches us, in whom we have a firm hope that he will also rescue us hereafter, does so not only because of his incomparable mercy, but also so that, just as through the prayers made for us by many persons he delivers us from every affliction, so also through many persons thanks may be given to him for us for so remarkable a benefit.

units.la: Vide, autem, quomodo per obliquum inducat eos ad agendum Domino pro se gratias. Et sanè omnium æquissimum est, ut post preces sequatur gratiarum actio. Qui pro liberando afflicto precatur ad Dominum, si precatur ex animo, utique pro liberato gratias aget liberatori, cuius antea opem implorauerat. Hodie quoque solenne est ut in cœtibus Ecclesiasticis publice oretur pro ægrotantibus, captiuis, & aliàs afflictis. Hæ preces fiunt communiter à multitudine fidelium, adhortatu ministri. Conuenit igitur, ut uicissim à multitudine fidelium gratiæ agantur Domino pro liberatis, quo donum propter multorum preces afflicto collatum multorum quoque gratitudine palam in Ecclesia deprædicetur.
