Verum, quemadmodū de leprosis dicebat Dominus: Nunquid decem mundati sunt, iam nouem ubi sunt? sic in hac quoque causa rarissimus quisque est, qui beneficio Domini propter fidelium suorum preces liberatus, redeat, & uel ipse gratias agat Domino uel quemadmodum orari pro se uoluit ab Ecclesia, ita & gratias ab illa pro se petat agi liberatori Domino. In hanc rem debebant incumbere ministri uerbi, ut quemadmodum hortatu suo authores sunt Ecclesiæ ad precandum pro afflictis, ita essent etiam illi authores ad agendum Domino gratias pro afflictorum liberatione.
units.tr: Notice, moreover, how he indirectly leads them to give thanks to the Lord for him. And indeed nothing is more fitting than that thanksgiving should follow prayer. Whoever prays to the Lord for the deliverance of one afflicted, if he prays sincerely, will certainly give thanks to the deliverer for the one delivered, whose aid he had earlier implored. Today too it is customary that in ecclesiastical assemblies prayer is offered publicly for the sick, the captive, and others afflicted. These prayers are made commonly by the multitude of the faithful, at the exhortation of the minister. It is fitting, therefore, that in turn thanks be given to the Lord by the multitude of the faithful for those delivered, so that the gift conferred on the afflicted through the prayers of many may also be openly proclaimed in the Church with the gratitude of many. But just as the Lord said of the lepers, "Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine?", so in this matter too there is very rarely anyone who, delivered by the Lord's benefit through the prayers of his faithful people, returns and either gives thanks to the Lord himself or, just as he wished to be prayed for by the Church, so also asks the Church to give thanks on his behalf to the delivering Lord. In this matter the ministers of the Word ought to apply themselves, so that just as by their exhortation they are the authors of the Church's prayer for the afflicted, so they may also be the authors of giving thanks to the Lord for the deliverance of the afflicted.

units.la: Quid est autem quod dicit: ex multis personis, & per multos? Refert ne quàm multi orent ad Dominum pro liberando afflicto, & quàm multi gratias agant pro liberato? Dicemus ne pluris facere Deum multorum preces quàm paucorum? Multi sunt vocati, inquit Dominus, pauci electi. Si orent multi vocati, citius ne exaudiet Deus, quàm si orent pauci electi.
units.tr: But what does he mean by saying "from many persons" and "through many"? Does it matter how many pray to the Lord for the deliverance of one afflicted, and how many give thanks for the one delivered? Shall we say that God sets more store by the prayers of many than of few? "Many are called," says the Lord, "but few are chosen." If many who are called pray, will God hear more quickly than if few who are chosen pray?

units.la: Respondeo. Multitudinem in se non moratur Deus, sed moratur synceritatem ex animo ad se orantium. Horum si multi sunt acceptior est oratio no ut multorum in se, sed ut multorum piorum. Causa hæc de qua loquitur Apost. sic erat comparata ut multos concerneret ipsius libe-ratio. Conueniebat igitur ut multi etiam pro illa precarentur ad dominum, & pro impetrata quoque multi gratias agerent domino. Huc respiciens dicit: ut ex multis personis, item per multos, &c. Et infrà cap. 4. Palàm dicit, beneficium exuberans, pluribus gratias agentibus, exuberare in gloriam Dei.
units.tr: I answer: God does not regard the multitude in itself, but regards the sincerity of those who pray to him from the heart. If these are many, the prayer is more acceptable, not because of the number of many people in itself, but because of the number of many pious people. This cause of which the Apostle speaks was so constituted that the deliverance concerned many. It was fitting, therefore, that many should also pray to the Lord for it, and that many should also give thanks to the Lord for what was obtained. Looking to this, he says "from many persons," likewise "through many," and so on. And below, in chapter 4: he openly says that the abounding benefit, with many giving thanks, overflows to the glory of God.

units.la: Nam gloriatio nostra hęc est, testimonium conscientię nostrę, quod cum simplicitate & synceritate Dei, non sapientia carnali, sed per gratiam Dei conuersati fuerimus in mundo, abundantius autem erga uos. Non enim alia scribimus uobis, quàm quæ recognoscitis, aut etiă agnoscitis. Spero autem quod usq; ad finem quoque agnoscetis, quemadmodum & agnouistis nos ex parte, quoniă gloria uestra sumus, quemadmodum & uos nostra in die domini Iesu.
units.tr: For our boasting is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and sincerity of God, not in fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have conducted ourselves in the world, and more abundantly toward you. For we write to you no other things than those which you read, or even acknowledge. And I hope that you will acknowledge to the end, as you have also acknowledged us in part, since we are your glory, as you are ours in the day of the Lord Jesus.

units.la: Quoniā nō dicit simpliciter gloriatio nostra, sed: Nam gloriatio nostra hęc est, testimonium conscietiæ nostræ, refereda sunt hæc ad præcedentia. Sunt qui referant ad spem Apostoli, de qua dixit: In quo spem fixa habemus, quod etiā posthac erepturus sit, quasi iam spei huius causam collocet non solum in misericordia Dei & preces fidelium, sed & in conuersationis suæ simplicitatem ac synceritatem, de qua ueraciter conscientiæ suæ possit testimonio gloriari. Sic & ueteres & recentiores nonnulli exponunt. Meo tamen iudicio non hoc agit in præsenti, ut spei suæ causam adferat aliam, quàm attulit in præcedentibus, sed magis tuetur innocentiam suam contra pseudapostolos, qui afflictiones ipsius odiose insectabàtur ac maliciose interpretabatur, quasi in culpa esset ipse, quod passim ubique afflictaretur. Contra horum maliciam citat primum suam ipsius deinde & Corinthiorum conscientiam, ac dat utrique, quod de conuersationis suæ simplicitate ac synceritate testetur sic dicit: Nam gloriatio nostra hæc est, testimonium conscientiæ nostræ. Quasi dicat: Tam enim abest, ut sinistro aliquo studio mortalium in me animos concitem simq; ipse mihi tot afflictionum causa improbe ac maliciose conuersando in hoc mundo, ut magis contra omnes meos inimicos de innocenti mea conuersatione certissimo conscientiæ meę posśim testimonio gloriari, quod simpliciter ac syncere conuersatus sim in mundo. Et de hac innocentia mea uos ipsi testificari poteritis, quibus maxime notum est, quomodo apud uos sim conuersatus.
units.tr: Because he does not say simply "our boasting," but "For our boasting is this, the testimony of our conscience," these words must be referred to what precedes. Some refer them to the Apostle's hope, of which he said: "in whom we have a firm hope that he will also rescue us hereafter," as if he now placed the cause of this hope not only in God's mercy and the prayers of the faithful, but also in the simplicity and sincerity of his conduct, about which he can truly boast with the testimony of his conscience. Both ancient and some recent writers explain it thus. In my judgment, however, he is not at present aiming to offer a different cause for his hope from the one he gave earlier, but rather to defend his innocence against the false apostles, who hostilely attacked his afflictions and maliciously interpreted them, as if he himself were to blame for being afflicted everywhere. Against their malice he cites first his own conscience and then that of the Corinthians, and gives to both the testimony of the simplicity and sincerity of his conduct, saying: "For our boasting is this, the testimony of our conscience." As if he said: "I am so far from stirring up minds against me by any sinister zeal of mortals, or from having brought so many afflictions upon myself by wickedly and maliciously conducting myself in this world, that I may rather boast, against all my enemies, of the most certain testimony of my conscience concerning my innocent conduct, that I have conducted myself simply and sincerely in the world. And you yourselves can bear witness to this innocence of mine, you to whom it is best known how I have conducted myself among you."

units.la: NAM gloriatio nostra hæc est, inquit, testimoniū conscientiæ nostræ.) Poterit hic quæri quomodo de suaipsius conscientia glorietur Apostolus, cum alibi dicat: Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. An in Domino gloriatur, qui de conscientia sua gloriatur?
units.tr: "For our boasting is this," he says, "the testimony of our conscience." Here it may be asked how the Apostle can boast of his own conscience, when elsewhere he says: "He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord." Or does he who boasts of his conscience boast in the Lord?

units.la: Respondeo. Refert quo animo de conscientia sua sit gloriatus Apostolus. Qui secundum carnem gloriatur, carnis quærit gloriam illiusque uires gloriando extollit. Si sic gloriatus est Apostolus, non est gloriatus in Domino. Verum quàm non sit gloriatus secundum carnem, abunde satis ex eo patet, quod tam insigni doxologia misericordias erga se Dei prædicauit, illisque omnem suam salutem acceptam tulit. Quare quod hic dicit: Nam gloriatio nostra hæc est, testimonium conscientiæ nostræ, non ad hoc dicit, ut aliquid gloriæ carni suæ uindicet, sed ut improbitati pseudapostolorum occurrat, per quos Satan cursum Euangelij Dei remorari satagebat. Et hoc faciens magis gloriam gratiæ Dei quàm suam ipsius quærit. Sic animatus non modo inculpabiliter sed & pie & utiliter de testimonio conscientiæ suæ contra Apostolos Satanæ gloriatur.
units.tr: I answer: it matters with what mind the Apostle boasted of his conscience. He who boasts according to the flesh seeks the glory of the flesh and by boasting exalts its strength. If the Apostle boasted in this way, he did not boast in the Lord. But that he did not boast according to the flesh is clear enough from the fact that he proclaimed God's mercies toward himself with such a remarkable doxology, and attributed all his salvation to them. Therefore, when he says here, "For our boasting is this, the testimony of our conscience," he does not say it to claim any glory for his flesh, but to meet the wickedness of the false apostles, through whom Satan was striving to hinder the course of the Gospel of God. In doing this he seeks the glory of God's grace more than his own. Thus inspired, he boasts of the testimony of his conscience against the apostles of Satan not only blamelessly, but also piously and profitably.

units.la: TESTIMONIVM, inquit, conscientiæ nostræ.)
units.tr: "The testimony of our conscience," he says.)

units.la: Pulchre testimonium coniungit cum conscientia. Non enim certius ullum potest esse testimonium quàm conscientiæ. Qui conscius est alicuius rei bonæ uel malæ, de illa utiq; omnium potest certissimum ferre testimonium. Et hanc testimonij certitudinem non infringit, sed magis confirmat, quod non de aliena, sed sua ipsius conscientia loquitur, dicens: Nam gloriatio hæc est, testimonium conscientiæ nostræ. Loquitur enim de testimonio, quo seipsum cum primis contra calumnias pseudapostolorum solabatur & obfirmabat. Nescit mentiri sibijpsi propria conscientia. Siue nos damnet siue de innocentia nostra testetur, non fallit. Quare cum diuini iudicij certitudinem & iusticiam uellet exprimere Rom. 2. conscientiarum nostrarum nos ipsos accusantium aut excusantium testimonia citat, secundum quorum calculos uel iudicandi simus in die Domini uel absoluendi. Non potuit igitur firmius testimonium inducere, quàm propriæ conscientiæ.
units.tr: Paul rightly joins testimony with conscience, for no testimony can be more certain than that of conscience. Whoever is aware of some good or evil deed can certainly bear the most reliable witness to it before everyone. Paul does not weaken this certainty but strengthens it, because he speaks not of another's conscience but of his own: "For this is our boast, the testimony of our conscience." He is speaking of the testimony by which he himself, above all, comforted and steadied himself against the slanders of the false apostles. One's own conscience cannot lie to oneself. Whether it condemns us or testifies to our innocence, it does not deceive. So when Paul wanted to express the certainty and justice of God's judgment in Rom. 2, he cites the testimony of our consciences, which either accuse or excuse us, and by whose reckoning we shall be either condemned or acquitted on the day of the Lord. He could not, therefore, have brought forward a firmer witness than one's own conscience.

units.la: Sed dices. Iustificat igitur se ipse propriæ conscientiæ testimonio? Quid ergo est quod 1. Corint. 4. dicit: Nullius mihi (intellige culpæ) conscius sum, sed non per hoc iustificatus sum? Qui me iudicat, Dominus est. Si non potuit propriæ conscientiæ testimonio iustificari, quorsum hic illud pro asserenda sua innocentia citat?
units.tr: But you will say: does he then justify himself by the testimony of his own conscience? What then does he mean in 1 Cor. 4 when he says: "I am conscious of nothing against myself (understand, of fault), yet I am not thereby justified; it is the Lord who judges me"? If he could not be justified by the testimony of his own conscience, why does he here cite it to assert his innocence?

units.la: Respondeo. Triplex est iudicij forum, in quo uita nostra uel accusatur uel excusatur.
units.tr: I answer: there is a threefold tribunal in which our life is either accused or excused.

units.la: Primum est nostrum ipsorum quod in nostris conscientijs singuli circumferimus, nec ullo modo fallere uel effugere possumus.
units.tr: The first is our own, which each of us carries about in his conscience, and from which we can in no way hide or escape.

units.la: Secundum est extra nos humanum illud, quo facta nostra iudicant homines, tam priuati quàm ordinarij iudices.
units.tr: The second lies outside us: the human tribunal, in which men, both private persons and public judges, weigh our deeds.

units.la: Tertium est diuinum, supremum, & ultimum. Quod primum attinet, habebat illud Apostolus pro se, in causa Apostolicę suæ conuersationis. Et huius testimonium opponit secunsecundi iudicij, humani uidelicet, foro. Quicquid in illo de Apostolatu suo iudicaretur, haudquàquam morabatur, fretus conscientiæ suæ testimonio. De hoc est quod loco citato dicit: Mihi uero pro minimo est, ut à uobis dijudicer, aut ab humano iudicio. Quod uero subiungit: Imò, nec me ipse dijudico: Nullius enim mihi conscius sum, sed non in hoc iustificatus sum, respicit ad forum iudicij Dei, in quo se non iustificari per hoc dicit, quod nullius sibi sit mali conscius. In eo siquidem etiam occultissima cordium nostrorum, à conscientijs nostris abscondita, si misericordia non accesserit, iudicantur. Iam quod præsentem locum concernit, citat conscientiæ suæ testimonium, non ad hoc, ut se coram Deo prorsus iustificet, sed ut innocentiam suam in seipso contra secundum, humani uidelicet iudicij, forum, in quo per pseudapostolorum calumnias impetebatur, fortiter defendat.
units.tr: The third is divine, supreme and final. As to the first, Paul had it on his side in the case of his apostolic conduct, and he sets its testimony against the second tribunal, the human one. Whatever was judged about his apostleship in that court, he did not much care, relying on the testimony of his conscience. Of this he says in the passage cited: "But it is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by human judgment." What he adds, "Indeed, I do not even judge myself; for I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not thereby justified," refers to the tribunal of God's judgment, in which he says he is not justified merely because he knows of no evil in himself. In that court even the most hidden secrets of our hearts, concealed from our consciences, are judged, unless mercy intervenes. But as to the present passage, he cites the testimony of his conscience not so that he may justify himself entirely before God, but so that, in the human tribunal, where he was being attacked by the slanders of the false apostles, he may vigorously defend his innocence.

units.la: Admonet igitur hic locus, quomodo conscientiæ nostræ debeamus usurpare testimonium. Sic uidelicet, ut innocentiam nostram contra improborum calumnias in nobisipsis tueamur, non ut per illud in conspectu Dei iustificemur.
units.tr: This passage therefore teaches us how we ought to use the testimony of our conscience: namely, to defend our innocence within ourselves against the slanders of the wicked, not to be justified by it in the sight of God.

units.la: QVOD cum simplicitate, inquit, & synceritate Dei, non sapientia carnali, sed per gratiam Dei conuersati fuerimus in mundo.) Profert & exponit conscientiæ suæ testimonium. Huius duo membra ponit. Vnum quadre: alterum, quid testificetur. Qua de re testificetur, in eo exprimit, quod dicit: Quod conuersati fuerimus in mundo. Ergo prolaturus est testimonium conscientiæ suæ, de conuersatione sua, qua in mundo conuersabatur.
units.tr: "That in simplicity and godly sincerity, not in fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have conducted ourselves in the world." He brings forward and sets out the testimony of his conscience. He gives two parts of it: one is the witness, the other is what it testifies. He states what it testifies in the words "that we have conducted ourselves in the world." So he is about to produce the testimony of his conscience concerning his conduct, by which he lived in the world.

units.la: Sed obsecro, refert ne quomodo Apostolus Christi conuersetur in mundo? An non est satis ad asserendam authoritatem Apostolicam, & titulus Apostolatus poterit ubilibet obtèdi?
units.tr: But I ask: does it matter how an apostle of Christ conducts himself in the world? Is it not enough for asserting apostolic authority, and can the title of apostle not be thrust forward anywhere?

units.la: Hodie quidem isto retinendæ authoritatis compendio utitur Apostolus Babylonis, meretricis illius magnæ, uerum olim, cum in uiuis essent ueri Christi apostoli, referebat plurimum, quomodo conuersarentur in mundo, ne quo pacto cuipiam essent offendiculo. Iam illorum successores, ut uideri uolunt, quamuis Curios simulent ac Bacchanalia uiuant, nihilo tamen minus usurpant illud Christi: Supra cathedram Mosis sedent Scribæ & Pharisæi, quæ dicunt facite, quæ faciunt facere nolite. Et illud: Qui uos audit, me audit. Et Coriphæus illorum, etiamsi innumera animarum millia secum ad inferos pessime uiuendo deducat, nó uult tamen iudicari à quoquam. Hisce notis uidere licet, quales iam habeat ecclesia apostolos, & quàm non debeat mirum uideri cuipiam, unde fit catholica ecclesiarum corruptio, postquam obtinuit hæc pestis in capitibus, ut iudicent non referre, quomodo conuersentur in mundo, modo à sede Romana confirmati titulos possint iactare dignitatum suarum ac prælatura.
units.tr: Today indeed the Apostle of Babylon, that great harlot, uses this shortcut for retaining authority. But once, when the true apostles of Christ were alive, it mattered greatly how they conducted themselves in the world, so that they might give no stumbling block to anyone. Now their successors, who wish to appear, though they affect to be scrupulous and live like Bacchanals, nonetheless claim that saying of Christ: "The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses' seat; so do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do." And that: "He who hears you hears me." And their chief, even though by living most wickedly he may lead countless thousands of souls with him into hell, does not want to be judged by anyone. From these marks one can see what sort of apostles the Church now has, and it should not seem strange to anyone whence comes the corruption of the catholic churches, now that this plague has taken hold among the heads, so that they judge it makes no difference how they conduct themselves in the world, provided that, confirmed by the Roman see, they can flaunt the titles of their dignities and prelacies.

units.la: Vtinam autem eiusmodi fuci non obtineant in ecclesijs ab Antichristianismo liberatis. Nam hic quoque lues ista radices agere cœpit, quæ non parum rigatur ab illis, qui non possunt de mysteriorum Dei dispensatione loqui, nisi pluribus inculcent, non referre qualis sit minister, & quomodo uiuat in ecclesia Dei, modo salua maneat dominica institutio. Scio & sciunt multi boni uiri, si de mysteriorum Christi integritate censendum sit, nihil ad illam facere ministri uitam, uerum interea quis non uidet, imò non palpat, etiamsi nihil de institutione dominica, quod ritus attinet, deteratur, illam ipsam tamen in multitudine fidelium propter ministrorum cōtemptum reddi clumbem & infrugiferam?
units.tr: Would that such shams did not hold sway in churches freed from Antichristianism. For this pestilence has also begun to take root here, and it is watered not a little by those who cannot speak of the dispensation of God's mysteries without repeatedly insisting that it does not matter what sort of minister he is, or how he lives in the Church of God, provided the Lord's institution remains safe. I know, and many good men know, that if the integrity of Christ's mysteries is to be judged, the life of the minister has nothing to do with it. Yet meanwhile who does not see, indeed who does not feel, that even when nothing is taken away from the Lord's institution as far as the rite is concerned, that very institution is rendered lame and unfruitful among the multitude of the faithful because the ministers are despised?

units.la: Alterum membrum testificantis est conscientiæ, quid illa de conuersatione ipsius testificetur. Exprimit hoc dicens: quod cum simplicitate ac synceritate Dei, non sapientia carnali, sed per gratiam Dei conuersati fuerimus in mundo. Reijcit hisce uerbis à conuersatione sua omnis doli, maliciæ, impostureæ, & insynceritatis calumnias, quibus pseudapostoli Apostolatum ipsius suspectum & odiosum reddere molicbātur. Etenim per ea, quæ conscientiam suam de conuersatione sua testificari dicit, satis ex oppositio indicat cuius nam generis calumnijs impetitus fuerit à pseudapostolis.
units.tr: The second part of the witnessing conscience is what it testifies about his conduct. He expresses this in saying: "that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not in fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have conducted ourselves in the world." By these words he rejects from his conduct all the slanders of deceit, malice, trickery and insincerity, by which the false apostles tried to make his apostleship suspect and hateful. For from what he says his conscience testifies about his conduct, the opposite makes it sufficiently clear what kind of slanders the false apostles attacked him with.

units.la: QVOD cum simplicitate, inquit, & synceritate Dei.) Vulgata habet, quod in simplicitate cordis. Licet in Græco tantum habeatur ἁπλότητι, id est, in simplicitate, loquitur tamen Apostolus non de alia quàm cordis simplicitate. Quare non est præter rationem dictio cordis ab interprete adiecta. Quid autem sit conuersari in mundo cum simplicitate cordis ac synceritate Dei, notius est quàm ut exponendum sit operosius. Simplicitas ac synceritas cordis est, qua omnia absque dolo malo candide ac fideliter aguntur. Duplicitas & insynceritas est, qua aliud foris simulatur uerbis ac gestibus, & aliud intus celatur in corde, atque ita imperitis imponitur. Synceritas est puritas, iuxta illud: Syncerum est nisi uas, quodcunque infundis acescit. Huic coniuncta est simplicitas. Cohærent enim ambæ, quemadmodum & duo contraria uicia, duplicitas & insynceritas sic cohærent, ut ubi locum habet altera, abesse nequeat altera. Etenim cor malis affectibus impuratum & insyncerum quicquid agit, agit cū maliciosa duplicitate, sic ut aliud pretendat foris, & aliud meditetur intus. Tales cum essent apostoli Satanæ in ministros Christi transfigurati, huius maliciæ insimulabant apostolos Christi, Paulum cum primis, à qua tamen illi omnium erant alienissimi.
units.tr: "That in simplicity and sincerity," he says, "of God." The Vulgate has "in simplicity of heart." Although the Greek has only ἁπλότητι [haplotēti], that is, "in simplicity," the Apostle is speaking of nothing other than simplicity of heart. So the translator's addition of the word "heart" is not unreasonable. What it is to conduct oneself in the world with simplicity of heart and godly sincerity is too well known to need a laborious explanation. Simplicity and sincerity of heart is that by which everything is done candidly and faithfully, without evil deceit. Duplicity and insincerity is that by which one thing is feigned outwardly in words and gestures, and another is hidden inwardly in the heart, and so is imposed upon the unwary. Sincerity is purity, as in the saying: "Unless the vessel is clean, whatever you pour into it turns sour." Simplicity is joined to it. The two go together, just as the two contrary vices, duplicity and insincerity, go together, so that where one has a place, the other cannot be absent. For a heart defiled and insincere through evil affections, whatever it does, it does with malicious duplicity, so that it presents one thing outwardly and plots another within. Since the apostles of Satan had been transformed into ministers of Christ, they accused the apostles of Christ, Paul above all, of this malice, though those apostles were most remote from it.

units.la: Quod autem nó simpliciter dicit: cum simplicitate & synceritate, sed, Cum simplicitate & synceritate Dei, exponunt alij de eo quod simplicitas ista ac synceritas Apostolo fuerit à Deo data, non ex carne nata, alij de eo, quod talis fuerit ac taliter conuersa. tus Apostolus respectu Dei quem perpetuo habuerit ob oculos. Vterque lensus uerus est. Nam hæ uirtutes & à Deo dantur, & ad conscientiam Dei in omnibus diriguntur. Commentarij qui Hieronymo dantur, habent: quoniam Deus simplex est & syncerus. Chrysostomus tamen nec legit nec exponit, & syncerita te Dei, sed simpliciter habet, quod cum simplicitate & syncéritate, non sapientia carnali, &c.
units.tr: But as for why he does not simply say "with simplicity and sincerity," but "with simplicity and sincerity of God," some explain that this simplicity and sincerity was given to the Apostle by God and not born of the flesh; others that he thus conducted himself with regard to God, whom he always kept before his eyes. Both senses are true, for these virtues are both given by God and directed to the awareness of God in all things. The commentaries that are given under the name of Jerome have: "because God is simple and sincere." Chrysostom, however, neither reads nor expounds "and sincerity of God," but has simply: "with simplicity and sincerity, not in fleshly wisdom," etc.

units.la: NON sapientia carnali, inquit, sed gratia Dei.) Quoniam utut magnum est in ministro Christi esse simplicem, integrum, syncerum & fidelem, haud tamen ad hoc est sufficiens, ut ministerium suum prudenter, competenter & utiliter exequatur, nisi accedat donum sapientiæ ac prudentiæ, adiecit hanc particulam Apostolus ad præcedentia, qua non adimit sibi sapientiam ueram Apostolo Christi necessariam, sed magis uindicat, uocans eam gratiam Dei: adimit uero eam quæ carnis est, quam sine dissimulatione in se nusquam agnoscit, magnificiebant autem pseudapostoli, illiusque nomine inflati magistros agebant magis quàm apostolos. Quod igitur dicit: non sapientia carnali, sed gratia Dei, hoc est, agnosco & fateor, simplicitati ac syncéritati meæ non esse coniunctam sapientiam illam carnis & mundi, de qua sibijpsis admodum placent magistri illi uestri ac pseudapostoli, uerum interea absque omni controuersia iure mihi loco sapientiæ uerè uindico gratiam Dei, quæ mecum operata est, & operatur ad finem usque in Apostolatu meo, sic ut plus cæteris omnibus laborauerim, & Euangelium Dei latius quàm illi propagauerim. Sic per gratiam Dei intelligit omnia illa charisimata spiritus, omnemque illius efficaciam & uirtutem, quibus instructus & adiutus Apostolatu suo non modo fideliter ac syncere, sed & sapienter & utiliter functus est. Quomodo uero mundi huius & carnis sapientiam inutilem esse regno Dei, imò contrariam, doceat, uidere licet, 1. Corinth. 1. 2.
units.tr: "Not in fleshly wisdom," he says, "but in the grace of God." Although it is a great thing for a minister of Christ to be simple, upright, sincere and faithful, this alone is not enough for him to carry out his ministry wisely, appropriately and usefully, unless the gift of wisdom and prudence is added as well. The Apostle appended this particle to what precedes it. It does not deny the Apostle of Christ the true wisdom he needs, but rather claims it for him, calling it the grace of God. It denies only that wisdom which belongs to the flesh, which he nowhere acknowledges in himself without pretence. The false apostles, however, were puffed up with it, and in its name they acted more as masters than as apostles. So when he says, "not in fleshly wisdom but in the grace of God," he means: I admit and confess that the wisdom of the flesh and the world, in which your teachers and false apostles take such pleasure, is not joined to my simplicity and sincerity. Yet meanwhile, without any dispute, I rightly claim for myself, in place of that wisdom, the grace of God, which has worked with me and still works until the end of my apostleship, so that I have laboured more than all the rest and spread the gospel of God more widely than they did. Thus by the grace of God he understands all those gifts of the Spirit and all their power and efficacy, by which he was equipped and aided, so that he discharged his apostleship not only faithfully and sincerely but also wisely and usefully. How he teaches that the wisdom of this world and of the flesh is useless to the kingdom of God, or rather opposed to it, may be seen in 1 Corinthians 1 and 2.

units.la: Chrysostomus hoc loco per carnalem sapientiam intelligit astutiam, uersutiam, artificium sermonis, & perplexa sophismata. Respicit ad pseudapostolorum sapientiam, quæ nihil erat aliud, quàm corruptæ carnis uafrum, & uersutum acumen.
units.tr: Chrysostom in this place understands by fleshly wisdom craft, cunning, the artifice of speech and tangled sophisms. He has in view the wisdom of the false apostles, which was nothing other than the sly and crafty sharpness of a corrupt flesh.

units.la: ABVNDANTIVS autem, inquit, erga uos.) Nusquam erat sui non similis, uerum apud Corinthios uersanti plus incubuerat necessitatis sic solicite per gratiam Dei agendi omnia, ut nullam permitteret pseudapostolis calumniandi uel contra se gloriandi occasionem. Et præterea quoniam multus erat domino in ea ciuitate populus, multa quoque illic cœlestis gratiæ uirtute annu egerat & menses sex, sicuti uidere est Actorum decimooctauo. Quare non immerito dicit: abundantius autem erga uos. Nam plus apud illos laborauerat, plusq; fructus domino attulerat quàm alijs in locis, unde & illis notius erat qualis esset ipse, & quomodo conuersaretur in mundo quàm alijs. Hoc autem dicens transfit à testimonio proprij, ad illorum conscientiæ de conuersatione sua testimonium: unde & subijcit.
units.tr: "But more abundantly," he says, "towards you." He was never unlike himself, but among the Corinthians he had laid more stress on the need to act in all things so carefully by the grace of God that he allowed the false apostles no occasion of slandering him or of boasting against him. Moreover, since there was a large people for the Lord in that city, he had also worked there for a year and six months by the power of heavenly grace, as may be seen in Acts 18. Therefore he rightly says, "but more abundantly towards you." For he had laboured more among them and brought more fruit to the Lord than in other places, so that they knew better than others what he was like and how he conducted himself in the world. In saying this he passes from the testimony about himself to the testimony of their conscience concerning his conduct, and so he adds:

units.la: NON enim alia scribimus uobis, quàm quæ recognoscitis, aut etiā agnoscitis, &c.) Summa est. De conuersatione mea non modo mea ipsius, sed & uestra ipsorum, idque præ alijs, testatur conscientia, quod cum simplicitate & syncéritate, non in sapientia carnali, sed gratia Dei conuersatus sim in mundo, amplius uero erga uos, quare quæ scribo, uos ipsi recognoscitis, & uera esse agnoscitis, & sicuti spero, ad finem usque agnoscetis. Neque enim alia uobis de conuersatione mea quàm uobis iam antea comperta scribo.
units.tr: "For we write to you nothing other than what you recognise, or even acknowledge, etc." The sum is this: my conscience bears witness, and yours too, and that more than others', concerning my conduct, that I have lived in the world with simplicity and sincerity, not in fleshly wisdom but in the grace of God, and most of all among you. Therefore you yourselves recognise what I write and acknowledge it to be true, and, as I hope, you will go on acknowledging it to the end. For I write to you about my conduct nothing other than what you have already learned.

units.la: Vetus interpres sic habet: Nō enim alia scribimus uobis, quàm quæ legistis & cognoscitis. Et Erasmus sic uertit, nisi quod reddidit in præsenti, quæ legitis autem, etiam agnoscitis. Sane quod in Græco est ἀναγινώσκετε, uerti potest, quæ legitis. Significat enim ἀναγινώσκειν aliquando legere. Et sic ueteres quoque legunt. Verum cum hoc uerbum proprie significet recognoscere, mirum est quomodo legendi sensu uertendum putauerint. Quid enim est: Non alia scribimus uobis, quàm quæ legitis? An periculum erat, ne ipse scriberet aliud, & ipsi legerent aliud? Nihil huius agit Apostolus. Significat se de simplicitate & integritate conuersationis suæ, & de gratia Dei non scribere ipsis noua quædam, affectata & causæ suæ accommodata, ipsis uero incognita, & talia quæ agnoscere non possint, sed quæ non recognoscant modo, sed & agnoscant. Quare cum hunc sensum ipse contextus offerat ultro, & uerbum ἀναγινώσκεις non repugnet, sed propria sua significatione pulchre astipuletur, uisum est nec ueterem nec recentiorem interpretem, sed ipsam ueritatem sequi, & sensum illius simplicem ac planum amplectendo uertere, non, quæ legitis, sed, quæ recognoscitis. Est autem ἀναγινώσκειν, si compositionem urgeas, renoscere quod antea aliquando cognoueramus, quod nos dicimus, recognoscere ἐπιγινώσκειν uero agnoscere significat, hoc est, ueritatem rei ad nos pertinentis, ubi expositā fuerit, probare & amplecti. Sic Corinthij quæ Paulus hoc loco scribebat, primum poterāt, ut antea reipsa experti, recognoscere, & ut ad se pertinentia, agnoscere & probare. Loquitur enim de eo quod dixit, abundantius autem erga uos.
units.tr: The old translator has: "For we write to you nothing other than what you have read and know." Erasmus translates in the same way, except that he renders in the present tense, "what you read, you also acknowledge." Certainly the Greek [ἀναγινώσκετε] can be rendered "what you read," for [ἀναγινώσκειν] sometimes means to read, and the ancients also read it so. But since this verb properly means to recognise, it is strange that they thought it should be taken in the sense of reading. For what does "We write to you nothing other than what you read" mean? Was there a danger that he might write one thing and they read another? The Apostle does nothing of the kind. He means that about the simplicity and integrity of his conduct and about the grace of God he is not writing to them anything new, contrived and suited to his own cause, and unknown to them, something they could not acknowledge, but things they not only recognise but also acknowledge. Therefore, since the context itself offers this sense readily, and since the verb [ἀναγινώσκεις] does not resist it but agrees well with its proper meaning, I have judged it right to follow neither the older nor the more recent translator but the truth itself. Embracing its plain and simple sense, I translate not "what you read" but "what you recognise." Now [ἀναγινώσκειν], if you press the compound, means to know again what we had once known before, which we call to recognise; but [ἐπιγινώσκειν] means to acknowledge, that is, when the truth of a matter that concerns us has been set out, to test it and embrace it. So the Corinthians could, as having formerly experienced these things themselves, first recognise what Paul was writing here, and then acknowledge and approve it as belonging to them. For he is speaking of what he has just said, "but more abundantly towards you."

units.la: SPERO autem, inquit, quod usque ad finem quoque agnoscetis, quemadmodum & agnouistis nos ex parte.) Ne dicat quisquam, talem quidem cognouimus, cum apud nos esses: uerum qualis iam sis, & qualem te exhibiturus sis in posterum, ignoramus, occupat dicens: Spero autem quod quemadmodum agnouistis nos hactenus & ex parte, sic agnituri sitis etiam usque ad finem, nec quicquam in nobis de præterita nostra conuersatione desyderaturi.
units.tr: "I hope," he says, "that you will acknowledge to the end, just as you have acknowledged us in part." So that no one may say, "Indeed we knew you such as you were when you were with us, but we do not know what you are now or what you will show yourself to be in future," he forestalls this by saying: "I hope that just as you have acknowledged us hitherto and in part, so you will go on acknowledging us even to the end, and will desire nothing in us beyond our past conduct."

units.la: Vide autem quàm loquatur modeste. Non dicit. Scio & affirmo uobis, sed, spero. Significat se bona teneri erga Deum fiducia, quod quemadmodum hactenus adfuerit sibi opegratiæ suæ, dederitque ut simpliciter & syncere conuersaretur in mundo, ita in posterum quoque & ad finem usque eandem sibi non sit denegaturus gratiam. Sic nihil de suis ipsius uiribus, quantumuis magnus Apostolus ac præclaris dotibus insignitus præsumit, nec de præterito securitatem in futurum, sed spem erga Deum concipit, & secundum hanc summa cum diligentia in cursu cœptæ conuersationis pergit ac perseuerat.
units.tr: See how modestly he speaks. He does not say, "I know and assure you," but "I hope." He means that he holds a good confidence towards God, that just as God has hitherto helped him by his grace and granted that he should live in the world simply and sincerely, so in future too, and to the end, God will not deny him the same grace. Thus he presumes nothing from his own strength, though he was a great apostle and endowed with excellent gifts. He does not infer security for the future from the past, but conceives hope towards God, and in accordance with this hope he presses on and persists with the greatest diligence in the course of the conduct he has begun.

units.la: QVOD usque ad finem quoque agnoscetis, quemadmodum & agnouistis nos ex parte.) Ad finem agnoscere, pro, ad plenum agnoscere dixit. Præteritæ conuersationis agnitionem uocat, ex parte, respectu eius quæ sit plena. Plena autem est, quæ ad finem usque sibi similis perdurat. Admonemur, luctandum nobis esse ad plenitudinem Christianæ conuersationis, ne conquiescamus in ea quæ ex parte adhuc est & imperfecta. Qui peregrè proficiscitur, irremisso labore tendit ad locum quem petit, nec cæset se peregrinationem suam absoluisse, si partem aliquam itineris confecerit, sed si quò uolebat ad plenum peruenerit. Scit enim omnem itineris laborem reddi inanem, si uel subsistat in illo, nec progrediatur, uel domum deserta profectione redierit. Consimili modo comparata est & nostrę conuersationis conditio. Bene cœpisse aliquid est, aliquousque prouectum esse, adhuc maius est: uerum frustra utrunque est, nisi ad finem usque perseuerantes, plenæ pietatis terminum cösequuti fuerimus. Cogitet quisque, si quod dedit inculpatæ conuersationis speci- men, summa sibi elaborandum esse cura, ut integritatem illius ad finem usque illibatam custodiat, præsertim si sit Christi minister. Quantum enim profuit præteritæ conuersationis syncęritate, tantum oberit & sibi & alijs, si secus aliquando quàm Christi deceat ministrum conuersari, ac pristinam simplicitatem ac syncęritatem deserere cœperit. Si Paulus aliter in Asia quàm antea in Achaia cöuersatus fuisset, haud tantum utilitatis attulisset regno Dei præterita synceritate, quantum damni dedisset illius immutatione.
units.tr: "That you will acknowledge to the end, just as you have acknowledged us in part." He said "to acknowledge to the end" for "to acknowledge fully." He calls the recognition of past conduct "in part," in comparison with that which is full. A conduct is full when it continues to the end, always like itself. We are warned that we must strive for the fullness of Christian conduct, and not rest in that which is still partial and imperfect. One who sets out on a journey presses on without slackening towards the place he seeks, and does not think his journey finished if he has covered some part of the way, but only when he has fully reached where he wished to go. For he knows that all the labour of a journey is rendered vain if he either halts on the way and does not advance, or, having abandoned his departure, returns home. Our conduct is in a similar condition. To have begun well is one thing, to have advanced some way is greater still; but both are in vain unless we persevere to the end and attain the goal of full piety. Let each one consider that, if he has given some example of blameless conduct, he must take the greatest care to keep its integrity unblemished to the end, especially if he is a minister of Christ. For as much as the sincerity of past conduct has profited, so much will it harm both himself and others if at some point he begins to live otherwise than becomes a minister of Christ and to abandon his former simplicity and sincerity. If Paul had conducted himself in Asia otherwise than he had in Achaia, his past sincerity would have brought as little benefit to the kingdom of God as the change would have brought harm.

units.la: QVONIAM gloria uestra sumus, inquit, quemadmodum & uos nostra, in die domini Iesu.) Non est in Græco δόξα, id est, gloria, sed καύχημα, id est, gloriatio. Quare uertendum erat: Quoniam gloriatio uestra sumus. Hoc est, quoniam talis sum uester Apostolus, & tam syncere & fideliter apud uos sum conuersatus, ut iure de me gloriari possitis, & uicissim tales uos estis meo ministerio per gratiam Dei facti, quos in Christo Iesu genui, ut habeam in uobis de quo glorier. Hanc uestram
units.tr: For we are your boasting, he says, just as you are ours, in the day of the Lord Jesus. In the Greek there is not δόξα, that is, glory, but καύχημα, that is, boasting. Therefore it ought to be translated: "For we are your boasting." That is, since I am such an apostle to you, and have lived among you so sincerely and faithfully, you may rightly boast of me; and in turn you are such through my ministry, made so by the grace of God, whom I have begotten in Christ Jesus, that I may have in you something to boast of. This boasting of you concerning me

units.la: A de me gloriationem totis uiribus illibatam, ad finem usque seruaturum me spero, nec admissurum quid unquam, unde uos mei pudeat. Poterat hic addere, idem uos quoque factuoros spero, nec tale quid admissuros unquam, unde gloriatio mea quam in uobis habeo, in pudorem & confusionem desinat: uerum maluit hoc tacita quàm expressa admonitione animis illorum insinuare. Addit, in die domini Iesu. Hoc dicendo, significat se de tali gloriatione loqui, quæ non sit iuxta sæculum uel inanis in se ac uana, de re uidelicet nihili, uel fluxa ac cito desitura, sed sit uera ac solida, & ad diem usque, in quo iudicaturus est dominus, duratura. Clanculum autem perstringit pseudapostolos, à quibus ipsius Apostolatus perpetuo suggillabatur. Quasi dicat: Quicquid magistri uestri de me sentiant, uester sum Apostolus, & sic me apud uos gessi, ut sim uestra gloriatio, & uos mea, id quod in die domini Iesu manifestabitur, ubi omnia occulta in lucem emergent, & unusquisque recipiet, secundum quod gessit in hac uita.
units.tr: I hope to keep whole with all my strength until the end, and I will never allow anything in myself of which you might be ashamed. He could have added here that I hope you too will do the same, and never allow anything of the kind by which my boasting in you would turn into shame and confusion; but he preferred to insinuate this into their minds by silent rather than explicit admonition. He adds: "in the day of the Lord Jesus." By saying this he indicates that he is speaking of a boasting that is not according to the world, nor empty and vain in itself, about a thing of no worth, nor fleeting and soon to cease, but true and solid, and lasting until the day on which the Lord will judge. Yet he also quietly strikes at the false apostles, by whom his own apostleship was constantly disparaged. As if to say: whatever your teachers think of me, I am your apostle, and I have so conducted myself among you that I am your boasting and you are mine; which will be made manifest in the day of the Lord Jesus, when all hidden things will come to light and each will receive according to what he has done in this life.

units.la: Hodie gloriatio episcoporum est, si amplissimas habeant dioceses, si sint iuxta sæculum nobiles, opulenti, & potentes, & de talibus episcopis suis gloriantur miseræ ac fascinatæ ecclesiæ, haud secus quàm olim habitatores Sichen & Israelitæ reliqui gloriabantur de rege suo Abimelech, & ille de ipsis lætabatur: perinde ac si ligna constituant super se rhamnum in regem, deque illo glorientur, & ille de ipsis, donec egrediatur ex rhamno ignis, & consumat tam ligna subiecta, quàm seipsum. Vide Iudicum nono. Quanto felicius habe-rent ecclesiæ Christi, si de legitimis ac fidelibus possent episcopis & pastoribus gloriari, & quanto melius ageretur cum episcopis, si sic instituerent ecclesias, ut esse possent ipsorum gloriatio, non in facie præsentis sæculi, sed in die domini Iesu, in quo reddituri sunt uillicationis suæ rationem? Gloria pastoris grex est, si sit bene pastus. Et gregis est, si sit syncerus, gloria pastor. Nunc cum lupi glorientur de ouibus, & oues de lupis transfiguratis, quid aliud expectandū est, quàm ut pars utraque confundatur ac pereat in die domini Iesu, in quo ueri pastores de ueris ouibus, & ueræ oues de ueris pastoribus ueraciter ac solidè gloriabuntur?
units.tr: Today the boasting of bishops consists in having very large dioceses, in being noble, wealthy and powerful according to the world; and the wretched and bewitched churches boast of such bishops of theirs, no differently than the men of Shechem and the rest of the Israelites once boasted of their king Abimelech, and he rejoiced in them: just as if the trees set a bramble over themselves as king, and boasted of him, and he of them, until fire came out of the bramble and consumed both the trees beneath and himself. See Judges chapter nine. How much more happily would the churches of Christ fare if they could boast of lawful and faithful bishops and ministers, and how much better would things go with the bishops if they so ordered the churches that they might be their boasting, not in the face of the present world, but in the day of the Lord Jesus, on which they are to render an account of their stewardship? The glory of the shepherd is the flock, if it is well fed; and the glory of the flock is the shepherd, if he is sincere. Now, since wolves boast of the sheep and sheep of wolves disguised as shepherds, what else is to be expected than that both parties be confounded and perish in the day of the Lord Jesus, on which true ministers will truly and solidly boast of true sheep, and true sheep of true ministers?

units.la: Poterit autem hic quæri, quomodo dicat Corinthios Apostolus gloriationem suam sore in die domini Iesu, cùm illorum ecclesia, & tum temporis, cum hæc scriberet, admodum esset corrupta, & in multis culpabilis, & tàdem sit in apostasiam Mahometicam, & seruitutem Turcicam abducta? An de tali poterit ecclesia gloriari in die domini?
units.tr: But here it may be asked how the Apostle says that his boasting will be in the day of the Lord Jesus concerning the Corinthians, since their church, at the time when he wrote this, was thoroughly corrupted and guilty in many respects, and in the end has been led into Mahometan apostasy and Turkish servitude. Can the church boast of such a thing in the day of the Lord?

units.la: Respondeo. Qualis qualis fuerit ecclesia: Corinthiorum tempore Apostoli, & qualis qualis sit postea facta, & in diem usque domini futura erat, & est, & erit gloria sui Apostoli, si respiciamus ad multum illum lum electorum populum, de quo dixit ad eum dominus: Noli timere, quia multus est mihi populus in hac ciuitate. Habuit ea ecclesia suû triticum, & simul paleas adiunctas, & quid uetat ne credamus adhuc hodie superesse in illa aliquid tritici, superq; futurum usque in diem domini, quantumuis sit seruituti Turcicæ subiecta? De hoc populo domini, quem initio genuerat in Christo, de hoc inquam tritico quod initio plátauerat, loquitur hic Apostolus, cum dicit: Quemadmodum & uos nostra gloriatio in die domini Iesu, non de reprobis, quos ipse non plantauit. Sic intelligendum est etiam quod 1. Thess.2. in calce scribit. Philip. 2. formathoc ipsum per modum adhortationis, dicens, ut gloriari posim in die Christi, quod non in uanum cucurrerim, nec in uanum laborauerim.
units.tr: I answer: whatever sort of church it was in the time of the Corinthian apostle, and whatever sort it later became, and whatever it is and will be until the day of the Lord, it is and will be the glory of its apostle, if we look to that great chosen people of whom the Lord said to him: "Do not fear, for I have many people in this city." That church had its wheat, and chaff mixed in with it; and what forbids us from believing that even today some wheat remains in it, and will remain until the day of the Lord, however much it is subject to Turkish servitude? It is of this people of the Lord, whom he had begotten in Christ at the beginning, of this wheat, I say, which he had planted at the beginning, that the Apostle speaks here when he says: "just as you are our boasting in the day of the Lord Jesus," not of the reprobate, whom he himself did not plant. In the same way must be understood what he writes at the end of 1 Thessalonians 2. In Philippians 2 he expresses this very thing by way of exhortation, saying: "that I may be able to boast in the day of Christ that I have not run in vain, nor laboured in vain."

units.la: Et hac fiducia uolebam ad uos uenire prius, ut geminam apud uos inirem gratiam, & per uos pertransfire in Macedoniam, & rursus à Macedonia uenire ad uos, ac à uobis deduci in Iudæam.
units.tr: And with this confidence I wished to come to you first, so that I might have a double grace among you, pass through you into Macedonia, return from Macedonia to you, and be sent on by you into Judea.

units.la: Commoda transitione dilabitur ad ea quæ aduentum ipsius concernebant. Dixit Corinthios suam esse gloriationem, & se illorû, usq; in diem domini Iesu. Sic de illis confidens cogitauerat secundo uenire ad eos Corinthum. Hoc est quod dicit: Et hac fiducia uolebâ ad uos uenire prius. Considebat illis cum primis omnium esse notissimum, quàm syncere conuersatus fuisset apud ipsos, licq; animatos esse ergasè, vt gloriarentur de se tanquam fideli & eximio suo Apostolo, quemadmodum ipse de illis tanquam filijs suis glorietur. Hac, inquit, fiducia motus, uolebam uenire ad uos.
units.tr: With a smooth transition he moves on to matters concerning his coming. He has said that the Corinthians are his boast and he is theirs, even unto the day of the Lord Jesus. Trusting them in this way, he had planned to come to them at Corinth a second time. This is what he means by "And with this confidence I wished to come to you first." It was above all clear to them how sincerely he had lived among them, and they were to be moved to glory in him as a faithful and outstanding apostle, just as he himself boasts of them as his children. "Moved by this confidence," he says, "I wished to come to you."

units.la: Est autem totus hic locus de ipsius aduentu quadrimembris. Nam primum aperit vnde motus uoluerit ad eos uenire. Deinde ad quid: tertio quomodo: quarto, quare non uenerit. Motum cõsilij huius attingit cum dicit: Et hac fiducia uolebam ad uos uenire prius. Sic commendat illis consilium aduentus sui. Poterat causam hanc seorsum exordio ingredi, & praetexere Apostolicam suam authoritatem, qua motus uenire ad eos uoluerit. Verum maluit per transitionē sic ad eam delabi, ut animi sui fiduciam, quam de ipsis conceperat, praetexeret, id quod omnino amicitiæ spirat ingenium, quæ sic est comparata, ut bene fidentes inter se reddat amicos. Fiducia uero pleraque praesumit, quæ non prudentia cauta tentanda iudicaret, id quod & Paulo accidit in hac causa, sicuti postea uidebimus.
units.tr: The whole passage about his coming has four parts. First, it reveals what moved him to want to come to them; second, for what purpose; third, by what route; fourth, why he did not come. He touches on the motive for this plan when he says, "And with this confidence I wished to come to you first." Thus he commends to them the plan of his visit. He could have entered on this cause separately at the start, and put forward his apostolic authority as the reason he wished to come to them. But he preferred to slide into it by a transition, so as to put forward the confidence he had conceived in them. This entirely breathes the spirit of friendship, which is so constituted that it makes those who trust each other into friends. Confidence, however, presumes many things which cautious prudence would not judge should be tested; and this also happened to Paul in this matter, as we shall see later.

units.la: Illud: Volebam ad uos uenire prius, satis indicat mutatam sibi eam tum fuisse voluntatem, ut iam non uellet quod uoluerat prius, intellige, cum ad ipsos de aduentu suo scriberet. Pristina quidem fiducia manebat, quam tota hæc spirat Epistola: uerum propositum ex illa natum meliori consilio mutauerat. Ergo & apostoli mutant sua consilia. Nec mirum, cum sit sapientis mutare consilium, non satis circumspecte uel ex amore, uel odio, uel praesenti aliqua occasione praesumptum.
units.tr: The words "I wished to come to you first" sufficiently indicate that his will had then changed, so that he no longer wished what he had wished earlier, namely when he was writing to them about his coming. The earlier confidence remained, and this whole Epistle breathes it; but he had changed the purpose born of it by a better counsel. So apostles too change their plans. Nor is this surprising, since it belongs to a wise man to change a plan that was presumed without sufficient caution, whether from love, or hatred, or some present occasion.

units.la: VT geminam, inquit, apud uos inirem gratiam.) Sic uertit Erasmus. Vulgata habet, ut secundam gratiam haberetis. In Graeco est, ἵνα δευτέραν χάριν ἔχητε, id est, ut alteram gratia haberetis. Legunt quidam χάριν, id est, gaudium, pro χάριν, id est, gratiam. Significat hac particula ad quid ad eos uenire uoluerit. Ad hoc uidelicet, ut rigaret apud eos altero suo aduentu, quod in primo plantauerat, hoc est, ut corrigeda corrigeret, prolapsa erigeret, infirma corroboraret, disiuncta ac diuulsa ad unitatem reduceret, pseudapostolorum & inflatorum non uerba, sed uirtutem consideraret, impoenitentes ad poenitentiam induceret, in fide ac uera pietate aliquousque progressos, ad ulteriora proueheret, synceros ac sanos communiret, &c. Haec omnia uocat alteram gratiam, propter quam etiam Timotheum ad eos miserat, & Apollon ut ad eos proficisceretur, admodum obsecrauerat. Hunc exitiimo esse germanum praesentis loci sensum. Quare malo legere, ut alteram haberetis gratiam, quemadmodum habetur in Graeco, quàm cum Erasmo, ut geminam apud uos inirem gratiam. Etenim gratiam apud aliquem inire, non est illi impertire, sed magis illius ambire ac consequi gratiam, quo sensu non loquitur hic Apostolus, & ipsa uerba dissentiunt. Quis enim non uidet aliud sonare, ut alteram apud uos inirem gratiam, & aliud, ut alteram habere-tis gratiam? Deinde, si legamus, ut geminam haberetis gratiam, poterit intelligi tam de duplici secundi aduentus gratia, quàm de altera post priorem ipsis collata. Ne ergo inquirat aliquis, quæ nam fuerit gemina illa gratia, quam fuerint Corinthij ex secundo habituri illius aduentu, exitiimo satius esse ut legamus, ut alteram, quàm ut geminam habetis gratiam. Scio Chrysostomum exponere de duplici gratia, vna quæ fuerit per epistolam, altera quæ euenisset ipsis ob illius praesentiam: uerum si cui haec expositio placet, illam per me licet retineat.
units.tr: "That I might have a double grace among you," he says. Erasmus translates it thus. The Vulgate has, "that you might have a second grace." In the Greek it is "that you might have a second grace [ἵνα δευτέραν χάριν ἔχητε]," that is, "that you might have another grace." Some read "joy [χαράν]" instead of "grace [χάριν]." This particle signifies the purpose for which he wished to come to them: namely, that by a second visit he might water among them what he had planted in the first. That is, he would correct what needed correcting, raise up the fallen, strengthen the weak, bring the divided and torn back to unity, weigh not the words but the power of the false apostles and the puffed-up, lead the impenitent to repentance, carry those who had advanced somewhat in faith and true godliness on to higher things, and strengthen the sincere and sound, and so on. He calls all these "another grace," and on account of it he had also sent Timothy to them and had earnestly urged Apollos to set out for them. I think this is the true sense of the present passage. Therefore I prefer to read "that you might have another grace," as it stands in the Greek, rather than with Erasmus, "that I might win a double grace among you." For to win grace among someone is not to impart it to them, but rather to seek and obtain their favour; in that sense this Apostle is not speaking here, and the words themselves disagree. For who does not see that "that I might win another grace among you" means something different from "that you might have another grace"? Further, if we read "that you might have a double grace," it could be understood either of a twofold grace from his second coming or of another grace conferred on them after the first. So, lest anyone ask what that double grace was which the Corinthians would have from his second visit, I think it better to read "another grace you might have" rather than "a double grace." I know that Chrysostom explains it as a double grace: one which came through the letter, the other which would have come to them from his presence. But if anyone likes that explanation, let him keep it, as far as I am concerned.

units.la: Consyderet hic lector, quantum discriminis sit inter ueros & falsos apostolos. Verus apostolus ob id inuisit ecclesias, ut conferat illis suo aduentu aliquid gratiae, non ut suoipsius consulat emolumento. Venit ad ecclesias ut pater ad filios, non ut auferat ab illis quicquam, sed ut de suo quod illis prosit, adferat. At falsus apostolus, legatus non Christi, sed Antichristi, non ad hoc uenit, ut adferat aliquid quod prosit ecclesijs, nisi forsan persequutionis crucem, sed ut auferat unde Romana nequitia sustentetur. Et interea compositis digitis fingit se spargere Apostolicam benedictionem, quasi propter illam sit missus, eū lōge agat aliud. Eiusmodi Apostoli Satanae debedebebant omnibus ubiq; portis obseratis excludi, quemadmodum antiquo prouerbio apud Germanos dicitur: wenn dir Rom für dein hauß kumpt, so schlüß die thür zuo.
units.tr: Let the reader consider how great is the difference between true and false apostles. The true apostle visits the churches so that by his coming he may bring them some grace, not so that he may consult his own advantage. He comes to the churches as a father to his children, not to take anything from them, but to bring from his own store what will profit them. But the false apostle, an envoy not of Christ but of Antichrist, does not come to bring anything that profits the churches, except perhaps the cross of persecution; he comes to carry off whatever the Roman wickedness is sustained by. Meanwhile, with fingers folded, he pretends to be scattering apostolic blessing, as if he had been sent for that purpose, while in fact he is doing something else entirely. Such apostles of Satan ought to be shut out, with every gate barred, just as the old German proverb says: when Rome comes to your house, shut the door on it.

units.la: ET per uos, inquit, pertransire in Macedoniam, & rursus è Macedonia uenire ad uos, ac à uobis deduci in Iudæam.) Hisce uerbis exponit quomodo ad eos uenire uoluerit. Sic uidelicet, ut in itinere, quo petiturus erat Macedoniam, ueniret primum Corinthum, non ut ibi hæreret, sed ut pertransiret in Macedoniam, indeq; reuersus rediret ad ipsos, & ab eis in Iudæam deduceretur. De hoc illius consilio legimus etiam Act.19. ad hunc modū. His aūt expletis proposuit Paulus in spiritu, ubi trāsisset Macedoniam & Achaiam ire Hierosolymam.
units.tr: "And to pass through you into Macedonia, and to come again from Macedonia to you, and be sent on by you into Judea." In these words he explains how he wished to come to them. Namely, on the journey by which he was going to make for Macedonia, he would first come to Corinth, not to stay there, but to pass through into Macedonia, and returning from there come back to them, and be sent on by them into Judea. We read of this plan of his also in Acts 19, in this way: "And when these things were completed, Paul purposed in the Spirit, when he had passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem."

units.la: Quæruntur hic quomodo ista conueniant cū ijs quæ cap.ultimo præcedentis Epistolæ scripsit, ubi sic legitur; Veniam autem ad uos cum Macedoniam transiero. Macedonia enim pertransiturus sum. Apud uos autem forte permanebo, aut etiam hybernabo, ut uos me deducatis quocunque proficiscar. Nolo enim uos nunc in transcursu uidere, sed spero tempus aliquantum mansurum me apud uos, si Dominus permiserit.
units.tr: Here it is asked how these things agree with what he wrote at the end of the last chapter of the preceding Epistle, where it is read thus: "But I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia. For I shall pass through Macedonia. But perhaps I will remain with you, or even winter, so that you may send me on wherever I go. For I do not wish to see you now in passing, but I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits."

units.la: Chrysostomus quæstioni huic sic satisfieri putat, si dicamus quæ hic Apostolus scribit, contraria quidem esse ijs quæ in priore scripsit Epistola, haud uero uoluntati ac proposito ipsius. At sic respondendo causam dat alteri quæstioni, an uidelicet aliud uoluerit Apostolus in hac causa, & aliud scripserit. Quare nobis sic respondendum esse uidetur, ut dicamus nihil prorsus hic esse contrarietatis in mente Apostoli, quamuis uerba in speciem ab eo quod antea scripserat diuersum quid præferre uideantur.
units.tr: Chrysostom thinks this question is answered if we say that what this Apostle writes here is indeed contrary to what he wrote in the former Epistle, but not contrary to his will and purpose. But in so answering he gives occasion to another question: whether the Apostle wished one thing in this matter and wrote another. So it seems to us we must answer that there is absolutely no contrariety in the Apostle's mind, although the words may appear to present something different from what he had written before.

units.la: Primum enim quod hic dicit per ipsos se in Macedoniam transire uoluisse, non est ei contrarium, quod in præcedenti Epistola dixit: Veniam autem ad uos cum Macedoniam transiero. Nam uerbum transiero, sic poterit accipi, ut non præteritæ, sed magis futuræ significationis sensu acceptum, referatur ad transitionem non præteritam, quasi tum demum ad eos uenire uoluerit, postquam Macedoniam transisset, sed ad futuram, ut significet se in itinere, quo Macedoniam petere constituerat, ad ipsos uoluisse uenire. Quare uerti poterat, ubi Macedoniam pertransibo. Deinde quod in præcedenti Epistola dicit: apud uos autem forte per manebo, aut etiam hybernabo, ut uos me deducatis quocunque proficiscar, nulla necessitate sic accipitur, ut dissentiat ab eo quod hic scribit. Etenim quod hic dicit, & rursus è Macedonia uenire ad uos, non sic intelligi debet, ut mansionem diuturniorem excludat, cuius mentionem facit in præcedenti. Postremo, quod illic dicit: Nolo enim uos nunc in transcursu uidere, quamuis uideri potest de Macedonico transitu dictum, potest tamen æquè intelligi de alio quopiam, qui tum fuerit illi faciendus, & cuius occasione ad illos uenire potuerit, sicut & in præcedenti Epistola annotauimus, præsertim cum non simpliciter dixerit ibi: Nolo enim uos in transcursu uidere, sed, Nolo enim uos nunc in transcursu uidere. Vbi ista consydero, puto nos recte ad præsentem posse respondere quæstionem, nihil utrobiq; esse tam hic quàm in præcedenti Epistola quod aliquid habeat contrarietatis.
units.tr: First, what he says here, that he wished to pass through Macedonia on the way to them, is not contrary to what he said in the preceding Epistle: "But I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia." For the word "when I have passed through" may be taken not in the past sense but in the future, and refer not to a past passage, as if he wished to come to them only after he had passed through Macedonia, but to a future one, to signify that on the journey by which he had determined to make for Macedonia, he wished to come to them. Hence it could be rendered "when I shall pass through Macedonia." Next, what he says in the preceding Epistle, "But perhaps I will remain with you, or even winter, so that you may send me on wherever I go," is not, by any necessity, taken to disagree with what he writes here. For what he says here, "and to come again from Macedonia to you," ought not to be understood as excluding the longer stay he mentions in the preceding. Lastly, what he says there, "For I do not wish to see you now in passing," although it can be seen as said of the Macedonian journey, can equally be understood of some other journey which would then have to be made by him, and on whose occasion he could come to them, as we also noted in the preceding Epistle; especially since he did not simply say there, "For I do not wish to see you in passing," but "For I do not wish to see you now in passing." Considering these things, I think we can rightly answer the present question: there is nothing of contrariety in either passage, here or in the preceding Epistle.

units.la: De eo quod dicit: & à uobis deduci in Iudæam, annotauimus in Epistola præcedenti.
units.tr: As for the words "and to be sent on by you into Judaea," I have commented on them in the previous epistle.

units.la: Hoc igitur cum in animo uersarem, num quo pacto leuitate sum usus? aut num quę cogito secundum carnem cogito? ut sit apud me etiam etiam, & non nō. Imo fidelis Deus, qd' sermo noster erga uos non fuit etiam & non.
units.tr: Therefore, when I was turning this over in my mind, did I use lightness in any way? Or do I plan what I plan according to the flesh, so that with me there is yes yes and no no? But God is faithful: our word to you was not yes and no.

units.la: Iam quarto loco trāsit ad reddendam rationem, quare ad eos non uenerit. Primum autem reijcit à se calumniam leuitatis, quam illi intentabant reprobi, quasi temerè ac leuiter promittat, postea uero promissum non seruet. Deinde uero subijcit rationem propter quam non uenerit. Hoc igitur cum in animo uersarem, inquit, num quo pacto (Græcè, μή τι ἄρα) leuitate sum usus? quasi dicat: quemadmodum mihi nonnulli impingunt. Aut, num quæ cogito, secundum carnem cogito? ut sit apud me etiam & non? quasi dicat: Absit à me huiusmodi consiliorum leuitas ac temeritas, quæ non ex spiritu, sed ex carne nata facit ut ubi expectatur etiam inueniatur non. Haud parum autem confidentius reijcit à se calumniam leuitatis, cum instando & urgendo dicit: Hoc igitur cogitas num quo pacto leuitate sum usus? aut num quæ cogito secundum carnem cogito? quàm si simpliciter diceret: non sum usus leuitate, cum hoc in animo uersarem, neq; secundum carnem cogito quę cogito. Perinde nanq; est ac si dicat: an adeo me leuis animi hominem iudicant apud uos nonnulli, ut quod ad uos uenire cogitaui, cogitarim temerè ac leuiter? & adeo esse carnalem, ut quæ cogito cogitem secundum carnem? adeoq; mendacem ut ubi dico etiam, ibi sit non? Absit à me huiusmodi leuitas. Vos me talem nulla unquam estis in re experti.
units.tr: Now in the fourth place he passes on to give the reason why he did not come to them. First, however, he rejects from himself the charge of lightness, which those wicked men were bringing against him, as if he made promises rashly and lightly and afterwards did not keep them. Then he adds the reason why he did not come. "Therefore, when I was pondering this," he says, "did I use lightness in any way?" [μή τι ἄρα] As if to say: as some men charge me. "Or do I plan what I plan according to the flesh, so that with me there is yes yes and no no?" As if to say: far be from me such lightness and rashness in counsel, which, born not of the Spirit but of the flesh, makes it so that where one expects yes, one finds no. He rejects the charge of lightness quite boldly, however, pressing and urging with "Therefore do you plan this, did I use lightness in any way? Or do I plan what I plan according to the flesh?" more than if he had simply said: I did not use lightness when I was pondering this, nor do I plan according to the flesh what I plan. For it comes to the same thing as if he said: Do some of you judge me so light of mind that I resolved to come to you rashly and lightly? And so carnal that I plan according to the flesh what I plan? And so lying that where I say yes, there is no? Far be such lightness from me. You have never found me such in any matter.

units.la: HOC igitur, inquit, cum in animo uersarem, num quo pacto leuitate sum usus?) Triplex est leuitas, uel, si mauis, tres sunt leuitatis gradus in homine carnali. Primus est in cogitationibus, secundus in uerbis, tertius in factis. Leuitas cogitationum est, quando ad quemuis leuem animi motum mox accedit in corde consensus, & fit concepta uoluntas, sine ulla seria dijudicatione. Leuitas in uerbis ex primo gradu assurgit. Ea est, qua cogitatio cordis leuiter concepta, leuiter profertur, ac uerbis temerè eximitur. Leuis enim cordis leuis ministra est lingua. Nihil hic est clausum. Nam domus eiusmodi, ut magnus Antonius de quibusdam loquacioribus fratribus dicebat, non habet ianuam, & qui uult intrat ac soluit asinum. Hinc leuiter non promittenda promittuntur, non effutienda sparguntur, non uituperanda uituperantur, non laudanda laudantur, non asse-renda afferuntur,non neganda negantur.
units.tr: "Therefore, when I was pondering this, did I use lightness in any way?" There is a threefold lightness, or, if you prefer, there are three degrees of lightness in carnal man. The first is in thoughts, the second in words, the third in deeds. Lightness of thought is when consent comes at once into the heart upon any light movement of the mind, and a resolve is formed without any serious deliberation. Lightness in words arises from the first degree. It is that by which a thought lightly conceived is lightly uttered and rashly let out in words. For the light tongue is the light servant of a light heart. Nothing here is guarded. For such a house, as the great Antony said of certain talkative brothers, has no door, and whoever wishes goes in and unties the donkey. Hence things that ought not to be promised are lightly promised, things that ought not to be blurted out are scattered abroad, things not to be blamed are blamed, things not to be praised are praised, things not to be asserted are asserted, and things not to be denied are denied.

units.la: Secundum hunc leuitatis gradum superat tertius, qui est factorum. In hunc enim usque exurgit leuis animi leuis uoluntas, quæ cum nullo fræno coerceatur pleno impetu ad id quod uult faciendũ properat, uel, ut est incon-stans omnis leuitas, facillimo negocio muta-tur, & diuersum tentat. Apostolus igitur leui-tatis notam ferre non ualens, ne primum qui-dem illius in fe gradum agnoscit,sed confiden-ter reijcit dicens:Hoc igitur cum in animo ver-farem,num quo pacto leuitate sum usus? Vti-nâ qui ad gubernaculâ ecclefiarũ Christi sedet, magni domini ac prælati, notas pessimorum non modo cogitatuum, sed & uerborũ & ope-rum tam possent conftáter à fe reijcere, q; con-ftanter Apostolus ne leuis quidem cogitatio-nis notam ferre ualens, grauitatem Apostolo dignam inculpatam sibi retinere sategit.
units.tr: Beyond this second degree comes the third, that of deeds. For the light will of a light mind rises to this, and since it is restrained by no bridle, it hurries with full impulse to do what it wants, or, since all lightness is inconstant, it is changed with the greatest ease and tries the opposite. The Apostle, therefore, unable to bear the mark of lightness, does not even acknowledge its first degree in himself, but confidently rejects it, saying: "Therefore, when I was pondering this, did I use lightness in any way?" Would that those who sit at the helm of Christ's churches, great lords and prelates, could reject from themselves the marks of the worst, not only of thoughts but also of words and works, as steadfastly as the Apostle, unable to bear even the mark of a light thought, strove to keep for himself, blameless, the seriousness worthy of an apostle.

units.la: AVT num quæ cogito fecundum carnem cogito,inquit.) Quemadmodũ Paulomaftig̃ ex eo quod non uenerat Corinthũ, iuxta præ-cedentis Epistolæ scriptum calumnias aduer-sus ipsum struebât, ita ipse eas eodem quo illi struebant ordine refutat. Colligebant autê illi ad hunc modum. Non uenit ut promisit. Ergo leuitate usus est, dum uenire ad nos cogitauit.
units.tr: "Or do I plan what I plan according to the flesh?" he says. Just as the men ill-disposed toward Paul were building up calumnies against him, on the ground that he had not come to Corinth as he had written in the preceding epistle, so he refutes them in the same order in which they built them. They drew their conclusions in this way: he has not come as he promised; therefore he used lightness when he thought of coming to us.

units.la: Deinde, quoniam leuitate usus est de aduê-tu suo ad nos cogitando,consequitur esse eum sic comparatum in uniuersum, ut quæ cogitat in alijs quoque rebus cogitet, non fecundum Deum,sed fecundum carnem.
units.tr: Then, since he used lightness in thinking about his coming to us, it follows that he is so constituted in general that what he thinks in other matters too, he thinks not according to God but according to the flesh.

units.la: Tertio & hinc necesse est,ut sermo ipsius nō fit ueritate firmus,sed desinat in mędacium, ut cū dicit etiá,inueniatur nō. Sic colligebât illi.
units.tr: Third, and from this it is necessary too that his word is not firm in truth, but ends in falsehood, as when he says yes and it is found to be no. Thus they reasoned.

units.la: Ipse igitur ut hanc illorum collectione refu-tet, eodem ordine reijcit primum calumniam leuitatis à cogitatione sua, qua ad ipsos uenire cogitauerat, deinde transit ad fecũdam calum-niam diluendam qua ipsum cogitationes suas omnes fecundum carne cogitare nugabantur.
units.tr: He therefore, to refute their conclusion, first rejects, in the same order, the charge of lightness in his thought, by which he had planned to come to them; then he passes on to refute the second charge, by which they were trifling that he thought all his thoughts according to the flesh.

units.la: Sic dicit:Aut num quæ cogito,fecundum car-nem cogito?quasi dicat: Absit. Tertio refutat etiam calumniam mendacij,cum subiungit, ut fit apud me etiam & non. Hæc autem par-ticula habetur in Græco ad hunc modum, ἵνα ἢ παρ' ἐμοὶ τὸ ναὶ ναὶ καὶ τὸ οὒ οὒ. i. ut fit apud me illud etiá etiam, & illud non non.Verum quæ mox subijciuntur palam declarant esse hic per errorē admissam superfluá duarũ istarum uo-cum,etiá & non,ingeminatione, illaq; sublata legendũ simpliciter.An quæ cogito fecundum carnê cogito,ut fit apud me etiam & non? Imo fidelis Deus,quod lermo noster ad uos factus non fuit etiá & non. Omnino reijcit à fe incon-stantiam illam qua carnales ac leues homines nunc affirmât, mox quod affirmarunt negant, sic ut sermo illorum nihil habeat firmitudinis, fitq; in illo etiam non etiam sed non.
units.tr: So he says: "Or do I plan what I plan according to the flesh?" as if to say: Far be it. Third, he also refutes the charge of falsehood, when he adds, "so that with me there is yes yes and no no." In the Greek this particle reads thus: [ἵνα ἢ παρ' ἐμοὶ τὸ ναὶ ναὶ καὶ τὸ οὒ οὒ], that is, "so that with me there is that yes yes, and that no no." But what is added immediately afterwards plainly shows that the superfluous repetition of these two words, "yes yes" and "no no," has crept in here through an error, and that it should be read simply without the repetition: "Do I plan what I plan according to the flesh, so that with me there is yes and no? But God is faithful, that our word to you was not yes and no." He altogether rejects from himself that inconstancy by which carnal and light men now affirm and presently deny what they have affirmed, so that their word has no firmness, and in it there is yes, not yes but no.

units.la: Quod fi cui ingeminatio uocum istarum, quæ in Græco est, retinenda uidetur, habet Chryfoftomum quem sequatur, qui sic expo-nit.An quæ cogito,fecūdum carnem tanquam homo carnalis cogito,ut fit παρ' ἐμοί, id est, in mea potestate,ut quod promitto præstē, quod nego constanter negem, quo meum etiam fit etiam, & meum non fit non,hoc est,ut mei sim iuris,ad eundum quólibet, & faciędum quidli-bet,sicuti solent carnales, qui non subsunt ma-gifterio ac ductui spiritus,sed pro suo ipsorum arbitrio libere cogitant, & faciunt omnia. Ve-rum longe alia est Apostolatus mei conditio. Subiectus sum spiritui,ut illius obedia uolun-tati. Vbi ille aliud uoluerit,meum etiá non est amplius etiam,ubi quod ego nolebam ipse uo-luerit,meum nó, non potest amplius esse non. Sic non est in mea potestate, ut etiam sit apud me constanter etiá,& non sit non,sed est in po-testate spiritus sanēti qui me gubernat, esset au-tem in mea potestate si liber essem à ductu spi-ritus,quemadmodum liberi ab illo sunt homi-nes carnales. Hic Chrysost. sensus nihil quidē habet incommodi & haud male conuenit cum uerbis Apostoli, si particulam hanc tantum in-spicias,uerum si quod mox subiungitur consy-deres,apparet aut reijciendam esse duarū ista-rum uocum,etiam & non, ingeminatione, aut exponēdam ad hunc modum: An quæ cogito secundum carnem cogito,ut quod nunc apud me est etiam etiam,hoc est,quod nunc etiá esso affirmo, paulo póst sit non non, id est, rursus constanter negetur. Vel cogitandū esse, desy-derari uoculam μή, & legēdum ut non sit apud me etiam etiam,& non non.
