units.tr: But if anyone thinks the repetition of these words, which is in the Greek, should be kept, he has Chrysostom to follow, who expounds it thus: "Do I plan what I plan according to the flesh, as a carnal man, so that it is in my power [παρ' ἐμοί], that is, so that what I promise I perform, and what I deny I deny constantly, so that my yes is yes and my no is no; that is, so that I am free to go anywhere and do anything, as carnal men are wont to do, who are not subject to the teaching and guidance of the Spirit, but think and do all things freely by their own judgment. But the condition of my apostleship is far different. I am subject to the Spirit, so as to obey his will. When he wishes otherwise, my yes is no longer yes; when he wills what I did not want, my no can no longer be no. So it is not in my power that my yes be constantly yes and my no constantly no; it is in the power of the Holy Spirit who governs me. It would be in my power if I were free from the guidance of the Spirit, as carnal men are free from it." This sense of Chrysostom has no inconvenience at all and agrees quite well with the words of the Apostle, if one looks only at this particle. But if one considers what is added immediately after, it appears that either the repetition of these two words, yes yes and no no, should be rejected, or it should be explained thus: "Do I plan what I plan according to the flesh, so that what is now with me yes yes, that is, what I now affirm as yes, shortly afterwards is no no, that is, is again constantly denied?" Or one must suppose that the little word [μή] is missing, and it should be read, "so that it may not be with me yes yes and no no."

units.la: Nos admonemur hoc loco, quàm non con-ueniat Christiano hæc leuitas, ut sit in uerbis eius,non,quod erat etiam,uel etiam,quod erat non. Qua de re monet & Iacobus cap. ultimo dicens: Sit uestrum est,est,non,non:ne in simu-lationem incidatis.Credi nō potest,quàm tur-pe sit Christiano homini,quem conuenit ueri-tatis esse discipulum, spiritu ueritatis imbutū, si carnali leuitate utendo, inconstans ac uanus deprehendatur in uerbis, sic ut etiam illius sit non,& non sit etiam.
units.tr: We are warned here how little this lightness suits a Christian, that his words should be "no" when they were "yes," or "yes" when they were "no." James also warns about this in the last chapter, saying: "Let your 'yes' be yes, and your 'no,' no, lest you fall into hypocrisy." It cannot be believed how shameful it is for a Christian man, who ought to be a disciple of truth and imbued with the Spirit of truth, if, indulging in carnal levity, he is caught inconstant and vain in his words, so that what is his "no" is also "yes," and what is "yes" is not "yes."

units.la: IMO fidelis Deus,inquit,quod sermo no-ster erga uos non fuit etiam & non.) Sic negat uerum esse quod maleuoli ex eo,quod non ue-nerat Corinthum,colligebant,esse apud ipsum etiam & non, ideoque nec ueri aliquid esse in ipsius fermonib. quos Corinthi habuerit. Ab-fit, inquit, ut sit apud me etiam & non. Imo sic fideliter egit mecū Deus, ut sermo meus, quo filium eius apud uos prędicaui,nó fuerit etiam & non,hoc est,nó fuerit uanus,sed multis mo-dis uerax & constans declaratus.Quod autem de sermone Euangelicæ suæ prædicationis lo-quatur,testantur sequentia. Intelligebat hanc esse maliciam pseudapostolorum, ut prętextu isto de non seruata promissione, omnem suam doctrinam uanitatis ac mendacij insimularet. Quare mox occurrens fidelem Deū ob id prę-dicat dicat & laudat, quod passus non sit ut sermo eum Christnum. 2 Sic prædicarunt apostoli ipsius apud Corinthios esset etiam & non.
units.tr: Nay, God is faithful, he says, that our word toward you was not "yea and no." Here he denies that what the malicious were gathering from the fact that he had not come to Corinth is true: that there was "yea and no" in him, and so nothing true in the words he had spoken at Corinth. "Far be it," he says, "that there should be 'yea and no' with me. Nay, God has dealt so faithfully with me that my preaching, in which I proclaimed his Son among you, was not 'yea and no,' that is, was not empty, but was shown in many ways to be true and steadfast." That he speaks of the word of his evangelical preaching is shown by what follows. He understood that this was the malice of the false apostles: under the pretext of a promise not kept, they would charge all his teaching with vanity and falsehood. So at once he calls God faithful and praises him for this, that he has not allowed the word preaching Christ to be "yea and no." In this way his apostles preached among the Corinthians.

units.la: Obseruandum nobis hic est, quantum periculi sit doctrinæ veritatis, si minister illius aliis in rebus, uel semel tantum leuis fuerit & uanus in uerbis deprehensus. Huc incubit Satan per suos apostolos, ut veritatem Dei, quam in se falsam esse coprobare non poterit, per occasionem uanitatis, si quam in ministris illius deprehenderit, uel deprehensam esse, cum non sit, praetexere poterit, suspectum de medacijs reddat. Nemo credit quantum damni res ista dederit & hodie quoque det ecclesijs. Quatumuis enim ueritas Euangelij Dei non ministri exi-stimatione, sed suaipsius firmitudine subsistat, reipsa tamen plurimum referre uidemus à quali ministro, graui ne uel leui, ueraci uel mendaci, praedicetur. Sciebat hoc Apost. ideoq; tā grauiter notā hanc leuitatis ab Apostolatu suo reiecit.
units.tr: We must observe here how great a danger there is to the doctrine of truth if its minister is found light and empty in his words, even once and only once, in other matters. Satan works through his apostles to this end: if he cannot prove the truth of God false in itself, he can, by taking occasion from any vanity he finds in its ministers, or pretending that he has found it there when it is not so, make the truth suspect of falsehood. No one believes how much harm this has done, and still does today, to the churches. For although the truth of the Gospel of God stands by its own firmness and not by the esteem of the minister, we nevertheless see in fact how much it matters by which minister it is preached: whether he is serious or light, truthful or lying. The apostle knew this, and therefore he so firmly rejected from his apostleship the mark of lightness.

units.la: Deinde obseruandum est q; competenter ac pertinenter in hac causa uocet Deum fidelem, propterea quod non permiserit, ut sermo Euangelij Dei, quem Corinthijs prædicauerat, fieret etiam & non. Sit hoc solatio Christi ministris, quod fidelem habet Deum, qui doctrinam veritatis deserere nō posit. Hoc elogio Dei usus est & Epistola praecedenti cap.10.
units.tr: Next we must observe that in this matter he fittingly and appropriately calls God faithful, because he did not permit the word of God's Gospel, which he had preached to the Corinthians, to become "yea and no." Let this be a comfort to the ministers of Christ, that they have a faithful God, who cannot forsake the doctrine of truth. He used this praise of God also in the previous epistle, chapter 10.

units.la: Nam Dei filius Iesus Christus, qui inter uos per nos prædicatus est, per me, & Siluanum, & Timotheum nō fuit etiam & non, sed etiam in illo fuit. Quotquot B enim sunt promissiones Dei, in ipso sunt etiam, & in ipso amen, Deo ad gloriam per nos.
units.tr: For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, by me and Silvanus and Timothy, was not "yea and no," but in him it has always been "yea." For all the promises of God are in him "yea," and in him "Amen," to the glory of God through us.

units.la: Porro qui confirmat nos unà uobiscū in Christū, & qui unxit nos, Deus est, qui etiam obsignauit nos, deditq; arrham spiritus in cordibus nostris.
units.tr: Now he who establishes us together with you in Christ, and who anointed us, is God, who also sealed us and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts.

units.la: Exponit quod sermone suum erga ipsos non fuisse dixit etiá & nō. Primo, refert illud ad sermonē Euangelij de Christo inter ipsos prædicati. Nam Dei filius, inquit, Iesus Christus, qui inter uos per nos prædicatus est. Et ne de sua tantum doctrina loqui uideatur, addit, per me, & Siluanum, & Timotheum. Duorum istorum opera fuerat usus ad rigandū quod in illa ecclesia plantauerat, quare illos sibi in defensione communis doctrinæ non immerito coniungit. Coiungit sibi utrunq; in subscriptione quoq; posterioris Epistolæ ad Thessa. Et Apost. Petrus mentionem facit Syluani. 1. Pet. cap. ult.
units.tr: He explains what he said, that his word toward them was not yes and no. First, he refers it to the word of the Gospel about Christ preached among them. "For the Son of God," he says, "Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us." And lest he seem to speak only of his own doctrine, he adds, "by me, and Silvanus, and Timothy." He had used the work of these two to water what he had planted in that church, so he rightly joins them to himself in defending the common doctrine. He joins both to himself also in the subscription of the later epistle to the Thessalonians. And the Apostle Peter mentions Silvanus, 1 Pet. last chapter.

units.la: NAM Dei filius, inquit, Iesus Christus, qui inter uos p nos prædicatus est.) Obseruemus hic quid prædicarit Paulus Corinthijs. Iesum, uidelicet, Christum filium Dei. Huic prædicationi insunt tria. 1 Primū diuinitatē Christi: secundum, humanitatē illius: tertium, fuscep-tam salutis nostrę dispensationem concernit. Diuinitatis in eo est, quod appellat eū filiū Dei. Humanitatis est, quod Iesum proprium illius nomē in circuncisione carnis impositū exprimit. Dispensationis suscepta est, quod uocat
units.tr: "For the Son of God," he says, "Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us." Let us observe here what Paul preached to the Corinthians: namely, Jesus, Christ the Son of God. Three things are contained in this preaching. First, the divinity of Christ; second, his humanity; third, the undertaken dispensation of our salvation. The divinity is in that he calls him the Son of God. The humanity is in that he names Jesus, his proper name, given at the circumcision of the flesh. The undertaken dispensation is in that he calls him

units.la: eum Christnum. 2 Sic prædicarunt apostoli Christum, uerum Deum, uerum hominē, & uerum nostrum domnū ac Seruatorē. In his tribus caput est Euangelicæ prædicationis, fides & confessio Christiana, quam exprimebat Petrus Matth.16. dicens: Et nos credimus & cognouimus, quod tu es Christus filius Dei uiui.
units.tr: "Christ." So the apostles preached Christ as true God, true man, and our true Lord and Saviour. In these three lies the heart of Evangelical preaching, the faith and Christian confession, which Peter expressed in Matth. 16, saying: "And we believe and know that you are Christ the Son of the living God."

units.la: 3 Huic fidei promissa est uita æterna. Ioan.3. Qui credit in filium, habet uitam æternā. Non est autem illa ex carne & sanguine, sed ex reuelatione cœlesti. Unde & Petro dicebat Christus: Caro & sanguis non reuelauit tibi, sed pater meus qui est in cœlis. 4 Et hæc fides & reddit ueros Christianos, & nota est uerorum Christianorum, nec de alia intelligendum est, quando sermo fit de fide catholica.
units.tr: To this faith eternal life is promised. John 3: "He who believes in the Son has eternal life." Yet this life is not from flesh and blood, but from heavenly revelation. Whence Christ also said to Peter: "Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." This faith both makes true Christians and is the mark of true Christians, and nothing else is to be understood when there is talk of the catholic faith.

units.la: NON fuit etiam & nō, sed etiam in illo fuit, inquit.) Negat sermonem suum, id est, doctrinam & prædicatione de Christo, fuisse inanem ac mendacem, quandoquidem ipse filius Dei Iesus Christus ab ipso prædicatus nō est, etiam & non, hoc est, uanus & falsus, sed etiam, uerus uidelicet Christus, & uerus filius Dei, nō alius reipsa quam qualis inter ipsos fuit prædicatus. Sic intelligo quod dicit: non fuit etiam & non, sed etiam in illo fuit. Non fuit etiam in prædicatione nostra, & non in seipso, sed est in illo fuit, quemadmodum à nobis est prædicatus. Romanus Pōtifex qui prædicatur à suis quod sit uicarius Christi & caput ecclesiæ, ille est etiá & non. Etiam, quatenus talis prædicatur, non, quatenus non est in ipso is qui prædicatur.
units.tr: "It was not yes and no, but in him was yes," he says. He denies that his word, that is, his teaching and preaching about Christ, was empty and false, since Jesus Christ the Son of God, preached by him, is not "yes and no," that is, vain and false, but "yes," that is, the true Christ and true Son of God, in reality no other than he was preached among them. So I understand what he says: it was not yes and no, but in him it was yes. It was not yes in our preaching and no in himself, but is yes in him, just as he was preached by us. The Roman Pontiff, who is proclaimed by his followers to be Christ's vicar and the head of the Church, is yes and no: yes, insofar as he is proclaimed as such; no, insofar as he is not in himself what is proclaimed.

units.la: Mahomet inter Turcos prædicatus, est etiá & non. Etiam, quatenus propheta Dei prædicatur uerbis, non, quatenus non est propheta Dei, sed seductor & propheta Satanæ. At Iesus Christus filius Dei inter Christianos prædicatus, ut prædicatur ita & est uerus Christus & uerus Dei filius. Quare in illo non est etiam & non, sed etiam tantum, ut in prædicatione, ita & reipsa.
units.tr: Mahomet, preached among the Turks, is yes and no: yes, insofar as he is proclaimed in words as a prophet of God; no, insofar as he is not a prophet of God but a seducer and prophet of Satan. But Jesus Christ the Son of God, preached among Christians, is as he is preached, the true Christ and true Son of God. Therefore in him there is not yes and no, but only yes, both in the preaching and in reality.

units.la: QVOTQVOT enim sunt promissiones Dei, inquit, in ipso sunt etiam, & in ipso sunt amen.) Veritate Christi Iesu filij Dei, propter quā in illo est non etiá & non, sed etiá, refert ad ueritatē promissionum Dei, quę tam sunt uera-ces, quàm uerax est Deus ipse. Intelligit autē de promissionibus Dei, quas protulit per prophetas suos in scripturis sanctis de filio suo, quarū meminit etiam, Rom.1. Nullam eximit, sed, quotquot sunt, inquit, etiam sunt & amen. Secundum hæc promissiones Dei prædicauit Iesum esse Christum filium Dei. Quare cōstanter colligit, sermones suos de Christo esse non etiam & non, sed etiam in Christo.
units.tr: "For as many as are the promises of God," he says, "in him are yes, and in him are amen." Referring to the truth of Christ Jesus, the Son of God, on account of which in him there is not yes and no but yes, he relates it to the truth of God's promises, which are as true as God himself is truthful. He means the promises of God that he delivered through his prophets in the holy Scriptures about his Son, of which he also speaks in Rom. 1. He excludes none, but says that however many there are, they are all yes and amen. According to these promises of God he preached Jesus to be Christ the Son of God. Therefore he constantly concludes that his sermons about Christ are not yes and no, but yes in Christ.

units.la: Quod autē dicit, in ipso sunt etiá, & in ipso sunt amen, quamuis tam ad Deū promittētem quàm ad Christum promissum referri queat, magis tamen placet, ut referamus ad Christum, in quo promissiones Dei ueraces esse deprehenduntur, dum de illo factæ in eo etiam sunt completæ. Sunt quidem ueraces in se, & erant quoq; ueraces priusquam in Christo ad-
units.tr: But when he says, "in him they are also, and in him they are Amen," although this could be referred both to God making the promise and to Christ to whom the promise was made, it pleases me more to refer it to Christ, in whom the promises of God are found to be true, since in him they have been fulfilled, having been made concerning him. They are indeed true in themselves, and they were also true before they were fulfilled in Christ; but since they were made concerning Christ the Son of God, they could not be fulfilled except in him. Therefore in Romans 15 he says that Christ was made a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers.

units.la: implerentur, uerum quoniam de Christo filio Dei factæ sunt, non potuerunt adimpleri, nisi in illo. Quare Rom.15. dicit Christum fuisse ministrum Circuncisionis pro veritate Dei, ad confirmandas promissiones patrum.
units.tr: But when he had said, "in him they are also," he added, "and in him they are Amen"; he did not do this because the Greeks call it nai and the Hebrews call it amen as if these were different things, but in order to affirm the truth more strongly he used two words meaning the same thing, one Greek and the other Hebrew. The first served the Greeks, the second the faithful Hebrews, to both of whom the truth of God's promises fulfilled in Christ was to be proclaimed and grasped with undoubting faith.

units.la: Quod vero postquam dixit: in ipso sunt etiam, subiecit, & in ipso sunt amen, non obid fecit, quod aliud sit esse ναί Græcis, & aliud אמן Ebræis, sed ad maiorem veritatis affirmationem duabus hisce vocibus, Græca una, Ebræa altera, idem significantibus, usus est. Priore seruiuit Græcis, posteriore Ebræis fidelibus, quibus utrisque veritas promissionum Dei in Christo adimpleta prædicanda erat, & indubitata fide apprehendenda.
units.tr: This passage must be carefully noted. It serves greatly to confirm our faith in Christ that he links his truth with the truth of God's promises, which cannot be proved false; so that it would be necessary first for God himself, the promiser, to be a liar, before what he promised could be shown to be a lie, and both of these are utterly impossible. Therefore it is the duty of a diligent Christian to have ready at hand the promises of God concerning Christ expressed in the Scriptures, so that by their infallible truth he may strengthen his faith in Christ the Son of God against all the temptations of Satan.

units.la: Locus hic diligenter notandus est. Plurimum in eo seruit fidei nostræ in Christum confirmandæ, quod veritatem eius annectit veritati promissorum Dei, quæ tam nequeunt falsitatis arguì, ut necesse sit prius ipsum Deum promittentem esse mendacem, quàm ea quæ promisit de medacio posse couinci, quod utrumque est prorsus impossibile. Quare diligetis Christiani est, promissiones Dei de Christo in scripturis expressas, habere in promptu, quo infallibili illarum veritate fidem suam in Christū filium Dei contra quasuis Satanæ tentationes communiat.
units.tr: "To the glory of God through us," he says. Here one may object: that the truth of God's promises fulfilled in Christ tends to the glory of God who promised, no one fails to acknowledge. For by common sense it is so ordered that the glory of the promiser depends on the truth of the promises.

units.la: DEO, inquit, ad gloriam per nos.) Dices hic. Quod veritas promissionum Dei in Christo adimpletarum faciat ad gloriam promittentis Dei, nemo est qui non agnoscat. Etenim communi sensu sic est comparatum, ut gloria promittentis pendeat à veritate promissorum.
units.tr: "To the glory of God through us" (inquit). You may say here: that the truth of God's promises fulfilled in Christ tends to the glory of the promising God, no one fails to acknowledge this. For by common sense it is so arranged that the glory of the one who promises depends on the truth of the promises.

units.la: Quod vero subiungitur ab Apostolo, per nos, quomodo per ipsos gloria ad Deum de veritate promissorum eius redierit non uideo. Nam per Christum hoc est factum in quo impletæ sunt promissiones Dei, non per Apostolos.
units.tr: But as to what the Apostle adds, "through us", I do not see how glory has returned to God through them concerning the truth of his promises. For this was done through Christ, in whom God's promises were fulfilled, not through the Apostles.

units.la: Respondeo. Si ista: Quotquot enim promissiones sunt Dei in ipso sunt etiā, & in ipso sunt amen, parenthesi incluseris ad hunc modum. Nam Dei filius Iesus Christus qui inter uos per nos prædicatus est, per me & Siluanum, & Timotheum, non fuit etiam & nō, sed etiam in ipso fuit (quotquot enim sunt promissiones Dei in ipso sunt etiam, & in ipso sunt amen) Deo ad gloriam, per nos poterit hæc particula referri ad ea quæ de prædicatione sua dixit, qua Christum filium Dei non falsum sed verum, ueraciter ad gloriā Dei inter Corinthios prædicauerit, atque ita nulla remanet quæstio. Sane quatenus ueritas promissionum Dei de Christo per Euangelij prædicationem declarata est ab Apostolis hactenus dici potest, quod gloria ueritatis illarum Deo per ipsos cesserit.
units.tr: I answer: if you enclose the words "For as many as are the promises of God, in him is the yes, and in him is the amen" in parentheses in this way: "For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, by me and Silvanus and Timothy, was not yes and no, but in him was yes (for as many as are the promises of God, in him is yes, and in him is amen)", then the phrase "to the glory of God through us" can be referred to what he had said about his own preaching, by which he preached Christ the Son of God among the Corinthians not as false but as true, truly, to the glory of God; and so no question remains. Indeed, insofar as the truth of God's promises concerning Christ has been declared by the Apostles through the preaching of the gospel, it can be said up to this point that the glory of their truth has passed to God through them.

units.la: PORRO qui confirmat nos, inquit, unà uobiscū in Christū & qui unxit nos, Deus est, qui etiā obsignauit nos, dedit& arram spiritus in cordibus nostris.) Quoniā prædicatiōis huius de Christo nec fides nec confessio nec profesio humanarū est uirium, sed omnino cœlestem gratiā requirit ne quid huius sibijpsi uindicare uideatur, in eo quod secūdo dixit: per nos trā fert ad Deum quicquid huius est, tribuitq; totam diuinæ confirmationi, unctioni, obsignationi, & oppignorationi dicens: Porro qui confirmat nos vnà uobiscum in Christū, & qui unxit nos, Deus est, &c. Omnia autem hæc, confirmat nos, unxit nos, obsignauit nos, & dedit arram spiritus in cordibus nostris, ad hoc dicuntur ut certitudo ueritatis Dei, quæ in Christo est, ex ipso esse Deo per spiritum suū in nobis operate significetur. Est uero scopus Apostoli non modo exprimere unde ipse in certitudine prædicationis suæ stabiliatur, sed & huius admonere ipsos Corinthios, ut eandē fidei suæ certitudinem uel habere se sciant, uel petant, non ex carne & sanguine sed ex ipso Deo. Et in hunc usum immiscuit particulam hāc unà uobiscum, quæ semel tantum posita ad sequentia · quoq; referri debet. Hos enim confirmat Deus in Christum quos unxit, obsignauit, & data arra spiritus sui oppignorauit. Etenim non sunt ista diuisa, sed cohærent.
units.tr: "Now he who establishes us with you in Christ," he says, "and who anointed us, is God, who also sealed us and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts." Since neither faith, nor confession, nor profession of this preaching about Christ is of human strength, but requires altogether heavenly grace, lest he seem to claim any of this for himself, in what he said second, "through us", he refers whatever is of this to God, and attributes it wholly to divine confirmation, anointing, sealing, and pledging, saying: "Now he who establishes us with you in Christ, and who anointed us, is God," etc. All these things, "establishes us", "anointed us", "sealed us", and "gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts", are said so that the certainty of the truth of God that is in Christ may be signified as coming from God himself, working in us through his Spirit. Moreover, the aim of the Apostle is not only to express whence he himself is established in the certainty of his preaching, but also to admonish the Corinthians themselves, that they may know that they either have, or should seek, this same certainty of their faith not from flesh and blood but from God himself. And to this end he has inserted the phrase "with you", which, though placed only once, ought also to be referred to what follows. For God establishes those whom he has anointed, sealed, and pledged by giving the pledge of his Spirit. Indeed these things are not separated, but cohere.

units.la: PORRO qui cōfirmat nos inquit.) Loquirur hic proprie, & eorū, quæ metaphoricis uocibus subijcit exprimit effectū. Huc enim ungimur, obsignamur, & oppignoramur, ut in fide Christi salutisque nostræ ac cœlestis gratiæ certitudine confirmemur.
units.tr: "Now he who establishes us," he says. He speaks here properly, and expresses the effect of those things which he subjoins in metaphorical words. For to this end we are anointed, sealed, and pledged, that we may be confirmed in the faith of Christ, in the certainty of our salvation and of heavenly grace.

units.la: VNA uobiscum inquit.) Non est otiosum quod non se tantum sed & Corinthios fideles, quibus scribit, diuinę huius cōfirmationis participes facit. Simul enim excitat eos, ut quoties propriæ infirmitatis sensu tanguntur, cogitent ab eodem se Deo confirmari, ubi necesse est, à quo confirmantur Apostoli, ideoq; minus impiorum hominum minas & persequutiones perhorrescant, cum sciant habere se Deum in cœlis, à quo confirmentur.
units.tr: But observe how modestly and cautiously he does not say, "who confirms you with me," but "who confirms us with you." For if he had said, "who confirms you with me," he would seem to join himself not to the weak Corinthians who are to be confirmed by God, but to God the confirmer himself, as if together with him he confirmed the weak Corinthians, not that he was confirmed by God together with them. Now, since he expressly says, "who confirms us with you," he places himself altogether in the same class of the weak who are to be confirmed by God. Indeed he so joins himself that he says he is confirmed by God together with them, not that they are his, but that he is theirs.

units.la: Vide autem quàm modeste ac caute non dicat: qui confirmat uos una mecum, sed, qui cōfirmat nos unà uobiscū. Etenim si dixisset: qui confirmat uos una mecū, uideretur se coniungere non Corinthijs infirmis à Deo confirmandis, sed ipsi Deo confirmatori, quasi unà cum illo confirmaret infirmos Corinthios, nō cum illis cōfirmaretur à Deo. Nunc cum diserte dicit: qui confirmat nos unà uobiscum, omnino se in eandem infirmorum & à Deo confirmandorum classem, conijcit. Imò sic annectit, ut non ipsos secum, sed se unà cum ipsis à Deo confirmari dicat. Et reuera non erant illi ipsius, sed ipse erat illorum.
units.tr: "In Christ," he says. In Greek it is eis Christon, that is, into Christ, yet nothing prevents us from reading, with the common reading, "in Christ." Although to be confirmed in Christ is also rightly said. For we are confirmed for this purpose, that we may remain firm in the faith of Christ and not allow ourselves to be torn from it by any adversities. Thus whoever is prepared to do and suffer all things for it may be said to be confirmed in the Gospel. Indeed, whoever has decided to follow Christ, unless he is confirmed by heavenly grace, will not be able to accomplish what he has decided. Hence that saying of Christ: "Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me."

units.la: IN Christum inquit.) Græce quidem est εἰς χριστὸν. i. in Christū, nihil tamen impedit quo minus cum uulgata lectione legamus, in Christo. Quanquam confirmari in Christū rectè & ipsum dicitur. Est enim ad hoc cōfirmari ut in fide Christi firmi permaneamus, & ab illa nos nullis aduersis auelli sinamus. Sic potest in Euangeliū confirmatus dici, quisquis propter illud paratus est facere ac pati omnia. Sane qui Christum sequi constituit, nisi cœlesti sit gratia confirmatus, quod cōstituit perficere nō potelse rit. Vnde illud est Christi: Qui uult uenire post {A}me abneget semetipsum, tollat crucem suam & sequatur me.
units.tr: "In Christ," he says. In Greek it is εἰς χριστὸν, that is, "into Christ"; nothing nevertheless prevents us from reading, with the common reading, "in Christ". Although it is also rightly said that one is confirmed in Christ. For it is to this end that one is confirmed, that we may remain firm in the faith of Christ and not allow ourselves to be torn away from it by any adversities. Thus one may be said to be confirmed in the gospel who is prepared for its sake to do and suffer all things. Indeed, one who has resolved to follow Christ, unless he is confirmed by heavenly grace, will not be able to carry out what he has resolved. Hence that saying of Christ: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me."

units.la: ET qui unxit nos inquit.) Per metaphorā unctionis, intelligit gratiā sanctificationis, ad similitudinem regum, prophetarum, & sacerdotū, qui oleo inaugurationis sanctificabātur. Vt enim illi externo oleo, ita nos interno quod spiritus est, inungimur, quemadmodum & Christus filius Dei non externa olei sed interna spiritus sancti unctione in regem ac sacerdotem unctus est & inauguratus, à qua nostra non differt, nisi in eo quod ipse supra omnem mensuram, nos uero in mensura spiritum ungentem nos ac sanctificantem accepimus.
units.tr: "And who anointed us," he says. By the metaphor of anointing he means the grace of sanctification, in likeness to kings, prophets, and priests, who were consecrated with the oil of inauguration. For just as those were anointed with external oil, so we are anointed with the internal, which is the Spirit; just as Christ, the Son of God, was anointed and inaugurated as king and priest not with the external oil but with the internal anointing of the Holy Spirit, from which our anointing does not differ, except in this, that he received the Spirit beyond all measure, while we have received him in measure, anointing and sanctifying us.

units.la: DEVS est inquit.) Nō caret emphasi. Quasi dicat: Quod in uobis agitur, non est meum sed Dei, non humanum sed diuinum opus. Deus operatur in uobis, vngens uos, obsignás & oppignorans. Dici non potest, quantum hinc lit alacritatis ad perferedum pro Christo omnia, si sentiamus Deum esse qui operetur in nobis ad salutem nostram omnia.
units.tr: GOD is (he says). There is emphasis here. As if he said: What is being done in you is not mine but God's; it is not a human but a divine work. God works in you, anointing you, sealing and pledging you. It cannot be said how much eagerness this gives to endure everything for Christ, if we feel that it is God who works in us all things for our salvation.

units.la: QVI etiam obsignauit nos inquit.) Potest hoc intelligi de obsignatione baptismatis. Est enim baptisma obsignatio qua uelut in oule ac peculium Dei obsignamur. Obsignationem hanc tribuit Deo, quia in illa magis opus spiritus quàm ministri baptizātis respicit. De Simone Mago non dicerem fuisse illum obsignatum à Deo cum baptizaretur. Quia in baptismate illius defuit opus spiritus. Dominus nouit qui {B}sui sint. Suos ipse obsignat, alienos nequaquā. Sic accepta de baptismate obsignationis metaphora nihil habet incommodi.
units.tr: WHO ALSO SEALED US (he says). This can be understood of the sealing of baptism. For baptism is a sealing by which we are sealed as God's own and special possession. He ascribes this sealing to God, because in it he looks more to the work of the Spirit than to the minister who baptizes. I would not say that Simon Magus was sealed by God when he was baptized, because in his baptism the work of the Spirit was lacking. The Lord knows who are his own. He seals his own, and certainly not aliens. So the metaphor of the sealing taken from baptism has nothing objectionable in it.

units.la: DEDITQVE arram spiritus, inquit, in cordibus nostris.) Nisi hæc detur à Deo ijs qui baptizantur, frustra per ministrū obsignantur. Poterat aute simpliciter dicere, deditq; spiritū suū in cordibus nostris. Nā de infusione illius loquitur. Verum placuit metaphora arræ, ut significet, quo nobis debeat esse loco datǫ à Deo & infusus in corda nostra spūs sanctus. Loco uidelicet arræ. Est autē arra oppignoratio, qua utrinque constringuntur tam qui dedit, quàm qui accepit. Cum dat spiritum suum Deus in corda nostra, hac se nobis subarratione cōstrin git, quod nolit nos deserere, sed pro suis agnoscere in sempiternū, & nos illi, dum arram hāc accipimus, in peculiū ipsius & ius proprietatis obstringimur, quod nolimus nos unquā possessionis ac iuri illius subducere, factamq; oppignorationem irritam reddere. Qui dat arram, tanquam precij partem, confirmat emptionem & contractum, seq; ad plenam solutionē constringit. Hoc intelligens August. dicit: Aliquid spiritus dedit pro pignore, ut ipsam plenitudinem desyderemus. Qui accipit arram, confirmat uenditionem, seq; obligat, quod nolit interuertere quod uēdidit. Hic usus est arræ, nisi circunstantijs inconuenientibus reddatur irrita. Huc respiciēs Apostolus dicit: deditq; arram spiritus in cordibus nostris. Arra pecunia-
units.tr: AND GAVE THE PLEDGE OF THE SPIRIT, he says, IN OUR HEARTS. Unless this is given by God to those who are baptized, they are sealed through the minister in vain. He could, however, have simply said: and gave his Spirit in our hearts. For he speaks of the infusion of it. Yet he chose the metaphor of a pledge, so that it might signify in what place the Holy Spirit, given by God and poured into our hearts, ought to be for us: namely, in the place of a pledge. A pledge is indeed a security by which both parties are bound, both the one who gives and the one who receives. When God gives his Spirit into our hearts, he binds himself to us by this pledge, that he is unwilling to forsake us, but to acknowledge us as his own forever; and we, while we receive this pledge, are bound to be his special possession and under his right of ownership, so that we are unwilling ever to withdraw ourselves from his possession and right, or to render the pledge made void. He who gives a pledge, as a part of the price, confirms the purchase and the contract, and binds himself to full payment. Understanding this, Augustine says: He gave something of the Spirit as a pledge, so that we might desire the fullness itself. He who receives the pledge confirms the sale and binds himself, so that he is unwilling to overturn what he has sold. This is the use of a pledge, unless it is rendered void by inconvenient circumstances. Looking to this, the Apostle says: and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts. As a pledge of money is put into a purse, so the pledge of the Spirit is poured into our hearts.

units.la: ria infertur loculis, arra spiritus in corda nostra infunditur. Loquitur autem non de donis spiritus, quorum metio fit in Epistola præcedente, quæ nonnunquam & reprobis cōferuntur, nec certum habent uerae salutis pignus, sed de gratia spiritus filiorum Dei, quæ in Christum filium Dei credentibus electis sic confertur, ut clament ad Deum abba pater, illiusq; moderatu regantur ac dirigantur.
units.tr: Not a pledge of money, but a pledge of the Spirit is poured into our hearts. He speaks, however, not of the gifts of the Spirit, which are mentioned in the preceding Epistle, and which are sometimes given even to the reprobate, and do not hold a certain pledge of true salvation; but of the grace of the Spirit of the sons of God, which is so given to the elect who believe in Christ the Son of God that they cry out to God, Abba, Father, and are ruled and directed by his guidance.

units.la: Vide autem quàm competenter ad causam quam agit post assertam promissionum Dei in Christo ueritatem, efficaciam doctrinæ Christi, quàm Corinthijs prædicauerat, in ipsis credentibus declaratam subijciat, ut duobus omnium certissimis testimonijs veritatis Dei in promissis, & efficaciæ doctrinæ Christi in credentibus comprobet, non fuisse in illa etiam & non, sed etiam & amen. Et ideo usus est verbis præteritis, unxit nos, obsignauit nos, & dedit arram spiritus in cordibus nostris, significans loqui se de efficacia prædicationis suæ virtute & operatione spiritus Dei in ipsis credentibus declarata. Confirmatio, unctio & obsignatio suffraganeorum fabula est, omni veritate destituta. Veri Christiani confirmantur, ungun-tur & obsignantur ab ipso Deo, à quo & arram spiritus accipiunt.
units.tr: Notice, however, how fittingly, for the cause he is pursuing, after asserting the truth of God's promises in Christ, he sets forth the efficacy of the doctrine of Christ, which he had preached to the Corinthians, as declared in the believers themselves, so that by the two most certain testimonies, the truth of God in his promises and the efficacy of Christ's doctrine in believers, he may prove that in him there was not "yes and no," but "yes and amen." And therefore he has used the past tenses: anointed us, sealed us, and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts, signifying that he is speaking of the efficacy of his preaching, declared by the power and operation of God's Spirit in the believers themselves. The confirmation, anointing and sealing by the suffragans is a fable, destitute of all truth. True Christians are confirmed, anointed and sealed by God himself, from whom they also receive the pledge of the Spirit.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM CAPITIS.
units.tr: Argument of the Chapter.

units.la: EST hoc caput trimembre. Primo reddit rationem, quare ad ipsos nondum uenerit. Secundo præcipit de scortatore in ecclesiam post pœnitentiam recipiendo, quem in Epistola præcedente excommunicari iusserat. Tertio, rursus incipit Apostolatum suum commendare.
units.tr: This chapter has three parts. First, it gives the reason why he has not yet come to them. Second, it instructs them to receive back into the Church, after repentance, the fornicator whom he had ordered to be excommunicated in the previous Epistle. Third, he again begins to commend his apostleship.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: Chapter 2

units.la: GO uero testem Deū inuoco in animam meam, quod parcens uobis nondum uenerim Corinthum, non quod dominemur uobis nomine fidei, sed quod adiutores sumus gaudij uestri, nā fide statis. Decreui uero apud memetipsum hoc, non iterum cum dolore uenire ad uos. Nam si ego mœrore uos affecero, quis est qui exhilaret me, nisi is qui mœrore afficitur ex me? Et scripsi uobis hoc ipsum, ne si uenirem ad uos, dolorem caperē ex ijs, de quibus oportebat me gaudere, fiduciam hanc habens erga uos omnes, quod meum gaudium, uestrum sit omnium. Nam ex multa tribulatione & anxietate cordis scripsi uobis per multas lachrymas, non ut mœrore afficeremini, sed ut cognoscere-tis retis charitatem, quam habeo abundantius erga vos.
units.tr: Moreover I call God as witness upon my soul that it was to spare you that I have not yet come to Corinth. Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are helpers of your joy, for by faith you stand. Indeed I have decided within myself not to come to you again in sorrow. For if I cause you sorrow, who is there to cheer me but the one who is made sorrowful by me? I wrote this very thing to you so that, when I came, I would not suffer grief from those over whom I ought to rejoice, having confidence in you all that my joy is the joy of you all. For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears, not so that you would be made sorrowful, but so that you might know the love I have for you, which is more abundant.

units.la: Hactenus reiecit à se calumniam leuitatis, idq; hoc maioreterio, quod illa ipsam quoque doctrinam Christi à se Corinthijs praedicatam inuoluerat, iam initio capitis huius subijcit quod desyderabatur, quia videlicet ratione nondum uenisset Corinthum. Poterat autem in genere dicere: Non fuit hactenus commodum ut uenirem ad uos. Et hoc dicens nihil dixisset alienum à uero. At interim non expresse id quod ipsum specialiter fuit remoratus, & quod eos scire uolebat. Quoniam autem rarum id erat, & pseudapostolos improbabile, protert in medium non simpliciter sed praemio iureiurando, quo plus mueniat fidei. Sic dicit: Ego uero testem Deum invoco in animam meam, quod parcens uobis nondum uenerim Corinthum. Ergo propterea nondum uenerat Corinthum, quod metuebat, ne si uenisset, praesens constitutus parcere non posset impoenitentibus, quibus tamen absens parcebat ipse futurae resipiscentiae. Hac de re infra in calce cap. 12. sic scribit. Nam metuo, ne qua fiat, ut si uenero non quales uelim reperiam uos, & ego reperiar uobis qualem nolitis, ne quomodo sint contentiones, aemulationes, irae, concertationes, obtrectationes, susurri, tumores, seditiones. Ne iterum ubi uenero, humile me faciat Deus meus apud uos, & lugeam multos eorum, qui ante peccauerunt, nec eos poenituit immunditiae, libidinisq; & impudicitiae quam patrarunt. Haec ibi. Vnde patet quid sit quod se ob id nondum uenisse Corinthum dicit, ut illis parceret. Quibus? Illis uidelicet, quos nondum poenitebat perpetratae immunditiae, libidinis & impudicitiae, deinde contentiosis, aemulatoribus, tracundis, obtrectatoribus, susurratoribus, tumidis ac seditiosis. Ergo post priorem quoque epistolam erat adhuc tales in ecclesia Corinthiorum. Sic malum pertinax non corrigebatur literis, quantumuis grauibus ac magno Apostolicae authoritatis scriptis, ac posse bat gra uiorem praesentis apostoli animaduersionem.
units.tr: Up to this point he has rejected from himself the charge of levity, and he does so all the more because that charge had also cast doubt on the very teaching of Christ which he had preached to the Corinthians. At the beginning of this chapter he now states what was being sought, namely the reason why he had not yet come to Corinth. He could have said in general terms: "It has not been convenient for me to come to you so far." Saying this, he would have said nothing false. Yet he would not have expressly stated the particular thing that had held him back, and which he wanted them to know. Since such a thing was rare, and the false apostles would not readily believe it, he brings it forward not simply but with an oath, so that he may win more confidence. He says: "Moreover I call God as witness upon my soul that it was to spare you that I have not yet come to Corinth." So he had not yet come to Corinth because he feared that, if he came and were present, he would not be able to spare the impenitent, whom, while absent, he was sparing in hope of their future repentance. On this matter he writes further on, at the end of chapter 12, as follows: "For I fear that, when I come, I may not find you such as I would wish, and that you may find me such as you would not wish: that there may be quarrels, jealousies, angers, rivalries, backbitings, whisperings, conceits, and disorders; that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may mourn over many of those who have sinned before and have not repented of the uncleanness, fornication and lewdness which they have committed." Thus far that passage. From this it is clear what he means when he says that he has not come to Corinth for this reason, that he might spare them. Spare whom? Clearly those who did not yet repent of the uncleanness, fornication and lewdness they had committed, and then the contentious, the jealous, the angry, the backbiters, the whisperers, the conceited and the disorderly. Therefore even after the earlier Epistle there were still such people in the Corinthian Church. So a stubborn evil was not being corrected by letters, however weighty and written with the great authority of an apostle, and it could be corrected only by the more severe correction of the apostle present in person.

units.la: Quare poterit hic quaeri, parcendum ne fuerit talibus, cum essent impoenitenter tales? Respondeo, nisi adhuc fore sperasset, ut manstu- dine ac longanimitate sua ad resipiscentiam provocarentur, non fuisset ratio parcendi talibus. Parcebat aut e. Sperabat igitur. Quod hac ratione parcebat, non erat culpabile, sed conforme exemplo diuinae patientiae, quae & ipsa longanimiter tolerando peccatores ad resipiscentiam inuitat, sicut uidere est Rom. 2. Hoc itaque parcendi genus magis salutis illorum desyderium ac spem futurae resipiscentiae quam negligentiam spirabat.
units.tr: Here it may be asked whether such people ought to have been spared, since they were impenitent. I answer: unless he had hoped that they might be brought to repentance by his gentleness and long-suffering, there would have been no reason to spare them. But he did spare them; therefore he hoped. That he spared them for this reason was not blameworthy, but in keeping with the example of divine patience, which also, by bearing with sinners patiently, invites them to repentance, as may be seen in Romans 2. This kind of sparing therefore breathed a desire for their salvation and a hope of future repentance rather than negligence.

units.la: Sed dices: Quid necesse erat propterea non uenire Corinthum, cum nihilo secius praesens quoque parcere posset?
units.tr: But you will say: Why was there any need to refrain from coming to Corinth, since he could have spared them just as well when present?

units.la: Respondeo. Sine contemptu authoritatis Apostolicae non potuisset praesens parcere im-
units.tr: I answer: Without contempt for apostolic authority, he could not have spared the impenitent when present,

units.la: poenitentibus, sicut potuit absens. Si praesens peperciisset talibus, tria magna mala euenissent.
units.tr: as he could while absent. If he had spared such people when present, three great evils would have followed.

units.la: 1 Primo nanq; authoritatem suam contemptui exposuisset, idq; non solum apud eos quibus peperciisset, sed & apud reliquam totam ecclesiam, atque ita omnis uigor Apostolici muneris elanguisset, cuius rei proh dolor non uno tantum loco hodie quoque exempla uidemus in ecclesijs, in quibus praesentia ministrorum omnium est despicatissima, propterea quod ad quaeuis flagitia praesentes conniuent.
units.tr: (1) First, he would have exposed his authority to contempt, and not only among those whom he had spared but also throughout the whole Church; and so all the vigour of the apostolic office would have grown feeble. Alas, we see examples of this even today in many churches, where the presence of all ministers is most despised, because they connive at every kind of scandal when they are present.

units.la: 2 Deinde impoenitentes illi quibus praesens peperciisset, omnem de resipiscentia cogitationem prorsus abiecissent, id quod facere nondum poterant, donec aduentum Apostoli solicit expectare cogebantur, nec sperare poterat fore ut praesens parceret perinde atque parcebat absens, praesertim cum iam secundo scribens haud parsurum se praesentem commi- naretur.
units.tr: (2) Second, those impenitent people whom he had spared when present would have altogether cast aside any thought of repentance, which they could not yet do; they were compelled to wait anxiously for the apostle's coming, and they could not hope that he would spare them when present just as he spared them while absent, especially since, writing a second time, he had threatened that he would not spare them when present.

units.la: 3 Tertio, non modo impoenitetes illi in peccatis suis & impoenitentia cordis obstinatiores fuissent facti, sed & saniores malo hoc exemplo haud parum fuissent corrupti, & impune serpenti labe infecti. Horum consyderatione cogitabat prudens Apostolus multo esse satus, ut parceret absens impoenitentibus, spe resipiscentiae futurae, quam ut praesens in illos animaduerteret quidem, uerum magis eos intempestiua animaduersione perderet, dum impoenitentes à corpore ecclesiae abscinderet, quam seruaret.
units.tr: (3) Third, not only would those impenitent people have been made more set in their sins and more hardened in the impenitence of their hearts, but also, being more sound, they would have been corrupted by this bad example and infected by a crawling plague that went unpunished. Considering these things, the prudent apostle thought it far better to spare the impenitent while absent, in hope of future repentance, than to take action against them while present, for by untimely correction he would destroy them more than save them, cutting off the impenitent from the body of the Church.

units.la: Hac prudetia spiritus utinam utantur nonnulli fratres, qui in ministerio suo longe diuersi a negligentibus ac torpidis, intempestiuo nonnunquam & parum utili zelo ad corripiendum peccantes feruntur.
units.tr: Would that some brethren would use this prudence of the Spirit, who, in their ministry, are far removed from the negligent and sluggish, yet are sometimes carried away by an untimely and little useful zeal in rebuking sinners.

units.la: Quid est autem quod dicit: quod parcens uobis, & non magis, quod parcens nonnullis ex uobis, cum tamen non de omnibus indiscriminatim, sed de impoenitentibus tantum intelligat?
units.tr: But what does he mean by saying "that I might spare you", and not "more" or "that I might spare some of you", since he does not mean indiscriminately all of them, but only the impenitent?

units.la: Scribit omnibus, alios laudat, alios reprehendit, & tamen utrunque nonnunquam facit in genere, relinquens utrorunque cum bonorum tum malorum conscientijs, ut sibi quisque quod ad se pertinet applicent. Quamuis subinde etiam specificanter loquatur, id quod & in hac causa infra cap.12. facit.
units.tr: He writes to all, he praises some and rebukes others, and yet he sometimes does both in general terms, leaving each of both the good and the bad to examine their own conscience, so that each may apply to himself what pertains to him. Although he sometimes speaks specifically as well, which he also does in this matter further on, in chapter 12.

units.la: Videndum etiam est quare non simpliciter dicat: Propterea nondum ueni Corinthum, quod uobis parco, sed iusiurandum praemittit dicens: Ego uero testem Deum inuoco in animam meam. Opus ne habebat coram Corinthijs testimonio Dei, ut non fuerit satis simpliciter id quod res erat proponere? Habebat sane propter pseudapostolos, qui omnia ipsius finistre interpretabantur. Illi culpam quod nondum uenisset, in ipsum re- iciebant, cum non ipsius esset, sed eorum quibus parcebat. Cum autem id non appareret in se uerosi- mile, & tamen conduceret senioribus ut crederetur, noluit simpliciter quod uerum esse sciebat, sed cum iuramento proferre, quo uel ab inuitis fidem extorqueret.
units.tr: We should also consider why he does not simply say: "For this reason I have not yet come to Corinth, because I spare you", but puts an oath before it, saying: "Moreover I call God as witness upon my soul." Did he need the testimony of God before the Corinthians, so that it was not enough to state plainly what was the case? Indeed he did, on account of the false apostles, who interpreted all his actions in a bad sense. They laid the blame for his not having come yet upon him, when it was not his fault but that of those whom he was sparing. Since this did not seem probable in itself, and yet it would serve the elders to be believed, he chose not to state simply what he knew to be true, but to bring it forward with an oath, by which he might extract belief even from the unwilling.

units.la: Sic dicit: Ego uero testem Deum inuoco in animam meam. Quasi dicat: Accusant me magistri uestri leuitatis, & cogitationum carnalium sermonum q; non ueracium, quod cum constituerim uenire Corinthum, nondum uenerim, ego uero usqueadeo alienus sum ab hac culpa, quam illi mihi impingunt, ut testem Deum innocem in animam meam, quod parcens uobis nondum uenerim Corinthum, atque ita non ego, sed uos in culpa sitis nondum praesti ti promissi.
units.tr: So he says: "Moreover I call God as witness upon my soul." As if he were saying: "Your teachers accuse me of levity and of carnal thoughts and untrue words, because, though I had determined to come to Corinth, I have not yet come. But I am so far from this fault which they impute to me that I call God to witness upon my soul that it was to spare you that I have not yet come to Corinth; and so it is not I but you who are at fault for the promised visit not yet having taken place."

units.la: EGO uero, inquit, testem Deum inuoco in animam meam.) Habemus hic non modo exemplum Apostolicum, quo legitima iuramenta licita esse comprobantur, qua de re uidere est in appendice de iuramento, quam Commentarijs nostris in psalmos adiecimus, sed & formam quandam pleni ac sufficientis iuramenti, cui nihil abest quod ad faciendam fidem desyderari debeat.
units.tr: "Moreover," he says, "I call God as witness upon my soul." Here we have not only an apostolic example by which lawful oaths are shown to be permitted, which may be seen in the appendix on the oath that we added to our Commentaries on the Psalms, but also a certain form of a full and sufficient oath, in which nothing is lacking that ought to be required to produce belief.

units.la: Citat Deum testem ueritatis omnium certissimum. Est enim ille secretorum omnium cognitor, & praeterea ueritatis amantissimus & omnis innocentiae iudex. Et ne videatur hoc sine suo uelle periculo impune facere, quod ab impijs fieri solet, sciens Deum esse omnis periurij ultorem, animam suam deponit, si falso testem Deum citet, dicens: ego uero testem Deum inuoco in animam meam, intellige, si mendax sim.
units.tr: He calls God as witness of the truth, who is most certain of all. For he is the knower of all secrets, moreover the greatest lover of truth and the judge of all innocence. And lest it seem that he may do with impunity what the impious usually do, knowing that God avenges every perjury, he puts his own soul at stake, if he calls God as witness falsely, saying: "But I call God as witness against my soul," that is, if I am lying.

units.la: Sane sic comparatum est omne iusiurandum, ut citetur Deus testis in animas illorum, qui quod falsum est, testimonio ipsius pro uero confirmari uolunt, atq; ita contestatione nominis ipsius impie abutuntur.
units.tr: Indeed every oath is so constituted that God is called as witness against the souls of those who want what is false confirmed as true by his testimony, and so by invoking his name they impiously abuse it.

units.la: NON quod dominemur uobis, inquit, nomine fidei, sed adiutores sumus gaudij uestri.) In Graeco est, οὐχ ὅτι κυριεύομεν ὑμῶν τῆς πίστεως, id est, non quod dominemur uestrae fidei, quemadmodum & uetus interpres reddidit.
units.tr: "Not that we lord it over you," he says, "in the matter of faith, but we are helpers of your joy." In the Greek it is "οὐχ ὅτι κυριεύομεν ὑμῶν τῆς πίστεως" [ouch hoti kyrieuomen hymōn tēs pisteōs], that is, "not that we lord it over your faith," as the old translator also rendered it.

units.la: Alij tamen subaudiunt uoculam, ἐν πίστει, ut sit, οὐχ ὅτι κυριεύομεν ὑμῶν τῆς πίστεως ἐν πίστει, id est, non quod dominemur uobis fidei gratia: & putant fieri non posse, ut quis cuiuspiam dominetur fidei. Meo iudicio non est tantum discriminis, inter utranque uersionem, ut à simplicitate Graeci contextus discedere debeamus.
units.tr: Others, however, supply the little word "ἐν πίστει" [en pistei], so that it reads "οὐχ ὅτι κυριεύομεν ὑμῶν τῆς πίστεως ἐν πίστει" [ouch hoti kyrieuomen hymōn tēs pisteōs en pistei], that is, "not that we lord it over you for the sake of faith," and they think it impossible that anyone should lord it over another's faith. In my judgment there is not so great a difference between the two renderings that we ought to depart from the plain sense of the Greek context.

units.la: Quoniam dominij speciem habere uidebatur, quod se illis parcere dixit, mox occupat dicens, non quod dominemur uestrae fidei, sed quod adiutores sumus gaudij uestri. Cui potestas est parcedi delinquentibus, eidem est potestas castigandi quoque delinquentes. Quare ne ex opposito oppositum, siniistro studio colligentes dominationis affectationem sibi impingerent maleuoli, negat statim hoc se ob id scribere, ut dominatum sibi in fidem ipsorum uindicet, sed ad hoc potius, ut adiutor sit gaudij ipsorum.
units.tr: Since he had said that he spared them, which seemed to have the appearance of lordship, he immediately adds, "not that we lord it over your faith, but that we are helpers of your joy." Whoever has the power to spare offenders has also the power to punish them. Therefore, lest the ill-disposed, gathering the opposite from the opposite with a malicious purpose, should charge him with an ambition to dominate, he at once denies that he writes this for the purpose of claiming lordship over their faith, but rather so that he may be a helper of their joy.

units.la: Vide solicitudinem ac cautionem Apostolo-
units.tr: See the concern and caution worthy of

units.la: lo Christi dignam. Loquitur de legitima sua & Apostolica potestate, quam habebat in eos qui delinquebant, & loquitur non de eo, quod uelit illa uti, sed de eo potius quod nolit ad praesens uti, & tamen ueretur, ne quam occasionem praebeat maleuolis, accusandi se de studio dominandi.
units.tr: the Apostle of Christ. He speaks of his lawful and apostolic power, which he had over those who did wrong, and he speaks not of his wish to use it, but rather of his unwillingness to use it at present, and yet he fears lest he give the ill-disposed any occasion to accuse him of a desire to dominate.

units.la: Hodie, bone Deus, quàm remoti sunt à mente Apostoli, qui successores uideri uolut apostolorum. Palam enim absq; ulla dissimulatione dominatum exercet in ecclesias Christi, in quo sic inualuerunt, ut & regibus & principibus co fidentissimè dominentur.
units.tr: Today, good God, how far removed from the mind of the Apostle are those who want to be seen as successors of the apostles! For they openly, without any disguise, exercise lordship over the churches of Christ, and in this they have so prevailed that they domineer most boldly over both kings and princes.

units.la: Quo praetextu? Praetextu fidei ac religionis: Homines carnalissimi, irreligiosissimi, à uera Christi fide, pietate, ac religione alienissimi, sacrarum scripturarum ignorantissimi, sumunt sibi dominitum in causa fidei ac religionis Christianae super omnes, usque adeo, ut mactét crudelissimè propter fidem Christi, quam non intelligunt, ueros fideles. O dominatores iniqui, quis aperiet uobis oculos mentis ut intelligatis iudicij diuini grauitatem, quod iamiam cerucibus uestris imminet?
units.tr: On what pretext? On the pretext of faith and religion. Most carnal and most irreligious men, most alien from the true faith, piety and religion of Christ, most ignorant of the holy Scriptures, claim for themselves lordship over all in the cause of faith and of Christian religion, to such an extent that they most cruelly slaughter, for the sake of the faith of Christ which they do not understand, the true faithful. O unjust lords, who will open your eyes of mind, that you may understand the gravity of the divine judgment, which now hangs over your necks?

units.la: Dicet quisquam. Ergo ne in ecclesia Christi liberum erit omnibus credere uel non credere quidlibet? Nemo ne erit qui à uera fide deficientes, & alios quoq; ad defectionem solicitantes, ordinaria potestate cohibeat, & in ordinem cogat?
units.tr: Someone will say: "Then in the Church of Christ will it not be free for everyone to believe or not to believe anything at all? Will there be no one who, by ordinary power, restrains those who fall away from the true faith and who also urge others to defection, and brings them into order?"

units.la: An no pastoris officium est, aberrantes oues in uiam, uel nolentes reducere ne pereant?
units.tr: Is it not the office of a shepherd to bring back straying sheep to the way, or unwilling ones, lest they perish?

units.la: Respondeo. Non perstringimus legitimum uerorum pastorum officium, quorum utique est, aberrantes oues in uiam reducere, sed dominatum, quem perstrinxit & improbauit primum Christus ipse, Lucae uigesimosecundo, deinde & apostolus Petrus in prioresua epistola cap. quinto, & in Veteri quoq; test. Deus ipse in falsis pastoribus, qui auferre gregi ipsius dominabantur. Verus pastor ouem erratem quae rit, inuentam humeris suis imponit; & ad ouile reportat ne pereat.
units.tr: I answer: We do not impugn the lawful office of true shepherds, whose duty it certainly is to bring straying sheep back to the way; but we impugn the lordship which Christ himself first condemned and rejected, Luke twenty-second, and then the apostle Peter in his first epistle, chapter five, and also in the Old Testament God himself, against the false shepherds who lorded it over his flock to snatch it away. The true shepherd seeks the straying sheep, and once found, he lays it on his shoulders and carries it back to the fold, lest it perish.

units.la: Falsus uero mactat & perdit. Sic nostri ecclesiarum domini, quos pro errantibus habent in ecclesia non instruunt, quia non possunt, imo non curant, sed cum imperio urgent, ut ueritatem abnegent, & ut uiolentia sua efficiant quod uolunt, torturis cogunt ad recantandum, & recantare nolentes atroeiter necant. An hoc non est dominari fidei in ecclesia Christi, quod tamen de se negat Paulus, idque in ecclesia quam non alius quispiam ante ipsum, sed ipse primus ante alios plantauerat, & in Christo genuerat? Hi nostri magni domini & non pastores, sed magistri ecclesiarum, in ecclesijs, quas nec plantarunt, nec rigant, sic dominantur fidei nostrae, ut non modo quid faciendum sit, quod attinet ritus nostrae religionis, sed & quid credendum sit, quod fidei dogmata concernit, admodum magistraliter non ex sacris scripturis & apostolorum Christi doctrina, sed de suo, & sic praecipiat
units.tr: But the false one slaughters and destroys. So our lords of the churches, whom they regard as erring persons in the Church, do not instruct them, because they cannot, or rather do not care to; but they press them with command, so that they deny the truth, and by their violence they bring about what they want; they compel them by tortures to recant, and those who are unwilling to recant they cruelly put to death. Is this not to lord it over the faith in the Church of Christ, which Paul nevertheless disclaims for himself, and that in a church which no one else before him, but he himself first of all, had planted and begotten in Christ? These great lords of ours, who are not shepherds but masters of the churches, in churches which they neither planted nor water, so lord it over our faith that they not only prescribe, in a most magisterial manner, what is to be done as regards the rites of our religion, but also what is to be believed as regards the doctrines of faith, not from the holy Scriptures and the teaching of the apostles of Christ, but from their own heads, and they command thus:

units.la: ut nisi credas quod ipsi credendum pro suo do minatu praescribunt, non sufficiat tibi ad hoc ut sis Christianus, omnis illa fides, quam praedicarunt in orbe Apostoli, praenunciarunt prophetæ, & Christus ipse ad hoc ut salvemur requisiuit, sed habendus sis pro haeretico, & igni comburendus. An hoc non est dominari fidei Christianorum? Dominari quid est aliud quàm non iure, non potestate legitima, non pro utilitate subditorum, quæ recta ac bona sunt praecipere, sed pro imperio, propria libidine, ad excedendum dominatum in subditos, & ostendendum maioritatis eminentiam, quiduis imponere credendum ac faciendum, idq; magno cum supercilio & fastu, & seueris comminationibus extorquere in omnibus obedientiam omnium seruilissimam, etiam reclamantibus fidelium conscientijs absque ulla contradictione praestandam? Si ab hoc dominatus genere alieni sunt ecclesiarum domini, restituant conscientias fidelium liberas à iugo magisterij humani, in libertatem Christianam, qua sint serui non hominum, sed eius à quo iunt precio magno redempti. Quod fidem Christianam ueram ac synceram attinet, plantanda illa est praedicatione Euangelica, è cuius auditu operante spiritu Dei in cordibus electorum nascitur, riganda est ac fouenda eodem uerbo unde est nata, dirigenda ac prouehenda prudenti cura ministrorum Christi, orationibus, operibus uerè bonis, & tolerantia afflictionum magis ac magis confirmanda, non humano magisterio ac dominatu in quidlibet abstorqueda. At hoc opus, hic labor est. Facilius est mille conscientijs subditorum frænum imponere dominationis, & dicere: sic uolo sic iubeo, quàm unius hominis conscientiam uera Christi fide docendo & instruendo ad salutem ædificare.
units.tr: that unless you believe what they, by their lordship, prescribe that is to be believed, all that faith which the apostles preached throughout the world, which the prophets foretold, and which Christ himself required for our salvation, does not suffice for you to be a Christian, but you must be held a heretic and be burned with fire. Is this not to lord it over the faith of Christians? What is it to lord it over, other than, not by right, not by lawful power, not for the benefit of subjects, to prescribe what is right and good, but by command and by one's own lust, in order to exceed the dominion over subjects and to show the eminence of superiority, to impose whatever one pleases to be believed and done, and to extort, with great haughtiness and pride and severe threats, the most servile obedience from all, to be rendered even while the consciences of the faithful protest, without any contradiction? If the lords of the churches are alien from this kind of lordship, let them restore the consciences of the faithful, free from the yoke of human teaching, to Christian liberty, by which they are servants not of men but of him by whom they were redeemed at great price. As far as true and sincere Christian faith is concerned, it is to be planted by the evangelical preaching, from whose hearing, the Spirit of God working in the hearts of the elect, it is born; it is to be watered and nourished by the same word from which it was born, directed and advanced by the prudent care of the ministers of Christ, by prayers, by truly good works, and by endurance of afflictions, to be confirmed more and more, not to be wrested into anything by human teaching and lordship. But this is the work, this is the labour. It is easier to put the bridle of domination on a thousand consciences of subjects, and to say: "Thus I will, thus I command," than to build up a single man's conscience to salvation by teaching and instructing him in the true faith of Christ.

units.la: AD interim illud est, o magni domini, satraparum Antichristi, hoc autem uerorum Apostolorum & ministrorum Christi, in opere Euangelij ac regni Dei fideliter & indesinenter laborantium.
units.tr: Meanwhile, that is the way of the great lords, the satraps of Antichrist; but this is the way of the true Apostles and ministers of Christ, who labour faithfully and unceasingly in the work of the gospel and the kingdom of God.

units.la: SED adiutores sumus, inquit, gaudij uestri.) Repete illud ὅπ, id est, quod, è praecedenti particula, & lege, non quod dominemur fidei uestræ, sed quod adiutores sumus gaudij uestri. Hoc est, non quod delectet nos dominatum exercere in uestram fidem, sed quod magis delectat paternam erga uos ostendere indulgentiam & storgiam, unde non contristemini, sed gaudeatis. Hoc animo parcens uobis nondum ueni Corinthum. Vide Apostolicum & paternum pectus. Hoc ingenio sunt domini, ut malint timeri, quàm amari. Oderint, inquiunt, modo metuant. Non delectantur gaudio subditorum, ideoque non sunt adiutores gaudij illorum, sed delectantur potius animis seruiliter oppressis, anxijs, & ad omnia tremebundis, uerbis mendaci adulatione supplicibus, gestibus seruiliter abiectis, & operibus nihil aliud quàm seruitutem spirantibus.
units.tr: "But we are helpers," he says, "of your joy." Repeat that "ὅπ" [hop], that is, "that," from the preceding particle, and read: "not that we lord it over your faith, but that we are helpers of your joy." That is, not that it delights us to exercise lordship over your faith, but that it delights us more to show paternal indulgence and affection toward you, so that you may not be saddened but rejoice. With this intention of sparing you I have not yet come to Corinth. See the apostolic and paternal heart. Such is the nature of lords that they prefer to be feared rather than loved: "Let them hate, provided they fear," they say. They do not delight in the joy of their subjects, and therefore they are not helpers of their joy; rather they delight in minds crushed in servile fashion, anxious and trembling at everything, in words which beg with lying flattery, in gestures abjectly servile, and in deeds breathing nothing but slavery.

units.la: Hæ sunt delectationes magnorum dominorum, quibus perinde afficiuntur ac si non sint amplius homines, sed dij quidà, ad hoc nati, ut in perium exerceant in homines uelut in bestias. Verùm uides hic longè aliter animatu esse Christi Apostolum. Non delectatur dominio, non tristitia & dolore fidelium, sed delectatur ztorgia paterna, & gaudio eorum quos in Christo genuit. Huius gaudij exhibet se adiutore, quoad eius fieri potest. Ideo parcit etiam delinquentibus, ipse relipiscentiæ, & eam ob causam nondum uenit Corinthum, ne quos cupit esse gaudentes reddat tristes ac dolentes.
units.tr: These are the pleasures of great lords, who are affected as though they were no longer men but a kind of gods, born to exercise rule over people as over beasts. But you see here that the apostle of Christ is minded very differently. He takes no delight in dominion, but in the sorrow and grief of the faithful; he delights instead in fatherly affection [στοργή] and in the joy of those whom he begot in Christ. He shows himself a helper of that joy, so far as it can be done. For this reason he even spares the offenders, waiting for their repentance, and for this reason he has not yet come to Corinth, lest he make those whom he wants to be joyful sad and grieving.

units.la: De quo autem gaudij genere loquitur? Est gaudium carnis & mundanum, quando quę uo lumus secundum carnis affectus cōsequimur, siue illa sint licita, siue illicita. Huius gaudij adiutor dubio procul nolebat esse Apostolus Christi. Loquitur ergo de alio genere gaudij. Hoc alibi sic expressit: Gaudete in domino semper, iterum dico gaudete. In eo cupiebat illos retinere. Ideo cauebat, ne qua austeritate caltigationis animos eorum in religione Christi cōtristaret. Sunt qui exponant de gaudio futurae uitæ. Verùm præter scopum Apostoli.
units.tr: But what kind of joy does he mean? There is a fleshly and worldly joy, when we obtain what we wish according to the desires of the flesh, whether those things are lawful or unlawful. Beyond doubt the apostle of Christ was not willing to be a helper of that joy. He is speaking, then, of another kind of joy. He expressed this elsewhere: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice." It was in this joy that he wanted to keep them. Therefore he took care not to sadden their minds in the faith of Christ by any harshness of correction. There are those who explain it as the joy of the life to come. But that is beside the apostle's purpose.

units.la: NAM fide statis, inquit.) Non satis perspicuum est, quò referenda & quomodo accipienda sit particulæ huius ἀπολογία. Si diceret, sed quod fumus adiutores gaudij uestri, quod habetis in fide, in qua statis, nihil esset obscuri. Iam cum postquam dixit: Non quod dominamur fidei uestræ, sed quod adiutores sumus gaudij uestri, per uoculam rationalem, ὅ, subijcit dicens: nā fide statis, incertum uidetur quo sit referendum, an ad proxime præcedens, sed quod adiutores sumus gaudij uestri, uel ad illud: Non quod do minemur fidei uestræ. Si ad illud, ergo significat se ob id non dominari ipsorum fidei, quod fide stent, unde mox consequi uidetur: ergo nisi fide stetissent, dominatus ipsis nomine fidei fuisset. Et hinc colligent inconsulti homines, non prohiberi dominatum episcoporum in ecclesia in eos qui fide non sunt firmi, sed in eos tantum, qui fide stant, quales sunt potiores, perfecti, ac religiosi, degetes in monasteriis, ut hoc nomine à iurisdictione episcoporum sint exempti. Hoc sensu dicant episcopi, ecclesiarum domini, ad monachos & monachas, homines religiosos, & in fide perfectos: Non dominamur fidei uestræ fratres, nam uos fide staris, sed dominamur fidei, consciëntijs ac locuhs iai corum. Nam illi fide non stant, sed ueluti prostrati iacent, quare oportet ut illis dominemur, ne unquam ad fidei rectitudinem ac libertate assurgant. Sensum hunc probare non possum. Nam nō ideo dominari uolebat Corinthijs Apostolus, quod fide starent, dominaturus si nō stetissent. Dominatus omnis alienus est à ueris apostolis. Non est illorum dominari, nec in stātes, nec in iacentes, nec in firmos, nec in infirmos. Reliquum igitur est, ut referamus ad proximè præcedens, quo se gaudij illorum adiutorem esse dixit. Vt hic sensus.
units.tr: "For you stand by faith," he says. It is not sufficiently clear to what this particle of explanation [ἀπολογία] should be referred, or how it should be taken. If he had said, "but we are helpers of your joy, which you have in the faith in which you stand," there would be nothing obscure. But since, after saying "not that we lord it over your faith, but that we are helpers of your joy," he adds, by the explanatory little word "for" (γάρ), "for you stand by faith," it seems uncertain whether this should be referred to the immediately preceding clause, "we are helpers of your joy," or to that clause, "not that we lord it over your faith." If to the latter, then he means that he does not lord it over their faith because they stand in faith, from which it seems to follow at once: therefore, had they not stood in faith, he would have lorded it over them in the name of faith. And from this uninstructed men would conclude that the lordship of bishops in the Church is not forbidden over those who are not firm in faith, but only over those who stand in faith, such as the more eminent, the perfect and the religious, who dwell in monasteries, so that by this name they are exempt from the jurisdiction of bishops. In this sense the bishops, lords of the churches, might say to monks and nuns, religious people perfect in faith: "We do not lord it over your faith, brothers, for you stand in faith; but we lord it over the faith, consciences and places of those who lie fallen." For those do not stand in faith, but lie as if prostrate, and therefore it is fitting that we should rule over them, lest they ever rise to the uprightness and freedom of faith. I cannot approve this sense. For the apostle did not wish to lord it over the Corinthians because they stood in faith, as if he would have lorded it over them had they not stood. All lordship is alien to true apostles. It is not theirs to lord it over those who stand or those who lie, over the firm or over the weak. It remains, therefore, that we refer the words to the immediately preceding clause, in which he said that he was a helper of their joy. Such is this sense.

units.la: Delector uestro gaudio. Et ut illud inconcuf sum retineam, adiutor illius esse studeo, quandoquidem in fide Christi statis, id est, constanter perseueratis & alacres estis in domino. Placet mihi hæc fidei uestræ constantia, & omnia ago, ut in illa sitis alacres & gaudentes. Hic sensus nihil habet incommodi. Nec male ex eo colligitur, ergo nisi fide stetisset, non erat futurus gaudij illorum adiutor. Nam planè sic dubio procul animatus est Christi Apostolus, ut haud facile sit gaudio eorum opitulaturus, qui à fide uera dilabentes gaudent, cum dolendum ipsis sit potius quàm gaudendum. Quis enim pius delectari poterit gaudio eorum, qui gaudent in malo, & exultant in rebus pessimis? Iuntque adeo phrenetici, ut de salute sua periclitantes rideant?
units.tr: "I take delight in your joy." And that I may keep that statement unshaken, I am eager to be its helper, since you stand in the faith of Christ, that is, you persevere constantly and are cheerful in the Lord. I am pleased with this constancy of your faith, and I do all things so that you may be cheerful and rejoicing in it. This sense has nothing unsuitable in it, and it is not wrongly inferred from it: "therefore, had he not stood in faith, he would not have been going to be a helper of their joy." For beyond doubt the apostle of Christ is so disposed that he would hardly be ready to help the joy of those who, slipping away from the true faith, rejoice, when they ought rather to grieve than rejoice. For what godly man could take delight in the joy of those who rejoice in evil and exult in the worst things? Or are they so frenzied that they laugh while endangering their salvation?

units.la: SED decreui, inquit, apud memetipsum hoc, non iterum cum dolore ad uos uenire.) Lege ad hunc modum. Decreui autem hoc mihijpsi, nō iterū cum tristitia uenire ad vos. Etenim non dicit diuersum quid à præcedēti, ut usurpanda sit vocula aduersatiua, sed, cum ea nec sit in textu Græco, ubi non est ἀλλὰ, id est, sed, sed est ἀλλ', id est aut, uero, nec accommodet sen sui. Deinde, nō est in Græco, apud memetipsum sed simpliciter ἐμαυτῷ, id est, mihijpsi.
units.tr: "But I have decided within myself," he says, "not to come to you again in sorrow." Read it in this way: "But I have decided this in myself, not to come to you again in sadness." For he does not say something different from what precedes, so that an adversative little word must be supplied; but since it is not in the Greek text, where there is not ἀλλά, that is "but," but ἀλλ', that is "or" or "truly," it does not suit the sense. Next, it is not in the Greek "within myself," but simply ἐμαυτῷ [ἐμαυτῷ], that is, "in myself."

units.la: Latius explicat quod dixit: sed adiutores sumus gaudij uestri. Gaudij huius erat hæc conditio, ut inuoluerent utrosque tam Apostolum quàm Corinthios fideles, mutua videlicet complexione, & συμπαθίᾳ charitatis, sic ut contristata Corinthijs gaudere non posset Apostolus, perinde ac si contristato filio pater, contristata charissima coniuge maritus cōtristetur. Hoc significaturus dicit: Decreui aut hoc mihijpsi, nō iterum cū tristitia venire ad uos. Hoc est: Hanc mihijpsi legem constitui, posteaquàm uos semel estis per me contristati, non esse committendum mihi, ut iterum ad uos cū tristitia ueniam, qua utriq; & ego & vos contristemur. Hoc enim si facerem, & meum & uestrum gaudium turbarem. Quod ait, non iterū omnino significat antea se cum tristitia uenisse ad eos. Non possumus aut exponere hoc de corporali adipsos aduentu. Quare exponendum est de literis prioribus, quas multis modis contristatus scripserat, & per illas cum tristitia ad eos venerat, quarum etiam mox mentionem faciet.
units.tr: He explains more fully what he said: "but we are helpers of your joy." The condition of this joy was that both the apostle and the faithful Corinthians should be bound together, namely by mutual embrace and by the sympathy [συμπάθεια] of charity, so that the apostle could not rejoice while the Corinthians were saddened, just as a father is saddened when his son is saddened, or a husband when his most beloved wife is saddened. Intending to signify this, he says: "But I have decided this in myself, not to come to you again in sorrow." That is: "I have laid down this rule for myself, that since I have once caused you sorrow through myself, it must not be committed by me that I come to you again in sorrow, by which both I and you would be grieved. For if I did this, I would disturb both my joy and yours." When he says "not again," it entirely signifies that he had previously come to them in sorrow. We cannot explain this of his bodily coming to them.
