Therefore it must be explained of the earlier letter, which he had written in great distress, and through which he had come to them in sorrow, a letter he will also mention shortly.

units.la: Vbi illarum seueritate sensit illos fuisse contristatos, decreuit sibijpsi, non uenire denuò ad eos cū tristitia, siue per literas, siue per seipsum. Sic animatus mitis scribit in hac Epistola, quā scripserat in priore.
units.tr: When he had perceived by its severity that they had been saddened, he decided within himself not to come to them again in sorrow, either by letter or in person. Thus disposed, he writes gently in this Epistle, as he had written harshly in the earlier one.

units.la: Dixerit hic quispiam, decretū hoc Apostoli, quo statuerat non venire iterū ad Corinthios cum dolore, fuisse nō satis consultū, propterea quod fieri poterat, ut ipsa hoc ecclesiæ corruptio poscoret, ut nihilo scriberet ad illos mitior quàm antea, imò ipse ad eos abiret, seuerius animaduersurus in impœnitentes ac sectarios, nisi opus domini in ea ecclesia prorsus desererre uellet.
units.tr: Someone here might say that this decision of the apostle, by which he resolved not to come again to the Corinthians in sorrow, was not sufficiently well considered, since it could happen that the corruption of that Church would require him to write to them no more gently than before, or even to go to them himself, to take more severe action against the impenitent and the factious, unless he wished to abandon the work of the Lord in that Church altogether.

units.la: Respondeo. Tria sunt decretorū genera. Primum est affectuū, quo secundum quod uel diligimus uel odimus aliquid facere penes nos ipsi decernimus. Secundum est opinionū, quo decernimus ea, quæ nostra opinione, decernen da uidentur, cum longe essent alia decernēda. Tertium est ueri ac certi iudicij, quo rite ac legitimè, necessario & vtiliter, quæ uel nostros uel aliorum usus concernunt, decernimus. Iam cogitet pius lector, ad quod nam triū istorū decretorum genus referendum sit præsens hoc Apostoli decretum. Meo iudicio referendum est ad decreta quæ promanant è fonte dilectio nis, quā tota hæc materia spirat. Diligebat eos ut filios, quare dolebat ipsi, quod in priore eos Epistola seuerius corripuerat & cōtristauerat, quapropter decreuerat non comittere, ut iterū ad eos cum tristitia ueniret. Hæc tamen ipsa charitas, & paterni pectoris storgia, unde præsens natum erat decretū, aliud erat decretura si salutis eorum conditio aliud poposcisset.
units.tr: I answer: there are three kinds of decisions. The first is of the affections, by which, according to whether we love or hate something, we decide within ourselves to do it. The second is of opinions, by which we decide those things which, in our opinion, seem to be decided, although they ought to have been decided otherwise. The third is of true and certain judgment, by which we rightly and lawfully, necessarily and profitably decide those things which concern our own or others' uses. Now let the godly reader consider to which of these three kinds of decision the present decision of the apostle should be referred. In my judgment it is to be referred to those decisions which flow from the fountain of love, which this whole matter breathes. He loved them as sons, and therefore he grieved that in the earlier Epistle he had rebuked them more severely and saddened them; wherefore he had decided not to commit himself to coming to them again in sorrow. Yet this very charity, and the fatherly affection [στοργή] of his heart, from which the present decision was born, would have decided otherwise had the condition of their salvation demanded otherwise.

units.la: NAM si ego mœrore uos affecero, inquit, quis est qui exhilaret me, nisi is qui mœrore afficitur ex me? Reddit rationem, quare ad eos non iterū cū tristitia uenire decreuerit. Ne uidelicet, inquit, meipse tristitia conficiam. Nam contristatis uobis contristor & ipse. Etenim læ titia spiritus mei pendet à uestra alacritate.
units.tr: For if I grieve you, he says, who is there to cheer me, except the one who is grieved by me? He gives the reason why he has decided not to come to them again in sorrow: namely, so that, he says, I do not wear myself out with grief. For when you are saddened, I am saddened too, since the gladness of my spirit depends on your cheerfulness.

units.la: Hanc si uobis ipse turbauero, quis erit qui me exhilaret, quandoquidem qui hoc possent, mœrore afficiuntur ex me? Hæc ratio, quid spirat aliud quàm ipsissimam uerę dilectionis sympathiam? Perinde est ac si maritus dilectissimæ cōiugi, nonnihil à se contristatæ dicat: Nolo te amplius contristare. Nam si ego te contristo, quis exhilaret me? Cum non sit qui me exhilaret, præter te, quæ contristaris à me.
units.tr: If I were to trouble you in this way, who would there be to cheer me, since those who could do so are grieved by me? What does this reasoning breathe except the very sympathy of true love? It is just as if a husband, whose most beloved wife had been somewhat saddened by him, were to say: "I do not want to grieve you any more. For if I grieve you, who will cheer me? There is no one to cheer me but you, and you are grieved by me."

units.la: Hunc ego puto esse sensum Apostoli. Qui tamen Chrysostomum sequūtur alium adferunt, eumq; diuersum. Hi sic exponunt: Nam si ego uos contristo, id est, dum ego uos corripio, & uos à me correpti contristamini, quis me exhilarat, nisi is qui propterea cōtristatur quod me contristatum intelligit, atq; ita contristatus resipiscit? Gaudeo enim quod si contristamini, ut resipiscatis. Verum hic sensus non bene conue nit cum eo quod præmisit dicens: Decreui aut non iterum cum tristitia uenire ad uos. Sic enim debebat potius dicere: Decreui denuò uenire ad uos cum tristitia. Quare? Quia dum uos contristo, ego exhilaror per eos qui ex me contristantur. Habent hic quod obseruent fideles in ecclesia Christi, quibus dono Dei datum est, ut pastores habeant, non magistros, sed patres. Hi quoniam fidei suæ commissos impense diligunt, pro ingenio dilectionis nulla re suaui us afficiūtur, quā si illos uideat in studio uerę pietatis alacres & gaudetes, & erga se amāter affectos. Sic animatus fidelis pastor non delectatur ulla seueritate. Quod si seueri aliquādo corripit, non est dādum ipsius auctoritati, à qua est natura sua alienus, sed peccantium, quam quærit, saluti. Quare non est ut corripienti succenseat quisquam, sed magis ut condoleant omnes. Nequit enim sine dolore obiurgare & corripere quos diligit, & tristes reddere, quos malit esse alacres & gaudentes, ut & ipse cum Apostolo dicere possit. Si ego uos cōtristo, quis exhilarat me, nisi uos qui contristamini ex me?
units.tr: I think this is the Apostle's meaning. Yet those who follow Chrysostom bring in another sense, and a different one. They explain it thus: "For if I grieve you, that is, while I correct you, and you, being corrected by me, are saddened, who cheers me, except the one who is grieved because he knows I am grieved, and so, grieved, comes to repentance? For I rejoice that you are saddened so that you may repent." But this sense does not fit well with what he said before, when he wrote: "I decided not to come to you again in sorrow." For he ought rather to have said: "I decided to come to you again in sorrow." Why? Because while I grieve you, I am cheered by those who are grieved on my account. Here faithful people in the Church of Christ, to whom it has been given by the gift of God to have ministers, not masters but fathers, have something to notice. Since they dearly love those committed to their faith, by the nature of love they are affected by nothing more sweetly than by seeing them eager and rejoicing in the pursuit of true godliness and loving towards them. So encouraged, a faithful minister takes no delight in any severity. If at times he corrects them severely, this must be attributed not to his authority, which is by its nature foreign to him, but to the salvation of the sinners, which he seeks. Therefore no one should be angry with the one who corrects, but rather all should grieve together with him. For one cannot rebuke and correct those whom one loves, and make sad those whom one would rather see cheerful and joyful, without pain. So he too can say with the Apostle: "If I grieve you, who cheers me, except you who are grieved on my account?"

units.la: ET scripsi uobis, inquit, hoc ipsum. ) Quaerunt ubi hoc ipsum scripserit. Verum, meo iudicio, desyderatur uocula, διὰ, ut legendum sit, διὰ τοῦτο ὅντο, id est, propter hoc ipsum. Neque enim quid, sed quare scripserit docet. Et scripsi uobis, inquit, propter hoc ipsum, ne si uenissem ad uos, tristitiam haberem ex ijs, unde me gaudere oportebat. Intelligo autem de Epistola praecedenti, de qua reddit rationem, quare illa scripserit. Ob eandem uidelicet causam, propter quam nondum ad ipsos uenerat. Scripserat propterea, ne cogeretur praesens exequi, quod per literas est executus. Nam si hoc fecisset, plurimum tristitiae perpessus fuisset praesens, idque ab ijs, de quibus magis erat ipsi gaudendum.
units.tr: "And I wrote this very thing to you," he says. People ask where he wrote this very thing. But in my judgment a small word is missing, διὰ, so that it should be read διὰ τοῦτο αὐτό, that is, "for this very reason." For he is explaining not what he wrote but why he wrote it. "And I wrote to you," he says, "for this very reason, so that if I came to you I would not have sadness from those from whom I ought to rejoice." I understand this of the previous Epistle, for which he gives the reason why he wrote it: namely, for the same cause for which he had not yet come to them. He had written so that he would not be compelled to do in person what he has done through letters. For if he had done this in person, he would have suffered much sorrow, and that from those in whom he ought rather to have rejoiced.

units.la: Sic dicit: Et scripsi uobis propter hoc ipsum, ne si uenissem ad uos, tristitiam haberem ex ijs unde me gaudere oportebat.
units.tr: Thus he says: "And I wrote to you for this very reason, so that if I came to you I would not have sadness from those from whom I ought to rejoice."

units.la: Sed dices. Si propterea praecedentem ad illos Epistolam scripsit, ne cogeretur proficisci Corinthum, ibique praesens contristari, quorsum in illa uenturum se ad eos promisit?
units.tr: But you will say: If he wrote the earlier Epistle to them for this reason, so that he would not be compelled to go to Corinth and be grieved there in person, why did he promise in that letter that he would come to them?

units.la: Respondeo. Fecit hoc spe resipiscentiae eorum, qui peccauerant. Sperabat enim fore, ut si resipuissent cum gaudio apud eos esse & aliquandiu manere posset. Verum cum hoc non per omnia fieret, sicuti uidere est infrà cap. 12. per inpoenitentiam illorum factū est, ut coactus fuerit mutare sententiam.
units.tr: I answer: He did this in hope of the repentance of those who had sinned. For he hoped that, if they repented, he could be with them with joy and remain for some time. But since this did not happen in every respect, as may be seen below in chapter 12, it came about through their impenitence that he was forced to change his plan.

units.la: In eo quod dicit: ne si uenissem ad uos, tristitiam haberem ex ijs, unde me gaudere oportebat, cogitandum nobis est, quàm sit graue ac molestum tristitiae genus, quo contristantur ij qui diligunt, ab illis quos impense diligunt, per quos magis gaudium quàm dolore expectant. Rerum tristium multa sunt genera. Quod attinet eos per quos contristamur, non est ullum tristitiae genus grauius quā quod nascitur nobis ex amicis & dilectis. Leue est, si cōtristent nos inimici, de quibus non nisi tristia expectauimus unquam. Hoc genus tristitiae facile concoquitur, uerum si contristemur, uel ab amicis, quod accidebat Dauidi à Saule socero ipsius, & Christo à discipulo, uel propter amicos, quod usuuenit Apostolo à plerisque Corinthiorum, hoc genus tristitiae zelo charitatis, quasi cote quadam exacuitur, & pectus amantis acutissime transuerberat. Quare non est praeter rationem quod uulgo dicitur: kein lieb on leid.
units.tr: In what he says, "so that if I came to you I would not have sadness from those from whom I ought to rejoice," we must consider how grievous and troublesome is the kind of sorrow by which those who love are saddened by those whom they love dearly, from whom they expect joy rather than pain. There are many kinds of sad things. As for those by whom we are grieved, there is no kind of sorrow heavier than that which arises for us from friends and beloved ones. It is light if enemies grieve us, from whom we have never expected anything but sad things. This kind of sorrow is easily digested. But if we are grieved by friends, as David was by his father-in-law Saul, and Christ by a disciple, or on account of friends, as happened to the Apostle at the hands of many of the Corinthians, this kind of sorrow is sharpened by the zeal of love, as if on a whetstone, and pierces most keenly the heart of the one who loves. Therefore it is not beside the point what is commonly said: "no love without sorrow" (kein lieb on leid).

units.la: Simul cogitent omnes ecclesiae Christi, quales conueniat eas esse suis apostolis, episcopis, ministris, & pastoribus. Tales uidelicet, quae possint illis esse gaudio. Loquitur autem Apostolus de gaudio, non carnis, sed spiritus. Inueniās hodie episcopos, quibus ecclesiae quas possident, haud modico sint gaudio, praesertim si sint pingues. Verum sic esse gaudio episcopis, parum facit ad salutem. Veris episcopis, & non quae sua sunt, sed quae Christi quaerentibus, esse gaudio, id denique confine potest esse menti Apostoli, & perinde habet, ac si liberi morigeri & honesti gaudio sint parentibus.
units.tr: Let all the congregations of Christ consider at the same time what kind they ought to be towards their apostles, bishops, ministers and pastors. Namely, such as can be a joy to them. But the Apostle is speaking of joy not of the flesh but of the spirit. Today you will find bishops who are not a little joyful over the churches they hold, especially if these are rich. But for bishops to take joy in this way contributes little to salvation. For the true bishops, and those who seek not their own things but the things of Christ, to be a joy to them: this, in short, can be what is in the mind of the Apostle, and it is as if children who are obedient, upright and honourable were a joy to their parents.

units.la: FIDVCIAM hanc habens, inquit, erga uos omnes, quod meum gaudium omnium uel trum fit. ) Considebat se amari ab illis quemadmodum abs se amabantur ipsi. Quare considebat simul hanc esse mutuam inter ipsos sympathiam, ut quemadmodum contristatis ipsis contristabatur & ipse, ita si gauderet ipse, gauderent & ipsi. Hac fiducia fretus scripsit ad eos, speras fore, ut resipiscentes mutarent tristitiam sua in gaudium, dū ferre nō possent, ut propter ipsos ulla tristitia afficeretur. Hoc illis significans dicit: Scripsi uobis propter hoc ipsum, ne si uenissem ad vos: tristitiā caperē ex ijs unde me gaudere oportebat, hāc erga vos oēs habes fiduciam, quod meum gaudium uel trum fit omnium.
units.tr: "Having this confidence," he says, "towards you all, that my joy is the joy of you all." He was confident that he was loved by them just as he himself loved them. Therefore he was confident that there was a mutual sympathy between them, so that just as he was saddened when they were saddened, so if he rejoiced, they too would rejoice. Relying on this confidence, he wrote to them, hoping that they, repenting, would change their sadness into joy, since they could not bear that anyone should be affected by sorrow on their account. Signifying this to them, he says: "I wrote to you for this very reason, so that if I came to you I would not have sadness from those from whom I ought to rejoice; I have this confidence towards you all, that my joy is the joy of you all."

units.la: Et ne ab hac sua fiducia quempiam illorum excludere videatur, nō simpliciter dicit: fiduciam hanc habens erga uos, sed, erga uos omnes, neque, quod meum gaudium uel trum fit, sed, quod meum gaudium omnium uel trum fit.
units.tr: And so that he may not seem to exclude anyone of them from this confidence of his, he does not simply say, "having this confidence towards you," but "towards you all"; and he does not say, "that my joy is your joy," but "that my joy is the joy of you all."

units.la: Atqui si vera sunt quae vtraq; hac scribit Epistola, non sic erant omnes erga ipsum animati, ut gaudium ipsius omnium ipsorum esset gaudium. Nequit enim hoc in illis fieri ecclesijs, in quibus sunt studia sectarum, & magistri obtinuerūt trahentes post se discipulos, quod malum utiq; in ecclesiam Corinthiorum irrepserat. Videmus igitur hoc exemplo rursus exprest sum charitatis ingeniū, quae omnia credit, & omnia sperat, & dum hoc facit in multis fallitur, quod Apostolo quoq; usu venit, qui quemadmodum plus diligens minus diligebatur, ita de omnib9 bene fidens in plurib. fallebatur. Cum hoc tā insigni acciderit Apostolo ab illis quos in Christo genuerat, & tanquam filios impense diligebat, nemo post illum Christi minister insolens esse putet, si in eandem fortem apud eos incidat, quos docendos suscepit, ut & ipse de omnibus bene sperans, uix in paucis aliquot in ueniat quod sperat. Et melius est sic animatum Christi ministrum diligendo & fidendo falli à multis, quàm neq; diligendo quemquam, nec fidendo cuipiam, prorsus à nemine falli. Prius enim bonorū est, posterius uero hominum infidorū, qui quemadmodum ipsi beneuolunt nemini, ita in animis suis de nemine bonam possunt concipere fiduciam.
units.tr: But if the things that he writes in this Epistle are true, not all of them were so disposed towards him that his joy was the joy of all of them. For this cannot happen in those churches in which there are factions and teachers who have won over disciples who follow them, which evil had certainly crept into the Church of the Corinthians. We see therefore by this example again the expressed nature of love, which believes all things and hopes all things, and while it does this it is deceived in many. This happened also to the Apostle, who, the more he loved, the less he was loved, and, trusting everyone well, was deceived in many. Since this has happened to the Apostle in so remarkable a way from those whom he had begotten in Christ and loved dearly as sons, let no minister of Christ after him think it strange if he falls into the same lot among those whom he has undertaken to teach; so that, hoping well of all, he may scarcely find among a few what he hopes for. And it is better for a minister of Christ to be thus disposed, and to be deceived by many through loving and trusting, than neither to love anyone nor to trust anyone and so to be deceived by no one at all. For the former belongs to good people, but the latter to faithless men, who, just as they wish well to no one, so in their minds they can conceive no good trust in anyone.

units.la: NAM ex multa afflictione, inquit, & anxietate cordis scripsi uobis, p multas lachrymas, &c.) Occupatio est. Dixerat: Nā si ego tristitia vos afficio, & quis est qui exhilaret me? Item, & scripsi uobis propter hoc ipsum, ne si uenissem ad vos, tristitiam caperem ex ijs unde me gaudere oportebat.
units.tr: "For out of much affliction and anguish of heart, I wrote to you, through many tears, etc." This is an occupatio. He had said: "For if I cause you sorrow, who is there who will cheer me?" Likewise: "And I wrote to you for this very reason, so that when I came to you I would not receive sorrow from those things over which I ought to rejoice."

units.la: Poterant hic dicere: ergo tristari nolens non uenisti. Iā si tristari nolebas, quorsum nos priore Epistola tantopere corripiēdo cōtristare uoluisti, luisti, si quidem lætitia tua pendet à nostra?
units.tr: Here they could say: "So you did not come, because you were unwilling to grieve. But if you were unwilling to grieve, why did you want to grieve us so much in the earlier Epistle by rebuking us so sharply, if indeed your joy depends on ours?"

units.la: Respondet: Scripsi uobis non ut tristitia uos afficerem, sed ut charitatē meā quam erga uos abundantius habeo, cognosceretis. Ea me siquidem impulit, ut scriberem ad uos cum multa tribulatione & anxietate cordis, cuius testes erant lachrymæ, quas cum scriberem largas & multas effundebam. Quare si quid seuerius scripsisse uideor, dabitis hoc neque irę, neq; fastui, neq; odio uestri, sed tribulationi & anxietati cordis mei, quam parit mihi charitas, qua uos abundantius diligo.
units.tr: He replies: "I wrote to you not so as to cause you sorrow, but so that you might know my love, which I have in greater abundance toward you. It was this that impelled me to write to you with much tribulation and anguish of heart, as the tears I shed in abundance and in great quantity as I wrote bear witness. So if I seem to have written somewhat more severely, you will attribute this not to anger, nor to pride, nor to hatred of you, but to the tribulation and anguish of my heart, which love brings upon me, the love by which I love you more abundantly."

units.la: NAM ex multa afflictione & anxietate cordis scripsi uobis, inquit, per multas lachrymas.) Obseruemus hic, quid discriminis sit inter magistros & patres ecclesiarum. Magistri, prælati, ac domini, succensere possunt peccantibus, illosq; seuerè corripere, & in corde contemnere, uerum contristari & angustiari in corde, ac lachrymas propter illos effundere non item. Quia quod faciunt, non faciunt ex charitate, à qua sunt alieni, sed uel ex pharisaica iustitia dedignationis plena, uel ex hyprocrisi, uel studio quæstus. Patres uerò, quoniam paterna sunt erga suos storgia affecti, ubi uident illos peccare, tribulatur & angustiatur in corde, & ubertim lachrymantur, atq; ita corripiunt, etsi acriter tamen amanter, & plus immiscent lachrymarum quàm exprobrationum.
units.tr: "For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you," he says, "through many tears." Let us observe here what difference there is between the masters and the fathers of the churches. Masters, prelates and lords can be angry with sinners, rebuke them severely and despise them in their heart, but to be saddened and distressed in heart and to shed tears over them is not something they do. This is because what they do they do not from love, from which they are estranged, but either from Pharisaic righteousness full of disdain, or from hypocrisy, or from a desire for gain. Fathers, however, since they are moved by paternal affection [στοργή] toward their own, when they see them sin, are troubled and distressed in heart and weep copiously. Thus they rebuke, sharply yet lovingly, and they mix in more tears than reproaches.

units.la: PER multas lachrymas, inquit.) An nō erat hoc admodum muliebre? Certè Stoicum non erat, ill achrymari nedum multū illachrymari.
units.tr: "Through many tears," he says. Was this not very womanly? Certainly it was not Stoic, for the Stoic did not weep, much less weep often.

units.la: Respondeo, citius muliebriter illachrymantur Christus & Apostoli, quàm cum Stoicis indurantur, quia citius perditione hominum contristantur quàm Stoici, contristantur autem citius, quia plus diligunt quàm illi, plus diligūt, quia diuinę sunt bonitatis cōfortes magis quā illi. Nec tetrici sunt cum pharisæis ac Stoicis, nec ridiculi cum Democrito Gelasio, sed magis cum Heraclito ad miseriarum humanarum conspectum illachrymantur.
units.tr: I reply: Christ and the Apostles weep womanly more readily than they are hardened like the Stoics, because they are saddened more quickly by the ruin of men than the Stoics are. They are saddened more quickly because they love more than those do, and they love more because they partake more of divine goodness than those do. Nor are they gloomy like the Pharisees and Stoics, nor ridiculous like Democritus or Gelasius, but rather, like Heraclitus, they weep at the sight of human miseries.

units.la: NON ut mœrore afficeremini, inquit.) Quare noluit, ut mœrore afficerentur, cum in pœnitētis animi & reprobi indicium fuisset, si correpti ab ipso nullo fuissent mœrore affecti?
units.tr: "Not that you might be afflicted with sorrow," he says. Why did he not want them to be afflicted with sorrow, since it would have been a sign of a penitent mind, and of a reprobate one if, rebuked by him, they had been affected by no sorrow at all?

units.la: Respondeo: Resipiscentiam quidem illorum quæsiuit ex animo, tristitiā uero non ita. Aliud est si respiciatur quid deceat filios delinquentes & aliud si cōsyderetur, quid querat pater corripiés illos, ac redarguens. Illos quidē decet ad paternam correptionem contristari, patris uero ingenium haud sic est comparatū, ut dele stetur illorum tristitia, quamuis gaudeat de illorum resipiscentia. In papatu à plerisq; pharisæis ac pœnitentiarijs hoc magis agitur, ut qui peccarunt tristitiā & dolorem, uel simulatū, ostentent, quā ut uerè resipiscant. Et ipsi pharisęi hypocritę sic sunt animati, ut tetricum quidem possint ostendere uultum, resipiscentiam uero nō item, quasi delectetur Deus mœrore ac vultu deiecto, & non magis resipiscentia.
units.tr: I reply: He sought their repentance from the heart, but not sorrow in itself. It is one thing if one considers what befits sinning children, and another if one considers what a father seeks when he corrects and reproves them. It befits them to be saddened by paternal correction, but a father's disposition is not so constituted that he delights in their sorrow, though he rejoices at their repentance. Under the papacy this is pursued much more by most Pharisees and penitentiaries, so that those who have sinned display sorrow and grief, even feigned, rather than truly repent. And the Pharisees themselves, the hypocrites, are so disposed that they can show a gloomy face but not repentance, as if God were delighted by mourning and a downcast countenance, and not rather by repentance.

units.la: SED ut cognoscceretis charitatem, inquit.)
units.tr: "But that you might know the love," he says.

units.la: Poterat dicere, sed ut perficerem erga uos opus charitatis. Verùm non id modo agebat, sed simul quod agebat cognosci ab illis uolebat, ideo dicit: sed ut cognosceretis charitatem. Sic non est satis amanti quod amat, sed id cognosci cupit ab eo quem amat.
units.tr: He could have said, "but that I might perform a work of love toward you." But he wanted not only to do this but also that what he did should be recognized by them. Therefore he says: "but that you might know the love." Thus it is not enough for the one who loves that he loves; he also desires to be recognized by the one he loves.

units.la: Deinde obserua, qua in re charitatem suam cognosci ab illis uoluerit. In paterna uidelicet correptione, quam Epistola illa spirabat. Pater enim quem diligit filium corripit. Verùm pauci sunt qui hinc intelligant se diligi, quod ubi peccarunt corripiuntur & castigantur.
units.tr: Next, observe in what matter he wanted his love to be recognized by them: namely, in paternal correction, which that Epistle breathed. For a father corrects the son whom he loves. But few are those who understand from this that they are loved when, having sinned, they are corrected and chastised.

units.la: QVAM habeo abundantius, inquit, erga uos.) Quasi dicat: Vt quo uos seuerius corripere, hoc ahūdātiorē charitatē erga uos ostēderē.
units.tr: "Which I have in greater abundance," he says, "toward you." As if he said: the more severely I rebuke you, the more abundant love I show toward you.

units.la: Dicet quisquā. Ecquid causę erat, qd Corinthios abundantius diligebat quàm alios?
units.tr: Someone will say: Was there any reason why he loved the Corinthians more abundantly than others?

units.la: Respondeo. Rationem dilectionis nemo ne ipse quidem diligens explicuerit. Quare nō est ut quæramus, quare Corinthios Apostolus plus cæteris dilexerit. Frequenter accidit, ut à filijs suis mater tenerius diligat unū, quàm cæteros, cuius tamē rei ratione si quæratur haud facilè reddiderit. Sic est ingeniū eorū qui diligunt, ut diligant ignari quare diligūt, & ut plus aliquē quā cæteros, & ipsos tamē charos, diligant, & hoc quoq;, quare faciant ignorantes.
units.tr: I reply: No one, not even the lover himself, can explain the reason for love. So we need not ask why the Apostle loved the Corinthians more than the rest. It often happens that a mother loves one of her sons more tenderly than the others, yet if asked the reason she would hardly be able to give it. Such is the nature of those who love: they love without knowing why, they love one more than the rest, though the rest are dear to them too, and they do this also without knowing why they do it.

units.la: Quod si quis tristitia affecit, non me tristitia affecit, nisi ex parte, ne aggrauē oēsuos. Sufficit istiusmodi hominī incre patio hæc, quæ facta est à pluribus: adeò ut ediuerso magis cōdonare debeatis & consolari, ne quomodo fiat ut immodica tristitia absorbeatur eiusmodi.
units.tr: "But if anyone has caused sorrow, he has not caused it to me except in part, lest I burden you all." Such a rebuke, made by many, is enough for such a man. So, on the contrary, you ought rather to forgive and comfort him, lest such a man somehow be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.

units.la: Quapropter obsecro uos, efficite ut ualeat in illū charitas. Nam & in hoc scripseram, ut cognoscerem probationem uestri, an ad omnia obedientes sitis. Cui uerò cōdonatis aliquid, cōdono & ego. Nam & ego si quid cui condonaui, propter uos condonauí in conspectu Christi, ne occupemur à Satana. Nō enim cogitationes illius ignoramus.
units.tr: Therefore I beg you, see to it that love prevails toward him. For I also wrote this so that I might know your proof, whether you are obedient in all things. Whomever you forgive anything, I also forgive. For I too, if I have forgiven anything to anyone, have forgiven it for your sakes in the sight of Christ, lest we be overreached by Satan. For we are not ignorant of his designs.

units.la: Pertinent istaad secundum capitis huius mēbrum, in quo rationem uoluit haberi scortatoris ex ecclesia eiecti, ne si ampliori tristitia afficeretur, prorsus periret.
units.tr: These things pertain to the second part of this chapter, in which he wished account to be taken of the fornicator cast out of the Church, lest, if he were affected with greater sorrow, he should utterly perish.

units.la: QVOD si quis tristitia affecit, inquit.) Loquitur de dicto iā scortatore, nō nominās eum, quoniā & persona & facinus & excōmunicatio illius, abūdē satis innotuerat ecclesię. Quare simpliciter ac moderatē dicit: Quod si quis contristauit. Poterat dicere: Quod attinet scortatoré illū, qui causam dedit tristitiæ, uerū quo niā aspirabat ad illius reconciliationē, maluit modestè de illo loqui, quā seuerè. Sic etiā ueluti per occasionē & non data opera ad causam illius transeat, sensim in illam illabitur, ne quid in animis illorum turbæ moueat, si studiosius exordium causæ huic præmittat. NON me contristauit, inquit, nisi ex parte.) Locus hic nonnihil habet obscuritatis. Quare & diuersimode legitur & exponitur.
units.tr: "But if anyone has caused sorrow," he says. He speaks of the fornicator already mentioned, without naming him, since his person, his crime and his excommunication were sufficiently well known to the Church. So he speaks simply and moderately: "But if anyone has saddened." He could have said: "As for that fornicator who gave cause for sorrow..." But since he aimed at the man's reconciliation, he preferred to speak of him modestly rather than severely. Thus he passes to the cause as if by occasion and not by design, gliding into it gradually, lest by a lengthy preface to this matter he stir some tumult in their minds. "He has not saddened me," he says, "except in part." This place has some obscurity, and so it is read and explained in different ways.

units.la: 1 Primo ad hunc modum. Non me contristauit tantum, sed & omnes uos, ex parte, ne aggrauem. Hoc est. Tristitiam communem intulit & mihi & uobis omnibus, ex parte tamen, id est, non omnino, ne ipsum hæc scribens aggrauem. Sic distinguit & exponit Chrysostomus. 2 Deinde sic. Non me contristauit, nisi ex parte, id est, secundum quid, non tali tristitia quæ me ratione priuarit, sed quæ nonnihil turbarit. 3 Tertio hoc pacto. Non me contristauit, quia me per resipiscentiam suam lætificauit, nisi ex parte, quatenus sibijpsi molestiam pœnitendi cöciliauit. Verum ne grauem uos omnes, si pereat is homo, sufficit illi increpatio hæc, &c. Sic nonnulli illud, ne aggrauem omnes uos, à præcedentibus auulsum coniungunt sequentibus. 4 Mihi simpliciter ad hunc modum exponendum uidetur. Quod si quis contristauit, hoc est, tristitiam in ecclesia excitauit, non me, quasi aduersum me speciali ter peccando, contristauit, nisi hac parte, quatenus solicitum reddidit, ne uos omnes propter illius peccatum aggrauare cogerer. Hactenus sanè contristauerat me. Cupiebam enim uobis parcere, ac nullam perturbationem imponere ecclesiæ. Hunc puto sensum esse Apostoli. Dili gebat ecclesiam illam admodum, cuius peculiari quadam ratione erat Apostolus, ideoque illi & parcebat ac metuebat plurimum, unde & in hac causa propter illam potissimum contristabatur, anxius erat, & cum lachrymis scribebat, cauere cupiēs, ne quid hinc ad illam uel mali, uel perturbationis serperet.
units.tr: 1. First, in this way: "He has not saddened only me, but also all of you, in part, lest I burden him." That is: he brought common sorrow both to me and to all of you, yet in part, that is, not entirely, lest by writing this I burden him. So Chrysostom distinguishes and explains it. 2. Then thus: "He has not saddened me, except in part," that is, in some respect, not with such sorrow as would deprive me of reason, but with sorrow that somewhat disturbed me. 3. Thirdly, in this way: "He has not saddened me, since by his repentance he has gladdened me, except in part, insofar as he brought upon himself the trouble of repenting. But lest I burden you all, if that man should perish, this rebuke is enough for him," etc. So some detach "lest I burden you all" from what precedes and join it to what follows. 4. To me it seems best to explain it simply thus: "But if anyone has saddened," that is, has stirred up sorrow in the Church, "he has not saddened me, as though by sinning specially against me, except in this respect, that he made me anxious lest I be compelled to burden you all because of his sin. Up to this point he had indeed saddened me. For I wished to spare you and to impose no disturbance on the Church." I think this is the Apostle's meaning. He loved that Church very much, and he was its Apostle in a peculiar way; therefore he both spared it and feared greatly for it. Hence in this matter he was especially saddened on its account, was anxious, and wrote with tears, desiring to guard lest any harm or disturbance creep from this into it.

units.la: SVFFICIT, inquit, istiusmodi homini increpatio hæc, quæ facta est à pluribus.) Incipit præscribere, de recipiendo peccatore. Principio, significat illi sufficere increpationem à pluribus, id est ab ecclesia factam. Non uult exclusionem illius excedere sufficientiæ modum.
units.tr: "It is enough," he says, "this rebuke which was given by many." (Sufficit ... quæ facta est à pluribus.) He begins to lay down rules about receiving the sinner back. First, he indicates that the rebuke given by many, that is, by the Church, is enough for such a man. He does not want the exclusion to go beyond the measure of what is sufficient.

units.la: Metitur autem illum non à quantitate & enormitate admissi facinoris, quam in superiori Epistola consyderari uoluerat, cum esset ferenda sententia, sed à qualitate personæ quæ peccauerat, & à grauitate increpationis, quam in ecclesia subierat. Qualitatem personæ expressurus non simpliciter dicit: Sufficit illi, sed, sufficit istiusmodi homini. Hoc dicens, dubio pro culuel aliquid infirmitatis in illo, cui parcendum fuerit, uel singularem aliquem mœrorem, quo ab ecclesia reiectus, conficiebatur, consyderandum proponere uoluit. Grauitatem increpationis notans non dicit simpliciter: Sufficit istiusmodi homini increpatio accepta, sed, increpatio hæc, inquit, quæ facta est à pluribus. Leuius siquidem est, increpari ab uno aliquo, idq; seorsim, extra multorum conscientiā, quā si id fiat palam à multitudine in unum cœtum congregata. Hic non pudor tantum subeundus est in publico omnium conspectu, sed & sustinendæ grauissimæ diuexationes & concuf-
units.tr: He measures this not by the size and enormity of the crime, which he had asked them to consider in the earlier letter when the sentence was to be pronounced, but by the quality of the person who had sinned and by the severity of the rebuke he had undergone in the Church. To express the quality of the person, he does not simply say, "It is enough for him," but "It is enough for such a man" (istiusmodi homini). In saying this, he wishes us to consider, with some doubt, either a weakness in the man who ought to be spared, or some unusual grief by which he, cast out by the Church, was being worn down. In noting the severity of the rebuke, he does not simply say, "The rebuke received is enough for such a man," but "this rebuke," he says, "which was given by many." It is indeed lighter to be rebuked by one person, and that in private, outside the knowledge of many, than if it is done openly by the multitude gathered into one assembly. Here he has to bear not only shame before the public gaze of all, but also the most grievous torment and agitation of conscience, feeling night and day the sentence of condemnation pronounced by many.

units.la: siones conscientiæ, còdemnationis sententiam à pluribus illatam noctes ac dies sentientis.
units.tr: And so, the sentence of condemnation pronounced by many, he feels night and day.

units.la: Admonemur itaque hoc loco, qua diligentia uigilandum sit omnibus illis, quorum curæ commissæ sunt fidelium animæ, ne in correctionibus & castigationibus eorum qui deliquerunt, modum excedant. Procliues sumus pro carnis ingenio ad seueritatem exercendam in peccantes, sicut ægrè nobis ipsis quantumuis grauì ac prolixa animaduersione satisfaciamus. Imo quo seuerius ferimur in peccantes, hoc iustiores uideri uolumus. Sic fit ut proclines sumus ad excedendum modum sine quo nō modo inutilis est, sed & noxia omnis disciplina & castigatio. Satagant igitur omnes Christi ministri, ut & intelligant illud ἱκανόν, id est sufficit, & ad illius mensuram omnia disponant & moderentur. Cordati homines satis intelligunt, quod hinc damni fit, non in religione tātum, sed & rebus alijs humanis, quod pauci sunt, qui norint uel etiam scire cupiant, quid sit illud, sufficit.
units.tr: We are therefore warned here how carefully all those must watch to whose care the souls of the faithful have been entrusted, lest in correcting and chastising those who have offended they exceed the measure. By the nature of the flesh we are inclined to exercise severity against sinners, just as we ourselves are hardly satisfied with any punishment, however heavy and prolonged. Indeed, the more harshly we are carried against sinners, the more just we want to seem. So it happens that we are inclined to exceed the measure, without which all discipline and correction is not only useless but harmful. Therefore let all ministers of Christ take pains both to understand that word "enough" [ἱκανόν], that is, "sufficient," and to arrange and regulate everything according to its measure. Sensible people understand well how much harm comes from this, not only in religion but also in other human affairs, that there are few who know, or even wish to know, what "enough" means.

units.la: Admonitioni huic annexum est & illud, non esse sufficientiæ modum metiendum ad grauitatem delicti, sed potius ad qualitatem personæ post delictum pœnitentis. Admonuit hac de re & Chrysostomus, cuius hæc sunt uerba.
units.tr: Attached to this warning is also this point: the measure of what is sufficient is not to be judged by the gravity of the offence, but rather by the quality of the person who repents after the offence. Chrysostom also gave warning about this matter, and his words are these.

units.la: Omnino ut imperitus medicus, modum dandi remedij nesciens, plus nocet quàm prodest, quales sunt qui medentur ad præscriptum Hippocratis & Galeni, magis quàm ad qualitatem patientis, ita & imperitus Christi minister, nō habes rationem personæ curandæ, sed ad delicti tantum grauitatem respiciens, Satanæ potius seruit quàm Christo, quia perdit magis quàm seruat. Quid igitur damni natum sit ex canonibus pœnitentialibus, quis unquam sufficienter pendit?
units.tr: Just as an unskilled physician, not knowing the proper amount of a remedy, does more harm than good, as do those who treat according to the prescription of Hippocrates and Galen rather than according to the condition of the patient, so too an unskilled minister of Christ, who takes no account of the person to be cured but looks only to the gravity of the offence, serves Satan rather than Christ, because he destroys rather than saves. What harm has arisen from the penitential canons? Who has ever sufficiently weighed this?

units.la: Animaduertendum & hoc est quod dicit, Sufficit istiusmodi homini increpatio hæc, &c. Proponitur nobis discrimen inter electos & reprobos. Electis sufficit increpatio ecclesiastica, ad hoc ut emendentur, reprobis uerò ne uniuersa quidem ecclesiæ disciplina, ex qua magis exacerbantur, quàm emendantur.
units.tr: We must also note what he says: "It is enough for such a man, this rebuke," and so on. A distinction is set before us between the elect and the reprobate. For the elect the ecclesiastical rebuke is enough, so that they may be amended; but for the reprobate not even the whole discipline of the Church is enough, since by it they are made more bitter rather than amended.

units.la: QVÆ facta est à pluribus, inquit.) Efficacia exprimitur ecclesiasticæ excommunicationis, quæ secundum superioris epistolæ præscriptum fiebat in medio multitudinis in cœtum sacrum congregatæ. Ab hac aliena est, quę sine consensu & conscientia multitudinis tentatur à prelatis ecclesiarum. Etenim non ita constringitur excommunicati conscientia per unius aut alterius in se latam sententiam non accedente publico multitudinis consensu, atque constringi illam necesse est, si unanimi & ministrorum & multitudinis uoluntate excommunicatus fuerit.
units.tr: "Which was given by many," he says. This expresses the efficacy of ecclesiastical excommunication, which, according to the rule of the earlier letter, was carried out in the midst of the multitude gathered into the holy assembly. Far from this is the excommunication attempted by prelates of the churches without the consent and knowledge of the multitude. For the conscience of the excommunicated person is not bound in the same way by a sentence pronounced against him by one or another person, if there is no public consent of the multitude; yet it must be bound if he has been excommunicated by the united will of both the ministers and the multitude.

units.la: ADEO, inquit, ut ediuersò magis condonare debeatis & consolari.) Postquam admonuit terminanterminandam esse peccatoris excommunicationem, subiungit de impertienda illi uenia & consolatione. Vult autem ut ad hanc propendeant magis quàm ad diuturniorem excommunicationis seueritatem. Ideo non simpliciter dicit: Vt condonare debeatis & consolari, sed, adeò ut ediuersò magis condonare debeatis & consolari, quasi dicat, quàm excommunicationem hanc ulterius extendere.
units.tr: "So much so," he says, "that on the contrary you ought rather to forgive and comfort." After he has admonished that the excommunication of the sinner must be brought to an end, he goes on to speak of granting him pardon and comfort. He wants them to incline to this rather than to a long continuation of the severity of excommunication. So he does not simply say, "That you ought to forgive and comfort," but "so much so that on the contrary you ought rather to forgive and comfort," as if to say, rather than extend this excommunication any further.

units.la: Obseruandum est hoc loco, quàm appositè ac pertinenter hæc duo uerba condonandi & consolandi usurpet. Videbantur magis propensi ad ulcisendum quàm ad remittendum, & per consequens ad affligendū potius quàm ad consolandum. Hortatur igitur eos, ut condonent magis delictum & consolentur afflictum, quàm ut in lata sententia diutius pergant.
units.tr: It must be observed here how fittingly and appropriately he uses these two words, forgiving and comforting. They seemed more inclined to punish than to pardon, and consequently more to afflict than to comfort. He therefore urges them to forgive the offence and comfort the afflicted man rather than to persist for long in the sentence pronounced.

units.la: Quæsierit quisquam, quare non ipsi Corinthij potius huc priores inclinauerint, ut poenitenti condonarent delictum & tristem consolarentur, eaque de re ad Apostolum scriberēt. Responderi potest paucis. Multum discriminis est inter stergiam patris erga filios, & fraternam filiorum cognationem. Pater propensior est ad misericordiam erga sua uiscera, quá frater erga fratrem. Pater erat Paulus. Tangebatur commiseratione & cura erga eum quem in Christo genuerat. Ab hac remotiores erant Corinthij, quare non pariformiter cum Paulo de salute fratris erant soliciti.
units.tr: Someone might ask why the Corinthians themselves did not rather incline first to forgive the penitent the offence and comfort the sorrowful man, and write to the Apostle about this matter. This can be answered briefly. There is a great difference between the affection of a father towards his sons and the fraternal kinship of brothers. A father is more inclined to mercy towards his own bowels than a brother towards a brother. Paul was a father. He was moved by compassion and care for the one whom he had begotten in Christ. The Corinthians were more distant from this, and so they were not equally anxious with Paul about the salvation of their brother.

units.la: NE quomodo fiat, inquit, ut immodica tristitia absorbeatur eiusmodi.) Iusticiarius dicit: nequaquam condonandum est peccatori, priusquam sufficienti poenitentia satisfecerit pro grauitate peccati quod perpetrauit. Satisfaciendum est iusticiæ Dei, & ecclesiæ quoq;, priusquam recipiatur peccator. Huc oculos intendunt seueri alienorum peccatorum magis quàm propriorum uindices. At uerus Christi Apostolus, Christi ubiq; spiritum, charitatem & misericordiam spirans, magis solicitus est de infirmitate ac tristitia poenitētis ne quo pacto fiat, ut si diuturnior sit tribulatio, immodica tristitia absorbeatur, hoc est, ad desperationem adigatur, illiusq; ui ueluti fluctibus adobruatur ac pereat, quàm de sufficienti satisfactione, siue iusticiæ Dei siue ecclesiæ præstanda. Rursus autem notat poenitentis infirmitatem, & monet illius habendam esse rationem, cum dicit, eiusmodi. Qui dura sunt ceruice & corde lapideo, non facilè absorbentur à tristitia, secus uerò comparati sunt infirmi, quos morsus conscientiæ modico negocio fatigant & conficiunt.
units.tr: "Lest somehow," he says, "such a one be swallowed up by excessive sorrow." The upholder of strict justice says: the sinner must by no means be forgiven before he has made sufficient satisfaction by penance for the gravity of the sin he has committed. Satisfaction must be made to the justice of God, and to the Church also, before the sinner is received. Severe avengers of the sins of others rather than of their own fix their eyes on this. But the true Apostle of Christ, breathing everywhere the Spirit, charity and mercy of Christ, is more anxious about the weakness and sorrow of the penitent, lest in any way, if the affliction lasts too long, he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow, that is, be driven to despair and, as if by the force of waves, be overwhelmed and perish, than about the sufficient satisfaction to be rendered either to the justice of God or to the Church. Again, he notes the weakness of the penitent and warns that account must be taken of it when he says "such a one." Those who are hard of neck and heart are not easily swallowed up by sorrow; but the weak, whom the bites of conscience wear down and exhaust with little effort, are of a different constitution.

units.la: Locus hic de immodica tristitia, diligenter obseruādus est omnibus, præsertim illis, quibus commissa est cura aliorum. Credi non potest, quantū hinc sit periculi, conscientijs maxime, sensu peccatorū quasi importabili quadam mole oppressis. Qui huiusmodi sunt, salutandi sunt amanter, affatuq; blando & amico frequenter erigendi, fundendæ sunt pro illis preces ad dominum, & si quo pacto fieri po A test, onus quo premuntur uel tollendum in uniuersum, uel aliquousq; diminuendum. Et hæc facienda sunt, priusquam per immodicam tristitiam absorbeantur. Etenim ubi fuerint absorpti, nihil uel certè parum profuerit quic quid tentetur, nisi singularis quedā gratia Dei absorptos è barathro desperationis extrahat.
units.tr: This passage about excessive sorrow must be carefully observed by all, especially by those to whom the care of others has been entrusted. It cannot be believed how much danger arises here, especially for consciences oppressed by the sense of sin as by an almost unbearable weight. Those who are in such a state are to be greeted lovingly, and often raised up with a gentle and friendly address; prayers are to be poured out for them to the Lord, and, if in any way it can be done, the burden by which they are pressed is to be either removed altogether or diminished to some extent. And these things must be done before they are swallowed up by excessive sorrow. For once they have been swallowed up, whatever is attempted will do little or no good, unless some singular grace of God draws the swallowed out of the pit of despair.

units.la: QVAPROPTER obsecro uos, inquit, efficite ut ualeat in illum charitas.) Quasi dicat. Quoniam sic est tristis ac lugubris factus, ut timendum sit, ne immodica hac tristitia prorsus absorbeatur, recipite eum per charitatem in ecclesiæ uestræ communionē, ut spiritus eius refocilletur. Efficite, inquit, ut ualeat in illū charitas. Græcè est, χυρῶσαι εἰς ἀπτὴν ἀγάπην, id est, ut publicis suffragijs decernatis ac cōfir metis in illū charitatem. Nā hoc significat uerbum χυρῶσαι, rē aliquam siue per suffragia siue aliàs legitima authoritate decernere, statuere, confirmare, & authenticam ratamq; reddere. Voluntas Pauli est, ut Corinthij in cœtu sacro communibus suffragijs decernant & confirment, recipiendum esse in ecclesiam per charitatem peccatorem poenitentem ac tristē, quēadmodum antea communib9 illum suffragijs excommunicauerant. Et hoc illis non imperat, sed ut faciant obsecrat, quia non uult ut ab inuitis sed potius uoluntarijs fiat, quo charitatis opus plenius à spōtaneis perficiatur, simulque innuit, quàm sit cupidus eius rei, propter quam illos obsecrare dignatur, quò reddat & illos unà secum in idem institu ti propensos.
units.tr: "Therefore I beg you," he says, "bring it about that love may prevail over him." As if he said: since he has become so sad and mournful that it is to be feared lest he be utterly swallowed up by this excessive sorrow, receive him by love into the fellowship of your Church, so that his spirit may be revived. "Bring it about," he says, "that love may prevail over him." The Greek is "κυρῶσαι εἰς αὐτὸν ἀγάπην," that is, that you should decide and confirm love towards him by public votes. For the verb κυρῶσαι signifies to decide, establish, confirm and make a thing authentic and valid by a legitimate authority, whether by votes or otherwise. It is Paul's will that the Corinthians in the holy assembly should decide and confirm by common votes that the penitent and sorrowful sinner is to be received back into the Church in love, just as they had earlier excommunicated him by common votes. He does not command them to do this, but begs them to do it, because he does not wish it to be done by unwilling people but rather by willing ones, so that a work of love may be more fully performed by those who are spontaneous; at the same time he hints how eager he is for the thing for which he deigns to beg them, so that he may make them also inclined, together with himself, to the same purpose.

units.la: Habemus ergo hic locum de recipiēdis excommunicatis, quando illi, & quomodo sint in consortium ecclesiæ recipiendi. Vbi uideli cet timendum est, ne immodica tristitia absorbeantur, recipiendi sunt in ecclesiam. Deinde recipiendi sunt communibus fidelium suffragijs, ad quem modum excōmunicandi quoq; sunt, qui enormiter peccarunt. Tertio, faciēda est hæc reconciliatio per charitatē fraternam. Poterat dicere. Obsecro, ut recipiatis eum ad uos. Verum quoniam multum refert, quomodo hoc fiat, maluit dicere: Obsecro ut decernatis in eū dilectionem. Dilectio nō simpliciter recipit in consortium, sed recipit tanquam dilectum & omnibus uerae dilectionis officijs amplexandum & confouendum.
units.tr: We have here, then, a passage about receiving excommunicated people back: when they are to be received into fellowship with the Church, and how. Here, namely, one must fear that they will be swallowed up by excessive sorrow, and they must be received back into the Church. Next, they must be received by the common votes of the faithful, in the same way that those who have sinned grievously must also be excommunicated. Third, this reconciliation must be made through brotherly love. He could have said, "I beg you to receive him back to yourselves." But since it matters a great deal how this is done, he preferred to say: "I beg you to resolve on love towards him." Love does not simply receive someone into fellowship, but receives him as one who is beloved, and as one to be embraced and cherished with every duty of true love.

units.la: NAM & in hoc scripseram, inquit, ut cognoscerem probationem uestri, nū ad omnia obedientes sitis.) Quoniam superiori epistola seuerè de peccatore hoccommunibus suffragijs excommunicando scripserat, poterant cogitare: ecquid hoc rei est? Quem antea tam graui ac seuero scripto Satanę tradi uoluit, hunc mutata iam sententia per charitatem uult recipi. Quæ est hæc inconstantia? Occurrit igitur dicens. Quę superiori epistola scripsi, non in hoc scripseram ut hominem hunc perderem, sed ut experimentum uestri caperem, sitis ne ad ea quæ scribo morigeri. Et sanè morigeri fuistis. Iam obsecro ut nunc quoq; sitis. Fuistis illic ad tradendum Satanæ hominem peccatorem. Sitis nunc ad recipiendum poenitentem, & ser uandum periclitantem. Nulla est hic inconstā tia. Quod illic egi, etiamnū ago. Quare & uos quemadmodum illic obediuistis, sic etiánum obedite. Sic retinebimus mutuū cōsensum, & simul seruabimus fratrem periclitantem.
units.tr: "For this too I wrote, that I might know your proof, whether you are obedient in all things." Since in the previous letter he had written severely about excommunicating this sinner by the common votes, they could think: what is going on here? The man whom he had earlier wished to be handed over to Satan with such a grave and severe writing, he now, having changed his mind, wants to be received through love. What is this inconsistency? So he answers, saying: what I wrote in the previous letter I did not write in order to destroy this man, but to test you, whether you would be compliant with what I write. And indeed you were compliant. Now I beg that you be so again. You were then obedient in handing the sinful man over to Satan; now be obedient in receiving the penitent man and saving him when he is in danger. There is no inconsistency here. What I did there, I still do. Therefore, just as you obeyed there, so obey again now. In this way we shall keep our mutual agreement and at the same time save our brother who is in danger.

units.la: VT cognoscerem, inquit, probationem uestri, an ad omnia obedientes sitis.) Ergo in hoc est uerorum ac probatorum fidelium experimentum, si scriptis Apostolicis per omnia sint obedientes. Loquor aut non de scriptis ac rescriptis apostolorum Babylonis, quæ authe tica sunt in ecclesia malignantium, ac pluspon deris habent, quàm uerorum apostolorum scripta. Abest: In illis nō est experimentum ue rorum fidelium, sed magis reproborum. Qua re non est, ut hunc locum pseudapostoli ac ma gistri ecclesiarum pro maioritate sua confirmā da citent, ac dicant, ubi est maioritas, ibi est mā dandi authoritas, cæteros manet obediendi necessitas. Nostra ætate in conuentibus Imp. cœperunt uocari obedientes, qui plus obedie tiæ Romano pontifici præstant, q; ipsi Christo & apostolis, & inobedientes, qui in causa reli gionis malūt obedire Deo quàm hominibus. Verum facilè intelligit homo cordatus hanc ueram esse ac Christianam obedientiam, qua probati fideles cognoscuntur, uerbo domini ac scriptis apostolorū eius per omnia & in o mnibus obedire.
units.tr: "That I might know your proof," he says, "whether you are obedient in all things." So the test of true and approved believers lies in this: whether they are obedient in all things to the apostolic writings. But I am not speaking of the writings and rescripts of the apostles of Babylon, which are regarded as authentic in the Church of the wicked, and which they hold in higher esteem than the writings of the true apostles. Far from it: in those things there is no test of true believers, but rather of the reprobate. Therefore it is not right for the false apostles and the teachers of the churches to cite this passage to confirm their majority, and to say: where there is a majority, there is the authority to command, and the rest remain under the necessity of obeying. In our age, at the imperial assemblies, those have begun to be called "obedient" who render more obedience to the Roman pontiff than to Christ himself and the apostles, and "disobedient" those who in matters of religion prefer to obey God rather than men. But a discerning person easily understands that this is the true and Christian obedience by which approved believers are recognized: to obey the word of the Lord and the writings of his apostles in all things and in every respect.

units.la: CVI uerò condonatis aliquid, inquit, & ego condono.) Quò ad plenum fiat rata & au thentica reconciliatio poenitentis peccatoris, illorum suffragijs cōiungit & suum assensum. Tribuit autem illis priore partem, cum dicit: Cui uerò condonatis aliquid, & ego cōdono. Poterat pro authoritate sua dicere: Cui uero ego condono aliquid, cōdonabitis & uos. Ve rum studio demulcet illorum animos, ne per id offendantur quod ad hoc se scripsisse dixit, ut cognosceret probationem ipsorum, an per omnia sint obedientes, quasi hoc dicens, seruo rum ipsos uelit habere loco. Sic cupit eos esse obedientes, ut simul sint non seruorum sed fra trum loco, & permittit illis primas in opere charitatis, quo perficiat illud non inuito sed li bero ac spontaneo spiritu.
units.tr: "But to whom you forgive anything, I also forgive." So that the reconciliation of the penitent sinner may be made firm and genuine, he joins his own assent to theirs by their votes. He assigns to them the first part, when he says: "But to whom you forgive anything, I also forgive." He could have said, on the strength of his authority: "To whom I forgive anything, you too shall forgive." But with care he soothes their minds, lest they be offended by what he said, that he wrote in order to know their proof, whether they are obedient in all things, as if saying that he wished to have them in the place of servants. Thus he desires them to be obedient, yet at the same time to stand in the place not of servants but of brothers, and he allows them the first place in the work of love, so that it may be carried out not with an unwilling but with a free and spontaneous spirit.

units.la: NAM & ego si quid cui condonaui, inquit, propter uos condonaui.) Græcè est, καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ εἴ τι κεχάρισμαι ᾧ, κεχάρισμαι δι᾽ ὑμᾶς ἐν προσώπῳ Χρι στῷ. Erasmus sic distinguit. Nā & ego si quid cō donaui, cui condonaui, propter uos cōdona ui. Meo iudicio simpliciter distingui potest ad hunc modum. Nam & ego si quid condonaui cuipiam, condonaui propter uos, ut sit in Grę co talis distinctio, καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ εἴ τι κεχάρισμαι ᾧ, κε χάρισμαι δι᾽ ὑμᾶς.
units.tr: "For I too, if I have forgiven anything to anyone, have forgiven it for your sake." In Greek it reads: καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ εἴ τι κεχάρισμαι ᾧ, κεχάρισμαι δι᾽ ὑμᾶς ἐν προσώπῳ Χρι στῷ. Erasmus punctuates it thus: "For I too, if I have forgiven anything to someone, to whom I have forgiven, have forgiven for your sake." In my judgment it can be punctuated simply in this way: "For I too, if I have forgiven anything to anyone, have forgiven it for your sake," so that the Greek division is: καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ εἴ τι κεχάρισμαι ᾧ, κεχάρισμαι δι᾽ ὑμᾶς.

units.la: Poterant dicere: Atqui iam antea, ut uide mus cōdonasti peccatori huic, priusquam nos illi cōdonemus. Quid igitur est quod scribis, si nos cui quid condonemus, condonare & te.
units.tr: They could say: "And yet, as we see, you had already forgiven this sinner before we forgave him. What, then, do you mean when you write that if we forgive anyone anything, you too forgive?"

units.la: Respondet. Verum est, iam illi condonaui, quod me attinet, in corde meo, & coram Chri sto, at feci hoc propter uos, non propter tuen dam meam authoritatem. Vestri potius ratio nem habeo in hac causa. Quare autem propter ipsos hoc fecerit, subiungens aperit. Ne occu pemur à Satana. Poterit retineri uulgata lectio, ne circumueniamur à Satana. Quanquam nō est præter rationem, quod Erasmus uertit, ne occupemur à Satana. Significat enim uerbum πλεονεκτεῖν superiores habere in re aliqua, atqi ita illam poslidere & occupare. Admonet ita-que, non agi hic priuati tantum hominis cau sam, sed & sibi & ecclesiæ communem. Ideo non dicit: Si quid cui condonaui, propter illū cōdonaui, ne occupetur à Satana, sed, si quid cui condonaui, propter uos condonaui, in cō spectu Christi, ne occupemur à Satana. Et sei psum includit, non dicens, ne occupemini à Satana, sed, ne occupemur à Satana, quo mi nus eos offendat.
units.tr: He answers: "It is true that I had already forgiven him, so far as I am concerned, in my heart and before Christ; but I did this for your sake, not to maintain my own authority. I am rather taking account of you in this matter." Why he did this for their sake he explains by adding: "lest we be taken advantage of by Satan." The reading of the Vulgate, "lest we be circumvented by Satan," could be retained. Yet what Erasmus translates, "lest we be overreached by Satan," is not unreasonable, for the verb πλεονεκτεῖν means to have the advantage over others in some matter, and so to get possession of it and seize it. He therefore reminds them that this is not a matter concerning only a private individual, but one that is common to himself and to the Church. Hence he does not say, "If I have forgiven anything to anyone, I forgave him for his sake, lest he be seized by Satan," but "If I have forgiven anything to anyone, I forgave it for your sake, in the sight of Christ, lest we be seized by Satan." And he includes himself, not saying "lest you be seized by Satan," but "lest we be seized by Satan," so that he may less offend them.

units.la: Illud, in conspectu Christi, uarie accipitur, quia varie accipi potest. Alius, in facie Christi, alius respectu Christi, alius coram Christo, alius in persona & uice Christi. Exi stimo hunc esse sensum: Si quid cui condonaui, condonaui in conspectu Christi, non in foro ecclesiæ. Vt au tem in ecclesiæ quoq; uestræ foro fiat hęc con donatio, peto ut & uos illi condonetis, & hoc facio propter uos quoq;, ne occupemur à Sata na. Dixerit quisquam. Ergo nisi condonassent pœnitenti peccatori Paulus & Corinthij, occu pati fuissent à Satana? Ipse quidé peccator de sperationé fuisset absorptus, uerū quomodo propterea Satan & Paulum & ecclesiam occu passet non uideo.
units.tr: The phrase "in the sight of Christ" is understood in various ways, because it can be understood in various ways: one takes it as "in the face of Christ," another as "with respect to Christ," another as "before Christ," another as "in the person and stead of Christ." I think this is the sense: "If I have forgiven anything to anyone, I have forgiven it in the sight of Christ, not in the court of the Church. But so that this forgiveness may also be made in the court of your church, I ask that you too forgive him; and I do this for your sake also, lest we be taken advantage of by Satan." Someone might object: "Then unless Paul and the Corinthians had forgiven the penitent sinner, would they have been seized by Satan?" The sinner himself would indeed have been swallowed up by despair, but I do not see how Satan would therefore have seized Paul and the Church.

units.la: Respondeo. Primum ea debet esse sympa thia fidelium in ecclesia Christi, ut uno pericli tante periclitari censeantur & alij. Hac ratio ne, ubi Satan occupat membrum unum eccle siæ, rectè ecclesiam occupare dicitur, quemad modum rectè corpus hominis uulneratum di cimus, ubi membrum illius aliquod est uulne ratum. Deinde, ubi nec pastor solicitus est de salute omnium, nec ipsæ oves mutuæ salutis, i mò ne suæ quæ libet propriæ rationem habet, an non timendū est, ne occupentur à falsis pa storibus & à lupis? Planè sic habet in ecclesia quoq;, in qua nec Apostolus de seruandis peri clitantibus aliqua cura afficitur, nec ipsi fide les de sua quiq; ac de fratrum sunt salute solici ti. Hic planè timendum est omnib; ne occupe tur à Satana. Obsecro, si timendū erat ecclesię Corinthiorū Apostolo adhuc superstite, à quo fuerat plantata, ne occuparetur à Satana, quid non timendum est reliquis omnibus ecclesijs, in quibus uel dormiunt pastores, uel pro libi dine sua dominantur?
units.tr: I answer: first, the sympathy of the faithful in the Church of Christ ought to be such that when one member is in danger, the others are considered to be in the same danger. For this reason, when Satan seizes one member of the Church, the Church is rightly said to be seized, just as we rightly say that a human body is wounded when one of its members is wounded. Next, where neither the minister is anxious about the salvation of all, nor the sheep themselves have regard for mutual salvation, or even for their own salvation, must we not fear that they will be seized by false ministers and by wolves? Clearly it is so in the Church as well, in which neither the Apostle is concerned with the preserving of those in danger, nor do the faithful each care for their own salvation and that of their brothers. Here everyone must clearly fear being seized by Satan. I ask you: if the Church of the Corinthians, which had been planted by the Apostle while he was still alive, had to fear being seized by Satan, what should not be feared by all the other churches, in which either the ministers are asleep or they rule according to their own pleasure?

units.la: NON enim cogitationes illius ignoramus, inquit.) Quare timeat, ne occupentur à Sata na, exponit hisce uerbis. Sensus est. Nō est fru stra, quod cauendum censeo, ne occupemur à Satana. Etenim clam nobis non est, quæ sint illius cogitationes. Græcè est νοήματα, quæ nō simpliciter cogitationes significat, sed potius consilia & ratiocinationes, quales esse solent astutorum & callidorum. Non dicit simpliciter, non enim ignoramus, quàm insidietur nobis Satan, sed: Non ignoramus quàm sint, & quæ, astuta illius consilia. Intelligebat Apostolus abundè, quo tenderent Apostoli Satanæ, imò Satan ipse in angelum lucis transformatus. Quod præsentem causam attinet, sub specie iustæ disciplinæ moliebatur perditionem non unius tantum peccatoris, sed totius quoque ecclesiæ. Et utinam episcopi & pastores ecclesiarum iam olim νοήματα Satanæ in angelum lucis transformati intellexissent, uel hodie saltem intelligerent.
units.tr: For I am not ignorant of his thoughts, he says. He explains by these words why he fears that we may be taken over by Satan. The sense is: it is not in vain that I think we should take care lest we be taken over by Satan. For his thoughts are not hidden from us. The Greek is νοήματα [noémata], which means not simply thoughts but rather plans and schemes, such as crafty and cunning men usually devise. He does not simply say, "we do not know how Satan lays snares for us," but, "we do not know how crafty his plans are and what they are." The Apostle understood very well what the aims of Satan's apostles were, indeed of Satan himself, transformed into an angel of light. As far as the present case is concerned, under the appearance of just discipline he was working for the ruin not only of one sinner but of the whole Church. And would that the bishops and ministers of the churches had long ago understood the νοήματα [noémata] of Satan, transformed into an angel of light, or would at least understand them today.

units.la: Cæterum cum uenissem Troadem in Euangelíü Christi, & ostium mihi esset apertum in domino, non habui relaxationem spiritui meo, eo quod non inuenissem Titum fratrem meum, uerùm ua ledicto illis, abij in Macedoniam.
units.tr: But when I came to Troas for the gospel of Christ, and a door was opened to me in the Lord, I had no rest for my spirit, because I had not found Titus my brother; but bidding them farewell, I went on into Macedonia.

units.la: Relicta aliquantisper causa peccatoris recôciliandi, meminit itineris sui Macedoniam uersus suscepti, de quo capite præcedenti dicere cœperat, ut per huius occasionem Titi quoq; mentionem faciat, quem Corinthum miserat. Cæterùm, inquit, cù uenissem Troadë. Troas ciuitas est Phrygiæ, olim Antigonia dicta, opposita Chersoneso. Et hinc transitus est in Europam. Addit in Euangelium Christi. Id est, propter Euangelium Christi ibi prædicandum. Licet iterin Macedoniâ instituerat, interim tamen in ea loca diuertit, in quibus occasionem prædicandi Euangelij inueniret. Est quidem ciuitas hæc in littore maris, & traiectum habes & portum, eratq; hanc ob causam commoda Paulo, cum ad iter quod instituerat, tum ad inueniendum Titum. Verum nô huius commoditatis sed Euangelij prædicandi potissimum gratia in illam se profectum fuisse dicit.
units.tr: Leaving aside for a while the matter of reconciling the sinner, he recalls the journey he had begun towards Macedonia, which he had started to speak of in the preceding chapter, so that on this occasion he may also mention Titus, whom he had sent to Corinth. "But," he says, "when I came to Troas." Troas is a city of Phrygia, formerly called Antigonia, opposite the Chersonese, and from there there is a crossing into Europe. He adds "for the gospel of Christ", that is, for the sake of preaching the gospel of Christ there. Although he had already founded churches in Macedonia, he nevertheless turned aside to those places where he might find an opportunity of preaching the gospel. This city lies on the shore of the sea, and has a crossing and a harbour, and for this reason it was convenient for Paul, both for the journey he had planned and for finding Titus. Yet he says that he went there not chiefly for the sake of this convenience but for the sake of preaching the gospel.

units.la: E T ostium, inquit, apertum mihi esset in domino.) Quid sit ostium apertum esse in domino, dictum est capite ultimo superioris epistolæ. Quod autem ostium Euangelio Christi in ea fuerit ciuitate apertum, uidere est Actorum uigesimo, ubi sic legimus. Hi cum præcessissent expectarunt nos Troade, nos uero abnauigauimus post dies azimorum à Philippis, & uenimus ad eos Troadem intra dies quinq;, ubi demorati sumus diebus septem. Vno autem die sabbatorum, cum conuenissent discipuli ad frangendum panem, Paulus differebat eis, profecturus postridie, &c. Hinc satis patet fuisse Troade discipulos, quos cum iret in Macedoniam Paulus domino lucrifecerat, quibus etiam, cum è Macedonia rediret & Iudæam peteret, in domino congregatis integram noctem disseruit, & adolescentem quendam ex illis nomine Eutychum è tertio cœnaculo delapsum ac mortuum, uitæ restituit.
units.tr: And a door, he says, was opened to me in the Lord. What it means for a door to be opened in the Lord was explained at the end of the last chapter of the earlier epistle. That a door was opened to the gospel of Christ in that city can be seen in Acts chapter 20, where we read as follows: "These, going before, waited for us at Troas; but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of unleavened bread, and came to them at Troas in five days, where we stayed seven days. And on the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached to them, intending to depart on the next day," and so on. From this it is quite plain that there were disciples at Troas whom Paul had won for the Lord when he went into Macedonia, and to whom, when he returned from Macedonia and was making for Judaea, he also spoke at length all night as they gathered in the Lord; and he restored to life a young man named Eutychus, who had fallen from the third storey and was dead.

units.la: N O N habui relaxationem, inquit, spiritui meo, eo quod non inuenissem Titum fratrem
units.tr: I had no rest, he says, for my spirit, because I had not found Titus my brother

units.la: meum.) Nisi retulisset hoc scire Corinthios, non scripsisset. Referebat autem plurimum. Miserat enim ad eos Titū, ut cognosceret per illum de statu ecclesiæ ipsorum. Et hunc speraverat se inuenturum Troade. Quo non inuento fatigabatur spiritus ipsius desyderio ad uentus illius, per quem se infrà capite septimo refocillatū fuisse scribit. Significat igitur, ufqueadeo sibi res ipsorum esse cordi, ut nulla sit spiritui suo refocillatio, nisi de illis audiat optata. Quare quod dicit: nô habui relaxationem, uel requiem, ἀνεσιν spiritui meo, eo quod non inuenissem Titum fratrem meum, non eo sensu dictum est, quo nonnulli exponunt: quasi non suffecerit duplici labori, prædicandi uidelicet ijs qui audire cupiebant, & resistendi hæreticis & infidelibus, cum esset solus, & Titum non inuenisset, cui unam laborum partem prædicandi uidelicet, imponere cupierit. Solū fuisse Troade, & si fuisset, solum non suffecit se laboribus, neutrū, meo iudicio, cum ratione dicitur. Puerilis admodum est hic sensus. Nec ratio esset, cur tale quid Corinthijs scribe ret Apostolus.
units.tr: I think he would not have written this unless he meant the Corinthians to know it, and it mattered a great deal. For he had sent Titus to them so that through him he might learn the state of their church. And he had hoped to find him at Troas. When he did not find him, his spirit was worn out by longing for his coming, through whom, as he writes later in chapter seven, he was refreshed. He means, therefore, that the affairs of the Corinthians were so dear to him that his spirit could find no refreshment unless he heard welcome news of them. So when he says, "I had no rest or relief (ἄνεσιν [anesin]) for my spirit, because I had not found Titus my brother," this is not to be taken in the sense that some explain it: as if it were not enough for him to bear a double labour, namely preaching to those who wished to hear and resisting heretics and unbelievers, since he was alone and had not found Titus, to whom he wished to hand over one part of the labour, namely the preaching. He was alone at Troas, and even if he had been alone, being alone was not, in my judgement, enough to tire him out; neither reading makes sense. This sense is quite childish, and there would be no reason for the Apostle to write such a thing to the Corinthians.

units.la: Cogitemus hic quàm iugis fuerit & assidua fatigatio spiritus Apostoli. Etenim si unius ecclesiæ tanta afficiebatur cura & solicitudine, ut relaxationem non inueniret spiritus ipsius, nisi optata de illa audiisset, quantum fuisse credendum est curarum cumulum, quibus propter reliquas, tam multas noctes ac dies tantū non enecabatur. Vt indefinentium persequutionum & afflictionum molestias taceam.
units.tr: Let us consider here how constant and unceasing was the weariness of the Apostle's spirit. For if he was so affected by the care and anxiety for a single church that his spirit found no relief unless he heard welcome news of it, how great a load of cares must be believed to have been upon him, by which, on top of the rest, he was almost killed day and night, not to mention the troubles of unending persecutions and afflictions.

units.la: Deinde hic quoq; uidemus fuisse illū humanis affectibus perinde atq; nos obnoxiū. Speyrabat, & affectabat, inuenturum se Titum, ubi Troadem uenisset. Sperabat aūt frustrà. Neq; enim iuuenit eum cum illo uenisset. Erat ergo spes hæc frustranea, qualis frequenter accidit in rebus humanis. Adhæc cum non inuenissset Titum Troade sicuti sperauerat, fatigabatur spiritu absq; ulla relaxatione. Et hoc humanū erat. Sic enim comparati sumus ut spe nostra frustrati turbemur & molestemur. Sunt hæc communia mortalibus. Illud tamen pium erat & Apostolicum, quod ista patiebatur ex solicitudine ecclesiarum Christi.
units.tr: Next we see here too that he was subject to human feelings just as we are. He hoped and expected to find Titus when he had come to Troas. But he hoped in vain: for he did not find him, since Titus had not come with him. This hope, then, was vain, as often happens in human affairs. Moreover, since he had not found Titus at Troas as he had hoped, his spirit was wearied without any relief. And this was human. For we are so made that when we are disappointed in our hope we are troubled and vexed. These things are common to mortals. Yet it was pious and apostolic that he suffered these things out of concern for the churches of Christ.

units.la: V E R V M ualedicto illis, abij in Macedoniam, inquit.) Supra cap. primo sic dicit: Et hac fiducia uolebam ad uos uenire prius, ut geminam gratiam haberetis, & per uos irem in Macedoniam. Hic dicit se, cum Titum non inuenisset Troade, adeoq; nulla esset spiritui suo relaxatio, abijsse in Macedoniam, significans ob id se minus uenisse Corinthum, quod ignoraret, quo in statu res ipsorum essent, propterea quod Titum Troade non inuenisset, ex quo se de illis cognitutum sperauerat.
units.tr: But bidding them farewell, he says, I went into Macedonia. Above, in the first chapter, he says this: "And in this confidence I wished to come to you first, so that you might have a double grace, and through you I might go on into Macedonia." Here he says that, since he had not found Titus at Troas, and therefore had no relief for his spirit, he went away into Macedonia, meaning that he had come less to Corinth for this reason: he did not know what state their affairs were in, because he had not found Titus at Troas, from whom he had hoped to learn about them.

units.la: Illud, ualedicto illis, Græcè est ἀποταξάμενΟ ἀυτοῖς. Erasmus uertit, dimisisillis. Vulgata habet: Valefaciens eis. Neutra uersio satisfacit메ti Apostoli, imò nec significationi ipsius uocis ἀποταξάμενΟ. Significat enim illa nô simpliciter citer uale dicere ac dimittere, sed magis ubi di scedendum ac ualedicendum est extrema dare mandata, & ordinare quę post discessum nostrū fieri uelimus, ut ἀπολύσεις recte uocetur Germanicè ein abscheid. Sic Paulus cū non inuento Tito Troadem relinquere & in Macedoniam abire uellet, ostium apertū in domino non neglexit, sed ijs qui credere coeperat, quae facerēt ac quomodo se, donec ad ipsos reuerteretur gererent, iam discessurus ordinauit ac praescripsit.
