Hoc significans, non simpliciter dicit: abij in Macedoniam, sed ὑποτάξαμην & αυτοῖς, id est, ubi illis constitui & ordinaui quae facerent, abij in Macedoniam. Quare nō est ut hic opero sam quæstione moucamus, quare Apostolus ostiū Euangelio Dei Troade apertū, propter absentiā Titi negligere uoluerit. Potiora agebat, & interim primordia recens iacta nō negligebat. Quare ad illa reuersus quod plantauerat diligenter rigauit. Amplitudinem curarū illius ingenij nostri angustia noncapit, quapropter neq; conuenit, ut de factis illius temere nobis iudicium sumamus.
units.tr: That phrase, "bidding them farewell", in Greek is ἀποταξάμενος αὐτοῖς [apotaxamenos autois]. Erasmus translates it "dismissing them", and the Vulgate has "saying farewell to them." Neither translation satisfies the Apostle's meaning, nor even the meaning of the word ἀποταξάμενος [apotaxamenos] itself. For that word signifies not simply to say farewell and dismiss, but rather, when one is about to depart, to give final instructions and to ordain what we wish to be done after our departure; so that the word ἀπολύσεις [apolyseis] is rightly rendered in German as "ein abscheid" (a farewell or parting order). So when Paul, not having found Titus, wished to leave Troas and go away into Macedonia, he did not neglect the door opened to him in the Lord, but, now about to leave, he laid down and prescribed for those who had begun to believe what they should do and how they should conduct themselves until he returned to them. Signifying this, he does not simply say, "I went away into Macedonia," but, having given them instructions and ordered what they should do, he went away into Macedonia. Therefore we need not raise here the laborious question why the Apostle, when the door of God's gospel was open at Troas, wished to neglect it because Titus was absent. He was engaged in more important work, and meanwhile he did not neglect the newly laid foundations. So, returning to them, he diligently watered what he had planted. The breadth of his mind's cares is beyond the narrowness of our wit, and therefore it is not fitting that we rashly pass judgement on his deeds.

units.la: Deo autem gratia qui semper triumphat per nos in Christo, & odorem noticię suę manifestat per nos in omni loco. Quoniā Christo bona fragrantia sumus Deo, in his qui saluī fiunt, & in his qui pereūt: his quidem odor mortis ad mortem, illis uero odor uitae ad uitam. Et ad haec quis idoneus? Non enim sumus ut plerique cauponantes sermonē Dei, sed uelut ex syncéritate, sed uelut ex Deo in conspectu Dei per Christum loquimur.
units.tr: But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ, and through us makes manifest the savour of his knowledge in every place. For we are to God the good savour of Christ, among those who are being saved and among those who perish: to the one an odour of death unto death, to the other an odour of life unto life. And who is sufficient for these things? For we are not, like many, peddlers of the word of God, but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God we speak in Christ.

units.la: Occasione eius quod dixit, & ostium mihi apertum esset in domino, rapitur in hanc doxologiam, qua & successum Apostolatus sui deprædicat, & nomine illius Deo gratias agit, tribuens illi omnem illius ut operationem ita & gloriam. Deo autem gratia, inquit, uox haec ex corde profecta, hominum est beneficia Dei agnoscētium, magnificantium, & cum gratiarum actione deprædicantium. Quid autē prædicat de Deo? Qui semper, inquit, triumphat per nos in Christo. In Graeco est τῷ πάντοτε θριαμβεύοντι ἡμᾶς, id est. Qui semper triūphat nos. Sic habet & uulgata additio. Verum quoniam ea lectio, incommoda est Latinis auribus, ideo legunt nonnulli, qui triumphare nos facit semper. Sanè uerosimile est Apostolū uerbo hoc Ebraico more in sensu hyphil esse usum, ut θριαμβεύω sit nō simpliciter triumphare sed facere ut triumphes. Qui uero cum Erasmo legūt: triumphat per nos, triumphantem constituūt non Apostolum sed Deum.
units.tr: Prompted by what he had just said, "and a door was opened to me in the Lord," he is carried into this doxology, in which he both proclaims the success of his apostleship and, in that name, gives thanks to God, ascribing to him all his work and all the glory of it. "But thanks be to God," he says. This voice comes from the heart of people who acknowledge God's benefits, magnify them, and proclaim them with thanksgiving. What does he proclaim about God? "Who always triumphs over us in Christ." The Greek is τῷ πάντοτε θριαμβεύοντι ἡμᾶς [τῷ πάντοτε θριαμβεύοντι ἡμᾶς], that is, "who always triumphs us," and the Vulgate addition reads the same. Since that reading is awkward to Latin ears, some read "who always makes us triumph." It is indeed likely that the Apostle used the verb in the Hebrew manner, in the hiphil sense, so that θριαμβεύω means not simply "to triumph" but "to cause to triumph." Those who read with Erasmus, "triumphs over us," make God, not the Apostle, the one who triumphs.

units.la: Quid est autem quod dicit, Ttriumphare? est uictoriā de hoste superato cū publica pompa, lætitia, & gloria referre. Simplicius est, ut hic intelligamus idem esse, quod, qui semper uictores nos reddit in Christo. Victoriae ac triumphi loco ducebat, quoties aliquos regno Satanae ereptos in castra Christi ducere dabatur. Et quoniam id vbiq; dabatur, quocunque uenisset, dicit se semper fieri triumphatorem in Christo.
units.tr: What does "to triumph" mean? It means to bring back a victory over a defeated enemy with public pomp, joy, and glory. It is simpler to understand here that the phrase means the same as "who always makes us victors in Christ." Whenever it was granted to him to lead some people snatched from the kingdom of Satan into the camp of Christ, he counted that as the place of victory and triumph. Since this was granted to him everywhere, wherever he came, he says that he is always made a triumphant one in Christ.

units.la: Mirabilis omnino triumphator, qui ut capite quarto superioris epistolae de seipse dicit, ipectaculum erat factus & mundo, & angelis, & hominibus, & ad id usque temporis eluricebat, sitiebat, nudus erat, colaphis cędebatur, incertis uagabatur sedibus, manibus proprijs operans laborabat, male audiebat, persequutione patiebatur, conuicijs afficiebatur, & uelut excrementum ac reiectamentum mundi quocunq; uenisset erat. Si hoc genus uitae triumphatori conuenit, sanè maximus erat triūphator. Verum quamuis afflictionum ista rum respectu omnium uidebatur esse miserrimus, & nusquam uincere sed vbique uinci, nihilo tamen minus nusquam uictus sed uictor ubiq; spolia auferebat hosti antiquo, animas uidelicet Christo credentium. Quare nō dicit: qui nos semper triumphare facit in mundo, sed, qui nos semper triumphare facit in Christo. Qui uictor discedebat in Christo, quasi uictus affligebatur in mundo. Hoc genus uictoriae Christianorum est, durans ad finem usque mundi, quo dum in mundo uidetur uinci, uincunt ipsi & Satanam & mundum. Vincunt enim, dum animas suas per omnis generis tribulationes virtute patientiae in fide Christi illibatas & inuictas seruant. Sic uincuntur tyranni occisores fidelium, & uincunt occisi. Tyrannus clamat, nega, nega. Cōfessor Christi uicissim, non nego, inquit, absit, sed Christianum me esse ad extremum usque halitum cōfiteor, & in extremo uictoriae articulo constitutus, Christum Seruatorem suum inuocat, illiquo spiritum suum commendat, quem tyrannus impius uictus & confusus blasphemat. Pugna est non de præsenti hac & momentanea uita, sed vtrum agnoscas & habeas dominum, Christum ne uel Satanam, ueritati ne Dei cum electis, uel mendacijs Satanae cum reprobis adhęreas, & uiuas ne ac saluēris in sempiternum cum Christo & sanctis omnibus, uel pereas in æternum cum diabolo & impijs omnibus. In hac pugna uincit, nō qui occidit, sed qui in ueritate ac fide Dei perstat inuictus, & uincitur non qui occiditur, sed qui quoniam non uincit, hoc est, quod uult non obtinet, inuictum & in fide domini sui permanentem occidit, atque ita non hilaris ē pugna sed iratus & confusus discedit, relicto in manu Domini quem secum in castra Satanae uelut in triumpho ducere proposuerat.
units.tr: A truly remarkable triumphant one! As he says of himself in the fourth chapter of the earlier letter, he was made a spectacle to the world, to the angels, and to men. Up to that time he was hungry and thirsty, naked, struck with fists, wandering without a fixed home, working with his own hands, reviled, suffering persecution, subjected to insults, and wherever he came he was treated like the filth and offscouring of the world. If this kind of life suits a triumphant one, then he was indeed the greatest triumphant one. Yet although in regard to these afflictions he seemed to be the most wretched of all, never conquering but everywhere conquered, nevertheless he was never defeated but everywhere a victor, and he carried off spoils from the ancient enemy, that is, the souls of those who believe in Christ. Therefore he does not say, "who makes us triumph in the world," but "who makes us always triumph in Christ." He departed a victor in Christ, though in the world he was afflicted as one defeated. This is the kind of victory of Christians, lasting until the end of the world: while in the world they seem to be conquered, they conquer both Satan and the world. For they conquer while they keep their souls, through every kind of tribulation, unharmed and unconquered by the power of patience in the faith of Christ. So tyrants who kill the faithful are conquered, and the slain conquer. The tyrant cries, "Deny, deny!" The confessor of Christ in turn replies, "I will not deny, far from it! I confess that I am a Christian to my last breath." Set at the final moment of victory, he calls upon Christ his Saviour and commends his spirit to him, while the impious tyrant, defeated and shamed, blasphemes. The struggle is not about this present and momentary life, but about whether you acknowledge and have the Lord, Christ or Satan; whether you cleave to the truth of God with the elect or to the lies of Satan with the reprobate; and whether you live and are saved forever with Christ and all the saints, or perish eternally with the devil and all the impious. In this struggle the one who wins is not the one who kills, but the one who stands unconquered in the truth and faith of God. And the one who is conquered is not the one who is killed. Rather, the one who does not conquer, that is, who does not obtain what he wants, kills one who remains unconquered and steadfast in the faith of his Lord. So he departs from the fight not cheerful but angry and shamed, having left in the hand of the Lord the one whom he had planned to lead with him into the camp of Satan as in a triumph.

units.la: ET odorem, inquit, noticiae suae manifestat per nos in omni loco.) Exponit quomodo triumphet ubique in Christo. Per sermonē videlicet scientiae & cognitionis Dei, hoc est, per Euangelium regni, quo scientia Dei, à mūdo abscōditam, manifestabat ubique. Loquitur
units.tr: "And he makes manifest," he says, "the fragrance of his knowledge through us in every place." He explains how he triumphs everywhere in Christ: namely, through the word of the knowledge and recognition of God, that is, through the gospel of the kingdom, by which he made known everywhere the knowledge of God hidden from the world.

units.la: B bulationes virtute ... (note marker B placed between columns on right page) tur autem de noticia Dei, non ea tantum qua unus cognoscitur ac solus uerus Deus, omnium conditor ac Seruator, quam sciētiam Dei uindicant sibi & Iudæi & Turci, & multi sapientes ex Gentibus haud ignorarūt, sed de ea qua mysterium ac ueritas Christi filij Dei cognoscitur, cuius scientia abscondita est à mundo, & ad cuius manifestationem singulari erat consilio Dei ab vtero matris segregatus, sicuti uidere est Gal.1. ubi dicit: qui segregauerat me ab vtero matris meæ, &uocauit per gratiam suam in hoc, ut reuelaret filium suum per me. Et Coloss.4. ubi petit à fidelibus, ut orent pro se ad Deum, ut aperiat sibi ostium sermonis, ad loquendum mysterium Christi, ut illud, sicuti oportet loquendo manifestet. Meminit huius & in ea quæ ad Titum est cap.1.
units.tr: He speaks of the knowledge of God, not only of that by which God is recognised as the one true God, the creator and Saviour of all, which the Jews and the Turks claim for themselves, and which many wise men among the Gentiles have not altogether been ignorant of. He speaks of that knowledge by which the mystery and truth of Christ the Son of God is known, whose knowledge has been hidden from the world, and for whose manifestation, by a singular plan of God, he was set apart from his mother's womb. This can be seen in Galatians 1, where he says, "who set me apart from my mother's womb, and called me by his grace, to reveal his Son in me." Also in Colossians 4, where he asks the faithful to pray to God for him, that he may open to him a door of speech to speak the mystery of Christ, so that he may make it manifest as he ought to speak. He mentions this also in the letter to Titus, chapter 1.

units.la: Quod autem non simpliciter dicit: & noticiam suam, sed, & odorem noticiæ suæ manifestat per nos, ad commendandum suaueolentiam cognitionis Dei facit, quæ in Christo est omnium iucundissima, & ad refocillandum abiectas conscientias efficacissima. Quod si quis uocem, odoris, positam esset censet ⁊p gustu: quasi dicat: & gustum, id est primum experimentum noticiæ suæ manifestat, per nos in omni loco, huic non admodum repugnarim. Nam ita habet. Quocunque ueniebat, gustum aliquem noticiæ Dei in Christo præbebat ijs, qui Euangelio Dei credere incipiebant, plenitudinem uero illius non ita. Magis tamen placet prior metaphoræ huius sensus, propter sequentia.
units.tr: Now, when he does not simply say "his knowledge" but "the fragrance of his knowledge," he is commending the sweet smell of the knowledge of God, which in Christ is the most delightful of all, and the most effective for reviving despairing consciences. If someone thinks that the word "fragrance" is used in place of "taste," as if he said "the taste, that is, the first experience of his knowledge, he makes manifest through us in every place," I would not greatly oppose this. For the sense is this: wherever he came, he offered to those who began to believe the gospel of God some taste of the knowledge of God in Christ, though not its fullness. Yet the former sense of this metaphor pleases me more, on account of what follows.

units.la: Illud, in omni loco, non est intelligendum aliter, quàm de locis in quibus prædicauit, ne cæterorum apostolorum labores irritos fuisse, Paulum uero solum toto terrarum orbe Christi ueritatem manifestasse dicamus. Quocunque ueniebat, ibi aliquem noticiæ Dei odorē prædicando, & si non apud multos, apud aliquos saltem tanquam primitias sequuturorū excitabat. Sic persequutiones illius quid erat aliud quam noticiæ Dei propagatio?
units.tr: "In every place" must be understood only of the places where he preached, lest we say that the labours of the other apostles were in vain and that Paul alone made the truth of Christ known throughout the whole world. Wherever he came, by preaching he gave some fragrance of the knowledge of God there, and if not among many, at least among some, as the first fruits of those who would follow. So what were his persecutions, if not the spreading of the knowledge of God?

units.la: QVONIAM Christi bona fragrātia sumus Deo, inquit, in his qui salui fiunt, & in his qui pereunt.) Explicat quod Deum odorem noticiæ suæ per se in omni loco manifestare dixit. Comparat Christum quem prædicabat in mundo unguento uel aromati suaueolentissimo, & se aromatario uel vnguētario, qui quouis loco existat, vnguenti quod secum gestat suaueolentiam spargit. Sic non simpliciter dicit: Quoniam bona fragrantia sumus, sed: Quoniam Christi bona fragrantia sumus, quib. uerbis bonam quam spargebat fragrantiam deputat Christo. Quatenus hunc & doctrina & uitæ conuersatione spirabat, hactenus illius bona erat fragrantia. Perinde ac si uoces Apostolos lucem Christi. Hoc dicens significat eos esse lucem, quatenus Christum lucem mundi euangelizando prædicant, & conscientias mortalium ueritate Dei illuminant.
units.tr: "For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God," he says, "among those who are saved and among those who perish." He explains what he said, that he makes the fragrance of his knowledge manifest everywhere through himself. He compares Christ, whom he preached in the world, to a most sweet-smelling ointment or spice, and himself to a perfumer or ointment-seller, who, wherever he stands, spreads the fragrance of the ointment he carries with him. So he does not simply say, "we are a good fragrance," but "we are the good fragrance of Christ," by which words he attributes to Christ the good fragrance that he spread. Insofar as Christ breathed out his fragrance through their teaching and manner of life, to that extent he was a good fragrance. It is as if he called the apostles the light of Christ. In saying this he means that they are light insofar as they preach Christ, the light of the world, in the gospel, and illuminate the consciences of mortals with the truth of God.

units.la: Quid est autem quod non simpliciter dicit? Quoniam Christi bona fragrantia sumus, sed addit Deo? Refert Apostolatum suum ad authorem Deum, qui per ipsum odorem noticiæ suæ manifestabat in omni loco. Pungit autem pseudapostolos, quibus Apostolatus ipsius nō bona Christi fragrantia authore Deo, sed pessimus quidam fœtor erat. Quasi dicat. Quantū uis Apostolatus nostER graueolentia quædam ac pessimus fœtor fit in naribus magistrorum ueltrorum, reipsa tamen scimus & experimur esse nos Deo authore suauem Christi odore. Quare subijcit dicens.
units.tr: But why does he not simply say, "we are the good fragrance of Christ," and instead add "to God"? He refers his apostleship to God as its author, who through this very fragrance of his knowledge makes himself manifest in every place. He also strikes at the false apostles, for whom his apostleship was not a good fragrance of Christ with God as its author, but a certain foul and wretched stench. As if he said: however much our apostleship seems to some heavy-smelling and a most wretched stench in the nostrils of your teachers, yet in fact we know and experience that we are, with God as its author, the sweet odour of Christ. Therefore he adds what follows.

units.la: In his qui salui fiunt, & in his qui pereunt, his quidem odor mortis ad mortem, illis uero odor uitæ ad uitam. Vbicunq; prædicabat Euangelium Christi, & bonam illius fragrantiā spirabat, diuersum euentum experiebatur. Alij enim probabāt & amplectebantur credētes. Hi erant electi & ad uitam æternā destinati. Alij reprobabant & auersabantur. Isti erat ex reprobis ac pereuntibus. Nihilominus suauis erat in se Christi odor, & authore Deo spargebatur per prædicationē Euangelij in toto mundo, licet alijs esset odor uitæ ad uitam, alijs uero odor mortis ad mortem. In illis operabatur propria uirtute uitam, in istis ipsorum uicio & culpa mortem.
units.tr: Among those who are saved and among those who perish, the fragrance of death is unto death for some, but the fragrance of life is unto life for others. Wherever he preached the Gospel of Christ and breathed out its good fragrance, he met with different outcomes. Some approved and embraced it by believing. These were the elect, destined to eternal life. Others rejected it and turned away. These belonged to the reprobate who perish. Yet the fragrance of Christ was sweet in itself, and by God's authority it was spread through the preaching of the Gospel throughout the whole world, though to some it was a fragrance of life unto life and to others a fragrance of death unto death. In the former it worked life by its own power, but in the latter it worked death through their own vice and fault.

units.la: Non debet autem mirum uideri, quod bonam Christi fragrantiam non solum in illis qui salui fiunt bonum odorem & odorem uitæ, sed & in reprobis qui pereunt mortis odorem uocat, cum Christus ut non ad iudicium ita nec ad mortem uenerit in hunc mundum. Etenim in rebus humanis quoque usitatissimum est, ut res eadem, in seipsa bona & utilis, aliis seruiat ad bonum, aliis ad malum, diuersumque & alienum sortiatur à natura sua in nonnullis effectum. Charitas omnia credens, omnia sperans, omnibus benefidens, omnibus mansueta & humana, omnibus benefaciens, utique bona est, & sibijpsi constans, similis, & eadem ubique. Et tamen ab alijs bene collocatur, ab alijs male, alios prouocat ad bonum, alijs cau-sa redditur contemptus & socordiæ. Medicina bona est in se, attamen pro diuersitate subiectorum redditur uel utilis uel noxia. Scientia, singulare donum Dei alios reddit utiles homines, alios uero inflatos & noxios. Opulentia quoque, & ipsa diuino munere constans, alios reddit beneficos, alios superbos. Solis splendor alios illuminat, alios occæcat. Bona fragrātia, sicut uidere est in apothecis aromatarijs & unguentarijs, alios recreat, alios reddit deiectos. Et Christus ipse alijs uenit in resurrectionem, alijs in ruinam. Ecquid aliud accideret Euangelio illius quàm hoc ipsum, ut alijs sit odor uitæ ad uitam, alijs odor mortis ad mortē, interim manens in seipso non diuersum sed idem, bonum uidelicet & natura sua diuinum & utile?
units.tr: Nor should it seem strange that he calls the good fragrance of Christ a fragrance of death, not only in those who are saved, where it is a good odour and a fragrance of life, but also in the reprobate who perish. Christ came into this world not for judgement, and so not for death either. Indeed, it is very common in human affairs that the same thing, good and useful in itself, serves some for good and others for harm, and in some cases produces an effect that is different and foreign to its nature. Charity, which believes all things, hopes all things, is kind to all, gentle and humane toward all, and does good to all, is certainly good, consistent with itself, the same and everywhere alike. Yet some receive it well and others badly; it stirs some to good, while for others it becomes an occasion of contempt and sloth. Medicine is good in itself, but according to the disposition of the patients it proves either useful or harmful. Knowledge, a singular gift of God, makes some men useful but others proud and hurtful. Wealth too, itself a gift of God's bounty, makes some generous and others arrogant. The brightness of the sun lights up some things and blinds others. A good fragrance, as can be seen in the perfumers' and ointment-sellers' shops, refreshes some and depresses others. And Christ himself came for the rising again of some and the fall of others. What else would happen to his Gospel than this very thing: that it is a fragrance of life unto life for some and a fragrance of death unto death for others, while remaining in itself not different but the same, namely good, divine by its nature and useful?

units.la: Non est autem præter rationem & scopum præfipræfixum quod diuersum hunc effectum Euâ{A} gelij Dei per metaphoram bonæ fragrantiæ exprimit. Si dixissent simpliciter: Quoniam Christi minister sum non solû in illis qui salui fiunt, sed & in alijs qui pereunt. Illis sum occasio uitæ ad uitam, illis occasio mortis ad mortem, admodum offendisset multos, Apostolatumque suum, quasi mortis minístrum, graui odio reddidisset obnoxium ac detestabilem. Prudenter itaque utitur metaphora bonæ fragrantiæ, cui nemo uicio dare potest, quod nô nullis nocet, cum natura sua iucunda sit & utilis. Sic non sua sed reproborum culpa fiebat, quod erat illis odor mortis ad mortē, qui per gratiam Dei electis erat odor uitæ ad uitam.
units.tr: Nor is it beyond reason or the purpose proposed that Paul expresses this differing effect of the Gospel of God by the metaphor of a good fragrance. If he had simply said: "Because I am a minister of Christ, not only to those who are saved but also to others who perish; to the former I am an occasion of life unto life, to the latter an occasion of death unto death," he would have offended many and made his apostleship, as a minister of death, hateful and detestable. So he wisely uses the metaphor of a good fragrance, to which no one can object that it harms some, since its nature is pleasant and useful. Thus it was not by its own fault but by the fault of the reprobate that what was a fragrance of death unto death to them was, through the grace of God, a fragrance of life unto life to the elect.

units.la: ET ad hæc, inquit, quis idoneus? Vel, quis sufficiens?) Quasi dicat. Conditio hæc Apostolatus mei, quę alijs est odor uitæ ad uitam, alijs odor mortis ad mortem, non est humanę facultatis. Nemo mortalium est, qui illam per se dispensét, uel dispensandæ sufficiat. Consequitur ergo dispensari eâ diuino consilio. Nec mihi imputandum est, quod bona Christi fragrantia odor uitæ ad uitam illis est qui saluantur, nec Euângelio Dei & mihi quod odor mortis ad mortem est ijs qui pereunt. Totum hoc diuina dispositione geritur.
units.tr: And to these things, he says, who is sufficient? Or, who is fit? As if he said: this office of mine, which is to some a fragrance of life unto life and to others a fragrance of death unto death, is not within human power. No mortal is able to dispense it by himself or to be sufficient to dispense it. It follows, then, that it is dispensed by the divine counsel. Nor is it to be imputed to me or to the Gospel of God that the good fragrance of Christ is a fragrance of life unto life to those who are saved, or that it is a fragrance of death unto death to those who perish. All this is carried out by divine disposition.

units.la: NON enim fumus, inquit, ut plerique, cauponantes sermonem Dei, sed uelut ex syncerita te, &c.) Sensus est. Nô enim est, ut me quisquam sermonem Dei negociando ac nundinâdo adulterare, atque ita in culpa esse dicat,{B} quod multis est odor mortis in mortem. Faciut hoc sane multi, quibus uerbum Dei abijt in quæstum, quorum Deus uenter est, & omnis prædicatio nihil aliud quàm turpis nundinatio & inanis gloriæ uenatio. Nos sermonem Dei prædicamus, ut est in se, purum & illibatum. Loquimur enim tanquam ex syncer itate, tanq̃ ex Deo, & coram Deo, in Christo.
units.tr: For we are not, he says, like many who peddle the word of God, but as of sincerity, etc. The sense is this: no one may say that I adulterate the word of God by trading in it and selling it at market, and so am at fault because to many it is a fragrance of death unto death. Many certainly do this, for whom the word of God has become a source of gain, whose god is their belly, and whose every preaching is nothing but shameful huckstering and a hunt for vainglory. We preach the word of God as it is in itself, pure and unadulterated. For we speak as of sincerity, as of God, and before God, in Christ.

units.la: Sic duo agit hisce uerbis. 1 Primum, perstringit pseudapostolos, quod sermonem Dei cauponando adulterent, hoc est, non syncere, non tanquam ex Deo, non coram Deo, sed ex suispsorum affectibus mundo sese non Deo accommodantes Christum prædicet. Et hos dicit esse nô paucos aliquos sed multos. Meo iudicio loquitur de ijs, qui ex circuncisione credentes circuibant, & non solum corde non integro sed peruerso Christum prædicabant, sed & impuritatem ex legis obseruationibus & traditionibus Euangelio immiscebant, trahentes post se discipulos, & totas domos subuertentes. Et forsan ex Gentibus quoque nônulli erant, qui sermoni Dei plurimum immiscerent ex fecibus philosophiæ ac mundanæ sapientiæ. Et hæc fiebant à multis, idque apostolis adhuc in uiuis exi stentibus, & conquerentibus. Tam scilicet est puræ doctrinæ uicia tio malum antiquum, malum subito inualescens, malum tenax & obstinatum, ut ne apo stolis quidem cedat. Et audent hodie iactare plerique, nunquam esse ecclesiam obnoxiam factam erroribus.
units.tr: So in these words he does two things. First, he censures the false apostles, who adulterate the word of God by peddling it, that is, who do not preach Christ sincerely, not as of God, not before God, but out of their own affections, accommodating themselves to the world and not to God. And he says these are not a few but many. In my judgement he speaks of those who came from circumcision, who went about believing, and who preached Christ not only with an unsound but with a perverse heart, mixing impurity from the observance of the law and from traditions into the Gospel, drawing disciples after themselves and overturning whole households. And perhaps some of the Gentiles too were among those who mixed a great deal into the word of God from the dregs of philosophy and worldly wisdom. And these things were done by many, and this while the apostles were still alive and complaining. So ancient, so suddenly strengthening, so tenacious and obstinate is the evil of corrupting pure doctrine, that it does not even yield to the apostles. And many today dare to boast that the Church has never been liable to errors.

units.la: 2 Alterum est, quod prædicationi ac doctrinæ suæ uindicat synceritatem, authoritatem, & conscientiam Dei in Christo. Sed loquimur, inquit, in Christo, tanquam ex synceritate, tanquam ex Deo, in conspectu Dei. In Christo loqui, est in nomine ac spiritu Christi loqui. Loqui tanquam ex synceritate, loqui est sicuti de cet eos, qui sine dolo syncere ac candide loquuntur. Loqui tanquam ex Deo, loqui est quemadmodum conuenit ei, qui authore Deo loquitur, quod ab illo in mandatis accepit. In conspectu Dei loqui, est sic loqui cum conscientia ac religione Dei, ac si loquendum fit in ipso conspectu Dei. Hæc uindicat doctrinæ suæ, non quærens inanem gloriam, sed resistens pseudapostolorum calumnijs, & consulens fidelibus præsertim infirmioribus.
units.tr: Second, he claims for his preaching and teaching sincerity, authority, and the conscience of God in Christ. But we speak, he says, in Christ, as of sincerity, as of God, in the sight of God. To speak in Christ is to speak in the name and spirit of Christ. To speak as of sincerity is to speak as those do who speak without guile, sincerely and candidly. To speak as of God is to speak as befits one who speaks by God's authority, as one who has received his commission from him. To speak in the sight of God is to speak with the awareness and reverence of God, as if one were speaking in God's very presence. He claims these things for his teaching, not seeking empty glory, but resisting the slanders of the false apostles and consulting the faithful, especially the weaker ones.

units.la: Habent igitur hic ministri Christi certas legitimi ministerij notas, numero quinque.
units.tr: Here, then, the ministers of Christ have certain marks of a lawful ministry, five in number.

units.la: 1 Prima est in eo quod dicit: loquimur. Excluduntur ergo muti ac personati episcopi nô loquentes sed dominantes.
units.tr: (1) The first lies in what he says: we speak. Thus dumb and masked bishops are excluded, who do not speak but lord it over others.

units.la: 2 Secundam exprimit cum dicit: in Christo. Excluditur omne genus doctrinæ, quod causam Christi non concernit.
units.tr: (2) He expresses the second when he says: in Christ. Every kind of teaching that does not concern the cause of Christ is excluded.

units.la: 3 Tertia in eo est quod dicit: tanquam ex synceritate. Græcè est ὡς ἐξ εἰλικρινείας. Exponunt autem εἰλικρινὴς, τὸ καθαρὸν καὶ ἀμιγὲς σπέρμα, id est, purū & nulla re alia mixtum. Ergo pure ac syncere prædicat Christum, qui nihil aliud doctrinæ Christi immiscet. Excluditur omnis mixtura, siue sit ex traditionibus humanis, siue ex obseruatijs legis, siue ex acumine humanæ sapientiæ. Quis autem omnia mixturæ genera recensuerit, quibus doctrinæ Christi puritas inde est ab apostolorum temporibus uiciata?
units.tr: (3) The third lies in what he says: as of sincerity. In Greek it is ὡς ἐξ εἰλικρινείας [hōs ex eilikrineias]. They explain eilikrinēs as the pure and unmixed seed [τὸ καθαρὸν καὶ ἀμιγὲς σπέρμα], that is, pure and mixed with nothing else. Therefore he preaches Christ purely and sincerely who mixes nothing else with the teaching of Christ. Every admixture is excluded, whether it comes from human traditions, from observances of the law, or from the subtlety of human wisdom. Who, then, could list all the kinds of admixture by which the purity of Christ's teaching has been corrupted from the times of the apostles onward?

units.la: 4 Quartam attingit dicens: sed tanquam ex Deo. Ergo requiritur, ut uerus Christi minister non humana sed diuina authoritate suffultus, loquatur in ecclesia Dei, quo tanquâ sermones & oracula Dei loquatur 1. Pet. 4.
units.tr: (4) He touches on the fourth when he says: but as of God. Therefore it is required that a true minister of Christ, supported not by human but by divine authority, speak in the Church of God, so that he speaks as the words and oracles of God, 1 Pet. 4.

units.la: 5 Quintâ exprimit dicés: in conspectu Dei. Aliud est loqui in conspectu ac respectu hominum, & aliud loqui in conspectu & respectu Dei ubique præsentis & omnia nostra uidentis & audientis. In conspectu hominum locum habet hypocrisis, fraus, & cauponatio, in conspectu Dei nequaquâ. Vbi hæ notæ desunt, non est ut Christi ministrum agnoscamus.
units.tr: 5. The fifth point he expresses by saying: "in the sight of God." To speak in the sight and presence of men is one thing; to speak in the sight and presence of God, who is present everywhere and sees and hears all that we do, is another. Hypocrisy, deceit and huckstering have their place in the sight of men, but by no means in the sight of God. Where these marks are absent, we ought not to acknowledge him as a minister of Christ.

units.la: ARGVMBNTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: VT pseudapostolorum nequiciam infringat, qui de lege Mosaica plurimum insolescebat, et syncritatem Euangelij Christi impurabant, Apostolatum suum tanquam Noui testamenti ministerium supra ministerium legis extollit.
units.tr: In order to break the wickedness of the false apostles, who boasted greatly of the Mosaic law and found fault with the sincerity of the gospel of Christ, he exalts his apostleship, as the ministry of the New Testament, above the ministry of the law.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: NCIPIMVS rursus nosipsos commendare? Num egemus, ut nonnulli, commendaticijs epistolis apud vos, aut à uobis commendaticijs? Epistola nostra uos estis, inscripta in cordibus nostris, quae intelligitur & legitur ab omnibus hominibus, dum declaratis, quod estis epistola Christi subministrata a nobis, inscripta non atramento, sed spiritu Dei uiuentis, non in tabulis lapideis, sed in tabulis cordis carneis.
units.tr: Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of commendation to you, or from you? You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts, which is known and read by all men, since you show that you are a letter of Christ, delivered through us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on the fleshy tablets of the heart.

units.la: Apostolatum suum supra legis Mosaicae ministerium euecturus, deque efficacia ipsius ac praestantia commemoraturus, mox initio calumniae pseudapostolorum occurrit, qui dubio procul dicturi erant: Ecce hominem gloriosulum & iactabundum, propriarumq; laudum ebuccinatorem. Incipit seipsum denuo commendare, quemadmodum in superiore epistola fecit. An non fatui sunt, qui seipsum commendanti credunt? Hoc illos dicturos praescienS. Incipimus rursus nosipsos commendare inquit. Quasi dicat, quemadmodu dicturi sunt uestri magistri, omnia nostra carpentes ac mali ciosè diuexantes. Hoc intelligens non simpliciter dicit: Non commendamus nosipsi. Neq; enim egemus commendatione apud uos, sed ut ueluti uerba pseudapostolorum exprimat: Incipimus inquit rursus nos ipsos commendare. Apostolatum suum tantopere non asseruisset, nisi improbissima pseudapostolorum malicia coegisset. Non quaerebat sibijpse nominis celebritatem in hoc mundo, id quod illi ipsi Magistri studiosissimè factitabant, sed fructum Apostolatus sui, salutem uidelicet credentium, quam Satan per suos ministros subuerte re moliebatur. Nec hoc agebat, ut scribedo sese Corinthijs commendaret, ac gratiam fauorem̄q; illorum ambiret, quibus integritatem suam & paternum affectum reipsa & euidentissimis argumentis comprobauerat.
units.tr: Paul, about to raise his apostleship above the ministry of the Mosaic law and to speak of its efficacy and excellence, at once at the outset meets the slander of the false apostles, who would undoubtedly say: "Look at this boastful, self-glorifying man, a trumpeter of his own praises. He begins to commend himself again, as he did in his earlier letter. Are not those fools who believe a man commending himself?" Foreseeing that they would say this, he writes: "We begin again to commend ourselves," as if to say: "This is what your teachers will say, carping at everything we do and tearing it to pieces with malice." Understanding this, he does not simply say, "We do not commend ourselves." Rather, in order to express the words of the false apostles, he says: "We begin, you say, to commend ourselves again." He would not have asserted his apostleship so strongly had the most shameless malice of the false apostles not compelled him. He was not seeking for himself fame in this world, which those very masters eagerly pursued, but the fruit of his apostleship, namely the salvation of believers, which Satan was trying to overthrow through his ministers. Nor was he doing this so that by writing he might commend himself to the Corinthians and seek their favour and goodwill, when he had already proved his integrity and fatherly affection to them by deeds and most evident arguments.

units.la: NVM egemus, inquit, ut nonnulli, commendaticijs epistolis apud uos, aut à uobis commendaticijs? In Graeco legitur, ει μη χρῃζομεν, quod sonat, si non egemus, uel, nisi egemus: quae lectio nō cōuenit sensui Apostoli, nisi exponas hoc pacto. Incipimus ne rursus nosipsos commendare? Quasi dicat: Minimè omnium. Nisi for-
units.tr: "Do we need," he says, "as some do, letters of commendation to you, or from you?" In the Greek it reads ει μη χρῃζομεν [ei mē chrēizomen], which means "if we do not need," or "unless we need." This reading does not agree with the Apostle's meaning unless you explain it thus: "Are we beginning to commend ourselves again?" as if to say, "By no means at all. Unless perhaps we need, as some do, letters of commendation to you."

units.la: san egemus, ut nonnulli, commendaticijs ad uos epistolis. Verum quoniam omnes interrogandi modo legunt. An egemus, ut nonnulli, commendaticijs epistolis ad uos: apparet legendum esse in Graeco: ει μη, per ita, non ει μη per epsilon iota, ut uerti possit, aut num egemus, ut nonnulli commendaticijs epistolis ad uos, aut à uobis commendaticijs? Utrouis modo legas nihil diuersi nascitur in sensu.
units.tr: But since all the interpreters read it as a question, "Do we need, as some do, letters of commendation to you?", it seems that in the Greek we should read ἦ μή [ē mē], spelled with the letter eta (ita), not with epsilon and iota, so that it can be rendered "or do we need, as some do, letters of commendation to you, or from you?" However you read it, nothing different arises in the sense.

units.la: Tria commendationum genera attingit, quae etiam procul à se reijcit. Primum est, quo se ipse Corinthijs commendare uidebatur. Hoc mox initio capitis refutat dicens: Incipimus ne rursus commendare nosipsos? Secundum, quo alios subordinare poterat, qui se Corinthijs commendarent. Tertium, quo ipsum Corinthij commendassent alijs. Utraque haec reijcit cum dicit: Num egemus commendaticijs epistolis apud uos? aut à uobis commendaticijs, hoc est, quibus me uos commendetis alijs?
units.tr: He touches on three kinds of commendation and rejects them all. The first is that by which he seemed to commend himself to the Corinthians. He refutes this at the very beginning of the chapter, saying: "Are we beginning to commend ourselves again?" The second is that by which he could have recommended others who would commend themselves to the Corinthians. The third is that by which the Corinthians might have commended him to others. He rejects both of these when he says: "Do we need letters of commendation to you, or from you?", that is, by which you would commend me to others?

units.la: Vide autem quomodo loquatur. Non dicit: Non quaerimus commendaticias epistolas ad uos, aut à uobis ad alios, sed: Num egemus commendaticijs, &c. Quasi dicat. Ad quid mihi opus est, ut uobis commender uel à meipso, uel ab alijs, uel à uobis ad alios? Nec dicit: Non egemus, sed, Num egemus? quod cum emphasi negationis dicitur. Quasi dicat. Iudicate uosipsi, an haec mea sit conditio, ut egeam literis commendaticijs, praesertim apud uos, quibus mea conuersatio omnium est notissima. Quis sanè mentis dicet patrem egere commendaticijs literis ad suos filios?
units.tr: Note, however, how he speaks. He does not say, "We do not seek letters of commendation to you, or from you to others," but, "Do we need letters of commendation?" and so on. As if to say: "What need have I to be commended to you either by myself, or by others, or by you to others?" And he does not say, "We do not need," but, "Do we need?", which is said with the emphasis of a negation, as if to say: "Judge for yourselves whether my condition is such that I need letters of commendation, especially among you, to whom my conduct is best known to all. Who, being in his right mind, would say that a father needs letters of commendation to his own sons?"

units.la: In eo autem quod non simpliciter dicit: Nū egemus commedacijs epistolis apud uos, sed addit, ut nonnulli: perstringit eos ex pseudapostolis, qui ut aliquid existimationis sortirentur in ecclesia, uenerant Corinthum cum epistolis commendaticijs, quas ut uerosimile est, à Hierosolymitanis nonnullis fratribus Mosaicae legis aemulatoribus ad hoc acceperant, ut Paulo negocium facesserent. Quasi dicat. Non mihi, sed magistris illis uestris opus est literis commendaticijs, quorum uobis syncericitas nec uitae est nec doctrinae perspecta.
units.tr: But in that he does not simply say, "Do we need letters of commendation to you?", but adds "as some do," he strikes at those among the false apostles who had come to Corinth with letters of commendation, in order to gain some standing in the Church. As is likely, they had obtained these from some brothers in Jerusalem, zealous for the Mosaic law, for the purpose of causing trouble for Paul. As if to say: "It is not I, but those teachers of yours, who need letters of commendation, whose integrity and whose life and teaching are not well known to you."

units.la: Hoc autem dicens, non damnat usum commendationis, qui perpetuò fuit in ecclesia & admodum utilis est, si rite ac legitime seruetur. Initio conuersionis suae opus erat & ipsi ut fratribus commendaretur, quod & factum est à Barnaba. Et ipse quam plurimos sibi, quàm Ecclesijs notiores in literis suis commendauit, praesertim eos, quos habebat cooperarios, quales erant Timotheus & Titus. Verum qui eam erat apud omnes ecclesias nactus authoritatem, ut merito pro commendatis haberentur, quos ipse commendasset, utique non egebat ut uel ipse se commendaret per literas, uel commendaretur ab aliis. Omnino argumentum habent literae commendaticiae hominis ignoti, illis saltem, quib. commendatur. Et quoniam periculum est, ne qui per aliorum A commendationem insinuatur ecclesijs, ubi admissus ac receptus fuerit, talis non inueniatur qualis fuerat commendatus, usi sunt maiores nostri magna cura & cautione in comendatione fratrũ. Hodie ut omnia agûtur leuiter ac temere, ita in dandis literis commédaticijs quoque plus est leuitatis quàm conuenit illis, quorum est testes esse ueritatis certæ & cognitæ, ne quo pacto usu ipsis ueniat, ut confusi dicát: non putaram.
units.tr: In saying this, however, he does not condemn the use of commendation, which has always existed in the Church and is very useful if it is kept properly and lawfully. At the beginning of his conversion, he too needed to be commended to the brothers, which was done by Barnabas. And he himself commended very many in his letters to the churches, especially those whom he had as fellow workers, such as Timothy and Titus. But because he had gained such authority among all the churches that those whom he commended were rightly regarded as recommended, he certainly did not need either to commend himself by letter or to be commended by others. Indeed, letters of commendation for an unknown man carry weight, at least with those to whom he is commended. And since there is a danger that someone may insinuate himself into the churches through the commendation of others, and once admitted and received there may not turn out to be what he was commended as, our forefathers used great care and caution in commending the brothers. Today, as everything is done lightly and rashly, so in giving letters of commendation there is also more levity than is fitting for those whose duty is to be witnesses of certain and known truth, lest it happen to them that, confused, they say: "I did not think so."

units.la: EPISTOLA nostra uos estis inquit.) Reddit rationem, quare non egeat epistolis commendaticijs. Quia uos, inquit, abunde mihi epistolis loco Epistolæ, qua commender. Quomodo erant autem Corinthij epistola Pauli? Neque quatenus erant homines, neque quatenus erant diuites, pauperes, sapientes, &c. sed quatenus erant Christiani, per uerbum Euangelij in Christo regenerati, hactenus erat illi epistola commendaticia. Per ipsius enim Apostolatum tales erat facti. Sic igitur uniuscuiusque episcopi opus in ecclesia Christi ipsius est Epistola, qua uel commédetur uel culpabilis declaretur. Ipsa uitæ conuersatio, ipsa Ecclesiæ uel ædificatio uel destructio certius de quolibet episcopo pronunciant, quàm ullæ literæ. Expressior scriptura est factorum quàm uerbo rum ac literarum.
units.tr: "You yourselves are our letter," he says. He gives the reason why he does not need letters of commendation: because you, he says, are enough for me in place of a letter by which I might be commended. How were the Corinthians a letter of Paul? Not insofar as they were human beings, nor insofar as they were rich, poor, wise, and so on, but insofar as they were Christians, regenerated in Christ through the word of the gospel; so far was he a commendatory letter to them. For through his apostleship they had become such. Thus the work of every bishop in the Church of Christ is a letter by which he is either commended or declared blameworthy. The conduct of his life and the building up or destruction of the Church declare more certainly about any bishop than any letters do. The writing of deeds is more expressive than that of words and letters.

units.la: INSCRIPTA, inquit, in cordibus nostris, &c.) Metaphorâ epistolæ prosequitur & expli cat. Declarandum enim erat qualib. esset char B tis uel tabulis, quali atramento, & à quo inscripta, deinde à quo subministrata, & à quibus, & quomodo legeretur & intelligeretur. Hæc explicaturus dicit: Inscripta in cordibus nostris. Quod in Graeco est, ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν, id est, in cordib. nostris, manifestũ habet errorem, in una litera hypsilon admissum, dum pro illa po sita est, ita. Legêdũ enim est, ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν. Scio Chrysostomũ quoq; cum alijs legere & exponere, in cordibus nostris, & alios referre ad eos qui cũ Paulo erant, alios uerò tâ ad Corinthios quàm ad Paulum. Verùm refipsa clarior est, quàm ut sit dubitandũ, de quorũ cordibus loquatur Apostolus, præsertim si sequetia consyderentur.
units.tr: "Written," he says, "on our hearts," and so on. He carries on and explains the metaphor of the letter. For it had to be declared what kind of writing material or tablets, what kind of ink, and by whom it was written, then by whom it was delivered, and to whom, and how it was read and understood. Intending to explain these things, he says: "Written on our hearts." What is in the Greek, ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν [en tais kardiais hymōn], that is, "on our hearts," clearly contains an error, a letter upsilon having been admitted in place of one of the other letters, so that it reads ὑμῶν [hymōn], "your," instead of ἡμῶν [hēmōn], "our." For it should be read ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν, "on your hearts." I know that Chrysostom also reads and explains it, with others, as "on our hearts," and refers some of them to those who were with Paul, and others both to the Corinthians and to Paul. But the thing itself is clearer than that there should be any doubt about whose hearts the Apostle is speaking of, especially if the following words are considered.

units.la: INSCRIPTA, inquit, in cordibus uestris.) Per epistolam intelligit Christianam fidem, mentem, ac pietatem. Hæc erat inscripta in ipsorũ cordibus, ueluti tabulis, & comendabat opus Pauli tanquam Apostoli ipsorũ, per quê Christiani facti fuerant. Quod in Graeco est ἐγγεγραμμένη, id est, inscripta, nonnullis idem est, quod, quæ circumfertur, quasi fit περιφερομένη. Video multis nocere, quod non satis inhæret apostoli uerbis. Quis non uidet aliud esse inscribi literas, & aliud circumferri?
units.tr: "Written," he says, "on your hearts." By the letter he understands the Christian faith, mind, and piety. This was written on their very hearts, as on tablets, and it commended the work of Paul as their apostle, through whom they had become Christians. What is in the Greek, ἐγγεγραμμένη [engegrammenē], that is, "written," is to some the same as "which is carried about," as if it were περιφερομένη [periphereomenē]. I see that it harms many that they do not adhere closely enough to the Apostle's words. Who does not see that to be written upon is one thing, and to be carried about is another?

units.la: QVÆ intelligitur, inqt, & legitur ab omnibus hominib⁹.) Manet in forma metaphoræ. Epistolæ, nisi legatur & intelligatur, nullus est ulus. Quare & hoc explicat. Prius autem est le gi, deinde intelligi, quę leguntur. Ordinê hunc nó curat apostolica gratuitas, cum notus sit omnibus. Quanquam sunt, qui legêdum putât, quæ cognoscitur & agnoscitur. Illi tamen ipsi receptam lectionem retinent.
units.tr: "Known and read by all men," he says. This remains in the form of a metaphor. A letter is of no use unless it is read and understood, and so he explains this as well. Reading, however, comes first, and understanding follows what is read. The apostolic freedom does not concern itself with this order, since it is familiar to everyone. Some think the word should be "known and acknowledged" instead of "read," but even they keep the accepted reading.

units.la: Quoniam genus epistolę, de quo scribit spirituale erat, ne quis nec legi nec intelligi possé dicat, asserit utrumq; dicés, quę & intelligitur & legitur. Rursus ne dicat quis, legitur quidem & intelligitur, sed à quibus? subiungit ab omnibus hominibus. Nô est igitur epistola hæc illegibilis, nec sic est perplexa, ut non possit à quolibet intelligi, cum talis sit, ut & legatur & intelligatur, hoc est, legi & intelligi potest ab omnibus hominibus. Significat igitur loqui se non de imaginaria aliqua epistola, quá nemo legere & intelligere potest, sed de tali, quam legant & intelligant omnes homines, eamq; ob causam non habeat opus alia, qua commédetur cuiquam.
units.tr: Since the kind of letter he is writing about is spiritual, lest anyone say that it can be neither read nor understood, he asserts both, saying that it is both understood and read. Again, lest someone say that it is indeed read and understood, but by whom? he adds: by all men. This letter, then, is not unreadable, nor is it so obscure that it cannot be understood by anyone. It is of such a kind that it is both read and understood, that is, it can be read and understood by all men. He therefore means that he is not speaking of some imaginary letter that no one can read or understand, but of one that all men can read and understand, and for this reason it needs no other letter to commend it to anyone.

units.la: DVM declaratis quod estis epistola Christi, inquit, subministrata à nobis. ) Exponit quomodo, ut epistolę ipsius legantur & intelligantur ab omnibus hominibus. Non dicit, dum estis epistola Christi, sed, dum declaratis quod estis epistola Christi. Hoc est, dum uos & fidei professione & uitæ conuersatione Christianos esse in omnium oculis declaratis. Hic non modo interna fides cordis, sed & uniuersa uitæ conuersatio, & manifesta religionis professio, Christiana prædicatur ab Apostolo, & epistola Christi uocatur, quæ legatur & intelligatur ab omnibus non fidelibus tantum, sed & quibusuis alijs hominibus. Sic est cõparata Christi epistola. Scripta est literis non imaginarijs & inuisibilibus, sed admodũ expressis & spectabilibus, sic ut legi & intelligi possit ab omnibus. At hodie inuenias Christianos, qui satis esse censeât, si Christiani sint in corde, sicut scriptura ipsorum abscondita sit à lectione & intelligentia cæterorum hominum, soliq; Deo cognita. Verùm Paulus aliter de epistola Christi scribit. Non dicit: quæ legitur & intelligitur à Deo, sed, ab omnibus hominibus: neque dicit, dum fidem habetis in Christum, sed, dum declaratis quod estis epistola Christi. Declaranda est hæc epistola Christi, non abscondenda, lux enim est, non tenebræ.
units.tr: "WHILE you declare that you are the letter of Christ," he says, "ministered by us." He explains how the letter is to be read and understood by all men. He does not say "while you are the letter of Christ," but "while you declare that you are the letter of Christ." That is, while you show before everyone's eyes that you are Christians, both by your profession of faith and by the conduct of your life. Here the apostle proclaims as Christian not only the inward faith of the heart but also the whole conduct of life and the open profession of religion, and he calls it the letter of Christ, which is to be read and understood not only by believers but by all other men as well. Such is the letter of Christ as it has been composed. It is written not with imaginary and invisible letters, but with very plain and visible ones, so that it can be read and understood by everyone. Yet today you will find Christians who think it enough if they are Christians in the heart, as though their writing were hidden from the reading and understanding of other men and known to God alone. But Paul writes otherwise about the letter of Christ. He does not say: which is read and understood by God, but by all men; nor does he say: while you have faith in Christ, but: while you declare that you are the letter of Christ. This letter of Christ must be declared, not hidden, for it is light, not darkness.

units.la: SVBMINISTRATA à nobis inquit.) Verba hæc incommodè diuiduntur ad hunc modum: quod estis epistola Christi, subministrata, à nobis inscripta. Verùm epistolam hanc Christi non simpliciter subministratam, sed à se subministratam dicit. Quare sic est legendum: dum declaratis, quod estis epistola Christi subministrata à nobis, inscripta non atramento, sed spiritu Dei uiuentis. Et Augustinus legit, per nos subministrata in libro de spiritu & litera. Dixit eos esse suam epistolam, & mox subiungit, dum declaratis, quod estis epistola Christi. Si Christi erant epistola, quomodo suâ esse dixit. Hactenus uidelicet, qd ipse illá tanquá Christi Apost. p Euágelij pdicatione subministrauerat. Erat hæc epistola Christi, tanq; ipsius Dni, erat Pauli tanq; ministri & apostoli, q ea subministrauerat. Constat ergo hæc epistola uoluntate & authoritate Christi, & submi-nistratione Apostoli, & propter illam Christi, propter hanc Apostoli est epistola. Sic cauet Apostolus, ne nimium sibijpse tribuere uideatur, vbi dicit: Epistola nostra uos estis, quare explicationem hanc subijcit, qua domino promissis ius assignat ecclesiæ, sibi uero submi-nistrationem. Hodie dominium sibi uindicat in ecclesias Christi, qui ne submi-nistrationem quidem illarum uindicare sibi possunt.
units.tr: "MINISTERED by us," he says. These words are wrongly divided in this way: "which you are, the letter of Christ, ministered, written by us." But he says that this letter of Christ was ministered not simply, but ministered by himself. So it must be read thus: "while you declare that you are the letter of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God." Augustine also reads "ministered through us," in his book On the Spirit and the Letter. He called them his letter, and immediately adds: "while you declare that you are the letter of Christ." If they were the letter of Christ, how did he call them his own? Clearly, so far as he had ministered it as the apostle of Christ through the preaching of the gospel. This letter was Christ's, as of the Lord himself, and it was Paul's, as of the minister and apostle who had ministered it. The letter is therefore established by the will and authority of Christ and by the ministry of the apostle, and it is Christ's on account of Christ and the apostle's on account of the apostle. The apostle is careful in this way, lest he seem to attribute too much to himself, when he says: "You are our letter." So he adds this explanation, by which he assigns ownership of the promises to the Church under the Lord, and the ministry to himself. Today men claim dominion for themselves over the churches of Christ, when they cannot even claim for themselves the ministry of them.

units.la: INSCRIPTA, inquit, non atramento, sed spiritu Dei uiuentis.) Discriminat inter epistolas pseudapostolorum, quibus commendari se Ecclesijs curabant & hanc suam, de Apostolatu suo testificantem. Epistolæ, inquit, Magistrorum uestrorum, quibus se admodum commendari putant, scribuntur atramento, literis mortuis, & scriptura humana. Has nacti, magni sibijpsis uidentur esse apostoli. At hęc mea epistola, qua meus commendatur Apostolatus, scripta est non atramento, non literis mortuis, non scriptura humana, sed spiritu Dei uiuentis. Estis igitur mihi non mortua sed uiua epistola, literis constans spiritualibus adeoq; & uiuis, non humana sed diuina, spiritum non hominis sed Dei uiuentis scripta, cuius opera non sunt mortua sed uiua.
units.tr: "WRITTEN," he says, "not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God." He distinguishes between the letters of the false apostles, by which they took care to commend themselves to the churches, and his own letter, which bears witness to his apostleship. "The letters of your teachers," he says, "by which they think they are greatly commended, are written with ink, with dead letters and with human writing. Having these, they seem to themselves to be great apostles. But this letter of mine, by which my apostleship is commended, is written not with ink, not with dead letters, not with human writing, but with the Spirit of the living God. You are therefore to me a letter not dead but living, consisting of spiritual letters, and so living, not human but divine, written with the Spirit not of man but of the living God, whose works are not dead but living."

units.la: Loquitur autem de spiritu Christi, quē Corinthij acceperant credentes, quotquot erant ex electis. Horum respectu uocat eos in communi epistolâ Christi, spiritu Dei uiuentis scriptam. Nolim tamen hic excludere charismata spiritus, quibus ea ecclesia, quemadmodum & aliæ potita fuerat, de quibus in superiori epistola mentionem fecit cap. 14. Nam & per illa, tanquam per uiuas spiritus Christi literas, declarabatur, esse ecclesiam illam epistolam Christi, spiritu Dei uiuentis scriptam, & per Apostolatum Pauli subministratam.
units.tr: He speaks, however, of the Spirit of Christ, whom the Corinthians received when they believed, all who were among the elect. With respect to these he calls them, in the common letter of Christ, written by the Spirit of the living God. Yet I would not wish here to exclude the gifts of the Spirit, which that church, like others, possessed, and of which he made mention in the earlier letter, chapter 14. For through these, as through living letters of the Spirit of Christ, it was made clear that that church was a letter of Christ, written by the Spirit of the living God and ministered through the apostleship of Paul.

units.la: NON in tabulis lapideis, inquit, sed in tabulis cordis carneis.) Incipit collimare ad discrimen Veteris ac Noui testamenti, quo Apostolatum suum cōtra pseudapostolos supra Mosaicæ legis ministerium extollat. Lex Mosis, qua parte erat optima, inscripta fuerat tabulis lapideis. At Euangelium Christi inscribitur non tabulis lapideis, sed cordibus, quæ tabulę sunt carneæ. Carneas uocat, ad differentiam lapidearum. Perstringit igitur pseudapostolos eti am hactenus, quatenus ministerium Mosaicæ legis tanti faciebant, ut ministerio Euangelij Christi opponendum esse censerent. Quasi dicat, uestri magistri legis æmulatores uideri uolūt, & huius nomine inflatur. Sic cęci sunt, ut non uideant uos uiuam esse epistolam, spiritu Dei uiuentis cordibus uestris multo efficacius inscriptam, quàm olim legem Mosis tabulis lapideis insculptam, atque ita impleri illud prophetæ. Quoniam hoc est fœdus quod feriam cum domo Israel: post dies istos, dicit Dominus, dabo legem meam in medio ipsorum, & super cor ipsorum inscribam eam, & ero ipsis in Deum, & ipsi erunt mihi in populum.
units.tr: "NOT on tablets of stone," he says, "but on tablets of flesh in the heart." He begins to aim at the difference between the Old and New Testaments, by which he exalts his apostleship against the false apostles above the ministry of the Mosaic law. The law of Moses, in its best part, was written on tablets of stone. But the gospel of Christ is written not on tablets of stone but on hearts, which are tablets of flesh. He calls them fleshly, to distinguish them from stony ones. He therefore also strikes at the false apostles, insofar as they valued the ministry of the Mosaic law so highly that they thought it must be set against the ministry of the gospel of Christ. As if he were saying: your teachers wish to seem to be emulators of the law, and they are puffed up in its name. They are so blind that they do not see that you are a living letter, written in your hearts by the Spirit of the living God far more effectively than the law of Moses was once engraved on tablets of stone, and thus that the saying of the prophet is fulfilled: "For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel: after those days, says the Lord, I will put my law in the midst of them, and I will write it upon their heart, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people."

units.la: Sic per collationem lapidearum ac carnearum tabularum tam ingens docet esse discrimen inter suum Apostolatum & doctrinam pseudapostolorum, quàm diuinius & præstantius est legem Dei inscribi cordibus hominum, quàm tabulis lapidum. Nec est ut dicat quisquam, multa uana cordibus hominum posse inscribi, ideoque non esse tanti momenti quod illis inscribitur noua aliqua doctrina, quales multæ in hoc mundo cordibus humanis insinuantur. Non loquitur de eo tantum, quod doctrinam suam cordibus Corinthiorum inscriperat, sed quod scriptura hæc constabat spiritu Dei uiuentis. Sanè multum refert non modo quid, sed & quomodo cordibus nostris inscribatur. Si humanæ tantum persuasionis calamo etiam id quod uerum est inscribitur, delebilis est & euanida scriptura, id quod nostra quoque ætate quotidiana docet experientia. Si uero literatura spiritus Dei uiuentis cordibus nostris impressa fuerit, id demum firmam, efficacem, & uiuam reddit scripturam, quæ legi & intelligi possit ab omnibus, deleri uero à nemine.
units.tr: Thus, by comparing the tablets of stone with the tablets of flesh, he teaches that there is as great a difference between his apostleship and the teaching of the false apostles as there is between the law of God being written on human hearts and its being written on tablets of stone, which is far more divine and excellent. Nor can anyone say that many empty things may be written on human hearts, and that therefore what is written on them, some new doctrine, is of no great importance, such as the many doctrines of this world that are insinuated into human hearts. He is not speaking only of the fact that he had written his teaching on the hearts of the Corinthians, but that this writing consisted of the Spirit of the living God. Indeed, it matters much not only what but also how a thing is written on our hearts. If what is true is written only with the pen of human persuasion, the writing is erasable and fades away, as our own age also teaches through daily experience. But if the writing of the Spirit of the living God has been impressed upon our hearts, it makes the writing firm, effective and living, something that can be read and understood by all, and erased by no one.

units.la: Quod autem non simpliciter dicit: sed in tabulis cordis, sed addit, carneis, respicit ad ea quæ Ezech. 11. & 36 de Noui testamenti gratia prædicta leguntur ad hunc modum. Et dabo uobis cor nouum, & spiritum nouum ponam in medio uestri, & auferam cor lapideum de carne uestra, & dabo uobis cor carneum, & spiritum meum ponam in medio uestri, & faciam ut in præceptis meis ambuletis, &c. Erant & sunt hodie quoq; corda gentis huius non carnea sed lapidea, hoc est, dura & obstinata, cœlestis doctrinæ haudquaquam capacia. Est igitur & hoc cū primis opus spiritus Dei, ut tollat corda lapidea, & substituat carnea, gratiæ Noui testamenti capacia. His itaque uocibus sic prædicat Noui testamenti prærogatiuam in Corinthijs declaratam, ut simul perstringat & inueteratam Iudaicæ gentis obstinationem ac duriciem, & Mosaicæ legis infirmitatem, quæ non potuerit ex lapideis cordibus corda facere carnea, sensum ad capiendam uitæ doctrinam habentia.
units.tr: Now, when he does not simply say "on tablets of the heart," but adds "fleshly," he refers to what is read in Ezekiel 11 and 36 about the grace of the New Testament, which is foretold in this way: "And I will give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit in the midst of you, and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh, and I will put my spirit in the midst of you, and I will cause you to walk in my precepts," and so on. The hearts of this people were, and today still are, not fleshly but stony, that is, hard and obstinate, in no way capable of heavenly teaching. Therefore it is above all the work of the Spirit of God to take away stony hearts and to substitute fleshly ones, capable of the grace of the New Testament. By these words, then, he so proclaims the prerogative of the New Testament, as it has been shown among the Corinthians, that at the same time he strikes at the long-standing obstinacy and hardness of the Jewish nation, and at the weakness of the Mosaic law, which could not make fleshly hearts out of stony ones, hearts having the sense to receive the doctrine of life.

units.la: Fiducia autem huiusmodi habemus per Christum erga Deum, non quod idonei simus ex nobis ipsis cogitare quicquam, tanquam ex nobis ipsis, sed si ad aliquid idonei sumus, id ex Deo est, qui & idoneos nos fecit ministros Noui testamenti, non literæ sed spiritus. Nam litera occidit, spiritus autem uiuificat.
units.tr: Such confidence we have through Christ toward God: not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves, but our sufficiency is of God, who also made us sufficient ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

units.la: Coepit magnificè de Apostolatu suo loqui, dum per se Deum odorem noticiæ suæ manifestafestare in omni loco, seq; Deo bonam Christi fragrantiâ, & Corinthios epistolam suam non atramēto, sed spiritu Dei uiuentis cordibus i-psorū inscripta esse dixit. Ideo quod supra di-xit. Et adhæc quis idoneus? repetens amplifi-cat, ne quid horum suis ipsius uiribus tribue-re uideatur. Sic dicit: fiduciam autem huiuf-modi habemus per Christum ad Deum, non qd̄ idoneī simus ex nobis ipsis cogitare quic-quam tanquam ex nobis, sed si ad aliquid ido-neī sumus id ex Deo est, &c. Quasi dicat, Pote-ro uideri confidentius loqui & plura mihi tri-buere quàm conueniat, uerùm quę loquimur, bona cum fiducia loquimur, quam non ex no-bis sed per Christum habemus ad Deum. In-gens nobis est & efficax fiducia erga Deum. Hanc autem gignit in nobis spiritus Christi, & certa experientia, qua Deum patrem causæ filij sui in omnibus efficaciter adesse experi-mur. Huiusmodi fiduciam Apostoli, tam fideli ter erga Christū affecti, in opere illius tam dili genter & indesinenter pergentis, tam multa p nomine illius patientis, tamq; ardenter ad ser uandum quosuis noctes ac dies anhelatis, qs dubitat in conspectu Dei maximi fuisse mo-menti propter Christum, sic ut impossibile fue-rit, posse fieri irritam & inefficacem?
units.tr: He began to speak magnificently of his apostleship, since through him God makes manifest the savour of his knowledge in every place, and he is to God the good fragrance of Christ; and he said that the Corinthians were his letter, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, on their hearts. Therefore, what he said above, "And who is sufficient for these things?", he repeats and amplifies, lest he seem to attribute any of these things to his own powers. He speaks thus: "Such confidence we have through Christ toward God, not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves, but our sufficiency is of God," and so on. As if he were saying: I may seem to speak too confidently and to ascribe more to myself than is fitting; but what we say, we say with good confidence, which we have toward God not from ourselves but through Christ. Our confidence toward God is great and effective. Now this confidence is produced in us by the Spirit of Christ and by sure experience, by which we learn that God the Father is effectively present in all things for the cause of his Son. Who can doubt that such confidence, in the apostles who were so faithfully disposed toward Christ, so diligently and unceasingly pressing on in his work, who suffered so much in his name and so eagerly strove to save whomever they could night and day, was of the greatest moment in the sight of the most high God on account of Christ, so that it would be impossible for it to be made void and ineffective?

units.la: NON quod idonei simus, inquit, ex nobis ipsis cogitare quicquâ, tanq ex nobis ipsis.) Hisce uerbis disertè negat sibi facultatem esse de suo, non modo operandi aliquid eorū quæ memorauit, sed ne cogitandi quidem. Simul etiam reijcit à se fiduciam carnis, quæ & ipsa multa sibi ipsi de Deo pollicetur, ubi se instru-ctam ad ea perficienda ac consequenda putat, quæ affectat. Ne de hac loqui uideatur, cum se fiduciam huiusmodi erga Deum habere dicit, non contentus eo quod dixit, per Christum, subijcit disertè omnimodam propriarum uiri-um abnegationem dicens: non quod idonei simus ex nobis ipsis cogitare quicquam tan-quam ex nobis ipsis: quasi dicat, fiduciam hu-iusmodi erga Deum nō ex eo habemus, quod existimemus nos instructos &idoneos esse ex nobis ipsis, ad cogitandum ea de quibus lo-quimur.
units.tr: "Not that we are sufficient," he says, "to think anything as of ourselves." In these words he plainly denies that he has any ability of his own, not only to perform any of the things he has mentioned, but even to think them. At the same time he also rejects from himself the confidence of the flesh, which likewise promises many things to itself from God, when it thinks itself equipped to accomplish and obtain what it desires. Lest he seem to speak of this, when he says that he has such confidence toward God, not content with having said "through Christ," he plainly adds a complete renunciation of his own powers, saying: "not that we are sufficient to think anything as of ourselves"; as if he were saying: we have this confidence toward God not because we think ourselves equipped and sufficient in ourselves to think the things we speak of.

units.la: SED si aliquid, inquit, idonei sumus, id ex Deo est.) Hoc dicens, omnē facultatem qua i-doneus erat ad faciendū ea de quibus scribit, Deo fert acceptam. Non dicit: sed quod ad tā magna & multa, sed, si ad aliquid idonei sum?. Quasi dicat, quantumuis minutum, id ex Deo est, non ex nobis. Quid suis ipsiusuiribus relin-quit, unde possit gloriari, qui disertè dicit: si a-liquid possumus, non est ex nobis sed ex Deo? Nihil prorsus.
units.tr: "But if we are sufficient for anything," he says, "that is of God." In saying this, he attributes to God every ability by which he was fit to do the things about which he writes. He does not say, "but our sufficiency is for such great and many things," but "if we are sufficient for anything." As if he were saying: however small it is, it is of God, not of us. What does he leave to his own powers from which he might glory, who plainly says: if we are able for anything, it is not of us but of God? Nothing at all.

units.la: ID ex Deo est, inquit.) Dicet aliquis. Etiam uires nostrae quas naturaliter habemus, non sunt aliunde quàm ex Deo. Respondeo, uerū est, at ut non loquitur de rebus humanis, natu-ralib. & usitatis, sed de efficacia ministerij sui, ita ex Deo esse hoc loco, non idem esse intelli-git, quod simpliciter esse ex Deo conditore &
units.tr: "That is of God," he says. Someone will say: even the powers we have by nature are not from anywhere but God. I answer: this is true; but he is not speaking of human, natural and ordinary matters, but of the efficacy of his ministry; and he does not mean by "being of God" in this place what it would simply mean to be of God as Creator and

units.la: gubernatore omniū, quatenus ex illo omnes nostræ sunt naturæ uires, sed esse ex singulari illius dignatione, ac dispensatione, qua Regnū suum dispensat in electis. Quare qd̄ dicit: non quod idonei simus ex nobis ipsis cogitare qc-quam, tanquam ex nobisipsis, &c. non est alio quàm ad præsentem causam de Apostolatus i-psius efficacia trahendum. Interea tamen ne-mo pius negat, in cæteris quoq; reb. quæcūq; nobis est uel cogitandi uel operandi facultas, aliunde illam non esse quàm ex Deo.
units.tr: Governor of all, by whom all the powers of our nature are, but being of God's singular favour and dispensation, by which he dispenses his kingdom among the elect. Therefore, when he says, "not that we are sufficient to think anything as of ourselves," and so on, this is to be taken only with reference to the present matter, the efficacy of his apostleship. Meanwhile, however, no pious person denies that in all other matters also, whatever ability we have either to think or to act, it is not from anywhere else but from God.

units.la: Est hic locus unus ex illis, qui opinionem li-beri arbitrij refellunt. Etenim si Apostolus, in lege Domini à puero institutus, & diligentis-sima pharifaicæ sectæ disciplina ad honestam uitæ conuersationem enutritus usq; adeo alie-nus est à rebus spiritualibus ac diuinis, ut ne ad cogitandum quidem aliquid illarum sit ido-neus ex seipso, quomodo facultatem liberi ar-bitrij ad bonum quæ sit ex uiribus naturæ, cæ-teris hominibus dabimus? Quod enim Paul? de Apostolatu suo dixit, id nos haud incómo-dè ad verampietatem, fidem, spem, dilectionē, timorem Dei, obedientiam, uitæ sanctimoni-am &c. accommodamus.
units.tr: This is one of those passages which refute the opinion of free will. For if the Apostle, instructed from boyhood in the law of the Lord and brought up to an honest manner of life by the most diligent discipline of the Pharisaic sect, was so alien to spiritual and divine things that he was not even sufficient from himself to think anything of them, how shall we grant to other men a faculty of free will for good, which is from the powers of nature? For what Paul said of his apostleship, we may not inappropriately apply to true piety, faith, hope, love, the fear of God, obedience, the holiness of life, and so on.

units.la: QVI &idoneos fecit nos ministros Noui te-stamenti, inquit.) Non negat igitur idoneum esse se ad ea quæ de ministerio suo prędicat, cũ hic se dicat à Deo factum esse idoneum, sed hoc tantum negat, quod alij sibijpsis tribuere solent, ex se ipso uidelicet esse idoneum.
units.tr: "Who also made us sufficient ministers of the New Testament," he says. He does not deny, then, that he is sufficient for the things he preaches about his ministry, since here he says that he was made sufficient by God; but he denies only what others are accustomed to attribute to themselves, namely, that they are sufficient of themselves.

units.la: Admonemur hoc loco primum, quis sit qui fa-ciat idoneos uerbi diuini ministros. Deus sci-licet, qui uocat eos etiam & mittit. Quē ille nō facit idoneum, in sempiternum non erit ido-neus, quantumuis sit doctus & eloquens. Pau-lus erat doctus in lege, institutus ad pedes Ga-malielis, & simul habebat insignem zelū Dei, & tamen idoneus Noui testamenti minister haudquaquam esse potuisset, nisi singulari gra-tia ad id fuisset muneris à Deo factus idone-us. Iam si eruditio & eloquentia non reddunt idoneum ecclesiæ ministrum, quomodo red-det illiterata barbaries? Quare non est ut di-cant ignaui homines. Vana est eruditio. Idō-neus est quem Deus facit idoneum. Valeant igitur literæ. Hic idem Apostolus & post uo-cationem suam literas non abiecit, & Timo-theum suum ad iugem est sacrarum scriptura-rum lectionem hortatus. Non cōuenit igitur, ut cœlestis gratiæ necessitas ignauiæ & infci-tię patrocinetur, quemadmodum nō cōuenit, ut eruditio & scientia gratiæ Dei necessitati deroget.
units.tr: In this place we are first reminded who it is that makes ministers of the divine Word sufficient: namely God, who also calls and sends them. Whom he does not make sufficient, he will never be sufficient, however learned and eloquent he may be. Paul was learned in the law, trained at the feet of Gamaliel, and at the same time had a remarkable zeal for God; yet he could never have been a sufficient minister of the New Testament, unless by a singular grace he had been made sufficient for that office by God. Now if learning and eloquence do not make a minister of the Church sufficient, how will unlettered barbarism make him so? Therefore it is not as lazy men say: "Learning is vain; he is sufficient whom God makes sufficient. Let letters go." This same Apostle, even after his calling, did not cast aside letters, and he urged his Timothy to the constant reading of the sacred Scriptures. It is not fitting, then, that the necessity of heavenly grace should be made a cover for laziness and ignorance, just as it is not fitting that learning and knowledge should detract from the necessity of the grace of God.

units.la: Nec ociosum est illud, quod non simpliciter dicit: qui idoneos fecit nos suos ministros, sed, qui idoneos fecit nos Noui testamenti mi-nistros. Quasi dicat, uestri Magistri urgent ob-seruantiam legis, quasi sint ueteris testamenti ministri, mihique uicio uertunt, quod diuer-sum doceo, at ego factus sum à Deo idoneus minister non Veteris sed Noui testamenti. Vi-derint ipsi quid sint, & quid à Deo facti uideri uelint.Et hoc dicens collimat ad collationem Veteris ac Noui testamenti, quò inter utriusq; ministeria discriminando præstantiam Noui ostendat.
units.tr: Nor is that idle which he does not say simply, "who made us his ministers," but "who made us ministers of the New Testament."
