As if he were saying: your teachers insist on observance of the law, as though they were ministers of the Old Testament, and they find fault with me because I teach otherwise; but I have been made by God a sufficient minister not of the Old but of the New Testament. Let them see for themselves what they are, and what they wish to appear to have been made by God. And in saying this he aims at a comparison of the Old and New Testaments, so that by distinguishing between the ministries of each he may show the excellence of the New.

units.la: NON literæ, inquit, sed spiritus.) Cum dicit se ministrum esse factum Noui testamenti, non literæ, sed spiritus, nö dat Nouo testamen to litera & spiritum, sic ut per literam intelligat doctrinam literis expressam, per spiritū uerò doctrinam uiua uoce & spiritu expromptâ, quasi dicat, non ut literis agam atramento scriptis, sed ut prædicem Euangelium. Etenim si hoc diceret, & sic inter doctrinam scriptam & uiua uoce prædicatam discriminaret, omnem eam doctrinæ suæ partem damnaret, quam literis utique atramento scriptis comprehēsam ad ecclesias misit, cuius tamen utilitas non minor fuit, & est hodie quoq;, quàm prædicationis uiua uoce expressæ, adeoq; non minus ex spiritu sancto profecta quàm illa. Quare Ecclesias in locis suis ut authoritatem ecclesiæ Romanæ supra sacras scripturas extollat, frustra hūc Apostoli locum citat. Neq; enim discriminat ille inter sacram scripturam & uiuâ prædicationis uocem.
units.tr: "Not of the letter," he says, "but of the Spirit." When he says that he has been made a minister of the New Testament, "not of the letter but of the Spirit," he does not set the letter and the Spirit against the New Testament in such a way that by the letter he understands doctrine expressed in writing, and by the Spirit doctrine delivered by living voice and spirit; as if he were saying: I do not act by writing with ink, but I preach the Gospel. For if he meant this, and so distinguished between doctrine written and doctrine preached by living voice, he would condemn that whole part of his teaching which he sent to the churches comprehended in writing with ink; yet its usefulness was no less, and is today also, than that of preaching expressed by living voice, and it proceeded no less from the Holy Spirit than that did. Therefore, those who cite this passage of the Apostle in vain, in order to exalt the authority of the Roman Church above the sacred Scriptures, are mistaken. For he does not distinguish between sacred Scripture and the living voice of preaching.

units.la: Nec probanda est eorum sententia, qui per literam sensum literalem, quem litera proprie intellecta legēti offert, & per spiritum sensum latentem & mysticum intelligendum esse iudicant. Licet enim sæpenumero occurrant sacræ scripturæ loci, in quibus non superficies literæ, sed quod in illius est inuolucro recondi-tum amplectendum sit, non est tamen hac in re Veteris ac Noui testamenti discrimē, & apostolici ministerij à legali posita differentia. Nā & in Veteri testamento multa sic dicuntur, ut non possint aliter quàm secundum proprium literæ sensum accipi, & in Nouo non pauca habentur, in quibus si literam sequamur, absurdū sensum accipiamus oportet. In ipsius Seruatoris nostri uerbis multa sunt figurate & parabolice dicta, & Apostolica doctrina multis est metaphorarum ac similitudinum inuolucris referta. Rursus in ueteri multa figurate, & in Nouo plurima proprijs & apertis loquutionibus proferuntur. Quare nec hunc possumus probare sensum.
units.tr: Nor can the view of those be approved who judge that by the letter we should understand the literal sense that the letter, read in its proper meaning, offers, and by the Spirit a hidden and mystical sense. For although passages of Scripture often occur in which what must be embraced is not the surface of the letter but what lies concealed within its wrapping, there is still no such distinction between the Old and New Testaments, nor such a difference between the apostolic ministry and the legal one, as this view supposes. In the Old Testament many things are said in such a way that they cannot be taken otherwise than according to the proper sense of the letter, and in the New Testament there are not a few passages in which, if we followed the letter, we would have to take an absurd sense. In the words of our Saviour himself many things are said figuratively and in parables, and apostolic doctrine is full of wrappings of metaphors and similitudes. Conversely, in the Old Testament many things are expressed figuratively, and in the New most things are stated in plain and open terms. Therefore we cannot approve this sense either.

units.la: Apostolus cum dicit se ministrum esse factum non literæ sed spiritus, nihil dicit aliud, quàm factum esse se ministrum non legis Mosaicæ, quamuis in illa sit natus & enutritus, sed gratiæ & efficaciæ spiritus, quam uocat spiritum, sicuti legem uocat literam, atque ita inter Vetus ac Nouum testamentum discernit, ut huic det spiritum, illi literam, & duabus hisce uocibus utriusque conditionem, id est illi us imbecillitatem, & huius uirtutem & efficaciam exprimat. Loquitur autem non de ea litera legis, quæ figuras continet & umbras, sed de ea, qua decalogus manifesta continens præcepta tabulis est lapideis inscriptus: sicuti patet in sequentibus. Et Nouo testamento Euangelio uidelicet regni Dei, dat spiritum, non ut
units.tr: When the Apostle says that he has been made a minister not of the letter but of the Spirit, he says nothing other than that he has been made a minister not of the Mosaic law, although he was born and brought up in it, but of the grace and efficacy of the Spirit, which he calls the Spirit, just as he calls the law the letter. In this way he distinguishes the Old Testament from the New, so that he gives the Spirit to the one and the letter to the other, and by these two words he expresses the condition of each: the weakness of the former and the power and efficacy of the latter. He is speaking, however, not of that letter of the law which contains figures and shadows, but of that letter by which the Decalogue, containing plain precepts, was inscribed on tables of stone, as is clear from what follows. And to the New Testament, namely the Gospel of the kingdom of God, he gives the Spirit, not in order to take away from the letters and from the use of the human voice,

units.la: literarum illi & humanæ uocis usum adimat, sed ut uirtutem & efficaciam gratiæ illius præstantioremq; dispensationem exprimat.
units.tr: but in order to express the power and efficacy of that grace and its more excellent dispensation.

units.la: Sunt qui legem ideo literam uocari sentiāt, quod per literas sit data, Euangelium uerò ac Noui testamenti dispensationem spiritû, ppte rea quod per infusionem spiritus sancti datū sit illius ministerium Apostolis. Verū si ob hāc causam legem uocat literam, Nouū testamentum spiritum, consequitur & ea quæ per apostolos habemus scripta esse scripturā legalem, & ministerium iudicandi in Israele fuisse spiritum, propterea quod luculento testimonio spiritus delectis illis 70. Viris datū fuisse legitur. Numeri undecimo. Quin & ministerium prophetandi in Veteri testamento hac ipsa ratione spiritus uocari posset, quantūuis prophetę legi Veteris Testamenti accenseantur. Quis enim negat prophetas spiritu Dei fuisse ad prophetandum inauguratos ac missos?
units.tr: There are those who think that the law is called the letter because it was given through letters, and that the Gospel and the dispensation of the New Testament are called the Spirit because their ministry was entrusted to the Apostles by the infusion of the Holy Spirit. But if the law is called the letter for this reason, and the New Testament the Spirit, it follows that the writings we have from the apostles are legal writings, and that the ministry of judging in Israel was the Spirit, since it is read that the Spirit was given to those chosen seventy men by a clear testimony (Numbers 11). Indeed the ministry of prophesying in the Old Testament could also be called the Spirit by this same reasoning, even though the prophets are reckoned among the law of the Old Testament. For who denies that the prophets were installed and sent by the Spirit of God to prophesy?

units.la: Rectius ergo dicemus legem ob id uocari literam, & Noui testamenti ministerium spiritum, quod lex nihil aliud confert, quàm litera lem intelligentiam faciendorum ac uitando-rū. hoc est, ad nihil fuerit aliud dispensata Israe li, quàm ut litera esset docens quid faciendum esset uel uitandum, atq; ita coscientias de peccato conuinceret ac damnaret. Noui uerò testamenti ministerium spiritum impertit credentibus, gratiam uidelicet & uirtutem Dei cordā innouantem ac conscientias iustificantem. Et hunc sensum Chrysostomus quoq; posuit, cū dicit: τὰ οὖν ἐκεῖνῳ ἐκ τῆς πνευματικὸς ὁ νόμῳ; πῶς οὖν φησιν, οἱ δάμεμ ὅτι ὁ νόμῳ πνευματικὸς ἔζι; πνευματικὸς μέν, ἀλλ' οὐ πνεῦμα παρέιχεν. οὐ γὰρ πνεῦμα ἐκόμωσε μωνὸς ἀλλὰ γράμματα. ἡμεῖς δὲ ἐπισεύθημεν πνεῦμα δἰδόναι. Hæc ille. Et ipsa Apostolorum acta satis docent, quomodo ministerium illorum spiritussancti gratiam contulerit in Christum credentibus.
units.tr: It is more correct, therefore, to say that the law is called the letter, and the ministry of the New Testament the Spirit, because the law confers nothing except a letter-knowledge of what is to be done and avoided; that is, the dispensation to Israel served for nothing else than that the letter should teach what was to be done or avoided, and so convict and condemn consciences of sin. But the ministry of the New Testament imparts the Spirit to believers, namely the grace and power of God renewing the heart and justifying consciences. Chrysostom also took this sense when he says: What then? Is the law not spiritual? How then does he say that the law is spiritual? Spiritual indeed, but it did not supply the Spirit. For it did not give the Spirit to men but letters. But we have promised to give the Spirit. [τὰ οὖν ἐκεῖνο ἐκ τῆς πνευματικῆς ὁ νόμος; πῶς οὖν φησιν, οἱ δὲ ἄνθρωποι ὅτι ὁ νόμος πνευματικός ἐστιν; πνευματικὸς μέν, ἀλλ' οὐ πνεῦμα παρέσχεν. οὐ γὰρ πνεῦμα ἔδωκε τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἀλλὰ γράμματα. ἡμεῖς δὲ ἐπηγγείλαμεθα πνεῦμα δώσειν.] That is his statement. And the very Acts of the Apostles sufficiently show how their ministry conferred the grace of the Holy Spirit upon those who believed in Christ.

units.la: NAM litera occidit, inquit, spiritus autem uiuificat.) Quoniā nō dicit: τὸ δὲ γράμμα. id est, Litera aūt, sed, τὸ δ γράμμα. id est, Litera enim occidit, existimo particulam hanc esse loco αἰπολογίας adiectam, ut rationem reddat, quare factū sit à Deo idoneus Noui testamenti non Veteris, spiritus, non literę minister, uel, quod magis placet, quare uoluerit Deus Noui testamenti ministerium, nō literæ esse sed spiritus. Propterea uidelicet, qd transierat tēpus mortificationis, aduenerat uerò uiuificatiōis, quapropter cessare oportebat ministerium literę, quod illa non nisi occidat, & inchoari ministerium spiritus, qui solus uiuificat. Quasi dicat. Quoniam uoluit me Deus esse ministrum nō Veteris sed Noui testamenti, simul me idoneum ministrum fecit non literæ sed spiritus. Litera nanq; ad Vetus testamentū pertinens occidit, Spiritus uerò qui per Noui testamenti ministerium confertur, uiuificat.
units.tr: "For the letter kills," he says, "but the Spirit gives life." Because he does not say τὸ δὲ γράμμα [but the letter], that is, "but the letter," but τὸ γράμμα [the letter], that is, "for the letter kills," I think this particle is added in the place of a causal particle, so as to give the reason why God made him a minister of the Spirit, and of the New Testament rather than the Old, not of the letter; or, which pleases me more, why God willed the ministry of the New Testament to be not of the letter but of the Spirit. Namely, because the time of mortification had passed and the time of quickening had arrived; therefore the ministry of the letter had to cease, since it kills and does nothing else, and the ministry of the Spirit, which alone gives life, had to begin. As if he were saying: since God willed me to be a minister not of the Old but of the New Testament, at the same time he made me a fit minister not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter, belonging to the Old Testament, kills; but the Spirit, which is conferred through the ministry of the New Testament, gives life.

units.la: NAM litera occidit inquit.) Opposita sunt dicet quisquam occidere & uiuificare. Si litera occidit, spiritus uerò uiuificat, ergo opposita sunt inuicem: Puto neminem hoc dicturum. Lex enim, quam hic per literam intelligit, sancta est, & spiritualis, nihil minus quam opposita spiritui. Quomodo igitur dicit litera occidere? Litera occides est litera continens sententiam condemnationis, qualia solent contra noxios esse rescripta principum; & qualis erat litera epistolæ Dauidis, quam Vriæ in castra ad Ducem exercitus perferendam dederat. Talis litera non est lex tabulis lapideis inscripta, quæ præcepta admodum pia, sancta & necessaria non ad mortem sed ad vitam data continet. Quare admodum inconueniens esse videtur ipsius & naturæ & scopo, quod Apostolus eam occidere dicit. Si diceret litera non viuificat, viuificat vero spiritus, daret infirmitatem & inefficaciam literæ, non occisionem, & nulla esset quæstio.
units.tr: "For the letter kills," he says. Someone might say that to kill and to quicken are opposites. If the letter kills and the Spirit quickens, then they are opposed to each other. I think no one will say this. For the law, which he here understands by the letter, is holy and spiritual, nothing less than opposed to the Spirit. How, then, does he say that the letter kills? The letter that kills is a letter containing a sentence of condemnation, such as the rescripts of princes usually are against wrongdoers; and such was the letter of David which he gave to Uriah to carry to the commander of the army in the camp. Such a letter is not the law inscribed on tables of stone, which contains precepts that are very pious, holy and necessary, given not for death but for life. Therefore it seems quite inconsistent with both its nature and its purpose that the Apostle says it kills. If he had said that the letter does not quicken but the Spirit does, he would be attributing weakness and inefficacy to the letter, not killing, and there would be no question.

units.la: Respondeo. Duplex est operatio legalis literæ. Vna propria, impropria & per accidens altera. Propria est præcipere bonū & prohibere malum, ac reddere intelligentem faciendorum & vitandorum. Est enim lux quædam, illuminans paruulos. Vnde & Apostolus dicit: Nescicbam concupiscentiā esse peccatum, nisi lex diceret: Non concupisces. Et Dauid: Lucerna, inquit, pedibus meis verbum tuū. Dum hoc facit litera legis, operatur quod conueniens est & proprium suæ naturę, perinde atque lux dū illuminat oculos, & disiectis tenebris visibilia reddit, quę antea fuerant caligine obducta. Et hactenus Apostolus legem sanctam & bonam ad vitam datam esse dicit Rom. 7.
units.tr: I answer: the legal letter has a twofold operation. One is proper, the other improper and incidental. The proper operation is to command what is good and forbid what is evil, and to make a person understand what is to be done and avoided. For it is a kind of light, illuminating little ones. Hence the Apostle also says: "I would not have known sin to be concupiscence, unless the law said, 'You shall not covet.'" And David: "Your word," he says, "is a lamp to my feet." While the letter of the law does this, it works what is fitting and proper to its nature, just as light, when it illuminates the eyes and drives away the shadows, makes visible what had been covered by darkness. And so far the Apostle says that the law is holy and good and given for life (Romans 7).

units.la: Impropria est & per accidens, dum auget vires peccati reddituq; transgressores & per consequens maledictos ac reos mortis, atque ita occidit. Vires peccati auget, dum cōcupiscentiam carnis nostræ prohibendo magis ac magis incendit. Et hoc facit nō suo sed carnis nostræ vicio, quæ sic est corrupta ut nitatur in ueritū, & quo magis prohibeas hoc ardētius cōcupiscat, quemadmodum accidit medicis, qui dum ægrotis potum aquæ negant, magis eos ad appetitum illius accendunt. Reddit transgressores, maledictos ac reos mortis, & sic occidit, non de suo, sed per accidens nostræ inobedientiæ ac maliciæ. Nisi enim lex esset, non esset transgresio. Sine transgresione non esset reatus mortis. Ettamen transgresionem non gignit lex, sed inobediens depravati cordis nostri malicia. Sic proprie quidem loquendo litera non occidit, occidit vero per occasionem aliunde allatam. Verum de tota hac materia copiosa est ipsius Apostoli explicatio in ea quę ad Romanos est cap. septimo, ubi de illa nonnulla annotauimus.
units.tr: The operation is improper and incidental when it increases the strength of sin and makes transgressors, and consequently accursed and liable to death, and so kills. It increases the strength of sin when, by forbidding our fleshly desire, it inflames it more and more. It does this not by its own fault but by the fault of our flesh, which is so corrupt that it strives after what is forbidden, and the more you forbid, the more eagerly it desires; just as happens to physicians who, when they deny water to the sick, only inflame their appetite for it. It makes transgressors, accursed and liable to death, and so kills, not from its own nature but incidentally, through our disobedience and wickedness. For if there were no law, there would be no transgression; without transgression there would be no guilt of death. Yet the law does not beget transgression; the disobedient malice of our depraved heart does. Thus, speaking properly, the letter does not kill; it kills only through an occasion brought in from elsewhere. But the Apostle's full explanation of this whole matter is in his Epistle to the Romans, chapter seven, where we have noted some things on it.

units.la: LITERA occidit inquit.) Non immerito quæsierit quisquam quos nam occidat litera legis, an in uniuersum omnes, uel aliquos tantum. Bonos quidem & morigeros nō occidit, sed qui sunt illi? Manet ergo quæstio de malis, an illos occidat omnes. Si hos omnes, ergo uniuersum genus humanū occidit, quia non est qui sit bonus & faciat bonum, ne unus quidem, teste Dauide, & Apostolo Rom. 3.
units.tr: "The letter kills," he says. It is not unreasonable for someone to ask which people the letter of the law kills: all men without exception, or only some. It does not kill the good and obedient, but who are they? So the question remains about the wicked, whether it kills all of them. If it kills all of them, then it kills the whole human race, since there is none who is righteous and does good, no, not one, as David and the Apostle testify (Rom. 3).

units.la: Respondendū est: occidere literā eos quibus est à Deo præscripta. Si præscripta est omnibus totius orbis nationibus, occiditomnes, quia omniū conscientias constringit. Si uero Iudæis tantū est data & illis qui ex Gentibus legi sese cum Iudæis subijciūt, sicut Apostolus legē illis loqui dicit, qui sunt sub lege, ergo Iudæos tantū occidit, quorum etiā tantum conscientias constringere potest. Conditio legis hæc est, ut obnoxios ad obediendū sibi faciat eos tantum, quibus est lata & præscripta. Est quidem Deus non Iudæorum tantum sed & Gentium Deus, ut iure suo posit legem figere omnibus totius orbis nationibus. Verum quemadmodum Israelis populum ex aliis sibi nationibus elegit, in quo nomen suum declararet, & unde nobis Seruatorem Christū mitteret, ita illi etiam singulari cōfilio legem præscripsit, qua conscientiæ ipsorum constringerentur & in obedietia retinerentur. Quod igitur illius litera per occasionem humanæ malicię occidit, non est referendum ad eos, quibus illa non est lata sed ad populum illum legalem tantum, & illius proselytos. Alioqui quorsum clamaret Apostolus dicens Galat. 5. Contestor omnem hominē qui circuncidītur, quod debitor est totius legis seruandæ? An hoc dicens, non liberat incircuncisos ab obseruātia legis illiq; circūcisos tantū subijcit? Si incircūcili aūt non sunt debitores legis, ergo non cōstringit eos litera legis, adeoq; nec occidit.
units.tr: The answer is that the letter kills those to whom it has been prescribed by God. If it has been prescribed to all the nations of the world, it kills all, since it binds the consciences of all. But if it was given only to the Jews, and to those Gentiles who subject themselves to the law along with the Jews, as the Apostle says he speaks to those who are under the law, then it kills only the Jews, whose consciences alone it can bind. The condition of the law is this: it makes obligated to obedience only those to whom it has been brought and prescribed. God is indeed the God not only of the Jews but also of the Gentiles, so he could by his own right impose the law on all the nations of the world. But just as he chose the people of Israel from among the other nations, in which he would make his name known and from which he would send us the Saviour Christ, so by a singular counsel he also prescribed the law to them, by which their consciences would be bound and held in obedience. Therefore, that his letter kills through the occasion of human wickedness is not to be referred to those to whom it was not given, but only to that legal people and its proselytes. Otherwise, why would the Apostle cry out, saying in Galatians 5: "I testify to every man who is circumcised that he is a debtor to keep the whole law"? Or, in saying this, does he not free the uncircumcised from observing the law and subject only the circumcised to it? If the uncircumcised are not debtors of the law, then the letter of the law does not bind them, and so it does not kill them either.

units.la: Dices. Ergo Gentes non sunt morti obnoxiæ, quia per literā legis non occiduntur, atq; ita melior est earū conditio quàm Iudæorum? Respondeo. Per peccatū mors intrauit inuoluens omnes homines. Rom. 5. Et capite secundo. Quicunque sine lege peccant, sine lege & pereunt, & quicunque in lege peccant per legem iudicātur. Et Gentes etsi scriptam legem non habent, habent tamen legem naturæ, per quam conscientię illarum accusantur & damnantur. Quare etsi non occidit eas litera tabulis lapideis insculpta, occidit tamen lex naturæ cordibus ipsarum inscripta.
units.tr: You will say: so the Gentiles are not liable to death, because they are not destroyed by the letter of the law, and so their condition is better than that of the Jews? I reply: through sin death entered in, enveloping all men (Rom. 5), and in the second chapter: "Whoever sins without the law will also perish without the law, and whoever sins in the law will be judged by the law." And although the Gentiles do not have a written law, they have the law of nature, by which their consciences are accused and condemned. Therefore, even if the letter inscribed on stone tablets does not kill them, the law of nature, written in their hearts, nevertheless kills them.

units.la: Adhuc cur talem legem, inquies, dedit populo suo Deus, cum sciret eam non uiuificatu ram sed occisuram? Respondeo. Non debemus consilia Dei in ius uocare. Magnam contulit ei genti prærogatiuam, in eo præcipue, quod manifestauit ei sua iudicia. Non fecit taliter omni nationi, inquit propheta. Quod si beneficium hoc per accidens occidit, non debemus propterea culpare Deum. Legem dedit bonā, iustam, & sanctā, cuius insigne utilitatem agnouerunt pij, sicuti uidere est psalm. 19. Vbi illius litera occidit, facit hoc peruersitate cordis humanis non sua natura. Ipsa bonitas Θεοῦ μακροθυμία Dei peruersis ad hoc facit, ut thesaurizent sibijpsi irā in die iudicij Rom. 2. Nunquid rogabimus, quare Deus sit bonus & μακροθυμος? Quanquā & illud non sine consilio
units.tr: Still, you will ask, why did God give such a law to his people, since he knew it would not give life but would kill? I reply: we ought not to call the counsels of God into question. He conferred a great privilege on that nation, chiefly in this, that he made known to them his judgments. "He has not dealt thus with any other nation," says the prophet. And if this benefit accidentally kills, we ought not on that account to blame God. He gave a good, just, and holy law, whose remarkable usefulness the godly have recognised, as may be seen in Psalm 19. Where its letter kills, it does so through the perversity of the human heart, not by its own nature. The very goodness, the forbearance of God [μακροθυμία], to the perverse only makes them store up for themselves wrath on the day of judgment (Rom. 2). Shall we ask why God is good and patient? Yet even this is not without the counsel of God, by which what the letter kills is directed to good, while the abundance of sin through the law serves the abundance of grace in Christ (Rom. 5).

units.la: {A} non est qui sit bonus & faciat bonum, ne unus quidem lio Dei ad bonum dirigitur, quod litera occidit, dum abundantia peccati ex lege, ad abundantiam gratiæ facit in Christo, Rom.5.
units.tr: {A} "There is none who is righteous and does good, no, not one" ... by the counsel of God what the letter kills is directed to good, while the abundance of sin through the law serves the abundance of grace in Christ (Rom. 5).

units.la: SPIRITVS uero uiuificat, inquit.) Vt occidere est uitam auferre, ita uiuificare est à morte liberare. Spiritus ergo uiuificat, dum nos à morte & peccato liberat. Liberat autem non eos tantū quos litera legis occidit, sed & reliquos omnes, qui participes illius efficiuntur. Efficiūtur uero participes illius quotquot uere in Christum credunt, iuxta illud Christi Iohan.7. Si quis sitit, ueniat ad me & bibat. Qui credit in me, sicut dicit scriptura, flumina de uentre eius fluent aquæ uiuæ, quod, interprete Euangelista, dixit de spiritu quem accepturi erant credétes in ipsum. Hunc enim uiuificantem suum spiritum promisit olim Deus per prophetas suos Noui testamenti temporibus, quem & luculenter præstitit per ministerium apostolorū, quò respicit Apostolus, dum se idoneum factum esse dicit Noui testamenti ministrum, non literæ sed spiritus, eo quod litera occidat, spiritus uero uiuificet.
units.tr: "But the Spirit gives life," he says. As to kill is to take away life, so to make alive is to free from death. The Spirit therefore gives life when he frees us from death and sin. He frees not only those whom the letter of the law kills, but all the rest who become partakers of it. And all who truly believe in Christ become partakers of it, according to that saying of Christ in John 7: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, out of his heart will flow rivers of living water," which, as the Evangelist explains, he said of the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive. For God long ago promised through his prophets in the times of the New Testament that he would give his life-giving Spirit, and he clearly performed this through the ministry of the apostles. This is what the Apostle has in view when he says that he has been made a fit minister of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit, because the letter kills but the Spirit gives life.

units.la: Quid est autem quod non dicit, non legis sed Euangelij, lex enim occidit, Euangelium uero uiuificat, sed, non literæ sed spiritus. Litera enim occidit, spiritus uero uiuificat? Non omnis lex occidit. Est enim lex etiam spiritus uitæ, quæ per Christum Iesum liberat à iure peccati & mortis Rom.7. quæ sane non occidit sed uiuificat. Ea uero lex quæ non spiritu in corda hominum, sed litera tabulis lapideis inscribitur, quatenus non habet nisi literam, hactenus occidit. Deest enim spiritus uiuificans, & interim constringit conscientias damnans inobedientes, & incendés prauam concupiscentiā. Deinde non mox uiuificat Euangelium omnes eos à quibus auditur, quia non omnes illi credunt. Qui sonū & literam illius accipit, non uiuificatur nisi credat & spiritum accipiat, imò occiditur magis qnàm uiuificatur. Nam super incredulos Euangelij auditores manet ira Dei, ut uitam habere nequeant. Iohan.3. Cum igitur ministerij sui efficaciam exprimere uellet, non dixit, nō legis sed Euangelij, lex enim occidit, Euangelium uero uiuificat, sed, non literæ sed spiritus, litera enim occidit, spiritus uero uiuificat. In litera fine spiritu infirmitas est, imò mors est. Tolle spiritum, mortua erunt omnia. In spiritu uis est uiuificádi. Tolle spiritū, quid erit totum Nouum testamentum aliud quàm litera & sonitus uocis, adeoq; & mors, non minus, quàm litera legis? Tolle spiritum, ipsa caro Christi, etiamsi corporaliter esset præsens in cœna, & corporaliter ederetur, quemadmodum fratres nonnulli contendunt, nihil prodesset tamen Christo ipso testificante ac dicente: Spiritus est qui uiuificat, caro non prodest quicquam, de quibus uerbis in Commentarijs nostris super Iohannem pleraq; diximus.
units.tr: But why does he not say "not of the law but of the Gospel", since the law kills and the Gospel gives life, and instead say "not of the letter but of the Spirit: for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life"? Not every law kills. There is also the law of the Spirit of life, which through Christ Jesus frees from the right of sin and death (Rom. 7), and which certainly does not kill but makes alive. But that law which is written not by the Spirit in the hearts of men but by the letter on stone tablets kills, insofar as it has nothing but the letter. For the life-giving Spirit is lacking, and meanwhile it binds consciences, condemning the disobedient and kindling depraved desire. Moreover, the Gospel does not immediately give life to all those who hear it, because not all believe it. Whoever receives only the sound and the letter of it is not made alive unless he believes and receives the Spirit; indeed he is killed rather than made alive. For the wrath of God remains upon those who hear the Gospel unbelievingly, so that they cannot have life (John 3). Therefore, when he wished to express the efficacy of his ministry, he did not say "not of the law but of the Gospel, for the law kills and the Gospel gives life", but "not of the letter but of the Spirit, for the letter kills and the Spirit gives life". In the letter without the Spirit there is weakness, indeed there is death. Take away the Spirit, and all things will be dead. In the Spirit is the power to quicken. Take away the Spirit, and what will the whole New Testament be but letter and sound of voice, and therefore death, no less than the letter of the law? Take away the Spirit, and the flesh of Christ itself, even if it were bodily present in the Supper and bodily eaten, as some brethren contend, would profit nothing, Christ himself testifying and saying: "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing" (John 6). Concerning these words I have said much in my Commentaries on John.

units.la: Porro, cum extra spiritū hunc uiuificantem mors sint omnia ea quæ data sunt ad uitam,
units.tr: Moreover, since apart from this life-giving Spirit all things that are given for life are death,

units.la: A uehementer stupendum est, quare tantæ sint inter doctos homines rixæ & contentiones de dogmatibus & opinionibus ad ueram uitam non facientibus, & non magis omnis huc cura & solicitudo impedatur, ut ministerium Noui testamenti etiamnum non sit litera sed spiritus, Spiritus uiuificat. Quod uiuificatum est spiritu, uitam habet pro qualitate & operatione spiritus, unde est uiuificatum. Huius uitæ indicia Gal.5. recensentur. Vtpote, charitas, gaudiū, pax, lenitas, benignitas, bonitas, fides, mansuetudo, temperantia, &c. quæ ibi fructus spiritus uocātur, de quibus nulla nunc est cogitatio, & interim fumus insignes Noui testamenti ministri. Multi sic certant de uerbis Christi, quæ spiritus sunt & uita, ut declarent se ne micam quidem habere spiritus Christi. Et cum tales sint indubitato, indubitatam sibi ueram illorum sententiam uindicant. Vtinam horum hominum morositas corrigi posset in ecclesia.
units.tr: It is greatly to be wondered at why there are such great quarrels and contentions among learned men over dogmas and opinions that do not lead to true life, and why all this care and anxiety is not rather spent on ensuring that the ministry of the New Testament is still not a letter but the Spirit, "the Spirit gives life." What has been made alive by the Spirit has life according to the quality and working of the Spirit by which it was made alive. The signs of this life are listed in Galatians 5: namely love, joy, peace, gentleness, kindness, goodness, faith, meekness, self-control, etc., which there are called the fruit of the Spirit. Of these there is now no thought at all, and yet there are plenty of distinguished ministers of the New Testament. Many contend so over the words of Christ, which "are spirit and life," that they show they do not have even a crumb of the Spirit of Christ. And since such men are without doubt, they claim for their own opinion an undoubted truth. Would that the stubbornness of these men could be corrected in the Church.

units.la: Quod si administratio mortis in literis, deformata in saxis, fuit in gloria, adeo ut non possent oculos intendere filij Israel in faciem Moysi, propter gloriam uultus eius, quæ aboletur, cur non potius administratio spiritus erit in gloria? Nam si administratio condemnationis gloria, multo magis excellit administratio iusticiæ in gloria. Quandoquidem ne glorificatum quidem fuit, quod glorificatum est in hac parte, propter eminentem gloriam. Etenim si quod aboletur fuit in gloria, multo magis id quod manet, est in gloria.
units.tr: But if the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not look steadfastly on the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, which was passing away, why should not the ministry of the Spirit rather be glorious? For if the ministry of condemnation was glorious, the ministry of righteousness far exceeds it in glory. Indeed, what was made glorious in this respect was not glorious at all, because of the surpassing glory. For if what was passing away was glorious, much more is that which remains glorious.

units.la: Pseudapostoli, licet Christum in speciem profiterentur, gloria legis tamen magis quàm Euangelici ministerij iactabant, immo per illam Apostolatum Pauli singulari studio fugilabat, quod ille legi uideretur iniquior, quam tamen magna cum gloria latam esse constaret. Horum maliciæ occurrens Paulus, non negat gloria administratæ legis, sed ab illa tanquam minore argumentatur necessario maiorem esse gloriam administrati Euágelij, cum tanta fuerit administratæ legis. Vt autē euidenter quod uult euincat, non dicit simpliciter: Si administratio legis fuit in gloria, cur non potius administratio Euangelij erit in gloria, sed conferens utriusque administrationis effectus, in quibus potissimum relucet utrius maior sit præstantia, argumentatur ad hunc modum: Quod si administratio mortis in literis deformata in saxis, fuit in gloria, &c. cur non potius administratio spiritus erit in gloria?
units.tr: The false apostles, though they professed Christ in appearance, boasted rather in the glory of the Law than in the glory of the Gospel ministry. Indeed, through the Law they sneered at Paul's apostleship with particular zeal, because he seemed more hostile to the Law, though it was well established that the Law had been given with great glory. Meeting their malice, Paul does not deny the glory of the Law as administered, but from it, as from a lesser thing, he argues by necessity that the glory of the Gospel as administered is greater, since the glory of the Law was so great. So that he may clearly prove what he intends, he does not simply say, "If the administration of the Law was glorious, why should not the administration of the Gospel rather be glorious?" Instead, comparing the effects of each administration, in which the greater excellence of each chiefly shines forth, he argues in this way: "But if the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones, was glorious, etc., why should not the ministry of the Spirit rather be glorious?"

units.la: Item, si administratio condemnationis gloriosa fuit, multo magis administratio iusticiæ excellit in gloria.
units.tr: Likewise, if the ministry of condemnation was glorious, the ministry of righteousness far surpasses it in glory.

units.la: Ad hæc, si quod aboletur fuit in gloria, multo mato magis id quod manet est in gloria. Vis argumenti huius est à praestantia dignitatis ad excellentiam gloriae. Cuius enim maior est dignitas,illi etiá maior competit gloria. Maiorem autè dignitatem maior euincit operationum praestantia. Quàm autem praestantius sit administrare uitam & iusticiam, quàm administrare condemnationem & mortem, nemo est cui non pateat.Cum ergo ministerium literae ministeriū sit mortis & condemnationis, Euangelij uero administratio sit spiritus & uitae, & absq; controuersia maior sit dignitas eius quod spiritum,iustitiā & uitam, quàm quod mortem & condemnationem ministrat, cōsequitur omnino maiorem competere gloriam administrationi Euangelij, quàm administrationi legalis literae. Cui accidit & illud, quod administratio literae iam tamē aboleba-tur,administratio uero spiritus permanet usq; ad finem.Quare quanto praestatius est id quod permanet eo quod aboletur, tanto praestatior est Euangelij quàm legis gloria. Haec est praesentis argumenti summa, quo Apostolus gloriationem pseudapostolorum de gloria legis sic inuertit, ut ex ea ipsa gloria Euangelij praestantiore esse conuincat, quàm sit gloria legis.
units.tr: Moreover, if what was passing away was glorious, much more is that which remains glorious. The force of this argument runs from the excellence of dignity to the splendour of glory: for whatever has the greater dignity also has the greater glory. And greater dignity is proved by the greater excellence of the works. Now, that it is more excellent to administer life and righteousness than to administer condemnation and death, no one fails to see. Since therefore the ministry of the letter is a ministry of death and condemnation, but the administration of the Gospel is a ministry of the Spirit and of life, and since without dispute the dignity of that which ministers the Spirit, righteousness and life, is greater than that which ministers death and condemnation, it follows altogether that greater glory belongs to the administration of the Gospel than to the administration of the legal letter. To this is added that the administration of the letter was already passing away, whereas the administration of the Spirit remains until the end. Therefore, the more excellent is that which remains than that which passes away, the more excellent is the glory of the Gospel than the glory of the Law. This is the sum of the present argument, by which the Apostle so turns the boasting of the false apostles about the glory of the Law that from that very glory he proves the glory of the Gospel to be more excellent than the glory of the Law.

units.la: Quod si administratio mortis in literis deformata in saxis. Vtitur periphrasi legis, sumpta ex ipso modo,quo fuit lata dum eam deformatam literis saxo insculptis fuisse dicit: Quod uerterunt,deformata in saxis, in Graeco est, ἐντετυπωμένη ἐν λίθοις, id est, insculpta & impressa saxis. Modus hic latae legis refertur ad decalogum & tabulas foederis,potissimam Mosaicae legis partem,ne qua sit de reliquis illius literis quaestio.
units.tr: "But if the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones": he uses a periphrasis for the Law, taken from the very manner in which it was given, since he says it was engraved in letters cut into stone. The phrase "engraved on stones" is, in the Greek, ἐντετυπωμένη ἐν λίθοις [entetypōmenē en lithois], that is, carved and impressed on stones. This manner of giving the Law is referred to the Decalogue and the tablets of the covenant, the principal part of the Mosaic Law, so that no question arises about the rest of its writings.

units.la: De tabulis autē hisce lapideis legitur Exo. 24.ad hūc modum. Dixit autem dominus ad Moysen: Ascende ad me in montem, & esto ibi, daboq; tibi tabulas lapideas & legem ac mandata,quae scripsi,ut doceas filios Israel.Et cap. 31. Deditq; dominus Moysi completis huiusmodi sermonibus,in monte Synai duas tabulas testimonij lapideas scriptas digito Dei. Et cap.32.Cumq;appropinquasset ad castra,uidit uitulum & choros, iratusq; ualde proiecit de manu tabulas,& confregit eas ad radicē montis.Et cap.34. Praecide tibi ait duas tabulas lapideas instar priorum , & scribam super eas uerba quae habuerūt tabulae quas fregisti,&c. Excidit ergo duas tabulas lapideas quales antea fuerant,& de nocte consurgēs ascendit in montem Synai,sicut praeceperat ei dominus, portans secum tabulas. Et ibidem. Dixitque dominus ad Moysen. Scribe tibi uerba haec, quibus tecum & filijs Israel pepigi foedus. Fuit ergo ibi cum domino Moyses quadraginta dies & quadraginta noctes, panē nō comedit, & aquam nō bibit,& scripsit in tabulis decem uerba foederis. Cumq; descenderet de monte Synai,tenebat duas tabulas lapideas testimonij,& ignorabat, quod cornea esset facies sua ex consortio sermonis domini. Videntes autē Aaron & filij Israel corneam Moysi faciem,timuerunt prope accedere. Vocatiq; ab eo, reuersi sunt tam Aaron quàm principes synagogae,& postquam loquutus est ad eos,uenerunt ad eum etiam omnes filij Israel. Quibus praecepit cuncta,quę audierat à domino in monte Synai. Impletisque sermonibus posuit uelamen super faciem suam. Qui ingressus ad dominum, & loquēns cum eo auferebat donec exiret, & tunc loquebatur ad filios Israel omnia quae sibi fuerant imperata. Qui uidebant faciem egredientis Moysi esse corneam, sed operiebat ille rursus faciem suam , quando loquebatur ad eos. Haec de tabulis lapideis, & gloria faciei Mosis ex scripturis huc retuli, propterea quod Apostolus ex illis hoc loco argumentatur.
units.tr: Concerning these stone tablets we read in Exodus 24, in this manner: "And the LORD said unto Moses, Come up to me into the mount, and be there: and I will give thee tablets of stone, and a law, and commandments, which I have written, that thou mayest teach them." And in chapter 31: "And he gave unto Moses, when he had made an end of speaking with him upon mount Sinai, two tables of testimony, tables of stone, written with the finger of God." And in chapter 32: "And it came to pass, as soon as he came nigh unto the camp, that he saw the calf, and the dancing: and Moses' anger waxed hot, and he cast the tables out of his hands, and brake them beneath the mount." And in chapter 34: "Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first: and I will write upon these tables the words that were in the first tables, which thou brakest." So he hewed two tables of stone like the former ones, and rising early in the morning went up unto mount Sinai, as the LORD had commanded him, bearing in his hand the two tables of stone. And the same chapter: "And the LORD said unto Moses, Write thou these words: for after the tenor of these words I have made a covenant with thee and with Israel." So Moses was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights; he neither did eat bread nor drink water, and he wrote upon the tables the words of the covenant, the ten commandments. And when he came down from mount Sinai with the two tables of testimony in his hand, he did not know that the skin of his face shone while he talked with the LORD. And when Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, behold, the skin of his face shone; and they were afraid to come nigh him. And Moses called unto them; and Aaron and all the rulers of the congregation returned unto him: and Moses talked with them. And afterwards all the children of Israel came nigh: and he gave them in commandment all that the LORD had spoken with him in mount Sinai. And till Moses had done speaking with them, he put a veil on his face. But when Moses went in before the LORD to speak with him, he took the veil off, until he came out; and he came out, and spake unto the children of Israel that which he was commanded. And the children of Israel saw the face of Moses, that the skin of his face shone: and Moses put the veil upon his face again, until he went in to speak with him. I have brought these things about the stone tables and the glory of Moses' face out of the Scriptures here, because the Apostle argues from them in this place.

units.la: Vide autem quomodo non dicat simpliciter: quod si administratio literae saxis impressae, sed, quod si administratio mortis in literis,impressa saxis. Colligit ex eo quod legem uocauit literam occidentem. Si litera occidés est lex,ergo administratio legis est administratio mortis literis impressa saxis. Dubio procul dura erant ista omnibus illis,qui zelo legis Mosaicae tenebantur, ne lucem ueritatis agno scerent. Verum duro nodo debebatur durus cuneus. Non erat grauius obstaculum Euangelio Dei,quàm praetextus legis, cuius tamen Iudaei infirmitatē ac dispensationis rationem non intelligebant.Quare ipsa necessitate coactus ad hunc modum de illa loquitur Apostolus,quo gloriam Euangelij Dei contra praepositeros legis aemulatores tueatur.
units.tr: Notice, however, that he does not simply say "if the ministry of the letter impressed on stones," but "if the ministry of death in letters impressed on stones." He draws this from the fact that he called the Law "the letter that kills." If the Law is the killing letter, then the administration of the Law is the administration of death in letters impressed on stones. Undoubtedly these words were harsh for all those who held to the zeal of the Mosaic Law, lest they should acknowledge the light of truth. But a hard knot needs a hard wedge. Nothing was a greater obstacle to the Gospel of God than the pretext of the Law, whose weakness, and the reason of God's dispensation, the Jews did not understand. Therefore, compelled by this very necessity, the Apostle speaks of it in this way, so that he may defend the glory of the Gospel of God against the proud rivals of the Law.

units.la: Non est autē ociosum quod dicit:ἐντετυπωμένη ἐν λίθοις,id est, insculpta & impressa lapidibus. Iam tum figurabatur legem parari cordibus lapideis, foreq; difficilem illius administrationem,perinde atque defficile est literas insculpere saxo. Nisi hoc innuissēt,poterat dicere,ἐγγεγραμμένη πλαξί,id est inscripta tabulis.
units.tr: It is not idle that he says ἐντετυπωμένη ἐν λίθοις [entetypōmenē en lithois], that is, carved and impressed on stones. Even then it was foreshadowed that the Law would be prepared for stony hearts, and that its administration would be difficult, just as it is hard to carve letters into stone. Had he not meant this, he could have said ἐγγεγραμμένη πλαξί [engegrammenē plaxi], that is, inscribed on tablets.

units.la: FVIT in gloria,inquit,adeo ut nō possent oculos intendere filij Israel in faciem Moysi, propter gloriam uultus eius.) Hoc est. Sic fuit illustris & splendida,ut non possent oculi filiorum Israel terre splendore uultus Moysi. Posuit enim uocem,gloriam,pro splendore.Non est autem praeter rationem à Deo factū, quod faciem Mosis uoluit ad hunc modū fieri isplen didam,quò diuini alloquij testimonium in facie sua omnium spectatium oculis ingereret, admonerentūrq; omnes,quantæ praerogatiuę sit propius accedere ad Deum, & ab illo accipere mandata populo ipsius proponenda, cum ne interpretis eiusmodi quidem faciem fine uelamine contueri possent.
units.tr: "Was in glory," he says, "so that the children of Israel could not look steadfastly on the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance." That is: it was so bright and splendid that the eyes of the children of Israel could not bear the brightness of Moses' face. For he used the word "glory" for "splendour." Nor was it beyond reason that God willed Moses' face to be made so radiant, so that the witness of the divine address might be set before the eyes of all in his face, and so that all might be reminded how great a privilege it is to draw near to God and receive from him commandments to be set before his people, since even the face of such an interpreter could not be looked upon without a veil.

units.la: QVÆ aboletur, inquit.) Series lectionis requirit ut referatur haec particula ad gloriam uultus Mosaici. Poterat igitur dicere καταργημένω,id est,quæ abolita est ac cessauit. Verum quoniā ea gloria,licet iā olim mortuus sit Moses,tandiu durabit, quandiu durabat administratio legis, maluit loqui in praesenti καταργουμένω. μίνλω, id est, quæ aboletur ac cessat, propterea quod ad initium Noui testameti lex illa adeoque & gloria Moysi administratoris illius iam aboleri cœpisset. Sic igitur agnoscit quidem magnam fuisse gloriam administratæ legalis literæ, uerum admodum imminuit illam, dum eam aboleri dicit: Locus hic esset dicendi de abrogatione legis Mosaicæ, uerum de ea in locis nostris uidebitur.
units.tr: "Which is passing away," he says. The sequence of the reading requires that this particle be referred to the glory of Moses' countenance. He could therefore have said καταργημένω [katargēmenō], that is, which has been abolished and has ceased. But since that glory, although Moses died long ago, would last as long as the administration of the Law lasted, he preferred to speak in the present tense, καταργουμένω [katargoumenō], that is, which is being abolished and ceasing, because that Law, and therefore the glory of Moses its administrator, had already begun to be abolished at the beginning of the New Testament. Thus he indeed acknowledges that the glory of the legal letter as administered was great, but he greatly diminishes it while saying that it is being abolished. This place would call for a discussion of the abrogation of the Mosaic Law, but that will be seen in its own place.

units.la: CVR nō potius administratio spiritus, inquit, erit in gloria? Magna, aiebant, est gloria legis. Non negat hoc Apostolus, sed infert: cur non potius administratio spiritus erit in gloria? Non dicit: cur non etiam, sed cur non potius. Nec dicit, administratio Euangelij, sed administratio spiritus, intellige, uiuificantis, ut opponat eam administrationi mortis. Iuxta rationem oppositorum dicendū erat, cur non potius administratio uitæ erit in gloria? Verū maluit ponere spiritum uiuificatorem, quàm ipsam uitam, propterea quod effusio illius in credentes tum temporis esset manifesta & miraculo plena, testimonium diuinæ uirtutis & gratiæ omnium oculis ingerens, idque multo illustrius quàm corneaMoysi facies, neminem illuminans, sed magis imbecilles spectantium oculos reuerberans.
units.tr: Why then, he says, will the ministration of the Spirit not rather be in glory? "Great," they used to say, "is the glory of the law." The Apostle does not deny this, but he draws an inference: why will the ministration of the Spirit not rather be in glory? He does not say "why not also," but "why not rather." Nor does he say "the ministration of the Gospel" but "the ministration of the Spirit," namely the Spirit who gives life, so that he may set it over against the ministration of death. According to the logic of opposites he ought to have said, "Why will the ministration of life not rather be in glory?" But he preferred to name the life-giving Spirit rather than life itself, because the outpouring of that Spirit upon believers at that time was manifest and full of miracle, presenting to everyone's eyes the testimony of divine power and grace, and this far more brilliantly than the horned face of Moses, which lit up no one but rather dazzled the weak eyes of the onlookers.

units.la: Quid est autem quod non dicit in præsenti: Cur non potius administratio spiritus sit in gloria, sed in futuro, cur non potius administratio spiritus erit in gloria? An non iam tum cum hæc scriberet & fuerat & erat in gloria? Vtiq;. Verum loquitur de gloriæ huius perennitate, qua duratura erat donec durat ipsum Euangelium, multo iustius quàm gloria uultus Moysi durabat, quandiu durabat ipsa lex.
units.tr: But why does he not say, in the present tense, "why is the ministration of the Spirit not rather in glory," but in the future, "why will the ministration of the Spirit not rather be in glory"? Was it not already in glory when he was writing this, and was it not then in glory? Certainly. But he speaks of the perpetuity of this glory, by which it was to endure as long as the Gospel itself endures, far more justly than the glory of Moses' face endured as long as the law itself endured.

units.la: NAM si administratio condenationis gloria, inquit, multo magis excellit administratio iusticiæ in gloria.) Nectit affinia & cognata. Etenim si litera legis mortis est administratio, consequitur illam condemnationis quoque esse administrationem. Nisi enim condemnaret inobedientes, non occideret. Nam sic sunt coram Deo iusto iudice affines & cognatæ mors & condemnatio, ut una posita, cohæreat & altera. Consimili modo cohærent in Euangelio spiritus & iusticia. Dicit itaque: Nam si administratio condenationis, id est, legis peccatores condemnantis, gloria, hoc est, gloriosa, uel in gloria est, multo magis excellit administratio iusticiæ in gloria. Hoc est, multo convenit excellentiorem esse gloriam administrationis Noui testam. quæ iusticiā administrat.
units.tr: "For if the ministration of condemnation," he says, "is glory, much more does the ministration of righteousness abound in glory." He links things related and kindred. For if the letter of the law is a ministration of death, it follows that it is also a ministration of condemnation. For unless it condemned the disobedient, it would not kill them. Death and condemnation are so bound together before the just Judge of God that, one being posited, the other clings to it. In the same way, in the Gospel, the Spirit and righteousness cohere. He therefore says: "For if the ministration of condemnation, that is, of the law condemning sinners, is glory, that is, is glorious or in glory, much more does the ministration of righteousness abound in glory." That is, it befits the ministration of the New Testament, which administers righteousness, to have a more excellent glory.

units.la: Potest autem illud, administratio iusticiæ, bifariam accipi, uel de administratione iustificationis, quę est per fidem in Christum, uel de iusticia uitæ eorū qui spiritum Dei acceperūt, & iam non secundum carnem sed secundum spiritum uiuunt. In Græco est uox δικαιοσύνη, quæ poterat iustificationis sensu uerti, quemadmodum in ea quę ad Romanos est uertitur capite quarto, octauo & decimo. Et ratio oppositionis uidetur hoc requirere, ut legatur, ad-ministratio iustificationis. Condemnationi quippe rectius opponitur iustificatio, quæ est liberatio & absolutio à reatu & condemnatione, quàm iusticia uitæ, cuius oppositum est iniusticia magis quàm condemnatio.
units.tr: The phrase "ministration of righteousness" can, however, be taken in two ways: either of the ministration of justification, which is through faith in Christ, or of the righteousness of life of those who have received the Spirit of God and now live not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. In Greek the word is δικαιοσύνη [dikaiosynē], which could be translated in the sense of justification, as it is in the Epistle to the Romans, chapters four, eight and ten. And the logic of the opposition seems to require that it be read as "ministration of justification." For justification, which is liberation and absolution from guilt and condemnation, is more properly set against condemnation than the righteousness of life, whose opposite is unrighteousness rather than condemnation.

units.la: Quod si placet legere, administratio iusticiæ, & intelligere non de imputata, sed ea quæ uitæ nostræ sit iustitia, cogitandū est, non coniuenisse Apostolo, ut iuxta seriem oppositorum diceret: Nam si administratio iniusticiæ in gloria est, multo magis excellit administratio iusticiæ in gloria. Sic enim tribuisset legi administrationem iniusticię, quæ cum natura illius pugnat. Condemnationem quidē & mortem transgressorum, iniusticiam uero transgredientium & peccantium non administrat.
units.tr: But if one prefers to read "ministration of righteousness" and to understand it not of imputed righteousness but of that which is the righteousness of our life, one must consider that the Apostle did not intend to say, following the order of opposites: "For if the ministration of unrighteousness is in glory, much more does the ministration of righteousness abound in glory." For in that case he would have ascribed to the law a ministration of unrighteousness, which conflicts with its nature. The law does not administer the condemnation and death of transgressors, but unrighteousness of those who transgress and sin.

units.la: Verum utrolibet modo legamus, siue administratio iustificationis, siue administratio iusticiæ, & uera sunt utraque attributa & conuenientia Euangelio Christi, & firmum est argumentum Apostoli. Queinadmodum enim gloriosius est liberare reos à condenatione & morte, interuentu regalis clementiæ, quàm condemnare eos sententia iudiciaria, & occidere gladio lictoris, ita omnino gloriosior est administratio iustificationis, & iusticiæ, quàm administratio condemnationis.
units.tr: But however we read it, whether "ministration of justification" or "ministration of righteousness," both are true attributes and agree with the Gospel of Christ, and the Apostle's argument is sound. For just as it is more glorious to free the guilty from condemnation and death, by the intervention of royal clemency, than to condemn them by judicial sentence and kill them with the executioner's sword, so the ministration of justification and of righteousness is altogether more glorious than the ministration of condemnation.

units.la: Vide autem quàm caute ac circumspecte non dicat: Si Moses administrator mortis & condemnationis in tanta fuit gloria, ut in faciem eius non possent intendere filij Israel, quáto magis Apostolus Christi administrator spiritus & iusticiæ erit in gloria? Sic enim dicendo uisus fuisset suam ipsius magis quàm Noui testamenti spectare gloriā, leq; supra Moysen euehere uelle, atq; ita calumnias pseudapostolorū cofirmasset magis quàm reprobasset. Quare cōsulto collatione hac sic adfert in medium, ut manifestū faciat, nō sua se, sed Noui testamenti adeoq; & ipsius Christi gloriā contra illius obscuratores pseudapostolos ac legis doctores tueri. Ideo inculcat administrationē Noui testamēti spiritus & iusticiæ præstantio rē esse ac maiore gloria dignā, quàm sitadministratio literæ occidētis & condenantis, quantumuis illa tātopere iactetur à pseudapostolis
units.tr: See how cautiously and circumspectly he does not say: "If Moses, the administrator of death and condemnation, was in such glory that the children of Israel could not fix their eyes on his face, how much more will the Apostle of Christ, the administrator of the Spirit and of righteousness, be in glory?" For by saying this he would have seemed to look to his own glory rather than that of the New Testament, and to want to raise himself above Moses, and thus he would have confirmed rather than refuted the slanders of the false apostles. Therefore he deliberately brings forward this comparison in such a way as to make it plain that he defends not his own glory but the glory of the New Testament, and indeed of Christ himself, against its disparagers, the false apostles and teachers of the law. Hence he insists that the ministration of the New Testament of the Spirit and of righteousness is more excellent and worthy of greater glory than the ministration of the letter that kills and condemns, however much the false apostles boast of it.

units.la: QVANDOQVIDEM ne glorificatū quidē fuit, inquit, quod glorificatū est in hac parte, propter eminentē gloriā.) Sensus est. Vsq; adeo excellit administratio spiritus & iustitiæ administratione mortis & condemnationis, ut gloria illa quę contigit Moysi, si conferatur ad eam quæ Noui est testamēti, non sit gloria, sed prorsus euanescat, propter excellentem Noui testamenti gloriam. Sic quod dicit: quod glorificatum est in hac parte, intelligendū est de parte Veteris testamenti, & de gloria quæ contigit faciei Mosis. Non negat simpliciter glorificatā illā fuisse, sed respectu superemi nentis gloriæ Noui testamēti: Quod perinde est, ac si quis splendore Lunæ splendorem esse neget, non simpliciter & seorsim cōsyderatū, sed collatum splendori Solis, propter immenfam illius excellentiam. Et reuera, quid aliud erat litera legis in Vet. testam. quàm quod est splendor Lunæ in nocte? si ad gloriam Noui testameti conferatur, in quo Sol iusticię Christus, non unum tantum unius gentis angulum utcunque, sed totum terrarum orbem excellentissimo splendore illuminat?
units.tr: "For indeed what was glorified was not glorified in this respect, on account of the surpassing glory," he says. The sense is this: the ministration of the Spirit and of righteousness so far excels the ministration of death and condemnation that the glory which came to Moses, when compared with that of the New Testament, is not glory at all but altogether vanishes, on account of the excellent glory of the New Testament. Thus when he says "what was glorified in this respect," it must be understood of the part of the Old Testament and of the glory that came to the face of Moses. He does not simply deny that it was glorified, but speaks with respect to the surpassing glory of the New Testament. This is just as if someone were to deny that the light of the Moon is light, not considering it simply and in isolation, but comparing it with the light of the Sun, on account of its immense excellence. And indeed, what else was the letter of the law in the Old Testament but the light of the Moon at night, when it is set beside the glory of the New Testament, in which the Sun of righteousness, Christ, illumines with most excellent radiance not merely one corner of one nation, however small, but the whole orb of the earth?

units.la: Et hæc ipsa excellens Noui testamenti gloria, per quam obscurata est gloria Veteris, cōsimili modo obscurabitur infinita illa futurę uitę gloria, in qua non modo apostoli gloriosi erunt, sed & omnes fideles instar Solis splendescet, non amplius spiritus & iusticia, nedum litera administrabitur, sed Deus ipse facie ad faciem exhibitus, omnia erit in omnibus. Sic crescit & paulatim assurgit in immensum gloria diuinæ dispensationis, qua salutem humani generis certis ac distinctis gradibus ante legem, in lege, post legem, & postremo in futuro sæculo dispensat. Quo magis ad præfixum terminum appropinquamus, hoc magis diuinæ erga nos dignationis gloria relucet, donec tandem ad plenitudinem illius pertingamus.
units.tr: And this very excellent glory of the New Testament, by which the glory of the Old is obscured, will in like manner be obscured by that infinite glory of the future life, in which not only the glorious apostles will be, but all the faithful will shine like the Sun; no longer will the Spirit and righteousness be administered, still less the letter, but God himself will be seen face to face, and will be all in all. Thus the glory of the divine dispensation grows and gradually rises to immensity, by which he dispenses the salvation of the human race by certain and distinct stages: before the law, under the law, after the law, and finally in the age to come. The nearer we approach the appointed end, the more the glory of the divine condescension towards us shines forth, until at last we attain its fullness.

units.la: ETENIM si quod aboletur, inquit, fuit in gloria, multo magis id quod manet, est in gloria.) Græcè est simpliciter ἐν δόξῃ, ut æque erit in gloria, atque est in gloria uerti queat. Quanuis nihil esset legis æmulatoribus intolerabilius, quàm quod de abolitione legis ac Veteris testamēti prædicabatur ab Apostolo, resipsa tamē sic agebatur diuinitus, & requirebat hoc propagāda Christi ueritas, ac dispensanda salutis nostrę doctrina, ut necessario adigeretur ad inculcandum ac prędicandū aduenisse Veteris testamenti finē Christum Seruatorē, & per Euágelij gratiā aboleri legis obseruantiā. Quare consultò non dicit: si quod abolendū est, sed, si quod aboletur, nec dicit, quod est, sed, quod fuit in gloria. Iam tum enim reipsa abolebatur administratio Mosaicæ legis per Euágelium regni Dei, & gloria illius fuerat, non erat amplius. Administratio uero spiritus & iusticiæ manet. Quare recte colligit, maiorem huius quàm illius esse gloriam.
units.tr: "For if what is abolished," he says, "was in glory, much more is that which remains in glory." In Greek it is simply ἐν δόξῃ [en doxē], so that it could be rendered "it will be in glory" just as "it is in glory." Although nothing was more intolerable to the emulators of the law than what the Apostle proclaimed about the abolition of the law and of the Old Testament, nevertheless the matter was so ordered by God, and the propagation of Christ's truth and the dispensing of the doctrine of our salvation required it, that they were necessarily compelled to insist and proclaim that Christ the Saviour had come as the end of the Old Testament, and that the observance of the law was abolished through the grace of the Gospel. Therefore he deliberately does not say "what is to be abolished," but "what is being abolished," and does not say "what is," but "what was in glory." For already then the ministration of the Mosaic law was in fact being abolished through the Gospel of the kingdom of God, and its glory had been, and was no longer. But the ministration of the Spirit and of righteousness remains. Therefore he rightly concludes that the glory of this is greater than that of the other.

units.la: MVLTO magis, inquit, id quod manet, est in gloria.) Poterit hic quæri, quomodo tribuat administrationi spiritus & iusticię per seuerantiā manēdi, cum omnino sit in fine mūdi cessatura. Ipse quidem spiritus & uera iusticia manent in sempiternum, uerum administratio utriusq;, cui seruierunt per Euágelium Apostoli, & hodie quoq; seruiūt ministri Christi, non manebit, sed per plenitudinem illam diuinæ uisionis, ueræq; iusticiæ ac felicitatis, qua in futuro sæculo fruemur, prorsus cessabit, non minus quàm ipsa legis administratio per gratiā est Noui testamenti abrogata. Quid igitur est, quod hic illā manere & ob id maiore eius gloriā q; administratæ legis esse dicit?
units.tr: "Much more," he says, "that which remains is in glory." Here someone may ask how he attributes permanence to the ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness, since it will certainly come to an end at the close of the world. The Spirit itself and true righteousness do indeed last forever. But the administration of both, which the apostles served through the Gospel and which the ministers of Christ still serve today, will not remain. It will cease entirely when we enjoy the fullness of divine vision, true righteousness and blessedness in the age to come, just as the administration of the law was abolished by the grace of the New Testament. What then does he mean by saying that this administration remains, and that for this reason its glory is greater than that of the administration of the law?

units.la: Respondeo. Dicit eam manere, non quod in futuro quoq; sit sæculo duratura, quo sensu in præcedenti epistola charitatem manere dixit, sed quod non sit eam subsequutura Noui cuiusdam alterius testamenti administratio, si cut ipsa Veteri testamento successit, sed duratura fit ad finem usq; mundi. Quod si simpliciter referas hæc uerba ad Vetus & Nouum testamentum, sic ut Vetus aboleri, Nouum uero manere dicat, nulla erit quæstio. Licet enim administratio Noui testamēti, qualis est instituta à domino, & per apostolos dispensata, ultra mundi huius finem mansura non fit, ipsum tamen testamentū Nouum æternum est Ebr. 13. ideoq; in sempiternum mansurum, quod de Veteri dici non potest.
units.tr: I answer: he says it remains not because it will last into the age to come, in the sense in which in the previous letter he said that love remains, but because no other new administration will follow it, as the present one followed the Old Testament. It will endure until the end of the world. If you refer these words simply to the Old and New Testaments, so that he says the Old is abolished and the New remains, there will be no problem. For although the administration of the New Testament, as it was instituted by the Lord and dispensed through the apostles, will not last beyond the end of this world, the New Testament itself is eternal (Heb. 13), and so it will remain forever. This cannot be said of the Old.

units.la: Itaq; cum habeamus huiusmodi spē, multa libertate utimur, & nō quemadmodum Moses ponebat uelamen in facie sua, ne intenderet filij Israel in finem eius quod abolebatur. Sed occæcati sunt sensus illorū. Nam usq; ad diē hodiernū idem uelamen in lectione Veteris testamēti manet, nec tollitur uelum, quod per Christū aboletur. Sed ad hūc usq; diem cum legitur Moses uelamen cordibus illorū impositū est. At ubi cōuersi fuerint ad dominū, tolletur uelamen. Dominus enim spiritus est. Porro ubi spiritus domini, ibi libertas. Nos autem omnes retecta facie gloriā domini in speculo repræsentantes ad eandem imaginem transformamur à gloria in gloriam, tanquam à domini spiritu.
units.tr: Therefore, since we have such hope, we use great boldness, and not as Moses put a veil over his face, so that the children of Israel would not look at the end of what was being abolished. But their minds were blinded. For to this day the same veil remains at the reading of the Old Testament, and the veil, which is abolished through Christ, is not taken away. Indeed, to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts. But when they turn to the Lord, the veil will be removed. For the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. But we all, with unveiled faces, reflecting the glory of the Lord in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord.

units.la: Hactenus absoluit argumentationem suam de excellentia Noui testamenti, qua legis Mosaicæ gloria longe superatur, & administratio spiritus & iusticiæ supra administrationē litera, mortis & condemnationis euidenti collatione extollitur. Iam consequeter ex eo quod dixit: Si quod aboletur fuit in gloria, multo magis id quod manet est in gloria, occasione sumit transfeundi ad perstringenda Iudæorum occæcationem, & prædicandam Noui testamenti lucem. Transit autem hoc pacto. Itaq; cum habeamus eiusmodi spem, multa libertate utimur. Loquitur de spe permanentis Noui testamenti. Quasi dicat: Itaque cum sperēmus Nouū hoc testamentū nō ut Vetus succedēte alio aliquo nouo cessaturū sed permansurum, & hactenus quoque maiore dignū esse gloria quàm Vetus, non agimus in administratione illius timide ac solicite, sed cum magna libertate & fiducia, quicquid de Apostolatu nostro nugentur uestri magistri ac legis doctores. Sic recte respondet illis qui dicebant: præsentia illius leuis, epistolæ graues, redditq; rationem, quare tanta cum libertate doctoribus legisrefistat. Chrysoft. exponit ad hunc modū. Quoniā igitur maioribus diuina dignatione potimur q; Moses, multa fiducia utimur, hoc est, cū libertate ubiq; loquimur, nihil celantes, nihil subtrahētes, nihil dissimulātes, sed manifeste loquentes, &c. Sic mihi magis placet, ut legamus,
units.tr: Up to this point he has completed his argument concerning the excellence of the New Testament, by which the glory of the Mosaic law is far surpassed, and the administration of the Spirit and of righteousness is exalted above the administration of the letter, of death and of condemnation, by clear comparison. Now, from what he said, "If what is abolished was in glory, much more what remains is in glory," he takes the occasion to pass on to censure the blindness of the Jews and to proclaim the light of the New Testament. He makes the transition in this way: "Therefore, since we have such hope, we use great boldness." He speaks of the hope of the abiding New Testament, as if he were saying: "Since we hope that this New Testament will not cease, as the Old did, to be succeeded by some other new covenant, but will remain, and that it is also worthy of greater glory than the Old, we do not act timidly and anxiously in its administration, but with great freedom and confidence, whatever your teachers and doctors of the law may babble about our apostleship." Thus he rightly answers those who said, "His presence is weak, and his letters are weighty" (2 Cor. 10:10), and he gives the reason why he speaks with such freedom against the teachers of the law. Chrysostom explains it in this way: "Since we enjoy greater things by divine favour than Moses did, we use much confidence, that is, we speak everywhere with freedom, concealing nothing, withholding nothing, dissembling nothing, but speaking plainly," and so on. I prefer to read it so: [the reading "we use much liberty" rendered as] "let us use much liberty," as Erasmus translates it, thinking that it is an exhortation to keep Christian liberty.

units.la: mus,multa libertate utimur,q;,multa libertate utamur,sicuti uertit Erasmus,existimās adhortationem esse ad retinendam Christianam libertatem.
units.tr: (Here the unit continues the reading just noted: whether we read "we use much liberty" or "let us use much liberty," as Erasmus translates it, he takes it as an exhortation to retain Christian liberty.)

units.la: Nos admonemur hic,non modo quæ deceat ministrū Christi loquendi libertas ac fidu cia,sed ut unde illa nascatur. Vtimur,inqt,multa libertate,loquendi videlicet. Decet hæc doctrinam ueritatis. Veritatem Dei dehonestat, qui de illa obscurè,timidè, & hęsitàter loquitur. Qui de mendacio & incertis opinionib⁹ loquitur,loquatur ille obscure,intricatè,incostanter,dubitanter,& dissimulàter. Doctorem ueritatis multa decet loquendi parrhefia.
units.tr: Here we are reminded not only of what freedom and confidence of speech are fitting for a minister of Christ, but also of where they come from. "We use," he says, "much liberty" of speech, namely. Such freedom befits the doctrine of truth. The one who speaks of God's truth obscurely, timidly and hesitantly dishonours it. The one who speaks of falsehood and uncertain opinions may speak obscurely, intricately, inconstantly, doubtfully and evasively. A teacher of the truth needs much freedom of speech.

units.la: Verùm plurimùm refert, unde nascatur loquédi fiducia. Qui potētes sunt in mŭdo, ufq; adeò liberè quod uolunt loquŭntur,vt perinde audiri uelint,ac si singula uerba singula sint tonitrua. Qui doɛti sunt ac sapientes iuxta sę culum, quemadmodum se solos sapere putát, ita & omnia dicunt confideter. Minister Christi,loquitur & ipse cum fiducia ac liberè,uerū neque potétia aliqua,neq; eruditionis ac sapientię opinione inflatus, sed ex certa ueritatis persuasione,& spe hac cuius meminit Apostolus, parrhefiam loquendi diuino munere naƈtus. Præclara est hęc Apostoli spes,qua dicit: Si quod aboletur,fuit in gloria, multo magis id quod manet erit in gloria. Administratio Euangelij stulticia erat Gentibus & offendiculů Iudęis,ac præterea grauissimis persequutionibus premebatur,ita vt ministri illius ueluut expurgamenta essent huius mundi, unde magna tentatio nascebatur infirmioribus conscientijs, quàm pseudapostoli calumnijs suis vehementer acuebant. Contra hanc obicit Apostolus,tam abesse,ut propterea quicq̄ de doctrina Euangelij sui subtrahere ac dissimulare uelit,quod ea passim probris ac calumnijs dehonestetur,ut magis in assereda illa vtatur magna libertate,hac spe fultus,quod cum euanecens iam legis doctrina fuerit in gloria,multo magis futura sit in gloria administratio Euangelij non euanescens sed permanens. Confimi li modo cogitet hodie quoq; Christi minister: Si quod nulla unquam gloria sed confusione potius dignum fuit tantum gloriæ reperit in hoc sæculo,multo magis erit in gloria quod digni tate sua meretur ut sit in gloria, quantumuis iā per reprobos hæreseos damnetur, & omnis generis ignominia dehonestetur. Hac spe fretus,aget liberè & magna cum fiducia in ministerio suo,quod accepit à domino.
units.tr: But it matters greatly where the confidence of speech comes from. Those who are powerful in the world speak so freely what they wish that they want to be heard as if each word were a thunderclap. Those who are learned and wise by the standards of this age speak with confidence in everything, just as they think themselves alone wise. The minister of Christ also speaks with confidence and freedom, but he is not puffed up by any power or by the reputation of learning and wisdom. Rather, from the firm persuasion of the truth and from that hope of which the Apostle speaks, he has obtained boldness of speech as a gift from God. This hope of the Apostle is outstanding, when he says: "If what was abolished was in glory, much more what remains will be in glory." The administration of the Gospel was foolishness to the Gentiles and a stumbling block to the Jews, and moreover it was pressed down by very grave persecutions, so that its ministers were like the scum of this world. From this a great temptation arose for weaker consciences, which the false apostles fiercely sharpened with their slanders. The Apostle answers this objection: far from wishing to withdraw or dissemble anything of his Gospel's teaching because it is everywhere disgraced by insults and calumnies, he uses greater freedom in asserting it, supported by this hope: since the teaching of the law, though now fading away, was in glory, much more will the administration of the Gospel, which does not fade but endures, be in glory. In the same way, let the minister of Christ today also reflect: if what never deserved glory but rather shame has yet found so much glory in this age, much more will that which by its dignity deserves to be in glory be in glory, although it is already condemned by the reprobate as heresy and dishonoured with every kind of disgrace. Supported by this hope, he will act freely and with great confidence in his ministry, which he has received from the Lord.

units.la: ET non quemadmodum Moses,inquit,ponebat uelamen in facie sua,ne intenderent filij Israel in finem eius quod aboleturs.) Græcè est ἀκαταργούμενον, quod nescio quare interpres reddere uoluerit,quod abolebatur,cum supra eandem dictionem reddiderit,quod aboletur. Vetus interpres consultius transtulit,quod euacuatur.De splendore Mosaici uultus admodum gloriebantur Iudęi, & interim mysterium obuelationis illius uel non intelligebant, uel
units.tr: "And not as Moses," he says, "put a veil over his face, so that the children of Israel would not look at the end of what was being abolished." In Greek it is "being abolished" [ἀκαταργούμενον]. I do not know why the translator chose to render it "was being abolished," when above he rendered the same word "is abolished." The Old Translator more carefully rendered it "is made void." The Jews greatly gloried in the brightness of Moses' face, and meanwhile they either did not understand the mystery of that veiling, or they stubbornly ignored it, although in fact it was being fulfilled in them.

units.la: constanter dissimulabant, cũm tamen in ipsis reipsa adimpleretur. Eam itaq; partem hoc cõ textu sic tractat,ut nisi occęcati essent,facilè & infirmitatem suam & legis obuelationem intelligerent. Quod igitur in faciem Mosis intedere non poterant Israelitæ,ipse uerò eam ob causam uelamen vultui suo,cum ipsis loquere tur,imponébat,accommodat presenti causæ, primò per dissimilitudinem,deinde per applicationem.
