Dissimilitudo est in eo quod dicit: Et non quemadmodum Moses ponebat uelamen in facie sua, ne intenderent filij Israel in finem eius quod aboletur, ubi subintelligendū est,ita nos luci doctrinæ Euangelij,uel, splendescenti faciei Christi uelamen imponimus, ne intendant in illam credentes electi ac filij Dei,sed manifestam illius lucem contemplamur oēs. Est ergo & hęc inter Mosen & Christum dissimilitudo,quod Moses populo tectá suam faciem,Christus uerò apertam : Moses doctrinam legis obuelatam & adumbratam, Christus autem clarum & manifestum Euangelium credentibus offert. Admonet hac dissimilitudine,quá oporteat infœlices esse & prorsus oꝰcæcatos eos omnes,qui pluris faciút obuelatum Mosen,quàm clarum & perspicuum Christum,gaudent umbris legis magis quàm manifesta gratię ac ueritatis Dei luce.
units.tr: Therefore this passage treats that part in such a way that, unless they were blinded, they would easily understand both their own weakness and the veiling of the law. So, since the Israelites could not look at Moses' face, and Moses for this reason put a veil on his face when he spoke with them, he applies it to the present case, first by dissimilarity and then by application. The dissimilarity lies in what he says: "And not as Moses put a veil over his face, so that the children of Israel would not look at the end of what is being abolished." Here one must understand: so we put a veil over the light of the Gospel teaching, or rather over the shining face of Christ, so that the elect and the children of God who believe do not look at it, but all of us behold its manifest light. There is therefore this dissimilarity between Moses and Christ: Moses covered his face from the people, but Christ shows his face openly; Moses offers the teaching of the law veiled and shadowed, but Christ offers the clear and manifest Gospel to believers. This dissimilarity warns how unhappy and utterly blinded are all those who value the veiled Moses more than the clear and plain Christ, who delight in the shadows of the law more than in the manifest light of grace and of the truth of God.

units.la: Illud,ne intenderent filij Israel in finē eius (sic est in Græco εἰς τὸ τέλος) qd aboletur cum sequentibus,applicationem habet ad præsentem causam.Non sic est autem accipiendum, quasi Moses data opera ac scienter ad hoc faciem suam obtexerit,ne aliquádo Israelitæ in finem legis,Christum uidelicet, mĕtis oculos intenderent,sed intelligendum est ad hûc modû. πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἀτενίσαι τοὺς υἱοὺς Ἰσραὴλ, &c.id est, ad hoc quod non essent filij Israel intentis oculis prospecturi in finē eius quod aboletur. Et hic sensus pulchrè aperit mysterium, quod in tecta Mosis facie præcessit. Fauet illi primum illud πρὸς τὸ, quod hic idem est,quod διὰ τὸ, id est, ppterea quod:deinde uerbum ἀτενίσαι, quod futuri temporis sensu positum est. Quare non sa tis circúspectè uerterűt,ne intenderent, cum uertendum esset, propterea quod non essent intentis oculis prospecturi filij Israel in finem eius quód aboletur.Quasi dicat,Ipse Moses iá tum cum faciem suam obuelaret, futurum significabat primum,vt non intenderét ac prospiceret filij Israel in Christum finem legis,deinde,vt gloria legis aboleretur. Sic obuelatio vultus Mosaici duo portědebat,cũ quod Israelitæ non essent agnituri Christum,tùm quod lex habitura esset finem & abolenda per Christum. Descendebat de monte Moses facie illustri. Et cum loquendum esset cum Deo claritatem uultus sui non tegebat. Cum verò ægendum esset cum filijs Israel ,uelum imponebat faciei prêter solitum splendescenti. Sic erat cö parata doctrina legis. In se erat doctrina Dei, erat bona,iusta & sanƈta,nec ullis erat in conspeƈtu Dei uelata umbris sed clara & manife-
units.tr: That they might not look intently at the end of it (in Greek εἰς τὸ τέλος) which is abolished along with what follows, applies to the present case. It should not be taken as though Moses deliberately and knowingly covered his face so that the Israelites would not fix their eyes on the end of the law, namely Christ. It must be understood in this way: πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἀτενίσαι τοὺς υἱοὺς Ἰσραὴλ, etc., that is, so that the sons of Israel would not look intently at the end of what is abolished. This sense clearly brings out the mystery that preceded in the veiling of Moses' face. First, the phrase πρὸς τὸ favours it, since here it means the same as διὰ τὸ, that is, because. Second, the verb ἀτενίσαι, which is placed in a future sense. So the translators did not render carefully enough with "that they might not," when it should have been rendered "because the sons of Israel were not going to look intently at the end of what is abolished." As if he were saying: already when he veiled his face, Moses was signifying two things: first, that the sons of Israel would not look and gaze at Christ, the end of the law; second, that the glory of the law would be abolished. So the veiling of the Mosaic face bore two meanings: that the Israelites would not recognise Christ, and that the law was to have an end and be abolished through Christ. Moses came down from the mountain with a shining face, and when he had to speak with God he did not cover the brightness of his face; but when he had to deal with the sons of Israel, he put a veil on his face, which shone beyond its usual state. Thus the teaching of the law was arranged. In itself the teaching of God was good, just and holy, and in the sight of God it was not veiled by shadows in any way, but clear and manifest.

units.la: sta.Aƈ sta. At populo proposita erat obuelata, {A}ppter illius imbecillitatem, propter quam & Moses velū faciei suæ imponebat. Quod itaq; magis ad pudore Israelis faciebat, iactabat pseudapostoli quasi inde multū ad ipsos rediret gloriæ.
units.tr: But it was set before the people veiled, on account of their weakness, for which reason Moses also put a veil on his face. Therefore what served rather to the shame of the Israelites, the false apostles boasted of as if much glory returned to themselves from it.

units.la: SED occæcati sunt sensus illorum, inquit.) Quasi roget quis, quomodo rem hanc non intelligant Iudæi, respondet: Occæcati sunt sensus illorum. Quasi dicat. Quomodo intelligerent ista, cum prorsus sint sensibus occæcatis? Sic vno verbo tollit uniuersum illud offendiculum, quod erat ex contradictione Israelis, qua Euangelio pertinacissimè repugnabat, ad quos peculiariter pertinebat Christus. Quis enim mirabitur eos qui occæcati sunt, non agnoscere sed repudiare veritatis lucem? Si videas in ipsa meridie impingere cæcos, facile intelligis culpā nō esse diurnæ lucis, sed eorū q præ cæcitate sua illā non vident. Nihilo magis miramur hodie, qui fiat, quod tam multi sapientes ac prudentes veritati Dei resistūt. Experimur enim reipsa, esse sensus illorum occæcatos, vt culpa sit ipsorum, non veritatis.
units.tr: "BUT THEIR MINDS WERE BLINDED," he says. As if someone were to ask how the Jews did not understand this matter, he answers: their minds were blinded. As if he said: how could they understand these things, since their minds are utterly blinded? Thus in one word he removes the whole stumbling block that arose from the obstinacy of Israel, by which they most stubbornly resisted the Gospel, although Christ belonged to them in a special way. For who will be surprised that those who are blinded do not recognise but reject the light of truth? If you see blind men stumbling in broad midday, you readily understand that the fault lies not in the daylight but in those who, because of their blindness, do not see it. We are no more surprised today at how it happens that so many wise and prudent men resist the truth of God. For we learn by experience that their minds are blinded, so that the fault is theirs and not the truth's.

units.la: NAM vsq; ad diem hodiernū, inquit, idem velamē in lectione Veteris testameti manet.) Explicat quod dixit, sed occæcati sunt sensus eorum, imo probat. Et est sensus. Quām enim occæcati sint eorū sensus, in eo abūde satis patet, quod ad hodiernū vsq; diem, dū Vetus testamentū legunt, non intelligunt illius scopū & finem, quare velamen illud Mosaicum adhuc manet. Ergo occæcatio Israelis, per ipsum Moysen praefigurata, inde ab eo tempore quo data est lex, ad Christum vsq; toto Veteris testamenti tēpore durauit. Et ne sic quidē dū cessauit. Quare? Quia uelum hoc non nisi per Christū tollitur, dum ille agnoscitur ac recipitur. Hoc significans dicit: nec tollitur uelū, quod p Christum aboletur. Quasi dicat. Et hæc Iudæorum occæcatio, nullis signis ac portentis, nullisq; quantumuis indefessis docendi ac contecтandi laboribus tolli poterit, quandiu Christum recipere detrectant, sed durabit tantisper dum ad illum conuersi fuerint.
units.tr: "FOR UNTIL THIS DAY," he says, "the same veil remains in the reading of the Old Testament." He explains what he said, "but their minds were blinded," or rather he proves it. And the sense is this: how blinded their minds are is clear enough from the fact that, to this day, while they read the Old Testament, they do not understand its scope and end, and so that Mosaic veil still remains. Therefore the blindness of Israel, prefigured by Moses himself, has lasted from the time the law was given until Christ, through the whole time of the Old Testament, and not even then has it ceased. Why? Because this veil is removed only through Christ, when he is recognised and received. Signifying this, he says: nor is the veil removed, which is abolished through Christ. As if he said: this blindness of the Jews cannot be removed by any signs or wonders, nor by any labours of teaching and exhortation, however untiring, as long as they refuse to receive Christ; but it will last until they are turned to him.

units.la: Sed ad hunc vsq; diē cum legitur Moses, inquit, uelamen cordib. illorum impositū est. Idē repetit vt inculcet, & simul quod dixit, uelamē in lectione Veteris testamenti manet: sic expo nit, ut referat nō ad ipsum Mosen, hoc est, ad legem Mosis, sed ad ipsorū corda. Velamen, inquit, cordib. illorū impositum est. Quasi dicat. Quanuis clara sit Veteris testamenti scriptura in se, haud tamen intelligūt eam dū legitur, propterea quod corda ipsorū obducta sunt velamento, à Mose præfigurato.
units.tr: "But to this day, when Moses is read," he says, "a veil lies upon their hearts." He repeats this to press it home, and at the same time, to explain what he said, "the veil remains in the reading of the Old Testament," he so expounds it that it refers not to Moses himself, that is, to the law of Moses, but to their hearts. "A veil," he says, "lies upon their hearts." As if he said: although the Scripture of the Old Testament is clear in itself, yet they do not understand it when it is read, because their hearts are covered with the veil prefigured by Moses.

units.la: Vide autem quàm prudenter cauet, ne quo pacto ipsam legē obscuritatis accusēt. Ideo omnē hanc culpam in ipsos Iudæos reijcit, dum sensus illorum occæcatos, & in lectione Veteris testamenti dum Moses explicatur, uelamen cordibus ipsorum impositum esse dicit, quod auferri nequeat, nisi per solum Christum. Idē respondeamus & hodie, omnibus illis qui sa-
units.tr: Note how prudently he takes care not to let them accuse the law itself of obscurity. Therefore he throws all this blame on the Jews themselves, since he says that their minds are blinded, and that when Moses is explained in the reading of the Old Testament a veil lies upon their hearts, which cannot be removed except through Christ alone. We should answer the same today to all those who

units.la: cram scripturam nō Veteris modo sed & Nouī testamenti obscurum esse causantur. Quod perinde est, ac si quis cæcutientes habens ocu los Solem causetur esse obscurum & caligino sum. Corda ipsorum sunt crassissimo uelamine obducta, eoq; non simplici sed multiplici, con texto uidelicet partim ex humanæ sapientiæ fi lo, partim ex respectu magnorum uirorum, partim ex catholica & inueterata tot sēculorū consuetudine, ut philautiam, quēstum, & uen tris inanisq; gloriæ studium taceam. His uelu ti squamis obducti ipsorum sensus, lucem ueri tatis in sacris scripturis splendescētem cerne re non possunt, nec poterunt vnquā, nisi Chri stum nudum & apertum recipiant, per quem solum omnis generis uelamenta à cordibus mortalium tolluntur.
units.tr: complain that Sacred Scripture is obscure, not only of the Old Testament but also of the New. This is just as if someone with weak eyes accused the sun of being dark and misty. Their hearts are covered with a very thick veil, and that not a simple one but a manifold one, woven partly from the thread of human wisdom, partly from respect for great men, partly from the Catholic and long-established custom of so many centuries, not to mention self-love, gain, and the pursuit of the belly and of empty glory. With these veils, as with scales, their minds are covered, so that they cannot see the light of truth shining in the sacred Scriptures, and they never will be able to, unless they receive Christ naked and open, through whom alone every kind of veil is removed from the hearts of mortals.

units.la: AT ubi cōuersi fuerint ad dominum, inqt, tolletur uelamen.) In Græco legitur nō in plurali, conuersi fuerint, sed in singulari ἐπιστρέψῃ. Vulgata interpres habet: cōuersus fuerit, quasi subintelligendum sit, Israel. Meo iudicio refe rendum est ad proximè præcedēs, cor uideli cet filiorum Israel, cui impositum est uelame. Quod enim interpres uertit, uelamen cordib. illorum impositum est, in Græco habetur, uela mē super cor ipsorum impositum est. Cui sub iungit: at ubi conuersum fuerit, intellige, cor i psorum, ad dominum, tolletur uelame. Significat hoc dicens populum hunc occæcatū, cor de esse auersum à domino, ideoq; fieri nō pos se, ut liberetur à velamine cordis, & illumine tur, nisi corde conuertatur ad dominū. Qui o culis auersis retrocedit à luce, utiq; seipse pri uat vsu lucis, donec ad illā conuersus illumine tur. Sic qui corde est auersus à domino, nisi ad illum cōuertatur, non poterit à cæcitate & ob uelatione cordis sui liberari.
units.tr: "BUT WHEN THEY SHALL HAVE BEEN TURNED to the Lord," he says, "the veil will be taken away." In the Greek it is read not in the plural, "they shall have been turned," but in the singular, ἐπιστρέψῃ. The Vulgate translator has "when he shall have been turned," as if Israel were to be understood. In my judgment it refers to the nearest preceding noun, namely the heart of the sons of Israel, on which the veil has been placed. For what the translator renders, "a veil lies upon their hearts," is in the Greek "a veil lies upon their heart." To this he adds: "but when it has been turned," understand the heart of them, "to the Lord, the veil will be taken away." By saying this he signifies that this blinded people has its heart turned away from the Lord, and therefore it cannot be freed from the veil of the heart and enlightened unless its heart is turned to the Lord. He who turns away his eyes from the light, certainly deprives himself of the use of light, until he is turned to it and enlightened. So he who is turned away in heart from the Lord cannot be freed from blindness and the veiling of his heart unless he is turned to him.

units.la: Sunt qui referāt hæc uerba ad id, quod Mo fes in deserto, quoties ad dominum accedendum erat, uelum de facie sua tollebat, quo nu da & aperta fronte cum illo loqueretur, quasi fit in Græco, ... id est, quādo uerò cōuerteba tur ad dominū, tollebatur uelamen. Verum cū Græca non ad præteritum sed ad futurum tēpus accommodata legantur ad hunc modum, ... id est, quandō uerò cōuersum fuerit ad dominum, tolletur velamen, malo intelligere de futura Israelis conuersione ad dominum, qua prorsus ab hac cordis obuelatiōe liberabitur, cuius præfiguratio quædam erat in facto Mo sis, quo dum à populo ad dominum conuerte batur, uelamē de facie sua auferebat, quō aper ta fronte loquentem sibi dominum uideret.
units.tr: There are some who refer these words to what Moses did in the desert: whenever he had to approach the Lord, he took the veil from his face, so that he might speak with him with bare and open brow, as in the Greek, ... that is, "but when it was turned to the Lord, the veil was taken away." But since the Greek is read, not in the past tense but in a form suited to the future, in this way, ... that is, "but when it shall have been turned to the Lord, the veil will be taken away," I prefer to understand it of the future conversion of Israel to the Lord, by which it will be wholly freed from this veiling of the heart, of which there was a certain foreshadowing in the deed of Moses, when, as the people was turned to the Lord, he took the veil from his face, so that he might see the Lord speaking with him with open brow.

units.la: De hac cōuersione Israelis uaticinatus est Mo ses Deu. 4. dicens: Nouissimo autem tempore conuerteris ad dominum Deum tuum & au dies uocem eius, quia Deus misericors domi nus Deus tuus est. Et Rom. 11. Apostolus quē dam de illa prædixit.
units.tr: Moses prophesied of this conversion of Israel in Deut. 4, saying: "But in the latter time you will turn to the Lord your God and hear his voice, for the Lord your God is a merciful God." And the Apostle in Rom. 11 foretold something of it.

units.la: Conuersionis huius spem faciens fidelibus, non dicit,si conuersum fuerit,sed, quando cō- uersum fuerit cor eorum ad dominum, tollē- tur uelamen, significans fore tempus à Deo præfinitum,quo Israel corde suo conuertatur ad dominum, & à cæcitate sua liberetur. Et hac spe motus patienter ferebat Iudæorum contra se furias,& eos qui ex credentibus cre- dunt instruit, ne animo sint erga eos inimico, neue quid desperatius contra eos præsumát.
units.tr: In holding out to the faithful the hope of this conversion, he does not say "if it shall have been turned" but "when their heart shall have been turned to the Lord, the veil will be taken away." This signifies that there will be a time appointed by God when Israel will be turned in heart to the Lord and freed from its blindness. Moved by this hope, he patiently endured the Jews' fury against him, and he instructs those who believe from among the believers that they should not be hostile in mind toward the Jews, nor presume anything more desperate against them.

units.la: DOMINVS autem spiritus est, inquit.) Exponuntur hæc aliter atque aliter. Alij sub- iectum uolút esse in uoce spiritus,sic ut de illo prædicetur quod sit dominus. Facit hoc Ly- ranus sic dicens:Dominus autem spiritus est, id est,Spiritus sanctus est liber & libertatis do- minus. Et ante hunc Augustinus quoque sic exposuit libro secundo de Trinitate, capite decimo. Cum etiā Spiritus sanctus, inquit,do minus dictus inueniatur, ubi Apostolus ait: Dominus autem spiritus est. Et ne quisquam arbitretur filium significatum, & ideo dictum spiritum propter incorpoream substantiam, sequutus contexuit,ubi autem spiritus domi- ni,ibi libertas. Spiritum autem domini nemo dubitauerit esse Spiritum sanctum. Hæc illæ. Si in Græco esset κύριος δὲ τὸ πνεῦμα ἐστίν, pos- set sic legi,dominus autem spiritus ille est, sic ut idem esset quod, spiritus autem ille domi- nus est. Iam cum sit ὁ δὲ κύριος τὸ πνεῦμα ἐστίν, non fauet Græca lectio sententiæ Augustini, quam & Chrysostomus refutat dicēs: At non dixit: Spiritus dominus, sed, dominus spiri- tus. Multum autē interest inter hanc & illam sermonis structurā. Hæc iste. Augustinus sen- tentiā hanc amplexus est propter hæreticos, qui corporeā in Christo domino substantiam negantes,præsentē Apostoli locum ad hoc u- surpabant,ut errori suo patrocinium prætexe- rent, & dominum secundum essentiam suam, perinde atque Deum,spiritum esse conuince- rent. Et ut hanc sententiam teneret, id fecisse uidetur, quod nō satis circumspecte Græcum textum consyderauit,sed Latina translatione contentus fuit. Illa sic est cōparata,ut perinde de spiritu quod sit dominus, atq; de domino quod sit spiritus prædicari uideatur. Si dicas: dominus autem paterfamiliās est, æque de pa- trefamiliās quod sit dominus, atque de domi- no quod sit paterfamiliās prædicare uidebe- ris.Sic cum hic legimus:Dominus autem spi- ritus est,non minus de spiritu quod sit domi- nus, quàm de domino quod sit spiritus præ- dicari non immerito putabimus. At Græca in- spicientibus diuersum apparet. Consimile ac- cidit & Basilio,qui ut argumento suo inseruī- ret,in opere de spiritu sancto cap.21.sic scribit. Itaq; audiat etiam alia testimonia,quæ palam spiritum dominum appellant. Dominus,in- quit,ipse spiritus est. Item,tanquam à domino spiritu.Sic ille. Alij subiectum ponunt in uo- ce,dominus.Et hi discrepant in eo à se inuicē, quod alij intelligunt de Deo simpliciter,iuxta illud: Iohan.4. Deus autem spiritus est,alij de
units.tr: "But the Lord is the Spirit," he says. These words are explained in different ways. Some wish the subject to be in the word "Spirit," so that it is predicated of him that he is Lord. Lyranus does this, saying: "But the Lord is the Spirit, that is, the Holy Spirit is the Lord of liberty and freedom." Before him Augustine too explained it this way in the tenth chapter of the second book of his On the Trinity. "Since the Holy Spirit," he says, "is also found to be called Lord, where the Apostle says: 'But the Lord is the Spirit.' And lest anyone think that the Son is signified, and that the Spirit is so called because of an incorporeal substance, he follows up and adds: 'Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.' No one will doubt that the Spirit of the Lord is the Holy Spirit." So far Augustine. If the Greek were κύριος δὲ τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστιν [kyrios de to pneuma estin], it could be read thus: "But that Spirit is the Lord," so that it would mean the same as "But that Spirit is the Lord." But since the Greek is ὁ δὲ κύριος τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστιν [ho de kyrios to pneuma estin], the Greek reading does not favour Augustine's interpretation, and Chrysostom also refutes it, saying: "He did not say 'the Spirit is Lord' but 'the Lord is the Spirit.' There is a great difference between this word order and that one." So far he. Augustine embraced this interpretation on account of the heretics, who denied that the Lord Christ had a bodily substance and used the Apostle's passage to support this error, and sought to prove that the Lord, according to his essence, was a spirit just as God is. To maintain this view, he seems to have done what was not sufficiently careful: he considered the Greek text insufficiently and was content with the Latin translation. That translation is so constructed that it seems to be predicated of the Spirit that he is Lord just as it is predicated of the Lord that he is Spirit. If you say "the Lord is the householder," you will seem to predicate of the householder that he is Lord just as much as of the Lord that he is householder. So when we read here "But the Lord is the Spirit," we shall not unreasonably think that it is predicated of the Spirit that he is Lord no less than of the Lord that he is Spirit. But to those who examine the Greek, the matter appears otherwise. Basil suffered something similar, who, in order to fit the passage to his argument, writes thus in his work On the Holy Spirit, chapter 21: "Therefore let him hear also other testimonies which openly call the Spirit Lord. 'The Lord himself,' he says, 'is the Spirit.' Likewise, 'as from the Lord the Spirit.'" So far he. Others place the subject in the word "Lord." These differ from one another in this, that some understand it simply of God, according to that passage in John 4: "God is Spirit," while others understand it of Christ the Lord.

units.la: Christo domino. Et postremum hoc mihi re- tinendum uidetur. Nihil enim impedit quin expeditus hic sit sensus. Dixit: At ubi con- uersum fuerit (cor eorum) ad dominum, tol- letur uelamen. Iam ut hoc explicet subiungit. Dominus autem spiritus ille est. Non simpli- citer,spiritus est,sed cum articulo, spiritus ille est,inquit. Loquitur autem de spiritu,cuius se supra ministrum esse, & quem uiuificare di- xit. Quasi dicat. Dominus autem,quem præ- dico,cuius sum minister & Apostolus,non est litera,sed spiritus, spiritus ille Noui testamen- ti,spiritus uiuificans. Dispensatio Noui testa- menti in Christo domino, perficitur nō litera occidente,sed spiritu uiuificante. Hoc dicens non prædicat de essentia Christi, quod sit spi- ritus,quemadmodum hæretici nonnulli intel- lexerunt(& utinā non sint hodie,qui talē no- bis Christum proponát) sed de dispensatione & administratione Noui testamenti, quæ est in Christo & à Christo domino.Quemadmo- dum enim cum dicit:cum legitur Moses, non de persona,sed de officio ac lege Mosis loqui- tur,ita cum hic dicit:Dns autē spiritus ille est, nō tam de persona Christi loquitur, quę secū- da est sanctæ Triadis hypostasis,q; de illius di- spensatione, qua Noui testamentū dispensa- tur & administratur, significās illā esse non li- teralem & mortuā,qualis est Mosaica in Vete- ri testamento, sed spirituale ac uiuificā. Si ubi dixit: Litera occidit, spiritus uero uiuificat, statim subiunxisset:Moses aut litera illa est,pu to neminē sic desipere, qui uel de essentia uel persona Mosis, & non potius de officio ac di- spensatione illius intelligendum esse putaret. Consimili modo cū hic dicit:Dns aut spiritus est,nō cōuenit ut de persona domini, sed po- tius de dispensatione illius , ad quā Noui per- tinet testamenti administratio, intelligamus.
units.tr: This last view seems to me the one to be retained, for nothing prevents this sense from being plain. He had said: "But when their heart shall have been turned to the Lord, the veil will be taken away." Now, to explain this, he adds: "But the Lord is that Spirit." He does not simply say "is Spirit" but, with the article, "is that Spirit," he says. He speaks of the Spirit over whom he has said he is a minister, and whom he has said gives life. As if he said: "The Lord, whom I preach, whose minister and apostle I am, is not the letter but the Spirit, that Spirit of the New Testament, the life-giving Spirit. The dispensation of the New Testament in the Lord Christ is carried out not by the letter that kills but by the Spirit that gives life." In saying this he does not predicate of the essence of Christ that he is Spirit, as some heretics understood it (and would that there were none of them today who set forth such a Christ to us!), but he speaks of the dispensation and administration of the New Testament, which is in Christ and from the Lord Christ. For just as when he says "when Moses is read" he speaks not of the person but of the office and law of Moses, so when he here says "But the Lord is that Spirit" he speaks not so much of the person of Christ, who is the second hypostasis of the holy Trinity, as of that dispensation by which the New Testament is dispensed and administered, signifying that it is not literal and dead, as the Mosaic dispensation is in the Old Testament, but spiritual and life-giving. If, where he said "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life," he had immediately added "but Moses is that letter," I think no one would be so foolish as to think this should be understood of the essence or person of Moses, and not rather of his office and dispensation. In the same way, when here he says "But the Lord is the Spirit," it is not fitting that we should understand it of the person of the Lord, but rather of his dispensation, to which the administration of the New Testament pertains.

units.la: Hic itaq; locus neq; adimit Christo domino corporea carnis nostræ substantiā, quā de se- ipse post resurrectione quoq; prædicat dicēs: Palpate & uidete, quoniam spiritus carnē & ossa non habet, sicuti me uidetis habere, neq; patrocinatur illis, qui ut probēt, tres esse sub- stantiali numero & gradu distinctos spiritus, ideoq; & Christū esse spiritū,dictum hoc Apo- stoli citât:Dns est spiritus.Sic uerbi superficiē ad se rapiunt , neglecto germano illius sensu.
units.tr: This passage therefore neither takes away from the Lord Christ the bodily substance of our flesh, which he himself also affirms after the resurrection, saying: "Handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me to have" (Luke 24:39). Nor does it favour those who, to prove that there are three spirits distinct in substantial number and rank, and that therefore Christ too is a spirit, cite this saying of the Apostle: "The Lord is the Spirit." Thus they seize upon the surface of the words, neglecting their genuine sense.

units.la: Sunt qui sic exponāt:Dns aut est spiritus il- le,hoc est,dns est spiritus & anima legis.Qua- re nisi cōuertatur Israel ad dñm, nihil habebit de lege præter litera mortuā & mortiferā. Vbi uero ad illū cōuersus fuerit, habebit legē uiuā & uiuificā,quia habebit spiritum legis, ipsum uidelicet dominum, sine quo mortua lex est.
units.tr: There are some who explain it thus: "But the Lord is that Spirit," that is, "the Lord is the Spirit and soul of the law." Therefore, unless Israel is turned to the Lord, it will have nothing of the law but the dead and deadly letter. But when it has been turned to him, it will have the living and life-giving law, because it will have the Spirit of the law, namely the Lord himself, without whom the law is dead.

units.la: Quomodo autē ad propositū faciat, quod dixit: Dominus autem spiritus ille est, patet in eo quod subijcit dicens : Vbi uero spiritus domini,ibi libertas. Israel conuersus ad do- minum, liberabitur à uelo pariter , quo ob- uelatum est cor ipsius , & à seruitute litē- ræ. Quare ? Quia dominus non est litera, sed spiritus, hoc est, non dispensat literâ occi- dentem, ut Moses, sed spiritum uiuificantem: ubi autem spiritus ille domini est, ibi est libertas. Hoc est, ibi aperiuntur & illuminantur mentes, & soluuntur uincula conscietiarum, quibus & legi & peccato adeoq; & morti fuerant obstrictæ. De hac libertate Christus ipse Ioan.8. nonnulla dixisse legitur: Si filius, inquit, uos liberauerit, uere liberi eritis. Vbi pleraq; huc pertinentia annotauimus.
units.tr: How this bears on the point he made, namely "But the Lord is that Spirit," is plain from what he adds: "But where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." Israel, turned to the Lord, will be freed equally from the veil with which its heart is covered, and from the bondage of the letter. Why? Because the Lord is not the letter but the Spirit; that is, he does not dispense the letter that kills, as Moses did, but the Spirit that gives life. Where that Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. That is, there minds are opened and enlightened, and the bonds of consciences are loosed, by which they had been bound both to the law, and to sin, and so to death. Christ himself is read to have said some things about this liberty in John 8: "If the Son shall have made you free, you will be truly free." Where I have noted many things pertaining to this.

units.la: Obseruet autem diligens lector, quod cum dixisset: Dominus autem spiritus ille est, non subiecit: ubi uero dominus spiritus est, sed, ubi uero spiritus domini est. Diuersa quidem dicitur, dominus spiritus, & spiritus domini: uerum in sensu Apostoli nihil habent diuersi, sed prius p posterius declaratur, ut intelligamus, propterea uocari dominum spiritum, quod spiritum uiuificante, ac liberos reddentem in Nouo testamento dispensat, cui sensui recte subijcitur: ubi uero spiritus domini est, quibus uer bis datur domino spiritus, quæ dispensat. Perinde ac si de Mose & litera eius dicas: Moses uero litera illa est. Vbi autem litera Mosis est, ibi est captiuitas ac seruitus conscientiæ. Hinc uelut ex oppositio satis liquere puto, quomodo intelligendum sit, & quàm nihil habeat diuersi quod dicit: Dominus autem spiritus est. Vbi uero spiritus domini est, ibi libertas. Tam enim recte utrunq; de Christo domino prædicatur, quod sit spiritus ille Noui testamenti, & quod ipsius sit ille spiritus, quàm recte de Mo- se dixeris, quod sit litera illa Veteris testamenti, & quod ipsius sit ea litera, nisi quod spiritum dispensat Christus non ut seruus, sed ut dominus, Moses uero literâ administrat non ut dominus, sed ut seruus. Sane nō immerito hoc dicitur esse Christus, quod ipse de suo peculiariter dispensat. Dispensat autem spiritum suum in corda credentium. Ergo recte spiritus hic ab Apostolo uocatur, & spiritus quem dispensat ipsius spiritus appellatur. Quod perinde est ac si de calore Solis dicas: frigus enecat, calor uero uiuificat. Sol autè calor ille est. Porrò ubi Solis est calor, ibi telluris est fœcunditas. Qui dicit: Sol calor est, non de substantia illius loquitur, sed de operatione quam habet pecu liarem, propter quam & calor recte dicitur, & calor quem emittit, Solis calor uocatur.
units.tr: But let the diligent reader observe that, when he had said "But the Lord is that Spirit," he did not add "where the Lord is the Spirit" but "where the Spirit of the Lord is." The expressions "the Lord is the Spirit" and "the Spirit of the Lord" are indeed different, but in the Apostle's sense they have no difference; rather the one is declared by means of the other, so that we understand that the Lord is called the Spirit because he dispenses in the New Testament the life-giving Spirit who makes free, and to this sense is rightly joined: "where the Spirit of the Lord is," by which words the Lord is given as the Spirit whom he dispenses. It is just as if you were to say of Moses and his letter: "But Moses is that letter. Where the letter of Moses is, there is captivity and bondage of conscience." From this opposition I think it is sufficiently clear how it is to be understood, and how far what he says, "But the Lord is that Spirit. Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty," has no difference in meaning. For it is as rightly predicated of the Lord Christ that he is that Spirit of the New Testament, and that the Spirit is his, as it would rightly be said of Moses that he is that letter of the Old Testament, and that the letter is his. But Christ dispenses the Spirit not as a servant but as Lord, while Moses administers the letter not as Lord but as a servant. Indeed it is not unreasonably said of Christ that he dispenses what is his own in a special way. He dispenses his Spirit into the hearts of believers. Therefore this Spirit is rightly called Spirit by the Apostle, and the Spirit whom he dispenses is called the Spirit of him. This is just as if you were to say of the heat of the sun: "cold kills, but heat gives life. And the sun is that heat. Moreover, where the heat of the sun is, there is the fruitfulness of the earth." He who says "the sun is heat" does not speak of its substance but of the operation it has peculiarly, on account of which it is rightly called heat, and the heat it sends forth is called the heat of the sun.

units.la: Priusquâ hinc transeamus, obiter admonédus est lector, ut cogitet, q; sint omnes omniù nationū religiones, cultus, ceremoniæ, & quic quid colendi numinis gratia præsumitur, uniuersa quoq; iusticiæ studia, extra Christū mor tua & seruilia, quandoquidem teste Apostolo, Christus est spiritus, & spiritus Christi liberas mentes & conscientias efficit, quod nō sic est dictum, quod præter Christū alius quisquâ sit, qui spiritū in corda hominū dispésset, aut alius sit spiritus, qui libertatè conferat, præter Christi spiritū, sed quod unus Christus spiritum in corda suorū effundat, & unus Christi spiritus seruitutem conscietiarum tollat, & libertatem conferat. Arguat igitur libertas conscientiarum & mentiū spiritum, & spiritus Christū, ac consequeter ueros Christianos. Quis enim ueros dicat esse Christianos, in quibus nulla apparét inhabitatis Christi argumenta? Qui spiritum Christi nō habet, hic nō est eius, inquit, apostol9
units.tr: Before we pass on from here, the reader is briefly reminded to consider what all the religions, worships and ceremonies of all nations are, and whatever is undertaken in the name of honouring the divine power, together with all the pursuits of righteousness, that lie outside Christ: they are dead and slavish. For, as the Apostle testifies, Christ is the Spirit, and the Spirit of Christ makes minds and consciences free. This is not said to mean that there is anyone other than Christ who distributes the Spirit into human hearts, or that there is some other spirit which confers liberty apart from the Spirit of Christ. It means that Christ alone pours out his Spirit into the hearts of his own, and that the one Spirit of Christ removes the slavery of consciences and confers liberty. Let the liberty of consciences therefore show the Spirit of minds and the Spirit of Christ, and consequently the true Christians. For who would call them true Christians in whom no signs of Christ's indwelling appear? "Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ," he says, "is not his," says the Apostle.

units.la: NOS autè, omnes, inquit, retecta facie gloriam domini speculantes ad eandé imaginem transformamur à gloria in gloriam, tanquam à domini spiritu.) Quod dixit: At ubi conuersum fuerit ad dominum, tolletur uelamé. Dominus autem spiritus ille est, porrò ubi spiritus domini, ibi libertas, probat per exemplum eorum qui conuersi sunt ad dominū, ac spiritum illius cōsequuti. Vel, quod magis placet, per contentionē opponit fideles Christi occæcatis Iudæis, quorū cordi uelum est impositum, sic ut in finē legis qui Christus est, intendere nequeant. Ad huc usq; diem, inquit, cum legitur Moses, uelamen cordibus illorū impositum est. Gloriam faciei Mosis inspicere non possunt. At nos omnes, intellige, quotquot ad dominum còuerfi & Christiani facti, spiritum illius accepimus, abfq; omni uelamine, facie retecta, gloriam non Mosis, sed ipsius domini speculamur. Deinde, illi etiâsi hodie gloriam Mosaici uultus cernerent, ad eandem tamen imaginem haudquaquam transformarentur, at nos omnes, qui gloriam domini facie retecta speculamur ad eandem quam speculamur imaginem trásformamur à gloria in gloriam, tanquam à spiritu domini, qui hanc in nobis transformationem operatur.
units.tr: "But we all," he says, "with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord." He had said: "But when it shall have turned to the Lord, the veil will be taken away. Now the Lord is that Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." He proves this by the example of those who have turned to the Lord and obtained his Spirit. Or, what pleases more, by contrast he sets the faithful in Christ over against the blinded Jews, on whose heart a veil has been laid, so that they cannot gaze at the end of the law, which is Christ. "To this day," he says, "when Moses is read, a veil lies upon their hearts. They cannot look upon the glory of Moses' face. But we all," understand, "as many as have turned to the Lord and become Christians, have received his Spirit, without any veil; with unveiled face we behold not the glory of Moses but of the Lord himself. Further, even if they today were to behold the glory of Moses' countenance, they would by no means be transformed into the same image; but we all, who behold the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image which we behold, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord, who works this transformation in us."

units.la: NOS autem omnes, inquit.) Dubio procul non de omnibus in uniuersum loquitur, quotquot Christianam religionem profitentur. Sunt enim multi, qui cum se dominū nosse dicant, factis diuersum ostendant, ut perspicuum sit, non esse eos ad imaginē Christi trásformatos, in quibus uerba ista locum habere non possunt. Quare necesse est, ut de ueris tantum Christianis intelligantur.
units.tr: "But we all," he says. Beyond doubt he does not speak of all in general who profess the Christian religion. For there are many who, though they say they know the Lord, show the opposite by their deeds, so that it is plain they have not been transformed into the image of Christ, and these words cannot apply to them. Therefore it is necessary that they be understood only of true Christians.

units.la: RETECTA facie, inquit, gloriam domini speculantes.) Amphibolum est, an de facie domini uel fidelium loquatur. Si domini faciem intelligit, sensus est. At nos omnes non Mosis quæ tecta est, sed ipsius domini retectâ faciem, inquit illa gloriam eius speculamur. Verum magis probatur, ut de fidelium gloriam domini speculantium facie intelligatur, ut sit sensus. Obijciunt illi Mosen, qui retecta facie gloriam domini speculando, claritate uultus sui à claritate domini sit adeptus. Erat is ex omni populo unus, cui hoc contigerit. At nos, non unus & alter, sed omnes aperta facie & à pristino uelamento liberati gloriam domini speculando participes ac conformes illi reddimur.
units.tr: "With unveiled face," he says, "beholding the glory of the Lord." It is ambiguous whether he speaks of the face of the Lord or of the faithful. If he means the face of the Lord, the sense is: "But we all, not like Moses whose face is veiled, but with the Lord's own face unveiled, behold his glory." The more probable meaning, however, is that the face is that of the faithful who behold the glory of the Lord, so that the sense is this. They object to Moses, who, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, obtained from the brightness of the Lord a brightness in his own countenance. He was one man out of the whole people to whom this happened. But we, not one or another, but all, with open face and freed from the former veil, by beholding the glory of the Lord are made partakers in it and conformed to him.

units.la: GLORIAM domini speculantes.) Quod in Græco est δόξαν, pro claritate positum est, quemadmodum & in sequentibus ubi dicit, ἀπὸ δόξης εἰς δόξαν, id est, à gloria in gloriam, pro, à claritate in claritatem. Loquitur autem non de dominici corporis claritate, qualem uiderunt apostoli ante pasionem eius in monte Thabor, Matth. 17. & qualem post resurrectionem in sempiternum retinet, cui etiam corpora nostra configurabuntur, sed de clara & perspicua illius reuelatione & cognitione, in qua gloria unigeniti Dei, domini ac redemptoris omnium, imo ipsius quoq; patris tanquam in ipsius filio relucet. Gloria Christi gloria est unigeniti Dei, in qua est plenitudo gratiæ ac veritatis Dei, quam se Ioannes uidisse, dicit ca. 1.
units.tr: "Beholding the glory of the Lord." The Greek word here is δόξαν [doxan], used for brightness, as also in what follows, where he says ἀπὸ δόξης εἰς δόξαν [apo doxēs eis doxan], that is, "from glory to glory," meaning "from brightness to brightness." He speaks not of the brightness of the Lord's body, such as the apostles saw before his passion on Mount Tabor (Matth. 17.), and which he retains for ever after the resurrection, and to which our bodies also will be conformed. He speaks of the clear and manifest revelation and knowledge of him, in which the glory of the only-begotten God, the Lord and Redeemer of all, and indeed of the Father himself, shines forth as in his Son. The glory of Christ is the glory of the only-begotten God, in which is the fullness of the grace and truth of God, which John says he saw (ch. 1.).

units.la: SPECVLANTES.) In Græco est κατοπτριζόμενοι. Erasmus uertit, in speculo repræsentantes, cum posset uulgatam uersionem retinere. Significat enim id uerbi non modo impressam imaginem referre, sed & propositam contemplari. Primum est gloriā domini revelata facie cōtemplari, deinde ad imaginē illius transformari, tertio illam exprimere ac repræsentare. De primo loquitur hic Apostolus. Quare uisum est uetere retinere uersionē.
units.tr: "Beholding." The Greek is κατοπτριζόμενοι [katoptrizomenoi]. Erasmus translates it "representing in a mirror," although he could have kept the Vulgate version. For this verb means not only to reflect an impressed image but also to contemplate what is set before one. The first step is to contemplate the glory of the Lord with unveiled face; then to be transformed into his image; third, to express and represent it. The Apostle speaks here of the first. Therefore it seemed good to retain the old version.

units.la: AD eandem, inquit, imaginē transformamur.) Hoc est, conformes reddimur imagini, quam in Christo contemplamur. Imago ueteris hominis est in corpore peccati, membra habens terrestria & mundana, stuprum, immunditiam, molliciem, concupiscentiam malam, & omnis generis impietatem erga Deum, & iniquitatem erga homines. Nouus homo, qui est ex spiritu Christi, formatur ad agnitionem & imaginem eius qui condidit ipsum, Christi uidelicet, cuius membra sunt cœlestia, in omni pietate, ueritate, iusticia, & nouæ uitæ sanctimonia. Hanc Christi imaginem non modo in ipso Christo præ oculis habent & contemplantur ueri fideles, sed & in seipsis repræsentant & exprimunt, pro mensura quisq; donationis Christi. Quare omnino desipiunt, qui nisi ligneam Christi imaginem præ oculis habeant, quam colant & adorent, nihil se Christi habere putant, & interim uiuam illius imaginem ad quam transformentur prorsus non curant, imo ignorant.
units.tr: "Into the same image," he says, "we are transformed." That is, we are made conformed to the image which we contemplate in Christ. The image of the old man is in the body of sin, having earthly and worldly members: fornication, uncleanness, softness, evil lust, and every kind of impiety towards God and iniquity towards men. The new man, who is of the Spirit of Christ, is formed to the knowledge and image of him who created him, namely Christ, whose members are heavenly, in all piety, truth, righteousness and the holiness of a new life. True believers not only have this image of Christ before their eyes and contemplate it in Christ himself, but also represent and express it in themselves, according to the measure of Christ's gift each one has. Therefore they are utterly foolish who, unless they have a wooden image of Christ before their eyes, which they worship and adore, think they have nothing of Christ at all; and meanwhile they care not at all for, indeed do not even know, the living image of him into which they ought to be transformed.

units.la: A GLORIA, inquit, ad gloriam.) Quidam sic. A gloria cognitionis & gratiæ, ad gloriā uisionis beatæ. Alij à gloria Moysi ad gloriā Christi. Adhuc alij ad hunc modū: A gloria in gloriā, id est, subinde ad maiorē ac maiorem gloriam crescentes. Quemadmodum intelligunt illud: ibunt de uirtute ad uirtutem. Potest & sic exponi, à gloria domini, quam retecta facie contemplamur, in gloriam transformationis quæ in nobis perficitur. Perinde atq; facies Moysi cum à claritate diuinæ uisionis inclaresceret, à gloria in gloriam transformabatur, ita & nos à gloria imaginis Christi transformamur in eiusdem imaginis gloriam.
units.tr: "From glory to glory," he says. Some take it thus: from the glory of knowledge and grace to the glory of the blessed vision. Others take it: from the glory of Moses to the glory of Christ. Still others understand it in this way: from glory to glory, that is, growing from time to time into greater and greater glory, as they understand that other text, "they will go from strength to strength." It can also be explained thus: from the glory of the Lord, which we contemplate with unveiled face, into the glory of the transformation which is brought about in us. Just as the face of Moses, when it shone with the brightness of the divine vision, was transformed from glory to glory, so we too are transformed from the glory of the image of Christ into the glory of that same image.

units.la: TANQVAM à domini spiritu, inquit.) Magna quidem est intentæ contemplationis uis, quæ plerunq; mentes nostras in ea transformat, quæ studiosius contemplamur. At hic transformationis huius gratia tribuitur ipsi spiritui domini. Ille nanque nos regenerat, &
units.tr: "As by the Spirit of the Lord," he says. Great indeed is the power of intent contemplation, which very often transforms our minds into the things we contemplate more eagerly. But here this transformation is attributed to the Spirit of the Lord himself, for he regenerates us

units.la: ad imaginem eius cuius gloriam contemplamur, transformat. Cogitandum hic est, quis sit ille spiritus, qui transformat alios ad imaginem Dominici, alios ad imaginem Francisci. Spiritus domini Christianos homines transformat ad gloriam & imaginem domini.
units.tr: and transforms us into the image of him whose glory we contemplate. Here one must consider what that spirit is which transforms some into the image of Dominic, others into the image of Francis. The Spirit of the Lord transforms Christian men into the glory and image of the Lord.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: Argument.

units.la: Dhuc uindicat Apostolatui suo syncéritatem & singularem cognitionis Christi lucem. Deinde meminit iterum afflictionum suarum, quibus & nonnulla de consolationibus suis attexit, per quas subinde confirmabatur, ne concideret.
units.tr: Still he vindicates for his apostleship sincerity and the singular light of the knowledge of Christ. Then he again recalls his afflictions, to which he adds some of his consolations, by which he was from time to time strengthened, lest he should collapse.

units.la: CAPVT IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 4.

units.la: ROPTEREA cum ministerium hoc habeamus, ut nostri misertus est Deus, haud degeneramus, sed reijcimus occulta dedecoris, no uersantes in astutia, neq; dolo tractantes uerbum Dei, sed manifestatione ueritatis commendantes nosipsos apud omnem conscientiam hominum, in conspectu Dei.
units.tr: Therefore, since we have this ministry, as God has had mercy on us, we do not lose heart. We renounce the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness nor handling the word of God deceitfully, but by the manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.

units.la: Postquam ministerium Noui testamēti supra dignitatem Veteris longè eminere ostendit, redit ad id quod supra dixit: qui & idoneos nos fecit ministros Noui testamenti, non literæ, sed spiritus, ac ministerium suum rursus contra pseudapostolorum calumnias ab omni fraudis ac doli suspicione uindicat. Propterea, inquit, cum ministerium hoc habeamus, ut nostri misertus est Deus, hoc est, consyderantes itaq; immensam hanc Noui testamenti dignitatem, & quàm excellens nobis sit concreditum ministerium, idq; nullo nostro merito, sed potius ex singulari misericordia Dei, totis uiribus ac summo studio cauemus, ne quid in illo admittamus, quod occultæ alicuius fraudis & astutiæ dedecus spiret. Non tractamus uerbum Dei dolo malo, sed per manifestam ueritatem commendamus ministerium nostrum omnium conscientiis, idque in conspectu Dei.
units.tr: Having shown that the ministry of the New Testament far surpasses the dignity of the Old, he returns to what he said above, "who also made us fit ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit," and again he defends his ministry against the slanders of the false apostles, from every suspicion of fraud and deceit. "Therefore," he says, "since we have this ministry, as God has had mercy on us." That is: considering this immense dignity of the New Testament and how excellent the ministry entrusted to us is, and that without any merit of ours but rather from the singular mercy of God, we take every care with all our strength and utmost zeal that we admit nothing into it that breathes the disgrace of some hidden fraud and cunning. We do not handle the word of God with evil deceit, but by manifest truth we commend our ministry to the consciences of all, and that in the sight of God.

units.la: PROPTEREA, inquid, cum ministerium hoc habeamus.) Vide quam nihil inanis gloriæ spiret. Non dicit, cum tam excellentem dignitatem consequuti simus, sed, cum ministerium hoc habeamus. Deinde, non dicit, ad quod nos elegit Deus, sed, ut nostri misertus est Deus. Quibus uerbis non sua merita, sed misericordiam Dei deprædicat, quasi dicat, eramus enim omnium indignissimi, qui ad hoc ministerium uocaremur, utpote hostes ac pertequutores nominis Christi. Digni eramus potius qui perderemur. Verū incomparabili miserifericordia Dei factum est, ut ex hostibus facti A simus ministri Christi. Plenam autem & expressam misericordiæ huius depræDicationem uidere licet in ea quæ est ad Timotheū prior, capite primo.
units.tr: "Therefore," he says, "since we have this ministry." See how nothing of empty glory breathes here. He does not say, "since we have attained so excellent a dignity," but "since we have this ministry." Then he does not say, "to which God has chosen us," but "as God has had mercy on us." By these words he proclaims not his own merits but the mercy of God, as if to say: we were the most unworthy of all to be called to this ministry, being enemies and persecutors of the name of Christ. We deserved rather to perish. But by the incomparable mercy of God it came about that we, from enemies, became ministers of Christ. A full and explicit proclamation of this mercy may be seen in the first letter to Timothy, chapter one.

units.la: HAVD degeneramus,inquit.) In Græco est οὐκ ἐκκακοῦμεν. Vetus reddidit, nō deficimus, quam lectionem & recentiores nonnulli sequuntur, nec ipse Erasmus improbat, quamuis reddiderit,haud degeneramus. Obseruet hic Christi minister, in quē usum subinde consyderanda sit Euangelici ministerij superemi-nentia. Apostolus quoties de excellentia Apostolatus sui cogitabat, non inflabatur corde, nec ob illam plus sibi supercilij sumebat, sed instigabatur, ut quo sublimius esset cōsequutus ministeriū, hoc in illo fidelius uersaretur, & minus deficeret. Debet hoc exemplo ministri Christi, quoties de ministerij sui dignitate cogitat, incitari non ad fastum, sed ad solicitudinem perseuerandi ac pergendi in fide ac synceritate, quæ à fideli ministro requiritur. Cui multum concreditur, ab illo multum repetitur. Qui fidem fallit in magnis, magnæ utique perfidiæ reus efficitur. Qui collocatur in sublimi, si deciderit, quò cadit altius, hoc cadit periculosius. Hæc & quæ alia sunt his consimilia cogitanda, merito solicitum reddunt & cautum Euangelij Dei ministrum.
units.tr: "We do not lose heart," he says. In Greek it is οὐκ ἐκκακοῦμεν. The Old translator rendered it "we do not faint," a reading some more recent writers also follow, and Erasmus himself does not disapprove, although he rendered it "we do not lose heart." Let the minister of Christ observe here how often the eminence of the evangelical ministry ought to be considered. Whenever the Apostle thought of the excellence of his apostleship, he was not puffed up in heart, nor did he assume more pride from it; rather he was spurred on, so that the more sublimely he had attained the ministry, the more faithfully he would conduct himself in it and the less he would faint. By this example, whenever the minister of Christ thinks of the dignity of his ministry, he ought to be stirred not to arrogance but to anxious care to persevere and press on in the faith and sincerity required of a faithful minister. Much is entrusted to him, and of him much will be required. Whoever deceives faith in great matters is certainly made guilty of great faithlessness. Whoever is placed on high, if he falls, falls the more dangerously the higher he falls. These and similar things, when pondered, rightly make the minister of God's Gospel anxious and cautious.

units.la: SED reijcimus occulta dedecoris,inquit.) Græcē est, ἀλλ' ἀπειπάμεθα. Vulgatus interpres habet,sed abdicamus. Erasmus uertit in præterito,sed reiecimus. Mihi quoq; præteritum pro præsenti, Ebreo more,positū uidetur. Loquitur enim de re, quæ non perficitur,si semel atque iterum fiat, sed indefinentem curam ac perfectione requirit. Reijcere quæ mala sunt, opus est totius uitæ nostræ studiū requirens.
units.tr: "But we have renounced the hidden things of shame," he says. In Greek it is ἀλλ' ἀπειπάμεθα. The Vulgate translator has "but we renounce" (abdicamus). Erasmus renders it in the past tense, "but we have rejected." To me the past tense seems to be used for the present, in the Hebrew manner. For he speaks of a matter that is not accomplished if it is done once or twice, but requires an unending care and perfecting. To reject what is evil is a work that demands the study of our whole life.

units.la: OCCVLTA dedecoris.) Græcē est, τὰ κρύπτα τῆς αἰσχύνης, quod Erasmus uertit, occultamenta dedecoris. Verti poterat, latebras turpitudinis. Intelligo omnis generis fraudem, astutiam, impostură,simulationem, & fucos. Significat se Apostolus usq; adeo studere synceritati in suo ministerio, ut reijciat à se nō modo ea dedecora, quæ sint in propatulo, & conscientijs hominum obuia,sed & quæ sint κρύπτα, i.abscōdita,secreta,&occulta,quālia sunt quæ dolo & impostu-ris agūtur. Sic animati sunt,qui quod agunt, syncere & candide agūt, suntq; ueritatis sic studiosi, ut illā etiam in occultissimis seruent. Vtinam posset hoc ἀπειπάμεθα τὰ κρύπτα τῆς αἰσχύνης, dici ab illis, qui apostolorum successores uideri uolunt. Quid dico? Vtinā reijceret à se τὰ φανερὰ τῆς αἰσχύνης, & exueret tandē frontem meretriciam erubescere nescia. At quomodo abijceret à se occulta dedecora, qui de manifestis in hunc usq; diem erubescere nescīunt? Olim dicebāt: Si non caste,tamē caute. At iam nec caste nec caute uiuere curāt. Verū sic tradidit eos domi-nus in reprobum sensum,ut faciant ea summa cum impudentia,unde palàm fiat omnibus, q
units.tr: "The hidden things of shame." In Greek τὰ κρύπτα τῆς αἰσχύνης, which Erasmus rendered "hidden disguises of shame." It could have been rendered "hiding-places of baseness." I understand every kind of fraud, cunning, imposture, pretence and deceit. The Apostle means that he so strives for sincerity in his ministry that he rejects from himself not only those disgraces which lie in the open and are obvious to men's consciences, but also those which are κρύπτα, that is, hidden, secret and concealed, such as are carried out by trickery and impostures. Those are animated who do what they do sincerely and openly, and are so zealous for the truth that they keep it even in the most hidden places. Would that ἀπειπάμεθα τὰ κρύπτα τῆς αἰσχύνης could be said by those who wish to seem the successors of the apostles! What am I saying? Would that they would cast from themselves τὰ φανερὰ τῆς αἰσχύνης, the open shames, and would at last cast off the harlot's brow that knows not how to blush! But how would they cast away hidden disgraces, when to this day they do not know how to blush at open ones? Formerly people said, "If not chastely, at least cautiously." But now they take care to live neither chastely nor cautiously. But the Lord has so given them over to a reprobate mind that they do these things with the utmost impudence, whence it is plain to all that

units.la: NON Christi,sed Antichristi sint apostoli.
units.tr: Not of Christ, but of Antichrist are these apostles.

units.la: NON uersantes,inquit,in astutia, neq; dolo tractantes uerbum Dei.) Occultum dedecus erat pseudapostolorum,ut exempli gratia dicā,qui ex circuncisione erant, quod,ut scan dalum crucis Christi effugerent, & discipulos post se trahentes in carne ipsorū gloriarentur, circuncisionem prædicabant,atq; ita uerbum Euangelij Dei dolose tractates in astutia, non in synceritate ambulabāt. Quod igitur se non ambulare in astutia, neque uerbum Dei dolose tractare dicit Apostolus,sic dicit,ut interim perstringat pseudapostolos illos , qui hæc faciebant, quasi dicat, quemadmodum ambulant, & uerbum Dei tractant uestri illi magistri, qui se & Ebræos, & Christi iactant esse apostolos.
units.tr: "Not walking," he says, "in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully." The hidden disgrace was that of the false apostles, for example those who were of the circumcision. In order to escape the scandal of the cross of Christ, and to glory in the flesh of those whom they drew after them as disciples, they preached circumcision, and so, handling the Gospel of God deceitfully, they walked in craftiness, not in sincerity. So when the Apostle says that he does not walk in craftiness nor handle the word of God deceitfully, he says it in such a way that meanwhile he strikes at those false apostles who were doing these things, as if to say: this is how your teachers walk and handle the word of God, who boast that they are apostles of the Hebrews and of Christ.

units.la: Sed obsecro, an non ambulant in astutia, & uerbum Dei dolose tractant, qui in ecclesia Dei fictis uerbis negociantur, & quæstus gratia iam Pontificiam potestatem,iam patrocinia sanctorum,iam purgatorium ignem,iam sacrificium Missæ pro peccatis uiuorum & mortuorū, iam ordinum suorum præroga-tiuas,iam Papales indulgētias,& innumera alia turpisimi quæstus commenta prætexunt?
units.tr: But I ask you: do not those walk in craftiness and handle the word of God deceitfully, who in the Church of God trade in fictitious words, and for the sake of gain put forward now papal power, now the patronage of the saints, now the fire of purgatory, now the sacrifice of the Mass for the sins of the living and the dead, now the prerogatives of their orders, now papal indulgences, and countless other inventions of most shameful gain?

units.la: Obserua uero, quomodo postquam dixit, non uersantes in astutia,subiecit, neque dolo tractantes uerbum Dei. Prius est, ambulare astute ac uersute, deinde studium sequitur uerbum Dei dolose tractandi. Qui ambulant ἐν πανουργίᾳ,id est,uersutia, quo uersuta sua studia quasi uelamento quodam obducant,& interim quod quærunt obtineant , prætexunt & ipsi uerbum Dei,sed dolose tractatum. Dolosa igitur hæc uerbi Dei tractatio , non est hominum imperitorum ac simplicium , sed πανουργῶν, id est, eorum qui ex quolibet facere possunt quidlibet,unde & πανοῦργοι,id est, omnia facientes uersuti illi uocātur,qui nihil non audent, & obtinent etiam , simulando , dissi-mulando,prætexendo, comminiscendo,&c. ubi uerbum Dei in hosce homines incidit,expectandum aliud nihil est, quàm ut dolose tractetur. Et utinam hæc πανουργία non regnaret in ecclesia tot iam sæculis , idque eo loco maxime, cui plenam tribuunt Apostolicæ sedis authoritatem. Toto terrarum orbe non inueniashomines in hac panurgia exercitatio-res. Iures ipsam panurgiam iam olim eo loco fixisse sedem, cui quicquid est in reliquo orbe hypocriticum,uafrum, uersutum , & sophistī-cum,facta conspiratione coniunctum est, quo mysterium illud iniquitatis , quod Apostolus præuidit,mutuis studijs perficiant.
units.tr: Observe, moreover, how after saying "not walking in craftiness," he added "nor handling the word of God deceitfully." First comes walking in craftiness and cunning; then follows the zeal of handling the word of God deceitfully. Those who walk ἐν πανουργίᾳ, that is, in cunning, cover their crafty aims as with a certain veil, and meanwhile obtain what they seek. They also put forward the word of God, but handled deceitfully. This deceitful handling of God's word, therefore, belongs not to unlearned and simple men but to πανουργῶν, that is, to those who can make anything out of anything. Whence those cunning men are also called πανοῦργοι, that is, doers of all things, who dare nothing short of everything and obtain their ends even by pretending, dissembling, pretexting, contriving, and so on. When the word of God falls into the hands of such men, nothing else is to be expected than that it be handled deceitfully. And would that this πανουργία had not reigned in the Church for so many centuries, and especially in that place to which they ascribe the full authority of the apostolic see. In the whole world you would not find men more practised in this panourgia. You may judge that this panourgia has long since fixed its seat in that place, to which everything in the rest of the world that is hypocritical, sly, crafty and sophistical has been joined by united conspiracy, so that they may bring to completion, by mutual zeal, that mystery of iniquity which the Apostle foresaw.

units.la: SED manifestatione ueritatis, inquit, cō-mendantes nosipsos apud omnem conscien-tiam hominum,in conspectu Dei.) Rursus inculcare uidetur, quod supra in calce capitis secundi dixit ad hunc modum:Non enim su-mus ut pleriq; cauponantes sermonem Dei, sed uelut ex synceritate , sed uelut ex Dec, in cōspectu Dei per Christum loquimur. Ve-rum rum non tantum in genere tribuit sibi studiū A lium nostrum,in his qui pereunt uelatū est, in quibus Deus huius sæculi excæ-cauit sensus incredulorum,ne illucescat illis lumen Euangelij glorię Christi,qui est imago Dei. Non enim nosipsos prę-dicamus, sed Christum Iesum dominū, nos autē seruos uestros propter Iesum. Quoniam Deus est qui iussit è tenebris lucem illucescere, qui luxit in cordibus nostris ad illuminationem cognitionis gloriæ Dei in facie Iesu Christi.
units.tr: "But by the manifestation of the truth," he says, "commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God." He seems again to press what he said above at the end of the second chapter: "For we are not, like many, peddlers of the word of God, but we speak in sincerity, as from God, in the sight of God, through Christ." Yet he does not ascribe zeal for sincerity and truth to himself in general only; it is veiled among those who perish, in whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelieving, lest the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine upon them. "For we do not preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus' sake. For God, who commanded light to shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ."

units.la: synceritatis ac ueritatis,sed in ijs potissimum, quæ pseudapostoli subuertere moliebantur. Loquitur enim præcipuè de abrogatione legis Mosaicæ,deq; incorporatione gentium in ecclesiam Dei,quâ utranq; non modo non docebant pseudapostoli, sed & quibus poterant modis impedire conabantur, & hanc ob causam plurimum ipsi negocij inter circuncifos facessebant,quibus ut sese cōmendarent, Mosen cum Christo coniungebant. Ipse uero ut Christum syncere ac fideliter prædicaret, ueritatē Dei,quam circuncifi ferre non poterant, manifestabat ubiq;, sic ut Petrum quoq; repre henderet, quod non recto pede ad ueritatem Euangelij ingrederetur, dum Gentes suo exemplo iudaizare cogebat.Galat.2.Magni momenti res erat,ueritatē Christi sic manifestare, ut in uno illo constaret omnem nostram sitam esse salutem, ad quem scopum Apostolus iste collimabat ubiq;, quò referendum esse iudico quod hic se ueritatem manifestare dicit.
units.tr: ...of sincerity and truth, but especially in those matters which the false apostles were striving to overthrow. For he speaks chiefly of the abrogation of the Mosaic law and the incorporation of the Gentiles into the Church of God. The false apostles not only did not teach either of these, but tried by every means to hinder them, and for this reason they caused Paul a great deal of trouble among the circumcised, to whom they recommended themselves by joining Moses with Christ. Paul, however, so that he might preach Christ sincerely and faithfully, made plain everywhere the truth of God, which the circumcised could not bear. So much so that he also rebuked Peter, because Peter did not walk on the straight path to the truth of the gospel, while he compelled the Gentiles by his example to Judaize (Gal. 2). It was a matter of great moment to make the truth of Christ so clear that it stood firm in this one thing, that all our salvation rests in him. Towards this goal the Apostle aimed everywhere, and to this, I judge, we should refer what he says here, that he makes the truth manifest.

units.la: COMMENDANTES nosipsos,inquit, apud omnē conscientiā hominū.) Hoc est,sistentes nos , quales simus, & quid sentiamus, cora conscietijs omniū. Non quærimus latebras,nō subterfugimus cuiusquà conscientiā, sed palam ac diserte coram omnibus ueritatem Dei docemus ac manifestamus. Sic intelligo quod in Græco est συνιστῶντες,& interpretes uer terū cōmendantes, ne quis quærendū putet, quomodo se per ueritatis huius manifestationem omniū conscientijs cōmendauerit Apostolus,cum propter illa quàmplurimis displi-cuerit,placuerit uero paucis.Non dicit se gra-tiam omnium hominum ueritatis huius manifestatione quærere, & hoc se illis proposito commendare, sed sistere se ac notum facere omnibus,quid uere & per omnia sentiat ac doceat,ideoq; ueritatem Dei absque omni dissimulatione manifestare omnibus.
units.tr: "Commending ourselves," he says, "to every man's conscience." That is, presenting ourselves as we are and as we think, before the consciences of all. We do not seek hiding places, we do not flee from anyone's conscience, but openly and plainly, before all, we teach and make manifest the truth of God. So I understand the Greek συνιστῶντες [synistōntes], which the translators render as commending. Lest anyone think it needs asking how the Apostle commended himself to the consciences of all by this manifestation of the truth, since on account of these things he displeased very many and pleased only a few: he does not say that he seeks the favour of all men by manifesting this truth, and that he commends himself to them with this aim. He says rather that he presents himself and makes himself known to all, as to what he truly and in every respect thinks and teaches. Therefore he manifests the truth of God to all without any pretence.

units.la: Qui uersute agunt,sic docent & scribunt,ut nullius hominis conscientiæ nudos se sistant. Veritatem enim Dei ,præsertim quatenus in controuersia est, & multorum odijs exposita, cumq; periculo coniuncta,non manifestát,sed uel dissimulát in uniuersum , uel uocibus ambiguis sic inuolutam tradunt, ut nemo facile intelligat,quid uere sentiat.Ab hac astutia scribit Apostolus esse se prorsus alienum.
units.tr: Those who act craftily teach and write in such a way that they do not present themselves naked to anyone's conscience. For they do not manifest the truth of God, especially where it is in controversy, exposed to the hatred of many and joined with danger. Instead they either dissemble it altogether, or hand it down wrapped in ambiguous words, so that no one easily understands what they truly think. From this cunning the Apostle writes that he is wholly removed.

units.la: Quàm autem religiose omniū se conscientijs per manifestationem ueritatis nudum ac manifestum exhibuerit, in eo exprimit, quod subijcit dicens:in conspestu Dei. Quasi dicat. Haud aliter, quàm si loquamur & agamus in ipso conspestu Dei,sitq; negocium nobis non cum hominum tantum conscietijs,sed & cum ipso Deo,in cuiusconspestu nihil loci est ullis imposturis,quibus utuntur illi, qui alieni sunt à religione Dei, & hoc tantum agunt, ut uel fallant conscientias hominum, uel se falso illis insinuent.
units.tr: How scrupulously he has shown himself naked and manifest to the consciences of all, through the manifestation of the truth, he expresses in what follows, saying, "in the sight of God." As if he said: "We speak and act just as if we were doing so in the very sight of God. Our business is not only with the consciences of men, but with God himself, in whose sight there is no room for those impostures which are used by people who are estranged from the religion of God, and who aim only either to deceive men's consciences or to insinuate themselves into them falsely."

units.la: Quod si adhuc uelatum est Euange-
units.tr: But if our gospel is still veiled

units.la: lium nostrum,inquit.) Græcè sic legitur: εἰ δὲ κεκαλυμμένον τὸ εὐαγγέλιόν ἡμῶν, id est, Si uero etiam uelatū Euangelium nostrū.Erasmus reddidit: Quod si adhuc, uocula, adhuc,non est in textu. Apparet euin legisse ἐν pro ἐπὶ. Deinde ambiguū est, an cum dicit:Euangeliū nostrum,sibijpsi specialiter uindicet Euangeliū quod prædicabat,uel sic illud uocet, quod cómune sit credentiū. Sane utrolibet sensu capi potest. Erat enim ipsius Euangelium, propterea quod ab ipso prædicabatur, & erat cómune ipsi cum Corinthijs,propterea quod ab illis esset acceptum, imò diuinitus ad eos missum.Sic idem Euangelium & Dei est,& Christi,&Apostoli & fidelium.Dei, à quo missum est,Christi,de quo , apostoli per quem prædicatur, fidelium, quibus diuinitus est destinatum,& ab illis etiam acceptum.'
units.tr: ...he says. In Greek it reads: εἰ δὲ κεκαλυμμένον τὸ εὐαγγέλιόν ἡμῶν [ei de kekalymmenon to euangelion hēmōn], that is, "But if our gospel is also veiled." Erasmus rendered it "But if still," but the word "still" is not in the text. It seems he read ἐν for ἐπὶ. Next, it is ambiguous whether, when he says "our gospel," he specially claims for himself the gospel that he preached, or calls it that because it is common to believers. Indeed it can be taken in either sense. It was his gospel, because it was preached by him, and it was common to him and the Corinthians, because it had been received by them, indeed sent to them divinely. So the same gospel is God's, and Christ's, and the Apostle's, and the faithful's: God's, by whom it was sent; Christ's, of whom it tells; the Apostle's, through whom it is preached; the faithful's, to whom it was divinely destined and by whom it was also received.

units.la: Quid est autem,quod non dicit:Si Nouum testamentū,uel si administratio spiritus, aut,si Christus uelatus est,sed,si Euangeliū, & quare nō dicit,si Euangeliū Dei, sed,si Euangeliū nostrū uelatū est?Has uoces Nouū testamētū, spirispiritus, Christus, non rapiebât pseudapostoli ad diuexandum, quemadmodum uocé Euangelij, sub nomine Pauli diuexabant, uocantes Euangelium Pauli, per singularem contemptum, eo uidelicet modo, quo nostra ætate aduersarij doctrinâ ueritatis Christi contumeliæ gratia Euangelium Lutheri uocare cœperunt. Haud igitur cædes illorum malitiæ uocat absque pudore doctrinam Christi quam prædicabat suum Euangelium, significâs se omnino illud absq; ullo pudore pro suo agnoscere, quantumuis ab illis proscinderetur.
units.tr: But why does he not say "if the New Testament," or "if the ministry of the Spirit," or "if Christ is veiled," but "if the gospel"? And why does he not say "if the gospel of God," but "if our gospel is veiled"? The false apostles did not seize upon these words, New Testament, Spirit, Christ, to deride them, as they derided the word gospel under the name of Paul, calling it "the gospel of Paul" out of singular contempt. In the same way our adversaries in our own age have begun to call it "the gospel of Luther" in order to insult the doctrine of Christ's truth. So he did not, out of spite, shamelessly call the doctrine of Christ which he preached "his gospel," signifying that he acknowledged it without any shame as his own, however much they tore it apart.

units.la: IN his qui pereunt, inquit, uelatum est.) Exponit qui nam illi sint, in quibus uelatum est Euangelium. Et hac expositione reijcit ab illo culpam ac transfert in eos, qui lucis illius participes fieri non poterant, & hos sic describit, ut liquido appareat causa, propter quam uelatum sit in ipsis Euangelium, quod tamen in multis alijs clarissima lux est. Poterat dicere, Si uelatum etiam est Euangelium nostrum, id quod mihi magistri uestri obijciût, uelatum est non in omnibus, sed quibusdam tantum, qui illud malo quodâ studio auersantur. Verum maluit eos sic describere, ut liquidum fit tales eos esse in quibus nequeat habere locû lux Euangelij. Sic dicit: In his qui pereunt uelatum est. Depingit autem eos tribus teterrimis coloribus, uocans eos incredulos, excæcatos, & pereuntes, ut mirû non sit in talibus uelatum esse Euangelium. Quod perinde est, ac si quis ludi literarij magistro cuipiam obiciat, disciplinâ ipsius esse inanè ac frustranea, ille autè respondeat: Si inanis est Scholæ meæ disciplina, inanis est in ijs q sunt immorigeri, obstinati, & tandè malo mortis gñe periturî.
units.tr: "Among those who perish," he says, "it is veiled." He explains who those are in whom the gospel is veiled. By this explanation he removes the blame from the gospel and transfers it to those who could not share in that light. He describes them so that the cause of its being veiled in them clearly appears, although in many others it is the clearest light. He could have said: "If our gospel is also veiled, as your teachers object, it is veiled not in all, but only in certain people who turn away from it with some wicked zeal." But he preferred to describe them so that it is plain they are such people in whom the light of the gospel cannot find a place. So he says: "Among those who perish it is veiled." He paints them in three most hideous colours, calling them unbelieving, blinded, and perishing, so that it is no wonder that the gospel is veiled to such people. It is just as if someone were to object to a schoolmaster that his teaching is empty and fruitless, and he replied: "If the discipline of my school is empty, it is empty among those who are unruly, obstinate, and who will at last perish by a kind of evil death."

units.la: IN his qui pereût, inquit, uelatû est.) Rem eandem in priore ad Corinthios capite primo alijs uerbis expressit dicens. Nam sermo crucis ijs quidem qui pereunt stultitia est, at nobis qui seruamur potentia Dei est. Quod illic uocat sermonem crucis, uocat hic Euangelium suum, & quod hic uelatum esse, illic stulticiam uocat. Utrunq; autè tribuit ἀπολλυμένοις, id est, pereuntibus. Qui uero sunt illi pereuntes? An non totum genus humanum in perditione est propter corpus peccati? Et quomodo ij perire dicuntur, qui Euangelium Dei non accipiût? Respondeo, Aliud est esse in condemnatione, ac perditione dignum, & aliud perire. Per peccatum facti sumus omnes digni qui perdamur in uniuersum. Verum non perduntur in sempiternum, quotquot per gratiam Christi à perditione seruantur, pereunt uero, quotquot illius participes non fiunt. Et hos uocat Apostolus pereuntes, non hic tantum, sed & supra cap. secundo, & primo Cor. 1. quibus opponit σωζομένοις, id est, eos qui seruantur. Quod autem Christus Lucæ 19. dicit: Venit filius hominis quærere & saluû facere quod perierat, non est de iltis ἀπολλυμένοις omne salutis gratiâ respuen tibus, ideoque incurabiliter pereuntibus, sed in uniuersum de toto humano genere intelli-
units.tr: "Among those who perish," he says, "it is veiled." In the first chapter of his earlier letter to the Corinthians he expressed the same thing in other words: "For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who perish, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God" (1 Cor. 1). What there he calls the word of the cross, here he calls his gospel; and what here he says is veiled, there he calls foolishness. He attributes both to τοῖς ἀπολλυμένοις [tois apollymenois], that is, to those who perish. But who are those who perish? Does not the whole human race stand in destruction on account of the body of sin? And how are those said to perish who do not receive the gospel of God? I answer: it is one thing to be worthy of condemnation and destruction, and another to perish. Through sin we were all made worthy to be destroyed, in general. But not all who are saved from destruction through the grace of Christ are destroyed for ever. Those perish who do not become partakers of that grace. These the Apostle calls perishing, not only here but also above in chapter 2, and in 1 Cor. 1, and he opposes to them τοῖς σωζομένοις [tois sōzomenois], that is, those who are being saved. As for what Christ says in Luke 19, "The Son of man came to seek and to save that which was lost," this is not to be understood of those ἀπολλυμένοις [apollymenois] who reject all the grace of salvation, and who therefore perish beyond cure,

units.la: gendû quod in Adamo morti ac perditioni facti erat obnoxium, de talibus uidelicet, qui gratiam salutis non recusant, sine qua omnino essent perituri.
