Quemadmodû igitur transgressioni primi nostri parétis debemus, quod perditione facti sumus digni, ita gratiæ Seruatoris nostri Christi acceptû ferre conuenit, quod nô sumus ex illis quos Apost. uocat pereútes.
units.tr: but in general of the whole human race, which in Adam had been made liable to death and destruction, namely of those who do not refuse the grace of salvation, without which they would certainly perish. Just as we owe to the transgression of our first parent that we were made worthy of destruction, so it is fitting that we ascribe to the grace of our Saviour Christ the fact that we are not among those whom the Apostle calls perishing.

units.la: Obserua uero quod non dicit: in his qui peribunt, quemadmodû non dicit, in his qui perierût, sed, in ijs qui pereunt. Sic perditionem omnimodam tribuit nec futuro iudicio, nec originali parentum nostrorum transgressioni, sed obstinatæ incredulitati gratiam oblatæ salutis pertinaciter respuenti, per quam solum à perditione liberamur.
units.tr: Observe, moreover, that he does not say "among those who will perish," just as he does not say "among those who have perished," but "among those who perish." So he attributes utter perdition neither to the future judgement nor to the original transgression of our parents, but to obstinate unbelief, which stubbornly refuses the grace of salvation offered, the only means by which we are freed from destruction.

units.la: IN quibus Deus huius sæculi, inquit, excæcauit sensus incredulorû.) Qui sint pereuntes illi, in quibus Euangelium uelatum est, consequenter explicat. Si diceret simpliciter, quorum sensus Deus huius sæculi excæcauit, ne illucesceat illis lux Euágelij, nô satis expeditus esset sensus. Iá cû dicit: in quibus Deus huius sæculi excæcauit sensus, & addit, incredulorû, significat quidé excæcatione hanc fieri in pereuntibus, uerû nonnisi talibus, qui sint increduli. Incredulus autem dici nô potest, cui nihil dû est prædicatû de Christo. Quomodo n. credi potest in eû de quo nihil est auditû? Quemadmodû hyeme de arbore iudicari nô potest, sterilis ne sit uel fertilis, donec æstate qualis sit deprehêdatur. Tempus enim fructificandi nô est hyeme sed æstate. Et quemadmodû noctur na durante caligine de cæcis iudicari non potest, in qua etiam ij qui uidendi facultatem habent, nil cernere possunt, ita de credulitate & incredulitate non potest ferri sententia, ubi nô sonat uox uerbi Dei, ubi Euangelium ne audi tum quidem, nedum fide est acceptum uel incredulitate reiectum. Quare uigilâter adiecit, incredulorû. Euenit ut & electi nonnunquam ad fidê Christi tardius accedât, sic ut auditum uerbi Dei aliquandiu respuant, imo & persequantur, id quod in hoc ipso accidit apostolo. Ea aût tergiuersatio nô potest uocari incredulitas, quia sequenti fide tollitur, sicuti tardior fructificatio nô recte uocaretur sterilitas, propter sequente fertilitatem. Imo etiamsi uoces eam temporariam incredulitatem, excæcatio ni tamen non est obnoxia, quæ contingit illis tantum incredulis, qui sunt ex reprobis & perituris, sicut hæc Apostoli uerba perspicue docet. Deus huius sæculi, inquit, excæcat sensus incredulorû. Quorû? Qui sunt ex pereûtibus. Dicit enim. In his qui pereût, in quibus Deus huius sæculi excæcauit sensus incredulorum.
units.tr: In whom, he says, the God of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers.) He next explains who those perishing people are in whom the Gospel is veiled. If he had simply said, "whose minds the God of this age has blinded, so that the light of the Gospel should not shine on them," the meaning would not be sufficiently clear. But since he says "in whom the God of this age has blinded the minds," and adds "of unbelievers," he signifies that this blinding happens to those who are perishing, but only to such as are unbelievers. Yet one cannot be called an unbeliever to whom nothing has yet been preached about Christ. For how can one believe in him of whom nothing has been heard? Just as in winter one cannot judge whether a tree is barren or fruitful, until its character is discovered in summer; for the time of bearing fruit is not winter but summer. And just as in the night, when the darkness is thick, one cannot judge the blind, since even those who have the power of sight can see nothing, so no verdict can be passed on belief and unbelief where the voice of the Word of God does not sound, where the Gospel has not been heard, much less received in faith or rejected in unbelief. Therefore he carefully added "of unbelievers." It happens that even the elect sometimes come to faith in Christ more slowly, so that for a time they reject the hearing of the Word of God, and even persecute it, as happened to the Apostle himself. But such shilly-shallying cannot be called unbelief, because it is removed by later faith; just as a slower fruiting would not rightly be called barrenness, on account of the later fertility. Indeed, even if you call that a temporary unbelief, it is not liable to blinding, which falls only on those unbelievers who are of the reprobate and the perishing, as these words of the Apostle clearly teach. The God of this age, he says, blinds the minds of unbelievers. Of whom? Those who are of the perishing. For he says: "In those who are perishing, in whom the God of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers."

units.la: Quapropter summopere cauendum est, ne temere pro excæcatis ac pereuntibus habeamus eos, quos hodie Euangelio salutis nostrę côtradicere & obluctari, uidemus. Adhuc qui dê uelatû illis est Euangeliû, ut ueritatê illius non uideant, at quandiu duratura sit in illis ista obuelatio, solus ille nouit qui quos uult &c. & quando uult ad ueritatis suæ cognitionem uocat, & uocatos illuminat: quemadmodum non debemus securi de omnium eorum esse salute, qui propere ac facilè doctrinâ Euangelij amplectuntur. Nam dubio procul multi sunt inter illos, qui ad tempus credant, & tentationis sint tempore recessuri, & hodie quoq; locum habet illud: primi nouissimi, & nouissimi primi. Hæc quidem satis sunt perspicua. Verùm non est concors omnium sententia, ne apud veteres quidem, quem nam sæculi huius Deum, incredulorum sensus excæcantem, uocet, dicens: in quibus Deus huius sæculi, uel qui, Græcè, αἰὼν ὁ τοῦτο, excæcauit, &c. Nam alij referunt ad Satanam, alij ad ipsum uerum Deum. Lyranus de utroq; exponi posse sentit, quemadmodum & Commentarij qui Hieronymo tribuuntur. Chrysostomus uero, Theophilactus & Ambrosius quoq; ad uerum Deum referunt. Et Augustinus lib. 21. cap. 2. contra Faustum Manichæum sententiam hanc sic quorundam esse dicit, ut si multa approbet, ac doceat, quomodo nō sit incōueniens uero Deo excæcare mentes incredulorum, ac tradere illos in reprobum sensum, & obdurare, & quæ alia illi consimilia palam in scripturis tribuuntur.
units.tr: Therefore we must take great care not to rashly regard as blinded and perishing those whom we see today resisting and struggling against the Gospel of our salvation. The Gospel is indeed veiled from them, so that they do not see its truth; but how long this veiling will last in them, only he knows who calls whom he wills, &c., and when he wills calls them to the knowledge of his truth, and enlightens those called; just as we must not be secure about the salvation of all those who quickly and easily embrace the doctrine of the Gospel. For without doubt there are many among them who believe for a time and will fall away in the time of temptation; and even today that saying holds: the first shall be last, and the last first. These things are quite plain. But the opinion of all is not in agreement, not even among the ancients, as to which God of this age it is who blinds the minds of unbelievers, when he says: "in whom the God of this age," or "who," in Greek, ὁ θεὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου, has blinded, &c. For some refer it to Satan, others to the true God himself. Lyra thinks it can be explained of either, as do the commentaries that are attributed to Jerome. But Chrysostom, Theophylact and Ambrose also refer it to the true God. And Augustine, in book 21, chapter 2, against Faustus the Manichaean, says that this opinion belongs to certain people in such a way that, while they approve and teach many things, it is not inconsistent for the true God to blind the minds of unbelievers, to hand them over to a reprobate mind, and to harden them, and other things like these that are plainly ascribed to him in the Scriptures.

units.la: Alij exponunt de Satana, præsertim recentiores, ex eo forsan moti, quod Satanam conuenientius quàm uerum Deum, sæculi huius Deum uocari existimant. Sanè quod me attinet, si uspiam in scripturis legerem uerum & unicum cœli ac terræ Deum, cum hac specifica tione uocari Deù huius sæculi, uel huius mundi, magis placeret Chrysostomi sententia, quàm alio rum quatenus de uero Deo locum hunc exponit. In Genesi quidem cap. 21. Versu. 33. de Abraham legimus, quod in Beersheba plantarit nemus, & inuocarit ibi nomen domini Dei sæculi. Et Esa. 40. uers. 27. legitur ad hunc modum. An ignoras? an nō audisti? De sæculi dominus, creator finium terræ. Verù quoniam uox עולם id est, sæculum, plerunq; pro sempiterno accipitur, ut עולם idem sit, quod Deus sempiternus, quàuis in Esaiæ loco haud incommode de hoc sæculo accipi queat, deinde Apostolus non simpliciter dicit: Deus sæculorum, sed, Deus huius sæculi, existimo simpliciter esse, ut de Satana exponamus, quæ & Christus mundi huius principem uocat, & hic Apostolus quoq; de illo Ephes. 2. ad hunc modum scribit: Et uos cum essetis mortui delictis ac peccatis in quibus aliquādo ambulastis iuxta sæculum mundi huius, iuxta principe, cui potestas est aeris, qui est spiritus, nunc agens in filijs contumacibus. Quo sensu princeps huius sæculi uocatur Satan, eo potest & Deus sæculi huius uocari. Tà enim proprie nō est princeps quàm non est Deus huius mundi, uocatur autem utrunq; propter reprobos, qui per sæculū hoc intelliguntur, in quibus agit, dominatur, ac regnat, quos habet sibi ad quæ vult omnia seruos ac morigeros, ut non sit quærendum,
units.tr: Others explain it of Satan, especially more recent writers, perhaps moved by this, that they think it more fitting to call Satan the God of this age than the true God. Indeed, as far as I am concerned, if I were to read anywhere in the Scriptures of the true and only God of heaven and earth being called by this specific designation, the God of this age or of this world, I would prefer Chrysostom's opinion to the others, insofar as they explain this passage of the true God. In Genesis chapter 21, verse 33, we read of Abraham that he planted a grove at Beersheba and called there on the name of the Lord, the God of the age. And Isaiah 40, verse 27, reads in this way: "Do you not know? Have you not heard? The Lord of the age, the creator of the ends of the earth." But since the word עולם, that is, age, is generally taken for everlasting, so that עולם means the same as the everlasting God; although in the passage of Isaiah it could quite fittingly be understood of this age; and since the Apostle does not simply say "God of the ages" but "God of this age," I think it is simply right that we should explain it of Satan, whom Christ also calls the prince of this world, and whom this same Apostle in Ephesians 2 describes in this way: "And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince who has power over the air, the spirit who now works in the sons of disobedience." In the sense in which Satan is called the prince of this age, God too can be called the God of this age. For neither is he properly the prince, since he is not the God of this world, yet both are so called on account of the reprobate, who are understood by this age, and in whom he acts, rules and reigns, whom he has as slaves and obedient servants for all that he wills, so that it is not to be asked

units.la: quomodo sensus illorum excæcare possit. De ipsa excæcatione nō est ut hic loquamur. Dixmus de illa Matth. 13. Ioan. 12. & Esa. 6. & de obdurationem cordiū Rom. 1.9.11. Alijs modis excęcat Deus ipse, alijs propheta Esa. 6. alijs Satan, alijs tenebrę mentiū. 1. Ioan. 2. alijs propria malitia Sap. 2. Quemadmodum & corporis excæcatio alia per Deum fit, alia per Solem, alia per tenebras, alia p homines, alia alio quopiā casu, sunt qui seipsi excæcauerint. Et illuminat corpus ipse Deus, illuminat Sol, illuminat dies, illuminat accensa lucerna. Mentes quoque Deus illuminat, Christus illuminat, Spiritussan stus illuminat, Apostolus illuminat, Euangeliū illuminat. Hæc omnia recte dicuntur, sic tamen ut à summo illo omnium rectore ac dispensatore Deo uel iustissimo iudicio uel clementissima gratia disponantur.
units.tr: how he can blind their minds. We are not here to speak about blinding itself. We have spoken of it in Matthew 13, John 12, Isaiah 6, and of the hardening of hearts in Romans 1, 9, 11. God blinds in one way, the prophet in Isaiah 6 in another, Satan in another, the darkness of lies in another (1 John 2), and one's own wickedness in another (Wisdom 2). Just as the blinding of the body also happens in different ways: some by God, some by the sun, some by darkness, some by men, some by another chance, and some have blinded themselves. God himself enlightens the body, the sun enlightens, the day enlightens, a lit lamp enlightens. God enlightens minds too; Christ enlightens, the Holy Spirit enlightens, the Apostle enlightens, the Gospel enlightens. All these things are rightly said, yet in such a way that they are ordered by that supreme director and steward of all, God, either by his most just judgment or by his most merciful grace.

units.la: NE illucescat illis lumen Euangelij gloriæ Christi, inquit, qui est imago Dei.) Quorsum Deus huius sæculi Satan sensus incredulorum excæcauerit, istis uerbis exprimit. Dubio procul, excæcationis illi finis est, ut salute eorum quos excæcat impediat, & miseros in perditione retineat. Hoc agenti opus est, ut omnibus modis caueat, ne ad cognitionem ueritatis perueniant, aut si aliquo pacto splendore lucis illius tangantur ex eo magis occæcétur quā illuminētur. Quare primum illius studiū est, ut caueat ne qua occasione illis lumen veritatis illucescat. Regnat enim in tenebris & sic miseros dementat, ut se in nescio qua luce uersari putent, cum toti sint errorum tenebris immersi.
units.tr: LEST the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine on them, he says.) By these words he expresses for what purpose Satan, the God of this age, has blinded the minds of unbelievers. Without doubt the end of this blinding is to hinder the salvation of those whom he blinds, and to keep the wretched in perdition. The one who is doing this must take every care to prevent them from coming to the knowledge of the truth; or, if they are touched in some way by the brightness of that light, to take care that they are blinded more by it than enlightened. Therefore his first concern is to take care that the light of truth does not shine on them by any opportunity. For he reigns in darkness and so drives the wretched out of their minds, that they think they are living in some light or other, when they are wholly immersed in the darkness of errors.

units.la: Hoc illius studium exprimit Apostolus dicens: ne illucescat illis lumen Euangelij gloriæ Christi. Etenim ubi lumen hoc mentib. hominum illucescit, illuminantur ad cognoscendū ueritatem Dei, perq; cognitione illi liberi redduntur è laqueis Diaboli, resipiscunt, credunt & seruantur. Vnde & Christus Ioan. 8. dixit: Si manseritis in sermone meo cognoscetis veritatem, & veritas reddet uos liberos. Et sic Apostolus 1. Timoth. 2. Qui uult, inquit, omnes homines saluos fieri, & ad cognitionem ueritatis uenire.
units.tr: The Apostle expresses this purpose of his when he says: lest the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ should shine on them. For where this light shines on men's minds, they are enlightened to know the truth of God, and through this knowledge they are set free from the snares of the devil; they repent, believe and are saved. Hence also Christ said in John 8: "If you abide in my word, you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free." And so the Apostle in 1 Timothy 2: "who wills that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth."

units.la: Et propter hanc metium illuminatione, quæ fit per veritatis Dei cognitione, nō dicit simpliciter, ne cognoscatur ab illis veritas Euangelij, sed utitur similitudine diurnę lucis, qua illucescente dispelluntur tenebrę noctis, redditur aperta rerum omnium facies, & aperiuntur oculi non ad uidendum modo, sed & ad iudicandum de singulis, quo iudicio damnantur nocturnarum imaginationum & opinionū errores, illisq; spretis apprehenditur ac tenetur veritas, ac secundū hanc humanę actiones diriguntur, & vitæ necessitatibus consulitur. Secūdum hanc similitudinem dicit: ne illucescat illis lux Euangelij gloriæ Christi. Hoc est, ne dispellantur illis tenebrę errorum, quibus mentes ipsorum sunt immersę, veniantq; ad lucem ueritatis Dei, quæ est in Christo Iesu.
units.tr: And because of this illumination of minds, which comes through the knowledge of God's truth, he does not say simply that the truth of the Gospel should not be known by them. Instead he uses the likeness of daylight: when it dawns, the darkness of night is dispelled, the face of all things is made plain, and the eyes are opened not only to see but also to judge of particular things. By this judgement the errors of nocturnal imaginings and opinions are condemned, and, these being rejected, the truth is apprehended and held, human actions are directed by it, and the needs of life are provided for. According to this likeness he says: lest the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ should dawn on them. That is, lest the shadows of error, in which their minds are immersed, be dispelled, and they come to the light of God's truth, which is in Christ Jesus.

units.la: Sic igitur comparat veritatem Euangelij lu ci diurnæ, ad ortū Solis illucescenti. Dies hic est Noui testamenti tépus, splendor Solis gloria, id est, charitas Christi, lux veritas Euangelij, qua mentes illuminantur. Quare quemadmodum ortu Solis tota terra illustratur, & singulis rebus natiua facies redditur, quæ in tenebris latuerat, ita per Euangelij lumen totū genus humanum illuminetur, & ad cognitionē veritatis perducatur necesseest. Nō est enim aliud lumē, quo mentes illuminentur, q humanæ sapientiæ magisterio magis occæcatur q illuminantur.
units.tr: Thus he compares the truth of the Gospel to the light of day, dawning at the rising of the sun. This day is the time of the New Testament, the splendour of the sun is the glory, that is, the love of Christ, and the light is the truth of the Gospel, by which minds are illuminated. Therefore, just as at the rising of the sun the whole earth is lit up and the natural face of each thing is restored, which had lain hidden in darkness, so the whole human race must necessarily be illuminated by the light of the Gospel and brought to the knowledge of the truth. For there is no other light by which minds are enlightened; rather, they are blinded more by the teaching of human wisdom than they are enlightened.

units.la: Obserua uerò, quod non simpliciter dicit: ne illucescat lumē Euágelij, sed, ne illucescat illis lumē Euangelij gloriæ Christi. Efficere non potest mundi huius princeps Satan, vt lux Euangelij obscuretur in se nec illucescat vspiā. Non dominatur ueritati, dū dominatur reprobis ac pereūtibus. Iusto Dei iudicio cauere potest, ne lux Euangelij illucescat mentib. reprobo-rum, præterea non habet quod faciat in hac causa. Sæuiat quantū potest, manet ac manebit in se lux ueritatis, nec manet tantum sed & illucescit mentibus electorum. Obscurat mentes Tyrannorum & incitat aduersus lucem Euágelij Christi. Et quid illi omni sua sæuitia efficiunt? An, ne veritas sit veritas? Absit. An ne illuminet illa mētes electorum? Nequaquam. Neutrum efficere possunt. Nolint uelint dies est, exortus Sol est, discernit rerum facies lux reddita terris. Illuminatos, ubi visum est domino, occidere possunt, ipsam ueritatis lucē tolle re non possunt.
units.tr: Observe, moreover, that he does not say simply: lest the light of the Gospel should dawn, but: lest the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ should dawn on them. The prince of this world, Satan, cannot bring it about that the light of the Gospel is obscured in itself, or that it nowhere dawns. He does not rule over the truth, but only over the reprobate and the perishing. By the just judgement of God he can prevent the light of the Gospel from dawning on the minds of the reprobate, but beyond that he has nothing he can do in this matter. He may rage as much as he can; the light of truth remains and will remain in itself, and it does not merely remain but also dawns on the minds of the elect. He darkens the minds of tyrants and stirs them up against the light of the Gospel of Christ. And what do they accomplish with all their savagery? Do they make the truth no longer true? Far from it. Do they keep that light from illuminating the minds of the elect? By no means. They can accomplish neither. Whether they will or not, it is day; the sun has risen; the light given to the earth distinguishes the faces of things. They can kill those who have been illuminated, when it seems good to the Lord, but they cannot take away the light of the truth itself.

units.la: QVI est imago Dei, inquit.) Non solet Apostolus quiescere ac subsistere in Christo, quoties quæ ad gloriam illius & nostram salutem spectant illi tribuit, sed lectorem per Christum quasi manuducit ad ipsum Deum patrem. Sic hoc quoq; loco, cum Euangelium lumen gloriæ Christi vocasset, mox subiungit, qui est imago Dei, vt admoneat, in filio nobis spectandū & agnoscendum esse patrem. Inuisibilis in se est Deus, quia figuram quæ spectari possit non habet. Vnde & Christus dicit: Deum nemo uidit unquam: vt igitur uideri & cognosci possit, misit uerbum suum in mundum, in quo sit ipsius imago, quæ sic illucescat mentibus electorum, ut in ea videatur & cognoscatur ipse. In hac autem imagine Dei, quæ Christus est, filius & vnigenitus Dei, exprimitur non figura aliqua corporea quæ in Deo non est, sed splendor diuinitatis, sapientiæ, potentiæ, voluntatis & gratiæ illius. Filius carnis imaginem carnalis sui parentis refert. At Christus vnigenitus Dei viuentis imaginem refert non carnalis parentis, quem nullum habet, sed cœlestis sui patris, cuius gloriæ splendor est, & substantiæ character, id est, expressa imago. Vnde ad Philippum dicebat: Philippe qui videt me, videt & patrem meum. Item, pater in me est & ego in patre. Et, pater in me manens ipse facit opera quæ ego facio. Deus lux est. 1. Ioan. 1. Lucem hanc in se videt nemo. Est enim inaccessa. Datur igitur spectanda in filio tanquam in ipsius imagine, propter quam dicit: Ego sum lux mundi. Ioannis 8. Gloria lucis splendor est cūcta illuminans. Sic Christus dum splendore suo mundum illuminat gloria patris est, cuius imaginem lucendo spectandam exprimit.
units.tr: "Who is the image of God," he says. The Apostle is not accustomed to rest and remain in Christ whenever he attributes to him those things that look to his glory and our salvation, but he leads the reader, as it were by the hand, through Christ to God the Father himself. So also in this place, having called the Gospel the light of the glory of Christ, he immediately adds, "who is the image of God," to warn us that the Father is to be looked at and recognised by us in the Son. God is invisible in himself, because he has no figure that could be seen. Hence Christ also says: "No one has ever seen God" (John 1:18). So that he might be seen and known, he sent his Word into the world, in which is his own image, which so shines on the minds of the elect that in it God himself is seen and known. But in this image of God, who is Christ, the Son and only-begotten of God, is expressed not some bodily figure, which is not in God, but the splendour of his divinity, wisdom, power, will and grace. A son bears the image of his carnal parent. But Christ, the only-begotten of the living God, bears the image not of a carnal parent, whom he does not have, but of his heavenly Father, whose glory is the brightness and the exact expression of his substance, that is, the express image (Heb. 1:3). Hence he said to Philip: "Philip, whoever sees me sees my Father also" (John 14:9). Likewise: "The Father is in me and I in the Father" (John 14:10), and "The Father dwelling in me does his works" (John 14:10). "God is light" (1 John 1:5). No one sees this light in itself, for it is inaccessible. It is therefore given to be looked at in the Son, as in his image; for this reason he says, "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12). The glory of light is a splendour illuminating all things. So Christ, while by his splendour he illuminates the world, is the glory of the Father, and by shining he expresses his image, to be looked at.

units.la: Perinde ac si Solem hunc uisibilem, vnde terrarum illuminatur orbis, uoces imaginem Solis inuisibilis, quatenus cuncta splendore suo illustrat.
units.tr: It is just as if you were to call this visible sun, from which the orb of the earth is illuminated, the image of the invisible Sun, inasmuch as it lights up all things with its splendour.

units.la: Quanuis hæc similitudo non satisfacit causæ de qua loquimur, aliquo tamen pacto ad illam accedit. Sunt in cœlo stellæ, & Luna, illustris admodum, sunt in terra varij generis lucernæ ac splendores, in quibus tamen omnibus nihil est, quod imaginem Dei, perinde atque Sol vnicus exprimere videatur. Vnicus est, splendidissimus est, adeo ut excellentiam splendoris eius haud ferre possit humanus oculus, perpetuo sibijpsi similis est, totum orbem percurrendo illustrat, similem non habet, & quæ alia in illo sunt prorsus eximia. In eo tamē deficit, quod ex creaturis est Dei, qd prin-cipium habet, quod mutabitur, quod non prę-sens est vbique, quod voluntate præditus non est, &c. At Christus sic est imago Dei uiuen-tis, vt non sit ex creaturis, nisi secundum carnem, secundum quam non est imago Dei, sed genitus ex Deo patre, principium non habēs, nec mutationi obnoxius, nec absens vspiam, nec voluntate destitutus, sed quem vult illuminans, patrem in se habens, & in patre existens semper, &c.
units.tr: Although this likeness does not fully fit the matter we are speaking of, it nonetheless approaches it in some way. In the heavens there are stars and the moon, very bright; on the earth there are lamps and lights of various kinds; yet among all of these there is nothing that seems to express the image of God as the one Sun does. It is unique and most splendid, so that the human eye cannot bear the excellence of its brilliance; it is always like itself, it illuminates the whole orb as it traverses it, it has no like, and it has other utterly remarkable features. Yet it falls short in this respect: it is one of God's creatures, it has a beginning, it will change, it is not present everywhere, it is not endowed with will, and so on. But Christ is so the image of the living God that he is not of the creatures, except according to the flesh, and according to the flesh he is not the image of God; rather, he is begotten of God the Father, has no beginning, is not subject to change, is nowhere absent, is not deprived of will, but illuminates whomever he wills, has the Father in himself, and always exists in the Father, and so on.

units.la: Dicet aliquis. Imago non est id ipsum cuius est imago. Si Christus est imago Dei, ergo nō est ipse Deus.
units.tr: Someone will say: an image is not the very same thing of which it is the image. If Christ is the image of God, then he is not God himself.

units.la: Respondeo. Relationes in diuinitate non pertinent ad illius essentiam, sed ad personas. Christus vt filius est imago Dei patris, non vt Deus. Nō enim Deus, ut Deus est imago Dei. Quare stabit argumentū si dicas: Christus est imago Dei patris, ergo nō est Deus pater. Homo gignit ad imaginē suam hominem filiū. Si dicas: Ergo filius imago hominis nō est homo, non recte colligis. Si vero ad hunc modū dixeris: Ergo filius imago patris non est pater, vel, filius imago hominis nō est is homo cuius est imago, stabit argumentatio. Homo non est imago hominis, nisi per relationem, qua filius homo imago est hominis patris. Maior igitur illa. Imago non est idipsum cuius est imago, non est simpliciter accipienda, sed limitanda per relationem. Imago enim natura potest esse eadem cum eo, cuius imago est, persona uero non ita. Sic filius idem est natura cum patre, cuius est imago, persona vero non idem. Christus igitur filius Dei, natura idē est qd Deus, persona vero filius est & imago Dei.
units.tr: I answer: relations in the Godhead do not pertain to his essence but to the persons. Christ, as Son, is the image of God the Father, not as God. For God, as God, is not the image of God. Therefore the argument would fail if you said: Christ is the image of God the Father, therefore he is not God the Father. A man begets a son in his own image, a man. If you say: therefore the son, the image of a man, is not a man, you do not infer correctly. But if you put it in this way: therefore the son, the image of the Father, is not the Father; or, the son, the image of a man, is not that very man of whom he is the image, the argument will hold. A man is not the image of a man except through the relation by which the son, a man, is the image of the father-man. So the major premise, "An image is not the very same thing of which it is the image," is not to be taken absolutely, but is to be limited by the relation. For an image can be the same as that of which it is the image in nature, but not in person. So the Son is the same as the Father, of whom he is the image, in nature, but not the same in person. Christ, therefore, the Son of God, is in nature the same as God, but in person the Son is also the image of God.

units.la: NON enim nosipsos pdicamus, inquit, sed Christū Iesum dominum, &c.) Quoniam non simpliciter dicit: non prædicamus nosipsos, sed: Non enim prędicamus nosipsos, merito quæritur, quò referenda sit uocula rationalis, lis, enim. Nam ad proxime praecedentia uidetur parū cōmodè posse referri, nisi intentè cōsyderes coherentiam. Dixit: Quod si adhuc uelatū est Euangelium nostrum, in his qui pereunt uelatum est, in quib. Deus huius saeculi excaecauit sensus incredulorum, ne illucescat illis lumé Euangelij gloriæ Christi. Quoniā doctrinam quam tradebat suum Euangelium uocauit, & tamen mox subiecit, ne illucescat illis lumen Euangelij, non mei, sed gloriæ Christi, particulæ huius rationem subnectit, dicens: Non enim nosipsos praedicamus, sed Christū Iesum dnm. Quasi dicat: Ideo dum sensus incredulorum excæcantur, ne illucescat illis lumen Euangelij, velatur in illis non nostrū, sed Christi Euangelium. Neq; enim nosipsos, sed Christum Iesum dnm praedicamus. Euangeliū nostrum, nō est nostrū, sed Christi Euangeliū.
units.tr: "For we do not preach ourselves," he says, "but Christ Jesus as Lord," etc. Since he does not say simply, "we do not preach ourselves," but "For we do not preach ourselves" (the particle "for," enim), it is rightly asked to what the little word "for" should be referred. For it seems that it cannot be referred conveniently to the immediately preceding words, unless you attentively consider the connection. He had said: "But if our Gospel is still veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing, in whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, lest the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ should dawn on them." Since he called the doctrine that he taught "our Gospel," and yet immediately added, "lest the light of the Gospel should dawn on them, not of mine but of the glory of Christ," he attaches the reason for this clause, saying: "For we do not preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord." As if he said: Therefore, while the minds of the unbelievers are blinded, lest the light of the Gospel dawn on them, what is veiled in them is not our Gospel but the Gospel of Christ. For we preach not ourselves but Christ Jesus as Lord. Our Gospel is not ours but the Gospel of Christ.

units.la: Potest autem particula haec etiā ad ea referri, quibusdam paulo supra uerbū Dei dolo tractare negauit, quasi illius ratione redditurus dicat: Nō enim nosipsos praedicamus, sed Christū Iesum dominum. Quasi dicat: Qui seipsos praedicantes quae sua sunt quaerunt, uerbum Dei tractant nō syncerè, sed dolo. At nos illud tractamus, non dolo, sed syncerè ac ueraciter, quia praedicamus haud nosipsos, sed Christū Iesum. Si haec est praesentis loci cōsequentia, q interme-dia sunt de excæcatione incredulorum, per parenthesin iunt inserta. Non est autem dubiū, quin hoc dicens iterum perstringat pseudapostolos, qui non Christū dūm, sed seipsos praedicabant, dū magistri haberi uolebant, & discipulos post se trahebant. Etenim qui tales sunt, etiamsi verbis proponant Christū, finis tamē & scopus praedicandi non est ipsis Christus, sed philautia, & inanis gloria & turpis in ecclesia negociatio. Consyderemus hodie quē praedicēt Antichristi mysteḡ, hoc est, quid praedicādo quaerant. Sub nomine Christi praedicat & extollunt Antichristū, sub quo negociantur in ecclesia, atq; ita praedicant non Christū, sed seipsos. Et utinam nemo ex illis, qui Euangelici uideri volūt, seipsum praedicet, dū Christū ipsum praedicare videtur, qd faciūt oēs q quidē ore sonāt Christum, sed quaerūt corde seipsos.
units.tr: This clause can also be referred to what Paul said a little above, when he denied that he handled the word of God deceitfully, as if he were giving the reason for that denial: "For we do not preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord." As if he said: those who preach themselves seek their own interests, and they handle the word of God not sincerely but deceitfully. But we handle it not deceitfully but sincerely and truthfully, because we preach not ourselves but Christ Jesus. If this is the connection of the present place, the matters in between, about the blinding of unbelievers, are inserted as a parenthesis. There is no doubt that in saying this he again attacks the false apostles, who preached not Christ the Lord but themselves, while they wanted to be held as masters and drew disciples after themselves. For those who are such, even if they set forth Christ in words, the end and aim of their preaching is not Christ but self-love, empty glory and shameful trade in the Church. Let us consider today whose mystery the Antichrist preaches, that is, what people seek by preaching. Under the name of Christ they preach and exalt Antichrist, under whose cover they trade in the Church, and so they preach not Christ but themselves. And would that none of those who wish to seem evangelical preached himself while seeming to preach Christ himself, as all do who indeed sound Christ with their mouth but seek themselves in their heart.

units.la: SED Christū Iesum dnm, inquit.) Non simpliciter Iesum Christū, sed Iesum Christū dnm praedicabat. Quid est praedicare Iesum Christū dominum aliud, quā omnia illi subijcere praedicando quae in caelo sunt, & in terra & quosuis ad illum tanquam ad unicū Seruatorem ac Redemptorem dirigere. Non possunt hoc facere, qui ipsi regnare ac pro dominis haberi uolunt in ecclesia.
units.tr: "But Christ Jesus the Lord," he says. He did not preach Jesus Christ simply, but Jesus Christ as Lord. What is it to preach Jesus Christ as Lord, other than by preaching to subject all things to him, whatever is in heaven and on earth, and to direct everyone to him as the only Saviour and Redeemer? Those cannot do this who wish to reign themselves and to be held as lords in the Church.

units.la: NOS autem seruos uestros propter Iesum, inquit.) An quemadmodum Iesum Christum dominum, ita se seruum Corinthiorum praedicabat. Non puto. Iesum Christū dominū petuo & praedicabat & inculcabat omnibus, propterea quod in illo sita est salus omniū. At seruum se Corinthiorū nō ita iactabat uerbis, sed agebat reipsa, idq; de se sentire eos cupiebat.
units.tr: "But we are your servants for Jesus' sake," he says. Did he preach himself as servant of the Corinthians in the same way as he preached Jesus Christ as Lord? I do not think so. He constantly both preached and impressed upon everyone Jesus Christ the Lord, because the salvation of all lies in him. But he did not boast of being servant of the Corinthians in words; he showed it in deed, and wished them to think of him in that way.

units.la: Seruiebat ipsis praedicando Christū dominū, nō iactabat illud potificiū, seruus seruorū, qd Rom. pontifices omnib. suis bullis & rescriptis praemittere consueuerūt, cū reipsa agant in ecclesia, nō seruos fideliū, sed dominos, & rerū & corporum & animarū. Praedicant se seruos seruorū, & esse uolūt domini dominantium. Praedicant se seruos, & non seruiunt, quia Christū Iesum dominū non praedicant, ideoq; non possunt addere illud, propter Iesum, & interim simulant se hoc inani titulo imitari apostolos.
units.tr: He served them by preaching Christ the Lord. He did not boast of that papal title, "servant of servants," which the Roman pontiffs are accustomed to put before all their bulls and rescripts, while in fact they act in the Church not as servants of the faithful but as lords of goods, bodies and souls. They proclaim themselves servants of servants, and wish to be lords of lords. They preach themselves servants and do not serve, because they do not preach Christ Jesus the Lord, and therefore cannot add the words "for Jesus' sake." Meanwhile they pretend to imitate the apostles by this empty title.

units.la: Quid est autē qd non potius dicit: Nos autē seruos Iesu propter vos. Cū enim praedicaret Christū Iesum dnm, quid conuenientius de se praedicare potuit, quā quod esset seruus Christi Iesu, quemadmodum in nonnullis etiam epistolis de se scribit. Respondeo, prius quidem est esse seruū Dei, deinde uero seruire illis quib. à Deo is destinatus. Sic erat quidem Apostolus prior loco seruus Iesu Christi, & secundario seruus Corinthiorū, uocat aut se hoc loco seruum illorum, ut & suspicionem dominatus à se reijciat, & interim pseudapostolos pstringat, q sic praedicabant Christum, ut sub illius praetextu magistri essent in ecclesia. Facile est cuilibet praedicare se seruum Christi, & interim agere dominū in ecclesia, idq; propter hoc ipsum, qd sit seruus Christi, perinde ac si seruus regis ob hoc ipsum agat dominū subditorum, quib. est ab illo praefectus, quod seruus est regis. At Paulus quanuis esset seruus Christi haud tamen agebat dominum in ecclesia, imo propter hoc ipsum quod seruus & Apostolus esset Christi Iesu, seruum agebat fidelium, ad quos erat ab illo missus. Ideo & subijcit, propter Iesum, hoc est, propterea quod seruus sum & Apostolus Iesu Christi aduos ob id missus, ut saluti uestrę seruiam. Hac puto illum ratione maluisse hoc loco dicere: nos aut seruos uestros propter Iesum, quā nos autem seruos Iesu propter uos.
units.tr: Why then does he not rather say, "But we are servants of Jesus for your sake"? For since he preached Christ Jesus the Lord, what could he more fittingly preach about himself than that he was servant of Christ Jesus, as he also writes about himself in some of his letters? I answer: it is first to be a servant of God, and then to serve those to whom one is sent by God. So the apostle was indeed first in rank a servant of Jesus Christ, and secondarily a servant of the Corinthians. But he calls himself here their servant, both so that he may reject from himself any suspicion of domination, and meanwhile to attack the false apostles, who so preached Christ that under his pretext they might be masters in the Church. It is easy for anyone to preach himself a servant of Christ and meanwhile act as lord in the Church, and precisely because he is a servant of Christ, just as if a king's servant, for that very reason, acted as lord over the subjects to whom he has been set by the king, because he is the king's servant. But Paul, although he was a servant of Christ, did not act as lord in the Church. Rather, precisely because he was a servant and apostle of Christ Jesus, he acted as servant of the faithful, to whom he was sent by him. Therefore he adds, "for Jesus' sake," that is, because I am a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, sent to you for this reason, that I may serve your salvation. I think he preferred for this reason to say here "but we are your servants for Jesus' sake" rather than "but we are servants of Jesus for your sake."

units.la: Sic igitur ministri uerbi serui sunt Iesu Christi, ut propter ipsum sint & serui fidelium, quorum saluti sunt destinati. Et ostendent uerius, quod serui sint Iesu Christi, si malint seruire, quā m propterea quod serui sunt Iesu insolescere in ecclesia. Interim tamen ualde iniquū est, quod hodie passim ministros Christi, haud alio videmus à magistratib. quā m seruorū habe ri loco. Quos debebant agnoscere pro seruis Iesu Christi, eoq; nomine habere in precio, habent pro suis seruis, & quę volunt, vel docenda, vel tacenda praescribūt. Et inuenias fucos inter ipsos ministros, qui vt gratificetur talib. magistratibus, & veris ministris negocium facessant, vociferatur: Minister est infra omnes, contrà reperias qui partim zelo cohonestandi ministerij, partim malo studio clament: minister est supra omnes. Dum haec fiunt in ecclesia, paucos inuenire licet, qui ex animo seruiāt fidelibus, & rarus quisque magistratus est, qui fidelem Christi ministrum competenti honore prosequatur.
units.tr: Thus the ministers of the Word are servants of Jesus Christ, so that for his sake they are also servants of the faithful, to whose salvation they are appointed. They will show more truly that they are servants of Jesus Christ if they prefer to serve rather than to grow insolent in the Church because they are servants of Jesus. Meanwhile, however, it is very unjust that today we see Christ's ministers held by magistrates everywhere as nothing other than servants. Those whom they ought to acknowledge as servants of Jesus Christ, and on that account hold in honour, they regard as their own servants, and prescribe what they wish to be taught or kept silent. And you will find drones among the ministers themselves who, to curry favour with such magistrates and to make trouble for true ministers, cry out: "The minister is beneath all." On the contrary, you will find others who, partly from zeal to uphold the ministry and partly from bad motives, cry: "The minister is above all." While these things happen in the Church, one may find few who serve the faithful from the heart, and there is scarcely any magistrate who honours a faithful minister of Christ with due respect.

units.la: QVONIAM Deus est, inquit, qui iussit è tenebris nebris lucem illucescere.) Etiam hic uidendū {A}est quò referre debeamus uoculā ὅτι.i.quoniā. Potest referri ad id quod paulo suprà dixit: si uelatum est Euangelium, uelatū esse ex eo quod Deus huius sæculi, Satā uidelicet, excæcet sen sus incredulorū, ne illucescat illis lumen Euā gelij gloriæ Christi, ut iam subiungat non esse hoc ex eo, quòd in se sit Euangelium obscurū, cum uoluerit Deus illud instar lucis è medijs tenebris ortę illucescere cūctis. Nam esset hic sensus incommodus, & pulchrè opponeret cō silium Dei malitię Satanæ, possetq; retineri, si simpliciter diceret: Quoniā Deus iussit è tene bris lucē illucescere. Verū cum nō simpliciter dicit: quoniā Deus iussit, sed quoniā Deus est qui iussit è tenebris lucē illucescere, rationem exprimi cēseo, quare prædicet nō seipsum, sed Christū Iesum dñm, se verò seruum illorū propter Iesum, quasi dicat: Quod autē prædico nō meipsum, sed Christū Iesum dñm, me verò seruum uεstrū propter Iesum, ex eo est, quod qui lucem hanc, cuius sum minister, è tenebris illu cescere iussit, Deo est, cuius gratiæ & voluntati consecratus ad hoc sum, vt seruiam & ipsi & vobis propter Christum.
units.tr: "For God is he," he says, "who commanded light to shine out of darkness." Here too we must see to what we ought to refer the little word ὅτι [hoti], that is, "for." It can be referred to what he said a little above: if the gospel is veiled, it is veiled because the god of this age, namely Satan, blinds the minds of unbelievers, so that the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ does not shine on them. Now he adds that this is not because the gospel is obscure in itself, since God has willed it to shine on all like light arising out of the midst of darkness. For this sense would be unsuitable, and it would set the counsel of God neatly against the malice of Satan, and could be retained if he simply said: "For God commanded light to shine out of darkness." But since he does not simply say "for God commanded," but "for God is he who commanded light to shine out of darkness," I think the reason is expressed why he preaches not himself but Christ Jesus the Lord, and calls himself their servant for Jesus' sake. As if he said: That I preach not myself but Christ Jesus the Lord, and myself as your servant for Jesus' sake, is because he who commanded this light, whose minister I am, to shine out of darkness is God, to whose grace and will I am consecrated for this, that I may serve both him and you for Christ's sake.

units.la: QVONIAM Deus est, inquit, qui iussit è te nebris lucem illucescere.) Vt per tenebras ig-norantiā Dei errorū plenā, in qua regnū est Sa tanę, ita per lucē cognitionem veritatis Dei, in qua regnū est Christi vnigeniti Dei, intelligit. Est itaq; sensus. Quoniā nō obsequor humano cōsilio, dū Christū prædico, sed voluntati ac mā {B}dato Dei, qui voluit ac iussit, ut veritas prædi-cetur inter Gētes, ibiq; instar lucis è medijs te-nebris illucescat. Loquitur omnino de eo qd̄ uocatus & constitutus erat diuinitus, ut esset Apostolus ac doctor Gentium, id quod Iudai-cam gentem habebat pessimè, & magna pars eorum qui crediderant ex circuncisione, hac erant opinione, nō esse Christum prædicandū Gentibus. Tuetur igitur Apostolātū suum au-thoritate diuina dicēs: Quoniam Deus est qui iussit è tenebris lucem illucescere. Quid erant Gentes toto terrarū orbe aliud, quod religio-nem ac scientiam Dei attinet, quàm crassissimæ quædam tenebrę? Erat enim sine Deo, Eph.2. in quo solo lux est mentū. Est tenebris illis lux veritatis ac scientiæ Dei per ministerium & prę dicatione Apostoli huius illuxit, dum scientia Dei & fides in Christum locum in illis inue-nit. Et hoc factum est iussu Dei: ideoq; ineffi-cax esse non potuit, nisi apud incredulos & ex cæcatos tantum perditioni destinatos ac pe-reuntes.
units.tr: "For God is he," he says, "who commanded light to shine out of darkness." He understands by darkness the ignorance of God, full of error, in which the kingdom of Satan lies; and by light the knowledge of the truth of God, in which the kingdom of Christ, the only-begotten of God, lies. The sense is therefore this: since I do not obey human counsel when I preach Christ, but the will and command of God, who willed and commanded that the truth be preached among the Gentiles and there shine forth like light out of the midst of darkness. He speaks altogether of that which he was called and appointed by God to be, namely apostle and teacher of the Gentiles. The Jewish nation took this very badly, and a great part of those who had believed from circumcision were of the opinion that Christ should not be preached to the Gentiles. He therefore defends his apostolate with divine authority, saying: "For God is he who commanded light to shine out of darkness." What were the Gentiles throughout the whole world, as far as the religion and knowledge of God are concerned, other than very thick darkness? For they were "without God" (Eph. 2), in whom alone is the light of minds. In that darkness the light of the truth and knowledge of God shone through the ministry and preaching of this apostle, since the knowledge of God and faith in Christ found a place among them. And this was done by the command of God; therefore it could not be ineffective, except among unbelievers and the blinded, destined only to perdition and perishing.

units.la: Quod autem mādatum hoc de illuminan-dis Gentibus, peculiariter datum fuerit Pau-lo, uidere est Actorum uigesimo sexto, in uer-bis ipsius Seruatoris cœlitus ad illū factis, ubi sic legitur: Ad hoc apparui tibi, ut constituam te ministrum, & testem eorum quæ uidisti, & eorum, quibus apparebo tibi, eripiēs te de po-pulis & Gentibus, ad quas nunc ego mitto te, ut aperiantur oculi eorū, & conuertantur è te-
units.tr: That this command concerning the enlightenment of the Gentiles was given to Paul in particular may be seen in Acts 26, in the words of the Saviour himself, spoken to him from heaven, where it is read thus: "For this purpose I have appeared to you, to appoint you a minister and a witness of the things you have seen, and of those things in which I will appear to you, rescuing you from the peoples and the Gentiles, to whom I now send you, to open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God."

units.la: nebris ad lucē, & de potestate Satanæ ad De-um. Sic intelligo quod hic dicit: qui iussit è te-nebris lucem illucescere, de illuminatione Gē tium facta iussu Dei per Euangelium à Paulo prædicatum. Alij illud, E' tenebris, ad ministe-rium humanum, alij ad umbras legis, alij alio referunt, uerùm res ipsa satis monet, dictū esse de tenebris Gentium.
units.tr: I understand what he says here thus: he who commanded light to shine out of darkness [namely] the enlightenment of the Gentiles, made by the command of God through the Gospel preached by Paul. Others refer "out of darkness" to the human ministry, others to the shadows of the law, others to other things. But the matter itself sufficiently shows that it was said of the darkness of the Gentiles.

units.la: Quicquid igitur lucis etiamnū est inter nos qui sumus Christiani ex Gentib. ex iussu Dei est: iussit Deus, factum est, nec fieri nō potuit. Et iussionis huius efficaciæ, debemus lucem Euägelij Christi, cui ne portæ inferorum qui-dem resistere poterunt. E' tenebris iussit Deus illucescere lucem. Quis faciet ne fit quod Deo esse iubet? Hæc diuina iussio firmior est quàm ut ullis possit Tyrannorum uiribus irrita red-di. Filij tenebrarum, lucis osores, doctrinę Pau-li, per quā maiores nostri ad cognitionē Chri-sti perducti sunt, infensissimè aduersantur. Est odium hoc antiquum, inueteratum, & incura-bile. At interim uirtute diuinæ iussionis lux Euangelij Dei è medijs tenebris illuxit, illuce-scit, & ad finem usq; illucescet, etsi non in om-nib.in ijs tamen qui præordinati sunt ad uitā, & ob id rectè filij lucis vocantur.
units.tr: Whatever light there still is among us who are Christians from the Gentiles is therefore from the command of God. God commanded, and it was done; it could not fail to be done. We owe the light of the Gospel of Christ, and the efficacy of this command, to which not even the gates of hell will be able to resist. God commanded light to shine out of darkness. Who will make it not happen, when God commands it? This divine command is too firm to be made void by any power of tyrants. The sons of darkness, haters of light, most bitterly oppose the teaching of Paul, through which our forebears were brought to the knowledge of Christ. This hatred is ancient, deep-rooted, and incurable. Yet meanwhile, by the power of the divine command, the light of God's Gospel has shone out of the midst of darkness, shines, and will go on shining to the end, although not in all, yet in those who are predestined to life; and therefore they are rightly called sons of light.

units.la: QVI luxit, inquit, in cordibus nostris, ad il-luminationem cognitionis glorię Dei in facie Iesu Christi.) Sensus est. Qui ad hoc in me lu-cem ueritatis excitauit, ut per me Gentes illu-minaret ad cognoscendā gloriā suam, in Chri-sto relucentem. Luxit Deus in corde Aposto-li, dum eum luce cognitionis Christi donauit, hoc est, oculos cordis ipsius ad uidendam ue-ritatis suæ lucem spiritu suo aperuit & illumi-nauit, quam illuminationem mentis per eā ad umbrauit, qua illi oculos corporis ministerio Ananię cū baptizādus esset aperuit. Act. 9. Lu-xit autē in corde illius ad illuminationē Gentiū per quā cognoscerent gloriam, i. claritatē Dei multo excellentius in facie Christi, quā cum lex daretur in facie Moysis relucentem. Hoc est uidelicet quod dicit: Ad illuminationē co-gnitiōis glorię Dei in facie Iesu Christi. Quod li quis ista præcedentis particulæ expositione habere, & ad eā esse illuminatione referenda putat qua cor Apostoli illuminatū fuit à Deo, eum sensum nullus reiecero.
units.tr: "Who has shone in our hearts, for the enlightenment of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." The sense is: he who has stirred up in me the light of truth for this purpose, that through me he might enlighten the Gentiles to know his glory shining forth in Christ. God shone in the heart of the Apostle when he gave him the light of the knowledge of Christ; that is, by his Spirit he opened and enlightened the eyes of his heart to see the light of his truth. This enlightenment of the mind he foreshadowed by that enlightenment by which he opened the eyes of Paul's body through the ministry of Ananias, when Paul was about to be baptized (Acts 9). He shone, moreover, in Paul's heart for the enlightenment of the Gentiles, so that they might know the glory, that is, the brightness of God, far more excellently in the face of Christ than when the law was given, shining in the face of Moses. This is clearly what he means: "for the enlightenment of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." If anyone thinks this should be understood from the explanation of the preceding particle, and referred to that enlightenment by which the heart of the Apostle was illumined by God, I would reject no such sense.

units.la: QVI luxit, inquit, in cordibus nostris.) Ob serua diligēter, quōd Apostolum suum Deus, per quem illuminaturus erat Gentes, prius il-luminauit, q̄ ad illuminandū alios emitteret. Nec mirum. Quis enim ita desipit ut per lucer-nam non accensam lucis aliquid præstari pos-se putet? Paterfamiliās lucernam, unde domē sticos suos illuminare constituit, primū accen-dit, deinde candelabro ardentem ac lucentem imponit, ut qui in domo sunt uideant. Sic De⁹ prophetas & apostolos, quos instar lucernarū çandelabris est in domo sua imposituru s, lu-ce sua, id est, uiuua ueritatis suæ cognitione, ac cendit & illuminat, quo per eos cæteros illu-minare possit. At, ô Christe, lux uera, unde il-lumiluminamur omnes, quales stát hodie in eccle- {A}sijs tuis lucernæ: Aliæ lychnos habent extin- stos & fumigantes, sic vt fœtorem fumi qui nō assueuerunt ægerrimè ferant, aliæ nunquam accensæ, nec scintillulam quidem ostendunt, & interim templa replent candelis ac lampadib. noctu ac die, non sine sumptu ardentibus, noctu cum nemo adest, nisi cæcæ imagines & vespertiliones, & bubones, interdiu, cum Sol il- le clarissimus omnium oculos splendore suo il luminat. Vnde mentes populi tui illuminen- tur nulla est illis cura, uindicant sibi claues sci entiæ Dei & regni cœlorum & interim nec v- tuntur illis ad aperiendum aliis, nec eos quos tu illuminas lucem abs te acceptam, aliis admi nistrare sinunt.
units.tr: "Who has shone in our hearts," he says. Observe carefully that God first enlightened his Apostle, through whom he was about to enlighten the Gentiles, before he sent him out to enlighten others. Nor is this surprising. For who is so foolish as to think that anything of light can be furnished by a lamp that is not lit? The householder first lights the lamp with which he decides to illumine his household, and then sets it, burning and shining, on a lampstand, so that those in the house may see. So God kindles and illumines the prophets and apostles, whom he will set in his house like lamps on lampstands, with his own light, that is, with the living knowledge of his truth, so that through them he may be able to enlighten the rest. But, O Christ, true light, by whom all are enlightened, what sort of lamps are those in your churches today! Some have lamps that are extinguished and smoking, so that they can scarcely bear the stench of the smoke to which they are unaccustomed; others were never lit and do not show even a tiny spark. Meanwhile they fill the temples with candles and lamps, night and day, burning at no small expense: by night, when no one is present except blind images, bats and owls; by day, when that most brilliant of all suns illumines the eyes of all with its splendour. Whether the minds of your people are enlightened is no concern of theirs. They claim for themselves the keys of the knowledge of God and of the kingdom of heaven, and yet they neither use them to open the way for others, nor allow those whom you enlighten to pass on to others the light received from you.

units.la: Quid est autem quod non dicit: qui luxit in mentibus nostris, sed, qui luxit in cordibus no stris? Cum lux ista sit perspicuitas cognitionis Dei, cognitio autem magis ad mentem quàm ad cor pertineat, dicendum magis fuisse videtur: qui luxit in mentibus nostris, quàm, qui luxit in cordibus nostris.
units.tr: But why does he not say "who has shone in our minds," but "who has shone in our hearts"? Since this light is the clarity of the knowledge of God, and knowledge pertains more to the mind than to the heart, it seems it should rather have been said "who has shone in our minds" than "who has shone in our hearts."

units.la: Respondeo. Si in luce hac cognitionis Dei præter scientiæ perspicuitatem ac claritatem, nihil esset aliud, conuenientius vtiq; dixisset: qui luxit in mentibus nostris, quàm, qui luxit in cordibus nostris. Verùm cum claritate scien- tiæ Dei coniunctus est, & fidei zelus, quæ sanè fides nō mētis est, sed cordis. Propterhāc rectè dixit: qui luxit in cordibus nostris: Cognitio- nem & fidē Christi cōiunctim exprimebat Pe- trus, cū Ioan. 6. diceret, Domine, ad quem ibi- mus? Verba uitæ æternæ habes, & nos credim9 & cognouimus, quòd tu es Christus filius Dei uiui. Sic in ueris fidelib9 lux ueritatis Christi, nec claritatē habet sine ardore, nec ardoré si- ne claritate, hoc est, nec cognitione sine fide, nec fidem sine cognitione Dei.
units.tr: I answer: if there were nothing in this light of the knowledge of God beyond the clarity and brightness of knowledge, he would surely have spoken more fittingly in saying "who has shone in our minds" than "who has shone in our hearts." But zeal of faith is joined with the clarity of the knowledge of God, and this faith belongs not to the mind but to the heart. For this reason he rightly said "who has shone in our hearts." Peter expressed knowledge and faith in Christ together, when in John 6 he said, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we believe and know that you are Christ, the Son of the living God." So in true believers the light of Christ's truth has neither clarity without ardour, nor ardour without clarity; that is, neither knowledge without faith, nor faith without knowledge of God.

units.la: AD illuminationē, inquit, cognitionis glo- riæ Dei.) Illuminatio uisionis proprie est illu- minatio oculorū ad uidendū: Sic illuminatio cognitionis, metaphoricè illuminatio est mē- tis ad cognoscendū. Vt igitur ne Solem quidē, quo clarius nihil in hac tota est cœli terræque machina uidere possunt oculi; nisi beneficio Dei accepta sint uidendi facultate illuminati, ita gloriam Dei in Christo, lōgè omnium cla- rissimè relucentem, humanæ nequeunt per se cognoscere mentes, nisi singulari gratia diui- næ illuminationis illustratæ.
units.tr: "For the enlightenment," he says, "of the knowledge of the glory of God." Enlightenment of sight is properly the illumination of the eyes for seeing; so enlightenment of knowledge is, metaphorically, the illumination of the mind for knowing. Just as the eyes cannot see even the sun, the brightest thing in the whole machine of heaven and earth, unless they have received the faculty of sight by the favour of God, so human minds cannot by themselves know the glory of God shining in Christ, most brightly of all, unless they are illuminated by the singular grace of divine enlightenment.

units.la: GLORIÆ Dei, inqt.) Poterat dicere, glo- riæ Christi, quemadmodū paulo ante Euage- lio lumē gloriæ Christi dedit dicens: ne illuce scat illis lumen Euágelij gloriæ Christi. Verū studio subinde mentionem facit Dei, ut quæ Christi sunt, cum Deo patre illi communia es- se admoneat.
units.tr: "Of the glory of God," he says. He could have said "of the glory of Christ," as he did just before, when he spoke of the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, saying "lest the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ should shine on them." But he makes frequent mention of God, to remind us that the things of Christ are common to him with God the Father.

units.la: Cogitet autem diligens lector, quid sibi ue- lit, quod toties uoculam δόξης, id est, gloriæ pro claritate ponit Apostolus: Sic comparatū est in rebus humanis, ut quicquid clarum est ac splendidum, pro glorioso & magnifico ha- {A}beatur. Vnde dum gloriosos appellare uolu- mus mundi huius potentes, uocamus illustris simōs & clarissimos. Quid autem clarius est & illustrius, quàm consilū illud Dei, quo per unigenitum suū totum se uoluit, quantus quā tus est ad saluandum genus humanū profun- dere: Sed hæc claritas non perspicitur oculis carnis, sed perspicitur oculis mētis, ab ipsa cla- ritate cognoscenda diuinitus illuminatis. Qui claritati igitur in rebus humanis multum tri- buunt gloriæ, leuent mentis oculos, ad conte- plandum claritatem Dei in Christo Iesu. Hanc si uel modicè contemplari cœperint, omnem huius mundi claritatem nihil minus, quā glo- riōsam esse iudicabunt.
units.tr: Let the diligent reader consider, however, what the Apostle means by so often using the little word δόξα [doxa], that is, glory, for brightness. It is so in human affairs that whatever is bright and splendid is regarded as glorious and magnificent. Hence when we wish to call the powerful of this world glorious, we call them illustrious and most famous. But what is brighter and more illustrious than that counsel of God, by which he willed to pour out himself wholly, in all his greatness, through his only-begotten Son, to save the human race? Yet this brightness is not perceived by the eyes of the flesh, but by the eyes of the mind, divinely illuminated so as to know that very brightness. Therefore let those who attribute much glory to brightness in human affairs lift up the eyes of their mind to contemplate the brightness of God in Christ Jesus. If they once begin to contemplate it even a little, they will judge all the brightness of this world to be no glory at all.

units.la: IN facie Iesu Christi, inquit.) Admirantur Iudæi claritatem, quæ ad tempus olim in facie Mosis illuxit, quàm tamen videre nō possunt, sed legunt duntaxat & audiunt, qualis olim fuerit. Vbi tamen litera nōn habet aliud, quàm quod fuerit cornea, longe inferior ea claritate quam in Sole hoc uisibili uidemus quotidie; nedum illa, qua gloria Dei in facie Christi uni geniti illius respiendet, illisq; tātum nota est, qui mentis illam oculis intuentur.
units.tr: "In the face of Jesus Christ," he says. The Jews marvel at the brightness that once shone for a time on the face of Moses, yet they cannot see it. They only read and hear what it was like. But the letter says nothing more than that it was horny, far inferior to the brightness we see every day in this visible sun, and much more so to that glory of God which shines in the face of Christ, his only begotten Son, and which is known only to those who behold it with the eyes of the mind.

units.la: Non loquitur autem de corporea Christi fa cie, sed de ea quæ salutis nostræ dispensatione spectandam proponit. Imago Dei Christus est. Facies imaginis huius spectanda proponi tur in uerbi incarnati mysterio in quo gloria unigeniti in mundum hunc pro salute generis humani missi uisenda exhibetur. Pictam Chri sti faciem ostentant Pontificij summa religio- ne uenerandam, quam uiuam uiderunt innu- meri sine aliquo salutis emolumento. Faciem hominis ostentant pro pictoris arbitrio deli- neatam, non ad uiuum expressam, in qua non gloria Dei, sed artificium pictoris & quæstus Pontificum spectatur, & interim faciem Chri- sti in qua imago Dei cernitur traditionibus & constitutionibus suis uelut obducto uelo ob- scurant & occultant.
units.tr: He is not speaking of the bodily face of Christ, but of that face which the dispensation of our salvation sets before us to be looked upon. Christ is the image of God. The face of this image is set forth to be looked upon in the mystery of the Word made flesh, in which the glory of the only begotten Son, sent into this world for the salvation of mankind, is displayed to be seen. The Papists display a painted face of Christ, to be venerated with the highest reverence, though countless people saw him alive without any benefit to their salvation. They display a face of a man, drawn according to the painter's judgment, not taken from life, in which one sees not the glory of God but the craft of the painter and the profit of the Popes. Meanwhile, by their traditions and constitutions, they veil and hide the face of Christ, in which the image of God is discerned, as if a veil had been drawn over it.

units.la: Habemus autem thesaurum hunc in testaceis uasculis, ut virtutis eminentia sit Dei & non ex nobis; dum in omnibus premimur, at non anxij reddimur, labo ramus, at non destituimur, persequutio nem patimur, at non deserimur, deiici- mur, at non perimus, semper mortificatio- nē domini Iesu in corpore circumserē- tes, ut & uita Iesu in corpore nostro ma nifestetur. Sēper enim nos qui uiuimus in mortem tradimur propter Iesum, ut & uita Iesu manifestetur in mortali carne nostra. Itaq; mors quidem in nobis agit, uita autem in uobis.
units.tr: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God and not of us. We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed; always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life of Jesus also may be made manifest in our body. For we which live are always delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, that the life also of Jesus may be made manifest in our mortal flesh. So then death worketh in us, but life in you."

units.la: Hactenus primam capitis huius partem absoluit, in qua de ministerij sui syncėritate & sin gulari luce quædam meminit. Subijcit iam al- teram de afflictionib. suis & consolationibus. HABEMVS autem thesaurum hunc in testaceis vasculis inquit.) Habet hoc in more, ut ubi de ministerij sui eminentia & efficacia loquitur, annectat quaedam uel de personae suae humilitate, uel de afflictionibus, quas indefinen-tes patiebatur, ne quid sibijpsi de gloria ministerij sui vindicare videatur. Facit hoc in praesenti quoq; materia: facit aut propter pseudapostolos, quibus hoc erat in consueto, ut exaf flictionibus ipsius argumentum captarent uilipendendi ipsius ministerium. Quare memi nit hic non simpliciter afflictionum suarum, sed annectit experimenta diuinę potentiae, quę in omnibus ipsius afflictionibus ubertim aedebatur. Sic mox initio comparat quidem se testaceo vasculo, quod & infirmum est, & fragile, & cuius fractura haud magnae iacturae aestimari solet. Verum addit, in hoc se testaceo uasculo thesaurum illum habere, de quo gloriatus est in praecedentibus.
units.tr: Here he finishes the first part of this chapter, in which he speaks of the sincerity of his ministry and of certain singular light. Next he adds the second part, concerning his afflictions and consolations. "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels," he says. It is his habit, when he speaks of the eminence and efficacy of his ministry, to add something about the humility of his person or about the afflictions which he endured without ceasing, lest he seem to claim anything of the glory of his ministry for himself. He does this in the present matter too, and he does it on account of the false apostles, for whom it was customary to seize upon his afflictions as an argument for despising his ministry. Therefore he does not simply mention his afflictions here, but adds the experience of divine power, which was shown abundantly in all his afflictions. So at the very beginning he likens himself to an earthen vessel, which is both weak and fragile, and whose breaking is usually reckoned to be no great loss. But he adds that in this earthen vessel he has that treasure of which he boasted in what went before.

units.la: HABEMVS aut thesaurum hunc, inquit, in testaceis vasculis.) Nō simpliciter thesaurum, sed hunc, inquit, thesaurum habemus. Quem? De quo videlicet loquutus est, dicens: Deus est, qui luxit in cordibus nostris ad illuminationem cognitionis gloriae Dei in facie Iesu. Illuminatio cordis ad cognoscendum gloriam Dei in Christo thesaurus est incoparabilis, & omnium preciosissimus. Quid enim preciosius eo poterit esse thesauro, in quo est nō caducum aliquod, sed aeternae uitae bonum. Haec est vita aeterna, inquit ipse Seruator, ut cognoscant te Deum patrē, & quem misisti Iesum Christum. Ioa. 17. Quantumuis magnus huius mundi thesaurus recondatur, praestantiori tamen usui accomodari seruireq; non potest, q presenti uitae uel seruandae uel redimendae: idq; non a Deo, sed ab hostibus. At ille cognitionis Dei thesaurus praxeuus est non temporariae huius, sed aeternae vitae. Quare illo tanto est preciosior, quato caducam hanc uitam excellit aeterna.
units.tr: "But we have this treasure," he says, "in earthen vessels." He does not say simply "a treasure," but "this treasure we have." Which one? Clearly the one he spoke of when he said: "God, who hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6). The illumination of the heart to know the glory of God in Christ is an incomparable treasure and the most precious of all. For what can be more precious than that treasure, in which is not something perishable, but the good of eternal life? "This is eternal life," said the Saviour himself, "that they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent" (John 17:3). However great a treasure of this world may be stored up, it cannot be applied to or serve any more excellent use than to preserve or redeem this present life, and that not from God but from enemies. But the treasure of the knowledge of God is profitable for the eternal life, not for this temporal one. Therefore it is so much more precious than this perishable life as eternal life excels it.

units.la: IN uasis testaceis inquit.) Non loquitur de corporis sui fragilitate, sed de personae suae humilitate, quam pseudapostoli diuexabant. Illa cōparat testaceo vasculo: quasi dicat: Vtut magni uestri Apostoli personae meae humilitatem contemnant, & contemptui coram omnibus exponant, nolint uelint, tamen relinquent mihi thesaurum hunc, quę mihi Dominus haud aliter, quā testaceo vasculo circumferendum credere dignatus est. Quid est autem, quod infirmitatem & humilitatem uasculi huius diue xant, & non magis thesaurum caelestem in illo reconditum agnoscunt? Quis adeo demens est, ut thesauro in testaceo uasculo reperto nō magis exultet propter thesaurum, quam quiri tetur propter humilitatem uasculi? Qui dodie praestantes Christi ministros, propterea quod externa sunt uitae huius conditione & fortuna non illustres, sed humiles, quantumuis ecclesijs Christi utiles existant, contemptui habet, sic non despiunt, ut si quis ipsis auri uel argenti, uel lapidum preciosorum thesaurum in vasculo
units.tr: "In earthen vessels," he says. He is not speaking of the frailty of his body, but of the humility of his person, which the false apostles were disparaging. He compares that person to an earthen vessel, as if to say: "However much your great apostles may despise the humility of my person and expose it to contempt before everyone, whether they wish it or not, they will still leave me this treasure, which the Lord has deigned to entrust to me to be carried about in no other vessel than an earthen one. But why do they disparage the weakness and humility of this vessel, and do not rather acknowledge the heavenly treasure hidden in it? Who is so foolish that, having found a treasure in an earthen vessel, he does not rejoice more over the treasure than complain over the humility of the vessel?" Those who today despise the excellent ministers of Christ, because by the outward condition and fortune of this life they are not illustrious but humble, however useful they may be to the churches of Christ, do not despise them in such a way that, if someone brought them a treasure of gold, silver or precious stones, hidden in a vessel

units.la: lo testaceo reconditum, & alicunde effossum adferat, propter vasculi vilitatē ipsum à se tho saurum reijciant, ac dicant: Quid mihi uasculo hoc testaceum? Et interea cœlestem thesaurū in vasibus figulinis reconditum propter exterē faciei humilitatem respuūt, non intelligen tes, quo consilio Deus thesaurum suum à sapi entibus mundi huius abscondat, & paruulis ma nifestet. Matth. 11.
units.tr: of earthenware and dug out from somewhere, they would reject that treasure on account of the cheapness of the vessel and say: "What is an earthen vessel to me?" Yet meanwhile they spurn the heavenly treasure stored in earthen vessels because of the humble outward appearance, not understanding for what purpose God hides his treasure from the wise of this world and reveals it to little ones (Matt. 11:25).

units.la: Scio Chrysostomū cum nonnullis alijs simi litudinem uasorum testaceorum referre ad hu manam fragilitatem, omnib9 communem. Sanè si illa imò & carnis nostrae origo cōsidere tur, quid est corpus humanum aliud, quàm testa ceū vasculū? An non est è limo terrae opificio Dei formatum? An nō sic est fragile, ut omnis ipsius gloria uix herbulae ac flori caduco pos sit comparari? Et in huiusmodi testaceis uasculis omnes illi thesauri donorum Dei, quae mor talibus conferuntur, utiq; habentur. Quisnā est Rex ille, qui Regiae potentiae gloriam non habeat in vasculo testaceo? uerum (quemad modum exposuimus) non respicit Apostolus hoc loco ad corporis sui fragilitatem, quam cū caeteris habebat mortalibus communem, sed ad personae suae humilitatem, in oculis mundi cōtemptibilem, perinde atq; in domibus diui tum inter uasa aurea, argentea & aenea viliora censentur testacea. Tales erant Apostoli in hoc mundo, nullis humanae sapientiae, potentiae, & fortunae praerogatiuis spectabiles. Non erant potentes, nobiles aut sapientes, sed homines vulgares, ac praeterea Iudaei, quae gens passim despicatissima habebatur. Hoc respectu sordebat Euangelium potentibus ac sapientibus huius mundi. Quod si quis expositionem Chrysostomi sequedam putat, per me id licet. Tandē ille tamen in hanc, quam ponimus, diferendo declinat.
units.tr: I know that Chrysostom, with some others, refers the likeness of earthen vessels to human frailty, which is common to all. Indeed, if the origin of our flesh is also considered, what is the human body other than an earthen vessel? Is it not formed from the clay of the earth by the workmanship of God? Is it not so fragile that all its glory can scarcely be compared to a little herb or a fading flower? And in such earthen vessels are contained all those treasures of God's gifts which are bestowed on mortals. What king is there who does not have the glory of royal power in an earthen vessel? But (as we have explained) the Apostle here does not look to the frailty of his body, which he had in common with other mortals, but to the humility of his person, which was contemptible in the eyes of the world, just as in the houses of the rich earthen vessels are judged of less worth than golden, silver and bronze ones. Such were the apostles in this world, conspicuous for no advantages of human wisdom, power or fortune. They were not powerful, noble or wise, but ordinary men, and moreover Jews, a people everywhere held in the greatest contempt. In this respect the gospel was despised by the powerful and wise of this world. But if anyone thinks Chrysostom's exposition is to be followed, that is up to him. Yet in the end Chrysostom himself turns aside to the interpretation we are setting forth.

units.la: VT virtutis eminentia fit Dei, inquit, & nō ex nobis.) Reddit rationem, quare thesaurum hunc Deus testaceis uasculis committere uoluerit: vide autem quam reddat. Poterat dicere, ut confundantur uasa preciosa, aurea, argentea, hoc est, sapientes ac potentes huius mundi, dum inanes relinquuntur, & thesaurū hunc in uasculis testaceis agnoscere non sustinent. In praecedenti Epistola, cum uocationem fidelium considerandam proponeret, quare Deus infirma mundi elegerit, hanc rationem reddidit, dicens, Vt confundat fortia. Eam poterat assignare & hoc loco perinde atque illic: uerum consultius, & argumento, quod tractabat uicinius, uisum est hanc reddere, quae minus pateret inuidiae, & facilius posset agnosci. Sic dicit: Vt virtutis eminentia fit Dei, & non ex nobis: hoc est, ut virtutis huius gloria, quae tam excellenter in efficacia Apostolatus mei passim ostenditur, nō ad nos, sed ad ipsum Deū referatur: uel, ut eminentia virtutis, id est, excellens haec ministerij nostri uirtus & efficacia agnoscatur esse ex Deo, & non ex nobis. Sanè etiamsi aureo uasculo thesaurum hunc impofuisset Deus, nihilominus in se fuisset illius efficacia, non ex uasculo, sed ex ipso. Quòd igitur posuit illum in uasculo testaceo, non ad id est factum, ut uirtus illius esset ipsius, sed ut esse ipsius perspicuè monstraretur. Sic est caro comparata, ut quamuis sit infirma, aspiret tamen ad gloriam operum Dei, quæ non ipsa, sed Deus operatur in ipsa.
units.tr: "That the excellency of the power may be of God," he says, "and not of us." He gives the reason why God wished to commit this treasure to earthen vessels; but see how he gives it. He could have said: "that the precious vessels, of gold and silver, that is, the wise and powerful of this world, may be put to shame, while they are left empty and cannot bring themselves to recognise this treasure in earthen vessels." In the previous letter, when he was setting forth the calling of the faithful to be considered, he gave the reason why God chose the weak things of the world, saying: "that he might confound the things which are mighty" (1 Cor. 1:27). He could have assigned that reason here too, just as there; but it seemed more prudent, and closer to the argument he was treating, to give this reason, which is less open to envy and can more easily be recognised. So he says: "That the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us": that is, that the glory of this power, which is so excellently displayed in the efficacy of my apostleship, may be referred not to us but to God himself; or, that the excellency of the power, that is, this outstanding power and efficacy of our ministry, may be acknowledged to be from God and not from us. Indeed, even if God had placed this treasure in a golden vessel, its efficacy would nonetheless have belonged to itself and to him, not to the vessel. Therefore, that he placed it in an earthen vessel was done not so that its power would be the vessel's own, but so that it might be clearly shown to be God's. Thus the flesh is so constituted that, although it is weak, it nevertheless aspires to the glory of God's works, which are not performed by it, but by God in it.
