units.la: Quare iustissimo consilio Deus sic suam in illa uirtutem operatur, ut Sole clarius fiat, non illius esse uirtutem in ijs quæ fiunt, sed Dei. Huc facit, quòd uirtutem suam exercet in uasculis non aureis, argenteis, eburneis, &c. sed testaceis, id est, sic infirmis, ut nulla illis posset ratione gloria eorum, quæ fiunt tribui, sed indubitatum sit, uni esse Deo adscribendam.
units.tr: Therefore God, by a most just counsel, so works his power in that frail vessel that it becomes clearer than the sun that the power in the things done is not theirs but God's. This is to the point, that he exercises his power not in golden, silver or ivory vessels, and so on, but in earthen ones, that is, in vessels so frail that the things done cannot in any way be ascribed to them, but must undoubtedly be ascribed to God alone.

units.la: Obsecro, quid uniuersa est orbis huius machina? cœlum, aër, aqua, ignis, terra, si conferatur ad eminentiam uirtutis, quam in illis diuina Maiestas, inde ab initio ad finem usque declarat? Est ne quid in illa, quod dignum & conueniens tantæ sit uirtutis operationibus? Si bestias non modò minutas, sed & grandes inspicias, meliores ne sunt testaceis uasculis? At quantam in illis & per illas uirtutem declaratopifex omnium Deus? Homo quid est, inquit Propheta, quod memor es eius? &c. Et uanitas uanitatum omnis homo uiuens.
units.tr: I ask you, what is this whole machine of the world? Heaven, air, water, fire and earth, if they are compared with the eminence of the power which the divine Majesty declares in them from the beginning to the end? Is there anything in it that is worthy of and fitting for the works of so great a power? If you look at beasts, not only the small ones but the large ones as well, are they better than earthen vessels? Yet how great a power does God, the maker of all things, display in them and through them? "What is man," says the Prophet, "that you are mindful of him?" (Ps. 8:4), and "Every man living is altogether vanity" (Ps. 39:5).

units.la: Nihilo tamen minus quantæ in illo diuinæ uirtutis operationes indesinenter relucent? Ipse uirginis uterus, unde natus est unigenitus Dei, quid erat aliud, quàm uasculum testaceum, in se consideratus? Quàtum ille thesaurum concepit, gestauit, aluit, ac peperit? Ipsæ natalium Christi, educationis, & conuersationis circumstantiæ, quàm fuerunt humiles in oculis mundi? At interim habebat cœlestium bonorum omnium thesaurum Christum filium Dei, humani generis Seruatorem.
units.tr: Nevertheless, how great are the operations of divine power that shine forth in him without ceasing? The very womb of the Virgin, from which the only-begotten Son of God was born, what else was it, considered in itself, than an earthen vessel? How great a treasure did it conceive, carry, nourish and bring forth? And the circumstances of Christ's birth, upbringing and manner of life, how humble were they in the eyes of the world? Yet meanwhile Christ, the Son of God, the Saviour of mankind, had within him the treasure of all heavenly goods.

units.la: Hæc, & quæ alia sunt eiusmodi omnia, ad quæ apostolorum humilitatem referimus, si considerentur, luce clariùs demonstrant, sic placere Deo, ut uirtute suam in rebus infirmis perficiat, quo, sicut Apostolus hic dicit, eminetia ac gloria illius ipsius sit, nō illarum. Quare uehementer peccant, qui operu Dei uirtute, uel contenunt propter testacea uasa, uel nō Deo, sed uasculis tribuunt, in quibus illa perficiuntur.
units.tr: These things, and all others of this kind, to which we refer the humility of the apostles, if they are considered, demonstrate more clearly than light that it pleases God to perfect his power in weak things, so that, as the Apostle says here, the eminence and glory may be his own and not theirs. Therefore those greatly err who either undervalue the work of God's power because of the earthen vessels, or ascribe it not to God but to the vessels in which it is accomplished.

units.la: DVM in omnibus premimur, inquit, at nō anxij reddimur.) Græce est, ἐν παντὶ θλιβόμενοι, ἀλλ' οὐ στενοχωρούμενοι. Illud, ἐν παντί, id est, in omni, desideras aliquid quòreferatur, siue locum, siue tempus. Si referas ad locum, idem est, quod ubique & passim, si ad tempus, sonat semper: uerum interpretes retulisse uidentur ad causas, res & negocia, dum reddiderunt, in omnibus. Deinde illud, ἀλλ' οὐ στενοχωρούμενοι, malim reddere, sed non in arctum redigimur, quàm, at non anxij reddimur. στενοχωρεῖσθαι, significat, loco esse sic angusto & arcto, ut nec progredi, nec retrocedere, nec ullum in latus declinare liceat.
units.tr: "Being pressed on every side," he says, "yet not distressed" (2 Cor. 4:8). In Greek it is "ἐν παντὶ θλιβόμενοι, ἀλλ' οὐ στενοχωρούμενοι" [in every way afflicted, but not cramped]. As to "ἐν παντί", that is, "in everything", you may ask what it refers to, whether place or time. If you refer it to place, it means the same as "everywhere and on all sides"; if to time, it means "always". But the translators seem to have referred it to causes, matters and affairs, when they rendered it "in all things". Next, I would prefer to render "ἀλλ' οὐ στενοχωρούμενοι" as "but are not brought into a narrow place", rather than "yet are not distressed". The verb "στενοχωρεῖσθαι" means to be in a place so narrow and confined that one can neither advance, nor go back, nor turn aside to either side.

units.la: Quoniam thesaurū se hunc Euangelicæ lucis in uasculis testaceis habere dixit, quo uirtutis eminentia non ex se sit, sed ex Deo, consequeter id reipsa comprobari declarat. Quasi dicat: Etenim quid aliud, quàm excellētia diuinæ uirtutis in eo declaratur, quòd dum premimur in omnibus, laboramus, persequutionem patimur, ac deijcimur, in arctū tamen nō redigimur, nō destituimur, nō deserimur, non perimus? Quàm facilè est, fictile uasculū premendo ac proijciendo confringere: tam esset facile modica nos pressura conquassari ac confringi, nisi diuina uirtute seruaremur in omnibus. Seruamur autè in hunc usq; diem, & contra omnium opinionem in tot, tamq; grauibus afflictionibus, pressuris ac persequutionibus duramus mundo ac Satana inuito. Quo igitur humiliores & abiectiores sumus, hoc magis in nobis diuinę uirtutis eminētia relucet. Humilitatem personæ meæ uident ac diuexant uestri magistri, quur uirtutem Dei construa-tricem illius non uident?
units.tr: Since he has said that he has this treasure of the gospel light in earthen vessels, by which the eminence of the power is not from themselves but from God, he consequently declares that this is shown in fact. As if he said: Indeed, what else is shown by the excellence of divine power in this, that although we are pressed on every side, we labour, suffer persecution and are cast down, yet we are not brought into a narrow place, we are not left without resources, we are not forsaken, we do not perish? How easily an earthen vessel is broken by pressing and throwing down; so easily would we be shaken and broken by a slight pressure, were we not preserved in all things by divine power. But we are preserved to this day, and, contrary to everyone's opinion, we endure under so many and so grievous afflictions, pressures and persecutions, the world and Satan being unwilling. Therefore the more humble and abject we are, the more the eminence of divine power shines forth in us. Your teachers see the humility of my person and harass it; why do they not see the power of God that builds it up?

units.la: DVM in omnibus premimur, inquit.) Particulæ huius expositio uidebitur infra, cap.12. Nos admonemur, quæ sit in hoc mundo sors & cōditio uerorū Christi ministrorū, ueritatis sunt ministri. At illa peregrina est in terris, & inter extraneos facilè inimicos sortitur, ut ille ait, Spiritū ueritatis, teste Christo, inūdus hic accipere non potest. Quid poterit igitur cōsequi aliud, qut minister Christi, spiritu ueritatis imbutus, nusquā nō in reprobos incurrat, à quibus premātur in omnibus? Imò ne à fratribus quidē securus sit perpetuò, inter quos multi sunt Caini, homines carnales, & odio fraterno laborantes.
units.tr: "Being pressed on every side," he says. The exposition of this phrase will be seen below, in chapter 12. We are reminded what is the lot and condition in this world of the true ministers of Christ. They are ministers of the truth. But the truth is a stranger on earth, and among strangers it easily meets with enemies, as he says: the world cannot receive the Spirit of truth, as Christ bears witness (John 14:17). What then can follow for a minister of Christ, imbued with the Spirit of truth, except that he everywhere runs into the reprobate, by whom he is pressed on every side? Indeed, he is not even always safe from his brothers, among whom there are many Cains, carnal men labouring under brotherly hatred.

units.la: AT non in arctū redigimur, inqt.) Qui pmi tur, hoc sine pmitur, ut in angustū redacti oppriamtur. Du potētes pmūt imbecilles, multi paucos, prudetes &astuti, simplices & idiotas, nihil expectatur aliud, qut opprimat quos pmūt, & opprimere satagūt. Sic ppetuo uidebatur, in oculis mūdi Christianismū stare nō posse, quādoquidē totius erat orbis potētū ac prudētū infestationib ac pßuris obnoxius. At in hūc usq; die perstitit: nec pstitit tantū, sed & in medijs pßuris creuit, & instar palmæ magis ac magis in sublime subnixus est. Quid hodie Antichristus agit aliud, qut pßuris, multis, uarijs, grauib, & irremisis in omnib regnis, triplici suo diadematis subiectis, ministros ueritatis opprimat? At illi beneficio Christi nondū sunt in arctū redacti. Redacti uidebātur, cū Euangelice pfessionis principes ac magistrat placitis aduersariorū manus dare cogerētur: uerū ibi quoq; diuina uirtu emicuit, dū pßuris illis termin impositū, & eos q in angustū redacti uidebatur, in spaciosa latitudine restituit. Hæc dices Apost. nō excludit animi afflicti pathos, siue anxietate, siue tristitia, siue metu: sed admonet nō sic se redigi i arctū, ut nusq; detur exitus: sed diuina uirtute ex omnib. se pßuris liberari.
units.tr: "But are not brought into a narrow place," he says. Whoever is pressed, is pressed so that, being driven into a narrow space, he may be crushed. The powerful press the weak, the many the few, the prudent and cunning the simple and unlearned; nothing else is to be expected than that they oppress those whom they press, and strive to oppress them. Thus it always seemed, in the eyes of the world, that Christianity could not stand, since it was exposed to the attacks and pressures of the mighty and wise of the whole world. Yet to this day it has persisted; and not only has it persisted, but it has grown in the midst of pressures, and like a palm tree it has been raised higher and higher. What else does Antichrist do today, with many, various, grievous and unremitting pressures in all kingdoms subject to his threefold crown, than oppress the ministers of the truth? Yet by the benefit of Christ they have not yet been brought into a narrow place. They seemed to have been brought into one when the princes and magistrates of the evangelical profession were forced to give their hands to the wishes of their adversaries; but there too the divine power shone forth, when it set a limit to those pressures and restored to a broad spaciousness those who seemed to have been brought into a narrow place. In saying this, the Apostle does not exclude the affliction of a troubled mind, whether anxiety, sadness or fear; but he warns that we are not so driven into a narrow place that no way out is given, but that by divine power we are delivered from all pressures.

units.la: LABORAMUS, inqt, & nō destituimur.) greçe é, [illegible, ~12 letters] Significat
units.tr: "We are perplexed," he says, "but not left without resources." The Greek is [illegible]. It signifies

units.la: ὑπορεῖσθαι inopem esse, & sumitur aliquando de consilij, aliquādo de rerum necessariarum inopia. Et hinc est expositionū, imò & lectionis variatio. Vetus interpres reddidit, aporiamur. Et Lyranus exponit, id est, depauperamur, & dicitur aporos graece, quod est pauper latine. Ambrosius sic: Inopiam passi, sed non destituti, i.e. in inopia positis affuit pastor Deus. Theophylactus utriusq; & consilij & rerum inopiae sententiam posuit. Germanicus interpres sic uertit. Vns ist bang, aber vuir verzagen nit. Erasmus, laboramus, inquit, usurpauit uerbū labo rādi, qd utriq; sensui cōuenire potest. Ipse Apostolus usus est hoc uerbo Galat. 4. dicens ἀπορούμενοι ἐν ὑμῖν, i. cōsilij inops sum in uobis. Et Ioā. 13. sic habetur. Intuētes alius aliū discipuli ἀπορούμενοι, i. hęsitātes, de quo nam diceret. Vero ἐξαπορηθῆναι usus est Apostolus & s. cap. 1. ad hunc modū, ὥστε ἐξαπορηθῆναι ἡμᾶς καὶ τοῦ ζῆν, id est, ut de uita quoque desperaremus. Placet igitur ut hic quoq; eundē uocū istarū sensum retineamus, ac legamus, perplexi, sed non desperabundi. Ipsam duarū istarum uocum allu sionē duabus latinis uocibus exprimere non possumus, Germanicis possemus & facilius & melius. Nolim tamen admodū reluctari illis, qui de rerum inopia intelligunt, qua, ut infrā cap. 11. uidebimus, Apostolus iste nonunquā laborauit. Sane quāuis esurie passus sit, nunquā tamē passus illā est ad extremū usq; discri men, sed semper illi in tempore diuina proui dentia succurrit. Sic diceremus Germanice, Vuir leide vuol hūger, vuerde aber nit vßgehungert, ut dictum sit ad similitudinem eorum qui in præsidijs obsessi fame & inopia rerū arctātur, & ad deditionem sollicitantur, qui tamē utut rerum omnium inopia pressi fidem principi suo seruates ad deditionem cogi non possunt, sed præstant & tandem liberantur. Consimili plane modo thesaurum Christi principis sui Apostolus tāta fide custodiuit, ut nulla posset rerū inopia ad proditionē illius adigi, atq; ita ὑπορηθῆναι quidem potuit, ἐξαπορηθῆναι uero non potuit. Ea uidelicet erat diuinæ uirtutis efficacia confirmatus.
units.tr: "ὑπορεῖσθαι" (to be without resources, to be in need), which is sometimes used of lack of counsel, sometimes of lack of necessary things. Hence comes the variation both of the explanations and even of the reading. The old translator rendered it "we are at a loss" (aporiamur). Lyra explains it as "we are impoverished", and in Greek "aporos" means what in Latin is "poor". Ambrose says: "Suffering want, but not forsaken; God, the shepherd, was present to those placed in want." Theophylact placed the sense both of lack of counsel and of lack of things. The German translator renders it thus: "Wir sind bang, aber wir verzagen nit" (We are anxious, but we do not despair). Erasmus used the verb "to be in labour" (laboramus), which can suit either sense. The Apostle himself used this verb in Galatians 4: "ἀπορούμενοι ἐν ὑμῖν" [I am perplexed about you], that is, I am without counsel concerning you. And in John 13 it is so: the disciples, looking at one another, were "ἀπορούμενοι" [in doubt], that is, hesitating about whom he meant. But the Apostle has used "ἐξαπορηθῆναι" in chapter 1 in this way: "ὥστε ἐξαπορηθῆναι ἡμᾶς καὶ τοῦ ζῆν" [so that we despaired even of life], that is, so that we even despaired of life. It pleases me, therefore, to retain the same sense of these words here as well, and to read "perplexed, but not despairing". We cannot express the allusion of these two words with two Latin words; with German words we could do so more easily and better. Yet I would not greatly object to those who understand it of lack of things, which, as we shall see below in chapter 11, this same Apostle sometimes suffered. Indeed, although he suffered hunger, he never suffered it to the utmost extremity, but always divine providence came to his aid in time. So we would say in German: "Wir leiden Hunger, wir werden aber nit ausgehungert" (We suffer hunger, but are not starved out), as said of those who, besieged in strongholds, are pressed by famine and want and are urged to surrender, yet who, though pressed by a lack of all things, keeping faith with their prince, cannot be forced to surrender, but hold out and at last are delivered. In quite the same way the Apostle guarded the treasure of Christ his Prince with such faith that no lack of things could drive him to betray it; and so he could indeed be "ὑπορηθῆναι" [in want], but he could not be "ἐξαπορηθῆναι" [utterly without resources]. Such was the efficacy of the divine power that strengthened him.

units.la: Si uerbum ἐξαπορηθῆναι desperādi sensu ac ceperimus nascitur quæstio, quomodo neget hic se fieri desperabundū, cū supra cap. 1. loco citato dixerit se adeo fuisse supra modū grauatum in Asia, ut de uitā quoq; desperaret? Ad hanc quæstionem respondemus, aliud esse desperare de uita hac præsenti & aliud desperare de causa ipsa propter quam in discrimen uenieris. De uita sua desperauit Paulus cū supra modū grauaretur in Asia, de ipsa uero causa propter quam grauabatur, nequaquam desperauit: aliās illā desperatione uictus deseruisset, deseruit autem nullo modo, sed ad finem usq; in fide & ministerio suo diuina uirtute suffultus perdurauit.
units.tr: If we take the word ἐξαπορηθῆναι [exaporēthēnai] in the sense of despairing, the question arises of how he can here deny that he was made to despair, when in chapter 1, cited above, he said that he was so greatly burdened in Asia that he even despaired of his life. To this question we reply that it is one thing to despair of this present life and another to despair of the cause itself for which one is put in peril. Paul despaired of his life when he was burdened beyond measure in Asia, but he did not in any way despair of the cause for which he was burdened. Otherwise, overcome by that despair, he would have abandoned it. But he did not abandon it at all; supported by divine power, he persevered in his faith and ministry to the end.

units.la: PERSEQVVTIONEM patimur, inquit, sed in ea nō deserimur.) Persequutionibus agitatū uasculū testaceūac fragile diu posse du-rare, uerosimile non est. At uolebat dominus ut duraret. Cum igitur per se durare non pos-set, assuit illi sua uirtute, & in medijs persequu-tionibus præter omnium opinionem seruauit. Erat igitur argumentum in eo diuinæ uirtu-tis, quod in persequutionibus tandiu durare poterat, id quod pseudapostoli egregiē disi-mulabant, & interim propter crebras perse-quutiones Apostolum Christi contemptui ex ponebant.
units.tr: "We suffer persecution," he says, "but we are not forsaken in it." It is not likely that a fragile earthen vessel, buffeted by persecutions, could endure for long. But the Lord wished it to endure. Since it could not endure by its own strength, he lent it his power and preserved it amid the persecutions, beyond everyone's expectation. There was therefore evidence of divine power in this, that it could hold out so long under persecutions. The false apostles pointedly ignored this, and meanwhile, on account of the frequent persecutions, they held the apostle of Christ up to contempt.

units.la: Quid si referas ista ad omnes Christi fide-les, qui pie in hoc mundo uiuere uolētes per-sequutionē patiūtur, & è quibus multi in per-sequūtionibus necātur? An de illis quoq; prę-dicari potest, quod persequutionem patiētes non deserāntur? Si suos Deus in persequutio nibus non deserit, quid est quod Christus ipse in cruce clamauit: Deus meus, Deus meus quare deseruisti me? Respondeo, deserendi duplex esse genus. Vnum quo suos Deus in persequutionibus sic seruat, ut è manibus im-piorū incolumes eripiantur, ac præter spem omniū in uita hac seruentur. Sic Apostolū suū & multos alios sępenumero præsenti ope ser-uauit & eripuit. Alterum, quō licet de uita pe-riclitantes in ipsa tamen causa, propter quam periclitantur, non deserit, sed constantes in fi-de seruat. Vtroq; modo Apostolum suum, po-steriore omnes eos fideles conseruat, qui in ipsis persequutionibus occiduntur.
units.tr: What if you apply these words to all the faithful of Christ, who, wishing to live piously in this world, suffer persecution, and of whom many are put to death in the persecutions? Can it be said of them too that, suffering persecution, they are not forsaken? If God does not forsake his own in persecutions, what is it that Christ himself cried out on the cross: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" I reply that there are two kinds of forsaking. The one is that by which God so preserves his own in persecutions that they are snatched unharmed from the hands of the impious and are kept alive in this life beyond everyone's hope. So he often preserved and rescued his apostle and many others by his present help. The other is that, although they are in peril of their lives, he does not forsake them in the very cause for which they are in peril, but keeps them steadfast in faith. By the first way he preserved his apostle; by the second he preserves all those faithful ones who are killed in the very persecutions.

units.la: DEIICIMVR, at nō perimus, inquit.) Lo-quitur ad similitudinem eorū, qui in conflictu καταβαλλόμεθα, i. deijciuntur ac prosternuntur ab hoste, & tamen sic seruatur & eriguntur, ut non pereat, sed rursus erecti in hoste uehātur. Sic ipse quoq; etiāsi frequenter, ueluti in ter-ram deijceretur, dū iam carceri includeretur, iam uirgiscēderetur, iam lapidaretur, iam alijs atq; alijs afflictionibus prosterneretur, haud-quaq; tamē peribat, sed ope diuina erectus for-tius in opere domini pergebat. Existimo eum non loqui de animi perculsi deiectione, sed ad similitudinē pugnantiū de uarijs affliotioibus, uelut ictibus, quib. in oculis mundi prosterni, ac uinci uidebatur. Et hac quoq; ratione ex-cellēs in eo uirtus Dei declarabatur, quod to-ties prostratus non peribat. Quis nō singulari felicitate usum dicat eum, qui aliquoties in cōflictu prelij prostratus nō modo non peri-rit, sed tandē & uictor euaserit? At reuera mul-to præclarior in Paulo uirtus declarata fuit, quod præter spem omnium è tam grauibus frequenter periculis liberatus uictor abibat.
units.tr: "We are cast down, but we do not perish," he says. He speaks in the likeness of those who in a conflict are καταβαλλόμεθα [kataballometha], that is, struck down and laid flat by the enemy, and yet are so preserved and raised up that they do not perish, but, raised again, ride on against the enemy. So he too, although often, as if thrown to the ground, was now shut up in prison, now beaten with rods, now stoned, now laid low by one affliction after another, nevertheless was not destroyed, but raised up by divine help, went on more boldly in the work of the Lord. I think he is not speaking of a dejection of a shaken spirit, but in the likeness of fighters who are struck down by various afflictions as by blows, and who seemed in the eyes of the world to be laid flat and conquered. In this way too the excellent power of God was made manifest in him, in that, though so often prostrated, he did not perish. Who would not say that he who, having been laid low several times in the battle line, not only did not perish but in the end emerged victorious, enjoyed singular good fortune? Yet in truth a far more striking power of God was shown in Paul, in that, delivered from such grave dangers so often, beyond everyone's hope, he went away a victor.

units.la: SEMPER mortificationem domini Iesu in corpore circumferentes, inquit, ut & uita Iesu in corpore nostro manifestetur. Semper enim nos qui uiuimus in mortem tradimur propter Iesum, &c.) Cohæret ista. Sensus est. Quid di-co? Ipsam mortificationem domini Iesu inde-sinēter circumfero in corpore meo. Vocat au-tem mortificationem domini Iesu, non quam dominus passus est in suo corpore, sed quam ipse propter dominum indesinenter subibat.
units.tr: "Always carrying about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life of Jesus also may be made manifest in our body. For we who live are always delivered unto death for Jesus' sake," etc. These words cohere. The sense is this: what do I say? I carry about in my body without ceasing the very dying of the Lord Jesus. He calls it the dying of the Lord Jesus not because the Lord suffered it in his own body, but because he himself, for the Lord's sake, unceasingly underwent it.

units.la: Sic enim exponens subijcit. Semper enim nos qui uiuimus in morte tradimur propter Iesum. Quemadmodū igitur suprà cap.1. afflictiões quas pro Christi nomine ferebat, Christi uocat afflictiões: ita hic mortificatione corporis sui, in quam propter dominū tradebatur quotidie, dni Iesu mortificationem appellat.
units.tr: For, explaining himself, he adds: "For we who live are always delivered unto death for Jesus' sake." Therefore, just as above in chapter 1 he calls the afflictions which he bore for the name of Christ the afflictions of Christ, so here he calls the mortification of his own body, into which he was daily delivered for the Lord's sake, the mortification of the Lord Jesus.

units.la: SEMPER, inquit, mortificatione dni Iesu in corpore circumferetes.) Quoniā crebris periculorum incursibus ad internecione ab impijs impetebatur, quid uidebatur aliud, quàm homo prorsus neci destinatus, qui ipsam mortem uelut umbrā insequente se circumferret: perinde atque ouiculae mactationi destinatae, siue sint in pascuis, siue in ouili, mactationem sui circumferunt. Sic loquitur non de ueteris Adæ corporis peccati ac membrorum ipsius, sed de carnis suæ mortificatione, hoc est, de ea qua corpus ipsius, tanquam testaceum uascu-lum, affligebatur propter dominum.
units.tr: "Always," he says, "carrying about the mortification of the Lord Jesus in the body." Since he was attacked by the impious with frequent assaults of dangers, to the point of destruction, what did he seem to be but a man utterly destined for slaughter, who carried about death itself, as a shadow following him? Just as little sheep destined for slaughter carry about their slaughter, whether they are in the pastures or in the fold. He speaks thus not of the body of sin of the old Adam and its members, but of the mortification of his own flesh, that is, of that by which his body, like a fragile earthen vessel, was afflicted for the Lord's sake.

units.la: Nolim tamen admodum digladiari, si quis mortificatione domini hoc loco eam intelligat, quam dominus ipse in corpore suo circumtulit, ut hanc circumferre in corpore suo dicatur, quisquis propter ipsum in mortem tradi-tus conformis illi redditur, quod alibi uocat compati cum Christo.
units.tr: Yet I would not wish to contend too fiercely if someone understands by the mortification of the Lord in this place that which the Lord himself carried about in his own body, so that whoever is delivered unto death for his sake, and is made conformable to him, is said to carry it about in his own body; this he elsewhere calls suffering with Christ.

units.la: VT & uita Iesu in corpore nostro manifestetur inquit.) Exponunt aliter atq; aliter. Potest primo exponi de uita Iesu, in qua ille contra omnium impiorum studia & furias uirtute diuina seruabatur, donec hora esset qua uolēs crucē subiret, & animā suam pro nobis daret. In eiusmodi hominis uita, quæ per omnis generis discrimina seruatur, luculentissimū est diuinæ uirtutis argumentum. Talis fuit uita Christi, talis post Christum extitit & uita Pauli, per quam in corpore ipsius uita Christi manifestabatur.
units.tr: "So that the life of Jesus also may be made manifest in our body," he says. They expound it in different ways. It can first be explained of the life of Jesus, in which he, against the schemes and furies of all the impious, was preserved by divine power until the hour came when he, willing it, would undergo the cross and give his soul for us. In the life of such a man, which is preserved through every kind of peril, there is a most striking proof of divine power. Such was the life of Christ; after Christ, such too was the life of Paul, through which the life of Christ was made manifest in his body.

units.la: Potest deinde & sic exponi, ut uita Iesu uita intelligatur hominis, nō in pace ac securitate, sed in afflictionibus & sub cruce uiuentis. Vt sit sensus. Exprobrat mihi uestri magistri crebras afflictiones, quas propter Christū perferro. Agnosco illas, imo gloriot de illis, tā abest ut uelim eas dissimulare. Dum enim illis indesinenter exercear, quid aliud facio, quàm quod mortificationem domini Iesu in corpore meo circumfero? Et hac circūferendo utiq; ipsam Iesu uitā in corpore meo adumbro, imo manifesto. Talis enim erat uita illius, ut semper morti destinata, & afflictionibus devota uideretur. Dum igitur afflictiões meas diuexat, quid aliud in me q; ipsam Christi uitā diuexat?
units.tr: It can then also be explained so that the life of Jesus is understood as the life of a man living not in peace and security but in afflictions and under the cross. The sense would be this: your teachers reproach me for the frequent afflictions which I endure for Christ. I acknowledge them; indeed I glory in them, so far am I from wishing to conceal them. For while I am unceasingly exercised by them, what else do I do than carry about in my body the mortification of the Lord Jesus? And by carrying this about, I surely shadow forth, indeed I make manifest, the very life of Jesus in my body. For such was his life, that it always seemed destined to death and devoted to afflictions. Therefore, while he harasses my afflictions, what else does he harass in me than the very life of Christ?

units.la: Tertiò, Chrysost. & post hunc Theophyl. huiusmodi sensum adferunt. Quod nos mortificatione domini Iesu, afflictiones uidelicet & quotidianas mortes in corpore nostro circūferimus, quid aliud est, quàm quòd & uita illius in corpore nostro manifestatur? Quis enim in quotidianis nos mortibus seruat, nisi is qui mortuus, & excitatus uiuit in sempiternum? Quòd dns Iesus, pro quo morior quoti-die, adhuc uiuat, in eo satis declaratur, qd' me in tam iugi mortificatione contra omniū opinionem seruat. Sic putat illi perstringi eos qui fide resurrectiōis mortuorū in dubiū uocabāt.
units.tr: Thirdly, Chrysostom, and after him Theophylact, offer a sense of this kind. That we carry about in our body the mortification of the Lord Jesus, namely afflictions and daily deaths, what else is it than that his life also is made manifest in our body? For who preserves us in our daily deaths, except him who, dead and raised up, lives forever? That the Lord Jesus, for whom I die daily, still lives, is sufficiently declared by the fact that he preserves me in such constant mortification against everyone's expectation. In this way, he thinks, those are rebuked who called into doubt, by the faith of the resurrection of the dead.

units.la: Quartò, sunt qui referunt ista ad futurū sæculum, in quo corpora nostra, quæ nunc mortificatione domini uarijs modis afflicta circumferunt, ad claritatem corporis Christi conformabuntur, ut quemadmodum hic mortis, ita illic & uitæ illius imagine sortiantur, ubi mortalitas ipsorum absorbebitur à uita. Exprimit hoc. 2.Tim.2. ad hunc modum. Certus termo. Si mortui fuerimus cum illo, uiuemus etiā cū illo, si sufferimus, regnabimus quoq; cum illo. Significat igitur hoc sensu cum dicit: Semper mortificatione domini Iesu in corpore circumferentes, ut & uita Iesu in corpore nostro manifestetur, quaspe tot afflictiões propter Christum sustineat. Hac uidelicet, fort post hanc uitam, ut quemadmodū mortificationis Christi particeps sit in hoc sæculo, ita particeps fiat illius quoq; uitæ in futuro.
units.tr: Fourthly, there are those who refer these words to the future age, in which our bodies, which now carry about the mortification of the Lord, afflicted in various ways, will be conformed to the glory of the body of Christ, so that, as they share in his death here, so there they may share in the image of his life, where their mortality will be swallowed up by life. Paul expresses this in 2 Tim. 2 in this way: "Faithful is the saying: for if we be dead with him, we shall also live with him; if we suffer, we shall also reign with him." He signifies therefore in this sense when he says: "Always carrying about in the body the mortification of the Lord Jesus, that the life of Jesus also may be made manifest in our body," namely because he endures so many afflictions for Christ's sake. Assuredly, perhaps after this life, so that just as he shares in the mortification of Christ in this age, so he may also share in his life in the age to come.

units.la: Quod autem uerbum manifestādi attinet, ubi dicit: Vt & uita Iesu in corpore nostro manifestetur, existimo referendū esse ad id, quod uita Iesu abscōdita est in electis ac credētibus, per formas mortificationis, quæ in corporib: illorū exercetur, donec in hac carne circumeunt, cū tamē in conspectu Dei nihil sit minus quàm abscōdita: manifestabitur uerò, ubi ipse Christus manifestabitur, qua de re Colos. 3. loquitur ad hunc modum. Itaque si resurrexistis unà cū Christo, superna quærite, ubi Christus est ad dexteram Dei sedēs, superna curate, nō terrestria. Siquidē mortui estis, & uita uestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo. Vbi Christus manifestatus fuerit uita nostra, tunc & uos cum illo manifestabimini in gloria.
units.tr: As for the word "manifested" (manifestandi), where he says "that the life of Jesus may be manifested in our body," I think it should be referred to the life of Jesus that is hidden in the elect and believers, through the forms of mortification exercised in their bodies for as long as they walk in this flesh. Yet in the sight of God nothing is less hidden. It will be manifested when Christ himself is manifested, and on this matter he speaks in Colossians 3 in this way: "If then you are risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; mind the things that are above, not the things that are on earth. For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, who is our life, is manifested, then you also will be manifested with him in glory."

units.la: SEMPER enim nos qui uiuimus, in morte tradimur ꝑpter Iesum, inq̈t, ut & uita Iesu manifestetur in mortali carne nostra.) Illud, q̈ uiuimus, Græce οἱ ζῶντες, i. uiuētes, nonnulli uertendū esse iudicāt, dū uiuimus. i. donec in hac carne ac psenti uita sumus. Verū, meo iudicio, magis facit ad mentē Apostoli, ut legamus, qui uiuimus, quàm, dū uiuimus. Loquitur adhuc de sua persona, & exponit quod in præcedenti se mortificatione domini Iesu in corpore suo circūferre dixit. Est autem hic sensus. Mortificatione domini Iesu semper in corpore nostro circumferimus. Quomodo? Quia nos, qui ecce adhuc uiuimus, semper in morte tradimur propter Iesum. Hoc infrà cap. 6. sic exprimit: Quasi moriētes, & ecce uiuimus. Tradebatur in morte semper propter Iesum, quod attinet studia & conatus impiorum, & indefinentia discrimina, & erat quasi moriens: & tamen ecce uiuebat interim, diuina uirtute seruatus. Considerandam igitur præsentem opem Dei proponit Corinthijs, per quam in tam crebris ac grauibus periculis, magno cum miraculo contra uim impiorum in uita seruabatur.
units.tr: "For we who live are always delivered to death for Jesus' sake," he says, "that the life of Jesus may be manifested in our mortal flesh." The phrase "we who live," in Greek οἱ ζῶντες [hoi zōntes], that is, "the living," some judge should be translated "while we live," that is, as long as we are in this flesh and in the present life. But in my judgment it fits the Apostle's meaning better to read "we who live" than "while we live." He is still speaking of his own person and explaining what he said in the preceding clause, that he bears the mortification of the Lord Jesus in his body. The sense is this: we always bear about in our body the mortification of the Lord Jesus. How? Because we, who even now are still alive, are always delivered to death for Jesus' sake. He expresses this below in chapter 6: "As dying, and behold we live." He was always being delivered to death for Jesus, as far as the schemes and efforts of the wicked and the unending dangers went, and he was as one dying; yet behold, he was meanwhile living, preserved by divine power. So he sets before the Corinthians the present help of God, by which, amid such frequent and grave dangers, he was kept alive against the violence of the wicked, to the great wonder of all.

units.la: VT & uita Iesu, inquit, manifestetur in mor-tali tali carne nostra.) Quod in præcedeti dixit,in corpore nostro,id iam sic clarius exprimit: in mortali carne nostra. Non simpliciter, in carne nostra, sed, in mortali carne nostra,inquit. Quod carnem suam mortalem uocat ad expri mendū illius infirmitatē ac fragilitatem facit, qua tam erat mortificatu facilis, quàm fractu facile est testaceum uasculum, quod eam ob causam fragile uocatur. Quemadmodum admirabile uideretur,si uas fictile quotidie ad frangendum traditum non frangeretur interim,sed illæsum perseueraret, ita uehementer mirabile erat, quod caro Apostoli semper in mortem propter Christum tradita non occidebatur sed uiuebat, cum tamen perinde atq; cæterorū hominum esset mortalis. Cum hoc palam & sic fieret,ut latere non posset, an non uita Iesu in mortali ea carne manifestabatur,si intelligas secundum primam expositionem huius particulæ, quam supra annotauimus:
units.tr: "That the life of Jesus," he says, "may be manifested in our mortal flesh." What he had said in the preceding clause, "in our body," he now expresses more clearly: "in our mortal flesh." He does not simply say "in our flesh," but "in our mortal flesh." By calling his flesh mortal he expresses its weakness and frailty, by which it was as easily mortified as a clay vessel is easily broken, which for that reason is called fragile. Just as it would seem remarkable if an earthen vessel, handed over daily to be broken, were not broken but remained unharmed, so it was greatly wonderful that the flesh of the Apostle, always delivered to death for Christ, was not killed but lived, although it was just as mortal as the flesh of other men. Since this happened so openly and in such a way that it could not be hidden, was not the life of Jesus manifested in that mortal flesh? This holds if you understand the first explanation of this phrase, which we noted above.

units.la: Vita Iesu omnino est,aut qua ille olim in mū do hoc costitutus sub cruce,humilitate & obe dientia patris sui uixit, aut qua iam in cœlis ui uit in gloria, aut qua Paulus in tot afflictionibus propter Iesum,uel qua per uirtutē uiuen tis in cœlo Iesu,siue qua conformiter uitę Iesu in carne mortali uixit, siue qua post hāc uitam corpore glorificato secundum imaginē clari ficati Christi uiɛturus est. Ex tot sententijs eli gat sibi leɛtor, quam existimat præsenti causæ cæteris esse accommodatiorem. Si cui uidebi tur,colligat ad hunc modum. Si mortificatio- nem domini Iesu semper in corpore suo Pau lus circumferebat , quatenus propter Iesum semper in morte tradebatur, consimili igitur ratione & uita Iesu in mortali eius carne ma nifestabatur, quatenus propter Iesum diuina uirtute per tot afflictiones & mortes mirabili ter seruabatur in uita, ut posset dicere, sumus quasi morientes,& ecce uiuimus.
units.tr: The life of Jesus is either that by which he once lived in this world, placed under the cross, in humility and obedience to his Father; or that by which he now lives in glory in heaven; or that by which Paul lived through so many afflictions for Jesus; or that by which Jesus lives through the power of the living one in heaven; or that by which he lived conformably to the life of Jesus in mortal flesh; or that by which he is to live after this life with a glorified body, according to the image of the glorified Christ. The reader may choose for himself from among so many opinions the one that he judges more suitable to the present matter than the others. If anyone thinks fit, let him reason in this way: if Paul bore the mortification of the Lord Jesus always in his body, inasmuch as for Jesus' sake he was always being delivered to death, then by a like reasoning the life of Jesus was manifested in his mortal flesh, inasmuch as for Jesus' sake he was wondrously preserved in life by divine power through so many afflictions and deaths, so that he could say, "we are as dying, and behold we live."

units.la: ITAQVE mors quidē in nobis agit, in quit,uita uero in uobis.) Et hæc particula ua rie exponitur. Chrysostomus & Theophyla ɛtus sic. Nos quidem in periculis sumus, uos autem uita fruimini, quæ ex periculis nostris constat,quippe quibus Euangelium prædica tum est,quo uitam uiuitis sempiternam, & in terim uiuuitis in pace, extra pericula, quibus nos obruimur quotidie. Et Ambrosius confi mili modo : Hæc dicit,inquit,quia pro salute eorum morti subijciebantur. Gentibus enim prædicantes inimicitias sibi excitabant tam à Iudæis q; à Gentibus usq; ad mortē. Exponit nō de Paulo tantū,sed & de reliquis apostolis. Hi tres in eo cōueniunt, quod uitā intelligūt, quæ est ex prædicatione Euangelij, nisi quod Chrysostomus adijcit, uos autē nō estis in tan tis periculis,sed quiete fruimini, & in illa po timini uita quæ est ex istis periculis.Hanc sen tentiam & recentiores quidā sequuntur. Hie ronymus per interrogationem dictum sentit ad hunc modū:Nunquid in nobis semper erit mors,& in uobis uita & futura & præsens:
units.tr: "So then death works in us," he says, "but life in you." This clause also is explained in various ways. Chrysostomus and Theophylactus explain it thus: "We are in dangers, but you enjoy life, which comes from our dangers, since the Gospel has been preached to you, by which you live eternal life; and meanwhile you live in peace, outside the dangers by which we are overwhelmed every day." Ambrosius, in a similar way: "He says this," he writes, "because they were being subjected to death for their salvation. For in preaching to the Gentiles they stirred up enmities against themselves, both from the Jews and from the Gentiles, even unto death." He explains it not only of Paul but of the other apostles as well. These three agree in understanding the life that comes from the preaching of the Gospel, except that Chrysostomus adds that "you are not in such great dangers, but enjoy quiet, and you partake in that life which comes out of those dangers." Some more recent writers also follow this opinion. Hieronymus thinks the statement is made by way of a question, in this manner: "Will death always be in us, and life in you, both future and present?"

units.la: Mea sententia cum illis est,qui hisce uerbis pseudapostolos falsè perstringi iudicát,qui in terea dum in medijs mortibus quotidie uersa retur ipse Apostolus, Christianismū talem cū suis meditabántur,in quo agerent absque ullo discrimine securi ac quieti. Hos igitur notans dicit:Itaq; mors quidē in nobis agit,dum quo tidie propter Christū in mortem tradimur, in uobis uero agit uita. Quasi dicat:Vos estis se curi,dū nos quotidie periclitamur,uidete qua les Christiani sitis. Verū non subsistit hoc lo co,sed breuiter notat pseudapostolos & eorū assectatores. In priore autē Epistola cap.4.idē agit fusius,ubi dicit:Iam saturati estis,iam dita ti estis,absq; nobis regnū adepti estis,atq; uti nam sane adepti sitis, & quæ sequuntur. Duo admittebant pseudapostoli in hac causa , pro pter quę merito perstringebātur ab Apostolo. Vnum erat, quod persequutiones & afflictio nesChristi fugientes,quo securius ac quietius agerent, circuncifionem & legis obseruantiā Euangelio Christi cōiungebant. Alterū,quod Apostolatum Pauli propter crebras illius affli ctiones cōtemptui exponebāt. Quare merito hoc illis obijcit, quod in se mors , in ipsis uita ageret. Aliàs frequēter hæc accidit in ecclesijs Christi diuersitas,ut dū alij uersantur in mor te,agant alij in uita, pace ac securitate.An non in fratribus nostris,qui sunt in Anglia, Gallia, Italia,Hispania agit mors,in nobis uero uita,q uersamur ijs locis Germaniæ,in quibus liber tas habetur Euágelicæ doɛtrinę ac religionis. Illi uarijs afflictionibus exagitantur,& uelut oues occisionis neci tradūtur propter Euáge liū Christi:Nos eidē adhęrētes Euágelio uiui m⁹ in pace ac securitate.Et utinā nō patiamur aliquando lōgę pacis mala. Potest hęc dinersi tas ex diuina dispositione in ecclesijs esse fide liū.Verū id excusari nō poterit, quod nonulli sic administrant Euangelium Christi,ut nullis fiant periculis obnoxij in hoc mundo, & inte rim eos qui ueritatis gratia afflictantur,pro ir requietis & seditiosis habēt, qui suapte culpa incidát in discrimina uitæ, quemadmodū nec eos probare possumus , qui cū phanatico spiri tu exagitati turbent ecclesias,& eā ob causam legibus Magistratuū coerceātur, ministros E uágelij uētris seruos uocát,&de afflictionibus suis gloriātes,improperát illis quieté ac pacé, quasi illā non diuino beneficio acceptam,sed malo corruptæ doɛtrinæ studio acquisitā ha beant. Verū argumentum corruptæ doɛtrinæ non est mox in quiete ac securitate uitæ, quē admodum non mox in afflictionibus ac per sequutionibus argumentū est doɛtrinæ sanæ.
units.tr: My opinion agrees with those who judge that the false apostles are rightly rebuked by these words, since, while the Apostle himself was daily exposed to deaths in the midst of them, they were devising for themselves and their followers a Christianity in which they could act securely and quietly, without any danger. Noting these men, he says: "So then death works in us," since daily for Christ's sake we are delivered to death, "but life works in you." As if he said: "You are secure while we are in danger every day; see what kind of Christians you are." Yet he does not dwell on this point, but only briefly marks the false apostles and their adherents. In the earlier Epistle, chapter 4, he treats the same matter more fully, where he says: "Now you are full, now you are rich, you have obtained the kingdom without us, and would indeed that you had obtained it," and what follows. In this matter the false apostles held two positions for which they were rightly rebuked by the Apostle. The first was that, fleeing persecutions and afflictions of Christ so that they might act more safely and quietly, they joined circumcision and observance of the law to the Gospel of Christ. The second was that they held Paul's apostleship in contempt because of his frequent afflictions. Therefore he rightly charges them with this: that death works in him and life in them. Elsewhere it often happens in the churches of Christ that, while some live in death, others live in life, in peace and security. Is not death at work in our brethren who are in England, France, Italy and Spain, while in us, who live in those regions of Germany where liberty of evangelical doctrine and religion is enjoyed, life is at work? They are harassed by various afflictions and, like sheep, are handed over to slaughter for the Gospel of Christ; we, adhering to the same Gospel, live in peace and security. And would that we did not someday suffer the evils of a long peace. This diversity can be among the faithful in the churches by divine disposition. But what cannot be excused is that some so administer the Gospel of Christ that they become liable to no dangers in this world, and meanwhile they regard as restless and seditious those who are afflicted for the sake of the truth, as if they brought the danger to their lives by their own fault. Nor can we approve of those who, stirred up by a fanatical spirit, disturb the churches, and for this reason are restrained by the laws of the magistrates; they call the ministers of the Gospel slaves of their belly, and, boasting of their own afflictions, reproach them with their quiet and peace, as if they had it not by divine benefit but had acquired it by the evil study of corrupt doctrine. But the sign of corrupt doctrine is not at once quiet and security of life, just as the sign of sound doctrine is not at once afflictions and persecutions.

units.la: Cæterū cū habeamus eundē spiritū fidei iuxta illud q̃d scriptū est: Credidi, & ideo loquutus sum:& nos credimus, quapropter & loquímur, sciētes quod qui suscitauít dominū Iesum, nos quo que per Iesum suscitabit,&cōstituet uo biscū, Nā omnia propter uos, ut beneficium quod exudauit pluribus gratias agetibus Deo exuberet in gloria Dei. Propterea no defatigamur, sed quanuis externus homo noster corrupitur, internus tame renouaturin dies lingulos. Nam momentanea leuitas afflictionis nostrę mire supra modum æternum pondus glorię parit nobis, dum no spe ctamus ea quæ uidetur, sed ea quæ non uidentur. Nam quę uidentur temporaria sunt, at quæ non uidentur æterna.
units.tr: But since we have the same spirit of faith, according to what is written: "I believed, and therefore have I spoken"; we also believe, and therefore we speak, knowing that he who raised up the Lord Jesus will raise us also through Jesus and will present us with you. For all things are for your sake, so that grace, abounding through the thanksgiving of many, may overflow to the glory of God. Therefore we do not lose heart; though our outward man is wasting away, yet our inward man is renewed day by day. For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, works for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory, while we look not at the things which are seen but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.

units.la: Legendum est non ut Erasmus uertit: Cæterum cum habeamus, quasi ad aliá materiam progrediatur, sed simpliciter ut est in Græco, id est, habentes autem eundem spiritum fidei. Sensus est: Quemadmodum autem Dauid olim spiritum habens fidei credebat, & ut credebat loquebatur, sicut scriptum reliquit: credidi & ideo loquutus sum, ita & nos eundem habentes fidei spiritum credimus, qua propter & loquimur. Videdum igitur est, unde sumpserit scripturæ locum quem adducit, & quid crediderit Dauid quidq; credendo loquutus sit, deinde quid ipse Apostolus crediderit, & quod nam fidei uerbum in præcedentibus protulerit.
units.tr: It must be read not as Erasmus translates it, "But since we have", as if the Apostle were passing on to another subject, but simply as it stands in the Greek, that is, "having, however, the same spirit of faith." The sense is this: just as David once, having the spirit of faith, believed, and as he believed he spoke, as he left in writing, "I believed, and therefore have I spoken", so we too, having the same spirit of faith, believe, and therefore we speak. Therefore we must consider where he took the passage of Scripture that he quotes, and what David believed and spoke in believing, then what the Apostle himself believed, and what word of faith he had set forth in the preceding verses.

units.la: Quod locum scripturæ attinet: Credidi, & ideo loquutus sum, habetur ille in Psalmo centesimo sextodecimo, secundum numerum Ebræorum, ubi legitur ad hunc modum המאמנתי B בי ארבר, id est, Credidi quod essem loquuturus. Vel, Credebam cum loquerer. Pagninus uertit: Credidi quando loquutus sum. Septuaginta verterunt: ἐπίστευσα διὸ ἐλάλησα, id est, Credidi, ideo loquutus sum. Quod in Ebraeo est בי, id est, quoniam, uel cum, illi reddiderunt per διό, id est, propterea, ideo propter quod. Et eam lectionem usurpauit Apostolus quod in magno usu & authoritate esset uersio Sept.
units.tr: As for the passage of Scripture, "I believed, and therefore have I spoken", it is found in Psalm 116 according to the Hebrew numbering, where it reads in this manner: הֶאֱמַנְתִּי כִּי אֲדַבֵּר [heemanti ki adabber], that is, "I believed that I was about to speak", or "I believed when I spoke." Pagninus translates: "I believed when I spoke." The Seventy rendered: ἐπίστευσα διὸ ἐλάλησα [episteusa dio elalesa], that is, "I believed, therefore I spoke." What is בִּי [ki] in the Hebrew, that is, "because" or "when", they rendered by διό [dio], that is, "therefore, for this reason." The Apostle used that reading because the version of the Seventy was in great use and authority.

units.la: Quid autem credes loquutus sit Dauid, diligens lector facile intelliget, si Psalmum ipsum attente legat. Circumdederunt me, inquit, laquei mortis, angustiæ infernales inuenerant me, angustiam & dolorem inueneram. Et nomen domini inuocabam (dicens) obsecro domine, eripe animam meam. Sic præmisit narrationem discriminis in quo fuerat, & nominis Dei inuocationem, iam audi uerba fidei. Benignus est dominus, & probus, & Deus noster misericors. Custodit paruulos dominus. Hæc erat illius de domino fides. Ex ea quid est loquutus? Sequitur attenuatus sum, at seruabit me. Reuertere anima mea in requiem tuam, quoniam dominus benefaciet tibi. Quoniam eripies animam meam e morte, oculos meos a lachrymis, pedem meum a lapsu. Versabor coram domino in terris uiuentium. Hęc ex fide, qua erat in dominum, loquutus subiugit. Credidi, cum hæc loquerer, uel, Credidi, ideo loquutus sum. Credebat dominum esse benignum, probum, misericorde, custodem ac Seruato-
units.tr: What David believed and so spoke, a diligent reader will easily understand if he reads the Psalm itself attentively. "The snares of death", he says, "compassed me; the pains of hell gat hold upon me; I found trouble and sorrow. Then called I upon the name of the LORD: O LORD, I beseech thee, deliver my soul." So he first sets out the account of the danger he was in, and the calling upon the name of God; now hear his words of faith: "Gracious is the LORD, and righteous; yea, our God is merciful. The LORD preserveth the simple." This was his faith concerning the Lord. What he spoke out of that faith follows: "I was brought low, and he helped me. Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the LORD hath dealt bountifully with thee. For thou hast delivered my soul from death, mine eyes from tears, and my feet from falling. I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living." Out of the faith he had in the Lord, he adds, as one speaking: "I believed when I spoke these things", or, "I believed, therefore I spoke."

units.la: rem paruulorum. Sic credens loquebatur uerba fidei, seruabit me, reuertere anima mea in requiem tuam, quia benefaciet tibi dominus. Item: Eripies animam meam e morte, &c. Et Versabor adhuc coram domino (id est, in atrijs domini, in medio Hierusalem, unde fuerat eiectus) in terris uiuentium.
units.tr: He believed the Lord to be kind, righteous, merciful, and the keeper and saviour of the simple. So, believing, he spoke the words of faith: "He will help me; return, O my soul, unto thy rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you." Likewise: "You will deliver my soul from death", and so on. And "I will still walk before the Lord" (that is, in the courts of the Lord, in the midst of Jerusalem, from which he had been cast out) "in the land of the living."

units.la: Sic credidit, & sic loquutus est Dauid, neutrum in uanum, sed ueraciter utrunq;, unde & secundum fidem suam liberatus e discrimine extremo redijt Hierosolymam in atria domini, inq; illis reddidit uota sua domino, quæ in discrimine constitutus uouerat, ac sacrificauit illi sacrificium laudis. Iam de Apostolo uideamus, quomodo scripturam hanc ad causam suam citet.
units.tr: So David believed and so spoke; neither was in vain, but both truly. Hence, also according to his faith, he was delivered from the utmost danger and returned to Jerusalem into the courts of the Lord, and there he paid his vows to the Lord, which he had vowed while in danger, and offered to him the sacrifice of praise. Now let us see from the Apostle how he cites this Scripture for his own cause.

units.la: HABENTES autem eundem spiritum fidei inquit.) Intellige, quem habuit Dauid. Est aut spiritus fidei, si loquutione hac urgeas, aut spiritus credens, uel, fidei seruans, aut spiritus fidem operans in cordibus hominum, aut donū fidei, ut spiritus, pro dono spiritus accipiatur, sicut spiritus patientiæ, donum est patientiæ, aut ingenium fidei, ut eundem habere fidei spiritū, idem fit habere fidei ingenium. Verum hoc loco spiritum fidei pro dono fidei posuit. Nec inuenio locum præter hunc unum, in quo hac fit locutione usus. Nobis autem diligeter obseruandum est, quod cum posset dicere: habentes autem eundem fidem, dixit, habentes autem eundem spiritū fidei. Meo iudicio, amplius quiddam est habere spiritum fidei, q; sim pliciter aliquid credere, quemadmodum amplius est habere spiritū sapientię, quàm aliquā in re sapere, ampliushabere spiritū spei, spiritū dilectionis, quàm simpliciter aliquando sperare, & aliquando diligere. Innumeros reperias, quos & si nonnunquam credere, sperare, diligere, & patientes esse uideas, spiritum tamen fidei, spei, dilectionis & patientiæ habere non facile dixeris, propterea quod & reliqua illorū uita à tam insigni dono disideat, & in eo qd' recte facere uidentur haud diu perduret, quorum neutrum in illis deprehenditur, qui spiritu sunt fidei, spei, charitatis & patientiæ imbuti, præsertim excellentius cæteris, quales extiterunt Dauid & Paulus, duo celeberrima uerę fidei exemplaria.
units.tr: "But having", he says, "the same spirit of faith." Understand it as David had it. Now the spirit of faith is, if you press the expression, either a spirit that believes, or a spirit that keeps faith, or a spirit that works faith in the hearts of men; or the gift of faith, the spirit being taken for the gift of the Spirit, just as "spirit of patience" is the gift of patience; or the disposition of faith, so that to have the same spirit of faith is the same as to have the same disposition of faith. But in this place he has put "spirit of faith" for the gift of faith, and I find no other place besides this one where this expression is used. We must carefully observe, however, that although he could have said, "having the same faith", he said "having the same spirit of faith." In my judgment, to have the spirit of faith is something more than simply to believe something, just as to have the spirit of wisdom is more than to be wise in some matter, and to have the spirit of hope and the spirit of love is more than simply sometimes to hope and sometimes to love. You will find countless people who, though you may sometimes see them believe, hope, love and be patient, you could not easily say that they have the spirit of faith, hope, love and patience, because the rest of their life is far from such a notable gift, and what they seem to do rightly does not last long. Neither of these is found in those who are imbued with the spirit of faith, hope, charity and patience, especially those who excelled the others, such as David and Paul, the two most famous examples of true faith.

units.la: IVXTA illud quod scriptum est: Credidi, & ideo loquutus sum.) Testificatur igitur de Dauide, quod spiritu fidei eodé quo ipse imbutus crediderit, & quæ credebat loquutus fit. Hūc fidei spiritū coeunit in uerbis & factis Dauidis perinde atq; Apostoli uigilater obseruare. Non in uerbis, inquá, duntaxat, sed & in factis. Etenim spiritus fidei non loquitur tantum uerba, sed facit etiam opera fidei. Eodem fidei spiritu, quo lingua credétium regitur ad loquendum, regitur & manus ad operandum. Non est eiusdem spiritus argumentum in illis, quorū lingua sonat Christū, manus uero expriműt antichristū, de quib. dici potest, uox quidé uox Iacob, manus uero manus sunt Esau. Quod ob id admoneo, ne quoniâ scriptum est: Credidi, & ideo loquutus sum, existime- mus, satis esse ad declarandū quod fideles si- mus, si uerba fidei in speciem proferamus, cre- dendūq; soli sit linguæ, quicquid agát manus.
units.tr: "According to what is written: I believed, and therefore have I spoken." He therefore bears witness concerning David that, with the same spirit of faith with which he himself was imbued, he believed, and he spoke what he believed. We must watch carefully that this spirit of faith is joined in the words and deeds of David, just as the Apostle does. Not in words alone, I say, but also in deeds. For the spirit of faith does not only speak words, but also does the works of faith. By the same spirit of faith by which the tongue of believers is governed to speak, the hand is also governed to work. There is no proof of the same spirit in those whose tongue sounds of Christ while their hands express Antichrist, of whom it may be said: "The voice indeed is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau." I warn of this so that, because it is written, "I believed, and therefore have I spoken", we may not think it enough to prove that we are faithful if we put forward words of faith in appearance, and that belief belongs only to the tongue, whatever the hand may do.

units.la: ET nos credimus, inquit, quapropter & loquimur.) Non est necessarium ut percurra- mus hic uniuersam Apostoli fidē, & quæcunq; ex illa loquutus est, sed manendum est in ter- mino causæ de qua disserit. Quid igitur in illa credit, & ut credit loquitur? Credebat se per diuinæ uirtutis gratiam non deseri, quantum- uis magnis periculis indesinenter inuoluere- tur, sed semper eripi. Et ut credebat ita est & loquutus, sicuti uidimus in præcedentibus. Quo pertinēt & ea quæ subijcit dicens: scien- tes quod qui suscitauit dominum Iesum, nos quoq; per Iesum suscitabit, & constituet uobi- scum. Hæc quoniā temerarie dicta uideri po- terant, tametsi reipsa coprobarentur frequen- ter, ex spiritu tamen fidei asserit à se dici.
units.tr: "And we believe", he says, "therefore we also speak." It is not necessary here to run through the whole faith of the Apostle, and all that he spoke out of it, but we must remain within the limit of the cause he is discussing. What, then, does he believe in that, and what does he speak as he believes? He believed that by the grace of the divine power he would not be forsaken, however much he was continually entangled in great dangers, but would always be delivered. And as he believed, so he also spoke, as we have seen in what goes before. To this pertain also the words that he adds: "knowing that he who raised up the Lord Jesus will raise us also through Jesus and will present us with you." Since these words could seem rashly spoken, even though they were frequently proved true in fact, he asserts that they are said by him out of the spirit of faith.

units.la: Citantur ista contra eos, qui ad salutis suæ rationem satis esse putant, si corde credant, etiamsi quod credunt altissime dissimulent, nec ullo modo confiteantur. Recte illis objici- tur ingeniū hoc fidei, quo sic coparati sunt qui uere credunt, ut quod credunt loquantur etiā & confiteantur, quo admoneantur, ne seipsi fallant, opinioné fidei pro uera fide amplexi, sed dum alieni ab illius efficacia deprehedun- tur in se reuersi pro dono uerę fidei clamēt ad dominum. Verum ea de re in Proscęro nostro.
units.tr: These things are cited against those who think it enough for their salvation if they believe in their heart, even though they utterly conceal what they believe and in no way confess it. The disposition of faith is rightly objected to them, by which those who truly believe are so equipped that they also speak and confess what they believe; so that they may be warned not to deceive themselves, embracing an opinion of faith in place of true faith, but, when they find themselves estranged from its efficacy, return into themselves and cry out to the Lord for the gift of true faith. But concerning this matter, see in our Proscerus.

units.la: Vtinam autē quod ab Apostolo hic dici- tur, & nos credimus quapropter & loquimur, uere posit ab omnibus uerbi Dei ministris di ci,in quibus inualescit illorū multitudo, quo- rum alij magis quæ opinantur, quàm quę cre- dunt ecclesijs pro uerbo Dei proponunt, alij quæ legunt in scripturis, non alio quàm literæ instinctu absque spiritu & fide in ecclesijs lo- quuntur. Priores admodum seducunt, poste- riores parum ædificant, animum auditoribus non facientes, quia animum ipsi non habent.
units.tr: Would that what the Apostle says here, "we believe, and therefore we also speak", could truly be said by all ministers of the Word. Among them the number grows of those who put forward to the churches as the Word of God what they rather think than believe, and of others who speak in the churches only what they have read in Scripture, moved by nothing but the letter, without the Spirit and without faith. The former greatly mislead, and the latter build up little, not stirring the minds of their hearers, because they have no mind of their own.

units.la: SCIENTES, inquit, quod qui suscitauit dominū Iesum, nos quoque per Iesum suscita- bit, & constituet uobiscum.) Quoniā uerbum credenti frequenter ab illis quoq; usurpatur, qui quod opinantur credere se dicunt, atq; ita affirmant, ac si sit omnium uerissimum, cum sit inanis opinio, ideo postquam dixit: Et nos credimus, quapropter & loquimur, ne ex ina- ni opinione, & non uera ac certa fide loqui ui- deatur, non dicit: Credētes, sed, sciētes, quod qui suscitauit dominum Iesum, nos quoq; per Iesum suscitabit & constituet uobiscum.
units.tr: "KNOWING," he says, "that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also through Jesus, and will present us with you." The word "believing" is often used by those who say that they believe what they only suppose, and who affirm it as the most certain truth when it is empty opinion. So, having said "We believe, and therefore we also speak", lest he seem to speak from empty opinion and not from true and certain faith, he does not say "believing" but "knowing": that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also through Jesus, and will present us with you.

units.la: Sunt autem hęc uerba sic comparata, ut bi- sariam exponi queant. Primo sic, ut intelligen da sint de suscitatione quę sit non è sepulchro, sed ex periculis mortis, cuius & supra capite primo meminit dicens: Quin ipsi in nobisipsis sententiam mortis acceperamus, ne confide- remus in nobisipsis, sed in Deo, qui ad uitam suscitat mortuos, qui ex tanta morte eripuit nos, & eripit, in quo spem fixam habemus, quod etiam posthac sit erepturus.
units.tr: These words can be explained in two ways. First, they may be understood of a raising that is not from the tomb but from the dangers of death. He mentioned this above in chapter 1, saying: "But we ourselves had the sentence of death within ourselves, so that we should not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead, who delivered us from so great a death, and does deliver us, in whom we have set our hope that he will also deliver us henceforth."

units.la: Quod illic se spem fixam habere dicit, quod erepturus sit ipsum Deus è morte, id in præ- senti sic exprimit, ut scire se dicat, quod qui do minum Iesum suscitauit, se quoq; sit per Iesum suscitaturus, hoc est, per uirtutem domini Iesu è discrimine mortis liberaturus. Et huic sensui pulchre conuenit quod addit: & constituet uo- biscum, hoc est, sic me liberum reddet, ut uo- bis restitui possim, quò & quod sequitur per- tinere uidetur, cum dicit: Nam omnia propter uos, ut beneficium quod exundauit pluribus gratias agentibus, exuberet in gloriam Dei.
units.tr: When he says there that he has his hope fixed on God delivering him from death, he now expresses it by saying that he knows that he who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise him through Jesus; that is, will free him from the peril of death by the power of the Lord Jesus. The words that follow agree well with this sense, "and will present us with you"; that is, he will so free me that I can be restored to you. What follows also seems to pertain to this, when he says: "For all things are for your sakes, so that the grace which abounds through the thanksgiving of many may overflow to the glory of God."

units.la: Deinde possunt exponi de futura resurre- ctione, ad hunc modum. Sciētes quod qui do- minū Iesum suscitauit è morte, nos quoq; per illum in die iudicij quo suscitaturus est mor- tuos, suscitabit è morte, & uobiscū constituet, ut in sempiternum coiungamur. Sic, inquam, exponi possunt, si separatim inspiciātur, secus uero, si à sequentibus non auellantur.
units.tr: Second, the words may be explained of the future resurrection, in this way: "knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus from the dead will also raise us from the dead through him on the day of judgment, when he is to raise the dead, and will present us with you, so that we may be joined together for ever." They can be explained thus, I say, if they are looked at separately; otherwise, if they are not detached from what follows.

units.la: Nascitur autē in hoc sensu, quem plerosq; post ueteres amplećti uideo, haud dissimulan da quæstio. Quæri nanq; potest, an post futu- ram resurrectionem, in statu futuri sæculi, con stituendus sit Paulus cum Corinthijs, & si sit, quare cum illis magis quàm cum cęteris fide- libus, quos & ipsos in Christo genuit, &, num cæteri quoq; apostoli, cum illis singuli coniun gendi sint, quos cum hic uiuerent ad fidē Chri sti conuerterunt. Et si hoc futurum sit, an non eiusmodi coniunctiones locum habituræ sint in cæteris quoq; statibus & ordinibus, ut qui in hac uita coiuncti sunt, in futura quoq; con- iunctim uiuant. Talia, & quæ annexa sunt ta- libus, quæri poterunt hoc loco præsertim à cu riosis, & nescio quas sibi futurarū rerum ima- gines somniatibus, quæ à præsentis sæculi sta- tibus ac moribus haud abludant. Hanc nos quęstionem, ut curiosam & infrugiferā, perq; solam futuræ uitæ experientiā explicabilem, curiosis hominibus relinquimus, & omnem futuræ nostri coniunctionis rationem & con- ditionem vni Deo committimus.
units.tr: In this sense, which I see most people embrace after the ancients, a question arises that must not be concealed. For it can be asked whether, after the future resurrection, in the state of the age to come, Paul is to be placed with the Corinthians; and if so, why with them rather than with the other faithful whom he also begot in Christ; and whether the other apostles too are to be joined individually to those whom they converted to the faith of Christ while they lived here. And if this is to happen, will not such joinings also take place in the other states and orders, so that those who were joined in this life will also live together in the life to come? Such questions, and others connected with them, may be raised here, especially by the curious, who dream up some images of future things that do not differ much from the states and customs of the present age. We leave this question, as curious and unfruitful, and explicable only by experience of the future life, to curious people, and we commit the whole manner and condition of our future union to God alone.

units.la: Illud autem obseruandum est, quod sensus superioris particulæ, qua se semper propter Iesum in morte tradi dixit, ut & uita Iesu in car ne ipsius mortali manifestetur, à sensu præsen tis loci dependet. Si prior expositio tenenda est, sicut apparet, consequitur & illic eam esse tenendam, quam primo loco posuimus. Si po sterior hic probatur, probanda est & illic, quæ postrema assignatur.
units.tr: It must also be observed that the sense of the earlier clause, in which he said that he is always delivered to death for Jesus' sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest in his mortal flesh, depends on the sense of the present passage. If the first explanation is to be held, as appears, it follows that the one we placed first must be held there too. If the second is approved here, it must be approved there too, the one assigned last.

units.la: SCIENTES, inquit, quod qui suscitauit dominū Iesum, nos quoq; p Iesum suscitabit.) Non dicit simpliciter: Sciētes, quod nos Deus suscitabit, sed, Sciētes quod qui suscitauit do- minum Iesum, nos quoque per Iesum suscita- bit. Sumit ergo scientiam hanc, quod se Deus suscitaturus sit, ex eo quod dominum Iesum suscitauerit. Sic fides resurrectiōis Christi cer- tā ipsi spem de sui quoq; suscitatiōe gignebat.
units.tr: "KNOWING," he says, "that he who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us through Jesus." He does not simply say, "knowing that God will raise us", but "knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us through Jesus." He therefore takes this knowledge, that God will raise him, from the fact that God raised the Lord Jesus. Thus faith in the resurrection of Christ begot in him a sure hope of his own resurrection too.

units.la: Dicet autem quisquam. Ecquæ est illa consequentia? Deus suscitauit dominū Iesum,ergo per hunc suscitare debuit & Paulū. Suscitauit pater filium suum,quid hoc ad Paulū? qui & si erat Apostolus,filio tamē multo erat inferior.
units.tr: Someone will say: what kind of inference is this? God raised the Lord Jesus; therefore he ought to raise Paul through him. The Father raised his own Son; what has this to do with Paul? Although he was an apostle, he was far inferior to the Son.

units.la: Respondeo.Non est in hac causa consyderada in se domini Iesu Christi præstantia & prerogatiua,qua cunctos non homines modo sed & angelos incoparabili dignitate antecellit, sed dignatio diuinæ maiestatis,qua filiū suum pro nobis dedit in mortem,& cum eum suscitaret,p nobis suscitauit,iuxta illud:Qui mortuus est propter peccata nostra, & resurrexit propter iustificationem nostri. Hac consyderatione omnino consequitur, ut ueraciter dicamus:Scimus quod qui suscitauit dominum Iesum,suscitabit & nos per Iesum,quandoquidem propter nos illum suscitauit.
units.tr: I answer: in this matter we must not consider the excellence and prerogative of the Lord Jesus Christ in himself, by which he surpasses all, not only men but also angels, in incomparable dignity. Rather, we must consider the condescension of the divine majesty, by which he gave his Son for us to death, and in raising him, raised him for us, according to that saying: "who was delivered for our sins, and was raised for our justification" (Rom. 4). From this consideration it follows altogether that we may truly say: we know that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also through Jesus, since he raised him for our sake.

units.la: Non est autem ociosum, quod non simpliciter dicit:nos quoq; suscitabit,sed,nos quoq; p Iesum suscitabit. Neq; enim sic eum propter nos suscitauit,ut nos quoq; propter ipsum suscitet,sed ut sit nobis ille æternæ uitæ author ac dominus,redemptor & Seruator,habeatq; potestatem suscitandi mortuos perinde atque pater. Quare uigilanter hic dicit Apostolus, nos quoq; per Iesum suscitabit. Et ipse dominus Iohan.quinto dicit: Sicut pater suscitat mortuos & viuificat,ita & filius quos uult uiuificat. Confulto tamen opus uiuificationis, sic tribuit Christo domino,ut sit patris , per ipsum operantis,cum dicit: Qui suscitauit dominum Iesum,nos quoq; suscitabit per Iesum. Et Christus dicebat:pater in me manens ipse facit opera.Ita conuenit nos à Deo patre expectare omnia,ut tamen expectemus per Christum,& sic per Christum accipere quæ accipimus,ut tamen à Deo patre dare ea sentiamus. Sol nos illuminat ac fouet,sed per suos radios. Per radios solares accipimus & lucem & calorem,uerum à Sole.
units.tr: Nor is it idle that he does not simply say, "he will raise us also", but "he will raise us also through Jesus." For he did not raise him for our sake in such a way that he would also raise us for his sake; rather, so that he might be to us the author and Lord of eternal life, the redeemer and saviour, and might have the power of raising the dead just as the Father has. Therefore the Apostle carefully says here, "he will raise us also through Jesus." And the Lord himself says in John 5: "As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills." Yet, on purpose, he attributes the work of quickening to Christ the Lord in such a way that it is the Father's work performed through him, when he says: "He who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also through Jesus." And Christ used to say: "The Father dwelling in me does the works himself" (John 14). So we ought to expect everything from God the Father, and yet to expect it through Christ, and to receive through Christ what we receive, yet to perceive that it is given by God the Father. The sun lights and warms us, but through its rays. We receive both light and heat through the rays of the sun, yet from the sun itself.

units.la: ET constituet uobiscum,inquit.)Diximus supra,quid quæstionis nascatur, si particulam hanc ad futuram uitam retulerimus , iam ubi eam de restitutione intelligimus,qua se Corinthijs Apostolus è discrimine grauium afflictionum liberatum restituendum fore dicit, quæsierit quisquam, quomodo se hoc scire dicat, cum non legamus usquam, quod post hasce literas Corinthum uenerit.Respondemus,non esse hic excludendum conditionem generalem illam, & in omnibus huiusmodi loquutionibus si non exprimitur,necessario subintellgedam,uidelicet,si ea uisam fuerit domino. Dubio procul,non sic de scientia sua præsumere uoluit,ut uoluntati ac dispositioni diuinę prejudicaret. Dixit se scire,quod qui dominum Iesum suscitauit,se quoq; sit per Iesum suscitaturus.Et adiecit:ac constituet uobiscum. Sensus est. Sic me suscitabit, ut si uidebitur uobiscum constitui possim. Quanquam non est satis firmum,quod nunquam postea uenerit Corinthum,etiamsi scriptum non legatur.
units.tr: "AND will present us with you," he says. We said above what question arises if we refer this clause to the future life. Now, when we understand it of the restoration by which the Apostle says he will be restored to the Corinthians, freed from the peril of grievous afflictions, someone may ask how he can say he knows this, since we do not read anywhere that he came to Corinth after this letter. We answer that the general condition is not to be excluded here, which in all such expressions, if it is not stated, must necessarily be understood: namely, if it shall seem good to the Lord. Without doubt, he did not wish to presume so much on his own knowledge as to prejudice the will and disposition of God. He said he knew that he who raised the Lord Jesus would also raise him through Jesus. And he added: "and will present us with you." The sense is: he will raise me so that, if it is seen fit, I may be presented with you. Although it is not sufficiently certain that he never afterwards came to Corinth, even if it is not written that he did.

units.la: NAM omnia propter uos,inquit.) Reddit rationem,unde sciat,quod suscitandus sit per Iesum,& cum ipsis constituendus. Poterat dicere: Nam æquum est ut suscitet per Iesum, quandoquidem propter Iesum in mortem trador quotidie.Verum maluit dicere: Nam omnia propter uos, quo rationem reddat non se sed ipsos concernentem, & non quid æquum sit coram Deo,sed quàm omnia ad ipsorum salutem disponantur à Deo exprimentem.Sensus est:Quod scio fore ut suscitet per Iesum,ac uobiscum constituat,ex eo est,quod scio propter uos geri omnia quæ mecum geruntur, quo gratiæ ac salutis,quæ in Christo est,fitis participes. Nihil dicit hic aliud,quàm quod supra cap.1.dixit ad hunc modum: Siue autem affligimur,id fit pro uestri consolatione ac salute, siue consolationem accipimus,pro uestri consolatione ac salute,&c.Idem 1.Cor.3.sic protulit:Itaq; ne quis glorietur in hominibus. Omnia nanq; uestra sunt. Magna omnino consolatio ueris pijs ac fidelibus ex eo est,quod sciunt propter se ac suo bono geri diuinitus omnia.
units.tr: FOR ALL THINGS ARE FOR YOUR SAKES, he says. He gives the reason by which he knows that he is to be raised up through Jesus and set with them. He could have said: "For it is fitting that he raise me up through Jesus, since for Jesus' sake I am daily delivered to death." But he preferred to say: "For all things are for your sakes," by which he gives a reason that concerns not himself but them, and states not what is fitting before God but how all things are ordered by God for their salvation. The sense is: that I know he will raise me up through Jesus and set me with you comes from this, that I know all the things that happen to me happen for your sake, so that you may be partakers of the grace and salvation that are in Christ.
