Here he says nothing other than what he said above in chapter 1, in this manner: "Whether we are afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation; or whether we receive consolation, it is for your consolation and salvation," etc. He expressed the same in 1 Corinthians 3: "Therefore let no one glory in men, for all things are yours." It is a great consolation to true, pious and faithful people that they know that all things are done by God's providence for their own sake and good.

units.la: Quomodo autem non omnia propter eos gererentur,propter quos non modo condita sunt hæc omnia,sed & uerbum illud æternum carnem nostrâ assumpsit,& Deus homo factus, inque mortem datus est? Et utinâ agnosceret hoc omnes Christi ministri,quod propter electos,uocatos sanctos, ac fideles dispensantur diuinitus omnia, & ea potissimum quæ cum ipsis geruntur,dubio procul, si ad hunc modū de fidelib.Christi, quibus præsunt, sentirent, possentq; ex animo cum Apostolo ad eos dicere:Propter uos sunt omnia,humilius paulò de se ipsis,& honorificentius de illis sentirent.
units.tr: Yet how would not all things be done for those for whose sake not only all these things were created, but also that eternal Word took on our flesh, and was made God and man, and was given over to death? And would that all Christ's ministers acknowledged this, that for the sake of the elect, the called, the saints and the faithful, all things are dispensed by God, and especially those things that happen to them. Undoubtedly, if they thought in this way about the faithful of Christ over whom they preside, and could say with the Apostle from the heart to them: "All things are yours," they would think more humbly of themselves and more honourably of them.

units.la: VT beneficiū quod exundauit,inquit,pluribus gratias agentibus Deo exuberet in gloriam Dei.) Reddit rationem præcedentium: Non est autem ea referenda ad id quod dixit: Nam omnia propter uos,sed ad illud,& constituet uobiscum, sic ut per parenthesim legantur ista ad hunc modum,scientes quod qui suscitauit dominum Iesum,suscitabit & nos per Iesum,& constituet uobiscum (nā omnia propter uos) ut beneficium quod exundauit, plu ribus gratias Deo agentibus,exuberet in gloriam Dei.Quasi dicat.Constituet nos Deus uobiscum,uelut è morte suscitatos , efficietque ut pro tam insigni abundantiaq; beneficio,quod in multorum usus exundauit, plures sibi gratias agant,cedatq; illud abundanter in ipsius gloriam.Sic per dictionem beneficij,intelligo suscitationem ac restitutionem ipsius,de qua utraque dixit,suscitabit & nos per Iesum & constituet uobiscum.Beneficium illud,uel gratia, ut est in Græco,non tam concernebat Apostolum quàm ecclesiā Corinthiorum. Quare uocat illud,beneficium exundans,in usus uideli cet plurimorum.Et reuera usque adeò exundans gratia est,qua Deus Apostolū suum tandiu contra impiorum furias seruauit, ac sæpenumero ueluti mortuum suscitauit ecclesijsq; restituit,ut in hunc illa diem ůsq; totus Chri- stianus orbis frui possit,modo uelit. Et hac no stra ętate an nõ huc Apostolũ suũ Deus tã ex uberáti gratia uelut è sepulchro suscitauit,no biśq; restituit,ut per ipsum lux ueritatis innu- meris illucescere cœperit ecclesijs.Iacebat se- pult⁹,tenebris Papisticę dominationis immer sus.Interea regnabat in ecclesia Simon,fictici- us ille Petrus.Huius larua mox suscitatus Pau lus detraxit,& Antichristi facie cunctis spectã dam ac detestandam proposuit.
units.tr: "That the grace which has overflowed," he says, "may abound through the thanksgiving of many to the glory of God." He gives the reason for what precedes: these words are not to be referred to what he said, "For all things are for your sakes," but to that, "and will set us with you." So they are read with a parenthesis in this way: "knowing that he who raised up the Lord Jesus will raise us also through Jesus, and will set us with you (for all things are for your sake), so that the benefit which has overflowed, through the thanksgiving of many to God, may abound to the glory of God." As if he said: God will set us with you, as if raised from death, and will bring it about that many give thanks to him for so remarkable an abundance of benefit, which has overflowed for the use of many, and that it may abound to his glory. Thus by the word benefit I understand his raising up and restoration, of which he spoke both in "will raise us also through Jesus" and "will set us with you." That benefit, or grace, as it is in the Greek, concerned the Apostle not so much as the Church of the Corinthians. Therefore he calls it a benefit overflowing for the use, namely, of very many. And indeed grace is so overflowing that God preserved his Apostle so long against the rages of the wicked, and so often raised him up as if dead and restored him to the churches, that the whole Christian world can enjoy it up to this day, if it wishes. And in our own age has not God in such abundant grace raised his Apostle again, as if from the sepulchre, and restored him, so that through him the light of truth has begun to shine on countless churches? He lay buried, sunk in the darkness of Papist domination. Meanwhile Simon, that fictitious Peter, reigned in the Church. Paul, raised up, soon stripped off his mask and set before all the Antichrist's face to be looked at and detested.

units.la: PLVRIBVS,inquit,gratias agétibus Deo, exuberet in gloriam Dei.) Rursus admonet Corinthios, ut erga tam luculentam gratiam Dei gratos sese exhibeant, ac Deum commu- ni gratulatione glorificent.Idem & supra cap. 1.hisce uerbis expressit:Vt ex multis personis, pro dono in nos collato per multos gratię a- gantur pro nobis.
units.tr: "Through the thanksgiving of many," he says, "may abound to the glory of God." Again he admonishes the Corinthians that they should show themselves grateful for so brilliant a grace of God, and glorify God with common thanksgiving. He expressed the same also above in chapter 1 in these words: "That from many persons, for the gift bestowed on us through many, thanks may be given for us."

units.la: Quod præsentem locum concernit, obser- uandum est, quod gratiarum actionem ad glo ria Dei facere dicit.Beneficia Dei quibus nos afficit,exuberat in gloria Dei p gratiarũactio- nem.Nec aliud est in nobis,quod benefactori Deo repędere possimus,quàm hoc unũ,ut gra tiam illius ex animo deprædicemus,& gratia- rumactione nomen illiusglorificemus.Et hoc est sacrificiū illud laudis,quod in Nouo testa- mento dominus instituit,ubi mortis suæ reme morationé in corporis ac sanguinis sui sacra- mento fidelibus suis commendauit. Quare ce lebrationem illius ueteres non immeritò Eu- charistiam uocandam esse censuerunt.
units.tr: As regards the present place, it must be observed that he says thanksgiving is made to the glory of God. The benefits with which God favours us overflow to the glory of God through thanksgiving. Nor is there anything in us which we can repay to the benefactor God, except this one thing: that we heartily proclaim his grace and glorify his name by thanksgiving. And this is that sacrifice of praise which the Lord instituted in the New Testament, where he commended to his faithful the remembrance of his death in the sacrament of his body and blood. Therefore the ancients rightly judged that its celebration should be called the Eucharist.

units.la: PROPTEREA,inquit,non defatigamur.) In Græco est,οὐχ ἐκκακοῦμεν,quod supra paulo post initiū capitis uertit,nõ degeneramus. Ve tus constanter habet:non deficimus. Hinc ad finem ůsq; capitis memorat, q̄ non frangatur animo propter crebras afflictiones, sed con- stanter in opere domini pergat. Quib⁹ autem respectib⁹ hoc faciat, simul explicat. Ponit autem triplicem respectum. Primum assignat cum dicit:Propterea non defatigamur: Qua- propter Quoniá scimus, quod qui suscitauit dominum lesum,suscitabit & nos per lesum, & constituet uobiscum, &c. Hac scientia con- firmati,nullis laboribus defatigamur, nec ul- lis afflictionibus frangimur. Hoc dicens, illo- rum quoq; animos ad consimilem fidei con- stantiam, infractamq; malorum tolerantiam excitat. Primus igitur respectus hoc illi loco erat scientia cuius meminit,qua sciebat haud- quaquam sibi defuturum dominum. Secun- dum mox subijcit dicens, sed quanuis exter- nus homo noster corrumpitur, internus tamē renouatur in dies singulos.Poterat dici:Quo- modo non defatigaris , cum tot afflictioni- bus ipsum corpus tuum atteratur quotidie? Respondet.Licet externus homo noster cor- rumpitur,internus tamē renouatur in dies sin gulos.Quare nō est ut defatigemur. Animum hunc meum nullæ afflictiones frangunt. Re- nouatur enim quotidie . Illo renouato nihil efficiunt corporis afflictiones, quâtumuis ma gnæ ac crebræ.
units.tr: "Therefore," he says, "we do not lose heart." In the Greek it is οὐκ ἐκκακοῦμεν, which a little after the beginning of the chapter he translated "we do not faint." The Vulgate constantly has "we do not fail." From here to the end of the chapter he mentions that he is not broken in spirit because of frequent afflictions, but persists steadfastly in the Lord's work. He also explains at the same time for what reasons he does this. He sets out a threefold reason. The first he states when he says: "Therefore we do not lose heart." Wherefore, "since we know that he who raised up the Lord Jesus will raise us also through Jesus, and will set us with you," etc. Confirmed by this knowledge, we are not worn out by any labours, nor broken by any afflictions. In saying this, he also stirs up their minds to a like constancy of faith and unbroken endurance of evils. The first reason, then, in that place was the knowledge he mentioned, by which he knew the Lord would by no means fail him. The second he immediately adds, saying: "but though our outward man is wasting away, yet our inward man is renewed day by day." One could say: "How do you not lose heart, when your body is worn down daily by so many afflictions?" He answers: "Though our outward man is wasting away, yet our inward man is renewed day by day." Therefore it is not the case that we lose heart. My spirit is not broken by any afflictions. For it is renewed daily. With it renewed, the afflictions of the body accomplish nothing, however great and frequent they be.

units.la: SED quanuis externus homo noster cor- rumpitur,inquit.) Per externum hominem corpus intelligit,cum illius conditionibus na turaliter annexis. Partem illam hominis quç ex carne est corporea,uisibilis,palpabilis,infir ma,alterationibus & corruptioni obnoxia,uo cat externumhominem,intelligens externam hominis partem.Neque enim duo sunt homi- nes in uno indiuiduo,sed duæ unius hominis partes,exterior & interior: exterior, corpus hocanimatum,interior spiritus.Duabus hisce partibus constat homo.Nos hic admonemur, etiam apostolorum corpora sic fuisse infirma, ut corruptioni essent obnoxia, & rebus aduer sis,ac temporis ętatisque iniurijs attereren- tur perinde atque cæterorum mortalium. Sic reliquias peccati originis in carne sua pertulé runt & ipsi.Quare conuenit,ut quoties exter- ni nostri hominis infirmitas pro præsentis hu ius uitæ conditionibus molestatur, illiusque corruptionem uiui adhuc experimur,commu nes hæsce ærumnas patienter feramus,cum il- las & apostoli in suis corporibus pertulerint, præsertim si hoc fiat in causa regni Christi có- munisq; nostræ salutis.
units.tr: "But though our outward man is wasting away," he says. By the outward man he understands the body with its conditions naturally attached. That part of man which is of flesh, corporeal, visible, palpable, weak, subject to alterations and corruption, he calls the outward man, understanding the outward part of man. For there are not two men in one individual, but two parts of one man, outward and inward: the outward, this animated body, the inward, the spirit. Man consists of these two parts. We are admonished here that the bodies of the apostles also were so weak that they were subject to corruption, and were worn down by adverse things and the injuries of time and age just as those of other mortals. So they too bore the remnants of original sin in their flesh. Therefore it is fitting that whenever the weakness of our outward man is troubled by the conditions of this present life, and we experience its corruption while still alive, we patiently bear these common hardships, since the apostles also bore them in their bodies, especially if this is done in the cause of Christ's kingdom and our common salvation.

units.la: INTERNVS tamen renouatur in dies sin- gulos,inquit.) Hoc est,spiritus tamen nouis quotidie consolationibus confirmatur.Chry- sost.exponit dicens:Quomodo renouatur? Fi de,spe,& animi alacritate. Quasi nouus spiri- tus est,quoties noui fidei ac spei auctibus cre- scit robustiorq; efficitur. Non est autem ocio- sum quod dicit ἡμέρα καὶ ἡμέρα,id est,in dies sin- gulos. Quoniá afflictiones quibus externus homo corrũpebatur,erát indefinetes & quoti diane,opus erat ut spiritus ecótra nouis quo- tidie consolationibus renouaretur . Nouit hoc diuina prouidentia,quare pro multitudi- ne afflictionum multiplicat pijs hominibus & consolationes,qua de re & supra capite primo meminit.
units.tr: "Yet the inward man is renewed day by day," he says. That is, the spirit is nevertheless strengthened daily by new consolations. Chrysostom explains, saying: "How is it renewed? By faith, hope and cheerfulness of mind." As if the spirit is new whenever it grows by new increases of faith and hope and becomes stronger. Nor is what he says, ἡμέρα καὶ ἡμέρα, that is, day by day, idle. Since the afflictions by which the outward man was wasting were unending and daily, it was necessary that the spirit, on the contrary, be renewed daily by new consolations. Divine providence knows this, and therefore in proportion to the multitude of afflictions it multiplies consolations for pious people as well; for which reason he also mentions it above in chapter 1.

units.la: Obseruandum uerò est, quod corruptioné externi hominis renouationi interni coniun- git.In sæculo diuersum cernitur. Illic ubi ex- ternus homo floret,animosus & inflatus est in ternus, ubi uerò languet & corrumpitur ex- ternus,languet etiam & concidit internus.Est enim internus in homine carnali sic compara tus,ut ,p qualitate externi uel sit alacer uel de- iectus,iuxta quod externus uel floret uel lan- guet . At in homine pio diuersimodè se ha- bet internus homo ab externo.Hic quò exter- nus pinguior est ac floridior , hoc magis ipse marcescit ac languet,cŏtra quò ille magis cor- rumpitur,hoc ipse magis per diuinæ consola- tionis gratiam renouatur.Ignorant hoc tyran ni.Ideo dum se per pressuras externi hominis internum expugnaturos putant, quò magis externum premunt, hoc magis causam dant interno,ut ualidior ad quæuis aduersa ferenda reddatur.
units.tr: It must be observed, moreover, that the corruption of the outward man is joined to the renewal of the inward man. In the world the opposite is seen. There, where the outward man flourishes, the inward is high-spirited and puffed up; but where the outward languishes and is corrupted, the inward too languishes and collapses. For the inward man in a carnal person is so constituted that by the condition of the outward it is either lively or dejected, according as the outward either flourishes or languishes. But in a pious man the inward man stands in a different relation to the outward. Here, the fatter and more flourishing the outward is, the more the inward itself withers and languishes; on the contrary, the more the outward is corrupted, the more the inward is renewed through the grace of divine consolation. Tyrants do not know this. Therefore, while they think they will overcome the inward man by pressing on the outward, the more they press the outward, the more they give cause to the inward to be made stronger for bearing any adversity.

units.la: NAM momentanea leuitas afflictionis no strae, inquit, mire supra modum aeternum pondus gloriae parit nobis.) Hic est tertius respectus, quo ad constantiam in ferendis afflictionibus permouebatur. Vtilitas uidelicet & fructus afflictionis patienter pro nomine Christi toleratae. Nam momentanea leuitas, inquit, afflictionis nostrae, &c. Non simpliciter dicit. Nam afflictio nostra parit nobis gloriam, sed & gravitatem afflictionis suae extenuat prorsus, & fructum illius amplificat in immensum. Extenuatio afflictionis est cum dicit: Nam momentanea leuitas afflictionis nostrae. Vt duplex est gravitas afflictionis, dum & molesta est in se, & diu durat, ita & duplicem ponit extenuationem, unam qua vocat afflictionem suam momentaneam, velut in momento ac puncto temporis transeuntem, alteram, qua dat illi leuitatem. Sic extenuans afflictiones suas animat fideles ad tolerantiam. Quis enim gravabitur pro nomine Christi tolerare aduersa, si cogitet quam sint omnia praesentis vitae mala respectu aeternorum leuia & momentanea?
units.tr: "For the momentary lightness of our affliction," he says, "wonderfully, beyond measure, produces for us an eternal weight of glory." Here is the third consideration by which he was moved to constancy in enduring afflictions: the usefulness and fruit of affliction patiently borne for the name of Christ. For he says, "the momentary lightness of our affliction," and so on. He does not simply say that our affliction produces glory for us. He both wholly diminishes the gravity of his affliction and immeasurably magnifies its fruit. The diminishing of affliction is in the words, "For the momentary lightness of our affliction." Just as the weight of affliction is twofold, since it is both grievous in itself and lasts a long time, so he sets down a twofold diminishing: one by calling his affliction momentary, passing in a moment, a point of time; the other by giving it lightness. In this way, by diminishing his afflictions, he encourages the faithful to endure. For who would be burdened to bear adversity for the name of Christ, if he considered how all the evils of the present life are light and momentary compared with eternal things?

units.la: Sed dices: Si leues ac momentanea erant afflictiones Apostoli, quomodo supra cap. 1. dixit se fuisse in Asia grauatum supra modum ac supra vires? Ad hanc quaestionem supra capite primo respondimus, quare non est ut hic respondeamus.
units.tr: But you will say: if the afflictions of the Apostle were light and momentary, how is it that in chapter 1 he said that he had been burdened in Asia beyond measure and beyond his strength? We answered this question above, at the first chapter, and there is no need to answer it again here.

units.la: Amplificat vero afflictionum suarum fructu, cum dicit: supra modu aeternu pondus gloriae parit nobis. Illud, mire supra modum, in Graeco est καθ' ὑπερβολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολήν, id est, secundum excellentiam ad excellentiam. Vetus red didit: supra modum in sublimitate, quasi duae sint diuersae uoces. Totus hic locus bimembri oppositione constat, qua afflictiones & fructus afflictionum inter se conferuntur: & utriqu par ti datur sua ὑπερβολή, id est, excellentia: ὑπερβολὴ afflictionum est in momentanea leuitate, ὑπερβολή futurae gloriae est in aeternitate. Ordina igitur lectionem ad hunc modum: Nam momentanea leuitas afflictionis nostrae secundum excellentiam, hoc est: Nam leuitas afflictionis nostrae, quae excellenter momentanea est, ad excellentem aeternitatem, uel, ad excellentia aeternam, pondus gloriae operatur in nobis. Sic in priori oppositionis membro est afflictio, momentanea leuitas & excellentia leuitatis uel breuitatis, in posteriori est gloria, quae afflictionis est pondus quod leuitati, est aeternitatis excellentia quae momentaneae breuitati opponitur. Et est sensus: Nam ex eo quod afflictiones in hac uita, excellenter momentaneas ac leues pro nomine Christi ferimus, nascitur nobis pondus gloriae ad excellentem aeternitatem, uel, ad excellentiam aeternam. Et commentarij qui Hieronymo tribuuntur de hoc sensu ita notant. Sic enim habet, uel quod tribulationum pondus, quae supra modum sunt in praesenti, sublimitatem gloriae aeternae perficiat. Graeca possunt sic legi, τὸ δὲ παραυτικὸν ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως
units.tr: He magnifies the fruit of his afflictions when he says: "beyond measure, produces for us an eternal weight of glory." The Greek for "wonderfully, beyond measure" is according to excellence unto excellence [καθ' ὑπερβολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολήν], that is, according to excellence to excellence. The old translator rendered it "beyond measure in sublimity," as if these were two different words. The whole passage rests on a two-part antithesis, in which afflictions and their fruits are set against each other, and to each part is given its own excellence [ὑπερβολή]: the excellence [ὑπερβολὴ] of the afflictions lies in their momentary lightness, the excellence [ὑπερβολή] of the future glory lies in eternity. Order the reading in this way: "For the momentary lightness of our affliction, in excellence," that is, "For the lightness of our affliction, which is excellently momentary, works in us a weight of glory for excellent eternity, or for eternal excellence." Thus in the first member of the antithesis there is affliction, momentary lightness and the excellence of lightness or brevity; in the second there is glory, which is the weight that answers to lightness, and the excellence of eternity, which is set against momentary brevity. The sense is: because we bear afflictions in this life for the name of Christ, which are excellently momentary and light, there arises for us a weight of glory for excellent eternity, or for eternal excellence. The commentaries ascribed to Jerome also note this sense in these words: "or because the weight of tribulations, which in the present life are beyond measure, brings to perfection the sublimity of eternal glory." The Greek may be read thus: but the momentary lightness of the tribulation [τὸ δὲ παραυτικὸν ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως].

units.la: {B} Dei aduersantur. Habemus in caelo dominum, qui sapientes ac prudentes in astucia ipsorum comprehendit, & omnia illorum consilia infatuat.
units.tr: {B} ... are opposed to God. We have in heaven a Lord, who takes the wise and prudent in their own craftiness and makes foolish all their counsels.

units.la: A ἡμῶν καθ' ὑπερβολὴν, id est, ἡ καθ' ὑπερβολήν, quae uidelicet secundum excellentiam est, qualis fuerat qua pertulerat in Asia, de qua supra capit. i. dixit, quod per illam καθ' ὑπερβολὴν fuerit grauatus. Et huic lectioni subdiuisio quae in Graeco post, καθ' ὑπερβολήν, habetur, fauere uidetur.
units.tr: The reading our excess [ἡμῶν καθ' ὑπερβολήν], that is, the excess [ἡ καθ' ὑπερβολήν], which is to say, according to excellence, is of the kind that he endured in Asia, of which he spoke in chapter 1, saying that he had been burdened beyond measure [καθ' ὑπερβολήν] by it. The subdivision that appears in the Greek after beyond measure [καθ' ὑπερβολήν] also seems to favour this reading.

units.la: Admonemur hac oppositorum collatione, quomodo in afflictionibus constituti praesentium tribulationum & futurae felicitatis diuersitatem & circunstantias consyderantes consolemur nosipsi, ne animo fracti ueritate Dei, in qua omnis nostra salus est, deseramus. Premit nos afflictio: cogitemus de futura gloria. Ignominiosa crux Christi est in hoc saeculo: at gloriosus erit illius fructus in futuro. Deinde cogitemus quanta leuitas quantum pariat podus gloriae. Momentaneae breuitati, aeternitatem gloriae opponamus. Si excellens est afflictio, quam excellens sit futurae felicitatis gloria cogitemus, atq; ita excellentiam excellentiae opponentes, afflictionum excellentiam, pe am quae infinitis modis excellit in momentaneam leuitatem redigamus. Aptissimum plane compendium est ad extenuandum omnia, quae in hoc saeculo contra dominum & fideles eius excellere uidentur. Est potetia Caesarum ac Regum excellens: Opponamus illi excellentissimam eius potentiam, qui dominus est dominantium, & aufert spiritum principum, ac dicamus: Si dominus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Excellunt sapientia ac prudentia qui ueritati Dei aduersantur. Habemus in caelo dominum, qui sapientes ac prudentes in astucia ipsorum comprehendit, & omnia illorum consilia infatuat. Excellit persequutio ac tribulatio: Excelletior erit futura felicitas. Excellit crucis Christi ignominia: Incomparabiliter excellet futura gloria. In summa, quicquid excellens est in hoc saeculo, respectu caelestium, quae longe sunt excellentiora, omnem excellentiae existimationem amittunt.
units.tr: This comparison of opposites admonishes us how, placed in afflictions, we should console ourselves by considering the difference between present tribulations and future happiness, and their circumstances, so that we do not, broken in spirit, abandon the truth of God, in which all our salvation lies. Affliction presses us: let us think of future glory. The cross of Christ is disgraceful in this age, but its fruit will be glorious in the future. Next, let us consider how great a lightness produces how great a weight of glory. Let us set eternity of glory against momentary brevity. If affliction is excellent, let us consider how excellent the glory of future happiness is, and so, setting excellence against excellence, let us reduce the excellence of afflictions, which in countless ways surpasses, to momentary lightness. This is plainly a most fitting shortcut for diminishing everything that seems to prevail in this age against the Lord and his faithful people. The power of Caesars and kings is great: let us set against it the most excellent power of him who is Lord of lords and takes away the spirit of princes, and let us say: "If God is for us, who can be against us?" The wisdom and prudence of those who oppose the truth of God prevail. We have in heaven a Lord, who takes the wise and prudent in their own craftiness and makes foolish all their counsels. Persecution and tribulation prevail: future happiness will be greater. The disgrace of the cross of Christ prevails: future glory will surpass it beyond comparison. In sum, whatever is excellent in this age, when set against heavenly things, which are far more excellent, loses all its reputation for excellence.

units.la: De illo admonuerunt alij, fructum huc afflictionum, gloriam uidelicet futurae uitae nec competere quibusuis afflictis, sed ijs tantum, qui propter Christum, ueritatem ac iusticiam Dei affliguntur, nec deberi afflictionibus nostris quasi merces meritis. Licet enim hic Apostolus dicat, quod momentanea leuitas afflictionum nostrarum aeternum nobis pariat gloriae pondus, haud tamen id aliter dicit, quam ut admoneat de gloria, quam pro sua bonitate Deus dabit electis ac fidelibus suis, secundum quam illos etiam ante hunc mundum ab aeterno elegit, & cuncta ad salutem eorum pertinentia dispensat. Alias si pondus hoc aeternae gloriae cum praesentis vitae afflictionibus conferatur, tanti illae ad hoc collatae non erunt, quati est aquae guttula imminenti pelago collata. Quare igitur impossibile est, ut guttula aquae pariat immensum pelagus, tam est impossibile, ut momentanea afflictio per se pariat aeternam gloriam. Non enim sunt pares praesentis tempo-ris ris afflictiones ad gloriam quæ reuelabitur er ga nos.
units.tr: Others have warned about this: that the fruit of afflictions, namely the glory of future life, belongs not to every kind of afflicted person but only to those who are afflicted for Christ, for the truth and righteousness of God, and that it is not owed to our afflictions as a reward for merits. For although the Apostle here says that the momentary lightness of our afflictions produces for us an eternal weight of glory, he does not say it in any other sense than to remind us of the glory which God, in his goodness, will give to his elect and faithful, according to which he also chose them from eternity before the world, and arranges all things that pertain to their salvation. Otherwise, if this weight of eternal glory is compared with the afflictions of the present life, those afflictions, set beside it, will be no more than a drop of water set beside the vast sea. Therefore, just as it is impossible for a drop of water to produce the immense sea, so it is impossible for a momentary affliction of itself to produce eternal glory. For the sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed toward us.

units.la: DVM non spectamus ea quę uidentur, inquit, sed ea quæ non uidentur.) Græcè est μὴ σκοπούντων ἡμῶν, id est, nō spectantibus nobis: quod admoneo, ne quis in uocula, dum, hæsitet, ac quærat, an afflictio tum nobis pariat gloriam, dum ea quæ non uidentur spectamus. Hactenus pertinét ista ad præcedentia, quatenus in illis æternitatem futuræ gloriæ momentaneæ afflictioni opposuit. Significat enim se, dum afflictionibus premitur, spectare non caduca præsentis uitæ uel mala uel bona, sed æternam, in futuro sæculo paratam gloriam, ac sempiternum reproborum exitium.
units.tr: "While we do not look at the things which are seen," he says. The Greek is while we do not look [μὴ σκοπούντων ἡμῶν], that is, "while we are not looking," which I note so that no one, in a small matter, hesitates and asks whether affliction then produces glory for us while we look at the things that are not seen. Up to this point these words pertain to what precedes, inasmuch as in them he set the eternity of future glory against momentary affliction. For he means that, while he is pressed by afflictions, he looks not at the perishable goods or evils of the present life, but at the eternal glory prepared in the future age, and at the everlasting destruction of the reprobate.

units.la: Et quoniam gloria hæc, quam gigni ex afflictionibus dicit, nec præsetis est temporis, nec uisibilis oculis carnis, ideoq; imperitiores cogitare poterant, nugas esse quę de illa dicit, pterea quod afflictiones quas pro Christo tolerabat, ignominiam ipsi magis quàm gloriam generet, occupat dicés, non spectantibus nobis quæ uidētur, sed ea quæ non uidentur. Quasi dicat. Scimus afflictiones Christi quas patimur multum nobis gignere ignominiæ in hoc sæculo, at nos nō spectamus ea quæ sunt carni ob oculos, sed potius ea quę ab illa nō uidetur. Quę náque ab illa uidentur caduca sunt ac trásitoria, quę uero non videntur, ęterna. Talis autem est gloria illa, quam pariunt nobis afflictiones Christi. Non est uisibilis carni, quia non est terrena ac uitę præsentis, sed cœlestis ac sęculi futuri.
units.tr: And since this glory, which he says is begotten from afflictions, belongs neither to present time nor to the eyes of the flesh, the unlearned could think that what he says about it is nonsense, because the afflictions which he bore for Christ produce for him disgrace rather than glory. He anticipates this, saying, "while we do not look at the things that are seen, but at the things that are not seen." As if he said: We know that the afflictions of Christ which we suffer produce for us much disgrace in this age; but we do not look at those things which are before the eyes of the flesh, but rather at those which are not seen by it. For the things that are seen by it are perishable and transitory, but the things that are not seen are eternal. Such is that glory which the afflictions of Christ produce for us. It is not visible to the flesh, because it is not earthly and of the present life, but heavenly and of the future age.

units.la: DVM non spectamus ea quę videntur, inquit.) In omnis generis actionibus aliquid est quod agentium animus spectat, ac ueluti scopum quendam collimando petit, quoque 're-fert quę agit omnia. Qui sęculi huius sunt filij, spectant ea quę sunt sęculi, quę sunt carnis, quę sunt terrena, uisibilia & præsentia. Qualia sunt opes, honores, voluptates, & id genus alia. Deinde fugiunt quoque nonnihil ea mala, quę cerni possunt ac sensibus carnis horrenda uidētur, ut sunt morbi corporis, paupertas, dolores carnis, persequutiones, carceres, & ad vltimum mors. Qui vero filij Dei sunt, & ad veram futurę uitę felicitatem electi, adeoque spiritu Dei aguntur, hi non spectant ea quę sunt mundi, non morātur ea quę uidentur, nō quę-runt quę sunt super terrā, sed potius quę sunt in cœlis, quę sunt spiritualia, cœlestia, inuisibilia & futura. Hęc spectando nullis afflictionibus quantumuis grauibus à sancto propositọ auocātur. Viderit igitur quisq; quid spectet, quid quęrat, quò animi sui intentionem dirigat. Qui terrena spectant, in confessione nominis Christi, si ingruat persequutio, durare nō poterūt. Qui spectant cœlestia, terrenis inhiare non possunt.
units.tr: While we do not look at the things which are seen: he says. In every kind of action there is something which the mind of the agent looks at, and aims at as a sort of target, by which it refers everything it does. Those who are sons of this age look at the things of this age, which are of the flesh, earthly, visible and present: such as wealth, honours, pleasures, and other things of that kind. Then they also shun, to some extent, those evils which can be perceived and which seem dreadful to the senses of the flesh, such as bodily sickness, poverty, pains of the flesh, persecutions, prisons, and at last death. But those who are sons of God, and chosen for the true happiness of the life to come, and so are driven by the Spirit of God, do not look at the things of the world, do not dwell on what is seen, do not seek what is upon the earth, but rather what is in heaven, what is spiritual, heavenly, invisible and future. By looking at these they are not turned aside from their holy purpose by any afflictions, however grievous. Let each one therefore see what he looks at, what he seeks, to what he directs the intention of his mind. Those who look at earthly things will not be able to endure in confessing the name of Christ if persecution rises up. Those who look at heavenly things cannot be captivated by earthly ones.

units.la: Est autem reuera magna ac singulari mentis illuminatione opus, vt propter inuisibilia non spectemus ea quę videntur. Reperias qui
units.tr: Indeed it is truly a work of great and singular illumination of the mind that, on account of the invisible things, we do not look at the things which are seen. You may find people who

units.la: & ipsi non admodum spectent ea quæ uidentur, & ab alijs impensissimè appetuntur, sicut alius non capiatur uoluptatibus ac delitijs carnis, sic agrestis, ut inter feras syluestres & natus & educatus uideatur: alius non quæratho nores, sed magis in fœcibus ignauię & inertiæ suæ manere cupiat. At Apostolus hic non simpliciter dicit: non spectantibus nobis quæ uidentur, sed addit, uerùm ea quę non uidentur. Spectare bona quæ non uidentur, & propter illa non spectare quæ uidentur, id demum hominis est non iam in terris sed in ipso cœlo cōuersantis. Etenim ubi oculus cordis, ibi cor, ubi cor, ibi ipsa uita, ubi uita est, ibi est & uitæ conuersatio. Qui terreni sunt, conuersantur in sæculo ubi sunt quæ diligunt, spectant & appetunt. Illis si proponas futurabona, regerunt, da mihi præsentia, serua tibi futura: si uocaueris eos ad spectanda quæ non uidentur, non obtemperant, sed dicunt, quæ uidentur certa sunt, quę non uidenturincerta, retinebo certa, tu persequere incerta. Et sic illi pulchrė sibi sapere uidentur, non modo non accipientes uera bona, sed & ridentes & exufflantes.
units.tr: themselves do not very much look at the things which are seen, and yet are most eagerly pursued by others; just as one man is not caught by the pleasures and delights of the flesh, yet is so rustic that he seems to have been born and raised among wild beasts; another does not seek honours, but would rather remain in the dregs of his own sloth and idleness. But the Apostle here does not simply say: while we do not look at the things which are seen; he adds: but at the things which are not seen. To look at good things which are not seen, and on account of them not to look at what is seen, that is truly the mark of a man who now lives not on earth but in heaven itself. For where the eye of the heart is, there is the heart; where the heart is, there is life itself; where life is, there too is the course of life. Earthly people live in the world where what they love is, they look at it and desire it. If you set future goods before them, they reply: give me present things, keep future things for yourself; if you call them to look at what is not seen, they do not obey, but say: what is seen is certain, what is not seen is uncertain; I will keep what is certain, you pursue what is uncertain. And so they seem to themselves to be wise, not only refusing the true goods, but also laughing at them and blowing them away.

units.la: NAM quæ uidentur, temporaria sunt, inquit, at quæ non uidentur ęterna.) Quanuis etiam si de omnibus uisibilibus loqueretur, uera esset sententia (nam cœlum, inquit dominus & terra transfibunt) existimo tamen intelligendū esse de ijs quæ uel appetuntur in hoc sæculo uel fugiuntur, ut sunt uisibilia tam bona quàm mala. Vt igitur rationem reddat, quare non spectet ea quæ uidentur, spectet uerò q non videntur, sic inter utraq; discernit, ut illa dicat esse temporaria, ista uerò æterna. Vocat autem temporaria, ad tempus dūtaxat durantia, æterna uerò fine fine in sempiternum permanentia, quanuis in Græco sit αἰώνια, id est, sæcularia, uel per sæcula durantia, qui sensus ad futurę uitæ statum non pertinet, in quo nō sunt sæcula, sed fine sæculis continua ac sempiterna felicitas. Cum Apostolus 1.Cor.10.dicit, in quos fines sæculorum inciderunt, satis admonet sæcula præsentis esse uitæ, & habere suos fines.
units.tr: For what is seen is temporary, he says, but what is not seen is eternal. Even if he were speaking of all visible things, the statement would be true (heaven and earth, says the Lord, shall pass away); yet I think it must be understood of those things which are either sought or shunned in this age, such as visible goods and evils alike. So that he may give the reason why he does not look at what is seen but looks at what is not seen, he distinguishes between the two, calling the former temporary and the latter eternal. He calls things temporary which last only for a time, and eternal those which remain forever without end, although in the Greek it is αἰώνια, that is, of the age or lasting through the ages; this sense does not apply to the state of the life to come, in which there are no ages, but a happiness continuous and everlasting without end to the ages. When the Apostle says in 1 Cor. 10, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, he sufficiently reminds us that the ages belong to the present life and have their ends.

units.la: AT quæ non uidentur, inquit, æterna.) Loquitur de illis bonis, quæ ut præsentis sæculi non sunt, ita & oculis carnis uisibilia non sunt. Aliàs multa sunt quę quanuis non uideantur æterna, tamen dici non possunt. Non uidētur quæ tenebris & latebris abdita latent, uideri autem possent, nisi laterent. Non uidetur quæ præsentia non sunt, sed procul dissita, natura tamen sic sunt comparata ut præsentia uideri possint. Non videntur quæ aliquando sunt futura, & ubi fuerint uidebuntur. Nihil horum æternum uocari potest. Imò ne ea quidem omnia æterna existunt, quæ natura sua sunt inuisibilia. Animam in pecore non uideo, neq; natura uisibilis est, æterna tamen non est. Ventū non uideo, qui & ipse inuisibilis est, & tamen æteræternus non est. Voces loquentiū, canentiū, ridentiū, eiulantiū quis uidet? Nemo tamen eas æternas esse dixerit. Non est igitur quod Apo‐stolus æterna esse dicit quæ non uidentur, ultra propositum, quod spectat, extendendum.
units.tr: But things which are not seen, he says, are eternal. He speaks of those good things which, as they do not belong to the present age, so also are not visible to the eyes of the flesh. Otherwise there are many things which, though they are not seen, cannot be called eternal. Things which lie hidden in darkness and concealment are not seen, yet they could be seen were they not hidden. Things which are not present but far off are not seen, yet by their nature they are so constituted that they could be seen if present. Things which will at some time be future are not seen, and when they are there they will be seen. None of these can be called eternal. Indeed not even all those things which are invisible by their very nature exist eternally. I do not see the soul in the beast, nor is it visible by nature, yet it is not eternal. I do not see the wind, which is itself invisible, and yet it is not eternal. Who sees the voices of those speaking, singing, laughing, or wailing? Yet no one would say that they are eternal. Therefore it is not right to extend what the Apostle says, that things which are not seen are eternal, beyond the purpose for which he speaks.

units.la: Vnde est autem quod homo mortalis quæ temporaria sunt negligens spectat æterna? Si quæ uidentur temporaria sunt, & temporaria transitoria, utique & homo temporarius est ac transitorius, quia ex ijs est & ipse quæ uidentur. Quorsum autem mihi æterna bona, cum sim ipse temporarius ac transitorius? Quæ mihi ex æterno est, uel esse potest utilitas, nisi sim & ipse æternus? Centum annorum bona, centum annos uiuenti abunde sufficiunt, quorsum illi opus diuturnioribus nedum æternis? An non mortuis omnia sunt mortua, siue temporaria siue æterna? Hæc cogitare potest homo animalis, consilium Dei in electis non intelligens, quo conditus est homo inexterminabilis, & sempiternæ uitæ destinatus. At nouus homo, qui ex Deo est, ac spiritu Dei ducitur, quemadmodum ad hoc est conditus, ut particeps sit æternæ uitæ, ita ad illius etiam æternitatem aspirat, adeoq; spectat no temporaria sed æterna, quia in sempiternum uicturo non sufficiunt temporaria quæ ipso usu consumuntur, & unà cum tempore etiam num usurpata transeunt. Argumentum itaq; æternitatis est in pijs & electis, quod temporaria bona contemnentes spectant æterna. Et hūc in illis sensum & affectum non impedit externi hominis mortalitas & corruptio. Licet enim secundum illum sint tēporarij, propter necessitatem moriendi, secundum noui tamen hominis conditionem sunt æterni, & per uirtutem futuræ resurrectionis etiam quod iam in illis est uisibile, infirmum, ac tēporarium corpus, in die domini suscitabitur, & ut æternitatis possit esse particeps mutabitur, qua de re prima Corinthiorum decimoquinto disseruit Apostolus, & initio sequentis capitis nonnihil attinget.
units.tr: But whence is it that mortal man, neglecting what is temporary, looks at what is eternal? If the things which are seen are temporary, and temporary things are transitory, then surely man too is temporary and transitory, since he himself is also of those things which are seen. But why should eternal goods matter to me, since I am myself temporary and transitory? What usefulness can there be for me from the eternal, unless I am eternal myself? Goods for a hundred years suffice abundantly for one who lives a hundred years; why would he need things that last longer, let alone eternal ones? Or are not all things dead to the dead, whether temporary or eternal? Natural man can think this, not understanding God's counsel concerning the elect, by which man was made imperishable and destined for everlasting life. But the new man, who is of God and led by the Spirit of God, just as he is made to share in eternal life, so also aspires to its eternity, and therefore looks not at temporary but at eternal things, since temporary things, which are consumed by use itself and pass away together with time as they are used up, are not enough for one who is to live forever. Therefore there is a token of eternity in the godly and elect, that despising temporary goods they look to eternal ones. And the mortality and corruption of the outward man does not hinder this sense and affection in them. For although according to that man they are temporary, on account of the necessity of dying, yet according to the condition of the new man they are eternal; and through the power of the future resurrection, even the visible, weak and temporary body which is already in them will be raised up on the day of the Lord, and will be changed so that it may share in eternity. On this matter the Apostle discoursed in the fifteenth chapter of the first Corinthians, and at the beginning of the following chapter he will touch on it somewhat.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: DE exuendo terreno domicilio ac novo quod è cœlis sit induendo disserit. Addit qua fide, qua spe, qua conscientia, ac desyderio erga dominum, cui reddenda est factorum ratio, conuersetur in ista præsentis uitæ peregrinatione, quamq; conueniat ut omnes uiuant ei qui pro omnibus mortuus est & resurrexit, sintq; in illo noua creatura. In calce de Apostolatu suo ac ministerio reconciliationis, quod pro Christi nomine obibat subiungit.
units.tr: He discusses putting off the earthly dwelling and putting on the new one that is from heaven. He adds with what faith, hope, conscience and longing toward the Lord, to whom an account of their deeds must be given, we should conduct ourselves during this pilgrimage of present life, and how fitting it is that all should live for him who died for all and rose again, and that they should be a new creation in him. At the end he adds a word about his own apostleship and the ministry of reconciliation, which he performed for the sake of Christ's name.

units.la: CAPVT V. SCIMVS enim quod si terrenum domicilium huius tabernaculi destructum fuerit, ædificationem ex Deo habemus, domicilium non manufactum, æternum in cœlis. Nam in hoc gemimus domicilio nostro quod e cœlo est, superindui desyderantes, si tamen induti non nudi reperiemur. Etenim qui sumus in hoc tabernaculo, gemimus onerati, propterea qd nolimus exui, sed superindui, ut absorbeatur mortalitas a vita. Qui vero parauit nos in hoc ipsum, Deus est, qui & dedit nobis arrabonem spiritus.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. For we know that if the earthly house of this tabernacle is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, longing to be clothed upon with our habitation which is from heaven, if indeed we shall be found clothed and not naked. For we who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened, not because we wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed upon, so that mortality may be swallowed up by life. Now he who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who also has given us the pledge of the Spirit.

units.la: Erat Apostolus corpore circundatus infirmo, corruptibili ac mortali, perinde atque ceteri homines, & atterebatur illud quotidie, non modo communibus molestijs, sed & singularibus ac grauibus afflictionibus, quas pro nomine Christi ferebat crebras & irremissas. Et interim non frangebatur animo, sed in opere domini pergebat ac durabat constanter, nec spectabat temporaria, sed æterna. Prius uidebatur mirum, posterius prorsus stultum. De priori mentionem fecit capite præcedenti, ubi dixit: Propterea non defatigamur, sed quamuis externus homo noster corrumpitur, internus tamen renouatur in dies singulos. De posteriori uero loquitur initio capitis huius dicens: Scimus enim, quòd si terrenum nostrum domicilium huius tabernaculi destructū fuerit, ædificationem ex Deo habemus, domicilium non manufactum, æternum in cœlis. Dixit se non spectare tēporaria sed æterna. Subijcit rationem, per occupationem. Quasi enim dicat aliquis. Atqui tu interim dum non temporaria sed æterna spectas quotidie morti appropinquas. Quorsum igitur æterna ei homini qui propediem est interituras? Respondet: Quòd moriturus sum breui, non impedit me, quò minus sperem ac spectem æterna. Etenim etiamsi terrenum hoc nostrum domicilium destructum fuerit, ob id tamen non prior bonorum æternorum fruitione, imò tum mihi demum accessus erit ad æterna. Scimus enim habere nos paratam à Deo ædificationem domicilij non manufacti, sed cœlestis & æterni.
units.tr: The Apostle was surrounded by a body that was weak, corruptible and mortal, just like other men, and it was worn down daily, not only by common troubles but also by particular and grievous afflictions, which he bore for the name of Christ, frequent and unrelenting. Yet in the meantime he was not broken in spirit, but went on and persevered steadfastly in the work of the Lord, and he looked not at temporal things but at eternal ones. The former seemed remarkable, the latter utterly foolish. He mentioned the former in the preceding chapter, where he said: "Therefore we do not lose heart, but though our outward man is wasting away, our inward man is being renewed day by day." About the latter he speaks at the beginning of this chapter, saying: "For we know that if the earthly house of this tabernacle is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens." He said that he did not look at temporal things but at eternal ones. He gives the reason by anticipating an objection. For as if someone might say: "But while you look at eternal things and not temporal, you are daily drawing near to death. Why then eternal things for a man who is soon to perish?" He answers: that I shall die soon does not prevent me from hoping for and looking to eternal things. For even if this earthly dwelling of ours is destroyed, I will not for that reason be deprived of the enjoyment of eternal goods; rather then, indeed, I will have access to eternal things. For we know that God has prepared for us a building, a dwelling not made with hands, but heavenly and eternal.

units.la: SCIMVS enim, inquit.) Iterum quod animalis homo nulla potest scientia comprehedere, sed sola fide capitur, scire se dicit. Est enim fides certa cōprehensio, & firma hypostasis earū rerum quę non uidentur, sed speratur. Nititur nanque uerbi Dei ueritate ac certitudine, multo certius quàm ulla humana ratio suis indagationibus & argumentis.
units.tr: "For we know," he says. Again, he says that he knows what the natural man cannot grasp by any knowledge, but is apprehended by faith alone. For faith is a sure grasp and a firm substance (hypostasis) of those things which are not seen but are hoped for. It rests on the truth and certainty of the Word of God, far more surely than any human reason with its inquiries and arguments.

units.la: QVOD si terrenum nostrum domicilium huius tabernaculi destructum fuerit, inquit.) Terrenum domicilium uocat suum corpus, quod cap.praecedenti externum hominem uocauit. Coparat se militi in luteo tuguriolo, uel si maiuis, tabernaculo militanti, & sic animato, ut si destructum sibi fuerit uile quod inhabitat tuguriolum, non admodum contristetur, propterea quod beneficio Regis sui perapta militia splendidum & eximium aedificium habiturum se speret.
units.tr: "But if our earthly dwelling of this tabernacle is destroyed," he says. He calls his own body an earthly dwelling, which in the previous chapter he called "the outward man." He compares himself to a soldier in a clay hut, or, if you prefer, a soldier in a tent, and one so disposed that if the lowly hut he lives in is destroyed, he will not be greatly saddened, because by the favour of his king, having served well in the campaign, he hopes to receive a splendid and excellent building.

units.la: Poterat simpliciter dicere: quod si occidar, scio me uitam habituram in coelis non temporariam sed aeternam, uerum ut significet non occidi se, sed corpus suum terrenum ac fragile destrui, quod tamen in caelestem & aeternum fit commutadum; dicit perinde fore illius destructionem, ac si domicilium terrenum ac luteum destruatur. Significat igitur Christiano hominis corpus esse loco lutei domicilij uel tabernaculi, ut illo occiso non occidatur ipse, sed deste ruat ipsius domicilium terrenum, luteum, terreum & fragile, in quo peregrinatus sit in hoc praesenti saeculo, ut corpus nostrum sit peregrinationis tabernaculum, cuius destructio non sit nostra destructio, sed peregrinationis nostrae terminatio, & ad coelestem uitam transitus.
units.tr: He could have said simply: "If I am killed, I know that I shall have a life in heaven, not temporary but eternal." But in order to signify that it is not he who is killed, but his earthly and fragile body that is destroyed, though it is to be changed into a heavenly and eternal one, he says that its destruction will be like the destruction of an earthly and clay dwelling. He means, therefore, that for the Christian the body is in the place of a clay dwelling or tent, so that when it is slain, he himself is not slain, but only his earthly, clay, earthen and fragile dwelling is torn down, in which he has been a pilgrim in this present age. Thus our body is the tent of our pilgrimage, whose destruction is not our destruction but the end of our pilgrimage and a passage to heavenly life.

units.la: Non est autem otiosum, quod corpus suum uocat non simpliciter domicilium, sed ἐπίγειον οἰκίαν, id est, terrestre domicilium, uel luteam domunculam. Respicit ad illud: Terra es, & ad terram reuerteris. Monet simul non esse adeo magnae iacturae dispendium, si corpus suum destruatur, cum sit terrestre ac luteum domicilium, fieriq; non possit, ut quale est, duret in sempiternum.
units.tr: It is not idle that he calls his body not simply a dwelling, but an earthly house (ἐπίγειον οἰκίαν) [epigeion oikian], that is, a terrestrial dwelling or a little clay house. He has in mind that word: "You are earth, and to earth you shall return." At the same time he warns that the loss is not of such great consequence if his body is destroyed, since it is a terrestrial and clay dwelling, and it cannot happen that what is such should last for ever.

units.la: HVIVS tabernaculi.) Non contentus, quod uocauit corpus suum terrestre domicilium, addit, huius tabernaculi, ut significet, esse illud tabernaculare quoq; domicilium, praeterquam quod est terrestre. Inter iustam domum & tabernaculum hoc est discriminis, quod domus eorum est qui certam & fixam habent mansionem, tabernaculum uero eorum qui in certis sedibus tanquam peregrini uel milites oberrant. Sic de Abrahamo Ebr. 11. memorat, quod quauis promissionem terrae Canaa haberet a Deo, in tabernaculis tamen habitarit cum Isaaco, peregrinum referens magis quam terrae illius haeredem. Significans igitur esse corpus suum tabernaculum, in quo non fixam habeat mansionem, sed incertam & transitoriam peregrinationem, uocem hac tabernaculi adiecit. Sic & Petrus corpus suum tabernaculum uocauit dicens: Attamen iustum arbitror, quandiu sum in hoc tabernaculo excitare uos per commonitionem, cum sciam breui futurum ut deponam hoc tabernaculum meum, &c. 2. Petri 1.
units.tr: "Of this tabernacle." Not content with calling his body an earthly dwelling, he adds "of this tabernacle," to signify that it is also a tent-like dwelling, besides being earthly. There is this difference between a proper house and a tabernacle: a house belongs to those who have a certain and fixed abode, but a tabernacle belongs to those who wander as pilgrims or soldiers in places not their own. So Hebrews 11 records of Abraham that although he had God's promise of the land of Canaan, he nevertheless dwelt in tents with Isaac, showing him to be a pilgrim rather than an heir of that land. Signifying, therefore, that his body is a tabernacle, in which he has not a fixed abode but an uncertain and transitory pilgrimage, he added the word "tabernacle." So also Peter called his body a tabernacle, saying: "Indeed I think it right, as long as I am in this tabernacle, to stir you up by reminding you, since I know that I shall soon put off this tabernacle of mine," etc. 2 Peter 1.

units.la: Quemadmodum Paulus morte hic tabernaculi sui destructionem, ita Petrus suam, tabernaculi depositionem uocauit.
units.tr: Just as Paul here called the destruction of his tabernacle its death, so Peter called his own the laying down of the tabernacle.

units.la: ÆDIFICATIONEM, inquit, ex Deo habemus, domicilium non manufactum, aeternum in coelis.) His uerbis exprimit, quare non impediatur destructione corporis sui, quo minus participes fiat aeternorum bonorum. Ob id uidelicet, quod parata sibi fit aedificatio longe melior & aeternae felicitati conuenientior, quam terrenum & tabernaculare domicilium. Quae illa 1 Primo uocat eam οἰκοδομήν, id est, aedificationem. Inter hanc & tabernaculum multum est discriminis. 2 Deinde uocat eam aedificationem ex Deo, & exponens addit, domicilium non manufactum. A Deo utiq; conditum est & corpus nostrum, nec est ullis hominum manibus factum, corpus inquam terrenum hoc, fragile, mortale & corruptibile. Quid est ergo praerogatiue futuri nostri corporis, prae hoc psenti, in eo quod dicit illud fore ex Deo & haud manufactum? Meo iudicio, futurum nostrum corpus ob id ex Deo & non manufactum fore dicit, quod immediate diuina uirtute, absque ulla humana cooperatione perficietur, id quod de terrestribus hisce nostris domicilijs dici non poterit, quae quoniam intercedente humana sunt cooperatione facta, manufacta, id est, huius creationis uocantur. Quibus illa medijs constent, & modis perficiantur, notum est omnibus. Quae habebimus in futura uita, omnino absque hisce medijs & modis sola diuina uirtute constabunt. Cauendum est aut, ne illud, ex Deo, alio sensu accipiamus, quam si dixisset, a Deo, ne locum demus haereticis, qui corpora nostra ex ipsa esse substantia Dei contendunt. Cum Christus dicit: Qui ex Deo est, uerbum Dei audit, propterea uos non auditis, quia ex Deo non estis, non loquitur de substantia Dei, sed de gratia electionis ac praedestinationis, secundum quam ex Deo sunt, qui ad uitam sunt electi ac praeordinati. Hic cum Apostolus corpora nostra, quae in futura uita habebimus, ex Deo & non manufacta fore dicit, ad differentiam eorum dicit, quae in hac uita circumferimus, quorum origo & ipsa quidem est a Deo, uerum non immediate, sed per media carnis ac sanguinis, humanae uidelicet cooperationis interuentu: illa uero immediate a Deo conditur, ut alia eorum origo, unde sint talia, assignari non possit, qua uirtus diuina. 3 Tertio addit, aeternum. Opponit hoc fragilitati ac mortalitati terrestris corporis, per quam fit, ut sit non aeternum sed temporarium, caducum, ac transitorium. At quod habebimus in futuro non transitorium erit sed aeternum. Neq; enim obnoxius erit tempori, morbis, morti, corruptioni, &c. sed ab his omnibus liberum interminabili uita & gloria fruetur. Huius spe ac respectu perdurat Apostolus in afflictionibus, & corporis sui destructionem tam non fert molestè, ut etiam cupiat illud dissolui, & ingemiscat, donec dissoluatur & interim non spectat quae videntur & transeunt, sed quae non videntur & in sempiternum permanent.
units.tr: "A building," he says, "we have from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens." By these words he expresses why the destruction of his body does not prevent him from sharing in eternal goods. This is evidently because a building is being prepared for him, far better and more suited to eternal happiness than the earthly and tent-like dwelling. Here, first, he calls it οἰκοδομήν [oikodomēn], that is, a building. There is much difference between this and a tabernacle. Second, he calls it a building from God, and explaining it he adds, a house not made with hands. Our body too was certainly created by God, and it is not made by any human hands: this body, I mean, which is earthly, fragile, mortal and corruptible. What then is the advantage of our future body over the present one, in that he says it will be from God and not made with hands? In my judgement, he says our future body will be from God and not made with hands because it will be perfected immediately by divine power, without any human cooperation; this cannot be said of our earthly dwellings, which, since they are made with human cooperation, are called "made with hands," that is, of this creation. By what means and methods they are constituted and perfected is known to all. What we shall have in the future life will be wholly without these means and methods, and will consist by divine power alone. We must take care, however, that we do not understand "from God" in another sense than if he had said "by God," lest we give room to heretics who contend that our bodies are of the very substance of God. When Christ says, "He who is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God" (John 8), he is not speaking of the substance of God, but of the grace of election and predestination, by which those are of God who are chosen and predestined to life. Here, when the Apostle says that the bodies we shall have in the future life will be from God and not made with hands, he says this in contrast with those we carry about in this life, whose origin is indeed from God, but not immediately: it is through the means of flesh and blood, that is, by the intervention of human cooperation. The future bodies, however, are created immediately by God, so that no other origin can be assigned for them, of what kind they are, than divine power. Third, he adds "eternal." He sets this against the frailty and mortality of the earthly body, by which it comes about that it is not eternal but temporary, perishable and transitory. But what we shall have in the future will not be transitory but eternal. For it will not be subject to time, sickness, death, corruption, etc., but free from all these will enjoy an endless life and glory. In hope of this and with this in view the Apostle persists in his afflictions, and bears the destruction of his body so little grievously that he even desires that it be dissolved, and groans until it is dissolved; and meanwhile he does not look at what is seen and passes away, but at what is not seen and remains for ever.

units.la: IN coelis, inquit.) Opponit hoc terreno terrestris corporis incolatui. In terris circumferimus corpus hoc mortale, gloriosum illud habebimus in coelis.
units.tr: "In the heavens," he says. He sets this against the earthly sojourn of the earthly body. "In earth we carry about this mortal body; we shall have that glorious one in the heavens."

units.la: Hactenus iuxta communem sensum praesentem lo-
units.tr: Hitherto, following the common understanding, we have explained the present pas-

units.la: Ioan. 8. tem locum de corpore glorificato, quo uestie-mur post resurrectionem exposuimus. Verum quoniam illo non statim post corruptibilis hu ius corporis nostri destructione potimur, sed expectâda est uniuersalis illa mortuorum resurrectio, demum in fine seculorum futura. Apostolus uero, cum dicit: Scimus quod si ter-renum nostrū domicilium huius tabernaculi destructum fuerit, ædificationem ex Deo habemus, &c. de tali ædificatione ac domicilio loqui uidetur, quod se statim post destructionem corporis sui accepturū sciat, non est præ-terrationem, quòd nonullis hic locus de cœlesti mansione ac statu beatæ uitæ, in quam electorum ac fidelium spiritus statim post de-structionem terreni corporis transferuntur, magis quàm de glorificatis nostris corporibus intelligedus esse uidetur. Horū igitur iudicio erit hic sensus. Scimus enim, quod ubi terrena nostra habitatio huius tabernaculi, corporis uidelicet, quòd iam circumferimus, destructa nobis fuerit, siue id fiat per manus aduersariorum uiolenter, siue matura ac tempestiua morte, mansionem habemus à Deo nobis paratam, nō hic in terris, sed in ipso cœlo, in quam recipiemur. Et huic expositioi fauere uidetur, quod nō in futuro habebimus, sed in præsenti, habemus dixit, & quod cœlesti illi domicilio æternitatem tribuit, idem esse appa-ret cum eo quod Christus dixit, ut recipiàt uos in æterna tabernacula. Cœlestes mansio-nes æternæ ob id dicuntur, quòd non solum durabunt in sempiternum, nunquâ destruen-dæ, sed & ob id quoque, quod paratæ sunt ab æterno. Deinde non manufactæ dicuntur, respectu terrenarum mansionum, quæ manibus hominū construuntur, & in cœlis parate sunt, cum istæ sint in terris. Lectoris iudicio relinquimus utrum sensum probet ac retineat. Si ueritas quæritur, ueri sunt utriq;. Tantum uidendum est, utrâ expositio uerbis sit ac menti Apostoli uicinior.
units.tr: sage concerning the glorified body with which we shall be clothed after the resurrection (Ioan. 8.). But since we do not obtain that body immediately after the destruction of this corruptible body of ours, but must await that universal resurrection of the dead which is to come at the end of the ages, the Apostle, when he says, "We know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle be destroyed, we have a building from God," and so on, seems to speak of such a building and dwelling, which he knows he will receive immediately after the destruction of his body. It is not out of place to note that for some this passage seems to be understood of the heavenly dwelling and state of the blessed life, into which the spirits of the elect and faithful are carried immediately after the destruction of the earthly body, rather than of our glorified bodies. Therefore, in their judgment, the sense will be this: "For we know that when our earthly habitation, that is, this tabernacle of the body which we now carry about, has been destroyed for us, whether this happens violently by the hands of enemies or by an early and timely death, we have a dwelling prepared for us by God, not here on earth but in heaven itself, into which we shall be received." This exposition seems to be supported by the fact that he says "we have" in the present, not "we shall have" in the future, and that the Apostle ascribes eternity to that heavenly dwelling, which appears to be the same as what Christ said: "that they may receive you into everlasting habitations." Heavenly dwellings are called eternal because they will not only endure forever, never to be destroyed, but also because they have been prepared from eternity. Then they are said to be "not made with hands," in contrast with earthly dwellings, which are built by human hands, and they are prepared in heaven, whereas these are on earth. We leave it to the judgment of the reader whether he approves and retains this sense. If truth is sought, both are true. It only needs to be considered which exposition is closer to the words and mind of the Apostle.

units.la: Quod posteriore sensum attinet, admonemur, quid efficiat in nobis fides ista, qua nos post terrenum hunc præsentis uitæ incolatum, in quo tabernacula manufacta incolimus, æternam in cœlo mansione habere scimus. Hoc uidelicet, ut nec quæramus ea quæ sunt huius mundi caduca & transitoria, sed æterna cœlestis uitæ bona, nec molesta sit corporis huius depositio, quocunq; illa modo & quàdocunq; fiat, sed molesta potius sit illius inhabitatio. Quis credat eum certum esse, quòd mansionem ἀmœnissimam habeat in infulis Fortu-natis, qui frigidum suum hyperborearum regionum incolatū cupide retinere satagit, nec priuari illo facile sustinet? Etenim natura sic comparati sumus, ut si detur optio, malimus amœna & iucunda, quàm inamœna ac tristia. Quare ubi tristia & inamœna cum iucundis & amœnis commutare detrectamus, manifesto ostendimus argumento, quod de commutationis huius certitudine dubitamus. Vitæ
units.tr: As for the latter sense, we are reminded what that faith effects in us, by which we know that after this earthly sojourn of the present life, in which we dwell in tabernacles made by hands, we have an eternal dwelling in heaven. This, of course, is that we should seek not the things of this world, which are perishable and transitory, but the eternal goods of the heavenly life; and that the laying aside of this body should not be grievous, however and whenever it happens, but rather that dwelling in it should be grievous. Who would believe that a man is sure of having a most pleasant dwelling in the Fortunate Isles, when he eagerly strives to hold on to his cold residence in the regions of the far north, and can hardly bear to be deprived of it? For we are so constituted by nature that, if the choice is given, we prefer pleasant and agreeable things to unpleasant and sad ones. Therefore, when we refuse to exchange sad and unpleasant things for pleasant and agreeable ones, we clearly show by this argument that we doubt the certainty of that exchange.

units.la: fumus cupidi omnes, & nemo est, qui non æternum quàm ad tempus tantùm uiuere malit. Verùm quotusquisq; est, qui temporariam hanc & miseram uitam cupide deponat? Unde hoc est, quàm ex eo, quod non omnes cum Apostolo dicere possumus: Scimus nos æternam mansionem habere in cœlis?
units.tr: We all desire to live, and there is no one who would not rather live forever than only for a time. But how few are there who eagerly lay down this temporary and wretched life? Whence is this, except that we cannot all say with the Apostle: "We know that we have an eternal dwelling in the heavens"?

units.la: NAM in hoc, inquit, gemimus, domicilio nostro quod è cœlo est, superindui desyderan-tes.) Rationalis uocula, nam, uel est hic o-ciosa, uel referenda est ad id quod in calce capitis præcedentis, non quæ uidentur, sed quæ non uidentur, ideoque æterna sunt, spectare se dixit. Hoc enim spectare cum gemitibus & magno eorum quæ spectatur desyderio, coniunctum est. Quare ut affectus animi æterna spectantis exprimat, unde pateat, quàm illa cupide & obnixe spectet, dicit: Nam in hoc gemimus, domicilio nostro quod è cœlo est, superindui desyderantes. Quid enim spectem, gemitus nostri testantur, quibus in hoc terrestri ac fragili domicilio ingemisco. Ingemisco siquidem impulsu desyderij, quo cœlesti domicilio superindui desydero. Sic illud, in hoc, accipio de terreno domicilio, corpore uidelicet. Non est enim in Græco ἐνταῦθα, ut legi possit, ad hoc, sed ἐν τούτῳ, id est, in hoc domicilio uidelicet, quod tum circunferebat.
units.tr: "For in this," he says, "we groan, desiring to be clothed upon with our habitation which is from heaven." The little word "for" (nam) is either idle here, or it must be referred to what he said at the end of the preceding chapter, that he looks not at the things which are seen but at those which are not seen, and therefore are eternal. For to look at these is joined with groanings and a great longing for what is looked for. Therefore, in order to express the feeling of a mind that looks upon eternal things, and to show how eagerly and earnestly he looks at them, he says: "For in this we groan, desiring to be clothed upon with our habitation which is from heaven." For our groanings bear witness to what we look for, since in this earthly and frail dwelling I groan. I groan indeed from the impulse of desire, by which I long to be clothed upon with the heavenly dwelling. So I take the words "in this" as referring to the earthly dwelling, that is, the body. For the Greek does not have ἐνταῦθα, which could be read as "in this place," but ἐν τούτῳ, that is, in this dwelling, namely the one which he was then carrying about.

units.la: Quid autem in terreno suo corpore constitutus gemuerit, exponit dicés: Domicilio nostro quod è cœlo est, superindui desyderâtes. Domicilium suum corpus illud uocat, quod accepturus est in resurrectione mortuorum. Vocat illud οἰκητήριον, non σκηνὴς, quod non ut in tabernaculo uagam & transitoriam, sed ut in domo certam ac permanentem in illo sit habiturus mansionem. Illo superindui desyderabat.
units.tr: What he groaned about while he was in his earthly body he explains by saying: "desiring to be clothed upon with our habitation which is from heaven." He calls that body his dwelling, which he is to receive at the resurrection of the dead. He calls it οἰκητήριον, not σκηνή, because he is to have it as a settled and permanent habitation, as in a house, rather than a wandering and transitory one, as in a tent. He longed to be clothed upon with that.

units.la: QVOD è cœlo est, inquit.) Quid? An corpora illa in quibus resurgemus, de cœlo in sepulchra nostra descendent? Etenim si corpus Pauli de cælo descensurum est, descésura sunt utiq; & nostra. Si sic sentiendum est, quomodo stabit fides nostra, qua carnis huius resurrectionem futuram credimus? Et quid de corporibus reproborum sentiendum est, quæ & ipsa reuiuiscent ac resurgent, de quibus dicere non possumus, quòd de cœlo sint descensura? Si illa resurgent immortalia ad æternas pœnas, quomodo non & nostra talia resurgent ad æternam uitam, ut non sit necesse nobis de cœlo corpora mitti?
units.tr: "WHICH IS FROM HEAVEN," he says. What then? Will those bodies in which we rise come down from heaven into our graves? For if Paul's body is to come down from heaven, then ours surely will also come down. If this is the sense, how will our faith stand, by which we believe that the resurrection of this flesh is to come? And what must be thought of the bodies of the reprobate, which will also be revived and raised, of which we cannot say that they will come down from heaven? If those rise immortal for eternal punishments, why should not ours also rise such for eternal life, so that there is no need for bodies to be sent to us from heaven?

units.la: Respondeo. Non dicit Apostolus, quod de cœlo descendet, sed, quod è cœlo, quod idem est ac si dicat, quod cœleste erit. Qualitatem futuri sui corporis exprimit, non descensum, cum dicit: quod è cœlo, opponens illam qualitati corruptibilis huius corporis, quod terrestre est ac luteum. Quanto autem amplior est cœli quàm terræ, tanto est amplior cœlestium corporum quàm terrestrium gloria. Hoc significans cœlestem futuri sui corporis gloriam terrestris humilitati opponit.
units.tr: I answer: the Apostle does not say that it will come down from heaven, but "which is from heaven," which is the same as saying "which will be heavenly." He expresses the quality of his future body, not its descent, when he says "which is from heaven," setting it against the quality of this corruptible body, which is earthly and of clay. But as heaven is greater than earth, so the glory of heavenly bodies is greater than that of earthly ones. In signifying this, he sets the heavenly glory of his future body against the lowliness of the earthly one.

units.la: SVPERINDVI defyderantes, inquit.) Vtitur metaphora uestiendi, coparans corpus uestimento, quod haftenus coparauit tabernaculo & domicilio. Sic pro sua diligentia rem eandem alijs atq; alijs figuris format, fpectandamq; proponit. Quomodo autem coelesti corpore quasi uestimento fuperindui defyderarit, exponit in sequentibus.
units.tr: "CLOTHED UPON, desiring," he says. He uses the metaphor of clothing, comparing the body to a garment, as he previously compared it to a tabernacle and dwelling. Thus, with his usual diligence, he forms and sets forth the same thing under different figures. How he desired to be clothed upon with the heavenly body, as with a garment, he explains in what follows.

units.la: SI tamen induti, inquit, non nudi reperiemur.) Expositionem fuperinduitionis subijcit. Qui prorsus nudi sunt, induuntur dum uestiuntur, qui uero nudi non sunt, sed induti, non induuntur, sed fuperinduuntur, dum adhuc aliquo alio ueftiu genere supra id quo induti sunt, uestiuntur & ornatur. Huc respiciens dicit: Si tamen induti, non nudi reperiemur. Indutus tum erat terrestri corpore, no nudus. Sic comparatus no poterat indui coelesti, perinde ac fi nudus, id est, terrestri corpore exutus fuisset. Quoniam uero futurū est, ut in die resurrectionis multi adhuc in uiuis agant, funtq; non nudi, sed induti, ideoq; coelestibus corporibus non induendi, sed fuperinduedi, illo respiciens dicit, fi tamen induti non nudi reperiemur. Quasi dicat: Si tame in die domini, quando resurgent mortui, inter uiuos non inter mortuos, inter eos qui adhuc terrenis erunt corporibus induti, non inter nudos, id est, corporibus suis exutos reperiemur. Hic sensus per sequentia confirmatur.
units.tr: "IF INDEED," he says, "we shall be found clothed, not naked." He adds an explanation of this being clothed upon. Those who are altogether naked are clothed when they are dressed; but those who are not naked, but already clothed, are not clothed but clothed upon, since while still wearing some other kind of garment over what they already have on, they are dressed and adorned. Looking to this he says, "If indeed we shall be found clothed, not naked." He was then clothed with the earthly body, not naked. Being so constituted, he could not be clothed with the heavenly body as if he were naked, that is, stripped of the earthly body. But since it will happen that at the day of resurrection many will still be alive, and they will be not naked but clothed, and so are not to be clothed with heavenly bodies but to be clothed upon, looking to this he says, "if indeed we shall be found clothed, not naked." As if he said: "If indeed in the day of the Lord, when the dead rise, we shall be found among the living and not among the dead, among those who are still clothed in earthly bodies and not among the naked, that is, those stripped of their bodies." This sense is confirmed by what follows.

units.la: Alij tamen aliter exponunt. Intelligūt eos fore uestitos, qui tum in ueste nuptiali, fide uidelicet Christi, adeoq; & ipso Christo reperientur. Nudos uero cæteros, qui fine hac ueste in die domini comparebunt. Illos coelesti gloria fuperinduendos, istos nequaquā. Sane quoniā omnes quidem mortui resurgent, tam reprobi quàm fideles, haud tamen omnes coelesti gloria decorabuntur, sed fideles tantùm, haftenus non nudi, sed uestiti fuperinduētur. Verū si sequētia consyderētur, prior sensus ad mentē Pauli propius accedere deprehedetur.
units.tr: Others, however, explain it otherwise. They understand that those will be clothed who are then found in the wedding garment, namely faith in Christ, and so in Christ himself. But the rest, who will appear on the day of the Lord without this garment, will be naked. The former will be clothed over with heavenly glory, the latter not at all. Indeed, since all the dead will rise, both the reprobate and the faithful, yet not all will be adorned with heavenly glory, but only the faithful; these, who were not naked but clothed until then, will be clothed over. But if the following words are considered, the former sense will be found to come closer to Paul's mind.

units.la: ETENIM qui fumus, inquit, in hoc taber naculo, gemimus onerati, propterea quod nolimus exui, sed fuperindui, ut absorbeatur mortalitas à uita.) Præcedentem particulam exponit, quomodo uidelicet, & quare dixerit, fi tamē induti nō nudi reperiemur. Rationem ex eo adducit, quòd omnes homines, pij quoque, morte corporis natura exhorrēt, ideoq; pij, quoniam immortalitatis quidem sunt appetentes, & tamē à morte corporis abhorret, mallent sic uiui deprehensi absq; morte coelestibus corporibus superindui, quàm per mortem ueteri corpore nudari, ac sic immortali ac nouo indui. Hoc sensu dicit: Etenim qui sumus in hoc tabernaculo, id est, quotquot pij terreno adhuc corpore circundamur, propter hoc gemimus onerati illius incolatu, quod licet nolimus illo per morte exui, à qua natura abhorremus, superindui tamē nouo ac coelesti cupiamus. Quomodo ? Sic ut absorbeatur inquit mortalitas, uel, ut in Græco est, & uetus æditio habet, quod mortale est, à uita. Id est, ut coelestis uita, quę cum nouo ac coelesti corpore datur, ueteris mortalitatē & corruptionem absq; gustu mortis absorbeat, & repente exter reno coeleste reddat. Eueniet hoc illis, qui uiui in die resurrectionis deprehendētur. Hunc sensum & Lyranus tradit, nec Burgensis reprehendit.
