Sic enim exponit: Si tamen uestiti & nō nudi inueniemur, id est, si absq; dissolutione corporis corruptibilis quo utitur anima, ut uestimēto posset superindui gloria, tunc absq; aliquo impedimento appetitus gratię in hoc ferretur, sed quia hoc est impossibile, ideo retardatur per naturalē appetitū dissolutionem corporis & animæ abhorrentis, propter quod subditur: Nā & q sumus in hoc tabernaculo. i. in hoc corpore mortali, ingemiscimus grauati de dissolutioe corporis & animę, eò quod noli m⁹ expoliari corpore uidelicet p morte, sed su puestiri. i. indui glorię uestimēto, &c. Hęc ille.
units.tr: "For we who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened, because we are unwilling to be unclothed but clothed over, so that mortality may be swallowed up by life." He explains the preceding clause: how and why he said, "if indeed we shall be found clothed, not naked." He gives the reason: all men, the godly too, naturally shrink from the death of the body. So the godly, although they desire immortality, shrink from bodily death, and would rather, if found alive, be clothed over with heavenly bodies than be stripped of the old body through death and so be clothed with the new and immortal. In this sense he says: "For we who are in this tabernacle," that is, as many as the godly are still encompassed by an earthly body, "on this account we groan, burdened by our sojourn in it; for although we are unwilling to be stripped of it through death, from which nature shrinks, yet we desire to be clothed over with the new and heavenly." How? "So that mortality may be swallowed up," or, as the Greek has it and the old edition reads, "what is mortal may be swallowed up by life." That is, the heavenly life, which is given along with the new and heavenly body, may swallow up the mortality and corruption of the old body without tasting death, and suddenly make what was earthly heavenly. This will happen to those who are found alive on the day of resurrection. Lyra also gives this sense, and Burgensis does not object. For he explains thus: "If indeed we are found clothed and not naked," that is, if, without the dissolution of the corruptible body which the soul uses, glory could be put over it as a garment, then the desire for grace would proceed without any hindrance; but since this is impossible, it is delayed by the natural aversion to the dissolution of body and soul. Hence it is added: "For we who are in this tabernacle," that is, in this mortal body, we groan, burdened by the dissolution of body and soul, because we are unwilling to be stripped of the body through death, but to be clothed over, that is, clothed with the garment of glory, and so on. So he says.

units.la: In eo quod dicit: Etenim qui sumus in hoc tabernaculo gemimus onerati, obseruandum est, apostolos quoq; humanæ sortis ac miserię esse participes, donec uiuūt in hoc terreno habitaculo, ut & ipsi oneretur illius molestijs, & onerati ingemiscát, liberationēq; appetát. Hu iusmodi gemitus ut sunt naturales, ita nihil habent culpæ, nedū si sint ex fide ac desyderio futurę corporū nostrorū redemptionis. Imò ipsa omnis creatura cógemiscit nobiscū, & unà parturit usq; ad id tēporis quo à seruitute corruptionis in libertatē gloriæ filiorū Dei liberabitur. Quare nihil minus habēt eiusmodi gemitus q̄ indicia impatientiæ. Ipsa patientia sanctorū plena est gemitibus ac suspirijs, quibus usq; adeo nō offenditur Deus, ut per prophetā dicat: Propter miseriā inopū, & gemitū pauperū nūc exurgā: ponā illis salutē, &c. Psal. 12. Et Ezec. 9. frōtes uirorū gementiū securitatis nota signari iubet. Et Ps. 102. gemitus cōpeditorū exaudiri ab illo canitur: quin ipse spūs postulat ̧p nobis gemitib. inenarrabilib. Ro. 8,
units.tr: In what he says, "For we who are in this tabernacle groan, burdened," it must be observed that the apostles too share in the human lot and misery as long as they live in this earthly dwelling, so that they too are burdened by its troubles and, being burdened, groan and seek deliverance. Such groanings, being natural, have no fault at all, much less when they arise from faith and desire for the future redemption of our bodies. Indeed the whole creation groans with us and labours together until the time when it will be freed from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the sons of God. Therefore such groanings are no less signs of impatience. The very patience of the saints is full of groanings and sighs, and God is so far from being offended by these that through the prophet he says: "Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise; I will set salvation for them," and so on. Ps. 12. And Ezek. 9 bids that the foreheads of men who groan be marked with the sign of security. And Ps. 102 sings that the groanings of prisoners are heard by him. Indeed the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings. Rom. 8.

units.la: PROPTEREA, inquit, quod nolimus exui, sed superindui.) Ergo & sanćti sic uellēt ad cœlestē futurę uitę gloriā peruenire, ut nō essent ipsis subeundi mortis dolores, & corpus hoc terrenū mortis interuētu exuendū. Nec est, ut existimemus sic animatos displicere dño, qui & ipse dicebat: Pater si fieri potest, transeat à me calix iste, ne bibā illū. Hic animus nō repugnat uolūtati Dei in sanćtis, quia non est obfirmatus in hac carnis infirmitate, obfirmatus uerò est in proposito obediendi diuinæ uoluntati, unde & dicebat dominus: Verunta- men non sicut ego uolo, sed sicut tu uis.
units.tr: "Therefore," he says, "because we are unwilling to be stripped, but clothed over." So also the saints would wish to attain the heavenly glory of future life in such a way that they would not have to undergo the pains of death, and this earthly body would not have to be stripped off through the intervention of death. Nor should we think that souls so disposed displease the Lord, who himself said: "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; let me not drink it." This disposition does not oppose the will of God in the saints, because they are not fixed on this weakness of the flesh; they are fixed rather on the purpose of obeying the divine will, whence the Lord also said: "Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will."

units.la: Deinde & id sanćtorū est, quòd nō simpliciter dicit: Propterea quòd nolimus exui, quasi amantes sint corporis terreni, & uitę quā in illo uiuunt, nolintq; illis priuari, quemadmodū animati sunt filij huius sæculi, sed addit quid uelint, si ita uoluntas esset domini, cū dicti: sed superindui. Hoc uotū nō est hominū carnaliū, qui cœleste hoc indumētnū, nec norunt, nec futufuturum credunt, multo minus appetunt, sed fidelium ac spiritualium tantùm, quorum conversatio non est in hoc sæculo sed in cœlis, ubi Christus est ad dexteram Dei.
units.tr: Moreover, this too is characteristic of the saints: he does not simply say, "because we are unwilling to be stripped," as if they were lovers of the earthly body and of the life they live in it, and unwilling to be deprived of it, as the children of this age are minded. He adds what they would wish if this were the will of the Lord: "but to be clothed over." This desire belongs not to carnal men, who neither know this heavenly garment nor believe it will come, much less desire it, but only to the faithful and spiritual, whose conversation is not in this age but in heaven, where Christ is at the right hand of God.

units.la: SED superindui inquit.) Ergo in die resurrectionis, qui in hisce corporibus uiui reperientur, & illa quæ habent corpora nostra non exuent sed retinebùt, & nouis illis ac cœlestibus superinducentur, ut corpora habeant duplicata, perinde ac si una uelte indutus superinduatur & altera, atq; ita duplici sit uelte indutus. Respondeo. Non est hic Apostoli sensus. Verbo superinduedi loquitur, nō de nouo quodā corpore ueteri coniungēdo, sed de gloria immortalitatis, ei corpori quod hic circumferimus superinduenda. Qualitate glorificati corporis comparat nouo indumento, nō noui corporis substantiam. Et id quod subijcit dicēs: ut absorbeatur mortalitas à uita, pulchre exponit, qd uerbo superinduedi intelligat. Nō dicit: ut absorbeatur uetus corpus à nouo, terrenum à cœlesti, mortuum à uiuo, sed, ut absorbeatur mortalitas terreni corporis à uita, ne sit mors ipsa gustanda. Mortalitas terreni corporis qualitas est non ipsa substantia. Vbi illa absorbebitur per cœlestem uitam in uiuis, quod subita mutatione in momento temporis fiet, non absorbebitur substantia corporis sed qualitas, qua mortale est & corruptibile.
units.tr: "But to be clothed over," he says. Therefore, on the day of resurrection, those who are found alive in these bodies will not strip off but retain the bodies they have, and will be clothed over with those new and heavenly ones, so that they have doubled bodies, just as if a man clothed in one garment were clothed over with another, and so doubly clothed. I answer: this is not the apostle's meaning. By the word "clothed over" he speaks not of some new body to be joined to the old, but of the glory of immortality to be put over the body which we carry here. He compares the quality of the glorified body to a new garment, not the substance of a new body. And what he adds, "so that mortality may be swallowed up by life," admirably explains what he means by "clothed over." He does not say, "that the old body may be swallowed up by the new, the earthly by the heavenly, the dead by the living," but "that the mortality of the earthly body may be swallowed up by life, lest death itself be tasted." The mortality of the earthly body is a quality, not the substance itself. When that is swallowed up by heavenly life in the living, which will happen by a sudden change in a moment of time, it is not the substance of the body that will be swallowed up but the quality by which it is mortal and corruptible.

units.la: VT absorbeatur mortalitas à uita inquit.) Græcè est τὸ θνητὸν, id est, mortale, quo corpora nostra sunt mortis capacia, imo morti obnoxia. Mortalitas hæc in omnem humani generis carnè per primi hominis communis nostri parentis peccatum peruenit, cuius meminit Apostolus Rom.5.
units.tr: "That mortality may be swallowed up by life," he says. In Greek it is τὸ θνητὸν [to thnēton], that is, what is mortal, by which our bodies are capable of death, nay, liable to it. This mortality came upon the whole human race through the sin of the first man, our common parent, which the apostle mentions in Rom. 5.

units.la: Non dicit autem, ut absorbeatur mors, sed ut absorbeatur mortalitas à uita. Per mortalitatem morti reddimur obnoxij. Illa absorpta nihil loci relinquitur morti. Imo mortalitate & incorruptibilitate corporū nostrorū sublata, ipsa quoq; mors sublata sit necesse est. Qua de re in priori ad Corinthios cap. 15. scribit ad hunc modum. Cum autē corruptibile hoc induerit incorruptibilitatem, & mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem, tunc fiet sermo qui scriptus est: Absorpta est mors in uictoriam.
units.tr: He does not say, however, that death is to be swallowed up, but that mortality is to be swallowed up by life. Through mortality we are made liable to death. When that is swallowed up, no place is left for death. Indeed, with the mortality and corruptibility of our bodies taken away, death itself must necessarily be taken away. Therefore in the first epistle to the Corinthians, ch. 15, he writes in this manner: "But when this corruptible has put on incorruptibility, and this mortal has put on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory."

units.la: Illud, à uita, nō est in Græco, ἀπὸ τῆς ζωῆς. sed cū articulo τὸ ἀπὸ τ̂ς ζωῆς, id est, ab illa uita. Nō enim de præsenti hac, sed cœlesti illa ac futura uita loquitur. Præsens hæc tam abest ut mortalitatem corporum nostrorum absorbeat, ut magis ab illa absorbeatur. Reipsa uidemus sic esse comparatū, quicquid uitæ in carne sub cœlo est, ut per mortalitatis ingluuiem absorbeatur. At ubi aduenerit immensa illa cœlestis uitæ uis perinde absorbebitur quicquid in nobis mortale est, quemadmodū nocturnas tenebras clarissimi solis exortu absorberi uidem9.
units.tr: The words "by life" are not in the Greek as ἀπὸ τῆς ζωῆς [apo tēs zōēs], but with the article, τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς ζωῆς [to apo tēs zōēs], that is, by that life. For he speaks not of this present life, but of that heavenly and future life. This present life is so far from swallowing up the mortality of our bodies that rather it is swallowed up by that. We see in fact that it is so constituted that whatever life there is in the flesh under heaven is swallowed up by the gulp of mortality. But when that immense power of heavenly life arrives, whatever in us is mortal will be swallowed up in the same way, just as we see nocturnal darkness swallowed up at the rising of the most bright sun.

units.la: Obseruemus igitur quantum discriminis sit inter præsentem hanc uitam, & eam quæ dabitur in futuro. Præsentem uidemus mortalitate absorberi, nec impedire possumus istā uoraginem, nec in nobis nec in ijs qui nobis sunt charissimi: futura uerò, quā expectamus, uiceuersa absorptricem hanc mortalitate absorbebit. Hanc rerum uicissitudinem pij homines considerabunt, quò sese contra mortalitatis adhuc regnantis ac quoquis uorantis ingluiem solentur.
units.tr: Let us therefore observe how great the difference is between the present life and the life that will be given in the future. We see the present life swallowed up by mortality, and we cannot prevent this abyss, either in ourselves or in those who are dearest to us. The future life, which we await, will in turn swallow up this mortality that devours us. Godly people will consider this exchange of circumstances so that they may console themselves against the devouring of mortality, which still reigns and consumes everyone.

units.la: QVI uerò parauit nos in hoc ipsum, inquit, Deus est.) Quoniam insolita, & humanū captum ac uotum quoque & cunctas nostras uires excedetia loquebatur, refert illorum perfectionem ad Deum dicens: Qui uerò parauit nos in hoc ipsum, Deus est. Græce est κατεργασάμενος, id est, qui perfecit nos. Vetus interpres habet, qui autē efficit nos. Placet tamen quod Erasmus tráftulit: qui parauit nos. Chrysostomus quoniā reperit in præterito: qui perfecit nos, retulit ad opificiū creationis ad hūc modum: Cum formaret nos ab initio è terra, non in hoc condidit, ut moreremur, sed ut nos immortales redderet. Verum non est insolens Apostolo uerbis præteritis uti pro præsentibus, ut hic legi possit, qui uerò parat nos in hoc ipsum, Deus est. Et magis probauero, si uerbum hoc parandi referamus ad operationem Dei, non generalem illam qua genus humanum condidit è terra, sed speciale, qua electos suos singulari gratia & uirtute ad gloriā immortalitatis parat. Vt sit sensus. Qualis qua lis sum in oculis mūdi, & utut pro reiectāmeto habear, & reuera per meipsum nihil horum de quibus loquor in meipso efficere possum, qui me tamen in hoc parauit Deus est, qui ut cœpit ita & perficiet. Is me suo tempore cœlesti & æterno immortalitatis indumento donabit. Alij tamen aliter exponunt. Quidam referunt ad naturalem affectum, quo se Paulus mortem horrere significat, quòd ille sit à Deo in nobis, qui nos tales condidit, ut morte fugiamus. Sensum hunc probare non possum. Licet enim affectus hic naturæ omnino sit à Deo, aliud est tamen si dicas: tales nos fecit Deus, & aliud si dicas cum Apostolo: qui nos in idipsum parauit Deus est.
units.tr: "Now he who has prepared us for this very thing is God." Since he was speaking of things unusual, beyond human understanding and desire, and beyond all our powers, he refers their accomplishment to God, saying: "Now he who has prepared us for this very thing is God." The Greek is κατεργασάμενος [katergasamenos], that is, "who has produced us" or "who has accomplished us." The old translator has "who makes us," but Erasmus's rendering, "who has prepared us," pleases me more. Chrysostom, since he found the past tense, "who has accomplished us," referred it to the work of creation, in this way: "When he formed us from the earth at the beginning, he did not make us for this, that we should die, but that he should make us immortal." But it is not unusual for the Apostle to use the past tense for the present, so that this can be read as "who prepares us for this very thing is God." I would prove this more fully if we refer this verb of preparing to God's working, not that general working by which he made the human race from the earth, but the special working by which he prepares his elect by his singular grace and power for the glory of immortality. The sense is this: whatever I am in the eyes of the world, and however much I may be regarded as refuse, and though I cannot of myself bring about in myself any of those things of which I speak, yet God, who has prepared me for this, is God; and as he has begun, so he will also finish. In his own time he will clothe me with the heavenly and eternal garment of immortality. Others, however, explain it differently. Some refer it to the natural feeling by which Paul signifies that he shrinks from death, on the ground that it is God who has made us such in ourselves, that we should flee death. I cannot approve this sense. For although this natural feeling is wholly from God, it is one thing to say, "God made us such," and another to say, with the Apostle, "Now he who has prepared us for this very thing is God."

units.la: Quidam ad desyderium futuræ immortalitatis referunt, quasi dicat Apostolus: qui nobis desyderium hoc indidit Deus est. Si legeretur ὁ δὲ ἐνεργασάμενος ἡμᾶς αὐτὸ τοῦτο, id est, qui inoperatur hoc ipsum in nobis, aliquid rationis haberet hæc expositio. Verùm quoniā dicit, ὁ δὲ κατεργασάμενος ἡμᾶς εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο, id est, qui perficiet, uel parauit, uel aptauit nos in hoc ipsum, existimo non loqui ipsum de desyderio futuræ immortalitatis, sed de operatione Dei in electis, qua suos parat ad immortalitatem, ad quam eos ab æterno destinauit. Dico, quid mihi uideatur. Liberū est lectori probare quam expositionem sequatur.
units.tr: Some refer it to the desire for future immortality, as if the Apostle said: "God is the one who has planted this desire in us." If the text read ὁ δὲ ἐνεργασάμενος ἡμᾶς αὐτὸ τοῦτο, that is, "he who works this very thing in us," this explanation would have some reason. But since it says ὁ δὲ κατεργασάμενος ἡμᾶς εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο, that is, "he who will perfect us, or has prepared or fitted us for this very thing," I think that the Apostle is not speaking of the desire for future immortality, but of God's working in the elect, by which he prepares his own for immortality, to which he destined them from eternity. I say what seems to me; the reader is free to approve whichever explanation he follows.

units.la: Obseruia uerò quòd nō in futuro dicit: qui parabit nos. Etenim ad immortalitatis indumentum acquirēdum non demum parabitur, ubi iā induendū erit, sed quāto terrenū ipsius corpȳ crebriorib. afflictionib. atterebatur quo-
units.tr: Observe, moreover, that he does not say "who will prepare us" in the future. For in order to acquire the garment of immortality, we are not prepared only when we are about to put it on; rather, the more our earthly body was worn down by frequent afflictions, the more

units.la: tidie, tanto magis illum dominus ad immoi ta litatis ac cœlestis uitæ gloriâ parabat.Perinde ac si architectus uetus tugurium demoliatur, non ut nulla supersit domus amplius, sed ut illo destructo locus nouo ædificio paretur. Quemadmodū illic ueteris tugurij destructio ad nouam est structurâ præparatio,ita & Apostolo eueniebat, ut dum terrenū ipsius domicilium destruebatur, ipse ad cœlestis & æterni domicilij consequutione diuinitus pararetur. Quid sunt igitur Tyranni illi, hostes & aduersarij Christi aliud, qui sanctos Dei mille modis affligunt, ac terrena illorum domicilia destruunt, quàm Dei illos ad immortalitatis gloriâ parâtis ministri facietesqdˢ non intelligūt?
units.tr: daily, the more the Lord was preparing us for the glory of immortality and the heavenly life. It is just as when a builder pulls down an old hut, not so that no house remains at all, but so that by its demolition a place is made ready for a new building. As in that case the destruction of the old hut is the preparation for the new structure, so it happened to the Apostle: while his earthly dwelling was being destroyed, he himself was being prepared by God to attain the heavenly and eternal dwelling. What, then, are those tyrants, the enemies and adversaries of Christ, who afflict the saints of God in a thousand ways and destroy their earthly dwellings, other than ministers who, without understanding it, make them ready for the glory of immortality?

units.la: QVI & dedit nobis arrabonē spiritus inquit.) Quasi dicat. Qui non solū opus suum operatur in nobis, parans nos ad futuram gloriam, sed & de illo certos nos esse uolens, dedit nobis arrabonem, ne quis dubitationi sit locus, spiritum uidelicet, quem in Christo accepimus,quem nobis esse uult loco arrabonis,quò de gratia sua & futura gloria certificemur. Sunt qui particulam hanc præcedenti sic esse subiectam existimant, ut modū illius exponat, quo uidelicet paret suos Deus ad cœlestē gloriam. Verùm,meo iudicio,simplicius est, ut sensum quē assignauimus retineamus. De eo uero,quòd spiritum uocat arrabonem, non est ut hic annotemus.Nam ea de re annotauimus supra circa calcem cap.primi,ubi eodem modo de spiritu loquutus est.
units.tr: "Who has also given us the pledge of the Spirit." As if he said: he who not only works his work in us, preparing us for future glory, but who also wishes us to be certain of it, has given us a pledge, so that there may be no room for doubt; namely the Spirit, whom we have received in Christ, and whom he wishes to be to us in place of a pledge, so that we may be assured of his grace and future glory. There are those who think that this clause is joined to what precedes in such a way that it explains the manner in which God prepares his people for heavenly glory. But, in my judgment, it is simpler to keep the sense we have assigned. As to his calling the Spirit a pledge, there is no need for us to comment on it here, for we made our comment on this matter above, near the end of the first chapter, where he speaks of the Spirit in the same way.

units.la: Itaq; bono animo sumus semper, & scimus, quòd cum domi sumus in corpore, peregrinamur à domino. Per fidem enim ambulamus, & non per speciem, Cōfidimus autē & probamus magis peregre abesse à corpore, & præsentes adesse apud Deū. Quapropter contendimus,siue domi præsentes, siue foris peregre agentes, ut illi placeamus. Omnes enim nos manifestari oportet coram tribunali Christi,ut reportet unusquisq; quæ per corpus sunt gesta, iuxta quod fecit,siue bonum siue malum.
units.tr: So we are always of good courage, and we know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord. For we walk by faith, not by sight. We are confident, and we prefer rather to be away from the body and present with God. Therefore we strive, whether at home or abroad, to be pleasing to him. For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what he has done through the body, whether good or evil.

units.la: Quod Græcam lectionem attinet, uidetur uerbum aliquod desyderari. Sic enim legitur: θαῤῥοῦντες οὖν πάντοτε καὶ εἰδότες ὅτι ἐνδημοῦντες ἐν τῷ σώματι, ἐκδημοῦμεν ἀπὸ τ κυρίου, διὰ πίστεως γὰρ περιπατοῦμεν οὐ διὰ εἴδους. i. semper igitur fidentes,uel,bono animo existētes,& sciētes,quod cum domi sumus in hoc corpore, peregrinamur à domino. Per fidem.n.ambulamus. Nōdū expressum est uerbū aliquod quod sermonem hiulcū cōpleat,ne quid desideret lectot. Vulgatus interpres simpliciter ut reperit,trástulit. Erasmus ut sermonē compleret,perinde reddidit ac si sit in Græco, θαῤῥοῦμεν οὖν πάντοτε καὶ εἰδότες, id est,Itaq; bono animo sumus sem-
units.tr: As regards the Greek reading, some word seems to be lacking. For it is read thus: θαῤῥοῦντες οὖν πάντοτε καὶ εἰδότες ὅτι ἐνδημοῦντες ἐν τῷ σώματι, ἐκδημοῦμεν ἀπὸ τοῦ κυρίου, διὰ πίστεως γὰρ περιπατοῦμεν οὐ διὰ εἴδους; that is, "therefore always being confident, or being of good courage, and knowing that while we are at home in this body we are away from the Lord. For we walk by faith." No word has yet been expressed that would complete the broken sentence and so leave the reader nothing lacking. The Vulgate translator simply rendered it as he found it. Erasmus, in order to complete the sentence, rendered it as if the Greek were θαῤῥοῦμεν οὖν πάντοτε καὶ εἰδότες, that is, "Therefore we are always of good courage and know," changing the participles into verbs. But in my judgment it was not necessary to do this. The context itself, if it is not carelessly torn apart, sufficiently remedies this difficulty, in this way: "Therefore always being confident, or bold, and knowing that while we are at home in this body we are away from the Lord (for we walk by faith and not by sight), we are rather confident and prefer to be away from the body and present with the Lord." Those who tore this sequence apart, separating the words θαῤῥοῦμεν δὲ καὶ ἐνδοκοῦμεν [tharroumen de kai endokoumen] from what precedes by placing a break between them, detached what belongs to the completion of what goes before.

units.la: per,& scimus. Sic participia in uerba ipsorum mutauit. Verùm,meo iudicio,non erat necesse hoc facere. Contextus ipse,si non imperite diuellatur,satis medetur huic incommodo,ad hunc uidelicet modum. Semper igitur fidentes uel audentes,& scientes, quod cum domi sumus in hoc corpore peregrinamur à domino (per fidem enim ambulamus, & non per speciē) magis confidimus & probamus peregrinari à corpore,& præsentes adesse apud dominum. Hanc seriem lectionis discerpserunt, qui uelut nouum ac separatum quid, illud θαῤῥοῦμεν δὲ καὶ ἐνδοκοῦμεν ἀ præcedentibus posito interstitio auulserunt, cum ad complementum præcedentium pertineat.
units.tr: by faith, and we know. So he changed the participles into verbs. Yet in my judgement it was not necessary to do this. The context itself, if it is not carelessly torn apart, sufficiently remedies this difficulty, in this way: "Therefore always being confident or bold, and knowing that while we are at home in this body we are away from the Lord (for we walk by faith, not by sight), we are the more confident and approve of being away from the body and of being present with the Lord." Those who have torn apart this sequence of the reading have, as if it were something new and separate, cut off the phrase "we are confident, and well pleased" [θαῤῥοῦμεν δὲ καὶ εὐδοκοῦμεν] from what precedes, placing an interval between them, although it belongs to the completion of what precedes.

units.la: Sensus autem est. Accepto igitur arrabone spiritus,certiŏ; facti parari nos à Deo ad recipiendum futuræ immortalitatis indumētum, semper quidem animo sumus confidenti, & contra quæuis discrimina audēti, quibus quo tidie appetimur & afflictamur, scientes nos dum domi sumus in hoc corpore,illudq; tanquam terrenum domicilium incolimus, non esse præsentes coram domino, sed ab illo peregrinari (nam in hac peregrinatione à domino ambulamus non per speciem, sed per fidem) Verum cōfidimus & probamus magis id qdˢ ab hac est peregrinatione diuersum, ut uidelicet à corpore hoc peregrinantes præsentes simus apud dominum. Huc sese uota nostra indesinenter extendunt. Hunc præsentis loci sensum existimo esse manifestum,cui lucis ali quid adferret,si uocula μὲν, id est,quidē, præmitteretur,cui postea δὲ, id est,uero,responde ret,ac legeretur: θαῤῥοῦντες μὲν οὖν πάντοτε,id est, igitur semper quidem confidentes, uel audentes ac scientes,&c.
units.tr: The sense, then, is this. Having therefore received the pledge of the Spirit, we are made certain that we are being prepared by God to receive the garment of future immortality. We are always indeed of a confident mind, and bold against whatever dangers daily assail and afflict us, knowing that while we are at home in this body, and dwell in it as in an earthly dwelling, we are not present before the Lord but are away from him (for in this absence we walk by faith, not by sight). But we are confident and approve rather of that which is different from this absence, namely that, departing from this body, we may be present with the Lord. Our desires extend ceaselessly toward this. I judge this to be the plain sense of the present passage, which would be given some light if the little particle "indeed" [μὲν] were placed before it, and "but" [δὲ] answered to it, so that it read: "Therefore being always indeed confident" [θαῤῥοῦντες μὲν οὖν πάντοτε], that is, therefore always indeed confident, or bold and knowing, and so on.

units.la: ITAQVE bono animo existētes semper, inquit.) Significat hoc dicens, nullis se afflictionibus sic premi, ut animum in causa Christi confidentem abijciat, sed quicquid malorū accidat, semper pergere,audere,ac conari.Ne que enim loquitur de animo per se, uel in se immoto ac firmo, quē nullæ possint afflictiones turbare,sed de animi sui confidentia & audacia, qua in ipsis afflictionibus ac periculis constitutus ea faciat docendo,prædicando,& fratrum animos erigendo : unde sibijpse præsentissimum exitium accersere uideatur. Hoc erat semper θαῤῥεῖν, quod ipsi loco dementię, temeritatis &spiritus irrequieti imputabatur. Quare Erafmus rectius uertisset. Itaq; confidenti animo, quàm itaq; bono animo sumus semper.Sane causam non habuit ueterem uer sionem hic loco mouendi,quæ habet, Audentes igitur semper.
units.tr: "Therefore, being of good courage always," he says. By this he means that he is not so weighed down by any afflictions that he gives up the confidence he has in Christ's cause; whatever evils befall him, he always presses on, dares, and strives. For he is not speaking of a mind that is firm and unmoved in itself, which no afflictions could disturb, but of his own confidence and boldness, by which, even in afflictions and dangers, he teaches, preaches, and raises up the spirits of the brothers, so that he seems to be bringing down the gravest ruin upon himself. This was always "to be confident" [θαῤῥεῖν], and it was imputed to him as madness, rashness, and a restless spirit. Hence Erasmus translated more accurately, "Therefore we are always of confident mind" rather than "of good courage." The older version, which reads "Therefore daring always," certainly had no reason to change this passage.

units.la: ET scientes, inquit, quod cum domi sumus in corpore, peregrinamur à domino.) Duæ Græcæ dictiones, quas hic ponit Apostolus, ἐνδημοῦντες,uidelicet & ἐκδημοῦμεν nō possunt duabus Latinis cōsimilibus pari elegātia reddi.ἐνδημοῦν significat agere in populo,ac domo sua ἐκδημοῦν uero diuersum significat,agere ui delicet inter alienos & exteros, in regionibus remotis, abesse à populo ac domo sua, & in summa, peregrinari. Quod igitur dicit: ἐνδημοῦντες ἐν τῷ σώματι, uerti potest, quod cum agimus ac uersamur in corpore, nec opus est, ut reddamus, cū domi sumus in corpore. Esse in corpore, agere in corpore, uersari in corpore, est ἐνδημοῦμεν ἐν τῷ σώματι.
units.tr: "And knowing," he says, "that while we are at home in the body [ἐνδημοῦντες ἐν τῷ σώματι] we are away from the Lord." The two Greek words the Apostle uses here, namely ἐνδημοῦντες and ἐκδημοῦμεν, cannot be rendered by two Latin words of similar sense with equal elegance. ἐνδημοῦν means to be among one's own people and at one's own home, whereas ἐκδημοῦν means the opposite: to be among strangers and foreigners, in distant regions, to be away from one's people and home, and in short, to be a sojourner. What he says, therefore, ἐνδημοῦντες ἐν τῷ σώματι can be rendered as "while we live and move in the body"; there is no need to translate it literally, "while we are at home in the body." To be in the body, to act in the body, to dwell in the body, is ἐνδημοῦμεν ἐν τῷ σώματι.

units.la: QVOD cum domi sumus in corpore, inquit, peregrinamur à domino, Quasi dicat. Scimus huius nostrae uitae incolatum quo uersamur in hoc corpore, sic esse comparatum, ut donec in illo sumus, peregrinemur à domino. Quaeriert autē hic quisquā, an corpus hoc nostrum tam sit remotū à domino, ut quotquot in illo agimus, propter illud excludamur à domino, simusque ab illo remoti ac peregrini, quemadmodum haec uerba Apostoli sonare uidentur. Ecquomodo haec sententia reliquis scripturis conueniat, quales sunt: An nescitis, quod corpora uestra membra sunt Christi? Item: An nescitis quod corpus uestrum templum est inhabitantis in uobis Spiritus sancti, quem habetis à Deo?
units.tr: "While we are at home in the body," he says, "we are away from the Lord." It is as if he said: We know that this sojourn of our life, in which we dwell in this body, is so arranged that, for as long as we are in it, we are away from the Lord. But someone might ask here whether this body of ours is so far removed from the Lord that all of us who live in it are shut out from him because of it, and are remote and absent from him, as the Apostle's words seem to suggest. How does this statement agree with the other Scriptures, such as: "Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?" And again: "Do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, whom you have from God?"

units.la: Respondeo. Non negat haec Apostolus. Neq; illa praesenti sententiae contradicūt. Corpora nostra non sunt aliena à Christo, cuius utiq; sunt membra. Et interea tamen multum discriminis est inter societatem qua Christo in hac terrena uita constituti coniungimur, & eam qua illi terreno corpore exuti, in caelesti uita coniungemur. Christus terrā hanc relinquens caelos ascendit, ad mansiones caelestes & aeternas, & futurum promisit, ut nos quoq; ad illas tanquam ad sedes patrias subuehat. Secūmq; habeat in sempiternū. Hic cum agat u q; ad diem iudicij, nos uero in corpore existentes terras incolamus, utiq; peregrinamur ab illo, idq; peregrinatione tam longinqua, q; longinquo spacio terra dirimitur à sede caeleste. Haec est simplex Christianorum theologia, quae à nonnullis contentiosis hodie mirum in modum discerpitur. Secundū hanc loquitur Apostolus cum dicit: Et scientes quod cum agimus in corpore, peregrinamur à domino.
units.tr: I answer: the Apostle does not deny these things, nor do they contradict the present statement. Our bodies are not alien to Christ, of whom they are indeed members. Yet there is still a great difference between the fellowship by which we are joined to Christ in this earthly life, and the fellowship by which we shall be joined to him in the heavenly life, when we are stripped of the earthly body. Christ, leaving this earth, ascended into the heavens, to the heavenly and eternal mansions, and promised that he would also bring us up to them, as to our fatherland's seats, and would keep us with himself forever. He remains there until the day of judgment, while we, existing in the body, dwell on earth, and so we are indeed away from him, and away by a journey as long as the distance by which the earth is separated from the heavenly seat. This is the simple theology of Christians, which some contentious people today tear to pieces in a remarkable way. It is according to this that the Apostle speaks when he says: "And knowing that while we live in the body, we are away from the Lord."

units.la: Caeterum duo haec simul sunt cogitanda: Vnum, quod licet peregrinemur à domino, ille tamen uirtute spiritus sui non deserit nos, sed corda nostra inhabitat, nobiscum existens usq; ad consummationē saeculi, sicq; fide lium suorum conuentus sanctificat, ut se in medio illorum fore promittat dicens: Vbicunq; fuerint duo uel tres in nomine meo congregati, ibi sum in medio eorum. Alterum, licet ille caelestes mansiones inhabitet, & nos hic peregrinemur corpore in terris, cordibus tamen usq; ad eum ascendimus, sic ut conuersatio nostra in caelis magis sit quàm in terris. Sic peregrinatione ista non impedimur, quo minus spiritalibus recreationibus subinde eri gamur, consortioq; fruamur, etsi non per omnia, ex parte tamen caelesti.
units.tr: These two things, however, must be considered together. First, although we are away from the Lord, he nevertheless does not forsake us by the power of his Spirit, but dwells in our hearts, remaining with us even to the end of the age; and so he sanctifies the gatherings of his faithful, promising that he will be in the midst of them, saying: "Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them." Second, although he dwells in the heavenly mansions and we are sojourning here on earth in the body, nevertheless in our hearts we ascend to him, so that our conversation is more in heaven than on earth. Thus this sojourn does not prevent us from being raised up from time to time by spiritual refreshments and from enjoying fellowship with him, even if not in every respect, yet in part, in a heavenly manner.

units.la: PER fidem enim ambulamus, inquit, non per speciem.) Parenthesis haec probationis est gratia inserta, ad comprobandū, quod nos in corpore existentes à domino peregrinari dixit. Quasi enim hoc audiens aliquis dicat: Quomodo peregrini sumus à domino, in quo uiuimus, & quem in nobis uiuente habemus? Peregrinari nos, inquit, à domino, dum in corpore ambulamus, uel per id abunde manifestum est, quod omnis haec uita nostra uita est fidei non speciei. Ambulamus quidem cum domino, uerum non in specie, id est, facie ad faciem, in ipso illius aspectu praesentes, quemadmodum cum illo erimus in uita futura, sed per fidem, qua illi adhaeremus, quia opem illius imploramus, qua futura speramus & expectamus, qua, in summa, non apparentia & non praesentia credendo ac fidendo apprehendimus, quae fides in futuro saeculo, ubi ambulabimus in specie, locum non habebit, sed praesentis tantum est uitae, ideoq; certo comprobat, donec per ipsam ambulamus, peregrinari nos à domino. Poterat alia comprobare ratione quod dicebat, uerum haec & Christiana est in Christianis tantum locum habens, & simul certo quod uult euincit. Perinde habet haec ratio, ac si filijs regis in regione aliena degetibus persuasurus quod peregrinentur à patre ac sede paterna dicas: Etenim ambulatis non in illius aspectu praesentes, sed in fide, qua creditis nuncijs ac literis quas ille ad vos mittit, & uicissim nuncijs ac literis cum illo agitis.
units.tr: "For we walk by faith," he says, "not by sight." This parenthesis is inserted for the sake of proof, to confirm what he said, that while we are in the body we are away from the Lord. For as if someone hearing this should say: How are we away from the Lord, in whom we live and whom we have living in us? He says that we are away from the Lord while we walk in the body, and this is made abundantly clear by the fact that all this life of ours is a life of faith, not of sight. We indeed walk with the Lord, but not in sight, that is, face to face, present in his very gaze, as we shall be with him in the future life; rather we walk by faith, by which we cling to him, because we implore his aid, by which we hope for and expect things to come; by which, in short, we grasp by believing and trusting things not seen and not present. This faith will have no place in the future age, where we shall walk in sight; it belongs only to the present life, and therefore it certainly proves that, as long as we walk by it, we are away from the Lord. He could have proved what he was saying by another reason, but this one is Christian and has a place only among Christians, and at the same time it certainly establishes what he wants. The argument is just like this: if you wished to persuade the sons of a king, who live in a foreign region, that they are away from their father and their father's seat, you might say: For you walk not in his presence before his eyes, but in faith, by which you believe the messengers and letters that he sends to you, and in turn you deal with him through messengers and letters.

units.la: Haec frequentia paternorum nunciorum, scriptorum ac rescriptorum, tam non est eorum qui in domo paterna agát, ut magis etiā comprobet, quod ab illa peregrinemini. Consimili modo habet & nostra conditio. In peregrinatione hac non destituimur paternę prouidentiae solatijs. Habemus illius uerbum & literas, & nuncios, & spiritum. Verum haec ipsa comprobant, non agere nos in illius aspectu, sicut agimus in futuro, sed peregrinari ab illo.
units.tr: This frequent exchange of paternal messages, writings, and replies is so far from belonging to those who live in the father's house that it proves even more that you are away from it. Our condition is similar. In this sojourn we are not deprived of the comforts of the Father's providence. We have his Word, his letters, his messengers, and his Spirit. Yet these very things prove that we do not live in his sight as we shall in the future, but are away from him.

units.la: CONFIDIMVS uero & probamus magis peregrinari à corpore, inquit, & praesentes esse apud dominum.) Aperit hisce uerbis perpetuum cordis sui desyderium, quo ex hac praesenti peregrinatione liberatus in caelis cū domino agere cupiebat, id quod alibi sic exprimit: Cupio enim dissolui & esse cum Christo. Peregrinationem qua in corpore suo peregrinabatur à domino, pro uoluntate domini patienter ferebat, at interim terminata illa apud dominum agere cupiebat. Videmus hic duo esse peregrinationum genera, sic à seinuicem diuisa, ut simul esse nequeant, sed necesse sit, durate altera alterā quiescere. Vna est praesentis uitae, qua peregrinamur à domino, altera post mortem, qua peregrinamur à corpore. Peregrinantes à domino non possumus peregrinari à corpore. A corpore peregrinantes peregrinari à domino non possumus.
units.tr: "Yet we are confident, and we rather prefer," he says, "to be away from the body and to be present with the Lord." In these words he discloses the constant desire of his heart, by which, freed from this present sojourn, he longed to be with the Lord in heaven, which he expresses elsewhere thus: "For I desire to depart and to be with Christ." The absence from the Lord which he endured in his body he bore patiently at the Lord's will, but meanwhile he longed to be with the Lord once that absence was ended. We see here two kinds of absence, separated from each other so that they cannot exist together, but of necessity one must cease while the other lasts. One is of the present life, in which we are away from the Lord; the other is after death, in which we are away from the body. Those who are away from the Lord cannot be away from the body; those who are away from the body cannot be away from the Lord.

units.la: Deinde uidemus sic comparatos esse sanctos, ut quoniam praesente in corpore uitam peregrinationis loco habent, cupiat eam terminari, minari, ac peregrinari à corpore, idq; non sim pliciter, sed desyderio agendi in conspectu domini. Quare non simpliciter dicit: probamus magis peregrinari à corpore, sed addit, & præsentes adesse apud dominum. Non mox præsens est apud dominum, quisquis peregrinatur à corpore. Nam & impij peregrinantur à corpore, ubi illo fuerint per mortem exuti, de quibus tamen credere fas non est, ut post mortem sint apud dominum, quemadmodum apud eum sunt electi. Paulus cupiebat peregrinari à corpore magis quàm à domino. Impij cupiunt peregrinari à domino magis quàm à corpore. Inuenias multos qui & ipsi à corpore peregrinari cupiant, apud ethnicos quoque, quorum nonnulli seipsi à corporis incolatu liberarunt, alius ne incideret in manus hostis, alius ne præsentem ignominiam quam horrebat, ferre cogeretur, alius ne dolores corporis, quibus premebatur diutius sustineret. Verum Apostolus alium finem spectans, non hoc tantum quærebat, ut corporis liberaretur molestijs, sed ut præsens esset apud dominum.
units.tr: Next, we see that the saints are so disposed that, since in the present life in the body they regard their life as a sojourn, they desire it to be brought to an end, to depart, and to be away from the body, and this not simply, but with a longing to live in the sight of the Lord. Hence he does not simply say, "We prefer to be away from the body," but adds, "and to be present with the Lord." Not everyone who is away from the body is at once present with the Lord. For the wicked also depart from the body when they have been stripped of it by death; yet we must not believe that they are with the Lord after death, as the elect are with him. Paul longed to be away from the body rather than from the Lord. The wicked long to be away from the Lord rather than from the body. You will find many who even among the heathen have desired to be away from the body, some of whom freed themselves from the dwelling of the body: one so as not to fall into the hands of an enemy, another so as not to be forced to endure the present disgrace which he dreaded, another so as not to bear longer the bodily pains by which he was oppressed. But the Apostle, looking to another end, did not seek only to be freed from the troubles of the body, but to be present with the Lord.

units.la: Est locus hic diligenter obseruandus. De statu mortuorum alius aliud somniat. Expedita hic illius ratio proponitur. Apostolus homo Christianus dum uotum ac desyderium suum exprimit, quo à corpore peregrinari cupit, quo præsens sit apud dominum, non hoc tantum ostendit, quid desyderare debeat Christiani, sed & quid certò sperare. Hoc uidelicet, ut post mortem hanc terreno corpore exuti apud dominum futuri sint præsentes. An debemus hoc dare Apostolo, quod rem in uotis habuerit haudquaquam futuram? aut quæ cæteris non sit speranda Christianis? Absit, quod credebat sperabat, quod sperabat optabat, nec scribebat Christianis de re ad ipsos haud commuiter pertinente.
units.tr: This passage must be carefully observed. Men dream differently about the state of the dead, and the reasoning on this point is set out plainly here. The Apostle, as a Christian, while he expresses his vow and desire to be away from the body and present with the Lord, shows not only what a Christian ought to desire but also what he may hope for with certainty: that after this death, stripped of the earthly body, they will be present with the Lord. Must we grant that the Apostle prayed for something that by no means would come about, or something other Christians should not hope for? Far from it. What he believed, he hoped for; what he hoped for, he wished for; and he did not write to Christians about a matter that in no way pertained to them in common.

units.la: Et illud obseruet diligens lector, quomodo uerbo peregrinandi utatur. Præsenti corporis uitæ tribuit peregrinationem, quæ sit à domino. Illa sanè nota est, quàm sit breuis. Deinde & eam uitæ nostræ partem, quæ inter mortem corporis & diem resurrectionis intercedit, peregrinationem uocat à corpore. Hæc nobis adhuc est incognita. Est enim cognitio illius non intellectu, sed sola experientia capienda. Quid igitur mors est corporis, quàm mutatio peregrinationis? Secunda illa peregrinatio nulla tertia mutabitur. Etenim illa finita, nec à domino nec à corpore peregrinabimur, sed utriq; & domino & corpori præsentes erimus in sempiternum.
units.tr: Let the diligent reader also notice how he uses the word "to be away" (peregrinari). He ascribes a sojourning away to the present life of the body, which is from the Lord, and everyone knows how brief that is. Then he calls that part of our life which lies between the death of the body and the day of resurrection a sojourning away from the body. This is still unknown to us, for knowledge of it is to be gained not by understanding but by experience alone. What, then, is the death of the body but a change of sojourning? That second sojourning will not be changed by any third. For when it is finished, we shall be away neither from the Lord nor from the body, but we shall be present to both the Lord and the body forever.

units.la: QVAPROPTER & contendimus, inquit, siue domi præsentes, siue foris peregrinantes ut illi placeamus.) Græca duabus dictionibus exprimuntur ad hunc modum: εἴτε ἐνδημοῦντες, εἴτε ἐκδημοῦντες, id est, siue domi agentes, siue peregrinantes. Vetus habet, siue absentes siue præsentes. Est autem amphibolum quò referas. Nã quod dicit, siue domi agentes, siue peregrinantes, referri potest tam ad domi
units.tr: "Wherefore we also strive," he says, "whether present at home or away sojourning, that we may be pleasing to him." The Greek is expressed in two words in this way: eite endēmountes, eite ekdēmountes [εἴτε ἐνδημοῦντες, εἴτε ἐκδημοῦντες], that is, whether living at home or living abroad. The Old (Vulgate) has "whether absent or present." The phrase is ambiguous as to what it should be referred to. For what he says, "whether at home or sojourning,"

units.la: num quàm ad corpus. Ad dominum sic, siue domi agentes apud dominum, siue peregrinantes ab illo. Ad corpus sic, siue domi agentes in corpore, siue à corpore peregrinantes.
units.tr: can be referred as much to the Lord as to the body. Referred to the Lord: whether at home, dwelling with the Lord, or sojourning away from him. Referred to the body: whether at home in the body, or sojourning away from the body.

units.la: Declarat quid ex dicto sibi uoto nascatur, quo probabat magis peregrinari à corpore, & præsens esse apud dominum. Hoc uidelicet, ut pro uiribus cōtendat placere domino, siue hic in peregrinatione, siue illic præsens apud ipsum constitutus. Principio non simpliciter dicit: contendimus, sed, quapropter & contendimus. Significans studium hoc placendi domino ex eo sibi potissimū nasci, quod aspirabat ad felicitatem illam, qua se apud dominum præsentem fore & sperabat & optabat. Quisenim nō cupiat impense illi placere, cum quo se in sempiternum feliciter actūrū sperat? Si gratificari studemus illis quibus ad horam uel coniungimur uel subijcimur, quanto magis faciendum hoc erga eum est, cum quo præsentes erimus in sempiternum? qui si dixerit: discedite à me, non noui uos, in æternum nos exitium abijciet?
units.tr: He declares what arises from the vow he has made, by which he showed that he rather wished to be away from the body and present with the Lord. Namely, that as far as his strength allows he strives to please the Lord, whether here in his sojourning or there, established in his presence. First, he does not simply say "we strive," but "wherefore also we strive," signifying that this zeal to please the Lord arises for him chiefly from the fact that he aspired to that happiness by which he both hoped and wished to be present with the Lord. For who would not desire earnestly to please him with whom he hopes to live happily forever? If we are eager to gratify those to whom we are joined or subject for an hour, how much more ought this to be done toward him with whom we shall be present forever? He who, if he says, "Depart from me, I do not know you," will cast us into eternal ruin.

units.la: Deinde non simpliciter dicit: Quapropter placere illi cupimus, ne hoc sibi in uotis tantum esse uideatur, sed: Quapropter contendimus, ut illi placeamus. φιλοτιμούμεθα, inquit, id est, magno studio conamur & annitimur. Qui sic contendunt, nihil non faciunt, quod ipsi placere, nihil nō omittūt, quod ipsi displicere iudicauerint, cui se in omnibus approbare cupiunt. Hoc perpetuū debet esse uerorū Christianorum studium, uerum sic, ut in meta uerbi dominici consistant, ne si extra illam præsumant, quibus domino gratificari se putauerint, audiant hoc ab illo: Frustra colunt me docentes doctrinas & mandata hominum.
units.tr: Next, he does not simply say, "Wherefore we desire to please him," lest this should seem to be merely in wishes, but "wherefore we strive that we may please him." He says philotimoumetha [φιλοτιμούμεθα], that is, we attempt with great zeal and exert ourselves. Those who strive in this way leave nothing undone that they think pleasing to him, and omit nothing that they judge displeasing to him, since they wish to approve themselves to him in all things. This should be the constant zeal of true Christians, but so that they remain within the limits of the Lord's word, lest, if they presume beyond it, they hear from him what they thought would please him: "In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men."

units.la: Tertio, non est otiosum, quod non simpliciter dicit, quapropter contendimus, ut illi placeamus, sed, quapropter cōtendimus, siue domi agētes siue peregrinātes, ut illi placeamus. Inuenias qui cupiant placere domino, ubi agendū est post mortē in illius præsentia, de hac præsenti uero uita, qua ab illo peregrinamur, parum sint soliciti. At uerus Christianus non minus illi placere contendit, dum adhuc ab illo peregrinatur, quàm dum præsens est apud illum futurus. Quare Apostolus satis uigilanter utrunque expresit. Etenim qui ex animo gratificari cuipiam studet, non minus absenti quàm præsenti placere contendit.
units.tr: Thirdly, it is not idle that he does not simply say, "Wherefore we strive that we may please him," but "wherefore we strive, whether at home or away sojourning, that we may please him." You will find people who want to please the Lord where something must be done after death in his presence, but about this present true life, in which we are away from him, they are little concerned. But the true Christian strives no less to please him while he is still away from him than when he shall be present with him. Therefore the Apostle expressed both with good care. For he who from the heart is eager to gratify anyone strives to please the absent no less than the present.

units.la: Verum nascitur hic quæstio, quomodo uer bū contendendi referri posset ad tempus, quo post mortē præsentes erimus apud dominum. Studium contedendi, ut placeamus domino, præsenti uitæ coueniat, futuræ quomodo conueniat, edicere non possum. Quare miru uidetur quo se Apostolus siue præsens in corpore, siue peregrinus à corpore cōtendere dicat, ut domino placeat. Respondeo. Si quod in Græco habetur simpliciter esset, ut habetur, uersu, nulla esset hic quæstio. Habetur aut in Græco adhuc modū, διὸ καὶ φιλοτιμούμεθα, εἴτε ἐνδημοῦν-
units.tr: But here the question arises of how the word "to strive" could be referred to the time when after death we shall be present with the Lord. The zeal of striving to please the Lord suits the present life; how it suits the future I cannot say. So it seems strange why the Apostle says he strives, whether present in the body or away from the body, to please the Lord. I answer: if what is in the Greek were simply as it stands in the verse, there would be no question here. But in the Greek there is also this phrase: dio kai philotimoumetha, eite endēmoun-

units.la: ΤΑ
units.tr: [ΤΑ]

units.la: {ε}ἐκδημοῦντες ἐνδημοῦσι αὐτῷ εἶναι). Hic uerbum con{A}tendimus, non sic est positum, ut necessario sit ad duo participia, ἐκδημοῦντες & ἐνδημοῦντες referendum, sed, ut ptineat ad id quod sequitur, ἐνδημοῦσι αὐτῷ εἶναι). Dicit enim se Apostolus conte dere, ut placeat domino, siue sit in corpore siue extra corpus apud dominum. Quare potest sic uerti. Ideo contendimus, ut illi siue domi agentes siue peregrinantes placeamus. Si dicas: Contendimus ut siue viui simus siue mortui, domino placeamus, vtiq; nulla datur occasio disputandi de eo, quomodo mortui cõtendere possint, ut placeant domino. Verū datur illa in uersione Erasmi, dum reddidit ad hunc modum: Quapropter contendimus siue domi præsentes, siue foris peregrè agetes, ut illi placeamus. Hac inconsulta uersione uerbum contendi quasi studio ad mox sequentia, siue domi præsentes, siue foris peregrè agentes, cõnectitur, & ab eo, ad quod pertinet, videlicet, ut illi placeamus, auellitur. Non insector inter pretem multis modis clarum, sed simplicitate uerborum Apostoli ab occasione friuolarū quæstionum uindico.
units.tr: ...tes, eite ekdēmountes, endēmousi autō einai [ἐκδημοῦντες ἐνδημοῦσι αὐτῷ εἶναι]. Here the verb "we strive" is not placed so that it must necessarily be referred to the two participles, ekdēmountes and endēmountes, but so that it pertains to what follows, endēmousi autō einai, "to be pleasing to him." For the Apostle says he strives to please the Lord, whether he is in the body or outside the body with the Lord. Therefore it can be rendered thus: "Therefore we strive, that whether dwelling at home or sojourning away, we may please him." If you say, "We strive that whether we are alive or dead we may please the Lord," then certainly no occasion is given for disputing how the dead can strive to please the Lord. But that occasion is given by Erasmus's translation, which he rendered thus: "Wherefore we strive, whether present at home or living abroad, that we may please him." By this ill-advised rendering the word "strive" is joined, as if by zeal, to what immediately follows, "whether present at home or living abroad," and is torn away from that to which it belongs, namely, "that we may please him." I do not attack the translator, who is clear in many respects, but I defend the simplicity of the Apostle's words from the occasion of trifling questions.

units.la: OMNES enim nos manifestari oportet coram tribunali Christi inquit, ut reportet unusquisque, &c.) Hactenus Corinthijs exposuit, quomodo erga præsentis uitæ incolatum animatus sit ipse, ac quo studio contedat, ut Christo domino siue in corpore siue extra corpus constitutus placeat: iam ut illis terrorem incutiat, animosq; eorum ad consimile studiū provocet, admonet eos futuri iudicij, in quo reddendum sit unicuiq; secundum quod gesslit in corpore siue bonum siue malum. Huius futuri iudicij respectum eo sibi facere dicit, ut summopere domino tanquam futuro omnium iudici placere studeat. Ideo cum dixisset: Quapropter contendimus ut siue domi præsentes, siue foris peregrè agentes illi placeamus, generalem hanc sententiam rationis loco subiecit, dicens: Nam omnes nos manifestari oportet coram tribunali Christi, ut reportet unusquisque quæ facta sunt per corpus, &c.
units.tr: "For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ," he says, "so that each may receive," etc. Hitherto he has set out for the Corinthians how he himself is disposed toward the sojourn of the present life, and with what zeal he strives to be pleasing to Christ the Lord, whether established in the body or outside it. Now, to strike terror into them and provoke their minds to a similar zeal, he warns them of the future judgment, in which each is to receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or bad. He says that regard for this future judgment makes him strive above all to please the Lord as the future judge of all. Therefore, having said, "Wherefore we strive, whether present at home or sojourning abroad, that we may please him," he added this general statement in place of a reason: "For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what has been done through the body," etc.

units.la: Dices: Conuenit ne metu iudicij futuri impellere Christianos, ut Christo domino tanquam iudici placere studeant, & non magis ad hoc alicere, ut ex charitatis affectu & Christiana obseruantia placere illi tanquam Seruatori ac redemptori contendant, ad quem modum animat erat ipse Apostolus? Respondeo. Non est propositum Apostoli spiritum timoris plătare in cordibus fidelium, ut illo ad qualecunq; studium religionis perducantur, sed accommodat se ecclesiæ Corinthiorum, in qua erant pseudapostoli illorumq; discipuli, quorū corda non erant integra erga dominum: erat multi carnales & impœnitentes, qui nihil agebant minus quàm ut domino placerent, quem nisi contepsissent, haudquaq; in impœnitentia sua perseuerassent. Illis omnibus terrore incutere uoles, mentione inducit futuri iudicij, in quo coram tribunali Christi manifestādi sint omnes.
units.tr: You will say: is it fitting to drive Christians by fear of future judgment, so that they strive to please Christ the Lord as judge, rather than to draw them to this by the affection of charity and Christian observance, so that they strive to please him as Saviour and Redeemer, the way the Apostle himself was disposed? I answer: it is not the Apostle's purpose to plant a spirit of fear in the hearts of the faithful, so that they are led by it to any kind of religious zeal. Rather, he adapts himself to the church of the Corinthians, in which there were false apostles and their disciples, whose hearts were not sound toward the Lord. There were many carnal and impenitent people, who did nothing less than try to please the Lord; had they not despised him, they would by no means have persisted in their impenitence. To strike terror into all of them, he brings in the mention of the future judgment, in which all must be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ.

units.la: Placuit autem illi uerbum manifestandi. Poterat dicere: Omnes enim nos sistemur coram tribunali Christi, quo uerbo usus est in Romanis cap.14. ubi eandem sententiam posuit. Verum appositissime usurpauit verbum manifestandi, dicens: Omnes enim nos manifestari oportet coram tribunali Christi, ut perstringat hypocrisim pseudapostolorum, qui se transfigurabant in apostolos Christi, & interea Apostolatum ipsius omnium contemptui calumnijs suis exponere moliebantur, cum essent ipsissimi Apostoli Satanæ. Hanc illorum maliciam in obscuro adhuc grassantem manifestari aliquando fore minatur, in die uidelicet domini, qui & ob id reuelationis dies uocatur, propterea quod in illo manifesta erūt consilia cordium. Huic manifestationi se quoq; & omnem suum Apostolatum subijcit dicens: Omnes enim nos manifestari oportet coram tribunali Christi. Idem fecit & 1.Cor.4. ubi dicit: Qui me uero iudicat, dominus. Proinde ne ante tempus quicquam iudicetis, donec uenerit dominus, qui & illustraturus est occulta tenebrarum, & patefaciet consilia cordium, ac tunc laus erit unicuiq; à Deo.
units.tr: He chose the word "manifested" for a reason. He could have said, "For we all shall stand before the tribunal of Christ," a phrase he used in Romans 14, where he expresses the same idea. But he used the word "manifested" most aptly when he said, "For we must all be made manifest before the tribunal of Christ." He thereby strikes at the hypocrisy of the false apostles, who disguised themselves as apostles of Christ while trying to expose his apostolate to contempt through their slanders, although they were themselves the very apostles of Satan. He threatens that this malice of theirs, still spreading in obscurity, will one day be made manifest, namely on the day of the Lord, which is therefore also called the day of revelation, because on that day the counsels of hearts will be made manifest. He subjects himself and all his apostolate to this manifestation, saying, "For we must all be made manifest before the tribunal of Christ." He did the same in 1 Cor. 4, where he says, "But he who judges me is the Lord. Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts, and then each one will have his praise from God."

units.la: Seruit igitur sententia hæc: omnes nos manifestari oportet coram tribunali Christi, illis potissimum temporibus, in quibus regnat in ecclesia reproborum hominum hyprocrisis, qua se pro apostolis Christi, uicarijs, episcopis, prælatis, ac pastoribus uenditant, cum sint lupi graues, non parcentes gregi, & interea contradicentes hæreseos damnant, & mille mortibus cruciandos ac necandos abijciunt. Hic uerus Christi minister securā conscientia causam suā contra pseudapostolos & contra impiam illorum condemnationem transferet ad futurum Christi tribunal, dicés: Omnes nos manifestari oportet coram tribunali Christi. Videt inimicos Christi hypocritas regnare in tenebris, & hinc fieri, ut qui falsi sunt pastores pro ueris, & qui ueri pro falsis habeantur. Occulta hæc tenebrarum coram tribunali Christi retegenda ac manifestanda sciens, omnes iniurias à reprobis illatas patienter tolerat, & causam suam diei reuelationis commendat.
units.tr: This sentence therefore serves, "We must all be made manifest before the tribunal of Christ," especially in those times when the hypocrisy of reprobate men reigns in the Church. These men pass themselves off as apostles of Christ, vicars, bishops, prelates and pastors, though they are grievous wolves, not sparing the flock; and meanwhile they condemn as heresy whatever contradicts them, and cast off those who are to be tortured and put to death a thousand times over. Here the true minister of Christ, with a clear conscience, transfers his cause against the false apostles, and against their impious condemnation, to the future tribunal of Christ, saying, "We must all be made manifest before the tribunal of Christ." He sees that the hypocrites, enemies of Christ, reign in darkness, and that as a result those who are false pastors are taken for true ones, and the true for false. Knowing that these hidden things of darkness will be uncovered and made manifest before the tribunal of Christ, he patiently bears all the injuries inflicted by the reprobate and commends his cause to the day of revelation.

units.la: ONNES nos, inquit, manifestari oportet.) Manifestatur quod antea fuerat obscurū. De manifestis non rectè dicitur, quod manifestetur. Iam si nos omnes manifestari oportet coram tribunali Christi, consequitur eos quoq; manifestandos esse, qui in concilijs pōtificum pro hæreticis publicantur ac manifestantur. Exēpli gratia: Iohannes Hus & Hieronymus Pragensis in concilio Constantiensi pro hæreticis declarati sunt ac manifestati. Et illis igitur restat tribunal Christi, coram quo manifestentur, si nos omnes coram illo manifestari oportet. Nemo igitur sententiæ Synodali iniquitatur, quasi per illā iusta sit manifestatio falsorum ac uerorum ministrorū, sed tribuat illam diei domini, in quo tandem ueraciter ac finaliter manifestabuntur omnes, id est, declarabuntur. rabuntur qui sunt & quales, detrahetur ipsis imposita larua, protrahetur in lucem qd' in oculis mūdi altissimis tenebris abditum latuit. Sunt aut manifestationis huius duæ partes. Vna, qua manifestabitur, nō esse nos eos, pro quibus habiti fuimus in sæculo. Altera, qua patefiet, qui simus.
units.tr: "We must all," he says, "be made manifest." What was hidden is made manifest. It is not correct to say that what is already manifest is made manifest. Now if we all must be made manifest before the tribunal of Christ, it follows that those too must be made manifest who are proclaimed and exposed as heretics in the councils of the pontiffs. For example, John Hus and Jerome of Prague were declared and exposed as heretics at the Council of Constance. For them too, therefore, the tribunal of Christ remains, before which they will be made manifest, if we all must be made manifest before him. Let no one, therefore, object to the sentence of the synod as though by it the manifestation of false and true ministers were justly made; rather let him ascribe it to the day of the Lord, on which at last all will be truly and finally made manifest, that is, declared: who and of what sort they are will be revealed, the mask imposed on them will be stripped off, and what lay hidden in the deepest darkness in the eyes of the world will be brought into the light. There are two parts to this manifestation. One is that it will be shown that we are not what we were taken to be in this age. The other is that it will be disclosed what we really are.

units.la: Non est autem transeundum, quod non simpliciter dicit: Omnes enim nos manifestabimur, sed: Omnes enim nos manifestari oportet. Quærendum hic fuerit quare nos omnes manifestari oportear coram tribunali Christi, quæ sit ista manifestandi necessitas. Si consideremus tam futuræ quàm præsentis huius vitæ circumstantias, diuinæ iustitiæ ƨquitatem, ac futuri iudicij rationem, facile patebit, quare sic fieri oporteat, vt omnium omnia coram tribunali Christi manifestentur. In hac præsenti vita res magnę humanorum iudiciorum tenebris obscurantur magis quàm manifestantur, ac studia mortalium simulationibus ac dissimulationibus obteguntur, atq; ita in hoc sæculo nec ante nec post mortem nostram reuelantur, sed abscondita ac sepulta iacent. Quoniam igitur non manifesta modo, sed occulta hominum consilia studia & facta iudicio Dei sunt obnoxia, necesse erit ut manifestentur, & manifestata iudicentur. In futura vita lux erit, cui non conueniet, vt occultum quid & abscondi ditum in filijs lucis esse sinat. Quare & illius respectu necessarium est, vt in iudicio Christi omnia manifestentur. Et ipsius iudicij ratio hoc poscit, vt iustum non modò fit, sed & iustū esse appareat in vniuersum omnibus. Huc faciet omnium manifestatio, per quam iudicij falsorum apostolorum omnium esse iustissimū declarabitur. Ipse etiam finalis segregatio bonorum ac reproborum, ouium & hædorum manifestationem hanc necessario requiret. In summa, sic dispensabitur extremum illud & universale iudicium vt iustitia & æquitas illius vltro omnium oculos incurrat, id quod manifestatio hæc efficiet.
units.tr: Nor must we pass over the fact that he does not simply say, "For we all shall be made manifest," but "For we must all be made manifest." Here one should ask why we must all be made manifest before the tribunal of Christ, and what this necessity of manifestation is. If we consider the circumstances both of the future life and of this present life, the equity of divine justice and the nature of the future judgment, it will readily become plain why it must be so, that the all things of all people be made manifest before the tribunal of Christ. In this present life great matters are obscured by the darkness of human judgments rather than made manifest, and the pursuits of mortals are covered over with pretences and dissimulations; thus in this age they are revealed neither before nor after our death, but lie hidden and buried. Since, therefore, not only the manifest but also the hidden counsels, pursuits and deeds of men are subject to the judgment of God, they must be made manifest, and once made manifest, judged. In the future life there will be light, and it will not be fitting that anything hidden and concealed be allowed to remain among the children of light. Therefore, with regard to that light too, it is necessary that all things be made manifest in the judgment of Christ. And the very reason of judgment demands that it not only be just but also be seen to be just by all. The manifestation of all things will serve this purpose, by which the judgment against all the false apostles will be declared most just. The final separation of the good and the reprobate, of the sheep and the goats, will likewise necessarily require this manifestation. In short, that last and universal judgment will be so ordered that its justice and equity will of their own accord strike the eyes of all, and this manifestation will bring that about.

units.la: CORAM tribunali Christi, inqt.) Quare nō dicit: coram tribunali Dei, sed, coram tribunali Christi? Quia nō de quouis iudicio Dei loquitur, qd' in hoc sæculo exercetur, sed speciali ter de iudicio extremo in quo semel palam & conspicuus omnib. in fine mundi sedebit ad iudicandum Christus dominus, iudicabitq; de omnibus tam mortuis quàm viuis. Huius tribunalis terrorem singulari studio inculcare illis voluit, quorum corda sentiebat non esse ega Christum fidelia & integra.
units.tr: "Before the tribunal of Christ," he says. Why does he not say "before the tribunal of God" but "before the tribunal of Christ"? Because he is not speaking of any judgment of God that is exercised in this age, but specifically of the last judgment, in which the Lord Christ, once and openly visible to all, will sit at the end of the world to judge, and will judge both the dead and the living. He wished to instil the terror of this tribunal with particular care into those whose hearts he perceived were not faithful and sincere toward Christ.

units.la: VT reportet vnusquisq;, inquit, quę per corpus sunt gesta, iuxta quod fecit, siue bonū siue malum. ) Hunc finem ponit manifestationis omnium, retributione uidelicet eorū quæ facimus in hac vita. Neq; enim satis erit manifestum fieri, sed vt iusti iudicij norma seruetur, retribuetur vnicuiq; secundū quod gessit bonum vel malum. Nemo uel hic excipitur. Vt reportet unusquisq; inquit. Omnes manifesta-
units.tr: "That each one may receive," he says, "the things done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil." He sets this end for the manifestation of all, namely the repayment of what we do in this life. For it will not be enough merely to be made manifest; so that the rule of just judgment may be kept, each one will be repaid according to what he has done, good or evil. No one is excepted, not even here. "That each one may receive," he says. We shall all be made manifest; we shall all receive back according to what we did in this life.

units.la: bimur, omnes reportabimus secundū quod in hac vita gessimus. Sed dices: Quis igitur seruabitur? An non Propheta deprecas iudiciū Dei dicit: Ne intres in iudicium cū seruo tuo domine, quia non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis viuens? Si iudicandū de nobis est secundū quod gessimus in corpore, ne vnū quidem pro mille respondere poterimus. Quid ergo consequetur aliud, quàm vt seruetur nemo, damnemur omnes? Et quæ vtilitas nobis ex eo est quod credimus in Christum vnigenitum Dei ac Seruatorem peccatorum? Deniq; quę veritas in verbo illius remanebit, quo dicit: Qui sermonem meum audit & credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam æternam, & in iudicium non venit, sed transiuit à morte in vitam? Et quid est quod hic Apostolus Rom.cap.8. nullam his dicit inesse condemnationē, qui insiti sunt Christo Iesu? Deniq; quomodo tota illa iustificatio nis doctrina consistet, quam hic Apostolus tā diligenter tradidit, si standum nobis erit uelcadendū in iudicio secundū factorum nostrorum exigentiam? Etenim licet Christiani fumus, à peccatis tamē nondū sic liberi sumus, ut nihil peccemus in vniuersum.
units.tr: But you will say: Who then will be saved? Does not the prophet, in pleading against the judgment of God, say, "Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord, for no living man will be justified in your sight"? If we are to be judged according to what we have done in the body, we shall not be able to answer for one in a thousand. What then will follow, except that no one is saved and all are condemned? And what advantage is it to us that we believe in Christ, the only-begotten Son of God and Saviour of sinners? Finally, what truth will remain in his word, where he says, "He who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life"? And what of the fact that the Apostle here, in Rom. 8, says that there is no condemnation for those who are grafted into Christ Jesus? Finally, how will that whole doctrine of justification, which this Apostle so diligently delivered, stand, if we must stand or fall in judgment according to the measure of our deeds? For although we are Christians, we are not so free from sins that we sin nothing at all.

units.la: Respondeo. Omnino sic habet. Reportabit in die iudicij vnusquisq; nostrū, iuxta qd' gessit siue bonum siue malum. Et tamen nihil dece dit ex eo doctrinæ gratiæ. Qui viri fideles sunt, opus Dei faciunt credentes in Christū. Iohan.6. Ex illo vtiq; reportabūt iustificationem & vitam æternam, secundum dominicā promissionem & doctrinam Apostolicam.
units.tr: I answer: Certainly it is so. On the day of judgment each one of us will receive back, according to what he has done, whether good or evil. And yet nothing is taken away from this by the doctrine of grace. Those who are faithful men do the work of God by believing in Christ (John 6). By that, surely, they will receive justification and eternal life, according to the promise of the Lord and the apostolic teaching.

units.la: Quæ subinde peccant, hic illis remittuntur p sanguinem ac propiciationem Christi.1.Ioha. 1.2. Bona quæ faciunt reportabunt clamante Christo: Venite benedicti patris mei, percipite regnum, quod paratum est vobis à constitutione mundi. Esuriui, & dedistis mihi cibum, sitiui, & dedistis mihi potum, &c. Qui vero reprobi sunt, mala quæ hic faciunt reportabunt & ipsi. Ite, inquiet maledicti in ignem æternū, qui paratus est diabolo & angelis eius. Esuriui enim & nō dedistis mihi cibum, &c. Sic reportabunt electi ac fideles fidei suæ fructus, reprobi verò perfidiæ suæ mercedem. Sic synceri Christi ministri, bonum reportabūt ex eo qd' fideles in opere domini fuerunt, audientqueilud: Euge serue bone & fidelis intra in gaudiū domini tui. Sic pseudapostoli, operarij iniquitatis, malū reportabunt ex eo quòd perfidi fuerunt in opere domini, audientq; illud: Discedite à me operarij iniqui. Non noui vos. Hæc futuri iudicij norma nihil incommodauit cœlesti gratiæ, qua per sanguinem Christi seruantur electi & veri fideles. Neq; enim remissio illa peccatorum, quæ per Euangelium Dei prędicatur, usq; ad tempus iudicij tantū durat, sed firma permanet in sempiternum.
units.tr: Whatever sins they commit from time to time are forgiven them here through the blood and propitiation of Christ (1 John 1 and 2). The good works they do will be repaid, Christ proclaiming, "Come, you blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink," and so on. But the reprobate will also receive back the evils they do here. "Depart," he will say, "you accursed, into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you gave me no food," and so on. Thus the elect and faithful will receive back the fruits of their faith, but the reprobate the wages of their faithlessness. So the sincere ministers of Christ will receive back good, because they were faithful in the work of the Lord, and will hear that word: "Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your lord." So the false apostles, workers of iniquity, will receive back evil, because they were faithless in the work of the Lord, and will hear: "Depart from me, you workers of iniquity; I never knew you." This rule of the future judgment does no harm to the heavenly grace by which the elect and true believers are preserved through the blood of Christ. For that forgiveness of sins, which is proclaimed through the Gospel of God, does not last only until the time of judgment, but remains firm for ever.

units.la: QVÆ gesta sunt per corpus, inquit, iuxta id quod fecit siue bonum siue malum. Quid est quod dicit: quæ sunt per corpus, iuxta id qd' fecit? An in die iudicij ea tantum reportabimus
units.tr: "Whatever has been done through the body," he says, "according to what one has done, whether good or evil." What does he mean by saying "whatever has been done through the body, according to what one has done"? Shall we on the day of judgement receive back only those things

units.la: quæ corpore ac manibus gessimus, opera cras sa & actu transeuntia, sic ut nulla habeatur ra-tio spiritualiū: qualia sunt fides, incredulitas, spes & desperatio, charitas & odium, patientia & impatientia, misericordia & immisericordia, humilitas & superbia, & quæ alia sunt huius-modi, unde vel boni vel mali censemur. Si hęc quoq; in iudicium venient, quid est quod di-cit: Quæ iusta sunt per corpus, iuxta quod fe-cit. Respondeo: Non diuidit Apostolus inter opera corporis, & affectus cordis: Illud enim τὰ διὰ τοῦ σώματος, idē ipsi hoc loco est, quod τὰ ἐν τῷ σώματι, i. quæ in corpore gesta sunt.
