Intelli-git enim omnia ea quę facimus in hac uita, dū in corpore hoc habitamus: Et verbū πράξω, quę pertinet ad affectus cordis atq; ad opera cor-poris: significat aliquid agere, siue id corde fiat, siue externo aliquo corporis organo.
units.tr: which we have done with the body and hands, works that pass away in deed and action, so that no account is taken of spiritual things: such as faith and unbelief, hope and despair, love and hatred, patience and impatience, mercy and unmercifulness, humility and pride, and other things of this kind, by which we are reckoned either good or evil? If these also come into judgement, what does he mean by saying, "whatever is done through the body, according to what one has done"? I answer: the Apostle does not divide between works of the body and affections of the heart. For the phrase [τὰ διὰ τοῦ σώματος] here means the same as [τὰ ἐν τῷ σώματι], that is, things done in the body. For he understands all the things we do in this life, while we dwell in this body. And the verb [πράσσω], which pertains both to affections of the heart and to works of the body, signifies to do something, whether this is done in the heart or by some outward organ of the body.

units.la: IVXTA id quod fecit, inquit, siue bonum, siue malum.) Non dicit: Vt reportet unusquis-que quod fecit, sed iuxta id quod fecit: id est, secundum qualitatem eorum quæ fecit. Non loquitur autem de qualitate operū nostrorū, qua digna vel indigna in se censeantur (alio-qui calix aquæ frigidę quanti erit faciendus?) sed qua bona bona sunt, mala mala. Vnde & ad-dit: Siue bonum, siue malū. Si boni quid sece-ris, reportabis illius fructū: eumq; nō sic ad me suratū, vt præcise dignitati boni operis re-pō-deat, sed secundum magnificentiam diuinę ma-iestatis, quæ minuta bona liberalissimè remu-nerat: si male egeris, recipies secundum men-suram iusticiæ ac iusti iudicij.
units.tr: "According to what he has done," he says, "whether good or evil." He does not say, "that each one may receive what he has done," but "according to what he has done," that is, according to the quality of the things he has done. He does not speak of the quality of our works by which they are judged worthy or unworthy in themselves (otherwise, how much would a cup of cold water be worth?), but of the quality by which good things are good and bad things bad. Hence he adds: "whether good or evil." If you have done something good, you will receive its fruit, and this will not be reckoned to me in such a way that it answers precisely to the worth of the good work, but according to the greatness of the divine majesty, which most generously rewards even small good deeds. If you have acted badly, you will receive according to the measure of justice and of the just judgment.

units.la: Sciētes igitur, terrore illum Domini suademus hominib. Deo uero manife-sti sumus. Spero autē nos & in cōscien-tijs uestris manifestos esse. Non enim i-terū commēdamus nosipsos uobis: sed occasionem damus uobis gloriandi de nobis, ut aliquid habeatis aduersus eos qui in facie gloriantur, & non in corde.
units.tr: Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men; but we are made manifest to God, and I hope that we are also made manifest in your consciences. For we do not commend ourselves to you again, but give you occasion to glory on our behalf, so that you may have something to answer those who glory in appearance and not in heart.

units.la: In præcedentibus significauit, quo sibi tri-bunalis Christi respectus seruiat: ad hoc vide-licet, vt in omnibus illi placere contendat. Iam de eo subijcit, quid hinc colligat proponendū & suadendum alijs. Sciētes igitur, inquit, ter-rorem illum Domini suademus hominibus. Sunt hæc verba amphibolicè posita. Possunt enim bifariam accipi. Primo sic: Sciētes igitur ista, timorem Domini suademus homi-nibus: hoc est, quoniam futurum scimus ut manifestari nos oporteat omnes coram tribu-nali Christi, vt reportet unusquisq; quæ gesta sunt per corpus, iuxta id quod gessit, siue bo-num siue malum, suademus hominibus docē-do, admonendo, hortando, instádo & urgēdo, ut timeant Dominum, illumq; in omnibus ob-seruent. Deinde ad hunc modum: Sciētes igitur timorem hunc Domini: hoc est: scientes igitur, q; sit timēdus Dominus, futurus omniū iudex, suademus hominibus, vt timentes illū
units.tr: In what precedes he has shown how the judgment seat of Christ serves as a reason for him to strive to please Christ in all things. Now he goes on to say what he infers from this, which must be set forth and urged on others. "Knowing therefore," he says, "the terror of the Lord, we persuade men." These words are ambiguous, for they can be taken in two ways. First, thus: knowing these things, we persuade men of the fear of the Lord; that is, since we know that we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what he has done through the body, whether good or evil, we persuade men by teaching, admonishing, exhorting, pressing and urging them to fear the Lord and to observe him in all things. Second, in this way: knowing this fear of the Lord, that is, knowing that the Lord, the future judge of all, is to be feared, we persuade men

units.la: pietati studeant. Vtrobiq; subintelligendum est aliquid. In priore sensu, illud: Sciētes igitur absoluēdum uidetur, si addas, ista. In posterio-re, illud, suademus hominibus, desiderare vi-detur, ut Dominum timeant & obseruent. Ni-hil est periculi; priorem ne uel posteriore am-plectamur. Prior tamen mihi magis arridet.
units.tr: to devote themselves to godliness, fearing him. In either sense something must be understood. In the first sense, the words "knowing therefore" seem to require something to complete them, such as "these things." In the second, the words "we persuade men" seem to want something like "that they may fear and observe the Lord." There is no danger in embracing either the former or the latter. Yet the former pleases me more.

units.la: SCIENTES igitur, timorem Domini sua-demus hominibus, inquit.) Obserua quod di-cit: Sciētes suademus. Hoc genus suadendi, quod ex certa scientia promanat, omnium so-let esse urgentissimum ac fortissimum. Non na- scitur ex supremis labris, non sumitur ex alio-rum scriptis, sed ex uiuo sensu veritatis, in quo nullus est dubitationi locus. Tales suasores cō-ueniet esse veros Christi ministros.
units.tr: "Knowing therefore the fear of the Lord, we persuade men," he says. Observe what he says: "knowing, we persuade." This kind of persuading, which springs from certain knowledge, is usually the most urgent and most forceful of all. It does not arise from superficial lips, nor is it taken from the writings of others, but from the living sense of the truth, in which there is no room for doubt. Such persuaders ought to be true ministers of Christ.

units.la: Vnde autem hæc erat illi sciētia, cū de re lo-quatur in fine demū mūdi futura, ad cuius cer-titudinem nulla humani ingenij ratio pertin-git: Scientiā pro fidei certitudine posuit. Qd certo futurum credebat, id se scire dicit. Sed hac de re diximus & antea.
units.tr: But whence came this knowledge to him, when he speaks of things that lie in the final end of the world, and to whose certainty no power of human intellect extends? He puts knowledge for the certainty of faith. What he believed would surely come to pass, he says he knows. But we have spoken of this matter before as well.

units.la: TIMOREM Domini suademus hominib. inquit.) Quid est quod non dicit: Suademus uobis, aut ecclesijs, uel fidelibus, sed homini-bus: Loquitur non de fidelibus tātum, sed de omnibus hominibus in genere, præsertim nō-dum credentibus in Christum. Habebat hoc in more, ut imprimis de Christo concionibus inculcaret hominibus futurum illud iudiciū, quo iudicaturus est dominus viuos & mor-tuos, quo animos eorum timore Domini per-celleret. Huius rei exépla videmus Actor. 17. & 24. Decimoseptimo differens ad Athenienses inter cætera dicit: Et tempora quidem huius ignorantiæ cum hactenus dissimularit Deus, nunc annunciat hominibus, vt omnes vbique resipiscant, eo quod statuit diem in quo iudi-caturus est orbe terrarum cū iusticia, per eum virum, per quem decreuit fide præstita omni-bus, cum excitarit illum ex mortuis. Vicesimo quarto capite sic legimus: Post aliquot autem dies cum adueniesset Felix cum Drufilla uxore sua, quæ erat Iudæa, accersiuit Paulum, & au-diuit ab eo fidem quæ est in Christum. Dispu-tante autem illo de iusticia & temperantia, & de iudicio futuro, tremefactus Felix respodit, In præsentia abi, &c. His exemplis satis mani-festē uidemus, quomodo hominibus Aposto-lus timorem Domini suasurus futurū iudiciū inculcarit. Et ad Ebr. 6. inter prima Christianę doctrinæ elementa recensetur & iudicium æ-ternū. Et Petrus in Act. cap. 10. hoc Domini post resurrectionem apostolis suis præcepisse dicit, ut prædicarent populo, ac testificaretur, quod ipse sit constitutus à Deo iudex viuorū ac mortuorum. Et hoc dubio procul diligen-tissimè perfecerunt. Hoc intelligēs Paulus di-cit: Scientes igitur oportere nos omnes mani-festari coram tribunali Christi, timore Domi-ni suademus hominibus. Vtinam autem per-suaderi nobis possit timor hic Domini, qui iá à maioribus nostris multis seculis fidē in Chri-stum stùm profitemur,uidemus reipsa paucissimos esse,qui uera religione Dominum timeant.
units.tr: "We persuade men," he says, "of the fear of the Lord." Why does he not say, "We persuade you, or the churches, or the faithful," but "men"? He speaks not only of the faithful but of all men in general, especially those not yet believing in Christ. It was his custom, above all in sermons about Christ, to impress upon men that future judgment in which the Lord is to judge the living and the dead, so that by the fear of the Lord he might pierce their minds. We see examples of this in Acts 17 and 24. In chapter 17, speaking to the Athenians, among other things he says: "The times of this ignorance God has indeed overlooked until now, but now he declares to men that all everywhere should repent, because he has appointed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, by that man whom he has appointed, having given assurance to all by raising him from the dead." In chapter 24 we read thus: "But after some days, when Felix came with Drusilla his wife, who was a Jewess, he sent for Paul and heard him concerning faith in Christ. But as he reasoned about righteousness and temperance and the judgment to come, Felix trembled and answered, 'Go your way for now,' etc." From these examples we see plainly how the Apostle, to persuade men of the fear of the Lord, impressed upon them the future judgment. And in Hebrews 6, eternal judgment is counted among the first elements of Christian doctrine. And Peter in Acts 10 says that the Lord after his resurrection commanded his apostles to preach to the people and to testify that he is appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead. And without doubt they carried this out most diligently. Understanding this, Paul says: "Knowing therefore that we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, we persuade men by the fear of the Lord." Would that this fear of the Lord could be persuaded upon us, for we who now for many centuries have professed faith in Christ, as handed down by our forefathers, see in fact very few who fear the Lord with true religion.

units.la: DEO uerò manifesti sumus, inquit, spero autē nos & in conscientijs uestris manifestos esse.) Habet ista occupationem. Dicturi erant pseudapostoli: Hic homo tribuit sibiipse plurimum. Occupat dicens: Suademus quę recta sunt hominibus: nos uerò quod attinet, Deo manifesti sumus, qui corda nouit omnium. Et quod uitam & doctrinam nostrā attinet, uobis quoque non sumus incogniti. Nam conscientijs uestris manifestos nos esse spero.
units.tr: "But we are made manifest to God," he says, "and I hope that we are also made manifest in your consciences." This verse has a purpose. The false apostles were going to say: "This man attributes a great deal to himself." He anticipates them, saying: "We persuade men of what is right; but as for us, we are made manifest to God, who knows the hearts of all. And as to our life and teaching, we are not unknown to you either. For I hope that we are made manifest to your consciences."

units.la: Obseruent, qui sic uitam suam instituunt in hoc sæculo, ut profundent sua cósilia abscondantq; ac dicant, Quis uidet nos? Stultissimū plane & impium est quod faciūt. Impiū, quòd non cogitat manifestos esse se Deo. Huiusmodi impietatē perstringit Propheta Psal. 94. ubi sic legimus: Et dicūt, non uidet Dominus, & non intelligit Deus Iacob. Intelligite insipientes in populo, & stulti quando eritis prudentes? An qui plantat aurem, non audit? qui formát oculū, non uidet? An qui castigat gentes, non redarguet? qui docet hominem scientiam. Dominus nouit cogitationes hominum quod uanæ sunt. Hæc ibi. Impietas ista & Esaię 29 reprehenditur. Stultissimum est, quòd à conscientijs hominū quoq; abscondi se posse putant, cum quib. uiuūt & agunt. Etenim etsi ad tempus fallunt, simulatio tamen omnis sic est comparata, ut non diu decipiat. Addo, manifestum etiam maliciæ argumentū esse in eo, qd conscientias hominum fallere satagunt. Si uiri boni essent, & rectè agerent omnia, dicerent utiq; & ipsi cum Paulo, Speramus nos esse in conscientijs hominū manifestos. In summa, admonet nos hic locus, fieri nō posse quin manifesti fiamus. Primùm enim manifesti sumus Deo semper, & in omnibus: deinde efficere non poterimus quin & hominibus, & si non omnibus, nonnullis tamen, & forsan ijs quib. omnium minimè uolumus, manifesti fiamus in hoc mundo: tertiò tandem in die iudicij manifestabimur omnibus & angelis & hominibus, ubi uel confusionem vel laudem reportabimus, & maximam, & sempiternam. Qui hæc considerat, facilè intelligit q̄ deceat nos sic agere in omnibus, ut & Dei & hominum cō scientias ferre possimus.
units.tr: Let those who order their lives in this world so as to hide their counsels deeply and say, "Who sees us?" consider this. What they do is utterly foolish and impious. It is impious, because they do not think that they are made manifest to God. The prophet, in Psalm 94, condemns this impiety, where we read thus: "And they say, the Lord does not see, neither does the God of Jacob understand. Understand, you foolish among the people, and you fools, when will you be wise? He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? He who formed the eye, shall he not see? He who chastises the nations, shall he not rebuke? He who teaches man knowledge. The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain." So far the psalm. This same impiety is rebuked also in Isaiah 29. It is foolish of men to think that they can hide themselves even from the consciences of those with whom they live and act. For even if they deceive for a time, all pretence is so constituted that it does not deceive for long. I add that it is also a clear sign of malice that they strive to deceive the consciences of men. If they were good men and acted rightly in everything, they would surely say with Paul also: "We hope that we are made manifest to the consciences of men." In sum, this passage admonishes us that it is impossible for us not to be made manifest. For first, we are always and in all things manifest to God; second, we cannot prevent ourselves from being made manifest in this world to men, if not to all, yet to some, and perhaps to those whom we least wish; third, at last, on the day of judgment we shall be made manifest to all, both angels and men, where we shall receive either confusion or praise, and very great and everlasting praise. He who considers these things easily understands how fitting it is for us to act in all things so that we can bear the scrutiny of the consciences both of God and of men.

units.la: NON enim iterū, inquit, nosipsos commendamus uobis.) Amouet suspicionem, qua uideri poterat, quòd se iterū cōmendet Corinthijs. Sensus est, quòd ista dico, non in hoc dico, ut me vobis commendem. Spero enim abundè nos manifestos esse vestris cōscientijs. Hic ordo eorū quæ dicit, inuersus est, secundū quem dicendum erat: Non autem iterū nosipsos cōmendamus uobis. Spero enim nos & in conscientijs uestris esse manifestos.
units.tr: "For we do not again commend ourselves to you." He removes a suspicion that might arise, namely that he is again commending himself to the Corinthians. The sense is: I say these things not to commend myself to you. For I hope that we are fully manifest to your consciences. The order of what he says is inverted; the order in which it ought to have been said is: "And we do not again commend ourselves to you. For I hope that we are also manifest in your consciences."

units.la: SED occasionem damus uobis, inquit, gloriandi de nobis.) Exponit quorsum præcedentia dixerit, quæ ad id dixisse uideri poterat, ut se Corinthijs commendaret. Non ut me uobis commendem hæc dico, inquit, sed ut occasionem vobis præbeam gloriandi de me: hoc est, officium & opus Apostolatus mei contra pseu dapostolos defendendi, dum me uestrum esse Apostolum & agnoscitis & gloriamini. Hoc sentiens addit:
units.tr: "But we give you occasion," he says, "to glory about us." He explains the purpose of what he has said, which might seem to have been said in order to commend himself to the Corinthians. He says: I say these things not so that I may commend myself to you, but so that I may give you occasion to glory about me; that is, to defend the office and work of my apostleship against the false apostles, since you both acknowledge and boast that I am your apostle. Thinking this, he adds:

units.la: VT aliquid habeatis aduersus eos, qui in facie gloriantur, & non in corde.) Perstringit pseudapostolos qui in faciem de se plura iactā bant, quum cordib. essent ab eis procul, de quibus gloriabātur. Gloriari in facie, & nō in corde, est ea coram hominib. verbis iactare, quæ conscientia ipsa agnoscere non potest. Verùm istorum iactantiam ipse infrà cap. 10. 11. & 12. retundet.
units.tr: "So that you may have something against those who glory in appearance, and not in heart." He censures the false apostles, who boasted much of themselves to their faces, while they were far from the hearts of those about whom they boasted. To glory in appearance and not in heart is to boast with words before men of things which the conscience itself cannot acknowledge. Yet he himself will refute their boasting later, in chapters 10, 11 and 12.

units.la: Vide modestiam Apostoli. Corinthijs sic erat manifestus, ut abundè ex ijs quæ certò cognouerant, ad hoc essent instrucţi, ut pseudapostolorum glorias refringerent, & ipsius existimationem tuerentur. Verùm dissimulans hoc cùm posset eos reprehendere, dicit se occasionem illis dare gloriandi de se, & subministrare aliquid aduersus improbos iactatores, quasi minus ad id sufficienter iam antea essent instructi, & non vltrò absq; monitu in hoc incumbendū ipsis fuerit. Sic parcebat illis, cùm merito eos posset confusione suffundere, & asperiter reprehendere.
units.tr: Note the modesty of the Apostle. He was so well known to the Corinthians that, from what they had certainly learned, they were sufficiently equipped to refute the glories of the false apostles and to defend his reputation. But although he could have rebuked them, he dissimulates this and says that he gives them occasion to glory about him, and supplies them with something against the wicked boasters, as if they were not sufficiently prepared for this beforehand, and as if they had not had to apply themselves to it of their own accord, without a reminder. In this way he spares them, although he could justly have overwhelmed them with shame and rebuked them sharply.

units.la: Nam siue insanimus, Deo insanimus, siue sani sumus, uobis sani sumus. Charitas enim Christi constringit nos, iudicātes illud, quòd si unus pro omnib. mortuus fuit, ergo oēs mortui fuerūt: & pro omnib. mortuus est, ut qui uiuunt post hac, non sibi uiuant, sed ei qui pro ipsis mortuus est & resurrexit. Itaq; nos post hac neminem nouimus secundum carnem. Sí uerò & Christum cognouimus secundum carnem, nunc tamē non amplius nouimus. Proinde si quis est in Christo, noua creatura est. Vetera præterierunt, ecce noua facta sunt omnia.
units.tr: "For whether we are beside ourselves, we are beside ourselves for God; or whether we are sober, we are sober for you. For the love of Christ constrains us, judging this, that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live henceforth should not live to themselves, but to him who died for them and rose again. Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh. And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him so. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old things have passed away, behold, all things have become new."

units.la: Non insaniebat Paulus, sed nunquam non sobria ac sana loquebatur. Verùm quoniam subinde sublimiùs philosophabatur, quàm uc à quibusl bet posset capi, hoc illi à maleuolis pro insania imputabatur. Cùm ergo fore præuideret, ut quæ hoc capite de terreno ac cœlesti domicilio disputauerat, insaniæ à pseudapostolis deputarētur, p occupatione ista subiecit, dicens: Nam siue insanimus, Deo insanimus, siue sani sumus, uobis sani sumus. Quasi dicat: Magistris uestris iam insanire, ubi sublimiora, iam sobriè loqui, ubi humiliora proferro, uideor. Verùm ubi sublimiora loquor, non insania, sed spiritussanći instinctu loquor: atque ita Deo insanio, ubi humiliora profero, atque tum demum sobrius esse videor, in uestram gratiam sic loquor: atque ita uobis sum sobrius ac sanus. Significat his uerbis Apostolus, esse sibi duplicē loquēdi respectū. Vnū, quo Deū ipsum, alterū, quo ecclesiā Dei respiciat. Sic nihil reseruat sibijpsi, sed totū sese Deo & ecclesiæ eius consecrat, quandoquidē ad gemi num hunc scopum dirigit omnia.
units.tr: Paul was not insane, but he always spoke soberly and wisely. But since he sometimes philosophised more sublimely than could be grasped by some, this was imputed to him as madness by ill-wishers. Therefore, since he foresaw that what he had argued in this chapter about the earthly and the heavenly dwelling would be counted as madness by the false apostles, he added this in anticipation, saying: "For whether we are beside ourselves, we are beside ourselves for God; or whether we are sober, we are sober for you." As if he said: Now, when I speak more sublimely, I seem to your teachers to be mad; when I bring forth humbler things, I seem to speak soberly. But when I speak in lofty terms, I am not mad, but speak by the impulse of the Holy Spirit; and so I am beside myself for God. When I bring forth humbler things, and then I seem at last to be sober, I speak thus for your benefit; and so I am sober and sane for you. By these words the Apostle signifies that he has a twofold respect in speaking: one by which he looks to God himself, the other by which he looks to the Church of God. Thus he reserves nothing for himself, but consecrates himself wholly to God and his Church, since he directs everything to this double purpose.

units.la: CHARITAS enim Christi constringit nos, inquit.) Vnde frequenter cohibeatur, ne sublimiora, sed submissiora proferat, exponit, dicens: Charitas enim Christi constringit nos. Loquitur autem de charitate Christi, qua ille nos dilexit, ac semetipsum pro omnib⁹ dedit, sicuti patet ex mox sequentibus. Hac se sic constringi dicit, vt omnia ad captum ecclesiæ attemperet. Huic dari vult sicuti sobrie loqui videatur. Sunt qui per charitatem Christi intelligunt eam, qua Apostolus Corinthios propter Christum diligebat. Chrysostomus tamen nobiscum sentit. Verbum συνέχει recte verteris, cohibet. Significat enim cohiberi se per charitatem Christi, ne sublimius pro dignitate cœlestis doctrinę euehatur, sed ad captum se imperitorum ac rudiū demittat. Magistri nostri sęcularem philosophiam magis quàm Christi ueritatem ipirates, si aliquo charitatis affectu præditi essent, cohiberentur & ipsi, ne gloriæ suæ potius rhetoricando ad populum, quàm saluti auditorum consulerent.
units.tr: "For the love of Christ constrains us," he says. He explains why he is often restrained, so that he does not utter lofty things but humbler ones, saying: "For the love of Christ constrains us." He speaks of the love of Christ, by which he loved us and gave himself for all, as is clear from what follows. He says that he is so constrained by this, that he adapts everything to the understanding of the Church. He wishes this to be given to him, so that he may seem to speak soberly. There are those who understand by the love of Christ that love with which the Apostle loved the Corinthians for Christ's sake. Chrysostom, however, agrees with us. The verb συνέχει [sunechei] is rightly rendered "restrains" (cohibet). For it signifies that he is restrained by the love of Christ, so that he is not carried aloft beyond the dignity of heavenly doctrine, but lowers himself to the understanding of the unlearned and rude. Our teachers, who pursue secular philosophy more than the truth of Christ, if they were endowed with some affection of love, would also be restrained, so that they would not seek their own glory by rhetoric before the people, rather than the salvation of the hearers.

units.la: IVDICANTES illud, inquit, quòd si vnus pro omnibus mortuus fuit, ergo omnes mortui fuerunt.) Exponit insignem Christi charitatem, & quid ipse in illa consideret exprimit. Charitas Christi est, quòd pro omnibus vnus ipse mori dignatus est. Maiorem vtique charitatem nemo habet, quàm vt animam suam ponat pro amicis suis. Christus verò non pro amicis tantum, sed & inimicis, nō pro quibusdam tantum, sed pro omnibus mortuus est. Hæc est immensa diuinæ dilectionis amplitudo. Ex hac vide quid colligat Apostolus. Si vnus, inquit, pro omnibus mortuus fuit, ergo omnes mortui fuerunt. Argumentum est à fine mortis Christi. Mortuus est pro nobis, vt ui tæ restitueremur. Eramus igitur mortui. Et sic mortuus est pro omnibus. Erant ergo omnes mortui. Sic Apostolus Ephes.2. dicit: Et vos cum essetis mortui delictis ac peccatis. Dicit itaq;: Charitas Christi cohibet & cogit nos, vt rationem habeamus salutis vestræ. Sic enim de illa iudicamus. Christus unus mortuus est pro omnib. Ergo erant omnes mortui: & ipse tanti fecit mortuos, vt semetipsum pro illis daret, quò vitæ restituerentur. Quantò magis conuenit, vt ipse quoq; omnem operam pro illis impendam, pro quibus ille mori dignatus est: & sic illis sermonem vitæ dispensem, vt capere illū possint. Hic est præsentis loci sensus.
units.tr: "Judging this," he says, "that if one died for all, then all died." He sets out the remarkable love of Christ, and expresses what he himself considers in it. The love of Christ is that he deigned to die alone for all. For no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends. But Christ died not only for friends, but also for enemies; not only for some, but for all. This is the immense breadth of divine love. From this, see what the Apostle concludes. "If one," he says, "died for all, then all died." The argument is drawn from the end of Christ's death. He died for us, so that we might be restored to life. We were therefore dead. And so he died for all. Therefore all were dead. So the Apostle says in Ephesians 2: "And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins." He says, therefore: The love of Christ restrains and compels us to take account of your salvation. For thus we judge concerning it: Christ alone died for all. Therefore all were dead; and he esteemed them so dead that he gave himself for them, so that they might be restored to life. How much more fitting is it that I too should expend all my effort for those for whom he deigned to die, and that I should dispense the word of life to them, so that they may be able to grasp it. This is the sense of the present passage.

units.la: Sunt tamē, qui illud, ergo omnes ἀπέθανον cū vulgata æditione legant, ergo omnes mortui sunt: & de morte exponant non peccati, à qua nos Christus morte sua liberare voluit, sed car nalium nostrorum affectuum, & ueteris in nobis Adæ, ad quam nos Apostolica doctrina ar-
units.tr: There are, however, those who read, with the Vulgate edition, "therefore all ἀπέθανον [apethanon]," that is, "therefore all are dead," and who explain the death not as death of sin, from which Christ wished to free us by his death, but as death of our carnal affections and of the old Adam in us, to which the apostolic teaching invites us by the argument

units.la: gumento mortis Christi inuitat. Sanè non cōsequitur, Christus mortuus est pro omnibus, ergo omnes mortui sunt sibijpsis, vt Christo viuant: consequitur autem illud: Christus vnus mortuus est pro omnibus, ergo mortui erant omnes, in peccatis videlicet: quemadmodum paulo ante ex epistola ad Ephesios admonuimus. Quare lectio vulgata, ergo omnes mortui sunt, non exprimit mentem Apostoli, nec satisfacit illius argumento. Rectius igitur est, vt cum Erasmo legamus: Ergo omnes mortui fuerunt.
units.tr: of Christ's death. Certainly it does not follow that "Christ died for all, therefore all are dead to themselves, that they may live to Christ"; what follows is rather this: "Christ alone died for all, therefore all were dead," namely in sins, as we noted a little earlier from the epistle to the Ephesians. Therefore the Vulgate reading, "therefore all are dead," does not express the mind of the Apostle, nor does it satisfy his argument. It is more correct, then, to read with Erasmus: "Therefore all were dead."

units.la: ET ,p omnib. mortuus est, inqt, vt qui viuūt posthac, non sibi viuāt, sed ei qui pro ipsis mortuus est & resurrexit.) Collimat ad parænesim, quâ subijciet. Exponit aūt finem mortis Christi. Hūc esse dicit, vt qui per illā sunt ab exitio mortis liberati ac viuificati, adeoq; iam viuūt, viuant in posterū non sibi, sed ei qui pro ipsis mortuus est & resurrexit.
units.tr: "And he died for all," he says, "so that those who live henceforth should not live to themselves, but to him who died for them and rose again." He aims at the exhortation which he will subjoin. He explains the end of Christ's death. He says this is its purpose: that those who have been set free by it from the ruin of death and made alive, and who now live, should henceforth live not to themselves, but to him who died for them and rose again.

units.la: ET pro omnibus mortuus est, inquit,) Repetit hanc particulam, vt vtilitatem illius ac finem illi annectat. In præcedenti necessitatem mortis Christi, quæ ex eo erat quòd mortui erant omnes, nec aliunde quàm ipsi morte viuificari poterant: in præsenti finē illius, ad quē luctandū nobis sit exprimit. Cauendum autem est, ne sic Christū pro omnibus mortuum esse sentiamus, vt mortis ipsius efficacia communiter peruenerit ad omnes. Illa siquidem non capitur à reprobis, incredulis, & impœnitentib. licet in se sufficiens sit pro vniuerso genere humano redimendo. Proponitur salus quæ ex illa est omnibus, & sufficit omnibus, modò capiatur ab omnib. Vniuersum mundum sic dilexit Deus, vt filium suum vnigenitum dederit, vt omnis qui credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Iohan.3. Sic mortuus est ille pro omnibus (quia mortui erant omnes) vt omnis credens in ipsum viuificetur ac seruetur.
units.tr: "And he died for all," he says. He repeats this phrase to join to it its usefulness and purpose. In the preceding verse he set out the necessity of Christ's death, which arose from the fact that all were dead, and that they could be made alive in no other way than by death itself. Here he sets out the end and goal of that death, which we ought to strive toward. We must take care, however, not to think that Christ died for all in such a way that the efficacy of his death reaches all alike. For it is not received by the reprobate, the unbelieving and the impenitent, although in itself it is sufficient to redeem the whole human race. The salvation that comes from it is offered to all, and it is sufficient for all, provided it is received by all. "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life" (John 3). So he died for all (because all were dead) so that everyone who believes in him might be made alive and kept safe.

units.la: VT qui viuūt, inquit.) Intellige, àmorte peccati per morte ipsius liberati ac viuificati. Vt qui viuunt, id est, qui beneficiū vitæ, quod ex morte ipsius est, fide in ipsum sunt consequuti. Non dicit, vt omnes post hac ei viuant, qui ipsis mortuus est: neq; enim fieri hoc potest, nisi ab illis qui morte ipsius sunt viuificati, sed, vt qui viuunt. In illis locū habet finis mortis Christi, uita uidelicet Christo consecrata. Qd igitur tam paucos Christianam uitam viuere uidemus, ex eo est vtiq;, quòd pauci sunt qui ex morte Christi viuant. Viuunt enim ex eo tionnisi veri fideles.
units.tr: "So that those who live," he says. Understand: those who have been freed and made alive from the death of sin through his death. "So that those who live," that is, those who have obtained by faith in him the benefit of life that comes from his death. He does not say that all should live afterwards for him who died for them, for this cannot happen except in those who have been made alive by his death; he says "those who live." In them the purpose of Christ's death takes effect, namely, that life is consecrated to Christ. So if we see so few living a Christian life, this is certainly because few live by the death of Christ. For only true believers live by it.

units.la: POST hac non sibi viuant, inquit.) Græcè est μηκέτι ἑαυτῶς ζῶσιν, id est, non amplius sibijpsis viuát. Sic igitur extra Christū mortui fuerunt, & sunt omnes, ut sibijpsis viuerent ac viuant. Viuere autem sibijpsi, est omnia facere secundum affectus carnis, nec vllam habere uel numinis uel iusticiæ rationē, & sibijpsi, in summa, totum addictum esse in omnibus. Hoc genus uitæ, præterquam quòd omnis generis vicijs peccatis ac sceleribus scatet, in se quoque abominabile est, & à vita Dei omnium alienissimum, ac prorsus diabolicum. Deus ipse non sibijpsi, sed omnibus quæ condidit uiuit. Non uiuunt sibijpsis cœlestes spiritus, sed uiuunt Deo ac nobis. Omnis reliqua creatura quicquid est nostro bono est, nobisque seruit. Solus Satan & homo hoc genus vitæ apprehenderunt, quo nec Deo, nec aliis creaturis, sed sibijpsis uiuant. Merito igitur ac salubri consilio requiritur ab illis, q morte Christi à morte peccati liberati sunt ac uiuificati, ut nō amplius sibijpsis uiuant. Abundè magna est gratia, qua pristinæ uitæ malicia remittitur, & exitium illius aufertur, ut merito requiratur ut redemptori viuentes posthac ad idem genus vitę nō redeamus.
units.tr: "They should no longer live for themselves," he says. The Greek is μηκέτι ἑαυτῶς ζῶσιν [mēketi heautois zōsin], that is, "no longer should they live for themselves." So all were dead, and are, outside Christ, so that they live and have lived for themselves. To live for oneself is to do everything according to the desires of the flesh, to have no regard for either God's will or righteousness, and, in short, to be wholly given over to oneself in all things. This kind of life, besides being full of every sort of vice, sin and wickedness, is in itself abominable and utterly alien to the life of God, and altogether devilish. God himself does not live for himself, but for all the things he has made. The heavenly spirits do not live for themselves, but live for God and for us. Every other creature, whatever it is, is for our good and serves us. Only Satan and man have taken hold of this kind of life, by which they live neither for God nor for other creatures, but for themselves. Rightly, therefore, and with wholesome purpose, it is required of those who have been freed and made alive from the death of sin through Christ's death that they no longer live for themselves. Great indeed is the grace by which the wickedness of our former life is forgiven and its ruin taken away, so that it is rightly required that, living now for our Redeemer, we do not return to the same kind of life.

units.la: SED ei, inquit, qui pro ipsis mortuus fuit & resurrexit.) Poterat simpliciter dicere, ut nō amplius sibijpsis uiuant, sed ipsi. Verùm ut æquitatem rei huius exprimat, adiecit, Qui ꝑ ipsis mortuus fuit & resurrexit. In morte siquidem redemptionis est præcium: in resurrectio ne uero, excitatio, uita, & iustificatio. Moriendo satisfecit pro peccatis nostris, resurgendo vitæ nos restituit, & iustificauit. Qui traditus est, inquit Rom.4. propter peccata nostra, & resurrexit propter iustificationem nostri. Quid igitur æquius censeri poterit, quàm ut saluberiter uiuamus ei, qui, quo salui simus, mori pro nobis uoluit?
units.tr: "But for him," he says, "who died for them and rose again." He could have simply said, "that they should no longer live for themselves, but for them." But to express the justice of this matter, he added: "who died for them and rose again." In his death there is the price of redemption; in his resurrection, indeed, there is awakening, life and justification. By dying he made satisfaction for our sins; by rising again he restored us to life and justified us. "He was delivered," he says in Romans 4, "for our sins, and rose again for our justification." What then could seem more just than that we should live usefully for him who was willing to die for us so that we might be saved?

units.la: Quid est autem uiuere Christo? Est ab illo pendere in omnibus: est omnia totius vitæ studia spiritui illius ac voluntati consecrare: est iuri ac potestati illius sese subdere in omnibus: est sic uiuere in summa, ut nec ipse exprimas aliud uiuendo, quàm Christi spiritum, nec aliud ex te sentiat, quibuscum uiuis, quà Christum. At hoc vitæ genus plane ex diametro pugnat cum eo, quo nobisipsis uiuimus. Quare ut hoc in nobis locum habere possit, requiritur ut ad illud non reuertamur amplius. Nequit enim fieri ut Christo uiuamus, donec nobisipsis uiuere pergimus. Ideo rectè non simpliciter dixit, Vt qui uiuunt, ei uiuat, qui pro ipsis est mortuus, sed interposuit, Non amplius sibijpsis uiuant: & ne hoc sufficere uideatur, adiecit: Sed ei qui pro ipsis mortuus fuit, & resurrexit.
units.tr: But what does it mean to live to Christ? It means to depend on him in all things; it means to consecrate all the pursuits of our whole life to his Spirit and will; it means to submit ourselves to his right and power in all things; it means, in short, so to live that you express nothing else in your living than the Spirit of Christ, and that those with whom you live perceive nothing in you but Christ. But this kind of life fights directly against that in which we live for ourselves. Therefore, if this kind of life is to have a place in us, it is required that we never return to the other. For it cannot happen that we live to Christ while we continue to live for ourselves. So he rightly did not simply say, "that those who live should live for him who died for them," but he inserted, "should no longer live for themselves"; and lest this seem sufficient, he added: "but for him who died for them and rose again."

units.la: ITAQVE nos posthac neminè nouimus secundū carnem, inquit.) Locus hic admodū obscurus est. Recitabo aliorum expositiones, deinde & meam adijciam.
units.tr: "AND so from now on we know no one according to the flesh," he says. This place is very obscure. I shall recite the explanations of others, and then add my own.

units.la: 1 Chrysostomus illud χτ' σάρκα, id est, secundum carnem, aliter in genere de quouis Christiano, & aliter in specie de Christo exponit.
units.tr: 1. Chrysostom explains the phrase κατὰ σάρκα [kata sarka], that is, "according to the flesh," one way in general of any Christian, and another way specifically of Christ.

units.la: Sic enim illud: Itaq; nos posthac neminem nouimus secundum carnem, exponit, ut Christo competere non possit: cum tamen perspicuum sit, particulam hanc, secundum carnem, non alio atque alio, sed eodem esse utrobique sensu ab Apostolo positam. Verba illius hæc sunt: Quod de nobis dicit, secundum carnem, est in peccatis esse, &, non secundum carnem, non esse in peccatis. In Christo verò, illud, secundum carnè, est in naturalib. esse passionibus, vt-pote, in siti, in fame, &c. Peccatu enim nō fecit, &c. Haud vero secundū carne esse, est ab eiusmodi passionib. esse liberū, non esse extra carnè. Cum illa nanq; venturus est ad iudicandū orbem. Hæc ille, què Theophylactus more suo sequitur.
units.tr: For he explains that sentence, "And so from now on we know no one according to the flesh," in such a way that it cannot apply to Christ, although it is clear that the Apostle used this phrase "according to the flesh" in the same sense in both places, not in different senses. His words are these: "What he says of us, 'according to the flesh,' means being in sins, and 'not according to the flesh' means not being in sins. In Christ, however, 'according to the flesh' means being subject to natural passions, such as thirst, hunger, and so on. For he did not commit sin, etc. Yet not to be according to the flesh means to be free from such passions, not to be outside the flesh; for he will come to judge the world." So far Chrysostom, whom Theophylact follows in his own manner.

units.la: 2 Ambrosius sic exponit, vt quod in genere concernit oēs, non attingat, & ea tantū exponat, quæ de Christo dicuntur. Verba eius assignabo. Itaq; nos ex hoc tempore neminē noui mus secundum carnem. Etsi cognouimus secundum carnem Christum, sed nunc iam non nouimus. Verum est, quia Christo resurgente à mortuis, iam cessat in eo carnalis natiuitas, cessat infirmitas corporis, cessat & passio mortis. Vsq; ad crucem enim suspicio fuit infirmitatis in Christo. Post aut apparuit esse qd non credebatur, sicut & ipse ait: Cùm exaltaueritis filium hominis, tunc cognoscetis quod ego sum. Hoc ergo idcirco Apostolus memorat, vt ostendat, qua deuotione obsequendū sit Christo. Pro salute enim hominum, non solum hominem nasci se dignatus est, sed & iniurijs agi & mori, vt intelligentes quà preciosa sit mors eius, propensiùs illi seruiant, non quasi homini vicem reddentes, sed Deo: quia unicuiq; ꝑ persona eius & meritis refundenda obsequia sunt. Hæc ille.
units.tr: 2. Ambrose explains it in such a way that he does not touch on what concerns all in general, and explains only those things that are said of Christ. I shall set down his words. "And so from this time on we know no one according to the flesh. Although we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him. It is true that, since Christ has risen from the dead, carnal birth ceases in him, weakness of body ceases, and the suffering of death ceases too. For up to the cross there was suspicion of weakness in Christ. But afterwards there appeared what was not believed, as he himself says: 'When you have lifted up the Son of man, then you will know that I am he.' Therefore the Apostle mentions this so as to show with what devotion we ought to serve Christ. For for the salvation of men he deigned not only to be born a man, but also to be treated with injuries and to die, so that those who understand how precious his death is may serve him more eagerly, not as repaying a debt to a man, but to God; for services are to be rendered to each person according to his person and merits." So far Ambrose.

units.la: 3 Et Augustinus de doctrina Christiana lib. 1. cap. 34. per carnem hoc loco humanitatem à Christo susceптam, & quæ in illa perfecta est, dispensationem intelligit.
units.tr: 3. And Augustine, in On Christian Doctrine, book 1, chapter 34, understands by "flesh" in this place the humanity assumed by Christ, and the dispensation that was perfected in it.

units.la: 4 Lyranus ad hunc modum exponit. Itaq; nos ex hoc neminē nouimus secundū carne, id est, cum nemine societate contraximus motu carnali affectione. Sed quia posset aliquis obiicere, quòd Apostoli multum dilexerunt Christum, etiam secundū præsentiam corporalem, ideo subdit Apostolus in persona apostolorum, qui cum Christo fuerunt corporaliter: Etiamsi cognouimus Christum secundum carnem, id est, affecti eius præsentia corporali, sed nunc iam non nouimus, illo scilicet modo, sed meliori. Hæc ille.
units.tr: 4. Lyra explains it in this way: "And so from now on we know no one according to the flesh," that is, we have formed no fellowship with anyone by carnal motion or fleshly affection. But because someone might object that the Apostles greatly loved Christ even in his bodily presence, the Apostle therefore adds, in the person of the apostles who were with Christ bodily: "Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh," that is, affected by his bodily presence, "yet now we no longer know him," that is, in that manner, but in a better one. So far Lyra.

units.la: 5 Recentiorum quidam sic exponunt, vt secundum carnem aliquē cognoscere, idem sit quod cognoscere eum carnaliter, studio & affectu carnis, quomodo caro facit. Et adferunt hunc sensum. Quoniam omnes vnà cum Christo mundi sumus ac carni mortui, non conuenit vt in posterum secundum carnē & carnaliter viuamus, & carnaliter quenquam, sed potius spiritualiter cognoscamus. Etenim carnaliter aliquem cognoscere, non est eum ultrà q caro potest cognoscere. Vltrà autem caro non valet, quàm vt quod suum est quærat in omnibus, quo pacto mundani homines sese mutuò cognoscunt, nos Christiani uerò non item. Et quemadmodum fratres nostros non cognoscimus carnaliter, sed spiritualiter: ita & Christum non carnaliter, sed spiritualiter cognoscimus. mus, quærentes in eo nó quæ carnis, sed quæ {A}spiritus sunt. Hanc expositionem nónnulli magnificiunt. At meo iudicio ad mentem Apostoli non accedit. Deinde infirmum est, quòd particulam hanc, secundum carnem, referunt ad cognoscentem, non ad eos qui cognoscuntur: quo sensu de Deo quoq; dici potest, quòd à multis secundum carnė, id est, carnaliter cognoscatur, cùm tamen carnem non habeat. Quàm multi siquidem sunt, qui & carnaliter de Deo sentiát, & quæ carnis sunt in illo quærant. At Apostolus hic de cognitione eorum loquitur, qui & carnem habent, & secundum carnem quam habent, cognosci possunt. Loquitur enim de Christianis, & Christo ipso.
units.tr: 5 Some of the moderns explain it so that to know someone according to the flesh means to know him carnally, with the fleshly zeal and affection that the flesh produces. They offer this sense: since we all have been dead together with Christ to the world and to the flesh, it is not fitting that in future we should live according to the flesh and know anyone carnally, but rather that we should know spiritually. For to know someone carnally is to know him only as far as the flesh can know him, and the flesh is capable of nothing beyond seeking what is its own in all things. This is how worldly people know one another, but we Christians do not. Just as we do not know our brothers carnally but spiritually, so also we know Christ not carnally but spiritually, seeking in him not the things of the flesh but the things of the Spirit. Some men extol this explanation, but in my judgment it does not agree with the mind of the Apostle. Moreover, it is weak to refer the phrase "according to the flesh" to the one who knows rather than to those who are known. On that sense it could also be said of God that he is known by many according to the flesh, that is, carnally, although he has no flesh. Indeed, there are many who think carnally about God and seek in him the things of the flesh. But the Apostle here speaks of the knowledge of those who do have flesh and who can be known according to the flesh they have. For he speaks of Christians, and of Christ himself.

units.la: 6 Nonnulli alij exponunt, cognoscere secundum carnem aliquem, esse illum cognoscere secundum externam laruam, apparentiam & dotes carnis. Et Christum cognoscere secundum carnem, esse illum secundum ea quæ in carne ad tempus gesìt cognoscere.
units.tr: 6 Some others explain knowing someone according to the flesh as knowing him according to his outward mask, appearance and bodily endowments. And to know Christ according to the flesh is to know him according to the things he did in the flesh for a time.

units.la: 7 Sentiat quisq; quod uero propius accedere putat. Mea sententia sic habet: Mente Apostoli in hisce verbis cogniturò opus est, ut quid ille hoc loco secundum carnem cognoscere, & quid novam creaturam vocet, accuratè intelligat. Infrà cap. II. perstringens pseudapostolos, quos perpetuos habebat hostes, impingit illis, quod gloriarentur secundum carnem. Et subijciens illorum glorias, dicit: Hebræi sunt? sum & ego. Israelitæ sunt? sum & ego. Semen Abrahæ sunt? sum & ego. Gloriabantur itaq; {B}secundum carnem, iactantes Ebræos esse se, Israelitas, & semen Abrahæ. Deinde & circumcisionem carnis urgebant, ut in carne circumcisorum gloriari possent, quasi secundum illam censendi sint Christiani. Et hinc fiebat, ut pro veris Christianis ij demum habendi viderentur, qui secundum carnem essent ex Israele, & circumcisi essent carne. Horum pestem ubiq; impugnans, diligenter monet, Christianum hominem non censeri secundum prærogatiuam carnis, sed secundum novam creaturam, quæ sit ex Christo Iesu. Sic Galatas in uiâ revocans, dicit: Nam in Christo Iesu neq; circumcisio quicquam valet, neque præputium, sed nova creatura. Huc respiciens, hoc quoq; loco dicit: Itaq; nos posthac neminem novimus secundum carnem: hoc est: Nos igitur posteaquam unus mortuus est pro omnibus, eo quòd mortui essent omnes, & ob id pro omnibus est mortuus, ut qui viuunt, non amplius sibijpsis, sed ei uiuant, qui pro ipsis est mortuus, & resurrexit, ab eo tempore neminem Christianum censemus ex ijs, quæ sunt secundum carnem, siue sit circumcisus, siue præputiatus, siue Græcus, siue Iudæus, siue Barbarus, siue Scytha, siue seruus, siue liber, siue carnalem legis obseruantiam teneat, siue minus. Hæc omnia carnis sunt. In carne quidem adhuc fumus qui Christo uiuimus: uetùm haudquaquam secundum carnem Christiani censemur. Vestri magistri prærogatiuam carnis admodum extollùt, & secundum hanc de Christianis iudicant. At nos, licet & ipsi ex Israele simus, posfimusq; de carne gloriari, nihilominus quàm ipsi, Christianum tamen neminem censemus secundum carnem, postquâ Christo fumus inserti. Hunc existimo germanum esse præsentis loci sensum, quem & Commentarij qui Hieronymo dátur, attingunt. Sic enim habent: Itaque nos ex hoc neminem nouimus secundum carnem, id est, carnaliter circumcisum, & carnales ceremonias seruantem.
units.tr: 7 Let each man feel as he thinks closest to the truth. My own opinion is this. To grasp the meaning of the Apostle in these words, we must carefully understand what he means here by knowing according to the flesh, and what he calls a new creature. Earlier, in chapter 2, he attacks the false apostles, whom he always had as enemies, and charges them with glorying according to the flesh. Answering their boasts, he says: "Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? So am I." So they gloried according to the flesh, boasting that they were Hebrews, Israelites and the seed of Abraham. Furthermore, they insisted on circumcision of the flesh, so that they could glory in the flesh of the circumcised, as if Christians were to be counted by it. From this it came about that only those seemed to be regarded as true Christians who were of Israel according to the flesh and circumcised in the flesh. Attacking this plague everywhere, he diligently warns that a Christian man is not judged according to the privilege of the flesh, but according to the new creature, which is from Christ Jesus. So, calling the Galatians back to the right way, he says: "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creature." Looking to this, he says also in the present passage: "Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh." That is: since one died for all, and therefore all died, and he died for all so that those who live should no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose for them, from that time on we judge no one a Christian by what belongs to the flesh, whether he is circumcised or uncircumcised, Greek or Jew, barbarian or Scythian, slave or free, whether he keeps the carnal observance of the law or less of it. All these things belong to the flesh. We who live to Christ are indeed still in the flesh, but we by no means count anyone a Christian according to the flesh. Your teachers greatly exalt the privilege of the flesh and judge Christians by it. But we, although we too are of Israel and can glory in the flesh, nevertheless count no one a Christian according to the flesh, as they do, since we have been grafted into Christ. I think this is the true sense of the present passage, and the commentaries that are given under the name of Jerome also touch on it. For they say: "Therefore from this we know no one according to the flesh, that is, one circumcised carnally and keeping carnal ceremonies."

units.la: ETIAMSI uero & Christum cognouimus secundū carnem, inquit, nunc tamen non amplius nouimus.) Sensus est. Obijciunt nobis Christum ipsum, quòd sit Iudæus, ex femine Abrahæ, & circumcisus, & quòd legè ipse quoq; seruarit, quòdq; in carne inter Israelitas uersante uiderint. Nos ista in Christo nó sic inora mur, ut ex illis regulam Christianæ religionis ac censuræ sumendam existimemus. Aliquando nos ipsi quoq; secundum carnem de Christo sentiebamus, sicq; carnem illius intuebamur, ac si secundū illius prærogatiuâ ad Israelem tantum pertineret. Verùm rectius in fide illius instructi, non amplius de illo secundum carnem iudicamus, sed potius secundum consilium Dei, quo datus est uniuerso generi humano Redemptor ac Seruator, ut in ipso uiuamus omnes, deq; spiritu ipsius censeamur omnes, non Israelitæ & Iudæi, sed ueri Christiani. Huic sententiæ concordat, quòd & Christus ipse nec matrem, nec fratres secundū carnem agnoscebat. Matt. 12. sed secundum obedientiâ, qua patris cœlestis uolùtati obeditur.
units.tr: Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, he says, yet now we no longer know him in that way. The sense is this. They object to us that Christ himself was a Jew, of the seed of Abraham, circumcised, and that he kept the law himself, and that they saw him living among the Israelites in the flesh. We do not so dwell on these things in Christ as to think that the rule of the Christian religion and its judgment should be taken from them. At one time we too judged Christ according to the flesh, and we regarded his flesh as if it pertained only to Israel by reason of its privilege. But now, instructed more rightly in his faith, we no longer judge him according to the flesh, but rather according to the counsel of God, by which a Redeemer and Saviour was given to the whole human race, so that we all live in him and all are counted by his Spirit, not as Israelites and Jews but as true Christians. The saying agrees with this, that Christ himself did not acknowledge his mother or his brothers according to the flesh (Matt. 12), but according to the obedience by which the will of the heavenly Father is obeyed.

units.la: PROINDE si quis est in Christo, inquit, nóua creatura est. Vetera præterierunt, ecce noua facta sunt omnia.) Absoluit, quòd neminē se secundum carnem cēsere dixit. Non est enim loquutus de cognitione, qua homine ut homi nem censemus, sed qua Christianum cognoscimus. Ideo colligendo non dicit: Si quis est homo, sed, si quis est in Christo. Hominē secundum carnem recte cognoscimus, Christianum uero non ita. Cum ergo Christianus nó sit secundum carnem cognoscēdus, reliquum est, ut ex noua creatura censeatur. Hæc.n.inter se opponuntur. In carne uetustas est, in Christia no uero noua creatura, nouus homo, secundū Deum è supernis conditus. Vnde addit: Vetera præterierunt, ecce noua facta sunt omnia. Præterierunt uetera, in quibus constabat carnis prærogatiua, & iusticia secundum legem. Præterierunt Noui testamēti successione, per quā noua facta sunt in Christo omnia. Nouus homo, nouus spiritus, noua uita, testamentum nouū, noua iusticia, &c. Hæc mea est de præsen ti loco sententia, quam iudico & menti Apostoli conuenire, & nihil discrepare à uerbis.
units.tr: Therefore, he says, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature: the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new. He concludes that he said no one is judged according to the flesh. For he did not speak of the knowledge by which we regard a man as a man, but of the knowledge by which we recognise him as a Christian. So in drawing the conclusion he does not say, "If anyone is a man," but, "If anyone is in Christ." We rightly know a man according to the flesh, but we do not know a Christian in that way. Since a Christian is therefore not to be known according to the flesh, it remains that he be judged by the new creature. For these are opposed to each other. In the flesh there is the old; in the Christian there is the new creature, the new man, created from above according to God. Hence he adds: the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new. The old things have passed away, those things in which the privilege of the flesh and righteousness according to the law consisted. They have passed away by the succession of the New Testament, through which all things have become new in Christ: new man, new spirit, new life, new covenant, new righteousness, and so on. This is my opinion on the present passage, which I judge to agree with the mind of the Apostle and not to differ from his words.

units.la: ITAQVE nos posthac neminē nouimus se cundū carné, inquit.) Admonet hic locus, nó esse Christianos cēsendos ex ijs q̄ sunt carnis. Loquitur quidē Apost.de prærogatiua carnis,
units.tr: Therefore, he says, from now on we know no one according to the flesh. This passage admonishes us that Christians are not to be judged by those things which belong to the flesh. The Apostle indeed speaks of the privilege of the flesh,

units.la: quam in Abrahamo, circucisione, & legis observantia iactabant pseudapostoli: verum nihil impedit, quo minus nos generaliore sententiam hinc struamus, pronunciantes, nullis carnis dotibus siue naturales hæ sint, siue religiosæ, siue fortuitæ, mentiendum esse Christianum, ut taceam ea quæ ad corruptionem carnis pertinent, è quibus est cultus eidolorū, qui inter opa carnis Gal. 5. numeratur. Nota, Christiani hominis non est statuenda ulla in re carnali, siue in sacro siue in prophano sit usu. Carnis sunt omnia, unde censetur Iudæus, unde Ethnicus, unde Turcus. Christianus ex his cognoscitur nemo. Carnis sunt omnes illi cultus templarij, serico, argento, auro, lapidibus preciosis, & cereis ardentibus splendentes. Secundum hos quoq; nemo censetur Christianus. Nemo enim secundum carne Christianus esse cognoscitur. At hodie his potissimum antiquos & catholicos Christianos metiūtur Pontificij.
units.tr: which the false apostles boasted of in Abraham, in circumcision, and in observance of the law. Nevertheless, nothing prevents us from drawing a more general conclusion from this, declaring that a Christian is not to be judged by any gifts of the flesh, whether these are natural, religious or accidental, not to mention those things which pertain to the corruption of the flesh, among which is the worship of idols, which is numbered among the works of the flesh in Gal. 5. Note: no judgment of a Christian man is to be founded on any carnal thing, whether it be in sacred or in profane use. All things are of the flesh by which a Jew is judged, by which a heathen is judged, by which a Turk is judged; no one is recognised as a Christian by any of these. Of the flesh are all those temple furnishings that shine with silk, silver, gold, precious stones and burning wax candles. No one is judged a Christian by these either, for no one is known to be a Christian according to the flesh. Yet today the Papists especially measure the ancient and catholic Christians by these things.

units.la: SI uero & Christū cognouimus secundum carne, inqt.) Potest hoc referri ad tempus, quo adhuc extra Christi erat cognitione Paulus in Iudaismo. Habebat tum quoq; aliquā de Christo futuro sententiam, queimadmodum de apostolis quoq; legimus, quòd & ipsi opinione sibi de illo conceperint, quòd liberaturus esset Israelem, illiq; regnum restituturus, & quòd se cundum morem sæculi esset regnaturus. Hæ sententiæ de Christo secundū carnem erāt, & prorsus Iudaicæ. Agnoscit hoc de se Apostolus, & fatetur, quòd aliquando de Christo secundū carne senserit. Admonemur hoc exemplo, candidi esse hominis nō dissimulare, multo minus negare, si aliquando in errore constitutus, aliter quàm ueritas habet, senserit.
units.tr: "But even if we have known Christ according to the flesh," he says. This can be referred to the time when Paul, still outside the knowledge of Christ, was in Judaism. He then held some opinion about the future Christ, just as we read that the apostles too had formed the view that he would free Israel and restore the kingdom to it, and that he would reign in the manner of the world. These opinions about Christ according to the flesh were entirely Jewish. The Apostle acknowledges this about himself and confesses that at one time he thought of Christ according to the flesh. We are warned by this example that it is the mark of an honest man not to conceal, and much less to deny, that he once held a view in error, thinking otherwise than the truth is.

units.la: NVNC tamen nō amplius nouimus. inqt.) Non negat se Christum cognoscere in carne. Absit. Cum enim alibi nihil se nisi Christū Iesum & hunc crucifixum, scire dicit, utiq; nouit Christū in carne, uerū hominem, uerè passum, & mortuū. Hoc ergo dicens, non adimit Christo ueram carnem, ueráq; carnis natura, quam sibi Christus ipse post resurrectionem uindicat, dicens: Palpate & uidete, quoniā spiritus carne & ossa non habet, sicuti me habere uidetis: sed negat se amplius de Christo sentire secundū carne, eo modo quo senserat de illo in Iudaismo. Quare locū hic non habet hostes ac negatores carnis Christi, siue prisci siue recentiores. Et illi quoq; qui Christū & Deum & hominē tempore Nestorij in ecclesia Constanti nopolitana consitebātur, impertinenter hæc Apostoli uerba cōtra presbyterū Anastasium usurparūt, cūm ille in ecclesia docens, diceret: Nemo Mariā Deiparā uocet: fuit enim homo Maria. Ex homine auté Deū nasci est impossibile. Qua de re sic legimus: Hoc auditum multos clericos & laicos, & pariformiter cunctos perturbauit. Sciebant enim oēs Christum esse Deum, & nullo pacto propter dispesationem susceptā tanquam homine à diuinitate separatum, fidem habentes Apostolicæ uoci, quę di-
units.tr: "But now we no longer know him," he says. He does not deny that he knows Christ in the flesh. Far from it. For when he elsewhere says that he knows nothing except Jesus Christ and him crucified, he certainly knows Christ in the flesh, a true man who truly suffered and died. In saying this, therefore, he does not take from Christ his true flesh or the true nature of the flesh, which Christ himself claims for himself after the resurrection, saying: "Handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have" (Luke 24). He says only that he no longer thinks of Christ according to the flesh, in the way he had thought of him in Judaism. Hence this passage gives no support to the enemies and deniers of Christ's flesh, whether ancient or more recent. Those too who in the time of Nestorius, in the Church of Constantinople, confessed Christ to be both God and man, misapplied these words of the Apostle against the presbyter Anastasius, when he, teaching in the church, said: "Let no one call Mary the Mother of God; for Mary was a man. But for a man to be born of God is impossible." Concerning this we read as follows: "When this was heard, it disturbed many clergy and laity, and indeed all alike. For all knew that Christ is God, and in no way, on account of the dispensation undertaken, did they hold that he was separated from the divinity as a mere man, adhering to the word of the Apostle which says:"

units.la: cit: Etiási cognouimus secundū carnem Christū, at iam nō amplius cognoscimus. Hæc Socrates Eccles. hist. lib. 7. cap. 32. Illis Christum cognoscere secundū carnem, est homine eum césere, & nō amplius cognoscere secundū carnē, césere Deū. Secundū eiusmodi sensum Apostoli nō cognoscebat amplius in Christo homine, sedDeū tatū. Verū sic labi cogūturq; uer ba Apostoli nō satis inspecta, temerè ūsurpāt.
units.tr: "Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him" (2 Cor. 5:16). So Socrates, Ecclesiastical History, book 7, chapter 32. For those people to know Christ according to the flesh is to regard him as a mere man, and not to know him according to the flesh any longer is to regard him as God only. In this sense the Apostle no longer knew Christ as a man, but only as God. But the words of the Apostle, not sufficiently examined, are thus forced into error and rashly misused.

units.la: PROINDE si quis est in Christo, inquit, nō ua creatura.) Obserua, quòd cūm dicendū esset: Si quis est Christianus, dixit, Si quis est in Christo. Ergo Christianum esse, est in Christo esse. ExtraChristū quisquis est, Christianus nō est. Facilè est participē fieri sacramentorū, nominis, ac professionis Christi: at in Christo esse, non ita. Nam id omnino nouū hominē requirit: unde & hic dicit: Si quis est in Christo, noua creatura est. Maxima pars Christianorū uetus adhuc creatura est. Nondum enim sunt spiritu Christi regenerati ac renouati. Cogniturī igitur Christianū, uitā illius, nō externam professione tantū inspiciamus. Ex uita discere licet, uetúsne sit adhuc uel noua creatura. Vbi uetus creatura in solidū retinetur, ibi omnino extra Christi spiritū uiuitur. In solidū di- co, ne teneras adhuc inChristo ac recētes plantulas propter ueteris creaturæ reliquias damnem. Vetus.n.creatura non ita subito exuitur, nec noua repēte tota induitur. Habet hęc mutatio suos gradus, & incremēta paulatim exuī gentia. Et interim tamen habet sua etiam indicia unde cognoscatur, quantumuis illa sint tenuiora. Quid sit autē in Christo esse, & quid esse Christum in nobis, in Commēnt. nostris super Ioannem fuse diximus.
units.tr: "Therefore if anyone is in Christ," he says, "he is a new creature." Observe that where he ought to have said, "If anyone is a Christian," he said, "If anyone is in Christ." So to be a Christian is to be in Christ. Whoever is outside Christ is not a Christian. It is easy to become a partaker of the sacraments, of the name and profession of Christ; but to be in Christ is not so easy. For that requires altogether a new man, and so he also says here: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature." The greater part of Christians are still an old creature. For they have not yet been regenerated and renewed by the Spirit of Christ. Let us therefore look at the life of a Christian, and not merely at his outward profession, if we wish to know him. From his life we can learn whether he is still an old creature or a new one. Where the old creature is wholly retained, there one lives altogether outside the Spirit of Christ. I say "wholly," lest I condemn the tender and still-young little plants in Christ on account of the remnants of the old creature. For the old creature is not put off so suddenly, nor is the new put on entirely all at once. This change has its stages, and the putting off of the old is a gradual process of increase. Meanwhile, however, there are also signs by which it may be recognized, however slight they may be. What it is to be in Christ, and what it is for Christ to be in us, we have discussed at length in our Commentaries on John.

units.la: VETERA præterierūt, ecce noua facta sunt omnia, inquit.) Vtiq; testamentū Vetus cum suis iusticijs carnis transijt, & Nouū succēssit. Erant & ueterā illa ex Deo: quare non debebant humano consilio è medio auferri. Rectè igitur dicit ἀφῄλθεν, id est, transierūt. Impleta illorum dispensatione, successione Noui testamenti transierūt, perinde ac si umbras noctis ad exortum Solis transfire dicas'. Veteres errores non eo sunt honore habendi, ut sponte sua transfire sinātur, sed studio auferendi. Vide & illud. Nō dicit: Ecce noua feciīmus omnia, sed: Ecce noua facta sunt omnia. Non immutarūt apostoli testamenta Dei, sed Deus ipse uirtute spiritus sui quem effuderat, antiquato Veteri, Nouum subiunxit.
units.tr: "The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new," he says. Certainly the Old Testament, with its righteousnesses of the flesh, has passed away, and the New has succeeded it. Yet those old things were also from God; therefore they ought not to have been removed by human counsel. Rightly, then, he says [ἀφῄλθεν], that is, "they have passed away." Once their dispensation was fulfilled, they passed away with the succession of the New Testament, just as you might say that the shadows of night pass away at the rising of the sun. Old errors are not to be honoured so far that they are allowed to pass away of their own accord, but they must be removed by zealous effort. Notice also this: he does not say, "Behold, we have made all things new," but, "Behold, all things have become new." The apostles did not alter the covenants of God; rather God himself, by the power of his Spirit which he had poured out, when the Old was made obsolete, joined the New to it.

units.la: Author Apocalypseos cap. 21. cūm uidisset in spiritu cœlum nouum & terram nouam, uocem hanc cœlitūs de throno audiuit: Ecce tabernaculū Dei cum hominibus, & habitabit cum eis. Et ipsi populi eius erunt, & ipse Deus cum eis erit eorum Deus. Et absterget Deus omnem lachrymam ab oculis eorum. Et mors ultrà nō erit, neq; luctus, neq; clamor, neq; dolor erit ultrā, quia prima abierūt. Et dixit qui sedebat in throno: Ecce noua facio omnia. Igitur moxinitio Noui testamēti, per spiritum Christi innouata sunt omnia, & in fine quoq;, quando mors abolita fuerit, noua per Christũ fient omnia. Prior innouatio testamenti est, & mentiũ nostrarum. In hac possunt adhuc omnis generis afflictiones innouatorum hominum exercere fidem ac patientiam. Posterior est totius cœli ac terræ machinæ, & allatura secum est plenam ac sempiternam felicitatem. Prior de posteriore nos certificat. Habet enim arrhabonem spiritus. Posterior priorem in ele ctis ac fidelibus absoluet & perficiet. Hic enim mentium fit innouatio, illic etiam corpora nostra innouabuntur.
units.tr: The author of the Apocalypse, chapter 21, when he had seen in the Spirit a new heaven and a new earth, heard this voice from heaven from the throne: "Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them. And they shall be his people, and God himself will be with them, their God. And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes. And death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more, because the former things have passed away." And he who sat on the throne said: "Behold, I make all things new." Therefore, at the very beginning of the New Testament, all things were renewed through the Spirit of Christ, and at the end too, when death has been abolished, all things will be made new through Christ. The first renewal is that of the covenant and of our minds. In this, the faith and patience of renewed men can still be exercised by every kind of affliction. The second is that of the whole machinery of heaven and earth, and it will bring with it full and everlasting happiness. The first assures us of the second, for it has the earnest of the Spirit. The second will complete and perfect the first in the elect and faithful. For here the renewal takes place in our minds, but there our bodies too will be renewed.

units.la: Omnia autem ex Deo, qui reconciliauit nos sibi per Iesum Christum, deditq; nobis ministerium reconciliationis: quandoquidem Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi, non imputans eis peccata sua, & posuit in nobis sermonem reconciliationis. Itaque nomine Christi legatione fungimur, tanquam Deo uos obsecrante per nos, rogamus pro Christo, reconciliemini Deo. Eum enim qui non nouit peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, ut nos efficeremur iustitia Dei per illum.
units.tr: "Now all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; for God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their sins to them, and he has placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we act as ambassadors in the name of Christ, as though God were exhorting you through us; we beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God. For he made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him" (2 Cor. 5:18–21).

units.la: Refert in Deum omnia quæ in præcedentibus dixit, simulq; exponit adhuc clarius, & interim addit de ministerio Apostolatus sui. To tam salutis nostrę rationem breui compendio digerit & exponit. Quare locus hic ab omnib. est fidelib. summo semper habendus in precio, & singulari studio menti penitus insinuadus.
units.tr: He refers all the things he said before to God, and at the same time explains them more clearly, and in addition speaks of the ministry of his apostleship. He sets out in a brief summary the whole account of our salvation. Therefore this passage should always be held in the highest esteem by all the faithful, and must be deeply impressed upon the mind with special care.

units.la: OMNIA autem ex Deo, inquit.) Suprà alicubi diximus, in more id esse Apostolo, ut quæcunq; Christo, tanquam Redemptori ac Seruatori ad salutem nostram pertinentia tribuit, ad Deũ patrem, tanquã illorum authorẽ ac fontem referat, quo certior nobis in omnibus fidei nostræ ratio cõstet. Hoc ipsum in præsenti quoq; facit, dicens: Omnia autem ex Deo. In genere quidem omnia sunt ex Deo, quæ in cœlo sunt, terra ac mari, & quæ fuerunt, sunt, & futura sunt, qua de re alibi admonet. Hic uero specialiter de ijs loquitur, quæ summam salutis nostræ concernunt: quorum in præcedentib. ex parte meminit, ubi unũ mortuum fuisse dicit pro omnibus, ut qui uiuũt, non amplius sibijpsis uiuãt, sed ei qui pro ipsis mortuus fuit & resurrexit: quibus uerbis opus redemptionis nostræ per Christum partæ expressit, id quod hic cum annexis suis omnibus Deo patri, tanquã authori asignat. Quare nõ simpliciter dicit πάντα, sed cum articuli specificatione, τὰ πάντα, id est, hæc autem omnia ex Deo. Specificationem hanc in sequentibus explicabit.
units.tr: "But all things are from God," he says. Elsewhere we have said that it is the Apostle's custom to refer to God the Father, as the author and fount of these things, whatever he attributes to Christ as Redeemer and Saviour pertaining to our salvation, so that the reasoning of our whole faith may be more certain for us. He does this here too, saying: "But all things are from God." In general all things are from God, whatever is in heaven, on earth and in the sea, and whatever has been, is, and will be; on which matter he gives advice elsewhere. Here, however, he speaks specifically of those things which concern the sum of our salvation, of which he has partly spoken in what goes before, where he says that one died for all, so that those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them. In these words he expressed the work of our redemption obtained through Christ, and this, with all its attachments, he here assigns to God the Father as its author. Therefore he does not simply say [πάντα], but with the specification of the article, [τὰ πάντα], that is, "these all things are from God." He will explain this specification in what follows.

units.la: QVI reconciliauit nos sibi per Iesum Christum, inquit.) Sic exponit illud, quod suprà unũ pro omnibus mortuum fuisse dicit. Quis tinus ille sit, aperit, dicens: Per Iesum Christũ,
units.tr: WHO HAS RECONCILED US TO HIMSELF THROUGH JESUS CHRIST, he says. He explains what he said above, that one died for all, and states who that one is, saying: through Jesus Christ.

units.la: A Ipsum opus quo ille pro omnibus mortuus fuit exponit, dicens: Qui reconciliauit nos sibi. Eramus omnes natura filij iræ, inimici, peccatores, abalienati à Deo, & in peccatis mortui. Quatenus peccatores, inimici, filij iræ & abalienati à Deo eramus, opus nobis erat reconciliatione cum Deo, nulla alias cuiquam potes rat ipes esse salutis. Quatenus mortui eramus in peccatis, poscebat ipsa necessitas mortis ui ctorem ac uiuificatorem. Vtrunq; igitur misericordissimus pater, reconciliatorem uidelicet ac uiuificatorẽ præstitit in filio suo Iesu Christo, dum illum pro nobis omnibus peccatum fecit, mortiq; tradidit, ut uictima esset & oblatio placationis, reconciliationis ac redemptionis.
units.tr: He explains the work itself by which he died for all, saying: who reconciled us to himself. We were all by nature children of wrath, enemies, sinners, estranged from God, and dead in our sins. Insofar as we were sinners, enemies, children of wrath, and estranged from God, we needed reconciliation with God, and there could be no other hope of salvation for anyone. Insofar as we were dead in sins, the very necessity of our death called for a conqueror of death and a giver of life. The most merciful Father therefore provided both, namely a reconciler and a giver of life, in his Son Jesus Christ, when he made him sin for us all and delivered him to death, so that he might be the victim and the offering of propitiation, reconciliation and redemption.

units.la: Obserua uero, quod non dicit: Qui reconciliatus nobis est per Iesum Christũ. Neque sic alienum, quid à uero dixisset, uerum propositio suo non seruisset. Quare dicere maluit, Qui recõciltauit nos sibi per Iesum Christũ. Sic reconciliationis nostrę opus per Christum, tanquam Mediatorem factũ, Deo patri tribuit, quod is nos sibi reconciliauerit. Magnum est, esse nos reconciliatos non angelis modo, sed ipsi Deo, maius est, factum hoc esse per ipsum filium Dei. Omnis uero maximum est, quod factum hoc est non extra uoluntatem & consilium patris, sed ab ipso sic uolente, constituente, ac filium suum ad id mittente, inq; mortem tradente. Non expectauit nos, dum ipsi reconciliationem suppliciter ambiremus: sed eius propositi inscios, imo auersos, & peccatis immortuos, ultrò suapte misericordia per filium sibijpse reconciliauit, & ad hanc quosuis reconciliationem uocauit & inuitauit. O' stupendæ bonitatis exemplum. Læsa maiestas prima sibi reconciliat inimicos. Discamus omnes, quæ spes debeat esse reconciliatis coræo, qui nos sibi ultrò cum inimici essemus, reconciliare dignatus est. Qui sic propensus fuit in inimicos, qualem esse credendum est in reconciliatos? Discamus item omnes, quid faciendum sit læsis & offensis. Non expectandum uidelicet, donec qui læsit suopte instinctu ueniat, & reconciliationem ambiat: sed ad exemplum hoc cœleste connitendum, ut qui læsus est, ipse sibi primus fratrem, à quo læsus est, reconciliet. Nihil huius facimus, quia fratres non diligimus: nõ diligimus autem, quia boni non sumus, sed à bonitate cœlestis patris alienissimi.
units.tr: Observe, however, that he does not say: who was reconciled to us through Jesus Christ. Nor would he have said anything false by that, but it would not have served his purpose. So he preferred to say: who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ. In this way he attributes the work of our reconciliation to God the Father, through Christ acting as Mediator, in that God reconciled us to himself.
