It is a great thing that we have been reconciled not only to angels but to God himself; it is greater that this was done through the Son of God himself. But the greatest thing of all is that this was done not against the will and counsel of the Father, but by him, willing it, decreeing it, sending his Son for this purpose and handing him over to death. He did not wait for us to beg him humbly for reconciliation. Rather, when we were ignorant of his purpose, indeed turned away from it and dead in sins, he of his own accord, through his mercy, reconciled us to himself through his Son, and called and invited us to accept this reconciliation. O example of wonderful goodness! The majesty that was offended first reconciles its enemies. Let us all learn what hope those who have been reconciled should have, since he who, when we were his enemies, deigned to reconcile us to himself of his own accord. If he was so inclined toward enemies, what must he be thought to be toward those reconciled? Let us also all learn what ought to be done by those who have been injured and offended. Clearly we should not wait until the one who wronged us comes of his own impulse and seeks reconciliation; rather, following this heavenly example, the one who was wronged should strive to reconcile to himself first the brother by whom he was wronged. We do none of this because we do not love our brothers; and we do not love them because we are not good, but are very far estranged from the goodness of the heavenly Father.

units.la: DEDITQVE nobis ministerium reconciliationis, inquit.) Non erat satis ad salutem, quod nos sibi clementissimus pater per Christum filium suum reconciliauit, nisi nos recon ciliationis huius redderemur capaces. Reconciliatio non poterat locum habere inter inimicos, sed utriusque partis assensum ac uoluntatem requirit. Nostri reconciliatio, quod ipsum Deum attinet, perfecta quidem est in morte Mediatoris Christi unigeniti Dei: uerum quod nos ex altera parte concernit, perfecta non est, nisi conditionibus illius nos ex animo accommodemus, ut capaces illius esse A Hoc est, remittes eis peccata ipsorum, propter posumus. Hę sunt respiscentia & fides in Christum. Sine his nemo reconciliationis huius potest esse capax. Excluduntur enim impoenitentes & increduli. Vt igitur participes illius efficeremur, misit Euangelium suum in orbe, per quod ad resipiscentiam ac fidem in Christum uocarentur omnes, quo reconciliationis huius gratia potirentur. Et id muneris commisit apostolis tanquam reconciliationis huius legatis. Hoc significans Apostolus dicit: Deditq; nobis ministerium reconciliationis. Non solì ipsi, sed & reliquis apostolis ministerium hoc dedit. Nihil tamen impedit, quo minus hic de suo Apostolatu loqui intelligatur, de quo pseudapostoli controuersiam improbissimè mouebant. Sic itaq; non modo ipsum reconciliationis opus, sed & dispensandæ illius ministerium Deo authori tribuit.
units.tr: AND HE HAS GIVEN TO US THE MINISTRY OF RECONCILIATION, he says. It was not enough for our salvation that the most gracious Father reconciled us to himself through his Son Christ, unless we were made capable of this reconciliation. Reconciliation could not take place between enemies; it requires the assent and will of both parties. As far as God himself is concerned, our reconciliation was indeed completed in the death of the Mediator Christ, the only-begotten God. But as far as concerns us on the other side, it is not complete unless we accommodate ourselves from the heart to its conditions, so that we may be able to receive it. These conditions are repentance and faith in Christ. Without these no one can be capable of this reconciliation, for the unrepentant and the unbelieving are excluded. So that we might be made partakers of it, he sent his Gospel into the world, through which all are called to repentance and faith in Christ, so that they may obtain the grace of this reconciliation. And he committed this office to the apostles as ambassadors of this reconciliation. The Apostle signifies this when he says: And he has given to us the ministry of reconciliation. He gave this ministry not only to himself but also to the other apostles. Nothing prevents us, however, from understanding that he is here also speaking of his own apostleship, over which the false apostles were wickedly raising controversy. Thus he attributes to God, the author, not only the work of reconciliation itself but also the ministry of dispensing it.

units.la: Obseruet uero diligēs lector, quàm elegantì ordine reconciliationem hanc nostri inter Deum, Christū, & apostolos diuidat. Deo tribuit illius authoritate, Christo opus, p quod, tanquam Mediatori, apostolis dispensandę illius ministerium, tanquam ministris ac legatis. Nusquā excluditur Deus, à quo sunt hæc omnia. Nec Christus sine Deo reconciliationis opus perfecit, nec Apostoli dispensationis illius ministerium sine Deo obiuerunt in mundo.
units.tr: The diligent reader should also observe how elegantly the Apostle divides this reconciliation among God, Christ and the apostles. He attributes to God its authority, to Christ the work, by which, as Mediator, he [assigns] to the apostles the ministry of dispensing it, as ministers and ambassadors. God, from whom all these things come, is nowhere excluded. Christ did not accomplish the work of reconciliation without God, nor did the apostles carry out the ministry of its dispensation in the world without God.

units.la: Quis autem satis perpenderit, quàm grato elogio prædicationem Euangelij exornet, dum uocat eam ministerium reconciliationis, utiq; & pacis? Nihil acceptius excogitari potest ijs, B qui sunt metu Dei ac morsu conscientiæ angustiati; quàm ministerium hoc reconciliationis: per quod non modo ad resipiscentiam & fidem in Christum uocantur, sed & certissimam reconciliationis ac pacis cum Deo promissionē accipiunt, per quam conscientiæ ipsorum à metu ac sensu iræ Dei liberantur, quę antea nullis modis excutere poterant, & tamē grauitatem illius ferendo non erant. Reuera speciem rebellionis habet, si quis ministerium hoc reconciliationis contemperit, ac fusq; deq; fecerit, nec expectandum est eiusmodi conteptoribus aliud, q exitium & certissimum & meritissimum.
units.tr: But who has weighed sufficiently how gracefully he adorns the preaching of the Gospel, in calling it the ministry of reconciliation, and of peace? Nothing can be imagined more welcome to those who are distressed by fear of God and by the gnawing of conscience than this ministry of reconciliation, through which they are not only called to repentance and faith in Christ, but also receive the most certain promise of reconciliation and peace with God. By this their consciences are freed from the fear and the feeling of the wrath of God, which they could in no way shake off before, and which they were not able to bear because of its weight. Truly, whoever despises this ministry of reconciliation and holds it cheap has the appearance of rebellion, and such despisers should expect nothing else than destruction, both most certain and most deserved.

units.la: QVANDOQVIDEM, inquit, Deus erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians sibi non imputans eis peccata ipsorum.) Declarationē eorū subijcit, quæ de opere & ministerio reconciliationis dixit. Sic illud: Qui nos sibi reconciliauit per Iesum Christū exponit, dicens: Quandoquidem Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi, non imputās eis peccata. Quasi dicat: Neq; enim Christus opus hoc reconciliationis per seipsum sine Deo præsumpsit, sed ipse Deus Christum filium suum inhabitans; & in omnibus dirigens, non nos modo, sed & mundum, id est, omne genus humanum, quod inde ab initio ad finem usq; mundi fuit, & est, & erit, sibi reconciliauit, dum filium in mortem pro omnibus dedit.
units.tr: SINCE, he says, GOD WAS IN CHRIST, RECONCILING THE WORLD TO HIMSELF, NOT IMPUTING THEIR SINS TO THEM. He adds a declaration of what he said about the work and ministry of reconciliation. Thus he explains the words who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, saying: since God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their sins to them. As if he were saying: Christ did not presume to undertake this work of reconciliation by himself without God, but God himself, dwelling in his Son Christ and directing him in all things, reconciled to himself not only us but also the world, that is, the whole human race, which from the beginning to the end of the world was, is, and will be, when he gave his Son to death for all.

units.la: NON imputás eis peccata ipsorum, inquit.)
units.tr: NOT IMPUTING THEIR SINS TO THEM, he says.

units.la: quæ abalienati ab ipso fuerant. Quid enim aliud est, non imputare peccata peccatori, q cle meter remittere? & quid remittere, q non imputare? Sic Propheta Psal.32. remissione, & non imputationem peccatorum pro eodem usurpat, dicens: Beatus, cui remittitur transgressio, & cui tegitur peccatum. Beatus homo, cui non imputat Dominus peccatum. Particulam hac Apostolus necessario adiecit: Neq; enim reconciliatio hæc mundi cum Deo fieri potuit, nisi omnibus peccatis nostris clementer remissis. Si peccata imputare uoluisset, locum reconciliatio no habuisset. Nemo nanq; erat ex omni genere humano, qui pro suis, nedum aliorum peccatis, iusticiæ Dei satisfacere, & hac ratione reconciliationem impetrare potuisset.
units.tr: (they who had been estranged from him). For what else is it not to impute sins to a sinner than to forgive them mercifully? And what is forgiving other than not imputing? So the Prophet in Psalm 32 uses forgiveness and non-imputation of sins as the same thing, saying: Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, and whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin. The Apostle necessarily added this phrase, for this reconciliation of the world with God could not have happened unless all our sins had been mercifully forgiven. If God had wished to impute sins, there would have been no place for reconciliation. For there was no one from the whole human race who could have satisfied the justice of God for his own sins, let alone for those of others, and by this means obtained reconciliation.

units.la: Ergo ne totum genus humanum reconciliatum est Deo per Christū, sic ut nemini mor talium peccata imputentur? Si hoc sentiendū est simpliciter, quid aliud consequitur, q perire neminē, saluari indiscriminatim omnes? Sanè ex hoc & consimilibus aliis locis nonnulli dogma de saluandis omnibus, etiā impijs nostra ætate renouare conati sunt. Verum est omnino quod dicit Apostolus: Mundum sibi in Christo Deus reconciliauit, non imputans eis peccata ipsorum, quantū attinet ipsum reconciliationis opus, toti generi humano reconciliādo paratū ac sufficiēs. Verum (quem admodū supra diximus) quoniam reconciliatio inter inuitos locum habere non potest, institutum est ab ipso Deo ministerium reconciliationis, quo cuncti ad hanc gratiam cupidè amplexandam uocetur & inuitentur. Hanc si totus mundus amplexaretur, utique totus mundus omni peccatorum imputatione reiecta cum Deo reconciliaretur, ac seruaretur, nec periret mortaliū quisquam. Cum id non fit, quid aliud restat, quàm ut generalis huius gratiæ participes fiant hi tantum, qui grati illam resipiscendo & credendo amplectuntur?
units.tr: Therefore has the whole human race been reconciled to God through Christ, so that no mortal's sins are imputed to anyone? If this is to be taken simply, what else follows but that no one perishes and all are saved without distinction? Certainly from this and similar passages some have tried in our own time to revive the dogma of the salvation of all, even of the wicked. It is entirely true what the Apostle says: God reconciled the world to himself in Christ, not imputing their sins to them; as far as the work of reconciliation itself is concerned, it is prepared and sufficient for reconciling the whole human race. But (as we said above) since reconciliation cannot take place between those who are unwilling, the ministry of reconciliation has been instituted by God himself, by which all are called and invited to embrace eagerly this grace. If the whole world embraced it, then surely the whole world, with the imputation of sins set aside, would be reconciled and preserved with God, and not one mortal would perish. Since this does not happen, what else remains but that only those become partakers of this general grace who embrace it gratefully by repenting and believing?

units.la: ET posuit, inquit, in nobis sermone reconciliationis. Græcè est, ὁ λόγος τῆς καταλλαγῆς. Non mutassem uetere uersione, quæ habet, & posuit in nobis uerbū reconciliationis, quòd usus huius uocis frequēs sit in scripturis in ecclesia receptis, nec tanta sit ratio, quur mutetur. Sit hoc minutū. Apostolus exponit quod supra dixit: Et dedit nobis ministerium reconciliationis. Quod ibi uocauit ministerium, id iam exponendi gratia uocat λόγον, id est, uerbum, intelligens prædicationem Euangelij. Generalius est ministerium reconciliationis. Possunt enim multæ esse ministerij species. At speciali us est uerbum reconciliationis. Nam hoc elogio exprimitur certus modus administrandæ reconciliationis. In papatu reconciliatione hac constituerunt aliam atq; alia, dum eam iā Missis suis, iam confessionibus priuatis, iam indulgentijs Pontificijs alligarunt, de quibus nulla extat d constitutionis authoritas. Quare diligenter obseruandū est, qd Apost. hic dicit: Et posuit Deus
units.tr: And he has placed in us the word of reconciliation. In Greek it is "the word of reconciliation" [ὁ λόγος τῆς καταλλαγῆς]. I would not have changed the old version, which reads "and has placed in us the word of reconciliation", since this term is common in the Scriptures received by the Church, and there is no strong reason to change it. This is a minor point. The Apostle explains what he said above: "And he has given us the ministry of reconciliation." What he there called the ministry, he now, by way of explanation, calls the word [λόγον], that is, the word, understanding the preaching of the Gospel. "Ministry of reconciliation" is the more general phrase, for there can be many kinds of ministry. "Word of reconciliation" is more specific, because this phrase expresses a definite mode of administering reconciliation. Under the papacy they have set up one form of this reconciliation after another, now tying it to their Masses, now to private confessions, now to papal indulgences, and there is no extant authority of any constitution for these. Therefore we must observe carefully what the Apostle says here: "And God has placed..."

units.la: A Hoc est ... B Cap. 2. v. 9. (marginal references as printed) Deus,id est,constituit, iniunxit, & mandauit, λόγον, id est, uerbum, prædicationem, & annunciationem reconciliationis, hoc est, de reconciliatione mundi, à Deo per Christũ facta. Palàm loquitur de prædicatione Euangelij, per quam reconciliationem hanc Deus toti orbi proponi uoluit. Hanc uiam dispensandæ illius nundinatores & cauponarij in ecclesia ferre non possunt: quam tamen apostoli, tanquam à Deo acceptam, fideliter & constanter tenuerunt. Mutatà à Deo non inuenio, ab Antichristo inuenio. Disputant de sacramentis, an non & per illa reconciliationis huius gratia applicetur. Si separatim inspiciantur absq; uerbo reconciliationis, non concedo, si illi incorporentur, concedo in baptismate, propter uerbum. Cœnsæ dominicæ alia est ratio.
units.tr: A: That is ... B: Chap. 2, v. 9. God (that is, has appointed, enjoined and commanded) the word [λόγον], that is, the word, the preaching and announcement of reconciliation, namely of the reconciliation of the world made by God through Christ. He is clearly speaking of the preaching of the Gospel, through which God wished this reconciliation to be offered to the whole world. The money-changers and hucksters in the Church cannot bear this way of dispensing it, though the apostles, as received from God, held to it faithfully and steadfastly. I do not find it changed by God; I find it changed by Antichrist. They dispute about the sacraments, whether through them too this grace of reconciliation is applied. If they are considered separately, apart from the word of reconciliation, I do not grant it; if they are joined to it, I grant it in baptism, because of the word. The Lord's Supper has a different reasoning.

units.la: Quòd autem sit uerbum reconciliationis, ex eo qd' præmissum est patet. Quid enim aliud prædicabat minister reconciliationis huius, quàm ipsam reconciliationem à Deo factam, & sic factâ, ut mundum sibi per Christum non imputans eis peccata ipsorum, reconciliarit. Hanc gratiam fideliter prædicare, & quosuis ad resipiscentiam & fidem in Christum uocare, est uerbum reconciliationis prædicare.
units.tr: That it is the word of reconciliation is clear from what has been said. For what else did the minister of this reconciliation preach than the reconciliation itself, made by God and made in such a way that, not imputing their sins to them, he reconciled the world to himself through Christ? To preach this grace faithfully, and to call anyone whomever to repentance and faith in Christ, is to preach the word of reconciliation.

units.la: ITAQVE nomine Christi legatione fungimur, inquit, tanquâ Deo uos obsecrâte p nos, rogamus pro Christo, reconciliemini Deo.) Quod lectione attinet, illa, in nomine Christi, &, pro Christo, in Græco nō sunt alijs atq; alijs uerbis posita, sed utrobiq; habetur ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ. Quare & utrobiq; constâter uertendum erat, pro Christo, uel, nomine Christi. Tâ enim recte legeris, rogamus noïe Christi, quàm, nomine Christi legatione fungimur, uel, ρ Christo legatione fungimur, quâ, rogamus ρ Christo.
units.tr: "Therefore we act as ambassadors in the name of Christ," he says, "as though God were exhorting you through us; we beg in the place of Christ: be reconciled to God." As to the reading: the phrases "in the name of Christ" and "in the place of Christ" are not expressed by different words in the Greek, but in both places there is ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ [for Christ]. Therefore it had to be translated consistently in both places, as "for Christ" or "in the name of Christ". For you may read "we beg in the name of Christ" as correctly as "we act as ambassadors in the name of Christ", or "we act as ambassadors for Christ", or "we beg for Christ".

units.la: Habent ista paraenesim, cuius summa est: Itaque rogamus uos reconciliemini Deo. Circumstantiæ sunt: rogamus autem non ut priuati homines, nostro ipsorum instinctu & arbitratu, sed ut legati Christi, nomine Christi, tanquam Deo ipso uos hortante per nos.
units.tr: These words contain an exhortation, whose summary is: "Therefore we beg you, be reconciled to God." The circumstances are these: we beg not as private men, by our own impulse and judgment, but as ambassadors of Christ, in the name of Christ, as though God himself were exhorting you through us.

units.la: ITAQVE pro Christo, inquit, legatioe fungimur.) Ex præmissis authoritate Apostolatus sui colligit. Dixit: Deditq; nobis ministerium reconciliationis. Item, & posuit in nobis ministerium reconciliationis. Hinc colligês: Itaque, inquit, quoniam Deo sic placuit, ut impo neret nobis recociliationis huius ministerium, nos mandato illius obedientes legatione hanc obimus pro Christo, id est, loco & uice Christi, perinde ac si Christus ipse ad uos ueniret. Qui legatus imperatoris in castris est, uices illius in castris gerit, sic ut omnis illius potestas ab ipso dependeat imperatore, pro quo legatione fungitur. Consimilem Apostolatui sui uindicans potestatem Apostolus, dicit se non modò ex constitutione & mandato Dei, sed & pro ipso Christo, uel, nomine Christi, legatione ad exequendum reconciliationis ministerium fungi. Magna semper habita est legatorum, præsertim regiorũ, dignitas, ad quam
units.tr: "Therefore," he says, "we act as ambassadors for Christ." From what has been said he draws a conclusion from the authority of his apostleship. He had said: "And he has given us the ministry of reconciliation"; likewise: "and has placed in us the ministry of reconciliation." Drawing the inference, he says: "Therefore, since it has pleased God so to impose on us the ministry of this reconciliation, we, obedient to his command, discharge this embassy for Christ, that is, in the place and stead of Christ, just as if Christ himself were coming to you. An envoy of the emperor in the camp bears the emperor's office in the camp, so that all his power depends on the emperor for whom he acts as envoy." Claiming for his apostleship a similar power, the Apostle says that he acts as envoy to carry out the ministry of reconciliation not only by the appointment and command of God, but also for Christ himself, or in the name of Christ. The dignity of envoys, especially royal ones, has always been held in great regard, and to this

units.la: legabantur non uulgares homines, sed selecti, non iuuenes, sed uiri uenerabili senecta suspiciendi. Vnde & πρεσβεῖς uocãtur. Nomina eorũ philosophorũ, qui olim cum Areobindo in Persiam pacis constituendæ gratia legati mittebantur, ad posteros honoris gratia tràsmissa sunt, quorũ meminit Suidas. Quanto dignius est ut legati cœlestis regis, reconciliationis gratia non in Persiam tantum, sed in totũ orbem amandati, perpetuò sint in omnium fidelium memoria, habeâturq; in precio, qui legatione eam post illos ex uoluntate Dei prosequûtur.
units.tr: not ordinary men were sent, but chosen ones, not young men, but men to be looked up to for their venerable old age. Hence they are also called πρεσβεῖς [elders]. The names of those philosophers who were once sent as envoys with Areobindus into Persia to establish peace have been handed down to posterity in honour, as Suidas records. How much more worthy it is that the envoys of the heavenly King, sent for the sake of reconciliation not only into Persia but into the whole world, should remain forever in the memory of all the faithful and be held in esteem: those who, after them, carry on this embassy by the will of God.

units.la: TANQVAM Deo uos obsecrâte per nos, in qt.) In Græco est, ὡς τοῦ Θεοῦ παρακαλοῦντος δι' ἡμῶν, id est, tanquam Deo exhortante per nos. Sic habet & uulgata. Verbum παρακαλεῖν aliquan-do quidem obsecrare significat, uerũ hic restius exhortandi sensu accipitur. Si quis tamen Chrysostomum sequutus malit legere, tanquam Deo obsecrante per nos, quòd existimet haud indecorũ esse Deo, si dicatur nos per apostolos suos obsecrare, per me licet sic sentiat, modò sciat eum sensum nõ necessario ex uerbo Græco nasci, quod non minus exhortari quàm obsecrare significat. Non contentus dixisse, itaque nomine Christi legatione fungi mur, mox de Deo ipso subijcit, illumq; uelut exhortantem quosuis ad amplexandã reconciliationem inducit. Tribuit illi quod ipse ex authoritate eius faciebat. Ipse exhortabatur, ipse obsecrabat & solicitabat quosuis. Et hoc tanti uult haberi, ac si a Deo ipso fiat, cuius rei duæ sunt causæ, diuini mandati una, spiritus altera. Neq; enim humanum, sed diuinum censeri debet, quod licet per hominem fiat, mandato tamè ac spiritu Dei impellête perficitur.
units.tr: "As though God were exhorting you through us." In Greek it is ὡς τοῦ Θεοῦ παρακαλοῦντος δι' ἡμῶν, that is, "as God exhorting through us". So also the Vulgate has it. The verb παρακαλεῖν sometimes means to beseech, but here it is rather taken in the sense of exhorting. If anyone, however, following Chrysostom, prefers to read "as God beseeching through us", because he thinks it not unfitting for God to be said to beseech us through his apostles, let him so understand it, as far as I am concerned, provided he knows that this sense does not necessarily arise from the Greek word, which means no less to exhort than to beseech. Not content to have said "therefore we act as ambassadors in the name of Christ", he immediately adds something about God himself, and brings him in, as it were, exhorting anyone to embrace reconciliation. He ascribes to God what he himself was doing by God's authority: he himself exhorted, he himself besought and urged anyone. And he wants this to be held of as much weight as if it were done by God himself, for which there are two causes, one a divine command, the other the Spirit. For what is done through a man, though it is done by a human being, but is carried out under the impulse of God's command and Spirit, ought to be counted not human but divine.

units.la: ROGAMVS nomine Christi, inquit, recon ciliemini Deo.) Græcè est, δέομαι. Significat autem uerbũ δέομαι indigere ac desiderare, & consequenter suppliciter pro re necessaria ac desiderata obsecrare. Haud igitur leuiter rogabat, ut Deo reconciliarentur; sed obnixè ac suppliciter, perinde ac si rẽ ageret sibijpsi omnibus modis necessariâ, cum tamen quicquid agebat, ipsorum salutis gratia ageret. Etenim si Deo reconciliari detreẞassent, utiq; suo ipsorum hoc, non apostoli, exitio fecissent.
units.tr: "We beg in the name of Christ: be reconciled to God." In Greek it is δέομαι. The verb δέομαι means to lack and to desire, and consequently to beg earnestly for something necessary and desired. He did not therefore beg lightly that they be reconciled to God, but earnestly and suppliantly, just as if he were pursuing a matter necessary to himself in every way, although whatever he did, he did for their salvation. For if they had refused to be reconciled to God, they would have done this to their own destruction, not to the apostle's.

units.la: Vides uerè paternum in Apostolo pectus. Emiserat apostolos suos dominus in hanc ipsam reconciliationis legationem, ut prædicarent Euangelium omni creaturæ, ac docerent omnes Gentes, baptizâtes eos in nomen patris & filij & spiritus sanctí: ut autẽ suppliciter obsecrarent homines, quo se Deo reconciliari sinerent, mandasse illum nõ legimus. At hic Apostolus nõ modò prædicat & docet in nomine Christi, sed & quosuis obnixè obsecrat, ut Deo recõcilientur. Sic Apostolatum suum nõ est pfunctorie exequutus, sed animo planè erga quosuis paterno, & salutis omniũ cupido. Perinde ac si qs reo cuipiá liberè dimittendo, si ignosci sibi supplex petat, pleẞedo uerò, si id facere detreẞet, ut salutæ suę ac uitæ cõsu lat persuasurus non simpliciter uolûtatem ac gratiâ principis exponat, sed & cunctatem ac tergiuersantem obnixè obsecret ac roget, ne tam insignem principis gratiam contemnat, sed uitæ suæ remissionem delictorum supplici-ter petendo consulat, & hoc eò faciat impensius, quo magis illum cunctari & exitio uicinio-rem fieri uiderit. Consimile mihi admodū uidetur, quod hic Apostolus scribit, dicens: Ro-gamus nomine Christi, reconciliemini Deo. Videbat quàm certo exitio tam insignis gratia contemneretur, & quàm certa salute resipi-scendo & credendo acciperetur: ideoq; tanto serio ad amplexandam illam quosuis obse-crando ac rogando solicitabat. Et quoniâ scie-bat Christo se ea in re summopere gratificari, tanquâ humanæ salutis unico reparatori, non simpliciter obsecrabat, sed in nomine Christi, cuius uices gerebat. Et quid obsecrat? Recon-ciliemini, inquit, Deo. Atqui Deum in Chri-sto fuisse, ac mundum sibi reconciliasse dixit. Quid ergo est quod hic se rogare dicit, ut Deo reconcilientur? Respondeo: Recôciliari Deo, hoc loco, non est reconciliari implacato, sed reconciliationem iam placati, in Christo filio ipsius factam, grato animo p resipiscentiâ ac fidé in sanguine reconciliationis amplecti. Qui hoc non faciunt, Deo reconciliati non sunt, quis ille mundum sibi in Christo reconciliarit.
units.tr: You see the truly paternal heart of the Apostle. The Lord had sent his apostles into this very embassy of reconciliation, that they should preach the Gospel to every creature, teach all nations, and baptize them in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; but we do not read that he commanded them to beg men suppliantly to let themselves be reconciled to God. Here, however, the Apostle not only preaches and teaches in the name of Christ, but also earnestly begs anyone whomever to be reconciled to God. Thus he did not perform his apostleship perfunctorily, but with a truly paternal mind toward all and a desire for the salvation of all. It is just as if someone, to persuade a guilty man that he should consult his own safety and life, were to set out not merely the prince's will and grace, which would freely pardon him if he asked forgiveness but would punish him if he refused to do so, but were also to beg and entreat earnestly the one who hesitates and shirks, not to scorn so remarkable a grace of the prince, but to provide for his life by humbly seeking remission of his offences; and he does this all the more urgently the more he sees him hesitating and drawing nearer to destruction. Something very like this seems to me what the Apostle writes here, saying: "We beg in the name of Christ, be reconciled to God." He saw how surely such remarkable grace would be despised to certain destruction, and how surely it would be received to salvation by repentance and faith; therefore he urged them with such earnestness, begging and entreating them to embrace it. And since he knew that in this matter he greatly pleased Christ, the sole restorer of human salvation, he did not simply beg, but did so in the name of Christ, whose office he bore. And what does he beg? "Be reconciled," he says, "to God." Yet he had said that God was in Christ and had reconciled the world to himself. What then does he mean in saying that he begs them to be reconciled to God? I answer: to be reconciled to God in this place does not mean to be reconciled to one who is still hostile, but to embrace with a grateful mind, through repentance and faith in the blood of reconciliation, the reconciliation already made in Christ, his Son, with the God who is now appeased. Those who do not do this are not reconciled to God, although he reconciled the world to himself in Christ.

units.la: Dices: Si ergo reconciliati sunt cum Deo, qui reconciliationis huius gratiam fide accipiunt, quorsum Corinthios, utique fideles & reconciliatos rogat, ut cum Deo reconcilientur, quasi nondum cum illo sint reconciliati?
units.tr: You will say: if those who receive the grace of this reconciliation by faith are already reconciled to God, why does he ask the Corinthians, who are certainly faithful and reconciled, to be reconciled to God, as if they were not yet reconciled to him?

units.la: 1 Respondeo. Erant adhuc inter illos multi, quos nondum peccatorum suorum poenitebat. Vtiq; illi cum Deo reconciliati non erant, quia reconciliationis gratiam per impoeniten-tiam à se reijciebant. Horum respectu non immerito dicit: rogamus, reconciliemini Deo.
units.tr: 1. I answer: there were still many among them whom repentance for their sins did not yet move. Those certainly were not reconciled to God, because by their impenitence they rejected the grace of reconciliation. With respect to these, he rightly says: "We beseech you, be reconciled to God."

units.la: 2 Deinde potest & hoc cogitari, quod hic dicit: rogamus in nomine Christi, recôciliemini Deo, nô sic dici, ut specialiter ad Corinthios pertineat, sed ut significet, q; ardéter ministerium hoc reconciliationis obeat, quosuis rogando, ac dicendo, reconciliemini Deo. Et huic sententiæ fauet, quod in Græco non est, tanquâ Deo uos exhortante, sed simpliciter, tanquam Deo exhortante per nos, ut possit referri ad omnes. Rogabat omnes Apostolus, quibus Christū initio prædicabat, dicens: Reconciliemini Deo, hoc est, gratiam reconciliationis, quam uobis Deus ipse per nos offert, cum poenitentia & fide in Christum cupide accipite, quo saluemini. In hoc sensu nihil loci habet dicta iam quæstio.
units.tr: 2. Next, this may also be considered: when he says here, "We beseech you in the name of Christ, be reconciled to God," it is not said in such a way as to pertain specifically to the Corinthians, but to show that he discharges this ministry of reconciliation with ardour, beseeching and urging everyone: be reconciled to God. This sense is also favoured by the fact that the Greek does not read "as though God were exhorting you," but simply "as though God were exhorting through us," so that it can be referred to all. The Apostle besought all to whom he first preached Christ, saying: "Be reconciled to God," that is, eagerly receive, with repentance and faith in Christ, the grace of reconciliation which God himself offers you through us, so that you may be saved. In this sense the question raised has no place.

units.la: EVM nanq; qui no nouit peccatū, pro nobis peccatum fecit, inquit, ut nos efficeremur iusticia Dei per illum.) Rursus primariâ causam urget, ob quam reconciliari Deo debea-mus, mortem uidelicet Christi, sic tamen, ut illâ exponat. Poterat dicere, dedit enim filiū suū in morte, quo per illū recóciliaremur. Ve-
units.tr: "For him who knew no sin he made sin for us," he says, "that we might be made the righteousness of God through him." Again he presses the chief cause for which we ought to be reconciled to God, namely the death of Christ, yet in such a way as to explain it. He could have said: "For he gave his Son in death, so that through him we might be reconciled." Ve-

units.la: rū pro eximia sua sapientia consilium Dei in hac causa exprimere uolens dicit: Eum nanq; qui peccatū non nouit, pro nobis peccatū fecit, ut nos efficeremur iusticia Dei per illum. Sic bi-membrem ætiologiam ponit, in cuius primo membro memorat quid in causa salutis nostrę fecerit Deus, in altero ad quid fecerit.
units.tr: But, with his singular wisdom, wishing to express God's counsel in this matter, he says: "For him who knew no sin he made sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God through him." So he gives a two-membered explanation: in the first member he records what God did in the cause of our salvation, and in the second, to what end he did it.

units.la: EVM nanq; qui peccatum non nouit, pro nobis peccatū fecit.) Suprà dixit: non imputans eis peccata ipsorum. Hic rursus peccatorum meminit, dum Deū filium suū pro nobis peccatū fecisse dicit. Loquitur enim de hostia pro peccatis, quâ more scripturæ peccatū uo-cat. Sic enim scriptura loquitur, ubi de sacrificio pro peccatis meminit, ut Exod.30. Et expiabit Aheron super cornua eius semel in anno, מדם חטאת בפרים, id est, de sanguine peccati expiationū. Hoc est, de sanguine hostiæ expiationū pro peccato oblatæ. Et Leuit. 4. Et educet iuuencū extra castra, & cóburet eum ibi, חטאת חטאת הוא, id est, peccatū ecclesiæ ipse est: pro, hostia pro peccato ecclesię ipse est. Adumbras illas legalium sacrificiorū, quibus hostia pro peccatis offerebatur respi-ciens, dicit Christum à Deo factum fuisse pro nobis peccatū, quod nihil est aliud, quàm factum eum fuisse hostiam ac sacrificium expia-torium pro peccatis nostris. Huius respectu Deus remisit nobis omnia peccata nostra, nec aliquod ex illis imputauit, quandoquidē ea filio suo tanquam hostiæ expiatoriæ in cruce portanda & expianda imposuit.
units.tr: "For him who knew no sin he made sin for us." Above he said: "not imputing their sins to them." Here again he mentions sins, in saying that God made his Son sin for us. For he speaks of the sacrifice for sin, which, in the manner of Scripture, is called sin. Scripture speaks thus wherever it mentions sacrifice for sins, as in Exodus 30: "And Aaron shall make atonement upon its horns once a year [מדם חטאת בפרים], that is, with the blood of the sin-offering of atonement," meaning with the blood of the victim offered for sin as an atonement. And in Leviticus 4: "And he shall take the bullock outside the camp and burn it there [חטאת הוא], that is, it is the sin of the congregation," meaning it is the sin-offering for the congregation. Looking to those shadows of the legal sacrifices, in which a sin-offering was offered for sin, he says that Christ was made sin for us by God, which is nothing other than that he was made the victim and expiatory sacrifice for our sins. On account of this, God forgave us all our sins and imputed none of them to us, since he laid them upon his Son, to be borne and expiated on the cross as an expiatory victim.

units.la: Ociosum autē non est, quod nô simpliciter dicit, Christum enim, sed periphrasticè, cum enim qui peccatū non nouit. Hoc dicens uin-dicat Christo innocentiâ singularem, qua non modò peccatum non fecit ullum, sed ne nouit quidem peccatū, id est, peccare nor nouit. Sic cauet, ne pro suo aliquo peccato crucifixus putetur, quo firmum sit, quod pro nostris pec-catis in cruce expiandis, peccatū à Deo factus est. Etenim si peccator fuisset & ipse, peccatū pro nobis fieri non potuisset. In huius rei figu-ram requirebatur in lege, ut immaculatus iu-uencus pro peccato offerretur. Sic igitur uin-dicat Christo innocentiam & iusticiā, sine qua peccatorum nostrorū expiatio nulla prorsus fuisset. Hunc unum nobis iustum & innocen-tem dedit Deus, in quo omnia totius generis humani peccata expiari possent.
units.tr: It is not idle that he does not simply say "Christ," but speaks periphrastically, "him who knew no sin." By saying this he vindicates for Christ a singular innocence, by which he not only committed no sin, but did not even know sin, that is, he did not know how to sin. Thus he guards against the thought that Christ was crucified for some sin of his own, so that it stands firm that for the expiation of our sins on the cross he was made sin by God. For if he himself had been a sinner, he could not have been made sin for us. To represent this in the law, an unblemished bullock was required to be offered for sin. Thus he vindicates for Christ innocence and righteousness, without which the expiation of our sins would have been altogether impossible. God gave us this one just and innocent man, in whom all the sins of the whole human race could be expiated.

units.la: Et uide quàm constàter hic quoq; ad Deū referat, quod pro nobis à Christo est factum. Non dicit: Is enim qui peccatum non nouit, peccatum se pro nobis fecit, sed: Eum enim qui peccatum non nouit, Christum uidelicet, pro nobis peccatum fecit: quis? Deus, de quo dixerat, reconciliemini Deo, cui mox subiun-xit, eum enim qui peccatum non nouit, pro nobis peccatum fecit. Magna planè consolatio est, quod Deus ipse innocenti suo filio omnia nostra peccata in cruce, extra portam, ex-pianda imposuit, atq; ita illum peccatum pro nobis fecit. VT nos efficeremur, inquit, iustitia Dei in ipso.) Exponit ad quid Deus filium suum innocentem ac iustum, peccatum pro nobis fecerit. Poterat dicere, ut in illo peccata nostra expiaret. Et hoc ipsum sanè agebat. Verũ placuit vti antithesi peccatorum nostrorum, & iustitiæ Christi. Nos peccatores eramus, ille iust. Vt commutatio fieret, nostra peccata imposuit filio iusto, ac vicissim iusticiam illius communicauit nobis peccatoribus. Propter aliena igitur peccata, factus ille peccatû est, & nos propter alienam iusticiam iustitia Dei facti sum. Sicut enim ille non suis, sed nostris peccatis peccatum à Deo, ita nos non nostra ipsorum, sed ipsi iusticia, iusticia Dei facti sum à Deo. Nihilo enim magis nostra est iusticia qua iusti ficamur, quàm ipsius sunt peccata, pro quibus expiandis mortem pertulit. Facta namq; commutatione peccata nostra sua, & iusticiam suâ nostram fecit. Hoc exprimere uolens Apostolus, dicit: Eum enim qui peccatum non nouit, pro nobis peccatû fecit, ut efficeremur iusticia Dei in ipso.
units.tr: See how consistently he here too refers to God what was done for us by Christ. He does not say, "He who knew no sin made himself sin for us," but "him who knew no sin, namely Christ, he made sin for us." Who did? God, of whom he had said, "Be reconciled to God," and to whom he soon added, "him who knew no sin he made sin for us." It is indeed a great consolation that God himself laid all our sins upon his innocent Son, to be expiated on the cross, outside the gate, and so made him sin for us. "That we might be made," he says, "the righteousness of God in him." He explains the purpose for which God made his innocent and just Son sin for us. He could have said: that he might expiate our sins in him. Indeed, this is what he was doing. But he chose to use an antithesis between our sins and the righteousness of Christ. We were sinners, he was just. That there might be an exchange, he laid our sins upon the just Son, and in turn communicated his righteousness to us sinners. Therefore he was made sin on account of others' sins, and we were made the righteousness of God on account of another's righteousness. For just as he was made sin by God not for his own sins but for ours, so we are made the righteousness of God, by God, not through our own, but through his. For our righteousness by which we are justified is no more ours than his sins were ours, for whose expiation he endured death. For by the exchange made, he made our sins his own and his righteousness ours. Wishing to express this, the Apostle says: "For him who knew no sin he made sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him."

units.la: Quid est autem quod non dicit: ut efficeremur iusti, sed, ut efficeremur iusticia Dei? Eadem ratione quæras, quid sit quod nó dicit: eũ q. peccatũ nõ nouit, p nobis peccatore fecit, sed pro nobis peccatũ fecit? Filiũ suũ Deus peccatore non fecit, sicuti nos peccatores sumus: peccatum uerò, id est, sacrificiũ expiatoriũ pro peccatis nostris fecit. Sic nos iustos non fecit, què admodum ille iustus est, ut nihil amplius sit peccati in nobis, sicut in illo nihil erat, nec est peccati, sed fecit nos iusticiam, id est, imputauit nobis iusticiam, idque non nostram, quæ nulla est, sed suam, gratuitam uidelicet & clementer à se imputatam, quam habeamus, non in nobis, sed in ipso filio. Ideo non simpliciter dicit Apostolus, vt nos efficeremur iusticia; sed, vt nos efficeremur iusticia Dei in ipso. Si dicas Christum à Deo factum esse peccatum Dei in nobis, vtique nõ intelligis de peccato, quod Deus fecerit, quemadmodum nos peccamus, sed de eo quod nostra illi peccata, tanq; hostiæ pro nostris peccatis, expiáda imposuit. Consimili modo, cum Apostolus dicit: factos nos esse iusticiam Dei in Christo, non loquitur de iusticia, quâ Deus ipse in se iust est, uel de ea quæ illius sit iusticiæ similis, sed de iusticia quâ nobis in Christo imputat, sicuti peccata nostra illi imputauit. Itaq; ut Christus in se iusticia Dei, in nobis peccatum factus est: ita nos in nobis peccatum; in Christo uerò iusticia Dei sumus. In hac commutatione omnis nostra salus est sita.
units.tr: But why does he not say "that we might be made just," but "that we might be made the righteousness of God"? By the same reasoning you might ask why he does not say "he made him a sinner for us," but "he made sin for us." God did not make his Son a sinner, as we are sinners; rather, he made him sin, that is, an expiatory sacrifice for our sins. Likewise he did not make us just in the way that he is just, so that there would be no more sin in us, as in him there was no sin, nor is there any. Rather, he made us righteousness, that is, he imputed righteousness to us, and not ours, which is nothing, but his own, freely and graciously imputed by him, which we have not in ourselves but in the Son himself. Therefore the Apostle does not simply say "that we might be made righteousness," but "that we might be made the righteousness of God in him." If you say that Christ was made sin by God in us, you certainly do not understand sin as sin that God committed, as we sin, but as that which he laid our sins upon as a victim to be expiated for our sins. In a similar way, when the Apostle says that we are made the righteousness of God in Christ, he does not speak of the righteousness by which God is righteous in himself, nor of that which is like his righteousness, but of the righteousness which he imputes to us in Christ, just as he imputed our sins to him. Thus as Christ in himself is the righteousness of God, so in us he was made sin; and so we in ourselves are sin, but in Christ we are the righteousness of God. In this exchange all our salvation lies.

units.la: Augustinus in Enchiridio, ad Laurentium cap. quadragesimoprimo, paucis hęc verbis expressit, dicês: Ipse ergo peccatû, & nos iusticia, nec nostra, sed Dei, nec in nobis, sed in ipso, sicut ipse peccatum nõ suum, sed nostrũ nec in se, sed in nobis factus est.
units.tr: Augustine, in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter forty-one, expressed this in a few words, saying: "He himself, therefore, was made sin, and we righteousness: not our own, but God's; not in us, but in him; just as he was made sin not his own, but ours, and not in himself, but in us."

units.la: ARGVMENTVM
units.tr: ARGUMENT

units.la: Occasione præcedentium hortatur Corinthios, ne gratiam Dei quam in Christum credentes receperant, culpatè uiuendo frustrancam reddant: & ad id studij suo illos exemplo prouocat. Deinde hortatur eos, ut consortia infidelium fugiant.
units.tr: Occasioned by what precedes, he urges the Corinthians not to render vain the grace of God, which they received as believers in Christ, by living sinfully; and by his own example he stirs them to zeal for this. Then he urges them to flee the company of unbelievers.

units.la: CAPVT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: VIN & adiuuātes obsecramus, ne in uacuũ gratiam Dei receperitis. Dicit enim in tēpore accepto exaudiui te, & in die salutis succurri tibi. Ecce nunc tempus acceptũ, ecce nunc dies salutis, nullã ullã in re dantes offensionem, ne reprehendatur ministerium, sed in omnib. cōmendantes nosipsos, ut Dei ministri, in tolerantia multa in afflictionibus, in necessitatibus, in anxietatibus, in plagis, in carceribus, in seditionibus, in laboribus, in uigiliis, in ieiunijs, in puritate, in scientia; in animi lenitate, in benignitate; in spiritu sancto, in charitate non simulata, in sermone ueritatis, in potentia Dei, per arma iusticiæ dextra ac sinistra; per gloriam & ignominiam, per conuitia, & laudes, quasi impostores, & tamē ueraces, quasi ignoti, & tamē noti, quasi morientes, & ecce uiuimus, quasi correpti, & nõ occisi, quasi dolētes, semper tamē gaudētes, quasi pauperes, multos tamē ditantes, ut nihil habentes, & tamen omnia possidentes.
units.tr: And working together with him, we beseech you that you do not receive the grace of God in vain. For he says: "In an accepted time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you." Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation. We give no offence to anyone in anything, so that the ministry is not blamed, but in all things we commend ourselves as ministers of God: in much patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, in stripes, in prisons, in tumults, in labours, in watchings, in fastings; in purity, in knowledge, in gentleness of spirit, in kindness; in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God; through the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left; through glory and dishonour, through reproach and praise; as deceivers, and yet true; as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold we live; as chastened, and not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.

units.la: Cohæret ista, quare incommodū uisum est eã diuidere. Proposuit Apost. in pcedētib. doctrinā salutis nostræ de reconciliatione à Deo ipso facta, qua sibi genus humanum per Iesum Christum reconciliauit, ac reconciliationis huius ministerium Apostolis imposuit. Iam initio capitis huius sexti paraenesim subijcit, qua Corinthios hortatur, ne tam insigniem gratiam male uiuendo inanem sibijpsi reddant. Sic itaque dicit:
units.tr: These things hang together, and so it seemed inconvenient to divide them. In the preceding chapters the Apostle set out the doctrine of our salvation, concerning the reconciliation made by God himself, by which he reconciled the human race to himself through Jesus Christ, and he laid the ministry of this reconciliation upon the Apostles. Now at the beginning of this sixth chapter he adds an exhortation, by which he urges the Corinthians not to make so remarkable a grace empty for themselves by living badly. He speaks thus:

units.la: QVIN & adiuuātes obsecramus, ne in uacuũ gratiã Dei receperitis. ) Græcè est: συνεργοῦντες καὶ παρακαλοῦμεν. i. Cooperātes uerò obsecramus etiam. Amphibolum est, cuiusnam sit cooperarium esse dicat. Solet aliàs Dei se uocare cooperarium. Agnoscit hoc & Chrysostomus: & tñ eò inclinat, ut referat ad ipsos Corinthios, exponēs, συνεργοῦντες ὑμῶν. i. Cooperātes uobis. Mihi simplicius uidetur, ut respectu pcedētiū intelligamus de ministerio illius, quo Deo in reconciliatione per Christum facta, ad hoc cooperabatur, ut ad illam quosuis inuitaret. Hoc faciens simul obsecrabat alios ut Deo reconciconciliarentur, alios ne gratiam Dei semel accep-tam inanem redderet. Copulam &, inter-pres non suo loco posuit, dum uertit: Quin & adiuuantes obsecramus. Nō sic loquitur Apo-stolus, sed ad hunc modum. Cooperantes au-tem etiam obsecramus. Cooperationi adijcit obsecrationem, non obsecrationi cooperatio-nem. Vulgata habet: Adiuuantes autem exhor-tamur. Is interpres copulam omisit, uel si red-didit, negligentia antiquariorum factum est, ut interciderit. Quale autem pectus in eo spi-ret Apostolus, quod ministerium suum nō mo-do docendo, sed & quosuis rogando & obse-crando exequutus est, supra admonuimus ca-pite praecedenti, ubi dicit: rogamus nomine Christi reconciliemini Deo.
units.tr: "And working together, we also beseech you that you do not receive the grace of God in vain." The Greek is: συνεργοῦντες καὶ παρακαλοῦμεν [working together and we beseech], that is, "But working together we also beseech." It is ambiguous what he means by being a fellow-worker. The Apostle elsewhere calls himself a fellow-worker of God. Chrysostom also recognises this, yet he inclines to refer it to the Corinthians themselves, explaining συνεργοῦντες ὑμῶν [working together with you], that is, "working together with you." It seems to me more simply, with respect to what precedes, that we should understand it of his ministry, by which he worked, in the reconciliation made by God through Christ, to invite everyone to it. In doing this he at the same time begged others to be reconciled to God, and others not to make empty the grace of God once received. The translator has put the conjunction "and" out of its place when he renders it, "And working together we beseech." The Apostle does not speak thus, but in this way: "Working together, moreover, we also beseech." He adds the beseeching to the working together, not the working together to the beseeching. The Vulgate has: "Working together, however, we exhort." That translator omitted the conjunction, or if he rendered it, it has been lost through the carelessness of the copyists. But what kind of spirit the Apostle breathes in this, that he carried out his ministry not only by teaching but also by asking and beseeching everyone, we noted above in the preceding chapter, where he says: "We ask in the name of Christ, be reconciled to God."

units.la: NE in uacuum, inquit, gratiam Dei receperi-tis.) In Graeco additur ὑμᾶς, i.uos. Quasi di-cat, Etsi multi à gratia Dei recidant, uos tamen, in quibus saluandis tantopere laboraui, obse-cro, ne quam amplexi estis gratiam Dei, in ua-cuum receperitis. Non dicit, ut gratiam Dei re-cipiatis, aut, reconciliemini Deo, quod utrūq; idem est. Loquitur enim ad Corinthios fide-les, qui gratiam Dei credetes receperant, illiq; reconciliati fuerant. Qui tales sunt, admonen-di ueniunt, ut acceptam gratiam bene collo-cent, ne illam sibijpsi inanem reddant.
units.tr: "Not in vain," he says, "have you received the grace of God." In the Greek ὑμᾶς [you] is added, that is, "you." As if he were saying: Although many fall away from the grace of God, yet I beseech you, for whose salvation I have laboured so greatly, that you do not receive in vain the grace of God which you have embraced. He does not say, "that you receive the grace of God," or "be reconciled to God," although both amount to the same thing. For he is speaking to the faithful Corinthians, who had received the grace of God by believing and had been reconciled to it. Such people need admonition so that they may put the grace they have received to good use, lest they make it empty for themselves.

units.la: Dices: Ecquomodo fieri potest, ut gratia Dei in vanū ac frustrà recipiatur, cū sitin illa omnis nostra salus sita, sicut Apostolus hic alibi dicit: Gratia saluati estis. Si gratia saluat, quomodo potest frustrà recipi? Respondeo. Saluat quidē gratia, uerum refert plurimum, quomodo acci-piatur & collocetur. Verbum Dei, uerbum gratiæ, reconciliationis ac salutis accipere, gra-tiam Dei recipere est, quam autem illud diuer-simode accipiatur, notum est ex parabola Do-minica, Mat. 13. Alij accipiunt quidem, sed non intelligunt, ideoque malus ille ueniens rapit quod erat in cordibus illorum seminatum. Alij protinus & cum gaudio accipiunt, uerum non permittunt, ut radices agat in cordibus i-psorum, sunt enim temporarij: atque ita fit, ut tribulatione propter uerbum gratiæ oborta, continuò offendantur ac relabantur. Alij & i-psi quidem accipiunt, uerum sic sunt curis hu-ius saeculi, fallacium opum studio, ac voluptā-tibus immersi, ut acceptū uerbū in cordib.illo rum suffocetur, & infrugiferum reddatur. An non hi omnes gratiam Dei frustrà recipiunt, etiamsi illud mox atque audierunt & cupidè, & cum gaudio recipiant? An hi demum utili-ter accipiunt, qui auditum intelligunt, intelle-ctum cordi tanquam terrae bonae syncera fide insinuant, ac fructum illius proferūt, alius me-diocrem, alius uberiorem, secundum mensurā donationis Christi?
units.tr: You will say: How can it happen that the grace of God is received in vain and to no purpose, since all our salvation lies in it, as the Apostle says elsewhere in this letter: "You have been saved by grace." If grace saves, how can it be received to no purpose? I answer: grace does indeed save, but it matters greatly how it is received and how it is placed. To receive the word of God, the word of grace, of reconciliation and of salvation, is to receive the grace of God; but that this word is received in different ways is known from the parable of the Lord, Mat. 13. Some indeed receive it, but do not understand it, and so that evil one who comes snatches away what had been sown in their hearts. Others receive it at once and with joy, but they do not allow it to take root in their hearts, for they are temporary; and so it happens that when tribulation arises on account of the word of grace, they immediately take offence and fall back. Others too indeed receive it, but they are so immersed in the cares of this age, in the pursuit of deceitful wealth, and in pleasures, that the received word is choked in their hearts and made unfruitful. Do not all these receive the grace of God in vain, even if they receive it eagerly and with joy as soon as they hear it? Or do those usefully receive it who understand what they hear, and who implant the understanding in the heart, like good ground, with sincere faith, and bring forth its fruit, one a modest amount, another a greater, according to the measure of the gift of Christ?

units.la: Cum itaque Apostolus Corinthios obse-crat, ne gratiam Dei in vacuū reciperent, satis indicat receptam esse in vacuum ac frustrà, si fructu suo destituatur. Perinde ac si terram frustrà bonum semen recepisse dicas, si uel au-
units.tr: When therefore the Apostle begs the Corinthians not to receive the grace of God in vain, he sufficiently indicates that it is received in vain and to no purpose if it is deprived of its fruit. Just as if you were to say that the ground had received good seed in vain, if it were either carried off by birds, or trampled under the feet of passers-by, or unable to put down roots, or choked by thorns, and so made unfruitful;

units.la: feratur ab auibus, uel transeuntium pedibus proteratur, uel radices agere nequeat, uel spi-nis suffocetur, atq; ita infrugiferum reddatur, & medicinam utut in se bonam, receptam esse in uanum, si sic recepta collocataq; fuerit, ut restituendae sanitati nihil conducat. Quantum autem ex eo fit exitij, si medicina, unde vale-tudini adeoque & uitae consulendum erat, ab-usu reddatur inefficax, nemo cordatus non intelligit.
units.tr: and that a medicine, however good in itself, has been received in vain, if it has been received and applied in such a way that it contributes nothing to restoring health. How great the harm is when a medicine, by which health and therefore life ought to be cared for, is made ineffective by misuse, no sensible person fails to understand.

units.la: Obsecro, quis satis perpederit, quàm sit cer-ta, quàm merita, quàm irrecuperabilis ex eo perditio, si gratiaDei, sine qua saluari potest ne-mo, sic inutiliter collocetur, ut in uacuū sit re-cepta? Leuius malum est non accepisse, quàm acceptam male collocasse. Satius est non co-gnouisse uiam iusticiæ, quàm à cognita ad pri-stinæ uitae uomitum more canum reuerti. Sic enim posteriora fiunt peiora prioribus. Admo-nitio hæc vehementer necessaria est omnibus illis qui Euágelio Christi, sermoni gratiæ Dei, nomen dederunt, quorum pars maxima, dum non Christo, sed sibijpsis viuunt, satis declarat gratiam se Dei parum recepisse utiliter.
units.tr: I ask you, who has weighed sufficiently how certain, how deserved, how irrecoverable the ruin is, if the grace of God, without which no one can be saved, is applied so uselessly that it is received in vain? It is a lesser evil not to have received, than to have received and applied it badly. It is better not to have known the way of righteousness than, having known it, to return to the vomit of one's former life like a dog. For in this way the latter end becomes worse than the beginning. This admonition is very necessary for all those who have given their name to the Gospel of Christ and to the word of the grace of God, of whom the greatest part, while they live not for Christ but for themselves, sufficiently show that they have received the grace of God to little profit.

units.la: DICIT enim. In tempore accepto exaudi-ui te, inquit, & in die salutis succurri tibi.) Citat locum hunc è promptuario prophetica-rum scripturæ, ex Iefhaiah uidelicet cap. 49. ubi sic legimus, [Hebrew], id est, Sic dicit Dominus: In tē-pore beneplaciti respondi tibi, & in die salutis succurri tibi. Quo sensu positum sit hoc à Pro-pheta uaticinium, in Commentarijs nostris su-per Ieshaiam diximus. Apostolus accommo-dat illud suo proposito, ut consideratione tam accepti ac salutiferi temporis Corinthios per-moueat, quo gratiam Dei non recipiant mo-do, sed & utiliter recipiant. Huc applicat illa, in tempore accepto, item, in die salutis, quod utrunque idem est, nisi quod prius per poste-rius exponitur.
units.tr: For he says: "In an accepted time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you." He cites this passage from the storehouse of the prophetic Scriptures, namely from Isaiah chapter 49, where we read thus: [Hebrew], that is, "Thus says the Lord: In a time of good pleasure I have answered you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you." In what sense this prophecy was uttered by the Prophet we have set out in our Commentaries on Isaiah. The Apostle applies it to his purpose, so that by considering so accepted and saving a time he may move the Corinthians, that they should not only receive the grace of God, but receive it usefully. To this he applies the words "in an accepted time" and likewise "on the day of salvation," both of which amount to the same thing, except that the former is explained by the latter.

units.la: Nam cætera, ut, exaudiui te, item, succurri tibi, non bene conuenient illis, quibus sic est ultrò gratia Dei per Euangelium oblata, ut de illa ne cogitarint quidem antea, nedum ad Deum pro illa clamauerint, ut clamantes ex-audiri potuerint, & ut exauditi liberari: qua-les utique fuerunt, qui ex Gentibus in Chri-stum crediderunt, è quorum numero erant & Corinthij, quo pertinet illud Esaiæ, Romano-rum decimo ab Apostolo citatum: Inuentus fui his qui me non quærebant, conspicuus fa-ctus sum his, qui de me non interrogabant. Dicimus igitur hunc locum proprie pertinere ad populum Israelis, quem Deus in exilio ad se clamantem, cum tempus liberandi uenisset, exaudiuit & liberauit. Apostolus uero accom-modat eum suo instituto, quatenus in illo me-tio fit temporis accepti, ac diei salutis. Vnde & subijcit:
units.tr: For the other words, "I have heard you" and likewise "I have helped you," do not fit well those to whom the grace of God has been offered through the Gospel so freely that they had not even thought of it before, much less cried out to God for it, so that, crying out, they could be heard, and being heard, be set free. Such indeed were those who from the Gentiles believed in Christ, and among their number were also the Corinthians, to which belongs that passage of Isaiah cited by the Apostle in Romans chapter 10: "I was found by those who did not seek me; I was made manifest to those who did not ask for me." We say therefore that this passage properly pertains to the people of Israel, whom God, when they cried to him in exile, and when the time of deliverance had come, heard and set free. But the Apostle adapts it to his plan, insofar as there is mention in it of an accepted time and a day of salvation. Hence he adds:

units.la: ECCE nunc tempus acceptum, ecce nunc dies salutis.) Vides hoc vnum ex isto loco ad propositum applicari, quod tempori gratiæ respon-
units.tr: Behold, now is the accepted time, behold, now is the day of salvation.) You see that this one statement from that passage is applied to his purpose, namely that it answers to the time of grace.

units.la: Respondet: Erat utiq; & tũ tempus benepla-citi diuini, & dies salutis, cum tempestiuum esset in conspectu Dei, afflictum suum populum ad se clamantem exaudire, & è captiuitate liberare. Verùm eius temporis felicitas, vix vm bra quædam fuit ad id temporis collata, in quo sibi mundum Deus per Christum reconciliauit, & sermonem reconciliationis per apostolos in totum orbem emisit, ac quosuis ad hanc gratiam vocauit. Vt huius temporis felicitate supra eā de qua propheta ad Israelem uaticinatus est, extollat, non simpliciter dicit, & nunc quoque tempus acceptum est, ac dies salutis, sed emphaticè: Ecce inqt, nūc, si vnquam uerè tempus acceptū est, ecce nūc tandem uerè dies salutis.
units.tr: It answers: that time too was indeed a time of God's good pleasure and a day of salvation, since it was the proper season in the sight of God to hear his afflicted people crying out to him and to deliver them from captivity. But the happiness of that time was scarcely a faint shadow compared with the time in which God reconciled the world to himself through Christ, and sent out the word of reconciliation through the apostles into the whole world, calling all men to this grace. So that he may exalt the happiness of this time above that of which the prophet prophesied to Israel, he does not simply say, "now too is the accepted time and the day of salvation," but emphatically: "Behold," he says, "now, if ever truly, is the accepted time; behold, now at last truly is the day of salvation."

units.la: Nullo unquam tempore Deus tantum beneplaciti erga genus humanum ostendit, nulla vnquam dies tantæ salutis ferax fuit, quantę est hæc præsens. Quare etiam atque etiam uidete, ne temporis huius gratiam & felicitatem contemnentes, aut non vtiliter collocantes, tam insigni uos opportunitate in posterū priuetis. Hac expositione cauemus, ne sensus prophetæ destruatur, & iuxtà ostendim, quo modo ista ab Apostolo ad institutum quod agebat, sint omnium pertinentissimè accommodata.
units.tr: At no time has God shown such good pleasure toward the human race, and no day has ever been so fruitful of salvation, as this present one. Therefore look again and again, lest by despising or misusing the grace and happiness of this time you deprive yourselves in future of so remarkable an opportunity. By this exposition we guard against destroying the sense of the prophet, and at the same time we show how the Apostle has most fittingly applied these words to the business he was then handling.

units.la: Obseruemus igitur hoc loco, quib. elogijs tempus gratiæ Dei, tępus Noui testamenti, & Euangelij exornet, uocat illud tępus יצרון, i.beneplaciti Dei, bonæ uoluntatis, cui concordat hymnus angelicus, quo in die nati Redemptoris cecinerunt: Gloria in excelsis Deo, & in terra pax, hominibus bona uoluntas εὐδοκία, quæ Ebręis est רצון.
units.tr: Let us observe, then, in this passage, with what epithets he adorns the time of God's grace, the time of the New Testament and of the Gospel. He calls it the time of [רצון], that is, of God's good pleasure and goodwill, with which the angelic hymn agrees, which the angels sang on the day of the Redeemer's birth: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill toward men" [εὐδοκία]. In Hebrew this is [רצון].

units.la: Quid est autem beneplacitum hoc Dei aliud, quàm quòd posita ira misertus est generis humani, illudque sibi in Christo filio reconciliauit, & omnimodam erga illud beneuolentiam induit? Beneplacitum hoc Dei trahit secū quæ in cœlo sunt & in terra omnia: quid dico? Ipsum unigenitum Dei, imò Deum ipsum. Da mihi beneplacitum principis, non erit in eo quicquam, quod simul cum illo non dederis.
units.tr: But what else is this good pleasure of God, than that, with wrath laid aside, he has had mercy on the human race, has reconciled it to himself in Christ his Son, and has put on toward it every kind of kindness? This good pleasure of God brings with it all things in heaven and on earth: what am I saying? The only-begotten Son of God himself, indeed God himself. Give me the prince's favour, and there will be nothing in it that you have not given along with him.

units.la: Sic Apostolus Rom. 8. Deum pro nobis esse dicit, contenditq; fieri non posse, ut à quoquam condemnemur.
units.tr: So the Apostle says in Rom. 8 that God is for us, and he argues that it is impossible for anyone to condemn us.

units.la: Deinde uocat hoc tępus Diẽ salutis, propterea quòd in illa salus est, & parta generi humano per Christum, & mundo per apostolos ministerio prædicationis Euangelicæ dispensari cœpta.
units.tr: Then he calls this time the day of salvation, because salvation is in it, and has been obtained for the human race through Christ, and has begun to be dispensed to the world through the apostles by the ministry of the preaching of the Gospel.

units.la: Vide autem quàm competenter, & q ordinatè hæc duo, tempus beneplaciti ac diem salutis, coniunxerit. Vt enim in beneplacito regis est uita, in ira uero mors: ita in beneplacito Dei salus, in ira uero pditio existit. Pulchrè igitur tempori beneplaciti Dei diem salutis coniunxit.
units.tr: See how fittingly and how orderly he has joined these two things, the time of God's good pleasure and the day of salvation. For as in the king's good pleasure there is life, but in his wrath there is death, so in God's good pleasure there is salvation, but in his wrath there is destruction. Rightly, therefore, he joined the day of salvation to the time of God's good pleasure.

units.la: NVLLAM ulla in re dantes offensionem in quit.) Sic habetur in Græco, μηδεμίαν ἐν μηδενὶ διδόντες προσκοπὴν. Vulgata habet, nemini dantes ullam offensionem. Erasmus vertit: Nè quam vsquam demus offensionem. Primùm vocula ne, nō est in Græco hoc loco, deinde, non est δῶμεν[?] demus, sed in participio, διδόντες, id est, dantes. Fefellit hunc interpretem, quòd existimauit ista per modum exhortationis esse dicta, cum de se loquatur Apostolus hinc ad finem usq; præsentis contextus. Quare ordinanda est lectio ad hunc modum. Cooperantes autem obsecramus etiam, ne in vacuum gratiam Dei receperitis (Dicit enim. In tempore accepto audiui te, & in die salutis succurri tibi. Ecce nunc tempus acceptum, ecce nūc dies salutis) nullam ulla in re dantes offensionem, ne reprehendatur ministerium, sed in omnibus commendantes nosipsos, ut Dei ministri, &c.
units.tr: "Giving no offence in anything" [μηδεμίαν ἐν μηδενὶ διδόντες προσκοπὴν]. This is how it stands in the Greek. The Vulgate has "giving no offence to anyone." Erasmus renders it "that we give no offence anywhere." First, the little word "that not" is not in the Greek here; second, the Greek is not "let us give" (δῶμεν), but a participle, διδόντες, that is, "giving." The translator was misled because he thought these words were spoken by way of exhortation, whereas the Apostle is speaking about himself from here to the end of the present context. Therefore the reading should be ordered in this way: "But we beseech you also, working together, not to receive the grace of God in vain (for he says: 'In an accepted time I heard you, and in a day of salvation I helped you. Behold, now is the accepted time, behold, now is the day of salvation'), giving no offence in anything, so that the ministry may not be blamed, but commending ourselves in all things, as ministers of God," and so on.

units.la: Sic ista post parenthesim connectenda sunt ei quod initiò dixit: Cooperantes autem obsecramus. Loquitur enim de studio suo, quo se in ministerio sic gessit inculpabiliter, ut absque offensione cunctis prodesse, & ad salutem cooperari posset. Quod si omnino participiū διδόντες in suum uerbum mutandum uidetur, melius est ut uertatur: Nullam ulla in re dantes offensionem, ut constet sibi sermo, quo de seipso loquitur Apostolus.
units.tr: Thus these words after the parenthesis are to be connected with what he said at the beginning: "But we beseech you, working together." For he is speaking of his own zeal, by which he so conducted himself in the ministry blamelessly that he could benefit all without offence and cooperate for their salvation. But if the participle διδόντες must in any case be changed into a finite verb, it is better to render it: "Let us give no offence in anything," so that the sense of the words in which the Apostle speaks of himself is consistent.

units.la: Non est autem præter rationem, quod adhortationi, de gratia Dei, cuius ipse minister erat, non in vanum recipienda, mox de ministerio suo subijcit, illiq; hoc synceritatis vindicat, quòd nemini ex eo aliqua obijciatur causa quur offendatur, sed magis exhibeatur in omnibus occasio agnoscendi ministrum Dei. Ete nim nisi eiusmodi integritate commendetur Christi minister, ut in ministerio suo inculpabilis reperiatur, planè clumbes sunt omnes illius adhortationes: & quàtumuis sedulò admoneat curandum esse omnib. ne gratiam Dei in vanū recipiant, ipse tamen gratiam Dei ineffi-caciter prædicat, & frustra de illa non in vanū recipienda hortatur.
units.tr: It is not out of place that, after urging that the grace of God, of which he himself was a minister, should not be received in vain, he immediately goes on to speak of his ministry and claims this sincerity for it, so that no cause for offence may be given to anyone through it, but rather that occasion may be given in all things of recognising a minister of God. For unless the minister of Christ is commended by such integrity that he is found blameless in his ministry, all his exhortations are plainly empty; and however earnestly he admonishes everyone to take care not to receive the grace of God in vain, he himself preaches the grace of God ineffectively, and urges in vain that it not be received in vain.

units.la: Vide autem quàm caute non dicat: neminem ulla in re offendentes, sed, nullam ulla in re dantes offensionem. Aliud est dare offensionem, hoc est causam offensionis, & aliud offendere maleuolos nulla data offensionis causa. Offensio est data & accepta, est data, & non accepta, est non data, & tamen accepta. Offensionē dare, alienū esse debet à fidelibus omnib. alienissimum à Christi ministro. Datā offensionem accipere, infirmorum est & incautorum, quorum potissimum habenda erat ratio.
units.tr: Note how carefully he does not say, "giving offence to no one in anything," but "giving no offence in anything." It is one thing to give offence, that is, to furnish a cause of offence, and another thing to offend the ill-disposed when no cause of offence has been given. Offence may be given and taken; it may be given and not taken; it may be not given and yet taken. To give offence ought to be most alien to all the faithful, and most alien of all to the minister of Christ. To take offence that has been given belongs to the weak and the careless, and it is especially their case that had to be considered.

units.la: Qui infirmus est in via Dei, licet ubique offensionum causæ occurrant, haud tamen offenditur, sed in offensione pede quo cœpit pergit. Non datam offensionem accipere, vel errantium est, uel maleuolorum. Errantium, ut in Papatu, si minister sit uxoratus, offenditur populus, si sit publicus scortator, non offenditur, quia talibus assueuit. Maleuolorum, quando prælati ecclesiarū puritate doctrinæ Christi
units.tr: He who is weak in the way of God, although occasions of offence present themselves everywhere, is not offended, but in offence he goes on with the foot he began with. Not to take offence when it has been given belongs to the erring or to the ill-disposed. It belongs to the erring, as in Popery: if a minister is married, the people are offended; if he is a public whoremonger, they are not offended, because they have become accustomed to such men. It belongs to the ill-disposed when the prelates of the churches are offended by the purity of the doctrine of Christ,

units.la: fti offenduntur, per quam dominatui, questui, ventri & ocio illorum derogatur.
units.tr: by which their lordship, gain, belly and idleness are diminished.

units.la: Postremum hoc offensionis genus minister Christi cauere non potest, imò nec debet. Offendebat illo Paulus innumeros ex Gentibus, & Iudæis, ex falsis Apostolis & falsis fratribus; cum tamen n emini iustam obijceret offensionis causam. Quod significans dicit, nullam ulla in re dantes offensionem, ne reprehendatur ministerium.
units.tr: A minister of Christ cannot guard against this last kind of offence, and indeed he ought not to. Paul gave offence in this way to countless people, both among the Gentiles and the Jews, among the false apostles and false brothers, although he never gave a just cause of offence to anyone. Signifying this, he says: "giving no offence in anything, so that the ministry may not be blamed."

units.la: NE reprehendatur ministerium inquit.) Sic uocat suum Apostolatum. Intelligit autem de ministerio reconciliationis à Deo sibi imposito, cuius capite præcedenti meminit. Nō dicit autem simpliciter, ne malè audiam ego, ne culper ac contemnar ego, sed, ne reprehen datur ministerium, uel, ne macula inuratur ministerio. Græcè μὴ μωμηθῇ ἡ διακονία. Significat autem μώμῳ maculam. Quamuis etiam suæ famæ rationem habeat Apostolus, magis tamen folicitus est pro ministerio suo, ne illud infamiæ maculam incurrat. Nouit enim admodum esse procliue, ut quæ persona ministri delinquit, ipsi impingantur ministerio, præsertim à μωμοσκόποις, qui in hoc sunt intentissimi, ut quærant undique occasionem uituperandi ministerij, quod magis odiunt quàm ministri personam.
units.tr: "So that the ministry may not be blamed," he says. So he calls his apostleship. He means the ministry of reconciliation imposed on him by God, which he mentioned in the preceding chapter. But he does not say simply "so that I may not be ill spoken of, so that I may not be blamed and despised," but "so that the ministry may not be blamed," or "so that no stain may be inflicted on the ministry" [μὴ μωμηθῇ ἡ διακονία]. The Greek word μῶμος means a stain. Although the Apostle also takes account of his own reputation, he is nevertheless more concerned for his ministry, lest it incur the stain of infamy. For he knew very well that it is easy for what a minister's person does wrong to be charged against the ministry itself, especially by the fault-finders [μωμοσκόποι], who are most intent on seeking from every side an occasion to disparage the ministry, which they hate more than the minister's person.

units.la: Sciens hoc, non modò ipse cauet, ne reprehensibilis inueniatur, sed & ab omnibus Christi ministris hanc uitæ ac ministerij integritatem requirit, ut sint irreprehensibiles, prima Timoth. tertio, Tit. primo. Ast hodie tangit paucos hæc cura ministros. Satis est non errare prædicando, quicquid fiat viuendo. Magna pars bibunt, ludunt, negociantur, fidem fallūt, vsuram accipiunt, odio fraterno inficiuntur, melioribus beneficijs, ut vocant, impudenti ambitu inhiant, & inueniuntur, qui ne ab adulterio quidem abstineant. Hi omnes parum curant, quomodo audiat ipsorum ministerium: quia parum sunt de gloria Christi, & salute fidelium soliciti.
units.tr: Knowing this, he not only takes care himself that he not be found blameworthy, but also requires this integrity of life and ministry from all the ministers of Christ, that they be blameless, as in 1 Tim. 3 and Tit. 1. But today this care touches few ministers. It is enough, they think, not to err in preaching, whatever they do in living. Most of them drink, gamble, do business, deceive the faithful, take usury, are stained with brotherly hatred, pant with shameless ambition after the better benefices, as they call them, and are found to be such that they do not even abstain from adultery. All these care little how their ministry is heard, because they are little concerned for the glory of Christ and the salvation of the faithful.

units.la: SED in omnibus, inquit, commendantes nosipsos, ut Dei ministri.) Non est satis Christi ministro, si nullam ulla in re det offensionem, ne ministerium reprehendatur, sed & hoc ab eo requiritur, ut se insinuet & commendet omnibus, idque non in re vna & altera tantum, sed in omnibus, tanquam Dei ministrum: hoc est, ut sic se gerat in omnibus, ut cau sam inueniant omnes agnoscendi ac probandi ministrum Dei, qui videlicet gloriam Dei, nō suam quærat in omnibus, qui spiritu Dei imbutus uoluntatem Dei fideliter proponat omnibus, quiq; omnes huc & verbo & vitæ studio inuitet, ut salutis suæ rationem habentes, gratiam Dei recipiant, & vtiliter collocet. Hoc sentiens Apostolus, postquam dixit, nullam ulla in re dantes offensionem, mox subiecit, sed in omnibus commendantes nosipsos, ut Dei ministri.
units.tr: "But in all things," he says, "commending ourselves, as ministers of God." It is not enough for a minister of Christ to give no offence in any matter, so that the ministry is not blamed. He is also required to insinuate and commend himself to all, and not in one or two matters only but in all things, as a minister of God. That is, he must so conduct himself in everything that all may find cause to acknowledge and approve him as a minister of God: one who seeks the glory of God and not his own in all things, who, imbued with the Spirit of God, faithfully sets forth the will of God to everyone, and who invites all to it both by his word and by his zeal for a good life, so that, taking account of their salvation, they may receive the grace of God and make good use of it. The Apostle, having this in mind, after saying "giving no offence in any matter," immediately added, "but in all things commending ourselves, as ministers of God."

units.la: Quemadmodum autem in præcedenti par-
units.tr: Just as we said in the preceding paragraph,

units.la: ticula diximus, aliud esse offendere maleuolos sine data offensionis causa, & aliud, dare offensionem, ita sentiendum est & hoc loco. Aliud est commendare se bonis, & aliud, studere quidem, vt commendes te omnibus, & tamen interea displicere multis.
