Apostolus cum hic dicit, commendantes nosipsos in omnibus, vt Dei ministri, non euentum exprimit, sed studium, quo se omnibus tanquam Dei ministrum commendare satagebat. Alias, ut innumeros offendebat, quamuis nemini offensionis causam daret, ita paucis se commendabat effectu, licet commendaret se omnibus studio.
units.tr: so the same must be understood here. It is one thing to give offence to ill-disposed people when no cause for offence has been given, and another thing to give offence. It is one thing to commend oneself to good people, and another to strive to commend oneself to all and yet meanwhile to displease many. When the Apostle says here, "commending ourselves in all things, as ministers of God," he expresses not the result but the effort by which he took pains to commend himself to all as a minister of God. Otherwise, although he gave no one cause for offence, he offended countless people; and so he commended himself with success to few, although he commended himself to all in zeal.

units.la: In tolerātia multa, inquit, in afflictionibus, in necessitatib. in anxietatibus, in plagis, in carcerib. in seditionibus, in laboribus, in uigilijs, in ieiunijs.
units.tr: In much patience, he says, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, in stripes, in prisons, in tumults, in labours, in watchings, in fastings.

units.la: Quomodo & quam constanter se tanquā minister Dei commendarit in omnibus, consequenter memorat. Et principio singularem tolerantiam considerandam proponit, quase sic obfirmauerat in opere domini obeundo, ut ab eo nullis posset aduersis & molestijs repelli. Sic dicit: in tolerantia multa, ac mox species quasdam rerum aduersarum, ac molestarum subijcit, quibus tolerantia ipsius in mini sterio Christi indesinenter exercebatur, cum dicit: in afflictionib. in necessitatibus, in anxietatibus, &c. Quod dicit, in afflictionibus, genus est, & coniungendum cum præcedenti, ut legatur, in tolerantia multa, in afflictionib^9, ac tum sequantur afflictionum & tribulationum species, necessitates uidelicet, anxietates, plagæ, carceres, seditiones, labores, uigiliæ & ieiunia.
units.tr: He next sets out, in order, how and how steadfastly he commended himself in all things as a minister of God. And first he puts forward his singular patience, as if he had so steeled himself in performing the Lord's work that no adversities or troubles could drive him from it. He says: "in much patience," and straightway he sets out certain kinds of adverse and troublesome things, by which his patience in the ministry of Christ was constantly exercised, when he says: "in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses," and so on. The phrase "in afflictions" is a general term and is to be joined with what precedes, so that it reads "in much patience, in afflictions," and then there follow the kinds of afflictions and tribulations: namely necessities, distresses, stripes, prisons, tumults, labours, watchings and fastings.

units.la: IN afflictionibus.) De afflictionibus ipsius, illarumq; grauitate & multitudine supra, ca.1. dictum est.
units.tr: "In afflictions." Concerning his afflictions, and their severity and number, has been said above, in chapter 1.

units.la: IN necessitatibus.) Græcè est ἐν ἀνάγκαις. Intelligit de rerum necessariarum penuria, cuius & infrà, cap. vndecimo mentionem faciet. Hanc quomodo tam insignis Apostolus inciderit, mihi non minus mirum est, quàm quomodo pertulerit. In hoc ipsius tolerantia commendatur, in illo turpissima eorum qui credere coeperant, ingratitudo notatur, demptis tamen illis, qui & ipsi consimili necessitate premebantur.
units.tr: "In necessities." In Greek it is ἐν ἀνάγκαις [en anankais]. He means want of necessary things, of which he will also make mention below, in chapter 11. How so distinguished an Apostle came to fall into this is to me no less wonderful than how he endured it. In this his patience is commended; in that, the most shameful ingratitude of those who had begun to believe is noted, though excepting those who were themselves pressed by the same necessity.

units.la: Videmus hodie quoq; non paucos Christi ministros cum egestate admodum despicabili luctari, cum interea ociosi ventres in ecclesijs delicatissimè saginentur. Antiquum hoc malum est, cui & prophetæ Dei in Veteri testamento, in ipso populo Dei obnoxij fuerunt, sicuti secundo Regum quarto, mox initio capitis uidere licet.
units.tr: We see today too that not a few ministers of Christ struggle with most contemptible poverty, while meanwhile idle bellies are most daintily fattened in the churches. This is an ancient evil, to which the prophets of God in the Old Testament were also subject, even among the people of God itself, as may be seen at the very beginning of 2 Kings 4.

units.la: IN anxietatibus, inquit.) Græcè est ἐν στενοχωρίαις. Significat autem στενοχωρία proprie locorum angustiam, in qua periclitari solent, qui in illam impelluntur, sicuti in prælijs fieri consueuit. sufcuit. Transfertur autē ea uox ad animi quo-que angustiam & anxietatem, quo sensu hic posita uidetur. Vel, intelligenda est de angu-stijs, quibus in periculis, undiq; circumuallan-tibus sic arctabatur subinde, ut nullum pateret effugium.
units.tr: "In distresses," he says. In Greek it is ἐν στενοχωρίαις [en stenochōriais]. Now στενοχωρία properly signifies the narrowness of places in which those are wont to be in danger who are driven into them, as usually happens in battles. The word is also transferred to narrowness and anxiety of mind, which seems to be the sense here. Or it must be understood of the straits in which, when surrounded on every side by dangers, one was at times so hemmed in that no way of escape lay open.

units.la: IN plagis inquit.) De uerberibus loquitur, quorum meminit infrà, cap. 11. dicens: A Iudeis quinquies quadragenas plagas una minus accepi. Ter uirgis cæsus fui.
units.tr: "In stripes," he says. He speaks of beatings, of which he makes mention below, in chapter 11, saying: "Five times I received from the Jews forty stripes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods."

units.la: IN carceribus, inquit.) De his videre est, Actorum 16. Sub his comprehenduntur & uincula.
units.tr: "In prisons," he says. Of these one may see Acts 16. Chains are included under this heading.

units.la: IN seditionibus.) Græcè est, ἐν ἀκαταστασίαις. Chrysostomus intelligit crebras eiectiones, per quas fit ut nequeas uspiam consistere, ac pedem figere. Et is sensus, nec alienus est ab ipsa dictione, nec malè conuenit ijs quæ Paulo sæpe numero acciderunt. Verùm uox eadem seditionem quoq; significat. Etenim seditione obtinente sic omnia turbantur, ut nihil ferè sit in statu publico, quod non loco & ordine suo moueatur, sic ut omnia confusa reddantur & incerta. Et ex Actis Apostolorum satis patet mal-lum hoc seditionum aliquoties expertum esse Apostolum.
units.tr: "In tumults." In Greek it is ἐν ἀκαταστασίαις [en akatastasiais]. Chrysostom understands frequent expulsions, through which it happens that you cannot stand anywhere or fix your foot. This sense is not foreign to the word, and it suits well what often happened to Paul. But the same word also signifies sedition. For when sedition prevails, everything is so thrown into confusion that scarcely anything in the public state is not moved from its place and order, so that all things become confused and uncertain. And from the Acts of the Apostles it is sufficiently clear that the Apostle more than once experienced this evil of sedition.

units.la: Quare uterq; sensus sic est comparatus, ut nihil sit periculi vtrum retineas. Admodum graue est, ac periculosum, infame etiā, pro eo haberi qui seditiosus homo sit, & author seditionum. Quid autem iniquius excogitari potest, quàm pro talibus habere eos, qui & pacis sunt studiosissimi, & omnibus ex æquo confulissimum esse cupiunt: quales fuerunt Christus & Apostoli, qui tamen à maleuolis pro seditiosis sunt habiti. Mox ad primum Euangelicæ lucis exortum per sua membra Satã tanquam tenebrarum princeps, seditiones excitat, ut harum authores esse uideantur in speciem, qui nouam & insolitam doctrinam adferunt, quo illa hac notetur infamia, quòd pariat seditiones. Nos huius rei nostra quoque ætate aliquod uidimus exempla. Hanc Satanæ malitiam minister Christi diligenter quo ad eius fieri potest obseruet & causeat. Quod si cauere non poterit, sic tamen se gerat, ut nullam seditioni dedisse causam constare possit, ipsam seditionē cum Paulo animo infracto ferat, oretque do-minum, ut motus à Satana excitatos compescat, largiaturq; pacis serenum, in quo ueritas Dei propagari queat.
units.tr: Both senses, therefore, are so related that there is no danger in retaining either. It is very grievous, dangerous and also infamous to be regarded as a seditious man and an author of sedition. What could be devised as more unjust than to regard as such those who are most zealous for peace and most desire to consult the good of all alike? Such were Christ and the Apostles, who nevertheless were held to be seditious by ill-disposed men. Soon, at the first rising of the light of the Gospel, Satan, as prince of darkness, through his members stirs up seditions, so that those who bring the new and unusual doctrine seem in appearance to be the authors of them, and so that the doctrine is marked with this infamy, that it produces seditions. We have seen some examples of this in our own age. The minister of Christ should diligently watch against this malice of Satan, and guard against it as far as it can be done. But if he cannot guard against it, let him so conduct himself that it can be established that he gave no cause for sedition. Let him bear the sedition itself with an unbroken spirit, as Paul did, and pray the Lord to restrain the disturbances stirred up by Satan and to grant the calm of peace, in which the truth of God may be spread abroad.

units.la: IN laboribus, inquit.) Laboriosa res est ministerium Apostolicum, episcopatus plus habet quietis. Laborib. Apostolatus ipse feruor Pauli magnum cumulum adiecit. Plus enim omnibus laborauit. Huc accessit operatio manuaria, unde se sustentaret, ne cui esset oneri. Sic vicissim apostolicis & manuarijs laboribus per mare, per terras discurrendo, prædicando, vnumquenq; separatim solicitando, & operando noctes ac dies fatigabatur, ut mirū sit quomodo tot tantéq; irremissorum laborum tolerantiæ sufficere potuerit.
units.tr: "In labours," he says. The Apostolic ministry is a laborious thing; the episcopate has more quiet. Paul's apostolic zeal itself added a great burden to his labours, for he laboured more than all. To this was added manual work, by which he supported himself so as not to be a burden to anyone. Thus, in turn, by apostolic and manual labours, running through sea and land, preaching, urging each one separately, and working night and day, he was worn down. So it is a wonder how he could be sufficient for the endurance of so many and such great unremitting labours.

units.la: IN vigilijs.) Duplex illi vigiliarum genus: unum erat, quo ad operandū, alterum, quo ad docendum vtebatur. Posterioris exemplū habetur in Actis, cap. 20. ubi memoratur, quomodo Troadæ totam noctem ad diluculum usq; in opus domini docēdo & exhortando insum pserit.
units.tr: "In watchings." He had a twofold kind of watching: one he used for working, the other for teaching. An example of the latter is in Acts 20, where it is recorded how at Troas he spent the whole night until daybreak in teaching and exhorting in the work of the Lord.

units.la: Quod illic fecit, dubio procul pro consuetudine sua fecit, qua noctu cœtum fidelium congregabat, quòd diurni cœuentus magno essent cum periculo coniuncti. Hinc vsus vigiliarum natus est in ecclesia inter primos Christianos, temporib. persequutionū, quem postea episcopi pacis quoq; tempore retinuerut, ac dieb. profestis deputarūt, perinde ac si tutum non esset interdiu congregare ecclesiam. Tandē nil aliud quàm nomen inane remansit.
units.tr: What he did there he undoubtedly did according to his custom, by which he gathered the assembly of the faithful at night, because daytime gatherings were attended with great danger. Hence the custom of night watches arose in the Church among the first Christians in times of persecution. The bishops later retained it even in a time of peace, and assigned it to working days, as if it were not safe to assemble the Church by day. In the end nothing remained of it but an empty name.

units.la: IN ieiuniis, inquit.) Græcè est, ἐν νηστείαις. Accipitur autem uox νηστεία frequentius quidem pro ieiunio religioso, ac sponte suscepto, uerū Actorum 27. pro necessario quoq; usurpatur, in historia uidelicet naufragij, in quo Paulus erat uinctus, ubi sic legitur: Multo autem tempore peracto, & cum esset iam periculosa nauigatio, διὰ τὸ καὶ τὴν νηστείαν ἤδη παρελθεῖν, id est, quod ieiunium iam præterisset. Erasinus uertit, ob id quoq; quòd iam ultra tempus stinuissent inediam, quasi sit διὰ τὸ καὶ τὴν ἀσιτίαν παρελθεῖν, qua uoce Lucas eodem postea sensu in eadem utitur historia, dicens, πολλῆς δὲ ἀσιτίας ὑπαρχούσης, id est, cum autem multa iam esset inedia. Vnde apparet usurpasse Lucam νηστείαν & ἀσιτίαν ex æquo, de ieiunio neq; religioso, neq; sponte suscepto, sed de necessario & inuoluntario, quale frequenter accidit militantib. nauigantibus, & inopia rerum necessariarum pressis.
units.tr: "In fastings," he says. In Greek it is ἐν νηστείαις [en nēsteiais]. The word νηστεία is taken more often indeed for religious fasting, undertaken voluntarily. But in Acts 27 it is also used of a necessary fast, namely in the story of the shipwreck, in which Paul was bound, where it is read: "Now when much time had passed, and the voyage was already dangerous, because the fast was already past" [διὰ τὸ καὶ τὴν νηστείαν ἤδη παρελθεῖν], that is, because the fast was already over. Erasmus translates it: "also because they had already gone beyond the time they had endured hunger." Luke uses the word ἀσιτία [asitia] in the same story later, saying "when there was now much want of food" [πολλῆς δὲ ἀσιτίας ὑπαρχούσης], that is, "when there was now much hunger." Hence it is clear that Luke used νηστεία and ἀσιτία interchangeably, of a fast that was neither religious nor voluntary, but necessary and involuntary, such as often befalls soldiers and sailors pressed by want of necessary things.

units.la: Iam quod præsentem locū attinet, scio alios exponere de uoluntario ieiunio, alios de necessario, alios de utroq;. Mihi rectius sentire uidetur, qui de necessario accipiunt, quod frequenter pertulit Apostolus, non inuitus quidē, patienter tamen, tanquam speciem afflictionum Christi. Sic sentire placet, quod præter rationem ac propositum Apostoli uidetur ieiunio voluntario, ac spōte suscepto tribuere tolerantiam. Cæterum de ieiunio in Matthæo nostro pleraq; diximus, cap. 4.
units.tr: As for the present passage, I know that some expound it of voluntary fasting, others of compulsory fasting, and others of both. It seems to me more correct to take it of compulsory fasting, which the Apostle often endured, not unwillingly but patiently, as a kind of the afflictions of Christ. I am pleased to hold this view, because it seems contrary to the Apostle's reasoning and purpose to ascribe endurance to voluntary and self-imposed fasting. Otherwise, we have said much about fasting in our commentary on Matthew, chapter 4.

units.la: IN puritate, inquit, in scientia, in animi lenitate, in benignitate, in spiritu sancto, in charitate non simulata, in sermone ueritatis, in potentia Dei.) Cœpit recensere, quibus se uirtutibus tā quam Dei ministrum commendet in omnibus. Inter has primum locum tribuit tolerantiæ afflictionum, quarum aliquot species adnumerauit. Iam consequenter tolerantiæ subijcit & reliquas uirtutes, haud quidem omnes, eas tamen in quibus abūdè sufficienter Dei possis agnoscere ministrum.
units.tr: "In purity," he says, "in knowledge, in kindness, in gentleness, in the Holy Spirit, in love unfeigned, in the word of truth, in the power of God." He began to list the virtues by which he commends himself in all things as a minister of God. Among these he first places endurance of afflictions, of which he has enumerated several kinds. Next he adds the remaining virtues, not all of them indeed, but those by which one may sufficiently recognise a minister of God.

units.la: IN puritate, inquit.) Græcè est, ἐν ἁγνότητι. Vulgata habet, in castitate. Loquitur de puritate uitæ, cuius oppositum est lasciuiarum & scortationū impuritas. Nō loquitur de virgini{A}tate, aut viduali continentia, sed de puritate, cuius seruantes esse possunt, ac debent etiam coniuges. Vbi Timotheum suum hortatur, vt sit forma fidelium in sermone, in conuersatione, in dilectione, in spiritu, in fide, ἐν ἁγνείᾳ, id est, puritate, non hoc agit, vt Timotheus suo exemplo quosuis ad virginalem castitatem prouocet, sed vt forma sit omnibus, etiam coniugibus vitae ab omni scortationum, ac libidinū immundicia purae. Et Tit.2. Vbi doceri vult adolescentulas, vt maritos suos diligant, vt liberos ament, vt sobriē sint, σώφρονας, inquit, id est, purae, &c. non requirit ab illis virginalem, sed coniugalem castitatem.
units.tr: "In purity," he says. In Greek it is ἐν ἁγνότητι [en hagnotēti]. The Vulgate has "in chastity." He speaks of purity of life, whose opposite is the impurity of lewdness and fornication. He is not speaking of virginity or the continence of widows, but of a purity which married people also can and should keep. When he urges his Timothy to be a pattern to the faithful in speech, conduct, love, spirit, faith, and ἐν ἁγνείᾳ [en hagneia], that is, in purity, he does not mean that Timothy should by his example urge everyone to virginal chastity, but that he should be a pattern to all, including married people, of a life clean from every impurity of fornication and lust. Likewise in Titus 2, where he wants young women taught to love their husbands and their children, to be sober, σώφρονας [sōphronas], he says, that is, chaste, and so on. He does not require virginal chastity from them, but conjugal chastity.

units.la: Notū est illud Paphnutij, nunquā satis in ecclesia obseruatū dictū, quoin concilio Niceno, cum episcopi nouam legem de adimendo ministris visu coniugij, in ecclesias introducere vellent, diserte testatus est, castitatem esse congressum viri cū uxore legitima. Vide Socratē libro primo Ecclef.hiftor. cap.11.Et hic ipse Apostolus, non modò coniugium honorabile inter omnes, sed & cubile coniugū impollutum esse dicit.
units.tr: There is the well-known saying of Paphnutius, never sufficiently observed in the Church, which he uttered at the Council of Nicaea, when the bishops wanted to introduce into the churches a new law removing marriage from the ministers. He plainly testified that chastity is the intercourse of a man with his lawful wife. See Socrates, Ecclesiastical History, book 1, chapter 11. And this same Apostol says that not only is marriage honourable among all, but also that the marriage bed is undefiled.

units.la: Cū igitur hic inter cæteras virtutes, in quibus se ministrum esse Dei comprobauit, ponit puritatem, significat se in Apostolatu suo vitæ puritatem studiosissimè custodiuisse, quod haud parum argumenti habeat impuritas vitæ, ministri non Dei, sed carnis & immundarum libidinum. Iam pontificij cum sint omnis generis libidinibus, palam & impudenter immersi, vitamque viuant omnium impurissimam, nihilo tamen seciùs pro Dei voluntate haberi ministris. Et interea impuritatis eos damnant, qui coniuges Christo domino, in Euangelio ipsius ministrant.
units.tr: Since, then, he here places purity among the other virtues by which he proved himself a minister of God, he means that in his apostleship he most zealously guarded the purity of his life. Impurity of life is a strong argument that a minister is not of God but of the flesh and of unclean lusts. Now the Papists, who are plunged openly and shamelessly into every kind of lust and live the most impure of lives, are nevertheless held by them to be ministers according to God's will. Meanwhile they condemn as impure those who serve the Lord Christ in the Gospel as married men.

units.la: IN scientia, inquit.) Dubium non est, quin non loquatur de scientia sæculari, quam sibi nusquam vindicat. Loquitur ergo de scientia rerum spiritualium, quemadmodum & infra cap.vndecimo, cum dicit: Licet imperitus sim sermone, ἀλλ' ἐν τῇ γνώσει, id est, non tamen scientia. Obsecro sine hac quomodo agnoscēs ministrum & interpretem Dei? Potest ἱκανότης uir esse probus, & Christianus: at Apostolus & minister sermonis vitæ esse non potest, cui nō est donum scientiæ rerū spiritualium, præsertim earum quę mysteria Christi concernunt. Cum ergo Apostolus scientiā hanc vbertim expromeret, vtiq; comprobabat se singularem esse Dei ministrum.
units.tr: "In knowledge," he says. There is no doubt that he is not speaking of worldly learning, which he nowhere claims for himself. He is therefore speaking of knowledge of spiritual things, just as in chapter 11 below, when he says: "Though I am unskilled in speech, but not in knowledge" [ἀλλ' ἐν τῇ γνώσει, all' en tē gnōsei]. I ask, without this knowledge, how will you recognise a minister and interpreter of God? A man may be an honest and upright Christian and yet lack ability; but an Apostle, a minister of the word of life, cannot be one who lacks the gift of knowledge of spiritual things, especially of those that concern the mysteries of Christ. Since, then, the Apostle set forth this knowledge abundantly, he plainly proved himself a singular minister of God.

units.la: IN animi lenitate.) Græcè est, ἐν μακροθυμίᾳ. Sonat autem μακροθυμία eam animi lenitatem, qua tardē ad iram est, & procul ab ὀξυθυμία, id est, excandescentia, quæ ex diametro μακροθυμία opponitur. De Deo testantur scripturæ, quod sit אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם, id est, μακροθυμὸς. Consequitur ergo nihil minus esse, quàm ministrum beneuoli Dei, qui ὀξύθυμος est, id est, præceps ad iram. Qui eiusmodi est, irati Dei minister esse potest, quales sunt tyranni: beneuoli ac ministis esse non potest. Cum ergo Apostolus minister esset gratiæ Dei, non conueniebat ut esset ad irā propensus, quare dono Dei factū est vt esset μακροθυμός, & ea se virtute ministrū placa ti ac beneuoli Dei esse comprobaret.
units.tr: "In gentleness of spirit." In Greek it is ἐν μακροθυμίᾳ [en makrothymia]. Makrothymia means that gentleness of spirit by which one is slow to anger, and it is far from ὀξυθυμία [oxythymia], that is, quickness to anger, which is the direct opposite of makrothymia. The Scriptures bear witness that God is אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם [erek appayim], that is, μακρόθυμος [makrothymos], long-suffering. It follows that nothing is less fitting for a minister of a kindly God than to be quick to anger. A man of this kind can be a minister of an angry God, as tyrants are; he cannot be a minister of a kindly God. Since, then, the Apostle was a minister of the grace of God, it was not fitting that he should be prone to anger. Therefore by the gift of God he was made long-suffering, and by this virtue he proved himself a minister of a gentle and kindly God.

units.la: IN benignitate.) Græcè est, ἐν χρηστότητι. Vulgata habet in suauitate. Nescio an Latina vox benignitas, Græcè χρηστότης ex æquo respondeat. Benignitas nanq; ea virtus est, qua quod datur, non maligne, sed benigne, id est, large datur. Vnde terra fructus large reddens benigna vocatur. χρηστότης vero animi ac morū placiditatem, comitatem, suauitatemque significat: quæ virtus admodum est insignis, ac mirum in modum ad commendationem ministerij facit.
units.tr: "In kindness." In Greek it is ἐν χρηστότητι [en chrēstotēti]. The Vulgate has "in sweetness." I do not know whether the Latin word benignitas corresponds exactly to the Greek χρηστότης [chrēstotēs]. Benignitas is that virtue by which what is given is given not grudgingly but kindly, that is, generously; hence the earth that yields its fruit abundantly is called benign. But χρηστότης signifies the calmness, courtesy and sweetness of disposition and manners. This virtue is very distinguished, and it greatly adds to the commendation of the ministry.

units.la: Opponit illi Apostolus Roma. 11. ἀποτομίαν, id est, seueritatē, dicēs: ἐπὶ οὖν χρηστότητα καὶ ἀποτομίαν θεοῦ. Hæc autem morum placiditas ac suauitas retineri non potest, nisi adsit μακροθυμία. Quare illam Apostolus præmisit, quemadmodum & 1.Corint.13. cum dicit: ἡ ἀγάπη μακροθυμεῖ, χρηστεύεται. Et Galat.5. μακροθυμία, χρηστότης. Certè altera non poterit sine altera consistere. Vbi ὀξυθυμία est, ibi χρηστότης esse non potest: rursus ubi χρηστότης est, ibi ὀξυθυμία locum non inuenit.
units.tr: The Apostle sets against it ἀποτομία [apotomia], that is, severity, in Romans 11, saying: "Behold therefore the kindness and the severity of God" [ἐπὶ οὖν χρηστότητα καὶ ἀποτομίαν θεοῦ]. But this calmness and sweetness of manners cannot be kept unless long-suffering is present. Therefore the Apostle put it first, as in 1 Corinthians 13, where he says: "Love is patient, is kind" [ἡ ἀγάπη μακροθυμεῖ, χρηστεύεται]. And in Galatians 5: "long-suffering, kindness" [μακροθυμία, χρηστότης]. Certainly the one cannot exist without the other. Where there is quickness to anger, there kindness cannot be; and again, where kindness is, quickness to anger finds no place.

units.la: IN spiritu sancto inquit.) Non incommode acceperis hoc de donis spiritus sancti, quę Græcè charismata.1 Corinthior.14. vocantur. Nam & illa plurimum faciebant ad commendandū ministerium. Haud tamen displicet, quod nonnulli spiritum accipiunt hic pro animo ac mente, vt significet Apostolus in omnibus se & erga omnes agere animo sancto, id est, simplici, candido, puro, & ab omni hypocrysi alieno. Et talis animō non est ex carne, sed ex dono spiritus sancti. Qualitas spiritus hominis abscondi constanter non poterit, sed leui momento proditur. Plurimum autem facit ad agnoscendum ministrum Dei, si in omnibus quæ agit, spiritum non prophanum, sed sanctum spiret.
units.tr: "In the Holy Spirit," he says. You may not wrongly take this of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which in Greek are called χαρίσματα [charismata], in 1 Corinthians 14. For these also greatly helped to commend the ministry. Yet it is not objectionable that some take spirit here for disposition and mind, so that the Apostle means that in all things and towards all he acts with a holy spirit, that is, a simple, sincere, pure mind, free from all hypocrisy. Such a disposition does not come from the flesh but from the gift of the Holy Spirit. The quality of a man's spirit cannot be hidden for long but is revealed in a short time. It greatly helps to recognise a minister of God if in all that he does he breathes a spirit not profane but holy.

units.la: IN charitate non simulata, inquit.) Et Christus ipse notā hanc posuit, qua discipuli ipsius cognoscantur. Et Deus cum sit charitas, vtiq; ministros suos spiritu charitatis imbuit, quibus ipse ministerium reconciliationis imponit. Et per hanc igitur ministrum se Dei declarauit Apostolus, & in omnibus sese commendauit, & approbauit illis, cum quibus egit. Non est autem ociosum, quod non simpliciter dicit: Et in charitate, sed addit: non simulata. Sic enim vindicat sibi veram charitatem, illamque à falsa distinguit. Vera eorum est, qui spiritu sunt veritatis regenerati, adeoque & filij Dei, & eorum quoque, qui veritatis sunt ministri. Falsa vero eorum, qui spiritu mendacij ducuntur, & cum primis pseudapostolorum, qui verbis dilectionem iactant, vt incautos fallant.
units.tr: "In love unfeigned," he says. Christ himself gave this as the mark by which his disciples are known. And since God is love, he surely imbues his ministers, to whom he entrusts the ministry of reconciliation, with the spirit of love. Through this, then, the Apostle showed himself a minister of God, and commended himself in all things, and approved himself to those with whom he dealt. It is not idle that he does not simply say "in love," but adds "unfeigned." For thus he claims for himself true love and distinguishes it from false love. True love belongs to those who are born again by the Spirit of truth, and so to the sons of God and also to those who are ministers of the truth. False love belongs to those who are led by the spirit of lies, and above all to the false apostles, who boast of love in words in order to deceive the unwary.

units.la: IN sermone veritatis, inquit.) Exponunt de doctrina. Sanè ministri Dei est q uera sunt docere. Et utiq; doctrina Apostoli sermo erat non mendacij, sed veritatis. Docuit quidem quæ vera sunt, & docuit ut minister Dei: at cū veritas illa Euangelij Dei peregrina fit in terris, & non nisi electis, ac credentibus probetur, ipse vero in omnibus sese non electis tantum, & fidelibus, sed & quibuslibet commendare scribat, easq; hic uirtutes recenseat, quæ incredulis quoque probantur, existimo quod dicit, in sermone veritatis, intelligedum esse de veritate omnium eorum, quæ ad cōuictum humanū pertinentia, cum quibuslibet loquebatur, ne quo pacto ulla in re uanus in uerbis deprehenderetur, quod genus uicij etiam infidelibus admodum improbatur. Nec fieri potest, ut credant eum in doctrina esse veracem, quem alias uanum ac mendacem in uerbis deprehendunt.
units.tr: "In the word of truth," he says. Some expound this of doctrine. Certainly it is the duty of a minister of God to teach what is true, and the Apostle's teaching was surely a word not of falsehood but of truth. He did indeed teach what is true, and taught as a minister of God. But since that truth of the Gospel of God is strange on earth and is approved only by the elect and believers, while he writes that he commends himself in all things not only to the elect and faithful but to anyone at all, and lists here those virtues which are also acknowledged by unbelievers, I think that by "the word of truth" we must understand the truthfulness of all those things that pertain to human intercourse, when he spoke with anyone at all, so that in no matter he might be caught being vain or false in words, a fault which even unbelievers strongly disapprove. Nor can it be that they believe him to be truthful in doctrine when they find him vain and lying in his words on other occasions.

units.la: Hunc itaq; sensum præsentis loci germanū esse iudico. Si tamen de doctrinæ veritate quisquam accipiendum esse putauerat, habet 2. Tim. 2. locum, ubi doctrina sermo veritatis ab Apostolo uocatur.
units.tr: I judge this to be the true sense of the present passage. Yet if anyone thinks it should be understood of the truth of doctrine, he has 2 Timothy 2, where the Apostle calls doctrine "the word of truth".

units.la: IN potentia Dei.) De potentia signorū ac miraculorū loquitur, quæ per ipsum ædebantur, ut sermo Euangelij quod prædicabat, confirmaretur. Hæc potentia exordijs erat Euangelicæ prædicationis addita, donec illa confirmaretur, postea cessauit, qua cessante subsequuta est operatio Satanæ, qua impostor ille per suos apostolos, falsis ac mendacibus signis orbem dementauit, qua de re 2. Thessal. 2. sic leginus: cuius est aduentus secundum operationem Satanæ, cum omni potentia & signis ac prodigijs mendacibus, & cum omni deceptione iniusticiæ, in ijs quæ pereunt, pro eo quod dilectionem veritatis non receperunt in hoc, ut salui fierent. De eiusmodi signis ac miraculis innumerosa uolumina in Papatu conscripta habentur, & à seductis religiosè, imò superstitiosè leguntur.
units.tr: "In the power of God." He speaks of the power of the signs and miracles that were done through him, by which the gospel he preached was confirmed. This power was added at the beginning of the evangelical preaching until that preaching was confirmed; afterwards it ceased. When it ceased, the working of Satan followed, by which that impostor, through his apostles, with false and lying signs, deluded the world. On this matter we read in 2 Thessalonians 2: "whose coming is according to the working of Satan, with all power and lying signs and wonders, and with all deception of unrighteousness, among those who perish, because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved." Countless volumes about signs and miracles of this kind have been written in the Papacy, and are read religiously, or rather superstitiously, by those who have been seduced.

units.la: PER arma iusticiæ, dextra ac sinistra, inquit, per gloriam & ignominiam, per conuicia & laudes.) In Græco est, διὰ τῶν ὅπλων τῆς δικαιοσύνης τῶν δεξιῶν καὶ ἀριστερῶν. Vulgata habet, à dextris & à sinistris: quoniam arma quæ sunt à dextris dextra, & quæ à sinistris sinistra, rectè uocantur, nihil discrepantiæ est in duabus hisce uersionibus.
units.tr: "Through the weapons of righteousness, on the right hand and on the left," he says, "through glory and dishonour, through evil report and good report." In the Greek it is: "through the weapons of righteousness, of the right hand and of the left" [διὰ τῶν ὅπλων τῆς δικαιοσύνης τῶν δεξιῶν καὶ ἀριστερῶν]. The Vulgate has "on the right and on the left". Since weapons that are on the right are rightly called right, and those on the left left, there is no difference between these two versions.

units.la: Comparat autem se militi sic armato, ut dextra gladium habeat, sinistra scutum, gladio impetat hostem, scuto ictus ac tela illius excipiat. Arma iusticiæ sunt, quibus iusticiæ contra iniusticiam militatur. Sic illa & Romanorum sexto, uocat. Hos se dicit utrinque instructum. Quare in eo quod dicit: per arma iusticiæ dextra ac sinistra, subaudiendū est, instructi. Quæ autem arma iusticiæ intelligat, puto accipiendum esse ex præcedentibus, sic ut sinistra sint, tolerantia, qua ut scuto ictus hostis, ita omnis generis afflictiones excipiuntur ac feruntur, dextra uero, puritas, scientia, animi lenitas, benignitas, spiritus sanctus, cha-
units.tr: He compares himself to a soldier so armed that he holds a sword in his right hand and a shield in his left: he attacks the enemy with the sword and receives the enemy's blows and missiles on the shield. The weapons of righteousness are those with which righteousness fights against unrighteousness; so he calls them in Romans 6 as well. He says that he is equipped on both sides. Therefore in the words "through the weapons of righteousness, on the right hand and on the left" we must supply "equipped". As for what he means by the weapons of righteousness, I think we should take them from what precedes: the left-hand weapon is endurance, by which every kind of affliction is received and borne, as the shield receives the enemy's blow; the right-hand weapons are purity, knowledge, gentleness of spirit, kindness, the Holy Spirit,

units.la: ritas non simulata, sermo veritatis, ac potentia Dei, quibus antiquus hostis, & omnes qui veritati Dei aduersantur, repelluntur. Sane his armis pugnando declarauit se militem ac ministrum esse Dei.
units.tr: unfeigned love, the word of truth, and the power of God, by which the ancient enemy and all who oppose the truth of God are driven back. Indeed, by fighting with these weapons he showed that he was a soldier and minister of God.

units.la: PER gloriam, inquit, & ignominiam, per conuicia & laudes.) Quidā ad hæc referunt, quod dixit, per arma iusticiæ, dextra ac sinistra, quasi gloria & laudes sint arma dextra, ignominia & conuicia sinistra, ueruin non uideo quomodo hæc sint arma iusticiæ, cū ignominia & conuicia magis iniusticiæ quàm iusticiæ conueniant. Nos hunc existimamus esse Apostoli sensum. His itaque uelut armis iusticiæ à dextris & à sinistris instructi, sic stationem nostram tuemur, ut inde, nec per gloriam, nec ignominiam, neq; per conuicia, neq; per laudes dimoueamur. Quare subaudiendum est uerbum aliquod, ut pote penetramus, ut legatur ad hunc modum.
units.tr: "Through glory," he says, "and dishonour, through evil report and good report." Some refer this to what he said, "through the weapons of righteousness, on the right hand and on the left", as if glory and praise were the right-hand weapons and dishonour and evil report the left. But I do not see how these are weapons of righteousness, since dishonour and evil report belong more to unrighteousness than to righteousness. We think this is the Apostle's meaning. Equipped with these weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, we hold our position so that we are moved from it neither by glory nor by dishonour, neither by evil report nor by praise. Therefore some word must be supplied, such as "we advance", so that it reads in this way:

units.la: PER arma hæc iusticiæ (habetur enim articulus in Græco διὰ τῶν ὅπλων) dextra ac sinistra instructi penetramus per gloriam & ignominiam, per conuicia & laudes. Quasi dicat: Sic ut nec gloria & laude efferamur, nec ignominia & conuicijs deijciamur. Sicubi laudamur & extollimur, non inflamur, sed commendamus nos hominibus benignitate, spiritu sancto, & charitate non simulata. Si ignominia & conuicijs impetimur, nec deijcimur animo, nec excandescimus, nec malum pro malo reddimus, sed commendamus nos tanquam ministrum Dei, tolerantia & animi lenitate.
units.tr: "Through these weapons of righteousness" (for the Greek has the article: διὰ τῶν ὅπλων) "equipped on the right and on the left we advance through glory and dishonour, through evil report and good report." As if to say: let us neither be lifted up by glory and praise, nor cast down by dishonour and reproaches. Where we are praised and exalted, we are not inflated, but we commend ourselves to people by kindness, by the Holy Spirit, and by unfeigned love. If we are assailed with dishonour and reproaches, we are neither cast down in spirit, nor flare up in anger, nor repay evil for evil, but we commend ourselves as ministers of God, by endurance and gentleness of spirit.

units.la: Quod autē post gloriā & ignominiam, adijcit conuicia & laudes, specificationem habet. Nam gloria & ignominia in genere, conuicia uero & laudes in specie dixit. Species enim gloriæ est laus, & species ignominiæ est conuicium. Significat igitur Apostolus idem sibi euenire quod Christo domino, qui & ipse ab alijs laudabatur, ab alijs uituperabatur. Nā alij de illo dicebant, bonus est, alij contrà, non, aiebant, sed seducit turbas. Ioan. 7. Et hæc communis sors est omniū uerorū Christi ministrorū, ut à bonis quidē laudentur, à reprobis uero innumeris conuicijs impetantur ac proscindantur. Quare cogitandum ipsis est, non esse discipulum supra magistrū, curandumq;, ut cū Apostolo armis iusticiæ, tā sinistris quàm dextris, muniti utrunq; cuentum sic excipiant, ut in utroque ueros se Christi declarent esse ministros.
units.tr: Moreover, the fact that after "glory and dishonour" he adds "evil report and good report" is a specification. For he spoke of glory and dishonour in general, and of good report and evil report in particular: praise is a species of glory, and reproach is a species of dishonour. The Apostle therefore means that what happened to Christ the Lord happens to him too, for Christ too was praised by some and reviled by others. For some said of him, "He is good"; others said on the contrary, "No, but he leads the crowds astray" (John 7). This is the common lot of all true ministers of Christ: they are praised by good people, but assailed and torn to pieces by countless reproaches from the wicked. So they must reflect that the disciple is not above his master, and take care that, armed with the weapons of righteousness, both left and right, they receive both kinds of report in such a way that in each they show themselves to be true ministers of Christ.

units.la: QVASI impostores, inquit, & tamen ueraces, quasi ignoti, & tamē noti, &c. In Græco est ὡς πλάνοι, καὶ ἀληθεῖς, ὡς ἀγνοούμενοι, καὶ ἐπιγινωσκόμενοι. i. ut impostores, & ueraces, ut ignoti, & cogniti. Omnino subintelligendū est aliquid, nec displicet, quod Eras. uertit, & tñ ueraces, & tamē noti. Quod dixit p ignominiā & conuicia explicat, recensens aliquot reproborum conuicia, quibus persona ipsius, & per cōsequens Apostolatum quoque obscurare nitebantur.
units.tr: "As deceivers," he says, "and yet true; as unknown, and yet well known," etc. In the Greek it is: "as deceivers, and true; as unknown, and known" [ὡς πλάνοι, καὶ ἀληθεῖς, ὡς ἀγνοούμενοι, καὶ ἐπιγινωσκόμενοι]; that is, "as impostors, and true; as unknown, and recognised." Something must certainly be understood, and Erasmus's translation, "and yet true, and yet well known", is not objectionable. What he said he explains through "dishonour and reproaches", listing some of the reproaches of the wicked by which they tried to obscure his person, and consequently his apostleship too.

units.la: Vocabant eum impostorem, hominem ignotum, morti deuotum, castigatum, tristem,
units.tr: They called him an impostor, a man unknown, devoted to death, chastised, sorrowful,

units.la: B ... pauperem, ac nihil habentem. Hisce conuitijs annectit singulis, quàm nihil sit minus, quàm quod illi sibi exprobrant. Sic dicit:
units.tr: ... poor, and having nothing. He attaches to each of these reproaches how far from the truth it is, compared with what they charged him with. He says:

units.la: QVASI impostores.) Hoc est, habemur pro impostoribus, suspecti reddimur, & auersandi, quasi simus seductores. Fiebat hoc à Iudeis, incredulis ex Gentibus, & pseudapostolis, præsertim illis, qui quæstum exercebát in sua religione, eráts; pessimi impostores. Nam hoc genus hominum sic animatu est, ut emergentem veritatis lucem, quam ferre non potest, impostura & hæresim, illiusque ministros impostores, & hæreticos uocet. Accidit hoc & ipsi Christo, de quo ad Pilatum dicebant: Recordati sumus, quod seductor & impostor ille dixit, Matth.27.
units.tr: "As deceivers." That is, we are regarded as impostors; we are made suspect and to be shunned, as if we were seducers. This was done by the Jews, by unbelievers among the Gentiles, and by false apostles, especially those who made gain out of their religion and were the worst of impostors. For this kind of men is so disposed that, whenever the light of truth rises which they cannot bear, they call it imposture and heresy, and its ministers impostors and heretics. This happened to Christ himself, of whom they said to Pilate: "We remember that that seducer and impostor said" (Matthew 27).

units.la: Quid ad hoc Apostolus? Et tamen, inquit, ueraces. Quasi dicat: Vtut habeamur pro impostoribus, impostores tamen non sumus, sed ueraces, ueritatem Dei fideliter docētes. Non dicit, & tamen ipsi sunt impostores, sed, & tamen ueraces, intellige sumus. Non hoc agebat, ut conuicia cóuitijs rependeret, sed & ministerium suum contra insimulationem impostura defenderet.
units.tr: What does the Apostle say to this? "And yet true," he says. As if to say: however much we may be regarded as impostors, we are not impostors, but true men, faithfully teaching the truth of God. He does not say, "and yet they themselves are impostors", but "and yet true"; supply "we are". He was not doing this to repay reproaches with reproaches, but to defend his ministry against the charge of imposture.

units.la: QVASI ignoti, inquit, & tamen noti.) Dicebant ignotus & obscurus homo est, nescimus quis sit, & unde sit. Quemadmodum canes ignotis allatrát: ita illi in eo erant, ut Paulo quasi ignoto oblatrarent omnes.
units.tr: "As unknown," he says, "and yet well known." They said: "He is an obscure man; we do not know who he is or where he comes from." Just as dogs bark at strangers, so they were all barking at Paul as if he were unknown.

units.la: ET tamen noti, inquit.) Si quisquam qualis esset notus erat, notus utique erat Paulus. Nam cum in omnibus ministrum se Dei esse comprobaret, utique ignotus & obscurus esse nō poterat, præsertim illis, qui ab ipso in Christo Iesu regenerabantur. Obscuritas familiæ ac natalium, quam ipsi obijciebant reprobi, nihil faciebat ad propositum, & interea celebritatem nominis ac ministerij, qua passim illustrabatur, egregiè dissimulabant: imò hæc ipsa erat, quâ obscurare moliebantur. At ipse hanc afferens, dicit: & tamen noti. Non affectabat nominis celebritatē, ac interea ad maliciam reproborum conniuere, & opus in se Dei dissimulare non poterat. Quod ipsi obijciebant pseudapostoli, poterat multo iustius illis obijcere, utpote hominibus sic obscuris & ignotis, ut opus haberent literis commendaticijs, cuius meminit supra, cap.3. Verùm nolebat uicariæ exprobrationis funem cum illis trahere, sed magis ministerij sui celebritatem tueri.
units.tr: "And yet well known," he says. If anyone was well known as to what sort of man he was, Paul certainly was. For since he proved himself a minister of God in all things, he surely could not be unknown and obscure, especially to those who were regenerated in Christ Jesus through him. The obscurity of his family and birth, which the wicked objected to him, had nothing to do with the matter; meanwhile they carefully concealed the fame of his name and ministry, which was everywhere illustrious. Indeed, this very fame was the thing they tried to obscure. But he, bringing it forward, says: "and yet well known". He did not seek the celebrity of his name, yet he could not wink at the malice of the wicked and conceal the work of God in himself. What the false apostles objected to him, they could have objected to themselves with much more justice, being men so obscure and unknown that they needed letters of commendation, which he mentions above in chapter 3. But he did not want to drag the rope of reciprocal reproach with them; he preferred rather to guard the fame of his ministry.

units.la: QVASI moriētes, & ecce uiuimus, inquit.) Supra cap.4. dixit se semper in mortem tradi propter Iesum. Hoc ipsi uicio uertebatur à reprobis ac pseudapostolis. At, inquit, nondum mortui sumus, sed, ecce uiuimus.
units.tr: As dying, and yet behold we live, he says.) Above, in chapter 4, he said that he was always being handed over to death for Jesus' sake. The reprobates and false apostles held this against him. But, he says, we are not yet dead; rather, behold, we live.

units.la: Nō simpliciter, uiuimus, sed, ecce uiuimus, inquit. Quasi dicat: Vident me frequenter tradi in mortem propter dominū, & id mihi exprobrant, quur non simul uident, quod interim adhuc uiuo? quur non uirtutem Dei, quæ me cōseruat, hac in re agnoscunt? Hanc supra quoque cap.4. considerandam propositum, dicens: Semper enim nos qui uiuimus, in mortem tradimur propter Iesum.
units.tr: He does not simply say "we live" but "behold, we live." As if he were saying: They see me being frequently handed over to death for the Lord, and they reproach me for it. Why do they not at the same time see that I am still alive? Why do they not recognise in this the power of God, which preserves me? He had already set out this point above, in chapter 4, saying: "For we who live are always delivered unto death for Jesus' sake."

units.la: QVASI correpti, & nō occisi.) Vulgata habet, ut castigati. Græcè est, ὡς παιδευόμενοι. Quēadmodū infrà cap.11. meminit. Virgis aliquoties cæsus fuerat. Id castigari uocat scriptura. Sic Pilatus, cum Christum flagellare ac sic liberare constituisset, dicebat, παιδεύσας οὖν αὐτὸν ἀπολύσω, id est, castigatum igitur dimittam. Maleuoli igitur castigationem hanc singularem iram Dei interpretabantur, & sic opprobrabat Apostolo, ac si flagiciosi hominis haberet argumentum. Ipse igitur regerit, at non occisi. Quasi dicat: Vtut exprobrent nobis quòd castigemur subinde, interim tamen uidere poterunt, haud esse nos occisos, sed uirtute Dei liberatos. Non est autem otiosum, quod se uiuere, & occisum non esse dicit. Sciebat id uehementer urere pseudapostolos, quod perpetuò seruabatur, & è tot discriminibus ereptus adhuc uiuebat.
units.tr: As chastened, and not killed.) The Vulgate has "as chastened." The Greek is ὡς παιδευόμενοι [hōs paideuomenoi]. He mentions this again below, in chapter 11: he had been beaten with rods several times. Scripture calls such beating chastisement. So Pilate, when he had decided to scourge Christ and then release him, said: "Having chastised him, therefore, I will release him" [paideusas oun auton apolysō], that is, "I will dismiss him once chastised." Ill-disposed people therefore interpreted this particular chastisement as a sign of God's anger, and they reproached the Apostle as if it were proof of a wicked man. He therefore replies: "but not killed." As if to say: however much they reproach us that we are chastised from time to time, they can at least see that we have not been killed but delivered by the power of God. Nor is it idle that he says he is alive and not killed. He knew that it burned the false apostles greatly that he was constantly preserved, and that, snatched from so many dangers, he was still alive.

units.la: QVASI dolentes, inquit, semper tamē gaudentes.) Cum crebris afflictionibus exerceretur, uidebatur in oculis mundi, uir esse dolorum ac tristiciarum, atq; ideo etsi uiueret, ut tam tamen uiuere miseram & infœlicem, cui mors ipsa sit præferenda.
units.tr: As sorrowful, he says, yet always rejoicing.) Since he was harassed by frequent afflictions, he seemed in the eyes of the world to be a man of sorrows and griefs; and so, even if he lived, he seemed to live a wretched and unhappy life, one for which death itself would be preferable.

units.la: Regerit igitur dicens: semper tamen gaudentes, quib. uerbis negat se propterea uirum esse dolorum, & infeliciter uiuere, quòd crebris afflictionibus exerceatur, cum potius iuguiter à domino refocilletur, & exhilaretur. Quemadmodum enim supra cap.1. dixit, sicut abundabant in ipso afflictiones Christi: ita & consolationes per Christum in ipso abundabant, usqueadeo, ut & alios afflictos consolari posset in domino.
units.tr: He therefore replies, saying: "yet always rejoicing." By these words he denies that he is a man of sorrows or lives unhappily because he is harassed by frequent afflictions. Rather, he is continually refreshed and cheered by the Lord. For, as he said above in chapter 1, "as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so also our consolation abounds through Christ," to such an extent that he could also comfort others who were afflicted, in the Lord.

units.la: QVASI pauperes, inquit, multos tamen ditantes.) Iuxta sæculum quidem diues non erat, at interim sic pauper non erat, ut egestatis necessitate adactus circuiret, & prædicaret, cuius ipsum insimulabant, dum paupertatem exprobrabant. Itaque sic à se paupertatis probrum reijcit, ut dicat se multos ditare, id quod pauperum esse non potest. Quomodo autem multos ditarit, non est ut quæramus. Thesaurum scientiæ Dei, gratiæ, ac salutis circumferebat. Ex illo multos utique, credentes uideli cet, non euanidis ac fallacibus, sed permanentibus, ac ueris opibus ditabat, hoc est, beatos reddebat.
units.tr: As poor, he says, yet making many rich.) According to the world he was indeed not rich, but still he was not so poor that, driven by the necessity of want, he went about and preached, which was what they accused him of while they reproached him with poverty. And so he throws off the disgrace of poverty in such a way as to say that he makes many rich, which cannot be the case for the poor. As for how he made many rich, we need not inquire. He carried about the treasure of the knowledge of God, of grace, and of salvation. From it he enriched many, namely believers, with riches that are not fleeting and deceptive but lasting and true; that is, he made them blessed.

units.la: VT nihil habentes, inquit, & tamen omnia possidentes.) Poterat regeri. Quomodo multos ditas, cum ipse nihil habeas? Respondet: Quomodo nihil habeo, cū omnia possideam? Sed dices, ecquomodo possidebat omnia? Possidebat omnia, nō ut Apostol, sed ut Christianus, Christianorum enim sunt omnia propter Christum. Sic 1. Corinth.3. dixit: Omnia uestra sunt, siue Paulus, siue Apollo, siue Cephas, siue mundus, siue mors, siue præsentia, siue futura, omnia, inquam, uestra sunt, uos autem Christi, Christus uero Dei. Vt Christia nus igitur posidebat omnia, ut Apostolus uerò ac dispensator misteriorum Dei ac thesaurarius Christi, ditabat multos.
units.tr: As having nothing, he says, and yet possessing all things.) It could be objected: How do you make many rich, when you yourself have nothing? He answers: How do I have nothing, when I possess all things? But you will say: how did he possess all things? He possessed all things not as an apostle but as a Christian, for all things belong to Christians because of Christ. So in 1 Corinthians 3 he said: "All things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or death, or the present, or the future: all things, I say, are yours; and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's." Therefore he possessed all things as a Christian, but as an apostle and a steward of the mysteries of God and a treasurer of Christ, he enriched many.

units.la: De Romanis apostolis dici nō potest, quòd sint quasi pauperes, cum regū opes ostentent, dici uerò potest, quod multos locupletět, uerum alio diuitiarum genere, quàm quo multos locupletarunt ueri Christi Apostoli, mundano scilicet ac perituro. Dici de illis non potest, quod sint quasi nihil habentes, dici uero potest, quod sint omnia posidentes, at non quemadmodum Christiani, sed ut domini, omnibus omnium conscientijs ac loculis manus inijcientes.
units.tr: It cannot be said of the Roman apostles that they are as poor, since they display the wealth of kings. But it can be said that they enrich many, though with a different kind of riches from those with which the true apostles of Christ enriched many, namely worldly and perishing riches. It cannot be said of them that they are as having nothing; but it can be said that they possess all things, yet not as Christians do, but as lords, laying their hands on the consciences and purses of all.

units.la: Os nostrum apertū est erga uos Corinthij. Cor nostrum dilatatū est. Non estis angusti in nobis, sed estis angusti in uisceribus uestris. Eandem autem remunerationem, ut à filijs exigo. Dilatemini & uos.
units.tr: Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted in us, but you are restricted in your own affections. Now as to the same recompense, I speak as to my children: be enlarged you also.

units.la: Diligebat eos, perinde atque pater diligit filios, ideoque illis pro affectu paterno liberè ac fiducialiter loquebatur. Agnoscit hoc, & simul unde fit exponit, perque eam occasionem reprehendit eos, quod sic erga ipsos affecto non responderent ex æquo, & ut id faciant requirit. Sic dicit: Os nostrum apertum est erga uos Corinthij.
units.tr: He loved them just as a father loves his children, and therefore he spoke to them freely and confidently out of paternal affection. He acknowledges this, and at the same time explains where it comes from, and on that occasion he rebukes them, because they did not respond equally to his feeling towards them, and he asks them to do so. He says: "Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians."

units.la: Hoc est, liberè ac fiducialiter uobis loquor, ô Corinthij, nihil celo, nihil dissimulo: sed ut affectus sum, & ut sentio, sic ad uos loquor. Ore aperto loqui, nihil est aliud quàm absque ulla dissimulatione quicquid est in corde pro loqui, id quod facere solemus, dum loquimur dilectis & amicis. Significat igitur, loqui se illis, tanquam dilectis. Ideo non simpliciter dicit: Os nostrum apertum est, sed addit, ergà uos ô Corinthij. Quasi dicat: Quos in domino diligo, & nihil rerum mearum celare possum.
units.tr: That is: I speak to you freely and confidently, O Corinthians; I conceal nothing and dissemble nothing, but I speak to you as I feel and as I am disposed. To speak with an open mouth is nothing other than to say, without any dissimulation, whatever is in the heart, which we are accustomed to do when we speak to beloved friends. He therefore signifies that he speaks to them as to beloved ones. So he does not simply say "our mouth is open" but adds "to you, O Corinthians." As if to say: Those whom I love in the Lord, and from whom I can conceal nothing of my affairs.

units.la: Obseruemus igitur hoc loco, quàm deceat ministrum Christi, ut in ecclesia Dei fratribus loquens liberè ac disertè ore non semiclauso, ac musitabundo, sed aperto loquatur. Habet & lupi, in pastores transformati, os apertum erga gregem domini: uerum non ut quæ salutis sunt liberè loquantur, sed ut oues domini discerpant, & omnia uorent.
units.tr: Let us therefore observe in this place how fitting it is for a minister of Christ, when speaking to brothers in the Church of God, to speak freely and plainly, with an open mouth, not half-closed and muttering, but open. Wolves, transformed into ministers, also have an open mouth towards the flock of the Lord; but not so that they speak freely of what concerns salvation, but so that they tear the sheep of the Lord apart and devour everything.

units.la: COR nostrum dilatatum est.) Hoc est, non sic sum angusto corde, ut uos non capiam omnes, & intra uiscera mea foueam, sed admodum dilatato & amplo, sic ut in me nulla uobis sit angustia. Nemo uestrùm excluditur, nemo arctatur in corde meo. Vnde & addit: Non arctamini in nobis. Græcè, sτενοχωρεῖσθε ἐν ἡμῖν. Significat se illos omnes amanter complecti in domino, nec quenquam illorum ferre grauatim.
units.tr: Our heart is enlarged.) That is: I am not of so narrow a heart that I cannot hold you all and cherish you within my bowels; rather, my heart is so greatly enlarged and spacious that there is no narrowness towards you within me. None of you is shut out, none is confined in my heart. Hence he adds: "You are not restricted in us." In Greek, στενοχωρεῖσθε ἐν ἡμῖν [stenochōreisthe en hēmin]. He signifies that he embraces them all lovingly in the Lord, and that he bears none of them with reluctance.

units.la: SED estis angusti in uisceribus uestris.) Græcè est, στενοχωρεῖσθε δὲ ἐν τῖς σπλάγχνοις ἡμῶν.
units.tr: But you are restricted in your own bowels.) In Greek: στενοχωρεῖσθε δὲ ἐν τοῖς σπλάγχνοις ἡμῶν [stenochōreisthe de en tois splanchnois hēmōn].

units.la: id est, arctamini uerò in uisceribus uestris. Sé-sus est: Corda uestra non sunt dilatata, sed angusta, estis in uobis angusti, sic ut me uicifim non capiatis, quemadmodum ego uos capio. Et huc facit subiecta expositio, qua dicit:
units.tr: That is, but you are restricted in your own bowels. The sense is: your hearts are not enlarged but narrow; you are narrow towards yourselves, so that you do not receive me in return as I receive you. The following explanation, in which he says, agrees with this:

units.la: EANDEM autè remunerationem, ut à filijs exigo, dilatemini & uos.)
units.tr: And for the same recompense, as I ask of my children, you also be enlarged.

units.la: In Græco est, τῷ δὲ αὐτῷ ἀντιμισθίαν ὡς τέκνοις λέγω, πλατυνθῆτε καὶ ὑμεῖς, quæ mihi coniungenda uidentur, uertendaq; ad hunc modum, de eadem autem remuneratione, tanquam filijs, dico, dilatemini & uos. Hoc est, hortor autem uos, ut dilectionì meæ erga uos respondetes sitis, & uos corde dilatato, meque complectamini amanter, quemadmodum ego uos complector. Et hoc posco à uobis tanquam pater à filijs, & posco tanquam æquam remunerationem.
units.tr: In Greek it is: "Now for the same recompense, I speak as to children: be enlarged, you also" [τῷ δὲ αὐτῷ ἀντιμισθίαν ὡς τέκνοις λέγω, πλατυνθῆτε καὶ ὑμεῖς]. These words seem to me to belong together and should be rendered in this way: "Now for the same recompense, I speak as to children: be enlarged, you also." That is, I exhort you to respond to my love for you and to enlarge your hearts, and to embrace me lovingly, just as I embrace you. This is what I ask of you as a father of children, and I ask it as a fair return.

units.la: Erasmus in annotationibus suis, per angu-stiam uiscerum intelligit superstitiosam legalium ceremoniarum, & humanarum traditionum obseruantia, per dilatationem uerò conscientiam ab illis in Christo liberam. Verùm illius sententiæ connexio uerborum istorum haud fauet.
units.tr: Erasmus, in his annotations, understands by the narrowness of the bowels the superstitious observance of legal ceremonies and human traditions, and by enlargement the conscience freed from these in Christ. But the connection of the words does not favour that sense.

units.la: Sunt autem duo hîc de ingenio charitatis obseruanda.
units.tr: There are two things to observe here about the nature of love.

units.la: 1 Vnum est, quomodo illa & cor reddat dilatatum, & os apertum. Tolle hanc, frigebunt & contrahentur omnia, cor erit angustum & contractum, os uel clausum uel semiapertum, nihil proferens integrum, nihil syncerum & candidum.
units.tr: 1. The first is how love makes the heart enlarged and the mouth opened. Take this away, and everything grows cold and shrinks: the heart becomes narrow and constricted, the mouth either shut or half-open, uttering nothing whole, nothing sincere and candid.

units.la: 2 Alterum est, quod charitas eandem ἀντιμισθίαν, id est, uicariam dilectionem, quæ sit loco remunerationis, poscit ab illis quos diligit. Non poscit eorum bona, sed cor pro corde, dilectionem pro dilectione. Eam ob causam alibi quæritur hic Apostolus, quod plus diligens minus diligatur. Verum hæc est ueræ dilectionis sors, ut raro ἀντιμισθίαν inueniat.
units.tr: 2. The second is that love asks from those whom it loves the same return, that is, a corresponding love, which takes the place of payment. It does not ask for their goods, but heart for heart, love for love. For this reason the Apostle complains elsewhere that the one who loves more is loved less. Yet this is the lot of true love: it rarely finds a return in kind.

units.la: Ne ducatis iugum cum incredulis.
units.tr: Do not be yoked together with unbelievers.

units.la: Quod enim consortiū iusticiæ cum iniusticia? aut quæ cōmunio luci cum tenebris? aut quæ cōcordia Christo cum Belial? aut quæ pars fidelí cum infideli? aut quid conuenit templo Dei cum simulacris? Nam uos templum estis Dei uiuentis, quemadmodum dixit Deus: Inhabitabo in illis, & inambulabo, & ero illorum Deus, & ipsi erūt mihi populus. Quapropter exite de medio illorū, & separemini ab illis, dicit dominus, & immundum ne tetigeritis, & ego suscipiam uos, & ero uobis loco patris, & uos eritis mihi uice filiorum, ac filiarum, dicit dominus omnipotens.
units.tr: For what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness? Or what communion has light with darkness? Or what concord has Christ with Belial? Or what part has the believer with the unbeliever? Or what agreement has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God, as God said: "I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Therefore come out from among them and separate yourselves from them, says the Lord, and touch nothing unclean, and I will receive you, and I will be a father to you, and you shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty."

units.la: Initio capitis huius cœperat exhortari, & obsecrare Corinthios, ut cauerent, ne gratiam Dei in uacuum reciperent. Eam exhortationem commemoratione ftu-dij sui, quo neminem offendere, sed omnibus sese commendare satagebat, parumper interrupit. Iam igitur ad illam redit, dehortaturque eos ab illicito infidelium commercio. Nam uix aliud quicquam erat quo citius abducerentur à gratia Dei quam acceperant, illiusq; efficacia & utilitate priuarentur, quàm quod illicitis ac noxijs infidelium commercijs nimium securi miscebantur. Dicit itaq; :
units.tr: At the beginning of this chapter he had begun to exhort and beseech the Corinthians to take care not to receive the grace of God in vain. He briefly interrupted that exhortation by mentioning his own zeal, with which he laboured not to offend anyone but to commend himself to all. Now therefore he returns to it, and dissuades them from unlawful dealings with unbelievers. For there was scarcely anything that could draw them away more quickly from the grace of God they had received, and deprive them of its power and benefit, than their rather careless mingling in unlawful and harmful dealings with unbelievers. So he says:

units.la: NE ducatis iugum cum incredulis.) Græcè est: μὴ γίνεσθε ἑτεροζυγοῦντες ἀπίστοις. Non dicit συζυγοῦντες, sed ἑτεροζυγοῦντες. Sunt enim συζυγοῦντες, qui pares eidem iugo ducédo submittuntur. At tales non sunt fideles & infideles, Christiani, & alieni à Christo. Sunt uerò fideles fidelibus, uel infideles infidelibus coniuncti. ἑτεροζυγοῦντες uerò sunt, qui cū disparibus ac diuersis iugum ducunt, perinde ac si equus & bos eidem iugo subdantur. Cum ergo auocare Corinthios uellet, ne iugũ ducerent cum infidelibus ipsi fideles, conuenienter usus est hac uoce, ἑτεροζυγοῦντες, qua illis mox initiò disparis commercij absurditate consideranda proponit, quod statim atq; oculos spectatium incurrit pro reprobo habetur. Infideles enim utiq; sunt ἑτεροι, id est, alij ac diuersi à fidelibus ut fieri nequeat quin sint ἑτεροζυγοῦντες ij fideles qui cum illis iugum ducunt.
units.tr: "Do not be yoked together with unbelievers." In Greek it is: "Do not become unequally yoked with unbelievers" [μὴ γίνεσθε ἑτεροζυγοῦντες ἀπίστοις]. He does not say "yoked together" [συζυγοῦντες] but "unequally yoked" [ἑτεροζυγοῦντες]. For those are "yoked together" [συζυγοῦντες] who are placed under the same yoke as equals. But believers and unbelievers, Christians and those alien to Christ, are not such. Believers are joined to believers, or unbelievers to unbelievers. But those are "unequally yoked" [ἑτεροζυγοῦντες] who draw the yoke with those who are unlike and different, just as an ox and a horse would be put under the same yoke. Therefore, since he wished to call the Corinthians away from drawing a yoke with unbelievers while they themselves were believers, he appropriately used this word, "unequally yoked" [ἑτεροζυγοῦντες], by which he sets before them at the outset the absurdity of such a mismatched association, which, as soon as it meets the eye of the onlooker, is judged to be wrong. For unbelievers are indeed "others" [ἕτεροι], that is, different and diverse from believers, so that those believers who draw the yoke with them cannot help being "unequally yoked" [ἑτεροζυγοῦντες].

units.la: Non dicit autem, cum Iudeis, uel, cum Gentibus, sed cum infidelibus, cum incredulis, ut discrimen illud exprimat, quo discernuntur à fidelibus tam Iudæi quàm Gentes, & propter quod alij ac diuersi sunt ab illis. Natum esse Iudæum uel Ethnicum non impedit, quo minus ineantur commercia. Quis enim Christianus est, qui non sit natione, uel Iudæus, uel Ethnicus? Verum infidelem esse, id demum reddit alium ac diuersum à Christianis, & impedit ineundæ societatis commercium, tanquam ἑτεροζυγίαν.
units.tr: He does not say, however, "with Jews" or "with Gentiles", but "with unbelievers", "with the faithless", so that he expresses the distinction by which both Jews and Gentiles are separated from believers, and on account of which they are other and different from them. Being born a Jew or a Gentile does not prevent association. For who is a Christian who is not, by birth, either a Jew or a Gentile? But being an unbeliever at last makes a person other and different from Christians, and hinders the entering of fellowship and dealings, as an unequal yoke would.

units.la: Ἄπιστος uerò, id est, infideles, uocat non eos simpliciter, qui fidem in corde non habent, quorum multi sunt in ecclesijs Christianorũ: qui tamen, quoniam baptizati sunt, & fidem Christianam ore profitentur, deque mysterijs Christi cum cæteris fidelibus externa communicatione participant, pro infidelibus non habentur, sed eos, qui ex professo à Christiana fide sunt, adeoque & à Christo & ecclesia Christi alieni, quales sunt hodie Turci & Iudei. Cũ illis non uult ut iugũ ducat Christianus. Quare loco hoc abutuntur omnes illi, qui ob qualemcunque dissensionem, & diuersam loci alicuius scripturæ intelligentiam, communicationem dissoluendam esse clamitant, uociferantes, Apostolus monet, ne iugum ducamus cũ infidelibus. Quasi mox infidelis sit, qui non in omnibus & per omnia nobiscũ sentit. Morbidi animi sunt, qui sic sentiunt. Tales nostra ætate deprehendimus Anabaptistas, quibus infideles habentur, quotquot sectæ ipsorum subscribere detrectant. Quid de Anabaptistis
units.tr: By "unbelievers" [ἄπιστοι] he means not simply those who do not have faith in their heart, of whom there are many in the churches of Christians. Since these have been baptized and profess the Christian faith with their mouths, and share in the mysteries of Christ with the other believers through outward communion, they are not regarded as unbelievers. Rather, he means those who have openly stood apart from the Christian faith, and are therefore alien both to Christ and to the Church of Christ, such as the Turks and the Jews today. A Christian must not wish to draw the yoke with these. Hence all those abuse this passage who, on account of some dissension of whatever kind, or a different understanding of some passage of Scripture, cry out that fellowship must be dissolved, shouting that the Apostle warns us not to draw the yoke with unbelievers. As if anyone who does not agree with us in all things and in every respect were at once an unbeliever. Those who think this way have sick minds. In our own age we have found such people among the Anabaptists, who count as unbelievers all who refuse to subscribe to their sect. But why speak of the Anabaptists?

units.la: dico? Malum hoc inde ab Apostolorum temporibus turbauit ecclesias.
units.tr: This evil has troubled the churches from the time of the Apostles.

units.la: Quid est autem ducere iugum cum infidelibus? Sunt qui referant ad imparia coniugia, quibus Christiani nubűt infidelibus. Illi uoce ἑτεροζυγῶντες mouentur. Verùm si in textu eo usque legendo progrediaris, ubi ijs quę in genere, ac per similia dixit specificationem subijcit, puto liquere, alió respicere Apostolum ἑτεροζυγίας ad imparia coniugia, quamuis nec illa probet, nec nos repugnemus, quominus ea uelut species ἑτεροζυγίας sub eo qd in genere dicit comprehendatur. Alij loci huius sensum nimis extendunt, referentes illum ad ea quoque quæ humani conuictus commercia concernunt. Nostra sententia est, loqui Apostolum de commercijs, quæ religionis possunt uiciare puritatem, siue illa immediatè ad religionem pertineant, quale erat quod eidolothitis cum infidelibus, idq; in templis & sacrificijs illorum, uescebantur, siue aliquo pacto ad uiciandam religionis puritatem faciant, quo referenda sunt, quod in spectaculis theatricis, cum infidelium colluuie sedebat, & quod nuptias cum infidelibus inibant, deinde & iudicia iudicum infidelium leuibus de causis non coacti sectabantur.
units.tr: But what is it to draw the yoke with unbelievers? Some refer it to unequal marriages, in which Christians marry unbelievers. They are moved by the word "unequally yoked" [ἑτεροζυγῶντες]. But if you read on in the text until you reach the specification that he adds to what he had said in general terms and by likenesses, I think it becomes clear that the Apostle has in view something other than unequal marriages. Yet I do not, on that account, reject them, nor do we oppose including them, as one form of unequal yoking, under what he says in general. Other interpreters stretch the sense of this passage too far, referring it also to those dealings that concern the common intercourse of human life. Our view is that the Apostle is speaking of dealings that can corrupt the purity of religion, whether they pertain directly to religion, as when they ate meat sacrificed to idols with unbelievers, and that in their temples and sacrifices, or whether in some way they serve to corrupt the purity of religion. To this class belong the sitting with the filth of unbelievers at theatrical shows, the entering into marriages with unbelievers, and the following of the judgments of unbelieving judges for trivial causes when they were not compelled to do so.

units.la: QVOD enim consortium iusticiæ cum iniusticia, inquit?) Absurditatem τῆς ἑτεροζυγίας antithesibus aliquot considerándam proponit, quo rationem reddat, quare dehortetur eos à consortio infidelium. Adducit autem earum rerum antitheses, quæ sic sunt sibi inuicem contrariæ, ut nullius sint cófortij capaces: ut sunt iusticia & iniusticia, lux & tenebræ, Christus & Belial. Et in hanc classem collocat, fideles etiam & infideles, templum Dei & simulacra, quo parenesim suâ confirmet. Sic dicit: Quod enim côfortium iusticię cum iniusticia? Quasi dicat: Nullum. Si nullum, ergo nec uobis cum infidelibus ullum debet esse côfortium. Alioqui eiusmodi uestro & infidelium consortio quantũ in uobis est, coniungetur iusticia cum iniusticia, dum iusti coniunguntur cum iniustis. Hunc sensum poscit, quòd non simpliciter dicit: Quod consortium, sed, Quod enim consortium iusticiæ cum iniusticiei? Quod autem infidelibus tribuat iniusticiam, facit non hoc tantum loco, sed & 1.Cor.6.cum dicit: Sustinet aliquis uestrum negocium habens, cum altero iudicari sub iniustis, & non magis sub sanctis? Et paulò infrà: Sed frater cum fratre litigat, idq; sub infidelibus. Vbi patet, infideles habendos esse pro iniustis. Videmus hodie nonnullos Euangelij ministros consortia sacrificulorum Papistarũ sectari. Possemus eodem illos argumento ab eiusmodi consortio dehortari, ut dicamus: Ne ducatis iugum cum seductoribus. Quod enim consortium uerita-ti cum mendacio? Vestro cum seductoribus consortio coniungitis, ueritatem cum mendacio, quæ tamen coniungi non possunt.
units.tr: "For what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness?" he says. By means of several antitheses he sets before us the absurdity of the unequal yoke, in order to give a reason why he dissuades them from fellowship with unbelievers. He brings forward antitheses of things which are so contrary to one another that they are incapable of any fellowship: such as righteousness and unrighteousness, light and darkness, Christ and Belial. And into this class he also places believers and unbelievers, the temple of God and idols, so as to confirm his exhortation. He says: "For what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness?" As if to say: none. If there is none, then neither should there be any fellowship between you and unbelievers. Otherwise, to the extent that it is in your power, by such fellowship of yours with unbelievers, righteousness would be joined with unrighteousness, as the righteous would be joined with the unrighteous. This sense is required by the fact that he does not simply say "What fellowship" but "For what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness?" That he ascribes unrighteousness to unbelievers he does not do only in this place, but also in 1 Cor. 6, where he says: "Does any of you, having a matter against another, dare to go to law before the unrighteous, and not before the saints?" And a little further on: "But brother goes to law with brother, and that before unbelievers." Here it is plain that unbelievers are to be regarded as unrighteous. Today we see some ministers of the Gospel pursuing the fellowship of the Papist priests. We could dissuade them from such fellowship by the same argument, saying: "Do not be yoked together with deceivers. For what fellowship has truth with falsehood? By your fellowship with deceivers you join truth with falsehood, which nonetheless cannot be joined."

units.la: Obserua. Si iusticia cum iniusticia coniungitur, ubi fidelis consortium init cum infideli, requirequiritur ergo,ut quemadmodū iniustus est infidelis,ita iustus sit fidelis, ut dum fidelis fideli iungitur,iusticia iusticiæ iungatur. Vnde autem dabūtur nobis hodie tales Christiani, in quibus hæc ratio posit consistere firma? Plerique enim sic comparati sumus, ut si iungamur Turcis,multo illis deprehendamur iniustiores.
units.tr: Observe. If righteousness is joined with unrighteousness when a believer enters into fellowship with an unbeliever, then it is required that just as the unbeliever is unrighteous, so the believer be righteous, so that when a believer is joined to a believer, righteousness is joined to righteousness. But where shall we find today such Christians in whom this principle can firmly stand? For most of us are so constituted that if we are joined to the Turks, we are found to be far more unrighteous than they.

units.la: AVT quæ communio, inquit, luci cum tenebris? Planè nulla. Nulla igitur esse debet fideli cum infidelibus. Est enim fidelis filius lucis, & infidelis filius tenebrarum, sic ut si fidelis iungatur infideli, quantū in ipso est lucem iungat cum tenebris. Ipse lucis ac tenebrarum aspectus clamat, nullius eas esse comunionis capaces. Quare & mox initio sic discretæ sunt ab opifice Deo,ut lux diem,tenebræ vero noctem separatim constituant. Significans igitur tam esse absurdum, si comunio fideli intercedat cum infideli,quàm absurdum est, si per im possibile communio intercedat inter lucem & tenebras. Habet autē Apostolus hoc in more,ut fideles vocet lucem, infideles vero tenebras,sicuti videre est Ephesiorum quinto, ubi dicit: Eratis aliquando tenebræ, nunc autem lux in domino. Tenebras vocat infideles propter ignorantiam Dei, ac cæcitatem cordium ipsorum, fideles vero lucem, propter scientiam Dei,qua corda illorum per spiritum sanctum illuminantur.
units.tr: "Or what fellowship," he says, "has light with darkness?" Clearly none. There ought therefore to be none for a believer with unbelievers. For the believer is a son of light and the unbeliever a son of darkness, so that if a believer is joined to an unbeliever, he joins, as far as in him lies, light with darkness. The very aspect of light and darkness cries out that they are capable of no fellowship. Wherefore also at the very beginning they were distinguished by God the Creator, so that light makes the day and darkness the night, each separately. Signifying, therefore, that it is as absurd for fellowship to arise between a believer and an unbeliever as it would be if, by impossibility, fellowship arose between light and darkness. The Apostle has the habit of calling believers light and unbelievers darkness, as may be seen in Ephesians 5, where he says: "You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord." He calls unbelievers darkness on account of their ignorance of God and the blindness of their hearts, and believers light on account of the knowledge of God by which their hearts are illumined through the Holy Spirit.

units.la: AVT quę concordia,inquit,Christo cū Belial,id est,cum Satana? Omnino nulla. Sunt enim hi duo hostilissimè inter se pugnantes. Christus enim author salutis , Belial author perditionis,Christus restaurator omniū, Belial vero destructor, Christus princeps lucis, Belial princeps tenebrarum est. Quare nulla prorsus inter eos potest esse concordia. Nulla igitur potest esse inter fideles quoq; & infideles. Nam fideles Christo,infideles vero Belial sunt insiti.
units.tr: "And what agreement," he says, "has Christ with Belial, that is, with Satan?" Certainly none. For these two wage the most hostile war against each other. Christ is the author of salvation, Belial the author of perdition; Christ the restorer of all things, Belial the destroyer; Christ the prince of light, Belial the prince of darkness. Therefore there can be absolutely no agreement between them. Therefore there can be none between believers and unbelievers either. For believers are engrafted into Christ, and unbelievers into Belial.

units.la: Vide autem quomodo uim argumentationis huius intendat. Hactenus duabus antithesibus iusticiæ & iniusticiæ, lucis & tenebrarum,absurditatem & impossibilitatem quoq; huius expressit. Iam vero quàm horribilis etiā sit & impia in eo declarat, quod Christum & Belial inducit.
