Quis enim fidelium non exhorresçat, si cogitet se Christum cum Belial coniungere, dum infidelium consortia sectatur?
units.tr: Note, however, how he presses the force of this argument. Thus far, by the two antitheses of righteousness and unrighteousness, light and darkness, he has expressed the absurdity and impossibility of such fellowship. Now he declares how horrible and impious it is, in that he brings in Christ and Belial. For who of the faithful would not shudder if he considered that, in pursuing the company of unbelievers, he was joining Christ with Belial?

units.la: Vocem Belial autē, quæ nullo alio loco in Nouo testamento legitur, è Veteris testamen. scripturis desumpsit, in quibus homines iniqui, praevaricatores, temerarij ac nullis disciplinis subiecti,filij Belial uocantur, sicuti uide re est 1.Samuel.25.de Nabal, & 1.Samuel.2.de filijs Samuelis,& 1.Reg.21.de duobus falsis testibus. Vocantur autem filij Belial, propterea quod sunt sine iugo. Nam ipsa uox בליעל idè sonat quod sine iugo,à בלי,id est, sine,& על, id est,iugum. Vnde & Hieronymus in uersione libri Iudic.cap.19. ubi hæc leguntur : Ecce
units.tr: The word Belial, which is read in no other place in the New Testament, he has taken from the Scriptures of the Old Testament, in which wicked, lawless, reckless men who are subject to no discipline are called sons of Belial, as may be seen at 1 Samuel 25 concerning Nabal, at 1 Samuel 2 concerning the sons of Samuel, and at 1 Kings 21 concerning the two false witnesses. They are called sons of Belial because they are without a yoke. For the word itself בליעל [Belial] literally means "without a yoke", being made up of בלי, that is, "without", and על, that is, "yoke". Hence also Jerome, in his version of the book of Judges chapter 19, where these words are read: "Behold,

units.la: uiri ciuitates, uiri filij Belial, adiecit de suo, id est,absq; iugo. Quare autē Satanam uocet Belial,non est ut quæramus. Omnium enim iniquissimus est, & omnis puaricationis author.
units.tr: men of the city, men, sons of Belial," he added of his own, that is, "without a yoke". Why he calls Satan Belial we need not inquire. For he is the most wicked of all and the author of every prevarication.

units.la: Illud lector per se obseruet, quod ubi uetus habet, Quæ conuentio,& Erasmus,quæ concordia,in Græco est τίς συμφώνησις, id est,quę consonātia. Sane sic natura comparati sumus, ut ubi concordia non est, ibi nulla fit consonantia,ut non immerito concordiam pro consonantia posuerit Erasmus.
units.tr: Let the reader observe for himself that where the old version has "what agreement" (quae conventio), Erasmus has "what concord", but the Greek is τίς συμφώνησις [tis symphōnēsis], that is, "what harmony". Indeed we are by nature so constituted that where there is no concord, no harmony arises; so Erasmus did not unreasonably put "concord" for "harmony".

units.la: AVT quæ pars fideli cum infideli? inquit) Hic rem ipsam quam amoliri cupit exprimit. Non dicit autem simpliciter,quæ societas, uel quæ cóiunctio,sed,quæ pars fideli cū infideli? Quasi dicat: Nulla. Ergo nec societas ulla. Etenim quibus pars nulla cum reprobis est, illis etiam societas cum reprobis debet esse nulla. Quibus sors & pars eadē est, iungātur utpote fideles cū fidelibus,infideles cum infidelibus.
units.tr: "What portion has a believer with an unbeliever?" he says. Here he expresses the very thing he wishes to remove. He does not say simply "what partnership or what union", but "what portion has a believer with an unbeliever?" As if to say: none. Therefore no partnership either. For those who have no portion with the reprobate ought to have no partnership with them either. Those whose lot and portion are the same may be joined: believers with believers, unbelievers with unbelievers.

units.la: Loquitur autē de participatione bonorum spiritualium & cœlestiū. In illis enim non participat infideles,uel si mauis, loquitur de perditione infidelium, in qua utiq; nulla pars est fideli cum infidelibus. Nam in rebus huius uite necessitatem concernentibus pars est fideli eadem cum infidelibus.
units.tr: He speaks, however, of the sharing of spiritual and heavenly goods, in which unbelievers have no share. Or, if you prefer, he speaks of the perdition of unbelievers, in which surely a believer has no portion with unbelievers. For in the matters of this life that concern necessity, a believer has the same portion as unbelievers.

units.la: AVT quid conuenit templo Dei cum simulacris? inquit) Rem propius,& uelut acu,ut in proverbio est,tangit. Multis quidē modis fieri potest, ut fidelis cum infidelibus illicitè,& cū religionis Christianæ detrimēto coniungatur. Verum ea demum societas immediate religioni Christianæ repugnat, qua templū Dei simulacris commiscetur & conspurcatur. Per simulacra nanq; immortalis & inuisibilis Dei gloria ad similitudinem mortalium,uel hominum,uel animaliū mutatur. Rom.1. Videmus autem hic quàm tenax sit hoc malum,præsertim ubi sæculorū aliquot est consuetudine inueteratū. In priore epistola correxit illud,nec dubium est,quin idem fecerit cum esset apud eos presens,& fidem in Christum initio in cor dibus eorum plantaret. Et tamen post hæc omnia necessarium est uisum,rursus eos à commercio simulacrorum avocare.
units.tr: "What agreement," he says, "has the temple of God with idols?" He touches the matter more closely, and, as the proverb says, with a needle. Certainly in many ways it can happen that a believer is unlawfully joined with unbelievers, to the detriment of the Christian religion. Yet that fellowship is directly opposed to the Christian religion by which the temple of God is mixed and defiled with idols. For through images the glory of the immortal and invisible God is changed into the likeness of mortal beings, whether men or animals. Romans 1. We see here how stubborn this evil is, especially when it has grown inveterate through the custom of several centuries. He had corrected it in the former epistle, and there is no doubt that he did the same when he was present among them and planted faith in Christ in their hearts at the beginning. And yet, after all these things, it seemed necessary to him to call them back again from the practice of idols.

units.la: Nō aūt simpliciter dicit: Quid conuenit uobis cū simulacris? sed: Quid conuenit templo Dei cum simulacris? In falsorum Deorū templis habentur ipsorum simulacra, quia dij ipsi nō habētur, qui ut uel prorsus nō sunt, uel dij non sunt,ita in templis suis præsentes esse nopossunt At templi dei longe diuersa est conditio. Tem plū enim ueri Dei nō absentis Dei poscit imaginem,sed ipsum Deū habet in se præsentem. Quare nihil illi potest esse inconuenientius,q usus simulacrorum.Hoc notans, dicit Apostolus: Quid conuenit templo Dei cum simulacris? NAM uos,inquit,templū estis Dei uiuētis.) Ne dicerent : Nos simulacra templo Dei non inferimus,subiungit:Nam uos templum estis Dei uiuentis. Si quis templo Dei, quod Hierosolymis erat,simulacrū intulisset, rem uisus fuisset facere omnibus modis abominandam: At interea ueriori quam illud erat templo Dei simulacrorum spurcitiem inferebant, cum se simulacrorum commercio de eidolothytis ue scendo conspurcarent. Hoc non consideran-tibus exponit, dicens: Nam uos templum Dei estis uiuentis.
units.tr: He does not, however, say simply, "What agreement have you with idols?" but "What agreement has the temple of God with idols?" In the temples of false gods their images are kept, because the gods themselves are not present; since they either do not exist at all or are not gods, they cannot be present in their temples. But the condition of the temple of God is far different. For the temple of the true God, which is not an absent God, does not require an image, but has God himself present within it. Wherefore nothing can be more incongruous for it than the use of images. Noting this, the Apostle says: "What agreement has the temple of God with idols?" For you, he says, are the temple of the living God. Lest they should say, "We do not bring idols into the temple of God," he adds: "For you are the temple of the living God." If anyone had brought an idol into the temple of God that was at Jerusalem, he would have seemed to do a thing abominable in every way. Yet meanwhile they were bringing into the temple of God a filth of idols that was more real than that, when they defiled themselves by partaking of idol-sacrifices through fellowship with images. He explains this for those who do not consider it, saying: "For you are the temple of the living God."

units.la: NON simpliciter templū Dei estis, inquit, sed addit uiuentis.) Perstringit templa falso-rum deorum, quę templa sunt nonuiuetium, sed mortuorum, aut certè nusquam extatium deorum. At populus fidelium templū est Dei non mortui, sed uiuentis. Est igitur discrimen hoc inter templa falsorum deorum, & templū ueri Dei, quod illa sine simulacris deorū tem-pla deorum esse nequeunt, hoc uero simulacra ufq; adeò nō requirat, ut per illa prophanetur etiam, propterea quòd habeat in se Deum ip-sum, non mortuum, sed uiuentem.
units.tr: "Not simply the temple of God are you," he says, but he adds "of the living." He strikes at the temples of false gods, which are temples not of living gods but of dead gods, or at least of gods who nowhere exist. But the people of the faithful is the temple of God, not of a dead God but of the living. There is therefore this difference between the temples of false gods and the temple of the true God: those temples cannot be temples of gods without images of the gods, whereas this one does not require images at all, and is even defiled by them, because it has within itself God himself, not dead but living.

units.la: QVEMADMODVM dixit Deus, inquit, inhabitabo in illis, & inambulabo, & ero illo-rum Deus, & ipsi erunt mihi populus.) Quo-niam rarum & insoles uidebatur, quod dixit: Nam uos templum estis Dei uiuentis, probat illud & confirmat per scripturas, easq; non quaslibet, sed in quibus Deus ipse loquatur. Sic dicit: Quemadmodum dixit Deus, inha-bitabo in illis & inambulabo, &c. Quę citat ex scripturis, nō uno habentur loco, si uelis om-nia ad finem usq; capitis coiungere. Quæ hic meminit ad comprobandū, quod populus fi-delium templū sit Dei, referunt nonnulli ad 37. caput Ezechielis, ubi tamen non leguntur nisi ista: Erit tabernaculū meum in eis, & ero eis Deus, & ipsi erunt mihi populus. Quare malo referre ad ea quæ Leuit. 26. leguntur ad hunc modū: Et ponam habitationē meam, in medio uestri, & nō abijciet uos animā mea. Et ambulabo in medio uestri, & ero uobis in Deū, & uos eritis mihi in populū. Locum hūc citat Apostolus, sic tamē, ut non ad uerbū. Magis enim sensum quàm uerbaspeƈtat. Quod il-lic est! Ponam habitationem meam in medio uestri, pro eo dicit: Inhabitabo in illis, persona etiam mutans, deinde illud, & nō abijciet uos anima mea, omittit, cætera satis plenè appen-dit, nisi quòd personam mutat.
units.tr: "As God said," he says, "I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people." Since it seemed rare and unusual that he said, "For you are the temple of the living God," he proves and confirms it from the Scriptures, and not just any Scriptures, but those in which God himself speaks. He says: "As God said, I will dwell in them and walk among them, etc." The passages he cites from the Scriptures are not found in one place, if you wish to join all of them to the end of the chapter. Some refer what he here recalls, to prove that the people of the faithful is the temple of God, to Ezekiel chapter 37, where however only these words are read: "My tabernacle shall be among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people." Therefore I prefer to refer it to what is read in Leviticus 26 in this manner: "And I will set my dwelling in the midst of you, and my soul will not cast you off. And I will walk in the midst of you, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people." The Apostle cites this place, yet not word for word, for he regards the sense rather than the words. Where there it reads "I will set my dwelling in the midst of you," he renders "I will dwell in them," changing the person as well; then he omits "and my soul will not cast you off"; the rest he weighs quite fully, except that he changes the person.

units.la: Probat igitur, fideles esse templum Dei ex ipsis uerbis Dei, quibus se in illis habitaturum & ambulaturum, ac Deum ipsorum futurum, eosq; pro populo suo habiturum dicit. Si rex quidam de populo suo dicat, habitabo in illo, & ambulabo in illo, & ero eis rex, & ipsi erunt mihi populus, inde colligi nō poterit, eum po-pulum esse aulam regis sui. Aliud enim est, au-lam regis esse in medio populi regni, & aliud, ipsum populum esse aulam regis, quod poste-rius fieri non potest, prius uero, regibus cōsue-tum, Deo est inconueniens. Non enim ille, ut homo, templis manufactis inhabitat, sicut rex in sua aula, sed ut Deus secundum naturā spi-ritus in cordibus suorum fidelium, quæ inha-bitat, dum spiritum illis suæ gratiæ infundit.
units.tr: Paul therefore proves from God's own words that the faithful are God's temple. In them, he says, God will dwell and walk, will be their God, and will hold them as his people. If some king said of his people, "I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their king, and they will be my people," it could not be inferred from this that the people is the king's palace. It is one thing for the royal palace to stand in the midst of the people of the kingdom, and another for the people itself to be the palace, which cannot happen at all. The first is customary for kings, but the second is unfitting for God. For God does not dwell in temples made by hands, as a human king dwells in his palace. He dwells as God, who by his nature is spirit, in the hearts of his faithful people, as he pours into them the Spirit of his grace.

units.la: Dices: At locus Leuit. 26. loquitur de taber-naculo quod in medio populi sui Deus, utiq; manufactum habuit.
units.tr: You will say: but the passage in Leviticus 26 speaks of the tabernacle, which God had in the midst of his people, and which was certainly made by hands.

units.la: Respondeo. Quem cœli cœlorum non ca-piunt, quomodo capiet tabernaculum manu-factum? Vide 1. Reg. 8. Cœlum mihi sedes est, & terra scabellum pedum meorum, inquit domi-nus ipse, quam ergo domum ædificabitis mi-hi? aut quis erit locus quietis meæ? Nonne ma-nus mea fecit hęc omnia? Esa. 66. Relinquitur ergo, non habitare Deum in templis manufa-ctis. Quare neq; in tabernaculo manufacto ha-bitauit, sed erat illud testimonij locò, quòd ha-bitaret Deus in medio sui populi, in illorū ui-delicet cordibus sedem sibi parans. Quapro-pter Apostolus locum hunc pertinenter pro-posito suo accommodauit. De eo autem quòd templum Dei sunt fideles, dictum est 1. Cor. 3. Quare non est ut hic plura dicamus.
units.tr: I answer: how will the tabernacle made by hands contain him whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain? See 1 Kings 8: "Heaven is my throne and the earth my footstool, says the Lord himself. What house then will you build for me? Or what will be the place of my rest? Has not my hand made all these things?" (Isa. 66). It follows, then, that God does not dwell in temples made by hands. Therefore he did not dwell in the tabernacle made by hands either. It was a sign and testimony that God would dwell in the midst of his people, preparing a seat for himself in their hearts. For this reason the Apostle has fittingly applied this passage to his purpose. That the faithful are the temple of God has been said in 1 Corinthians 3, so there is no need to say more here.

units.la: INHABITABO in illis inquit.) In quibus? Præmisit Leuit. 26. Si in præceptis meis ambu-laueritis, & mandata mea custodieritis, & sece-ritis ea, & postea inter cætera subiecit: Ponam habitationem meā in medio uestri, & non ab-ijciet uos anima mea. Ambulabo in medio ue-stri, & ero Deus uester, & uos eritis mihi popu-lus. Ergo promissio hæc non habet locum in immorigeris, sed in ijs tātum qui in præceptis Dei ambulant. i. uolūtati se domini Dei sui ac-commodant, illiq; bona fide adhærent. At ta-les esse non possunt, nisi electi ac fideles.
units.tr: "I will dwell in them," he says. In whom? He has premised from Leviticus 26: "If you walk in my precepts, and keep my commandments, and do them," and afterwards, among other things, he adds: "I will set my dwelling in the midst of you, and my soul will not cast you off. I will walk in the midst of you, and I will be your God, and you will be my people." This promise therefore does not apply to the disobedient, but only to those who walk in God's precepts, that is, who conform themselves to the will of the Lord their God and cling to him in good faith. Yet such people cannot exist unless they are the elect and the faithful.

units.la: Verbum autem inhabitandi, metaphorico sensu transfertur ad Deū. Nō inhabitat Deus aliquem locū ut homo, sed inhabitare dicitur, quando per spiritum suum corda electorum perpetuitate gratiæ suæ dirigit ac moderatur in omnibus. Quod in textu est, ἐν αὐλοῖς, in Le-uitico est, בתוכם, i. in medio uestri uertunt, nonnulli, inter uos. Malle intra uos, uel simpli-citer, in uobis. Neq; enim Deus sic inter nos est, ut non sit & intra nos, quandoquidem ha-bitat in cordibus nostris. Sumus in ædificio templi huius lapides uiui, utiq; propter spiri-tum uiuificantē, qui est in nobis, & propter ea ius operationem uiui lapides sumus. Quare sic in medio nostri habitat Deus, ut sit in o-mnibus tepli sui lapidibus, illosq; singulatim pariter & coniunctim inhabitet, quod de rege dici nō potest, qui non aliter regiam suam in-habitet, quàm ut extra ligna & lapides, unde illa constructa est, maneat, & ambulet in ua-cuo, nec aliquid illis uitalis spiritus conferat.
units.tr: The verb "to dwell" is transferred to God in a metaphorical sense. God does not dwell in a place as a human does. He is said to dwell when, through his Spirit, he directs and governs the hearts of the elect in all things by the continuing power of his grace. What in the text is [ἐν αὐλοῖς] ("in the courts"), in Leviticus is [בתוכם], which some translate "in the midst of you," others "among you." I would prefer "within you," or simply "in you." For God is not so among us as not also to be within us, since he dwells in our hearts. In the building of this temple we are living stones, certainly because of the living Spirit who is in us, and because of his working we are living stones. Thus God dwells in the midst of us so that he is in all the stones of his temple, and dwells in each of them individually and together. This cannot be said of a king, who dwells in his palace only in such a way that he remains outside the wood and stones from which it was built, and walks in an empty space, conveying no living spirit to them.

units.la: E T inambulabo inquit.) Metaphora est sumpta à rege in medio regiæ suæ ambulatis, & quę considerandā sunt consiferantis ac cu-rantis. Sic Deus nō est ociosus in suo templo. Non stat in illo clauis perinde atque Marpesia cautes fixus & immotus, quemadmodum o-ciosa & muta simulacra in templis Papistarū, imò factitium Christū sacrario inclusum, stare uidemus. Deus uerus ac uiuēs ambulat in suo templo, hoc est, omnia illius lustrat, dirigit ac moderatur, nihil minus quàm ociosus & im-motus motus inhabitator, qualem imperiti homines sibi ipsis confingunt.
units.tr: "And I will walk among you," he says. This is a metaphor taken from a king walking in the midst of his palace, and it implies the care and attention of one who guards and looks after. So God is not idle in his temple. He does not stand fixed and motionless in it like a nail driven into the Marpesian rock, as we see the idle and mute images standing in the temples of the Papists. Indeed, they set up a made-up Christ shut up in the sanctuary. The true and living God walks in his temple, that is, he surveys, directs and governs all its parts. He is in no way an idle and motionless inhabitant, such as unskilled people imagine for themselves.

units.la: Et ero illorum Deus, inquit, & ipsi erunt mihi populus.) Quorsum in illis habitare & inambulare velit exponit. Ad hoc videlicet, ut sit illorum Deus, & moderetur seruetq; eos, tá quam suum populum. Deum enim esse alicuius, est illius esse Seruatorem: & populum Dei esse, est illi fide & obedientia obstrictum esse, ac nomini eius sanctificatum. Quantæ autem felicitatis sit populum esse Dei, nemo unquam satis perpendit. Cogitans hoc propheta dicit: Beatus populus, cuius dominus Deus est. Psal. 144. Reuera sic est. Tantū felicitatis habemus, quantum coniunctionis cum uero Deo, extra quem euanida sunt omnia, quæ stultus hic mundus cupidissimè sectatur.
units.tr: "And I will be their God," he says, "and they will be my people." He explains what he means by dwelling and walking in them: namely, so that he may be their God, and may govern and preserve them as his own people. For to be someone's God is to be his Saviour, and to be God's people is to be bound to him in faith and obedience, and consecrated to his name. But no one has ever considered enough how great a happiness it is to be the people of God. The prophet, thinking on this, says: "Blessed is the people whose God is the Lord" (Ps. 144). Truly it is so. We have as much happiness as we have communion with the true God, outside of whom all those things vanish which this foolish world eagerly pursues.

units.la: QVAPROPTER, inquit, exite de medio illorum, & separemini ab illis dicit dominus, &c.) Posteaquam dehortatus eos est, ne iugū ducant cum infidelibus, eo quod eiusmodi societas prorsus sit absurda, impia, & horrenda, iam subijcit adhortationem, admonens & colligens ex præmissis, reliquum esse, ut ab infidelium consortio separentur. Hanc autem parænesim non suis, sed ipsius Dei uerbis exprimit, parte illius ex Ieshaiah capit. 25. desumpta, ubi legimus ad hunc modum: [Hebrew] id est: Recedite, recedite, exite inde, immundum ne tetigeritis, exite de medio eius, mundamini portantes vasa domini. Hac inclamatione propheta reliquias Israelis hortatur, ut è medio Babylonis exeant ac discedant, caueantq; ne immunditiis illius polluantur. Eam applicat Apostolus suo proposito, ut significet hanc esse voluntatem Dei, ut populus liberationis populus in gratiam Dei assumptus, à consortio impiorum, infidelium, & immundorum discedat, ne contaminetur, & à gratia Dei excidat. Rursus autem non inhæret uerbis, sed sensum proponit.
units.tr: "Therefore," he says, "come out from among them, and be separate from them, says the Lord," and so on. Having urged them not to be yoked with unbelievers, because such fellowship is altogether absurd, impious and dreadful, he now adds an exhortation, admonishing them and drawing the conclusion from what has gone before, that they must separate themselves from the company of unbelievers. He expresses this exhortation not in his own words but in God's own, taken in part from Isaiah 52, where we read as follows: [Hebrew], that is: "Depart, depart, go out from there, do not touch the unclean thing, go out from the midst of it, be cleansed, you who carry the vessels of the Lord." By this cry the prophet exhorts the remnant of Israel to come out and depart from the midst of Babylon, and to take care not to be polluted by its uncleanness. The Apostle applies it to his purpose, to show that this is the will of God: that the people freed and taken into God's grace should withdraw from fellowship with the wicked, the unbelieving and the unclean, lest it be contaminated and fall from God's grace. Yet he does not cling to the words but sets out their meaning.

units.la: QVAPROPTER, inquit, exite de medio illorum.) Dices: Ergo exeundū fidelibus erat ex omnibus locis, in quibus habitabant infideles, atq; ita deserendus totus orbis. Nam occupabant illi mundum, & erant fideles admodum pauci.
units.tr: "Therefore," he says, "come out from among them." You will say: then the faithful would have had to leave every place in which the unbelievers lived, and so the whole world would have to be abandoned. For they occupied the world, and the faithful were very few.

units.la: Respondeo. Non hoc requirit Apostolus, ut loca infidelium deserant fideles, unde nulla contaminatio est, sed ut à ritibus ac moribus illorum separetur, qui partim erant impij, partim flagitiosi ac scelerati. Humanum interim conuictu, qui necessarius est tam fideli quàm infideli, non soluit. Immo ne mensæ quidem, modo prophanæ, communicationem reijcit, sicuti videre est 1. Cor. 10. Quare quod dicit: Exite de medio eorum, & separemini ab illis, in hac causa quam tractat Apostolus, non est trahendum ultra illius propositum. Et nos hodie, dū quosuis fideles hortamur, ut secundum illud Apoca. 18. cecidit cecidit Babylon magna, &c. Exite de illa populus meus, ne participes sitis
units.tr: I answer: the Apostle does not require that the faithful leave the places where unbelievers live, since there is no contamination in that alone. He requires that they be separated from the rites and morals of those who were partly impious and partly shameless and wicked. Meanwhile he does not dissolve human fellowship, which is necessary for the faithful and unbelievers alike. Indeed he does not even reject eating together, provided the meal is not profane, as can be seen in 1 Cor. 10. So what he says, "Come out from among them, and be separate from them," in the matter that the Apostle is treating here, should not be stretched beyond his purpose. And we today, when we exhort any faithful people, do so in accordance with that passage of Apoc. 18: "Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, &c. Come out of her, my people, lest you be partakers of her sins and receive of her plagues."

units.la: A delictorum eius, & de plagis eius ne accipiatis, deserant Babylonem, non requirimus locala separationem, nisi illa tū periculo sit uel cōscientiæ uel vitæ coniuncta, sed eam, qua impij cultus & adulterina dogmata vitentur.
units.tr: We do not require a local separation, that they should leave Babylon, unless that separation is bound up with danger either to conscience or to life. Rather we require that separation by which the cults of the impious and adulterous doctrines are avoided.

units.la: ET immundum ne tetigeritis, inquit.) Nō simpliciter dicit: ne impuremini, vel, ne immundum quid faciatis, sed, & immundum ne tetigeritis. Quasi dicat: Visq; adeo ab immunditiis in fidelium abstineatis, ut ne tactum quidem illorum vobis permittatis. Non loquitur autem de corporalibus immunditiis, sed de spiritualibus quibus conscientia impuratur, de falsis videlicet cultibus, deq; communicatione gentilium sacrificiorum. Superstitiosas eorum traditiones, qui cibos à Deo creatos vitados docent, quasi sint immundi, cū teste Christo quoque, non inquinet hominē, quod intrat per os in stomachum, reprehendit Colos. 2. dicens: Si mortui estis cum Christo, quid quasi viuentes in mundo decretis tenemini? Ne tetigeris, ne gustaris, ne contrectaris, quæ omnia ipso pereunt vsu. Hoc genus hominū quæ immunda non sunt pro immundis habet, & intersis cultibus, Simonia, fornicatione, adulterijs, & consimilibus alijs immergitur.
units.tr: "And do not touch the unclean thing," he says. He does not simply say, "do not defile yourselves," or "do not do anything unclean," but "do not even touch the unclean thing." As if he said: "Abstain from the uncleannesses of the faithful to such a degree that you do not even allow yourselves to touch them." He speaks, however, not of bodily uncleannesses but of spiritual ones, by which the conscience is defiled, namely false worship and the communion of pagan sacrifices. Christ himself also bears witness that what enters through the mouth into the stomach does not defile a man, and Col. 2 rebukes those superstitious traditions which teach that foods created by God are to be avoided as if they were unclean. It says: "If you have died with Christ, why, as though living in the world, are you held by decrees? Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle," all of which perish in the using. This kind of people considers things that are not unclean to be unclean, and yet plunges itself into the cults, simony, fornication, adulteries and other such things.

units.la: ET ego suscipiam uos, inquit, & ero uobis loco patris, & vos eritis mihi vice filiorum ac filiarum dicit dominus omnipotens.) Vnde hæc citet Apostolus non satis liquet. In præmisso Esaiæ loco non habentur, nisi forsan quod illic legitur [Hebrew], i.& colliget vos Deus Israel, per id exprimere voluit, quod dicit: & suscipiam uos.
units.tr: "And I will receive you," he says, "and will be to you in place of a father, and you will be to me in place of sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty." It is not altogether clear where the Apostle takes these words from. They are not found in the passage of Isaiah cited above, except perhaps that the Hebrew there, [Hebrew], "and God of Israel will gather you," is meant to express what he says: "I will receive you."

units.la: Illud, & ero uobis loco patris, ex Hieremiā cap. 31. sumptum videri potest, vbi legitur: Et factus sum Israel pater. Item: Ero Israeli in patrē. Quod vero annectit, & vos eritis mihi vice filiorum ac filiarum, unde citet non video. Sanè ipsa relationis ratio sic habet, vt quorum Deus pater est, hi illi vicissim sint loco filiorū & filiarum, vt de re ipsa non sit dubiū. An vero vim hanc relationis de suo voluerit exprimere, vel alicubi scriptum adducere, incertū qui dem videtur, mihi tamen verosimile apparet: quoniā addit, dicit dominus omnipotens, & ista in forma loquentis Dei ponit, esse hæc alibi non occurrat.
units.tr: The phrase "and will be to you in place of a father" may seem to be taken from Jeremiah 31, where we read, "And I have become a father to Israel," and again, "I will be a father to Israel." But I do not see where he takes the words "and you will be to me in place of sons and daughters." Certainly the logic of the relation itself is such that those whose God is a father are, in turn, in place of sons and daughters to him, so that there is no doubt about the matter itself. Whether he meant to express this force of the relation from his own mind, or whether he is citing something written somewhere, seems uncertain, though it appears likely to me, since he adds "says the Lord Almighty," and puts these things in the form of God speaking, and this does not occur elsewhere.

units.la: Nobis obseruandum est, auersari Deum immundicijs spiritualibus inquinatos. Cum dicit: ego suscipiā uos, & ero vobis loco patris, &c. quibus verbis significat, nolle se impuros suscipere, nec patris illis esse loco. Hoc tamen non sic est intelligendum, quòd neminem suscipiat, qui aliquando fuerit factus immundus. Immundum fuisse non excludit à gratia, sed obstinatè immundum esse. Pristina immundities deletur resipiscentia & fide, per remissionem peccatorum, & iusticiæ imputationem. Vnde Petro dicebatur diuinitus: Quod Deus purifi cauit
units.tr: We must observe that God turns away from those who are defiled with spiritual uncleanness. When he says, "I will receive you, and will be to you in place of a father," etc., by these words he signifies that he is unwilling to receive the impure, nor to be a father to them. This, however, is not to be understood as meaning that he receives no one who has at some time become unclean. Having been unclean does not exclude from grace; what excludes is being obstinately unclean. Former uncleanness is wiped out by repentance and faith, through the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness. Hence the word was spoken to Peter from heaven: "What God has cleansed, do not call unclean."

units.la: {A} Vide supra cap. 5. cauit, tu ne immundum dixeris. Ea uero manet, & à Deo separat, quæ omnem resipiscentiam respuit.
units.tr: {A} See above, chapter 5: "What God has cleansed, do not call unclean." But that which rejects all repentance remains, and is separated from God.

units.la: Deinde obserua, quomodo diuinâ ergo nos dignationem amplificet. Suprà, illud, & ero illorum Deus, & ipsi erunt mihi populus, citatuit, iam concludens adfert id quod multò est amplius uidelicet, & ero vobis loco patris, & vos eritis mihi uice filiorum ac filiarum.
units.tr: Next, observe how he magnifies the divine condescension toward us. Above he cited "and I will be their God, and they will be my people"; now, concluding, he brings forward what is far greater, namely, "and I will be to you in place of a father, and you will be to me in place of sons and daughters."

units.la: ARGVMENTVM
units.tr: ARGUMENT

units.la: HOrtatur statim initio ad sanctimoniā uitæ. Deinde rursus memorat, quo sit erga eos animo, quo affectu, quaq; fiducia, & quantū consolationis per Titū ab ipsis ad se reuersum acceperit. Tertiò exponit quid utilitatis ex ea prouenerit trifticia, qua per priorem fuerant epistolam contristati. Postea redit ad consolationem, ex aduentu Titi acceptam.
units.tr: At the very beginning he exhorts them to holiness of life. Then again he recalls what his attitude, feeling and confidence toward them was, and how much consolation he received from them through Titus when Titus returned to him. Thirdly he sets out what benefit has come from that sorrow by which they had been saddened through the earlier letter. Afterwards he returns to the consolation received from the arrival of Titus.

units.la: CAPVT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: AS igitur promissiones cū habeamus charissimi, mundemus nosipsos ab omni inquinamento carnis ac spiritus, perficientes sanctimoniam cum timore Dei.
units.tr: Since therefore we have these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.

units.la: Paraenesis ista, quoniam ex praecedentibus infertur, & prorsus ad eandem materiam pertinet, quæ in illis tractata est, inconuenienti dimissione ab illis diuulsa est, & ad principium capitis huius translata. Has igitur promissiones cum habeamus charissimi inquit. Quas? Quibus pollicitus est Deus, quod habitare & ambulare in nobis tanquam in suo templo, quod Deus noster esse, nosq; pro suo populo habere, immò quod nos filiorum filiarumq; loco suscipere, patrisq; loco nobis esse uelit. Hæ promissiones utiq; amplissimæ sunt ac tales, vt nec felicius nobis nec maius quicquam contingere queat.
units.tr: This exhortation follows from what precedes and belongs entirely to the same subject treated there. Through an inappropriate break it has been separated from those passages and moved to the beginning of this chapter. He says, "Since we have these promises, dearly beloved." Which promises? Those God has pledged: that he will dwell and walk in us as in his own temple, that he will be our God, that he will hold us as his people, indeed that he will receive us in the place of sons and daughters and be a Father to us. These promises are most ample, and nothing more happy or greater could befall us.

units.la: Quid est autem quod dicit: Has igitur promissiones cū habeam? Cū res promissas adepti essent, & iam haberent fideles quibus scribit. Nā utiq; suscepérat eos Deus in Christo, vt essent illorū & Deus & pater, & habitabat in eis gratia & virtute sui spiritus, mox atq; credentes fuerant facti.
units.tr: But what does he mean by saying, "Since we have these promises"? The faithful to whom he writes had already obtained the promised things and already possessed them. For God had indeed received them in Christ, so that he was their God and Father, and from the moment they believed, he dwelt in them by his grace and by the power of his Spirit.

units.la: Respondeo. Promissiones habentur bifariam. Primò, spe futurę acquisitionis. Sic habemus promissiones futurę resurrectionis, æternæ vitæ & gloriæ cum Christo in sempiternum possidendæ. Ipsa promissa bona nondum habemus, sed credentes ac sperantes expectamus. Deinde promissiones quasdam sic habemus, ut ipsa quoq; simus promissa consequuti.
units.tr: I answer: promises are held in two ways. First, by the hope of a future acquisition. So we hold the promises of the future resurrection, of eternal life and of glory to be possessed with Christ forever. We do not yet have the promised good things themselves, but we await them in faith and hope. Second, there are promises which we hold in such a way that we have already obtained the very things promised.

units.la: In hanc classem referendæ sunt promissiones quarum hic meminit Apostolus. Hæ nanq; in præsenti uita fide acquiruntur. Pertinent enim ad præsentē gratiam, qua electos suos ac fideles dignatur Deus, mox atq; vocationis ac iustificationis fuerint facti participes. Quare conuenientius verteretur ad hunc modum. Hæc igitur promissa cum habeamus, id est, adepti simus ac possideamus. Quasi dicat. Cū igitur simus iam templum Dei, habitantis & ambulantis in nobis, sitq; ille Deus ac pater noster, & nos illius populus filij ac filiæ. Quid hinc infert ac faciendum admonet?
units.tr: The promises the Apostle mentions here belong to this second class. They are acquired by faith in the present life. For they pertain to the present grace by which God deigns to favour his elect and faithful, as soon as they have become partakers of calling and justification. So the sentence would be better rendered thus: "Since we have these promised things," that is, since we have obtained and possess them. As if he said: "Since therefore we are already the temple of God, in whom he dwells and walks, and since he is our God and Father, and we are his people, sons and daughters, what does he infer from this and what does he admonish us to do?"

units.la: CHARISSIMI, inquit, mundemus nosipsos ab omni inquinamento carnis ac spiritus.) Significationem paternæ dilectionis immiscet, dum eos vocat charissimos, quo & moueat eos ad obsequendum, & quæ subiecturus est præmolliat. Mundemus nosipsos inquit. Respicit ad id quod in promissione Dei, veluti conditionis vice requiritur, vbi dicit: immūdum ne tetigeritis. Quasi dicat. Quandoquidem hoc est promissioni gratiæ, quā adepti sumus annexum, vt ab omni immundo sic abstineamus, vt ne tangamus quidem quod immundū est, ne polluamur, summopere curandum nobis est, ut nosipsos ab omni inquinamento mundemus, ne tā insigni gratia indigni reperiamur.
units.tr: "Dearly beloved," he says, "let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit." He mingles a sign of paternal love when he calls them dearly beloved, both to move them to obedience and to soften what he is about to say. "Let us cleanse ourselves," he says. He looks to what is required in God's promise, as though it were the condition of the promise, where it says: "Touch no unclean thing." As if he said: since it is attached to the promise of grace which we have obtained that we abstain from every unclean thing, so that we do not even touch what is unclean, lest we be defiled, we must take the greatest care to cleanse ourselves from every defilement, lest we be found unworthy of so great a grace.

units.la: Vide autem quàm caute non dicat: mundate vosipsos, sed mundemus nosipsos, quo tolerabiliorem reddat admonitionem, sic propositā, vt se quoq; concernat perinde atq; ipsos, ne vi deantur ipsi soli opus habere, ut mundentur. Pharisæorum est, sic monere alios, ut ad se pertinere non putent admonitionem, qua alios faciendorum ac vitandorum admonent. Verus Christi minister, licet ex officio quosuis ad veræ pietatis studiū exhortetur, quoniam tamen & ipse eadem cum alijs est carnis infirmitate circumdatus, dū admonet alios, seipsum quoque una cum alijs eorum quæ facienda sunt, admonet.
units.tr: Notice how cautiously he does not say, "Cleanse yourselves," but "let us cleanse ourselves," so that he makes the admonition more bearable, set forth in such a way that it touches himself also, as it touches them, lest they seem to be the only ones in need of cleansing. It belongs to the Pharisees to admonish others in such a way that they do not think the admonition pertains to themselves, though they admonish others about what must be done and avoided. A true minister of Christ, although by his office he exhorts anyone whatsoever to the pursuit of true godliness, since he too is surrounded by the same weakness of the flesh as others, when he admonishes others he admonishes himself too, together with them, about what must be done.

units.la: AB omni, inquit, inquinamento carnis & spiritus.) Per carnem & spiritum intelligit corpus & animam. Sunt autem carnis inquinamenta, quibus corpus ipsum immundis actibus polluitur, vt sunt, externi simulacrorum cultus, quibus ante illa procumbitur in genua, leuantur oculi, extenduntur manus, pedibus ad eius modi cultus itur ac reditur. His actibus omnino membra corporis polluuntur. Deinde impuratur corpus scortatione, incestu, adulterio & alijs infandis libidinibus: Polluitur etiam ebrietate, qua sanè mirum in modum defœdatur. Spiritus inquinatur immundis, affectibus ac prauis concupiscentijs, ira etiam, inuidia, & odijs, & cum primis diffidentia, cui opponitur fides, qua corda purificantur. Et quoniam multæ sunt eorum species, quibus caro & spiritus inquinantur, non simpliciter dicit, ab inquinamento, sed, ab omni, id est, ab omnis generis inquinamento carnis & spiritus. Neque enim mundus esse poterit, qui etsi unam & alteram impu-
units.tr: "From every filthiness," he says, "of the flesh and spirit." By flesh and spirit he understands body and soul. The defilements of the flesh are those by which the body itself is polluted by unclean acts, such as external worship of images, before which men kneel, raise their eyes, stretch out their hands, and go and return on foot to such worship. By these acts the members of the body are wholly defiled. Then the body is defiled by fornication, incest, adultery and other unspeakable lusts. It is also polluted by drunkenness, which indeed disgraces it in a wonderful way. The spirit is defiled by unclean emotions, by depraved desires, also by anger, envy and hatreds, and above all by distrust, which is opposed by faith, by which hearts are purified. And since there are many kinds by which flesh and spirit are defiled, he does not simply say "from defilement," but "from every," that is, from every kind of defilement of flesh and spirit. For a man cannot be clean who, though he avoids one or another kind of impurity, is still defiled by the rest.

units.la: impuritatis speciem uitat, ceteris tamen inqui{A}natur. Quare requiritur, vt ab omni nos inquinamento mundemus. Nec carnis tantum, sed & spiritus, nec spiritus modo, sed simul & carnis puritatem poscit, quo toti simus in conspectu domini mundi, non foris tantum in corpore, sed & intus in spiritu.
units.tr: Therefore it is required that we cleanse ourselves from every defilement. He demands purity not only of the flesh but also of the spirit, and not of the spirit only but at the same time of the flesh, so that we may be wholly clean in the sight of the Lord, not only outwardly in the body but also inwardly in the spirit.

units.la: Dicet quisquam. Ergo ne immundi adhuc erant fideles, quib. scribit, vt opus haberent ab omni inquinamento carnis & spiritus mundari? Quid igitur est quod 1. Cor. 6. ad eosdem scribit dicens: Atq; haec eratis quidem sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis, sed iustificati estis in nomen domini Iesu, & per spiritum Dei nostri. Si abluti iam erant & sanctificati, vtiq; non erant omnis generis inquinamento immundi. Si immundi non erant, quorsum attinebat admonere eos, vt seipsos ab omni inquinamento carnis & spiritus mundarent?
units.tr: Someone will say: "Then were the faithful to whom he writes still unclean, that they needed to be cleansed from every defilement of flesh and spirit? What then is the meaning of what he writes to the same people in 1 Cor. 6: 'And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God'? If they were already washed and sanctified, they certainly were not defiled by every kind of impurity. If they were not defiled, why was it necessary to admonish them to cleanse themselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit?"

units.la: Respondeo. Abluti quidem erant & sanctificati, verum haud pariformiter omnes. Nam quod attinebat sacramentum ablutionis ac sanctificationis, baptisma videlicet, eos quidem sacramentaliter erant mundati, verum quod vitae puritatem cocernebat, qua non sacramentaliter tantum, sed & realiter mundi essent, nondum erant mundi omnes. Quare ad eos qui adhuc carnales erat, adeoq; & immundi, referenda est haec admonitio, vt quod erant facti sacramentaliter, esse curarent & realiter. Quin & alij, qui reipsa esse satagunt, quod secundum gratiam sacramenti facti sunt, non sic sunt perfecte mundi, ut nul{B}lo inquinamenti genere vita ipsorum impure tur. Quapropter & illis opus est, ut hac admonitione ad plenam mundiciam persequenda stimulentur.
units.tr: I answer: they were indeed washed and sanctified, but not all alike. For as far as the sacrament of washing and sanctification is concerned, namely baptism, they were indeed cleansed sacramentally; but as far as the purity of life is concerned, by which they would be clean not only sacramentally but in reality, not all of them were yet clean. Therefore this admonition is directed to those who were still carnal, and hence still unclean, so that they might take care to make real what they had become sacramentally. Moreover, others who strive in reality to be what they have become according to the grace of the sacrament are not so perfectly clean that their life is not defiled by some kind of impurity. So they too need to be stirred by this admonition to pursue full cleanness.

units.la: PERFICIENTES, inquit, sanctimoniā cū timore Dei.) Declarat quomodo seipsos ab omni inquinamento mundare debeant. Sanctificati erat per sacramentū sanctificationis & nomen Christi, in quod erat, initiati perq; spiritum Dei, quem acceperant credentes. Ea sanctificatio initialis erat perfecta quidem quod gratiam sanctificantis Dei, perficiedaq; uero ad huc, quod uitam sanctificatorum attinet. Ad hanc illos perfectionem sic hortatur, ut perficientes coeptam in ipsis sanctificationem ab omni inquinamento carnis & spiritus abstineant, uel si mauis, ab omni inquinamento abstinentes sanctificationem perficiant.
units.tr: "Perfecting," he says, "holiness in the fear of God." He declares how they ought to cleanse themselves from every defilement. They had been sanctified through the sacrament of sanctification and the name of Christ, into which they had been initiated, and through the Spirit of God, whom they had received by believing. That sanctification was initial; it was perfect as far as the grace of God who sanctifies is concerned, but still needed to be perfected as far as the life of the sanctified is concerned. To this perfection he so exhorts them, that by perfecting the sanctification begun in them they should abstain from every defilement of flesh and spirit; or, if you prefer, by abstaining from every defilement they should perfect their sanctification.

units.la: Videmus igitur hoc loco, quid de sacramentali sit sanctificatione sentiendum. Quod illa concernit sumus omnes sancti, quotquot baptizati sumus in Christo. Verum ea sanctificatio ut est initialis, ita perfectionis studiū a nobis requirit. Est enim adhuc imperfecta, donec quic quid in carne ac spiritu nostro apphanū est & impurum, expurgetur. At haec perfectio non absoluitur, nisi spiritus e corpore liberatus ad caelestia fuerit translatus.
units.tr: We see here, therefore, what is to be thought about sacramental sanctification. As far as that goes, we are all holy, as many of us as have been baptized into Christ. But that sanctification, while it is initial, requires of us a striving after perfection. For it is still imperfect until whatever in our flesh and spirit is stained and impure is purged away. This perfection, however, is not complete until the spirit, freed from the body, has been carried up to heavenly things.

units.la: ADDIT, cum timore Dei.) Respicit ad carnales, quibus hoc procliue est, ut de gratia Dei persuasi parum timoris Dei retineat in corde,
units.tr: He adds, "in the fear of God." He looks to carnal people, for whom it is easy, once persuaded of the grace of God, to retain little fear of God in the heart.

units.la: id quod nostra hac aetate nimis manifestum est in multis, qui vbi Papisticis superstitionibus per verbum Dei liberati fuere, vna cum super stitione omnem timorem Dei abiecerunt, atq; ita sese omnis generis inquinamentis commaculat, & sanctificationem qua ex verbi Dei potiti fuerant prophanant. Idem eueniebat plerisque in ecclesia Corinthiorum. Quare hortatur eos, vt acceptam sanctificationem cum timore Dei perficiant. Reuera merito timemus eum, qui nisi misericorditer ignoscere voluisset, iustissimo nos poterat iudicio damnare in sempiternum, & damnaturus etiam est omnes eos qui gratiam suam aut spernetes non accipiunt; aut acceptam male collocant.
units.tr: This is only too evident in our own age in many who, once freed by the word of God from Papist superstitions, have cast off along with superstition all fear of God, and so defile themselves with every kind of impurity and profane the sanctification which they had received through the word of God. The same thing happened to many in the church of Corinth. Therefore he exhorts them to perfect the sanctification they have received with the fear of God. Indeed we rightly fear him who, had he not been willing to pardon us in mercy, could have condemned us to eternal damnation by most just judgment, and who will condemn all those who either despise his grace or do not receive it, or who misuse it once received.

units.la: Capaces estote nostri: neminem laesimus, neminem corrupimus, neminem fraudauimus. Non hoc ad condemnatione uestri dico. Siquidem ita ante dixi uobis, qd in cordib. nostris estis ad commoriendum & conuiuendum. Multa mihi fiducia erga uos, multa mihi gloriatio de uobis, impletus sum consolatione, uehementer exundo gaudio in omni afflictione nostra. Etenim cum uenissemus in Macedoniam nulla habuit relaxatione caro nostra, sed in omnibus afflige-bamur. Foris pugnę, intus terrores. Verum qui consolatur humiles, consolatus est nos Deus per aduentum Titi. Non solum autem per aduentum illius, verum etiam per consolationem, quam ille accepit de uobis, cum annunciaret nobis uestrum desiderium, uestrum fletum, uestrum pro me studium, adeo ut magis gauisus fuerim.
units.tr: Make room for us in your hearts. We have wronged no one, corrupted no one, defrauded no one. I do not say this to condemn you, for I have already told you that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together. Great is my confidence in you, great is my boasting about you; I am filled with comfort, and I overflow with joy in all our affliction. For when we came into Macedonia our flesh had no rest, but we were troubled on every side: fightings without, fears within. But God, who comforts the humble, comforted us by the coming of Titus. And not only by his coming, but also by the comfort he received from you, when he reported to us your longing, your mourning, and your zeal on my behalf, so that I rejoiced all the more.

units.la: Sunt haec admodum pathetica, ubiq; singularis dilectionis affectus spirantia. Summa contextus istius haec est. Poscit ab illis vicissim diligi, ac significat quo sit erga ipsos affectu, quaque fiducia, & quam sit per aduentum Titi recreatus & exhilaratus. Capaces estote nostri, inquit, vel vt vulgata habet, capite nos. Locum poscit in illorum cordibus, vt quemadmodum eos corde dilatato complectabatur omnes, ita illi se vicissim in cordibus suis capiat & complectantur. Sentiebat enim eos cordib. erga se esse angustis, sicuti & supra cap. precedenti conquestus est, dicens: Cor nostrum dilatatum est. Non estis angusti in nobis, sed estis angusti in visce ribus uestris. Eandem autem remunerationem vt a filijs exigo.
units.tr: These words are very emotional, breathing a singular affection of love. The sum of this passage is this: he asks them in return to love him, and shows what affection and what confidence he has toward them, and how much he was refreshed and cheered by the coming of Titus. "Make room for us," he says, or, as the Vulgate has it, "receive us." He asks for a place in their hearts, so that just as he embraced them all with an enlarged heart, they in turn might receive and embrace him in their hearts. For he perceived that they had narrow hearts toward him, as he complained in the previous chapter, saying: "Our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted in us, but you are restricted in your own affections." Now, as a return, I ask the same from you as from children.

units.la: NEMINEM laesimus, inquit, neminem corrupimus, neminem fraudauimus.) Hoc est, nulla in re cuiquam ex vobis causam dedimus, quo minus nos amanter corde suo complecta tur. Quod nonnulli ex uobis me fastidiunt, & interim sectarum magistros in precio habent, faciunt hoc absq; mea culpa. Neminem enim ex uobis aliqua iniuria affecimus (hoc est qd' dicit, οὐδένα ἠδίκησαμεν) neminē corrupimus, id est, nullius integritatem per falsam doctrinam à studio recti abduximus & uiciauimus, neminē fraudauimus, Græcē, οὐδένα ἐπλεονέκτησαμεν, id est, neminem studio auariciæ circumuenimus. Perstringit obliquè in pseudapostolis dominatum, à ueris apostolis alienum, corruptelas falsæ doctrinæ, & studiū auariciæ, quo bonis fidelium insidiabantur: dominatum, in eo quod dicit, neminem iniuria affecimus, corruptelas falsæ doctrinæ in eo quod subiungit dicens, neminem corrupimus, studium auariciæ, quo bonis fidelium fraudulenter insidiabantur, in eo quod addit, neminem fraudauimus. Verùm hac de re infrà cap.ii. manifestius dicturus est.
units.tr: "We have wronged no one," he says, "we have corrupted no one, we have defrauded no one." That is, in nothing have we given any of you cause to embrace us less warmly in his heart. That some of you despise me while meanwhile holding the leaders of factions in esteem, they do without any fault of mine. For we have done no injury to any of you (this is what he says: οὐδένα ἠδίκησαμεν [we wronged no one]); we have corrupted no one, that is, we have not led anyone's integrity away from zeal for the right by false doctrine and spoiled it; we have defrauded no one, in Greek οὐδένα ἐπλεονέκτησαμεν [we took advantage of no one], that is, we have not circumvented anyone out of greed. He obliquely strikes at the domination of the false apostles, alien to the true apostles, at the corruptions of false doctrine, and at the zeal for gain by which they laid snares for the goods of the faithful: the domination in what he says, "we have wronged no one"; the corruptions of false doctrine in what follows, "we have corrupted no one"; the zeal of greed by which they fraudulently laid snares for the goods of the faithful in what he adds, "we have defrauded no one." But he will speak of this more plainly below, in chapter 11.

units.la: Nos hic discrimen uerorum ac falsorum apostolorum obseruemus. Veri, ut alieni sunt à dominatu, à falsa doctrina & à studio auariciæ & quæstus: ita nemini inferunt iniuriam, nemi nem corrumpunt, neminem auariciæ studio circumueniunt, falsi uerò quemadmodum infecti sunt spiritu dominationis, falsæ doctrinæ, & auariciæ ac quæstus, ita iniuriis eos afficiūt quibus dominantur, corrumpunt quos docēt, circumueniunt incautos, è quibus aliquid potest esse lucri. Inspice Romam, & uide quid de fede Apostolica quam sibi vindicant, iudicare debeas. Si reperis eam liberam à dominatu, à corruptelis falsæ doctrinæ, ab inexplebilis auariciæ quæstu, ut possit dicere, nemini iniuriam intuli, neminem corrupi, neminem fictis uerbis negociando circumueni, bene, agnosce Apostolicæ synceritatis imitationem, si uero dominatricem, corruptricemac circum uentricem deprehenderis, cognosce sedem Antichristi, & execrabilem imposituram Satanæ sub prætextu sedis Apostolicæ in ecclesia regnantem.
units.tr: Here let us observe the difference between true and false apostles. True apostles, as they are alien to domination, to false doctrine, and to the love of gain and profit, so they do injury to no one, corrupt no one, and circumvent no one through greed. False apostles, as they are infected with the spirit of domination, of false doctrine, and of greed and profit, so they inflict injuries on those they lord over, corrupt those they teach, and circumvent the unwary from whom some gain can be got. Look at Rome, and see what you ought to judge about the see of the Apostles which it claims for itself. If you find it free from domination, from the corruptions of false doctrine, and from the gain of insatiable greed, so that it can say, "I have done injury to no one, corrupted no one, circumvented no one with feigned words in trade," then acknowledge an imitation of apostolic sincerity. But if you find it domineering, corrupting, and circumventing, recognise the seat of Antichrist and the detestable imposture of Satan, reigning in the Church under the pretext of the apostolic see.

units.la: NON hoc ad condemnationem uestri dico, inquit.) Græcè simpliciter est, οὐκ πρὸς κατάκεισιν λέγω, id est: Non ad condemnationem dico. Id est, non dico ut quempiam ex uobis accusem & condemnem. Non sic innocentiam meam defendo, ut uos condemnem. Videbatur eos accusare, quod innocentem se fastidirent & aerfarentur. Verùm non hoc agebat, sed simpliciter eos innocentiæ suæ admonet, ut cogitent, non esse causam quur se fastidiant. Et hoc agens quoniam ueretur, ne plus eos offendat, occupatione tollens, quod suspicari poterant, dicit: Non ad condemnationem dico. Vide modo destiam Apostoli. Quamuis eos acriter obiurgare, & propter tot tamque magna beneficia, quibus eos affecerat, ingratitudinis accusare posset, nihil huius faciens, sola innocentiæ suæ defensione contentus est, & sic quoq; ueritus, ne quo pacto offendat, negat se quæ dicit, adipsorum dicere condemnationem. Erant plane condemnabiles, uerùm quæ dicebat, non ob id dicebat ut eos condemnaret.
units.tr: "I do not say this to condemn you," he says. In Greek it is simply οὐκ πρὸς κατάκεισιν λέγω [I do not speak for condemnation], that is: "I do not speak for condemnation." That is, I do not say this so that I may accuse and condemn any of you. I do not defend my innocence in such a way as to condemn you. It might seem he was accusing them, since they despised and abhorred him though he was innocent. But he was not doing that; he simply reminds them of his innocence, so that they may consider there is no cause for despising him. And since he fears he may offend them further, he forestalls what they might suspect and says: "I do not say this to condemn." See the moderation of the Apostle. Although he could sharply rebuke them, and accuse them of ingratitude for the many great benefits with which he had favoured them, he does none of this. Content with the defence of his innocence alone, and fearing lest he offend them in any way, he denies that what he says is spoken for their condemnation. They were plainly condemnable, but he did not say what he said in order to condemn them.

units.la: SIQVIDEM iam ante dixi, quod in cordibus nostris estis ad commoriendum & conuiuendum.) Reddit rationem, qua probet se nō hæc dicere, ut ipsos condemnet. Siquidē iam ante dixi inquit, quod in cordibus nostris estis ad commoriendum, &c. Quasi dicat. Vsque adeò uos diligo ut paratus sim uobiscum ferre ac pati omnia, quæ uobis ferenda fuerint, siue ad vitam, siue ad mortem, sic estis in cordibus nostris, ut separare nos nec mors possit nec vita, tam abest, ut condemnare uos cupiam. Siquidem iam ante dixi inquit, ubi hoc dixerat antea. Capite præcedenti ubi dixit. Os nostrum apertum est erga vos. Cor nostrum dilatatum est. Non estis angusti in nobis. Quod illic obscurius innuit, hic clarius exprimit. Sic autem habet veræ dilectionis ingenium, ut nullo se pacto separari sinant qui diligunt ab ijs quos corde sunt complexi. Non possunt deserere mortuos, non possunt seiungi à viuis. Reperti sunt catelli usq; adeò herorum suorum amantes, ut à latere uiuorum non discederent, à sepulcro mortuorum auelli non possent. Vtinam sic coparati simus & ipsi erga Christum, ut à dilectione illius nec vita nec morte separari possimus. Sine huiusmodi dilectionis spiritu nemo pastor ad ouiculas domini ueracirer dicturus est, In cordibus nostris estis ad commoriendum & conuiuendum.
units.tr: "For I have already said that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together." He gives the reason by which he proves that he does not say these things to condemn them. "For I have already said," he says, "that you are in our hearts to die together," and so on. As if to say: I love you so much that I am ready to bear and suffer with you all that must be borne by you, whether to life or to death. You are in our hearts so that neither death nor life can separate us; so far am I from wishing to condemn you. "For I have already said," he says, referring to what he had said earlier in the preceding chapter: "Our mouth is open toward you. Our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted in us." What he hinted at there more obscurely, he expresses here more clearly. Such is the nature of true love, that those who love never allow themselves to be separated from those whom they have embraced in their heart. They cannot desert the dead; they cannot be parted from the living. There have been dogs so fond of their masters that they would not leave the side of the living and could not be torn from the grave of the dead. Would that we too were so disposed toward Christ, that neither life nor death could separate us from his love. Without this spirit of love, no minister would truly be able to say to the Lord's little sheep, "You are in our hearts, to die together and to live together."

units.la: Obserua uerò solicitam Apostoli prouidentiam. Quoniam sic statuerat, cum hæc ad Corinthios scriberet, quod nollet eos scribendo offendere, sed magis conciliare & sibi & interipsos mutuò. priusquam ad innocentiæ suæ defensionem diceret, neminem lesimus, neminem corrupimus, neminem circumuenimus, præmisit de sua erga eos dilectione, qua omnes amanter gestabat & fouebat in corde, quo cum minore offensione quæ dicturus erat acciperent, & si quid tristius diceret, dilectionis affectui tribuerent. Iam postquam tale quid protulit, unde offendi poterant, non contetus præmissa cautione, rursus quàm diligat eos commemoras, refricat quæ antea dixerat. Sciebat uidelicet, q leui momento præcedens serenitas obliuioni tradatur, ubi uel modica nubecula uelatur. Ipsa dilectionis opera mox obscurātur, si uel uerbulum proferas quod offendat, nedum significatio illius verbis prolata. Quare haud absque ratione hac est usus diligentia qua dicta iam antea refricaret dicens: Siquidem iam ante dixi, quod in cordibus nostris estis, &c.
units.tr: Observe, moreover, the careful foresight of the Apostle. He had decided, while writing to the Corinthians, that he did not wish to offend them by writing, but rather to win them over, both to himself and to one another. So before he said in defence of his innocence, "we have wronged no one, corrupted no one, circumvented no one," he first spoke of his love toward them, with which he embraced and cherished them all in his heart, so that they might receive what he was about to say with less offence, and if he said anything harsher, they might attribute it to the feeling of love. Now, after he had put forward something from which they could take offence, he was not content with the caution he had given; he again recalls how much he loves them, and renews what he had said before. He knew that a previous calm is quickly forgotten, and that even a slight cloud covers it. The very works of love are soon obscured if you utter a single word that offends, let alone a declaration of it in words. So it was not without reason that he took this care, renewing what he had said before: "For I have already said that you are in our hearts," and so on.

units.la: MVLTA mihi fiducia erga uos, inquit, multa mihi gloriatio de uobis.) Græcè est, πολλή παρρησία, quod hic legimus, multa fiducia. Fiduciæ multæ sunt species, at παρρησίαν cōstat esse libertatem ac fiduciam loquendi, qua citra hæsitationem liberè ac fiducialiter loquimur, & quæ admonenda uidetur admonemus, quasi sit παντὸς ῥησία. Hæc parrhesia tum rectè loquēdi libertas uocatur, quando sine metu liberè loquimur, ubi tamen metuendum esset periculum. lum. Vbi vero amicos fiducialiter monemus, bona præditi fiducia, quod respectu amicitiæ boni sint liberam admonitionem consulturi, tum recte eiusmodi parrhesiam fiduciam loquendi uocamus. Et hanc intelligit Apostolus cum dicit: Multa mihi parrhesia erga vos. Quod enim supra capite precedenti dixit, Os meum apertum est erga vos, hoc ipsum alijs hic verbis exprimit.
units.tr: "Great is my confidence toward you," he says, "great is my boasting about you." In Greek it is πολλή παρρησία [much boldness], which here we read as "great confidence." There are many kinds of confidence, but παρρησία is known to be the freedom and confidence of speaking, by which we speak without hesitation and frankly, and admonish where admonition seems needed, as if it were παντὸς ῥησία [free speech in all things]. This parrhesia is rightly called freedom of speaking when we speak freely and without fear, where there would nevertheless be danger to fear. But when we frankly admonish friends, endowed with good confidence, because out of friendship they are good people about to offer free admonition, then we rightly call such parrhesia confidence of speech. This is what the Apostle means when he says: "Great is my parrhesia toward you." For what he said in the preceding chapter, "My mouth is open toward you," he here expresses in other words.

units.la: NON ad condemnationem, inquit, hęc dico, nam diligo vos, & habeo in corde meo ad con moriendum & ad conuiuendū, sed quæ dico pro mea parrhesia dico, quę mihi multa est erga vos.) Et hoc dicens, iterū exprimit dilectionis ingenium, quę sic comparata est, vt existimet sibi liberè admonendum esse, si quid sit admonendum, idq; iure amicitiæ. Opposita huic est assentatio, quæ falso amicitiam simulat, dū omnia laudat in faciem, etiam quæ laudanda nō sunt, sed corrigenda.
units.tr: "I do not say this to condemn you," he says, "for I love you, and you are in my heart, to die together and to live together. But what I say, I say out of my frankness, which toward you is great." In saying this, he again expresses the nature of love, which is so disposed that it judges it must speak freely, if anything needs admonishing, and does so by the right of friendship. Opposed to this is flattery, which falsely feigns friendship while it praises everything to a person's face, even what should not be praised but corrected.

units.la: MVLTA gloriatio de vobis, inquit.) Quasi dicat. Quamuis ad vos liberè, quia multa cum fiducia loquor, interim tamen ad alios de vobis multum glorior, tam abest ut quæ dico, ad condemnationem vestri dicam. Non enim tan topere de vobis gloriarer, si non diligerem, si improbarem, si accusarem, si condemnarem. Rursus ingenium veręr dilectionis expressum uides, quæ in faciem liberè monet & corripit dilectū, de quo tamē ad alios impēse gloriatur, honesteq; & amanter loquitur. Contra assentatrix illa κολακεία in facie adulatur, à tergo ob loquitur, in faciem simulat amicitiam, à tergo spirat hostiles inimicitias. Nec dubito quin hoc ingenio fuerint pseudapostoli, quibus hic Paulus integritatem suam & veræ dilectionis experimenta opponit.
units.tr: "My boasting about you is great," he says. It is as if he said: although I speak to you freely, because I speak much and with confidence, nevertheless I boast much about you to others. So far is what I say from being said to your condemnation. For I would not boast about you so much if I did not love you, if I did not approve of you, if I accused you or condemned you. Again you see the true character of love, which admonishes and rebukes the beloved frankly to his face, and yet speaks of him to others with great pride, honourably and lovingly. The flatterer, by contrast, [practises] κολακεία: she flatters to the face, backbites behind the back, feigns friendship in the presence, and breathes hostile enmity behind the back. I have no doubt that the false apostles had this disposition, and against them Paul sets his own integrity and the proofs of true love.

units.la: IMPLETVS sum consolatione, inquit, uehementer exundo gaudio in omni afflictione nostra.) Transit ad ea quæ de aduentu ad se Titi dicturus est. Loquitur enim de consolatione & gaudio, quibus per illū affectus fuit, qd ob id facit, ut ostendat, quàm non frustra de illis multum glorietur.
units.tr: "I am filled with comfort," he says, "I overflow exceedingly with joy in all our affliction." He passes to what he is about to say concerning Titus's coming to him. For he speaks of the comfort and joy with which he was affected through him, and he does this to show how not in vain he boasts so much about them.

units.la: IMPLETVS sum, inquit, consolatione.) Non simpliciter dicit: accepta consolatione gaudius sum, sed, ut abundantiam dilectionis suę erga eos considerandam proponat, dicit se impletum esse consolatione, & vehementer exundare gaudio, nec sic contentus, addit in afflictione nostra, immo, in omni afflictione nostra, vt uim consolationis & gaudij tantam esse significet, ut omnem afflictionum suarum molestiam ac tristitiam absorbeat. Vnde autem tantum consolationis & gaudij acceperit mox exponet.
units.tr: He does not simply say, "Having received comfort, I am glad," but, so that he may set before them the abundance of his love towards them to be considered, he says that he is filled with comfort and overflows exceedingly with joy. Not even content with this, he adds "in our affliction", or rather "in all our affliction", to signal that the power of the comfort and joy was so great that it swallowed up all the discomfort and sadness of his afflictions. He will soon explain where he received so much comfort and joy.

units.la: VEHEMENTER, inquit, exúdo gaudio.) In Græco est, ὑπερπερισσεύομαι, quod uetus inter pres simpliciter uertit, superabundo. Haud displicet uero, quod Erasmus transtulit, uehementer exundo. Videtur enim Apostolus loqui de multa gloriatione, cuius iam meminit, per quam gaudium de Corinthijs acceptum uelut exun-
units.tr: "I overflow exceedingly," he says, "with joy." In Greek it is ὑπερπερισσεύομαι [I overabound exceedingly], which the Old Translator rendered simply as "I abound". Erasmus's rendering, "I overflow exceedingly", is not unwelcome. For the Apostle seems to speak of the great boasting he has already mentioned, through which the joy received from the Corinthians was, as it were, overflowing.

units.la: dabat. Sic est natura cordis humani, vt impletū affectibus vel gaudij uel tristiciæ, uel dilectiōnis uel odij exundet in apertū, unde illud est, ex abundantia cordis os loquitur.
units.tr: Such is the nature of the human heart: when it is filled with emotions, whether of joy or sadness, of love or hatred, it overflows into the open. Hence that saying: "Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks."

units.la: IN omni afflictione nostra, inquit.) Sic hic quoq; impleri significat quod moxinitio cap. primi, gloriando & cum gratiarum actione de Deo prædicauit dicens: Benedictus Deus & pater domini nostri Iesu Christi, pater misericordiarum & Deus omnis consolationis, qui consolatur nos in omni afflictione nostra, ubi quæ cogitanda sint admonuimus.
units.tr: "In all our affliction," he says. So here too he signifies that he is filled with what he proclaimed at the very beginning of chapter 1, when, boasting and giving thanks, he spoke of God: "Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction", where we have already noted what must be considered.

units.la: ETENIM cum venissemus in Macedoniā, inquit, nullam habuit relaxationem caro nostra, sed in omnibus affligebamur. Foris pugnę, intus terrores.) Exponit paucis quod dixit: in omni afflictione nostra. Referunt hæc nonnulli ad ea quæ illi Actorum 16 & 17. euenisse leguntur. Verum series historiæ repugnat. Etenim quæ illic memorantur, euenerunt illi cum primum in Macedoniam euangelizandi gratia venissent. Quæ vero hic memorat euenerunt cū post Corinthiorum & Ephesiorum conuersionem Macedoniam confirmationis gratia reuisteret, quā de re videre est Actorum decimonono, & vigesimo, & suprà cap. 1. Quod ita dicit: Etenim cum venissemus in Macedoniā, non loquitur de primo in illam aduentu, sed de secundo. Quas autem in illo perpessus sit afflictiones, specialiter quidē non exprimit, in genere tamen significat dicens: nullam habuit relaxationem caro nostra, sed in omnibus affligebamur. Per carnem intelligit externum hominem, quem innumeri labores fatigabant, & simul impiorum hominum insectationes affligebant, sic ut nulla illi contingeret relaxatio. Nam non afflictionibus tantum, sed & timoribus exercebatur. Sic dicit: Foris pugnæ, intus terrores. Foris impugnabatur ab aduersarijs incredulis, qui ueritati Christi contradicebant, & ministros illius persequebantur. Intus cruciabatur timoribus, quibus timebat infirmioribus, ne vel à pseudapostolis seducerentur, vel persequutionibus à professione nominis Christi abstrerrerentur. Sic in omnibus affligebatur foris & intus, vt nulla daretur carni ipsius relaxatio.
units.tr: "For when we had come into Macedonia," he says, "our flesh had no rest, but we were troubled on every side. Without were fightings, within were fears." He explains briefly what he said: "in all our affliction". Some refer these words to the events recorded in Acts 16 and 17. But the sequence of the history opposes this. For what is recorded there happened when they first came into Macedonia to preach the gospel. But what he mentions here happened when, after the conversion of the Corinthians and Ephesians, he revisited Macedonia to strengthen the churches, as may be seen in Acts 19 and 20, and above in chapter 1. That he says, "For when we had come into Macedonia", shows he is not speaking of his first arrival there, but of the second. The afflictions he suffered on that occasion he does not specify in particular, but he signifies them in general, saying: "our flesh had no rest, but we were troubled on every side." By "flesh" he means the outward man, whom countless labours wearied, and at the same time the attacks of wicked men troubled, so that no rest came to him. For he was exercised not only by afflictions but also by fears. Thus he says: "Without were fightings, within were fears." Outwardly he was attacked by unbelieving opponents who contradicted the truth of Christ and persecuted its ministers. Inwardly he was tormented by fears, fearing for the weaker brethren, lest they be seduced by the false apostles or driven away from the profession of the name of Christ by persecutions. Thus he was troubled on every side, outwardly and inwardly, so that his flesh was given no rest.

units.la: Conuenienter autem carnem & relaxationē coniungit. Caro nanq; p infirmitate sua facile fatigatur laborib. & persequutionibus, fatigata vero nihil æque appetit atq; relaxationē. Hanc in se quoq; carnis infirmitatem & naturā experiuntur prophetæ, apostoli, & sancti, donec in hac vita laboribus & omnis generis molestijs exercentur.
units.tr: He rightly joins "flesh" and "rest". For the flesh, by its weakness, is easily worn down by labours and persecutions, and when worn down it desires nothing so much as rest. The prophets, apostles and saints also experience this weakness and nature of the flesh in themselves, as long as in this life they are exercised by labours and by every kind of trouble.

units.la: FORIS pugnæ, inquit, intus terrores.) In Græco est, ἔξωθεν μάχαι, ἔσωθεν φόβοι, id est, deforis pugnę, abintus, ut ita dicā, timores. Nō dicit simpliciter, ἔξω μάχαι, ἔνδον φόβοι, id est: Foris pugnę, intus timores. Quare cum dicit ἔξωθεν, intelligendum est de ijs qui foris erant, alieni à fide Christi, & cum addit ἔσωθεν, referendum ad fideles qui erant intus, quemadmodum & 1. Cor.6.illos Ἰδιὸς ἐξω, istos Ἰδιοὶ ἔσω vocat. Quasi dicat, Impugnabar ab illis qui sunt foris, & timores mihi incutiebantur ab ijs qui sunt intus. Hæc volui lectionis gratia indicare, præsertim cum faciant ad perspicuitatem sensus.
units.tr: "Without were fightings," he says, "within were fears." In Greek it is ἔξωθεν μάχαι, ἔσωθεν φόβοι [outside fights, inside fears], that is, fights from without, and fears, so to speak, from within. He does not simply say ἔξω μάχαι, ἔνδον φόβοι [fights outside, fears inside]. Therefore, when he says ἔξωθεν, it must be understood of those who were outside, strangers to the faith of Christ; and when he adds ἔσωθεν, it refers to the faithful who were inside, just as in 1 Cor. 6 he calls the former οἱ ἔξω and the latter οἱ ἔσω [those outside, those inside]. It is as if he said: I was attacked by those who are outside, and fears were struck into me by those who are inside. I have wished to point this out for the sake of reading, especially since it helps the clarity of the sense.

units.la: VERVM qui consolatur humiles, inquit, consolatus est nos Deus per aduentum Titi.) Qui dixerat, impletus sum consolatione, uehementer exundo gaudio, id iam consequenter exponit. Duo autem dicit. Vnum, quis se, alterum, unde sit consolatus. Primum tribuit Deo, alterum aduentui Titi. Verùm, inquit, consolatus est nos Deus. Consolationes quibus subinde in afflictionib. recreabatur, vt coepit initiò epistolæ, ita in progressu quoq; constanter adscribit Deo. Non dicit autem simpliciter consolatus est nos Deus, sed præmittit, qui consolatur humiles. Sic exprimit ingenium & naturam Dei, qua vsqueadeo bene vult humilibus, ut singulari quodam studio laborantibus illis succurrat, superbos uerò sic detestatur, ut resistat illis ex diametro. Non loquitur autem de illis qui animo sunt humili & modesto, sed de abiectis ac depressis. Neque enim dicit: τὸς ταπεινοφρονοῦντας, sed, τοὺς ταπεινοὺς, quia non loquitur de uirtute modestiæ, sed de afflictionibus, quibus pij in hoc sæculo ab impijs deprimuntur & humiliantur, quod & ipsi passim experiebatur. Quod ergo dicit: Qui consolatur humiles, nihil est aliud, quàm qui consolatur afflictos ac depressos. Significat autem talem se fuisse factum, cum in omnibus afflictaretur, id est, adfuisse sibi consolatorem humilium & afflictorum, Deum uidelicet, seq; esse abunde consolatum.
units.tr: "But he who comforts the lowly," he says, "God comforted us by the coming of Titus." He who had said, "I am filled with comfort, I overflow exceedingly with joy", now sets out consequently what this was. He says two things: one, who comforted him, the other, by what means he was comforted. He attributes the first to God, the second to the coming of Titus. "But," he says, "God comforted us." The comforts by which he was refreshed from time to time in his afflictions, he consistently ascribes to God, just as he did at the beginning of the letter and so continues as he goes on. But he does not simply say "God comforted us", but puts in front "who comforts the lowly". In this he expresses the character and nature of God, who so well wishes to the lowly that he helps them with a singular zeal when they labour, but so opposes the proud that he sets himself directly against them.
