He does not speak of those who are humble and modest in spirit (τοὺς ταπεινοφρονοῦντας [the humble-minded]), but of the lowly and downcast (τοὺς ταπεινοὺς [the lowly]), because he is speaking not of the virtue of modesty but of the afflictions by which the godly in this age are cast down and humbled by the ungodly, which he himself experienced everywhere. So what he says, "who comforts the lowly", is nothing other than "who comforts the afflicted and downcast". He signifies, moreover, that he himself had been made such a person when he was troubled in all things, that is, that the comforter of the lowly and afflicted, namely God, was present to him, and that he himself had been abundantly comforted.

units.la: PER aduentum Titi, inquit.) Meminit unde sit se consolatus Deus. Per aduentum uidelicet Titi. Miserat hunc Corinthum cum nonnullis aliis fratribus, sicuti uidere est capite sequenti, & cum Macedoniam reuisurus uenisset Troadem, ibique illum non, ut sperauerat, inuenisset, spiritu fatigabatur, ideoque relicta Troada abijt in Macedoniam, interim cupide aduentum illius expectans. Cum ergo interea temporis admodum afflictaretur, beneficio domini factum est, ut aduenien te illo recrearetur & exhilararetur. Sic dicit: consolatus est nos Deus per aduentum Titi. Erat is ipsi acceptissimus, propterea quod fidus esset omnium laborum socius, illiusq; absentiam ægrè tulisset, quare plurimum lætabatur, quod saluum eum receperat. Paucos habebat cooperarios in opere domini fideles. Nam plerique non quæ domini, sed quæ sua ipsorum erant quærebant, ut non immeritò solicitus fuerit pro Tito isto, ac plurimum consolationis & gaudij ex reditu illius acceperit.
units.tr: "By the coming of Titus," he says. He mentions the means by which God comforted him: namely, by the coming of Titus. He had sent Titus to Corinth with some other brethren, as may be seen in the following chapter. When he came to Troas, intending to revisit Macedonia, he did not find him there, as he had hoped; he was worn down in spirit, and so, leaving Troas, he went on into Macedonia, meanwhile eagerly awaiting Titus's arrival. Therefore, while he was greatly troubled in the meantime, by the Lord's kindness it came about that on Titus's arrival he was refreshed and cheered. So he says: "God comforted us by the coming of Titus." Titus was most dear to him, because he was a faithful partner in all his labours, and Paul had taken his absence hard, so he rejoiced greatly that he had received him back safe. He had few fellow-workers in the Lord's work who were faithful, for most sought not the things of the Lord but their own. So it is no wonder that he was anxious for this Titus, and that he received much comfort and joy from his return.

units.la: NON solum autem per aduentum illius, inquit, uerumetiam per consolationem quam il le accepit de uobis, &c.) Vt maneat in proposito, significat magnam partem consolationis huius & gaudij ab ipsis esse profectam, ne in solo Titi aduentu conquiescere uideatur, quod ad ipsos parum pertinere videri poterat. Haud dissimulat exhilaratu se fuisse aduentu Titi. Quare non dicit: Non per aduentu illius, sed: Non solum aut per aduentum illius, uerùm potissima consolationis suæ causam transfert in ipsos, sicuti mox patebit.
units.tr: Not only through his coming, he says, but also through the comfort which he received from you, etc. To keep to his purpose, he means that a large part of this comfort and joy came from them, so that he does not seem to rest in Titus's arrival alone, which might seem to concern them little. He does not hide that he was cheered by Titus's arrival. So he does not say "not through his coming" but "not only, or not through his coming," and he shifts the chief cause of his comfort onto them, as will soon become clear.

units.la: VERVMETIAM per consolationem, inquit, quam ille accepit de vobis.) In Græco est, παρεκλήθη ἐφ' ὑμῖν, id est, qua consolatus, uel, si mauis, refocillatus est in uobis. Quid consolationis verò Titus consequutus sit à Corinthijs, infrà circa calcem capitis huius memorabit. Hic obiter subijcit, quid nunciarit sibi de ipsorum erga se desiderio, fletu ac studio, dicens, cum annunciaret nobis uestrum desiderium, uestrum fletum, uestrum pro me studium, adeò ut magis gauisus fuerim. Tria ponit: desiderium, fletum, ac studium, Græcè ζῆλον, desiderium Corinthiorum erat quo præsentiam Pauli desiderabant ij, qui inter illos erant synceri. Hoc promissione aduentus sui in priore epist. cap. ult. admodum exacuerat. Fletus erat, quo lugebat propter correptionem, qua priore ipsos epistola admodum contristauerat, qua de re mox subijciet. Zelus pro ipso erat, quo se pseudapostolis & ipsorum sectatorib. nomen Paulo infamantibus opponebant. Hæc igitur cum audisset ex Tito, magis adhuc gaudebat. Intelligebat enim ex illis, tanquam certis argumentis, esse se cordi adhuc Corinthijs, adeoq; & opus domini, quod in ipsis cœperat, consistere salutem & integrum, quantumuis illud pseudapostoli in omnium cordibus viciare conarentur. Hinc itaq; afferebatur ipsi maioris gaudij occasio, qua plurimum recreabatur spiritus ipsius, quod eos illorum amantissimus, ac salutis ipsorum cupidissimus. Et alioqui sic est comparatu dilectionis ingenium, ut exhilaretur plurimum qui diligit, si certis argumentis intelligat, esse se charum illis quos diligit. Qualia uerò essent dilectionis argumenta, desiderium, fletus, & zelus, in seipso potissimum experiebatur Apostolus, qui & ipse præsentiam Corinthiorum desiderabat, cum lachrymis ad illos scribebat, & ut infrà capite 11. scribit, zelotypus erat erga eos, Dei zelo accensus. Vix certiora habentur amoris indicia, quàm quæ hic memorantur, desiderium, fletus, & zelus. Vtinam istis nos argumentis charitatem Christi Seruatoris nostri testatam reddere possimus.
units.tr: BUT ALSO THROUGH THE COMFORT, he says, WHICH HE RECEIVED FROM YOU. In the Greek it is was comforted through you [παρεκλήθη ἐφ' ὑμῖν], that is, he was comforted, or, if you prefer, refreshed, by you. What comfort Titus received from the Corinthians he will relate later, near the end of this chapter. Here he adds in passing what Titus reported to him of their longing for him, their weeping and their zeal, saying: when he reported to us your longing, your weeping, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced the more. He lists three things: longing, weeping and zeal (in Greek zeal [ζῆλον]). The longing of the Corinthians was that those among them who were sincere desired Paul's presence; he had greatly stirred this by the promise of his coming at the end of the first epistle. The weeping was grief over the rebuke by which his earlier letter had greatly saddened them, which he will mention presently. The zeal for him was the way they set themselves against the false apostles and their followers, who slandered Paul's name. Hearing these things from Titus, he rejoiced all the more. For from them he understood, as from sure evidence, that the Corinthians still held him dear, and that the work of the Lord which had begun among them was still whole and safe, however much the false apostles tried to corrupt it in everyone's hearts. Thus an occasion of greater joy was offered him, by which his spirit was greatly refreshed, because he loved them most dearly and longed for their salvation. Indeed, love is so constituted that one who loves is greatly gladdened if he understands by clear signs that he is dear to those whom he loves. The Apostle himself experienced, above all in himself, what the signs of love were: longing, weeping and zeal. He longed for the presence of the Corinthians, wrote to them with tears, and, as he writes below in chapter 11, was jealous over them, kindled with the zeal of God. Scarcely any clearer tokens of love are found than those mentioned here: longing, weeping and zeal. Would that by such signs we could show the love of Christ our Saviour.

units.la: Nā etiamsi contristati uos per epistolā, non me pœnitet, tametsi pœnituerat. Video nanq; quod epistola illa, tametsi ad tempus, contristauit uos. Nunc gaudeo, nō quod contristati fueritis, sed quod contristati estis ad pœnitentiam. Nam contristati estis secundum Deum, sic ut nulla in re detrimento sitis affecti per nos. Nam quæ secundum Deum est tristitia, ea pœnitentiam ad salutem haud pœnitenpœnitendam parit, mundi uero trifticia morte operatur. Ecce enim istuc ipsum quod secundū Deum cōtristati fuistis, quātam in uobis operatum est solicitudinē, imò satisfactionem, imò indignationem, imò timorem, imò desiderium, imò uindictam. Siquidem ubique com medastis uosipsos, quod puri sitis in eo negocio. Proinde tametsi scripsi uobis, non eius id causa feci qui læserat, nec eius causa qui læsus fuerat, sed ob id, ut palàm fieret studium uestrum pro nobis apud uos in conspectu Dei.
units.tr: For even if I saddened you by the letter, I do not regret it, although I did regret it. For I see that that letter, though only for a time, grieved you. Now I rejoice, not that you were grieved, but that you were grieved to repentance. For you were grieved according to God, so that you suffered no loss through us in anything. For the sorrow that is according to God produces a repentance not to be regretted, leading to salvation, but the sorrow of the world produces death. For see, this very thing, that you were grieved according to God, how much earnestness it has worked in you, yes, self-defence, indignation, fear, longing, even punishment. For in every way you have shown yourselves to be pure in this matter. Therefore, although I wrote to you, I did not do so for the sake of him who had done the wrong, nor for the sake of him who had been wronged, but so that your earnest care for us might be made plain to you in the sight of God.

units.la: Per occasionē eius quod fletus Corinthiorum meminit, ob quem se magis adhuc gaudere dixit, transit ad exponendum utilitatem, quam illis ea tristicia pepererat. Videbatur enim inconueniens esse, & alienum ab ingenio dilectionis, propterea gaudere quod tristes agrant ac flebant Corinthij, quos tantopere se diligere asseuerabat. Cum sit dilectioni conuenientius, flere cum flentibus, cum gaudētibus uero gaudere. Quare cum desiderio ac zelo illorum fletum coniunxisset ac dixisset, cum annunciaret nobis uestrū desiderium, uestrū fletum, uestrū pro me studium, adeò ut magis gauisus fuerim, essetque uerosimile cogitaturos illos, ergo quo tristiores nos fumus, hoc tu magis gaudes: mox subijcit expositionem, qua qd dixerat declaret, rationēq; reddat, qua re ipse ppter fletū eorū magis fuerit gauisus.
units.tr: On the occasion of his mention of the weeping of the Corinthians, because of which he said he rejoiced the more, he passes on to explain the benefit which that sorrow had brought them. For it seemed out of place, and foreign to the nature of love, to rejoice because the Corinthians, whom he declared he loved so greatly, were sad and wept. Yet it is more fitting for love to weep with those who weep, and to rejoice with those who rejoice. So, having joined their weeping to their longing and zeal, and having said: when he reported to us your longing, your weeping, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced the more, and since it was likely that they would think: the sadder we are, the more you rejoice, he now adds an explanation to clarify what he had said and to give the reason why he rejoiced the more because of their weeping.

units.la: NAM etiamsi cōtristaui uos per epistolam, inquit, non pœnitet me.) Sic exponit quod de fletu Corinthiorum dixerat, significans se loqui de tristicia, qua priore fuerant epistola contristati. Videbatur autem dolendum ipsi esse, quod eos quos diligebat contristasset. Et sane doluisset, nisi tristiciam illorū ad salutem ipsis conducere intellexisset. Sic dicit: Nam etiamsi contristaui uos per epistolam, non pœnitet me. Quare autem non pœnituerit ipsum, consequenter exponet. Interim tamē fatetur, quod contristarit eos per præcedentem epistolam, cum supra capite secūdo negauerit, se ad hoc scripsisse ut contristarentur. Non delectabatur illorum tristicia, ideoq; nō ob id scripserat, ut contristarentur, sed ut solicitudini suæ erga eos satisfaceret, salutisq; ipsorum rationem haberet. Et tamen agnoscit epistolam suam in causa illis fuisse, ut contristarentur, cuius se iam haudquaquam pœnitere dicit.
units.tr: FOR EVEN IF I SADDENED YOU BY THE LETTER, he says, I DO NOT REGRET IT. He explains in this way what he had said about the weeping of the Corinthians, meaning that he speaks of the sorrow with which they had been saddened by his earlier letter. It might seem that he ought to grieve that he had saddened those whom he loved. And indeed he would have grieved, had he not understood that their sorrow was for their salvation. So he says: For even if I saddened you by the letter, I do not regret it. Why he does not regret it he will explain in sequence. Meanwhile he admits that he had saddened them by the previous letter, although in chapter 2 above he denied that he had written in order that they should be grieved. He took no pleasure in their sorrow, and therefore he had not written in order that they might be grieved, but to satisfy his care for them and to take thought for their salvation. Yet he acknowledges that his letter had been the cause of their grief, and he says that he no longer regrets it at all.

units.la: Illud, tametsi pœnituerat, Chrysost. legendū esse putat, etiàsi pœnituisset. Sic enim exponit <bl>ἐκ τῶν πρότερον μὲν μελομένων, νῦν δὲ μεταμέλο μαι, ἀλλὰ πῶς: εἰ μεταμέλομαι νῦν, εἰ καὶ μεταμελόμην</bl> Absurdum uidetur, si dicat Apostolus, antea pœnituisse se, quod eos cōtristasset, quasi non Spiritus sancti, sed humano illos consilio per epistolam contristarit. Ideoq; legendum hic iudicat: non pœnitet me, etiamsi pœnituisset.
units.tr: Chrysostom thinks that the words "although I did regret it" should be read as "even if I had regretted it." For he explains it thus: [ἐκ τῶν πρότερον μὲν μελομένων, νῦν δὲ μεταμέλομαι, ἀλλὰ πῶς: εἰ μεταμέλομαι νῦν, εἰ καὶ μεταμελόμην]. It seems absurd, if the Apostle were to say that he had previously regretted that he had grieved them, as if he had grieved them by the letter through human counsel and not through the Holy Spirit. Therefore he judges that here one should read: I do not regret it, even if I had regretted it.

units.la: VIDEO nanq;, quod epistola illa, inquit, tametsi ad tēpus, cōtristauit uos.) Dixit: Nam etiamsi contristaui uos per epistolam, non me pœnitet, tametsi pœnituerat. Iam si consequēter legamus: Video nanque quod epistola illa grauauit uos, etiamsi ad tempus, apparet referendum esse ad fletum, de quo nūciauerat Titus. Q.d. Quod enim cōtristauerit uos epistola illa, quamuis ad tēpus, ex eo uideo quòd mihi Titus nunciauit. Et hæc lectio cum Græco cōtextu cōuenit. Vulgata tamē habet, uidens quod epistola illa, etsi ad horam, uos contristauit. Hæc lectio mihi cōuenire uidetur cum eo quod dixit, tametsi pœnituerat, ut ratio subijciatur, quare ipsum pœnituerit: uidēs, inquit, id est, cum uiderem, quod epistola illa contristauerit uos, licet factum sit hoc ad horā, id est, ad modicū tēpus. Hanc lectionē nō ausim reijcere. Pulchrè nāq; ei qd̄ p̄missum est coh̄eret.
units.tr: FOR I SEE THAT THAT LETTER, he says, THOUGH ONLY FOR A TIME, GRIEVED YOU. He said: For even if I saddened you by the letter, I do not regret it, although I did regret it. Now if we read the sequence consistently: For I see that that letter grieved you, even if only for a time, it appears that this must be referred to the weeping of which Titus had told him. That is, "For I see from what Titus has reported to me that that letter grieved you, though only for a time." And this reading agrees with the Greek context. The Vulgate, however, has: seeing that that letter, though for an hour, grieved you. This reading seems to me to agree with what he said, although I did regret it, so that a reason is added why he had regretted it: seeing, he says, that is, when I saw that that letter had grieved you, although this happened only for an hour, that is, for a short time. I would not dare to reject this reading, for it fits nicely with what was previously said.

units.la: Non est autē ociosum quod dicit: <bl>εἰ καὶ πρὸς ὥραν</bl>, id est, licet ad horam, intellige, tantū. Sic enim extenuat tristiciam Corinthiorum, non in se, sed respectu sequūtæ illā utilitatis. Nos admonemur conducere hoc saluti delinquentium, ut ad tempus, utut modicum, contristentur, quo contristati resipiscant. Modicum tristiciæ, si prudenter disponatur, plurimū non-nunquam adfert utilitatis.
units.tr: It is not idle that he says εἰ καὶ πρὸς ὥραν [even if for an hour], that is, although for an hour, understand: only that. For in this way he lessens the sorrow of the Corinthians, not in itself, but in view of the benefit that followed it. We are reminded that it serves the salvation of offenders that they be grieved for a time, however short, so that, being grieved, they may repent. A little sorrow, if it is wisely arranged, often brings very great benefit.

units.la: NVNC gaudeo, inquit, non quòd cōtristati fueritis, sed quod contristati sitis ad pœnitentiā.) Quasi dicat. Pœnitebat me, quod quamuis modico tepore contristassem uos per epistolā; nunc uero, ubi ex Tito cognoui, quanta emolumenti ex ea uobis fit tristicia natū, gaudeo, tā abest ut eius me pœniteat amplius. Et quoniā audire poterat, ergo de tristicia nostra sumis tibi materiā gaudij: exponens subijcit, nō quod cōtristati fueritis, sed quod cōtristati sitis ad pœnitentiā. Quasi dicat: Exhilarat me nō tristicia vestra, quasi illa delectar, cū illa me magis turbarit, sed pœnitetia quā tristicia ista peperit. Aliud est tristari simpliciter, & aliud, tristari ad bonū aliquē fine. Nemo delectatur tristicia eius quē diligit, delectarū uero oēs salute eorū quos diligimus, adeoq; & medū placet quoad illa peruenīūt, etiamli sit in se tristē & austerum. Inhumani sunt admodū, quibus uolupe est, si quem tristem & anxium red dere poterūt, etiamsi uiderint illū nullo ipsius bono, imò cum magno malo cōtristari.
units.tr: NOW I REJOICE, he says, NOT THAT YOU WERE GRIEVED, BUT THAT YOU WERE GRIEVED TO REPENTANCE. It is as if he said: I was sorry that I had grieved you by the letter, though only for a short time; but now, since I have learned from Titus how great a benefit has arisen for you from that sorrow, I rejoice, so far is it from being the case that I regret it any more. And since they could ask: therefore you take matter for joy from our sorrow, he explains by adding: not that you were grieved, but that you were grieved to repentance. As if he said: it is not your sorrow that cheers me, as if I took pleasure in it, since it has troubled me more, but the repentance which that sorrow has brought forth. To be grieved simply is one thing, and to be grieved for some good end is another. No one takes pleasure in the sorrow of one whom he loves, but all delight in the salvation of those whom they love, and so even a medicine pleases, insofar as it achieves its end, though in itself it is bitter and harsh. They are very inhuman who take delight if they can make someone sad and anxious, even when they see him grieved to no good of his own, but rather to great harm.

units.la: SED quod contristati sitis, inquit, ad pœnitentiā. ) Græcē est εἰς μετάνοιαν, i. ad resipiscentiam, cuius uocis sensum latina uox pœnitentia nō exprimit, quamuis Erasmus illi eundē sensum affingere molitur, dū pœnitere idē esse putat, quod pone tenere, i. potiū factū intelligere. Valla rectius, duo, inquit, uocabula græca μετάνοια & μετάμελια differūt à nostro. Nā pœnitētia dicta est à pœnitet, quod est, tædet uel piget. Græca uocabula dicta sunt à sensu retractādo, & cura in melius mutāda, elegātior dictio, ut ait Lactantius, q̄ nostra: Itaq; in nostro uerbo significatio est, tristicia cōmisi, in Græcis, mē tis emēdatio. Hæc ille. Quare si legas hoc loco, sed quod cōtristati sitis ad pœnitētiā, perinde sonat, ac si dicas, sed quod cōtristati sitis ad tristicia, siquidē pœnitentia dolor est & tristicia de eo quod est admissum. Malo itaq; legere ad resipiscentiā, secundū uim Græcę uocis, q̄, ad pœnitentiā. Quale aūt resipiscētiā tristicia hæc pepererit, Corinthijs paulo post memorabit. Supra alicubi monuimus, nō esse apostolos similes pharisæis, qui tristiciā in ijs qui deliquerūt magis spectāt q̄ uerā resipiscentiā. Apostolus hic diserte significat non delectari se tristicia Corinthiorum, delectari uero resipiscentia.
units.tr: "But that you were made sorry, he says, to repentance." In Greek it is εἰς μετάνοιαν [eis metanoian], that is, to repentance in the sense of change of mind, and the Latin word poenitentia does not express the meaning of this word. Erasmus nevertheless tries to attach this same meaning to it, since he thinks that poenitere means the same as ponitentem tenere, that is, rather to understand what has been done. Valla is more accurate: he says that the two Greek words μετάνοια [metanoia] and μεταμέλεια [metamelia] differ from our word. For poenitentia is named from poenitet, which means "it causes sorrow or grief." The Greek words are named from reconsidering a matter and changing one's care for the better, a more elegant expression, as Lactantius says, than ours. Thus in our word the meaning is sorrow for a wrong committed, while in the Greek it is amendment of mind. So far Valla. Therefore, if one reads here, "but that you were made sorry to repentance," it sounds just as if one were to say, "but that you were made sorry to sorrow," since repentance is grief and sorrow for what has been committed. I prefer, then, to read "to repentance [resipiscentia]," according to the force of the Greek word, rather than "to penance." What kind of repentance this sorrow brought forth, he will mention to the Corinthians shortly after. We have noted elsewhere that the apostles are not like the Pharisees, who look more at the sorrow of those who have sinned than at true repentance. The Apostle here clearly signifies that he does not take pleasure in the sorrow of the Corinthians, but takes pleasure in their repentance.

units.la: NAM cōtristati estis secūdū Deū, inquit, sic ut nulla in re detrimēto sitis affecti per nos.) Sensus est. Gaudeo quod ad resipiscentiā cōtristati fuistis. Id nāq; declarat, cōtristatos fuisse uos ex eo, quod Deū uos offendisse intelligxistis. Sic rationalem ꝓ, ad precedens refero, quo dixit eos cōtristatos fuisse ad resipiscētiā. Contristati, inquit, estis ad resipiscentiā, quod ex eo est, quod secundū Deū cōtristati estis. Existimo aūt cōtristari secundū Deū, nihil hic esse aliud, q̄ cōtristari ob id quod Deū offende ris. Alijs idē esse uidetur, qd ex Deo cōtristari.
units.tr: "For you were made sorry according to God," he says, "so that in nothing you were harmed through us." The sense is: I rejoice that you were made sorry to repentance. For this declares that you were grieved because you had understood that you had offended God. So I refer the rational particle to what precedes, where he said that they were grieved to repentance. You were grieved, he says, to repentance, which comes from this, that you were grieved according to God. I think that to be grieved according to God here means nothing other than to be grieved because you have offended God. To others it seems to be the same as to be grieved from God.

units.la: Illud, sic ut nulla in re detrimēto sitis affecti per nos, exponūt ad hūc modū. Sic secundum Deū ad resipiscentiā cōtristati estis per nostrā epistolā, ut ex ea nihil acceperitis detrimenti, sed magis adiuti sitis plurimū. Cōmentarij qui Hieronymo dātur, hūc sensum adferūt: Cōtristati estis secundū Deū ut in nullo detrimētō patiamini ex nobis, hoc est, ne ueniētes aliquē ex uobis dānaremus, intellige, si non effetis secundū Deū ad resipiscentiā contristati. Vetus interpres, meo iudicio, cauti⁹ uertit, ut in nullo detrimento patiamini ex nobis, quàm Eras. qui quod in Græco est, ἐν μηδενὶ, reddidit nulla in re, cum apostolus non de rebus, sed de hominibus ad ecclesiā Corinthiorū pertinētibus loquatur, dicatq; eos sic cōtristātos esse secūdum Deū ad resipiscentiā, ut in nemine ex fratribus, ne in eo quidé, qui tam enormiter peccauerat, ut excōmunicatione meruerit, detrimentū ex ipso accipiat. Etenim pro detrimēto reputat ecclesiæ, si quisquā ē numero fidelium uelut membrū à corpore propter impœnitentiam authoritate apostolica abscindatur. Erat hoc euenturū Corinthijs nisi ad resipiscentiā cōtristati fuissent. Huiusmodi detrimenti sensus hodie prope nullus est in ecclesiā, etiamsi multa Christianorū millia palā, ac prorsus quotidie perire cernamus. Romani Pōtifices sæpe numero integra regna ab Ecclesiæ cōmunioe, quātū ī ipsis fuit, nullas iustas ob causas, absq; hoc ecclesiastici detrimēti sensu absciderunt.
units.tr: As for the words "so that in nothing you were harmed through us," they explain them in this way: "In this way you were made sorry according to God to repentance through our letter, so that from it you received no harm, but were rather helped greatly." The commentaries that are attributed to Jerome bring forward this sense: "You were made sorry according to God so that you suffered no harm from us, that is, so that we would not condemn any of you when we came, understand, if you had not been made sorry according to God to repentance." In my judgement the old translator rendered more cautiously, "that you might suffer no harm from us," than Erasmus, who rendered what is in the Greek, ἐν μηδενὶ [en mēdeni], as "in nothing," since the Apostle is not speaking about things but about persons belonging to the church of the Corinthians, and says that they were so grieved according to God to repentance that, in no one of the brothers, not even in him who had sinned so enormously that he deserved excommunication, would the church suffer harm from him. For he counts it as harm to the church if anyone from the number of the faithful were cut off by apostolic authority from the body, like a limb, because of impenitence. This would have happened to the Corinthians unless they had been made sorry to repentance. Today there is almost no sense of such harm in the church, even though we see many thousands of Christians perishing openly, and indeed daily. The Roman Pontiffs have often cut off whole kingdoms from the communion of the church, as far as lay in them, for no just causes, without any sense of this ecclesiastical harm.

units.la: NAM quæ secundū Deū est tristicia, ea resipiscentiā ad salutē haud pœnitendam operatur, mundi uero tristicia mortē operatur.) Ad resipiscentiam eos cōtristatos esse dixit, ex eo, qd' cōtristati sint secundū Deū. Huius iā ratio nē subijcit, dicēs: Nā quæ secundū Deū est tristicia, resipiscentiā ad salutem operatur, mūdi uero tristicia mortem operatur. Hæc est ueluti maior, minor uero, cōntristati estis secundum Deū. Argumentatur enim ad hūc modū. Quæ secundū Deū est tristicia, resipiscentiam parit. Vos aūt cōtristati estis secundū Deū. Ergo cōtristati estis ad resipiscentiā. Est aūt maior hæc bimēbris, cōstans antithesi duplicis tristiciæ, eius uidelicet quæ sit secundum Deū, & eius quę sit secundū mundu, & exprimes diuersam utriusq; operationē. Tristicia secundū Deum hoc loco esse diximus, qua qui peccauit ob id contristatur, quod Deum offendit, perinde ac si filius contristetur quod offenderit patrem. Huic tristiciæ tribuit, quod resipiscentiam gignat. Etenim cui dolet, quod Deum offendit, utiq; peccatū suum agnoscit ac damnat, atque ita mutata sententia resipiscit. Sic tristicia quę secundum Deum est, resipiscentiam gignit. Vbi autem uera resipiscentia est, ibi est & salus. Reddit enim illa gratię Dei capaces, iuxta illud: Si conuersus fuerit peccator, &c. uita uiuet, & non morietur. Et conuertimini ad me & salui eritis. Et: Nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut conuertatur & uiuat. Ad Deum autem resipiscendo conuertimur. Hoc intelliges dicit: ea resipiscentiam ad salutem operatur. Et addit, haud pœnitendā. Græcē est, ἀμεταμέλητον, quę uox nescio an Latinè posit unica uoce proprie reddi. Sumpta est à μεταμέλεια, qd' cura, sicuti μεταμέλεια sensus mutatione significat. Hinc sunt ἀμεταμέλητος & ἀμεταμελήτως, quorum prior uox id sonat, quod curæ, posterior uero quod sensus mutationem non recipit. Rom. 2.
units.tr: "For the sorrow that is according to God works repentance unto salvation, which is not to be regretted, but the sorrow of the world works death." He said that they were grieved to repentance because they were grieved according to God. Now he adds the reason for this, saying: "For the sorrow that is according to God works repentance unto salvation, but the sorrow of the world works death." This is as it were the major premise, and the minor is, "You were grieved according to God." For he argues in this way: "The sorrow that is according to God brings forth repentance. But you were grieved according to God. Therefore you were grieved to repentance." This major premise, which has two members, is a double antithesis of sorrow, namely of that which is according to God and of that which is according to the world, and it expresses the different working of each. We have said that sorrow according to God here is that by which one who has sinned is grieved because he has offended God, just as a son is grieved that he has offended his father. To this sorrow he attributes that it begets repentance. For he who grieves that he has offended God surely acknowledges and condemns his sin, and so, having changed his judgement, repents. Thus the sorrow that is according to God begets repentance. Where there is true repentance, there is also salvation. For it makes men capable of the grace of God, according to that: "If the sinner is converted, etc., he shall live and not die" (Ezek. 18), and "Turn to me and you will be saved," and "I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live." Now we are turned to God by repenting. You will understand this when he says, "it works repentance unto salvation." And he adds, "not to be regretted." In Greek it is ἀμεταμέλητον [ametamelēton], a word that I do not know whether can be properly rendered in Latin by a single word. It is taken from μεταμέλεια [metamelia], which means care, just as μεταμέλεια signifies a change of sense. Hence come ἀμεταμέλητος [ametamelētos] and ἀμεταμελήτως [ametamelētōs], of which the former word means what is not a matter of care, while the latter means what does not admit a change of sense. (Rom. 2.)

units.la: Cor obstinatum & occæcatū, ab omni resipi- scentia alienum, uocat ἀμεταμέλητον καρδίαν. Capite II. charismata Dei uocat ἀμεταμέλητα. Inter pretes utrobiq; impœnitetiæ significationem reponunt. Nam χαρδίαν ἀμεταμέλητον, uertūt cor pœnitere nescium, & cor impœnitens, & χαρίσματα ἀμεταμέλητα dona sine pœnitentia. Et dona quorum illum pœnitere nō posit, cum uox impœnitentiæ uim uocum istarū non exprimat, sitq; inter illas luculentum discrimen. Si ordinem ueræ conuersionis inspicias, primum locum habet tristitia, secundum Deum, quæ ex auditu uerbi Dei, operante spiritu sancto acquiritur. Hanc consequitur μετάνοια, id est, immutatio mentis, quam resipiscentiam uocamus. Ex illa nascitur μεταμέλεια, id est, curæ quoque mutatio, omnia totius uitæ studia complectens. Donec mentis fascinatio durat, fieri non poterit, ut curæ ac studia in melius mutentur. Vbi uero locum reperit μεταμέλεια, ibi mutatum sensum sequitur mutatio curæ. Hæc breuiter de duabus istis uocibus.
units.tr: He calls a stubborn and blinded heart, alien to all repentance, "an unrepentant heart" [ἀμεταμέλητον καρδίαν]. In chapter 11 he calls the gifts of God "irrevocable" [ἀμεταμέλητα]. The translators in both places put the meaning of impenitence. For they render ἀμεταμέλητον καρδίαν as a heart unable to repent and an impenitent heart, and χαρίσματα ἀμεταμέλητα as gifts without repentance, and gifts which he cannot regret, since the word for impenitence does not express the force of these words, and there is a clear difference between them. If you look at the order of true conversion, sorrow according to God comes first, which is gained from hearing the Word of God, the Holy Spirit working. This is followed by μετάνοια [metanoia], that is, change of mind, which we call repentance. From it arises μεταμέλεια [metamelia], that is, a change of care also, embracing all the pursuits of the whole life. As long as the bewitchment of the mind lasts, it cannot happen that cares and pursuits are changed for the better. Where μεταμέλεια finds its place, there a change of care follows the changed sense. These are brief remarks on those two words.

units.la: Quod præsentem Apostoli locum attinet, non displicet, qd uetus interpres ἀμεταμέλητον reddidit stabilem. Nec Valla reprobat. Illud autem ambiguum est, an eam uocem ad resipiscentiam uel ad salutem referre debeamus. Valla ad salutem pertinere negat. Meo iudicio nihil est periculi, siue ad resipiscētiam, siue ad salutem referas. Nam ad utranque referri potest. Etenim resipiscentia, quam tristicia secundum Deū parit, ut uera est & syncera, ita est & ἀμεταμέλητον. Qui secundum Deum tristatur & resipiscit, huius resipiscentia studiorum in melius emendationem non mutat, sed retinet. Et salus, quam uera resipiscentia conciliat, sic est comparata, ut curæ Dei, qua resipiscentes saluare constituit, mutationem non recipiat. Si quis tamen accuratius rem ipsam perpendat, inueniet forsan μεταμέλεια, rectius dici μεταμέλητον, quam ἀμεταμέλητον, eò quod metis mutatio curarum quoq; mutationem gignit, atq; ita epitheton hoc referendum esse ad salutem, ut quemadmodū dona Dei ἀμεταμέλητα, Rom. II. ita hic & salus Dei ἀμεταμέλητον uocetur. Sed obseruationum gratia repetamus ipsa uerba.
units.tr: As for the present passage of the Apostle, it does not displease me that the old translator rendered ἀμεταμέλητον [ametamelēton] as "stable." Nor does Valla disapprove. But it is uncertain whether we ought to refer that word to repentance or to salvation. Valla denies that it pertains to salvation. In my judgement there is no danger, whether you refer it to repentance or to salvation. For it can be referred to either. Indeed, the repentance that sorrow according to God brings forth, insofar as it is true and sincere, is also ἀμεταμέλητον. He who is grieved and repents according to God, his repentance does not change the amendment of his pursuits for the better, but keeps it. And the salvation that true repentance procures is so constituted that it does not admit a change of the care of God, by which he has determined to save the repentant. If anyone, however, weighs the matter more accurately, he will perhaps find that μεταμέλεια ought more correctly to be called μεταμέλητον than ἀμεταμέλητον, because a change of mind also brings about a change of cares, and thus this epithet is to be referred to salvation, so that just as the gifts of God are ἀμεταμέλητα (Rom. 11), so here also the salvation of God is called ἀμεταμέλητον. But for the sake of observation let us repeat the words themselves.

units.la: NAM quæ secundū Deum est tristicia, inquit.) Dubium nō est, quin tandem à Deo exhilaretur, quisquis secundum Deum contristatur. Sunt autem eiusmodi tristitiæ quatuor species, quæ in præsenti occurrunt. Prima est, cuius meminit hoc loco Apostolus. Et huic soli cōpetit, quod ea resipiscentiæ dicit esse effectricem. Secunda est, qua pius homo propter nominis Dei ignominiam contristatur. Hoc genere tristitiæ contristantur quotidie, qui uiuunt uel inter alienos à fide Dei, uel inter falsos Christianos, eidololatras, & uerbi Dei hostes. Sic uiuebant illi, qui pij cum essent, & uiuerent in medio populi Dei in ipsa Hierusalē, super abominationibus quæ fiebant, gemebat & dolebant, de quibus legere licet Ezech.9.
units.tr: For whoever is grieved according to God, there is no doubt that he is at last cheered by God. There are four kinds of this godly sorrow that present themselves here. The first is the one the Apostle mentions in this place, and it belongs to this alone that he says it produces repentance. The second is that by which a pious man is grieved because of the disgrace to the name of God. People who live among those who are strangers to the faith of God, or among false Christians, idolaters and enemies of the Word of God, are grieved daily by this kind of sorrow. Those who were godly and who lived in the midst of the people of God in Jerusalem itself were like this, groaning and grieving over the abominations that were being committed, as may be read in Ezekiel 9.

units.la: Illi utiq; tristabātur secundum Deum, quemadmodum & ij quibus idem accidit in Babylone, in Assyria, & aliis gentium locis. Tertia est, qua contristantur omnes illi, qui iniurias, conuicia, & persequutiones propter nomen Dei patiuntur. Ad hanc pertinet locus 1.Pet. 2.ubi sic dicit: Nam hæc est gratia, si quis propter conscientiam Dei sufferit molestias, præter meritum affectus malis. Quarta est, nata ex desiderio apparendi in conspectu Dei, quando spiritus hominis fidelis & amantis Dei propter peregrinationis suæ prolongatione contristatur. Figura huius erat, quod Dauidi in exilio cōstituto accidit, cuius mētio fi t in Psal. 42. ubi dicit: Quemadmodum desiderat cervus ad fontes aquarum, ita desiderat anima mea ad te Deus. Quàm autē desiderium hoc cum tristicia fuerit coniunctum, satis aperit, cum dicit: Fuerunt mihi lachrymæ meæ panes die ac nocte. Item: Quare tristis es anima mea, & quare conturbas me? Hunc affectum ipse quoque Apostolus expertus est, sicut in eo patet, quod dicit, cupió dissolui, & esse cum Christo. Hæ sunt tristitiæ species, quæ secundum Deum est. Plures recenseri possunt, sed existimo hasce in præsenti sufficere. Et utinam locum in nobis habeant.
units.tr: Those people were indeed grieved according to God, as were also those to whom the same thing happened in Babylon, in Assyria and in other places of the nations. The third kind is that by which all those are grieved who suffer injuries, reproaches and persecutions for the name of God. To this belongs the passage in 1 Peter 2, where he speaks thus: "For this is grace, if someone for conscience toward God endures sorrows, suffering wrongfully." The fourth arises from the desire to appear in the sight of God, when the spirit of a faithful man who loves God is grieved because his pilgrimage is prolonged. The figure of this was what befell David when he was in exile, as is mentioned in Psalm 42, where he says: "As the deer longs for the water brooks, so longs my soul for you, O God." How closely this longing was joined with sorrow the psalm makes plain enough when it says: "My tears have been my bread day and night." Likewise: "Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me?" The Apostle himself also experienced this feeling, as is clear from what he says: "I desire to depart and to be with Christ." These are the kinds of sorrow that are according to God. More could be listed, but I think these are enough for the present. And would that they had a place in us.

units.la: EA resipiscentiam, inquit, ad salutem haud pœnitendam parit.) Tria obserua. Primum, quod tristicia quæ secundum Deum est, parit resipiscentiam. Ea autem nō est omnium. Et enim nisi diligas ac magnifacias Deum in corde, non contristaberis quod peccádo eum offendisti. Quare hoc genus tristiciæ eorū tantum est, qui sunt ex Deo. Reproborum esse nō potest. Ergo nec uera resipiscentia est omniū. Secundum, quod uera resipiscētia facit ad salutem. Non loquor de quauis pœnitētia (nam & Iudam proditionis suæ pœnitebat, sed fructra) sed de uera resipiscentia, quæ est ex tristicia secundum Deum. Sed hac de re iam dixi mus. Tertium, quod salus resipiscentibus per gratiā Dei cōceísa, non est μεταμέλητον, sed stabilis & firma. Non enim mutatur Deus ut homo.
units.tr: "It produces repentance," he says, "not to be repented of, leading to salvation." Note three things. First, that the sorrow which is according to God produces repentance. But this is not the lot of everyone. For unless you love and esteem God in your heart, you will not be grieved that you have offended him by sinning. Therefore this kind of sorrow belongs only to those who are of God; it cannot belong to the reprobate. So true repentance is not found in all people. Second, that true repentance leads to salvation. I am not speaking of any repentance whatever (for Judas also repented of his betrayal, but in vain), but of true repentance, which arises from the sorrow that is according to God. But I have already spoken of this matter. Third, that the salvation granted to the repentant through the grace of God is not metamelēton, but stable and firm. For God does not change as man does.

units.la: MVNDI uero tristicia, inquit, morte operatur.) Est hoc alterum genus tristitiæ, prio ri oppositum, tanquam & natura & effectu diuersum. Vocat illud tristitiam mundi. Non intelligit autem de mundo, quatenus ille humanum genus cōplectitur, in quo ut multa sunt tristia, ita multum quoque est tristitiæ, cui nō competit, quod hic tristitiam mundi mortem operari dicit. Intelligit igitur de mundo, quatenus sub ea uoce corruptio huius sæculi, àdeoque & homines mundani, à sensu Dei alienati intelliguntur. Huius tristitiam gemino sensu uocare possumus. Primo, ut sit mundi tristitia, qua mundus ipse, uel, quomodo mundus contristatur. Tristatur autem mundus, quando illi quæ cupiditatibus eius sunt contrariæ, eueniunt, quemadmodum gaudet si illæ ex animi sententia succedant. Altero, ut sit tristitia mundi, qua carnaliores homines propter mundum ob religionis causam offensum & inimicum contristantur. Vtrunque tristitiæ genus, quemadmodum & ex opposito gaudium mundi, morte operatur. Pius homo tristatur secundum Deum, dum dolet illi quod Deum peccando offendit. Filius huius sæculi tristatur, quando studium peccandi nō ex uoto succedit. Et carnalis Christianus tristatur, sentiens se sustinere inimicitiam mundi. Huius generis tristicia salutem impedit, ac morti reddit obnoxium. Etenim quando resipiscet, qui de peccato non tristatur, nisi quando impeditur, quo minus pro libidine sua peccet. Quando tristabitur ille secundum Deum, ut resipiscat, qui de offensa Dei non tristatur, tristatur uero de offensa & inimicitia mundi. Credibile est aut inter Corinthios eiusmodi fuisse Christianos, qui mundū in cordibus suis nondum reliquerint, & ab illius amicitia ægrè a- uelli sustinuerint, quales utiq; erant qui cū infidelibus in eidolio conuiuabantur, quorum gratia seriam illam dehortatione capite præcedeti de fugiendo infidelium consortio posuit.
units.tr: "But the sorrow of the world," he says, "works death." This is the second kind of sorrow, set against the first, as being different both in nature and in effect. He calls it the sorrow of the world. But he does not mean the world insofar as it embraces the human race, in which there is much that is sad, and also much sorrow to which it does not apply that this sorrow of the world works death. So he means the world insofar as under that word are understood the corruption of this age, and therefore worldly men, alienated from the sense of God. We may describe this sorrow in a twofold sense. First, it may be the sorrow of the world, by which the world itself is grieved, or the way in which the world is grieved. The world is grieved when things contrary to its desires come about, just as it rejoices when they turn out according to its wishes. Second, it may be the sorrow of the world, by which more carnal men are grieved because of the world's hostility and enmity on account of religion. Both kinds of sorrow, just as the joy of the world on the opposite side, work death. The pious man is grieved according to God when he laments that he has offended God by sinning. The son of this age is grieved when his zeal for sinning does not succeed as he wishes. And the carnal Christian is grieved, feeling that he endures the enmity of the world. This kind of sorrow hinders salvation and makes a man liable to death. For he who is not grieved over sin will repent only when he is prevented from sinning as his lust desires. He who is not grieved over the offence against God, but is grieved over the offence and enmity of the world, will be grieved in such a way that he will repent. It is likely that among the Corinthians there were Christians of this sort, who had not yet left the world in their hearts and had borne with difficulty being torn away from its friendship. Such indeed were those who feasted with unbelievers in the idol temple, and for whose sake the Apostle set down that grave exhortation in the preceding chapter about shunning the company of unbelievers.

units.la: ECCE enim, inquit, istuc ipsum, quod secundum Deum contristati fuistis, quantam in uobis genuit solicitudinem. ) In Græco est σπεύδω, id est, studiū. Declarat quod tristiciam secundum Deum, resipiscentia ad salutem gignere dixit. Declarat autem recensione fructuum, quos sic contristati ac resipiscētes protulerunt Corinthij. Hos recenset numero septem: solicitudinem uidelicet, satisfactionem, indignationem, timorem, desiderium, zelum, & uindictam. Ecce enim, inquit, istuc ipsum quod secundum Deum contristati fuistis. Nequit satis inculcare, quanti debeant facere tristiciam, quam expriore ipsius epistola conceperat. Non simpliciter dicit: Quod secundum Deum cōtristati fuistis, magnam in uobis genuit solicitudinem, sed cum nota admirationis: Ecce enim, inquit, istuc ipsum quod secundum Deum contristati fuistis, quantam in uobis genuit solicitudinem, &c. Quasi dicat: Ecce tristicia illa uestra, quæ uidebatur molesta & acerba, non uobis modo, sed & mihijpsi, quàm fuerit uobis utilis, & quàm egregios protulerit in uobis uerę resipiscentiæ fructus.
units.tr: "For behold," he says, "this very thing, that you were grieved according to God, how much earnestness it produced in you." In Greek it is spoudē, that is, zeal. He shows that the sorrow according to God produces repentance leading to salvation. He shows this by enumerating the fruits which the Corinthians, grieved and repentant in this way, brought forth. He lists seven of them: namely earnestness, defence, indignation, fear, desire, zeal, and vengeance. "For behold," he says, "this very thing that you were grieved according to God." He cannot sufficiently press how greatly they ought to value the sorrow which he had caused by his earlier letter. He does not simply say: "That you were grieved according to God produced great earnestness in you," but with a mark of admiration: "For behold," he says, "this very thing that you were grieved according to God, how much earnestness it produced in you," and so on. As if he were saying: "Behold that sorrow of yours, which seemed troublesome and bitter, how useful it has been, not only to you but to me too, and how splendid the fruits of true repentance it has brought forth in you."

units.la: QVANTAM in uobis, inquit, genuit solicitudinem.) Σπουδή Græcis est, studium & solicitudo, qua in res serias diligenter & indesinenter incumbimus. Fuerant Corinthij antea remissi ac socordes, præsertim in causa scortatoris. Verùm ubi correpti fuerunt ab Apostolo, socordiam ac negligentiam suam in magnam solicitudinem commutarunt.
units.tr: "How much," he says, "it produced in you earnestness." In Greek spoudē is zeal and anxious care, by which we apply ourselves diligently and unceasingly to serious matters. The Corinthians had previously been careless and negligent, especially in the case of the fornicator. But when they were rebuked by the Apostle, they changed their carelessness and negligence into great earnestness.

units.la: IMO satisfactionem, inquit.) Græcè est ἀπολογίαν. Vulgata habet, defensionē. Malim purgationem. Et ea uox pulchrē conuenit sequentibus, ubi dicit: Siquidem ubiq; commendastis uosipsos quod puri sitis in eo negocio. A uoce satisfactionis periculum est imperitis & incautis, ne Apostolū de Papistica satisfactione loqui existiment, cum illi uox apologia quæ hic habetur, miniimè omnium conueniat. Nec defensio satis quadrat causæ de qua agitur. Defendere se dicitur, qui per iniuriam iniquè impetitur ac læditur. Quomodo id Corinthijs hoc loco detur ab Apostolo, nō uideo. Arbitramur itaq; uertendum esse, imò purgationem. Quomodo autem purgauerint se Corinthij, in sequentibus exponet.
units.tr: "Nay, defence," he says. In Greek it is apologian. The Vulgate has "defence." I would prefer "clearing." And this word agrees well with what follows, where he says: "For you have shown yourselves in every way to be pure in this matter." There is a danger in the word "satisfaction" for the unlearned and the careless, that they may think the Apostle is speaking of Papistical satisfaction, though the word "apology" here fits least of all. Nor does "defence" quite suit the matter under discussion. A man is said to defend himself when he is wrongly attacked and injured unjustly. I do not see how this can be applied to the Corinthians in this place by the Apostle. We judge therefore that it should be translated "clearing," indeed "purgation." How the Corinthians cleared themselves, he will explain in what follows.

units.la: IMO indignationem.) Qua uidelicet suc- censebant sibijpsis, & indignè ferebant, quod in tam enormi scelere tam egissent negligenter, simulque indignabantur scortatori, quod Christiani nominis professionem tanto dedecore infamem reddidisset. Hoc genus indignationis sanctum est, & uehementer utile ad corrigēda tam nostra quàm aliorum peccata. Etenim qui non succenset peccatis, quādo ad illorum emendationem mouebitur. Non laudat Apostolus Pharisæorum seueritatem, qua illi peccatis se indignari simulant magis quàm indignantur, dum propriæ iusticiæ opinione inflati, peccatores dedignantur, sed loquitur de sancta illa indignatione, quam tristicia secundum Deum in illis, qui ueraciter resipi- scunt, operatur.
units.tr: "Nay, indignation." Namely, that they were angry with themselves, and took it badly that they had acted so carelessly in so enormous a crime; and at the same time they were indignant with the fornicator, because he had brought the profession of the Christian name into infamy by so great a disgrace. This kind of indignation is holy, and very useful for correcting both our own sins and those of others. For he who is not angry at sins, when will he be moved to amend them? The Apostle does not praise the severity of the Pharisees, by which they pretend to be indignant at sins more than they really are, while, puffed up with the opinion of their own righteousness, they disdain sinners; but he speaks of that holy indignation which sorrow according to God works in those who truly repent.

units.la: IMO timorem.) Nō intelligit alium quàm Dei. Et reuera non erat præter rationē quod per admonitionem & correptionem Apostoli in seipsos reuersi cognita admissorum grauitate sensu timoris Dei percellebantur. Et præterea conueniens erat, ut securitatem ac socordiam sensus timoris Dei expelleret.
units.tr: Nay, fear.) He means nothing other than the fear of God. And indeed it was not unreasonable that, through the Apostle's admonition and rebuke, they had come back to themselves and, recognising the seriousness of what had been committed, were struck with a sense of the fear of God. Moreover, it was fitting that he should drive out of them the complacency and carelessness that lacked the sense of the fear of God.

units.la: IMO desiderium.) De hoc paulò suprà dictum est, ibi, cum annunciaret nobis uestrum desiderium. Tam aberat, ut accepta per epistolam correptricem tristicia, desiderio Apostoli in fidelibus extingueret, ut magis accenderet etiam. Erat enim tristicia secundum Deum.
units.tr: Nay, longing.) This was said a little earlier, where he wrote, "when he announced to us your longing." So far was the sorrow received through the corrective letter from extinguishing the Apostle's longing among the faithful that it actually kindled it more. For it was a godly sorrow.

units.la: IMO zelum.) Et de hoc dictum est suprà, quatenus pro Apostolo suo contra obtrectatores illius singularem zelum ostendebant. In præsenti uerò uidetur de zelo loqui, quo pro ecclesia repurganda incaluerant.
units.tr: Nay, zeal.) This too was mentioned above, where they showed their singular zeal for their Apostle against his detractors. In the present passage, however, he seems to speak of the zeal with which they had burned to cleanse the Church.

units.la: IMO uindictam.) Zelò subijcit uindictam, qua scortatorem excommunicauerant. Nam fecerant hoc ex zelo Dei, quo erant accensi. Aliud est uindictam sumere de reprobis, quoniam sic imperat potestas superior, & aliud, facere hoc ex zelo Dei ac iusticiæ. Scripserat illis Apostolus de excōmunicādo scortatore, ac ueteri fermento expugnando. Si hoc fecissent non nisi Apostoli iussu, ex zelo utiq; non fecissent, nec fuisset id operis fructus resipiscētiæ.
units.tr: Nay, vengeance.) He adds vengeance to zeal, namely that by which they had excommunicated the fornicator. For they had done this out of the zeal of God by which they were inflamed. It is one thing to take vengeance on the reprobate because a higher power so commands, and another to do it out of zeal for God and righteousness. The Apostle had written to them about excommunicating the fornicator and purging out the old leaven. If they had done this only at the Apostle's command, they would certainly not have done it out of zeal, and the fruit of repentance would not have followed.

units.la: SIQVIDEM ubiq; commendastis uosi- psos, inquit, quod puri sitis in eo negocio.) postquam fructus tristiciæ Corinthiorum & certa indicia uerę resipiscentiæ recesuit, quid ipse ex illis colligat ac pronunciet, hisce uerbis exponit, cum dicit: Siquidem ubiq; commendastis uosipsos quod puri sitis in eo negocio. Rationalis siquidem non est in Græco, sed simpliciter ad hunc modū: ἐν πάντι σωσαίωσ ἑαυτοὺς ἁγνοὺς ἐν τῷ πράγματι. i. Per omnia commendamendastis uosipsos, quod puri sitis in eo nego cio. Per omnia, intelligit de indicijs ueræ resipiscentiæ, quæ iam recensuit. Quasi dicat. Nihil desidero in uobis amplius. Sic uos exhibuistis in hac causa solicitos, sic uos purgastis, sic indignati estis, sic timore perculsi fuistis, sic præsentiâ meam desideratis, sic zelo Dei accensi fuistis, sic ulti estis admissum facinus, ut mihi satisfeceritis per omnia, declarâueritisq; ab omni uos culpa alienos esse in eo negocio, quo de uobis scripsi, sic ut consensu admissi flagitij haudquâquam fueritis polluti.
units.tr: "For you have everywhere commended yourselves," he says, "that you are pure in this matter." After recounting the fruit of the Corinthians' sorrow and the sure signs of true repentance, he sets out in these words what he himself gathers and declares from them, saying: "For you have everywhere commended yourselves, that you are pure in this matter." The Greek does not read exactly this way, but simply thus: ἐν παντὶ συνεστήσατε ἑαυτοὺς ἁγνοὺς εἶναι ἐν τῷ πράγματι, that is, "in every way you have commended yourselves, that you are pure in this matter." By "in every way" he means the signs of true repentance that he has just recounted, as if to say: "I want nothing more from you. So earnestly have you acted in this affair, so have you cleansed yourselves, so have you been indignant, so have you been struck with fear, so have you longed for my presence, so have you been inflamed with the zeal of God, so have you avenged the crime committed, that you have satisfied me in every respect and shown that you are free of all guilt in the matter about which I wrote to you, so that by consenting to the shameful deed you were not at all defiled."

units.la: Hic audire poterat: Quur ergo totam ecclesiam propter unius hominis facinus tantopere contristare uoluistis? Respondet:
units.tr: Here someone might object: "Why, then, did you want to grieve the whole Church so greatly on account of one man's crime?" He answers:

units.la: PROINDE tametsi scripsi uobis, nô id feci eius causâ qui læserat, nec eius qui læsus fuerat, sed ob id, ut palàm fieret studium uestrum pro nobis apud uos in conspeƈtu Dei. Quasi dicat. Scripsi quidem uobis communiter omnibus, uerùm potissimâ causâ cur scriberem, non erat, ut unius aut alterius rationem habe rem, illorumq; nomine uos coutristarem omnes, sed ut certo experimento notum fieret apud uos, quomodo essetis erga nos affeƈti, idque in conspeƈtu Dei. Hoc uidelicet cum primis agebam, cum scriberem, & iam quod queràbâ, luculentissimis est argumentis â uobis probatum & comprobatum. Sic, meo iudicio, obiectioni occurrit, & consilium suum exposuit, quo ad eos scribere uoluerit.
units.tr: "Therefore, although I wrote to you, I did not do it for the sake of him who had done the wrong, nor for the sake of him who had been wronged, but so that your zeal for us might be made plain among you in the sight of God." As if to say: "I indeed wrote to you all together, but the chief reason for writing was not to take account of one or another person and so grieve you all on their behalf, but that by a sure test it might become known among you how you were disposed toward us, and this in the sight of God. This, of course, was my chief aim in writing, and what I was seeking has already been proved and confirmed by you with the clearest evidence." In my judgment, this is how he meets the objection and sets out the purpose for which he wished to write to them.

units.la: Sunt tamen quibus lectio Chrysostomi, cui & Ambrosius concordat, non displicet. Illa sic habet: sed ob id, ut palàm fieret studiû nostrû pro uobis apud uos. Ea lectio cõuenit cum eo quod supra cap. 2. paulò post initium dixit ad hunc modum. Nam ex multa afflictione & anxietate cordis scripsi uobis per multas lachrymas, nô ut mœrore afficeremini, sed ut cognosceretis charitatem quam habeo abundâtius erga uos. Idem enim est cum eo quod hic secundum Chrysostomi lectionem dicit: sed ob id, ut palàm fieret studiû nostrum pro uobis. Et facilis sanè lapsus est, in duobus hisce pronominibus ὑμῶν, id est, uestrum, & ἡμῶν, id est, nostrum: item, ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν, id est, pro uobis, & ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, id est, pro nobis. Verum quæ iam in usu est lectio, sic ad causam quam agit Apostolus hoc loco accommoda est, ut non uideatur quùr mutari debeat.
units.tr: Yet there are those who do not dislike the reading of Chrysostom, with which Ambrose also agrees. It runs thus: "but so that our zeal for you might be made plain among you." That reading agrees with what he said above in chapter 2, shortly after the beginning, in these words: "For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you through many tears, not that you should be grieved, but that you might know the love I have more abundantly toward you." This is the same as what he says here, according to Chrysostom's reading: "but so that our zeal for you might be made plain." It is certainly an easy slip between these two pronouns, ὑμῶν, that is "your," and ἡμῶν, that is "our," and likewise between ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν, that is "for you," and ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, that is "for us." Yet the reading now in common use fits the Apostle's argument in this place so well that there seems no reason why it should be changed.

units.la: PROINDE inquit, etsi scripsi uobis.) Hoc est, etsi communes ad uos omnes literas scripsi. Emphasis est in pronomine uobis. Videbatur enim propter unius priuati peccatum non debuisse scribi communiter omnibus.
units.tr: "Therefore," he says, "although I wrote to you." That is, "although I wrote a letter common to you all." The emphasis falls on the word "to you." For it seemed that because of the sin of one private person, the letter should not have been written to everyone together.

units.la: NON id feci eius causa qui læserat, inquit, nec eius qui læsus fuerat.) Dices hic. Ergo unius & alterius salutem tanti non faciebat, ut propter ipsos scriberet ad ecclesiam? Atqui bonus pastor nonagintanouem iustis reliƈtis, unicam ouiculam errantem, ne pereat, diligenter quærit. Num melior est discipulus magistro, & seruus suo domino?
units.tr: "I did not do it for the sake of him who had done the wrong," he says, "nor for the sake of him who had been wronged." Here someone will say: "Then did he hold the salvation of one or another so cheap that he did not write to the Church on their account? And yet the good shepherd, leaving the ninety-nine just sheep, diligently seeks the one straying sheep, lest it perish. Is not the disciple above his teacher, and the servant above his lord?"

units.la: Respondeo. Salutem peccatoris non neglexit Apostolus, cuius ratione in Epistola priore habuisse negari non potest. Verum non fuerat ipsi primaria causa scribendi unius & alterius, sed potius totius ecclesiæ respeƈtus. Non hoc egerat scribendo, ut propter unius peccatum totam contristaret ecclesiam, sed ut manifestum fieret in ea causa, quomodo essent erga se affeƈti Corinthij. Si legas igitur, non id feci eius causa tantum qui læserat, nec eius qui læsus fuerat, non erit locus quæstioni. Quòd si non placet uoculam, tantum adijcere uel subintelligere, reliquum erit ut intelligamus, non de eo simpliciter loqui Apostolum, quod scripserat communiter omnibus, sed quod scribendo sic contristauerat omnes, ac si constituerit unius hominis facinus imputare omnibus. Hic negat se propter unum & alterum ad eum modum scripsisse omnibus, ut omnes contristaret: sed consilium sibi eius instituti fuisse, ut comprobaretur, quo essent erga se studiô.
units.tr: I answer: the Apostle did not neglect the salvation of the sinner, and that he took account of it in the former letter cannot be denied. But the primary reason for his writing was not the concern for one or another person, but rather regard for the whole Church. He did not write in order to grieve the whole Church because of one man's sin, but so that it might become clear in this affair how the Corinthians were disposed toward him. If, then, you read, "I did not do it for the sake of him who had done the wrong alone, nor for the sake of him who had been wronged," there will be no room for the question. But if the little word "alone" is not wanted, either to be added or understood, what remains is that we understand the Apostle to be speaking not simply of what he had written to them all together, but of how by writing he had grieved them all, as if he had decided to impute one man's crime to everyone. Here he denies that he wrote to them all in that way, grieving them all, because of one or another person; rather, the purpose of his undertaking was to test how eager they were toward him.

units.la: NON id feci, inquit, eius causa qui læserat, nec eius qui læsus fuerat.) Licet nonnulli referant hæc ad ea quæ 1. Cor. 6. sic legunțur. Itaque iam quidem omnino delictum in uobis est, quod lites habetis inter uos inuicem. Cur non potius iniuriam patimini? Cur nô potius damnum accipitis? Imò uos iniuriam facitis, & damno afficitis, idque fratres: quasi dicat, se Apostolus non horum gratia scripsisse, qui uel affecerint alios, uel ipsi ab alijs affeƈti sint iniuria, unde lites sint inter ipsos nate: mihi tamen illi rectius sentire uidentur, qui referunt ad scortatorem, & eum qui facinore illius læsus fuerat, siue is fuerit ipsius pater, siue alius quisquâ, cui mulier post obitû patris nupserit.
units.tr: "I did not do it," he says, "for the sake of him who had done the wrong, nor of him who had been wronged." Although some refer these words to what is read in 1 Cor. 6: "Therefore it is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather accept loss? But you do wrong and cause loss, and that to brothers." As if to say, the Apostle did not write for the sake of those who had either harmed others or been harmed by others, which gave rise to the lawsuits among them. Yet to me those seem to take the matter more rightly who refer it to the fornicator and to the man who had been wronged by his deed, whether he was the woman's father or some other man whom she married after her father's death.

units.la: SED ob id, inquit, ut palàm fieret studium uestrû pro nobis apud uos in conspeƈtu Dei.) Ergo ne ob id scripsit, ut uideret quam se obseruarent, quam q; diƈto suo essent obedientes? At id erat quærere seipsum, nô illorû salutem.
units.tr: "But so that," he says, "your zeal for us might be made plain among you in the sight of God." Then did he write not so that he might see how they respected him and how obedient they were to his command? But that would be seeking himself, not their salvation.

units.la: Respondeo. Absit. Quomodo seipsum quesiuisset, qui per tot discrimina cûctis prodesse studebat? Sciebat eos tëtari per pseudapostolos, sciebat inter illos esse studia seƈtarum, sciebat seƈtarios puritatem traditæ â se doƈtrinæ labefaƈtare, sciebat nomen suum per illos obscurari, ita ut parum adhuc inter illos existimationis habere uideretur. Cum ergo hæc ad destrucțione purae fidei in Christum, adeoq; ad ipsorum quoque perditionem facere possent, ut luculento experimento manifestum fieret, quales essent adhuc in uera doƈtrina, fide ac pietate, sani he uel corrupti, cogitabat illis obijcere occasionem per epistolâ correptricem, unde inter ipsos palàm fieret quomodo essent erga se ipsorû Apostolû affeƈti. Hoc suum consilium quod scribendo sequutus fuerat exposnit, dicens: Etsi scripsi, nô eius causa scripsi qui læserat, nec eius qui læsus fuerat, sed ob id ut palàm fieret studium uestrum pro nobis apud uos, id est, in uestra ecclesia, in conspeƈtu Dei. Non erat res ista leuis momenti. Non agebat curio. ruriosè,ut ipsi intelligeret,quid adhuc autho-ritatis haberet apud Corinthios,sed eo magis spectabat,ut si declararent illi esse se adhuc in fide & obedientia syncerōs,& honorificè erga suū apostolum affectōs,pseudapostolorum ex eo & sectariorum improba studia infirmarentur,ac languida redderentur,perinde ac si maritus domo absens,& castitati uxoris suæ ab impuris hominibus metuės, luculento aliquo exemplo in ciuitate sua manifestū ab illa fieri cupiat,quàm sit erga se constās in fide & amore coniugali,quo posteà minus sit spei reliquū nebulonibus pudicitiā illius sollicitandi. Talem mihi apparet fuisse apostolo Corinthiorum curam,ac tale consilium in hac causa.
units.tr: I answer: far from it. How could he be seeking himself, who through so many dangers was eager to benefit everyone? He knew they were being tempted by false apostles; he knew that factions were among them; he knew the sectarians were undermining the purity of the doctrine handed down by him; he knew that his name was being obscured by them, so that he seemed to have little standing among them still. Since these things could contribute to the overthrow of the pure faith in Christ, and so to their own ruin, he meant, by a clear test, to make plain what they were still like in true doctrine, faith and piety, whether sound or corrupted. He therefore considered offering them, through a corrective letter, an opportunity by which it would become openly evident among them how they were disposed toward their Apostle. He explains this plan that he followed in writing, saying: "Although I wrote, I did not write for the sake of him who had done the wrong, nor of him who had been wronged, but so that your zeal for us might be made plain among you, that is, in your Church, in the sight of God." This was no trivial matter. He was not acting like a busybody, to learn what authority he still had among the Corinthians; rather, he looked to this, that if they showed that they were still sincere in faith and obedience and honourably disposed toward their apostle, the shameless zeal of the false apostles and sectarians would be weakened and made feeble. It was as when a husband, away from home and fearing for his wife's chastity from impure men, wishes to have some striking example shown in his city of how steadfast she is in faith and conjugal love, so that afterwards the scoundrels have less hope of tempting her chastity. Such, it seems to me, was the Apostle's concern for the Corinthians, and such was his purpose in this matter.

units.la: Illud,in conspectu Dei,non est otiosè adiectum. Non hoc quærebat,ut coram Deo manifestum fieret,quales essent Corinthij, cum illa nota sint omnia omnium, sed ut absq; ulla hypocrisi,ueraciter,ac religiosè cum conscientia Dei manifestum facerent,quales adhuc essent in accepta fide,religione ac pietate.
units.tr: This was not added idly, in the sight of God. The apostle did not mean that it should be made plain before God what sort of people the Corinthians were, since all their characteristics were already known to everyone. He meant that they should show, sincerely and devoutly, without any pretence and in the sight of God's conscience, what they still were in the faith they had received, in religion and in piety.

units.la: Idcirco consolatione accepimus ex consolatione uestra,magis uero abundantius gauisi sumus ob gaudium Titi, propterea quòd spiritus eius refocillatus est ab omnibus uobis: quod si quid apud illum de uobis gloriatus sum, nō sum pudefactus,sed ut omnia cum veritate loquuti sumus uobis, ita & gloriatio nostra,qua usus eram apud Titū veritas facta est. Et uiscera illius maiorem in modum erga uos affecta sunt, dum recolit omnium uestrum obedientiam, quemadmodum cum timore ac tremore re exceperitis ipsum. Gaudeo quòd in omnibus confido uobis.
units.tr: Therefore we have received comfort from your comfort, and we rejoiced all the more abundantly at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by all of you. For if I boasted anything to him about you, I have not been put to shame; but just as we have spoken all things to you in truth, so our boasting, which I made before Titus, has also proved true. His heart is drawn to you all the more, as he recalls the obedience of all of you, how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice that in all things I can trust you.

units.la: Redit ad ea quæ suprà dicere coeperat, ubi dixit:uerum qui consolatur humiles consolatus est nos Deus per aduentum Titi, non solū autem per aduentum illius, uerum etiam per consolationem quam ille accepit de uobis,cū annunciaret nobis uestrū desiderium, uestrū fletum, uestrum pro me studium, adeo ut magis gauisus fuerim.Hanc consolationem de illis per Titum acceptam hactenus explicuit & amplificauit:iam repetens illam trāfit ad eam, quaTitus ipse apud eos recreatus fuit,memoratque quanto per hanc fit affectus gaudio. Id circo inquit,consolatione accepimus ex consolatione uestra. Hoc est, Cum igitur ad eum modum per omnia cōprobaueritis quòd puri sitis in hoc negocio, refocillati quidè sumus ex hac uestra cōsolatione, quam attulit nobis Titus, uerum id nobis maioris adhuc gaudij materiam peperit,quòd Titus tantopere apud uos exhilaratus est, & spiritus eius per uos omnes refocillatus.
units.tr: He returns to what he had begun to say above, where he said: "But God, who comforts the humble, has comforted us by the coming of Titus, and not only by his coming, but also by the comfort which he received from you, when he reported to us your longing, your weeping, and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced all the more." Having so far explained and enlarged on this comfort which Titus received from them, he now repeats it and passes on to the matter in which Titus himself was refreshed among them, and he recounts how greatly he was moved with joy through this. Therefore, he says, "we have received comfort from your comfort." That is: since you have thus in all things shown yourselves pure in this affair, we indeed have been refreshed by this comfort of yours, which Titus brought us; but this has given us yet further matter for joy, that Titus was so greatly cheered among you, and his spirit was refreshed by you all.

units.la: IDCIRCO, inquit, consolatione accepimus ex consolatione uestra.) Obserua quæ sit
units.tr: "Therefore," he says, "we have received comfort from your comfort." Observe what kind of comfort and refreshment a true minister of Christ has, by which he consoles his labours in the ministry.

units.la: consolatio ac recreatio ueri Christi ministri qua labores suos soletur in ministerio. Si uide licet populum habeat in causa pietatis sollicitum peccatis indignantem, Dei timētem, ergase studiosum ac morigerum. Eiusmodi consolatio à populo fidelium profecta, solata est olim apostoli labores & afflictiones,dubio procul solatur & hodie fidele Christi ministrum nihil in ministerio suo quaerente aliud, quàm ut multum fructus adferat suo Domino. Secus animati sunt, qui uel uentris uel loculorum farciendorum curam agunt.
units.tr: If he has a people who are anxious in matters of piety, indignant at sins, fearing God, and devoted and obedient to him, then such comfort, coming from a faithful people, once consoled the apostle's labours and afflictions; and without doubt it still consoles today a faithful minister of Christ, who seeks nothing in his ministry except that he may bring much fruit to his Lord. Those are of a different spirit who are concerned only with filling their belly or their purse.

units.la: MAGIS uero abundantius gauisi sumus ob gaudium Titi.) Hoc dicens,non prefert illis Titum,quasi pluris fecerit illius gaudiū quàm ipsorum refipiscentiam, sollicitudinem, purgationem, indignatione, timorem, desiderium & zelum, adeoq; & salutem,quod admodum fuisset inconueniens ipsius Apostolatui,cuius omnes labores & afflictiones ad hunc finem tendebant,ut pararet Domino populum fidelem ac promissae salutis capacem. Imò si rectè inspiciantur quæ hic memorat abundantia consolationis,quam se ob gaudiū Titi confequutum dicit,dilectionem ipsius ac curam nō tam erga Titum quàm erga ipsos Corinthios commendant,quemadmodum mox patebit.
units.tr: "But we rejoiced all the more abundantly at the joy of Titus." In saying this, he does not place Titus above them, as if he had valued Titus's joy more than their repentance, their anxiety, their purging of the offence, their indignation, their fear, their longing and zeal, and so their salvation. That would have been quite unbecoming to his apostolic office, whose labours and afflictions all aimed at this end: to prepare for the Lord a faithful people capable of the promised salvation. Indeed, if we look rightly at the abundance of comfort which he says he obtained from Titus's joy, it commends his love and care not so much for Titus as for the Corinthians themselves, as will soon be clear.

units.la: QVOD refocillatus sit spiritus eius ab omnibus uobis,inquit.) Quid sit spiritū laborantis, & in multis molestijs ac periculis uersantis refocillari, notius est quàm ut sit admonendum. Titus absq; dubio non modò cum labore ac periculo,sed & cum cura ac sollicitudine nō modica Corinthū ab apostolo missus uenit, cum sciret eam ecclesiam studio pseudapostolorum scissam esse in studia sectarū, me tueretq; sibi ab insidijs falsorum fratrum non minus quàm exterorum & infidelium: uerùm cum uenisset Corinthum,ab eiusmodi cura ac sollicitudine pio erga se fidelium studio refocillatus est ipsius spiritus, uerùm id infrà apertius exprimet.
units.tr: "Because his spirit has been refreshed by all of you," he says. What it is for the spirit of a man who labours and lives amid many troubles and dangers to be refreshed is too well known to need pointing out. Titus, without doubt, came to Corinth sent by the apostle not only with labour and danger, but also with no small care and anxiety, since he knew that this church had been torn into factions by the zeal of the false apostles, and he feared the snares of false brethren no less than those of outsiders and unbelievers. But when he came to Corinth, his spirit was refreshed from such care and anxiety by the pious goodwill of the faithful towards him; yet the apostle will express this more plainly below.

units.la: Vide uerò quàm non simpliciter dicat: qd' refocillatus sit spiritus eius, quasi in eo conquieuerit gaudij ipsius abundantia,sed addat, ab omnibus uobis,in qua particula uis est gaudij huius sita. Non dicit à Deo, cum tamen omnis consolatio piorum sit à Deo,sed refocillationem hanc deputat Corinthijs, non dicēs à nonnullis ex uobis, neque simpliciter,à uobis,sed ab omnibus uobis. Non ob id tantopere gaudebat, quòd spiritus Titi refocillatus fuerat,sed propterea,quòd refocillatus fuerat ab omnibus Corinthijs fidelibus, quòd uideli cet reperisset eos omnes erga se amater ac reueréter affectos:& per omnia morigeros,inqu eo studio concordes. Timuerat enim ne forsan inueniret eos studijs sectarū sic immersos ac diuisos,ut paucos esset habituros qui se audirent,& monitis suis obtemperarent.
units.tr: See how he does not simply say that his spirit was refreshed, as if the abundance of his joy had rested in that alone, but adds "by all of you," and in that little phrase lies the force of this joy. He does not say "by God," although all the comfort of the godly is from God; but he attributes this refreshment to the Corinthians, not saying "by some of you," nor simply "by you," but "by all of you." He did not rejoice so greatly because Titus's spirit had been refreshed, but because it had been refreshed by all the faithful Corinthians, since he had evidently found them all warmly and reverently disposed towards him, and obedient in all things, and united in this zeal. For he had feared lest he should find them so immersed and divided in the factions of the sectarians that there would be few who would listen to him and obey his admonitions.

units.la: QVOD si quid apud illum de uobis gloriatus sum,non sum pudefactus, inquit:sed ut omnia cum ueritate loquuti sumus uobis, ita & gloriatio nostra, qua vsus eram apud Titum, veritas facta est.) Quasi dicat: Non ob id tantum gauisus sum maximopere, quod sic Titû acceperitis concorditer omnes, ac reuerenter tractaueritis, vt refocillatus sit à vobis omnib. spiritus eius, sed hanc quoque ob causam qd gloriationes meas de vobis, quib. omnes vos Tito cum illi proficiscedum esset, ad vos com mendaui, non fuisse à vero alienas declarastis, vt hic quoq; verax inueniar, perinde atq; in aliis, quæ ad vos sum loquutus. Hæc vestra laus est, qua vos & Deo & mihi & pijs omnibus ac ceptos redditis.
units.tr: "But if I boasted anything to him about you, I have not been put to shame," he says, "but just as we have spoken all things to you in truth, so our boasting, which I used before Titus, has become true." It is as if he said: I did not rejoice so greatly only because you all received Titus with one accord and treated him with reverence, so that his spirit was refreshed by you all; but also for this reason, that you have shown that the boasts I made about you, when I commended you all to Titus as he was about to set out for you, were not foreign to the truth, so that I may be found truthful here too, just as in the other things I have said to you. This is your praise, which makes you acceptable both to God and to me and to all the godly.

units.la: Chrysostomus sic exponit, vt ratio reddatur eius quod dixit spiritum Titi refocillatum fuisse ab ipsis omnibus, sitq; sensus. Refocillatus est spiritus eius à vobis omnib. in eo, quod pudefactus non sum ob ea quæ de vobis sum gloriatus, sed in omnibus verax inuentus.
units.tr: Chrysostom explains it in such a way as to give the reason for what he said, that Titus's spirit was refreshed by all of them, and the sense is: "His spirit was refreshed by you all in this, that I have not been put to shame over what I boasted about you, but have been found true in all things."

units.la: Verum prior mihi expositio Germanior esse videtur.
units.tr: Yet the former explanation seems to me more German.

units.la: Quod itaq; dicit: quod non sum pudefactus, non resipit affectum apriæ gloriæ studiosum, sed magis gloriæ ac salutis Corinthiorum cupidum.
