Etenim ex eo quod sic se gesserunt erga Titû, vt quæ de ipsis gloriatus fuerat ipsorum Apostolus reipsa ostenderint esse vera, non tam gloriato Apostolo, quàm ipsis laude ac gloria gaudebat, quemadmodum & econtrario ipsis potius ignominiam peperisset, quàm Apostolo, si diuersum quid apud eos reperisset Titus, quà ab illo acceperat. Nihil enim habet, quod dedecori confine sit, si præceptor discipulorû suorum amans laudet eos, deq; illorum obedientia ac studijs glorietur. Quod si illi in peius mutati uituperio magis, quàm laude digni fuerint inuenti, ipsis hoc exprobrandum est, nõ præceptori. Si vero gloriationi præceptoris responderint, deq; eo gauisus ille fuerit, gaudium eiusmodi magis de illorum quàm ipsius laude prouenire censendum est, sicut & dolor, si ipso rum culpa pudefactus fuerit, ex illorum potiꝰ, quàm ipsius illi confusione ac dedecore nascitur. In summa & dolor & gaudium amantis ex amore nascuntur, & concernunt potius amatum, quàm amantem. Secundum humanã nor mam iudicandum est de tota hac causa, qua de scribit hic Apostolus.
units.tr: When he says, therefore, "that I have not been put to shame," this does not savour of an eagerness for vain glory, but rather of a desire for the glory and salvation of the Corinthians. For from the fact that they so conducted themselves towards Titus that they showed in fact that what their apostle had boasted about them was true, he rejoiced not so much in his own boasting as in their praise and glory; just as, on the contrary, if Titus had found among them something different from what he had heard from the apostle, it would have brought shame upon them rather than upon the apostle. For there is nothing disgraceful in a teacher who loves his disciples praising them and boasting of their obedience and zeal. But if they had changed for the worse and been found deserving of blame rather than praise, this would have to be laid to their charge, not to the teacher. If indeed they answered their teacher's boasting, and he rejoiced over them, that joy must be judged to arise from their praise rather than from his own; just as sorrow, if he had been put to shame through their fault, would arise from their confusion and disgrace rather than from his own. In short, both the grief and the joy of a lover arise from love and concern the beloved rather than the lover. The whole of this matter, about which the apostle writes here, must be judged according to human custom.

units.la: SED ut omnia loquuti sumus vobis cũ veritate, inquit.) Apparet quidem intelligendũ hoc esse in genere de tota doctrina, quam illis cum veritate vtiq;, tanquam ipsissimam veritatem Dei tradiderat, verum si sic intellexerimus, mox quæri poterit, an quæcunq; de Corinthijs gloriatus fuerat, sic fuerint per omnia vera, sicuti vera est doctrina Christi, quam illis prædicauerat.
units.tr: "But just as we have spoken all things to you in truth," he says. It appears indeed that this should be understood in general of the whole doctrine, which he had handed down to them in truth, as the very truth of God; but if we understand it so, it may at once be asked whether all the things he had boasted of concerning the Corinthians were in every respect as true as the doctrine of Christ which he had preached to them.

units.la: Quare Chrysostomo vsum est, intelligenda hæc esse, non de doctrina, sed de omnibus quæ apud Corinthios de Tito fuerat gloriatus. Sic enim exponit, εἰκὸς γὰρ αὐλὸν ἡ περὶ Τίτῳ πολλὰ ἀν τοῖς ἐπιτην ἐγκώμια. Dicit itaque hoc sensu. Sed quèadmodû cũ apud uos essemus, ac Titum
units.tr: Therefore he follows Chrysostom, holding that these words are to be understood not of the doctrine but of everything he had boasted about Titus among the Corinthians. For Chrysostom explains: "It is likely that he praised Titus to them in many ways" [εἰκὸς γὰρ αὐτὸν ἡ περὶ Τίτου πολλὰ ἂν τοῖς ἐπαινεῖν]. He therefore means this: "But just as, when we were with you and commended Titus to you,

units.la: A uobis commendaremus, veraciter de illo dixi mus omnia, sic ut talem experti sitis, qualè vo bis prædicauimꝰ, ita vicissim & eaq; Tito de vo bis gloriando diximus, vera sunt inuenta.
units.tr: we spoke the truth about him in everything, so that you found him to be the kind of man we had described to you; and in the same way, when we boasted of you to Titus, what we said has been found true."

units.la: Alij exponunt ad hunc modum: sed ut om nia loquuti sumus vobis cum veritate, hoc est, vt nulla nos in re falso quid loquutos deprehendistis, sed veraces in omnibus. Verû Chrysostomi expositio magis placet. Videtur hanq; Apostolus de utroq; gaudere, cùm quod Titꝰ inuentus esset Corinthijs, qualem ipsis prædicauerat, tum quod Corinthij tales se præbuissent Tito, quales eos esse gloriatus apud illum fuerat.
units.tr: Others explain it in this way: "But just as we spoke to you in truth in everything," that is, you have found us in nothing to have spoken falsely, but truthful in all things. But Chrysostom's explanation pleases me more. It seems that the Apostle rejoiced in both: that Titus was found by the Corinthians to be what he had preached to them, and that the Corinthians had shown themselves to Titus to be what he had boasted they were.

units.la: Illud, veritas facta est, Ebraismus est, pro, verax inuenta est. Ebrei sic loquuntur, quia adiectiuis carent. Quin & nobis Germanis in vsu est hæc loquutio, ut dicamus, Es ist die warheit, pro, Es ist war. Interim obserua quod non dicit, veritas fuit, sed, veritas facta est. Quę dicimus, prædicamus, gloriamur, ac promittimus, tum demum vera siunt, quando reipsa vera esse declaratur. Promiserat Tito fore ut inueniret Corinthios per omnia morigeros. Ea de illis gloriatio ac promissio tũ est facta veritas, cũ se talēs Tito exhiberent.
units.tr: The phrase "the truth has become" (veritas facta est) is a Hebraism, meaning "has been found truthful." The Hebrews speak this way because they lack adjectives. Indeed, we Germans also use this expression, saying Es ist die warheit instead of Es ist war. Notice in the meantime that he does not say "it was true" but "it has become true." What we say, preach, boast of, and promise becomes true only when it is shown in fact to be true. Paul had promised Titus that he would find the Corinthians obedient in all things. That boast and promise became true when they showed themselves to Titus as such.

units.la: ET uiscera illius, inquit, maiorem in modū erga uos affecta sunt.) Commendat illis & hac in re Titum, quo magis eos in officio, & in eo quod erga illum ostenderant, studio retineat. Et uiscera illius, inquit. Per uiscera intelligit diledionis affectum, quem Græci σπλάγχνα uocãt, eo quod ille sedem suam in intimis cordis penetralibus habeat. Sic sedes amoris pro ipso amoris affectu ponitur, ut veritas illi exprimatur. Multa est in conuiƈtu humano dilectiõis simulatio in verbis & factis, ubi nihil expenetra libus uiscerũ proman at, ideoq; nec uiscerũ appellationem meretur, quæ soli uerę dilectioni competit, in qua nullus est simulationi locus. Hanc ut commendet in Tito, non dicit: Et ille admodum gloriatur de vobis, ac multa præclara de vobis loquitur, sed, Et uiscera illius maiorem in modum erga uos affecta sunt.
units.tr: "And his inward parts," he says, "are poured out toward you in greater measure." He commends Titus to them in this matter too, so that he may keep them more firmly in their duty and in the eagerness they had shown toward him. "And his inward parts," he says. By "inward parts" he means the feeling of love, which the Greeks call σπλάγχνα [splanchna], because that feeling has its seat in the innermost recesses of the heart. Thus the seat of love is put for love itself, so that the truth is expressed. In human society there is much pretence of love in words and deeds, where nothing comes forth from the deepest inward parts; and so it does not deserve the name "inward parts," which belongs only to true love, in which there is no room for pretence. He does not say, to commend this in Titus: "He also boasts greatly of you and speaks many fine things about you," but "And his inward parts are poured out toward you in greater measure."

units.la: MAIOREM in modum.) Græcè est, περισσοτέρως, id est, abundantius. Non hoc tantum dicit, quod admodũ sint uiscera Titi erga eos affecta, sed quod affecta sint abundantius adhuc quàm antea. Significat illum & antea quidem abunde dilexisse eos, uerũ iam abundantius affici erga eos illius uiscera. Diligit minister Christi fideles, quibus præest in uerbo: primũ quidem propterea quod sunt Christi, deinde quod sunt curæ suæ ac fidei commissi, præterquam quod sunt eiusdem fidei ac salutis cõsortes, uerũ ea dilectio plurimũm accipit incrementi, & abundantius affici illius uiscera, si se in causa pietatis p omnia exhibeant obedientes ac ductiles, perinde atque pater filios suos primum quidem ob id diligit, quæ sunt ipsiꝰ pignora, tũ vero adhuc abundantiori dilectione prosequitur, ubi uiderit eos in omnibus ergà se reuerêtes esse, obseruantes q; & morigeros. Tale quid accidit Tito, & vsuuenit omnibus uerbi ministris, syncerè erga Christum & ecclesiam eius affectis.
units.tr: "In greater measure": in Greek it is περισσοτέρως [perissoterōs], that is, more abundantly. He does not merely say that Titus's inward parts are very much affected toward them, but that they are affected even more abundantly than before. It signifies that he had indeed loved them abundantly before, but now his inward parts are moved toward them more abundantly still. The minister of Christ loves the faithful over whom he presides in the Word: first indeed because they belong to Christ, then because they are entrusted to his care and charge, besides the fact that they share the same faith and salvation with him. But that love grows greatly, and his inward parts are moved more abundantly, if they show themselves in everything obedient and teachable in the cause of godliness. Just as a father loves his sons first because they are his own pledges, and then pursues them with still greater love when he sees them respectful toward him in all things, observant and compliant, so it happened to Titus, and it happens to all ministers of the Word who are sincerely affected toward Christ and his Church.

units.la: DVM recolit omnium uestrûm obedientiâ inquit.) Sic laudat illorum obedientiâ, ac tantopere extollit, vt vel recordatio illius viscera Titi suauiter afficiant. Hac laude cupit eos retinere in coepta obedientia constantes. Dum recolit, inquit, Vides ingenium animi cádidi in Tito. Memoriam obsequiorum, quib. vsus fuerat apud Corinthios, secum asportauit in pectore, illamque postea frequenter recolendo refricuit.
units.tr: "While he recalls the obedience of you all," he says. So he praises their obedience and extols it so highly that even the memory of it stirs Titus's inward parts sweetly. By this praise he wishes to keep them steady in the obedience they have begun. "While he recalls," he says. You see the candid spirit of Titus. He carried in his breast the memory of the services he had received among the Corinthians, and by recalling it often afterward he kept it fresh.

units.la: Simul obserua quæ sit efficacia recordationis, in eo qui diligit. Viscera, inquit, illius abundantius erga uos affecta sunt. uel, quod magis probaré, afficiuntur, quandoquidem in Græco quoq; nô preteriti temporis, sed præsentis, verbum habetur. Quando afficiuntur?
units.tr: At the same time, observe the power of remembrance in one who loves. "His inward parts," he says, "are poured out toward you in greater measure." Or, what I would rather approve, "are being poured out," since in the Greek too the verb is in the present tense, not the past. When are they poured out?

units.la: DVM, inquit, recolit omnium vestrûm obedientiam. Sic recordatio tantum potest in animo diligentis, vt viscera afficiat Titus, cum recoleret obedientiam Corinthiorum, reuerentiamq; & obseruantiam erga se, sic de illa ex intimis visceribus amanter loquebatur, ut ipsa illius uiscera affici sentiret Apostolus. Eandem uim recordationis requirit à nobis dominus, cum tradita corporis sui communicatione, dicit: Hoc facite in mei commemorationem. Et hac omnino sentiremus in nobisipsis, si vel tantum de Christo, quantum habebat de Corinthijs Titus, in pectore nostro resideret. Iam cū hic admodum deficiamus, fit vt mortua sint in nobis omnia. Et interea magnis contentionibus de præsentia corporis domini in pane, quę in cordibus nostris esse debebat, cœlum ac terram miscemus.
units.tr: "While he recalls," he says, "the obedience of you all." So remembrance can have such power in the mind of one who loves that it moves Titus's inward parts: when he recalled the obedience, reverence, and respect of the Corinthians toward him, he spoke of it so lovingly and from the depths of his inward parts that the Apostle himself felt those inward parts moved. The Lord requires the same power of remembrance from us, when, having given the communion of his body, he says: "Do this in remembrance of me." And we would certainly feel this in ourselves if we had in our breast even as much of Christ as Titus had of the Corinthians. But since we are so utterly lacking in this, it comes about that all things in us are dead. And meanwhile, in great contentions about the presence of the Lord's body in the bread, which ought to be in our hearts, we stir up heaven and earth.

units.la: QVEMADMODVM, inquit, cum timore ac tremore exceperitis ipsum.) Solicitâ & anxiam diligentiam in excipiendo Titum declaratam, uocat timorem ac tremorem. Non est autem præter rationem, quod nominatim me minit, quomodo illum Corinthij exceperint, & quod viscera Titi recordatione eius tantopere affecta fuerunt. Etenim solicitus & anxius ad eos profectus fuerat, & forsan nihil minus sperauerat, quàm ut tam ab illis exciperetur reuerenter & amanter. Quare quam initio statim expertus fuerat illorum erga se in excipiendo reuerentiam, penitius imbiberat, ideoq; recordatione illius, cum primis afficiebatur. Possum exèmplum de eo adducere in medium quod mihi contigit, cũ anno millesimo quingentesimo tricesimo primo, Augustâ non sine molesta solicitudine & cura, quantumuis uocatus uenissem, quanta me populus eius ecclesiæ, tanquam Euangelicæ doctrinæ sitientissimus, cũ alacritate & reuerentia exceperit, etiam num sine viscerum affectu, recordari non possum. Multis me officijs per annos decem & octo prosequutus est postea, uerùm principia illius erga me studij, ut primum in corde meo locum obtinuerunt, ita & penitius inhærent, & plus re
units.tr: "As," he says, "you received him with fear and trembling." He calls the anxious and careful diligence shown in receiving Titus "fear and trembling." It is not beside the point that he specifically mentions how the Corinthians received him, and that Titus's inward parts were so greatly moved by the memory of it. For Titus had gone to them anxious and troubled, and perhaps had hoped for nothing less than to be received by them so reverently and lovingly. Therefore the reverence they showed him in receiving him, which he experienced at the very beginning, sank more deeply into him, and so he was especially moved when he recalled it. I can bring forward an example from my own experience: in the year 1531, when I came to Augsburg, though called there, not without troubling anxiety and care, I cannot, even now, recall without a stirring of the inward parts how the people of that church, as most thirsty for the Evangelical doctrine, received me with eagerness and reverence. Afterward they showed me many kindnesses over eighteen years. But the first beginnings of their zeal toward me, once they had gained a place in my heart, have stuck more deeply there in the same way, and they move me more than any of the later things I have mentioned.

units.la: memorata mouent. Oro dominum, ut eam ecclesiam in gratia sua illibatam conseruet.
units.tr: I pray the Lord that he keep that church unharmed in his grace.

units.la: GAVDEO, inqt, qd in omnibus confido uobis.) Nó est in Græco, ὅτι ἐν πᾶσιν θαῤῥῶ ὑμῖν, id est, quod omnibus uobis confido, sed, ὅτι ἐν πασῃ θαῤῥῶ ἐν ὑμῖν, id est, quod in omni, uel per omnia confido uobis. His uerbis significat se integrâ ac plenam de illis concepisse fiduciâ, ac bene de eis sperare in omnib. ad verâ pietate pertinentib. Sensus est. Exhilarat me multũ, quod tales vos pbueritis, cũ apud uos essem, in præsentia mea, & nũc quoq; in absentia mea erga Titũ: sic uos gesseritis diligentes, reuerentes, & obedientes, ut nulla posthac incidere possit tentatio, ac difficultas, in qua non possim uobis confidere. Et hac conclusione termi nat causam istam, qua de præsenti capite diligenter egit.
units.tr: "I rejoice," he says, "that in all things I am confident of you." It is not in the Greek ὅτι ἐν πᾶσιν θαῤῥῶ ὑμῖν [hoti en pasin tharrō hymin], that is, "that I am confident of you in all things," but ὅτι ἐν πάσῃ θαῤῥῶ ἐν ὑμῖν [hoti en pasē tharrō en hymin], that is, "that in every way, or in all respects, I am confident in you." By these words he signifies that he has conceived a full and complete confidence in them, and that he hopes well of them in all matters pertaining to true godliness. The sense is this: "It greatly cheers me that you have shown yourselves such, both when I was with you in person and now also in my absence toward Titus, conducting yourselves so lovingly, reverently, and obediently, that no temptation or difficulty can arise hereafter in which I cannot have confidence in you." With this conclusion he ends the cause that he has carefully treated in this chapter.

units.la: Nó est autem hinc leuis materia gaudij omnibus illis, quibus commissa est moderandorum aliorũ cura, si sic se gerant obedienter subditi, ut nihil incidat occasionis, quantumuis insidiosæ ac lubricæ, in quo de illorum possint integritate, & constantia dubitare. Quàta hinc fit curarum releuatio, experiuntur quotidie pa tresfamiliâs. Rursus quâtus cumulus accedat hinc ad necessarias curas, si tales sint subditi, vt parum illis possis confidere, notissimum est illis, qui molestiam hanc experiuntur. Bona erga subditos fiducia omnium est laborum, & carum releuatio, magniq; gaudij materia. Qua re præter rationem non est, quod Apostolus causam istam hac clausula terminat, ut dicat: Gaudeo, quod in omnibus confido vobis.
units.tr: This is not a slight matter for joy for all those to whom the care of governing others is committed, if their subjects so conduct themselves obediently that no occasion arises, however insidious and slippery, in which they might doubt their integrity and constancy. How great a relief from cares this brings, fathers of families experience every day. Again, how great a burden is added to necessary cares if the subjects are such that one can place little confidence in them, is well known to those who experience this trouble. A good confidence in one's subjects is the relief of all labours and of cares, and a great matter for joy. Therefore it is not beside the point that the Apostle ends this cause with this clause, saying: "I rejoice that in all things I am confident of you."

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: Exemplo ecclesiarum Macedoniæ exhortatur Corinthios ad eleemosynam, in usus sanctorum qui Hierosolymis erant, conferendam.
units.tr: By the example of the churches of Macedonia he exhorts the Corinthians to contribute alms for the use of the saints who were in Jerusalem.

units.la: CAPVT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 8.

units.la: ERTIORES autem uos facio fratres, de gratia Dei quæ data fuit in ecclesiis Macedoniæ: quoniâ per multâ probationem afflictionis exuberauit gaudium ipsorum, & profunda illorum paupertas exundauit in diuitias simplicitatis ipsorum. Nam pro uiribus, testor, etiam supra uires prompti fuerunt, multa cum obtestatione rogantes nos, ut beneficium & societatem ministerij suscipere mus in sanctos: ac non quatenus sperabamus, quin etiã semetipsos dediderunt primùm domino, deinde & nobis per uoluntatem Dei, in hoc, ut adhortaremur Titum, ut quemadmoadmodum ante coepisset, ita & consum{A}maret hac quoq; erga uos beneficentia. Imo quemadmodum ubiq; abundatis fide, & sermone, & scientia, & omni diligentia, & in ea quae ex uobis erga nos est charitate, facite, ut in hac quoq; beneficentia abundetis.
units.tr: Moreover, brothers, I make known to you the grace of God that has been given in the churches of Macedonia: that in a great trial of affliction their abundance of joy and their deep poverty have overflowed into the riches of their generosity. For, I bear witness, beyond their means they were willing, even beyond their strength, begging us most earnestly to accept the gift and the fellowship of the ministry to the saints. And they did not merely do as we hoped; they first gave themselves to the Lord and then to us, by the will of God, so that we would urge Titus that, just as he had begun before, so he would also complete this generous act toward you. But just as you abound in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all diligence, and in the love for us that is in you, see that you abound in this generous act too.

units.la: Existimo materiam hanc de eleemosyna, ac contributione in sanctos facienda, admodum esse prudenter, veluti parenthesim quandam in medio epistolae inserta, ut quae & ante & post de synceritate Apostolatus sui, contra pseudapostolos, tam multis inculcat hoc, uelut interstitio tolerabiliora redderentur legentibus, & a fastidio liberarentur. Et in priore epistola ca. vlt. causam hanc attigit, verum in praesenti tractat ea fusius, duob. videlicet hisce capitibus, octauo & nono.
units.tr: I think this subject of almsgiving and of contribution for the saints is very wisely placed, like a parenthesis inserted in the middle of the letter. Before and after it, he insists on the sincerity of his apostleship against the false apostles, and this interruption makes the rest more bearable for readers and frees them from weariness. In the earlier letter, at the end of the last chapter, he touched on this cause, but in the present letter he treats it more fully, namely in these two chapters, the eighth and the ninth.

units.la: CERTIORES autem uos facio fratres, de gratia Dei, quae data est, inquit, in ecclesijs Macedoniae.) Excitat animos eorum, ut quae dicturus est auidius audiat, cum sic orditur: Certiores autem uos facio fratres, de gratia Dei q data est in ecclesijs Macedonię. Etenim cū sic scribimus amicis, quod certiores eos reddamus, videmur aliquid dicturi; quod nesciant: & tamen scire ipsos referat. Idem facit hic Apostolus. Intendit autem excitationem hanc, per id quoq;, quod no simpliciter dicit: Certiores uos facio de eo qd geritur in ecclesijs Macedoniae, sed, Certiores uos facio de gratia Dei, quae data est in ecclesijs Macedoniae. Sic enim loquens significat dicturum se de re non vulgari, sed de tali quae ex singulari gratia data sit ecclesijs Macedoniae.
units.tr: "Moreover, brothers, I make known to you the grace of God that has been given," he says, "in the churches of Macedonia." He stirs their minds so that they will listen more eagerly to what he is about to say, when he begins thus: "Moreover, brothers, I make known to you the grace of God that has been given in the churches of Macedonia." For when we write to friends that we are informing them of something, we seem about to say something they do not know, and yet it reports something they already know. The Apostle does the same here. He intends this stirring also by not simply saying, "I inform you about what is happening in the churches of Macedonia," but, "I inform you of the grace of God that has been given in the churches of Macedonia." For in speaking thus he signals that he will speak not of an ordinary matter, but of something given to the churches of Macedonia by singular grace.

units.la: Gratia Dei & multifaria est, & multis etiam modis, praesertim in ecclesijs Dei, secundum mensuram dispensationis spiritus, dispensatur. Videmus hic ecclesijs Macedoniae concessam fuisse gratiam, quę sic nondum erat concessa fidelibus ecclesiae Corinthiorum, ut necessariu duceret Apostolus, de illa ad eos scribere, qd ad aemulationem prouocarentur. Et vigilantes, hoc est, ministri Christi, si quod singulare donum Dei alicui concessum sit ecclesiae, de illo certiores eos facere, qui suae sunt curae commissi, quo congratulentur fratribus, & gratias agant domino; consimilemq; ab illo gratiam supplciter petant.
units.tr: The grace of God is manifold, and it is dispensed in many ways, especially in the churches of God, according to the measure of the dispensation of the Spirit. Here we see that grace was granted to the churches of Macedonia which had not yet been granted to the faithful of the Corinthian church. The Apostle thought it necessary to write to them about it, so that they might be provoked to emulation. And watchful men, that is, ministers of Christ, if some singular gift of God has been granted to a church, ought to inform those committed to their care about it, so that they may rejoice with their brothers, give thanks to the Lord, and humbly ask him for a similar grace.

units.la: QVÆ data est, inquit, in ecclesijs Macedoniae.) Quid est quod non dicit: quae data est ecclesijs, sed, in ecclesijs Macedoniae? Gratia haec de qua in praesenti loquitur Apostolus, dupliciter in ecclesijs data est. Primum a Deo fidelibus qui in ecclesijs erant. Deinde, per hos sanctis qui erant Hierosolymis, quorum necessitatibus subseruiebatur. Sic gratia Dei in alijs quoq; donis dupliciter datur in ecclesijs. Primum, illis in quos donum effunditur, deinde per hos & reliquis, ad quos utilitas illius pertingit. Perinde atque in corpore nostro, quae
units.tr: "Which has been given," he says, "in the churches of Macedonia." Why does he not say "given to the churches" but "in the churches of Macedonia"? This grace of which the Apostle speaks here has been given in the churches in two ways. First, by God to the faithful who were in the churches; then, through these, to the saints who were in Jerusalem, whose needs were being served. So also the grace of God in other gifts is given in the churches in two ways: first to those into whom the gift is poured, then through these to the rest, to whom its benefit reaches. Just as in our body, the gifts divinely granted

units.la: sunt dotes diuinitus concessae, datae sunt primum membris singularibus, aliis aliae, ut oculis donum videndi, auribus audiendi, &c. deinde & toti corpori, ad cuius illa visus seruiunt. Nec impedit hunc sensum, quod sancti Hierosolymitani, quibus haec gratia deputabatur, non erat in ecclesijs Macedoniae. Corpore quidem in illis non erant, erant vero communicatione spiritus, qua vnum fiunt omnes omnium ecclesiarum fideles.
units.tr: are given first to individual members, some to some, as the gift of sight to the eyes, of hearing to the ears, and so on, and then to the whole body, which they serve. Nor does it hinder this sense that the holy men of Jerusalem, to whom this grace was assigned, were not in the churches of Macedonia. They were indeed not present in body, but they were present by the communion of the Spirit, by which all the faithful of all the churches become one.

units.la: Et illud obseruandum est, quod non in vna & altera tantum ecclesia gratiam hanc, sed in genere in ecclesijs Macedoniae datam esse dicit. Singularis hoc quoq; gratiae erat, quod communiter omnibus eius prouinciae ecclesijs concessa erat haec gratia. Multum quidem in seculari-bus negocijs ad conformitatem praestat lo-corum vicinitas, & eiusdem regionis incolat: verum in donis Dei, si qua reperitur conformitas in vnius prouincię ecclesijs, tribuendum hoc potius est, & cum primis singularis dispensatio Dei, cuius rationem nec inquirere debemus, nec reddere possumus. Si quaeras unde sit, quod in ecclesijs Germaniae data est singularis haec gratia renouatae ac restitutae doctrinae Christi, qua nondum tanta libertate potiuntur aliarum prouinciarum ecclesiae; no possumus eam referre alio, quam ad singulare consilium Dei, quo dona sua, ut vult, dispensat: Interea negandum non est, uti Deum mediis quidem litati doni sui conuenientibus, inter quę recte numeratur & uis vicini exempli, quemadmodum & sedulitas fideliū ministrorum. Sed videamus quae nam sit gratia illa Dei, de qua certiores facit Corinthios.
units.tr: It must also be noted that he says this grace was given not in one or another church only, but generally in the churches of Macedonia. This too was a mark of singular grace, that it was granted in common to all the churches of that province. Certainly in worldly affairs the nearness of places and residence in the same region produce much conformity; but in the gifts of God, if any agreement is found among the churches of one province, this should rather be ascribed to the singular dispensation of God, whose reasons we neither ought to inquire into nor are able to give. If you ask why this singular grace of the renewed and restored doctrine of Christ has been given in the churches of Germany, which the churches of other provinces do not yet enjoy with such freedom, we cannot refer it to anything but the singular counsel of God, by which he dispenses his gifts as he wills. Meanwhile it must not be denied that God uses means suited to his gift, among which the force of a neighbouring example is rightly counted, as is the diligence of faithful ministers. But let us see what that grace of God is, of which he informs the Corinthians.

units.la: QVONIAM per multam probationem affliction is exuberauit gaudiu illorum, & profunda paupertas illorum, exundauit in diuitias simplicitatis ipsorum, inquit.) In Graeco est, ὅτι ἐν πολλῇ δοκιμῇ θλίψεως, id est, quoniam in multa probatione afflictionis. Et sic legere malo, q quoniam per multam probationem afflictionis. Exprimit quae sit illa gratia Dei, quam in ecclesijs Macedoniae datam dixit. Sensus autem eorum est qd dicit, quod Macedones admodum afflicti, admodum pauperes & simplices, abunde contribuerint in vsus sanctorum. Per gaudium nonnulli intelligunt illorum largitione. Mihi videtur simpliciter intelligendum esse de gaudio spirituali sancti, quo in medijs afflictionibus recreabantur, & hilares erant ad dandum, cuius meminit i. Thess. 1. dicens: Et vos imitatores nostri facti estis, & domini, recipientes sermone cum afflictione multa, cum gaudio spirituali, vbi perinde atq; hic multae Macedonum afflictioni gaudiū coniungit. Legatur itaq; ad hunc modum, secundum Graeci contextus seriem: Quoniam in multa probatione afflictionis abundatia gaudij ipsorum, & profunda paupertas ipsorum, exundauit in diuitias simplicitatis ipsorum. Hoc est, quoniam abundas illorum gaudium quo alacres sunt, quauis in multis afflictionibus, quibus probantur, & iuxta ingens pauper-tas, pertas,quam ex spoliatione bonorum suorum contraxerunt,sic exundarunt in cōtributione in vsus sanctorū facta, vt opuleter contribue-rint.Hanc itaq; Macedonū contributionē non proponit Corinthijs simpliciter, sed cum am-plificatione ex circūstantijs desumpta.Vtpote quod dederint cū gaudio. i. hilares & alacres ad dandū,quod ob id memorat, vt Corinthij intelligant sibi quoq; dandū esse cum gaudio. Nam hilarem datorem diligit Deus. Deinde, quod alacritatem hanc contribuendi ostende-rint in multis afflictionib.constituti. Tertiò, quod gaudiū hoc fuerit in illis nō modicū, sed copiosum & abundans.Quartò,ut quod dede-rint admodū pauperes.Quintò ,quod non de-derint tenuiter,sed largiter & opulenter. Sic ornat,cohonestat, & commendat eleemosynā Macedonū,vt manifestū faciat,esse illam singu-larem quandam gratiam datā à Deo, ac dignā, quæ omnibus ecclesijs loco exempli propo-natur.
units.tr: "Since in a great trial of affliction their joy has overflowed, and their deep poverty has overflowed into the riches of their simplicity," he says. In Greek it is "hoti en polle dokime thlipseos" [ὅτι ἐν πολλῇ δοκιμῇ θλίψεως], that is, "since in much proving of affliction." I prefer to read it thus rather than "since through much trial of affliction." It expresses what that grace of God is, which he said was given in the churches of Macedonia. Its sense is what he says: that the Macedonians, very afflicted, very poor and simple, contributed abundantly for the use of the saints. Some understand "joy" as their generosity, but it seems to me it should be understood simply of the spiritual joy of the saints, by which they were refreshed amid afflictions and were cheerful in giving. He mentions this in 1 Thess. 1: "And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, receiving the word with much affliction, with spiritual joy," where, just as here, he joins joy to the great affliction of the Macedonians. So let it be read in this way, following the order of the Greek text: "Since in much proving of affliction the abundance of their joy, and their deep poverty, has overflowed into the riches of their simplicity." That is: since their joy, by which they are eager although tried by many afflictions, and their great poverty, which they contracted from the plundering of their goods, have thus overflowed in the contribution made for the use of the saints, so that they contributed richly. So he presents this contribution of the Macedonians to the Corinthians not simply, but with amplification drawn from the circumstances: namely, that they gave with joy, that is, cheerful and eager to give. He mentions this so that the Corinthians understand they too must give with joy, for God loves a cheerful giver. Second, that they showed this eagerness in giving while placed in many afflictions. Third, that this joy in them was not moderate but abundant and overflowing. Fourth, that they gave though very poor. Fifth, that they did not give meanly but largely and richly. Thus he adorns, honours and commends the almsgiving of the Macedonians, to make clear that it was a singular grace given by God, and worthy to be set before all the churches as an example.

units.la: Est igitur diligenter obseruandū, quòd eiusmodi eleemosynam,gratiā Dei in ecclesijs da-tam vocat.Iudicio carnis videtur illis tantum impartiri gratiam,quib.eleemosynā datur. At iudicio spiritus,nō minus, imò magis eorum est hæc gratia,qui dant eleemosynam quā qui accipiunt.Beatius siquidem est dare,quā acci-pere.Accipere possunt oēs,dare verò non oēs, sed ij tātū,quib.data est gratia à Deo, ut det ex animo,det cū gaudio,det largiter. Hoc genus dandi eleemosynā nō habetur in ecclesijs, nisi per singularē gratiam Dei,quia magis beneuo-lentiā Christianā,quàm terrenarū facultatū a-bundantiam requirit.Sed ipsa uerba ex ordine inspiciamus.
units.tr: Therefore it must be carefully observed that he calls such almsgiving a grace of God given in the churches. By carnal judgment it seems that grace is bestowed only on those to whom alms are given. But by the judgment of the Spirit this grace belongs no less, indeed more, to those who give alms than to those who receive them. For it is more blessed to give than to receive. Everyone can receive, but not everyone can give; only those to whom God has given grace to give from the heart, to give with joy, to give generously. This kind of giving alms is not found in the churches except through the singular grace of God, because it requires Christian goodwill more than an abundance of earthly means. But let us examine the words themselves in order.

units.la: QVONIAM in multa probatione afflictio-nis,inquit.) Non simpliciter,in multa afflictio-ne,sed,in multa probatione afflictionis.Non af-ligebantur tantū,quod accidere potest omni-bus,sed afflictiones patiēter pro Christi nomi-ne ferentes,probati reddebantur.Sic Rom. 5. afflictioni patientiā,patientiæ probatione tri-buit.Et hoc piorum & electorum est tantū.Nā impij ac carnales,dū affliguntur, nō probati patientiam redduntur,sed per impatientiā po-tius reprobi deprehenduntur.
units.tr: SINCE IN A GREAT TRIAL OF AFFLICTION, he says. He does not simply say "in great affliction," but "in a great trial of affliction." They were not merely afflicted, which can happen to anyone, but by bearing their afflictions patiently for the name of Christ they were proved genuine. So in Romans 5 he attributes patience to affliction and proof to patience. This belongs only to the pious and the elect. For the impious and the carnal, when they are afflicted, are not proved and made patient; rather, through their impatience they are exposed as reprobate.

units.la: Obserua verò,quod non simpliciter dicit: quoniam in probatione,sed,quoniam in mul-ta probatione afflictionis. Ergo non obiter se-mel atq; iterū,sed grauiter, & in multis ac fre-quenter per afflictiones fuerant probati Mace-dones.Sic solet dominus,quos alijs in exēplū probatæ fidei,ac patientiæ proponere constitu-it,multis & grauibus afflictionib. exercere, ac singulari probatione conspicuos reddere, quales hic Macedones fuisse videmus.
units.tr: Note, however, that he does not simply say "since in a proof," but "since in a great trial of affliction." The Macedonians, therefore, were proved not once or twice in passing, but severely, and in many and repeated afflictions. The Lord is accustomed to exercise with many and grievous afflictions those whom he has appointed to be set before others as examples of tested faith and patience, and to make them conspicuous by a singular proof, as we see the Macedonians were here.

units.la: ABVNDANTIA gaudij ipsorū. )Nihil hic mediocre.Probatio afflictionis multa, & gau-dium probatorum non modicum,sed abūdās. Ea est dignatio Dei in eos, quos tribulationi-bus exercet.Multitudini afflictionis abundan-tia coniungit gaudij,ac consolationis . Sic Da-
units.tr: THE ABUNDANCE OF THEIR JOY. Nothing here is moderate: the proof of affliction is great, and the joy of those who are proved is not small but abundant. This is the favour of God toward those whom he exercises with tribulations. Abundance of joy and consolation goes together with the multitude of affliction. So David says:

units.la: uid:Secundum multitudinem dolorum meo-rum consolationes tuæ,inquit, lætificauerunt animam meam.Et Apostolus de seipso , supra cap.1.Quoniam,inquit,sicut abundāt afflictio-nes Christi in nobis,ita per Christum abundat & consolatio nostra.
units.tr: "According to the multitude of my sorrows, your consolations have gladdened my soul" (Ps. 94 [Vulgate 93]). And the Apostle says of himself, above in chapter 1: "For as the afflictions of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds."

units.la: ET profunda paupertas ipsorum .) Nō erat illorū qualiscunq; paupertas,sed quā ad fundū usq; erant exhausti,vt nihil superesset, quā re-liquiæ quędā modicę,velut in imo fundo reli-ctę.Qui sic cōparatisunt,ad eorū potius uiden-tur pertinere numerū,quib. sit impartien-dum ab alijs,quā à quibus in usus aliorū expe-ctanda sit aliqua cōtributio.An pauperes adeò fuerint,priusquam crederent in Christum , vel postea propter nomen Christi spoliati pauper-tate hanc incurrerint,non exprimit Apost.quē admodum nec illud,an omnes fuerint paupe-res,vel maior pars tantum . Si priusquā crede-rent tales fuerant,cogitandum est de eo quod 1.Cor.1.legimus,elegisse Deū imbecilles & igno-biles,ut cōfunderet robustos & nobiles. Si ve-rò antea diuites,rapinam bonorum suorū, ꝑ-pter Christum passi,facti fuerant pauperes,co-gitemus quàm absimus ab hoc exēplo , qui iu-xta fortunam sæculi,pauperes diuitias,sub no-mine Christi quærimus.Sic animati,ne obolū quidem cū gaudio amittimus, ne dum omniū fortunarum detrimentū,propter Christum ala-cri animo subimus.
units.tr: AND THEIR DEEP POVERTY. Their poverty was not of just any kind, but they had been drained to the bottom, so that nothing remained except some small leftovers, as if left at the very bottom of a vessel. People so situated seem to belong rather to the number of those to whom something must be given by others than to those from whom some contribution for the use of others is to be expected. The Apostle does not state whether they were so poor before they believed in Christ, or whether they became poor afterward, stripped of their goods for the name of Christ; nor does he say whether all of them were poor or only the greater part. If they were such before they believed, we must consider what we read in 1 Corinthians 1, that God chose the weak and the base to shame the strong and the noble. If, however, they had been rich before, and became poor after suffering the plundering of their goods for Christ, let us consider how far we are from this example, we who, in the manner of the world's fortune, seek riches while we are poor, under the name of Christ. Yet we, so inspired, would not lose even a penny with joy, much less bear the loss of all our fortunes for Christ with a ready mind.

units.la: EXVNDAVIT,inquit,in diuitias simplici-tatis ipsorū.)Mirū quomodo exundare possit quod ad fundū vsq; exhaustū est.Exūdatio nō exhaustorū,sed ad summū usq; repletorū est. Deinde qd' adhuc amplius est, haud qualiter-cunq; profundam Macedonū paupertatē, sed ad diuitias usq; exundasse dicit.Videntur hæc esse impossibilia,si ad litera vrgeantur.Verū in hac causa duo cōsideranda veniunt. Vnum est quod Chrysostomus annotat dicens: ... Et Christus cum viduam quę duos obo-los in gazophylatium dederat plus, quā diui-tes dedisse dixit:nō quantū,sed quo animo de-derit expressit,ac circūstantias expendit,quod illa de necessario,diuites de abundāti conferret.Sic modicā Macedonū contributionem ex undantiam,Apost.propter conferendi alacrita-tem,diuitias verò propter profundæ paupertatis illorū respectum uocat.
units.tr: HE OVERFLOWED, he says, INTO THE RICHES OF THEIR SIMPLICITY. It is strange how that which has been drained to the bottom can overflow. Overflowing is not of things exhausted, but of things filled to the brim. Moreover, what is still more, he says the Macedonians' deep poverty overflowed not merely into abundance but into riches. These things seem impossible if pressed literally. But two things must be considered in this matter. One is what Chrysostom notes, saying: "...". And Christ, when he said that the widow who had put two mites into the treasury had given more than the rich, did not express the amount but the spirit in which each gave, and weighed the circumstances: that she gave from necessity, the rich from abundance. So the Apostle calls the Macedonians' small contribution an overflowing, because of their eagerness to give, and calls it riches because of the regard for their deep poverty.

units.la: Alterū est, singularis Apostoli bonitas, & e-pijcia,qua tam benignē interpretatur fidelium fortunas,ac beneficentiæ studia. Sic afficieba-tur Macedonū inopia,vt iudicaret eam esse ꝑ-fundam,& modicū quod dabat diuitias estima-ret.Hoc ingenio sunt boni,mali verò pro mali cia ingenij sui,omnia maligne interpretantur. Si hæc cōsideremus,facile intelligemus, quo modo profundam Macedonū paupertatem in diuitias exundasse dicat.
units.tr: The other is the singular goodness and kindness of the Apostle, who so kindly interprets the fortunes of believers and their zeal in beneficence. He was so moved by the poverty of the Macedonians that he judged it deep, and considered what they gave to be riches. Good men are of this disposition, while evil men, according to the malice of their own nature, interpret everything maliciously. If we consider these things, we shall easily understand how he can say that the deep poverty of the Macedonians overflowed into riches.

units.la: IN diuitias,inquit,simplicitatis eorum.)Ne uideatur copiam in contributione eorum, & non magis animū depræcdicare, nō simpliciter
units.tr: INTO THE RICHES, he says, OF THEIR SIMPLICITY. Lest it be thought that the stress lies on the quantity of their contribution rather than on commending their disposition, he does not simply say

units.la: dicit:exundauit in diuitias, sed ,exundauit in diuitias simplicitatis ipsorum. Loquitur autè de simplicitate animi, qua simpliciter & cădide, abiq; omni simulatione ac duplicitate, ut afficiebantur, erga sanctos & ipsos pauperes, ita & alacriter quantū poterât,dederât.Huiusmodi simplicitatem in eleemosyna largienda, in Romanis quoque cap.12. requirit,dicés,qui impertit in simplicitate.
units.tr: "he overflowed into riches," but "he overflowed into the riches of their simplicity." He speaks of the simplicity of mind, by which they gave, as they were moved toward the saints and the poor themselves, simply and sincerely, without any pretence or duplicity, and as eagerly as they could. In Romans 12 also he requires this simplicity in giving alms, saying: "He who gives, let him do it in simplicity."

units.la: Ergo Corinthijs Apost.iuxta seculū diuitibus,exemplum Macedonum pauperū proponit,ut illorum imitatione discant, nō quātum, sed quanta cum alacritate,ac simplicitate dare debeát. Si diuites Corinthij Macedonib. egenis,ad imitandum proponerētur, esset inimita bile exēplum.Respectu enim nō esset ad beneuolentiá,sed ad largiēdi magnificētiá,in qua diuiti pauper respōdere nō potest. Quare singulari consilio Dei sic cohonestatur piorum hominum paupertas,vt in causa eleemosynæ exemplo proponatur diuitibus,eoq; tali, vt citius illi, vt multum dent inducantur, quàm ut pauperum alacritati, ac simplicitati ex æquo respondeant.
units.tr: Therefore the Apostle sets before the Corinthians, who were rich according to the age, the example of the poor Macedonians, so that by imitating them they may learn to give not how much, but with how much eagerness and simplicity. If the rich Corinthians were set before the needy Macedonians for imitation, the example would be inimitable. For the regard would not be to goodwill, but to magnificence in giving, in which a poor man cannot match a rich one. Therefore, by a singular counsel of God, the poverty of the pious is so honoured that in the matter of almsgiving it is set before the rich as an example, and that in such a way that they may be led more quickly to give much, than to match the eagerness and simplicity of the poor.

units.la: NAM pro viribus,testor,etiam supra uires propti fuerunt ,inquit.) Declarat quę dixit. Referт aūt ea ad promptitudinem animi, non ad multitudinem contributorū,dicens: Nam pro uiribus,imò supra uires prompti fuerunt. Loquitur de uiribus facultatum . Græcè est χ?
units.tr: FOR ACCORDING TO THEIR MEANS, I bear witness, and beyond their means they were willing, he says. He explains what he said. He refers these words to the readiness of mind, not to the number of contributors, saying: "For according to their means, indeed beyond their means, they were ready." He speaks of the means of their resources.

units.la: Si dicas.Quomodo pauperes exhausti exundare potuerunt in diuitias? Respondet.Dando secundum ipsorum facultatem,quantum dare potuerūt.Imò,inquit,etiá supra quā potuerūt dare cupiendo.Rursus dices. Quomodo fieri potuit,vt supra uires darent? Quis enim dare poterit plura q̄ habeat? Respondeo.Nō dicit: etiam supra uires dederunt,sed etiam supra uires prompti fuerunt . Maior est pauperum ad dandū pròptitudo,q̄ facultas.In Græco est,αὐ-θαίρετοι.Significat autem αὐταίρετῳ, cum qui suapte voluntate motus,non ab alio, sed à seipso elegit sibijpse quod faciat.Et quoniam qui tales sunt,promptè faciunt, quod faciendum suapte sponte elegerunt,fit vt αὐταίρετος uocět proptos.Hac itaq; voce præoccupat Apostolus,ne dicat quisquam: Quod pro uiribus dederunt,imò supra uires dare uoluerunt,tua factū est authoritate, qui sic eos solicitado urseris,& ad contribuêdum impuleris.Vltro,inquit,suapte sponte,nò à me impulsi pro virib.dederūt, imò supra vires dare cupiebant.Et hæc nó sim pliciter de illis narrat,sed quo plus inuenirent fidei,testor,inquit.Q.d.quæ vidi ac certò sum expertus , testimonio meo uobis confirmo. Tanti momēti res est uolūtaria & alacris,quā tumuis in se modica piorum,pauperum ac sim pliciú hominum eleemosyna,ut dignetur eam Apostolus,non simpliciter, sed uelut adiurat testificando commemorare.
units.tr: If you say: how could the impoverished poor overflow into riches? He answers: by giving according to their ability, as much as they were able to give. "Indeed," he says, "even beyond what they could give, by desiring to." Again you will say: how could it happen that they gave beyond their means? For who can give more than he has? I answer: he does not say they gave beyond their means, but that they were ready beyond their means. The readiness of the poor to give is greater than their resources. In the Greek it is self-willed [αὐθαίρετοι]. This word signifies those who, moved by their own will, not by another but by themselves, choose for themselves what they do. And since those who are such do promptly what they have freely chosen to do, the ready are called self-willed. By this word the Apostle anticipates anyone saying: "What they gave according to their means, and wished to give beyond their means, was done at your instigation, since you urged and pressed them to contribute." No, he says, of their own accord, not impelled by me, they gave according to their means, indeed they desired to give beyond their means. And he tells this not simply of them, but so that he may find more faith for it: "I bear witness," he says, that is, "I confirm by my testimony to you what I have seen and know for certain." So great a matter is a willing and eager alms, even though it is small in itself, of pious, poor and simple people, that the Apostle thinks it worthy to recall it not simply, but as if adjuring them by testifying.

units.la: MVLTA cum obtestatione rogātes nos,in-
units.tr: WITH MUCH EXHORTATION, begging us,

units.la: quit,ut beneficiū & societatē ministerij suscipe rem in sactos.) Græcè est, μετὰ πολλῆς παρακλήσεως δεόμενοι ἡμῶν, id est,multa cum obsecratione rogantes nos. Vulgata habet:cum multa exhortatione obsecrantes nos.Chrysost.legit hic ḡdam,quæ nos non habemꝰ. Sic enim ille habet, μετὰ πολλῆς παρακλήσεως δεόμενοι ἡμῶν, ἐν θλι λεύοντες ἐν πνεύμα. Deinde illud,ut beneficiū & societatem ministerij susciperem in sanctos, in Græco sic legitur: τὴν χάριν καὶ τὴν κοινωνίαν τῆς διακονίας τῆς εἰς τοὺς ἁγίους διακονέω ἡμᾶς. i. Vt gratia & communicatione ministerij, qd est in sanctos susciperem. Qd testatur eos fuisse in hac causa αὐταίρετος, exposit hisce verbis,vnde idin illis cognouerit.Quoniā,inqt,nō expecta runt,vt super hac re solicitaretur à nobis,sed ipsi nos vltrò plurimū obsecrantes,rogarūt, vt gratiam & communicatione suā quam ad ministerium,quod fit in usus sanctorum iam contri buerant , in nostram curam ac fide suscipere mus.Hinc videlicet facilè cognouit,quā essent in hoc negocio αὐταίρετοι,alacres & propti,vt ea de re bona fide testificari posset.
units.tr: he says, that we would receive the grace and the fellowship of the ministry toward the saints. In the Greek it is "with much entreaty begging us" [μετὰ πολλῆς παρακλήσεως δεόμενοι ἡμῶν], that is, "asking us with much urging." The Vulgate has "with much exhortation beseeching us." Chrysostom reads here something that we do not have; for he has, "with much entreaty begging us, in the Spirit..." Then the clause "that we would receive the grace and the fellowship of the ministry toward the saints" is read in the Greek thus: "that we would receive the grace and the communion of the ministry which is toward the saints" [τὴν χάριν καὶ τὴν κοινωνίαν τῆς διακονίας τῆς εἰς τοὺς ἁγίους]. This shows that they were self-willed in this matter, and he explains by these words how he knew this about them. For, he says, they did not wait for us to be urged about this business, but they themselves, of their own accord, begged us very much and asked us to take into our care and faithfulness the grace and fellowship of the ministry, which they had already contributed for the use of the saints. From this he could easily know how self-willed, eager and ready they were in this business, so that he could bear good faith witness to it.

units.la: Quid aūt multa opus erat obsecratioe in re tam pia,erga Apostolū Christi,qui & vltrò ad ministrandū sanctis propēdebat,& pterea admonitus erat ab apostolis , vt memor esset pauperū? Nisi initio detrectasset communicatione hanc ab illis suscipere, vlteriore rogatu, & obsecrādi instātia,opus utiq; nō fuisset.Quare detrectasse illū,idq; non leuiter,sed obsirma tius aliquātò,multa illorū obsecratio conuincit. Quur aūt detrectarit ex eo primum patet, qd tribuit illis profundam paupertatem, & contributione usq; adeò spontaneā vt vires ipsorū excederet dādi alacritas.Cū videret eos admodum pauperes,& in cōtributione hac nó habere tenuitatis suæ ratione, inconsultum iudicabat à talib. quicūq̄ accipere, quantūuis in vsus sanctorū collatum:ideoq; quáuis illi obsecra ret,vt acciperet,haud tamē cōsestim, ac facilē consensit,donec multa esset obsecratione permotus.Hodie qui questū in ecclesię sectantur, nullis viduis,nullis orphanis,nullis pauperib. parcūt,sed vndecunq; coaceruant, quo luxui, libidini,& ocio suo satisfaciát. Et interim successores sunt Apostolorum.
units.tr: But why was there any need of much entreaty in a matter so pious, toward the Apostle of Christ, who was himself eager of his own accord to minister to the saints, and had moreover been admonished by the apostles to remember the poor? Unless at first he had shrunk from receiving this contribution from them, there would surely have been no need of further request and insistent entreaty. That he did shrink from it, and not lightly but with some firmness, is proved by their great entreaty. Why he shrank from it first appears from the fact that the Apostle attributes to them deep poverty, and a contribution so spontaneous that their eagerness to give exceeded their strength. Seeing that they were very poor, and had in this contribution no regard for their slender means, he judged it unwise to receive anything whatever from such people, however much was gathered for the use of the saints. Therefore, although they begged him to receive it, he did not agree immediately or readily, but only after he had been moved by much entreaty. Today those who pursue gain in the church spare no widows, no orphans, no poor, but heap up riches from every quarter, so that they may satisfy their luxury, lust and idleness. And meanwhile they are the successors of the Apostles.

units.la: VT gratiā,inquit,& cōmunicatione ministe rij,qd fit in sanctos susciperemus.) Contributa in vsus sanctorum,vocat gratiá & communicatione.Gratiá,propter beneficentiá,ex gratia & fauore ,pfectá. Sic &1Cor. ult. eleemosynā in sanctos collectam gratiam vocauit dicens: ubi venero,quoscunq; probaueritis,per episto las eos mittā,vt perferant gratiam uestram Hie rosolymam.Cōmunicatione vero,quōd cōmunicāda essent sanctis egenis.Sic vocat eleemosynam in sanctos,& Ro.15.& infrà cap. sequenti.Addit,ministerij quod fit in sanctos.Ministerium uocat hoc loco, administrationem eleemosynæ huius,qua colligebatur,& Hierosolymá deportabatur.Hāc igitur gratiā & communicationē Macedones adferebant ad Paulum, obnixè rogátes,ut eâ in curâ suam suscipęret,& sanctis administraret.De vocibus istis,gratia& communicatione diximus 1.Cor.vlt.
units.tr: "That we would receive the grace and the fellowship of the ministry which is performed for the saints." He calls the contributions for the uses of the saints both grace and fellowship. He calls them grace because of the beneficence, which proceeds from grace and favour. So also in 1 Cor. last chapter he called the alms collected for the saints grace, saying: "When I come, whomever you approve, I will send by letters, to carry your grace to Jerusalem." He calls them fellowship because they were to be shared with needy saints. So he calls the alms for the saints fellowship in Rom. 15 and in the following chapter of this letter. He adds "of the ministry which is performed for the saints." Here he calls ministry the administration of this alms, which was collected and carried to Jerusalem. The Macedonians therefore brought this grace and fellowship to Paul, earnestly asking that he take it into his care and administer it to the saints. We discussed these words, grace and fellowship, at 1 Cor. last chapter.

units.la: AC non quatenus sperabamus, quinetiâ semetipsos dederûnt primû dño, deinde & nobis voluntatem Dei.) Hoc est,tâta fuit eorû propitudo in hac causa,ut plura derint,quâ spe raueramus.Sperauerat modicâ aliquâ cótributione,qd̄ sciret eos esse pauperes admodû. At illi,inqt,nô modò de substantiola quisq; sua in vsu sanctorû,pro viribus cótulerunt,sed & semet ipsos obtulerunt,dño primû in quê credere cœperunt,deinde & nobis,si qua nobis in re adiumento esse possent,per voluntatem Dei.
units.tr: "And not as we hoped, but they gave themselves first to the Lord, and then to us, by the will of God." That is, their readiness in this matter was so great that they gave more than we had hoped. He had hoped for some modest contribution, knowing they were very poor. But they, he says, not only each gave from his little substance for the use of the saints, according to his means, but also offered themselves: first to the Lord, in whom they had begun to believe, and then to us, if they could be of help to us in any matter, by the will of God.

units.la: AC non quatenus sperabamus.) Ergo erra-uit Apost.minus de beneuolêtia fidelium Macedonû sperâdo,quâ habebat veritas? Errauit utiq;,sed pter culpâ. Min⁹ bene de fratrib. spe-rare,quâ res ipsa poscit, potest fieri dupliciter. Primò p sinistrâ suspicionê,uel diffidentiâ,q na scitur in animo insyncero,& à spiritu charitatis alieno,quod sine culpa fieri non potest.Qui sic animati sunt erga fratres, de animo illorum ac voluntate nô bene sentiût,ideoq; de illis min⁹ bene sperât.Deinde,respectu tenuitatis,quan-do rerû penuria premuntur.Hic nihil est culpę, si qs in causa fraterne cótributionis minus spe-rat de pauperib.quâ de opulêtis. Accidit hoc a-postolo: Qd̄ aût falsus est,falsʼ est ut homo,cui nô sunt mox nota omnia,q̄ Deus in suis est ele-ctis,singulari gratia operaturus.In ijs vero quæ fratris cócernunt animû,ac voluntate charitas plerunq; plura sperat,quâ habeat res ipsa, atq; ita sperando fallitur frequenter. Verùm satius est multo falli ad hunc modû,quâ cum diffiden-tib.ac reprobis,minus sperare de fratrib. quàm conueniat charitati fraternæ.
units.tr: "And not as we hoped." So did the apostle err in hoping less of the goodwill of the Macedonian believers than the truth warranted? He erred indeed, but not without fault. To hope less well of brothers than the matter requires can happen in two ways. First, through a sinister suspicion or distrust, which arises in an insincere mind, alien to the spirit of charity, and this cannot happen without fault. Those so disposed toward the brothers do not think well of their minds and wills, and so hope less well of them. Second, with respect to their poverty, when people are pressed by a lack of goods. Here there is no fault if someone in the matter of a brotherly contribution hopes less of the poor than of the wealthy. This happened to the apostle. That he was wrong, he was wrong as a man, to whom not all things were at once known, which God would work in his elect by singular grace. In those matters which concern the mind and will of a brother, charity often hopes for more than the thing itself contains, and so by hoping it is frequently deceived. Yet it is far better to be deceived in this way than, with the distrustful and the reprobate, to hope less of brothers than brotherly charity ought.

units.la: QVIN etiâ semetipsos dederunt primû dño, deinde & mihi.) Adiceit quidem hoc per auxe sim,verûm pulchrè facit ad uerę pietatis cõple-mentû,cuius pars tantum est,liberalè esse ac be-neficû in subleuandis sanctorum necessitatibus, id qd̄ Macedones supra quâ sperasset, fecisse p dicauit.Plenitudo pietatis trib.hisce partib.có-prehêditur.Prima,ut nosipsos demus primum domino,secunda,ut demus nos & ministris do-mini per voluntatem Dei ,tertia ,ut diligamus fratres , ac necessitatibus illorum pro uiribus succurramus.
units.tr: "Indeed they gave themselves first to the Lord, and then to me." He adds this by way of amplification, but he does well to complete true piety, of which a part only is being liberal and generous in relieving the needs of the saints. This he declared the Macedonians had done beyond what he had hoped. The fullness of piety is comprised in three parts. First, that we give ourselves first to the Lord. Second, that we also give ourselves to the Lord's ministers, by the will of God. Third, that we love the brothers and help their needs according to our means.

units.la: QVIN & semetipsos,inquit, dederût primû dño.) Semetipsum dare dño,est totum se illius voluntati ac gratiæ,non modò permittere,sed & ex animo offerre,consecrare & addicere, pa-ratumq; esse non solum facere, sed & pati pro-pter illum omnia.At hoc fieri nô poterit,nisi ab-negemus nosipsos,ut iam nô nobis,sed dño ui-uamus.Macedones quoniam totos se dederât dño,absq; vlla tergiuersatione pro nomine illi-us ferebant quicquid afflictionum inferri pos-set.Deinde,inquit,& nobis. Obserua distribu-tionem.Primû dño,inquit,deinde & nobis.Pri-mum dño,vt dño,deinde Paulo nô ut dño, sed ut dñi seruo & Apostolo.Aliter dño, aliter ser-
units.tr: "Indeed they gave themselves, he says, first to the Lord." To give oneself to the Lord is to surrender oneself wholly to his will and grace: not merely to permit it, but to offer it from the heart, to consecrate and devote oneself, and to be ready not only to act but also to suffer everything for him. This cannot happen unless we deny ourselves, so that we live no longer to ourselves but to the Lord. Since the Macedonians had given themselves wholly to the Lord, they bore without any evasion whatever afflictions could be laid upon them for his name. "And then," he says, "to us." Observe the order: "first to the Lord," he says, "and then to us." First to the Lord, as Lord; then to Paul, not as Lord, but as the Lord's servant and apostle. Otherwise to the Lord, otherwise to the servant.

units.la: uo,domino tâquâ ei in cuius fumus iure ac po-testate,tanquâ Deo,redêptori ac seruatori no-stro.Seruo tanquâ dominicę gratiæ ac volû-tatis erga nos ministro,Macedones post dñm de derût seipsos.Paulo,tâquâ dñi Apostolo,ut do-ctrinæ illius sese pberent morigeros, ac ductî-les.Nô est autê ociosum,qd̄ addit, p volûtatem Dei.Significat eos hoc fecisse secundû voluntâ-tê,non suâ,sed Dei.Dei voluntas est, ut audian-tur cû obedietia,quos ipse verbi sui ministros & interpretes mittit,idq; perinde habet, ac si ip-se audiatur.Vnde illud Christi est:Qui vosau-dit,me audit,,quæ verba haudquaquâ eos con-cernût,qui falsi sunt, non veri Christi apostoli. De eo quoq; cogitet diligês lector,qd̄ nô dicit, per voluntatê dñi,sed per uoluntatê Dei.Apo-stolatû suum,rursus per voluntatem Dei authê-ticum esse monet,quo totam dispensatione re-gni Christi,cuius erat minister, ad voluntatem Dei patris referat,id quodpro suo more frequê-ter facit,sicuti videre est1.Cor.1.supra cap.1.E-phe.1.Col.1.&2 Tim.1.
units.tr: To the Lord, as to the one in whose power and right we are, as to God our redeemer and saviour. To the servant, as the minister of the Lord's grace and will toward us, the Macedonians gave themselves after the Lord. To Paul, as the apostle of the Lord, so that they might present themselves as obedient and pliable to his teaching. It is not idle that he adds "by the will of God." It signifies that they did this according to the will of God, not their own. It is God's will that those whom he sends as ministers and interpreters of his word be heard with obedience, and he holds this just as if he himself were heard. Hence that saying of Christ: "He who hears you hears me." Those words by no means concern those who are false, not true apostles of Christ. Let the diligent reader also consider that he does not say "by the will of the Lord" but "by the will of God." Again he reminds us that his apostleship is authentic through the will of God, by which he refers the whole dispensation of Christ's kingdom, whose minister he was, to the will of God the Father. He does this frequently in his manner, as can be seen at 1 Cor. 1, above in chapter 1, Eph. 1, Col. 1, and 2 Tim. 1.

units.la: Voluntas hæc Dei perpetua est ad finem uf-què mundi perdurans,qua constituit, ut veris Christi ministris obsequantur ij , qui ab illis in fide ac vera pietate instituuntur: obsequantur, inquam,non ad quæuis,sed ad ea quę ministe-rium illorum, & Christi doctrinam ipsorumq; salutem concernunt.Qui in Papatu sunt,seruili ter obediunt falsis apostolis &pastoribus,ad o-mnem illorum,tam tyrannidem , quàm impo-sturam:qui verò de Euangelio Christi glorian-tur maiore ex parte,nec domino se, nec illi⁹ mi-nistris dederunt,sed suopte arbitrio indulgent in omnibus.
units.tr: This will of God is perpetual, lasting until the end of the world, and by it he has ordained that those who are instructed in faith and true piety by the true ministers of Christ should obey them. They should obey, I say, not in every matter, but in those which concern the ministry, Christ's doctrine, and their own salvation. Those in the Papacy obey false apostles and ministers slavishly, in all their tyranny as well as their imposture. But those who for the most part boast of the Gospel of Christ have given themselves neither to the Lord nor to his ministers, but indulge their own choice in everything.

units.la: IN hoc,inquit,ut adhortaremur Titû,ut quê admodum antê cœpisset, ita & consummaret hanc quoq; erga vos beneficentiam.) Hacten⁹ gratiâ Dei,quâ in ecclesijs Macedoniæ datâ es-se dixit,expositi,amplificauit, & cômendauit, iam ad propositû,quod agere ᵗ ôstituit transit. Sensus est,Macedonû hæc alacritas ac pietas, qua non modò sanctis largiter côtribuerût,sed & semetipsos primùm dño,deinde & nobis de derunt,perpulit nos,vt Titû adhortaremur, cû ad vos eum mitteremus,vt gratiam hanc, quâ apud vos cœpit cõsummaret.Cum dicit,se Ma-cedonum exemplo motum, ut Titum hortare-tur,quo apud ipsos,eandem beneficentiam an-tea cœptam côsummaret,prouocat eos,vt eo-dem ipsi quoq; moti,consimilem in sanctos be-neficentiam ostendant.
units.tr: "In this, he says, that we might exhort Titus, that as he had begun before, so he might also complete this beneficence toward you." Having thus far explained, amplified and commended the grace of God, which he said had been given in the churches of Macedonia, he now passes to the matter he had set out to treat. The sense is this: the eagerness and piety of the Macedonians, who not only gave generously to the saints but first gave themselves to the Lord and then to us, moved us to exhort Titus when we sent him to you, that he might complete among you this grace which he had begun. When he says that he was moved by the example of the Macedonians to exhort Titus, so that Titus might complete among them the beneficence begun earlier, he challenges them to be moved by the same example and to show a similar beneficence toward the saints.

units.la: VT quemadmodum antè cœpisset, inquit.) In sequentibus patet cœpisse Corinthios iam antea,anno videlicet præcedenti, contribuere in vsus sanctorû. Hic apparet factum id fuisse studio,&adhortatu Titi.Sanè si verba inspicias cœperat Titus Corinthios,non hac in causa tâ-tum,sed & in alijs instituere.Vnde non simpli-citer dicit:ita hâc beneficentiâ, sed, ita & hanc quoq; beneficentiâ erga uos cõsummaret.Illud erga uos,Græce est, ᾱὶς ὑμᾶς.i.in vos. Sic loquê-do significat cœptâ gratiâ,si côsûmetur cessurâ in emolumētū ipsorū Corinthiorū,ideoq; Titū cōsummaturū eā erga ipsos nō minus, q̄ erga sanctos, in quorū usus erat cōtribuendum.
units.tr: "That as he had begun before, he says." It is clear from what follows that the Corinthians had already begun earlier, in the previous year, to contribute for the uses of the saints. Here it appears this was done through the zeal and exhortation of Titus. Indeed, if you look at the words, Titus had begun among the Corinthians not only in this matter but in others as well. So he does not simply say "so in this beneficence," but "so also in this beneficence he might complete it toward you." The Greek for "toward you" is [εἰς ὑμᾶς], that is, "into you." Speaking thus signifies that the grace begun, if it is completed, will turn to the advantage of the Corinthians themselves; so Titus would complete it toward them no less than toward the saints, for whose use the contribution was to be made.

units.la: Obiter obserua, quod consummationé cœptæ beneficentiæ urget. Cœperant Corinthij, sed remissiores facti cœptá contributioné nō complebant. Sic solent, qui quod faciunt, non faciunt ex animo, non ἀυλαρίσιοι, sed aliūde impulsi. In medio cursu subsistunt, longè disimiles à Macedonibus, qui quoniá suaptè sponte cōtribuebāt, cōtributioné cōplebant. Tantum refert, quo animo quod bonū est facere incipias. Quo fit autē habédū loco opus in se quidem bonū, & bene cœptum, uerum per socordiam, negligentiá, ac fastidiū desertum & imperfectū, nō est opus ut admoneamus. Ipsa nos natura in rebus, quas quotidie nasci uidemus abundè docet, imperfecta esse inutilia. Quare frustra incœperis quod bonū est, nisi cōpleas.
units.tr: Incidentally, observe how he presses the completion of the beneficence begun. The Corinthians had begun, but growing more remiss they did not finish the collection they had started. So it is with those who do what they do not from the heart, not of their own accord [αὐθαίρετοι], but impelled by something else. They stop halfway, very unlike the Macedonians, who, since they contributed of their own accord, completed the contribution. So much depends on the spirit in which you begin to do what is good. Hence a work that is good in itself and well begun, but deserted and left unfinished through sloth, negligence and disgust, need not be urged on us. Nature itself, in the things we see born every day, amply teaches that what is unfinished is useless. Therefore you begin in vain what is good unless you complete it.

units.la: IMO, inquit, quemadmodū ubiq; abūdatis fide, & sermone & scientia, & omni diligētia, & in ea quę in uobis erga nos est charitate, facite ut in hac quoq; beneficētia abūdetis.) In Graeco est ἀλλὰ, uulgatə interpres reddit: Sed sicut in omnibus, &c. Erasmus uero, imò quemadmodū ubiq;. Neutra uersio cōmoda uidetur. Ipsa graeca uox multę significationis est, & ut uariè usurpatur, ita & uariè redditur. Mihi reddēda hoc loco sic uidetur, ut sit cōmoda transitioni, qua Apost. ab exēplo Macedo. ad exhortationem quam instituit trāfit. Quare existimo cōmode uerti posse ad hūc modū. Sanè quemadmodū ubiq; abūdatis fide, &c. Quod si redditur. Sed, vel at, uel, uerū quēadmodū ubiq; abūdatis fide, &c. omnino subaudiēdū uenit aliqd, utpote, uerū quicquid sit de exēplo Macedonū, curandum uobis est, ut sicut abundatis fide, &c.
units.tr: "Indeed, he says, as you abound in everything: in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all diligence, and in that charity toward us which is in you, see that you abound in this beneficence too." The Greek has [ἀλλὰ], "but," which the Vulgate renders "But as in all things," and Erasmus "Indeed, as in every way." Neither rendering seems suitable. The Greek word has many meanings and is used and rendered in various ways. Here it seems to me best rendered so that it fits the transition by which the apostle passes from the example of the Macedonians to the exhortation he now undertakes. So I think it can fitly be rendered thus: "Indeed, as you abound in faith, and so on." If it is rendered "but," "yet," or "however," then something must be understood, such as: "However things stand with the example of the Macedonians, you must take care that, as you abound in faith, and so on."

units.la: Sanè quemadmodū ubiq; abundatis fide, &c. Exhortationē quā subijcit exēplo Macedonum orditur prudēti cōsilio à laude Corinthiorū, qua tribuit illis excellētiam in fide, uerbo, scientia, diligentia, & charitate, quā erga se ostēdebant. Primūm in genere dicit eos ubiq; excellere, intellige de uarijs dotibus, quas in Christo acceperāt, quibus supra cæteras eccle sias eminebāt. Magna sane laus, ut nō immerito exordiū exhortatiōis suæ hic sumat Apost. Deinde qd' in genere dixit explicat p species, quas recēset dicēs, fide, uerbo, scientia, & omni diligētia, & in ea quę ex uobis erga nos est charitate. Fide intelligit generaliter, qua credebāt unū esse Deū, Christū esse dominū, & quæ historiā dispēsationis Christi concernūt, & quæ alia sunt eiusmodi, quibus fides miraculorum quoq; coniungi potest. Neq; enim uerosimile est loqui ipsum de fide iustificāte, in qua Macedones potius quàm Corinthios excelluisse appa ret. De fide dictū est, 1. Cor. 12. & 13. Per sermonem uel uerbū, intelligit ḡonū sermonis sapiētiæ ac scientiæ, cuius meminit 1. Cor. 12. Per scientiā cognitionem rerū spiritualiū, qua de mentione fecit 1. Cor. 8 mox initio capitis. Illud, in omni diligētia, Grecè est, ἐν πάσῃ σπουδῇ,
units.tr: Indeed, "as you abound in everything, and so on." He begins the exhortation he adds, modelled on the Macedonians, with a wise approach: he praises the Corinthians, attributing to them excellence in faith, speech, knowledge, diligence, and the love they showed toward him. First he says in general that they excel everywhere. This is to be understood of the various gifts they had received in Christ, by which they stood out above the other churches. It is certainly a great commendation, and the Apostle rightly takes it as the opening of his exhortation. Then he explains by particulars what he had said in general, listing "in faith, in speech, in knowledge, and in all diligence, and in the love from you toward us." By "faith" he understands it broadly: the belief that there is one God, that Christ is Lord, and what concerns the history of Christ's dispensation, and other things of this kind, to which the faith in miracles may also be joined. For it is not likely that he is speaking of justifying faith, in which the Macedonians seem to have excelled the Corinthians rather than the reverse. Faith is discussed at 1 Cor. 12 and 13. By "speech" or "word" he understands the gift of the word of wisdom and knowledge, which he mentions at 1 Cor. 12. By "knowledge" he means knowledge of spiritual things, which he touched on at 1 Cor. 8, at the beginning of that chapter. The phrase "in all diligence" is in Greek "ἐν πάσῃ σπουδῇ,"

units.la: quam uocē cap. præcedēti solicitudinē uertit, ad quē modum hic eam uetus interpres reddit. Existimo autē intelligendam esse de solicitudine, quam cap. præcedenti ex tristicia, quæ secundum Deum erat, natam illis fuisse dixit. Auxesim autem laudis huius habet, quod omnis generis solicitudinem illis tribuit.
units.tr: a word which in the preceding chapter he rendered as "care," and which the old translator renders in the same way here. I think it should be understood of the care which, in the preceding chapter, he said had arisen in them from the sorrow that was according to God. He intensifies the praise by attributing to them every kind of care.

units.la: ET in ea quę ex uobis erga nos est charitate, inquit.) Ergo tribuit illis & charitatē, imò excellētiam in charitate. Tribuit quidem, uerum cum specificatione, dicēs, quæ erga nos est. At causa de qua scribit, poscit charitatē fraternā erga omnes Christi fideles. Hanc illis non tribuit istis uerbis. Erat quidem laude dignum, quod amanter erant affecti erga suum Apostolum, uerum id genus dilectionis nō satisfacit dominico præcepto, quo nos inuicē diligere iubemur. Inuenias etiā in sæcularibus discipulis eiusmodi discipulos, qui præceptores quidē suos admodū diligant, se inuicē uero non ita. At Christiana disciplina non contenta hoc dilectionis genere, mutuam inter ipsos discipulos, hoc est, Christi fideles charitatē reqrit, ad quā Apost. ubiq; sedulo hortatur, præsertim in epistola priore. Agnoscit tñ ac laudat hanc Corinthiorū erga se dilectionē: uerū facit hoc in eum finē, ut inde occasionē sumat inducendi eos ad plenę & integræ charitatis studium.
units.tr: "And in the love which is from you toward us," he says. So he attributes to them love as well, indeed excellence in love. He does attribute it, but with a qualification, saying "which is toward us." Yet the matter he is writing about calls for brotherly love toward all Christ's faithful. He does not grant them this in these words. It was certainly praiseworthy that they were warmly affected toward their Apostle, but this kind of affection does not satisfy the Lord's command by which we are bidden to love one another. You will find among secular disciples such pupils, who indeed dearly love their teachers, but not one another. Christian discipleship, however, is not content with this kind of affection: it requires mutual love among the disciples themselves, that is, among Christ's faithful, and the Apostle urges this everywhere with earnestness, especially in the first epistle. Nevertheless he acknowledges and praises this love of the Corinthians toward himself, but he does so to this end: that he may take from it an occasion of leading them to a zeal for full and complete love.

units.la: FACITE, inquit, ut in hac quoq; beneficentia abundetis.) Nō cōuenit, ut hic p gratia legamus beneficētia, quod fieri posset, si diceret, χάρις, id est, & in gratia quoq; abundetis. Sic enim dicendo distingueret gratiam à dotibus cæteris, in quibus excellebant Corinthij, ut rectè pro beneficentia posita intelligeretur. Iam cum dicit: ut in hac quoq; gratia abundetis, perspicuum est, quòd subintelligēdum sit, sicut in cæteris, quæ tamen pro beneficentijs accipi nō possunt. Gratia erat fides, gratia sermo, gratia scientia Corinthiorum, quæ tamen non rectè beneficētiam uocaueris, licet beneficētia inter species gratiæ referatur. Hortatus eos, non ad modicam & uulgarem beneficentiam, sed ad excellētem, qualis erat Macedonum, proposuit eis excellentiam, non aliena rum uirtutum, siue Macedonū, siue aliorū, sed propriarum, & tum demū subiecit: sic faciete, ut in hac quoq; gratia abūdetis. Q.d. Quāuis egregium sit Macedonū exemplum, ac diguum, ad cuius imitationē prouocentur omnes ecclesiæ, haud tamen ad illud uos exigo, sed ad uestrarū uirtutū excellentiam, qua cæteras ecclesias excellitis. Hanc uobis imitandam propono. Voluit uos dominus excellere fide, sermone, scientia, studio ac diligentia, & dilectione erga me uestrū Apostolum, iam uobis etiam atque etiam uidendum est, ut in hac quoq; gratia abundetis, ne cæteri s qui tantam charismatum excellentiam non habent, inferiores in hac causa reperiamini, in qua uos supra cæteros eminere conueniebat.
units.tr: "Do this," he says, "that you may abound in this grace also, in the giving." It would not fit to read here "beneficence" for "grace," which might be possible if he had said "χάρις," that is, "that you may abound in grace also." For by saying this he would distinguish grace from the other gifts in which the Corinthians excelled, so that it would rightly be understood as "beneficence." But since he says "that you may abound in this grace also," it is clear that one must supply "as in the others," though these cannot be taken as acts of beneficence. Faith was a grace, speech was a grace, knowledge was a grace of the Corinthians; yet you would not rightly call these "beneficence," although beneficence is counted among the kinds of grace. Having urged them to not a modest and common beneficence, but to an excellent one such as the Macedonians had, he set before them an excellence not of other men's virtues, whether of the Macedonians or of others, but of their own. Only then does he add: "Do this, that you may abound in this grace also." That is to say: although the example of the Macedonians is outstanding and worthy, and all churches should be prompted to imitate it, I do not require you to conform to it, but to the excellence of your own virtues, by which you surpass the other churches.
