This I put before you to imitate. The Lord willed you to excel in faith, speech, knowledge, zeal, and diligence, and in love toward me, your Apostle. Now you must consider again and again that you abound in this grace also, lest you be found inferior in this matter, when those who do not have such excellence in gifts stand below you, and in which you ought to have stood out above the rest.

units.la: Argumentū exhortationis huius multū habet ponderis, si rectè inspiciatur. Cui multum datum est, ab illo multū requiritur. Corinthijs multū erat à dño datū, sic ut supra cæteras ecclesias abundarent fide, sermone, scientia & diligentia, ut cætera charismata taceā. Erat igitur consequens, ut in studio quoq; uerę pietatis multū ab illis requireretur. Quo uinea diligentius est culta, hoc plus fructus ex illa requritur. Fides, sermo, scientia, & id genus alia charismata, instar sunt cultus. Fructus est omnis generis beneficētia, ex uera charitate profecta. Quare nō est ut dicas: Quid opus erat Corinthijs, ut abundarent in beneficentia? An non satis erat, quod abundabant fide, sermone ac scientia? An hęc est Christianorum conditio, ut qui in uno abūdat, abundare debeat in omnibus? Distinguendū est inter ea, quę necessariò tanquā bonę arboris fructus requirūtur ab omnibus, quale est studiū charitatis, & ea quæ non ita poscūtur necessariò, qualia sunt, quorū hic excellentia Corinthijs tribuit, non quod nullus sit illorū usus, cum, ut diximus, sint instar cultus, unde uerę pietatis fructus crescat, sed quod nemo Christianus, secundum mensuram illorū, uel magnā uel paruā, magis uel minus pius in cōspectu domini cēsetur. Macedones in illis, nō ita excellebāt (sic pono) ut Corinthij, excellebant uero in operibus charitatis, tanquam ueris fructibus, unde arbores bonæ cēsemur. Non lego Apostolū adhortatū illos esse, ut quemadmodū abundaret in hac fraterna beneficentia, ita abundaret etiā in fide, sermone & scientia, donis etiā linguarū, & cæteris charismatibus, sicuti lego adhortatū esse Corinthios, ut sicut in istis excellebant, ita excellerent in studio quoq; beneficentiæ fraternæ erga sanctos, ac pauperes declarandæ. Corinthios itaq; Apost. nō hortatur hoc loco ad studiū excellendi in omnibus, qđ carni solet esse agnatū, sed quoniam beneficio domini, in ijs excellebant, quæ ad profectum uerę pietatis facere debebāt, in necessarijs uero deficiebāt, admonet eos necessariò, ut quo plus accepe-rāt gratiæ, hoc abundatius etiā ueros pietatis fructus proferāt. Cōsimili ratione admonēda est Germania nostra, ut quemadmodum in fide, sermone & scientia, dono Dei excellit, ita excellat, & studio uerę pietatis, charitatis, ac beneficentię, nō modo erga indigenas, sed & aduenas, propter Euangelii Christi exulātes.
units.tr: The argument of this exhortation carries much weight, if it is rightly examined. "To whom much has been given, from him much will be required." Much had been given by the Lord to the Corinthians, so that they abounded above the other churches in faith, speech, knowledge, and diligence, not to mention the other gifts. It followed, then, that much would also be required of them in the zeal for true godliness. The more diligently a vineyard is tended, the more fruit is expected from it. Faith, speech, knowledge, and gifts of that kind are like cultivation. The fruit is every kind of beneficence, arising from true love. So do not say: "What need was there for the Corinthians to abound in beneficence? Was it not enough that they abounded in faith, speech, and knowledge? Is it the condition of Christians that whoever abounds in one thing must abound in all?" One must distinguish between those things which are necessarily required of all, as the fruit of a good tree, such as the zeal of love, and those which are not necessarily demanded, such as those gifts in which the Corinthians are here credited with excellence. This is not because these have no use, since, as we have said, they are like cultivation by which the fruit of true godliness grows; rather, it is because no Christian is judged more or less pious in the sight of the Lord according to the measure of these gifts, whether great or small. The Macedonians did not excel in these (as I suppose) as the Corinthians did, but they excelled in the works of love, as true fruits, by which trees are judged good. I do not read that the Apostle urged them that, just as they abounded in this brotherly beneficence, so they should also abound in faith, speech, and knowledge, and in the gifts of tongues and the other charismata. But I do read that the Corinthians were urged that, just as they excelled in those gifts, so they should excel also in zeal for showing brotherly beneficence toward the saints and the poor. Therefore the Apostle does not in this place urge the Corinthians to a zeal for excelling in everything, which is wont to be akin to the flesh; but since by the Lord's kindness they excelled in those things which ought to advance true godliness, and were lacking in what was necessary, he admonishes them of what is needful: that the more grace they had received, the more abundantly they should also bring forth the true fruits of godliness. In a similar way our Germany is to be admonished: that, as she excels in faith, speech, and knowledge by the gift of God, so she should excel also in zeal for true godliness, love, and beneficence, not only toward natives, but also toward strangers, who are exiles for the sake of the Gospel of Christ.

units.la: Non secundum imperium loquor, sed per solicitudinem erga alios, etiā ueltrę dilectionis synceritatē approbans. Nostis enim beneficentiam dni nostri Iesu Christi, qđ propter uos pauper factus sit, cum esset dives, ut uos illius pauper tate ditesceretis. Et consilium in hoc do, nam hoc uobis cōducit: qui quidē non solū facere, uerum etiā uelle iam cœpistis anno superiore. Nunc autem & illud quod facere cepistis, perficite, ut quem admodū uoluntas propta fuit, ita & perficiatis ex eo qd potestis. Etenim si prōadsit animi promptitudo, ea iuxta quic quid illud est, quod posside aliquis, accepta est, nō iuxta id qd non possidet.
units.tr: "I speak not by way of command, but by way of concern for others, also proving the sincerity of your love. For you know the beneficence of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor, so that by His poverty you might be made rich. And I give counsel in this matter, for this is profitable for you: you who not only began to do, but also to will, a year ago. Now, however, complete also what you began to do, so that, as the willingness was ready, so also the completion may be from what you have. For if the readiness of mind is present, it is accepted according to what anyone has, and not according to what he does not have."

units.la: Quoniā dixit, & in hac gratia abundate, ne uideatur, hoc uelut imperando dicere, atq; ita uel ab inuitis beneficetiam iStam extorquere, occupatione suspicionem hanc cauet, dicens:
units.tr: Since he had said, "and abound in this grace also," lest it seem that he is saying this as a command, and so wrest this kindness from unwilling people, he anticipates that suspicion by adding:

units.la: NON secundū imperium loquor. Non est ut disputemus hic, potestatem ne habuerit imperandi illis, uel minus. Ipsa causa de qua loquitur, sic est comparata, ut imperium non capiat. Requirit enim datorem non coactum & inuitum, sed spōtaneum & hilarē. Magna laus est eleemosynæ Macedonicæ, quod ne hortatu quidē, nedum imperio Apostoli, sed sponte sua, tam liberaliter cōtribuerunt. Haud igitur præter rationē est, quod non modo nihil impe-rat in hac causa Corinthijs, sed & diserte se nō imperando hæc loqui testatur, ne non impe-rans, uel in specie imperare uideatur. Hæc est Apostolica diligētia, qua hodie nō habēt opus Ro. Apostoli, qui omnem suum Apostolatum mandandi & imperandi potestate metiuntur.
units.tr: "I speak not by way of command." We need not argue here whether he had the power to command them or not. The very matter he is speaking of is not of a kind that admits command. It calls for a giver who is not compelled or unwilling, but spontaneous and cheerful. The Macedonian almsgiving deserves great praise, because they contributed so generously, not even at the urging, much less the command, of the Apostle, but of their own accord. It is therefore not unreasonable that in this matter he not only commands the Corinthians nothing, but also expressly declares that he is speaking without command, lest, while not commanding, he should seem to command in appearance. This is apostolic diligence, which the Roman apostles today have no need of, since they measure their whole apostleship by the power of commanding and ordering.

units.la: SED per solicitudinē, inquit, erga alios etiā ueltrae dilectionis synceritatē approbās. Græce sic legitur: ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς ἑτέρων σπουδῆς, καὶ τὸ τῆς ὑμετέρας ἀγάπης γνήσιον δοκιμάζων. i. (sed per aliorū studium, etiā ueltrę charitatis synceritatem comprobans. Potest hoc bifariā intelligi. Primo ad hunc modū, sed per curā, qua de aliorū, j. sanctorū, sum necesitatib. solicitus, hæc adu-os scribo, quo explorē, quām sitis in hac charitate ingenui ac synceri. Et hūc sensum Erasmus exprimere uoluit, dum uertit, sed per solicitudinē erga alios etiā ueltrę dilectionis synceritatē approbās. Deinde sic: Sed ut per aliorū, id est, Macedonū studium, cuius mentionem feci, ueltrā quoq; dilectionem, quām sit ea ingenua cōprobem. Posterior hic sensus mihi magis arridet. Loquitur non de suo, sed Macedonū studio, quod illis in precedētibus diligēter amplificando commendauit, ac dicit, se illius exemplum ad hoc proposuisse, ut comprobet quām sint ipsi quoq; erga studiū charitatis synacere & ingenue affecti. Haud illibēter autem assentior Chrysost. qui sentit Apostolū nō loqui de cōprobatione, qua ipse synceritate charitatis Corinthiorū experiatur, sed qua illam alijs reddat certā & comprobatam. Neq; enim faciebat ad cautionē apostolicā, si se certo experimēto cogniturum diceret, quām essent in charitate synceri erga fratres. Quin magis sic loquitur, ut significet se ad hoc Macedonū induxisse exemplū, ut charitatem ipsorū, sibi nota tam, alijs comprobatā redderet. Et sic sentiebat de illis. Cōfidebat eis in omnib: idq; cum gaudio, sicuti supra dixit, in calce cap. præcedētis: Gaudeo, quod in omnib. cōfido uobis.
units.tr: "but through the earnestness of others, also proving the sincerity of your love." In Greek it reads: "ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς ἑτέρων σπουδῆς, καὶ τὸ τῆς ὑμετέρας ἀγάπης γνήσιον δοκιμάζων" [but through the zeal of others, also proving the genuineness of your love]. This can be understood in two ways. First, thus: "but through the care I have for others, that is, the saints, whose needs concern me, I write these things to you, so that I may test how sincere and genuine you are in this love." Erasmus wished to express this sense when he translated: "but through the earnestness toward others also proving the sincerity of your love." Second, thus: "But so that, through the zeal of others, that is, of the Macedonians, whom I have mentioned, I may prove how genuine your love also is." This latter sense pleases me more. He is speaking not of his own zeal but of the zeal of the Macedonians, which he had commended in the preceding verses with careful amplification, and he says that he has set their example before them so that he may prove how genuinely and sincerely you too are disposed toward the zeal of love. I do not, however, entirely agree with Chrysostom, who holds that the Apostle is not speaking of a proof by which he himself would test the sincerity of the Corinthians' love, but of a proof by which he would make that love certain and attested to others. For it would not suit apostolic caution if he said he would come to know by certain experience how sincere they were in love toward the brothers. Rather, he speaks so as to indicate that he has brought forward the Macedonian example in order to make their love, which was known to him, attested to others as well. And so he judged of them. He trusted them in all things, and this with joy, as he said above at the end of the preceding chapter: "I rejoice that I have confidence in you in all things."

units.la: Apparet Apostolum erga Corinthios perinde fuisse affectum, atq; præceptor literarius erga discipulum, singulari ingenio præditum, de quo glorietur apud omnes. Ille, si qua spe- cimina eruditiôis ab alijs discipulis œdita fue- rint, mox ea singulari suo discipulo æquali de- xteritate exprimenda proponit: nô ut ingenij illius uires experiatur ipse, cum habeat eas in comperto, sed ut ostendat alijs, se nô frustra de discipulo illo gloriari, & ingenij illius dexteri tatem depræðicare. Consimili modo Apost. exemplum Macedonicarũ ecclesiarum Corin thijs suis, de quibus admodum gloriabatur, ad hoc proposuit, ut extimulati declararent, q̃ & ipsi ad studiũ charitatis ingenuè essent affecti.
units.tr: It is clear that the Apostle felt toward the Corinthians just as a schoolmaster feels toward a pupil endowed with exceptional talent, of whom he boasts before everyone. If some examples of learning have been produced by other pupils, he immediately sets them before his outstanding pupil to be matched with equal skill, not in order to test that pupil's abilities himself, since he already knows them, but to show others that he does not boast of that pupil in vain, and to proclaim the pupil's skill. In a similar way the Apostle set the example of the Macedonian churches before his Corinthians, of whom he was very proud, so that, being spurred on, they might show that they too were genuinely disposed to the zeal of love.

units.la: Obseruet autè diligēs lector, quod ab Apo- stolo in charitate requiritur τὸ γνῶσις. Significat autem ea uox, id quod est natiuũ, quasi sit γνώσιος. Quæ natiua sunt, syncera sunt, tanquã haud corrupta, nulloq; mixturæ adulterio uiciata, aut nullo afciticio colore deformata. Na tiuus corporis decor γνώσι@ est: sic charitatis syncęritas est, quæ nullis est fucis, & impostu- ris uiciata, sed pro ingenio uerę charitatis pu- ra & simplex. Requirit igitur Apostol in Chri stianis charitatem γνώσιον, i. simplicem, puram, synceram & illibatam, in qua nihil sit simula- tum, fucatum ac fictum. Ea syncęritas depræ- hęditur in ueris fructibus charitatis, quos hic Apostolus à Corinthijs declarari poscit.
units.tr: Let the diligent reader also observe that the Apostle requires in love what is "γνήσιον" [genuine]. This word signifies what is native, as if it were "γνήσιος" [of true birth]. Things that are native are sincere, as if unspoiled, not defiled by the adultery of any admixture, nor disfigured by any borrowed colour. Natural bodily beauty is "γνήσιον"; so the sincerity of love is free from all paint and deceit, and is pure and simple according to the nature of true love. The Apostle therefore requires in Christians a love that is "γνήσιον", that is, simple, pure, sincere and unblemished, in which nothing is feigned, painted or pretended. This sincerity is discerned in the true fruits of love, which the Apostle here asks the Corinthians to display.

units.la: NOSTIS enim beneficentiâ, inquit, domi- ni nostri Iesu Christi.) Qui in multis excellũt, haud facile aliqua in re æqualium suorum mo- uentur exèplo: putant enim sine detrimento gloriæ suæ fieri nô posse, ut eos imitętur, quos ipsi excellũt in multis, & quorũ duƈtores esse debuerint potius, quàm secƈatores. Qui sic ani mati sunt ex singularium uirtutum suarũ con- scientia, nô tam æqualiũ, quàm præstãtiorum exemplis mouentur, à quibus excelli se in om nibus negare non possunt. Tale quid uidetur Apost. metuisse in Corinthijs, ideoq; post in- duƈtũ Macedonũ exemplũ ipsius Christi gra- tiam suspiciendâ & imitandam in omnib. pro- posuisse, dicens: Nostis enim gratiâ domini nostri Iesu Christi, quod propter uos pauper factus fit, &c. Quasi dicat: Quicquid uobis de exèplo Macedonũ uideatur, saltè ipsius Chri- sti imitatores sitis. Huius enim gratiam utiq; nostis, quam & exosculari, & pro uiribus imi- tari uos conuenit, ut nullis hac in re opus ha- beatis præceptis. Ipsa nanq; per se abundè suf- ficit ad excitandum imitationis studium, non in uobis tantum, sed & in alijs omnibus.
units.tr: "For you know the kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ." Those who excel in many things are not easily moved in any matter by the example of their equals. They think it impossible, without loss of their own glory, to imitate those in whom they themselves excel in many things, and of whom they ought rather to be leaders than followers. Those who are so disposed, from consciousness of their singular virtues, are moved not so much by the examples of their equals as by those of their superiors, whom they cannot deny they fall short of in every respect. The Apostle seems to have feared something of this kind in the Corinthians. Therefore, after the example of the Macedonians, he sets before them the grace of Christ Himself, to be admired and imitated in all things, saying: "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor," etc. As if he were saying: "Whatever you think of the example of the Macedonians, at least be imitators of Christ Himself. For you certainly know His grace, which you ought to embrace and, as far as you can, imitate, so that in this matter you need no precepts at all. For this alone is more than enough to arouse the zeal of imitation, not only in you but in all others as well."

units.la: Poterat dicere: Nostis enim præceptũ do- mini nostri Iesu Christi, quo iubet, ut diliga- mus nos inuicem, sicut ipse dilexit nos. Quare licet ego uobis hic nihil imperem, constringit tamen uos imperàtis Christi authoritas. Verũ maluit eos prouocare exemplo, quàm urgere præcepto Christi, quo esset cõtributio ipsorũ nô coaƈta, sed uoluntaria. Sic ubiq; accômodat se causæ quam agit. Et reuera in animis uero- rũ fidelium multum habet efficaciæ, si conside- rent non doƈtrinâ modò, sed & ipsam Christi uitâ, tanquã uiuam eorũ imaginê, quæ uerbo
units.tr: He could have said: "For you know the precept of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which He commands that we love one another as He has loved us. So although I command you nothing here, the authority of Christ's command binds you nonetheless." But he preferred to provoke them by example rather than to press them by the precept of Christ, so that their contribution would be not compelled but voluntary. Thus he everywhere adapts himself to the cause he is pleading. And indeed, it has great power in the hearts of true believers if they consider not only the doctrine but also the very life of Christ, as a living image of themselves, which is set before them in His word.

units.la: illius proponũtur, ut non fit frustra, quod Co- rinthijs hic ab Apostolo dicitur: Nostis gra- tiâ domini nostri Iesu Christi. Sic in alijs quoq; ad ueram pietatem necessarijs dicendum nobis est, nostis mansuetudinem domini nostri Iesu Christi. Nostis patientiâ, nostis humilitatę, no stis charitatę, &c. Domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: Therefore it is not in vain that the Apostle says to the Corinthians here: "You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ." So in other matters also necessary to true piety we must say: "You know the gentleness of our Lord Jesus Christ. You know His patience, you know His humility, you know His love," and so on, "of our Lord Jesus Christ."

units.la: QVOD propter uos, inquit, pauper fa- stus est, cum esset diues, ut uos illius pauperta te ditésceretis.) Hęc est gratia domini nostri Ie su Christi, quã si penitius inspexissent Corin- thij, nô habuissent opus admonitione Aposto lica. Tria dicit. Primum, quod Christus cum diues esset, factus fit pauper. Secũdũ, propter quos. Tertiũ ad quid. Quod pauper factus est, inquit, cum esset diues. Diues erat tanquã uni genitus Dei, & hæres omnium. Pauper factus est, nô amittêdo diuitias suas, sed non utendo. Cũ dominus esset omniũ, factus est omniũ ser uus, uenies in mundũ, ut nô ministraretur sibi, sed ut ipse ministraret omnibus. Cũ ius habe- ret omniũ quæ in cœlo sunt & in terra, à pos- sessioe & usu illorũ ad tępus abstinuit, usque adeo, ut minus possideret in terra, q̃ uulpes ac uolucres cœli. Sic.n. Matt. 8. dicit: Vulpes fo- ueas habet, & uolucres cœli nidos, filius autê hominis nô habet, ubi caput suũ reclinet. Pa- rentũ ipsius, natalium, educationis, & conditio- nis humilitas singulare paupertatê ostêdit. Sic exinaniuit semetipsum sumpta forma serui, u- nâ cũ summa humilitate, ac paupertate. Inte- rea tamen omniũ erat ditissimus in ipsa etiam paupertate cõstitutus, ut multo uerius ipsi cô- petat illud, quasi pauperes, multos tamê ditan tes, ut nihil habêtes, & tamê omnia possidêtes q̃ Paulo. Pauper factus est. Propter quos? Pro- pter uos, inqt. Quare nô dicit in gne, propter nos oës? An ,ppter Corinthios tãtû factus est pauper xps? Dũ generalê Christi gratiã Corin thijs specialiter applicat, nô facit hoc, ut cæte- ris ea fidelib. auferat, istis uerò solis deputet, sed ut seruiat causæ quâ agit. Fortius urget si beneficiũ Christi cõsideretur, non ut generale est omniũ, sed ut in nos specialiter est collatũ. Si audias sic dilexisse Deũ hûc mundũ, ut uni- genitũ suũ daret, tãtû efficaciæ ad cõmouêdũ animũ nô senties, quãtũ experiris, si absq; ulla dubitatione cũ Apostolo de beneficio Christi dicas: Qui dilexit me, ac tradidit semetipsum pro me. Hoc consilio Apost. maluit hic dicere, qd propter uos, q̃, qd propter nos oës pauper faƈt9 est, quo uidelicet gratiâ hác psius cõside- rátes, efficaci9 ad imitationẽ illi9 ꝑmoueretur VT uos, inqt, illi9 paupertate ditésceretis.) Hoc est, nô ut uos quoq; pauperes essetis, sed ut p ipsi9 paupertatê ditésceretis. Sic exprimit ad quid pauper factus fit Christus. Nô hęret in eodem paupertatis, ac diuitiarũ geniere. Pau- pertatem tribuit Christo, nô spiritualem, quæ opposita fit spiritualib. diuitijs, sed terrenâ: di- uitias uerò tribuit fidelib. Christi, paupertate ipsius partas, non terrenas, quæ oppositæ sint terrenæ ipsius paupertati, sed spirituales. Spiritualis paupertas locum in Christo habere non potuit. Et si habuisset, neminē prorsus spiritualiter ditasset. Habuit uerò terrena, quæ spiritualēs diuitias non excludit. Rursus terrenas diuitias fidelib.suis assumpta terrena paupertate, nec quæsiuit, nec suppeditauit, quæ nō sunt hę dignæ cœlesti gratia, & uocatione, nec reddūt homines uere felices, sed spirituales, quibus ditati felices sint in sempiternum. Quare Christi paupertate non sunt partę opes illæ pontificū, episcoporum, cardinalium, & cæterorū prælatorū, quamuis locum hunc Apostoli sibi potisimum competere putant, quasi propter ipsos pauper fit factū Christus, ut ipsi terrenis regum ac principū opibus abundent in hoc sæculo. Non possunt hæc de Christo sine grandi illius contumelia dici, nō minus q; si dicant: Christus factus est pro nobis humilis, ut nos simus sublimes & elati in hoc sæculo. Christus factus est sub lege, ut nos absq; lege uiuamus omnium liberrimè. Christus factus est pro nobis Deo patri obediens, ut nos nec Deo, nec hominib. obedeamus. Christus pro nobis omnis generis afflictiones, ac tentationes subiuit, ut nos in omnis generis uoluptatibus ac delicijs uiuamus. Adiungant & illud: Christus pro nobis ascendit ad cœlos, ut nos descendamus in ignem æternum. Verum relictis illis, inspiciamus mentem Apostoli.
units.tr: "That though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich." This is the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, which the Corinthians would not have needed an apostolic admonition about if they had looked into it more deeply. He says three things. First, that Christ, though He was rich, became poor. Second, for whose sake. Third, for what end. That He became poor, he says, though He was rich. He was rich as the only-begotten Son of God and heir of all things. He became poor not by losing His riches but by not using them. Though He was Lord of all, He became the servant of all; coming into the world, He was not ministered to but came to minister to all. Though He had a right to all that is in heaven and on earth, He abstained for a time from the possession and use of them, so much so that He possessed less on earth than the foxes and birds of the heavens. For thus Matthew 8 says: "Foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head." The lowliness of His parents, His birth, His upbringing and His condition show singular poverty. So He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, together with the greatest humility and poverty. Yet in that very poverty He was the richest of all, so that it applies to Him far more truly than to Paul: "as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing all things." He became poor. For whose sake? For your sake, he says. Why does he not say, "for our sake, all of us"? Did Christ become poor only for the sake of the Corinthians? When he applies the general grace of Christ specially to the Corinthians, he does not do so to take it away from the other faithful and assign it to these alone, but to serve the cause he is pleading. It urges more strongly if the benefit of Christ is considered not as general to all, but as conferred on us specifically. If you hear that God so loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son, you will not feel as much power to move your heart as you will if, without any doubt, you say with the Apostle of Christ's benefit: "who loved me and gave himself for me." For this reason the Apostle preferred to say here "for your sake" rather than "for all of us," so that, considering this grace of His, they might be more effectively moved to imitate it. "So that you," he says, "by his poverty might become rich." That is, not so that you also should be poor, but that you might become rich through His poverty. Thus he expresses for what purpose Christ became poor. He does not cling to the same kind of poverty and riches. He ascribes to Christ a poverty that is not spiritual, which is opposed to spiritual riches, but earthly; and he ascribes to the faithful of Christ riches gained through His poverty, not earthly ones, which are opposed to His earthly poverty, but spiritual ones. Spiritual poverty could not have a place in Christ; and if it had, He would have enriched no one spiritually at all. But He had earthly poverty, which does not exclude spiritual riches. Again, by taking on earthly poverty He neither sought nor supplied earthly riches to His faithful, which are not worthy of heavenly grace and calling and do not make men truly happy, but spiritual riches, by which those enriched are happy forever. Therefore the wealth of the popes, bishops, cardinals and the other prelates is not gained from Christ's poverty, although they think this passage especially belongs to them, as if Christ became poor for their sake, so that they might abound in the earthly riches of kings and princes in this age. These things cannot be said of Christ without great dishonour to Him, no less than if they were to say: "Christ became lowly for us, so that we might be lofty and exalted in this age. Christ became subject to the law, so that we might live most freely without law. Christ became obedient to God the Father for us, so that we might obey neither God nor men. Christ for us underwent every kind of affliction and temptation, so that we might live in every kind of pleasure and delight." Let them add this too: "Christ for us ascended into heaven, so that we might descend into eternal fire." But setting those things aside, let us look at the mind of the Apostle.

units.la: Poterat gratiā Christi, quæ multifaria est, sub alia specie, quām paupertatis ac diuitiarū proponere, utpote Christus uenit in hūc mundum, ut nos ad cœlos euheret, uel, Christus factus est pro nobis filius hominis, ut nos filios Dei efficeret: uel: Christus mortuus est pro nobis, ut nos per ipsum uiuamus, & quæ alia multa eiusmodi adferri poterant, quę omnia species quædam sunt generalis Christi gratiæ, uerū prudenti consilio eam illius speciem proposuit, quę coueniret causæ quam agebat. Erat Corinthij diuites charismatū spiritualiū. Eas diuitias acceperat beneficio Christi. Erat iuxta sæculum quoq; diuites. Conabatur eos inducere, ut pauperes sanctos, qui Hierosolymis erant, liberali cōtributione iuuarent. Itaq; ne paupertatis gratia, diuites ipsi cōtemnerēt pauperes sanctos, proponit ipsis paupertatem Christi, cum illius ratione & utilitate, quo admonerētur, uenerandā esse, nō contemnēdam sanctorum paupertatem, idq;duplici nomine, primū propter Christū, qui pro ipsis factus sit pauper, deinde, propter utilitatē, quam ex illius paupertate fuerant consequuti. Duabus hisce rationibus admonemur & nos, ne populum domini pauperē & egenum propter paupertatis despectū cōtemnamus, quę fors solet esse pauperū in hoc sæculo, iuxta illud: Nil habet infœlix paupertas duri⁹ in se, quām quod ridiculos homines facit. Magna paupertatis utilitas, ex Christo & apostolis redijt ad genus humanum. Contra maxima detrimenta, cūm pietatis, tum felicitatis prouenerunt ex opulentia Antichristi, ac fallorū illius apostolorū.
units.tr: Christ's grace, which is manifold, could have been set forth under some other aspect than that of poverty and riches. For example: Christ came into this world to raise us up to heaven; or, Christ was made the Son of man for us, that he might make us sons of God; or, Christ died for us, that we might live through him. Many other statements of this kind could also have been adduced. All of them are certain general aspects of Christ's grace, but with prudent judgment he set forth that aspect which suited the cause he was pleading. The Corinthians were rich in spiritual gifts, and they had received those riches by the benefit of Christ. They were also rich according to the world. He was trying to induce them to help the poor saints at Jerusalem with a generous contribution. So that the grace of poverty would not lead the rich themselves to despise the poor saints, he sets before them the poverty of Christ, together with its reason and usefulness, so that they would be admonished that the poverty of the saints is to be honoured and not despised. He gives a double reason: first, on account of Christ, who became poor for their sake; second, on account of the benefit they obtained from his poverty. By these two reasons we too are admonished not to despise the Lord's people, who are poor and needy, on account of their poverty, which is usually the lot of the poor in this world, according to the saying: "Unhappy poverty has nothing harsher in it than that it makes men ridiculous." Great benefit for the human race has come from Christ and the apostles through poverty. On the other hand, the greatest losses, both to piety and to happiness, have come from the wealth of Antichrist and of his false apostles.

units.la: Dices. Ecquomodo terrena Christi pauper tas spirituales nobis peperit diuitias? Respondeo. Non ex eo quod pauper est factus, sed ex eo quod pro nobis pauper est factus, quo nobis seruiret in carne humili, cūm docendo ac mirabilia operando, tum mortem pro peccatis nostris subeundo. Per paupertatem enim illius subintelligenda uenit, tota suscepta pro nobis dispensationis humilitas.
units.tr: You will ask: how did Christ's earthly poverty bring us spiritual riches? I answer: not from the fact that he became poor, but from the fact that he became poor for us, so that he might serve us in lowly flesh, both by teaching and working miracles, and by undergoing death for our sins. For through his poverty is to be understood the whole humility of the dispensation he took up for us.

units.la: Comunis locus hic est, extra Christū totum genus humanū, ueris esse diuitijs destitutum, ac omnimodæ perditioni obnoxiū: eos uero solos esse reuera diuites, qui ditati sunt à dño, & in dño. Deinde terrena paupertate nemini esse Christiano probrosam, propter pauperē Christum, qui sua paupertate paupertatem fidelium suorum consecrauit, & à contemptu uindicauit. Quod tandē ecclesię potētia ac diuitijs excellere cœperūt: quemadmodū id factū est præter consilium domini, ita male etiam cesit. Vnde illud Hieron. est, in uita Malchi capiui monachi, postquam ecclesia ad Christia nos principes uenit, potentia quidem & diuitijs maior, uirtutibus uero minor est facta.
units.tr: This is a commonplace: apart from Christ, the whole human race is destitute of true riches and liable to every kind of ruin, and only those are truly rich who have been enriched by the Lord and in the Lord. Next, earthly poverty is shameful to no Christian, on account of poor Christ, who by his own poverty consecrated the poverty of his faithful people and rescued it from contempt. As for the fact that the Church began to excel in power and riches, just as this happened beyond the counsel of the Lord, so it has also turned out badly. Hence that saying of Jerome, in the Life of Malchus the captive monk: "After the Church came to Christian princes, it became greater indeed in power and riches, but lesser in virtues."

units.la: ET consiliū in hoc do, inquit, nā hoc uobis conducit: qui quidē non solum facere, uerumetiā uelle iam cœpistis anno superiore, &c.) In hoc, inquit, negocio non imperō, sed consulo, non cogo, sed prouoco, quia non inuitos, sed uoluntarios requiro. Dicet quisquā, ubi consiliū datur, ibi nō est obediendi necessitas, sed uel obed³diʼ, uel nō obediendi libertas. Ergo charitatis synceritas, quā in Corinthijs comprobare cupiebat Apostolus, ex rebus liberis est, quæ sine culpa tā possunt nō haberi, quām haberi. Quid igitur est qd' dominus præcipit, dices: Hoc est præceptū meū, ut diligatis uos inuicē? An non hoc præcepto synceritate ueŗ charitatis requirit? Respondeo. Non loquitur hic Apost. de ipsa charitatis synceritate in se, cum dicit: Et consiliū in hoc do, sed sicuti sequētia docent de perficiēda cōtributione. Ad hāc hortaturus dicit se illis non imperare, sed consiliū dare. Simul tamen cauendū est, ne putemus consilium Apostoli sine culpa ac noxia posse à fidelibus contēni. Licet enim uim præcepti nō adæquet cōsiliū, quod attinet ipsam consulentis Apostoli moderatione: peccat tamen quisquis illud contemnit, & saluti suę admodū male consulit, qui nihil sibi faciendum ducit, nisi ad quod expresso mandato astringitur. Nec fieri potest, ut præceptis ex animo obediat, qui consilia salubria secure cōtemnit.
units.tr: "And I give counsel in this matter," he says, "for this is profitable for you, who indeed began a year ago not only to do but also to will," etc. "In this matter," he says, "I do not command but advise; I do not compel but urge, because I seek not unwilling but willing givers." Someone will say: where counsel is given, there is no necessity of obeying, but only the freedom either to obey or not to obey. Therefore the sincerity of love, which the Apostle wished to prove in the Corinthians, belongs to things that are free, and which can be had or not had without fault. What then, you will ask, does the Lord command when he says: "This is my commandment, that you love one another"? Does he not require sincerity of true love by this command? I answer: the Apostle is not speaking here of the sincerity of love in itself when he says, "And I give counsel in this matter," but of bringing the contribution to completion, as the following words show. He says that he is urging them, and that he is not commanding them but giving counsel. At the same time we must take care not to think that the Apostle's counsel can be despised by the faithful without fault and harm. For although the counsel does not have the force of a precept, as far as the Apostle's own moderation in advising is concerned, nevertheless whoever despises it sins, and gives very poor counsel to his own salvation, who considers nothing to be done unless he is bound by an express command. Nor can one obey the precepts from the heart if he carelessly despises wholesome counsel.

units.la: NAM hoc uobis coducit, inquit.) Q.d. Cōsuledo uobis, nō tām aliorū cōmodum, q; uestrā salutē spectō. Ergo qui cōsulit fidelibus, ut largiter cōtribuant, ad succurrendū necessitatibus pauperū, consulit ipsorum utilitati, licet pauperū cōmodis cōfulere uideatur. Quid.n. cōsulit aliud, quàm, qd Christus dixit, ut paret sibi amicos, quorū gratia recipiantur in æterna tabernacula: atq; terrenas opes in cœlestes thesauros conuertat, ut haud immerito dicat
units.tr: "For this is profitable for you," he says. That is: I advise you, looking less to the advantage of others than to your own salvation. Therefore whoever advises the faithful to contribute liberally to relieve the needs of the poor, advises their own benefit, although he seems to be advising the advantage of the poor. For what else does he counsel than what Christ said, that they should make for themselves friends, through whom they may be received into the eternal tabernacles, and turn earthly wealth into heavenly treasures? So the Apostle rightly says:

units.la: hic Apostolus:Nam hoc uobis conducit.Emphasis est in pronomine VOBIS. Quasi dicat: magis quàm illis quibus estis daturi.
units.tr: "For this is profitable for you." The emphasis is on the pronoun YOU: as if he said, "more than for those to whom you are going to give."

units.la: QVI quidè non solù facere, inquit,uerumetiã uelle iam coepistis anno superiore.) Erat quidè hoc in illis repræhésibile, quod bonum opus intermiserat, cuius tamé anno superiore initiù fecerant, id quod manifestum habebat inconstantiæ argumentum, uerum nó erat in eo Apost. ut inconstantiâ eorum reprehenderet,sed ut quod coeptum erat ad perfectionem perduceretur. Huc usurpat non modò exépla Macedonum,& ipsius Christi, sed & ipsorum præiudiciû,quo & facto, & uoluntate iam antea testati fuerant, esse contributionem hanc in usus sanctorû faciendam. Huius eos admonens,dicit:Nam hoc uobis conducit, qui quidem iam antea non solum facere,uerumetiam uelle coepistis anno superiore. Q.d. Quid opus aliorû exemplis in causa,quâ ipsi,& piâ,& uobis utilé esse,iam antea declarastis, dum anno superiore non modò cóntribuere, sed & ad còtribuêdum uoluntarij esse coepistis ? Exi-stimo autem hoc factum esse post priorem epistolâ. Nam in illa cap. ult. quædam de collecta hac faciêda scripserat, quibus lectis,uerosimile est eos confestim cótribuere coepisse, at in coepto non perstitisse,quemadmodum solet, qui non ἀυταιρέλοι aliquid facere incipiunt,sed aliorum hortatu inducti.
units.tr: "Who indeed began a year ago not only to do but also to will." Indeed this was blameworthy in them, that they had abandoned a good work which they had begun the year before; and this was a clear proof of inconstancy. But the Apostle's purpose was not to reprove their inconstancy, but to bring to completion what had been begun. For this he uses not only the examples of the Macedonians and of Christ himself, but also their own former judgment, by which, both in deed and in will, they had earlier shown that this contribution ought to be made for the use of the saints. Admonishing them of this, he says: "For this is profitable for you, you who indeed began a year ago not only to do but also to will." That is: why need examples of others in a cause which you yourselves have already shown to be both pious and useful to you, since a year ago you began not only to contribute but also to be willing to contribute? I think, moreover, that this happened after the earlier letter. For in its last chapter he had written something about this collection to be made; and when they had read it, it is likely that they at once began to contribute, but did not persevere in what they had begun, as happens with those who begin something not of their own accord [αὐθαίρετοι] but urged on by the exhortation of others.

units.la: Quid est autem quod dicit,qui nô solum facere,sed & uelle iam coepistis ? An prius est facere,quàm uelle? Legitimo quidè ordine prius est uelle, quàm facere:uerum frequenter accidit, ut faciamus quod nolumus, quodq; non delectat ubi uoluntas,nec præcedit factû, nec sequitur.Nonnunquam etiam usuuenit, ut factû sequatur uoluntas, & approbans illud, & continuâs,sicuti fieri uidemus in adolescentibus,qui literis operâ dare coacti,faciût id quidem,sed aliquandiu nolentes, donec tandem literarum dulcedine capti, quod antea inuiti fecerant,uolentes facere incipiât,& studia sua cum delectatione prosequantur: uerùm quod præsente causam attinet, Corinthij nô modò contribuere coeperant anno superiore, sed & uelle,hoc est, contribuerant non inuiti,sed uolentes,atq; ita factum suum uoluntate approbauerant. Huius eos admonens dicit,qui quidem non solum facere, sed & uelle iam antea coepistis anno superiore. Minus habet leuitatis mutare factum,ad quod non accessit uoluntas,id uerò admodum leue est,si in causa bona nô factum modò,sed & uoluntas, quæ factum approbauerat, mutetur. Animus in bono constans quod uelle ac facere coepit,nec uelle,nec facere definit donec perficiatûr. Quod si à facto impeditur,uoluntate tamen faciendi constanter retinet, donec faciendi facultatem recipiat.Hæc erant,meo iudicio, de quibus Corinthios Apostolus hisce uerbis admonere uoluit. Vnde & subijcit:
units.tr: But what does he mean by saying, "you who have begun not only to do, but also to will"? Is doing before willing? In the proper order, willing comes before doing. Yet it often happens that we do what we do not want to do, and what does not please us: the will neither precedes the deed nor follows it. Sometimes, too, the will follows the deed, approving it and continuing in it, as we see in young people who are forced to devote themselves to their studies. They do so, but at first unwillingly, until at last, captured by the sweetness of letters, they begin to will what they had earlier done against their inclination, and pursue their studies with delight. But as far as the present matter is concerned, the Corinthians had not only begun to contribute the year before, but also to will it. That is, they had contributed not unwillingly but willingly, and so by their will they had approved what they did. Admonishing them of this, he says, "you who have begun not only to do, but also to will, last year." It is less fickle to change a deed to which the will has not joined itself, but it is truly very fickle if, in a good cause, not only the deed but also the will that approved the deed is changed. A mind constant in good begins to will and to do, and it ceases neither to will nor to do until the work is finished. If it is hindered from the deed, it nevertheless steadfastly keeps the will to do, until it receives the opportunity to act. These, in my judgment, were the things about which the Apostle wished to admonish the Corinthians in these words. Hence he adds:

units.la: NVNC uero & illud quod facere coepistis,
units.tr: "NOW, indeed, also perform the doing of what you have begun,"

units.la: perficite,inquit.) Græcè sic, ῥωνὶ ἢ χαὶ τὸ ποιῆσαι ἐπιτελέσαι. i. nunc uero & facere perficite. Quasi dicat, nûc uobis incûbit, ut quod uelle coepistis,etiam facto perficiatis. Non simpliciter dicit, ῥωνὶ ἢ τὸ ποιῆσαι ἐπιτελέσαι,id est,nunc autem facere perficite,sed adiecta copula, ῥωνὶ ἢ χαὶ τὸ ποιῆσαι. i. nunc autem etiam facere perficite,ubi subintelligendû est, quod uelle coepistis. Vulgatus interpres habet: nûc uero & facto perficite. Nô displiceret,si in Græco esset, χαὶ τῷ ποιῆσαι. i.& faciedo, quemadmodum ille legisse uidetur. Hortatur itaque eos ut bonum opus,quod & facere, & uelle coeperant,faciendo perficiant. Volûtas quidem pro facto coram Deo accipitur, si desit faciendi facultas : uerum ubi illa uolêtem non destituit, ibi non probatur inefficax, & ignaua uoluntas. Cû ergo nihil impediret Corinthios,quo minus quod & facere,& uelle coeperant,perficerent,rectè admonentur ab Apostolo, ut quod bene coeperant,perficiant.
units.tr: Perform it, he says. In Greek it reads: νῦν δὲ καὶ τὸ ποιῆσαι ἐπιτελέσαι [nun de kai to poiēsai epitelesai], that is, "now also to perform the doing." It is as if he said: now it is incumbent on you that, just as you began to want it, you also complete it by deed. He does not simply say "now to perform the doing" (that is, "now perform the doing"), but adds the conjunction, "now also to perform the doing," where "what you began to wish" must be understood. The Vulgate translator has: "now also perform it by deed." It would not be objectionable if the Greek had καὶ τῷ ποιῆσαι [kai tō poiēsai], that is, "and by doing," as he seems to have read it. He therefore urges them to complete by doing the good work that they had begun both to wish and to do. Before God, the will is indeed accepted in place of the deed when the ability to act is lacking; but where the will does not fail, it is not approved as an ineffective and idle will. Since nothing hindered the Corinthians from completing what they had begun both to wish and to do, the Apostle rightly admonishes them to finish what they had well begun.

units.la: VT quemadmodû uolûtas própta fuit,inquit, ita & perficiatis ex eo quo potestis.) In Græco sic legitur: ὅπως χαλάσωμεν ἡ προθυμία τὸ θέλειν, ὥσως χαὶ τὸ ἐπιτελέσαι τῶν ἐχ τοῦ χειν, ubi omnino deest prepositio ἐκ, id qd' uel in Chrysostomo uideri poterat,qui sic legit: ὅπως χαὶ ἀπὸ ἢ προθυμία ἐκ τοῦ θέλειν, ὥσως χαὶ τὸ ποιῆσαι ἐκ τῆς ἐχεω.i. Vt quemadmodû animi propensio ex uoluntate, ita & factum ex facultate. Vbi nos habemus τὸ ἐπιτελέσαι, ibi legit ille τὸ ποιῆσαι. Sensus igitur est. Quod iâ antea uoluistis,faciêdo quoq; perficite, ut quemadmodû animi propensionem uolêdo declaraftis, ita & perfectione operis ex eo qd' habetis ac posidetis, declaretis. Sic puto manifestû esse, corruptâ nos habere lectione in Græco,ubi legimus: τὸ θέλειν, pro ἐκ τοῦ θέλειν. Non simpliciter dicit: ὅπως χαλάσωμεν ἡ προθυμία ἐκ τοῦ θέλειν, ὥσως χαὶ τὸ ἐπιτελέσαι ἐκ τοῦ ποιῆσαι. i. ut quemadmodû ex uolûtate est animi propensio, & alacritas, ita fit & perfectio operis ex facto, sed, ita fit & perfectio ἐκ τῆς ἐχεω.i.ex eo quod habetis. Hoc dicens cauet ne immoderatâ, ac nimiâ contributione, quæ facultates ipsorû excedat,poscere uideatur.Et id in sequetibus fusius explicat. Interim tamé admonet eos tacitè, perfectione eleemosynæ nô esse simpliciter ex qualicûq; cótributione, sed ex tali, quę facultatib.respôdeat, ut quemadmodû nô requritur nimia,ita & probáda non fit ea, quæ minor est,q; ut facultati dâtis respôdeat. Et hæc ratio non in eleemosyna tantum, sed & in cæteris bonis est operibus spectâda. Bonû opus nô perficitur simpliciter,& utcûq; faciendo,sed faciendo pro uiribus.Qui minus facit quá ꝓ uiriib. palâ testatur facere se non ex animi proptitudine, sed obiter ac pfunctorie: atq; ita bonû opus nô perficit, qa factû ipsius & proptitudine destituitur, & ad metâ facultatis non pertingit.Quare admodum prudenter Apost.ut secundû uolûtate animi propensione, ita secûdû facultate operis perfectione metitur.Sic.n.nec grauat tenuiores, poscedo plura,quam ra quàm præstare posint, nec approbat tenaciores, poscedo minus, quàm pro facultatum ipsorum mensura contribuere queant.
units.tr: "As the readiness of mind was present, so also let the completion be from what you have," he says. In Greek it reads: ὅπως καθάπερ ἡ προθυμία τὸ θέλειν, οὕτως καὶ τὸ ἐπιτελέσαι τῶν ἐκ τοῦ ἔχειν [hopōs kathaper hē prothumia to thelein, houtōs kai to epitelesai tōn ek tou echein], where the preposition ἐκ is wholly lacking. This might seem to be found in Chrysostom, who reads: ὅπως καθάπερ ἀπὸ ἡ προθυμία ἐκ τοῦ θέλειν, οὕτως καὶ τὸ ποιῆσαι ἐκ τῆς ἐξεως [hopōs kathaper apo hē prothumia ek tou thelein, houtōs kai to poiēsai ek tēs hexeōs], that is, "as the eagerness of mind comes from the will, so also the deed comes from the ability." Where we have τὸ ἐπιτελέσαι [to epitelesai], that writer reads τὸ ποιῆσαι [to poiēsai]. The sense, then, is this: just as you have already shown by wanting it, so also complete it by doing, so that as you have declared the eagerness of your mind by willing, so you may also declare the completion of the work from what you have and possess. So I think it is clear that our Greek text is corrupt where we read τὸ θέλειν [to thelein] in place of ἐκ τοῦ θέλειν [ek tou thelein]. He does not simply say: "as the eagerness of mind comes from the will, so also completion of the work comes from the deed," but "so also completion comes ἐκ τῆς ἕξεως [ek tēs hexeōs], that is, from what you have." In saying this he guards against seeming to demand an immoderate and excessive contribution that would exceed their means. He explains this more fully in what follows. Meanwhile, however, he tacitly warns them that the completion of almsgiving does not consist in any contribution whatever, but in one that corresponds to their resources. Just as an excessive gift is not required, so a gift smaller than their means allow is not to be approved. This principle must be observed not only in almsgiving but in all good works. A good work is not completed simply by doing it in any way at all, but by doing it according to one's strength. Whoever does less than his strength allows clearly shows that he does it not from eagerness of mind, but casually and perfunctorily; and so such a work is not completed, because it lacks both its doer's eagerness and does not reach the measure of his ability. Therefore the Apostle very wisely measures the completion of the work by the readiness of mind in the will and by the means of the one who works. Thus he neither burdens the poorer by demanding more than they can give, nor approves the more tight-fisted by demanding less than they could give according to the measure of their resources.

units.la: ETENIM, inquit, si prius adsit animi promptitudo, ea iuxta, quicquid illud est, quod possidet aliquis accepta est, nō iuxta id quod non possidet.) Reddit rationem eius quod perfectionem eleemosynę mesura facultatis terminans dixit, ita sit & perfectio, secundū id quod habetis. Et est sensus. Vbi enim animi propensio in propatulo est (hoc significat <bl>εἰς προθυμίαν προκείμενον</bl>) est illa accepta & grata, secundū id qd quis habet, ac præstare potest, nec supra illud poscitur amplius quicquā. Sic requiruntur hæc tria in eleemosyna, velle, posse, dare. Tertiū sine medio non requiritur, sine primo non probatur: Primum probatur sine tertio, ac sufficit, si desit secundum. In secundo mensura tertij consistit. Vide autē prudentiā Apostoli. Quamuis perfectio eleemosynæ non solum ultra uires nihil poscit, sed & liberalitate requirit uirib. respondente, de posteriori tamē nullā facit mentionē, quoniā molestum, & cū sinistra suspitione cōiunctum fuisset, sed in eo qd acceptius erat consistens inculcat, non requirit plura, q cuiusq; possit præstare facultas. Ideo nō contētus eo quod dixit, iuxta id qd quis possidet accepta est, addit, nō iuxta id quod non possidet. Quantū aut quisq; possideat cōscientijs illorū relinquit. Nec determinat quantū de quāto sit dandū: sed simpliciter monet, non requiri multum ab eo qui parum possidet, sed acceptū esse munus, qd & promptò aio detur, & dantis facultatē non excedat
units.tr: "For if the readiness of mind is present first," he says, "it is accepted according to whatever a person possesses, not according to what he does not possess." He gives the reason for what he said, that the completion of almsgiving is limited by the measure of one's means: "so also the completion, according to what you have." The sense is this: where readiness of mind is set before them (this is what the Greek εἰς προθυμίαν προκείμενον [eis prothumian prokeimenon] signifies), it is accepted and pleasing according to what someone has and is able to give, and nothing further is demanded beyond that. Thus three things are required in almsgiving: willingness, ability, and giving. The third is not required without the first, and the first is not approved without the third. The first is approved without the third, and it suffices if the second is lacking. The measure of the third depends on the second. See the Apostle's prudence here. Although the completion of almsgiving not only demands nothing beyond one's strength, but requires a generosity that matches one's strength, he makes no mention of the latter, since it would have been burdensome and linked with a sinister suspicion. Instead, he dwells on what was more acceptable and presses it home: he does not require more than each person's means can supply. So, not content with saying "accepted according to what someone possesses," he adds "not according to what he does not possess." He leaves to each person's conscience how much he possesses. Nor does he set how much should be given out of how much; he simply advises that much is not required of one who has little, but that a gift is acceptable if it is given with a ready mind and does not exceed the giver's means.

units.la: Non enim ut alijs sit relaxatio, uobis autē angustia, sed ut ex æquabilitate in præsenti tēpore uestra copia illorū succurrat inopię, & illorū copia uestrae succurrat inopiæ, ut fiat æquabilitas, quē admodum scriptū est: Qui multū habebat, huic nihil superfuit, & qui paululum habebat, is nihilominus habuit.
units.tr: "For it is not that others may have relief while you have hardship, but that by equality, in the present time, your abundance may supply their want, and their abundance may supply your want, so that there may be equality, as it is written: He who had gathered much had nothing left over, and he who had gathered little had no lack."

units.la: Quare nō requiratur eleemosyna, quæ mesuram possessæ facultatis excedat, istis uerbis primum declarat, deinde subijcit qualis requiratur. Accepta est, inquit, animi propensio, secundum id quod quis possidet, nō secundū id quod nō possidet. Quare nō secundū id quod quis non possidet? Quia nō hoc requiritur, inquit, ut alijs sit relaxatio, uobis autē angustia. Hoc est, non talis quæritur contributio, quæ sanctis Hierosolymis agentibus pro sua copia quietem gignat, ac relaxatione molestiarum: uos uero grauet, propterea qd ultra uires deteritis, & usibus uestris quæ necessaria sunt detraxeritis, ut tribulationem incurratis.
units.tr: By these words he first makes clear why an almsgiving that exceeds the measure of one's means is not required, and then he adds what kind is required. "The readiness of mind is accepted," he says, "according to what someone possesses, not according to what he does not possess." Why not according to what someone does not possess? Because this is not what is required, he says, "that others may have relief while you have hardship." That is, the kind of contribution sought is not one that, out of its means, brings rest and relief from troubles to the saints at Jerusalem, while burdening you, because you would spend beyond your strength and take away what is necessary for your own use, so that you would fall into tribulation.

units.la: Dicet quisquam: Si talis eleemosyna non quæritur, quare paulo supra Macedones ea ob causam laudauit, quod supra uires propti fuerint ad dandum. Respondeo. Aliud est, non requirere, & aliud, si non quæsitum fiat, laudare.
units.tr: Someone may object: if such an almsgiving is not sought, why did he praise the Macedonians a little above for this very reason, that they were eager to give beyond their strength? I reply: it is one thing not to require, and another thing to praise when something is done that was not asked for.

units.la: Inhumanū uidetur hoc requirere à quopiam, ut quibus ipse opus habet, alijs largiatur, quo illi lautè uiuant, ipse autem interim cum fame luctetur, ac miserè uiuat. Et tamen si quis hoc ex abundantia charitatis fecerit, quis non laudet? A Macedonibus nunquā requisiuit Apostolus, ut tantū daret, quantū suapte spōte dederunt, ubi dederūt ultrò singulare illorū charitatem laudauit. Quis ausus fuisset unquā petere hoc à diuina Maiestate, ut filius Dei pauper fieret pro nobis, quo nos illius paupertate ditescerēmus? Nemo hoc sine gradi impudentia ac diuinæ Maiestatis iniuria, peti posse iudicasset. Et tamē cum ultrò sit à filio Dei factū, quis fideliū non supra omnes cœlos extol lit? quis satis celebrare poterit? Quod itaq; dicit Apost. nō ut alijs sit relaxatio, uobis autem angustia, nō sic dicit, ut inde colligēdū sit, esse culpabile factū, si quis sic seruiat alijs, ut ipse sibi molest: á ascisçat, quo alijs cōmode uiuere liceat, cū id laudis potius habeat materiā, sed, quod nequeat tale quid citra pudorem peti à quoquam. Sic multa fiunt in rebus humanis, quæ nemo facile petat, uel cuiquam suadeat, & tamen, ubi facta sunt, impense laudantur.
units.tr: It seems inhuman to ask someone to give to others what he himself needs, so that they may live in comfort while he struggles with hunger and lives wretchedly. And yet if someone does this out of an abundance of love, who would not praise him? The Apostle never asked the Macedonians to give as much as they gave of their own accord; when they gave freely, he praised their exceptional love. Who would ever have dared to ask of the divine Majesty that the Son of God should become poor for us, so that we might be enriched by his poverty? No one would have judged that this could be asked without great shamelessness and an injury to the divine Majesty. And yet, since it was done of his own accord by the Son of God, what faithful person does not exalt him above all the heavens? Who could celebrate it sufficiently? So when the Apostle says, "not that others may have relief while you have hardship," he does not say this so that one may infer that it is a blameworthy act if someone serves others to the point of making himself miserable, in order that others may live comfortably. That would rather be a matter for praise. Rather, he means that such a thing cannot be asked of anyone without shame. Many things are done in human affairs that no one would easily ask for, or advise anyone to do; yet when they have been done, they are highly praised.

units.la: SED ut ex æquabilitate, inquit, in præsenti tempore, uestra copia illorū succurrat inopiç, & illorum copia uestræ succurrat inopiæ.) Vt nihil iniqui peti significet, limitat usum eleemosynæ & contributionis æquabilitate, quæ si uspiā, certe inter Christianos, tanquā fratres ac filios Dei, locum habere debet. Sed ut ex æquabilitate, inquit. Repetendū est illud <bl>ἵνα</bl> ex præcedēnti particula, ac legendum <bl>ἀλλὰ ἵνα ἐξ ἰσότητος</bl>. i. Sed ut ex æquabilitate. Alias in Greco est, <bl>ἀλλ' ἐξ ἰσότητος</bl>, id est, Sed ex æquabilitate. Est autem hic, ex æquabilitate, nihil aliud, quàm ex studio æquabilitatis.
units.tr: But that there may be equality, he says, in the present time, your abundance may succour their want, and their abundance may succour your want. To show that nothing unfair is sought, he limits the practice of almsgiving and contribution by equality, which, if it has a place anywhere, ought certainly to hold among Christians as brothers and sons of God. But he says, "that there may be equality" [ἀλλὰ ἵνα ἐξ ἰσότητος]. The "ἵνα" must be carried over from the preceding particle, and one should read "ἀλλὰ ἵνα ἐξ ἰσότητος", that is, "But that there may be equality." Elsewhere the Greek reads "ἀλλ' ἐξ ἰσότητος", that is, "But out of equality." Here "out of equality" means nothing other than "out of zeal for equality."

units.la: IN præsenti tépore, inquit.) Particula hæc aliter atq; aliter accipitur. Alij referūt eā ad tēpus præsentis uitę, hoc sensu, Vestra copia quā habetis in præsenti tépore, quasi qd in Græco est legēdū sit ad hūc modū: <bl>τὸ ὑμῶν περισσεῦμα ὁ ἐν τῷ νῦν καιρῷ, cū sit, ἐν τῇ νῦν καιρῷ τὸ ὑμῶν περισσεῦμα.</bl> Sane sic quidem habet præsentis sæculi cursus, ut in illo alius abūdet opibus, alius penuria premutur, uerū Apost. huc nō spectauit. Alij referūt ad id temporis, in quo Apost. hæc scripsit, & sancti in ecclesia Hierosolymitana, & Iudææ magna famis molestia premebātur. Et hic mihi sensus magis probatur. Voluit. n. Corinthios habere ratione præsentis calamitatis, ac simul innuit cōtributionē illā, quadescribebat, nō sic posci, ut sit perpetua, sed ut præsenti dūtaxat necessitāti sanctorū succurrat. Ideo nōtāter particulā hāc, in præsenti tēpore, inseruit, cui etiā uox <bl>καιρῷ</bl> cōcordat, quę magis articulū temporis, quàm tēpus significat.
units.tr: "In the present time," he says. This phrase is taken in different ways. Some refer it to the time of the present life, in this sense: "Your abundance, which you have in the present time," as if the Greek ought to be read thus: "τὸ ὑμῶν περισσεῦμα ὁ ἐν τῷ νῦν καιρῷ", whereas it reads "ἐν τῷ νῦν καιρῷ τὸ ὑμῶν περισσεῦμα." Certainly the course of the present age is such that in it one man abounds in wealth while another is oppressed by poverty; but the Apostle was not looking to this. Others refer it to the time in which the Apostle wrote this, when the saints in the church of Jerusalem, and the people of Judea, were oppressed by a great distress of famine. This sense seems to me the more probable. For he wished the Corinthians to have regard to the present calamity, and at the same time he hints that the contribution he was ordering was not to be sought as a permanent thing, but only to succour the saints in their present necessity. Therefore he deliberately inserted this phrase, "in the present time," to which the word "καιρῷ" also agrees, which signifies a point of time rather than a period.

units.la: VESTRA copia. inquit, illorū succurrat inopiæ.) Græcè est <bl>τὸ ὑμῶν περισσεῦμα</bl>, id est, Vestra abundantia. Non dicit simpliciter, succurratis illis, sed, ut uestra abundantia succurrat illorum inopiæ, quibus uerbis duo facit.
units.tr: "Your abundance," he says, "may succour their want." The Greek is "τὸ ὑμῶν περισσεῦμα", that is, "your abundance." He does not say simply, "you should help them," but "that your abundance may succour their want," and in these words he does two things.

units.la: Primum
units.tr: First

units.la: ¶ Primùm cauet, ne molesta videatur futura contributio, in eo quod ex abundantia illorum aliquid dandū esse significat. Etenim qui dat ex abundanti, necessitatibus suis nihil incommodat, quia de ijs quibus ipse habet opus, nihil detrit.
units.tr: First he guards against the contribution seeming burdensome, in that he signifies that something must be given from their abundance. For one who gives from abundance does not harm his own needs, since he takes nothing from what he himself has need of.

units.la: Dices: At eiùsmodi cōtributio nō laudatur à domino, sed ea potius, quę fit ex necessarijs, si cuti uidere est Luc. 21. vbi duo minuta œra à vidua in gazophylaciū missa præferūtur à Christo omnib. diuitum mulieribus: propterea qd illi ex abundantia, ipsa uero ex sua penuria qd habebat dederat. Quid igitur est quod Apostolus Corinthios docet eleemosynam dare de abundanti?
units.tr: You will say: but such a contribution is not praised by the Lord; rather the one that is made from necessities is. As one can see in Luke 21, where the two small coins put into the treasury by the widow are preferred by Christ above all the gifts of the rich women, because they gave from their abundance, but she from her poverty gave what she had. Why then does the Apostle teach the Corinthians to give alms from abundance?

units.la: Respondeo. Causam hanc studio sic moderatur, vt Corinthios reddat voluntarios, inducatque eos ad contribuendū haudgrauatim sed alacriter. Cū ergo dixisset acceptam esse contributionē quę sit & voluntaria, & secundū id quod quisq; possidet, ne videatur requirere, ut quod quisq; necessarium habet, alijs elargiatur, moderationem hanc subiecit, qua requirat non nec essaria sed quę deriter ex abundantia. Sic mitigat omnia, sciens se agere non cum Macedonib. sed cum opulētis Corinthijs. Interea tamē si illi exemplum Macedonum sequuti non ex abundanti tantum sed & ex necessarijs contribuisset, nihilo hoc secius in illis quàm in Macedonibus laudasset.
units.tr: I answer: he moderates this cause with such care as to make the Corinthians willing, and to lead them to contribute not grudgingly but cheerfully. Since he had said that the contribution is acceptable which is both voluntary and according to what each possesses, lest it seem that he requires each to give to others what he needs himself, he added this moderation, by which he asks not for what is necessary but for what comes from abundance. Thus he softens everything, knowing that he is dealing not with the Macedonians but with the wealthy Corinthians. Meanwhile, if they had followed the example of the Macedonians and contributed not only from abundance but also from necessities, he would nonetheless have praised this in them no less than in the Macedonians.

units.la: 2 Deinde, in eo quod inopiæ sanctorum meminit, cui Corinthiorum abundantia succurre B re debeat, significat vrgentem esse causam, propter quàm hæc contributio requiratur, necessitatem videlicet egentiū sanctorū, cuius debeat cōmiseratione tanquā fratres ad succurrendū permoueri. Nos admonemur, in quos debeat nostra liberalitas ubertim conferre. In egenos videlicet & inopes fratres. Inopiam, non sancti tatem ac merita sanctorū proponit, cui sit alacriter succurrendum. Postea cœperūt impostores ac quæstores ptexere sanctitatē monachorum & Nonnarū, hominum religiosorum ut aiebant spiritualium, Deo soli viuentiū, mundo mortuorum, pro omnium salute vigilantiū, præcantium ac psallentium. Et sub hoc ptextu corrasæ sunt ingentes opes, vt iam dici non posit, quod inopiæ talium succurratur, sed quod luxui potius & ocio fomenta subministrentur.
units.tr: Second, in that he mentions the want of the saints, which the abundance of the Corinthians ought to succour, he signifies that the cause for which this contribution is sought is urgent, namely the necessity of the needy saints, by whose compassion they ought to be moved to help as brothers. We are reminded to whom our liberality ought to be bountifully bestowed: namely on needy and poor brothers. He sets before us their want, not the sanctity and merits of the saints, to whom help is to be given willingly. Afterwards impostors and quaestors began to cloak the sanctity of monks and nuns, religious people, as they called themselves, spiritual, living to God alone, dead to the world, keeping watch for the salvation of all, praying and chanting psalms. And under this pretext immense riches have been amassed, so that it can no longer be said that the want of such people is relieved, but rather that the supplies go to luxury and idleness.

units.la: Quare quod hic Apostolus dicit: vt uestra abundantia illorum succurrat inopiæ, inuertendum est ac dicendum, vt uestra inopia illorum abundantiæ subseruiat. Huius inuersionis exempla omnium sunt manifestissima in reditibus ac tributis, quæ singulis annis in monasteria & Canonicorum collegia ex labore ac sudore plebis conferuntur.
units.tr: Therefore what the Apostle says here, "that your abundance may succour their want," must be turned round and said thus: "that your want may serve their abundance." The most obvious examples of this reversal are in the revenues and tributes which are conferred every year on monasteries and colleges of canons from the labour and sweat of the common people.

units.la: ET illorum copia, inquit, uestræ succurrat inopiæ.) Particulam hanc communiter omnes sic exponunt, ut copia pauperum sanctorum, quib9 contributio fratrum succurrere debuit, sit bonorum spiritualium, quæ ab illis proueniunt ad Corinthios, & cæteros quoque qui ex
units.tr: "And their abundance," he says, "may succour your want." All commonly expound this particle thus: that the abundance of the poor saints, to whom the brothers' contribution ought to have given help, consists of spiritual goods which come from them to the Corinthians, and to the others too who

units.la: Gentibus in Christum crediderunt (nam verbum domini ex Sion egressum peruenit ad Gentes) uel, quæ in posterū ad Corinthios ab illis prouenire potuerint, per communicationem videlicet singularis pietatis ac iusticiæ, in quibus ipsi non abundauerint, sed inopes fuerint. Verum, meo iudicio, nihil horum cogitauit Apostolus, cū hæc scriberet. Etenim, primùm nō dicit, quemadmodū illorum copia uestrę succurrit inopię, sed, ἵνα ἡ τὸ ἐκείνων περίσσευμα ... id est, vt & illorum abundantia subueniat uestræ inopiæ. Quare patet nō esse intelligendū de eo quod verbū domini è Sion ad Gentes iā tum erat egressum, & ad Corinthios quoq; allatū, sed de futura aliquā bonorū communicatione. Deinde si de bonis spiritualibus, quæ sint pietas & iusticia, quarū potuerint communicatio peruenire ad Corinthios fideles, locum hunc expōsuerimus: mox ꝗstio nascitur an Christiani qui Hierosolymis erant sic abundanter fuerint pij ac iusti, vt de abundantia iusticiæ ac pietatis suę inopiæ credentiū Corinthiorum succurrere potuerint. Dicant hoc quicunq; voluerint, ego nunquam dixero. Scib esse communicationem fideliū in bonis spiritualibus, de qua non est ut hic dicamus, verum non video, quare danda sit ecclesiæ Hierosolymitanæ abundantia, Corinthiacæ vero inopia pietatis & iusticię. Nec conuenit hic sensus prudenti moderationi, qua Apostolus causam hanc sic tractat, ne quo pacto Corinthios suos offendat. Quomodo autem hoc offenderet, si Hierosolymitanis daret abundantiam pietatis ac iusticiæ, ipsis uero inopiam, eamq; talem, cui per illos fit succurreduim, modo ipsi de terrenorum suorum bonorum abundantia aliquid illis impertiant? In summa, nec veritati, nec prudentiæ Apostoli conuenit hic sensus, & interim fenestras aperit eorum imposturę, qui sanctorum merita, si detur aliquid, ex quadam illorum abundanti pietate ac iusticia alijs nūgantur esse communicabilia. Quare cogor à receptis huius loci expositionibus discedere, eamq; sequi, quæ & simplicior est, & veritati metiq; apostoli vicinior, nec fenestras reproborum hominū impostur is aperit. Hanc esse iudico, si exponamus non de diuersorum bonorum, corporaliū ac spiritualium, sed eo rundem, corporaliū scilicet, communicatione, ad hunc modum. Vt uestra copia in præsenti tempore, quo rerum necessariarum penuria Iudea laborat inopiæ illorum succurrat, vt in posterum, ubi per vicissitudinem rerum uos cœperitis egere, illi uero melius habere quā nūc, illorum copia uicissim uestrę succurrat inopiæ. Hoc sensu admonet Corinthios, esse rerum uices, sic ut non semper abundent, qui ad tempus abundare uidentur, nec semper inopes sint qui iam penuria rerū laborat, unde cogitēt, quod sibi in tali casu fieri velint, id faciant & alijs, nec insolescant propter luculentiorem modici temporis fortunam, nec contemnant fratres propter præsentem egestatem, cuius & ipsi olim sint incommoda experturi. Hæc sententia mihi hoc loco probatur, iudicent cordati.
units.tr: believed in Christ from among the Gentiles (for the word of the Lord went forth from Zion and reached the Gentiles), or of what could come in future from them to the Corinthians, namely by the communication of singular piety and righteousness, in which they themselves did not abound but were poor. But in my judgment the Apostle thought of none of these things when he wrote this. For first, he does not say "as their abundance succours your want," but "ἵνα ἡ τὸ ἐκείνων περίσσευμα ...", that is, "that their abundance also may come to the aid of your want." Hence it is clear that this is not to be understood of the word of the Lord, which had already gone out from Zion to the Gentiles and had also been brought to the Corinthians, but of some future communication of goods. Next, if we were to expound this place of spiritual goods, which are piety and righteousness, whose communication could come to the faithful Corinthians, a question immediately arises: whether the Christians who were at Jerusalem were so abundantly pious and just that out of the abundance of their piety and righteousness they could succour the want of the believing Corinthians. Let whoever wishes say this; I shall never say it. I know there is a communion of the faithful in spiritual goods, but that is not what we are discussing here; and I do not see why the abundance of the church of Jerusalem should be given to the Corinthians as the want of piety and righteousness. Nor does this sense agree with the prudent moderation by which the Apostle handles this cause, so as in no way to offend the Corinthians. For how would he offend them if he gave the Jerusalemites an abundance of piety and righteousness, but they a want, and such a want as must be succoured by them, provided they impart something of the abundance of their earthly goods? In sum, this sense agrees neither with the truth nor with the prudence of the Apostle, and at the same time it opens windows to the imposture of those who babble that the merits of the saints, if something is given, can be communicated to others out of a certain abundance of their piety and righteousness. Therefore I am compelled to depart from the received expositions of this place, and to follow that which is both simpler and closer to the Apostle's meaning, and which does not open windows to the impostures of reprobate men. I judge this to be the case if we expound it not of the communication of different goods, bodily and spiritual, but of the same goods, namely bodily, communication, in this way: that your abundance, in the present time, in which Judaea labours in want of necessary things, may succour their want; so that in future, when by the turn of events you begin to be in need and they to be better off than now, their abundance may in turn succour your want. In this sense he admonishes the Corinthians that there are changes of fortune, so that those who seem to abound for a time do not always abound, nor are those who now labour in poverty always needy; whence let them consider what they would wish done for themselves in such a case, and do it for others, nor let them grow proud because of the more brilliant fortune of a short time, nor despise their brothers because of present want, the discomforts of which they themselves will one day experience. This view I approve in this place; let the judicious decide.

units.la: VT fiat æquabilitas, inquit.) Hoc est, ut removeatur à Christianis inæqualitas illa, qua uidemus inter incredulos & alienos à Christo, alios agere in luxu ac delicijs, alios contrà fame torqueri, nec esse ullam communicationem rerum necessariarum, nec commiserationem erga inopes & afflictos, q; inæqualitas inter Christianos locum habere non debet, inter quos regnat non φιλαυτία, sed φιλαδελφία, quarum altera æquabilitatis, altera uero inæqualitatis est mater. Vtiq; ueris Christianis cor est vnum & anima vna. Vbi hæc est vnitas, ibi non est alius dives, alius pauper, sed suppetit singulis unde uiuant, propter fraternam bonorum communicationem, sicut in exemplo primorum Christianorum Act. 4. uidere licet. De hac æquabilitate loquitur hic Apostolus, quæ sine communicatione rerum necessariarum locum in hoc sæculo habere nō potest. Deus enim sic mundum hûc dispensat, ut non reddat omnes ex æquo diuites, neq; omnes pariter pauperes, sed alios diuites, alios pauperes, ut sint in quibus liberalitatis suæ, ac rursus in quibus disciplinæ suæ exempla uisenda proponat, detq; diuitibus occasionem exercendæ erga proximos pauperes fraternæ dilectionis ac beneficentiæ, pauperibus uero materiam fiduciæ, qua à prouidentia sua pendeant, & ut interim in patientia comprobentur & exerceantur.
units.tr: "That there may be equality," he says. That is, the inequality which we see among unbelievers and those estranged from Christ should be removed from Christians: some live in luxury and pleasures, while others on the contrary are tormented by hunger, and there is no sharing of necessities or compassion towards the needy and afflicted. Such inequality ought not to exist among Christians, among whom reigns not self-love [φιλαυτία] but brotherly love [φιλαδελφία]. The one is the mother of inequality, the other of equality. Indeed, among true Christians there is "one heart and one soul." Where this unity is, there is no one rich and another poor; rather, each has enough to live on, because of the brotherly sharing of goods, as may be seen in the example of the first Christians in Acts 4. It is this equality of which the Apostle speaks here, which cannot exist in this age without the sharing of necessities. For God so arranges the world that He does not make all equally rich or all equally poor, but some rich and some poor: so that there may be those in whom His generosity is shown, and others in whom the examples of His discipline are to be seen; and so that He gives the rich an opportunity to exercise brotherly love and beneficence towards their poor neighbours, and gives the poor a ground of trust, by which they depend on His providence, and so that meanwhile they may be proved and exercised in patience.

units.la: Quis autem sufficiëter perpendere poterit, quantum momenti æquabilitas ista ad hoc aderat, ut animi sic inuicem de bonis, suis communicantium inter se coalescant, & cor vnum & anima una esse in duo pergat? Hic fieri nō potest ut dives fastidiat pauperē, quē pauperē esse nō finit, sed communicatione fraterna æqualem sibi reddit. Rursus fieri non potest, ut pauper diuiti opes quas habet inuideat, cū eas ppter fraternam communicationem non minus suas q; illi9 esse uideat. Verùm ab hac æquabilitate nostra hæc tempora omnium sunt alienissima, in quibus albū & nigrum tam sibi inuicem dissimilia non sunt, atq; inæquales inter se sunt qui opibus abundant & qui inopia laborant.
units.tr: But who could sufficiently weigh how much importance this equality had, so that, sharing their goods with one another, their minds might be joined together, and they might continue to be "one heart and one soul"? Here it cannot happen that the rich man despises the poor man, whom he does not allow to remain poor, but makes equal to himself by fraternal sharing. Again, it cannot happen that the poor man envies the rich man the wealth he has, since, because of the fraternal sharing, he sees it to be no less his own than the other's. But this equality is utterly alien to our times, in which black and white are not so unlike one another, and those who abound in wealth and those who labour in want are unequal to one another.

units.la: QVEMADMODVM scriptū est, inqt: Qui multū habebat huic nihil superfuit, & qui paulum habebat, is nihilominus habuit.) Locum hunc citat ex ijs quæ de Mana Exodi 16. legun tur ad hunc modum. Hic est sermo quem præcepit uobis dominus. Colligat unusquisque ex eo quantum sufficit ad vescendum, Gomer per singula capita, iuxta numerum animarum uestrarum quę habitat in tabernaculo sic tolletis. Feceruntq; ita filij Israel & collegerūt, alį plus, alius minus, & mēsi sunt ad mensuram Gomer, ולא תעדיף המרבה וחמעיט לא החסיר איש ולבי אבלי לקטו i.& non abundauiʒ qui multū, neq; eguit qui modicum collegerat, singuli quantum ad edendum satis erat collegerunt.
units.tr: "As it is written," he says, "He who had much had nothing over, and he who had little had nonetheless enough." He cites this passage from what is read about the manna in Exodus 16, in this manner: "This is the word which the Lord has commanded you. Let each one gather from it as much as is sufficient for eating, an omer for each head, according to the number of your souls that dwell in the tent, so you shall take it." And the sons of Israel did so, and gathered, some more, some less, and they measured by the omer; "and he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no lack; each gathered as much as was enough to eat." [ולא תעדיף המרבה וחמעיט לא החסיר איש ולבי אבלי לקטו]
