units.la: Hanc historiam inducit Apostolus, & propositio suo accommodat, quatenus in illa declara-tur q placeat dño æquabilitas alimenti necessarij in suo populo, quod ipse illi pro sua bonitate suppeditat, & contrà q displiceat auaricia eorū, qui cum detrimento proximorū suorum ne cessitatis mensuram excedentes, plura sibi coaceruant quàm vsus necessarius postulat. Æquabilitas exprimitur in eo quod dicit Moses, & non abundauit qui multum, neq; eguit qui modicum collegerat. Quomodo autē factum hoc sit, declaratur mox ubi subiicit: singuli quantū satis erat ad edendum collegerunt. Etenim qui numero domesticorum cæteros superabant, necessario quidem plus cæteris, qui uero numero erant pauci, minus quam illi colligebant, & tamen nec illi abundabant, nec isti egebant, propterea quòd singulis Gomer unum deputatum fuerat, tam in numerosa quàm in minus nu merosa familia, tam diuitibus quàm pauperib. Etenim secundum numerum capitum cuiusq; domus colligebatur & numerus Gomer, quem admodum præscriptum ac determinatum fuerat à Domino.
units.tr: The Apostle brings in this history and adapts it to his purpose, in that it shows how pleasing to the Lord is an equal supply of necessary food among His people, which He Himself in His goodness provides for them; and, on the contrary, how displeasing is the avarice of those who, to the detriment of their neighbours, gather more for themselves than the measure of necessity and necessary use demands. The equality is expressed in what Moses says: "he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no lack." How this came about is explained immediately after, where he adds: "each gathered as much as was enough to eat." For those who outnumbered the others in their households necessarily gathered more than the others, while those who were few in number gathered less than they; yet neither did the former have excess nor did the latter lack, because one omer had been assigned to each person, in a large household as in a smaller one, to the rich as to the poor. For the amount gathered was reckoned according to the number of heads in each household, and the measure of the omer was that which the Lord had prescribed and determined.

units.la: Dices, ergo si qui plus collegissent quàm pro numero capitum, atque ita necessarij alimenti mensuram excessissent, culpabiles fuissent tanquam præscripti diuini transgressores. Deinde æquabilitas ista non constabat mutua contributione, quæ locum non habet, ubi nemo est qui egeat. Atq; ita hæc historia damnat abundantes, & nullos habet egentes, adeoq; & nullam contributionem. Quare impertinenter ab Apostolo ad causam quam agit adducta uidetur, in qua sunt egentes, & non requiritur, ut nemo opibus abundet, sed hoc tantum, ut qui abundat, egenti de abundantia sua communicet. Respondeo. Scopus est Apostolo commendare fidelibus æquabilitatem. Et quoniam illa pulchrè fuerat in populo Israel, cum cœlitùs per Manna pasceretur, diuino præscripto instituta historiam illius hactenus applicat suæ causæ, quatenus simpliciter exemplum habet æquabilitatis, non quatenus singulari præscripto Dei certa colligendi cibi moderatio fuerat determinata, non quod aliis modis non posset fieri æquabilitas, vel quod per se illicitum sit esse diuitem, vel domino displiceat, si in populo ipsius sint pauperes, sed quod ea mode ratio tum temporis conueniret circumstantijs & loci in quo agebant annis 40. & alimenti quo de cœlo comuniter omnes pascebātur, & pædagogię, qua rudis populus manifesto & quotidiano diuinæ erat prouidentiæ experimento in fide Dei instituendus. Is modus instituendæ ac seruandæ æquabilitatis mutatus postea est, ubi ipsam promissam terram incolere, agros serere, vineas plantare, vrbes & pagos inhabitare, & consueta humano generi commercia inter se exercere coeperunt. Ibi alia poscebatur æquabilitatis retinendæ ratio. Ea nimirum, quæ charitate & contributione fraterna constaret, qua de eidem est populo præscriptum Deut. 15. ad hunc modum. Non deerunt pauperes in terra habitationis tuæ, idcirco ego co ego præcipio tibi, ut aperias manum fratri tuo egeno ac pauperi, qui tecum uersatur in terra. Hanc rationem & primá ecclesia Christiano rum amplexa est Hierosolymis; & Apostolus ubique in scriptis suis urget: quæ ob id est præstantior ea quæ fuit in deserto, quod exercitio mutuę charitatis constat, quæ nos cum Deo coiungit, ac diuinæ bonitatis consortes reddit, à qua illa fuit aliena. Neq; enim occasionem dabat mutuę charitatis per contributionem exercendæ, cum nec abundare nec egere quenquá sineret, quod necessarium alimentum concernebat. Quod reliquam substantiam auri & argenti & pecorum attinebat, erant vtique in populo, cum in solitudine quoq; ageret, multi diuites, cæteris opulétiores, uerùm in necessaria uitę sustentatione nec diues abundabat, nec pauper egebat. Nam & uestimenta omnium ex æquo infracta durabant in deserto, & calciamenta pedum omnium nulla uetustate absumebantur, & quotidie singulis non minus tenuiorib⁹, quàm ditioribus æqua mensura Gomer alimoniæ gratia cœlitùs dabatur. Quare cum æquales essent in uictu & amictu, nec ulla esset cuiquam alterutrius penuria, æquabilitas ista charitatis & mutuæ contributionis exercitio desi tuebatur, conuenientior populo rudi, quàm ei qui sit in verbo domini institutus, ac spiritu uerę dilectionis imbutus.
units.tr: You will say: then if some had gathered more than the number of heads required, and so had exceeded the measure of necessary food, they would have been guilty as transgressors of the divine precept. Moreover, this equality did not depend on mutual contribution, which has no place where no one is in need. And so this history condemns those who abound and has no needy persons, and therefore no contribution. Hence the Apostle seems to have brought it in inappropriately to the cause he is pleading, in which there are needy persons, and it is not required that no one abound in wealth, but only that whoever abounds share from his abundance with the needy. I reply: the Apostle's aim is to commend equality to the faithful. And since this equality had been finely maintained among the people of Israel, when they were fed from heaven by the manna, established by divine precept, he applies that history to his cause so far as it simply offers an example of equality, and not insofar as by a particular precept of God a fixed moderation in gathering food had been determined; not because equality could not be achieved by other means, or because it is in itself unlawful to be rich, or displeasing to the Lord if there are poor persons among His people; but because that mode of arrangement suited the circumstances of that time and place, in which they lived for forty years, and the food by which all were fed in common from heaven, and the schooling by which the untutored people was to be taught to trust in God through the manifest and daily experience of divine providence. That mode of establishing and maintaining equality was changed later, when they began to dwell in the promised land itself, to till fields, plant vineyards, inhabit cities and villages, and carry on among themselves the customary commerce of mankind. There another way of maintaining equality was required: namely, one that consisted in charity and fraternal contribution, which was prescribed to the same people in Deuteronomy 15 in this manner: "There shall not be lacking poor in the land of your habitation; therefore I command you, that you open your hand to your brother who is needy and poor, who dwells with you in the land." The first church of the Christians in Jerusalem also embraced this principle, and the Apostle everywhere urges it in his writings. This is more excellent than that which existed in the wilderness, because it consists in the exercise of mutual charity, which joins us to God and makes us partakers of divine goodness, from which that earlier arrangement was far removed. For it did not give occasion for the exercise of mutual charity through contribution, since it allowed no one either to abound or to lack in what concerned necessary food. As for the remaining substance of gold, silver and flocks, there were certainly, even while they were in the wilderness, many rich people among the people, wealthier than the rest; yet in the sustaining of necessary life the rich man had no excess and the poor man no lack. For the garments of all lasted unworn in the wilderness, and the sandals of all were worn away by no age, and every day to each person, to the poorer no less than to the richer, an equal measure of the omer was given from heaven for nourishment. Therefore, since they were equal in food and clothing, and no one lacked anything of either, that equality was maintained without the exercise of charity and mutual contribution, which was more fitting for an untutored people than for one instructed in the word of the Lord and imbued with the Spirit of true love.

units.la: Verùm deplorandum hoc est admodũ, quod usq; adeò inter nos, qui Noui testaméti populus sumus, charitas & quæ ex charitate est mutua contributio refriguit, ut multo plures sint causæ, propter quas eiusmodi æquabilitas in uictu & amictu diuinitùs nùc datur, qualis fuit in deserto, quá fuerint olim in populo rudi & nodũ in uerbo domini instituto. Alias ad finem usq; mundi sperandum non est, ut æquabilitatis commodis potiamur in hoc sæculo.
units.tr: But it is deeply to be lamented that among us, who are the people of the New Testament, charity and the mutual contribution that arises from charity have so grown cold that there are far more reasons why an equality in food and clothing of the kind that existed in the wilderness is now given by God, than there were once among the untutored people, who were instructed in the word of the Lord. Otherwise, we should not hope until the end of the world to enjoy the advantages of equality in this age.

units.la: Gratia autem Deo qui dedit eádem solicitudínem pro uobis in corde Titi. Nam exhortationem quidem accepit, uerùm cum diligentior esset, suapte sponte ad uos abijt. Misimus autem una cum illo fratrem eum, cuius laus est in Euangelio per omnes ecclesias: nec id solum, uerumetiam delectus est ab ecclesijs comes peregrinationis nostræ, cũ hac gratia quæ administratur à nobis ad ipsius domini gloriam, & animi uestri promptitudinem: declinates hoc, ne quis nos carpat in hac exuberantia quæ administratur à nobis, procurantes honesta nõ tantum coram domino sed etiam coram hominibus. Misimus autem una cum illis fratrem nostrum quem probauimus in multis sæpenumero diligentê, nũc autem multo diligentiorem ob multam fiduciam quam habeo erga uos, siue Titi
units.tr: But thanks be to God, who put the same earnest care for you into the heart of Titus. For he indeed accepted our exhortation, but since he was more diligent, he went to you of his own accord. We sent with him the brother whose praise is in the gospel throughout all the churches; and not only that, but he was also chosen by the churches to travel with us in this grace which is administered by us to the glory of the Lord himself and to show your readiness of mind. We do this so that no one may blame us for this abundance which is administered by us, providing for what is honourable not only before the Lord but also before men. We sent with them our brother, whom we have often tested in many things and found diligent; but now he is much more diligent, because of the great confidence I have in you,

units.la: nomine qui socius meus est & erga uos adiutor, siue aliorũ qui fratres nostri sũt & legati ecclesiarũ, gloria Christi. Proin de documentũ charitatis uestrę, & nostræ de uobis gloriationis in eos demonstretis, etiam in conspectu ecclesiarum.
units.tr: whether on behalf of Titus, who is my partner and your helper, or of our other brothers who are the messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ. Therefore show them the proof of your love and of our boasting about you, even in the sight of the churches.

units.la: Toto hoc contextu laudat & commendat Corinthijs legatos, quos ad eos propter hanc contributionis causam miserat, ut contributa ab illis accepta ad se adferrent. Meminit autem trium: Titi videlicet, & duorum aliorum, sic ut singulorum encomia seiunctim ponat: Gratia autem Deo, inquit, qui dedit eandem solicitudinem pro uobis in corde Titi: Hunc cæteris duobus præponit, propterea quòd esset Corinthijs notus, imò iam antea haud parum apud eos in opere domini laborasset. An illis præstantior quoq; fuerit nostrum non est pronunciare: Orditur autem commendationem eius à ἀξιολογία Dei, laudans diuinã bonitatem, quod cor illius in eandem curam ac solicitudinem excitarit, qua ipse erga Corinthios admodum afficiebatur. Poterat simpliciter dicere: Abijt ad vos Titus, plenus eiusdem solicitudinis pro uobis qua ego distineor; uerùm ut significaret illis, causam hanc geri diuinitus, atq; ita animos eorum propensos ad illam redderet, dixit: Gratia autem Deo agatur videlicet, uel, agenda est à vobis, qui dedit eandem solicitudinem pro uobis in corde Titi:
units.tr: Throughout this whole passage Paul praises and commends the messengers whom he had sent to the Corinthians on account of this matter of the contribution, so that they might bring to him what had been collected from them. He mentions three: namely Titus, and two others, and he gives the praise of each one separately. "But thanks be to God," he says, "who put the same earnest care for you into the heart of Titus." He places Titus before the other two, because he was known to the Corinthians, and indeed had already laboured not a little among them in the work of the Lord. Whether he was also superior to them, it is not for us to pronounce. He begins his commendation with the praise of God, blessing the divine goodness that stirred up his heart to the same care and concern with which Paul himself was greatly moved toward the Corinthians. He could have simply said: "Titus has gone to you, full of the same concern for you with which I am occupied." But in order to show them that this matter is carried on by divine appointment, and so to make their minds more inclined to it, he said: "But thanks be to God," that is, it must be given thanks by you, "who put the same earnest care for you into the heart of Titus."

units.la: Nobis obseruandũ est, quod solicitudinem institutiendæ contributionis, qua necessitatib⁹ sanctorum Hierosolymitanorum consulendũ erat, uocat solicitudinem pro ipsis Corinthijs, quos ad contribuendum solicitabat, quib. uerbis significat se magis ipsorum quàm Hierosolymitanorum ratione habere in hac causa; sed huius admonuimus & antea. Deinde, eiusmodi solicitudinem cândidam ac syncerã esse donum Dei, qui illam dat in corda uerorum uerbi sui ministrorum. Nisi ille det tales animos, nihil purum erit in omnibus omnium ecclesiarũ eleemosynarijs ministris, uel potius dominis. Nam domini esse cœperunt, qui olim ministri fuerunt.
units.tr: We must observe that the concern for organising the contribution, by which relief was to be provided for the needy saints in Jerusalem, he calls concern for the Corinthians themselves, whom he was urging to contribute. By these words he shows that in this matter he is considering their good more than that of the Jerusalemites; but we have noted this also before. Next, that such a sincere and pure concern is a gift of God, who gives it into the hearts of the true ministers of his Word. Unless he gives such minds, nothing will be pure among all the almoners of all the churches, or rather, their lords. For those who were once ministers have begun to be lords.

units.la: NAM exhortationem quidé accepit, inquit, uerùm cum diligentior esset, suapte sponte ad uos abijt.) Declarat unde cognouerit eandé solicitudinem in corde Titi datam esse à domino. Nam, inquit, cum exhortarer eum ut ad vos contributionis huius gratia proficisceretur, deprehendi eum voluntarium ac spontaneum, & in id negocij ultro & vsq; adeò propensum, ut manifestum esset curam hac à dño cordi ipsius esse inditam. Suprà meminit unde motus Titũ adhortatus sit, ut hanc quoq; gratiam erga Corinthios expediret. Hic significat, quàm uoluntarium eum ad id negocij inuenerit. Habemus ergo exemplum hic uoluntariæ obedientiæ, quam Apostolus in Tito suo deprædicat. Commendat in eo, quod fuerit ἀντιμέτρῳ, ἀπονδυσόμενος, adhortationem acceperit & Corinthum abiecit. abierit. Hæc sunt ornamenta syncerę obedien- tiæ, esse videlicet voluntarium, adhortatione suscipere, solicitum esse, &ad id quod faciendū est abire. In his est verę obedientiæ plenitudo. Falsa est, vbi adhortatio quidem aure accipitur verum quod faciendum est non perficitur, vel ab inuitis, & neglectim perficitur.
units.tr: "For he indeed accepted our exhortation," he says, "but since he was more diligent, he went to you of his own accord." He explains how he knew that this same concern had been given to Titus's heart by the Lord. For, he says, when I exhorted him to go to you for the sake of this contribution, I found him willing and spontaneous, and so eagerly inclined to the business that it was plain that this care had been implanted in his heart by the Lord. Earlier he mentioned from what motive he had exhorted Titus to carry out this grace toward the Corinthians as well. Here he indicates how willing he found him for the task. We therefore have here an example of willing obedience, which the Apostle proclaims in his Titus. He commends in him that he was [ἀντιμέτρῳ, ἀπονδυσόμενος], that he received the exhortation and set off for Corinth. These are the marks of sincere obedience: to be willing, to receive exhortation, to be diligent, and to go to do what must be done. In these is the fullness of true obedience. It is false where the exhortation is indeed heard by the ear, but what must be done is not carried out, or is carried out by unwilling people and carelessly.

units.la: SVAPTE sponte, inquit, ad vos abijt.) Paulo antè ab illis ad Paulum redierat, illiq; respiscentiam, solicitudinem & obedientiam eorū deprædicauerat, sicuti cap. præcedēti uidim⁹. Iá ad illos denuò mittitur, propter unā hāc causam, vt cœptam apud eos contributionem expediat, & cōtributa secum ad Paulum adferat. Constituerat enim ille Hierosolymam profici sci, & sanctis illic gratiam & cōmunicatione ecclesiarū ex Gentib. offerre. Abit aūt spōte, quia cordi ipsi erant ecclesiarū cōmoda, & prēterea paulo antè corā respiscentiā & obedientiam Corinthiorum expertus fuerat.
units.tr: "Of his own accord," he says, "he went to you." Shortly before he had returned from them to Paul, and had praised their repentance, concern and obedience, as we saw in the preceding chapter. Now he is sent to them again for this one reason: to complete the contribution begun among them and bring the collected gifts back with him to Paul. For Paul had resolved to set out for Jerusalem and to offer to the saints there the gift and the fellowship of the churches from among the Gentiles. And Titus went of his own accord, because the welfare of the churches was dear to his heart, and besides, he had shortly before experienced the repentance and obedience of the Corinthians in person.

units.la: Meminit aūt huius de Tito, non tā laudandi il lius gratia, quā ad hoc, vt intelligerent esse illū erga ipsos amanter affectū, propter præteritā obsequentiā, qua se illi ad omnia morigeros ex h buerant, & hinc in ipsa causa propter quam ad ipsos redibat, eò se ductiliores ac magis propensos præberent. Poterat alia in illo commēdare, verùm quoniam ipsis iam abundē notus erat, tacitis virtutibus quibus erat præditus, hoc vnum significat, quod sponte ad ipsos abijssēt, quo animum illius erga se beneuolum agnoscerent.
units.tr: He mentions Titus here not so much to praise him, as to make them understand that he had a loving affection for them, on account of the past compliance by which they had shown themselves obedient to him in all things; and so that in this very matter, for which he was returning to them, they might show themselves more pliant and more inclined. He could have commended other things in him, but since they were already well acquainted with him, and with the unspoken virtues with which he was endowed, he mentions only this one thing, that he went to them of his own accord, so that they might recognise his goodwill toward them.

units.la: MISIMVS autem, inquit, vnà cum illo fratrem eum, cuius laus est in Euangelio per omnes ecclesias.) Quod Titum non solum misit, sed duos illi fratres adiunxit, non est sine consilio factum, sicuti videbimus mox infrà. Quis autem fuerit frater iste, de quo prædicat, quòd laus illius sit per omnes ecclesias, & quod deletus fuerit comes peregrinationis suæ, non est cōcors omnium sententia. Alij Lucam, alij Barnabam intelligūt. Chrysost. de Barnabba intelligit, propterea quod ille comes fuerit peregrinationis Pauli, & præterea clarus propter Euangelij prædicationem. Et huic assentiūtur nonnulli ex recentioribus. Sophronius verò præsentē locū de Luca exponit. Sic enim de illo scribit, Ἀυκας ἰατρὸς ... Et huic sententiæ Hieron. cōsentit. Sanè de Luca vel ex Actis apost. cōstat, qd' comes fuerit peregrinationis Pauli. Nec dubiū est, quin multū laudis consequutus sit in omnibus ecclesijs, præsertim gentiū, pro pterea quòd Euangelicam historiam singulari fide ac diligentia Græco sermone conscripsit. Probabile nanq; est qd' nihil huius inscripto ante illum communicatum fuerit Græcis ecclesijs. Matthæus nanq; Ebraicè historiā Christi contexuit, quę à Græcis legi non potuit, do
units.tr: "We sent," he says, "with him the brother whose praise is in the gospel throughout all the churches." That he did not send Titus alone, but joined two brothers with him, was not done without purpose, as we shall see shortly below. Who that brother was, of whom he declares that his praise is throughout all the churches, and that he was chosen as the companion of his journey, is not a matter on which all agree. Some understand Luke, others Barnabas. Chrysostom understands Barnabas, because he was the companion of Paul's journey, and besides was famous for preaching the gospel. Some of the more recent writers agree with him. Sophronius, however, explains the present passage of Luke. For he writes of him thus: [Λουκᾶς ἰατρὸς ...]. And Jerome agrees with this opinion. Certainly it is established from the Acts of the Apostles that Luke was the companion of Paul's journey. Nor is there any doubt that he gained great praise in all the churches, especially among the Gentiles, because he wrote the gospel history in Greek with singular faith and diligence. For it is probable that nothing of this kind had been made known to the Greek churches before him.

units.la: nec è Græco idiomate couerteretur. Et de Iohane cōstat quod post cæteros scripserit. Marci Euangelio vt epitomen habet eiꝰ qd' à Matthęo scriptum est, ita post illud contextū esse patet. Quod ille Græcè scripserit, & non Ebraicè vel Ægyptiacè, quomodo probetur non video. Hiïce coniecturis existimo verosimilius sentire eos qui hæc de Luca quàm qui de Barnabba exponunt.
units.tr: For Matthew wrote the history of Christ in Hebrew, which could not be read by the Greeks, nor could it be translated from the Greek idiom. And it is certain that John wrote after the others. It is clear that Mark's Gospel, which has the character of an epitome of what Matthew wrote, was composed after that. How it can be proved that he wrote in Greek and not in Hebrew or Egyptian, I do not see. On these conjectures I think that those who explain these words of Luke rather than of Barnabas are more probably right.

units.la: Mea sententia sichabet. Quod hic Paulus dicit, fratrem illum quem vnà cū Tito Corinthū miserat, comitem fuisse peregrinationis suę ab ecclesijs delectum, intelligendum est non in vniuerium de tota illius peregrinatione, sed ea tantum, qua collectas ecclesiarum quæ erant inter Gētes Hierosolymam deportare constituerat. Ad hanc perficiendam delecti fuerunt ab ecclesijs nonnulli fratres, qui vnà cum ipso proficiscerentur. Ex his fuisse Barnabbā mihi haud quaqua ,pbabile videtur. Etenim postq; ille diuulg fuit à Paulo, ob dissidiū inter ipsos propter Marcum exortū, non legitur amplius cum eo fuisse coniunctus. De separatione illorum legimus Act. 15. quo tempore nec Corinthij, nec Macedones ad Christum fuerat conuersi, Macedonum siquidem conuersio postea subsequuta est, sicut videre est Act. 16. & Corinthiorū adhuc post illam, vt Act. 18. habetur. Cū igitur legatio hæc ad Corinthios facta fit non ante illorum conuersionem sed diu postea, & Barnabbas antequā illi conuerterentur à Paulo fuerit segregatus, nec illi postea cōiunctus legatur, quomodo ab eo Corinthū cum Timotheo potuit, in causa, cuius administrationis principium Act. 19. demum inchoatur. Lucam vero in ea peregrinatione Hierosolymam cū Paulo profectū esse, ex ipsius profectionis narratione omnib. abunde redditur manifestum. Quare qui verba hęc Apostoli de Barnabba exponūt, non satis causam hanc inspex isse uiden tur. Respexerunt ad ea quæ de societate Pauli & Barnabbę Act. 13.14 & 15. leguntur, & nō ad ea tempora, in quib. hæc sunt à Paulo scripta, ad quæ si respexissent, non amplius Barnabbā in comitatu Pauli fuisse deprehendissent.
units.tr: My view is as follows. What Paul here says, that the brother whom he sent to Corinth with Titus was chosen by the churches as the companion of his journey, must be understood not generally of his whole journey, but only of that part in which he had resolved to carry the collections of the churches which were among the Gentiles to Jerusalem. To carry this out, some brothers were chosen by the churches to set out together with him. That Barnabas was one of these seems to me by no means probable. For after he was separated from Paul, because of the dispute that arose between them over Mark, we no longer read that he was joined with him. We read of their separation in Acts 15, at which time neither the Corinthians nor the Macedonians had been converted to Christ; for the conversion of the Macedonians followed later, as may be seen in Acts 16, and that of the Corinthians was still later still, as is recorded in Acts 18. Since therefore this embassy to the Corinthians was made not before their conversion but long afterwards, and Barnabas had been separated from Paul before they were converted, and is not read to have been joined with him afterwards, how could he have been sent to Corinth by him together with Timothy, in a matter whose beginning is only narrated in Acts 19? But that Luke went up to Jerusalem with Paul on that journey is made abundantly clear to all from the account of the journey itself. Therefore those who explain these words of the Apostle about Barnabas do not seem to have examined this matter sufficiently. They looked to what is read about the partnership of Paul and Barnabas in Acts 13, 14 and 15, and not to the times in which these things were written by Paul; had they looked to those times, they would not have found Barnabas any longer in Paul's company.

units.la: CVIVS laus est, inquit, in Euangelio p omnes ecclesias.) Bene de omnibus ecclesijs meritus, merito ab omnib. ecclesijs laudatur. Lucas conscribendo Euangelium bene est de omnibus ecclesijs meritus. Ergo, &c. Quod maiorem attinet, admonentur ecclesiæ, ut bene de illis sentiant ac loquantur, qui laboribus suis bene de ipsis sunt meriti. Magis optandum est hoc vt fiat, quā prædicandū quod fiat. Sic sunt nostra tempora. Quod minorem concernit, ad monentur cordati omnes, quid promereantur illi qui scriptis suis regnū Christi ac doctrinam veritatis pro suis quilq; uiribus, & mensura donationis spiritus, scribendo ac lucubrando illustrant, eoq; laborum genere omnibus, quantum in ipsis est, ecclesijs in causa pietatis ac uerę salutis prosunt. De Luca scribunt nonulli, quod fuerit pictor. Quod si imaginū visus qui nunc est, apostolorum tempore fuisset in eccle mini fieri non posset. Ecótrà igitur ignominiò sa est omnis auaritia & tenacitas.
units.tr: Of whom, he says, the praise is in the Gospel throughout all the churches. He who has done well by all the churches is rightly praised by all the churches. Luke, by writing the Gospel, has done well by all the churches. Therefore, and so forth. As for the major premise, the churches are admonished to think and speak well of those who by their labours have deserved well of them. This is more to be wished for than it is to be expected, and so it is in our own times. As for the minor premise, all thoughtful people are reminded what they owe to those who, by their writings, illuminate the kingdom of Christ and the doctrine of truth, each according to his own powers and the measure of the gift of the Spirit, by writing and studying late into the night, and who by this kind of labour benefit all the churches, so far as lies in them, in the cause of piety and true salvation. Some write that Luke was a painter. But if the use of images, as it is now, had existed in the churches in the time of the apostles, this could not have happened. On the contrary, all covetousness and meanness is then disgraced.

units.la: sijs, & ille picta simulacra Seruatoris, beatę vir ginis, Iohánis Baptistę, & apostolorū ad eccle-sias misisset, an non dicendū potius fuisset Apo-stolo cuius laus est in pictura imaginū sanctorū quá cuius laus est in Euangelio, per oēs ecclesi-as: verum hic pictor, Christi & apostolorum imá-gines non corporeas penicillo, sed spirituales scripto Euangelico depinxit, atq; ita mirum in modū profuit ecclesijs, & laudem, quæ etiam-num durat, est promeritus, vt veraciter potue-rit Apostolus dicere, cuius laus perpetua in o-mnibus erit ecclesijs.
units.tr: If he had sent to the churches painted likenesses of the Saviour, the blessed Virgin, John the Baptist and the apostles, would it not rather have been said to the Apostle whose praise lies in painting pictures of the saints than to the one whose praise lies in the Gospel throughout all the churches? But this painter depicted the images of Christ and the apostles, not corporeal ones with a brush, but spiritual ones with the written Gospel, and so profited the churches in a remarkable way and has earned a praise which endures even now. Hence the Apostle could truly say: whose praise will be perpetual in all the churches.

units.la: NEC id solum, inquit, verumetiā delect9 est ab ecclesijs comes peregrinatiōis nostrę.) Quo niá qd' dixit, cuius laus est in Euangelio, gene-ralius erat q vt ad propositum faceret, subiūgit ista tāquā propius ad causam quā agebat facien-tia. Diximus aūt paulo suprà, non loqui ipsum de vniuersa peregrinatione sua, sed ea tantum, qua profecturus erat Hierosolymam, & sanctis contributionem ecclesiarum ex Gentib. unà cū quibusdam fratribns ab ecclesijs ad id nego-cij delectis assignaturus. Ex hisce erat hic Lu-cas, quē ideo unà cum Tito Corinthum misit, vt aliarum ecclesiarū præiudicio Corinthiosin duceret ad credendum suas collectas, viris istis ablq; vlla hæsitatione fide dignis, quorū priori psis erat iam antea notus, deq; ipsisoptime me-ritus, secundus reliquarum ecclesiarū iudicio & electione dignus, de cuius fide prorsus nihil addubitarent.
units.tr: "Nor that alone," he says, "but he was also chosen by the churches to be the companion of our journey." For since what he had said, whose praise is in the Gospel, was too general to serve his purpose, he added these words, which bear more directly on the cause he was pleading. We said a little above that he is not speaking of his whole journey, but only of that journey on which he was about to go to Jerusalem, to hand over to the saints the contribution of the churches from the Gentiles, together with certain brethren chosen from the churches for this business. Of these was this Luke, whom he therefore sent to Corinth together with Titus, so that, without prejudice to the other churches, he might lead the Corinthians to believe that their collections were safe in the hands of men who were beyond any doubt trustworthy: the first of them was already known to them, and had deserved well of them, while the second was worthy of the judgement and choice of the other churches, so that they should have no doubt whatever about his faith.

units.la: CVM hac gratia, inquit, quæ administratur à nobis ad ipsius domini gloriam, & animi ue-stri promptitudine.) Declarat cuius peregrina-tionis suę comes delectus ab ecclesijs fuerit fra-ter ille quem miserat cum Tito. Eius uidelicet, in qua cum gratia, id est, cum collecta ecclesia-rum, quam administrandam suscepera t, Hiero-solymam erat profecturus. In eam profectione delectus erat Lucas vt vnà cum ipso proficisce-retur. Commendat autem causam hanc non ex eo solum, quod singularis existimationis uiros Corinthum miserat qui illam ifthic expediret, sed ex eo quoq;, quod ipse eam administrandā susceperat, de cuius fide dubitare non poterat, ad hæc, quod administraturus eam esset nō mo-dò ad refocillationem pauperum, sed & ad do-mini gloriam, & ipsorum promptitudinem. Hæc eo faciebant, vt de causa hac non leuiter sed piè ac religiosè sentientes, quo pluris eam facerent, hoc alacriores ac liberaliores ad con-tribuendum redderentur.
units.tr: "With this grace," he says, "which is administered by us to the glory of the Lord himself and the readiness of your mind." He declares who was the brother, chosen by the churches to be the companion of his journey, whom he had sent with Titus. That is, the journey on which he was about to go to Jerusalem with the grace, that is, the collection of the churches, which he had undertaken to administer. Luke had been chosen to set out with him on that journey. He commends this cause not only because he had sent men of singular repute to Corinth to settle it there, but also because he himself had undertaken to administer it, and his faith could not be doubted; moreover, because he would administer it not only for the relief of the poor, but also for the glory of the Lord and for their readiness. He did this so that the Corinthians, thinking about this cause not lightly but in a pious and religious spirit, might value it more and so be made more eager and generous in giving.

units.la: AD ipsius dñi gloriam, inquit.) Erasmus red-didit: ad eiusdem domini gloriam. Sanè sic red-di potest quod in Græco legitur, ὡς ... δόξαν. Nec est ociosa lectio. Pertinenter nanq; admonet eundem ipsis cum ecclesia fra-trum Hierosol. esse dominum, ad cuius sit glo-ria factura ipsorum cōtributio & contributio-nis administratio. Ergo gloriosum in se est, si frater fratri, eiusdem fidei cōsorti, de bonis suis sicubi necessitas postulauerit, liberali & alacri animo communicet. Alioqui ad gloriam do-
units.tr: "To the glory of the Lord himself," he says. Erasmus rendered it: "to the glory of the same Lord." Indeed what is read in Greek [ὡς ... δόξαν] can be rendered in that way, and the reading is not idle. For he appropriately reminds them that the same Lord is theirs together with the church of the brethren at Jerusalem, and that their contribution and the administration of the contribution will be to his glory. Therefore it is glorious in itself if one brother, a fellow sharer in the same faith, shares his goods with another, wherever necessity demands it, with a generous and eager mind. Otherwise, to the glory...

units.la: ET ad animi uestri pròptitudinē, inquit.) Vulgata lectio habet: & destinatā uoluntatem nostram, & exponit Lyranus, ad exequendum nostrę uoluntatis ordinationem. Verum in Græco est τὴν ... προθυμίαν ὑμῶν. Tribuit illis pro-ptitudinem & alacritate animi, qua propensi fuerint ad contribuendū. Et hoc faciens incitat eos ad maiorem alacritatem, præsertim cum se gratiam hanc non modò ad gloriā dñi, sed & ad promptitudinē ipsorū declarandā ac testifican-dam administraturū dicit. Satis quidem incita-menti homini pio ad hoc est, ut quod bonū est alacriter operetur, si intelligat opus suū factu-rum ad gloriā domini Dei ac redeptoris sui, ue-rum sciens negociū sibi esse cū imperfectis ad-huc & rudib. adiecit particulam hanc de laude promptitudinis ipsorū, qua vt homines affice-rentur & ad ampliorem contribuendi alacrita-tem incitarentur. Prudentiam hanc imitentur ministri uerbi, ut duplici hoc affectuum genere & ipsi fideles cū ut pios, tum ut homines ad pie-tatis studium excitent.
units.tr: "And to the readiness of your mind," he says. The Vulgate reading has: "and our determined will", and Lyranus explains it as "for carrying out the ordering of our will". But in Greek it is [τὴν ... προθυμίαν ὑμῶν], "your readiness". He ascribes to them readiness and eagerness of mind, by which they were inclined to contribute. In doing this he urges them towards greater eagerness, especially since he says that he will administer this grace not only to the glory of the Lord but also to the declaring and attesting of their readiness. This is certainly enough of an incitement for a godly man to work eagerly at what is good, if he understands that his work will be to the glory of the Lord God and his Redeemer. But since he knew he had to do with people who were still imperfect and untaught, he added this particle about the praise of their readiness, so that they might be moved by it and stirred to greater eagerness in contributing. Let the ministers of the Word imitate this prudence, so that by this double kind of appeal they may stir the faithful both as pious people and as human beings to a zeal for piety.

units.la: DECLINANTES hoc, inquit, ne quis nos carpat in hac exuberantia, quæ administratur à nobis.) Quo consilio non miserit Titum so-lum sed illi adiūxerit duos fratres probatę fidei uiros, hisce verbis aperit. Declinantes, inquit, hoc, ne quis nos carpat. Si coniungas ista præce-dentibus, quibus dixit, quę administratur à no-bis, dicendum potius fuerat, ἐκκλινόμενοι, id est, de-clinantibus, quam ἐκκλινόμενοι, id est, declinantes. Iam cum legatur ἐκκλινόμενοι, manifestum est refe-rendum esse ad illud quod paulo suprà dixit: Misimus autem vnà cum illo fratrem, cuius laus est in Euangelio, &c. ut sequatur ratio, de clinantes hoc, ne quis nos carpat. Quasi dicat, Ideo misimus hunc fratrem, propter Euange-lium laudatum in omnibus ecclesijs, & præte-rea delectum ab ecclesijs, ut sit peregrinationis huius nostrę comes, quo declinemus maleuo-lorū morsus cauentes ne quis nos carpat, quasi tam exuberantis pecuniae collectam non satis {A}fideliter administremus.
units.tr: "Avoiding this," he says, "lest anyone find fault with us in this abundance which is administered by us." By what plan he sent not only Titus but added to him two brethren of tried faith, he reveals in these words: "avoiding this," he says, "lest anyone find fault with us." If you join this to what precedes, where he said "which is administered by us", it ought rather to be [ἐκκλινόμενοι], that is, "avoiding" in the dative, than [ἐκκλινόμενοι] in the nominative as the text has it. But since the Greek is [ἐκκλινόμενοι], it is clear that it refers to what he said a little above: "we have sent with him the brother whose praise is in the Gospel," and so on, so that the sense follows: "avoiding this, lest anyone find fault with us." As if he were saying: "We have therefore sent this brother, on account of the Gospel praised in all the churches, and moreover chosen by the churches to be the companion of this our journey, so that we may avoid the bites of evil men, taking care that no one finds fault with us as if we did not administer so large a sum of money faithfully enough."

units.la: PROCVRANTES, inquit, honesta non tantum coram domino sed etiam coram hominib.) Quo modo declinet malorum hominum detractionem, ac sinistram de ministerio suo suspicionem, haec dicens declarat. Procurando videlicet honesta. Graece est, προνοούμενοι, id est, providentes. Significat sibi hoc esse curae, ut administrationem hac neq; leviter, neq; modis suspectis, sed honestè & fideliter obeat, ideoq; non misisse vulgarem aliquê hominê, minus notū, neq; Titum solum, quantumuis virum probatum, ipsisq; cum primis cognitum, sed adiunxisse illi etiam alios viros honestos & fidei probatae, ne quem locum relinqueret cuipiam carpendi se in hac causa. Locus hic diligenter observandus est illis qui in ecclesia Dei aliqua in re ministrant, praesertim pecuniaria, quo syncerita tem, fidem, & cautionem apostoli imitetur. Principio, videm hic q; ille non fusq; deq; faciat, quid de se loquatur ac iudicent alij, carpat ne uel laudet. Declinantes, inquit, ne quis nos carpat in hac exuberantia, quae administratur à nobis. Agnoscit exuberantem esse pecuniarum summam, quam administrandam susceperit, cogitat quàm facile fit, ut sinistra suspicione propter illam graeuetur, & quâ eiusmodi suspicio indigna sit suo Apostolatui, & noxia futura causae Christi & sanctorum egenorum, ideoq; declinat illâ studiosissimè. Hodie nulla est nec mica quidè eiusmodi solicitudinis in animis Romanorum pontificum, de Petri & Pauli successione gloriantium. Administrandam susceperunt annatarum, ut uocant, pecuniam, multo numerosiore quâ fuerit collectarum, de quibus loquitur hic apostolus. Carpuntur ob illius abalienatio nê in ipsis Imp. comitijs, nedum multorum piorum hominum sermonibus & querelis, uerũ fraus meretricis perfricta erubescere nescit. Bonis ecclesiae pro libidine in omnis generis luxum abutuntur, ob quam perfidiâ hodie palam accusantur, uerum accusatores suos faltidiosissime exufflant. Deinde, quomodo declinat & cauet, ne à quopiam in administratione tam copiosae pecuniae carpatur? Non legib, minis & execrationibus sicuti solent pontifices.
units.tr: "Providing for things honest," he says, "not only before the Lord but also before men." By saying this he declares how he avoids the detraction of evil men and the sinister suspicion about his ministry. That is, by providing for honest things. In Greek it is [προνοούμενοι], that is, "providing". It signifies that he takes care that this administration be carried out not lightly nor in suspicious ways, but honestly and faithfully; and therefore he did not send some ordinary man, less known, nor Titus alone, however approved a man and especially known to them, but added to him other honest men of tried faith, so as to leave no place to anyone for finding fault with him in this matter. This passage is to be carefully noted by those who serve in any way in the Church of God, especially in money matters, so that they may imitate the sincerity, faithfulness and caution of the apostle. First, we see here that he does not care a fig what others judge or say of him, whether they find fault or praise. "Avoiding this," he says, "lest anyone find fault with us in this abundance which is administered by us." He acknowledges that the sum of money he has undertaken to administer is abundant; he considers how easily it may be burdened by a sinister suspicion because of it, how such suspicion is unworthy of his apostleship and harmful to the cause of Christ and of the needy saints; and therefore he avoids it most diligently. Today there is no trace, not even the smallest, of such concern in the minds of the Roman pontiffs, who boast of the succession of Peter and Paul. They have taken on the administration of the annates, as they call them, a sum far larger than the collections of which the apostle here speaks. They are criticised for its alienation even in the imperial diets, not to mention the complaints and grumbling of many pious men; but the brazen deceit of a harlot does not know how to blush. They misuse the goods of the Church at their pleasure for every kind of luxury, and for this treachery they are openly accused today; but they scoff at their accusers most disdainfully. Next, how does he avoid and guard against being found fault with by anyone in the administration of so great a sum of money? Not with laws, threats and curses, as the pontiffs are wont to do.

units.la: Quomodo ergo? Modo prorsus Apostolico & efficaci. Hunc ponit bimembrem, Primo, συλλό μενοι, inquit. Nő dicit συλλόντες, sed συλλόμενοι. συλλω inter alia significat ordinare ac contrahere, quod legibus & minis fieri solet à tyrannis: συλλομαι vero in passiuo contrahi metu ac cauere, quod eorum est, qui honestatis & innocentiae sunt studiosi. Sic contrahebatur Apostolus, & cauebat, ne incideret in maleuolorum hominum detractrices & carpentes linguas. Deinde προνοούμενοι, inquit, καλά, id est, solicita providentia procurantes honesta. Quomodo? Non tantum coram domino, inquit, sed etiam coram hominibus. Hoc est, non solum in veritate quę nota sit conscientiae Dei, sed & in specie ueritatis & honestatis, qua satisfiat conscientijs hominum. 1. Thess. 5. iubemur abstinere ab omni
units.tr: How then? In a way that is altogether apostolic and effective. He sets out this two-part method. First he says συλλόμενοι [sullomenoi], not συλλύντες [sullyntes]. The verb συλλύω [sullyō] means among other things to put in order and to gather together, which tyrants usually do by laws and threats. But συλλόμενοι in the passive means to be drawn together by fear and to take care, which belongs to those who are zealous for honesty and innocence. In this way the Apostle drew himself together and took care not to fall into the slanderous and carping tongues of ill-disposed men. Then, he says, προνοούμενοι καλά [pronooumenoi kala], that is, providing for honourable things with anxious foresight. How? "Not only before the Lord," he says, "but also before men." That is, not only in the truth as it is known to the conscience of God, but also in the appearance of truth and honesty, by which the consciences of men are satisfied. In 1 Thess. 5 we are commanded to abstain from every appearance of evil, not only from evil itself.

units.la: specie mala, nedum à malo ipso. Primũ quidè est approbare se conscientiae Dei, verùm sic animati sunt qui hoc veraciter faciūt, ut & coram hominibus quae honesta sunt diligenter procurent, ne quo pacto cuiquâ sint offendiculo. Nullius sibi fraudis ac perfidiae conscius erat Apostolus, sed syncerè coram domino agebat omnia, verùm quo & ecclesiae Dei satisfaceret, legationem hanc virorum fide dignorum ac selectorum Corinthũ mittit, quo coram hominibus quoq; honestè ageret. Hoc exemplũ Apostoli prorsus est omnib. Christi ministris imitandũ.
units.tr: Certainly the first thing is to approve oneself to the conscience of God. But those who do this sincerely are also so disposed that they diligently provide, before men too, for what is honourable, so that in no way they may become a stumbling block to anyone. The Apostle was conscious of no fraud or treachery, and he acted sincerely before the Lord in all things. Yet, so that he might satisfy the Church of God, he sends this embassy of trustworthy men chosen from the Corinthians, so that he might also act honourably before men. This example of the Apostle is altogether to be imitated by all ministers of Christ.

units.la: MISIMVS
units.tr: We sent

units.la: aút, inquit, vnà cum illis fratre nostrũ, quę probauimus in multis sæpenumero diligente.) Hunc tertiũ cõmendat à cõprobata diligentia. Quem probauimus diligenté, inquit, non semel atq; iterum sed sępenumero, non in modicis ac paucis, sed in multis. Sic ex primit non vulgarem sed singularem in hoc fratre diligentiam. Inuenias qui per occasionem, aut respectu proprij alicuius cõmodi, in vno & altero negocio diligentes sese offendant, quos propterea non vocamus ἀπροσκόπους, i. diligentes ac solicitos, quia qd' faciunt, faciunt non ex animo sed perfunctorie, & per occasionem alicuius lucri. Qui uero uel natura uel dono Dei uere sunt diligentes, illi in multis, in magnis & parvis, & semper sunt diligentes. Hi autem aptissimi sunt rebus gerendis, praesertim quae singularem solicitudinem ac diligentiam requirunt.
units.tr: "And with them," he says, "we sent our brother, whom we have often proved diligent in many matters." He commends this third man for his proven diligence. "Whom we have proved diligent," he says, not once or twice but often, not in small and few matters but in many. So from this he shows that the diligence of this brother was not ordinary but outstanding. You will find people who, on some occasion or from regard for some private advantage, show themselves diligent in one or another business; we do not call these ἀπροσκόπους [aproskopous], that is, diligent and careful, because what they do they do not from the heart but perfunctorily and for the sake of some gain. But those who are truly diligent, by nature or by the gift of God, are diligent in many things, in great and small matters, and always. Such men are most fit for managing affairs, especially those that require unusual care and diligence.

units.la: Quare fratrem hunc, propterea quod inuenerat eum saepenumero diligentem, causae huic vnà cum Tito & Luca praefecit. Quis aút frater hic fuerit, haud facilè conijci poterit. Neq; necessarium est vt conijciatur. Optandũ fuerit eiusmodi multos esse in ecclesia, qui curae, diligentiae, sedulitatis, ac solicitudinis dono diuinitus praediti, negocijs ecclesiasticis vtiliter gerendis praefici possint.
units.tr: Therefore he set this brother over this business together with Titus and Luke, because he had often found him diligent. Who this brother was can hardly be conjectured, nor is it necessary that he be conjectured. It would be desirable that there were many such men in the Church, endowed by God with the gift of care, diligence, zeal and concern, who could be usefully placed in charge of ecclesiastical business.

units.la: NVNC aút diligentiore, ob multa fiduciam quam habeo erga vos, inquit.) Illud, nunc aút diligentiorem, sic positũ est, vt ambiguũ sit, ad praecedentia ne sit vel ad sequentia referendũ. Si ad praecedentia, sensus erit. Misimus aút vnà cum illis fratre nostrũ quę probauimus in multis sepe diligentem, nunc vero, i. in hac causa, diligentiore deprehendimus, vel fore confidimus. Misimus aút eum ob multam fiduciam quam habemus erga vos. Si ad sequetia, quod mihi magis spbatur, exponendum erit ad hunc modum, qui nunc, in causa hac vestra, propter quã cum primis duob. mittitur, plus adhuc solicitudinis ac diligentiae pollicitus est, ob multam fiduciam, quã me erga vos habere intellexit. Vide aút prudentiam Apostoli. Dum hanc reddit rationẽ quare frater iste diligentior futurus sit in hoc Corinthiorum negocio, quod videlicet multũ sibi fiduciae erga ipsos esse intellexerit, simul eos incitat, vt eiusmodi fiduciae promptitudine & liberalitate contribuendi respondeant. Etenim vix aliquid magis improbũ ac dedecorosum videtur, quàm bene de nobis sperantium fallere fiduciam.
units.tr: "But now much more diligent, because of the great confidence I have in you," he says. The phrase "but now much more diligent" is so placed that it is unclear whether it refers to what precedes or to what follows. If to what precedes, the sense will be: "We sent with them our brother, whom we have often proved diligent in many matters; but now we have found him, that is, in this business, more diligent, or we trust he will be. We have sent him because of the great confidence we have in you." If to what follows, which seems to me more probable, it should be explained thus: he who now, in this your business, for which he is sent together with the first two, has promised even more care and diligence, because of the great confidence which he understood I have in you. Notice the prudence of the Apostle. While he gives the reason why this brother will be more diligent in this business of the Corinthians, namely that he has understood there is great confidence in them, at the same time he urges them to answer such confidence with readiness and generosity in giving. For scarcely anything seems more wicked and shameful than to disappoint the confidence of those who think well of us.

units.la: SIVE Titi nomine, inquit, qui socius meus est, & erga uos adiutor, siue aliorū qui fratres nostri sunt,& legati ecclesiarū,gloria Christi.) Græca sic habent, εἴτε ὑπὲρ Τίτου κοινωνὸς ἐμὸς εἰς ὑμᾶς συνεργός, εἴτε ἀδελφοὶ ἡμῶν, ἀπόστολοι ἐκκλησιῶν, δόξα Χριστοῦ. i. Siue pro Tito,socius meus, & erga uos adiutor, siue fratres nostri, legati ecclesiarū, gloria Christi. Omnino subintelligendum est aliquid, quod sententiam compleat. Chrysostomus sic habet, τί ἔστιν, εἴτε ὑπὲρ Τίτου· εἰ δὲ τι ἀπαύθν, φησί. i. Quid est, siue pro Tito? Sic dicendum est aliquid, inquit, hæc dicere possum, quod socius meus sit, & erga uos adiutor, siue de aliis audire quid uultis, & ipsi fratres nostri sunt, & legati ecclesiarum. Si cui hęc lectio placet, habebit hunc sensum. In summa, siue de Tito, siue de reliquis duobus quid sentire debeatis, quæritis. Titus socius meus est, & erga uos cooperarius, cæteri duo fratres nostri sunt, & præterea legati ecclesiarum, gloria Christi. Huic sensui competit, ut illud, εἴτε Τίτου uertatur, de Tito.
units.tr: "Whether on behalf of Titus," he says, "who is my partner and fellow-worker toward you, or of the others who are our brethren and messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ." The Greek reads: εἴτε ὑπὲρ Τίτου κοινωνὸς ἐμὸς εἰς ὑμᾶς συνεργός, εἴτε ἀδελφοὶ ἡμῶν, ἀπόστολοι ἐκκλησιῶν, δόξα Χριστοῦ. That is: whether for Titus, my partner and fellow-worker toward you, or our brothers, messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ. Something must certainly be supplied to complete the sense. Chrysostom reads: τί ἔστιν, εἴτε ὑπὲρ Τίτου; εἰ δὲ τι ἀπαύθν, φησί. That is: "What is it, whether on behalf of Titus?" He says: one must say something; I can say these things, that he is my partner and fellow-worker toward you, or, if you want to hear about the others, they too are our brothers and messengers of the churches. If one likes this reading, it will have this sense: in short, whether you are asking what you ought to think of Titus or of the other two, Titus is my partner and fellow-worker toward you, the other two are our brothers and besides messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ. The sense fits best if εἴτε Τίτου is rendered "concerning Titus."

units.la: Verum uersio Erasmi cum hoc sensu non concordat, neq; uulgata, quæ habet, siue pro Tito, qui est socius meus, &c. Hic erit Græca lectio sic compleda, εἴτε ὑπὲρ Τίτου, ὃς ἐστὶν κοινωνὸς ἡμῶν, καὶ εἰς ὑμᾶς συνεργός, εἴτε ὑπὲρ ἄλλων, οἱ εἰσὶν ἀδελφοὶ ἡμῶν, &c. ac uertenda. Siue pro Tito, qui est socius meus,&c. siue pro aliis qui sunt fratres nostri, ut sit sensus. Misimus autem unà cum illis fratrem nostrum, quem probauimus in multis sæpenumero diligentem, nunc uero multo diligentiorem ob multa fiduciam quam habeo erga uos, siue pro Tito, siue pro cæteris duobus, qua confido uos illum, tanquam socium meum, & erga uos cooperarium, & istos tanquam fratres nostros & legatos ecclesiarū, propter Christū, cuius sunt gloria, amanter ac cepturos, ac fidem illis indubitatam nō minus quàm mihi, si ad uos uenirem, præbituros. Lectori liberum sit iudicium. Vtrum sensum ex his probauerit, nihil est periculi.
units.tr: But Erasmus's translation does not agree with this sense, nor does the Vulgate, which has "whether for Titus, who is my partner, etc." Here the Greek would have to be completed thus: εἴτε ὑπὲρ Τίτου, ὃς ἐστὶν κοινωνὸς ἡμῶν, καὶ εἰς ὑμᾶς συνεργός, εἴτε ὑπὲρ ἄλλων, οἱ εἰσὶν ἀδελφοὶ ἡμῶν, etc., and it should be translated: "whether for Titus, who is my partner, etc., or for others who are our brothers," so that the sense is: "We have sent with them our brother, whom we have often proved diligent in many matters, but now much more diligent, because of the great confidence I have in you, whether for Titus or for the other two. I trust that you will receive them lovingly, as you would receive me, for the sake of Christ, to whom belongs the glory; Titus as my partner and fellow-worker toward you, and these as our brothers and messengers of the churches; and that you will show them no less unshaken trust than you would show me if I came to you." The reader is free to judge. Whichever sense he chooses, there is no danger.

units.la: SIVE pro Tito, inquit, qui est socius meus, & erga uos cooperarius meus.) Titus erat Apostoli discipulus, & tamē uocat eum socium suum. Quare? Quia erat illius cooperarius. So cius erat igitur laborum illius, non ipsius Apostolatus, & Apostolicæ authoritatis. Qua in re uidemus Apostoli modestiam, qua discipulum simpliciter uocat socium suum.
units.tr: "Whether for Titus," he says, "who is my partner and my fellow-worker toward you." Titus was the Apostle's disciple, and yet he calls him his partner. Why? Because he was his fellow-worker. He was therefore a partner in his labours, not in the apostleship itself or in apostolic authority. In this we see the modesty of the Apostle, who simply calls his disciple his partner.

units.la: SIVE aliorum, inquit, qui sunt fratres nostri, & legati ecclesiarum.) Nō dicit, qui sunt legati nostri, sed, qui sunt fratres nostri, & legati ecclesiarum. Tanta modestia causam hanc agit, ut authoritatem Apostolatus sui nō prætexat, sed magis respectū ecclesiarū, à quibus fratres isti ipsi erant coniuncti, ut ipsarum essent in hac causa legati. Vocat & Rom. Pontifex, quos secū habet Cardinales, suos fratres: uerum quos ad reges ex illis, & principes mittit, nō ecclesiæ legatos, sed legatos à latere appellat, quo suam in illis authoritatem uenetandam ac suspiciendam esse moneat. Nec immerito. Non enim ecclesiarum Christi, sed sua per illos agit negocia.
units.tr: "Whether of the others," he says, "who are our brothers and messengers of the churches." He does not say "who are our messengers," but "who are our brothers and messengers of the churches." He handles this matter with such modesty that he does not put forward the authority of his apostleship, but rather points to the churches, from which these brothers were sent, so that they were messengers of the churches in this business. The Roman Pontiff also calls the cardinals he keeps with him his brothers; but those whom he sends from among them to kings and princes he does not call messengers of the Church but legates a latere, so that they may be reminded to revere and esteem his authority in them. Nor undeservedly. For they carry on not the business of the churches of Christ but his own through them.

units.la: GLORIA Christi.) Siue duos illos fratres siue unà cum illis & Titum gloria Christi uocat, nobis obseruandum est, quos debeamus in ecclesia ministros habere in precio, amăter amplectì, ac reuereri. Eos uidelicet, qui sic ministrant solicitè ac fideliter, & sic præterea uiuunt, ut sint Christo suo domino non dedecori, sed gloriæ. Qui diuersum agunt, non Christo, sed uentri suo seruiêtes, quæstū in ecclesia sectantes, oues Christi non pascentes, sed perdentes, ac simul turpissimè uiuentes, ut non sunt gloria Christi, sed nominis illius ignominia, ita non sunt uenerādi, sed tanquam sal infatuatus contemnendi & abijciendi. PROINDE documētum charitatis uestrę, inquit, & nostræ de uobis gloriationis, in eos demonstretis, etiam in conspectu ecclesiarū.) Sic claudit cōmendationem trium istorū legatorum, per paraenesim ultro illam consequentem. Etenim cum tales essent quales eos commendauit, consequebatur dignos esse quos amanter susciperet, illisq; reuerenter obsequentur. Sic itaq; concludit. Proinde documentum charitatis uestræ, & nostræ de uobis gloriationis, in eos demonstretis. Hortatur eos, ut duo cōprobent ac demonstrent erga tres hosce fratres ac legatos, quæ utraq; ipsis maximę laudi & ornamento poterant esse futura. Vnum est, ut quàm sint charitate Christi præditi, legatos istos amanter ac reuerēter suscipiēdo declarent. Alterū, ut gloriationē suā de ipsis ueram fuisse comprobēt. Hoc est, ut promptè ac largiter in usus sanctorū contribuant. Hoc enim illos factuios speri fecerat, & Tito & fratribus reliquis & Macedonibus quoque gloriando de illis, quàm essent ad hanc causam animo prompto & alacri. Vide autem quomodo loquatur. Non dicit simpliciter: Proinde suscipite eos reuerenter ac placidè, & largiter cōtribuite, sed, τῶν ἔργων τῆς ἀγάπης ὑμῶν, id est, ostensionem, demonstrationem dilectionis uestræ, & nostræ de uobis gloriationis in eos ἐνδείξασθε. i. ostendite, demonstrate. Q.d. Scio uos diligere Christum & Christi ministros, ac propensos esse ad succurrendū egentibus sanctis. Quare nō hor tor ut tales sitis, sed ut quod estis, erga uiros istos esse uos demonstretis, quo & charitatē nō quàuis, sed uestrā, & pręptitudinē iuuādi patu peres, qua estis secundum gloriationē meam de uobis præditi, cōprobetis ac manifestā faciatis. Magnam ubiq; prudentiam spirat scripta Apostoli, uerum in iis potissimum, quæ ad Corinthios istos scripsit, si singula diligenter inspicias. Vtinam habeamus tales medicos & animarū & corporū, qui tanta solicitudine ac prudentia utantur erga curandos infirmos. Illud, etiá in conspectu ecclesiarū, in Græco est, εἰς πρόσωπον τῆς ἐκκλησίας. i. & in faciem ecclesiarū. Chrysostomo idè est quod εἰς δόξαν καὶ τιμὴν ἐκκλησίας. i. in gloriam & honorem ecclesiarum. Hoc sensu, in facie ecclesiarū aliquid facere, idé est quod respectu ac reuerentia ecclefiarũ facere. Etenim, inquit, si hos uiros honore afficeritis, cedet is honor ecclesijs, à quibus sunt missi. Non displicet hic sensus. Potest tamen etiâ sic exponi. Charitate uestram, & cóprobatione gloriationis nostrę de uobis, ostendite in eos nõ seorsim modo & priuatim, sed & in facie ecclefiarũ uestrarũ. Lyranus exponit, ut & alijs ecclesijs innotescat charitas uestra ad ædificationẽ fideliũ. Quoniâ non determinat de quib. ecclesijs loquatur, fit ut alij de ecclesijs exponant, quarũ fratres istos dixit esse legatos, alij de ecclesijs Achaiæ, ad quas illi mittebantur, alij in genere de omnib. ecclesijs, ad quas rumor de liberalitate Corinthiorum pertingere poterat. Quomodocunq; exponamus, uidemus Apostolũ requirere à Corinthijs, ut ecclesiarum habeant rationem.
units.tr: GLORY of Christ.) Whether he calls those two brothers, or Titus along with them, the glory of Christ, we must observe which ministers we ought to hold in esteem in the church, embracing and revering them with love: namely, those who minister so diligently and faithfully, and who live in such a way that they are a disgrace to no one but a glory to Christ their Lord. Those who act otherwise, serving not Christ but their belly, seeking gain in the church, not feeding but destroying Christ's sheep, and at the same time living most shamefully, are not the glory of Christ but a disgrace to his name; so they are not to be revered, but, like salt that has lost its savour, to be despised and cast out. THEREFORE show to them, he says, the proof of your love and of our boasting about you, even in the sight of the churches. So he closes the commendation of these three envoys, with an exhortation that follows directly from it. For since they were such as he has commended, it followed that they were worthy to be received with love and obeyed with reverence. So he concludes: Therefore show to them the proof of your love and of our boasting about you. He urges them to demonstrate two things toward these three brothers and envoys, both of which would be of the greatest praise and ornament to them. The first is that by receiving these envoys lovingly and reverently they should declare how much they have the love of Christ. The second is that they should prove that their boasting about them was true; that is, that they contribute promptly and generously to the needs of the saints. For he had led Titus, the other brothers and the Macedonians too to expect this, by boasting of how ready and eager they were for this cause. Note, however, how he speaks. He does not simply say: therefore receive them respectfully and gladly, and give generously; but he says, τῶν ἔργων τῆς ἀγάπης ὑμῶν, that is, the showing, the demonstration of your love, and of our boasting about you, in them ἐνδείξασθε, that is, show, demonstrate. As if he said: I know that you love Christ and Christ's ministers, and that you are inclined to help the needy saints. Therefore I do not exhort you to be such, but to show toward these men what you are, so that you may prove and make manifest the love, not of some sort but your own, and the readiness to help, which you possess, as my boasting about you has declared. The writing of the Apostle breathes great prudence throughout, but especially in those things which he wrote to these Corinthians, if you examine each part carefully. Would that we had such physicians of souls and of bodies, who use such care and prudence toward the sick they are to heal. The phrase, even in the sight of the churches, in Greek is εἰς πρόσωπον τῆς ἐκκλησίας, that is, in the face of the churches. Chrysostom has, for this, εἰς δόξαν καὶ τιμὴν ἐκκλησίας, that is, to the glory and honour of the churches. In this sense, to do something in the face of the churches is the same as to do it out of respect and reverence for the churches. For, he says, if you honour these men, that honour will return to the churches from which they were sent. This sense is not unpleasing. Yet it can also be explained thus: show in them your love and the confirmation of our boasting about you, not only separately and privately, but also in the face of your churches. Lyra explains that your love may also become known to the other churches, for the edification of the faithful. Since he does not determine which churches he means, some expound it of the churches whose brothers he called these men to be envoys of; others of the churches of Achaia, to which they were being sent; others in general of all the churches to which the report of the Corinthians' generosity could reach. However we explain it, we see the Apostle asking the Corinthians to take account of the churches.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: Eandem materiam prosequitur, quam capite præcedenti cœpit.
units.tr: He pursues the same subject that he began in the preceding chapter.

units.la: CAPVT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: AM de subministratione qui dē quæ fit in sanctos superuacuũ est mihi scribere uobis. Noui enim promptitudinem animi uestri, quâ de uobis iacto apud Macedones: quod Achaía parata sit ab anno superiore, & uestrũ exemplũ prouocauit cõplures. Misi tamẽ hos fratres, ne gloriatio nostra qua glorier de uobis, inanis fiat in hac parte: ut quemadmodum dicebam, parati sitis, ne quo pacto fiat, ut si mecũ uenerint Macedões, & offenderint uos imparatos, nos pudore suffundamur, ut ne dicam uos, in hoc argumento gloriationis. Proinde necessarium arbitratus sum adhortari fratres, ut prius accederent ad uos, & præpararẽt iam ante promissam bonam collationem uestram, ut ea sit in promptu, sic tâquam bona collatio, & non tanquam fraudatio.
units.tr: Concerning the ministry that is performed for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you. For I know the readiness of your mind, of which I boast among the Macedonians: that Achaia has been prepared since last year, and your example has provoked very many. Yet I have sent these brothers, so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this respect; so that, as I was saying, you may be ready, lest by any chance, if the Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we be put to shame, not to mention you, in this matter of boasting. Therefore I have judged it necessary to exhort the brothers to go on ahead to you and to prepare beforehand your promised generous gift, so that it may be ready, as a gift that is generous and not as an extortion.

units.la: Cohærent ista cum præcedẽtibus, à quibus non erat distinctione hac noui capitis auellenda. In calce præcedentis dixerat: Proinde documentũ charitatis uestræ, & nostræ de uobis gloriationis in eos demonstretis, & in conspectum ecclefiarũ. Iam postremæ huius particulæ, & in conspectũ ecclefiarũ, ratione subijcit, dicens: Nam de subministratione quidem quæ fit in sanctos, superuacuũ est mihi scribere uobis. Q_d. Quod uos hortor, ut documentũ charitatis uestræ & nostræ de uobis gloriationis in legatos hosce demonstretis, nõ hoc animo facio, ut ipse experiar, quomodo hac in re sitis
units.tr: These things cohere with what precedes, and this division of a new chapter must not tear them apart. At the end of the previous chapter he had said: Therefore show to them the proof of your love and of our boasting about you, and that before the churches. Now he gives the reason for this last phrase, and before the churches, saying: For concerning the ministry that is performed for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you. That is, I urge you to show these envoys the proof of your love and of our boasting about you; I do not do this with the intention of testing for myself how you are disposed in this matter, as if I doubted your love.

units.la: affecti, quasi de uestra charitate dubitẽ. Nã mihi quidẽ, id est, quod me attinet, non est opus, sed superuacuum, ut scribam uobis de subministratione hac quæ fit in sanctos. Verũ quod scribo, ob id facio, ut ecclesijs cæteris innotescat uestra charitas, manifestumq;fiat, q nõ frustra de animi uestri simus promptitudine gloriati. Etenim mihi illa satis est perspecta. Sic postquâ dixit: Nã mihi quidẽ superuacuũ est scribere uobis de subministratione hac quę fit in sanctos, mox subiecit: Noui enim promptitudinem animi uestri, quam de uobis iacto apud Macedones. Verbórũ itaq; istorũ emphasis est in pronomine MIHI, & ordinanda est lectio ad hunc modum: Nam de subministratione hac quæ fit in sanctos, mihi quidẽ superuacuum est scribere uobis. Vocula, quidem, non est otiosè posita, id quod infrà patebit, ubi dicit: Misi tamen hosce fratres. Quod si tamen illam ut posita est acceperis, ac legeris: Nã de subministratione quidẽ q fit in sanctos, &c. ne sic qdẽ impeditur sensus quẽ ostedim. NAM de subministratione quidem, inquit, quæ fit in sanctos.) In Græco est ἀπὸ μὲν γὰρ τῆς διακονίας. Loquitur de suo ministerio, quo in usus sanctorũ cõtributa à fidelibus colligebat. Quamuis nonnulli exponunt de subministratione contribuentium nõ colligẽtis Apostoli. Notum tamẽ est, quomodo uoce hac διακονία, in hac causa utatur. In priore epistola cap. ulti. mo, cum de modo colligendi fidelium contributa admonere uellet, uocem λογίαν usurpauit, dicens, ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς λογίας τῆς εἰς τοὺς ἁγίους. i. De collecta uero quę fit in sanctos. Ipsam uero contributionem, & cõtributa, uocat, χάριν & κοινωνίαν & εὐλογίαν, id est, gratiam, communicationem & benedictionem. De eo quod dicit: quę fit in sanctos. 1. Cor. ult. diximus.
units.tr: For as far as I am concerned, that is, for my part, there is no need, but it is superfluous, to write to you about this ministry that is performed for the saints. But what I write, I do so that your love may become known to the other churches, and that it may be made clear that we have not boasted about the readiness of your mind in vain. For I have had sufficient proof of it. So, after saying: For it is superfluous for me to write to you about this ministry that is performed for the saints, he immediately added: For I know the readiness of your mind, of which I boast among the Macedonians. The emphasis of these words lies in the pronoun ME, and the reading should be ordered in this way: For concerning this ministry that is performed for the saints, it is indeed superfluous for me to write to you. The little word indeed has not been placed idly, as will appear below, where he says: Yet I have sent these brothers. But if you take it and read it as it stands, For concerning the ministry indeed that is performed for the saints, etc., the sense is not hindered, as I will show. FOR concerning the ministry indeed, he says, that is performed for the saints. In Greek it is: ἀπὸ μὲν γὰρ τῆς διακονίας. He speaks of his own ministry, by which he collected contributions from the faithful for the use of the saints. Although some explain it as the ministry of those who contributed, not of the Apostle who collected. It is well known, however, how he uses the word διακονία in this matter. In the first epistle, in the last chapter, when he wished to advise about the manner of collecting the contributions of the faithful, he used the word λογία, saying: ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς λογίας τῆς εἰς τοὺς ἁγίους, that is, concerning the collection that is made for the saints. But the contribution itself, and the contributions, he calls χάρις, κοινωνία and εὐλογία, that is, grace, communication and blessing. On the phrase that is performed for the saints we have spoken in our commentary on 1 Corinthians, at the end.

units.la: SVPERVACVVM est mihi scrbere uobis, inquit.) Et tamen interim prolixè scribebat, quamuis sciret illorum promptitudinem, hoc agens, ut illa innotesceret ecclesijs ad ædificationẽ. Admonétur hic ministri uerbi, ut etiâsi sciât ipsi quomodo animati sint fidelesquibus præsunt, urgeat tñ eos, ut id manifestũ faciant ipsis operibus, quo & alij ædificentur. Deinde & illi, qui propterea quod quę faciêda sint noruṇt, ægre ferũt si de illis admoneãtur sæpius, habet hic quod cogitét. Superfluũ quidem uideri, si sæpius audiant iam antea cognita, uerũ nihilo secius admonẽdos esse se, ut quę sciunt, opere quoq; præstent, ac scire se declarent.
units.tr: IT IS SUPERFLUOUS for me to write to you, he says. And yet meanwhile he wrote at length, although he knew their readiness, doing this so that it might become known to the churches for their edification. Here the ministers of the Word are admonished that, even if they know how the faithful over whom they preside are disposed, they should still urge them to make it plain by their works, so that others may be built up as well. Then also those who, because they know what must be done, are displeased if they are admonished often, have here something to consider: it may seem superfluous if they hear again what they already knew, yet they must nonetheless be admonished, so that they may also perform by their deeds what they know and show that they know it.

units.la: NOVI enim, inquit, promptitudine animi uestri.) Vnde illam sciebat. Suprà cap. præcedẽti dixit: qui nõ solũ facere, uerumetiá uelle iam cœpistis anno superiore. At interea decies mutari poterát, & προθυμία ipsorũ desinere in μιλαθυμίαν, id quod in rebus humanis quotidie fieri uidemus. Sanè quod Galatis accidit, accidere potuit & istis. Verũ ꝑ ingenio charitatis meliora sperabat, credẽs eos eadẽ adhuc esse pròptitudine præditos in hac causa, qua præditi fuerant anno superiore. Cum ergo diuersum quid de illis nesciret, hâc se scire dixit.
units.tr: FOR I know, he says, the readiness of your mind. From where did he know it? Above, in the previous chapter, he said: who not only have begun to do, but also to will, last year. Yet in the meantime their readiness could have changed ten times over and turned from προθυμία into μιλαθυμία (sluggishness), as we daily see happening in human affairs. Certainly what happened to the Galatians could have happened to these too. But he hoped for better things from the disposition of charity, believing that they were still endowed with the same readiness in this matter with which they had been endowed the year before. Since, therefore, he did not know anything different about them, he said that he knew this.

units.la: QVAM de uobis iacto, inquit, apud Macedones.) At Macedonibus opus non erat, ut exemplo Corinthiorum ad promptitudinem contribuēdi prouocarentur, cum usqueadeo <bl>ζηλωταί</bl> essent, ut ipsorum promptitudinem initio capitis praecedentis Corinthijs imitandam proponēs, satis comendare & depraedicare nequiuerit. Quorsum ergo promptitudinem Corinthiorū tantopere apud eos iactare voluit? Respondeo. Duo fines erant ipsi gloriandi de alacritate eorum, qui se promptos in hac causa & consimilibus alijs ostendebant. Vnus erat, ut alios ad imitationem illorum prouocaret. Hoc consilio Macedonum promptitudinem admodum eximiam iactauit in hac Epistola apud Corinthios. Alter erat, ut eos qui iam propti erant, & <bl>ζηλωταί</bl>, in promptitudine quam habebant aliorum exemplis confirmaret, etsi fieri posset, magis adhuc prouocheret, & ad ampliora incitaret. Sic promptitudinem Corinthiorum hic apud Macedones iactare se dicit.
units.tr: WHICH I boast of among the Macedonians, he says. But the Macedonians had no need to be provoked to readiness in contributing by the example of the Corinthians, since they were so zealous that, when at the beginning of the previous chapter he proposed their readiness for the Corinthians to imitate, he could not commend and extol it enough. Why, then, did he wish to boast so much of the readiness of the Corinthians among them? I answer: there were two purposes for boasting of the eagerness of those who showed themselves ready in this matter and in similar others. One was to provoke others to imitate them. With this design he boasted, in this Epistle, among the Corinthians of the very remarkable readiness of the Macedonians. The other was that those who were already ready and zealous might be confirmed in the readiness they had by the examples of others, and, if possible, be provoked even more and urged on to greater things. So here he says that he boasts among the Macedonians of the readiness of the Corinthians.

units.la: QVOD Achaia parata sit ab anno superiore, inquit.) Hoc uidelicet iactabat apud Macedones. Nō dicit qd Corinthus, sed, qd Achaia parata sit. Nō enim de Corinthiorū tantum ecclesia, sed & de caeteris quae in ea regione erant, loquens, paratas eas esse iactabat. Achaiae metropolis est Corinthus. Quare dū eam nominabat, simul & Corinthū complectebatur. Et interim de Achaia iactando apud Macedones, non Philippenses tantum, uel Thessaloni censes, qui metropolitani erat in Macedonia, sed totam Macedoniam exemplo Achaiae in promptitudine contribuendi confirmabat.
units.tr: THAT Achaia has been prepared since last year, he says. This, of course, he was boasting among the Macedonians. He does not say that Corinth has been prepared, but that Achaia has been. For speaking not only of the church of Corinth but also of the other churches in that region, he was boasting that they were ready. Corinth is the metropolis of Achaia. So when he named Achaia, he at the same time embraced Corinth as well. And meanwhile, in boasting of Achaia among the Macedonians, he was strengthening not only the Philippians or the Thessalonians, who were the metropolitan city in Macedonia, but the whole of Macedonia, by the example of Achaia, in readiness to contribute.

units.la: ET uestrum exemplū prouocauit plures, inquit.) In Graeco est, <bl>ὁ τῶν ὑμῶν ζῆλος</bl>, id est, & zelus qui ex uobis. Vulgata habet, & aemula tio uestra. Apparet non esse frustra quod non dicit, <bl>ὁ ὑμῶν ζῆλος</bl>, id est, & uester zelus, sed, <bl>ὁ ἐξ ὑμῶν ζῆλος</bl>, id est, & zelus qui ex uobis, subintellige, nascebatur. Loquitur enim, meo iudicio, non de Corinthiorum zelo, sed Macedonum, quem illorum complures ex gloriatione ipsius conceperat, qua Achaiam dicebat esse paratam. Quare uulgata rectius haberet, & aemulatio uestri, quàm, & aemulatio uestra.
units.tr: AND YOUR EXAMPLE has provoked many, he says. In Greek it is ὁ τῶν ὑμῶν ζῆλος, that is, and the zeal which comes from you. The Vulgate has and your emulation. It is clear that it is not without reason that he does not say ὁ ὑμῶν ζῆλος, that is, and your zeal, but ὁ ἐξ ὑμῶν ζῆλος, that is, and the zeal which comes from you, understand: was arising. For he speaks, in my judgment, not of the zeal of the Corinthians but of the Macedonians, which many of them had conceived from his boasting, by which he said Achaia was prepared. Therefore the Vulgate would more correctly have and the emulation of you, rather than and your emulation.

units.la: Quid est autem, quod Macedones hic exemplo Corinthiorum prouocatos dicit, cum initio praecedentis capitis tantopere de illis praedicauerit, quod fuerint <bl>ζηλωταί</bl> in hac causa, illorumq; promptitudinem Corinthijs exempli loco propositurit?
