Respondeo. Non dicit, prouocauit omnes, sed, prouocauit plures, significans esse inter eos plures, quibus occasio nem aemulationis de Achaia gloriando praebuerit. Interea nō aufertur caeteris gloria, quā illis supra tribuit. Vide autem quàm prudenter prouocet eos Macedonum iitorum exemplo, ut & ipsi uicissim per illud ad aemulationem permoueantur.
units.tr: But why does he here say that the Macedonians were provoked by the example of the Corinthians, when at the beginning of the previous chapter he had praised them so highly, because they were zealous in this matter, and had set their readiness before the Corinthians as an example? I answer: he does not say that he provoked all, but that he provoked many, signifying that among them there were many to whom he had given the occasion of emulation by boasting about Achaia. Meanwhile the glory which he had attributed to the others above is not taken away. Notice, moreover, how prudently he provokes them by the example of the Macedonians, so that they in turn may be moved to emulation through it.

units.la: MISI tamen hos fratres, inquit.) Hacte-nus ab initio capitis exposuit, quomodo non ad hoc de submi-nistratione quae fit in sanctos ad ipsos scribat, ut ipse cognoscat quàm sint prompto erga illam animo, quod id esset superuacuum, quandoquidē abunde sciat, qua sint promptitudine, sed ad hoc potius ut eam declarent erga legatos istos, & ecclesijs manifestam faciant, qua de re iam subijcit, dicens: Misi tamen hos fratres, &c. In Graeco est, <bl>ἔπεμψα δὲ</bl>, id est, sed misi, uel, misi uero, ubi <bl>ἀπέστειλα</bl> respondet <bl>εἰμί</bl>, quod initio capitis habetur ad hunc modū, <bl>ἐπεὶ μὲν γὰρ τῆς διακονίας</bl>, id est, nam de ministerio quod fit in sanctos, superuacuū quidem est mihi scribere uobis, &c. misi tamen hos fratres.
units.tr: "I have nevertheless sent these brothers," he says. Up to this point, from the beginning of the chapter, he has explained that he is not writing to them about the ministry that is done for the saints so that he himself may learn how eager they are for it. That would be superfluous, since he already knows well how ready they are. He writes rather so that they may show this eagerness toward these envoys and make it plain to the churches. He now adds this point, saying: "I have sent these brothers," etc. The Greek is ἔπεμψα δὲ [ἔπεμψα δὲ], that is, "but I have sent," or "yet I have sent," where ἀπέστειλα answers to εἰμί. This is found at the beginning of the chapter in this form: ἐπεὶ μὲν γὰρ τῆς διακονίας [ἐπεὶ μὲν γὰρ τῆς διακονίας], that is, "for concerning the ministry that is done for the saints, it is indeed superfluous for me to write to you," etc. "Yet I have sent these brothers."

units.la: NE gloriatio nostra, inquit, qua glorior de uobis, inanis fiat in hac parte.) Fusius exponit ad quid fratres istos miserit. Summa est, metuebat ne si imparati deprehenderentur, una cum ipsis confusioni exponeretur, quādoquidem paratos esse fuerat gloriatus. Hoc significans, dicit: Ne gloriatio nostra qua de uobis glorior, intellige, quod parata sit Achaia, inanis fiat. Inane est, quod uero destitutū est. Veritas igitur sola est, quae omnia nostra dicta & facta solida reddit, sic ut sine illa prorsus sint inania. Magna est haec gloria ueritatis. Iam cū mendax sit omnis homo, quid consequitur aliud, quàm uanum & inanem esse omnem hominem, quatenus ueritate destituitur? Quare si uanitatis dedecus fugimus, necesse est, ut ue-ritati studeamus.
units.tr: "That our boasting," he says, "in which I boast about you, may not be made empty in this respect." He goes on at more length to explain why he sent these brothers. The sum is this: he feared that if the Corinthians were found unprepared, he himself would be exposed to shame together with them, since he had boasted that they were ready. Meaning this, he says: "that our boasting, in which I glory about you (understand: that Achaia is ready), may not be made empty." What is empty is what is found to lack its substance. Truth alone, therefore, is what makes all our words and deeds solid, so that without it they are altogether empty. This is the great glory of truth. Since every man is a liar, what else follows, except that every man is vain and empty, insofar as he is destitute of truth? Hence, if we flee the disgrace of vanity, we must be zealous for truth.

units.la: INANIS, inquit, fiat in hac parte.) Gloriabatur de illis non hoc tantum, quod parati essent ad contribuendum, sed & quod abundarent fide, sermone, scientia, ac diligentia. Quare ne uniuersam suam de illis gloriationem in hac causam arctare uideretur, ubi dixit, ne gloriatio nostra qua glorior de uobis, inanis fiat, adiecit, in hac parte, ut reliquá gloriationem ad hanc causam non pertinentem excluderet. De illa siquidē certior erat quàm de ista. Erat autem pars ista non minoris momenti, imò hoc maioris, quàm illa, quo magis quàm illa Christianae habebat charitatis documentum, sine qua inanis est omnis fides & scientia, id quod adijcere poterat, uerum parcebat illis, sciens quanti facerent fidei, sermonis, & scientiae, quam habebant, excellentiam.
units.tr: "May be made empty," he says, "in this respect." He was boasting about them not only because they were ready to contribute, but also because they abounded in faith, speech, knowledge and diligence. So that he would not seem to restrict his whole boasting about them to this one matter, when he said, "that our boasting in which I glory about you may not be made empty," he added "in this respect," in order to exclude the rest of his boasting, which did not pertain to this matter. For he was more certain of that boasting than of this one. Yet this part was of no less importance, indeed of greater importance than the other, inasmuch as it gave more proof of Christian love, without which all faith and knowledge is empty. He could have added this, but he spared them, knowing how highly they valued the excellence of the faith, speech and knowledge that they had.

units.la: VT quemadmodum dicebam, inquit, paratī sitis.) Ad hoc scilicet misérat legatos istos. Quid autem est illud, quemadmodum dicebam? Quid dixerat? Achaiam dixerat esse paratam ab anno superiore. Ne hoc non ueraciter dixisse uideretur, misit legatos hosce, ut paratos se redderent.
units.tr: "As I was saying," he says, "that you may be ready." He had sent these envoys for precisely this purpose. But what is "as I was saying"? What had he said? He had said that Achaia had been ready since the previous year. Lest he seem not to have spoken truly in this, he sent these men so that they might make the Corinthians ready.

units.la: Sed dices. Ergo nondum erant parati, & uerum non erat, quod Achaiam parata esse fuerat gloriatus. Respondeo. Quoniam anno superiore & facere & uelle coeperant, sicuti cap. praecedenti dixit, ideo Achaia parata esse gloriabatur, nō quod in uniuersum parati iam essent, sed quod studio parandi se, & opere ipso essent occupati. Sic solemus de illis gloriari, quos uidemus opus aliquod alacri animo aggredi, ut dicamus illud esse iam factum propterea, quòd sic animatos haudquaquam cessaturos esse confidimus, donec quod tam cupide coeperunt, opere compleant. Accidit hoc Apostolo in causa Corinthiorum. Quare non est uanitatis accusandus ob id, quod Achaiam hoc sensu dixit esse paratam.
units.tr: "But you will say: then they were not yet ready, and it was not true that he had boasted that Achaia was ready." I answer: since they had begun both to act and to will in the previous year, as he said in the preceding chapter, Achaia was therefore boasted of as ready, not because they were already ready in every respect, but because they were occupied with eagerness to prepare themselves and with the work itself. We commonly speak in this way about those whom we see taking up some task with a willing mind: we say that it is already done, because we are confident that such people, once so inspired, will not cease until they finish with work what they have so eagerly begun. This happened to the Apostle in the case of the Corinthians. Therefore he is not to be accused of vanity because he said in this sense that Achaia was ready.

units.la: NE quo pacto fiat, inquit, ut si mecum uenerint Macedones, & offenderint uos imparatos, nos pudore suffundamur; ut ne dicá uos, in hoc argumento gloriationis.) Quoniam apud Macedones paratam esse Achaiam fuerat gloriatus, & apud illos agebat cum haec scirent, esset que probabile, fore in ipsius comitatu cum discederet, nonnullos Macedones ab ecclesijs ad id officij delectos, ut ipsum deducerent & comitarentur, metuebat ne si Corinthū una cum illis ueniret, & imparatos offenderet, pro gaudio pudore suffunderetur.
units.tr: "Lest by any means," he says, "if the Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we be put to shame, not to say you, in this matter of boasting." Since he had said among the Macedonians that Achaia was ready, and was dealing with them while they knew this, and since it was likely that some Macedonians, chosen by the churches for this duty, would be in his company when he departed to escort and accompany him, he feared that if he came to Corinth together with them and found the Corinthians unprepared, he would be covered with shame instead of joy.

units.la: VT si mecū, inquit, uenerint Macedones.) Quod Cotinthū postea uenerit, non legimus. Constituit quidem illò proficisci, ut hic & alijs in locis apparet, uerùm certis de causis quod decernebat, non perfecit. Cum hic dicit, ut si mecum uenerint Macedones, quasi de suo ad illos aduentu nihil dubitans, de comitatu Macedonum tantū dubitáter loquitur, tanquam de re etsi non certo futura, tali tamen quae fieri probabiliter posset. Qua in re cum neutrum sit postea factum (nam è Macedonia recta contendit Hierosolymam, idque festinanter, ut illic esset in die Pentecoft. habens in comitatu suo Macedones quatuor, sicuti uidere est Act. 20.) nobis obseruandum est, non modò non semper euenire quae sancti decernunt, sed & nonnunquam metuere eos frustra, ne eueniat quae futura non sunt, atque ita probabili euentuum opinione decipi, perinde atque caeteros homines. Cum haec acciderint ipsis apostolis, sunt à nobis patienter ferenda, tanquam humana, quibus admoneamur, ut quo minus cer ti de futuris euentibus sumus, hoc maiore fide à certitudine diuinę prouidentiae in omnibus pendeamus.
units.tr: "If the Macedonians come with me," he says. We do not read that he afterwards came to Corinth. He did indeed resolve to set out there, as appears here and in other places, but for certain reasons he did not carry out what he had decided. When he says here, "if the Macedonians come with me," he speaks of his coming to them as if he had no doubt about it, but he speaks with hesitation only about the Macedonians' accompanying him, as about a matter which, though not certain to happen, could probably come about. Since neither of these things happened afterwards (for from Macedonia he made straight for Jerusalem, and in haste, so as to be there on the day of Pentecost, having in his company several Macedonians, as may be seen in Acts 20), we must observe that what the saints decide does not always come to pass, and that sometimes they fear in vain that what is not going to happen might happen, and are thus deceived by a probable opinion of outcomes, just as other men are. When such things have happened to the apostles themselves, they are to be borne by us patiently as human things, by which we are admonished that the less certain we are about future events, the more firmly, with greater faith, we should depend in all things on the certainty of divine providence.

units.la: ET offenderint uos, inquit, imparatos, nos pudore suffundamur.) Quo animo ab hoc fi-bi pudore metuerit, & qualis ille fit, suprà in calce capitis septimi annotauimus, ubi dixit: Quod si quid apud illum de uobis gloriatus sum, non sum pudefactus.
units.tr: "And find you," he says, "unprepared, we be put to shame." With what feeling he feared this shame for himself, and what sort of shame it was, we noted above at the end of the seventh chapter, where he said: "If I have boasted anything to him about you, I have not been put to shame."

units.la: VT ne dicam uos, inquit.) Hac particula admonet, cum pudorem non sibi tantum, sed & ipsis Corinthijs euenturum, si imparati offendantur. Sed ea quoque de re loco iam citato diximus.
units.tr: "Not to say you," he says. By this particle he warns that the shame would fall not only upon himself but also upon the Corinthians themselves, if they were found unprepared. But we have already spoken about this point in the passage cited above.

units.la: IN hoc, inquit, argumento gloriationis.) In Graeco est, ἐν τῇ καυχήσει ταύτῃ τῆς καυχήσεως, Vulgatus interpres reddidit, in hac substantia. Admonent nonnulli uertendum esse: in hac fiducia gloriationis, eo quod καυχήσις non solum substantiam, sed & audaciā & confidetiam Budaeo teste significet. Sane haec lectio nō ma-
units.tr: "In this matter of boasting," he says. The Greek is ἐν τῇ καυχήσει ταύτῃ τῆς καυχήσεως [ἐν τῇ καυχήσει ταύτῃ τῆς καυχήσεως]. The Vulgate translator rendered it "in this substance." Some suggest it should be rendered "in this confidence of boasting," since καυχήσις signifies not only substance but also boldness and confidence, according to Budaeus. Certainly this reading does not agree badly

units.la: lè conuenit praesenti causae. Etenim quod gloriatus fuerat de Corinthijs Apostolus, esse ilos paratos, magis fecerat ex bona erga eos fiducia, qua quod facere coeperant perfecturos sperabat, quàm ex certa scientia. Apparet tamen hanc uocem & hic & infrà cap. II. usurpatam esse pro καυχήσει, quae uox propositū, causam, materiam & argumentum significat. Vtut sit, nihil dicit aliud, quàm quod paulò ante dixit, ἐν τῇ μέρει τούτῳ, id est, in hac parte. Idè enim cauere uoluit hoc loco quod illic.
units.tr: with the present case. For the Apostle's boasting about the Corinthians, that they were ready, arose more from his good confidence in them, by which he hoped they would complete what they had begun, than from certain knowledge. It appears, however, that this word is used here and in chapter 11 in the sense of καύχησις, which signifies the purpose, the matter, and the subject. Whatever the case, he says nothing other than what he said a little before, ἐν τῷ μέρει τούτῳ [ἐν τῷ μέρει τούτῳ], that is, "in this respect." For here he wished to guard against the same thing that he had guarded against there.

units.la: PROINDE necessarium, inquit, arbitratus sum adhortari fratres, ut prius accederent ad uos.) Quare necessarium? An necessariū erat Apostolo cauere, ne si Macedones uenirét, imparati offenderentur Corinthij & confusioni unà cum ipsis exponeretur? Sic ipse animatus erat, & sic sentiebat. Hodie nihil uidetur minus esse necessariū, quam uitare confusionem & pudorem, ne ministerium uerbi infametur. Nihil enim minus quaeritur, quàm quod summopere quaerendum ducebat Apostolus, & ut ducebat ita & sedulo quaerebat, aedificationem uidelicet ecclesiarum & Regni Christi propagationem, quae eiusmodi offendiculis ex comperta mendaciorum uanitate natis, mirum in modum destruitur. Quare praeter ratione non erat, quod ad uitādum hoc offendiculum necessarium iudicabat mittere fratres, qui quod adhuc curādum erat curarent.
units.tr: "Therefore," he says, "I judged it necessary to exhort the brothers that they should go to you first." Why necessary? Was it necessary for the Apostle to take care lest, if the Macedonians came, the Corinthians should be found unprepared and he should be exposed to confusion together with them? Such was his feeling, and such was his judgment. Today nothing seems less necessary than avoiding confusion and shame, lest the ministry of the Word be brought into disrepute. For nothing is sought less than what the Apostle thought ought to be sought above all, and what he sought diligently as he thought it: namely, the edification of the churches and the propagation of the kingdom of Christ, which is destroyed in a wonderful way by such stumbling-blocks, born from the known vanity of lies. Therefore it was not without reason that he judged it necessary to send brothers to avoid this stumbling-block, who would attend to what still needed attention.

units.la: ADHORTARI fratres, inquit.) Non satis pro authoritate apostolica loquitur, quam ho die Romani mandando & imperando fortiter exercendam esse iudicant. Poterat dicere, misi fratres, uerum quemadmodum miserat eos non mādando, sed hortando, ita se illos etiam misisse scribit, ut modestiam & facto & scripto spiret.
units.tr: "Exhort the brothers," he says. He does not speak with full apostolic authority, which the Romans today think should be exercised forcefully by commanding and dictating. He could have said "I have sent the brothers," but as he had sent them not by command but by exhortation, he writes that he sent them in a way that breathes modesty in both deed and writing.

units.la: VT prius, inquit, accederent ad uos.) Romanus Pontifex citasset eos peremptorie, ut ad se uenirent Romam, non misisset fratres, qui ad eos accederent. Verum diuersum apostolatū diuersi mores comitantur. Verus Christi Apostolus, omnia studiosissimè uitans, quę aliquam poterant dominatus praeferre speciē, non uocauit ad se Corinthios, sed misit ad eos fratres, qui quod agendū erat curarent, priusquam ipse cum Macedonibus ad eos uenisset.
units.tr: "That they may come to you beforehand," he says. A Roman Pontiff would have summoned them peremptorily to come to Rome and would not have sent brothers to go to them. But different conduct accompanies different kinds of apostleship. The true Apostle of Christ, avoiding with the utmost care everything that might carry any appearance of lordship, did not summon the Corinthians to himself but sent brothers to them to attend to what needed doing, before he himself came to them with the Macedonians.

units.la: ET praepararet, inquit, iam ante promissam bonam collationem uestram.) Ad quid eos miserit hisce uerbis tandem exprimit. In Graeco est, καὶ προεπαγγείλωνται, id est, prius perficiāt, absoluant, & expediant, iam ante promissam bonam collationem uestram. In Graeco est: εὐλογίαν ὑμῶν, id est, benedictione uestram. Sic autem uocat collectam, quae in usus sanctorū parari debebat. Eam iam anno superiore promiserant non uerbis modo, sed & facto & uoluntate. Ideo uocat eam ante promissam, ut plus ponderis habeat & legatio fratrum, & praesens hoc scriptum. Nam ut uulgo dicitur, omne promissum cadit in debitum. De debito tamen tacens, promissionis meminit, quasi illius fiducia fretus, fratres istos miserit, ut collectam promissam præpararent.
units.tr: "And that they may prepare beforehand your promised generous gift," he says. Here at last he states what he sent them to do. The Greek is καὶ προεπαγγείλωνται, that is, that they may first complete, finish and arrange your promised generous gift beforehand. The Greek has εὐλογίαν ὑμῶν [your blessing], that is, your benediction. He calls the collection by this name because it had to be prepared for the uses of the saints. The Corinthians had promised it already the year before, not only in words but also in deed and in willingness. He calls it "promised beforehand" so that both the mission of the brothers and this present letter may carry more weight. For, as the common saying goes, every promise becomes a debt. Yet, saying nothing of the debt, he mentions the promise, as if relying on its trust he had sent these brothers so that they might prepare the promised collection.

units.la: VT ea sit in promptu, inquit, sic tanquâ bona collatio, & non tanquâ fraudatio.) In Græco est, χαὶ μὴ ὡσπερ πλεονεξίαν. Vulgata versio habet, non quasi auaritiam. Vox πλεονεξία significat nimiam illam cupiditatẽ, qua plura quàm par sit cupimus, à plus habedo. Ideo uetus interpres uertit, auaritiam. Ambiguum autẽ est intelligendum ne sit de cupiditate Corinthiorum uel fratrum istorum, quos miserat Apostolus. Sanè poterat ex utraq; tam dantium q; accipientium parte peccari. Qui dat, si det tenacius, facit hoc pleonexiæ uicio. Qui accipit, si accipiat cupidius, æquo & plura appetat q; coeuniat, facit hoc & ipse per pleonexiā. Existimo tamen significasse Apostolū Corinthijs, tum demum fore contributionem ipsorum ἐπαγγελία, id est, paratam ac promptam, si sit non parca ac tenaciter collata, sed largiter, sicuti de cet eulogiam, in usus sanctorum promissam. Et huic sensui fauent sequetia. Chrysostomus tamen alteri sententiæ adstipulatur. Nam sic exponit: μὴ νομίσωμεν, φησί, ὅτι ὡς πλεονεκτοῦντες αὐτῷ λαμβάνομεν, ἀλλ' ὡς αὐτοι γενέσθαι ὑμῖν ἐυλο-γίας. Erasmus quoq; sic sensisse uidetur, dum reddidit: & non tàquam fraudatio. Hoc sensu feré omnes maiorum nostrorum eleemosynæ in pleonexiam degenerarunt.
units.tr: "So that it may be ready, he says, as a generous gift and not as a grudging exaction." The Greek is καὶ μὴ ὡσπερ πλεονεξίαν [and not as covetousness]. The Vulgate version has "not as covetousness." The word πλεονεξία signifies that excessive desire by which we want more than is fitting, from plus habendo, having more. Therefore the old translator rendered it "covetousness." It is ambiguous whether it refers to the desire of the Corinthians or of those brothers whom the Apostle had sent. Certainly one could sin on either side, both of those giving and of those receiving. The one who gives, if he gives too tightly, does this by the vice of covetousness. The one who receives, if he receives too eagerly and seeks more than is fair and than agrees, does this too through covetousness. I think, however, that the Apostle meant to tell the Corinthians that their contribution would be ἐπαγγελία [ready and prepared] only if it were not given sparingly and grudgingly, but generously, as befits a blessing promised for the uses of the saints. The following words favour this sense. Chrysostom, however, supports the other opinion. For he explains it thus: μὴ νομίσωμεν, φησί, ὅτι ὡς πλεονεκτοῦντες αὐτῷ λαμβάνομεν, ἀλλ' ὡς αὐτοι γενέσθαι ὑμῖν ἐυλογίας [let us not suppose, he says, that we take it as those who covet, but as being a blessing to you]. Erasmus also seems to have understood it this way, when he rendered it "and not as an extortion." In this sense nearly all of our forefathers' almsgivings degenerated into covetousness.

units.la: Illud autem dico, Qui semetem facit parce, is parcè quoq; metet, & qui semè facit in benedictionibus, in benedictionib. quoq; metet: unusquisq; secundum propositū cordis, non ex molestia aut necessitate. Nam hilarem datorem diligit Deus. Potens est autẽ Deus efficere, ut tota gratia in uos exuberet, ut in omnibus omnem sufficientiã habentes, exuberetis in omne opus bonum: quemadmodum scriptũ est: Dispersit, dedit pauperibus, iustícia eius manet in sæculum sæculi.
units.tr: But this I say: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessings will also reap in blessings. Let each one give as he has purposed in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to make all grace abound toward you, so that always having in all things sufficiency, you may abound to every good work, as it is written: "He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains forever."

units.la: Exponit quare admoneat Corinthios, ut contributionem faciant non in pleonexia, sed in benedictione. Hoc se exponere uelle significat, dicens, τοῦτο δέ, id est, hoc autem, scilicet, est quod dico, uel, quod specto. Quid? Qui par ce seminat, inquit, is parce quoq; metet, & qui seminat in benedictionibus, in benedictionibus quoque metet. Quasi dicat. Propterea ue- lim collectam uestram parari non parcè ac tenaciter tanquam pleonexiam, sed liberaliter ac large tanquam benedictione, quod ijs qui parcè contribuunt, parcè, qui largè, largè quo que retribuetur à Deo. Poterat sic simpliciter rem ipsam exprimere, uerùm maluit simili tudine uti omniũ & notissima & conuenientissima, sumpta de ijs qui terrenam sementem faciunt, & ex illa uitæ suæ alimenta colligunt, ut admoneat, eandem esse conditionem dan-
units.tr: He explains why he admonishes the Corinthians to make the contribution not in covetousness but in blessing. He signifies that he wishes to set this out, saying τοῦτο δέ, that is, "but this," namely, this is what I mean, or what I have in view. What is it? He who sows sparingly, he says, will also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessings will also reap in blessings. As if to say: therefore I would have your collection prepared not sparingly and grudgingly, as in covetousness, but liberally and largely, as a blessing; because God will repay those who give sparingly sparingly, and those who give largely largely. He could have stated the matter itself plainly like this, but he preferred to use a comparison, the most familiar and most suitable of all, taken from those who sow an earthly seed and gather from it the nourishment of their life, so as to remind us that giving alms is in the same condition as sowing seed,

units.la: tis eleemosynam, quæ est facientis sementem. Qui seminat, id quod ex benedictione domini acceperat antea, partim in usus domesticos impendit, partim sementi deputat, & telluri committit. Facit autem hoc non grauatim ingemiscendo, sed alacriter bene sperando, manu non contractiore, sed aperta, semen suum proiicit in agrum uacuum, nihil habentem, & ex se nihil reddere ualentem, nec proiicit tantum, sed & occando operit, ac uelut in agri uisceribus sepelit, ubi hoc opus suũ perfecit, incrementum illius domino committit, & ab illius munificentia fructum expectat.
units.tr: for he who sows, out of the blessing of the Lord which he had received before, partly spends it on household needs and partly sets it aside for sowing, and commits it to the earth. He does this not with reluctance and groaning, but cheerfully, hoping well; with an open hand, not a tight one, he casts his seed into the empty field, which has nothing and cannot give anything back of itself. Nor does he merely cast it, but he also covers it with a harrow and buries it, as it were, in the bowels of the field. When he has completed this work he commits its increase to the Lord and expects the fruit from the Lord's bounty.

units.la: Cosimili modo qui dat eleemosynam, non dat nihil exijs quæ & ipse antea de manu diuinæ benedictionis accepit (excluditur in hac causa, quod iniquis est modis acquisitū) quorum alia suis ac suorum usibus accommodat, alia pauperibus consecrat. Et dum hoc facit, non ingemiscedo grauatim, nec parca, sed larga manu facit. Et quod dat ueluti semen in ua cuum agrum, sic in famelicum pauperem proijcit, ac totum gratiæ Dei commendat, sciens non perire quod in uiscera pauperum sepelitur: qui sic benigna manu seminat eleemosynam, benignam uicisim diuinæ remunerationis messem sortietur.
units.tr: Likewise, he who gives alms does not give away anything that he himself had earlier received from the hand of divine blessing (in this matter it is excluded that it was acquired by unjust means), some of which he applies to his own and his family's uses, and some of which he consecrates to the poor. And while he does this, he does it not groaning with reluctance, nor sparingly, but with a generous hand. And what he gives, as it were seed into an empty field, so he casts into the needy poor man, and commends the whole to the grace of God, knowing that what is buried in the bowels of the poor does not perish. He who thus sows alms with a generous hand will in turn receive a harvest of generous divine reward.

units.la: QVI sementem facit, inquit.) Ergo semen est eleemosyna, idq; non ut in horreo recondi tum, sed ut in agro seminatum, & qui dat eleemosynam, sementem facit. Sementem autem facere, non est frustra res nostras dilapidare, sed cum fœnore multiplicare.
units.tr: "He who sows seed," he says. So the seed is alms, and not to be stored away in a barn but to be sown in the field, and he who gives alms makes a sowing. To make a sowing, however, is not to squander our goods in vain, but to multiply them with interest.

units.la: PARCE, item, in benedictionibus.) Videmus hic, seminare in benedictionibus, & seminare parcè, esse opposita, quare benedictionis uocem pro copiosa contributione usurpatam esse patet. Vnde hoc fit, annotarunt ante me alij. Sensus hic conuenientior est Ebrææ uoci בְּרָכָה, quàm uel Græcæ εὐλογία, uel Latinæ, benedictioni.
units.tr: "Sparingly, likewise, in blessings." Here we see that sowing in blessings and sowing sparingly are set in opposition, so it is clear that the word "blessing" is used for a copious contribution. How this comes about, others have noted before me. This sense agrees better with the Hebrew word בְּרָכָה [berakah] than with the Greek εὐλογία or the Latin benedictio.

units.la: Obserua uero quàm cautè non dicat: Qui modicum, sed, qui parcè seminat. Etenim licet in terrena satione sic habeat, ut qui parum seminat, parum etiam metat, siue id faciat parcè per tenacitatem, siue modicè per penuriã seminis, in hac tamen spirituali plurimum discri minis est inter eum qui parcè cum largè pos- set, si uellet, & eum qui parum, cum multa non habeat, in usus pauperum seminat. Etenim qui modicum habens, modicum largitur pauperibus, si id ex animo facit, non modicum largitur, sed multum. Vt enim iniuriæ, ita & beneficia animo constant.
units.tr: But observe how carefully he does not say "he who sows a little" but "he who sows sparingly." For although in earthly sowing it is the case that he who sows little also reaps little, whether he does it sparingly through tightness or meagrely through a lack of seed, yet in this spiritual sowing there is a great difference between one who sows sparingly when he could sow generously if he wished, and one who sows little when he has not much, into the uses of the poor. For he who, having little, gives little to the poor, if he does it from the heart, does not give little but much. For just as injuries, so too benefits are measured by the intention.

units.la: PARCE metet, inquit, item, in benedictionibus, id est, copiosè, metet.) Hoc dicens, promittit cœlestem remunerationẽ, tanquâ mes- sem. Qui metit sementem quam fecit, ubi illa matura est, agrum cum falce ingreditur, & sata sua demetit, demessa colligit, inque horrea sua recondit. In hac spirituali messe nihil quæ- ritur ex agro, id est, ex pauperibus, quibus se- men nostrum concredidimus, nihil etiam ab ips ipso Deo, agri huius domino, reposcitur, sed A quæ ille suo tempore pro liberali sua bonitate rependit, metuntur, id est, grato animo de manu illius recipiuntur.
units.tr: "He will reap sparingly," he says, "likewise, in blessings," that is, he will reap abundantly. In saying this he promises heavenly reward as a harvest. He who reaps the seed he has sown, when it is ripe, goes into the field with a sickle, cuts down his crops, gathers what he has cut, and stores it in his barns. In this spiritual harvest nothing is sought from the field, that is, from the poor to whom we have entrusted our seed, nor is anything demanded back from God himself, the lord of this field; but in His own time, in His generous goodness, He repays, and they are reaped, that is, received from His hand with a grateful heart.

units.la: Rependit autem ille parcè, ijs qui parcè, in benedictione ijs qui in benedictione, nihil ijs qui nihil seminarunt, ut quisque secundum sationis suę mensuram recipiat, cuius rei imaginem in terrena satione uidemus. Cum nihil illis rependi dico, qui nihil in agro pauperum seminarunt, non loquor de illis, qui non tenacitate & immisericordia, sed paupertate impediuntur, quo minus aliquid egenis largiantur, sed de tenacibus & immisericordibus, qui cum habeant unde dare possent, uiscera sua erga pauperes, & cum uisceribus ipsas quoque manus claudunt. Istis sanè nihil reponditur aliud quàm iudicium sine misericordia: illis uerò ut uoluntas est pro facto, ita non minus rependitur, quàm si permulta dedissent.
units.tr: He repays sparingly to those who sow sparingly, and generously to those who sow generously. He repays nothing to those who have sown nothing, so that each person receives according to the measure of his sowing, an image of which we see in earthly sowing. When I say that nothing is repaid to those who have sown nothing in the field of the poor, I am not speaking of those who are kept from giving to the needy by poverty rather than by stinginess and want of mercy. I mean the miserly and merciless, who, though they have the means to give, shut their bowels against the poor, and with their bowels they also shut their hands. For such people nothing is laid up except judgement without mercy. But to those whose will is ready, the deed is counted as done, and they receive no less than if they had given a great deal.

units.la: In eo quod dicit: Qui parcè seminat, parcè & metet: obseruandum est, quàm nullum bonum irremuneratum diuinæ bonitatis abundantia relinquat. Qui parcè dat, quoniam hoc facit uel ex tenacitate, uel ex diffidetia, uel ex defectu charitatis, uel ex fastidio & contemptu pauperum, dignus esset prorsus, cui nihil rependeretur. Ea tamen est natura diuinę bonitatis, ut & illorum eleemosynam, etsi parcè, remuneret tamen.
units.tr: In what he says, "He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly," we must observe how the abundance of divine goodness leaves no good deed unrewarded. Someone who gives sparingly, because he does so out of stinginess, or distrust, or lack of love, or disdain and contempt for the poor, would truly deserve to receive nothing in return. Yet such is the nature of divine goodness that it rewards even the alms of those who give sparingly.

units.la: Deinde obserua, quod cum dicendum uideretur, qui seminat multum, is & multũ metet, dixit: Qui seminat in benedictionibus, in benedictionibus quoque metet. Aliud enim est, multum dare manu, & aliud, multum dare corde syncero ac uoluntario. Qui manu dat multum, sic dare potest, ut parum sit in conspectu domini. Qui syncero corde dat largiter, copiose dat in oculis domini. Et hoc est in benedictione dare.
units.tr: Next, notice that where one might have expected him to say, "He who sows much will also reap much," he said instead: "He who sows in blessings will also reap in blessings." For it is one thing to give much with the hand, and another to give much with a sincere and willing heart. A person may give much with his hand and yet give in such a way that it is little in the sight of the Lord. Whoever gives generously with a sincere heart gives abundantly in the eyes of the Lord. This is what it means to give in blessing.

units.la: VNVSQVISQUE, inquit, secundum propositum cordis.) Particulam hanc adiecit, ne quoniam parcè messurum dixit eum qui parcè seminat, multum à singulis requirere uidea tur. Ideo benedictionem quàm requirit, refert ad προαίρεσιν cordis, non ad abundantiam dato rum. Hoc faciens cauet suspicionem pleonexiæ. Est autem προαίρεσις id quod penes nosipsos in corde prius eligimus ac statuimus, ad faciendum accingamur. In eiusmodi autem proposito est αὐθαίρεσις, quà Macedonibus capite præcedeti tribuit, libera uidelicet & spontanea uoluntas. Huic liberum permittit, ut det quantum ipsa statuerit, nihil requirens aliud, quàm ut libera ac uoluntaria contributio fiat. Nequit autem fieri, ut non detur liberaliter, ubi datur uoluntate non reluctate, sed ultro ad dandum propensa. Et hic est fons eius eleemosynæ, quæ sic detur liberaliter, ut possit non modò beneficentia, sed & benedictio uocari.
units.tr: "Each one," he says, "according to his purpose of heart." He added this phrase so that, having said that the one who sows sparingly will reap sparingly, no one should think that he requires much from each person. So he refers the blessing he requires to the purpose of the heart [προαίρεσιν], not to the abundance of what is given. In doing this he guards against any suspicion of greed. A purpose [προαίρεσις] is what we first choose and resolve within ourselves, in our hearts, before we set about doing something. In such a purpose there is also a self-determination [αὐθαίρεσις], which in the preceding chapter he attributed to the Macedonians, namely a free and spontaneous will. He allows this will to give freely as much as it has decided, asking for nothing more than that the contribution be free and voluntary. Nor can it happen that a gift is not given generously where it is given with a will that is not reluctant but readily inclined to give. And this is the source of that alms which is given so freely that it can be called not only a kindness but also a blessing.

units.la: NON ex molestia, inquit, aut ex necessitate.) Græcè est, μὴ ἐκ λύπης, id est, nō ex tristicia: Aperit quare dixerit: Vnusquisque secundum
units.tr: "Not out of grief," he says, "or out of necessity." In Greek it is "not out of sorrow" [μὴ ἐκ λύπης], that is, not out of sadness. He explains why he said: "each one according to his purpose of heart." That is, he means that a contribution should not be made with sadness, as if it were extracted by compulsion.

units.la: propositum cordis. Ne uidelicet contribut. si fiat cum tristicia, & uelut ex necessitate coacta. Talis autem fiat necesse est, ubi non datur uoluntario cordis proposito. Quasi dicat. Nemo hic cogitur, neminì ex necessitate quantũ dare debeat, præscribitur. Quare non est ut quisquam ex uobis det tristis & inuitus. Qui non sponte potest dare, non est ut det inuitus, cum neque sit qui cogat, neq; tristis & coacta eleemosyna probetur. Per necessitatem intelligit coactionem, quæ coacti facimus, facimus inuiti, adeoq; & tristes. Alias nō omnia necessaria reddunt coactos & inuitos. Necessariò comedimus, bibimus ac dormimus. Nihil tamen horũ coacti & inuiti facimus. Necesse est ad acquirendâ salutem, ut resipiscamus, & credamus Euangelio. Nemo tamen uere credens ac resipiscens, inuitus credit & resipiscit. Necesse est, ut Deum timeamus, diligamus, & colamus super omnia & in omnibus. Et tamen fiunt ista à pijs animo non coacto, sed uoluntario, & in lege Dei meditante dies ac noctes. Sic necesse est, ut diligamus proximos propter mandatum domini. Nec ista necessitas recipit animũ coactum. Quis enim coactus & inuitus diligit? Verum si necesse sit, ut quę tua sunt des ei quem non diligis, eiusmodi necessitas reddit coactum & inuitum, nō natura sua, sed tuo uicio. Si nanq; diligeres, non dares inuitus, sed αὐτάρκης. Etiam tamen atq; etiam animaduertendum est, qualis sit ista coactio, & quatenus demus inuiti. Si carne quidem reluctante, spiritu uero uolente & cogente dederimus, eiusmodi eleemosyna non est prorsus & sic coacta, ut ab inuitis data dici possit. Neq; enim iudicandum est de illa secundum carnis, sed magis secundum spiritus uoluntatem. Ea uero tota coacta est & reproba, quam toti tam spiritu quàm carne damus inuiti.
units.tr: Such a contribution must necessarily be made where it is not given from the willing purpose of the heart. It is as if he said: "No one is forced here, and no one is told by necessity how much he ought to give. So none of you should give sadly and unwillingly. Whoever cannot give willingly should not give unwillingly, since there is no one to compel him, and an alms given sadly and under compulsion is not acceptable." By necessity he means compulsion, which we do when we act under constraint and therefore unwillingly and even sadly. Otherwise, not everything that is necessary makes us compelled and unwilling. We necessarily eat, drink and sleep, yet we do none of these things under compulsion or against our will. It is necessary for the sake of gaining salvation that we repent and believe the Gospel, yet no one who truly believes and repents does so unwillingly. It is necessary that we fear, love and worship God above all things and in all things, yet the godly do these things not under compulsion but willingly, meditating on the law of God day and night. So too it is necessary that we love our neighbours for the Lord's command, yet this necessity does not admit a compelled mind. For who loves under compulsion and against his will? But if it were necessary that you give what is yours to someone you do not love, such a necessity would make you compelled and unwilling, not by its own nature but by your own fault. For if you loved, you would not give unwillingly, but would be self-sufficient [αὐτάρκης] in giving. Yet we must consider carefully what kind of compulsion this is, and to what extent we give unwillingly. If we give with the flesh resisting but the spirit willing and driving us on, such an alms is not altogether compelled, so that it could be said to be given by unwilling people. For it must be judged not according to the will of the flesh but rather according to the will of the spirit. But that alms is wholly compelled and worthless which we give unwillingly with the whole of ourselves, both spirit and flesh.

units.la: NAM hilarè datorem diligit Deus, inquit.) Reddit rationem, quare nō sit dandum ex tristicia aut ex coactione. Quia uidelicet non placent Deo, qui dant tristes & inuiti, eò quod ille diligat datorem hilarem. In promptu uero causa est, hilarem cur ille datorem diligat. Nō tam munus ipsum quàm dantis animum spectat. Animi enim in dando hilaritas, multo est præstantior auro. Et sic comparati sunt, quotquot homines sunt ingenui, ut magis delectentur dantis beneuolentia, quàm doni magnitudine. Parum iucunditatis habet munus cum tristicia datum, unde & in ea quæ ad Rom. est cap.12. dicit: qui miseretur, faciat hoc in hilaritate. Et Ecclesiasticus cap.35. dicit, ἐν πάσῃ δόσει ἱλάρωσον τὸ πρόσωπόν σου.
units.tr: "For God loves a cheerful giver," he says. He gives the reason why it should not be given in sadness or under compulsion: God is not pleased with those who give sadly and unwillingly, because he loves a cheerful giver. The reason why he loves a cheerful giver is readily apparent. God looks not so much at the gift itself as at the mind of the giver. The cheerfulness of mind in giving is far more precious than gold. And all men of good character are so disposed that they take more pleasure in the goodwill of the giver than in the greatness of the gift. A gift given with sadness brings little delight, and so in Romans 12 he says: "he who shows mercy, let him do it with cheerfulness." And Ecclesiasticus 35 says: "in every gift show a cheerful face" [ἐν πάσῃ δόσει ἱλάρωσον τὸ πρόσωπόν σου].

units.la: Vide autem quàm prudeter non dicat: nos enim hilares datores diligimus, uel, nam hilarem datorem diligunt pauperes sancti, sed, nì hilarem datorem diligit Deus, quo plus moueat ad spontaneam & hilarem contributionem. Poterat dicere, nam plus gratiæ habet donum hilariter datum, quàm quod datur cum tristicia. Verùm prouocare uoluit eorum pietatem tatem quibus cordi erat placere Deo. Qui nan que sic animati sunt, nihil cum maiore faciunt delectatione, quàm quod Deo placere sciunt. Nec otiosum est, quod non dicit: Munus hilariter datum, sed, hilarem datorem diligit Deus. Munera non spectat Deus; qui omnib. bonis abundat, & omnia ipse donat, sed bonitate eorum qui hilariter necessaria tribuut egenis, eaque in re diuinæ sese naturæ conformant.
units.tr: Notice how wisely he does not say, "We love cheerful givers," or "The holy poor love a cheerful giver," but "God loves a cheerful giver," so that he might move them more strongly to a voluntary and cheerful contribution. He could have said, "A gift given cheerfully has more grace than one given with sadness." But he wished to stir up the piety of those whose heart was set on pleasing God. Those who are so disposed take no greater delight in anything than in knowing that they please God. Nor is it idle that he does not say "a gift given cheerfully" but "God loves a cheerful giver." God does not regard gifts, since he who abounds in all good things and gives all things himself; rather, he regards the goodness of those who cheerfully supply the needy with what is necessary, and in this they conform themselves to the divine nature.

units.la: POTENS est autem Deus efficere, inquit, vt tota gratia in vos exuberet.) Iam illud explicat, quod dixit, qui in benedictionibus seminat, in benedictionibus quoq; metet. Ratio hæc non potest aliter iudicare, quàm depérditum esse quod erogatur in pauperes, nihil rependere valentes, non minus quàm si in sterilem proijciantur semina harenam. Quare non videt unde fit messurus qui bona sua profundit in egenos. Ei cogitationi occurrens inducit Deum qui rependat. Huius potentiæ memor nit dices. Potens est autem Deus efficere, &c. quo carnem reprimat, quæ dicit: impossibile est vt aliquid ex eo metatur, quod à pauperib: sic absumitur, vt nihil superfit residui. Quasi dicat. Etsi pauperibus impossibile est, vt retribuant, Deo tamen non est impossibile, vt totâ vestram gratiam, id est, gratuitam eleemosynam in uos exuberare faciat, quemadmodum uos illam vbertim profunditis in pauperes.
units.tr: "God is able," he says, "to make all grace abound toward you." He now explains what he said: "he who sows in blessings will also reap in blessings." Reason of this kind cannot judge otherwise than that what is spent on the poor, who cannot repay anything, is lost, no less than if seeds were cast on sterile sand. So the one who pours out his goods on the needy does not see from where he will reap. Meeting this thought, Paul brings in God as the one who repays. Reminding them of this power, he says: "God is able to make..." etc., so as to restrain the flesh, which says: "It is impossible that anything be reaped from what is so consumed by the poor that nothing remains." It is as if he said: "Even if it is impossible for the poor to repay you, it is not impossible for God to make all your grace, that is, your free alms, abound toward you, just as you pour them out abundantly upon the poor."

units.la: Studio autem non simpliciter dicit: vt de gratia vestra portio aliqua, sed, vt tota gratia, nec dicit, ad vos redeat, sed, in uos exuberet, hoc est, cum fœnore vbertim ad vos redeat. Loquitur ad similitudinem largæ sationis. Illa Deus sua potentia totam in agricolam exuberare facit, sic vt non modo quantum seminauit, sed multò adhuc plura magno cum fœnore metat. Qui hoc singulis annis vbiq; terrarum tam ergo malos quàm bonos facit, quomodo non faceret erga semententem eorum quos diligit, quæ semen tem facit charitas, per spiritum sanctum cordibus electorum infusa.
units.tr: But he does not simply say "that some portion of your grace," but "all your grace," and he does not say "may return to you," but "may overflow in you," that is, may return to you abundantly with interest. He speaks by way of likeness to a generous sowing. By his power God makes the farmer's harvest overflow, so that he reaps not only as much as he sowed but much more, with a great return. God does this every year, everywhere on earth, for both the evil and the good. How then would he not do it for the sowing of those whom he loves, the sowing that charity makes, poured into the hearts of the elect through the Holy Spirit?

units.la: VT in omnibus, inquit, omnem sufficientiâ habentes, exuberetis in omne opus bonum.) Exponit quomodo Deus totâ gratiâ eorû qui succurrunt egenis exuberare in ipsos faciat. Vt in omnibus, inquit, omnem sufficientiam habentes, exuberetis in omne opus bonum. Adhuc loquitur ad similitudinem agricolæ, qui quod seminauit, benedictione domini auctum metit, inquit horreum suum colligit. Hic benedictionem domini experitur primum in eo, quod ex messe sua sufficienter recipit, unde cum suis viuat, deinde in eo quoq; quod ultra eam sufficientiam adhuc recipit, quod & seminet, & pauperioribus quoq; impertiat. De sufficientia propriæ alimoniæ loquitur cum dicit, ut in omnibus, intellige, ad victum & amictum necessariis, omnem αὐτάρκειαν, id est sufficientiam vobis satisfacientem habetes. De reliqua abundantia, unde ad largiendum egenis sufficiat, loquitur cum subijcit, exuberetis in omne opus bonum. Hoc est, abunde simul habeatisvn
units.tr: "So that in all things, having all sufficiency, you may abound to every good work." He explains how God makes his whole grace overflow upon those who help the needy. "So that in all things," he says, "having all sufficiency, you may abound to every good work." He still speaks by likeness to the farmer, who reaps what he sowed, increased by the Lord's blessing, and gathers it into his barn. Here the blessing of the Lord is experienced first in this, that from his harvest he receives enough to live on with his own, and then also in this, that beyond that sufficiency he still receives something that he can both sow and share with the poorer. He speaks of the sufficiency of one's own maintenance when he says "in all things": understand, for food and clothing that are necessary, having all self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκειαν], that is, enough to satisfy you. He speaks of the remaining abundance, by which there is enough to give to the needy, when he adds "may abound to every good work." That is, you should have enough at once and be able to practise every kind of good work, such as feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, and so on.

units.la: de omne genus boni operis exerceatis, vtpote esurientes pascatis, nudos vestiatis, &c. Est hæc benedictio domini insignis, & propria piorum sic videlicet quæ in domesticos vsus necessaria sunt habere, vt iuxta abundet, unde beneficentiam exerceamus in pauperes. Vox αὐτάρκεια diligenter obseruanda est hoc loco. Promittit pio homini non quæ ad luxum & voluptates, sed quæ ad necessarios vsus sufficiant, quibus possit esse contentus. Unde αὐτάρκεια nonnunquam pro frugalitate, & αὐτάρκης pro contentum esse ponunt. Huius limites qui excedunt, incidut in vicium πλεονεξίας, & inuoluut se tentationibus innumeris, redduntq; prorsus ad omne bonum opus steriles & infrugiferos. Quare Apostolus magna ratione cum αὐτάρκεια abundantiam ad omne opus bonum sufficien tem coniunxit. Metienda est autem αὐτάρκεια non multitudine bonorum, sed animo frugali necessario rerum vsu contento, quem Apostolus alibi determinat, dicens: Est autem quæstus magnus, pietas μετ' αὐτάρκειας, id est, cum sufficientia (Erasmus reddidit, cum animo sua sorte contento) Nihil enim intulimus in hunc mundum, videlicet nec efferre quicquam possumus; ἀρκέσθησόμεθα, id est, contenti erimus. Animo sic comparato, non opus est magna bonorum copia, ad istam αὐτάρκειαν, sed modica sufficient: Est enim & ipsa natura minimis contenta. Si ad mensuram αὐτάρκειας viueremus, nunquam redde emur pauperes. Iam quoniam pars maxima insaniæ ἐξ πλεονεξίας indulget, alter alterum in vicia trudimus, & ad extrema illac abundantiæ, hac egestatis exorbitamus, atq; ita vitæ nostræ cursum multis nobis molestijs aggravamus, cum si ad αὐτάρκειαν spectaremus, facillima nobis viuendi ratio, opitulante nos diuina bonitate, constare posset.
units.tr: This blessing of the Lord is remarkable and proper to the godly: to have what is necessary for domestic use, and besides that to have abundance, from which we may exercise beneficence towards the poor. The word self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκεια] must be carefully observed in this place. He promises the godly person not what suffices for luxury and pleasures, but what suffices for necessary uses, with which one can be content. Hence they sometimes use self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκεια] for frugality, and self-sufficient [αὐτάρκης] for being content. Those who go beyond these limits fall into the vice of greed [πλεονεξίας], and entangle themselves in countless temptations, and become utterly barren and unfruitful for every good work. Therefore the Apostle with good reason joined abundance sufficient for every good work with self-sufficiency. But self-sufficiency is to be measured not by the multitude of goods, but by a frugal mind, content with the necessary use of things, which the Apostle elsewhere defines, saying: "Now godliness with contentment is great gain," that is, with sufficiency (Erasmus rendered it: with a mind content with its lot) [μετ' αὐτάρκειας]. "For we brought nothing into this world," clearly we can carry nothing out; "we shall be content" [ἀρκέσθησόμεθα], that is, we shall be satisfied. When the mind is so disposed, there is no need of a great abundance of goods for that self-sufficiency, but a modest amount is enough, for nature itself is content with very little. If we lived by the measure of self-sufficiency, we would never be made poor. But since the greater part of mankind indulges in the madness of greed, we push one another into vices, and we are carried from the extreme of abundance to the extreme of want, and so we weigh down the course of our life with many troubles, whereas if we looked to self-sufficiency, a very easy way of living could be maintained for us, with the divine goodness helping us.

units.la: QVEMADMODVM scriptum est, inquit: Dispersit dedit pauperibus, iustitia eius manet in saeculum.) Locum hunc scripturæ citat ex Psalmo 112. vbi prosperitas viri iusti ac timentis Dei inter alias & ista prædicatur, quæ quam uis bona sua dispergat in egenos, ppetuo tamen habeat quo pauperibus succurrat. Id in Ebræo sic legitur, מזר נתן לאביונים צדקתו עומדת לעד, id est: Dispergit, dat pauperibus, iustitia eius perstat perpetuo. Verbo dispergendi non prodigam bonorum profusionem ac dilapidationem, sed largam ac liberalem erogationem, in morem eius qui semen suum aperta manu dispergit in agrum, significat. Liberaliter, inquit, dispergit sua bona, nõ tenaciter ac parce, dum largitur ea pauperibus. Et tamen hæc illius iustitia non perit dispergendo, sed firma & continua perstat perpetuo. Iusticiam autem intelligit bonitatem ac benignitatem egenis subuenientem, quo sensu vox צדקה in scripturis frequenter ponitur. Illam non consumit larga distributio quæ fit in pauperes, sed magis conseruat, perinde atq; agricolæ non perit semen quod seminet, ex eo quod singulis annis ma- {Nn} gnam feminis sui partem dispergit in terram, sed magis ex eo sic illi feminis copia paratur, vt quo plus seminauit, hoc plus habeat quod porrò seminet. Igitur hoc scripturæ loco tanquam fide digno spiritusiancti testimonio cóprobat illud quod dixit: Potens est autem Deus efficere, vt tota gratia in vos exuberet, vt in omnibus omnem sufficientiam habentes, exuberetis in omne opus bonum. Huius rei imago in fontibus quoq; relucet, qui quo largius fluunt ipsorum aquæ, vel hauriuntur crebrius, hoc aquarum scaturigines habent & expeditiores & copiosiores. Sic comparata est diuinæ prouidentiæ bonitas, vt organis illis, quibus ad succurrendum necessitatibus nostris vtitur, hoc plus suppeditet facultatis, quo plus illa in usus nostros erogant. Parca & sordida & tenacia & illiberalia pectora digna sunt, quæ tanquam sterilia, etiam ijs quæ habent priuentur, & inania reddantur.
units.tr: "As it is written," he says: "He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever." He cites this passage of Scripture from Psalm 112, where the prosperity of the righteous man who fears God is proclaimed among other things, including this: that although he scatters his goods among the needy, he still always has something by which to help the poor. In the Hebrew it reads thus: מזר נתן לאביונים צדקתו עומדת לעד [mizar natan le'evyonim tzidqato 'omedet le'ad], that is: "He scatters, he gives to the poor; his righteousness stands forever." By the word "scatters" is signified not a prodigal pouring out and squandering of goods, but a generous and liberal distribution, after the manner of one who scatters his seed with an open hand over the field. "He scatters," he says, "his goods liberally, not tightly and sparingly, while he gives them to the poor. And yet his righteousness does not perish by scattering, but stands firm and continual forever." By righteousness he understands the goodness and kindness that helps the needy, in which sense the word צדקה [tzedaqah] is often used in the Scriptures. Large distribution to the poor does not consume it, but rather preserves it, just as the farmer does not lose the seed he sows, although every year he scatters a great part of his seed on the earth; rather, from this a supply of seed is so prepared for him that the more he has sown, the more he has to sow again. Therefore, by this passage of Scripture, as by the testimony of the Holy Spirit worthy of belief, he confirms what he said: "God is able to make all grace abound toward you, so that having all sufficiency in all things, you may abound to every good work." An image of this shines forth also in springs, which, the more largely their waters flow, or the more often they are drawn, have their sources both more ready and more abundant. So the goodness of divine providence is arranged so that it supplies more means to those instruments, by which it helps our needs, the more they distribute to our uses. Stingy, sordid, tight-fisted, and illiberal hearts deserve to be deprived even of what they have, as barren things, and to be made empty.

units.la: Illud, iustitia eius manet in sæculum, exponunt veteres de æterno iustitiæ præmio, quod dabitur in futuro. Verùm conformior menti apostoli est expositio quam posuimus.
units.tr: The old writers explain the words "his righteousness endures forever" of the eternal reward of righteousness, which will be given in the future. But the explanation we have given is more in keeping with the mind of the Apostle.

units.la: Qui uero suppeditat semen seminanti, is (potens est) & panē in cibū suppeditare ac multiplicare sementē uestrā, & augere prouētus iusticię uestrę, ut in omnib.locupletemini in omnē simplicitatem, quę per nos efficit, ut gratię agā- tur Deo. Nam functio huius ministerij nō solum supplet ea quę desunt sanctis, uerū etiam exuberat in hoc,qd per multos gratiæ agantur Deo,qui per probationem ministerij huiusglorificant Deū super obedientia consensus uestri in Euangelium Christi,&de simplicitate cō municationis in ipsos,&in omnes,&in illorum oratione pro uobis,qui desiderant uos propter eminētem gratiā Dei in uobis. Gratia autem Deo,super ineffabili suo munere.
units.tr: "He who supplies seed to the sower, he (will supply) also bread for food, and will multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness, so that you may be enriched in all simplicity, which through us works thanksgiving to God." For the function of this ministry not only supplies what the saints lack, but also overflows in this, that many give thanks to God, who through the proof of this ministry glorify God for the obedience of your confession to the Gospel of Christ, and for the simplicity of the fellowship shared with them and with all, and in their prayer for you, who long for you because of the surpassing grace of God in you. Thanks be to God for his unspeakable gift.

units.la: Id quod in præcedenti dixit adhuc clarius exprimit, vsq; ad ea verba quibus dicit: Nam functio huius ministerij. Qui vero suppeditat semen seminanti inquit. Ab exemplo incremeti diuini, quo seminanti agricolæ semen quod in agrum proiecit, copiosé multiplicatur, vt vberem messem sortiatur, fidem facit ei quod dixit: Potens est Deus efficere vt tota gratia in uos exuberet, &c. Nequit cœptæ similitudini satis immorari, qua vix aliud ad præsente causam accommodatius adduci potuit. Pro eo qd in præcedenti dixit: Potens est Deus, reponit hic periphrasim istam Dei: Qui suppeditat semen seminanti, in qua nos admonet eius potentiæ simul ac prouidentiæ Dei, qua feminatibus nobis, plantantibus, ac rigantibus increμentum largitur, quo fata nostra multiplicentur.Potest autem quod dicit, Qui suppeditat semé, exponi tam de semine quod seminatur ab agricola, quàm de eo quod ab illo metitur. Nam vtrunq; à Deo est, virtute benedictionis illius suppeditatum qui suaipsius dona multiplicat dum quod satu à nobis est copioso fœnore restituit.
units.tr: What he said in the preceding verses he expresses still more clearly, down to the words in which he says: "For the function of this ministry." "He who supplies seed to the sower," he says. From the example of the divine increase, by which the seed that the farmer has cast into the field is multiplied abundantly, so that he obtains a rich harvest, he gives assurance of what he said: "God is able to make all grace abound toward you," and so on. One cannot dwell long enough on the likeness he has begun, for hardly anything more suitable to the present cause could have been brought forward. In place of what he said earlier, "God is able," he here puts this periphrasis of God: "who supplies seed to the sower," in which he reminds us of God's power and at the same time of his providence, by which he gives increase to us as we sow, plant, and water, so that our harvests are multiplied. Moreover, what he says, "who supplies seed," may be explained both of the seed that is sown by the farmer and of that which is reaped from it. For both are from God, who by the power of his blessing supplies seed and multiplies his own gifts, while he restores with abundant interest what was sown by us.

units.la: IS,inquit, (potens est) & panem in cibum suppeditare,&c.) In Græco est, [illegible, ~40 letters], i. & panem in cibum suppeditare,& multiplicare sementem vestram, & augere germina iustitiæ vestræ,&c. Hæc tria infinita,suppeditare,multiplicare,augere,quo niam sensum non complent,alij legùt in futuro,suppeditabit,multiplicabit,& augebit,quemadmodum vetus interpres reddidit: alij in optatiuo,suppeditet,multiplicet, & augeat, sicuti vertit Erasmus,quem sensum & Chrysostomi sequutus est,& post Chrysostomum recentiores aliquot. Mihi vero cogitanti,quàm sit præter morem Apostoli infinita ponere pro futuris vel optatiuis,apparet illud ex præcedentibus,δύναται, i.potes est,repetendum esse,accedendum: Qui vero suppeditat semen seminanti,potens est & panem in cibū suppeditare, & multiplicare sementem vestram,& augere germina iustitiæ vestræ,&c.
units.tr: "He is able," he says, "to supply bread for food," etc. In the Greek it is [text missing in the scan], that is, "and supply bread for food, and multiply your seed, and increase the shoots of your righteousness," etc. Because these three infinitives, supply, multiply and increase, do not complete the sense, some read them as futures, "will supply, will multiply, and will increase," as the old translator rendered them; others read them as optatives, "may supply, may multiply, and may increase," as Erasmus translated, following Chrysostom's sense, as did several more recent writers after Chrysostom. But when I consider how contrary to the Apostle's custom it is to put infinitives for futures or optatives, it seems that δύναται [dynatai], "is able," must be repeated from the preceding words and understood: "He who supplies seed to the sower is able also to supply bread for food, and to multiply your seed, and increase the shoots of your righteousness," etc.

units.la: IS potens est,inquit,& panē in cibum suppeditare.Facit hoc dum semen suppeditat seminanti. Verùm hic de illis loquitur, qui seminant non in agro luteo sed in agro pauperum, quibus de bonis suis communicant. Ne illi solliciti sint ac dicant: Vnde viuemus nos & nostri,postquá facultates nostras insumimus in pauperes? dicit Deum, qui semen suppeditat seminanti, posse ipsis & panem suppeditare in cibum. Sic carnis diffidentiæ ac solicitudini occurrit. Est autem argumentum à minori ad id quod multo est maius. Minoris momenti est sementis quam facit agricola, quàm fit ea quà facit Christicola, qui semen suum in agrū Christi, pauperes videlicet sanctos, larga manu dispergit. Cumergo Deus agricolæ sementi sic vbertim benedicat, vt copiosam messem ex ijs quæ seminauit colligat, quomodo Christicolæ sementem sic deferere poterit, vt ne panè quidem illi suppeditet in cibum? Per panem autem in cibū, intelligeἀυτάρκειαν rerū necessariarum, cuius in præcedentibus meminit.
units.tr: "He is able," he says, "also to supply bread for food." He does this by supplying seed to the sower. But here he speaks of those who sow not in muddy soil but in the field of the poor, to whom they give a share of their goods. So that they will not worry and say, "How will we and our families live, once we have spent our resources on the poor?", he says that God, who supplies seed to the sower, can also supply them with bread for food. In this way he meets the distrust and anxiety of the flesh. The argument runs from the lesser to the greater. The seed a farmer sows is of less importance than the seed a Christian sows, who scatters his seed with a generous hand in the field of Christ, that is, among the holy poor. Since God so abundantly blesses the farmer's seed that he gathers a plentiful harvest from what he has sown, how could he fail to supply even bread for food to the Christian who sows in this way? By "bread for food" he means sufficiency of necessary things, which he mentioned in the preceding verses.

units.la: AC multiplicare sementem vestram,inquit, & augere prouentus iustitiæ vestræ.) Idem bis dicit,nisi quòd prius per posteri exponit. Neq; enim terrenam ac triticeam sementem intelligit,cum dicit,ac multiplicare sementem vestram,sed contributionem in vsus pauperū faciendam,quam ideo sementem uocat, quod pauperibus elargiri non sit detrimentum lacere,sed lucrum. De hac se loqui significans subiungit,& augere ,puent iustitiæ vestræ. In Græco est,τὰ γενήματα, id est germina. Vocat autem germina iustitiæ Corinthiorum, eandem contributionē quà sementem ipsorum appellauit.
units.tr: "And to multiply your seed," he says, "and increase the yield of your righteousness." He says the same thing twice, except that he explains the first by the second. For when he says "and multiply your seed," he does not mean earthly and wheat seed, but the contribution to be made for the use of the poor. He calls it seed because giving to the poor is not a loss but a gain. To show that he is speaking of this, he adds "and increase the yield of your righteousness." In the Greek it is τὰ γενήματα [ta genemata], that is, the shoots. He calls the Corinthians' contribution "the shoots of righteousness," the same contribution he had called their seed.

units.la: Dicit Deum hanc posse multiplicare & augere, quo persuadeat ipsis, reijciendam esse solicitudinem carnis, quae dicit: quo plus impendero egenis, hoc magis facultates meas imminuo. Tá abest, inquit, ut in pauperes facta contributio bonorum vestrorum futura sit diminutio, ut nullo possint illa meliori ac feliciori compendio multiplicari & augeri. Est enim illa sementis, germina habens vestrae iustitiae, q Deus & multiplicabit & augebit: Iusticiam ipsorum bonitatem ac benignitatem ipsorum vocat, respiciens ad locum quem supra ex Psa. IIx. citauit. Huic autem admodum pulchrè tribuit germina, quae sunt opera charitatis, misericordiae, & beneficentiae, qualia sunt quae in pauperes impenduntur. Quid ergo uocabimus thesauros diuitum auarorum ac tenacium, quos arcis inclusos magna solicitudine in star formicarum Indicarum custodiunt? Si iusticia piorum hominum sic est fœcunda, ut quae tribuunt pauperibus, sint illius sementis & germina, quid aliud thesauros auarorum uocabimus, quàm inanes ac steriles iniusticiae aiistas?
units.tr: He says that God can multiply and increase this, to persuade them that they must reject the anxiety of the flesh, which says, "The more I spend on the needy, the more my resources shrink." Far from it, he says: the contribution made to the poor will not diminish your goods, but they can be multiplied and increased by no better or more fortunate means. For that seed, bearing the shoots of your righteousness, God will both multiply and increase. He calls their righteousness their goodness and kindness, looking back to the passage he cited above from Psalm 112. He very aptly ascribes to this righteousness the shoots, which are works of love, mercy and beneficence, such as those spent on the poor. What, then, shall we call the treasures of the rich, the greedy and the stingy, which they guard with great care, shut up in chests like Indian ants guarding gold? If the righteousness of pious people is so fruitful that what they give to the poor is its seed and shoots, what else shall we call the treasures of the greedy than empty and barren ears of unrighteousness?

units.la: VT in omnibus locupletemini, inquit, in omnem simplicitate. ) In omnibus locupletari, nihil est hic aliud, quàm quod paulo supra dixit: Ut in omnib. omnem sufficientiâ habetes. Nec illud, in omne simplicitate, aliud est quàm qd' illic dixit, in omne opus bonum. Cap. praecedenti eádem simplicitatem tribuit Macedonib. vbi eam esse diximus, qua candidè ac simpliciter absq; omni hæsitatione ac simulatione synceri homines pauperū inopiæ larga contributione succurrunt.
units.tr: "That you may be enriched in everything," he says, "in all simplicity." To be enriched in everything is here nothing other than what he said a little above: "that in everything you may have all sufficiency." Nor is "in all simplicity" anything other than what he said there: "in every good work." In the previous chapter he ascribed the same simplicity to the Macedonians, and we said there that it is the quality by which sincere people, candidly and simply, without any hesitation or pretence, relieve the poverty of the needy with a generous contribution.

units.la: QVÆ per nos efficit, inquit, ut gratiae agantur Deo.) Nonnulli legunt, quae per vos. Nihil est autem periculi, vtrolibet modo legamus. Hactenus prouocauit Corinthios ad hilarem ac largam contributionem, & diffidentiae carnis occurrit, quae perpetuò deperire putatque impenduntur egenis, & paupertatis seincommoda incursuram veretur, si largius illis tribuat. Iam subijcit de gloria Dei, quae ex contributione illorū sequutura fuerit. Quae, inqt, simplicitas largiedi hoc p nos est effectura, ut gratiæ agantur Deo. Est aut gratiarumactio, ipsissim cultus Dei. Quare de illa non frustra quae sequuntur subiecit, quibus materiam hanc eo fine claudit, ad quem omnia nostra dicta ac facta tendere debent.
units.tr: "Which," he says, "through us brings it about that thanks are given to God." Some read "which through you." It makes no difference which way we read it. Hitherto he has urged the Corinthians to a cheerful and generous contribution, and he meets the distrust of the flesh, which always fears that its goods are perishing when they are spent on the needy, and dreads that the hardships of poverty will befall it if it gives more liberally. Now he adds what glory to God will follow from their contribution. "This simplicity of giving," he says, "will bring it about through us that thanks are given to God." Thanksgiving is itself the very worship of God. So what follows was not added in vain, and with it he closes this subject, to which end all our words and deeds ought to be directed.

units.la: NAM functio huius ministerij, inquit, non solùm supplet ea quae desunt sanctis, &c.) In Græco est, ὅτι ἡ διακονία τῆς λειτουργίας ταύτης, i. Nam ministerium officij huius. Vox λειτουργία sonat publicum officium ac ministerium: quo sensu hic ab Apostolo de ministerio curandarum collectarum vsurpatur. Exponit praecedetem particulam, qua simplicitatem Corinthiorum per se dixit efficere, ut Deo agantur gratiae. Tribuit hoc dicto iam ministerio suo. De illo haec duo praedicat quae Deo sunt acceptissima. Vnum, quod supplet ea quae desunt sanctis,
units.tr: "For the function of this ministry," he says, "not only supplies what is lacking to the saints," etc. In the Greek it is ὅτι ἡ διακονία τῆς λειτουργίας ταύτης [hoti he diakonia tes leitourgias tautes], that is, "For the ministry of this service." The word λειτουργία [leitourgia] means public office and ministry; in this sense the Apostle here uses it of the ministry of administering the collections. He explains the preceding particle, by which he said that the simplicity of the Corinthians brings it about that thanks are given to God. He now ascribes this to his own ministry, and he asserts two things of it that are most acceptable to God. The first is that it supplies what is lacking to the saints,

units.la: hoc est, quod pauperum fidelium, qui Hierosolymis & in Iudaea erant, necessitatibus succurrat. Quoniam aut hoc non tam est in cospectu contribuentiū q in oculis Dei praeclarū, non dicit simpliciter: Nam functio ministerij huius supplet ea q desunt sanctis, sed, non solum, inquit, supplet ea quae desunt sanctis, atq; ita adiungit alterū: Verumetiam exuberat in hoc, quod per multos gratiae agantur Deo. Neq; dicit simpliciter, quod gratię agâtur Deo, sed, qd' gratię p multos agantur Deo, significans quo liberalior fit eleemosyna hoc plurimum necessitatibus succurri, ideoq; plures adgratias agendas Deo permoueri, & sic fieri, vt à pluribus celebretur ac glorificetur Deus.
units.tr: that is, that it relieves the needs of the faithful poor who were at Jerusalem and in Judea. Since this is not so conspicuous in the eyes of the contributors as it is in the eyes of God, he does not simply say, "For the function of this ministry supplies what is lacking to the saints," but, "not only," he says, "supplies what is lacking to the saints," and so he adds the other point: "Moreover, it also abounds in this, that through many thanks are given to God." He does not simply say that thanks are given to God, but that thanks are given to God through many, signifying that the more generous the alms, the more the needs are relieved, and therefore more people are moved to give thanks to God, and so it comes about that God is celebrated and glorified by many.

units.la: Larga itaq; fideliū eleemosyna, praeterquā qd' egregium habet fidei & charitatis exerciti um, duos hosce fructus in illis parit, quib. per ipsam succurritur, si sint sancti, i. Christiani ac pij, sustentatione videlicet pauperum sanctorum & glorificationem Dei. De primo dicit: Non solū supplet ea quae desunt sanctis. Et sanctis dū in hac vita degunt, multa desunt, quae fraterna potest supplere charitas, non solū in corporali bus sed & spiritualib. Verùm superstitio Papistica imperitam Christi plebem à viuis & mul torum egenis sanctis ad mortuos colendos auertit, quorum defectus etiamsi qui essent, impleret tamen non posset. In illos maximos sumptus facere consueuerunt, viuis interea & egetibus sanctis egregiè neglectis. Cæci homines non vident quàm diuinum sit opus, defectus im plere sanctorum. Donec sumus in hac vita, communi huic conditioni subiacemus, vt in multis deficiamus, quae nostra ipsorum nequeam facultate supplere. Nemo ex omnibus est mor talibus qui sibi ipse sufficiat in omnibus, ut alio rum non habeat opus subsidio. Sic res humanas diuina prouidentia constituit ac disposuit, quo necessario mutuis veluti vinculis constricti coalescamus & conglutinemur, coniungat quae vel mutua necessitas quos non mox coniungit mutua charitas. Qui igitur sic animati sunt, vt defectus fratrum supplere gestiant, plane diuini homines sunt ad diuinae naturae hactenus consortes quatenus diuino charitatis spiritu ducuntur.
units.tr: Therefore the generous alms of the faithful, besides being an outstanding exercise of faith and love, bring forth two fruits in those who receive them, provided they are holy, that is, Christian and pious: the sustaining of the holy poor and the glorifying of God. Of the first he says, "not only supplies what is lacking to the saints." While the saints live in this life, many things are lacking to them, which fraternal love can supply, not only in bodily but also in spiritual matters. But the superstition of the Papists turns the unlearned people of Christ away from the living and needy saints to the honouring of the dead, whose defects, even if they had any, it could not supply. They are accustomed to spend the greatest sums on these, while the living and needy saints are shamefully neglected. Blind men do not see how divine a work it is to supply the defects of the saints. As long as we are in this life we are subject to this common condition, that we fall short in many things, which we cannot supply from our own resources. No one among all mortals is sufficient to himself in everything, so as not to need the help of others. Thus divine providence has constituted and arranged human affairs, so that we, bound together as if by mutual ties, cohere and are joined together, and mutual need joins those whom mutual love does not yet join. Therefore those who are so animated that they eagerly supply the defects of their brothers are truly divine people, sharers in the divine nature so far as they are led by the divine spirit of love.

units.la: Ad alterum pertinet quod dicit: veruetiam exuberat in hoc, quod per multos gratiae agantur Deo: in quo obserua gratitudinem sanctorum, qua pro corporali quoqi alimento gratias agunt Deo, agnoscentes illius esse bonitatem ac prouidentiam, quod per fratres necessitatibus ipsorum subuenitur. Hanc non ita agnoscunt, qui opibus in hoc saeculo abundantes in delitijs ac luxu viuunt.
units.tr: The next point concerns the words, "Yes, it even abounds in this, that through many thanksgivings are offered to God." Note here the gratitude of the saints, who give thanks to God even for bodily food, acknowledging that it is his goodness and providence that their needs are relieved through their brothers. Those who live in luxury and pleasure, abounding in wealth in this world, do not acknowledge this.

units.la: QVI per probationem ministerij huius, inquit, glorificant Deum super obedientia consensus vestri in Euangelio Christi, & super simplicitate communicationis in ipsos, & in omnes.) Dixit ministerium hoc collectarum exuberare in hoc quoq;, quod per multos agatur Deo gratiae. Id iam fusius explicat dicens: Qui videlicet multi, per probationem, hoc est, certum experimentum, ministerij huius, fructum illius sentientes, glorificant Deū. quapropter: propter obedientiam videlicet consensus vestri in Euangelium Christi, & propter simplicitatem communicationis in ipsos & in omnes. Probationem ergo & euidens experimentum ministerij sui, in hac causa, statuit primùm in eo, quòd sancti Hierosolymitani per illud cognouerant, & adhuc amplius cognituri erant, q; essent fideles ex Gentibus concorditer Euangelio Christi subditi, deinde & in eo quoque qd'experiebantur reipsa, quā candidè ac largè cōtribuerent in suos & aliorū omnium vius. Propter hæc duo glorificabant Deum, quod tantum incrementi dedisset Euangelio Christi inter Gentes, de quibus nulla spes, vel certè parum admodū fuerat spei, qd' vnquā essent ad cognitionem vnius veri Dei in Christo domino peruenturæ. Obseruemus hoc loco quando susceptum à nobis Euangelium Christi cedat ad gloriā Dei. Glorificant, inquit, Deū super obedientia, uel, subiectione, consensus vestri in Euangelium Christi, & super simplicitate communicationis in ipsos & in omnes. Ergo, tum demum causas damus glorificādi Deum propter nos, quando concordi obedientia consentimus in Euangelium, i. in doctrinam Euangelij Christi, præbentes nos communiter morigeros ac ductiles illius apostolis ac ministris, & per charitatem de bonis nostris communicamus egenis fratribus. Qui ad hunc modum se accommodant Euangelio Christi, veri sunt Euangelici, propter quos ab omnibus pijs meritò glorificatur Deus. Verùm ubi tales hodie repepиemus ecclesias, in quibus nulla sit erga Christi Euangelium αὐτοπαγὴ & ἐπεροδοξία, imò & ἀλλὰ λογία. Illud, & in omnes, commendat generalem beneficentiam, qua nō in aliquos tantum sed in omnes fidei consortes studium communicandi ac benefaciendi ueri Christiani exercet. Vide autem quomodo liberet sanctos à suspicione φιλαυτίας dū prædicat de illis qd' Deum glorificent non ob id tantum, quod defectibus & egestati ipsorum succurrebatur à fidelibus ex Gentibus, sed &, imò cum primis, quod essent illi subditi Euangelio Christi, idq; concordi consensu.
