Deinde, dumnon simpliciter dicit: & super simplicitate communicationis in ipsos, sed addit, & inomnes, ne in hac doxologia Dei proprium emolumentum quod adferebatur ex contributione ecclesiarum magis quàm ipsum Euangelij & ueræ charitatis profectum spectare viderentur, id quod alienum fuisset à sanctis.
units.tr: "Who, through the proof of this ministry, glorify God for the obedience of your confession to the gospel of Christ, and for the simplicity of your contribution to them and to all." He says that this ministry of the collection abounds also in this, that through many people thanks are given to God. He now explains this more fully, saying: "who, namely many, through the proof, that is, the sure experience, of this ministry, perceiving its fruit, glorify God," for the obedience of your agreement to the gospel of Christ, and for the simplicity of your contribution to them and to all. So the proof and clear evidence of his ministry in this matter he locates first in this: that the saints of Jerusalem had come to know, and would come to know still more, that the believers from the Gentiles were in harmony subject to the gospel of Christ; and then in this also, which they experienced in fact, how openly and generously they contributed to their own people and to all others. For these two things they glorified God, because he had given such an increase to the gospel of Christ among the Gentiles, from whom there was no hope, or at least very little hope, that they would ever come to the knowledge of the one true God in Christ the Lord. Let us observe here when the gospel of Christ, once received by us, redounds to the glory of God. They glorify, he says, God for the obedience, or subjection, of your agreement to the gospel of Christ, and for the simplicity of your contribution to them and to all. Therefore we then give cause for God to be glorified on our account when we agree in harmonious obedience to the gospel, that is, to the teaching of the gospel of Christ, showing ourselves together compliant and pliable to its apostles and ministers, and through love share our goods with needy brothers. Those who accommodate themselves to the gospel of Christ in this way are truly evangelical, and on their account God is rightly glorified by all the godly. But where, today, shall we find such congregations, in which there is no self-will [αὐτοπαγὴ], no otherness of opinion [ἐπεροδοξία] towards the gospel of Christ, and even less strange speech [ἀλλολογία]? The words "and to all" commend a general beneficence, by which the true Christian exercises his zeal for sharing and doing good not only to some but to all who share the faith. Note also how he frees the saints from the suspicion of self-seeking, while he says of them that they glorify God not only because help was given to their defects and poverty by the believers from the Gentiles, but also, and indeed above all, because they were subject to the gospel of Christ, and with harmonious agreement. Next, since he does not simply say "and for the simplicity of your contribution to them," but adds "and to all," so that in this giving of glory to God their own advantage, which came from the contribution of the churches, should not seem to be the main concern rather than the advance of the gospel itself and of true love, which would have been alien to the saints.

units.la: ET in illorum, inquit, orationē pro uobis.) Duobus præcedentibus ministerij huius fructibus addit & tertium, orationem videlicet sanctorum pro fidelibus Corinthiorum, necessitatib. ipsorum subuenientibus. Non est autē hæc particula referenda ad proximè præcedētia, sed ad id quod paulo suprà dixit: Verum etiam exuberat in hoc, quod per multos agātur gratię Deo, &c. ut hic subiungatur, & in illorū oratione pro uobis, subintelligē, exuberat funētio videlicet ministerij huius. Sic tribuit eleemosynario huic ministerio tria supplementum scilicet indigentiæ sanctorum, gratiarumactionem, & orationē pro contribuentib. Hæc est igitur retributio ac gratitudo pauperū, qua sub uenientib. sibi vices reddunt, nō tēporaria pro tēporarijs repēdentes, sed Deogratias agentes & pro ipsis ad illū orantes. Cogitet autē pius homo, quā sint hæc tria corā Deo magni momenti, & omnib. sacrificijs externis potiora, cui sancti, quos ipse in filio suo per spiritū gratiæ suæ sanctificauit, propter ipsum afflicti & depauperati omnium sunt acceptissimi.
units.tr: "And in their prayer for you," he says. To the two preceding fruits of this ministry he adds a third, namely the prayer of the saints for the faithful of Corinth, who were helped in their needs. This particle should not be referred to what immediately precedes, but to what he said a little above: "Yes, it even abounds in this, that through many thanksgivings are offered to God," etc., so that there is added here, "and in their prayer for you," where one must understand, "abounds," namely the function of this ministry. In this way he attributes three things to this charitable ministry: the supply of the saints' need, thanksgiving, and prayer for those who contribute. This, then, is the return and gratitude of the poor, by which, when they are helped, they repay the favour, not returning temporal things for temporal things, but giving thanks to God and praying to him on their behalf. Let the godly man consider how great these three things are before God, and how much better they are than all external sacrifices; for the saints whom he has sanctified in his Son through the Spirit of his grace are most acceptable to him, precisely because they are afflicted and impoverished.

units.la: Non est aut ociosum quod non dicit: Et in illorum αυτοσυνχῶ, id est, oratione, sed Αἴτσεσ. Significat autem Αἰτέω indigeo, unde est Αἴτησις, quæ uox precationem sonat obnixam & urgētem, qualis esse solet indigentium, dum necessitate compulsi pro ijs orant, sine quibus consistere non possunt. Tales significat esse precationes sanctorum pauperum pro illis, quorum beneficentia subleuantur, quas ego pluris fecero, q; omnes omniū sacrificorum horas, vt vocant canonicas, siue eas cantēt coniūcti, siue murmuret separati, oēs item omnium missarum orationes & collectas. Vnius pauperculę uiduę precatione cum orphanis suis ad Deū pro benefacientium sibi salute orantis, omnibus istis præferendam duxero. Hasce egentium sanctorum preces expetat quisquisapit, & interea in tercessiones diuorum in cœlis existētiū, quas fingunt & vendunt negociatores tēplarij, supfticiosis relinquat. De illis nihil certo constat, de istis constat. Obtemperantes ergo ei qui viliter ac prudenter cōsulens dicit: Tene certū & relinque incertum, exerceamus opera Christianæ charitatis in egenos sanctos, non in diuos, quibus nihil commodare possumus, & p illorum certas & vrgentes preces gratiæ Dei commendari petamus.
units.tr: Nor is it idle that he does not say "in their intercession" [ἐντεύξει], that is, prayer, but "request" [αἴτησις]. Now aitein means to be in need, whence comes aitēsis, a word that signifies an urgent and insistent entreaty, such as is typical of those in need when, compelled by necessity, they pray for those without whom they cannot survive. He indicates that such are the prayers of the poor saints for those by whose beneficence they are relieved, and these I would value above all the hours of all the sacrifices, as they call them canonical, whether they are sung together or murmured in private, and likewise all the prayers and collects of all the masses. I would prefer above all these the prayer of a single poor widow, who, with her orphans, prays to God for the salvation of her benefactors. Let whoever is wise seek the prayers of the needy saints, and meanwhile leave the intercessions of the saints in heaven, which the merchants of the temple invent and sell, to the superstitious. Of those nothing is certain; of these, something is. Therefore, obeying him who advises wisely and prudently, "Hold to what is certain and leave what is uncertain," let us practise the works of Christian love towards needy saints, not towards the saints in glory, to whom we can give nothing, and let us seek that, through their sure and urgent prayers, we be commended to the grace of God.

units.la: QVI desiderant uos, inquit, propter eminētem gratiam Dei in uobis.) Significat sanctos qui Hierosolymis erat, præclarè de Corinthijs sentire, sic ut desideret eos, intellige, videre. Roma.1.1.Thess.3.& 2.Timoth.1. uerbū ἰδεῖν, id est, videre, cum verbo desiderandi expresse coniungit. Hic verò & Philip.1.& 2. non exprimit, vbi tamen subintelligendum venit. Desiderių sanctorum, quo Corinthios uidere gestiebant, argumentū erat, quod honorifice esset erga eos affecti. Sic nanq; comparati sumus, vt quos magnifacimus absentes, videre cupiamus præsentes. Quare autem magni eos facerent, exprimit cū subiungit, propter eminentē gratiā Dei in uobis. Nō dicit, propter liberalitatē vestram in ipsos, sed, pptersupereminentē gratiā Dei in uobis, quibus uerbis duo facit. Primò ingeniū sanctorū exprimit, qui gratiā Dei in credentibus magis suspiciunt ac venerātur, q propriū emolumentū spectāt. Sancti Hierosolymitani non tā propter refocillationē, quā acceptuaccepturi erant ex liberalitate Corinthiorum, q̄ pter singulare gratiā Dei, in illis relucente, desiderabā eos videre. Deinde, dū p dicat super eminente in illis gratiā Dei, quæ desiderium uidendi ipsos excitet in sanctis, qui Hierosolymis erat, prouocat eos ad liberaliorē contributionem, quo & gratiæ Dei & sanctorū de se exi stimationi & desiderio competenter respondeant. Nō possum satis Apostoli diligentiā, prudētiā, fidem, & zelum in hac epistola admirari.
units.tr: "Who long for you," he says, "because of the surpassing grace of God in you." He signifies that the saints who were at Jerusalem thought very highly of the Corinthians, so that they longed to see them. Romans 1, 1 Thessalonians 3, and 2 Timothy 1 join the verb "to see" [ἰδεῖν], that is, "to see," expressly with the verb "to long for." Here, however, and in Philippians 1 and 2, he does not express it, though it is to be understood. The longing of the saints, with which they eagerly wished to see the Corinthians, was a sign that they were honourably disposed towards them. For we are so constituted that we desire to see present those whom we hold in high esteem when they are absent. Why they held them in such esteem he expresses when he adds, "because of the surpassing grace of God in you." He does not say "because of your generosity towards them," but "because of the surpassing grace of God in you," and by these words he does two things. First, he expresses the disposition of the saints, who regard and honour the grace of God in believers more than they look to their own advantage. The saints of Jerusalem longed to see them, not so much for the refreshment they were receiving or were about to receive from the Corinthians' generosity, but because of the singular grace of God shining out in them. Then, since he speaks of the surpassing grace of God in them, which stirs up in the saints of Jerusalem a desire to see them, he urges them to a more generous contribution, so that they may respond fittingly both to the grace of God and to the esteem and longing of the saints for them. I cannot sufficiently admire the diligence, prudence, faith, and zeal of the Apostle in this letter.

units.la: GRATIA aūt Deo, inquit, super inenarrabi li suo munere.) Habet hæc verba exclamatione, qua consideratione tam insignis gratiæ Dei, tā Corinthijs quā sanctis in Iudæa cōcessæ, in δοξολογίαν hāc erūpit, & materiā duob. iistis capitib9 8. & 9. tractatam concludit. Sic aūt nō modo suum erga vtranq; ecclesiam tam Hierosolymitanam quā Corinthiacam affectū ostendit, sed & Corinthiorū animos ꝓuocat, vt & ipsi gratiā Dei vtrobiq; singulare & excellente lecu magnificiāt. Et reuera donū Dei est ἀνεκδιήγητον i.qd nemo satis exponere ac depræ dicare queat, si ecclesiæ Christi ad hunc modum inter se sint comparatæ, sicut de Corinthiorum & Hierosolymitanorum ecclesijs Apostoli in hac materia commemorare videmus. Nam dona Dei inenarrabilia uocat fructus illos, quos ex contributione ecclesiastica tam dantibus, quam accipientibus prouenire meminit.
units.tr: "But thanks be to God," he says, "for his inexpressible gift." These words have the form of an exclamation, by which, in consideration of so remarkable a grace of God granted both to the Corinthians and to the saints in Judea, he breaks out into this doxology [δοξολογίαν] and concludes the matter treated in these two chapters, 8 and 9. In this way he not only shows his own affection towards both churches, that of Jerusalem and that of Corinth, but also stirs the minds of the Corinthians, so that they too may magnify the grace of God, which is singular and excellent in both places. And truly it is a gift of God that is inexpressible [ἀνεκδιήγητον], that is, something no one could sufficiently describe or proclaim, if the churches of Christ were thus related to one another, as we see the Apostle recall in this matter concerning the churches of Corinth and Jerusalem. For he calls inexpressible gifts of God those fruits which he remembers arising from the ecclesiastical contribution, both for those who give and for those who receive.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: Vthoritatem ac potestatē Apostolatus sui contra pseudapostolorum calumnias tuetur.
units.tr: He defends the authority and power of his apostleship against the calumnies of the false apostles.

units.la: CAPVT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: AETERVM ipse ego Paulus obsecro uos per lenitatē & mansuetudinē Christi, qui iuxta faciē quidē humilis sum inter uos, absens tamen audax sum erga uos. Rogo aūt uos, ne præsens audeam ea fiducia qua existimor audax fuisse in quosdam, qui putant nos ueluti secundum carnē ambulare: nam in carne ambulantes non secundū carnem militamus. Siquidem arma militiæ nostræ non sunt carnalia, sed potentia Deo, ad demolitionē munitionū, quib. consilia demolimur, & omnem celsitudinem quę extolitur aduersus cognitionē Dei, & captiuam ducimus omnem cogitationē ad obediendum Christo, & in promptu habemus uindictā aduersus omnē inobedientiā, cū impleta fuerit uestra obedientia.
units.tr: Now I, Paul myself, beseech you by the gentleness and meekness of Christ, I who am humble in your presence, but bold toward you when absent. I ask that when I am present I need not be bold with that confidence with which I am thought to be bold against some, who suppose that we walk according to the flesh. For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh. The weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but mighty before God for the pulling down of strongholds: we pull down counsels, and every height that is raised up against the knowledge of God, and we bring every thought captive to the obedience of Christ; and we are ready to avenge all disobedience, when your obedience is complete.

units.la: Diximus initiò capitis octaui, materiam de contributione in sanctos facienda insertā esse uelut in medio epistolæ, vt quę de syncieritate Apostolatus sui tractauit antea, & iam in posterum tracturus est, hoc quasi tolerabiliori interstitio nonnihil mitigarentur. Hac iam abiuluta, redit ad ea quæ nonnullis ante octauum capitibus, ad defensionem Apostolatus sui prientia subinde attigerat, quod ea causam nondum satis expediuisse iudicaret, cū magni esset momenti, magnaq; necessitate ad resistendum pseudapostolorum improbitati, & ad defendendum Apostolatus sui autoritatē impelleretur. Hac nanq; labefactata, nihil poterat sequi aliud, quàm vt omnis illius fructus tam partus q̄ adhuc pariendus interiret.
units.tr: At the start of chapter eight we noted that the matter of the contribution for the saints was inserted, as it were, in the middle of the letter, so that the matter he had treated earlier, and would treat again later, concerning the sincerity of his apostleship, might be somewhat softened by this more bearable interlude. With that now set aside, he returns to what he had touched on several times before the eighth chapter in defence of his apostleship. He judged that this cause was not yet sufficiently settled, since it was of great importance, and he was driven by great necessity both to resist the wickedness of the false apostles and to defend the authority of his apostleship. For if this were overthrown, nothing else could follow than that all the fruit of his labour, both that already brought forth and that yet to be brought forth, would perish.

units.la: Orditur aūt exordio admodū emphatico dicens: Ipse autem ego Paulus obsecro vos per lenitatē & mansuetudinē Christi, &c. Emphasis in eo primùm est, quod non simpliciter dicit: Obsecro aūt vos, sed: Ipse aūt ego Paulus qui iuxta faciem quidē humilis sum inter uos, absens tamen audax sum erga vos. Mox initiò perstringit pseudapostolos illorumq; sectatores, qui in nomen ipsius ludebāt, quod & re & nomine esset modicus ac modici momenti Apostolus (Sonat enim Paulus modicum) detrahebant; illi, quod cum in faciem esset humilis & abiectus, absens audaciam scriptis in ipsos spiraret. Hæc notans dicit, Ipse ego Paulus ille, cuius nomen nonnulli apud uos exsufflant & irridper, & quem tantæ dicunt esse temeritatis, vt cum præsens ob personæ humilitatem despicabilis apparearem, absens quosuis per epistolas terrere præsumam, quicquid illi dicat, & quantūuis in nomē meū ludāt, obsecro vos, qui saniores estis, &c: Deinde & in eo est emphasis, quod non dicit, simpliciter obsecro vos, sed addit, per lenitatē & mansuetudinem, uel, ut Vulgata habet, per mansuetudinē ac modestiam Christi. Hoc dicens, non modò obtestatur eos ferio per nomen Christi, sed admonet eos, quantā oporteat eorum esse peruersitatem qui mansuetudinē & modestiā in Apostolo contemptui exponāt, cum Christus ipse, Apostolo suo infinito maior, maluerit mānsuetus & modestus versari inter homines q̄ splendidus & magnificus: cuius tamen mānsuetudinē & modestiam nemo Christianus in argumentū contemptus rapiat, admirentur vero & suspiciant omnes. Sic existimo hæc verba, q iuxta faciē quidem humilis sum, absens tamen audax in vos, nō sic esse posita, quod ea ipse de se prædicet Apostolus, sed quod maleuoli ea ipsi improperarent, quibus mox per obliquum humilitate, mansuetudinē ac modestiam Christi dñi objicit, in quo videant, q̄ non sit in Apostolo persone spectanda claritas, cum illa non fuerit in apostolorum domino.
units.tr: He begins with a very emphatic opening, saying: "Now I myself, Paul, beseech you by the gentleness and meekness of Christ, etc." The emphasis lies first in the fact that he does not simply say "I beseech you," but "I, Paul myself, who am humble in your presence, but bold toward you when absent." Right at the start he strikes at the false apostles and their followers, who made sport of his name, belittling him as a small and insignificant apostle in both fact and name (for Paul means "small"). They said that while he was humble and abject in appearance, he showed boldness in his letters when absent. Noting this, he says: "I am that Paul whose name some among you sneer at and mock, and whom they say is so rash that, though I appear despicable in person when present, I presume to terrify anyone by letters when absent. Whatever they say, and however much they make sport of my name, I beseech you, who are the more sensible, etc." Again, the emphasis lies in the fact that he does not simply say "I beseech you," but adds "by the gentleness and meekness," or, as the Vulgate has it, "by the meekness and modesty of Christ." In saying this he not only solemnly adjures them by the name of Christ, but also warns them how perverse those people must be who hold the meekness and modesty of the apostle in contempt, when Christ himself, infinitely greater than his apostle, chose to live among men meek and modest rather than splendid and magnificent. Yet no Christian should take this meekness and modesty of Christ as a pretext for contempt; rather, all should admire and esteem it. I think these words, "who am humble in your presence, but bold toward you when absent," were not put this way because the apostle himself was declaring them about himself, but because ill-wishers were throwing them at him. Then, by an indirect route, he sets against this the meekness and modesty of the Lord Christ, so that they may see that in an apostle the splendour of his person is not to be regarded, since it was not present in the Lord of the apostles.

units.la: IPSE aūt ego Paulus, inquit.) Obseruà fidu ciam hanc in Apostolo. Quo magis pseudapostoli nomen ipsius subsannabant, & in significationem illius ludebant, hoc ipse de illo minus erubescebat, sed quasi gloriando esse se Pauli profitebatur. Nulla erat in nomine hoc ignominia, nulla in ipsius persona, nulla in Apostolatu, latu, quare de nullo horu erubescebat. Admonetur hoc exèplo ministri Christi ut cosimili fiducia obfirmati, neutiquà cedat aduersariorum nequiciæ, qua vel nomina ipsorum, vel psonas, vel fortunas, vel officia ludibrijs exponere moliuntur, scientes se contra eiusmodi maliciam & veritate doctrinæ & innocentia vitæ abunde esse munitos.
units.tr: "But I myself, Paul," he says. Observe the boldness in this apostle. The more the false apostles jeered at his name and made sport of its meaning, the less he himself was ashamed of it, but openly professed himself to be Paul, as if it were a matter for boasting. There was no disgrace in this name, none in his person, none in his apostleship, and so he was ashamed of none of these. By this example the ministers of Christ are admonished, steadied by a like confidence, not to give way at all to the wickedness of their adversaries, who try to expose to ridicule their names, their persons, their fortunes or their offices, knowing that they are amply armed against such malice, both by the truth of their doctrine and by the innocence of their lives.

units.la: OBSECRO uos, inquit, per lenitatè & mâ suetudinem Christi.) Lenitate ac mansuetudine erga peccatores Christus dominus uti maluit quâ seueritate. Quare in omnib. tâ uerbis quâ factis mitis apparuit & mâsuetus. Et huiusmodi medicu poscunt conscientiæ sensu peccatorum perculsę, quibus pacandis nihil minus accommodum est quâ pharisaica seueritas, q malum magis exasperatquâ curat. Sciens hoc Apostolus imitatus est exemplum dni, quo plures mansuetudine ac lenitate lucrifaceret, & huius Tim. quoq; admonuit, dicens: Seruum domini oportet non pugnare, sed placidum esse erga omnes, propensum ad docendum, tolerante malos cum mâsuetudine, &c. Cum ergo nihil sit & acceptius & magis necessarium pec catorib. hac Christi mansuetudine ac lenitate, non debemus eam contemnere in illius ministris, sed propter dominicu exemplu, & necessitates nostras cupidè amplecti, procul ab ingenio pharisæorum & iusticiariorum qu b. seueritas & peccatorum dedignatio magis arridet quâ dominica mâsuetudo, qua se peccatoribus mitem ac placidu etiam vsq; ad mensæ communicationem præbuit. Non aut probanda nobis tantum est hæc mansuetudo dei, sed & v q; adeo suspicienda ac veneranda, vt de illa admoniti non minus flectamur ad refipiscentiam, q si de ira ac iusto iudicio Dei, ipsa quoq; gehenna admoneamur.
units.tr: "I beseech you," he says, "by the gentleness and meekness of Christ." The Lord Christ chose to use gentleness and mildness toward sinners rather than severity. Therefore he showed himself mild and meek in all things, both in words and in deeds. Such a physician is needed by consciences struck with a sense of sin, and for calming them nothing is less suitable than Pharisaic severity, which exasperates the wound rather than healing it. Knowing this, the apostle imitated the example of the Lord, by which he won more people through meekness and gentleness, and he also admonished Timothy of this, saying: "The servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle to all, apt to teach, patient, bearing with evil men in meekness, etc." Since nothing is more acceptable and more necessary for sinners than this gentleness and meekness of Christ, we ought not to despise it in his ministers, but to embrace it eagerly for the sake of the Lord's example and our own needs, far from the disposition of the Pharisees and self-righteous people, who are more pleased by severity and disdain of sinners than by the Lord's meekness, by which he showed himself gentle and mild to sinners, even to the point of sharing their table. Nor is this meekness of God only to be approved by us; it is also to be so esteemed and revered that when we are admonished by it we are no less moved to repentance than if we were warned by the wrath and righteous judgment of God, and by gehenna itself.

units.la: QVI iuxta faciem quidem humilis sum inter uos, inquit, absens tamen audax sum inter vos.) Obserua ingenium hominum maleuolorum. Humilitatem præsentis Apostoli rapiebant in argumentum contemptus & oppro bationis, correptione epistolarem interpretantur audaciam absentis, quasi audacia sit, si minister Christi in faciem humilis, & erga omnes mansuetus, absens per literas corripiat deinquentes quos in Christo genuit. Humilitas oppositá est superbia personæ sublimis. Si despicienda est humilitas, ergo fulpiciêda est superbia. At coram Deo abominatio est, quicquid altum est coram hominibus. Et coram hominib. quoq; non est admodu grata superbia, siue illa sit externi status, siue personæ, siue morum. Quare humanæ conditioni magis amica & grata est humilitas quâ superbia. Verum ut febres palatum reddunt amarum, sic odia iudicia rerum corrupûtur, ut culpetur quod alienum est à culpa, & probetur quod natura sua est improbabile.
units.tr: "Who am humble in your presence," he says, "but absent am bold toward you." Observe the disposition of ill-wishers. They twisted the humility of the apostle present into a pretext for contempt and reproach, and they interpret the boldness of the absent apostle in his letter of rebuke as if it were audacity, as though it were boldness if a minister of Christ, humble in person and meek toward all, rebukes by letter those sinning against him whom he begot in Christ. Humility is opposed to the pride of a lofty person. If humility is to be despised, then pride must be admired. But whatever is lofty before men is an abomination before God. Pride is not very pleasing even to men, whether it is pride of outward status, of person, or of morals. Therefore humility is more friendly and welcome to human nature than pride. But just as fevers make the palate bitter, so hatred corrupts judgments of things, so that what is free from fault is blamed, and what is by its nature not blameworthy is approved.

units.la: ABSENS, inquit, audax sum erga uos.) Vbi Romanus pontifex bullis suis iniquissimis excommunicat integras ecclesias, prouincias & regna, & detonat in reges ac principes, illos que de sedibus suis deiicit, non accusatur audacia. Quare? Quia non est in facie humilis, sed admodum superbus triplo diademate corona tus, non incedit ut homo, sed baiulatur ut eidolu, ac sedet in templo tanquâ in maiestate Dei extollitur; supra omne quod dicitur Deus.
units.tr: "Absent," he says, "I am bold toward you." Where the Roman pontiff, by his most iniquitous bulls, excommunicates whole churches, provinces and kingdoms, and thunders against kings and princes, casting them down from their thrones, he is not accused of boldness. Why? Because he is not humble in face but very proud, crowned with a triple diadem; he does not walk as a man but is carried as an idol, and he sits in the temple as if exalted to the majesty of God, above everything that is called God.

units.la: Vbi ad hunc modum alienissimus ab humilita te Apostolica, & supra quamcunq; regiam sub limitatem sublimis ac superbissimus omnium ipsum orbem fastidiosissimè damnat, non habetur audax. At cum nostra ætate frater quidâ humilis in oculis mundi quæstuosissimas superbi ac Simoniaci pontificis indulgentias luce verbi Dei reprobabiles ac uitandas esse ostenderet, accusabatur audaciæ, quod fratercu lus obscurus in angulo Saxonicolatens non ipsum modo sanctissimum, sed & omnes Christiani orbis populos, sanctissimi indulgentias & probantes & ementes, reprobare non dubitaret, quasi unus plus omnibus saperet. Verum humilitas fraterculi illius sic erat veritate Dei munita, ut Rom. superbiæ prorsus esset inexpugnabilis.
units.tr: Where someone so utterly alien to apostolic humility, and so proud and lofty above every royal height, most disdainfully condemns the whole world, he is not held to be bold. Yet in our own age, when a certain humble brother showed to the world's eyes that the most profitable indulgences of a proud and simoniacal pontiff were to be rejected and avoided in the light of God's Word, he was accused of boldness, because this obscure little brother, lurking in a corner of Saxony, dared to condemn not only the most holy pontiff himself but also all the peoples of the Christian world, who both approve and buy the most holy indulgences, as if he alone knew more than everyone. But the humility of that little brother was so fortified by the truth of God that it was utterly impregnable to the pride of Rome.

units.la: ROGO autem uos, inquit, ne præsens audeam ea fiducia qua existimor audax fuisse in quosdam.) Quæ hactenus à principio capitis dixit imperfectum sensum habent, neq; enim expressum est, quid obsecret Corinthios. Id iâ subijcit, cum repetitione obsecrationis dicês: rogo autem uos, ne præsens audeam, &c. ut sic impleatur sensus. Ipse autem ego Paulus qui iuxta faciem humilis sum inter uos, absens tamen audax in uos, obsecro uos per lenitatem & mansuetudinē Christi, imo rogo uos, ne me cogatis, vt præsens audeam ea fiducia,. &c.
units.tr: "I beg you," he says, "that when I am present I may not have to dare with that boldness by which I am thought to have been bold against certain people." What he has said so far, from the beginning of the chapter, has an incomplete sense, for he has not stated what he is urging the Corinthians to do. He therefore adds it, repeating the entreaty and saying: "I beg you, that when I am present I may not dare," and so on, so that the sense is completed. "But I, Paul myself, who am humble in person among you, yet bold toward you when absent, beseech you by the gentleness and meekness of Christ. Indeed, I beg you, do not make me, when present, dare with that confidence," and so on.

units.la: Sic illud, Νόμω ἀξ, per auxesim esset positum. Nec inconueniens esset si quod initiò est παρα-καλῶ ὑμᾶς, verteretur, hortor & admoneo uos, vt quodsequitur, Νόμω ἀξ, per auxesim legatur imo obsecro ac rogo vos. Omnino plus emphasis est in uerbo Νόμω quam in uerbo παρα-καλῶ, siquti plus est obsecrare ac rogare quàm admonere & hortari. Videtur igitur sic dicere uoluisse: Ipse aut ego Paulus, hortor vos per lenitatem ac mansuetudinem Christi, imo non hortor tantu sed & rogo, ne me cogatis, ut audeam præsens, quod absens tantum audere putor, nolitis experiri quid possim præsens.
units.tr: So that phrase [Νόμω ἀξ] is placed there by way of amplification. Nor would it be out of place if the first word, [παρα-καλῶ ὑμᾶς], were rendered "I exhort and admonish you," so that what follows, [Νόμω ἀξ], is read by amplification as "nay, I beseech and beg you." Certainly the emphasis lies more in the word [Νόμω] than in [παρα-καλῶ], since to beseech and beg is more than to admonish and exhort. It seems, then, that he meant to say this: "I, Paul myself, exhort you by the gentleness and meekness of Christ; nay, I do not merely exhort but also beg you, do not make me dare, when present, what I am thought to dare only when absent. Do not wish to test what I can do when present."

units.la: Hoc dicens, deprecatur quidem necessitatem seuerius agendi cum immorigeris & contumacibus, uerum simul minatur eam seueritatem si admonitionem, obsecrationem & mansuetudinem suam contemnere pergant. Vnde & subijcit, qua λογίζομαι, id est cogito audere in quosdam, qui putant nos uelut secundu carne ambulare, &c. Erasmus & uetus interpres uerbum λογίζομαι, sensu passiuo reddiderunt, existimor. Verum rectius uertisset sensu actiuo, cogito, quo uerbo minatur cogitare se de seueritate exercenda in reprobos, nisi emendetur. Annotat Chrysostomus, quod non dicit, parătus iâ sum, uel, decreui, sed, cogito. Significat ficat autem λογίζομαι non simpliciter, sed ratio cinando de re aliqua uel facieda, uel omittenda cogitare, ad quem modū se Apostolus hoc loco cogitare dicit, si pergāt esse contumaces, fore sibi praesenti aliquando in eos audēdum.
units.tr: In saying this, he indeed deprecates the necessity of acting more severely toward the disobedient and stubborn; yet at the same time he threatens that severity if they persist in despising his admonition, entreaty and gentleness. Hence he adds the words [λογίζομαι], that is, "I reckon I shall dare against certain people, who think that we walk as if according to the flesh," and so on. Erasmus and the old translator rendered the verb [λογίζομαι] in the passive sense, "I am thought." But it would have been more correctly rendered in the active sense, "I reckon," a word by which he threatens that he is reckoning on exercising severity against the reprobate, unless they mend their ways. Chrysostom observes that he does not say "I am prepared" or "I have decided," but "I reckon." The verb [λογίζομαι] signifies not simply to think, but to think about something to be done or left undone, by reasoning. In this sense the Apostle here says that he reckons that, if they persist in being contumacious, at some time he will have to dare against them when present.

units.la: QVI putant nos veluti secundum carnem ambulare, inquit.) Perstringit eos, in quos sibi audendum esse cogitabat. Non dixit, qua cogito audere in uos, sed, qua cogito audere in quosdam, eos uidelicet, qui cogitant nos ambulare secundū carnem. Ambulare secundum carnem, carnalium est hominum, & latissimè patet. Est autem non spiritus, sed carnis studere sensibus, consilijs & affectibus, & secūdum hanc facere omnia. In praesenti uero, meo iudicio, cogitabant pseudapostoli Paulum ambulare secundum carnem, indulgendo suis affectibus, & secundū illorum impulsum seuerius scribendo, pluraque sibi sumendo, quàm humiliati personę ipsius conueniret, ac sustinere posset. Sane & hoc ingenio caro est, ut ubi seueritatē induit, multo acrius insectetur uicia aliorum, quàm ferat ipsius conditio, & interea tamen zelum iustitiae simulet. Erat Apostolus in faciem humilis secundum carnem, infirmus & modicae existimationis. Quare iudicabant eum nec esse, nec posse, nec praestare alia, nedum plura quàm sit, possit, & praestet caro, quamq; esset, appareret, & praestaret praesens in carne: ideoq; seueritate illam, qua grandia quaedam detonaret absens in epistolis, esse inanem & inefficacem carnalis temeritatis B praesumptionem. Communiter fere exponunt in genere de carnis affectibus ac desiderijs. Chrysost. species quasdam expressit, dicens: τίνας δὲ τότε φησὶ οἷς ἀνάγκῃ... Ergo dicebant eum ambulare secundum carnem, propterea quod iudicarent eum esse hypocritam, uersutum, & arrogantem. Sic intellexit Chrysost.
units.tr: "Who think that we walk as if according to the flesh," he says. He sets against those whom he reckoned he must act boldly toward. He did not say "I reckon I shall dare against you," but "against certain people," namely those who think that we walk according to the flesh. To walk according to the flesh belongs to carnal men and has a very wide application. To be concerned with the things of the flesh, rather than of the Spirit, in one's judgments, counsels and affections, and to do all things according to this, is the thing in question. In the present case, in my judgment, the false apostles thought that Paul walked according to the flesh, by indulging his own feelings and writing more severely under their urging, and by claiming more for himself than befitted the humble person he was and could bear. Indeed, it is the nature of the flesh that, when it puts on severity, it attacks the faults of others much more sharply than its own condition allows, while all the while it pretends a zeal for righteousness. The Apostal was humble in person according to the flesh, weak and of little esteem. Therefore they judged that he neither was, nor could, nor performed anything beyond what the flesh is, can and performs, and what it was and showed itself to be when present in the flesh. And so they held that the severity with which, when absent, he thundered certain great things in his letters, was empty, and that the boldness of his carnal rashness and presumption was ineffective. Most expositors explain this generally, of the affections and desires of the flesh. Chrysostom expressed certain particulars, saying: [τίνας δὲ τότε φησὶ οἷς ἀνάγκῃ...]. Therefore they said he walked according to the flesh, because they judged him to be a hypocrite, crafty and arrogant. So Chrysostom understood it.

units.la: Obsecro, si Paulus in oculis pseudapostolorum uisus est ambulare secūdum carnem, cuius omnia Christum in ipso loquentem ac uiuentem spirabant, quis nam post illum sic spiritualiter ambulabit, ut à reprobis nō dicatur ambulare secundum carnem. Maledica reprobórum ora nemo Christi minister effugiet, quae ne Christus quidem ipse effugere potuit, quo minus audiret seductor, comedo, uini potor, publicanorum amicus, & peccatorum socius. Hodie matrimonia ministrorū Christi sic infamant homines spurcissimi, scortatores publici, adulteri, incestuosi, & adhuc scelestioribus libidinibus absorpti, ut uocēt ea scortatione, dicantq; nubentes ambulare secundum carne. Has calumnias minister Christi haud plurisfaciat quàm latratu canum, ac cogitet hoc genus hominum sic esse comparatum, ut de rebus bonis & honestis bene loqui nesciat.
units.tr: I ask you, if Paul seemed in the eyes of the false apostles to walk according to the flesh, although in him all things breathed of Christ speaking and living in him, who after him will walk so spiritually that he will not be said by the reprobate to walk according to the flesh? No minister of Christ will escape the slanderous mouths of the reprobate, which Christ himself could not escape, so that the seducer, the glutton, the wine-drinker, the friend of tax-collectors and the companion of sinners was still heard of him. Today the marriages of Christ's ministers are so defamed by the most filthy men, public whoremongers, adulterers, incestuous men, and men swallowed up in still more wicked lusts, that they call that whoring, and say that the married walk according to the flesh. A minister of Christ should set no more store by these calumnies than by the barking of dogs, and should reflect that this kind of men is so constituted that it knows not how to speak well of good and honourable things.

units.la: NAM in carne ambulantes, inquit, non secundum carnem militamus.) Vocula γάρ, id est, nam, indicat particulam hanc per aetiolo-
units.tr: "For though we walk in the flesh," he says, "we do not war according to the flesh." The little word [γάρ], that is, "for," shows that this particle is placed as a causal explanation.

units.la: giam esse positam. Pseudapostoli iudicabant Paulum ambulare secundum carnem. Quare? Quia in carne ambulantes, inquit, non secundum carnem militamus. Ergo ne ob id dicebant eum ambulare secundum carnem, quod in carne ambulans, non secūdum carnem ambulasimilem? Atqui hoc minus debebant eum hujus insimulare quod secundum carnem ambulare. Non est igitur particulae huius aetiologia ad id referenda, quod proximè praecedit, quia non reddit rationē, quare Pseudapostoli Paulum secundum carnem ambulare cogitarint, sed ad id qd dixit, qua cogito audere in quosdam, ut rationem redderet, quare cogitaret in eos audere, qui se secundum carnem ambulare cogitabant. Ob id uidelicet, quod hoc falsò de se iudicabant. Nam licet in carne ambulare ut homo carne amictus, secundum carnem tamen non ambulabat. Ergo nō ideo cogitabat audere in eos quod id de se cogitarent, sed quod falsò cogitarent. Neq; enim æquum est ut propterea ultionem cogites in eum qui male de te loquitur, quod id facit, si merito fecerit. Si secundum carnem ambulasset Paulus, admodum fuisset iniquum de ultione eorum cogitare, qui id dixissent.
units.tr: The false apostles judged that Paul walked according to the flesh. Why? Because, he says, though we walk in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh. Then did they say he walked according to the flesh for this reason, that walking in the flesh he did not walk in a fleshly manner? Yet they ought the less to have accused him of walking according to the flesh on this ground. Therefore this causal particle is not to be referred to what immediately precedes, since it does not give the reason why the false apostles thought Paul walked according to the flesh; rather it refers to what he said, "I reckon I shall dare against certain people," to give the reason why he reckoned he would act against those who thought he walked according to the flesh. This, namely, because they judged this falsely of him. For although he walked in the flesh, as a man clothed with flesh, he did not walk according to the flesh. Therefore he did not reckon he would act against them because they thought this of him, but because they thought it falsely. Indeed it is not fair that you should plan vengeance against one who speaks ill of you merely because he does so, if he has spoken rightly. Had Paul walked according to the flesh, it would have been altogether unjust to plan vengeance against those who had said so.

units.la: Dices, Atqui ne sic quidem coueniebat Apostolo de inimicorum suorum ultione cogitare, cum Rom.12. doceat alios, non esse quaerendam propriae iniuriae uindictam, sed domino permittendam, dicenti: Mihi uindictam, & ego retribuam. Respondeo: Vt non quae sua sed quae Christi & aliorum essent, quaerebat: ita hic quoq; non propriae iniuriae uindictam, sed reprobórum hominum repressionem meditabatur, qui omnem Apostolatus sui cursum subuertere, & fructum Euangelicae doctrinae in ecclesia Corinthiorū disipare moliebātur.
units.tr: You will say: but neither was it becoming for the Apostle to plan vengeance against his enemies in this way, since in Romans 12 he teaches others that the vengeance of their own injury is not to be sought but left to the Lord, saying: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay." I answer: just as he sought not what was his own but what was Christ's and others', so here too he was meditating not vengeance for his own injury but the repression of reprobate men, who were striving to overturn the whole course of his apostleship and to scatter the fruit of the Gospel teaching in the Corinthian Church.

units.la: Obserua uero hic, quod fatetur quidem ambulare se in carne, humili uidelicet & infirmā, uerum iuxta negat se ambulare secundum carne. Ergo aliud est, uiuere in carne, & aliud, uiuere secundum carnem, aliud ambulare in carne, aliud ambulare secundum carnem. In carne uixit & ambulauit Christus ipse, tanquam uerus homo uiuens & circuiens inter homines, edens, bibens, dormiens, & quae alia ad carnis infirmitatem pertinēt sustinens, secundum carnem tamen nec uixit, nec ambulauit. Etenim secundum carnem uiuere & ambulare, est omnia secundum carnis desideria, consilia, & corrupta studia facere, quę locum in illo non habuerunt. In Apostolo habere potuissent, nisi illa uirtute spiritus Christi in se repressisset.
units.tr: Observe here that he confesses indeed that he walks in the flesh, that is, in humility and weakness, yet he denies that he walks according to the flesh. Therefore it is one thing to live in the flesh and another to live according to the flesh; one thing to walk in the flesh, another to walk according to the flesh. Christ himself lived and walked in the flesh, as a true man living and going about among men, eating, drinking, sleeping, and enduring whatever else pertains to the infirmity of the flesh; yet he neither lived nor walked according to the flesh. For to live and walk according to the flesh is to do all things according to the desires, counsels and corrupt aims of the flesh, which had no place in him. They could have had a place in the Apostle, had he not repressed them by the power of the Spirit of Christ.

units.la: Non est autem otiosum, quod cum dicendum uideretur: non secundum carnem ambulamus, dixit, non secundū carnem militamus. In carne circuibat orbem, humilis & despicabilis in oculis mundi, & circuitus ipsius non erat uagatis, otiosi, ac curiosi hominis, sed primarij ducis, Christo domino militātis. Vt hoc significaret, dixit se militare. Et ut militiā suam separaret. separararet à militia sæculi, negauit se militare {A}secundum carnem. Non militabat mundano alicui regno, sed regno Christi, in mundo hoc propagando, quod ut mundanum non est, sed spirituale, ita non poscit illius militia uires carnis, sed uirtutem & operationem spiritus.
units.tr: It is not idle that, where it seemed he should have said "we do not walk according to the flesh," he said instead "we do not war according to the flesh." In the flesh he went about the world, humble and despised in the eyes of the world; and his going about was not that of a wandering, idle and curious man, but that of a leader serving under the Lord Christ. To signify this, he said that he served as a soldier. And in order to separate his warfare from the warfare of the world, he denied that he warred according to the flesh. He did not serve some worldly kingdom, but the kingdom of Christ, to be propagated in this world; and since this kingdom is not worldly but spiritual, its warfare does not require the strength of the flesh, but the power and working of the Spirit.

units.la: SIQVIDEM arma militię nostrę non sunt, inquit, carnalia, sed potétia Deo.) Quoniā negauit se militare secúdum carnem, ideoq; aliquod sibi militiæ genus uindicauit (quemadmodum & Christus coram Pilato cum dixisset, Regnum meum non est de hoc mŭdo, non regem se, sed mundanum regem esse negauit, ideoq; à Pilato audiuit, Ergo rex es tu) consequenter, & probat se à qualitate armorum non militare, secundum carnem, & simul militiæ suæ genus & uires exponit, dicens: Siquidem arma militiæ nostræ non sunt carnalia: quasi dicat, uel à qualitate armorum quibus utor in hac militia, constare potest non militare me secundum carnem. Videtis enim me nō esse accinctum more mundi armis carnalibus. Qualibus ergo? Subdit, sed potentia Deo. Dicendum uidebatur, sed, spiritualia, uerum ut contra contemptum infirmitatis, quam in oculis mundi circumferebat carne, armorum suorum robur opponeret, dixit, sed potentia, nec simpliciter potentia, sed, potentia Deo: quasi dicat, cui milito, qui illis per me tanquâ suis utitur. Transfer hæc ad nostros Pontifices, & uide num illi quoq; cum Apostolo Christi dicere possint, non secundum carnem militamus. Siquidem arma militiæ nostræ non sunt carnalia, sed potentia Deo. Pro mundano regno belligerantur, & qualitati belforum ad quę ac cinguntur, conueniunt ipsorum arma. Mundanum regnum quærunt carnalibus armis, quibus & Romanos Pontifices & Cardinales illorum, & equestres episcopos, accinctos ad belligerandum uidere licuit.
units.tr: FOR our weapons of warfare, he says, are not carnal, but mighty through God. Since he denied that he fought according to the flesh, he claimed for himself a kind of warfare of his own, just as Christ, when he had said before Pilate, "My kingdom is not of this world," denied that he was a king in a worldly sense, and so heard from Pilate, "You are a king then." Consequently, he proves from the nature of his weapons that he does not fight according to the flesh, and at the same time sets out the kind and the power of his warfare, saying: "For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal." It is as if he said: from the nature of the weapons I use in this warfare, it can be established that I do not fight according to the flesh. For you see that I am not girded with carnal arms in the manner of the world. With what, then? He adds, "but mighty through God." One might have expected "but spiritual," but in order to set against the contempt for weakness that he bore in the sight of the world on account of his flesh, he states the strength of his weapons: "but mighty," and not simply "mighty," but "mighty through God." It is as if he said: the God whom I serve uses these weapons through me as his own. Apply this to our Pontiffs and see whether they too can say with the Apostle of Christ, "We do not fight according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God." They wage war for a worldly kingdom, and their weapons suit the kind of war for which they gird themselves. They seek a worldly kingdom with carnal arms, and we have seen the Roman Pontiffs and their Cardinals, and the bishops who ride to battle, girded for fighting.

units.la: NON sunt carnalia, inqt, sed potétia Deo.) An carnalia & potétia arma sibi sunt inuicem oppositæ? Sic apparet ex hisce uerbis. Poterat igitur dicere, non sunt infirma, sed potentia Deo, nisi hęsisset in termino carnis, secundum quam à reprobis ambulare dicebatur. Interim tamen ex oppositione potentiū armorum satis intelligimus, infirmitate tribui carnalibus armis. Sunt aut arma carnalia non modo ferrea, lignea, ænea, lapidea, sed & ea quibus sapientia, prudetia, ratio & sciet a carnis utitur, qualib. pugnát philosophi, sapiétes, doćti, rhetores, &c. In summa, infirma est omnis armatura carnis, & ea demum uerè potens, quę est spiritus Dei, qui suos armat uirtute diuina, uerbo uitæ, ueritate, zelo fidei, ardore charitatis, patientia afflictionū. & constátia spiritus inexpugnabili. His armis olim muniti episcopi expugnarūt omnis generis hæreses, maximè gladio uerbi Dei. Iam uero abiectis illis, usurpant sibi arma carnalia, gladios, laqueos, igne, aquâ, carceres, &c. & his se apprime munitos putát, & fortes ad extirpanda doctrinâ Euágelij. Ve{B}
units.tr: NOT carnal, he says, but mighty through God. Are carnal and mighty weapons set against each other? It seems so from these words. He could therefore have said "not weak but mighty through God," had he not stuck on the word "flesh," according to which the reprobate are said to walk. Yet from the opposition between mighty weapons and carnal ones, we understand well enough that weakness is ascribed to carnal arms. Carnal weapons are not only those of iron, wood, bronze or stone, but also those which the flesh uses in wisdom, prudence, reason and learning, with which philosophers, wise men, learned men, rhetoricians and the like fight. In sum, every armour of the flesh is weak, and that alone is truly mighty which is the Spirit of God, who arms his own with divine strength: with the word of life, with truth, with zeal for the faith, with the fire of love, with patience under affliction, and with a spirit that cannot be overcome. Bishops armed with these weapons once overthrew every kind of heresy, above all with the sword of the word of God. But now that these have been cast aside, they take up carnal weapons, swords, snares, fire, water, prisons, and the like, and think they are most thoroughly armed with these, and strong enough to root out the doctrine of the Gospel. But in fact they will find out that carnal weapons are too weak to overcome the truth.

units.la: rum reipsa experientur, arma carnalia esse infirmiora, quæ ut ueritatem expugnare ualeant.
units.tr: Indeed, they will find that carnal weapons are too weak to be able to overcome the truth.

units.la: AD demolitionem munitionū, inquit, quibus consilia demolimur, & omnem celsitudinē, quę extollitur aduersus cognitionem Dei, & captiuâ ducimus omnem cogitationem ad obediendum Christo.) In Græco sic legitur, πρὸς καθαίρεσιν ὀχυρωμάτων, λογισμὸς καθαιροῦντες, ὑπέρωμα ἐπαιρόμενον τῆς γνώσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἐχμαλωτίζοντες πᾶν νόημα. i. ad destructionem munitionū consilia destruentes, & omnē celsitudinē quæ extollitur aduersus scientiā Dei, & captiuantes omnem intellectum, &c. Participia illa, destruentes, captiuantes, & in promptu habentes, si ad proximè præcedentia referas, uidelicet, Nam arma nostra non sunt carnalia, sed potentia Deo, ad demolitionē munitionum, nec Græci nec Latini sermonis constructioni conueniunt. Quare coniungenda sunt paulò superioribus, & lectio ordinada ad hunc modum. Nam in carne ambulantes non secundum carnem militamus (siquidem arma militiæ nostræ non carnalia sunt, sed potentia Deo) militamus autem ad demolitionem munitionum, consilia demolientes, &c. Sic puto beneficio parenthesis & repetitione uerbi militamus Græcam posse saluari lectionem.
units.tr: FOR the pulling down of strongholds, he says, by which we pull down counsels, and every height that is raised against the knowledge of God, and bring every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ. In the Greek it reads: πρὸς καθαίρεσιν ὀχυρωμάτων, λογισμὸς καθαιροῦντες, ὑπέρωμα ἐπαιρόμενον τῆς γνώσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἐχμαλωτίζοντες πᾶν νόημα, that is, "for the destruction of strongholds, destroying counsels, and every height that is raised against the knowledge of God, and taking captive every understanding," and so on. If you refer those participles, "destroying" and "taking captive," to the words immediately before, namely "For our weapons are not carnal, but mighty through God, for the pulling down of strongholds," they fit neither the Greek nor the Latin construction. They must therefore be joined to the somewhat earlier words, and the reading should be arranged thus: "For though we walk in the flesh, we do not fight according to the flesh (for the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God). We fight, however, for the pulling down of strongholds, destroying counsels," and so on. In this way, I think, by means of the parenthesis and the repetition of the word "we fight," the Greek reading can be preserved.

units.la: Potentiā & efficaciam militiæ suæ exponit, tribuēs illi expugnatione regni Satanæ, & captiuatione mentiū in obedientiā Christi, deniq; & ultione aduersus omnē inobedietiam. Militamus, inqt, ad demolitione munitionū. Loquitur ad similitudine mundanæ militiæ, per quā hostiū munitiones expugnatur ac destruūtur, & qui in illis deprehenduntur captiui abducūtur. De quibus aút munitionib. loquatur, euestigio subiūgit dicės: λογισμὸς καθαιρῶν-τες. Vertūt aút λογισμούς cōsilia. Vox ipsa sonat ratiocinatione. Intelligit de consilijs ratiocinationis humanę, non syncerę, sed corruptę, in qua potissimum Satan regnat inter homines. Chrysost. exponit, τὴ τῦφον ἐπλλωικὸν καὶ σφισμάτων, καὶ συλλογισμῶν πλῶ ἰσχύν. Hæc getilis philosophiæ ac sapientiæ munitiones uirtute spiritus Christi per Euágelij prædicatione in cordib. hominū destruūtur. Hoc pertinet & illud qd sequitur: Et omnē celsitudiné, quæ extollitur aduersus scientiā Dei. Per celsitudinē intelligunt gloriā & potentiā mūdi. Nihil tamē uetat quo minus idē intelligamus qd per munitiones. Quod si de gloria mūdanæ potētię exposuerimus, obseruandū est, qd non simpliciter dicit, & omnē celsitudiné, sed addit, quę extollitur aduersus scientiā Dei, ne putemus Euágeliū omni simpliciter aduersari potētię regū ac principū. Legitimā illorū celsitudinē nō tollit, sed eā q sciētię Dei aduersatur, destruit. In summa, omnē celsitudinem Deo aduersantē, siue sit spūalis siue mūdana, siue sapiētię siue gloriæ, siue potētię, demolitur uirtus Euangelij. Quomodo? Nō ut nulla talis sit amplius in mundo, sed ut sit inefficax, & ut in illis qui credunt, prorsus destruatur. Alias illud Psal. 2.
units.tr: He sets out the power and efficacy of his warfare, ascribing to it the overthrow of Satan's kingdom, the taking captive of minds into obedience to Christ, and finally vengeance against all disobedience. "We fight," he says, "for the pulling down of strongholds." He speaks in the likeness of worldly warfare, in which the enemy's fortifications are stormed and destroyed, and those found within them are taken captive and led away. As to what strongholds he is speaking of, he immediately adds: λογισμὸς καθαιροῦντες. They translate λογισμούς as "counsels," though the word itself suggests reasoning. He means the counsels of human reasoning, not as they are in their purity, but as they are corrupted, and in which Satan above all reigns among men. Chrysostom explains it as [τὸ τῦφον ἐπηρμένον καὶ σοφισμάτων καὶ συλλογισμῶν πλῆθος ἰσχύν], that is, the strength of swollen pride, of sophisms and of syllogisms. These fortresses of pagan philosophy and wisdom are destroyed in men's hearts by the power of the Spirit of Christ through the preaching of the Gospel. This also applies to what follows: "and every height that is raised against the knowledge of God." By "height" they understand the glory and power of the world. Nothing prevents us from understanding the same thing by "height" as by "stronghold." But if we explain it of the glory of worldly power, we must observe that he does not simply say "every height," but adds "that is raised against the knowledge of God," lest we think that the Gospel simply opposes every power of kings and princes. It does not take away their lawful height, but destroys that which sets itself against the knowledge of God. In sum, the power of the Gospel overthrows every height that opposes God, whether it be spiritual or worldly, whether of wisdom, of glory, or of power. How? Not so that no such thing remains in the world any more, but so that it is made ineffective, and is wholly destroyed in those who believe. Otherwise that passage of Psalm 2 would still hold:

units.la: Quare fremunt gentes, &c. Assistunt reges terræ, & principes coëeniunt in unum aduersus dominum & aduersus Christum eius, inde ab initio Euangelij in orbe prędicati ad finem usque durat in mundo.
units.tr: "Why do the nations rage," and so on. "The kings of the earth set themselves, and the princes take counsel together against the Lord and against his Anointed." This has lasted in the world from the beginning of the Gospel's preaching throughout the earth until its end.

units.la: ET captiuam ducimus, inquit, omnem cogitationem ad obedien dum Christo.) Pertinet hoc ad secundam partem militaris uirtutis, captiuos, regno aduersario ereptos abducere, & in obedientiam ac peculium legitimo regi asserere. Concernit hoc electos, qui per Euangelium è captiuitate Satanæ & peccati liberantur, & Christo uero suo ac legitimo regi ad obediendum adducŭtur. Horum mens, uel, ut in Græco est νόημα, id est, intellectus, captiuatur luce ueritatis de errore conuicta, & Christo ad obediendum sistitur. Quare quod dicit, πᾶν νόημα, id est, omnem intellectum, nō est referendum uniuersaliter ad omnes homines, sed limitandum secundum id quod sequitur, ad obediendum Christo, quod non nisi de electis potest & credentibus exponi. Tutius ac simplicius igitur est, ut uertamus, totum intel lectum, quàm, omnem intellectum: intelligamusq; intellectum, qui prius obcæcatus fuerat in tenebris errorum, accepta ueritatis luce totum in unoquoq; credentium ad obediendum Christo adduci.
units.tr: AND we bring into captivity, he says, every thought to the obedience of Christ. This pertains to the second part of military power, which is to lead away captives snatched from the adversary's kingdom, and to claim them for obedience and possession of their lawful king. This concerns the elect, who through the Gospel are freed from the captivity of Satan and sin, and are brought to obey Christ their true and lawful king. Their mind, or, as the Greek has it, νόημα, that is, understanding, is taken captive by the light of truth, convicted of error, and is brought to stand before Christ in obedience. Therefore the words πᾶν νόημα, that is, "every understanding," are not to be referred universally to all men, but restricted by what follows, "to the obedience of Christ," which can only be explained of the elect and believers. It is safer and simpler, therefore, to translate "the whole understanding" rather than "every understanding," and to understand that the understanding, which had previously been blinded in the darkness of errors, once the light of truth is received, is brought in its entirety in each believer to obey Christ.

units.la: ET in promptu, inquit, habemus uindictam aduersus omnem inobedientiam.) Tertiam militaris uirtutis partem exprimit, pertinentem ad rebelles, dignos in quos uindicta propter inobedientiam exerceatur. Et hanc militiæ suæ uindicat, ne quid illi desit, sed plena sit, ad perfectă uictoriam instructa & efficax. Dicit hanc esse sibi in promptu, paratam uidelicet, sic ut illa possit expedite uti, si quando necessitas poposcerit. Ponit autem eam indeterminate, quare tam de excommunicatione quàm de corporali uindicta intelligi potest, quali usus est in Elymam Magum, & Petrus in Ananiam & Sapphyram. Nec loquitur de una inobedientię specie, sed in genere de omnibus, & omnium inobedientium, cum non simpliciter dicit, aduersus inobedientiam, sed, aduersus omnem inobedietiam. Quasi dicat, Qualencunq; & qualiuncunque etiam eorum qui apud uos inobedientes esse malùt, quàm obedire. Interim tamen non loquitur de alia inobedientia, quàm quæ rebellis sit aduersus ueritatem Euangelij Christi.
units.tr: AND we have in readiness, he says, vengeance against all disobedience. He expresses the third part of military power, which applies to rebels who deserve to be punished for their disobedience. He claims this vengeance as part of his warfare, so that nothing may be lacking to it, but it may be full, equipped and effective for complete victory. He says that it is ready for him, that is, prepared, so that he may use it readily whenever need demands. He states it indefinitely, so it can be understood both of excommunication and of bodily punishment, such as he used against Elymas the magician, and Peter against Ananias and Sapphira. Nor does he speak of only one kind of disobedience, but in general of all, and of all disobedient persons, since he does not simply say "against disobedience," but "against every disobedience." It is as if he said: whoever and whatever kind of people among you prefer to be disobedient rather than obey. Yet he does not, in the meantime, speak of any disobedience other than that which rebels against the truth of the Gospel of Christ.

units.la: CVM impleta fuerit uestra obedientia, inquit.) Adiecit hoc respectu eorum qui in ecclesia Corinthiorum inobedientes esse coepe-rant, quibus spe resipiscentiæ parcebat, donec ecclesia perfectă obedientiam in causa, de qua duobus præcedentibus capitibus egit, & in cæteris quoq; ostendisset. Et hæc dicens, minando terret immorigeros Apostolatus sui contemptores.
units.tr: When your obedience has been fulfilled, he says. He added this with regard to those in the Corinthian church who had begun to be disobedient, whom he spared in hope of their repentance, until the church had shown perfect obedience in the matter treated in the two preceding chapters and in the rest. In saying this, he threatens by menace those unruly despisers of his apostleship.

units.la: {A} arma militiæ nostræ non sunt carnalia, sed potentia Deo, ad demolitionem munitionū, consilia demolientes, & omnem celsitudinē, quæ extollitur aduersus cognitionem Dei, &c. quę eximia & sublimia sunt in rebus, uiribus, & facultatibus humanis, siue sint λογισμοὶ sapientiæ, siue ύψώματα iusticiæ, glorię ac potetiæ humanæ, esse munitiones Regni Satanæ, per Euãgelicæ prædicationis uirtutem demoliendę.
units.tr: {A} "The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God, to the pulling down of strongholds, casting down counsels and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God," etc. Those things which are excellent and lofty in human matters, resources and abilities, whether they are reasonings [λογισμοὶ] of wisdom or heights [ύψώματα] of righteousness, glory and human power, are strongholds of the kingdom of Satan, to be pulled down by the power of the preaching of the gospel.

units.la: Ί Et hic locus de efficacia Apostolicæ militiæ admodum insignis, in quo diligens lector obseruabit, primum in eo quod dicit, siquidē
units.tr: This passage on the efficacy of the apostolic warfare is most remarkable. In it the diligent reader will observe, first, in what he says, "since indeed".

units.la: ἀ Deinde obseruandum est quod dicit, quæ extollitur aduersus scientiam Dei, ubi uidemus fastum & superbiā hominum impiorum non submittere se, sed aduersari scientiæ Dei. Donec regnat superbia, fieri nō potest, ut obediatur scientiæ Dei. Quare nemo miretur, quì fiat quod qui sublimes sunt in hoc sæculo, & mente & conditione elati, tantopere ueritati Dei aduersantur. Humilibus facile persuadetur, ut obediat ueritati, superbis nequaquam.
units.tr: Next, we must observe what he says: "that exalts itself against the knowledge of God." Here we see that the pride and haughtiness of wicked men do not submit themselves but oppose the knowledge of God. While pride reigns, it cannot happen that the knowledge of God is obeyed. Therefore let no one wonder why those who are lofty in this age, elated in mind and station, so greatly oppose the truth of God. The humble are easily persuaded to obey the truth; the proud by no means.

units.la: Quid rationis auré est, quod non dicit, quæ extollitur aduersus Deum, sed, quæ extollitur aduersus scientiam & cognitionem Dei? Regnum Satanæ regnum est tenebrarū & ignorătiæ Dei. Huic nihil magis aduersatur quàm doctrina scientiæ Dei. Ideo instigantur manci pia Satanæ, ut huic sese opponāt. Et quoniam hypocrisi maliciam suam obtegunt, nolunt uideri tales qui contra Deum extollătur, quem apprimè se colere simulant, at interim doctrinæ scientiæ Dei manibus & pedibus obsistūt. Obsecro quid aliud faciunt hodie qui uerbum scientiæ Dei tanta cum pertinacia repellunt, & plebem Christi à lectione sacrarum scripturarū sic arcēt, ut codices ipsos sacrarū scripturarum è manibus fidelium raptos igni tradāt? An non sedent in sublimi qui hoc faciunt? An non extolluntur aduersus scientiam Dei?
units.tr: What reason is there, pray, that he does not say "that exalts itself against God," but "against the knowledge and understanding of God"? The kingdom of Satan is a kingdom of darkness and of ignorance of God. Nothing opposes this more than the teaching of the knowledge of God. Therefore the ministers of Satan are stirred up to set themselves against it. And since they cover their malice with hypocrisy, they do not want to appear to be those who exalt themselves against God, whom they pretend above all to worship; yet meanwhile they resist with hands and feet the teaching of the knowledge of God. I beseech you, what else do those do today who repel the word of the knowledge of God with such obstinacy, and keep the people of Christ so far from reading the holy Scriptures that they hand over to the fire the very codices of the holy Scriptures snatched from the hands of the faithful? Do not those who do this sit on high? Are they not exalted against the knowledge of God?

units.la: ȝ Tertiò, in eo quod dicit: & captiuum ducimus omnem intellectum ad obediendū Christo, adsto, admonemur sic nos esse per veritatem Dei liberatos è regno & potestate Satanæ, ut interim mentes nostræ non sint liberæ ad cogitandum & faciendum quæ nobis adlubescât, sed captiuatæ in obedientiam Christo redemptori præstandam
units.tr: Third, in what he says, "and we take captive every thought to obey Christ," we are reminded that we are thus freed by the truth of God from the kingdom and power of Satan, yet that meanwhile our minds are not free to think and do whatever pleases us, but are taken captive to render obedience to Christ the Redeemer.

units.la: 4 Quarto, cum dicit: in promptu habentes uindictam aduersus omnem inobedientiam, cum impleta fuerit uestra obedientia, admonemur de prudentia Apostolica in ultione rebellium exercenda. Nolebat Apostolus ulcisci in rebelles, donec impleta esset obedientia reliquorum, unde certus redderetur, non esse multitudinem fidelium sociam rebellionis, atque ita sine disturbatione status ecclesiastici in paucos rebelles exerceri posse uindictam.
units.tr: Fourth, when he says, "having in readiness vengeance against all disobedience, when your obedience shall have been fulfilled," we are reminded of apostolic prudence in exercising vengeance on rebels. The Apostle did not want to punish the rebels until the obedience of the rest was complete, so that it would be certain that the multitude of the faithful was not a partner in the rebellion; and thus vengeance could be exercised on a few rebels without disturbing the state of the church.

units.la: Quę in conspectu sunt uidetis: Si quis de seipso confidit quod Christi sit, illud rursum perpendat ex seipso, quod quemadmodū ipse Christi est, ita & nos Christi sumus. Nam si & amplius quippiam glorier de potestate nostra, quam dedit nobis dominus in ædificationem, & non in destructionem uestri, non pudebiam. Ne uideat ceu perterrefacere uos per epistolas. (Nam epistolæ, inquiunt, graues sunt & robustæ, ac præsentia corporis infirma, & sermo contemptus) Hoc cogitet qui istiusmodi est, quod quales sumus sermone per epistolas cū absumus, tales sumus etiam præsentes facto.
units.tr: "You look at what is before your eyes. If anyone trusts in himself that he is Christ's, let him reckon again from himself that, just as he is Christ's, so also are we Christ's. For even if I boast somewhat more of our authority, which the Lord gave us for building you up and not for pulling you down, I shall not be ashamed. Let him not think that I seem to terrify you by letters. (For, they say, the letters are weighty and strong, but the presence of the body is weak and the speech contemptible.) Let him who is such consider this: that what we are in word by letters when we are absent, such we are also in deed when present."

units.la: Causam quam initio capitis coepit, prosequitur. Quę in conspectu sunt uidetis: inquit. Græcè est: τὰ κατὰ πρόσωπον, id est, quæ secundū faciem sunt. Deinde, uerbum uidetis, sic est in Græco, ut uerti possit, tam uidete in imperatiuo, quàm uidetis in indicatiuo. Vetus interpres uertit, uidete. Et exponunt: uidete uel facta mea, quæ in oculos uestros incurrentia, omnium sunt manifestissima, & ex illis iudicate, num ambulem secundum carnem, & intelligite militiæ meæ cum qualitatem, tum uirtutem. Hoc sensu illud τὰ κατὰ πρόσωπον, id est, quæ secundū faciē sunt, idē est, quod quæ manifesta sunt & euidetia. Chrysostomus tamen per interrogationem legit, Quæ secundū faciē sunt uidetis: & in sensu exprobrationis exponit ad hunc modum, ... Et hic mihi sensus probatur, quamuis nec alter quicquā habeat incōmodi.
units.tr: He pursues the cause he began at the start of the chapter. "You look at what is before your eyes," he says. In Greek it is "the things according to the face" [τὰ κατὰ πρόσωπον], that is, things that are according to the appearance. Next, the verb "you look" is in Greek such that it can be translated either as "look" in the imperative or as "you look" in the indicative. The old translator renders it "look." And they explain: "look at my deeds too, which, falling under your eyes, are most manifest to all, and judge from them whether I walk according to the flesh, and understand both the quality and the power of my warfare." In this sense, "the things according to the face," that is, things according to appearance, is the same as what is manifest and evident. Chrysostom, however, reads it with a question, "Do you look at things according to the face?" and explains it in the sense of reproach in this manner: ... And this sense seems right to me, although the other has no inconvenience either.

units.la: Dicit itaq;. Quoniam iuxta faciem humilis appareo, quod mihi nonnulli obijciunt, & hinc occasionem contemnendi Apostolatus mei sumunt, estis ne uos adeo spiritualium rerum imperiti, ut & ipsi de me non secundum
units.tr: He says therefore: "Since I appear humble in person, as some object to me and take from this an occasion of despising my apostleship, are you so inexperienced in spiritual matters that you too judge of me not according to

units.la: ueritatem & efficaciam Apostolatus mei, sed secundum faciem, id est, personæ meæ humilitatem iudicetis: & gloriosulos illos in faciem eximios uestros magistros magnificatis: Est itaq; malum hoc, personarum uidelicet & facierum respectus, quod per omnes ubique regnat ecclesias, non recens, sed admodum antiquum, & in ipsis Apostolicis ecclesiis exortum, tamq; ualidum, ut Apostolicam quoque supereminentiam, imò Christum ipsum, in contemptum coniecerit.
units.tr: the truth and efficacy of my apostleship, but according to the face, that is, the humility of my person; and do you magnify those glorious-seeming, outwardly distinguished teachers of yours?" This evil, namely the respect for persons and faces, reigns everywhere through all the churches. It is not recent but very ancient, and it arose even in the apostolic churches themselves, and it is so powerful that it has cast into contempt even the apostolic pre-eminence, indeed Christ himself.

units.la: SI quis de seipso confidit, inquit, quod Christi fit, illud rursum perpendat ex seipso, quod quemadmodū ipse Christi est, ita & nos Christi sumus.) Quamuis non asseueranter dicit: Sunt apud uos, qui se Christi esse dicant, sed: Si quis de seipso confidit quod Christi sit, non dubito tamen fuisse inter pseudapostolos, qui sic se dicerent & iactarent esse Christi, ut hoc nomine aduersus Apostolum insolesceret, cuius rei argumentum est quod 1. Corin. 1. inter schismaticos etiam illi numerātur, qui se Christi esse dicebant: Significatum est mihi de uobis, inquit, fratres mei, quod contentiones sunt inter uos. Dico autem illud, quod unusquisq; uestrum dicit, alius quidem, ego sum Pauli, ego uero Apollo, ego uero Cephæ, ego uero Christi, &c. Vbi exposuimus, quomodo fieri possit, ut se Christi quisquam esse schismaticè dicat. Planè probabile est, uenisse Corinthum pseudapostolos, qui ob id quod Christum in carne uidissent, & aliquid forsan consuetudinis cum discipulis illius habuissent, aut è numero illorum extitissent, admodum gloriati sint esse se peculiariter Christi discipulos; illosque hic perstringi ab Apostolo, cum dicit: Si quis de seipso confidit quod Christi sit, illud rursum perpendat, quod quemadmodum ipse Christi est, ita & nos Christi sumus. Vide autē quàm modestè loquatur. Non contendit Christi eos non esse, imò non dicit: uideat uerè ne Christi sit uel secus. Neque enim mox Christi est, qui se illius esse gloriatur, ad quæ modum iactatiam eorum restringere poterat, sed quasi concedens esse eos Christi, unum hoc agit, ut se quoque Christi esse contendat, ad quem sco pum unicè spectat, nec imprudenter. Etenim nemo ob id Christi se esse euicerit, si alios Christi non esse probauerit: quemadmodum nemo propterea bonus est, quod alios probat esse malos, sicuti cacabus ex eo se album ac nitidum esse non euincit, si ollæ dicat, Væ tibi tu nigra.
units.tr: "If anyone trusts in himself," he says, "that he belongs to Christ, let him reckon again from himself that, just as he is Christ's, so also are we Christ's." Although he does not say assertively, "There are among you those who say they are Christ's," but "If anyone trusts in himself that he is Christ's," I do not doubt that among the false apostles there were some who called themselves and boasted that they were Christ's, so as to become arrogant against the Apostle by this name. The evidence for this is that in 1 Cor. 1 those who said they were Christ's are also counted among the schismatics: "It has been signified to me concerning you, my brothers, that there are contentions among you. I mean this, that each one of you says: I am of Paul, I indeed of Apollos, I of Cephas, I of Christ," etc. There we explained how it can happen that someone calls himself Christ's in a schismatic way. It is plainly probable that false apostles came to Corinth who, because they had seen Christ in the flesh and perhaps had some familiarity with his disciples, or had come from their number, gloried greatly that they were Christ's disciples in a special way; and that these are the ones the Apostle here attacks when he says: "If anyone trusts in himself that he is Christ's, let him reckon again that, just as he is Christ's, so also are we Christ's." But see how modestly he speaks. He does not contend that they are not Christ's; he does not say "let him see whether he truly is Christ's or not." For one who boasts that he is Christ's is not at once Christ's, so he could not restrain their boasting in this way. Instead, as if conceding that they are Christ's, he presses only this, that he too contends to be Christ's, which is the goal at which he alone looks, and not without reason. For no one proves himself to be Christ's by showing that others are not Christ's; just as no one is good because he proves others to be bad, and a pot does not prove itself white and shining by saying to another pot, "Woe to you, you black one."

units.la: ILLVD, inquit, rursum ex seipso perpédat, quod quemadmodū ipse Christi est, ita & nos Christi sumus.) Non simpliciter dicit, illud perpendat, sed, illud rursum ex seipso perpendat, neq;, quod & nos Christi sumus, sed, quod quemadmodū ipse Christi est, ita & nos Christi sumus. Sic emphaticè posuit ista, rursum ex seipso, &, quemadmodum ipse Christi est. Argumentum est ab æquo. Vir bonus & æquus non sic de se bene sentit, ut de alijs male sentiat. tiat,sed quod de se honestè iudicat,idem iudi-cat & de alijs. Est enim admodum iniquum, sine magnis & euidentibus causis non tribue-re alijs quod tibijpse tribuendum esse iudicas. Sic dicit hic Apostolus: Si quis sibijpse tribuit quòd Christi sit discipulus, hoc de seipso sen-tiens,sentiat & de nobis. Nec est, ut id audiat & cognoscat ex nobis. Si uir bonus est,quem-admodū ex seipso de se iudicat quòd sit Chri-sti,ita ex seipso de nobis quoque sentiat,quòd Christi simus. Argumentum hoc æquitatis,lo-cum habet in illis qui eiusdem religionis pro-sessione iunguntur:secus uero in illis qui ma-nifesta dissensione ac professionis diuersitate à se inuicem disidsent,quales sunt iudǫi,Gen-tes & Christiani.De Iudǫo incredulo, & à pro-sessione nominis Christi alieno, nemo Chri-stianus sentiet, quòd sicut ipse Christi est, ita Christi sit & ille, qui non modò ad Christum non pertinet,sed & palàm se alienum ab illo esse profitetur. Pseudapostoli & sectarij Chri-sti se esse gloriabantur. Idem faciebat & Pau-lus.Iâ si satis illis erat professio nominis Chri-sti ad hoc,ut Christo accenserentur, debebant hoc ipso iudicio uti & de Paulo, & reliquis Christianis.Si præter publicam Christianæ re-ligionis professionem uel fidei,uel dilectionis ac zeli,uel ministerij gratia Christi se esse con-sidebant, poterant ac debebant ex seipsis eas-dem ob causas de Paulo quoq; iudicare quòd Christi esset & ipse. Hac æquitatis norma si u-teremur hodie in ecclesia, minus haberemus B schismatum, minus temerarij iudicij , minus item persequutionum.
units.tr: He says further, let him weigh this again from his own case: just as he himself is Christ's, so we too are Christ's. He does not simply say, let him weigh that, but, let him weigh this again from his own case, and not merely that we too are Christ's, but that just as he himself is Christ's, so we too are Christ's. In this way he puts these words emphatically: again from his own case, and just as he himself is Christ's. The argument is from equity. A good and fair man does not think well of himself in a way that makes him think ill of others; rather, what he judges honestly about himself he judges also about others. For it is very unfair, without great and evident causes, to deny to others what you yourself judge should be attributed to you. So the Apostle says here: If anyone attributes to himself that he is a disciple of Christ, let him think the same of us too, judging from his own feeling.
