Nor is it that he should hear and learn this from us. If he is a good man, then just as he judges from himself that he is Christ's, so from himself let him also think of us, that we are Christ's. This argument from equity has its place among those who are joined in profession of the same religion, but not among those who are plainly divided by open dissent and difference of profession, such as Jews, Gentiles and Christians. No Christian would think of an unbelieving Jew, a stranger to the profession of the name of Christ, that just as he himself is Christ's, so that man too is Christ's, since he not only does not belong to Christ but openly professes himself alien to him. The false apostles and sectarians of Christ boasted that they were his. Paul did the same. Indeed, if the profession of Christ's name was enough for them to be counted among Christ's people, they ought to use this same judgment about Paul and the other Christians. If they reckoned themselves to be Christ's, apart from public profession of the Christian religion, by reason of faith, or love and zeal, or the ministry, then for these same reasons they could and ought to judge from themselves that Paul too was Christ's. If we used this rule of equity today in the Church, we would have fewer schisms, less rash judgment, and likewise fewer persecutions.

units.la: Dicet quisquam. Si negocium hoc erat A-postolo cum pseudapostolis, quomodo dicit se Christi esse quemadmodū illi sint Christi? An nō aliter Christi est uerus Apostolus,quàm falsus? Respondeo. Nō dicit se sic esse Christi, sicut illi sint Christi, sed iniquum illorum de se iudicium perstringens, æquitatis eius illos admonet, qua quemadmodum de seipsis iudi-cabant quòd Christi essent, ita iudicent de se quoq; quod &ipse sit Christi.Si mulier hone-sta à minus honesta diffamata dicat: Si confi-dis te mulierem esse honestam,ex te ipsa idem de me quoque sentias,ut quemadmodum ho-nestam te iactas,ita honesta sim & ego. Hoc di-cens non comparat se mulieri minus honestę, sed iniquum illius de se iudicium ad æquitatis normam reuocat & reprimit.Quare,ubi dicit, quod sicut ipse Christi est,ita & nos, subaudi-endum est si uere Christi est,Christi sumus.
units.tr: Someone will say: if this was the Apostle's dispute with the false apostles, how can he say that he is Christ's as they are Christ's? Is not the true apostle Christ's in a different way from the false one? I answer: he does not say that he is Christ's in the same way as they are Christ's, but in condemning their unfair judgment of him, he admonishes them by their own sense of equity: just as they judged about themselves that they were Christ's, so let them judge about him too, that he also is Christ's. When an honest woman is slandered by a less honest one, if she says: If you trust that you are an honest woman, then think the same of me, so that just as you boast of being honest, I too may be honest, she does not compare herself with a less honest woman, but calls back and restrains that woman's unfair judgment of her by the rule of equity. Therefore, where he says that just as he himself is Christ's, so are we, the words "if he is truly Christ's" must be understood: we are Christ's.

units.la: NAM si & amplius, inquit, quicquam glo-rier,de potestate nostra, quam dedit nobis do-minus in ædificationem,& non in destructio-nem uéstri, non pudefiam.) Non simpliciter dicit: Si amplius,sed : Nam si etiam amplius quicquam glorier,&c. Quare exponendū est tanquam æciologia eius quod præcessit. Po-test autem trifariam exponi.Primò sic,ut referatur ad ea quæ paulò supra de virtute & effi-cacia Apostolatus sui scripsit, dicês: Siquidem arma militiæ nostræ non carnalia sunt,sed po-tentia Deo ad demolitionem munitionū,qui-bus consilia demolimur,&c. quasi adhuc am-plius quiddam sit, potestatem habere ędifican di, de qua si gloriari uelit,non pudesiat. Verū hic sensus non satis, meo iudicio, probabilis est.Deinde, ut referatur ad proximè præceden-tia,quibus dixit, debere eum qui se Christi es-se confidit,quemadmodum ipse Christi est,ita ex seipso reputare,quod ipse quoq; sit Christi, hoc sensu. Sic enim comparatum esse se, ut si ultra id quod Christi est, tanquâ Christianus; de potestate sua quoq; gloriari uelit,quâ à do-mino tanquam Apostolus accepit, non sit pu-defaciendus.Etenim amplius quiddam est,nõ solum fidelem esse Christi, sed & Apostolum. Tertiò, sic quoq; non incómode expoueris: Etenim etiamsi amplius quippiam quàm ipsè sibi uindicare queat, de potestate nostra glo-rier,quam nobis dominus dedit,non pudesiá. Quare merito,qui talis est,duplici me nomine Christi esse cogitabit,si de seipso confidere po-test, quod sit Christi.
units.tr: "For if I should boast even more of anything," he says, "concerning our power, which the Lord gave us for edification and not for your destruction, I shall not be ashamed." He does not simply say, "if more," but, "For if I should even boast more of anything," and so on. Therefore this must be explained as an explanation of what went before. It can be explained in three ways. First, so that it refers to what he had written a little above about the virtue and efficacy of his apostleship, saying: For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds, by which we pull down counsels, and so on, as if there were something still more: to have the power of building up, of which, if he wished to boast, he would not be ashamed. But this sense seems to me not sufficiently probable. Second, so that it refers to the things immediately preceding, in which he said that whoever trusts that he is Christ's ought to reckon from himself, just as he himself is Christ's, that he too is Christ's, in this sense: that he is so constituted that, beyond what he has as a Christian who is Christ's, he may wish to boast also of his power, which he received from the Lord as an apostle, and he will not be put to shame. For it is something more to be not only a faithful man of Christ but also an apostle. Third, this too may be explained not inappropriately: even if I should boast of something more than he himself can claim for himself, concerning our power which the Lord gave us, I shall not be ashamed. Therefore whoever is such a man may rightly think that he is Christ's in a twofold respect, if he can trust about himself that he is Christ's.

units.la: Non dicit autè simpliciter,de potestate nõ-stra,sed addit,quâ dedit nobis dom'nus. Vin-dicat Apostolatui suo non audaciam ac teme-ritatē humanæ præsumptionis,id quod pseud apostoli faciebant, sed potestatem legitimam ab ipso Christo acceptam,cuius demonstratio erat in efficacia manifesta, sic ut de ea gloriâ-do non pudesieret. Qui hodie de potestate A-postolica gloriantur, probent eam sibi datam esse à domino,deinde sic eam comprobent ef-ficaciter, ut gloriando de illa non pudesiant. Ostendant ueritatem gloriationis suæ ipsiùs operis efficacia. Potestatem quam dat domi-nus,non sinit esse uanâ & inefficacem, sed mu-nit, & instructam reddit eam uirtute spiritus.
units.tr: He does not, however, say simply "our power," but adds "which the Lord gave us." He claims for his apostleship not the boldness and rashness of human presumption, which the false apostles practised, but the lawful power received from Christ himself, whose demonstration was in its manifest efficacy, so that he would not be ashamed to boast of it. Those who today boast of apostolic power should prove that it was given them by the Lord, and then should prove it so effectively that they need not be ashamed to boast of it. Let them show the truth of their boasting by the efficacy of their own work. The power that the Lord gives he does not allow to be empty and ineffective, but fortifies it and makes it equipped with the strength of the Spirit.

units.la: Addit, in ædificationem,& non in destru-ctionem uéstri, quibus uerbis potestatis suæ usum & finem expressit. Quod autem d cit, non in destructionem, nõ aduersatur ei quod supra arma militiæ suæ potētia dixit esse Deo ad destructionem munitionum. Duo erant in ipsius Apostolatu, quæ à Deo acceperat, po-tentia uidelicet & potestas.Priorem Græci uo-cant δωάμιν,posteriorem ἐξουσίαν. Potentiá de-putat militiæ,datq; illi usum destruendi muni-tiones ac celsitudinem regni Satanæ, captí-uasque menres ducendi in obedientiam Chri-sti,qua de loquutus est in præcedentibus. Po-testatem deputat ædificationi fidelium, cuius hoc loco meminit. Cum ergo hic dicit: quam dedit nobis dominus in ædificationem,& nõ in destructionem, non contradicit priori Apo-stolatus sui officio,sed distinguit inter illud & posterius,separans usum potestatis ab usu po-tentiæ:ideoq; non simpliciter dicit, & non in destructionem,sed addit,uéstri. Vsus siquidē destructricis potentiæ locum habet in impijs & infidelibus, nõ in pijs ac fidelibus, quorum fides ac pietas ędificanda est,non destruen-da. Prius autem est,destruere per potentiam Dei omnem uim Satanæ, & captiuare mentes in obedientiam Christi. Posterius uero ędificare per potestatem à Deo acceptam. Hęc duo destruendi primùm, deinde & ædificandi officia non Apostolica modò, sed & prophetica fuerunt. Sic enim Hieremiæ dictum est à Deo: Ecce dedi verba mea in ore tuo, ecce constitui te hodie super Gentes & super regna, ut euellas & destruas, & disperdas, & dissipes, & ędifices ac plantes. Vtraq; incumbunt nostris quoque temporibus omnibus illis qui ministerio verbi præficiuntur in ecclesia, quæ si fideliter exequi voluerint, infensissimos experietur Pontifices & episcopos, & omnes eos, qui Romanæ tyrannidi sunt devoti: qui nec destructionem impietatis, superstitionis, ac regni sui, nec ædificationem fidelium ferre possunt. Curabunt autem, ut non modò fortiter verbi potentia ad destruendum uim aduersariam, sed & prudenter potestate sua ad ædificandum fideles utantur, sic ut sint ambidextri una manu destruentes destruenda, altera ædificantes ædificanda. Inuenias qui perpetuò destruant, nunquam uero ædificent: rursus qui ex opposito toti sint ad ædificandum intenti, & interea quæ destruenda sunt non destruant. Qui sic verbum domini administrant, inutiliter in opere domini sudant. Illi uero omnium sunt peruersissimi, & ipsissima Satanæ organa, qui non modò nec ædificant ædificanda, nec destruunt destruenda, sed quod omnium est pessimum, quæ potentia verbi destruenda erant, potestate illegitimè præsumpta ædificant & extruunt, & quæ legitima potestate ædificanda erant, potentia brachij sæcularis, quantum in ipsis est, destruunt. Destruere debebat omnem impietatem, eidololatriam, superstitionem, cæcitatem, & uim Satanæ uerbo Dei aduersantem: uerum hæc magis ædificant. Ædificare debebant in cordibus fidelium fidem in Christum, ueram fiduciam, pacem conscientiarum, spem futurorum, timorem & obedientiā Deo unicè præstandam, &c. at ista pertinacissime quantum possunt destruunt. Et interim sunt Apostolici, catholici & orthodoxi.
units.tr: He adds, "for edification and not for your destruction," words by which he expresses the use and purpose of his power. But when he says "not for destruction," this does not contradict what he said above, that the weapons of his warfare are mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds. In his apostleship there were two things he had received from God, namely might and authority. The Greeks call the former dynamin [δύναμιν] and the latter exousian [ἐξουσίαν]. He assigns might to his warfare, and gives him the use of pulling down strongholds and the height of Satan's kingdom, and of leading captive minds into obedience to Christ, which he spoke of in the preceding words. He assigns power to the edification of believers, which he mentions in this place. Therefore when he says here: which the Lord gave us for edification and not for destruction, he does not contradict the former office of his apostleship, but distinguishes between that and the latter, separating the use of power from the use of might. Hence he does not simply say "and not for destruction," but adds "of you." For the use of destructive might belongs to the wicked and unbelieving, not to the godly and faithful, whose faith and piety are to be built up, not destroyed. But the first task is to destroy, by the power of God, every force of Satan and to lead minds captive into the obedience of Christ; the second is to build up by the power received from God. These two offices, first of destroying and then of building up, were not only apostolic but also prophetic. For thus the Lord said to Jeremiah: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, I have set you this day over the nations and over the kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to throw down, to build and to plant (Jer. 1). Both of these fall upon all those in our own times who are set over the ministry of the Word in the Church. If they wish to carry them out faithfully, they will find the Pontiffs and bishops, and all who are devoted to Roman tyranny, most bitterly hostile: men who can bear neither the destruction of their impiety, superstition and kingdom, nor the building up of the faithful. They will take care, however, not only to use the power of the Word boldly to destroy the hostile force, but also to use their authority wisely to build up the faithful, so that they are ambidextrous, destroying what must be destroyed with one hand and building what must be built with the other. You will find some who always destroy but never build, and again others who are wholly intent on building and in the meantime do not destroy what must be destroyed. Those who administer the Word of the Lord in this way toil in the Lord's work to no purpose. But those are the most perverse of all, and the very instruments of Satan, who neither build what must be built nor destroy what must be destroyed, but, what is worst of all, build up and set up by an illegitimately presumed authority what the power of the Word had to destroy, and, as far as in them lies, destroy by the might of the secular arm what was to be built up by lawful authority. They ought to destroy all impiety, idolatry, superstition, blindness, and every force of Satan opposed to the Word of God; but these men rather build them up. They ought to build up in the hearts of the faithful faith in Christ, true trust, peace of conscience, hope of things to come, and fear and obedience to be rendered to God alone, and so on; but these men most stubbornly destroy all these as far as they can. And meanwhile they are called apostolic, Catholic and orthodox.

units.la: NE uidear inquit, ceu perterrefacere uos per epistolas.) Particula hæc sic posita est, ut tam sequentibus quàm præcedentibus possit accómodari. Chrysostomus refert ad sequentia. Mihi placet, ut referatur ad præcedentia, hoc sensu. Non pudefiá, etiámsi amplius quiddam glorier de potestate mea, quam dedit mihi dominus. Verū cohibeo me, gloriando non tantum, quantum ueraciter possem. Quare: Ne uidear uos per epistolas perterrefacere, atque ita confirmare id quod nonnulli cauillantur, dicentes: Epistolæ sunt graues & robustæ, at præsentia corporis infirma, & sermo cõtemptus. Sic desideratur aliquid, uidelicet, sed tepero mihi, uel, quod dico, ne uidear ceu perterrefacere uos per epistolas. Romani Pontifices procul absunt ab hac Apostolica modestia ubi per minaces bullas horrendum sonantes
units.tr: "Lest I seem," he says, as if I would frighten you through letters. This particle is placed so that it can be attached to both what follows and what precedes. Chrysostom refers it to what follows. I prefer to refer it to what precedes, in this sense: I shall not be ashamed even if I should boast somewhat more of the power the Lord gave me. But I restrain myself, and boast not as much as I truly could. Therefore: "lest I seem to frighten you through letters," and so confirm what some carp, saying: "The letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible." So something is wanted here, namely, "but I spare myself," or "what I say is, lest I seem as if to frighten you through letters." The Roman Pontiffs are far removed from this apostolic moderation, when through threatening bulls sounding horribly

units.la: omnem uim... temptus.) Ad eam præsentiam corporis refe-ro, quod dicebant maleuoli, at præsentia corporis infirma, & sermo contemptus, qua primo illis Christum prædicauit. At tû non erat causa, quur se grauem ostenderet erga fideles, sed potius resipsa omnem poscebat manuetudinem ac lenitatem. Posteaquam uero reprobi opus domini in absentia ipsius uiciare mo-liebâtur, & sectæ essent in ecclesiam cum omnis generis corruptelis introductæ, poscebat ipsa necessitas, vt scriberet ad eos grauius ac se uerius, quàm se initio apud eos gessisset. Quare iniquissimè faciebât, qui id ipsi uicio uerte bant, præsertim cum causa seueritatis huius est ex ipsis.
units.tr: "all power ... contemptible." I refer to that bodily presence what the ill-disposed were saying: "his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible," which he first preached to them in Christ. But at that time there was no reason for him to show himself severe towards the faithful; rather, the situation itself demanded all gentleness and mildness. But after the reprobate began to corrupt the work of the Lord in his absence, and sects with all kinds of corruptions had been introduced into the Church, necessity itself required him to write to them more gravely and sharply than he had behaved among them at the beginning. Therefore those acted most unjustly who turned this against him as a fault, especially since the cause of this severity lay in them.

units.la: Deinde & illud cogitemus. Erat Apostolus iuxta sæculû non illustris & gloriosus sed humilis. At sic comparatus est Deus, vt humilibus det gratiam. Euenicbat igitur vt in præsentia constitutus propter personæ humilitatem à carnalioribus ac reprobis despiceretur, qd' ipsi quoq; Christo accidit, atq; ita gratia Dei in ipso minoris momenti reputaretur. Et hoc nô Paulo tantum accidit, sed hodie quoq; vsuenire videmus illis, qui cû scriptis suis magnam sibi partim eruditionis, partim pietatis existimationem concilient, ubi præsentes spectâtur humiliores opinione apparent, ut rectè dicas: Sæpe uiri magni minuit præsentia famam. Sic comparatum est hoc sæculum, ut non æstimet magni, nisi eos quorum & persona est spectabilis, & sermo splendidus ac gloriosus, humiles uerò mox primo aspectu fastidiat. Sic fit, vt in formis humilitatis gratia Dei respuatur. At aurum in quocunq; cœno ac luto repertû aui de colligunt, quod eius studiosiores exi stant quàm gratiæ Dei.
units.tr: Next let us also consider this. The Apostle, according to the world, was not illustrious and glorious but humble. Yet God is so disposed that he gives grace to the humble. It therefore happened that when he was present, he was despised by the more carnal and reprobate on account of the lowliness of his person; which also happened to Christ himself, and so the grace of God in him was regarded as of little importance. This did not happen to Paul alone; we see it happening today too with those who, by their writings, win for themselves a great reputation partly for learning, partly for piety, but when present appear lower than their reputation. So one may rightly say: "The presence of a great man often diminishes his fame." This age is so constituted that it esteems only those whose person is impressive and whose speech is splendid and glorious, while it immediately despises the humble at first sight. Thus it happens that in humble forms the grace of God is spurned. Yet gold, wherever it is found in any mud or filth, men gather with eagerness, so much more diligent are they about it than about the grace of God.

units.la: HOC reputet, qui istiusmodi est, quod qua les sumus sermone per epistolas cum absum⁹, tales sumus & cû adsumus facto.) Cogitabant ac dicebant quoq;, Quæ scribit, grauia quidè sunt & fortia, sed interim nihil sunt nisi uerba hominis in absentia audentis, in præsentia ue rò humilis & abiecti. Quæ minatur absens, nû quam tentabit præsens. Occurrit dicens: Qui istiusmodi est, hoc est, qui de nobis ad hûc mo dum iudicat, hoc reputet ac sibijpse persuade-at, qd' quales sermone sumus per epistolas dû absumus, tales sumus & cum adsumus facto, hoc est, quod absentes scribimus, hoc præsentes facere possumus potestate & efficacia quâ accepimus à dño. Sic intelligendû est quod dicit: tales sumus cum adsumus facto, non de prima illa præsentia, qua Christum initio Corinthi prædicauerat, in qua non erat causa, ut talis esset facto, qualem se postea per epistolas ostendit sermone, sed de futura, si coactus à re probis denuò ad eos uenisset.
units.tr: "Let him who is such reckon this": that as we are in word by letters when absent, such we are also in deed when present. They also thought and said: "What he writes is indeed weighty and strong, but meanwhile it is nothing but the words of a man who is bold when absent, but humble and abject when present. What the absent man threatens, the present man will never attempt." He meets this by saying: "Let him who is such," that is, who judges of us in this way, "reckon this and persuade himself," that as we are in word by letters when we are absent, so we are also in deed when we are present; that is, what we write while absent, we can do when present, by the power and efficacy which we have received from the Lord. So what he says, "such we are in deed when present," must be understood not of that first presence in which he had preached Christ at Corinth, when there was no cause for him to be in deed what he later showed himself to be in word by letters, but of a future presence, if he were compelled by the reprobate to come to them again.

units.la: Obseruα verò, quod in singulari dicit: Hoc reputet qui istiusmodi est, quemadmodum & in præcedentibus: Nam epistolæ, inquit, graues sunt, &c. ubi uni cuidam, quisquis ille fuerit, id obloquutióis datur, quoepistolas ipsi⁹ graues
units.tr: Observe, however, that he says in the singular, "Let him who is such reckon this," just as in the preceding verses: "For his letters, he says, are weighty," etc. Here this objection is given to a certain single person, whoever he may be, who says that his letters are weighty

units.la: A præsentiam verò infirmam & sermonem contemptibilem esse dixerit. Apparet venisse Corinthum à Iudæa pseudapostolû aliquem qui spiritu liuoris impulsus Apostolo sese opponere tentauerit, id quod & capite sequenti innuitur, vbi dicit: Nam si is qui uenit alium lesum prædicat, &c.
units.tr: but that his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible. It appears that some pseudo-apostle had come to Corinth from Judea, who, impelled by a spirit of envy, tried to set himself against the Apostle; this is also hinted at in the following chapter, where he says: "For if he who comes preaches another Jesus," etc.

units.la: Deinde & illud obseruemus, quod dicit, q talis est, pro eo quod dicendum erat, qui hoc dicit. Qualis quisq; est talia dicit & facit. Quare ex verbis & factis proditur quisq; qualis sit, bonus ne uel malus, amicus uel inimicus, pius, uel impius, sapiens uel stultus, iustus uel iniustus. Ideo rectè hic dicit: Hoc reputet qui talis est, i. qui sic erga me maligné animatus est, ut & præsentiam meam & epistolas diuexet. Vbi audimus aliquem proximi sui dicta & facta ob loquendo diuexátem, facilè qualis erga illum sit intelligimus.
units.tr: Next let us also observe that he says "such a one is" in place of what should have been said, "he who says this." Whatever sort of person someone is, such things he says and does. Therefore from words and deeds it is revealed what each person is like, whether good or bad, friend or enemy, pious or impious, wise or foolish, just or unjust. Rightly, then, he says here: "Let him who is such reckon this," that is, who is so maliciously disposed towards me that he vexes both my presence and my letters. Where we hear someone reproaching his neighbour's words and deeds with abuse, we easily understand what he is like towards him.

units.la: De eo quoq; cogitandû est, quod dicit, quà les sumus sermone per epistolas cû absumus, tales sumus & cum adsumus facto, vbi admonemur quid viro graui, honesto, probo ac uera ci competat. Hoc videlicet, inter cætera, vt sit sibijpsi nusquâ dissimilis, nonalius absens & alius præsens, sed & absens sit qualis est præsens, & præsens qualis est absens, tanquâ alienus ab omni hypocrisi, instar auri, quod non aliud est in loculis & aliud extra loculos, non aliud in manu diuitis & aliud in manu pauperis sed ubiq; sibijpsi constanter simile. Deinde, vt non iactet sermone plura, quâ possit præstare facto, ne pudefactus inanis ac vanus deprehêdatur. Multo tutius est minus pmittere verbis, & plª q promiseris præstare factis. Etenim nemo hinc leuitatis arguitur, quod nequit magnifica præstare facto, si magnifica non promiserit, sed id demum leuitatis est pudori obnoxium, si plura promiseris quâ opere præstare possis, præsertim si accesserit iactantia.
units.tr: We must also think about what he says: that as we are in word by letters when absent, so we are in deed when present. Here we are reminded what befits a grave, honourable, upright and truthful man. This, among other things, is that he should never be inconsistent with himself, not different when absent and another when present, but that he be when absent what he is when present, and when present what he is when absent, free from all hypocrisy, like gold, which is not one thing in the purse and another outside the purse, not one thing in the rich man's hand and another in the poor man's hand, but everywhere constantly like itself. Next, that he should not boast in words more than he can perform in deeds, lest he be caught out as empty and vain, put to shame. It is much safer to promise less in words and to perform more in deeds than you have promised. For no one is convicted of levity because he cannot perform great things in deed if he has not promised great things; but it is precisely levity that is liable to shame if you promise more than you can perform by work, especially if boasting is added.

units.la: Non enim, inquit, sustinemus inserere aut conferre nosipsos cû quibusdam qui seipsos cômendât. Sed isti nô intelligunt quod ipsi inter sese seipsos metiûtur & cõparât semetsibi. At nos nô in immensû gloriabimur, sed iuxta mensurâ regulę, qua partitus est nobis Deus, mēsura pertingendi etiam usq; ad uos. Nô enim quasi nô pertingamus usq; ad uos, extendimus nosipsos supra modû. Nam usq; ad uos quoq; peruenimus in Euangelio Christi, nô in immēsum gloriantes super alienis laborib. sperantes futurû, ut subolescente fide uestra in uobis, magnificemur iuxta regulam nostram in exuberantiam, ut ijs quoq; regionibus, quæ ultra uos sunt, euangelizem, non per alienam regulâ, ut de his quæ parata sunt gloriemur. Verùm qui gloriatur, in domino glorietur. Nō enim qui se ipse cōmendat ille probatus est, sed is quē dominus cōmendat.
units.tr: "For," he says, "we do not dare to insert or compare ourselves with some who commend themselves. But these do not understand that they measure themselves among themselves and compare themselves with themselves. But we will not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the rule by which God has apportioned to us a measure to reach even as far as you. For we do not stretch ourselves beyond measure, as if we did not reach as far as you. For we have come even as far as you in the Gospel of Christ, not boasting beyond measure in other men's labours, hoping that, as your faith grows in you, we shall be magnified according to our rule abundantly, so that we may also preach the Gospel in those regions which lie beyond you, not in another's rule, that we may glory in things already prepared. But he who glories, let him glory in the Lord. For it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom the Lord commends."

units.la: Dixit se talem esse facto praesentem, qualis sit sermone per epistolas absens. Iā quae subiūgit declarant, alienum ipsum esse ab ea uanitate, qua plura de se iactet uerbis, quā opere praestare posit, ad quem modū pseudapostoli ina niter de seipsis gloriari soleant. Sic dicit: Non enim sustinemus inserere aut conferre nosipsos cum quibusdam qui se ipsos commendant. In Graeco est, id est, nō enim audemus, quod nihil est aliud, quàm: Non enim sic uani ac temerarij sumus, ut illis nos iungamus ac similes reddamus, qui seipsos cōmendant, hoc est, studio inanis gloriae plura de se iactant quàm ueraciter praestare queant. Quare Erasmus non infeliciter uertit, Non enim sustinemus, ne uideatur Apostolus sic magnificare gloriosos illos Thrasones, ut non ausit se illis comparare, aut albo illorum inferere. Honesta matrona non audet inserere se ac comparare leuibus mulierculis, quę & uerbis & factis impuri cordis lasciuiā spirant. Hoc genus ἀπολμίας honesti animi indicium habet. Sic quod non audebat Apostolus comparare se uanis Thrasonibus, illorumq; se numero inferere, qui inani ia statione insolescebant, argumentum habebat animi ueritatis studiosi, & ab inani iactantia abhorrentis. Quare uanissimum erat, quod in simulabat eū, quisquis fuit, eius leuitatis, qua grauiora sonaret epistolis absens, quàm facto praestare posset praesens.
units.tr: He has said that he is in deed present such as he is in word by letters when absent. What he goes on to add declares that he is far from that vanity by which men boast in words of more than they can perform in deeds, which is the manner in which pseudo-apostles are accustomed to glory about themselves. So he says: "For we do not dare to insert or compare ourselves with some who commend themselves." In the Greek it is, that is, "for we do not dare," which is nothing other than: "For we are not so vain and rash as to join ourselves to them or make ourselves like those who commend themselves," that is, who by a zeal for empty glory boast of themselves more than they can truly perform. Therefore Erasmus has rightly rendered: "For we do not dare," lest the Apostle appear to magnify those glorious braggarts so much that he would not dare to compare himself with them or insert himself into their number. An honourable matron does not dare to insert herself or compare herself with frivolous little women who breathe lust in both words and deeds of impure heart. This kind of modesty [ἀπολμίας] is a sign of an honourable mind. Thus, that the Apostle did not dare to compare himself with vain braggarts or insert himself into the number of those who grew arrogant in empty pretence, was evidence of a mind eager for truth and abhorrent of empty boasting. Therefore it was most vain of that man, whoever he was, to pretend to such levity that he sounded weightier when absent in his letters than he could perform in deed when present.

units.la: SED isti non intelligunt, inquit, quod ipsi inter sese seipsos metiuntur, & coparant semet sibi.) In Graeco est, ἀλλὰ αὐτοὶ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἑαυτοὺς μετροῦντες καὶ συγκρίνοντες ἑαυτοὺς ἑαυτοῖς οὐ συνιᾶσιν, id est: Sed ipsi in se ipsis seipsos metientes, & coparantes seipsos sibijpsis nō intelligunt. Vulgata uero uersio sic babet: Sed ipsi in nobis nosmetipsos metientes, & coparantes nosmetipsos nobis. Hic interpres refert ista ad ipsum Apostolū, quasi nō de gloriosulis Thrasonib. pseudapostolis, sed de seipso loquatur, & illud οὐ συνιᾶσιν, id est, nō intelligunt, omittit. Chrysostomus hic dicit, ἢ περὶ ἑαυτῶ τοῦτο φχοὶ, ἢ περὶ ἐκείνων. Verum certius est, ut referamus ad eos quorum inanes glorias perstringit, hoc sensu: Non ausimus nos coparare & inferere illis qui seipsos commendant: Verum illi nō intelligunt, quam sit turpe quod faciūt, propterea quod metiuntur sese nō nisi ad seipsos, & coparant se nō ad perfectiores, sed ad seipsos, hoc est, sic placēt sibijpsis, ut neminē esse putēt cum quo sint coferendi. Non obseruant, quibus donis à Deo ornati sint alij, sed se ipsos tantum spectantes existimant non inueniri parē nedum potiorem. Si saperent, conferrent ea, de quibus gloriātur, cum donis ac dotibus aliorum, & hoc facientes facile intelligerēt, nō esse sibi causas insolescendi, gloriandi, & alios praese fastidiendi, sed potius modeste ac sub-
units.tr: "But they do not understand," he says, "that they measure themselves among themselves and compare themselves with themselves." In the Greek it is: "But they, measuring themselves among themselves and comparing themselves with themselves, do not understand" [ἀλλὰ αὐτοὶ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἑαυτοὺς μετροῦντες καὶ συγκρίνοντες ἑαυτοὺς ἑαυτοῖς οὐ συνιᾶσιν]. The Vulgate version reads: "But they, measuring themselves among us and comparing themselves with us." This translator refers these words to the Apostle himself, as if he were speaking of himself and not of the boastful false apostles, and he omits the phrase οὐ συνιᾶσιν, that is, "do not understand." Chrysostom says here that he speaks either about himself or about those others [ἢ περὶ ἑαυτῶν τοῦτο φησὶν, ἢ περὶ ἐκείνων]. It is more certain, however, that we refer the words to those whose empty glory he censures, in this sense: "We do not dare to compare ourselves with, or set ourselves among, those who commend themselves. But they do not understand how shameful is what they do, because they measure themselves only against themselves and compare themselves not with better men but with themselves. That is, they so please themselves that they think there is no one with whom they ought to be compared. They do not notice with what gifts of God others have been adorned, but looking only at themselves they suppose that no equal, let alone a superior, can be found. If they were wise, they would compare the things they boast of with the gifts and endowments of others, and in doing so they would easily understand that they have no reason for arrogance, boasting, and despising others, but rather reason to act modestly and humbly.

units.la: missius agendi. Ergo illi perinde faciebant, atque sciolos nonnullos facere videmus, qui quo niam nec legūt aliorum scripta, nec audiunt alios, sed instar testitudinis suoipsius succo contentæ, suamipsorum duntaxat eruditione inspiciunt, illamq; pluris faciunt decuplo, q̄ sit in seipsa, atq; ita opinione scientiæ inflantur: qua stulticia liberari possent, si se non cum seipsis sed cum alijs conferrent. Consimilem planè stulticiam perstringit hoc loco Apostolus in Thrasonib. illis qui seipsi cōmendabant, iactantes admodū, quod essent Ebrei, Israelitæ, semē Abrahę & Christi ministri, sicut capite sequēti uidebimus, & horum consideratione aduersus alios, ipsum quoq; Paulū inflabantur, quasi non & ipse Ebræum se, Israelitam, semen Abrahæ, Christiq; ministrum iactare posset.
units.tr: So those men acted just as we see some half-learned persons acting. Since they neither read the writings of others nor listen to others, but, like a tortoise content with its own juice, look only at their own learning, they value it at ten times what it is worth in itself, and so they are puffed up with the conceit of knowledge. They could be freed from this folly if they compared themselves not with themselves but with others. The Apostle here censures a very similar folly in those boasters who commended themselves, glorying greatly that they were Hebrews, Israelites, the seed of Abraham and ministers of Christ, as we shall see in the following chapter. By considering these things against others, they were puffed up against Paul himself, as if he could not likewise boast that he was a Hebrew, an Israelite, the seed of Abraham and a minister of Christ.

units.la: Admonemur horum exemplo, ut de nobis ipsis iudicaturi non nostras tantum uirtutes, si quæ conceßæ sunt diuinitus, sed & aliorū inspiciamus, nosq; non cum nobisipsis, sed cum alijs, præsertim potioribus, cōferamus, ne per stulticiam inlolescamus, inflemur, & alios contemnamus. Hæreat in mentibus nostris quod dicit: οὐ συνιᾶσιν, id est, non intelligunt, ne in putidam hanc stulticiam incidamus.
units.tr: By the example of these men we are warned, when we judge ourselves, to look not only at our own virtues, if any have been granted us by God, but also at those of others. We should compare ourselves not with ourselves but with others, especially with better men, so that we do not become arrogant through folly, puffed up, and despise others. Let what he says stick in our minds: οὐ συνιᾶσιν, that is, "they do not understand," so that we do not fall into this foul folly.

units.la: Scio à nonnullis locum huc sic exponi: Sed isti, cum sui similibus sese conferunt, & mutuū muli scalpunt belle sibi mutuo placentes. Et hoc uolunt esse, quod dicit, sed isti ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἑαυτοὺς μετρῶντες, ideoq; ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, i. in seipsis, reddunt, inter sese, cum uerti possit, intra sese. Verum sensus quem posuimus, meo iudicio, uerbis est vicinior.
units.tr: I know that by some people this passage is explained thus: "But those men, when they compare themselves with their own kind, and scratch one another like mules, delight themselves greatly with one another." And they want this to be the meaning of what he says, "But they, measuring themselves [ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἑαυτοὺς μετρῶντες]," and therefore they render ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, that is, "in themselves," as "among themselves," whereas it could be rendered "within themselves." In my judgment, however, the sense I have given is closer to the words.

units.la: AT nos non in immensum gloriabimur, inquit, sed iuxta mensuram regulę, qua partitus est nobis Deus mensurā pertingendi etiam uf que ad uos.) Quod in Græcis exemplarib. est, q nobis sunt in manu, ἡμεῖς σιμμ ὁ θεὸς μέτρα ἐφικέσθαι ἀχρι ὑμῶν, existimo pro μέτρα legendum esse μέτρον, i. mensuram, quemadmodū in Chrysostomo expositione, in exemplari Veronensi legitur, & vulgata lectio Latina habet. Postquam stulticiam pseudapostulorum perstrinxit, qua seipsi uane iactabant, opponit ia ad finem usq; capitis moderatione suam, qua ipse non gloriabatur ultra mensurā donationis Christi, quo lector uideat, quā iniquè egerint pseudapostoli, quōd insimularunt ipsum eius uanitatis, qua plura sibi tribueret scribendo absens, quam præstitisset faciendo præsens, cum ipsi eo uicio laborarent, ut iactarent de se temerè magna, quorum nihil præstitissent, nec præstare possent. Sic dicit: at nos non in immesum gloriabimur. Gloriari, εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα, est gloriari ultra modum & mensuram eorū quæ præstiteris uel præstare posis. Ideo subijcit, sed iuxta mensuram regulæ, qua partitus est nobis Deus mensura pertingendi etiā usque ad uos. Apparet pseudapostolos gloriatos fuisse, quod in longinquum prædicationis suæ cursum extendissent, & quasi totum orbe prædicando peragrassent, quod & Chrysostomus anmus annotat, qui dicit: ἡ γὰρ εἰχὸς ἵνα ... Ea gloriatio erat inanis, & in immensum extæfa. Apostolus uero nō gloriabatur vltra regulá gloriandi, quæ est, ut secundū mēsuram donationis Christi, & non vltra gloriemur. Hanc sibi à Deo datam esse dicit, ut ad ipsos Corinthios quoq; prædicando Christum pertigerit.
units.tr: "But we," he says, "will not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the rule by which God has apportioned to us a measure to reach even as far as you." In the Greek copies that are in our hands, the reading is "we [ἡμεῖς δὲ] ... God [ὁ θεὸς] ... a measure [μέτρον] to reach as far as you [ἐφικέσθαι ἄχρι ὑμῶν]." I think that for μέτρα we should read μέτρον, that is, "measure," as in Chrysostom's exposition, and as the Veronese copy has it, and as the Latin reading of the Vulgate has. Having censured the folly of the false apostles, who vainly boasted of themselves, he sets against it, to the end of the chapter, his own moderation, by which he did not boast beyond the measure of Christ's gift. Thus the reader may see how unjustly the false apostles acted when they accused him of that vanity by which he claimed more for himself in writing from afar than he had accomplished in person when present, although they themselves suffered from that vice, rashly boasting of great things which they had not accomplished and could not accomplish. So he says: "But we will not boast beyond measure." To boast εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα is to boast beyond the due limit and measure of what you have done or are able to do. Therefore he adds: "but according to the measure of the rule by which God has apportioned to us a measure to reach even as far as you." It appears that the false apostles boasted that they had extended their preaching over a long course, and had, as it were, traversed the whole world by preaching, as Chrysostom also notes, who says: "For it is likely that ..." [ἡ γὰρ εἰκὸς ἵνα ...]. That boasting was empty and stretched beyond all measure. But the Apostle did not boast beyond the rule of boasting, which is that we should boast according to the measure of Christ's gift and not beyond it. He says that this measure was given to him by God, so that by preaching Christ he might also reach the Corinthians themselves.

units.la: Obserua, quod non dicit: nos non gloriabimur, sed, nos nō in immensum gloriabimur. Ergo nō diffitetur in vniuersum se quoq; gloriari. Vnde rectè colligimus non esse in se illicitū sanctis, ut glorientur. Illicitum uero & culpabile est, si quis glorietur non veraciter sed falso, iactans ea, in quibus nihil est veri, vel, non de suo sed alieno, uel non moderatè, sed ultra mēsuram à dño acceptam, uel non certa & vtili ratione sed inaniter ac frustrà, uel non in domino, sed in carne siue sua siue aliena. Nihil horū in gloriationibus sanctorum reperitur, qui gloriantur ueraciter, de suo, moderatè, prægnanti ratione, & in domino.
units.tr: Observe that he does not say, "We will not boast," but "we will not boast beyond measure." Therefore he does not deny that he boasts at all. Hence we rightly conclude that it is not in itself unlawful for the saints to boast. It is unlawful and culpable, however, if someone boasts not truthfully but falsely, claiming things in which there is nothing true; or boasts not of his own but of another's; or not moderately, but beyond the measure received from the Lord; or not for a sure and useful reason, but emptily and in vain; or not in the Lord, but in the flesh, whether his own or another's. None of these faults is found in the boastings of the saints, who boast truthfully, of their own, moderately, with sound reason, and in the Lord.

units.la: Deinde obsetua quod dicit: sed secundum mensuram κανόνα, i. regulæ, qua partitus est nobis Deus mensuram, &c. uides hic non modo dari à Deo quæ bona sunt, & rectè gerun-tur, sed & partiri illum unicuiq; suâ mensurâ, alij plus, alij minus, nemini nihil, nemini om-nia. Adhæc, partitioni huic uides assignari canonem, certam videlicet regulam. Quis canon ille sit, secundum quem Deus unicuiq; dona sua secundū mensuram partitur, nō exprimit. Neq; certò potest exprimi. Quia secreto diuinæ prouidentiæ constat, quæ omnia sapiēter, vtiliter, & sufficienter pro uniuscuiusq; neces-sitatib. siue uitæ sustentandæ siue obeundi ministerij distribuit. Et hic Canō seruādus est omnib. illis, quos Deus aliis in hac uita uel aliis educandis, uel instituendis, uel gubernandis ac protegendis præfecit, ut & ipsi unicuiq; suam mensuram necessitatibus ipsius competentem subministrent.
units.tr: Next, observe what he says: "but according to the measure of the rule [κανόνα], that is, of the rule by which God has apportioned to us the measure," and so on. Here you see that God gives not only good things but also the right ways of acting, and that he apportions to each person his own measure: to some more, to others less; to no one nothing, to no one everything. Moreover, you see that a rule, that is, a certain fixed standard, is assigned to this apportioning. The author does not state what that rule is, according to which God apportions his gifts to each one in measure, and it cannot certainly be stated. It rests in the secret of divine providence, which distributes all things wisely, usefully and sufficiently, according to the needs of each person, whether for sustaining life or for performing a ministry. And this rule must be kept by all those whom God has set over others in this life, whether to bring them up, instruct them, govern them or protect them, so that they too may supply to each one his own measure, suited to his needs.

units.la: Illud quoq; animaduertendum est, quod dicit: pertingendi etiam vsq; ad vos. Magnis labo-rib. & crebris periculis per multas Gentes & vrbes inde à Iudæah Corinthū usq; euangeli-zando puenerat. Et ea de re sic gloriatur, illāq; singulari dono Dei adscribit, ac si maximo suo cū emolumento cursum huc perfecisset. Tantus videlicet inerat pectori illius propagandi regni Christi ardor, ut quo latius illius gratia excurrere dabatur, hoc magis singularem in se gratiam Dei agnosceret.
units.tr: This also must be noted, what he says: "to reach even as far as you." After great labours and frequent dangers, he had come through many nations and cities, from Judaea as far as Corinth, preaching the gospel. And for this reason he boasts, and he ascribes it to the singular gift of God, as if he had completed this course hither to his own very great advantage. Such was the ardour for spreading Christ's kingdom in his heart that the wider the way his grace was allowed to run, the more he acknowledged the particular grace of God towards himself.

units.la: NON enim, inquit, quasi non pertingamus usq; ad uos, extendimus nosipsos supra modū. Nam vsq; ad uos quoq; peruenimus in Euan-gelio Christi.) Exponit quod in præcedentib. dixit: at nos non in immensum gloriabimur, &c. Gloriari in immensum uocat hic extêdere se supra modum, intellige, gloriādo. Et negat se hoc facere, dū ad Corinthios usq; pertigisse cursum suū gloriatur, dicēs: Dū gloriamur de
units.tr: "For we do not," he says, "as if we did not reach as far as you, extend ourselves beyond measure; for we came even as far as you in the gospel of Christ." He explains what he said before: "But we will not boast beyond measure," and so on. Here he calls extending oneself beyond measure boasting beyond measure, understand, by boasting. And he denies that he does this while he boasts that his course reached as far as the Corinthians, saying: "While we boast about you, that we have come as far as you in the gospel of Christ, and that we are your Apostle, we do not boast beyond measure, nor do we extend ourselves beyond measure, as if we had not come as far as you, and so attribute more to ourselves by boasting than we have accomplished in deed, far from it; for also as far as you..."

units.la: uobis, quod ad uos usq; in Euangelio Christi peruenerimus, vesterq; Apostolus simus non gloriamur in immensum, nec extēdimus nosi-pios supra modum, quasi ad uos usq; nō perue-nerimus, ideoq; plura nobis gloriando tribua-mus quàm opere præstiterimus, absit, nā & ad uos usq; Christum uobis euangelizando per-uenimus. Nō simpliciter autē dicit: Nam usq; ad uos peruenimus, sed, nam usq; ad uos quo-que peruenimus, queadmodū & in præceden-tibus dixit, qua partitus est nobis Deus men-suram pertingendi etiam usq; ad uos. Sic lo-quēdo significat se non sic ad eos usq; uenisse, ut inde à Hierosolymis Corinthū usq; nullis præterea Gentibus ac populis euangelizauerit, nisi ipsis solis, sed potest multas alias regiones peragratasad ipsos quoq; pertigisse, quare glo-riari se non ultra mensuram cursus sui quoties de ipsis glorietur. Et illud haud ociose adie-ctum est, quod dicit: in Euágelio Christi. Du-bio procul multi erát ex Iudeis, qui & ipsi Co-rinthū uenerát. Nam ibi synagoga Iudæorum habebatur, ut uidere est Act. 18. Vt significet i-gitur uenisse Corinthū se non ut Iudæū aut a-lias simpliciter ac uulgariter, sed ut Apostolū Christi ad prædicandū illic Euangeliū Christi, cum dixisset: Nam usq; ad uos quoq; peruenimus, addit, in Euangelio Christi, id est, in præ-dicatione Euagelij Christi, in Apostolatu præ-dicandi Euangelij Christi. Obserua hoc loco uerbum καυχᾶσθαι. Locum habet in illis qui modū tenere nesciunt, sed mimia uel lucri, uel uoluptatis, uel inanis gloriæ cupiditate rapti perpetuò sese ultra mensurā recti, honestatis & modestiæ, si factis nequeunt, uerbis saltem ac uotis extendunt. Et hoc ingenio feré sum omnes, nisi quod gratia spiritus Dei electos cohibet, ne quod ipsorū quoq; est carni agna-tum, vnà cum reliqua multitudine sequantur.
units.tr: "...that we have come to you in the gospel of Christ, and that we are your apostle, we do not boast beyond measure, nor do we stretch ourselves beyond due bounds, as though we had not come as far as you, and so by boasting claim more for ourselves than we have accomplished by our work. Far be it! For we have indeed come even to you, evangelizing Christ to you." He does not say simply, "For we have come as far as you," but "For we have come even as far as you," as he also said above, where God has allotted us a measure for reaching even as far as you. By speaking this way he signifies that he did not come to them in such a way that, from Jerusalem onward to Corinth, he evangelized no other nations or peoples apart from them alone. Rather, he may have traversed many other regions and still have reached them too, so that he does not boast beyond the measure of his course whenever he glories in them. The addition "in the gospel of Christ" is not idle. Beyond doubt there were many Jews who also came to Corinth, for a synagogue of the Jews was there, as may be seen in Acts 18. So, to signify that he came to Corinth not as a Jew or as an ordinary person, but as an apostle of Christ to preach the gospel of Christ there, after saying "For we have come even as far as you," he adds "in the gospel of Christ," that is, in the preaching of the gospel of Christ, in the apostleship of preaching the gospel of Christ. Note the word καυχᾶσθαι [καυχᾶσθαι] here. It applies to those who do not know how to keep measure, but, carried off by an excessive desire for gain, pleasure or empty glory, constantly stretch themselves beyond the bounds of what is right, honourable and modest, if not in deeds then at least in words and boasts. Nearly all people are of this disposition, except that the grace of God's Spirit restrains the elect from following the rest of the crowd in what is kin to their own flesh.

units.la: NON in immensum gloriátes super alienis laboribus inquit.) Paulo supra quinq; posuim illicitæ gloriationis species, inter quas eā quoq; recensuimus quā hic ponit Apostolus, negās se gloriari super alienis laboribus. Quia ubi se Corinthum quoq; in Euangelio Christi peruenisse dixit, idem poterant in speciem iactare pseudapostoli, eam illis gloriatione adimit ne-gans se gloriari super alienis laboribus; dū Co-rinthū se prædicādo peruenisse dicit. Venerat quidē Corinthū etiam illi, & dubio procul ibi prædicabāt, uerūm quod ibi fidelium Christi repererunt ecclesiam non poterāt suis tribuere laborib. Nam debebatur hoc laborib. Apostoli, qui primus Corinthios ad fidē in Christū conuerterat, & ecclesiā ibi costituerat. Quare cum se Corinthiorū gloriaretur esse Apostolū, non gloriabatur super alienis sed super pprijs laborib. Et hoc dicens putidam reddit illorū iactantiam, quase Corinthum usq; peruenisse gloriabantur. Verum infrà adhuc plura hac de re subijciet.
units.tr: "NOT boasting beyond measure in other men's labours," he says. A little above, we set out five kinds of unlawful boasting, among which we also counted the one the Apostle mentions here, denying that he boasts in other men's labours. For when he said that he had come even to Corinth in the gospel of Christ, the false apostles could, in appearance, boast of the same thing. By denying that he boasts in other men's labours, he takes away from them that kind of boasting, since he says that he came to Corinth by preaching. Certainly they too had come to Corinth, and beyond doubt they preached there; but since they found a church of Christ's faithful there, they could not credit it to their own labours. For this was owed to the labours of the Apostle, who had first converted the Corinthians to faith in Christ and established the church there. So when he boasts that he is the apostle of the Corinthians, he does not boast in other men's labours but in his own. By saying this, he makes their boasting appear foul, since they boasted of having come even to Corinth. But he will set out more on this matter further on.

units.la: SPERANTES futurum, inquit, vt subole-scēte fide vestra in vobis magnificemur iuxta regulam nostram in abundantiam, vt ijs quoq; regioregionibus; quæ ultra uos sunt euangelizem.) Ne uideatur metam Apostolici sui cursus sistere in Corinthijs, dicit sibi spem esse extendédi illum adhuc usq; ad ulteriores populos. Hoc est, quod cum dixisset: Nam usq; ad uos quoq; peruenimus in Euangelio Christi, non in immensum gloriantes super alienis laboribus, subiùgit, sperantes futurum, ut ijs quoque regionibus quæ ultra uos sunt euangelizé. Vulgata editio non exprimit sensum Apostoli. Sic enim habet, Spem autem habentes crescentis fidei uestræ in uobis magnificari secúdum regulam nostrā in abundantia, etiam in illa quæ ultra uos sunt euangelizare. Non enim loquitur Apostolus de spe fidei Corinthiorū qua fore sperauit, ut illa crescat, sed de spe Euangelij ad ulteriores quoq; Gètes prædicatione iua pro pagádi. Quare quod in Græco est αὐξανομένης τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν, non debebat uerti in genitiuo, sed dei uestræ, sed in ablatiuo, crescète fide uestra in uobis. Sensus est. Non sic de uobis glorior, quasi prædicationis meæ cursus in uobis terminetur, sed spero futurum, ut ubi fides uestra paulo fuerit facta in uobis uegetior ac firmior secundum regulam nostram, illum ex abundâ ti, ad ulteriores quoque Gentes, quę ultra uos sunt, euangelizando extendamus. Verbum μεγαλυνθῆναι, id est, magnificari, sic est positū ut tam ad præcedens, ἐν ὑμῖν, id est, in uobis, q; ad sequentia possit referri. Si referas ad præce dens sensus erit: Spero fore ut magnificemur in uobis ubi fides uestra adoleuerit. Si ad se- quentia, significat sperare se ut secúdum abun dantiam regulæ suæ magnificetur, ubi ulterio ribus quoque Gentibus euangelizauerit.
units.tr: "HOPING, he says, that as your faith grows, I may be magnified among you according to our rule, abundantly, so as to preach the gospel also in the regions beyond you." Lest the goal of his apostolic course seem to stop at the Corinthians, he says that he has the hope of extending it still further, to more distant peoples. This is what he means: after saying "For we have come even as far as you in the gospel of Christ, not boasting beyond measure in other men's labours," he adds, "hoping that I may preach the gospel also in those regions which lie beyond you." The Vulgate edition does not express the Apostle's sense. It reads: "But having hope that your growing faith may magnify us among you according to our rule, abundantly, even to preach the gospel in those places that lie beyond you." For the Apostle does not speak of a hope, held by the Corinthians, that their faith would grow; he speaks of his own hope that the gospel would be spread by his preaching to more distant nations too. So the Greek αὐξανομένης τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν [αὐξανομένης τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν] ought not to be rendered in the genitive, "of your faith," but in the ablative, "your faith growing." The sense is: I do not glory in you as if the course of my preaching ended among you; rather I hope that, when your faith has become somewhat stronger and firmer among you, according to our rule, we may extend our preaching abundantly, to the more distant Gentiles beyond you. The verb μεγαλυνθῆναι [μεγαλυνθῆναι], that is, "to be magnified," is so placed that it can refer both to what precedes, "among you" [ἐν ὑμῖν], and to what follows. If you refer it to what precedes, the sense is: I hope to be magnified among you when your faith has grown. If to what follows, it signifies that he hopes to be magnified, according to the abundance of his rule, when he has preached also to the more distant Gentiles.

units.la: SPERANTES futurum inquit.) Non affirmat, sed sperare se dicit, fore ut adhuc la tius Euangelij cursum extendat. Terminus enim illius erat in scientia ac manu Dei, à cu ius dispensatione totus pendebat.
units.tr: Hoping for the future, he says. He does not affirm this but says he hopes that the course of the Gospel will extend still further. Its limit lay in the knowledge and hand of God, on whose disposal the whole depended.

units.la: VT subolescéte fide uestra in uobis, inquit) An cursum Euágelij nō poterat ad ulteriores Gentes extêdere, nisi fides Corinthiorū prius adoleuisset? Quid si prorsus non credidissent? An ipsorum incredulitas regnum Christi impediuisset, quo minus ad ulteriores populos propagari posset? Respondeo. Incredulitas illorum cursum Euangelij haudquaquā remo rata fuisset, remorabatur uero fidei illorū im becillitas. Etenim si Euágeliū nō recepissent, potuisset excusso pedum suorū puluere transi re ad ulteriores, id uero facere non potuit po steaq; credere cœperant, nisi prius fide illorum aliquousq; corroborata. Hoc scilicet est quod dicit: ut subolescente fide uestra in uobis, &c.
units.tr: "So that, with your faith growing up in you," he says. Could he not have extended the course of the Gospel to more distant nations unless the faith of the Corinthians had first grown? What if they had not believed at all? Would their unbelief have hindered the kingdom of Christ from spreading to further peoples? I answer: their unbelief would by no means have hindered the course of the Gospel, but the weakness of their faith did hinder it. For if they had not received the Gospel, he could have shaken the dust from his feet and passed on to other peoples. But once they had begun to believe, he could not do so unless their faith had first been strengthened to some degree. This is evidently what he means: "so that, with your faith growing up in you," and so on.

units.la: MAGNIFICEMVR, inquit, iuxta regulam nostram in exuberantiâ.) Sensus est, ut adhuc ampliorem gloriandi materiâ acquiramus. Id uocat magnificari secúdum regulam suam in abundantiâ. Regulam eádem intelligit quam suprà uocauit mensurâ regulæ. Suam eam uo cat quod à Deo sibi sit constituta. Verbo autem magnificandi non utitur carnali affectu, quasi appetat ac sperat inanis gloriæ augmētū, sed usurpat illud & accômodat propósito suo cô tra pseudapostolos, quorum improbitatē re fellere cœpit. Obserua obiter, quod Canonem diuinæ admesurationis uocat suū Canonem. Talis erat Canonicus Paulus militans ac ser uiens sub Canone. i. regula, nō Francisci, non Bernhardi, non Dominici, sed ipsius domini. Regula sit non modò ministro, sed & cuilibet fideli, mensura diuinæ constitutionis ac uoca tionis, ut secundum hanc se religiosè ac fideli ter gerat. Est autè regula hæc duplicis condi tionis. Alia nanq; est ἐγγραφος, alia ἀγγραφος, id est, nō scripta, erat ea qua de loqui tur hic Apostolus. Neq; enim aliquo erat scri pturæ loco expressum quousq; propagaturus esset Euangelium Christi: ἐγγραφος uero est, qua ipsa doctrina præscribitur Euangelij mi nistris: & qua fidelibus omnibus ac singulis constituitur quid credere ac uiuere debeant. Hoc sensu sunt omnes Christiani, tam fideles q; ministri Canonici, ministrantes ac uiuentes sub regula Dei, à qua si declinauerint multò uerius ac perniciosius irregulares fiunt, quàm si monachus cucullaẗ à sua regula exorbitet.
units.tr: "We shall be magnified," he says, "according to our rule, in abundance." The sense is that we may acquire still greater matter for glorying. He calls this being magnified according to his rule in abundance. By rule he means the same thing he called above "the measure of the rule." He calls it his own because God had established it for him. He does not use the word "to be magnified" out of a carnal feeling, as if he desired and hoped for an increase of empty glory. Rather, he takes the word and adapts it to his purpose against the false apostles, whose wickedness he had begun to expose. Observe in passing that he calls his own rule the canon of divine measurement. Such was the canonical Paul, serving and fighting under the canon, that is, under the rule, not of Francis, Bernard or Dominic, but of the Lord himself. The rule should be the measure of divine ordinance and calling not only for a minister but for every believer, so that each may conduct himself religiously and faithfully according to it. This rule is of two kinds. One is engraphos [ἔγγραφος], the other agraphos [ἄγραφος], that is, unwritten. It was the unwritten rule of which the Apostle speaks here, for it was not expressed in any place of Scripture until the Gospel of Christ was to be spread abroad. The written rule is that doctrine itself which is prescribed to the ministers of the Gospel, and which sets out for all the faithful, each one, what they ought to believe and how they ought to live. In this sense all Christians, both the faithful and the canonical ministers, minister and live under the rule of God. If they depart from it, they become irregular far more truly and perniciously than a hooded monk who strays from his rule.

units.la: VT ijs quoq; regionibus, inquit, quæ ultra uos sunt, euangelizem.) Non exprimit eas re giones, quibus ultra Corinthum sitis sperat se prædicaturum Euangelium. Nec id referebat admodum. Si cursum illius quo inde à Hiero solymis Corinthum usq; peruenit considereres, ultra Corinthum utiq; erat Macedonia, in qua tamē priusquam Corinthū uenissęt Christum prædicauerat. Quin in ea quę ad Rom. est cap. 15. gloriatur se ad Illyricū usq; impleuisse Chri sti Euangelium, quæ extrema pars est Mace doniæ. Tandem & Romā usq;, licet captiuus, peruenit, & ibi quoq; biennió euangelizauit.
units.tr: "And that I may preach the Gospel also in those regions," he says, "which lie beyond you." He does not name the regions beyond Corinth where he hopes to preach the Gospel, nor did this much matter. If you consider the course by which he came from Jerusalem to Corinth, then beyond Corinth lay Macedonia, where, however, he had preached Christ before he reached Corinth. Indeed, in Romans 15 he boasts that he had fulfilled the Gospel of Christ as far as Illyricum, which is the farthest part of Macedonia. Finally he came even to Rome, though as a captive, and there too he preached the Gospel for two years.

units.la: NON per aliena regulam, inquit, ut de his quæ parata sunt gloriemur.) Dixit, sperantes futurum, ut magnificemur per regulā nostrā. Iam quorsum id dixerit exprimit subijciens, non per alienam regulā in ijs quæ parata sunt, intellige, ab alijs, gloriando. Dicit se nolle glo riari de alienis laboribus, de locis in quib. alij Christū prædicauerint, sed de suo labore para tis. Nequit hoc satis inculcare, gloriari se non de alieno, sed de suoipsius labore, nō secundū alienam sed secundum suam regulam, non de ijs quæ ab alijs, sed quæ à se sint parata. Sic & Rom. 15. dicit: Nō ausim loqui quicquā eorum quæ nō effecit Christus per me, in obedientiā gentiū. Et paulò pōst: ita porro annitens prę dicare Euangelium, non ubi nominatus erat Christus, ut ne super alienum fundamentum ædificarem, sed quemadmodum scriptum est: Quibus non est annunciatum de eo, uidebūt, & qui non audierant, intelligent. Hæc dicen do perstringit pseudapostolos ac subintroeun tes fratres, laboribus suis insidiantes, deq; alie no impensè gloriantes.
units.tr: "Not by another's rule," he says, "so that we glory in things already prepared." He said, "hoping that we shall be magnified by our rule." What he meant by this he makes clear by adding: not by another's rule, in things already prepared, that is, prepared by others, in glorying. He says that he does not wish to glory in the labours of others, in places where others have preached Christ, but in his own labour in places prepared by him. He cannot stress enough that he glories not in another's labour but in his own, not according to another's rule but according to his own, not in what others have prepared but in what he himself has prepared. So also in Romans 15 he says: "I dare not speak of anything that Christ has not accomplished through me, for the obedience of the Gentiles." And a little later: "Thus I strive to preach the Gospel not where Christ was already named, so that I do not build upon another's foundation; but as it is written: 'They to whom nothing was announced concerning him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand.'" In saying this he censures the false apostles and the intruding brethren, who lay snares for the labours of others and glory extravagantly in what is another's.

units.la: Et utinam id genus hominum nullum post se reliquisset seminariū, neq; tātopere in ea ur be post Pauli labores inualuisset, q; improbisi me ecclesiarū Christi constituere magistrā. Et Anaba-
units.tr: And would that this kind of men had left no seed behind them, nor had prevailed so greatly in that city after Paul's labours, the most shameless of men, who dared to set themselves up as mistress of the churches of Christ. And the Anaba-

units.la: Anabaptistæ quid aliud faciunt, quàm quod in eas ecclesias, in quibus iam est Euangelicæ doctrinæ fundamentû ab alijs magno cum labore positum, subrepunt, & de suis erroribus superstruunt, unde quod positum est fundamentum subuertatur. Nec Anabaptistæ tantû hoc faciunt. Inuenias siquidem Euangelicos ministros, qui in ecclesijs hodie, quas alij non sine multo discrimine ab impietate ac seruitute Papistica liberarunt, & ad Euangelij lucem ac libertatem perduxerunt, haud secus insolescant, quàm si ipsi illarum primi sint apostoli, & quod adhuc peius est, labores antecessorû, quibus ipsi bene utuntur, iniquissimis conuicijs proscindant, ac nomina eorum per quos populus primùm Euangelio credere coepit, odiosa reddere conentur. Pseudapostoli iactabant Hierosolymam & Petrum & Iacobû magnos apostolos. Papistæ iactant Romam & Petrum. Et isti quoque habent unde se iactent, haud plus de proprio gloriantes quàm illi.
units.tr: What else do the Anabaptists do than creep into those churches in which others, at great labour, have already laid the foundation of evangelical doctrine, and build upon it their own errors, so that what was laid as the foundation is overthrown? Nor do the Anabaptists alone do this. You will find evangelical ministers today who, in churches which others freed, not without great danger, from Papist impiety and servitude, and brought to the light and liberty of the Gospel, swell up no less than if they themselves were the first apostles of those churches. And, what is worse still, they tear to pieces with the most unjust reproaches the labours of their predecessors, of which they themselves make good use, and they try to make odious the names of those through whom the people first began to believe the Gospel. The false apostles boasted of Jerusalem, and of Peter and James as great apostles. The Papists boast of Rome and of Peter. These men too have something to boast of, and glory no less in what is their own than those did.

units.la: VERVM qui gloriatur, inquit, in domino glorietur.) Generalem paraenesim ponit, ad omnes pertinentem communiter. Verum inquit, quisquis ille sit qui gloriatur, & undecunque glorietur, hoc ab illo cumprimis requiritur, ut glorietur in domino. In priore epistola ad Cor. cap. 1. eandem paraenesim tribuit scripturis dicens: Vt quemadmodû scriptû est, Qui gloriatur, in domino glorietur, respiciens opinor ad nonû caput Hieremiæ. Gloriari autem in domino, est nihil eorum de quibus gloriamur, nostris tribuere uel uiribus uel sapientiæ uel iustitiæ, sed omnia diuinæ prouidetiæ adscribere, & illius tantum nô nostram gloriando spectare gloriam. Qui sic animati sunt, non poterunt gloriari secundum carnem, ideoque nec supra mensuram suam, nec de falso, nec de alieno gloriabuntur, quemadmodû faciebant pseudapostoli, qui quonam inanis gloriæ studio tenebâtur, in domino gloriari nô poterât.
units.tr: "But he who glories," he says, "let him glory in the Lord." He lays down a general exhortation that pertains to all alike. "But," he says, whoever he is that glories, and whatever he glories in, this above all is required of him: that he glory in the Lord. In the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 1, he attributes the same exhortation to the Scriptures, saying: "As it is written, 'He who glories, let him glory in the Lord,'" looking, I think, to the ninth chapter of Jeremiah. To glory in the Lord, however, is to ascribe nothing of what we glory in to our own strength, wisdom or righteousness, but to attribute all to divine providence, and in glorying to look to his glory alone, not our own. Those who are so disposed will not be able to glory according to the flesh, and therefore they will glory neither beyond their measure, nor in what is false, nor in what belongs to another, as the false apostles did. Held by a desire for empty glory, they could not glory in the Lord.

units.la: Quisquis gloriatur, tria haec gloriando facit. 1 Primo, gaudet & exultat in seipso, super ijs de quibus gloriatur. De tristibus, unde dolemus, nemo gloriatur, sed de laetis, de bonis, ac praeclaris. Loquor de cordatis & honestis hominibus: carnales siquidem de carnalibus, & mali de malis laetantur. Sic Pro. 2. Laetâtur, inquit, cum malè faciunt, & in peruersitatibus maliciæ exultant. 2 Deinde gaudium suum non continent in conscientiæ suæ secreto, sed praedicant & iactât apud alios. Hinc est, quod iactantia pro gloriatione sumitur. Et id faciût non leuiter sed ore pleno, nô semel atqui iterû, sed frequenter, praesertim qui gloriantur in rebus uanis ac nihili. 3 Tertio laudé & gloriâ iactando quaerunt, unde uerbû est gloriari Latinis, & καυχάομαι Graecis. Et hic studia in contraria scinduntur pij ac reprobi. Pij gloriando non suamipsorum sed Dei gloriam quaerunt, quemadmodum in illo exultât quoque, & non suas uirtutes, sed Dei in se bona & gratiam de praedicant, & sic gloriantur non in se sed in domino. Reprobi uerò dum gloriantur, suâ ipsorum gloriam ac laudem uenantur, non Deum sed seipsos laudantes. Hinc Ebraeis est uerbû, התהלל, quod seipsum laudare significat, & tamé ad eorum quoque gloriationem usurpatur, qui gloriando non tuam, sed Dei gloriam quaerunt, & non in carne, sed in domino Deo suo exultât, sicuti uidere est Hier. 9. ubi sic legitur, כה אמר יהוה אל יתהלל החכם בחכמתו ראל יתהלל הגבור בגבורתו אל יתהלל עשיר בעשרו בי אם בזאת יתהלל המתהלל השכל וידע אותי בי אני יהוה עושה חסד משפט וצדקה בארץ כי באלה חפצתי נאם יהוה, id est: Sic dicit dominus, ne glorietur uel, ne laudet se, sapiens in sapientia sua, ne glorietur uir robustus in robore suo, ne glorietur dives in diuitijs suis. Quin magis in hoc glorietur qui gloriatur, quod intelligit ac cognoscit me, quod ego sum dominus faciens misericordiam, iudicium & iustitiam in terra. Nam illis delector, dicit dominus. Ex hac itaq; distinctione facile uidere est, qui sint qui in domino, & qui in carne gloriantur.
units.tr: Whoever glories does three things in glorying. First, he rejoices and exults in himself over the things of which he glories. No one glories in sad things, over which we grieve, but in joyful, good and excellent things. I speak of sensible and honest men; for carnal men rejoice in carnal things, and wicked men in wicked things. So Prov. 2: "They rejoice," it says, "when they do evil, and exult in the perversities of wickedness." Second, they do not keep their joy hidden in the secret of their conscience, but proclaim it and boast of it before others. Hence boasting is taken for glorying. And they do this not lightly but with full mouth, not once but again and again, especially those who glory in vain and worthless things. Third, by boasting they seek praise and glory; hence the Latin verb gloriari and the Greek kauchaomai [καυχάομαι]. Here the efforts of the godly and of the reprobate are divided in opposite directions. The godly, in glorying, seek not their own glory but God's; they exult in that same boasting, and proclaim not their own virtues but the good things and grace of God in them. So they glory not in themselves but in the Lord. The reprobate, however, when they glory, hunt after their own glory and praise, praising not God but themselves. Hence the Hebrews have the verb hithallel [התהלל], which signifies to praise oneself, yet it is also used of those who, in glorying, seek not their own but God's glory, and exult not in the flesh but in the Lord their God. This may be seen in Jeremiah 9, where it reads thus [כה אמר יהוה אל יתהלל החכם בחכמתו ראל יתהלל הגבור בגבורתו אל יתהלל עשיר בעשרו בי אם בזאת יתהלל המתהלל השכל וידע אותי בי אני יהוה עושה חסד משפט וצדקה בארץ כי באלה חפצתי נאם יהוה]: "Thus says the Lord: let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, let not the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches. But let him who glories glory in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who does mercy, judgment and righteousness on earth; for in these things I delight, says the Lord." From this distinction it is therefore easy to see who they are that glory in the Lord, and who glory in the flesh.

units.la: NON enim qui seipsum commendat, inquit, ille probatus est, sed is quem dominus commendat.) Reddit rationem quare debeat qui gloriatur gloriari in domino. Sumit autem eam ex oppositio & illius uanitate. Commendare seipsum, inducit tanquam oppositum gloriationi quae fit in Deo. Etenim qui seipsum commendat, gloriatur utiq; in seipso, & gloriâ quâ uindicat sibijpsi, detrahit Deo, quod maxima est in conspectu Dei iniquitas. Vanitas huius est, quod non praestat id quod ab eo qui seipsum commendat quaeritur. Vult enim probatus haberi, & in hunc se finem gloriâdo commendat. At propria commendatio probatum reddit neminem, sed suspectû potius de impostura, magisq; contemnendum ac fugiendum quàm sus piciendum. Hoc significans dicit: Non enim qui seipsum commendat ille probatus est.
units.tr: For it is not he who commends himself, he says, who is approved, but he whom the Lord commends. He gives the reason why the one who boasts ought to boast in the Lord, and he takes it from the contrast with the vanity of the other. To commend oneself is set up as the opposite of the boasting that is done in God. For whoever commends himself boasts in himself, and by the glory he claims for himself he takes glory away from God, which is the greatest iniquity in God's sight. The vanity of this lies in the fact that it does not deliver what is sought from the one who commends himself. For he wants to be held approved, and he commends himself with that end in view. But self-commendation makes no one approved; rather it makes him suspected of imposture, and to be despised and avoided rather than trusted. Signifying this, he says: For it is not he who commends himself who is approved.

units.la: Iudiciû hoc de ijs qui seipsos commendant ac uenditant quasi admodum sint probati, de quorû fide & integritate dubitare debeat nemo, summopere necessarium est in ecclesijs, praesertim ubi locum habent hypocritæ qui singulari hypocrisis studio insinuât se ac commendant imperitis & incautis, & obtinent etiam ut pro iustis, sanctis, ac probatis habeantur, cûm sint nequissimi impostores. Si maiores nostri cautione hac fuissent usi, ut cogitassent, secundum Apostoli sententiam probatos non esse eos qui seipsi commendant, minus fuissent seductionibus facti obnoxij.
units.tr: This judgment about those who commend and puff themselves up, as if they were thoroughly approved, when no one ought to doubt their faith and integrity, is very necessary in the churches, especially where hypocrites hold sway. They work their way in and commend themselves to the inexperienced and the incautious with a singular zeal for hypocrisy, and they even manage to be regarded as just, holy and approved, though they are the most wicked impostors. If our forebears had used this caution, and had considered that, according to the Apostle's saying, those who commend themselves are not approved, they would have been less exposed to seduction.

units.la: QVEM autem probatum pronunciat? Sed is, inquit, quem dominus commendat.) Non dicit, quem alij commendant, sed, quem dominus commendat. Humana commendatio probatum non reddit. Commendabátur pseudapostoli commendaticijs aliorû epistolis, quemadmodum supra cap. 4. uidimus, & tamé non erant probati, sed impostores reprobandi. Nemo minem potest homo talem reddere qualem commendat. Dum autè commendamus aliquem uirtutis alicuius nomine, fit ut saepenumero fallamur, bonû existimantes esse eum qui no-
units.tr: But whom does he pronounce approved? But he, he says, whom the Lord commends. He does not say whom others commend, but whom the Lord commends. Human commendation does not make a man approved. The false apostles were commended by letters of recommendation from others, as we saw above in chapter 4, and yet they were not approved but were impostors to be rejected. No man can make another to be what he commends him as. But when we commend someone on account of some virtue, it often happens that we are deceived, thinking him good when he is in fact

units.la: bis inscijs & non satis circumspectis malus est ac reprobandus. Imo, quod adhuc peius est, haud raro commendamus eum què indignū esse scimus qui commendetur, dum illi magis cupimus esse consultum quàm quibus eum commendamus. Non igitur præter rationem est, quod poëta monet dicens, Qualē cōmendes etiā atq; etiā aspice, ne mox Incutiant aliena tibi peccata pudorem. Fallimur, & quendā nō dignū tradimus: ergo Quē sua culpa premit, deceptus omitte tueri, Vt penitus notum si tentent crimina seruos Tuerisq; tuo fidentem præsidio.
units.tr: evil and to be rejected, by people who are unaware and not sufficiently watchful. Indeed, what is worse still, we often commend someone whom we know to be unworthy of being commended, because we want to serve the one we recommend him to rather than those to whom we commend him. It is therefore not beside reason that the poet advises, saying: Look again and again at the man you would commend, lest soon the faults of others bring shame upon you. We are deceived and hand over someone unworthy: therefore, let him whom his own fault weighs down be dropped, deceived, lest his crimes, if they become fully known, should attack the servant who trusts in your protection.

units.la: Vbi autem dominus aliquem commendat, ibi nec fallitur ipse, nec fallit quenq;, quare ne cesse est, ut sit probatus. Cōmendat ille nō ut homo, significans qualis sit quem commédat, nec commendat uerbis sed manifestis argumentis, ipsis uidelicet operibus ac donis suis, quibus talem reipsa reddit, qualem uult haberi. Sic cōmendabat Paulū tanquam insignem Apostolum, reddebatq; eum probatū magna Apostolatus ipsius efficacia. Hoc genere com mēdationis destituebātur pseudapostoli, quare quo probati uiderentur, magnas de se scientiæ, sapientiæ, eloquentiæ iactabant ampullas, & Paulum præ se tanquā humilem & idiotam sermone fastidiebant. Hac regula diuinæ commendationis instructi iudicemus de ministris Christi, probati ne sint, uel secus. Si donis Dei ad ministerium necessariis fuerint instructi, idq; manifestis argumentis declarauerint, agnoscamus in illis commendationem Dei, habeamusq; eos tanquam probatos in precio. Nulla arbor uerborum commendatione probata redditur, redditur uero bonorum fructuum fertilitate. Sic in ministris quoque iudicandis ac probandis, discamus ex structibus cognoscere arborem.
units.tr: But where the Lord commends someone, there he is neither deceived himself nor deceives anyone, so it is necessary that such a person be approved. He commends not as a man, indicating what sort of person he commends, nor does he commend by words but by clear evidence, namely by his own works and gifts, by which he really makes a person what he wants him to be held to be.
