So he commended Paul as an outstanding apostle, and he made him approved by the great effectiveness of his apostleship. The false apostles were without this kind of commendation, which is why, in order to appear approved, they boasted great bubbles of knowledge, wisdom and eloquence about themselves, and despised Paul in their speech as a humble and unlearned man. Instructed by this rule of divine commendation, let us judge the ministers of Christ, whether they are approved or not. If they have been equipped with the gifts of God necessary for the ministry, and have shown this by clear evidence, let us recognise in them the commendation of God, and hold them in high esteem as approved. No tree is made approved by the commendation of words; it is made so by the fertility of good fruits. So also in judging and testing ministers, let us learn from the fruits to know the tree.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: Ox initio significat, quàm cupiat se à Corinthijs patienter audiri, & quare tam sit pro ipsis solicitus, quãq; nullam dederit ipsis causam, ob quã se fastidire debeant, ac tum fiducialiter ac libere contra pseudapostolos dimicat, suamq; gloriationem illorum iactantiæ opponit.
units.tr: At the beginning he signifies how much he wishes to be heard patiently by the Corinthians, and why he is so anxious on their behalf, and that he has given them no cause for which they ought to be disgusted with him. Then he fights boldly and freely against the false apostles, and sets his own boasting against their boastful pretensions.

units.la: CAPVT XI.
units.tr: Chapter 11

units.la: VTINAM tolerassetis me paulisper in insipientia mea, imò & suffertis me: nam zelotypus sum erga uos Dei zelo. Adiunxi enim uos uni uiro, ut uirginem castam exhiberetis Christo, sed metuo, ne qua fiat, ut quēadmodū serpēs Euan decepit uersutia sua, ita corrumpātur sensus uestri à simplicitate quæ erat erga Christum. Nam si is qui uenit aliū Iesum prædicat, quē non prædicauimus, aut si spiritū alium accipitis, quem non accepistis, aut Euangelium aliud, quod nō accepistis, recte sustinuistis. Arbitror enim me nihilo inferiorem fuisse eximijs apostolis. Si uero idiota etiam sim sermone, non tamen scientia.
units.tr: Would that you bore with me a little in my foolishness; but indeed you do bear with me. For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God. I have betrothed you to one husband, so that I might present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear that, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity that is toward Christ. For if someone comes preaching another Jesus, whom we have not preached, or if you receive another spirit, which you have not received, or another gospel, which you have not received, you bear it well. For I consider that I am not in any way inferior to the most eminent apostles. But even if I am unskilled in speech, I am not so in knowledge.

units.la: VTINAM, inquit, tolerassetis me paulisper) In Græco quidē sic est, ὀφελον ανειχεσθε μου, id est: Vtinam tolerassetis me, uerum cōuenientius est, ut legamus, utinā toleretis me. Neq; enim respicit præteritum aliquod tempus, in quo debuerint ipsum tolerare, nō tolerauerint autem, sed loquitur de præsenti causa quam tractat, gloriatione uidelicet cūm sua tum pseudapostolorū, & optare se dicit, ut in illa se patienter audiant, cui sensui non conuenit præteritum tolerassetis, sed præsens, toleretis. Sensus aut est. Esto, uidear uobis quoq; insipiēter gloriari. Boni hoc consulens id saltē optarim, ut hanc insipientiam meā paulisper toleretis, dum rationem & æquitatem illius explicem.
units.tr: "Would that," he says, "you bore with me a little." In the Greek it is ὄφελον ἀνείχεσθε μου [ophelon aneicheste mou], that is, "Would that you bore with me." It is more fitting, however, to read "would that you might bear with me." For he is not looking back to some past time in which they ought to have borne with him and did not, but is speaking of the present matter he is treating, namely his own boasting and that of the false apostles, and he says he wishes that they would hear him patiently in it. For this sense the past tense "you bore" does not fit, but the present "you might bear" does. The meaning, then, is this: "Granted, I may seem to you to boast foolishly as well. Being kind, I would at least wish that you would bear with this foolishness of mine for a little while, while I set out the reason and justice of it."

units.la: Tolerantia rerū est nōn lætarū, non desideratarum, nō spectabilium & magnificarū, sed tristium, molestarū & ineptarum. Tale autē nihil eorum uideri debebat Corinthijs, quę scribit ad ipsos Apostolus. Verū quoniā, ut puerbio dicitur, propria laus sordet, futurū prēuide bat, ut gloriādo insipiēs factus uideretur: & tamē ipsa hoc poscebat, imò extorquebat, pseudapostolorum improbitas, ut Apostolatū suū cōtra illos tutaretur & gloriatione sua iactātiā illorū reprimeret, id saltem erga se poscit obseruantiæ, ut si uideatur desipere gloriādo, in ea ab ipsis insipientia toleretur paulisper. Nec optat hoc ac petit ab illis, tanq; à filijs suis immerito. Debent enim filij parentibus, subditi præpositis, discipuli magistris, non modò dilectione ac uoluntariam obedientiā, sed & tolerantiam, sicubi uel per ignorantiā, uel tentatione aliqua uicti, uel senio aut morbo deficiētes, in re aliqua ineptiant & hallucinētur, quēadmodū & parōtes, præpositi & magistri multa tolerāt in ijs qui ipsis sunt subiecti. Sine hac quippe mutua tolerantia conuictus humanæ uitæ nec in prophanis nec in sacris subsistere poterit, quandoquidem nemo est tam in præpositis quàm in subditis, tam sapiēs, tā bonus, tam in bono constās ac perfectus, ut nō subinde labatur, & ineptiat. Nō ineptiebat Apostolus, sed utitur cōcessione in hoc loco, & simul poscit tolerantiā, quā sibi debebant etiāsi reue ra alicubi desiperet. Cauendū tamē est, ne patrociniūm hoc loco permittamus falsis doctoribus, qui ut plebē Christi sub seruitute Antichristi detineant, argumētātur ad hūc modū. Etiāsi erret & desipiat aliqua in re Apostolica sedes & ecclesia, non debet tamē ob id deseri, sed tāquā mater ecclesiarū obseruāter ac reue renter tolerari, & quicquid huius est, ipsius senio attribui. Nos respondemus, in Rom. ecclesia damnari à nobis non lœuia quædā & anilia deliria, sed grauissimas abominationes in cultibus, inferenda flagicia in moribus, & improbissimum dominatū Antichristianamq; tyrānidem nidem in regimine omnium iniquisimo. Si mater esset, & non meretrix Babylonica, si tantum alicubi deliraret, facile illa toleraremus. Est modus in rebus, sunt certi denique fines: Vt quos citraque nequit consistere rectum, ut inquit ille. Idem statuendum est etiam in hac tolerantia, quae legitima esse non potest, ubi modus illius excedVitur, quod fit, ubi feruntur in ecclesia falsi cultus verbo Dei repugnates, simonia prima illa omnium haeresis, grauissima sententia ab ipso apostolo Petro damnata, cuius se Simoniaci gloriantur esse successores, superbissimus dominatus, dogmata non modo erronea, sed & impia, ut vitae spurcissimae sordes taceam. Hic patientem esse culpabile est, non laudabile. Simus tolerates, ubi nec gloriae Dei, nec puritati fidei nostrae, nec saluti animarum quicquam incommodatur.
units.tr: Tolerance applies to things that are not pleasant, not desired, not impressive and splendid, but sad, troublesome and foolish. Nothing of this kind should have appeared to the Corinthians in what the apostle writes to them. But since, as the proverb says, self-praise is distasteful, he foresaw that by boasting he would seem foolish. Yet the wickedness of the false apostles itself demanded this, indeed forced it from him: that he should defend his apostleship against them and check their arrogance by his own boasting. He asks from them, as a mark of respect toward himself, at least this much: that if he seems to be foolish in boasting, he be borne with in that foolishness for a little while. Nor does he wish or ask this from them as if he had not earned it, as though they were his sons. Children owe their parents, subjects their rulers, and disciples their teachers not only love and willing obedience, but also tolerance, whenever they, overcome by ignorance, some temptation, old age or sickness, blunder and wander in some matter. Likewise parents, rulers and teachers bear with much in those who are subject to them. Without this mutual tolerance, human life, whether in secular or sacred matters, could not endure, since no one among rulers or subjects is so wise, so good, so steadfast and perfect in goodness, that he does not from time to time slip and blunder. The apostle did not blunder, but he uses a concession in this passage and at the same time asks for the tolerance they owed him, even if he were in fact somewhere playing the fool. Yet we must take care that we do not allow this passage to become a patronage for false teachers, who, in order to keep the people of Christ under the slavery of Antichrist, argue in this way: "Even if the apostolic see and the Church should err and go astray in some matter, it ought not for that reason to be abandoned, but as the mother of churches it should be respectfully and reverently tolerated, and whatever is amiss in it should be ascribed to its old age." We reply: in the Roman Church we condemn not some trivial and childish follies, but the most grievous abominations in worship, shameful crimes in morals, and the most wicked domination and Antichristian tyranny in government, which is most unjust of all. If she were a mother and not the Babylonian harlot, if she merely went astray somewhere, we would easily tolerate it. There is a measure in things, and there are certain limits, beyond which, as that poet says, what is right cannot stand. The same must be decided also about this tolerance, which cannot be lawful when its measure is exceeded. That happens when false worship opposed to the word of God is brought into the Church; when there is simony, that first of all heresies, condemned by the apostle Peter himself in the gravest sentence, of whose successors the Simoniacs boast; when there is the most arrogant domination; when there are doctrines that are not only erroneous but impious, not to mention the filth of the most foul life. Here to be patient is blameworthy, not praiseworthy. Let us tolerate only where nothing is detracted from the glory of God, from the purity of our faith, or from the salvation of souls.

units.la: IMO & suffertis me, inquit.) Graece est, ἀλλὰ ἡ ἀνέχεσθέ με: quod, ut alij quoq; annotarunt, uerti potest tam imperandi modo, tolerate, quàm indicandi toleratis me. Vtrolibet modo legamus, sensus est: Verum quid opus uotis in hac causa? Nihil enim iniqui peto, & uos alioqui fertis me, uel, quare tolerate me paulisper.
units.tr: "Indeed, you bear with me," he says. The Greek is ἀλλὰ ἀνέχεσθέ με [alla anechesthe me], which, as others have also noted, can be rendered either as an imperative, "bear with me," or as an indicative, "you bear with me." Whichever way we read it, the sense is: "But why need there be prayers in this matter? For I ask nothing unjust, and you in any case bear with me," or, "Why do you not bear with me for a little while?"

units.la: NAM zelotypus sum, inquit, ergà uos, Dei zelo.) Rationalis est haec particula. Si referas eam ad id quod uersum est, Imo & suffertis me, non uidetur quadrare. Neque enim Corinthij illi, quorum gratia haec scribit, tolerabant ipsum, alioqui quorsum opus erat optione? deinde etiamsi tolerassent, non ideo tamē tolerassent, quod zelo Dei erga ipsos zelotypus esset, sed tolerare ob hanc causam debebant. Quare commodius uidetur, ut legamus in imperatiuo, Imo & tolerate me, ut sequatur ratio, cur debeant ipsum tolerare. Proptereà uidelicet, quòd sit erga ipsos zelotypus. Quasi dicat, Quoniam quod facio, non facio inanis gloriae studio, sed impulsu zeli, quo erga uos afficior non modico, sed admodum magno & singulari, ideo tolerate me paulisper, cogitantes quae sit cura & solicitudo zeli. Vox zelotypiae non est in Graeco, sed simpliciter, ζηλῶ γὰρ ὑμᾶς θεοῦ ζήλῳ quod uulgatus interpres uertit: Aemulor enim uos Dei aemulatione. Zelotypus est proprie qui propter pulchritudinem formae solicitus est, ne rivalem sortiatur in mulierc ula. Hac uoce non est usus Apostolus usquam.
units.tr: "For I am jealous over you," he says, "with the jealousy of God." This particle is causal. If you refer it to what has just been said, "Indeed, you bear with me," it does not seem to fit. For those Corinthians, for whose sake he writes, were not bearing with him; otherwise why would there be any need to ask? Moreover, even if they had borne with him, they would not have done so because he was jealous over them with God's jealousy, but they ought to have borne with him for this reason. So it seems more suitable to read the imperative: "Indeed, bear with me," so that the reason follows why they ought to bear with him. Namely, because he is jealous over them. As if he said: "Since what I do, I do not do out of a desire for empty glory, but from the impulse of the zeal with which I am affected toward you, not in a small measure but very great and singular, therefore bear with me a little, considering what the care and concern of zeal is." The word for jealousy is not in the Greek; it has simply ζηλῶ γὰρ ὑμᾶς θεοῦ ζήλῳ [zelo gar hymas theou zelo], which the Vulgate translator renders "For I am jealous of you with a jealousy of God." A jealous man, properly speaking, is one who is anxious, because of the beauty of his beloved, lest she obtain a rival in some woman. The apostle nowhere uses this word.

units.la: Addit, Dei zelo, quo zelum suum erga Corinthios secernat ab eorum zelo, qui no Deu, sed seipsos zelando respiciunt, quia non Dei, sed sui sunt ipsorum amantes, ac propriae gloriae studiosi. Pro ecclesia Corinthiorum zelabatur Apostolus, non quod sibi illam uindicaret, sed quod esset Dei. Hodie Pontifices dum pro regno suo dimicant, & innoxios trucidant, zelum domus Dei praetexunt, uerum reliqua illorum uita & corruptissima studia satis arguunt, quo zeli genere ferantur. Zeli fons amor est, at quis celabit amorem? Nam studijs uitae prodiitur omnis amor.
units.tr: He adds "with the jealousy of God," by which he distinguishes his zeal toward the Corinthians from the zeal of those who look not to God but to themselves in their zeal, because they love not God's things but their own, and are eager for their own glory. The apostle was zealous for the Church of the Corinthians not because he claimed it for himself but because it belonged to God. Today the Pontiffs, while they fight for their own kingdom and slaughter the innocent, put forward the zeal for God's house as a pretext. But the rest of their lives and their thoroughly corrupt pursuits sufficiently show what kind of zeal drives them. The source of zeal is love, but who will hide love? For every love is revealed by the pursuits of one's life.

units.la: ADIVNXI enim uos uni uiro, inquit, ut uirginem castam exhibeatis Christo.)
units.tr: For I have betrothed you to one husband, he says, that I may present you as a pure virgin to Christ.)

units.la: Exponit zeli sui rationem, explicans quod dixit, Dei zelo. Poterat dicere: Conuerti enim uos ab erroribus ac uanitatibus uestris ad Deum uiuum, uerum quo magis accommodaret se causae, quam aduersus pseudapostolos agebat, Christum inducit, & despösationis similitudinem, quo conuenientius subijciat, quid nam ipsis mali à pseudapostolis timeat, qui cum Iudaei essent, nō tam erant in eo ut unius Dei, quàm ut Christi fide in Corinthijs labefactarent. Sic dicit: Adiunxi enim uos uni uiro, ut uirginem castam exhibeatis Christo, uel, exhibeam ac sistam Christo. Quod enim in Graeco est, ... Vtroque modo uerti potest, tam ut uirginem castam exhibeā, quàm ut uirginem castam exhibeatis Christo. Et uerbum ... non simpliciter adiungere, sed perinde atque ossa in corpore iunctuis suis coaptantur, coadunare & compingere significat, atq; ita ad coniugalem quoq; coniunctionem transfertur.
units.tr: He explains the reason for his zeal, spelling out what he meant by "with the zeal of God." He could have said, "For I have turned you from your errors and vanities to the living God," but in order to suit his words more closely to the cause he was pleading against the false apostles, he brings in Christ and the likeness of a betrothal. By this comparison he shows more fittingly what harm he feared for the Corinthians from the false apostles. Since these men were Jews, their concern was less with the faith in the one God than with undermining the faith in Christ among the Corinthians. So he says: "For I have betrothed you to one husband, that I may present you as a pure virgin to Christ," or "that I may present and set you before Christ." The Greek can be rendered either way: "that I may present a pure virgin," or "that you may be presented to Christ as a pure virgin." The verb does not simply mean "to join"; like bones fitted together in a body, it means to join closely and fit together, and so it is carried over to the joining of marriage.

units.la: ADIVNXI enim uos, inquit, uni uiro.)
units.tr: For I have betrothed you, he says, to one husband.)

units.la: Loquitur ut minister Christi, cui impositum erat ministerium reconciliationis, ut quosuis ad fidem in Christum per Euangelij praedicationem adduceret, illiq; coniungeret, ac ueluti desponsaret. Non simpliciter autem dicit, Induxi enim uos ad cognitionem ac fidem Christi, quod tamen uerè dicere poterat, sed quod adhuc maius quiddam est, adiunxi, uel desponsaui uos, ut uetus habet, uni uiro ut uirginem castam exhibeam uel sistam Christo. Cognitio Christi, & fides in Christum, utrăque quidem aeternae habent uitae promissionem, uerum desponsatio hęc, qua Christo tanquam uni sumus uiro in unam carnem connubiali coadunatione arctissimè coniuncti, plus habet diuinae dignationis erga genus humanum, plus dignitatis & honoris, & plus felicitatis. Poterat dicere, subiecti uos uni domino, ut illi obediatis & fidem seruetis. Verum sic dicendo summam illam nostri cum Christo coadunationem, dignitatem ac felicitatem non exprésisset. Vide simul quàm singulari dignitate Apostolatum suum ornet, dum se nō simpliciter ministrum, sed & pronubum Christi facit. Non est hoc cuiusuis serui, ut regi suo uirginem aliquam desponsET, sed eius qui propter singularem fidem ac familiaritatem id in mandatis accepit à rege. Et competente quoque ei dignitati fidem exprimit, cum dicit: Vt uirginem castam exhibeam Christo. Non erat contentus qualicunque desponsatione, sed talis incumbebat, qua Christo sisteret, non maritatam, alij uiro coniunctā, sed uirginem, eamque non immundo aliquo amore pollutam ac uiciatam, sed castam. Cum dicit, Virginem, loquitur de statu uirginitatis, in quo puella libera est ab omni maritali commercio, nulli nec legitimo uiro, nec scortatori coniuncta. Cum addit, castam, loquitur de puritate tate & integritate fidei sponso suo seruandæ. Exprim t igitur hac desponsationis metaphora, uerorum Christi fidelium mispat & conditiones. Requirit enim ab illis, ut quod fidé ac religione attinet, nemini sint obstricti, nemini spirituum siue bonorum siue malorum, & nemini hominum quorumcunq;, nisi uni Christo, deinde, ut uni Christo fidei castitatem illibatam seruent & integram.
units.tr: He speaks as a minister of Christ, to whom the ministry of reconciliation had been entrusted, so that through the preaching of the gospel he might bring anyone to faith in Christ and join them to him, as it were betrothing them. He does not simply say, "For I have brought you to the knowledge and faith of Christ," though he could truly have said that. He says something greater: "I have joined you, or betrothed you," as the older text has it, "to one husband, that I may present, or set before Christ, a pure virgin." The knowledge of Christ and faith in Christ both carry the promise of eternal life. But this betrothal, by which we are most closely joined to Christ as to one husband, in one flesh, by the union of marriage, carries more of God's condescension toward the human race, more dignity and honour, and more happiness. He could have said, "I have subjected you to one Lord, that you may obey him and keep the faith." But by saying so he would not have expressed that supreme union, dignity and happiness of ours with Christ. Notice also with what singular dignity he adorns his apostleship, when he makes himself not merely a minister but the groomsman of Christ. It is not the task of just any servant to betroth some virgin to his king. It belongs to one who has received such a commission from the king because of his special faith and intimacy. He also expresses faith befitting his office when he says, "that I may present a pure virgin to Christ." He was not content with any sort of betrothal; he aimed at one by which he might present to Christ not a married woman, joined to another man, but a virgin, and one not polluted and corrupted by any unclean love, but chaste. When he says "virgin," he speaks of the state of virginity, in which a girl is free from all marital dealings, joined neither to a lawful husband nor to a lover. When he adds "chaste," he speaks of the purity and integrity of faith to be kept for her bridegroom. By this metaphor of betrothal he therefore sets forth the duties and conditions of true believers in Christ. He requires that in matters of faith and religion they be bound to no one, neither to any spirits, good or evil, nor to any men whatever, but only to the one Christ; and then that they keep the chastity of their faith undefiled and whole for the one Christ.

units.la: ADIVNXI, uel, desponsaui uos uni uiro, inquit.) Desponsatio per subarrationem confirmari solet. Desponsauit Apostolus Corinthios Christo. Qua igitur subarratione confirmauit eā despōsationem? Supra cap.1.sic dicit: Porrò qui confirmat nos unà uobiscum in Christū, & qui unxit nos, Deus est, qui etiam obsignauit nos, deditq; arrā spūs in cordibus nostris. Ergo desponsationis huius cōfirmatio per arram spiritus Christi constat, cuius sacramentum est baptismus. Ipse Apostolus tanquā pronubus, ecclesiā fidelium sacramēto despōsa-tiōis, Deus uerō spū suo tanq̄ arra cōfirmauit.
units.tr: "I have betrothed you," or "I have betrothed you to one husband," he says. A betrothal is usually confirmed by an earnest. The Apostle betrothed the Corinthians to Christ. By what earnest, then, did he confirm this betrothal? Above, in chapter 1, he says: "Moreover, he who establishes us with you in Christ, and who has anointed us, is God, who also has sealed us and given the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts." So the confirmation of this betrothal consists in the earnest of the Spirit of Christ, whose sacrament is baptism. The Apostle himself, as groomsman, betrothed the church of believers to Christ by the sacrament of betrothal, and God confirmed it with his Spirit as the earnest.

units.la: VT uirginē castá, inquit, exhibeā Christo.) Quid est qd' nō pluraliter dicit, ut uirgines castas, sed in singulari, ut uirginē castā exhibeam Christo? Si per uirginē intelligit ecclesiā, quę sponsa est Christi, quomodo tribuit hoc nomi nis ecclesię Corinthiorum, quasi illa sit sponsa Christi, cum ecclesia quæ Christi sponsa est, sit unica, quā uocāt catholicā? Respondeo. Quan do ecclesia sponsa Christi unica consideratur, non respicitur ulla particularis, siue Romana, siue Hierosolymitana, siue Corinthiorū, sed catholica, toto terrarū orbe d̄ sperfa, tanquá unicū Christi corpus, oēs ubiq; fideles unitate spiritus ac fidei sub uno capite Christo complectēs. Hic uero loquitur Apostolus ad ecclesiā Corinthiorū specialiter. Nō loquitur igitur de catholica ecclesia, sed particulari, quā Christo despōsauerat. Ergo unaquæq; particularis ecclesia recte Christo despōsata dicitur, ut illi tanquā casta uirgo sistatur. Sunt autē eiusmodi in numeris. Ergo innumeræ sunt uirgines, quæ Christo regi post reginā ipsius, catholicā uide licet ecclesiā, adducūtur ac desponsantur, ut im pleatur illud Psal. 45. Adstat regina à dextris tuis cum masla auri Ophir. Audi filia, & uide, & inclina aurē tuam, & obliuiscere populi tui & domus patris tui. Et concupiscet rex decorē tuū, quoniā ipse dns tuus, & adorabis eum. Et filia Tyri cum munere, uultū tuū deprecabūtur diuites populi. Tota gloriosa filia regis ab interioribus, ex interfertionibus deauratis indumentū eius. Vestibus Phrygianis deducitur ad regē, uirgines post eā, sociæ eius, adducūtur tibi. Adducūtur cū gaudio & exultatione, ingrediuntur palatiū regis, &c. Tales uirgines sunt particulares ecclesię, quæ sociæ catholicæ; post illā Christo adducūtur ac dispensantur, è quarū numero erat & Corinthiorū ecclesia, quā se hic Apostolus Christo desponsasse dicit, ut eā illi castā exhiberet, ac sisteret uirginē.
units.tr: "That I may present," he says, "a pure virgin to Christ." Why does he not speak in the plural, "pure virgins," but in the singular, "a pure virgin to present to Christ"? If by the virgin he means the church, which is the bride of Christ, how does he attribute this name to the church of the Corinthians, as if it were the bride of Christ, when the church which is the bride of Christ is one, the one called catholic? I answer: when the church is considered as the one bride of Christ, no particular church is in view, whether Roman, Jerusalemite, or Corinthian, but the catholic church, spread over the whole orb of the earth, as the one body of Christ, embracing all the faithful everywhere in the unity of the Spirit and of faith under the one head, Christ. But here the Apostle speaks specially to the church of the Corinthians. Therefore he does not speak of the catholic church but of a particular church, which he had betrothed to Christ. Hence each particular church is rightly said to be betrothed to Christ, so that it may be presented to him as a chaste virgin. There are, moreover, many such churches. So there are countless virgins who, after the queen, that is the catholic church itself, are brought to Christ the King and betrothed to him, in fulfilment of Psalm 45: "The queen stands at your right hand in gold of Ophir. Hearken, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house. And the king shall greatly desire your beauty, for he is your Lord, and you shall worship him. And the daughter of Tyre with a gift, the rich among the people shall entreat your favour. The whole glorious daughter of the king is within, her clothing is of interwoven gold. She shall be led to the king in embroidered garments; the virgins after her, her companions, shall be brought to you. They shall be brought with gladness and exultation; they shall enter the king's palace," and so on. Such virgins are the particular churches, which, as companions of the catholic church, are brought after her to Christ and given in marriage. The church of the Corinthians was one of their number, and the Apostle says he had betrothed it to Christ, so that he might present it to him as a chaste virgin.

units.la: VT uirginē castā, inquit, exhibeā Christo.) Non dicit, gloriosam, pulchrā, nō habentē ma-culam aut rugā, sed ἀγνὴν, id est, castā. Christus ipse exhibet sibi ecclesiam gloriosam & perfectā, sicuti uideri est Eph. 5. Vt adhibeat eā, inquit, sibijpsi gloriosam ecclesiā, nō habētem maculā, aut rugā, aut quicquā eiusmodi, sed ut sit sancta & irreprehensibilis. Talis in hac uita reperitur nulla ecclesia, sed perfectio ista seruatur in futurū sæculū, ad quā tamen cōniten-dum est omnibus. At castā uirginē sistere Christo satagebat Apostolus, totus in eo, ut in fide esset lyncera, & fideliter affecta, queadmodū casta uirgo erga sponsum suum afficitur, & in fide illius lyncera & constans permanet, licet non sit prorsus ab omnib. uicijs ac defectibus libera. Hæc fidei castitas vinculum est despon-sationis, operitq; uicia reliqua adhuc in ani-mo & moribus hærentia, quæ paulatim per spiritū sanctificationis expurgātur. Nullę sunt uirtutes, quæ perfidiā in uirgine corā sponso illius uenialem reddant, sunt uero uicia multa quæ per fidei syncericatem ac castitatem ve-nialia reddantur. Quare præter rationem non est, quod castitatem hanc in ecclesijs tanquam uirginib. Christo sistendis requirit Apostolus.
units.tr: "That I may present," he says, "a pure virgin to Christ." He does not say glorious, beautiful, without spot or wrinkle, but ἁγνήν [hagnēn], that is, chaste. Christ himself presents to himself a glorious and perfect church, as may be seen in Ephesians 5: "That he might present to himself the church glorious, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind, but that it should be holy and blameless." No church is found like this in this life, but that perfection is reserved for the age to come, and toward it all must strive. But the Apostle was anxious to present a chaste virgin to Christ, wholly intent that the church should be sincere in faith and faithfully disposed, just as a chaste virgin is disposed toward her bridegroom and remains sincere and constant in faith toward him, although she is not entirely free from all vices and defects. This chastity of faith is the bond of the betrothal, and it covers the other vices that still cling to the mind and conduct, which are gradually purged away by the sanctifying Spirit. No virtues can make unfaithfulness in a virgin before her bridegroom venial, but there are many vices which are made venial through the sincerity and chastity of faith. Therefore it is not without reason that the Apostle requires this chastity in the churches, to be presented to Christ as virgins.

units.la: SED metuo, ne qua fiat, inquit, ut quemad-modum serpens Euā decepit sua uersutia, ita corrumpātur sensus ueštri à simplicitate quæ est erga Christum.) Hortatus est eos, ut se to-lerent. Prætexuit zelum suū erga ipsos, adiecit rationē zeli, iam metum illius exponit, dicēs: Sed metuo, &c. Metuebat non sibi, sed ipsis, quos zelabat. In zelo metus est, quemadmodū res est soliciti plena timoris amor. Quid autē illis metuebat? Ne corrumpantur, inquit, sen-sus uestri à simplicitate quę est ergaChristum. In Græco est simpliciter, [?]ἁπλότης τῆς ἀπλότητος τῆς εἰς Χριστόν[?]. id est, à simplicitate quæ erga Christum, uel in Christū. Eras. uertit quæ erat erga Christum. Vetus, quæ est in Christo Iesu. Nec erat, nec est, in Græco habetur. Quare æquè uerti potest, quę esse debet erga Christū. Timebat igitur fidelis Apostolus, ne animi ac sensus Corinthiorū corrumperentur à simplicitate, quā uel habuerat initio cōuersionis erga Christū, uel tū adhuc habebāt, uel certē habere de-bebāt. Simplicitas autē erga Christum est inte-gritas mentis, quā Ebraei uocāt [?]תמימות[?]. Hanc Deus erga se à populo suo, hanc maritus ab u-xore sua requirit. Ea est, bene sentire de Chri-sto, bene fidere Christo, & bona ab illo pendē-re cū fiducia: ideoq; nihil esse minus quàm cu-riosum ac scrupulosum in illius uerbo, sed illi simpliciter absq; omni curiosa inquisitione ac scrupulositate credere. Eiusmodi simplicitas corrúpitur, uel, metes credentiū ab illa corrú-pūtur, quādo uel proprijs motibus, uel alienis suadelis incipiūt nōnihil de eo dubitare, quod antea indubitato crediderunt, & inquirere in qd antea nō inquisierat, pter Christū ac uerbū eius admirari etiā alia, & paulati pferre quoqi, nolle amplius stultefcere credēdo, sed sapere inuestigādo ac sciēdo. Vbi hæc locū inueniūt in animis credentiū, mox simplicitas, quę fue-rat erga Christū, corrúpitur, hoc ē, syncerita-te suaum
units.tr: "But I fear," he says, "lest somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is toward Christ." He had exhorted them to bear with him, and he has pleaded his zeal for them; now he sets out the reason for his zeal and explains his fear, saying: "But I fear," and so on. He feared not for himself but for them, whom he loved with zeal. Fear is contained in zeal, just as love full of anxiety is full of dread. What, then, did he fear for them? "Lest your minds be corrupted," he says, "from the simplicity that is toward Christ." The Greek simply has ἁπλότης [haplotēs], that is, simplicity, "from the simplicity toward Christ" or "in Christ." Erasmus translates "which was toward Christ"; the Vulgate, "which is in Christ Jesus." Neither "was" nor "is" appears in the Greek, so it can equally be rendered "which ought to be toward Christ." The faithful Apostle therefore feared that the minds and understanding of the Corinthians would be corrupted from the simplicity which they had had toward Christ at the beginning of their conversion, or which they still had, or at least ought to have. Now simplicity toward Christ is integrity of mind, which the Hebrews call תמימות [temimut]. God requires this from his people toward himself, and a husband requires it from his wife. It means to think well of Christ, to trust Christ, and to expect good things from him with confidence; and therefore nothing is further from it than being curious and scrupulous about his word, but simply to believe him without any curious inquiry or scruple. This simplicity is corrupted, or rather the minds of believers are corrupted from it, when, either by their own impulses or by the persuasions of others, they begin to doubt something about which they had formerly believed without doubt, and to inquire into what they had not inquired into before; when they begin to admire other things besides Christ and his word, and gradually to be unwilling to be foolish any longer by believing, preferring instead to be wise by investigating and knowing. Where such things find a place in the minds of believers, at once the simplicity that had been toward Christ is corrupted, that is, it loses its sincerity,

units.la: suam amittit, perinde ac si liquor preciosus natiuam suam integritatem mixtura aliqua uiciatus perdat. Corinthij simplicem ac puram Euangelij de Christo doctrinam initio ab Apostolo acceperant, illiq; simpliciter & candidè crediderant, & credentes Christo adhærere cœperát, deq; Apostolo suo bene tanquam de Christi ministro senserant. Huic illorum simplicitati metuens dicit: Sed metuo ne sensus uestri à simplicitate quæ erga Christum est, corrumpantur.
units.tr: Just as a precious liquor loses its natural purity when some admixture spoils it, so the Corinthians had at the beginning received the pure and simple doctrine of the Gospel concerning Christ from the Apostle. They had believed him simply and sincerely, had begun to cleave to Christ as believers, and had thought well of their Apostle as a minister of Christ. Fearing for this simplicity of theirs, he says: "But I fear lest your minds be corrupted from the simplicity that is towards Christ."

units.la: Vnde autem hoc metuebat? Tribus de causis. Prima erat ab exemplo, primæúæ seductionis, qua prima parens nostra Eua per Satanæ astutiam seducta est. Secunda ab insidijs pseudapostolorum, qui Corinthum uenerat. Tertia ab eo quod aures illis accommodare, & impostturam eorum tolerare cœperant. Primam exprimit dicens, ut quemadmodum serpens Euam decepit uersutia sua. Nota est deceptionis huius historia, quam in Genesi cap.3. fusè expositimus. Significat antiqui Serpentis maliciam ac uersutiam etiamnum esse cauedam, ideoq; se timere Corinthijs, quod nō ignoret perseuerare illum in uersutia sua, qua initio uti cœpit. Non dicit, quemadmodum Satan Euam potentia sua perdidit, sed, quemadmodū Serpens Euā uersutia sua decepit. Citius manifestum malum etiam admodum uiolētum, q deceptio uersuti impostoris cauetur. Quare uel ipso decipiendi uerbo, & mentione uersutiæ, admonet simplices & imperitos periculum ipsis imminere, nisi admoniti caueant sibi B non modo à manifestis tyrannis & impijs hostibus, sed & ab impostoribus, aliud prætendentibus in speciem, & aliud occultè machinantibus. Qua usus est autem Satanas uersutia ad decipiendam Euam?
units.tr: Why did he fear this? For three reasons. The first was the example of the first seduction, by which our first parent Eve was seduced through the cunning of Satan. The second was the snares of the false apostles who had come to Corinth. The third was that the Corinthians had begun to lend them their ears and to tolerate their imposture. He expresses the first when he says: "as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness." The history of this deception is well known, and we have expounded it at length on Genesis chapter 3. It signifies that the malice and craftiness of the ancient Serpent must still be guarded against, and therefore he fears for the Corinthians, knowing that the serpent persists in the craftiness with which he began. He does not say "as Satan destroyed Eve by his power," but "as the Serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness." An evil that is obvious, even very violent, is guarded against more quickly than the deception of a crafty impostor. Therefore, by the very word "deceive" and by the mention of craftiness, he warns the simple and unskilled that danger threatens them, unless, being warned, they take care not only against open tyrants and impious enemies but also against impostors who pretend one thing in appearance and secretly contrive another. But what craftiness did Satan use to deceive Eve?

units.la: Principio, non est aggressus ipsum Adamum, sed Euam, tanquam mulierem, infirmiorem, & ad curiositatem ac credulitatem proclivorem. Sic solet etiamnum. Infirmiores tentat præ cæteris. Adam, inquit alibi, non est seductus. Quare? Quia uerbis serpētis ab ipsa Euah expositis, non credidit, sed seductæ uxori obsequutus est. Astute igitur non ipsum, sed Euam tentando est aggressus. Neq; enim fore sperabat, ut mendacibus ipsum uerbis seducere ret, sicut de Eua sperabat.
units.tr: First, he did not attack Adam himself but Eve, as the weaker woman, more prone to curiosity and credulity. He still does the same: he tempts the weaker ones above the rest. "Adam was not seduced," he says elsewhere. Why? Because he did not believe the serpent's words as Eve herself reported them, but yielded to his seduced wife. Craftily, then, Satan attacked not Adam but Eve. For he did not hope to seduce Adam with lying words, as he hoped to do with Eve.

units.la: Deinde & illud astutè fecit, quod solam in absentia Adæ aggressus est. Metuebat enim ne frustra illa tentaret, si id præsente uiro faceret.
units.tr: Next, he acted craftily in attacking her alone, in Adam's absence. For he feared that his attempt would be in vain if he made it in the presence of her husband.

units.la: Tertiò, uersuto & illud consilio fecit, quod earuatus opera serpentis usus est, unde minus uidebatur esse periculi.
units.tr: Thirdly, he also acted with crafty design in using the serpent as his instrument, so that there seemed to be less danger.

units.la: Quartò, uersutè simulauit beneuolētiam, qua honori ac felicitati primorum hominum ex animo faueret.
units.tr: Fourthly, he craftily feigned goodwill, as if he favoured from his heart the honour and happiness of the first human beings.

units.la: Quintò, tale erat & illud, quod nō in re aliqua leuicula, sed in ea illā tentauit, unde si uinceret, in exitium genus humanum conijceret.
units.tr: Fifthly, this too was of the same kind: he tempted her not in some trifling matter but in that very thing, by which, if he won, he would hurl the human race into ruin.

units.la: Sextò, suadendo etiā ac promittendo, quæ curiosæ carni adlubescere poterant.
units.tr: Sixthly, he tempted her by persuading and promising even what could please the curious flesh.

units.la: Septimò, uerbo Dei quoq; detrahendo.
units.tr: Seventhly, he also detracted from the word of God.

units.la: 8 Vltimò, à fide & obedientia Dei abducendo. Hæc omnia consideranda proponit, dum Euam per Serpentis uersutiam deceptā fuisse dicit. Et quid aliud agebat Satan in ecclesia Corinthiorū, q ut plane consimili uersutia per organa sua, laruatos uidelicet apostolos, simpliciores mendacibus uerbis deceptos, in absentia Apostoli à simplici doctrina ac fide, in qua salus existit, abduceret, corrüperet ac perderet? Hæc illius ✶ in hunc usq; diem nimis efficax, nota debebat esse fidelibus omnibus, præsertim Christi ministris.
units.tr: 8 Lastly, he drew her away from the faith and obedience of God. He sets all these before us for consideration when he says that Eve was deceived by the craftiness of the Serpent. And what else was Satan doing in the church of the Corinthians, than, by the very same craftiness and through his instruments, namely masked apostles, deceiving the simpler ones with lying words in the Apostle's absence, drawing them away from the simple doctrine and faith in which salvation lies, corrupting and destroying them? This craft of his, so very effective even to this day, ought to be known to all the faithful, and especially to the ministers of Christ.

units.la: NAM si is qui uenit, inquit, aliū Iesum prædicaret, quem non prædicauimus, aut si spiritum alium acciperetis, quæ non accepistis, aut Euangelium aliud, quod non accepistis, rectè sustineretis.) Pertinent hæc ad secundam & tertiā causam, propter quas metuebat, ne sensus illorum à simplici doctrina & fide Christi abalienarētur & corrüperentur. Primā esse diximus uersutiam Satanæ, qua olim Euam seduxit. De illa hactenus loquutus est. Secunda, insidias pseudapostolorum, qui Corinthum in ipsius absentia uenerant, ut secūdum parabolam dominicam zizania in ecclesia illa, perinde atq; in alijs seminaret. Tertiam, quòd Corinthij aures illis prebere ac improbitatem eorum tolerare cœperát. Hæ duæ posteriores hisce uerbis notantur. Secunda, in eo quod dicit: Nam si is qui uenit aliū Iesum prædicaret, &c. Tertia in eo quòd addit, rectè toleraretis. Tolerabát ergo pseudapostolum, qui ad ipsos uenerat, sed non rectè, ac præter rationē. Quare? Quia non poterat adferre aliud Euāgeliū, alium Iesum, & alium spiritum, quàm ipse illis attulerat iam antea, & credentes etiam accepe rant, ideoq; causa non erat fastidiendi doctrinam acceptam, contemnendi Apostolū Christi, à quo fuerant ad fidem Christi conuersi, & alios superuenientes admirari, suspicere, & illi præferre, quasi multo ab illis acciperent potiora quā hactenus accepissent. Hoc significās tate quæ est erga Christum corrumpantur, nō facio præter causam. Nā toleratis insolentiam noui Apostoli qui ad uos uenit, cum nulla sit ratio quur id faciatis. Neq; enim adfert uobis aliū Iesum, aliud Euangeliū, aliúmue spiritum, quàm attulimus nos, & à nobis accepistis. Fateor, si meliora adferret quàm nos, rectè nobis negleētis ipsum toleraretis. Sed meliora uobis nec adfert nec adferre potest. Quare nō recte, ac nulla de causa ipsum toleratis. Et hæc uestra curiositas metū hunc mihi incutit, quo anxiè timeo, ne si tales esse pergatis breui corrūpamini, & simplicitate Christiana amittatis.
units.tr: "For if he who comes," he says, "preached another Jesus, whom we have not preached, or if you received another spirit, which you have not received, or another Gospel, which you have not received, you would bear it rightly." These words concern the second and third causes for which he feared that their minds would be estranged and corrupted from the simple doctrine and faith of Christ. We have said that the first was the craftiness of Satan, by which he once seduced Eve, and of that he has spoken so far. The second was the snares of the false apostles who came to Corinth in his absence, to sow tares in that church, as in the Lord's parable, just as they did elsewhere. The third was that the Corinthians had begun to lend them their ears and to tolerate their wickedness. These last two are marked by these words: the second in "For if he who comes preached another Jesus," and the third in "you would bear it rightly." They were therefore tolerating the false apostle who had come to them, but not rightly, and without reason. Why? Because he could not bring another Gospel, another Jesus, or another spirit than what he had already brought them earlier and what they had received and believed. There was therefore no cause to despise the doctrine they had accepted, to slight the Apostle of Christ by whom they had been converted to the faith of Christ, and to admire, look up to and prefer those who arrived later, as though they would receive from them far better things than they had received until then. Signifying this, he says: I am not acting without cause in fearing that your minds will be corrupted from the simplicity that is towards Christ. For you tolerate the insolence of the new apostle who has come to you, when there is no reason for you to do so. For he brings you neither another Jesus, nor another Gospel, nor another spirit, than we brought, and which you have received from us. I grant that if he brought better things than we did, you would rightly tolerate him and set us aside. But he neither brings nor can bring better things to you. Therefore you do not tolerate him rightly, and for no reason. And this curiosity of yours instils in me the fear by which I anxiously dread that, if you continue to be such, you will soon be corrupted and lose your Christian simplicity.

units.la: NAM si is qui uenit, inquit.) Græcè est, ✶ ✶ ✶. Est autē ✶ uox accepsic ut usurpari posit, perinde in præteriro aut futuro, atq; in præsenti tempore, ac uenti, ueniens, uel qui uenit, uel qui uenturus est. Hic autem usurpata est in præterito, de eo qui iam ad Corinthios uenerat, nouus & aduentitius Apostolus. Vtitur hac uoce Apostolus lus non ociosé,sed emphaticè uocans nouum illum Apoitolû,de quo pleriq; admodû gloria bantur,ἐρχόμενον,id elt,aduenti:ciû,quod neq; miísus à domino,neq; uocatus ab ecclesia,suo pte studio Corinthû uenisset,ideoq; indignus qui Apostoli, id est, legati sibi titulû uendica-ret, nihil uocandus aliud, q ἐρχόμενον, id est, aduenticius,ad eorû numerû pertinês,de quibus conqueritur Deus dicés,currebat, & ego nô miserâ eos, & quos Christus uitare nos iubet,dicés:Cauete uobis à falsis prophetis, qui ueniûtad uos in uestimetis ouiû. Non dubito pseudapostolû illum,ubi à curiosis suspici coepit,digitis fuisse monstratum, idq; his uerbis, ἰδὺ ὧδε ὁ ἐρχόμενος. i. Ecce hic est, q uen t. Quare Apostolus ut hanc illorû curiositate ac leuitate perstringat, rectè eû uocat ἐρχόμενον.
units.tr: "For if he who comes," he says. In Greek it is "ho erchomenos" [ἐρχόμενος]. The word [ἐρχόμενον] can be used of the past, the future or the present alike, as "coming," "one who comes," "the one who comes," or "the one who is about to come." Here it is used in the past tense, of one who had already come to the Corinthians as a new and newly arrived apostle. The Apostle uses this word not idly but emphatically, calling that new apostle, of whom very many boasted greatly, "ho erchomenos" [ἐρχόμενον], that is, "the newcomer" or "the arrival," because he had come to Corinth of his own zeal, not sent by the Lord nor called by the church. He was therefore unworthy to claim the title of Apostle, that is, legate, and deserved to be called nothing but "the newcomer," belonging to the number of those of whom God complains, saying: "I did not send these prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied," and whom Christ bids us avoid, saying: "Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing." I do not doubt that when that false apostle began to be looked upon with curiosity, he was pointed out with fingers, and with these words: "Behold, here is he who comes" [ἰδοὺ ὧδε ὁ ἐρχόμενος]. Hence the Apostle, to rebuke their curiosity and levity, rightly calls him "ho erchomenos" [ἐρχόμενον].

units.la: ALIVM Iesum prædicaret,inquit (uulgata habet,aliû Christû) aut si spiritû alium, aut Euangelium aliud.) Obserua hoc loco,quę potissimû requirat,magniq; facienda moneat Apostolus,Iesum uidelicet,spiritum & Euangeliû, sic ut qui uerû Iesum,ac uerû Euágelium, non adulterinum prædicant,& ex quorû prædicatione ij qui credût nô alium quàm uerum spiritû Dei accipiunt,etiamsi cætera sint insolêtes,tolerari tamê & in precio haberi debeât: secus uero, si diuersum à uero prædicet Iesum & Euágeliû, & ex doctrina ipsorum adulterinus accipiatur spiritus,etiâsi nomê Christi, Euangelij,& spiritus prætexant, titulumq; sibi uendicent apostolorû Christi. Non est aût ut hinc se tueâtur Papistæ,dicêtes: An nô & ipsi uerû Iesum,unigenitû Dei,& filiû uirginis Mariæ, & uerû Euágeliû confitemur & prædicamus? An nô spiritû S. quoq; tertiâ sanctæ Trinitatis personâ esse docemus? Quare ergo nô tolleramur,etiâsi in nônullis culpabiles simus? Nô mox Iesum prędicat,qui nô talê prędicat,qualis nobis est à Deo patre ad salutê nostrâ datus. Viderint ipsi qualê Iesum habeant,ac sibi ipsis & aliis fingant,an nô, ut Erasmus hoc loco annotat,onustû opibus,onustû imperio,dition, uoluptatibus , & quicquid hic mundus habet præstigiarum,ad hęc cæremonijs plus q Iudaicis obsitû,cum uerus ille ab omnibus hisce rebus fuerit purissimus? Iesum habet in sacrario obseratû & inclusum, in sacrario inquâ lapideo & manufacto, in quod ille, secundum scripturas,ingressus nô est, sed in ipsum cœlû, ut appareat uultui Dei pro nobis.Iesum habet prorsus ociofum & exauthoratû, ut qui potestatem suam omnê cœlestis ac terreni imperij transtulerit in omniû teterrimû Romanę sedis môstrum, quod se uicarium illius esse contendit, & omnê hanc sibi potestatê in cœlo, terra & inferis uindicat,atque ita Antichristum esse se coprobat. Sub hoc Iesu ditescunt in sæculo, & sæculi principes adæquât. Sub hoc Iesu uen dût omnia sacra,cœlum,& Iesum ipsum. Sub hoc Iesu deliciâtur in carne, & horrêdis libidi nibus immergûtur. Sub hoc Iesu dominantur in ecclesia,& in ouiculas ueri Iesu tyránidé ad sanguinê usq; qué fundunt exercent. Sub hoc
units.tr: "Preach another Jesus," he says (the Vulgate has "another Christ"), "or another spirit, or another Gospel." Observe here what the Apostle especially requires and bids us value greatly: namely Jesus, the Spirit and the Gospel. Those who preach the true Jesus and the true Gospel, not an adulterated one, and from whose preaching believers receive nothing but the true Spirit of God, should be tolerated and held in esteem even if other things about them are unusual. Otherwise, if someone preaches a Jesus and a Gospel different from the true ones, and from his teaching an adulterated spirit is received, then even if they pretend the name of Christ, of the Gospel and of the Spirit, and claim for themselves the title of Christ's apostles, they must not be tolerated. There is no reason for the Papists to shelter themselves here, saying: "Do we not also confess and preach the true Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God and of the virgin Mary, and the true Gospel? Do we not also teach that the Holy Spirit is the third person of the holy Trinity? Why then are we not tolerated, even if we are at fault in some points?" Not everyone who preaches Jesus preaches him as he was given to us by God the Father for our salvation. Let them see what kind of Jesus they have, and what kind they feign for themselves and others: whether, as Erasmus notes here, one loaded with riches, loaded with empire, dominion, pleasures, and whatever illusions this world has, and besides that covered with ceremonies more than Jewish, when that true Jesus was most pure of all these things. They have Jesus shut up and enclosed in a sanctuary, a stony, man-made sanctuary, into which he did not enter, according to the Scriptures, but into heaven itself, to appear before the face of God for us. They have Jesus utterly idle and deposed, since he transferred all his power of heavenly and earthly dominion to that most foul monster of all, the Roman see, which contends that it is his vicar, claims all this power in heaven, on earth and in hell, and so proves itself to be Antichrist. Under this Jesus they grow rich in the world and equal the princes of the world. Under this Jesus all holy things are sold: heaven, and Jesus himself. Under this Jesus they revel in the flesh and are plunged into horrible lusts. Under this Jesus they dominate in the church and exercise tyranny, even to the shedding of blood, over the little sheep of the true Jesus. Under this Jesus

units.la: Iesu omnê Christianæ pietatis synceritatê cor rumpunt, & in impias superstitiones & eidolomanias peruertunt. Quisquis cordatus hæc considerat,facile intelligit qualis habeatur Iesus in Papatu,uerus ne uel ficticius.
units.tr: Under this Jesus they corrupt all the sincerity of Christian piety and turn it into impure superstitions and idolatries. Anyone of sense who considers these things will easily see what Jesus is held to be in Papistry, whether a true one or a fictitious one.

units.la: De spiritu quid dicam? Non respicio quid de spiritu sancto in specie loquantur, sed qualem habeant ipsi spiritum,& qualem accipiant qui sub iugo illorum detinentur, & dogmatis illorû acquiescunt. Vbi ficticius Iesus habetur, spiritus ueri Iesu haberi nô potest. Non est spiritus ueri Iesu spiritus Antichristi, sed Christi, nô est spiritus mêdacij,sed ueritatis: non detinet homines in impietate , superstitionibus, eidololatria & falsis cultibus, sed corda illorû uera in Christum fide renouat,& ab hisce omnibus liberat: non est sanguinarius in erratês, sed mansuetus. Vnde & uerus Iesus ad discipulos suos dicebat: Nescitis cuius spiritus sitis: Venit filius hominis seruare animas, non perdere. Quid autem crudelius unquam excogitari poterit,quàm quod ab illis in eos exerceri uidemus, qui ab Antichristi iugo deficiunt?
units.tr: What shall I say about the Spirit? I am not looking at what they teach about the Holy Spirit in name, but at what kind of spirit they themselves have, and what kind is received by those who are held under their yoke and submit to their doctrines. Where a fictitious Jesus is held, the Spirit of the true Jesus cannot be had. The Spirit of the true Jesus is not the spirit of Antichrist but of Christ; it is not a spirit of lying but of truth. It does not hold men in impiety, superstitions, idolatry and false worship, but renews their hearts in true faith in Christ and frees them from all these things. It is not bloodthirsty toward the erring but gentle. Hence the true Jesus also said to his disciples: "You do not know what spirit you are of. The Son of man came to save souls, not to destroy them" (Luke 9:55-56). What cruelty could ever be devised that is greater than what we see them inflict on those who fall away from the yoke of Antichrist?

units.la: Quale uero prædicent Euangelium, nihil est causæ cur admoneam. Tale habent Euangelium,quod ne literam quidem ueri Euange lij iuxta se ferre queat: unde & codices Euangelij Christi fideliû manibus ereptos, igni tradunt. Prolixum est recensere Euangelij ipsorum dogmata, &forsan tædiofum quoque lectori,cum sint omnium notissima,quorum ne usum quidem in uero Christi Euangelio conti​netur. Et interim in Missis suis murmurant uel cantât Euangelium, sed lingua populo incognita,lum naria oculis corporis lucentia ac cendunt:& lucem Euangelij, qua mentes audientium illuminari debebant extinguût. De concionibus illorû quid dicam,in quibus maxima partem obtinent Aristoteles, Sophistæ, Scotistæ, Thomistæ, merita mortuorum sanctorû,& doctrina de purgatorio , de Missæ sacrificio, de potestate Papæ,de intercessione & cultu sanctorum,de indulgentijs Romanis,de meritis bonorû operum,de Decimis,de oblationibus,& quę alia sunt eiusmodi innumera. Quæ Christo dantur, dantur obiter,in specie, ad hoc tantum, ut sub ipsius nomine regnent, non ut ipse regnet in cordibus credentium.
units.tr: There is no need for me to warn about what kind of gospel they preach. They have such a gospel that cannot bear even a letter of the true Gospel beside it; hence they also hand over to the fire the copies of the Gospel of Christ taken from the hands of the faithful. It would be lengthy to recount their gospel doctrines, and perhaps tedious to the reader too, since they are known to everyone, and of these not even the use is found in the true Gospel of Christ. Meanwhile in their Masses they mutter or sing the Gospel, but in a tongue unknown to the people; they light candles that shine for the eyes of the body, and they extinguish the light of the Gospel by which the minds of the hearers ought to be enlightened. What shall I say of their sermons, in which the greatest part is taken up by Aristotle, the sophists, the Scotists and the Thomists, the merits of dead saints, the doctrine of purgatory, the sacrifice of the Mass, the power of the Pope, the intercession and cult of the saints, the Roman indulgences, the merits of good works, tithes, offerings, and countless other things of this kind? Whatever is given to Christ is given in passing and in outward show, only so that they may reign under his name, not so that he may reign in the hearts of believers.

units.la: Cum ergo talem habeant Iesum,talem spiritum,tale Euangelium, non verum,sed ficticium,non est ut præsenti se loco tueantur, sed competit ipsis potius quod Galat.primo dicit Apostolus ad hunc modum: Cęterûm etiamsi nos, aut angelus è cœlo prædicauerit uobis Euaugelium , præter id quod prædicauimus uobis,anathema sit.Quemadmodum antè diximus,& nunc iterum dico , si quis uobis prędicauerit Euangelium,præter id quod accepi stis,anathema sit.Locus ille,quoniam mentio nem illius feci , non aduersatur huic præsenti. Cum hic dicit, recte toleraretis eû qui ad uos uenit, si alium Iesum prædicaret,quê nô prędicauimus,& aliud Euangeliû,quod nô acce pistis,per aliud Euangeliû & aliû Iesum,intel-
units.tr: Since, then, they have such a Jesus, such a spirit and such a gospel, which are not true but fictitious, they cannot defend themselves in the present place; rather, what the Apostle says in the first chapter of Galatians applies to them: "But even if we, or an angel from heaven, preach to you a gospel other than what we have preached to you, let him be accursed." And as I said before, and now say again: "If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than what you have received, let him be accursed" (Gal. 1:8-9). That passage, since I have mentioned it, does not conflict with this present one. Here he says that you would rightly tolerate the one who comes to you if he preached another Jesus, whom we have not preached, and another gospel, which you have not received. By "another gospel and another Jesus" he means the true one; but there, by "another gospel" he means one alien to the truth.

units.la: ligit uerũ,illic uero, per aliud Euangeliũ,intel ligit alienũ à uero.Hic dicit: Sinô ego uerũ uo bis Iesum & Euangeliũ prædicaui,sed falsum, ille uero aliũ uobis Iesum,& aliud Euágelium, uerum uidelicet, prædicat, rectè me faltiditis, & illum toleratis. Illic uero, constanter sibi ue rum tribuit Euangeliũ, & pseudapostolis sal- sum,ideoq; anathema pronunciat omnẽ eum, qui aliud ab illo prædicat. Anathematis huius grauitatem experiẽtur olim omnes illi,qui E- uangelium Christi dogmatum suorum mixtu ra corruperũt. Sed redeamus ad Apostolum.
units.tr: Here he says: "If I have not preached to you the true Jesus and Gospel, but a false one," while that man preaches to you another Jesus and another gospel, which is evidently a true one, then you rightly reject me and tolerate him. But there, he consistently claims the true Gospel for himself and calls the false one that of the pseudo-apostles, and therefore pronounces anathema on anyone who preaches something other than what he preaches. All those who have corrupted the Gospel of Christ by mixing in their own doctrines have already experienced the gravity of this anathema. But let us return to the Apostle.

units.la: ARBITROR enim me, inquit, nihilo in- seriorem fuisse eximijs apostolis.) Græcè est, λογιζομαι γαρ μηδεν υστερηκεναι των υπερλιαν αποστολων, id est,arbitror enim me nihilo inferiorem,uel, nihilo posteriorem fuisse (nam utrunque legi potest) illis qui plusquã ualde, uel, supra mo- dũ, sunt apostoli. Vulgata habet, Existimo.n, me nihil minus fecisse à magnis apostolis.Sen sus est.Nô aût rectè eũ toleratis,quandoquidẽ neq; aliũ ille Iesum prædicat, quẽ ego nô prædi cauerim : neq; aliũ spiritũ accipitis, quẽ antea ex prædicatioe mea nô acceperitis: neq; aliud Euágelium ab illo accipitis, ideoq; nihil in A- postolatu meo desiderare potestis.Arbitror e- nim me sic illo functum esse apud uos, ut nul- la in re posterior ac minor fuerim illis,qui pro ualde magnis & excellẽtibus habẽtur apostolis. Nemo illorũ quantus quantus sit plus uo- bis fidei,plus scientiæ & cognitioũ Dei, & plus charismatũ spiritus attulisset. Quare prorsus nihil est causę cur aduenticiũ illũ tantopere su spiciatis, illiusq; infolétiá toleretis, quasi plus fructus ex illius q̃ ex nostra doctrina acqratis.
units.tr: "For I reckon," he says, "that I was not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles." In Greek it is: "λογιζομαι γαρ μηδεν υστερηκεναι των υπερλιαν αποστολων" [logizomai gar meden hysterēkenai tōn hyperlian apostolōn], that is, "for I reckon that I was nothing inferior, or nothing later (for either reading is possible), to those who are apostles beyond measure, or, above measure." The Vulgate has, "I think I have done nothing less than the great apostles." The sense is this: you rightly tolerate him not, since he does not preach another Jesus than I have preached, nor do you receive another spirit than you received before through my preaching, nor do you receive from him another gospel; therefore you can find nothing lacking in my apostleship. For I reckon that I have so discharged my office among you that in no respect have I been later or lesser than those who are regarded as very great and excellent apostles. None of them, however great, would have brought you more faith, more knowledge of God, or more gifts of the Spirit. Therefore there is absolutely no reason why you should so greatly suspect this newcomer, or tolerate his arrogance, as if you gained more fruit from his teaching than from ours.

units.la: Illud , eximijs apostolis,sic positũ est, ut re- ferri possit tam ad pseudapostolos illos glorio sos ac iactabundos, quàm ad Petrũ, Iacobũ & Ioannem. Si referẽdũ est ad ueros apostolos, argumento est,sub illorũ se nominibus uendi tasse pseudapostolos illos, cũ quib. Paulus lu- ctatur, ut sit sensus, etiamsi magni ac præcipui apostoli ad uos ipsi uenissent, nihilo plus uo- bis contulissent,quàm cõtulerim ego.Neq;.n. ulla in re minꝰ uobis cõtuli, quá uestra popo- scerit salus & necessitas,& quâ illi prestare pos sint.Quare nõ est ut sub illorũ nominibus su- cũ uobis fieri sinatis.Verum mihi probabilius est,referendũ esse ad pseudapostolos, nõ qd' il li eximij fuerint apostoli,sed quod à Paulo per ironiá υπερλιαν αποστολοι. i. supra modũ apostoli ob id uocetur, qd' se supra modũ efferrent, & excellẽtis Apostolatus glorias efflaret. Nõ ui- deo alioqui,qd sibi uellet Apostolus , si Petrũ, Iacobum & Ioannem υπερλιαν αποστολυς uocaret.
units.tr: The phrase "the chiefest apostles" is so put that it can be referred both to those boastful and vainglorious pseudo-apostles and to Peter, James and John. If it is referred to the true apostles, it is evidence that those pseudo-apostles with whom Paul contends sold themselves under their names, so that the sense is: even if the great and pre-eminent apostles themselves had come to you, they would have contributed no more to you than I have. For I have contributed nothing less to you in any respect than your salvation and need demanded, and than they are able to supply. Therefore you should not allow yourselves to be taken in under their names. Yet it seems more probable to me that it should be referred to the pseudo-apostles, not because they were excellent apostles, but because Paul calls them, by irony, "hyper-eminent apostles" (υπερλιαν αποστολοι [hyperlian apostoloi]), that is, apostles beyond measure, because they exalted themselves beyond measure and boasted of the glories of their excellent apostleship. Otherwise I do not see what the Apostle would mean if he called Peter, James and John "hyper-eminent apostles."

units.la: Nos obseruemus hoc loco,nõ esse de mini- stris Christi cẽsendũ aliter,quâ secundũ mini- sterij ipsorũ fructus.Quantũuis in facie humi- lis sit,quẽ dns spiritu suo ad ædificatione eccle się reddidit instructũ, nô est propter persoñæ humilitatẽ inferior cẽsendus illis,q supra mo- dũ sunt in ecclesia episcopi,Pontifices, & præ- lati,imò præferendus etiá, quatenus ad utili-
units.tr: We should observe at this point that ministers of Christ are not to be judged by any standard other than the fruit of their ministry. Although a man may be humble in appearance, if the Lord has equipped him with his Spirit for the building up of the Church, he is not on account of his humble person to be considered inferior to those bishops, pontiffs and prelates who are above measure in the Church; indeed he is to be preferred to them, insofar as he is better equipped, by the grace of God, for the benefit of the churches of Christ.

units.la: tatem ecclesiarum Christi per gratiam Dei in- structior. Nec insoles uideri debet, si qui eius- modi est nihilo seipse inferiorem illis esse, & sentiat & liberè asserat, præsertim si se inflata illorum authoritate grauari senserit.
units.tr: Nor should it seem arrogant if such a man judges himself in no way inferior to them, and feels and freely asserts this, especially if he has perceived himself burdened by their inflated authority.

units.la: SI uero idiota etiá sim sermone,inquit,non tamẽ scietia.) Quoniã dicebãt,præsentia cor- poris infirma,& sermo contemptus,sicuti cap. præcedẽti uidimus, atq; ita Apostolatũ ipsius extenuare, sese q; cõptioris sermonis prætex- tu supra illũ efferre moliebatur, quasi quo splẽ didior est sermo, hoc superior & excellentior sit Apostolus, etiá isti calũniæ respõdet,dicẽs: Si uero idiota etiá sim sermone, ut illi mihi im pingũt,inde tamẽ nõ cõsequitur, esse me ipsis inferiore, quádoquidẽ scietia nõ sum idiota & imperitus.Non dicit se esse idiotam sermone, neq; erat etiá,sed per cõcessionẽ,etiási sim, in- quit,idiota sermone, ubi subaudiendũ est,sic- ut ipsi mihi opprobrát. Aliàs Act.14. ducé illũ sermonis fuisse legimus, ita ut ab ethnicis pro Mercurio haberetur. Et tamẽ non pugnat pro gloria elegatioris sermonis,quâ pseudaposto- li magnificiebant: quandoquidem in ecclesia Christi nô tâ requiritur à ministro,ut splẽdidẽ rhetoricetur,quàm ut sciens sit rerũ diuinarũ & necessariá scietiá uerbis intelligibilibus gra uiter & fideliter proponat. Sæculare eloquen tiá alij affectant,alij exercẽt inutiliter in eccle- sia.Notũ est illud philosophi, qui post longá e- ruditorũ episcoporũ concertatioñe, qua nihil efficiebatur cũ pij cuiusdá & idiotę Senis simplicè sermonẽ religiosè ac cordatè prolatũ au disset,illoq; in cõscientiá sua uiĉtus tenerẽtur, dicebat:Donec mecũ agebatur uerbis, uerbis ego uerba rependi, & quę dicebantur dicẽdi arte subuerti, ubi uero pro uerbis uirtus pro- cessit ex ore dicẽtis,nõ potuerũt uerba resiste re uirtuti,nec homo aduersari potuit Deo.Vi- de in Ecclesiast.hist.Ruffini,lib.1.cap.3. Nolim tamẽ patrocinari illis, qui ad hoc quidem sunt parati,ut puritatem sermonis nihili faciant, & egregiæ sint idiotæ,uerum interea de scientia Dei, ad docendũ necessaria, nihilo plus sunt soliciti,sermone idiotæ & scientia bardi,
units.tr: "But even if I am rude in speech," he says, "yet not in knowledge." For they were saying that his bodily presence was weak and his speech contemptible, as we saw in the preceding chapter; and so they were trying to diminish his apostleship and to exalt themselves above him by the pretext of a more polished speech, as if the more splendid the speech, the more superior and excellent the apostle. He answers this slander too, saying: "But even if I am rude in speech, as they throw in my face, it does not follow that I am inferior to them, since I am not untaught and unskilled in knowledge." He does not say that he is rude in speech, nor was he, but by way of concession: "even if I am," he says, "rude in speech," where one must supply: "as they reproach me." Elsewhere we read that Paul was the leader in speech, so that he was taken by the Gentiles for Mercury (Acts 14:12). And yet he does not contend for the glory of more elegant speech, in which the pseudo-apostles prided themselves; for in the Church of Christ it is required of a minister not so much that he speak splendidly in rhetorical style as that he be knowledgeable in divine matters and set forth what is necessary, in intelligible words, gravely and faithfully. Others aim at worldly eloquence, and others use it uselessly in the Church. The saying of that philosopher is well known: after a long contest among learned bishops, in which nothing was achieved, when he heard a simple speech delivered religiously and wisely by a certain pious and unlearned old man, and was overcome by it in his conscience, he said: "As long as the contest was carried on with words, I answered words with words, and what was said was overturned by the art of speaking; but when power came forth from the mouth of the speaker in place of words, the words could not resist the power, nor could the man oppose God." See Rufinus's Ecclesiastical History, book 1, chapter 3. I would not, however, defend those who are ready to make nothing of purity of speech and to be outstandingly unlearned, while at the same time being no more concerned with the knowledge of God necessary for teaching, being unlearned in speech yet learned in ignorance.

units.la: Verum ubiq; manifesti sumus in om nib. ergauos. Num peccaui, quod me ipsum humiliaui, ut uos exaltaremini? quod gratuito Euangelium Dei prædi cauí uobis? Cæteras ecclesias depręda tus sum,accepto ab illis stipendio, quo uobis inseruiré.Et cum apud uos essem & egerê, nõ fui onerosus cuiquã. Nam quod mihi deerat, suppleuerũt fratres, qui uenerant à Macedonia:& ín omni- bus sic me seruabam, ne cui essem one- rosus,atq; ita seruabo. Est ueritas Chri- sti ín me, qd hæc gloriatio nõ ínterrum- petur contra me in regionibus Achaiæ. Quapropter an quod nõ diligam uos? Deus nouit. Verum quod facio, idem & facia, ut amputem occasione ijs, qui cupiunt occasione, ut in eo de quo gloriatur, reperiantur quèadmodū & nos.
units.tr: Yet in every way we have made ourselves known among all of you. Did I sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted? Did I sin in preaching the Gospel of God to you free of charge? I plundered other churches, taking wages from them in order to serve you. And when I was with you and in need, I did not burden anyone; for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked. In all things I kept and will keep myself from being a burden to anyone. As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia. Why? Is it because I do not love you? God knows. But what I do, I will go on doing, so that I may cut off the opportunity from those who desire an opportunity, that they may be found to boast in the same way as we do.

units.la: VERVM ubiq; manifesti sumus, inquit, in omnibus erga uos.) Græcè est, ἀλλ' ἐν πάντι φανερωθέντες ἐν πᾶσιν εἰς ὑμᾶς. i. At in omni manifestati in omnibus in uos. Vulgata lectio sic habet: In omnibus autem manifestus sum uobis. Sic posita est hæc particula, ut tā ad præcedentia, q̃ ad sequentia referri possit. Si ad præcedentia referas, sensus erit. Arbitror enim me nihilo inferiorem fuisse eximijs apostolis. Etiamsi autem idiota sim sermone, non tamen scientia. Verum haud opus mihi est, ut ista coprobem apud uos, quibus abunde & in omnibus sum manifestus. Qualem me gesserim in omnibus erga uos, manifestum est. Et ipsa Apostolatus mei efficacia sic est in uobis manifesta, ut iure glorier, nihilo me inferiorem esse illis, qui supra modum sunt Apostoli, nec idio tam esse scientia, etiamsi me sermone idiotam esse dicant. Sic apparet hæc uerba connectenda esse præcedētibus. Si uero referas ad sequētia, ne sic quidem incomodus erit sensus, si legas ut in Græco est, absq; uerbo sumus uel fuimus, ad hunc modum. Verū ubiq; manifestati in omnibus erga uos, an peccaui quod meipsum humiliarim? Hoc est: Verū cum ubiq; & in omnib. sim erga uos manifestatus tanquam uerus Christi Apostolus, an ideo peccaui, & inferior sum nouis illis uestris apostolis, quod meipsum uestro bono humiliaui, ut uos exaltaremini? an ob id contemptibilis est meus Apostolatus, quod uobis Euangelium Dei gratuito prædicaui? Quasi dicat, An adeo estis peruersi, ut qd' ad commendationem Apostolatus mei facere debebat, ad illius extenuationem peruertatis? An qui se uestro bono humiliat, dignus uobis uidetur, qui contemnatur? An quo minus uos graduai, hoc inferior sum Apostolus? qua si hæc sit Apostoli conditio, ut hoc sit excellentior Apostolus, quo maioribus sumptis molestum reddit ac sumptuosum Euangelium, & quo plus accipit à fidelibus, hoc illis plus de cœlesti gratia impertiat? Si sic sentitis, toto cœlo erratis. Humiliare seipsum aliorum bono, ad exemplum Christi, & gratis prædicare Euangelium, non inferiorem reddit, sed magis ornat & commendat Apostolum. Et hæc posterior expositio uerbis, ut in Græco habentur, conuenientior uidetur.
units.tr: "But we have been made manifest in every way" he says. In Greek it is "ἀλλ' ἐν πάντι φανερωθέντες ἐν πᾶσιν εἰς ὑμᾶς", that is, "But having been made manifest in everything, among all, toward you." The Vulgate reads: "But I am made manifest to you in all things." The particle is placed so that it can be referred both to what precedes and to what follows. If you refer it to what precedes, the sense is: "For I think I was in no way inferior to the most eminent apostles. Even if I am unskilled in speech, I am not so in knowledge. But there is no need for me to prove these things to you, among whom I have been abundantly and in all respects made manifest. The way I have conducted myself among you in all things is plain. And the very effectiveness of my apostleship is so evident among you that I may rightly boast that I am in no way inferior to those who are apostles beyond measure, nor unskilled in knowledge, even if they say I am unskilled in speech." It appears, then, that these words should be joined to what goes before. But if you refer them to what follows, the sense is not awkward either, provided you read it as it is in the Greek, without supplying "we are" or "we were", thus: "But having been made manifest in all things among you, did I sin in humbling myself?" That is: "But since I have been made manifest everywhere and in all things among you as a true apostle of Christ, did I therefore sin, and am I inferior to your new apostles, because I humbled myself for your good so that you might be exalted? Is my apostleship therefore contemptible because I preached the Gospel of God to you free of charge?" As if he said: "Are you so perverse that you twist into a disparagement of my apostleship what ought to have commended it? Does one who humbles himself for your good seem worthy of contempt to you? Am I a lesser apostle because I do not burden you? If this is the condition of an apostle, that he is the more excellent the more burdensome and costly he makes the Gospel, and the more he receives from the faithful, the more heavenly grace he imparts to them, then you are wrong, utterly wrong. To humble oneself for the good of others, after the example of Christ, and to preach the Gospel freely, does not make an apostle inferior, but adorns and commends him all the more." And this latter explanation seems more agreeable to the words as they stand in the Greek.

units.la: VERVM cū ubiq; manifesti simus, inquit, in omnibus erga uos.) Gloriatur iam secundo, supra cap. 5. & hic esse se Corinthijs manifestum in omnibus, quo omnem illis excusationem adimit. Quomodo enim uel errorem uel ignorantiam ptexere poterit, qui in re non simpliciter, sed sibi cum primis, & non ex parte, sed omnino manifesta mendacium pro ueritate sectatur? Vides exemplū synceri Christi ministri, qui ubicunq; agit, lux est, nō solū do-
units.tr: "But since we have been made manifest in every way among all of you," he says. He now boasts a second time, as above in chapter 5, that he has been made manifest to the Corinthians in all things, by which he removes from them every excuse. For how could one who pursues a lie for the truth, in a matter not simply but chiefly known to him, and not in part but altogether plain, cover up his error or ignorance? You see an example of a sincere minister of Christ, who wherever he acts is a light, not only by teaching,

units.la: cēdo, sed & cōuersando, nō ex parte tantū, sed in omnib. quę à Christi ministro requiruntur, ne quo pacto fiat, ut fideles à pseudapostolis seducti, inueniant quod errori suo prætexant.
units.tr: but also by his conduct, not in part only but in all the things that are required of a minister of Christ, so that in no way should it happen that the faithful, seduced by false apostles, find something to use as a pretext for their error.

units.la: NVM peccaui, inquit, quod meipsum humiliauit, ut uos exaltaremini? In Græco est, ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐποίησα. i. num peccatum feci. ἁμαρτία est, quando à scopo præfixo aberratur, quod nos Germani ein fehler uocamus, & ἁμαρτίαν ποιεῖν ein fehler thuon. Est autem hoc loco peccatū facere, contra mispat, decorū & scopū ueri apostoli, tale quid facere ob quod merito contemnare, ut si sis superbus, arrogans, ac proprij nominis studiosus, aut uentris seruus, uel turpis lucri cupidus, uel dominij in ecclesia appetes, aut doctrinâ Christi nec fideliter nec prudēter tradens. Non dicit autē simpliciter, nō peccaui, sed num peccaui? ad hoc interrogās & urgens, ut conscientias ipsorū appellet, num seipsum humiliādo peccauerit. Q.d. Adeo ne stultipidi & incogitates estis, ut peccatū esse putetis, si seipsum humiliauerit Apostolus Christi, cum illi magis peccet, qui seipsos exaltant, & quantum in ipsis est, alios humiliant?
units.tr: "Did I sin," he says, "in humbling myself so that you might be exalted?" In Greek it is "ἢ ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησα", that is, "Did I commit a sin?" Sin [ἁμαρτία] is when one strays from the set goal, which we Germans call ein fehler, and to commit sin [ἁμαρτίαν ποιεῖν] is ein fehler thuon. Here, however, committing a sin means doing something contrary to the office, decorum and aim of a true apostle, something for which one would rightly be despised, such as being proud, arrogant, and eager for one's own name, or a slave of the belly, or greedy for base gain, or seeking dominion in the church, or handing on the teaching of Christ neither faithfully nor prudently. He does not say simply, "I did not sin," but "Did I sin?" He asks this in a challenging way, appealing to their consciences, whether he sinned by humbling himself. As if he said: "Are you so foolish and thoughtless that you think it is a sin if an apostle of Christ humbles himself, when those who exalt themselves, and as far as they are able make others lowly, sin far more?"

units.la: Humiliare uero seipsum, est gerere se non secundum statum ac dignitatis suæ amplitudinē, sed quę infra illam sunt facere, perinde ac si dominus posita dominationis suæ dignitate ac potestate, agat ea quæ sunt serui. Huc facit exemplū Christi, q cū esset dominus ac magister, usq; ad pedes discipulorum seipsum lauādo illos ac tergēdo humiliauit. Quomodo aūt humiliauerit seipsum Apostolus, mox exponet.
units.tr: To humble oneself, however, is to conduct oneself not according to the rank and greatness of one's dignity, but to do those things that lie beneath it, just as a lord, setting aside the dignity and power of his lordship, does the things that servants do. The example of Christ bears on this, who, though he was lord and master, humbled himself by washing and wiping the feet of his disciples. How the apostle humbled himself, he will explain shortly.

units.la: VT uos, inquit, exaltaremini.) Nō dicit, ut exalter, sed, ut uos exaltaremini.
