Vafrū genus humiliantium se est, qui, quoniam dictum est à domino: Qui seipsum humiliauerit, exaltabitur, ad hoc se humiliant, imò speciem humilitatis præferunt, ut exaltentur, quale est quod Rom. Pontifex sic se seruū seruorū Dei uocat, ut supra oēs in ecclesia dominetur & exaltetur. Verus Christi Apostolus humiliādo se nō fui, sed aliorū quærebat exaltatione: quemadmodū & Christus ob id humiliauit seipsum, ut nos ad dignitatem filiorū Dei exaltaremur. Et ei dignitati Apostolus quoq; humiliādo se seruiuit. Ob id enim submisse ac modeste agebat apud Corinthios omnia, ut hoc facilius eos ad cognitionem ueritatis & fidem in Christum induceret, unde omnis nostra salus est, felicitas, gloria & dignitas.
units.tr: "That you might be exalted," he says. He does not say "that I might be exalted" but "that you might be exalted." There is a crafty kind of people who humble themselves: since it has been said by the Lord, "Whoever humbles himself will be exalted," they humble themselves for this very purpose, or rather they put on a show of humility so that they may be exalted. This is the case with the Roman Pontiff, who calls himself "servant of the servants of God" so that he may rule and be exalted above all in the church. The true apostle of Christ, in humbling himself, did not seek his own exaltation but that of others, just as Christ too humbled himself so that we might be exalted to the dignity of the sons of God. And the apostle also served that dignity by humbling himself. For this reason he acted humbly and modestly in all things among the Corinthians, so that he might more easily lead them to the knowledge of the truth and to faith in Christ, from which comes all our salvation, happiness, glory and dignity.

units.la: QVOD gratuito, inquit, Euangelii Dei prædicatui uobis.) Græcè est, quod gratuito Euangelium Dei euágelizaui vobis. Euágeliū Dei euágelizare, est felicissimū à Deo nunciū, salutis videlicet, & æternæ uitæ per Christum partæ, mortalib. magno gaudio annúciare ac prædicare. Hoc Corinthijs annunciauerat gratuito. Dices: quid hoc magni erat, quod non uēdiderat illis Euangeliū, sed gratuito obtulerat, cum non emisset illud, sed gratuito accepisset & ipse: ideoque contra mandatum Christi fecisset, dicentis: Gratis accepistis, gratis date, nisi gratuito prædicasset? Quod Romanus Pontifex uēdit claues, altaria, Christum ipsum, nihil habet infolentię. Nam uendere iure potest, eo quod emerit, & ipse prius. Verum alia est apostolorum Christi conditio.
units.tr: "Because I preached the Gospel of God to you free of charge," he says. In Greek it is "ὅτι δωρεὰν τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ εὐαγγέλιον [εὐηγγέλισα] ὑμῖν", that is, "that I announced the Gospel of God to you freely." To announce [εὐαγγελίζειν] the Gospel of God is to proclaim with great joy to mortals the most happy message from God, namely of salvation and eternal life obtained through Christ. This he had announced to the Corinthians freely. You may ask: what was so great about it, that he did not sell them the Gospel but offered it free, since he himself had not bought it but had received it freely, and so would have acted against the command of Christ, who said, "You have received freely, give freely," unless he had preached freely? The Roman Pontiff, who sells keys, altars and Christ himself, has nothing unusual about him. For he can rightly sell what he himself first bought. But the condition of the apostles of Christ is different.

units.la: Respondeo. Nec emit Pontifex quod se uēdere simulat, nec uēdit etiam, quia gratia Dei nec emi potest, nec uendi, sed turpis simoniæ fabulam ludit in ecclesia, donec tempus aduenerit iusti iudicij, quod nō dormit. Quod Paulum attinet, non loquitur ille de gratuita prædicatione, cuius oppositum sit, nundinatio simoniaca, sed de ea qua nec cibū quidem, qui laboranti debetur, à Corinthijs acceperat, quo omnibus modis δἰὰ τιαυον illis exhiberet Euangelium, eoq; omnem tergiuersandi, & oblocquendi causam amputaret.
units.tr: I answer: the Pontiff neither buys what he pretends to sell, nor does he sell it at all, since the grace of God can be neither bought nor sold; rather he plays out the shameful farce of simony in the church, until the time of the just judgment comes, which does not sleep. As for Paul, he is not speaking of free preaching in the sense opposed to simoniacal haggling, but of that kind in which he did not even accept from the Corinthians the food that is owed to a labourer, so that by every means he might present the Gospel to them without cost, and thereby cut off every cause of evasion and objection.

units.la: Videtur autem hic exponere, quomodo seipsum humiliarit, ut ipsi exaltarentur. Gratuito uidelicet Euangelium Dei prędicando. Est enim non modica humilitatis species sic operari, ac seruire, ut ne cibum quidem accipias, cuiuis operanti debitum, sed ab eo iure sic abstineas, ac si ne cibo quidem dignum sit, quod operaris, ad quem modum eorum labores extenuare uolentes, qui nec utiliter nec grauiter operātur, ne cibum quidem eos promereri dicimus. Nihil unquam geri potest in hoc mundo, & utilius, & preciolius, quodq; maiore dignius sit honore, quàm quod Apostolus gratuito egit apud Corinthios, uerum ea humilitas non ipsius modo personæ, sed & ipsi Euangelio Dei, quod gratuito prædicauerat, cōtem ptū peperat. Quale est quod hodie in Euangelicis ecclesijs usuuenire uidemus, in quibus quo minore sumptu constat totum Euangelij ministerium, hoc minoris æstimatur. In papatu magnifice de nugis illis sentiebamus, quæ nonnisi emendo acquiruntur. Hæc est carnis nostrę peruersitas. Ipsum cœlum uilescit, si gratis offeratur, nec de Deo magnifice sentitur, nisi bona sua uendat, uel bene meritis tantum impertiat.
units.tr: It seems that here he sets out how he humbled himself so that they might be exalted, namely by preaching the Gospel of God free of charge. For it is no small mark of humility to work and serve in such a way that you do not even accept the food owed to any worker, but abstain from that right as though what you do were not even worth food. In the same way, we say that those who labour without usefulness or seriousness do not even deserve food, wishing to belittle their labours. Nothing can be done in this world that is more useful, more precious, and more worthy of honour than what the Apostle did free of charge among the Corinthians. But that humility brought contempt not only upon his person but also upon the Gospel of God itself, which he had preached free of charge. This is what we see happening today in the Evangelical churches, where the less the whole ministry of the Gospel costs, the less it is esteemed. In the Papacy we thought highly of those trifles that are acquired only by buying. This is the perversity of our flesh. Heaven itself becomes cheap if it is offered freely, and God is not thought highly of unless He sells His goods or bestows them only on the well deserving.

units.la: CAETERAS ecclesias, inquit, depręda tus sum, accepto ab illis stipēdio, quo uobis inseruirem.) Quoniam mox audire poterat, unde ergo necessarios sumptus accepisti? Subiūgit Cæteras ecclesias depręda tus sum, accepto ab illis stipendio, quo uobis inseruiré. Quid hoc est? Licet ne Apostolo depręda ri ecclesias Christi? Æquum ne est, alios depręda ri, ut alios diuites reddas? An par est depręda ri pauperiores, ut gratis seruias ditioribus?
units.tr: "I plundered other churches," he says, "receiving wages from them so that I might serve you." Since one might immediately ask, "Then where did you get the necessary expenses?" he adds: "I plundered other churches, receiving wages from them so that I might serve you." What is this? Is it lawful for the Apostle to plunder the churches of Christ? Is it fair to plunder some so that you may make others rich? Or is it right to plunder the poorer so that you may serve the richer for nothing?

units.la: Respondeo. Neminem more militari, aut prædonum depręda tus est Apostolus. Rem ipsam simpliciter in sequentibus exprimit dicens: Cum essem apud uos, & egerem, non fui onerosus cuiquā. Nam quod mihi deerat, suppleuerunt fratres, qui uenerant è Macedonia. Ergo liberam, ac spontaneam cōtributionem Macedonum, qua egestati ipsius succurrerāt, cum seruiret Corinthijs, uocat depręda tionem ac stipendium, non quod adeo multum
units.tr: I answer: the Apostle did not plunder anyone in the manner of soldiers or robbers. In what follows he expresses the matter plainly, saying: "When I was with you and was in need, I was not a burden to anyone. For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked." So he calls the free and voluntary contribution of the Macedonians, by which they relieved his need while he served the Corinthians, "plunder" and "wages." This is not because he received so much from them that it could rightly be called plunder,

units.la: ab illis, ut recte prada uocari potuerit, accepe rit, sed quod, ut ipse erat animatus, etiam modicum à pauperioribus acceptum magni facere, ac instar prędæ habere soleret. Laborabat manibus suis, ne cui esset oneri. Verū non potuit simul pro se & socijs, quos secum habebat, sic sufficere laborando, ut non adhuc egeret. Ei necessitati subueniebant Macedones qui seipsos primū Deo, deinde ipsius Apostolo dederant, sicuti supra cap. 8. meminit. Hoc igitur illorum supplementum, quo id quod deerat supplebatur, nec adeo multum, nec coactum, sed spontaneum, uocat depręda tionem significans usq; adeo se propter pseudapostolos, noluisse quempiam Corinthiorum grauare in hac causa, ut citius alias ecclesias depręda turus fuerit, quàm cuipiam Corinthiorum futurus oneri, quod illud citra Macedonū offendiculum fieret, hoc uero citra offendiculū Corinthiorum fieri non posset, propter pseudapostolorum insidias.
units.tr: but because, being minded as he was, he was accustomed to regard even a small sum received from the poorer as great and to treat it as if it were spoil. He laboured with his own hands so as not to be a burden to anyone. Yet he could not, by working, support himself and the companions he had with him so as not to be still in need. The Macedonians, who had first given themselves to God and then to the Apostle himself, as he mentioned above in chapter 8, came to that need. So this supply of theirs, by which what was lacking was made up, not large and not compelled but voluntary, he calls plunder, signifying that he was so unwilling, because of the false apostles, to burden any Corinthian in this matter, that he would sooner plunder other churches than become a burden to any Corinthian. For what could be done without offence to the Macedonians could not be done without offence to the Corinthians, because of the snares of the false apostles.

units.la: Non dicit autem simpliciter: alias ecclesias depręda tus sum, sed addit, accepto ab alijs sti pendio, παρὰ τῶν ὑμῶν διακονίαν, id est, ad uestri ministerium. Secernit depręda tione suam ab ea quæ prædonum est, qua illi nemini seruiētes, sed in quosuis grassantes ociosi ex pręda uiuunt, & confert eam militi, cui debetur militare pro ministerio ipsius stipēdium, siue id accipiat ab illis quibus militādo seruit, siue àuiētis. Ad posterius hoc respicere uidetur, comparans Macedonū fideles, iam uiētis, atq; ita quod ab illis accipiebat, prędæ ac stipendij loco ducens: prędæ, respęctu uiētoriæ, stipēdij, respęctu militiæ suæ ac ministerij, præsertim cum Corinthij nihil darent, quibus expugnandis, ac domino asserendis inseruiebat.
units.tr: He does not, however, simply say, "I plundered other churches," but adds, "receiving wages from others," παρὰ τῶν ὑμῶν διακονίαν, that is, "for your ministry." He separates his plunder from that of robbers, who serve no one but, idly attacking whomever they meet, live off the spoil. He compares it instead to a soldier, to whom pay is due for his service, whether he receives it from those for whom he fights or from the conquered. He seems to refer to the latter, comparing the faithful Macedonians, who were now conquered, and so treating what he received from them as both spoil and pay: spoil with respect to victory, pay with respect to his warfare and ministry, especially since the Corinthians gave nothing, though he was serving them by conquering them and winning them to the Lord.

units.la: Nos hinc admonemur, qua prudentia ac discretione uti debeat fidelis Christi minister, in illis locis, ubi primùm populis seductis Euangelium Dei prædicat, quod attinet laboris ipsius stipēdium. A Macedonibus accepit, etiá absens & alijs seruiēs Apostolus, à Corinthijs & præsens & ipsis ministrans nō accepit. Faciebat hoc prudenter, discernens inter Macedones & Corinthios. Macedones dño se iam dederant, illumq; plena fide amplexi erant, & prꝛterea non erant ad rem intenti, sicuti erant Corinthij, sed simplices ac frugi homines, frugaliter uiuentes, ideoq; magis ad dandū q ad accipiendum proclives. Corinthij nondū pleno pede ad Eugelium accesserant, & cum essent diuites, simul erant & tenaciores, adeoq; ad accipiendum magis quàm ad dandum propensi: quare consultum non erat, ut stipēdium ab ipsis peteret, consultius uero, ut ultro à Macedonibus oblatum acciperet. Ad hunc modū hodie quoque Christi minister discernat inter eos, qui nomen Christi dederunt Euágelio, & eos qui ad cognitionem ueritatis nondum uenerunt, nec professionē illius adhuc sunt amplexi, sed primùm audire cœperūt. Ab illis accipiat stipendium, ab istis nondum. Debetur quidem
units.tr: Here we are reminded what prudence and discretion a faithful minister of Christ ought to use, in those places where he first preaches the Gospel of God to deceived peoples, as regards his wages for labour. The Apostle, though absent and serving others, received from the Macedonians; the Corinthians, though present and ministering to them, he did not receive from. He did this prudently, discerning between the Macedonians and the Corinthians. The Macedonians had already given themselves to the Lord and had embraced him with full faith; moreover, they were not intent on worldly gain as the Corinthians were, but were simple and thrifty people, living frugally, and therefore more inclined to give than to receive. The Corinthians had not yet come to the Gospel with full step, and, being rich, were at once more grasping and more disposed to receive than to give. Therefore it was not advisable for him to ask wages from them, but more advisable to accept what the Macedonians offered of their own accord. In the same way today the minister of Christ should distinguish between those who have given their name to the Gospel of Christ and those who have not yet come to the knowledge of the truth, nor have yet embraced its profession, but have only begun to hear. From the former he should accept his wages; from the latter not yet.

units.la: quidé uictus laboranti ministro, uerũ multum refert, à quibus, & quomodo accipiatur. Roma nus pontifex ministrás nemini omnes depræ datur ecclesias, de cuius prædis quid attinet meminisse, cum nullorum prędonum tam sint manifestæ, quàm sunt illius. Illi omnium mini mè conuenit, præsens hoc Pauli exemplum, conuenit uero laborantibus, ac ministrantib. fratribus, qui ad illius sese imitatione accom modare possunt, & in loco debent etiam, si fi deliter domino seruire uoluerint.
units.tr: Certainly food is owed to a labouring minister, but it matters greatly from whom and in what manner it is received. The Roman pontiff, who ministers to no one, plunders all the churches; there is no need to recall his plunder, since none of the robbers are as manifest as he is. This present example of Paul does not suit him at all, but it does suit labouring brothers who ministers, who can accommodate themselves to his imitation, and who ought to do so in their place too, if they wish to serve the Lord faithfully.

units.la: ET cum apud uos essem, inquit, & egerem, non fui onerosus cuiquam.) Exponit quod se alias ecclesias depræ…datū esse, & ab illis stipen dium, ut ipsis inseruiret accepisse dixit. Ne uideretur stipendiũ hoc accepisse ab alijs, ut Co rinthijs prędicaret, priusquá Corinthũ uenif-set, cum iam Macedonià deserere cŏstituisset, dicit: Et cũ apud uos essem, intellige, Euágeli-zans & ministrans uobis, passus sum egestate: & quamuis egerem, nolui tamen oneri cuipiá esse ex uobis. Egerat apud eos docēdo annum & menses sex. Operabatur autem cū apud eos esset, manens apud Aquilam & Priscillā, quod eiusdē esset cum illis artifici, skηνοποιὸς uidelicet. Credibile est autē & illos fuisse tenuis fortunæ, præsertim cū essent exules, à Claudio Imp. cum alijs iudæis pulsi, & artificium ipso rum nō esset de cōmuniter necessarijs, adeoq; minus lucrosum, ut mirū nō sit, eguisse ipsum aliquádiu, donec à Macedonib9 quod deerat suppleretur. Neq; enim refertis loculis à Ma-cedonibus Corinthum uenerat. Sic intelligo factum fuisse, ut egeret prędicans Corinthijs, quandoquidem illi nihil conferebant.
units.tr: "And when I was with you," he says, "and was in need, I was not a burden to anyone." He explains that he had been plundering other churches and had received wages from them in order to serve them. So that it might not seem that he had received this wage from others in order to preach to the Corinthians before he had come to Corinth, since he had already resolved to leave Macedonia, he says: "And when I was with you," understand: evangelising and ministering to you, "I suffered need; and although I was in need, I nonetheless did not wish to be a burden to any of you." He had taught among them for a year and six months. He worked while he was with them, staying with Aquila and Priscilla, because he was of the same craft as they were, namely tent-making [σκηνοποιός]. It is credible that they too were of slender means, especially since they were exiles, driven out with the other Jews by the Emperor Claudius, and since their craft was not among the most necessary and so was not very profitable. It is no wonder that he himself was in need for some time, until what was lacking was supplied by the Macedonians. For he had not come to Corinth with purses full from the Macedonians. Thus I understand that it happened that he was in want while preaching to the Corinthians, since they contributed nothing.

units.la: Illud: Non fui onerosus cuiquam, in Græco est: ἀ καταναρκῶ ὑσὶν ⳙ. Est autē καταναρκῆν tor pedine, ac segnicie sua alijs esse onerosum, & de aliena uiuere quadra, prorsus segnè & in-utilem, qualium innumeram καταναρκώντων prælatorum, cenonicorum, ac monachorum multitudinem ecclesiæ bona deuorare uide-mus, cum interea laborantibus ministris, uix arido pane uiuere detur.
units.tr: That phrase, "I was not burdensome to anyone," reads in the Greek: [οὐ καταναρκῶ ὑμῖν]. Now καταναρκᾶν means to be a burden to others through one's own sluggishness and idleness, and to live off another's purse: utterly slack and useless. We see an innumerable multitude of such sluggards (καταναρκώντων) among the prelates, canons and monks, who devour the goods of the Church, while meanwhile the ministers who labour can scarcely be allowed to live on dry bread.

units.la: Obserua uero, quod nō simpliciter dicit: cũ egerē, nihil accepi à quoq̄, sed, nó fui onerosus cuiquá, quibus uerbis satis exprimit, quare nó acceperit quicquá à Corinthijs. Quod uideli-cet metueret, ne molestũ hoc illis esset & one-rosum. Sic animati sunt homines ingenui, ut ægrè cuiquá sustineant esse oneri. Et præterea cogitabat, q̄ nó facturū id esset, ad propagádũ Euangeliũ apud eos, quibus molestũ fore me tuebat, si aliab ipsis aliquandiu deberet. Hoc ingenio erat, & hac modestia præditus. At ob-secro, quáti sumpt9 fuisset alere Christi Apost. nullo nec equestri, nec pedestri satellitū comi-tatu sũptuosũ, qualeshodie uidem9 episcopos & pōtifices, ꝑlatos & abbates onera terræ, sed uno & altero cooperatore cōtentũ, & omniũ frugalissime uiuētẽ. Sed hæc sors est uerorum Christi ministrorũ, ut apuddiuites Corinthios magis q̄ apd' pauperes Maced.egere cogātur.
units.tr: Observe, however, that he does not simply say, "When I was with you I received nothing from anyone," but "I was not a burden to anyone." By these words he sufficiently expresses why he received nothing from the Corinthians: he was evidently afraid that this would be troublesome and burdensome to them. Such are noble-minded men: they are reluctant to be a burden to anyone. Moreover he reflected that it would not help to spread the Gospel among them if he were a trouble to them, if he should owe anything to them for any length of time. Such was his disposition, and such his modesty. But I ask you, how great an expense it would be to feed a minister of Christ without any retinue of attendants, whether mounted or on foot, which is costly; such as we see today among bishops and pontiffs, prelates and abbots, who are burdens on the earth, whereas he was content with one or two fellow-workers and lived most frugally of all. But this is the lot of the true ministers of Christ: that among the rich Corinthians they are more often compelled to go in want than among the poor Macedonians.

units.la: NAM quod mihi deerat, inquit, suppleue: ũt fratres, qui uenerant è Macedonia.) Qui nam illi fuerint, nó exprimitur. In Act. quidē ca. 18. Silas ac Timotheus è Macedonia Corinthum ad Paulum uenisse leguntur, uerum incertum est, an de illis loquatur, uel alijs quibusdam. Si supplementum illud, quo egestati ipsius sub-ueniebatur, fratres isti de suo cótulerunt, exi-stimo nó posse ad Silam ac Timotheũ referri. Si uero non de suo, sed de contributione eccle-siarũ defeƈtus Pauli suppleuerunt, nõ est absi-mile uero, accepisse hos duos ab ecclesijs Ma-cedonię quo necessitatibus illius succurreret. Et hic sensus, meo iudicio, probabilis est, pro-pter præcedentia, quibus se alias ecclesias de-prędatũ esse dixit, quo Corinthijs inseruiret.
units.tr: "For what was lacking to me," he says, "the brethren who came from Macedonia supplied." It is not stated who these were. In Acts 18 we read that Silas and Timothy came to Paul at Corinth from Macedonia, but it is uncertain whether he means them or some others. If the brethren supplied the shortfall from their own means, I do not think it can refer to Silas and Timothy. If, however, they made up Paul's deficiency not from their own resources but from the contributions of the churches, it is not unlikely that these two received gifts from the churches of Macedonia so that they might relieve his needs. In my judgment this sense is probable, given what precedes, where he says that he had plundered the other churches in order to serve the Corinthians.

units.la: Non dicit: ἀνεπληρώσαν, id est, repleuerũt, sed προσαναπληρῶσαι. Significat uero προσαναπλη-ρῶν, non simpliciter aliquid ab integro implę-re, sed id quod rei non sufficienter impletæ, adeoq; adhuc aliquid ad iustam impletionem desideranti deest, facta ad ea quæ adsunt ad-iectione aliqua supplere, sic ut nihil desit am-plius. Ergo non integram & omnimodam su-stentationem sui, sed portiunculam tantum, quæ deerat à Macedonibus accepit, reliquam uero parte operando manibus suis acquisiuit. Non quod illi plura conferre nolliet, sed quod ipse plura accipere detractaret, quàm quæ ad supplementum necessarij uictus sufficerent.
units.tr: He does not say ἀνεπληρώσαν [anepleρōsan], that is, "they filled up," but προσαναπληρῶσαι [prosanaplērōsai]. The word προσαναπληροῦν means not simply to fill something up from the beginning, but to supply, by some addition to what is already there, what has been insufficiently filled and so still lacks something for a full filling, so that nothing is lacking any more. Therefore he received from the Macedonians not the whole and complete support of himself, but only the small portion that was lacking, and by working with his own hands he got the rest. This was not because they were unwilling to contribute more, but because he himself was reluctant to accept more than what sufficed to make up the necessary provision of his livelihood.

units.la: Hac autē in re uideo in ecclesijs peccari gra uiter, primùm ab illis magistratibus, qui bona ecclesiæ non modo suę potestati subiecerunt, sed & stipędia ministris uerbi debita adeo de-curtarunt, ut illi necessitate cogente singulis prope annis eorum quæ desunt supplementũ ab ipsis precario, ac suppliciter expetere cōpel-lätur, eamq; προσαναπληρῶσιν, admodum graua tim præstant, imò nonunquá petentes uacuos à se, non sine contumelijs abijciunt. Quàm aut illi diuersimode animati sint à Macedonibus, qui non de alieno, sed de suo, non sibi, sed alijs ministranti Apostolo, ea quæ deerant suapte sponte suppleuerũt, iudicet cordati. Deinde à prælatis illis & cenonicis, qui cũ de patrimo-nijs suis abunde habeàt unde uiuere possent, non tamen contenti sunt aliquo supplemẽto, sed integra præbendarum suarum corpora, ut uocant, de bonis ecclesię exigunt, absumunt, non ut sufficientem duntaxat alimoniã, sed & opum abundantiã habeant, unde & pars ma-gna insumi in scorta, equos, mulos, canes, & reliquũ uitæ luxum, & simul in thesauros cu-mulus aliquis pecuniarum reponi possit.
units.tr: In this matter I see that the churches sin gravely. First, by those magistrates who not only have subjected the goods of the church to their own power, but have so cut down the stipends owed to ministers of the Word that the ministers, under the pressure of necessity, are almost every year compelled to beg and entreat them humbly for a supplement to what is lacking; and these magistrates grant it with great reluctance, and sometimes, when asked, they dismiss the petitioners empty-handed and with insults. How differently they have been moved than the Macedonians, who of their own accord, not from what belonged to others but from their own, supplied what was lacking to the Apostle, who was serving not himself but others, let any sensible person judge. Second, by those prelates and canons who, although they have ample means of their own on which they could live, are not content with any supplement, but demand and consume the entire bodies of their prebends, as they call them, from the goods of the church, not merely to have sufficient sustenance but an abundance of wealth, so that a large part of it can be spent on harlots, horses, mules, dogs and the rest of the luxury of life, and at the same time some heap of money can be laid up in treasuries.

units.la: ET in omnibus sic me seruabam, inquit, ne cui essem onerosus, atq; ita seruabo.) Quod di-xit, cum apud uos essem, & egerem, non fui onerosus cuiquá, id iam fusius explicat, sic ut proxime præcedentia: nam quod mihi deerat suppleuerũt fratres, qui uenerât è Macedonia, per modum parenthesis posita esse uideantur. Explicat autē huius facti sui studiũ, propositũ, propositi constantiam, specificationem & ra-tionem tionem. Studium exprimit dicens: Et in omnibus sic seruabam ἐμαυτὸν, id est, meipsum ne onerosus essem ὑμῖν, id est, uobis. Non in causa uictus tantum, inquit, sed & in reliquis omnibus, in quibus uti poteram meo iure, cohibui me, ac seruaui, uiuens parcissime, ne essem uobis oneri. In uerbo, seruandi, dicens, seruabam meipsum, studium exprimit facti sui, studium uidelicet abstinentiae, non ab illicitis tantum, sed ab ijs quoq;, quibus licite ac iure Apostolatus sui potuisset uti, ἐξουσίαν ἔχειν ὡς χρῆσθαι ἀποστόλῳ, sicut 1. Thess. 2. dicit: Virtus haec seruandi, ac cohibendi seipsum, insigne donum Dei est, ad hoc pijs datum, ut abstinentiae bono cum iusticiae ac commodati uitae suae studere, tum charitati proximorum inseruire ualeant. Iusticię, abstinendo ab illicitis: commoditati uitae, ne si affectibus suis indulgeant sibijpsis innumeras molestias ascisant: charitati fraternae, abstinendo ab omnibus, quibus fratres, uel laedi, uel grauari, uel offendi poterunt, etiam si illis iure queant uti, quo praesens Apostoli facit exemplum.
units.tr: "And in all things," he says, "I so kept myself, so that I would be burdensome to no one, and so I will keep myself." What he said, "when I was with you and was in need, I was burdensome to no one," he now explains more fully, so that the immediately preceding words, "the brethren who came from Macedonia supplied what was lacking to me," seem to be placed as a parenthesis. He explains the zeal of this action of his, the purpose, the constancy of his resolve, its specification and its reason. He expresses his zeal by saying: "And in all things I so kept ἐμαυτὸν [emauton], that is, myself, that I would not be burdensome to ὑμῖν [hymin], that is, to you." Not only in the matter of food, he says, but in all the other things in which he could have used his right, he restrained and kept himself, living most sparingly, so that he might not be a burden to you. In the word "kept," when he says "I kept myself," he expresses the zeal of his action, namely a zeal for abstinence, not only from unlawful things but also from those things which he could have used lawfully and by right of his apostleship, ἐξουσίαν ἔχειν ὡς χρῆσθαι ἀποστόλῳ [exousian echein hōs chrēsthai apostolōi], as he says in 1 Thessalonians 2. This virtue of keeping and restraining oneself is a distinguished gift of God, given to the godly for this purpose: that by the good of abstinence they may be able to attend both to justice and to the convenience of their life, and to serve the love of their neighbours. Justice, by abstaining from unlawful things; convenience of life, lest by indulging their passions they bring countless troubles upon themselves; brotherly love, by abstaining from all those things by which brethren can be hurt, burdened or offended, even if they could use them rightly. The present example of the Apostle shows this.

units.la: Ad propositum ipsius pertinet quod dicit, atq; ita seruabo. Nô erat illi satis seruasse se aliquâdiu, nè cui esset oneri, nisi id sibi in futurū quoq; faciendū censeret, ac porro facere ꝑpponeret. Nam ratio propositi talis erat, ut nô minus futurū quàm praeteritū abstinentiae huius studium requireret. Sic affecti sunt, quorū studia non sunt perfunctoria, sed ex animo ad iustum fine spectante profecta: Illis non est satis semel sese atq; iterum cohibuisse, ne quâ offensionem praebeant causae, quam agendâ suscepe-runt, sed à coepto studio nô resiliunt, donec quod agedum est perficiatur, ideoq; quod aliquandiu fecerunt, ad finem usq; facere cōtendut. Sic animatus Apost. postquâ dixit, in omnibus me sic seruabâ, ne uobis essem onerosus, adiecit de suo ꝑpposito dicēs, atq; ita seruabo.
units.tr: What he adds, "and so I will keep myself," pertains to his purpose. It was not enough for him to have kept himself for some time so as not to be a burden to anyone, unless he judged that he must do the same in the future too, and proposed to continue doing so. For the reason for his resolve was such that the zeal for this abstinence required it no less in the future than in the past. Those whose zeal is not perfunctory, but proceeds from the heart with a just end in view, are so disposed. For them it is not enough to have restrained themselves once and again, lest they give offence to the cause they have undertaken to carry out; they do not withdraw from the zeal they have begun, but strive to do to the end what must be done, and so they make every effort to continue to the finish what they have done for some time. So the Apostle, having said, "in all things I so kept myself, so as not to be burdensome to you," added on his own part his purpose, saying: "and so I will keep myself."

units.la: AD constātiam propositi huius facit, quod subiungit: Est ueritas Christi in me, quod haec gloriatio nô interrumpetur contra me.) Non simpliciter dicit: Et hoc ꝑppositū haud abijciā, sed gloriatio haec non interrūpetur cōtra me. Voce gloriationis significat, se ista dicere non exprobrandi, sed gloriādi affectu, ne grauatim hoc tulisse uideatur, quod nihil in usus suos cōferrent Corinthij. Etenim nemo sic animatus est, ut molestè ferat, id de quo gloriatur, uel ut glorietur de re aliqua, quâ grauatim ferat. Imò nô modò uoce gloriationis hoc significat, sed & per id quod dicit: non interrumpetur cōtra me, significans contra se, nô pro se fore si quid ab ipsis accipiat, & gloriationem hanc, quod gratuito praedicauerit ipsis Euangelium Christi amittat. Quod autem interpres uertit: non interrumpetur contra me: Graece est, ἐκφραγήσεται εἰς ἐμέ, quod reddi potest: nô obturabitur in me. German. interpres sic uertit: so soll mir diser ruom nit gestopfft VVerden, quasi dicat: non obturabitur gloriatio hęc in ore meo, uel non obturabitur mihi os, ne glorier gratui-
units.tr: To the constancy of this purpose belongs what he adds: "There is the truth of Christ in me, that this boasting will not be stopped against me." He does not simply say, "I will not abandon this purpose," but "this boasting will not be stopped against me." By the word "boasting" he signifies that he says these things not from a desire to reproach, but from a feeling of glorying, lest he seem to have taken it hard that the Corinthians contributed nothing to his needs. For no one who is so disposed is annoyed at what he boasts of, or boasts of something at which he is vexed. Moreover, he signifies this not only by the word "boasting," but also by what he says, "will not be stopped against me," meaning that it would be against himself and not for himself if he received anything from them, and that he would lose this boasting, that he had preached the Gospel of Christ to them freely. As for the translator's rendering, "will not be stopped against me," the Greek is ἐκφραγήσεται εἰς ἐμέ [ekphragēsetai eis eme], which can be rendered "will not be stopped up in me." The German translator renders it thus: "So soll mir diser ruom nit gestopfft werden," as if he said: this boasting shall not be stopped up in my mouth, or my mouth shall not be stopped, so that I may not boast that I preached the Gospel to you freely.

units.la: to me praedicasse nobis Euangelium. Quàm uero constanter in eo se propositó cōfirmarit, in eo exprimit quod iureiurando dicit: Est ueritas Christi in me, quod haec gloriatio nō obturabitur in me. Habet enim particula haec formā iuramēti, quasi dicat: Per ueritatem Christi quae in me est iuro, quod gloriatio haec, &c. uel: Quàm certo est in me ueritas Christi, tam certo non obturabitur gloriatio hxc in me. German. interpres reddidit ad hunc modum: So gwiß die vuarheit Christi in mir ist. Iurat ergo Apostolus p ueritate Christi, quod nolit quicquam à Corinthijs accipere, ne obturetur in ore ipsius hęc gloriatio, quod Euangelium illis gratuito praedicauerit. Sic iurando cauet, ne ob id ista scribere putetur, ut Corinthij pudefacti de conferendo aliquid cogantur, quo notam ingratitudinis à se abstergant.
units.tr: How firmly he confirmed himself in this purpose he expresses in what he says with an oath: "There is the truth of Christ in me, that this boasting will not be stopped up in me." For this particle has the form of an oath, as if he said: "By the truth of Christ which is in me I swear that this boasting," and so on; or: "As surely as the truth of Christ is in me, so surely will this boasting not be stopped up in me." The German translator rendered it in this way: "So gwiß die vuarheit Christi in mir ist" (as surely as the truth of Christ is in me). The Apostle therefore swears by the truth of Christ that he is unwilling to receive anything from the Corinthians, lest this boasting, that he preached the Gospel to them freely, be stopped up in his mouth. By swearing thus he guards against being thought to have written these things so that the Corinthians, shamed, would be compelled to contribute something, in order to wipe away from themselves the mark of ingratitude.

units.la: Vide autē quàm conuenienter formula hac iuramenti Apostolus Christi utatur dicēs: Per ueritatem Christi quae in me est. Iuramēti mispat, hoc est, ut iuremus per ea quae nobis sunt admodum in precio, hac cōditione, ut si iuremus falso, damno illorū mulctemur. Cum ergo ueritas Christi omniū esset Apostolo charissima, & maximi momēti, per eā iurauit potissimum, ut significaret tā se nolle in uanum iurare, quàm nollet ueritate Christi, quā singulari beneficio Dei acceperat, priuari. Hoc affectu conuenit omnes erga Christi ueritatem prēditos esse ministros, ut nihil in toto illi mūdo praeferat, & studio illius ab omnis generis medacijs in uniuersum abstineant. Verū quotus quisq; illorum est, qui in gratiam ueritatis Christi, quam praedicādam suscepit, in omnibus suis sermonibus à mendacio sibi caueat, illudq́ue ex animo detestetur ac fugiat?
units.tr: Notice how fittingly the Apostle of Christ uses this form of oath, saying: "By the truth of Christ which is in me." It is the custom of oaths that we swear by those things which are very precious to us, on the condition that if we swear falsely we are punished by the loss of them. Since, therefore, the truth of Christ was most dear to the Apostle and of the greatest importance, he swore chiefly by it, to signify that he was as unwilling to swear in vain as he was unwilling to be deprived of the truth of Christ, which he had received by the singular benefit of God. It is fitting that all ministers should have this disposition toward the truth of Christ, so that they prefer nothing in the whole world to it, and by zeal for it abstain entirely from every kind of lie. But how few there are of them who, for the sake of the truth of Christ which they have undertaken to preach, guard themselves in all their sermons against falsehood, and detest and flee it from the heart?

units.la: Erat autē ueritas Christi in Apostolo uarijs modis: Primò, quatenus erat in illo spiritus Christi, qui spiritus est ueritatis, & à mundo capi non potest. Deinde in scientia & intelligentia mysteriorum Christi, qua ueritas illius cognoscitur. Tertiò, in affectu cordis, quo cognitam amabat, ac plurimi faciebat. Quartò, in ore per ministerium uerbi, quod de Christo praedicabat. Tres priores modi communes sunt fidelibus omnibus, quartus ad ministerium uerbi pertinet. Quanquā nec alienus prorsus est à fidelibus, qui & ipsi ueritate Christi habent in ore; dum gratiam ac ueritatem à Christo factā laudibus extollūt ac depraedicāt.
units.tr: Christ's truth was in the Apostle in several ways. First, insofar as the Spirit of Christ, who is the Spirit of truth and cannot be received by the world, was in him. Second, in the knowledge and understanding of Christ's mysteries, by which that truth is known. Third, in the disposition of his heart, by which he loved the truth he knew and held it in highest esteem. Fourth, in his mouth, through the ministry of the Word, which he preached concerning Christ. The first three ways are common to all the faithful; the fourth belongs to the ministry of the Word. Yet it is not entirely foreign to the faithful either, who also have Christ's truth in their mouths when they extol and proclaim the grace and truth made by Christ with praises.

units.la: IN regionibus Achaiae, inquit.) Specificatio est propositi, uel, si mauis, limitatio. Non enim cōstituerat nūsquam accipere quicquam, sed à Corinthijs tantum. Ideo dicit: In regionibus Achaiae, inter quas erat & Corinthus. Alioqui acceperat à Macedonibus, & aliis quoque, ubi id citra offendiculum fieri poterat. Quare in promptu est, quod respondeatur illis, qui ex hoc Apostoli facto, generalem omnibus ministris regulam praescribere conantur, debere uidelicet eos gratuito praedicare omnibus. Apostolus hoc non fecit ubique, quanquandoquidem non dicit, quod hæc gloriatio non obturabitur in me in toto orbe, sed in regionibus Achaiæ. Et ne in illis quidem præiudicauit hoc suo facto sequuturis post ipsum episcopis ac ministris, quasi nec ipsis aliquid ab Achaicis fidelibus accipere liceat, quanto minus in cæteris. Quare adiecta hęc limitatio generalis regulæ præscriptum non admittit.
units.tr: "In the regions of Achaia," he says. This is a specification of his purpose, or, if you prefer, a limitation. For he had not resolved to receive anything anywhere except from the Corinthians. Therefore he says, "in the regions of Achaia," among which was Corinth. Otherwise he had received from the Macedonians too, and from others also, wherever this could be done without offence. Hence the answer is ready for those who try to draw from this act of the Apostle a general rule for all ministers, namely that they ought to preach freely to everyone. The Apostle did not do this everywhere, since he does not say that this boasting will not be stopped in me throughout the whole world, but in the regions of Achaia. Nor did he, even in those regions, lay down a precedent for bishops and ministers who would follow him, as if they too were not permitted to receive anything from the faithful of Achaia, much less from elsewhere. So this added limitation does not allow the general rule to be prescribed.

units.la: QVAPROPTER, inquit: An quod non diligam uos? Deus nouit. Verum quod facio, idem & faciam, ut amputem occasionem ijs qui cupiunt occasionem, ut in eo de quo gloriantur reperiantur quemadmodum & nos.) Pertinent ista ad rationem propositi huius. Hanc uero non ponit simpliciter, sed per occupationem. Videbatur enim mirum, quare ab Achaicis nihil prorsus accipere constituisset. Quare cum fore cogitaret, ut ratio huius requireretur, præoccupās ponit eā ipse ad hunc modum: Quapropter? An quod non diligam uos? &c. Non modo quæsituros eos de ratione hac, sed & alienam à uero suspicaturos cogitabat, quemadmodum fieri solet. Et talem inducit ipse, ac refellit priusquam uerum exprimat.
units.tr: "THEREFORE," he says, "is it because I do not love you? God knows. But what I do, I will also continue to do, that I may cut off the occasion from those who desire an occasion, so that in the matter they boast of they may be found just as we are." These words pertain to the reason for this purpose. But he does not state this reason plainly; he states it by anticipation. For it seemed strange why he had resolved to receive nothing at all from the Achaians. So, expecting that the reason for this would be demanded, he anticipates it and puts it himself in this form: "Therefore? Is it because I do not love you?" and so on. He foresaw that they would not only ask about this reason but would also suspect a motive foreign to the truth, as usually happens. He brings in such an objection himself and refutes it before he expresses the truth.

units.la: QVAPROPTER, inquit.) Hoc est. Quam ob causam nolo, ut hæc mihi gloriatio obturetur in regionibus Achaiæ? Quid rationis est, quod tā constanter nihil à uobis accipere constitui? An ideo hoc facio, quod nō diligā uos? Hæc erat falsa ratio, quam ob id adducit, quod timendum erat, ne illam in causa esse suspicarentur. Dices, Et quomodo uerosimile erat hoc eos suspicaturos? Etenim ut argumētum dilectionis non est in eo, si quis accipiat ab aliis pro labore suo unde uiuat, ita contemptus argumentum in eo non est, si gratuito quis laboret, nolitque pro labore suo accipere quicquam. Respondeo. Quoniam acceperat à Macedonibus, à Corinthijs uero non modo non acceperat, sed & nunquam accepturum se affirmabat, uidebatur uel non tanta apud eos dilige ntia laborasse in opere domini, ut aliquid pro labore suo accipiendum esse sibi censeret, minus uero diligenter laborasse, ob id quod eos cōtemneret, & tanto non esset amore prosequutus, quanto affectus fuerit erga MacedonES. Sic timendum erat, ne propositum hoc ipsius sinistre interpretarentur, & in argumentum contemptus sui raperent. Poterant cogitare & hoc modo,
units.tr: "THEREFORE," he says. That is: "For what cause do I not want this boasting to be stopped in the regions of Achaia? What reason is there that I have so firmly resolved to receive nothing from you? Is it because I do not love you?" This was a false reason, which he raises because it was to be feared that they would suspect it to be the cause. You may ask, "And how was it likely that they would suspect this?" Indeed, just as the sign of love does not lie in whether someone receives from others the means of living for his labour, so contempt does not lie in whether someone labours freely and does not wish to receive anything for his labour. I answer: since he had received from the Macedonians, but from the Corinthians not only had he not received, but he also declared that he would never receive, it might seem either that he had not laboured among them in the Lord's work with such diligence that he thought he ought to receive something for his labour, or that he had laboured less diligently because he despised them and did not pursue them with as much love as he had for the Macedonians. Thus there was a danger that they would misinterpret his purpose in an unfavourable sense and take it as proof of his contempt for them. They could think in this way too:

units.la: Quare accepit à Macedonibus, à nobis uero tantopere nihil accipere cōstituit? An quia illi sunt opulenti, nos uero pauperes? Sed hoc in causa esse non potest. Sunt enim pauperiores nobis, etiam ipsius testimonio. Restat igitur ideo nolle eum accipere à nobis, quod minus habeat erga nos fiducię, accepisse uero ab illis, quod magis ipsis fidat, quàm nobis, atq; ita plus eos etiam diligat, quàm nos. Quatenus igitur contemnere, ac diffidere argumentū habent cordis non diligentis, hactenus poterat cogitare. Non vult à nobis accipere, quia non diligit, sed contemn t nos, tantumq; fiducię erga nos non habet, quantū habet erga Macedones. Ne sic itaq; colligerent, occupatione cauens dicit: An quod non diligam vos? Deus nouit. Subintellige, quod diligam uos. Citat Deum teste dilectionis suę, quo suspicionem hanc, & sinistram propositi sui interpretatione reijciat. Poterat dicere nequaquam, sed diligo vos. Verùm quoniam cupiebat illis esse perlua sissimum, quod ipsos diligeret, maluit Deum, quàm seipsum citare testem.
units.tr: "Why did he receive from the Macedonians, but has so firmly resolved to receive nothing from us? Is it because they are wealthy and we poor? But this cannot be the cause, for they are poorer than we are, by his own testimony. It remains, then, that he is unwilling to receive from us because he has less trust in us, and has received from them because he trusts them more than us, and so loves them more than us." Therefore, insofar as they had grounds to think him contemptuous and distrustful, that is, of a heart that does not love, so far could they reason. He does not wish to receive from us because he does not love us, but despises us, and has no more trust in us than he has in the Macedonians. Lest they should draw this conclusion, he forestalls it and says: "Is it because I do not love you? God knows." Supply: "that I love you." He calls God as witness of his love, so that he may reject this suspicion and the unfavourable interpretation of his purpose. He could have said simply, "No, but I love you." But since he wished it to be most clearly shown to them that he loved them, he preferred to call God rather than himself as witness.

units.la: VERVM qd' facio, idé & faciá (in Græco non est idem, sed simpliciter, i. & faciā, vt subintelligendum sit, ad hoc facio) vt amputem occasionem ijs qui cupiūt occasionem.) Reiecta pseudologia, quam ex facto ipsius colligere poterant in speciem, subijcit verā rationem, propter quā nihil à Corinthijs ac reliquis Achæis accipere constituerat. Eam exprimit primùm in genere dicens: Verùm quod facio, & facturussum, ob id facio, ut amputem occasionem ijs qui cupiunt occasionem. Dictum est hoc generaliter. Specificadi verò gratia addit: ut in eo de quo gloriantur, reperiantur, quemadmodum & nos.
units.tr: "BUT what I do, I will also do" (in the Greek it is not "I will also do" but simply "and I will do," so that "to this end I do it" must be understood) "in order that I may cut off the occasion from those who desire an occasion." Having rejected the false reasoning which they could in appearance draw from his action, he adds the true reason for which he resolved to receive nothing from the Corinthians and the rest of the Achaians. He expresses it first in general terms, saying: "But what I do, and will do, I do for this reason: that I may cut off the occasion from those who desire an occasion." This is stated generally. In order to specify it, he adds: "that in the matter they boast of they may be found just as we are."

units.la: VT amputé, inquit, occasionem.) Occasionem amputare, uel præscindere, est causas & principia sequuturæ rei veluti radices excindere. Græcè est: ἵνα ἐκκόψω τὴν ἀφορμὴν. Est autè ἀφορμὴ ea causa quæ à facto, vel consilio aliquo nata occasionem gerendi, vel conandi saltem aliquid præbet, quod aliàs ne tentaretur quidem. In huiusmodi ἀφορμαῖς, tam præbendis, quàm amputandis, tanque captandis, quàm fugiendis omnino situm est multum. Multum nocuit, qui occasionem mali, præsertim incautis & imperitis obiecit. Multum ècontra profuit, qui occasione vel boni præbuit, vel mali amputauit. Magnam gerendæ rei commoditatem nactus est, qui occasionem illius uigilàter captauit. Facilè sequuturum malum vitat, qui occasionem illius præscindit. Principijs obsta inquit ille, sero medicina paratur. Dum mala per longas inualuere moras. Hac prudentia vsus Apostolus, nolebat à Corinthijs fumere stipendiū, ne quam si sumeret, pseudapostolis hoc suo facto abutendi occasionem obijceret.
units.tr: "THAT I may cut off," he says, "the occasion." To cut off or cut away an occasion is to root out, as it were, the causes and beginnings of a thing that is to follow. In Greek it is: ἵνα ἐκκόψω τὴν ἀφορμὴν [so that I may cut off the occasion]. An occasion [ἀφορμή] is that cause which arises from a deed or some plan and offers the opportunity to act, or at least to attempt something which otherwise would not even be tried. Much depends on such occasions, both on offering them and on cutting them off, on seizing them and on avoiding them altogether. One who offers an occasion of evil, especially to the incautious and inexperienced, does great harm. On the contrary, one who offers an occasion of good, or cuts off an occasion of evil, does great good. He who has seized an occasion of carrying out a matter diligently has gained a great advantage. He who cuts off an occasion avoids an evil that would easily follow. "Resist the beginnings," says the poet; "the remedy is prepared too late when the evils have grown strong through long delays." The Apostle, using this prudence, was unwilling to take a salary from the Corinthians, lest by doing so he should offer the false apostles an occasion to abuse this act of his.

units.la: Vide autem quomodo loquatur. Non dicit simpliciter, ut amputem occasionem pseudapostolis, cum tamen de illis intelligat, sicut in sequentibus mox patebit, sed, vt amputem occasionem ijs qui cupiunt occasionem. Græcè est, ἵνα ἐκκόψω τὴν ἀφορμὴν τῶν θελόντων ἀφορμὴν, i. vt amputem occasionem eorum, qui volunt occasionem. Genitiuum interpres mutauit in datiuum. Occasio, si quæratur quorum sit, est & dantium, & accipientium, & rerum unde sumitur. Græcus contextus tribuit hic occasionem captantibus. Si verò quæratur, quibus amputetur occasio, amputatur alia dantibus, alia captantibus. Cum ergo Apostolus hoc egerit, ut occasioné & captantiū & captantibus ampuamputaret, nihil est periculi utrolibet modo legamus, siue, ut amputè occasionem eorum, qui uolunt occasionem, siue, ut amputem occasionem iis qui cupiunt occasionem. Tribuit igitur Pseudapostolis hanc maliciam, imò maliciæ studium, ut non solum oblatis occasionibus abusi sint ad malū, sed & offerri sibi occasiones cupuerint. Cupere occasionem nocendi inimicorum est; studiosissime insidiantium. Illis écontra pari studio, & uigilantia omnis est amputåda occasio. Si hoc egissent episcopi, tantum occasionis non esset datum Satanæ occasionem undiq; uenanti, tam spurcis ac fœdis libidinibus, ecclesias conspurcandi, cuius futuri mali occasionem Paphnutius in concilio Niceno præscindendam esse prudentissimè quidem, uerum frustra monebat.
units.tr: But see how he speaks. He does not simply say, "that I may cut off the occasion from the false apostles," although he means them, as will soon become plain in what follows; but he says, "that I may cut off the occasion from those who desire an occasion." The Greek is ἵνα ἐκκόψω τὴν ἀφορμὴν τῶν θελόντων ἀφορμὴν [that I may cut off the occasion of those who desire an occasion]; that is, "that I may cut off the occasion of those who want an occasion." The translator changed the genitive into the dative. When one asks whose occasion it is, it belongs both to those who give it, to those who receive it, and to the things from which it is taken. The Greek text here assigns the occasion to those who seize it. If one asks from whom the occasion is cut off, it is cut off from some givers and from others seizers. Since the Apostle acted so as to cut off the occasion from both the seekers and the givers, there is no danger whichever way we read it, whether "that I may cut off the occasion of those who want an occasion," or "that I may cut off the occasion from those who desire an occasion." He therefore attributes this malice to the false apostles, or rather an eagerness for malice, so that they not only abused the occasions offered to do evil, but also wished for occasions to be offered to them. To desire an occasion of harming is the mark of enemies who lie in wait most eagerly. Against such people, the occasion must be cut off with equal eagerness and vigilance. If the bishops had done this, Satan, hunting everywhere for occasions, would not have been given so much opportunity to defile the churches with such filthy and foul lusts. Paphnutius, at the Council of Nicaea, rightly and most prudently warned that the occasion of this future evil ought to be cut off, but he warned in vain.

units.la: Dicet quisquam, Æquum ne est, ut ne occasionem inueniat qui cupit occasionem, abstineam ab eo quod in se est bonum? An quemadmodum non sunt facienda mala, ut eueniant bona, ita etiam non sunt facienda bona, ne eueniant mala? Si hoc dicimus, quod nam opus tam bonum esse, tanq; bene fieri poterit, quod mali, non ad occasionem mali abripiant, ideoque fieri à nobis nō debeat? Bonū autem esse iustum & æquum, ut minister in opere domini laboras de labore suo accipiat unde uiuat, præter ipsius Christi, & Apostoli quoq; testimonium ipsa naturalis æquitas, & communis omnium consensus comprobat. Quid igitur necesse erat Apostolo, ut tam confirmato animo nihil acciperet à Corinthijs, ne occasioné permitteret illis, qui occasionem cupiebant? Sic nascitur quæstio, an quod bonum est ac rectū, si fiat, ob id sit uitandū, ne mali ex eo sumatur occasio? Nos respōdemus, diuidendū esse inter bona necessaria, & bona licita quidem, uerum nō necessaria. Bonum necessariū est prædicare Euangelium Christi. Væ mihi, inquit, si non euangelizauero. Omittendum hoc non est, etiam si mille ex eo malorū occasiones sumantur à reprobis. Bonum licitum æquum & iustum est, prædicantem sumere uictū & amictum ab illis, quibus prædicat. Potest hoc omitti, si cessurum uidetur ad occasionem mali, propter reproborum insidias. Non peccat, qui iure suo non utitur, si usus illius causæ Christi nociturus uidetur. Imò, q Christo fideliter seruit, nūquam uolet uti iure suo, si uiderit ex eo occasionem fore reprobis, ut ueritati Dei negocium facessant. Non faciebat Apostolus malum, ut eueniret bonum, uel uitaret malum, cum stipendium debitū à Corinthijs accipere nolebat, sed omittebat bonum licitum, ne per maliciam pseudapostolorum eueniret ex eo malum.
units.tr: Someone will say: is it not fair that a man who seeks an occasion should not find one, so that I should refrain from something good in itself? Or, just as evil things should not be done so that good may come, so good things should not be done so that evil may not come? If we say this, what good thing could ever be done well, if evil men might seize on it as an occasion for evil, and therefore it ought not to be done by us? That it is good and just that a minister in the Lord's work should receive from his labour the means to live, the natural justice itself and the common consent of all confirm, besides the testimony of Christ himself and of the Apostle too. Why, then, was it necessary for the Apostle, with his mind so firmly set, to take nothing from the Corinthians, lest he give an occasion to those who were seeking one? So the question arises: if a thing is good and right, should it be avoided, when done, for the sake of not giving the wicked an occasion from it? We answer that a distinction must be made between goods that are necessary and goods that are lawful but not necessary. It is a necessary good to preach the Gospel of Christ: "Woe is me," he says, "if I do not preach the Gospel." This must not be omitted, even if a thousand occasions of evil are taken from it by the reprobate. It is a lawful good, just and fair, for the preacher to receive food and clothing from those to whom he preaches. This may be omitted if it seems likely to become an occasion of evil, because of the snares of the reprobate. He does not sin who does not use his own right, if its use seems likely to harm the cause of Christ. Indeed, one who serves Christ faithfully will never wish to use his right if he sees that it will give the reprobate an occasion to hinder the work of God's truth. The Apostle was not doing evil that good might come, or to avert evil, when he refused to receive the wages due to him from the Corinthians; rather he was omitting a lawful good, lest through the malice of the false apostles evil should come of it.

units.la: VT in eo, inquit, de quo gloriātur, reperiātur quemadmodum & nos.) Supra particulam hāc specificationem habere diximus, cuius uidelicet rei occasionem pseudapostolis permittere noluerit. Vt reperiantur, inquit, quemadmodum & nos. In quo? In eo, inquit,
units.tr: "That in the thing about which they boast they may be found even as we are." I have said above that this clause is a specification of what he was unwilling to allow the false apostles an occasion for. "That they may be found," he says, "even as we are." In what? "In that," he says,

units.la: de quo gloriātur. Quod nam erat illud? Appàret illos nó accepisse stipendium, quo Corinthios sibi deuinctiores redderent, eaque in re præstantiores Paulo inuenirētur, si stipēdium ille pro labore suo sumeret, & hāc illis gloriationem noluisse permittete Paulum, ideoque nec ipsum stipēdium accipere uoluisse, quo in hac causa non excellerent, sed tales inueniren tur, qualis erat & ipse. Sic pleriq; tam ueteres quàm recentiores exponunt.
units.tr: "about which they boast." What was that? It appears that they had not received wages, by which they would have bound the Corinthians more closely to themselves and would have been found superior to Paul in this respect, if he had taken payment for his labour; and that Paul did not want to allow them this boasting, and therefore did not wish to receive the wages himself, lest in this matter they should excel, but should be found such as he himself was. Thus most writers, both ancient and recent, explain it.

units.la: Sunt tamen hæc uerba sic posita, ut bifariam exponi queant. Primò, quemadmodum iam exposuimus, ut amputem, inquit, occasionem ijs, qui cupiunt occasionem: amputem autem ob id, ut in quo gloriantur, nó excellentiores, sed quales & nos sumus, inueniantur. Inuenirentur autem excellentiores nobis, si nos sumptuosum redderemus Euangelium, accipiendo stipendium à uobis, illi uero gratuitum, nō accipiendo à uobis quicquam. Hanc illis occasionem nunquam permittemus, ideoq; nihil à uobis unquam accipere costituimus. Côstaret hæc expositio, si côstaret pseudapostolos gratuito prædicasse Corinthijs. Deinde exponi possunt hoc pacto: ut amputem occasione ijs qui cupiūt occasionem. Quam occasione cupiūt? Per quam uidelicet in eo de quo gloriātur reperiātur quemadmodum & nos, ne minores nobis, ac minus grati propterea inueniantur, quod stipendium accipiunt à uobis, sed pares, si & ipsi stipendium acciperemus. Quare nolo à uobis accipere quicquā, ne pares nobis inueniantur. In priore expositione uerba hæc, ut in eo de quo gloriantur, reperiātur quemadmodum & nos, ratione habent, quare Apostolus occasionem pseudapostolis amputare uoluerit. In posteriore uero, exponunt quā occasione pseudapostoli dari sibi cupierint. Et hāc sequuntur est Ambrosius. Sic enim ille exponit: Gloria pseudapostolorum in pecunijs erat ac cupiēdis. Ideo Apostolus hoc refutauit, ne illis similis uideretur, qa nisi hoc ab Apostolo fuisset uitatū, maior illis occasio data fuisset accipiendi, aut magis extorquendi, quando in hac re formam ab Apostolo data, ostenderet. Hæc ille. Ergo quod in textu est: in eo de quo gloriātur, intelligit de stipēdio apostolico quo de gloriati sint pseudapostoli, quasi in illo uerorū sit Apostolorum argumentum. Sanè accepisse eos à Corinthijs, infrà in hoc ipso capite patebit. Quare uerosimile non est, fuisse eos de gratuita Euangelij prædicatione gloriatos, ut quod dicit, ut in eo de quo gloriantur, reperiantur quemadmodum & nos, de illa posset intelligi, quamuis & Chrisostomus de ea exponat, non diligens alioqui in exponendis Apostoli sensibus. Annotat ille quàm non sit otiosum quod non dicit: ut in eo quod faciunt, sed, ut in eo de quo gloriantur. Neq; enim simpliciter illi uel accipiebant, uel gratuito prædicabant, sed ad ostētationem sese comparabant, cuius uanitatem in uerbo gloriandi perstringit. Quorsum gloriarentur in eo quod simulabant, bant, abundè intelligebat, ideoq; & occasione quam quaerebant diligenter illis amputabat.
units.tr: Yet these words are so phrased that they can be explained in two ways. First, as we have already set out: that I may cut off, he says, the occasion from those who seek an occasion; and I cut it off so that in the thing about which they boast they may be found not superior, but such as we are. They would be found superior to us if we made the Gospel costly by receiving wages from you, while they made it free by receiving nothing from you. We will never allow them this occasion, and therefore we have resolved to receive nothing from you ever. This explanation would stand if it were certain that the false apostles preached to the Corinthians for nothing. Second, the words can be explained thus: that I may cut off the occasion from those who seek an occasion. What occasion do they seek? Namely, that by it they may be found, in that about which they boast, even as we are: lest they be found inferior to us, and less esteemed, because they take wages from you, but equal to us if they too took wages. Therefore I am unwilling to receive anything from you, lest they be found equal to us. In the first explanation the words "that in that about which they boast they may be found even as we are" give the reason why the Apostle wanted to cut off the occasion from the false apostles. In the second, they explain what occasion the false apostles had desired to be given them. Ambrose follows this second explanation. For he explains it thus: "The boast of the false apostles lay in money and in the desire for it. Therefore the Apostle refuted this, lest he should seem similar to them; for unless this had been avoided by the Apostle, a greater occasion would have been given them of receiving, or of extorting more, since the Apostle, in this matter, showed the pattern he had given." So he. Therefore, by what is in the text, "in that about which they boast," he understands the apostolic wages, about which the false apostles boasted, as if in that lay the proof of true apostles. That they did in fact receive wages from the Corinthians will become clear later in this same chapter. So it is not likely that they boasted about preaching the Gospel without payment, so that what he says, "that in that about which they boast they may be found even as we are," could be understood of that. Although Chrysostom explains it of this, he is otherwise not careful in expounding the Apostle's meaning. He observes how far from idle it is that he does not say "in that which they do," but "in that about which they boast." For they did not simply either take wages or preach for nothing, but they presented themselves for display, and he touches on their vanity in the word "boast." He understood well enough what they would boast of in what they pretended, and therefore he diligently cut off from them the occasion they sought.

units.la: Siquidè istiusmodi pseudapostoli operarij dolosi sunt sumpta persona apostolorum Christi: atq; haud mirum, quando quidè ipse Satanas transfiguratur in angelum lucis. Nō magnū est igitur, si & ministri illius persona in se transferunt, quasi sint ministri iusticiæ, quorum finis erit iuxta opera ipsorum.
units.tr: For such false apostles are deceitful workers, who have assumed the character of the apostles of Christ; and no wonder, since Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light. It is no great thing, then, if his ministers also transform themselves, as though they were ministers of righteousness, whose end will be according to their works.

units.la: 1 Primò exprimit qui nā sint illi qui occasionē cupiāt. Pseudapostoli videlicet: Siquidē istiusmodi pseudapostoli, inquit.
units.tr: 1. First he sets out who those are who seek an occasion: the false apostles, namely. "For such false apostles," he says.

units.la: 2 Deinde ratione reddit, quare occasionem quam cupiūt amputare illis studeat. Quia dolosi sunt operarij, inquit.
units.tr: 2. Then he gives the reason why he takes care to cut off the occasion they seek: "Because they are deceitful workers," he says.

units.la: 3 Tertiò, dolū illorū exponit dicens: transfiguratēs se in apostolos Christi, & in ministros iusticiæ.
units.tr: 3. Thirdly, he explains their deceit, saying: transforming themselves into apostles of Christ, and into ministers of righteousness.

units.la: 4 Quartò, dicit eos imitari ingenium Satanæ, tanquam illius ministros.
units.tr: 4. Fourthly, he says that they imitate the nature of Satan, as his ministers.

units.la: 5 Quintò, minatur illis meritū exitiū. Sed vi deamus singula.
units.tr: 5. Fifthly, he threatens them with a fitting destruction. But let us look at each point.

units.la: SIQVIDEM istiusmodi pseudapostoli, inquit.) Quoniam obscurū adhuc erat, quos nā intelligeret dicēs, vt amputē occasionem illis, qui cupiunt occasionē, non simpliciter dicit: Nam sunt illi operarij dolosi, sed: Nā istiusmodi pseudapostoli operarij dolosi sunt. Hac nota non solum qui sint aperit, sed & fugiendos eos esse monet. Véditabant se pro apostolis Christi, verùm non erant ἀληθαπόστολοι, sed ψευδαπόστολοι. Est aut pseudapostolus falsus legatus qui credentes sibi seducit, & si id in causa salutis fiat, prorsus perdit. Notæ huius sunt istæ. Primò, non est ritè missus, sed suapte spōte currit. Deinde, vel prorsus falsa nūciat, vel veris falsa immiscet, quo sub specie veritatis seducat. Tertiò, seipsum quærit in omnib. vt nō modò falsus, sed & suijpsius rectè vocari possit Apost. Quartò, iactabundus est & gloriosul, seipse magnificans, & veros apostolos contēptos reddere satagēs. Planè tales erat, quos hic perstringit Apost. Contrà, verus Apostolus est, qui nō à seipso currit, sed missus est à dño, non alia nūciat, quàm quæ in mandatis accepit, non seipsum quærēs, sed dñm cuius est Apostolus, nec iactabundus de suo, sed gloriāns in dño, nec veros alios apostolos contēnens, sed magnificāns & extollens.
units.tr: "For such false apostles," he says. Since it was still unclear whom he meant, in saying that he cuts off the occasion from those who seek an occasion, he does not simply say, "For they are deceitful workers," but: "For such false apostles are deceitful workers." By this mark he not only reveals who they are, but also warns that they are to be shunned. They put on the appearance of apostles of Christ, but they were not true apostles [ἀληθαπόστολοι] but false apostles [ψευδαπόστολοι]. A false apostle is a false envoy, who seduces believers, and if this is done in a matter of salvation, he utterly destroys them. The marks of such a person are these. First, he has not been rightly sent, but runs of his own accord. Second, he either announces utterly false things, or mixes false things with true, so as to seduce under the appearance of truth. Third, he seeks himself in everything, so that he may be rightly called not only false but also an apostle of himself. Fourth, he is boastful and vainglorious, magnifying himself and striving to make the true apostles despised. Clearly these were the sort the Apostle is here rebuking. On the contrary, a true apostle is one who does not run of his own accord, but is sent by the Lord; who announces nothing other than what he has received in his commission; who seeks not himself but the Lord whose apostle he is; who is not boastful about his own things, but glories in the Lord; and who does not despise the other true apostles, but magnifies and exalts them.

units.la: OPERARII dolosi sunt, inquit.) Hinc erat Apostolo cautio ac solicitudo amputandi illis occasionē, quā quærebant. Sciebat eos omnia agere ac moliri dolo improbo. Ea res reddebat ipsum cautum, ac vigilantem. Nō dicit simpliciter, dolosi sunt, sed operarij dolosi sunt. Operabātur & ipsi, sed animo doloso, nō syncero. Videm hic referre plurimū, quo animo quis operetur in ecclesia dñi. Operari palā mala & noxia, minū habet periculi. Ociari quoq; itidē minus est periculosum. Verū operari cū dolo & in speciem, ea quæ videntur esse bona, reipsa uero animo seducendi, admodū est periculosum. Tales vocātur in scripturis ..., operarij iniq., quos & Christus ipse notat, Mat. 7. dicens: Multi dicet mihi in illo die: Dñe, dñe nonne per nomē tuū prophetauimus? & p nomen tuū dæmonia eiecimus? & per nomen tuū multas virtutes præstitimus? Ac tum confitebor illis, nunquā noui vos: Discedite à me, q operamini iniquitatem.
units.tr: "The workers are deceitful," he says. From this the Apostle had reason to be cautious and watchful, so as to cut off the occasion they were seeking. He knew they did everything and schemed with wicked deceit, and this made him careful and alert. He does not say simply that they are deceitful, but that they are deceitful workers. They did work, but with a deceitful heart, not a sincere one. Here we see how much it matters with what intention a person works in the Church of the Lord. To work openly at evil and harm carries less danger, and idleness is likewise less dangerous. But to work with deceit and under a show of what seems good, while really intending to mislead, is very dangerous. Scripture calls such people "workers of iniquity," and Christ himself marks them in Matthew 7, saying: "Many will say to me on that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in your name, cast out demons in your name, and done many mighty works in your name? And then I will profess to them, I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity."

units.la: SVMPTA, inquit, psona apostolorū Christi.) Græcè est μεταςχηματιζόμενοι εἰς ἀποστόλους χριστοῦ. i. transfigurati in apostolos Christi. Vulgata habet transfigurātes se in apostolos Christi. Verbum μεταςχηματίζεσθαι, tertio habetur in hoc contextu. Erasm. reddidit, iā sumpta persona, iā transfiguratur, & tertio, persona in se transferunt. Vulgatus interpres abfq; ostentatione copiæ constanter reddidit per verbū transfigurandi, non magis culpabilis in vnius Latini, q Apostolus in vnius Græci verbi repetitione. Si verbū transfigurādi semel vsurpatū satisfacit Græco verbo μεταςχηματίζεσθαι, poterat & secundo & tertio satisfacere.
units.tr: "Taking on the persona of the apostles of Christ," he says. The Greek is μετασχηματιζόμενοι εἰς ἀποστόλους Χριστοῦ [metaschēmatizomenoi eis apostolous Christou], that is, "transfigured into the apostles of Christ." The Vulgate has "transfiguring themselves into the apostles of Christ." The verb μετασχηματίζεσθαι occurs three times in this context. Erasmus rendered it at one time "taking on a persona," at another "is transfigured," and a third time "transfer the persona to themselves." The Vulgate translator, without any show of variety, consistently rendered it by the one word "transfiguring." It is no more open to blame in a Latin translator to repeat one word than it is in the Apostle to repeat one Greek word. If the word "transfiguring," used once, suffices for the Greek μετασχηματίζεσθαι, it could have sufficed also the second and third time.

units.la: Quoniā vocavit pseudapostolos operarios dolosos, exponit illorū dolū dicēs, transfiguratēs se in apostolos Christi. Ttransfigurare se, eit natiuę ac verę formę, falsam ac fictā superinducere, illamq; fallēdi gratia oftētare. Erant pseudapostoli reipsa, quos hic perstringit. Hęc erat vera illorū figura, ac proprius color. Cū ergo dolosi essent, verę figurę superinducebāt falsā, fingentes se apostolos esse Christi. Hæc transfiguratio veram illorum figuram abscondebat quidem, verū non auferebat, & figurā apostolorum Christi præferebat quidē, at veros ex illis Christi apostolos non reddebat. Quare pertinenter admodum vsus est verbo, transfigurādi, quod sic differt ... quod hæ voces essentiæ ac substantiæ mutationem, illud verò figuræ alienæ assumptionem, vel fictione significat, quo sensu positum est hoc loco. Neq; enim veram Apostolorum Christi figuram veraciter assumebāt, sed falso simulabant ac fingebāt, quemadmodum neq; pseudoprophetę, de quib. Christus Mat. 7. prę monuit, vestimenta ouium, cum sint lupi rapaces, veraciter assumunt, sed fingunt ac simulāt. Et hoc genus falsorum apostolorum in apostolos Christi transfiguratorum Romam post Paulum venisse, eamque ecclesiam viciasse in viciata & corrupta, sub prætextu nominis Petri Apostolicam sedem falsò nominatā miris artibus fundasse, ac mysterium iniquitatis in illa cooperante Satana, cuius erant mini stri, efficaci successu operari cœpisse, prorsus nihil addubito. Quod Romæ apostolum Petrū iactarūt, illiusq; autoritatem prætexuerūt, vt Pauli existimationem supprimeret, improbissimo studio & antea in alijs quoq; ecclesijs fecerant, sicut in epistolis Pauli patet. Et hanc subdolam & noxiam transfigurationem ad successores suos tam efficaciter transmiserunt, vt cordacordatus quisq; si consideret illam intentius, ipsissimam Satanæ operationé agnoscere cogatur. Sub hoc Sole nanq; nihil uisum est unquam magis hypocriticū ac dolosum, magisq; ad fallendum, & ad inuadendum omnium ecclesiarum magisterium instructum.
units.tr: Since he has called the false apostles deceitful workers, he explains their deceit by saying, "transfiguring themselves into the apostles of Christ." To transfigure oneself is to lay a false and feigned form over one's true and natural form, and to show it for the sake of deceiving. The false apostles, whom he here censures, were in truth what they were, and this was their real figure and proper colour. Since they were deceitful, they laid a false figure over their true one, pretending to be apostles of Christ. This transfiguration did indeed hide their true figure, but did not remove it; it presented the figure of the apostles of Christ, yet did not make them true apostles of Christ. So the Apostle used the word "transfiguring" very aptly. Words of this kind differ: the one signifies a change of essence and substance, while the other signifies the assumption, or pretence, of a foreign figure, which is the sense intended here. For they did not truly assume the true figure of the apostles of Christ, but falsely simulated and feigned it, just as the false prophets, of whom Christ warned beforehand in Matthew 7, do not truly assume the sheep's clothing, though they are ravening wolves, but feign and counterfeit it. And I have no doubt at all that this kind of false apostle, transfigured into the apostles of Christ, came to Rome after Paul, and that it corrupted the Church in that corrupted state; under the pretext of Peter's name it founded, by wonderful arts, the falsely named Apostolic See, and began to work with effective success the mystery of iniquity, with Satan cooperating in it, whose ministers they were. They boasted that the apostle Peter was at Rome and pretended his authority, so that Paul's reputation might be suppressed, and with the most wicked zeal they had done the same before in other churches as well, as is clear from Paul's epistles. And they handed down this crafty and harmful transfiguration to their successors so effectively that anyone who considers it more attentively is compelled to recognise the very working of Satan. For under this sun nothing has ever been seen more hypocritical and deceitful, or better equipped to mislead and to seize the teaching office of all the churches.

units.la: ATQVE haud mirū, inqt, quādoquidē ipsē Satanas transfiguratur in angelū lucis.) Quoniā imperitiorib. res admodū miranda, & incredibilis uidetur, fieri posse, ut pseudapostolus transfiguretur in apostolū Christi, ut admoneat nō debere hoc uideri mirū, ipsius Satanę exemplū inducit, quod & cognitu necessariū est fidelibus omnibus, & tale, de quo dubitari nō potest: & tamen si cōsideretur multo est mirabilius. Tantū enim discrepātiæ inter pseudapostolum, & uerum Christi apostolū non est, quantum est inter Satanam extremæ maliciæ spiritū & angelum lucis, & tamen in hunc ille pessimus impostor transfiguratur. Quare mirum non est, inquit, si pseudapostoli transfigurantur in apostolos Christi. Hoc dicens, significat eos imitari ingenium Satanæ.
units.tr: "And no wonder," he says, "since Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light." Because it seems a very wonderful and incredible thing to the unskilled that a false apostle should be transfigured into an apostle of Christ, he advises that this should not be regarded as a marvel, and brings forward the example of Satan himself. This example is necessary for all the faithful to know, and it is of such a kind that it cannot be doubted; yet if it is considered, it is far more marvellous. For there is not so great a difference between a false apostle and a true apostle of Christ as there is between Satan, the spirit of extreme malice, and an angel of light; and yet that most wicked impostor is transfigured into this. Therefore, he says, it is no wonder if false apostles are transfigured into apostles of Christ. In saying this, he signifies that they imitate the cunning of Satan.

units.la: Non dicit autē simpliciter, transfiguratur in angelū, sed, in angelū lucis. Natura ipsus est Satā, quēadmodū & angeli lucis. Angelus nō est, nisi quando mittitur à Deo ad operis alicuius exequutionē: sonat enim angelus nunciū. Angelus erat spiritus ille malus, q mittebatur ad seducēdū impiū regē Achab, ut esset spūs mendax in ore omniū, quos habebat prophetarū. Missio hęc reddebat eū angelū, uerū nō angelū lucis, sed tenebrarū & errorū. Angelus lucis, minister est ueritatis, & gratiæ Dei nūcius. Talis erat Gabriel, ad beatā uirginē missus, tales erāt angeli, quos pastoribus euangelizasse legimus: tales erant, qui mulieribus resurrectione Christi nunciabāt, nec alij erāt, qui patriarchis, prophetis, Christo & apostolis apparuerūt. In eiusmo di angelum mutari non potest Satan, transfigurari potest. Sic spiritus ille seductionis, ut falleret Achab, quem punire uolebat Deus, transfigurabat se in angelū lucis, quasi esset spiritus ueritatis. Hæc transfiguratio Satanæ inuexit in ecclesias omnis generis errores, impietatē, superstitiones, falsos cultus, & eidolomaniā, pro pterea qđ neglectis sanctis scripturis episcopi, Satanā nisi nigrū & manifestū cognoscere noluerūt: transfiguratum uero, ac dealbatum in speciem, pro angelo lucis sunt amplexi.
units.tr: He does not, however, say simply "transfigured into an angel," but "into an angel of light." Satan's nature is that of an angel of light, as is also the case with angels of light. A being is an angel only when he is sent by God to carry out some task, for "angel" means messenger.
