units.tr: "Three times I suffered shipwreck," he says. We read that he suffered shipwreck once, in Acts 27, which the reader may consult in its place. Where else he suffered shipwreck we do not read.

units.la: NOCTEM ac diē in profundo egi,inquit.) Ambrosius sic exponit:Hoc factum est quan-do missus est Romam,cum appellasset Casa-rem,tunc desperatione vitæ in alto,hoc est, in profundo maris fuit,mortem ante oculos ha-bens.
units.tr: "A night and a day I have spent in the deep," he says. Ambrose explains it thus: this happened when he was sent to Rome, after appealing to Caesar. Then, in despair of life, he was on the deep sea, that is, in the depths of the sea, with death before his eyes.

units.la: Qq bens. Sic enim scriptum est in ipso loco: ita ut de A sperarem9 nos etiá viuere. Lyran9 illud, noc̈te ac die, idé esse iudicat, qd̃ p magnū tēp9, quasi dicat se Paulus crebrò hinc inde per mare naui-gasse. Citat præterea aliorū sententiā, qui putant Paulum sub aquis in ipso fundo maris no stem ac diem stetisse, diuinaq́ue fuisse virtute feruatū ac restitutum. Chrysostom9 sic sentit, [Greek] . Putat ergo Paulum no stem ac diem natasse in mari. Erasmus, quoniam in Græco non est, in profundo maris, sed simpliciter [Greek] , i.e. in profundo, putat ęquè de carceris atq; maris posse profundo exponi. In re quę aliis atq; aliis modis fieri potuit, non inuenio quid certò affirmari possit, nec libet affirmare ubi cóiecturis tantum relictus est locus. Sequatur lector quod vero putauerit esse propius.
units.tr: ...for so it is written in the very passage: "so that we despaired even of life." Lyra judges that "a night and a day" is the same as "for a long time," as if to say that Paul had often sailed hither and thither across the sea. He also cites the opinion of others, who think that Paul stood a night and a day under the water, at the very bottom of the sea, and was preserved and restored by divine power. Chrysostom takes it that Paul swam a night and a day in the sea. Erasmus, since the Greek does not say "in the depth of the sea" but simply "in the depth," thinks it may equally be explained of the depth of a prison as of the sea. In a matter that could have happened in various ways, I do not find anything that can be affirmed for certain, nor do I wish to affirm where only conjecture leaves room. Let the reader follow whatever he judges nearer the truth.

units.la: IN itineribus sæpe, inquit.) Positū est hoc absolutè pro crebris profectionib. quib. in oēs regiones inde à Hierusalē ad Illyricū vsq; excurrerat. Quantæ autem sit molestiæ vt pericula taceā, per alienas prouincias & regiones peregrinum hominem crebrò proficisci, norūt qui vel modicè sunt experti, præsertim si id fiat in causa odiosa, qualis est in hoc sæculo causa Euangelij Christi.
units.tr: "In journeys often," he says. This is said absolutely of frequent journeys, by which he ranged through all regions from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum. How great a trouble it is, to say nothing of the dangers, for a foreign man to travel often through foreign provinces and regions, those know who have had even a little experience, especially if this is done in a hateful cause, such as in this age is the cause of the Gospel of Christ.

units.la: IN periculis fluminum, inquit.) De periculis in mari mentionem feorsim faciet. Recitat B pericula quæ non modica sed multa crebrò itineranti euenerunt. Exundantia flumina vix sine discrimine traijciuntur. In eiusmodi pericula sæpe incidit.
units.tr: "In perils of rivers," he says. He will mention the dangers at sea separately. He recounts the dangers which befell him, not few but many, as he often travelled. Flooded rivers can scarcely be crossed without peril. He often fell into such dangers.

units.la: PERICVLIS latronum.) Latrocinia exercentur potißimum in peregrinos & inermes. Quare probabile est Paulum quoq; nó semel in illa incidisse.
units.tr: "In perils of robbers." Robberies are committed chiefly against foreigners and the unarmed. Therefore it is probable that Paul too fell into them more than once.

units.la: PERICVLIS ex genere, inquit.) Id est, ex Iudeis, ex quorū gente erat natus. De illorū insidijs & infestationib. quib9 vbiq; Paulū opprimere moliebantur in Actis legitur.
units.tr: "In perils from my own kind," he says, that is, from the Jews, from whose nation he was born. Their plots and harassments, by which they everywhere tried to overwhelm Paul, are read of in Acts.

units.la: PERICVLIS ex Gentib.) Quib9 videlicet prædicabat, & quorū falsos cultus reprobabat. Et de illis in Actis. Iudei illū persequebantur, velut apostatā à lege ac populo Dei. Gētes vero tanquā deorū aduersariū & hostem. Sic omnium vbiq; tā Iudæorū quā Gentiū erat odijs & insidijs expositus.
units.tr: "In perils from the Gentiles." Namely, those to whom he preached, and whose false worship he rejected. And of them Acts says: the Jews persecuted him as an apostate from the law and people of God, the Gentiles as an adversary and enemy of their gods. Thus he was everywhere exposed to the hatred and plots of both Jews and Gentiles.

units.la: PERICVLIS in ciuitate, inquit.) Ambrof. de ciuitate Damascenorū exponit, cuius infrà mentionē faciet. Chrysost. rectius [Greek] , inquit. Neq; enim Damasci tantū, sed & in multis alijs ciuitatib. periclitatus fuit. Intelligit autē opinor, precipuè de seditionib. quas per ciuitates impij tam ex Iudæis quàm ex Gentibus aduersus ipsum excitarunt.
units.tr: "In perils in the city," he says. Ambrose refers this to the city of the Damascenes, which he will mention below. Chrysostom says this more correctly, for he was in danger not only at Damascus but in many other cities. I think he means chiefly the seditions which the impious, both Jews and Gentiles, stirred up against him in the cities.

units.la: PERICVLIS in deserto, inquit.) Deserti pericula sunt post latrocinia, errores fames, sitis, arenæ exagitatio quæ fit in tempestatibus, qua sæpenumero viatores magnis arenæ cumulis adobruntur & obteguntur, & bestiaerum incursus, quibus solitudines sunt refertæ.
units.tr: "In perils in the desert." The dangers of the desert are, after robbers, wandering, hunger, thirst, the buffeting of sand which happens in storms, by which travellers are often overwhelmed and buried under great heaps of sand, and the attacks of wild beasts, with which the wastelands are full.

units.la: PERICVLIS in mari, inquit.) Præter naufragia & tempestatum violentiam, qua naues in loca remota plerumq; abijciuntur multum periculi nauigantib. in mari à piratis est, & picib. quoq; marinis, & Charybdi, & Scylla, & Syrti, & scopulis.
units.tr: "In perils at sea." Besides shipwrecks and the violence of storms, by which ships are often cast onto remote shores, sailors at sea are in great danger from pirates, from sea monsters too, and from Charybdis, Scylla, the Syrtes and the rocks.

units.la: PERICVLIS inter falsos fratres, inquit.) Hæc tanto sunt periculosiora, quanto minus propter familiaritatem fraterna caueri possunt. Loquitur aut de illis potißimū, qui ex circumcisione erant, & propter Mosaicæ legis æmulationem odio ipsum prosequebantur, quamuis & ipsi pro Christianis haberi vellet. Quid hodie pijs hominibus à falsis fratribus accidat plus nimio manifestum esse videmus. De falsis fratribus uide Gal. 2.
units.tr: "In perils among false brothers." These are all the more dangerous, the less they can be guarded against because of the familiarity of brothers. He speaks chiefly of those who were of the circumcision and who, out of zeal for the Mosaic law, pursued him with hatred, although they wished themselves to be regarded as Christians. How much more than enough what happens today to godly men from false brothers we see clearly. On the false brethren see Gal. 2.

units.la: IN labore, inquit, & molestia, in vigilijs sæpe in fame & siti, in ieiunijs sæpe, in frigore & nuditate.) De laboribus dictum est supra. Labores illos irremissos quos propter Euangelium obibat, comitabantur in sæculo hoc ingrato & impio, molestiæ vigiliarum, famis, sitis, ieiuniorum, frigoris ac nuditatis, quarum singulæ sufficiunt ad molestandum hominem quantùis laborum patientem. De vigilijs & ieiunijs supra quoque mentionem fecit cap. 6. De fame, siti ac nuditate, cui coniunctum est frigus, vide 1 Cor. 4.
units.tr: "In labour and toil, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness." Of labours it was said above. The unceasing labours he undertook for the Gospel were accompanied, in this ungrateful and impious age, by the troubles of watchings, hunger, thirst, fastings, cold and nakedness, each of which is enough to trouble a man, however much he may be able to endure labours. He also mentioned watchings and fastings above, in chapter 6. On hunger, thirst and nakedness, to which cold is joined, see 1 Cor. 4.

units.la: PRÆTER ea quæ extrinsecus accidunt, inquit.) Græcè est, [Greek] . Quoniam [Greek] aliquando extra, aliquando præter significat, fit vt particula hæc aliter atq; aliter accipiatur. Alij nanq; legunt, præter ea quæ extrinsecus accidunt, sicuti vertit Erasmus, alij præter ea quæ prætereo, quemadmodū exponit Chrysostomus, dicens, [Greek] . Vulgatus interpres tertiam lectionem posuit. Vertit enim præter illa quæ intrinsecus sunt. Si legas, præter ea quæ extrinsecus accidunt, quærendum uidetur, an non pleraq; quæ hactenus recensuit extrinsecus ipsi acciderint? Item quomodo cura & solicitudo ecclesiarum extrinsecus illi acciderit. Ad vitandam hanc quæstionem, existimo legendum esse in Græco, [Greek] , id est, præter ea quæ sunt extra ista. Nisi dicturi sumus quæ sequuntur non pertinuisse ad munus Apostoli, vt extrinsecus dictum sit respectu eorum quæ ad curam ipsius pertinebant. Vulgatus interpres respexit ad naturam curarum, quæ vt externæ molestiæ corpus, ita ipsę cor affligunt: atque ita quę hactenus recensuit pro externis quæ vero subijcit pro internis reputauit. Hoc sensu illud [Greek] ad præcedentia referendum esset. Quasi dicat, Præter dicta iā exterioră, sunt & interiora quæ me affligunt, vtpote incumbens mihi quotidiana cura omnium ecclesiarum, &c.
units.tr: "Besides those things that come from outside," he says. The Greek preposition sometimes means "outside" and sometimes "besides," so the particle is taken in different ways. Some read "besides those things that happen from without," as Erasmus translates; others read "besides those things that I pass over," as Chrysostom explains. The Vulgate translator adopted a third reading, rendering "besides those things that are within." If you read "besides those things that happen from without," it seems to be asked whether most of what he has so far listed did not also happen to him from without, and likewise how the care and anxiety of the churches came to him from without. To avoid this question, I think the Greek should be read as "besides those things which are outside these," that is, besides those things that lie beyond these, unless we are going to say that what follows did not belong to the apostle's office, so that it is called external with respect to the things that pertained to his care. The Vulgate translator looked to the nature of the cares, which, as external troubles afflict the body, so they afflict the heart itself; and so he reckoned what he had listed so far as external, and what he adds next as internal. In this sense the phrase would refer to what precedes, as if he said: besides the external things already mentioned, there are also internal things which afflict me, namely the daily care of all the churches, and so on.

units.la: INCVMBENS, inquit, mihi quotidiana cura omnium ecclesiarum.) Græcè sic legitur, [Greek] , incursum, instatia & conspiratio nem tionem significat. Vulgata lectio habet, instantia mea. Erasmus vertit, incumbens mihi. Et vtriq; interpretes illud, καθ' ἡμέραν, id est, quotidiana, coniunxerunt cum sequenti particula, cura omnium ecclesiarum, cum tamen illa distinctè sit à praecedenti posita. Malim ego sic legere: Incursus meus qui quotidianus est, cura illa omnium ecclesiarum. Germanicus interpres melius reddidit ad hunc modum. On was sich sonst zutregt (sic vertit illud χωρὶς τῶν παρεκτὸς) Das ich teglich wyrdt angelauffen, vnd trag sorg fur alle gmeine. Sic pulchrè illud ἡ ἐπισύστασις μου, i. incursus ille meus, ne actiuè sed passiuè accipiatur, verbaliter trauftulit. Das ich teglich wyrdt angelauffen. Loquitur aut non de hostili, sed de negociorum incursu ac multitudine, quib. singulis diebus vel aduentu fratrum, vel salutationi bus aut consultationib. praesentium fidelium, vel literis absentium molestabatur, quorum in definens multitudo & cumulus vrgens recte ἐπισύστασις vocatur. Quis autem adeo stupidus est, ut non intelligat, quàm magna quamq; mo leftam fuisse necesse sit negociorū multitudinem, quorum illi moles quotidie incubebat.
units.tr: "Pressing upon me," he says, "every day, the care of all the churches." The Greek word signifies an onset, insistence or crowding in. The Vulgate reading has "my instance." Erasmus renders it "pressing upon me." Both translators joined the word for "daily" with the following phrase, "care of all the churches," though it is set apart from what precedes. I would prefer to read: "my onset, which is daily, that care of all the churches." The German translator rendered it better: "What else befalls me, that I am daily assailed, and bear care for all the congregations." He thus expressed neatly that "my onset" should be taken not actively but passively: "that I am daily assailed." He speaks not of hostile attack but of the onslaught and multitude of business, by which he was troubled every day, either by the arrival of brothers, or by the greetings and consultations of the faithful present, or by the letters of absent ones. The crowd and pressing heap of these, in its accumulation, is rightly called an onset. Who is so dull as not to understand how great and how burdensome the multitude of business must have been, the weight of which lay on him every day?

units.la: Cum interea pseudapostoli ociosè deliciarentur. Vidi specimen huius quoddam, in viris illis qui primi in opus reformandarum ecclesiarum incubuerunt, uerum quid illi censeri poterunt Paulo collati? Sanè admodū negocio sus ac frequens est incursus Romanorum Pontificum, uerùm iuxta non molestus, quia lucro sus, ac talis qui & ocio, & luxui, & opibus, & regno ipsorū plurimū adferat fomenti. In curia Romana ἐπισύστασις quotidiana est non eorum qui Apostolū Christi vel Petrum vel Paulum, sed qui Simonem negociatorem ac venditorē Christi quaerunt.
units.tr: While meanwhile the false apostles idled in luxury. I have seen some sign of this in those men who first set to work on reforming the churches, but what could they be compared with Paul? Certainly the assault of the Roman Pontiffs is frequent and busy, yet it is not troublesome in the same way, because it is profitable to them and brings much fuel to their leisure, luxury, wealth and rule. In the Roman court there is a daily uprising, not of those who seek the apostle of Christ, whether Peter or Paul, but of those who seek Simon, the merchant and seller of Christ.

units.la: Illud cura omniū ecclesiarū, appositorie ad iectū esse videtur, vt exponatur, de qua ἐπισύστασις loquatur. Ea videlicet, quae ad curam ecclesiarum omnium pertinebat. Nulla negligere poterat. Habebat omnes in precio. Et quia reces adhuc erat illarū plantatio, adeoq; multa euenidebat vel ad instructionē imperitorū, vel ad confirmationē infirmorum, vel ad consolationem afflictorum, vel ad correctionē delinquētium pertinentia, cura hac quā in pectore gerebat, excutere non poterat.
units.tr: The phrase "the care of all the churches" seems to be added to explain what kind of uprising is meant: namely, the one that pertained to the care of all the churches. He could neglect none, and he held them all in esteem. Since their planting was still recent, many matters arose that pertained either to the instruction of the unlearned, or the strengthening of the weak, or the consolation of the afflicted, or the correction of offenders, and he could not shake off the care of these things that he bore in his heart.

units.la: Vindicat sibi & Romanus Pontifex omniū ecclesiarum cura, non vt illis consulat, sed vt regnum suū amplificet, & omniū loculis laqueos injiciat. Gerebat Paulus omniū ecclesiarū cura, quas ipse videlicet plantauerat & in Christo genuerat, perinde atq; pater curam liberorum suorum gerit, & curam gerebat, qua saluti ipsarum consuleret, non qua eas domino suo subijceret. At Romanus ille Simon vindicat sibi cura ecclesiarum, quarum nullam nec plantarit, nec rigauit, nec verbo pietatis pauit, & talem vindicat, quae non ad salutem animarum, sed magis ad perditionem faciat. Quae vero fit natura, quae solicitudo, & quae sedulitas curae, non est vt hic memoremus, cum id experian-
units.tr: The Roman Pontiff too claims for himself the care of all churches, not to advise them, but to enlarge his kingdom and cast snares into everyone's purse. Paul bore the care of all the churches which he had planted and begotten in Christ, just as a father bears the care of his children; and he bore that care to provide for their salvation, not to subject them to his own lord. But that Roman Simon claims for himself the care of churches, none of which he planted, watered, or fed with the word of godliness, and he claims a care that tends not to the salvation of souls but rather to their destruction. What the nature of that care is, and what the diligence and earnestness of it is, we need not describe here, since

units.la: tur in seipsis, quotquot aliorū veram ac fidelē curam gerunt.
units.tr: those who truly and faithfully care for others experience this in themselves.

units.la: QVIS infirmatur, inquit, & ego non infirmor? Quis offenditur, & ego non vror?) Ad eurā ecclesiarū pertinet nō modo ecclesias in gene re sed & singula illarum mebra curare. Erat aut in recentib. adhuc ecclesijs multi infirmi fratres, quorū imbecillis erat ac tenera fides. Erant item multae offendiculorū occasiones, quib. innumeri à sana doctrina & fide absterre bantur. Haec omnia pectus Apostoli cruciabat. Non abijciebat infirmos in fide, sicuti facit falsus pastor. Non damnabat eos qui offendebantur, sed illis compatiebatur: de istorū offensione admodū dolebat. Videmus hodie innumeros haud parum infirmari fide, quamplurimos etiam sic offendi, vt à recepta doctrina & fide prorsus resiliant, societatem fidelium deserat, & ad pristinas abominationes perinde atq; canis ad vomitum relabantur. Verùm quotusquisque reperitur ex pastoribus, qui cum in firmis infirmetur, & propter eos qui offensi re siliunt vratur?
units.tr: "Who is weak," he says, "and I am not weak? Who is offended, and I do not burn?" It belongs to the care of churches to look after not only the churches in general but also each of their members. In the churches, still recent, there were many weak brothers whose faith was feeble and tender. There were also many occasions of stumbling by which countless people were turned away from sound doctrine and faith. All these things tormented the Apostle's heart. He did not cast off the weak in faith, as the false minister does. He did not condemn those who were offended, but had compassion on them, and he grieved greatly at their offence. Today we see countless people weakened in faith, not a few, and very many so offended that they utterly withdraw from the received doctrine and faith, forsake the fellowship of the faithful, and relapse into their former abominations like a dog returning to its vomit. But how few are found among ministers who are weakened with the weak and burn over those who withdraw through offence?

units.la: Obserua uero, quod non simpliciter dicit: Cum infirmis infirmor, & propter eos qui offenduntur vror, sed: Quis infirmatur, & ego non infirmor? Quis offenditur, & ego non vror? Si gnificat se omnes Christianos ex aequo amanter complecti, nec discernere inter diuitem & pauperem, inter nobilem & ignobilem, inter doctum & idiotam, sed de omnium pariter esse salute solicitū. Quasi dicat, Quis nam adeo est despicabilis, cuius infirmitati non compatiar, & de cuius relapsu non excrucier? Qui nō ad hunc modum sunt animati, quemadmodū potiorum tantum, nobilium, diuitum, doctorum, &c. rationem habent, illorumq; offensas cauere studient, ita nullam gerunt curam ignobilium, pauperum, & idiotarum, deque horū salute parum sunt soliciti, quia nec Christum nec oues Christi fideliter, sed seipsos perfidè quaerunt.
units.tr: Observe, however, that he does not simply say, "I am weakened with the weak, and I burn over those who are offended," but: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is offended, and I do not burn?" He signifies that he embraces all Christians equally with love, and does not distinguish between rich and poor, noble and ignoble, learned and unlearned, but is equally anxious for the salvation of all. As if he said: Who is so contemptible that I do not sympathise with his weakness, and am not tormented by his fall? Those who are not moved in this way, who take account only of the more powerful, noble, rich and learned, and strive to guard against their offences, but bear no care for the ignoble, poor and unlearned, and are little anxious for their salvation, because they seek neither Christ nor the sheep of Christ faithfully, but themselves faithlessly.

units.la: SI gloriari oporteat, de his quae infirmitatis meae sunt gloriabor, inquit.) Iterum significat se non ex animo in materiam hanc, sed necessi tate adactum descendisse cum dicit: Si gloriari oportet. Per se non erat necesse gloriari, verū quoniā pseudapostoli perinde gloriabātur in ecclesia Corinthiorū, ac si studium gloriādi insignioris haberet Apostolatus argumentum necessario & ipse gloriari cogebatur, quo glori as illorum extingueret. Hoc significans dicit: Si gloriari oportet.
units.tr: "If I must glory, I will glory of the things that concern my infirmity," he says. Again he signifies that he came down to this subject not of his own will but driven by necessity, when he says, "If I must glory." In itself there was no need to glory; but since the false apostles boasted in the church of the Corinthians, as if their zeal for boasting were the mark of a more distinguished apostleship, he himself was necessarily compelled to glory too, so as to extinguish their boasting. Signifying this, he says, "If I must glory."

units.la: DE his quae infirmitatis meae sunt gloriabor.) Absurdum est gloriari de infirmitatibus. Gloriandi siquidē materia in ijs potius est quae decori sunt & ornamento, quàm in ijs quae contemptum generant ac despectum. Quare gloriandum magis fuisse videtur in fortitudineac potentia, quàm in infirmitate. Est enim omnis infirmitas despicabilis, gloriosa nulla. Quid igitur est quod se gloriaturum dicit in infirmitatibus suis? Respondeo. Gloriabantur pseudapostoli
units.tr: "I will glory of the things that concern my infirmity." It is absurd to glory in infirmities, for the matter of glorying lies rather in things that are becoming and an ornament than in those that produce contempt and scorn. Wherefore it seems he ought rather to have gloried in strength and power than in infirmity, for every infirmity is despicable and none is glorious. What then does he mean by saying he will glory in his infirmities? I answer: the false apostles gloried in their singular knowledge, in the splendour of their speech, and in their fleshly privilege, that they were Hebrews, Israelites and the seed of Abraham.

units.la: poitoli de singulari scientia, de splendore sermonis de progatiua carnis, quod essent Ebrei Israelitæ ac seme Abrahę. Vt horū glorias obli què perstringat, negat se de talib. gloriaturum non qd veraciter de illis gloriari nó posset, sed quod eiusmodi gloriatio nihil faceret ad veri Apostolatus commendationem, facteret autè potius, si quis ob fidelem ac sedulam Euangelij prædicationem multis sit laboribus, afflictionibus, periculis ac curis obnoxius, & interim tamen ope diuina adiutus strenuè in opere Euangelij pergat. Gloriá potentię, qua in omnibus periculis & laboribus tandiu perdurabat, non sibi, sed Deo referuans, sibijpsi tribuit nihil, quà & carnis & spiritus infirmitatè. Carnis, quam experiebatur in externis laboribus & periculis: spiritus, quá sentiebat in cura & solicitudine ecclesiarum.
units.tr: To blunt their glories, he says he will not glory in such things, not because he could not truly glory in them, but because such glorying contributes nothing to the commendation of true apostleship. It would contribute, rather, if someone, for the faithful and diligent preaching of the Gospel, were exposed to many labours, afflictions, dangers and cares, and yet, helped by divine aid, persevered vigorously in the work of the Gospel. The glory of power, by which he endured through all dangers and labours for so long, he reserved not for himself but for God, and attributed to himself nothing but the infirmity of flesh and spirit: of the flesh, which he experienced in external labours and dangers; of the spirit, which he felt in the care and anxiety of the churches.

units.la: Hoc genus gloriationis aut gloriam non ipsius sed Dei comendabat. Etenim quo magis infirmů se esse gloriabatur, hoc magis virtute operâtis in se Dei extollebat, iuxta illud supra cap. 4. Habemus aut thesaurū hunc in testaceis vasculis, ut uirtutis eminentia sit Dei & nō ex nobis, dum in omnib. premimur, at non arctamur, laboramus, at nondestituimur, &c. Omnium itaq; conuenientissimè postquam laborum periculorumq; suorum catalogū recensuit, ne de tot ac tantorū discriminum ac mole stiarum tolerantia gloriari ac tantam fortitudinem, qua in hisce omnib. infractus perstiterit, sibijpsi tribuere videatur, subijcit dicens, Si gloriari oportet, de his quę infirmitatis meæ sunt, gloriabor. Quasi dicat, Non de fortitudine, non de victoria, non de constantia, non de tot laborum meorum fructu, sed de infirmitate mea gloriabor, quo horum omniū virtus so li Deo cedat. Sanè pati aduersa, laborare, affligi, molestari, esurire, sitire, iactari, curis angi & quæ huiusmodi sunt alia, quæ propter Euangelium Christi in Apostolatu suo patiebatur, non sunt fortitudinis sed infirmitatis. Fortitudinis potius est, nullū hisce permittere locum, sive ea sit naturalis, sive singulari dono Dei cō cessa.
units.tr: This kind of glorying commended the glory not of himself but of God. For the more he gloried that he was weak, the more he extolled the power of God working in him, according to that passage above, chapter 4: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us; we are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair," and so on. Therefore, most fittingly, after he had recounted the catalogue of his labours and dangers, lest he seem to attribute to himself the endurance of so many and great trials, and the fortitude by which he stood unbroken in all these things, he adds: "If I must glory, I will glory of the things that concern my infirmity." As if he said: I will glory not in my courage, not in my victory, not in my constancy, not in the fruit of my many labours, but in my infirmity, so that the virtue of all these things may fall to God alone. Indeed, to suffer adversities, to labour, to be afflicted, troubled, hungry, thirsty, buffeted and distressed with cares, and other such things which he suffered in his apostleship for the sake of the Gospel of Christ, belong not to fortitude but to infirmity. It is rather the mark of fortitude to allow these things no place, whether that fortitude be natural or granted by a special gift of God.

units.la: Obseruemus igitur hoc loco quid discrimi nis sit inter gloriationis pseudapostolorum & veri apostoli. Gloriantur illi de ijs quæ splendida sunt & plausibilia, Apostolus vero de infirmitatibus suis gloriatur. Quare tam diuersi modè gloriantur? Quia gloriam illi non Dei sed suam, ille vero gloriam non suam sed Dei gloriando quærit.
units.tr: Let us observe, then, in this place what difference there is between the glorying of the false apostles and that of the true apostle. They glory in things that are splendid and showy; the Apostle glories in his infirmities. Why do they glory in such different ways? Because they seek glory for themselves, not for God, in their glorying; while he seeks glory not for himself but for God.

units.la: Deus & pater domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui est benedictus in sæcula, nouit quod non mentiar. In Damasci ciuitate gētis præfectus nomine Aretę regis excubi as posuerat in Damascenorū urbe, cupiens me comprehendere, ac per fenestram in sporta demissus fui per mœnia, effugiq; manus eius.
units.tr: "God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ever, knows that I lie not. In Damascus the governor under Aretas the king kept the city of the Damascenes with a garrison, desiring to apprehend me; and through a window, in a basket, was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands."

units.la: Quoniam de infirmitatib. suis gloriari constituit, inducit historiam, in qua quàm fuerit infirmus mostratur. Et quoniam illa mox initio Apostolatus ipsius facta fuerat, cum neminem secū haberet eorum, quos postea & comites & testes accepit eorum quę ipsi euenerunt, indu cit eam non simpliciter, sed cū iuramento & cō testatione conscientię Dei, dicens: Deus & pa ter domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui est benedictus in sæcula, nouit quod non mentiar. Propter Apostolicam authoritatem satis erat corā fidelib. fide dignus, vt non esset necesse vsurpare contestationem Dei: verūm quoniam versabatur in materia contentiosa, & dimicabat cū pseudapostolis, quos habebat infensissimos ac versutissimos hostes, propter illorum sectatores iureiurando confirmat ea quæ dicit ab omni esse mendacio aliena.
units.tr: Since he has resolved to boast of his weaknesses, he introduces a narrative in which it is shown how weak he was. And since this event had taken place at the very beginning of his apostleship, when he had none of those with him whom he later took as companions and witnesses of what happened to him, he introduces it not simply, but with an oath and an appeal to the testimony of God's conscience, saying: "God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever, knows that I do not lie." Because of his apostolic authority he was credible enough before the faithful, so there was no need to invoke God as witness; but since he was dealing with a contentious matter, and fighting against false apostles, whom he had as most hostile and crafty enemies, he confirms by an oath, on account of their followers, that what he says is free from all falsehood.

units.la: DEVS, inquit, & pater domini nostri Iesu Christi.) Poterat simpliciter dicere Deus nouit qd non mentiar, quèadmodum cap. sequenti dicturus est aliquoties: Deus nouit, verùm haud præter rationē est quod elogijs illis ornat Deū, vocans eum patrem domini nostri Iesu Christi, & benedictum in sæcula. Visus est illis initio quoq; præsentis epistolæ ad propositum, in quo tum versabatur perinde atq; hic.
units.tr: "God," he says, "and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." He could simply have said, "God knows that I do not lie," as he will sometimes say in the following chapter, "God knows." Yet it is not without reason that he adorns God with those titles, calling him the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ and blessed forever. These seemed fitting to him, at the start of this letter, for the purpose he was then pursuing, just as here.

units.la: Quarenon est vt iterum de illis annotemus, ni si quod illud: qui est benedictus in sæcula, sic positum est, vt referri possit tam ad Christum Iesum dominum nostrum, quàm ad Deum patrem. Ad Christum refert palàm in Rom. cap. 9 vbi sic dicit: ex quibus est Christus secundum carnem, qui est in omnibus Deus benedictus in sæcula, Amen.
units.tr: Nor is there any need to note again that this phrase, "who is blessed forever," is so placed that it may be referred both to Christ Jesus our Lord and to God the Father. He clearly refers it to Christ in Romans chapter 9, where he says: "of whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever. Amen."

units.la: IN Damasci ciuitate, inquit, gentis præfectus nomine Aretæ regis, &c.) Historiam hanc Lucas Act. 9. narrat ad hunc modū. Saulus autem multo magis inualescebat & confundebat Iudæos, qui habitabant Damasci, affirmans qd is esset Christus. Expletis autem diebus, complu ribus iimerunt inter se Iudæi consiliū, vt illumoc ciderent. Sed intellectæ sunt Saulo insidię eorum. Asseruabantq; portas die ac nocte, vt eum interficerent. Accipientes autem eum discipu li nocte, per murum demiserunt submittentes in sporta.
units.tr: "In the city of Damascus," he says, "the governor of the nation under King Aretas, etc." Luke narrates this history in Acts 9 as follows: "But Saul increased all the more in strength and confounded the Jews who lived at Damascus, affirming that this man was the Christ. And when many days were past, the Jews took counsel together to kill him. But their plot became known to Saul. And they watched the gates day and night, that they might kill him. But his disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket."

units.la: Videntur ista hactenus discrepare à verbis Pauli quod is insidias contra se factas, & vrbis custodiā refert ad præfectum Aretæ regis, Lucas vero ad Iudæos qui habitabat Damasci, sic vt nullā præfecti huius mentione faciat. Verū nulla hic est discrepantia. Lucas reijcit totam hanc causam in Iudæos, quod illi consiliū occidendi Paulū coepissent, eiusq; maliciæ primi authores fuissent. Paulus vero deputat eā præfecto regis, quod is ad instantiam Iudęorū vrbem clausisset, & custodias sua potestate portis adhibuisset, quo ipse comprehenderetur & occideretur.
units.tr: These accounts seem hitherto to differ from Paul's words: he says that the plot against him and the guarding of the city were the work of the governor under King Aretas, whereas Luke attributes them to the Jews who lived at Damascus, and makes no mention of this governor at all. But there is no real discrepancy here. Luke places the whole cause on the Jews, because they had begun the plan to kill Paul and were the first authors of his malice. Paul, however, ascribes it to the king's governor, because at the instance of the Jews he had shut the city and, by his authority, set guards at the gates so that Paul might be seized and killed.

units.la: Sed oritur hic quæstio, quid nam sit in hac historia, vel sic incredibile, vel ita ad gloriationem Pauli faciens, ut dignum duci debuerit, cuius gratia Deum citaret testem. Facilè credi potuit, pfectum Aretæ regis excubias posuisse in ciuitate Damascenorum vt ad instantiā Iudæorum ipsum caperet & occideret. Deinde nec illud difficile erat creditu, quod per fenestram demissus à discipulis, manus eius effugerit. Hæc duo manifesta erant in ipsa historia: quare non erat ratio, vt diuinæ conscientiæ contestatione confirmarentur. Ad hanc quæstionem respondemus, duo esse in hac historia præcipua, quorum fidem operæprecium erat iureiurando confirmari. Vnum, quod salua uritate quam præ', dicabat ex tricis illis euaserit. Huc facit euasionis modus. Etenim si recantasset, opus non fuisset per fenestram vrbicorum mœniorum demissum effugere. Alterum, quod nulla sua virtute, sed magis vt infirmus consilio & prouidentia Dei adiuta euaserit. Etenim ad hunc modum effugere infirmitatis est, non fortitudinis. Et tamen in ciuitate clausa, & ex cubijs diligenter ab ipso præfecto regio positis non posse capi, sed præter opinionem euadere argumentum habet auxilij diuini. Citat itaq; historiam hanc tanto serio, vt in illa & infirmitatem suam & præsentem opem Dei considerandam proponat, quam vtranq; in reliquo periculis ipsius concurrisse videre licet. Ad id vero, fuerit ne decorum Apostolo Christi, hoc pacto periculum effugere, responderut ante me alij. De rege Areta, quis fuerit, videlicet Iosephus lib. 18. antiquitatum Iudaicarum cap. 9 & 11.
units.tr: But here a question arises: what in this history is either so incredible, or so suited to Paul's boasting, that it ought to have been thought worthy of God being summoned as witness? It was easy to believe that the governor under King Aretas had posted guards in the city of the Damascenes, so that at the instance of the Jews he might seize and kill him. Nor was it difficult to believe that, let down through a window by the disciples, he escaped the hands of the governor. These two points were plain in the history itself; so there was no reason why they should be confirmed by an appeal to the testimony of divine conscience. To this question we answer that there are two main points in this history, the belief in which it was worth confirming by an oath. The first is that he escaped those snares while keeping the truth he preached; the manner of his escape bears on this, for if he had recanted there would have been no need to be let down through a window in the city wall to flee. The second is that he escaped not by any virtue of his own, but as a weak man, helped by the counsel and providence of God. For to escape in this way belongs to weakness, not to strength. And that, in a closed city, with guards carefully posted by the king's own governor, he could not be taken but escaped beyond expectation, is evidence of divine help. He therefore cites this history with such seriousness, so that in it his weakness and God's present help may be considered together, both of which are seen to have met in the rest of his perils. As to whether it was fitting for an apostle of Christ to escape danger in this way, others have answered before me. Concerning King Aretas, who he was, see Josephus, Jewish Antiquities, book 18, chapters 9 and 11.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT

units.la: Prosequitur gloriationes suas, & post mentionem visionum ac reuelationum gloriatur denuò de infirmitatibus suis. Deinde causam gloriationis suæ reijcit in Corinthios. Tertiò innocentiam suā, & eorum quos ad ipsos miserat asserit. Quartò significat illis quid metuat, si ad ipsos reuertatur.
units.tr: He pursues his boasts; and after mentioning visions and revelations, he boasts again of his weaknesses. Then he refers the cause of his boasting back to the Corinthians. Third, he asserts his own innocence and that of those whom he had sent to them. Fourth, he indicates to them what he fears if he returns to them.

units.la: CAPVT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: GLORIARI sanè non expedit mihi. Veniam enim ad visiones ac reuelationes domini. Nouì hominē in Christo ante annos quatuordecim, an in corpore, nescio, an extra corpus, nescio, Deus nouit, raptum huiusmodi in tertium usq; cœlum: & scio huiusmodi hominem, an in corpore, an extra corpus, nescio, Deus nouit, raptum fuisse in paradisum, & audisse arcana verba, quæ fas non sit homini loqui. Super huiusmodi homine gloriabor, de meipso uero nō gloriabor, nisi super infirmitatibus meis.
units.tr: Indeed, it is not expedient for me to glory. For I will come to the visions and revelations of the Lord. I know a man in Christ who, fourteen years ago, whether in the body or out of the body I do not know (God knows), was caught up to the third heaven. And I know that such a man, whether in the body or out of the body I do not know (God knows), was caught up into paradise and heard secret words which it is not lawful for a man to utter. On behalf of such a man I will glory, but on my own behalf I will glory only in my infirmities.

units.la: GLORIARI sanè non expedit mihi, inquit.) Vulgata lectio habet: Si gloriari oportet, non expedit quidem. At Græca exemplaria, quæ in manib. habentur non habent, ... sed, ... i. Gloriari sanè nō expedit mihi. Sic legit & Chrysost. Quoniam commemoraturus iam erat, non ad infirmitatem suam, sed ad singularem & eximiam dignationem Dei pertinetia, ne studio de illis gloriari videretur, præmisit hæc verba quibus testaretur, agnoscere se, quàm non sit vtile sibi, de visionibus ac reuelationibus gloriari. Gloriari sanè non expedit, mihi, inquit. Et vt significaret, de quo gloriationis genere loquere tur, veniam enim, inquit, ad visiones ac reuelationes domini. Quibus verbis separat hoc genus gloriationis ab eo quo de infirmitatibus suis fuerat gloriatus, de quibus non dixerat, quod sibi de illis gloriari non expediret. Quare autem de visionibus ac reuelationibus gloriari non expedierit ipsi, infrà uidebitur. Dices, Vt quid ergo gloriatur, si non expedit gloriari?
units.tr: "Indeed, it is not expedient for me," he says. The Vulgate reading has: "If I must glory, it is indeed not expedient." But the Greek copies that are now in hand do not have that; they read simply "Indeed, it is not expedient for me to glory." Chrysostom also reads it this way. Since he was about to speak of things that pertain not to his weakness but to the singular and remarkable favour of God, he prefaced these words, by which he testifies that he recognises how unprofitable it is for him to glory in visions and revelations, lest he seem to glory in them by design. "Indeed, it is not expedient for me to glory," he says. And so that he might indicate what kind of glorying he was speaking of, he adds: "For I will come," he says, "to the visions and revelations of the Lord." By these words he separates this kind of glorying from that in which he had gloried concerning his infirmities, and of which he had not said that it was not expedient for him to glory. Why it was not expedient for him to glory in visions and revelations will be seen below. You will ask: why then does he glory, if it is not expedient to glory?

units.la: Respondeo. Nō simpliciter dicit, gloriari nō expedit, sed, gloriari nō expedit mihi. Si simpliciter non expediuisset gloriari, nequaq; ad hoc gloriationis genus descendisset. Quod sibi quidem nō expedire sciebat, fecit propter alios quibus profuturum sperabat.
units.tr: I answer: he does not say simply that glorying is not expedient, but that glorying is not expedient for me. If glorying had simply been inexpedient, he would never have descended to this kind of glorying. He knew it was not expedient for himself, but he did it for the sake of others, whom he hoped it would benefit.

units.la: VENIAM enim, inquit, ad visiones ac reuelationes domini.) Quid discriminis sit inter visiones & reuelationes admonuerunt alij. Visionum tria genera assignantur ab Augustino, corporale videlicet, spirituale & intellectuale: vide de Genesi ad litera cap. II. Vbi vir ille prolixam & intricatam de visionib. ac præsenti loco disputationem habet. Visiones esse possunt tam spirituales quàm corporales in quib. nulla sit reuelatio, nisi separatim contingat. Corporalis visio erat, qua Balthasar articulos manus in pariete scribentis vidit Dan. 5. & tamen quod videbat non intelligebat, quia visio erat sine reuelatione, quam posteà per Danielè est consequutus. Spirituales visiones erat quas viderunt Eunuchi Pharaonis in custodia constituti Gen. 40. & quas vidit Pharao cap. 41. in quibus nulla erat reuelatio, donec ea daretur per Iosephum. Spiritualis visio erat cum adiuncta reuelatione, quam Daniel vidit cap. 7. Et reuelationes sæpenumero contingunt absq; visionibus, per internum spiritussanctì instinctum. Iam de quarū visionum ac reuelationum generibus hic loquatur Apost. cum dicit, Veniam enim ad uisiones ac reuelationes domini, patet in sequentibus.
units.tr: "For I will come," he says, "to the visions and revelations of the Lord." Others have pointed out what the difference is between visions and revelations. Augustine assigns three kinds of vision: bodily, spiritual and intellectual. See his book On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapter 12, where that man gives a lengthy and intricate discussion of visions, and also in the present passage. There can be visions, both spiritual and bodily, in which there is no revelation unless it comes separately. The bodily vision was that in which Belshazzar saw the fingers of a hand writing on the wall (Dan. 5), and yet he did not understand what he saw, because it was a vision without revelation, which he later obtained through Daniel. The spiritual visions were those which the eunuchs of Pharaoh saw while held in prison (Gen. 40), and those which Pharaoh saw (ch. 41), in which there was no revelation until it was given through Joseph. A spiritual vision came with an added revelation, as Daniel saw (ch. 7). And revelations very often occur without visions, through the inward prompting of the Holy Spirit. That the Apostle is speaking here of these kinds of visions and revelations, when he says "For I will come to the visions and revelations of the Lord," is clear from what follows.

units.la: NOVI hominem in Christo, inquit.) Hominem in Christo idem esse sentio quod homine Christi, Christianum, ad Christum pertinentem. Chrysostomus nec legit, in Christo, nec exponit. Si verò particulam hanc, in Christo, non ad præcedentia, noui hominem, sed ad sequentia referas, legasq; ad hunc modum: Noui homine ante annos quatuordecim in Christo
units.tr: "I know a man in Christ," he says. I take "a man in Christ" to mean the same as "a man of Christ": a Christian, one belonging to Christ. Chrysostom neither reads nor explains the words "in Christ." But if you refer this particle "in Christ" not to what precedes, "I know a man," but to what follows, and read it in this way: "I know a man fourteen years ago in Christ"

units.la: B sto raptû in tertiũ vsq; cœlum, idem erit quod in causa & virtute Christi. Vtrunq; uerum est. Et Christianus erat homo iste, & in causa pariter & uirtute Christi in tertium vsq; cœlû raptus fuit. Probabile est planè, visiones hasce ac reuelationes pertinuisse ad singularem Christi cognitionē, qua singularis Apostolus Christi erat imbuendus.
units.tr: "...caught up to the third heaven," it will be the same as "in the cause and power of Christ." Both are true. That man was a Christian, and he was caught up to the third heaven both in the cause and equally in the power of Christ. It is clearly probable that these visions and revelations pertained to the singular knowledge of Christ with which he, as a singular apostle of Christ, had to be imbued.

units.la: ANTE annos quatuordecim.) Libenter illis assentior qui visiones istas Apostolo circa Apostolatus ipsius principium vel non multo post contigisse censent, ut pillas ad futuros laDores & iunumera pericula subeúda instructior redderetur, eiusq; tempori cōuenire, qd hic dicit, ante annos quatuordecim. Sic nanq; solet Deus pcipua sua organa, quibus uti ad res magnas & periculosas cōstituit, pcurrentib; aliquot visionib. instruere ac cōmunire, sicuti videre est Hier. 1. & Ezec. 1. Reliquis apostolis non ita opus erat spiritualibus visionib. ac reuelationib. quoniam per ipsius Christi præsentiam abûde erant in cognitione ipsius instructi, opus autem erat Paulo, post ascensionē Christi demum conuerso.
units.tr: "Fourteen years ago." I gladly agree with those who think these visions came to the Apostle near the beginning of his apostleship, or not long after, so that he might be made better equipped to undergo the innumerable labours and dangers ahead; and that this fits the time he mentions here, "fourteen years ago." For God is accustomed to equip and fortify with some preceding visions those chief instruments of his whom he appoints to great and dangerous tasks, as can be seen in Jer. 1 and Ezek. 1. The other apostles did not need spiritual visions and revelations in the same way, since through the very presence of Christ they were abundantly instructed in the knowledge of him. But Paul needed them, being converted only after the ascension of Christ.

units.la: AN in corpore nescio, an extra corpus, nescio, Deus nouit.) Argutatur Augusti. in hisce verbis Apostoli, quomodo nescierit in corpore ne uel extra corpus raptus fuerit, cū nescire nequiuerit corporalia ne uel spiritualia in raptu isto viderit: nec illud ignorauerit, corpora lia extra corpus, & spiritualia in corpore non posse videri. Verū argutando remipsam nihilo reddit clariorem. Quin ibi rectius dicit, cū inquit, quis audeat dicere se scire, quod se nescire Apostolus dixit? Quare meo iudicio non est vt scrutemur ea quæ Apostolus non nouit, no uit uero Deus solus.
units.tr: "Whether in the body I do not know, or out of the body I do not know; God knows." Augustine makes a fine argument from these words of the Apostle: how could he not know whether he was caught up in the body or out of it, since he could not fail to know whether in that rapture he had seen bodily or spiritual things, nor be ignorant that bodily things cannot be seen outside the body, nor spiritual things within it? But by arguing in this way he makes the matter no clearer at all. Indeed, he speaks more rightly when he says: who would dare to say that he knows what the Apostle said he did not know? Therefore, in my judgement, we should not inquire into those things which the Apostle did not know; God alone knows them.

units.la: Sidicas, ad quid ergo particulam hanc ponere uoluit, cum sine illa rēipsam ponere possit? respōdeo, vt significaret visiones hasce tā fuisse sibi claras & euidentes, vt in dubio hęrearet extra ne corpus uel in corpore cōstituto cōtigerint. Dubitationi quippe huiusmodi non fuisset locus, si momētaneę & obscurę somnio quàm visionibus similiores extitissent.
units.tr: If you ask why, then, he wished to add this particle when he could have stated the matter without it, I answer: to indicate that these visions were so clear and evident to him that he was in doubt whether they had occurred outside the body or while he was in it. For there would have been no room for such doubt if they had been momentary and obscure, more like dreams than visions.

units.la: Nō dicit, nescieba Deus vero sciebat, sed ne scio, Deus nouit. Quæ corporalib. oculis uidemus in corpore nos videre ac vidisse scimus. Quæ uel in somnijs vel in raptu & ecstasi uidemus, interea quidē dū ea videmus, extra corpus ea videri à nobis ignoram⁹, postquā uero nobisipsis restituti sumus haud ignoram⁹ amplius. At Apostolus non modò cum in ipso esset raptu, sed & postquam ad se reuersus esset, in corpore ne uel extra corpus vidisset ea quę viderat ignorauit. Magna hæc est sui ignorantia. At in illa clarissimis uisionib. instruebatur Apostolus, quę illi hoc fuere magis perspicuę, quo magis sibijpsi fuerat ereptus.
units.tr: He does not say "I did not know," but "I do not know; God knows." What we see with our bodily eyes we know we see and have seen in the body. What we see in dreams, or in rapture and ecstasy, we do not know, while we are seeing them, whether we see them outside the body; but once we have been restored to ourselves, we no longer remain ignorant. Yet the Apostle, not only while he was in the rapture itself but even after he had returned to himself, did not know whether he had seen in the body or outside the body the things he had seen. This is a great ignorance of himself. But in those most clear visions the Apostle was instructed, and they were all the more plain to him the more he had been snatched away from himself.

units.la: RAPTVM huiusmodi, inquit, ad tértium vsque cœlum.) Non simpliciter raptum, sed raptum huiusmodi inquit. Cuiusmodi? Cuiusmodi ego sum. Loquitur quidem de seipso, ue
units.tr: "Such a man was caught up," he says, "to the third heaven." He does not say simply "caught up," but "such a man was caught up." Of what kind? Of the kind I am. He does indeed speak of himself, but in such a way that he might seem to be speaking of someone else, which he does for the sake of modesty. That he is speaking not of another but of himself will become clear below.

units.la: rū sic, vt de alio quopiā loqui uideri possit, id qd modestiæ gratia facit. Quod autem non de alio, sed de seipso loquatur infrà patebit.
units.tr: (cont.)

units.la: IN tertiū vsq; cœlū, inquit.) Mihi dubiū nō est voluisse Apostolum ad interiora se & secretiora sublimioraq; cæli secreta fuisse raptū significare. Quare non est vt anxiè de numero cœlorum disputemus. Id sanè constat vnius cœli multos esse gradus qui cœli nomine in scripturis vocantur. Sic cœlum est aereum, à quo volucres, cœli volucres vocantur. Sic cœlum est syderium in quo est Sol, & Luna, & stellæ. Sic cœlum est crystallinū, quod διαφανὲς vocāt Et empyreum, i. igneum. Erit aliquando, vt de cœlis melius quàm nūc de terris iudicare possimus. In eam felicitatis nostræ cōditionē scrutationem cœlorum differendam esse censeo.
units.tr: "Into the third heaven," he says. There is no doubt in my mind that the Apostle meant to signify that he was caught up into the more inward and secret and higher secrets of heaven. Therefore we need not anxiously dispute about the number of heavens. It is certainly agreed that within the one heaven there are many grades, which are called heavens in the Scriptures. Thus the heaven is the air, from which the birds are called "birds of heaven." Thus the heaven is the starry heaven, in which are the sun, the moon and the stars. Thus the heaven is the crystalline heaven, which they call transparent [διαφανὲς], and the empyrean, that is, the fiery heaven. A time will come when we may judge of the heavens better than we can now judge of the earth. I think the investigation of the heavens should be deferred until our happy condition of life.

units.la: ET scio huiusmodi hominem, inquit, an in corpore, an extra corpus, nescio, Deus nouit, raptum fuisse in paradisum.) Dixit, ueniam enim ad visiones ac reuelationes domini. Ex visionibus vnam subiecit, quæ potior erat, vbi raptus, in tertium vsq; cœlum meminit. Iam re uelationum quoq; vnam ex multis subiectur dicit: Et scio huiusmodi hominē, an in corpore an extra corpus, nescio, Deus nouit, raptum fuisse in paradisum, & audisse arcana verba, q fas non sit homini loqui. Disputat Augustin an idem sit hoc loco per paradisum, quod per tertium cœlum intelligendum. Et Lyranus idem esse asserit, quem & recentiores nonnulli sequuntur. Verum ipsa narratio duorum raptuum sic est distincta, vt liquidum fit, non esse de vno & eodem tantum raptu intelligenda quæ dicit. In tertium cœlum raptus fuit, vt videret gloriam Dei & gloriam regnantis in cœlo Christi. In paradisum uero, hoc est, in sedem beatorum spirituum, patriarcharum ac prophetarum, vt nō modò quò & ipse post dissolutionem corporis venturus esset, videret, sed & archana quædam audiret, vnde ad Apostolatum suum instructior rediret. De paradiso autem diximus in Commentarijs no stris super Genesim cap. 2. ibi. Plantauerat autem dominus Deus paradisum, &c. Sic sentiendū esse puto simpliciter absq; vlla scrupulositate, præsertim cum in re tam abstrusa obtusior sit mentis nostræ acies, quàm vt ad certitudinem illius indagando pertingere possit. Quantum ac quale discrimen sit inter tertium cœlum & paradisum discutiendum mihi non sumo, donec in hoc mortali corpore detineor, ipe tamē vtriusque cognitionem in futurum expecto. Interim tamen sic nolim inter tertium cœlum & paradisum cœlestem, beatorum spirituum mansionem, distinguere, vt eos qui in paradiso sunt à Christo seperarem, cum ad latronem ille dixerit: Hodie mecum eris in paradiso, & hic ipse Paulus dissolui & esse cum Christo in uotis habuerit.
units.tr: "I know a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, (whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) such an one caught up to the third heaven." He says, "For I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord." Of the visions he adds the one that was the more important, in which he speaks of being caught up even to the third heaven. Then, of the revelations, he adds one of many: "I know such a man, (whether in the body, or out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth,) how that he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter." Augustine discusses whether "paradise" here means the same as the third heaven. Lyra asserts that it does, and some more recent writers follow him. But the narrative itself separates the two rapturous experiences so clearly that it is plain the things he describes cannot be understood of one and the same rapture. He was caught up to the third heaven to see the glory of God and the glory of Christ reigning in heaven. But he was caught up into paradise, that is, into the abode of the blessed spirits of the patriarchs and prophets, so that he might see there what he himself would also come to after the dissolution of the body, and hear certain secrets, from which he might return better instructed for his apostleship. We have spoken of paradise in our Commentaries on Genesis, chapter 2, at the words "And the Lord God had planted a garden," etc. I think this should be taken simply, without any anxious scruple, especially since in so obscure a matter the edge of our mind is too dull to reach certainty by inquiry. How great and what kind of difference there is between the third heaven and paradise I do not claim to discuss while I am held in this mortal body; yet I look forward to knowing both in the future. Meanwhile, however, I would not wish to distinguish the third heaven and the heavenly paradise, the dwelling of the blessed spirits, so as to separate from Christ those who are in paradise, since he said to the thief, "Today you will be with me in paradise," and this same Paul had it as his desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.

units.la: ET audisse, inquit, archana uerba, quæ fas non sit homini loqui.) Propter uerbum audiendi refero ista ad reuelationes, quæ factæ sint Paulo in exstasi constituto. Non est autem A quaerendum quibus modis uerba fiant in paradiso coelesti, cum sint in illo nō corpora, sed beatorum spiritus. Quemadmodum extra se constitutus formas se corporales uidere, & uerba corporaliter prolata audire putauit, cum tamen in coelesti illa mansione non sint corpora, sed spiritus, ita etiam hominem illum uerba quaedam in paradiso audisse dicit.
units.tr: "And heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter." Because of the word "heard," I refer these things to the revelations made to Paul while he was in an ecstasy. We should not inquire by what means words are formed in the heavenly paradise, since there are there not bodies but the spirits of the blessed. Just as, placed outside himself, he thought that he saw bodily forms and heard words uttered bodily, although in that heavenly dwelling there are not bodies but spirits, so he says that the man heard certain words in paradise.

units.la: ET audisse, inquit, arcana uerba.) Graecè est ἄρρητα ῥήματα, id est, uerba quae uel nō possint, uel non debeant dici, quod sint uel auersanda & turpia, uel mystica, ac propter misterium celáda, uel impia, uel prohibita. Nos haec uerba nō sic ἄρρητα fuisse censemus quod dicit nequiuerint, sed quod extra paradisum inter homines & ab homine dici non debeât. Vnde & subijcit, quae fas non sit homini loqui. Hoc dicens, omnem nobis cognoscendi ea curiositatem amputat.
units.tr: "And heard unspeakable words." In Greek it is ἄρρητα ῥήματα [arrhēta rhēmata], that is, words which either cannot or ought not to be spoken, either because they are repugnant and shameful, or mystical and to be hidden on account of their mystery, or impious, or forbidden. We do not think these words were called unspeakable because they could not be expressed, but because they ought not to be spoken outside paradise, among men, or by a man. Hence he adds, "which it is not lawful for a man to utter." By saying this he cuts away from us all curiosity to know them.

units.la: Quare autem fas nō sit homini ut ea loquatur, si quis quaerat, cum fas fuerit Paulo, ut ea audiret, non est quod respondeamus aliud, quàm quod non ad praesentis uitae conditionem, sed ad paradisi secreta pertinuerint.
units.tr: If someone asks why it is not lawful for a man to speak them, when it was lawful for Paul to hear them, we need only answer that they pertained not to the condition of the present life but to the secrets of paradise.

units.la: Rursus, si quaeras, ad quid ergo Paulo profuerit ea audire, respondeo, nisi profuisset ipsi, ad cognitionem eorum admissus non fuisset. Secretorum cognitio ut non conducit omnibus, ita non pertinet ad omnes: conducit autem selectis, quos diuina dignatio tanquam singularia gratiae suae organa elegit. Horum enim animos ad res arduas & grauia sustinenda discrimina conscientia coelestium secretorum admodum confirmare poterit.
units.tr: Again, if you ask what good it did Paul to hear these things, I answer: unless it had profited him, he would not have been admitted to knowledge of them. Knowledge of secrets, as it does not benefit all, so it does not belong to all; it benefits the chosen, whom divine condescension has picked out as singular instruments of his grace. For the awareness of heavenly secrets can greatly strengthen the minds of these men to sustain difficult things and grave dangers.

units.la: Rursus dices. Atqui Christus dicit: Omnia quae audiui à patre meo nota feci uobis. An maiora & secretiora fuerunt quae Paulus audiuit in paradiso, quàm quę Christus unigenitus Dei audiuit à patre suo? Si fas fuit Christo loqui de illis omnibus quae audiuit ex patre, cur fas non fuit Paulo loqui de ijs quae audiuit in paradiso? Respondeo. De hoc reddat rationem ipse Paulus, qui diserte dicit: & audiuit arcana uerba quae fas non est homini loqui. Quę Christus audiuit ex patre, audiuit ut Mediator inter Deum & homines: & ideo audiuit, ut ea generi humano reuelaret. Haec conditio non fuit Pauli. Ad haec quae Christus audiuit à patre, audiuit non ad hoc ut ipsi conducerent: Paulus uero in paradisum raptus audiuit archana uerba, non quae alijs exponerentur, sed quae ipsi prodessent.
units.tr: Again you will say: but Christ says, "All things that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you." Were the things Paul heard in paradise greater and more secret than those the only-begotten Son of God heard from his Father? If it was lawful for Christ to speak of all those things he heard from the Father, why was it not lawful for Paul to speak of those things he heard in paradise? I answer: Paul himself must give the reason for this, since he plainly says, "and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter." What Christ heard from the Father, he heard as Mediator between God and men, and therefore he heard it in order to reveal it to the human race. This condition was not Paul's. Moreover, what Christ heard from the Father, he heard not so that it might be of use to himself; but Paul, caught up into paradise, heard unspeakable words, not to be expounded to others, but to be of profit to himself.

units.la: Adhuc dices: Cum Actorum 20. nihil se subtraxisse dicat, quo minus omne consilium Dei Ephesijs annunciauerit, quomodo hic sibi quae in paradiso audierat, loqui dicit esse illicitum?
units.tr: You will press further: since in Acts 20 he says that he had kept back nothing that would prevent him from declaring to the Ephesians the whole counsel of God, how does he now say that it is unlawful to speak of what he heard in paradise?

units.la: Respondeo, loquitur ibi de ijs rebus quae consilio Dei ad utilitatem erant ac salutem fidelium scitu necessariae, non in uniuersum de secretis omnibus. Vnde & eodem loco dicit, ut nihil subtraxerim eorum quae essent in rem uestram, quin annunciarem uobis.
units.tr: I answer: there he speaks of those things which, according to God's counsel, were necessary to know for the benefit and salvation of the faithful, not of all secrets in general. Hence in the same place he also says, "that I kept back nothing that was profitable to you, but declared it to you."

units.la: SVPER huiusmodi, inquit, homine gloriabor, de meipso uero non gloriabor, nisi super infirmitatibus meis.) Videtur adhuc loqui de alio quopiam homine, qui raptus fuerit in tertium coelum, & in paradisum, cum tam distincte dicit, Super huiusmodi homine gloriabor, de meipso uero non gloriabor, quibus uerbis arrogätiam quidem cauet, ne seipse efferre & gloriando iactare uideatur, interea tamē subtili quodam modo seipsum diuidit in hominem alium atq; alium, de quorum altero gloriari uelit, de altero nolit, nisi quod infirmitates illius attinet, imò quorum alterum huiusmodi hominem, alterum seipsum uocet, quasi alter ille de quo gloriari uelit, nō sit ipse, sit uero is de quo gloriari nolit. Quid autem hoc aliud est, quàm gloriari super felicitate sua, cuius per diuinam dignationem in utroq; raptu gustum quedam perceperat, super uirtutibus uero suis, & praerogatiuis carnis nolle gloriari? Quare? Quia in Paulo in tertium usq; coelū & in paradisum rapto, gloria non carnis sed gratiae Dei relucebat. In Paulo uero Ebraeo, Israelita & femine Abrahae gloria erat carnis, de qua sine detrimento gratiae Dei gloriari nō poterat. De eo quod dicit, nisi super infirmitatibus meis, dictum est supra.
units.tr: "Of such a man will I glory; but of myself I will not glory, but in my infirmities." He seems still to speak of some other man who was caught up to the third heaven and into paradise, since he says so distinctly, "Of such a man will I glory, but of myself I will not glory." By these words he guards against arrogance, lest he should seem to exalt himself and boast by glorying. Yet in a subtle way he divides himself into one man and another man, of whom he wishes to glory in the one and not in the other, except as regards his infirmities. Indeed, he calls one "such a man" and the other himself, as if that other, of whom he wishes to glory, were not himself, but he of whom he is unwilling to glory were himself. But what else is this than to glory in his happiness, of which he had received a certain taste in both raptures through divine condescension, while being unwilling to glory in his own virtues and the privileges of the flesh? Why? Because in Paul, caught up to the third heaven and into paradise, the glory of grace and not of the flesh shone forth. But in Paul the Hebrew, the Israelite and the seed of Abraham, there was the glory of the flesh, of which he could not glory without detriment to the grace of God. What he says, "except in my infirmities," has been explained above.

units.la: Nam si uoluero gloriari non ero insipiens, veritatem enim dicam: sed parco uobis, ne quis de me cogitet, supra id quod uidet esse me, aut quod audit ex me. Et ne excellentia revelationum supra modū efferrer, datus fuit mihi stimulus per carnem, nūcius Satanae, ut me colaphis caederet ne supra modum efferrer. Super hoc ter dominū rogaui, ut discederet à me, & dixit mihi: Sufficit tibi gratia mea, nam uirtus mea per infirmitatē perficitur. Libentissime igitur gloriabor potius super infirmitatib. meis, ut inhabitet in me uirtus Christi. Quāobrē placeo mihi in infirmitatib. in contumelijs, in necessitatib. in persequutionibus, in anxietatib. pro Christo. Cum enim infirmus sum, tunc robustus sum.
units.tr: "For if I should desire to glory, I shall not be foolish, for I shall speak the truth; but I forbear, lest any man should think of me above that which he sees me to be, or hears from me. And lest I should be exalted above measure by the abundance of revelations, there was given me a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure. For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said to me: My grace is sufficient for thee; for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me. Wherefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ. For when I am weak, then am I strong."

units.la: Quoniam dixit, de meipso uero non gloriabor, ne hoc sic dictum acciperet, quasi etiamsi quammaxime uellet nihil in se haberet, unde ueraciter gloriari posset, significat non ob id gloriari se nolle de seipso, quod nō possit, sed quod satius esse ducat, ut abstineat à gloriationibus, quàm ut more pseudapostolorū glorietur. Sic dicit: Nam si uoluero gloriari, &c. Legendum est, Nam si uellem gloriari non essem insipiens, ueritatē enim dicere, uerū abstineo.
units.tr: Since he said, "But I will not boast of myself," lest anyone take this as though, even if he wished to, he had nothing in himself of which he could truly boast, he makes clear that he did not refrain from boasting about himself because he could not, but because he judged it better to abstain from boasting than to boast in the manner of the false apostles. So he says: "For if I should wish to boast, etc." The reading should be: "For if I wished to boast I would not be foolish, for I would be telling the truth, but I refrain."

units.la: SI uellem gloriari, inquit.) Atqui gloriabatur. Verum nō de seipso gloriabatur, nisi quod infirmitates ipsius attinebat. Subintelligendum igitur est, de meipso.
units.tr: "If I wished to boast," he says. And yet he did boast. But he did not boast about himself, except in so far as it concerned his weaknesses. So "about myself" must be understood.

units.la: NON essem insipiens, veritatem enim dicerem.) Ergo qui citra veritatem gloriatur, insipiens est. Poterat dicere, non essem mendax, non essem impudens. Etenim etiam qui vera de seipso praeter rationem iactando gloriatur, insipiens est, quia facit quod vanum est ac stultum: qui vero falsa de se iactat, non modo insipienter, sed & impudenter gloriatur. Verum moderatius loqui voluit, propter eos quos perstringebat, qui de seipsis non modo quae carnis erant, sed & pleraque falsa iactabant, id quod pro sua modestia deputat insipientiae.
units.tr: "I would not be foolish, for I would be telling the truth." Therefore whoever boasts without truth is foolish. He could have said, "I would not be a liar, I would not be shameless." For even one who boasts of true things about himself beyond reason is foolish, because he does what is vain and senseless; but one who boasts of false things about himself is not only foolish but also shameless. He chose to speak more moderately, however, on account of those he was rebuking, who boasted about themselves not only of the things of the flesh but also of many false things. Because of his modesty, he counts this as folly.

units.la: SED parco vobis, inquit.) Vobis, non est in Graeco, sed simpliciter φείδομαι ὑμῶν, quod nulla necessitate versum est, parco autem, cum φείδεσθαι non solum parcere, sed & cavere & abstinere significet. Quare rectius est, ut vertamus, sed abstineo, nec addamus, vobis, quia ut adiectae rationes indicant, non tam illorum quàm sua gratia à gloriationibus abstinebat. Nobis hic observandum est abstinentiae admodum Christianae exemplum. Poterat Apostolus veraciter de multis suis virtutibus ac gestis gloriari, verum abstinebat: non quod esset illicitum, sed quod inutile & cum periculo coniunctum esse sciret. Sic Christianus non modo ab illicitis, sed & à licitis abstinet, quae nec sibi nec aliis profore novit.
units.tr: "But I spare you," he says. "You" is not in the Greek; the text simply has φείδομαι ὑμῶν [I spare you], which has been rendered without any necessity. Yet "I spare" [φείδεσθαι] means not only to spare but also to take care and to abstain. So it is better to translate "but I abstain," and not to add "you," because, as the reasons that follow show, he abstained from boasting less for their sake than for his own. Here we must notice a most Christian example of abstinence. The Apostle could truly have boasted of his many virtues and deeds, but he refrained, not because it was unlawful, but because he knew it was useless and attended with danger. So a Christian abstains not only from unlawful things but also from lawful things which he knows will profit neither himself nor others.

units.la: NE quis de me cogitet, inquit, supra id quod videt esse me, aut quod audit ex me.) Incipit rationem reddere, quare de seipso magnifica iactare nolit. Reddit autem geminam, unam quae alios, alteram quae se concernat. Alios concernit quod dicit, ne quis de me cogitet supra id quod videt esse me, aut quod audit ex me. Graecè est, μήτις εἰς ἐμὲ λογίσηται, ὑπὲρ ὃ βλέπει με id est, ne quis in me reputet, supra id quod videt me, ubi subintelligendum est ἄνω, id est, esse. Cavebat igitur, ne si magnificè de seipso gloriaretur maioris fieret, quàm esse videbatur, aut quàm essent ea quae ex ipso audiebantur. Nō dicit, supra id quod sum, sed, supra id quod videt esse me, aut quod audit ex me. Erat Apostolus Christi, minister ac dispensator mysteriorum Dei. Id erat manifestum. Videbantur & audiebantur ex eo certe huius experimenta. Supra id non vult tribui sibi quicquam 1.Cor.4. dicit: Sic nos æstimet homo, ut ministros Christi, & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. Ne pluris fieret sedulo cavebat. Notum est quid acciderit ipsi ac Barnabae. Act.14. cum claudum hominem in pedes erexisset.
units.tr: "Lest anyone think of me," he says, "beyond what he sees me to be, or what he hears from me." He begins to give the reason why he is unwilling to boast grandly about himself. He gives a twofold reason, one concerning others and the other concerning himself. The one concerning others is what he says: "lest anyone think of me beyond what he sees me to be, or what he hears from me." The Greek is μήτις εἰς ἐμὲ λογίσηται, ὑπὲρ ὃ βλέπει με [lest anyone reckon concerning me above what he sees in me], where ἄνω [above] must be understood with "to be." He was therefore taking care that, if he boasted grandly about himself, he would not be thought greater than he appeared, or greater than the things heard from him warranted. He does not say, "beyond what I am," but "beyond what he sees me to be, or what he hears from me." The Apostle was a minister of Christ and a steward of the mysteries of God. This was plain. From him, certainly, there were visible and audible proofs of this. He does not wish anything beyond this to be attributed to him. Compare 1 Cor. 4: "Let a man so regard us, as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God." He carefully took care that he would not be esteemed more highly. What happened to him and to Barnabas is well known, when he raised up the lame man on his feet (Acts 14).

units.la: Admonemur hoc exemplo, ut non minus caveamus ne pluris quàm, ne minoris quàm sumus habeamur. Qui suopte studio maioris quàm par sit aestimatur, fallit alios, quod probi hominis non est, & odiosum se reddit Deo: qui eiusmodi superbiam detestatur, denique periculo sese magni contemptus exponit, quę incurret mox atq; detecta fuerit ipsius vanitas. Qui vero minoris reputatur quàm debeat, ad tempus quidem obscurius degit inter homines, Deo autem apprime manifestus est:
units.tr: We are admonished by this example to take no less care that we are not valued more than we are, or less than we are. The one who by his own eagerness is esteemed more highly than is fitting deceives others, which is not the mark of an honest man, and makes himself odious to God. The one who detests such pride, finally, exposes himself to the danger of great contempt, which he will incur as soon as his vanity is detected. But the one who is reckoned less than he ought to be lives for a time in more obscurity among men, yet is most clearly known to God.

units.la: ubi vero manifestationis ipsius tempus adveneri t, modici temporis contemptus indelebili laude commutatur.
units.tr: But when the time of his manifestation has come, contempt for a short time is exchanged for lasting praise.

units.la: Simul observa in eo quod uidendi & audiendi uerba usurpat, unde iudicium nobis de homine constare debeat. Ex ijs uidelicet, quę in illo uidemus, & ex illo audimus. Non solū, quod audit ex me, inquit, sed & quod uidet in me. Nec dicit, quod audit de me, sed, quod audit ex me. Quae de homine audiuntur ex alijs, nihilo plus sunt fide digna, q digna est fama. Quae vero ex ipso homine de quo iudicandum est audiuntur, coiuncta ijs quae in illo uidentur, ueluti duplici testimonio iudicium de illo confirmant. Quare admodum impudentes sunt, qui cum Bacchanalia uiuant, & ipsam impudicitiam ore spirent, nihilo tamen secius pro Curijs haberi uolunt, cum & uerbis & operibus omnium sint carnalissimi, pro spiritualibus tamen sese uenditant.
units.tr: At the same time, observe in his use of the words "to see" and "to hear" how we ought to be able to form a judgment about a man: from those things which we see in him and hear from him. He says not only "what he hears from me," but also "what he sees in me." And he does not say "what he hears about me," but "what he hears from me." What is heard about a man from others is no more trustworthy than his reputation is worthy of trust. But what is heard from the very man whom we must judge, joined with what is seen in him, confirms the judgment about him as if by a double testimony. Hence those are most shameless who live in Bacchanalian fashion and breathe out immodesty with their mouths, and yet nonetheless wish to be regarded as Curii, while in both words and deeds they are the most carnal of all, and yet they offer themselves as spiritual men.

units.la: ET ne excellentia reuelationum supra modum efferrer, inquit, datus fuit mihi stimulus per carne, nuncius Satanae ut me colaphis caederet, ne supra modum efferrer.) Habet haec alteram rationem, quae ipsum cocernebat, ob quam non conducebat, ut magnificè de seipso gloriaretur. Erat enim ipsi alioqui periculum, ne propter reuelationum excellentiam supra modu efferretur. Id istis uerbis exprimit, quibus ad hoc sibi datum esse angelum Satanę dicit, à quo colaphis caedatur, ne propter excellentiam reuelationum in superbiam efferatur.
units.tr: "And lest I be lifted up beyond measure by the excellence of the revelations, a thorn was given to me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, to buffet me, lest I be lifted up beyond measure." This contains a second reason, which concerned himself, why it was not expedient for him to boast grandly about himself. For otherwise there was a danger to him that he might be lifted up beyond measure on account of the excellence of the revelations. He expresses this in these words, in which he says that an angel of Satan was given to him for this purpose, by whom he is buffeted, so that he would not be puffed up with pride on account of the excellence of the revelations.

units.la: ET ne excellentia reuelationum supra modum efferrer, inquit.) Patet ex hoc loco pertinere ad ipsum, quae in praecedentibus de homine in tertium usque coelum & in paradisum rapto gloriatus est. Etenim si de alio loquutus esset, nihil ipsi periculi fuisset, ne propter excellentia alienarum reuelationum s modu efferretur.
units.tr: "And lest I be lifted up beyond measure by the excellence of the revelations," he says. It is clear from this passage that what he boasted of in the preceding verses, about the man caught up to the third heaven and into paradise, pertains to himself. For if he had spoken about another man, there would have been no danger to him of being lifted up beyond measure by the excellence of someone else's revelations.

units.la: Cogitandum est hic pio homini, quàm propter qualemcunq; prerogatiuam infletur ac superbiat. Etenim si hoc erat Apostolo tot laboribus ac periculis depressō, usqueadeò timendū, ut singulari quodam antidoto opus haberet, per quod contra tentationē superbię in humilitate ac modestia contineretur, quid nobis nō est multo timendum amplius, qui etsi parē reuelationū excellentiā consequuti non sumus: multò tamen minus habemus roboris ac resistendum tentationibus superbiae, quantumcunq; leuibus ac minutis, quàm habuerit ille contra tam graues superbiendi occasiones.
