Quare admodum defipiūt qui studio dignitates ac honores in hoc seculo ambiunt, non considerantes quantis se ipsi periculis obnoxios reddant.
units.tr: Here a godly man should consider how easily he is puffed up and swollen with pride on account of any kind of prerogative whatever. For if this was so dangerous for the Apostle, who was weighed down by so many labours and perils, that he needed a certain singular antidote, by which he might be kept against the temptation of pride in humility and modesty, how much more must we fear, who, even though we have not attained an equal excellence of revelations, nonetheless have far less strength and resistance against temptations to pride, however slight and trivial, than he had against such grave occasions of being puffed up. Therefore those are utterly foolish who eagerly pursue dignities and honours in this age, not considering how great the dangers are to which they expose themselves.

units.la: NE supra modū efferrer, inquit.) Graecè est, ἵνα μὴ ὑπεραίρωμαι. Significat ὑπεραίρεσθαι supra q par est ac conuenit efferri, ὑπεραίρεια Apostolus, si magnificentius de se ipse sentiat, uel ab alijs sentiatur, quàm conueniat ministro Christi, quamq; uel in ipso uidetur, uel ex ipso auditur. De Antichristo secunda Thess. secundo,
units.tr: "Lest I be lifted up beyond measure," he says. The Greek is ἵνα μὴ ὑπεραίρωμαι [that I may not be lifted up beyond measure]. To be lifted up [ὑπεραίρεσθαι] signifies being lifted up beyond what is fitting and proper. The Apostle means that if he were to think of himself more grandly than is fitting for a minister of Christ, or if others were to think so, judging from what is seen in him or heard from him, then he would be lifted up beyond measure.

units.la: futurum praedixit Paulus, ut efferatur supra omnem qui dicitur Deus aut numen, adeo ut in templo Dei sedeat, ostetans seipsum esse Deum, quo loco uocem καθαρόμενον legimus. Est autem id reuera supra modum efferri. Etenim unicuique datus est a Deo uel excellentiae uel humilitatis modus, supra quem si quis extollitur, utiq; supra modum sibi uidelicet competentem, extollitur.
units.tr: Paul foretold that Antichrist would be lifted up above every so-called god or object of worship, so that he would sit in the temple of God, showing himself to be God (2 Thess. 2). There we read the word [καθαρόμενον]. To be lifted up beyond measure is indeed exactly this. For to each one God has given a measure of excellence or of humility, and if anyone is raised above it, he is clearly raised beyond the measure proper to himself.

units.la: DATVS fuit mihi stimulus per carnem, inquit, nuncius Satanae, ut me colaphis caederet, ne supra modum efferrer.) Quod stimulum uertit, Graece est σκόλοψ, quae uox sonat palum, paxillum, & sudem, lignum uidelicet in acie praeustum & acutum. Huius apud ueteres, & forsan adhuc apud plerasque nationes alius atque alius usus est, sic ut alijs fit uice stimuli ad impellendum boues, alijs uice cuspidis in conflictu militari, alijs ad conficiedum sepem ac uallum, alijs ad crucifigendum sceleratos. Vtitur hac uoce Apostolus sensu non proprio, sed metaphorico. Quid autem per illam intelligat, significat cum subiungit, nuncius Satanae: Quis ille fuerit, non est eadem omnium sententia. Alius adfert κολαφισμόν, qua frequenter laborarit Apostolus, alius iliacam passionem, alius incitamenta carnalis concupiscentiae, alius terrores Satanae, alius omne genus tentationis, alius quosdam daemonas: Chrysostomus uero propius ad sensum Apostoli, meo iudicio accedes, exponit de aduersarijs, qui illum crebris iniurijs, contumelijs & persequutionibus afflixerint, inter quos nominatim recefet Alexandrum aerarium, Hymenaeum & Philetum. Sane de Alexandro 2. Tim. 4. singulariter conqueritur, quod multa sibi mala intulerit, uerbisq; suis ualde restiterit. Exist i mo tamen loqui Apostolum hoc loco de singulari quoda & infigniter malo aduersario, quem angelum Satanae singulariter uocet: qualis fuit Alexander, qui non uno tantum loco molestus ipsi extiterit, sed ubilibet infensissime aduersatus fuerit. Hunc comparat sudi ac paxillo, quod quemadmodum sudes praeacuta carnem pungendo affligit, sic fit illius infestationibus ueluti punctionibus afflictatus. Sic intelligo illud, datus est mihi stimulus carni, ut idem sit quod datus est mihi ueluti stimulus carnem pungens, angelus Satanae. Non placet ut legamus stimulus carnis, uel, stimulus in carne, aut, stimulus per carnem, sed ut in Graeco est, stimulus carni, quasi sit ἐδόθη μοι, ὅστε ἄγγελος σατανᾶ, ἀγγελ... i. datus est mihi nuncius Satanae, qui sit mihi instar stimuli quo caro pungitur. Dico quid mihi uideatur, sic tamen, ut nemini praeiudicare cupiam. Crediderim autem aduersarium illum fuisse expseudapostolis, quos cap. praecedenti uocauit ministros Satanae.
units.tr: "A thorn was given to me in the flesh," he says, "a messenger of Satan, to buffet me, lest I be lifted up beyond measure." The word that he translates as "thorn" is σκόλοψ in Greek, which means a stake, a pointed post, or a stake hardened by fire and sharpened, that is, a piece of wood sharpened in the fire. Among the ancients, and perhaps still among many nations, this has had various uses: for some it serves as a goad for driving oxen, for others as a spear in military combat, for others for making a hedge or rampart, and for others for crucifying criminals. The Apostle uses this word not in its proper sense but metaphorically. What he means by it he indicates when he adds, "a messenger of Satan." What this was has not been understood in the same way by everyone. Some understand it as the buffeting [κολαφισμός] which the Apostle often suffered; others as a rising of fever (ilíaca passio); others as incitements of carnal lust; others as terrors sent by Satan; others as every kind of temptation; others as certain demons. Chrysostom, however, in my judgment comes closer to the Apostle's meaning, and explains it of adversaries who afflicted him with frequent injuries, insults and persecutions, among whom he names Alexander the coppersmith, Hymenaeus and Philetus. Indeed, in 2 Tim. 4 he complains particularly of Alexander, that he did him many evils and strongly opposed his words. I think, however, that the Apostle here speaks of a certain single and remarkably evil adversary, whom he calls singularly a messenger of Satan, such as Alexander was, who was troublesome to him not in one place only, but who opposed him most bitterly wherever he was. He compares this man to a stake or post: just as a sharpened stake afflicts the flesh by piercing it, so he was afflicted by this man's assaults as by pricks. This is how I understand the words "a thorn was given to me for the flesh," so that it means the same as "there was given to me, as a thorn piercing the flesh, an angel of Satan." I do not care for reading "a thorn of the flesh," or "a thorn in the flesh," or "a thorn through the flesh," but rather, as it is in the Greek, "a thorn to the flesh," as if it were ἐδόθη μοι, ὅστε ἄγγελος σατανᾶ [there was given to me a messenger of Satan], that is, there was given to me a messenger of Satan, who would be to me in the manner of a thorn by which the flesh is pricked. I say what seems to me, yet in such a way that I wish to prejudge no one. I would believe, moreover, that this adversary was one of the false apostles, whom in the preceding chapter he called ministers of Satan.

units.la: Dicit autem non simpliciter esse sibi stimulum, sed esse sibi datum stimulum, utique non aliunde quam a Deo ipso, idq; non ad punien dum, sed ad conseruandum, loco uidelicet antidoti, quod a medico contra periculu pestis
units.tr: He says that the thorn was not simply in him, but was given to him, certainly by no other source than God himself, and this not for punishment but for preservation, that is, as a kind of antidote, such as a physician gives against the danger of plague.

units.la: datur. Quare uidentur mihi non satis perpendere studium Dei in Paulum, qui uerbu ἐδόθη sic exponunt. Permisit Deus, ut Satan adhiberet mihi stimulum. Chrysost. forsan ueritus ne Deo mali quicquam tribuatur, sic exponit, σωσχώρησον τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ... Verum Apostolus non utitur uerbo permittendi, sed diserte dicit: datus est mihi stimulus. Vt signi ficet illum reputari a se pro singulari Dei dono. Hoc genus exponendi sacras scripturas, quo uerba, dandi, tradendi, obduradi, excaecandi, occidendi, perdendi, &c. Deo tributa, per uerbum permittendi exponuntur, meo iudicio, nec menti spiritus sancti satisfacit, nec quod cauere conatur, cauet.
units.tr: Therefore they seem to me not to weigh sufficiently the care of God for Paul, those who explain the word "was given" (ἐδόθη) thus: God permitted Satan to inflict a thorn on me. Chrysostom, perhaps fearing lest anything evil be attributed to God, explains it thus: "concede to people..." But the Apostle does not use the word "permit"; he plainly says: "a thorn was given to me." He means that it is to be reckoned by him as a singular gift of God. This manner of explaining the sacred Scriptures, by which words of giving, delivering up, hardening, blinding, killing, destroying, and so on, which are ascribed to God, are explained by the word "permit," in my judgment neither satisfies the mind of the Holy Spirit nor guards against what it attempts to guard against.

units.la: VT me colaphis caederet, inquit.) Intelligit de probris, conuicijs, blasphemijs, & contumelijs, quibus ipsum angelus ille Satan afficiebat, ac contemptum reddere moliebatur. Colaphis & alapis caedi contemptus & ignominiae notam habet, quemadmodum & capite praecedeti annotauimus. Quare usurpat illud Apostolus pro contumelijs ac probris, quae sibi aduersarius contemptus gratia inferebat.
units.tr: "That he might strike me with fists," he says. He means reproaches, insults, blasphemies and abuse, with which that angel Satan assailed him and tried to bring him into contempt. To be struck with fists and slaps carries the mark of contempt and disgrace, as we noted also in the preceding chapter. So the Apostle uses it for insults and reproaches which his adversary inflicted on him for the sake of contempt.

units.la: Ergo ad hoc contumelijs afficiebatur ab angelo Satanae, ut contra periculum elationis ac superbiae in humilitate conseruaretur, cauereturq; ne ex Apostolo Christi fieret Apostolus Satanae. Tanto bono seruiebat ipsi angelus ille Satanae, imo Satan ipse, non intelligens cor filium Dei: sed cursum Euangelij Christi hoc se pacto impedire posse putans, si Apostolum illius condigna exi stimatione priuatum, contumelijs ac probris contemptibilem redderet. Sic infatuatus Satan dum obesse molitur, magis etiam prodest, & quod impedire conatur, expeditum potius reddit quam impeditum. Gloria haec est sapientiae ac prouidentiae Dei, quam non satis illustrat Chrysost. hoc loco, dum Deum Satanae permisisse dicit, ut per nuncium suum colaphis caederet Paulum.
units.tr: Therefore he was subjected to insults from the angel of Satan for this purpose: that he might be preserved in humility against the danger of pride and arrogance, and that he might be guarded lest the apostle of Christ become an apostle of Satan. That angel of Satan, or rather Satan himself, served so great a good, not understanding the heart of the Son of God, but thinking he could hinder the course of the gospel of Christ in this way, if he deprived the Apostle of due esteem and made him contemptible through insults and reproaches. Thus Satan, infatuated, while he labours to harm, actually benefits more, and what he tries to hinder he makes more free rather than hindered. This is the glory of the wisdom and providence of God, which Chrysostom does not sufficiently illustrate in this place, when he says that God permitted Satan to strike Paul with fists through his messenger.

units.la: NE supra modum efferrer, inquit.) Particula haec abundat hoc loco. Nam initio periodi huius posita sic satisfacit praesenti causae, & consilium Dei exprimit, ut lector illam haud quaquam denuo desideret. Crediderim ab aliquo inconsulto repetitam. Si dicat princeps aliquis, ne per excellentiam potestatis supra modum efferar, datus est mihi peculiaris hic morbus, qui humanae me conditionis admoneat, puto non requiri, ut denuo dicat, ne supra modum efferar. In uulgata editione non reperitur, & ne quis Graeca exemplaria praetexat, a Chrysostomo quoq; non repetitur.
units.tr: "Lest I be exalted above measure," he says. This particle is superfluous in this place. For placed at the beginning of this sentence it already satisfies the present cause and expresses the counsel of God, so that the reader by no means desires it again. I would believe it was repeated by someone careless. If some prince should say, "lest I be exalted beyond measure by the excellence of my power, this peculiar affliction has been given to me, which reminds me of my human condition," I think it is not required that he say again, "lest I be exalted beyond measure." It is not found in the Vulgate edition, and lest anyone pretend Greek copies, it is not repeated by Chrysostom either.

units.la: SVPER hoc ter dominum rogaui, inquit, ut discederet a me, & dixit mihi: Sufficit tibi gratia mea, nam uirtus mea per infirmitatem perficitur.) Hactenus duas rationes expo-suit, quare non conducat sibi ut de seipso, sicuti faciebat pseudapostoli, glorietur. Iam ut con-filium Dei erga se in hac causa, cuius in posteriore ratione meminit, plenius exponat, subiungit quomodo se erga aduersarium suum angelo angelù Satanæ colaphizantem se, gesserit. Prin A cipiò dicit se confugisse ad preces. Nō est conatus suijpsius sese uiribus contra illum tueri, sed dominum ipsum precando implorauit. Super hoc, inquit, dominum παρεκάλεσα, id est, in auxilium inuocaui. Id enim sonat hoc loco uerbum παρακαλεῖν. Videbat ac sentiebat non hominis se, sed ipsius Satanæ malicia impeti: quare cesebat maiori sibi quàm sit humanum opus esse auxilio, ideoq; ad preces conuersus, opem domini implorauit. Ergo precibus contra aduersarios pugnare piorum est, magis quàm uindictam moliri.
units.tr: "Concerning this I besought the Lord three times," he says, "that it might depart from me, and he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." Thus far he has set out two reasons why it is not profitable for him to glory in himself, as the false apostles did. Now, in order to explain more fully God's counsel toward him in this matter, of which he spoke in the latter reason, he adds how he conducted himself toward his adversary, the angel of Satan who struck him. First he says that he took refuge in prayer. It was not an attempt by his own strength to defend himself against that one, but he implored the Lord himself by prayer. "Concerning this," he says, "I besought the Lord" (παρεκάλεσα), that is, I called upon him for help. For the word παρακαλεῖν in this place means exactly that. He saw and felt that he was attacked not by a man, but by the malice of Satan himself; therefore he yielded that he needed a help greater than human, and so, turning to prayer, he implored the help of the Lord. Therefore to fight against adversaries by prayer is the part of the godly, rather than to plan revenge.

units.la: Deinde meminit quid à domino petierit: ut discederet, inquit, à me. Petijt igitur liberari ab infestatore illo angelo Satanæ.
units.tr: Then he mentions what he asked of the Lord: "that it might depart from me," he says. He therefore sought to be freed from that troubler, the angel of Satan.

units.la: Licet quidem orare ad dominum, ut nos liberet à malis, quibus infestamur: uerùm poterit hic quæri quare Paulus petierit à domino, ut discederet à se aduersarius, à quo colaphizabatur, cum sciret illum ad hoc sibi datum, ut per eum humiliaretur ne propter reuelationũ excellentiam supra modum efferretur? Quis sanæ mentis petierit auferri à se antidotum, quod à medico contra uenenum accepit? Angelus autem ille Satanę quid aliud erat Paulo, quàm antidotum contra uenenum superbiæ?
units.tr: Indeed it is lawful to pray to the Lord that he deliver us from the evils by which we are troubled. But here it may be asked why Paul asked the Lord that his adversary, by whom he was struck, should depart from him, since he knew that this one had been given to him so that through him he might be humbled, lest he be exalted above measure because of the excellence of the revelations. Who of sound mind would ask that the antidote which he received from a physician against poison be taken away from him? Yet what else was that angel of Satan to Paul than an antidote against the poison of pride?

units.la: Respondeo. Fieri potuit ut consilium domini in ea causa non intelligeret, priusquà illud accepto à domino responso cognouisset. Verum esto, intellexerit etiam priusquam orare, nihil tamen orando admisit, quod domino B displicuerit: quandoquidem & ipse dominus cum passionis suæ calicem deprecaretur, utiq; id deprecatus sit, quod sibi ad totius humani generis salutem perferendũ esse sciebat. Quare non est ut culpemus Apostolum in eo, quod à domino ipso factum reprehendere non possumus.
units.tr: I answer. It may have happened that he did not understand the counsel of the Lord in this matter before he learned it from the Lord's answer. But grant that he understood it even before he prayed; nevertheless in praying he did nothing that displeased the Lord, since the Lord himself, when he prayed against the cup of his passion, certainly prayed against what he knew he had to endure for the salvation of the whole human race. Therefore we need not blame the Apostle for that, which we cannot blame the Lord himself for having done.

units.la: Tertiò, addit etiam quoties hoc à domino petierit. Non semel tantum ac secundò, sed tertiò. Ter, inquit, dominũ rogaui. Existimo hoc non ita esse ab illo factum, quod non sæpius fuerit oraturus, nisi accepto responso frustra se hoc petere intellexisset, sed quod ab ulterio re instantia oraculo domini post tertiam precationē fuerat auocatus. Et Christus ipse cum calicem passionis suæ deprecaretur, tertiò orauit, postea ab angelo confortatus destitit. Non est itaq; quod dicit: ter dominum rogaui, exponendum, sæpius dominũ rogaui. Cum semel rogasset, nec impetrasset, rogauit secundò, cum ne tum quidem quod petebat consequutus esset, orauit tertiò, atq; ibi per oraculũ Dei admonitus, cessauit. Nobis hic nõ prescribitur regula, quoties precari debeamus, quia exemplum hoc non est tale, quod unicuique competat, sed singulare. Generale uerò est quod Luc.18. semper orare, ac non deficere ab orando docemur.
units.tr: Thirdly, he adds also how many times he asked this of the Lord. Not once only, or a second time, but a third time. "Three times," he says, "I besought the Lord." I think he did not do this in such a way that he would not have prayed more often, unless he had understood by the answer that he was asking in vain, but because, after the third prayer, he was called away from more persistent insistence by the oracle of the Lord. And Christ himself, when he prayed against the cup of his passion, prayed three times, and afterwards, strengthened by an angel, he ceased. Therefore what he says, "I besought the Lord three times," is not to be explained as "I besought the Lord more often." Having asked once and not obtained, he asked a second time; when even then he did not obtain what he sought, he prayed a third time, and there, admonished by the oracle of God, he ceased. For us no rule is laid down here as to how often we ought to pray, because this example is not such as fits everyone, but is singular. What is general is what we are taught in Luke 18: that we should always pray and not faint in prayer.

units.la: ET dixit mihi, inquit.) Dominus uidelicet, ad quem orauerat. Quomodo loquutus sit illi dominus, an per uisionem, uel per inter-
units.tr: "And he said to me," he says. That is, the Lord to whom he had prayed.

units.la: nam spiritus sancti reuelationem, uel per ministeriũ alicuius sancti ac fidelis hominis, certò statui non potest: nec refert admodum ut modum sciamus quo loquutus sit illi dominus, sed satis est scire quid illi, & à quo sit responsum, & quod aures domini non sint surdæ ad preces fidelium, etiamsi petant per imprudentiam quæ noxia magis essent si darentur quàm utilia, nedum si utilia & necessaria petant.
units.tr: In what manner the Lord spoke to him, whether through a vision, or through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, or through the ministry of some holy and faithful man, cannot be determined with certainty; nor does it greatly matter that we know the manner in which the Lord spoke to him, but it is enough to know what answer was given to him, and by whom, and that the ears of the Lord are not deaf to the prayers of the faithful, even when they ask through ignorance things which would be more harmful if granted than useful, much less when they ask for things both useful and necessary.

units.la: SVFFICIT tibi gratia mea, inquit.) Hoc est, non est opus, ut auferatur abs te angelus Satanæ, quasi in cursu Apostolatus tui pergere nequeas, nisi ille à te discedat, sed quàtumuis ille insaniat, sufficit tamen gratia spiritus mei ad conseruandum te, & operandum per te, ad quæ missus es à me. Sic puto loquutum esse dominum de gratia spiritus sui quem Paulo dederat, & à quo ille dirigebatur, & per quê efficaciter in Apostolatu suo pergebat. Si Dauid, cum à Saule exagitaretur, orasset ad Deũ, ut discederet ille à se, cessaretq; ab improbitate persequendi se, respondisset q; illiDeus istis uerbis: Sufficit tibi gratia mea, utique nihil dixisset aliud, quàm sine ut persequatur te Saul quantum uolet, nihil enim efficiet, sed gratia mea qua te conseruo, abunde sufficit ad eneruandum illius conatus. Vsurpet isto sensu dictum hoc domini, quotquot à reprobis infestantur in hoc seculo, ut dicant & ipsi: Sæuiát impij quantum uoluùt, mihi gratia domini sufficit, per quam abunde contra illorum maliciam conseruari possum.
units.tr: "My grace is sufficient for you," he says. That is, there is no need that the angel of Satan be taken away from you, as though you could not continue in the course of your apostleship unless he departed from you; but however much he rages, the grace of my Spirit is sufficient to preserve you and to work through you, for which purposes I have sent you. Thus I think the Lord spoke concerning the grace of his Spirit which he had given to Paul, by which he was guided, and through which he effectively continued in his apostleship. If David, when he was harassed by Saul, had prayed to God that he might depart from him and cease from the wickedness of pursuing him, and God had answered him with these words, "My grace is sufficient for you," he would certainly have said nothing other than: let Saul pursue you as much as he wishes, for he will accomplish nothing, but my grace, by which I preserve you, is abundantly sufficient to weaken his attempts. Let all who are troubled by the reprobate in this age use this saying of the Lord in this sense, that they too may say: let the wicked rage as much as they will, the grace of the Lord is sufficient for me, through which I can be preserved abundantly against their malice.

units.la: NAM uirtus mea, inquit, per infirmitatem perficitur.) Græcè non est, διὰ ἀσθενείας, id est, per infirmitatem, sed ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ, id est, in infirmitate. Virtus Dei per infirmitatem Apostoli illustrabatur quidem, uerum nõ perficiebatur per illam, sed per spiritum Dei in illa. Reddit rationem, imò magis exponit, quomodo gratia ipsius suffecerit Paulo. Nam, inquit, ἡ ἐμὴ δύναμις μου. i. potentia mea, qua per Apostolatum tuum operor, ac te in omnis generis periculis conseruo, perficitur nõ in fortitudine tua, sed magis in infirmitate. Etenim si tuopte robore ad gerenda omnia, tuiq; conseruationem sufficeres, non esset locus potentiæ meæ. Iam quàto tu es infirmior, & pluribus periculis obnoxius, hoc plus est loci potentiæ meæ ad operandum in te, & ad conseruandũ te, ne tot periculis adobrutus pereas. Quare sine ut colaphizet te angelus ille Satanę, super quo rogas, ut discedat à te. Nihil efficiet, imò quo magis insanit, hoc plus occasionis ad illustrandã potentiam meam adferet: quemadmodum quo maior est morbus, hoc uirtus medicinæ reddi tur illustrior.
units.tr: "For my power," he says, "is made perfect through weakness." In Greek it is not διὰ ἀσθενείας, that is, "through weakness," but ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ, that is, "in weakness" [ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ]. The power of God was indeed displayed through the Apostle's weakness, but it was not made perfect through it; it was made perfect by the Spirit of God within that weakness. He gives a reason, or rather explains more fully, how his grace sufficed for Paul. For, he says, ἡ ἐμὴ δύναμις [ἡ ἐμὴ δύναμις], that is, my power, by which I work through your apostleship and preserve you in every kind of danger, is made perfect not in your strength but rather in your weakness. For if you were sufficient by your own strength to accomplish everything and to preserve yourself, there would be no room for my power. Indeed, the weaker you are and the more exposed to dangers, the more room there is for my power to work in you and to preserve you, lest you perish, overwhelmed by so many dangers. Therefore let that angel of Satan buffet you, about whom you ask that he depart from you. He will accomplish nothing; rather, the more he rages, the more occasion he will give to display my power, just as the greater the disease, the more distinguished the power of the medicine becomes.

units.la: Nos admonemur hac gnoma, qua uirtutem suam dominus in infirmitate perfici dicit, quo cõsilio suo Deus totum genus humanum tot infirmitatibus obnoxiũ reddere uoluerit, præsertim quod carnem nostram attinet, de qua dominus ipse testatur quod sit infirma. Ad hoc uideuidelicet,ut sit uelut officina quædam potentiæ ipsius, in illa & exerendæ & declarandæ, magis quàm in ipsis angelis. Huius admonea{A}mur quoties propriæ infirmitatis molestijs afficimur, ne unde ad laudandum prouidetiam erga nos creatoris nostri permoueri debeamus,inde ad impatientiam impellamur.
units.tr: We are admonished by this saying, in which the Lord says that his power is made perfect in weakness, as to the purpose for which God wished the whole human race to be subject to so many infirmities, especially as regards our flesh, of which the Lord himself testifies that it is weak. Namely, so that it may be, as it were, a certain workshop of his power, in which that power is both exercised and displayed, rather than in the angels themselves. We are reminded of this whenever we are troubled by the vexations of our own infirmity, so that we may not be driven to impatience from the very source from which we ought to be moved to praise the providence of our Creator toward us.

units.la: LIBENTISSIME igitur gloriabor potius super infirmitatibus meis, ut inhabitet in me uirtus Christi.) Quid ex accepto oraculo domini collegerit,ac quomodo per illud affectus sit,subiungit,dicens:Igitur, id est, cum hæc sit ratio afflictionum & infirmitatum mearum, ut propter eas inhabitet in me uirtus Christi, libentissime super illis gloriabor, tam abest, ut illarum me pudeat. Non dicit ante simpliciter,Libentissime igitur gloriabor,sed ,Libentissime igitur magis gloriabor super infirmitatibus meis. Potest uero illud μᾶλλον,id est,magis alió atque alió referri. Vtpote,magis quàm antea, uel, magis quàm ut me illarum pudeat, uel,magis quàm super uirtutib. ac factis meis. Posterior hic sensus magis placet. Videtur enim perstringere pseudapostolos. Quasi dicat, Glorientur illi super prærogatiuis suis, dignitatibus,uirtutibus,ac factis,ego magis, idque libentissime gloriabor super infirmitatibus meis. Quare ? uel,ad quid?
units.tr: "Most willingly therefore I will glory rather in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me." He adds what he gathered from the Lord's oracle and how he was affected by it, saying: "Therefore," that is, since this is the reason for my afflictions and infirmities, that on account of them the power of Christ may dwell in me, I will most willingly glory in them, so far is it from being the case that I am ashamed of them. He does not say simply, "Most willingly therefore I will glory," but "Most willingly therefore I will glory rather in my infirmities." The μᾶλλον, that is, "rather," can, however, be referred in different ways: namely, more than before, or more than that I am ashamed of them, or more than in my virtues and deeds. The last sense pleases me more, for it seems to strike at the false apostles. As if he said: let them glory in their prerogatives, dignities, virtues and deeds; I will glory more, and that most willingly, in my infirmities. Why? Or, to what end?

units.la: VT inhabitet,inquit,in me uirtus Christi.) Græcè est, ἵνα ἐπισκηνώση ἐπ' ἐμὲ, quod mihi non satis pertinéter uerti uidetur,ut inhabitet in me,sed uertendum esse potius,ut incumbat supra me,ut protegat me, ut me quasi quodà {B}tabernaculo obumbret. Meo iudicio non loquitur de inhabitatione, sed magis de protectione & operatione uirtutis Christi. Vt incúbat supra me uirtus Christi, inquit. Ergo nisi gloriarus esset in infirmitatibus suis, non protexisset ipsum uirtus Christi? Sic apparet. Verum colligendum est ad hunc modum. Libentissime igitur gloriabor potius in infirmitatibus, quàm cum pseudapostolis in uirtutibus meis,ne destituar uirtute Christi. Ergo uirtute Christi destituuntur, qui de proprijs uirtutibus gloriantur.
units.tr: "That the power of Christ may dwell in me." In Greek it is ἵνα ἐπισκηνώση ἐπ' ἐμέ [ἵνα ἐπισκηνώση ἐπ' ἐμέ], which seems to me not quite appropriately rendered "that it may dwell in me," but should rather be rendered "that it may rest upon me, that it may protect me, that it may overshadow me as with a tabernacle." In my judgment he speaks not of indwelling but rather of the protection and working of Christ's power: "That the power of Christ may rest upon me," he says. Therefore, unless he gloried in his infirmities, would the power of Christ not have protected him? So it appears. But the conclusion should be drawn in this way: "Most willingly therefore I will glory rather in infirmities than with the false apostles in my virtues, lest I be deprived of the power of Christ." Therefore those who glory in their own virtues are deprived of the power of Christ.

units.la: QVAMOBREM placeo mihi in infirmitatibus,inquit,in contumelijs, in necessitatibus,in persequutionibus, in anxietatibus pro Christo.) Placere sibi & gloriari coniuncta sunt. Nemo enim sibi displicens de seipso gloriatur: ac rursus nemo de seipso glorians, sibi displicet. Significat igitur gloriari se de infirmitatibus suis non obiter ac simulanter, sed prorsus ex animo, sic ut placeat sibi in illis. Et ut exponat quid per infirmitates suas intelligat, subiungit in contumelijs, in necessitatibus,in persequutionibus, in anxietatib. pro Christo,toleratis uidelicet. Per se parum iucunditatis ac præstantiæ habet, unde sibi placere quis queat,contumeliæ,necessitates,persequutiones,& anxietates,sed magis plurimum molestiæ ac contemptus: quare non simpliciter dicit, in contumelijs, in necessitatibus,in persequutionibus, in anxietatibus, sed addit pro Christo. Qua in re uides q eodé sint affectu erga Christū præditi apóstoli Act.5. de ceteris apostolis legitimus ad hūc modum: Et illi quidem ibant gaudentes à conspectu concilij, quod digni habiti essent, ut pro nomine eius contumelia afficerentur. Illis magnæ dignitatis loco erant contumeliæ pro Christi nomine illatæ,sic ut propter illas admodum gauderet. Paulo pariformiter erga Christū affecto tanti erant,ut sibi placeret in illis. Hunc in illis animum gignebat amor,quo erga Christum ardebant,cuius tanta uis erat, ut quæ carni suntacerbissima,spiritui fierent dulcissima: & quæ in mundo sunt ignominiosissima & infelicissima, ipsis essent gloriosissima & felicissima. De necessitatibus & anxietatibus dictum est supra cap. 6. Contumeliæ & persequutiones notæ sunt. Cótumelias priore loco posuit,respiciens ad angelum Satanæ à quo contumelijs,calumnijs,blasphemijs, probris ac conuicijs perinde atq; colaphis cædebatur.
units.tr: "Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities," he says, "in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ." To take pleasure in oneself and to glory are joined together. For no one who is displeased with himself glories in himself; and again, no one who glories in himself is displeased with himself. He means, therefore, that he glories in his infirmities not casually or in pretence, but altogether from the heart, so that he takes pleasure in them. To explain what he understands by his infirmities, he adds: "in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses, endured for Christ," of course. In themselves, reproaches, necessities, persecutions and distresses have little pleasantness or excellence by which anyone could take pleasure in himself, but rather much annoyance and contempt. Therefore he does not simply say "in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses," but adds "for Christ." In this you see that the apostles, endowed with the same affection toward Christ, are described thus in Acts 5: "And they indeed went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to be dishonoured for his name." For them, reproaches inflicted for the name of Christ were a matter of great dignity, so that they rejoiced greatly on account of them. In the same way Paul, being affected toward Christ, valued these things so highly that he took pleasure in them. Love gave rise to this disposition, by which they burned toward Christ, and its power was such that things most bitter to the flesh became most sweet to the spirit, and things most shameful and unhappy in the world became to them most glorious and most happy. About necessities and distresses it was said above in chapter 6. Reproaches and persecutions are well known. He placed reproaches first, looking to the angel of Satan, by whom he was struck with reproaches, slanders, blasphemies, insults and abuse just as with blows.

units.la: CVM enim infirmus sum,inquit,tunc robustus sum.) Græcè est δύναλος εἰμι, id est, potens sum. In ipso oraculo rationem reddidit dominus,quare Apostolo gratia ipsius sufficiat, qd uidelicet uirtus ipsius in infirmitate perficiatur. Iam ipse quoq; Apostolus, quare placeat sibi in infirmitatibus suis, contumelijs uidelicet,necessitatibus,persequutionibus & anxietatibus,rationem reddit, dicens : Cum enim infirmus sum, tunc potens sum.
units.tr: "For when I am weak," he says, "then I am strong." In Greek it is δυνατὸς εἰμι [δυνατὸς εἰμι], that is, I am powerful. In the oracle itself the Lord gave the reason why his grace suffices for the Apostle, namely that his power is made perfect in weakness. Now the Apostle himself also gives the reason why he takes pleasure in his infirmities, namely reproaches, necessities, persecutions and distresses, saying: "For when I am weak, then I am powerful."

units.la: Videtur prorsus esse paradoxon quod dicit. Primum enim, quando non erat infirmus cum homo esset? Homo semper infirmus est. Apostolus homo erat infirmitati adhuc obnoxius.Ergo semper infirmus erat. Quid est igitur quod dicit: Cum infirmus sum,tunc robustus sum? Semper ergo robustus erat. Deinde cum infirmum esse,ac rursus esse potentem,idq; simul inter se sint oppositá, sic ut qui infirmus est,ob id non sit potens,quod est infirmus , & qui potens est,ideo non sit infirmus , quod est potens,uidetur contradictio esse in hisce uerbis:cum enim infirmus sum , tunc potes sum:
units.tr: What he says seems entirely a paradox. For first, when was he not weak, since he was a man? Man is always weak. The Apostle was a man still subject to infirmity; therefore he was always weak. What then is the meaning of "when I am weak, then I am strong"? So he was always strong. Next, since to be weak and again to be powerful are opposites, so that one who is weak is for that reason not powerful, and one who is powerful is for that reason not weak, there seems to be a contradiction in these words: "for when I am weak, then I am powerful."

units.la: Respondeo ad primum obiectum. Quemadmodū contumelias,necessitates,persequutiones & anxietates propter Christum illatas uocat suas infirmitates:ita tunc se dicit esse infirmum , quando contumeliis,necessitatibus, persequutionib.& anxietatibus afficitur.Qua re non debet quod dicit ad perpetuam humanæ naturæ infirmitatem trahi.
units.tr: I answer the first objection. Just as he calls the reproaches, necessities, persecutions and distresses inflicted for Christ's sake his infirmities, so he says he is then weak when he is afflicted with reproaches, necessities, persecutions and distresses. Therefore what he says should not be drawn out to the perpetual infirmity of human nature.

units.la: Ad alterum respondeo. Infirmum esse ac simul esse potentem alio atque alio respectu uidelicet, ut dicit ab Apostolo dici. Infirmum se dicit respectu eorum quæ à reprobis illata mala patiebatur:potentem uero respectu uirtutis Christi per quam in infirmitatibus suis confirmabatur & conseruabatur.Propter Christum infirmus reddebatur,per eundem Christū reddebatur potens. Quare nulla contradictio est in hisce uerbis : Cum infirmus sum,tunc potens sum. |Consimili ratione recte dicet Christianus: Cum stultus sum, tunc sapiens sum. Cum peccator sum, tunc iustus sum. Cū miser sum, tunc felix sum. Cum inglorius sum, tum gloriosus sum. Cū occidor, tum uiuificor. Diuersis ista respectibus absque ulla contradictione recte dicuntur non à quolibet, sed à Christiano, qui in mundo stultus, in Christo sapiens, in seipso peccator, in Christo iustus, propter carnis ærumnas miser, propter gratiam Christi felix, in mundo inglorius, in Christo gloriosus est, in carne occiditur, spiritu uiuificatur. In Christo constitutis sunt paradoxa ista uera omnia, extra Christum uero falsa.
units.tr: To the other I answer. To be weak and at the same time to be powerful is true in different respects, as the Apostle says. He calls himself weak with respect to the evils inflicted by the reprobate, which he suffered; but powerful with respect to the power of Christ, by which he was strengthened and preserved in his infirmities. He was made weak for Christ's sake, and by the same Christ he was made powerful. Therefore there is no contradiction in these words: "when I am weak, then I am powerful." By a similar reasoning a Christian may rightly say: When I am foolish, then I am wise; when I am a sinner, then I am righteous; when I am wretched, then I am happy; when I am without glory, then I am glorious; when I am killed, then I am made alive. These things are rightly said, without any contradiction, in different respects, and not by just anyone but by a Christian, who in the world is foolish but in Christ is wise; in himself is a sinner but in Christ is righteous; on account of the miseries of the flesh is wretched but on account of Christ's grace is happy; in the world is without glory but in Christ is glorious; in the flesh is killed but in the Spirit is made alive. For those established in Christ all these paradoxes are true, but outside Christ they are false.

units.la: Factus sum insipiēs gloriando. Vos me coegistis.
units.tr: I have become foolish in boasting; you have compelled me.

units.la: Nam ego debueram à uobis commendari. Nulla enim in re inferior fui summis Apostolis, tametsi nihil sum. Signa quidē Apostoli peracta sunt inter uos cū omni patientia & signis & prodigiis & potentibus factis. Nam quid est, in quo fuistis inferiores ceteris Ecclesijs, nisi quod ipse ego nō fuerim uobis onerosus? Condonate mihi hanc iniuriam. Ecce tertio propensus animo sum, ut ueniam ad uos, nec ero uobis onerosus. Nō enim quæro quæ uestra sunt, sed uos. Non enim debent filij parentibus recōdere, sed filijs parētes. Ego uero libentissimè impendam & expendar pro animabus uestris, licet uberius uos diligens minus diligar.
units.tr: For I ought to have been commended by you. In nothing was I inferior to the chief apostles, though I am nothing. The signs of an apostle were indeed wrought among you with all patience, by signs and wonders and mighty deeds. For in what were you inferior to the other churches, except that I myself was not a burden to you? Forgive me this wrong. Behold, I am now minded to come to you for the third time, and I will not be a burden to you. For I do not seek what is yours, but you. For children ought not to lay up treasure for their parents, but parents for their children. I for my part will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls, although, loving you more abundantly, I may be loved the less.

units.la: Poterat insipiens uideri, quod tam multis gloriationis suæ causam prosequeretur. Excu sat se de eo, uerum sic ut quod cōcedit, dicens, Factus sum insipiens gloriādo, mox per translationem à se reijciat in ipsos Corinthios, imputās illis insipientiæ huius culpam, cum dicit: uos me coegistis. Quod agnoscit uiciofum esse, & notā habere insipientiē, quod tam prolixè gloriationibus suis immoratus esset, documento nobis esse debet, quàm non debeamus impudenter negare, si quid à nobis sic gē ritur, ut speciem uicij alicuius præferat, sed agnoscere quicquid id sit uicij. Agnitio quippe uicij multum de culpa illius deterit, impudēs uero pernegatio multum illi adijcit ponderis. Quod uero culpam tràsfert in Corinthios, & ipsum obseruandum uenit, omnibus uideli cet illis qui per alienam culpam inducti sunt, ut admittant quod sit uiciofum. Illi quemadmodum exemplo Pauli admonentur, ut quod uiciofē gesserunt candidè agnoscant, ita excu santur etiam, si ad tuendam innocētiam suam culpam non agnoscant, sed in authores illius reijciant. Obserua interim, quod non simpliciter dicit, uos mihi occasionem dedistis, & uos in causa estis, sed, uos me coegistis. Græcè est, ἀναγκάσεις, id est, necessitatem mihi instalistis.
units.tr: He might seem foolish, since he pursued the cause of his boasting at such length. He excuses himself for it, but in such a way that, while he concedes it, saying, "I have become foolish in boasting," he at once shifts the blame by a transfer onto the Corinthians themselves, imputing the guilt of this folly to them when he says, "you have compelled me." That he acknowledges it to be a fault, and to bear the mark of folly, that he dwelt so long on his boasts, ought to be a lesson to us: we must not shamelessly deny it if anything done by us bears the appearance of some vice, but must acknowledge whatever vice it is. For the acknowledgment of a fault greatly diminishes its guilt, whereas shameless denial adds much weight to it. But that he transfers the blame onto the Corinthians is also to be noted: it seems to be for all those who are led on by another's fault to admit that it is a vice. Just as they are admonished by Paul's example to frankly acknowledge what they have done wrongly, so they are also excused, if, in order to defend their innocence, they do not acknowledge the fault but throw it back on its authors. Observe meanwhile that he does not simply say, "you gave me occasion, and you are the cause," but "you have compelled me." The Greek is ἀναγκάσεις [ἀναγκάσεις], that is, "you have imposed necessity upon me."

units.la: A Nulla externa ui coegerat ipsum, sed sic se gesserat, ut ipsi necesse esset, materiā hāc gloriatio nis præter animi sententiā ingredi & tractare.
units.tr: No external force had compelled him, but he had so conducted himself that it became necessary for him to enter upon and handle this matter of boasting, contrary to his own inclination.

units.la: NAM ego debueram à uobis commendari, inquit.) Exponit quomodo se coegerint. Quod uidelicet se non commendauerant ipsi sicuti debuerant. Quasi dicat, Si uos me commedassetis sicuti debebatis, nulla mihi fuisset necessitas commendandi meipsum. Cum id non feceritis, necessitas tuendi Apostolatus mei ad hanc me proprię gloriationis insipientiam adegit, cuius culpa in uobis residet. Ergo ufqueadeo necessarium ducebat Apostolus, ut commendaretur, hoc est, in existimatione competenti apud fideles haberetur, ut cum id nō fieret à Corinthijs, existimationem suijpse gloriando tueretur. Hoc faciens non inanem gloriam, sed Apostolatus sui efficaciam ac frū ctū quærebat. Deinde uidemus hoc loco, ubi quis non facit quod debet, cogi alios ut id faciant, & esse illum in culpa, si qui id faciunt, uicij aliquid admittant. Vt exempli gratia. Si legitimus pastor oues fidei suæ commissas non pascat, cogitur quisquis neglectarum ouium domino fidelis est, officium ac curam pascendi subire: quod si id uiciofum & temerarium uidetur, in culpa est pastor, qui quod ex officio facere debebat, non facit, non is, qui deser tarum ouium saluti ac commodis domini sui consulere uoluit.
units.tr: "For I ought to have been commended by you," he says. He explains how they compelled him: namely, that they had not commended him as they ought. As if he were saying: if you had commended me as you were bound to do, there would have been no necessity for me to commend myself. Since you have not done so, the necessity of defending my apostleship has driven me to this folly of boasting about myself, the fault for which lies with you. Therefore the apostle thought it so necessary to be commended, that is, to be held in due esteem among the faithful, that when the Corinthians did not do this, he defended his standing by boasting of himself. In doing so he sought not empty glory but the efficacy and fruit of his apostleship. Next we see here that when someone does not do what he ought, others are compelled to do it, and that he is at fault, while those who do it admit some vice. For example: if a lawful minister does not feed the sheep committed to his faith, whoever is faithful to the neglected sheep is compelled to take up the office and care of feeding them. But if this seems a vice and a rash act, the fault lies with the minister who does not do what he ought to do from his office, not with the one who wished to provide for the safety and welfare of the abandoned sheep of his Lord.

units.la: NVLLA enim in re, inquit, inferior fui summis apostolis, tametsi nihil sum.) Poterat audire, Commendassemus te, si par esses magnis illis Apostolis, qui post te uenerunt. Quare quod te non commendauimus, non nobis, sed tibijpsi imputare debes. Occupatione igitur cauet ne tale quid illi regerere possint, dicēs: Nulla enim in re inferior fui summis apostolis. Hoc illis iam secundò inculcat. Nam supra quoq; capite præcedenti dixit: Arbitror enim me nihilo inferiorem fuisse τῶν ὑπερλίαν sολῶν, id est, illis qui plus quàm ualde sunt apostoli, quemadmodnm & hic dicit. Idem ergo cum sit utrobique sensus, non est ut illum denuò ponamus.
units.tr: "For in nothing," he says, "was I inferior to the chief apostles, though I am nothing." They could have heard: "We would have commended you, if you were equal to those great apostles who came after you. Therefore, that we did not commend you, you must impute not to us but to yourselves." He therefore takes care, by anticipation, that they cannot throw such a thing back at him, saying: "For in nothing was I inferior to the chief apostles." He presses this on them a second time. For he also said in the preceding chapter: "For I consider that I am not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles" [τῶν ὑπερλίαν ἀποστόλων], that is, those who are apostles more than exceedingly, as he says here too. Since the sense is the same in both places, we need not set it out again.

units.la: Erát igitur Corinthij culpabiles in eo quod Apostolū nō cōmendabát, cū nulla in re summis esset apostolis inferior, tū demū extra culpam futuri, si inferiorem eum esse comprobare potuissent. Cōsimili modo culpabiles esse mus, quotquot hodie titulares illos episcopos, ecclesiarum dominos, haud commendamus, si illi nulla essent in re ueris episcopis inferiores. Iam cum ab illis ... dissideant, sic ut ueraciter cōmendari nequeant, extra culpam sumus nos, ipsi uero in culpa sunt, quod pro ueris episcopis non agnoscuntur.
units.tr: The Corinthians were therefore at fault in that they did not commend the apostle, since he was in nothing inferior to the chief apostles; they would have been free of blame only if they could have shown him to be inferior. In a similar way, we are blameless, as many as do not commend today those titular bishops, lords of churches, if they are in nothing inferior to true bishops. Since they differ from them ... in such a way that they cannot truly be commended, we are without fault, but they themselves are at fault, in that they are not recognised as true bishops.

units.la: Illud, tametsi nihil sum, bifariam accipi potest. Primùm, ut nihil se esse agnoscat & fateatur, si extra Apostolatus à domino accepti cminētiam & uirtutem spiritus Christi in ipso operantem consideretur. Hoc sensu rectè ueterūt interpretes, tametsi nihil sum. Hoc dicēs omnem gloriam Apostolatus sui à se in ipsum dominum reijcit, ne hanc sibijpsi tàtopere gloriando quæsisse videatur. Deinde, vt non dicat se nihil esse, sed, etiamsi nihil sit, sicuti de ipso censebant pseudapostoli, nihilo tamé inferiorem esse se illis, qui plusquam valde sunt apostoli. Si hoc sensu dicit ὑστερήκα, vertendum non est, tametsi nihil sum, sed, etiâsi nihil sim. Quasi dicat, Quèadmodû me nonnulli ex vobis, magnis illis apostolis collatû nihil esse iactant. Sic posterior hic sensus percócessionem esset expressus. Priorem alij, alij posteriorem amplectuntur. Meo iudicio parum refert vtrû accipiamus, tametsi prior mihi magis arridet. Quèadmodû nec in eo periculi aliquid est; quod particulam hanc vulgatus interpres cû sequentibus, Erasmus vero cum praecedentib. coniunxit.
units.tr: The words "though I am nothing" can be taken in two ways. First, that he acknowledges and confesses that he is nothing, if he is considered apart from the eminence of the apostleship received from the Lord and the power of the Spirit of Christ working in him. In this sense the interpreters have rightly rendered it, "though I am nothing." By saying this he refers all the glory of his apostleship away from himself and onto the Lord himself, lest he should seem to have sought it for himself by boasting so greatly. Second, that he does not say that he is nothing, but "even if I am nothing," as the false apostles judged of him, yet that I am in no way inferior to those who are more than exceedingly apostles. If he uses the verb ὑστέρηκα [ὑστέρηκα] in this sense, it should not be rendered "though I am nothing," but "even if I am nothing." As if he were saying: "just as some of you boast that I am nothing when compared with those great apostles." In this way the latter sense would be expressed with concession. Some embrace the former, others the latter. In my judgment it matters little which we take, although the former pleases me more. Nor is there any danger in this, whether the Vulgate translator joined this particle with what follows, or Erasmus with what precedes.

units.la: Nobis hic cogitandum est quid reputandû sit homo extra Christum, quantumuis sit potens, diues, sapiens, & iustus. Paulus homo erat. Verùm quid est homo? inquit propheta. Ebræus erat, Israelita ac semen Abrahæ erat, & præterea pharisæus fuerat, ac præcipuus legis æmulator, qua de re vide Phil. 3. Hæc tamé omnia illic reputat vt stercora, hic nihil esse dicit. Quid minus nihilo? Seruiat hæc cogitatio ad humiliandum carnis typhum.
units.tr: Here we must consider what is to be reckoned of a man outside Christ, however powerful, rich, wise and righteous he may be. Paul was a man. But what is man? says the prophet. He was a Hebrew, an Israelite and seed of Abraham, and moreover had been a Pharisee and a chief zealot of the law; on this matter see Phil. 3. Yet there he reckons all these things as dung, and here he says he is nothing. What is less than nothing? Let this thought serve to humble the pride of the flesh.

units.la: SIGNA quidem Apostoli, inquit, perácta fuerût inter vos, cû omni patiētia, & signis, & prodigijs, & potentibus factis.) Quia nihilo le summis illis apostolis inferiorem esse dixit, subijcit illius comprobationem ex ijs quæ Corinthi tanquam verus Christi Apostolus gesserat, quæ ipsi Corinthij, tum inter ipsos gesta essent, ignorare non poterant. Sic dicit: Signa quidem Apostoli perácta fuerunt inter uos. Signa hic uocat certa indicia, de vero Christi Apostolo testantia. Moderatè autem non dicit, peregi, sed, perácta fuerunt inter uos, ne quid hic sibi vindicare videatur, quasi quicquam illorum suapte virtute peregerit. Quę erant autem illa signa?
units.tr: "Indeed the signs of an apostle," he says, "were wrought among you, with all patience, and by signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds." Because he said that he was in no way inferior to those chief apostles, he adds the proof of this from the things he did at Corinth as a true apostle of Christ, things which the Corinthians themselves, since they were done among them, could not be ignorant of. So he says: "The signs of an apostle were indeed wrought among you." Here he calls signs certain indications that bear witness to a true apostle of Christ. He does not say modestly, "I wrought," but "were wrought among you," lest he seem to claim for himself anything of those works as if he had accomplished them by his own power. But what were those signs?

units.la: CVM omni patientia, inquit, & signis, & prodigijs, & potentibus factis.) Duo genera signorum ponit, quibus Apostolatus ipsius inter Corinthios, quemadmodum & alijs locis obsignatur ac declaratus fuit. Prius est omnis generis afflictionum tolerantia, quam uocat hic omnem tolerantiam. Omnis toleratia est, qua quicquid aduersi propter Christum accidit, constanter toleratur. Hanc suprà quoq; cap. 6. primo loco inter ea recensuit, quibus sese in omnibus tanquam Christi ministrum commendabat, dicens: Sed in omnibus commendamus nosipsos ut Dei ministros, in multa tolerantia, in afflictionibus, &c. Signum hoc veri Apostoli non est simpliciter in tolerantia malorum, sed in tolerantia qua propter Christum omnis generis mala alacri animo perferuntur. Aliàs habet & Satan suos martyres. Posterius signum tribuit signis, prodigijs, & potentibus factis, quæ per ipsum virtute & operatione spiritus
units.tr: "With all patience," he says, "and by signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds." He sets down two kinds of signs by which his apostleship among the Corinthians was attested and declared, as also in other places. The first is endurance of afflictions of every kind, which he here calls all patience. This is all patience, by which whatever adversity befalls on account of Christ is endured steadfastly. He also listed this above, in chapter 6, first among those things by which he commended himself in all things as a minister of Christ, saying: "But in all things we commend ourselves as ministers of God, in much patience, in afflictions," and so on. This sign of a true apostle lies not simply in patience under evils, but in patience by which every kind of evil is borne with a willing mind for the sake of Christ. Otherwise Satan too has his martyrs. The second sign he assigns to signs, wonders and mighty deeds, which were wrought through him by the power and working of the Spirit

units.la: Christi fuerat perácta inter Corinthios. Signa intelligit hic miracula, qualia erant restitutiones morbidorum, cęcorum, claudorum, & leprosorum, expulsiones dæmonum, & excitationes mortuorum. Nec alia intelligit per τέρατα & δυνάμεις, id est, portenta & virtutes aut potentias. Miracula illa quæ per apostolos diuina fūt operatione ædita, signa ob id vocantur, quod significabant doctrinam Euangelij, cui erant annexa, cœlitus esse à Deo missam in mundū; deinde & qualitate sua quosuis admonebant, esse illam missam ad salutem generis humani. τέρατα, id est, portenta & prodigia ob id vocantur, quod praeter consuetum ordinem naturæ fiebant, erantq; instar monstrorum. δυνάμεις vocabantur, quod nonnisi singulari potentia Dei gerebantur. Sic diuersis respectibus eadem miracula signa, prodigia, & potentiae appellantur.
units.tr: The works of Christ had been performed among the Corinthians. Here he means by signs miracles of the kind that were the restoring of the sick, the blind, the lame and the lepers, the casting out of demons, and the raising of the dead. By portents and powers [τέρατα and δυνάμεις] he means nothing other than these, that is, portents, and virtues or powers. The miracles that were wrought through the apostles by divine operation are called signs because they signified that the doctrine of the gospel, to which they were attached, had been sent into the world from heaven by God; and then, by their very nature, they reminded everyone that it had been sent for the salvation of mankind. They are called portents and prodigies [τέρατα] because they happened outside the customary order of nature and were like monsters. They are called powers [δυνάμεις] because they were performed only by the singular power of God. So the same miracles are called signs, prodigies and powers, according to different points of view.

units.la: Posterius hoc signorum genus unde Apostolus Christi cognoscitur, non est simpliciter situm in miraculosis factis, sed in miraculis, prodigijs, & potentijs, quæ Christi sint & inter falsa computari nequeat. Alioqui & de Antichristo, apostolo Satanæ 2. Thes. 2. legitur, quod adventus ipsius sit insignis, prodigijs & potentijs, verum additur, mendacibus, quæ sint secundum operationem Satanæ, qui mendax est ab initio. Mendacium signorum & operationum Satanæ plenus iam olim est Papatus Romanus.
units.tr: This latter kind of sign, by which the apostle of Christ is recognised, does not consist simply in miraculous deeds, but in miracles, prodigies and powers which belong to Christ and cannot be counted among false ones. Otherwise, it is also read of the Antichrist, the apostle of Satan, in 2 Thessalonians 2, that his coming is marked by signs, prodigies and powers; but it is added that they are lying ones, which are according to the working of Satan, who is a liar from the beginning. The Roman Papacy has long been full of the lying signs and works of Satan.

units.la: NAM quid est, inquit, in quo fueritis inferiores cæteris ecclesijs, nisi quod ipse ego non fui vobis onerosus? ) Sufficientiam signorum Apostolatus sui per collationem reliquarū ecclesiarū astruit. Quasi dicat, Inspicite reliquas ecclesias, quas cæteri plantarūt apostoli, de quibus admodū pseudapostoli gloriantur, & videte, nū in illis plusculum aliquid, quod ad veri Apostolatus comprobationem pertineat, repriatis, quod in vestra ecclesia desiderari queat. Et quoniam de re comperta loquitur summa cum fiducia, non dicit. Nihil est, in quo fueritis inferiores cæteris ecclesijs, sed per interrogationem vrgendo & instando, Nam quid est in quo cæterae vos ecclesię excellant, quod mi nisterium Apostolicum attinet? Quasi dicat, Sitis vosipsi iudices, num signa veri Apostoli plura & luculentiora in cæteris ecclesijs quàm in vestra reperiantur. Si nihil est in illis, quod in vestra desiderari possit, qd causæ est, qd adventicios illos apostolos me fastidito, tanto pere suspicitis & magnificatis?
units.tr: FOR what is there, he says, in which you were inferior to the other churches, except that I myself was not a burden to you? He establishes the sufficiency of the signs of his apostleship by comparison with the other churches. As if he were saying: Look at the other churches, which other apostles planted, and of which the false apostles boast so much, and see whether you find in them anything more, pertaining to the proof of a true apostleship, that could be wanting in your church. And since he speaks of a matter that is known, he speaks with great confidence, and does not say, "There is nothing in which you were inferior to the other churches," but, pressing and insisting by a question: For what is there in which the other churches surpass you, as far as the apostolic ministry is concerned? As if he were saying: Judge for yourselves whether more and clearer signs of a true apostle are found in the other churches than in yours. If there is nothing in them that could be wanting in yours, why is it that you so greatly admire and magnify those foreign apostles and despise me?

units.la: Ergo si ecclesia inferiorem se cæteris ecclesijs in ijs quæ uerum ac fidelem Christi ministrum coprobant reperiat, non immeritò Apostolum ac doctorem suum fastidit, & eos qui potiores sunt in opere domini præillo suspicit. Est autem ecclesia alio atq; alio modo cæteris vel inferior uel superior. Primò, in ijs quę doctrinam & reliqua ministerij specimina cognunt. In hisce nullis alijs ecclesijs cedebat ecclesia Corinthiorum. Quare magnam illorū curio.
units.tr: So if a church finds itself inferior to other churches in those things which prove a true and faithful minister of Christ, it is not without reason that it despises its apostle and teacher, and admires those who are more eminent in the work of the Lord. A church, however, may be inferior or superior to others in different ways. First, in those things which concern doctrine and the other specimens of the ministry. In these the church of the Corinthians yielded to no other churches. Therefore that curiosity and fickleness of theirs, by which they despised their apostle, must have been great.

units.la: {Rr} curiositate ac leuitatem fuisse necesse est, qua Apostolu suum fastidiebant. Deinde in fructibus legitimi ac sufficientis ministerij, qui à fidelibus requiruntur. In illis Corinthij inferiores erant ecclesijs Macedoniæ. Verùm cum illas quoq; plantarit Paulus, sua ipsorum culpa erant illis inferiores.
units.tr: Secondly, in the fruits of a lawful and sufficient ministry, which are required of the faithful. In these the Corinthians were inferior to the churches of Macedonia. But since Paul had planted those too, they were inferior to them through their own fault.

units.la: NISI quod ipse ego, inquit, non fui uobis onerosus.) Exceptio est, non ad veritatem causæ, sed ad sinistrum Corinthiorum iudiciu ac commodata. Etenim quod non fuerat ipsis onerosus, ad maiorem potius ipsius exi∫timatio nem quàm ad opinionem defectus facere poterat, nisi fuissent per pseudapostolos fascinati. Tale est & illud quod capite præcedenti dixit: Nũ peccaui, quod meipsum humiliaui, ut vos exaltaremini? quod gratuito Euangelium Dei prædicaui vobis? & quæ ibi sequuntur. Con simili modo nonnullis hodie ecclesijs dici potest: Quid est in quo defeceritis in causa ueræ religionis, cum Christum apud uos prædicaremus? Nisi forsan quod nulli annuli aurei digitos nostros amiciebant, nec ulla catena aurea ornati ac torquati incedebamus, neque sericis vestiebamur, quales post nos adepti estis episcopos, magnos dominos magis quàm veros pastores.
units.tr: UNLESS that I myself, he says, was not a burden to you. This is an exception, not one that goes to the truth of the case, but one adapted to the Corinthians' perverse judgement. For the fact that he had not been a burden to them could make them esteem him more highly rather than suspect any defect, unless they had been bewitched by the false apostles. Something similar is what he said in the preceding chapter: "Did I sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached the gospel of God to you free of charge?" and what follows there. In a similar way it can be said today to some churches: What is it in which you have failed in the cause of true religion, since we preached Christ among you? Unless perhaps it is that no golden rings adorned our fingers, nor did we walk about decked and adorned with golden chains, nor were we clothed in silks, such as you have obtained as bishops after us, great lords rather than true ministers.

units.la: CONDONATE mihi hac iniuriam, inqt.) Quasi dicat, Si iniuste factum est à me, quod onerosus uobis non fui, condonate mihi τὼ ἀδικί αν ταύτῳ, i. hanc iniusticiã. Nec iniuste egerat, nec petit serio, ut condonent sibi factum hoc tanq; iniustũ, sed accommodat se causæ quam agit, & hac ironia Corinthios haud parũ pungit. Solemus illa uti, quoties nos illis displicere videmus, quos amamus, & quib. optimè cõ sultum cupimus, ut ingratitudinem illorũ per stringamus. Sic dicimus: an in eo peccaui, qd te domi meæ tandiu alui, quod tato studio ad id honoris in quo es euexi? &c. Condona mihi hanc iniuriam, si tam es excors factus, ut non cogites quàm rebus tuis consulere voluerim. Habet hæc ironia ualdè salsam ingrati animi reprehensionem.
units.tr: PARDON me this wrong, he says. As if he were saying: If I have done wrong in not being a burden to you, pardon me this wrong. He had not acted wrongly, nor does he seriously ask that they pardon him for the deed as if it were wrong; but he adapts himself to the case he is pleading, and by this irony he stings the Corinthians not a little. We are accustomed to use such irony whenever we see those whom we love, and whom we most wish to be well advised, displeasing us, so that we may rebuke their ingratitude. So we say: Did I sin in that I fed you in my house for so long, or that I raised you with such zeal to the honour in which you now stand? etc. Pardon me this wrong, if you have become so foolish that you do not consider how much I have wished to look after your interests. This irony contains a very sharp rebuke of an ungrateful mind.

units.la: ECCE tertio, inquit, propensus animo sum, vt veniam ad vos, nec ero vobis onerosus.) Capite præcedenti cum dixisset, In omnibus sic me seruabam, ne cui essem onerosus, adiecit, atq; ita seruabo: Id iam denuo inculcat, ne animum ac consilium suum mutasse uideatur. Sic dicit: Ecce tertio propensus animo sum, vt veniam ad vos, nec ero vobis onerosus. Non dicit: Ecce tertio veniam, sed: Ecce tertio propensus animo sum, vt veniam ad uos. Adhuc enim incertus erat, uenturus ne ad eos esset vel secus. Quod numerum ternarium attinet, existimant quidam venisse eum antea ad eos, secundo & cum hæc scriberet, tertio venire ad eos constituisse. Non repugno. Videtur tamen non de aduentu suo ad eos siue primo, siue secundo, uel tertio, sed de proposito veniedi ad eos loqui, quo iam cũ ista scriberet, tertio Corinthum proficisci constituerit. De eiusmodi
units.tr: BEHOLD, he says, for the third time I am minded to come to you, and I will not be a burden to you. In the preceding chapter, when he had said, "In all things I have so kept myself that I should be a burden to no one," he added, "and so I will keep." He now presses this again, so that he may not seem to have changed his mind and purpose. He says: Behold, for the third time I am minded to come to you, and I will not be a burden to you. He does not say: Behold, for the third time I will come, but: Behold, for the third time I am minded to come to you. For he was still uncertain whether he would come to them or not. As for the number three, some think that he had come to them before, a second time, and that while writing this he had determined to come to them a third time. I do not object. It seems, however, that he speaks not of his coming to them, whether the first, second or third time, but of his intention of coming to them, which, as he was writing this, he had decided should be a third visit to Corinth. Of such an

units.la: propositolegimus 1. Corinth. ultimo, & supra cap. 1.
units.tr: purpose we read in 1 Corinthians 16, and above in chapter 1.

units.la: NEC ero uobis onerosus, inquit.) Atqui iá condonari sibi petijt hanc iniuriam, quod one rosus ipsis non fuerat. Quid est igitur quod iá denuò dicit, nec ero vobis onerosus? Quis ita condonari sibi petit admissum, vt mox idem constanter admissurum se, & non magis nõ am plius admissurum dicat? Respondeo, Duplex modus est condonandi aliquid. Primus est, quo condonamus delictum, adiecta hac conditione, ne tale quid in posterum admittatur amplius. Sic dicebat adulteræ dominus: Vade & iam amplius noli peccare, Iohan. 8. Hic condonandi modus seruandus est in remissione grauium peccatorum, flagiciorum ac scelerũ. Alter est, quo defectus leues, ac vicia non enormia sic condonamus, ut in homine illa aliàs non malo toleremus, etiamsi quotidie admittantur. Hoc genus condonandi locum habet in illis qui sic coiuncti sunt, vt leui de causa diffungi nec possint nec debeant, quales sunt coiuges, quorum alter alteri multa condonare cogitur, ne vinculum coniugij rumpatur.
units.tr: NOR will I be a burden to you, he says. And yet he had already asked them to pardon him this wrong, namely that he had not been a burden to them. What then is the point of his saying again, "nor will I be a burden to you"? Who asks pardon for a fault in this way, and then says that he will commit the same fault constantly, and not rather that he will not commit it any more? I answer: There are two ways of pardoning something. The first is that by which we pardon an offence on this condition, that such a thing is not committed again in future. So the Lord said to the adulteress: "Go, and sin no more," John 8. This manner of pardoning must be observed in the remission of grave sins, crimes and wickedness. The other is that by which we pardon slight faults and defects, which are not enormous, in such a way that we tolerate them in a man who is otherwise not bad, even though they are committed every day. This kind of pardoning applies to those who are so joined together that they can and ought not to be separated for a slight cause, such as spouses, one of whom is obliged to pardon the other many things, lest the bond of marriage be broken.

units.la: Ad posteriorem hunc condonandi modũ, non ad priorem pertinet quod Apostolus hic dicit, Condonate mihi hanc iniuriam, & tamè mox subdit, Ecce tertio propensus animo sum, ut veniam ad uos, nec ero uobis onerosus. Quasi dicat: Si hoc uos offendit, quod nulli ex vobis onerosus fui cum apud vos essem & egere, condonate id mihi ac tolerate me, quandoqui dem mutare non possum. Nam etiamsi tertio ad vos uenirem, adhuc nemini ex uobis onerosus essem.
units.tr: The apostle's words here, "Pardon me this wrong," belong to the second of these modes of pardoning, not the first; and yet he immediately adds, "Behold, for the third time I am minded to come to you, and I will not be a burden to you." As if he were saying: If this offends you, that I was a burden to none of you when I was with you and in need, pardon it to me and bear with me, since I cannot change. For even if I came to you a third time, I would still be a burden to none of you.

units.la: NON enim quæro quæ vestra sunt, inquit, sed vos.) Suprà capite præcedenti rationem assignauit, ob quam nulli Corinthiorum onerosus esse voluerit. Hanc videlicet, vt amputaret occasionem ijs qui cupiebant occasionem, ut in eo de quo gloriabantur, reperirëtur quèadmodum & ipse. Hic vero adhuc aliam ponit, dicens: Non enim quæro quæ vestra sunt, sed uos. Non est insolitum facere rem eandem plures ob causas. Prior ratio cócernebat pseudapostolos, posterior hæc affectum paternæ dilectionis, qua Corinthios prosequebatur, exprimit. Hoc enim illius ingenium est, ut magis filiorũ, qui pater est, quàm suis ipsius commodis studeat. Et id est non quærere quæ illorum sunt, sed ipsos. Dilectio non inhiat bonis dilectorum, quia non illa sed ipsos potius diligit. Quod quisq; diligit, id vnicè quærit, faluumq; esse cupit. Sic animatus erga Corinthios Paulus nolebat illis esse oneri, quia non bona illorum sed ipsos quærebat. Quærebat autem ipsos tanquam verus Christi Apostolus non pecuniarum, sed hominum piscator constitutus, & quærebat non ut sibi eos subijceret, sicuti facio bant, & hodie quoque faciunt pseudapostoli, sed vt Christo adduceret, adductosq; in gratia illius ac uera salute conseruaret. Vtinam intelligat fideles Christi, quid quærat qui ad ipsos veniunt legati Romani Pontificis, monachi, quæstuarij, & qui pasturas & episcopatus ipsorum ambiunt.
units.tr: "For I seek not what is yours, but you" (2 Cor. 12:14). Earlier, in the preceding chapter, he gave the reason why he did not want to be a burden to any of the Corinthians: namely, to cut off the opportunity of those who were looking for an opportunity, so that in the matter they boasted of they might be found just as he was. Here, however, he gives another reason, saying: "For I seek not what is yours, but you." It is not unusual for one thing to be done for several reasons. The first reason concerned the false apostles; this second one expresses the feeling of fatherly love with which he regarded the Corinthians. For it is the nature of a father to care more for his children than for his own advantage. And this is what it means not to seek what is theirs but them. Love does not covet the goods of those loved, because it loves not their goods but the people themselves. Whatever a person loves, he alone seeks and wishes to see safe. So Paul, disposed toward the Corinthians in this way, did not want to be a burden to them, because he sought not their goods but them. He sought them as a true apostle of Christ, appointed a fisher of men and not of money, and he sought them not so that he might subject them to himself, as the false apostles did and still do today, but so that he might bring them to Christ and keep them, once brought in, in his grace and true salvation. Would that the faithful of Christ understood what is sought by those who come to them as legates of the Roman Pontiff, monks, and pardon-sellers, and by those who court their pastorates and bishoprics.

units.la: Sed dices. Paulus gratuito prædicauit Euangelium Corinthijs, quia non quæ ipsorum erant, sed ipsos quærebat. Ergo qui non gratuito Christum prædicant, sed victum & amictū, ac quæ præterea necessaria sunt, ab illis quibus prædicant, accipiunt, non ipsos sed quæ ipsorum sunt quærunt. Respondeo. Sic colligendo damnamus no modo reliquos apostolos, qui de labore suo vixerunt, sed & doctrinam Pauli, quam tradidit 1. Cor. 9. imo ipsius Christi, q operarium cibo suo dignum esse dicit Matth. 10. Absit. Non sequitur si colligas ad hunc modum: Petrus à fidelibus, quibus prædicabat Euangelium, necessarios sumptus accepit, ergo non illos sed quæ ipsorum sunt quæsiuit.
units.tr: But you will say: Paul preached the gospel to the Corinthians free of charge because he sought not what was theirs but them. Therefore those who do not preach Christ free of charge, but receive food and clothing and whatever else is necessary from those to whom they preach, seek not them but what is theirs. I answer: by such reasoning we condemn not only the other apostles, who lived by their own labour, but also the teaching of Paul, which he delivered in 1 Cor. 9, and indeed the teaching of Christ himself, who says that a workman is worthy of his food (Matt. 10). Far be it. The inference does not follow if you argue in this way: Peter received necessary support from the faithful to whom he preached the gospel; therefore he did not seek them but what was theirs.

units.la: Aliud enim est accipere necessaria debita, ad hoc, ut porro labores ac prosis, & aliud quære re ut accipias, & inhiare bonis aliorum. Neque sic recte collegeris. Paulus gratuito prædicauit Corinthijs, quia non quærebat ipsorum bona sed ipsos, ergo si quid ab illis accepisset iam non ipsos, sed bona ipsorum quæsiuisset. Non sequitur. Vt quid ergo non & ipse accepit in quies? Respondeo. Non erat ipsi hoc tantum agendum, vt singularem in illos dilectionem declararet, sed simul cauendum erat, ne pseudapostolis, quos habebat improbissimos aduersarios, occasionem quærentibus occasionem permitteret.
units.tr: For it is one thing to receive necessary things that are owed, so that one may go on labouring and be useful, and another to seek to receive and to covet the goods of others. Nor would you reason rightly in this way: Paul preached to the Corinthians free of charge because he sought not their goods but them; therefore if he had received anything from them he would then have sought not them but their goods. That does not follow. But why then did he not also receive something from them? I answer: it was not his only aim to show his singular love for them; he also had to take care not to give the false apostles, who were his most wicked adversaries, an opportunity, since they were looking for an opportunity.

units.la: NON enim debent filij parentibus recondere inquit, sed filijs parentes. ) Diuino sic est & naturali ordine constitutum, vt parentes filijs, non vt filij parentib. quæ necessaria sunt, in futurum recondant. Non dicit autem simpliciter, Non thesaurizant, sed, non debent, i. nullo iure tenentur recodere parentib. Quare? Quia non est sic diuinitus constitutum, deinde, quia præstare hoc non possunt. Neq; enim loquitur de filijs adultis, & parentibus senio confectis, necessariaq; illorum sustentatione, ψ νόμω φιλαστ γυκ, sed de liberis nondum educat s, ac parentum illorum prouidentia, futuris ipsorum necessitatibus prospiciente. Cum ergo dicit, Non enim debent filij parentibus recondere, sed filijs parentes, reddit rationem, quare no quærat bona Corinthiorum sed ipsos, propterea vt delicet, quod sit ipsorum pater, patris aut non sit inhiare bonis liberorum, sed magis necessitatibus illorum quoad eius possit prospicere, etiamsi id sine magno suo detrimento facere nequeat. Vnde & subijcit:
units.tr: "For children ought not to lay up for their parents, but parents for their children" (2 Cor. 12:14). By divine and natural order it has been so established that parents lay up for their children what is necessary for the future, not children for their parents. He does not say simply, "they do not store up," but "they ought not," that is, they are bound by no right to lay up for their parents. Why? Because it has not been so ordained by God; and further, because they cannot provide it. For he is not speaking of grown children and parents worn out with old age, whose support is a matter of [οὐ νόμῳ φιλαστοργίας] by the law of natural affection, but of children not yet grown, whose parents' foresight provides for their future needs. So when he says, "For children ought not to lay up for their parents, but parents for their children," he gives the reason why he seeks not the goods of the Corinthians but them: namely, because he is their father, and a father does not covet the goods of his children but rather looks out for their needs as far as he is able, even if he cannot do so without great loss to himself. Hence he adds:

units.la: EGO vero libentissimè impendam, & expendar pro animabus vestris. ) Reperias nonnunquam parentes qui sint erga liberos suos prosus astorgi, & μισοτέκνοι magis quam φιλοτέκνοι, in quibus id quod in genere dixit, debere parentes recondere filijs, locum non habet, eo quod nulla cura de liberorum necessitatibus procurandis afficiantur, sed sic res suas agant, ut pauratiores sint ad accipiendum ab illis
units.tr: "I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls" (2 Cor. 12:15). You will sometimes find parents who are utterly unnatural toward their children, child-haters [μισοτέκνοι] rather than child-lovers [φιλοτέκνοι], in whom what he said in general, that parents ought to lay up for their children, has no place, because they are not concerned to provide for their children's needs, but manage their affairs so as to be more eager to receive from their children

units.la: quàm ad dandum, ad quem modum affecti erga Corinthios erat pseudapostoli, vitrici, non veri parentes. Horum respectu dicit, Ego vero libentissimè impendam, & expendar pro animabus vestris.
