Quasi dicat: Etiamsi reperias eiusmodi parentes, qui liberis suis ne tantillum quidem recondant, imo magis ad hoc sint pronpensi, ut ab illis accipiant, quos magistri vestri pseudapostoli imitantur, ego tamen, a quo estis in Christo geniti, sic sum erga vos animatus, vt libentissimè impendam mea omnia, imo ex pendar ipse totus pro animabus vestris. Signi ficat naturalem parentum storgiam erga liberos ipsorum citius deficere posse, quam suam erga eos quos in Christo genuit. Talis locus est & Esaiae quadragesimonono ubi ad Israelē dicit dns: An obliuisci potest mulier infantis sui, ut non miseretur filij vteri sui? Et tamen etiamsi illa oblita fuerit, ego tamen tui non obliuiscar.
units.tr: than to give to them. This was the disposition of the false apostles, the stepfathers, not true parents, toward the Corinthians. With regard to them he says: "I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls." As if to say: Even if you find parents of this kind, who do not lay up even the smallest thing for their children, and who are rather inclined to receive from them, the very people your teachers, the false apostles, imitate, I, by whom you have been begotten in Christ, am so disposed toward you that I will most gladly spend all that I have, indeed I will be spent myself entirely for your souls. He signifies that natural parental affection toward their children can fail more quickly than his own toward those whom he begot in Christ. Isaiah 49 has a similar passage, where the Lord says to Israel: "Can a woman forget her infant, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Yet even if she forgets, I will not forget you."

units.la: Excellentiam autem dilectionis suae erga eos in eo exprimit, quod non simpliciter dicit ἀπαρνίσω, sed addit, ἐκ ἀπαρνίσασθαι: ἀπαναλίσκω simpliciter sumptu facere & impedere aliquid, ἐκ ἀπαναλίσκωμαι vero, omnia sic expedere significat, vt prorsus nihil retineas, sed omnes tam vires quàm facultates insumas, reddarisque exhaustus totus.
units.tr: He expresses the excellence of his love for them in this, that he does not simply say [ἀναλώσω], "I will spend," but adds [ἐξαναλωθήσομαι], "I will be spent out." [ἀναλίσκω] means simply to spend or lay out something at cost, whereas [ἐξαναλίσκομαι] means to expend everything in such a way that you retain nothing at all, but use up all your strength and resources and are yourself wholly exhausted.

units.la: Quare vero paratus sit expendere omnia, in eo significat, quod addit, p animab. vestris.
units.tr: Why he is ready to spend everything he indicates in what he adds: "for your souls."

units.la: Quasi dicat Citius quàm patiar periclitari animas vestras, expendam pro illis omnia, & exhauriar prorsus. Hinc tamen nemo colligat, ergo poterat Apostolus animas Corinthiorum seruare, si seipsum pro illis expendisset, atq; ita nō solus Christus Seruator est animarum sed & Apostoli. Absit. Non dicit: Seruabo animas vestras, sed libentissimè expendar pro animabus vestris. Quasi dicat. Sic vos diligo vt si animarum vestrarum perditionem cum vitę meę dispendio cauere possem, libentissimè expendarem meipsum. Sic Rom. 9. optabat anathema esse à Christo pro Israelitis. Quis non cupi at charissimorum suorum pignorum vitam magnis pecuniae sumptibus redimere? Vnde tamen non sequitur: ergo possunt parentes vitam liberorum suorum pecunia redimere & à morte seruare. Aliud est velle facere si possis, & aliud posse.
units.tr: As if to say: Rather than suffer your souls to be endangered, I will spend everything for them and be utterly emptied. Yet no one should infer from this that the apostle could have saved the souls of the Corinthians if he had spent himself for them, and so that Christ alone is not the Saviour of souls but the apostles too. Far be it. He does not say, "I will save your souls," but "I will most gladly be spent for your souls." As if to say: I love you so much that, if I could prevent the destruction of your souls at the cost of my own life, I would most gladly give myself up. Likewise in Rom. 9 he wished to be accursed from Christ for the sake of the Israelites. Who does not wish to redeem the life of his dearest children at great expense of money? Yet it does not follow from this that parents can redeem their children's lives with money and save them from death. It is one thing to wish to do something if you can, and another to be able to do it.

units.la: LICET vberius vos diligens minus diligar inquit.) Tria dicit. Primum, quod diligat eos περισσοτέρως, id est, copiosius & abundantius. Aperit hic fontem omnis storgiae qua erga ipsos afficiebatur. Secundum, qd ab illis minus diligatur. Hoc non sine dolore conqueritur. Verum ea sors est impense amantium, ut plus diligentes minus diligantur. Hanc communem habent cum Deo, qui & ipse nos incomparabiliter diligens; minus à nobis diligitur. Verum hoc peruerso sumus ingenio ut quos adn odum diligere debebamus minus diligamus, & quos odisse conueniebat, impense diligamus, ut recte dicat Basilius in epistola quadam: ἐβά λως οἱ ἀνδρωποι ἐμισῶσι τὰς ἐχθίστους, ἢ φιλῶσι τὰς χείρονας. Tertiū: Neq; sic tamē impediri se, quo minus libentissimē totum se pro animab. ipso rum expedat. Ea videlicet erat abundantia dilectionis qua ipsos prosequebatur. Huius tanta vis est, vt omnia vincat, omnia deuoret ac cōcoquat, vnde extingui poterat, vt nō immerito dictum sit illud, Amor omnia vincit. Sanè id citiùs facit, quàm ut vincat seipsum.
units.tr: "Though loving you more abundantly, I may be loved less" (2 Cor. 12:15). He says three things. First, that he loves them [περισσοτέρως], that is, more copiously and abundantly. Here he reveals the source of all the affection with which he was moved toward them. Second, that he is loved less by them. He complains of this not without pain. But such is the lot of those who love intensely: the more they love, the less they are loved. Men share this with God, who, though he loves us beyond comparison, is loved less by us. But we are so perverse in our nature that we love less those whom we ought most to love, and love intensely those whom it would be fitting to hate, as Basil rightly says in a certain letter: men [ἐμισοῦσι...] hate their most hateful enemies, or love their worse ones. Third, that he is not thereby hindered from spending himself wholly and most gladly for their souls. Such was the abundance of the love with which he pursued them. Its power is such that it conquers all things, devours and digests all things; and yet it could be extinguished, so that the saying "love conquers all" is not without reason. Surely it does this more quickly than it conquers itself.

units.la: Sed esto, ipse nō grauaui uos, uerūm cū essem astutus dolo uos coepi. Nū per quenquam eorū quos misi ad uos, expilaui uos: Rogaui Titum, & unà cū illo misi fratrem. Num quid à uobis extorsit Titus: An non eodem spiritu ambulauimus: an non ijsdem uestigijs:
units.tr: "But grant it: I did not burden you myself, but, since I was crafty, I caught you by guile. Did I defraud you through any of those whom I sent to you? I asked Titus, and sent a brother along with him. Did Titus extort anything from you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not walk in the same footsteps?"

units.la: Vt erant sectatores pseudapostolorū admodum ad comminiscendum calumnias instructi, verosimile erat illos ad ea quæ iam dixit Apostolus maliciosè obiecturos ad hunc modum, οὐ μὲν ἐκ κατεβάρησας ὑμᾶς, ἀλλ' ὑπάρχων πανουργὸς δόλῳ τέτῳ ἐλαβες ὑμᾶς. Hoc est: Tu quidè non fuisti nobis oneri, uerūm cum sis astutus dolo nos isto coepisti, & in nassam tuam pellexisti. Huic cauillo occurrit dicens: Sed intelligo quid nonnulli inter uos dicat. Esto fuerim astutus, ad hoc non grauans uos, ut eiusmodi uos dolo caperem. Si sic sentitis, age num per quenquā eorū, quos ad vos post discessum me um misi, expoliaui uos: Etenim si non syncerè sed dolosè vobiscum in eo egi, quod neminem ex uobis grauaui, ad hoc ut uos inscarem & caperem, quibus postea dominarer, dolum eiusmodi post discessum meum cohibere non potui, quin proderem per illos, quos ad uos misi. Verùm vosipsos conuenio, an per quenquam eorū quos ad vos misi, aliquid ex vobis extorserim, vosq; expilauerim. Cum autem ne per illos quidem expilauerim uos, an non manifestum relinquitur, quod egerim uobiscum nullo dolo, sed syncerè ac candidè, dū nulli ex uobis onerosus esse uolui?
units.tr: Since the followers of the false apostles were very skilled at inventing slanders, it was likely that they would raise against him, in this way, the points the Apostle has just made: "Indeed, he did not burden you [οὐ μὲν ἐκ κατεβάρησας ὑμᾶς], but being crafty he caught you by this guile [ἀλλ' ὑπάρχων πανουργὸς δόλῳ τέτῳ ἐλαβες ὑμᾶς]." That is: "He was indeed no burden to us, but since he is crafty, he caught us by this trick and enticed us into his net." Paul meets this objection by saying: "But I understand what some of you are saying. Grant that I was crafty, and that by not burdening you I meant to trap you in this way. If you think so, then tell me: did I defraud you through any of those whom I sent to you after my departure? For if I did not deal with you sincerely but deceitfully, by not burdening any of you in order to ensnare you and catch you, so that I might afterwards lord it over you, then I could not have kept such a deceit hidden after my departure, but would have betrayed it through those whom I sent to you. But I appeal to you yourselves: did I extort anything from you through any of those whom I sent to you, and so defraud you? Since I did not defraud you even through them, is it not clear that I dealt with you without any guile, sincerely and openly, since I wished to be a burden to none of you?"

units.la: SED esto, inquit.) Cōcessionis figura est, quam tamen mox refellit, tam abest, ut hæc de se per affirmationem dicat. Concedit autem, quod maleuoli de facto suo cauillabātur, quo gloriam illius obscurarent. Id exprimit dicēs: Sed esto ipse non grauaui vos, uerūm cum essem astutus dolo uos coepi. Cum dicit: ipse nō grauaui vos, exprimit concessionem pseudapostolorum, qui quod negare non poterant fatebantur quidem, verùm sinistra interpretatione adiecta, odiosum reddebant dicentes, haud quidem ipse vos grauauit, uerum fecit hoc astutè, vt eiusmodi uos dolo caperet, sibique in posterum deuinctos redderet. Sic solet maleuoli. Quod negare non possunt, sinistris interpretationibus maliciosè obscurant. Est hoc frequentissimum apud eos, qui spiritu liuoris ducuntur. Sic Pharisæi cum gloriam ac lucem operum Christi ferre non possent, quo
units.tr: "But grant it," he says. This is a figure of concession, which he refutes at once; so far is he from saying these things about himself by way of affirmation. He concedes, however, what the ill-willed were carping about his conduct, by which they would obscure his glory. He expresses this in saying: "But grant it: I myself did not burden you, but, since I was crafty, I caught you by guile." When he says "I myself did not burden you," he expresses the concession of the false apostles, who admitted what they could not deny, but, by adding a malicious interpretation, made it hateful, saying: "He indeed did not burden you himself, but he did this craftily, so that he might catch you by guile and bind you to himself for the future." So the ill-willed do. What they cannot deny, they maliciously obscure with sinister interpretations. This is very common among those who are driven by a spirit of envy. Thus the Pharisees, since they could not bear the glory and light of Christ's works, carped by a sinister interpretation, since they could not deny that these things were done without manifest shamelessness, saying that they were done by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.

units.la: A niam ea negare sine manifesta impudentia ne quibant, per sinistram interpretationem cauil labantur, fieri illa per Beelzebub principe dæmoniorum. Nostris temporibus infinita maliciæ huius exempla in illis uidere licet, qui veritati Euāgelij Christi aduersantur. Verùm ne mini id mirū uideatur. Etenim si non Paulo tātum, sed & Christo ipsi malicia hæc negocium facere tentauit, non debet insolens videri si virus suū in nos quoq; effundat. Illi ipsi, qui per astuciam suā dolo maiores nostros circūuene runt, coeperunt, & in seruitutem omnium seruilissimam coniecerūt, quod ipsi faciunt, illius nos insimulant. Quàm omnis generis dolo coeperint ecclesias Romani Pontifices, episcopi, & monachi, obscurum erat, cum omnia essent caligine catholicæ ignorantiæ obducta, iá verò restituta ueritatis luce, uix quicquā magis est perspicuum.
units.tr: In our own times one can see countless examples of this malice in those who oppose the truth of the gospel of Christ. But let no one think this strange. For if this malice tried to do its work not only against Paul but against Christ himself, it should not seem unusual if it pours out its poison against us too. Those very men who, by their cunning, deceived our forefathers and cast them into the most servile slavery, accuse us of doing what they themselves do. How the Roman pontiffs, bishops and monks deceived the churches by every kind of guile was obscure while everything was clouded in the darkness of Catholic ignorance; but now that the light of truth has been restored, scarcely anything is more evident.

units.la: Tria hæc ex ordine subsequuntur, vbi locus datur pseudapostolis, dolus videlicet, captura, & dominium. Dolus varijs modis proponi tur imperitis, & incautis, in eo tamen conueni tur, quod omnis generis doli specie pietatis ac sanctimoniæ obuoluuntur, quo non modo la teant, sed & incautos fallant & capiant. Huc appositi sunt homines astuti, quibus in promptu est quidlibet fingere, simulare, ac dissimulare, quales nobis innumeros dedit ea natio, quæ ante Christum quoq; ad totius orbis primatum aspirauit. Quàm illi nos Germanos præcipuè dolo admodum insigni coeperint, causa imperij ad nos translati, si penitus inspiciatur, abunde declarat, ut ea quæ religionem concernunt taceam. Eo dolo capta est Germania, & vnà cum suo imperio Romanorum Pontificum libidinibus subiecta fefellerunt, coeperunt, suoque dominio insignem hanc nationē subiecerunt, quam nostra ætate dominus singulari beneficio ad libertatem reuocare digna tur, modò intelligant, qui in illa sunt principes ac magistratus.
units.tr: These three things follow in order, where room is given to the false apostles: guile, that is, trickery; capture; and domination. Guile is presented to the unskilled and the incautious in various ways, yet they agree in this, that every kind of deceit is wrapped in the appearance of piety and sanctity, so that it not only hides but also deceives and ensnares the unwary. Crafty men are suited to this, men who readily feign, simulate and dissemble anything. Such men that nation, which aspired even before Christ to the primacy of the whole world, has given us in countless numbers. How, with a guile especially remarkable, they began to take hold of us Germans, after the seat of empire was transferred to us, is abundantly clear if one looks closely, not to mention what concerns religion. By this guile Germany was captured, and together with its empire it was subjected to the lusts of the Roman pontiffs. They deceived, they began to rule, and they reduced this distinguished nation to their dominion. In our own age the Lord deigns, by a singular benefit, to call it back to liberty, provided that those princes and magistrates who are in it understand this.

units.la: NVM per quēquam eorum, inquit, quos misi ad vos, expilaui vos?) Græcè est, ἐπλεονέκτησα ὑμᾶς, vulgat interpres vertit, circūueni uos. Et Erasmus suprà cap. 9. πλεονεξίαν vertit fraudationem, vbi illam cupiditatē plura habendi significare diximus. Sic refutat cauillum male uolorum. Poterat dicere, Atqui non modò ipse nihil, sedneq; per quenquam eorū quos misi ad vos, aliquid à vobis accepi. Verum quo conscientias ipsorum appellet, confidenter dicit, Num per quenquam eorum quos misi ad uos expilaui vos? Quasi dicat: Age dicite vos ipsi, si dolo prædicaui uobis gratuito, quo caperem uos, & postea per meos commodius uos expilarem, an per quenquam eorum hoc fecerim, quos misi ad uos?
units.tr: "Did I defraud you through any of those whom I sent to you?" The Greek is ἐπλεονέκτησα ὑμᾶς [I defrauded you]; the Vulgate translator renders it "circumvented you," and Erasmus, above in chapter 9, renders πλεονεξίαν as "defrauding," where we said that this word signifies the desire to have more. So he refutes the calumny of the ill-willed. He could have said: "Indeed, not only did I take nothing, but neither did I receive anything from you through any of those whom I sent to you." But in order to appeal to their consciences, he says confidently: "Did I defraud you through any of those whom I sent to you?" As if to say: "Come, tell me yourselves: if I preached the gospel to you freely in order to catch you, and afterwards to fleece you more conveniently through my men, did I do this through any of those whom I sent to you?"

units.la: ROGAVI Titum (verti poterat, hortatus sum Titum) & unà cum illo misi fratrem. Num quid à uobis extorsit Titus? An non eodem spiritu ambulauimus? an non ijsdem uestigijs?) Suprà capite octauo dixit Titum se esse adhortatum, tatum,ut quemadmodum ante coepisset,ita & consummaret coeptū apud Corinthios opus. Huius hic mentionem facit,dicens : Hortatus sum Titum, ubi subintelligenda sunt quę iam ex cap.8.citauimus.
units.tr: "I asked Titus" (it could be translated "I exhorted Titus") "and sent a brother along with him. Did Titus extort anything from you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? In the same footsteps?" In chapter eight he said that he had exhorted Titus so that, just as he had begun earlier, so he would also complete the work he had started among the Corinthians. Here he mentions this, saying: "I exhorted Titus," where what we cited above from chapter 8 must be understood.

units.la: ET una cum illo misi fratrem,inquit.) Misérat cum Tito duos , quare quæsierit quisquam,quare unius tantum mentionem faciat, & utrum ex illis intelligat. Verum facilis est est reponsio. Duos quidem cum Tito miserat, uerum unus ex illis magis Ecclesiarum, quàm ipsius fuerat legatus, sicuti capite octauo uidere licet. Quare unius tantum recordatur,idque alterius,quem non ecclesiæ,sed ipse misérat.
units.tr: "And sent a brother along with him," he says. He had sent two with Titus. Someone may ask why he mentions only one, and which of the two he means. But the answer is easy. He had indeed sent two with Titus, but one of them had been the envoy of the churches rather than of Paul himself, as can be seen in chapter eight. So he recalls only one, and that the one whom he himself had sent, not the one sent by the churches.

units.la: NVM quid à uobis extorsit Titus?) Atqui ad hoc illum miserat, ut pecunias ab ipsis acciperet. Verum uon ut sibi,nec ut ipsi,sed ut in usus sanctorū acciperet. Deinde ut acciperet non ab inuitis, sed à spontaneis, idq; non ad παλιστέλμ,sed ad ευλογίαν. Quare nihil hic actū fuit à Tito,quod contra ipsius esset propositū.
units.tr: "Did Titus extort anything from you?" Yet he had been sent for this purpose, to receive money from them; but not for himself, nor for his own benefit, but to receive it for the use of the saints. Further, he was to receive it not from the unwilling but from the willing, and that not as πλεονεξίαν [covetousness] but as εὐλογίαν [a blessing]. Therefore nothing was done by Titus here that was contrary to his purpose.

units.la: AN non eodem spiritu ambulauimus, inquit? an non ijsdem uestigijs?) Hoc est: An non ille erga uos perinde animatus fuit atque ego? An non pariformiter non uestra quæsiuit,sed uos? Sed dices : Quid autem, si diuerso ille spiritu, alijsque uestigijs ambulasset, id ne Paulo imputandum fuisset? Nemo sic sentierit opinor. Neque enim conuenit ut quæ faciunt posteri, illorum maioribus, uel, quæ faciunt discipuli, illorum præceptoribus imputentur. Nec est ut dicas,Paulus miserat Titum B ad Corinthios, quare si is diuersum quid ab instituto ipsius egisset, ipsi utiq; imputandum fuisset. Etenim miserat quidem illum, uerum non ad expilandum, sed ad ædificandum Corinthios. Si illos expilasset, haud leue quidem offendiculū Apostolatui ipsius paperisset,ipse tamen extra culpam fuisset, propterea quod nec ipsius hoc ille iussu fecisset, nec post factū in comitatum ipsius receptus fuisset. Romanus pontifex mittit legatos suos in orbe Christianum ad ecclesias,reges ac principes. Accipiunt illi quæcunq; emungere possunt. Si faciunt hoc spiritu non eodem, sed diuerso, declaret hoc Pontifex competenti correptione & emendatione. Verum quis non uidet similes habere labra lactucas,hoc est, eodem illos spiritu, & ijsdem uestigijs ingredi? Qua in re uidemus legitimam episcoporum successionem non in eo simpliciter consistere, si perpetua imitatione succedentes præcedentium uestigijs ingrediantur. Stabilis quidem in eo & nullo discrimine interrupta successio monstratur: uerum non legitima, quæ non est pseudepiscoporum, sed uerorum ac legitimorum. Simon ille,unde orta est in ecclesia Simoniaca hæresis,suos habet successores, eodem spiritu, & ijsdem uestigijs ingredientes. De illorum successione glorientur pseudepiscopi,de legitima gloriari non possunt.
units.tr: "Did we not walk in the same spirit," he says, "and in the same footsteps?" That is: Was he not animated towards you in the same way as I am? Did he not likewise seek not your possessions but you yourselves? But you will say: "What if he had walked in a different spirit and in other footsteps? Would that have been imputed to Paul? No one, I think, would think so. For it is not fitting that what posterity does should be imputed to their forefathers, or what disciples do to their teachers. Nor can you say: Paul sent Titus to the Corinthians, so if he had done something different from his instructions, it would certainly have been imputed to Paul himself. For he had indeed sent him, but not to plunder, but to build up the Corinthians. If he had plundered them, he would indeed have brought no slight offence upon Paul's apostleship, yet Paul himself would have been free of blame, because he would not have done this by his command, nor would he have received him into his company after the deed." The Roman pontiff sends his legates throughout the Christian world to churches, kings and princes. They take whatever they can squeeze out. If they do this in a spirit that is not the same but different, let the pontiff declare it with fitting rebuke and correction. But who does not see that they have lips like lettuces, that is, that they walk in the same spirit and in the same footsteps? In this matter we see that legitimate succession of bishops does not consist simply in this: that those who succeed walk in the footsteps of their predecessors by perpetual imitation. A succession that is unbroken and without any break is indeed shown in this, but it is not a legitimate one, since it belongs not to true and lawful bishops but to false ones. That Simon, from whom the Simoniacal heresy arose in the Church, has successors who walk in the same spirit and the same footsteps. False bishops may glory in that succession; they cannot glory in a legitimate one.

units.la: Illud obseruandum est obiter, quod primo loco eundem spiritū,secundo uero eadem uestigia posuit. Admonemur non esse expectandum ut ijsdem uestigijs ingrediantur, qui non sunt eodem præditi spiritu. Diuersa uestigia diuersitatem spiritus arguunt. Est tamen consideratio ista cautè ac moderatè accipienda: Etenim non possumus tribuere Paulo, quod diuerso ab Apostolis spiritu ambulauerit, ubi ecclesias ab æmulatione Mosaicæ legis auocauit magis,quàm faciebant Apostoli, Petrus, Iacobus & Ioannes. Nam frequenter hoc accidit, ut eodem spiritu præditis, necesse sit alijs atq; alijs modis rem eandem usurpare ac tractare,propter circunstātiarum ac respectuum diuersitatem.Quale & illud est,quod cum cæteri apostoli uictum sumerent propter prædicandi laborem, Paulus à Corinthijs accipere detrectabat.In eadem uero causa,ubi nulla est circumstantiarum varietas,alijs atq; alijs uestigijs ingredi,qualis erat de quahoc loco scribit Apostolus, non est eorum qui eodem sint spiritu præditi.
units.tr: This point should be noted in passing: he first says "the same Spirit" and then "the same footsteps." We are reminded that those who do not have the same Spirit should not be expected to walk in the same footsteps. Different footsteps show a difference of spirit. Yet this observation must be taken carefully and moderately. We cannot say that Paul walked in a spirit different from the Apostles when he called the churches away from zeal for the Mosaic law more than Peter, James and John did. Often, when men have the same Spirit, they must still use and handle the same thing in different ways, because of the variety of circumstances and considerations. This is also why, while the other apostles took food because of their labour in preaching, Paul refused to receive it from the Corinthians. But where there is no variety of circumstances, to walk in different footsteps, as the Apostle writes about in this passage, is not the mark of those who have the same Spirit.

units.la: Rursum arbitramini, quod nos uobis excusemus? In conspectu Dei, in Christo loquimur, sed omnia, charissimi, pro uestra ædificatione. Nā metuo, ne qua fiat,ut si uenero, non quales uelim reperiā uos, & ego reperiar uobis, qualem nolitis, ne quomodo sint contentiones,æmulationes,irę, concertationes,obtrectationes,susurri,tumores,seditiones.Ne iterū ubi uenero,humilem me faciat Deus meus apud uos, & lugeā multos eorū qui ante peccauerunt, nec eos pœnituit immunditiæ, libidinisq; & impudicitiæ quam patrarunt.
units.tr: Again, do you think that we are excusing ourselves to you? "In the sight of God we speak in Christ, but all things, beloved, for your edification. For I fear lest, when I come, I should find you not such as I would wish, and I should be found by you such as you would not wish: lest there be contentions, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, seditions. And lest, when I come again, my God humble me among you, and I mourn many of those who sinned before and have not repented of the uncleanness, fornication and lewdness which they have committed."

units.la: Quoniā tanta diligentia innocentiā suā in hac epistola aduersus pseudapostolorū calumnias tuetur,ut uideri possit ad morē eorū, qui quod malè gesserunt excusare moliuntur,ubi factū negare nō possunt,studiosius sese purgare,ut ei cogitationi occurrat,dicit:Rursum arbitramini quod nos uobis excusemus? Vetus interpres uertit:Olim putatis, cum sit in Græco non πάλαι.i.olim,sed πάλιν.i.iterum. Quoniam in præcedentibus aliquoties materiam hanc attigerat,non dicit simpliciter, Arbitramini,sed,Rursum arbitramini.Erat enim uero simile & antea eos tale quid cogitasse.
units.tr: Since he defends his innocence in this letter with such great care against the slanders of the false apostles, it might seem that, like those who try to excuse what they have done badly, he is zealously clearing himself, where he cannot deny the deed. To meet this thought, he says: "Do you think again that we excuse ourselves to you?" The old translator renders it, "Do you think of old," but the Greek has not πάλαι, that is, "of old," but πάλιν, that is, "again." Since he had touched this matter several times before, he does not say simply, "You think," but "Again you think." For it was indeed likely that they had thought such a thing before as well.

units.la: QVOD nos uobis excusemus,inquit.) Græcè est ὅτι ὑμῖν ἀπολογούμεθα. Significat autē hoc uerbum adductis rationibus sese purgare & excusare. Negat autem hoc se facere, propterea quòd qui sese excusant, plerunq; adferant ea quæ magis sint accommodata causæ quam agunt,quàm in se uera. Ideo subijcit:
units.tr: "That we excuse ourselves to you," he says. In Greek it is ὅτι ὑμῖν ἀπολογούμεθα. This verb means to clear oneself and to excuse oneself by bringing forward reasons. He denies that he does this, because those who excuse themselves usually bring forward arguments that suit their cause better than they are true. Therefore he adds:

units.la: IN cospectu Dei in Christo loquimur.) Sensus est: Nihil fingimus excusationis gratia,sed quę uera sunt loquimur. Hoc significans dicit, se in conspectu Dei in Christo loqui.Hic enim non est locus fictionibus. In conspectu Dei loqui, est loqui in conscientia Dei tam religiose, ac si id fiat in conspectu divinae maiestatis. Addit in Christo, quod exponi potest, vel, in causa Christi, id est, Christum concernente, vel in spiritu Christi, vel sub testimonio Christi. Non debemus autem particulam hanc de praesenti tantum causa exponere, sed generaliter de omnibus quae in Christo loquebatur. Quasi dicat, Non est mei moris ut excusationibus utar, quae fictis rationibus conflari solent, sed itafum comparatus, ut quecunque in causa Christi praecipue loquor, loquar non temere ac leviter, sed magna cum religione, tanquam in conspectu Dei constitutus.
units.tr: "In the sight of God we speak in Christ." The sense is: we invent nothing for the sake of an excuse, but we speak what is true. In saying this, he means that he speaks in the sight of God, in Christ. For there is no place for pretence here. To speak in the sight of God is to speak in the awareness of God, as religiously as if it were done in the sight of the divine majesty. He adds "in Christ," which may be explained as "in the cause of Christ," that is, concerning Christ, or "in the Spirit of Christ," or "under the witness of Christ." We should not explain this particle only with respect to the present cause, but generally, concerning everything he spoke in Christ. As if he said: it is not my custom to use the excuses that are usually contrived with fabricated reasons. Rather I am so disposed that whatever I speak especially in the cause of Christ, I speak not rashly or lightly, but with great reverence, as one who stands in the sight of God.

units.la: SED omnia charissimi pro vestri aedificatione.) Graece est non ἀλλά, sed, quemadmodum Erasmus hic vertit, sed; τὰ δὲ πάντα, id est, omnia vero. Vetus melius reddidit, Omnia autem. Si legas, sed omnia charissimi pro vestri aedificatione, omnino desiderabitur aliquid. Vtpote: In conspectu Dei in Christo loquimur, nihil adferentes pro nostri purgatione, sed omnia pro vestri aedificatione. Si vero, omnia autem pro vestri aedificatione, expositio erit, quorsum ista tam multis, tamque religiose in conspectu Dei loquutus sit, Pro ipsorum videlicet aedificatione. Quasi dicat. Non spectato meipsum, neque in hac praesenti causa, neq; in aliis, sed ut non vestra, sed vos quaero, ita & omnia pro vestri aedificatione, non pro nostri excusatione loquor. Multa scripsit in hac epistola, quibus in speciem sui ipsius uideri poterat habere rationem, utpote contra adversarios pugnado, tam multis gloriando, Apostolatus sui authoritatem asserendo, suamque innocentiam defendendo, &c. Verum in omnibus quae scripsit, nihil minus quam seipsum quaesiuit: sed omnia ad hunc finem direxit, ut Corinthij in fide ac synceritate erga Christum ac vera pietate aedificarentur. Hoc significas dicit: Omnia vero charissimi pro vestri edificatione.
units.tr: "But all things, beloved, for your edification." In Greek it is not ἀλλά, but, as Erasmus renders it here, "but"; τὰ δὲ πάντα, that is, "but all things." The old translator rendered it better: "But all things." If you read "but all things, beloved, for your edification," something would have to be supplied, namely: "In the sight of God we speak in Christ, bringing nothing forward for our own purgation, but everything for your edification." But if you read "but all things for your edification," the explanation is why he spoke so much and so religiously in the sight of God: namely, for their edification. As if he said: I do not look to myself, either in this present cause or in others, but I seek you, not what is yours; so also everything I say is for your edification, not for my own excuse. He wrote many things in this letter which might seem to have some regard for himself, as when he fights against adversaries, boasts of so many things, asserts the authority of his apostleship, and defends his innocence. Yet in all that he wrote, he sought nothing less than himself; he directed everything to this end, that the Corinthians might be built up in faith, in sincerity towards Christ, and in true piety. This is what you signify when he says: "But all things, beloved, for your edification."

units.la: NAM metuo, inquit, ne qua fiat, ut si venero, no quales velim reperiam vos, & ego reperiar vobis quale nolitis.) Sane neutrum istorum ad aedificationem Corinthiorum fecisset. Quare cum utrunq; metuendum sibi esse cerneret, in omnes sese formas mutabat, omnéq; lapidem movebat, ne quod pseudapostoli coeperant, ad destructionem ecclesiae perficerent. Hoc sentiens dicit: Nam metuo, ne qua fiat ut si venero, non quales velim reperiam vos, & ego reperiar vobis qualem nolitis.
units.tr: "For I fear," he says, "lest by some means, when I come, I shall find you not such as I wish, and I shall be found by you such as you do not wish." Certainly neither of these would have served the edification of the Corinthians. So, since he saw that he had to fear both, he changed himself into every form and moved every stone, so that the false apostles would not accomplish what they had begun, to the destruction of the Church. Feeling this, he says: "For I fear lest by some means, when I come, I shall find you not such as I would wish, and I shall be found by you such as you would not wish."

units.la: NAM metuo, inquit.) Paterni pectoris curam ac solicitudinem per verbum metuendi exprimit. Solicitudo paterna erga liberos sine metu esse no potest. Perpetuo siquidem timet solicitum parentis pectus, ne quid admittant liberi quod sit inhonestum, aut accidat illis quod sit noxium. Huiusmodi metus solicitum Apostoli pectus indefinetr molestauit. Quid autem metuebat?
units.tr: "For I fear," he says. By the word "fear" he expresses the care and anxiety of a father's heart. A father's anxiety for his children cannot be without fear. Indeed, a parent's anxious heart constantly fears that the children may admit something dishonourable, or that something harmful may befall them. Such fear troubled the anxious heart of the Apostle without measure. But what did he fear?

units.la: NE qua fiat, inquit, ut si venero. (non est in Graeco, si venero, sed μὴ πως ἐλθὼν, id est ne quo pacto veniens, quod uptrendu est, ne quo pacto ubi venero. Vulgatus interpres habet, cum venero) non quales velim reperiam vos, & ego reperiar uobis qualem nolitis.) Quoniam in ipsius absentia subingresi fuerant pseudapostoli, metuere coepit, ne per illorum astutia decepti, loge in alios quam quales reliquerat, mutarentur: atq; ita fieret, ut ubi ad eos venisset, inueniret quales nollet; & per consequens ipse reperiretur qualem ipsi nollent. Sane metus hic non est praeter rationem, nec frustra fatigat eorum animos, qui a suis quos diligunt, aliquandiu abesse coguntur. Etenim raro accidit, ut domum reuersi reperiant illos quales ublut, sic ut nihil acciderit domi ipsorum, unde contristetur. Quare uehementer cu'pa biles sunt, qui nulla necessitate coacti domo, uxore, ac liberis relictis, mercenariam militiā sectantur. Hic saepenumero euenit, ut coniuges quas castas reliquerant, domum reuersi corruptas reperiant, ut taceam quae liberis interea, ac rebus domesticis incommoda accidere solent. Haec licentia in militia excurrendi in Republica bene constituta ferri non debet.
units.tr: "Lest by some means," he says, "when I come" (it is not in the Greek "if I come," but μὴ πως ἐλθὼν, that is, "lest by some means coming," which should be rendered "lest by some means when I come"; the Vulgate translator has "when I come"), "I shall not find you such as I would wish, and I shall be found by you such as you would not wish." Since the false apostles had crept in during his absence, he began to fear that, deceived by their cunning, they might be changed far from what he had left them, and so it would happen that when he came to them he would find them not as he wished, and consequently he himself would be found by them not as they wished. Certainly this fear is not beyond reason, nor does it needlessly trouble the minds of those who are forced to be away from those they love for some time. For it rarely happens that, having returned home, they find them just as they were, with nothing having happened in their households to cause sorrow. Therefore those are deservedly blamed who, without any necessity, leave home, wife and children behind and pursue mercenary soldiering. Often it happens that wives whom they left chaste are found corrupted when they return home, not to mention the harms that usually befall children and domestic affairs in the meantime. This licence to go off to war should not be tolerated in a well-ordered commonwealth.

units.la: ET ego reperiar uobis, inquit, qualem nolitis.) Habet haec particula minas sequuturae severitatis, quam experturi sint Corinthij, si alij quam conueniat reperti fuerint. Quemadmodum in ludo literario si praeceptor discipulos reperiat quales nolit, mox consequitur, ut reperiatur & ipse alius quam ipsi uelint, dum uirgain eos qui deliquerunt, animaduertit: ita metuens Apostolus, ne ubi uenerit Corinthu, reperiat eos quales nolit, annectit hanc particulam, dicens: & ego reperiar uobis qualem nolitis. Vtrunq; metuebat, quia nec ferre poterat illorum corruptelas, nec sine dolore in delinquentes animaduertere. Qui amat, quemadmodum laetatur, non modo si qualem uult habeat eum quem amat, sed & si habeatur ab illo qualem is cupit, ita uiceuersa no solum ob id contristatur, quod reperit eum qualem non non uult, sed & ob id quod sentit se alium esse quam ille cupiat. Honesto marito uix poterit tristius quicquam accidere, quam si coniugem suam aliam quam uult reperiat, & uicissim alium quam ipsa uelit, praestare se cogatur. Sic enim omnis coniugalis societatis suauitas e medio tollitur, ac tristi acerbitate commutatur. Hoc genus mutuae contristationis metuens Apostolus dicit: Metuo nanque, ne qua fiat, &c.
units.tr: "And I shall be found by you," he says, "such as you would not wish." This particle carries the threat of severity to follow, which the Corinthians would experience if they were found other than they ought to be. Just as in a school, if the teacher finds his pupils not as he wishes, he soon proceeds to be found himself other than they wish, when he punishes those who have done wrong with the rod, so the Apostle, fearing that when he came to Corinth he would find them not as he wished, adds this particle, saying: "and I shall be found by you such as you would not wish." He feared both, because he could neither bear their corruptions nor punish the offenders without grief. As one who loves rejoices not only when he has the one he loves as he wishes, but also when he is regarded by him as he desires, so conversely he is saddened not only because he finds the beloved not as he wishes, but also because he feels that he is other than the beloved desires. Scarcely anything more sorrowful can happen to an honourable husband than to find his wife other than he wishes, and to be forced in turn to show himself other than she would like. For thus all the sweetness of the marriage bond is removed and changed into bitter sorrow. Fearing this kind of mutual grief, the Apostle says: "For I fear lest by some means, etc."

units.la: NE quomodo sint contentiones, inquit, aemulationes, irae, concertationes, obtrectationes, susurri, tumores, seditiones.) In Graeco desideratur aliquid. Sic enim habetur, μή πως ἔρις, ζῆλοι, &c. idest, ne quomodo contentiones, aemulationes, &c. ubi subaudiendum est, sint inter uos. Exponit consequenter utramque metus sui partem. Dixit: Nam metuo, ne qua fiat, ut ubi uenero, non quales uelim reperiam uos. Iam quales eos reperire nolit ac metuat, ne tales eos sit reperturus, aperit, dicens: Ne quomodo sint inter uos contentiones, æmulationes, irę, concertationes, obtrectationes, susurri, tumores, seditiones. Erat du bio procul & alia multa uicia, quibus Corinthij laborabant, quorum etiam alibi meminit. Verum quoniam in hac epistola contra pseudapostolos potissimum dimicat, ea hic recenset, quæ instar malorum malæ arboris fructuum ex sectis nascebatur, quas pseudapostoli plantauerat. Harum primarius fructus est mutuæ charitatis extinctio, quam consequuntur eue-stigiò quæ hic memorantur, contentiones, æ-mulationes, irę, &c.
units.tr: "Lest somehow there be contentions, he says, emulations, wraths, quarrels, detractions, whisperings, swellings, seditions." The Greek lacks something here. It reads "lest perhaps strife, jealousies, etc. [μή πως ἔρις, ζῆλοι, &c.]", that is, "lest somehow contentions, emulations, etc.", where "among you" must be supplied. He then goes on to set out both parts of his fear. He said: "For I fear that somehow, when I come, I will not find you as I would wish." Then he makes clear what sort of people he does not want to find and fears he will find, saying: "Lest there be among you contentions, emulations, wraths, quarrels, detractions, whisperings, swellings, seditions." There were, of course, many other vices among the Corinthians, which he mentions elsewhere. But since in this letter he fights chiefly against the false apostles, he lists here those fruits which, like the bad fruit of a bad tree, sprang from the sects that the false apostles had planted. The chief of these fruits is the extinction of mutual love, which is immediately followed by the things mentioned here: contentions, emulations, wraths, etc.

units.la: CONTENTIONES, æmulationes, irę, concertationes.) Habent quædam exemplaria in singulari ἔρις, id est, contentio. Gal. 5. numeratur hæc uicia inter opera carnis hoc ipso ordine quo hic recensentur. Sic enim ibi legitur, ἔρεις, ζῆλοι, θυμοί, ἐριθεῖαι. 1 Cor. 1. contentionum meminit ad hunc modum: Significatū est mihi de uobis fratres mei à familiaribus Chloæ, quod contentiones sint inter uos.
units.tr: "Contentions, emulations, wraths, quarrels." Some copies have the singular in the Greek, ἔρις [eris], that is, contention. In Gal. 5 these vices are counted among the works of the flesh in the same order in which they are listed here. For there it reads: "strifes, jealousies, outbursts of anger, rivalries" [ἔρεις, ζῆλοι, θυμοί, ἐριθεῖαι]. In 1 Cor. 1 he mentions contentions in this way: "It has been reported to me, my brothers, by those of Chloe's household, that there are contentions among you."

units.la: Dico autem illud, quod unusquisq; ueltrū dicit: Ego qui de sum Pauli, ego uero Cephę, ego uero Christi, &c. Et 1. Cor. 3. Siquidė, inquit, cum in uobis sit æmulatio, & contentio, & factiones, nonne carnales estis? Ergo cum priorem ad illos epistolā scriberet, tales erant, quales si ad eos uenisset, reperturū se metuebat, cum hæc scriberet. Qua in re uidemus ne apostolis quidė sic ipsorum successisse scripta, admonitiones & correptiones, ut curis, metu ac solicitudine scribendo liberarentur.
units.tr: "I mean this, that each of you says: I am of Paul, I of Cephas, I of Christ, etc." And in 1 Cor. 3: "For since, he says, there is among you jealousy and contention and factions, are you not carnal?" So when he wrote his earlier letter to them, they were such as he feared he would find if he came, and that was why he was writing this. In this we see that not even for the apostles did their writings, admonitions and rebukes succeed in such a way that they were freed from care, fear and anxiety when writing to their people.

units.la: Quamuis hic Apostolus in priore epistola morbum hunc sectarum studiosissime reprehenderat, in hac posteriore tamen metuere se scribit, ne ubi uenerit ad Corinthios, reperiat inter eos contentiones, æmulationes, &c. Loqui autem ipsum de contentionibus, æmulationibus, concertationibus, obtrectationibus, &c. sectariorum, puto ex priore epistola abunde esse manifestū. Contentio & zelus erat, quod dicebant, alius ego sum Petri, alius ego sum Pauli, &c. Contendebat quisq; pro eo quem æmulabatur ac sectabatur. Et ex eiusmodi contentione ac zelo nascebantur quę sequuntur, irę, concertationes, obtrectationes, susurri, tumores, id est, tumidę animorum inflationes, quibus alij aduersus alios inflabantur, seditiones, uel factiones, quas 1. Cor. 1. & Galat. 5. uocat διχοστασίας, hic ἐπιλασσοτ, quam uocem Erasmus prima Corinthiorum decimoquarto, confusionem terret, ubi de illa diximus. Quam miserabilis autem sit ecclesiarum status, in quibus obtinent studia contentionum, æmulationum, irarum, concertationum, obtrectationum, susurrorū, inflationum ac factionum, quis satis unquam perpendit?
units.tr: Although in the earlier letter this apostle had most earnestly rebuked this disease of the sects, in this later one he writes that he fears that when he comes to the Corinthians he will find among them contentions, emulations, etc. That he is speaking of the contentions, emulations, quarrels, detractions, etc. of the sectarians, I think is clear enough from the earlier letter. The contention and zeal lay in what they said: "I am of Peter, I of Paul," etc. Each contended for the one whom he emulated and followed. And from such contention and zeal there arose what follows: wraths, quarrels, detractions, whisperings, swellings, that is, the swollen puffings-up of minds by which some were inflated against others; and seditions or factions, which in 1 Cor. 1 and Gal. 5 he calls divisions [διχοστασίας], and here [ἀκαταστασίαν], disorder, a word which Erasmus renders "confusion" in 1 Cor. 14, where I discussed it. But who has ever sufficiently weighed how wretched is the state of churches in which the pursuits of contentions, emulations, wraths, quarrels, detractions, whisperings, swellings and factions prevail?

units.la: Illud obiter annotādum puto. Sunt in hoc uiciorū catalogo duę uoces idem significātes, ἔρις uidelicet & ἐριθεῖαι, quas tamen haud sine aliquo discrimine posuit Apostolus. Vtraque contentione significat. ἔρις Suidas sic definit ἔρις ἡ διὰ λόγων ἐπὶ ἀξίᾳ φιλονικία. Consimili modo & ἐριθεῖαν definit, dicens: ἐριθεία, ἡ διὰ λόγων φιλονικία. Mihi apparet ἔρις, sic primo esse loco positū, ut in genere significet omne illud disidiū, quod inter Corinthios erat, ad quem modum & pacis nomine generaliter subinde utimur, quādo nihil contentionis, nihil odiorū, nihil bellorum, &c. esse significantes, pacem esse dicimus.
units.tr: I think this should be noted in passing. In this catalogue of vices there are two words with the same meaning, namely ἔρις [eris] and ἐριθεῖαι [eritheiai], which the Apostle nevertheless did not use without some distinction. Both signify contention. Suidas defines ἔρις thus: contention is rivalry for honour carried on through words [ἡ διὰ λόγων ἐπὶ ἀξίᾳ φιλονικία]. He defines ἐριθεία in a similar way, saying: ἐριθεία is rivalry carried on through words [ἡ διὰ λόγων φιλονικία]. It seems to me that ἔρις is placed first so that it signifies in general all that discord which existed among the Corinthians, just as we commonly use the word peace in a general sense, when we say there is peace where there is no contention, no hatred, no wars, etc.

units.la: Sic timebat Paulus, ne inter Corinthios reperiret nō pacē, sed contentionē. Quę uero sequuntur uelut explicatione habet eorū malorū, quę in contentione regnant, ac ueluti partes illius existunt. Inter illa numeratur & ἐριθεῖα, eo uidelicet sensu, quē Hieronymus Gal. 5. ad hunc modū exponit. Est autē ἐριθεῖα, cum quis semper ad contradicēdum paratus, stomacho delectatur alieno, & muliebri iurgio contendit, & prouocat contendentē. Hæc ille. Ergo ἐριθεῖαν Apostolus posuit hoc loco pro rixa. Erasmus uertit hic concertationem. Ad exprimendum hoc discrimen pulchrē facit quod in singulari dicit: μὴ ἀωσ ἔρεις, id est, ne quo pacto sit inter uos contentio, ac tū in plura li ueluti mebra contentionis subijcit, ζῆλοι, θυμοί ἐριθεῖαι, &c. Exiistimo autē haud necessariū esse, ut singula explicando persequamur, maxime nostra hac ætate, in qua plus satis hæc monstra ecclesijs Christi negocium faciunt, ac terribilibus suis formis piorum animis horrorem incutiunt. Ipse illorum catalogus uix potest ab homine Christiano citra horrorem legi:
units.tr: So Paul feared that he would find among the Corinthians not peace but contention. What follows is, as it were, an explanation of the evils that reign in contention and exist as its parts. Among these is ἐριθεία, in the sense which Jerome gives on Gal. 5 in these words: "ἐριθεία is when someone, always ready to contradict, takes pleasure in another's ill temper, and contends with womanly brawling, and provokes the one who contends. So far he." Therefore the Apostle here uses ἐριθεία for quarrelling. Erasmus renders it here as "conflict." To bring out this distinction, it is useful that he says the singular first, μὴ πως ἔρις [lest somehow strife], and then adds in the plural, as if they were limbs of contention, ζῆλοι, θυμοί, ἐριθεῖαι, etc. I think it is not necessary to pursue each of them one by one, especially in our own age, in which these monsters cause more than enough trouble for the churches of Christ and with their dreadful forms strike horror into pious minds. Their very catalogue can hardly be read by a Christian without horror.

units.la: NE iterum ubi uenero, inquit, humilem faciat me Deus meus apud uos.) Hactenus priorem metus sui partem expositū, iam subiungit posteriorē, quæ ex priore nascebatur. Ea erat quod metuebat, ne Corinthijs suis ubi ad eos uenisset, nō qualē uellent reperiretur. Ad hāc pertinet quod dicit: Ne iterum ubi uenero, humilē me faciat Deus meus apud uos, & lugeā multos, &c. Humilitas quædam est omnis tristitia. Ideo mox subijcit: Et lugeā multos eorū qui antē peccauerūt, nec eos pœnituit immundiciæ, libidinisq;, & impudicitiæ, quā patrarūt. Hoc genus humilitatis futurū sibi metuebat, secus uero animatus erat erga persona suę humilitatē. Quod autem nō simpliciter dicit, ne humilis fiam, sed, ne humiliet me Deus meus apud uos, puto intelligēdum esse de eo, quod propter Deum, & uenire Corinthum cōstituebat, & si eo uenisset propter eos, qui impœnitentes erant, luctu habituros esset. Sic dicit facturum Deum, quod sibi propter Deum euenturū metuebat. Ergo à Deo humiliatur, propter Deū, & in causa Dei humiliatur: & rursus à Deo glorificatur, propter Deū glorificatur.
units.tr: "Lest again, when I come, my God humble me among you." Having explained so far the first part of his fear, he now adds the second, which arose from the first. This was what he feared: that when he came to his Corinthians he would not find them as they wished. To this belongs what he says: "lest again, when I come, my God humble me among you, and I mourn many," etc. All grief is a kind of humbling. Therefore he immediately adds: "and I mourn many of those who sinned before and did not repent of the uncleanness, lust and impurity which they committed." He feared this kind of humbling would be his lot, whereas he was otherwise minded about the humbling of his own person. As for the fact that he does not simply say "lest I be humbled," but "lest my God humble me among you," I think it must be understood of this: he had resolved to go to Corinth on account of God, and if he went there on account of those who were impenitent, he would have cause for mourning. So he says that God would do what he feared would happen to him on God's account. Thus he is humbled by God, on account of God, and in the cause of God; and again he is glorified by God, on account of God.

units.la: ET lugeam multos eorum, inquit, qui antė peccauerunt: nec eos pœnituit immunditiæ, libidinisq;, & impudicitiæ, quā patrarūt.) Nō puto referre, siue de priuatō Apostoli, siue de publico ecclesiæ luctu intelligamus. Si Corinthum uenisset, luxisset utique, & ecclesiam ad lugendum una secum induxisset. ET lugeam multos.) Non perstringit omnes, sed ex omnibus aliquos. Ergo non omnes tales erant, propter quos lugendum fuisset Apostolo. Nec dicit, Et lugeam aliquos, sed, Et lugeam multos. Erant igitur in ea ecclesia, quà tantopere diligebat, non pauci aliqui, sed multi impœnitentes, quorum gratia lugendum fuisset Apostolo, si ad ipsos uenisset.
units.tr: "And I shall mourn many of them, he says, who sinned before, and did not repent of the uncleanness, lust and impurity which they committed." I do not think it matters whether we understand this of the Apostle's private grief or of the public grief of the church. If he had come to Corinth, he would certainly have mourned, and would have drawn the church along to mourn with him. "And I shall mourn many." He does not condemn all, but some out of all. Therefore not all were such that the Apostle would have had to mourn on their account. Nor does he say "I shall mourn some," but "I shall mourn many." There were therefore in that church, which he loved so greatly, not just a few but many impenitent people, for whose sake the Apostle would have had to mourn had he come to them.

units.la: QVI ante peccauerunt, inquit.) An sit hoc intelligendum de peccatis ante baptismum patratis, uel de illis quæ post receptâ Christiani nominis professionem admiserant illi nō pauci, sed multi, non puto posse certò statui. Fieri potuit, ut in absentia Pauli multi ex Corinthijs ad professionem quidem Christianismi uenerint, uerum sine resipiscentia præcedentium peccatorum. Rursus uerosimile est fuisse in illorum ecclesia multos, qui post baptismū quoque in consueta immundicia citra resipiscentiam pergerent.
units.tr: "Who sinned before," he says. Whether this is to be understood of sins committed before baptism, or of those which, after the profession of the Christian name had been received, not a few but many had committed, I do not think can be determined with certainty. It may have happened that during Paul's absence many of the Corinthians came to the profession of Christianity, but without repentance for their earlier sins. Again, it is likely that in their church there were many who, even after baptism, persisted in their customary uncleanness without repentance.

units.la: NEC eos pœnituit, inquit, immunditiæ libidinisque & impudicitiæ quam patrarunt.) Quod hic Erasmus libidinem uertit, in Græco est πορνεία, quæ uox scortationē significat, quemadmodum & ipse illam Galatis 5. trāstulit, ubi inter opera carnis recēsentur, μοιχεία, πορνεία, ἀκαθαρσία, ἀσελγεία. i. adulterium, scortatio, immundicia, & impudicitia, uel ut ibi uertit Erasmus lasciuia. Immundicia & impudicitia generales uoces sunt, quarū multæ sunt species, adulterium uidelicet, incestus, stuprum, scortatio, & quæ contra naturam admittuntur. Lyranus immundiciam accipit pro Sodomia, & impudicitiā pro deploratione uirginum, quā tamen Gal. 5. refert ad exteriorem inhonestatem in aspectu, gressu, tactu, & huiusmodi quæ procedunt ex impudicitia cordis. Annotant nonnulli per ἀσελγείαν intelligi Græcis atrociorem petulantiam, quam sonet Latinis lasciuia. Ab Æsch. ponitur pro flagitiosa & obscœna consuetudine stuprandi. Verum uideamus quæ sint hoc loco obiter obseruanda.
units.tr: "Nor did they repent," he says, "of the uncleanness, lust and impurity which they committed." What Erasmus renders here as lust, the Greek has as fornication [πορνεία], a word which signifies fornication, just as he himself translated it in Gal. 5, where among the works of the flesh are listed adultery, fornication, uncleanness, and impurity [μοιχεία, πορνεία, ἀκαθαρσία, ἀσελγεία], that is, adultery, fornication, uncleanness and impurity, or, as Erasmus there renders it, lasciviousness. Uncleanness and impurity are general words, of which there are many species: adultery, incest, rape, fornication, and those acts which are committed against nature. Lyranus takes uncleanness to mean sodomy and impurity to mean the deflowering of virgins, though in Gal. 5 he refers it to outward immodesty in look, gait, touch and such things, which proceed from impurity of heart. Some note that by lasciviousness [ἀσελγείαν] the Greeks understand a more atrocious wantonness than the Latin word lasciviousness suggests. Aeschines uses it for a shameful and obscene habit of debauchery. But let us see what is to be observed here in passing.

units.la: 1 Principio obserua quod non dicit, & castigem, uel, excommunicem, sed, & lugeam. Castigare & excommunicare peccates facile est, præsertim iusticiarijs & magnis magistris: lugere uero non ita. Id enim eorum est tantum qui diligunt, & paterna sunt storgia etiam erga delinquentes præditi. Ad luctū uideo non nullos hodie non tam esse appositos, quàm ad excommunicandum: neq; tam esse propensos ad colligendum, quàm ad excludendū. Citantur exempla Pauli, uerum affectus Paulinus paucis est cordi. Citius excommunicantem quàm lugentem sequimur.
units.tr: 1. First, observe that he does not say "and I will rebuke" or "and I will excommunicate," but "and I will mourn." Rebuking and excommunicating sinners is easy, especially for judges and great magistrates. But mourning is not so easy. It belongs only to those who love, and to those endowed with a fatherly affection [στοργή] even toward wrongdoers. I see that today some are not so inclined to mourning as they are to excommunicating, nor so eager to gather in as to shut out. Examples of Paul are cited, but the Pauline affection is little valued among them. We follow the excommunicator more quickly than the one who mourns.

units.la: 2 Deinde quid opus erat luctu, cum absens quoq; multos illos impœnitentes perinde atque unicum illum, quo de 1. Cor. 5. legimus, ex communicare posset, ac fermentum illud expurgare, ne reliqua massa corrumperetur? Nō est uidelicet prudēti pastori temerē úsurpāda quorumuis excommunicatio, sed etiam atq; etiam uidendum, ad ædificationem ne & re-
units.tr: 2. Next, what need was there for mourning, when he could have excommunicated, even while absent, the many impenitent people just as he did that one man we read of in 1 Cor. 5, and could have purged out that leaven so that the rest of the lump would not be corrupted? Clearly the prudent minister must not rashly assume the excommunication of anyone whatever, but must consider again and again whether the step will serve for edification and as a remedy for the evils, or the reverse.

units.la: medium malorum factura fit, uel secus. Pericu lose autem præsumitur, ubi non unus & alter, idq; propter enorme & omnibus detestabile flagitium, quale erat scortatoris illius, cuius iam mentionem fecimus, sed multi & ob nicia communiora, excommunicatur. Nam periculum illic est, ne multi illi schisma constituat in ecclesia, & malum nō emendetur, sed in peius mutetur. Hoc timens Apostolus, non dicit: Congregatis uobis & meo spiritu, excommunicate multos illos qui antè peccauerunt, &c. sed, & lugeam multos, &c.
units.tr: Excommunication is presumptuously undertaken when it is applied not to one or two people, and that for a monstrous crime detestable to all, like that of the fornicator we have already mentioned, but to many people for more common offences. For there is danger there, lest those many people create a schism in the Church, and the evil is not corrected but changed for the worse. Fearing this, the Apostle does not say: "When you are gathered together with my spirit, excommunicate those many who sinned before," etc., but "and I will mourn for many," etc.

units.la: 3 Tertiò, cum usus excommunicationis sit non modò ut emēdetur qui peccauit, & ecclesiam peccato enormi offendit nec desistit, sed & ut reliqui cautiores reddantur, uidemus id in ecclesia Corinthiorum nō succesisse, quam uis scortator ille iussu esset Apostoli ab ecclesia excommunicatus, quandoquidem adhuc multi in illa erant, de peccatis suis haudquaquam resipiscentes, quos utiq; exemplum excommunicati, & metus excommunicationis ad resipiscentiam non permouit.
units.tr: 3. Third, since the purpose of excommunication is not only that the one who has sinned and persists in offending the Church with a gross sin may be corrected, but also that the rest may become more cautious, we see that this did not succeed in the Corinthian church. Although that fornicator had been excommunicated by the Apostle's command, many still remained in that church who by no means repented of their sins, and the example of the excommunicated man and the fear of excommunication did not move them to repentance.

units.la: 4 Quartò, non simpliciter dicit, qui antè peccauerunt, sed addit, nec eos pœnituit immundiciæ, &c. Ergo non tam lugubre est peccasse, quàm nulla peccati pœnitentia duci. In peccatore resipiscēte non est materia luctus, sed gaudij potius, idq; in cœlis inter ipsos angelos Lucæ 15. Qua in re obseruandum nobis est, quanta sit resipiscentiæ utilitas, & rursus quantum impœnitentiæ malum.
units.tr: 4. Fourth, he does not simply say "who sinned before," but adds "and they did not repent of the uncleanness," etc. Therefore it is not so much a matter for mourning that people have sinned, as that they are not led by any repentance for their sin. In a sinner who repents there is no matter for mourning, but rather for joy, and that in heaven itself among the angels, Luke 15. In this matter we must observe how great is the usefulness of repentance, and again how great is the evil of impenitence.

units.la: Loquitur autem de resipiscentia uera, qua peccatum non ad tempus suspeditur, sed prorsus abijcitur. In Papatu simulât se sacrifici pœnitentia immunditiæ, scortationis ac lasciuiæ suæ duci, dum scorta & concubinas suas una & altera septimana, tempore quadragesimæ, quam uocant, ædibus suis excludunt, & mox ad pristinam immunditiam reiterandam resumunt, quod genus pœnitentiæ impudentissima est illusio Dei. Verum meliore digni non sunt, qui legitimi cöiugij honestatem propter terrenas ocij ac uentris cōmoditates abiurāt.
units.tr: He speaks, however, of true repentance, by which sin is not put off for a time but is utterly cast away. Under the Papacy their priest pretends to be led to repentance for his uncleanness, fornication and lewdness, while for one or two weeks in the season of Lent, as they call it, he shuts his mistresses and concubines out of his house, and soon takes them back to resume the former uncleanness. This kind of repentance is the most shameless mockery of God. But those who renounce the honourable state of lawful marriage for the sake of earthly leisure and the comforts of the belly are not worthy of better.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM.
units.tr: ARGUMENT.

units.la: MInatur hoc capite non parsurum se illis qui antè peccauerunt, sed declaraturum loquentis in se Christi uirtutem, quandoquidem experimentum illius quærebant. Tandem epistolam claudit.
units.tr: In this chapter he threatens that he will not spare those who sinned before, but will show the power of Christ speaking in him, since they were seeking proof of it. Finally he closes the epistle.

units.la: CAPVT XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 13.

units.la: HIC tertius erit aduentus meus ad uos. In ore duorū testium aut triū constitue tur omne uerbum. Prædixi & prædico, ut præsens cum essem iterum, ita & absens nunc scribo
units.tr: "This is my third coming to you. Every word is established by the mouth of two or three witnesses. I have foretold, and I foretell, as though I were present for the second time, and now, though absent, I write"

units.la: ijs,qui ante peccauerũt,& reliquis omnib.quod si uenero denuo, nō parcam. Quandoquidē experimentū quaeritis in me loquētis Christi, qui erga uos nō est infirmus,sed potes est in uobis. Nā quauis crucifixus fuit ex infirmitate,uiuit tamē ex uirtute Dei. Siquidē &nos infirmi sumus in illo,sed uiuemus cū illo ex uirtute Dei erga uos. Vosipsos tentate,nū sitis in fide, uosipsos probate. An non cognoscitis uosmetipsos,qd Iesus Christus in uobis est? Nisi sicubi reprobi estis. At spero uos cognituros, quod nos non simus reprobi.
units.tr: "to those who sinned before and to all the rest, that if I come again I will not spare them. Since you seek proof of Christ speaking in me, who is not weak toward you but is powerful among you. For though he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives by the power of God. For we too are weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God toward you. Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? Unless perhaps you are reprobates. But I hope you will recognise that we are not reprobates."

units.la: HIC tertius erit aduentus meus ad uos,inquit.) In Graeco est, τρίτον τοῦτο ἔρχομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς, i.Tertia hac vice venio ad vos. Vulgatus interpres vertit:Ecce tertio hoc uenio ad vos. Ex hoc & eo qui in capite praecedenti est loco,existimant nonnulli Paulum priusquam haec scriberet,secundo inuisisse Corinthios. Dixi supra ei me sententiae non repugnare. Haud tamē video quomodo illa ex verbis istis necessario concludatur. Etenim quid impedit,quo minus secundo se ad eos uenisse dicat, cum priorem ad ipsos epistolam mitteret,& iam per alteram hanc tertio praesertim cum hic simplici ter dicat: Tertio iā uenio ad uos. Si dixisset, Tertio uenturus sum ad uos, probabilior esset illa sententia. Verū cum dicat τρίτον Φρο, i. Tertio hoc,uel,tertio iam,apparet ipsum loqui de aduētu qui fiebat per epistolā quam scribebat.
units.tr: "'This is my third coming to you,' he says. The Greek reads τρίτον τοῦτο ἔρχομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς [tritonn touto erchomai pros hymas], that is, 'For the third time I am coming to you.' The Vulgate translator renders it: 'Behold, for the third time I am coming to you.' From this and from the passage in the preceding chapter, some think that Paul had visited the Corinthians a second time before he wrote this letter. I said above that this opinion does not conflict with my own view. Yet I do not see how it is necessarily concluded from these words. For what prevents him from saying that he had come to them a second time, since he had sent them an earlier letter, and now, by this second one, is coming for the third time? Especially since he says simply, 'Now for the third time I am coming to you.' If he had said, 'For the third time I am about to come to you,' that opinion would be more probable. But since he says τρίτον τοῦτο [triton touto], that is, 'this third time,' or 'now the third time,' it is clear that he is speaking of the visit that was taking place through the letter he was writing."

units.la: Non est autem otiosum quod se iā tertio ad eos uenire dicit. Etenim hoc dices notat impoenitentium duriciem,qua fiebat,ut semel atque iterum admoniti haud resipiscerent, & simul minatur,si tertiam quoq; hanc admonitionem contempserint,tentaturum se seueriora, unde & mox subijcit,
units.tr: "Nor is it idle that he says he is now coming to them for the third time. For this expression marks the obstinacy of the impenitent, by which they did not repent even when admonished once and again. At the same time he threatens that, if they despise this third admonition too, he will proceed to harsher measures. Hence he immediately adds:"

units.la: IN ore duorum testium ac trium constitue tur omne verbum.) Locum huc citat ex Deu. cap.19.ubi sic legitur, על פי שנים עדים או על פי שלשה עדים יקום דבר, id est: Super ore duorum testium,uel,super ore trium testium stabit uerbum. Est autem stare verbum, idem quod firmari causam de qua testimonia feruntur,si duo uel tres de illa conformiter fuerint testificati. Hanc legem accommodat suo proposito. Qua si dicat,iam tertio conuenio uos, ac redarguo impoenitentes. Quare nihil illis excusationis relinquetur in posterum,si tertiam hanc redarguetionem contempserint, sed quemadmodū in ore duorum uel trium testium,iuxta legem, condemnatur rei,firmaturq; iudicium, ita tertia hac admonitione fiet,ut tanquam sufficienter admoniti,merito condemnentur, eo quod manifestum sit,constituisse eos pertinaciter in impoenitentia sua pergere,si ne sic quidem resipuerint. Cōsimile est illud Christi Matth.18. ubi trina admonitione sufficiētiam correptionis terminat,dicens: Si peccauerit in te frater
units.tr: "'In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word is established.' He cites this place from Deuteronomy 19, where it is read thus: עַל פִּי שְׁנַיִם עֵדִים אוֹ עַל פִּי שְׁלֹשָׁה עֵדִים יָקוּם דָּבָר [al pi shenayim edim o al pi shelosha edim yakum davar], that is: 'By the mouth of two witnesses, or by the mouth of three witnesses, the word shall stand.' To stand, however, means the same as to have a matter confirmed about which testimony is given, if two or three have testified to it in agreement. He applies this law to his purpose. As if he said: 'Now I come to you a third time, and I rebuke the impenitent. Therefore they will have no excuse left in future if they despise this third rebuke. Just as, by the mouth of two or three witnesses, the accused is condemned according to the law and the judgment is confirmed, so by this third admonition it will happen that, having been sufficiently admonished, they are rightly condemned, since it will be plain that they have resolved to persist obstinately in their impenitence, if not even so they repent.' Similar to this is the saying of Christ in Matthew 18, where he limits the sufficiency of correction to three admonitions, saying:"

units.la: tuus,uade & argue eum inter te & ipsum solum. Si te audierit lucratus est fratrem tuum: sin uero te non audierit, adhibe tecum adhuc unum aut duos, ut in ore duorum aut trium testium consistat omne verbum. Quod si non audierit eos,dic ecclesiae. Quod si ecclesiam non audierit, sit tibi uelut ethnicus & publicanus. Sic in foro iudiciario contumaciae damnatur, si quis tertio legitime citatus non comparuerit.
units.tr: "'If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother; but if he does not hear you, take with you one or two more, so that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand. And if he does not hear them, tell the Church. And if he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector.' Thus in the court of law a person who, legitimately summoned three times, does not appear is condemned for contumacy."

units.la: Itaq; secundum hanc Apostoli sententiam, tot testibus cōuenitur & accusatur peccator, quod uicibus siue per unū siue per alios atq; alios admonetur, ac redargutus ad resipiscentiam uocatur. Deinde uidemus hic sufficienti bus testimonijs omni excusatione priuari eos qui secundo ac tertio admoniti,praesertim per eos quorum sunt curae subiecti, resipiscere detrectant. Quod si ex abundanti saepius redarguuntur, facit hoc ad condemnationis illorum auxesim,perinde ac si pluribus testibus quam tribus qui in iudicio accusatur, de flagitio admisso conuincatur.
units.tr: "Therefore, according to this sentence of the Apostle, a sinner is confronted and accused by so many witnesses, since he is admonished repeatedly, whether through one person or through others and others again, and, having been rebuked, is called to repentance. Next we see here that those who, though admonished a second and third time, especially by those under whose care they are placed, refuse to repent, are deprived of every excuse by sufficient testimonies. And if they are rebuked more often than necessary, this contributes to the increase of their condemnation, just as if a person accused in court were convicted of a committed crime by more witnesses than the three required."

units.la: PRAEDIXI, inquit, & praedico, ut praesens cum essem, iterum ita & absens nunc scribo, &c.)
units.tr: "## 'I have foretold,' he says, 'and I foretell, as though I were present for the second time, and now, though absent, I write,' etc."

units.la: In Graeco sic legitur, προειρηκα καὶ προλέγω, ὡς παρὼν τὸ δεύτερον, καὶ ἀπὼν νῦν γράφω, id est, Praedixi & praedico ut praesens, secundo & absens nunc scribo. Itaq; Erasmus de suo adiecit,cum essem,&,ita,& δεύτερον, id est, secundo, uertit, iterum. Augustinus libro 3.contra epistolā Parmeniani cap.2.legit ad hunc modum: Praedixi & praedico sicut praesens, secundo & nunc absens,his qui ante peccauerunt. Et Ambrosius sic:Praedixi enim & praedico ut praesens secundo aduentu, & absens nunc his qui ante peccauerūt. Vulgatus interpres habet,ut praesens uobis.Pro δευτέρῳ reddidit uobis, & uerbum γράφω omisit, quemadmodum illud nec Augustinus nec Ambrosius legerunt. Et uidetur commodius omitti posse,quam legi.
units.tr: "The Greek reads: προειρηκα καὶ προλέγω, ὡς παρὼν τὸ δεύτερον, καὶ ἀπὼν νῦν γράφω [proeirēka kai prolegō, hōs parōn to deuteron, kai apōn nyn graphō], that is, 'I have foretold and I foretell, as present the second time, and now absent I write.' Erasmus, therefore, added from his own resources 'as I was,' 'and,' and 'so,' and translated δεύτερον [deuteron], that is 'second,' as 'again.' Augustine, in the third book against the letter of Parmenian, chapter 2, reads it in this way: 'I have foretold and I foretell, as present, a second time, and now absent, to those who sinned before.' Ambrose also reads: 'For I have foretold and I foretell, as present at a second coming, and now absent, to those who sinned before.' The Vulgate translator has 'as present to you.' For δευτέρῳ [deutera] he rendered 'to you,' and he omitted the verb γράφω [graphō], just as neither Augustine nor Ambrose read it. And it seems more suitable to omit it than to read it."

units.la: Exponit quorsum legem illam, in ore duorum uel trium testium, &c. citarit. Quasi primum testimonium fuisse significat,quod praedixerat cum secundo apud eos esset, alterum uero quod nunc denuo inculcat, quid? quod nō sit parsurus ubi ad ipsos uenerit. Sic dicit: Praedixi & praedico, praedixi cum essem praesens secundo, praedico etiam nunc cum sum absens:praedico autē ijs qui ante peccauerunt, & reliquis omnibus,qd si uenero denuo non parcam. Si ad hūc modum exposuerimus, apparet ipsum secundo uenisse Corinthū,ac praesentem redarguisse peccantes. Verum si illud & praedico ὡς παρὼν τὸ δεύτερον καὶ ἀπὼν νῦν, con iunctim acceperimus ad hunc modum,perinde ac si presens sim secundo,nunc quoque absens hoc praedico,non poterit firmū esse,quod secūdo praesens fuerit apud Corinthios. Etenim non simpliciter dicit, παρὼν τὸ δεύτερον. i. cū psens essem secūdo, sed ὡς παρὼν τὸ δεύτερον, id est,perinde ac si sim praesens secundo. Dein de ista iūgit nō cum praeterito uerbo praedixi, sed cum praesenti,praedico. Verum non contedo,sed diligēte lectore quid cogitet moneo. Quibus autem prædixit, & nunc quoq; præ-dicit: Illis, inquit, qui antè peccauerunt, & re-liquis omnibus. Vbi dicit, ijs qui antè pecca-uerunt, subintelligëdum est illud ex calce ca-pitis precedentis, nec eos pœnituit immundi-ciæ, libidinisq; & impudicitiæ quâ patrarunt. Neque enim loquitur in genere de omnibus qui antè peccauerant, sed de illis speciali-ter, quos peccatorum suorum non pœnitebat.
units.tr: "He explains to what end he cited that law, 'in the mouth of two or three witnesses,' etc. He indicates that the first testimony was what he had foretold when he was with them the second time, and the second is what he now repeats: what? That he will not spare when he comes to them. He says: 'I have foretold and I foretell: I foretold when I was present the second time; I foretell also now that I am absent. I foretell to those who sinned before and to all the rest that if I come again I will not spare.' If we explain it in this way, it appears that he came to Corinth a second time and rebuked the sinners in person. But if we take 'and I foretell' together with ὡς παρὼν τὸ δεύτερον καὶ ἀπὼν νῦν [hōs parōn to deuteron kai apōn nyn], as though he were present the second time, and now also absent, in this way: 'as if I were present a second time, now also absent I foretell this,' it cannot be firmly established that he was present with the Corinthians a second time. For he does not simply say παρὼν τὸ δεύτερον [parōn to deuteron], that is, 'when I was present the second time,' but ὡς παρὼν τὸ δεύτερον [hōs parōn to deuteron], that is, 'as if I were present a second time.' Then he joins 'I foretell' not with the past tense 'I have foretold' but with the present. However, I do not contend the point, but I advise the careful reader to consider what he thinks. To those to whom he had foretold, and now foretells again, he says: 'to those who sinned before, and to all the rest.' Where he says 'to those who sinned before,' it must be understood from the end of the preceding chapter: that they did not repent of the uncleanness, lust and impurity they had committed. For he is not speaking generally of all who had sinned before, but specifically of those whose sins they did not repent of."

units.la: Illud, & reliquis omnibus, ad hoc adiecit, ut etiam eos qui non ita peccauerant, nec pec-cabát in præsenti cum ista scriberet, neque de impœnitentia accusari poterant, cautos red-deret, ne exemplo peccantium & impenitentium seducti securius agerent, & in idem malum inciderent. Admonētur hoc exemplo mi-nistri Christi, quàm non eos modò qui delin-quunt corripere & ad resipiscentiam uocare, sed & cæteros cautos ac uigilantes reddere debeant, ne & ipsi peccando à studio innocen-tiæ exorbitent. Quid autem illis prædicit?
units.tr: "The words 'and to all the rest' he added so that he might also make cautious those who had not sinned in this way, nor were sinning at the present time when he wrote, nor could be accused of impenitence, lest, led astray by the example of sinners and the impenitent, they should act too securely and fall into the same evil. By this example the ministers of Christ are admonished that they ought not only to correct those who offend and call them to repentance, but also to make the others cautious and watchful, lest they too, by sinning, turn aside from zeal for innocence. But what does he foretell to them?"

units.la: QVOD si uenero, inquit, non parcam.) Est hæc comminatio paterna. Sensus est: Si me coe-geritis ut ad uos denuo ueniam, non ueniam frustra, sed animaduertam in eos qui non resi-puerunt. Dices: Quorsum opus erat iterû hoc atque iterum prædicendo comminari? Respon-deo, quia adhuc illis parcebat, conabaturq; eiusmodi comminationibus paterna erga ipsos stiorgiam spirantibus, eos qui peccauerát, fle-ctere ad resipiscentiam, ne seuerius aliquid in eos tentare cogeretur, à qua seueritate uehe-menter abhorrebat, qua de re & suprà cap. pri-mo meminit, dicens: Ego uero testem Deum inuoco in animam meam, quod parcens uo-bis nondum uenerim Corinthum, & quæ ibi sequuntur. Augustinus contra Donatist. dimi-cans lib.3. aduersus epist. Parmen. cap.2. locû hunc sic propositô suo accommodat. Ideoque idem Apostolus cum iam multos comperisset & immunda luxuria & fornicationibus inqui-natos, ad eosdem Corinthios in secunda epist. scribens, non itidem præcipit, ut cum talibus nec cibum sumeret. Multi enim erant, nec dici de his pot-rat, si quis frater nominatur forni-cator, aut eidolis seruiens, aut auarus, aut ali-quid tale, cum eiusmodi nec cibum quidem simul sumere, sed ait, Ne iterum cum uenero ad uos humiliet me Deus, & lugeam multos ex his qui antè peccauerunt, & non egerût pœ-nitentiam super immunditia, & luxuria, & for-nicatione quam gesserunt: per luctum suum potius eos diuino flagello coercedos minans, quàm per illam correptionem, ut ceteri ab eo-rum coniunctione se contineant. Consequen-ter enim dicit: Ecce tertio hoc ueniam ad uos, ut in ore duorū uel triū testium stet omne uer-bum. Prædixi & prædico, sicut præsens, secu-do & nunc absens his qui antè peccauerût, & cæteris omnibus: quia si uenero iterū non par-cam, quia probatione quæritis ejus qui in me loquitur Christus.
