Quid aliud dixit hic, nō par-cam, nisi quod superius ait, Et lugeâ multos, ut luctus eius impetraret flagellum à domino,
units.tr: "'If I come,' he says, 'I will not spare.' This is a paternal threat. The sense is: If you compel me to come to you again, I will not come in vain, but will take action against those who have not repented. You will say: 'Why was it necessary to threaten repeatedly by foretelling it again and again?' I reply: because he was still sparing them, and was attempting by threats of this kind, which breathe paternal affection toward them, to win over those who had sinned to repentance, so that he would not be compelled to attempt something more severe against them, a severity from which he strongly shrank. On this matter he also mentions it above in the first chapter, saying: 'But I call God to witness upon my soul that it was to spare you that I have not yet come to Corinth,' and what follows there. Augustine, contending against the Donatists in the third book against the letter of Parmenian, chapter 2, adapts this passage to his purpose in this way: 'And so the same Apostle, when he had already discovered many who were defiled by unclean lust and fornications, writing again to the same Corinthians in the second letter, did not similarly command that one should not even eat with such persons. For there were many, and it could not be said of them: if anyone is named a brother, a fornicator, or a servant of idols, or covetous, or anything of the kind, do not even eat together with such a person. Instead he says: "Lest again, when I come to you, God humble me, and I mourn over many of those who sinned before and did not repent of the uncleanness, lust and fornication which they committed."' By threatening that they should be restrained by divine scourging through his mourning, rather than by that correction, so that the others might keep themselves from fellowship with them. For he says consequently: 'Behold, I am coming to you for the third time, so that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand. I have foretold and I foretell, as present, a second time, and now absent, to those who sinned before and to all the rest, because if I come again I will not spare, since you seek proof of him who speaks in me, Christ.' What else did he mean here by 'I will not spare' than what he said above, 'and I will mourn over many,' so that his mourning might obtain a scourge from the Lord"

units.la: quo illi corriperentur, qui iam propter multi-tudinem non poterant ita corripi, ut ab eorū coniunctione se cæteri continerent, & eos eru-bescere facerent, sicut faciendum est, si quis fra-ter in aliquo ceteris dissimili crimine nomina-tur. Et reuera si contagio peccandi multitudi-nem inuaserit, diuinæ disciplinæ seuera miseri-cordia necessaria est: nam consilia separationis & inania sunt & perniciosa atq; sacrilega, quia & impia & superba fiunt, & plus perturbant in firmos bonos, quàm corrigant animosos ma-los. Hæc ille, quæ vtinam considerent diligen-tius fratres illi, qui meo iudicio, imprudentius aliquanto ad separationis consilia propendet.
units.tr: by which those were rebuked who, because of their number, could no longer be corrected in such a way that the rest held themselves back from fellowship with them and made them blush, as ought to be done when some brother is named for a crime unlike the others. And indeed, if the contagion of sin has seized a multitude, the severe mercy of divine discipline is necessary. For plans of separation are both empty and harmful and sacrilegious, since they become both impious and proud, and they disturb the weak believers more than they correct the wicked who are obstinate. Thus he. Would that those brothers would consider this more carefully, who, in my judgment, incline somewhat too rashly toward plans of separation.

units.la: QVANDO QVIDEM experimentum quę-ritis, inquit, in me loquentis Christi, qui erga uos non est infirmus, sed potens est in uobis.) Contemni se videbat, perinde ac si nulla esset virtute Christi præditus, atq; ita contemni in se Christum. Cum hoc facerent impœnitentes & securè in peccatis suis pergentes, nec qquâ- sibi à Christo per Apostolum ipsius metuētes, eam securitatem molestè ferens, interpretatur nihil esse aliud, q̃ tentationem Christi in se lo-quentis, & per hanc tépestiuum fieri dicit, ut quod experiri q̃ deprecari malunt, reipsa expe-riantur. Sic cum dixisset, quòd si venero non parcam, subiungit, quandoquidem, vel vt Au-gustinus legit, quia probationem quæritis lo-quentis in me Christi. Minas ipsius securi ride-bant, non credétes eas fieri per spiritū Christi, nec fore per virtutem illius efficaces, id quod nihil erat aliud, q̃ experimentū quærere, Chri-ftus ne per ipsum minas eas proferret, vel ef-sent inania tantum terriculamenta, nihil viriū habentia. Dicit itaq; mallem vobis parcere, i-deoq; nondum veni ad uos Corinthum, sed li-teris in uiam uos reducere molior. Verū quo-niam admonitiones meas quæ per literas fiūt perinde cōtemnitis, ac si sint hominis infirmi ac contempti, & non ipsius Christi, atq; ita ex-perimentum quæritis loquetis in me Christi, age vbi uenero, faciam ut quod quæritis inue-niatis. Neq; enim parcam amplius, sed declara-bo vobis, q̃ sit Christi in me loquêtis potetia.
units.tr: "Since you seek proof," he says, "of Christ speaking in me, who is not weak toward you, but is mighty among you." He saw himself being despised, as though he were endowed with no power of Christ, and thus Christ himself despised in him. When the impenitent did this, going on securely in their sins and not fearing the threats which Christ had made to them through his Apostle, Paul, bearing that security with displeasure, explains that it is nothing other than a testing of Christ speaking in him, and he says that through this it comes about in good time that they actually experience what they preferred to experience rather than to avoid. So, having said, "If I come, I will not spare," he adds, "since indeed," or, as Augustine reads it, "because you seek a proof of Christ speaking in me." They mocked his threats carelessly, not believing that they were made by the Spirit of Christ, nor that they would be effective through his power, which was nothing other than seeking proof whether Christ would bring these threats forth through him, or whether they would be empty frightening words, having no force. He therefore says: I would rather spare you; and so I have not yet come to you at Corinth, but I am striving to bring you back to the way by letters. But since you despise my admonitions, which are made by letter, as though they were those of a weak and contemptible man, and not of Christ himself, and so you seek proof of Christ speaking in me, well then, when I come, I will make you find what you seek. For I will spare you no longer, but I will show you what the power of Christ speaking in me is.

units.la: Haud quidē studio ac volentes id agebant impœnitentes Corinthij, vt certò cognosceret admonitiones Pauli, Christi esse in ipso loquē-tis, uerùm quoniam illis non credebant, sed cō-temptim in impœnitentia sua pergebant, dicit id nihil esse aliud q̃ velle experiri veritatem ac virtutem in se loquentis Christi, quatenus vi-delicet non credere minis, sed pergere in malo nihil est aliud q̃ condignas velle experiri pla-gas, perinde ac si præceptor immorigero disci-pulo, quem nullis admonitionib. acquiescere uidet, dicat, quandoquidem experimentū q̃-ris uirgæ, quam in potestate mea habeo, age si monitis hisce meis non parueris, non parcam amplius, sed faciam, ut quod quæris inuenias, ostendamq; tibi quæ sit illa mea potestas, cu-ius admonitiones nihili facis.
units.tr: The Corinthian impenitent certainly did not do this with zeal or willingly, so that they would know for certain that the admonitions of Paul were of Christ speaking in him; but since they did not believe them, and went on contemptuously in their impenitence, he says that this is nothing other than wishing to experience the truth and power of Christ speaking in him, insofar as they, not believing the threats, but persisting in evil, are nothing other than wishing to experience deserved blows. It is as if a teacher, seeing that an obstinate disciple does not heed any admonitions, said: "Since you seek proof of the rod which I hold in my power, well then, if you do not obey these my warnings, I will spare you no longer, but I will make you find what you seek, and I will show you what that power of mine is, whose admonitions you make nothing of."

units.la: Hunc existimo germanum esse præsentis loci sensum, ut experimentum q̃rere, sit per-tinaci tinaci impœnitentia exequutione minarũ con tra se prouocare, vt quod quis credere detre- ctat,reipsa experiatur: deinde illud, loquentis in me Christi, de admonitionibus & commina tionib. per ipsum factis, intelligatur, licet enim vniuersa Euangelij doctrina quam prædicabat non esset ipsius, sed loquentis in ipso Christi, specialiter tamen hic de potestate sua quam à Christo acceperat, loquitur, ex qua ipsos admonebat & corripiebat, quam impœnitentes contemnebant.
units.tr: I think this is the true sense of the present passage: that to seek proof is, by obstinate impenitence, to provoke against oneself the execution of threats, so that one actually experiences what one shrinks from believing. Next, the words "of Christ speaking in me" should be understood of the admonitions and threats made through him. For although the whole doctrine of the Gospel which he preached was not his own, but that of Christ speaking in him, nevertheless here he speaks especially of his power, which he had received from Christ, by which he admonished and rebuked them, and which the impenitent despised.

units.la: QVI erga vos non est infirmus, inquit, sed potens est in vobis. Transfert cōtemptum potestatis suæ in ipsum Christum, & vt admonea-ut, quàm non sit excusabilis, reuocat illis in me-tem, quanta sit efficacia & potentia loquentis in se Christi inter ipsos declarata. Sic dicit: Qui erga vos non est infirmus, sed potens est in vo-bis. Non simpliciter dicit, qui non est infirm' sed potens. Neq; enim in genere de potentia Christi loquitur, cum illa sit infinita, sed specia-liter de ea, quæ erga ipsos fuerat declarata lo-quens: qui erga vos, inquit, non est infirmus sed potens est in vobis.
units.tr: "Who is not weak toward you," he says, "but is mighty among you." He transfers the contempt of his power to Christ himself, and, in order to show how inexcusable they are, he calls back to their mind how great the efficacy and power of Christ speaking in him had been shown among them. He says: "Who is not weak toward you, but is mighty among you." He does not simply say, "who is not weak, but mighty." For he is not speaking generally of the power of Christ, since that is infinite, but specially of that power which had been displayed toward them, when he says: "who is not weak toward you, but is mighty among you."

units.la: Fuerat aût illa in ecclesia Corinthiorũ bifa-riam declarata. Primò, in ministerio prædica-tionis ipsius per virtutē cooperantis spiritus Christi, in variis charismatibus, signis ac portē-tis, de quib. cap. præcedenti dixit, Nulla enim in re inferior fui summis apostolis, tametsi ni-hil sum. Signa quippe Apostoli perącta fuerũt inter vos cum omni patientia, & signis & pro-digijs & potentibus factis. Sanè per hæc abū-dè satis declaratū fuerat inter Corinthios, nō minus quàm in reliquis ecclesijs, nō esse Chri-stum infirmum, sed potentem in apostolorum suorum ministerio. Deinde per castigationē necessariam, qua corripiendi sunt peccantes. Ea quoq; virtus Christi comprobata fuerat in Corinthijs, priusquam priore ad illos epistolá scripsisset. Sic enim cap.11. legimus: Nam qui edit & bibit indignè, iudicium sibijpsi edit & bibit, non dijudicans corpus domini. Propter hoc inter uos multi imbecilles & inualidi, & dormiunt multi. Etenim si nosipsos dijudicas-semus, haudquaquam iudicati fuissemus. At cum iudicamur, à domino corripimur, ne cum mundo condemnemur. Quibus verbis satis in nuitur immisisse dominum virgam paternam illis, qui sacramento corporis & sanguinis ipsi us ad iudicium vsurpabant, eaq; in re declara-tum fuisse, non esse Christum sic infirmum, ut nequeat in eos animaduertere, qui admonitio-num apostolorum ipsius cōtemptores esse ma-lunt quàm obsequutores, sed satis potentem ad castigandam fidelium suorum impœniten-tiam. Quod itaq; dicit, qui erga vos non est in-firmus, sed potens est in vobis, non incommo-dè ad vtranq; Christi virtutem inter Corinthi-os declaratam referri poterit. Nam vtrăq; sic in-ter illos declaratæ fuerant, ut sufficerent sin-gulæ ad redarguendum inexcusabilem impœ-niten- um contemptum.
units.tr: Now that power had been displayed in the Corinthian church in two ways. First, in the ministry of his preaching, through the power of the Spirit of Christ working together with it, in various gifts, signs and wonders, of which he spoke in the preceding chapter: "For I am not in any way inferior to the chief apostles, though I am nothing." For "the signs of an apostle were wrought among you with all patience, by signs and wonders and mighty deeds" (2 Cor. 12). Surely by these things it had been made clear enough among the Corinthians, no less than in the other churches, that Christ is not weak, but mighty, in the ministry of his apostles. Second, through the necessary correction by which sinners are to be rebuked. That power of Christ had also been proved among the Corinthians before he wrote the earlier letter to them. For so we read in chapter 11: "For he who eats and drinks unworthily, eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the Lord's body. For this reason many among you are weak and sickly, and many sleep. For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged. But when we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, so that we are not condemned with the world" (1 Cor. 11:29–32). By these words it is sufficiently indicated that the Lord had sent his fatherly rod upon those who used the sacrament of his body and blood for judgment, and that it had been shown in this matter that Christ is not so weak as to be unable to punish those who prefer to despise rather than obey the admonitions of his apostles, but is powerful enough to chastise the impenitence of his faithful. Therefore, when he says, "who is not weak toward you, but is mighty among you," this can not unfitly be referred to both powers of Christ displayed among the Corinthians. For each of them had been shown among them in such a way that either alone would suffice to refute their inexcusable impenitent contempt.

units.la: Habet hic vnde se solentur Christi ministri, vbi se apud eos quoq; quibus Christum prædi-cant, nihil authoritatis habere vident. Etenim si id accidit Paulo, per cuius prædicationem Christus inter Corinthios potens declaratus fuerat, quid mirum est, si ipsis idem vsueniat, cum nulla tanta fit ipsorum prædicationi vir-tus Christi coniuncta, quanta coniuncta erat Apostolatui Pauli, multis signis ac portentis illustrato?
units.tr: Here Christ's ministers have something to console them, when they see that they have no authority even among those to whom they preach Christ. For if this happened to Paul, through whose preaching Christ had been shown to be mighty among the Corinthians, what wonder is it if the same happens to them, since no such power of Christ is joined to their preaching as was joined to the apostleship of Paul, which was made illustrious by many signs and wonders?

units.la: NAM quamuis crucifixus fuit, inquit, ex in firmitate, viuit tamen ex virtute Dei.) Vindi-cat gloriam potentiæ Christi contra contem-ptum crucis. Quoniam prædicabat Christum crucifixum, videbatur prædicare Christū non potentem sed infirmum, qui sine periculo pof sit contemni. Occurrit, non negans infirmita-tem carnis in crucifixione ac morte illius ma-nifestatam, sed agnoscens quidem illam, uerū sic vt afferat illi vitam, non amplius infirmitati vt antea, obnoxiam, sed diuina virtute glorifi-catam, qua se ab omni possit contemptu poten-ter afferere. Quasi dicat, An ideo contemnitis Christum in me loquentem quod mortuus est per infirmitatem carnis? Mortuus quidem su-it ex infirmitate, verùm non est mortuus am-plius, sed virtute Dei à morte excitatus viuit, & viuit non adhuc infirmus, sed potentia Dei præditus. Et hæc ipsius potentia abundè inter vos est declarata, vnde cognoscere potestis, habere nos Christum neq; mortuũ, neq; infir-mum, sed viuum ac potentem.
units.tr: "For though he was crucified," he says, "through weakness, yet he lives by the power of God." He vindicates the glory of Christ's power against the contempt of the cross. Since he preached Christ crucified, he seemed to preach a Christ who was not mighty but weak, one who could be despised without danger. He meets this objection, not denying that the weakness of the flesh was shown in his crucifixion and death, but acknowledging it indeed, yet in such a way as to bring to him life, no longer subject to weakness as before, but glorified by divine power, by which he can powerfully assert himself against all contempt. As if he said: Do you therefore despise Christ speaking in me because he died through the weakness of the flesh? He indeed died through weakness, but he has not remained dead; by the power of God he has been raised from death and lives, and lives not still weak, but endowed with the power of God. And this power of his has been abundantly shown among you, whence you can know that we have a Christ who is neither dead nor weak, but living and mighty.

units.la: De eo quod Christum ex infirmitate cruci-fixum esse dicit, annotarunt alij, quomodo in-firmitatis vocabulo de veritate carnis huma-næ, ab illo salutis nostræ gratia suscepte admo-neamur, contra eos qui non naturæ ac condi-tioni suscepte carnis, sed singulari dispensatio-ni tribuunt, quod mori potuit. At Apostolus diserte dicit: Nam crucifixus est ex infirmita-te, quod sanè non potest alió referri, quàm ad carnem illius sic infirmam ut mori posset. Diui-na quidem dispensatione factum est, vt verbũ illud æternum per quod condita sunt omnia, caro fieret, verùm talis caro, quæ infirma esset nostræque dempto peccato, natura & condi-tione similis, imò ὁμοίως. Et hęc carnis infir-mitas haud quidem intulit Christo moriendi necessitatem, cum mortuus sit, quia voluit, & quia pater sic constituerat, verùm naturæ suæ infirmitate suscepte, pro nobis dispensationi accommodata seruiuit. Ad hoc enim talem su-scepit, vt quoniam nos carni & sanguini sum- obnoxij, ipse similiter particeps eorundem fa-ctus per mortem aboleret eum, qui mortis ha-bebat imperium. Non ob id est crucifixus ex infirmitate, quod nequiret infirmam suam car-nem reddere firmam, & seruare à necessitate moriendi, si ita voluisset pater, sed quod obe-diens Deo patri, infirmam suam carnem spon-te sua tradidit, vt mortem gustaret in cruce.
units.tr: Others have remarked on the statement that Christ was crucified through weakness, noting how the word "weakness" reminds us of the truth of human flesh, which he took up for the sake of our salvation. They argue against those who ascribe his capacity to die not to the nature and condition of the flesh he assumed, but to a special dispensation. The Apostle plainly says: "For he was crucified through weakness," which certainly cannot refer to anything but his flesh, so weak that it could die. By divine dispensation it came about that the eternal Word, through whom all things were made, became flesh. But this flesh was weak and, sin excepted, like ours in nature and condition, indeed "in like manner" [ὁμοίως]. This weakness of the flesh did not bring Christ the necessity of dying, since he died because he willed it and because the Father had so appointed. Rather, having taken up the weakness of his nature, he served the dispensation suited to us. For he assumed such flesh so that, since we are subject to flesh and blood, he himself, likewise made a partaker of them, might by death destroy him who had the power of death. He was crucified through weakness not because he could not make his weak flesh strong and preserve it from the necessity of dying if the Father had so willed, but because, obedient to God the Father, he of his own accord gave up his weak flesh so that he might taste death on the cross.

units.la: Quare nec moriendi necessitate damus Chri-sto ex carnis illius infirmitate, nec sic dispensa-tionem tionem susceptam agnoscimus, vt infirmitatē carnis in illo negemus. Oportuit Christum sic pati, non propterea quod infirmus erat carne, sed quia sic ab æterno disposuerat pater. Infirmus autē factus est carne, vt nostras infirmitates portare, proq; peccatis nostris crucifigi posset ac mori, de his, sicuti dixi, annotarunt ante me alij, volui autem & ipse de illis admonere, vt sententia mea ipsorū annotatis coniungā.
units.tr: Therefore we do not attribute to Christ a necessity of dying from the weakness of that flesh, nor do we so acknowledge the dispensation he took up that we deny the weakness of the flesh in him. It was necessary for Christ to suffer in this way, not because he was weak in the flesh, but because the Father had so arranged from eternity. Yet he was made weak in the flesh so that he could bear our infirmities and be crucified and die for our sins. Others before me have noted these things, as I have said, but I too wished to remind readers of them, so that I might join my own view to their remarks.

units.la: Et illud, viuit tamen ex virtute Dei, cautè accipiendum est, ne intelligamus tribui Christo, quod non suapte, sed sic Dei virtute viuat, quemadmodum nos toti quanti quāti sumus, virtute non nostra, sed Dei viuificabimur. Viuit ille virtute Dei, sua videlicet, quatenus verus Deus est, diuinaq; potestate quā habet animam, quam posuerat pro nobis recepit, quem admodum & ex infirmitate sua, vt homo, crucifixus fuit. Idem Christus ex sua mortuus est infirmitate, humana videlicet, & ex diuina sua virtute viuit. Verbum autem viuendi non posuit simpliciter, sed emphaticè, vt idem sit qd᷑, viuendo triumphat ac regnat, virtutemq; sua declarat.
units.tr: The words "yet he lives by the power of God" must be taken carefully, lest we understand them as if it were ascribed to Christ that he lives not by his own power but by God's, just as we shall all be made alive not by our own power but by God's. He lives by the power of God, namely his own, insofar as he is true God, and by the divine power which he has over the soul that he laid down for us and took up again. Just as he was crucified in his weakness as man, so the same Christ died through his human weakness and lives by his divine power. He did not use the verb "to live" in a plain sense, but emphatically, so that it means: by living he triumphs and reigns and displays his power.

units.la: SIQVIDEM & nos infirmi sumus in illo, in quit, sed viuemus cum illo ex virtute Dei erga uos.) Græcè est, ὅτι γὰρ ἡμεῖς, i. Etenim nos, quasi quod hic dicit vel rationem vel cōprobationē habeat præcedentium, quæ de Christi dixit in firmitate, & virtute. Rationem habere non potest. Neq; enim ideo Christus crucifixus est ex infirmitate, & viuit ex virtute Dei, quod Paulus infirmus postea in ipso victurus erat cum ipso, ex uirtute Dei erga Corinthios, sed ijs potius quæ de Christo prædicat, ratio assignari potest eorum, quæ hic loquitur de seipso.
units.tr: "For we also are weak in him," he says, "but we shall live with him by the power of God toward you." In Greek it is "for we" [ὅτι γὰρ ἡμεῖς], as if what he says here gave a reason or proof for the preceding words, which spoke of Christ's weakness and power. But it cannot give a reason. Christ was not crucified through weakness and does not live by God's power because Paul, weak, was afterwards to live with him by God's power toward the Corinthians. Rather, a reason for what he says here about himself can be found in what he proclaims about Christ.

units.la: Cum ergo illud καὶ γὰρ nequeat hic uim habere αἰτιολογίας, restat vt positum sit sensu comprobandi. Iam quod de Christo dixit, crucifixum illum fuisse ex infirmitate, nullam comprobationem requirebat, tanquam per se alioqui manifestum. Reliquum igitur est, ut referendum sit ad id quod dixit, Viuit tamen ex virtute Dei. Huius comprobandi gratia subijcit: Etenim nos infirmi quidem sumus in illo, sed viuemus cum illo ex uirtute Dei erga vos.
units.tr: Since, therefore, the "and for" [καὶ γὰρ] here cannot have the force of giving a reason, it remains that it is placed in a confirming sense. As for what he said about Christ, that he was crucified through weakness, this needed no confirmation, being evident in itself. What remains, then, is that it must refer to what he said: "yet he lives by the power of God." To confirm this, he adds: "For we indeed are weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God toward you."

units.la: Quasi dicat: Vbi senseritis nos viuere ac posse erga uos per virtutem Dei cum Christo, qui iā infirmi in illo & nihil posse erga uos uidemur, tum comperietis non esse illum infirmum in nobis, sed potentem erga vos, adeoq; non cōtemnendum in nobis sed religiosissimè reuerendum. Hunc sensum poscit uocula γὰρ. Nisi illa esset, appareret ista dicta esse ad exprimendam conformitatem eorum quæ Apostolo si milia acciderunt cum Christo, legendaq; & exponenda ad hunc modum. Et nos (consimiliter) infirmi quidem sumus in illo, uerū uiuemus cum illo ex uirtute Dei erga vos. Quasi di cat. Quemadmodum ille crucifixus est ex infirmitate, ita & nos in illo multis afflictionibus obnoxij sumus & infirmi: & sicuti ille viuit ex virtute Dei, potensque est erga uos, ita
units.tr: As if he said: When you perceive that we live with Christ and are able toward you by the power of God, though we now seem weak in him and to have no power toward you, then you will find that he is not weak in us, but powerful toward you; and so he is not to be despised in us, but most reverently revered. The little word "for" [γὰρ] demands this sense. Were it not there, these words would seem to express the conformity of what happened to the Apostle with what happened to Christ, and should be read and explained in this way: "And we (similarly) are indeed weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God toward you." As if he said: just as he was crucified through weakness, so we too are in him subject to many afflictions and are weak; and just as he lives by the power of God and is powerful toward you,

units.la: & nos cum illo, vbi ad uos redierimus, ex virtute Dei erga uos viuem⁹, potétesq; erimus. Hic sensus stare posset, nisi esset vocula γὰρ.
units.tr: so we too, when we have returned to you, shall live with him by the power of God toward you, and shall be powerful. This sense could stand, were it not for the little word "for."

units.la: Quoniam non simpliciter dicit: viuemus cū illo ex virtute Dei, sed addit, erga vos, manifestum est non esse intelligendum de futura vita qua cum Christo viuemus in gloria, sed de ea, qua se potentem erga Corinthios, vbi ad eos venerit, ad castigandum impœnitentes fore di cat. Quare quorundam expositio, qui hæc de futura gloria exponunt, & impertinens est ad præsentem causam, & ipsis verbis non conue-nit. Minatur adhuc id ipsum quod supra dixit, quod si uenero denuò non parcam. Ei commi nationi exequendæ propter formas infirmitatis, quas varijs modis afflictus præferebat, impar videbatur. Comminatur igitur illis fore, vt cum Christo satis sit erga eos viuax & potens ad castigandum immorigeros, quantumuis in oculis ipsorum infirmus & contemptibilis appareat.
units.tr: Since he does not simply say "we shall live with him by the power of God" but adds "toward you," it is clear that this is not to be understood of the future life in which we shall live with Christ in glory, but of the power by which he says he will be mighty toward the Corinthians when he comes to them, to punish the impenitent. So the exposition of those who explain these words of future glory is irrelevant to the present case and does not fit the words themselves. He still threatens the very thing he said above: "if I come again I will not spare." To carry out that threat, he seemed unequal to it because of the forms of weakness which, afflicted in various ways, he displayed. He therefore threatens them that, living with Christ, he will be sufficiently strong and powerful toward them to punish the unruly, however weak and contemptible he may appear in their eyes.

units.la: VOSIPSOS tentate inquit, num sitis in fide, vosipsos probate.) Trāstert causam de qua agit ad ipsorū cōscientias. Quasi dicat, Quod si virtute viuentis Christi in me nō agnoscitis, agnoscite illā saltem in vobis. Probate & examinate vosipsos, nū declarata sit in vobis virtus Christi. Si illam in vobis deprehenditis, quomodo in me non agnoscitis, per quem illa vobis contigit? Hæc est summa præsentis loci. Sed videamus ipsa verba.
units.tr: "Test yourselves," he says, "whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves." He transfers the matter he is dealing with to their consciences. As if he said: If you do not recognize the power of Christ living in me, at least recognize it in yourselves. Prove and examine yourselves, whether the power of Christ has been displayed in you. If you find it in yourselves, how do you not recognize it in me, through whom it came to you? This is the sum of the present passage. But let us look at the words themselves.

units.la: VOSIPSOS tentate, inquit.) Græcè est πειράζετε. Significat πειράζειν Græcis immaturo a liqd & frustraneo conatu aggrediendo tētare. Hoc sensu nō loquitur hic Apostolus, sed simpliciter iubet eos experimentū capere de seipsis. Quare verti poterat: Explorate vosipsos uel, experimentum capite de uobisipsis.
units.tr: "Test yourselves," he says. In Greek it is "try" [πειράζετε]. Among the Greeks, "to try" [πειράζειν] signifies to attempt something rashly and to no purpose. The Apostle does not use the word in that sense here, but simply bids them take a trial of themselves. Hence it could be translated: "Explore yourselves," or "take a test of yourselves."

units.la: NVM sitis in fide.) εἰ ἐστε ἐν τῇ πίστει, i. si estis in fide. Sic habet & vulgata ædition. Non iubet eos periculū de seipsis facere, num sint in fide, sed, nū sit in ipsis Christus, id quod paulo post exprimet. Dicit. Si estis in fide, i. si estis fideles & viri Christiani, experimentum de vobisipsis capite. Nondum exprimit, cuius rei periculū in seipsis facere debeant. Quare expositio eorum impertinēs est, qui sic exponunt: Volmet ipsos tentate, i. facta vestra examinate, antequā veniam ad vos iudicandum. Non poscit ut sua ipsorum facta examinent, sed ea potius, quæ o-perabatur in ipsis virtus Christi.
units.tr: "Whether you are in the faith." In Greek it is "if you are in the faith" [εἰ ἐστε ἐν τῇ πίστει], that is, "if you are in the faith." The Vulgate edition also has it so. He does not bid them make trial of themselves to see whether they are in the faith, but whether Christ is in them, which he will express a little later. He says: "If you are in the faith," that is, if you are faithful and Christian men, take a test of yourselves. He does not yet state what matter they must put to the test in themselves. So the exposition of those is irrelevant who explain it thus: "Test yourselves," that is, examine your deeds before I come to judge you. He does not require them to examine their own deeds, but rather those things which the power of Christ worked in them.

units.la: VOSIPSOS probate.) Repetitio ista confidentiam exprimit qua causam hanc ad ipsorum conscientias transfert. Alioqui nihil aliud intelligit, per verbum δοκιμάζετε quàm per πειράζετε.
units.tr: Prove yourselves.) This repetition expresses confidence, by which he transfers the matter to their own consciences. Otherwise he understands nothing else by the word δοκιμάζετε [dokimazete] than by πειράζετε [peirazete].

units.la: AN non cognoscitis uosmetipsos, quòd Iesus Christus in vobis est?) Tandem exprimit quod volebat, & cuius experientiam de seipsis capere debeant. Profert autem id cum quadam stupiditatis exprobartione, dicens: An' nō cognoscitis uosmetipsos, quod Iesus Christus in vobis est? Quasi dicat, Adeo' ne stupidi estis ne
units.tr: Do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?) At last he states what he wanted, and the experience of themselves that they ought to take. He puts it, however, with a certain rebuke of stupidity, saying: "Do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?" As if he said, "Are you so stupid that you do not even know yourselves, in what matter?"

units.la: {A} carnis in illo negemus. vt ne vosipsos quidem cognoscatis? qua in re? Quod videlicet Iesus Christus in vobis est, hoc est, quod virtus Iesu Christi agit in vobis, dū tot charismatibus spiritus per fidem in ipsum, ac nominis ipsius professione cumulati estis? Unde est vobis sermo sapientiæ, & scientiæ? Unde fides? Unde dona sanationum? Unde prophetia? Unde discretiones spirituum? Unde genera linguarum? Unde interpretatio linguarum? An non hæc & eiusmodi alia virtutem agentis in vobis Christi declarant? Si tam potes igitur in vobis est Iesus Christus, quomodo illum in me nonnisi infirmum esse putatis? Vel ex vobisipsis perpendite, quid de Apostolatu meo sentire debeatis.
units.tr: "...that we deny in him according to the flesh." Namely, that Jesus Christ is in you, that is, that the power of Jesus Christ works in you, while you have been loaded with so many gifts of the Spirit through faith in him and by the profession of his name? Whence is the word of wisdom and of knowledge to you? Whence faith? Whence the gifts of healings? Whence prophecy? Whence the discerning of spirits? Whence kinds of tongues? Whence the interpretation of tongues? Do not these and other such things declare the power of Christ working in you? If, then, Jesus Christ is so much in you, how do you think he is only weak in me? Or judge from yourselves what you ought to think of my apostleship.

units.la: Illud, quod Iesus Christus in vobis est, exponunt nonnulli de gratia Christi, per quam credentes regenerantur ac iustificantur, & conscientiæ ipsorum pacificantur. Verum hæc illorum sententia abludit à scopo causæ in qua Apostolus versatur. Neq; enim de gratia iustificante agit hoc loco, illisq; dotibus spiritus, quæ hanc concomitantur, sed de potentia Christi, per cuius timorē impœnitētes ad pœnitentiam reuocare moliebatur.
units.tr: Some expound the words "that Jesus Christ is in you" of the grace of Christ, through which believers are regenerated and justified, and their consciences are pacified. But this opinion of theirs is far from the aim of the matter with which the Apostle is dealing. For he is not treating here of justifying grace nor of those gifts of the Spirit which accompany it, but of the power of Christ, by the fear of which he was striving to call back the unrepentant to repentance.

units.la: Haud tamen negarim non incomodè locum hunc ad id vsurpari posse, vt admoneamur singuli, quo nosipsi exploremus, simúsne in fide Christi, & habitet in nobis Christus per fidē, vel secus. Sunt enim certa experimenta fidei, vnde cognoscam, sit ne Christus in cordib. nostris per spiritum ipsius vel minus, quandoquidem nequit otiosa esse vera in Christū fides: qua de re in locis nostris videre licebit, vbi vt lente domino in lucem prodibunt.
units.tr: Yet I would not deny that this passage can be fittingly applied to admonish each of us to examine ourselves, whether we are in the faith of Christ, and whether Christ dwells in us through faith or not. For there are sure tests of faith, by which I may know whether Christ is in our hearts through his Spirit or not, since true faith in Christ cannot be idle. On this matter we shall be able to see in our places, where, as the Lord slowly brings them to light.

units.la: NISI sicubi reprobi estis, inquit.) Græcè est, ei μήτι ἀδόκιμοί ἐστε, i.nisi in aliquo, aliquatenus, vel aliqua ex parte, reprobi estis. Moderatius loquitur, quàm si simpliciter diceret, nisi reprobi estis, quo minus offendat, & tamen interim solicitos in hac causa reddat. Dixit, An non cognoscitis vosmetipsos, quod Iesus Christus in vobis est? Hic adjicit exceptionem omnium vrgentissimam, dicens, nisi ex parte reprobi estis. Sensus est: Christus in vobis est, agens in vobis per suum spiritum, idq; virtute tam manifeste, vt in dubium vocari non possit, nisi non eper omnia synceri infide, sed nonihil reprobi. Ergo non est in reprobis Christus. Fugit enim spiritus Christi animam insynceram.
units.tr: "Unless perhaps you are reprobate," he says.) In Greek it is "ei mēti adokimoi este" [εἰ μήτι ἀδόκιμοί ἐστε], that is, unless in some respect, in some measure, or in some part, you are reprobate. He speaks more moderately than if he simply said, "unless you are reprobate," so that he might give less offence, and yet meanwhile make them anxious in this matter. He had said, "Do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?" Here he adds the most pressing exception, saying, "unless you are reprobate in part." The sense is: Christ is in you, working in you through his Spirit, and that by power so manifest that it cannot be called into doubt, unless you are not wholly sincere in the faith but somewhat reprobate. Therefore Christ is not in the reprobate. For the Spirit of Christ flees from an insincere soul.

units.la: AT spero vos cognituros, inquit, quod nos non simus reprobi.) Quia dixit, nisi ex parte reprobi estis, quoniam id in nonnullis nimis verum esse apparebat, in quibus testimonium hoc & experimentum conscientiæ propriæ quod Christus in ipsis esset, ad quod eos provocauit, locum non habebat, redit ad ea quæ de seipso in præcedentibus dixit. Est autē sensus. Quicquid sit de plerisq; vestrum, etiamsi reprobi sint & alieni à Christo, illiusque virtute ac spiritu, spero tamen vbi ad vos venero, sic fore experimentum loquentis in me Christi,quod quæritis, manifestum, vt cogniturii sitis, haud esse me reprobum, sed verum Christi Apostolum.
units.tr: "But I hope you will know," he says, "that we are not reprobate." Because he had said "unless you are reprobate in part," since this seemed all too true of some, in whom this testimony and the experience of one's own conscience that Christ was in them, to which he had called them, had no place, he returns to what he had said about himself earlier. The sense is this: whatever may be the case with most of you, even if they are reprobate and alien from Christ and from his power and Spirit, I nevertheless hope that when I come to you, the experience of Christ speaking in me, which you seek, will be so manifest that you will know that I am not reprobate, but a true Apostle of Christ.

units.la: Potest igitur fieri, vt verus sit ac syncerus Christi minister in ecclesia Dei, etiam si audito res sint reprobi. Et hæc cura cōpetit ministris Christi, vt quales quales sortiantur auditores, ad hoc ipsi contendant, ut non modò non sint reprobi, sed & reprobi non esse cognoscantur. Id autem obtinere poterunt, si nihil omittant eorum quæ fidelis ministri officium concernunt, sic vt omnis culpa resideat in auditoribus perinde atq; in sterilib. arboribus, quæ nulla quantumuis diligenti cultura frugiferæ reddi possunt. Fit nonnunquam vt diligentia ministrorum degeneres ac reprobos auditorū animos arguat, dum frustra ad excolendos eos laboratur, è contra frequenter accidere videm, vt sterilitas auditorum arguat indiligentiā ministrorum. Verum ea demum felix est ecclesia, in qua profectus auditorū, fidem, curam ac diligentiam veri ministri Christi commendant.
units.tr: It is therefore possible that a true and sincere minister of Christ may be in the Church of God, even if those who hear him are reprobate. And this care belongs to the ministers of Christ, that, whatever sort of hearers they obtain, they should strive for this, that they not only be not reprobate, but be recognised as not reprobate. They will be able to obtain this if they omit nothing of those things which pertain to the office of a faithful minister, so that all the fault resides in the hearers, just as in barren trees, which can by no care however diligent be made fruitful. Sometimes it happens that the diligence of ministers exposes the degenerate and reprobate minds of hearers, while labour is spent in vain to cultivate them; on the other hand, we frequently see that the barrenness of hearers exposes the negligence of ministers. But that Church is truly happy in which the progress of the hearers commends the faith, care and diligence of the true minister of Christ.

units.la: Opto aūt apud Deum, ne quid mali faciatis, nō quo nos probati appareamus, sed ut uos quod honestū est faciatis, nos uerò ueluti reprobi simus. Non enim possumus quicquam aduersus veritatem, sed pro veritate. Gaudemus enim cū nos infirmi fuerimus, uos uerò validi fueritis. Hoc autem insuper optamus uestram integritatem. Propterea hæc absens scribo, ne cum præsens fuero rigidus sim iuxta potestatem, quam dedit mihi dominus in extructione, & non in destructionem.
units.tr: I pray to God, however, that you do no evil, not so that we may appear approved, but that you may do what is honourable, and that we may be as reprobate. For we can do nothing against the truth, but only for the truth. For we rejoice when we are weak and you are strong. Moreover, we also pray for your integrity. For this reason I write these things while absent, so that when I am present I may not be harsh, according to the power which the Lord gave me for building up and not for tearing down.

units.la: Quod Erasmus hic vertit: Opto autem ad Deū, Græcè est, εὐχομαι δὲ πρὸς τὸν θεόν, qd ver ti poterat: Oro aūt ad Deū, quemadmodū & vulgata lectio habet, & Germanicus interpres reddidit. Totus ardebat studio ædificandi Corinthios, omnibus suis laboribus, nihil quærens sibi proprij vel commodi vel nominis. Cū ergo dixisset: At spero uos cognituros, quod nos non simus reprobi, ne hoc dicendo suæ tantū existimationis studium spirare videretur, quic quid esset de Corinthijs, occurrēs eiusmodi suspicioni subijcit confestim: Oro aūt ad Deum ne quid mali faciatis, nō quo nos probati appareamus, sed vt vos quod honestum est faciatis, nos vero veluti reprobi simus. Quibus verbis diserte significat, alienū esse se à studio proprię existimationis: nec quærere aliud in tota hac causa, quàm vt ipsi probati inueniantur, etiāsi ipse pro reprobo habeatur.
units.tr: Erasmus here translates: "But I pray to God," which in Greek is "euchomai de pros ton theon" [εὐχομαι δὲ πρὸς τὸν θεόν], which could be rendered, "But I pray to God," as the Vulgate reading also has, and the German translator has rendered it. He burned with zeal to build up the Corinthians, in all his labours seeking nothing for himself, neither gain nor honour nor reputation. Therefore, when he had said, "But I hope you will know that we are not reprobate," lest by saying this he should seem to breathe only a zeal for his own reputation, whatever might be the case with the Corinthians, he immediately meets such a suspicion by adding: "But I pray to God that you do no evil, not so that we may appear approved, but that you may do what is honourable, and that we may be as reprobate." In these words he clearly signifies that he is far from any zeal for his own reputation, and that in this whole matter he seeks nothing other than that they themselves be found approved, even though he himself be held as reprobate.

units.la: ORO autem, inquit, ad Deum.) Non modò scribebat, & fratres mittebat, quo in viam reducerentur Corinthij, sed & orabat pro illis ad Deum. Nec immerito. Sciebat enim nihil
units.tr: "But I pray," he says, "to God." He not only wrote and sent brothers, so that the Corinthians might be brought back to the way, but also prayed to God for them. And not undeservedly. For he knew that nothing is accomplished by the one who plants, nothing by the one who waters, unless the increase and the efficacy of the work be given by God.

units.la: hil efficere plantantem, nihil riganté, nisi incre mentū & efficacia operis detur à Deo. Quare scitè admodum dictum est alicubi ab Augusti no de ministro verbi: Sit prius orator quàm di ctor. Oret ad Deum Christi minister non modo pro dono intelligentiæ ac sermonis, sed & pro incremento fructificationis. Oret non solum in ecclesia cum cœtu fidelium pro more vsitato, sed & domi suæ secreto, pro zeli sui ardore, quo fiat, vt & in ecclesia ardentius & effi cacius loquatur. Frigidum est os docentis, cuius pectus non ante sermonem spiritu & ardore orationis incaluit, animumque ad dicendū ardentem concepit, quo & audientibus animū faciat.
units.tr: Hence it has been very aptly said somewhere by Augustine of the minister of the Word: "Let him be a pray-er before he is a teacher." The minister of Christ should pray to God not only for the gift of understanding and of speech, but also for the increase of fruitfulness. Let him pray not only in the Church with the assembly of the faithful according to the customary manner, but also at home in private, for the ardour of his zeal, so that it may come about that he speaks in the Church more fervently and more effectively. Cold is the mouth of a teacher whose breast has not before the sermon grown warm with the Spirit and the fervour of prayer, and has not conceived a mind burning to speak, by which he also kindles the minds of the hearers.

units.la: Oro, inquit. Ad quem? Ad Deum. Papistici doctor orat & ipse pro suggestu, & plebem ad orandū secū inuitat. Rectè quidem facit qd orat. Testatur enim orando non esse sui arbitrij, neq; facultatem neq; efficaciam docendi, quantumuis magnus sit liberi arbitrij doctor, sed aliunde petendam esse vtranq;. Verum ad quem orat? Paulus: Oro, inquit, ad Deum. An & ipse ad Deum? Ad Deum quidem, sed non solum. Simul nanq; orat etiam ad non Deum dum orat ad beatam virginem. Neq; enim illa Deus est, ideoque quod Paulus à Deo petit, ipsa præstare non poterit. In summa: Paulus orat ad Deum, Paulus ille doctor Gentium, Papisticus doctor orat etiam ad non Deum. Paulus petit aquam è fonte, ille petit & è fonte & è cisterna, in qua non est aqua, nisi infundas.
units.tr: "Pray," he says. To whom? To God. The Papist teacher prays also himself from the pulpit, and invites the common people to pray along with him. He does rightly in that he prays. For by praying he testifies that the ability and the efficacy of teaching are not at the discretion of himself, however great a teacher of free will he may be, but must be sought from elsewhere, from both. But to whom does he pray? Paul: "I pray," he says, "to God." Does he too pray to God? To God indeed, but not only. For at the same time he also prays to what is not God, while he prays to the blessed virgin. For she is not God, and therefore what Paul asks from God she will not be able to grant. In sum: Paul prays to God; that Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles; the Papist teacher prays also to what is not God. Paul seeks water from a spring; he seeks both from a spring and from a cistern in which there is no water, unless you pour it in.

units.la: Audite inuocatores diuorum. Deificate primum quos inuocatis, ac tum demum ad eos o rate, veroque Deo adorando coniungite, ne si tis adoratores eorum qui dij non sunt. At deificare, hoc est, ex non Deo Deum facere non poteltis, nec potest hoc Romanus vester Pontifex mortuorū canonizator. Cessate igitur ab illorū inuocatione, quos fatemini nec esse nec fieri posse deos, & cū omnib. electis, sanctis ac veris fidelib. adorate & inuocate Deum verū & vnicum, patrem filium ac spiritumsanctum, cuius estis sacramento in baptismate obsignati ac sanctificati.
units.tr: Hear me, invokers of the saints. First deify those whom you invoke, and only then pray to them and join them to the true God in worship, lest you be worshippers of those who are not gods. But to deify, that is, to make God out of a non-God, you cannot do, nor can your Roman Pontiff, the canonizer of the dead, do it. Cease therefore from invoking those whom you yourselves admit can neither be nor become gods, and with all the elect, holy and true faithful, adore and invoke the one true God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, by whose sacrament you were sealed and sanctified in baptism.

units.la: Quid autem petit à Deo Paulus? Oro, inquit, ad Deū, ne quid mali faciatis. Quorsum hoc petebat à Deo, si per liberū arbitrium potest homo vitare malum & quod bonum est facere? Si suppetit nobis ex libero arbitrio facultas vitandi mali, suppetebat ex eodem illa & Corinthijs. Verum Apostolus cum sciret nō esse in carne nostra bonum, nec esse quenquā mortalium, qui ex suisipsius virib. bonū faciat & non peccet, orauit ad Deū pro Corinthijs unde est omne bonū, qui operatur in nobis & velle & perficere, ut per gratiā suam custodiret illorum animos ne quo mali genere delinquerent, & Euangelium Christi dedecore afficerent, seq; ipsos perderent.
units.tr: What then does Paul ask of God? "I pray to God," he says, "that you do no evil." Why would he ask this of God, if by free will man can avoid evil and do what is good? If the power of avoiding evil is available to us from free will, it was equally available to the Corinthians. But the Apostle, knowing that nothing good dwells in our flesh, and that there is no mortal who from his own powers does good and does not sin, prayed to God, from whom is every good thing, who works in us both to will and to accomplish, that by his grace he would keep their minds from falling into any kind of evil, from disgracing the Gospel of Christ, and from ruining themselves.

units.la: Non est autem otiosum, quod non simpliciter dicit: ne faciatis malum, sed, μὴ ποιῆσαι
units.tr: It is not idle, however, that he does not simply say "that you do evil," but "that you not do" [μὴ ποιῆσαι].

units.la: μὴ ποιῆσαι ὑμᾶς κακὸν μηδὲν, i.ne faciatis vos vllum malum. Poterat dicere, μὴ ποιῆσαι ὑμᾶς κακόν τι, verū quo significaret nihil prorsus admittendū esse fide lib. quod sit malum, voluit ad hunc modum loqui, μὴ ποιῆσαι ὑμᾶς κακὸν μηδὲν. Etenim qui in vno offendit, omnium reus est.
units.tr: "That you do no evil at all" [μὴ ποιῆσαι ὑμᾶς κακὸν μηδὲν], that is, "that you do no evil thing." He could have said μὴ ποιῆσαι ὑμᾶς κακόν τι, but to signify that nothing at all that is evil must be admitted by the faithful, he chose to speak thus: μὴ ποιῆσαι ὑμᾶς κακὸν μηδὲν. For whoever offends in one point is guilty of all.

units.la: Sed dices. Quomodo fieri potest, vt prorsus nihil faciamus quod sit malum? cū non sit homo qui non peccet, & Dauid dicat: Ne intres in iudicium cum seruo tuo dñe, quia non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo vllus viuens. Cum ergo fieri nequiret, quod à Deo petebat Apostolus, consequitur quod rem impossibile frustra petierit.
units.tr: But you will say: how can it come about that we do absolutely nothing that is evil, since there is no man who does not sin, and David says: "Enter not into judgment with your servant, O Lord, for in your sight no living man will be justified"? Since therefore what the Apostle asked of God could not be done, it follows that he asked in vain for something impossible.

units.la: Respondeo. Deo, à quo hoc petebat, non est impossibile, vt tales nos reddat, qui prorsus nihil mali faciamus. Quare non petijt ab illo rem impossibilem. Deinde, perfecta hæc innocentia, quæ ab omni sit malo libera, quemadmodum grata est Deo, & ad gratiæ illius ornamentum plurimum faceret, ita debet omnibus instar scopi cuiusdam esse præfixa, vt ad illam comitamur pro viribus. Hoc studij omnibus modis requiritur à nobis, quantumuis ne mo sit in hac vita, qui scopum hunc sic feriat, vt nusquam ab illo exorbitet. Qui hoc studio prædigi ad præfixam innocentiæ metam cum timore domini collimant, etiamsi non consequuntur quod cupiunt, sed subinde aberrant, hoc tamen illis propter gratiam Christi, & propter studium pietatis, haud imputatur sed misericorditer condonatur. Quare Apostolus rectè hoc à Deo petijt, vt custodiret Corinthios ne quid mali facerent, idque ipsis scripsit quo ad solidum veræ innocentiæ studium prouocarentur.
units.tr: I answer: it is not impossible for God, from whom he asked this, to make us such that we do absolutely no evil. Therefore he did not ask of him something impossible. Next, this perfect innocence, free from all evil, is as pleasing to God and would greatly add to the adornment of his grace; so it ought to be set before all as a kind of goal, so that we strive toward it with all our strength. This zeal is required of us in every way, although there is no one in this life who so strikes this mark that he never strays from it. Those who, eager in this zeal, aim at the set goal of innocence with the fear of the Lord, even if they do not attain what they desire but from time to time go astray, this is nonetheless not imputed to them on account of the grace of Christ and their zeal for piety, but is mercifully pardoned. Therefore the Apostle rightly asked this of God, that he would keep the Corinthians from doing any evil, and he wrote it to them so that they would be provoked to a solid zeal for true innocence.

units.la: Adhuc dices: Cum scriptura dicat: Define à malo & fac bonum, sitque vera ac perfecta pietas non in ea tantum sita, si nihil mali faciamus, sed requirat etiam vt quod bonum est faciamus: quemadmodum non est satis arbori, si nullos malos fructus ferat, nisi ferat bonos quid est quod Apostolus pro eo tantum ad Deum orauit, vt daret Corinthijs, ne quid mali facerent?
units.tr: You will still object: since Scripture says, "Depart from evil and do good," and true and perfect piety consists not only in doing no evil but also requires that we do what is good, just as it is not enough for a tree to bear no bad fruit unless it also bears good fruit, why did the Apostle pray to God only that he would grant the Corinthians not to do any evil?

units.la: Respondeo. Prima pars pietatis est innocentia, sine qua ad alterā, quę est in studio bonorū operū, peruenire potest. Cū ergo tales adhuc esent Corinthij, vtpote carnales, quib. nondum esset prorsus exemptū studium mali, timendūque esset ne faciendo quæ mala essent offendiculum gignerent Euangelio, ac seipsos cœlesti gratia priuarent, visum fuit summopere necessarium, vt pro dono vitæ innocuę orarét ad Deum, non quo in primo illo gradu consisterent, sed vt per hunc ad alterum quoq; coinuitaren tur, ad quem nemo ascendere poterit, nisi primum desistat à malo.
units.tr: I answer: the first part of piety is innocence, without which one cannot attain to the other, which lies in zeal for good works. Since the Corinthians were still such, being fleshly, and zeal for evil had not yet been altogether removed from them, and since it was to be feared that by doing what was evil they would create a stumbling block to the Gospel and deprive themselves of heavenly grace, it seemed highly necessary to pray to God for the gift of an innocent life. Not that they would remain in that first stage, but that through it they would also be drawn on to the other, to which no one can ascend unless he first desists from evil.

units.la: NON quo nos probāti appareamus, inquit, sed vt uos quod honestum est faciatis, nos uerò veluti reprobi simus.) Potest id quod in se bonū est animo fieri sic in syncero, ut non modò do laudabile non sit, sed & culpabile. Bonum in se erat orare ad Deum pro Corinthijs, ne quid mali facerent. Verum culpabile fuisset, si hoc Paulus ob id à Deo petijsset, ut recte se gerentibus illis ipse gloriam inde reportaret, prọq; magno ac probato Apostolo haberetur. Sic enim nec Corinthiorum salutem, nec gloriam nominis Christi, sed suamipsius spectasset, & insignem hypocritam in conspectu Dei gesisset. Sciens igitur hoc ingenio praeditam esse carnem, ut in eo quoque, quod per se bonum est seipsum magis quaerat, quàm vel gloriam Dei vel salutem eorum, quorum ratione in specie habere videtur, ne quod se orare ad Deum dixit, ne Corinthij mali quid faciant, sinistro hoc animo facere videretur, occupatione hac cauit dicens: non quo nos probati appareamus, sed ut uos quod honestum est faciatis. Quasi dicat. Cum autem id peto à Deo, non quaero meam gloriam in uobis, sed uestrà salutem, ne gratiam Dei in uanum accipientes, & illam amittatis & uofipsi perdatis.
units.tr: "Not that we may appear approved," he says, "but that you may do what is honourable, while we may seem as reprobates.") What is good in itself can be done with a mind so unsound that it is not only not praiseworthy but even blameworthy. It was good in itself to pray to God for the Corinthians that they do no evil. But it would have been blameworthy if Paul had asked this of God for the reason that, with them behaving rightly, he himself might gain glory from it and be regarded as a great and approved Apostle. For then he would have looked to neither the salvation of the Corinthians nor the glory of Christ's name, but to his own, and would have acted as a notorious hypocrite in the sight of God. Knowing therefore that the flesh is so constituted that even in what is good in itself it seeks itself more than either the glory of God or the salvation of those on whose account it seems to act, lest his saying that he prayed to God that the Corinthians do no evil should seem to be done with this sinister mind, he guarded against it with this caution, saying: "not that we may appear approved, but that you may do what is honourable." As if he said: "When I ask this of God, I do not seek my own glory in you, but your salvation, lest, receiving the grace of God in vain, you lose it and destroy yourselves."

units.la: Refert igitur plurimum nō modò quid, sed & ad quem finem ad Deum orando petas. Inuenias hodie qui orent ad Deum pro ecclesia, ut discordiam hanc qua illa turbatur ac scinditur, auferat, detq; illi pacem ac tranquillitatem. Hoc genus orationis si fiat à priuato Christiano, non est obnoxium suspicioni, quod aliud quaerat quàm ecclesiæ bonum. Si uero fiat ab illis qui dominantur in ecclesia, & non nisi uentris ac quæstus gratia orát & psallunt, quis dubitat quæri à talibus concordiam & pacem ecclesiæ, non ecclesiæ, sed suoipsorum respectu? Si pater à Deo petat, ne filij ipsius mali quicquam faciant, probabile est peti hoc ad illorum salutem propter affectum paternum, qui totus filiorum commodis inseruire solet. Si uero pædagogus aliquis oret, ne discipuli quos non genuit sed instruendos acceperit, immorigeri sint & indociles, orat quidem rem in se bonam, uerum admodum in dubio est, posit ne ueraciter cum Paulo dicere: non quo ego probatus appareaм, sed ut ipsi in uiros eruditos, & tam ecclesiæ quàm patriæ utiles euadant. Non nego reperiri præceptores sic erga discipulos suos animatos, & uelim tales esse non præceptores tantum, sed & pastores in uniuersum omnes. Verum quod Paulus 1.Cor.4.dixit: Etiamsi innumeros pedagogos habeatis in Christo, non multos tamen habetis patres, id hodie quoque nimis ueraciter dici potest.
units.tr: Therefore it matters greatly not only what you ask in praying to God, but also to what end. Today you will find those who pray to God for the Church, that he would take away the discord by which it is troubled and torn apart, and give it peace and tranquillity. If this kind of prayer is made by a private Christian, it is not open to suspicion that he seeks anything other than the good of the Church. But if it is made by those who rule in the Church, and who pray and sing psalms only for the sake of belly and gain, who doubts that such men seek concord and peace in the Church not with regard to the Church, but with regard to themselves? If a father asks God that his sons do nothing evil, it is probable that this is asked for their salvation, on account of paternal affection, which is wont to serve wholly the advantage of the sons. But if some tutor prays that his pupils, whom he did not beget but received to instruct, may not be disobedient and unteachable, he prays indeed for a thing good in itself; yet it is very doubtful whether he can truthfully say with Paul: "not that I may appear approved, but that they may become learned men, useful both to the Church and to the fatherland." I do not deny that there are teachers so disposed toward their pupils, and I would wish that all such men were not only teachers but also ministers in the full sense. But what Paul said in 1 Cor. 4: "Though you have countless tutors in Christ, yet you do not have many fathers," can be said even today all too truly.

units.la: NON quo nos probati appareamus, inquit.) Non dicit: non quo nos probati simus, sed, non quo nos probati appareamus. Aliud est esse, & aliud non esse, sed apparere probatum. Probatum uelle uideri magis quàm esse, non uerum probitatis studium, sed hypocrisis est, & Deo & hominibus detestabilis. Ad hoc luctari, ut uerè sis probatus, hominis est fidem ac ueritatem amantis.
units.tr: Not that we may appear approved, he says. He does not say "not that we may be approved", but "not that we may appear approved." Being approved is one thing, and appearing approved is another. To wish to seem approved rather than to be so is not a true zeal for integrity but hypocrisy, which is detestable both to God and to men. To struggle to be truly approved belongs to a man who loves faith and truth.

units.la: SED ut uos quod honestum est, faciatis, inquit.) Græce elt, τὸ καλὸν. quæ uox aliquando bonum significat, quemadmodum & uulgatus interpres uertit: sed, ut uos quod bonum est faciatis, uerum magis proprie sonat pulchrum, egregiū & honestum. Habet Christiana professio suum, ut ἀγαθὸν ita & καλὸν. Sua cuiq; statui peculiaris honestas est, & praeterea est honestas omnium publica, ne quid indecenter geratur. Verum hac de re non est ut hic dicamus.
units.tr: BUT THAT YOU MAY DO WHAT IS HONOURABLE, he says. In Greek it is τὸ καλὸν [to kalon], a word which sometimes means "good," as the Vulgate translator also renders it: "that you may do what is good." But the word more properly means beautiful, noble and honourable. The Christian profession has its own version of this, as it has of ἀγαθὸν [agathon] and καλὸν. Each rank has its own peculiar honour, and there is also a public honour common to all, so that nothing is done unbecomingly. But we need not discuss this matter here.

units.la: Non dicit autem: Vt uos quod honestum est, sciatis, sed, ut uos quod honestum est facia tis. Scientia boni & honesti acquiritur ex sedula ac diligenti instructione doctoris. Nihil huius desiderabatur in Corinthijs. Verum ut honestum quod sciebant, opere facerent, nō poterat dari ab Apostolo, sed à solo Deo, qui dat & uelle & perficere, quare hoc ab illo petebat, sciens ad condemnationem magis quàm ad salutem facere scientiam honesti, ubi meliora cognoscuntur, & deteriora perpetrantur.
units.tr: He does not say, however, "that you may know what is honourable," but "that you may do what is honourable." Knowledge of the good and the honourable is acquired through the careful and diligent instruction of a teacher. Nothing of this was lacking in the Corinthians. But that they should actually do in deed what they knew to be honourable could not be given by the Apostle, but only by God alone, who gives both the willing and the doing. So he asks this of God, knowing that the knowledge of what is honourable tends more to condemnation than to salvation, when better things are known and worse things are committed.

units.la: NOS uero ueluti reprobi simus.) Ergo ne illorum gratia cupiebat esse reprobus, ut ipsi probati inuenirentur? Non dicit simpliciter: nos uero reprobi simus, sed, nos uero ueluti reprobi simus. Aliud est esse reprobū, & aliud esse ueluti reprobum. Esse autem ueluti reprobum, bifariam accidit. Primum, si qua species hominis reprobi, qui tamen reprobus non sit, in conuersatione uitę uel uerbis, uel moribus, uel factis non rite intellectis apparėat. Vt exempli gratia: Species hominis reprobi erat, cum Christus cum publicanis & peccatoribus conuiuaretur. Deinde, si quis pro reprobo habeatur, cum neque sit reprobus, neque aliquid faciat, propter quod pro reprobo haberi debeat. Tale quid intelligit hic Apostolus, cum dicit: nos uero ueluti reprobi simus, id est, perinde habeamur & æstimemur ac si simus reprobi. Perstringit hoc dicens pseudapostolorum maliciam, à quibus inter Corinthios insimulabatur, quasi esset non uerus sed reprobus Apostolus. Quasi dicat, parum me moueret, quod in oculis pseudapostolorum pro reprobo habeor, si uos nihil mali facientes probati deprehenderemini. Sic fidelis præceptor animatus est erga suos discipulos, ut æquo animo ferret, si pro indocto haberetur, modò ipsi docti euaderent. Et est huius sententiæ magna ratio. Erat Paulus uerus Christi Apostolus, non ob id ut ipse probatus haberetur, sed ut Christo quamplurimos lucri faceret, multumq; fructus ferret. Vbi ergo id præstare dabatur, conueniebat ut esset contentus, quicquid de se sentirent reprobi, sic tamen ut nullam illis causam malè de se sentiendi obijceret.
units.tr: BUT WE MAY SEEM AS IF WE WERE REPROBATE. Did he then desire to be reprobate for their sake, so that they might be found approved? He does not simply say "we are reprobate," but "we may seem as if we were reprobate." To be reprobate is one thing, and to seem as if one were reprobate is another. Now to seem reprobate happens in two ways. First, when some appearance of a reprobate man shows itself in one's manner of life, whether in words, conduct or deeds, which are not rightly understood. For example, Christ had the appearance of a reprobate man when he feasted with publicans and sinners. Second, when someone is held to be reprobate although he is not reprobate and does nothing for which he ought to be held so. It is this sort of thing the Apostle means when he says, "we may seem as if we were reprobate," that is, we may be regarded and esteemed just as if we were reprobate. He is striking at the malice of the false apostles, by whom he was accused among the Corinthians, as if he were not a true but a reprobate apostle. As if he were saying: "It would matter little to me that in the eyes of the false apostles I am held to be reprobate, if you, doing nothing wrong, were found to be approved." So a faithful teacher is so disposed towards his disciples that he bears with equanimity being held unlearned, provided that they themselves become learned. And there is a great reason for this view. Paul was a true apostle of Christ, not so that he himself might be held approved, but so that he might win very many for Christ and bear much fruit. Where that was granted, it was fitting that he should be content with whatever the reprobate thought of him, yet so that he gave them no cause to think ill of him.

units.la: Magna admodum ignominia est audire hæreticus, apostata, schismaticus, seductor, &c. quæ non præter rationem prisci s patribus intoleranda uisa est, è quibus Hieronymus nem- minem minè uult esse in suspicione hæresèos patien- tem. Verùm fidelis Christi ministri pectus studio ac zelo lucrifaciendi mortales ardens, ex animo dicet cum Apostolo: oro ad Deum ne quid mali faciant, quibus Euangelium Christi annuncio: non quo ipse probatus, uerus, & orthodoxus doctor appareà, sed ut ipsi quod honestum & uerè Christianum est, facientes, probati inueniâtur, ego uero ueluti reprobus hæreticus, schismaticus, & seductor interim habear. Neq; enim mea refert, quid de me sen- tiant ac iudicent hostes ueritatis, quorū quæ- stui ac uentri uniuersa Christiana religio serui re cogitur, quibus Christus ipse cum suis apo- stolis, si modò ut olim in terris ageret, pro hæ- reticissimis seductoribus haberentur. Quod enim me attinet, parum mihi est, ut iudicer ab humano die, cum habeam iudicem in cœlis.
units.tr: It is a very great disgrace to be called a heretic, an apostate, a schismatic, a seducer, and so on; the ancients, not without reason, regarded this as intolerable. Among them Jerome wished no one to be exposed to even the suspicion of heresy. But the faithful minister of Christ, whose heart burns with zeal for winning mortals, will say from his heart with the Apostle: "I pray to God that they do no evil, I who proclaim the gospel of Christ," not that I myself may appear a approved, true and orthodox teacher, but that they, doing what is honourable and truly Christian, may be found approved, while I, meanwhile, be held as a reprobate, a heretic, a schismatic and a seducer. For it matters little to me what the enemies of the truth think and judge of me. The whole Christian religion is compelled to serve their gain and their belly, and if Christ himself with his apostles were to live on earth as once he did, they would be held the most heretical seducers. As for me, it is enough for me to be judged by the human day, since I have a judge in heaven.

units.la: NON enim possumus aliquid aduersus ue- ritatem, inquit, sed pro veritate.) Non simpli- citer dicit; se non posse quicquam aduersus ueritatem, sed subijcit hoc præcedentibus lo- co rationis, cum dicit: Non enim possumus a- liquid aduersus ueritatem. Quare uidendum est non modò quid dicat, sed & quomodo id faciat ad rationem præcedentium. Vox veritas latè patet, quod & Pilatus sentiebat, cum ad dominum diceret, Quid est veritas? Existi- mo autem usurpatam hic esse de veritate Christi, Christianæq; professionis, ad quam pertinet, ut qui Christiani sunt, ab omni malo abstineant, & quod bonum m honestumq; est faciant. Etenim qui diuersum faciunt, alieni sunt à veritate Christi. Cum igitur dixisset, orare se ad Deum pro Corinthijs, ne quid mali faciat, non quo ipse probatus appareat, sed ut illi quod honestum sit, faciant, consequenter adijcit hæc uerba, non enim possumus aliquid aduersus veritatem Dei, ut significet, si veritati Christi studentes inculpate se gerant, nihil se in ipsos posse, eo quod nihil potestatis acceperit à domino aduersum eos, qui se rectè gerât, sed magis pro illis, ut eos magis ac magis ædificet & confirmet. Loquitur ut Apostolus Christi, nihil sibi in quenquam sumens, quod non sit secundum potestatem à domino acceptam.
units.tr: FOR WE CAN DO NOTHING AGAINST THE TRUTH, he says, BUT FOR THE TRUTH. He does not simply say that he cannot do anything against the truth, but he attaches this to what precedes, as a reason, when he says: "For we can do nothing against the truth." Therefore we must consider not only what he says but also how it bears upon what goes before. The word "truth" has a wide range, as Pilate also understood when he said to the Lord, "What is truth?" I think, however, that here it is used of the truth of Christ and of the Christian profession, to which it belongs that those who are Christians abstain from every evil and do what is good and honourable. For those who act otherwise are estranged from the truth of Christ. Therefore, having said that he prays to God for the Corinthians, that they do nothing wrong, not so that he himself may appear approved, but so that they may do what is honourable, he goes on to add these words: "for we can do nothing against the truth of God." He means that, if they who are zealous for the truth of Christ conduct themselves blamelessly, he has no power against them, since he has received from the Lord no power against those who behave rightly, but rather power for them, to build them up and confirm them more and more. He speaks as an apostle of Christ, claiming for himself nothing that is not according to the power received from the Lord.

units.la: Poterat dicere, Non enim possumus quic- quam contra iustos, pios, ac fideles. Verù quo niam veritatis Christi minister & Apostolus erat, ad hunc modum loqui uoluit, ut significa ret potestatem sibi nō esse aduersus alumnos veritatis, qui veritati studeat, cuius ipse sit mi- nister. Consequitur eos impugnare veritatem Christi, qui uéros Christianos uel probris pro scindunt, uel aliàs persequûtur, dum & fidem & uitam eorum insectantur. Romanus Ponti- sex si uerus esset Apostolorum successor, nec ipse quicquam potestatis haberet aduersus ue- ritatem Christi, quam hodie persequitur. Ha- bet autem, sicuti manifestum apparet. Ergo non est uerus apostolorum successor, nec ue- ritatis, sed mendacijs ac seductionis minister,
units.tr: He could have said, "For we can do nothing against the just, the pious and the faithful." But since he was a minister and apostle of the truth of Christ, he wished to speak in this way, so as to signify that he has no power against the followers of the truth, who strive for the truth, whose minister he himself is. It follows that those who attack the truth of Christ are those who either tear true Christians apart with reproaches or otherwise persecute them, while they assail both their faith and their life. If the Roman Pontiff were the true successor of the Apostles, he would have no more power against the truth of Christ than he has today, when he persecutes it. But he does have power, as is plainly evident. Therefore he is not the true successor of the apostles, nor a minister of the truth, but of lies and seduction,

units.la: potentia præditus eius, cuius est minister & Apostolus, Satanæ uidelicet, in angelum lucis transfigurati. Quare quemadmodum Christi Apostolus hic dicit, non enim possumus aliquid aduersus veritatem, sed pro veritate, re- spiciens ad Apostolatus sui potestatem à do- mino acceptà, ita ille rectè contrarium dicet: Non .n. possumus aliquid pro veritate, sed ad- uersus veritatè, uel: Non possumus aliquid ad uersus mendacium, sed pro mendacio, si lo- quendum ipsi sit secundum id quod à suo do- mino accepit. Quod autem non loquitur ad hunc modum, in causa est, quia loqui ipsum oportet non secundum veritatem, sed secun- dum mendacium, tanquam transfiguratus A- postolus, ut mysterio transfigurationis suæ, & iræ Dei corruptis ecclesijs debitæ seruiat. Nō est igitur expectandum, ut Apostolus hic men dacij ac seductionū aliud unquam meditetur ac faciat, quàm ut mendacio contra veritatem Christi omnes suas uires impendat. Hoc fe- cit hactenus, facit hodie, & facturus est usq; ad tempus destructionis ipsius, non palàm & ex professo, sed modis transfigurationi ipsius conuenientibus.
units.tr: endowed with the power of him whose minister and apostle he is, namely Satan, transformed into an angel of light. Therefore, just as the Apostle of Christ here says, "For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth," looking to the power of his apostleship received from the Lord, so the other would rightly say the opposite: "For we can do nothing for the truth, but against the truth"; or "we can do nothing against a lie, but for a lie," if he were to speak according to what he has received from his lord. That he does not speak in this way is because he must speak not according to the truth but according to the lie, as a transformed apostle, so that by the mystery of his transformation he serves the wrath of God owed to the corrupted churches. Therefore it is not to be expected that this Apostle ever devises or does anything other than spend all his strength in lying against the truth of Christ. He has done this hitherto, he does it today, and he will do it until the time of his own destruction, not openly and avowedly, but by means fitting to his transformation.

units.la: GAVDEMVS enim, cum nos infirmi fue- rimus, uos autem ualidi fueritis, inquit.) Ad- huc aliam rationem adijcit: ut prior sumpta est à qualitate Apostolicæ potestatis, ita posterior hæc à studio quo erat erga eos plane paterno. Non modò non uindicabat sibi quicquam po- testatis animaduertendi in ipsos, si in veritate Christi inculpabiles se fore præstitissent, sed nec delectabatur animaduersione, etiamsi necessa- ria esset. Gaudebat igitur, si ipsi rectè se in Christo gererent, ut ut ipse infirmus, quasi ni- hil posset, uideretur. Quoniam tandiu parce- bat ipsis, spe resipiscentiæ, dabatur hoc infir- mitati ipsius, propter quam, & , ut fieri solet, contemnebatur. Hoc se tam non laturum mo- leste dicit, ut gaudisurus sit etiam, modo ipsi re- cte ualeant in Christo, sic ut nihil aduersus ipsos posset. Poterat adijcere: Si uero deseren tes Christi ueritatem, quæ mala sunt facere perrexeritis, cogar nolim uelim reipsa declara re, quàm sim in Christo potens erga eos qui male agunt. Verum de hoc in præcedentibus satis meminerat.
units.tr: "For we rejoice when we are weak and you are strong," he says. He adds another reason, and while the first was drawn from the nature of apostolic authority, this second one comes from his genuinely fatherly affection towards them. He did not merely refrain from claiming any power to punish them, provided they had proved blameless in the truth of Christ; he did not even take pleasure in punishing, even when it was necessary. So he rejoiced if they conducted themselves rightly in Christ, even though he himself appeared weak, as if he could do nothing. Because he had spared them so long, in hope of their repentance, this was granted to his weakness, and on account of it he was, as usually happens, despised. He says that he will not bear it so badly that he would not rejoice, provided they were doing well in Christ, so that he would have no power against them. He could have added: "But if you abandon the truth of Christ and persist in doing evil, I shall be forced, whether I like it or not, to demonstrate in deed how powerful I am in Christ against those who act wickedly." But he had said enough about this in what precedes.

units.la: Ergo infirmum esse Apostolum est officio castigationis uel non posse uti, quod in rectè agentes nihil potestatis eiusmodi habeat, uel non uti per negligentiam, aut propter spem futuræ resipiscentiæ. Prior ac posterior modus locum habuerunt in Apostolo, medius non habuit.
units.tr: So to be weak as an apostle, in the office of correction, is either not to be able to use authority of this kind, since it has no force against those who act rightly, or not to use it through negligence or because of hope of future repentance. The first and the second mode applied to the Apostle; the middle one did not.

units.la: Deinde ualidum esse fidelem in Christo, est saluum & integrum esse in fide, ueritate ac pietate, sic ut nihil mali, sed quod honestum est faciat.
units.tr: Then, to be strong as a believer in Christ is to be sound and whole in faith, truth and piety, so that one does nothing wrong but whatever is honourable.

units.la: HOC autem insuper optamus, uestrâ inte- gritatem.) Hoc est, non modò gaudemus ubi fueritis ualidi, sed optamus etiam ut sitis ualidi & integri. Græcè est τὸ ὑμῶν καταρτίσθητε. Sonat autem καταρτισμὸς restitutionem membrorum luxatorum, & laceri corporis redintegrationem. Vsus est hac uoce admodum conuenienter. Erant enim membra ecclesiæ Corinthiorum separatis à se inuicem diuulsa & luxata. Quare optat ut se dicit, ut suis quæq; locis restituantur, atq; ita corpus ipsorum redintegretur. Optamus & nos ecclesiarum καταρτισμὸν, quas non Euangelij Dei ueritas, sed doctrina mendaciorum discerptas ac luxatas reddidit: optamus autem ueram quæ sit in unitate fidei ac spiritus sub capite Christo.
units.tr: "This too we pray for, your perfection." That is, not only do we rejoice when you are strong, but we also pray that you may be strong and whole. The Greek is "τὸ ὑμῶν καταρτίσθητε" [to hymōn katartisthēte]. The word "καταρτισμὸς" [katartismos] means the setting of dislocated limbs and the restoration of a torn body. He has used this word most fittingly. For the members of the Corinthian church were torn apart and dislocated from one another. Therefore he prays that they may be restored, each to its own place, and so their body be made whole again.
