We too pray for the "καταρτισμὸς" [katartismos] of the churches, which the truth of the Gospel has not torn apart and dislocated, but the teaching of lies; and we pray that they may be made true, in unity of faith and spirit under Christ the head.

units.la: PROPTEREA hæc absens scribo, inquit, ne cum præsens fuero, rigidus sim iuxta potestate quam dedit mihi dominus in extructionem, & non in destructionem.) Tandem conclusurus epistolam, exprimit rationem ac con silium suum, quare hæc absens ad eos, priusquâ Corinthû aliquâdo ueniat, scribere uolue rit. Pseudapostoli dicebant: Epistolæ quidem graues sunt, at præsentia corporis infirma: hoc est, ubi præsens est, nihil potest eorū, quæ minatur in epistolis. Quare ad id tantum intonat scribendo, ut epistolaribus minis absterritos, sub potestate sua contineat. Ipse contrà. Propterea, inquit, hæc absens scribo, nō quod neqUeam si præsens fuero, rigidus esse in immorigeros, sed ne sim rigidus, id est, ne cogar uti seueritate iuxta potestatem quam dedit mihi dominus, &c. Non agebat rigidè, quia parcebat, illi dicebant, quia non potest. Minatur ergo illis futurum, ut, nisi hoc se scripto in ordinem redigi patiantur, non parcat amplius, sed præsens agat rigidè. Quare cum dicit, Propterea hæc absens scribo, ne cum præsens fuero, rigidus sim, subaudiendum est, ut quæ emendanda sunt, priusquam ueniam, emendetis, ut tû sequatur, ne cum præsens fuero, & inemendatos reperero, rigidus sim iuxta potestatem, &c. Græcè est μὴ ἀποτόμως χρήσωμαι. i.ne seuerè, rigidè, truncatim, præcisè, utar, quod idem est, atq; μὴ τῇ ἀποτομίᾳ χρήσωμαι. i.ne seueritate, rigore, præcisione ac truncatione utar. ἀποτομία est, quando incuncanter compendiosa seueritate utimur, & quæ in ordiuem redigi emendariq; nullis modis possunt, abscindimus. Hanc abscisione minari uideretur impœnitentibus, nisi aduerbium ἀποτόμως plerunq; idem significaret simpliciter quod sæuerè ac rigidè.
units.tr: "Therefore I write these things while absent," he says, "so that when I am present I may not be harsh, according to the power which the Lord gave me for building up and not for destruction." Concluding the letter at last, he sets out his reason and purpose for why he wished to write these things to them while absent, before he came to Corinth at some time. The false apostles were saying: "The letters are indeed weighty, but the bodily presence is weak"; that is, when he is present he can do nothing of what he threatens in his letters. So he thunders in writing only to restrain them under his authority by frightening them with threats in letters. He, on the contrary, says: "Therefore I write these things while absent, not because I shall not be able, if present, to be harsh towards the disobedient, but so that I may not be harsh, that is, so that I may not be forced to use severity according to the power which the Lord gave me," and so on. He was not acting harshly because he was sparing them; they said that this was because he could not. So he threatens them with what will happen: unless they allow themselves to be brought into order by this writing, he will spare them no longer, but when present will act harshly. Therefore, when he says "Therefore I write these things while absent, so that when I am present I may not be harsh," it must be understood: "so that you may correct the things which need correcting before I come, that I may not, when I am present and find you uncorrected, be harsh according to the power," and so on. The Greek is "μὴ ἀποτόμως χρήσωμαι" [mē apotomōs chrēsōmai], that is, "that I may not use severity, harshness, abruptness, or cutting off," which is the same as "μὴ τῇ ἀποτομίᾳ χρήσωμαι" [mē tē apotomia chrēsōmai], that is, "that I may not use severity, rigour, cutting off and truncation." "ἀποτομία" [apotomia] is when we use a swift and summary severity and cut off those who cannot in any way be brought into order and corrected. It would seem that he threatens the impenitent with this cutting off, were it not that the adverb "ἀποτόμως" [apotomōs] usually means simply the same as "severely" and "harshly."

units.la: Addit, iuxta potestatem. Græcè κατὰ τὸ ἐξουσίαν, qua uoce significat se nihil acturum ex commoti animi impetu ac proprio arbitratu, sed ex officio potestatis Apostolicæ. Et ut hac sibi esse dicat non temerè usurpatam, more pseudapostolorum, sed legitimam & authenticam, subijcit: quam dedit mihi dominus in extructionem, & non in destructionē. Sed de his uerbis supra cap.10. diximus, quare non est ut hic illis immoremur.
units.tr: He adds "according to the power." The Greek is "κατὰ τὴν ἐξουσίαν" [kata tēn exousian], by which word he signifies that he will do nothing from the impulse of an excited mind or by his own judgement, but from the office of apostolic authority. And so that he may say that this authority is not rashly assumed by him, in the manner of the false apostles, but lawful and genuine, he adds: "which the Lord gave me for building up and not for destruction." But we spoke about these words above, at chapter 10, so there is no need to dwell on them here.

units.la: Quod superest fratres, ualete, integri estote, consolationē habete, unanimes
units.tr: Finally, brethren, farewell; be made perfect; be comforted; be of one mind;

units.la: sitis, in pace agite, & Deus charitatis ac pacis erit uobiscum. Salutate uos mutuo osculo sancto. Salutant uos sancti omnes. Gratia domini lefu Christi, & charitas Dei, & communicatio spiritus sancti sit cum omnibus uobis. Amen.
units.tr: live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints salute you. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. Amen.

units.la: Concludit epistolam admodum copetenter & appositè, idque conclusione necessarijs membris sic absoluta, ut uix aliquid desiderari possit. Insunt enim illi primùm summaria adhortatio, deinde promissio, tertiò salutatio, & quartò Apostolica apprecatio.
units.tr: He concludes the letter very fittingly and aptly, and with a conclusion so complete in its necessary parts that scarcely anything more could be desired. For it contains, first, a summary exhortation; secondly, a promise; thirdly, a greeting; and fourthly, an apostolic blessing.

units.la: QVOD superest, inquit, fratres.) Quasi dicat, Hactenus scripsi uobis quæ necessaria uidentur, iam nihil restat aliud quàm ut scriptis meis obedientes rectè ualeatis, &c.
units.tr: "Finally, brethren," he says. As if to say: "Hitherto I have written to you what seemed necessary. Now nothing remains except that you, obeying my writings, may fare well in the right way," and so on.

units.la: VALETE, inquit.) Græcè est χαίρετε, quod sonat proprie gaudete, quemadmodû & uulgatus interpres uertit, & Chrysost. quoq; exponit, dicens: Cótristasti, terruisti, anxios reddidisti, tremere fecisti ac metuere, & quomodo gaudere iubes? Propter hoc ipsum gaudere iubeo. Etenim si ijs quæ ego feci, ea quę uobis cópetunt, subiecceritis, nihil impediet quo minus gaudeatis. Etenim quicquid potui feci. Longanimis fui, distuli, non excidi, adhortatus sum, consului, terrui, comminatus sum, quo uos omnibus modis ad fructû resipiscentiæ in unum colligerem. Iam restat, ut quod uestrum est faciatis: quod si feceritis, immarcessibile uobis gaudium erit. Hæc ille. unde manifestum est, quod gaudendi sensu uerbum hoc χαίρετε acceperit. Nec uspiam inuenio positum ab Apostolo pro ualete, quantumuis Erasmo uertendum magis uisum fuerit ualete, quàm gaudete.
units.tr: "Farewell," he says. The Greek is "χαίρετε" [chairete], which properly means "rejoice," as the Vulgate translator also renders it, and Chrysostom expounds it, saying: "You have grieved, terrified, made anxious, made to tremble and fear; and how do you bid them rejoice? For this very reason I bid them rejoice. For if you submit to those things which I have done and which are fitting for you, nothing will prevent you from rejoicing. For I have done whatever I could. I was long-suffering, I delayed, I did not cut off, I exhorted, I counselled, I frightened, I threatened, so that by every means I might gather you into one for the fruit of repentance. Now it remains that you do what is yours; if you do, your joy will be unfading." Thus he. From this it is clear that he took the word "χαίρετε" [chairete] in the sense of rejoicing. Nor do I find it anywhere used by the Apostle for "farewell," although it seemed more fitting to Erasmus to translate it "farewell" rather than "rejoice."

units.la: INTEGRI estote.) Pertinet ista χαίρετε, καταρτίζεσθε, παρακαλεῖσθε, τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖτε, εἰρηνεύετε, ad summariâ adhortationem quinq; articulis ueluti digitis cõprehensam, & morbis Corinthiorû accômodatam. Illud καταρτίζεσθε, uertit Erafmus, integri estote, & uulgatus interpres, perfecti estote. Diximus supra quid sit καταρτισμὸς, unde satis patet, quid hic uelit Apostolus, quod nec Erafmus in Annotationibus suis dissimulat. Hortatur uidelicet, ut corpus ecclesiæ lacerum ac luxatum integritati suæ, reliĉto sectarum studio restituant.
units.tr: "Be whole." These words, "χαίρετε, καταρτίζεσθε, παρακαλεῖσθε, τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖτε, εἰρηνεύετε" [chairete, katartizesthe, parakaleisthe, to auto phroneite, eirēneuete], belong to the summary exhortation, which is gathered up as with five fingers and adapted to the diseases of the Corinthians. Erasmus translates "καταρτίζεσθε" [katartizesthe] as "be whole," and the Vulgate translator as "be perfect." We have said above what "καταρτισμὸς" [katartismos] is, whence it is sufficiently clear what the Apostle wishes here, which Erasmus himself does not conceal in his Annotations. He urges, namely, that they restore the torn and dislocated body of the church to its wholeness, by giving up their zeal for factions.

units.la: CONSOLATIONEM habete, inquit.) Quod in Græco est παρακαλεῖσθε adhortâdi sensum perinde habere potest atq; consolandi, ut idem sit quod adhortatione meam accipite, ac bene collocate, qui mihi sensus præsenti proposito magis conuenire uidetur. Chrysost. tamè putat referendū esse ad cŏsolationes cùm mutuas, tum suas, quibus erigendi ueniebant propter crebras tentationes ac pericula.
units.tr: "Be comforted," he says. The Greek "παρακαλεῖσθε" [parakaleisthe] can carry the sense of exhorting just as well as of comforting, so that it means "receive my exhortation and act upon it well," which seems to me the meaning more suited to his present purpose. Chrysostom, however, thinks it should be referred to comforts, both mutual and their own, by which they were to be raised up on account of frequent temptations and dangers.

units.la: VNANIMES sitis.) Τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖτε. i. idem sentite. Potest referri uel ad dogmata, ne in illis discreparent, uel ad animorum in charitate mutua cõsensum. Tale est quod 1. Cor.1. dicit: Idem Idé dicite omnes, & nó sint inter uos dissidia. IN pace agite.) Εἰρηνεύετε. Rectius, paci studete, pacifici estote. Vulgatus interpres habet pacem habete. Verum in pace agere, & pacem habere, optionis magis est quàm adhortationis. Nos Germani dicimus, neminé plus pacis habere, uel in pace magis agere posse, quàm per uicinos liceat. At paci studere piorum est ac pacificorum, ad quod genus studij Corinthios hic hortatur Apostolus. Paci studere possunt Christiani, etiamsi uiuát inter eos qui oderunt pacem, quemadmodum de se canit Dauid, Cum illis qui oderunt pacem, eram pacificus. Reuocat Corinthios à se inuicem dissentientes ad studia pacis.
units.tr: "Be of one mind." The Greek is "τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖτε" [to auto phronēte], that is, "think the same." It may refer either to doctrines, so that they should not disagree among themselves, or to the agreement of minds in mutual love. Similar is what he says in 1 Cor. 1: "Speak all the same thing, and let there not be divisions among you." "Live in peace." "Εἰρηνεύετε" [eirēneuete]. More correctly, "be zealous for peace, be peacemakers." The Vulgate translator has "have peace." But to live in peace and to have peace is more a wish than an exhortation. We Germans say that no one can have more peace, or live more peacefully, than his neighbours allow. But to be zealous for peace belongs to the godly and the peacemakers, and it is to this kind of zeal that the Apostle here exhorts the Corinthians. Christians can be zealous for peace even if they live among those who hate peace, as David sings of himself: "With those who hate peace I was peaceable." He recalls the Corinthians, who were at odds with one another, to the pursuits of peace.

units.la: ET Deus charitatis & pacis erit uobiscū.) Hactenus adhortatione absoluit, cui iam promissionem diuini fauoris subijcit, si idem sentire ac paci studere coeperint. Deus, inquit, erit uobiscū. Hoc est, nō destituet uos gratia & ope sua, sed fouebit uos præsenti spiritus sui auxilio. Nec simpliciter dicit, Deus erit uobiscum, sed, Deus charitatis & pacis erit uobiscum. Quare? Quia ut non est odiorū ac dissidiorū, sed charitatis ac pacis Deus, hoc est, & amans & author uerae charitatis ac pacis, ita deserere non potest charitati ac paci studentes. Etenim similes similibus congaudent.
units.tr: AND the God of love and peace will be with you.) Up to this point he has finished his exhortation, and now he adds the promise of God's favour, if they begin to think alike and pursue peace. God, he says, will be with you. That is, he will not forsake you, but will sustain you by his grace and help, and cherish you with the present aid of his Spirit. He does not simply say, "God will be with you," but "the God of love and peace will be with you." Why? Because God is not the God of hatred and dissension but of love and peace, that is, both the lover and the author of true love and peace, so he cannot abandon those who pursue love and peace. For like rejoices with like.

units.la: Dices: Ergo fieri potest ut priusquam nobi scum sit Deus, sine illius gratia & ope diligamus nos mutuò, idem uelimus ac nolimus, ac paci studeamus, atq; ita Deo causam demus, ut sit nobiscū, cum uerosimilius sit, nihil nos horū posse, nisi ipse nos gratia & ope sua præueniat. Respondeo, Sic est. Ipse nos præuenit spiritu gratiæ suæ, & corda nostra ad charitatem & pacem sectādam imbuit, ac tales reddítos magis ac magis amanter complectitur. Si quis diligit me, inquit Christus, sermonem meum seruabit, & pater meus diliget eum, & ad eum ueniemus, & mansionem apud eum faciemus. At unde homini, ut diligat Christū & sermonem eius seruet? nisi ex gratia diligentis nos Dei? Diligit Deus prior, & ut nos quoque diligamus, infundit spiritum suum in corda nostra, atq; ita regeneratos ac uicissim diligentes arctius & ampliore gratia complectitur. Nec mirū. Est enim Deus charitas, quemadmodum Ioannes in Canonica sua testatur: ideoq; qui manet in charitate, in Deo manet, & Deus in eo.
units.tr: You will say: then it can happen that before God is with us, we can love one another, agree or disagree, and pursue peace without his grace and help, and so give God a reason to be with us. Yet it is more likely that none of these things is possible unless he himself anticipates us with his grace and help. I reply: it is so. He anticipates us by the Spirit of his grace, imbues our hearts to seek love and peace, and then embraces those so renewed more and more lovingly. "If anyone loves me," said Christ, "he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him" (John 14:23). But how does a man come to love Christ and keep his word, unless from the grace of God who loves us? God loves first, and that we too may love, he pours his Spirit into our hearts; and so, regenerated and in turn loving, we are embraced more closely and with greater grace. Nor is this surprising. For God is love, as John testifies in his Epistle: therefore whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him (1 John 4:16).

units.la: SALVTATE uos mutuò osculo sancto. Salutant uos sancti omnes.) Pertinent hæc ad salutationis officiū, ad quod proclives debent esse Christiani, tanquam ad uerum ac syncerū dilectionis exercitium ac symbolum, quo de aliàs diximus, cuiusquam fuerit studiosus hic Apostolus in epistolis ipsius, præsertim ea quam ad Romanos scripsit, uidere licet.
units.tr: GREET one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.) These words pertain to the duty of greeting, to which Christians ought to be inclined, as to a true and sincere exercise and token of love. That this Apostle was careful about this in his letters, especially in the one he wrote to the Romans, may be seen.

units.la: De eo quod dicit, Salutate uos mutuò ofcu-lo sancto, dictum est 1.Cor. ultimo, & Rom. ultimo. De osculo sancto Chrysost. sic annotat: τί ἔστιν ἁγίῳ; μὴ ἀσπάζου μὴ δόλερῷ, κ) ἀσπάζου ὁ Ἰούδας τ. χείσου ἐφίλησεν. Addere debebat ὁ ἐπὶ διὰ τὸν χρι τὸν Χ ἐν χείσῳ φιλοῦντων.
units.tr: On his words, "Greet one another with a holy kiss," it was said at 1 Cor. last chapter and Rom. last chapter. Chrysostom comments on the holy kiss thus: [τί ἐστιν ἁγίῳ; μὴ ἀσπάζου δόλῳ, καὶ ἀσπάζου ὡς Ἰούδας τὸν Χριστὸν ἐφίλησεν]: "What is 'holy'? Do not kiss deceitfully, and kiss as Judas kissed Christ." He ought to have added: [διὰ τὸν Χριστὸν … ἐν Χριστῷ φιλούντων]: for the sake of Christ, of those who kiss one another in Christ.

units.la: De eo quoque quod subijcit, Salutant uos sancti omnes, dictum est 1.Cor. ultimo, ubi dicit, Salutát uos fratres omnes, quos hic uocat sanctos. Vtrunque tam sanctorum quàm mutuum salutandi officium tale est, ut nequeat ueraciter usurpari à disidentibus. Quare hortatus eos priusest, ut idem sentiant omnes, ac paci inter se studeant, ac tum de salutationibus subiecit.
units.tr: As for what he adds, "All the saints greet you," it was said at 1 Cor. last chapter, where he says, "All the brothers greet you," whom here he calls saints. Both the duty of greeting the saints and the duty of greeting one another are such that they cannot truly be practised by those who are at odds. Therefore, having first exhorted them that all should think alike and pursue peace among themselves, he then added words about greetings.

units.la: GRATIA domini Iesu Christi, & charitas Dei, & communicatio sancti spiritus, sit cum omnibus uobis, Amen.) Hæc est apprecatio, qua epistolam claudit Rom. ult. & 1.Cor. ult. simpliciter dicit, Gratia domini nostri Iesu Christi, sit cum omnibus uobis, quibus uerbis omnia quæ ad salutem nostram pertinent, breuiter complexus est. Neque enim ubi gratia Christi locum habet, charitas Dei & communicatio spiritus deesse poterūt, quas hic tamē propter pseudapostolos exprimit, ut innuat quibus bonis illi priuent ecclesiam Christi, dum eam in sectas discindunt. Deinde non erant illi in doctrina & fide sanctæ Triadis sans, Iudaismum adhuc magis quàm uerū Christianismum spirantes. Quare patris, filij ac spiritus sancti mētionem facit, de filio priore loco, non quod is patre sit maior, sed quod sit mediator, per cuius mediationis gratiam charitas Dei patris, & communicatio spiritus locum in nobis inueniunt, qua de re Caluinus, dilectus in domino frater, ante me annotauit.
units.tr: THE grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, be with you all. Amen.) This is the blessing with which he closes the letter, Rom. last chapter and 1 Cor. last chapter. He simply says, "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all," and in these words he has briefly embraced everything that pertains to our salvation. For where the grace of Christ has its place, the love of God and the fellowship of the Spirit cannot be lacking; yet he names them here because of the false apostles, to hint at the blessings those men deprive the Church of when they tear it into sects. Moreover, those men were not sound in the doctrine and faith of the holy Trinity, still breathing Judaism more than true Christianity. Therefore he mentions the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and names the Son first, not because the Son is greater than the Father, but because he is the Mediator, through whose mediating grace the love of God the Father and the fellowship of the Spirit find their place in us. On this point my beloved brother in the Lord, Calvin, has already made a note before me.

units.la: Non autem sic tribuit gratiam filio, patri charitatem, & spiritui communicationem, ut singulæ singulis tantum conueniant, & neque sit filij charitas & communicatio, neque patris gratia & charitas, absit. Sunt enim, ut recte annotat Chrysost. τὰ τῆς τελάδ ἀδιαίρετα, quemadmodum & multis in locis uidere licet, ubi quam hic filio asignat gratiam, & patri & spiritui, & quam charitatem hic patri tribuit, filio ac spiritui, & quam comunicationem adscribit spiritui, filio quoq; dare deprænditur. In huiusmodi donis non est distinctio personarum: est uero in hypostasibus, quarum unicuiq; sua est propria, de quibus non est hic dicendi locus.
units.tr: Nor does he so assign grace to the Son, love to the Father, and fellowship to the Spirit, that each belongs only to one, so that the love and fellowship are not of the Son, nor the grace and love of the Father; far from it. For, as Chrysostom rightly notes, [τὰ τῆς θεότητος ἀδιαίρετα], the works of the Godhead are undivided. This may be seen in many places, where the grace he here assigns to the Son is also shown to be given by the Father and the Spirit, the love he here ascribes to the Father is also given by the Son and the Spirit, and the fellowship he attributes to the Spirit is also shown to be given by the Son. In such gifts there is no distinction of persons; there is a distinction in the hypostases, each of which has its own property, but this is not the place to speak of them.

units.la: Quomodo ex hoc loco refellendi sint hæretici, qui Spiritus sancti diuinitatem negant, annotatum est à Chrysostomo.
units.tr: How heretics who deny the divinity of the Holy Spirit are to be refuted from this passage has been noted by Chrysostom.

units.la: Θεῷ δόξα.
units.tr: To God be glory.

units.la: Gratia sit Christi tecum, charissime Lector, Cui me commendes, dum mea scripta legis.
units.tr: Grace of Christ be with you, dearest reader, to whom I commend myself while you read my writings.
